# EUSEBIUS PAMPHILUS’ LIFE OF THE MOST BLESSED EMPEROR CONSTANTINE

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0009]

[Col. 0009] **SUMMARY.**—**CHAPTER I.** Preface, on the death of the Emperor Constantine.—**II.** On his sons as emperors.—**III.** On God’s honouring pious rulers and punishing tyrants.—**IV.** That God honoured Constantine.—**V.** That he reigned for thirty years, but lived more than sixty.—**VI.** That he was God’s servant and victor over the nations.—**VII.** Comparison of him with Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Alexander, king of the Macedonians.—**VIII.** That he subdued almost the entire world.—**IX.** That the son of the pious emperor left the Empire to his sons.—**X.** That this the households of tyrants.—**XIII.** On his father Constantius, who did not wish to persecute Christians as Diocletian and Maximian did.—**XIV.** How, when Diocletian reproached Constantius for his obtained the Empire by God’s determination.—**XXV.** Constantine’s victories over the Britons and barbarians.—**XXVI.** How he resolved to free Rome from Maxentius’ tyranny.—**XXVII.** That, considering the ruin of the pagans, Constantine chose Christianity instead.—**XXVIII.** How God, in answer to prayer, showed him a vision in heaven at midday: namely, a radiant cross with an inscription directing him to conquer by this sign.—**XXIX.** How Christ appeared to Constantine in a dream and commanded him to employ in war a sign made in the form of a cross.—**XXX.** The making of this sign in the likeness of a cross.—**XXXI.** Description of the cross-shaped sign which the Romans call the *labarum*.—**XXXII.** How Constantine became a catechumen and read the sacred himself in the dress of a slave.—**LIX.** How Maximinus, blinded by the violence of disease, issued a law on behalf of Christians.

## CHAPTER I. Preface on the death of the Emperor Constantine

[Col. 0009A]

Recently, indeed, the whole human race celebrated, with festivities and banquets recurring at fixed intervals, the second and third decennial anniversaries of our great Emperor. We ourselves also recently paid homage to that same victor and triumpher, surrounded by the assembly of God’s servants, by delivering an encomium at his twentieth anniversary. And, weaving crowns of orations for his thirtieth anniversary, we recently crowned his sacred head in the palace itself.

But now I hesitate in perplexity of mind: desiring, indeed, to offer something according to my accustomed practice, yet wholly ignorant where to turn, struck dumb by the spectacle of an unprecedented event. For wherever I direct the eyes of my mind—whether toward the rising [Col. 0009B] of the sun, toward its setting, over the entire world of lands, or toward heaven itself—I behold the most blessed ruler present everywhere. I observe that his children, like new lights of a kind, fill every region of the earth with their father’s rays; [Col. 0010A] and that he himself still lives in authority and power, governing human affairs far more nobly and powerfully, since he has been diffused and enlarged through the succession of his sons. Formerly they had been invested with the honour of Caesars; now, however, having wholly assumed their father, they have been proclaimed emperors and Augusti because of the outstanding virtue of their religion, displaying all their father’s ornaments.

## CHAPTER II. Preface on Constantine’s sons as emperors

And when I see him who a little while ago was beheld in a mortal body and lived among us, by some admirable arrangement enjoying even after death the same royal palaces, honours, and praises, [Col. 0010B] I am overwhelmed with incredible amazement. Moreover, when I extend the vision of my mind even to the vaults of heaven, and consider that there his most blessed soul dwells with God himself—freed indeed from its earthly and mortal covering, but clothed [Col. 0011A] in a garment of most radiant light—and understand that it no longer moves through these perishable abodes in the short course of time, but has been granted a crown forever flourishing, immortal life, and a blessed age, I stand speechless and utterly deprived of the use of tongue and reason.

I can utter no word; but, of my own accord condemning my inadequacy and imposing silence upon myself, I yield this office to one more powerful, that he may set forth praises proportionate to the merits: namely, to him who, being the immortal God and God’s Word, alone can establish and make valid his own declarations.

## CHAPTER III. On God’s honouring pious rulers and punishing tyrants

For, having foretold that those by whom he had been worshipped and honoured would in return be recompensed by him with the greatest rewards, [Col. 0011B] while those who had declared themselves his enemies and adversaries would bring destruction upon themselves, he demonstrated the truth of his promises and words already from this life onward. He set before our eyes the detestable ends of impious tyrants hostile to God; while to his servant he granted not merely life but even a most fortunate death, worthy of the highest praises, so that he deserved also to be celebrated in the accounts of all posterity and honoured not only with perishable but with immortal honours.

The human race, having devised some consolation for deadly destruction, has customarily honoured the memories of eminent persons by consecrated images, as though with immortal honours. Some, indeed, have represented the likenesses of men in the shadowed colours of encaustic painting; others [Col. 0011C] have expressed them in sculpture of lifeless material; some, cutting letters deeply into wooden or stone tablets, have resolved to consecrate to the everlasting memory of posterity the virtue of those whom they honoured. Yet all these things are perishable and vanish with the passage of time, since they express the form of mortal bodies, not the image of the immortal soul. Nevertheless, they seemed sufficient to those who had conceived in their minds no hope of any good after departing from this mortal life.

But God—God, I say—the common Saviour of all things, who has stored up with himself for lovers of piety goods greater than can be grasped by human thought, gives in advance in this age, as a pledge, the first fruits of future rewards, in some manner displaying and presenting to mortal [Col. 0011D] eyes the hope of immortal things. This the ancient oracles of the Prophets committed to writing openly proclaim. This the still-celebrated memory among posterity of men dear to God, who shone with various virtues, confirms. This is proved most true by the testimony of our own age, since Constantine alone of all who have ever ruled the Roman Empire, acceptable to God, the supreme King of all, has been set before all people as a splendid example of a religious life.

## CHAPTER IV. That God honoured Constantine

Finally, God himself, whom Constantine worshipped, demonstrated this by manifest testimony, since he was always gracious and favourable to him not only at the beginning, but also in the progress and at the end of his reign; for he had set him before humankind as a model for instruction in divine worship. This one man, certainly, among all emperors of whom we have ever heard, God appointed—as some most brilliant radiance, and as a herald of true religion proclaiming with the greatest voice—having heaped innumerable benefits upon him.

## CHAPTER V. That he reigned for thirty years, but lived more than sixty

He honoured the period of Constantine’s reign by completing three cycles of ten years and somewhat more; [Col. 0012B] but he bounded the period of his whole life among human beings by a span twice as great. Moreover, wishing to set him forth as an image of his own sole sovereignty, he made him victor over every kind of tyranny and destroyer of the impious Giants, who, driven by the audacity of a desperate mind, had raised the banner of impiety against God himself, the supreme King of all.

But those men arose for a moment and likewise were destroyed in a moment, more swiftly than speech. God, however, who is one and alone, having armed his servant alone against many with divine armour, and having through his agency cleansed and freed the world from the multitude of impious people, made him the teacher of his worship to all nations; declaring in a clear voice before all who heard him that he recognized the true [Col. 0012C] God and rejected the error of false divinities.

## CHAPTER VI. That he was God’s servant and victor over the nations

And he, like a good and faithful servant, did and proclaimed this, openly calling himself a servant and not being ashamed to confess himself the servant of the supreme King. God in turn immediately rewarded him, making him lord and conqueror, and alone among all emperors who have ever existed, ever unconquered and invincible. Because of his victories and trophies he made him so great an emperor as no one recalls any emperor to have been in former memory: so fortunate and dear to God, so pious and prosperous, that he brought more peoples and nations under [Col. 0012D] his rule than earlier emperors had done, and retained an empire free from every trouble until his last day.

## CHAPTER VII. Comparison of him with Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Alexander, king of the Macedonians

Ancient history relates that Cyrus, king of the Persians, shone above all who had ever existed. But he is said to have attained no fortunate end of life, but rather a shameful and disgraceful one, being killed by a woman. The Greeks proclaim that Alexander, king of the Macedonians, subdued innumerable peoples; yet, before reaching mature age, exhausted by revelry and drunkenness, he perished by an untimely death.

He completed the course of his entire life in thirty-two years, of which the period of his reign claimed no more than a third. He raged with slaughter like lightning, cruelly subjecting whole peoples and cities to slavery without distinction of age. But while he was scarcely in the flower of life and grieving for his beloved, death suddenly came upon him and extinguished him—childless, established by no offspring and no household—on foreign and hostile soil, lest he devastate humankind any longer. Soon his kingdom was torn into various parts, as each of his officers strove to seize and carry off a share for himself. Yet he is extolled with praises despite evils of this kind.

## CHAPTER VIII. That he subdued almost the entire world

[Col. 0013B]

Our emperor, however, began to reign at the age at which that Macedonian died. His life was twice as long as Alexander’s, and his reign three times as long. Moreover, having fortified his army with the gentle and moderate precepts of religion, he carried his standards into Britain and among those who inhabit the Ocean itself, which spreads far and wide toward the setting of the sun. He joined to his Empire all Scythia, lying beneath the very north, divided into very many peoples differing in name and customs.

Then, having extended his Empire to the farthest boundaries of the south—to the Blemmyes and Ethiopians themselves—he judged that those too who dwell toward the rising of the sun ought to be brought under his authority. Finally, even to [Col. 0013C] the furthest limits of the mainland—that is, to the remotest Indians and peoples surrounding them—illuminating all mortals who inhabit the whole world with the most radiant rays of piety, he held the petty kings, prefects, and satraps of barbarian peoples subject and obedient to himself. Of their own will and gladly they hailed him, sent ambassadors with gifts to him, and held his acquaintance and friendship in the highest esteem. Thus each honoured him in his own province, partly by publicly dedicated images and partly by statues; and Constantine alone among emperors was known and celebrated everywhere on earth. Therefore, in royal addresses he proclaimed his God with complete freedom even to these peoples.

## CHAPTER IX. That the son of the pious emperor left the Empire to his sons

Moreover, [the Latin is materially corrupt here: it says that he did not accomplish this in words but “was frustrated in the thing itself”]. Yet, exercising himself in every kind of virtue, he abounded in various fruits of piety: binding friends to himself by great benefits, governing his subjects by laws of clemency, and making his Empire peaceful and desirable to all. At length, after a long course of years, God, whom he had worshipped, rewarded him with the prizes of immortality after he had been wearied by various struggles, and transferred him from the mortal kingdom to immortal life prepared with himself for holy souls, raising up an offspring of three sons to succeed him in the Empire.

Thus imperial dignity, transmitted from his father, came to him; and by the law of nature it was preserved for his children [Col. 0014A] and grandchildren and thereafter propagated forever as a kind of paternal inheritance. God himself, who exalted that most blessed ruler with divine honours while he still lived with us on earth and adorned him in dying with a certain exceptional prerogative of dignity, would alone be a fitting writer of his life, since he consecrated his contests and glorious deeds in heavenly tablets.

## CHAPTER X. That this history is necessary and useful for forming character

For my part, although I understand that it is exceedingly difficult to say anything worthy of the felicity of so great a man, whereas silence is safe and free from danger, I nevertheless judge it necessary to consecrate for the everlasting memory of posterity an image of this most pious ruler, expressed in the colours of words as in the likeness of a mortal painting, so that we may dispel from ourselves the charge of sloth and indolence.

Indeed, I should be ashamed of myself if I did not devote all my diligence and ability, however slight and limited it may be, to him who worshipped the divine Majesty with the highest reverence. I trust, moreover, that this work, which comprises the deeds of the noblest emperor, acceptable to God, the emperor of all, will be useful for human life in common and especially necessary for me. For how would it not be shameful that the memories of Nero and of other impious tyrants, far worse than he, should not have lacked most diligent writers? They adorned evil subjects in elegant language and set them down in many volumes of histories; whereas we should remain silent, though God has permitted us to obtain such an emperor as no age ever saw, and to come into his presence, acquaintance, and conversation.

## CHAPTER XI. That the author will narrate only Constantine’s deeds that concern piety

Therefore, if this is fitting for anyone else, it is especially fitting for us to report the many and great goods that we have heard of to those whose minds are stirred by the example of good works toward the love of God. For others, having undertaken to write the lives of men of no importance and deeds altogether useless for correcting character—whether from favour or hatred toward certain persons, or to display their own learning—have magnified the accounts of most shameful crimes with a grand apparatus of words beyond what was fitting, making themselves teachers of the worst deeds to those who, by God’s singular favour, had been free from evils, deeds which ought to have been enveloped in forgetfulness and darkness.

Our discourse, however unequal it may be to the greatness of the undertaking, can seemingly be made illustrious by the narration of noble deeds alone. The commemoration itself of deeds acceptable to God will provide, for those at any rate whose minds are rightly disposed, a reading not useless [Col. 0015A] but especially fruitful. Therefore I judge that I must now pass over the many other things which may be narrated concerning this ruler: conflicts and battles, brave deeds and victories, trophies and triumphs gained over enemies, and whatever else he established for the benefit of individuals; laws enacted for the advantage of subjects and the commonwealth; and, finally, the many other labours of rule which he bore, things that are on everyone’s lips and in everyone’s memory. For the subject of the work I have undertaken admonishes me to pursue in speech and writing only those matters which concern the worship of God.

Yet since even these are almost infinite in number, I shall select from those that have come to our knowledge only the most suitable and most worthy of remembrance by posterity, and set them forth as briefly as I can. For the present time itself now grants us freedom to proclaim the praises of the most blessed ruler openly in every style of discourse (Eccles. II). Formerly it was by no means permitted to do so, because we are forbidden to pronounce anyone blessed before death, owing to the uncertain changes of life. Accordingly, I invoke God as my helper and entreat his heavenly Word to be pleased to inspire me in this work. I shall begin, then, with his earliest age, in the following manner.

## CHAPTER XII. That Constantine, like Moses, was brought up in the households of tyrants

Ancient history relates that the Hebrew people were once oppressed by most cruel [Col. 0015C] tyrants; and that God, when he had looked kindly and favourably upon the oppressed, provided that the prophet Moses, who was then still an infant, should be brought up amid the households of the tyrants and in their very bosom, and should learn thoroughly all the wisdom found among them.

Later, when in the course of time he had reached mature age, and divine justice, which is accustomed to aid the oppressed, demanded penalties from unjust tyrants, then God’s prophet went forth from the tyrants’ own households and rendered his service to the divine will. He opposed, in deed and word, the tyrants themselves by whom he had been brought up; but chose as friends and close companions those who truly were his brothers and kinsmen. Thereafter, when God had made him leader of the whole nation, he freed the Hebrews from their exceedingly bitter slavery among enemies; and through him exacted vengeance upon the race of tyrants by punishments inflicted from heaven.

This ancient history, I say—accepted by many as a fable—has filled the ears of all mortals. But now God has permitted us to behold with our own eyes miracles greater than all fables, a kind of spectacle considered among those who have seen it recently to be more trustworthy than every report. For in our age tyrants who had undertaken to wage war against God, the supreme King of all, grievously oppressed his Church. Constantine, however, who later became the slayer of tyrants, while still an adolescent and adorned with youthful down, lived among them, like that former servant of God, Moses, in the very [Col. 0016A] households of the tyrants.

Yet, though very young, he did not follow the same customs as the impious. For already from that age, his excellent natural disposition, moved by the divine Spirit, urged him toward a pious life acceptable to God. Emulation of his father also supplied incentives, by which the young man was summoned to the imitation of virtue and good actions. For his father was Constantius—for it is fitting opportunely to renew this man’s memory also—the most distinguished of the emperors of our time. We must briefly set forth certain things about him which bear upon the commendation of his son.

## CHAPTER XIII. On his father Constantius, who did not wish to persecute Christians as Diocletian and Maximian did

[Col. 0016B] When the Roman Empire was governed by four Augusti, Constantius, pursuing a way of life different from that of his colleagues, alone established peace with God, the ruler of all things. For they undertook to assault the churches of God, levelled them with the ground, and destroyed places of prayer together with their very foundations. He, however, kept his hands pure and unstained by their wicked impiety and in no way made himself like them.

They polluted the provinces subject to them with the slaughter of worshippers of God, both men and women, as though in some civil war. He always kept his mind pure and inviolate from a crime of that sort. They, heaping together the evils of most impious superstition, first enslaved themselves and then all their subjects to the deceits of most wicked demons. [Col. 0016C] He, the author and standard-bearer of profound peace within the boundaries of his Empire, permitted his subjects to devote themselves to divine worship without any trouble.

Finally, by crushing all mortals with most burdensome exactions, they gave them a life scarcely deserving to be called life and more bitter than any death. Constantius alone, presenting a gentle and tranquil government to his subjects, cherished them with something like a father’s care and concern. Since innumerable other virtues of this man are likewise proclaimed by everyone, we shall recall one or two of his actions, from which a judgment may be formed concerning what is passed over in silence, and then proceed to the proposed subject of our writing.

## CHAPTER XIV. How, when Diocletian reproached Constantius for his poverty, he filled the treasury and afterwards returned the money to those who had contributed it

[Col. 0016D]

When this ruler was celebrated in frequent talk among people for being gentle and mild, excellent and most loving toward God, and for having no money stored in his treasuries because of his incredible indulgence toward his subjects, the emperor who at that time held the highest rank in the Empire sent certain persons to him. He rebuked Constantius’ negligence in administering the commonwealth and reproached him with poverty, grounding the charge especially on the fact that he had nothing stored in his treasuries.

But Constantius asked the men who had come from the emperor to remain with him for a little while. Then he summoned from all provinces obedient to his rule every person of wealth and informed them that he needed money, and that this opportunity had been offered in which each should voluntarily declare his goodwill toward his ruler. Those men, since they had long wished for an occasion to be offered to testify to their devotion toward him, immediately upon hearing this filled his treasuries with gold, silver, and other wealth. They eagerly competed among themselves to surpass one another in generosity, and all did this with cheerful and glad countenances.

Afterward Constantius ordered the persons sent to him by the senior Augustus to view his treasuries and report what they had seen. He had, he said, gathered these things with himself for the present; but they had long been held for him by their own masters, as by faithful guardians of deposited wealth. They were struck with admiration at this matter. After their departure, however, the most humane ruler is said to have summoned the owners of the wealth; and, having highly praised their obedience and their devotion toward himself, to have ordered them, after receiving all their property, to return home.

This, then, is one action of that ruler by which his singular humanity is plainly shown. Another action offers an illustrious indication of his piety toward God.

## CHAPTER XV. On the persecution stirred up by others

The governors of provinces throughout the whole world, by command of the emperors, persecuted men devoted to divine worship. First of all, from the imperial palaces themselves came forth martyrs most devoted to God, who underwent contests for religion, courageously enduring fire, swords, the deepest abysses of the sea, and every kind of death. Thus, within a short time, all the emperors’ palaces were emptied of worshippers of God.

This was especially the reason why the authors of that crime remained deprived of God’s presence and aid. For while they persecuted the worshippers of the divine Majesty, they thereby drove away the prayers customarily made for themselves.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Constantius, pretending that he worshipped images, expelled those who were ready to sacrifice, but retained in his palace those who preferred to profess themselves Christians

[Col. 0017D]

Constantius alone conceived a wise plan. The matter which he carried out is indeed wonderful to hear; yet it is far more wonderful in its execution. To all the palace officials serving in his court, even to judges established in the highest offices, he gave the choice and offered this condition: if they sacrificed to demons, they might remain in the palace and enjoy their customary honours; but if they refused to do so, they were to be excluded from his presence and to depart removed from his acquaintance and intimacy.

When all had thus been divided in two, [Col. 0018A] one person going to this side and another to that, and the purpose and decision of each had been examined, the outstanding ruler disclosed the plan that had until then been concealed. He condemned the cowardice and excessive self-love of the former, but strongly approved the latter for their conscience devoted to the divine Majesty. Then he judged the former, as betrayers of God, unworthy even of a ruler’s service. “For how,” he said, “will those who are found faithless toward God preserve faith toward their ruler?” He therefore decided that men of that sort must be banished far from the royal residence.

But of those whom the testimony of truth itself showed to be worthy of God, he declared that they would have the same disposition toward their ruler; and he appointed them protectors and [Col. 0018B] guardians of his Empire, saying that such people ought to be reckoned among the foremost and most necessary of friends and valued far more highly than treasuries of immense wealth.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the affection and love of the same Constantius toward Christ

Such, as we have briefly indicated, was Constantine’s father. What end of life befell him when he had shown himself such toward God, and how great a distinction the God whom he worshipped wished to make between him and the remaining partners in the Empire, anyone who considers the matter itself more attentively will readily understand.

For after he had for a very long time furnished many proofs of royal virtue, recognizing the one supreme God of all, condemning the impiety of those who worshipped many gods, and having fortified his household on every side by the prayers of holy men, he is said to have spent the remainder of his life readily and tranquilly, with the highest glory. He possessed that happiness which is commonly said to consist in neither being troubled by others nor troubling others oneself.

In this way, throughout the entire period of his reign, which was continually even and peaceful, he consecrated his whole household—namely, his wife and children with all his servants—to God, the one King of all. Thus the multitude of those living together in his palace differed in no respect from the Church of God. Among them were also ministers of God, who worshipped God with unceasing prayers for the ruler’s safety, although among others it was generally not even permitted to utter the name of a worshipper of God.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That, after the abdication of Diocletian and Maximian, Constantius was the first Augustus, distinguished by numerous offspring

For these reasons he not long afterward received his reward from God, so that he obtained the first place in the Empire. For when the senior Augusti had, by some means unknown to me, abdicated the Empire—a sudden change which happened to them in the year following the destruction of the churches—Constantius alone was thereafter proclaimed first Augustus.

At first, adorned with the diadem of the Caesars together with Galerius, he had held the higher rank; later, when he had given an excellent proof of himself in that dignity of Caesar, he attained the highest summit of honour among the Romans and, among the four who were subsequently appointed, was called first Augustus.

He also surpassed the remaining emperors in the distinction of numerous offspring, surrounded by a great company of children of both sexes. Finally, when he was in extreme old age, about to pay what was owed to common nature and depart from this light, there God again displayed his admirable power to him, providing that his eldest son Constantine should be at hand to assume the Empire when he was on the point of death.

## CHAPTER XIX. On his son Constantine, who while still a youth came with Diocletian into Palestine

[Col. 0019B]

For Constantine lived with the emperors who were colleagues of his father, and dwelt among them as that ancient prophet of God, Moses, did, as we have already said. When his childhood was over and he had now entered the years of adolescence, he was held in the highest honour by the aforementioned emperors.

We too saw what he was like when he passed through the province of Palestine together with the senior Augustus. Standing at his right hand, he appeared pre-eminent among all who were eager to see him, already giving indications of a certain royal loftiness of spirit. For in beauty and stature of body no one could be compared with him. [Col. 0019C] He was so outstanding in bodily strength among his peers that they even feared him. But he was far more illustrious in virtues of mind than in bodily endowments. First, modesty adorned his mind; then liberal learning; and both inborn prudence and wisdom divinely bestowed cultivated him to no ordinary degree.

## CHAPTER XX. Constantine returns to his father because of the plots of Diocletian and Galerius
But the emperors of that time, seeing the young man noble and brave, and endowed with greatness and loftiness of spirit, began to be tormented alike by envy and fear on that account. They therefore watched for a suitable occasion [Col. 0019D] to inflict harm and disgrace upon the youth. When he understood this—for snares had been laid for him once and again, and had been exposed by God’s will—he sought safety in flight, imitating in this also the great prophet Moses. Moreover, God assisted him in all things, so ordering everything by His providence that he might be ready to succeed his father in the Empire.

## CHAPTER XXI. The death of Constantius, who left his son Constantine as emperor.

Having therefore escaped the treacherous snares, he hastened with swift course to his father; and after a long interval he came into his father’s presence. But at [Col. 0020A] about that time the last day of Constantius’s life was at hand. When he saw his son unexpectedly present, he sprang from his bed and embraced him with both arms. Declaring that the one grief which distressed him—the grief arising, that is, from his son’s absence—had now been utterly cast out from his heart, he gave the greatest thanks to God, testifying that henceforth death was for him preferable to every immortality. Then, having arranged his affairs according to his own judgment, and having bidden farewell to his children of both sexes, who surrounded him on every side like a kind of chorus, he lay in the palace and in the royal bedchamber; and, having placed the administration of the Empire, as natural order requires, in the hands of his eldest son, he departed from this life.

## CHAPTER XXII. How, after Constantius had been borne forth, Constantine was acclaimed Augustus by the soldiers.

[Col. 0020B]

Yet the commonwealth was not thereby left without an emperor. For Constantine, clothed in his father’s purple and coming forth from his father’s house, presented Constantius his father to all as though restored to life and still reigning in his son. Thereafter, preceding his father’s funeral with a vast multitude of his father’s friends—some going before and others following—he celebrated with most splendid ceremony the obsequies of the prince devoted to God. All accompanied the most blessed emperor with acclamations and praises; and with one accord of mind they judged that the dead ruler had been restored and recalled to the light in the person of his son. With auspicious acclamations they immediately, at the first impulse, hailed the new ruler as emperor, [Col. 0020C] Augustus. These voices of those praising the son brought honour to the dead father; while they proclaimed blessed the son who had been declared successor to so great a father. All the provinces subject to his rule were likewise filled with the greatest joy and inexpressible delight, since they had perceived that they had not been deprived of imperial providence even for the smallest moment of time. Thus God showed to all persons of our age, in the Emperor Constantius, what is the end of pious men and lovers of God.

## CHAPTER XXIII. A brief notice of the destruction of the tyrants.

What end befell the others who attacked the Churches of God as though in a declared war, I have thought it by no means proper to recount here; nor ought the memory of the good to be violated by an appended commemoration of evils. The events themselves surely suffice to check and restrain those who have received through their own eyes and ears the entire spectacle of the calamities which befell each of those men.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That Constantine obtained the Empire by God’s will.

In this manner God, the author of all things and governor of the whole world, Himself advanced Constantine, born of such a father, to be prince and emperor; so that, whereas all the rest obtained this dignity through the support of others, he alone was one of whose advancement no mortal could boast. [Col. 0021A]

## CHAPTER XXV. Constantine’s victories over the Britons and Barbarians.

Once he had been established in the Empire, he first began to provide for the portions of the realm transferred to him by his father, traversing with the greatest humanity all the provinces formerly under his father’s administration. He also subdued to his dominion all the Barbarians settled along the Rhine and the western Ocean who had dared to stir up fresh disturbances, rendering the savage gentle. Others he was content to restrain, driving them away from the borders of his Empire as wild beasts: namely, those whose incurable minds he perceived could in no way be brought over to a tranquil and peaceful manner of life. Having subdued these according to his desire, and setting the remaining parts of the world before his eyes, he meanwhile crossed against the British peoples situated in the recesses of the farthest ocean. When he had subdued them, he turned his eyes toward other parts of the world, in order to heal those which stood in need of his aid. [Col. 0021B]

## CHAPTER XXVI. How he resolved to free Rome from the tyranny of Maxentius.

Thereafter, embracing in his mind the whole inhabited world as though it were one vast body, and seeing the city which was the head of the whole world and mistress of the Roman Empire oppressed by tyrannical domination, [Col. 0021C] he first yielded the task of vindicating and liberating it to those who possessed the remaining portions of the Roman Empire, as being his elders. But when none of them could bring aid, and indeed those who had attempted it had met with a disgraceful end, he declared that life itself would not be life to him if he looked on while the mistress of all cities was afflicted by so great a malady; and he girded himself to extinguish the tyranny.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That Constantine, considering the ruin of those who had worshipped images, chose Christianity instead.

Now, understanding that besides military forces he needed some more excellent aid, because of the wicked arts and magical deceptions which the tyrant zealously [Col. 0021D] pursued, he sought God as his helper. He placed the equipment of arms and the forces of soldiers in second rank, being persuaded that the aid of the divine power was invincible and unconquerable. He therefore began to consider within himself what God he should adopt. While he anxiously investigated this matter, the following thought came to him: among the many who had held imperial power before him, those who had placed their hope in a multitude of gods and worshipped them with sacrifices and offerings had first been deceived by prophecies composed for flattery and by oracles promising every good fortune, and had at last perished by an unhappy kind of death. Nor had any of the gods been at hand to deliver them from the destruction divinely brought upon them. His father alone, [Col. 0022A] he reflected, had taken a course contrary to those men: condemning their error, he had worshipped throughout his life the one supreme God of all, and had possessed Him as saviour, guardian of the Empire, and author of every good.

When he weighed these matters within himself, he rightly observed that those who had placed confidence in a multitude of gods had fallen into a multitude of destructions, so that no trace of their race and offspring, lineage and name, or memory remained among humankind. On the other hand, the God of his father had furnished him with many and illustrious proofs of His power. Moreover, he considered that those who had previously led forces against the tyrant had gone into battle with a multitude of gods and had met a shameful end: one had withdrawn disgracefully with all his forces without accomplishing anything; the other had been slain in the midst of his army, becoming, as it were, the prey of a chance death. [Col. 0022B] Taking all these things into account, he judged it the height of madness to trifle by worshipping gods who were nowhere to be found, and, after so many and such great proofs, still to be carried away by blind error. He therefore decided that the God of his father alone was to be worshipped by him.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How God, in response to his prayer, showed him at midday a vision in the sky—namely, a luminous cross with an inscription instructing him to conquer by this.

He therefore began to implore that God’s help, praying and entreating Him to make Himself known to him and to stretch forth a helping hand in his present affairs. As the emperor prayed and made his supplication, a certain wondrous sign sent by God appeared to him. If this were reported by anyone else, listeners would scarcely find it easy to believe. But since Victor Augustus himself, long afterwards, when we had come into his acquaintance and intimacy, related it to us and confirmed the account by the solemnity of an oath, who could thereafter hesitate to give credence to this narrative? Especially since the time which followed confirmed the truth of this account by its own testimony. At the midday hours, as the sun was declining toward the west, he declared that he had seen with his own eyes in the sky a trophy in the form of a cross, composed of light and set above the sun, bearing this inscription: “By this conquer.” At this sight both he himself and all the soldiers [Col. 0022D] who were following him on some journey or other and had witnessed the miracle were greatly astonished.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How Christ appeared to Constantine in a dream and commanded him to use in war a sign made in the form of the cross.

Meanwhile, as he said, he began to wonder what this apparition might mean for him. While he pondered it and considered it long and deeply within himself, night at last came on. Then Christ of God appeared to him while asleep with that sign which had been shown in the sky, and commanded him to have made a military standard resembling that which he had seen in the sky, [Col. 0023A] and to use it in battles as a saving protection.

## CHAPTER XXX. The making of that sign in the likeness of the cross.

At the first light of dawn he rose and disclosed the whole secret to his friends. Then, summoning craftsmen in gold and precious stones, he sat among them, described in words the appearance of the sign, and ordered them to reproduce its likeness in gold and gems. We ourselves remember having seen it on several occasions.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Description of the cross-shaped sign which the Romans call the labarum.

It was as follows. A long spear, covered with gold, had a transverse bar in the form of a cross. Above, at the very summit [Col. 0023B] of the spear, a crown was fixed, interwoven with gems and gold. In it was the sign of the saving Name: that is, two letters indicated Christ’s name by its initial characters, the letter rho (ρ) crossed in its middle. The emperor was afterwards accustomed to wear these letters also upon his helmet. From the crossbar, which was set obliquely through the spear, hung a cloth: a purple textile covered with precious stones joined together and dazzling the eyes by the brilliance of their light, while the abundant gold interwoven with it afforded beholders an indescribable appearance of beauty. This cloth, attached to the crossbar, had its width equal to its length. The upright spear itself, extended in great length from its lowest part, bore in its upper part, beneath the very sign of the cross and above the top of the cloth painted in various colours, a golden, half-length image of the God-beloved emperor and his children. [Col. 0023C] The emperor always used this saving sign as a defence against the opposing forces of every enemy, and ordered standards made in its likeness to be carried before all his armies.

## CHAPTER XXXII. How Constantine, having become a catechumen, read the sacred Scriptures.

But these things came later. At that time, astonished by the marvellous vision, and having determined that no God other than the one he had seen was to be worshipped by him, he summoned to himself priests instructed in the mysteries of that secret doctrine. [Col. 0023D] He asked them who that God was and what the vision of the sign meant. They told him that this was God, the only Son of the one and only God; and that the sign which had appeared was a symbol of immortality and the trophy of the victory which He, while formerly dwelling on earth, had won over death. At the same time they taught him the causes of His coming, setting forth for him a careful account of the incarnation. He listened eagerly to these words in his desire to learn. Yet he remained held by wonder at the divine presence displayed before his eyes. When he compared that heavenly vision with the interpretation of the priests’ words, his mind was confirmed, since he was certain that knowledge of these things had been imparted to him by the instruction of God Himself. From then on he applied himself personally to the reading of the divine books; and, having taken priests of God as his associates, he judged that the God whom he had seen should be worshipped with every observance. Thereafter, fortified by the good hope which he had placed in Him, he undertook to quench the blaze of tyrannical fury. [Col. 0024A]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the adulteries committed by Maxentius at Rome.

For he who had seized the imperial city through tyranny had advanced to such impiety and wickedness that he boldly undertook every impious and unclean deed. He violated wives separated from their husbands by divorce, and sent them back violated to their husbands. Nor did he inflict this form of outrage upon obscure and low-born persons, but upon the foremost members of the Roman senate themselves. [Col. 0024B] Although he shamefully violated almost countless freeborn women, he could nevertheless by no means satisfy the unrestrained lust of his mind. But after he began to solicit Christian women, he could accomplish by no means that he might enjoy intercourse with them. For they preferred to expose their souls to death rather than surrender their bodies to him for defilement.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How the wife of a prefect took her own life in order to preserve her chastity.

One of these women, married to a man of senatorial rank who held the prefecture, learned that the attendants whom the tyrant employed as servants of such crimes were at the doors. Her husband, compelled by fear, had permitted them to seize and carry her away. [Col. 0024C] She was a Christian woman. She requested that a short time be granted her to adorn her body with customary dress. Entering her chamber and finding herself left alone, she plunged a sword into her breast; and immediately dying, she left her corpse to those who had come to carry her off. By her deed, which speaks more loudly than every voice, she declared to all mortals now living and yet to come that chastity, among Christians alone, is invincible, impregnable, and not subject to death. Such was her course of action.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The slaughter of the Roman people by Maxentius’s order.

All, therefore, fearing him as he rushed with every audacity into crimes of this kind—commoners and magistrates alike, nobles and obscure persons alike—were oppressed by a most grievous tyranny. Though they kept quiet and endured the bitterest slavery patiently, they could not even thus escape the tyrant’s bloody cruelty. Finally, on one day and for the slightest cause, he delivered the Roman people to be cut down by the Praetorian soldiers. Thus an innumerable multitude of the Roman populace was slaughtered in the middle of the city by the spears and weapons, not of Scythians and Barbarians, but of their own fellow citizens. How great, moreover, were the slaughters of senators, committed in order that their possessions might be seized, cannot possibly be counted; for every day very many were put to death on various fabricated charges. [Col. 0024D]

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Maxentius’s magical arts and the scarcity of provisions at Rome.

[Col. 0025A]

At last the tyrant set, as it were, the crowning height upon his crimes: the deceptions of magical art. At one time he cut open pregnant women; at another he examined the entrails of infants newly brought into the light; he sometimes slaughtered lions; and he performed certain impious rites to summon demons and to avert the war which was now imminent. By these arts he hoped to obtain victory. While he exercised tyranny at Rome, it can scarcely be said how many and how great evils he inflicted upon and imposed as slavery on his subjects. They were driven into an extreme scarcity of provisions, such as no memory of any person of our age recalls ever having existed in Rome before.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The defeat of Maxentius’s forces in Italy.

[Col. 0025B]

Moved by grief and compassion at all this, Constantine equipped himself with every military preparation against the tyranny. Having adopted as his protector the supreme God of all and invoked Christ His Son as saviour and helper, and having placed before his soldiers and bodyguards the trophy of victory—that is, the saving sign—he set out with his whole army, intending by his intervention to restore to the Romans the liberty they had received from their forefathers. Maxentius, however, trusting more in the deceptions of magical arts than in his subjects’ goodwill, did not dare even to proceed outside the city gates. Yet he had fortified on every side, with an innumerable multitude of armed men and armies positioned for ambush, all the places, towns, and districts around the city of Rome and throughout Italy which he held crushed beneath the yoke of slavery. Trusting in divine aid, the emperor attacked the tyrant’s first, second, and third battle-lines; immediately at the first onset he routed and put them all to flight, and penetrated into the interior of Italy. [Col. 0025C]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The death of Maxentius at the bridge of the Tiber.

At last he came nearer to Rome itself. But lest he should have to attack all the Romans on account of one tyrant, God drew that man, as though bound with certain chains, as far as possible beyond the city gates. [Col. 0025D] At the same time He proved by the event itself to all believers and unbelievers who saw with their own eyes the miracle that we shall recount, that the ancient miracles wrought against the impious and contained in the sacred volumes—though many dismiss them as fables, while they seem worthy of belief to the faithful—were wholly true. For just as in the time of Moses and the pious nation of the Hebrews, God cast Pharaoh’s chariots and army into the sea, submerged in the Red Sea his choicest warriors fighting from chariots, and covered them with the waves, so indeed Maxentius and all the soldiers and guards about him fell like a stone into the deepest abyss. [Col. 0026A]

This occurred when, driven into flight while divine power aided Constantine’s cause, he crossed the river which lay in his way. There he had constructed, over boats firmly planked together, a bridge—and had devised a mechanism for his own destruction, hoping by such a trick to ensnare the prince beloved by God. But God whom he worshipped came to that prince’s aid. The impious man, wretchedly, prepared hidden devices against his own head. Thus it could deservedly be said of him: “He opened and dug a pit, and fell into the hole which he made. His labour shall return upon his own head, and his injustice shall fall upon his own crown.” Accordingly, when the mechanisms constructed on the bridge were unexpectedly broken apart together with their hidden trap, the crossing began to collapse; and the boats suddenly sank together with the men themselves. [Col. 0026B] That most wretched man was the first of all to fall, and then all the guards and attendants whom he had around him, as the divine oracles had foretold, fell like a mass of lead into the deepest abyss.

Thus the soldiers who then gained victory by the aid of the divine Power, like the Israelites of old whom that great servant of God Moses led, might deservedly sing against this impious man, if not in words, at least by their deeds, the very same things that they had formerly sung against impious Pharaoh:

> Let us sing to the Lord, for He has been gloriously glorified.  
> Horse and rider He has cast into the sea.  
> He has become my helper and protector unto salvation.

And again:

> Who is like You among the gods, O Lord? Who is like You?  
> Glorified among the holy ones, wonderful in glory, working wonders.

[Col. 0026C]

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Constantine’s entry into the city of Rome.

When Constantine at that time, imitating the great servant of God Moses, had sung these things and other true counterparts of them in deed to the praise of God, ruler of all and author of victory, he entered Rome in triumph. All alike, from the senate and the equestrian order, as though liberated from the custody of a prison, received him with the whole Roman people, with cheerful faces and auspicious acclamations, with inexhaustible joy from the depths of their hearts. All—men and women with their children and an innumerable multitude of servants—hailed him with an incredible and unrestrainable cry as liberator, saviour, and author of good things. [Col. 0026D] But he, bearing piety toward God as though implanted and innate within him, was not elated by such acclamations or praises. Rather, understanding clearly that God’s help had been with him, he immediately and humbly rendered thanksgiving to the author of victory.

## CHAPTER XL. On Constantine’s statue holding a cross, and its inscription.

By a loud proclamation and inscriptions upon monuments, he announced the saving sign to all people. Having erected this trophy against the enemy in the midst of the imperial city, and having engraved in characters that would never perish this saving sign, which is the safeguard of the Roman Empire and of the whole [world: text defective, `t[.....]tius`] [Col. 0027A]—he immediately ordered a tall spear in the form of a cross to be placed beneath the hand of his statue in the most frequented place of the city, with the following inscription in Latin beneath it:

> By this saving sign, which is the proof of true power, I saved your city, liberated from the yoke of tyrannical domination. Having restored the senate and people of Rome to liberty, I restored to them their ancient honour, nobility, and splendour.

## CHAPTER XLI. The rejoicing of the provinces and Constantine’s benefactions.

In this manner the emperor most devoted to God, openly displaying the confession of the victorious cross, freely and candidly proclaimed the Son of God to the Romans. All those dwelling in the city, both senate and people, [Col. 0027B] freed from bitter and tyrannical domination, seemed somehow to breathe again, enjoy the rays of a purer light, and be born anew into a kind of new life. All the nations bounded by the western Ocean, likewise liberated from their former evils, celebrated festival days with every joy, continually praising Constantine as victor, friend of God, and benefactor toward all. With one mouth and one voice all declared that a common good, granted to humankind by God’s kindness, had dawned upon them. The emperor’s letters were also posted and read everywhere: by them those despoiled of their property recovered possession of it through the prince’s favour, and those unjustly exiled were restored to their homes. Those afflicted by tyrannical cruelty were freed also from chains and from every danger and fear. [Col. 0027C]

## CHAPTER XLII. Honours bestowed on bishops and the building of churches.

The emperor himself treated the ministers of God whom he had summoned with every service and honour. Since they were consecrated to the God whom he worshipped, he received them humanely not merely in words but in deeds. Accordingly, men outwardly contemptible in appearance and dress were admitted to his table, though he judged them by no means contemptible; for he looked not upon a person’s external appearance, which is subject to the eyes, but upon God Himself. Moreover, wherever he travelled, he took them with him, being certain that the God whom they worshipped would therefore also be propitious to him. [Col. 0027D] He even supplied the Churches of God with numerous benefits from his own treasuries: in part enlarging and raising their sacred buildings on high, and in part adorning the august sanctuaries of the churches with many offerings.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Constantine’s beneficence toward the poor.

Finally, by various distributions of money he relieved the poverty of those in need. He further showed himself humane and generous toward strangers who approached him. For those miserable and destitute persons who begged in the marketplace, he ordered that not only money and food necessary for living should be supplied, but clothing also to cover bodily nakedness. To those who had formerly been freeborn and wealthy but had later, through a change of fortune, fallen into the utmost calamities, he granted more abundant means of subsistence. Bestowing truly royal and magnificent gifts upon persons of this kind, he gave estates to some and adorned others with various dignities. He cared, as a father, for those who had fallen into the misery of orphanhood; and, relieving the loneliness of widowed women, he supported them with his patronage. He even gave in marriage to wealthy men and his own friends maidens bereft of parents. He did this only after first giving the brides whatever they ought to bring to their husbands. [Col. 0028A]

Finally, just as the sun, rising above the earth, freely bestows the rays of its light upon all, so Constantine, going forth from the palace at first dawn and in some sense rising together with the heavenly radiance of the sun, bestowed the rays of his beneficence upon all who came to him. No one ever approached him who did not carry away the fruit of some benefit; nor were those who expected any aid from him ever disappointed in their hope. [Col. 0028B]

## CHAPTER XLIV. How he attended synods of bishops.

In general, he showed himself such toward all. But taking especial care for the Church of God, whenever some persons disagreed with one another throughout the various provinces, he, as though appointed by God the common bishop of all, assembled councils of God’s ministers. He did not think it beneath him to be present and sit among their assembly, sharing in the examination of matters and promoting everything that concerned the peace of God. [Col. 0028C] He sat in the midst as one among many, keeping all guards and bodyguards at a distance, but surrounded by the fear of God and the goodwill of faithful friends. He particularly approved all whom he observed to agree with the sounder view and to be inclined toward peace and concord, openly showing that he especially delighted in the unanimous agreement of all. Those who were obstinate and disobedient, however, he disliked.

## CHAPTER XLV. How he endured foolish persons.

He even patiently endured certain persons who had attacked him too harshly, instructing them in a gentle and composed voice [Col. 0028D] to behave more moderately and not stir up seditions. Some of these, respecting his admonitions, abandoned the stubbornness of their minds. Others, whom no remedy could recall to soundness of mind, he left, entrusting them to God, never ordering anything harsher against anyone. For this reason, as is credible, those who stirred up sedition in Africa broke out into such wickedness as to attempt certain desperate deeds. It seems that the demon, stirred by envy at the abundance of present blessings and inciting people to certain grave and atrocious crimes, did so in order to inflame the emperor’s mind against them. Yet envy achieved nothing, since the emperor judged what was being done to be laughable and said that he recognized the prompting of the malignant demon. [Col. 0029A] Such actions, he said, did not belong to sound-minded persons, but either to persons wholly mad or to those driven by the goads of a most wicked demon; such people were deserving of pity rather than punishment. For it is not as great an act of justice to rise up to punish the frenzy of mad people as it is an act of the utmost humanity to grieve for their condition.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Victories won over the Barbarians.

In all his actions, then, the emperor thus rendered worship to God, the beholder of all things, and provided for His Churches with unshaken care. God in return subjected almost all barbarian peoples [Col. 0029B] beneath his feet, so that he raised trophies over enemies everywhere. He proclaimed him victor among all mortals with illustrious praise; He made him terrible to enemies and foes, although by his own nature he was not at all such a man, but rather the gentlest, mildest, and most humane of all mortals.

## CHAPTER XLVII. The death of Maximian and of others whose plots Constantine detected when God revealed them.

While he was doing these things, one of those who had abdicated the Empire, having prepared a plot to kill him, was detected and perished by a most disgraceful death. He was the first whose images and statues, as of an impious and criminal man, and other monuments of that kind customarily erected as marks of honour, were cast down throughout the world. After him others also, connected by kinship, were detected while secretly plotting against him; for God in a wondrous way disclosed all their plans to His servant through visions. [Col. 0029C] He also deigned frequently to display His presence to him, the divine form appearing through the greatest miracle and suggesting to him foreknowledge of future events. Those inexplicable miracles of divine grace which God Himself deigned to bestow on His servant can scarcely even be comprehended in speech. Protected by these, he passed the rest of his life in the greatest security: taking the greatest pleasure both in the goodwill of his subjects and in seeing all those subject to his Empire living in the highest tranquillity and joy, and especially rejoicing with incredible gladness at the splendour of the Churches of God. [Col. 0029D]

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Constantine’s decennial celebrations.

While he was in this condition, the tenth year of his reign elapsed. On that account, festival days having been celebrated throughout the Roman world, he offered to God, King of all, prayers with thanksgiving as pure sacrifices, free from fire and smoke. He took the greatest delight in these things; but not so much as he was troubled by the reports brought to him concerning the devastation of the provinces of the East.

## CHAPTER XLIX. How Licinius afflicted the East.

[Col. 0030A]

For it was reported that a certain monstrous beast was plotting against both the Church of God and the other provincials there, while the most wicked demon, as though inflamed by rivalry, endeavoured to do things contrary to those done by the emperor devoted to God. Thus the Roman Empire, divided into two parts, seemed to all like night and day. A darkness of night oppressed the inhabitants of the East, while the brightest day illuminated those who inhabited the western regions. Since these enjoyed countless good things procured for them by God, the envy of the malignant demon, hostile to every good, could not endure it. Nor did the tyrant who oppressed the other part of the Roman world under his rule consider it tolerable. [Col. 0030B] Though he saw his own affairs prospering and had been honoured with kinship to so great a prince, he neglected to follow the example of the religious emperor and instead made it his aim to imitate the practices and depraved ways of the impious. Although he had seen with his own eyes the pitiable end of their lives, he preferred to follow their counsels rather than remain in friendship and concord with one who was superior and more powerful.

## CHAPTER L. How Licinius plotted against Constantine.

He therefore waged an inexpiable war against a man who had deserved well of him, recalling neither the duties of friendship, nor the sanctity of oaths, nor the bond of kinship, nor treaties. For Constantine, as a prince of the utmost generosity, in order to give him the surest proof of sincere goodwill, had shared with him the nobility of his paternal stock and the splendour of an imperial lineage distinguished from his ancestors onward, by giving him his sister in marriage. He had also allowed him to share in the whole Roman Empire. [Col. 0030C] Licinius, on the other hand, entertaining thoughts wholly opposite to these, employed hidden devices against his superior, repeatedly devising various kinds of plots in order to repay good service with evils. At first, indeed, while feigning friendship, he did everything by deception and fraud, hoping that his plans would remain hidden. But God revealed to His servant the snares being secretly laid. When Licinius was detected in his first attempts, he had recourse to further deceits: now pretending fidelity in friendship, now gaining trust through the sanctity of treaties and oaths; then suddenly violating the agreements, again asking forgiveness through ambassadors, and anew shamefully mocking with lies. Finally, he openly declared war; driven on by the desperate audacity of his mind, he thereafter began to bear arms against God Himself, whose worship he knew the Emperor Constantine had embraced. [Col. 0030D]

## CHAPTER LI. Licinius’s plots against bishops and his prohibition of synods.

First, Licinius covertly and cunningly ensnared the ministers of God living under his rule, though they had never committed any offence against his empire [Col. 0031A], seeking out various accusations against them. And since no charge was available to him and he had nothing he could bring against those men, he enacted a law ordering that bishops should nowhere confer with one another about any matter; that none of them should be allowed to visit the church of his neighbour; or hold synods and councils concerning common affairs. But he sought this as an opportunity to harass us. For if our people violated the law, they had to undergo punishment; but if they obeyed the command, the laws of the Church were overthrown. For controversies of greater importance cannot be settled otherwise than through synods. Moreover, the tyrant, hostile to God, and striving in all things to oppose the emperor who loved God most dearly, imposed these measures upon our people. For Constantine [Col. 0031B] summoned the priests of God together for the sake of peace and mutual concord, and did so in honour of Him to whom they offered sacred rites. Licinius, however, while endeavouring to overthrow every excellent thing, attempted to disturb the harmony of the Churches.

## CHAPTER LII. The exile and proscription of Christians.

And because Constantine, beloved by God, gladly admitted the servants of God into his palace, Licinius, the enemy of God, holding entirely opposite views, expelled from the palace all worshippers of God who lived under his rule; and those whom he had in his retinue as most faithful and devoted persons he especially banished into exile. Those whom he had previously [Col. 0031C] adorned with some honour or dignity on account of their outstanding deeds, he commanded to serve others and perform the duties of servants. Having seized the property of all as though it were gain offered to him, he finally even threatened death to those who assumed the saving name of the Christian religion.

Moreover, having given himself over to every form of lust and sensuality, and committing many adulteries and other crimes of detestable obscenity, he judged that the honour of chastity and self-restraint could by no means be maintained by human beings, making the worst possible judgement about human nature from his own disease.

## CHAPTER LIII. Licinius’ edict forbidding women to assemble in church with men.

[Col. 0031D]

For this reason he enacted another law, ordering that men should not assemble in the church of God together with women for prayer; that women should not come to the venerable schools of virtue for instruction; and, finally, that bishops should not impart the precepts of divine religion to women, but that women chosen for this purpose should be appointed over the instruction of women. When these provisions were ridiculed by all, he devised something else for the destruction of the churches. He ordered the regular assemblies of the people to be held outside the gates, on open ground, alleging that the free air outside the gates was much more suitable for crowds than oratories situated within the city.

## CHAPTER LIV. How he dismissed from military service those who refused to sacrifice, and forbade prisoners to be fed.

[Col. 0032A]

But when he saw that they did not obey him even in this, at last, casting aside evasions and, as the saying goes, speaking plainly, he decreed that soldiers attached in each city to the governors’ courts should be removed from the service of the provincial administration unless they preferred to sacrifice to demons. Accordingly, the offices of magistrates throughout the provinces were stripped of pious and religious men. Yet he himself who enacted this law was stripped by the prayers of the holy men from whom he had deprived himself.

What need is there further to relate how he ordered that no one should humanely provide food to wretches detained in prison [Col. 0032B], and that no one should show compassion to persons wasting away from hunger in chains? That is, he ordered that no good person should exist at all, and that those whom nature itself moves to pity their neighbours should do no good deed. This was indeed an openly shameless and most savage law, easily surpassing every ferocity of character. Indeed, this penalty was added to the law: those who gave alms to prisoners were to suffer the same punishment as the prisoners themselves; they were to be cast into prison and chains and undergo the same penalty as criminals, though they had performed duties of humanity toward them.

## CHAPTER LV. On the injustice and avarice of Licinius.

[Col. 0032C]

Such were the enactments of Licinius. But what need is there to recount what innovations he introduced in matters of marriage or concerning the dying—daring to abolish the ancient laws of the Romans, rightly and wisely established, and to substitute in their place certain barbarous, savage, wholly unlawful, and unjust laws? Further, he devised a thousand kinds of exactions against his subjects. Accordingly, he invented new surveys of land, so that he might assess a larger measurement upon a small field, through his insatiable desire for excessive exactions. He therefore entered in the tax registers the names of peasants who were no longer alive but had long since died, seeking from this a profit of shameful gain. For the sordid parsimony of the man knew no [Col. 0032D] limit, nor did any satiety end his desire for possessions. Thus, though he had filled his treasuries with gold, silver, and an immense abundance of wealth, he groaned and complained of his poverty, afflicted by a kind of Tantalus-like disease.

Why should I mention the exiles to which he condemned innocent men? Why confiscations of property? Why men of noble and eminent rank led away to prison, whose wives he handed over to certain criminal slaves to be violated? Why enumerate married women and virgins, upon whom he, though already advanced in age, attempted to inflict violence? There is no need to linger longer in recounting these things, since the gravity of his final crimes made these earlier ones seem light and almost insignificant.

## CHAPTER LVI. How he finally stirred up persecution against Christians.

[Col. 0033A]

At last he proceeded to such madness as to wage war against the Churches and attack the bishops themselves, whom he understood to be especially opposed to him, regarding as enemies those who were friends of the greatest emperor, most beloved of God. For this reason above all he sharpened his fury against us, abandoning right reason. Nor did he call to mind the example of those who had persecuted Christians before him, or those whom he himself had been appointed avenger and destroyer to punish for their impious deeds. Nor did he recall in mind and thought the things of which he himself had been a witness, when he beheld with his own eyes that standard-bearer of all evils—whoever he may have been [Col. 0033B]—struck by a divinely inflicted plague.

## CHAPTER LVII. How Maximian, overcome by a fistulous and verminous ulcer, wrote a law in favour of Christians.

For when this man had begun to assail the Churches and had first stained his soul with the slaughter of the righteous and the worshippers of God, divine vengeance deservedly seized him, beginning with his very flesh and advancing even to his soul. Suddenly an abscess arose in the midst of his more hidden bodily parts; then a deep fistulous ulcer. The incurable ravaging of both consumed his innermost organs. From these burst forth an incredible multitude of worms, exhaling a deadly [Col. 0033C] stench. For the entire bulk of his body, through an excessive abundance of food, had been converted into an enormous mass of fat; this, it is reported, then dissolved into corruption and presented to those standing by a dreadful and intolerable spectacle.

Thus, shattered by so many evils, he finally began to understand the crimes he had committed against the Church. Thereupon, confessing his error to God, he restrained the persecution of Christians; and by issuing imperial edicts and laws he ordered their churches to be rebuilt as swiftly as possible, and Christians themselves to perform their sacred rites according to their customary practice and offer prayers to God for the emperor.

## CHAPTER LVIII. How Maximinus, persecutor of Christians, concealed himself in flight under a slave’s dress.

[Col. 0033D]

This man, then, who had been the author of the persecution paid penalties of this kind. But Licinius, of whom we now speak, was a witness and spectator of these events and had learned all things accurately through experience itself. Yet he suddenly forgot everything: he neither reflected upon the punishment inflicted upon the former man [Col. 0034A], nor upon the penalties which divine justice had exacted from the latter. Striving ambitiously to surpass the former, as in some contest of crimes, he gloried in devising new punishments against our people.

Fire and sword did not suffice him; neither did impalement upon nails, the tearing of beasts, or the gulfs of the deepest sea. In addition to all these, he himself devised a new kind of punishment: by an enacted law, he ordered the mutilation of the limbs by which we receive the use of light. Immediately, therefore, dense crowds not only of men but also of boys and women, disabled in their right eyes and the joints of their feet, partly by the sword and partly by cautery, were sent to the mines, to be afflicted there by prolonged labour [Col. 0034B].

For this reason divine justice also avenged itself upon him not long afterward: when, trusting in demons—whom he thought to be gods—and relying on an innumerable multitude of armed men, he joined battle. Then, entirely deprived of hope for divine help, he cast off the imperial garb, which was by no means fitting for him; then, mixing himself with a crowd of common people, he sought safety in flight, utterly fearfully and cowardly. Hiding himself through fields and villages, he thought he could remain concealed under a slave’s dress. But he could not escape that great eye of Providence which beholds all things. For when he judged that his safety had at last been placed beyond danger, struck by the burning dart of God, he fell prone upon the ground; and his whole body was so consumed by a plague inflicted from heaven [Col. 0034C] that every appearance of his former form was obliterated, and only dry bones remained, like some image.

## CHAPTER LIX. How Maximinus, blinded by the force of disease, issued a law in favour of Christians.

Moreover, as the plague of God raged more fiercely, at length his eyes protruded and, torn from their own sockets, left him blind: most justly suffering the same punishments that he had first devised against the martyrs of God. Thereafter, though still breathing, he too begged pardon from the God of the Christians, openly confessing that he had waged war against divinity. Nor did he recant otherwise than the former man: by issuing laws and constitutions, in which he frankly confessed his error in worshipping those whom he had believed to be gods, and testified that he had learned by experience to know the one God [Col. 0034D] of the Christians.

Although Licinius learned these things not from another’s account but perceived them in the events themselves, nevertheless, as though his mind had been covered by a dense darkness, he undertook the very things those men had done.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0033]

How, grieved by sedition, he urged peace.—LXIX. Whence the controversy between Arius and Alexander arose, and that such matters ought not to have been investigated.—LXX. An exhortation to concord.—LXXI. That there should not have been stubborn contention over certain trivial expressions.—LXXII.
