## CHAPTER I. The secret persecution of Licinius and the murder of bishops at Amasia, a city of Pontus.

[Col. 0035A]

In this manner the aforesaid Licinius rushed headlong into the abyss of the impious; and, imitating to his own destruction the example of those whose ruin for impious acts he himself had seen with his own eyes, he rekindled the persecution of Christians, like a fire already extinguished, and kindled a blaze of impiety much more grievous than those before it. At first, like an evil beast and a twisting serpent coiled around itself, breathing fury and hostile threats against God, he did not dare openly to wage war against the Churches of God established under his rule, for fear of Constantine. But concealing the poison of his wickedness [Col. 0035B], he prepared secret attacks against bishops only in certain places; and, by charges fabricated through provincial governors, put to death every one among them of proven excellence. The manner of their murder, moreover, was new and never known before. Certainly, what occurred at Amasia surpassed every measure of cruelty.

## CHAPTER II. Churches demolished and bishops slaughtered.

In that city, some churches of God were once again levelled to the ground after the earlier attack; others were closed by the provincial governors, so that none of those accustomed to attend them might assemble there or offer the regular worship to God. For the man who commanded these things did not suppose that prayers were offered there for him, being brought to that belief, plainly enough, by his conscience. [Col. 0036A] Instead, he persuaded himself that we performed everything and offered supplication to the divine power for Constantine.

But the governors, as flatterers and sycophants, certain that they were doing something pleasing to the emperor, condemned to capital punishment the best leaders of the Churches. Thus men who had committed no evil were carried away without any cause and punished just as though they were murderers. Some underwent a new kind of death: their bodies were cut piecemeal into many parts, and, after that cruel spectacle more horrible than any tragic fiction, they were thrown into the deepest sea to provide food for fish.

After this, the worshippers of God again began to flee. Again fields, again wildernesses received the servants of God. While these things were thus succeeding for the tyrant, he next resolved to stir up persecution against all Christians. And without doubt he would have achieved his desire, and nothing would have prevented him from bringing the matter to its conclusion, unless God, defender of His servants, swiftly forestalling what was to happen, had suddenly displayed His servant Constantine like a brilliant ray of light amid deep darkness and the blackest night, and had led him, as if by the hand, into these regions [Col. 0036B].

## CHAPTER III. How Constantine was moved on behalf of the Christians whom Licinius was preparing to persecute.

When he learned that news of such events had reached his ears, he understood that he must no longer dissemble. He summoned the strength of his sober mind; and blending severity of character with his innate clemency, he hastened to bring help to those oppressed [Col. 0037A], judging it a pious and holy act that, by removing one man from the midst, almost the whole human race might be preserved unharmed.

For he reasoned thus within himself: if he himself exercised the utmost clemency and showed mercy to a man deserving no mercy, it would profit that man nothing, since he would by no means depart from his perverse habits and practices, but rather would intensify his rage against his subjects; while to the oppressed no further hope of salvation would remain. Having considered this, the emperor resolved without delay to extend a saving right hand to those who had fallen into the most extreme calamities.

He assembled a great array of military forces and arms. All the troops, both cavalry and infantry, were already present, gathered together in one place. Before them all went the emblems of confidence in God: namely, the sign mentioned above [Col. 0037B].

## CHAPTER IV. How Constantine prepared for war with prayers, but Licinius with divinations.

Understanding that he then needed prayers more than ever before, he took with him the priests of God, believing that they should be present before him and remain with him as the best guardians of his soul. When the tyrant heard that Constantine was preparing to win victory over his enemies only with divine power assisting him; that those of whom I spoke were continually present and remained with him; and that the sign of the saving Passion went before both him and his whole army—he, as an impious man, judged these things worthy of ridicule, mocking Constantine and assailing him with insulting words.

He himself, however, associated with himself diviners and Egyptian seers, sorcerers and impostors, and finally the priests and prophets of the false gods he worshipped. Then, appeasing by sacrifices those whom he thought gods, he inquired of them what outcome the war would have. They answered without hesitation that he would be victor over his enemies and superior in war, as all the oracles everywhere with one accord promised him this in lengthy and elegant verses [Col. 0037C]. Interpreters of dreams through dreams and haruspices through the movement of entrails likewise affirmed that similar things were portended. Inflated by their deceitful promises, he advanced to the camp with great confidence and arrayed himself for battle.

## CHAPTER V. What Licinius said about images and Christ while sacrificing in a sacred grove.

When he was about to begin the war, he gathered the most distinguished among his protectors and more honoured friends in a certain place which they themselves regarded as sacred. It was a watered and shady grove, in which were seen many stone-carved statues of those whom he considered gods. Having lit candles before these and sacrificed according to the customary rite, he is said to have spoken as follows:

“Friends and fellow soldiers, these whom we worship, and whom we have received from our most remote ancestors as objects of worship, are ancestral gods. But he who leads the forces of the opposing party, violating the customs and institutions of his ancestors, has apostatized to the impious opinion of those who believe in no gods, rashly embracing some foreign God sought from I know not where. Indeed, he dishonours his army with that most shameful sign; and, trusting in it, he goes forth armed not so much against us as against the very gods whom he has violated [Col. 0038A].

“The present day, therefore, will plainly show which of us is led by blind error and will render judgement concerning the gods worshipped among us or by the people of the opposing party. For either victory granted to us will rightly and deservedly declare our gods to be true saviours and helpers; or, if that one God of Constantine, coming from I know not where, should prove superior to our gods, who are extremely numerous and now surely surpass Him in number, let no one thereafter call into question which God ought to be worshipped. Rather, let him approach the more powerful and offer Him the reward of victory.

“And if that foreign God whom we now hold in derision appears victorious, we too must acknowledge and worship Him, dismissing and bidding farewell henceforth to those for whom we light candles in vain. But if our gods prove superior—which, indeed, cannot be doubtful to anyone—then, after gaining victory in this place, we shall undertake to wage war against the impious despisers of the gods.”

Such words Licinius addressed to those around him before the battle began. Not long afterward, those very persons who had been present at his speech related them to us who write these things. Having delivered such an address, he ordered the soldiers to enter battle [Col. 0038B].

## CHAPTER VI. Apparitions seen in the cities subject to Licinius: Constantine’s soldiers pursuing Licinius’ forces.

While these things were occurring, an altogether marvellous apparition is reported to have appeared in the cities subject to the rule of that tyrant. Various companies of Constantine’s soldiers were seen at midday, passing through the cities as though victory had been won. These things were seen, although no one actually appeared anywhere; rather, divine power, through the vision presented to the eyes, foreshadowed what was to happen.

When the armies were now preparing to engage, the man who had broken the covenants of concord began the battle first. Then Constantine, calling the Saviour and supreme God of all to his aid and giving his soldiers this sign, routed the enemy in the first battle. Not long afterward, when a second battle was joined, he again departed victorious and won a far greater triumph, while the saving trophy of the cross went before his army [Col. 0038C–D].

## CHAPTER VII. That wherever the sign of the cross was present in battles, victory was won.

Certainly, wherever this sign had been seen, the enemy immediately fled, their backs pressed by the victors. When the emperor learned this, whenever he noticed that some division of his army was being hard pressed, he immediately ordered the saving trophy to be brought forward as a most efficacious talisman for securing victory [Col. 0039A]. Once this had been done, victory followed at once, divine power surely strengthening the courage and strength of the combatants.

## CHAPTER VIII. That fifty men were chosen to carry the cross.

Accordingly, selecting from the protectors all who seemed distinguished by bodily strength, courage of spirit, and the principles of true religion, he imposed this single duty upon them: that they should continually take care of this sign. There were fifty men in all. Their sole duty was to stand around and guard the sign with their escort; each carried it in turn upon his shoulders.

The emperor himself related these things to us who write this history, during a period of leisure, long after they had occurred; and he added at the same time a matter most worthy of remembrance [Col. 0039B].

## CHAPTER IX. That among the bearers of the cross, the one who fled was killed, but the one who remained faithfully escaped unharmed.

“For,” he said, “when in the midst of battle a great uproar had thrown the army into confusion, the man carrying this sign upon his shoulders, struck with fear, handed it to another to carry, in order that he himself might escape the danger. Hardly had the other received the sign to carry when, behold, the man who had slipped away and abandoned the guarding of the sign was struck in the belly by a missile and died. Thus he lay there lifeless, paying the penalty for his cowardice and faithlessness.

“But the saving trophy of the cross preserved unharmed the man who bore it aloft. Though missiles were hurled upon him from every direction, the standard-bearer himself escaped safely; the spear-shaft of the saving trophy, however, received the missiles [Col. 0039C]. It was a spectacle greater than every miracle: all the enemy missiles fell within that very narrow span of the shaft. While they struck and remained fixed in the shaft, the standard-bearer was preserved unharmed. Thus none of those performing this service was ever struck by any missile.”

This is not our own account, but that of the emperor himself, who among other matters also related this to us. Having ascribed his earlier victories to the help of almighty God, he afterward advanced further, moving his army forward in battle array.

## CHAPTER X. Various battles and Constantine’s victories.

When the leaders of the opposing side could not withstand his first assault, they threw down their arms and prostrated themselves at the emperor’s feet. He preserved them all unharmed, taking great pleasure in the preservation of human lives. But others who remained under arms prepared themselves for battle. The emperor invited them to surrender; but when he saw that friendly addresses could not bend them at all, he sent his army against them. They immediately turned their backs and fled. Some were captured as they fled and killed by the law of war. Others, colliding with one another, were slain by their own swords [Col. 0039D].

## CHAPTER XI. The flight and magical arts of Licinius.

But their leader, seeing that he had been deprived of the aid of his attendants and that all the forces he had assembled, both soldiers and auxiliaries, had vanished; and being convinced by the event itself that the hope he placed in the gods he worshipped was entirely vain, took to a most shameful flight. Escaping in this way, he removed himself from danger, because the emperor who loved God most dearly did not at once wish his men to pursue and press upon the fugitive’s rear, in order that the fugitive might escape [Col. 0040A].

For he hoped that Licinius, having finally recognized the most unhappy condition of his affairs, would depart from his former audacity and madness and return to a sounder mind. Such was Constantine’s judgement, owing to his exceptional humanity: he had resolved to bear injuries patiently and to grant pardon even to one undeserving of it. But Licinius was so far from abandoning his former wickedness that, instead, piling evil upon evil, he undertook worse deeds each day. Indeed, resorting again to the detestable arts of magicians, he began to behave with greater insolence. Of him, then, one might rightly say what was said of that ancient tyrant: that his heart had been hardened by God [Col. 0040B].

## CHAPTER XII. How Constantine, praying in a tent, gained victory.

Thus Licinius, binding himself with the chains of such crimes, plunged headlong into the abyss of destruction. Constantine, however, seeing that he needed another battle, devoted himself diligently to the worship of his Saviour. He pitched the tent of the cross outside the camp; dwelling there purely and chastely, he offered prayers to God, after the example of that ancient prophet whom the divine oracles testify set up a tent outside the camp [Col. 0040C].

A few persons of tested faith, piety, and goodwill constantly attended him there. He was accustomed always to do this whenever he was about to enter a contest. He was not rash, choosing always what was safer. Moreover, he was accustomed to conduct all things according to God’s counsel. When he diligently and earnestly prayed to his God, God always deigned to manifest His presence to him. Thereupon, as though moved by a more divine impulse, he would spring from the tent; and, once he had given the signal to advance, he immediately commanded the soldiers without delay to draw their swords. They then charged the enemy at once and slew all who met them without distinction of age [Col. 0040D], until, in a brief moment of time, they had gained victory and raised trophies over their conquered enemies.

## CHAPTER XIII. Constantine’s humanity toward captured soldiers.

This was the way in which the emperor was accustomed, even previously, to conduct himself and train his army before the clash of battle. He always placed God before his own life, endeavoured to do all things by God’s command and counsel, and regarded the slaughter of many human beings as a religious scruple. Consequently, he took thought for the safety of enemies no less than for that of his own soldiers.

Accordingly, once his men had gained victory, he ordered them to spare the defeated and to remember that they were human beings born into a shared human nature [Col. 0041A]. If he happened to see the soldiers stubbornly inclined to slaughter, he restrained them by a distribution of gold, ordering that whoever captured an enemy alive should receive a fixed weight of gold. The emperor’s ingenuity thus devised this inducement to preserve human lives. As a result, very many even among the barbarians were saved, since the emperor’s gold had redeemed their lives.

## CHAPTER XIV. Again, concerning prayer in the tent.

The emperor was accustomed on other occasions as well to do these and many other similar things. But at that time, before engaging in battle, he withdrew into the tent and, as was his custom, devoted himself to prayer, abstaining from every amusement and more luxurious manner of life, wearing down his body by fasting and other such exercises [Col. 0041B], and appeasing God with supplications and prayers, so as to have Him gracious and favourable as the helper of his cause and to carry out the things He suggested to his mind.

Thus Constantine maintained a vigilant care for the commonwealth, making prayers not more for the salvation of his own men than for that of his enemies.

## CHAPTER XV. Licinius’ feigned friendship and worship of idols.

Because Licinius, who had shortly before taken flight, now employed dissimulation and again requested that friendship and treaties be renewed, the emperor, judging this to be in the interest of the commonwealth and beneficial to the human race, did not refuse to grant him peace on certain conditions. Licinius, to all outward appearance, pretended that he gladly accepted the laws [Col. 0041C] and confirmed his good faith by oath. But secretly he prepared military forces and planned again to make war and renew the conflict.

He also sought barbarian auxiliaries from every quarter and searched everywhere for new gods, having been deceived by the former ones. He did not recall what he had said shortly before in his public address about the gods. Nor was he willing to acknowledge the God who had fought for Constantine; instead, he began, not without laughter and derision, to seek many more and newer gods.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Licinius instructed his soldiers not to attack the sign of the cross.

Thereafter, when he had learned by experience that a certain secret and divine power resided in the saving trophy, [Col. 0041D] by whose aid Constantine’s army had been accustomed to win victory, he warned his soldiers not to engage it face to face, nor rashly and casually to cast their eyes upon it. For he said that this sign possessed incredible power, and was personally hostile and adverse to himself; and that therefore they must beware of entering battle against it. Having thus arranged matters, he resolved to fight against one who, in his innate clemency, hesitated and deferred the destruction impending over him. The followers of Licinius, indeed, trusting in the multitude of their gods, advanced with immense forces, carrying before them, as a means of protection, I know not what images of the dead and lifeless statues. Constantine, however, clothed with the breastplate of piety, set before the multitude of his enemies the saving and life-giving sign of the cross, [Col. 0042A] as a certain terror and a most powerful safeguard for repelling evils. At first he held back, sparing the sword for the time being, lest he should appear to have begun the battle first—and this out of reverence for the treaties which he had made.

## CHAPTER XVII. Constantine’s victory.

But when he saw that the enemies persisted obstinately and were now drawing their swords, he was moved with indignation and, by a shout alone and in the briefest moment of time, put all the enemy forces to flight, winning victory alike over demons and enemies.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The death of Licinius and the triumphs celebrated over him.

[Col. 0042B] Thereafter he subjected the enemy of God himself and his associates—condemned according to the law of war—to fitting punishment. Thus they were led away together with the tyrant; and all who had urged him to wage war against God paid the due penalty of death. Those who shortly before had been uplifted by vain hope now in fact embraced Constantine’s God and professed that only then at last did they acknowledge him as the one true God.

## CHAPTER XIX. Public joy and festivity.

The impious having thus been removed from the midst, the pure and clear rays of the sun were thereafter visible, as though the cloud of tyrannical rule had been driven away. All parts of the Roman Empire were joined into one body: the eastern [Col. 0042C] provinces being united with the West, and the whole body of the Empire shining forth under one ruler as a kind of head, whose sole dominion embraced all humankind. Those who had formerly sat in darkness and in the shadow of death were then granted bright rays of piety and joyful days. Nor did any recollection of past evils remain, since everywhere all celebrated the victor with praises and professed that they acknowledged his saving God alone.

Our victorious Constantine, excelling in every form of piety—for this was the surname most fittingly acquired by him, because of the victories everywhere granted him by God over his foes and enemies—recovered the East and reduced the Roman Empire, solid and united as it had once been, under his sole authority. [Col. 0042D] He was the first to proclaim to all the sole rule of the one God; while himself holding the unique sovereignty of the Roman world, he governed the entire human race. Every fear of the evils under which all people had been oppressed had now utterly vanished. Those who had formerly been sorrowful then looked upon one another with cheerful faces and joyous eyes. With choirs and hymns they celebrated without intermission, first the King of all, God, as they had been instructed; then the victorious Augustus, and his most moderate children, the Caesars beloved of God. No memory remained of former calamities or impiety; rather, people enjoyed the fruits of present blessings together with hope and expectation of those to come.

## CHAPTER XX. How Constantine enacted laws on behalf of the Confessors.

[Col. 0043A]

Then among us too, as previously among those inhabiting the other part of the world, there were published the emperor’s edicts, full of humanity; and laws breathing a sincere and religious observance of God promised, with undoubted hope, various goods of every kind. They granted to provincials what concerned their own advantage and established what was fitting and appropriate for the Churches of God. First, those who, because they had refused to sacrifice to idols, had been banished by provincial governors and compelled to leave their homeland, were recalled home. Then those who for the same reason had been assigned to municipal councils were released from public [Col. 0043B] duties; and those who had been despoiled of their possessions were ordered to have their property restored. Moreover, all who during the persecution, strengthened by divine power, had given a conspicuous example of courage and steadfastness—whether they had been condemned to the mines, to be worn down there by unceasing labor, or deported to an island, or assigned to public works—were suddenly freed from all these hardships and obtained liberty.

Likewise, all who had been deprived of military rank because of outstanding constancy in maintaining their religion were restored by the emperor’s generosity from this disgrace. He left it to their own choice and will either to recover their former offices and enjoy their previous rank of honor, or, should they prefer a quiet life, to remain henceforth exempt from every public duty. Finally, all who had been consigned to the women’s workshops (*gynaecea*) as a mark of disgrace, the emperor granted freedom no less than to the rest.

## CHAPTER XXI. How he also enacted laws concerning martyrs and Church property.

The emperor established by written laws these measures concerning those who had suffered such things. As regards their property, moreover, the emperor’s law made the fullest provision. He ordered that the possessions of the holy martyrs of God who had died in their confession should pass to their nearest relatives. If no person related to them by blood could be found, their inheritance was to be transferred to the Churches. The imperial letter of clemency further directed that property which had passed to others from the treasury, whether by sale or donation, or which had remained in the treasury, must be restored to its owners. [Col. 0043D] Such benefits did the prince’s kindness confer upon the Church of God, through laws sent into every province.

## CHAPTER XXII. How he also restored the peoples.

The emperor’s generosity bestowed far more and greater gifts upon peoples alien to our faith and upon all the provinces. Accordingly, all inhabitants of our regions, who previously, on hearing of what was occurring in the other part of the Roman Empire, had called blessed those who received such benefits and fervently wished that they too might one day enjoy the same goods, now seeing these things with their own eyes did not hesitate to call themselves [Col. 0044A] happy. They testified that a new miracle had occurred, such as no age under heaven had ever seen: namely, that so great an emperor had shone forth upon the human race. Such, then, was their view.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That he proclaimed God the author of blessings, and concerning his laws.

But the emperor himself, after reducing all things beneath his authority by the power of God the Savior, publicly made known to all the one who had bestowed these blessings upon him. He declared that this one, not he himself, had been the author of his victories. He proclaimed this in letters written in both Latin and Greek and sent to every province. Whoever reads the letters themselves will readily recognize the force and excellence of the discourse. There are two: one addressed to the Churches of God, the other to the peoples of individual cities who were alien to our religion. Since the latter is especially suited to the present subject, I have judged it necessary to insert it here, both so that copies of it, preserved in historical records, may endure perpetually among posterity and so that the reliability and truth of our narrative may be confirmed. It was copied from the authentic exemplar of the imperial law preserved among us. The subscription appended in the emperor’s own hand attests the truth of our account as with a seal.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Constantine’s law concerning piety toward God and the Christian religion.

(For this law, which extends from Chapter XXIV through XLIII, see below, where the sequence of Constantine’s works is given.)

## CHAPTER XLIII. How Constantine confirmed by deeds what he had enacted by laws.

Such were the provisions of the first letter sent to us by the emperor. What had been enacted by law was immediately put into execution, and in every respect measures contrary to those undertaken by tyrannical cruelty were carried out. Those to whom the law granted it enjoyed the emperor’s beneficence.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How he promoted Christians to govern provinces and forbade pagans to sacrifice.

Thereafter the emperor seriously set his hand to the work. First, he sent as governors into the individual provinces, for the most part, men devoted to the saving faith. If any of them appeared devoted to Greek superstition, they were forbidden to sacrifice. The same law was imposed also upon those who surpassed governors in rank, and indeed upon those who held the highest summit of honors and the authority of the praetorian prefecture. For if they were Christians, he allowed them to act consistently with the designation of their name; but if their disposition was otherwise, he commanded them not to sacrifice to images.

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning the laws by which sacrifices were forbidden and Churches ordered to be built.

Thereupon two laws were issued at one and the same time. One prohibited the detestable sacrifices of idol worship formerly performed everywhere in cities and fields, so that thereafter no one might dare either to set up statues of gods, or to undertake divinations and similar vain arts, or to slaughter victims. The other law directed that houses of prayer be raised on high and that Churches of God be made greater both in breadth and length—as though all people, so to speak, were hereafter going to approach God once the mad observance of many gods had been removed from their midst.

Religious observance of the divine Majesty impelled the emperor to hold these views and to write them to the governors of every province. The law further provided that they should not be sparing in disbursing funds, but that expenses for the construction of sacred buildings should be drawn from the imperial treasuries. Indeed, letters of this sort were written to the bishops of the Churches in every locality; and he deigned to write such a letter even to me. He addressed the first of these letters expressly to me by name.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Constantine’s letter to Eusebius and the other bishops concerning the building of Churches through the governors’ agency, and the restoration of old ones and construction of larger ones.

(See this letter below.)

## CHAPTER XLVII. That he wrote against the worship of idols.

The emperor, daily increasing his piety and reverence toward God, sent to all provincials an address concerning the error of image-worship in which Roman emperors before his time had been entangled. [Col. 0045C] With admirable eloquence he exhorted his subjects to acknowledge the supreme God of all and to accept his Son, Christ, as their Savior. I have also judged it necessary to translate these letters, written in his own hand, from Latin into Greek and to weave them into the present work, so that we may seem in some measure to hear the emperor himself crying aloud in these words to the ears of all mortals.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Constantine’s edict to the provincials concerning the false worship of many gods. Opening concerning virtue and vice.

(For this edict, which extends from Chapter XLVIII through LXI, see below.)

## CHAPTER LXI. How controversies arose in the city of Alexandria because of Arius.

[Col. 0045D]

The emperor, like a herald of God endowed with a very great voice, cried aloud these things to all provincials through his letters, seeking to recall his subjects from the error of demons and to urge them to embrace the true worship of God. While he rejoiced exceedingly for these reasons, news was brought to him of no small disturbance that had seized the Churches. Struck by this report, he began to devise a remedy.

The origin of the disturbance was this. The people of God flourished and applied themselves with a certain eagerness and exultation to honorable actions. [Col. 0046A] There was no powerful fear to cause disturbance; for, through the benefaction of God most good and great, a pleasant and profound peace surrounded the Church on every side. Yet envy, laying snares for our prosperity, had taken up its position. First creeping in secretly, it afterward danced in the midst of the assembly of the saints. Finally it set bishops against one another, stirring up tumult and dispute among them under the pretext of divine doctrines.

Then, as though from a slight spark, a most serious conflagration blazed forth. Beginning from the Church of Alexandria as from a head, it afterward spread through all Egypt, Libya, and Upper Thebaid. It also consumed the remaining cities and provinces, so that one could see not only the bishops of the Churches fighting one another with words, [Col. 0046B] but even the people themselves divided, some embracing the party of these men and others that of those. The spectacle of what was occurring advanced to such a pitch of disgrace that, in the very theaters of unbelievers, the venerable doctrine of divine preaching was subjected to the foulest laughter and mockery.

## CHAPTER LXII. Concerning Arius and the Meletians.

These persons were obstinately contending in the city of Alexandria itself over matters of the highest importance. Others, throughout all Egypt and Upper Thebaid, meanwhile disagreed over a certain controversy that had arisen earlier, so that Churches everywhere were torn apart. While the body of the Church suffered from such a disease, all Libya likewise fell ill at the same time, and the remaining parts of foreign provinces were seized by the same sickness. For those in Alexandria sent delegates to the bishops of the individual provinces. These, divided into one party or the other, also joined in the sedition.

## CHAPTER LXIII. How he sent an envoy with letters to restore peace.

Hearing this, the emperor was struck with deepest grief. Considering the matter to be like a domestic calamity, he immediately sent to Alexandria one of the worshipers of God who were about him, a man whom he knew to be esteemed for the modesty of his faith and to have been distinguished above others in the preceding time for his confession of religion, in order that he might restore peace among those who disagreed there. He gave him letters to the authors of the contention, above all useful and necessary. Since these furnish an illustrious example of the care and concern which he bore for the Churches of God, it will not be unfitting to insert them themselves into this narrative concerning him. They are as follows.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Constantine’s letter to Alexander the bishop and Arius the presbyter.

(This letter, extending from Chapter LXIV through LXXIII, may be seen below.)

## CHAPTER LXXIII. That contention persisted even after these imperial letters.

[Col. 0047A]

In this manner the emperor beloved of God sought, by sending a letter, to restore peace to the Church of God. Moreover, the good man and outstanding worshiper of God of whom I spoke above rendered excellent service not only in delivering the letter but also in [Col. 0048A] carrying out the will of him who had sent him. Yet the affair was too great to be quieted by the ministry of a letter. Thus the quarrel of the contending parties increased day by day, and the force of the evil pervaded all the provinces of the East. This was the work of envious jealousy and of the malignant demon, ever ill-disposed toward the Church’s prosperity, plotting our ruin.
