## CHAPTER I. Comparison of Constantine’s piety with the wickedness of the persecutors.

[Col. 0047B]

In this way the demon, the enemy of every good, who is accustomed always to envy the Church’s prosperity, stirred up tumults and civil wars within it in a time of peace and joy. Meanwhile the emperor beloved of God neglected none of the duties incumbent upon him, striving to do in every respect the opposite of what tyrannical cruelty had shortly before undertaken. By this means he prevailed over all his foes and enemies.

For first, those men, alien from the worship of the true God, compelled all mortals by various means and by force to worship false divinities. He, however, proving both by word and deed that those were not gods at all, exhorted everyone to acknowledge him who alone is God. Moreover, they reviled Christ of God with impious utterances; he wrote that the very thing which impious people especially assailed with curses was the safeguard of salvation, glorying in the trophy of the Lord’s passion. [Col. 0048B] They persecuted Christ’s worshipers and drove them from house and home; he recalled all from exile and restored them to their dwellings. They branded them with dishonor; he increased their honors and made them, in everyone’s judgment, fortunate and blessed. They unjustly confiscated and plundered the property of God’s worshipers; he not only restored their possessions to them but also enriched many with additional benefits. They published written enactments full of calumnies against the heads of the Churches; he, on the contrary, exalted and honored these men and, by issuing edicts and laws, made them more illustrious than before.

They utterly demolished houses of prayer, razing them from their very roofs to the ground; he ordered those still remaining to be raised higher and new ones to be constructed with magnificent adornment, the expenses being supplied from the imperial treasury. They ordered divinely inspired oracles to be destroyed by fire; he commanded copies of the sacred volumes to be multiplied at the expense of the imperial treasury and adorned with splendid equipment. [Col. 0049A] They forbade bishops to dare convene synods anywhere; he summoned bishops to himself from every province and not only admitted them within the palace and into his innermost chamber, but even wished them to share his table and roof. They honored demons with votive offerings; he exposed their deceptions and permanently distributed the material of the votive offerings, now dedicated to no use, to those who could use it. They ordered the temples of gods to be magnificently adorned; he utterly overthrew those things which superstitious persons worshiped with special reverence. They subjected God’s servants to disgraceful punishments; he pursued those who had perpetrated these acts and inflicted upon them deserved punishment, while never ceasing to honor the memorials of God’s holy martyrs.

They expelled men devoted to divine worship from the palace; he placed special confidence in such men, understanding that above all others they were well-disposed and faithful toward him. They, excessively eager to amass money, had enslaved their minds to a certain Tantalus-like craving; he opened all the treasuries with royal magnificence and distributed their contents freely and generously. Finally, they committed countless murders in order to plunder and confiscate the possessions of those they killed; but for as long as Constantine ruled, the sword hung idle and always unstained with blood for all judges, since in every province peoples and municipal councillors were governed by a kind of paternal authority rather than by force and compulsion. [Col. 0049C]

Whoever considers these things attentively will rightly say that a new age at last seemed to have appeared, an unfamiliar light suddenly shining upon the human race after long darkness. And such a person will confess that this was wholly God’s work: that God had set this religious emperor as an antagonist against that multitude of impious men.

## CHAPTER II. Again, concerning Constantine’s piety in freely professing the sign of the cross.

For since those men had proved to be such as none had ever been seen to be, and had dared to commit against the Church deeds which no one had ever heard, from the remotest memory of humankind onward, to have been committed, God rightly brought forth into public view an unprecedented miracle—namely Constantine—and through him performed things neither ever heard of nor seen with the eyes. What miracle, indeed, was newer and more unprecedented than the excellence of our emperor, whom God’s wisdom bestowed upon the human race? For with all confidence and freedom he continually proclaimed Christ of God to all and did not blush to be identified by the saving name. Rather, glorying greatly in this, he made himself known to all: now marking his face with the saving sign, now glorying in the triumphant trophy.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning Constantine’s image, above which was the cross and below it a dragon.

[Col. 0050A]

He also displayed for all to see, upon a lofty panel placed before the vestibule of the palace, the saving sign set above his own head; below it, the enemy and foe of humankind, who had attacked the Church of God through impious tyrants, falling headlong in the form of a dragon. For the divine oracles in the books of the prophets called him the dragon and the winding serpent. Therefore the emperor wished the dragon, pierced through the middle of its belly by darts and cast into the deep gulfs of the sea, to be depicted and displayed for all beneath the feet of himself and his sons, in wax melted by fire. [Col. 0050B] In this way he signified the hidden enemy of the human race, declaring that he had been thrust down into the abyss of destruction by the force and power of that saving trophy which had been set above his own head.

The image silently indicated this in its various colors. I, however, am moved to admire the emperor’s extraordinary understanding: impelled by a kind of divine inspiration, he expressed in painting what had long before been foretold in the utterances of the prophets concerning that beast—namely, that God would bring a great and terrible sword upon the dragon and the fleeing serpent, and would kill the dragon that is in the sea. Thus the emperor depicted their image, with the painting altogether imitating the reality itself.

## CHAPTER IV. Again, concerning the controversies in Egypt stirred up by Arius.

[Col. 0050C]

These things he carried out willingly. But jealous envy, which was still troubling the Churches of God in the city of Alexandria, together with the pestilential schism of the Thebans and Egyptians, distressed his mind not a little. For bishops in every city were fighting against bishops, peoples rising against peoples, and, colliding like the Symplegades, falling in mutual ruin by their own wounds. At last, driven to frenzy and desperation, they dared to commit certain impious acts and even to violate the emperor’s own images. Yet these things could move the prince not so much to anger as to grief, [Col. 0050D] for he deeply lamented the madness of ruined people.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the disagreement over the feast of Easter.

Another and much more serious disease, older than these, lay beneath them: namely, disagreement concerning the saving feast. Some maintained that the custom of the Jews ought to be followed; others said that the time itself must be observed accurately and that no agreement should be made with those in error, who in this matter also stood apart from evangelical grace. Thus, while peoples everywhere had long been divided among themselves and the rites of our sacred religion thrown into confusion—for diversity of timing in one and the same feast caused the greatest division among those keeping the festival, since some wore themselves down with fasts and hardships while others gave themselves to leisure and joy—there was no mortal able to provide a remedy for this evil, because the controversy among the disputants seemed to hang in an evenly balanced scale on both sides. Only almighty God could very easily heal these evils.

There was, moreover, one man upon earth, Constantine, who appeared suited to be God’s minister for accomplishing these benefits. When he heard of the matters just mentioned and learned that he had achieved nothing by the letters sent to the Alexandrians, he roused the resourcefulness of his own mind and said that he must undertake a new war against the invisible enemy who was disrupting the Church’s order.

## CHAPTER VI. How he ordered the Synod of Nicaea to be held.

[Col. 0051B]

Then, as though arraying a divine phalanx against him, he convened a general synod, inviting bishops from every quarter by honorable letters to be present as soon as possible. Nor was this merely a simple and bare command: the emperor’s generosity also contributed much to the undertaking. He provided some with access to the public post, while abundantly supplying others with the use of beasts of transport. A most suitable location was also assigned to the synod: Nicaea, a city in Bithynia named after victory.

Once the emperor’s command had been conveyed to all provinces, everyone immediately hastened there with the utmost eagerness, as though released from a starting-gate. They were drawn by the hope of blessings, the opportunity for present peace, and finally the spectacle of a new miracle—of so great an emperor. When they had assembled together, it became evident that what was happening was God’s work. For those who had been separated by the greatest distances not only in mind but also in body, regions, places, and provinces were then seen gathered into one; and one city held them all, like a great priestly crown woven from the fairest flowers. [Col. 0051C]

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the universal Council, to which bishops came from every province.

For from every Church that filled all Europe, Africa, and Asia, those holding the foremost rank among God’s ministers assembled together. One sacred building, as though enlarged by God’s will, enclosed within its compass Syrians and Cilicians, Phoenicians and Arabs, Palestinians, Egyptians, Thebans and Libyans, and others arriving from Mesopotamia. A bishop from Persia also attended the synod, nor was even a Scythian absent from this choir. Pontus likewise, Galatia, Pamphylia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Phrygia supplied each its choicest representative. Thracians also, Macedonians, Achaeans, Epirotes, and those situated far beyond them were nevertheless present. From Spain itself, that man celebrated in the speech of all likewise sat with the rest. The bishop of the imperial city was absent because of old age, [Col. 0052A] but presbyters were present to fulfill his role.

Constantine alone, the only emperor in all history, dedicated to Christ his Savior this crown, bound and united by the bond of peace, as a divine memorial of gratitude for the victories he had gained over foes and enemies—having convened in our own time this most distinguished assembly, as a kind of image of the apostolic choir.

## CHAPTER VIII. That, as Acts of the Apostles says, they assembled from diverse nations.

For in the time of the Apostles, devout men are said to have come together from every nation under heaven. Among them were Parthians, Medes, [Col. 0052B] Elamites, and inhabitants of Mesopotamia, Judaea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; also visitors from Rome, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs. Yet in their case the following limitation existed: not all who assembled were ministers of God. In the present gathering, however, more than two hundred and fifty bishops were present. The number of accompanying presbyters, deacons, acolytes, and many others can scarcely be reckoned.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the virtue and age of the two hundred and fifty bishops.

Among these ministers of God, some excelled in eloquent wisdom; others in the gravity of their life and endurance of labors; others were adorned with modesty and graciousness of character. Some were held in the highest honor because of advanced age; some shone in the youthful vigor both of body and mind. Some had only very recently entered upon the course of their ministry. The emperor had ordered abundant daily provisions to be supplied to them all.

## CHAPTER X. The synod held in the palace, where Constantine entered and sat with the bishops.

Moreover, when the day appointed for the council arrived, on which the controversies had to be decided, and all those of whom the Synod consisted were present, they entered the very middle hall of the palace, which seemed to surpass all the rest in size. Very many seats having been arranged in order along either side of the hall [Col. 0052D], all who had been summoned entered and took their respective places. After the whole synod had seated itself with becoming restraint, all were at first silent, awaiting the emperor’s entrance. Soon one of the emperor’s closest attendants entered, then another and a third. Others also went before him—not, as was customary, from the ranks of soldiers and guards, but only those friends who professed faith in Christ. When the signal was given announcing the emperor’s entrance, all rose; then at last he himself arrived, walking down the middle like some angel of the heavenly God, dazzling the eyes of all by the brightness of his purple garment and shining with certain fiery rays, adorned moreover with the extraordinary splendor [Col. 0053A] of gold and precious stones.

Such, indeed, was his bodily adornment. But as regards his soul, it was sufficiently evident that he was adorned with fear of God and piety. This was indicated by his lowered eyes, the blush upon his face, and the movement of his body and his gait. So too was the rest of his bodily appearance: namely, the height by which he far surpassed all those around him. He excelled the others not only in stature, but also in beauty of form, in a certain graceful majesty of his whole body, and finally in unconquered strength. Yet all these qualities, tempered by admirable modesty and imperial gentleness, revealed the exceptional excellence of his mind, greater than all praise.

When the emperor came to the head of the benches, he first stood in the middle. A low chair of wrought gold having been placed before him, he did not sit down [Col. 0053B] until the bishops had signaled him to do so. All the others did likewise after the emperor.

## CHAPTER XI. The silence of the Council, after Bishop Eusebius had said a few words

Then the bishop occupying the foremost place on the right rose and addressed the emperor in a brief speech, offering thanks and praise to almighty God on his account. When he too had sat down, all immediately fixed their eyes upon the emperor and kept silence. He looked upon them all with cheerful eyes and a serene countenance; then, collecting his thoughts, he spoke words of this kind in a gentle and measured voice.

## CHAPTER XII. Constantine’s address to the Synod concerning peace

[Col. 0053C]

(See this address below.)

## CHAPTER XIII. How he recalled the bishops, when they were contending with one another, to concord

After he had spoken these things in the Latin language, which someone else interpreted into Greek, he then gave the floor to the presidents of the council. Thereupon some began to accuse their neighbors; others replied to the accusers and in turn lodged complaints. Thus, when many charges had been advanced on both sides and great controversy had arisen at the very outset, the emperor listened to everything with the greatest patience, received the questions presented with attentive mind, and, reinforcing and assisting in turn what was said on either side [Col. 0053D], gradually reconciled those who contended too obstinately. Addressing all of them gently, and using the Greek language—for he was not ignorant even of that language—he was most gracious and agreeable: drawing some, persuaded by force of argument, to his own view; entreating and winning over others; praising those who had spoken rightly; and encouraging all toward concord. At last he made them unanimous and in agreement concerning all the matters over which they had previously disputed.

## CHAPTER XIV. The unanimous judgment of the Synod concerning the faith and Easter

Thus not only did agreement in one faith prevail among all, but one and the same time for the celebration of the saving feast was also established by all [Col. 0054A]. What had been agreed upon in common was committed to writing and confirmed by the subscriptions of each individual. These things having been accomplished, the emperor declared that he had won this second victory over the enemy of the Church, and celebrated a triumphal festival in honor of God.

## CHAPTER XV. How Constantine entertained the bishops at a banquet on his twentieth anniversary

At the same time the twentieth year of his reign was being completed. Since public celebrations were held for this occasion in all the provinces, the emperor invited God’s ministers to a banquet; and, dining with them now reconciled among themselves, he offered this to God through them as a fitting sacrifice. No bishop [Col. 0054B] was absent from this imperial banquet. The event itself far surpassed every power of description. Guards and soldiers stood in a circle, swords drawn, protecting the entrance to the palace. Yet the men of God passed through their midst without any fear and entered as far as the innermost chambers of the palace. Some of them then reclined at table with the emperor; others reclined upon couches arranged on either side. It seemed altogether as though an image of Christ’s kingdom were being sketched out, and the reality itself seemed nearer to a dream than to truth.

## CHAPTER XVI. Gifts bestowed upon the bishops and letters written to all

When the banquets had been celebrated with the most splendid display, the emperor received all generously and, in accordance with his magnificence [Col. 0054C], added this further act: he honored each person with gifts according to merit and rank. He also informed by letter those who had not attended this synod concerning what had been done in it. I shall set forth these letters in this work, as though inscribed upon a tablet. They are as follows.

## CHAPTER XVII. Constantine’s letter to the Churches concerning the Synod of Nicaea

(See this letter, which occupies this and the following three chapters, below.)

## CHAPTER XXI. He counsels the departing bishops to preserve concord

Moreover, when the Synod was about to be dissolved, the emperor addressed the bishops in order to take leave of them. He summoned them all together on an appointed day. When they were present, he urged them to be zealous in preserving peace among themselves [Col. 0054D], to flee obstinate disputes, and not to envy any bishop among them if he flourished in the praise of wisdom and eloquence. Rather, they should regard each person’s virtue as the common good of all; nor should those who are more eminent exalt themselves above their inferiors. For it belongs to God to judge the true virtue and excellence of each person.

It was more fitting, he said, that the more eminent should accommodate themselves to the weaker with a certain indulgence and gentleness, especially since it is altogether most difficult to find anything perfect in every respect. Therefore they ought mutually to grant pardon for another’s slight fault [Col. 0055A], and to forgive whatever had been committed through human weakness, always giving great consideration to mutual concord; lest, while they themselves stirred up dissensions among one another, an occasion for mockery be afforded to those prepared to assail the divine law with curses.

Nevertheless, they themselves should give the greatest consideration to such people, since they could easily be preserved if what takes place among us appeared to them exceptional and admirable. Nor, indeed, was it obscure to them that abundance of discourse brings no benefit to all people. Some rejoice when resources useful for the support of life are supplied to them; others are accustomed to seek protection. Some love those by whom they are kindly received; others, honored with small gifts, are moved [Col. 0055B] to enter into friendship. Very few are true lovers of discourse, nor is one zealous for truth easily found. For this reason one must accommodate oneself to all, and, like a physician, administer what is useful for each person’s health, so that saving doctrine may be honored by all in every respect.

These were the emperor’s first instructions to them. Finally, he added that they should also diligently offer prayers to God for him. Having thus taken leave of them, he thereafter gave all permission to return to their homelands. They therefore returned home with the greatest joy; and thereafter one opinion prevailed among all, confirmed by the emperor’s own presence and by the common agreement of all, since those who had long been divided from one another had grown together, as it were, into [Col. 0055C] one body.

## CHAPTER XXII. How he exhorted some, wrote to others, and distributed money

Delighted by so great a success, the emperor offered by letter a most welcome benefit to those who had not attended the synod. He also ordered a great sum of money to be distributed to all peoples, both those living in the countryside and those living in cities, thus celebrating the public festival for the twentieth year of his reign.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How he wrote to the Egyptians and exhorted them to peace

[Col. 0055D] But while all others cultivated peace among themselves, among the Egyptians alone the fury of implacable contention burned, so that they indeed caused trouble to the emperor, yet did not thereby provoke him to anger. For honoring them in every way as fathers—or rather, as prophets of God—the emperor summoned them again before him; again he acted as their arbiter; again he honored them with presents and gifts. He also communicated by letter the judgment he had rendered as arbiter, confirming and ratifying what had been decreed by the Synod; and he exhorted them to pursue concord and not to wish to divide and tear apart the body of the Church, but to reflect in their minds upon the coming judgment of God. These matters the emperor conveyed to them in a special letter.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How he frequently wrote religious letters to bishops and peoples

[Col. 0056A]

He wrote many other letters of this kind and composed almost innumerable epistles: now prescribing to bishops what concerned the welfare of the churches of God; now addressing the peoples themselves by letter and calling the peoples of the Church his brothers and fellow servants—the most blessed man. But perhaps there will be leisure at another time to gather these together in a separate volume, lest the course of this history be interrupted.

## CHAPTER XXV. How he commanded a church to be built at Jerusalem in the holy place of the Lord’s resurrection

After these events, the emperor beloved of God undertook in Palestine another work especially worthy of remembrance. What was it? He judged it his duty to make the most blessed place of the Lord’s resurrection at Jerusalem illustrious and venerable to all mortals. He immediately ordered a house of prayer to be built there—not prompted to this without God’s will, but with the Savior himself stirring his mind.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How the impious had covered the Lord’s tomb with ruins and images placed over it

For once impious men—or rather, the whole race of demons, through the agency of impious men—had sought utterly to envelop in darkness and oblivion that venerable monument of immortality [Col. 0056C]. I mean that monument to which the angel, once descending from heaven and shining with marvelous light, rolled away the stone from the minds of those who were truly stony and who still imagined that the living Christ lay among the dead; bringing glad tidings to the women and removing the stone of unbelief from their minds, in order to establish the belief in the life of him whom they sought.

Certain impious and profane men had therefore resolved utterly to destroy this saving cave, foolishly supposing that in this way they would conceal the truth. Thus, not without immense labor, they brought earth from elsewhere in great quantity, heaped it up, and filled the whole place. Having raised it to a moderate height and paved it with stone, they covered the sacred cave beneath that great heap [Col. 0056D]. Then, as though nothing more remained for them to do, they built upon that ground a burial-place truly baleful to souls, constructing a dark cavern of dead images in honor of the licentious demon whom they call Venus. There they offered execrable sacrifices upon profane and unclean altars.

They thought that they would accomplish their purpose only if they buried the saving cave beneath such impure filth. Miserable men! They could not understand that it was altogether impossible for him who had won victory over death to leave this crime of theirs hidden—just as it is impossible for the sun, shining over the earth and pursuing its accustomed course in heaven, to escape the knowledge [Col. 0057A] of the whole human race. The power of our Savior, shining with a far more excellent light and illuminating not bodies, as the sun does, but the minds of human beings, was already filling the whole world with its rays.

Nevertheless, what impious and profane men had contrived against the truth remained for a long time. None among governors, commanders, or even emperors was found fit to overthrow so great a crime, save one ruler most acceptable to God, the king of all. Inspired by the divine Spirit, he was indignant that the aforesaid place had been deceitfully blocked by opponents with every kind of refuse and filth and entirely consigned to oblivion; and, judging that he ought not to yield to the wickedness of those who had devised this, he invoked the power of God his helper and commanded it to be cleansed. He considered that the very portion of the ground which the adversaries had defiled ought, through his work and service, to enjoy divine magnificence. As soon as this was commanded by the emperor, those works prepared for deception were immediately cast down from on high to the ground, and the buildings constructed to deceive people were demolished and scattered along with their statues and demons [Col. 0057B].

## CHAPTER XXVII. How Constantine commanded the building materials and ruins of the temple to be thrown very far away

Yet the emperor’s zeal did not rest here. He further commanded that the demolished materials and ruins be removed and thrown as far as possible beyond the boundaries of the region. This command too was immediately carried out. But even having proceeded thus far [Col. 0057C], the emperor did not consider himself satisfied. Rather, impelled by a kind of divine ardor, he ordered the place to be excavated to a great depth and the soil itself—defiled, as it were, by the expiatory rites of demons—together with the earth that had been dug out, to be carried as far away as possible.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The discovery of the most holy tomb

Without delay, this too was done as commanded. After another level of ground, namely the place lying at the bottom, had appeared, then beyond all expectation the august and most holy monument of the Lord’s resurrection itself shone forth. The cave—that which may truly be called the Holy of Holies—presented a kind of image of our Savior’s resurrection [Col. 0057D], when, after the darkness and concealment beneath which it had lain, it came again into the light and most clearly displayed to those who had gathered to see it the history of the miracles formerly performed there, testifying by the events themselves, which speak more clearly than any voice, to the resurrection of our Savior.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How he issued letters to governors and to Bishop Macarius concerning the building of the church

These things having been accomplished in this manner, the emperor immediately issued decrees and provided liberal funds, ordering a temple worthy of God to be erected with royal magnificence around the saving cave. For he had long before resolved upon this in his own mind, and with a certain divine zeal had foreseen what was to come [Col. 0058A]. He commanded the governors of the eastern provinces to carry out that great, spacious, and magnificent work, providing abundant expenditure. To the bishop who at that time governed the church of Jerusalem he gave a letter of this kind, in which he affirmed in the clearest words the doctrine of saving faith, writing as follows:

## CHAPTER XXX. Constantine’s letter to Macarius concerning the building of the Martyrium of our Savior

(See this letter, which occupies this and the following two chapters, below.)

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How the Church of the Savior was built, which the prophets had called the new Jerusalem

[Col. 0058B]

These things, then, were written by the emperor. But the result immediately followed the words themselves: at the very site of our Savior’s martyrion there was built a new Jerusalem, opposite that celebrated old Jerusalem which, after the impious killing of the Lord, had suffered final desolation and paid the penalty for the impiety of its inhabitants. Against this, therefore, the emperor raised with splendid adornment a trophy of the victory which our Savior had won over death. Perhaps this was that recent and new Jerusalem proclaimed in the prophecies of the prophets, concerning which so many praises are uttered in the sacred books by the divine Spirit himself.

First, therefore, he adorned that sacred cave as the head of the whole work: the divine monument [Col. 0058C], beside which an angel once shining with heavenly light had announced to all the regeneration manifested through the Savior.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Description of the structure of the holy tomb

This monument, I say, as the head of the whole work, the emperor’s magnificence first of all adorned with outstanding columns and the greatest splendor, illuminating it with ornaments of every kind.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Description of the courtyard and colonnades

From there he proceeded to a vast place open to the sky. Its ground he paved with shining stone [Col. 0058D], adding long colonnades on every side along three sides.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Description of the walls, roof, decoration, and gilding of the Basilica itself

For on that side opposite the cave and facing the rising sun stood the basilica: a work plainly admirable, raised to an immense height and extended to great length and breadth. Its interior was covered with variegated marble veneers; the exterior surface of its walls, adorned with polished stones carefully joined together, displayed an exceptional beauty, in appearance not at all inferior to marble.

As for the roof [Col. 0059A] and vaulted ceilings, he fortified the exterior roofing with lead, as with a very strong defense against winter rains. The interior roof, however, was made up of carved coffers and, like a vast sea, extended throughout the whole basilica in panels fitted together; covered entirely with the purest gold, it made the whole basilica gleam as though with rays of light.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Description of the double colonnades on both sides and the three eastern doors

Moreover, on each side double colonnades, both subterranean and rising above ground, matched the entire length of the basilica; their vaults were likewise varied with gold. Those in front [Col. 0059B] of the basilica were supported by huge columns; the inner ones were supported by doorposts richly decorated externally. Three doors, suitably arranged toward the eastern sun, received the crowds entering.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Description of the apse and the twelve columns with bowls

Opposite these doors was the apse (*hemisphaerium*), the crown of the entire work, extending to the very summit of the basilica. It was encircled by twelve columns, corresponding to the number of the holy apostles of our Savior. Their capitals were adorned with very large silver bowls, which the emperor had dedicated to his God as a most beautiful offering.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Description of the courtyard, halls, and entrances

[Col. 0059C]

Proceeding from here toward the approaches before the church, he placed an open court between them. In that place were first a courtyard, then colonnades on either side, and finally the gates of the courtyard. Beyond these, the entrances to the whole work, richly adorned in the very middle of the street where the market for goods was held, offered passersby from outside a view, not without a certain amazement, of the things visible within.

## CHAPTER XL. On the number of votive offerings

The emperor therefore built this church as a testimony to the saving resurrection [Col. 0059D], and adorned it with a magnificent and truly royal display. It cannot be told with how many and how great ornaments and votive offerings, some of gold and silver, others of gemstones, he beautified it in diverse ways. There is no leisure here to set forth individually their equipment, remarkable for supreme craftsmanship, size, number, and variety.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the building of the Church at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives

He also undertook to adorn with splendid magnificence other places in the same region made famous by two sacred caves. He honored appropriately the cave in which our Savior first manifested his divine presence [Col. 0060A] and deigned to be born in the flesh. In the other cave he honored the memory of the Lord’s ascension, which had formerly occurred on the summit of the mountain. In adorning these places with splendid decoration, he also consecrated to the everlasting remembrance of posterity the name of his mother, through whose labor and service so great a good was being provided for the human race.

## CHAPTER XLII. How Helena Augusta, Constantine’s mother, went to Bethlehem to pray and built these churches

For when she had resolved to render to God, the King of all, the due service of her pious devotion, and had determined that she ought to offer thanksgiving with supplications to God for her son, so great an emperor, and for his sons, the Caesars most beloved by God—her grandsons—although already advanced in age, she hastened with a youthful spirit. This woman of singular prudence went to visit the land worthy of veneration and to inspect the provinces, cities, and peoples of the East with a kind of royal care and foresight.

After she had venerated our Savior’s footsteps with the worship due to them, as prophetic speech had once foretold: “Let us worship,” it says, “at the place where his feet stood,” she immediately left to posterity also the fruit of her piety [Col. 0060B].

## CHAPTER XLIII. Again concerning the Church at Bethlehem

For she at once dedicated two churches to the God whom she had worshiped: one at the cave in which the Lord was born, and the other on the mountain from which he ascended into heaven. For Emmanuel, which means “God with us,” deigned to be born beneath the earth for our sake; and the place of his birth was called Bethlehem by the Hebrews. Therefore the Augusta, most devoted to God, adorned the childbirth of the Virgin God-bearer (*deipara Virgo*) with outstanding monuments, embellishing that sacred cave with every kind of decoration.

Not long afterward the emperor honored that same birth of the Lord with royal offerings, adding to his mother’s magnificence various monuments of gold and silver, and embroidered hangings [Col. 0060C]. Moreover, the emperor’s mother, in memory of the ascension of Christ, the Savior of all, erected lofty buildings upon the Mount of Olives, raising a sacred house with a church on the very summit of the mountain. Here, reliable history attests, Christ, the Savior of all, initiated his disciples into hidden mysteries in the cave itself. The emperor too worshiped the King of all in this place with various ornaments and votive offerings.

Thus Helena Augusta, the most devout mother of a devout emperor, dedicated to God her Savior these two august and most beautiful monuments, worthy of immortal remembrance, in the two sacred caves, as tokens of pious devotion, while her son supplied her with the resources of imperial power. Not long afterward the aged woman received a reward worthy of her labors. For, having passed the whole course of her life in supreme happiness up to the first threshold of old age, and having borne abundant fruits of the divine commandments both in word and deed [Col. 0061A], and consequently having lived free from suffering with complete health of mind and body, she at last obtained from God, even in this life, an end fitting for her piety and the recompense of good works.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On Helena’s greatness of spirit and beneficence

As she traveled throughout the whole East with royal magnificence, she heaped countless benefits upon cities and upon private persons who approached her, and distributed countless gifts with a generous hand to the military ranks. To the poor, the naked, and those deprived of every aid and consolation she gave very much, supplying money in abundance to some and clothing to others to cover the nakedness of their bodies. She also released some oppressed by chains or the hardships of the mines [Col. 0061B]; freed others crushed by the violence of the powerful; and recalled still others from exile.

## CHAPTER XLV. How Helena conducted herself devoutly in the churches

Although by works of this kind she won great glory for herself, she did not neglect piety toward God. She frequently attended church in the sight of all and adorned sacred buildings with outstanding ornaments, not despising even the chapels of the smallest towns. Thus one could see a woman altogether admirable, conducting herself in modest and becoming dress together with the rest of the multitude, and declaring her devotion toward God by every kind of pious work.

## CHAPTER XLVI. How, at eighty years old, having made her will, she died

[Col. 0061C]

Now when, after a sufficiently long span of life, she was called to a happier lot, at about her eightieth year, and was at the very threshold of death, she made a will and declared her final wishes. She left as heir her only son, the sole emperor and lord of the whole world, together with his most noble sons, the Caesars, her grandsons. Among each of them she divided the property which she possessed throughout the whole world.

Having made her will in this way, she closed her final day, with such a great son present and standing by her, cherishing his mother with every kind of filial service and embracing her hands. Thus it seemed to those of sound judgment that the most blessed woman did not die at all, but rather exchanged this perishable life [Col. 0061D] for immortal life. Her soul, therefore, transformed into an incorruptible and angelic substance, was taken up to God her Savior.

## CHAPTER XLVII. How Constantine buried his mother and how he honored her while she lived

Her body, however, was accorded by no means ordinary honor. Conveyed to the royal city with a vast company of attendants, it was there placed in a royal tomb. Thus the emperor’s mother ended her life: a woman most worthy of everlasting remembrance, both because of the religious acts by which she distinguished herself [Col. 0062A] and because of that most excellent and admirable offspring born from her. On account of his other qualities, but above all on account of his devotion toward his mother, it is fitting to proclaim him blessed.

For although she had not previously been a worshiper of God, he made her so pious and devout that she seemed to have been instructed by the common Savior of all. He adorned her with royal honors to such a degree that, in all the provinces, she was called Augusta and empress by both pagans and soldiers, and gold coins were stamped with her image. Constantine had even granted her control over the royal treasuries, to use them as she chose and according to the judgment of her own mind. In this respect too he made his mother conspicuous and blessed in the judgment of all.

Therefore, among the matters relevant to making her memory illustrious [Col. 0062B], we have not without reason included these acts which the emperor, out of his exceptional filial devotion, performed in honor of his mother, while obeying the divine laws that enjoin upon children the duties owed to parents. Such most beautiful works the emperor built in Palestine, as we have said. In the other provinces too, building new churches from their foundations, he made them far more august than those that had existed before.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. How he built martyria at Constantinople and abolished all worship of idols

When he undertook to raise the city bearing his name to the highest glory, he adorned it with very many houses of prayer, with most spacious martyria, and with most splendid buildings constructed partly in the suburbs and partly within the city itself [Col. 0062C]. In this way he both honored the memory of the martyrs and consecrated his city to the God of the martyrs.

Finally, wholly aflame with the wisdom of God, he desired the city which he had resolved to distinguish with the appellation of his own name to be so completely free from every worship of idols that nowhere in it should images of false gods be worshiped in temples; that no altars stained with the blood of victims, no sacrifices consumed by fire, no festivals of demons, nor any of those things customary among the superstitious should be seen or performed there.

## CHAPTER XLIX. The sign of the cross in the palace and the image of Daniel in the fountains

You could see, therefore, in the fountains situated in the middle of the forum [Col. 0062D], images of the Good Shepherd, well known to those versed in the divine oracles, and likewise an image of Daniel with lions, rendered in bronze and gleaming with gold leaf. So great a love for the divine majesty had occupied the emperor’s mind that, in the most elevated chamber of the whole palace, upon a great panel spread in the middle of the gilded ceiling, he caused the sign of the Lord’s passion to be fixed, fashioned from gold and precious stones. This, it seems to me, the most devout ruler established as a defense and safeguard for the empire.

## CHAPTER L. On the churches which he built at Nicomedia and elsewhere

With these ornaments he adorned the city bearing his name [Col. 0063A]. He adorned the chief city of Bithynia with the monument of a most beautiful and magnificent church, erecting at his own expense in honor of his Savior trophies also in that place, commemorating the victory he had won over the enemies and adversaries of God. In the remaining provinces too, he made the foremost and most famous cities illustrious through the magnificence of houses of prayer—for example, the metropolis of the entire East, the city which derived its name from Antiochus.

There, as at the summit of all the provinces of that region, he consecrated to God a singular work, remarkable alike for size and beauty. He enclosed the whole church externally with a very long circuit. Within, he raised the basilica itself to the greatest height, constructed in an octagonal form and surrounded on every side by very many rooms and halls, both subterranean spaces and upper chambers [Col. 0063B]. This basilica he adorned most abundantly with a great deal of gold and bronze and other precious materials.

## CHAPTER LI. That he built a church at the place called Mamre

These, then, are the most outstanding monuments which the emperor dedicated to God. But when he learned that the very Savior who had lately dwelt upon earth had long before manifested the presence of his divinity in Palestine to certain men most devoted to God, beside the oak called Mamre, he commanded a basilica to be built there also. Accordingly, imperial authority was sent to the governors of the provinces, letters being given to each of them, ordering them to hasten [Col. 0063C] to bring the work entrusted to them to completion.

To us who write this history, moreover, he sent an exposition full of wisdom. A copy of it seems to me fitting to insert here, so that the care and diligence of this ruler most devoted to God may be more certainly known. Rebuking us, therefore, for what he had learned was being done in the aforesaid place, he wrote the following word for word.

## CHAPTER LII. Constantine’s letter to Macarius concerning Mamre

(See this letter, contained in this and the following chapter, below.)

## CHAPTER LIV. Temples and images everywhere destroyed
These things the emperor pursued with every effort for the glory of Christ’s saving power [Col. 0063D], and in this manner he did not cease to worship God his Saviour. Yet he also strove by every means to refute the superstitious error of the gentiles. Accordingly, in certain cities the porticoes of temples were stripped bare, their doors removed by imperial command; the roofs of others were broken up, their tiles taken away. The revered bronze statues of some, which the error of the ancestors had for many years grandly vaunted, were set before every eye in the public squares of the city named after the emperor. Thus, exposed to the ridicule and contempt of spectators, here stood Pythian Apollo, there Sminthean Apollo, and in the circus itself the Delphic tripods; while the Heliconian Muses stood in the palace. Finally, that city bearing the emperor’s name [Col. 0064A] was everywhere filled with bronze images, fashioned with elegant workmanship and formerly dedicated throughout the several provinces.

Men afflicted with the disease of error had, over a long period, vainly offered hundreds of victims and burnt offerings to these, as though to gods. But at last they learned wisdom, when the emperor began to employ them for the amusement and diversion of onlookers. He punished images fashioned from gold, however, in another manner. For, observing that the ignorant multitude, like children, vainly trembled before such masks of error fashioned from gold and silver, he judged that they ought to be removed from their midst. They were, as it were, fragments of stones cast before the feet of people walking in the midst of darkness; and henceforth the level and even course of the royal road ought to be opened for all [Col. 0064B].

Having considered this, he did not think that military force or an army was needed to suppress these things. One or two of his household officials sufficed for the task; with scarcely more than a nod, he dispatched them throughout all the provinces. Trusting both in the emperor’s piety and in their own reverence toward God, they made their way through densely gathered crowds and populous multitudes, abolishing everywhere, in cities and in the countryside, the ancient error. First, not without laughter and disgrace, they compelled the priests themselves to bring forth their gods from certain dark recesses. Then, stripping those same gods of their outward adornment, they exposed to the view of all the inward ugliness concealed beneath the painted image. Finally [Col. 0064C], after scraping off the useful material, casting it into the fire, and melting it down, they set aside and retained for themselves whatever appeared useful and necessary. Whatever was superfluous and altogether useless, they left to the superstitious as a perpetual memorial of disgrace.

The prince, worthy of every admiration, performed another action as well. At the same time that images of the dead, made of precious material, were being despoiled in the manner described, he had the remaining images, made of bronze, brought together. Thus those gods celebrated by the delirious fables of the Greeks were dragged along bound with ropes.

## CHAPTER LV. Destruction of the temple at Aphaca in Phoenicia, and the abolition of sexual immorality.

[Col. 0064D]

After this, the emperor, as though raising a brilliant torch from some watchtower, looked about on every side with royal eyes, to see whether any hidden remnants of error might perhaps still survive. And just as an eagle, borne aloft to the very heavens upon its wings and endowed with exceedingly sharp sight, easily looks down from on high upon things far distant on earth, so he, while residing in the palace of his most beautiful city, perceived as though from a watchtower a destructive snare of souls lying hidden in Phoenicia.

It was a sacred grove and temple, situated neither in the midst of a city nor in a forum or street, such as many structures ambitiously erected for ornament may be seen in cities; but remote, far from crossroads and public ways, consecrated to the foulest demon, whom they call Venus, on part of the summit of Mount Lebanon near Aphaca [Col. 0065A]. There was there a kind of school of wickedness, open to every impure person and to those who had corrupted their bodies with every license. Certain effeminate persons—more properly called women than men—having renounced the dignity of their sex and submitting to feminine practices, propitiated the demon. Moreover, unlawful intercourse of women, adulteries, and foul and impious crimes were committed in that temple, as though in a place devoid of every law and governor. No one observed what was being done there, because no grave and modest man dared to approach it.

But the crimes perpetrated there could not remain hidden even from the greatest emperor. When he himself had inspected them with the eye of imperial foresight [Col. 0065B], he judged that such a temple was unworthy even to be illuminated by the sun’s rays. Accordingly, he ordered it, together with its images and votive offerings, wholly razed to its foundations. At once, therefore, the contrivances of wanton error were scattered at the emperor’s command, the soldiers devoting their labour to cleansing the place. And those previously given over to licentiousness, terrified by the emperor’s threats, learned to behave modestly. In the same manner those superstitious gentiles, who imagine themselves very wise, were taught to behave more modestly. They too learned in fact their own foolishness and vanity.

## CHAPTER LVI. Destruction of the temple of Aesculapius at Aegae.

[Col. 0065C]

For when the greatest and most widespread error of superstition had seized vain people concerning that Cilician demon, and almost countless persons admired him as a saviour and physician—for he would sometimes appear to those sleeping in the temple, sometimes cure the illnesses of the sick (yet he was in truth a deceiver of souls, drawing people easily deceived away from the true Saviour and dragging them into the false error of impiety)—the emperor, in accordance with his custom and settled purpose, since he had set before himself the worship of God, who is both zealous and the true Saviour, ordered this temple also to be levelled to the ground.

Without delay, at a single nod of the emperor, the temple which eminent philosophers had so greatly revered lay upon the ground, overthrown by military force [Col. 0065D]; and with the temple fell the very being hidden within it—not a demon or a god, but a certain deceiver of souls, who for a very long time had led people into fraud. Thus he who promised to free others from evils and calamities found no remedy by which to protect himself, no more than when the tales pretend that he was struck by lightning. But the deeds of our emperor, above all acceptable to God, were not similarly fabulous. Rather, by the manifest power and might of the Saviour himself, this temple, together with the rest, was uprooted so completely that not even a trace of the former madness remained there.

## CHAPTER LVII. How the gentiles, when their images had been condemned, acknowledged God.

[Col. 0066A]

Therefore all who had formerly been devoted to the superstitious worship of demons, when they saw with their own eyes their error refuted and beheld everywhere the devastation of all temples and images, some turned to the saving teaching of Christ. Others, although unwilling to do the same, nevertheless condemned the rites of their ancestors as vain and empty, and ridiculed those whom they had formerly considered gods. Indeed, how could they think otherwise when, beneath the external appearance of images, they saw such filth hidden within? For there were either bones of corpses, or dried skulls secretly introduced by impostors’ deceit; or filthy rags full of shameful [Col. 0066B] uncleanness; or, finally, heaps of hay and straw.

When they saw these things amassed within the inner chambers of lifeless images, they reproached both their own extreme madness and that of their parents—especially when they observed that within those sanctuaries and images there was no inhabitant: no demon uttering oracles, no god declaring future events, as they had previously persuaded themselves, indeed not even a dim and shadowy apparition. Therefore every cave, however dark, and every most hidden recess lay readily open to those sent by the emperor; places formerly entered and inaccessible alike, even the innermost chambers of temples, were trodden by soldiers’ feet. Thus the blindness of mind that had long held all the gentiles entangled was discovered and laid open to the eyes of all [Col. 0066C].

## CHAPTER LVIII. How, after destroying Venus’s temple at Heliopolis, he first built a church there.

And these things deserve to be reckoned among the emperor’s illustrious deeds, as do those which he established individually in different provinces. Such was what we saw accomplished by him in Heliopolis, a city of Phoenicia. In that city the gentiles, who attach obscene lust to the name of the goddess Venus, had granted their wives and daughters permission to admit sexual violation with impunity. But now the emperor issued a new law full of modesty, providing that none of the practices formerly customary should henceforth be presumed.

He also sent them written instructions, as one appointed by God especially for this purpose: to imbue all mortals with the precepts of self-control [Col. 0066D]. Therefore he did not disdain to address even these people by letter, exhorting them to come speedily to the knowledge of God. Immediately he added actions corresponding to his words, constructing in that very place a great basilica for Christian worship. Thus what had nowhere been heard from the remotest memory of humankind was then for the first time fulfilled in actual deed: a city of persons devoted to the superstitious worship of demons was deemed worthy to possess God’s Church, presbyters and deacons; and a bishop consecrated to the supreme God of all presided over the people of that place.

Moreover, foreseeing with provident mind that very many would come to faith in Christ, the emperor bestowed abundant gifts there for the relief of the poor [Col. 0067A]. In this manner too he attracted and invited people to the saving teaching, almost uttering the very words of Paul: “Whether through pretext or through truth, Christ is proclaimed.”

## CHAPTER LIX. On the disturbance stirred up at Antioch concerning Eustathius.

But truly, while on account of these things all were living in the greatest joy and the Church of God was being exalted everywhere among all nations in every way, again the envy of the demon, which always lays snares for good things, began to rise against so great a prosperity of our affairs. It supposed that the emperor, provoked by our disturbances and insolence, would perhaps at last become alienated from us in mind [Col. 0067B].

Accordingly, having kindled a great conflagration, it filled the Church of Antioch with certain tragic calamities, so that the whole city almost came to total ruin. For the people of the Church were divided into two parts, while the rest of the city, together with the magistrates and soldiers, was in hostile dissension among itself. Matters had come to swords, had not divine providence and fear of the emperor restrained the people’s violence.

Here again the prince’s clemency, like that of the Saviour and physician of souls, applied the medicine of speech to sick people. He sent there one of those held in esteem around him, a most faithful man honoured with the rank of count, addressing the people as it were through a conciliatory embassy. And in letter after letter he exhorted them [Col. 0067C] to seek peace, teaching them how to act in a manner consistent with divine religion. At last he persuaded them, and excused them in his letters, asserting that he had heard in person the very author of the whole sedition.

I would have placed here these letters of his, filled with no ordinary teaching and usefulness, had they not branded the guilty with a mark of disgrace. Therefore I shall omit them for the present, since I have no intention whatever of renewing the memory of evils. I shall insert only those which he wrote, rejoicing and congratulating them concerning the peace and concord of others. In these letters he exhorts them not to claim for themselves the bishop of another place, through whose intervention they had made peace among themselves; but rather, according to the custom of the Church, to elect as bishop the one whom the common Saviour of all [Col. 0067D] himself has designated. He writes both to the people and to the bishops as follows.

## CHAPTER LX. Three letters of Constantine: the first to the Antiochenes, that they should not draw Eusebius away from Caesarea; the second to Eusebius, concerning his refusal of Antioch; the third to the Synod of Antioch, that Eusebius should not be removed from Caesarea.

(See below the letters contained in this and the two following chapters.)

## CHAPTER LXIII. How he endeavoured to eradicate heresies.

In giving these commands to the bishops of the Churches, the emperor exhorted them to do everything for the advancement of the praise of divine religion. But after removing dissensions [Col. 0068A] and restoring God’s Church to concord and a harmonious unanimity of teaching, he proceeded to judge that another kind of impious people—namely, a pestilential poison of the human race—must be eliminated. These were certain destructive people who devastated cities under a false appearance of modesty and gravity. The Saviour somewhere calls them false prophets and ravening wolves, in these words: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves. By their fruits you will know them.”

Accordingly, by sending an order to the provincial governors, he drove away and expelled this class of people. Beyond the law itself, the emperor also sent them personally a saving instruction, exhorting them to repent as soon as possible; for God’s Church would be for them a harbour of salvation [Col. 0068B]. Hear, then, how he addresses them in his letter.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Constantine’s ordinance against heretics.

(See below the ordinance contained in this and the following chapter.)

## CHAPTER LXVI. How, after impious books were discovered among heretics, very many of them returned to the Catholic Church.

Thus the dens of heretics were scattered by imperial command, and the beasts themselves—that is, the authors of their impiety—were driven into flight. Of those who had been deceived by them, some, terrified by the emperor’s threats, crept into the Church with a certain spurious and counterfeit disposition, cleverly dissembling for the time. For since the law ordered their books to be sought out, all who practised forbidden arts were discovered. For this reason they resorted to pretence, doing everything in order to secure safety for themselves.

Others, however, sincerely and wholeheartedly passed over to the hope of better things. The bishops of the Churches, after a careful examination of both groups, drove far away those who tried to approach deceitfully under sheep’s skins [Col. 0068C]. But those acting sincerely, after testing them for some time, admitted them, following suitable proof, to the number of those allowed into the sacred assemblies. Such, then, was the treatment of the abominable heretics.

Those, however, who displayed no impiety in their doctrines but had been separated from the common fellowship through the fault of certain schismatics, were received into the Church without delay. Thus they returned in groups, as from a foreign land; they regained their homeland by right of return and acknowledged the Church as their mother. Having wandered far from her for a very long time, they at last returned to her joyful and glad after a long interval. The members of the whole body were joined to one another by a common bond, and a single structure grew together. The one catholic Church of God alone shone forth in harmonious unity, with no association of heretics or schismatics left anywhere among the nations [Col. 0068D]. And of this illustrious achievement our emperor, most acceptable to God—the only one among all emperors who have ever existed—was the author.
