## CHAPTER I. How he honoured very many persons with gifts and promotions.

[Col. 0069A]

While the emperor was accomplishing so many and such great things for the enlargement and glory of God’s Church, administering all matters with the purpose that the teaching of our Saviour might receive the highest praise from all, he by no means neglected civil affairs in the meantime. Rather, in this sphere too, he never ceased to benefit the inhabitants of all provinces with diverse and continuous acts of generosity: sometimes publicly displaying toward all a kind of fatherly concern; sometimes privately adorning individual members of his household with various dignities; and, with abundant generosity of spirit, bestowing everything upon everyone.

No one who sought a benefit from the emperor ever failed of his aim [Col. 0069B], nor did anyone who had hoped for some good from him depart disappointed. Some obtained money; others estates. Some were adorned with consular rank, others with senatorial dignity. Certain persons were appointed consulars, and more were appointed governors. Of counts, some were made of the first rank, some of the second [Col. 0070A], and some of the third. Countless others received the rank of *perfectissimus* and many other such titles of dignity. For the emperor had devised various ranks in order to honour the greater number.

## CHAPTER II. Remission of a fourth part of taxes.

How greatly he strove to provide the whole human race with a cheerful and tranquil life may be seen even from this one example, most useful above all to human life and extended generally to all, which is still celebrated in everyone’s common speech. From the annual taxes paid on account of land, he remitted a fourth part and gave it to landowners. Thus, if one calculates this annual remission [Col. 0070B], the produce of the estates was free from tax payment every fourth year. This measure, established by law and confirmed for the future, afforded not only those then living but also their children and descendants a perpetual beneficence of the emperor, never to be erased by any oblivion.

## CHAPTER III. Equalization and relief of tax assessments.

[Col. 0071A]

Moreover, since some criticized the land registers and tax assessments made by previous emperors and complained that their estates were excessively burdened, this prince too, obeying the laws of justice, sent assessors to remove the injury from those petitioning him.

## CHAPTER IV. How, in financial cases, he gave from his own resources to those who had lost their case.

Furthermore, whenever he had pronounced judgment between two litigants, lest perhaps the party who lost the case should leave more sorrowful than the one in whose favour the suit had been decided, he gave from his own property to the defeated party—sometimes estates, sometimes money. Thus he ensured that the defeated party returned home no less glad than the party who had won, since he had been deemed worthy to come before the prince. For he considered that no person who had stood before so great a prince ought ever to depart gloomy and sad. Therefore each litigant left the court with a cheerful and smiling countenance; and all admired the emperor’s greatness of spirit [Col. 0071B].

## CHAPTER V. The subjugation of the Scythians, conquered through the sign of the cross.

What need is there to mention, as though incidentally, how he brought barbarian peoples under the dominion of the Roman Empire? How he was the first to put beneath the yoke the nations of the Scythians and Sarmatians, previously unsubdued and accustomed never to obey anyone; and how by force he brought them to acknowledge the Romans as masters even against their will? Previous emperors paid tribute to the Scythians, and the Romans were in fact subject to barbarians, paying an annual sum. But the emperor could not endure this indignity, nor did he think it fitting for a victorious prince to pay what earlier princes had paid.

Therefore, relying on the aid of his Saviour and bringing against them also the triumphant sign and trophy, he quickly subdued them all. He overcame the resisting and obstinate by arms; the rest he softened through prudent embassies, leading them from a savage life without laws to a humane and civilized one. In this manner the Scythians at last learned to obey the Romans [Col. 0071C].

## CHAPTER VI. The Sarmatians subdued when slaves rebelled against their masters.

[Col. 0071D]

God himself placed the Sarmatians beneath Constantine’s feet, and subdued people swollen with barbarian arrogance in the following manner. When the Scythians made war upon them, the Sarmatians armed their slaves to resist the enemy. After victory over the enemy had been won, the slaves began to turn their weapons against their masters and drove them all from their ancestral homes. These people found no harbour of safety other than Constantine. Accustomed to save people, he received them all within the boundaries of the Roman Empire. Those fit for military service [Col. 0072A] he enrolled in the forces; to the rest he assigned lands to cultivate for the necessities of life. Thus they themselves acknowledged that their calamity had turned out fortunately for them, since they had exchanged barbarian savagery for Roman freedom. In this way God added many barbarian peoples to his empire.

## CHAPTER VII. Embassies from various barbarians and gifts bestowed upon them by the emperor.

For envoys continually came to him from every region, offering him whatever gifts were most precious among their own peoples. We ourselves at times saw before the palace gates various figures and costumes of barbarians standing in order: their clothing and ornament were different, as were their hair and beards [Col. 0072B]. Their appearance was grim, barbarous, and fear-inspiring; their bodies extraordinarily tall. Some had ruddy faces, others were whiter than snow itself; others had some intermediate complexion.

Among the barbarians mentioned were Blemmyes, Indians, and Ethiopians, who, as Homer says, live divided in two at the extremity of the earth. Each separately brought to the emperor those things esteemed among his own people, as we commonly see them portrayed in paintings. Some brought golden crowns; others diadems set with gems; others boys conspicuous for blond hair; some barbarian garments woven with gold and flowers; these horses, those shields, long spears, arrows, and bows. By these gifts they signified that they offered the emperor obedience and an alliance in arms, should he wish it.

Receiving and setting aside the offerings made by each, he in turn gave them such abundant gifts that in a moment he made rich those who had brought presents [Col. 0072C]. He also adorned the noblest among them with Roman dignities, so that many of them, forgetting any return to their homeland, preferred to remain here among us.

## CHAPTER VIII. That he wrote to the king of Persia, who had sent envoys to him, on behalf of Christians living there.

Furthermore, when the king of the Persians also sought acquaintance with Constantine through envoys and sent him gifts as tokens of peace and friendship, intending thereby to make a treaty with him, the emperor likewise displayed an exceptional greatness of spirit. He far surpassed in magnificence of gifts the man who had first honoured him. And when he learned that the Churches of God were numerous among the Persians and that a great multitude of people had been gathered within Christ’s sheepfolds, he was greatly pleased by this report. Like a common protector and guardian of all people living everywhere, he extended his providential concern even to those regions, labouring for the good of all [Col. 0072D].

## CHAPTER IX. Letter of Constantine to Sapor, king of the Persians, confessing God and Christ with the highest piety.

(See below the letter contained in this and the following four chapters.)

## CHAPTER XIV. How peace was granted to Christians through Constantine’s continual prayers.

[Col. 0073A]

In this manner, while all nations everywhere were governed, as by the skill of one helmsman, and gladly embraced the empire and religion of God’s servant, and no one any longer disturbed the Roman Empire, all thereafter lived a tranquil and peaceful life. The emperor, believing that the prayers of pious people contributed greatly to the welfare of the state, considered that he must necessarily secure these prayers for himself. Therefore he himself supplicated and implored God’s aid, and commanded the leaders of the Churches to offer prayers to God for him.

## CHAPTER XV. That he ordered himself to be portrayed on coins and images in the posture of prayer.

[Col. 0073B]

How great a force and power of divine faith had taken root in his mind may easily be inferred from this one fact: he ordered himself to be represented on gold coins with his face lifted toward heaven and his hands outstretched in the manner of one praying. Coins of this type circulated throughout the entire Roman world. In the imperial palace itself, beside certain doors, he was depicted in images placed at the very summit of the vestibule, standing with eyes fixed upon heaven and hands spread out in the fashion of prayer.

## CHAPTER XVI. That by law he prohibited the placing of his images in temples of idols.

[Col. 0073C]

Thus he represented himself as supplicating God even in painted panels. Indeed, by an enacted law he prohibited his images from being dedicated in temples of idols, lest they should be defiled, even merely in outward appearance, by the error of forbidden superstition.

## CHAPTER XVII. Prayers in the palace and reading of the sacred Scriptures.

But anyone who wishes to attend closely will perceive deeds much more august than these: how he established in the palace a kind of Church of God. He surpassed all enrolled in that church in diligence and eagerness; taking the sacred codices into his hands, he meditated attentively upon the oracles uttered by God. Afterwards [Col. 0073D], with the whole company of courtiers, he recited the customary prayers.

## CHAPTER XVIII. He orders the Lord’s Day and Friday to be honoured.

He appointed as a day appropriate for prayer that which is first and chief among the rest, and which is truly the Lord’s Day and saving day. Furthermore, he appointed as guardians of the entire household deacons and ministers consecrated to God, adorned with gravity of life and other virtues. Finally, his faithful guards and attendants, armed with the weapons of goodwill and faith, had the emperor himself as their teacher in piety; they likewise honoured the saving and Lord’s Day, and on that day offered to God prayers pleasing to the emperor [Col. 0074A].

The most blessed prince also urged all other mortals to do the same, since he above all desired gradually to make all people worshippers of God. For this reason he commanded all living under Roman rule to rest on the Lord’s Day, and likewise to honour the day before the Sabbath, in memory, it seems, of the things said to have been done on those days by the common Saviour of all. Moreover, while he trained the entire army in the religious observance of the saving day called by the name of light and sun, he granted those who had embraced the divinely inspired faith leisure and opportunity to devote themselves, without any impediment, to prayers according to the custom and practice of God’s Church [Col. 0074B].

## CHAPTER XIX. How he taught even gentile soldiers to pray on Sundays.

For the rest, who had not yet received instruction in the doctrine of the divine faith, he prescribed by another law that on Sundays they should proceed into an open field and, at a signal, all together offer to God the prayer which they had previously learned. For they were not to place their confidence in spears and armour, nor in bodily strength, but were to acknowledge the supreme God of all, the author of all good things and indeed of victory itself; and were to render him their customary prayers, with their hands raised toward heaven and with the eyes of their minds lifted higher, even to the King of heaven himself [Col. 0074C]. In their prayers they were to invoke him as the author of victory, their saviour, guardian, and helper. He himself gave all the soldiers a form of prayer, ordering them all to recite it in the Latin language as follows.

## CHAPTER XX. Form of prayer given by Constantine to the soldiers

“We acknowledge you alone as God; we confess you as King; we invoke you as our helper. It is by your gift that we have gained victories and overcome our enemies. For the benefits already bestowed we now give you thanks, and from you we hope for those to come. We all beseech you and ask that you preserve for us our Emperor Constantine, together with his most pious children, safe and victorious for a very long time.”

He ordered these things to be done by the military units on the day of the sun [Sunday], and these words to be uttered by them while praying [Col. 0074D].

## CHAPTER XXI. He orders the sign of the Lord’s cross to be represented on the soldiers’ arms

Moreover, he ordered the sign of the saving trophy to be engraved even upon the arms themselves. And he commanded that before the army drawn up under arms there should be carried not golden standards and images, as had formerly been customary, but the trophy of the cross alone.

## CHAPTER XXII. His zeal for prayer and observance of the Paschal feast

As one initiated into the sacred mysteries, he would daily, at fixed hours, shut himself away in the innermost chambers of his palace [Col. 0075A]; removing all witnesses, he conversed alone with God alone. Prostrating himself on his knees, he sought in supplicatory prayer those things which he needed.

During the very days of the saving festival, intensifying the rigor of disciplines and exercises, and gathering all the powers of mind and body, he performed the office of priest and hierophant. He himself led all others in the celebration of the feast. He transformed the sacred vigil into the brightness of day, having, through those assigned to the task, columns of candles lit throughout the whole city. Lamps too, once kindled, illuminated every place far and wide, so that this mystical vigil was made more splendid than even the brightest day.

As soon as daylight came, desiring to imitate the beneficence of our Saviour [Col. 0075B], he stretched forth a generous hand to all nations, provinces, and peoples, giving rich gifts to everyone.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How he prohibited the worship of idols but honoured the feasts of the martyrs

In this way, then, he offered worship to his God. Moreover, throughout the Roman Empire, among common people as well as soldiers, the doors of image-worship were closed and every kind of sacrifice was forbidden. A law was also sent to provincial governors, requiring that they too should honour the Lord’s day. By the emperor’s command they observed the feast-days of the martyrs and duly honoured the seasons of ecclesiastical festivals. All these things were done with the emperor’s greatest joy [Col. 0075C].

## CHAPTER XXIV. His statement that he was, as it were, bishop of external affairs

Accordingly, when on one occasion he was entertaining bishops at a banquet, he said—not inappropriately—that he too was a bishop, using approximately these words in our presence: “You are bishops, indeed, of matters within the Church; but I have been appointed by God as bishop of matters conducted outside it.” Therefore, forming counsels consistent with his words, he governed all those subject to his empire with episcopal concern, and encouraged them by every means in his power to pursue true piety.

## CHAPTER XXV. The prohibition of sacrifices and initiations, and the abolition of gladiators and the impure priests of the Nile

[Col. 0075D]

For this reason, by frequent laws and enactments, he forbade everyone to sacrifice to images, consult diviners with inquisitive intent, erect images, or perform secret rites; finally, he forbade cities to be polluted by the bloody spectacles of gladiators.

And since the Egyptians and Alexandrians had been accustomed to worship their river through the ministry of certain effeminate men, a law was issued to them also, requiring that the entire race of androgynes be removed as something spurious, and that those afflicted with the disease of such indecency should nowhere be seen. But because superstitious persons thought that thereafter the Nile would by no means irrigate their fields as usual, God, favouring the emperor’s law, brought about precisely the opposite of what they expected [Col. 0076A]. Those who polluted the cities by their obscenity indeed ceased to exist; but the river itself, as though the whole region had been cleansed and purified, flowed more abundantly than ever before and, overflowing with a fuller supply of waters, irrigated all the fields. In this way it taught and admonished foolish people in actual fact that they ought to reject the impure, while favourable events should be ascribed to God alone, the author of all good things.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The amendment of the law against the childless, and of the law concerning wills

[Col. 0076B]

But truly, since acts of this kind, almost beyond number, were performed by the emperor in individual provinces, anyone who undertook to record them more fully would certainly have abundant material. Such, for example, was his replacing many old laws with new ones directed toward greater holiness. The character of this may be made clear by one or two examples.

The ancient laws punished childless persons by depriving them of their paternal inheritance. This law was indeed exceedingly harsh, since it penalized persons lacking children as though guilty of some crime. But the emperor, abolishing this rule of law, enacted a holy and religious law. Those, he said, who sinned voluntarily and deliberately ought to be punished suitably. Yet nature has denied children to many persons who, though they desired numerous offspring, remained childless because of bodily infirmity [Col. 0076C]. Others lived without children, not because they did not wish to have children as successors, but because, out of a most ardent love of philosophy, they shunned intercourse with women and embraced that form of continence.

Moreover, many women consecrated to the worship of God cultivated chastity and complete virginity, dedicating both mind and body to a life most pure and holy. What then? Ought this to be regarded as deserving punishment, or rather admiration and approval? For even the attempt itself deserves the highest praise; while its accomplishment exceeds the powers of human nature. Thus those to whom natural infirmity denied children, however earnestly they desired them, ought to be treated with compassion rather than punished [Col. 0076D]. One who is led by the love of a higher philosophy is worthy not of a fine but of universal admiration. In this manner the emperor corrected that law with the greatest equity.

Furthermore, ancient laws had provided that persons dying and, so to speak, drawing their last breath should draw up their wills scrupulously in certain prescribed words; formulas, solemnities, and words which had to be added were stipulated. Consequently, very many frauds were committed in order to frustrate the intention of the dying. When the emperor observed this, he amended this law also, establishing that dying persons might make a will in plain words and in whatever form of speech, and declare their final intention in any written document [Col. 0077A]; or, if they preferred to testify without writing, they might do so provided only that suitable witnesses were present who could preserve the truth without falsehood.

## CHAPTER XXVII. His law that Jews should not possess Christian slaves; that the decrees of councils should be valid; and other matters

He also enacted a law that no Christian should be enslaved by Jews. For it was not right, he held, that those redeemed by the Lord should be subjected to the yoke of servitude under the slayers of the prophets and of the Lord. If any slave of the Christian religion were found in the possession of a Jew, he ordered that the slave should be granted freedom and the Jew fined money.

He also confirmed by his authority the decisions of bishops promulgated in councils [Col. 0077B], so that provincial governors were not permitted to overturn episcopal decrees. For priests of God were to be preferred to any judge. He promulgated almost countless laws of this kind for his subjects; to set them out in a separate volume, in order that the emperor’s prudence might be perceived in this respect also, would require greater leisure.

Why should I now recount how, devoting himself to the supreme God of all, he carefully sought from dawn until evening those among every class of people upon whom he might confer benefits, and showed himself equitable and humane toward all, doing good to everyone?

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Gifts bestowed upon churches, and money distributed to virgins and the poor

[Col. 0077C]

Above all, however, he bestowed very many gifts upon the churches of God, now granting estates, now provisions for the support of the poor, widows, and orphans. Finally, by attentive provision he took care that clothing should be made for naked persons. But above all others he honoured most highly those who had devoted themselves wholly to divine philosophy. He almost venerated the most holy company of God’s perpetual virgins, since he firmly believed that God himself, to whom they had consecrated themselves, dwelt in their minds.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Constantine’s night studies and public addresses

He sometimes spent whole nights awake [Col. 0077D], himself instructing his mind by meditation on divine matters. In his leisure he applied himself to writing speeches and delivered frequent public addresses, believing it to be his duty to govern the peoples subject to him by the precepts of reason and make his rule an empire of reason.

Accordingly, he himself summoned an audience. Yet an innumerable crowd assembled to hear the emperor philosophize. If, while speaking, an occasion happened to arise for discussing theology, he immediately stood with a grave expression and lowered voice, and appeared to initiate his hearers into the mysteries of divine doctrine with singular reverence and modesty. When all applauded him with auspicious cries, he signalled to them to lift their eyes upward [Col. 0078A] and render distinctive worship and admiration to that one supreme King of all.

He arranged the divisions of his addresses in this manner: first he laid, as it were, a foundation in refuting the error of the pagans in worshipping many gods, proving by decisive arguments that their superstition was mere fraud and a bulwark of impiety. After this he discoursed on the sole sovereignty of God. Then he spoke concerning providence, by which both the universe and individual things are governed. From there he advanced to the saving dispensation, showing that this too had been accomplished by a necessary and fitting rationale. Continuing the course of his discourse, he undertook a discussion of divine judgment.

At this point he reproved the minds of his hearers with the greatest severity, denouncing plunderers, violent men, and those who had enslaved themselves to an insatiable desire for money [Col. 0078B]. He even scourged with the whip, as it were, of his speech certain members of his own household who were present, compelling them, driven by the stings of conscience, to lower their eyes. In a clear voice he solemnly declared to them that they would render to God an account of their actions. The governance of the world, he said, had been entrusted by God to himself; and he, following the example of the divine power, had entrusted to them the administration of portions of the empire; but all would eventually render an account of their deeds to the supreme King.

These were the things he continually declared; these he impressed upon them; with these teachings he imbued them. He himself, trusting in the sincerity of his faith, both thought and proclaimed such things. But they remained unteachable and, as it were, deaf to these most excellent instructions: with their tongues indeed, applause, and acclamations they approved what was said, yet in fact, through insatiable greed, disregarded it [Col. 0078C].

## CHAPTER XXX. How he marked out the dimensions of a grave for a certain greedy man, to shame him

Accordingly, on one occasion he took a member of his household by the hand and addressed him in these words: “How long, you there, are we to extend our greed?” Then, with the spear which he held in his hands, he traced on the ground the stature of a human body: “Even if,” he said, “you acquired for yourself all the riches of this age, indeed the whole world, you will carry away no more land than this space which I have marked out—if even this is granted you.”

Yet the most blessed emperor, though he both did and said these things, recalled no one from his former wickedness [Col. 0078D]. Rather, the actual outcome of events proved most clearly that the emperor’s warnings resembled divine oracles rather than mere words.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How he was mocked because of excessive clemency

Since there was no fear of capital punishment to deter evil men from crimes—the emperor being wholly inclined to clemency, and none of the provincial governors restraining offences—it came about that the public administration incurred no slight reproach. Whether rightly or wrongly, let each person decide as seems fit [Col. 0079A]. Meanwhile, let it be permitted to me to set forth the truth of the matter in writing.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Constantine’s discourse addressed to the assembly of saints

The emperor composed his discourses in Latin. Interpreters, to whom this task had been assigned, afterwards translated them into Greek. From these discourses translated into Greek I shall append to this work, by way of example, one which he entitled *To the Assembly of Saints*, calling that work a nocturnal composition for the Church of God, lest perhaps our testimony concerning these matters should seem to anyone an empty and groundless tale.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How he listened standing to Eusebius’ panegyrical addresses on the Saviour’s tomb

[Col. 0079B]

The remarkable act performed by the emperor in our presence seems to me by no means to deserve omission. Trusting in his extraordinary piety toward God, we once asked that he would be willing to hear us speak concerning the tomb of our Saviour; he most gladly lent us his ears. And although a great multitude of hearers stood around within the imperial palace itself, he stood with the others and listened to the discourse.

Although we asked him to sit upon the imperial throne placed nearby, he could never be induced to sit. Rather, attentively weighing what was said, he confirmed by his own testimony the truth of theological doctrines [Col. 0079C]. When we had already consumed much time and the speech had become rather long, we wished to conclude. But he encouraged us to continue until the discourse had been brought to its end. When we again begged him to sit, he gently resisted and sought to persuade us, at one time saying that it was improper to listen in a relaxed and comfortable manner when a discussion concerning God was undertaken; at another, affirming that this was useful and beneficial to himself. “For it is pious and religious,” he said, “to hear matters divine while standing.”

When these things had been completed, we returned home and resumed our customary studies and exercises.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. His letter to Eusebius concerning Pascha and the sacred books

[Col. 0079D]

Ever providing for the churches of God with provident mind, he wrote us a letter concerning the production of sacred books and the Paschal feast. For after we had dedicated to him a certain book in which the hidden meaning of that feast was expounded, the following letters of his show how, in return, he honoured us with his response.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Two letters of Constantine to Eusebius: the first concerning Eusebius’ discourse on Pascha; the second concerning the production of sacred books

(See below the letters contained in this and the following chapter.)

## CHAPTER XXXVII. How the books were produced

[Col. 0080A]

These were the emperor’s instructions. His words were immediately followed by the work itself, when we sent him, in splendidly ornamented volumes, sets of three and four [books or quires; *terniones et quaterniones*]. This will be attested by the emperor’s second reply. In it, having perhaps been informed that the city of Constantia in our region, formerly devoted to image-worship, had been moved by a certain impulse of the most holy religion to cast off its former error of superstition, he expressed his joy and his strong approval of the deed.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. How the Market-place of the Gazaeans became a city because of Christianity and was named Constantia

[Col. 0080B]

By this time, indeed, the Palestinian city of Constantia, having embraced the saving religion, was adorned with the prerogative of highest honour, both from God and from the emperor. For it received the name of a city, though it had previously been a village; and its former name was changed for the more distinguished name of the emperor’s most religious sister.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How a city in Phoenicia became Constantina, and idols were destroyed and churches built in other cities

The same was done in many places. For example, in a certain city of Phoenicia which is called after the emperor: its inhabitants cast innumerable images into the fire and embraced the saving religion [Col. 0080C]. In the other provinces too, innumerable persons, crowding together to the saving knowledge of God, destroyed throughout cities and countryside various images crafted from every kind of material, which they had formerly regarded as sacred. They demolished their temples and shrines, raised to immense height, with no one ordering them to do so. Building churches from their foundations, they changed their former judgment—or rather, their error.

But to recount individually the deeds of the emperor beloved of God belongs not so much to us as to those who were granted continual association with him. Since we have briefly set forth in this work what came to our knowledge, we shall pass on to the final period of his life.

## CHAPTER XL. After making his three sons Caesars at his three decennial celebrations, he celebrated at Jerusalem the dedication of the Martyrium

[Col. 0080D]

The thirtieth year of his reign was now being completed. His three sons had been proclaimed partners in his rule at different times. The first, bearing his father’s name, received this honour about the tenth year of his father’s reign. The second, bearing his grandfather’s name, was declared Caesar around the twentieth anniversary of his parent’s reign. The third, Constans—whose name signifies presence and stability—was raised to this rank around the thirtieth year of his father’s rule.

Thus, having raised up three sons beloved of God in a certain likeness of the Trinity, and having admitted the same into partnership in the empire at each successive decade [Col. 0081A], he considered the time of his tricennalia especially fitting for giving thanks to the supreme King of all. He judged it best, moreover, to celebrate the dedication of the martyrial church which he had built at Jerusalem with exceptional zeal and magnificence.

## CHAPTER XLI. Amid these events he ordered a synod to be held at Tyre over certain controversies in Egypt

But the envious demon, enemy of all good things, like some dense cloud setting itself against the brightest rays of the sun, attempted to disturb the splendour of this celebration, again convulsing the condition of the Egyptian churches by its contentions [Col. 0081B]. Yet the emperor beloved of God, gathering once more a synod of very many bishops, like a divine army led out to battle, set it against the malicious demon. He ordered bishops from all Egypt and Libya, and likewise from Asia and Europe, to assemble: first, to settle the controversy; then, to attend the dedication of the aforesaid martyrium.

Accordingly, he commanded them to resolve the disputes on their way in the city that is the capital of all Phoenicia. For it was not permissible that they should approach divine worship in mutual discord of mind, since divine law forbids those at variance to offer their gifts to God before they have settled their disputes with one another and pledged peace and friendship. The emperor turned these saving teachings of our Saviour over continually in his mind [Col. 0081C], and by a letter whose terms are as follows urged them to undertake the proposed task with complete concord and harmony of mind.

## CHAPTER XLII. Constantine’s letter to the synod assembled at Tyre

(See below this letter.)

## CHAPTER XLIII. How bishops from every province assembled for the dedication of the Church at Jerusalem

While these commands were being carried out, another messenger from the emperor arrived. Presenting imperial letters, he urged the synod, without delay, to hasten as quickly as possible to Jerusalem [Col. 0081D]. Therefore all departed from the province of Phoenicia and began to make their way by the public post to the appointed destination.

At last the entire place was filled with a great assembly of God, as distinguished bishops from every province came together at Jerusalem. The Macedonians had sent the bishop who held the first rank among them; and the Pannonians and Moesians had dispatched the choicest flower of God’s recruits and the chief ornament of their nation. There was also present an ornament of the Persian bishops, a holy man highly trained in the divine Scriptures. The Bithynians and Thracians likewise adorned the assembly by their presence. Nor were the most eminent bishops of Cilicia absent. Those of Cappadocia who excelled in learning and eloquence shone forth in the midst of the gathering [Col. 0082A]. In addition, all Syria, Mesopotamia, Phoenicia, Arabia, and Palestine itself; Egypt also, Libya, and those who inhabit the Thebaid—all gathered together and formed that great choir of God. An innumerable multitude of people from all the provinces followed them.

There was, moreover, for all these persons the attendance appropriate to a royal appearance; certain men of proven worth were sent from the imperial palace, to enhance the festival with expenses supplied by the emperor.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How they were received by the notary Marianus, money distributed to the poor, and gifts given to the Church

Over all these matters presided a man especially useful to the emperor, distinguished for faith, religion, and knowledge of sacred letters [Col. 0082B]. During the time of the tyrants he had become renowned through many confessions in defence of piety; nor without merit was the arrangement of these affairs entrusted to him.

Obeying the emperor’s commands with complete integrity, he honourably received the assembly of bishops with exceptional kindness and with most magnificent meals and banquets. To needy and naked persons, and to an innumerable multitude of poor people of both sexes suffering want of food and other necessities, he distributed a great quantity of money and very much clothing. Finally, he magnificently adorned the entire basilica with royal gifts. Such was the service which he performed.

## CHAPTER XLV. The bishops’ addresses at the gatherings, including those of Eusebius himself, the author of this work

[Col. 0082C]

The priests of God adorned the festival partly with prayers, partly with discourses. Some celebrated in praise the religious emperor’s kindness toward the Saviour of all and described in an address the magnificence of the martyrium. Others provided their hearers with a spiritual banquet by presenting the sacred doctrines of theology adapted to the present celebration. Some interpreted readings from the sacred volumes, bringing to light their hidden and mystical meanings. Those unable to aspire to these things propitiated God with unbloody sacrifices and mystical oblations, humbly offering prayers to God for the common peace, for the Church of God, for the emperor—the author of so many benefits—and for his most pious children.

There too we, to whom benefits greater than our merits had fallen [Col. 0082D], adorned the solemnity by delivering various public addresses: now describing in writing the beauty and magnificence of the imperial structure; now interpreting suitably and appropriately the meaning of prophetic oracles in relation to the present forms and images. Thus the solemnity of the dedication was celebrated with the greatest rejoicing during the emperor’s own tricennalia.

## CHAPTER XLVI. How he later recited before the emperor his description of the Martyrium and his discourse on the tricennalia

As for the form of the basilica of the Saviour, the appearance of the sacred cave, the beauty and elegance of the work, and the many gifts fashioned partly from gold and silver and partly from precious stones—we set all these forth in a separate work dedicated to the emperor [Col. 0083A]. We shall suitably publish that book at the end of this work, adding also that discourse on the tricennalia which, shortly afterward, having gone to Constantinople, we recited before the emperor himself, then for the second time proclaiming in the palace with praises the supreme God and Lord of all.

As the emperor beloved of God heard it, he seemed to leap for joy. He himself acknowledged this at the conclusion of the address, when he entertained the bishops who were present at a banquet and honoured them in every manner.

## CHAPTER XLVII. The Synod of Nicaea occurred at Constantine’s vicennalia, while the dedication of the Jerusalem basilica occurred at his tricennalia

[Col. 0083B]

The emperor assembled at Jerusalem this second synod, the greatest of all those known to us, after that first synod which he had convened in the most renowned city of Bithynia. The first, however, was triumphal: at the twentieth anniversary of his reign, in the city named Victory, he paid prayers and vows for his victory over enemies. This latter adorned the festival of his tricennalia, when the emperor dedicated, as a kind of peace-offering to God, the martyrium at the very monument of our Saviour, God the author of all good things.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. How he received someone’s excessive praises with displeasure

[Col. 0083C]

After all these matters had been concluded and the emperor’s virtue was celebrated in everyone’s speeches, one of the priests was not afraid to pronounce him blessed in his presence: because, he said, he had been deemed worthy both to attain in this life the supreme rule of the whole Roman world and to reign in the age to come together with the Son of God. The emperor bore such words with great displeasure, warning the man not to presume to use such language, but rather to make supplication to God that he might be accounted worthy, both in this life and in the future, to be numbered among God’s servants.

## CHAPTER XLIX. The marriage of his son Constantius Caesar

When the thirtieth year of his reign had been completed, he celebrated the marriage of his second son, having long before celebrated the marriage of the eldest [Col. 0083D]. Thus feasts and banquets were provided, the emperor himself leading out his son the bridegroom and receiving, in splendid display, the gatherings of men separately from those of women. Most splendid gifts were also distributed among the cities and peoples.

## CHAPTER L. Embassy and gifts sent by the Indians

At the same time ambassadors arrived from the Indians who inhabit the region toward the rising sun, bringing gifts: various jewels of exceptional brilliance and value, and beasts altogether unlike ours in shape and nature. Presenting all these to the emperor, they testified that his authority extended even to the Ocean [Col. 0084A], and that the princes and lesser kings of the Indian people, having erected paintings and statues in his honour, acknowledged and professed him as their emperor and king.

At the very beginning of his rule, the Britons, situated by the western Ocean, were the first of all to submit themselves to his authority; now the Indians dwelling toward the rising sun did the same.

## CHAPTER LI. How Constantine divided the empire among his three sons and trained them in both the art of rule and the duties of piety

Having thus brought both extremities of the world under his power, he divided the whole of the empire among his three sons, distributing it among his relatives as a kind of paternal inheritance. He gave the ancestral portion to the eldest; to the second, the empire of the East; and to the third son, the middle portion of the realm between these two [Col. 0084B].

Desiring to prepare for his children the best inheritance, and one especially useful for the salvation of the soul, he sowed the seeds of piety in their minds: partly instructing them himself through divine teachings, partly appointing for them teachers who were men of proven religion. He also set over them teachers most skilled in secular disciplines. Some trained them in the knowledge of military art, others in the precepts of civil affairs, and others in jurisprudence.

Each was assigned a royal retinue: shield-bearers, spearmen, protectores, military legions and units, and their commanders—centurions, tribunes, and generals—men whom their father had found most experienced in military affairs and endowed with special loyalty and goodwill toward his sons.

## CHAPTER LII. How, when they had entered manhood, he taught them piety

[Col. 0084C]

While the Caesars were still of tender age, ministers and advisers attached to them governed the state. But when they had reached manhood, the instruction of their father alone was sufficient for them. Sometimes he urged them in person, through private admonitions, to emulate him, setting before them his own piety as an example for imitation; sometimes he conveyed imperial instructions to them while absent by letters.

The first and greatest of these instructions was that they should prefer knowledge and worship of God, the supreme King of all, to all riches and even to imperial power itself. Finally, he allowed them independently to conduct whatever was useful for the state [Col. 0084D]; and before all else he expressly commanded that they should care for the Church of God and openly profess themselves Christians.

In this manner he trained his sons. They, however, stimulated not so much by their father’s admonitions as by their own inclination, surpassed their parent’s commands with eager spirit. They always kept the observance of divine religion before their eyes and maintained the holy rites of the Church in the very palace with their entire household. For this too had been a work of paternal foresight: that he entrusted to his sons no household servants or companions except Christians. The commanders of the chief units, to whom the care of public affairs had been entrusted, were likewise worshippers of God. For he trusted in persons professing faith in God as in certain most secure walls [Col. 0085A].

When the most blessed emperor had arranged these matters also in this way, God, dispenser of all good things, judging that, all affairs of the state having been excellently ordered by the emperor, the fitting time had finally come for him to be transferred to a better lot, imposed the fated end of his life.

## CHAPTER LIII. After ruling for thirty-two years and living more than sixty, he was always in sound health

He completed the course of his reign in thirty-two years, apart from a few months and days; the span of his life was nearly twice as long. At that age his body was free from every disease and blemish, untouched by any infirmity, and stronger than any youthful body [Col. 0085B]. It was handsome in appearance and powerful for every activity. Thus he practised military exercises, rode, walked, fought, raised trophies over conquered enemies, and won those bloodless victories in his customary way.

## CHAPTER LIV. Those who abused his exceptional humanity for greed and feigned piety

Likewise, his mind had reached the highest summit of human perfection, being adorned with every excellent quality, and especially with humanity. Yet many criticized him for this, because of the excessive wickedness of bad men, who ascribed their own depravity to the emperor’s forbearance.

Certainly we ourselves saw that two vices had become especially prevalent at that time: the violence of utterly wicked men, inflamed by insatiable greed, who afflicted nearly all mortals; and the deceitful pretence of those who craftily entered the Church and falsely, and only outwardly, bore the name of Christians [Col. 0085C]. But the emperor’s innate humanity and goodness, and his sincerity of faith and character, led him to believe in the feigned appearance of piety displayed by those persons who were considered Christians and who, with crafty minds, simulated sincere goodwill toward him.

Since he trusted himself to them, he perhaps sometimes stumbled into actions not entirely becoming; the envy of the malicious demon sprinkling this, as it were, as a stain upon his other praises.

## CHAPTER LV. How until the very last day of his life he wrote discourses
Divine justice, however, not long afterward visited those men with the punishment they deserved. But the Emperor had so trained his mind in the knowledge of discourse that, until the very last day of his life, he continued, as was his custom, to compose speeches, deliver addresses, and instil divine teachings into his hearers; likewise he constantly enacted laws, now on civil affairs, now on military matters; in short, he devised everything for the advantage and benefit of humankind. Nor should this by any means be passed over in silence: when the final day of his life was already impending, he delivered in his customary audience chamber a kind of funeral oration. [Col. 0086A] And, having prolonged his discourse at some length, he spoke in it concerning the immortality of souls, those who had lived piously, and the blessings laid up with God Himself for the friends of God. Conversely, by many arguments he clearly demonstrated what end awaited those who had adopted a contrary way of seeing, describing the ruin and destruction of the impious. As he asserted this gravely and earnestly, he seemed to be reproaching those nearest and dearest to him. Indeed, he asked one of them, puffed up with a vain opinion of wisdom, what he thought of what had been said. The man testified that all of it was most true and, though unwillingly, highly praised the arguments against the worship of many gods. By delivering such addresses to his intimate associates before his death, he appeared himself to be [Col. 0086B] smoothing his way toward a better life.

## CHAPTER LVI. How, setting out for the Persian war, he took bishops with him and prepared a tent in the likeness of a church.

This too must by no means be passed over: about this time, when news had been brought of a movement among the barbarians dwelling toward the rising sun, he declared that this victory over them still remained for him, and resolved to wage war against the Persians. Having decided to do this, he summoned military forces from every quarter; and he shared with the bishops who were with him his plan for the expedition, foreseeing with prudent judgment that men necessary for divine worship ought continually to accompany him. They, for their part, affirmed that they would follow [Col. 0086C] him gladly and would not leave him, but would serve as soldiers with him and fight alongside him by continual prayers to God. Greatly delighted by this reply, he indicated to them the route by which they were to proceed. He then prepared for the purposes of this war a tent, elaborately furnished in the likeness of a church, in which he had determined to offer prayers to God, the author of victory, together with the bishops.

## CHAPTER LVII. How, having received Persian envoys, he kept vigil with the others on the feast day of Easter.

Meanwhile, when the Persians learned that the Emperor was preparing war and greatly feared an encounter with him, they sent envoys to request peace from him. [Col. 0086D] Accordingly, the Emperor, a most ardent lover of peace, graciously received the Persian embassy and willingly concluded peace and friendship with them. The great solemnity of the Paschal feast was now at hand; in it the Emperor, paying his vows to God, kept vigil together with the others.

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the construction at Constantinople of the martyrium of the Apostles.

After this he began to build, in memory of the Apostles, a martyrium in the city named after himself. Having raised the whole church to an immense height, he made it splendid with varied kinds of stone, covering it from floor to vault with marble facing. Moreover, [Col. 0087A] covering the vault with coffered work of the finest workmanship, he overlaid it entirely with gold. Above, bronze laid in place of roof tiles provided the whole building with protection against rain. This likewise gleamed, being covered with abundant gold, so that it dazzled the eyes of those looking from afar when the sun’s rays were reflected from the bronze. The entire roofline was enclosed by certain latticed reliefs, skilfully fashioned of bronze and gold.

## CHAPTER LIX. Description of the same martyrium.

The church itself was thus adorned by the Emperor’s great zeal. Around the church was an immense court, open and exposed to the sky above. Along its four sides were porticoes [Col. 0087B] joined to one another, enclosing the court situated in the middle together with the church itself. In addition there were basilicas, baths, lodging-houses, and very many other dwellings for the use of those who guarded the place, attached to the porticoes and matching their length.

## CHAPTER LX. That he also built a tomb for himself in that church.

The Emperor dedicated all these things with the intention of commending to posterity forever the memory of the Apostles of our Saviour. But he built that sanctuary with another purpose also in mind, one at first obscure but finally made known to all at the end. For he had designated this place for himself after death, foreseeing with incredible eagerness of faith that his body might, after death, receive a common appellation [Col. 0087C] with the Apostles; that is, that even in death he might share in the prayers to be celebrated there in honour of the Apostles. Therefore, having erected there twelve chests, like certain sacred columns, in honour and memory of the apostolic college, he placed his own sarcophagus in the middle, with six chests of the Apostles arranged on either side. And in the place where his own body was to be fittingly laid after death, he made most careful provision. Having long beforehand arranged these matters with prudent foresight, he dedicated the sanctuary to the Apostles, firmly persuading himself that their memorial would bring no small benefit to his soul. Nor did God disappoint him of his desire and expectation. For, after he had performed the first observances of the Paschal feast and had made the very day of our [Col. 0087D] Saviour joyful and glad both for himself and for all others, God—by whose aid he carried out all things—at last saw fit, in due season, to transfer him, still occupied with such matters and persevering in such works until the end of life, to a better lot.

## CHAPTER LXI. The Emperor’s illness and prayers at Helenopolis; also concerning his baptism.

At first an irregular bodily indisposition, and afterwards illness, overtook him. He therefore went to the hot springs of his own city; from there he was conveyed to Helenopolis, a city named after his mother. There, in the [Col. 0088A] church of the martyrs, he remained for a long time and offered supplications and prayers to God. When he sensed that his final day of life was now imminent, he judged that the time had at last come to expiate the sins of his whole life, most firmly believing that whatever he had sinned through human frailty was to be wholly removed by the efficacy of the sacred words and the saving washing. Reflecting thus within himself, he fell prostrate on the ground with bent knee and humbly begged pardon from God, confessing his sins in the very martyrium. There, for the first time, he was judged worthy to receive the laying on of hands with solemn prayer. From there he went to the suburbs of Nicomedia and, summoning the bishops, spoke to them as follows.

## CHAPTER LXII. The words in which Constantine asked the bishops to confer baptism upon him.

[Col. 0088B]

> “This is the time that I have long hoped for, when I burned with incredible desire and longed, with all my prayers, to attain salvation in God. Now is the time for us also to receive that sign which confers immortality; now is the time to become partakers of the saving seal. I had indeed formerly resolved to do this in the River Jordan, in which the Saviour Himself is remembered to have received washing as an example for us. But God, who best knows what is beneficial for us, deigns to grant us this same thing in this place. Therefore let every doubt be removed. For if God, the arbiter of life and death, wills that I should live here longer, and if it has once been decreed that henceforth I be mingled with the people of God and, received into the Church, become with all the rest a participant in prayers, [Col. 0088C] I promise that I shall prescribe for myself such rules of life as are worthy of God.”

When he had said this, they performed the divine ceremonies according to the solemn rite; and, having imposed on him whatever was necessary, they made him a participant in the sacred mysteries. Thus Constantine alone of all emperors who had ever existed was reborn and perfected in the martyr-shrines of Christ; endowed with the divine seal, he exulted in spirit, was renewed, and filled with divine light. In his soul he derived the greatest pleasure from the excellence of faith; and, astonished, he marvelled at the most manifest greatness of divine power. After everything had been duly completed, he was clothed in white and royal garments, shining like light, and reclined upon a most white bed; [Col. 0088D] nor was he willing any longer to touch the purple.

## CHAPTER LXIII. How after baptism he praised God.

After this, raising his voice more loudly, he gave thanks to God in prayer; and, when his prayer was ended, he added:

> “Now I know that I am truly blessed; now that I have been made worthy of immortal life; now that I have been made a partaker of divine light.”

He also said that those deprived of such great blessings were wretched and unhappy. When tribunes and commanders of the military forces entered, lamenting in their turn that he was leaving them bereft and praying for a longer life for him, he answered them too that only now had he attained true life, and that he alone knew fully [Col. 0089A] how great were the blessings of which he had become a partaker. Therefore, he said, he was hastening and would delay his departure to his God by no evasion. He then arranged each matter according to his own judgment. To the Romans dwelling in the imperial city he bequeathed certain annual gifts. To his own children he left the empire as a paternal inheritance, settling everything as seemed good to him.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Constantine’s death, at noon on the feast day of Pentecost.

All these things occurred during that great solemnity of venerable and most sacred Pentecost, which, adorned by the sevenfold number of weeks, is marked by unity. Sacred Scripture testifies that on it both the common Saviour’s ascent [Col. 0089B] into heaven and the descent of the Holy Spirit to earth took place. Having thus received the things we have mentioned during that solemnity, the Emperor at last, on its final day—one which, if anyone called it the greatest of all festivals, would in my judgment be by no means mistaken—departed to the Lord about noon. He left to mortals the mortal part of himself, but joined to his God that part of the soul endowed with understanding and love of God. Such was Constantine’s end of life. But let us proceed to the rest.

## CHAPTER LXV. The lamentation of the soldiers and tribunes.

The protectores and the entire company of his guards immediately tore their garments, threw themselves face down upon the ground, struck their heads against the earth, and uttered wailings and lamentations amid beating of the breast and cries. They called upon him as lord and Emperor—not as a lord, but as most dutiful children call upon a father. The tribunes and centurions proclaimed him their saviour, protector, and benefactor. The rest of the army, like flocks, longed for their best shepherd with every mark of restraint and reverence. The populace too ran throughout the whole city, abundantly expressing the deepest grief of their hearts in cries and shouts. Many, from grief, appeared like men stunned; each regarding this as his own particular calamity and lamenting himself, since the common good of all had been taken from this life.

## CHAPTER LXVI. How the body was brought from Nicomedia to Constantinople, into the palace.

[Col. 0089D]

After this, the soldiers lifted the body from the bed, placed it in a golden sarcophagus, covered it with a purple garment, and conveyed it to Constantinople. There they placed it aloft in the principal chamber of the imperial palace. Then, with lamps lit everywhere upon golden lampstands, there was presented to those who looked on a marvellous spectacle, such as had never been seen on earth in the case of any mortal since the creation of the world. For in the middle chamber of the royal palace the Emperor’s corpse lay aloft in a coffin or bier, adorned with royal insignia—namely, purple and diadem—while many guards standing around kept watch by night and day.

## CHAPTER LXVII. How even after death he was honoured by the comites and the rest, as though alive.

[Col. 0090A]

Moreover, the commanders of the whole army, the comites, and the other judges and magistrates who had previously been accustomed to pay homage to the Emperor, in no way altering their former observance, entered at fixed hours and, bending the knee, saluted the Emperor laid in the sarcophagus after his death as though alive and breathing. After those leading men, the senators and all dignitaries who entered did the same in turn. Then an innumerable multitude of common people, together with children and women, came to behold this sight. These things were continually done over a long period, the soldiers having decreed that the body should lie and be guarded in this manner [Col. 0090B] until the Emperor’s sons arrived and themselves conducted their father’s funeral with due honour. Thus the most blessed ruler alone continued to rule even after death; all affairs were administered in the customary manner as though he still lived. This honour was granted by God to him alone within human memory. For because he alone, beyond other emperors, had honoured God, king of all, and Christ His Son by acts of every kind, he alone was deservedly honoured in this way. The supreme God of all deigned to grant him this: that his corpse should retain sovereignty upon earth. By this sign God clearly indicated to those who were not altogether dull and stupid that his soul enjoyed everlasting and immortal dominion. And these things were done in this manner.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. How, by the judgment of the army, his sons were named Augusti.

[Col. 0090C]

Meanwhile, the tribunes sent to the Caesars certain men selected from the military units, who had formerly been esteemed by the ruler for their loyalty and goodwill, to report to them everything that had occurred. This was what they did at that time. But all armies everywhere, as if moved by some divine spirit, as soon as Constantine’s death was announced, unanimously resolved—as though the greatest Emperor were still surviving—that they would have no ruler of the Roman Empire other than his children. Not long afterwards, they wished them to be called not Caesars but Augusti, a name which is, as it were, a badge of supreme sovereignty. The armies communicated their votes and acclamations to one another by letters; and the unanimous agreement of the legions became known at one and the same moment to all wherever they were.

## CHAPTER LXIX. Rome’s mourning for Constantine’s death, and the images decreed for him.

In the imperial city, when the senate and people of Rome learned of the Emperor’s death, regarding the grievous news as more bitter than any calamity, they imposed no limit upon mourning. The baths and markets were closed, as were public shows and all the other pleasures of life that people at leisure [Col. 0091A] are accustomed to pursue. Those who had formerly abandoned themselves to luxuries now walked mournfully through the streets. All proclaimed the Emperor blessed, beloved of God, and altogether most worthy of empire. Nor did they declare these things merely in empty words: by dedicating images, they honoured the dead man as though he survived. In these images, having depicted a likeness of heaven on a panel, they painted him resting above the heavenly vaults in an ethereal dwelling. They even named his children alone emperors and Augusti, without the association of anyone else; and with loud cries demanded that they should possess their Emperor’s body and lay it in the imperial city.

## CHAPTER LXX. How the body was laid to rest at Constantinople by Constantius.

[Col. 0091B]

The Romans too paid this honour to the ruler honoured by God. When the second of his sons arrived for his father’s funeral, he conveyed it into the city named after his father, himself leading the funeral procession. Military units, arranged in companies and ranks, went before. Behind followed an innumerable multitude of people. Spearmen and shield-bearers surrounded the Emperor’s body in the middle. When they arrived at the church of the Apostles of our Saviour, they laid down the sarcophagus there. In this manner the new Emperor Constantius, both by his arrival and by his other services, rendered honour to his father and performed the funeral rites as was fitting.

## CHAPTER LXXI. The liturgy celebrated in the martyrium of the Apostles at Constantine’s funeral.

[Col. 0091C]

When Constantius had departed with the military units, the ministers of God came forth into the midst with the crowds and the whole body of the faithful, and performed the rites of divine worship with prayers. The blessed ruler, lying on a lofty platform, was then celebrated with praises. An innumerable people, together with God’s priests, offered prayers to God for the Emperor’s soul, not without groaning and tears, rendering to the pious ruler a most welcome service. In this too God declared His lasting goodwill toward His servant: He granted succession to the paternal empire to his most beloved and legitimate sons; and He granted him the place he had most earnestly desired, beside the memorial of the Apostles, [Col. 0091D] so that the dwelling-place of that most blessed soul might enjoy participation in the apostolic name and honour; might be joined to the people of God in the church; and might be counted worthy to partake of divine rites, the mystical sacrifice, and the communion of holy prayers. He himself, moreover, retaining sovereignty even after death and governing the whole world as though restored to life, Victor Maximus Augustus, continued to rule the commonwealth under his own name.

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the phoenix bird.

Not like that Egyptian bird which, being the only one of its kind, is said to die upon a heap of spices, offering itself as though a victim, and then soon to be reborn from its own ashes, borne aloft on wings and seen in the same form as before; but rather after the example of his Saviour, who, like a grain of wheat sown, spreading Himself from one seed into many, brought forth an ear through God’s help and blessing and filled the whole world with His fruits. In this manner the most blessed ruler became many from one through the succession of his children, so that in every province images of him are erected for honour together with his sons, and the familiar name of Constantine is used even after his death.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. How on coins they depicted Constantine as ascending to heaven.

[Col. 0092B]

Moreover, coins were struck in this form: on the obverse displaying the blessed ruler with his head veiled; on the reverse, seated like a charioteer in a four-horse chariot, and received up to the heavenly beings by a hand extended to him from heaven.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. That, having worshipped God, he was deservedly also honoured by God.

By setting before our eyes these wonders in Constantine, who alone among all former emperors had openly professed himself a Christian, the supreme God of all sufficiently and more than sufficiently declared how great the difference was between [Col. 0092C] those who had been worthy to worship Himself and Christ His Son, and those who had embraced the opposite sect and opinion. Having made war upon the Church of God, they made God their adversary and enemy. Certainly the destruction of each of them demonstrated by the surest proof how great was the divine displeasure against them, just as, in Constantine’s death, certain pledges, as it were, of God’s goodwill toward him appeared openly to all.

## CHAPTER LXXV. That Constantine surpassed all preceding emperors in piety.

Since he alone among Roman emperors worshipped God, king of all, with a certain outstanding piety; [Col. 0092D] since he alone openly proclaimed Christ’s teaching to all; since he increased God’s Church in honour and glory as no one had done before; and since he alone overthrew the error of those who worshipped many gods and refuted all rites and forms of such superstition: he alone also deserved to attain, both in this life and after death, such things as no one is reported ever to have attained, either among Greeks or among barbarians. Nor can anyone among those ancient Romans, from the latest times back to the earliest, be reckoned who is comparable with this Constantine of ours.

[Col. 0093]

# PART ONE OF ALL THE WRITINGS OF CONSTANTINE THE GREAT, COMPRISING ALL EXTANT DECREES AND CONSTITUTIONS.

(ALL ARE EXTRACTED FROM THE EXCELLENT EDITION OF THE THEODOSIAN CODE BY GUSTAV HAENEL, UNLESS A DIFFERENT SOURCE IS EXPRESSLY NOTED.)

In the year of the Lord 312. Constantine Augustus, consul for the second time, and Licinius Augustus, consul for the second time.

[Col. 0093A]

[Note: [Col. 0093B] a Aur. Lugd. erroneously has *Realtionibus* (“reports/referrals”).]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Claudius Plautianus, Corrector of Lucania and Bruttii.

[Note: [Col. 0093B] b Cuj. 2, 2* has *Brutiorum*.]

After other matters: Concerning the few issues which cannot be decided by judicial [Note: [Col. 0093B] c Fol. 179 [ [Col. 0093B] a Aur. Lugd. erroneously has *Realtionibus*.] codex 4.] decision, you must consult Our Majesty, without interrupting Our occupations, since litigants retain the lawful option of appealing from a judgment. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, [Note: [Col. 0093C] d Aur. Lugd. has June, in error.] at Trier. [Note: [Col. 0093C] e I have added the year on the authority of Go., who nevertheless in the *Chronicle* gives: “Given on the third day before the Kalends of January,” from chapter 1 ff. of this title. In either place either “sixth” or “third” must have been written.] (312). Received on the eighth day before the Ides of February at Regio [Note: [Col. 0093C] f Be. has *Regii*.], under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the third time and Licinius for the third time (313).

## ON APPEALS AND THEIR PENALTIES, AND ON CONSULTATIONS.

[Note: [Col. 0093C] g 4 has *appelationibus*. 21, Sich.: *appellatione*. Some codices omit “and their penalties.” 32 and the Code of Justinian omit it.]

[Note: [Col. 0093C] h 6–8, 12, 17, 20, 21, 33, 36, 38, 40, 42 have *consolationibus* or *consolacionibus* (“consolations”). 44, in the index rubric: *consulacionibus*. 10, 14, 18: *conlationibus*. Sich.: *Collationibus*.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Claudius Plautianus, Corrector of Lucania and Bruttii.

[Note: [Col. 0093C] i Cuj. 2, 2* has *Bruttiorum*.]

If in a civil matter, after hearing the actions of both parties, [Col. 0093B] you have pronounced judgment and intend to refer the matter to Our cognizance, [Note: [Col. 0093C] j Go.–Be.: *utriusque* (“of each party”); Go. emends to *utrinque* (“on both sides”). Til.–Cuj. 2*, from codex 4, has *utrisque*, which I have restored.] you shall order a copy of the consultation to be issued to the litigants in the official records within ten days, so that, if anyone thinks your referral insufficient or contrary, [Note: [Col. 0093C] k Codex 4 has feminine *relaturam*; an earlier hand corrected it to masculine *relaturum*.] he may likewise submit to you in the official records, within five days, a petition in refutation, after [Note: [Col. 0093C] l Fol. 180 [ [Col. 0093B] b Cuj. 2, 2* has *Brutiorum*.] codex 4.] you have furnished him a copy of your consultation. [Note: [Col. 0093C] m Aur. [Note: [Col. 0094C] a See chapter 1 above in this title, note.]

[Note: [Col. 0094C] b The subscription in chapter 1 above in this title is fuller.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to the council of the province of Africa. A husband, without a mandate, shall have free authority to intervene in his wife’s affairs, subject to formal surety and other required observance, so that women may not, under the pretext of pursuing litigation, be assailed with disrespectful intrusion to the dishonour of matronly modesty and compelled to attend meetings of men or courts of justice. But if he has accepted a mandate, even though he is her husband, he must execute only what the issued procuration has prescribed. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of March at Hadrumetum, under the second consulship of Constantine Augustus and Licinius Caesar (312). (From the Code of Justinian.)

Emperor Constantine Augustus to all provincials. Executors appointed by any judge to recover debts—those debts sought under civil law—shall not remove from estates, as pledges, enslaved farmworkers, plough-oxen, or agricultural implements, since the payment of taxes is thereby delayed. If, therefore, any intermediary, creditor, prefect of a district or village, or decurion is discovered in this matter, he shall be subjected to such punishment as the judge, after assessment, determines. Given on the third day before the Nones of June at Sirmium, under the consulship of Constantine Augustus and Licinius (312). (From the Code of Justinian.)

In the year of the Lord 313. Constantine Augustus, consul for the third time, and Licinius Augustus, consul for the third time.

[Col. 0094C]

He therefore thinks Heraclea in Gaul is intended and that either May should be read instead of March, or, more correctly, the consuls of 315 should be given (Constantine IV and Licinius IV, Augusti, consuls); he assigns it in the *Chronicle* to 315. To that excellent man I wish to offer the thanks due to him, though I shall never be able to match the greatness of the benefit received. This leaf ends with the words *saepius habita hor…*, below, title IX of this book, chapter 2.] wrote [Note: [Col. 0097C] h In codex 4 *quam* is absent, but was added by an ancient hand. The Code of Justinian and some of its editions have *ante conscribebamus*. Cf. Go. on this chapter, note h, who proposes *quamquam antea scribebamus*, against P. Faber, who emended *quae ante cum scribebamus.]—“with the adjoining property, slaves, livestock, produce, and every right belonging to it”—so that [Note: [Col. 0097C] i Some editions of the Code of Justinian read *et*. Go. rightly defends *ut*, but nevertheless prefers *ut et ea*; I, 4, *eaq.*; but in codex 4 *ea quae* was corrected in red ink.] those things which belong to the equipment of the possession or house are to be handed over.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of March, at Milan [Note: [Col. 0097C] j The Code of Justinian has *Mediolani*. Morinus, *On Ecclesiastical Liberty*, vol. II, ch. 12, p. 329, corrects *Mai* for *Mart.*; Go. printed “I. Constantio.”], in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third consulship of Licinius [Note: [Col. 0097C] k Be. rightly wishes III to be added. Aur. Lugd.: “in the consulship.”] (313).

## ON DECURIONS

[Note: [Col. 0097C] l Some codices have *curionibus*; others add: “that is, concerning curiales [municipal councillors]” or “concerning curiales and receivers,” or “that is, that they undertake public functions not privately but in the presence of others.” Sich., in the marginal index of titles, p. 80: “Curiales.” Code of Justinian: “On decurions and their sons, those who are reckoned as decurions, and the ways in which they may be released from the burden of the curia.”]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Evagrius, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0097D] m Most codices read Const. or Constant. Evagrius’s rank is absent in codex 4, but without any indication of a lacuna; it is absent from the editions, the Code of Justinian, and very many Breviary and Alaric codices. Go. and Ri. mark a lacuna with five dots, Ri* with three. Go. and Be. in their notes require the abbreviation for *praefectus praetorio*; I restored it from codices 28, 32, 33, 36, and 40, where *ppo.* is added. The same abbreviation lies hidden in the reading of codex 15, which has: “Emperor C. [omitting Augustus, to] Evagrius, prefect of the city.” 26: “to Vigarius”; 34: “to Euarius”; 37: “to Euantius.”]

No judge [Note: [Col. 0097D] n 20: *Nullus*, according to Ri., from the Interpretation.] shall attempt to grant exemption from civic public services to any curialis [Note: [Col. 0097D] o 13: “and exemption”; 26: “by exemption.”], [Col. 0098A] or release anyone from the curia by his own discretion. For if anyone has been reduced by misfortune of this kind [Note: [Col. 0098B] a 20: “shall attempt, [to grant exemption] to a curialis.” Code of Justinian omits “from civic … shall attempt,” or reads otherwise.] [Note: [Col. 0098B] b 6, 7, 9, 10, 14, 17, 18, Code of Justinian: *huiusmodi*, “of this kind”; 20: “in this kind”; 25: “in theft”; 15 omits *eius modi*.] [Note: [Col. 0098B] c Rein. conjectures *degravatus*, “weighed down”; 8: “as he ought.”] that he ought to be relieved, a report concerning him must be made to our attention, so that for a fixed period [Note: [Col. 0098B] d 25: “a period.”] an exemption from civic public services may be granted to him [Note: [Col. 0098B] e 7, 16: “and exemption”; 9: *euacatio*; 10, 18: “and wandering”; 20: *vagacio*; 21: “and” in place of “to him.”] [Note: [Col. 0098B] f The Summary of the Theodosian Code adds: “also here, how records are to be drawn up before municipal authorities.” But concerning the drawing up of records before municipal authorities, the Theodosian Code has nothing in this passage.].

Posted [Note: [Col. 0098C] g 8, 9, 20, 29, 30, 33, 34, 38, 40, L. R. U.: “Given”; but 8, 42: “given on the Ides of March”; 20: “given on the day before the Ides of March”; 30: “given on the sixth day before the Ides of March”; 33, 34: “given on the sixth day before the Kalends of March”; 10, 18: “ordered on the Ides of March”; 40: “posted on the day before the Ides of March.”] on the Ides of March, in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0098C] h 7, 10, 13, 14, 16–18: “on the sixth”; 15, 20: “on the fourth”; 8 omits “Constantine … consuls.”] and the third consulship of Licinius [Note: [Col. 0098C] i 9, 42: “and Honorius”; 13, 15, 28, 36, 40, and Sich. in the margin: IV; 38: II; 6, 7, 10, 14, 16, 18, 20, 31–34, 39, 43 omit III. Codex 24 adds *aa.* after III. Some codices omit “consuls.”] (313 [Note: [Col. 0098C] j Go. gives 312, whether by error I do not know, since this law is entirely absent from the Chronicle.]).

**INTERPRETATION.** [Note: [Col. 0098C] k Go. wishes to add, “This law says the following,” and codex 38 has this; but it can readily be omitted.] No judge shall grant an undue exemption to a curialis, nor [Note: [Col. 0098C] l 20: “for not”; Sich.: “lest he.”] seek to release him from his office. For if the resources of any curialis are so slight and [Note: [Col. 0098C] m Sich., Cuj. 1–Lugd. omit “and.” Shortly afterwards some codices read *facultate*, “resources.”] exhausted that he is not thought able to bear the necessity of a public burden [Note: [Col. 0098C] n 6, 7, 20, 21, 43, 44, and many other codices, and Sich.: *honoris*, “office”; some codices: *honeris*, “burden.”], information concerning this must be referred to the emperor’s command [Note: [Col. 0098D] o Go. notes: “Read *ius sit* [‘let it be right’]: although *iussit* [‘he commanded’] can be maintained, namely, this law.” 6, 7: “is commanded.”].

## ON THE CENSUS OR REGISTRATION

The same Augustus [Note: [Col. 0098D] p 4: “The same Augusti.” Editions before Be.: “The same Augusti”; Go., in his commentary, and Pag., *Critique on Baronius’s Annals*, year 314, no. 10, approve. Code of Justinian: “Emperor Constantine Augustus.” Be. rightly restores the singular Augustus; for although Licinius was also Augustus at this time, no preceding constitution bears the names of both emperors, Constantine and Licinius. There is therefore no basis for referring *AA.* to them. Nor do I recall finding anywhere in the Theodosian Code a constitution of those two emperors together. Go. has already said that such constitutions occur in the Code of Justinian. Cf. ch. 8 of the Code of Justinian, *On Judgments* (III, 1); ch. 2, *If There Are Several Guardians* (V, 40); ch. 41, *On the Condition of Freedom* (VII, 16). Aur. Lugd.: “Eusebius.”] to Eusebius, vir perfectissimus, governor of Lycia and Pamphylia [Note: [Col. 0098D] q 4, Til.–Ri*: *Pamfyliae*. Code of Justinian: *Pamphiliae*.].

The urban populace, as is also observed in the eastern provinces, shall by no means be assessed in the censuses for its poll-tax [Note: [Col. 0098D] r 4, Til.: *conveniantur*, “shall assemble.”], but shall be held exempt under this command of ours [Note: [Col. 0098D] s The following is absent from the Code of Justinian. Go.: “Just as.”], just as the same urban populace had also been exempt under our lord and father Diocletian the elder Augustus.

Given on the Kalends of June, in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third consulship of Licinius (313).

## ON CERTIFICATES FOR FORMER TRIBUNES AND PROTECTORES

[Note: [Col. 0099B] a Cuj. 1–Lugd., Go., Ri*: “former tribunes”; Cuj. 2, 2*: *Extribunis*.]

[Col. 0099A]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Rufinus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0099B] b Cuj. 1–Lugd. have *ppo* and the codex; Cuj. 2, 2*: PPO, that is, Praetorian Prefect; Go.: P. P. O.; Ri., Ri*: PP. o. Go., *Chronology*, p. X, conjectures prefect of the city, incorrectly. Moreover, the codex has *Rufinus*, but the final *s* has been deleted.]
