It cannot be tolerated that men who have neither seen a battle line, nor beheld military standards, nor handled arms should insinuate themselves into the rank [Note: [Col. 0099B] c Go. prefers *in titulum*, or rather *in titulos*, “into the ranks,” and Reinesius does likewise.] of military distinction. Therefore, if any former protectores, former commanders, or former tribunes [Note: [Col. 0099B] d Aur. Lugd. omits “or former commanders.” Cuj. 1; Cuj. 2–Ri*: “if any former protectores [thus also Aur. Lugd.] or former commanders or former tribunes [also Aur. Lugd.].”] receive certificates, they shall not possess the privilege deserved [Note: [Col. 0099C] e Reinesius adds *nisi*, “unless.” The codex has “to insinuate themselves … the military order.”] by those who have attained this honor after completing the grades of military service amid the toil of arms.

Posted on the fourth day before the Ides of August, at Sirmium [Note: [Col. 0099C] f Thus the codex and Cuj. 1–Ri*. But Be.: Sirmii. With the subscription begins the second page of fol. LXXVII of the codex.], in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third consulship of Licinius [Note: [Col. 0099C] g Go. conjectures: “in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the fourth consulship of Licinius,” that is, the year 315. See also Go., *Chronology*, year 315, p. 10, who says that Morinus incorrectly attributed this law to Licinius, *History of Constantine*, part 2, p. 361. The year-number is absent in Go.–Ri*. Aur. Lugd., however, incorrectly has Licinius.] (313).

## ON THE OFFICE OF THE PROCONSUL AND LEGATE

Emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0099C] h Cl.: “the most illustrious Constantine,” but corrected to Constantine.] Augustus to Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa.

You shall hear publicly all civil cases, and especially those matters, including criminal business, which are more prominent by reason of public notoriety; and you shall order the proceedings to be completed on the third day, or at latest the fourth, or certainly the fifth. [Note: [Col. 0099C] i Pu., following Hu.’s conjecture: *debes*, “you must,” printed by Schro.] [Note: [Col. 0099C] j 5: *Velvel*. Cl., Pu.: *vel[vel]*.] [Col. 0099B] [Note: [Col. 0099C] k 5: “to be completed.”] Legates also, admonished under threat of coercion, shall observe all these provisions.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of November, at Trier, in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third consulship of Licinius [Note: [Col. 0099C] l 5 incorrectly: “in the thirteenth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the fourth consulship of Licinius.” The number XIII is entirely false; nor does IV fit, since it denotes the year 315, when Constantine was neither staying at Trier nor was Aelianus proconsul of Africa, but rather Probianus was (see Go., *Prosopography*, under “Aelianus,” and Bou., cited work, p. 745). Constantine did, however, stay at Trier in 313, under the consuls Constantine Augustus III and Licinius III; in the same year Aelianus was proconsul of Africa. Thus copyists could easily err in the numbers, and Cl., in correcting the text (for the edition has Lic. IV), rightly adapted the subscription to 313. For the same reasons Go. already wishes the chapters 1 and 2 mentioned above to be referred to 313; since they were issued almost on the same day as this constitution, they are undoubtedly all fragments of one larger constitution dismembered in the Theodosian Code. Cl., Pu.: A[A].] (313).

## ON THE GRAIN SUPPLY AND TAXES

[Note: [Col. 0099D] m Code of Justinian: “On annonae and tributes.” Some codices have *tribus* for *tributis*, arising from the abbreviation *trib.* Others: “On the distribution of grain”; 4: *tributus*, but corrected in red ink to *tributio*.]

Emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0099D] n See note i. Aur. Lugd. incorrectly: Constantivus.] Augustus to Proclianus. [Note: [Col. 0099D] o The rank is absent; nor does Go. wish Probianus, proconsul of Africa (see ch. 3 of Theodosian Code, *On Appeals*, XI, 30), to be read in place of Proculianus, whom he believes, because King Arsaces is mentioned in this law, to have been Praetorian Prefect of the East. Beck follows Go. Proculianus is named as tribune and Master of Offices in ch. 1 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Sale of Pledges* (XI, 9); hence Rein. wishes Proculianus, tribune and Master of Offices, to be read here, not wrongly; for the Code of Justinian also has Proculianus.]

Apart from our private estates, the catholic churches, the household of Eusebius of most illustrious memory, former consul and former master of horse and foot, and that of Arsaces, king of the Armenians, no one shall, by our order, be assisted from the principal revenues of the patrimonial estate. Datianus, a most illustrious man and patrician, who had formerly obtained this favor, requested with as much insistence that it be withdrawn from him as others customarily employ in requesting it. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0100B] a “All shall be obliged” begins ch. 4 of the cited Code of Justinian.] all shall be obliged to pay what is assigned by delegations of our hand [Note: [Col. 0100B] b Code of Justinian: “of our hand.” But our text is correct according to Go.], and no more shall be demanded [Note: [Col. 0100B] c The Code of Justinian adds: “or the power to remit [it] shall exist”; Cujacius, in his commentary on ch. 4 of the cited Code of Justinian, cited passage, p. 248, Contius, and Go. already held that these words must be deleted, since they are absent from the ancient manuscript books of the Code of Justinian. Cf. Dirksen, cited work, p. 497. Shortly afterward the Code of Justinian has *quis*, “anyone.”]. For if any vicar or provincial governor has already believed that anything should be remitted to anyone, whatever he has remitted to others [Note: [Col. 0100B] d Code of Justinian: “to another.”] he shall be compelled to provide from his own resources.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, at Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0100B] e Go. already saw that the city’s name has intruded here; Constantinople did not yet exist. The error arose from the emperor’s name which follows. The Code of Justinian rightly omits *Constantinopoli* throughout.], in the fourth consulship of Constantius Augustus and the fourth consulship of Licinius [Note: [Col. 0100C] f Valesius rightly says that the subscription is false; nevertheless, I do not wish, with him, on this sole ground—that Arsaces is mentioned—to attribute the law to Constantius, since Constantius removed the immunity which this law grants to catholic churches. See ch. 15 of the Theodosian Code, *On Bishops* (XVI, 2), and Go.’s commentary on this chapter. Valesius’s emendation also destroys the sequence of constitutions observed by the compilers of the Theodosian Code. Nor is Go.’s opinion certain, resting as it does on the mention of Eusebius, Arsaces, and Datianus, whose names fall in the time of Constantius. I see no reason for doubt. Valesius and Go. commit the error often made, and still made, by editors of ancient writers: when they find a name which is not altogether certain or does not seem to accord with the time under discussion in a book, driven by zeal to harmonize events they prefer to overturn the writer’s words and chronology completely rather than admit uncertainty about the name. This is precisely what has happened here to Valesius and Go.; for Eusebius, together with Rufinus, was suffect consul in 311 (see Go.’s commentary and Reland, cited work, preface, p. 16); Arsaces too, as Go. himself concedes, is mentioned during the reign of Constantine the Great; nor is Datianus’s name wholly unknown in Constantine’s age. Although I have not found the Datianus named here in any of the other writers of this age whom I have examined, that is not enough to disturb, on that ground alone, the order of the constitutions in the Theodosian Code. Among ancient writers distinguished men of the same name but of different times are frequently found; if someone were to merge all of them into one, he would certainly produce a monster dreadful to describe. The case here is no different. This constitution is therefore a law of Constantine. Whether it was issued under the consuls named here may indeed be asked, but cannot be affirmed, since chapter 2 of this title is later, and, as appears from the passages cited in the preceding note, belongs to the year 313. Therefore, lest the order and sequence of the constitutions be overturned, I maintain that this chapter too was issued in 313, in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus and Licinius.] (315?).

[Col. 0101A] The same Augustus to Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa. [Note: [Col. 0101C] a “When possessors have satisfied…” begins fol. 123 of codex 4 [ [Col. 0101C] b Til.–Lugd.: *sexaginari*, “sixty-men.”].]

When landholders have satisfied the public assessment, they shall bring their vouchers to the public record-keepers, so that the record-keepers, or *sexagenarii* [officials of sixty; Note: [Col. 0101C] b Til.–Lugd.: *sexaginari*.], mindful of their own liability, may receive them from the contributors who are to convey each month to each city the specific goods owed from their storehouses, lest the delivery of taxes be ascertained solely from false or imaginary receipts [*apochis*; Note: [Col. 0101C] c 4: *apocis*, and so frequently; I note this once for all.], etc.

Given on the Kalends of November, at Trier, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the fourth consulship of Licinius (315? [Note: [Col. 0101C] d Go., in his *Chronicle*, transfers this chapter to the year 313, correctly. Bou., cited work, p. 745, agrees with Go. Aur. Lugd.: “in the consulship.”]).

## ON TAX COLLECTIONS

[Note: [Col. 0101C] e Code of Justinian: “On Collectors of Taxes.”]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Aelianus, Proconsul [Note: [Col. 0101C] f 4: PU; Til.–Lugd.: P. V. In Cuj. 2, *Procons.* was silently restored from the Code of Justinian, correctly. Cf. ch. 1 of the Theodosian Code, *On Praetors* (VI, 4), note u, and below XI, 16, 1, note m. Code of Justinian omits “After other matters.”] of Africa.

After other matters: Officials of two hundred, one hundred, or sixty shall not first proceed against any debtor until they have received from the city record-keeper named lists [*breves*; Note: [Col. 0101C] g Cf. the final chapter of the Theodosian Code, *On the Office of the Count of the Sacred Largesses* (I, 10), note e.] [Col. 0101B] of the debts. This collection must indeed be conducted without any extortion [Note: [Col. 0101C] h Here begins fol. 137 verso of codex 4. The following is omitted from the Code of Justinian.], so that if anyone complains in court that he has been unlawfully compelled to pay [Note: [Col. 0101C] i 4: “having complained that unlawfully,” but *indebite* was corrected above the line.] or has suffered any harassment, and can prove this very fact, a severe judgment shall be pronounced against the collectors.

Given on the Kalends of November, at Trier, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0101D] j Go.: III. He wishes “in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third consulship of Licinius” (313), under whose consuls he places this chapter in his *Chronicle*, p. VII. See ch. 1 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Office of Provincial Governors* (I, 12), note i, and Go., *Prosopography*, under “Aelianus.” Code of Justinian: Treveris.] and the fourth consulship of Licinius (315).

## ON BISHOPS, CHURCHES, AND CLERGY

[Note: [Col. 0101D] k 11: “or clergy”; 15 omits “churches.” Some Breviary and Alaric codices: “On bishops, clergy, and churches.” Code of Justinian, book I, title 2: “On the Most Holy Churches and their property and privileges”; and title 3: “On Bishops, Clergy, Orphanages, Hostels, Foundling Homes, Poorhouses, Ascetic Houses, Monks, and their Privileges; on Military Peculium; on the Redemption of Captives; and on Clerics’ Marriages, Forbidden or Permitted.”]

Emperor Constantine Augustus . . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0101D] l 4, Til.–Cuj. 2*, Ri.–Be. give no indication of a lacuna. Go. believes this was addressed to a provincial governor, and specifically to Anullinus, Proconsul of Africa.]

We have learned that, through the faction of heretics, the clergy of the catholic Church are so harassed that they are burdened, contrary to the privileges granted them, by nominations or assumptions of office of some sort, which public custom requires. [Note: [Col. 0101D] m Go. here and below, and Ri., incorrectly have *palcet* for *placet*.] Therefore it is our pleasure that, if your gravity finds anyone so harassed, another person be substituted for him [Note: [Col. 0101D] n Fol. 395 [ [Col. 0101C] b Til.–Lugd.: *sexaginari*.] of codex 4.], and that thereafter persons of the above-mentioned religion be prevented from suffering injuries of this kind.

Given on the day before the Kalends of November, in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third consulship of Licinius [Note: [Col. 0102B] a 4 adds C., and the editions “Caesar,” or C. Be. notes: “Delete *Caesar*, for Licinius is to be understood not as Caesar but as Augustus.” Correctly; and, with the agreement of codices 15, 50, and 51, I have deleted *Caesar*.] (313 [Note: [Col. 0102B] b Lab.: 315.]).

## ON PENALTIES

Emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0102B] c Til.: “Emperor Constantine.” Be.: Constantius, incorrectly.] Augustus to Catulinus. [Note: [Col. 0102B] d Fol. 55 [ [Col. 0102B] a 4 adds C., and the editions “Caesar,” or C. Be. notes: “Delete *Caesar*, for Licinius is to be understood not as Caesar but as Augustus.” Correctly; and, with the agreement of codices 15, 50, and 51, I have deleted *Caesar*.] of codex 4. Following Rein. and Be., add from the Justinian codices: “Proconsul of Africa.” Against Go., who believes that Catulinus, because of the town of Hadrumetum where the law was received, was consul of Byzacena in this year and only in the following year proconsul of Africa. See Go. on this chapter, note b. It is troublesome that in the other laws connected with this chapter the rank too has fallen out. I therefore hold that it was supplied in the Code of Justinian from another source. 4, Till.–Be.: Catullinus. Cf. Theodosian Code II, 1, 1, note o. 10, 18: Catolinus; 15: “Augustus to Catulinus”; 26: Catholinus; 17, 28, 40 omit “to Catulinus.”]

Anyone who is to pronounce judgment [Note: [Col. 0102C] e 6, 7, 10, 12–14, 18: “is to give [judgment].”] shall observe this moderation: he shall not pronounce a capital and severe sentence upon anyone unless, in a charge of adultery, homicide, sorcery [*maleficium*], [Note: [Col. 0102C] f Thus rightly Be. from the Code of Justinian, with which 16, 20, 7, 12, 14 agree: “charges, as their own.” 8: “charges, when giving [judgment], as their own.” The rest: singular “charge.” 20: “charge or in his own.”] he has been convicted either by his own confession or at least by a convergent and concordant conclusion of all who have been subjected to torture or interrogation [Note: [Col. 0102C] g 15: “or.”] [Note: [Col. 0102C] h 6–8, 12, 14, 16: “and concord”; 6, according to Ri.: “breathing as one”; 20: “concordant and convergent”; Sich.: “converging and agreeing,” as 20 above the line reverses the order. Code of Justinian: “convergent and concordant.” Go. conjectures “of those converging and agreeing.”] [Note: [Col. 0102C] i 6–8, 12, 16, Go.: *fine*, “by a conclusion”; 10: “conclusion, having overcome.”], and has thus been caught in the alleged offense [Note: [Col. 0102C] j 15: “thus caught in the offense alleged.”] so that scarcely even he himself [Note: [Col. 0102C] k Cuj. 2–Ri*: “already”; 15 omits “himself.”] can sufficiently deny the acts which [Note: [Col. 0102C] l Sich., in the margin: “who.”] he committed.

Given on the third [Note: [Col. 0102D] m 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 32, Sich.: fourth. L. R. U. V.: 17, 40 omit III; 13: III–XV.] day before the Nones of November, at Trier [Note: [Col. 0102D] n 38: Ravenna; 42, L. (?) in Be.: Ravenna. Most codices: Triu.; others *trium* for *triu.*; 20: *triverim*. Code of Justinian: Treveris. 8 omits “Trier … Hadrumetum … and the year.”] (313 [Note: [Col. 0102D] o The year in which the law was given is omitted by the editions and the Code of Justinian, although Go. and Be. already require it.]). Received on the fifteenth [Note: [Col. 0102D] p 10, 18: V; 21: XII; 15 omits “Received … Hadrumetum.”] day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0102D] q Go., in his *Chronicle*, emends March.] at Hadrumetum [Note: [Col. 0102D] r Almost all codices: *adrometo*; 38: *alromitti*; 42: *alromiti*; Sich.: Adrumetum; 4: Hadrumet, with *i* added in red ink.], in the consulship of Volusianus [Note: [Col. 0102D] s Most codices: Volosianus. Be. wishes II to be added.] and Annianus [Col. 0102B] [Note: [Col. 0102D] t 12: Avianus; 10, 18, 20, 21, 38, 40, other codices, and Cuj. 2–Ri*: Anianus, printed by Be.; Sich.: Anienus.] [Note: [Col. 0102D] u Aur. Lugd.: “in the consulship.”] (314).

**INTERPRETATION.** A judge examining [Note: [Col. 0102D] v 6, 7: “discussing.”] a criminal shall not pronounce a capital sentence before either the accused himself confesses or he is more clearly proved guilty, whether by innocent witnesses or by accomplices in his crime [Note: [Col. 0102D] x Sich.: “or, having been convicted, by.”] [Note: [Col. 0102D] y Sich.: “consciousness.”], of having committed homicide, adultery, [Col. 0103A] or sorcery [*maleficium*] [Note: [Col. 0103B] a 6, 7: “is manifest”; 20: “is ascertained,” but corrected above the line.].

## ON APPEALS

Emperor Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0103B] b Breviary and Alaric codices, Sich., and Code of Justinian: “Emperor Constantine Augustus”; but 8: “Emperor Augustus.”] to Catulinus. [Note: [Col. 0103B] c 4, Til.–Be.: Catullinus. Breviary and Alaric codices: Catulinus, as Sich. Code of Justinian: Catolinus, Catholinus; only 15: “Augustus to Catulinus.” 28, 36, 40 omit “to Catulinus,” and some codices add “After other matters.” See Theodosian Code II, 1, 1, note o, and IX, 40, 1, note c.]

After other matters: It is by no means lawful that, when petitions of appeal have been submitted in a civil case [Note: [Col. 0103B] d 12 omits *ut*, “that.”] [Note: [Col. 0103B] e 26 omits *oblatis*, “submitted.” Sich.: “with appeal-petitions submitted.”], an appellant should suffer the torments of imprisonment [Note: [Col. 0103B] f In codex 4 *cruciatus* is written so that the letters *u* and *s* in the syllable *tus* are confused, and consequently it may at first sight be read *cruciatis*. For clarity, *tus* was corrected in red ink. 10, 18: “the torments of any person”; 26: “torments or any person.”] or any kind of injury, torture, or even insult [Note: [Col. 0103C] g 20: “tortures or insults.”] [Note: [Col. 0103C] h 20, above the line: “the appellee”; 26: “the appealed.”]. Criminal cases are excepted [Note: [Col. 0103C] i Fol. 181 [ [Col. 0103B] a 6, 7: “is manifest”; 20: “is ascertained,” but corrected above the line.] of codex 4. Go. notes: “Differently from criminal cases, etc.” 20: “apart from these criminal [cases].”], in which, even if they may [Note: [Col. 0103C] j Codex 15 adds *rei*, “defendants.” Code of Justinian: “may appeal … must … remain.” 26: “in which they may prove.”] appeal, they must nevertheless remain in such a condition [Note: [Col. 0103C] k 4, 12: *statutum*, “ordinance.” In codex 4, *statum* was corrected in red ink.] that after making an appeal they continue in custody [Note: [Col. 0103C] l Go. notes: “so that also after.” 9: “after the appeal.”] [Note: [Col. 0103C] m Code of Justinian adds: “if he does not have the means of providing a suitable surety.” 16: “into custody.”] [Note: [Col. 0103C] n 6: “have remained.” See above, note e. What follows is absent from the Code of Justinian. 12: “they remain,” and from ch. 16: “in that custody.”].

This moderation being observed, the appeals of those shall be received [Note: [Col. 0103C] o 20, above the line: “considered”; 26: “snatched away.”] who are known to have lodged them not as a prejudgment [Note: [Col. 0103C] p 8, 12, 14, 15, 17 omit *a*, “as”; 9: “not as a pre-”; 10, 13, 18: “not to prejudice”; 20: “who [lodged] the same gifts as a prejudgment”; 26: “who [lodged] them not.”] and not before the case has been examined and determined, but after the entire matter has been concluded by a peremptory prescription [Note: [Col. 0103C] q 4, 12, 15, Sich.–Lugd., Cuj. 2, 2*, in the corrections: *praescribtione*; 9, 12, 20, 21, 26, Cuj. 2–Ri*: *perscribtione*; Be.: *perscriptione*; the remaining codices: *proscriptione*. Go. interprets *perscriptione* as “that is, by a judgment”; yet *praescriptione* is not unsuitable. It is, moreover, clear that *perscriptione* intruded by error into Cuj. 2 and from it into the other editions. 20: “completed.”], or [Note: [Col. 0103D] r 26 omits *vel*, “or”; 8, 12: *per*; 18: *ut per*, “so that through.”] after proceeding through all its parts [Note: [Col. 0103D] s 6–8, 12, 14, 16, 17, 21, Sich.: *discusso*, “having been examined”; 9, 18, 26: *discurso*; 10: *discorso*; 20: *decursa*.], against the judge [Note: [Col. 0103D] t 15 omits “against the judge.” Shortly afterwards some codices have “lodged.”] they are known to have been lodged [Note: [Col. 0103D] u 6–8, 10, 12, 13, 16–18, Sich.: “are known.” Sich. omits “etc.,” as do some Breviary and Alaric codices.], etc.

Given on the third [Note: [Col. 0103D] v 6–8, 10, 12, 13, 17, 18, 20, 21, 27, 28, 33, 36, 38, 40, Sich., L. R. U.: fourth.] day before the Nones of November [Note: [Col. 0103D] x In Sich. “November” has fallen out.] at Trier [Note: [Col. 0103D] y Breviary and Alaric codices: Triu., Triueris, Treueris. 12, 28, 36, 40 omit “Trier,” and 8 omits “Trier … Hadrumetum.” I supplied the year at the urging of Go. and Be.] (313). Received on the fifteenth [Note: [Col. 0103D] z 30, 33: tenth; 20: “in August, on the sixteenth”; 28, 36, 40 omit XV.] day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0103D] aa 20: *mard*; 40: *mad*. Go., in his *Chronicle*, emends March. Cf. Theodosian Code IX, 40, 1, note nn.] [Col. 0104A] at Hadrumetum [Note: [Col. 0104B] a 4, Til.–Ri*: Hadrumetum. Be.: Hadrumeti. 15, 21: *adrumeto*; 10, 18: *adrumetulos*; 16: *adrumetu*; 6: *adrumetii*; 7, 14, and many other codices, Sich.: Adrumeti; 28, 36, 40, 43, 44: *adromito*; 20: Rome.], in the consulship of Volusianus [Note: [Col. 0104B] b Most codices: Volosianus; 20: Volocianus. Be. rightly wishes II to be added.] and Annianus [Note: [Col. 0104B] c 8 omits “and Annianus”; 32: “and Aelianus”; 20: “Annonianus”; nearly all other Breviary and Alaric codices, and Cuj. 2–Ri*: Anianus.] [Note: [Col. 0104C] d Very many codices omit “consuls.”] (314).

**INTERPRETATION.** This law prescribes [Note: [Col. 0104C] e Some codices: “This law prescribed.”] that an appellant ought not to be restrained by imprisonment or by the affliction of any injury [Note: [Col. 0104C] f 42, Aur. Lugd.: “injury.”], except in criminal cases [Note: [Col. 0104C] g 6, 7: “individual.”], in which a like condition of punishment and custody binds both accuser and accused [Note: [Col. 0104C] h 20: “and custody.” The editions: “will bind.”]. It says that their appeals should be received, but in such a way that the person who has appealed is kept in custody [Note: [Col. 0104C] i 20: plural, “those who have appealed … are kept.”] until the crimes charged reach another judge [Note: [Col. 0104C] j 10, 18: “are reached”; 21: “will reach.”], so that, after all matters have been fully examined, he receives a final sentence either of acquittal or of condemnation [Note: [Col. 0104C] k Some codices omit *de*, “of.”] [Note: [Col. 0104C] l Go. emends “definitive,” but all codices have “final.”].

## WHOSE APPEALS ARE NOT TO BE RECEIVED

[Note: [Col. 0104C] m Code of Justinian: “are received.”]

Constantine Augustus to Catulinus. [Note: Most manuscripts: Catolinus. 15: Catolino. 4, Til.–Be.: Catullinus. See Cod. Theod. II, 1, 1, note o. The title is absent in all manuscripts. See Cod. Theod. IX, 40, 1, note c.]

It is not fitting that dilatory and futile appeals [Note: 6, 7, 10: frustratoriasquae. 9: prostratoriasquae. 15: frustrationesque. 16: frutatoriasquae. 18: frustratoriasquem.]—mere mockeries rather than appeals [Col. 0104B]—should be admitted. For just as assistance ought not to be denied to those who appeal rightly, [Note: 8, 25: negare; 20: denegare. Shortly before, 14: sicut boni.] so it is not proper that judgments rightly rendered should be delayed for persons against whom judgment has deservedly been given and who appeal without purpose. [Note: 6–8, 14, 16, 17, 20, 21, Sich.: quos contra; 20: meritum. 20: provocantur deferri. Also 9: deferri. 6, Sich.: debent. 16: det.]

Accordingly, where a murderer, adulterer, evildoer, or poisoner—crimes of the utmost atrocity [Note: 21: homicida and 20: veneficia. Sich. omits vel mal.; 15: vel venef.; Go. and Ri*: vel adult. Then Ri*: Maleficium, vel Veneficium. Br. Al. manuscripts, Sich., Cuj. 2, 2*: facinora.]—has been exposed by his own confession, or by clear and most fully substantiated investigation of the truth through proofs and arguments, [Note: 6–8, 10, 14, 16–18, 21, R.: adlucida. 20: adlucidam et probatissimam veritatem. Sich.: lucida. The reading *et* is printed by Be. from Sich. and Cuj. 2, 2*, with which agree 6, 7, 12–17, 20, 21, 25, 50. Cod. 4, Til.–Lugd.: exprobatissima. Go.–Ri*: ex probatissima. Go. prefers et exploratissima. 9: ut prob. 10, 18: vel prob. R.: vel ex prob. 8 omits et. Do not be troubled by *probatissima probationibus*; see c. 4 of this title, *manifestis probationibus adulterio probato*. 16: quaestionibus.] [Col. 0105A] appeals ought not to be entertained; for it is evident that they hold out no hope of refuting what has been done, but rather attempt to defer it. [Note: 15: Detraxerit. 21: detecta sunt. 9: provocatis. 12: probationes. Sich.: appellationes. Fol. 206, cod. 4, 21, Sich. add *et*. Sich. in margin: speciem. 8 omits spem. 15: temptare differre; some manuscripts: deferre.]

Those who differ concerning various disputes and cases [Note: 4, 6–8, 10, 12, 14, 16–18, 21, 25, 50, Sich.: qui; 9: q.; only a few manuscripts have *quae*, as corrected by an early hand in cod. 4 and thence transmitted into the editions Til.–Be. Go. notes: “The following sentence is corrupt, and perhaps even intrusive, unless we suppose these words are to be restored thus, etc., [that is, *et caetera*], *quae de variis litibus causisque disserantur*: so that these are words of the compilers of the Theodosian Code, cutting from the complete constitution matters that did not yet make the title.” *Qui* has been restored on the evidence of the manuscripts, whose best and oldest witnesses have it, and from the sense of the passage; for the words *Qui—dissentiunt* must necessarily be joined to the following *nec—debebunt*. For this reason a full stop was placed after *tentare*, and, in place of the full stop added after *dissentiunt* in the editions Go.–Be. (*dissentiunt. Nec*), less complete punctuation was restored.] must not appeal rashly, nor from interlocutory judgments and prejudicial decisions, [Note: 10, 12, 18: ne tem.; 20: nec timore, but *temere* above the line. 20: praejudicibusque nec ab eis. Some manuscripts: praejudiciis quae; others have *hiis* both above and here, as Sich.] nor from matters that have been justly decided. If, however, a defendant in a charge of murder, sorcery, adultery, or poisoning can derive support for his defence from witnesses and an inquiry that have been proposed, but seems likely to be overwhelmed and accused on the other side, [Note: 20: rei and omits in; Ri. originally: *in*. 4: homidii, with *ci* added by the scribe. 15: hom. vel ad. vel mal. (omitting vel veneficit) crim. partem. 20: partem and later quaestionique. The reading *parte* is that of 4, 15, Til.–Be.; 6–8, 13, 20, 21, Sich.: partim; the remaining manuscripts: partem. Nor is this incorrect.] then, upon an appeal lodged by that person, [Note: Br. Al. manuscripts nearly all, Sich., Be., jub., Go.: *interposita*, correctly. 4, 15, Til., Cuj. 1, Cuj. 2, 2*: superinposita. Aur. Lugd.: super imposita. Go.–Ri*: super imposita. 25: superposita. 20 omits *tunc super interpositam appellationem*. Go. also conjectured *insuper posita*. In legal sources *interposita appellatio* is frequent; I do not recall *impositam appellationem*. Then cod. 15 omits sibi.] [Col. 0106A] who maintains that the evidence favorable to himself ought to avail him more than the evidence that has harmed him, full discretion shall be left to Our deliberation. [Note: 20: posse for pro se. Sich.: ipsam. 18: noscere for nocere. Some manuscripts: deliberationis; 14: liberatione. 15: relinquatur arbitrium.]

Given on the third day before the Nones of November at Trier, [Note: 24, 27, 28, 34, 36, 40: III; the remaining manuscripts and editions: IV. Go., initially, wishes III restored by joining this law with c. 1 and 2. Some manuscripts: Treveris, Triveris. 4, Til.–Lugd. omit Trev.–Maii. 20: Acc.–Hadrum.; 8: Trev.–Hadrum.; Cuj. 2–Ri*: Trev., but Go. adds in note. The year 313 is also absent in Go.–Be.] A.D. 313; received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May at Hadrumetum, [Note: Go. in the Chronicle prefers March, and 32 has this. Some manuscripts: Mad. See c. 2 cited, note u. 28, 36, 40 omit Maii. L. R. U.: Dat. XV kal. Mad.] in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, A.D. 314. [Note: Some manuscripts: adrometo; others Adrumeto, as Sich.; still others Arometo. B. adds II in the note. Some manuscripts: Volosiano and later Aniano, as Sich., Cuj. 2–Ri*; 6–8, 10, 18, 34 omit et Anniano.]

**INTERPRETATION.** In civil cases or lesser crimes not included in the laws, the delay provided by the laws must be granted to an appeal, [Note: 6–8, 10, 18, 20, and others: appellatione. These words seem to have been added by the interpreter, since they are absent from the law itself, unless perhaps they explain the law’s words *Nam—oportet*. Cf. Carl von Savigny, loc. cit., vol. I, 262, note 27 (1st ed.); 305, note g (2nd ed.).] and the judge’s sentence must be suspended by the appeal. But murderers, adulterers, [Note: Cuj. 2, 2*: sententiae. Sich., Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2*: homicidiis, adulteriis, as in certain Br. Al. manuscripts. 6, 7: Ad for At. Sich. omits quos.] and the rest whom this law comprises, if they have been convicted and confessed and wish to appeal, are to be denied delay; rather, in manifest crimes, once they have been convicted, the judge’s sentence is to be pronounced at once; [Note: 6–8, 10, 18, 20, 21, 42, 43, and others: convictus.] or, certainly, in grave crimes and cases involving persons of higher rank, the matter must be referred to the Emperor’s cognizance. [Note: Go. says that this interpretation is false. 42: def. est notitiam.]

**EDICT CONCERNING FREEDOM OF RELIGION.**

(From Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* X.5.) [Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0105C] Since long ago We had considered that freedom of religion ought not to be denied, but that authority should be given to the judgment and will of each individual to attend to divine matters according to his own choice, We had commanded each person, including Christians, to preserve the faith of his own sect and religion. But since [Col. 0105D] many and various sects seemed to have been expressly added to that rescript in which this authority had been granted to the same persons, perhaps some of them soon afterward withdrew from such observance.

Accordingly, when I, Constantine Augustus, and I, Licinius Augustus, had come propitiously to Milan and were considering all matters bearing upon public advantage and utility, among the remaining matters that seemed beneficial in every way to all, We judged—or rather, before all other matters, decreed—that those things should be established which concerned reverence and worship toward the Divine: [Col. 0107A] namely, that We should grant both Christians and all others free choice to follow whatever religion they may wish, so that whatever divinity or heavenly power there may be may be able to be favorable to Us and to all who live under Our authority.

Therefore, by sound and most right reasoning, We have decreed this Our will: that authority to follow and choose the Christian observance or religion shall be denied to no one whatsoever, and that authority be given to every person to devote his mind to that religion which he himself judges suitable for himself, so that the Divine may be able in all things to grant Us its customary favor and beneficence.

It was accordingly consistent for Us to write in reply that, with all the provisions [Col. 0107B] contained in Our former letters sent to your Devotion concerning the Christians—provisions which seemed entirely harsh and alien to Our mildness—wholly removed, every person who has adopted the same purpose of observing the Christian religion may now observe it freely and without deviation, without any disturbance. We have decreed that these matters be made fully clear to your diligence, so that you may know that We have granted these same Christians free and unrestricted authority to practice their own religion. Since your Devotion sees that this has been granted to them freely by Us, it is evident that authority has also been given to others who wish to pursue their own observance and religion. This is plainly consistent with the tranquillity of Our times: [Col. 0107C] each person is to have authority to choose and practice whatever divinity he wishes. This has been done by Us so that We may not seem to have diminished in any way any form of worship or religion.

Moreover, with regard to the Christians, We decree as follows: their places in which they formerly customarily assembled—and concerning which a different provision had been prescribed in letters previously sent to your Devotion—if any persons appear to have bought them either from Our treasury or from any other person, shall be restored to those same Christians without payment and without any demand for reimbursement of the price paid, without delay or hesitation. And if any persons have received the same places as a gift, they shall restore them as quickly as possible to those same Christians. [Col. 0107D] Thus, if either those who bought the same places or those who received them by gift seek anything from Our beneficence, they shall approach the provincial governor administering justice, so that provision may also be made for them through Our kindness.

All these places must be transferred, without any delay, directly through your zeal to the body of Christians. And since the same Christians are known to have possessed not only the places in which they customarily assembled but also other places belonging not to each of them individually, but to the right of their corporate body—that is, of the Christians—you shall order all these things, under the rule We have stated, to be restored without any dispute whatsoever to the same Christians, that is, to their body and to the association of each of them. [Col. 0110A] The foregoing arrangement is, of course, to be observed: those who restore the same places without payment, as We have said, may expect compensation for their loss from Our beneficence.

In all these matters you ought to give the aforesaid body of Christians the most effective assistance, so that Our command may be fulfilled with the greatest speed, and so that in this also provision may be made through Our kindness for the common and public tranquillity. For by this policy, as has already been stated, divine favor toward Us—which We have already experienced in many matters—will remain secure throughout all time. And in order that the terms of this Our legislation and beneficence may be brought to the knowledge of all, it is proper that these Our written instructions be posted everywhere and brought to everyone’s knowledge, [Col. 0110B] so that the legislation of this Our beneficence may escape no one.

[Col. 0106C] Long ago, indeed, when We perceived that freedom of religion ought not to be restrained, but that every person should be permitted, according to his own judgment and will, to apply himself to divine matters according to the dictates of his own mind, We decreed that all persons, Christians as well as others, should retain the faith and observance of their own sect and religion. But since [Col. 0106D] in that Rescript in which this permission had been granted to them, many and diverse sects seemed to have been expressly and specifically added, some of them perhaps shortly afterward abandoned such observance for this reason.

Wherefore, when We, Constantine and Licinius Augusti, had come to Milan under favorable auspices and were carefully investigating whatever concerned the advantage and utility of the commonwealth, among the other things which We judged in many respects useful to all, or rather which We considered should be established before all other things, [Col. 0108A] We judged that those matters should be settled which concerned the worship and reverence of the Divine Majesty: namely, that free authority be granted by Us to Christians and all others to follow whatever religion they wish, so that whatever divine and heavenly Majesty there may be may be propitious to Us and to all who live under Our rule.

We have therefore promulgated this Our will by sound and most upright counsel: that to no person whatsoever shall permission to follow or choose Christian observance and religion be denied. Rather, each person may devote his mind to the religion which he judges advantageous to himself, so that the Divine Majesty may show toward Us in all things its favorable care and beneficence. Furthermore, it was consistent that We should write in reply that this is Our determination: that, with every sect [Col. 0108B] contained in Our earlier letter concerning the Christians sent to your Devotion entirely removed, together with those provisions which seemed altogether sinister and alien to Our clemency, henceforth everyone who has decided that the Christian religion ought to be observed by himself may retain it freely and steadfastly, without any molestation or impediment.

We considered it proper that these matters be made known to your diligence, so that you may understand that We have granted Christians free and absolute permission to practice their religion. And since this has been simply and absolutely granted to them by Us, your Devotion understands that it has likewise been granted to others who wish to follow their own observance and worship. This clearly accords with the tranquillity of Our times, [Col. 0108C] namely, that every person should be free to choose and observe whatever mode of worshiping the divine power he wishes. We have done this so that We might not seem to have taken anything away from any divine worship or honor.

Further, We decree in favor of the Christians that their places in which they formerly customarily assembled—concerning which a different arrangement had been established at an earlier time in letters previously sent to your Devotion—if any persons seem to have purchased them either from Our treasury or from anyone else, shall restore them to the Christians themselves without any payment and without any claim for repayment of the additional price, promptly and without any evasion. And if anyone has received the same places as a gift, he shall immediately restore them to the Christians. If those who purchased those places or received them as gifts wish to seek anything from Our clemency, [Col. 0108D] they shall apply to the governor who administers justice in that province, so that their case may be considered by Our Serenity.

Your care and diligence must ensure that all these things are restored at once and without any delay to the corporate body of Christians. And since the same Christians are known to have possessed not only those places in which they customarily assembled, but also other places belonging not privately to individual members, but to the right of their corporate body, you shall order all these things, after the law mentioned by Us, restored without any doubt to the same Christians—that is, to each of their corporate bodies and associations—while observing, of course, the arrangement stated above: that those who restore those places without reimbursement of the price, as has been said, may expect indemnification from Our beneficence.

And [Col. 0109A] in all these matters you must offer, as far as possible, your assistance and diligence to the aforesaid corporate body of Christians, so that the command may be completed most speedily, and that through Our clemency provision may thereby also be made for common and public tranquillity. For by this policy, as We have already said, God’s care and favor toward Us, which We have experienced already in many affairs, will remain firm and stable forever. Furthermore, so that the purport of this Our law and beneficence may be conveyed to the knowledge of all, these Our letters should be posted everywhere and brought to the notice of everyone, lest the ordinance of Our beneficence be wholly unknown to anyone.

In the year of the Lord 314, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus.

[Col. 0109B]

**CONCERNING THE JULIAN LAW OF TREASON.**

Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Prefect of the City. [Note: According to Be., Volusianus was more likely Prefect of the City in this title, and perhaps Maximus was Praetorian Prefect of the City; or, as Go. wishes, Prefect of the Praetorium. Klenze, loc. cit., p. 65, thinks Maximus was either deputy Prefect of the City or Vicar. I am prevented from thinking him a Vicar by the words of lines XXVIII–XXX of the Constantinian law, cited above. Klenze supplies the inscription, but without the abbreviation of rank.]

If anyone brings against another an accusation of treason, then, once someone has been convicted in a matter of this kind, [Note: Klenze in the supplement omits in. Constantine’s Edict: ejus modi objectis, and omits re.] no privilege of rank shall protect anyone from a more rigorous investigation; [Note: Constantine’s Edict: quemquam privilegium. Cod. Justinian and Constantine’s Edict: strictiore, though the latter has astrictiori. Be.: ab strictiore. The remaining editions, following cod. 4: adstrictiore or ad strictiore, incorrectly.] he shall know that he too is to be subjected to torture if he cannot establish his accusation by other manifest indications. [Note: Cod. 4 begins on fol. 11a with the letters ne. The following through comprobare are bracketed in Til.–Ri*. Constantine’s Edict, following the second copy in the Ambrosian manuscript: indiciis . . . ut argumentis accusationem.]

The person found guilty of such rashness [Note: Constantine’s Edict: cum in eo. Cod. 4: tum eo, but corrected by an ancient hand to cum eo. Moreover, I have fully punctuated before *Cum*, and, because this was done, placed only a comma after *deprehenditur*. This punctuation, first proposed by Cujacius in his commentary on Cod. Just., loc. cit., and approved by Klenze, loc. cit., p. 63, is criticized by Go., who refers the words *qui h. esse tem. deprehenditur* to the defendant in a treason case. The editions Till.–Be. read: *comprobare, cum eo—deprehenditur. Illum.* Cod. Justinian: hujusmodi. Constantine’s Edict, following the Ambrosian manuscript: dipraehendetur. Cod. Justinian: reus deprehenditur. Go. conjectures reprehenditur.] must likewise be subjected to torture, [Note: Constantine’s Edict: illud. Constantine’s Edict: *torm. erui oporteat*. The learned Vesmius, in a most kindly letter to me, approves the reading of Constantine’s Edict, which I have given in notes e, h, i.] as must the person through whose advice and instigation he appears to have entered upon the accusation, [Note: Go. in annotation: cujus is. Constantine’s Edict: videatur.] so that the established punishment may be exacted from all who were privy to the offense. [Note: Constantine’s Edict adds tanti. *Statuta* is absent in Constantine’s Edict; Cod. Justinian has *instituta*, incorrectly. Constantine’s Edict adds: *sententia: . . . autem quod: . . . veniat subjugari.* See above. Klenze, loc. cit., p. 60, believes that what follows was corruptly written in the Theodosian Code and for this reason omitted in Cod. Justinian. Correctly; see below, notes r, t.]

§ 1. In the case also of slaves or freedmen who attempt to accuse or denounce their masters or patrons, [Note: Constantine’s Edict: sive. Constantine’s Edict: vel. Constantine’s Edict: *temptant ejus . . . juxta antiqui quoque juris statutum observandam esse censuimus, ut scilicet . . . m atrocis.*] the declaration of such atrocious audacity [Note: Cod. 4: audacia, but corrected by an ancient hand to audaciae.] must be suppressed at the very outset of the act itself by the judge’s sentence; and, with the audacity denied, it must be affixed to the gallows. [Note: Go. remarks: “This expression is unusual, *professio (audientia) patibulo affigatur*, unless you read *affigantur*.” Correctly. Go. provides more in his commentary on this chapter. The doubts are resolved by Constantine’s Edict, where the person who proceeds to such desperation is affixed, “that he may provide an example to others, lest anyone hereafter be found guilty of like audacity”; for the preceding words see note r.]

Posted on the day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, A.D. 314. [Note: Be. would add II. The name of the city is absent also in the Pinellian copy of the Edict, from whose words *beatitudo urbis Romae* Muratori supplied *Romae*.]

**CONCERNING THE CURATORS OF THE MUNICIPAL REGISTER OF DEBTS** [Note: 4, Til.–Lugd.: Kalendariis. Cod. Justinian, title XXXII, is entitled *Concerning Debtors of Cities*. Go. says that the same heading should have been placed in the Theodosian Code in place of that used by its compilers. Rein.: Al. *Concerning the curator of the commonwealth and examiner of public money.* Vat. fr. §128.] **AND THEIR SURETIES.**

Constantine Augustus to his own Locrio Verinus, greetings. [Note: Cod. Theod. II, 19, 1; XIV, 4, 2: Lucrius Verinus. See c. 1 cited, note y. Cod. Justinian omits Locrio and suo. Go. omits quos.]

In the case of persons whom you ascertain to be alive and solvent, or whose heirs retain intact estates, [Col. 0111A] the principal sums entered in the municipal debt-register must remain in force, provided, however, that they pay annual interest at the proper times; for it is both advantageous to the municipality to retain solvent debtors and beneficial to the debtors themselves that the accumulation of debt not be increased. [Note: The reading *retinent* is that of 4 and Cod. Justinian. The editions have retinere, namely dependent on pervideris. In cod. 4 the word retinent is clearly discernible but has almost disappeared; a corrector has written retinere over it in red, incorrectly. Cod. Justinian: reipublicae. Cod. Justinian: ipsis sit commodum. Go.: “That is, *sit*, from the common construction.”]

§ 1. And because it is unlawful for municipalities to be defrauded through the alienation of liable estates, it has been decided that, if a debtor of a municipal commonwealth has given away, sold, or transferred to another by any means anything from the estate which he possessed when he borrowed public money, then, after the nature of the property alienated has been examined and all the debtor’s means considered as they stood when the money was lent to him, [Note: Fol. 286, cod. 4. In cod. 4, corrected in red from *nec fas*. Cod. Justinian: si quis. Go.–Ri*: debtor of the commonwealth. Cod. 4: alienate, corrected by the scribe to alienatae. Cuj. 2, 2*: alienare. Cod. 4: credideretur, corrected in red to crederetur.] principal and interest shall be demanded proportionately from the person who retains anything from the debtor’s resources. [Note: Cod. 4: detinent ex orte, corrected in red to detinet ex sorte.]

Accordingly, whenever the estate of a person whose name is found liable in the municipal debt-register proves insufficient, the judge must investigate with every care and diligence [Note: Cod. Justinian: *cujus nomen civitati alicui invenitur obnoxium*. Cod. Justinian: *judex omni diligentia et sollicitudine*. Go.–Ri.: iniquirere.] to whom the debtor’s resources have passed under whatever legal condition, so that the individual holders, after an equitable valuation, may be sued proportionately according to the property which they possess; they will have a personal action against the debtor, who is released when they pay. But from the person from whom it is clear that the greater part of his property has passed away, the remaining portion which has stayed with him must also be transferred to a solvent person. [Note: Cod. 4: transierit debitores, restored in red to transierint debitoris. Go.: porsonalem, incorrectly.]

§ 2. If any debtor of a municipal commonwealth has made way for Our fisc, purchasers who have bought from Our fisc plainly ought, according to ancient law, the rescripts of the deified emperors, and Our constitutions, [Note: Fol. 286, cod. 4. Cod. Justinian: purchasers who bought from Our fisc. Go. also interprets ex as a. Cod. Justinian adds principum, but Cujacius omits it. Emperors are rarely simply called *divi*.] to suffer no inconvenience, since in such cases it has been decided that the commonwealth should bear accidental losses. [Note: Cod. Justinian omits what follows through exigantur.] But those who have received anything from the same estate by imperial bounty will, under the law enacted, be liable to the commonwealth. Consideration having been given to the debtor’s total means as they stood when he borrowed public money, [Col. 0112A] they shall be required, in proportion to the estate which they retain through Our generosity, to pay the appropriate part of principal and interest. [Note: 4, Til.–Ri*: fuerat, incorrectly. Be. correctly restores fuerant. Cod. 4: publice, corrected in red to publicae.]

§ 3. If a debtor does not appear, or has so consumed all his property that no one possesses anything from his estate, this debt too must be regarded as a loss belonging to the commonwealth. [Note: Go.: debitores, incorrectly. 4, Til., Be., Cod. Justinian: non comparuerit, correctly. Cuj. 1–Ri*: conparaverit, ineptly; Rein. and Go. emend conparuerit. Cod. Justinian: omnia sua ita. Cod. Justinian omits quoque. Cod. 4: publice.] Therefore, at the risk of the curator of the debt-register, the magistrates, and those who appoint them, money must be placed with solvent persons or with owners of rural estates. [Note: Cod. 4: kalendari, corrected in red to kalendarii. Cod. Justinian substitutes: “Therefore, through the care of the father of the city, [money must be placed] with solvent persons.”]

Posted on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, A.D. 314. [Note: Be. would add II. Go.–Ri*: Aniano.]

**CONCERNING DELAYS.**

Constantine Augustus to Ursus, Vicar. [Note: 15: Urso Vicario. 27: ad adversum vic. Go. wishes in the commentary to restore *ad Verum Vi. Clarium* [a most distinguished man], or *ad Verum Vicarium*, and in the notes *Vi. Clarum*, i.e. *Virum Clarissimum*; and in the Chronicle for A.D. 314, V.C. He thinks, because of Constantine’s letter to Caecilian in Eusebius X.6, that this Ursus was rationalis of Africa.]

Whenever anyone has obtained a rescript addressed to an extraordinary judge, delay must be wholly denied to him. But the person summoned into court must be given time to prove the falsehood of the petitions, or to produce documents or witnesses, since a person drawn unexpectedly before an unfamiliar judge could not have been prepared. [Note: 15: neganda. Cod. Justinian: improbanda, by error; cf. Gebauer and Dirksen, loc. cit., p. 417. Cod. Justinian: judicium. 15: jud. trahebatur.]

Given on the second day before the Nones of March, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, A.D. 314. [Note: Cuj. 1–Be.: Volusi, but Cuj. 2 in correction: Volusiano. Be. would add II. 15, W., Cod. Justinian: Volusiano. 27: Volosiano.]

**INTERPRETATION.** Whenever an order has been procured from some prince in order to draw one’s adversary, for a hearing, before a judge other than the one to whom he has been assigned, just as the petitioner must not receive a postponement if he requests one, [Note: 15: al. principis p. f. surrepta and omits ab. 15: debuit.] so neither should a requested delay be denied to the person brought into court, that he may more easily prove, by writing or witnesses, that the person by whom he has been sued obtained what he requested by a false petition. [Note: 15: debita.]

**CONCERNING SHIPOWNERS.** [Note: Cod. Justinian: *Concerning shipowners or nauclers who transport public supplies, and concerning the abolition of the contribution in lustral gold.*]

Constantine [Note: 4 and editions: Constantius. Go., Rein., and Be. emend to Constantinus, which is restored, since the scribe of cod. 4 plainly erred in writing Constantius.] Augustus to Volusianus . . . [Note: The title is omitted in cod. 4 and the editions; Go.–Ri* mark the gap by five dots; the rest indicate no lacuna. Go. and Be. add in the note: Prefect of the City. See C. Th. V, 6, 1, note z.]

If a shipowner is a *levamentarius* by origin, [Col. 0113A] he shall nevertheless remain permanently among the same persons with whom his parents are seen to have been. [Note: Go. remarks: “It should be written separately, *nihilo minus*, that is, equally, similarly to his parents.”]

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, A.D. 314. [Note: Add II, as Be. had already wished. Aur. Lugd., Cuj. 2, 2*: Cons.]

**CONCERNING THE ADMINISTRATION AND LIABILITY OF GUARDIANS AND CURATORS.** [Note: 39 omits Et Periculo; 15: Et Curatorum. “Concerning the administration, transfer, and liability, etc.” 28: et virorum; 31: et viatorum. Pu.: Tuorum, a typographical error. Cod. Justinian V.37: “Concerning the administration [omitting *and liability*] of guardians or curators, and the lending or depositing of wards’ money.”]

Constantine Augustus [Note: Sich.–Lugd. omit A. Sich., Cuj. 1–Be.: Constant.] . . . . . . . [Note: 8, 12, 21, Sich., Cuj. 1–Ri* add *et Julianus Caes.*, which cannot stand. Go. thinks Licinius should be written for Julianus, but the manuscripts oppose the conjecture. 6, 7, 9, 13, 14, 16, 17, 25–29, 32, 33, 36–40, 42, Til. add et c. [et Caesar or et Caes.]; 34: et consl.; 10, 18: et cet. Perhaps Crispus Caesar is meant, whom Constantine, when setting out against Licinius, had put in charge of Gaul, where the constitution was given. I do not doubt that cod. 15 supplies the true inscription: *Imp. Const. Aug. Basso ppo*; but since it is the reading of only one manuscript and it is uncertain whether Bassus was prefect in this year, I did not adopt it. Cod. Justinian: Constantine Augustus to Euphemiana, but I do not know whence this name arose.]

For the performance of a guardian’s or curator’s administration, if they are debtors, their property is pledged as if by right of pledge; wards are not prohibited from claiming it for themselves. [Note: 10, 18: tutores v. curatores—tit. oblita minoris semet. 14 omits vel curatoris. 21: tutores vel curatores b. se debit. 26: deb. et exist. Cod. Justinian adds: “The same applies if a guardian or curator has been appointed and has not administered the property of wards.”]

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of April at Trier, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, A.D. 314. [Note: 8, 19, 28, 36, 40, Sich. in margin: V; 31: VIII; 32, 38, 29 and manuscripts of Go.: VI. Most manuscripts: Triv. 15: trium. 33, 34: tribus. Sich.–Ri*, Cod. Justinian: Treveris. Then many manuscripts: Volosiano et Aniano, the latter appearing in Sich., Cuj. 1–Ri*. Other manuscripts omit Trev. or et Anniano. Be. wishes II inserted after Volusianum.]

**INTERPRETATION.** Every guardian or curator who, through negligence in his administration, is proved to be debtor to minors must know that his property is so pledged that, if he does not make satisfaction after an accounting has been made, [Col. 0113B] his property is held by the minors in the place of a pledge.

**CONCERNING THE CLAUDIAN SENATORIAL DECREE.** [Note: P. omits the heading; in Pu. it is enclosed in brackets; it is also absent in Cod. 1, which presents only the final part of the title.]

Constantine Augustus to Probus. If any free women have been joined, against their will, to persons of servile status after suffering violence either from slaves or from any other persons, they shall obtain redress under the appropriate severity of the laws. [Note: Aur. Lugd.: severitatem, and later custodire.]

§ 1. But if any woman is forgetful of her own honor, [Col. 0114A] she shall lose her freedom, and her children shall be slaves of the master whose slave’s concubinage (*contubernium*) she joined. [Note: Georgius d’Arnaud, *Variae Coniecturae*, book I, ch. 20, attempted *cujus servi se contubernio*; but that *contubernium* here denotes the slave is shown by Go. in the note to this chapter and by Cramer, *Dispunctationes juris civilis*, ch. XIII, p. 117.] This law must also be observed with respect to the past.

Posted on the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, A.D. 314. [Note: Be. would add II. Cuj. 1–Ri*: Aniano.]

**INTERPRETATION.** A woman joined by force and against her will to another’s slave obtains redress. But if she becomes a slave woman voluntarily, her children too are slaves.

**CONCERNING FREEBORN PERSONS WHO SERVED IN THE TIME OF THE TYRANT.** [Note: Maxentius, defeated by Constantine in A.D. 312, is meant. Some manuscripts: *Tirannis Servierint*. 6, 7: Servierint. 15 omits Temp. Tyr.]

Constantine Augustus to Volusianus. [Note: 37: Volucrum. Some manuscripts: A Volusiano. 40 omits ad Volus. Volusianus’s rank is absent from all manuscripts except 32, where he is called prp. It is also absent in c. 1, C. Th. *Concerning Shipowners* XIII.5. In c. 2, Cod. Just. *Concerning Dignities* XII.1, he is called Praetorian Prefect; but Prefect of the City is restored, because that abbreviation occurs in c. 2, C. Th. *Concerning Persons Whose Appeals*, XI.36, promulgated in A.D. 315. See Go. in commentary on this chapter and Corsini, loc. cit., p. 169. According to Go. and W., Volusianus seems in the same year 314 to have served both as consul and prefect.]

Let all strive in the spirit of devotion to restore to their birth-status those whom they recognize, either from their own conscience or from others’ evidence, to have been born free and to have lost their freeborn status under the tyrant, [Note: 20: Si quis. Then 12, 16: procreatis. 10, 18: Ingenuitatis amissae. 6, 7: amissae. 16: manumisse. Sich.: ingenuitate amissa. 9: Proprie. Ri. notes that it is not to be changed to convicti. 20: Aliarum indices recognoscant. Sich., Til., Aur. Lugd.: judiciis. W.: Naturalibus, a typographical error.] without awaiting the intervention of a judge. [Note: 19, 21: *Nec exspectent jud. interpellationes*; 21: exspectant. 1: interpellationem—certissimam, incorrectly. Go. has nec for non.]

For if anyone persists, contrary to his conscience or the most certain testimony of many persons, in the same tenacity of avarice, [Note: 6–8, 10, 13, 14, 16, 18, 20, 21 add id. In cod. 20, a later hand places *per* above *conscientiam* and *certissima*. The reading *in eadem avaritiae tenacitate* is that of 1, 6, 7, 10, 13–19, 21, Sich., Til.; W. rightly defends it against the vulgate of the editions Cuj. 1–Pu.: *avaritia et tenacitate*. 12: avaritiam tenacitatem; 20 originally avaritie et ten., but corrected to avaritia.] he shall be punished with the most severe penalty. [Note: 1: Siverissimam, corrected to severissima. 12: severissima testimonia mult.] It is further decided that those too shall be subjected to liability who knowingly conceal the fact that freeborn persons endure the necessity of slavery through wrong. [Note: Pu. omits autem. 1: Subjudari, incorrectly. Then Sich.: scienter. In the words servit..., the eighth leaf of cod. 1 breaks off, and P., Pu. end. Sich.: necessitate. 6, Sich., Cuj. 1–Lugd.: incuriam, incorrectly. 20: injurias.]

Posted on the eighth day before the Kalends of May at Rome, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, A.D. 314. [Note: Many manuscripts: Dat., but PP. is more correct, because Constantine was not at Rome at this time. 24: Dat. prop. 19: Prid.; 20: VII; 36, 40: IV; Anian. And. in Go.: XVIII. 19, 20: Mad.; 32, 38, 43 and the excellent note of Anianus in Go.: Mart. or Mar. Some manuscripts omit Rom. 20 adds III. Add II, as Be. had already wished. Many manuscripts: Volosiano. 8, 20 omit et Ann. Most manuscripts and Sich.: Aniano.]

**INTERPRETATION.** Freeborn persons who were assigned to slavery in the tyrant’s time [Note: Nearly all manuscripts: tyr. temp. The editions: temporibus—though Sich., Cuj. 1–Lugd.: tempore—tyr.] shall be restored to freeborn status. If anyone knowingly keeps in slavery a freeborn person assigned in this manner, [Note: 21: Adjecti, but corrected in the margin to addicti. Again the manuscripts, with few exceptions: hoc ordine; the editions: hoc ord. sciens. Sich.: tenuerint.] let him know that the laws will exact punishment from him.

## On the Privileges of Those Who Have Served in the Sacred Palace

Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Palatines who have rendered good service, greetings. From the Palatines—both those who have performed blameless duties in our service and those who have been employed in our bureaux, that is, those of records, letters, and petitions—we order that every accusation or nomination be kept far away; and that this benefit pass to their sons and grandsons by the very order of blood, and that they remain exempt from all burdensome and personal public services, together with all their movable property and urban slaves; nor are any injuries to be inflicted upon them by anyone. Thus, whoever disregards these provisions shall be required to pay the penalties due, without distinction of rank. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of November at Trier, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus (314).

> Note [Col. 0115C] j: Cujacius, second edition; Ri* in the index of titles: “On privilege.” The Code of Justinian subsequently has “those who serve.”
>
> Note [Col. 0115C] k: The word *and*, added by V., Cujacius 1–Ri*, is absent, probably rightly, in Gothofredus’s text of the Code of Justinian and, according to Gothofredus, in the Lugdunensis manuscript; for these reasons it was rightly deleted by Be. It is not in the codex.
>
> Note [Col. 0115C] l: The Code of Justinian omits “their.” The same manuscript has *S.* in place of “Greetings.” Next, the codex reads *tam in his*. Thereafter folio XLI of the codex begins with “...lorumque versati sunt.”
>
> Note [Col. 0115C] m: The codex reads *sanguinis vervenire*, corrected to *pervenire* by a later hand. Shortly afterward the codex has *unversis*, corrected to *universis*.
>
> Note [Col. 0115C] n: Gothofredus has *injuria*, erroneously; and the Code of Justinian has this in place of *haec* (“these things”).
>
> Note [Col. 0115C] o: Be., in a note, adds *ad* without reason. See Theodosian Code VI.26.14, note b; VIII.1.1, note f; X.20.2; and the First Novel of Theodosius, “On Those Removed from Military Service” (Berlin edition, p. 1236). The Code of Justinian reads *poenas debitas exsolvat* (“let him pay the due penalties”). Cramer printed this in his *Works*, p. 85, note 2; nor does *ad*, which Be. wishes to add, seem probable to him, although the Haffuiensis and Gottingensis manuscripts so read.
>
> Note [Col. 0115D] p: The codex and Cujacius 1–Ri* have *Triveris*; the Code of Justinian, *Treveris*. Gothofredus, in his Chronicle for this year, considers a different month or place-name to be required.
>
> Note [Col. 0115D] q: Be. emends to “Volusianus, consul for the second time.”
>
> Note [Col. 0115D] r: Gothofredus gives 316.

## On the Extortions of Advocates or Court Officials

> Note [Col. 0115D] s: The Code of Justinian: “On the Profits of Advocates and the Extortions of Offices or Court Officials”; a heading composed from this and the preceding title of the Theodosian Code.

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa.

If anyone knows himself to have been wronged by officials of ducenarian or centenarian rank, and especially by advocates of the fisc, let him not delay in approaching the courts and proving the wrong, so that suitable severity may be exercised against the person convicted. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of November at Trier. Received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March at Carthage, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315?).

> Note [Col. 0115D] t: “Aelianus” is absent from the manuscripts and editions before Be., without any mark of a lacuna. It was restored by Be., at Gothofredus’s recommendation, from chapter 1 of the Theodosian Code, “On the Advocates of the Fisc,” cited here, and from the Code of Justinian, which nevertheless addresses Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa.
>
> Note [Col. 0115D] u: Chapter 1 of the Theodosian Code, “On the Advocates of the Fisc,” adds: “After other matters.”
>
> Note [Col. 0116B] a: The Code of Justinian reads: “If anyone knows himself to have been wronged by ducenarians or centenarians, or advocates of the fisc.” The Lugdunensis codex has *fisi advocatus*. Codex I has “especially.”
>
> Note [Col. 0116B] b: Aurelius and Lugdunensis: *adiri* (“to be approached”). My copy of Cujacius 1 has *judicia* (“the courts”). The Code of Justinian: “the courts and prove.”
>
> Note [Col. 0116B] c: Codex Lugdunensis has *competensti*, but codex I corrects it to *competenti*; another reading is *competente severitate*.
>
> Note [Col. 0116B] d: The Code of Justinian, though Cujacius agrees with the Theodosian Code, gives: “Given on the Kalends of November,” consistent with Theodosian Code, “On Annona and Tribute,” chapter 2, and “On the Collection of Taxes,” chapter 1. Gothofredus wishes the consuls of 313 to be restored in his Chronicle, p. VII. See Theodosian Code I.12.1, note i, and chapter 1 “On the Advocates of the Fisc,” cited above, note m.
>
> Note [Col. 0116C] e: Codex Lugdunensis, Cujacius 1–Ri*, and seemingly codex I have *Triveris*; the Code of Justinian has *Treveris*.
>
> Note [Col. 0116C] f: “Received ... at Carthage” is omitted in chapter 1 of the Theodosian Code cited above and in the Code of Justinian, except in Cujacius; Ri* has “Constantius.”

## On the Advocate of the Fisc

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa. After other matters:

An advocate of the fisc, fearing punishment, shall take care not to conceal fiscal advantages; nor, when no case exists, shall he dare, in the name of the fisc, to stir up vexatious accusations against private persons. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of November at Trier, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315?).

> Note [Col. 0116C] g: Codex 4 has *advocatio*, but this was corrected in red ink. The Code of Justinian has “advocates.”
>
> Note [Col. 0116C] h: Sichardus and many manuscripts have *Elianus*; some have *Helianus*. Manuscript 15 has *leliano*; 25, *Velaiano*; 39, *aliano*.
>
> Note [Col. 0116C] i: Manuscript 4 and Pu., Til.–Lugd. have *PV*. See Theodosian Code X.9.3, note c. Some manuscripts abbreviate *proconsuli* as *ppo.* or *po.*; manuscripts 6, 7, and 8 omit “Proconsul.”
>
> Note [Col. 0116C] j: Some manuscripts, Br. and Al., and the Code of Justinian omit “After other matters.”
>
> Note [Col. 0116C] k: Manuscripts 6 and 7 read *necve nullo*; 10, 18, 25, and the Code of Justinian, *neve ullo*; 9 and 12, *ne ullo*; 15, *nec ullo*; 20, *nevel ullo*; Sichardus, *in ullo*. Be. notes: “I was unwilling to alter the reading defended by Gfr., although it seems less preferable.” It is surprising that Be. should hesitate here. Gothofredus rightly explains *nullo negotio* as “where there is no cause, no litigation, no subject-matter of litigation,” i.e. he must not dare, in the name of the fisc, to bring vexatious accusations against private persons where no suit exists.
>
> Note [Col. 0116D] l: Manuscript 21 and Sichardus: *existentes*.
>
> Note [Col. 0116D] m: Manuscript 20: *calumniam*; Sichardus, *calumniis*.
>
> Note [Col. 0116D] n: Manuscripts 15, 20, 21, 38, and 42 have VII; 30, VIII. In manuscript 6, L., R., and U., the numeral is omitted.
>
> Note [Col. 0116D] o: Gothofredus, in a note, gives “Kalends of November.” Without doubt he had in mind XI.1.2 and XI.7.1. The Epitome of the Monk reads: “Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of November.” Subsequently Sichardus, with many manuscripts, has *Treveris*; others, *Triu*.
>
> Note [Col. 0116D] p: In one manuscript or another, a consular numeral is absent. Manuscript 21 and Sichardus have “Licinius Caesar” in place of “IV,” as consuls; 15 has “At Trier, under the consuls mentioned above”; 20, “Constantius XIV”; the Epitome of the Monk, “and Merobaudes, consuls.” Gothofredus refers the law to 313, to which year it is assigned in the Chronicle and in the Code of Justinian, correctly. Bon. agrees with Gothofredus, cited work, p. 745. See Theodosian Code I.12.1, note i, and VIII.10.1, note above.

### Interpretation

Those who protect the advantages or benefit of our fisc ought to observe this limit: they must not be negligent concerning what is lawfully due to us, nor prove to be vexatious accusers of provincials while, in the name of the fisc, they unjustly demand something from them.

> Note [Col. 0116D] q: Some manuscripts have *nec* (“nor”).
>
> Note [Col. 0116D] r: Sichardus and Cujacius 1–Cujacius 2* have *hiis*; some manuscripts, *his*. Manuscript 21 has *injusta* and omits “from them.” Sichardus, Cujacius 1–Lugdunensis, has *injusto*.

## On Various Rescripts

> Note [Col. 0117C] a: In the margin of the first leaf of codex 1, the following words are written in small letters concerning this chapter: “…ni p…dultum | …sum exemplum | …graec lib. V. Cod. Just. D. D. R. Et Pragmaticis Sanctionibus.” [Materially uncertain OCR in the fragmentary wording.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Antiochus, Prefect of the Watch.

It does not please us that our annotations be admitted without a rescript; and therefore let the office of your gravity observe, as has always been maintained, that you are to consider our rescripts—or rather our letters—rather than annotations alone, to be heard. Given on the third day before the Kalends of January at Trier, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus (314).

> Note [Col. 0117C] b: “Augustus” is absent in codex 1.
>
> Note [Col. 0117C] c: Codex 1 has *Vigilium*.
>
> Note [Col. 0117D] d: P. supplies the letters *eo* that have been cut away in codex 1.
>
> Note [Col. 0117D] e: W. has *ipsas* (“the very [ones]”), erroneously; but the correction changes it to *nostras* (“our”).
>
> Note [Col. 0117D] f: Codex 1 has *Adnotitiones*.
>
> Note [Col. 0117D] g: Codex 1, *Triv.*; P., *Triveris*; Pu., *Triberis*.

## On Long Prescription of Time, Which Is Pleaded for Freedom and Not Against Freedom

A copy of the sacred letter of Constantine and Licinius, Augusti, to Dionysius, acting as Vicarius of the Praetorian Prefecture.

It accords with equity that the rights of freedom ought by no means to be impaired merely by the length of time, even if a period of sixty years has elapsed. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus (314). (From the Code of Justinian.)

## On Acquiring and Recovering Possession

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maternus.

No one doubts that there are two aspects of possession: one resting upon law, the other upon physical control. Both, however, are lawful only when they are established by the silence and acquiescence of all opponents. But once an objection and controversy have arisen, a person cannot be understood to be possessor who, although he physically holds possession, nevertheless, because of a challenge having been lodged and the cause brought into court, wavers and is uncertain concerning the right of possession. Posted on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February at Trier, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus (314). (From the Code of Justinian.)

In the year of the Lord 315, Constantine and Licinius Augusti being consuls for the fourth time.

## On the Public Post, Compulsory Transport-Service, and Supplementary Requisitions

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Constantius.

If anyone travelling should lead away an ox not assigned to the post but devoted to ploughing, he shall be seized by the stationarii and those in charge of the public post with due force, and either presented to the judge, if he is at hand, or handed over to municipal magistrates for appropriate punishment and sent on through their agency. Or, if he is of such rank that it would by no means be fitting to proceed against him with such force, a report concerning him shall be made to our Clemency. For whoever has reached a posting-station, if he happens not to have oxen, must remain there until they are supplied by those administering the public post; nor may he take away animals employed in tilling the land. Received on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February at Caralis, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315).

> Note [Col. 0117D] h: Manuscript 16 has “on compulsory requisitions”; Sichardus and the Code of Justinian have “and compulsory requisitions.” Sichardus and Til. likewise have this in the index of titles.
>
> Note [Col. 0117D] i: Some manuscripts read *perangariis*; others omit “and supplementary requisitions”; still others add, “this is concerning one who takes a post-horse.” Codex Lugdunensis has *Paranga*, with *riis* added above the line.
>
> Note [Col. 0117D] j: Gothofredus and Be., in notes, add “Praetorian Prefect,” correctly. In his Chronicle for this year Gothofredus understands him to be governor of Sardinia.
>
> Note [Col. 0117D] k: Be. notes: “Gfr. rightly corrected the punctuation of Cujacius 1 and 2, which lack commas and produce an entirely different sense.” The punctuation before *stationarios* was already as it is now in Aurelius Lugdunensis.
>
> Note [Col. 0117D] l: Be. emends *aut* (“or”) to *at* (“but”), not badly, though unnecessarily. I have judged the punctuation of the earlier editions to be restored; for Be. punctuates: *transmittatur. Aut.*
>
> Note [Col. 0118C] a: The codex has *explecaverit*. Aurelius Lugdunensis: *qui ... explicaverit*. Gothofredus emends to *applicaverit* and proposes various explanations of *explicaverit*, a word also suspected by Reinesius. He also recommends *appellere ad mansionem* (“to arrive at a station”), especially Ri. in note f to chapter 15 of this Theodosian Code title. But Ritter’s explanation should not be accepted either; he takes *explicare mansionem* to mean departing from the ordinary station of the public post to another place where the post does not stop, relying on the words of Theodosian Code VI.29.2 §1: “although this necessity is unfolded in public canals”—words which do not fit this passage at all. *Explicare mansionem* seems to mean nothing other than arriving at a station, having completed some stretch of the road (*Station zurücklegen*). Similarly Pliny, *Letters* VIII.1: *iter commode explicui*, “I completed the journey comfortably.”
>
> Note [Col. 0118C] b: Gothofredus and Reinesius aptly emend *egerunt* to *gerunt*.

## Whose Appeals Are Not to Be Received

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Volusianus, Prefect of the City.

Whoever appeals from a preliminary judgment or from the executors of matters previously determined, and prematurely seeks the adjudications of another tribunal, shall be fined thirty folles; and you yourself shall hear and decide the whole case without delay, since you will appear to make the case your own if, through connivance, you admit an appeal of this kind. If you discover that appeals have been lodged concerning any case whatsoever, you must observe in their examination what has already long since been most clearly established by us. Posted on the fifth day before the Kalends of March at Rome, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315).

> Note [Col. 0118C] c: Ri* has *Xolusianum*.
>
> Note [Col. 0118C] d: Gothofredus erroneously has *staturarum*.
>
> Note [Col. 0118C] e: Gothofredus notes: “Perhaps rather *altioris* (‘of a higher tribunal’)? I do not think so.”
>
> Note [Col. 0118C] f: Gothofredus and R. have *praepopere*.
>
> Note [Col. 0118D] g: Cujacius 1 and Cujacius 2–Ri* have *discinguas*. Folio 207 of codex 4 begins with the letters *cingas*.
>
> Note [Col. 0118D] h: Manuscript 4 and Til.–Ri* have *conhibentiam*, as almost always; I refrain from mentioning this further below. Gothofredus already records that *conhibentiam* was written for *conniventiam*.
>
> Note [Col. 0118D] i: Gothofredus maintains that this law, which was earlier than the first law, has perished.

## On Various Offices and Court Officials, and Their Certificates

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Versennius Fortunatus, Consular Governor of the Aqueducts.

The order of promotion must be observed, so that the first in the office is the person who was first in obtaining the imperial favor. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of March at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315).
