## If a Partner in a Petition Dies Without an Heir

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Mygdonius, Treasurer of the Sacred Palace.

If any one of those who have jointly obtained from our Clemency a grant of something should happen to die, leaving no surviving successors, it is our pleasure that the share of the person who has died intestate or without children should pass not to any outside person whatever, but to his partner or co-participant. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April at Antioch, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315).

> Note [Col. 0119B] a: Manuscripts 10 and 32 have “inheritance”; 15, “If he has died”; 24, “If the occasion of the petition has failed”; 38, “If the partner in recovery has failed without an heir.” The Code of Justinian: “If a partner in imperial generosity dies without an heir.”
>
> Note [Col. 0119B] b: Most Br. and Al. manuscripts have *Migdonem*; 17, 20, 28, 36, and 40, *Macedonium*; 15, “Mygdonius, Treasurer”; 25, *migonio castrensi*.
>
> Note [Col. 0119B] c: Manuscripts 17, 28, 36, 40, and Sichardus omit “Treasurer of the Sacred Palace,” as do most Br. and Al. manuscripts. Manuscript 4 and Til.–Lugd. have only *S.* In the Code of Justinian, except Cujacius, the heading and subscription of this chapter have been conflated with the text of the following law; see especially Gothofredus.
>
> Note [Col. 0119C] d: Sichardus has: “The military peculium: if anyone”; especially Gothofredus. Sichardus drew into the law words belonging to the heading, having wrongly interpreted the abbreviation *Castr. P.*
>
> Note [Col. 0119C] e: Manuscripts 12 and 25 have *impetraverint*.
>
> Note [Col. 0119C] f: Manuscripts 6, 7, 8, and 16 have *reliquit*; 10, 15, 18, 20, 21, and Sichardus, *reliquerit*; 25, *reliquerint*.
>
> Note [Col. 0119C] g: Manuscripts 12 and 20 add *ad*.
>
> Note [Col. 0119C] h: Manuscripts 6–8, 10, 12–14, and 18 have *filiis*.
>
> Note [Col. 0119C] i: Manuscripts 4, 21, and Sichardus–Lugdunensis have “has met his day without children”; 25 and Cujacius 2–Ri* have “has met his day.”
>
> Note [Col. 0119C] j: Other manuscripts have *Anthiociae* or *Antiocia*. Manuscript 4 and editions of the Code of Justinian have *Antiochiae*. Gothofredus proposes Antigonia near Stobi in Macedonia, or else considers “Given” to stand for “Proposed,” or for “Issued”; see Gothofredus on this chapter, note l, and in the Chronicle for this year.
>
> Note [Col. 0119C] k: Cujacius 2 and 2* have III.
>
> Note [Col. 0119C] l: In manuscripts one consular numeral or another is absent. Gothofredus–Ri* omit IV after Licinius; manuscript 21 and Sichardus omit Augustus after Constantine; 17, 28, 36, and 40 have Licinius III. Some manuscripts have *Lycinio*.

### Interpretation

If any person has died to whom our generosity has made a grant by name, and is known neither to have made a will nor to have left children, it is our pleasure that the share of that person be acquired by the one with whom the deceased received it jointly—that is, by his partner. For the partner is rightly preferred where it is known that no person of children has intervened.

> Note [Col. 0119D] m: Aurelius Lugdunensis, with many manuscripts, has *iis*; Sichardus, Cujacius 1, and some manuscripts, *hiis*; the rest, *his*.
>
> Note [Col. 0119D] n: Manuscript 20 has *ut*.
>
> Note [Col. 0119D] o: Sichardus omits *is* (“that person”).
>
> Note [Col. 0119D] p: Manuscripts 6–8, 10, 18, 20 (after correction), and 21 have *pater*; in manuscript 20 it formerly read *parte*, and in 21 *pr*.
>
> Note [Col. 0119D] q: Manuscript 20 has *accipiat*; other manuscripts, *acquirat*. Subsequently some manuscripts, including Sichardus, omit “his”; codex 20 omits “children”; 21 has “no person of children.”
>
> Note [Col. 0119D] r: Many manuscripts have “where no person [of children].”

## On Penalties

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Eumelius.

If anyone is condemned to the games or to the mines according to the nature of crimes established, let no writing be made upon his face, since the penalty of condemnation can be recorded by a single inscription on his hands and calves; so that the face, which is formed in the likeness of heavenly beauty, may not be defiled. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April at Chalon-sur-Saône, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315).

> Note [Col. 0119D] s: The rank of Eumelius is absent even in the Code of Justinian. Gothofredus reports that he was Vicarius of Africa.
>
> Note [Col. 0119D] t: The Code of Justinian has: “If anyone has been condemned to the mines,” omitting “to the games” and “or.”
>
> Note [Col. 0119D] u: The Code of Justinian has *cum*.
>
> Note [Col. 0120C] a: Aurelius Lugdunensis and the Code of Justinian have *inscriptione*.
>
> Note [Col. 0120C] b: The Code of Justinian has *est coelestis* (“is heavenly”).
>
> Note [Col. 0120C] c: Manuscript 4 has *Cavilluno*, corrected in red ink to *Cabilluno*. Be. has *Cabilluni*; the Code of Justinian, *Cabiluno*. Constantine was in Pannonia this year, not in Gaul. Gothofredus therefore emends in his commentary to Cabalin, a city of Thrace, approvingly according to Bou.; but in the Chronicle he gives Cabyle near Byzantium.
>
> Note [Col. 0120C] d: Aurelius Lugdunensis has *Cons.*

## On Treasures

Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Rationales.

Whoever finds a treasure and voluntarily brings it to the fisc shall receive one half of what he has found and shall hand over the other half to the fiscal accounts; provided, however, that every fiscal accusation shall cease, without the disturbance of an inquiry. For it is right that faith be placed in those who have voluntarily offered what they found. But if anyone refuses to report riches he has found and is exposed by any means, he must be excluded from the indulgence stated above. Given on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315).

> Note [Col. 0120C] e: Cujacius 2 and 2* have *ficalis*, erroneously.
>
> Note [Col. 0120C] f: Be. has *noluerint*, erroneously. With the words “and by some means,” folio 108 of codex 4 begins.

## On Cohortales, Principes, Cornicularii, and Primipilares

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Constantius, Praetorian Prefect.

Since the tyrant most unjustly established that those who had earned honorable discharge from cohortal military service and exemption for their property should serve in civil offices and the obligations of the municipal council, it is our pleasure, this law being abolished, that those who leave cohortal military service after completing twenty years of service shall thereafter be summoned to no civil public duties or curial obligations. This is likewise to be observed with respect to the officials of provincial governors. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315).

> Note [Col. 0120C] g: The Code of Justinian has *ac* (“and”).
>
> Note [Col. 0120C] h: See Vatican Fragments §§141, 143. The Code of Justinian has *Primipilariis*, but Cujacius, *Primipilaribus*.
>
> Note [Col. 0120C] i: Aurelius Lugdunensis has “Constantius,” erroneously.
>
> Note [Col. 0120C] j: Be. notes: “The usual reading [i.e. Ri., and likewise Ri*] is *PP. O.*; but the codex has *PP. o.* or *PPO.*; Cujacius 1, 2, and 2*, *PPO*; Gothofredus, *PP. O.*; and Aurelius Lugdunensis, *ppo.* These abbreviations amount to the same thing and signify the Praetorian Prefect. See above VII.13.9 and VII.14.1.”
>
> Note [Col. 0120D] k: Gothofredus doubts whether Maxentius—whom the sole law of Theodosian Code V.6, “On Freeborn Persons Enslaved in the Time of a Tyrant,” given in 314, concerns—or Licinius is intended. But in his commentary, agreeing with Glück, cited work, vol. XXXI, p. 427, he thinks Licinius must be meant, as he had been defeated in battle at Cibalae in the preceding year. Certainly the discussion concerns some lost constitution. The codex has *niquissime*, corrected to *iniquissime*.
>
> Note [Col. 0120D] l: Gothofredus’s edition from the manuscript has XXV. Cujacius 1–2* have *viginti*; especially Co. But the codex has XX years of service.
>
> Note [Col. 0120D] m: Aurelius Lugdunensis has *Cons.* Folio LXXXVI of the codex begins with the numeral “IV Kalends.”

Emperor Constantine Augustus, in his edict to the Africans.

It has been commanded to the stationarii of the primipilares, whose assigned places are plain, that if they extort anything beyond measure, they are to know that they will be punished by death. Furthermore, they must not maintain a prison; no one may hold a person in custody before them for an evident crime; nor may anyone have more than two muleteers from the province with him, or attach any to himself from Numidia; nor may he have a muleteer from other provinces, or one who has already been the servant of another stationarius. Posted on the sixth day before the Ides of May at Carthage, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the sixth time (315).

> Note [Col. 0120D] n: The Code of Justinian, because this is the first law of the title, has simply “Emperor Constantine.”
>
> Note [Col. 0120D] o: Gothofredus aptly emends *loca* (“places”) to *lucra* (“profits”). His other conjecture is *loca curarum* for *loca, coram*. If *loca* is correct, it means stations or boundaries.
>
> Note [Col. 0121C] a: The codex has *agason ex provincia*.
>
> Note [Col. 0121C] b: The codex has *nue*, with the letter *e* added over *n*. Shortly afterward Ri* has *provincias*, erroneously.
>
> Note [Col. 0121C] c: Editions have *alicui*. Gothofredus emends *alicujus*, rightly. The codex has *alicui) jam*. Less commendable is Gothofredus’s alternative conjecture, which substitutes *stationario* for *stationarii*.
>
> Note [Col. 0121C] d: In the Code of Justinian this chapter is deformed as follows: “All stationarii shall neither dare excessive exaction nor maintain a prison, nor shall anyone hold a person in custody, even for an evident crime ... knowing that, if anything of the kind has been committed, he is to be punished by death.”
>
> Note [Col. 0121C] e: The codex and editions before Be. have *Mai*; the Code of Justinian, *Maii*.
>
> Note [Col. 0121C] f: Editions before Be. have *Kartag.*; the Code of Justinian, *Carthag.*
>
> Note [Col. 0121C] g: Gothofredus wrongly omits IV before “consuls.” Aurelius Lugdunensis erroneously has *Cons.*, and likewise in the following law.

## On Support Which Indigent Parents Must Seek from the Public Treasury

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Ablavius.

Let a law be written on bronze tablets, whitened boards, or linen sheets and displayed throughout all the cities of Italy—a law which restrains the hands of parents from parricide and turns their inclination toward what is better. Let this concern engage your office: if any parent presents a child whom he cannot rear because of poverty, there must be no delay either in supplying food or clothing, since the upbringing of newly born infancy cannot endure delay. For this purpose we have ordered both our fisc and the imperial private estate (*res privata*) to furnish assistance without distinction. Given on the third day before the Ides of May at Naissus, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius Augustus for the fourth time (315).

> Note [Col. 0121C] h: The rank is absent; in its place Gothofredus–Ri* have six dots. Gothofredus wishes “Vicarius of the Praetorian Prefect” to be added, and Be. “Vicarius, Praetorian Prefect.” In the Chronicle for this year Gothofredus notes: “He seems to have acted in place of the Praetorian Prefect.”
>
> Note [Col. 0121D] i: Folio 173 of codex 4 begins with the words “a muleteer from the province.”
>
> Note [Col. 0121D] j: Gothofredus notes: “Perhaps *adserat*? It matters little.”
>
> Note [Col. 0121D] k: *Pro* (“because of”) is absent in codex 4 but added above the line by the scribe.
>
> Note [Col. 0121D] l: Manuscript 4 has *educare* twice, but the second occurrence is deleted by dots written beneath it.
>
> Note [Col. 0121D] m: Reinesius notes: “Heraldus says the following of this passage in *Daily Matters and Questions of Law*, book I, chapter 6, §12: Constantine wished by more extensive provision to prevent child-exposure; he was silent concerning exposed children. I do not know whether this law long exercised its force. I think it was temporary, and for that reason it was not received into the body of law collected by Justinian.”
>
> Note [Col. 0121D] n: Be. has *Naissi*.

## On Shipowners

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Amabilianus, Prefect of the Grain Supply.

Shipowners assigned to the association of urban bakers, and not bound to the bakers by any succession of inheritance, must be released from this duty. But if they happen to be bound to the bakers by hereditary right, they shall have the option, should they prefer, on account of the right of claim (*ob vindicias*), either to restore the inheritances of bakers to that same corporation or to yield them to any relatives of the deceased, so that they themselves may be freed from association with the bakers. But if they accept the inheritance, they must, by reason of succession, assume the partnership of the baking duty and bear from their own resources the burdens of shipowners, with the distinguished Prefect of the City of course deciding this matter. Given on the Kalends of June at Trier, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315).

> Note [Col. 0121D] o: Reinesius emends to “Annibalianus.”
>
> Note [Col. 0122B] a: Manuscript 4 has *vendicias*, corrected by the scribe to *vindicias*. Gothofredus reports that Mainardus conjectured *obventitias*. Gothofredus defends the common reading *ob vindicias*, i.e. because of the right belonging to the corporation of bakers to claim property bound to the bakers. See Theodosian Code XIII.6.5–6, “On the Estates of Shipowners.” Although *obventitias* is a word of very late Latin, and although codex 4 has *obvendicias*, differing only slightly in the letters *d* and *t*, I would not doubt that it should be adopted, had not the scribe himself corrected it.
>
> Note [Col. 0122B] b: Manuscript 4 has *corporis*, deleted in red ink. Folio 306 of codex 4 begins with the letters *ris*.
>
> Note [Col. 0122B] c: Manuscript 4 has *Prf.*
>
> Note [Col. 0122B] d: From Theodosian Code chapter 4 “On Appeals,” cited above, which has “Posted on the third day before the Kalends of January,” Gothofredus wishes in the Chronicle that “third day before the Kalends of January” be restored here so that the two chapters may be joined, since Constantine was at that time not at Trier but in Mysia, Dacia, or Pannonia. Yet this is insufficient: Gothofredus should also have restored *PP.* (“Posted”) for *Dat.* (“Given”). It seems to me that an error lies in *Dat.*; if *PP.* is restored in its place, everything is sound. Manuscript 4 and editions before Be. have *Triu.*; Ri*, *Triv.*

## On Pledges

Emperor Constantine Augustus to All Provincials.

Intercessors appointed by provincial governors to collect civil debts take slaves who are cultivators, or plough-oxen, from estates as pledges, and thereby payment of taxes is delayed. Therefore, if any intercessor, creditor, prefect of the peace, or decurion is discovered in this matter, he shall be subjected by the provincial governors to a capital sentence. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of June at Sirmium, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time (315).

> Note [Col. 0122C] e: Manuscript 26 adds “for a military rather than fiscal debt.” Some manuscripts, including 16 and Til., have “On Pledges,” and subsequently *pigneris*. The Code of Justinian (VIII.14) adds “and Mortgages.”
>
> Note [Col. 0122C] f: Some manuscripts omit “to all provincials.”
>
> Note [Col. 0122C] g: Manuscripts 10 and 18 have “Intercessors ... appointed”; 6, 7, 14, 16, 17, and 21, *datis*; 8 and 16, “and governors”; 21, “by senators”; 19 and 20 omit *a*. The Code of Justinian has “Executors appointed by any judge.”
>
> Note [Col. 0122C] h: Thus all manuscripts and Til., owing to the following phrase “whereby payment of taxes is delayed,” as Gothofredus and W. rightly approve. Manuscript 21 and all editions except Til. add *non*.
>
> Note [Col. 0122C] i: Manuscripts 6, 7, 14, 16, 17, 21, Sichardus, and Til. omit “cultivators or oxen.” See Cujacius, *Observations* IV.20. Manuscript 8 has “cultivating slaves or oxen,” from the interpretation; 10 and 18, “or oxen.”
>
> Note [Col. 0122D] j: Sichardus adds “veterans,” but the margin has *vercararios*. The Code of Justinian has “plough-oxen or agricultural implements [are] pledged.”
>
> Note [Col. 0122D] k: Thus manuscripts 6–8, 10, 14–19, Til.–Gothofredus; but in a note he judges either that *non* must be deleted or that *abstrahant* should be written. See note g. Manuscript 20 has *abstrauntur*; the remaining manuscripts and editions have *abstrahant*. The Code of Justinian has *non abstrahant*.
>
> Note [Col. 0122D] l: Manuscript 16 has “payment is handed over”; 19 and 20, “is rendered”; 9 adds *ut*.
>
> Note [Col. 0122D] m: Manuscripts 6–8, 10, 14–18, 20, Til., and the Code of Justinian have *vel* (“or”). W. conjectures *curator* in place of *creditor*.
>
> Note [Col. 0122D] n: Thus all manuscripts and editions except Be., who, on the authority of Gothofredus’s note and the Code of Justinian, gives *pagi* (“of the district”). The Code of Justinian has “of a district or village.” Cujacius, in his commentary on Code of Justinian X.1.9, wishes *pagis* to be read. The reading *pacis* (“of the peace”) is confirmed by the Gothic interpretation, which has *curator pacis* (“curator of the peace”), and by the *Basilica*, where the passage has εἰρηνάρχος (*eirēnarchos*, “peace officer”). W. approves *pacis*, since *praepositi pacis* (“officers of the peace”) are also mentioned in Theodosian Code XII.1.48 §2, “On Decurions,” where Gothofredus emends to *pagis*. Officers of villages and granaries are mentioned in Theodosian Code VII.4.1, “On the Distribution of Military Annona”; the superintendency of granaries and villages in XII.6.8, “On Tax Collectors.” See Gothofredus and W. on this passage.
>
> Note [Col. 0123B] a: Manuscript 15 has “the decurion in this”; 8 omits “in.”
>
> Note [Col. 0123B] b: Manuscript 8 has *subjetiatur*; 9, “is subjected by sentence”; 6 according to Ri., and 10, 14, 17, 18, “by sentence”; 19 and 20, “is judged by sentence.” The Code of Justinian has “shall be subjected to punishment assessed by the judge.”
>
> Note [Col. 0123B] c: Some manuscripts have VI; 28, 30, 33, 34, 38, the best manuscripts of the Anianic Interpretation according to Gothofredus, and the Code of Justinian have III. Subsequently 28 and 40 omit “June”; 33 has January; 20, July.
>
> Note [Col. 0123C] d: Thus most manuscripts and the editions Til.–Ri*; some have *Syrmio*; 21 and Sichardus, *Firmio*; Be. and W., *Sirmii*.
>
> Note [Col. 0123C] e: Some manuscripts and the Code of Justinian have “Constantine Augustus and Licinius”; 10, *cilinio*; 18, *cilmio*; others, *Lycinio*. Moreover 40 has Constantine Augustus III; Gothofredus, Ri., and Ri* omit IV after Constantine; 20 has “Constantinople IV.”

### Interpretation

Many presume, for a fiscal debt, to remove from estates slaves who cultivate the land or plough-oxen as a pledge; taxes are paid from their labor. Therefore, if any creditor, curator of the peace, municipal councillor, or any collector whatsoever presumes to do this, he shall be punished by the provincial judge.

> Note [Col. 0123C] f: Manuscript 20 has *intercessor*.
>
> Note [Col. 0123C] g: Some manuscripts, such as 10, 18, and 42, have *cura*; others, such as 21 in the margin, 36, 40, and the editions Sichardus, Cujacius 1, Aurelius Lugdunensis, have *curator*. The rest have *curam*. Subsequently manuscript 20 has “or councillor.”

## On Maternal Property, the Maternal Line, and the Abolition of Formal Acceptance

> Note [Col. 0123C] h: With the heading of this title folio CXX of codex Lugdunensis begins. Some manuscripts, such as 31–33 and 39, have “paternal.” The Code of Justinian: “On Maternal Property.”
>
> Note [Col. 0123C] i: Manuscripts 6, 7, 8, 16, other manuscripts, and Til. add “on.”
>
> Note [Col. 0123C] j: Some manuscripts have “paternal.” Many manuscripts have either “maternal” or “paternal”; codex 15 omits the words “and maternal line.”
>
> Note [Col. 0123C] k: Some manuscripts add “On.” Sichardus has *excretione* in place of *et cretione*. Til. omits *et* (“and”), though its rubricary index agrees with Sichardus. Some manuscripts erroneously have *creatione*. The Code of Justinian omits “and formal acceptance abolished”; manuscript 20, “abolished.”

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the consuls, praetors, tribunes of the plebs, and Senate, greetings.  
[Col. 0123D, note l: “Augustus” is absent in Sichard and in “Consuls, etc.” in certain manuscripts; in others: “to the Senate, greetings.”]  
[Col. 0123D, note m: 14 omits “of the plebs.” In the Lyon manuscript the syllables *ribus, Tribunis ple-* are almost obliterated.]  
[Col. 0123D, note n: 15 and 33 add “his own.”]  
[Col. 0123D, note o: *dicit* (“says”) is omitted in certain manuscripts and in the Code of Justinian: “20 Greetings. It has pleased [Us] to say.”]

It has pleased Us, while preserving the reverence and devotion due to sacred names  
[Col. 0123D, note p: 6–8 and other manuscripts have the erroneous *debitam*. Moreover, 8 reads “devotion, you, sacred.”]  
that the power and right of enjoying the property  
[Col. 0123D, note q: 20 has *in*, but corrected.]  
[Col. 0123B]  
[Col. 0123D, note r: 21 reads “indeed of it”; Sichard, “indeed all.”]  
of their children who are under sacred constitutions [*in sacris constitutorum*], in respect only of maternal property, shall remain with fathers; but that their licence to disinherit their children shall be withdrawn.  
[Col. 0123D, note s: Corrected to *rebus* (“property”) from manuscripts 15 and 19 instead of *res*, which the remaining manuscripts, including Lyon, and editions have.]  
[Col. 0123D, note t: 8 has *constitutionum*; 10 and 18, *constituti eorum*. Subsequently 8 has “all fathers,” and 21, “in paternal [property].”]  
[Col. 0123D, note u: *liberorum* is absent in Sichard; 10, 18, and 21 have *ei* (“to him”).]  
[Col. 0123D, note v: 15 has *denegetur* (“be denied”), not badly; 19, “licence be withdrawn from them.”]

§ 1. Therefore, in successions concerning maternal property alone, let the contrivance of formal acceptance (*cretio*) cease;  
[Col. 0124A]  
[Col. 0124B, note a: Incorrectly, 6–8, 10, 12–14, 17, and 18 have *conventum*. For *commentum* means a fiction. See Goez in the *Glossary of Legal Names*, and Dirksen, *Manual of Sources of Roman Civil Law*, under *Commentum*. Moreover, 20 reads “property concerning succession.”]  
and let property which has devolved upon children through succession from their mother be so within the power and ownership of their parents that the parents have the right of enjoyment, but are denied the licence of alienation.  
[Col. 0124B, note b: Here begins chapter 1 of the cited Code of Justinian, in which §§ 1 and 2 and the beginning of § 3 of this chapter are abridged as follows: “Property which has devolved upon children from their mother’s succession, whether by will or intestacy, shall be so in the power of their parents that they have only the faculty of using and enjoying it for their lifetime, while its ownership belongs, of course, to the children. But the parents, with whom, etc.”]  
[Col. 0124C, note c: 19 and 20 read “parents’ will and power or ownership.”]

For it has pleased Us that children under paternal power shall have as their own special property, and without participation by anyone else, the maternal estate which has accrued to them, when, upon their father’s death, they have become independent persons (*sui iuris*).  
[Col. 0124C, note d: 10 and 18 read “which [accrues] in the children.”]  
[Col. 0124C, note e: 12 has *subvenerit* (“has come to their aid”).]  
[Col. 0124C, note f: 14, 16, and Goez erroneously have the singular *fuerit*. 10 and 18: “they were the principal [thing]”; 20: *precium*, corrected to *praecipuam*; 9: *praecipuam*. A little later 21 has *consortium*.]

§ 2. But if a father, wishing to see his son as a head of a household (*paterfamilias*), emancipates him, he must make over to him the maternal estate,  
[Col. 0124C, note g: Valentinian and Justinian mention this law.]  
[Col. 0124C, note h: 19 reads *filium suum*; 20 omits *filium*.]  
[Col. 0124C, note i: Thus the manuscripts, Sichard, Tilius, and Beatus; Goez and Ritter have *iubet* (“orders”); Cujas 1 through Ritter’s first edition have *repraes. et*, with *et* explained by Goez as *etiam* (“also”).]  
[Col. 0124C, note j: 9, 16, 19–21, and Sichard have *debet* (“must”), which is equally admissible. 6–8, 12–14, and 17 have *habebit* (“will have”), incorrectly. Ritter has *debebit*.]  
so that the son, having received the gift of freedom and become owner of his own property,  
[Col. 0124C, note k: 15 reads corruptly “freedom, property acquired, lord.” The Lyon manuscript has *dominos*. Goez erroneously has *dominum*.]  
may, lest he appear ungrateful, offer to his parent, as a gift, a third part of the property kept for him. The valuation, if the things begin to be divided, shall be left to the judgment of worthy men; and, if he prefers, the father shall have free power also to alienate that third part.  
[Col. 0124C, note l: 20 has above the line *custodiat ve*, and later *aestimationem*, where 9 has *aestimatio nisi*. 6 and 7 have *muneres*; 12, “property for himself by numbers.”]  
[Col. 0124D, note m: Goez rightly criticizes those who prefer *nequierint* or *nescierint*. 19: “has begun—to be permitted.”]  
[Col. 0124D, note n: 6, 7, 10, and 18 read *virorum bonorum*.]  
[Col. 0124B, note o: 9, 19, 21, and Sichard have *habet*.]

§ 3. Before emancipation, however, parents in whose hands lies the power of using and enjoying maternal property must employ every diligence in preserving the property;  
[Col. 0124D, note p: Some manuscripts, such as 6 and 7, have *emancipatione*; 10 and 18, *an emancipatione*.]  
[Col. 0124D, note q: 19 and 20 have *patres* (“fathers”), but in 20 *parentes* or *parentibus* is added above the line.]  
[Col. 0124D, note r: The second page of folio 120 of the Lyon manuscript begins with the letters *narum*.]  
[Col. 0124D, note s: The Code of Justinian adds *tantum* (“only”).]  
[Col. 0124D, note t: 12 reads “must sell.” Subsequently 8 omits *adhibere*.]  
they must pursue in court what is legally due to their children, meet expenses diligently out of the fruits, resist those who bring suit, and conduct everything as though they had acquired complete and perfect ownership and legal standing.  
[Col. 0124D, note u: 6–8, 10, 18, and other manuscripts read *et*. The Code of Justinian: “pursue in court either personally or through an agent, and [meet] expenses out of [the fruits].”]  
[Col. 0124D, note v: 6–8, 12–14, and 16–18 have *facile*; Ritter correctly emends it to *impigre*. Similarly 10 has *fale*. 20 has above the line *integrare*.]  
[Col. 0124D, note x: 19 has “thus everything.”]  
[Col. 0125A]  
[Col. 0125A, note a: Goez proposes *dominum*, and 10, 18, and 20 have it, but nothing should nevertheless be changed. Moreover, 20 restores *dominium*.]  
[Col. 0125B: The Code of Justinian adds “had been acquired by them.”]  
[Col. 0125B, note b: 6–8, 13, 14, and 17 have *gerent*; 10 and 18, *gerint*.]  
[Col. 0125B, note c: 6–8, 13, 14, and 17 omit *ita*.]

Thus, if at any time they wish to alienate property, the purchaser, or the person to whom the property is given, shall take care not to receive, whether knowingly or unknowingly, any part of that property which it is forbidden to alienate.  
[Col. 0125B, note d: 20 has “to buy another’s property,” but a second hand adds above the line “they wish to alienate.” In Sichard, at the bottom margin of the second page of folio 55, *voluerint* is correctly read; but the first line of folio 56 begins corruptly with *voluerit*. In the upper margin of that page appears, incorrectly, “Book Five”; write “Book Eight.” Subsequently some manuscripts have *emptori* or *his*.]  
[Col. 0125B, note e: 19 and 20 have *donantur*.]  
[Col. 0125B, note f: The Code of Justinian has *unquam* (“ever”).]  
[Col. 0125B, note g: 15, 21, and Sichard read *alienare*.]

For the father must prove that the thing he gives or sells is his own by legal right; and the purchaser may, if he wishes, receive a guarantor or surety, because he will be unable to plead any prescription against the children whenever they claim their own property.  
[Col. 0125B, note h: 6–8, 10, 12–14, and 16–18 read “is his own when he gives”; this can stand if understood of the time when the gift is made.]  
[Col. 0125B, note i: 19 and 20 omit *et*.]  
[Col. 0125B, note j: The Code of Justinian omits “guarantor or.”]  
[Col. 0125B, note k: 10 and 18 have *perscriptionem*.]  
[Col. 0125B, note l: Some read *quandoquidem* (“since”); the Code of Justinian, *quandocunque* (“whenever”).]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August at Aquileia.  
[Col. 0125C, note m: 20, 31, 33, 34, L, R, U, and V have the sixth day before the Kalends; 32, the sixth. In 39 and 43, “fifteenth” is omitted; manuscript 8 has “Aquileia—Vettius,” and manuscript 19, “Read aloud.”]  
[Col. 0125C, note n: Editions and the Code of Justinian have *Aquileiae*. 16 and 21 read *Aquilino*. The Code of Justinian adds: “in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus (316); see below note x.”]

Read aloud before Vettius Rufinus, Prefect of the City, in the Senate, on the Nones of September, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time and Licinius Caesar. (319).  
[Col. 0125C, note o: Many manuscripts, Sichard, Tilius, and the Code of Justinian have *Vectium*. Some manuscripts have *Vetitum, Vetium, Vitium,* or *Vercium*. 20 has “August: read at Aquileia,” but in Ricius, “before Rufinus.” On the name see above, IV.13.1, note n. This Vettius is mentioned in Vatican Fragment §273, in the law of 315: “therefore [we appoint] Vettius Rufinus, most distinguished man, Prefect of the City, our friend.” In certain manuscripts the rank-sign is omitted; in others *ppo* is incorrectly given. Sichard likewise has “Prefect of the Praetorium.” 28 and 40, in X, read “in the Senate” and omit Vettius Rufinus, Prefect of the City.]  
[Col. 0125C, note p: Sichard has in the margin “Nones; 32 (which omits ‘in the Senate’) Prefect of the Praetorium, eighth day before the Kalends of September.” In 8 the text ends: “most distinguished men in the Senate.” 20 has corruptly “in judging, born September.” Nevertheless, all manuscripts and editions have Nones, although by Augustus’ institution the Senate was usually convened on the Kalends or Ides. See chapter 2 of this title.]  
[Col. 0125D, note q: In many manuscripts, Tilius, and the Code of Justinian, “fifth” is omitted. 19, 21, and Sichard have “second”; Sichard has “fifth” in the margin; 15, “sixth.” Some manuscripts read Constantinople for Constantine.]  
[Col. 0125D, note r: “Caesar” is also omitted in many manuscripts, in Goez through Ritter’s first edition, and in the Code of Justinian. Other manuscripts have *vir clarus*, *vir clarissimus*, *V.C.*, as Tilius, or *Vic.*]  
[Col. 0125D, note s: In Goez through Ritter’s first edition and in the Code of Justinian the year is omitted. Goez thinks that, because Vettius Rufinus is not known as Prefect of the City in this year, but is named Prefect in 315 and 316 (see above notes n and o), the consuls named here intruded by error from the following law; accordingly, the consuls of 316 should be restored from the Code of Justinian. In this he agrees with Valesius; Beatus seems to follow Goez’s opinion concerning Vettius Rufinus’ prefecture and emends to “Constantine Augustus IV and Licinius IV (315).” This is not bad, but it is contrary to the authority of the manuscripts, of which Goez too is deprived. I therefore judged that, in an uncertain matter, one must adhere to the received text, which all manuscripts, apart from errors, support. Moreover, on the inscription and subscription of this constitution and chapter 12 of the Theodosian Code, *On Jurisdiction* (II.1), compare Zirardinus, cited work, p. 379.]  

## INTERPRETATION

The remaining part of this law is contained in other laws.  
[Col. 0126A]  
[Col. 0126B, note a: 19, 20, and other manuscripts read *habetur*; shortly afterwards, “will have more.”]

This alone it has in addition to the other laws: fathers who have been ordered to administer their children’s property must conduct their business with the utmost care and integrity, so that nothing may perish to the children through their negligence; rather, they must cause the fruits of maternal property to be collected or sold without any negligence, so that at the appropriate time, as the Novella says, the children may receive their portions without any diminution.  
[Col. 0126B, note b: The Aurora and Lyon manuscripts have *gubernari* (“to be governed”).]  
[Col. 0126B, note c: 20 has above the line *habere*. 6, 7, Sichard, Cujas 1 through Lyon omit *agere*, and 10 has “their [business]—let them manage.” *Ut* is absent in manuscripts 19–21, 42, and others, and in Sichard.]  
[Col. 0126C, note d: 6 and 7 have *paternarum* (“paternal”), incorrectly.]  
[Col. 0126C, note e: That is, Theodosian Novella XIV, *On Paternal or Maternal Property* (Berlin edition, p. 1246).]  
[Col. 0126C, note f: Many manuscripts have *dicet*; some, such as 10 and 18, omit *lex*.]

Fathers may not alienate their children’s property; that is, they may neither sell nor give it away. But if perhaps a father should presume to do so, the purchaser, or the person to whom the gift is made, must guard themselves with great solicitude and care, lest they receive property of the children sold or given away by the father, whether knowingly or unknowingly. They shall compel the father—who has been seller or donor and keeps the children’s property in his own control—to prove that what he has delivered is his own. Further, to remove his suspicion, the purchaser shall obtain from the father-seller a surety, who shall not cause loss to the purchaser by an obligation upon his own property. For after the father’s death, the children may reclaim into their ownership their own property from any persons whatever, whether it was sold or given away by their father.  
[Col. 0126C, note g: Some manuscripts have *ut nec*. Moreover, above, Sichard, Cujas 1 through Lyon have *licet* (“it is permitted”).]  
[Col. 0126C, note h: Many manuscripts have *praesumpserit—accesserint—custodiat*. Goez through Ritter’s first edition likewise have *accesserint*. I print *accesserit* from Sichard, Cujas 1 through Cujas 2*. Sichard and Cujas 1 through Lyon have shortly afterward “or care.” Moreover, 20 has “neither to give nor alienate. But if they should presume—and the purchaser or he to whom the property is given should come.”]  
[Col. 0126C, note i: Most manuscripts, including 6–10, 20, 21, 42, 43, Sichard, and Cujas 1 through Lyon, have *comparatas* (“purchased”), but in the law the word *emptor* corresponds.]  
[Col. 0126C, note j: Sichard has *compellent*. Shortly below some manuscripts have *retineat*.]  
[Col. 0126B]  
[Col. 0126C, note k: 6 and 7 have *tradit*; 9, 42, and 43, *tradet*. Subsequently certain manuscripts have *posset*.]  
[Col. 0126C, note l: 20 has *suscipiant*, corrected to *percipiat*, followed by *quia*. Other manuscripts, such as 9, 21, and 43, have *percipiant*.]  
[Col. 0126D, note m: 20 has *faciant et*, as also 6, followed by *quia*.]  
[Col. 0126D, note n: Some manuscripts omit *a*.]

## CONCERNING THE LEX FABIA

[Col. 0126D, note o: Folio 28 verso of manuscript 4. Most manuscripts read *Faviam*. See Reland, p. 850. Some have *Fufiam*, and 33, 34, and 37, *Juliam*. The Code of Justinian adds “concerning kidnappers.” In the Breviary manuscripts of Alaric cited by Sichard, and in Cujas 2 through Beatus, is added: “That is, those who steal the children of others,” from the interpretation of the titles; on this see the edition of the Breviary which I am preparing. I have therefore deleted those words, which are spurious and end in manuscript 4, but which Beatus encloses in brackets as suspect. 15 has “Concerning those who steal the children of others,” a heading which the copyist fabricated from the heading of the Breviary of Alaric. Cujas 2 through Ritter’s first edition add “concerning kidnappers” in the index of titles; if it occurs in any manuscript, I do not doubt that it should be admitted.]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Domitius Celsus, Vicar of Africa.  
[Col. 0126D, note p: 8 has “to Domitius, consul,” and omits “Vicar of Africa.” 28, 36, and 40 omit Celsus and “Vicar of Africa”; 38 has “Africa.” Most manuscripts read *Africae*. 20, 33, 34, and 39 have *Domitianum* or *Domicianum*; 20 reads “The Emperors Constantine and Constans Augustus, to Domicianus and Celsus, vicar of Africa.”]

Kidnappers (*plagiarii*), who inflict upon parents the pitiable bereavement of living children, were held liable to punishment in the mines, together with the other previously established penalties.  
[Col. 0127A]  
[Col. 0127B, note a: Ritter’s first edition incorrectly has *plagiari*.]  
[Col. 0127B, note b: 21 has *inventium*, and subsequently 8 has *infigunt*.]  
[Col. 0127B, note c: Sichard has *cognitionem* (“examination”), and this reading of the Theodosian Code was already known to Alciatus. Goez, in his note e on this chapter, contends that Alciatus wrote this wrongly, but he himself is mistaken. In manuscript 15, “with the other penalties after examination” is omitted.]  
[Col. 0127B, note d: 6–8, 10, 12, 14–16, 18, 20, 21, Sichard, Cujas 2 and 2*, and the Code of Justinian have *teneantur* (“shall be held”), incorrectly. See Goez’s commentary.]

But if anyone charged with such an offence is brought forward, after the crime has become manifest, a slave or freedman shall be exposed to beasts at the very first spectacle; a free person, however, shall be sent to a gladiatorial school on this condition: before he does anything whereby he may be able to defend himself, he shall be put to death by the sword. We order that those who have already been sent to the mines for this crime shall never be recalled.  
[Col. 0127B, note e: 20 has “But if anyone of this kind”; the Code of Justinian, “of this kind.” There is scarcely need, as Goez did, to warn that *tamen* should not be changed into *tandem*.]  
[Col. 0127C, note f: 10 has *postea* and omits *quam*; Tilius through Lyon have *postea, quam*.]  
[Col. 0127C, note g: Sichard in the margin and the Code of Justinian have *claruerit* (“has become clear”); Goez incorrectly prints it. 20 adds above the line *aparuit*. In the same place shortly afterward it omits *vel*.]  
[Col. 0127C, note h: Goez conjectures *quoquo* without necessity. 15 omits *quoque*, and the Code of Justinian has “at the first spectacle.”]  
[Col. 0127C, note i: The Code of Justinian reads *subjiciatur* (“be subjected”), then “but a freeborn man shall be put to death by the sword,” and the rest ends.]  
[Col. 0127C, note j: 20 reads *super hanc formam*; 27, “but freedom under this condition.”]  
[Col. 0127C, note k: 6–8, 14, and Sichard have *gladiatorum*; 12 has corruptly *defendetur gladiorum*; 27, *gladatorio*.]  
[Col. 0127C, note l: 6–8, 10, 14, and 18 have *aliud* (“something else”). 15: “anything whereby he may be able to defend himself, he shall do with the sword.” Subsequently 20 has *quod se*.]  
[Col. 0127C, note m: Some manuscripts have *metallo*; 12 omits *in*.]

Given on the Kalends of August, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the fourth of Licinius. (315).  
[Col. 0127C, note n: 39 and 43 have “third”; 24, “ninth”; 8 and 36 omit “Constantine—and.”]  
[Col. 0127C, note o: Some manuscripts have *Lycinio*; 38, *Nicinio*.]  
[Col. 0127C, note p: 13 and 15 have “third”; 28, “in the consulship of Licinius and Constantine”; 39 and 43, “Licinius IV.” Numerous manuscripts and the Code of Justinian omit “IV”; Aurora and Lyon have *Cos.*]

## INTERPRETATION

Those who have stolen the children of others and carried them away anywhere, whether freeborn or slaves, shall be punished with death.  
[Col. 0127B]  
[Col. 0127D, note q: Numerous manuscripts, including 6–10, 18, 21, 42, and Sichard, have the singular “whether he be freeborn or slave, let him be punished”; 20 has “whether he be freeborn or slave.” Manuscript 6 seems to have *puniantur*, and some manuscripts read *punietur*. Moreover, 20 has *furtim* (“secretly”).]

## CONCERNING THE DUTY OF A PROVINCIAL GOVERNOR

[Col. 0127D, note r: 19 has “of governors.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Rufinus Octavianus, Corrector of Lucania and Bruttium.  
[Col. 0127D, note s: 5 reads “To Rufinus Octavianus, correctors of Lucania and Bruttium.” Cl. and Pu. print “Augustus to R. and O., correctors,” etc. W. omits “Augustus” and corrects *correctoribus* to *correctori*, proving from Theodosian Code XVI.2.2 and VII.22.1, addressed in 319 to the same Octavianus, and from other constitutions sent by Constantine to other correctors of Lucania and Bruttium—such as Theodosian Code IX.19.1, XI.29.1, XI.30.1, XII.2.3—that there was only one corrector of Lucania and Bruttium. See also Theodosian Code VIII.3.1 and Panciroli on chapter 54 of the *Notitia Dignitatum* of the West. Thus Octavianus’ complete name, previously unknown, was Rufinus Octavianus; this led the copyist to interpret the abbreviation *corr.* as *correctoribus*.]

Whoever has procured an extraordinary hearing from prefects or vicars, or has already procured one, you shall not permit his opponents and the persons necessary to the case to go or be transferred to the office of the prefects or vicar. Rather, with all parties and persons present, you yourself shall hear every case in your court, during the period which you shall reckon from the day on which the case began to be initiated in your court. Only then, if the person who requested the extraordinary hearing is dissatisfied with your judgment, shall he suspend it by an appeal lodged in accordance with the order of the laws, and proceed to his own judge.  
[Col. 0128A]  
[Col. 0128B, note a: 5 has *Judicum*.]  
[Col. 0128B, note b: 5 reads “persons necessary to the case.” Cl., followed by Pu. and W., reads *causae necessarias*, unnecessarily; for *causa* is an ablative of instrument.]  
[Col. 0128B, note c: 5 has *de homini*. Cl. incorrectly has *de hominis*. Pu. and W., from Hu.’s conjecture, have *de omni*. The copyist’s error seems to have arisen from aspiration in *omni*.]  
[Col. 0128C, note d: I have written thus, although Schroeder prints with manuscript 5, which nevertheless has *personis*. Cl. and Pu. print *ita his*, in which Hu. and Bijdr. think *statis* lies concealed; Schroeder proposes *personis iustis*, and W. emends to *usitatis*, with Schroeder’s approval. All these conjectures depart too far from the manuscript’s reading.]  
[Col. 0128C, note e: Pu. has *quo ex causa*.]  
[Col. 0128C, note f: 5 has *extraordinariorum*.]  
[Col. 0128C, note g: Thus rightly Pu. from Hu.’s conjecture, approved by Schroeder. 5 has *interposita ea provocationis*. Cl. has *interposita causa provocationis*. W.: *interposita provocatio causam*.]  
[Col. 0128C, note h: Schroeder conjectures “to the superior judge.”]

Given on the third day before the Nones of August at Trier, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the fourth of Licinius. (315).  
[Col. 0128C, note i: “IV” is absent in manuscript 5, but added by Cl.]

## CONCERNING VARIOUS RESCRIPTS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People.  
[Col. 0128B]  
[Col. 0128C, note j: Manuscript 1, the Alarician Breviary manuscripts, W., and older editions—in which this is the first chapter of the title—have “The Emperor Constantine Augustus.”]  
[Col. 0128C, note k: 26 and 36 omit “to the People.”]

Rescripts contrary to law shall have no force, however they may have been obtained. For judges ought rather to follow the public laws, which lay down the rules.  
[Col. 0128C, note l: 1, 19, 33, 38, and others have *perscribunt*.]

Posted on the fourth day before the Kalends of September at Rome, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the fourth of Licinius Caesar. (315).  
[Col. 0128C, note m: Some manuscripts have *Proposita* (“Posted”). 21 and 44 have *pp.*; 20 has in the margin “to the people,” followed by *data*. Sichard has *P. P.*; manuscripts 1, 20, 28, 40, and 41, together with R., P., and Pu., have *Data*. 33 has *propensio*.]  
[Col. 0128D, note n: 1 and Pu. omit “posted, IV”; 24, 30, and 33 have “III.”]  
[Col. 0128D, note o: Sichard, Tilius, Cujas 1, Aurora, Lyon, Cujas 2 and 2*, in the margin, have “March”; likewise Goez, Ritter, and Ritter’s first edition in annotation, and 36 and 40. But 31 and the Angers manuscript cited by Goez have “February,” and 41, June. Subsequently 20 has *Romano*, others *Roma*.]  
[Col. 0128D, note p: Some manuscripts have “III.”]  
[Col. 0128D, note q: “IV” is omitted by 8, 10, 18, 20, 24, 30, 33, 38, and 42; some of these omit Licinius, “most distinguished men,” and “Caesar.” 9 and 14 have “III”; 40, “Litio Jul., augusti, consuls”; 43 and 44, “Licinius Augustus IV, consul.”]  
[Col. 0128D, note r: *Caes.* first appears in manuscript 1, as it is read in Code of Justinian II.9.3, *On the Advocate of the Fisc*.]

## INTERPRETATION

Whatever rescripts have been obtained from emperors contrary to the laws shall have no force.  
[Col. 0128D, note s: 20 has in the margin “rescripts.”]  
[Col. 0128D, note t: Some manuscripts, Sichard, Cujas 1, Aurora, and Lyon have singular “from the emperor”; Sichard has “from emperors” in the margin. 20 and 21: “have been obtained from the emperor”; 5, 42, and 43: “have been obtained from emperors.”]

## CONCERNING APPEALS

[Col. 0129A]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Probianus, Proconsul of Africa.  
[Col. 0129C, note a: See Theodosian Code, chapters 5 and 6 of this title.]

You must hear cases of appeal that are adjudicated by you in Our tribunal—you to whom We entrust the function of Our examination—in such a way that you comply with the edict already generally established for bringing appellate business to an end, and dispose of those same matters as promptly as possible.  
[Col. 0129C, note b: 4 has “these cases which”; an earlier hand, perhaps the copyist’s, deletes *has* by points placed above it.]  
[Col. 0129C, note c: Thus 4 and Tilius; the rest have *vestro* (“your”). Cujas first silently corrected it to *nostro* in Cujas 1, rightly, because of what follows: “to whom We entrust the office of Our examination.” Yet it should not be understood of the tribunal over which the emperor himself presides, but of any tribunal held in the emperor’s name or place—here, the proconsul’s tribunal in Africa. Compare Theodosian Code XI.36.3: “Your Sublimity, who represents Our person in judicial hearings.”]  
[Col. 0129C, note d: 4 and Tilius have *id*. Cujas first silently corrected it to *ita* in Cujas 1, correctly. Subsequently Beatus has *negotiis*.]

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September at Rom[?], in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the fourth of Licinius. (315).  
[Col. 0129C, note e: Beatus notes: “Gothofred understands Romansianum near Naissus. Perhaps the same is indicated by *Rom.* in Theodosian Code I, which never expresses Rome in that manner. Yet I think *Rom.* and *Rum.* sometimes indicate Ravenna.” Goez proposes *Romansianam*, not *Romansianum*, but in his Chronicle says: “Therefore Constantine was at Rome at this time.” He thus disagrees with himself. What Beatus says of the spelling *Rom.* is wholly false.]

## CONCERNING THE LAW OF THE FISC

The Emperor Constantine Augustus and Caesar to the People.  
[Col. 0129D, note f: According to Goez, Pag., and Reland, p. 295, [the Caesar is] Licinius. Shortly afterward Goez erroneously reads “to Polus.”]

If any property is to be seized by the fisc, or hereafter granted by Us in consideration of an individual’s merits and services, or sold by the same [fisc], those who believe that their own property has been unjustly acquired by the fisc shall bring proceedings against it within a year, all others abstaining either from the claim or from the acquisition. Let them know and rejoice that annual periods within which they may recover their property have been granted; and, if they prove that justice supports their claim, let them recover it and hold it restored through Our favour.  
[Col. 0129D, note g: Goez proposes *occupatum* (“seized”), but does not reject *occupandum* or “to be seized henceforth.” He also has *vel* in place of *et*, and so forth.]  
[Col. 0129D, note h: Aurora and Lyon have *de ce cetero*.]  
[Col. 0129B]  
[Col. 0129D, note i: Goez emends *corporatas* or *occupatas*.]

Given on the Ides of September at Rome, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the fourth of Licinius. (315).  
[Col. 0129D, note j: Goez brackets “Given” in favor of “Posted,” since Constantine was not residing at Rome at this period.]

## CONCERNING CENTONARII AND DENDROPHORI

[Col. 0129D, note k: 3, 4, and Tilius through Ritter’s first edition have *Dendroforis*, and below *dendrofori*. Goez conjectures *centenariis* in his commentary.]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Evagrius, Prefect of the Praetorian Guard. Your Gravity should send letters to all judges directing that, in whatever towns there are *dendrophori* (“tree-bearers”), they be attached to the guilds of the *centonarii* and craftsmen, since it is expedient that these corporate bodies be enlarged by a multitude of people.  
[Col. 0129D, note l: From manuscript 3, which has *colligiis*. 4 and Tilius through Beatus omit *collegiis*. Panciroli, *Thesaurus* I.52, approved by Reinesius, plausibly conjectures *collegio*; Goez proposes *corporibus* or *corpora*, a proposal rejected by Maius; Beatus has *corporibus*.]  
[Col. 0129D, note m: Folio 344 of manuscript 4. Subsequently Beatus has *Naissi*.]

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October at Naissus; received on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the fourth of Licinius. (315).  
[Col. 0130A]

## CONCERNING DECURIONS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Crispinus . . . . .  
[Col. 0130B, note a: The official title is absent in manuscript 4 without any indication of a lacuna, and likewise in the editions from Tilius through Cujas 2* and in Beatus; Goez and Ritter indicate the omission by five points, Ritter’s first edition by six; I have restored five.]

## CONCERNING JEWS, COELICOLAE, AND SAMARITANS

[Col. 0130C, note g: 15 omits “Coelicolae and Samaritans.” The Code of Justinian has “Concerning Jews and Coelicolae,” omitting Samaritans. We wish it to be made known to the Jews, their elders, and their patriarchs that if anyone, after this law, should dare to assail with stones or by any other frenzied means—as We have learned is now occurring—someone who has fled their deadly sect and turned to the worship of God, he shall immediately be consigned to the flames and burned together with all his accomplices.  
[Col. 0130C, note j: Aurora and Lyon incorrectly have *patiarchis*.]

§ 1. But if anyone of the people should join their impious sect and attach himself to their assemblies, he shall suffer the penalties they deserve along with them.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November at Murgillum, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the fourth of Licinius. (315).

## CONCERNING THE GRAIN SUPPLY OF CARTHAGE

[Col. 0131B, note a: Cujas 1 through Lyon have *Chartag.*; Goez, *Carthaginensi*; the rest, *Carthag.*]

[Col. 0131A]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Catulinus, Proconsul of Africa.  
[Col. 0131B, note b: Aurora, Lyon, and Beatus have *Catullinum*. See Theodosian Code II.1.1, note o. Goez has “the emperors.”]  
[Col. 0131C, note c: 4 has *PU*; Tilius through Lyon, *P.V.* See Theodosian Code XI.16.1, note m. Goez says someone conjectures *Pf. P.*]

If anyone has divested himself of properties liable for the *aeneum* grain levy, he shall be free from every claim, even though he possesses or has purchased other properties free from the burden of *aeneum* grain.  
[Col. 0131C, note d: Goez rejects the emendation *poeno* and, on the unproved derivation of *aeneus* from Greek αἰνόν (*ainon*, “dreadful”), as though it meant “burdensome,” attempts in his commentary *oenaeo* or *oneto* grain—grain which one was compelled to sell outside the ordinary procedure, elsewhere called *synoneton*—or *oeneum*, from οἶνος (*oinos*, “wine”), grain so called because it was dedicated to Bacchus’ priests and attendants; or *aerinum*, as *aerina farina* in Pliny, *Natural History* XXII.25.58, which is made from αἶρα (*aira*, “darnel”). For other explanations see Goez, cited work, and Cironius, *Observations on Canon Law* IV.3. Might one write *aeno* or *aeneo*, so that *aenum frumentum* was named from bronze measures—that is, from the material of the vessel by which grain was measured? Thus *aenum* means, of course, a vessel fit for receiving and heating water, and receives its name from the material. Nor does the other conjecture cited by Goez displease me: that *aeneum frumentum* was so called in the same sense as cash grain-allowances (*aerariae annonae*), which were rendered in monetized money, not in kind. Reinesius conjectures *annuo*.]  
[Col. 0131C, note e: Goez emends *distraxerit* (“has sold”), plausibly, since purchasers seem to be contrasted with this word.]  
[Col. 0131D, note f: Folio 359 verso of manuscript 4. Goez: “Let him possess.”]  
[Col. 0131D, note g: The manuscript has *aeneis*, restored in red ink to *aenei*.]

For purchasers of encumbered properties must be held liable in proportion to the property they have acquired, even if they acquired it otherwise than by gift. But because many magistrates liable for payment of the *aeneum* grain levy have, while in office, substituted others for themselves, or, after being bought out on behalf of others, appointed still others, the substitutions shall be annulled and they shall be held liable for payment of the same *aeneum* grain levy. Only those among the substitutes must remain who are shown to possess sufficient means and not to have been substituted in place of persons of insufficient means by magistrates who had bought themselves out.  
[Col. 0131D, note h: Thus manuscript 4 and the editions; Goez and Beatus emend *liberalitate* to *liberalitatem*: that is, by a burdensome, not gratuitous, title. Reinesius, thinking an error lay hidden in *extra*, conjectures *ex mera*. I agree with Goez.]  
[Col. 0131D, note i: 4 has singular *fuerit*.]  
[Col. 0131B]

## CONCERNING EMPHYTEUTIC ESTATES AND THEIR LESSEES

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Cypitus. If anyone, without prejudice to the law of the fisc, gives estates held by emphyteutic right without the authority of a judge, the gifts shall be valid, provided that he is compelled, at the proper times, to render the payments due to the fisc.

Posted on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July at Trier, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third of Licinius. (310).  
*(From the Code of Justinian.)*

In the year of the Lord 316, in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus.

[Col. 0135D] **Textual note l:** No manuscript reads *Sebero* (or *Severo*), which Go., because of chapter 25 of the Justinian Code, “Concerning Gifts,” wishes to introduce in order to obtain the year 323—implausibly, according to Be. and W. ## Interpretation

If, in matters which may be given to minors, through the negligence or collusion of a tutor, the formalities or condition of the gift have not been fulfilled, he shall be compelled to pay from his own property what the minor has lost.

[Col. 0135D] **Textual note m:** Cuj. 2–Ri* omit *vel conditio*, which nearly all manuscripts contain. Shortly afterward manuscripts 6 and 21 read *deperiet* for *deperierit*, but 21 corrected it.

[Col. 0135D] **Textual note n:** Many manuscripts read *cogetur*; Sich., Cuj. 1, and Aur. Lugd., *cogatur*.

## Concerning Gifts

[Col. 0135D] **Textual note o:** This is part of a larger constitution of Constantine the Great concerning gifts. See the note to title “Concerning Pacts” II, 9, and the note above to chapter 2, “Concerning the Administration of Guardians” III, 30. According to Hollweg’s recension, its beginning is as follows:

“§ 249. Constantine and the Caesars. We have often learned of controversies arising from gifts, in which things merely sketched are treated as expressed, things begun as completed, or very many things as all things; since the apparent claims of litigants, through ingenuity and power of speech, either distorted things completed or completed those begun, the law became uncertain and the decrees of judgments fluctuated according to the impulse of those speaking, Maximus, dearest and most delightful. Hence, after certain persons had recently been excepted, a law was declared in which the highest legal right and a will free to all, perfected by the customary solemnity, enrich their beginnings by the present gift; timely care of ordinary gifts thereafter followed. Once those matters had been settled which are first because they are more important in religion, we turned our mind to the whole class of gifts, determining that all their kinds should be stamped with signs and names, so that in human contracts they might distinguish their differences through the proper character of their appellations. Accordingly, whether that gift …”

## Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect

A gift—whether made outright,

### § 1

In drawing up gifts, the name of the donor, the legal right, and the property must be recorded;

[Col. 0136D] **Textual note u:** The Vatican Fragment reads *praestabunt*. “Thus fear of personal loss will spur even the more sluggish to prepare these instruments. Then, in drawing up the same instruments, especially the name of the donor …”

[Col. 0137A] **Textual note a:** Manuscripts 6, 7, 12–14, and 16–18 read *ejus*; 19, *hujus*.

and this shall not be done secretly, by unskilled persons, or privately,

The Vatican Fragment omits *privatim*: “For through these things clandestine fraud has often induced people, by pretending that what was done was undone and what was written was erased, and by making gifts successively to different persons, often attracting many by the hope of possession, to join in an attack upon ownership. Therefore the tablets …” Manuscript 12 and the Justinian Code read *aut tabula*, which Go. approves and Be. correctly first restored to the text. The Vatican Fragment agrees, though it has the plural *tabulae prescribantur*. The remaining manuscripts, Br. and Al., Codex Lugdunensis, and editions before Be., read *ut tabulae*, although Sich. corrected it in the margin to *aut*, as in manuscript 19 and the Interpretation. Perhaps *ut* arose from the abbreviation for *vel*. Br. and Al.’s reading can also be accepted if *perscribantur* is read for *perscribatur*, an easy correction. The Interpreter, who found the false reading *perscribatur* in the copy he used, understood *tabulae* as a dative. Shortly afterward some manuscripts read *quocumque*, others *quoscunque*.

or on whatever other kind of material time may provide, by the donor himself or by one whom chance may have supplied, with many persons knowing of it, it shall be written out.

performed in the presence of neighbours and with arbitrators present,

[Col. 0138B] **Textual note b:** The Justinian Code adds: “where the laws require this.” The Vatican Fragment adds a lengthy passage: “and so that there may be no opportunity for insertion or theft, when it is advantageous to either party, let the same magistrates record the truth in examples. Thus, by the conscience of many, by the monuments of judicial decisions and the records of the people, or by the public dissemination of lawsuits, the faith will not be hidden from anyone. Such must be the beginnings of ownership, whose long possession often violates the lawful rights of properties; such the honour of liberality, which, proclaimed everywhere to the families of recipients and donors, may complete its praise of liberality and favour. At the same time, since it is an excellent thing to have gained each gift by deserving it, let its delight not be diminished by the sadness of litigation. But if the cause must be awaited and the judgment pronounced, and a liberality deprived of public testimony has revealed blind favour and obscure gatherings, since fraud alone is known, the claim to the things said to have been donated must not rashly be accepted, but by that alienation …, its rejection or … efforts having been turned aside, rightly … concerning the right by which each thing was donated … with that completion being made … thereafter of the words … anything according to the law having been changed … in making … nor any … to combine with future law … so that everyone may recognize … your … is to be preferred.”

Given on the third day before the Nones of February,

## Interpretation

A gift is either outright or made *mortis causa*.

[Col. 0138D] **Textual note h:** Nonnian manuscripts omit *aut*.

[Col. 0138D] **Textual note i:** Manuscript 20 adds *sibi reservat* above the line.

An outright gift is one in which the donated thing is delivered immediately.

[Col. 0138D] **Textual note j:** Manuscripts 6, 7, and 20 and others read *donatio directa*, but the present reading is preferable because of the antithesis.

A gift *mortis causa* is one in which the donor, while alive, retains the thing which he gives, writing: “If I die before you, my property shall pass to you,”

[Col. 0138D] **Textual note k:** Manuscripts 6 and 7 read *adviveret*.

[Col. 0138D] **Textual note l:** Manuscript 20 and others read *donavit*, followed by *ad illum cui donata est*.

so that afterward the donated property passes to the person to whom it is given, not to the heirs of the donor.

[Col. 0138D] **Textual note m:** The passage is corruptly written in the manuscripts: *quantum aut quam tunc*.

[Col. 0138D] **Textual note n:** Manuscripts 20, 43, and 44 and other manuscripts and Sich. read *donantis*, but Sich. corrected this in the margin to *donatoris*.

But if the person to whom the property has been given *mortis causa* dies first, the property remains in the legal ownership of the donor.

[Col. 0138D] **Textual note o:** Manuscripts 21, 26, and 42 and many others read *moritur*.

[Col. 0138D] **Textual note p:** Manuscript 20 reads: “the thing which was donated, that which was donated, remains in the legal ownership.”

There is also another kind of gift in which the donor binds the person to whom he gives to do or not do something—for example, if he orders something to be done which is judged impossible or contrary to morality; or if he orders something to be done which is honourable and can be fulfilled.

[Col. 0138D] **Textual note q:** Manuscript 20 reads *don. quae donatur*.

[Col. 0139B] **Textual note a:** *Quod* is omitted in many manuscripts.

For a gift is invalid when conditions that are honourable and possible have not been fulfilled.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note b:** This is the reading of many manuscripts; the editions less correctly read *posset*. Manuscript 21 omits *et*.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note c:** Many manuscripts read *possibiles*. Manuscript 20, following Ri., reads *honestates possibiles*, approved by Ri. Other manuscripts read *honestate*. Sich. adds *et* after *hon.*

But if dishonourable and impossible conditions are imposed, the conditions being removed, the gift is valid.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note d:** Manuscript 20 reads *honestae*, but according to Ri. it should be *honesta*, an error of Ri.; 21 reads *inhonestatem*.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note e:** Nonnian manuscripts read *donaciones pon.* Sich. reads *componatur*, but corrected it in the margin to *ponantur*.

There is likewise another kind in which the donor reserves to himself a definite period of possession.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note f:** *Est* is absent from many manuscripts, including 20, and *et* is found in Sich., Cuj. 1, and Aur. Lugd. Manuscript 21 reads *aestimet*, but the margin has *item est*.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note g:** Manuscript 20 above the line, and manuscripts 43 and others, read *donacionis*.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note h:** Sich., Cuj. 1, and Aur. Lugd. read *servat*. Nonnian manuscripts read *reservet*.

All the aforesaid gifts, however, are invalid if they exceed the limit prescribed by law, so that specified persons may bring an action concerning an excessive gift; that is, if the donor has not reserved for himself one quarter of his property, they shall not be valid.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note i:** Go. says that the Interpreter adds this sentence from his own source.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note j:** Manuscript 21 reads *modica*, but the margin has *immodica*. According to Go., the Interpreter adds this sentence from his own source.

Moreover, a gift is contrary to law if anyone gives property involved in litigation which is being claimed, or makes a gift in due legal form while setting down in the gift a condition contrary to good morals—that is, the occasion of any crime.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note k:** Aur. Lugd. reads *reperitur*, incorrectly.

[Col. 0139C] **Textual note l:** Go. wants *haud*, incorrectly; no manuscript has *haud*. Many manuscripts read *directo* for *recto*, which is acceptable. Shortly afterward Go. reads *conscribet*, and manuscript 20 *in donationem*.

If anything has been offered or transferred by gift to minors by anyone, their tutors or curators must take care that nothing be lacking for the validity of the gift.

[Col. 0139B] **Textual note m:** *A quocunque* is absent from manuscripts 6 and 7. Shortly afterward manuscript 21 reads *tutores sive*.

If, through their negligence, the gift has not been brought into effect, the loss shall fall upon them, so that whatever the minors have lost through the gift shall be restored to them by the curators or tutors from their own resources.

[Col. 0139D] **Textual note n:** Manuscripts 6 and 7 read *firmitatis donationis derogent*; other manuscripts, *firmitatis donationi*.

[Col. 0139D] **Textual note o:** Manuscripts 20 and 21 read *tutores vel curatores illorum*; 21 has *illis*.

In drawing up gifts, the following order shall be observed: the gift shall first contain the name of the donor or of the person to whom the gift is made;

[Col. 0139D] **Textual note p:** Manuscript 20 adds *eorum* and shortly afterward *donationis* after *contineat*.

[Col. 0139D] **Textual note q:** Aur. Lugd. reads *continuat*. Sich. adds *ac*. In manuscript 20 the words *donatio nomen prius* were written twice, but one occurrence seems to have been erased by a line beneath it.

next, the things given—whether lands, slaves, or any other things and property—shall be specifically entered in the gift,

[Col. 0139D] **Textual note r:** Manuscripts 6 and 7 read *deinde de his*. Shortly afterward, from other manuscripts, I have restored *donantur*, where the common reading is *donatur*.

[Col. 0139D] **Textual note s:** Manuscript 21 reads *integris*, but this was emended in the margin to *in agris*.

[Col. 0139D] **Textual note t:** Go. emends this to *nominatim donationes*, contrary to the manuscript evidence.

not secretly but publicly, not privately or in concealment,

[Col. 0140A] but either upon tablets,

[Col. 0140C] **Textual note a:** Aur. Lugd. reads *secreto*.

or on sheets, or wherever the gift may be read as having been made.

[Col. 0140C] **Textual note b:** Manuscripts 9 and 44 and others, and Cuj. 1–Aur. Lugd., read *ut in tabulis*; 20, *ut aut tabulis*; 6, 7, and 21, *ut aut in tabulis*.

If he knows letters, the donor himself shall subscribe the gift; if he does not know them, he shall select, in the presence of many persons, someone to subscribe on his behalf;

[Col. 0140C] **Textual note c:** Manuscripts 6 and 7 read *in quam*.

[Col. 0140C] **Textual note d:** Manuscript 21 reads *cognovit*, corrected in the margin to *novit*.

and the formal record and physical delivery shall then follow upon the gift itself,

[Col. 0140C] **Textual note e:** Some manuscripts add *in*.

[Col. 0140C] **Textual note f:** Manuscripts 9, 20, 21, and 44 read *gestorum*.

so that, if movables are given, they shall be delivered in the presence of many persons; but if a field or house is given, which cannot be moved, the donor shall withdraw from it and the thing given shall stand open to the new owner,

[Col. 0140C] **Textual note g:** Sich. reads *et*.

if the donor has not reserved to himself the usufruct of these things.

[Col. 0140C] **Textual note h:** According to Go., the Interpreter adds this from his own source. Manuscript 20 changes the order but reads *usumfr. s. de his rebus*. Records of gifts must be presented either before a judge or before the curia.

## Constantine Augustus to Cassius, Praetorian Prefect

[Col. 0140D] **Textual note q:** Go. says in his *Chronicle*, p. XII, that Vettius Rufinus was still Praetorian Prefect under these consuls, that Ovinius Gallicanus succeeded him, and that only in 318 did he know Julius Cassius as acting in the place of Bassus as Praetorian Prefect. He therefore wishes the annotation to this chapter to read *P. P. V.*, that is, “in place of the Urban Prefect.” Be. incorrectly follows him, affirming that Corsinius lists this Cassius among the Urban Prefects.

Bucch. attacks Wenck’s opinion because of the word *dudum*, “long ago,” which the emperor uses here. It would be more plausible that W. is right in thinking that the emperor refers to some lost law mentioned in chapter 1 of the Theodosian Code, “Concerning Betrothals” (III, 5). Compare Haubold, *Works*, volume I, preface, p. 53; Francke, *Civilistic Essays*, p. 42, note 29; and also Rudorff, dissertation *On the Cincian Law*, Berlin, 1825, octavo, p. 44.

[Note: [Col. 0141C] g 15 omits *Temp.* C. Et. 28. 36: “On—Restoration—and Summonses.” Likewise 40: “On—R. and Summonses.” Cod. Just. (VII, 63): “On Times and the Restoration of Appeals or Consultations.”]

[Col. 0141B] Emperor Constantine Augustus to Julianus, *vir clarissimus* [Note: [Col. 0141C] h 6, 9, 10, 14, 17, 27, 44: R. An. Reg. and And. in Go. Til. margin, “Julio Vero.” 16, 18, 19, 42, “Julio Viro.” [Col. 0141D] 38, “Julio Viro Urbo.” 25, “Nilio Viro,” as Put. in Go. 8, “Julio Auriliano.” 21, 44, “Jul. most distinguished man.” 7. 15, 39: “Julio,” omitting V. C., which other manuscripts also omit. 29 omits Julianus and what follows.] Governor of Tarraconensis [Note: [Col. 0141D] i 20, Sich.: “of Tarraco”; other manuscripts, “Taraconensis,” “Terraconensis.”].

When a case has once been removed from its prescribed times either through necessity or accident [Note: [Col. 0141D] j 20, 21, Sich.: “If, when.”] [Note: [Col. 0141D] k 6, 7, 9, 10, 14, 17–19 omit *vel*, “or.”] [Note: [Col. 0141D] l 20, 21, Sich.: “excepted.”], and afterward restoration is granted through the indulgence of our clemency [Note: [Col. 0141D] m 8: “redeemed grace is granted”; 9: “returning grace is granted”; 19: “has been granted.”], the litigants must be allowed, at the discretion of the judge, four months and no longer [Note: [Col. 0141D] n 15: “judges”; 21: “for judges.”] [Note: [Col. 0141D] o 15: “and not longer”; 8: “of another.”] [Note: [Col. 0141D] p 8, 20, 21: “he should allow”; 10, 18, R. An. Reg. in Go.: “to allow”; Sich. Cui. 1. Aur. Lugd.: “it may be open,” but Cui. 1. Aur. Lugd. margin: “to be allowed.”], even if by surreptitious means they have obtained something from us through a repeated petition [Note: [Col. 0141D] q Thus Til. Be. W. and almost all manuscripts; 21, Sich. Cui. 1–Ri*: singular, “has obtained.”].

Given on the day before the Nones of May [Col. 0142A], at Vienne [Note: [Col. 0142C] a 8 Med. 30: “Given, 4 May.”] [Note: [Col. 0142C] b 6, 7, 10, 14, 17–19, 24, 42: “Vianae”; 30: “Mannae”; 8: “Vihemine”; 9: “aviane”; 26: “Viano”; 20: “bienes.”], in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus [Note: [Col. 0142C] c 20, 21, Sich.: “Ambrosius and Rufus,” but Sich. margin: “Sabinus and Rufinus.” Til.: “Severus and R.” 38 omits “and R.” Many manuscripts: “Savino and Rufino.”] [Note: [Col. 0142C] d 15 adds: “It requires no explanation.”] (316).

**Interpretation.** When, through intervening necessity [Note: [Col. 0142C] e 20: “necessity occurring.”] or accident, the appointed [Note: [Col. 0142C] f Sich. Cui. 1. Aur. Lugd.: “permitted”; 6, 7: “previously appointed,” but corrected by a second hand in manuscript 7.] time has elapsed, and a litigant has obtained by imperial favour its restoration, judges shall grant the litigants no more than four months for the determination [Note: [Col. 0142C] g Sich. Cui. I. Aur. Lugd.: “for finishing.”] of the case. Once these have elapsed, they shall by no means be heard, even if they have obtained another favour from the lords [Note: [Col. 0142C] h Sich. margin, Cui. 1. Aur. Lugd.: “favour.”] [Note: [Col. 0142C] i Sich. 20 and many manuscripts: singular, “has obtained,” “shall be heard.” 6, 7: “is heard.”].

## ON THE PUBLIC POST

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Titianus [Note: [Col. 0142C] j The rank is absent both here and in Cod. Just.; nor, according to Go., is there another law of Constantine in C. Th. addressed to this Titianus. Be. considers him Prefect of the Praetorian Guard. [Col. 0142D] In the Chronicle Go. calls him Tatianus. Cod. Just.: “Emperor Constantine Augustus to Titianus.”].

Since many people, with knotted and very stout clubs, compel public animals, at the very beginning of their course, to expend whatever strength they possess, it is our pleasure that absolutely no one use a club in driving, but rather a switch [Note: [Col. 0142D] k Manuscript: *viga*, but an *r* is placed above the letter *g*.] or at least a whip, at whose tip a short point is fixed, which may stimulate the sluggish limbs by harmless [Col. 0142B] pricking—not to demand of them as much as their strength cannot sustain. Whoever acts contrary to this ordinance, if he is a promoted official, shall be punished by the humiliation of reduction in rank [Note: [Col. 0142D] l The words “if promoted—shall be punished” are read in Cuiacius’s commentary on c. 3 of the cited Cod. Just.], while a *munifex* shall incur the penalty of deportation [Note: [Col. 0142D] m In Cod. Just. this constitution reads: “We decree that horses assigned to the public post are not to be driven with logs or clubs, or merely with whips; and punishment shall not be lacking against one who does otherwise.”].

Given on the day before the Ides of May, in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus (316).

## ON APPEALS

Emperor Constantine Augustus sends greetings to Petronius Probianus [Note: [Col. 0142D] n Cod. Just. adds *dicit*, “says.” Reines.: “He was then, he says, proconsul of Africa, as Augustine calls him in I. III *Against Cresconius*, c. 7; this appears from the subscription, where he published this law at Theveste.” See also c. 3 under this title.].

From the time at which [Note: [Col. 0142D] o Cod. Just.: “from which.” See c. 8 under this title: “from that day on which—or from which.”], in civil cases brought between private parties, you have promised that you will seek an imperial consultation or make a report [Note: [Col. 0142D] p Cod. Just.: “will seek consultation.”], or the formalities of an appeal lodged by you have been completed, you are henceforth to hear nothing whatsoever that is special or requested, or that in any way advances the favour of partiality; rather, you must observe that, with the customary formal procedure set aside in accordance with earlier enactments [Note: [Col. 0142D] q See c. 1 under this title.], all records are sent to the imperial court, etc.

Given on the Ides of August at Arles [Col. 0143A] [Note: [Col. 0143C] a Be.: “at Arles.”]. Published on the Ides of October at Theveste [Note: [Col. 0143C] b 4: “Teueste.”], in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus (316).

Emperor Constantine Augustus sends greetings to Petronius Probianus [Note: [Col. 0143C] c Cod. Just.: “Emperor Constantine Augustus to Probianus.”].

It is not permitted to petition while a case is pending, unless perhaps a copy of an opinion has been denied to the person concerned [Note: [Col. 0143C] d Fol. 182 [ [Col. 0143C] a Be.: “at Arles.”] of manuscript 4.], or the transmission of the entire record has been withheld. If this is done, the crime of sacrilege shall threaten the judge who, by this act, imposes upon the litigant the necessity of petitioning. A person who petitions otherwise shall be fined half the value of the matter in dispute, to be paid into the fisc in an amount determined by the judge.

Likewise, whoever attempts by solicited influence to reopen a question settled by rescript or consultation [Note: [Col. 0143C] e 4: *consulatione*, corrected by an earlier hand to *consultatione*.], since he commits a more serious crime, is to be condemned forthwith in the entire assessed value of the litigation; and, under the observance of an oath [Note: [Col. 0143C] f Go. in commentary: “The words ‘under the observance of an oath’ troubled me for some time. But by these words Constantine the Great undoubtedly appears, in his customary manner, to bind himself by the sacred obligation of an oath.—So likewise—law 4, *On Accusations*” (IX, 1).], all pardon is to be denied if anyone attempts to petition contrary to these provisions [Col. 0143B] [Note: [Col. 0143C] g In Cod. Just. this constitution reads: “It is not permitted to petition—unless either a copy of the records or of the judgment is denied. But whoever attempts to reopen a settled—question by solicited influence” (omitting “since—crime”), “shall forthwith be condemned to his adversary in the entire assessed value of the litigation; and all pardon—if anyone attempts [to petition].” Cf. Dirksen, cited work, p. 355, and Hermann on cited c. 2, notes 12 ff.].

Given on the Ides of August at Arles [Note: [Col. 0143D] h Be.: “at Arles.” Herrm., from the Pistoria manuscript: “at Arles.”]. Published on the Ides of October at Theveste, in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus (316).

## ON VARIOUS RESCRIPTS

Emperor Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0143D] i 1: “The same emperors.” Cod. Just.: “Emperor Constantine Augustus to Bassus, Prefect of the City,” but P. U. is absent in many manuscripts; others have PP., as Nbg.] to Septimius Bassus, Prefect of the City. Whenever we are specially entreated to soften or mitigate the rigour of the law [Note: [Col. 0143D] j 1: *regorem*, corrected to *rigorem*—*linire*, “to smear,” for *lenire*, “to soften.”] [Note: [Col. 0143D] k 1: singular, corrected to plural *exoramur*.], the following shall be observed: rescripts obtained before the promulgation of an edict shall retain their validity, and an earlier rescript shall not be derogated from by a later one.
