Whenever a specific agreement concerning a future marriage has been made between betrothed persons, and the man has, either with the consent of the parents or himself, if he is independent, drawn up a gift of betrothal generosity for his betrothed woman of his own will, and has confirmed it with every formality of written instruments, [Note: [Col. 0180B] a Some MSS: “all these things.”] [Note: [Col. 0180B] b 29: “has solemnly bound it by the strength of documents.” Aur., Lugd.: “the document.”] so that both the legally performed acts are shown and entry into possession of lands or delivery of things follows, [Note: [Col. 0180B] c 6: “or and”; 20 omits “and.”] whatever has passed to the right and ownership of the betrothed woman through such a solemn gift, [Note: [Col. 0180B] d Some MSS: “also.” Then 42 omits “gift and which.”] [Note: [Col. 0180C] e 21 in margin: “of her.”] if the man afterward voluntarily refuses to take as wife the woman whom he has rejected, [Note: [Col. 0180C] f 6–9, 20, 42–44 and many others omit “afterward,” which may indeed be absent. MS 21 adds it in a second hand.] [Note: [Col. 0180C] g 20: “concerning whom.”] [Note: [Col. 0180C] h Some MSS: “rejected,” “depicted.” Sich.: “agreed upon and subscribed,” but “rejected” written above in the margin.] after the aforementioned solemn documents have been executed, he shall not reclaim anything that has been delivered. [Note: [Col. 0180C] i 20: “documents.” Some MSS: “may be.” 42: “endowed,” corrected to “delivered.”] [Note: [Col. 0180C] j 6, 7: “things delivered are reclaimed.”] And if he is found to retain anything of the things named, so solemnly given and delivered, [Note: [Col. 0180C] k 42: “will be known,” corrected to “is known.” Aur., Lugd.: “is known.”] it shall without any delay be transferred into the ownership of the betrothed woman whom he refused to take. [Note: [Col. 0180C] l Sich.: “be brought.”] It was not necessary to explain the remaining provision of this law, [Note: [Col. 0180C] m Many MSS: “of this law.”] [Col. 0180B] [Note: [Col. 0180C] n 6, 7 and other MSS, Sich., Cuj. 1–Lugd.: “necessary.” Then many MSS: “to be explained.”] because it is voided by subsequent laws. [Note: [Col. 0180C] o 8: “lower.”]

## CONCERNING BISHOPS

[Note: [Col. 0180C] p MSS 50, 51 add in the margin: “Clerics must abstain from public burdens.” Where this chapter is repeated, it is written thus: “This ruling is repeated.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Octavianus, Corrector of Lucania and Bruttium. [Note: [Col. 0180D] q Br. Al. MSS: “Emperor Constantine,” “Constantine,” or “Const.,” as in Sich.; 50, 51: “Emperor Constantine aaa.”] [Note: [Col. 0180D] r Cuj. 2–Ri*: “Octavius,” improbably. Go., who in his note wishes “Octavianus” restored from earlier editions. 4: “corrector.” Some MSS: “to Octavianus, Corrector.” 28, 42 omit “Corrector of Lucania and Bruttium.”] [Note: [Col. 0180D] s 11: “Lucania.” 16: “Licaniæ.”] [Note: [Col. 0180D] t Many MSS: “Brutium,” as Sich. 20: “of tributes” for “and Bruttium”; elsewhere “and Bruttium” is omitted.] Those who devote the services of religion to the divine cult—that is, those who are called clerics—[Note: [Col. 0180D] u 4: “diunio,” corrected by a second hand to “divino.” 6, 7: “of the divine.” 8: “of divine worship.” 26: “If any persons the ministry of divine worship … this one.”] shall be excused from all public burdens whatsoever, [Note: [Col. 0180D] v 25 omits “from.” 20: “ominously” for “wholly.”] lest, through the sacrilegious malice of certain persons, they be withdrawn from divine services. [Note: [Col. 0180D] x 15: “are excused, nor.” 26, 50, 51: “are excused.” Go. rightly denies that “nor” should be substituted for “and.”] [Note: [Col. 0180D] y Ri. omits “from,” and 12 has “from divine.”] [Note: [Col. 0180D] z 20, Sich.: “be withdrawn from services.” 11: “by sacrilege … be summoned.”] Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, [Note: [Col. 0181B] a 8, 16 omit “twelfth.”] in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time and Licinius Caesar (319). [Note: [Col. 0181B] b 28, 36, 40, L.R.U.: December; 34 omits “November”; 8, 50, 51 omit “Constantine … consuls.” Other MSS omit either “Augustus and fifth” or “Caesar, consuls,” or “Caesar,” as in Sich. 12: “Constantinople [Col. 0181C] Constantine.” 32: “at Constantinople, Augustus fifth.” 43: “Constantine Augustus or Licinius.” 15: “November, under the same Augusti as consuls.”]

INTERPRETATION. This law by a special enactment commands that no one whatsoever should presume, by a sacrilegious appointment, to make tax-collectors or persons enrolled for public service out of clerics; rather, it commands that, free from every public burden—that is, from every office and every compulsory service—they should serve the Church. [Note: [Col. 0181C] c 8: “specially.”] [Note: [Col. 0181C] d Many MSS and Aur., Lugd.: “commanded.”] [Note: [Col. 0181C] e Many MSS, Sich.–Lugd., Lab.: “neither tax-collectors nor enrolled persons.” Aur., Lugd. omits the second “nor.” Other MSS: “allured,” “enrolled,” and below “whomsoever.”] [Note: [Col. 0181C] f 20: “serve.”]

## CONCERNING THE DUTY OF THE GOVERNOR OF A PROVINCE

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Felix, Governor of Corsica. [Note: [Col. 0181C] g Code of Justinian omits “Governor of Corsica.”] Once six months have elapsed, written summaries of all business, drawn up by your staff, shall be sent to the record offices of the most eminent prefecture, so that, after these have been reviewed [Note: [Col. 0181C] h 5: “you review.”] and forwarded to our record offices, it may be made clear which judges have rendered faithful service, and in the dispatch of which cases; [Note: [Col. 0181C] i 5 and editions: “has rendered” for “will have rendered.”] thus the worthy may obtain a reward, and the negligent may incur punishment. [Col. 0181B] The provincials are granted the right to approach your court concerning negligence or avarice on the part of your staff. [Note: [Col. 0181C] j Thus 5, Ba., Pu.; Cl. and W. wrongly add “in.”] [Note: [Col. 0181C] k 5: “in approaching.”] [Note: [Col. 0181C] l 5: “avarice.”] But as for a person who has given a wrongful judgment because he was corrupted by a price or favor, the injured party shall be afforded redress against him not only through losses of reputation, but also by the risk of litigation. [Note: [Col. 0181C] m Chapter 2 of the cited Code of Justinian begins here, where “but” is omitted.] [Note: [Col. 0181C] n 5: “they have judged; him whom they have injured.”] [Note: [Col. 0181C] o Code of Justinian: “loss of valuation” (Hal., G.: “loss of reputation”).] [Note: [Col. 0181C] p Code of Justinian: “risk.” The same sense is contained in the reading of MS 5 if it is punctuated as we have done. Editions: “whom he has injured. Not … risk shall be afforded.”] Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of November [Note: [Col. 0181D] q Code of Justinian: eighth, but read ninth.] at Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0181D] r Thus 5, according to my copy. Cl., Pu., W.: “at Sirmium.” Code of Justinian incorrectly: “at Constantinople.”] in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time and Licinius Caesar (319). [Note: [Col. 0181D] s 5: “Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius Caesar for the fourth time, consul,” whose consulship falls in 315. This would make the present constitution earlier than the preceding one, which is impossible. Moreover, in that year Licinius was not Caesar, as Go. notes in his chronology for 317, but Augustus and consul with Constantine. Accordingly Cl. rightly prints: “Constantine Augustus for the fifth time and Licinius (for the fourth time), Caesar, consuls.” Pu. and W. omit “fourth” after Licinius; with that correction agree chapter 2 of the cited Code of Justinian and chapter 2 of the Theodosian Code, On the Reckoning of Time.]

## CONCERNING THE RECKONING OF TIME

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Felix, Governor of Corsica. [Note: [Col. 0181D] t 8: “Cursia”; 25: “Tuscia.” Some MSS omit “Corsica”; others have “after other matters” or “C.” after “other matters.”] After other matters: If claimants prove that, though repeatedly making applications, they have been delayed, [Note: [Col. 0181D] u 15: “making applications themselves.” Sich.: “that they themselves had been applied to.”] [Note: [Col. 0181D] v 21: “brought forward.”] and have thereby incurred a lapse of time [Col. 0182A] through negligence and indolence because your highness has postponed a hearing, [Note: [Col. 0182C] a 10–18 omit “and … negligence.”] [Note: [Col. 0182C] b Thus 8, 12, 14, 15, 17–19, R.; to these Ri. adds MS 6 and certain MSS cited by Go. 16: “to your highness.” 9: “by indolence, your highness.” 7, 20, 21 and editions: “of your highness.”] [Note: [Col. 0182C] c 14: “hearing.”] [Note: [Col. 0182C] d Thus 6, 7, 9, 10, 14–16, 18, 19: “postponing.” 8, 17, 20, 21: “postponed.” Editions: “of the postponing one.”] the claimant’s indemnification, proportionate to the case brought into dispute, [Note: [Col. 0182C] e 20: “cases.”] [Note: [Col. 0182C] f 6–8, 10, 14, 16–21, Til.: “into dispute.”] [Note: [Col. 0182C] g 8: “assigned.” 19: “have been brought.” 20, 21: “have been assigned.”] shall be made good out of your property. [Note: [Col. 0182C] h 9 adds “shall be given” after “property.” 17: “property to be done.”] [Note: [Col. 0182C] i 8, 10, 14–16 and MSS cited by Go.: “will be made good.” 19: “will be made good” plural.] Given on the ninth day [Note: [Col. 0182C] j Thus 6 according to Ri., 8, 10, 14–19, 29, 42, R., Til., and cited chapter 3 of the Theodosian Code, On the Duty of Provincial Governors. 6, 7, 9, 20, 21, 26, 28, 33, 40, 41, Sich., Cuj. 1–W.: fourth; 24, 27, 30, 31, 35, 38, 44, all MSS according to Go., and Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2 in margin: eighth; 36 omits ninth.] before the Kalends of November at Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0182D] k Sich. in margin: “Not July. At Firmium,” as in 40. Some MSS according to Go.: December. Most MSS and editions, Sich., Til.–Ri*: “at Sirmium.” Some: “Sermium,” “Syrmium.” 30, 33: “Remedium.” 38: “Siromium.” The rest: “at Sirmium.”] in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time and Licinius Caesar (319). [Note: [Col. 0182D] l Many MSS omit “fifth.”] [Note: [Col. 0182D] m 8, 26: “Licinianus.” 38: “Linius.”] [Note: [Col. 0182D] n 24, 30, 33: “fifth Caesar.” Many MSS, Sich.–Lugd. omit “Caesar.”] [Note: [Col. 0182D] o 15 adds: “The title has been explained.”]

## CONCERNING ADVOCACY

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Antiochus, Prefect of the Watch. The regulation is abolished by which a fixed number of advocates was assigned to individual tribunals; all shall have the freedom to strive, each according to the ability of his talent, for distinction in this profession before whatever court he chooses. [Note: [Col. 0182D] p 1: “which certain. … all … will … be.” P. restored letters cut off at the ends of lines. Then 1: “by the power of their talents.”] Given on the Kalends of November at Serdica, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time and Licinius Caesar (319).

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Antiochus, Prefect of the Watch. Cases are abandoned and fail at their proper times while advocates are drawn away among many offices and diverse departments. Therefore we have decreed that those who have once declared that they will conduct cases before you shall not have the power to plead before another judge. [Note: [Col. 0182D] q 1: “his own. … departments are … drawn … to … power.” P. restored letters cut off.]

Published on the Kalends at Serdica, in the consulship of Constantine and Licinius Caesar (319).

## CONCERNING EXACTIONS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Pacatianus, Vicar of the Britains. [Note: [Col. 0182D] r 4: “Britannias.”] Every decurion shall be proceeded against in proportion to the share for which either he himself, or his colonus or taxpayer, is liable and collects; [Note: [Col. 0182D] s Herald, Questions of Law I.9.4, Rein. emends to “possession,” incorrectly according to Go.] and no one shall in any respect be proceeded against on behalf of another decurion or territory. For it is manifest that this is prohibited and must henceforth be observed, so that under this provision of ours no one may suffer [Col. 0183A] injury on behalf of another. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0183B] a Be., conjecturally; Co. in the annals adds “fifth,” correctly. Then Go.–Ri*: “consuls.”] and Licinius Caesar (319).

## CONCERNING ABOLITIONS

[Note: [Col. 0183B] b Br. Al. MSS add, from the explanation of titles: “abolition is the forgetting of an alleged crime.” But it should be noted that in some MSS the word “forgetting” has fallen out, or this clause has been partly altered; I shall discuss this in the edition of the Breviary of Alaric.]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Januarius, Prefect of the City. [Note: [Col. 0183B] c Go., in his Chronicle, following probably Corsini, cited work p. 175, and Be., thinks that because Maximus was then Prefect of the City, “Prefects” (that is, deputy prefect or vicar) ought to be written instead of “Prefect of the City,” on account of chapter 3 of the Theodosian Code, Concerning the Famous, IX.34, given the following year and addressed to Januarinus acting as vicarial prefect. Conversely, in his note on this law and chapter 2 of the Theodosian Code, Concerning Accusations, IX.1, given under the same consuls as this law, Go. maintains that Januarius was Proconsul of Achaea, because that chapter 2 is said to have been received at Corinth. Many MSS: “ppo” or “ppm,” as L. (?) cited by Be. I restored “Januarinus” from 4, Til.–Cuj. 2*; the remainder have “Januarius.” See Theodosian Code IX.1.2, note x; IX.21.2, note y; IX.34.3, note u. 26: “Gennarius.” It is noteworthy that the rank of this same Januarinus is not mentioned in chapter 2 of the Theodosian Code, Concerning Counterfeit Coin, IX.21. Folio 49 of MS 4.] If, after the disturbance caused by an accusation has arisen, abolition is sought, the ground for this new act of mercy must be investigated, [Note: [Col. 0183C] d 15: “arisen without lot.”] [Note: [Col. 0183C] e 6, 7, 10, 18, 25: “the case.”] so that, if this is done without an agreement, [Note: [Col. 0183C] f 20: “without secret contempt.” 25: “by agreement.” Sich.: “agreement.” See Theodosian Code II.10.4, note f. Code of Justinian: “deception,” but Cuj., Observations II.15, supports “agreement.”] the requested humanity may be granted. But if any suspicion should arise that an obvious guilty party is being withdrawn from the laws by an agreement entered into, the plea of purchased mercy shall by no means be admitted; rather, after investigation, the appropriate punishment shall be inflicted upon the guilty accused person. [Note: [Col. 0183C] g 10, 18: “and,” and below “manifest guilty persons.” MS 20 omits “but … withdrawn.”] [Note: [Col. 0183C] h 13: “suspicion.”] [Note: [Col. 0183C] i 8, 15, Sich.: “by which.”] [Note: [Col. 0183C] j 15: “agreement.” 25, Sich.: “agreement.”] [Note: [Col. 0183C] k 25 omits “purchased … admitted.”] [Note: [Col. 0183C] l 20: “be carried out.” In the Code of Justinian this passage is altered as follows: “Abolition, after hearing the case in the presence of the parties, should be sought not from the emperor but from the competent judge; that is, if one has rushed into accusation through error, rashness, or passion. For if the accuser explains this, he will make room for abolition. But if, through deception or after being bribed by the accused, he comes to seek abolition: ‘purchased … appropriate punishment shall be imposed.’ Yet those who defend an injury done to themselves or their own people, and those who bring their relatives to accusation, are by no means prohibited from seeking abolition.”] Given on the sixth day [Note: [Col. 0183D] m 6: third; 31, 33, 34: seventh; Code of Justinian: sixteenth; L.R.U.: before the Kalends of September.] before the Kalends of December at Serdica, [Note: [Col. 0183D] n Thus most MSS; 4, editions, and Code of Justinian: “at Serdica.” 32: “Syrditia.” 20, 39, 43: “Sirdice.” 42: “Serditie.” 8 omits “Serdica … and.”] in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time [Note: [Col. 0183D] o In very many MSS either “Augustus” or “fifth” is omitted.] and Licinius Caesar (319). [Note: [Col. 0183D] p “Caesar” is absent from MS 4, the Code of Justinian, and many Br. Al. MSS.]

INTERPRETATION. If someone regrets having brought a criminal accusation [Col. 0183B] and having filed an indictment concerning something which he could not prove, [Note: [Col. 0183D] q 6–8, 10, 18, and other MSS: “If anyone … criminally … concerning that … could.” Also 20: “could”; 21: “will be able”; 42: “had been able.”] and if he reaches an agreement with the innocent accused person, they shall mutually absolve one another. But if the judge has found the person accused to be guilty, and if the accused and the accuser have agreed through corruption upon absolution from guilt, the person proved guilty shall, with collusion set aside, undergo the punishment established by law. [Col. 0184A] [Note: [Col. 0184B] a 6, 7: “they have agreed … accuser.”] [Note: [Col. 0184B] b Some MSS: “him.”] [Note: [Col. 0184B] c 21: “correction.” Sich.: “correction.” 7, 8: “the accuser’s corruption,” but in 7 the received reading has been restored by a second hand.] [Note: [Col. 0184B] d 6, 7: “undertake”; 21: “receive.”]

## CONCERNING INFORMERS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People. Let the one greatest evil of human life be suppressed: the detestable destruction wrought by informers. Let it be strangled among its first attempts in its very throat, and let the tongue of envy, cut off at the root, be torn out, so that judges may admit neither the calumny nor even the utterance of any informer. But if anyone is found to be an informer, he shall be subjected to a capital sentence. [Note: [Col. 0184B] e Br. Al. MSS and Sich.: “Emperor Coustantinus Augustus.”] [Note: [Col. 0184B] f 16: “Let … greatest evil,” omitting “one.” 20: “the greatest evil here of informers.”] [Note: [Col. 0184C] g 8 omits “detestable.” 10: “of informers,” omitting “destruction.” Shortly below, “of envy” is absent in 20; there likewise: “shall be strangled.” 4: “shall be strangled.”] [Note: [Col. 0184C] h 14, 25: “be torn out.” Rein. proposes “be removed.” See Interpretation.] [Note: [Col. 0184C] i 21: “neither tongue nor utterance.” Then some MSS: “informing.”] [Note: [Col. 0184C] j 4, 45: “but if anyone”; but in 4 the rubricator corrects it to “but if anyone,” and so 9, 20, 21, 25, Sich.–Lugd.; 13: “but anyone”; the remainder omit “if.”] [Note: [Col. 0184C] k 6, 7, 10, 18, 20, 21, 25: “by a capital sentence.” 20: “shall be added.”] Given and published in the Forum of Trajan [Note: [Col. 0184C] l 6–9, 12, 14, 16, 20, 21, 29, 31–34, 38, 42–44, Sich., and L. cited by Be. add “of the Deified.” 33: “of Marcian”; 40: “of Trajan.” Moreover, some MSS omit “and” after “given”; others place below “or fifth and Caesar,” or one or the other, or “Caesar, consuls.” MS 17 lacks “and … consuls.” L.R.U.: “Given on the Kalends of September.” 21: “third day before the Kalends.” Many editions further have “Constantius.” Go. assigns this law to 312, apparently because Constantine was not at Rome in 319 but in Pannonia, and thus this law could not have been given at Rome, as chapter 1 of the Theodosian Code, Concerning the Property of Decurions, V.2, given the same day at Sirmium, also demonstrates. But although Go. seems correct in judging that the integrity of this subscription has been damaged, I disagree with him in the remainder. For this law thereby becomes earlier than the first law under this title, which cannot be allowed unless we suppose that the day was already corrupt in the law itself, which is not probable. It is therefore likely that part of the subscription after “given” dropped out of the manuscripts, so that perhaps in the same year, 319, the law was given at Sirmium, Serdica, Sabaria, or finally Naissus, and afterward published at Rome. If that is so, this law need not be referred to in chapter 1 under this title.] on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time and Licinius Caesar (319). [Note: [Col. 0184D] m MS 21 adds “third.”]

[Col. 0184B] INTERPRETATION. Informers are those who either betray another’s property or attack another’s life. [Note: [Col. 0184D] n 6, 7, 10, 18: “attacks.” 9, 20, with insertion above the line, 21, other MSS, and Sich.: “attack.” 42: “may attack.”] Whoever is found to be an informer in any matter shall, at the very beginning of his betrayal, be seized by the local judge and immediately strangled; and his tongue shall be cut out at the root and removed, [Note: [Col. 0184D] o Some MSS omit “matter.”] [Note: [Col. 0184D] p Sich. adds “guilty.”] [Note: [Col. 0184D] q 6, 7 omit “and.” Shortly before, 21: “be strangled.”] so that, if anyone is going to be a betrayer, neither his calumny nor his voice may be heard. [Col. 0185A] [Note: [Col. 0185B] a 6: “so that if any”; 7, 10, 18, 20, 42–44 and other MSS: “so that he who.”] [Note: [Col. 0185C] b 6, 7: “his own.”]

## CONCERNING THE PROPERTY OF DECURIONS

[Note: [Col. 0185C] c Some MSS omit “Concerning the Property” and write “Concerning the Curions [or Decurions], that is, curiales.” Likewise in the margin of Aur., Lugd.: “Concerning the property of curions, that is, curiales.” These words, “that is,” etc., are transferred from the explanation of titles, of which I shall speak in the edition of the Breviary of Alaric. 15 and the Code of Justinian: “Concerning the Inheritances of Decurions.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Rufinus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0185C] d See chapter 1 of the Theodosian Code, Concerning Betrothals, III.5, note I.] If a decurion dies intestate and without children, and has neither a last will supported by the laws [Note: [Col. 0185C] e 15: “will,” not falsely.] [Note: [Col. 0185C] f 9: “performed”; 16: “law alone.”] nor an heir in the nearest degree by another legal right, [Note: [Col. 0185C] g Cuj. 2–W. add “by which,” which 6, 7, 10–14, 18, 21, Sich.–Lugd. omit; 8 omits “right”; 9, 15, 19, 20 correct “some.” Then 21: “shall fall.”] his property shall pass to the benefit of his own council, that is, shall accrue to the advantage of the order from whose body he has been removed by the necessity of fate. No one shall be permitted to petition for this property as vacant property from our clemency, even if it is truly proved that both a will and a lawful successor are lacking; and any privilege that may have been obtained shall immediately be annulled. [Note: [Col. 0185C] h Some MSS: “removed, with no one.” 8: “of offering.” 9: “to be deprived.”] [Note: [Col. 0185C] i 6, 7, 9, 13, 14, 17, 19–21, 25, Sich.: “or”; incorrectly Ri.] [Note: [Col. 0185C] j 19, 20: “every benefit … annul.”] [Note: [Col. 0185C] k 9: “if to anyone.” 6, 10, 18–20: “just as.” 15, Sich.: “if anything.” 25: “is proved, also all things just as it had been.”] [Note: [Col. 0185D] l Many MSS: “commanded.”] Given on the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 0185D] m 36, 40, Sich. add “fifth”; 20, 39: tenth.] at Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0185D] n Thus the MSS and Sich.–Ri*; but 21, 40, Sich. in margin: “at Firmium.” Be. and W. correct to “at Sirmium.”] in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time [Col. 0185B] [Note: [Col. 0185D] o Many MSS omit either “Augustus, fifth” or “fifth.” 10: “Constantine prefect Augustus fifth.” 15: “Augustus second.” 40, Sich. in margin: seventh.] and Licinius Caesar (319). [Note: [Col. 0185D] p Many MSS and Til. omit “Caesar” or “Caesar, consuls.”]

INTERPRETATION. If a curialis dies intestate, leaving neither children nor near relatives, the council from whose order he is removed shall claim whatever he leaves, so that no one may dare to request it from the emperors as though it were vacant property. If anyone does so, it shall have no force; for this law grants curiales the power to make a will. [Note: [Col. 0185D] q Some MSS: “dies.”] [Note: [Col. 0185D] r 6, 7, 10, 18, 21 and others, Sich.: “will be removed.” 8: “is subjected.” 9, 42, 44 and others: “is covered.” 20: “is subjected.” 43: “is removed.” Many MSS, Sich., Cuj. 1–Lugd.: “to whose order”; the remainder: “by whose order.”]

## CONCERNING VARIOUS RESCRIPTS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Crepereus Donatianus. [Note: [Col. 0185D] s 8, 10, 16, 18, Til. in margin: “Crepereius.” 5, 42: “Creperius.” 19: “Decrepitus.” 27: “Creperitius.”] [Note: [Col. 0185D] t 27 omits “Donatianus.” 29, 42: “Donatianus, Augusti.”] Heirs may invoke rescripts of which those who depart unto death have not availed themselves, so that benefits properly obtained may be secured for successors. [Note: [Col. 0185D] u 16: “had been.” 20 inserts above the line: “their parents.” Then certain MSS: “are brought together.”] [Col. 0186A] [Note: [Col. 0186B] a 19: “may be acquired.” 5, 38: “may acquire.” 8: “may secure.” 20, 21, Sich., Til.: “their successors may be permitted to pursue them,” from the Interpretation; but Til. in margin has our reading.] Published [Note: [Col. 0186C] b 5: “given.” Most MSS, Sich., Til., Cuj. 1, Aur., Lugd.: “given.” Til. in margin: “published.”] on the Ides of December, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time and Licinius Caesar for the fifth time (319). [Note: [Col. 0186C] c Thus W. prints it to avoid ambiguity, lest anyone interpret V.C. as *vir consularis*, “a man of consular rank.” Sich., Cuj. 2, 2*, Go., Ri., Ri*, Be.: “V.C., consuls.” Cuj. 1, Aur., Lugd.: “Licinius Caesar, consuls.” Most MSS and Til. omit “V.C.”]

INTERPRETATION. The benefits of emperors which those who had earned them did not obtain because death intervened may be pursued by their successors, so that heirs may receive the benefits obtained from their predecessors. [Note: [Col. 0186C] d Go. writes “executed” in Greek letters.]

## CONCERNING THE DUTY OF A PROCONSUL AND LEGATE

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Proculus, Proconsul of Africa. [Note: [Col. 0186C] e 5: “Ppculu.” Cl. rightly prints “Proculus,” which cited chapter 2 also has. Likewise Cl. rightly supplies “Proconsul of Africa,” omitted in both chapters; this is required both by the title and by Theodosian Code XV.3.1, Concerning Official Travel, and VI.35.2, Concerning Their Privileges, which are addressed to the same Proculus. Perhaps the words “Proculus, Proconsul” are concealed in the date-marking of MS 5.] It concerns public discipline, and is fitting to proconsular dignity, that you bring under your authority the care and knowledge of public exactions and of other matters, so that you may not rest content with the information and deceptive assertions of officials, but may learn the care and report of the judges themselves, of the prefect of the grain supply, [Note: [Col. 0186C] f On the Prefect of the Grain Supply see Go., *Notitia Dignitatum*, Code of Theodosius.] and of the rationales, if that information is trustworthy. [Note: [Col. 0186C] g W. maintains that “if” is put here for “so that,” whence he conjectures: “care and report.” Schr.: “that it may be trustworthy.”] For thus assistance can be given to provincials against unjust exactions. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time and Licinius Caesar (319).

## CONCERNING A MATTER ADJUDICATED

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Proculus. [Note: [Col. 0186D] h 8, 12, 23 add “petitions and.” 11, 14: “the petition is.” 17: “he petitioned,” in which either the rank of Proculus, who was Proconsul of Africa (see cited chapter 2 of the Theodosian Code, Concerning the Duty of a Proconsul, I.12), is concealed, or the text should be read: “Emperor … to Proculus. Petitions and rescripts obtained.” Go., Ri., Ri*, in order to indicate that the title of Proculus is missing, placed points after “Proculus.”] Obtained rescripts are not to be admitted if cases have once been decided by a judicial sentence which no appeal has suspended; rather, those who have obtained such a rescript are to be excluded even from the threshold of the courts. [Note: [Col. 0186D] i 14, 17: “to obtain.”] [Note: [Col. 0186D] j 8: “judicial”; 23: “of a judicial.” 11: “judicially.”] [Note: [Col. 0186D] k 11: “those vital”; 23: “those as such.” Code of Justinian: “those who have obtained such rescripts.”] [Note: [Col. 0186D] l Code of Justinian’s received text: “light,” incorrectly according to W.] Given on the seventh day [Note: [Col. 0186D] m 8, 12 omit “seventh.” Code of Justinian: sixth, incorrectly according to Go.] before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the fifth time and Licinius Caesar (319). [Note: [Col. 0186D] n 8 omits “fifth and Licinius Caesar”; it wishes “Caesar” added after Licinius, correctly. Compare cited chapter 2 of the Theodosian Code, Concerning the Duty of a Proconsul. Code of Justinian: “Constantine and Licinius Augusti, consuls (312),” with which the subscription of MS 11 nearly agrees, adding “Augustus” after Licinius; but the number “fifth” shows that “Caesar” must be added.]

## CONCERNING PROCURATORS

[Col. 0187A]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Bassus, Prefect of the City. Once procurators have been appointed and, after joinder of issue, have become masters [of the action], those who gave them the mandate shall have no power to pursue the business, unless mortal enmity, illness, or another necessary cause has intervened; for then the suit may be transferred even against their will. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, Constantine Augustus and Licinius Caesar, each for the fifth time, consuls (319). (From the Code of Justinian.)

## WHETHER, OF SEVERAL GUARDIANS OR CURATORS, ALL OR ONE MAY ACT FOR A MINOR OR BE SUED.

The Emperors Constantine Augustus and Licinius Caesar to Symmachus. If the risk of administration has been apportioned among provinces, it is proper that notice be given to all and that suit be brought by those alone who discharge the office of guardianship or curatorship in that province, lest defenders of minors be brought to court from other provinces. Given on the day before the Kalends of February, Constantine Augustus, for the fifth time, and Licinius Caesar, consuls (319). (From the Code of Justinian.)

## CONCERNING FREEDMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Prefect of the City. If an emancipated slave proves ungrateful toward his patron, and through some arrogance or contumacy raises his neck against him, or incurs the fault of a slight offence, he shall again be placed under subjection and control by his patron, if the patron’s complaint, established in court or before inferior judges, shows him to be ungrateful; and his children born thereafter shall also be slaves. For the offences of parents do not harm those who are established to have been born while their parent enjoyed freedom.

Moreover, if one who was freed by the rod in our council, after correction, proves himself worthy through repentance, so that Roman citizenship may be restored to him, he shall not enjoy the benefit of freedom unless his patron obtains this by submitting petitions. Given on the Ides of April at Rome, Constantine Augustus, for the fifth time, and Constans Caesar, consuls (319). (From the Code of Justinian.)

## CONCERNING THE SLAVES AND COLONI OF PATRIMONIAL, SALTUS-LAND, AND EMPHYTEUTIC ESTATES.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus. Coloni burden the emphyteutic lessees by appropriating, contrary to custom, lands which they have not brought under cultivation at all; although established practice permits them to touch only what has been planted by their own labour, whether olive groves or vineyards. They also attempt to appropriate the flowing waters of springs, the produce of which belongs to the emphyteutic lessees alone. It has therefore been decided that henceforth the rights and powers over waters shall remain with the emphyteutic lessees, and that only so much shall be allotted from them to the coloni as is plainly sufficient for cultivating those lands which they themselves cultivate. In proportion to the surplus irrigation which they have appropriated beyond their own cultivation, they shall furnish payments and additional contributions to the emphyteutic proprietors. Posted on the seventh day before the Ides of March at Carthage, Constantine Augustus, for the fifth time, and Licinius, both consuls (319). (From the Code of Justinian.)

In the year of the Lord 320, Constantine Augustus, for the sixth time, and Constantius Caesar, consuls.

[Col. 0188A]

## CONCERNING THE RESCISSION OF THE *LEX COMMISSORIA*.

[Note: [Col. 0188B] a In certain manuscripts: “Concerning the rescission of a *commissuria* or *commissura*.” Manuscript 38: “Concerning its repeal.” In the heading, certain manuscripts omit “to the People.” Code of Justinian VIII.35: “Concerning pledges and the rescission of the *lex commissoria* in pledges.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People. Since, among other abuses, the harshness of the *lex commissoria* has grown especially severe, it is our pleasure that it be invalidated and that all memory of it be abolished for the future.

[Note: [Col. 0188B] b The Code of Justinian adds “of pledges,” which V., following Go. and Be., received in brackets, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and earlier editions and notwithstanding the heading, which speaks generally “Concerning the rescission of the *lex commissoria*.” Hence W. rightly deleted *pignorum*; cf. Bijdr., p. 321. Moreover, W. rightly observes that here “creditors” themselves are signified by the *lex commissoria* in pledges, and that the interpreter understood it in no other way; the authors of the Theodosian Code included the enactment here because the *lex commissoria* attached to a pledge dissolves a sale. [Col. 0188C] Many manuscripts have *commissuriae*. Moreover, the manuscript of Lyons has: “Since.”]

Therefore, if anyone is oppressed by such a contract, let him breathe again under this enactment,

[Note: [Col. 0188C] c Manuscript 20: “all its memory obliterated”; others, “abolished.” Go.: *memoram*, by error.]

which removes present as well as past burdens and prohibits future ones.

[Note: [Col. 0188C] d Manuscript 20, above the line: “has done.”]

[Note: [Col. 0188C] e Manuscripts 19 and 20: “whatever.”]

[Note: [Col. 0188C] f Manuscript 19: “the present.”]

For we order creditors, once the thing has been lost, to receive back what they gave.

[Note: [Col. 0188C] g The Code of Justinian has “repels,” but some manuscripts, as here.]

[Note: [Col. 0188C] h Manuscript 19: “the matter sent.”]

[Note: [Col. 0188C] i The Code of Justinian has “recover,” but Hal. has “receive.”]

Given on the day before the Kalends of February at Serdica, Constantine Augustus, for the sixth time, and Constantine Caesar, consuls (320).

[Note: [Col. 0188C] j Certain manuscripts and the Code of Justinian: “second.”]

[Note: [Col. 0188C] k Manuscripts 28, 40, and Sich. in the margin: “in the month of September”; manuscript 36 omits “February.”]

[Note: [Col. 0188C] l Manuscript 21 omits “at Serdica”; manuscript 28: “Serdica—consuls”; manuscripts 15, Sich., and Cuj. 1 through Go.: “Sardica”; Ri. and Ri*: “Sardicae.” The manuscripts also read *Syrdicie, Serdicie, Syrcidie, Serditiae, Sirdici,* and *Serdice*. Til. and Go. think it should be supplied: “Posted on the Kalends of April at Rome,” from the sole constitution of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning the mitigation of celestial penalties* (VIII.16).]

[Note: [Col. 0188C] m Thus manuscripts 6–8, 10, 12, 14, 16–21, 36, 40, and editions from Sich. through Ri*. Manuscripts 24 and 32: “second”; 27: “seventeenth”; 33: “eighth”; 39: “thirteenth”; 43: “third.” The Code of Justinian, followed by Be. and W., and Sich. in the margin, has “seventh,” so that this constitution is referred to the year 326. But, apart from the fact that we do not know Constantine to have been at Serdica in that year, the law fits the year 320, together with those constitutions which, as I have said, should be joined to it. See also note k on the sole constitution of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning the petition for an inheritance* (II.22).]

C., consuls”; manuscript 20, “Thed., consul”; manuscript 10, “Theod., illustrious consul”; and manuscript 18, “Theodosius, illustrious C.,” corruptly. Manuscript 33 omits “and Constantine Caesar.” Hence only a few manuscripts and all editions have “Constantius,” erroneously. Manuscripts 32, 34, 38, 40 omit “Caesar.” Certain manuscripts put “A” for “Caesar.”]

### Interpretation

*Commissory* stipulations are called those in which a debtor promises, by a written stipulation made under necessity, to sell to his creditor the thing which he has pledged to him for a time.

[Note: [Col. 0188D] o Manuscript 20: “for necessity.”]

[Note: [Col. 0188D] p Certain manuscripts: “a written stipulation” or “by a written stipulation.” Cuj. 1 through Lugd.: “of a written stipulation.”]

[Col. 0189A]

This law revokes what has been done and utterly forbids its being done.

[Note: [Col. 0189C] a Manuscript 21, in the margin, and Sich.: “permits,” but Sich. in the margin has “promises.”]

[Note: [Col. 0189C] b Thus most manuscripts; editions have “utterly to be done” first.]

Thus, if anyone appears under such a pretext to have bought a debtor’s property from the creditor, he is not to flatter himself on the basis of his documents; rather, as soon as the person who, oppressed by debt, sold wishes it, he shall repay the money and recover his possession.

[Note: [Col. 0189C] c Manuscripts 6, 7, and others: “who”; manuscripts 10, 18: “what.”]

[Note: [Col. 0189C] d Manuscript 20: “the property from his debtor under.”]

[Note: [Col. 0189C] e Sich.: “to sell.”]

[Note: [Col. 0189C] f I have emended thus on the authority of the manuscripts. The editions have “revoke,” which is unsuitable.]

## CONCERNING THE INVALIDATION OF PENALTIES FOR CELIBACY AND CHILDLESSNESS.

[Note: [Col. 0189C] g With this heading begins folio CXIX of the Lyons manuscript. The Code of Justinian adds: “and concerning the abolition of the *decimarii*.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People. Those who under the old law were regarded as unmarried shall be freed from the impending terrors of the laws; and they shall live as though they were supported by the marriage bond in the number of married persons, and there shall be an equal condition for all in acquiring what each deserves.

[Note: [Col. 0189C] h The Code of Justinian: “The Emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, three Augusti,” improbably received by Go. and Heineccius in *On the Julian and Papian-Poppaean Law*, II.21 (Amsterdam, 1731, quarto, p. 345). Yet Heineccius adds: “unless you prefer to suspect with me that the sons confirmed their father’s edict in almost the same words, as usually happens.”]

[Note: [Col. 0189C] i Thus Be., following Go. on the authority of the Code of Justinian; the rest, with the Lyons manuscript, have “whence,” incorrectly.]

Nor shall anyone be regarded as childless: the losses imposed upon that designation shall not harm him.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] j The Code of Justinian: “and proposed.”]

§ 1. We make the same judgment concerning women, and we release for all alike the commands of law laid upon their necks, as though they were certain yokes.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] k The Code of Justinian: “judge,” adopted by Go.]

[Note: [Col. 0189D] l The Aur. Lyons manuscript has *inpositi*, an error.]

§ 2. Yet the exercise of this benefit shall not be open between husbands and wives, whose deceptive blandishments are scarcely restrained even by the opposing rigour of law; rather, the ancient authority of the laws shall remain among those persons.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] m The following passage is absent from the Code of Justinian.]

[Note: [Col. 0189D] n Go. in his commentary: “vigour.”]

Given on the day before the Kalends of February at Serdica. Posted on the Kalends of April at Rome, Constantine Augustus, for the sixth time, and Constantius Caesar, consuls (320).

[Note: [Col. 0189D] o Thus Go.; the rest have “at Serdica.” Go. in his *Chronicle*, p. XVIII: “Or, at Sardica.”]

[Note: [Col. 0189D] p According to Be., “Constantine” should be restored, rightly; see ch. 1 of the Theodosian Code cited, note e. The Code of Justinian: “Given on the Kalends of April at Rome, Constantius, for the second time, and Constans, Augusti, consuls”; and Spangenberg, add. 239, adds this in error.]

## CONCERNING EXACTIONS.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People. Let no one fear imprisonment, lashes from leaded scourges, weights, or other punishments devised through the insolence of judges, in the collection of debts, whether from perverse or angry judges. Prison is for punishment; prison is for criminal persons and officials, and—with public marking—for those judges whose coercive measures ought to be more prompt by reason of their office, who have acted contrary to this law.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] q Til. through Cuj. 2*: “Prison is for criminal persons and officials, and with public marking of those judgments whose, etc.” Cuj. 2 through Ri*: “and with public marking of those judges whose, etc.” The passage is difficult; Cuj. vainly attempted to restore it. The Code of Justinian: “Prison is for criminal persons and officials, and—whose [persons] should be more informed, or corrected, by reason of their office.” Go. emends: “and [the prison] of officials (with public marking of those judges whose officials ought to have been more prompt in enforcing restraint), who [that is, the officials] have acted contrary to this law.” Go. reads erroneously *eoram officio* and Ri. *citatores*. Bynkershoek, saying that Go.’s emendation and explanation are bad and worse, defends the reading of the Code of Justinian. Though difficult more through the construction of the words than through corruption, he explains it thus: “Prison is for officials, and with punishment or infamy for judges of this sort, who, not having discharged their duty, have acted contrary to this law. For the words *de officio debere certiores esse* signify not to discharge one’s duty.” Gutherius interprets the passage, leaving everything untouched: “That is, a stain or mark upon reputation should be imposed upon those judges whose restrained exactors ought more promptly to have been summoned—that is, brought more swiftly before the tribunal to pay their deserved penalties; for defendants summoned by the voice of a herald to the judicial tribunal are called *citati rei*: Papinian, I.10, Digest, *On Public Judgments* (XLVIII.1).” Go. thinks that nothing more discordant could be imagined than this interpretation. Cf. Dirksen, cited work, p. 498 ff. For my part, I think that the Code of Justinian’s reading should be adopted: “is for criminal persons and is for officials,” and thereafter that *coercitiones* should be read for *coerciti citatiores*. The manuscripts of the Code of Justinian commend this emendation, where they have: “whose coercions ought to be by reason of their office.” Another conjecture also occurs to me: “Prison is for punishment; prison is for criminal persons. The judgment of officials and, with public marking, of those whose officials are [the persons concerned], ought to be coercions, who, etc.” In V., *coherciti* begins folio 138 of manuscript 4.]

Let payers proceed safely in accordance with it. Or at least, if anyone is so alien from human feeling as to abuse this indulgence for contumacy, let him be confined in an open and free military custody, established for human use.

[Note: [Col. 0190C] a The Code of Justinian: “beside the governor,” approved by Bynkershoek, but rejected by Cuj. and Go. Cuj. approves the reading of the Theodosian Code; Go. emends it to “him,” namely prison. “It” must be retained, i.e. “in accordance with the law.” Justinian adapted the law to his own age.]

[Note: [Col. 0190C] b The Code of Justinian: “for use . . . established.”]

[Note: [Col. 0190C] c Thus Ri* and Be., following Go. on the authority of the Code of Justinian; manuscript 4 and Til. through Ri.: “military.” Moreover, the Code of Justinian has “if anyone in,” and Til. through Cuj. 2*: “military, if”; Go. through Ri*: place “of colonists” after “military.”]

If he persists in hardened wickedness, let his fellow-citizens take possession of his property and all his substance, undertaking the obligation of payment together with ownership of the substance.

[Note: [Col. 0190C] d The Aur. Lyons manuscript omits “his.” The Code of Justinian: “let the exactor proceed against the substance”; see preceding note. Bynkershoek approves it, but Cuj. and Go. reject it. In the following constitution it is said: “with a perpetual security of possession given to purchasers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0190D] e Bynkershoek prefers “undertaking the obligation of payment with the substance in proportion,” incorrectly.]

Once this power has been granted, we believe that all will be more ready to pay those things demanded for the needs of our army, for the common safety.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] f In certain editions of the Code of Justinian “to the exactor” is added, rightly rejected by Cuj. and Go.]

[Note: [Col. 0190D] g Manuscript 4: “and those things.”]

[Note: [Col. 0190D] h The Code of Justinian: “need.”]

Given on the Kalends of February, Constantine Augustus, for the sixth time, and Constantine Caesar, consuls (320).

[Note: [Col. 0190D] i Go. rightly restores, from laws to be joined with this constitution: “Given on the day before the Kalends of February at Serdica. Posted on the Kalends of April at Rome.” Manuscript 4, Til. through Lugd., and the Code of Justinian wrongly add “and Constantius Caesar.”]

## CONCERNING PUBLIC WORKS.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Flavianus, Proconsul of Africa.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] j Go. corrects to “Constantius.”]

[Note: [Col. 0190D] k Manuscript 4: “Flavianus, Prefect of the City of Africa”; Til. through Lugd.: “Flavianus, Prefect of the City, Africa.” Cuj., in Cuj. 2 and 2*, silently corrects to “Proconsul of Africa,” rightly. A similar error occurs in Theodosian Code VIII.5.10, note x, and XIV.25.1. Rein. proposes “to Aelianus,” etc., rightly. See following note.]

No one should think that cities ought to be stripped of their own ornaments; for it is not lawful for a city to lose the distinction received from its ancestors, as though it were to be transferred to the walls of another city. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of February at Milan; received on the eighth day before the Ides of July; Constantine Augustus and Constantine Caesar, consuls (320).

[Note: [Col. 0191C] a Go. and Be. omit the year. Go. transfers this constitution to the year 357, when Constantius Augustus was consul for the ninth time and Julian Caesar for the second, because Flavianus was Proconsul of Africa at about that time; see Theodosian Code I.12.4, note t, and VIII.5.10, *Concerning the Public Post*. Yet the sequence of constitutions opposes Go.’s view, since it is thereby overturned and confused: this constitution would have to be placed after ch. 6 of this title. Be. assigns it to 320—Constantine Augustus, for the sixth time, and Constantine Caesar, consuls—rightly, provided Rein.’s correction, “to Aelianus,” is correct. I do not doubt that it is, since no mention is made of Flavianus at the time to which the order of the constitutions suggests this should be assigned, whereas several laws were addressed to Aelianus in 320. See Go., *Prosopography*, V, “Aelianus,” and Theodosian Code I.12.3, *Concerning the Office of Proconsul.*]

## CONCERNING DECURIONS.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Edict. We order that the sons of decurions, when they have reached the vigorous age of eighteen years, be enrolled for civic duties throughout the province of Carthage. For it is not necessary to wait until they are released from the family and disengaged from the sacred rites, since the wishes of fathers ought not to prejudice the interests of cities.

[Note: [Col. 0191C] b Go., in the notes: “or even”; in the commentary on this constitution: “For it is not necessary to wait, etc.; if the word *enim* is correct here, it may seem possible to infer from this law that sons under paternal power in the province of Carthage were generally released from their fathers and freed from paternal power when they reached greater age.”]

[Note: [Col. 0191D] c Rein. emends “be attached.” Vatican Fragments §248: “released from sacred rites.”]

Posted on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, Constantine Augustus, for the sixth time, and Constantius Caesar, consuls (320).

[Note: [Col. 0191D] d Ri. through Be. omit “tenth,” erroneously.]

[Note: [Col. 0191D] e Be. in the note: “Constantine” should be restored, rightly. See Reland, cited work, p. 306. Aur. Lugd.: “consuls.”]

## CONCERNING DEFAMATORY LIBELS.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] f Manuscript 4, Til. through Ri*: “Helianus.”]

Although copies of the libels submitted in Africa are kept in your office and that of the vicarius, nevertheless permit those whose names they contain to enjoy freedom from fear and security; merely warn them to hasten to remain free not only from every crime but also from every plausible suspicion. For whoever has the confidence to accuse must prove his charge and not conceal what he knows, since he will deservedly attain public vindication worthy of praise.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] g Manuscript 4 and Til. through Cuj. 2*: “vicarii.”]

[Note: [Col. 0191D] h Folio 45 of manuscript 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0191D] i According to Go. in his commentary, some restore: “since he will be praiseworthy for public vindication.” Reinesius is among them. Nevertheless, Go. defends the received reading. See ch. 7 of this title: “he shall obtain the highest praise and reward.”]

Posted on the fifth day before the Kalends of March at Carthage, Constantine Augustus, for the sixth time, and Constantius Caesar, consuls (320).

[Note: [Col. 0191D] j Be., both here and in the following constitution, emends to “Constantine.” Aur. Lugd.: “consuls.” The subscription to Theodosian Code, *Concerning Appeals*, ch. 3, reads: “Posted on the sixth day before the Kalends of May at Carthage, Constantine Augustus, for the seventh time, and Constantius Caesar, consuls (326).” Yet ch. 2 of this title cannot, because of the sequence of laws, be drawn down to 326, unless one prefers with Go., in the *Chronicle* under 326, to bring the cited ch. 3 back to 320 by altering the month and consuls.]

## CONCERNING VETERANS.

[Col. 0192A]

The Emperor Constantine . . .

[Note: [Col. 0192B] a To indicate the lacuna I added the dots; apart from Go., no edition has them. “Magistrates” is absent also in the Code of Justinian, which has “The Emperor Constantine Augustus.” Nor is there any indication of a lacuna in the manuscript.]

When he had entered headquarters and had been greeted, the prefects, tribunes, and men of highest rank cried out: “Augustus Constantine, may the gods preserve you for us; your safety is our safety; truly we say it, under oath we say it.” The assembled veterans cried out: “Augustus Constantine, to what end have you made us veterans if we have no indulgence?” Constantine Augustus said: “I ought to increase rather than diminish the prosperity of my fellow veterans more and more.” The veteran Victorinus said: “Let us not be subjected anywhere to public duties and burdens.” Constantine Augustus said: “State more plainly: what are the principal duties that oppress you harshly?” All the veterans said: “You yourself surely see.”

[Note: [Col. 0192C] b The Code of Justinian: “when they had entered,” but Cuj.: “when he had entered.”]

[Note: [Col. 0192C] c See *Acts concerning the Recovery of the Theodosian Code*, p. 83, note y; Rob. Schneider, *Index of All Matters and Opinions Contained in the Body of Justinian Law*, vol. 1, fasc. 1, Leipzig, 1837, quarto, p. 40, under “Acclamatio”; and the Index of Latinity appended to the Theodosian Code. Acclamations are also mentioned above at I.16.6 and VI.9.2.]

[Note: [Col. 0192C] d The Code of Justinian: “May God preserve you for us.” The manuscript has “may your [plural] preserve,” and below “Victurinus.”]

Constantine Augustus said: “Let it now be clear that by my generosity this has been granted to all veterans: that none of them shall be subjected to any civic duty, nor to public works, nor to any contribution, nor by magistrates, nor by tax collectors.

[Note: [Col. 0192C] e The Code of Justinian: “greatest,” but Cuj.: “magnificence,” wrongly adopted by Go.]

[Note: [Col. 0192C] f The Code of Justinian omits “surely.”]

[Note: [Col. 0192C] g Thus Be.’s edition, following Go.: “that it be.”]

[Note: [Col. 0192B] h The Code of Justinian has “from the Code of Justinian,” though it has “them in any.” The manuscript and Cuj. 1 through Ri*: “none.” Yet Go. now concedes that examples of the double negative are not lacking. [Col. 0192D] See §1 of this constitution, “we have prohibited that none at all should trouble any of them,” and Theodosian Code VII.8.10, note o.]

[Note: [Col. 0192D] i Thus Be., on the authority of the Code of Justinian and Go. The manuscript and Cuj. 1 through Ri*: “no.” See preceding note. The words “by magistrates” begin folio LXXIV of the manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0192D] j The Code of Justinian: “nor in . . . shall he be subjected, nor to any contribution, nor by magistrates, nor by tax collectors.” Moreover, in Cuj. 1 through Cuj. 2* there is no punctuation between “tax collectors” and “in,” and the sentence proceeds: “nor by tax collectors in whatever . . .”]

At whatever markets they attend, they shall not be obliged to pay any charge imposed on account of sale. Tax farmers also, as they are accustomed to press upon agents, shall be kept away from these veterans; let them enjoy perpetual tranquillity after their labours.

[Note: [Col. 0192D] k The Code of Justinian: “at whatever markets they attend, they shall have to pay any charge for sale.”]

[Note: [Col. 0192D] l Thus Be., following Go. on the authority of the Code of Justinian. The manuscript and Cuj. 1 through Ri* incorrectly: “to tax farmers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0192D] m The Code of Justinian: “are accustomed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0192D] n The Code of Justinian: “supply,” but Cuj.’s old book has “superpellere.” Go.: “super-compellere.”]

[Note: [Col. 0192D] o The Code of Justinian: “the same persons.”]

[Col. 0193A]

§ 1. We have also forbidden our fiscus by the same letter to trouble any of them whatsoever; but they may buy and sell, so that their unbroken benefits may enjoy the tranquillity and peace of our age, and their old age may enjoy rest after its labours.

[Note: [Col. 0193B] a The Code of Justinian: “also our fiscus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0193B] b The Code of Justinian: “we forbid,” approved by Go., but rejected by Be. because of the separate verb “should trouble.” Cuj.: “we have forbidden.”]

[Note: [Col. 0193B] c The Code of Justinian: “should trouble,” but Cuj. has the reading of the Theodosian Code. Shortly afterward its manuscript has “them” for “him.” In the same place, above: “you see,” but corrected to “you perceive.”]

[Note: [Col. 0193B] d The Code of Justinian adds here: “to conduct money dealings and trade in the best businesses, and not merely”—omitting “that”—“unbroken”;]

[Note: [Col. 0193B] e Thus also the Code of Justinian. If this is so, “may enjoy” must here be taken in a passive sense. Similarly, Theodosian Code VIII.18.1: “the power and right of enjoying the property of children . . . shall remain.” See Juretus on Symmachus, *Letters* II.21. Go. conjectures “may be borne”; Be. “may remain,” or something similar. No doubt *perfruantur* arose by repetition of *perfruatur*: formerly another word seems to have stood here, which may be conjectured in different ways. Perhaps “may be bestowed”?]

[Note: [Col. 0193C] f The following has been expanded in the Code of Justinian as follows: “but we also permit that they be burdened with no civic duty, that is, bodily, personal, or transport burden”; and what follows to the end is absent.]

§ 2. Let the contests that were in the person of their father also defend their sons; and let those whom we earnestly desire to flourish not, if they can be proved contumacious after the same veterans, be decimated by these judgments, when they are attached more suitably to the governor’s staff by my command.

[Note: [Col. 0193C] g Go.: “Does it mean, ‘Let their sons also pay the contests?’ Or, ‘Let the contests descend upon their sons also?’ Nothing of the sort pleases me: the reading must be retained here.” Compare Vatican Fragments 195.]

[Note: [Col. 0193C] h Go. wishes either “and them” or “whom,” or “and which,” or “that which”—namely, “contests.”]

[Note: [Col. 0193C] i Go. conjectures “more quickly than usual,” because of what follows. See following note.]

[Note: [Col. 0193C] j Thus all editions and Go.’s manuscript: “lest, if they can be proved contumacious . . . by my command.” Go. emended the sufficiently obscure passage rather boldly: “For if they can be proved contumacious after the same veterans, they shall be attached to the governor’s staff in the tenth year of age and the sixth [year of service?], by my suitable command,” or “more suitably according to my command.” Be. wishes “through my command.” It seems to me that the text should read: “lest, if they can be proved . . ., they be excluded from these judgments and be attached to the governor’s staff more suitably by my command.” The sense would be: the sons of veterans should themselves serve and flourish, lest, if they stubbornly wish to evade military service, they be excluded from the benefits of privileges and be ordered instead to serve on governors’ staffs.]

The stationing soldiers of each local cohort shall therefore take care to send them, together with their parents’ despair, without any delay to the sanctity of my presence, so that they may be safe when they receive the penalties of indulgence which are consonant with *senuas* [reading materially uncertain].

[Note: [Col. 0193D] k Go. conjectures: “and their parents and despair,” or “investigating their despair, send them”; Be. prefers “their parents and despair to,” plausibly.]

[Note: [Col. 0193D] l Go. emends this corrupt passage thus: “so that, if they are safe, they may receive penalties of indulgence consonant with them.” I do not know a better emendation.]

Given on the Kalends of March in the city of the Velovoci, Constantine Augustus, for the sixth time, and Constantius Caesar, consuls (320).

[Note: [Col. 0193D] m The Code of Justinian omits “in.”]

[Note: [Col. 0193D] n The Code of Justinian: “Belovaci,” wrongly adopted by Go. Some learned men made it “Belovaci” from this, but Bou. p. 746 proves that this opinion cannot be accepted, because Constantine had already departed Gaul in 316. Bou. agrees with Go., who conjectures “of the Velani” in Upper Moesia. Moreover, see Reland, cited work, p. 307.]

[Note: [Col. 0194B] a Be. believes that “Constantine” should be restored here also and in the following laws.]

## CONCERNING PRAETORS AND QUAESTORS.

[Note: [Col. 0194B] b The manuscript: “PAETORIB.,” erroneously. Likewise shortly afterward *um* for *cum*.]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Aelianus, Prefect of the City.

[Note: [Col. 0194B] c Aelianus is not found as Prefect of the City in this year. Go. therefore conjectures either that it should be written “to Julianus, Prefect of the City,” and in the subscription: “Constantine Augustus, for the eighth time, and Constantine Caesar, for the fourth time, consuls (329),” in which year Julianus was Prefect of the City; or “to Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa,” which I think more correct, and Go. himself seems to concede it; other laws of this year have this address: Theodosian Code I.12.3, *Concerning the Office of Proconsul*, and IX.34.2, *Concerning Defamatory Libels*. The abbreviations PC and PU could easily have been interchanged by a copyist, especially if the province’s name had been omitted in the address. Besides improperly rejecting “Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa,” Be. conjectures “P., Prefect of the City,” which I do not understand.]

Persuaded by the honourable representations of the most distinguished senate, we decree that quaestors shall enjoy the same prerogative as consuls and praetors: thus, if anyone is nominated while absent before his sixteenth year, when the presentation of the office is being celebrated, he shall not be bound by the obligations of a grain condemnation, because it is our pleasure that this privilege support the age mentioned. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of March at Sirmium, Constantine Augustus, for the sixth time, and Constantius Caesar, consuls (320).

[Note: [Col. 0194C] d Aur. Lugd. incorrectly: “we decree” in a corrupt form.]

[Note: [Col. 0194C] e Thus Cuj. 2 through Ri*; the manuscript and Cuj. 1 through Lugd.: “at Sirmi.” Be.: “at Sirmii.”]

[Note: [Col. 0194C] f Go. and Be. rightly wish “Constantine” restored. A similar error occurs in ch. 2 of the cited Theodosian Code.]

## CONCERNING THE ABDUCTION OF VIRGINS OR WIDOWS.

[Note: [Col. 0194C] g The Code of Justinian: “Concerning the abduction of virgins or widows and likewise holy women.” The heading has been compounded from this and the following title of the Theodosian Code.]

[Note: [Col. 0194C] h Manuscript 20: “Concerning abduction,” with “Abductions” above the line. Manuscript 15: “Concerning the abduction of women.” Very many manuscripts have “abduction.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People. If anyone, having previously made no agreement with the girl’s parents, carries her off against her will, or abducts her with her consent, hoping for protection from her reply—though the ancients have altogether excluded her, on account of the weakness and instability of her sex and judgment, from pleadings, testimony, and every judicial proceeding—her reply shall afford her no benefit under the ancient law; rather, the girl herself shall be bound as an accomplice in the crime.

### Interpretation

If anyone has made no prior settlement with the parents of a girl, so that he ought to join her to himself in marriage, and carries her off either against her will or with her consent, if the girl agrees with the ravisher, both shall be punished alike. But if any of the girl’s friends or household, or perhaps her nurses, have given counsel for the abduction or offered an opportunity for carrying her off, they shall receive molten lead in mouth and throat, so that the part of the body from which encouragements to the crime are known to have been supplied may deservedly be closed.

>

Lugd.: “lest any.” MS. 42 and other manuscripts: “are known to supply … that woman … she is carried off unwillingly … she has cried out … assisted … may be able … to her.” MS. 21 omits “to the unwilling woman be denied.” Below, Cuj. 2 and 2*: “have protested against the abduction.”  

But those who are carried off unwillingly, and who have not cried out against the ravisher so that they might be delivered with the assistance of neighbors or parents, shall be denied succession to their parents. A convicted ravisher may not appeal, but shall be punished by the judge immediately at the opening stages of the inquiry. If, however, the ravisher perhaps comes to an agreement with the girl’s parents and vengeance for the abduction has been omitted through the silence of the parents, if a slave reports these matters, he shall receive Latin freedom; if he is a Latin, he shall become a Roman citizen. But parents who have assented to the ravisher in this matter shall be condemned to exile. Those, however, who have rendered aid to the ravisher, whether men or women, shall be burned by fire.

## If Anyone Corrupts Her Whose Guardian He Has Been

> [Col. 0197C] h Sich.: *fuerat* (“had been”) and corrupts the title index accordingly. MS. 20: *corripuerit* (“seizes”).  

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Bassus, Vicar of Italy.

> [Col. 0197C] i MSS. 28, 36, 40, Sich. in the margin: Catulinus. Some manuscripts omit Italy or Vicar of Italy.  

After other matters: When a girl has reached the years of adulthood and has begun to aspire to marriage, guardians must prove that the girl whose union is sought retains her virginity unimpaired. To prevent this rule from being extended too broadly, this obligation alone ought to bind the guardian: that he prove himself free of injury to her violated chastity. Once this has been established, he shall, free from all fear, enjoy the desired union; the office shall ensure that, if the offense of violated chastity rests upon him, he is punished with deportation, and all his property is claimed by the powers of the fisc, although he ought to suffer the punishment which the laws impose upon a ravisher.

> [Col. 0197C] j *Post alia* is omitted in many manuscripts, including MS. 4 and those of Sich.–Lugd., and in Codex Justinianus.  
>   
> [Col. 0197C] k MS. 4, Til. omit *et*.  
>   
> [Col. 0197C–D] l Breviary manuscripts of Alaric and Sich.: “when girls … have attained … have begun.” MS. 21: “begins to aspire to marriage.” Because of the words “free from all fear … shall enjoy,” appearing below, Go. conjectures: “and the guardians begin to aspire to marriage, they must prove [it],” a conjecture approved by Ri. Yet I do not hesitate to add my support to Go.’s opinion. For by this law the emperor seeks to prevent guardians from corrupting their wards and, by corrupting them, compelling them to contract marriages with the guardians themselves. For this reason it is said below: “that he prove himself free from injury to violated chastity.” These words no longer conflict with the later phrase, “free from all fear he shall enjoy the desired union.” Perhaps, therefore, with the Breviary manuscripts of Alaric, the text should read: “When [girls] have attained [adulthood], and guardians have begun to aspire to marriage, they must ….”  
>

>

>

### Interpretation

When girls living under a guardian first reach marriageable age and any suitor approaches, the girl shall not be joined in marriage until it has been proved that her virginity has been preserved by her guardian. For if her virginity is proved to have been violated by the guardian himself, he shall immediately be condemned to exile, and the fisc shall take all his property.

## On the Right of the Fisc

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Domitius Dracontius, Master of the Private Estate in Africa. When the fisc either endures or initiates litigation, a period of one year must be observed for deciding the case, because this is sufficient for preparing it; and private persons ought not to be harassed longer without profit to the fisc.

## On the Custody of Defendants

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Florentius, Rationalis. In any case in which a defendant has been produced, whether an accuser is present or he has been brought forward by the concern of the public authority, an investigation must immediately take place, so that the guilty may be punished and the innocent acquitted. But if the accuser is temporarily absent, or the presence of accomplices appears necessary, that must indeed be arranged as swiftly as possible. Meanwhile, the man who has been produced must not have iron manacles placed upon him, clinging to his bones, but rather longer chains, so that torture is absent while secure custody remains. Nor should one confined endure the darkness of an inner cell, but should be refreshed by admitted light; and when night has doubled the confinement, he should be received in the vestibules of prisons and in healthy places, and, when day returns, brought out at first sunrise into the public light, lest he perish through the punishments of prison—a fate known to be pitiable for the innocent and not sufficiently severe for the guilty.

> [Col. 0198D] o MS. 4: *publice*.

>

## On Clerics

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Bassus, Praetorian Prefect. Since the issued constitution directs that henceforth no decurion, no descendant of a decurion, nor anyone possessing adequate property and suited to the performance of public obligations, may take refuge in the title and service of clerics; but that thereafter only persons poor in fortune and not bound by civic public obligations be appointed in the places of deceased clerics: we have learned that even those persons are being disturbed who joined themselves to the fellowship of clerics before the promulgation of the law. Therefore we order that they be freed from every annoyance; but those who, after the law was enacted, evaded public services by fleeing into the number of clerics are to be removed far from that body, restored to the orders of the curia, and made to perform civic services.

## On the Office of a Proconsul and Legate

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa. Legates shall hear not only civil but also criminal cases, so that, if they see that a sentence must be pronounced against defendants, they shall not delay in sending them to the proconsuls. For all judges must observe this: after a suitable amount of time has been calculated, in which the necessary preparation of a criminal case may be completed, the guilty person shall receive prompt punishment, or the innocent person acquittal.

## On Veterans

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to all veterans. In accordance with our command, veterans shall receive vacant lands and possess them perpetually exempt from taxes; and they shall receive twenty-five thousand *folles* in coin for purchasing necessities for rural life, a pair of oxen, and one hundred modii of mixed grain. But any person who desires to engage in business, we permit to possess an exempt capital of one hundred *folles*. Therefore, apart from those occupied with homes or business, all of you who are without employment and conduct no business ought to resort to this remedy, lest you suffer want.

> [Col. 0201D] h The manuscript has *eademenda*. Go., in the commentary, because of constitution 8 of this title, conjectures *vagantes* (“wandering”); he also prefers *pecunias* below, without reason. Nor does Reinesius improve matters by conjecturing “in money.”  
>   
> [Col. 0201D] i Aur.–Be.: *nummum*. The manuscript and Cuj. 1 have *nummu*, incorrectly; but in the manuscript the syllable *mu* is not unlike *mo*. Go. conjectures *in nummis*. Following Cuj. 1 and the manuscript’s writing, *nummo* is more probable, and I adopt it. Someone wished to read *immunis*, wrongly according to Go. Schultz, cited work, pp. 617 and 629, emends “tax-exempt money of twenty-five thousand, or folles.” The manuscript has *militia* for *milia*.  
>   
> [Col. 0201D] j Cuj. 1: *aut*, i.e. *autem*. Codex 4 often has this scribal abbreviation in constitution 4 of this title. The second page of folio LXXIV of the manuscript begins at “or business.”  
>

Given on the third day before the Ides of October at Constantinople, Constantine Augustus, consul for the sixth time, and Constantius Caesar, consuls (320).

## On Defamatory Libels

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Januarinus, Acting Vicarial Prefect. Just as patience must be afforded to accusers if they wish to prosecute someone in court, so no credence should be given to defamatory libels, nor should any report concerning them be made to our knowledge, since such libels ought immediately to be destroyed by flames when no author of them exists.

## On Pagans, Sacrifices, and Temples

> [Col. 0202C] f Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2*. Lab.: “On pagans, sacrifices, and temples,” incorrectly according to Go., who restored a comma after *Paganis*, as Til. already has and Codex Justinianus. See Go.’s note on this title and Fabrotus, cited work.  

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus. If anything in our palace or in other public works is found to have been struck by lightning, according to the retained custom of ancient observance, the meaning of the portent shall be sought from haruspices, and a written report, diligently compiled, shall be referred to our knowledge. Permission to employ this practice shall also be granted to others, provided that they refrain from domestic sacrifices, which are specifically prohibited.

§ 1. Know that we have received the report and interpretation written concerning the striking of the amphitheater, about which you had written to Heraclianus, tribune and master of offices.

## On the Military Peculium of All Palatine Officials

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Severus, Prefect of the City. We decree that all Palatine officials, upon whom the definite privileges of our edict have long since been conferred, shall possess as a military peculium whatever property they acquire while serving in our palace, whether acquired through their own thrift or received through our gifts. For what is so much derived from the camp as that which is acquired with our knowledge and almost under our eyes? Nor are those strangers to the dust and toil of camps who accompany our standards, who are always at hand for our affairs, and whom the length of journeys and the difficulty of expeditions train, attentive and instructed in their duties. Therefore our Palatine officials, who have been able to use the privileges of the edict, shall retain as privileged their peculia which, while established in our palace, they have acquired—as stated—either by their own labor or by our gift.

Published on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, Constantine Augustus, consul for the sixth time, and Constantius Caesar, consuls, 320. (From Codex Justinianus.)

In the year of the Lord 321, Crispus II and Constantine II, Caesars, consuls.

**INTERPRETATION.** When a judge has begun to hear a case, let him receive patiently the assertions and responses of the litigants and investigate everything by a full examination. Nor [Note: [Col. 0204C] i 20: *ne*.] should he wish to oppose the litigants with his own judgment before they themselves [Note: [Col. 0204D] j Thus 8, 9, 42 and others, Sich., Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2*. 43: “he himself.” 6, 7, 20 and other manuscripts, and Go., Ri., Ri*: “to them.”], after everything has been completed, have nothing further [Note: [Col. 0204D] k 20, Sich.: “if already.”] [Note: [Col. 0204D] l Most manuscripts, Sich., Cuj. 1, Aur. Lugd.: “already” (omitting “nothing further”)—“do not have … to put forward” (omitting “and the action should be debated so long”): “until when.”] to put forward in the dispute; and the action should be debated until the truth of the matter is discovered [Note: [Col. 0204D] m Thus 6, 7; 8: “will be discovered.” 10, 18: “discovers”; others: “is reached.” Many manuscripts and editions: “may be reached.” Cuj. 1, Aur. Lugd. in margin: “may be investigated.”]. They must be questioned frequently, lest perhaps something omitted remain; for, if the case is to be concluded before the judge himself, he ought to know the whole matter. But if [Note: [Col. 0204D] n Many manuscripts: “if.”] the matter truly so requires [Note: [Col. 0204D] o Some manuscripts: “is required”; others: “will require.”] that it be referred to the emperor’s knowledge [Note: [Col. 0204D] p Some manuscripts: “be referred—given.”], the report submitted must be complete, after every matter has been examined [Note: [Col. 0204D] q Sich.: *suggessio*, an error.], etc.

[Col. 0204B] The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Prefect of the City [Note: [Col. 0204D] r The office is absent in the Code of Justinian. Go. wishes Prefect of the Praetorium to be added, approved by Be. Cf. C. Th. 1.4.1, note e. I have indicated the lacuna by dots.]. To the place. A person who knowingly has neglected to appear in court shall be punished by the judge as contumacious. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, at Sirmium, in the consulship of Probianus and Julianus (322).

## On Appeals

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus . . . After other matters: Let no one heap up in a rebuttal anything which he neglected to assert in his claim [Note: [Col. 0204D] s Go. mistakenly: *neglexererit*. The same commentator notes: “That is, in the dispute, as is said immediately below, or in the court.”]. This indeed often occurs by design: if someone despairs that a point can be proved, he conceals it in the present dispute, confident that he will be refuted if he puts forward fabricated and fictitious allegations. For this reason, each party must also be compelled to produce in court everything [Col. 0205A] [Note: [Col. 0205D] [ [Col. 0205A] This note appears at the foot of column 205, but the callout number (i) has not been printed in the text.] i Be.: “at Sirmium.”] which they consider conducive to the substance [Note: [Col. 0205C] a Folio 184 [ [Col. 0206C] a Go. mistakenly printed *separatam*.] manuscript 4.] of the suit; and they must be pressed in such a way that they know they are not permitted by the authority of this law to introduce in a rebuttal [Note: [Col. 0205C] b Go. notes: “And insert.”] anything which they did not dare to make public before the judge. For if, as We command, a complete assertion is set forth by the litigant in court, and the entire body of evidence is placed in the order of the consultation [Note: [Col. 0205C] c Cuj. 2, 2*: “unadvised.” *Consulti*, i.e. “of the consultation,” according to Go.], what Our judgments have rescripted will stand as settled and trustworthy. No ground for complaint will be afforded, nor any occasion for petitioning Us to order overturned and shaken those matters which We have decreed upon the report of one who submitted neither true nor complete information. Therefore, all allegations of the parties, the entire record, and copies of all documents shall be transmitted. This must be observed by all judges, but especially by Your Sublimity, who represents Our role in judicial hearings [Note: [Col. 0205C] e 4, Til., Cuj. 1, Cuj. 2–Ri*: “then.” Be., following Go., correctly emends to “but,” which is already found in the Aur. Lugd. editions.] [Col. 0205B].

§ 1. Complaints also arise among litigants because the aids of appeal are rejected by you who receive the image, or representation, of the imperial judicial hearing [Note: [Col. 0205C] f Folio 184 [ [Col. 0205C] b Go. notes: “And insert.”] manuscript 4. Only § passed into the Code of Justinian, where it reads: “Those also who receive the image of the imperial judicial hearing must be allowed the aids of appeals.”]. This must be prohibited. For what is more bitter and more unworthy than that someone, granted authority, should become so insolent through arrogance that the benefit of appeal is scorned, the issuance of a judicial opinion is denied, and the opportunity for rebuttal rejected?
