As though appeal had been devised as an insult to the judge rather than as a privilege of the litigant; or as though in this matter not the fairness of the judge but the advantage of the litigant [Note: [Col. 0205C] g The words “invented—litigant” are written twice in manuscript 4, but deleted by points in the second occurrence.] [Note: [Col. 0205C] h Go., in his commentary on this law, emends *utilitas* (“advantage”) to *vilitas* (“lowness”), i.e.: “Since in this matter the fairness of the judge—whether he has judged well or badly—is to be considered, and not the litigant’s lowliness, which is to be held in contempt or scorn in comparison with the judge’s authority and majesty.” I know that interchange between these words, *vilitas* and *utilitas*, has occurred; but in this passage Go.’s opinion is plainly false. The sense is this: appeal does not insult the judge, but is the litigant’s privilege; and it is not so much the judge’s fairness that is distrusted as provision that is made for the litigant’s advantage.] ought to be considered.

Given on the day before the Ides of June, at Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0205D] j Code of Justinian omits “Caesars.” Aur. Lugd.: “consuls.”] in the consulship of Crispus for the second time and Constantine for the second time, Caesars, consuls (321).

## On Honorary Codicils

[Col. 0205C] The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Severus, Prefect [Note: [Col. 0205D] l Severus is not recorded as Prefect of the City in this year; rather, Valerius Maximus is. Only from the day before the Nones of January 325 is Severus said to have been Prefect of the City. Accordingly Go. wishes the subscription to be restored as “Crispus III and Constantine III, consuls” (324), and in the Chronicle commands that, for this year, “to Maximus, Prefect of the City” be read, or else that this constitution be assigned to 326. Yet Severus is also called Prefect of the City in the final constitution of C. Th. 6.35, issued in 320; and in C. Th. 3.32.1, which belongs to 322, Severus’s office is omitted, although the subject of the law, which chiefly concerns the prefecture of the City, appears to require “Prefect of the City” to be restored in the address. For these reasons every alteration is hazardous. Be. conjectures “prefects” (*propraefecti* or vicars), wrongly. In the manuscript, “V.” has perished.] of the City. If anyone maintains that he has obtained codicils by Our judgment, and both the superior impression of the codicils and the internal writing support the claim, nevertheless, if it is established that he expected money for this, he shall none the less be rejected back into the plebs and deprived of office, inasmuch as he attempted to extort more. For only those who have served within the palace or have discharged public administrations ought to be admitted to offices of honour [Note: [Col. 0206C] b Go. at one time proposed *erigi*, *evehi*, or *exciri*, but later changed his view.], all others being excluded and restored to their own status.

Yet, if any persons, recommended by the support of worthy men and without payment of money, have been distinguished before Our eyes by undertaking an embassy for a province, they do not decline to discharge the other public burdens after obtaining the duumvirate, local curatorships, and testimony on behalf of a province [Note: [Col. 0206C] c The word “these” is absent from the edition but, according to Go., is present in the manuscript; correctly.] [Note: [Col. 0206C] d Go. emends to *testimonio*, which may readily be dispensed with. He first placed commas after *duumviratus* and *curas*, for in Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2* the words “duumvirates—obtained” are written continuously.]. But those who, after purchasing procuratorial posts [Note: [Col. 0206C] e Go., in a note: “procuratorial posts or administrations,” incorrectly.] and obtaining profits from the fisc, have earned exemption [Note: [Col. 0206C] f The manuscript: *meruerunt*. Editions: *meruerint*.], whether they are *perfectissimi* [Note: [Col. 0206D] g Be. prefers “are.”] or have acquired standing and place in the order of the *egregii* [Col. 0206B] [Note: [Col. 0206D] h Go. conjectures “within”; but see below, C. Th. 6.37, sole constitution: “have held a position in some office.”] [Note: [Col. 0206D] i Go. incorrectly: *constiterit*. The manuscript has “decurions, and below conceal themselves.”], shall be entered among the decurions. To these must also be added those who hold no administrative office and yet conceal themselves under the rank of *perfectissimi* [Note: [Col. 0206D] j According to Go., “for administrators,” correctly if this is the explanation.].

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, at Sirmium [Note: [Col. 0206D] k Be.: at Sirmium. Subsequently Aur. Lugd. wrongly: “Crispus II” (omitting “and”), “Constantinople II.”], received on the Nones of April, in the consulship of Crispus II and Constantine II, most distinguished Caesars [Note: [Col. 0206D] l See preceding column, note l.] (321).

## On an Undutiful Will

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Claudius, Governor of Dacia [Note: [Col. 0206D] m 6, 7: Dacia. 20: Datia. 8: Dacinia. 10, 18, Code of Justinian: Achaia. Pr.: province of Dacia.]. Although the authority of the laws has wished the burden to fall upon the persons of sons rather than mothers [Note: [Col. 0206D] n 19: “although.”] [Note: [Col. 0206D] o 8 omits “rather.”] [Note: [Col. 0206D] p 26: “the laws ought to take the burden,” whence; 33: “the laws wish,” and “concerning.”], so that those bringing an action for an undutiful will may, within the prescribed periods, show [Note: [Col. 0206D] q 6–8, 10, 16–18: “in no respect.” 19, 20: “may be shown.”] that through no fault of their own they gave their parents offence [Note: [Col. 0206D] r 10, 18: “nor.”], but that they continually obeyed and, as reverence for nature itself required, preserved their conduct unimpaired and without offence [Col. 0207A], so that, once these points have been proved [Note: [Col. 0207B] a 20: “had preserved, so that in consequence of their being deprived”; 33: “had reserved the offence brought upon them.”], they may set aside their parents’ intention [Note: [Col. 0207B] b 9, 15, 19, 20, Sich., Cuj. 1–W.: “may be able to have the parents’ wills removed.” 6–8, 10, 14, 16–18, Til.: “may remove the parents’ intention, wills”; the true reading lies hidden here, but, with Best, p. 41, *testamenta* should be removed, especially since the vulgate reading derives from manuscript 20, a manuscript which often contains glosses. Ri., defending the manuscript reading, thinks that the sense may be restored by adding punctuation: “they may preserve conduct unimpaired, without offence, so that, once these points have been proved, they may remove the parents’ intention. But wills, if the mother,” etc. See Ri., Preface to vol. I, p. XIV.]: nevertheless, if a mother [Note: [Col. 0207B] c This sentence has been altered in the Code of Justinian as follows: “Children who bring a complaint of an undutiful will against their parents’ will must furnish proof that they have continually rendered their parents the obedience due, as reverence for nature itself required, unless the instituted heirs prefer to show that the children were ungrateful toward their parents. But if a mother,” etc. Moreover, 6–8, 14, 17: “mother.”] brings an action for an undutiful will against the will of her son, We order a careful inquiry whether the son, having been injured by no just cause [Note: [Col. 0207C] d Thus all manuscripts, Sich.–Cuj. 2*, Code of Justinian; but Go.–W. omit *ex*.], has injured his mother by his final disposition [Note: [Col. 0207C] e Code of Justinian adds “in.”] and left her neither a mourning portion nor a lawful portion [Note: [Col. 0207C] f 9 adds “that.” Code of Justinian: “because he left her neither a mourning nor lawful [portion].” Hal. nevertheless omits the words “because.”], so that, the will having been set aside [Note: [Col. 0207C] g Code of Justinian: “rescinded.” 16: “the husband’s will removed for the mother.” 20, 33: “the mother’s will having been set aside.”], succession may be conferred upon the mother—provided that no consanguineous agnates of the deceased survive [Note: [Col. 0207C] h 20, Sich.: “and born.”] [Note: [Col. 0207C] i Thus the manuscripts, Sich., Cuj. 1–Ri*; Til., Be., W.: “are.”] [Note: [Col. 0207C] j In the Code of Justinian the words “provided that—survive” are omitted, and a new sentence begins here: “If, however, the mother.” Moreover, the change of moods in what follows should be noted.]; or whether the mother perhaps beset her son with dishonourable actions and improper desires [Note: [Col. 0207D] k 19, 20, Sich.: “needy.”] [Note: [Col. 0207D] l 15 omits “desires.” Code of Justinian: “schemes.”], attacked him by either secret or open plots [Note: [Col. 0207D] m Most manuscripts: “attacked.” 20: “sought” and “or.” 15 omits “perhaps.”], joined her friendship to his enemies, and otherwise conducted herself in such a manner [Note: [Col. 0207D] n Some manuscripts: “if she was turned.”] that she was considered an enemy rather than a mother [Note: [Col. 0207D] o 6–9, 14, 15, 33, Code of Justinian add “his.”]. Once this has been proved [Note: [Col. 0207D] p Thus 6, 7, 10, 14, 16–18, Til., Code of Justinian; 9, 15, 19, 20, Sich., Cuj. 1–W.: “so that this”; 20 subsequently: “further proved.” The Code of Justinian also has “unwillingly.”], even unwillingly she shall acquiesce in the will of her injured son [Note: [Col. 0207D] q 19, 20, Sich. add “of the injured,” from Interpretation 20: “will.”].

Given on the eighth [Note: [Col. 0207D] r 15: ninth; other manuscripts: seventh. Code of Justinian: third. Subsequently Sich. and some manuscripts: Sardica; other manuscripts, Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2*: Serdica.] day before the Ides of February, at Serdica, in the consulship of Crispus [Note: [Col. 0207D] s 6, 7: Crispus Caesar. Many manuscripts omit “Caesar,” as does the Code of Justinian, or have “Caesar II.”] Caesar II and Constantine [Note: [Col. 0207D] t Many manuscripts omit either “II” or “Caesar,” as do Sich.–Lugd., or read “II, Caesar, consuls.” Code of Justinian: “Const[antine], Caesar II.” Moreover Sich., Cuj. 1–Ri*: Constantius; but Ri., from manuscript 6, proposes Constantine. Cuj. 2–Ri*: “Caesars, consuls.”] II, Caesar, as consuls (321).

**INTERPRETATION.** Although the laws have granted sons greater power to bring suit than mothers if they have been passed over in a will [Col. 0208A], so that they may bring an action concerning their mother’s undutiful will—that is, if a fourth of his due share [Note: [Col. 0208C] a 20: “will—whence—will.”] [Note: [Col. 0208C] b Some manuscripts, such as 20, 42: “due.” 43 omits “his own.”] has not been left to the son [Note: [Col. 0208C] c Aur. Lugd.: “bestowed.”]—yet this is so only if they can prove that they have in no respect injured their mother’s filial devotion, but have rendered her the obedience which was fitting [Note: [Col. 0208C] d Some manuscripts, such as 9, 19, 20, 44: singular, “has been able—has injured”; others subsequently: “has been.”] [Note: [Col. 0208C] e 43: “has rendered,” corrected and subsequently written above the line: “passed over—had said.”]. Thus their mother’s will, in which they were passed over, shall not be valid.

For if a mother brings suit against her son’s will, alleging it to be undutiful [Note: [Col. 0208C] f 20: “undutiful.”], careful inquiry must be made [Note: [Col. 0208C] g 9, 20, 42, Sich., Cuj. 1, Aur. Lugd.: “inquired.”]. If [Note: [Col. 0208C] h 9, 44, and others omit “if.”] it is proved that the mother did nothing against her son, or that she perhaps did not attempt to injure him by any plots, openly or secretly, lest perhaps [Note: [Col. 0208C] i Many manuscripts: “nor.”] she entered into a plan [Note: [Col. 0208C] j 20: *conludium*.] against her son with his enemies [Note: [Col. 0208C] k Some manuscripts add “the mother.”] [Note: [Col. 0208C] l 20, Sich., Cuj. 1, Aur. Lugd. add “and,” approved by Ri.; but most manuscripts and Cuj. 2–Ri* omit it.]—an impious thing—and furnish assistance [Note: [Col. 0208C] m 9, 19, 20, Sich., Cuj. 1, Aur. Lugd.: “also,” approved by Ri.; but 20 after correction and Cuj. 2–Ri*: “and assistance.”] [Note: [Col. 0208D] n What follows is lacking in 40; there the text of constitution 3 is added from the words “Whence it is clear,” together with the subscription of constitution 3.]. If this has not occurred, a mother who has been passed over may set aside the will, because her son did not leave her a fourth portion of his property in the will which the son made [Note: [Col. 0208D] o 43: “if he shall have made.”], provided that the son is not proved to have brothers [Note: [Col. 0208D] p 10, 18: “of the son.” 6, 7, 20: “the son of a brother.”] who are consanguineous agnates—that is, born of one father—or their sons in the male line [Col. 0208B]. For if, as stated above, the mother is shown to have been passed over because of manifest enmities [Note: [Col. 0208D] q Some manuscripts: “enemies.”] of her own [Note: [Col. 0208D] r What follows is lacking in 28, 40, 41, and there follows the text of constitution 3 from the words “Whence it is clear,” together with its subscription.], she shall, though unwilling, acquiesce in the will of her injured son [Note: [Col. 0208D] s Many manuscripts: “will.”].

## On the Property of Persons Proscribed or Condemned

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Petronius Probianus [Note: [Col. 0208D] u Rein. adds Prefect of the City, from C. Just. 9.24.9; Emperors Arcadius and Honorius Augusti to Caesarius, Prefect of the Praetorium, from constitution 15 under this title.]. The property of a wife which had legally come to her, before the charge, by any succession, purchase, or even by the husband’s gift, I order to remain untouched when her husband is condemned. Nor is the wife to be bound by the misfortune of another’s crime [Note: [Col. 0208D] v In C. Just. 9.24.24 is added: “and dies as a result of the penalty, or is reduced to servile status by the nature of the punishment.”] [Note: [Col. 0208D] x C. Just. 9.24.24: *adstringi*, improperly according to Go.], since it is just that she should enjoy her paternal, maternal, and personal property [Note: [Col. 0208D] y C. Just. 9.24.24: “enjoy her own property.”] under the unimpaired condition of the laws [Note: [Col. 0208D] z C. Just. 9.24.24: “legal settlement.”].

And a marital gift bestowed on the wife before the time of the crime and accusation, because it was granted as the reward of chastity, must be preserved, as though nature rather than punishment had taken the husband away from her [Col. 0209A] [Note: [Col. 0209C] a C. Just. 9.24.24: “must be preserved—the husband.”] [Note: [Col. 0209C] b C. Just. 9.24.24: “taken away. But if he has been forbidden fire and water, or deportation has been imposed, while death has not followed as a penalty, gifts bestowed by the husband upon the wife remain in suspense, since marriage is not dissolved in cases of this kind; thus, if the husband has not revoked them up to the time of his death, they are confirmed by his death, and Our fisc shall thereafter have no share in the same property.”], having regard, of course, to the privilege and measure of her capacity to receive, so that it may be considered what she was able to receive.

§ 1. If it is clear that a father conferred anything upon emancipated children before the time of the crime and accusation, it shall be preserved for them whole and free from disturbance [Note: [Col. 0209C] c From here begins § 1 of C. Just. 9.24.9.] [Note: [Col. 0209C] d 4, Til.–Ri*: “for these same persons.” C. Just. 9.24.9: “for them without.”].

§ 2. But whatever neither the wife [Note: [Col. 0209C] e Folio 62a, manuscript 4.] nor emancipated children can claim, I direct that it be seized and incorporated, and specifically reported to Me, with this added: whether the condemned person has children, and likewise whether those same children have claimed anything in their own possession by reason of a gift [Note: [Col. 0209C] f C. Just. 9.24.9: “seized by public officials and thus.”] [Note: [Col. 0209C] g 4, Til.–Cuj. 2*, Ri., Ri*: “the same.” Go.: “likewise,” but in the note: “those same.”].

§ 3. But concerning those bound in fiscal proceedings and proscribed and condemned on account of accounts, it has been decided that whatever property a wife has [Note: [Col. 0209C] h From here begins § 2 of C. Just. 9.24.9.] [Note: [Col. 0209C] i C. Just. 9.24.9: “has had.”], or has received from her husband, to the extent that she could receive it [Note: [Col. 0209C] j In C. Just. 9.24.9 the words “to the extent that she could receive” are omitted.], before the beginning [Col. 0209B] of the proceeding [Note: [Col. 0209D] k Thus Be. from the Code of Justinian; 4, Til.–Ri*: “act.” Go. emends “commencement.” Summaries of the Theodosian Code, p. 11: “before the beginning of the action.”], from which the origin of the fraud and wrongdoing was brought before a court; and whatever was subsequently bestowed by gift upon emancipated children, before the bond arose, shall remain unimpaired in the recipients’ rights, lest fraud be attempted as a means of escape rather than generosity [Note: [Col. 0209D] l Code of Justinian: “was bestowed before the crime arose, unimpaired,” omitting, as Go. says, the most elegant reasoning contained here. Til.–Lugd.: “bestowed before than.” Ri., Ri*: “bestowed, before than.”]. Nor shall anything be liable to the fisc in any case except what he possessed in his own ownership when the obligation arose [Note: [Col. 0209D] m Code of Justinian: “began to be obligated, possessed.”], or what the person conducting affairs acquired in his own name or in the name of his wife, children, or anyone else [Note: [Col. 0209D] n 4: “doing,” but corrected to “conducting affairs” by the scribe himself, apparently.] [Note: [Col. 0209D] o Code of Justinian: “his own wife or children—shall have acquired.”].

§ 4. Except only Caesarians [Note: [Col. 0209D] p Folio 62b, manuscript 4.] [Note: [Col. 0209D] q Code of Justinian adds “or Catholiciani.”], who are excluded from every benefit of law [Note: [Col. 0209D] r Cuj. 2, 2*: *exluduntur*, incorrectly.], unless their accounts have been examined and cleared by Me, so that they may have permission to transmit what they have held without wrongdoing [Note: [Col. 0209D] s 4: “have held without wrongdoing,” but corrected by an earlier hand.].

Given on the third day before the Kalends of March, at Serdica [Note: [Col. 0209D] t C. Just. 9.24.24: Sardinia, wrongly. 4 and editions of the Theodosian Code: Serdica.], in the consulship of Crispus II and Constantine II, Caesars (321) [Note: [Col. 0209D] u C. Just. 9.24.24 omits “Caesars.” C. Just. 9.24.9 has the subscription of constitution 15 under this title. Aur. Lugd.: “consuls.”].

## On Their Privileges

[Col. 0210A]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Julius Verus, Vicar of Italy. Upon Our Palatines, who have been granted retirement because of their approved service, certain persons rashly impose the endurance of degrading public burdens and an unworthy obligation, under the pretext of payments customarily rendered. Although this offence deserves a more severe penalty, We nevertheless wish it to be remedied in this manner: Your Gravity shall request from the office of accounts a copy of the statute, and shall cause the provisions of this law to be entered in its official registers [Note: [Col. 0210B] a Go. emends “formed” to “drawn up.” I prefer “its [i.e., the statute’s] established text.”], so that, if they suffer anything of this kind, they may immediately have recourse to them, as to remedies at hand, and be freed from the burden imposed.

Published on the Ides of March, in the consulship of Crispus II and Constantine II, most distinguished Caesars [Note: [Col. 0210B] b Cuj. 1–Be.: “consuls.” The manuscript: *otenu* (corrected to *obtentu*)—*plectendum*—*iliquo*—*abq. ab int.*] (321).

## On Collectors, Superintendents, and Treasurers

[Note: [Col. 0210B] c 4: *prepositis*. Some manuscripts: *Propositis*; others: *Archariis*. Cuj. 2, 2*, in the index of titles: *arcaris*. 34 omits “superintendents and treasurers.” Sich., in the margin of the index of titles prefixed to this book and in the margin of this title’s rubric, reads: “On Superintendents, Exactors, and Treasurers of the State.” In manuscript 43, from the *Explanatio*, is added: “that this should not be done by public tax-collectors without the knowledge of the judge.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Edictum [Note: [Col. 0210C] d Rein. notes: perhaps “to Ecdicius,” or “Ecducus”; see law 2 (law 3), *On Extraordinary and Degrading Public Burdens*. See C. Th. 11.16.3 and 5.14.1, note b.]. If it is established that a collector has ruined the accounts [Col. 0210B], and is not solvent, his appointing authority shall be held under this obligation: whatever the collector dissipated, the appointing authority himself shall restore from his own resources, and shall be compelled to make good all the loss which would have been inflicted [Note: [Col. 0210C] e 4: *ac*, with an *h* added above in red.] [Note: [Col. 0210C] f Go. wishes either “or not” or “postponed by rescript” to be added. He prefers the former, approved by Be. and by me.] if a suitable examination had been applied in appointing solvent persons [Note: [Col. 0210C] g According to Go., for “had been.”].

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Crispus II and Constantine II, Augusti [Note: [Col. 0210C] h Til.–Lugd.: singular Augustus. Correctly Be. restores “Caesars” in place of “Augusti” in a note. Cuj. 2–Ri.: “consuls,” and Rit. 421.] (324).

## On Those Who Have Obtained Relief on Account of Age

[Note: [Col. 0210C] i Numerous manuscripts, in the titles and index of editions of Sich. and Til., and the Code of Justinian: “have obtained.” 9, 42: “obtain.” 19: “shall have obtained.” 20: “will command.”]

Constantine Augustus to Verinus. [Note: [Col. 0210C] j MS 38: *ppo.*; Codex Justinianus: *PP.*, disapproved by Gothofredus, who wishes *Pf. U.* to be placed, because MS 15 has this, and thinks that the subscription should be corrected to “Crispus III and Constantine III, consuls,” that is, 324; for Constantine was staying at Thessalonica in that year, but not in 321 (see C. Th. *On Shipowners*, XIII.5.4), and Lucius Verinus was Prefect of the City. Hence he also judges that the inscription and subscription of C. Th. *On the Hereditary Property of the Family*, II.24.1, should be amended. Although this conjecture is probable, it could not move me to alter anything, since not a single manuscript, either here or in the cited law *On Family Hereditary Property*, confirms the subscription proposed by Gothofredus. Moreover, the fact that MS 15 gives *ppm. urbis* is not weighty enough to require a different subscription against the authority of all the manuscripts. Baudius wishes either that *PPf. U.* be added or that the consuls be changed; but Verinus is nowhere mentioned as Prefect of the City in this year, Maximus holding the prefecture of the City in that year. It should further be noted that “Thessalonica” is absent in the cited law 1. Besides, Constantine’s rescript to Verinus, Vicar of Africa, dated A.D. 321, is mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, in the index to Conference 3, chapters 548–552, vol. I of Hardouin’s edition of the Councils, p. 1143; and by Augustine in the end of the third day of his *Breviculus*, and after the Conference, chapters 31 and 33, and Letter 52. See Gothofredus on C. Th. *On Infamous Libels*, IX.34, vol. III, p. 262.]

All young men [Col. 0211A] who are endowed with uprightness of character and wish more properly to manage, in town or country life, the paternal estate or the patrimonies of their ancestors [Note: [Col. 0211B] a MS 20: “who in honourable …”; temporal preface 33: “the aforesaid.” b Codex Justinianus: “grandfathers.” c Codex Justinianus omits “rural mode of life, more properly”; MS 20: “by a less proper administration of life they desire”; MS 19: “administration.”], and have begun to need imperial assistance [Note: [Col. 0211B] d Codex Justinianus adds “in this matter.” e MS 33: “imperial counsel,” and below “may dare.” f MS 20: “have begun to live.”], may dare to obtain dispensation from age only when the age of adolescence, having completed its twentieth year, has begun to open for them the door to entry upon most established youth [Note: [Col. 0211C] g MS 20: “with twenty years completed”; MS 15: “when the twentieth year is completed”; MS 9: *clause*; MSS 14 and 16: *causa*. Codex Justinianus: “when they have completed the limits of twenty years,” for “when … entry.” h MS 20: “and.”].

Thus, after obtaining dispensation from age, they themselves, invoking the imperial benefit, shall prove not only the number of years prescribed [Note: [Col. 0211C] i MSS 6, 7, 10, 14, 16, 17 omit “entry … themselves”; MSS 10 and 18 have “themselves” in place of “they themselves.” Baudius, following Ritter, says that these words are omitted in MS 6 as far as “thus,” through error. MSS 6, 7, and 16: “in themselves.” Some manuscripts: “the same persons themselves,” or “himself.” Codex Justinianus adds “by themselves.” j MSS 6–8, 14, 19: *perscriptorum*; MS 20: *pscriptoribus*; MSS 10 and 18: *perscripturarum*. Codex Justinianus: “by a writing,” incorrectly, although this reading occurs in some of its editions and manuscripts, as here. k MS 33 omits “number.”], but also, after calling witnesses endowed with honourable or equal or higher rank, shall establish by the testimony of a more honourable life the habits of their character and the integrity of their mind [Note: [Col. 0211C] l MS 16 omits “but … honourable.” Codex Justinianus omits “honourable … endowed.” MSS 6, 7, and 33: “equal or higher”; MSS 8 and 16: “equal”; MSS 9: “equal in rank”; MSS 10 and 18: “higher”; MS 20: “equal, as they were able, or higher.” m Codex Justinianus adds “suitable.” n MS 20: “and integrity of mind, testimony”; Codex Justinianus: “and testimony”; MS 33: “of the year.”].

When they have accomplished this subject to that condition [Note: [Col. 0211D] o Many manuscripts: “more honourable”; MS 33: “they establish honourably”; MS 20: “more honourable.”], they shall obtain in the alienation of landed estates only such right of age as the measurements of years, the laws of times, and nature customarily confer upon each individual [Note: [Col. 0211D] p MS 33: “had accomplished.” q MSS 9, 15, 19, 20, 33, and Sichard add “lawful.” r Thus MSS 9, 10, 18–20 and the margin of Cujas 1–Cujas 2*. MSS 6–8, 14, 16, and 17 have “of law and nature,” which is the same through a common scribal error. MS 33, which reads “laws and also nature,” shows the proper interpretation. MS 15: “laws and natures.” Sichard–Ritter*: “of the law of nature.” Baudius and Wenck: “laws, nature,” contrary to the evidence of all manuscripts. The manuscripts usually have “differ.” Codex Justinianus omits “When … customarily.”].

§ 1. We likewise decree that women, whose age precedes that of men by two years in reaching puberty—not late in puberty—may, once this interval of time has likewise been observed and after they have passed their eighteenth year, obtain the lawful right of age [Note: [Col. 0211D] s Some manuscripts: “two years, a husband,” or “indeed”; MS 33 omits “men.” t MSS 6, 7, 16: masculine *egressos*; MS 14: *egressus*; MSS 10, 18, and the Aureliensis/Lugdunensis edition: singular feminine. [Col. 0212A] a All manuscripts and Sichard–Ritter* have “we decreed,” but Baudius and Wenck print “we decree” from Codex Justinianus, which reads: “We decree that women who are commended solely by integrity of character, once they have passed their eighteenth year, may obtain dispensation from age. But on account of them …”].

But this applies to women whom integrity of character and acuteness of mind, whom an established reputation, recommends [Note: [Col. 0212B] b MS 20 and the margin of Sichard: “if.” c MSS 19 and 20: “age.” d Thus MSS 6–10, 14, 18, 20, and 15: “whom integrity … whom acuteness … whom established [reputation].” Sichard–Lugdunensis: “as though,” approved by Ritter; Cujas 2–Wenck: “and an established reputation.”]. On account of their modesty and reserve, we do not compel these women to be presented in a public gathering before witnesses [Note: [Col. 0212B] e MSS 6, 7, 10, 15, 16, 18, and Codex Justinianus: “and.” f MSS 16, 20, and Sichard: future “we shall compel”; MS 33: “now we shall compel”; MSS 10 and 18: “we did not know,” but “precepts”; Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: “precepts.” Sichard and Tilius: “to present.” Codex Justinianus: “but we do not compel those women, on account of the modesty and reserve of women, to be presented to a public gathering.” MS 15: “we do not compel [them] before witnesses.”], but, once dispensation from age has been obtained, we permit them, through an appointed procurator, to prove only their years by documents or witnesses [Note: [Col. 0212C] g MSS 6–8 and 14: “by little tablets or witnesses”; MS 9: “they should prove by them”; MSS 10, 15, 18: “to prove by them”; MS 20 and Sichard: “prove by witnesses or by them or witnesses”; MS 33: “prove by tablets or garments”; MS 19 omits “or witnesses.” h Codex Justinianus: “that their years of age alone can be proved by five witnesses or documents, an appointed procurator being sent; so that they themselves also …”; MS 9: “we permit her herself to …”].

Thus they too shall have, in all contracts [Note: [Col. 0212C] i Codex Justinianus: “business affairs.”], the same right which we have prescribed that men shall have [Note: [Col. 0212C] j Codex Justinianus: “and such as males [have]”; MS 15 omits “to have.” k MSS 6–8: *perscripsimus*; MSS 10, 18, 33: *proscriptum*; MSS 19 and 20: “we command.” Codex Justinianus adds: “provided, however, that they do not alienate landed estates without a decree,” from the final section.].

§ 2. Senators shall accordingly instruct the office of Your Gravity concerning their character and honourableness; persons of the rank *perfectissimus* shall do so before the vicariate prefecture; Roman equestrians and the rest before the Prefect of the Watch; shipowners before the Prefect of the Grain Supply [Note: [Col. 0212C] l MS 20 and Sichard: “and concerning honour.” m MSS 6, 7, 14, 16, 17 omit the second “and”; MS 15: “and the rest.” n MS 15: “before the Prefect of the City, shipowners”; MS 19: “Prefect of the Watch, chamberlain”; MS 20: “Prefect of the pre-watch, chamberlain.” Otherwise the manuscripts read “of the Watch.” MS 33 omits “of the Watch … Prefect.”].

§ 3. To this age—because between full and completed adolescence and most robust youth there lies the intermediate designation of established age [Note: [Col. 0212C] o MS 20: “grain supply of the city”; MS 19: “to which age.” Codex Justinianus instead has: “But senators of the rank *clarissimus* residing in this imperial city shall indeed [Col. 0212D] [make their representations] before Your Sublimity; the rest before the praetor; and in the provinces all shall do so before their governors concerning their character and honourableness.” Then, omitting everything else except the subscription, it adds: “Those who obtain dispensation from age from the imperial clemency contrary to the aforementioned provision should know that it has no force.” p MSS 10, 14, 17, 18: “and.” q MSS 6, 7, and Sichard: “of firmness”; MSS 10 and 18: “firm”; MS 19: “the intermediate firmness of most robust youth”; MS 20: “intermediate firmness”; MS 33: “the intermediate firmness.” r MS 15: “designation of age”; MS 19: “by designation”; MS 14: “we establish the designation.”]—we assign the following order: the first age shall be childhood; the next, adolescence; this established age shall be the third; the fourth, lawful age; and the fifth shall be regarded as old age [Note: [Col. 0212D] s MS 33 omits “that.” t MSS 15, 33, and Sichard: “childhood follows, adolescence follows”; MS 20: “the one following (corrected from *se quis*) adolescence, established.” Sichard: “established,” but in the margin “second and established.” u MS 19: “the established [age] shall be third.” v MSS 6 and 7: “of old age.”].

§ 4. This designation must also be entered in the contracts themselves, so that not the bare name of the seller is inserted in the deeds of purchase [Note: [Col. 0213B] a MS 20: “and.” b MSS 6–8 and 17: “of the person selling”; MS 16: plural; MS 18: “of the claimant.” c MSS 6, 7, 10, 16–18 add “in.”], but it is indicated that the buyer is a person who is regarded as of established age and of honourable status, and that the seller is of established age [Note: [Col. 0213B] d MSS 6–10, 15, 16, 18–20, and Tilius add “is.” Otherwise MS 9, 20, and 33 have “is of firmness of age,” as does Cujas 1. Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: “of firmness of age.” MS 14 omits “and honourable … age.” e MSS 10 and 18: “has.”]. Yet this shall be so provided that, since the opportunity for bad faith has been removed, those who have deserved the imperial benefit shall continue to exercise greater care in selling landed estates and shall not alienate estates without a decree [Note: [Col. 0213C] f MSS 20, 33, Sichard, and Aureliensis/Lugdunensis have “firmness,” but MS 20 interlinearly and Sichard in the margin have “established.” MS 9: “of firmness, thus”; MS 10: “firm age”; Tilius: “age, thus.” Cujas 1–Cujas 2*: “age. Thus.” Ritter and Ritter*: “age. Thus.” Gothofredus, Baudius, and Wenck place a section sign before “thus,” which we have deleted. g Ritter*: “exempted,” by error. h MSS 6–8, 10, 14, 16, 18: “bad faith.” i Sichard: “because,” but in the margin “and.” MS 15: “and they are to be more diligent in selling estates”; MS 10: “in securities”; MS 20: “of the seller.” j MSS 15 and 33: future perfect “shall have deserved.” k MS 8: “and lest.”].

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of April, at Thessalonica; published on the third day before the Kalends of June, at Rome, under the consulship of Crispus II and Constantius II, Caesars (321). [Note: [Col. 0213C] l Corrected to “V” on the authority of MSS 6, 7, 9, 10, 14–19, 24, 26, 27, 29, 30, 33, 42, rather than “VI,” which Sichard from MS 20 and the other editions retain. Codex Justinianus omits “V … published.” Gothofredus in his Chronicle wishes the consuls of 324 to be placed. m MS 15: “Kalends.” n MSS 9, 20, 29, 42, and Sichard: “IV”; MS 38 omits “III.” o MSS 9, 19, 20, 38, 40: “Kalends of January”; MS 35 and Codex Justinianus: “July.” p MSS 6–8, 14, 16, 18, Aureliensis/Lugdunensis, and Codex Justinianus: “Constantine”; MS 33, omitting “published … Crispus II,” has “Constantius …” and omits II. q Some manuscripts and Tilius: “both Caesars, consuls”; MS 19: “II Caesars, consuls”; MS 20: corrupted; MS 9 omits “both Caesars, consuls”; MS 15: “II Caesars”; MSS 26, 28: “II Caesars, consuls”; MSS 29, 31, 38, 40, Sichard, Cujas 1, and Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: “Caesars.” Codex Justinianus: “Caesar II.”]

**INTERPRETATION.** Young men who are proved to be of honourable character and desire to have a suitable legal capacity for administering their property must first, before attaining lawful age—that is, when [Col. 0213B] a man has begun to be twenty years old—implore the aid of the emperor; and, having received this benefit, must make their representation in public testimony in such order as to prove that they have completed the course of twenty years and live in honourable conduct [Note: [Col. 0213D] r MS 20: “has been proved to be of twenty years of age.” s Some manuscripts, including MSS 20 and 44, Sichard, Cujas 1, and Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: “honourable conduct.”], and thus have free power to transfer their estates into another’s rights, provided, however, that a decree intervenes [Note: [Col. 0213D] t MSS 6 and 7: “if.” u MS 20 adds “to transfer.” v Many manuscripts: singular “has”; below, MS 20: “are less.”].

Women, however, as they are two years younger in respect of puberty, so too, after the two-year period has elapsed, when they reach their eighteenth year, are not to be compelled publicly to prove their years, provided that they are women whom reputation commends for character and honourableness [Note: [Col. 0213D] x MSS 6, 7, 9 and others: “after it has been withdrawn”; MS 42: “after it has been added.” y Many manuscripts, including MSS 6, 7, 20, 42, omit “and”; MS 42 has “honours,” corrected to “honourableness.” z Most manuscripts: “they are to be compelled publicly to prove their years.”]. Rather, by sending a procurator, they shall establish in writing that they possess the years mentioned above and shall have a capacity in contracts similar to that of men. Thus, whatever sort of or however worthy a person she may be, she must establish these matters before the appropriate judge [Note: [Col. 0214C] a Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: “has”; some manuscripts: plural “must.”].

Therefore, when after adolescence they have been confirmed at this age, they shall also describe themselves in the writings or instruments of sale as honourable persons established in age. Yet this is permitted only to those who, as we have said, have deserved the emperor’s benefit for confirmation of age, so that they may not presume to alienate their estates without the command or decree of a judge, which is issued upon the judges’ direction or with the consent of the curiales [Note: [Col. 0214C] b MSS 6, 7, 9, 20, 42, and others: “nor.” c Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: singular “may presume,” as MSS 42–44; MS 42 corrected “may presume.”].

## ON PUBLIC WORKS

Constantine Augustus to Menander … [Note: [Col. 0214C] d Menander’s rank is absent in MS 4 and in the editions. See C. Th. IV.12.2, note a, and VIII.5.4, note a. On account of the wording of this law, Gothofredus wishes the abbreviation of the Praetorian Prefect to be restored, approved by Baudius.]

Because of the negligence of judges who delay imperial commands, we have sent different persons into the several provinces [Note: [Col. 0214B] e Folio 360 of MS 4.], so that they may report to Our knowledge what they see advanced by diligence or find impaired through negligence [Note: [Col. 0214D] f Reinesius ingeniously conjectures “think.” Gothofredus: “they may see and blame.” But “they may blame” is also suitable.].

Judges who are bound to restore public works must be admonished to report to Our knowledge concerning works completed rather than begun, unless perhaps it is right to request that provision be made for the expense accounts of some persons, should they perhaps be lacking [Note: [Col. 0214D] g Cujas 2 and 2*: *forre* for *forte*.]. With regard to matters of chief and greatest importance, they ought to solicit Our counsel, not concerning any matters whatever of the most trivial kind.

Given on the third day before the Ides of April, at Sirmium, under the consulship of Crispus II and Constantine II, most noble Caesars (321). [Note: [Col. 0214D] h MS 4 and Tilius–Lugdunensis: “Sirmi”; Baudius: “Sirmii.” i Baudius restores “Caesars,” correctly. See Reland, cited place, p. 308. Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: “consuls.”]

## ON THE ASSESSMENT OF PATRIMONIAL OR EMPHYTEUTIC ESTATES AND OF THE PRIVATE IMPERIAL ESTATE

[Note: [Col. 0214D] j MS 4: *enfytheuticorum*. Gothofredus: *emphiteuticorum*. Codex Justinianus: “patrimonial and emphyteuticary [estates],” omitting “and of the private imperial estate.”]

Constantine Augustus to Domitius Dracontius. [Note: [Col. 0214D] k According to Gothofredus and Baudius, Master of the Private Imperial Estate in Africa. See above, X.1.4.]

Whenever several persons possess a patrimonial estate, each shall not be forbidden to make the payment in proportion to his share [Col. 0214C]. For the proven industry of some may restrain the fault of the others [Note: [Col. 0214D] l Gothofredus: “industry”; in the rest, an error.].

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May at Sirmium; received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June at Carthage, under the consulship of Crispus II and Constantine II (321). [Note: [Col. 0214D] m MS 4 and Tilius–Lugdunensis: “Sirmi”; Baudius: “Sirmii.” n Folio 160 of MS 4. o Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: “consuls.”]

## ON MANUMISSIONS IN CHURCH

[Note: [Col. 0214D] p MS 8: “church”; MSS 6, 7, 19, and the Guelpherbytan Epitome add “performed.”]

Constantine Augustus to Bishop Hosius. [Note: [Col. 0214D] q Codex Justinianus: “The same Augustus,” since it is the second law under this title. r MS 9: “to the first bishop.” In Codex Justinianus “to the bishop” is absent. It was first restored by Bynkershoek and Hermann from C. Th.]

Those who, in a religious spirit, grant to their little slaves (*servuli*) within the bosom of the Church the freedom they have deserved shall be regarded as having bestowed the same by the same law by which Roman citizenship is customarily conferred after the prescribed formalities have been completed [Note: [Col. 0215B] a Codex Justinianus: “slaves,” but the majority of manuscripts, Pl. 1, and Gothofredus: “little slaves.” b Baudius and Wenck correctly restored the plural here and below in “may be regarded,” from Sichard and Codex Justinianus, with which MSS 9, 12, 14, 15, 17, 19, 21 agree. The remaining manuscripts and editions write singular “has granted … may be regarded,” except MSS 6, 7, 10, 18, which have singular “has granted” with plural “may be regarded.” c The same reading occurs in Codex Justinianus, manuscripts Pl. 1 and 2, Hal., Russ., *Cont.* 62, and Hermann; but MS Bg., the Nuremberg and Schöffer editions, *Cont.* 66 and the rest read “by that law.” d Labbe: “of Rome”; Sichard and Cujas 1–Cujas 2*: “Roman.” e MSS 6–8, 10, 12–14, 16, 17, and Tilius: “solemn.”].

But we have decided that this relaxation applies only to those who have granted [freedom] in the presence of bishops [Note: [Col. 0215C] f Most manuscripts, Tilius, and Codex Justinianus: “to these”; Sichard: “to these.” g Gothofredus adds “freedom” in the note. MSS 6, 7, 10, 14, 16, 18: singular “has granted.”].

§ 1. We grant still more to clerics: when they confer freedom upon their household slaves, they shall be said to have conferred the full benefit of liberty not only in the sight of the Church and of the religious people [Note: [Col. 0215C] h MS 15: “their household slaves.” i MSS 6–8, 12, 14, 17: “religious public.” j MS 15: “the benefit of liberty”; many manuscripts: “of liberty.”], but also when they have granted freedom by their final testament, or have directed that it be given in any words whatever [Note: [Col. 0215C] k Codex Justinianus: “have granted liberty.” l Sichard and Tilius: “but.” m Codex Justinianus, Nuremberg, Hal., Russ., *Cont.* 66 and subsequent editions: “to any persons whatsoever”; but manuscripts Pl. 1, 2, Bg., Gt., the Schöffer editions, *Cont.* 62, and Hermann: “in any words whatever.”]. Thus, from the day on which the will is published, direct freedom shall take effect without any witness or interpreter of the law [Note: [Col. 0215C] n MSS 6–8, 10, 12, 14, 16–18, 21, Sichard, Tilius–Lugdunensis: “commanded, or”; but in the margin of Cujas 1–Lugdunensis: “read: ‘thus, from the day [of] the published [will],’” undoubtedly from manuscripts, which passed into later editions and is found in some manuscripts, such as MSS 15 and 19. MS 14 and Labbe omit “thus.” o MSS 6–8, 10, 14, 16, Sichard–Lugdunensis, and Labbe: “public,” but Labbe notes “read: published.”].

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, under the consulship of Crispus II and Constantine II (321). [Note: [Col. 0215D] p MS 15: XIII; MS 30: VIII; MS 31: XVIII. The numeral in Codex Justinianus is found in Russ. in the margin, Bynkershoek, and Hermann. q Some manuscripts: “Crispolus”; others omit II. r MS 38: “Constantius Augustus, most illustrious consul”; MSS 6, 7, 10: “II, most illustrious consuls”; some manuscripts omit II.]

**INTERPRETATION.** Whoever has the desire to manumit in the most sacred Church [Col. 0215B] should know that, if he wishes to release his slaves in the presence of priests, they become Roman citizens upon receiving freedom [Note: [Col. 0215D] s Thus most manuscripts, Sichard, and Cujas 1–Lugdunensis; “have” in Cujas 2–Ritter*, printed by Gothofredus. t MSS 6 and 7: “desire.” u Labbe omits “that.” v Gothofredus notes: “Let him release [them].” x Gothofredus notes: “And let him know.”]. For if clerics wish to grant freedom to their slaves, even if they do so outside the presence of priests or the slaves are released orally without a document, their liberty shall remain complete and full, as it does for Roman citizens [Note: [Col. 0215D] y Gothofredus notes: “For ‘but.’” z MSS 6, 7, 9, 10 and many manuscripts: plural “freedoms.” aa MS 21 in the margin and Sichard: “even if not before the presence,” but MS 21: “they have done.”].

## ON THE RUNNING OF TIME

Constantine Augustus to Bassus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0216A] a Thus MSS 8, 9, 15, 19, 21 and Sichard, approved by Gothofredus, Baudius, and Wenck. MSS 10 and 18: “Publius.” The remaining manuscripts and editions have “Prefect of the City” or *pu.* See Corsini, p. 173, and C. Th. *On the Legitimate Heirs*, V.1.1, note c.]

Where one of the litigants has died while the suit is pending, the running of time must be renewed, as is contained in laws enacted long ago [Note: [Col. 0216B] b MSS 6–8, 10, 14, 15, 18, 19: “must be renewed.” c MS 6: “given.”].

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June at Sirmium, under the consulship of Crispus II and Constantine II, Caesars (321). [Note: [Col. 0216B] d MSS 9, 28, 29, 36, 40, 42 and Sichard in the margin: XII; MS 24: XIV; MSS 7, 17 and Tilius: XVI, as some manuscripts cited by Gothofredus; MS 33: III. e MSS 9, 24, 33: January. f Thus most manuscripts and Sichard–Ritter*, but Sichard has “Firmium” in the margin; MSS 33, 40: “Firminum”; Baudius and Wenck: “Sirmii.” g MS 24: Crispus I; MS 26: Crispus V; MSS 28, 40, 41: “Crispolus and”; MSS 29, 30, 33: “Crispinus and”; MS 42: “Crispinus II and”; MSS 31, 35 omit II. h Many manuscripts omit “II, Caesar,” or have “Caesar,” or “II Caesar”; MSS 24, 30, 33: “most illustrious consuls.”]

**INTERPRETATION.** If one of the litigants—whether defendant or claimant—perhaps departs this life within the period established in writing, the periods that had been fixed shall be renewed for his successors [Note: [Col. 0216B] i Sichard in the margin: “reclaimant.” MSS 6, 7: “the person claimed against.” j MSS 20, 24, Cujas 1, and Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: “within the established and prescribed period”; Sichard: “within the prescribed established period”; Cujas 1 and Aureliensis/Lugdunensis have this in the margin. k MSS 6, 7, 9, 20, 42–44 and many others omit “this life.” l Sichard, Cujas 1, and Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: “has departed.” m Sichard adds “by them.”].

## ON LEGITIMATE HEIRS

[Note: [Col. 0216C] n Thus corrected on the authority of the majority of manuscripts; likewise Sichard–Lugdunensis. But MS 21 in a second hand, and Cujas 2–Wenck, have “On inheritances.”]

Constantine Augustus to Bassus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0216C] o The editions read “Prefect of the City.” Baudius and Wenck, following Gothofredus, think either the common inscription or the subscription erroneous, since at the time this law was proposed, that is promulgated, Valerius Maximus Basilius had already held the office of Prefect of the City. They therefore direct that either “Praetorian Prefect” be restored in the inscription for “Prefect of the City,” or that different consuls, those of 317 or 318, be put in the subscription. But they themselves retreat from the former conjecture, because Bassus is expressly called Prefect of the City in law 2 under this title and in the *Lex Romana Burgundionum*, cited place. Wenck even conjectures, without adducing any evidence, that Bassus for some time held the urban and praetorian prefectures simultaneously. Finally Baudius thinks it possible that “to Basilius (Maximus), Prefect of the City” was written. But none of these conjectures is necessary: “Praetorian Prefect” must be corrected, as the chronology demands and as very many and the best manuscripts recognize both here and in law 2 under this title (see law 2, note u). Moreover, the other laws of this year, such as those with which this constitution must be joined, and C. Th. *On Evildoers*, IX.16.3, have *ppo.*, that is, Praetorian Prefect, not Prefect of the City, where this reading is written on the authority of the best manuscripts. That Bassus is called Prefect of the City in the *Lex Romana Burgundionum* does not seem important enough to create doubt, when so many manuscripts of the Theodosian Code support our emendation. Who does not know the frequent confusion of the abbreviations *ppo.*, *ppum.*, and *ppu.*, after examples of it have been published by us from the manuscripts in almost every constitution? The *Lex Romana Burgundionum* must therefore yield to the authority of the Theodosian Code itself. For *ppo.*, i.e. Praetorian Prefect, occurs in MSS 8, 9, 12, 14, 17, 19, 25–28, 32–34, 38, 39, 43, 44; “Publius” in MSS 10, 18; *ppm.* in MSS 15, 36, 40; and “prefect” in MS 29. Thus very few manuscripts agree with the editions in “Prefect of the City.”]

Where a mother does not have the *ius liberorum* [the legal privilege of children], even though an uncle on the father’s side and the others intervene, among whom the undiminished rights of agnation extend in order, and whatever agnates there may subsequently be, by whose right of blood relationship the mother could be excluded, it is Our pleasure that, whenever succession is intestate, a third share of all the son’s property be conferred upon the mother [Note: [Col. 0216D] p MS 15: “father.” [Col. 0217A] a Aureliensis/Lugdunensis: “intervening.” b Some manuscripts: “recognition.” c MS 15: “the rights endure, and”; MSS 8, 10, 13, 14, 16–18, 20: “are corrected,” but MS 20 has “are extended” above the line. d MS 19: “it may please [us] for all children.”].

The same one-third share shall be conferred upon the mother by an equal benefit even in the case of a paternal uncle, his son, or only his grandson, where agnation no longer continues—if, perhaps, blood relationship has been diminished through someone’s emancipation—although the mother has the *ius liberorum* [Note: [Col. 0217C] e MSS 10, 12–15, 18: “also” or “and now”; the rest and editions: “and so.” f Thus MSS 6–10, 12–14, 16–21. MS 15: “to the son and grandson alone, [though] agnation …” The editions read “to the son, as also to the grandson,” less correctly because of what follows: “it has not pleased Us to extend Our benefit beyond the degree of grandson.” g MS 20: “action indeed,” but corrected above the line as here. h Some manuscripts and Tilius: “diminished.” i MS 16: “would be conferred on the father.” j MSS 19 and 20 add “and.”].

Nor is this without reason: whenever the mother is supported by the aforesaid privilege, and agnation has been dissolved, it has not pleased Us to extend Our benefit beyond the degree of grandson, lest, when many persons are called, more appear to be taken from the mother than added to her [Note: [Col. 0217C] k MS 19: feminine “aforesaid.” l Nearly all manuscripts: “plundered.” m Sichard: “the benefit of rights beyond the degree”; MS 19: “by Our benefit.” n MS 15 omits “not.” [Col. 0217D] o MSS 19 and 20: “nor”; below, some manuscripts: “of the mother,” and MS 8: “offered.” p MS 15: “and less entered.”].

Accordingly, whether there is one paternal uncle or several, and whether there are his son or sons and grandsons or granddaughters, no more than a single third of all the property is to be conferred on all together, or upon each separately according to the degree of each [Note: [Col. 0217D] q MS 15 adds “paternal uncle.” r MSS 13, 21: “their sons or even daughters”; MS 15, omitting “even”: “grandson.” Many manuscripts: “or granddaughter.” MS 9: “grandson or grandsons.” MS 20: “their sons … and granddaughters.” Other manuscripts have “sons,” a frequent alteration of the letters *u* and *o*. s Cujas 1–Ritter*: “of the property together, to all.” MS 21: “all the property.” MSS 10, 18 omit “of all the property.” t MS 20: “defended” for “to be conferred”; MS 19 omits “degrees.”].

Similarly, if there are several persons by whom the mother can be excluded, no more than one third of the property shall belong to the mother against them all [Note: [Col. 0217D] u MSS 10, 15, 18 omit “and.” v MS 14: “were.” x Some manuscripts: accusative “one third.” y MS 16 omits “to the mother … indefinitely”; MS 18: “all against.”].

Therefore, where agnate persons of the aforesaid line exist in indefinite succession, We have determined that aid be given to the mother against all of them, although this aid is not granted against the mother to all persons, but only to the specified persons described above [Note: [Col. 0217D] z MSS 19, 20: “must … exist.” aa MS 12: “the mother, specified above”; MS 15: “the mother under specified [persons].”].

Thus, even without a request for possession of the estate—for this is the benefit of this law, not of the praetor [Note: [Col. 0217D] bb MS 12: “of the claimant.”]—as soon as the day on which the share is conferred upon them has arrived, they shall obtain full ownership of the share conferred upon them by a simple act of acceptance, by taking hold of any object belonging to the property or by making known their intention [Note: [Col. 0218B] a MS 21 and Sichard: “as if given”; MSS 9, 19, 20: “as if conferred,” but MS 20 has “when” above the line; MSS 10, 18: “as if delayed”; MS 15 omits “upon them.” b Thus MSS 9, 15, 19, 20, Baudius on Gothofredus’s conjecture, and Wenck. The rest: future “they shall obtain,” incorrectly printed by Wenck.].

They shall be granted perpetual capacity, for so long as they live, to enter upon the portion of the succession conferred upon them [Note: [Col. 0218B] c MS 12 omits “to them”; MS 19: “they live”; Sichard, Tilius, Cujas 1: “so long as they shall live”; Gothofredus: “so long as they shall live.”].

For We order that nothing pass to those who will be their successors unless the inheritance has first been acquired by those whom the scope of Our indulgence embraces; rather, it shall remain with those among whom it could have remained before this law [Note: [Col. 0218B] d MS 20: “successions,” but “successors” above the line. Earlier, MS 6: “of their own cession” for “of succession.” e MSS 6–8, 10, 18–20: “themselves.” f I have restored “embraces,” and nearly all manuscripts and Baudius have this, on the authority of Gothofredus, rather than “will embrace,” found in MS 21 and in Sichard–Ritter*. Wenck, to whom the future seems much more serious here, again prints “will embrace.” [Col. 0218C] g MS 20: “hold” above the line; the same manuscript: “among” for “with.” h Thus MSS 7, 8, 10, 13, 14, 17, 18 and Wenck, approved by Gothofredus and Baudius in their notes. MS 9: singular “could have”; the rest: plural “could have,” incorrectly printed by Wenck, unless perhaps “all things” has fallen out above, so that it would read “but all things [shall] remain with those ….” Yet emperors often use a plural verb after *quicquam* and a similar collective pronoun; therefore “could have” in the plural is not wrong.].

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June at Sirmium, under the consulship of Crispus II and Constantine II, Caesars (321). [Note: [Col. 0218C] i Thus corrected, following the evidence of very many manuscripts and required by the constitutions with which this law must be joined. The common reading is “published on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January.” MS 15: IV; an excellent note in Gothofredus: XV, Ritter XIV by error; MS 20: XIII. Gothofredus in his Chronicle: “X, others XIII.” Remarkable is the subscription in MSS 36, 40 and in Sichard’s margin: “the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.” j I have written “at Sirmium” on the authority of MSS 13, 14, 17 and as required by the laws with which, as I said, this must be joined. The other manuscripts read Rome or *Rom.*; MSS 30, 33, 34 omit Sirmium; the editions read Rome. Thus the manuscripts contain a double subscription to this law: that adopted by us concerns the time and place at which the law was issued; the other, hitherto known, concerns the time and place at which it was promulgated. [Col. 0218D] k Some manuscripts: III, through scribal negligence. l MSS 6, 7, 13, 14, 16, 17 omit “and Constantine II”; MSS 8, 12 omit “and … consuls”; MSS 10, 18 omit “and … Caesars”; MSS 36, 40: II; MSS 33, 34: “Constans,” omitting II Caesars; MS 42 omits Caesars; MS 9: “Caesars, consuls.” Otherwise MS 29, 39: “Constantius.” In MS 15 the subscription of the following law is placed here: “promulgated on the fourth day before the Kalends of January at Constantinople, under the consulship of Valentinian and Victor.” Tilius omits “Constantine II.” Otherwise Sichard–Ritter*: “Caesars”; MS 20: “Caesar.”]

**INTERPRETATION.** If a mother does not have the *ius liberorum*, that is, if she is freeborn and has not borne three living children, or is a freedwoman and has not borne four, and if she perhaps loses her only son intestate, and the dying son leaves with his mother one or more paternal uncles, or certainly sons or several grandsons of a paternal uncle or paternal uncles, who nevertheless have not been emancipated, the mother shall succeed to one third of the intestate son’s inheritance, while the uncle shall claim two shares; or, if there are several uncles, their sons or grandsons shall claim them [Note: [Col. 0218D] m “and” in the excerpt in Ritter and Ritter*, but added in correction in some manuscripts: “freedpersons.” n MSS 6, 7 omit “not.” o MSS 36, 40, Sichard, Cujas 1–Lugdunensis: “perhaps intestate.” p Some manuscripts: “uncle.” q MSS 6–8, 10, 18, 21, and others omit “or”; some manuscripts: “sons.” [Col. 0219A] a MS 20 omits “in”; MS 21: “in the third share.”].

But if the mother has the *ius liberorum*, and an uncle or uncles survive together with the mother, even if they have been emancipated, the mother who has the *ius liberorum* shall receive two shares of the property of her son dying intestate, and the uncle or uncles the third [Note: [Col. 0219B] b Many manuscripts: “right of children”; MSS 9, 10, 18 omit “right.” [Col. 0219C] c MS 20: “they have survived … have been.” d Sichard: “shall acquire,” but in the margin “shall receive”; MS 43: present “receives.”].

If the uncles are lacking, the sons of the paternal uncles, however many there may be, shall make equal shares for themselves, per capita. If the sons of the paternal uncles are lacking, the grandsons of the paternal uncles shall likewise succeed by a similar division [Note: [Col. 0219C] e MSS 19, 20, 42–44 and others add “uncles.” MS 43: “but if.” f Some manuscripts add “in the same manner” after “also” and after “of the paternal uncles.” Likewise, some manuscripts below have “succeed … mother shall suffice … and uncles.”].

But in this succession the present constitution alone suffices, so that possession of the estate is presumed among the mother, the uncles, and their sons and grandsons. If the inheritance has perhaps not been entered upon, and those who ought to have entered upon it die, this law excludes their heirs from succession to the inheritance not entered upon, because it expressly provides that an inheritance not entered upon does not pass to heirs [Note: [Col. 0219C] g MS 20: “but if perhaps added.” h MSS 6–9, 19, 20, 42, 44 and others, Cujas 2, 2*, and Gothofredus omit “inheritance,” incorrectly printed by Ritter. i Ritter*: “and these.” j MS 20: “to succession”; MS 21 omits “from.” k Some manuscripts, both here and above: “entered upon,” “entered upon.” l MSS 6, 7: “exclude.” m Thus most manuscripts; editions: “that law.” MS 9 omits “this.” n MSS 6–8, 20 and others add: “Here something concerning the law should be added. See the interpretation of law 3 under this title.”].

## IF DEATH OCCURS WHILE AN APPEAL IS PENDING

[Note: [Col. 0219C] o Some manuscripts: “a pending appeal”; MS 16: “a petitioner.” p Tilius, in the index of titles: “occurs”; MS 34: “has entered.”]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Bassus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0219D] q 4 *pu.* 6, 7, 20, 21, editions *P. V. s. Pf. U.*, that is, *Praefectus urbanus* [Urban Prefect], as in the Code of Justinian. Go. and Be. emend correctly to *P. P.* See above, cited chapter 3, note v, and V, 1, 1, note c. Our reading is confirmed by manuscripts 8, 12, 14, 17, 25, 39, 43, where *ppo* occurs; to these may be added 9, 15, 29, 38, 42 with the abbreviation *ppm*. 16 omits *Pf. P.* and several manuscripts do likewise. After other material, as in the Verona manuscript.]

After other matters: When judges consult whether, in hearing an appeal, they ought to extend fresh periods to the heirs of a litigant who has died in the course of litigation before the expiry of the period, or compel them to plead an unfamiliar case within the remaining days, it has been decided that, when appeals are adjudicated, if one of the litigants has died during the litigation, four months shall be renewed and fresh periods extended, lest persons ignorant of the proceedings, or even uncertain concerning acceptance of the inheritance, be compelled to suffer loss before they derive any benefit. [Note: [Col. 0219D] r 15 omits *de*.] [Note: [Col. 0219D] s 4, 10, 16, 18 have *litigatores* [litigants], and 16 *cognoscuntur*. 9, *litigatoribus*. 20, *litigatorum*. Go., *litigatoris*.] [Note: [Col. 0219D] t 15, *elapsum*.] [Note: [Col. 0219D] u Cuj. 2–Be., *defecerit*.] [Note: [Col. 0219D] v 9 omits *an*; 16 has *an eos cogere*.] [Note: [Col. 0219D] x 6, 7, 16, *cognitum*.] [Note: [Col. 0219D] y 20, *prerogare*. Then 16, *alterum ex*.] [Note: [Col. 0219D] z Fol. 206a of manuscript 4; then 4 has *defucto*, but corrected by the scribe.] [Note: [Col. 0220B] a Several manuscripts: *innovari … prorogare nec ign. … adeundam haereditatem.*] [Note: [Col. 0220B] b 20, *alicoquid quomodo*; above the line *aliquid*. Other manuscripts also have *quomodo* in place of *commodum*.] [Note: [Col. 0220B] c 20, *affligi*, with *affici* above the line. In the Code of Justinian this chapter is written as follows: “If one of the litigants dies while the appeal is still pending, his heirs shall have not merely the remaining time, but also another four months. But if a fixed period is granted for deliberation over the inheritance, after that period has elapsed [Verona manuscript: after the same period has elapsed], an interval of four months shall be counted [Verona manuscript omits *spatium*, ‘interval’], lest persons ignorant of the case … be compelled.”]

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, at Sirmium, during the second consulships of Crispus and Constantine Caesars (321). [Note: [Col. 0220C] d 4, 16, 21, 24, 31, editions before Be., and the Code of Justinian, *PP.*—that is, *proposita* [published]; the remaining manuscripts have *Dat.* [given]. Be., by Go.’s command, prints *Dat.*, correctly. See cited chapter 3. 10, 18, *Praecepta*.] [Note: [Col. 0220C] e 8, 34, Epitome of the Monk, XII. 12, 15, 20, 27, 31, 35, 44, XIV. 24, XX. Verona manuscript, III.] [Note: [Col. 0220C] f 24, July. Epitome of the Monk, January.] [Note: [Col. 0220C] g 4, Til.–Lugd., Verona manuscript, *Sirmi*. Be. and the Code of Justinian, *Sirmii*. Several manuscripts and Br. Al.: *Sermio*, *Firmio*, *Syrmio*; others, including 21, omit *Sirmio*.] [Note: [Col. 0220C] h 8, 28, 36, 30 omit *Crispo-coss.*; others have *II Caess. Cos.* or *Caess.*, and there are manuscripts in which *Constantius* or *AA.* [the Augusti] is written, as in the Sichard edition, or *aug.* instead of *Caess.*]

**INTERPRETATION.** [Note: [Col. 0220C] i 8, 20 add: “This law says the following.”] If, while an appeal is still pending, the death of the litigant who is appealing intervenes, four months must be granted for conducting the case to the heirs of the person who appealed—the person whose author has died; nor should he be hurried into stating the case, lest through ignorance of litigation which he has not handled in full he appear to incur loss. [Note: [Col. 0220C] j 28, 36, 40, and Sich. in the margin: *impendente appellatione* [while an appeal is impending]. 20: “If an appeal is still pending.”] [Note: [Col. 0220C] k 42, *invenerit*; and several manuscripts, “litigants appealing.” 6, *appellatis*.] [Note: [Col. 0220C] l 20 omits *est*, but adds it above the line.] [Note: [Col. 0220C] m Nearly all manuscripts read thus; editions, *debent*.] [Note: [Col. 0220D] n 20: *nec enim d. ad praestandam … incurre.* Cuj. 2–Go., *dicendum*.]

## On Malefactors

Emperor Constantine Augustus and Caesar to Bassus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0220D] o In the Br. Al. manuscripts and in Sichard, the emperor’s name is given. 15 and 40 omit it; C. 10 and 18 incorrectly add “and consul.”] [Note: [Col. 0220D] p The abbreviation for Praetorian Prefect occurs in manuscripts 8, 9, 14, 15, 27, 29, 38, 39, 42–44; Go. and Be. also preferred it. See III, 17, 1. It is omitted in manuscripts 26, 32. The remaining manuscripts, editions, and the Code of Justinian have *Pf. U.* [Urban Prefect].]

The knowledge of those persons must be punished and, with utmost severity, rightly prosecuted by the laws who, equipped with magical arts, have either plotted against human safety or led chaste minds astray toward lust. [Note: [Col. 0220D] q 6, 8, 12, 14, 16: “Their licence must be punished and vindicated by the most stringent laws” (16, *puniendum*; 6, *severissimis*). 7, “their knowledge must be punished.” 10, *licentia*. 18, “their licence must be punished.”] [Note: [Col. 0220D] r 6–8, 10, 12, 16, *vindicandam*. 14, 20, *vindicandum*. Above the line in 20, *marito*.] [Note: [Col. 0220D] s Code of Justinian: *contra salutem hominum moliti artes* [having devised arts against human safety]. 20, *molesti sal aut pudicus*.] [Note: [Col. 0221B] a 4, 7, 9, 10, 13–15, 18, 21, Sich.–Lugd., and Code of Justinian, *deflexisse* [led astray]. 20, *defluxisse*. 8, 12, 16, *deflexis*. Cuj. 2–Be.: *defixisse* [bound by magical spell], apparently conjectured by Cujas. Yet Go. too defends *defixisse* in his commentary from many other writers, as though *defigere* were a verb especially proper to sorcerers. Although this is true, I did not wish to depart from the manuscripts, which unanimously indicate that *deflexisse* was the genuine reading of the Theodosian Code. Further, minds are said with equal propriety to be turned aside from chastity toward lust. 6–8, 10, 12, 16, *animo*. 20, *animus*. 15, *deteguntur*. 20, *detegitur*. Then several manuscripts: *Nullus*. Code of Justinian: *pudicos animos ad libidinem deflexisse*.]

But remedies sought for human bodies, or harmless aids employed in rural places, are not to be implicated in any accusations: for example, so that ripe vintages may not fear rain, or be battered by the stoning of falling hail; aids by which neither anyone’s safety nor reputation is harmed, but by which their labours prosper, lest divine gifts and human labours be laid low. [Note: [Col. 0221B] b 4, *remedi*, corrected by a later hand with *a*. 21, *remedio*.] [Note: [Col. 0221B] c 6–8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 21, *humanitatis*, but 20 has *humanis* above the line.] [Note: [Col. 0221B] d The following is found in the Code of Justinian: “places, harmlessly employed as aids, so that ripe … might not be … shaken by rains or winds and hailstones, by which no one’s, etc.” 15: “ripe vintages [might fear] rain,” and omits *metuerentur* [might fear], in place of which V. in manuscript 7 adds above the line, in a recent hand, *paterentur* [might suffer]. Go. proposes *mitterentur*.] [Note: [Col. 0221C] e 6–10, 12, 14, 18, 20, *rore*. 21, *rore ne gr.* 13, *imb. obruere ne gr.* 16, *aurore gr.* Sichard, *venti et*.] [Note: [Col. 0221C] f 20, *lap. gr. quererentur innocentes*. 12, 21, *innocentes*.] [Note: [Col. 0221C] g 6–8, 10, 14, 18, *cujuscumque*. 20 and the Code of Justinian, *cujusquam*, preferred by Go. In what follows, the manuscripts and Code of Justinian have *existimatio*; others, *profecerint laboris*.] [Note: [Col. 0221C] h 8, *tererentur*.]

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, at Aquileia, during the consulships of Crispus and Constantine Caesars (321). [Note: [Col. 0221C] i 29, 42, XI; 32, 39, 43, and manuscripts cited by Go., L. R. U., XV; 15, 24 omit X.] [Note: [Col. 0221C] j 4, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 20, 21, 24, 29, 42, Sich.–Lugd., and Code of Justinian, June; but Sichard has July in the margin, as do the rest.] [Note: [Col. 0221C] Aquileia is read by many manuscripts, Cuj. 2–Ri*; 4, Til.–Lugd., *Aquilino*, incorrectly, and Go. initially printed it. 20, *aquilegia*. Be. and Code of Justinian, *Aquileiae*.] [Note: [Col. 0221D] l 6, 7, 10, 16, 18, *Crispino*. 8, *Crispiano*.] [Note: [Col. 0221D] m Sich.–Ri*. Code of Justinian: *Constantio*, as do 4, 10, 18, 21. But Be., supported by Go. and manuscript 6, with which most manuscripts agree, correctly restores *Constantino*. Several manuscripts have *Const.*; others, such as 8, 28, 36, 40, omit *et Const.*; many manuscripts have either *Caess.* or *Caess. Coss.* 21 and Sichard have *A.* for *Caess.* 4, Til.–Ri*, *Caes.* Moreover, Go. and Be. already observed that *II* should be added to each consul.]

**INTERPRETATION.** Malefactors, enchanters, those who send storms, or those who disturb human minds by invocation of demons, shall be punished by every kind of penalty. [Note: [Col. 0221D] n Thus nearly all manuscripts. Editions: “by every kind of punishment.”]

## On Customs Duties and Forfeitures

[Note: [Col. 0221D] o The heading is faint in manuscript 1; therefore P. Pu. enclosed it in brackets. But since the first law supplied by manuscript 1 is the same as the law that has hitherto been the sole law under this title, there can be no doubt that the remaining laws also belong here.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Junius Rufus, Consular Governor of Aemilia. [Note: [Col. 0221D] p 25, *Juvianum*. 28, 40, Sichard in the margin, *Julium*. 10, 34, *Juvium*. 33, *Juvinum*. 20 has *Jovinum* above the line. 8 omits “to J. R.”; the Code of Justinian, *Junium*.] [Note: [Col. 0221D] q Thus manuscript 1. 15, 28, 34, 40, 43, the Angers manuscript cited by Go., [Col. 0222B] the Code of Justinian, Sichard in the margin, P. Pu., W.: *Rufum*. The rest, *Rufinum*. Several manuscripts omit *Rufum*.] [Note: [Col. 0222B] a 9, 15—which has *consulem*—19, 44, *Italiae*. 39, 43, and the Angers manuscript cited by Go. add “and Liguria,” approved by Go. in his commentary on this title. 27 adds *et legat aliae* in place of *Italiae*, and 32 *edejure*. 28, 29, 33, 34, 36, 40 omit *Aemiliae*, as do 37, 42, and the Code of Justinian, which has *Cons. Aem.* In manuscript 18 these words are wrongly joined to the text as follows: *Consolare memilitiae penes*. Many manuscripts have *emelie*.]

The customs duties must remain with the person who has been highest in the bidding, provided that the lease is concluded for no less than three years and that the prescribed period for collecting the duties is interrupted in no way. [Note: [Col. 0222B] b 1, 8, *Poenis*. 16, *Poene*.] [Note: [Col. 0222B] c 9, *litigatione*.] [Note: [Col. 0222B] d 17, *aut*. Then 18 omits *quam*.] [Note: [Col. 0222B] e 14, *concludetur*.] [Note: [Col. 0222B] f 20, *exigendi*. 10, 18, *praestitum cum peractio*. 8, *quo cum peracto*. 6, 7, 14, 17, *cum peracto*.]

Once that period has elapsed, the rights of bidding and of contracting must be renewed, and placed in like manner with others; and the person who is found to have exacted from provincials anything more than has been fixed shall be subjected to capital sentence. [Note: [Col. 0222B] g Thus 1, 20, P. Pu., W., and the Code of Justinian, although 1 has *conductionumque*. The rest have *conductionemque*. Similarly, 9, 12, *conductio neque*. Moreover, 12, *creari*. 20, *segregari*, corrected to *recreari*. 9, *licitationo jura*.] [Note: [Col. 0222C] h 1, 9, 10, 15, 18, Code of Justinian, P. Pu., W., *ac*; several manuscripts, including 1, *hac*. 19, 20, *ad hanc*; the rest, *et hanc*, which must refer to *conductionemque*, except 6–8, 21, where *et* is absent, and Go., who omits *ac … subjugando*.] [Note: [Col. 0222C] i Most manuscripts, *conlocare*. 20, *alios c.* The following material is absent from the Code of Justinian.] [Note: [Col. 0222C] j Thus 1, 9, 12, 14, 15, Be. from Til. and conjecturally Go., P. Pu., W.; 16, *subjugantium*. The rest, *subjugandum*. Be. says it should be *sententiae*, rightly. See following chapter. Then 6, 7, *provinciales*.]

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, during the second consulships of Crispus and Constantine (321). [Note: [Col. 0222C] k Nearly all manuscripts—except 27–29, 36, 40, 43, 44—P. Pu., and W. omit the number X; it was added here in the editions and in the Code of Justinian. What follows varies greatly in the manuscripts. Some omit *Const. II*; others, such as Sich.–Lugd., P. Pu., and the Code of Justinian, have only the number after *Const.*; others put both numbers after the consuls’ names. Again, some manuscripts—24, 28, 29, 42, 44, Sichard, Cuj. 1–Lugd., and the Code of Justinian—add *Caes.* after *Cr.*; 30, 33, 38 instead have “Crispus, most illustrious,” though 38 has *clar. III*. Others, including 1, 24, 28, and Be. in his note, P. Pu., have the same abbreviation after *Const.*, or add *a*, as do 30, 32–34. Finally, some manuscripts read *Constantio* and omit it in the editions of Sichard, Cuj. 1–Ri.*, and before *Const.*]

**INTERPRETATION.** Customs duties are those payments rendered to the treasury for the conveyance of goods by vehicles: that is, goods are transported either by ships in coastal places or by vehicles through different regions. The law directs that the contract for this activity shall be held by capable persons for three years, and that thereafter this levy shall continually be entrusted anew to others who have offered the larger sum of payment. [Note: [Col. 0222D] l Go. notes that, contrary to necessity, he reads *vehiculorum* for *vehiculorum*, and shortly afterwards *deportantur*.] [Note: [Col. 0222D] m 20, *in littore his*, but *in littoreis* above the line. 21, in the margin, *littoris*.] [Note: [Col. 0222D] n 6–8, 10, 18, and others: *locis conductoribus*. 20, *loc. navibus conductoribus*.] [Note: [Col. 0222D] o 6–8, 10, 18–20, and other manuscripts, Sichard, Cuj. 1–Lugd., *extraneas*.] [Note: [Col. 0222D] p Many manuscripts and Sichard, *praecepit*.] [Note: [Col. 0222D] q 6, 7, 9, 20, 42, 44, *obtulerit*, though 42 corrects it to *obtulerint*.]

If, from this contract or levy, anyone attempts to exact more than has been prescribed, so that he begins to burden either a merchant or a provincial under this exaction, he shall know that he is liable to condemnation to capital punishment. [Note: [Col. 0223B] a 6–8, 21, and many other manuscripts, *si qui*. 20, *is qui*. 42, *si plus*.] [Note: [Col. 0223B] b Thus with manuscripts 6, 7, 20, 21 and most manuscripts; editions, *aut merc. aut*.] [Note: [Col. 0223B] c 6–8, 21 omit *coeperit*, but manuscript 21 adds *voluerint*. 20, *gravaverit peric.* 42 and Sichard, *gravare voluerit*.] [Note: [Col. 0223B] d Many manuscripts have *noverint esse damnandos*. Sichard: “he shall know that he will undergo the danger of capital punishment,” but in the margin, *damnandum*. 20, *captis*.]

[Note: [Col. 0223C] j The Code of Justinian adds *enim* [for], which Be. thinks seems to have fallen out here; but 4, 15, 50, 51 omit *enim*.]

## On Pardons for Crimes

Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People. Let everyone, when dying, have the right to leave to the most holy and venerable Catholic council whatever of his property he has wished. Let final declarations not be void. Nothing is owed to human beings more than that, after they can no longer will anything else, the expression of their last will should be free, and their decision—which cannot return again—unrestricted. [Note: [Col. 0223B] e Code of Justinian: “Emperor Constantine.”] [Note: [Col. 0223B] f Code of Justinian, *Catholico*. 51, *sanctissimae*. *Catholicae*, namely of the faith, religion, or church. See Theodosian Code XVI, 5, 52, note n.] [Note: [Col. 0223C] g 50, 51, *venerabilisque concilii*. 15: “Let everyone dying have the right [to leave] to the holy Catholic Church and venerable council whatever property he has wished,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0223C] h Code of Justinian, *relinquere*, and Go.: “perhaps also *optabit* [he will wish].”] [Note: [Col. 0223C] i 15: “Let final judgments not be void,” not wrongly. Ri. Ri*: *concilio decens bonorum quod optavit relinquere. Non ede sint cassa judicia*, corruptly.] [Note: [Col. 0223C] k Thus 15, 50, 51, and Code of Justinian; 4 and editions, *debetur*, which is not false.] [Note: [Col. 0223C] l 15, 50, 51: *quam suprema voluntas*, omitting *ut*.] [Note: [Col. 0223C] m 15, *postquam jam aliud*.] [Note: [Col. 0223C] n 15, 50, *libens*. Code of Justinian, *licitum*.]

Published on the fifth day before the Nones of July, at Rome, during the second consulships of Crispus and Constantine Caesars (321). [Note: [Col. 0223C] o 15, 50 omit *Caess.* Til.–Ri*. Lab., *Caess.*; but 4, Be., and Code of Justinian, *Caess.* 51: *pp. a. V. non.*]

## On Holidays

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Elpidius. [Note: [Col. 0223C] q Thus most manuscripts; others, *Hilpidio*, *Helidio*, *Adilpidio*, [Col. 0223D] *Helydio*. 38, *Hlpidio ag. cons.* 29 omits *Elpidio*. Sichard, *Helvidio*. The rest, *Helpidio*. But see Go. in the *Prosopography*. The title is omitted. In chapter 6 of the Code of Justinian, *On Private Buildings* (VIII, 10), addressed to the same Elpidius and issued in the same year on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, he is called acting deputy of the Praetorian Prefect. For this reason I do not think he was governor of Sardinia, as Go. seems to have believed because this law is said to have been published at Caralis, a town of Sardinia.]

Just as it seemed most unworthy that the day of the sun, celebrated by its own veneration, should be occupied by contentious disputes and nocturnal conflicts of factions, so it is welcome and pleasing that on that day matters especially suited to vows should be completed. [Note: [Col. 0223D] r 20, 21, Sichard: *ut diem*, but manuscript 20 has *ut* written above the line.] [Note: [Col. 0223D] s 15, “which we call the Lord’s Day.” See Selden, *De iure naturali et gentium iuxta disciplinam Ebraeorum*, III, 19, and Go., note d on this passage.] [Note: [Col. 0223D] t Thus Be. and W. from Go.’s conjecture and manuscripts 6, according to Ri., 8, 10, 15–19, R.; 6, 7, 14, *venerationem sui*. 9, *venerationi suae*. 20, 21, Sich.–Ri*., *venerationis suae*.] [Note: [Col. 0223D] u 20, 21, Sichard, *celebrent*.] [Note: [Col. 0223D] v 20, 21, *jurg. innoxiis*; Sichard, *in noxiis*. Then Sichard, *occupati*.] [Note: [Col. 0224B] a Be., *gradum*, corruptly.] [Note: [Col. 0224B] b Editions before Be., except Aur. and Lugd., *jocundum*, as do most manuscripts. Several manuscripts also have *et iuc.*] [Note: [Col. 0224B] c On this word see Go., note i on this passage. 19, *vota impleri* [vows to be fulfilled].]

Therefore all shall have leave on the feast day to emancipate and manumit, and official instruments concerning these matters shall not be prohibited.
