[Note: [Col. 0224B] d In these words begins the final part of chapter 8 of the Code of Justinian and of the cited chapter 2 of the *Collectio Ans. ded.*: “In these matters, however, also [in cases] of emancipation.”] [Note: [Col. 0224B] e 8, *ac manumittendi*.] [Note: [Col. 0224B] f 15, *manumitt. cuncti d. f.* Code of Justinian and *Collectio Ans. ded.* omit *die festo*.] [Note: [Col. 0224B] g 20, 21 omit *et*; 16 has *et* above *his*. Code of Justinian and *Collectio Ans. ded.* omit *rebus*.] [Note: [Col. 0224C] h 30, 24, Sichard, Cuj. 1, Aur., Lugd., Go., Ri., Ri*., Lab., *actus*, which Go. defends in his commentary. Cuj. 2, 2*, *actu*.] [Note: [Col. 0224C] i 20, 21, Sichard, *prohibeatur*.]

Published on the fifth day before the Nones of July, at Caralis, during the second consulships of Crispus and Constantine (321). [Note: [Col. 0224C] j 10, *publio*. 19, 31, 26, 28, 40, Sichard, and the *Annales Regii* cited by Go., *Dat.*; “published” for *PP.* 20, *ppo*.] [Note: [Col. 0224C] k Several manuscripts omit V and subsequently *Non.* 18, IV. 38, VI.] [Note: [Col. 0224C] l 8, *id.* 26, *kal.*] [Note: [Col. 0224C] m Thus nearly all manuscripts; Sichard in the margin, Til. and Cuj. 1 in the margin, Aur., Lugd., where *Julii calis* occurs for *Julii Caralis*. 20, 21, Sichard, Cuj. 1–W., June, or *Junii*.] [Note: [Col. 0224C] n 8 and Til. omit *Caralis*. 21, Be., *Carali*.] [Note: [Col. 0224C] o Several manuscripts, *Crispoli*, omit II, or have *Crispoli II*. 38, *Pristo Ulpiano*. 20, *Crispio*.] [Note: [Col. 0224C] p 10, 15, 18, 38, *Constantio*.] [Note: [Col. 0224C] q Many manuscripts omit II or *Coss.* 14, 24, 38, *II CC. Coss.* 19, *II ces. css.* 31, 35, III. 38, *VC. Coss.* In the Code of Justinian the subscription is entirely different.]

**INTERPRETATION.** Although we have ordered that all lawsuits and claims shall cease on the holy Lord’s Day, we nevertheless do not prohibit emancipation and manumission; and we permit official instruments concerning these matters to be drawn up under the same arrangement. [Note: [Col. 0224C] r 6–8, 20, 42–44, and many other manuscripts, Cuj. 2, 2*, “on the holy day of the Lord.” Then 6, according to Ri., *iussimus*.]

## On Customs Duties and Forfeitures

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Menander. [Note: [Col. 0224C] s *Menandrum*, whose rank is omitted here and in the following constitution, also in the Code of Justinian. Go. thinks he was Praetorian Prefect of Italy, but P. [thinks him] Count of Africa; W. incorrectly.] All provincials, in respect of things which they carry in for their own use or for the fisc, or carry back for the purpose of cultivating land, shall pay no customs duties to stationarii [customs-station officers]. But things carried outside the aforesaid purposes, or for trade, we subject to the customary payment. [Note: [Col. 0224D] t 1, *provincialis*. W., following P., observes that the words “all provincials” are nominatives absolute. I do not wish to recognize nominatives absolute in the law, but rather understand the same construction of *exigere* [to exact] as in Gellius, *Attic Nights* XV, 14: *exigor portorium*, that is, “customs duty is exacted from me.” Otherwise the reading of the Code of Justinian cannot be defended either.] [Note: [Col. 0224D] u Pu., *iuris*.] [Note: [Col. 0224D] v Thus P., probably W., and Pu. 1: *nulla vectigal stationariis*, omitting *a*. Code of Justinian: *nullum vectigal a stationariis exigantur*.] [Note: [Col. 0224D] x 1, *praedictis*.] [Note: [Col. 0224D] y The Code of Justinian adds *vel pensitationi* [or assessment], followed by material transferred from chapter 3 of this title in the Code of Justinian into a fifth chapter compounded from both Theodosian constitutions. The subscription is absent from the Code of Justinian.]

Given on the third day before the Ides of July, during the second consulships of Crispus and Constantine (321).

## On Customs Duties and Forfeitures

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Menander.

We do not permit customs duty to be exacted from country people carrying back things necessary for their own use or the cultivation of land; the penalty of death is proposed for stationarii, urban soldiers, and soldiers of the Third Augustan Legion, whose avarice is shown to attempt this. But for other things which they purchase for gain and intend to sell, they must acknowledge the customary customs duty. [Note: [Col. 0225B] a 1, *rusticanousibus*. P. Pu., *Rusticani*, which W., because of the following *exigi non sinimus*, rejects; he correctly emends to *Rusticanos*.] [Note: [Col. 0225B] b From this has been taken the clause in the cited law 5 of the Code of Justinian: “with capital punishment proposed for stationarii, urban soldiers, and the other persons whose avarice is shown to attempt this”; but, according to W., awkwardly, since mention of those subject to customs duties immediately precedes.] [Note: [Col. 0225C] c P. notes on this word: “In fact the first letter of the word is *e*, but it seems to hang from an *o*, and therefore I supplied *oportet*.”]

Given on the Kalends of August, during the second consulships of Crispus and Constantine (321).

## On Physicians and Teachers

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Volusianus . . . [Note: [Col. 0225C] e His rank is absent both here and in the Code of Justinian. Go. believes that Volusianus was indeed Praetorian Prefect in this year, but does not determine where he served. Be. says that perhaps *Pf. P.* should be added. The same scholar had previously written *Rein.* in the margin. Nothing appears in 4, Til., Cuj. 2*, Be., or the Code of Justinian to indicate a lacuna; Go.–Ri*. mark it with four dots. The Montpellier Code adds: “Book XIII, Laws.” It likewise adds immediately afterwards: “Physicians and grammarians.”]

We direct that physicians, grammarians, and other teachers of letters shall be exempt, together with the property which they possess in their own municipalities; and [that they] discharge public offices; we also prohibit their being summoned into court or suffering injury, so that anyone who harasses them shall pay one hundred thousand nummi into the treasury, the sum to be exacted by magistrates or quinquennales, lest they themselves bear this penalty. [Note: [Col. 0225C] f Thus also the Montpellier manuscript. In manuscript 4 it seems formerly to have read *fulgi*; a later hand substituted *n* for *l*. Til.–Lugd.: *praecipimus: et honoribus fungi, in ius.* Cuj. 2–Ri*.: *praecipimus: et honoribus fungi: in* (Go.: *in*) *ius*. Be.: *praecipimus; et honoribus fungi, in ius.* Be. remarks: “And the words *et h. f.* do not seem to be joined with *praecipimus*, to be governed by the verb *prohibemus*, because of what occurs at the end of the law, unless someone prefers to suppose that *honores* is used in a different sense, or that the preceding words were wrongly inserted by a copyist.” Correctly; for *honor* is a municipal magistracy carrying a rank of dignity, such as a duumvirate or aedileship, which the legislator wishes physicians and the like to undertake only voluntarily. Add that these words cannot be separated from what follows because of the word *etiam* [also], which immediately follows—unless perhaps in the reading *fulgi* there lies *fulgere* [to shine]. Then one should write: *praecipimus et honoribus*—that is, distinction—*fulgere. In ius*, etc. In the Montpellier manuscript these words are indeed joined with what precedes; nevertheless, since the following material down to *retinendo* is absent, no argument can be drawn from it.] [Note: [Col. 0225D] g Fol. 299b of manuscript 4. Til., *exact’*. Baronius conjectures *exactoris*. Til.–Cuj. 2*, Be.: *inferat a magistratibus, vel q. e.* Go.–Ri*.: *inferat, a Magistratibus, vel Q. e.*]

§ 1. If a slave injures them, he must be beaten with whips by his master in the presence of the person whom he injured; or, if the master consented, he shall pay twenty thousand nummi to the fisc, the slave being retained as a pledge until this sum is paid.

§ 2. We further direct that their fees and salaries be paid.

§ 3. Since [the text is materially uncertain] parents, masters, or guardians ought not to possess the most burdensome dignities, we permit them to undertake public offices if willing; we do not compel them if unwilling. [Note: [Col. 0225D] h A desperate passage. Be. notes: “Gfr. wishes *graves ins.* in I know not what sense. I myself think there is no room even for conjectures, since they are wholly without a sound basis. I once conjectured: *praecip., quo iam graviss. d. ut p. v. domini deesse non debeant. Et ut tut.*, etc.” Neither conjecture repairs the passage, although Go. also conjectures *Quinetiam, quoniam autem*, and *quoniam*. It seems to me that one or two lines are missing, unless all this material down to *debent* is to be regarded as a gloss, since neither the Code of Justinian nor the Montpellier manuscript indicates that anything of this kind occurred in this chapter. This deserves notice, although much is omitted in the Montpellier manuscript. In the Code of Justinian the passage has been altered as follows: “We direct that physicians, and especially archiatri [chief physicians], or former archiatri, grammarians, other teachers of letters, and teachers of law”—the latter disapproved by Cujas at the cited passage, p. 315, and by Go.; see chapter 5 of this title—“together with their wives and children, and also with the property which they possess” (from chapters 1 and 2 of this title), “shall be exempt from every function and from all civic and public burdens; and that they shall neither receive guests in the provinces nor perform any public service” (from chapter 1 of this title), “nor be brought to judgment, removed, produced, or suffer injury, so that anyone who harasses them shall be punished at the judge’s discretion. We order their fees and salaries also to be paid” (from chapter 3 of this title), “so that they may more easily instruct many persons in the liberal studies and the arts mentioned.” In the Montpellier manuscript §2 of this chapter reads: “We direct that their fees and salaries also be paid; we permit them, if willing, to perform public offices; we do not compel the unwilling,” and the subscription is absent.]

Published on the Kalends of August at Sirmium, during the consulships of Crispus and Constantine, the two Caesars (321). [Note: [Col. 0226C] a Go. prefers *Dat.* [given], but the Code of Justinian too has *PP.* [published].] [Note: [Col. 0226C] b Be. and Code of Justinian, *Sirmii*.] [Note: [Col. 0226C] c Thus also the Code of Justinian; Ri. emends: “Crispus Caesar II and Constantine Caesar II,” and Be.: “Constantine II Caesar, consuls.”] [Note: [Col. 0226C] d 4, Til.–Lugd., *C. Coss.* Cuj. 2–Ri*., *Caess. Coss.*, though Rein. emends *Caesaribus* and adds the note “322.” Be., *Caess. Coss.* Code of Justinian, *CC. Conss.*]

## Division of the Family Estate

[Note: [Col. 0226C] e Manuscripts have either *De Familia Herciscunda*, as in the indexes of the editions of Sichard and Cuj. 1–Ri*., or *Erciscunda*, as in editions before Be., except Til.; or *De Familia Erciscunde*, as in 20, 24, 25, 39, 42—in the index—43, 44; or *De Familiae Erciscunde* or *Herciscundae*, as in 5–7, 9, 16, 17, 42, Til. *Familiae Erciscundae*. Be., W., and the Code of Justinian: *Familiae Herciscundae*.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Verinus. [Note: [Col. 0226D] f See the title “On Those Who Obtain Relief from Age,” II, 17, note s.]

When property is to be divided, there can be no doubt that consent must be given by one’s heirs without any controversy. But with respect to documents of this kind, in which the intention of deceased persons is found to have been such that it may be understood that only a will was contemplated: even if the law seems to oppose it, such writings also ought to be valid only among the decedent’s own heirs, just as simply commenced writings are valid, although no supports of formal solemnity defend them, being sustained solely by the roots of intention. [Note: [Col. 0226D] g Many manuscripts, *dividundae*. 9, *divident haeres*.] [Note: [Col. 0226D] h 15 omits *suis*. 6, *ac h. s.*, by error. W. requires *a suis her.* Bijdr. conjectures *haeredibus tiis*, that is, *testamentis*.] [Note: [Col. 0226D] i 19, 20, Sichard, *concessum*.] [Note: [Col. 0226D] j Most manuscripts and Sichard, Til., *exspectat*, a common spelling in old manuscripts for *spectat*.] [Note: [Col. 0226D] k All manuscripts except 9 and 20 have *fuisse mens inven.*] [Note: [Col. 0226D] l 8 omits *ut … intelligatur*. 20, *intelligetur*.] [Note: [Col. 0226D] m Sichard and Til., *inscriptiones, inter*. Cuj. 1, Aur., Lugd., *inscriptio, inter*.] [Note: [Col. 0226D] n 20, *quos*.] [Note: [Col. 0227B] a 20 adds *vel*.] [Note: [Col. 0227B] b 6, 7, 14, 16, 19, 20, *nexae*. 10, 18: “no solemnities … harm.” 15, *nixas*.] [Note: [Col. 0227B] c 8, *voluntas*.]

For although, having been begun under the designation of a will, they appear to have lapsed because they have not been completed and cannot in any way be called otherwise, nevertheless final dispositions, presenting a plausible image of law, ought more justly to call forth in themselves the favourable inclination of the laws. [Note: [Col. 0227B] d 20, *cepti*.] [Note: [Col. 0227B] e Most manuscripts, *dispositionis*.] [Note: [Col. 0227B] f 6, 7, *coloratum i. imagine*. 14, *coloratu i. imagine*.] [Note: [Col. 0227B] g 15, *praeferentes*.] [Note: [Col. 0227C] h 20, *legem vel procl.*] [Note: [Col. 0227C] i 6, 7, 14, 47, *debeat*. Then 15 omits *cum*.]

Accordingly, since the succession of a deceased person is conferred upon sons and grandsons as his own heirs by civil law or by the aid of the praetor, it is decided that the intention should be considered specifically and immediately followed when property is divided, even if the will is said to have been begun but not completed, or if the writing is said to be void through the ineffectiveness of its wording or through a defect in legal solemnity. No more shall be retained than is shown to have been written for each individual person, so that the memory of the deceased parent may not be violated and occasions for lawsuits may be removed. [Note: [Col. 0227C] j 6, 7, 14, *civilis*. 10, 18, *civiles*.] [Note: [Col. 0227C] k 19, 20, *cum*. 15, *suis ut her.*] [Note: [Col. 0227C] l 6–8, 14, 16, 17: *defunctis accessio deferretur* or *deferetur*. 9, *defertur*. 20, *defunctis*. 10, 18, *deferretur*.] [Note: [Col. 0227C] m Thus 6–10, 14, 16–19, Til., or *ceptum*, which is the same. Editions, *inceptum*. 20, *ac si inceptum*.] [Note: [Col. 0227C] n 15, *completum e. t. memoratur*.] [Note: [Col. 0227C] o In the margin of Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2*, perhaps “or through verbal subtlety,” which I would have received had the manuscripts confirmed it. Go. conjectures “through subtlety or futility.”] [Note: [Col. 0227C] p Several manuscripts, *inani*. 20, *considerare*.] [Note: [Col. 0227C] q Thus 6–8, 17, approved by Go. 9, 10, 14–16, 20, *detegitur*, which comes to the same thing. Editions, *detegatur*.] [Note: [Col. 0227C] r 9, *violenter p.* 10, 20, *violent. parentes*. Sichard, *violentur parentes*.] [Note: [Col. 0227C] s 10, 18, *derimentur*. 19, *derimatur*.]

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, during the second consulships of Crispus and Constantine (321). [Note: [Col. 0227D] t 9, 29, 38, 42, VI. 17, 19, 24, and in the margin of Sich.–Cuj. 2*, III.] [Note: [Col. 0227D] u 28, 36, 40, December. 33, February.] [Note: [Col. 0227D] v Several manuscripts, *Crisponi*. 38, *Crispoli*; several omit II.] [Note: [Col. 0227D] x 8, 15, 29, *Constantio*. Many manuscripts and Sichard, Til. omit II, for which others have I. 6, 7, *Const. C.* in place of *C. II. Coss.* 19, “during the second consulships of the most illustrious.” See also the title “On Those Who Obtain Relief from Age,” II, 17, note s.]

## On Those Who Have Suffered Sentence, Been Restored, and Their Children

[Note: [Col. 0227D] y 15, “On Those Restored from Exile.” 26, “Freedmen,” omitting “and Their [Children].” Other manuscripts omit *Restitutis* [restored], as do the Code of Justinian and *Liberis eorum* [their children]. 20: “On those who have suffered sentence and been prestituted” [an evidently corrupt reading].]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Prefect of the City. [Note: 26: “to Maximinianus, praetorian prefect.” 15: “Augustus to Maximus.” Cujacius 2, 2*, Ri., Ri*: “praetorian prefect”; improperly Go. and Ri. Go.: “prefect of the people.” Many manuscripts: “praetorian prefect,” without “most eminent.” See *C. Th.* I.4.1, note e.]

In the question of a will which the son of a deportee had made while his father was returning, we decree—setting aside the criticisms of Ulpian and Paul upon Papinian—that Papinian’s opinion shall stand: namely, that the son shall be under the authority of his father, whose rank and property have been restored. [Note: 20: “the deported [man].” Sichard: “while he was deported.” 6–8, 12, 14, 16: “while he was returning.” 20: “while he remained [away].” Gothofredus conjectures “while remaining,” i.e. while situated or delayed in deportation. Shortly afterward, 20: “had made.”]

[Col. 0228A] [Note: 15: “setting aside the criticisms of Paul and Ulpian upon Papinian.” Many manuscripts read “Papian,” both here and in the interpretation. Manuscript 4: “Papinian,” but with *r* added above the *n* in yellow ink: “Papirian.” 13: “Ulpian’s.” See *C. Th.* I.4.3, *On the Responses of Jurists*.] [Note: 20: “opinion.”] [Note: 6–8, 14, 16: “whose.”]

§ 1. Yet this shall be so arranged that the acts performed by the son, whose lawful age had made his decisions valid, shall remain valid when the son returns to paternal authority; lest their rescission bring about the utterly absurd result that, at the same time, someone should have been under neither his father’s authority nor his own. [Note: 10, 18 add “have been.”] [Note: 6–8, 12, 14, 16: “whose trustworthiness.” Vatican Fragments §69.] [Note: 10, 18: “shall have made valid.” 12: corrupt reading.] [Note: 6–8, 14 omit “shall remain valid”; 16 has it.] [Note: 4, 6–10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 21: “into paternal authority”; 20: “of the father.” Manuscript 4 originally read “returning,” corrected in red ink.] [Note: Correctly so Be., supported by Go., from Sichard and the Code of Justinian; 4, 6–8, 10, 12–16, 18, 20, 21, Til.–Ri*: “nor.” Shortly afterward 9: corrupt; 20: “withdrawal.”] [Note: 15: “that no one was under his own authority or his father’s.” Some manuscripts: “authority.”]

§ 2. For minors are legally forbidden to transact anything. [Note: In manuscripts 6–8, 10, 12, 14–16, 18, “by law” is omitted.] [Note: Leaf 71b of manuscript 4.] If, when the father had been condemned, a guardian was appointed for them, that guardian must withdraw from his office when the person returns who ought not merely to return in name, but also to furnish his children with his own office, uncorrupted by any depravity, so as to protect and increase their property. [Note: Code of Justinian: “withdraw from his own office.”] [Note: In the editions, the words “father … whom” were printed twice in the Aur. Lugd. edition. In manuscript 14, *is* is absent after *datus*; in manuscript 8, *ut* is absent after *est*.] [Note: 20 has “to restore” written above the line.] [Note: At “uncorrupted by any depravity” begins folio XI of manuscript I, section XXXV of the whole Turin palimpsest, discovered by the distinguished Vesmius; it continues as far as the words “sleep within the time,” in constitution 4, *On Those Who Take Refuge in Churches* (IX.45).] [Note: 9, 20: “that they may protect and increase.”]

For if he abuses paternal authority for the license of wasting and squandering the patrimony, then, like a madman, an insane person, or likewise a spendthrift—a slave to all lusts and vices—the children’s money is not to be entrusted to him; he is to be removed from administration, he is not to cease to be guardian, and he himself is to make good from his own losses every loss suffered by the minor. [Note: 6–8, 12, 14, 16: “squandering”; 9: “offending.” In 20, *ad* before “wasting” is absent.] [Note: Go. and manuscript I omit “so that” before “madman.” 6, 7: “abuses.” Code of Justinian: “may abuse.”] [Note: 20: “abusing the license … insane, that is” (the latter written above the line), “spendthrift.” Code of Justinian: “and likewise a spendthrift.” Shortly afterward manuscript I: “lusts.”] [Col. 0228B] [Note: 6, 7: “and vices.” Sichard: “a slave to all vices.”] [Note: *est* is absent in manuscript 16. 20: “is not to be entrusted to the slave.”] [Note: Sichard: “common money.”] [Note: Be., from Sichard. The Code of Justinian adds *quin*, absent from Til.–Ri* and manuscripts I, 4, 6–10, 13–16, 18. 20: “from which”; 21: “which.” Sichard, in the margin: “who.”] [Note: 6, 7 read “to” for “from,” a reading excepted in manuscript 16. 8: “from administration.” 20: “from administration, as fugitive.”] [Note: 13: “and flee.” 15 omits “nor.” This sentence does not connect well.] [Note: 4: “and all,” corrected in red. Elsewhere this passage is corruptly written in the manuscripts: 6, “nor let the guardian’s seats be ignored, all that”; 7, “nor let the guardian designate himself, all that”; 8, “nor let the guardian, but designate, all that”; 12, “of the guardian, but designated.” A little below, 20: “make good.”]

But the sentence of deportation shall not diminish the father by any prejudice. [Note: 6, 7, 10, 16, 18: “the opinion”; shortly afterward 6, 7, 12: “father”; 9, 20: “by the father,” though 20 has “obey” above the line. 18: “of the father.”] If his established integrity has restored him to his children both by nature and by duty, the helm of affairs must be entrusted to him whose custody has been provided, following the model of public law. [Note: 6–8, 12, 16: “diminished, in what way.” 10, 18: “diminished, to what extent.” 14: corrupt.] [Note: 6–8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 omit “as by nature.” 15: “of nature,” as in the Code of Justinian, improperly Go.] [Note: 15, 16: “both by duty and to his children.” 16: “had restored.”] [Note: 14 omits “to him.”] [Note: 6: “of this man, for correction.” 12: “of this kind, for correction.” Also 8, 15, 16: “for correction.”] Unless this is granted to good fathers, their return will be more grievous than their departure. [Note: 15: “custody was provided—return will be more fruitful.” 20: “return.” Code of Justinian: “the return to the children will be grievous.”]

§ 3. Therefore indulgence shall avail for restoration only so far as the sentence availed for correction. [Note: 12, 16, 20: “reproof.” Leaf 72a of manuscript 4.] [Note: 4: “wished,” corrected by a later hand. 16: “wished also.” I: “and which”; 21: “as which.”] And just as the very name of deportation is, in itself, the stripping away of all things, so the return of indulgence is the recovery, under one designation, of all property and rank that have been lost. [Note: Cujacius 2–Ri*: “itself,” incorrectly and improperly Go.; I, 4, Br. Al. manuscripts, Sichard–Lugd., Be.: “the very.”] [Note: 6, 12, 16 omit “name.” 7: “the name of all things.” 10, 18: “of all things.”] [Note: 10, 18 omit “stripping … of all.” 20: “despoiling.”] [Note: Thus Be., from Go.’s correction in the edition from manuscript 6. So also 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18; the rest, including I and 4, have “of indulgence,” which can be tolerated. Similarly, “the return of favor” is said. Code of Justinian: “restoration by indulgence.” Sichard in the margin: “restoration.”] [Note: 6, 7: “rank.” 15 adds “and.” 29: “the single designation of rank.”] [Note: 6–8, 12: corrupt forms of “lost”; 14 likewise; 20: “about to lose.”]

And let children seek emancipation from their fathers by dutiful services, so that they may possess liberty as evidence not of condemnation but of paternal kindness. [Note: “Not” is absent in Cujacius 2, 2*. Shortly afterward manuscript I: “kindness.”]

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October at Sirmium, in the second consulship of Crispus and the second consulship of Constantine Caesars (321). [Note: 9, 12–15, 21, 24, 25, 38, 42, 43, Sichard, Cujacius 2, 2*, Go. in the Chronicle: seventeenth. 17, 28, 40, Sichard in the margin: sixth; this differs slightly from the date of constitution 1, *On the Responses of Jurists* (I.4). 20, 39: seventh. In manuscript I “eighteenth” has been erased, with a marginal mark.] [Col. 0229B] [Note: Some manuscripts: “Sermium,” “Sermii.” Sichard: “Syrmium.” 4, Til.–Lugd.: “Sirmi.” Be., Code of Justinian: “Sirmii.” 8 omits Sirmium.] [Note: Some manuscripts read variants of Crispus; manuscript I omits “second.”] [Note: Very many manuscripts omit “second,” as does Sichard, or “Caesars,” as does I, or both. 17, 28, 36, 40: corrupt consular subscriptions. Sichard: “Constantine, Caesars, consuls.” 21: “Constantine Augustus, twice consul.” 20: “Augustus” for “Caesars.”]

**INTERPRETATION**

If a father sent into exile has left his son at an age of majority, whatever the son has done concerning his own property shall, in accordance with the opinion of Papinian, remain settled and valid; nor is the father, after his return, permitted to proceed against either his son’s will or his settlement. [Note: Many manuscripts: “exile … at greater age … and whatever.”] [Note: 21: “did concerning his own [property],” corrected. Shortly afterward 6: “settled, valid.”] [Note: 7: “nor”; 9, 44: “or against a will.” 42 omits “or.”] [Col. 0230A] [Note: 20: “having returned.”]

Certainly, when the father returns, if he finds his son alive, he shall receive the son back into his own legal authority and paternal power. [Note: 6–9, 20, and other manuscripts omit “if.”] [Note: In manuscript 20 and in Sichard, “the son” is absent. Aur. Lugd.: “into his own paternal authority.”] [Note: 20, 42, 44: “shall receive.” 7, 8: “receives.” Sichard: “he shall receive him into his own paternal authority, and if indeed again concerning his own property, which [was done] in his absence.” 42 likewise: “which [was done] in his absence.”]

But whatever the son did concerning his own property while the father was absent, the father upon returning shall not be able to revoke. Whatever children under age have done shall be wholly invalid. Yet if, on account either of their age or their father’s absence, they have received guardians or curators, the returning father shall receive his children back, after the curators or guardians have been removed, together with all their property; but on this condition: that he administer and govern the children’s property in such a manner that they suffer not merely no loss, but that through the father’s diligence the children’s estate and resources may increase. [Note: 6–10, 18–20, 21, 42, 44: “or on account of the father’s absence,” and omit “or”; 20: “or.” Sichard: “of guardians or curators.”] [Note: 21: “son.” Sichard: “to the children.” 20: “when the father returns, the son [is] received back from guardians or curators.”] [Note: 42: “shall receive.” 20: “shall be received.”] [Note: 6–8, 10, 18, 20, 21 omit “however.”] [Note: 20: “may suffer.” 7, 8 omit “not,” but “not” was restored by a second hand in manuscript 7.] [Note: 6–8, 21, 43: “or.”]

But if the father is proved to be either prodigal, negligent, destructive, or given to lust, and is found to waste and dissipate the children’s property impiously and madly, the children of such a father shall, as though he were dead, remain under a guardian or curator. [Note: 6, 7, 20, 21: “is proved.” 8 omits “shall be proved … dissipate.”] [Note: 6, 7, 9: “indecently.”] [Col. 0230B] [Note: 6–8, 20, 21, 42: “is found.” 42: “to tear apart, is found.” Shortly afterward some manuscripts have “such” and “parts.”] [Note: Aur. Lugd.: “shall remain.”]

For as it is equitable that a good and useful father should receive the management and administration of his children’s property, so it is inequitable that, to the children’s loss, a returning father should tear apart by insane ruin resources preserved by guardians or curators. [Note: 6–20, 18, and other manuscripts: “as it is good [that] an equitable and useful father …”; also 20, 21, 42, 44: “and useful.” Editions: “and useful.”] [Note: Some manuscripts: “to the loss.”] [Note: 6–8, 21: “preserved”; other manuscripts: “by curators,” omitting “or.” Sichard omits “or by curators.”]

**ON THE RESPONSES OF JURISTS** [Note: Some manuscripts: “jurists,” with variant spelling.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Prefect of the Praetorium. [Note: Themis has “Augustus—Praetorian Prefect.” Cl. states, p. 128, note 20, that inscriptions of the year 321 and the following year call Maximus now praetorian prefect, now prefect of the city; therefore Maximus perhaps held both prefectures. I think “Prefect of the City” should be read, as the manuscripts also have in the sole constitution of *C. Th.*, *On Persons Condemned* (IX.43), and this is confirmed by the ancient author *On the Prefect of the City* in Cuspinianus. Scribes very frequently confuse the abbreviations of the two offices, Praetorian Prefect and Prefect of the City; there are hundreds of examples of this error. Our scribe seems to have made such an error in constitution 5, *On the Division of Rescripts* (I.2), where he wrote *ppo* for *PF. V.*; further examples will be found below in constitutions 2, 4–6, and 12, *On the Office of the Prefect of the City* (I.6).]

Desiring to remove the perpetual disputes of jurists, we order the notes of Ulpian and Paul upon Papinian to be abolished; for, while pursuing the glory of their intellect, they chose not so much to correct him as to corrupt him. [Col. 0231A] [Note: 5: “Papian, pursuing—correct.”] [Note: Themis: “to be corrupted.”] [Note: 5: “we order.”]

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, at Sirmium, in the second consulship of Constantine and the second consulship of Crispus (321). [Note: Themis: “third.”] [Note: Adds “at Sirmium.”] [Note: Pu.: “Crispus.” 5: “October, and in the consulship of Constantine and Crispus, designated second consuls.” In other constitutions of this year: “Crispus II and Constantine.”]

**ON COUNTERFEIT COINAGE**

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Januarinus. [Note: Manuscripts I and 4: “Januarinus,” which I have adopted. Editions: “Januarius,” as in the Code of Justinian. His office is absent also from both laws of the Code of Justinian and from the Collection of Canons of Ansegisus. Go. rightly observes that in the preceding year he is called acting vicar of the prefecture in constitution 3, *On Famous Libels* (IX.34), but he is called Prefect of the City in constitution 1, *On Abolitions* (XIX.37), issued in 319. Be. conjectures “Praetorian Prefect.”]

Since certain mint-workers engage in counterfeit coinage through clandestine crimes, let all know that they are under an obligation to seek out persons of this sort, so that, once found, they may be handed over to the courts, immediately revealing under torture those aware of the deed, and thus be subjected to fitting punishments. [Note: Thus Be. from both passages in the Code of Justinian, and it did not displease Go.; I, 4, Til.–Ri*: “with counterfeit coinage.” Shortly afterward manuscript I: “practices,” corruptly.] [Note: Code of Justinian: “court.”] [Note: Folio 32b of manuscript 4. At the bottom of the page a letter marks the number of the gathering. Shortly afterward manuscript I: “worthy || … punishments.”]

§ 1. We also grant immunity to their accusers; its amount, since estates differ in value, shall be fixed by us in each case. [Col. 0231B] [Note: Go. prefers “we promise,” plausibly but incorrectly. For *permittimus* stands for *remittimus*: that is, “we bestow, donate, grant,” as Go. himself admits.] [Note: Code of Justinian: “estate,” but Go. considers our wording more elegant.] [Note: Code of Justinian: “is fixed,” improperly Go.]

We also grant Roman citizenship to slaves who report this matter, so that their masters may receive their value from the treasury. [Note: 1: “who reports this matter,” corruptly.] [Note: The Code of Justinian omits “We also grant slaves … from the treasury,” but this sentence has been incorporated into constitution 2 of the Code of Justinian, *For What Causes Slaves [May Be Freed]* (VII.13): “Slaves who publicly report mint-workers engaged in producing counterfeit money through clandestine crimes shall be granted Roman citizenship, so that their masters may receive their value from the treasury”; and the following subscription belongs to this constitution.]

§ 2. But if any soldier causes a person apprehended in such a matter to leave custody, he shall be punished capitally. [Note: Code of Justinian: “suspected,” but Go. defends our reading as legitimate. On the custody of apprehended persons, above IX.3.5.]

§ 3. A private person shall also be denied permission to appeal. But if a soldier or a person promoted in rank incurs a crime of this kind, a report concerning his name and rank shall be made to us. [Note: Code of Justinian adds “in rank.”] [Note: Go.: “incurs,” erroneously.] [Note: Code of Justinian: “be referred to the competent judges.”]

§ 4. [Note: The following provisions in the Code of Justinian have partly been altered and partly enlarged from constitution 4 under this title: “But a house or estate in which these acts have been committed, if the owner is nearby—whose carelessness or negligence must be punished—even if he is ignorant, shall be claimed by the treasury; unless the owner, previously ignorant, as the Collection of Canons of Ansegisus has it, reports the perpetrated crime as soon as he discovers it. For then his estate or house shall by no means be subject to the injury of proscription. But if he has been very far from that house or possession, he shall suffer no loss; the manager of the estate, slaves, residents, or tenant-farmers who rendered assistance for this purpose shall, together with the perpetrator, suffer capital punishment.” Then follow: “We believe widows … so that … may remain” (see constitution 4 under this title); “But minors … their age” (omitting “if, however,” etc., from constitution 4); “what he sees … have been nearby, since … the property of the ward … so that from the property … as much as was to be imposed upon the ward” (improperly Go. in the notes to constitution 4). The date follows, and then the subscription of constitution 2, *C. Th.*]

If the owner of an estate or house is proved to have known, he must be deported to an island, with all his property immediately confiscated. But if the crime was committed without his knowledge, he must lose the estate or house in which the crime was committed. [Col. 0232A] [Note: Manuscript I: “with all his property confiscated—the crime committed,” as below “that crime was committed.”]

The manager of the estate, slave, resident, or tenant-farmer who rendered this assistance shall be punished capitally together with the person who committed the act; the estate or house shall nevertheless be claimed for the resources of the treasury. [Note: Go., in the note: “in this,” “for this.” The Code of Justinian likewise has “for this.”]

§ 5. But if the owner, previously ignorant, reports the perpetrated crime as soon as he discovers it, his estate or house shall by no means be subject to the injury of proscription; rather, the capital penalty shall overtake the author and agent of the offense. [Note: Leaf 33a of manuscript 4. Shortly afterward manuscript I: “reports the perpetrated [crime].”] [Note: Ri*: “proscribition.” I: “injury.”]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, at Rome, in the second consulship of Crispus and the second consulship of Constantine Caesars (321). [Note: Go. gives “issued” in place of “given,” or “published.” Manuscript I: “Given … Crispus and Constantine, twice Caesars, consuls.” Collection of Canons of Ansegisus: “Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends, at Rome, in the consulships of Crispus and Constantius.”]

**ON JEWS**

Emperor Constantine Augustus to the decurions of Agrippina. [Note: 11: “the same [emperor] to those of Agrippina.” Cujacius 2, 2*: “Agrippinians.” Go. in the Chronicle: “Agrippinensians.”]

We grant to all municipal orders by a general law the authority to call Jews to the curia. [Col. 0232B] [Note: 4, Til.: “to be called,” which is grammatically correct.] Yet, that something may be preserved for them as a consolation for their former observance, we allow two or three to remain exempt by perpetual privilege from all nominations. [Note: Aur. Lugd.: “and.”] [Note: 11: “observances.”] [Note: 11: “we endure by privilege, none,” and Cujacius 2, 2*: “we endure by privilege, none,” etc., improperly Go., who punctuates: “we allow them to remain exempt; we do not allow any [to be occupied].” He says: “This passage must be investigated; hence some have believed it faulty, because they understood *perpeti* here in the sense of *pati*.” Everything in this passage is sound. Til.–Lugd.: “we allow [them] to remain exempt, none …”]

Given on the third day before the Ides of December, in the second consulship of Crispus and the second consulship of Constantine Caesars (321). [Note: Go. in the Chronology: fourth, but notes “elsewhere third.” Below, 11 omits “Caesars, consuls.”]

**ON DONATIONS**

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Petronius Probinus. I order that the property of a wife which had come to her by any succession, purchase, or even the husband’s gift before the accusation shall, where the husband has been condemned (and has died as a penalty, or has been reduced to servile status because of the nature of his punishment), remain untouched; nor shall the wife be burdened by the misfortune of another’s crime. For it is right that she should enjoy her paternal, maternal, and own property under the unimpaired ordinance of the laws. And a marital gift conferred upon the wife before the time of the crime and accusation must be observed, because it was granted as a reward for chastity, as though nature, not punishment, had taken her husband away.

But if he has been interdicted from water and fire, or deported, while death has not followed as punishment, gifts made by the husband to the wife shall remain pending; for marriage is not dissolved in cases of this kind. Thus, if the husband does not revoke them during his lifetime, they shall be confirmed by his death; and our treasury shall thereafter have no share in those same things.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of March, in Sardinia, in the second consulship of Crispus and the second consulship of Constantius (321). [Col. 0233B] [From the Code of Justinian.]

**ON CONCUBINES**

Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People. No one shall be granted permission to keep a concubine while a marriage continues.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, with Constantine father and son as consuls (321 or 324). [From the Code of Justinian.]

**IF AN APPEAL IS PENDING**

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Bassus, Prefect of the City, after other provisions. If one of the litigants dies while an appeal is still pending, his heirs shall have not merely the remaining portion of the period, but also an additional four months. But if a fixed period is allowed for deliberation concerning acceptance of the inheritance, the four-month period shall be counted after its expiration, so that persons ignorant of the litigation, or even uncertain whether to enter upon the inheritance, may not be compelled to suffer losses before receiving any benefit.

Published on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, at Sirmium, in the second consulship of Crispus and the second consulship of Constantine Caesars (321). [From the Code of Justinian.]

**ON PRIVATE BUILDINGS**

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Elpidius, acting in the capacity of Praetorian Prefect. If anyone, after this law, transfers to rural estates ornaments—that is, marble or columns—from a city that has been stripped, he shall be deprived of the possession which he has thus adorned.

But if anyone wishes to transfer marble or columns from his own houses in one city to his own houses in another city, where walls are collapsing, he may do so freely, since their presence in either place is a public ornament. The same permission is given to transfer such ornament from one estate to another estate, even though it is necessary to transport it across walls or even through the middle of a city; provided only that articles brought into cities be exported.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, at Viminacium, in the second consulship of Crispus and the second consulship of Constantine (321).

**ON SEEKING DEFENDANTS**

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Januarius. Whoever, from the day on which he has been summoned as a defendant in court, refuses to appear for trial within a year, shall have his property claimed by the treasury. If he is later found and discovered guilty, he shall be subjected to a more severe sentence. But if by evident arguments and clear proof he establishes his innocence, his resources shall nevertheless remain with the treasury.

Given on the Ides of January, in the fifth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the consulship of Licinius Caesars (321). [From the Code of Justinian.]

**ON PARTITION OF THE FAMILY ESTATE**

[Col. 0234A]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Bassus. Published. Among all one’s heirs only—those who, though coming through any degree, are nevertheless seen to be equal, or emancipated children whom the praetor calls to succession—whether a will has been begun but not completed, or a codicil or letter of a parent is said to exist, or dispositions are found in any other manner of writing, in whatever words or indications they may have been left, the disposition of the deceased shall be preserved by the action for partition of the family estate, with the aid of the senatorial decree retained, even if such disposition has lacked the solemnity of the laws, although children are called to succession intestate.

But if among the children designated in such a testamentary intention another person is intermixed, it is certain that the intention shall be held void only insofar as concerns that intermixed person. [Col. 0234B]

Given at Rome, on the Kalends [month omitted], in the second consulship of Crispus and the second consulship of Constantine Caesar (321).

In the *Authenticum*, *On the Third and the Half*, § “And what often [occurs],” column 3, title 5, Novel 18, chapter 7:

Provided only that this document bears the subscription either of the parent himself or of all the children among whom the division is made. [From the Code of Justinian.]

In the year of the Lord 322, with Probianus and Julianus consuls.

**ON ACCUSATIONS**

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Agricolanus. [Note: 4, Til.: “Africolanus.” 20, 25: “agriculanus.” 42: “agriculam.” An. adds: “Correctly Proculus?” See Go. in the note.] … Since the law is clear and manifest that women have the capacity to institute a public criminal accusation only for specific causes—that is, if they pursue an injury done to themselves or their own—what was established of old must be observed. [Note: The earlier portion of this constitution seems to have passed into constitution 12 of the Code of Justinian, *On Those Who May Not Accuse*: there it is read from the beginning as follows: “A woman is not permitted to accuse in a crime belonging to public proceedings, except for specified causes—that is, if she pursues an injury to herself or her own—only according to the statutes of ancient law,” etc.] [Note: 4, Til. omit “law,” but manuscript 4 has it added above the line by an ancient hand. 12: “his.” Shortly afterward Go.: “manifest.”] [Note: Br. Al. manuscripts: *intentandi*, like Sichard, with variants; all are different forms of the same word. Ri. approves *intentandi*. We retain *intendendi*. See constitution 11 under this title, “if he does not prove what he has alleged,” and constitution 13, “indeed, of the examination to be instituted.”]

For it is not lawful that women should indiscriminately have the capacity to accuse; otherwise, in public inquiries, either proof or the authority of the accuser was sometimes admitted. [Col. 0234C] [Note: 9, 19, 20: “lost.” Go. improperly proposes in the commentary “integrity” for “proof.”]

Advocates, too, must be warned not recklessly to take up women, perhaps rushing into an unlawful action because of the security of their sex, for the sake of gain. [Note: 8–10, 12, 16: “regard,” and 16: “woman.” 20 has “severity” written above the line for “security.”] [Note: 20: “accession,” corrected to “action.” 15: “into a public action.” 6: “distinguished.” 19: “unlawful.”]

Published on the fifth day before the Ides of February, in the consulship of Probianus and Julianus (322). [Note: 8: “Kalends” for “Ides”; 24: “the day before”; 40: “published February”; 28, 40 omit “fifth day before the Ides”; 19: “Ides of February, tenth, published.”] [Note: 42: “and Valentinian, consul.” Go. deliberately assigned the year 325; improperly Ri.]

**INTERPRETATION**

Women shall not be permitted to accuse anyone except in a case concerning themselves or their own, because the laws prohibit them from undertaking other persons’ cases. [Col. 0235A] [Note: 6: “who by undertaking”; 21: “which by undertaking”; other manuscripts: “undertaking.”]

Advocates must likewise be warned not to undertake contrary to the laws the representation of women wishing to litigate in others’ cases. [Note: Many manuscripts, including 6 and 7: “advocates … must be warned not.” 19, 20: “An advocate must be warned.”] [Note: 6: “they shall undertake contrary to law.” In some manuscripts and in Sichard, “in” is omitted. Shortly afterward some manuscripts: “cases.”]

**ON NOTICE, OR THE EDICT, OF A RESCRIPT**

2. Emperor Constantius Augustus to Maximus, Prefect of the City. We decree that notice shall be given either before provincial governors or before those who have the right to draw up official records, so that a private attestation, written in the names of the dead, of persons absent in distant lands, or of persons who are nowhere in the world, may not attach false credit to transactions that never occurred. [Note: 6, 7, 14, 16: “to governors.” Shortly afterward some manuscripts: “authors.” Aur. Lugd., in the margin from the interpretation: “litigation,” omitted by a mark in the text, which seems to refer to “notice.”] [Note: 10, 18: “of completing.”] [Note: Aur. Lugd.: “and private testimony.”] [Note: Sichard: “litigation contestation.”] [Note: Some manuscripts omit “in.”] [Note: 5: “are.”] [Note: 19 omits “not.”] [Note: Thus W. from Go.’s conjecture. 5: “attach.” 6, 7, 14, 16, 19, 21, Cujacius 2–Cl.: “attach.” 10, 18: plural. 20, Sichard–Lugd.: plural, but Sichard–Lugd. in the margin: “may feign.” 8, 9, 15: “afflict.”]

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, at Sirmium, in the consulship of Probianus and Julianus (322). [Note: Manuscripts 26, 33, 35, 38 omit “tenth”; 24: twelfth, eleventh.] [Note: Thus corrected by the author of manuscripts 5–8, 10, 14, 17–20, 26, 38, 42, 44, R., and by constitution 2, *C. Th.*, *On Summoning Judges*, which itself has June. The remaining manuscripts and editions have July; 24, 30, 33: January.] [Note: Thus most manuscripts and editions; Be., W.: “at Sirmium”; 20: “Sirmia.”] [Note: 8: “Jovinian,” omitting Probianus; 15: “consuls.” The explanation needs none.]

**INTERPRETATION**

We order that litigation be formally contested before provincial governors, defenders, or all persons before whom official records are prepared, so that no one may admit into the contestation of a suit the name of an absent or dead person, or of one who cannot be found, lest an occasion for falsity arise. [Note: 20, Sichard: “about to contest.”] [Col. 0235B] [Note: Some manuscripts and R.: “nor.”] [Note: 6, 7: “will be able”; others: “will be able.”] [Note: 5 omits “in”; 43: “into that litigation.”] [Note: Aur. Lugd.: “receives.” 7, 20: plural, but in manuscript 7 corrected by a second hand to singular.] [Note: Some manuscripts, such as 42: “false witnesses.”] [Note: Many manuscripts, such as 9, 42: “accusation.”]

**ON JUDGMENTS**

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Prefect of the City. Concerning place. A person who knowingly neglects to appear for judgment shall be fined by the judge as contumacious. [Note: 11 and F. 6: “Emperor Constantine … Prefect of the City.”] [Note: 11: “is fined a penalty.”]

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June at Sirmium, in the consulship of Probianus and Julianus (322). [Note: 11 omits “June.”] [Note: Editions: “at Sirmium.”] [Note: 11 adds “From the Theodosian Corpus.”]

**ON THE FREE-STATUS CASE** [Note: The rubric is taken from Br. Al., whence it passed into the editions, except P., which has: “On the Case of Freedom.”]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Prefect of the City. [Note: W. restored the inscription, though omitting “Augustus,” from the Code of Justinian; but changed it, because the following constitution has “Prefect of the City,” from “Praetorian Prefect,” which the standard editions have. Manuscripts Bg., Montispes. H.82 support W.’s alteration. P. adds “Fragment of Law IV,” and Pu. “Constitution 4, Fragment.”] … [Col. 0236A] … [Note: Here begins the sixth Turin folio. That this is the fourth constitution under this title is clear because the number VI was placed on the reverse side of the folio for the constitution which until now was second. Therefore, as the Dutch scholars have conjectured, only one folio seems to have been lost between the fifth and sixth Turin folios; it contained, besides the concluding part of title six, title seven and the first three constitutions under this title together with the beginning of this constitution. P. wishes to supply “he had said,” approved in *Bijdr.*; W. proposes to add “he had adjudged.”]

…ixisset, an opportunity for the judgment of all those persons would be afforded. [Note: P.: “was done,” corruptly.] They interpreted this to mean that, after all persons had been drawn into litigation, and the claims had already been arranged and disposed of, and the judge’s inquiry almost completed, if births should occur among the persons who were the subject of the inquiry, they asserted that the times of law should be renewed, as though these births were additions to the necessary absence of a person whose presence was expected. [Note: Thus I, P., Pu.; but P. in the note wishes *quidam*, adopted by W. without necessity.] [Note: From P.’s conjecture; for in manuscript I this word has been torn away.] [Note: Pu.: “all claims having also been arranged,” contrary to manuscript I.] [Note: Thus P., Pu., W. by conjecture; in manuscript I the letters *qu* in “if” and *sen* in “occur” have been torn away. Hence the Dutch scholars, in the cited place, p. 334, wish to read “if a birth should occur to anyone.” But “additions” must necessarily refer to “births,” and therefore the text is to be read as printed.] [Note: I, P., Pu.: “assert,” improperly W., who changes it to “may assert,” though in the notes proposes “asserted.”]

But since absence is one thing and not yet having been born another, we have decided that those who are born shall enjoy the condition and legal status of their mothers, from whose wombs they are soon brought forth; and that the time of trial shall not be renewed because someone has been born. [Note: Here begins constitution 42 of the Code of Justinian cited above, which Go. thought should be combined with constitutions 5 and 6 under this title.] [Note: “And legal status” is absent in the Code of Justinian.] [Note: The words “and that … renewed” are absent in the Code of Justinian.]

But all persons born before suit shall be called into the inquiry in their own name, because only those who are born during the litigation must be included in every fortune of their mothers and either be delivered to their rightful owners or enjoy freedom together with those who gave them the light of day; for they can have no defense more proper or truer than that of their mothers. [Note: Code of Justinian: “Before the suit,” and shortly afterward, “all in their own name.”] [Note: 1: “who are born into litigation,” improperly P.] [Col. 0236B] [Note: Thus I and W.; but P., Pu., from the Code of Justinian: “will be in every,” omitting “in.” *Complecti* is often used in a passive sense.] [Note: The conjunction is absent in the Code of Justinian, though not in all its manuscripts.] [Note: Code of Justinian: “enjoy freedom with the authors of light,” and omits what follows.]

Given on the day before the Ides of June, at Sirmium, in the consulship of Probianus and Julianus (322). [Note: Code of Justinian: “Given on the day before the Ides of July,” and omits what follows.] [Note: I, P.: “Sermium, Provianus.” Pu.: “Sermii, Provianus.”]

**ON MAINTENANCE**

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Menander. … We have learned that provincials suffering from want of food and scarcity of sustenance sell or pledge their children. Therefore, whoever is found to be of this sort, unsupported by any substance of household property and scarcely and with difficulty maintaining his children, shall be assisted from our treasury before he becomes subject to calamity. [Note: Compare *C. Th.* VIII.5.4, note.] [Note: 4, Til.–Lugd.: “maintain,” erroneously. Aur. Lugd.: “and difficultly.”]

Thus proconsuls, governors, and rationales throughout all Africa shall have authority, and shall distribute necessary assistance to all whom they observe to be in miserable want, and immediately grant them suitable provisions from the granaries. [Note: Go. prefers “that,” not badly, but without necessity.] [Note: Leaf 173b of manuscript 4.]

For it is contrary to our customs that we should permit anyone to be consumed by hunger or driven into an unworthy deed.

Given on the day before the Nones of July, at Rome, in the consulship of Probianus and Julianus (322). [Note: Go. has “given” in place of “reported” or “received,” or wishes another location to be supplied. Constantine was in Pannonia in this year. See Go. in the Chronicle for this year and in the note to this constitution, note k.]

**ON THE FREE-STATUS CASE**
Imperator Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Prefect of the City. [Note: 13, 15, 21, 29, 32, 33, 39, 42, 44 and certain manuscripts, following Gothofredus, give the abbreviation for praetorian prefect instead of Prefect of the City, incorrectly. 15: “to Maximus.” 25: “to Maximus the procurator.” Moreover, the Breviarium Alaricianum manuscripts and editions have before “P.”: “Emperor Constantine Augustus” instead of “[the] same Augustus.” But now, from manuscript 1, where constitution 2 is by the same emperor, the heading had to be altered.]

If anyone brings into jeopardy of free birth persons enjoying freedom [Note: 15: “if anyone.”] and possessing it [Note: Sichardus: “possessing [singular].” 6–8, 21: “freedom.”] unexpectedly [Note: 1, Sichardus: “unexpected [singular].”], and if an *assertor*—an advocate or claimant of their free status—should happen to fail them, a public leading-about shall be provided while an *assertor* is sought [Note: Til. through Cujacius 2: “to be sought.” Sichardus: “and the assertor,” in the heading, not “the assertor,” as is said in R. 21: “assertor, who if,” in the heading. 10, 18: “is sought.”] by a written notice indicating the title [or claim], [Note: 1, P., Pu.: “indicating [plural],” printed by W.; on this reading W. argues at length against Gothofredus. 10, 18: “declaring.”] lest the case [Note: 6–10, 14, 17, 18, 21: “cases.” 19: “cause.”] be unknown through silence [Note: 9: “by the litigation itself.” 15: “through silence [of the] case.”] or even absurdly proclaimed [Note: Editions before W. wrongly print “proclaimed,” so that the following words, “that those who—should be compelled,” depend upon “proclaimed.” For these are the actual words of an absurd proclamation apparently employed by certain magistrates. W. was therefore entirely right to remove the brackets in which Be. had enclosed the words “lest—proclaimed,” since the following “that those who,” etc., cannot be joined with “indicating” and otherwise have no antecedent.]—namely: “that those who had begun [Note: 6, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, Til.: “had discovered.”] should wish [Note: Correctly P., Pu., W., with Til. and most manuscripts; Sichardus, Cujacius 1 through Be.: “should wish [subjunctive],” less suitably because of the following “should be compelled.”] to assert [their status], [Note: Til. omits “to assert.” 15: “to assert and should wish.” 10, 18: “should be compelled.” Gothofredus approves hesitantly in his note; Wenck disapproves.] or even those hesitating should be compelled [to do so]; and lest, if an *assertor* is lacking, they who are known by many to be free should be led away in chains by their masters, [Note: 1, 8, 10, 13–18, manuscripts cited by Gothofredus, and editions from Sichardus through Cujacius 1, P., Pu., W.: “bound.” Below they are called “confined.” 6, following R.: “bound [singular]”; rather, “bound [plural].” Aur. and Lugd.: “having been bound.” Cujacius 2 through Be.: “conquered,” defended by Gothofredus. 15: “defended by many, free.”] [Note: 1: “to masters.” 10, 16, 18, 21, and editions from Sichardus through Lugd.: “to all” or abbreviated “to all”; but in the margin of Cujacius 1 through Lugd.: “read: ‘deserted by masters,’” which R. has. Read “by masters,” not “to masters,” as manuscript 1 indicates. Moreover 9: “in the house.”] [Note: I have restored “should be led.” Cujacius 2 through Be., W.: “should be conducted away.” “Should be led” is preferable, because all manuscripts and editions from Sichardus through Lugd., P., and Pu. have it; Romans customarily use it in the judicial sense found here.]

§ 1. Therefore we enact: if anyone, poor and unknown in respect of an *assertor*, [Note: Cujacius and Gothofredus; Gothofredus demonstrates in his notes that “of an assertor” must be read. This is confirmed by manuscript 1, whence “assertor’s” passed into the editions of P., Pu., and W.; manuscript 15 likewise gives the true reading: “we enact that, if anyone [is] without an assertor.” Following Gothofredus, some have attempted “from an assertor,” which manuscripts 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 18 and R. give; manuscript 16: “from an assertor”; 21: “assertors.” The remaining manuscripts and editions of Cujacius 1 and Cujacius 2 through Be.: “an assertor.” Sichardus and Til.: “to an assertor.” Aur. and Lugd.: “assertor.”] after the people of the province have been searched, is abandoned, he shall be handed over to the person who has called him a slave—not with his freedom destroyed, [Note: 12: “not broken”; 19: “of broken and erased freedom.”] but postponed—so that, once the *assertor* has been found, he may recover strength [Note: 8: “may gather.” 9: “may recover [plural].” 15: “may gather strength.” 19: “who may recover things,” and omits “and.”] and, renewing his defenses, resist in court, supported by the right and privileges of a possessor, [Note: 6–9: “supported.” 10, 18: “support.” 14: “supported [plural].” 21: “possessors, supported by right and privileges.”] although he came forth from that man’s household. [Note: 1: “Although—from the household.” P. supplies “from the household,” which Pu. and W. accept; manuscript 15 has this plainly. Manuscript 6, following R.: “although he [is] that man’s slave”; but 6–8, 10, 13, 16, 18: “although and [is] that man’s slave.” The remaining manuscripts and editions: “although from that man’s household.”]

For that possession is not one received permanently, [Note: 1, 21: “received [plural].”] but an expectation of the *assertor* during the time when he has not been found. Thus, if the litigation is renewed and the parties are restored to their respective rights, [Note: Pu.: “his.”] and judgment is rendered for freedom, [Note: 15 omits “for freedom.”] the opponent shall, on account of his wrongful and shameless conduct, be fined a corresponding number of slaves [Note: 10, 18: “an equal number of slaves.”] for every person [Note: Manuscript 1 had “because,” but a second hand wrote “every” above it; hence P., Pu., W. and the editions: “every.” The remaining manuscripts have “because” or “how many because,” the latter of which editions before P. print.] sought for enslavement. [Note: Sichardus: “they shall have.” 21: “they shall be”; 9 and 15: “they were.”] But those born during the litigation itself [Note: 1, P., Pu.: “these”; 21, as here; the remaining manuscripts: “they,” as Til., or “these,” as Sichardus, incorrectly.] shall not be included in the condemnation. [Note: Thus manuscript 1 and W., as Gothofredus had long conjectured. 14: “they shall be condemned.” The remaining manuscripts and editions before W.: “they are condemned”; but the margin of Cujacius 2 through Lugd.: “read: ‘they shall be contained’ or ‘shall be counted,’” and the margin of Cujacius 2, manuscript 2: “read: ‘they shall be contained,’ or ‘shall be counted,’ or ‘computed.’” Similarly the interpreter: “these not being counted.” Be.: “repeat instead: ‘those—shall be condemned’ or ‘shall be condemned [plural].’” W. attacks the vulgar reading “are condemned,” since the verb has no referent; earlier, however, “the opponent” is spoken of.] [Note: Thus Sichardus, Til., P., Pu., W. instead of the singular “was,” which manuscript 1 has. Manuscripts 7 and 13 agree with W. The remaining manuscripts have either “were” or “had been,” as the editions.]

§ 2. But if anyone dies before the *assertor* is found or before judgment, [Note: Sichardus and Cujacius 1: “before judgment.” 6: “before [the] assertor.”] then, if his heirs prove the case of his status, [Note: 8: “established.” 19: “of established [status].” 15 omits “status.”] a slave shall be handed over by way of penalty, [Note: 10: “a fine whose.” 15: “a fine,” omitting “slave.” 18: “very speedily fined.” 19: “of the fined person.” Sichardus: “very speedily fined.”] and the heirs of the person who had rashly attacked freedom, if they show an implacable disposition, [Note: What P. says—that manuscript 1 has “if implacable”—cannot be seen in the copy.] shall remain subject to the same rule and condition concerning slaves. [Note: Thus clearly 1, 9, 15, 19, 21, and editions from Sichardus through Lugd., P., Pu., W. 16: “shows.” The remaining manuscripts, the margin of Cujacius 2, and Be.: “show,” approved by Gothofredus, who dislikes “say,” which passed from Cujacius 2 into the editions of Gothofredus, R., and R*.] But if [Note: Thus written with the manuscripts; editions except P. and Pu. have “but if.” 15: “if indeed [they allow them] free.”] they allow free those whom they find confined, the wrongs perish with the persons. [Note: Thus manuscript 1, P., Pu., W. The rest: “they shall escape.”] [Note: Many manuscripts and Sichardus: “chosen.” 6: “wrong [singular].” R. wrongly says that Sichardus has “chosen.” Moreover Sichardus and Til.: “they shall escape [punishment], with the persons against whom the wrongs were committed.”]

§ 3. The guardians of minors shall remain liable to the same penalty in slaves; [Note: 1, P., Pu.: “of guardians,” which is certainly not false. Cf. P. 14, Sichardus: “of a guardian.”] and, if those whom they had defended demand an accounting in court, [Note: 1: “and court those whom they defended.”] an assessment of the improperly managed affair shall be made. [Note: 8: “debtor.” 12: “is owed.”]

§ 4. Since the *assertor* has done this at his own risk, [Note: 19: “in.” 1: “have done.”] promising that the matter will remain secure, [Note: Some manuscripts: “safe,” and soon after others: “a great [sum] returned.” 1: “redemption.” 6, following R.: “that it may be sufficient.”] he shall likewise receive security for repayment of the penalty. [Note: Thus most manuscripts, including 1. For “that” and “thus” belong together. The words “Since—the assertor” refer to the preceding provisions. Editions and the remaining manuscripts: “promises.” Shortly afterward, 6: “a great [sum].”]

§ 5. The dominion of victors deprived defeated enemies of freedom; but laws punish the unjust [Note: 1: “inflict.” Some manuscripts: “punishment inflict.” Shortly afterward 6, 7, and others: “the laws punish the unjust.” 15: “the laws affix punishment to the unjust.” 10, 18: “may hold the unjust liable.” 21: “the laws [punish] the unjust.”] and deprive them of reputation. [Note: 8 omits “and”; 10: “and [of] fame.” Gothofredus conjectures: “those who despoil [others] of reputation.” 18 omits “reputation.”] A saying uttered in a quarrel [Note: Thus 1, P., Pu., W. The rest omit “in.” Many manuscripts: “quarrel.”] against an adversary, if thrown out more immoderately and wantonly, compels the speaker to undergo punishment; [Note: Aur. and Lugd.: “against an adversary.” 9: “having been wantonly thrown.” 19: “uttered and wantonly poured forth.”] and [Note: Thus 1, 16, P., Pu., W. The remaining manuscripts, Til., and the margin of Cujacius 1 through Cujacius 2: “will be compelled,” except 6, which has “would be compelled,” and 21, which has “they compel”; this is in editions from Sichardus through Be. Gothofredus wishes “they compel.”] the undermining and attack upon freedom will not go unpunished, [Note: Many manuscripts have “and whence W., in E. L. L. 1824, p. 1905 and in his edition, emends to ‘but indeed,’ which Pu. accepts in place of ‘and,’ found in the remaining manuscripts and editions except manuscript 1 and Til., which have ‘and.’ Gothofredus attempted ‘certainly not’ or ‘equally not’; but ‘and’ need not be altered, since the construction is not: ‘and it is more unjust—to have received; therefore it will not be punished’; rather, the sentence ‘the laws—compels’ continues with ‘and.’ 9 omits ‘and—undermining,’ and 15 omits ‘not.’ 13: ‘pledging.’] which is also punished in cases established by proof. [Note: P.: “of freedom. Which,” from conjecture.] [Note: 1: “convic….” P. and Pu., conjecturally; Gothofredus and the editions: “in abusive speeches,” approved by Bijdr.; the other editions: “in cases established by proof.” Likewise most manuscripts: “convictis”; but 8, 10, 18: “convinctis,” which can be read either “joined” or “convicted,” and perhaps conceals the true word. Soon afterward many manuscripts and Pu.: “is placed.” The following passages are disfigured by errors in manuscripts and editions.]

It is unjust, moreover, to have received another as a slave [Note: 1, 6–8, 12, 13, 16, 21: “another, moreover, [has] received [him] to himself”; similarly P. and Pu., although Pu. has “another’s.” They nevertheless insert themselves after “to,” approved by Bijdr., p. 335. 9: “another” before “slave.” 10, 18: “another slaves.” 19: “another’s,” omitting “moreover.” Gothofredus orders “a slave” to be written, approved by Be. “For enslavement” is proposed in the margin of Cujacius 1 through Cujacius 2. Moreover Pu.: “more unjustly,” from Gothofredus’s conjecture.] [Note: 1, P.: “had received.” P. punctuates the entire passage thus: “of freedom. What in abusive speeches—is [this]: another, however, had received [him] to himself as a slave; and another’s, etc.” In these P. thinks, less plausibly, that he has found as many parts of syllogisms. R. and R*: “another’s; to.” One or two words have dropped out.] and he is condemned for abducting another person’s slave. [Note: 8: “to.” 15: “from.” Gothofredus, in his note: “And therefore another’s.”] [Note: Thus 1, 6–10, 12, 15–18, 21, editions from Sichardus through Lugd., P., Pu., W.; but 8: “abduction.” Cujacius 2 through Be.: “assignment,” defended by Gothofredus and criticized by P. and W.] [Note: 6, 7, 13, 14, 16: “condemned [masculine].” 18: “condemned [plural].” 9: “condemned [neuter].”]

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, at Sirmium, [Note: 8: eleventh; 10, 15, 16, 18, 24, 39, 43: fourteenth; 32–34, Gothofredus, R., R*: twelfth.] [Note: Thus most manuscripts. Some: Sermium or Firmium. 40: Firmi. Be. and Pu.: at Sirmium. 8 omits “August—and.”] in the consulship of Probianus [Note: Some manuscripts and Sichardus in the margin: Probinus. 1, Pu.: Provianus. 16: Privianus.] and Julianus [Note: 9: Juvinus.] (322).

### INTERPRETATION

If anyone attempts to consign to slavery a person in a state of freedom, [Note: 21: “placed,” and in the margin “is compelled to be consigned.” Sichardus: “If anyone placed in freedom” [in the margin: “a person placed”] “is compelled to be assigned to slavery” [in the margin: “attempts to consign”]. Other manuscripts: “placed—assigned.” Cujacius 1 through Lugd.: “to bring.”] it commands that the person thus attacked be led, by the judge’s order, among the people and in public, [Note: Sichardus and Cujacius 1 through Lugd. omit “in.”] so that he may find a defender of his status; and, when the *assertor* has been found, he is to request him from the judge by a written document, lest free birth be oppressed by silence. [Note: 21, in the margin; Sichardus and Cujacius 1 through Lugd.: “suppressed.”]

But if he can neither appear on his own behalf nor find an *assertor*, he shall be handed over to the master for reclamation into slavery, not for penal punishment. Yet by this handing-over he shall not entirely [Note: 21: “and entire,” but in the margin “entirely.”] lose hope of freedom, provided that, when he has opportunity and an *assertor* has been found, he may assert his free status and be heard according to the laws.

But if, after the lawsuit has been restored in this manner, those who are attacked prove themselves freeborn, [Note: Some manuscripts: “the person attacked proves himself freeborn.”] then the man by whom their free birth had been unjustly assailed shall be compelled to give to those whom he had called to slavery as many slaves of the same age and sex [Note: 10, 18, 42, and others omit “to those—compelled.”] as the persons concerned; but those who are proved to have been born during the pending litigation shall not be counted in the condemnation. [Note: Sichardus and Cujacius 1 through Lugd.: “for condemnation.” 6, 7, 21: “whom they called to slavery—these not being counted in the condemnation, while the case is prolonged.” Most manuscripts: “is prolonged.”] [Note: Many manuscripts: “into litigation.”]

But if any of those called to slavery die while the case is delayed because an *assertor* must be sought [Note: “Is called [to slavery] while [waiting] for an assertor.”] or for another reason, [Note: 6, 7: “or another occasion.” 44: “through another occasion.”] and their heirs establish their status of free birth, compensation for the person who died during the litigation [Note: Many manuscripts omit “during.”] shall be rendered to his heirs by the person who attacked him, just as it would be for those still living.

But if the person who attempted to consign free persons to slavery dies [Note: Cujacius 1 through Lugd.: “to bring.” In my copy, Cujacius 1 has been corrected in a recent hand to “to carry away.”] and leaves sons or heirs, if they wish to pursue [Note: Some manuscripts: “prosecute.”] [Note: 44 adds “them.”] the case which their father or originator [Note: Sichardus, with many manuscripts: “actor.”] had begun, and are defeated, they shall be liable for the compensation written above, so that they may satisfy those improperly attacked with an equal number of slaves. [Note: Sichardus has “they are: or [else],” but in the margin “so that.”]

But if they do not wish to proceed or attempt to pursue them, but instead release those whom their originator had reduced to custody, [Note: Many manuscripts: “having been reduced into custody by the actor.”] [Note: Here manuscript 20 begins again. See C. Th., title *On Marriages* (III, 7), constitution 2, note p.] they shall be free from condemnation to a penalty, [Note: 20 omits “from.”] [Note: Some manuscripts: “penalty.”] because they have not persisted in their originator’s wrongdoing. [Note: 6, 7, 21, 42, and others: “wrong.”] [Note: Many manuscripts: “have stood forth.”]

But if they are perhaps minors, [Note: 6–9, 12, 14, 17, 19, and many others: “unless perhaps.”] and their tutor or curator [Note: 20: “originator,” written above the line.] wishes to pursue their cases contesting their free birth [Note: 20: “to pursue.”] and is defeated, he himself shall be liable to satisfaction out of his own property.

But if, after the lawsuit has been restored a second time, the *assertor* found wishes at his own risk [Note: 6–8: “his own.” 20: “at his own risk.”] to have the case of the persons assigned [to slavery] reopened, [Note: Cujacius 1 through Lugd., in the margin: “brought.” In my copy, Cujacius 1 has been corrected in a recent hand to “carried away.”] he must promise that, if he is defeated, [Note: Thus 6, 7, 20, 42, 44, and others; Sichardus and Cujacius 1 through Lugd.; approved by R. The remaining manuscripts: “if he is vindicated.”] he will restore the peculium or services [Note: Some manuscripts: “service.”] of those received [Note: 20: “of those subscribed,” corrected by a second hand to “of those received.” 21: “of those about to receive,” but in the margin “of those received.”] or the persons themselves. [Note: 20: “the persons [feminine].” Sichardus: “the person.” Some manuscripts: “the persons.”] Likewise, the person who attacks them, having given a surety, [Note: Some manuscripts: “having given sureties.”] shall promise that, if defeated, he will provide the stated number or value of slaves [Note: Cujacius 1 through Lugd. omit “or value.”] [Note: 12: “slaves.”] or [Note: Certain manuscripts: “or.”] satisfy whatever he claims from them [Note: Many manuscripts: “them.”] from their peculium. [Note: 20, 21 in the margin, Sichardus and Cujacius 1 through Lugd.: “from” instead of “in”; but in the margin of Cujacius 1 through Lugd.: “in.”] [Note: 44, Sichardus, Cujacius 1 through Lugd.: “what he claims, when defeated, he shall satisfy.” 6, 7: “what he claims to satisfy when defeated.”]

## CONCERNING CONSTITUTIONS

[Note: In the Breviarium Alaricianum a memorandum precedes this title. Although it does not belong to the Theodosian Code, I thought it should nevertheless be added in the notes of this edition because of the Visigothic Interpretation received here, from the recension of Karl von Savigny.

**Authoritative copy of King Alaric.** In this corpus are contained laws, or species of law, selected from the Theodosian [Code] and diverse books and, as commanded, explained, in the twenty-second year of the reign of the lord King Alaric, under the direction of the illustrious man Goiaric, Count. Authoritative copy. Memorandum to Timotheus, *vir spectabilis*, Count.

Considering the welfare of our people through propitious divine favor, we also correct, by better deliberation, whatever appeared inequitable in the laws, so that every obscurity of Roman laws and ancient law, with priests and noble men brought in, may shine forth when brought into the light of clearer understanding, and nothing may remain ambiguous against which the protracted or varying objection of litigants may direct its attack. All these matters having been clarified and gathered into one book by the selection of learned men, the assent of venerable bishops or our chosen provincials has confirmed what has been excerpted, with a clearer interpretation composed [thereupon].

Accordingly, our clemency has ordered the subscribed book, which is preserved as a collected work on tablets, to be sent to Count Goiaric for the determination of disputes, so that every prosecution of cases may be settled according to its sequence. No one may be allowed to introduce for debate anything else from laws or legal right except what the order of the dispatched book, subscribed by the hand of the *vir spectabilis* Anianus, contains, as we have commanded. You must therefore ensure that in your forum no other law or formula of law is presumed to be produced or received. If this should be found to have happened, know that it shall bring either peril to your life or loss of your property. We have ordered this injunction to be attached to the dispatched books, so that both discipline and penalty may bind all persons to our ordinance.

Anianus, *vir spectabilis*, by command of our Lord, the most glorious King Alaric, has issued and subscribed at Aduris this code selected from the laws of Theodosius, legal opinions, and diverse books, in the twenty-second year of his reign. We have reviewed [it]. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the twenty-second year of King Alaric, at Toulouse. And again in the twentieth year of the reign of Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. You will find more in the edition of the Breviary of Alaric that I am preparing.]

## CONCERNING THE EDICTS OF EMPERORS

[Note: 5 omits the rubric. Code of Justinian: “Concerning laws, codes, and edicts.”]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Lusitanians. [Note: 8, 26, 28: “Lusians”; others: “Lusitanian,” “Lusetanians.” Sichardus: “to the Lusian,” in the manuscript “to the Lusitanians”; Code of Justinian: “Lysitanians,” which does not displease R. Manuscript books of Pistoia, Vatican, Pl. 1, 2, Bg., and edition of Nuremberg: “Lisitanians.” Cont. reports that some address it to Bassus, Praetorian Prefect. Certain manuscripts omit “Augustus.”] If any edicts [Note: 19 omits “any.” Most manuscripts: “these” or “this.” Sichardus, Til., Cujacius 1, Aur., Lugd., Hincmar: “these.”] or constitutions [Note: 14, 16, 30: “said”; 39, 43: “issued,” omitting “or”; 18: “have been issued”; 32 omits “edicts or”; 5: “or consul.”] shall hereafter be discovered without date and consul, [Note: Code of Justinian: “If any personal grants [are found] without ….”] [Note: 8, 9, 19–21, 27, 30, 32, 33, 37–39, 44: “discovered [feminine].” 14: “comprehended.”] they shall lack authority.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of August [Note: 10, 14, 41, 44, in the royal Anianus manuscript—that is, the royal Paris manuscript of the Breviarium Alaricianum—cited by Gothofredus, and in the manuscript book of Pistoia: sixth; 16, Til., the manuscript of Cujacius 1, Aur. and Lugd., and the Code of Justinian: fifth; but Hal. Russ.: seventh day before the Kalends of April; Pistoia manuscript: April.], at Savaria, [Note: 10, 18: “at Savario, in the consulship of Probianus.” 19: Salaria; 38: Sabine; 39: Sabriae.] in the consulship of Probianus [Note: 21 omits “Probianus, consuls.” 8: “and likewise Provianus.” Some manuscripts: Provianus. 28, 36: Prolatio. 40: Problatio. 20: Sichardus has Robianus, but Sichardus in the margin: Problutio.] and Julianus, the most illustrious consuls. [Note: 6, 10, 16, 18 omit “and Julianus, the most illustrious.” 14 omits “and Julianus.”] [Note: Most manuscripts omit “the most illustrious.”] (322).

### INTERPRETATION

Whatever laws have been promulgated without date and consul [Note: Certain manuscripts: “brought forth.”] shall not be valid.

## CONCERNING PARDONS FOR CRIMES

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: Gothofredus and Be. emend in the notes to “Prefect of the City,” correctly. See C. Th. II, 4, 2, note c.] On account of the birth of Crispus and Helena [Note: Gothofredus, with much learning in his commentary on this constitution, emends: “on account of the preparations of Crispus and Helena,” or “the equipment,” that is, equipment for the journey to the city of Rome. He also conjectured “agreement.”] we grant pardon to all, except poisoners, murderers, and adulterers. Received on the third day before the Kalends of November, at Rome, in the consulship of Probianus and Julianus (322).

## CONCERNING THE ESTATE OF MINORS WITHOUT A DECREE
