[Note: Code of Justinian: “Concerning the estates and other property of minors which may not be alienated or encumbered without a decree.”]

Emperor Constantine Augustus [Note: W. omits “Augustus,” which 1, P., and Pu. have.] to Severus. [Note: The abbreviation of rank is omitted in manuscript 1; P. and W. wish “Prefect of the City” restored. Pu.: “Sreverus,” a typographical error.] Minors under twenty-five years of age [Note: 1: “age.”] may reclaim an estate or rural slave [Note: The letters of “with” have been torn away in manuscript 1. Only rural estates and slaves are mentioned here. Four years later Constantine the Great also legislated concerning urban estates and slaves in C. Th., *On the Administration and Liability of Guardians*, III, 30, constitution 3.] alienated without the intervention of a decree, even without a petition for restoration to the former condition; [Note: P. restores the italicized letters; Bijdr. prefers “of restitution,” referring to the rubric of C. Th., *On Restoration in Full*, II, 16, contrary to necessity and manuscript 1, where “in” lies hidden in the letter m of “petition.”] provided that, if, after this law has been published, [Note: 1: “set before [the public].”] so much time remains until the limits of the twenty-fifth year [Note: At this place P. supplies letters cut away from the parchment, followed by Pu.: “yet up to”; W. disapproves and reads “such time,” both in E. L. L. 1824, p. 1084, and in his edition of the Theodosian Code. Since both alternatives displease me, I have preferred the conjecture of the Dutch scholars. See Bijdr., cited passage, p. 325, and C. Th., *On Restoration in Full*, II, 16, constitution 2.] [Note: P. says: “In the palimpsest the scribe first wrote ‘five hundred,’ then erased the syllable ‘hundred.’”] that a lawsuit already begun cannot be concluded before the end of that year, [Note: 1: “begun.”] [Note: “Within” has been restored by P.] the action once initiated may be extended. [Note: 1: “Inquatalis.” It is not uncommon in manuscripts for *inchoata* to be written incorrectly as *incoata*, *incuata*, and similarly.] [Note: P. most correctly restores “may be extended,” where manuscript 1 has a torn passage: “may … … … di.”]

Moreover, those whom the same law finds, after completion of the twenty-fifth year, within their twenty-sixth year [Note: 1: “twentieth.”] must not delay to commence their actions, since the time for a lawsuit thus initiated is limited to the twenty-sixth year. [Note: 1: “finds, to begin—twentieth.”] Therefore, whoever attempts to bring an action after this period shall be barred, so that the possessor may thereafter be secure and certain. [Note: In manuscript 1, after “who,” there is a gap of about five letters. P. and Pu. supply “therefore”; W. reads “therefore,” which I prefer.]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, at Serdica, in the consulship of Probianus [Note: 1: Provianus.] and Julianus [Note: 1: “ru. and the rest”; P. supplies “lianus, consuls,” and in the edition of this constitution itself, “Ju[liano consuls].”] (322).

*Emperors . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .* [Note: [Col. 0244B] It is regrettable that both the inscription and subscription of this constitution have perished. Had they been preserved, great difficulties arising from the fact that two laws of the Code of Justinian—c. 18, *On the Estates of Minors* (V, 71), and c. 17, *On Appeals* (VII, 62)—appear to have been drawn from this constitution, but bear different inscriptions and subscriptions, would be removed. Thus c. 18 in Spangenberg’s edition bears the inscription: “Emperors Constantine Augustus and Constantine Caesar to the Senate”; whereas c. 17 is inscribed: “The same Augustus (i.e. Constantine the Great) to Julianus, Prefect of the City.” Their subscriptions differ as follows: c. 18 reads, “Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, under the consulship of Probianus and Julianus (322)”; c. 17, “Given on the third day before the Nones of August, at Heraclea, under the seventh consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third consulship of Constantius Caesar (326).”

W. would explain this diversity of subscriptions by holding c. 17 to be a repeated form of this constitution, issued some years later, were it not that the mention of the Constantinian praetor shows that the constitution was given to the East; while the latter portion concerns the prefecture of the city mentioned in c. 17, which, according to the testimony of the best writers, was instituted at Constantinople only by Constantius in A.D. 360. An additional obstacle is that Julianus is named in the inscription of c. 17; Gothofredus and Corsinius, in the cited passage, p. 179, demonstrate that he was prefect at Rome. W. therefore left the matter for more learned persons to decide.

The Dutch scholars (*Bijdragen* [*Contributions*], p. 327) attempted to remove the difficulty differently. They deny that c. 17 was derived from this constitution, since the purport of the two laws differs: c. 17 orders appeal to the prefect of the city, whereas this constitution forbids it unless, while the question is being heard before either praetor, one party has interposed the remedy of appeal. The considerable verbal similarity in the two laws, they maintain, is insufficient to show that c. 17 was drawn from c. 2 of this title, since similar expressions are not infrequently found in earlier and later laws.

This extremely ingenious conjecture at first greatly pleased me. If accepted, c. 17 conflicts neither with this constitution nor with c. 18 of the Code of Justinian; and what c. 17 says concerning the urban prefecture must be understood of the prefecture of the city of Rome, not of Constantinople. Yet statutes otherwise differing in subject matter often have very similar wording: this is shown by comparing constitution 18 of the Code of Justinian, drawn from this law, with c. 16 of the Theodosian Code, *On Praetors* (VI, 4). This comparison led Go. to think c. 18 was derived from c. 16, although the Turin parchment shows that this was mistaken.

But the following prevents me from adhering to this view: even if accepted, it does not remove all difficulties. For the names of two legislators are prefixed to c. 18, which is only three days later than c. 1 of this title, where only one emperor is mentioned. Who could suppose that such a great difference in the imperial names can be admitted in two constitutions separated by only three days—perhaps by no interval at all, since copyists not infrequently interchange XII and XV? I therefore think that the entire difficulty lies not in the words of the law but in the fact that in both codes both inscriptions and subscriptions are corrupt.

Go. had already perceived this corruption. Seeking to assign c. 18 to Constantius and Julianus Caesar and to connect it with c. 16 of the Theodosian Code, *On Praetors*, he defended, against the evidence of the manuscript books of the Code of Justinian, the inscription *to the Senate*, received since the Contian edition of 1571, in place of the earlier reading *to Severus*. Herrmannus, the highly esteemed editor of the Code of Justinian, kindly allowed me to inspect these manuscripts. Codices Pl. 1, Bg., Vat., and Pist., collated by Blume, and Montpellier H. 82 and 83, inspected by me, all read *ad Severum* (“to Severus”) or *Severo* (“to Severus”), not *ad Senatum* (“to the Senate”).

That both inscriptions and subscriptions are corrupt is demonstrated by the Turin parchment. There the copyist left a gap of seven letters after *Emperors* in the inscription, although this is insufficient to receive the rest of the inscription; and in the subscription, after *Given*, another gap of eighteen letters, not counting five letters which have been torn away. It follows that the compilers of the Theodosian Code themselves already doubted the true inscription and subscription of the law. Perhaps this doubt arose because c. 2 was compounded from two constitutions: one issued by Constantine the Great to Julianus, the other by Constantius and Constans. Certainly a law of two emperors is indicated by the abbreviation *Imp.* in codex 1.

When the compilers of the Theodosian Code hesitated, in drafting it, as to which constitution’s inscription or subscription should be received, they received neither. The compilers of the Justinian Code, however, who restored those laws to their former form, incorrectly supplied the inscriptions and subscriptions of both laws from elsewhere. Perhaps the subscription of c. 17 should be assigned to c. 18, if, by an easy correction of the imperial and consular names, the year 354 is restored and the text read:

> Emperors Constantius Augustus and Constans Caesar to the Senate.—Given on the third day before the Nones of August, at Heraclea (!), under the seventh consulship of Constantius Augustus and the third consulship of Constans Caesar (354).

But I do not wish to insist upon these conjectures. Moreover, what c. 17 says of the urban prefecture is no obstacle, since it is an interpolation.—Pu. restores the inscription from the cited c. 18, though adding brackets.]

Even if [Note: [Col. 0245C] Codex 1 reads *etsi* (“although”), which indicates that this constitution is a fragment of a larger law; W. thinks it adapted to removing a doubt concerning the jurisdictions of magistrates, which this law settled. P. and Pu.: “If [taken] from c. 18 of the Code of Justinian.”] minors are found liable, whether in their father’s name or their own, solely on account of pressing fiscal debts [Note: [Col. 0245D] Code of Justinian: “urgent”; nevertheless manuscripts have “pressing” (*ingruentibus*) with the Theodosian Code.], or under private contracts [Note: Code of Justinian: “may be found” (*reperiantur*).], the interposition of a decree [Note: Pu.: “when a decree has been interposed,” incorrectly.] is to be carried out by the Constantinian praetor, after the grounds have been thoroughly proved [Note: Code of Justinian: “examined and proved.”], so that, once the truth of the facts has been disclosed, the sale may remain valid [Note: Here c. 18 of the Code of Justinian ends. What follows as far as “if” belongs to codex 1. In the preceding text certain words were cut out in codex 1, and P. restored them from c. 18.].

This being so [Note: P. supplied the eight letters torn from codex 1. Pu. and W. also accepted the supplement, which I retain, though it seems unsuitable; I have found nothing better. Earlier W. conjectured: “When this [i.e. certainty] is lacking.” Cramer conjectured: “While these things are being done.”], suspected guardians also are to be proceeded against under his examination, and a counter-action [Note: This supplement is due to W., who, on account of Digest XXVII, 4, law 4, thinks this concerns the *actio contraria* to be granted to a removed guardian, and to be instituted not before the Constantinian praetor but before the official having ordinary jurisdiction. P., followed by Pu., restored *postul(ari, at tibi)*; W. first adopted this reading. In his note P. prefers *actio est* for *actione*.] is likewise to be granted; so that only then may recourse be had to your Experience (*experientiam tuam*) [Note: P. restored the torn letters *erienti* in codex 1, appealing to c. 16 of the Theodosian Code, *On Petitions* (X, 10). W. doubts whether this was right: there *experientia tua* has its genuine meaning, whereas here it expresses a formula hitherto unknown. Go. explains “either praetor” as the urban and peregrine praetors; the interlinear gloss of codex Pl. 1 does the same. W. states that the functions of the two praetors are nowhere else distinguished in either Code. P. thinks of the tutelary praetor established by M. Antonius and the Constantinian praetor, who, he believes, jointly heard cases of suspected guardians; W. refutes this, interpreting *utrumque* as “either,” concerning which sense see Savigny, *Recht des Besitzes* (*The Law of Possession*), p. 345 n. r. Rudorff, III, p. 179 n. 2, understands the two praetors at Byzantium instituted by Constantine, on the basis of Lydus, *On Magistracies* II, 30: “he decided that two praetors should suffice” (*δύο πραίτορσιν ἀρκεσθῆναι συνεῖδε*).], in accordance with the laws, if [Note: Here begins c. 17 of the Code of Justinian, though its final words are altered: “If . . . an appeal is made to the sacred judgment of the prefecture of the city, let it be observed.”] while the question is being heard before either praetor, one party has interposed the remedy of appeal, in order that you, the exalted adjudicator, may weigh the merits of the appeal. Given . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0246C] Here ends the fourth Turin parchment, on the lower part of which the copyist adds in uncial letters: “THEOD. BOOK III, ESPL-,” from which the end and number of the titles of Book Three are established.]

In the year of the Lord 323, under the consulship of Severus and Rufinus.

## ON THE CAUSE OF FREEDOM

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus [Note: [Col. 0246C] Codices 15 and 26: “to Maximus”; some manuscripts: *M. ppo.* or *ppm.*; so too cited c. 3 of the Code of Justinian. “Praetorian Prefect.” Be. wishes it to be read thus; otherwise 6 and 7 read: “the same Augusti.”] Prefect of the City. Freedom [Note: Codices 19 and 20: “freedpersons”; 16: “freedperson.” P.: “of freedom,” a typographical error.] has been so greatly valued by our forefathers [Note: 8: “by minors”; 15: “only by a greater [person].”] that even fathers, to whom the power of life and death over their children was granted [Note: Many manuscripts: “and not those things which”; 19 and 20: “and not those to whom”; 15: “power of life and death over children.”], were not permitted to take freedom away [Note: The Code of Justinian formerly read: “had been granted; they were not permitted to take freedom away,” and ends here in the cited c. 10. Go. wishes to read: “had been granted.”].

§ 1. If any person [Note: 15: “if therefore anyone”; 19 and 20: “but if anyone”; 17: “thus anyone”; 6–8 and 14: “anything.”] sold while a minor has, after becoming an adult, performed the transaction [Note: 6–8, 14, and 20: “transactions”; this can stand in 6–8 and 14 because of the preceding “anything,” and Ri. does not dislike it. Go. adds “servile.” 20: “as an adult.”], then, because a minor’s sale does not bind him merely through his knowledge of it [Note: Some manuscripts: “because,” and later “so that”; Sich.: “binds”; 15: “bound,” omitting “him.”], the prescription arising from the purchase and from the transaction performed by him as an adult [Note: 10 and 18: “and an adult transaction”; 1: “by an adult”; 16: “to an adult.”] shall not hold him when he comes to freedom [Note: 10 and 18 omit “when he comes.” 20: “the purchase.”] [Note: Many manuscripts read *perscriptio*; 19 and 20, *perscritione*. Codex 1 has a damaged *praescriptiono . . . catur tenebit*, but *catur* is erased by dots above it.].

§ 2. Nor indeed [Note: Be., because of the following “shall not be alleged,” proposes *nor also* or *nor less*, or wishes to delete *not* before “shall be bound”; he himself prefers the latter, and W. approves, since Sich. reads “the prescription shall not be alleged.” Nothing need be changed, however, if we suppose that the emperor wished the earlier, rather remote negation to be recalled. Sich., through Go., punctuates: “permitted, if . . . shall not hold. Nor indeed.”] shall a person who has been brought up by someone as a slave [Note: Codex 1, P., Pu., and W.: “is brought up”; the remaining manuscripts and editions: “was brought up,” a meaning equally good and apparently preferable. See *C. Th.*: “If anyone sold while a minor.”], and, having become an adult, acquiesced in the seller as though in a master [Note: 1: “of selling”; 6, according to Ri.: “having become an adult through selling,” preferably “having become an adult and sold”; 8, 13, 17, and Til.: “having become an adult and sold”; 10 and 18: “having become an adult and having been sold”; 14: “having become an adult and of selling”; 16: “having become an adult and of the sold [person].” Most manuscripts then have *velut*, *aut*, or *velud*.] and, after performing the transaction, has now almost relegated his freedom to the furthest remove [Note: 9: “chosen”; 10 and 18: “binds again”; 20: “binds again.” 21 and Sich.: “has brought himself back to extreme freedom,” though Sich. has “to slavery” in the margin. Earlier 10 and 18 omit “now.”]. For neither, after becoming an adult, did he know his origin [Note: 6–9, 12–14, 16, and 17: “had known.”], nor, by submitting to the sale of which he was unaware, is he to be deemed to have abandoned his status [Note: 1, P., Pu., and W. correctly read “of which he was unaware”; the remaining witnesses, “which he was unaware of.”] [Note: 19, 21, and Sich.: “of the sale.”]. Like a minor, he shall not be bound by the same prescription arising from the purchase and the transaction performed; rather, an assertion of freedom shall be granted to both [Note: 20: “performing”; Be. and W. think *not* superfluous. Many manuscripts read *perscriptione*.] [Note: Many manuscripts and Sich.: “shall be alleged”; 9: “shall be bound.”] persons [Note: Codices 1, 9, 10, 15, 18, Sich., and Cuj. 1 through W. read “to both”; 19 and 20, “to both groups”; the other manuscripts and Til., “in any event.” “To both” is retained: that is, both to the minor sold and to the person brought up as a slave. *Utique* arose from the abbreviation *utque*, which copyists misunderstood.].

§ 3. The same provisions [Note: 8, 10, 12–14, 17–20: “equal”; 15: “equal also.”] shall apply also to freedpersons [Note: 8: “of them”; 15: “shall be.” Aurelius of Lyons omits “among” after “also.”] who, through some gain, relapse into the same slavery [Note: 1 and 14: “the same”; 10, 13–15, 19, 20, Til., P., Pu., and W. from codex 1: “again into slavery”; the rest: “into slavery again.” Some manuscripts and Til. have *rursum*; codex 14 has “from slavery.”]. But [Note: 6–8, 12, 13, 16, 17, and Til.: “thus.”] their case [Note: 1: a corrupt *earu*, etc.] must be distinguished by this exception [Note: 20 has, above the line, “assertion.”]: persons manumitted before their fourteenth year [Note: 14: “among boys”; 20: “as adults,” omitting “who,” but “minors” is added above the line. The same witness shortly thereafter has “years.” 21: “of a minor.”] and thereafter retained in slavery, who because of their ignorance do not exercise their freedom [Note: 14, 16, 17: “is ignorant of freedom”; 12 and 13: “are ignorant of freedom”; 21: “ignorant or freedom”; 6 and 7: “is ignorant.”], and persons sold after reaching adulthood who perform the transaction [Note: Sich.: “adults who are sold”; 15 omits “sold”; 8 and 17: “perform a transaction”; 15 and Sich.: “perform.”], are not to be barred from an assertion of freedom. For ignorance or forgetfulness of the freedom granted to that age has been excused [Note: 9, 10, 15, 18–21, and P., Pu., W. from codex 1 read “or”; Go. conjectures the same. The others read “so that.” Be. wishes “and.” 6, 7, 13, 17, Til.: “ignorant law”; Til. adds “so that [there is] abolition.” 8: “abolition of ignorance”; 12: “ignorant law abolition”; 14: “ignorant law absolution”; 20: “to those ignorant,” corrected above the line to “ignorance”; 21 and Sich.: “since to those [with] freedom assigned by age, ignorance as forgetfulness, not . . .”; earlier Ri. A number of witnesses have “to freedom.”] [Note: 15: “may be.”]. But one who, with memory intact and not unaware of a sale subsequently made [Note: 9: “completed”; 20: “after the sale was made.”], binds himself shall lack the benefit of this law.

§ 4. And since relief must in turn also be provided for those who entrusted property to such persons [Note: P., Pu., and W. from codex 1: “those who entrusted property to them”; other editions: “property to them”; 10 and 18: “to those persons who entrusted property”; 19 and 20: “to whom property was entrusted”; 15: “also to those who entrusted property”; 6, 7, 12, 14, and 16 omit “property,” which Til. therefore brackets.], if anyone among all those described above proclaims himself to be free [Note: Here begins cited c. 3 of the Code of Justinian: “If anyone in a proclamation of freedom [declares] that what is in his possession,” etc. Codex 1 is corrupt. 9, 10, 18–21: “proclaim themselves.” 6, 7, 10, 13, 16, 18, 21, Sich., and Til.: “into freedom.”], he shall declare that what he has in his possession [Note: The Turin leaf ends at the syllable *es*, and this constitution ends here in P. and Pu. Pu.: “has with him for him.” 15: “the one who says himself [to be] his master”; Cuj. 1 through Cuj. 2*: “belongs to him who . . .”] belongs to the person who calls himself his master. Since there is no dispute about that [Note: 21: “would declare.” Sich.: “declares, since,” but “when” in the margin. Ri*: “since.” 8: “what.”] [Note: Code of Justinian: “there is no doubt about it.” 20 has “says” above the line.], the judge shall immediately order it restored and returned [Note: 6, 7, 10, 12, 14, and 16–19: “ordered.”].

§ 5. But if what is claimed [Note: 6 and 7: “but the claimant.” Code of Justinian omits “what.”] is disputed in connection with the business transaction [Note: 19 and, in the margin, Sich.; Cuj. 1 through Cuj. 2*: “denial.” 20: “if it has been present [in] denial [and is] disputed.” Code of Justinian: “is doubtful through denial,” a reading which W. thinks the context favors: for what is disputed through denial seems to be contrasted with what someone declares to be in his possession. The scholia on the *Basilica* support it, since, though the text itself gives the law’s sense more freely, VI, p. 478 translates: “But if what is demanded becomes doubtful by reason of denial” (*ὅπερ δὲ ἀπαιτεῖται ἐὰν γένηται τῇ ἀρνήσει ἀμφίβολον*), etc. Yet W. did not dare alter the reading, since *negotiatione* may, with Go., mean the business in which the slave had been placed by his master as an agent and for which he had not yet rendered accounts. The following text and the Visigothic interpretation confirm this explanation. Codices 10 and 18: *negociatio*; 12: “if business is lacking.”] it shall be preserved by a security furnished by the claimant of freedom, as provided in another law [Note: 6–8, 10, 13, 14, 17, 18, and Til.: “as another matter is lawfully comprehended.” The words “of the claimant . . . is” end in the Code of Justinian. According to Go., the other law is c. 1 of this title; according to W., the preceding §4.], and the claim shall be deferred [Note: 21 and Sich.: “is preserved, [and] the claim,” but there is no following verb in Sich.; perhaps this relates to the conjecture *negatione* which Sich. places in the margin, rather than to the word *ac*, as Ri. says. Ri.: *petititio*. 14: “shall be deferred”; 15 and the Code of Justinian: “shall be deferred,” approved by W.; 9, 10, 18, and Sich.: “shall be brought,” omitting “so that” in 10 and 18.], so that, if his own freedom is established [Note: 15 and the Code of Justinian omit “own.” 6 according to Ri.: “having established these as his own”; 6, 7, 16, and Til.: “having established those [things] as his own”; 8, 13, 14, 17: “having established these [as] his own”; 9: “freedom despoiled”; 19 and 20: “freedom stripped away”; 10: “freedom bound”; 18: “lawful freedom.” In the margin of Cuj. 1 through Lugd.: “and stipulated, elsewhere despoiled”; Cuj. 2 and 2* add in the margin: “elsewhere made his own.” Ri*: “freedperson.” Here the Code of Justinian adds from above: “since relief must also be given to those who entrusted property to them.”], an account of the transactions carried out by that person [Note: 19 adds “and.”] and everything owed [Note: 10 and 18 add “this”; 6 and 7: “all.” 14, 19, 20, and the Code of Justinian: “is owed.”] shall be required from him, so that the person deprived of his claim to servitude [Note: 9, 15, 19, and the Code of Justinian: feminine “slavery having been removed”; similarly the *Basilica* and its scholiast. 20: “slavery having been repelled.” Go. defends the masculine; I prefer the feminine, which suits this place better.]—who had formerly stood as master [Note: 20: “who had been entrusted, may have.”]—may retain what he had bestowed under the law of mastership upon him as upon a slave [Note: 6–8, 14, 16, 17, 20, Til., Russ. in the margin, and the Code of Justinian: “a slave,” approved by Spangenberg; but the Basilican scholium has “as to a slave” (*ὡς δούλῳ*). 9: “a slave”; 10 and 18: “as slaves, the master”; 13 and 15: “as a slave, the master”; Code of Justinian: “of ownership.” The Basilican scholium: “by right of mastership” (*δικαίῳ δεσποτείας*). W. defends our reading.] and what has been acquired from the profits and fruits of those things [Note: Go., Ri., and Ri* omit “things,” through a typographical error, but add it in Ri.’s corrections. Code of Justinian: “gathered.”], and what has been secretly taken [Note: The conjunction is missing from every manuscript except 15, and also from editions from Sich. through Ri*. Be. restores “and” from the Code of Justinian; Go. conjectures “and whatever.”] and obtained from illicit gains [Note: 10 and 18: “carefully taken”; 9, 16, 19, 20, and the Code of Justinian: “prepared”; 14: “divided”; 20 has “seized” above the line.]; for what the master had placed with a slave under the name of a peculium [Note: 10 omits “under the name.”] ought not to become free.

§ 6. But things acquired by will or gift [Note: 19, 20, and the Code of Justinian: “or.”], or purchased and made from the proceeds of those things [Note: 9: “so that those things”; 8: “or which from the proceeds of the same thing”; 20: “of the same”; 6 and 7: “of the same thing.”], shall be assigned to that same freeborn person.

§ 7. All these things, however, must remain in sequestration until the completion of the proceeding concerning freedom [Note: 7, 8, 10, 14, 16–18, and Til.: “until the proceeding concerning freedom has been completed”; 6: “until the proceeding concerning freedom”; 9: “but all these things [until] the exaction of freedom’s proceeding”; 21 and Cuj. 1 through Cuj. 2*: “concerning liberality.” Go., in his note: “concerning the proceeding of freedom.”], by which they are distinguished from the things mentioned above [Note: 9 and 15: “which,” the latter omitting “from”; 20: “because,” above the line. Code of Justinian: “so far as.” W. says *quo* is used for *quoad*, “until”; Go. understands it as “up to the point at which,” or wishes *quoad*.] [Note: 15: singular “is distinguished.”], so that, after these have been deducted by both sides [Note: Many manuscripts, Sich., and Cuj. 1 through Ri.: “these”; Ri*: “those.” Go. conjectures “separated.”] and placed in a neutral legal position [Note: W.: the common reading of the Code of Justinian is “placed in the middle,” omitting “legal.” But the Basilican scholium has “in a legal middle” (*ἐν μέσῳ δικαίῳ*), and Cujacius, *Observations* XII, 6, attests that old manuscripts of the Justinian Code read “placed in legal custody,” adducing another similar passage. 20 has “to the same [things]” above the line.], each may contend for their ownership [Note: 9: plural “may contend”; 19 and 20: “may grant”; 6–8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18: “may grant.”].

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0250C] 9, 15, 19, 24, 30, 33, 34, 36, 40, 44, Cuj. 2 through Ri*, and the margin of Sich. and Cuj. 1 through Lugd.: January; 27–29, 31, 42, and cited c. 10 of the Code of Justinian: June; Be. wishes “Praetorian Prefect” restored in the inscription in place of “Prefect of the City,” as W. prints. 35: July; 21: May.], at Thessalonica [Note: Most manuscripts read *Dessalonica*; some omit *Thess-*; others have *Thess.* or *Thessal.*, as editions before W.; W. himself, with the Code of Justinian, reads “at Thessalonica.” Shortly afterward several codices read Rufus for Rufinus.], under the consulship of Severus and Rufinus (323).

### INTERPRETATION

If a person sold while a minor, after reaching twenty-five years of age and becoming an adult [Note: 6–9, 19–21, 42, 44, and others add “if.”], has served or has been appointed steward of the purchaser’s property or manager of any undertaking, and then proclaims his free birth [Note: 9, 10, and 18 omit “appointed . . . proclaims.”], he shall be heard without prejudice from the service he performed [Note: Sich.: “slavery.”]; nor shall it prejudice him that, after reaching adulthood, he appeared to have administered the household or interests of the person by whom he was bought [Note: 20 and 21, in the margin: “as a minor.”].

This law likewise commands that the same rule be observed concerning freedpersons: if they were manumitted before their fourteenth year [Note: Some manuscripts: “their interests . . . commands [this] to be observed,” or “or whoever . . . was manumitted.” 20: “of the proposal.” The same witness later: *patronorum*, corrected from *patronum*. Cuj. 2 and 2*: thirteen for fourteen.] and, after reaching adulthood, managed their patrons’ affairs, their acts of service shall not prejudice their freedom. But whenever they wish, they may bring actions concerning their free birth or freed status [Note: 6–9, 20, and 21 omit “or,” but 21 adds it in the margin.] [Note: 20 omits “concerning.”] within the periods fixed by law.

Likewise, if a freeborn minor has been brought up by anyone and, unaware that he is free, has been sold by his foster-parent [Note: Some manuscripts: “a freeborn minor . . . free . . . has been dragged down.”] and has acted as a slave in administering the affairs or interests of the person who bought him, he shall have the right to protest before being bound by the prescription of thirty years [Note: 20: “to proclaim.” 21: “as if by a minor prescription.”]; and, as though a minor, before the prescribed periods are completed, he shall recover the freedom he lost [Note: 6, 7, 20, and 21: plural “recover.”].

Whatever the person by whom they were bought gave or donated to them, or whatever profit accrued through the administration of his property [Note: 6–9, 20, 21, 42, and 44: “he gave or donated to them . . . whatever.”], he shall have the power wholly to retain and reclaim. But if anything has been bestowed upon persons of this kind by any others, whether by will or donation [Note: 20: a corrupt *proficer—persona*.], they, now free, shall claim that alone for themselves. For whatever a freedperson acquired from the property of his patron, or a freeborn person from that of his purchaser, while serving [Note: Some manuscripts: “a will or donation . . . acquires.” 21: “freedpersons.”], the freedperson restored to liberty shall return to his patron and the freeborn person to his purchaser.

But those who, having reached adulthood [Note: Ri*: “but indeed those,” omitting “in.”], knowingly allow themselves to be sold, knowing themselves to be freeborn or freedpersons [Note: 20 adds “or.” Codices 8–10, 18, and others omit “freeborn or freedpersons”; 6, 7, 20, 21, and Sich. in the margin: “freedpersons.”], shall remain in the slavery into which [Note: 20: “the seller . . . into the same [slavery]”; 21: “if selling,” but “allow themselves to be sold” in the margin.] they knowingly pass of their own will.

## ON APPEALS

[Col. 0251A]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Florentinus . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0251B] A title of office is absent also in cited c. 8, where he is called not Florentinus but Florentius, as Reinesius writes him here. C. Th. IX, 3, 1 is inscribed “to Florentius, *rationalis*”; C. Just. I, 56, 1, drawn from cited C. Th. c. 8, reads “to Florentius, Praetorian Prefect.” Go. therefore doubts whether *rationalis* or “Praetorian Prefect” should be added here. In his annotation to this constitution he chooses the former, because this text and c. 8 concern collection of the grain levy; in his *Chronicle*, with Reinesius, he seems to prefer the latter. Reinesius also restores “Praetorian Prefect” in c. 8, but restores *rationalis* here.]

If anyone nominated for a magistracy objects, this shall be called not an appeal but a complaint; for the term “appeal” ought to be used in more important matters. Likewise, if a person appointed to collect the grain levy complains of an injustice, this shall be considered not an appeal but a complaint. Therefore the time limits for appeals need not be observed, but such complaints shall be heard immediately [Note: Cuj. 2 and 2*: incorrectly, “time.” Fol. 185 of codex 4 repeats the preceding note.].

Given on the Ides of April, at Constantinople [Note: The same reading occurs in cited C. Th. c. 8. Constantinople did not yet exist in that year: the city was Byzantium. Although Go. deletes “at Constantinople,” with Be. approving, and calls it a copyist’s error, supposing that the compilers of this Code substituted Constantinople for Byzantium, I concur and suspect that the compilers of the Theodosian Code themselves exchanged the city’s old name for the later name, better known in their own day. Historically, it is certainly not incredible that Constantine was at Byzantium in 323. Nor is this contrary to what my very kind friend Heimbach taught me: Justinianic and later writers customarily wrote “Constantinople” when referring conventionally to an eastern city, but used the old name Byzantium instead of Constantinople when mentioning the city in ordinary speech. Compare Heimbach’s edition of Athanasius Scholasticus, p. 11, notes 49 and 56. The mention of Constantinople fits the year of the law no better in C. Th. II, 24, 2, *On Partitioning an Inheritance*; VII, 20, 3, *On Veterans*; XII, 1, 8, *On Decurions*; XIII, 5, 3, *On Shipowners*; and Sirmondian c. 1, 17. See cited c. 2, note m; cited c. 3, note b; cited c. 1, note a; and cited c. 17, note t. Aurelius of Lyons: *Cons.*], under the consulship of Severus and Rufinus (323).

## ON DECURIONS

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Florentius . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0251D] The title of office is absent in codex 4 and in Till.–Cuj. 2*. Be. prints it without any mark of a lacuna. Go.–Ri* place five dots to indicate the gap; Be. only four. The Code of Justinian reads: “Emperor Constantine Augustus to Florentinus, Praetorian Prefect.” Reinesius likewise adds “Praetorian Prefect.” See C. Th. XI, 30, 12, note g.]

Decurions must be appointed to a magistracy [Note: Ri*: incorrectly, “Cagistracy.”] or to the collection of grain levies three months or more in advance, so that, if their complaint appears just, another may be substituted without impediment in the place of the person to be released.

Given on the Ides of April, at Constantinople [Note: See c. 12 cited above, note i. Aurelius of Lyons: *Cons.*], under the consulship of Severus and Rufinus (323).

## ON MILITARY AFFAIRS

[Note: Some manuscripts add “and On Plundering,” transferred from the exposition of titles. This also shows why in other manuscripts, such as 43 and several cited by Go., “On Plundering” was written in place of “On Military Affairs.” In codex 43, however, the true title was restored by a second hand. Go. explains this from the fact that the interpretation of this law and title alone was received in the Breviary of Alaric. On the interpretation of the rubric appended to the title in certain manuscripts, including 5, see my edition of the Breviary of Alaric.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus and Caesar [Note: Sich.: “Constantine”; Cuj. 1 through Cuj. 2*: “Constantine Augustus,” omitting “and Caesar,” words likewise absent in codices 15 and 25 and, according to Go., in the archetypal manuscript of this Code. Go. correctly reports that the addressee is absent; but C. Just. XII, 43, 1, *On Leave*, derived from c. 1 of this Theodosian title and to be joined with this constitution, is addressed to Leontius, Praetorian Prefect. Go., however, does not approve this; Spangenberg’s annotation makes clear that there is also extensive variation in the Code of Justinian here. Reinesius adds “to Proculus.” Go.–Ri* place five dots after “Caesar”; Be. only four.] . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . If anyone [Note: 9, 15, 16, 19, 20, 25, and 42 add “with”; Ri. thinks this taken from the Interpretation, though it can stand.] by a criminal conspiracy with barbarians [Note: 6–8, 10, 12–14, 17, 18: singular “a barbarian”; Ri. originally printed it so.] has afforded them the opportunity [Note: 42, corrected from “action”; 10 and 18: “satisfaction.”] of plundering [Note: 19 and 20: “of resources”; 25: “by opportunity.”] Romans [Note: 6, 7, 10, 18: “for plundering”; 8, 13, 19, 20: “by plundering.”] or if anyone has otherwise shared out plunder thus taken [Note: 9: “has surrendered”; 25: plural “have given.” 42: “has done [this] to Romans,” earlier “has defected.” Go. notes: “Let someone try [to read] ‘on Roman soil’: it is unnecessary.”] [Note: 15: “in some way”; Sich. and Til.: “or if in some other way.” 21 and Cuj. through Lugd., against manuscript authority: “has divided a deed”; 9: “divided things done”; 12: plural “have divided.”], he shall be burned alive [Note: 8, 10, 12, 14, 17, 18, 20, 25, the Code of Justinian, and Capitularies I, c.: “burned”; the remaining witnesses: “kindled,” not unprecedented but less fitting, and easily arising from *comburatur*. “Alive” is added by a second hand in codex 20.].

Given on the fourth [Note: 19 and 20: fifth; Ri. originally printed this. 13 and 40: third; 42: eighth; some manuscripts omit the number.] day before the Kalends of May [Note: 39: March; 43: *Mar.*; 20: “Mad.”], under the consulship of Severus [Note: 38: “Reverus”; some manuscripts: “Siviro”; 8 and 40 omit “Severus . . . consuls.”] and Rufinus (323).

### INTERPRETATION

If anyone has carried off booty with any enemies [Note: Go. notes: “wrongly.”] or shared booty with robbers, he shall be consumed by fire.

## ON LEAVE
Emperor Constantine, Augustus and Caesar.  
[Note: [Col. 0252C] *Thus the codex, Cuj. 1—Go.; but Ri., Ri*, and Be. omit “Imp.” without cause.*]  
[Note: [Col. 0252C] *Aur. Lugd. wrongly has Constantius.*]  
[Note: [Col. 0252D] *Thus Be., supported by Go. and c. 1 de Re milit., cited by Cuj. 1—Ri*. “A. etc.” (= *et cetera*), which abbreviation Go., by separating the letters, takes for “et C.,” i.e. “and Caesar,” correctly; for the codex has A ETC. Thus the stroke used as an abbreviation has been extended a little. Go. further observes in the Chronicle for this year: “The inscription of this law bears Constantine A. Caes.” Cod. Just.: “Emperors Constantine and Constans, Augusti, to Leontius, Praetorian Prefect.” See cited C. Th. c. 1, note i. Moreover, since the rubric of this title begins on folio LXII [Col. 0252B: at 6–8, 10, 12–14, 17, and 18, *barbarus*, incorrectly printed by Ri.] of the codex, at the bottom of whose page the quire-number XL is found.*]

Let it be permitted to none of the commanders or decurions [Note: [Col. 0252D] *Cod. Just. omits “or decurions.”*], or tribunes of cohorts [Note: [Col. 0252D] *Cod. Just. adds: “or their deputies and household officials during an expedition.”*], on any pretext whatever, to grant any soldier leave to depart from the camp and standards [Note: [Col. 0252D] *Thus Cod. Just. (probably G.) and Be. In the codex and Cuj. 1—Ri*, “from” is omitted, less suitably.*], or from those places in which they are posted [Note: [Col. 0252D] *Cod. Just. reads: “and the standards, or even from the places in which,” omitting the second “from.”*] [Note: [Col. 0253B] *The codex, Cuj. 1—Ri*, has “pertendant.” But Be., on Go.’s authority from Cod. Just., reads “praetendant,” which Val. also has. See Go.’s lengthy discussion in his commentary on this word.*]. [Note: [Col. 0253B] *Go. has “to learn” instead of “to depart,” an error. Shortly afterward Cod. Just. reads “contrary to this law.”*] But if anyone should dare to act contrary to the law and dismiss a soldier in defiance of the proclaimed order [Note: [Col. 0253B] *Cod. Just. has “interdictum,” approved by Reinesius; but Go. defends “indictum,” that is, the law or constitution.*] concerning leave [Note: [Col. 0253B–C] *Thus the manuscript, approved by Go., whose reading Be. restored. The codex has “sent away on leave,” but an “a” was placed by the scribe above “sent away.” Cuj. 1—Ri* read “sent the leave down,” as also does Cod. Just.; Go. printed this incorrectly.*], then, if there is no enemy outbreak at that time, let him be punished by deportation together with confiscation of his property. But if some incursion of barbarians has arisen [Note: [Col. 0253C] *Cod. Just. reads “dismissed him at a time when there was an incursion of barbarians” and lacks the words from “there is no outbreak” through “some.”*], and anyone is absent at the very time when soldiers ought to be present in camp and at the standards [Note: [Col. 0253C] *Aur. Lugd. incorrectly has “arque.” Go. prefers “ought formerly to have been,” without cause.*], let him be punished capitally [Note: [Col. 0253C] *The codex and editions before Be. have the spelling “afuerit”; likewise in the following constitution.*]. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, under the consulship of Severus and Rufinus [Note: [Col. 0253C] *Aur. Lugd. has “Ruffinus.”*] (323).

## On Extraordinary Burdens

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Ulpius Flavianus, consular governor of Aemilia and Liguria. Let patrimonial and emphyteutic estates [Note: [Col. 0253C] *“enfitheuticarii,” 4.*] situated throughout our Italy be held [Note: [Col. 0253C] *Folio 150 of codex 4 begins with the syllable “antur” of “habeantur.”*] exempt from every extraordinary burden [Note: [Col. 0253C] *In the margin Cuj. 1—2*: “restored burdens,” incorrectly printed Go. See below, c. 9 of this title. Cujacius’s conjecture is indeed ingenious, but not necessary.*], so that they pay only the canonical and customary payments, after the model of landholders in Africa. [Note: [Col. 0253C] *See C. Th. c. 9 of this title.*] Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June; read into the official acts under the consulship of Severus and Rufinus (323).

## On Bishops

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Elpidius . . . [Note: [Col. 0253C] *Edition 4 has Helpidius and omits “rank” without any mark of a lacuna. Go. supposes that he was Vicar of the City and Italy; Be. agrees. See C. Th. II.8.1, note y; XIII.5.4, note q.*]

Since we have learned that certain ecclesiastics and other servants of the Catholic sect are compelled by persons of different religions [Col. 0254A] [Note: [Col. 0254B] *Folio 396 of codex 4 begins here.*] to celebrate the sacrifices of lustral rites, we enact by this sanction [Note: [Col. 0254B] *Til.—Cuj. 2* and Ri* read “are compelled. By this”; Go. and Ri. report “are compelled, by this” and “compels. By this.”*] that, if anyone should think that those who serve the most holy law ought to be compelled to the rite of an alien superstition, he shall, if his condition permits, be publicly beaten with rods; but if consideration of rank shields him from such an injury, he shall suffer condemnation to a very heavy fine, which shall be claimed for the municipalities [Note: [Col. 0254B] *The editions have “rebus publicis.” Go.: “Does he mean cities and the resources of each commonwealth, so that we should here read *rebuspublicis* as one word? Or fiscal resources? The latter is supported by a similar example in law 2 above, On Judges (II.18.3).” I have written with the codex, which confirms Go.’s conjecture. [Col. 0254C] *rebuspublicis*, Summary of C. Th.: “the fisc.”*]. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, at Sirmium [Note: [Col. 0254C] *Edition 4, Til.—Cuj. 2*, and Lab. have “Sirmi”; Go.—Ri* have “Sirm I”; Be. has “Sirmii.”*], under the consulship of Severus and Rufinus (323).

## On the Sale of Pledges Held on Account of Tribute

[Note: [Col. 0254C] *Cod. Just.: “On the seizure and sale of pledges on account of tribute.”*]

Emperor Constantine Augustus . . . [Note: [Col. 0254C] *Go. thinks the inscription, as in the following law, should be “to the governor of Baetica.” There is no indication of a lacuna in codex 4 or Til.—Ludg.; Cuj. 2—Ri* have an asterisk.*]

Since the letters of your predecessor sent to Proculianus [Note: [Col. 0254C] *Above the letters “li” in the word, codex 4 has an e added by a second hand: Proculeianus.*], tribune and master of offices, state that the slaves of certain provincials were seized as pledges and retained under official custody because they had not provided canonical garments or horses [Note: [Col. 0254C] *The editions before Be. punctuate: “were retained, because.”*]; and since neither their masters recovered these slaves after paying their debts, nor did others buy them [Note: [Col. 0254C] *Til.—Cuj. 2* punctuate: “bought them, fearing that.”*], fearing that this sale might be annulled [Note: [Col. 0254C] *Aur. Lugd. incorrectly has the present tense, “may be annulled.”*]: we order that the masters of the slaves [Note: [Col. 0254C] *Folio 144 of codex 4 begins with the letters “cipiorum” of “mancipiorum.”*] be granted a period of two months to pay the debts, so that, when the debts of the transaction have been paid [Note: [Col. 0254C] *Cuj. 2 and 2* incorrectly have “may pay.”*] [Note: [Col. 0254C] *Cuj. 1—2* and Go.’s notes emend “unless, after the transaction,” approved by Be., correctly.*], whoever comes forward to purchase them may securely buy the slaves [Note: [Col. 0254C] *Go. incorrectly has the singular “slave.”*]. Posted on the day before the Kalends of January, at Castulo, under the consulship of Severus and Rufinus (323).

# Constantine’s Law Concerning Piety toward God and the Christian Religion

[Note: [Col. 0253] *The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.*]

Victor Constantine, Greatest Augustus, to the provincials of Palestine.

## I

It had long ago become evident among those who think rightly and wisely concerning God, through a manifest distinction removing every doubt, how great the difference is between zealous observers of the venerable Christian religion and its opponents and despisers. But now, through clearer proofs and deeds far more illustrious, both the absurdity of doubt itself and the greatness of the power of the supreme God are made plain. For those who faithfully observe the venerable law and dare violate none of its commands have an abundance of all good things, and suitable strength, with good hope and confidence, for accomplishing what they undertake. But those who have embraced an impious disposition have met with results corresponding to their conduct. For who, while failing to acknowledge God as the author of good things and refusing to honour him with due worship, could ever obtain anything good? The facts themselves certainly establish the truth of our words.

### Greek Version

Victor Constantine, Greatest Augustus, to the provincials of Palestine.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] *“To the provincials of Palestine.” In the Medicean codex I found written “to the Palestinian provincials.” Moreover, I began chapter 35 from these words, following the authority of the Royal and Fuket manuscripts. “To the provincials” is also read in the old copies.*]

[Note: [Col. 0254D] *“Removing all [doubt].” Write from the Medicean codex “and removing all [doubt].” And a little later, from the same codex, one should read “the observance of Christianity,” as is also read in the Royal copies and the Fuket codex.*]

[Note: [Col. 0255D] *“Those who hold it in contempt.” The Medicean codex has “those who wish to hold it,” which seems more correct to me.*]

[Note: *“And the outcomes.” The reading of the Medicean codex is much more correct: “The outcomes too corresponded. For who could obtain any good,” etc. And after “willing,” it also has the interrogative mark.*]

[Note: *“Proof to the.” Much more elegantly the Medicean codex writes: “and the deeds furnish proof of what has been said.”*]

I. From the beginning and long ago, among those who hold right and prudent opinions about the higher power, the distinction was evident, removing every doubt from afar: how great was the difference between exact observance of the most venerable service of Christianity and those who had made war upon it and held it in contempt. But now, through deeds more conspicuous and achievements more splendid, both the irrationality of doubt has been demonstrated and the greatness of the power of the great God: when those who faithfully revere the most holy law and dare not annul any command have abundant good things, excellent strength for their undertakings, and the attendance of good hopes; whereas for those who adopted an impious disposition, the outcomes too correspond to their choices. For who could obtain any good while neither recognizing God, the cause of good things, nor being willing to render him due worship? The deeds too furnish proof of what has been said.

## An Example from Ancient Times

### II

If anyone should review in thought the times extending from the past down to our own day, and contemplate in mind events long ago accomplished, he will certainly find that those who made justice and integrity the foundation of their actions attained a happy outcome to their plans, and, as though from some sweet root, gathered every sweetest fruit. But those who rashly attempted unjust acts, who in madness of mind exalted themselves against God himself, and had no sense of piety toward humankind, but inflicted exile, disgrace, confiscation of property, slaughter, and very many things of that sort; and who never repented or recalled their minds to a better course, received a corresponding recompense. Nor do these things happen irrationally or contrary to reason.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] *“From above down to here.” The particle “and” is absent in the Medicean codex, nor is it especially necessary. Next, where “and the actions formerly done” is read, that codex has “and the actions ever done.” Likewise, for “the end of the undertaking,” it writes “they brought their undertakings to an end,” as I also found written in the copies and the Fuket codex.*]

[Note: [Col. 0256D] *“And toward the human race.” This passage was mutilated; from the Medicean codex it must be restored as follows: “either having madly raged without understanding against the higher power, or having conceived no holy thought toward the human race,” etc.*]

[Note: *“Not irrationally.” The Medicean codex writes: “would not irrationally, nor contrary to reason, occur.” The Royal codex certainly also has “would occur.”*]

### Greek Version

II. If, then, anyone should run in thought through the times extending from the beginning down to the present, and contemplate in mind the deeds previously accomplished, he would find that all who laid a just and good foundation for their affairs brought their enterprises to a good and advancing end and, as it were, gathered sweet fruit from a certain pleasant root. But those who attempted unjust deeds with audacity, either raged senselessly against the higher power or conceived no holy thought for humankind, but dared exile, dishonour, confiscations, slaughter, and many such things; and never repented nor turned their minds to better things, received an equal recompense in return. And this did not happen irrationally or contrary to reason.

## On Those Who Suffered Persecution and on Persecutors

### III

For all who undertake actions with a just purpose, keep continually before their eyes the fear of God, retain steadfast faith in him, and do not value the threats and dangers of this present life above the hope of future good things—even though they may experience many bitter and grievous things for a short time—nevertheless, firmly believing that greater rewards are stored up for them, bear the evils that come upon them without distress. And the more severe the calamities they experience, the more illustrious the glory they win. But those who despised justice and equity, neither acknowledged God himself nor hesitated to afflict with insults and most bitter punishments those who faithfully worshipped God; nor did they think themselves wretched for punishing persons brought to trial on such grounds, but considered happy and blessed those who nevertheless maintained inviolate piety toward God amid such great evils: the armies of these men were partly slain and partly put to flight. Finally, defeated in every battle, they themselves at last succumbed.

[Note: [Col. 0256D] *“For all who.” I began this chapter from these words on the authority of the Fuket codex and Royal copies.*]

[Note: *“But all who dishonoured justice.” The Medicean codex reads more correctly: “But all who either dishonoured justice or failed to recognize the higher power.” This is what he said above in chapter 25, as I noted there: “those who attempted unjust deeds, either madly raged without understanding against the higher power, or conceived no holy thought toward humankind.”*]

[Note: *“They punished on pretexts.” The Medicean codex reads, more correctly in my view: “because they punished them on such pretexts.” Next, the same codex has, as in the text printed above, “ended in utter defeat.”*]

### Greek Version

III. For all who undertake actions with a just purpose, continually keep in mind the fear of the higher power, preserve steadfast faith in it, and do not value present fears and dangers above those hopes which are to come: even if for a time they experience certain hardships, because they believe that greater honours are laid up for them, they do not bear what befalls them heavily, but attain glory more splendid in proportion as they experience more grievous sufferings. But all who dishonoured justice or did not acknowledge the higher power, and dared subject those who faithfully pursued it to insults and incurable punishments, did not judge themselves miserable because they punished people on such grounds, but considered blessed and fortunate those who preserved their piety toward the higher power even in such circumstances. Many of their armies fell, many were turned to flight, and every battle-line of theirs ended in utter defeat.

## That Persecution Was the Cause of Evils for Those Waging War

### IV

From such crimes arose grievous wars and ruinous devastations. Hence came scarcity of the things necessary for the daily use of life, and an abundance of impending evils. Hence the authors of such great impiety, falling into extreme calamities, either perished utterly by an unhappy end or, living amid the highest disgrace, confessed that life was more bitter than any death and repaid their unjust deeds with, as it were, proportionate punishments. For each of them was afflicted by evils proportionately more severe as he had, in extreme madness, more violently undertaken, as he hoped, to overthrow the divine law. Thus not only did the evils of this life seem grievous to them, but the fear and expectation of punishments in the world below tortured them much more bitterly.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] *“Of impending evils.” The Medicean codex has “of impending terrors.” A little earlier the same codex reads “from such things arise,” etc.*]

[Note: *“Utterly destructive.” The Medicean codex reads, as does our text, “they met with an utterly ruinous death.” A little later it writes, undoubtedly more correctly, “each found so great a measure of misfortune.”*]

### Greek Version

IV. From such things arose grievous wars and utterly destructive devastations. Hence came shortages of what is necessary for daily needs and an abundance of impending evils. Hence the leaders of such great impiety, either enduring the utmost calamities, met with an utterly ruinous death; or, living a most shameful life, recognized it to be more grievous than death and received punishments, as it were, proportionate to their injustices. For each encountered so great a measure of misfortune as, in his irrationality, he had been driven to make war, as he supposed, upon the divine law. Thus not only were matters of life grievous to them, but they also expected with the utmost terror the punishments beneath the earth.

## That God Chose Constantine as Minister of Good Things

### V

When such grave impiety had taken hold of humankind, and the commonwealth, as though a deadly pestilence were spreading, had been brought into extreme danger of destruction and therefore required great care and saving aid, what comfort, what remedy did God then devise to deliver us from these evils? By “God” I mean him who alone truly is God and holds everlasting power throughout all ages. Nor is it arrogance for one who acknowledges benefits bestowed by God to speak magnificently. For God sought my ministry as suitable for accomplishing his will, and decided to employ my service. Beginning from the British Ocean and from those regions where a necessary decree ordains that the sun should set, I, by a certain heavenly power, expelled and dispersed all the evils that occupied the world: both so that humankind, instructed and formed by our ministry, might be recalled to the observance of the most holy law, and so that the blessed faith, under God’s guidance, might increase.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] *“Having occupied humankind.” The Medicean codex has “human affairs.” A little later it has “and requiring much saving treatment,” without the conjunction.*]

[Note: *“It must be understood.” The Medicean codex has the simple form “it must be understood,” instead of the compound, which is less harsh. The same codex then has “which alone both is and truly exists.”*]

[Note: [Col. 0258D] *“It would surely be boastfulness.” The Medicean codex reads more correctly: “It would surely not be boastfulness for one who acknowledges the beneficence from the higher power,” an emendation confirmed by Sozomen, book I, chapter 8, where he summarizes this law of Constantine.*]

[Note: *“For my ministry.” The Medicean codex omits “for,” which seems to me wholly superfluous.*]

[Note: *“By a certain higher power.” The last two words are absent in the Medicean codex, and “higher” refers to the preceding word, “necessity.”*]

[Note: *“All evils.” After these words the Fuket, Turnebus, and Savile manuscripts add “removed them from the way.” Christophorson reads thus, as is clear from his very confused translation here. I, however, think the words “he who, beginning from that sea by Britain,” etc., are said of Constantine himself, not of God, as Musculus and Christophorson thought. There is therefore no need of “removed them from the way,” which is read neither in the Medicean nor Royal codex nor in the old copies—especially because “I proceed even to the eastern regions” follows shortly afterward.*]

### Greek Version

V. When such grave and heavy impiety occupied human affairs, and public matters were in danger of being utterly ruined as though by some pestilential disease, and required great and saving treatment, what relief, what deliverance from evils did the divine power devise? By “the divine” one must certainly understand that which alone truly exists and has enduring power throughout all time. Yet it would surely be boastfulness for one who acknowledges beneficence from the higher power to speak magnificently; for it sought and judged my ministry suitable for accomplishing its own will. Beginning from that sea by Britain, and from the regions where by a certain necessity the sun is appointed to set, impelled by a higher power and dispersing all the evils that occupied everything, so that humankind, instructed through my ministry, might at once be recalled to the service of the most holy law, and blessed faith might at once increase under the guidance of the higher power.

## Constantine’s Pious Words Concerning God and Praise of the Confessors

### VI

For I shall never be ungrateful or forgetful of the benefit bestowed. Since I firmly believed that this most excellent ministry had been granted me as the highest gift, I at last reached the eastern regions. As they were afflicted by more grievous calamities, they demanded from us a greater remedy. I most firmly believe that my whole soul, all that I breathe, and whatever is moved in the inmost recesses of my mind, are owed by me to the supreme God. I know well that those who rightly and sincerely pursue the hope of heavenly things and have firmly and especially established it in God’s dwelling have no need of human favour, since they obtain honours greater in proportion as they have withdrawn themselves farther from the faults and crimes of mortality. Nevertheless, I judge it my duty to remove as far as possible from persons wholly free of blame and accusation the most bitter necessities temporarily imposed upon them and the wholly undeserved tortures. Otherwise it would be most absurd that their courage and steadfastness should have been tested and recognized while those who had resolved to persecute them for worshipping God were reigning, but that, when a servant of God administers the empire, their glory should not be advanced to a more illustrious and blessed height.

[Note: [Col. 0259C] *“For I shall not be ungrateful.” The Medicean codex reads “for I should never be grateful,” correctly, if one restores “ungrateful.” These words should be understood parenthetically. The Fuket and Turnebus manuscripts read “for I should not be ungrateful.”*]

[Note: [Col. 0259D] *“The most excellent.” The Medicean codex writes this entire passage far more correctly: “Believing this most excellent ministry to be a gift graciously bestowed upon me, I proceed even to the eastern regions,” etc. Moreover, these words conclude the entire period beginning with “he who, from the sea by Britain” in the preceding chapter, which the translators did not perceive. Nor could I ever have discovered it without the aid of the Medicean codex.*]

[Note: *“Distinctively and securely.” The Medicean codex has “distinctively and royally, securely,” etc. Emperor Constantine calls the hope of the children of God “royal,” because it surpasses all human things.*]

[Note: *“In proportion as they themselves.” Before I obtained the Medicean codex, I had seen that this must be the reading; the codex completely confirmed my conjecture. It also has “so much the more,” with *n* written below.*]

[Note: *“To something more splendid.” In the Medicean codex I found: “that their glory should be raised to a more splendid and blessed condition.”*]

### Greek Version

VI. For I shall not be ungrateful for the favour due; believing this most excellent ministry to be a gift graciously bestowed on me, I proceed even to the eastern regions, which, held by more grievous calamities, called aloud for a greater remedy from us. I have firmly believed that my entire soul, everything whatsoever that I breathe, and, generally, whatever stirs in the inmost recesses of my mind are owed by me to the greatest God. I know accurately that those who rightly pursue heavenly hope and establish it distinctly and securely in divine places have no need of human favour, obtaining honours greater in proportion as they have separated themselves from earthly deficiencies and evils. Yet I think it fitting for us now to remove as far as possible from those who are free of all blame and liability the necessities imposed on them for a time and the undeserved tortures. Otherwise it would be most absurd that, under those eager to persecute these persons on account of worship of the divine, their soul’s endurance and steadfastness should have been adequately recognized, whereas under a servant of God their glory should not be raised to something more splendid and blessed.

## A Law Releasing Persons from Exile, Municipal Enrollment, and Confiscation of Property

### VII

Therefore all who exchanged their native country for foreign soil because they refused to betray the worship and faith of God to which they had devoted themselves with their whole minds, having been condemned by cruel judicial sentences at whatever time; and all who were entered on the roll of the curia despite not previously being among the curiales: now restored to their paternal estates and customary leisure, let them give thanks to God, liberator of all. Likewise, whoever was stripped of property and punished by the loss of all possessions, and has hitherto led a most miserable life: let these also, restored to their former homes, families, and possessions, joyfully enjoy the beneficence of God.

[Note: [Col. 0260C] *“Judicial decisions.” The Medicean codex has “judgments,” and shortly afterward “were enrolled together in the lists,” as in the text printed above. The Royal copies have “were enrolled,” as does the Fuket codex.*]

[Note: [Col. 0260D] *“Paternal estates.” The Medicean codex more correctly reads “restored also to paternal estates.” The Royal codex certainly likewise has “restored.” Eusebius here calls paternal lands ancestral estates. For those bound to curiae—usually the wealthiest were enrolled in them—had their lands made over to the curiae. Thus, though they withdrew themselves by flight, they gained nothing, since the curia seized their estates. Constantine therefore decreed by this constitution that those assigned to curiae because of Christian faith, provided that they were not curiales by origin, should recover their paternal property which the curia had seized. Christophorson therefore translates wrongly “native residences.” Turnebus amended in his codex to “having been restored.” But the Fuket codex has “having restored themselves,” as do Savile and Christophorson.*]

[Note: *“Having been afflicted.” The Medicean codex has “having been struck,” which is preferable. It is a term of civil law. The phrase “to be struck by a fine” occurs frequently in imperial constitutions.*]

### Greek Version

VII. Therefore, if any exchanged their native country for residence abroad because they did not disregard the honour and faith toward the divine power to which they had consecrated themselves with whole souls, having been subjected to harsh judicial decisions at whatever times; and if any were enrolled among municipal councillors despite not previously completing their number: let such persons, restored to paternal estates and customary leisure, offer thanksgivings to God, the liberator of all. And if any have been deprived of their possessions and, struck by the loss of all their property, have hitherto led a most miserable life, let these also, restored to their former dwellings, families, and estates, joyfully enjoy the beneficence bestowed by the higher power.

## Likewise, Those Relegated to Islands

### VIII

We further command that all who are held on islands against their will shall enjoy the benefit of this provision, so that those who until now have been confined by mountain ruggedness and by the surrounding sea, freed at last from gloomy and inhuman solitude, may restore themselves to their relatives and friends and fulfill their wishes and desires. And those who have long lived in the utmost poverty and miserable squalor, obtaining return as though a prize were offered them, and released thereafter from anxieties, may live among us without fear. For that anyone should live in fear under us as rulers, who both boast and believe that we are servants of God, is a thing most absurd even to hear of, much less to believe. For we are so disposed as to correct the wrongs of others.

[Note: [Col. 0261C] *“Families.” The Medicean codex has the singular “family.” Shortly afterward, as in our text, “may joyfully enjoy.”*]

[Note: [Col. 0261D] *“Whom islands hold against their will.” He did not say “against their will” without reason, on account of monks who lived a solitary life on islands.*]

[Note: *“So that those until now.” The Medicean codex presents a different text: “so that at long last [those confined] by mountains,” etc.; a little later, “might give them back”; likewise, “those who lived poorly,” etc.*]

[Note: *“Odious squalor.” In the Medicean codex I found “disgraceful squalor,” which may perhaps be more correct. It means squalor bearing a certain odious stigma.*]

[Note: [Col. 0262C] *“Not in fear with us.” The entire passage is written very differently in the Medicean codex. It places a full stop after “released.” It then reads: “For to live in fear under us, who boast and believe ourselves to be servants of God, would be one of the most absurd things even merely to hear of, much less that anyone should endure either the hardships of mines or service in public works.” That reading seems to me sounder and plainer than the received text.*]

### Greek Version

VIII. Yet we also command that all whom islands hold against their will shall enjoy this provision: so that those hitherto shut in by mountain fastnesses and the encircling sea, once freed from gloomy and inhuman solitude, may restore themselves to their loved ones, fulfilling their desired longing. And those who have long led a poor life amid a certain odious squalor, treating their return as though it were some prize, and freed henceforth from anxieties, may live among us without fear. For to live in fear under us, who boast and believe ourselves servants of God, would be among the most absurd things even merely to hear of, still less to believe, since we are naturally disposed to correct the sins of others.

## Likewise, Those Who Had Been Condemned Dishonourably to Mines and Public Works

### IX

Whoever has been condemned either to the laborious work of mines or to service in public works, let them exchange continuous labours for sweet leisure and henceforth lead a lighter life according to their own wishes, bringing the hardships of immoderate toil to an end in gentle and tranquil rest. And although some have lost their common liberty and been marked by infamy, let them joyfully recover their former dignity—separated from them, as it were, by a long exile—and hasten to return to their native country.

[Note: [Col. 0262D] *“Sweet leisure.” The Medicean codex has “pleasant”; the Fuket manuscript, “sweeter.”*]

[Note: *“Even if they have fallen from common [freedom].” Write from the Medicean codex “but even if,” much more correctly. Turnebus had emended his codex to “and if they have fallen from common civil standing,” etc. But the reading of the Medicean codex is truer and is confirmed also by the Fuket codex.*]

### Greek Version

IX. Those who have been condemned either to toil in wretched mines or to perform services in public works, exchanging continuous labours for sweet leisure, may lead a lighter life, like those now living with freedom of choice, bringing the excessive distastefulness of their toils to a gentle relief. But even if some have fallen from common civil standing and suffered dishonour, let them, with fitting joy, recover their former dignity—separated from them, as it were, by a long journey—and hasten to their own native countries.

## On Confessors Who Had Served in the Army

### X

Furthermore, those who were formerly distinguished by military rank and lost it on a cruel and unjust pretext—namely, because, professing the worship of God, they preferred it to their rank—shall be free to choose whichever they prefer: either to resume military service and remain in the same position that they formerly held, or to live freely under honourable discharge. For it is equitable and consistent with reason that one who has shown such greatness and constancy of spirit in enduring tortures inflicted on him should, as he chooses, obtain either leisure or rank.

[Note: [Col. 0262D] *“In military ranks.” The Medicean codex has “in military offices.” Shortly afterward: “because of the cruel,” etc.*]

[Note: *“They preferred.” The Medicean codex reads: “they held knowledge of the higher power more highly than the rank they possessed; let it be according to their choice.”*]

[Note: [Col. 0263C] *“To live in freedom.” From the Medicean codex one should write “to live in honourable free leisure.” This is confirmed by Sozomen, book I, chapter 8, where he summarizes this law of Constantine. In the Fuket codex I found “to live in honourable freedom.” The Medicean, however, has “to live in honourable free leisure.”*]

### Greek Version

X. Moreover, for those who had once held military rank and fell from it because of a harsh and unjust pretext—because, confessing knowledge of the higher power, they preferred it to the rank which they possessed—let it be left to their choice either to remain in military service in the rank in which they had been, if they approve military service, or to live in honourable discharge and freedom. For it would be fitting and consistent that one who displayed such greatness of soul and endurance in the dangers brought upon him should, according to his choice, enjoy either leisure or honour.

## On the Liberation of Those Assigned to Women’s Workshops or Given into Slavery

### XI

Whoever was forcibly stripped of noble birth and subjected to a judicial sentence of this sort—being cast into women’s workshops or linen-weaving establishments to endure harsh and wretched labour, or treated as servants of the fisc, though their former splendour of birth had availed them nothing—let them rejoice both in the honours they formerly enjoyed and in the privilege of freedom, recover their former dignity, and henceforth pass their lives in complete happiness. And whoever exchanged liberty for slavery through the unjust and inhuman audacity of a seller, and repeatedly lamented services unfamiliar to him, perceiving himself, as by a sudden transformation, made a slave instead of a free person: now, by our command, recovering his former liberty, let him restore himself to his parents and undertake labours suited to a free person, having wholly erased from his mind the memory of the unsuitable services which he formerly performed.

[Note: [Col. 0263C] *“And indeed all who.” The Medicean codex has “and indeed also all who.”*]

[Note: *“Harsh and wretched.” In the Medicean codex I found “unaccustomed and,” from which, despite the corrupt word, I immediately recognized the true and genuine reading of this passage. I therefore write “unaccustomed and wretched.” For such service in women’s workshops and weaving establishments is unfamiliar to freeborn persons. The same codex has “labour,” not “toil.”*]

[Note: *“Though it had availed them nothing.” The Medicean codex more correctly has “though it had availed them nothing.” Shortly afterward it correctly reads from the same manuscript “rejoicing in noble things.”*]

[Note: [Col. 0263D] *“And he who exchanged slavery for liberty.” The Medicean codex adds the word, as follows: “and he who exchanged slavery for liberty,” correctly in my view. The emperor distinguishes two classes of persons: some noble persons were assigned to women’s workshops or made servants of fiscal estates, a more honourable sort of slavery; others, of lower condition, were sold to private persons. The Fuket codex has “and he who exchanged liberty for slavery.”*]

[Note: *“By the recklessness of a citizen.” The Medicean codex has “by the recklessness, of course,” but he means the audacity and cruelty of the judge who deprived a free person of liberty because he confessed the true divinity. In the Royal copies I found “of a seller”; Fuket has “of a seller.”*]

[Note: *“Lamenting.” The Medicean codex more correctly has “having lamented.”*]

[Note: [Col. 0264C] *“In which he formerly toiled.” The Medicean codex more elegantly has “which he formerly endured,” and shortly afterward “having expelled [them] from his memory,” as is also read in the Royal copies and Fuket codex. These words make sufficiently plain what I said: in this latter passage Constantine speaks of persons of lower and plebeian condition who had been sold by judicial sentence. For of those who were distinguished by splendour of birth Constantine says that they may now recover their former dignity. The latter he directs instead to the ordinary services and labours of free people.*]

### Greek Version

XI. And indeed all who, forcibly deprived of noble birth, suffered such a judicial judgment that, cast into women’s workshops or linen-weaving establishments, they endured harsh and wretched toil, or were regarded as servants of the treasury, their former birth having given them no help: let them rejoice in both the honours which they formerly enjoyed and the blessings of liberty; having recovered their accustomed dignities, let them henceforth live in complete joy. And he who exchanged liberty for slavery through the unlawful and inhuman recklessness of a seller, repeatedly lamenting unfamiliar services and recognizing himself as suddenly made a slave instead of free, now recovering his former liberty by our command, let him restore himself to his parents and undertake labours suited to a free person, casting from memory the unsuitable services in which he formerly toiled.

## On the Succession to the Property of Martyrs, Confessors, Exiles, and Those Whose Property Was Taken into the Treasury

### XII

We ought not to pass over in silence the property of which individuals were deprived for various reasons. Therefore, if any, undergoing the excellent and divine contest of martyrdom with fearless and confident spirit, were stripped of their possessions; or if, having become confessors, they acquired hope of eternal goods; or if, compelled to leave their native country because they refused to yield to persecutors by betraying their faith, they too were deprived of possessions; finally, if any, though not condemned by a capital sentence, nevertheless suffered loss of property: we order that the inheritance of all these persons be granted to their nearest relatives. Since the laws expressly prescribe that the nearer relatives receive the inheritance, it is easy to determine to whom the inheritance is due. Moreover, it accords with reason that those should enter upon the succession who would have been the nearer heirs had the persons concerned died their own deaths.

[Note: [Col. 0264C] *“For which each.” Write from the Medicean codex: “the property of which each was deprived for various reasons.” Shortly afterward: “having undergone the excellent and divine contest.” But the words “for which” are not found in the Royal copies either. I found the beginning of this period variously written in old books. The Medicean codex has “nor must the matter of property be passed over”; the copies, “nor must the matter be passed over”; Turnebus had emended his codex to “nor should it be passed over”; the Fuket codex has “nor must the matter of property of which each,” etc.; and the Royal codex also has “nor must it be passed over.” There is therefore no doubt that this is the true reading, which I do not know why Robert Estienne altered.*]

[Note: [Col. 0264D] *“And having become confessors.” The Medicean codex reads “or if any, having become confessors,” which I do not doubt is more correct. For, having spoken earlier of martyrs, he now speaks of confessors. Shortly afterward write from the same codex: “having been compelled because they did not yield to their persecutors by disregarding the faith, they were deprived of their possessions,” etc.*]

[Note: *“Or if indeed any were not.” Christophorson omitted this section because it seemed a merely superfluous repetition of what preceded. But since these words are also read in the Medicean codex, they should not rashly be deleted. For after the emperor has spoken of martyrs, confessors, and exiles who had left their country through fear of a capital sentence pronounced against them, he now treats those who, though not condemned by capital sentence, had nevertheless been deprived of property.
