They were not among martyrs or confessors, since they had not been brought to trial. Nor were they exiles, but remained in their native country while being forcibly stripped of their possessions. Certainly four classes of persons are listed in the title of this chapter. But Christophorson omitted the fourth. In the following chapter, however, the emperor lists only three classes, wholly passing over these last persons.*]

*Inherited source boundary: the supplied source ends here, in the middle of the editorial discussion.*
[Col. 0265C] “The laws prescribe that the nearer among the nearest kin [shall inherit].” In intestate successions, the law calls each nearest agnate to the inheritance, if there are no heirs in his own power, as Gaius teaches in the sixteenth title of his *Institutes*. Hence in law they are called legitimate agnatic heirs, because the law devolved the inheritance upon these alone. Cognates, indeed, could not be heirs by civil law, but were called to the inheritance only by praetorian law, as the jurists teach. Moreover, among cognates the nearest received the inheritance, just as among agnates; but the difficulty in this place is which persons are meant by the term *anchisteōn* [“of the nearest kin”]: agnates or cognates. Certainly, if by “laws” we understand the laws of the Twelve Tables, agnates must be meant. Sozomen has: “to those nearest in kin.”

“And that.” In the Royal manuscript one reads “and further,” a reading which I have followed in my translation. Yet “that” was formerly written in that manuscript, and was subsequently corrected to “further” by a later hand.

“Who would also have been more closely related, had those persons met their end naturally.” In the Medicean manuscript one reads: “who might have been more closely related.” The sense of this passage is quite obscure. Christophorson indeed translates it thus: “And it is evident that it is also reasonable that those should succeed who are more closely connected by domestic association, especially since the martyrs themselves met death not upon conviction for any crime, but led thereto by their own will.” But much in this translation is open to criticism. First, *automaton telos* [a “natural end”] cannot be said of martyrs. [Col. 0266C] Secondly, the discussion here is not of martyrs alone, but also of confessors and refugees who had died a natural death. It is therefore better to translate it here as “by their own natural death.” For the Greeks commonly speak thus, and Eusebius in particular, unless I am mistaken. Finally, he has translated *oikeioterous* very badly as “more closely connected by domestic association,” whereas it means “nearer relatives.” I therefore translate the whole passage as follows: “It is consonant with reason that those should come to the succession who would have been nearer relatives, had those persons died a natural death.” Our interpretation is confirmed both by what I have said above and by the Emperor’s saying “who would have been more closely related,” not “are.” By “those persons,” moreover, he means the martyrs.

[Col. 0263B] XII. Nor must the matter of the estates of which each person was deprived on various pretexts be passed over. If any persons, having endured the noble and divine contest of martyrdom, were deprived of their possessions through a fearless and resolute disposition and, having become confessors, secured for themselves eternal hope; and if any, compelled to migrate because they had not yielded to their persecutors by betraying the faith, were likewise deprived of their possessions; or if some, though not condemned to death, nevertheless unhappily suffered deprivation of their property: we order that their inheritances be assigned to their relatives by kinship. Since the laws prescribe that the nearer among the nearest kin [shall inherit], it is easy to determine to whom the inheritances properly belong, and that these would rightly have come to the succession, since they would have been nearer relatives, had those persons met their end naturally.

## THAT, WHEN KINSMEN ARE LACKING, THE CHURCH SHALL TAKE THE INHERITANCE, AND THAT BEQUESTS SHALL REMAIN VALID

[Col. 0265]

[Col. 0265A] XIII. But if no kinsman survives to take, as reason requires, the inheritance of those whom I have mentioned above—namely martyrs and confessors, or those who migrated from their native country for such a reason—we decree that the Church of each locality shall enter upon the inheritance. Nor indeed will this be burdensome to the deceased, if the Church for whose sake they underwent every hardship should obtain them as its heir.

[Col. 0265B] It must also necessarily be added that, if any of those mentioned above have given any portion of their goods to anyone, ownership shall, as is equitable, remain firm and valid to that recipient.

[Note: Col. 0266D]

“It shall not in every case.” Write, from the Medicean manuscript, “but it shall not in every case.” A little earlier the same manuscript writes “neither of the confessors,” more correctly, as in chapter 35. Likewise, “nor of the migrants indeed, of the …,” etc.

“Moreover, it must be laid down.” I would prefer to write “it must moreover be added,” as Turnebus and Savile emended it. And thus it is written in the Fuketian manuscript. A little later, the Medicean manuscript reads: “as if any of those previously mentioned …”

[Col. 0266A] XIII. But if none of the nearest kinsmen should remain to become, as reason would require, heir of any of those previously mentioned—neither, I mean, of the martyrs, nor of those who confessed, nor of those migrants who departed for such a reason—let the Church in each locality always be appointed to succeed to the inheritance. Yet this will certainly not be burdensome even to the departed, if the Church for whose sake they endured all their sufferings should happily become heir. Moreover, this too must be laid down: if any of those previously mentioned gave any of their possessions to persons whom they wished, it is reasonable that ownership remain valid to those persons.

## THAT THOSE WHO HAVE OCCUPIED SUCH PLACES, HOUSES, OR GARDENS SHALL RESTORE THEM, WITH THE EXCEPTION OF THE PROFITS

[Col. 0265]

[Col. 0265B] XIV. Further, so that no ambiguity may appear in our ordinance, but what is lawful may be readily known to anyone, let all understand that, whether they hold an estate, houses, a garden, or anything else among the possessions of those whom I mentioned above, they will act rightly and properly [Col. 0265C] if they voluntarily come forward and restore the property without any delay. And although some may appear to have received large profits from those properties on no just title of possession, nevertheless we judge that it is by no means equitable to reclaim those profits from them.

[Note: Col. 0266D]

“Therefore, even if in the highest degree.” In the Medicean manuscript one reads: “For even if some should appear to have profited greatly from them …” And a little later the same manuscript has: “having profited, and that a claim for these things should be made,” etc. This is excellent, in my judgment. For this is the second member of the period. The final member is “nevertheless, however,” etc., which in the printed editions has been wrongly severed and transferred to the following chapter.

[Col. 0266B] XIV. But so that no confusion may appear in the ordinance, and what is just may be readily known by all, let all see that, if they possess an estate, a house, a garden, or anything else belonging to those previously mentioned, it is good and advantageous for them both to acknowledge this and to restore it with [Col. 0266C] all speed. Therefore, even if some of them should appear to have reaped much profit from unjust possession, we judge it unjust that a claim should be made for those profits.

## HOW PETITIONS CONCERNING THESE MATTERS OUGHT TO BE SUBMITTED

[Col. 0265]

XV. But let them themselves candidly declare from what sources and how great profits they have collected, and request that pardon for this offense be granted them by us: so that both their former avarice may be cured by such amendment, and God Most High, accepting this satisfaction as a kind of repentance, may graciously forgive their errors. Yet perhaps those established as masters of these possessions—if indeed they either deserve or can be called by that name—will offer the following in their defense: that it was altogether impossible for them then to refrain from those things, when a manifold spectacle of every kind of evil lay before their eyes: when persons were brutally driven out and mercilessly destroyed; when possessions lay ruined and recklessly scattered here and there; when there were frequent proscriptions of the innocent, an insatiable frenzy of persecutions, and [Col. 0268B] sales of property.

But if any should perhaps rely upon such arguments and persist in excuses for their own avarice, they will find that this will not go unpunished, especially since it is precisely by this means that we render our service and ministry to God Most High. Whatever destructive necessity formerly compelled them to receive, it is now dangerous to retain. Moreover, insatiable desires must in every way be diminished, partly by reason and partly by examples.

[Note: Col. 0267C]

“May avarice be dissolved.” More correctly, the Medicean manuscript reads: “may avarice be healed.”

“Being brutally driven away, mercilessly destroyed, carelessly cast aside, frequent confiscations of those guilty of nothing,” etc. This passage was formerly read very differently elsewhere; but the reading of the Medicean manuscript, retained in this text, deserves greater approval. Anyone who compares the different modes of constructing the phrase, both among themselves and with what precedes and follows, will perceive this at first sight. The Fuketian manuscript agrees with the Medicean.

“They might persist in exhortations.” I corrected this passage with the aid of the Medicean manuscript, in which “purposes” is expressly written.

“Whatever, therefore, formerly.” The Medicean manuscript has “as those things formerly,” etc., and soon after, “to be dangerous.” I approve this more. For this period must be joined with the preceding one. Then, where “and otherwise” is read, the final particle is more correctly absent in the Medicean manuscript.

[Col. 0266C] XVI. Nevertheless, let them themselves acknowledge both how much and whence they collected, and request that pardon for this offense be granted them by us; so that at once, by such correction, their previous avarice may be healed, and at once God Most High, accepting this as though in place of some repentance, may become gracious toward the errors committed. For perhaps those established as masters of such possessions—if indeed that designation is worthy or possible in their case—will say in defense that it was impossible to refrain at that time, when there was a manifold spectacle of all evils: persons being brutally driven away, mercilessly destroyed, carelessly cast aside; frequent confiscations of those guilty of nothing; insatiable persecutions and sales of possessions. If, then, any should insist upon such arguments and persist in their insatiable purposes, they will find this not unpunished for themselves, especially since in this way our own contributions [Col. 0267B] are being offered in the service of God Most High. Whatever destructive necessity had formerly compelled persons to receive, it is now dangerous to retain. Besides, it is necessary in every way to lessen greed by arguments and examples.

## THAT THE TREASURY SHALL RESTORE ESTATES, HOUSES, AND GARDENS TO THE CHURCHES

[Col. 00267]

[Col. 0268B] XVI. For not even the treasury shall be permitted firmly to retain anything of what I have mentioned above if it possesses it. Rather, without daring even to raise an objection against the sacred churches, it shall rightfully relinquish to the churches what it has unjustly held for some time, [Col. 0268C] and shall finally restore it. Therefore we order that everything which may rightly appear to belong to the churches—whether it be a house and a possession, fields, gardens, or anything else whatsoever—be restored, with no right pertaining to ownership diminished, but all things remaining safe and intact.

[Note: Col. 0267D]

“For not even the treasury.” In the Medicean manuscript “for” is absent; and a little later in the same manuscript, as in our text, is written “nor even to reply.”

“Daring.” I write “having dared,” as in the Fuketian manuscript. [Col. 0268D] This is confirmed by the Medicean manuscript, where “they dared” is written. In the same manuscript, after the word “churches,” there is added “a gap,” that is, some words are missing.

“May rightly appear.” More correctly the Medicean manuscript reads: “may appear rightly.”

“To this commonwealth.” The correction of this passage is due to the Medicean manuscript, in which we expressly find written [Col. 0268D] “to ownership,” excellently. For the Emperor intends that all places and estates taken from Christians be restored to them in good faith, together with their rights. Thus if some servitude were owed to an estate or field—for example, a right of passage, a path, or a road—it is to be returned to Christians with the same right unimpaired in any respect. Therefore, if anyone had mortgaged an estate taken from a Christian, or granted it in emphyteusis, or imposed some burden or servitude upon it by sale, all these things are rescinded by this edict of Constantine. A little later, where “we order that they be resisted” was read, we corrected it from the same manuscript to “we order that they be restored.” The Fuketian, Turnebus’, and Savile’s manuscripts, however, have “that they be relinquished,” not badly.

[Col. 0267B] XVI. For not even the treasury, if it should hold anything of the things previously mentioned, shall be permitted to hold it securely; rather, as not even daring to speak against the sacred churches, it shall rightly relinquish to the churches those things which it unjustly held for a time. Therefore, everything which may rightly appear to belong to the churches—whether the property happens to be a house, or certain fields and gardens, or whatever other things—without any right belonging to ownership being diminished, but with all things remaining unimpaired, we order to be restored.

## THAT MARTYRIA AND CEMETERIES SHALL BE RETURNED TO THE CHURCHES

[Col. 0267]

[Col. 0268C] XVII. And as for those places which have been honored by the bodies of martyrs, and which preserve memorials of their glorious departure, who could doubt that they belong to the churches? Indeed, who would not order this, since no gift can be better, no labor more pleasing and more beneficial [Col. 0269A] than, under the prompting of the divine Spirit, to devote care to these matters: so that things taken away under wicked pretexts by unjust and most evil men may, having been most justly restored, again be preserved for the holy churches of God.

[Note: Col. 0268D]

“And indeed also.” In Moreau’s book the margin emends this to “yes, indeed also,” which is preferable.

[Col. 0269C] “Having great benefit.” The sense requires the reading “having greater benefit.” Moreover, after these words the Medicean manuscript contains the words “another would become,” which are lacking in the printed editions.

“Under the prompting of the divine Spirit.” The Medicean manuscript has “of the divine nod,” and “to devote diligence concerning such matters.” But “to devote” is also read in the Fuketian manuscript and those of Turnebus and Savile.

“By the most wicked.” In the Medicean manuscript one reads: “by unjust and most wicked [men].”

[Col. 0267C] XVII. And indeed those very places which have been honored with the bodies of martyrs, and which stand as memorials of their glorious departure—who could doubt that they belong to the churches, or who would not order it? Since there can be no gift better, nor any other labor more pleasing and bringing greater benefit, than, under the prompting of the divine Spirit, to devote care to these matters; and that things which were taken away under evil pretexts by most wicked men, when justly restored, should again be preserved for the holy churches.

## THAT THOSE WHO BOUGHT CHURCH PROPERTY OR RECEIVED IT AS A GIFT SHALL RESTORE IT

[Col. 0269]

[Col. 0269A] XVIII. Since it is characteristic of complete and perfect providence not to pass over in silence even those who have purchased something from the treasury by right of purchase, or possessed it as granted to them under the title of a gift, vainly extending their insatiable desire to such property, let all such persons know that, even though by the things which they dared to purchase they have earnestly tried to alienate our clemency from themselves, our kindness nevertheless [Col. 0269B] will not fail them insofar as this can and should be done.

[Note: Col. 0269C]

“Since [it is] of complete [providence].” I began a new chapter with these words and also supplied a heading, which was absent in the Genevan and Robert Estienne Paris editions. We supplied it, however, from both the Fuketian manuscript and the old papers of the Royal Library.

“By a lawful purchase.” The Medicean manuscript disclosed to us the true reading of this passage, where one reads “by the right of purchase.” I write “by right or title of purchase,” that is, by right or title of purchase. Certainly, to call this purchase just is foreign to Constantine’s thought, since he calls these purchases unjust and impious presumptions.

“Vainly, and to such things.” Long ago I conjectured that the particle “and” should be deleted; the Medicean manuscript expressly confirms this conjecture. The Emperor speaks of those who had requested that these places be granted to them by emperors. Christophorson did not see this. Soon after, the same manuscript reads “let such persons know,” etc., more correctly than the printed editions’ “as many as are such.” In the Fuketian manuscript and Turnebus’ text one reads “as many therefore as are such,” most badly.

[Col. 0270A] XVIII. Since complete providence would consist also in not passing over in silence those who either purchased something from the treasury by right of purchase or held it as vainly granted by gift, extending insatiable desires to such things, let such persons know that, although by what they dared to buy they tried to make our goodwill toward them alien, they will nevertheless not fail to receive it insofar as is possible and fitting. Let this, then, be carried thus far.

## EARNEST EXHORTATION TO WORSHIP GOD

[Col. 0270]

[Col. 0269B] XIX. But let it suffice to have spoken thus far of these matters. Further, since by most evident and certain proofs it has been shown that the distress and bitterness which formerly occupied human affairs have now been driven from the whole world, partly by the power and might of almighty God, partly by the exhortations and aids which He desires to be frequently rendered by me, all together and each individually perceive by diligent reflection what and how great is that power and grace which has utterly destroyed and swept away the stock of utterly evil men, while restoring the cheerfulness and joy of the good and spreading it widely throughout all regions; and which grants all persons free ability both to worship again [Col. 0269C] the divine law with due reverence and to honor fittingly [Col. 0272A] those who have consecrated themselves to the ministry of that law. Emerging, as it were, from a certain deep darkness and receiving clear knowledge of realities, they will henceforth show due observance toward this law, and pious and harmonious reverence. Let it be posted in our eastern regions.

[Note: Col. 0269D]

“Since therefore.” The Medicean manuscript has “but since.”

“It has been shown, by the power of Him who is able to do all things,” etc. Formerly one read “the power has been shown,” etc. More correctly, as the Medicean manuscript reads here; it also seems necessary to write “of almighty God.”

“Together with exhortations.” In the Medicean manuscript one reads “and together with exhortations.” Also absent in that manuscript are “through which” and “has now happened,” all of which were added by persons who did not understand this discourse. The entire passage must therefore be translated thus: “Further, since by most certain and evident proofs it has been shown that the distress and bitterness which formerly occupied human affairs have now been driven from the entire world, partly by the power and might of almighty God, partly by the exhortations and aids which He desires to be frequently rendered by me,” etc. What could be clearer or more certain than this reading? In place of “which [are] on my behalf,” I think one must certainly write “which [are] by me” or “from me.” For Constantine means his own ministry, which he offered to God in accomplishing matters of this kind. Not without reason does he boast of this at the beginning of this edict.

“The power.” In the Medicean manuscript the article is absent, and after these words these words are added: “what grace.” They cannot be absent without great damage to the entire sense. For “power” is what he above called “the power of God”; “grace” is the benefit bestowed upon human beings through Constantine’s aid and ministry.

“Which [destroyed] the seed of the most evil.” The Medicean manuscript has “which [destroyed] the seed of the evil and most wicked.” Further, one must write “which,” as is read in the Royal and Fuketian manuscripts and in the papers.

“Of deep darkness.” The Medicean manuscript reads “of deepest [darkness],” and the end of this edict is framed thus: “they will henceforth show due worship toward it and harmonious honor. Let it be posted in our eastern [Col. 0271C] regions,” that is, “Let it be posted in our eastern regions.” This is the subscription which Eusebius testifies in chapter 24 was appended to this edict in Constantine’s own hand. For emperors were accustomed to add “Let it be posted” in their own hand to edicts which they issued, and thereby to command the praetorian prefects, as appears from the Novels of Valentinian and Majorian. Certainly the single word “our” sufficiently indicates that this subscription was added in Constantine’s own hand. For the Emperor himself speaks and calls the eastern regions his own. Emperors were accustomed to speak thus, especially when they were discussing a province newly brought under their dominion. Thus Constantine, in his Letter to Elafius and in his Letter to Probianus, Proconsul of Africa, calls Africa “our Africa”; and in the first law of the Theodosian Code, *On Veterans*, [he says] “at our Nicomedia.” Thus in the sole law of the Theodosian Code, *On Those Who Are Bloodstained*, etc., Emperor Constantine says “to his Italians.” Finally, Constantius Caesar speaks in this way in the Letter to Eumenius, which Eumenius reports in his oration on behalf of the schools: “Our Gauls deserve,” etc. Moreover, this edict of Constantine is found in the Medicean manuscript after the books of Ecclesiastical History, with this heading: “Copy of the ordinance of the emperor beloved by God, which, after overthrowing the tyrants, he composed in the Greek tongue and sent to the peoples subject to him.” That is: “Copy of the constitution which the emperor dear to God, having defeated the tyrants, wrote in Greek and dispatched to his provincials.”

“Having received knowledge of the writings.” The Medicean manuscript has “of realities.” I found no other reading in the Royal manuscript, the old papers, and the Fuketian manuscript. Robert Estienne’s emendation must therefore be rejected.

[Col. 0270B] XIX. Since, therefore, it has been demonstrated by most evident and clear proofs—both by the power of God, who is able to do all things, and at the same time by the exhortations and aids which He deigns frequently to make through me—that the distress formerly holding all human affairs has already been driven out from the entire world beneath the sun, all persons, individually and collectively, perceive with earnest consideration what that power is, what grace it is, which, so to speak, has destroyed and annihilated the seed of the most wicked, while recalling the joy of the good and extending it abundantly throughout all regions; and which gives everyone complete freedom again to worship the divine law itself with all fitting reverence and to honor as is due those who have consecrated themselves to it. They, having risen as if from a deep darkness and received bright knowledge of realities, will henceforth show toward it due worship and pious, harmonious honor. Let it be posted in our eastern regions.

## EDICT OF CONSTANTINE TO THE PROVINCIALS CONCERNING THE FALSE WORSHIP OF MANY GODS. PREFACE ON VIRTUE AND VICE

(From Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, II, chapters 48, 60.)

[Note: Col. 0271] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0271]

Victor Constantine, Greatest, Augustus, to the eastern provincials.

[Col. 0272A]

I. Whatever is contained within the firmest laws of nature affords everyone sufficient awareness of divine providence and understanding in the ordering of all things. Nor is there any doubt for those whose minds are led by the straight path of knowledge toward that goal that the apprehension of sound reason and the accurate perception of sight itself, both tending and inclining by one impulse of true excellence, lead to knowledge of God. Therefore no prudent person will ever be disturbed on seeing the multitude carried along by contrary dispositions of life. For the grace of virtue would lie wholly useless unless vice set in opposition a perverse and desperate way of life. Therefore a crown is set before virtue, while God Most High presides over the judgment and punishment of vice. As far as I can, I shall try to set forth to you most plainly the hope and expectation that I hold concerning future things.

[Col. 0271A] Victor Constantine, Greatest, Augustus, to the eastern provincials.

[Note: Col. 0272C]

“By one impulse of true excellence.” Here virtue seems to be taken for perfection, both that which belongs to sight and that which belongs to intellect. For each power and perfection tends toward the same end: namely, knowledge of truth. Sense advances to the truth of sensible things; intellect proceeds from the truth of sensible things themselves to intelligible truth, [Col. 0272D] and thence gradually ascends to knowledge of the highest God. In this place *aretē tou alēthous* may also mean the force and power of truth. What follows, however, confirms that this passage must be understood of moral virtue.

“Useless.” I read “foolish,” as in the Fuketian manuscript and the books of Moreau and Gruter. A little later I write: “therefore a crown is set before virtue.” These matters are very obscure and involved, which must be attributed partly to Constantine himself, who, being superficially learned (*epsimathēs*), was more obscure in expression, and partly to Eusebius, or whoever else made Greek even more obscure from obscure Latin. In Fuketius’ manuscript one reads “useless,” and “therefore [a crown is set] for virtue,” etc., excellently.

I. Everything contained within the most authoritative laws of nature provides all persons with sufficient perception of providence and contemplation according to the divine ordering. Nor is there any doubt for those whose mind is led by a straight path of knowledge toward that goal, that the accurate apprehension of sound reason and of sight itself, by a single movement of true virtue, leads up to knowledge of God. Therefore no intelligent person would ever be disturbed at seeing the multitude carried along by contrary dispositions. For the grace of virtue would lie unnoticed and useless if vice had not set before it, directly opposite, the life of perverse madness. Therefore a crown is set before virtue, while God Most High holds authority over judgment. And I shall attempt, as plainly as possible, to declare to all of you my hopes concerning myself.

## CONCERNING CONSTANTINE’S PIOUS AND MOST GOD-LOVING FATHER, AND CONCERNING DIOCLETIAN AND MAXIMIAN, THE PERSECUTORS

[Col. 0271]

II. As for the emperors who preceded [my father], I always regarded them as alien and estranged because of the savagery and brutality of their character. My father alone pursued gentleness and mildness, invoking God the Father with marvelous reverence in all his actions. The rest, however, being in no way sound of mind, pursued brutality rather than clemency; they nourished it marvelously throughout the whole time of their rule, overthrowing true doctrine. Moreover, the fury of their wickedness was so greatly inflamed that, although all divine and human affairs were established in the deepest peace, they stirred up civil wars.

[Note: Col. 0273D]

“Civil wars.” He calls the persecutions of Christians civil wars. For nothing is more like civil war than when Christians in individual cities were driven out and slaughtered by the assaults not of enemies or barbarians, but of their own fellow citizens.

[Col. 0271C] II. I regarded the emperors who had arisen before this as estranged because of the savagery of their dispositions. My father alone practiced works of gentleness, invoking God the Father with wonderful reverence in all his actions. But all the rest, their minds being unsound, cared for brutality rather than mildness; and they nourished it lavishly during their own times, perverting the true doctrine. The violence of their wickedness was inflamed to such a degree that, although all divine and human affairs alike were at peace, civil wars were stirred up by them.

## THAT THE PERSECUTION WAS STIRRED UP BY AN ORACLE OF APOLLO, WHO COULD NO LONGER GIVE RESPONSES BECAUSE OF RIGHTEOUS MEN

[Col. 0273]

[Col. 0273A] III. At that time Apollo was said to have issued an oracle from a cave and some dark recess, rather than from a human mouth. In it he said that righteous men living upon the earth prevented him from speaking truth, and that for this reason false oracles were given from the tripod. On this account Apollo let down his unkempt hair and, with the art of divination expelled, lamented such a great evil among human beings. [Col. 0273B] But let us see what end these things had.

[Note: Col. 0273D]

“This made him, being downcast, let down his locks.” One should write: “This made his prophetess,” or, if you prefer, “his downcast priestess,” let down her hair; this is the reading I followed in my translation. Portesius and Morin also understood these words of the Pythia or priest of Apollo. Yet in Fuketius’ excellent manuscript the entire passage is written thus: “This made him, being downcast, let down his locks; and when divination was expelled,” etc.; Savile’s manuscript agrees. Soon afterward these same manuscripts read: “to what end it came.”

[Col. 0274A] III. At that time Apollo, they said, delivered an oracle from a certain cave and dark recess, not from a human being: namely, that the righteous on earth impeded him from speaking truth, and that for this reason he made the oracles from the tripods false. This made him, downcast, let down his locks; and, divination being driven away, he lamented the evil among humankind. But let us see to what end these things [Col. 0274B] came.

## HOW CONSTANTINE, WHILE STILL A YOUTH, HEARD THAT CHRISTIANS WERE RIGHTEOUS

[Col. 0273]

[Col. 0273B] IV. I now call you as witness, God Most High. You know how, when I was then very young, I heard the man who at that time held the foremost place among the Roman emperors—wretched, truly wretched, deceived by a false error of mind—curiously inquire of his guards who those righteous persons living upon the earth were; and how one of the sacrificers about him replied that they were Christians. He greedily swallowed the man’s answer as though it were honey, and drew the swords prepared for punishing crimes against sanctity free from all reproach. Immediately, therefore, he wrote bloody edicts with, so to speak, blood-stained sword-points, and commanded the judges to direct their natural ingenuity toward devising more severe [Col. 0273C] punishments.

[Note: Col. 0273D]

“Being quite a child.” It would be more correct to write “a young man.” For Constantine was not a child when he lived as a hostage in Diocletian’s court. His father Constantius handed him over to Diocletian in the year of Christ 291, when Constantius had been made Caesar by Diocletian. At that time Constantine was about fifteen years old. He died in the year of Christ 337, in the sixty-second year of his life.

“Having gulped honey.” In the Fuketian and Savile manuscripts one reads more correctly “having swallowed”; the Royal manuscript has no other reading.

“With murderous points.” He alludes to the point of a stylus. Constantine speaks elegantly when he says that those laws for persecuting Christians were written with bloody sword-points. Some ancients similarly said that Draco’s laws were written in blood, not ink.

“He exhorted [them] to stretch.” I would prefer to say “to exert,” as Eusebius commonly speaks.

[Col. 0274B] IV. I now call upon you, God Most High. I heard, while still quite a child, how he who at that time held the first place among the Roman emperors—wretched, truly wretched, his soul deceived by error—was inquisitively asking those who attended him who the righteous persons upon earth might be. And one of the sacrificers about him replied: “Surely they are Christians.” He, having swallowed the answer as though it were honey, stretched against blameless holiness the swords devised for crimes. Immediately, then, he composed edicts of blood with, so to speak, murderous points, and urged the judges to direct their natural acuteness toward discovering harsher punishments.

## HOW MANY KINDS OF TORTURES AND PUNISHMENTS WERE DEVISED AGAINST CHRISTIANS

[Col. 0273]

[Col. 0273C] V. At that time, I say, one could see with what freedom that venerable devotion to God endured, through the continual succession of cruelty, not merely ordinary daily outrages. For the self-restraint which not even enemies had ever injured was made an incidental object of insult by enraged fellow citizens. What fire, what kind of pain and torture, what kind of rack was not indiscriminately applied to every body and every age? At that time the earth itself undoubtedly shed tears; while the heaven enclosing all things within its circuit groaned, polluted with blood. Daylight itself was darkened by grief and horror at so great a portent.

[Note: Col. 0274D]

“Became an incidental object of insult.” Thus Eusebius said of Severus Caesar in Book I, “he became an incidental object of death”; see there what we have noted concerning this expression. For the interpreters saw nothing here.

“And every age.” The Fuketian manuscript gives “not every age.” A little later, in the same manuscript and in the Royal papers, the text reads as in ours: “the day itself was veiled by grief at the portent.”

[Col. 0274C] V. Then, then, it was possible to see with how great liberty that venerable devotion to God endured, through the uninterrupted succession of cruelty, not commonplace insults on each day. The sobriety which none of its enemies had ever injured became an incidental object of abuse by angry fellow citizens. What fire, what tortures, what type of rack was not indiscriminately applied to every body and every age? Then the earth undoubtedly wept; the world which encompasses all things, stained with blood, lamented aloud. Daylight itself was veiled by grief at the portent.

## HOW THE BARBARIANS RECEIVED CHRISTIANS

[Col. 0275]

[Col. 0276A] VI. But why do I recount these matters? The barbarians now boast of those persons who at that time fled from our regions, whom they received and held in captivity with humanity. For they allowed them not only to preserve their lives but also to retain among themselves the undiminished practice of their religion. Thus the Roman people now bears this perpetual mark of disgrace, which Christians, driven at that time from the Roman world and fleeing to [Col. 0276B] barbarians, impressed upon them.

[Col. 0275A] VI. But why [speak of] these things? The barbarians now boast concerning those who fled from us at that time, whom they received and kept in a most humane captivity. For they enabled them to retain in safety not only their lives but also the things belonging to their venerable religion. And now the Roman race bears this enduring stain, which the Christians driven from the Roman world at that time, fleeing to barbarians, fastened upon it.

## HOW THOSE WHO STIRRED UP THE PERSECUTION THROUGH THE ORACLE WERE PUNISHED BY DIVINE VENGEANCE

[Col. 0276B] VII. But what need is there to recount at greater length those lamentations and the common grief of the whole world? Afterward, the authors of so great a crime perished by a shameful end, hurled into the abyss of Acheron for everlasting punishments. For, dashed together in civil wars, they left behind no memory either of their name or of their race. This surely would never have happened to them, if that impious prophecy of Pythian Apollo had not possessed a certain false and counterfeit force.

[Col. 0275B] VII. But why must I remember at greater length those lamentations and the common grief of the inhabited world? Those authors of hatred have now gone, given over with a shameful end to the abysses of Acheron for everlasting punishment. For, caught up in civil wars, they have left behind neither name nor lineage. This would certainly not have happened to them if that impious prophecy of the Pythian oracles had not possessed counterfeit force.

## CONSTANTINE ASCRIBES GLORY TO GOD, CONFESSES THE SIGN OF THE CROSS, AND PRAYS FOR THE CHURCHES

[Col. 0276C] VIII. Now I pray and beseech you, God Most High: be gentle and favorable toward your eastern peoples; be favorable toward all the provincials, worn down by long calamity, and be willing through me, your servant, to grant them healing. Nor do I ask this of you without cause, Lord of all and holy God. For under your guidance and auspices I have undertaken and accomplished salutary enterprises. Displaying your sign everywhere, I have led a victorious army. Whenever public necessity requires it, following the standards of your power, I advance against the enemy. For these reasons I have dedicated my soul to you, rightly tempered with love and fear together. For I sincerely love your name, while I reverently fear the power which you have shown by many proofs and by which you have confirmed my faith. Therefore I hasten, myself placing my shoulders beneath the task, to restore anew your most holy house, which those profane and impious persons devastated by their criminal [Col. 0276D] overthrow.

[Note: Col. 0275D]

“Your most holy house.” He means the Catholic Church, which in chapter 56 he calls the house of truth. In the sacred books it is called the pillar and foundation of truth. A little later, following the Fuketian and Savile manuscripts and the Royal papers, one reads: “which those abominable men,” etc.

[Col. 0276C] VIII. I now pray to you, God Most High: may you be gentle and favorable to your eastern peoples; may you extend healing through me, your servant, to all your provincials crushed by long calamity. And I ask these things not unreasonably, O Lord of all, holy God. For under your guidance I undertook salutary enterprises and brought them to completion; displaying your seal everywhere, I led a most victorious army. And whenever some public need calls, following the same tokens of your power, I advance against the enemy. For these reasons I have dedicated my own soul to you, purely blended with love and fear. For I genuinely love your name, and I reverence the power which you have shown by many proofs and by which you have made my faith firmer. Therefore I hasten, myself putting my shoulders beneath the task, to renew your most holy house, which those abominable and most impious men devastated by the wickedness of its destruction.

## HOW HE WISHED ALL TO BE CHRISTIANS, BUT COMPELLED NO ONE

[Col. 0276D] IX. I desire your people to live in peace and remain free from all discord, for the common good of the whole world and all mortals. Let those who are entangled in the error of paganism likewise gladly receive, along with believers, the same enjoyment of peace and tranquility. For this restoration of mutual communion and fellowship [Col. 0277A] is of great force in bringing persons back to the right way. Let no one trouble another. Let each do what he wishes. Yet among those who think rightly, this must remain fixed and settled: that those alone shall live holily and purely whom you yourself have called to rest in your sacred laws. Let those who withdraw themselves have their shrines of falsehood, if they so wish. We retain the most splendid house of your truth, which you gave us according to nature. We pray this also for them: namely, that through the common harmony and concord of all, they too may attain the greatest joy.

[Note: Col. 0276D]

“It has power to lead [them] to the straight way.” In Fuketius’ manuscript one reads “power.” But the true reading is “will have power,” which I found in the old papers of the Royal Library. This is certainly far more elegant.

[Col. 0277D] “Let each do what his soul wishes.” That is, let each observe whatever religion he wishes. By these words Constantine left his subjects entire freedom to worship divinity as each wished. For that most religious prince greatly desired that all mortals should pass over to the faith of Christ; nevertheless, he never compelled anyone to do so. Indeed, he wished the pagans freed from their former error; yet he did not prohibit the ceremonies and sacrifices of the temples, as he himself testifies below in chapter 59.

[Col. 0275D] IX. I desire your people to be at peace and remain free from dissension, for the common good of the inhabited world and the benefit of all human beings. Let those who are astray gladly receive the same enjoyment of peace and quiet as believers. For this restoration of communion has power to lead toward the straight way. Let no one harass another. Let each do what his soul wishes. But those who think rightly must be convinced that they alone will live holy and pure lives whom you call to rest in your holy laws. Let those who draw themselves away, if they wish, possess the shrines of false speech; we possess the most splendid house of your truth, which you have given according to nature. This we pray also for them: that through common concord they too may attain gladness.

## HE ASCRIBES GLORY TO GOD, WHO THROUGH HIS SON ENLIGHTENED THOSE WHO WERE ASTRAY

[Col. 0277]

[Col. 0277B] X. For our religion is neither new nor recent. From the time when we believe the fabric of this world to have stood in fitting order, you established this religion together with the due observance of your divinity. But the human race, led astray by various errors, stumbled. Yet you, so that this evil might not increase further, raised up through your Son a most bright light and reminded all persons concerning the worship of your divinity.

[Note: Col. 0277D]

“For it is not new.” Eusebius writes likewise concerning the origin and antiquity of the Christian religion at the beginning of his *Ecclesiastical History* and in the books of the *Evangelical Demonstration*.

[Col. 0278B] X. For what concerns us is neither new nor anything recent. Rather, from the time when we have believed that the ordering of all things came firmly into being, you ordained this together with the reverence fitting for you. But the human race went astray, led away by errors of every kind; yet through your Son, lest evil become more oppressive, you raised a pure light and reminded all persons concerning yourself.

## AGAIN HE ASCRIBES GLORY TO GOD FROM THE MINISTRY OF THE WHOLE WORLD

[Col. 0277]

[Col. 0277B] XI. Your works furnish proof of this. Your power makes us innocent and faithful. The sun and moon proceed in fixed and determined courses; nor do the stars revolve without order around the axis of the whole world. The alternations of the seasons return according to a fixed law. By your word the firm stability of the earth stands fast; the winds move at their appointed time; and the rush of waters flows onward in an unceasing current. The sea is held within immovable bounds. And whatever extends over land and ocean has been fashioned for great and wonderful uses. Unless this were governed in accordance with the decision of your will, so great a diversity and manifold division of power would undoubtedly have brought ruin upon the whole world and human affairs. For those who have made war against one another would surely have fought more fiercely against the human race. And this indeed they do, though they are not seen by the eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0277D]

“According to the imposed season.” I read *κατὰ τὸν ἐπεισαχθέντα*, “according to the season brought in,” as Christophorson seems to have read it. And the codex of Fuket and Savile likewise presents this reading.

“Manifold division of power” (*πολλὴ τῆς ἐξουσίας διάκρισις*), that is, manifold divinity—of the sun, moon, stars, and elements, of which he spoke above. For each of these, unless governed by the will and power of the one God, would surely be gods. Thus *ἐξουσία* means power subject to no dominion, what is commonly called independence, which belongs to God alone.

“For those who fought against one another.” He means the gods of the Gentiles, as I said above: namely, the sun, moon, and the other elements of the world, which antiquity worshipped as gods. Immediately write, from the Fuketian codex, *τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ ἐμάχοντο γένει*, “they fought against the human race,” as is also read in the Royal manuscripts.]

[Col. 0278B] XI. Your deeds attest these things: your might makes us innocent and faithful. The sun and moon have a lawful course; nor have the stars a disorderly revolution in their orbit around the world. The alternations of the seasons revolve again according to law. The earth’s fixed station has been established by your word; and the wind makes its movement at the appointed season. The rushing course of the waters proceeds onward in the measure of an inexhaustible stream. The sea is enclosed by fixed limits. And whatever is spread out along with land and ocean, all this is wrought for certain marvellous and useful benefits. If this were not done according to the judgment of your will, undoubtedly such great diversity and the manifold distinction of independent powers would have wrought harm upon all life and affairs. For those who wage war against one another would have fought more fiercely against the human race. This they do even though unseen.

## HE PRAISES GOD, WHO ALWAYS TEACHES WHAT IS GOOD AND HONOURABLE

[Col. 0277]

[Col. 0277C] XII. We render you abundant thanks, Lord of all and supreme God. For the more human nature is recognized amid conflicting pursuits, the more firmly the teaching of divine religion is established among those who think more rightly and cultivate genuine virtue. But whoever refuses to be healed must not lay this to another’s charge. For the medicine which presides over healing is openly set before all. Only this must be guarded against: that no one violate that religion which the facts themselves attest to be pure and undefiled. Therefore let us all enjoy fellowship in this good granted to us, that is, the pleasantness of peace; and let us separate the conscience of our mind from everything contrary to it.

[Note: [Col. 0278D]

“Those who cultivate genuine virtue.” In the codex of Fuket and Savile, *γνησίως*, “genuinely,” is read.

[Col. 0279D] “Let him not impute this to another.” That is, whoever refuses to be healed and freed from the disease of idolatry must blame himself, since the remedy is at hand. Christophorson wrongly translates this passage as follows: “let him not blame another who wishes to be healed.” Of Portes I say nothing, since he nearly everywhere departs from the true sense. Musculus, certainly, translates this not unsuccessfully.]

[Col. 0278C] XII. Abundant thanks to you, master of all, supreme God. For insofar as humanity is recognized amid diverse pursuits, so much more are the teachings of the divine word established among those who think more rightly and cultivate genuine virtue. But whoever prevents himself from being healed must not impute this to another; for the art of healing presides over remedies, being openly set before all. Only let no one injure that which the facts attest to be undefiled. Therefore let all people avail themselves of the common share of the good bestowed, that is, the good of peace, separating conscience from everything contrary to it.

## EXHORTATION AT THE END OF THE EDICT THAT NO ONE SHOULD MOLEST ANOTHER

[Col. 0279]

[Col. 0280A] XIII. Moreover, let no one harm another on account of that which he himself has embraced in his mind. But whatever anyone may understand and know, let him, if possible, help his neighbour by it; if this is impossible, let him leave it alone. For it is one thing voluntarily to undertake the contest for immortality, [Col. 0280B] another to compel by force of punishments. I have said these things, and have discussed them more fully and at greater length than the purpose of our clemency required, because I did not wish to conceal or disguise the truth of the faith. Especially since some, as I hear, assert that the rites and ceremonies of the temples, and the power of darkness, have been utterly removed. I should indeed have recommended this to all persons, had not the violent presumption of depraved error lodged too deeply in the minds of some, to the destruction and injury of the restoration of the human race.

[Note: [Col. 0279D]

“That which he has shown himself to have accepted in persuading himself.” In the Royal codex *ἀναδέδεκται* is written above it in the same hand. Either reading can certainly be accepted.

“The faith of truth,” that is, the true faith. For this is the same as if he had said, “the truth of faith.” He speaks thus again below in chapter 69.

“The power of darkness.” The words are drawn from the Epistle of Paul. Moreover, just as here he calls Hellenism the power of darkness, so elsewhere he calls Christianity the power and efficacy of light.

“Insurrection” (*ἐπανάστασις*). This word properly signifies conspiracy and rebellion, which is most aptly said of idol worship. For idol worship is defection from the true God.

“Of the common resurrection.” It seems that *ἀνορθώσεως*, “restoration,” should be written. For the received word appears to have been repeated from the preceding line. Moreover, at the end of this edict there was doubtless appended the subscription, of which I have spoken much above: “Let it be posted in our eastern regions.” For this subscription properly belongs to this edict, since it was sent to the provincials of the East.]

XIII. But let each person not harm another by that which he has shown himself to have adopted in persuading himself. Whatever another has seen and understood, let him benefit his neighbour with it, if possible; if impossible, let him pass it by. For it is one thing voluntarily to take up the contest for immortality, another [Col. 0279B] to compel with punishment. I have said these things, and treated them at greater length than the purpose of my moderation required, because I did not wish to hide the faith of truth—especially because some, as I hear, say that the customs of the temples and the power of darkness have been removed. I would have advised this to all people, if the violent uprising of wicked error had not been excessively implanted in the souls of some, to the harm of the common restoration.

## CONSTITUTION OF CONSTANTINE AGAINST HERETICS

*(From Eusebius, Life of Constantine, III, chapters 64–65.)* [Note: [Col. 0279] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0279]

Victor Constantine the Great, Augustus, to the Heretics.

[Col. 0279B] I. Now recognize, by the benefit of this law, O Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionists, Paulianists, and all to whom the name of Cataphrygians [Col. 0280C] has been given—in short, all who establish and fill heresies by private assemblies—by how many falsehoods the vanity of your opinion is entangled, and with how destructive poisons your doctrine is imbued; so that through you a most grievous disease is brought upon the healthy, and perpetual death upon the living. O enemies of truth, foes of life, counsellors of destruction: everything among you is contrary to truth, suited to the most shameful crimes, and filled with absurdities and fictions. By these you establish falsehoods, oppress the innocent, and deny light to believers. Continually sinning under the pretext of divinity, you defile everything, wound the pure and undefiled consciences of men with deadly blows, and almost, one might say, snatch away daylight itself from human eyes. Why enumerate each particular, [Col. 0280D] when neither the shortness of time nor the greatness of our occupations [Col. 0281A] permits us to speak of your crimes in terms commensurate with them? For your offences are so grave and immeasurable, so foul and overflowing with every atrocity, that not even a whole day would suffice to set them forth. Besides, it is fitting to turn ears away from such matters and avert one’s eyes, lest the pure and sincere zeal of our faith be defiled by their particular exposition. Why, then, should we tolerate evils of this sort any longer? Especially since long endurance causes even those who are healthy and strong to be infected, as it were, with this pestilential disease. Why then do we not immediately root out the sources of such wickedness by public action?

Victor Constantine, the Greatest, Augustus, to the Heretics.

[Col. 0279B]

[Note: [Col. 0280D]

“A thing” (*χρῆμα*). In the codices of Fuket, Savile, and Turnebus I find *χαίροντα*, “rejoicing,” written, as Scaliger, Christophorson, and others found in their books.

0

[Col. 0281D] “Long indulgence” (*μακρὰ παρεπιθύμησις*). Perhaps *παρενθύμησις*, that is, neglect and dissimulation. In the codices of Fuket, Savile, and Turnebus, *ὑπέρθεσις*, “delay,” is read. A little later I write from the Fuketian codex: *διὰ δημοσίας ἐπιστρεφείας*, “by public correction.”]

[Col. 0279B] I. Learn now through this legislation, O Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionists, Paulianists, those called Cataphrygians, and, in general, all of you who fill up heresies by your own associations, in how many falsehoods the vanity among you is entangled, and how your teaching is held together by certain venomous drugs: so that by you the healthy are led into sickness, and the living into unending death. O enemies of truth, foes of life, and counsellors of destruction: everything among you is contrary to truth, consonant with shameful wickedness, a thing full of absurdities and fictions. By these you establish falsehoods, oppress the innocent, and deny light to believers. Always committing offences under the appearance of divinity, you defile all things, wound innocent and pure consciences with deadly blows, and, almost one may say, rob human eyes of daylight itself. Why need each matter be stated, [Col. 0279D] when neither brief time nor our occupations permit us [Col. 0282A] to speak worthily of your evils? For the enormities among you are so extensive and boundless, so hideous and full of every harshness, that not even an entire day suffices for their description. Moreover, it is fitting to turn ears aside from such things and avert the eyes, lest the sincere and pure zeal of our faith be polluted by a detailed narration. Why then shall we endure such evils any further? But long indulgence, like a pestilential disease, causes even the healthy to be corrupted; why, then, do we not at once cut out, as it were, the roots of so great a wickedness by public correction?

## ON THE ABOLITION OF THE ASSEMBLY-PLACES OF HERETICS

[Col. 0281]

[Col. 0281B] II. Therefore, since it is not possible to bear any longer this destruction arising from your ruinous wickedness, by this law we declare beforehand that none of you shall dare henceforth to assemble. Accordingly, we have ordered that all your houses in which you hold these meetings be taken away. Our concern has proceeded so far that the gatherings of your superstitious madness shall not run together merely in public, but not even in a private house or in places of any private right. But, what is far more honourable and excellent, all of you who are devoted to the true and pure religion should come to the Catholic Church and share in its holiness, through which you will be able to attain the truth. Let the deceit of your perverted mind—by which I mean the guilty and utterly ruinous discord of heretics and schismatics—be wholly separated from the prosperity of our times. For it befits the blessed condition which we enjoy with God that those who live in good hope should be led from every disorderly error onto the straight path, from darkness to light, from vanity to truth, and finally from death to salvation. And in order that the force of this remedy may become necessary and effective, we have ordered, as already stated, that all the meeting-places of your superstition—that is, the prayer-houses of all heretics, if indeed they ought to be called prayer-houses—be taken from them without objection and handed over without delay to the Catholic Church. The remaining places, however, are to be assigned to public ownership; and no facility for assembling is to be left to you hereafter, so that from this present day your unlawful associations may dare to gather in no place whatsoever, public or private. Let it be posted.

[Note: [Col. 0281D]

“Under all the assemblies of your superstition.” The first word should be deleted as superfluous. In the codices of Fuket, Savile, and Turnebus *ἐπὶ πάντα* is read; perhaps *ἐπίπαντα*, “all,” etc.

“Having been taken away.” Christophorson wrongly translates this “having been demolished.” For Constantine does not order the basilicas of the heretics to be destroyed, but to be taken from them and delivered to the Catholic Church. Similar imperial constitutions occur in the Theodosian Code, under the title *On Heretics*. Moreover, the Novatians had previously been excepted from this law of Constantine, as appears from law 2 under the same title. Yet by this final enactment of Constantine, they were included with the other heretics and [Col. 0282D] schismatics.

“Of assembling.” More correctly the Fuketian codex writes *τοῦ συνάγειν*. For *συνάγειν* is the proper word for this matter. The Latins use the single word *colligere*, “to gather,” as can be shown by many examples. Hence they call a *collecta* what in Greek is a *σύναξις*, “assembly.” Optatus, in Book 2, where he speaks of Donatist bishops in the city of Rome: “But because certain Africans had chosen to reside in the city, and appeared to have gone out from you, they themselves requested that someone should be sent from here to gather them.” And shortly after: “For the few who had no place where they might gather among the more than forty basilicas could not be called a flock or people.”

“May dare; let it be posted.” Christophorson did not understand the last word, which used to be appended to laws and imperial constitutions, sometimes in the emperors’ own hand. Thus in Theodosius’ novella on the restoration of the right to bear arms one reads: “And in the divine hand: Let it be posted for our most beloved Roman people.” And at the side: “Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of July at Rome, in the consulship of Valentinian and Anatolius.”]

[Col. 0282B] II. Therefore, since it is impossible to bear further this destruction of your utter ruin, we proclaim in advance by this law that none of you may dare henceforth to assemble. For this reason we have ordered all your houses in which you conduct these meetings to be taken away, our concern proceeding so far that the associations of your superstitious folly may not gather, not only in public, but not even in a private house or in any privately owned places. But, since it is much better, all of you who cultivate true and pure religion, come to the Catholic Church and communicate in its holiness, through which you will be able to attain truth. Let the deception of your perverted mind be wholly removed from the fortunate condition of our times—I mean the guilty and utterly destructive discord of heretics and schismatics. For it accords with the blessed state that we enjoy with God that those who live in good hopes should be led from every disorderly error to the straight path, from darkness to light, from vanity to truth, and from death to salvation. In order that this remedy may also have necessary force, we have ordered, as has been said, that all your superstitious meeting-places—I mean the houses of prayer of all heretics, if indeed it is fitting to call them houses of prayer—be taken away without contradiction and delivered to the Catholic Church without any delay. The remaining places are to be assigned to public uses; and no facility for assembling is to be left to you in future, so that from the present day your unlawful associations may dare to gather in no place, whether public or private. Let it be posted.

## ON MUNICIPAL MAGISTRATES

[Col. 0283A]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Florentinus, Praetorian Prefect. Decurions must be nominated for magistracy or for the collection of grain supplies three months, or more, in advance, so that, if their complaint appears just, others may be substituted without impediment in the place of the person to be relieved. Given on the Ides of April at Constantinople, in the consulship of Severus and Rufinus (323). *(From the Code of Justinian.)*

In the year of the Lord 324, in the consulship of Crispus III and Constantine III, Caesars.

## ON THOSE WHO HAVE EARNED EXEMPTION BY THE NUMBER OF THEIR CHILDREN OR BY POVERTY

[Note: [Col. 0283C] a 4: “On those who [by] the free number of children.”]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Dalmatius. Since we have learned that some persons, presenting to our view children belonging to others as their own, have obtained from us exemption from personal public services, we order that, once this has been proved, they be deprived of the benefit granted. But those who have five children of either sex shall retain an exemption once obtained, [Col. 0283B] provided that, if among this number a son of lawful age is found, he is immediately assigned to perform public services in his father’s stead. Fathers who have had five sons or daughters are to retain the immunity promised by the laws. § 1. If anyone has earned exemption on account of a slender census-rating and proves this, he shall enjoy the benefit, if, because of straitened means, he was called to personal services. Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February at Sirmium, in the consulship of Crispus III and Constantine II [uncertain: the accompanying note discusses whether “III” or “II” is correct] (324).

Constantine Augustus to Hilarianus, Proconsul of Africa. If any decurion is compelled, either for his own affair or for that of the municipality, to approach our court, he shall not depart before obtaining leave to travel upon making known to the judge his desire to depart. If anyone, through his own audacity, makes light of this order, he shall incur the penalty of deportation. Posted on the seventh day before the Ides of July at Carthage, in the consulship of Crispus III and Constantine III (324).

## IF THE POSSESSION OF AN ABSENT PERSON HAS BEEN DISTURBED BY FORCE OR OTHERWISE

[Col. 0285A]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Severus. Judges shall undertake in court the persons of absent persons who have been deprived of possession of any property, and shall deploy the formidable ministry of their authority. Thus they shall protect absentees, carefully inquiring only whether the possession of a person travelling abroad in any manner has been taken away—a possession which a kinsman, relative, next of kin, friend, tenant farmer, freedman, or slave held under any title. Nor shall they exclude from bringing an action those who have been dispossessed while holding in the name of absent persons, because no decision of the case was entrusted to them; nor, if they are slaves, shall they reject their persons in court because persons of that status are not permitted to plead cases. But even after the legally prescribed periods for recovering possession have elapsed, it is proper that they be allowed to bring suit, so that they may be restored without any delay to immediate possession, just as though the owner himself had returned and litigated. Yet we grant to the owner, whenever he returns, an action for recovery of possession, since restitution may meanwhile be delayed because of unfaithful slaves or negligent kinsmen, relatives, next of kin, friends, tenant farmers, or freedmen. For the elapsed period established by law for recovery of possession must not prejudice absentees. Rather, once the state of affairs wrongfully removed has been restored, everything remaining for adjudication of the dispute shall remain unimpaired, with judgment reserved for the proper and lawful persons—[Col. 0285C] since it is quite sufficient that those holding possession in the name of absentees be assisted against the violence of persons present. Given on the 10th day before the Kalends of November at Constantinople, in the consulship of Constantine VII and Constans Caesar III (324). *(From the Code of Justinian.)*

In the year of the Lord 325, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus.

Below, the Aurelia-Lyons edition reads “of infirmity.”] and his judges having been invalidated, let no one seek through calumny to overturn what he himself did voluntarily, nor what was lawfully done. Given on the day before the Ides of February, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus (325).

## ON THE OFFICE OF A VICAR

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Silvius . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0285D] g Thus 5. Therefore nine letters have dropped out at the end of the line after *Silvium*, showing that the text is corrupt. In the Theodosian Code Silvius’ dignity seems to have been indicated [Col. 0286B] after *Silvium*, so that Paulus is not the name of Silvius but another person.] Paulus, magistrate of Italy [Note: [Col. 0286B] a *Mag.* can signify either *magistrum*, “master,” as W. edits it, or *magistratum*, “magistrate,” as Pu. has it. Both appear doubtful: there is nowhere mention of a “Master of Italy,” and, as regards *magistratum*, although there were certainly magistrates in the regions of Italy, such as consular governors and governors, I do not recall *magistratus Italiae*, “magistrate of Italy,” being used in legal inscriptions for the office itself, for example for the rank of consular or corrector. Cl. has “Vicar of Italy,” but this is too far from the abbreviation of the codex. Perhaps the codex wrote *pm*, from which the copyist made *paulum mag.* This plausible conjecture is supported not only by the words “your gravity,” but also by the fact that no other praetorian prefect of Italy is known for this year. Nevertheless, in a doubtful matter I thought it necessary to retain the very reading of the codex.]

After other matters: So that your gravity, distracted by other occupations, may not be burdened with piles of such rescripts, it has seemed good to assign to your gravity only those cases in which a more powerful person may oppress an inferior or lesser judge, or in which such a matter arises that it is not lawful for it to be settled in the court of a provincial governor, so that what has long been handled by those same governors may be settled before you. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March at Nicomedia, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus (325).

## ON INTEREST

[Note: [Col. 0287B] b In the *L. R. B.*, cited work, the following is read; since it is not found in the Theodosian Code, it is clear that at least one chapter of this title has perished: “If anyone has stipulated, or has permitted to be stipulated, two hundredths as interest upon a security, he shall be punished also by loss of the money which he lent, according to the Theodosian law on interest.”]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Dracilianus [Note: [Col. 0287C] c 6–8, 10, 14, 17, 18, Til. in margin, Cujacius edition 1, Aurelia-Lyons: *Traciliannm*; but see Gothofredus on this passage, note b. 15, 28, 40: *Gracilianum*; 16, 25: *Racilianum*; 38: *Dracidiano*; 42: *Dracidianum*.] acting as deputy for the Praetorian Prefect. P.* many have *vicar.* or *vicarium ppo*; some, “the vicariate prefecture” or “vicar, praetorian prefect.” 9 and 20 have “agent acting in the place of the praetorian prefect”; 28, “agent acting in the place of the praetorian prefect at Caesarea.” Sichard and Til. print “Prefect of the Vicariate,” but Til. in the margin: “Vicar.”]

Whoever lends wet or dry produce to persons in need shall receive, in the name of interest, an excess of one third; that is, if the amount lent was two modii, he shall receive one additional modius. But if the creditor, having been summoned, refuses to receive the debt because of the benefit of interest, he shall be deprived not only of the interest but also of the amount of the debt. This law applies only to produce. For a creditor is forbidden to receive for money more than one hundredth. Posted at Caesarea on the fifteenth day before the [Col. 0287B] Kalends of May, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus (325).

### INTERPRETATION

Whoever lends wet fruits—that is, wine and oil—or any kind of provisions to another shall receive from him, as interest, no more than one third; that is, the person who has received two modii shall return a third modius in addition. But if the person who lends is summoned and, for the sake of greater interest, refuses to receive from the debtor his debt with the third modius added, he shall lose even the principal debt. We decree that this provision applies only to produce. For when money has been lent, we do not order more than a single hundredth to be demanded by creditors.

l Most codices: *super*, “over.”

n Aurelia-Lyons omits *modios*, “modii.”

o 19 and 20: “he shall lose his own [debt] after rejecting the third modius, to receive from his own debtor”; 21: “third modius … even his own [debt],” in a second hand.

p The Lex Visigothorum: “Which law.”

q Many codices: *praecipimus*, “we decree.”

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Severus [Note: [Col. 0288B] c The Code of Justinian: “Emperor Constantine.” 6, 16, and Anianus of Rheims, according to Gothofredus’ chronology for the year 325: “Severianus”; likewise Til. through Cujacius edition 2 in the margin, 6 according to Ri., note b on this law, 10, 18, and R.: “Severinus.” But see Gothofredus on this passage, note b, and in the Prosopography under Severus.] Urban Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0288B] d 10, 18, and R.: “Publius”; 19, 20: *po*; 5, 20: *ppo*; 21: “praetorian prefect.” Most manuscript books, the Code of Justinian, and Nuremberg: “P. P.”; but Pl. 1 omits “Severus, Urban Prefect,” while Montpellier H. 82 has “Urban Prefect.” Sichard, Til., Cujacius edition 1, Aurelia-Lyons, Cujacius editions 2 and 2*, but in margin “P.V.” See Reland, cited work, p. 318.]

Whenever, by our rescript, a prejudicial ruling or a suspensory prescription is remitted, the way of petition shall be open. But that which removes examination of the entire matter and exhausts the force of the principal case cannot be overturned without serious loss to the other party. Therefore let no relaxation of a peremptory prescription be sought, nor let petition be made against the edict. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June at Nicaea, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, most distinguished consuls (325).

[Note: [Col. 0288C] e 21 and Sichard: after *judicium*, “judgment”; but Sichard, in corrections p. 178, from the Augsburg codex: *nostri praejudicii*, “of our prejudicial ruling.” The Code of Justinian omits *pr.* or *vel*. Most codices have *praejudicio*, while others have *moratoriam*, “suspensory.”

f Sichard through Lyons and some codices: *perscriptio*, erroneously.

g 8, 9, 20 corrected, 21, and Sichard: *remittetur*, “will be remitted”; but Sichard, in corrections p. 178, has *emittetur*, “will be issued,” from the Augsburg codex. The Code of Justinian, better manuscripts, Nuremberg edition, Schöffer edition, and the Auredanian manuscript cited by Char. Herm. agree with the Theodosian Code; others even have *petitur*, “is sought,” but Halander and the rest have *permittitur*, “is permitted.”

h Some editions of the Code of Justinian: *supplicanti*, “to the petitioner.”

i 20, 21, and Sichard: *jus negoti*, “right of the matter”; but 20 has the gloss “or force” inserted between the lines, and Sichard corrects to our reading.

j 20 and Sichard: *principales*; 8: *principaliter*. Codex 21 omits “examination … principal.” Codex 35: “and the force of the principal … matter”; Sichard, in corrections: *principalis*.

k 20, 21, and Sichard: “cannot be overturned by authority without …”

l 20, 21, Sichard: “a peremptory relaxation may be sought”; [Col. 0288D] “nor rescription” (Sichard: “against rescriptions”), “therefore, nor.” Til.: “may [it] be, a peremptory relaxation be sought.” “Let no relaxation of a peremptory prescription therefore be sought, nor …”

m 16, 20, 21, and Til. add *sublimium*, “of exalted [persons].” The Code of Justinian omits “nor against the edict,” supplied here.

n 26, Halander, and Russ. omit X; 32 and 39: XI.

o 19, Halander, and Russ.: July. Immediately after, some codices: Nicaea, Pollinus, Julinianus. Sichard, Cujacius edition 1, Aurelia-Lyons, Bæhrens, W., and the Code of Justinian: Nicea; W. in corrections: Nicaea, as also Constitution 62, 66, 76; Cujacius editions 2 and 2*, Gothofredus, Ri., and Ri.*: Nicia.

p “VV. CC.” is omitted in most codices and in the Code of Justinian.]

INTERPRETATION. A delaying prescription [Note: [Col. 0288D] q Many codices, Sich., Cuj. 1, and Aur. Lugd. read *perscriptio* here and below, incorrectly. In the margin of codex 20 these words are added: “A delaying prescription, which prolongs the case, may be granted by the prince to petitioners; a peremptory one, which removes the principal case, cannot be granted, or, if granted, has no force.”] is called one that prolongs the case, that is, when a litigant requests a stay from the Emperor; a peremptory prescription is one that removes the principal case [Col. 0288B], that is, if a litigant wishes to extinguish the case without trial by the Emperor’s favor. Therefore, by an imperial rescript a delaying prescription may be granted to petitioners; a peremptory one cannot be granted, and, if it has been granted by the Emperor, it shall have no force.

## CONCERNING VETERANS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Prefect of the City. [Note: Go. emends *PP.* in this place as *Pro---Praef.*; or, as in c. 12 [Col. 0289C] C. Th. *de Decur.* (XII, 1), “Vicar of the East,” since Maximus’ urban prefecture falls in the years 319–323. Cf. Schultz on this constitution, cited work, p. 640.]

Comitatensian and riparian soldiers, and protectors, shall exempt their own head, that of their father and mother, and that of their wife, provided that they have all these persons surviving, if they are entered upon the tax-registers. But if they lack any of these persons, or lack them all, they ought to exempt from their own property only as much as they could have exempted on behalf of those same persons had they not been absent; provided nevertheless that, having made an agreement with others and simulated ownership, they do not exempt another’s property, but truly their own resources.

§ 1. We decree that veterans, after letters of discharge upon completion of service, shall exempt both their own head and that of their wife; but [Note: The codex and Go. incorrectly read *aut* (“or”). Earlier the codex reads: *post temeritate missionis epistolas tam suo quam*.] if they have earned an honorable discharge, they shall exempt their own head only. We command that all other veterans, from whatever army, together with their wives, enjoy exemption of one [Note: Although Go. admits that the received text may be correct, he prefers *sui unius*.] head.

§ 2. But a riparian veteran [Col. 0289B] [Note: The editions read *Ripenses autem veteranos*, but the codex has *Ripensis autem veteranos*, whence it is evident that Go. and Be. rightly emend to *Ripensis autem veteranus* [Col. 0289D]; I have adopted this, for we have often observed that *o* and *u* are confused in the codex.] who under a previous law, after twenty-four terms of service [Note: According to Go., this earlier law does not survive. A little later the codex has *missionem imp.*] and having obtained an honorable discharge, enjoyed exemption of one head, shall, even if after completing twenty terms he has earned an honorable discharge, exempt one head after the example of comitatensian soldiers. [Note: Go. prefers *excuset*, and, without any adequate reason, writes it within brackets as *excuseT*.] If discharged before twenty terms as well, since the infirm and disabled are not assigned to the tax-registers, he shall enjoy the same benefit. [Note: I have written *utatur*, on the authority of Aur. Lugd. and Go. Be. The codex, Cuj. 1, and Cuj. 2–Be. incorrectly read *utantur*. Moreover, the codex reads: *invecilli---halares---propri---adque uxores ei* (corrected to *uxoris et*) *ripensib. indiscretae---dimissus*.]

§ 3. Alares and cohortales, while serving, shall exempt their own heads; veterans also shall enjoy the same relief of exemption, whenever and in whatever regions [Note: Go. incorrectly reads *patribus*.] they have obtained their discharge, if they have been discharged from comitatensian [Note: At the letters *tatensi* (for *comitatensi*) begins folio LXXV of the codex. In the same place, a little later, the codex has *causa admisse*, but an *i* is added above the line after *d*, and an *i* is placed above *e* (*causa adimissi*).] military service on account of old age or disability: they shall exempt two heads, namely their own and their wife’s, without distinction as to the number of terms of service; and riparian veterans shall likewise enjoy the same privilege without distinction, if [Col. 0289C] they prove that they were discharged because of wounds received in war. Thus, if any of them leaves military service after fifteen terms but before twenty-four years, [Note: Go. incorrectly reads *malitia*.] he shall enjoy exemption only of his own [Col. 0290A] head; for the wife of a riparian veteran, if [Note: Thus Aur. Lugd., Be., and Cuj. 1. Cuj. 2, 2* in the margin; the codex, Cuj. 1, Cuj. 2–Ri*. omit *si*. Go. conjectures *uxorem etiam Ripensis militia*, which I do not understand.] he leaves military service, [his own head only shall enjoy exemption] [Note: Go. and Be. have already observed that the words *sui---excusatione* have been transferred here from the preceding line [Col. 0290C] and must be removed. Be. first enclosed them in brackets.] must be exempted after twenty-four years.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, at Antioch, [Note: Go. incorrectly has *Antiochiae*. The codex reads *Antiochiae*, as almost always.] in the consulship of Paullinus and Julianus (325).
