## CONCERNING DECURIONS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus . . . . . [Note: In codex 4 and in the editions the official rank is absent, and in codex 4 there is no indication of a gap. Til.–Cuj. 2*. Be.; Go.–Ri*. have five dots, as we do. Go. and Be., from c. 12 of this title and Cod. Just. XI.49.1, restore “Vicar of the East.” In the inscription of c. 1 C. Th. *de Gladiatoribus* (XV, 12), he is called P. P.; Go. interprets this abbreviation as *Propraefectum*, i.e. Vicar. See Go.’s notes on this constitution, the cited c. 1, and his commentary on c. 15 C. Th. *de Paganis* (XVI, 10), and above on cited c. 4 (where the inscription is Pf. U.), note d.]

Since we have granted to various persons that they be assigned to legions or cohorts, or restored to military service, whoever produces a benefit of this kind shall be investigated to determine whether he is of decurional stock or was previously named to a curia; so that, if anything of this kind is proved, he shall be restored to his curia and city. This rule should be observed concerning all those who have long since been approved in military offices, or are secured by the military oath after restoration to service, [Note: In codex 4 the scribe corrected *muniuntur* for *muniantur*, which had previously stood there and was accepted in the editions. Reinesius emends *nominantur*, incorrectly. Go. says *muniuntur* is better.] or will later be approved through recommendations.

Posted on the fifth day before the Ides of July, at Antioch, in the consulship of Paullinus [Note: Codex 4 and the editions have *Paulino* here and in the following constitution.] and Julianus (325). [Note: Either XV Kal. must be written here, or V Id. in cited c. 4, so that both constitutions fall on the same day and can be connected with one another.]

## CONCERNING RECEIVERS, OFFICIALS IN CHARGE, AND TREASURY CLERKS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Euphrasius, rationalis of the three [Note: Folio 274 [ [Col. 0290B] Note b: The words *sui---excusatione* have been transferred here from the preceding line [Col. 0290C] and must be removed, as Go. and Be. have already observed. Be. first enclosed them in brackets.] of codex 4, at the bottom of which is the quire-mark Λϛ. Codex 4 and the editions read *Eufraxium*. Cod. Just.: “The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Eufraxius.” (Cuj.: *Eufras.*)] provinces.

After other matters: For many estates, even situated in diverse places, [Note: Til.–Lugd., Go.–Ri*: *Pro multis etiam, et in diversis locis*. In Cuj. 2 and 2* all punctuation is absent. See above XI, 36, 18, note *, and XII, 1, 183, note i.] it shall be lawful to pay in a weight of gold at one time, [Note: Go. omits *simul*.] so that security may be given, upon issued guarantees, for all estates, [Note: Aur. Lugd. incorrectly reads *inferre*.] lest, when gold is exacted separately from each individual, [Note: Cuj. 1 has *ac unoquoque*, a typographical error.] the advantage of provincials be exhausted by many and continual additional charges. [Note: Go. forbids emendation to *intrimentis* or *intertrimentis*, having interpreted *incrementa* as *epimetra* [supplementary exactions]. Correctly. See below XII, 13, 4 and Go.’s commentary on this constitution.]

§ 1. We add this also: each person shall pay what he owes within the limits of the year, at whatever time he wishes, and the payment shall be recorded through the official register-clerk; [Col. 0291A] [Note: Cuj. 1 has *apparitorem in ratio*, a typographical error. Go. not only emends but prints *tabularium apparitorem*. Yet Til. has *tabularium*. Correctly. See c. 27 and 30 of this title. I have therefore restored *tabularium*. The others have *tabellarium*, as does codex 4.] the gold being received without any delay, [Note: Go. incorrectly reads *suspiciendo*.] lest anyone incur expenses in a foreign city or, what is more serious, [Note: The words *quod est gravius* are surrounded by brackets in codex 4 and the editions by a later hand.] incur the penalty prescribed for the offence through frustration of the law. [Note: Cod. Just., in the cited place, begins: “We decree that public receivers shall receive gold without any delay, lest anyone be compelled to incur expenses on this account.”] For if a person wishing to pay is disregarded by the receiver, he must, after calling witnesses, submit a formal protest; so that, once this has been proved, he himself, freed from the bond of the offence, shall receive the due security together with its proceeds, [Note: Codex 4 reads *Liberatis*, corrected in red ink to *liberatus*.] and the person who neglected to receive it shall be compelled, through the force of your office, to pay into the accounts of the fisc twice the weight that was owed. [Note: Cod. Just. reads: *officii Praesidiis inferre cogatur*. “But if receivers have been negligent, with the judge concerned neglecting his duty, the loss shall be made good out of that judge’s own resources,” Go.’s first edition.]

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Paullinus [Note: Codex 4, Thil., Aur.–Be., and Cod. Just. read *Paulino*. Cuj. 1 has *Pulino*, incorrectly. Ri* adds 425.] and Julianus (325). [Note: C. 1 C. Th. *de Ponderatoribus* (XII, 7) has *PP.* The reading should be either *Dat.* or *PP.* in both places, so that this constitution and c. 1 may be connected. Go. thinks these constitutions were issued either at Nicaea or Nicomedia.]

## CONCERNING WEIGHERS AND THE PAYMENT OF GOLD

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Euphrasius, [Note: Codex 4 and the editions read *Eufraxium*.] rationalis of the three provinces.

If anyone wishes to weigh coined gold solidi, [Note: The editions have *Si quis*; codex 4 has *Si qui*, corrected in red ink to *Si quis*.] he shall weigh seven [Note: Codex 4 has *coeti*, corrected in red ink to *cocti*. In editions before Be. an asterisk occurs here (*auri * cocti*), which Go. wishes removed and Reinesius rightly removes.] solidi of four scruples each, [Col. 0291B] stamped with our images, for each ounce; fourteen, however, for two ounces, and by this standard shall pay in the entire sum of the debt. [Note: Cuj. 2 and 2* have *dediti*, an error, corrected in the *Corrigenda*.] The same method shall be observed also if anyone pays in bullion, so that he may be deemed to have paid solidi. But the gold that is paid in shall be received on an even balance and with equal weights, [Note: C. 1 Cod. Just. is written thus: “Gold paid in by contributors, whether anyone wishes to weigh solidi or bullion, shall be received on an even balance and with equal weights.”] namely, so that the upper end of the string is held by two fingers, [Note: Codex 4: *summittas*.] while the remaining three fingers are free and project toward the receiver, and do not depress the weights; [Note: Folio 284 [ [Col. 0291B] Note a: Cuj. 1 has *apparitorem in ratio*, a typographical error. Go. not only emends but prints *tabularium apparitorem*. Yet Til. has *tabularium*. Correctly. See c. 27 and 30 of this title. I have therefore restored *tabularium*. The others have *tabellarium*, as does codex 4.] of codex 4. Go., in his note: “Read *deprimat*, namely, the receiver.”] with no balance-weight of the scale being held, and without [Note: Gironius, *Observ. jur. Can.* IV, 5, conjectures *sed*, rightly rejected by Go. For *nec* refers to the preceding *nec* and to *nullo*.] the scale hanging in equal and matching [Note: Codex 4: *equis*, corrected in red ink to *aequis*.] moments, [Col. 0292A] etc.

Posted [Note: See c. 2 C. Th. of this title, note b. Go. criticizes those who conjecture that this constitution was issued at Antioch, since Constantine at this time was in Bithynia, either at Nicaea [Col. 0292C] or Nicomedia.] on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Paullinus [Note: Codex 4, the editions, and Cod. Just. read *Paulino*.] and Julianus [Note: Aur. Lugd. has *Cons.*] (325).

## CONCERNING JUDGMENTS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Severus, Prefect of the City. [Note: 8, 19, 29, 38, 42: *ppo.* Sich.: Pf. P.]

Absolutely no hearing shall be afforded to anyone who divides the unity of a case [Note: 16, 19: *causam*. 20: *continentia*.] and, by the prerogative of an imperial favor, wishes to litigate before different judges what could have been concluded in one and the same court: the following penalty being prescribed for anyone who petitions [Note: Cod. Just.: “with a penalty threatened ex officio by the judge against the person who …”] contrary to this enactment and requests one judge concerning possession, [Note: Some codices: *possessionem*. 20: “another concerning possession, another concerning the principal issue.” 33 omits *atque---postulaverit*, as does Cod. Just. all words after *postulaverit*. Aur. Lugd. omits *alium super poss.*] and another concerning the principal issue, that, after deduction made according to the full valuation of the thing sought, [Note: Thus 6–8, 14, 16, 17. 19: “that the things sought.” 20: “that the thing sought”; the remaining codices and editions: “was sought.”] he shall pay one fifth into the public treasury of the city [Note: 20: *civitati*.] within whose territory [Note: 33: *de cujus*, omitting *finibus*.] the property in dispute is situated.

Posted [Note: Many codices and Sich.–Lugd.: *Dat.* Some omit III.] on the third day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Julianus and Paullinus [Note: 15, 19, 20, 24, 29, 30, 33, 38, 40–42, 44, Sich., and Cod. Just.: *Paul. et Jul.* 9 omits *Jul. et*; others: *et Paul.*] (325).

[Col. 0292B] INTERPRETATION. Let no one at all be heard who wishes to divide the presentation of one case before two judges, so as to set forth the principal matter before one and ask that a more advantageous point be confirmed for him by another. If anyone should perhaps presume to do this, he shall know that he is to be condemned to such a penalty [Note: 6, 7, 43, and others: *se p. nov.*] that he shall by no means recover what he claims, and shall surrender to the public treasury of that city one fifth of his property, from [Note: 19, 20, Sich., Cuj. 1, and Aur. Lugd. omit *de*.] whatever he possesses there, [Note: Many codices, Sich., Cuj. 1, Aur. Lugd.: *possidere pojerit*. 20: *possidere poterat*.] within whose territory the property in dispute is situated.

## CONCERNING THE OFFICE OF THE PRAETORIAN PREFECTS [Note: Some codices, Sich., Til.: *Praetorii*. 9 omits *Praetorio*. In Cod. Just. there are two titles: *de Officio Praefecti Praetorio Orientis et Illyrici* (I, 26), and *de Officio praefecti praetorio Africae* (I, 27).]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Constantius, [Note: 5 reads *Constantinum*, but Cl., Pu., and W. read *Constantium*, rightly, since Constantius held the prefecture in this year and often. See Cl. p. 128, note 23.] Praetorian Prefect. [Note: 5: *pu*, that is, *praef. urbi* [Prefect of the City].]

By edict we admonish all provincials that, if they have been disregarded after petitioning their own governors, they shall petition Your Gravity, so that, if it is established that this has occurred through the fault or negligence of the governors, Your Gravity shall immediately report it to our knowledge, [Note: 5: *scienciencia*, not *sciencienciec*.] in order that they may be suitably punished.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, at Antioch, in the consulship of Paullinus and Julianus (325).

## CONCERNING THE CREDIBILITY OF WITNESSES AND DOCUMENTS [Note: 20: “Concerning the credibility of witnesses and charters, that is, instruments.” Likewise L. R. U. 15 omits *et instrumentorum*.]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Aurelius Helladius. [Note: Go. infers from c. 5 Cod. Just. *de Postulando* (II, 6; C. Th. II, [Col. 0293D] 10, 3) that Helladius was governor of a province. Go. is mistaken: Constantine.]

Although the definition of ancient law and the rescripts of earlier emperors have imposed in court upon the claimant of a thing the necessity of proving the thing which he claims, nevertheless, moved by equity and justice, we order that, if such a case should arise, the claimant must at the outset, according to the rule of law, prove [Note: With the letters *bare* begins folio 216 [ [Col. 0293C] Note a: 5: *dicto*.] of codex 4. Above, 4: *quamdo*.] the basis on which the thing belongs to him. But if his side fails in proofs, [Col. 0293B] then and only then shall the possessor be placed under the necessity [Note: Go.: *inponitur*.] of proving the basis on which he possesses or the right by which he holds, [Note: Ri*. incorrectly: *eeneat*.] so that the truth may thus be examined.

Given at Naissus [Note: Be.: *Naissi*. Thereafter codex 4 and the editions: *Paulino*.] on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Paullinus and Julianus (325).

## CONCERNING ACCUSATIONS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to all Provincials.

If there is any person, of whatever place, rank, or dignity, who is confident that he can truthfully and openly prove against any of my judges, counts, friends, or palace officials [Note: Folio 2 [ [Col. 0293C] Note a: 5: *dicto*.] of codex 4.] something that appears not to have been conducted rightly and justly, [Note: Ri. incorrectly: *manifenifeste*, and shortly afterward *vedeatur*.] let him come forward fearless and secure; let him petition me. I myself shall hear everything; I myself shall investigate; and, if it is proved, I myself shall exact vengeance.

Let him speak confidently, and let one whose conscience is clear speak. If he proves it, as I have said, I myself shall exact vengeance upon the person who until this time has deceived me by feigned integrity. But the man who has disclosed and proved this I shall enrich both in honors and in property. So may the supreme divinity always be favorable to me and preserve me safe, as I desire, with the republic most prosperous and flourishing.

Posted [Note: According to Go., in the *Chronicle*, p. XXV, *PP.* is written in place of *Data*; if adopted, this constitution was issued on the same day as c. 1 C. Th. *de Fide test.* (XI, 39), though that one was issued at Naissus.] on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, at Nicomedia, in the consulship of Paullinus [Note: Codex 4 and the editions: *Paulino*.] and Julianus (325).

## CONCERNING GLADIATORS [Note: Cod. Just. adds: “To Be Entirely Abolished.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: Go. believes *Propraefecto Praetorio* should be read. See C. Th. XII, 1, 10, note e; VII, 20, 4, note d; and Boecking’s arguments against Go. in his annotations to the *Notitia Dignitatum*, eastern part, p. 125.]

Bloody spectacles do not please us in civil leisure and domestic tranquility. Therefore, since [Note: Cod. Just. omits *qui*.] we absolutely forbid men to be gladiators, [Col. 0294A] [Note: What follows is absent from Cod. Just.] you shall rather cause those who formerly used to incur this condition and sentence on account of offences to serve in the mines, [Note: Folio 388 [ [Col. 0294B] Note a: What follows is absent from Cod. Just.] of codex 4. Below Be., Cod. Just.: Berytus; and 4, Til.–Be., Cod. Just.: *Paulino*.] so that they may acknowledge the penalties of their crimes without bloodshed.

Posted at Berytus, on the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Paullinus and Julianus (325).

## CONCERNING DECURIONS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Constantius, Praetorian Prefect.

Since, after the curiae have been reviewed, some persons flee to the protection of military service, we command that all who are not yet found liable to the office of primipilus shall be released from military service and return to the same curia. Only those shall remain in military service [Note: Folio 222 [ [Col. 0294B] Note a: What follows is absent from Cod. Just.] of codex 4.] who, by reason of their place and rank, already belong to a part of your [Note: Thus 4 and the editions; in the margin of Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2*: “perhaps, *primipilatui*,” which Ranconetus attempted, incorrectly according to Go. Here, probably Be. emends *pastui*. See C. Th. XI, 16, 18; VIII, 4, 8; and the *Gloss. Nom.* I agree with Go. Shortly afterward Aur. Lugd.: *Cons.*] [reading uncertain].

Given on the Nones of October, in the consulship of Paullinus and Julianus (325).

## CONCERNING THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE MILITARY ANNONA [Note: With the rubric of this title begins folio XLIX of the Lugdunensis codex.]

[Col. 0294B] The Emperor Constantine [Note: Cuj. 2 and 2*: *Constantius*, but in the *Corrigenda* restored to *Constantinus*.] Augustus, greetings, Felix, most dear to us. [Note: Codex: *HABE Felix*. Cuj. 1–Lugd.: *HABE Felix*. R. NB., Cuj. 2–Ri.: *HABE Felix k. NB.* Ri*, Be.: *habe* (Be.: *have*) *Felix k. nb.* Similarly in the inscriptions above, c. 9 *de Off. rect. prov.* (I, 15), c. 1 *Qui petant* (III, 18), and c. 4 *de Oper. publ.* (XV, 1).]

Tribunes or officers in charge who are responsible for our soldiers ought not to leave in the granaries the annonae due to them, as recorded day by day, [Note: Cuj. 1–Lugd.: *judicio*, rightly rejected by Go., for the codex has *indicio*.] so that procurators, receivers, or officials in charge of districts and granaries may procure them. [Note: Go. and Be. emend *eam* to *eas*, though Go. thinks *eam* can be defended. *Eas* is preferable. Cf. c. 1 C. Th. *de Pignor.* (II, 30), note n.] For this results in the said persons demanding not annonae but money from provincials, while the provisions themselves remain [Note: Go. notes: “Read *remanentibus*. Or the reading may be defended as though it were written: ‘and the annonae remain, with the provisions spoiled’; perhaps in the same sense *ipsae* should be substituted for *ipsis*.” Reinesius emends *remanentibus*, to which conjecture the reading of the codex, which has *remanent*, perhaps also lends support.] spoiled and corrupted. [Note: Cuj. 2 and 2*: *adque*—as also the codex, Cuj. 1–Lugd., Go.–Ri*—*corruptae*. Reinesius corrects to *corruptis*.]

We therefore decree that the fisc shall claim the benefit of annonae left behind, and that the subscript-clerk and the optio shall be struck with the sword, since it cannot happen [Note: Be. conjectures *ferri*, not implausibly, but not truly.] that either provincials are burdened with a repeated levy, or corrupted provisions [Note: Thus Be. from the manuscript of Go. and Go.’s authority; correctly. Reinesius likewise emends thus; the rest read *corruptis*. Perhaps Cujacius wished to place here the reading of Cuj. 2 and 2*, indicated by us in note g.] are distributed to the soldiers, [Col. 0295A] while the said persons refuse to take on the appointed day the annonae appropriate to their rank. [Note: Go.’s manuscript: *detractationibus*. Thus it is in the codex.] If anyone is caught in this offence, he is not to be defended either by the merit of his person or by the eminence of his office.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, at Aquae, [Note: Go. conjectures in the *Chronicle*: *Aplis*.] in the consulship of Paullinus [Note: The editions, as also the codex, read *Paulino*.] and Julianus (325).

## CONCERNING DECURIONS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Vicar of the East. [Note: 20: *vicarium orientalem*. Some codices: *vecario et horient.* 10, 18: *vicariu. honorium*. 16: *uc orient.* Cod. Just.: “The Emperor Constantine Augustus … Vicar of the City,” incorrectly. See preceding note e. Boecking therefore does not seem to have sufficiently established, in his annotation on the *Notitia Dignitatum* in the Eastern Regions, p. 125, what Go. says concerning the Vicar of the East.]

If anyone derives his origin from either a greater or a lesser city, [Note: Thus 4, Til.–Ri*; Be., from codices 6, 20, Sich., and Cod. Just., prints *Si quis*, with the remaining Br. Al. codices agreeing. Cod. Just.: “If anyone, since he derives his origin from …,” omitting *si*, apparently as Go. approves. But this sort of expression is common, as in this title, c. 6: “But if an owner … concealed, if indeed … there is an estate,” etc. Shortly afterward 20: *inquolatus occasionem*.] and, desiring to evade that city, has transferred himself to another city on the pretext of residence, and concerning this has either attempted to submit petitions or to employ any fraud [Note: Go.: *fraudi*.] in order to evade the origin [Note: 10, 18 add *ducit*. With the word *proprii*—thus—begins folio 1 of codex 11.] of his own city, [Note: 16: *civitaje se luat*. 20: *eludit*, but corrected.] he shall bear the burdens of decurional office in two cities, [Note: 11 omits *civitatum*. Shortly afterward most Br. Al. codices: *honera*.] in one by reason of choice and in one [Note: Thus 4, Til.–Lugd., Cod. Just., and the Br. Al. codices except 11, which has *alia*, as Sich.; Cuj. 2–Be.: *altera*, from Cujacius’s conjecture. Be. wrongly says *alia* occurs in codex 20; it has *una*, but omits *in*. Moreover Cod. Just. has *voluntatis, et in una or. gr.*] by reason of origin.

Posted [Note: 10, 18: *praecepta*. 20, 29, 42: *dat. s. Data*, but 20: *PP. data*.] on the eighth [Note: 11: VII. 20: V. 28, 36, 40: VI.] day before the Kalends of January, [Note: 32, 35, 43: June. 4 and the editions: *Paulino*.] in the consulship of Paullinus and Julianus (325).

[Col. 0295B] INTERPRETATION. If any curial wishes to transfer from the city in which he was born to another [Note: 20 adds *civitatem*.] city, [Note: Some codices add *et*.] he shall in no way be able to escape the condition owed to the curia; nor, if he attempts to obtain this very thing by a submitted petition, [Note: Thus 6, 7, Sich., Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2*, and almost all Br. Al. codices. 11 and Go.–Ri*: *meriti*. 20: *ipso m.*] nor by any device, [Note: Many codices: *nullum argumentum*; others: *temptaverit ut nec u. a.*] shall he be able to evade the obligations [Note: The editions and almost all codices: *necessitatis*. I print *necessitates* from codex 42, though a later hand corrected it to *necessitatis*. 20 omits *aut*. Shortly afterward 44: *habitationem suam*.] or services of his city because he wished to change his residence. For whoever does this and transfers himself to [Col. 0296A] another city [Note: 6, 7: *aliena civitate*, as in C. Th.; 11, 43, and many other codices: *alia civitate*.] is commanded to serve in both cities, [Note: 6, 7, 21 omit *ut*, and some codices omit *in*.] that is, [Note: Thus almost all codices, including 6, 7, 20, 21. The editions: *hoc est*; 6, 7, 21 omit *in una*. 11: *id est ut in una*.] in one according to the condition of his birth and in the other according to his voluntary residence.

In the year of the Lord 326: Constantine Augustus, for the seventh time, and Constantius Caesar, consuls.

## TO THE CLAUDIAN SENATE

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People.

Since ancient law compels freeborn women joined in cohabitation (*contubernium*) with servants of the fisc to suffer degradation of birth-status, without any indulgence being granted either for ignorance or for age, it is our pleasure that the bonds of such unions indeed be avoided. But if a freeborn woman, whether in ignorance or even willingly [Note: According to Go., some conjecture *nolens* (“unwillingly”), which Go. rightly rejects.] cohabits with a fiscal servant, she shall suffer no loss of free status; but the offspring born of a fiscal-servant father and a freeborn mother shall hold an intermediate condition, so that, as the children of slaves and illegitimate children of free persons, they shall be Latins, who, although released from the necessity of slavery, shall nevertheless remain bound by the privilege of a patron.

We wish this law to be observed with respect both to fiscal servants and to those arising from the estates [Note: Cuj. 1–Be.: *patrimoniorum*. W. adopts the highly plausible conjecture of Go. and Be., *patrimonialium*. But I did not wish to alter a text owed to one only, and indeed lost, codex, considering it enough to indicate the matter.] of the imperial patrimony, and with respect to emphyteutic lands and those belonging to the bodies of our private property. For we take nothing away from the municipalities under the old law; nor do we wish to associate with the scope of this law the servile persons of any cities, [Note: Cuj. 1–Be.: *legis volumus---copulamus*, producing an impeded construction. W. therefore, following Go.’s conjecture, put *ullatenus* in place of *volumus*. Be. wishes to restore: *legis urbium---copulamus; volumus*. Both conjectures are too arbitrary. I have no doubt that *copulari* should be read. The confusion arose from an abbreviation in writing.] so that cities may retain the full force of the old prohibition. If [Note: Go.–Be. incorrectly omit *Si*, though Ri. notes that Cujacius has *Si vel*. Be. wishes to supply either *aut si* or *quae*; W.: *Si quam vel Si quas*.] either unforeseeing error, simple ignorance, or the lapse of tender age has driven persons into these snares of cohabitation, such cases shall be excepted by our enactments.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, at Serdica, [Note: Cuj. 1–Ri*: *Sardicae*, but Be., W., and Go.’s authority: *Serdicae*.] in the seventh consulship of Constantine Augustus [Note: Go. orders VI to be restored and this constitution referred to the year 320, so as to join it to the laws named above. Although this is not without plausibility, I have not adopted it, for the same reason concerning the construction repeated in the editions.] and the consulship of Constantius Caesar (326).

## CONCERNING THE PETITION FOR AN INHERITANCE [Note: 9: *Petitiones*. Sich. and Til., in their indexes of titles: *De haereditatum petitione*. Cod. Just.: *de Petitione hereditatis*.]

[Col. 0296C] The Emperor Constantine [Note: Some codices, according to Go.: *Constantius*, incorrectly.] Augustus and Caesar [Note: 15, 39, 40, and other codices omit *et Caesar*, both here and in the subscription; 20 omits *et*. 10, 18, and the others: an error arising from the abbreviation *et c.*] to Maximus, Prefect [Col. 0297A] of the City. [Note: 8 omits U. 10, 18: *publium*. 15: *praepssito*. Some codices: *ppo.* Sich.: PF. 20: *pfectu.*]

If one who, having lost the dignity [Note: Some codices: *dignitatem*, and shortly afterward *emissa* or *amissam---omnem*.] of Roman citizenship, has become a Latin, [Note: 15: *eff. si in*.] dies in that same status, all his peculium shall be claimed by his patron, or by [Note: Thus 6, 7, 10, 14, 17, 18. The other codices and editions omit *a*, except 19, which has *ad patronum vel ad patroni*, and 20, [Col. 0297C] which has *ad patronum vel p.*] the sons or grandsons of his patron, [Note: Many codices: *si vel*.] who have in no respect lost the right of agnation. [Note: 16: *admiserint*. 15: *agnat. jus, am.* 14: *neq. ejus agnitiones*.] Nor may his sons enter into a dispute as though it were [Note: 20: *litis vel haered.* 19: *disc. vel litis haered.* Sich.: *disceptationem litis, vel ut*. Til.: *velut*, as do most codices; Cuj. 1 and Aur. Lugd.: *vel ut*.] an hereditary controversy, [Note: 6–8, 10, 16, 18: *hereditario*, but 10, 18 add *et*.] since the status in which he died must especially be considered, not that which he acquired through the benefit of granted freedom, [Note: Aur. Lugd.: *libertati*.] but [Note: 15: *sortitus sit sed*.] the status [Note: Sich., Cuj. 1, Aur. Lugd. add *vindicetur*, a gloss which in 20 stands above the line within brackets over the words *in quo munere*—namely, *vindicetur*—and, having been admitted by Sich. into the text, passed into Cuj. 1–Lugd.] in which he died.

Given on the third [Note: 15, 24: IV.] day before the Kalends of February, at Serdica, [Note: The codices mostly have *Sirdicae*, some *Sirdiciae*. Sich., Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2*: *Serdice*.] in the seventh consulship of the Emperor himself [Note: Some codices omit *Aug.*] and of the Caesar (326). [Note: Go., followed by Be., wishes VI (320) to be written, since there is no record of Maximus as Prefect of the City in this year. Constantine does not appear to have stayed at Serdica in this year, but did so in 320, when he issued several laws from that city in the same month. Go. also wishes this constitution to be joined with others; on this see c. 3 C. Th. *ad Sc. Claud.* (IV, 11), preceding note, and note h. 33: VIII (i.e. 329), 28 August (omitting VII), and *tesunt*.]

INTERPRETATION. If a Roman citizen, being a freedman, has through an intervening fault become a Latin freedman, and dies in that Latin status without restoration of his former [Note: 20, Sich., Cuj. 1, Aur. Lugd.: *primi*.] condition, his property [Note: 6, 7, 44, and others: *facultatem*.] shall be claimed for themselves by his patron, or by the sons or grandsons of his patron, provided that they descend through the male line and have not been emancipated. Nor, if he has perhaps left sons whom he begot as a Roman citizen, [Note: 9, 20, Sich.: *Nec sibi fil.*, but Sich. in the margin: *filii*.] may they lay claim to anything from his inheritance, because it is not to be asked [Note: 6–10, 14, 17, 18, 44, and others: *quaerendum*. 20: *requirenda*.] in what freedom-status they were born, but in what condition their father was when he died.

## TO THE JULIAN LAW CONCERNING ADULTERIES [Note: Some codices, including 4, Til.–Ri*, and Sich. in the index of titles, have *adulteris*, which Ri. incorrectly explains from the ancient practice of writing *adulterIs*. 15: “Concerning the Julian Law on Adulteries.” 36, 40: “To the Julian Law on Adultery.” 37 omits *de Ad.* Cod. Just. adds “and fornication.”]

[Col. 0298A]

Imp. Constantine Augustus to Africanus, *vir clarissimus*. [Note: [Col. 0298B] b Many manuscripts (among them 4), Sichardus—Lugdunensis, and the Code of Justinian omit *V. C.*; 10, 18: “the consuls.” Others: “to Africanus.”] A woman who has committed adultery [Note: [Col. 0298B] c 19, 20, above the line: “He who has committed adultery.” 12: *commiserit*.] must be investigated as to whether she was the mistress of an inn [Note: [Col. 0298B] d 4, 10, 18: *cauponi* [of an innkeeper], or at least; but in manuscript 4 *i* was corrected by an earlier hand to *e*, with a transverse stroke (*ae*), and the letter *a* was added above in red by a later hand. Til.—Lugd.: *cauponia* [female innkeeper]. 19: “whether, as mistress, she managed an establishment.” 20: “mistress of a tavern, administering it.” Otherwise 10: “master.”] or a serving-woman, and whether she performed servile attendance [Note: [Col. 0298B] e 15: “and if she thus performed servile attendance.”] such that she herself commonly provided the wines of intemperance [Note: [Col. 0298B] f 19, and above the line; 20: *jura* [laws/rights].] [Note: [Col. 0298B] g 20: “human,” but *vina* [wines] above the line. 19: “provided.” Gothofredus objects to the conjecture “provided a way for intemperance” [Col. 0298C] or “opened it.”]—so that, if she was the mistress [Note: [Col. 0298C] h 10, 18: *ut sit domina*; 19: *ut si et domina*; 20: *et in domina t. fuerint* (printed by Ritter), but corrected to *ut si a domina*.] of the tavern, she is not exempt from the bonds of law; [Note: [Col. 0298C] i 20: *suscepta*. Folio 12 of manuscript 4.] but if she supplied service to drinkers, [Note: [Col. 0298C] j 16: “of drinkers.” 19: “to such persons.”] then, because of the low condition [*vilitas*] [Note: [Col. 0298C] k Code of Justinian: *praebuerit* [has supplied].] [Note: [Col. 0298C] l 4: *bilitate*, corrected in red to *vilitate*. 8: *virilitate*. Aur.—Ri*: *utilitate* [utility], undoubtedly an error propagated from the Aur. edition into subsequent editions. Gothofredus therefore rightly corrected and restored *vilitate*, as in the editions of Sichardus through Cujacius I. See below, “whom the low condition of their life,” and the Interpretation: “If she performed the office of so lowly a service.” The manuscripts also oppose *utilitate*: apart from manuscript 8, which reads *vilitate*, they have not *utilitate*. Yet the confusion of the two words is not rare in manuscripts.] of the woman brought into accusation, [Note: [Col. 0298C] m 12, 15: “is brought.” 19: “will be brought, with care excluded, free persons who …”] the accusation being excused, the free persons accused shall withdraw. For chastity is required of those women who are held by legal bonds; [Note: [Col. 0298C] n Sichardus: *hiis*, as in the manuscripts; *ab* is absent in manuscript 9.] but these women are exempt [Note: [Col. 0298C] o 6, 7, 9, 10, 18: *haec*; 15: “held, but these are”; 19, 20: “these nevertheless [are] exempt.” Code of Justinian: “are held and possess the designation *materfamilias*. *Hae*,” probably Gothofredus.] from judicial severity, [Note: [Col. 0298D] p 19, 20 omit *a*.] [Note: [Col. 0298D] q Some manuscripts: *praestantur*. Code of Justinian: “are exempt from the severity both of stuprum and of adultery.”] since the low condition of their life [Note: [Col. 0298D] r 4: *bilitas*. 20: “the utility, dignity of life.” Code of Justinian: “the low condition of life.”] did not deem them worthy of observance of the laws. [Note: [Col. 0298D] s 19: *lesum*. 14: *obseratione*.] [Note: [Col. 0298D] t 6, 7, 10, 12–20: *crediderit*. Code of Justinian: “with respect to the matters written above.”] Given on the third day before the Nones of February at Heraclea, [Note: [Col. 0298D] u 10, 18, 27, 33, 34: fourth; 38: sixth. In some manuscripts the third is omitted.] [Note: [Col. 0298D] v 20: “at the town of Herculaneum and under Constantius.” In other manuscripts too the city’s name is badly rendered: *Heracliae* (thus also the Code of Justinian), *Heracle* (thus 6, 7), *Aricliae Eracliano*.] when Constantine Augustus was consul for the seventh time [Note: [Col. 0298D] x 6, 7, 10, 12–14, 16, 18, 20, 39, 40, 43: sixth, i.e. 319. 15: ninth. 8 omits Constantine; 28: Constantine fifth, in that year; 38: fifth. In some manuscripts “seventh” is omitted, in others “Augustus.”] and Constantius [Note: [Col. 0298D] y 15: Constans. 24: “Constantius, *vir clarissimus*, consul.” In many [Col. 0299B] manuscripts C. is omitted. In manuscript 40 the subscription reads: “At Heraclea, Constantine sixth year and Constantius consul, sixth year.” Gothofredus once conjectured that this law should be assigned to Constantius and emended the subscription: “Constantius Augustus, seventh time, and Constans Caesar, consuls” (534); but he himself did not approve this view.] Caesar were consuls (326).

[Col. 0299A] INTERPRETATION. The mistress of an inn—i.e., the innkeeper’s wife—[Note: [Col. 0299B] a 20: “the female innkeeper’s mistress”; Aur.—Lugd.: *domina*, erroneously.] if found in adultery, may be accused. But if her maidservant, or a woman who supplied service [Note: [Col. 0299B] b Some manuscripts: *ministerio*. 20: “or he who.”] in the inn, has been caught in adultery, [Note: [Col. 0299B] c Very many manuscripts: *adulterium*, and shortly below *dimittitur*.] she shall be dismissed because of her low status. But [Note: [Col. 0299C] d 21 omits *sed*. 6–8, 12, 14, 17, 21, 42, 44, and other manuscripts; Cujacius II—Gothofredus: *sed et si*. 20: *sed si et*.] even the innkeeper’s wife herself, if [Note: [Col. 0299C] e 6–8, 12, 14, 17, 20, 21, 40; Cujacius II—Gothofredus omit *si*. 21 has *et* for *si*.] she has performed the office of so lowly a service, and has been caught in adultery, [Note: [Col. 0299C] f Many manuscripts: *egerit et in*, which ought to have been accepted. Editions: *Egerit, in*. 42, corrected from *egerit* to *ut in*. Other manuscripts: *adulterium*. Moreover, according to Gothofredus, the interpreter added this on his own account.] cannot be accused by her husband. [Note: [Col. 0299C] g Very many manuscripts: *poterit*, not improperly.]

## On the Custody of Accused Persons

Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0299C] h Codices of Justinian: “the same Augustus”; and Cujacius, Ritter’s first edition.] to Evagrius, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0299C] i I have added the official title on the authority of Gothofredus and Baehr, from the Code of Justinian. *Pf. P.* is omitted in manuscript 4 and in Til.—Baehr. Gothofredus conjectured in a note *PPP.*, that is, *propraefectis praetorio*; in the Chronicle, *Pf. U.* [Urban Prefect]; but he himself rejects the former conjecture.] If anyone is caught in a fault or crime which appears deserving of prison confinement and the squalor of custody, [Note: [Col. 0299C] j 4: *clautris*, but corrected; Code of Justinian: “by which he appears deserving …”] after being heard on the record, and when the offense has been established, [Note: [Col. 0299C] k Aur.—Lugd.: *amisso* [loss].] he shall undergo the punishment of imprisonment; and thereafter, once brought out, he shall be heard on the record. [Note: [Col. 0299C] l Cujacius I—Lugdunensis: “once brought out, he shall be heard on the record.”] Thus, as though under public testimony, a record of the offense committed shall be made, so that a certain moderating restraint may appear to have been applied [Note: [Col. 0299C] m 4: *immodicae*, but corrected in part in red.] [Note: [Col. 0299C] n 4: *quidam*, corrected in red to *quaedam*.] [Note: [Col. 0299D] o Til.—Lugd.: *ad temperies*. Code of Justinian: *temperies*. Ritter prefers *temperies*, to whom *adtemperies* seems to have arisen through copyists’ carelessness, misled by the following word. Dirksen shows that the latter word occurs nowhere else.] to judges acting with excessive severity.

Given on the third day before the Nones of February at Heraclea, [Note: [Col. 0299D] p Code of Justinian: *Heracliae*.] when Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0299D] q Folio 9 [ [Col. 0299B] a 20: “the female innkeeper’s mistress”; Aur.—Lugd.: *domina*, erroneously.] of manuscript 4.] was consul for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar [Note: [Col. 0299D] r Code of Justinian: “and Constantius Caesar, consuls for the second time,” correctly printed by Ritter; see him, note k.] was consul (326).

## On the Public Post

Constantine [Note: [Col. 0299D] s Here begins folio XCII of the Lugdunensis manuscript.] Augustus to Acindynus [Note: [Col. 0299D] t Cujacius I—Ri*: *Acindinum*. Code of Justinian: *Acyndino*. Gothofredus prefers to attribute this constitution to Constantius and assign it to 339.] Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0299D] u Baehr notes: “but it was also written to the remaining Praetorian Prefects.” He does not add on what grounds he maintains this.] The right to use a train of draft animals or post-horses [*agminales seu paraveredi*] [Note: [Col. 0299D] v The manuscript, Gothofredus, and the Code of Justinian read *respublica* [the commonwealth], and the Code of Justinian shortly below, consistently with this reading, *subministrat* [supplies], incorrectly nevertheless in Cujacius. In Gothofredus the singular seems to have arisen from an error; for in his commentary on this constitution he explicitly says that the plural is the reading of this law and the singular that of the Justinian Code.] shall be denied to governors, rationales, and others who on that account supply public services, grain rations, and fodder for animals; [Note: [Col. 0300A] a The words *agminalis seu* are absent from the Code of Justinian.] [Note: [Col. 0300B] b The word *licentia* seems to have been taken by editors from the Code of Justinian, for the Lugdunensis manuscript has *diligentia*, which could very easily arise from repetition of the syllable *di*.] [Note: [Col. 0300B] c From this point the Code of Justinian continues: “But neither shall anyone have permission to travel by another road than that on which the public post is known to be established; except, of course, Your Sublime Office, for whom the public post, permission to travel by it, and, wherever need demands, are available.”]

Nor do we permit them to demand anything from provincials outside the prescribed order; only those whose reliability is known may make such demands when necessity requires it. [Note: [Col. 0300C] d Gothofredus incorrectly: *poscant*; shortly afterward the manuscript and editions before Baehr read *hii*, and Aur.—Lugd.: *tatum*.] Wherever need demands, the public post is available to your gravity; [Note: [Col. 0300C] e Gothofredus conjectures *gravitati*; unless, with Baehr, one wishes to refer *gravitatis* to *ratio*. The Code of Justinian supports Gothofredus’ conjecture.] if you must turn aside from the public road onto some military route where no transport authorization is available, use public draft animals, but moderately and temperately, [Note: [Col. 0300C] f The manuscript has *temporate*, but it is corrected to *temperate*; below Cujacius I, II—Ri* conjecture likewise.] and only those necessary for your own use.

If this provision is neglected, you will incur a mark against your reputation, while the governors will bear the risk, since inspectors have already been dispatched concerning this matter. For the harms inflicted on our provincials may also be inferred from the fact that, for our journeys, which public utility sets in motion, [Note: [Col. 0300C] g In the manuscript this passage is written: *enim potest* (but above the line has been added *mala*), *quod nostris itinerib. provincialib.*, which words are nevertheless deleted by the copyist, except for the words *enim mala* and *nostris provincialib.* It is evident that some words were drawn back here by the copyist from the following sentence.] [Note: [Col. 0300C] h Read: *quae publica utilitas movet*. The manuscript: *moret*. Editions: *monet*.] with great and anxious preparation scarcely can a number of twenty teams of draft animals be supplied. [Note: [Col. 0300B] i The manuscript: *magminalium*, but the copyist has deleted *m* in the syllable *mag*.]

Posted on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, when Constantine Augustus was consul for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar was consul (326).

## On Pleading

Constantine [Note: [Col. 0300C] j The editions and manuscripts here give “Constantine Augustus,” because in them this is the first constitution under this title. 27: “Valentinian Augustus.”] Augustus to Bassus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0300D] k 6, 7, 16, 20, 42 (by a second hand), and several manuscripts cited by Gothofredus: *Pf. U.* [Urban Prefect], who wishes either to assign this passage to 320 or to understand the Vicar of Italy as Pro-Praetorian Prefect in 326. See Gothofredus on this constitution, note b, and in the Prosopography under Bassus; but see below, note v. 15: “to Bassus, PPO.” 10, 18: Publius.] We order that advocates [Note: [Col. 0300D] l 8, 10, 18–21, Sichardus: singular *Advocatus*. Constitution 5 of the Justinian Code, addressed by Constantine to Helladius in 323, is similar.] who, by criminal agreements, [Note: [Col. 0300D] m 8, 10, 18, *Annales Regii* in Gothofredus: “whoever [deals] with criminals.” 16, 19, 20, Sichardus: “with criminal …”] [Note: [Col. 0300D] n 8, 9, 14, 15, 20, 31, Sichardus, Til.—Lugd.: *depactionibus*.] strip and despoil persons in need of their aid, [Note: [Col. 0300D] o 6, 14: *opere*. 7, 19: *opes*.] [Note: [Col. 0300D] p 6: *gentes*. 15: *agentes*. Aur.—Lugd.: *regentes*.] [Note: [Col. 0300D] q 19–21, Sichardus: singular *expoliat*. 15 adds *eos*.] [Note: [Col. 0300D] r 19–21, Sichardus: singular *denudat*. 6–10, 14, 16, 18, Til.: *nudant*.] not by the legal merits of the case, [Note: [Col. 0300D] s 20, 21, Sichardus: *juratae*.] [Note: [Col. 0300D] t 19: *causa*.] but after considering the character and value of estates, livestock, and slaves, [Col. 0301A] [Note: [Col. 0301B] a 8: *fedorum p. emancipiorum qualitatem rationemq.*] and, while seeking their principal possessions, [Note: [Col. 0301B] b 19: *passunt*. 21, Sichardus: singular *poscit*.] compel them to convey these to themselves by an agreement extorted under duress, [Note: [Col. 0301B] c 19–21, Sichardus: *in quo acta*.] [Note: [Col. 0301B] d 19: “to write over from.” 20, 21, Sichardus: “transferred from.”] shall be excluded from the company of honorable persons and from the sight of the courts. [Note: [Col. 0301B] e 6–8: “and from the courts.” Til.: “the sight of the courts.”] [Note: [Col. 0301B] f 14: *conscriptu*. 20: *conspectis*.]

Posted [Note: [Col. 0301B] g 10, 15, 18–21, 26, 29, 36, 40, 42, Sichardus: “Given.”] on the eighth day before the Ides of March [Note: [Col. 0301B] h 20, 21, Sichardus: sixth, i.e. 320, probably Gothofredus. 19: the day before. 15 omits eighth. 26, 36, 40, Sichardus in the margin: seventh.] at Constantinople, when Constantine [Note: [Col. 0301B] i 6–8, 10, 14, 16, 17, Til.—Ri*: third. 19–21, Sichardus, Baehr, W.: seventh, i.e. 326; but 15, 24, 30, 31, [Col. 0301C] 35: eighth, i.e. 329, which is the truer reading, for in that year Bassus was Praetorian Prefect of Italy. See Gothofredus, Prosopography, under Bassus. 40: “to Constantine the prefect.” 26: Constantine first, and omits both *et* and *augustus*. 36 omits seventh—Caesar. 33 omits Constantine—consuls.] Augustus was consul for the eighth time and Constantius [Note: [Col. 0301C] j Some manuscripts: Constantine.] Caesar [Note: [Col. 0301C] k Many manuscripts omit Caesar, or read “Caesar, consuls”; some read “*V. C.*, consuls.” Add: fourth.] were consuls (329).

INTERPRETATION. Advocates—that is, persons conducting cases—[Note: [Col. 0301C] l Sichardus in the margin: *dicentes* [speakers], as manuscript 40.] who, through unjust greed, first compel those whose cases they undertake [Note: [Col. 0301C] m 19–21, Sichardus, Cujacius I, Aur.—Lugd.: “of those whose case they have undertaken,” and omit *quorum*.] [Note: [Col. 0301C] n Most manuscripts, Sichardus, Cujacius I, Aur.—Lugd.: “whose cases they are to conduct.”] [Note: [Col. 0301C] o 40, Sichardus, Cujacius I, Aur.—Lugd.: *cogantur* [are compelled].] to enter into an agreement concerning their possessions through an instrument of this kind, [Note: [Col. 0301C] p 9: *placitis et ut*.] so that everything better among their lands, [Note: [Col. 0301C] q *In* is absent from the editions, but added in almost all manuscripts.] slaves, or livestock may come to the advocates under a promised defense; [Note: [Col. 0301C] r 20, Sichardus: *definitione*, but Sichardus in the margin: *defensione*. It should further be observed that after *perveniant* no apodosis follows.] and therefore we order that those found to have acted so criminally against persons to whom they promised advocacy be excluded from the assembly of honorable men and from fellowship in the courts. [Note: [Col. 0301D] s Many manuscripts add *a*.]

## On Restoration in Full

[Note: [Col. 0301D] t 14, 19–21, 25, 26, Sichardus: “On Restorations in Full”; others, such as 38, 40, 42: “On Restoration in Full.” Code of Justinian (II, 22): “on restoration in full of persons under twenty-five years.”]

[Col. 0301B]

Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0301D] u Code of Justinian: “the emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, Augusti,” wrongly; but the Halle edition has our reading.] to the People. There is no doubt that, through the protection of enactments, provision has been made in restoration in full for minors against fictitious sales and the plots of guardians; [Note: [Col. 0301D] v 20, Sichardus: “restoration in full.” 6–8, 14–19, 33: *restitutionem*.] [Note: [Col. 0301D] x Code of Justinian adds “or curators.”] [Note: [Col. 0301D] y 20: *inducias*.] and it is declared that minors have been protected by the fraudulent-transfer interdict if those same persons should perhaps be shown to have alienated anything of their own in fraud of the guardianship. [Note: [Col. 0301D] z Sichardus: *cautam*.] [Note: [Col. 0301D] aa What follows is absent from the Code of Justinian.] [Note: [Col. 0301D] bb Many manuscripts, Til.—Ri*: *idem*. 20, Sichardus: *eidem*. 33 omits *iidem*. Baehr and W.: *iidem*, on Gothofredus’ authority, which accords with manuscript practice, since they very frequently have *idem* for *iidem*.] [Note: [Col. 0301D] cc Many manuscripts: *in fraude*.] [Note: [Col. 0302C] a 10, 18, Sichardus: *docentur*. 33: *ducentur*.]

Given on the third day [Note: [Col. 0302C] b Thus some manuscripts. See constitution 3, *C. Th.* On the Administration of Guardians (III, 30), note q.] before the Ides of March at Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0302C] c Thus most manuscripts, Sichardus—Ri*; Baehr and W.: *Sirmii*. Shortly afterward some manuscripts—VI, 26, 40—omit Sirmium through consuls.] when Constantine Augustus himself was consul for the seventh time and Constantius [Note: [Col. 0302C] d 6, 7, 14, 34 omit Constantius Caesar fourth; 16 omits “and—consuls”; others—9, 15, 19, 20, 29–31, 42, Sichardus—read “Constantius and fourth”; 10, 18 omit Caesar fourth. Til.—Baehr: Constantine, but Baehr in a note proposes our reading from Gothofredus’ Chronicle for this year.] Caesar [Note: [Col. 0302C] e 9, 42, 44: “and Caesarius.” Code of Justinian: “Constantius, second time, and Constans, Caesars, consuls” (339), a reading inconsistent with the subscriptions of the other constitutions to be joined to this one and with constitution 2 under this title, which would thus be older than the first constitution. See Glück, cited work, vol. XXXII, p. 476, [Col. 0302D] note 26.] was consul for the fourth time (326).

INTERPRETATION. It is established that the laws have made extensive provision for those under age. Therefore, against guardians’ frauds or sales which they have extorted from minors by some contrivance, [Note: [Col. 0302D] f At this word ends folio 25 of manuscript 24; the following folio begins with constitutions 2 and 3 under this title.] [Note: [Col. 0302D] g 20: “which if by contrivance …,” but *si* added above the line.] or against anything they have unjustly done under the name of guardianship, [Note: [Col. 0302D] h 20, Sichardus: *quicquam*, but Sichardus in the margin: *quicquid*.] [Note: [Col. 0302D] i Some manuscripts, such as 9, 44: *tali*.] they should know that it is to be revoked by the benefit of the law.

## On the Administration and Liability of Guardians

Constantine Augustus to the People. The law which compelled guardians and curators, as a matter of necessity, to sell gold, silver, gems, clothing, and other valuable movables, also urban estates and slaves, houses, baths, granaries, and everything situated within a city, and to convert all these into cash—apart from landed estates and rural slaves—[Col. 0302B] is gravely contrary to the interests of minors. [Note: [Col. 0302D] j Against those who understand here the oration of Severus partly preserved in Digest I.2, *On the Property of Those under Guardianship or Curatorship* (XXVII, 9), W. cites Haubold’s *Dissertatio historico-juridica de rebus eorum etc.* (Leipzig, 1798, quarto), chap. 2, §1, pp. 27–29 (*Opera*, vol. 2, pp. 184–190). In what follows I have nevertheless retained W.’s annotations, though briefer.]

We therefore order that it shall not be lawful for any guardian or curator to sell any of these things, unless perhaps under the same necessity and legal procedure by which it was formerly permitted to sell or pledge a rural estate or slave, or to give it as a donation in contemplation of marriage [*propter nuptias*] [Note: [Col. 0302D] k Constantine undoubtedly wrote *ante nuptias* [before marriage], since the term *donatio propter nuptias* came into established use only under Justinian.] or as dowry: namely, through a judicial inquiry, proof of the cause, and issuance of a decree, so that no room may exist for fraud.

Above all, urban slaves, who have knowledge of the whole household equipment, must always be retained in the inheritance and in the house. Good slaves will prevent fraud from being committed; bad slaves, if the matter requires it, may be put to the question and disclose the truth. Thus they will safeguard everything, [Note: [Col. 0302D] l W., to whom this scarcely seems fitting for slaves, especially bad ones, conjectures *observabuntur* [everything will be safeguarded].] so that the guardian cannot diminish the inventory, alter it, or remove anything from it. This is necessary concerning clothing, pearls, gems, vessels, [Col. 0302C] and the rest of the household equipment.

And, should it happen thus, it is more tolerable for slaves to die while belonging to their own masters than to serve strangers. Their flight is rather imputed to the guardian, whether he allows discipline to be relaxed through negligence, or subjects them to harshness, hunger, and beatings. For slaves do not curse their masters, but rather love them; hence this law too is better than the old one. For then, once the supervision of slaves had been removed, even the lives of minors were more frequently betrayed.

Nor shall it be lawful to sell the house in which the father died, in which the minor grew up, and in which it is sufficiently grievous either not to see the images of ancestors set up, or to see them torn down. Therefore, both the house and all other immovables shall remain in the property of minors; and no kind of building which the inheritance delivered intact shall perish through a guardian’s fraud.

Further, if a parent, or the person of whom the minor is heir, has left a building in disrepair, the guardian shall be compelled to restore it by attestation concerning the work itself and by the assurance of many persons. For annual revenues will thus contribute more to minors than prices diminished through fraud. [Note: [Col. 0303C] a Basilica, cited passage: “For income is better for a minor than the money of the price” (*κρεῖττον γὰρ ἐστι τῷ ἀνήβῳ ἡ πρόσοδος, τῶν τοῦ τιμήματος ἀργυρίων*). Rusardus incorrectly has *praedia demolita* [demolished estates].]

Slaves who possess some craft shall devote their labor to the minor’s advantage; and the rest, who cannot be employed by their minor master and possess no craft, shall be supported partly by their labor and partly by an allowance for maintenance. [Note: [Col. 0303C] b Basilica: *ἢ διὰ τῶν διαρίων αὐτῶν ἀποτρέφεσθωσαν*, i.e., “or let them receive fixed maintenance for each day.” A new period begins in what follows, for the words “For the law,” etc., concern not merely the immediately preceding matter but the entire subject of the law. Basilica: *Καὶ οὐ μόνον* [“And not only …”].]

For the law has made provision for minors not only against guardians, but also against immoderate and intemperate women, who commonly consign to new husbands not only the property of their children but even their lives. To this is added the fact that the practice of lending at interest the money itself—in which the ancients placed the whole strength of estates—is scarcely lasting, scarcely continuous or stable; when it fails, and money is often lost, minors’ estates are reduced to nothing.

Accordingly, no sale by a guardian shall be valid without issuance of a decree, except only in the case of garments worn out by use or corrupted so that they cannot be preserved by being kept. [Note: [Col. 0303C] c At this point the Code of Justinian immediately continues with the words “Animals …” But the Turin folio, beginning with *vel* [or], proves that something has been omitted in the Code of Justinian. Since the following word clearly must be referred to garments, Winkius rightly restored the connection conjecturally by inserting two words, distinguished in print.] Even a diligent guardian [Note: [Col. 0303D] d The final part of the law is formulated in constitution 4, Code of Justinian, *When a Decree Need Not Be Obtained* (V, 72), as follows: “And without issuance of a decree we permit guardians and curators of any persons to sell worn-out garments and superfluous animals.”] or curator, though he inspect them repeatedly to ensure that they remain sound, [Col. 0303C] shall not be forbidden to sell superfluous animals belonging to minors. [Note: [Col. 0303D] e Thus manuscript 1. Code of Justinian: “although [they belong] to minors.” Perhaps read: “Animals [belonging] to minors, lest they be sold, we do not forbid.”]

Given on the third [Note: [Col. 0303D] f Thus manuscript 1; but the Code of Justinian in both places (constitution 22 and constitution 4 cited), and constitution 1, *C. Th.* On Restoration in Full (II, 16), omit “third.”] day before the Ides of March at Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0303D] g Manuscript 1: *Sir.* P. Pu.: *Sirmi*. W.: *Sirmii*, as in constitution 1 of the Theodosian Code cited; but the Code of Justinian in both places has Constantinople, which W. rightly considers an error of copyists arising from the following names.] when Constantine Augustus was consul for the seventh time and Constantius [Note: [Col. 0303D] h Thus manuscript 1 and constitution 4 of the Code of Justinian cited; but constitution 22 of the Code of Justinian cited has Constantine, wrongly. Moreover, the letters *cogni* [in *recognitione*], *quin v* [in *veneant*], and *A. VII. e(t)*, torn away from the Turin parchment, were restored by P. from the Code of Justinian.] Caesar [Note: [Col. 0303D] i Constitution 4 of the Code of Justinian adds “fourth.”] were consuls (326).

## On the Lex Cornelia concerning Forgery

[Col. 0304A]

Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0304C] a From the Code of Justinian, “the same Augustus” should be restored.] to Maximus, Urban Prefect. Since in the past this practice was observed in the courts—that when documents were produced, if anyone alleged them to be forged, the judge would refrain from deciding the civil dispute—and since it consequently occurred that an impending accusation, unrestricted by any limitation period, would frustrate the claimant or possessor, [Note: [Col. 0304C] b Folio 29 [ [Col. 0303C] b Basilica: *ἢ διὰ τῶν διαρίων αὐτῶν ἀποτρέφεσθωσαν*, i.e., “or let them receive fixed maintenance for each day.” A new period begins in what follows, for the words “For the law,” etc., concern not merely the immediately preceding matter but the entire subject of the law. Basilica: *Καὶ οὐ μόνον* [“And not only …”].] of manuscript 4.] we have thought it expedient that, even if one or the other litigant raises an allegation of forgery, the authority of the documents produced shall nevertheless confer its force upon the claimant or possessor; [Note: [Col. 0304C] c 4: *strumentorum*, corrected in red.] so that, once the civil litigation has been concluded, a subsequent action for forgery may follow.

§ 1. Therefore we will that the formal accusation first cease. [Note: [Col. 0304C] d Baehr incorrectly reads *nunc* [now].] [Note: [Col. 0304C] e Here begins constitution 22 of the Code of Justinian cited.] But when an examination of forgery arises, then, in accordance with the ancient practice, after the civil inquiry has been concluded by judgment, [Note: [Col. 0304C] f The words “in accordance with the ancient practice—concluded” are absent from constitution 22 of the Code of Justinian. They are included in constitution 23 of the same title; see constitution 4 under this title, note n.] the strictest investigation shall be made by arguments, witnesses, [Col. 0304B] comparison of writings, and other traces of truth. Nor shall the inquiry rest upon the accuser alone, nor shall the entire burden of proof be imposed upon him; [Note: [Col. 0304C] g 4: *indigatur*, corrected by a later hand.] rather, the judge shall stand between the two parties and shall disclose by no interlocutory ruling what he thinks, [Note: [Col. 0304C] h 4: *ullaq.*; Code of Justinian: “and shall disclose by no interlocutory ruling what he thinks.”] but, as in imitation of a reference which mandates only the duty of hearing, [Note: [Col. 0304C] i Til.—Lugd.: *mandato officium praebeat*.] shall conduct the inquiry, revealing in his final judgment what appears clear to him.

§ 2. We limit to the period of one year the final term of criminal contention, which it is unlawful for a litigant and disputant to exceed. [Note: [Col. 0304D] j Code of Justinian: “We limit criminal [proceedings] within a short period, which it is unlawful for a litigant … to exceed, and the beginning of which will arise from the initiation of an accusation formally entered before the competent judge; after proof, by capital punishment, if it …,” etc.; thus also Cujacius II—Gothofredus. “*Contestatae*,” probably Gothofredus in the commentary.] Its beginning shall arise from an action attested before the competent judge; after proof, the person who committed forgery shall be liable to capital punishment, if the gravity of the offense requires it, or to deportation. [Note: [Col. 0304D] k Folio 30 of manuscript 4.]

Posted on the eighth day before the Kalends of April in the Forum of Trajan, when Constantine [Col. 0304C] Augustus was consul for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar were consuls (326). [Note: [Col. 0304D] l Gothofredus—Ri*, and the Code of Justinian omit the year, because Maximus is not found as Urban Prefect in this year. In a note, Gothofredus restores the consuls of 320. Baehr observes: “Gothofredus wishes [the reading] ‘sixth, and Constantine’; and indeed 326. Maximus had already been Praetorian Prefect. But if this subscription is correct, we must suppose that the law was addressed to the Praetorian Prefect and further sent also to the Urban Prefect.” I do not understand this. The law seems to have been issued in one year and posted in the Forum of Trajan in another.]

## On Swine Contractors

Constantine Augustus to Lucrius Verinus . . . [Note: [Col. 0304D] m The official title is absent in manuscripts and editions, with no indication of a lacuna. Gothofredus, Reinesius, and Baehr wish to add “Urban Prefect”; see note o.] A landholder shall have it in his own choice not to pay money to the swine contractor. This is permitted in order that swine contractors may not be afforded an opportunity for abuse in estimating the weight of pigs. [Note: [Col. 0304D] n Gothofredus: “We permit.”] But if the swine contractor has fairly assessed the pigs, the landholder—who has been granted the option of either mode of payment—shall pay him money. [Col. 0305A] [Note: [Col. 0305B] a Gothofredus: “of one or the other.”] [Note: [Col. 0305B] b Gothofredus: “if he wishes.”]

But lest the swine contractor suffer any loss in receiving payment, [Note: [Col. 0305B] c Cujacius II, II*: *detrimenta*. Reinesius corrected to *detrimenti*. Gothofredus: *deferatur* for *adferatur*.] the landholder shall pay each year such prices for pork as the usage of public commerce has established. And because prices do not always have one and the same rate in every place, payments in kind shall be made at the prices appropriate to the different places and times, [Note: [Col. 0305B] d Folio XXXIX of manuscript 1 ends in the letters *locorumette*. See constitution 18 of the preceding title, note above. Cujacius I: *Diversitate*.] [Note: [Col. 0305B] e See note above on this constitution. Gothofredus: “according to the commodity.”] unless pork itself is supplied.

The judges of the regions are to be instructed that every year they report to your knowledge the prices of pork in the several places, [Note: [Col. 0305C] f Folio 337 [ [Col. 0305B] b Gothofredus: “if he wishes.”] of manuscript 4.] [Note: [Col. 0305C] g 4: *adscient ad scientiam*, but *adscient* deleted in red.] so that, after this information has been considered by your gravity, the swine contractors may then travel through the various places [Note: [Col. 0305C] h 4: *tuncdemsuarii*. Ri*: *nunc* for *tunc*.] and receive the prices which you have learned prevail in those regions. For swine contractors will be unable to complain, [Note: [Col. 0305B] i 4, Til.—Lugd.: *Quaeri* [to be complained of].] because it makes no difference whether they purchase more dearly or more cheaply, since they receive from the landholder the price that they must pay. [Note: [Col. 0305C] j 4: *quatum pretium*.] And landholders will be moderate in selling commodities, because they know that the higher the prices they demand for meat, the more they must pay to the swine contractors.

Given on the third day before the Ides of April, when Constantine Augustus was consul for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar were consuls (326).

## On the Correction of Slaves

The same [Note: [Col. 0305C] k Aur.—Lugd.: “the consuls.” Because Lucrius Verinus was Urban Prefect in 323 and 324, whereas Anicius Julianus held that office in 326, Gothofredus wishes to assign this constitution to 324. Baehr likewise, following Gothofredus, considers the subscription false.] Augustus [Note: [Col. 0305C] l Manuscripts of the Breviary and Sichardus give the emperor’s name.] to Maximilianus [Note: [Col. 0305C] m I have restored *Maximiliano*, for this is read by manuscripts 1 and 4, the two surviving examples of the genuine Theodosian Code; likewise by manuscripts 13, 15 (and this manuscript frequently agrees with authentic exemplars of the Theodosian Code), 29, 37, 38 (but this one reads *ad Maximiliano*), 40, 42, Til.—Lugd.; Gothofredus in the Chronicle from manuscript 4. Likewise 21: *ad Maxaemilianum*. Cujacius II—Baehr: *Maximiano*. Constitution [Col. 0305D] 1, *C. Th.* On Aqueducts (XV, 2), is addressed to Maximilianus, consular governor, where Gothofredus notes: “Is he the same man called Maximilianus Macrobius, to whom constitution 2 above, On the Correction of Slaves, is addressed? But a Julius Maximilianus, Count, is also mentioned in an ancient inscription on the Caelian Hill at Rome, made by him in honor of Helena, mother of Constantine and grandmother of Constans and Constantius. It appears in Gruter’s *Corpus Inscriptionum*, CCLXXXIV.1.” Hence it is clear from these passages that the name Maximilianus was not unknown to the Romans and was only later corrupted by scribes into Maximianus, Maximus, *ad Maximianum* (as in Sichardus), and *ad Maximum*. Moreover, 20, 27, 32, 33, 37, 39, 43: *ad et* (“to Maximus and Macrobius,” or “to Maximianus and Macrobius,” as Sichardus has).] Macrobius. [Note: [Col. 0305D] n This name too has been corrupted by scribes: 6–8, 12 read *Nirotio*; 10, 18 *Nirutio*; 14 *Nirocio*; 25 *Magroino*; 26 *Machoronio*; 40 *Nicrovio*; 1, 20, 32, 38, 43 *Macrouio*; 13 *Macrobii*.] . . . Whenever the beatings [Note: [Col. 0306B] a 12: *verba* [words], and shortly afterward some manuscripts: *tales*.] [Col. 0306A] administered by masters are accompanied in the case of slaves by such an outcome that they die, [Note: [Col. 0306B] b 10, 18: *morientur*. 4, 12: *moriatur*.] those who, while correcting the worst faults, wished to secure better conditions for their own home-born slaves [*vernuli*] are free from blame. [Note: [Col. 0306B] c Sichardus: “are to be blamed.”] [Note: [Col. 0306B] d Thus all manuscripts, including manuscript 1; for P. notes: “*Vernu***. Therefore it was *vernulis*,” etc. Manuscript 4 alone reads *vernullis*, but it is corrected in red to *vernulis*. The reading *vernolis* in some manuscripts concerns only orthography. Sichardus—Lugdunensis likewise read *vernulis*. Cujacius II—Baehr wrongly: *vernaculis*. Gothofredus nevertheless found a rationale to explain *vernaculis*, but I do not accept it.] [Note: [Col. 0306B] e 12: *voluerunt*. 13: *voluerant*. 20: *voluerint*, corrected to *voluerunt*.]

Nor [Note: [Col. 0306B] f Thus the manuscripts, among them manuscript 1, and Sichardus; approved by W. Manuscript 4 alone has *Nam* [for], which passed into the editions Til.—Baehr. Retaining *Nam*, constitution 1 under this title is supplemented; with *Nec* it is corrected. For the emperor declares that if a slave, chastised with beatings for the purpose of correction, dies when fatal necessity threatens, it need not be investigated whether the master wished to kill the slave or merely to chastise and correct him.] do we wish inquiry to be made in a case of this sort, in which it is in the master’s interest to have his own slave unharmed, whether the punishment appears to have been inflicted with the intention of killing a human being or simply for correction. [Note: [Col. 0306C] g 4: *requirere*, corrected to *requiri*. 6 omits *in*.] [Note: [Col. 0306C] h 12 omits “in which,” and 10, 18: *domini*. 6, 7, 10, 18: *incolumi*. 20: “we have wished—incolomis.”]

For we do not think that a master should be pronounced guilty of homicide because of the death of a slave as often as he exercises domestic authority in simple examinations. [Note: [Col. 0306C] i Folio 19 [ [Col. 0306B] a 12: *verba* [words], and shortly afterward some manuscripts: *tales*.] of manuscript 4.] [Note: [Col. 0306C] j Sichardus: “For so often indeed it does not please [us] that the master [be held] guilty because of the death …” 15 omits *morte*.] [Note: [Col. 0306C] k 12: *dominicam exerceat*. 9: *exercitata*. 15: *exercet*.] Therefore, whenever slaves depart from human affairs because of the correction of beatings and imminent fatal necessity, [Note: [Col. 0306C] l 6–8, 10, 12–16, 18: *correptione*.] [Note: [Col. 0306C] m Sichardus: “slaves, correction of beatings, imminent, fatal, nor …” In Til.—Cujacius II* no comma is placed here. 20: *imminenter*. 4: *fa tali*, though one letter seems to have been erased.] [Note: [Col. 0306C] n 20: *excluduntur*.] masters need fear no inquiry. [Note: [Col. 0306C] o 8: *metuunt*.]

Given on the fourteenth day [Note: [Col. 0306C] p 6–10, 12, 16, 18, 20, 21, 24, 27, 29–31, 33, 34, 38, 39, 42, and the Epitome of Mon.: omit fourteenth. 13: thirteenth. 36, 40: eleventh. Sichardus: twelfth. 35: “Given on the second day before the Kalends of October at Agrippina, under Valentinian and Valens as consuls,” from the sole constitution, *C. Th.* That Provincial Damage Not Be Inflicted (XI, 11). L. R. U.: “Given on the tenth.” In manuscript 1 Peyron could not read the subscription. It is most corrupt in the manuscripts, as Ritter already noted. See this and the following notes.] before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0306D] q Thus 4, 6, 7, 10, 13, 15, 18, 43, Til.—Lugd., Gothofredus—Ri* in the Chronicle; L. R. U., Mad. The rest: March.] at Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0306D] r Manuscripts: *Sirmio, Sermio, Syrmio*, not *Sirmii*, as Baehr has. 21: *fir.* 4. 15, Til.—Lugd. omit Sirmium; 8: “at Sirmium, Constantine …”] when Constantine [Note: [Col. 0306D] s 6, 7, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 21, 24: “Constantius Augustus and Quintus [or fifth] as consuls,” and the rest is absent. 13: sixth. Sichardus: “Constantine Augustus fifth.” 29 omits seventh—consuls. 20, 38, 42: seventh—C.; 30, 31, 39: Augustus—C.; 33, 34: “and Constantius Caesar”; 40: “seventh and C.”; and Sichardus: “C.”] Augustus was consul for the seventh time and Constantius [Note: [Col. 0306D] t Some manuscripts, among them 4, Til.—Ri*: Constans; others: Constantine. Thus Ritter, following Pagius, *Dissertationes Hypaticae* and *Critica ad Annales Baronii* for 326, rightly criticizes these manuscript corruptions, partly repeated by Baronius, ordering the reading: “Constantine Augustus, seventh time, and [Col. 0307A] Constantius [Col. 0307B] Caesar, first time, consuls.”] Caesar were consuls (326).

[Col. 0306B] INTERPRETATION. If a slave dies while his master is punishing an offence, [Col. 0307A] the master is not liable for the crime of homicide, because he is guilty of homicide only if he is proved to have wished to kill. For correction is not counted as a crime.

[Note: [Col. 0307B] a In MS 35, fol. 47, the text ends with the words “has died”; fol. 48 begins with the words “interpret in the interest of his own work,” c. 1, C. Th. *Ne damna prov.* (XI, 11). Some quires have therefore perished.]

[Note: [Col. 0307B] b Thus the greater number and the best manuscripts; the rest and the editions: “while the master is punishing an offence, if he dies, the master is not liable,” or “is not to be held liable” (as Sichard, Cujas I–Lugdunensis), “for homicide.”]

[Note: [Col. 0307B] c Cujas I–Lugdunensis: “who.”]

[Note: [Col. 0307B] d MS 21: “is summoned.”]

## CONCERNING THE JULIAN LAW ON ADULTERIES

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Evagrius, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0307B] e MSS 4, 6–10, 13, 15–18, 21, 25, 29, 38–40, 42, and 44, and Sichard–Lugdunensis; the Code of Justinian omits “Praetorian Prefect.” MS 20 has “Praetorian Prefect at Nicomedia,” with the letter V added above the *o* (*Pfum*). MS 15: “The same Augustus to Evagrius.” MS 32: “Evagium.”] Although the crime of adultery is classed among public offences, [Note: [Col. 0307B] f MS 4: “the crime among all public offences,” but the words “among all,” which could easily have been transferred here from the following line, are deleted in red.] the bringing of accusations for which [Note: [Col. 0307B] h MS 20: *diligatio*, corrected to *dilatio*.] is granted to all alike without any distinction laid down by law, [Note: [Col. 0307B] g MSS 6–8, 10, 13, 16–18: “is brought.”] nevertheless, lest persons acting on a whim be allowed rashly to defile marriages, [Note: [Col. 0307C] i Sichard: “be allowed rashly to defile”; MS 20: “to be defiled.”] we have decided that the opportunity to accuse be granted only to the nearest and necessary persons: that is, to the father or cousin, and especially to the brother related by blood, [Note: [Col. 0307C] j MS 4 has “to the father or cousin, etc.”; but “or son” is added above the line in red, making the phrase “to the father or son or cousin.” The editions Tillet–Lugdunensis have the same wording; in Sichard’s edition, however, a comma is placed after *consanguineo* (“related by blood”). Br., Al., their manuscripts, Sichard, and Cujas II–Bœcking read “to the paternal cousin, cousin”; MSS 19 and 20, “to the paternal uncle [and] cousin”; and this is absent from MSS 6–8, 10, 12, 14, 17, and 18. MS 15 reads “to the paternal cousin—to the blood-relative and full brother.” The Code of Justinian reads: “to the father, brother, and likewise paternal uncle and maternal uncle,” with which the Basilica agrees. The Interpretation has: “full brother, paternal cousin, paternal uncle, and cousin.”

On this corrupt passage I hold the following view. Without doubt the individual persons included by the Julian Law among the nearest and necessary persons to whom the right of accusation belonged were listed in Constantine’s law. The first was the father, the last the cousin, and so forth. Now the compilers of the Theodosian Code named only the first and the last, introducing between the two persons some sign indicating the omitted matter (“father—cousin”), since they thought it enough to have mentioned necessary persons in general, because everyone knew what those persons were. [Col. 0307D] But it happened that in MS 4 and other copies of the Theodosian Code that intervening sign was omitted by scribes. The Visigothic epitomizer, to whom it was obscure why father and cousin were joined together, supposing that he had detected an error, changed “to the father or” into “to the paternal cousin.” His Interpretation shows that the epitomizer hesitated over what to make of it. The Code of Justinian agrees with our conjecture: it enumerates the individual persons in a manner appropriate to its own customs and period, but in such an order that the father is named first. Therefore, in MS 4, which I have followed, the genuine reading of the Theodosian Code lies concealed, provided that the omission is indicated by that sign. The words “or son,” added in the Tillet–Lugdunensis editions, are merely Tillet’s conjecture. Gothofredus did not judge correctly in his commentary on this passage.]

—whom genuine grief impels to bring an accusation. [Note: [Col. 0307D] k MSS 6–8, 12, 14, and 17: “whom indeed”; MS 16: “which indeed”; MS 9: “husbands,” and this is accordingly emended in MS 7. Sichard: “late,” and below, “these.”]

But upon these persons also we impose the requirement that they restrain the charge by withdrawal. [Note: [Col. 0308B] b At fol. 13 of MS 4, following note a; MS 21: “we shall impose.” The Code of Justinian: “we impose [this requirement], that, if they wish, they restrain the charge by withdrawal.” Gothofredus improperly prints this in his commentary.] Above all, the husband ought to be the avenger of the marriage-bed; [Note: [Col. 0308B] c MS 12: “of the marital bed.” Sichard: “of the bed.”] he is not forbidden even, on suspicion, [Note: [Col. 0308B] d MSS 6, 8, 10, 12–14, and 16–18 omit “on suspicion.” The Code of Justinian: “and on suspicion.”] to make his wife the accused party, [Note: [Col. 0308B] e MS 12: “the accused male”; MS 20: “the matter”; MS 19 omits “the accused woman.”] nor did the former emperors permit him to be bound within fixed periods by the obligation of filing an accusation. [Note: [Col. 0308C] f Sichard adds “although”; the Code of Justinian has “although,” or: “and he is not forbidden to retain her with him if he merely suspects her”; and it omits “nor within fixed periods.”]

[Note: [Col. 0308B] a MS 20: “compels”; MSS 10 and 18 omit “But.” In others it is omitted also after “But.” The Code of Justinian: “But also.”]

[Note: [Col. 0308C] g MS 8: “Not within”; MS 20: “not beyond.” Many manuscripts: “of the written charge.”]

[Note: [Col. 0308C] h MS 4 omits “fixed,” but it is added by an early hand.]

[Note: [Col. 0308C] i Sichard: “to be held.” The Code of Justinian adds: “although by the husband’s right he might accuse.”]

[Note: [Col. 0308C] j MS 19: “have refused.”]

But we decree that outsiders be kept far from this accusation. [Note: [Col. 0308C] k MS 20 and the Code of Justinian omit “this.”] For although the necessity of formal registration binds every kind of accusation, some persons nevertheless act wantonly and disfigure marriages with false reproaches. [Note: [Col. 0308C] l The Code of Justinian adds: “But violators of marriages ought to be punished by the sword.” Cujas, Gothofredus, and P. Faber think that this has been taken, or stitched on, from c. 4, C. Th. *Quorum appellationes* (XI, 36). Goldastus, in the omitted notes to Valerianus, p. 484, thinks that it has been omitted here; Gothofredus rightly rejects this view. See him both here and in his notes on the cited c. 4.]

Published at Nicomedia, [Note: [Col. 0308D] n MSS 19 and 20 omit “at Nicomedia.” MSS 38 and 40 and other manuscripts have “Nicomedia” or “Nicomidia.”] [Note: [Col. 0308C] m MSS 9, 19, 20, 29, and 42: “Given” instead of “Published”; MS 8: “Near.” Some manuscripts omit “Published.”] seven days before the Kalends of May, [Note: [Col. 0308D] o Thus MSS 4, 15, 38, 44, the Code of Justinian, and Tillet–Lugdunensis; MSS 33 and 34 have “four”; the rest, “three.” In MS 21 and in Sichard, “seven” is absent; but Sichard’s margin notes “three days before the Ides,” and this is also found in MS 40.] under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time [Note: [Col. 0308D] p MSS 6, 7, 10, 14, 16, 17, 28, 31, 32, 35, 39, and 40: “sixth.” See c. 1 of this title, note x. MS 12: “Augustus for the third time”; MS 19: “at Constantinople, Augustus for the fifth time”; MS 8 omits “Augustus—consuls”; MS 13: “Augustus for the seventh time”; MSS 20, 38, and 43: “seventh”; MS 29: “Constantine.”] and Constantine Caesar. [Note: [Col. 0308D] q Many manuscripts omit “Caesar,” or “Caesar, consuls.” The Code of Justinian: “and Constantius Caesar, consuls, for the fourth time.”] (326).

INTERPRETATION. [Note: [Col. 0308D] r Some manuscripts read “adultery” in the accusative. Shortly below, MS 20 has “born,” and MS 21 “known.”] No one may accuse an unrelated woman of adultery; rather, those relatives to whose dishonour it pertains may do so: namely, a full brother, paternal cousin, paternal uncle, [Col. 0308B] and cousin. Yet before formal registration, if the accused woman acquiesces, they may obtain pardon by satisfaction. [Note: [Col. 0308D] s MSS 6–10 and many others: “may.”] All the rest are excluded from accusation.
