[Note: [Col. 0308D] t I have deleted the “indeed” which the authority of most manuscripts and the editions Cujas II–Gothofredus V supports, but which the remaining editions retain. Shortly below, MS 21 has “excusing oneself.”] Husbands, however, are also permitted to accuse on suspicion. [Note: [Col. 0308D] u In Sichard and Cujas I–Lugdunensis, “also” is omitted.]

## CONCERNING APPEALS WHICH ARE NOT TO BE RECEIVED

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa. Since it was previously established by a law on appeals [Note: [Col. 0309C] a Gothofredus understands this as c. 1 of this title and c. 2, C. Th. *De appellationibus* (XI, 30).] that no one should lodge an appeal from a preliminary judgment or from execution, [Note: [Col. 0309C] b MS 4: “excusal,” corrected by a scribe to “execution.”] and that an appeal of this kind should not be admitted by those who judge in our stead, [Note: [Col. 0309C] c MS 4: “in its stead,” corrected by a scribe to “in our stead.”] lest lawsuits be prolonged to the ruin [Note: [Col. 0309C] d Gothofredus wrongly reads “of the emperor.”] of many by appeals lodged from preliminary judgments, or by introducing certain delaying evasions, [Note: [Col. 0309C] e Cujas I: “introduced.”] it has now seemed good to add a penalty, so that all may understand that they ought to establish their cases in the examination of the principal issue, [Note: [Col. 0309C] f The editions read “examinations”; MS 4, “of the examination,” corrected by a scribe to “in the examination,” not “examinations.” Gothofredus too corrected it to “in the examination.” I have restored *disceptatione*. Perhaps the word *se* (“themselves”) lies concealed in the letter *s*, and can suitably be inserted here: “in the examination [they must] establish their cases.”] and should not appeal, as it were, from the very beginnings of an initial interlocutory ruling or from executions. [Note: [Col. 0309C] g MS 4: “of the interlocutory ruling,” with an *n* added by a scribe above *is*.] For those who have impatiently thought that they must appeal at that stage [Note: [Col. 0309C] h At the letters *verint*, fol. 207 of MS 4 begins, following note b.] may appeal after the whole case has been heard; and those who appeal late from executions have not been denied the right of appeal.

Therefore, if anyone using such an appeal is found in your court, you shall fine him thirty folles; and you shall disentangle the whole case—but only that of the person [Note: [Col. 0309C] i Gothofredus notes: “only the person,” which is unnecessary. I have removed the brackets with which Bœcking enclosed the words “of the person—who has appealed.”] who has rashly appealed from a preliminary judgment or execution—without any delay. [Note: [Col. 0309D] j MS 4 and Tillet–Lugdunensis: “you shall disentangle.”] For no delay should be granted in our tribunal, [Note: [Col. 0309D] k Aur. Lugd. omits “in.”] since the time occupied by the appeal affords litigants sufficient time to bring forward the fullest presentation of their case. [Note: [Col. 0309D] l The Summary of the Theodosian Code adds something absent from this constitution: “Similar to the preceding law; but this is added here, that one appealing against a judgment pronounced by a judge must appeal within three days.”]

Published six days before the Kalends of May at Carthage, under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantine Caesar [Note: [Col. 0309D] m The year is absent in Gothofredus–Ritter*. Gothofredus therefore assigns this constitution to 320 (“Constantine VI,” etc.). See cited c. 2, note t. Aur. Lugd.: “consuls.”] (326).

## CONCERNING DECURIONS

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Evagrius, Praetorian Prefect. Since we have learned that municipal councils are being deserted [Note: [Col. 0309D] n Cujas II and II* wrongly print “deserted,” corrected by Reinesius to “to be deserted.” Shortly below, Ri. and Ri.* have “origin,” wrongly.] by persons liable by origin, who seek military service for themselves by petition and hasten to the legions or to various offices, we order that all councils be warned that, if they discover persons who, within twenty years of service in offices, [Note: [Col. 0309D] o Gothofredus and Bœcking rightly conjecture “they discover,” with the councils as subject, in place of “he discovers,” which the editions have. In fact, in MS 4 a scribe has added *n* above the syllable *rit* (*deprehenderint*), which I have restored.] have either fled their origin or enlisted themselves in military service despite having been nominated, [Note: [Col. 0309D] p See c. 10 of this title.] they shall bring them back to the council, and shall know that this is henceforth to be observed.

And anyone who, having abandoned the council, has served in the army, shall be recalled to the council, not only if he is a native decurion, but also if, possessing property fit for public burdens, he has fled to military service [Note: [Col. 0310C] a Aur. Lugd. has “wickedness,” and below “consuls.”] or has been released by our favour. [Note: [Col. 0309D] q Gothofredus wishes “is to be observed, that”; but since a new chapter begins with the words “And anyone,” we can readily dispense with this conjecture. At the words *vandum* (“be observed”) and “fol. 222 begins,” MS 4 has only the words following note b. Only the words “Anyone who, having abandoned the council—shall be recalled to the council” are received into the Code of Justinian, all the rest being omitted. Editions before Ritter have “henceforth.”]

Given sixteen days before the Kalends of July, under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantine Caesar (326).

## CONCERNING PHYSICIANS AND PROFESSORS

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Rufinus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0310C] b Rufinus is nowhere found as praetorian prefect in this year except in this single law; for this reason Gothofredus seems in his Chronology to have assigned this constitution to 354. Yet no law addressed to Rufinus occurs in that year. Moreover, Gothofredus’s conjecture conflicts with the sequence of laws.]

All chief physicians (*archiatri*) and *exarchiatri* [Note: [Col. 0310C] c Tillet–Cujas II*: “exarchiatris.”] shall remain free and exempt from all duties of decurions, senators, counts, and persons of perfectissimate rank, and from the services which are often imposed upon those who have discharged an administrative office; they shall likewise be free from public contributions. Nor shall they be summoned to any contribution of gold, silver, or horses which may perhaps be assigned to the aforesaid orders or ranks. We decree that the benefit of this enactment shall extend also to their sons.

Given twelve days before the Kalends of June, under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

## CONCERNING ACCUSATIONS

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Urban Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0310C] d MS 4 and Tillet–Lugdunensis: “Maximinus,” wrongly printed by Gothofredus; MS 15: “idem Augustus to Maximus.” Many manuscripts have *ppo.* in place of Urban Prefect.]

At one time [Note: [Col. 0310C] e MS 20: “at some time.” Gothofredus notes: “By the rescript of Antoninus, last law below, *Ad legem Corneliam de falsis*. Indeed also by Constantine’s law 2 of this title.”] it was allowed that not a written subscription, but a declaration of a charge in a single utterance issuing from the mouth, [Note: [Col. 0310D] f MS 17: “a saying to set forth [that] flees”; MS 20: “a saying, wife, [that] flees.”] should compel both accuser and accused to contend, under the peril of trial, concerning country, children, property, and finally life itself. [Note: [Col. 0310D] g MS 20: “that he under”; MS 9: “undergoing trial—concerning freedmen.”] Therefore [Note: [Col. 0310D] h MSS 10 and 18: “has sought”; MS 9: “the due property—to compel.” “And the same.”] we wish that, once the licence and rashness of a mere oral declaration have been removed, [Note: [Col. 0310D] i Sichard: “removed.” Shortly after, MS 21 has “this” for “to.”] accusation be returned to the form and procedure of written subscription, [Note: [Col. 0310D] j At the letters *ritate*, fol. 2 of MS 4 begins, following note b.] so that all may employ the ancient law in bringing criminal charges: that is, after anger has subsided [Note: [Col. 0310D] m MS 4 adds “through,” but this is deleted by an early hand; MSS 16 and 19: “sudden anger.”] and tranquillity of mind has returned through this interval, [Note: [Col. 0310D] n MS 15: “through intervals of time”; MS 20, above the line after *haec spatia* (“this interval”).] they may come to final action with reason and deliberation. [Note: [Col. 0310D] o MS 15: “with reason and deliberation they may come.”]

[Note: [Col. 0310D] k “To” is absent from some manuscripts. MS 20: “to undertake the death or accusation,” corrected. Ritter* also wrongly prints “death.”]

[Note: [Col. 0310D] l MSS 15, 50, Vatican 1283, and 52: “be brought.” Many manuscripts have *ref.* or *aut.* MS 20 omits “that.”]

Given eleven days before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 0310D] p MSS 20, 28, 32, 38, 40, and Sichard’s margin: July; MSS 24, 31, and 35: January.] at Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0310D] q Some manuscripts: Syrmium. Bœcking: “at Sirmium.”] [Col. 0311A] received at Rome, [Note: [Col. 0311B] a Some manuscripts: “Rome”; MS 20: “received,” omitting “Rome”; MS 52: “received, published at Rome.”] under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time [Note: [Col. 0311B] b Some manuscripts omit “seventh.”] and Constantius [Note: [Col. 0311B] c Some manuscripts: “and Constantine”; MS 4 and Tillet: “Constans”; MSS 50 and 52: “Constantine.” Gothofredus omits the year, as also Ri. and Ri.*, and because Maximus is Urban Prefect wishes to restore the consuls of 320, Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantine Caesar, which Bœcking approves; cf. C. Th. sole c., *De hereditatis petitione* (II, 22), note k. But the sequence of constitutions opposes this correction, since this law, the fifth in this title, would be older than chapters 3 and 4.] Caesar, [Note: [Col. 0311C] d Many manuscripts, including MS 4 and Tillet, omit “Caesar.”] consuls (326).

INTERPRETATION. If anyone in anger rashly throws some accusation [Note: [Col. 0311C] e Some manuscripts: “rashly some accusation”; MS 21: “an accusation which.”] against anyone, the insult is not to be treated as an accusation; rather, after time has been allowed for deliberation, he must declare in writing that he will prove what he said in anger. [Note: [Col. 0311C] f MS 21: “declares.”] But if, perhaps coming to his senses after anger, he does not wish to repeat or perhaps to write what he said, [Note: [Col. 0311C] g Most manuscripts: “what he said—does not perhaps wish to write.” The editions: “what he said—does not wish perhaps to write.”] he is not to be held liable as an accused person in respect of the crime.

## CONCERNING THEIR PRIVILEGES

[Note: [Col. 0311C] h The position in which this law occurs in the Theodosian Code is suspect. On account of the consuls in its subscription it necessarily ought to have been placed between chapters 4 and 5 of this title, not at the end of the title. Nor does it belong to this title, as both its subject matter and the heading prefixed to the same law in the Code of Justinian show: *De Castrensi Omnium Palatinorum Peculio* (XII, 31), “Concerning the camp peculium of all palatines.” I therefore do not doubt that this heading dropped out in the Lugdunensis manuscript, although there is no sign of a gap here. I would have restored it, had not each following title possessed its own number.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Severus, Urban Prefect. We direct that all palatine officials, on whom the specific privileges of our edict have long since been bestowed, shall hold as a military peculium whatever property they have acquired while staying in our palace, whether by their own thrift or through our gifts. [Note: [Col. 0311D] i The manuscript and Cujas I–Ritter* add “if,” which the Code of Justinian and Bœcking rightly omit, and which displeases Gothofredus.] For what is more military than what is acquired with our knowledge and almost beneath our eyes? Nor are those strangers to the dust and labour of military camps who accompany our standards, who are always ready for official duties, and whom the length of journeys and the difficulty of expeditions exercise while they are intent upon learned pursuits. [Note: [Col. 0311D] j The Code of Justinian: “sustained and trained,” but Gothofredus approves the reading of the Theodosian Code.] Accordingly, our palatine officials who have been able to use the privileges of the edict [Note: [Col. 0311D] k The Code of Justinian: “have been able,” wrongly, according to Gothofredus.] shall retain as privileged property their peculia, acquired while established in the palace [Note: [Col. 0311D] l The Code of Justinian adds “our.”] either, as stated, by their own labour or by our favour. [Note: [Col. 0311D] m The Code of Justinian: “gift,” but Gothofredus prefers the Theodosian reading.]

Published ten days before the Kalends of June, under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the sixth time [Note: [Col. 0311D] n Gothofredus, approved by Bœcking, although “sixth” is also in the Code of Justinian, corrects it to “seventh”: for in 320, under Constantine Augustus VI and Constantine Caesar—that is, the year which the Code of Justinian also has—Severus was not Urban Prefect, but Valerius Maximus. Cf. C. Th. VI, 22, c. 1, note a. In the Chronology for 320 Gothofredus notes: “In place of Prefect V above, A.D. 319.”] and Constantius Caesar, consuls (326).

## CONCERNING WOMEN WHO HAVE JOINED THEMSELVES TO THEIR OWN SLAVES

[Note: [Col. 0312B] a MSS 6–8, 32, and 40: “who,” but in MS 7 corrected to “women who.” MS 15: “Concerning those who marry their slaves.” Many manuscripts and Aur. Lugd. omit “themselves.”]

[Note: [Col. 0312B] b Some manuscripts: “have joined,” others “have united” or “have united themselves.” MS 21 and Sichard: “Concerning women who have joined themselves to their own slaves.” The Code of Justinian: “Concerning women who have joined themselves to their own slaves.”]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People. If any woman is discovered secretly to have had an affair with a slave, [Note: [Col. 0312B] c The Code of Justinian adds “her own,” as likewise Anthemius in the cited law: “their own slaves.”] she shall be subjected to capital punishment, [Note: [Col. 0312B] e Thus MS 15 and Bœcking from Sichard and the Code of Justinian. MS 14: “by a sentence.” MS 21 is not distinctly written; all the rest have “sentence,” and MSS 6–8, 13, 16, and 17, “capital sentence.”] the *verbero*—a slave—being committed to the flames. [Note: [Col. 0312C] g MSS 6 and 7: “virverone …”; MS 10: “virone”; MSS 18: “by fires, man to man …”; MSS 20 and 21: “to the *verbero*.”] Everyone shall have the right to charge this public crime; the official staff shall have authority to report it; [Note: [Col. 0312C] h Sichard: “and everyone”; MS 19: “the office”; MSS 6–8, 10, and 18: “the opportunity.”] and a slave too shall have leave to denounce it. [Note: [Col. 0312C] j MS 19: “to bring”; MS 20: “to bring”; MSS 6–8 and 14: “to defer,” and MSS 7 and 17: “leave.”] If he proves the crime, freedom shall be given him; but a false accusation shall incur punishment. [Note: [Col. 0312C] k The Code of Justinian omits “but a false accusation—relegated.” MSS 13 and 20: “of accusation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0312B] d MS 4 has “secret,” with *e* written above the *a* in red, and an *m* later added in yellow by a second hand, then deleted by a recent hand. MS 14: “a secret affair.” MS 15: “is discovered secretly to have had the affair.” MS 12: “is discovered.”]

[Note: [Col. 0312C] f MS 20: “shall be joined,” corrected to “shall be subjected,” as in MS 19.]

§ 1. A woman married in such a union before this law [Note: [Col. 0312C] l MS 15: “before this law.”] shall be separated from it, deprived not only of her home [Note: [Col. 0312C] n MS 15: “home”; MS 19: “at home”; MS 21: “husband.”] but also of communion with the province, and shall lament the departure of her beloved, now relegated. [Note: [Col. 0312C] p MS 4: “absence,” corrected in red to “departure.” MSS 10 and 18: “at departure.” MS 19 has “shall lament,” and the manuscript ends with this word; MS 20: “are relegated.”]

[Note: [Col. 0312C] m MS 4 and Tillet: “marital,” but in MS 4 an early hand adds *at* above *i*, producing “married in such [a union].” MS 9: “a married woman”; MSS 10 and 18: “marital.” MSS 19 and 20 have “before the law” above “such,” while MS 20 has “married” above the line. MS 15: “and,” after “separated,” very well. Sichard: “union.”]

[Note: [Col. 0312C] o MSS 6 and 7: “communion.”]

§ 2. The sons whom she has had from this union [Note: [Col. 0312D] q MS 21 and Sichard: “The sons also whom she has had from this union.” Tillet–Ritter*: “The sons, also whom,” etc., wrongly. MS 12: “ranks,” and Gothofredus wrongly reads “nor.”] shall be stripped of every mark of rank and remain in bare freedom; neither directly nor through an intermediary [Note: [Col. 0312D] r MS 9 omits “directly nor.” MS 21 has “and” inserted; some manuscripts, “whatever.”] shall they receive, under any form of testamentary disposition, anything from the woman’s property. [Note: [Col. 0312D] s MSS 6, 7, 16, and 17: “shall receive”; MS 14: “shall receive,” singular. Shortly below Sichard has “resources,” wrongly.]

§ 3. The intestate succession of the woman [Note: [Col. 0312D] t At fol. 16 of MS 4, following note a.] shall be assigned either to her children, if they are legitimate, [Note: [Col. 0312D] u MS 15: “Her succession shall be assigned either to children.”] or to her nearest relatives and cognates, or to the person whom legal principle admits; [Note: [Col. 0312D] v MS 6: “loses”; MS 21: “may lose”; Sichard: “may admit.”] so that both what that man, formerly beloved, [Note: [Col. 0312D] z MS 21, Sichard, and the Code of Justinian: “who has been condemned,” wrongly according to Gothofredus. MS 20: “has been condemned.”] is seen to have had in his own estate, and what the children born from him are seen to have had in their own estate by whatever chance, shall be claimed, as joined to the woman’s ownership, by the aforesaid successors. [Note: [Col. 0313B] a The Code of Justinian: “may be seen.” MS 6: “their own.”]

[Note: [Col. 0312D] x MS 15, 20, 21, and Sichard omit “so that”; MS 13: “so that,” but Sichard’s margin: “But this from the Code of Justinian.”]

[Note: [Col. 0312D] y MSS 6–10, 12, 14, 16, and 17 omit “that.” MS 20 has “that,” with “also” above the line. The Code of Justinian: “But this also, which that man.”]

[Note: [Col. 0313B] b MSS 6–8: “estate, lordship”; MSS 10 and 18: “estate”; MSS 12 and 20: “ownership”; MS 14: “lord.” The Code of Justinian: “the woman’s ownership.”]

[Note: [Col. 0313B] c MS 10: “joined”; MS 18: “joined by the aforesaid”; MS 8: “successions”; Ritter*: “by the aforesaid.”]

§ 4. All this is to be observed even if the woman or her beloved died before the law, [Note: [Col. 0313B] e MSS 6, 7, 10, 12, 14, 17, and 18: “departed”; MS 15: “shall have died”; MSS 20 and 21: “departed.”] because even one author of the offence incurs censure. [Note: [Col. 0313B] f MS 10: “the beloved, who is not”; MS 20: “or lovers,” but above the line “or the beloved.”] [Note: [Col. 0313B] g MSS 6–8, 10, 17, and 18: “will incur”; MS 20: “may incur,” and above “life” for “offence”; MS 15: “the force of censure incurs.”]

[Note: [Col. 0313B] d Sichard: “All these following passages are absent from the Code of Justinian.”]

§ 5. But if both have already died, [Note: [Col. 0313B] h MS 20: “have departed,” but Ritter II has “has departed,” wrongly.] we spare the offspring, [Note: [Col. 0313C] i MS 20: “we shall spare”; Sichard: “the offspring are spared.” Many manuscripts and Tillet–Ritter*: “we spare the offspring.” In MS 4 “offspring” has been restored in red.] lest it be burdened by the faults of deceased parents. Let the children be heirs of the succession left behind; let them take precedence over brothers, nearest relatives, and cognates. [Note: [Col. 0313C] j MS 21: “but children, but [they] take precedence”; Sichard: “may they be burdened; if there are children, let [them] take precedence”; MS 8: “over more powerful [persons]”; MSS 18: “more powerful”; MS 20: “may they be burdened without children,” but above the line “if there are children.” Some manuscripts: “cognates and succession.”]

§ 6. For we punish with death those who commit this act after the law. [Note: [Col. 0313C] k MS 21: “are punished”; MS 6: “committing.”] But those who, having been separated by law, secretly meet again and renew forbidden intercourse [Note: [Col. 0313C] m MS 20: “is forbidden,” with “forbidden” above the line; and shortly below “the investigating office—delay.”] shall, if convicted by the report of slaves, [Note: [Col. 0313C] n MS 8: “these slaves in judgment.”] by the report of an investigating official staff, or by denunciation of relatives, suffer a like punishment.

Given four [Note: [Col. 0313C] o MSS 12, 20, 21, 24, 28, 30, 32–34, 38, 43, 44, and Sichard: “three,” though Sichard’s margin corrects it to “four.” MSS 28, 31, 32, 35, 39, 43, 44, and Cujas II–Ritter*: July.] days before the Kalends of June at Serdica, [Note: [Col. 0313C] p Manuscripts: Serdice, Sirdice, Syrdicae, Serditiae, Serdicie.] under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time [Note: [Col. 0313C] q Gothofredus omits the year and wishes to restore the consuls of 320, Constantine Augustus VI; Baronius agrees. Pagius, Reland, and Ritter disagree; see Ritter’s disputation against Gothofredus in note r to this law. I would have restored it if Gothofredus’s conjecture were confirmed by manuscripts, especially since in 320 Constantine was not at Serdica in this month but at Milan. See C. Th. IX, 21, c. 3, *De falsa moneta*. The fact that many manuscripts have “Constantine” for “Constantius” somewhat confirms Gothofredus’s view, but not sufficiently to grant us licence to change the year; for MS 16 alone has “sixth.” MS 30: “Constantius II”; MSS 28, 40, and Sichard’s margin: “fifth”; MSS 33 and 34: “Constantius IX”; Epitome Monacensis: “fourth.” MSS 20 and 38 omit “seventh,” and MS 8 omits “at Serdica—and.” All the rest have “seventh.” See further C. Th. IX, 25, c. 1, note i. Moreover, the imperial names here show the same scribal errors which we have seen elsewhere. Many manuscripts omit “Caesar.” Epitome Monacensis: “and Constantius V Caesar, consuls.”] and Constantius Caesar, consuls (326).

INTERPRETATION. If any freeborn woman secretly has intercourse with her own slave, she shall be punished capitally. A slave convicted of adultery with his mistress [Note: [Col. 0313D] r Some manuscripts: “convicted of joining in adultery with [his] mistress.”] shall likewise be burned. Whoever wishes may accuse this kind of crime. Slaves or maidservants, if they bring an accusation concerning this crime, shall be heard, [Note: [Col. 0313D] s In Sichard the following is written: “Slaves have power to accuse this crime, so that, if they report it, they may be heard.”] provided that, if they prove it, they obtain freedom, but if they deceive, they are punished. [Note: [Col. 0314C] a Aur. Lugd. adds, from the Aegidian Summary: “because the law orders the wicked to be punished.”] [Note: [Col. 0314C] b Ritter and Ritter* add “themselves.”] [Note: [Col. 0314C] c Aur. Lugd. adds, from the Aegidian Summary: “And those born from such a union shall remain in merely bare freedom, and in every respect become strangers to their mother’s inheritance.”] The inheritance of a woman who has stained herself with such a crime shall be assigned either to her children, [Note: [Col. 0314C] d MS 20: “child,” and MS 21: “if there are.”] if they were born of her husband, or to relatives entitled by law.

## CONCERNING BISHOPS

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Ablavius, Praetorian Prefect. Exemption from public duties shall not be granted by popular consent or to just any applicants under the pretext of clerical status; nor shall people be rashly and without limit attached to the clergy. [Note: [Col. 0314C] e MS 4: “attached,” corrected in red to “attached together.”] But when a cleric has died, another shall be enrolled in the place of the deceased, [Note: [Col. 0314C] f In the margin of Cujas’s copy and of Cujas II and II*: “another is to be chosen”; in the margin of Aur. Lugd.: “another will be chosen.” Thus, when preparing Cujas I, Cujas used, besides the manuscript from which he supplied Book XVI, another manuscript, which I do not doubt was MS 11. See the Preface to the Theodosian Code, c. 43 of this title, and c. 62 *De Haereticis* (XVI, 5), note b. Gothofredus rightly defends “shall be enrolled.”] provided that he is neither of municipal descent nor possessed of such abundance of property as can most easily bear public functions. [Note: [Col. 0314D] g MS 4: “public—who may,” etc. From the words “public functions” onward some matters can be discerned in MS 11.] Thus, if a dispute arises between the city and clergy [Note: [Col. 0314D] h MS 11: “clerics.”] concerning a person, and equity draws him to public service because he is found to be a municipal by descent or qualified by property, [Note: [Col. 0314D] i At fol. 397 of MS 4, following note a. MS 11: “equity or.”] he shall be removed from the clergy and handed over to the city. [Note: [Col. 0314D] j MS 4: “is found,” corrected in red to “is recognised.”] For the wealthy must undergo the obligations of the world; the poor must be supported from the riches of the churches.

Published on the Kalends of June, under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constans Caesar [Note: [Col. 0314D] k Bœcking requires “Constantius.” Aur. Lugd.: “consuls.”] (326).

## CONCERNING THE PUBLIC POST

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Menander. [Note: [Col. 0314D] l The Lugdunensis manuscript has “idem Augustus to Menander. By reliable …”; Menander’s rank is therefore absent. It is absent likewise from all Theodosian laws addressed to Menander. See C. Th. IV, 12, cc. 2 and 3; below XI, 27, c. 2, and XV, 1, c. 2. For this reason learned men dispute Menander’s rank. See C. Th. IV, 12, c. 2, note a.]

We have learned by reliable reports that many persons sell at a fixed price compulsory transport-services (*angariae*) obtained as though for themselves and their own needs. [Note: [Col. 0314D] m Gothofredus–Ritter* wrongly punctuate: “obtained, compulsory transport-services.”] Therefore, although travel warrants (*evectiones*) are henceforth to be granted rarely and only to the deserving, all persons everywhere bound to the supervision of the public post [Note: [Col. 0314D] n Reinesius conjectures “bound.”] shall investigate whether anyone can be apprehended in this sort of crime, so that buyer and seller alike may be relegated to an island; those also ordered to supervise are to suffer the same punishment for concealment or negligence. [Note: [Col. 0314D] o Here begins the second page of folio XCII of the Lugdunensis manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0314D] p The manuscript has *luiturius*, wrongly.]

§ 1. It is not improper, however, if one who has a supply of compulsory transport takes someone with him, for the protection of life [Note: [Col. 0315B] a Gothofredus conjectures “of the road,” approved by Bondam in *Animadversiones criticae ad loca quaedam iuris civilis depravata* (Oelrichs, *Thesaurus novus Dissertationum juridicarum*, vol. II, tome II, p. 221). Gothofredus’s conjecture is attractive, but I do not know whether it should be adopted.] or to undertake the labour of a journey, [Note: [Col. 0315C] b Gothofredus notes: “Perhaps *adimendum* [‘to be taken away’]: but I change nothing rashly.” Bondam conjectures *obeundum* [‘to be undertaken’]. Nothing should be changed.] as a companion for comfort. For this act deserves pardon and cannot escape the notice of investigators; [Note: [Col. 0315C] c The manuscript has “investigator,” but an *s* is added above *e*.] that other act must be punished by the penalty stated above. On this matter the proconsuls, provincial governors, prefects of transport-vehicles, and all who preside over the public post should be warned. [Note: [Col. 0315C] d Gothofredus notes: “This passage must be punctuated thus. For the learned man errs who imagines prefects of provinces here in place of governors; rather, the prefects of vehicles here are different persons.”]

Given ten days before the Kalends of July, under the consulship of Constantine [Note: [Col. 0315C] e Reinesius corrects “Constantius.”] Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

## CONCERNING PUBLIC WORKS

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Secundus, Praetorian Prefect. We direct that provincial judges be warned that they must know that they ought not to order any new construction [Note: [Col. 0315C] f Gothofredus and Bœcking correct *ordinari* to *ordinare*, rightly. Perhaps *a se* (“by themselves”) may be written instead of *se*. Ritter* omits “ought.” Below, Aur. Lugd.: “consuls.”] before they have completed what was begun by their predecessors, except only the construction of temples.

Given three days before the Kalends of July, under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

## CONCERNING COUNTERFEIT COINAGE

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Tertullus, Proconsul of Africa. [Note: [Col. 0315C] g MS 4 and the editions have the title “Urban Prefect.” Gothofredus and Bœcking correct it to *PC*, that is, proconsul; rightly, for manuscript I has *pc*. I have therefore written “Proconsul.” The Code of Justinian: “Urban Prefect of Africa,” wrongly and rightly rejected by Gothofredus.]

If anyone has produced a coin by false casting, [Note: [Col. 0315C] h The Code of Justinian: “coins.”] we order that all his property be assigned to the fisc [Note: [Col. 0315D] j The Code of Justinian adds “our.”] and that he himself be restrained by lawful severity, [Note: [Col. 0315D] l The Code of Justinian omits “and that he himself—severity.” Gothofredus wishes comparison with cc. 1 and 2 of this title.] so that the business of minting coin may be carried on only in our mints. [Note: [Col. 0315D] m The Code of Justinian: “For we wish that the business of minting coin be carried on only in our mints,” and adds: “who commit the crime of treason, liable to …”; and “by reward” (from c. 5 of this title)—“may be discovered, or by whomever he may be”—“shall be handed over,” followed by the subscription of c. 3 of the Theodosian Code. See Gothofredus on c. 5 of this title, note a.]

[Note: [Col. 0315D] i MS 4: “confirmed,” but corrected in red by a later hand to “produced.”]

[Note: [Col. 0315D] k MS 4: “We order.” The Code of Justinian: “we order [them] to be assigned.”]

Given on the day before the Nones of July [Note: [Col. 0315D] n Tillet, *l. c.*, tome IV, p. 91, note 1, and *Notes*, p. 137, corrects this to June.] at Milan, under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar [Note: [Col. 0315D] o The Code of Justinian adds “for the fourth time,” wrongly; the law would then be later than the following one. Moreover Ritter has “Constantine—and Constantius.”] (326).

## CONCERNING THE INVALIDATION OF ACTS PERFORMED UNDER TYRANTS OR BARBARIANS

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Antiochus, Prefect of the Watch. [Note: [Col. 0315D] p Gothofredus wrongly reads “Virgil.”] Whatever a tyrant has rescripted contrary to law [Note: [Col. 0316C] a Gothofredus, in his commentary, thinks this constitution was neither issued by Constantius nor concerns the tyrant Maxentius, but was rather issued by Constantine against Licinius.] we order to have no force; his lawful rescripts are not to be challenged.

Given eight [Note: [Col. 0316C] b Although this constitution bears the name of Antiochus, Prefect of the Watch, while the following c. 4 is addressed to the Senate, Gothofredus wishes either that “eight” be deleted here or that “eight” be supplied in the subscription of the following chapter, so that the two chapters might be joined. I deny that this may be done.] days before the Ides of July at Rome, under the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Senate. Concerning those senators whom the tyrant [Licinius] reduced to the compulsory service of ship-owner, and who request restoration to their birth-status, it has pleased us to entrust judgment and examination to Your Sanctity, so that you may select those who correspond to your splendor in the resources of their estates, honorable conduct of life, and dignity of birth. For it is unfitting to commit the decision concerning so great a dignity to another rather than to your votes and judgments. Let the Prefect of the City report to us the names of those whom you have selected as worthy, that we may approve your judgment. Given on the Ides of July, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (329).

> Note [Col. 0316C]:  
> c. “by the tyrant Licinius.”  
> d. Manuscript 4 has *hac*; the *h* was deleted in red ink, yielding *ac* (“and”).  
> e. Manuscript 4 has *judicum* (“of judges”), corrected in red to *judicium* (“judgment”).  
> f. Gothofredus emends: “honorable conduct of life corresponds to the dignity of birth”; no emendation is necessary.  
> g. Gothofredus erroneously reads *elegeretis* (“you had selected”).  
> h. See above, note b.  
> i. Ritter and Ritter’s second edition read *Constantino* in error.

## HOW CIVIL PUBLIC BURDENS ARE ASSIGNED

> Note [Col. 0316C]:  
> j. The Code of Justinian: “How civil public burdens are imposed.” The Lyon manuscript’s index has *judicantur* (“are adjudged”). With the inscription, chapter 1 begins on folio 273 of manuscript 4.  
> b. Although this chapter bears the name of Antiochus, Prefect of the Watch, while the following chapter 4 is addressed to the Senate, Gothofredus wishes either that “VIII” be deleted here or that “VIII” be supplied in the subscription of the following chapter, so that the two chapters may be joined. I deny that this can be done.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Tiberianus, Count in Africa. Those magistrates who make nominations for the appointment of duumvirs to office in the coming year must, in view of their own liability, take care that, although in Africa nomination is customarily conducted also by popular vote, they themselves strive and labor no less to ensure that those nominated may be found suitable. For equity requires that, if unsuitable persons have been nominated, those upon whom the risk rests should themselves be held accountable. Given at Nicomedia, three days before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constans Caesar (326).

> Note [Col. 0316D]:  
> k. The editions read *iam* (“now”). Gothofredus conjectures *nam* (“for”), correctly and with the support of manuscript 4, in which the letter N, though pale, is plainly written and has also been repeated above the line in red by a later hand.  
> l. Gothofredus thinks that something is missing from this subscription, and I likewise have no doubt that it is mutilated; for the place is mentioned before the day and month. Moreover, Constantine was not at Nicomedia in this year. Gothofredus therefore assigns this constitution, in the *Chronology*, pp. XXV and XXVII, to 325: “Given … at Nicomedia, in the consulship of Paullinus and Julianus, most illustrious men, three days before the Kalends of August, etc.” In his notes, however, he assigns it to either 325 or 329. I think the former is correct. See C. Th. IX.1.4, concerning accusations. One may adopt either conjecture and write *Constantino*. The Aurélian and Lyon consular lists support this.

## CONCERNING THE SONS OF MILITARY ATTENDANTS AND VETERANS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Severus …

> Note [Col. 0316D]:  
> m. Although there is no gap in the manuscript, I have added dots. Gothofredus alone wishes him to be Prefect of the Praetorium; Beatus, denying that Severus was already Prefect of the Praetorium at this time, conjectures Prefect of the City.

We do not permit the sons of veterans to remain exempt because of privileges granted to their parents. Rather, after a public proclamation has been posted in every city, we order that they be diligently sought out and compelled to one of two alternatives: either to obey the obligations of the decurionate or to serve in the army. Your devoted office shall ensure that those approved are between twenty and twenty-five years of age.

§ 1. But if sons of veterans who have performed cavalry service wish to be approved among the cavalry, they shall have permission, provided that they are assigned to the aforesaid service, each with one suitable horse.

§ 2. If anyone has two horses, or one suitable horse and one slave, he shall serve with the rank of *circitor* and receive two *annonae*, a grade bestowed upon others after service.

§ 3. Let the decurions of individual cities be informed that they are not to delay in summoning to curial service sons of veterans of the aforesaid age, if they are unwilling to serve in the army or are found less suitable, provided, however, that they are known to be suitable by reason of their estates.

§ 4. Of those who wish to serve, any who are less fit for cavalry service because of a deficiency of their limbs [the transmitted phrase *deficiente calamitate membrorum* is problematic], but are known to be suitable for legionary service, shall be registered and sent to the *protector* dispatched for this purpose.

Given three days before the Kalends of August at Aquileia, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus and Constantius Caesar (326).

> Notes [Col. 0317C]:  
> a. Ritter has *proptet*, in error. The manuscript shortly afterwards has *programmatae*.  
> b. Gothofredus conjectures *id efficiente* (“with this producing the result”), which suits the sense. Beatus conjectures that a word is missing. One may also write *deficiente alacritate* (“through a lack of vigor”) or *qualitate membrorum* (“through the condition of the limbs”), or a similar expression; Reinesius conjectures *qualitate*. The words *idonei esse noscuntur* begin the second page of folio 78 of the manuscript; at the foot of the page is the quire-number 42.  
> c. Gothofredus orders the substitution of *congrui esse* (“to be suitable”), but this is unnecessary.  
> d. Gothofredus conjectures April in his chronology for this year, so that this may be joined with C. Th. IX.8, sole chapter, “If anyone [the woman] of whom he is guardian”; but see note n to that chapter.  
> e. Thus the manuscript and Cujas’s first through second revised editions. Gothofredus through Beatus read *Aquileiae*.  
> f. Aurélian and Lyon consular lists.

## CONCERNING VACANT PROPERTY

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Severus, Prefect of the City. Those to whom we have granted something for their services and merits are not to be harassed; rather, while they remain in their legal right—that is, free from the trouble of litigation—the instigator of proceedings who has attempted to create disturbance must be brought before your tribunal, so that, without troubling the possessor, he may establish his own right by clear proofs. You yourself shall undertake the role of the resisting party, since the benefit of our liberality is being attacked.

By this law we decree that whoever brings complaints of this kind shall establish his right according to the aforesaid procedure. The matters found established are to be reported to our knowledge, so that, while the ownership of possessors remains secure—those to whom, as stated, firmness of possession in perpetuity has been acquired—it may be for our decision how those who have proved their allegations should receive assistance from outside through the benefit of our clemency.

Read on the third day before the Nones of August in the Palace, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

> Notes [Cols. 0317D–0318C]:  
> g. Manuscripts of the *Breviarium Alaricianum* and the printed editions: “The Emperor Constantine Augustus.” Sichard: “The Emperor Constantantinus,” omitting Augustus.  
> h. Several manuscripts have *ppo.* or *ppm.*  
> i. Manuscripts 6, 7, 10, 14, 16, and 18: “Let not these persons harass”; manuscript 8: “Let them not”; manuscript 9: “those harassing”; manuscript 12: the corrupt reading *Nec interpellanti avibus*; manuscript 13: “Let them not harass, nor these persons.”  
> j. Sichard reads *emeritis pro ac meritis* (“for earned services instead of for merits”), printed by Gothofredus; but Sichard’s margin has *et meritis* (“and merits”).  
> k. Manuscripts 7–10, 12, 14, 16, and 18: *donavimus* (“we granted”); the future-perfect *donaverimus* should be restored from manuscripts 1, 4, 6, 13, 15, 20, 21, Sichard, Tilius, and Ritter’s second edition. See below, “whoever has attempted to create disturbance,” and chapter 1 of this title, “which we shall have granted.”  
> l. Manuscript 4 has *sine* (“without”), corrected by a recent hand to *sed in* (“but in”).  
> m. Manuscripts 6, 7, 12, 16, 20, and 21: “that is, in trouble”; manuscript 9: “that is, into trouble.” Ritter’s second edition mistakenly has *licitis* for *litis*.  
> n. Manuscript 20: *concitare*, with *judices* above the line. Cujas’s first edition incorrectly prints *judidicii*.  
> o. Manuscript 20 has *tentaverint* (“they have attempted”) above the line.  
> a. Manuscript 12: an abbreviation for *praesentari*; manuscript 20: *praesentare*, corrected above the line. Some manuscripts then read “so that the possessors may …”; manuscript 20, “they may establish.”  
> b. Manuscript 4 has *modestiam* (“moderation”), corrected in red to *molestiam* (“trouble”).  
> c. Manuscripts 6, 7, 10, 13, 18, 20, 21, and Sichard: *reluctantes* (“resisting persons”).  
> d. Manuscripts 1, 10, and 18: *suscipiens*; manuscript 20: *suscipias*.  
> e. Manuscript 1 omits *enim* (“for”).  
> f. Manuscripts 9, 20, and 21: *veniunt* (“come”).  
> g. Manuscript 20 adds *manifestis* (“clear”).  
> h. Manuscript 20 has *qui* (“who”), corrected above the line to *quae* (“the things which”), and *fuerit* (“has been”) for *fuerint* (“have been”); manuscript 8 omits from “the matters which” through “the benefit of clemency.”  
> i. Manuscript 20: “so that [there may be] secure … ownership.”  
> j. Manuscript 12: “to whom it has been handed over.”  
> k. Manuscript 21: *sint* (“may be”).  
> l. Manuscript 20: “their [allegations] to those who have proved … to assist”; manuscript 21: “of ours and from outside.” The word *subveniri* begins folio 88 of manuscript 4, in the letters *niri*.  
> m. Manuscript 14: “Read”; manuscripts 17, 28, 29, 36, 38, 40, and 42: “Given”; manuscript 44: “at the palace.” Many manuscripts of the *Breviarium Alaricianum*, and Sichard: the fourth day before the Nones; manuscript 8: the seventh. Manuscript 31 places here the subscription of C. Th. X.4.2.  
> n. Manuscript 17 omits from “in” through “the consuls”; the Epitome of Monza has “in the Palace.” Manuscripts 33 and 34: July.  
> o. Manuscripts 15 and 27 add “at Constantinople.”  
> p. Manuscripts 20, 24, 28, 36, and 40: sixth; manuscript 27: fourth; manuscript 32: seventeenth. In many manuscripts Augustus and then Caesar, or “Caesars, consuls,” are omitted.  
> q. Most manuscripts read *Constantino*, as does Sichard. The Aurélian and Lyon consular lists follow.

### Interpretation

Those to whom we have granted anything for their labor are not to be disturbed; rather, all things which we have bestowed are to remain established in their own right. Whoever wishes to disturb them shall be brought before a judicial hearing, so that the claimant may establish his right without any inconvenience to the possessor. Everything done in this matter between the aforesaid parties is to be reported to our knowledge, so that the person disturbed may also be assisted by our remedies.

> Notes [Cols. 0318C–0318D]:  
> r. Many manuscripts read *hi* (“these persons”); Sichard, *hii*. The same manuscript shortly afterwards has *donamus* (“we give”).  
> s. Manuscripts 6–10, 18, 20, 21, 42, others, Sichard, Cujas’s first edition through the Lyon edition: “which we have bestowed upon these persons”; manuscript 6 omits “all.”  
> t. Manuscript 44 omits *positis* (“established”); Sichard has *ipso*.  
> u. The manuscripts have *his* or *iis* (“him/them”), a few *ii* (“they”), and accordingly shortly afterwards *illi* (“that person”): “whoever shall have wished … let him be brought or drawn.” Thus manuscripts 6–8, 10, and 18. We accordingly restore, in agreement with the law itself, the singular number in place of the plural printed in the editions. Manuscript 43 has *pertrahatur* (“let him be drawn through”).  
> v. Manuscripts 6–8, 10, 18, 20, 21, 44, and others omit *ut* (“so that”); manuscript 43 has *et* (“and”).  
> x. Manuscript 6 omits *possidentis* (“of the possessor”); several manuscripts have *possidentes* (“possessors”); manuscript 20, *possidens*.  
> y. Manuscripts 6–9, 20, 21, 43, 44, and others: *pulsatus* (“the person attacked”).  
> z. Manuscripts 6, 7, 9, 21, 42, and 43: “concerning this matter.”  
> aa. Manuscripts 6, 7, 10, 18, and 43: “private persons.” Sichard: “and all things which have been done concerning this matter between private persons.”  
> bb. Some manuscripts have *referendi*, *referenda*, or *praeferendis*.  
> cc. Gothofredus, in his note, reads *inquietator* (“disturber”).

## CONCERNING APPEALS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Julianus, Prefect of the City. Certain judges of lower rank, aggrieved that the remedy of appeal is lodged against their judgments, bring it about that unnecessary and presumptuous reports from them are submitted to us. Therefore, when an appeal has been made from their judgments, we will that they by no means refer to Our Clemency the matter concerning which, once the appeal was lodged, they ceased to be judges; rather, they shall await the sacred hearing of Your Gravity, to whom we have entrusted our own place.

Given three days before the Nones of August at Heraclea, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar for the third time (326).

> Notes [Col. 0319B]:  
> a. Tilius, Cujas’s first edition, and Cujas’s second and second revised editions have *aegreferentes*.  
> b. Gothofredus through Ritter’s second edition omit the year. Since an unknown author on the Prefects of the City writes that Anicius Julianus did not take up the urban prefecture until the Ides of November in 326, Gothofredus proposes either the consuls of 329—Constantius Augustus for the eighth time and Constantine for the fourth time—or, preferably, those of 327, Constantine and Maximus. He inserts it into both years in his chronological constitution-list. These conjectures are opposed both by C. Just. 17, which must be coordinated with this law and agrees in every respect with its subscription, and by chronology and the sequence of laws, which Gothofredus has reversed. Beatus seems to have perceived this when he wrote: “But perhaps either the date is not correct, or the law reached Rome only after the Ides of November, from which time Julianus begins to be urban prefect.” Correctly. Reinesius thinks the numeral III should be deleted. Manuscript 4 reads *Haeracleae*.

## TO THE SENATUS CONSULTUM CLAUDIANUM

The Emperor Constantine … [the source text is lost] … on the Kalends of September at Serdica, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

> Note [Col. 0319C]:  
> c. The seventh Turin folio begins with this subscription of a lost constitution of Constantine. W. invented the inscription “The same Augustus,” which, though not false, is not found in the manuscript. Puchta and the Dutch editors in the *Bijdragen* think that this subscription belongs to the third, that is, the preceding, chapter of this title; if that conjecture were accepted, this title would contain one fewer constitution, and one would have to write either February or September in both subscriptions. But nothing should be attempted against the manuscripts, especially since there are examples of two or three laws on the same subject issued in the same year by the same emperors to the same magistrate. See chapters 2 and 3 of the following title. Puchta prints “1” instead of “I.”

## CONCERNING HERETICS

> Note [Col. 0319D]:  
> d. The Code of Justinian: “Concerning Heretics, Manichaeans, and Samaritans.”

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Dracilianus …

> Note [Col. 0319D]:  
> e. Manuscript 15: “to Archilianus”; similarly manuscripts 50 and 51: “to Darchilianus.” Ans. and the Code of Justinian have “to Gracilianus,” though some editions have “to Dracilianus.” Compare Witte, “Richter’s Critical Yearbooks for German Jurisprudence,” vol. I, p. 19. The official rank is absent not only from the Theodosian Code and its manuscripts, but also from the Code of Justinian. Compare C. Th. II.33.1, concerning interest, and Constantine’s letter to Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem, in *Life of Constantine* III.30 ff., in Socrates I.9 and Theodoret I.17. From these passages Gothofredus infers that the words “acting in the place of the Prefect of the Praetorium in the East” should be added. Beatus wishes “Prefect of the Praetorium” to be added, and Reinesius “acting in the place of the Prefect of the Praetorium.” Paris manuscript 1 of the Code of Justinian adds the corrupt phrase *perfectum perturio*. Dots have been inserted to indicate the gap.  
> f. Manuscript 2: “in consideration of the law,” a word drawn here from the following words.  
> g. Thus manuscripts 2, 11, 15, 50, 51, and the Code of Justinian, which reads: “Heretics [we will] not only [to be deprived] of these …” The editions read “not merely.” Manuscripts 11, 50, and Cujas’s editions spell *scismaticos*.

Privileges granted in consideration of religion ought to benefit only observers of the catholic law. But we will that heretics and schismatics be not only excluded from these privileges, but also bound and subjected to various public burdens.

> Note [Col. 0320B]:  
> a. Manuscript 11 reads *voluimus* (“we willed”) instead of *volumus* (“we will”).

Posted on the Kalends of September at Gerastus, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

> Notes [Col. 0320C]:  
> b. The passage through “at Gerastus” ends in manuscript 11. The Code of Justinian reads: “we will, but [that they be subjected] to contrary burdens,” etc.  
> c. Cujas’s editions have *subici*, as do manuscripts 50 and 51; Gothofredus through Ritter’s second edition also print it.  
> d. Manuscript 15: February.  
> e. Cujas’s first edition through Ritter’s second: *Lab. Generasto*; Beatus and the Code of Justinian: *Generasti*. Because of the mention of Dracilianus, who acted with praetorian-prefectural authority over Palestine and neighboring provinces, Gothofredus emends *Gerae asto*, “posted at Gera.” He argues that Gera lay near Pelusium in the Mareotis, close to Palestine. He also conjectured Gennesaret, that is, Tiberias, but rejected Geraestus. Finally he retained *Gerae-asto* and supplied “Given at Rome”; manuscripts 2, 50, and 51 read *Gerasto*, and manuscript 15 *Gerasio*. At Witte’s urging I have restored *Gerasto*, which nearly agrees with Gothofredus’s conjecture. The Pistoian manuscript cited by Herrmann in his edition of the Code of Justinian, note 9, has *Gerasti*.  
> f. Manuscript 50 has *Constantino*. The siglum C., missing in Gothofredus and Beatus, has been supplied from manuscripts 15, 50, and 51. In the edition it is missing, as it is in manuscript 11 and the Code of Justinian.

## CONCERNING THE SENATUS CONSULTUM CLAUDIANUM

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Ablavius, Prefect of the Praetorium. We decree that all ship-owners throughout the world shall be secure, free, and exempt for all time from every burden and public duty, whatever their locality or rank—whether decurions, plebeians, or persons of some other higher dignity—so that, freed from assessments and every contribution, they may perform the service of ship-owner with their estates intact.

§ 1. Nor is it fitting that their ships, whatever their size, be detained against their will for another public service at any shore they may enter. Guardians of the shores, officials set over taxes, collectors, decurions, *rationales*, and judges shall know that whoever violates this law shall suffer capital punishment.

Given fourteen days before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

> Notes [Col. 0320D]:  
> g. See preceding note c.  
> h. The Aurélian and Lyon lists have a defective *Na icularios*. Ritter’s second edition has *cujusque* (“of each”) for *cujuscumque* (“of whatever”); manuscript 4 and editions before Beatus read *plebei*.  
> i. Manuscript 4 and Tilius: “or from assessments”; the remaining editions have a corrupt text.  
> j. Ritter’s second edition omits *decurionibus*.

## CONCERNING HERETICS

> Note [Col. 0320D]:  
> k. Manuscript 11 reads: “The same Augusti to …”

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Bassus …

> Note [Col. 0320D]:  
> l. The official rank is absent from manuscripts and editions. Gothofredus believes Bassus to have been Vicar of Italy in this year, on the strength of C. Just. IX.10.1, “If anyone [the woman] of whom he is guardian.” Reinesius’s chronological constitution-list in Cujas’s second edition prefers “Prefect of the City, or rather Vicar of Italy.” Beatus supplies Prefect or Prefects of the Praetorium. See Gothofredus, *Prosopography*, under “Bassus.” I was the first to insert dots to indicate the gap.  
> m. From manuscript 2, approved by W.; manuscript 11 and the editions omit *adeo* (“so”).  
> n. Gothofredus dislikes the conjecture *perdamnatos* (“utterly condemned”).

We have not found the Novatians so wholly condemned that we thought what they requested should by no means be granted to them. Accordingly, we decree that they shall firmly and without disturbance possess their church buildings and places suitable for burials—namely, those which they have held from long usage, through purchase, or by acquisition in any manner whatsoever. Care must nevertheless be taken that they do not attempt to appropriate anything from those things which are manifestly known to have belonged, before the schism, to churches of perpetual sanctity.

Given seven days before the Kalends of October at Spoleto, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

> Notes [Cols. 0320D–0321C]:  
> o. Manuscript 11 reads, with several corruptions: “what they requested, we believed should be granted … churches … burial-place … we decreed; namely whatever they have held from … time.” Cujas’s first edition through the Lyon edition read *exempto* (“excepted”) for *ex empto* (“from purchase”).  
> a. Manuscript 11 and Cujas’s first edition: “in any manner. Care must be taken”; the Aurélian edition through Cujas’s second revised edition: “in any manner. Care must be taken.” The remaining editions: “in any manner. Care must be taken.” Gothofredus conjectures “Therefore it must be considered,” or “Moreover it must be considered.” Beatus thinks that *sed*, *at*, or a similar word has fallen out. Gothofredus had already perceived that some such word was lacking, but manuscript 2 supplies it: “Certainly care must be taken.” I have followed manuscript 2.  
> b. Manuscript 11 and the editions read ninth; because Constantine remained at Rome at this time until five days before the Kalends of October, and is said in the Constantinian Calendar to have departed from Rome only on that day, Gothofredus proposes the fourth or the day before, to join this constitution with C. Just. I.19.3, concerning petitions to the imperial office. He mistakenly thinks this possible, since that chapter was given at Rome eight days before the Kalends of October and addressed to the people, whereas this was given at Spoleto to Bassus. I have restored the seventh from manuscript 2.  
> c. Manuscript 11: *Spoliti*; see also below under “consul.”  
> d. I have supplied C. from manuscript 2; it is absent from manuscript 11 and the editions. Gothofredus and Beatus already wished it supplied. Cujas’s chronological constitution-list wrongly transfers this constitution to 354, followed by Reinesius.

## CONCERNING THE *UNDE VI* INTERDICT (RECOVERY AFTER FORCIBLE DISPOSSESSION)

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Severus.

> Notes [Col. 0321C]:  
> e. The official rank is absent here and in the Code of Justinian; but manuscripts 8, 33, and 34 have *ppo.*, incorrectly. Read *pu.*, that is, Prefect of the City, as Gothofredus conjectures and W. approves. Manuscript 25: “The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Senate,” not implausibly. See Gothofredus’s commentary on this chapter. Manuscripts 6, 16, 17, and 38 have *Severus*; manuscripts 6 and 7 correct it from *Severu*; manuscript 37 omits Severus.  
> f. Manuscript 15 omits from “of absentees” through “have been deprived.”  
> g. Manuscript 15 adds “of absentees”; the Code of Justinian has the plural *personas*; manuscript 42, *personae*.  
> h. Manuscript 14 omits *suae* (“their own”).  
> i. The Code of Justinian reads: “Thus let them protect absentees, so that they may investigate carefully only this,” etc., omitting “Yet these judges” through “substantive matters.”  
> j. Manuscript 15 omits *judices*; manuscript 8: “Yet these—not judges.”  
> k. Manuscripts 10 and 18: *quod* (“that”), and shortly afterward “officials … function”; manuscript 42: “whom [we ordered] to assume the role of those learning justice … functions.”  
> l. Manuscript 15: *abs diximus*, perhaps a scribal corruption.  
> m. Other manuscripts: *terminus* (“boundary”).  
> n. Manuscript 15: “with all things untouched and entire”; W. prefers “with all things entire”; both are correct.  
> o. Manuscript 42: “only that crime”; manuscript 12: “that they may investigate only.”  
> p. The Code of Justinian: *an* (“whether”).  
> q. Beatus and W. follow Tilius and manuscript 6, with which most manuscripts agree. Manuscripts 9, 19, 20, 42, Sichard, Cujas’s first edition through Ritter, and the Code of Justinian read “the possession of him who is abroad, by whatever means”; the Code has *modo* (“way”) for *pacto* (“means”). Manuscripts 15 and 21 omit *qui*.  
> r. The Code of Justinian: *sit* (“has been”).  
> s. The Code of Justinian adds “relative or parent, neighbor or friend, tenant or freedman, or slave”; manuscript 13 has *servus*.  
> t. Manuscript 6, according to Ritter, has the corrupt reading *Ore hos*. Manuscripts 6–8, 10, 13, 14, 18, 21, and Tilius: “lest they”; manuscript 20: “lest to these”; manuscripts 9, 15, 42, 50, and the Code of Justinian: “nor them”; manuscript 19: “nor of them.” Sichard through Cujas’s second revised edition place a comma after *retinebat*; Gothofredus, Ritter, and Ritter’s second edition a colon.

Judges shall assume in law the person of absentees who have been deprived of possession of any thing whatsoever, oppose the formidable agency of their authority, and thus protect absentees.

Yet we confine within these limits the function of those judges whom we have ordered to represent absentees: while all internal matters of the principal case remain untouched and entire, they shall investigate carefully only whether the possession of one who is abroad has been taken away by any means, although it was held under any title by a relative, friend, or slave.

They shall not exclude from the remedy those who, having been ejected, hold possession in the name of absentees, because the pleading of the case has not been entrusted to them; nor, if they are slaves, shall they reject their representation in law, because persons of such status are not permitted to plead cases. Even after the periods fixed by law for recovery of possession have elapsed, when such persons bring suit, relief must be granted, so that they may be restored without delay to summary possession, just as if the owner himself, having returned, had litigated.

Nevertheless, we have granted to the owner, whenever he returns, an action for recovery of possession, since restoration may meanwhile be delayed through unfaithful slaves or negligent relatives, friends, or tenants. For elapsed time, prescribed by law for recovering possession, ought not prejudice an absentee. But once the condition wrongfully removed has been restored, all matters remaining shall remain unimpaired for the litigation of the dispute; judgment is reserved for the proper and lawful persons, since it sufficiently assists those holding possession in the name of absentees against the violence of persons present.

Given ten days before the Kalends of November at Milan, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

> Notes [Cols. 0322B–0323C]:  
> a. Thus the manuscripts; nor does the Code of Justinian differ substantially, where it has “decision of the case,” although Halander and others read *dictio*. The editions read “the pleading of the case.” Manuscript 8 omits *dictio*. Manuscripts 6, 13, 14, and 16–20 have *ipsius*; manuscript 15: “not to them,” and manuscript 21 correctly has *sit*, while manuscript 42 has *est*.  
> b. Most manuscripts and Tilius: *experiundo rei*; manuscript 6: *experiundae rei*.  
> c. Some manuscripts have *seducant* (“separate”); manuscript 21 has an additional word, but its margin corrects it to *secludant*.  
> d. Manuscripts 9 and 42: “exclude, and if they are slaves”; manuscript 20: *sunt*; manuscripts 10, 12, and 18 have *sine* for *sint*, in error; manuscript 21 has the corrupt reading *servis in eorum*.  
> e. Manuscripts 6, 7, 10, 12, 17, 18, and 20, above the line, and Tilius have *requirant*. It may be from this that the bad interpretation of the passage arose. It seems, therefore, that the verb *requirendi* had already entered some manuscripts of the Theodosian Code through scribal error.  
> f. Manuscripts 6, 7, 12, 15, 18, 20, 50, and Tilius: *personam*; the Aurélian and Lyon editions read “if they are theirs, let them reject.”  
> g. Manuscripts 15, 19, 20, and the Code of Justinian: *huiusmodi*.  
> h. Some manuscripts: *orire* or *oriri*; the Code of Justinian: *perorare*. Compare Dirksen, *Civilistische Abhandlungen*, vol. II, p. 479.  
> i. Manuscripts 10 and 18: *postea* (“afterwards”); Gothofredus incorrectly wishes *sed et p.*  
> j. The corrected reading of most manuscripts and the authority of the Code of Justinian; manuscript 13 has “recovery [of] possession in the law.” Recent editions read *possessioni*.  
> k. Manuscripts 9, 10, 18, 19, and 42 read *praestet* (manuscripts 9 and 42, *praestent*) followed by *ut ad* (manuscripts 10 and 18, *a*) before *litigium*.  
> l. Manuscripts 10, 18, 42, and the Code of Justinian: *convenit*; manuscript 20: *largire*.  
> m. Many manuscripts have *possessionis*; the Code of Justinian adds “without any delay.”  
> n. The Code of Justinian adds *domino*; manuscript 21 has *quod libet*.  
> o. Manuscript 42: *recompensandae*; the Code has *possessionis recuperandae*, rejected by W.  
> p. The Code of Justinian: *indulgemus*; manuscript 8 adds *hic*.  
> q. Cujas’s first edition has *servulo*, incorrectly; the Code of Justinian has *servos*.  
> r. The Code of Justinian: *Absentibus* (“to absentees”).  
> s. Manuscript 9: *efficere*; manuscript 14: *sufficere*; manuscript 42: *officere*, but above the line *hoc facere*.  
> t. Manuscripts 9 and 42: *debent*; manuscript 12: *debebit*; manuscript 16: *dabit*.  
> u. Manuscript 19: *emersum*. Compare Dirksen, cited above.  
> v. Manuscripts 19 and 20, and Ritter’s second edition: *possessionis*; manuscript 19 has “recovery fixed by law”; manuscript 20, *praestitum*. Ritter’s second edition has *reformato*.  
> x. Manuscript 20: *sublevatus*, corrected above the line to *sublatus*; Gothofredus’s note has *ablatus*.  
> y. Manuscripts 7, 8, 13, 20, and 21: “from litigation”; manuscript 42: “for administration.”  
> z. Manuscripts 19 and 20: *immaculata* (“unstained”).  
> a. The Code of Justinian: *servato*; manuscript 19 has the corrupt reading *res. juste*.  
> b. The Code adds “to absentees,” rejected by W. Compare Dirksen, cited above. Manuscript 42: *legitimis qui*; the Aurélian and Lyon editions: *ligitimisque*.  
> c. Some manuscripts have “names … violence … assistance”; the Aurélian and Lyon editions likewise have *subvenire*.  
> d. Manuscripts 24, 31, 35, 38, and 39 omit X.  
> e. Manuscript 40 and Sichard’s margin: December.  
> f. Most manuscripts have *Mediolano* or an abbreviation. Editions: *Mediol.* Manuscripts 8 and 16 omit from Milan through “the seventh”; manuscript 32 has Milan. The Code of Justinian gives Constantinople, from which W. supposes the law was promulgated in both halves of the Empire. I think the place-name is an error arising from the following *Constantino*, examples of which have already been seen in earlier constitutions.  
> g. Some manuscripts and Tilius omit Augustus.  
> h. Manuscripts 13, 19, and 20: sixth; 33 and 34: ninth; 28, 36, 40, and Sichard’s margin: third; 42: *Vicr.*; 44: eighth. In some manuscripts the numeral is absent.  
> i. Some manuscripts: Constantine; the Code of Justinian: Constans.  
> j. Manuscripts 6, 7, 10, and apparently 18: *claro*; manuscript 19: “most illustrious man”; manuscript 21: “Constantius, illustrious, consuls.” The Code: “Caesar for the third time.” Some manuscripts, Sichard through the Lyon edition, omit Caesar.

### Interpretation

We specially admonish all judges that no one may presume, while owners are absent, to seize their property; rather, against wicked persons all things are to be recovered through the agency of the judge, while the principal matter remains intact.

If anyone alleges that he has a claim against an absentee, then even if there is someone to whom those who are abroad entrusted the management of their property, neither their agent nor procurator nor any of their slaves shall be compelled to plead the case on behalf of an owner who is absent or has issued no instruction. But if anything has been taken from them, it shall immediately be restored to those who, while the owner was absent, were excluded, once they make application.

If the owner himself has perhaps not recovered the property through his slaves’ negligence, then, when he has returned from abroad, he is in no way forbidden to recover his possession by the benefit of summary relief, even if a year has elapsed. Once everything taken during his absence has been fully restored, the action in the case shall proceed unimpaired, but only between lawful persons of full age. For it is fitting that we should thus provide for absentees against the malice of those who are present.

> m. The editions have *hiis*, except Ritter’s second edition, which has *iis*.  
> n. Manuscript 20: “the owner absent.”  
> o. Sichard has *a*, but his margin corrects it to *de*.  
> p. Manuscripts 21, 42, and 44 add *nullatenus* (“in no way”).  
> q. Manuscript 20: “he shall restore … by benefits.”
