> t. Manuscript 42: *opponatur* (“be opposed”).  
> u. Manuscript 20: *integritate* (“integrity”).  
> v. Manuscripts 6, 7, and 42: *aliter* (“otherwise”).

## CONCERNING THE ESTATES OF SHIP-OWNERS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus, in response to the decree of the ship-owners. We do not permit alienations of estates made by ship-owners for the purpose of evading their compulsory service to prejudice you. Therefore we will that purchasers of the aforesaid estates, upon application to the Prefect of the Annona, be compelled to perform the service to which they have made themselves liable.

Given five days before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

> Notes [Cols. 0323D–0324B]:  
> x. Code of Justinian: “Concerning the estates and all property of ship-owners.”  
> y. Manuscript 4 and the editions read Constantius, manifestly in error; its origin has often been explained. Before me, Gothofredus and Beatus restored Constantine in their notes.  
> a. Manuscript 4 has *it*, corrected in red to *id*.  
> b. Aurélian and Lyon consular lists.

## CONCERNING VARIOUS OFFICES

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Philippus, Prefect of the Praetorium. Officials who are found to have obtained letters from various offices by virtue of having been *protectores* are to be restored to their former military service.

Given three days before the Nones of November at Arles, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar (326).

> Notes [Cols. 0324B–0324D]:  
> c. Gothofredus, approving Bol., attributes this law to Constantius. But since P. indicates no variation in the writing, manuscript 1 too appears to agree with the printed texts. In accordance with the altered inscription, Gothofredus also emends the subscription in his chronology for 326 and 353, pp. XXVII and LI, and in his commentary on chapter 3 of this title. His words are: “The same judgment applies to law 2: Constantius is its author, both from the designation of Philippus, Prefect of the Praetorium, in the inscription, and from the place subscribed, Arles. Thus it appears referable to the consulship of Constantius for the sixth time and Constans Caesar for the second time, that is, A.D. 353, when Constantius was indeed at Arles, as Athanasius testifies in *To Those Living the Solitary Life*, p. 641, and Ammianus Marcellinus, book 14, pp. 9 and 25. Unless we should rather refer it to A.D. 346. Philippus’s prefecture falls approximately at that time; certainly law 1 below, ‘That a transfer of assessment [shall not occur],’ was given to him in 346. Yet the subscription, ‘Given at Arles,’ would oppose this, for in 346 Constantius the emperor was not in Gaul but in the East. And so, as I have said, it must be referred to A.D. 353.” See Gothofredus, *Prosopography*, under “Philippus.” Beatus thinks everything sound; I do not hesitate to agree, because manuscript 1 agrees with the common reading. Certainly this constitution may not be referred to 353, since the following chapter 3 would then be later, contrary to the arrangement of the Theodosian Code.  
> d. Thus the Lyon manuscript and editions before Beatus, who reads *Arelati*. Manuscript 1 seems to agree with our reading.  
> e. Gothofredus, uncertain to which year this constitution should be assigned, omits the year; it is also omitted by Ritter and Ritter’s second edition.

## CONCERNING DECURIONS
[Col. 0324B] Emperor Constantine Augustus to . . . . . Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0324D] f The name of the praetorian prefect to whom this law is addressed is lacking. Go. and Be. think that it was directed to all praetorian prefects, as chapter 18 of this title; I think otherwise, because the distinguished senate of the City is mentioned here. It therefore appears to have been addressed to the praetorian prefect of Italy; and in this year Bassus held that office. “Id. A. ad ppo.” in Til.—Go. places an asterisk after “ad.” Ri.—Be. do not mark a lacuna. We have inserted dots.] Some time ago our Clemency established by a promulgated law [Note: [Col. 0324D] g This law of Constantine, according to Go., is not extant.] that the sons of counts [Note: [Col. 0324D] h Of military affairs.] and governors, and of rationales and masters [Note: [Col. 0324D] i Go. notes: “That is, apparently, of the res privata.” See chapter 120 of this title and XI, 30, 49.] of the privy purse—provided nevertheless that they descend by origin from curiales—should be bound to the municipal orders. We now order that those who, [Note: [Col. 0324D] j Go. notes: “This word may seem suspect; one might prefer *quiqui*, that is, ‘whoever’; or *singuli*, ‘individual persons’; or finally *illi*, ‘those.’” Cuj. 1 has *cui*. Cui. 2, 2* have “should be bound; we now order that those who,” etc. Aur. Lugd. has “should be bound: now [Col. 0325B] we order that those who,” etc. Go.—Ri* likewise. See following note.] after performing public duties, have been found suitable [Col. 0325A] for the judgment of our Clemency to approach offices of honour, may, when summoned, attain honourable promotions. [Note: [Col. 0325B] a The editions read: “having been found suitable in public duties, to approach by the judgment of our Clemency, and shortly thereafter to honours, when summoned…” Til.—Cuj. 2* read: “honours; summoned to,” where Rein already places a comma before *ad*. Go. prefers *sunt* (though this is unnecessary), and punctuates thus: “we order that those who—who (Ri.’s edition, *quiqui*)—having performed public duties, have been found suitable by the judgment of our Clemency to approach offices of honour, may, when commanded (or excepted), attain honourable promotions.” I moved the comma which stood between *sint* and *judicio* to after “offices of honour,” and deleted the comma after *praecepti*.] But those whom the imperial authority does not know [Note: [Col. 0325C] b Ri* has *vos* (“you”); above, note 4 has *praecepti*.] we have entrusted to the judgment of the prefecture, so that they may restore to their proper municipal orders those who appear to be of curial stock and less fitted for imperial judgment, [Note: [Col. 0325C] c Thus 4, Til.—Lugd., Be. and Go.; Cuj. 2—Ri* erroneously read *restituent*, “they shall restore.”] while ensuring that those whom we have promoted by our judgment remain untouched; provided, however, that their heirs are assigned to the curiae. If indeed any decurion, overthrowing [Note: [Col. 0325C] d Folio 223 of manuscript 4.] the fiscal advantages, fleeing the curia, has by influence gained admission to the distinguished senate of the City, [Note: [Col. 0325C] e Editions before Be. read *orbis*, “world”; rightly, at Go.’s direction, Be. restored *urbis*, “of the City,” and manuscript 4 likewise has this. The error of the editions arose because the letter *u*, with its upper strokes somewhat bent, is not unlike *o*, and deceived Til. The City is Rome. Constantinople had not yet been made the seat of the Empire.] he shall by no means be admitted. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar being consuls (326).

## On Wills and Codicils

[Note: [Col. 0325C] f Cod. Just. VI, 23: “On Wills and the Manner in Which Wills Are Opened.” Chapter 15 omits “and Codicils.” Many manuscripts have *codicellis*.]

. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0325C] g See below, note i.]

[Col. 0325B] Emperors Constantine Augustus and Constantius [Note: [Col. 0325C] h Thus corrected from manuscripts 10, 18, and 25. Constantius is omitted in manuscripts 8, 19, 27, 36, and 40. The remaining manuscripts usually have *Cost.* The editions have *Constans*.] Caesar . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0325D] i W. first indicated the lacuna by dots. The passage is corrupt. Manuscripts 8, 12, 14, and 17 add *Aeterio*, as though Aetherius had been urban prefect. Yet I find Aetherius nowhere invested with that office. Should one write *Asterio*? Manuscript 15: “Constans to the People”; the rest omit it. Manuscripts 9, 29, and 42: “Constantius Augusti,” omitting “Caesar, Urban Prefect.” Manuscripts 10 and 18: “C. copu.” Manuscript 25: “C. aa. Caes. urban prefect.” Manuscripts 33 and 34: “Emperors Constantine and Constantius Augusti, men of clarissimate rank, of the City.” Manuscript 37 omits Caesar; 40 omits Urban Prefect. Manuscripts 8, 21, 26, 39, 42, and, according to Go., manuscript Til.: “praetorian prefect.” Be., following Go., prefers to attribute this constitution to Constantius and date it to 354. Hence in the subscription he also restores Constantius in place of Constantine.] Urban Prefect. In codicils not preceded by a will, as in testamentary dispositions [Note: [Col. 0325D] j Manuscript 16 has *voluntate*, “disposition.”], the participation of seven witnesses [Note: [Col. 0325D] k Manuscript 19 adds “succession.” Manuscript 6: *septe t.*] or five [Note: [Col. 0325D] l Manuscript 19 has *interventu*, “participation.”] must not be lacking; thus [Note: [Col. 0325D] m Manuscripts 10, 16, and 18 have *fit*, “is done.”] the successions of testators [Note: [Col. 0325D] n Manuscripts 6, 7, 16, and 17 have the singular *successioni*.] will be preserved without any legal defect. [Note: [Col. 0325D] o Manuscript 14 has *captivatione*, “captivity.”] Whenever, therefore, the required number of witnesses is lacking, the instrument of codicil shall be held invalid. The same has been decided for observance in other testamentary dispositions.

[Col. 0326A] Given on the eleventh [Note: [Col. 0326B] a Manuscripts 28, 30, 36, and 40: “Given on the tenth”; 31: “Given on the twelfth”; 8 omits “eleventh” and later “seventh.” Go.: “elsewhere, fifth.”] day before the Kalends of January, [Note: [Col. 0326B] b Manuscripts 24 and 35 have June, which Go. also conjectures.] Constantine Augustus for the seventh time [Note: [Col. 0326B] c Manuscript 19: “at Constantinople, Arcadius Augustus”; 38 and 34: “Constantine Augustus for the fourth time”; 38 and 42: “Constantius Augustus for the seventh time,” which Go. had already conjectured.] and Constantius [Note: [Col. 0326B] d Manuscripts 10, 18, and 25: “and Constantius.” The remaining manuscripts have *cost. s. Constant.*, but 21 and the editions have Constans.] Caesar being consuls (326).

### Interpretation

If anyone has not made a will but has made a codicil in place of a will, [Note: [Col. 0326B] e Thus corrected from the best manuscripts; Sich., Cuj. 1—Lugd. and the authoritative text have “but in place of.” The remaining editions read “but in the manner of.”] in which codicil a lawful appointment of an heir is contained, and has that codicil itself confirmed by the same number of witnesses—that is, by seven or five subscriptions [Note: [Col. 0326B] f Some manuscripts: “inheritance … that is … shall confirm,” and later “of the disposition.”]—it cannot be valid if there are fewer than five, just as other testamentary dispositions cannot be. For according to the preceding law, [Note: [Col. 0326C] g Thus most manuscripts. The editions have *leg. sup.* “preceding law.” Moreover, this passage shows that some law has fallen out, to which the interpreter refers. Cf. Go. in his commentary.] if, after a will had been made, a codicil was subsequently drawn up [Note: [Col. 0326C] h Many manuscripts have simply *post*, “after.”] and the testator wished therein to name an heir other than the one he had made in the will, the appointment of an heir in that codicil shall not be valid.

## On the Appointment of Guardians and Curators

[Note: [Col. 0326C] i W., following Go., notes that this law is confirmed by Emperor Leo in Cod. Just., V, 30, chapter 3, On Legal Guardianship; Bijdr., loc. cit., p. 323, rather refers it to another, lost law of Constantine concerning agnates.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus and Caesar [Note: [Col. 0326C] j Manuscripts 10, 18, and others: “and Caesar.” Manuscripts 15 and 21 omit it. Manuscripts 28, 40, and Sich. in the margin: Valens. Manuscript 32: “the same Augustus, Emperor and Caesar.” The Caesar meant is Constantius, who was consul this year (Go. says Constantine).] to the People [Note: [Col. 0326C] k Manuscript 30: “to the peculium.” Go. notes: “of the City of Rome.”]. In the case of women, a blood-related paternal uncle shall not decline legal guardianship. [Note: [Col. 0326C] m Manuscripts 6, 7, 14, 16, and 17 add *et*, “and,” not improperly; for this constitution was severely abridged by the Visigoths. Moreover, manuscripts 6, 7, and 17 have “blood-related paternal uncles”; manuscript 6 spells it *sanguinios*. Manuscripts 8 and 18: “legal guardianship, blood-related paternal uncles.” Manuscript 10: “legal guardianship, blood-related fathers.” Manuscript 42: *censanguineis*, corrected to *consanguineus*. In the margin of Cuj. 1—Lugd.: γρ., “read: or paternal uncle”; Vetranius Maurus, *On the Law of Children*, chapter 31, adopted this in Go.’s edition; so too, besides Glück, loc. cit., vol. XXVIII, p. 455, note 90, Rudorff, *The Law of Guardianship*, vol. I, p. 215, note 35. Manuscript 8 omits “day before the Kalends of January”; others add “and Caesar.” Heineccius, *Commentary on the Julian and Papian Laws*, p. 237, suggests “or patron,” against Glück, loc. cit.] [Note: [Col. 0326C] l Go. conjectures *in feminas*, “over women.” Manuscripts 6, 7, 14, 16, and 17 add *et*, “and,” not improperly; for this constitution was severely abridged by the Visigoths. Moreover, manuscripts 6, 7, and 17 have “blood-related paternal uncles”; manuscript 6 spells it *sanguinios*. Manuscripts 8 and 18: “legal guardianship, blood-related paternal uncles.” Manuscript 10: “legal guardianship, blood-related fathers.” Manuscript 42: *censanguineis*, corrected to *consanguineus*. In the margin of Cuj. 1—Lugd.: Greek *vel patruus*, “or paternal uncle,” which Vetranius Maurus, *On the Law of Children*, chapter 31, received in the edition of Go.; besides Glück, loc. cit., vol. XXVIII, p. 455, note 90, Rudorff, *The Law of Guardianship*, vol. I, p. 215, note 35. Manuscript 8 omits “day before the Kalends of January”; others add “and Caesar.” Heineccius, *Commentary on the Julian and Papian Laws*, p. 237, suggests “or patron,” against Glück, loc. cit.] Given on the day before [Note: [Col. 0326D] n Some manuscripts have “second”; Sich. “first Kalends,” but in the margin “day before.” Manuscript 28: July; 30, 33, 36, 40: June.] the Kalends [Note: [Col. 0326D] o “At Sirmium” is added.] of January, Constantine Augustus himself for the seventh time [Note: [Col. 0326D] p Manuscript 19: “Augustus for the sixth time and Caesar for the second time, consuls.” Manuscript 32 omits “seventh”; 36: “the prefect himself for the seventh time.” Be. wishes to insert “Constantius” after *et*.] and Caesar being consuls (326).

This law requires no exposition. [Note: [Col. 0326D] q Cuj. 1—Ri.: “This requires no interpretation.” Some manuscripts: “This law needs no exposition.”]

## On the Right of the Treasury

Emperor Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0326D] r Thus manuscript 4, Til.—Lugd., and the magistracy is absent. Go. therefore plausibly adds “to the People” from chapter 2, On Guardians, cited above, and joins it with this law. Another conjecture of Go., by which he dates this law to 315, is less preferable. For, apart from the fact that it would then be older than chapters 2–4 of this title contrary to the order of the Theodosian Code, the inscription “The same to Volusianus, Urban Prefect,” found in Cuj. 2—Be., was transferred by Cujas from the Justinian Code into the Theodosian Code, as Go. himself admits in his Chronicle for this year. That Volusianus is not known as urban prefect in this year is thus not important enough to compel alteration of the subscription, since the error must be attributed not to the Theodosian Code but to the corrupted text here in the Justinian Code. Nor, therefore, is it necessary to change “Urban Prefect” into “Praetorian Prefect,” as Rein. wishes; nor to write with Go., in his Chronicle for this year, “to Anicius Julianus, Urban Prefect,” a conjecture pleasing to Be., who in his notes emends it to “the most illustrious Julianus”; nor, finally, to assign this constitution to 354, a conjecture Go. proposed in his Chronicle but himself attacks there.] . . . . . . . . The opportunity for defence [Col. 0327A] must be granted to those upon whom the treasury brings any disturbance, since, while the controversy is still pending, it is not lawful for their property to be disturbed or entered in an inventory. [Note: [Col. 0327C] a Folio 79 of manuscript 4.] Whenever, therefore, a controversy arises and the treasury claims someone’s estate, the investigation shall be conducted before the person with whom all the property is situated, so that, when the outcome of the case has proved that it ought to be claimed, [Note: [Col. 0327D] b Thus correctly Be. from the Justinian Code; manuscript 4 and the editions have *vindicare*, “to claim.” Go. says *vindicare* can stand.] it may then at last be lawful to pursue the property; and an inquiry shall be held concerning the extent of the estate and assets, [Note: [Col. 0327D] c Ri* erroneously has *habere*, “to have.”] to be investigated through conditional slaves, so that, if anything has been concealed, it may be exacted, and, in addition, a further sum as a fine equal to that which had been fraudulently taken away. [Note: [Col. 0327D] d The Justinian Code adds *integrum*, “whole.” Dirksen, loc. cit., p. 492.]

§ 1. But if, in an inquiry of this kind [Note: [Col. 0327D] e Go.—Ri* and the Justinian Code have *hujusmodi*. Be., from Til.—Cuj. 2*, restores the reading of manuscript 4, retained by Go. in his commentary.], the name of a Caesarian official arises, [Note: [Col. 0327D] f Cuj. 2 and 2* incorrectly have *nomine*, “by the name.”] he shall not be allowed recourse to this constitution; for the habitual frauds by which the aforesaid persons have customarily dared to corrupt everything have earned them this exception. [Note: [Col. 0327D] g Manuscript 4 has *meruerit*, and so Go.; Be. emends to *meruerint*, which passed from an old correction in manuscript 4 into Til.—Be.; the Justinian Code has *meruit*.] Given on the day before the Kalends of January, [Note: [Col. 0327D] h Go. has not only June, but proposes it in the note as well.] at Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0327D] i Be. and the Justinian Code have *Sirmii*, “at Sirmium,” and the Justinian Code: “Constantius Augustus for the seventh time.”] Constantine Augustus for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar being consuls (326). [Note: [Col. 0327D] j Cuj. 2—Go. have Constantine, erroneously. Go. conjectures: “Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and Licinius Caesar, consuls (315),” but see the preceding note.]

## On Farmers, Registered Taxpayers, and Coloni

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Aemilianus, Praetorian Prefect. Farmers engaged in sowing or gathering crops shall never be drawn away for extraordinary burdens; since it is the task of provident administration to satisfy such needs at an appropriate time. Read on the seventh day before the Ides of March, Januarius and Justus being consuls (328). (From the Justinian Code.)

In the year of the Lord 327. Constantine Caesar for the fifth time and Maximus being consuls.

## On the Office of the Praetorian Prefects

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0327D] k Cf. Theodosian Code, chapter 2, On the Responses of Jurists (I, 4), note m.] Those who complain about governors’ decrees, because they judge them to have been issued to the detriment [Col. 0328A] [Note: [Col. 0328B] a Schr. conjectures *detrimentum*, without cause. b Thus manuscript 5; Cl. has *arbitrentur*.] of the laws, shall cause the matter to come before the judgment of your authority, [Note: [Col. 0328B] c Thus manuscript 5; Cl. and W. have “shall make come,” though Cl. and W. in *Opp.*, p. 441, emend it at the end.] so that, once *(labe) factatis* [“when the stain has been …”; materially uncertain] and overthrown [Note: [Col. 0328B] d Manuscript 5 has *factatis*, before which the word I supplied could easily have dropped out. It is certainly more appropriate to the sense than *frangere*, “to break.” Ba. conjectures *jactatis*, “having been cast down.” Cl., Pu., and W. have *fractis*, “having been broken,” which departs too far from manuscript 5. The same manuscript is subsequently erroneous.] those things which have improperly been imposed, they may not retain even the name of a judgment. [Note: [Col. 0328B] e Bijdr. emends *impressa*, “imposed,” to *expressa*, “expressed,” comparing Theodosian Code XII, 1, chapter 47, On Decurions; but *imprimere* here seems to mean “to effect by imposition.” See Code II, 20, chapter 11, On Matters Done through Force or Fear, and Manutius on Cicero’s *Letters to Friends*, V, 2, under *Impressione*.] Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, Constantine Caesar for the fifth time [Note: [Col. 0328C] f Cl. corrects to Constantius. g “Caesar for the fifth time,” absent from manuscript 5, correctly added by Cl.] and Maximus being consuls (327).

## Without a Census Registration

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Acacius, Count of Macedonia. Slaves entered upon the tax registers shall be transferred within the boundaries of the province, and those who have acquired ownership by purchase shall recognize that the census is to be inspected on their behalf. [Note: [Col. 0328C] h Go. and Be. think that *censum*, “the census,” has dropped out because of the nearly identical final syllables of the preceding word; yet in the Glossary Go. and Glück, loc. cit., vol. XVI, p. 134, explain *inspicere* as “to recognize the taxes.” Perhaps *inspiciendum* may be explained thus: “they shall know that inspectors must be sent, who assess the owner.” Cf. Theodosian Code XI, 1, chapter 31, On the Grain Supply: “the selected persons … may be assessed.”] It is reasonable that the same be observed also with respect to landed property; [Note: [Col. 0328C] i Go. emends *est* to *ut* or *et*, “that” or “and”; unnecessarily, provided that the punctuation is complete.] once their agreements have been removed, the public burdens and payments shall concern the responsibility of those to whose ownership [Note: [Col. 0328C] k Ri* erroneously has *dominium*, “ownership.”] the same properties have passed. [Note: [Col. 0328C] j According to Go., add *emptorum*, “of the purchasers”; or rewrite *earumdem onera*, “the burdens of the same properties.” Westphal, *On Purchase and Sale*, §630, approves this. Nothing need be altered. *Eorumdem* means “of those who made the agreement.”] Given on the third day before the Kalends [Note: [Col. 0328D] l According to Go., read “given” rather than “published.” Thessalonica was the metropolis of Macedonia, to whose count this law is addressed.] of March at Thessalonica, [Note: [Col. 0328D] m Manuscript 4, Til., Cuj. 1, 2, and 2*: *Thessal.*; the others: *Thessal.*] Constantine [Note: [Col. 0328D] n Be. correctly emends Constantius to Constantine. See Theodosian Code XI, 7, 4. Aur. Lugd. subsequently has Const.] and Maximus being consuls (327).

## On Praetors

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Julianus, Urban Prefect. We also relieve persons under twenty years [Note: [Col. 0328D] o The manuscript, according to Go., has “under twenty-five,” which Go. and Ri* retain; Cuj. 1—2* and Be. have “under twenty.” Aur. Lugd. has *vigenti*. The Lugdunensis manuscript has “under twenty-two,” or “under twenty”; I seem to have found both readings in the manuscript. I have therefore restored “twenty” with Cujas, since legal age is not at issue here. It cannot indeed be denied that the numerals II and V in ancient manuscripts such as the Lugdunensis scarcely differ in shape; but because “twentieth” is then written out in full, I thought the reading XX should be retained. It is well known that *minoris* is an accusative plural according to the old manner of writing.] of age, weak by reason of their youth, by this remedy: they shall by no means be bound under the title of that obligation by whose snares are bound [Note: [Col. 0329B] a Go. has *vinciuntur*, without reason.] [Col. 0329A] those who, after their twentieth [Note: [Col. 0329B] c Folio 4 of the manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0329B] b See note y. Editions before Be. have *vicensimum* from the manuscript, which soon after has *sciaenicis*, though that was corrected.] year of age, being abroad across the sea and dwelling in the provinces, do not make themselves available for presenting circus and theatrical games [Note: [Col. 0329B] d The Lugdunensis manuscript has *faciant*.], and are therefore subjected to a fixed kind of penalty. [Note: [Col. 0329B] e Be. wishes to restore *generi*, “to a kind,” i.e. “subjected to a kind of fine, exposed.” Correctly.] Given on the day before the Nones of March, received at Rome, Constantius [Note: [Col. 0329C] f Go. emends to “Constantine Caesar for the fifth time”; Be. to Constantine.] and Maximus being consuls (327).

## On Decurions

Constantine Augustus to Annius Tiberianus, Count. [Note: [Col. 0329C] g Rein. adds “through Africa,” approving Go. in the Chronicle. See Theodosian Code XII, 5, chapter 1, On the Manner of Performing Civic Duties. Cuj. 2 in the Chronicle has “to Anna” (Rein. corrects “Junius”) “Tiberianus, Count,” erroneously.] Having notified all provincial governors that our Clemency has determined that the sons of veterans are to be bound to curial duties, so that even those who flatter themselves with the honour of perfectissimate rank shall be thrust into the curia [Note: [Col. 0329C] h Til. has *incuria*, “in negligence.” Shortly before, manuscript 4 and editions before Be. have *hii*.] and serve in the necessary public offices. [Note: [Col. 0329C] i Go. omits *publicis*.] Posted on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May at Carthage, Constantius [Note: [Col. 0329C] j Be. wishes to restore Constantine. See XI, 7, 4, note u.] and Maximus being consuls (327).

## On Exactions

[Col. 0329B] Constantine Augustus [Note: [Col. 0329C] k Br., Al. manuscripts, Sich., and the Justinian Code have “Emperor Constantine Augustus.”] to the Africans. [Note: [Col. 0329C] l The Justinian Code adds “provincials.” Manuscripts 10 and 18: “to the African.”] Since you have rightly requested by your acclamation [Note: [Col. 0329C] m Manuscripts 10 and 20: “your petition”; 25: “our petition”; manuscript 4, Go.—Be.: *subclamatione*, “acclamation”; 21: “under condemnation”; Til.—Cuj. 2*: “under a cry.”] that no relaxation concerning others [Note: [Col. 0329D] p Manuscripts 10, 18, and 25 have *deferunt*; 15 omits *reliquorum*. q Manuscripts 6–8, 10, 14, and 16–18 have *labitas*, and manuscript 10 *provenerit*; 20 has *provenire* and above the line *vel possit*.] should accrue to those who defer payment of fiscal contributions, [Note: [Col. 0329C] o Manuscript 20: “that no one under payment”; 15: “that no [relaxation] for those contributions”; 16: “of contribution”; 21 omits “who.”] we specially order that the property of those who obstinately defer satisfying fiscal debts [Note: [Col. 0329D] r Here begins the Justinian Code. s Manuscripts 10 and 18 have *defecerunt*; 25, *deferant*. The Justinian Code: “may possess with perpetual security,” omitting *etc.*] be sold, with perpetual security of possession granted to the purchasers, etc. [Note: [Col. 0329D] t With “Given” begins folio 138 of manuscript 4, at the bottom margin of which is the quire-sign ΙΘ.] Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 0329D] u Manuscripts 28, 34, and 36 have July.] at Serdica, [Note: [Col. 0329D] v Some Br. and Al. manuscripts have Sirdica, Syrdica, Sirdice, Serditiae, Sirice. Manuscript 8 omits Serdica.] Constantine [Note: [Col. 0329D] x Add “Caesar for the fifth time” in the Justinian Code, as in Theodosian Code I, 4, chapter 2, On the Responses of Jurists, and II, 7, chapter 2, On Delays. I think “Caesar for the fifth time” should everywhere be deleted. Manuscripts 4, 6, 7, 10, 15, 16, 18, 20, 21, 36, Sich.—Lugd. have Constantius; Ri. prints it. 34 and 38 have Constantinople, erroneously; others have Conscio. Manuscripts 10, 18, and 29 add Augustus, and 16 “the two Caesars” after Maximus. Aur. Lugd. subsequently has *Cons.*] and Maximus being consuls (327).

[Col. 0330A] ### Interpretation

Whoever scorns to discharge the taxes on his lands, the lands of him who scorns to pay his taxes shall be sold by the collector; [Note: [Col. 0330B] a Go.—Ri*: “those who scorn; lands … he scorns.” [Col. 0330C] Ri* omits *qui* after *ejus*, and subsequently has *exactione*, “by exaction,” for *exactore*, “by the collector.” Subsequently 20, 21, and the editions have *firmo*, “firm.”] and those who purchase them shall possess what they have bought in this manner by a most secure right.

## On the Division of an Inheritance

Constantine Augustus to Constantius, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0330C] b Thus most manuscripts, including 20 and the Anicianus and Puteanus manuscripts cited by Go.; manuscript 25: “Augustus Constantius.” Manuscripts 10, 18–20, Sich.—Ri*: Constantine.] No one is granted permission to appropriate the goods of living persons [Note: [Col. 0330C] c Manuscript 42, corrected; manuscripts 8 and 20 have *ppu.*; 25 and the Anicianus and Puteanus manuscripts cited by Go. have *proc.*. d Manuscript 20 and Sich. have *observandis*, “preserving”; Sich. has *usurpandis* in the margin. e Manuscripts 10, 18–20 have *virorum*, “men.”] or to divide them contrary to good morals. But if, at their mother’s direction, her children have divided her goods among themselves [Note: [Col. 0330C] f Manuscripts 6–8, 10, 14, and 16–18 have *diviserunt*.], it has pleased us in every way [Note: [Col. 0330C] g Manuscripts 9 and 19 have *ob nefariam*; 20, *benefariam*. Sich. in the margin: *omni forma*.] that such a division should remain valid, provided it is shown that the same intention persisted until the end of her life. [Note: [Col. 0330C] h Manuscripts 6–8, 14, and 16: “provided also.”] Given on the third day before the Ides of June [Note: [Col. 0330C] i Thus most manuscripts, Til., and the margin of Cuj. 1—Cuj. 2*, approved by Go. Manuscript 16: January; 17: July. Some manuscripts and editions: fourth day before the Kalends of June; but Sich. in the margin has third.] at Constantinople, [Note: [Col. 0330C] j Go. says this word intruded through the occasion of the following “Constantine Caesar for the fifth time,” since Constantinople was founded three years later.] Constantine [Note: [Col. 0330D] k Manuscripts 9, 10, 18, 19, 24, 27, 29, 32, 33, 35, 44, Sich.—Ri*: Constantius, printed by Go., who proposes Constantine Caesar for the fifth time.] and Maximus being consuls (327).

[Col. 0330B] ### Interpretation

Although it is unjust for the goods of living persons [Note: [Col. 0330D] l Manuscript 20 and Capit. have *virorum*, “men.”] to be divided, nevertheless, if a mother while alive has directed and permitted her property to be divided among her sons, [Note: [Col. 0330D] m Manuscripts 6–8, 44, and many others: “her property … to be divided.”] and has persisted in the same intention until the end of her life, [Note: [Col. 0330D] o Some manuscripts: “until her end … the same intention.” Aur. Lugd.: *perstiteri*, “has persisted.”] the division made among the sons shall endure. [Note: [Col. 0330D] p Manuscripts 6, 7, and many others have the present *perdurat*, “endures.” Aur. Lugd.: “shall not be valid.”]

## On Delays

Emperor Constantine to Julianus, Urban Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0330D] q Manuscript 15 omits “Urban”; 27: “to Julianus, praetorian prefect.”] With the periods for requesting restoration in full observed, as has already been established, [Note: [Col. 0330D] r Cuj. 1, Aur. Lugd., and the Justinian Code omit *ut*, “as.”] if a delay is requested by the plaintiff, which can be confined within the limits fixed by law, [Note: [Col. 0330D] s The Justinian Code has “within the limits of restoration it is valid.”] it ought, whatever person requests it, to be granted after the facts have been heard. But if periods are requested [Note: [Col. 0330D] t Manuscript 15 reads: “the same ought to be granted. For, after the facts have been heard, whatever litigant requests it, such periods are sought.” u The Justinian Code omits *lege*, “by law.” Cf. Dirksen, loc. cit., p. 402.] which cannot be shortened within the span allowed by law [Col. 0331A] [Note: [Col. 0331C] a Manuscript 15: “cannot.”]—that is, if they are requested at the boundary of the lawful time [Note: [Col. 0331C] b Manuscript 15: “at the boundary of the aforesaid time they are requested,” omitting “and.”] and would extend its limits—the delay should be refused to the plaintiff; [Note: [Col. 0331C] c Manuscript 15: “would extend. Therefore delay [should be] refused to the plaintiff.”] for it was within his discretion to bring suit [Note: [Col. 0331C] d Manuscript 13 has *litigia*, “lawsuits.”] when the interval of the requested delay could still be included within the remaining period. [Note: [Col. 0331C] e Manuscript 15: “the remaining period.”]

§ 1. But if the defence of possessors requests the benefit of a delay, [Note: [Col. 0331C] f The Justinian Code has *rei*, “the defendant.” g Cuj. 2 and 2*: *suffragio*, singular; the Justinian Code: *suffragium*.] we decree that it be granted upon the cause being stated, without impediment from time [Note: [Col. 0331C] h Manuscript 15 has *dari*, “be given”; Aur. Lugd., *ferri*; the Justinian Code, *differri*, “be deferred.”], because it was by no means within the possessor’s power when he would be summoned to litigation [Note: [Col. 0331C] i Manuscript 15: “it had not stood in his power.”]. It must therefore be granted, even if the period obtained extends beyond the rule of the constitution. [Note: [Col. 0331C] j The Justinian Code has “beyond the definition of time.”] When such a delay, if obtained by the possessor [Note: [Col. 0331C] k Manuscript 15 has *et si*, “and if.”], the plaintiff too is not thereby prevented from seeking evidence. [Note: [Col. 0331D] n The Justinian Code has *prohibebitur*, “will be prevented.”] [Note: [Col. 0331D] l The Justinian Code has “by the defendant.” m Manuscript 15: “is obtained, and now plaintiff.”] Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, posted [Note: [Col. 0331D] o The Justinian Code omits *PP.*] at Rome, [Note: [Col. 0331D] p Manuscript 15 adds “to the Senate,” and 27 “from the Senate.”] Constantine Caesar for the fifth time and Maximus being consuls (327).

[Col. 0331B] ### Interpretation

Although it has been established that four months [Note: [Col. 0331D] r Manuscript 15 has *liquet*, “it is clear.” Go. wishes to restore: “Although it has been established that four months…”] are granted to applicants for seeking every restitution, [Note: [Col. 0331D] s Thus manuscripts 15, 27, and 28; but 40, 41, and the editions add *sit*, which perverts the sense.] if the period requested is that which has been granted—that is, one which cannot exceed four months—it ought to be allowed. [Note: [Col. 0331D] u Manuscript 15: “shall be allowed.”] But if delays are sought which exceed the time fixed by law, the delay must be denied to the plaintiff, because he ought to have known that his action must be concluded within the prescribed time. [Note: [Col. 0331D] v Manuscript 15: “denied, who.”] But if the person in possession should perhaps ask for time, what is granted to plaintiffs must absolutely be granted to him without limitation of time, [Note: [Col. 0331D] x Manuscript 15: “must be granted.”] because he could not know when his opponent would summon him to a case; and therefore the possessor shall receive time in which to answer. [Note: [Col. 0331D] y Manuscripts 40, 41, and Sich. omit “by … and therefore”; manuscript 15 adds “when.”] The plaintiff too may provide what is necessary for his own case. [Note: [Col. 0331D] z Manuscript 15: “may receive time; the plaintiff too may provide necessary things.”]

[Col. 0331C] Constantine Augustus to Victor, Rationalis of the City of Rome. Since certain debtors to the treasury, when ordered to pay the sum due, evade the force of execution by introducing the aid of an appeal, and no longer take care to seek a copy of the opinion or offer petitions in rebuttal, [Col. 0332A] [Note: [Col. 0332B] a “To seek a copy of the opinion; to offer petitions in rebuttal.”] it has been decided [Note: [Col. 0332C] b Folio 185 of manuscript 4.] that if, within the [Note: [Col. 0332C] c The summary of the Theodosian Code adds twenty.] days fixed for completing the formalities, [Note: [Col. 0332C] d The Justinian Code manuscripts omit *complendis*, “for completing.”] the appellant has failed through neglect to do these things, his appeal shall be deemed abandoned and the debt shall immediately be exacted. [Note: [Col. 0332C] e The Justinian Code has *existimetur*, “shall be deemed.”] Given on the day before the Kalends of August, Constantine [Note: [Col. 0332C] f Manuscript 4, Til.—Ri*, and the Justinian Code have Constantius. See above XI, 7, 4, note u. Aur. Lugd. subsequently has Const.] and Maximus being consuls (327).

## On the Responses of Jurists

Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0332C] g Cl., p. 128, note 21, says that no praetorian prefect named Maximus is found for this year. In the following year a constitution is extant addressed to a certain Maximus, but without title; Go. supposes him to have been praetorian prefect of Gaul. See Theodosian Code VII, 20, chapter 5, On Veterans.—A Maximus, praetorian prefect, is also mentioned in Theodosian Code I, 5, chapter 2, On the Office of the Praetorian Prefect; consequently I think there can be no doubt that he was praetorian prefect.] Everything [Note: [Col. 0332C] h Manuscript 5 has *Inuisa*.] contained in the writings of Paulus must be confirmed with accepted authority and held in every reverence. Therefore there is no doubt that his books of *Sentences*, composed with the fullest clarity, the most perfect expression, and the most just reasoning of law, are valid when produced in judgments. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of October at Treves, [Note: [Col. 0332C] i Cl., loc. cit., note 22, explains this as “published,” since Constantine was not in Gaul this year, comparing Go. in the Chronicle for 325, 328, 331, and 389, and the constitutions there cited. In this Cl. followed Go. on chapter 5 of the Theodosian Code cited above, vol. II, p. 438, note h, who, although he understands Treves as in Gaul, thinks perhaps a place among the Triballi and in Dacia, where Constantine was active at this time, is indicated. j Manuscript 5: *Treverunt*. Them.: *Trevesunt*. In his corrections Cl. wishes to read Constantius, which Pu. also has.] Constantine Caesar for the fifth time [Note: [Col. 0332D] k “Caesar for the fifth time” is absent from manuscript 5 and Them.] and Maximus being consuls (327).

In the year of the Lord 328. Januarius and Justus being consuls.

## On Oil Tables

[Col. 0332B] Emperor Constantine Augustus to Cerealis, Prefect of the Grain Supply. Oil tables which have become so vacant that no one can attach himself to their ownership are sold through the office for twenty folles apiece. [Note: [Col. 0332D] l Manuscript 4, Til.—Lugd.: “so that no one can attach himself to ownership.” Cuj. 2—Ri*: “so that no one can attach himself to ownership,” where Go., approving the change of *nullus*, “no one,” into *nullius*, “of no one,” silently made in Cuj. 2, wishes *possint*, plural, in place of *possit*. Be., following Go., prints: “so that they may attach themselves to no one’s ownership,” though he does not deny that Til.’s reading can stand; correctly, since “of them,” namely the oil tables, is understood. I restored the manuscript reading. A little later manuscript 4 has *concruam*.] But if anyone sells an oil table bought for the aforesaid folles at a higher price, he shall be bound in iron chains and sent to Illyricum, there to suffer an appropriate punishment. If anyone, however, retaining an oil table in his ownership, completes the course of life, that same table may pass by hereditary right to his own successors together with his other property. [Note: [Col. 0332D] m Aur. Lugd. omits *suis*, “his.”] Judges rightly consider that an injury is done to them if a litigant whose case has been injured by a judgment, *a prindein* [materially corrupt], receives from middling and lower persons what is to be furnished. [Col. 0333A] [Note: [Col. 0333B] a Here begins chapter 1 of the cited Justinian Code: “Emperor Constantine … Posted. Farmers never engaged in sowing or gathering crops shall be drawn to extraordinary burdens; since … satisfy,” and the rest ends. Go. defends *praestantur*, “are supplied,” if someone emends it to *praesignentur* or *praestituantur*, “are prescribed.”] [Note: [Col. 0333B] a Here begins chapter 1 of the cited Justinian Code: “Emperor Constantine … Posted. Farmers never engaged in sowing or gathering crops shall be drawn to extraordinary burdens; since … satisfy,” and the rest ends. Go. defends *praestantur*, “are supplied,” if someone emends it to *praesignentur* or *praestituantur*, “are prescribed.”] Nor shall a farmer engaged in accounts [Note: [Col. 0333C] b Thus manuscript 4, Til.—Ri*. Cuj. in the Justinian Code and Basilika, where Greek: *peri logismous*, “concerning accounts.” The glosses too know the reading *rationibus*, “accounts.” It therefore appears that *rationibus* is the true reading, and that *sationibus*, “sowing,” was restored in the Justinian Code at a later time. Be., by direction of Go. and Bic., adopts *sationibus* from the Justinian Code. Cf. the commentary on the Theodosian Code, Ri. edition, vol. IV, p. 121. Rein. notes: “the best reading will be *arationibus*, ‘ploughings,’ rather than *pastionibus*.” Dirksen, loc. cit., p. 156. According to Cujas, the sense is: “Coloni attached to the accounts of estates or to agriculture cannot at any time be summoned for transport-services or other extraordinary burdens,” except when, being free from accounts or from gathering crops, they have a suitable time to satisfy extraordinary burdens. Against this, Go. uses the words “a farmer engaged in accounts” and Justinian Code III, 12, chapter 3, On Holidays, for his opinion that an agent alone, not a farmer, is engaged in accounts; Go.’s view is not to be rejected, but because of the agreement of the sources and the purpose of this edition, *rationibus* should have been written. Leunclavius supports Go., *Notes*, book II, chapter 231, in Ottonis, *Thesaurus*, vol. III, p. 1551.] or gathering crops be drawn away for extraordinary [Note: [Col. 0333D] c At the syllable *ordinaria* begins folio 150 of manuscript 4.] burdens, since it is the duty of provident administration to satisfy such needs at a suitable time. If this provision is neglected, it touches the honour of your vicars; [Note: [Col. 0333D] d Cuj. 2—Ri* read “to satisfy; which … touches. To”; Be. rightly omits *ut*, “that.”] but proceedings shall be taken against the heads of the governors’ offices. The governors themselves shall also be required to write in their own hand what is needed, and in what necessity, for each heading: how many transport-services, how much labour, or what supplies and in what quantity must be furnished, so that they may record that they have examined it; [Note: [Col. 0333D] f Til.—Cuj. 2*: “they are: so that … may write, of the exaction.”] observing in the aforesaid order of exaction the distinction among richer, middling, and poorer persons. Read on the seventh day before the Ides of May at Rome, Januarius [Note: [Col. 0333D] g The Justinian Code has Januarius. Go. in the Chronicle: sixth day before the Ides; Aur. Lugd. subsequently has *Cons.*] and Justus being consuls (328).

[Col. 0333B] Constantine Augustus to all Palatines. Certain persons attempt to distort privileges granted to those who, after completing the offices of faithful service, have attained public posts of administration; nor do they understand that those advanced to the heights of promotion ought by no means to be stripped of their lawful distinction. We have therefore ordered that our Palatines, when they have completed the duty of faithful service and have been raised to the ranks of dignities, shall lose nothing of their privileges, but that their immunity shall be enlarged by the increase of their dignities. On this matter we have sent written instructions to the praetorian prefects and to the prefect of the city. Given on the third day before the Nones of July, at Yscoi [reading uncertain], in the consulship of Januarinus and Justus (328).

[Note: Col. 0333D h Go., Ri.: “The same Augusti.” Ri.: “The same Augusti.” Codex offici… but corrected to officia; a leaf begins, with the words fidelis….  
i The codex and Cuj. 1–Ri. have praecepimus, which can be retained if one considers the present text to have been written in epistolary form. Be., conjecturally with Go., reads praecipimus.  
j In the codex the numeral III has been cut away.]

## CONCERNING DEFAMATORY LIBELS

[Col. 0334A]

Constantine Augustus to Dionysius. A notorious written libel which lacks the name of an accuser is not to be examined at all, but is to be utterly destroyed. For whoever relies upon bringing an accusation ought to summon another’s life to judgment by an open charge rather than by a deceptive and secret writing. Posted at Tyre, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Januarinus and Justus (328).

[Note: Col. 0334B a Ms. 4 and Til.–Ri. have Tyro. Go. in the Chronology: the eleventh day before the Kalends.]

Constantine Augustus to Secundus, Praetorian Prefect. We order that records in criminal cases be made available as in civil cases: that is, where men’s safety is brought into jeopardy, neither is a request for the records to be awaited nor is the matter to be delayed by the accuser’s artifice, so that it may depend on the judge’s integrity and fairness. Given on the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Januarinus and Justus (328).

[Note: Col. 0334B b Go. observes: “Correctly; for one would err in substituting judicandi, ‘of judging.’ Nor should judicantis, ‘of the judge,’ be written.”  
c Aur. Lugd. omits Dat. Cuj. 1 has Kaen for Kalen. Aur. Lugd. Cons. and Go. (commentary, p. 12), owing to the resemblance between this law and c. 3, *On the Office of Provincial Governors* (I.19), regard the two laws as one, changing the emperor’s and consuls’ names. They would therefore write: “Emperor Julian … in the consulship of Julian and Sallustius (363),” in place of “Emperor Constantine … Januarinus and Justus.” But Go. did not judge these laws correctly. They were issued to different magistrates named in their inscriptions: c. 3 to Mamertinus, this one to Secundus, who was praetorian prefect under Constantine, not Julian. Further, the chronology does not permit this emendation, since the following c. 7 was issued in 338, and thus much earlier than this law if Go. is followed.]

## CONCERNING THE OFFICES OF PROVINCIAL GOVERNORS

[Col. 0334B]

The same Augustus to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect. Provincial governors ought, if anyone of the more powerful persons should prove excessively insolent and they themselves cannot punish, investigate, or pronounce judgment upon him, to report his name to us or at least to the attention of Your Gravity, so that provision may be made for the maintenance of public discipline and the protection of injured persons of lower station, etc. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, at Trier, in the consulship of Januarinus and Justus (328).

[Note: Col. 0334C–D d Ms. 5 has: “The same Augusti to Maxima, formerly [governor] of provinces. It is necessary.” Cl. Pu.: “The same Augustus to M., Provincial Governor. It is necessary.” Codex Justinianus: “Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, governor of a province. Provincial governors ought….” W. reads: “The same Augustus to Maximus … Provincial governors,” so that the beginning of the law lies in the words “Provincial governors,” not in “ought.” Examples of such transposition have already been seen in c. 2, *C. Th. On the Office of the Augustal Prefect* (I.14), and c. 10, *C. Th. On the Office of Vicars* (I.15). For, W. argues, it is unprecedented for anyone to be called “governor of provinces” without mention of the province over which he presides. Moreover, the following words—“report to us or to the attention of Your Gravity”—do not suit a provincial governor, nor do the words which the Codex Justinianus has in their place: “or at least report to the attention of the praetorian prefecture.” Finally, the words in cited c. 5, “provincial governors ought to refer [such matters] to your judgment,” clearly show that Maximus was not then a governor. For these reasons W., together with Go. on the cited c. 5, conjectures that this Maximus was praetorian prefect of Gaul; I think that conjecture is confirmed, in addition to c. 2 *C. Th. On the Responses of Jurists*, by c. 2 *C. Th. On the Office of Praetorian Prefects*, addressed to Maximus, praetorian prefect, on a similar matter and issued in the preceding year. Moreover, W. shrewdly observes that the defective inscription had already entered the Codex Justinianus at the time it was compiled, since the alteration to “the attention of Your Gravity” can scarcely have been made for any other reason than to make those words conform to the inscription. There is a remarkable diversity of readings in editions and manuscripts of the Codex Justinianus: the manuscripts Montisp. H. 82, Pist., Cas., Vat., Pl. 2, Bg., and the editions Schf., Bk., Herm. give Maximum; Pl. 1, Hal., and the rest, Maximianum. The rank of Maximus is omitted in Montisp. H. 82, Pist., Cas., Vat., Pl. 1 and 2, Bg., and the Nbg. editions.  
e Thus Ms. 5, Taf., Pu.; Cl. and W., from the Codex Justinianus, have potentiorum, “more powerful persons.”  
Col. 0335B a Schr. wishes judices, “judges,” to be added.  
b Ms. 3: Vindicari. Codex Justinianus: vindicare, but Pl. 1: judicare.  
c Codex Justinianus: “or at least to the attention of the praetorian prefecture.”  
d Thus Ms. 5. Codex Justinianus: tenuioribus, “persons of lower rank,” which is opposed to the earlier potentioribus. But here minoribus is opposed to potioribus.  
e Codex Justinianus before Bk.: “Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Probianus and Julianus,” placing this law in 322. But Maximus should then be written prefect of the city, since Maximus is mentioned as urban prefect in 322; see below, Chronology of Constitutions, for 322. Our subscription is confirmed by c. 5 *C. Th. On Veterans*. Cl. V. interprets Data as “Delivered,” since Constantine was not in Gaul in this year. See Go. in the Chronology for this year and on cited c. 5 *On Veterans*. Ms. 5 omits et.]

Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect. Care must be taken that veterans invested with the rank of protectores, or those who have received various honours for their merits, are not harassed by unsuitable injuries. If anyone is caught in this crime, the provincial governors ought to refer the matter to your judgment and send the aforesaid persons to your office, so that the act may most readily be punished according to its character. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, at Trier, in the consulship of Januarinus and Justus (328).

[Note: Col. 0335C f The rank of Maximus is absent from the manuscript and editions, including the Codex Justinianus. Only the Cui. edition has P. P., correctly and probably, according to Go., who added dots to indicate a lacuna. The rank has been supplied from cited c. 4, with which this law must be connected. See also above I.4.2. The manuscript Jd. has: “Augusti … concerning veterans,” corruptly.  
g Codex Justinianus: “veterans who [have been invested] with the rank of protector, or honours.”  
h Codex Justinianus: quod si quis, “but if anyone.”  
i Thus also Codex Justinianus. But Go. correctly says: “Either this word must refer to the earlier part prefixed to this law—in which some specified crime has been dealt with—or quo, that is, aliquo, ‘some,’ must be substituted for it.”  
j In the Codex Justinianus the following reads: “the provincial governors, investigating the deed within their jurisdiction, shall punish them according to the nature of the matter,” followed by the subscription.  
Col. 0335D k Codex Justinianus: Iun.  
l Ms. Go.: Triverei; rather Triveros, as Cui. 1. Cui. 2–Ri.: Triveris; Aur. Lugd. and Be.: Treviris. Go., in the notes, Chronology p. XXX, Prosopography p. 67, and Bon. p. 746 n. g, because Constantine was not in Gaul this year, conjecture either that a place outside Gaul—perhaps among the Triballi or in Dacia—must be substituted, or, as they prefer, that Data must be understood as “Delivered.” See also c. 2 *C. Th. On the Responses of Jurists* (I.4), note m.]

In the year of the Lord 329. Constantine Augustus, consul for the seventh time, and Constantine Caesar, consul for the fourth time.

Constantine Augustus to Secundus, Praetorian Prefect of the East. The authority of an ordinary judge, a provincial governor, or a vicar ought, like a watchman, to correct wrongful acts; but it is our pleasure that the officials of Your Sublimity and of the vicariate authority be removed from exactions, and that all taxes be collected through the provincial offices and the governors. For if the collection is not duly carried out, the person responsible, when brought before our tribunal, shall undergo danger to his life and to all his property. Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the eighth time and Constantius for the fourth time (329).

[Note: Col. 0335D m Ms. 5: “Augusti”; Cl., Pu.: A[A].  
n Thus Pu.; W. prefers this because of the following debet, “ought.” Ms. 5 and Cl.: iudices pr. reetores [corrupt]. Hu. conjectures iudicis.  
o Thus Pu. and W. in *E. L. L.* 1826, p. 1899. Ms. 5, Cl., W.: vicaria.  
p Cf. c. 6 *C. Th. On the Office of the Urban Prefect*: quasi in specula, “as if on a watchtower.”  
Col. 0336C a Ms. 5, Cl.: placeat. Pu. and W., conjecturally following Hu.: placet.  
b Cl. and Pu. conjecture vestrum, “your,” less correctly, W. noting that the praetorian prefect judged in the emperor’s sacred vice; see Haubold, *On the Imperial Consistory*, ch. III §4 (*Works*, vol. I, pp. 241 ff.).  
c Ms. 5: “at Constantinople … Constantine Augustus VIII and Constantius”; Ap. and Pu. omit “Constantine Augustus VIII and Constantius.”  
d Read Constantine Caesar IV, consul. See c. 2 *C. Th. On Restoration in Full* (II.16), note v.]

## CONCERNING COUNTERFEIT COINAGE

Constantine Augustus to Elpidius. It was formerly enacted that, if counterfeit coin were secretly struck on an estate or in a house, even without the owner’s knowledge, the fisc should claim the scene of the offence as its own property. We now direct that a distinction be made: if the owner was present nearby, whose carelessness or negligence must be punished, the earlier enactment shall remain valid; but if he was very far away from that house or estate, he shall suffer no loss.

§ 1. We have judged widows and wards worthy of special indulgence: a widow, even if present nearby, shall not lose her house or estate if no guilt of so grave a consciousness resides with her; wards, however, even if they were aware of it, shall suffer no loss, because their age, provided that they are under puberty, does not know what it sees. Their guardians, nevertheless, if they are nearby—since they ought not to be ignorant of what is done in the ward’s affairs—shall await this penalty: from their own property, if they are solvent, as much shall be paid to the fisc as would have been taken from the ward. These provisions having thus been amended, let the law be transmitted under all its headings. Given on the Kalends of March at Nicomedia; received on the eighth day before the Ides of April at Rome, in the consulship of Januarinus and Justus (328).

[Note: Col. 0336C e See above c. 1 *On Holidays* (II.8), note y. I.4, fourth edition: Helpidio.  
Col. 0336D f See c. 2 under this title.  
g Ri.: figuraratus.  
h Ri.: Non, an error.  
i Ms. 4 and editions before Be.: afue ir, but read abfuerit.  
j Leaf 33 in Ms. 4. Cuj. 2–Ri. wrongly omit autem. The learned Vesmius says nothing about Ms. I. If autem is absent in Ms. I, then vero should rightly also be omitted below.  
k Ms. 4 has indulgentiam, but it has been corrected in red ink to indulgentia.  
l Omit vero.  
m I have added in before omnibus from Ms. I; this preposition is absent from Ms. 4 and the editions. Yet I do not criticize the reading of Ms. 4. Til.–Cui. 2: emendatis omn. capitulis lex etc., incorrectly.  
n Go. and Rie.: Januario.]

## CONCERNING EXTRAORDINARY OR SORDID BURDENS

[Col. 0336C] Constantine Augustus to Aemilianus, Praetorian Prefect. The allocation of extraordinary burdens is not to be entrusted to the leading persons (principales). Provincial governors must therefore be instructed to make this allocation themselves, write it out with their own hand, and append the names without deception; and the rule previously enacted shall be observed, namely that [the burdens begin] with the more powerful persons. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of May, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the eighth time and Constantius for the fourth time (329).

[Note: Col. 0336D o Aur. Lugd. has ad twice.  
Col. 0337B a See *C. Th.* c. 2 under this title.  
b Ri. wrongly has VII. Go. in the Chronology: “Given on the third [elsewhere fourth] day before the Nones of March.”  
c Be. rightly wishes C. to be added. In Ms. 1, “ntio IV Coss.” has been cut away with the margin. Vesmius wishes the subscriptions of this year to read Constantio Caes. II.]

## CONCERNING PUBLIC WORKS

Constantine Augustus. Hail, Felix, most dear to us. All persons within one hundred feet in the vicinity of granaries shall be kept away; and if anything has been constructed, it shall be demolished, since very recent experience has openly shown that fiscal stores have suffered from fires in buildings adjoining granaries. But if anyone, through love of building, disregards public loss, we order that not only what he has built, but all his property and everything which he possessed by his own right, shall be adjudged to the fisc. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, at Sirmium, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus [repeated in the source, with corrupt numerals] and Constantine Augustus [repeated in the source, with corrupt numerals] and Constantius Caesar, consuls (329).

[Note: Col. 0337B d Ms. 4 has Habe, the b altered in red ink into u (Haue). The same is true in the following constitution. Cf. VII.4.1, note c.  
e Cuj. 2–Be.: K. NB. for karissime nobis.  
f Go.: “Those, namely, who are erecting or building structures, of whatever rank or dignity.” Ms. 4 first has arceatur, corrected in red ink; the editions have arceantur. What if one should read: “Every neighbouring property within one hundred feet shall be kept away”? For vicinitus occurs nowhere else, and with it admitted the sentence seems defective. Go. says that some emend vicinitates.  
Col. 0337C g The letter tum begins leaf 361 of Ms. 4.  
h Go. wishes et to be added. Ms. 4: construxit.  
i Be.: Sirmii.  
j Go.–Ri. add the year 329—“in the consulship of Constantine Augustus VIII and Constantius Caesar IV,” or, according to Vesmius, “and Constantius Caesar II”—although Go. in the Prosopography, under Felix, assigns this law to 328. Be. assigns it to 326, “Constantine Augustus VII and Constantius Caesar,” but chronology opposes this, since Constantine had moved from Sirmium to Italy before 11 Kalends of August. Manso, *The Life of Constantine the Great*, differing little from He., seeks consuls who had held the consulship before 329; thus, considering the order of constitutions, either the consuls of 326 or those of 328. I do not see what prevents restoration of the year 329, omitted by Be. Aur. Lugd. Cons.]

[Col. 0337B] Constantine Augustus to Bassus, Praetorian Prefect. It has been decided that, after the completion of the twenty-fifth year, from the day on which the twenty-sixth year begins, the periods for lodging a contestation shall be extended: in the city of Rome, as far as the hundredth milestone from Rome, until the last day of the thirtieth year, provided that the case is to be judged by judges sitting at Rome; throughout all Italy, until the end of the twenty-ninth year; and in all other provinces, until the completion of the twenty-eighth year. When that period has passed, let all plainly know that thereafter the safeguards of the laws are denied them, since, after removing the necessity of a contestation, we have enclosed actions for restitutio in integrum and causes to be decided within a fixed scheme.

§ 1. The same calculation of time should also be observed if anyone has obtained from our favour a dispensation from age: from the day on which our indulgence has been announced in the competent court and administration of his own property has been opened to him, he shall have the prescribed continuous period in which to pursue restitutions in full and bring his cases to conclusion.

§ 2. If a minor should at any time succeed to the rights of a minor, he shall not be prohibited, when he has passed the twenty-fifth year of his age, from using the benefit of restitutio in integrum, with the period unimpaired.

§ 3. But if a minor has acquired the rights of a person of full age, then, with respect to those actions which he has obtained through the person of that adult, he must receive for bringing forward restitutions in full and deciding cases as much time as remained to the deceased whose heir or possessor of goods he is shown to have been.

§ 4. But when an adult has acquired the succession of a minor, if he succeeds by civil law, whether intestate or under a will, then, as soon as the inheritance has been entered upon or accepted; but if by praetorian law, then from the time at which possession of the goods has been accepted: upon examining the matter of restitutio in integrum, the full periods, without any diminution, shall be reckoned. We order that these periods be observed not according to the places, districts, and provinces in which the heirs or possessors of goods reside, but according to those in which the deceased had established their domiciles. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, at Naissus; posted at Rome on the Nones of October, in the consulship of Constantine Caesar [the consular formula is corrupt] (329).

### INTERPRETATION

It seems just that, after the twenty-fifth year, when the twenty-sixth year has begun, a person who wishes to have restored to him, sound and whole, on account of the weakness of his age, those things which were wrongly done during his minority, either by himself or through guardians or curators, should seek this by lodging a contestation before the judge. Only in these provinces, if he has lodged his contestation before the twenty-eighth year, the things which he had wrongly lost shall be restored to him intact, without prejudice to the principal action.

For a person who believes that he must petition Our Serenity for a dispensation from age should know that this is granted him: without prejudice to our indulgence, which is comprehended in the following law, he shall have freedom until the period fixed above to have restored to his ownership the property which he had wrongly dealt with. But if a minor should perhaps succeed to the inheritance of one who himself died in minority, he must not be prohibited, when he reaches the twenty-sixth year, from seeking by a lodged contestation recovery in respect of matters which were available to that person. But if a minor receives the inheritance of one who died in full and complete age, then, once he has been restored in full, he shall pursue in his affairs the periods which were available by law to the deceased adult.

But when an adult succeeds to a minor, either by will or by whatever right, as soon as the inheritance of the deceased comes to him, whatever could have belonged to the ward for restitution in full shall pass into that person’s action; so that he shall follow the forum of that province in which the deceased minor is known to have resided.

Constantine Augustus to the Council of the Province of Africa. [The beginning is missing.] … has appealed in the principal case, which is neither new nor foreign to judicial proceedings. Therefore, after the principal matter has been heard, a litigant shall be permitted to obtain relief for his case through the remedy of law; and judges must take care not to send appellants to prison or have them guarded by soldiers. Posted on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, at Carthage, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the eighth time and Constantine Caesar for the fourth time (329).

### INTERPRETATION

This law commands that provincial judges ought not to take against themselves the assertions of appellants, because this is known to be neither new nor foreign to judicial proceedings. It therefore commands that a litigant be permitted to obtain relief for a flawed case through the remedy of appeal. It also specially orders that an appellant be sent neither to prison nor into any form of custody, but that he remain free while attending to his case.

## CONCERNING THOSE WHO HAVE ACCEPTED BLOOD-RELATIVES BOUGHT OR TO BE REARED

[Note: Col. 0341D p Ms. 15: emptos susceperunt, omitting vel nutriendos. Many manuscripts have emptis vel nutriendis, or one alternative or the other. Some also have acceperunt. Ms. 37: susceperint. Ms. 8 omits His, Qui; Mss. 6, 7, 16: His; Ms. 2: Emptos.  
q Another law of Constantine on the same subject, addressed to Provincials but lacking a subscription, is contained in c. 2 Codex Justinianus, *On Fathers Who Have Sold Their Children* (IV.43), which W. does not doubt was formerly in this place in the Theodosian Code itself, but was omitted by the Visigoths. Also relevant is Constantine’s rescript, Vatican Fragments §34, expressed in these words: “Augustus and Caesar to Flavia Aprilla. Since you declare that you have purchased for a specified sum a slave from among blood-relatives, whose price you say you paid and established by documents: we formerly prescribed that, if he should wish to recover his lawful free person, then he should give a slave to the owner in his place or pay the amount for which he was worth. Even now, if you purchased him from his parents for a fixed price, you are considered to possess the right of ownership. Yet no person from among gentiles may be proved free.” Subscribed on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus (313). Zimmern, cited work, vol. I, p. 670.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to his Italians. In accordance with the enactments of earlier emperors, if anyone has lawfully purchased an infant from among blood-relatives, in whatever manner, or has undertaken to rear him, he shall have the power to retain his service; provided that, if anyone after a succession of years claims him again for freedom or asserts that he is a slave, he shall provide another person of the same kind or pay the price that he may be worth. For one who has paid the proper price after drawing up an instrument ought to possess [him] securely, so that he also has unrestricted power to sell [him] for his own debt; and those who attempt to act against this law shall be subject to punishment. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, at Serdica, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the eighth time and Constantine Caesar for the fourth time (329).

[Col. 0343A] **INTERPRETATION.** If anyone has purchased an infant *a sanguine* (“from the blood [of birth]”) and reared him, he shall have unrestricted authority to keep and possess him. Certainly, if the master or father of the person reared should wish to reclaim him, he shall either give the foster-parent a slave of equal value, or the foster-parent shall receive the price for which the person reared is valued.

If persons nominated to a magistracy have fled, they shall be sought out; and, if it becomes clear that they are hiding with obstinate purpose, their property shall be granted to those who at the present time were being called in their place to the duties of the duumvirate. The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Bassus, D. U. Governors shall subscribe petitions not through assessors but personally. If any governor permits an assessor to subscribe without our knowledge, the assessor who subscribed shall immediately be punished with exile; and we order that the governor’s name be reported to us, so that punishment may be exacted from him more severely. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the sixth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the consulship of Constantine Caesar, 329.  
[Col. 0344B] *(From the Code of Justinian.)*

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Januarius. It is our pleasure that slaves possessing different crafts, who belong to the state, remain in those same cities. If anyone entices such a slave away, or thinks that he should be removed, he shall restore him together with another slave and pay twelve solidi to the municipality of the city whose slave he has taken away. Freedmen who are craftsmen likewise, if they have been enticed away, shall be returned to the municipality under the same arrangement. Thus, if a fugitive slave has not been sought out and recalled through the diligence of the *defensor*, that same *defensor* shall be required to provide two substitute slaves; and henceforth neither imperial favour nor sale shall have force in the case of such a person. Given on the twenty-first day before the Kalends of March, in the fifth consulship of Constantine Augustus and Licinius. [Col. 0344C] *(From the Code of Justinian.)*

In the year of the Lord 330, in the consulship of Gallicanus and Symmachus.

## CONCERNING BISHOPS

Constantine Augustus to Valentinus, consular governor of Numidia. Readers of the sacred writings, subdeacons, and the remaining clerics who have been summoned to the curia through the wrongdoing of heretics shall be released; and henceforth, after the pattern of the East, they shall by no means be summoned to curiae, but shall enjoy the fullest immunity. Given on the Nones of February at Serdica, in the consulship of Gallicanus and Symmachus (330).

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Tertullianus, *vir perfectissimus*, Count of the Diocese of Asia.

If anyone first lodges a complaint concerning places belonging to his own legal right which have been invaded, and that complaint is connected with a dispute over boundaries and ownership, the question of possession shall first be settled; then a land-surveyor shall be ordered to go to the places, so that, once the truth has been disclosed, litigation of this kind may be terminated.

But if the other party, having obtained dominion over the places, causes delays by evasion so that the controversy cannot be decided in the prescribed order concerning the places, a chosen land-surveyor shall be sent to the places. If a reliable inspection proves that the holder possesses the place, the claimant shall withdraw defeated; but if the claim of the person who first brought the case is established, that invader shall be subject to the penalty prescribed by the edict, provided it is established that he invaded those same places by force. For if places given up through the owner’s error or negligence have been occupied by others, they must yield to those owners alone. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of March at Verona, in the consulship of Gallicanus and Symmachus (330).

## CONCERNING BETROTHALS

Constantine Augustus to Valerianus, acting vice-prefect.

> [Col. 0346C] g Justinian Code: “The Emperor Constantine Augustus.”  
> [Col. 0346C] h MS 19: “to the vice-prefect”; MS 20: “vice-prefect”; the Pistoriensis, Casinensis, Vaticanus, Pluteus 2, Bg., Hal., and Russ. manuscripts: “to Valerianus, vice-prefect”; Pluteus 1 and the Nuremberg edition omit the office.

Although the law is not ordinarily accustomed to assist women ignorant of their legal rights in matters of gain, earlier enactments of the emperors declare that this rule has no place against age which is still imperfect. Therefore, lest anything inhumane be established after marital affection has been dissolved, we rule that, if property has been given and delivered at the time of marriage to persons below age who are to become spouses, it cannot for that reason be revoked because the husband at that time did not wish to record the gift in official documents. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Gallicanus and Symmachus (330).

## CONCERNING AQUEDUCTS

> [Col. 0347B] d Many manuscripts: *Concerning an Aqueduct*.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximilianus, Consular of the Waters.

> [Col. 0347B] e Cujas 2 and 2* wrongly read “the Emperors Constantine Augustus.”  
> [Col. 0347B] f Compare above IX.12.2, note r. Here too the manuscripts of the Theodosian Code agree with the Justinian Code.  
> [Col. 0347B] g MS 3 reads “consular of the owners of waters,” and MS 4 “consul of the owners of waters”; therefore both manuscripts do not distinguish the words. The editions have “Consular of the Waters. Owners,” etc., and so does the Justinian Code. Rein. wrongly adds “Picenianus” in his chronological list of constitutions of Cujas 2, under 330, from inscriptions published on p. 471, no. 8; but correctly, in the same chronology and on this law, he draws *Aquarum*, “of the Waters,” which in the editions is the first word of the law, back into the address: “To Maximilianus, Consular of the Waters. Owners,” etc. He agrees here with Go. (see the commentary on chapter 1, Theodosian Code, *Concerning Vacant Property*, X.8, Ri. edition, vol. III, p. 447, and the commentary on this constitution), whose words it is not useless to repeat here:
>
> “This law is addressed to the Consular of the Waters. For the word *Aquarum*, ‘of the Waters’—as Pancirolus also correctly indicated in his discussion of the Consular of the Waters in the *Notitia*, folio 122—must be drawn back into the address, and one should read: ‘To Maximilianus, Consular of the Waters.’ Then the law begins with the word ‘Owners.’ For no private persons are owners of public aqueducts; rather, as is immediately stated, the water-channel runs across the boundaries of owners’ estates. Therefore, out of fear of this point, the Interpreters absurdly interpret ‘owners of waters’ here as owners of estates through which water flows. And indeed, both the complete law and specifically the words at its end, ‘your office observing,’ show that Maximilianus, to whom this law is addressed, was Consular of the Waters. Another law of this Code, law 1 above, *Concerning Various Offices* (VIII.7), was likewise addressed to a Consular of the Waters—given in 315 by the same Constantine the Great to Versennius Fortunatus, Consular of the Waters—and there too mention is made of the office of the Consular of the Waters. The *Notitia Imperii* also mentions the Consular of the Waters, folio 118 (*Notitia Imperii Occidentalis*, chapter IV, ‘Under the disposition of the most illustrious Prefect of the City of Rome: the Consular of the Waters,’ Böcking edition, p. 16, no. 9). Indeed, two inscriptions concerning a Consular of the Waters survive in Gruter, LIV.6 and CCCCLIX.7. We note several similar instances of words of a law being drawn back into its heading under their own heading in the Prolegomena; meanwhile see law 1 above, *Concerning Vacant Property* (X.8), and also above I.7.4, note *; I.14.2, note r, and elsewhere. Therefore, there was a Consular of the Waters at Constantinople in this period. At Rome, however, Curators had long since been in charge; concerning them see Frontinus, *On Aqueducts*, chapter 97, pp. 170 ff. of Poleni’s edition, where he enumerates all Curators down to his own time.”
>
> Nothing prevented us, following Go., from printing: “To Maximilianus, Consular of the Waters. Owners,” etc.

Owners through whose estates the channels of the conduits pass shall be exempt from extraordinary burdens, so that, by their labour, watercourses choked with filth may be cleaned; and no additional burden in another matter shall be imposed upon those same owners, lest, occupied with other affairs, they fail to carry out the cleansing of the channels. If they are negligent, they shall be punished by loss of their estates. For the fisc shall obtain the estate of the person through whose negligence ruin has accumulated for the channel. Furthermore, those through whose lands the conduit passes must know that they may have trees, provided that fifteen feet are left clear on the right and left of the channels themselves. Your office shall see to it that, whenever they sprout, they are cut down, lest their roots damage the structure of the channel. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Gallicanus and Symmachus (330).

## SETTLEMENT OF BOUNDARIES

The same Augustus to Bassus, Prefect of the Praetorium.

> [Col. 0348C] j Sichard, Til., and Be. read “The Emperor Constantine Augustus,” from Breviary and Alaric manuscripts and their copies. The reading has been corrected, as Go. already suspected in his chronology under 330, on the authority of MSS 9, 14, 15, 17, 19, 20, 27, 32, 38–40, 43, 44, and 50, with which several constitutions of the preceding and following year agree, bearing the address “Bassus, Prefect of the Praetorium.” The remaining manuscripts and editions read “Prefect of the City,” first printed by Go., because Bassus is not found as prefect of the city in this year, but Petronius Probianus is. This induced Go. to think that the subscription should be changed to “Gallicanus and Bassus, consuls,” that is, the year 317, when Bassus was prefect of the city—contrary to the authority of all manuscripts and the order of the laws. This would make the present constitution the first constitution under this title, as W. has already observed.

If it is established that a person who has brought a boundary dispute wished, before anything had been determined by judgment, to usurp for himself something belonging to another, he shall lose not only what he was improperly claiming, but also—so that everyone may be more content with his own property and not seek property belonging to another—he who has been defeated in litigation as an intruder upon lands shall lose as much land as he attempted to seize. Read into the official records on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Gallicanus and Symmachus (330).
