In Cuj. 1–Lugd., an asterisk follows “The same Augustus.”] If, after the claim and defence have been arranged, another asks to be brought into court, [Note: [Col. 0369C] f Go.: *adsciri*, i.e. “to be admitted.” But in his commentary he proposes *adsciri* or *adscisci*.] the claim and defence shall indeed be arranged among all parties; but he himself shall be compelled to pay into the fisc as many slaves as he claimed. If the claimant fails, he shall either acknowledge the aforesaid fine or, if poverty prevents him from paying it, be sent to the mines. The same rule is to be observed concerning defenders of minors when a case of free status is being tried, etc. Given on the seventh [Note: [Col. 0369C] g Either read third, as in cited C. Th. V, 9, c. 1, or seventh there, which is preferred. See its note n. According to Go.’s chronology for this year: “elsewhere, Given on the third.”] day before the Kalends of November, at Constantinople, [Note: [Col. 0369C] h Cuj. 1–Be.: *CP.* W.: *Constantinop.*] in the consulship of Pacatianus and Hilarianus (332).

### INTERPRETATION

[Col. 0369B] If, after the claim and defence have been arranged, another person, claiming to be the owner, asks that the person be produced in court, the claim shall indeed be arranged among all parties, but he himself shall be liable to a fixed penalty. The same applies to the claimant and to defenders of minors.

## CONCERNING FUGITIVE COLONI, INQUILINES, AND SLAVES

[Note: [Col. 0369C–D] i 15 omits “and slaves.” In the rubric of the index in Sich. and Til., “inquilines and slaves” is omitted. Some manuscripts read “and slaves,” “slaves and servants,” or “slaves or servants.” A passage in L. R. B., from which it appears that this title was truncated by the Visigoths, reads: “But if anyone knowingly fails to present to the judges a slave or colonus belonging to another, residing in his house or on his estate, at least within our territory; or, having been warned by the owner of the fugitive, neglects to surrender him, he shall incur the fine for harbouring him, AS IT IS LAID DOWN IN THE LAST LAW OF THE THEODOSIAN CODE: CONCERNING FUGITIVE COLONI, INQUILINES, AND SLAVES, GIVEN TO FLORENTIUS, COUNT OF THE SACRED LARGESSES.” We seek that law here in vain. The first mention of this passage occurs in the margin of Aur. Lugd. at c. 2 under this title. See below, note p. Go., followed by Ri., makes it the last constitution of this title, adding the heading: “Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian Augustus to Florentius, Count of the Sacred Largesses.” W.’s notes correctly state that this was done without warrant, since no definite place can be assigned to this law, although Florentius, Count of the Sacred Largesses, is mentioned in the years 364–366 and 385; consequently this law seems to be inserted between cc. 1 and 2 under this title. Go. wishes to connect it with Code of Justinian XI, 67, c. 4.]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Provincials. [Note: [Col. 0369D] j Sich., Cuj. 1–Cuj. 2*: Constantine. In several manuscripts “to the Provincials” is omitted.] Wherever a colonus belonging by law to another is found, the person with whom he is found shall not only restore him to his origin, but shall also acknowledge the capitation-tax for the period in question. [Note: [Col. 0369D] k 6–8, 10, 18: *eosdem*, plural. In 21: “himself to his origin, and shall acknowledge capitation-tax concerning them.” Sich. subsequently: *captationem*, incorrectly; Ri. similarly. l 6, 7, 10, 12–14, 16, 17, 21: *agnoscant*, plural. 18: *agnoscunt*. 6, 7 also have “concerning them.”]

[Col. 0370A] § 1. The coloni themselves who contemplate flight [Note: [Col. 0370C] a Go. conjectures *meditabantur*, “were contemplating.”] shall also appropriately be bound in iron into a servile condition, [Note: [Col. 0370C] b 10, 18 omit *in*. 19, 20: “in servile condition.” c W. silently corrected *conveniet* to *convenit*; 10, 18 have the latter, but all other manuscripts and Sich.–Be. have *conveniet*, which has been restored. 20 subsequently: “and office . . . deserved.”] so that, by the deserved sentence of slavery, they may be compelled to perform the services appropriate to free persons. [Note: [Col. 0370C] d Sich.: *cogantur*, “may be compelled,” but in the margin *compellantur*. 9, 29: *compellatur*, singular.] Given on the third [Note: [Col. 0370C–D] e 21, Sich., Cuj. 1–Lugd.: sixth, but third in the margin. 35 and other manuscripts: seventh, correctly, as in cited c. 8; this does not differ much from manuscript 21 and the Sich.–Lugd. edition. 9: “third Ides.”] day before the Kalends of November, [Note: [Col. 0370D] f Add “at Constantinople.” See cited C. Th. c. 8.] in the consulship of Pacatianus [Note: [Col. 0370D] g Some manuscripts corruptly have Pagatianus, Pacatius or Pacacius, Patianus, Pecationus, Pascianus; others subsequently “and the treasury.” 8 omits “Pacatianus and.”] and Hilarianus (332).

### INTERPRETATION

If anyone knowingly keeps another’s colonus in his house, he shall first restore the man himself to his owner and be compelled to pay his taxes for as long as he was with him. But the colonus himself, who refused [Note: [Col. 0370D] h Some manuscripts: “into his house . . . refused,” and subsequently “into slavery.” Sich., Cuj. 1–Lugd. and some manuscripts: *noluerit*, “shall have refused.”] to remain what he was born, shall be reduced to slavery.

## CONCERNING FUGITIVE SLAVES AND FREEDMEN

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Tyberianus, Count of the Spains. When someone claims a fugitive slave and another, in order to evade the law that imposes a specified penalty upon those concealing slaves, sets up ownership as an objection or encourages him to assert freedom, the utterly worthless fellow concerning whom the dispute exists shall immediately be subjected to torture, so that, once the truth has been made clear, the dispute may be ended. This will benefit not only both litigants but may also deter slaves from flight. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Pacatianus and Hilarianus, 332. (From the Code of Justinian.)

## CONCERNING CODICILS

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect. If codicils could do what wills could, why should a different name be assigned to these instruments when one and the same force and authority united them? Therefore, the authority to institute heirs and substitutes by codicils has not been granted by legal authority. Given on 3 June, in the consulship of Pacatianus and Hilarianus, 332. (From the Code of Justinian.)

In the year of the Lord 333, in the consulship of Dalmatius and Zenophilus.

[Col. 0370C]

## CONCERNING THE ADMINISTRATION AND LIABILITY OF TUTORS AND CURATORS
Imp. Constantine Augustus to Felix.

[Note: [Col. 0370D] i Here too, and in what follows, many passages have been cut out in codex 1; since P. has supplied them from Ritter’s edition, I refrain from indicating them. Some manuscripts address Felix, whom Go. in note b thinks was Praetorian Prefect, but in the Chronology of the Constitutions, at this year, [he regards him as] Proconsul of Africa.]

Since, through the negligence or betrayal of guardians and curators, possessions held by emphyteutic right, through the fault of a forfeiture having intervened, are removed from the fortunes of minors, it is our pleasure that a guardian or curator who, while his office continues, has lost through an offence entailing forfeiture the prerogative of a minor’s possession held by emphyteutic right, shall restore to the minors, from his own property and under threat of official coercion, as much as the property is shown to have been worth.

[Note: [Col. 0370D] j 8 “Because.” Immediately afterward, some manuscripts read “negligence.”]

[Note: [Col. 0370D] k 10, 18 “to betray.”]

[Note: [Col. 0370D] l Pu. *possesiones suris*, erroneously. Aur. Lugd.: *possessionis juris* (“of a possession by right”).]

[Note: [Col. 0370D] m Here and a little later 1 has *enfateutici*; P. *enfileutici*; [Col. 0371B] Sich. *emphiteutici*. Cuj. 1—Lugd.: *emphit.*, as also shortly afterward W.]

[Col. 0371A] e

[Note: [Col. 0371B] a 19 “and.”]

[Note: [Col. 0371B] b 1 *cujusq.*; first edition of W. *cujusque*, although the reading *cujusque* does not disturb the sense of the law. [Col. 0371C]]

[Note: [Col. 0371C] c 1 “by possession.” 15 omits “possession.” In codex 21 a second hand puts *traditiones* (“deliveries”) in place of *possessio*.]

[Note: [Col. 0371C] d Pu., in the note, *praerogativam*, erroneously.]

[Note: [Col. 0371C] e 1 “…diderint”; 9 *perdiderint*. 19 has *praerogativa—perdiderint*. W. observed that this plural does not suit the passage; nevertheless it does suit if one reads “possessions—have lost,” just as at the beginning of the law it says “possessions—are removed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0371C] f Thus 1, 6, 7, 14, 16, 17, Til., P., Pu., W., the editions, Sich., Cuj. 1—Be.; *quantum* (“as much as”).]

[Note: [Col. 0371C] g 1, 14: *constavit*. The entire constitution is so corrupted in the Code of Justinian:

“If through the fault or fraud of a guardian or curator, because they had been unwilling to pay the rent imposed upon an emphyteutic estate, the estate of a minor has been lost, the damage that befell him must be made good from their substance.”]

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May,

[Note: [Col. 0371C] h 15, 24, 29, 40, Sich. in the margin, and Code of Justinian: the thirteenth; 28, 30, 33, 34: the fourth.]

at Constantinople,

[Note: [Col. 0371D] i 10, 18: March; 24, 39, 43: March; 8 omits “Constantinople, Dalmatius and.”]

in the consulship of Dalmatius and Zenophilus.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] j 6, 7: *Zenopilo*; 10, 18, 42: *Zenofilio*; 14, 15: *Zenofilo*; 38: *Zemopilo*; 1, 38, P.: *Genofilo*, although P. in the note has *Zenophilo*; 40, Sich. in the margin: *Azemopilo*; Code of Justinian: *Xenophilo*; Pu.: *Genophilo*.]

(333).

## INTERPRETATION

If it should happen that minors hold, subject to any payment, a possession held by emphyteutic right,

[Note: [Col. 0371D] k Cuj. 1—Lugd.: *emphiteutici*; Sich.: *enphit.*]

that is, one which their parents had deserved to hold from the property of the fisc, and this has either been diminished or certainly taken away through the negligence or betrayal

[Note: [Col. 0371D] l 6: *proditione*.]

of a guardian

[Note: [Col. 0371D] m 42 adds between the lines: “or procurator.”]

or curator,

[Note: [Col. 0371D] n 42 adds above the line: “or procurator.”]

whatever has perished must be restored by the guardian or curator.

## ON GIFTS

[Col. 0371B]

Imp. Constantine Augustus to Severus, Count of the Spains. By a law issued long ago we established

[Note: [Col. 0371D] o Go.: “By a law,” a typographical error. Go. doubts whether chapter 1 or chapter 3 of this title is intended, though he thinks the latter is more likely. I think chapter 1 is meant: being earlier, it is the one to which the emperor himself refers in chapter 3 of this title.]

that gifts must be declared by the attestation of official records.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] p Compare Dirksen, cited passage, p. 483.]

This ought especially to be observed among persons joined by the closest and most necessary ties,

[Note: [Col. 0371D] q Code of Justinian: *conjunctasque* (“and united”).]

since through clandestine and domestic frauds anything whatever can easily be fabricated to suit the occasion of the transaction, or what was truly done can be obliterated. Therefore, since our law does not exclude even children and parents from the drawing up of official records,

[Note: [Col. 0371D] r Code of Justinian: “nor.”]

the provision which we necessarily established long ago concerning gifts to be made in the records shall bind all persons,

[Note: [Col. 0371D] s What follows is lacking in the Code of Justinian; in its place the final part of chapter 8 [Col. 0372B] of this title has been transferred there: “But records concerning things transferred even elsewhere may be drawn up wherever this suffices.”]

[Col. 0372A] while preserving, nevertheless, the privilege of law which supports children and parents: namely, that the formality of delivery or mancipation

[Note: [Col. 0372B] a Cuj. 1, Cuj. 2, 2*: *mancipantionis*.]

need not be required. Given on the fourth

[Note: [Col. 0372B] b Code of Justinian: the third; first edition of Ri.: the third.]

day before the Nones of May, at Constantinople,

[Note: [Col. 0372B] c In the Code of Justinian, “Constantinople” is omitted.]

in the consulship of Dalmatius and Zenophilus.

[Note: [Col. 0372B] d Codex, Cuj. 1, Ri.*: *Zenophilo*.]

(333).

## ON THE CREDIBILITY OF WITNESSES AND DOCUMENTS

Imp. Constantine Augustus

[Note: [Col. 0372B] e 7, 14, 20, 38, 42, 43: *Constantinus*. Most Br. and other manuscripts: *Constant.* or *Const.*]

and Caesar

[Note: [Col. 0372B] f 6—8, 10, 16, 18, 20, 21, 37, 43 omit “and Caesar,” as in chapter 5 of C. Th. *On Gifts*, cited above. Further evidence is supplied by chapter 3 of this title, which is addressed to Constantine alone both in the Theodosian Code and the Code of Justinian. 33 and the corrected Sich.: “Emperor Constantine Augustus and Caesar.” [Col. 0372C] Be.: “Caesars,” from the Code of Justinian, at Ri.’s instruction, who notes: “Rather, CC., that is, Constantine the younger and Constantius. For Constans was made Caesar only at the end of this year.” Yet in the common editions of the Code of Justinian one reads “the same Augusti and Caesars,” that is, Diocletian and Maximian, first edition of Go. This wording passed from the Theodosian Code into the Code of Justinian. The compilers of the Code of Justinian did not notice that the emperor’s name ought to be restored, since this was Constantine’s first law. Be. corrected both heading and subscription in the Code of Justinian from the Theodosian Code.]

to Severus, Count

[Note: [Col. 0372C] g 15: “to Severus, Count.” Some manuscripts: “of the Spains,” “of Spain”; 36 omits “Spain.”]

of the Spains. Different documents and

[Note: [Col. 0372C] h The Code of Justinian omits “and.” Go. asks whether “and” should be taken as “or”; he explains it, together with what follows, as “different.”]

mutually undermining one another’s credibility, when produced by one party,

[Note: [Col. 0372C] i Code of Justinian: “produced by one and the same party.” 8: *probatoe*; 32 begins *nullus f.*]

could have no validity.

[Note: [Col. 0372C] j 6—8, 10, 13, 14, 16—18: “can”; 21, 32, Sich., Code of Justinian: “will be able to.”]

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of May,

[Note: [Col. 0372D] k 9, 29, 42: January; 16, 28: March; 30, 50: “Given on the third.”]

at Constantinople,

[Note: [Col. 0372D] l 8 omits “Constantinople—consuls,” and 20 omits “Constantinople.”]

in the consulship of Dalmatius

[Note: [Col. 0372D] m Many manuscripts: *Dalmacio*; 38: *almatio*; 40: *Dalfagio*.]

and Zenophilus.

[Note: [Col. 0372D] n 4 and nearly all Br. and other manuscripts, and editions before Be.: *Zenofilo*; 28, 36, 40: *anelofilo*; Sich. in the margin: *Anelophilo*; 21: *Zonofilo*; 38: *genofilo*; 42: *Zynofilo*.]

[Note: [Col. 0372D] o The common editions of the Code of Justinian have, incorrectly: “Given on the Kalends of May at Viminacium, in the consulship of the Caesars.” At Go.’s suggestion, Be. restored in place of this subscription the true subscription of the Theodosian Code.]

(333).

## INTERPRETATION

If anyone, wishing to secure

[Note: [Col. 0372D] p 6—8 and other manuscripts: “to remain secure by a multiple document”; 10, 18: “multiple documents”; 9: “against the transaction”; 21, Sich.: “to remain secure.” Many manuscripts: “to be secured.”]

his contract by multiple documents, produces concerning one matter a sale and a gift, or whatever other instruments, [Col. 0372B] all shall be annulled,

[Note: [Col. 0372D] q 6, 7: “whoever—are annulled”; 21: “are annulled.”]

because this law forbids documents which attack

[Note: [Col. 0372D] r 20 adds above the line: “assailing.”]

one another from being admitted.

## ON FINANCIAL CLERKS AND ACTUARIES

Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect. Urged by utility, we have ordered that annona officials and actuaries shall be attached to a permanent service,

[Col. 0373A]

[Note: [Col. 0373C] a Thus Go. from the codex; the rest: “we order.”]

that they shall also be assisted with grain allowances,

[Note: [Col. 0373C] b Go., incorrectly: *adjuvari* (“be assisted”).]

and that the poll-tax of those who are registered

[Note: [Col. 0373C] c Codex and editions before Be.: *censeti*. The same occurs a little below. Be., following Go., corrected it to *censiti*.]

shall be held exempt. Therefore your diligence shall instruct

[Note: [Col. 0373C] d Cuj. 1: *amonebit*; Cuj. 2, 2*: *amonebit*, through an error caused by the preceding letter *a*. Aur. Lugd.: *admonebit*. Go. restored *monebit* from the codex; Ri., Ri.*, and Be. adopted it.]

the appropriate offices to furnish immediately two annona allowances to actuaries and one to annona officials, and shall ensure that the poll-tax is held exempt only for those among them who are registered,

[Note: [Col. 0373C] e Do not conjecture *faciant* (“they shall ensure”).]

so long as they remain in active service; for afterward either merit and rank will honour them, or, if they are found guilty, punishment will attend them. Issued on the third day before the Nones of May, in the consulship of Dalmatius and Zenophilus.

[Note: [Col. 0373C] f Codex, Cuj. 1—Lugd.: *Zenofilo*.]

(333).

## ON PHYSICIANS AND TEACHERS

Imp. Constantine Augustus to the People. Confirming the benefits granted by the former deified emperors, we order that physicians and teachers of letters, together with their wives and children, shall be free from every public function and all public burdens; that they shall neither be enrolled for military service, receive guests, nor perform any office, so that they may more easily train many persons in the liberal studies and the aforementioned arts. Published on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Dalmatius and Zenophilus.

[Note: [Col. 0373C] g 4: *Zenofilio*; Aur. Lugd.: “consuls.”]

(333).

## ON VARIOUS RESCRIPTS

Imp. Constantine to Barbarus P. A.

[Note: [Col. 0373C] h Ri*: *Rarbarum*, incorrectly. The Code of Justinian omits “Barbarus.” [Col. 0373D] 25 omits “Pompeianus,” for which a manuscript of the Code of Justinian, Pl. 1, Montpellier H. 82, and the Nuremberg edition read “Pontianus.”]

Pompeianus, consular governor

[Note: [Col. 0373D] i 6: *pc.*; Til. in the margin: *Proc.*; 9, 10: “prefect”; 18: *pfectum*; 27, 48 omit “consular of Campania”; 9: *Campanioe aug.*]

of Campania. Although not judicial investigation but execution is commanded,

[Note: [Col. 0373D] j 19, interlinear note: “excusing oneself.”]

the truth of petitions must nevertheless be investigated, so that, if fraud has intervened,

[Note: [Col. 0373D] k W., with the Code of Justinian: “has intervened”; the other editions and most manuscripts: “intervenes.” 5: “and—intervenes.”]

the whole case may be investigated. Given on the third

[Note: [Col. 0373D] l 33: the fourth. Some manuscripts: “Kalends.”]

day before the Ides of November, at Aquis

[Note: [Col. 0373D] m On *Aquis*, see Go., *Chronology*, p. XXIII and at this place, note k, where he conjectures *Apris*, though without rejecting the common reading. Hal. and Russ. omit “Aquis.”]

in the consulship of Dalmatius and Zenophilus,

[Note: [Col. 0373D] n 8: *Genesio*; 19: *signafilo*; the remaining manuscripts: *Zenofilo, Genofilo, Genofilio, Genofalo, Jenufico*. Sich.: *Signophilo*; 20: *Signofilo*, and after the Interpretation repeats the consuls’ names, incorrectly writing *Zenonifilio*.]

most distinguished consuls.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] o Most manuscripts and the Code of Justinian omit “most distinguished men” (*VV. CC.*), but 28, 37, 40, 41 have “and—consuls.”]

(333).

## INTERPRETATION

Whatever a false, rather than a true, petition has obtained from the Emperor shall not be valid, because fraud has intervened.

## ON THE SONS OF SOLDIERS

[Col. 0373C]

Imp. Constantine Augustus to Ablavius, Praetorian Prefect. The sons of veterans, or of those who have been commanders or protectores, or who have held any other grade of military service, if they are infirm and weak, wherever they may be, are to be enrolled in the curiae, [Col. 0374A] so that those enjoying family property and unfit

[Note: [Col. 0374C] a It is clear that *re* is to be written, as Go. and Be. wished.]

[Note: [Col. 0374C] b Codex, Cuj. 1—Ri.*: *inaptos*. Above, the codex has *et* after *filii*, but corrected to *vel*; and *imbecillis*.]

for military service shall be joined to the association of the curiae. We have ourselves also done this in our presence to those whom we perceived to have been enervated by luxurious rearing. Therefore, those among them who are heads of households and fit for public duties shall be selected

[Note: [Col. 0374C] c Codex: *patrisfamilias s. et indoneis*. Aur. Lugd.: *eligatur*, incorrectly.]

to increase the number of curiales.

[Note: [Col. 0374D] d Cuj. 1; Aur. Lugd., incorrectly: *munerum* (“of duties”).]

The councils of individual cities are to be admonished

[Note: [Col. 0374D] e Thus Go.—Be., which seems more suitable to me than *commovendis*, the reading of the codex and Cuj. 1—Cuj. 2*. Compare, among other passages, chapter 13 *On Veterans* (VII.20). Below the codex has *defendende—sungolorum*, but the scribe corrected it to *singulorum*.]

not to hesitate to name those whom they know to be suitable, except those whom vigour and strength make fit for the defence of the state. For we have also instructed the commanders of the several frontiers that henceforth no useless son of a veteran shall be bound by military oath. They shall carefully inspect those who have already been approved as well, so that those found less fit

[Note: [Col. 0374D] f Cuj. 2, 2*: *idoni*, incorrectly. Here begins leaf LXXIX of the codex.]

may be released from the oath and sent to Your Gravity. Given and published on the Ides of November, in the consulship of Dalmatius and Zenophilus.

[Note: [Col. 0374D] g Codex, Cuj. 1—Ri.*: *Zenofilo*.]

[Col. 0374B] (333).

## ON APPEALS AND CONSULTATIONS

Imp. Constantine Augustus to Albinus. In both greater and lesser matters there is a right of appeal. A judge ought not to consider that an injury has been done to him because a litigant has fled for aid to an appeal. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Marcellinus and Probinus. Given on the Kalends of August; published on the Kalends of September; in the consulship of Constantine, Bassus, and Balbinus, 333. (From the Code of Justinian.)

In the year of the Lord 334, in the consulship of Optatus and Paulinus.

## ON SWINE-SUPPLIERS, CATTLE-SUPPLIERS, WINE-RECEIVERS, AND OTHER CORPORATE BODIES

[Note: [Col. 0374D] h The Code of Justinian omits “cattle-suppliers,” and then reads “and the rest.” Aur. Lugd.: *Suaris*.]

Imp. Constantine Augustus to Pacatianus, Praetorian Prefect. Since the corporation of swine-suppliers has been reduced to a few, we order them, in the presence of the Roman people, to state to whom exemption has been granted and upon whom the burden has fallen, so that, once this has been publicly made known for the public account,

[Col. 0374C]

[Note: [Col. 0374D] i Thus 4 and the editions; and, though P. is silent, codex 1. Go.: “and led out.” Be. prefers “led out.” “Made known” can be maintained; earlier there is “to state.”]

the example of the shipping corporation may be set before them. Accordingly, let them recognize that the private property of swine-suppliers is liable for the duty, and let them choose one of two alternatives: either they shall retain the property bound to the swine-supplying function and themselves remain obligated to swine-supplying service, or they shall nominate suitable persons whom they wish, who shall likewise satisfy the obligation.

[Note: [Col. 0374D] j 4 and the editions: *idem*; and much more corruptly 1: *idest*, unless *idem* was written there. Rep.: *iidem*. Go. proposes *iidem* or *eidem*; Be.: *iidem* or *item*. Our reading comes very close to…]

For we permit no one to be exempt from the burden of this function. But whether they have escaped by advancement to honours or through any kind of evasion, we order that they be recalled, and that this very matter be carried out with the Roman people as witness and hearer, and that we be consulted concerning them, so that we may take action

[Col. 0375A]

[Note: [Col. 0375B] a What follows is corrupt in codex 4 and in the editions, where it reads:

“that we may take action against those who, by this evasion, [with exemption] to be granted to absolutely no one, anyone who may have crept in, after the privilege has been invalidated, is also about to undergo danger to his life.”

In the margin of Aur. Lugd., for the restoration of the passage, these words are added at *tribuendas*: “For. *tribuenda, se subripere voluerit. p. b. in s. e. p. subituros.*” [Col. 0375C]

Go. employed this correction in order to conjecture: “that we may take action against them: he who, through this evasion, with it to be granted to absolutely no one, may otherwise have crept in,” etc.; and adds: “*Caeteroqui*, in place of *ideoqui*, that is, hereafter, otherwise.” But now leaf XXX of codex 1 comes to hand; its lines at this place are:

> *madu . . . . amusineosquihactergiversationeu si sunt*  
> *derelicofunctionishujussuacationempenitus tribuen*  
> *damsedeumquisubriperepotueritpostbenef icium*  
> *infirmatumsalutisetiampericulumsubitu . . . . . .*

(Pu. has five dots; W. seven.) P. read it thus:

“that we may take action against those who have employed this evasion; henceforth exemption from this function is to be granted to absolutely no one; but he who has procured it surreptitiously shall, after the privilege has been invalidated, also undergo danger to his life.”

W. says: “It is therefore apparent that the words *de reliquo—vacationem*, which the parchment supplies to complete this place, were elsewhere omitted because of the similar endings *tergiversatione, vacatione*; conversely, in the palimpsest—if P e y r o n has correctly rendered the letters—*nulli*, without which the passage cannot stand, has dropped out. Moreover, I think that not accusatives, with P e y r o n, are to be retained, but absolute ablatives, very common with emperors, must be restored; and that the whole passage must now be written thus:

‘that we may take action against those who have employed this evasion; henceforth, exemption from this function being granted to absolutely no one, he who may have procured it surreptitiously shall, after the privilege has been invalidated, also undergo danger to his life.’

Although this reading departs a little from the palimpsest, it is confirmed by the common reading: *ideo—subituro*.”

I have adopted what W. restored, especially since *tribuendasedeo* is contained in the reading *tribuendasideo* of codex 4. I do not say that *subrepere*, emended by Go. and restored by Be., is false.] 

against those who have employed this evasion; henceforth exemption from this function is to be granted to absolutely no one; but he who has obtained it surreptitiously shall, after the privilege has been invalidated, also incur danger to his life. Given

[Note: [Col. 0375D] b Go. has “Given” in place of “Published” or “Accepted.”]

on the eighth day before the Ides of March, at Rome, in the consulship of Optatus and Paulinus.

[Note: [Col. 0375D] c 1, 4, editions: *Paulino*.]

(334).

## ON MATERNAL PROPERTY

Imp. Constantine Augustus to Severus, Count of the Spains. It has been reported that certain fathers, bereft of the union of their first marriage,

[Note: [Col. 0375D] d Codex Lugd.: *conjugi*, but corrected to *conjugii*. A little below: *orbita*, but restored to *orbitate*.]

hasten, beyond the mercy due to blood, toward the ruin of their children; and, after contracting other marriages, claim for themselves a greater standing in their children’s property. Since they appear to have remained usufructuaries in this property, they presume to appropriate and squander it, so that those who remain in orphanhood are afforded no opportunity either to possess or to litigate. Therefore it is our pleasure that no father, after entering subsequent marriages, shall think himself entitled to assert a right in property which belonged to his former wife, except in the capacity

[Col. 0375B]

[Col. 0376A]

[Note: [Col. 0376B] a Codex Lugd.: *vicem* (“in the capacity [accusative]”).]

of a guardian, until the minors are shown to have reached the approved age. Our moderation orders that all these things be preserved and restored to them. Published

[Note: [Col. 0376B] b Go. emends “Corduba,” or wishes “Given” to be restored in place of “Published.” Otherwise the codex and editions have “Paulinus.”]

on the third day before the Kalends of April, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Optatus and Paulinus (334).

rationalis of the three provinces.

remains intact.

For who could endure

and

if, to anyone,

care must be taken lest, throughout the province,

day before the Kalends of May

In the division

of patrimonial or

Imp. Constantine Augustus

to Veronicianus,

governors,

[Note: [Col. 0377C] j Cuj. 1: *obsequntur*.]

must be checked in such a way that, as we previously enacted,

[Note: [Col. 0377C] l Codex, Cuj. 1—Lugd.: *sancxerimus*; Cuj. 2—Ri.*: *sanxerimus*. Go. in the note emends: *sanximus* or *sanxeramus*. Be. restores *sancivimus* from the Code of Justinian, though Cujacius there has *sanximus*.]

## ON THINGS SOLD OR GIVEN AWAY TO OFFICIALS

Imp. Constantine Augustus

[Note: [Col. 0377D] o Br., Al., Sich., Til. manuscripts: “Emperor Constantine Augustus.”]

to Veronicianus,

[Note: [Col. 0377D] p 15: *Feronicianum*; 16: *Verocinum*; 20, 35, 43: *Verocianum*; 25: *Verotiano*; 26: *Vericianum*; 21, Sich., Til.: *Veranicianum*; Aur. Lugd.: *Veronicinianum*; 27: *Nicianum*. Similarly 10, 18: “to Vero Nicianus.” 28: “Emperor Augustus to Julian Constantine”; 36: “Emperor Augustus to Julian Constantine”; 48: “Emperor Theodosius to Julian Constantine.” Some manuscripts read “vir clarissimus” instead of “Vicar”; others mark “Vicar.” “Of Tuscia.”]

Vicar of Asia. After other provisions:

[Note: [Col. 0377D] q “After other provisions” is absent in many manuscripts.]

We grant provincials the right

[Note: [Col. 0377D] r 20: “power.” Immediately afterward some manuscripts: “whatever.”]

so that anyone who has complained that sales were extorted from him by financial clerks

[Note: [Col. 0377D] s Sich., Til.: “money-changers,” first edition of Ri.; 21 omits “by.”]

who serve different governors,

[Note: [Col. 0377D] t 10, 18: “robbers.”]

[Col. 0378A]

may render such sales void and ineffective,

and improperly sold property shall revert to the ownership of the seller, while illicit and detestable purchasers are punished also by forfeiture of the price.

[Note: [Col. 0378B] e Some manuscripts: *praejudicii* (“prejudice”) in place of *pretii* (“price”), and “and” for “also.”]

Given on the fourteenth

[Note: [Col. 0378B] f 9, 27, 42, L., R., U. apud Canc.: the thirteenth; codex Pip.: the eighteenth, and S. Gall. as ours; 17: the seventeenth; 30: the fourth; 10: “Given, title, fourteenth.”]

day before the Kalends of June,

[Note: [Col. 0378B] g 10, 20, 39: January.]

in the consulship of Optatus

[Note: [Col. 0378B] h Some manuscripts: *Obtata*; others: *Obtoto*.]

THIS LAW DOES NOT REQUIRE EXPLANATION.

[Note: [Col. 0378B] j These words of the interpreter are absent in Cuj. 1—Cuj. 2*; Go., Ri., and Ri.* read “does not require interpretation,” but in Go.’s edition *interpretatio* was inserted into the middle of note a through a printer’s oversight. 21, Sich.: “This law.” After the Interpretation in Sich. there appears a trace of a new law:

“Emperor Theodosius Augustus to Julian Constantine. *Interpretation.* [Col. 0378C] Whoever complains that sales have been extorted from him by money-changers who serve different governors, they shall be rendered void and ineffective, and improperly sold property shall revert to the ownership of the seller, while illicit and detestable purchasers are punished also by forfeiture of the price.”

In the margin of Sich.’s edition is noted: “In the Strasbourg codex we discovered the beginning of another law, to which this Interpretation was attached; yet it differs not even a word from the preceding law.” Now, if it is asked whether an unknown law lies hidden in these words, I maintain that this must be denied. For the source has become known. The Strasbourg codex is the Bern manuscript (40), in which I found these very words of Sichard with the heading; but they are written so that they indicate not another law omitted from the other copies, but stand in place of the law itself received in Br. and Al. The same is true in codices 28 and 36. Thus this passage is nothing other than a corrupt interpretation of the law itself, with a corrupt heading: Constantine’s name was transposed, as codices 28 and 36 show; in its place the scribe of codex 40, noticing the gap after *Imp.*, substituted Theodosius; *Julianum* arose from *Veronicianum*. Sichard, however, having not carefully examined the heading of codex 40, took it as evidence of a lost law.]

Imp. Constantine Augustus to Andronicus.

## ON THE ADVOCATE OF THE FISC

Imp. Constantine Augustus to Pacatianus, Praetorian Prefect. Although the cause of private persons has greater weight with us than the protection of the fisc, nevertheless we order that, if several persons have received from us appointments as advocates of the fisc, the one who, upon examination of his trustworthiness, is found to be better, more eminent in integrity, and more accomplished in letters than the rest shall be preferred, even if he received this benefit from our clemency later than the others.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] y 4 and the editions: *reportabit*. Go. emended to *reportavit*; Be.: *reportavit* or *reportaverit*. One or the other necessarily had to be emended.]

Given on the third

[Note: [Col. 0379D] z Cuj. 2, 2*, Go.: the second, erroneously.]

day before the Nones of July, at Singidunum.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] aa Be.: *Singiduni*; Scrib.: *Singiduno*.]

In the consulship of Optatus and Paulinus.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] bb 4, Til.—Ri*: *Paulino*. Aur. Lugd.: “consuls,” both here and in chapters 3 and 4 of this title.]

(334).

## ON THE CREDIBILITY OF WITNESSES AND DOCUMENTS
The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Julianus, Governor.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] Chapter 16: Julianus, governor, in the Tarraconensian province, according to Reinesius’s marginal note. [Col. 0380A] Gothofredus says that some think otherwise. Chapter 23 of the Theodosian Code, *On Decurions* (XII.1), addressed to Julianus, was issued in 338; Gothofredus there notes: “I do not doubt that this Julianus [Col. 0380B] was governor of some province; indeed, four years earlier Law 3, under *On the Credibility of Witnesses*, was addressed to Julianus, Governor.” In his notes on the present chapter he doubts whether this is the same Julianus, or whether Cejonius Julianus is rather meant, whom Vopiscus mentions in the *Life of Firmus*, ch. 1 (2). In the *Prosopography*, however, he considers Julianus the former vicar, whom Ammianus Marcellinus, XXII.11, relates to have been killed in the consulship of Mamertinus and Nevitta (362). The matter is uncertain; yet the chronology does not permit us to understand here the same Julianus mentioned by Vopiscus or Ammianus Marcellinus. But I do not doubt that he is the same as the man in the cited ch. 23. Code of Justinian: Emperor Constantine Augustus.]

We have long since ordered that witnesses, before they give testimony, be bound by the sanctity of an oath, [Note: [Col. 0380B] In manuscripts 6, 7, 10, 13, 16, and 18: “religionem”; and in some manuscripts: “testis.” Manuscript 20: “in religione.”] and that greater credence be accorded to witnesses of higher rank. [Note: [Col. 0380B] Manuscript 4: “adhibeant”; manuscript *a*, corrected by a later hand: “perhibeant.” Manuscript 25: “praebeant.”]

§1. By the same practice [Note: [Col. 0380C] Thus manuscripts 4, 6–8, 10, 13, 14, 16–18, 21, 25, 50, Sichard through Ritter; the *Collectio Anselmi*, “ded.” Manuscript 12: “similes mores.” The remaining manuscripts, Beatus from manuscript 20, and the Code of Justinian: “modo.” Manuscript 15: “sim. s. modo ut.” I have restored *more*. *Mos* is used for “reason,” “method,” or “example.” Otherwise Tillet through Cujas, second edition: “habeatur, simili more.”] we have enacted [Note: [Col. 0380C] Manuscripts 6–8, 10, 12–18, 20, 21, and Sichard: “sancimus.”] that no judge shall readily permit the testimony of a single person to be admitted in any case whatsoever. [Note: [Col. 0380B] Manuscript 20: “adstare,” but above the line “arctari.” Gothofredus correctly reads thus. Beatus, from Sichard and certain editions of Justinian; manuscripts 4, 6–8, 10, 16–18, 20, 21, 25, 50; Tillet through Ritter, and the Code of Justinian in Spangenberg’s edition: “praecipimus.” The remaining manuscripts read “praecepimus.” Gothofredus through Ritter read “praecipimus”; Etienne likewise. Manuscript 8: “ut et.” Manuscript 20: “adhibeatur.” Code of Justinian: “testibus fides adhibeatur.”]

And now we expressly enact that the statement of one witness alone shall not be heard, [Note: [Col. 0380C] Manuscripts 4, 6–8, 10, 12–14, 17, 18, 21, and Tillet through the Lyons edition read: “et ut.” Thus Tillet through Cujas, second edition, first printing: “et ut honestioribus potius fides testibus habeatur, simili more sanximus, et …” Cujas, second and second revised edition, perhaps read and punctuated “et ut,” together with these editions. With this punctuation, V. refers “sanximus” to the preceding words “et … habeatur.” Manuscripts 16 and 25 omit “ut.” Manuscript 18 incorrectly has “injuste” for “unius.”] even if that witness shines with the honour of an illustrious municipal council. [Note: [Col. 0380D] Manuscripts 10 and 18: “in quocumque”; manuscript 20: “in quemcunque,” omitting “caussa.” Manuscript 4: “fiscale,” corrected in red ink to “fiscali.” Tillet through the Lyons edition read “fiscale,” correctly rejected by Gothofredus in his commentary; the remaining manuscripts, Sichard, and the Code of Justinian support “quacumque.” Gothofredus prefers “At nunc,” while not denying that “et nunc” can be defended. Manuscript 15: “non admittatur.” Sichard: “ne unius omnino testis responsio audiatur.” Manuscripts 6 and 7: “audeatur.” Above, the *Collectio Anselmi*, “ded.”: “omni modo testis.” Manuscripts 15, 50, and Sichard: “in m. praeclaro”; thereafter some manuscripts read “cure.” Manuscript 12: “refulgeat.”]

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, at Naissus, in the consulship of Optatus and Paullinus (334). [Note: [Col. 0380D] Manuscripts 24, 50, and the Aurelia-Lyons edition: ninth day; manuscript 21 omits “VIII”; manuscript 20: fifth day. Manuscript 39: December. Manuscript 34: “Nauso”; manuscript 38: “Neso”; manuscript 39: “Naissio.” Beatus: “Naissi.” Manuscript 8 omits “Naisso” and “et … Coss.” Manuscript 4 and other manuscripts and editions read “Paulino.”]

## INTERPRETATION

Witnesses, before they are questioned concerning a case, must be bound by an oath, [Note: [Col. 0380D] So nearly all manuscripts, including 6–10, 12, and 16–18.] so that they swear that they will say nothing false. This also provides that greater credence is to be accorded to witnesses of higher rather than lower rank. [Note: [Col. 0381B] Manuscript 20: “false … dico.” [Col. 0381C] Manuscript 9 omits “testibus.”] But the testimony of one person, however distinguished and suitable that person may appear, is in no way to be heard. [Note: [Col. 0381C] Manuscript 20: “quamlibet et splendida.” Sichard and Cujas, first through Lyons editions: “quamvis.”]

## ON THE EXEMPTIONS OF CRAFTSMEN

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Felix . . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0381C] The official title is also lacking in ch. 6 of the cited Theodosian Code title *On Shipowners* and in the Montpellier manuscript, which reads in Book XIII: “Law: The same emperor to Felix.” Gothofredus believes that Felix, here addressed as “Your Sublimity,” was praetorian prefect, specifically of Italy. Relying on this conjecture, Beatus, in the added notes to the *Praefatio*, and Gothofredus through Ritter indicate the missing title by six dots; the rest give no mark.]

There is need of very many architects; but because they are lacking, Your Sublimity shall induce in the African provinces to undertake this study those who, at approximately eighteen years of age, have acquired a taste for liberal learning. [Note: [Col. 0381C] Folio 304b of manuscript 4. The Montpellier manuscript omits “sublimitas tua” and “in provinciis Africanis.” Gothofredus: this word appears superfluous.]

In order that this may be agreeable to them, we wish both them and their parents to be exempt from those obligations customarily imposed upon persons; and an appropriate salary shall be established for those who are learning. [Note: [Col. 0381C] Manuscript 4: “iniugi,” an error. Gothofredus conjectures “docent,” because a salary was provided to teachers, not learners. But the tenor of the entire constitution, as preserved in the Theodosian Code, is that those who apply themselves to the study of architecture are to be attracted by rewards and advantages. The Montpellier manuscript also has “discent.”]

Posted on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, at Carthage, in the consulship of Optatus and Paullinus (334). [Note: [Col. 0381D] The cited ch. 6 has: “Posted on the seventh day before the Ides”; for this reason I deny that this constitution should be joined to that chapter. Gothofredus, in the *Chronicle*, reads “VII,” but adds: “Others, VI.” Thereafter manuscript 4 and the editions read “Paulino.” The Montpellier manuscript lacks the subscription. See the preceding note c.]

## ON SHIPOWNERS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Felix . . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0381D] Gothofredus and Ritter print six dots, Rike four; the rest do not indicate a gap.]

That arrangement seemed advantageous to us which expressly organized shipowners in this order: that, not indiscriminately but by duly observed rotations, they should undertake continuous voyages and complete the small voyages, [Note: [Col. 0381D] Folio 307a of manuscript 4. Manuscript 4: “currus,” corrected by the scribe to “cursus.” Gothofredus conjectures *exagogas* or *exagogios*, but does not alter “exiguos.”] so that by the relief of alternating assistance the circumstances of all, and especially of the poorer, might be strengthened, and there should be no necessity for some always to travel longer routes and become exposed to very many hazards. [Note: [Col. 0381D] Manuscript 4 reads, with corruption: “tenuioribus um potissimum confirmen nec.” A later hand placed a red asterisk after “um” and after “confirmen.” Tillet through the Lyons edition print: “tenuioribus * um potissimum confirmen *, nec.” Cujas’s conjecture, first printed in the second and second revised editions, is: “tenuioribus tum potissimum confirment, nec”; subsequent editors adopted it, though Gothofredus through Ritter retained the asterisk after “confirment.” They would more correctly have adopted Cujas’s other conjecture, noted in the margin of Cujas’s first through second revised editions and approved by Gothofredus and Beatus: “tenuiorum potissimum confirmentur,” omitting *potissimum* in the Aurelia-Lyons edition. I have preferred this, since manuscript 4 plainly contains a scribal error, though I have changed the present tense into the imperfect.]

To prevent this from happening again, let equal and just labour be assigned to all, and let assistance be provided according to the same principle, so that the poorer may not fall into complaints of fruitless lamentation.

Posted on the seventh day before the Ides of September, at Carthage, in the consulship of Optatus and Paullinus (334). [Note: [Col. 0382D] Ritter’s revised edition omits “VII.” Manuscript 4 and the editions read “Paulino.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Shipowners of the East.

For the advantage of the city which, by God’s command, we have endowed with an eternal name, we have judged that these privileges should be granted to you: that all shipowners shall be exempt from civic public duties, burdens, and compulsory services; nor shall they be compelled to undertake even civic honours from which they might suffer any inconvenience. [Note: [Col. 0382D] Gothofredus’s note reads “lubente,” but in his commentary he rightly defends “jubente.”]

They shall also be exempt from the administration of guardianship, whether statutory or imposed by magistrates or provincial governors. [Note: [Col. 0382D] Manuscript 4: “jus,” corrected by an earlier hand to “ejus.”] And they shall enjoy exemption from the Julian and Papian law, so that, even where there are no children, husbands may take in full under the wills of their wives, and the entire testamentary disposition of husbands may pass to their wives. [Note: [Col. 0382D] Cujas, in the margin of the first through second revised editions; Gothofredus and Beatus rightly emend “liberis,” for “lucris.”]

If they are sued concerning ownership, inheritance, or any other civil cause, they shall not be summoned, even by our rescript, before an extraordinary tribunal; rather, they shall answer claimants in their own forum. Following the example of the Alexandrian fleet (*stolus*), they shall receive four hundredths in grain and, for every thousand, one solidus, so that, encouraged by all these benefits and expending almost nothing from their own resources, they may diligently maintain maritime transport by their care. [Note: [Col. 0382D] Above *stoli*, an ancient hand wrote “cursus” in yellow ink in manuscript 4, doubtless to explain *stoli*. A later hand enclosed it in brackets drawn in red ink.]

Received on the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Optatus and Paullinus (334). [Note: [Col. 0382D] See preceding note b.]

## ON THE SOLDIER’S WILL

[Col. 0382C]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People.

Soldiers engaged on campaign, if by the disposition of their last will they wish to benefit their wives, children, friends, comrades-in-arms, or finally persons of any class whatsoever, may make a will in whatever way they can and wish. Nor, when their wives or children have obtained their father’s intended disposition, shall their merit, freedom, or rank be questioned. Accordingly, just as it has been permitted by legal principles and always will be permitted, if they have marked anything in writing upon a scabbard or shield with their blood glowing red, or inscribed it in the dust with their sword, at the very time when in battle they relinquish life’s lot, such a declaration of will must remain valid.

Given on the third day before the Ides of August, at Nicomedia, in the consulship of Optatus and Paullinus (334) (from the Code of Justinian).

## WHEN THE EMPEROR HEARS CASES INVOLVING WRETCHED PERSONS

[Col. 0383A]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Andronicus.

If a judgment of our clemency has been obtained against minors, widows, or persons exhausted and weakened by prolonged illness, those named shall not be compelled by any of our judges to appear before our court. Rather, within the province where the litigant, witnesses, and documents are located, they shall try the fortune of litigation; and every precaution shall be observed so that they are not compelled to cross the boundaries of their provinces.

But if minors, widows, or others rendered wretched by the injury of fortune petition for the judgment of our Serenity, especially when they dread another person’s power, their adversaries shall be compelled to appear before our tribunal.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Optatus and Paulinus (334) (from the Code of Justinian).

In the year of the Lord 335, in the consulship of Constantine and Albinus.

## ON PETITIONS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Provincials.

We direct all judges to be vigilant and to punish informers. [Note: [Col. 0383C] Manuscripts 10 and 18 omit “et ut,” as does the Code of Justinian. The Code of Justinian adds: “denouncing without an advocate of the fisc.”] For it is a most evident rule of law that whatever from anyone’s estate has fallen into forfeiture shall, both under the laws and according to the established order of prior law, be claimed by the advocates of the fisc acting on its behalf. [Note: [Col. 0383C] Manuscripts 10, 13, and 18: “apertissime.” Manuscript 20 and the Code of Justinian: “cujusque.” Manuscripts 6, 7, 10, 16, 18, and 31: “in casu.” Sichard’s marginal reading, “in cassum,” is approved by Dirksen, cited work, p. 495. All manuscripts except 8, 14, and 16, and Sichard, read “retro”; yet manuscript 4 has “recto,” corrected in red ink in the margin, as in Tillet through Beatus and the Code of Justinian. “Retro” is correct. Compare likewise ch. 16 of the Theodosian Code, *On Physicians* (XIII.3): “by the authority of sanctions previously enacted.” See the Glossary under *Retro* and Dirksen, cited work.]

But because some persons rashly do not cease to denounce estates possessed according to law, we grant to all who consider themselves injured the right to invoke the judges’ unsheathed severity against informers. [Note: [Col. 0383C] Manuscripts 10 and 18 omit “nulli.” Manuscript 20, corrected, reads “nonnullos”; it prescribes “esse” and shortly afterwards “differre.” [Col. 0383D] In manuscript 4, folio 91a begins with the letters “sessa.” Manuscript 4: “laesis,” corrected in red ink to “laesos.” Manuscripts 10 and 18: “lesos aestimant.” Manuscript 15: “damus omnibus qui se lesos aestimant licentiam contra.” Similarly the Code of Justinian, which adds *licentiam* after *omnibus*, though Dirksen thinks we can easily dispense with that word in the passage cited above. Manuscript 15 omits “ferro destrictam.” Many manuscripts, Sichard, and the Code of Justinian read “districtam.” What follows is absent from the Code of Justinian.]

For no one can recognize an informer better than the person who has suffered injury through that informer’s wickedness. [Note: [Col. 0383D] Manuscript 12: “prius.” Manuscripts 10 and 18 omit “ejus.” Manuscript 13 thereafter reads “sustinebit.”]

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Constantius and Albinus (335). [Note: [Col. 0383D] Manuscripts 4, 13, 33, 34, and Tillet through the Lyons edition: eleventh day; manuscripts 6–10, 12, 16–18, 20, 21, 24, 27–29, 31, 36, 40, 42, 44, and Sichard: tenth day; manuscript 15: twelfth day; Cujas through Beatus: second day. The remaining manuscripts omit “XI.” Gothofredus, in the *Chronicle*, reads third day; even the manuscripts and editions of the Code of Justinian differ among themselves. Very many manuscripts and Cujas’s second and second revised editions read “Constantino”; some manuscripts omit “Constantinopoli.” Manuscripts 17, 28, and 40: “et Licinio Coss.” Manuscript 20: “Abieno Coss.”]

## INTERPRETATION

[Col. 0384A]

Safeguarding justice, we pursue the names of informers, [Note: [Col. 0384B] Manuscript 20: “persequitur,” but above the line “persequantur.” [Col. 0384C] Sichard: “nomina persequamur.” Manuscript 44: “nomina pers.”] so that, when informers have been identified and convicted, they shall be punished by the sword.

## ON THE PROFITS OF OFFICES

[Note: [Col. 0384C] The Code of Justinian: “On the profits of advocates and extortions by offices or their staff”; a heading composed from this and the preceding title of the Theodosian Code.]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Pacatianus. [Note: [Col. 0384C] Gothofredus, Reinesius, and Beatus in the notes to the *Praefatio*.]

The ranks of the decuries of scribes, clerks, and consular lictors obtained by their petitions that, in civil cases and in the submission of petitions, they should perform the customary formal duties of their offices, as has been observed from ancient times; and this prerogative extends so far that military interference shall keep entirely apart from liberal causes. [Note: [Col. 0384C] The Lyons codex: “Ordinis.” Cujas’s first through second revised editions and Ritter’s revised edition: “decuriarum scribarum.” Codex 1: “Scr . . . . . batur.” The Lyons codex: “librarorum,” emended to “librariorum.” Thereafter Codex 1: “consolaris.” The Lyons codex: “utusq.” The editions read “hucusque.” I have adopted from Codex 1 “eo usque.” Codex 1 thereafter omits *a* after *usque*. The Lyons codex: “umilitares,” with *t* supplied above *u*. Below, the same codex has “contineat.” The Lyons codex: “oservabunt,” with *b* supplied above *o*.]

Provincial governors shall therefore observe what we have ordered.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Constantius and Albinus (335).

## ON DECURIONS

[Col. 0384B]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Felix, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0384C] Manuscript 4 reads “pp.” The copyist commonly writes “ppo.”]

Since African curiales have complained that certain persons in their body, after attaining the honour of the flamen and completing the insignia of priesthood or magistracy, are being compelled to become supervisors of lodgings—a duty which men of the next rank and merit in each curia have customarily performed—we order that no one distinguished by the aforesaid honours be compelled to perform the said service, lest an injustice seem to be done by our judgment. [Note: [Col. 0384C] Manuscript 4: “conquaesti.” Gothofredus emends “e” to “in.” Manuscripts 4 and Tillet through the Lyons edition: “flamonii.” Summary of the Theodosian Code: “Those made flamines Diales—‘flamines’ corrected by second hands to ‘flamones’—or priests ought not to be made supervisors of houses.” [Col. 0384D] Manuscript 4: “dicio,” incorrectly.]

Given on the day before the Nones of August, at Viminacium, in the consulship of Constantius and Albinus (335). [Note: [Col. 0384D] Beatus: “Viminacii.” Gothofredus thinks Viminacium was in Moesia, from which Constantine returned to Constantinople. Pagius, however, in the Prolegomena to the *Dissertation on the Consular Lists*, no. 24, because Constantine was at Constantinople at this time, takes *Dat.* to mean *Redd.*—that is, “issued” or “delivered.” Ritter rightly observes that a law concerning Africans ought to have been issued in Africa, not in Serbia; the error is not in *Dat.* but in *Viminacio*, a word corrupted by copyists.]

## ON THE JEWS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Felix, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0384D] Br. Al. manuscripts, Sichard, and Tillet in Br. Al.: “Emperor Constantine Augustus.” Manuscript 11: “Idem AA.” Manuscript 21 and others: “Constant.” Some Br. Al. manuscripts read “praepositum”; others omit “Pf. P.” After *alia*, to which words Gothofredus observes: “The matters contained in the cited Law 1, to which these words should be appended.” He understands that cited ch. 1 must be joined to the present chapter.]

After other matters: Jews shall not be permitted to harass, or to assail with any injury, one who has become a Christian from Judaism; such an outrage is to be punished according to the character of the offence committed, etc. [Note: [Col. 0384D] Manuscripts 29, 38, 39, 42, 50, 51, and L. in Beatus read “Judaeis”; manuscript 43: “Judaeus.” [Col. 0385A] Manuscripts 25, 33, 34, and 37: “inquietari”; manuscript 38 adds “a”; L. reads “eum,” as does the corrector of manuscript 42. Manuscripts 9, 14, 15, 32, 38, and 39 read “Judaeis”; Gothofredus also conjectures this, although he does not reject the received reading. At first glance the passage seems difficult, and editions therefore punctuate it differently: “inquietare Judaeos, non liceat,” or, in Sichard through Cujas’s second edition and Labbe, “inquietare Judaeos non liceat”; or, in Gothofredus through Beatus. Baronius explains it as though Jews were protected from injury by proselytes. But Christians, not Jews, are protected from injury. The passage is sound; its construction, though unusual, is entirely complete: “It shall not be permitted for Jews to harass or assail with any injury one who has become a Christian from Judaism.” Sirmondian ch. IV: “For by this same enactment we decree that, if anyone among the Jews, opening the door of eternal life, has committed himself to holy rites and has chosen to be a Christian, he shall suffer no harassment or annoyance from Jews. But if any Jew judges that a person made Christian from Judaism ought to be assailed with injury, we desire that the contriver of such an insult be subjected to avenging penalties according to the character of the offence committed, dearest parent Felix. Therefore, in affection for Your Divinity, we trust that he will ensure its observance throughout the Roman world by all, with fitting reverence; and we desire that Your Exalted Sublimity, by letters circulated through the diocese entrusted to it, urgently admonish the judges [Col. 0385C] that this due reverence be preserved.” Thus this passage has been greatly altered by the compilers of the Theodosian Code through a passion for alteration. Certain Br. Al. manuscripts read “alia” or “aliquid.” Manuscript 11: “pulsari et contumelio.” Thereafter certain manuscripts read “commissus.” Manuscripts 20 and 25 add “est”; manuscript 24: “finienda.” Many manuscripts read “ponienda”; in others *etc.* is absent, as it is in Sichard.]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, at Constantinople (335). [Note: [Col. 0385C] Manuscripts 24 and 34: tenth day; Sirmondian ch. IV and manuscript 38: twelfth day; the rest: eleventh day. I have followed the cited Sirmondian ch. IV.]

Posted on the eighth day before the Ides of May, at Carthage, in the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus (336). [Note: [Col. 0385C] Manuscripts 9, 29, 42, and L. in Beatus: “accepta”; manuscripts 10 and 18: “praecepta.” Labbe in the margin: “That is, promulgated.” Manuscripts 6, 7, 10, 12–14, 17, 18, 20, 21, Sichard, and Tillet in Br. Al.: “pridie” or “prid.” Manuscript 38 omits “VIII.” Sirmondian ch. IV: seventh day. Manuscripts 9, 27, and 29: “Kl.”; L. in Beatus: “Kal.” Manuscript 38: “Non.” Sirmondian ch. IV: March. Certain Br. Al. manuscripts and Mad.: “Karthagine.” I have added “Karthagine” from ch. 1, which must be joined to this chapter, and from Sirmondian ch. IV. I have also added the year after Constantinople, as Beatus already wished to do; for the consuls of the year in which this law was issued have fallen out. [Col. 0385D] Many manuscripts read “Neputiano” or “putiano”; Aurelia-Lyons: “Neapotiano.” Manuscript 4: “Facundococoss.” Manuscript 11 omits “Coss.”]

## THIS LAW REQUIRES NO INTERPRETATION

[Note: [Col. 0385D] Some manuscripts: “Ista lex et indiget,” as in Sichard; and “explicatione” for “interpretatione,” as Gothofredus through Ritter note in parentheses: “interpretatione [otherwise explicatione] non.”]

## THAT A JEW SHALL NOT HAVE A CHRISTIAN SLAVE

[Note: [Col. 0385D] Some manuscripts: “That a Jew shall not have a Christian slave.” The Code of Justinian: “That a heretic, pagan, or Jew shall not have, possess, or circumcise a Christian slave.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Felix, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 0385D] Sichard in the margin reads “Constantius” for “Constantinus.” Some manuscripts: “A. Felici.” Manuscript 11: “Felice”; others: “praepositum”; others omit “Pf. P.,” as does manuscript 21. Manuscript 20: “pfu.” Sichard: “PF. V.”]

If any Jew, having purchased a Christian slave or one of any other sect, has circumcised him, [Note: [Col. 0385D] Sirmondian ch. IV: “Indeed, the most salutary sanction of our constitution has long since been promulgated; we confirm it by the reverence due to our repeated law, and desire that, if anyone …” [Col. 0386B] The cited ch. IV continues: “shall not have shrunk from circumcising him, the circumcised person, having received freedom under the measure of this enactment, shall enjoy its privileges. It shall not be lawful for a Jew who has circumcised him to retain in servile obedience a slave of the aforesaid kind.” Certain Br. Al. manuscripts read “mercatur” for “mercatus” and “servitutem.”] he shall by no means retain the circumcised person in slavery; rather, the person who has suffered this shall enjoy the privileges of freedom, etc. [Note: [Col. 0386C] Manuscript 11: “servitute deserviat circumcisum si.” Manuscript 20: “pivilegiis.” Sichard: “haec” for “hoc.” Some manuscripts read “sustinuit potiantur” or “patiatur”; Sichard omits *etc.*]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, at Constantinople (335). [Note: [Col. 0386C] Sirmondian ch. IV and manuscripts 9, 16, 30, and 44: thirteenth day; the rest: eleventh day. In some manuscripts the whole subscription “Given … Constantinople” is absent.]

Posted on the eighth day before the Ides of May, at Carthage, in the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus (336). [Note: [Col. 0386C] Some manuscripts have “Dat.,” as do L., R., and U.; others “Acc.,” as L. in Beatus. In some manuscripts “Dat. … Karth.” is absent. Sirmondian ch. IV, manuscript 20, and Sichard: seventh day; Sichard corrects in the margin to eighth day. The Piper manuscript, L. R. U., has eighth day. Manuscript 9 omits “VIII … Coss.” Thereafter certain manuscripts and Mad. omit “Karthag.” The Anician codex cited by Gothofredus has March, like Sirmondian ch. IX. Further spellings include Nepucianus, Nebucianus, Ebucianus, Epucianus, Pontianus; and in manuscripts 11 and 20, “Carthagine Pociano,” with “Coss.” omitted in manuscript 11.]

## INTERPRETATION

If any Jew purchases and circumcises a Christian slave or a slave of any other sect, that slave, removed from the Jew’s power, shall remain free. [Note: [Col. 0386C] Some manuscripts omit *et* and write “a Judaeis.” Manuscript 11: “christianum servum … a judices ipsius.”]

## ON THE DUTY OF A GOVERNOR

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Pericles, Governor.

We have given you authority to punish officials of prefects who ravage the public post or devise wrongful schemes contrary to the public interest, provided that you inform the prefects of their fault.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, at Nicopolis, in the consulship of Constantius and Albinus, 335 (from the Code of Justinian).

In the year of the Lord 336, in the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus.

## ON NATURAL CHILDREN AND THEIR MOTHERS

[Note: [Col. 0386C] Most of this title is contained on the fifth folio of the Turin palimpsest. Although the heading, together with the first part of the title, is missing, the fact that among the intervening constitutions there appears the one which, in editions before W., was the first constitution of this title permits the conclusion that all constitutions on that folio are to be assigned to this title. The Code of Justinian adds: “and the causes by which they are made legitimate.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0386D] The superscription is absent in Codex 1. P. adds: “Fragment of Law III enacted by Constantine.” Pu. adds: “Fragment of Constitution 2, enacted by Emperor Constantine.” P., Pu., and W. correctly supply the emperor’s name by conjecture. But I have not been able to recover by conjecture the name of the magistrate to whom the law was sent. W. judges that he was the same Gregorius to whom, in the same year, ch. 3 of this title and ch. 3 of the Theodosian Code, *On Annual and Tributary Payments* (XI.1), were sent. This conjecture seems probable to me, less on account of Gregorius’s rank—W. asserts on Gothofredus’s authority that he was praetorian prefect of Africa, for in the same year several laws were also sent to Felix, praetorian prefect, [Col. 0387B] and posted at Carthage; see ch. 1 of the Theodosian Code, *That a Christian Slave …* (XVI.9), and Sirmondian ch. 4—than because of the mention in the present constitution of the same Licinianus who occurs in ch. 3 of this title.]

. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . [Col. 0387A] …ri fecit [incomplete reading], [Note: [Col. 0387B] The fifth Turin folio begins with the words “ri fecit.” P. supplies: “If a father gave something to natural children, or caused it to be given”; W. approves. W. nevertheless thinks that the greater part of this constitution has perished.] or if he purchased something in their name, the legitimate offspring shall recover the whole.

But if there are no legitimate children, nor a consanguine brother or sister, nor a father, the whole shall be claimed by the power of the fisc. [Note: [Col. 0387C] The second line of the Turin folio ends with the syllable *fra*; the third, from which certain letters have been cut away, begins with the syllable *con*. P., followed by Pu., therefore supplies “fra[ter aut] consanguineus.” W., rejecting *aut* in P.’s supplement, observes both that there is no one who can here be called *consanguineus* in the emphatic sense, *kat’ exochēn* (κατ’ ἐξοχήν, “pre-eminently”), and that, just as Constantine preferred consanguine brothers to uterine brothers in bringing an action challenging an undutiful will, he here wished a consanguine brother, but not a uterine brother, to be preferred to the fisc. Nothing had to be added concerning a sister, who necessarily had to be consanguine, since it is established that no other sister was admitted to civil succession. For this passage see W.’s lengthy note on Constantine’s views concerning natural children, and Batavians in *Bijdragen*, cited work, p. 329.]

Accordingly, all property shall also be taken from the son of Licinianus, who by a most sacred rescript attained the summit of rank, and shall be adjudged to the fisc under this law; he himself is to be beaten, bound in fetters, and reduced to the first beginnings of his origin. [Note: [Col. 0387C] Manuscript 1 reads fragmentarily: “verbe. . . . . compedib. … primordiaredi. . . . .” P., followed by Pu., restores: “verbe[ribus et] compedibus … primordia redi[gatur].” This reading is rejected by W., who objects that someone is said to be bound with beatings and that *redigatur* has no noun to which it can refer. W., with the approval of *Bijdragen*, p. 330, reads: “et ipso verberando, compedibus vinciendo et ad … primordia redigendo.” In that conjecture the conjunction *et* has been added without necessity; it is missing in Codex 1 in the middle of a line, not at its end.]

Read on the third day before the Kalends of May, at Carthage, in the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus (336). [Note: [Col. 0387D] P. prints 388, a typographical error.]

## ON SHIPOWNERS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Severus . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0387D] The official title is absent in manuscript 4 and in the editions, with no indication of a gap. Gothofredus reconstructs it from ch. 5 of the Theodosian Code, *On Donatists* (VIII.12), ch. 3, *On Maternal Property* (VIII.18), and ch. 2, *On the Credibility of Witnesses and Documents* (XI.39), as “Count of the Spains”; Beatus approves.]

The shipowners of the Spains must neither be bound to extraordinary services nor, when detained somewhere, suffer delays; but they must receive from the receivers, within ten days, the acknowledgements for goods delivered. And whenever they have arrived at any islands, ports, shores, or stations, upon producing the acknowledgements they shall suffer no disturbance whatsoever. [Note: [Col. 0387B] Manuscript 4, folio 308a, begins at the letters *tudinem*.]

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus (336).

## ON BETROTHALS

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Tiberianus, Vicar of the Spains. [Note: [Col. 0387D] Manuscripts 6–8, 14, 16–18, and Tillet read “Hispaniae”; manuscript 15, “Hisp. vic.”; manuscript 10, “viro claro Hisp.”; manuscript 25, “Vic. Vices Hisp.” Some manuscripts read “Span.” Manuscript 8 omits “Vic.”; manuscript 42 omits “Hisp.”]

If, after the bridegroom has bestowed gifts upon the bride and a kiss has intervened before the wedding, it happens that either he or she dies, we direct that half of the things given shall belong to the survivor, and half to the heirs of the deceased man or woman, of whatever degree they may be and by whatever right they succeed; so that the gift shall be considered to stand as to one half and to be dissolved as to one half. [Note: [Col. 0387D] Manuscript 15 omits “ab.” Manuscripts 6–10, 12, 14, and 17–20: “sponsoribus sponsae.” Manuscript 15: “sponsalibus donatis sponsae interv. osc.” [Col. 0388C] Manuscript 17: “vel hunc”; manuscript 19: “vel puellam”; manuscript 20: “vel puella.” Aurelia-Lyons: “susperstitem.” Manuscript 12: “quicunque.” Manuscript 8: “non.” Manuscript 8 reads: “dimidia … dimidia”; manuscript 12: “dimidia … dimidia”; manuscript 15 omits “ut donatio … videatur.” Manuscript 9: “media teneatur.”]

But where no kiss has intervened, whether bridegroom or bride dies, the whole gift shall be invalidated and restored to the donor—the bridegroom—or to his heirs. [Note: [Col. 0388C] Some manuscripts: “donatoris.” Manuscripts of Justinian: “vel.” Manuscript 20: “sive sponso vel her.”]

§1. But if the bride, whether a kiss has intervened or not, has bestowed something upon the bridegroom under the title of betrothal gifts—which rarely occurs—and it happens that either he or she dies before the wedding, then, with the whole gift invalidated, ownership of the given things shall pass to the donor-bride or to her successors. [Note: [Col. 0388C] Manuscript 14 omits “vel.” Manuscripts of Justinian: “donationis.”]

Given on the Ides of July, at Constantinople. Received on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, at Hispalis, in the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus (336). [Note: [Col. 0388C] The Code of Justinian omits “Dat. … Constant.” Beatus, approving W., wishes to add “in the consulship of Constantius and Albinus (335),” because a law could not have been received before it was issued, nor read on the Ides of January. [Col. 0388D] Nearly all manuscripts, Sichard through Cujas’s second revised edition: fourteenth day; manuscripts 39 and 43: seventeenth day; Sichard in the margin, Gothofredus through W., and the Code of Justinian: thirteenth day. Some manuscripts omit “Hispali”; manuscript 21 and Sichard: “Spalis,” corrected in the margin to “Hispali.” Many manuscripts: “Hispalis” or “Spalis.” Manuscript 20: “spaniis neposiano.” The Code of Justinian: “Pacato,” incorrectly.]

## INTERPRETATION

If, when a betrothal has been celebrated and a kiss has intervened, the bridegroom gives something to the bride and perhaps dies before the wedding, then the surviving girl may claim one half of the things formally given, and the heirs of the deceased shall acquire the other half, however remote the degree by which they come in the order of succession. [Note: [Col. 0388D] Thus many manuscripts; manuscript 21 and the editions: “aliqua … forsitan sponsus.” Manuscript 20: “potuerit.” Manuscripts 19 and 20, Sichard, and Cujas’s first through Lyons editions: “aequirant.” Manuscript 8: “quoscunque per gradus.” Manuscript 20: “quoc. gradus p. gr.”]

But if no kiss has intervened, the girl can claim none of the things given or delivered to her when the bridegroom dies. [Note: [Col. 0388D] Manuscript 8: “osculo non interveniente.” Some manuscripts: “intervenit.” Some manuscripts: “potuerit.”]

If, however, something has been given by the girl to the bridegroom and she dies, then, whether a kiss has or has not intervened, the girl’s parents or relatives shall recover all that she had given. [Note: [Col. 0388D] Some manuscripts add “forsitan.” Most manuscripts and the editions read “aliquid sponso.” Manuscripts 8, 20, and 21: “aut interc. osc. aut non totum.” Manuscript 20 adds “sibi.”]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Gregory.

Senators or [Col. 0389A] *perfectissimi*,

the quinquennal office,

Accordingly, whether it was given by the person who is called the father himself, or through another,  
[Note: [Col. 0390B] a 1: *aliam*, erroneously.]

## Concerning Decurions

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Evagrius, Praetorian Prefect. Since decurions, the sons of decurions, and those born from them  
[Note: [Col. 0390D] r Aur., Lugd.: *genitis*, “born”; the same editions below have *Cons.*]  
flee into various military services, we order that those serving in whatever offices be released from military service and restored to the curia, except those already employed in the offices of our palace. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus (336).

## Concerning the Annona and Taxes

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Gregory, Praetorian Prefect. All judges, by their own hand and at their own risk, shall make a written registration specifying fixed quantities and stated measures of the annona supplies and the other things due under the indiction. The advantage of this observance will be that, even after their succession,  
[Note: [Col. 0391B] a Go. rejects the conjecture *secessionem* for *successionem*.]  
it may readily be determined whether collectors wished to extort from the property of provincials anything beyond what was proper.  
[Note: [Col. 0391B–C] b Go.: *provinciarum*, “of provinces,” erroneously. c Cuj. 2, 2*: *excludere*, “exclude,” but corrected in the errata.]  
Given on the seventh day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus (336).

## Concerning the Order of Proceedings

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Calphurnius. Since, when civil litigation has been interrupted, it often happens that judgment is first given concerning a crime—which, being more serious, is rightly preferred to the lesser matter—when the criminal inquiry has ceased in whatever manner, the civil case must be determined as though newly brought before the court. Thus the conclusion of the criminal proceeding shall give a beginning to the civil action from the day on which judgment has been rendered between the parties. Given on the Ides of March, in the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus, 336. (From the Code of Justinian.)

In the year of the Lord 337, in the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus.

## Concerning Contracting a Sale

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Gregory.  
[Note: [Col. 0391C–D] d Some manuscripts read *Graeg.* Add Ps. P. 38: “Likewise another to Gregory.” In the Vatican Fragments the following words alone stand as the inscription: “Augustus and Caesar,” with neither the name of the official to whom it was given nor that of the emperor. The subscription there also differs; see the following note. Wenckius, in his edition of C. Th., p. 152 ff., note a; A. de Buchholtz, edition of the Vatican Fragments, p. 323; and Schilling, *Bemerkungen über römische Rechtsgeschichte*, p. 392, note 1090, discussed the question. The editor thinks that the second law under this title is a repetition of the Constantinian law preserved in the Vatican Fragments, with its inscription and subscription altered; Roman examples of this are numerous.]

Whoever purchases shall ascertain the tax assessment of the thing purchased; nor shall anyone be permitted either to purchase or to sell a thing without its assessment.  
[Note: [Col. 0391C–0392B] e The Vatican Fragments precede these words with the following passage: “With no interval of modesty or repose, nor any delay whatsoever for hesitation, now individuals, now whole peoples, rushing before our eyes, poured forth complaints so uniform in almost the same expressions that neither could the credulity of the petitioners be answered nor the nature of their allegations distinguished, most dear and most affectionate parent” [V.: *parens carissime atque amantissime*; Mai and Buchholtz: *parens karissime atque augustalis*]. “For by an equal example consuls and multitudes loudly declared that their property had not been justly sold; that, while others possessed it, they themselves paid fiscal dues; and, finally, with repeated entreaty they sought a remedy. We were greatly moved by this, fearing that persons persuaded by the crafty profit of certain adversaries might sell their property without its assessment and afterwards seek the aid of our clemency; and that, when contrivances of cunning were intermingled with their artifices, we might, without suspecting the hidden designs of deceivers, judging others by the character of our own innocence, relieve persons guilty of harming the tax assessment. These frauds, these deceits, these subtleties we prohibit by law and exclude by constitution; and therefore, after deliberate consideration of just providence, we enact that absolutely whoever,” etc. Schroeter, III. cited work, p. 349, wishes the entire paragraph from the Vatican Fragments to be restored to the Code itself; but see Wenckius, *E. L. L.* 1826, no. 136, p. 1084 (*Opp.*, p. 439).]

Public or fiscal inspection must be required by this law, so that if anything is sold without assessment and is reported by another, the seller shall lose possession, while the purchaser shall lose the price he gave, the fisc claiming it.  
[Note: [Col. 0392B–C] a Code of Justinian: “since it is necessary that he who has purchased should know the assessment of the thing purchased, nor may …”; Vatican Fragments: “he who purchases shall know the right and assessment of the thing purchased, nor may …” b Code of Justinian: *cuiquam*. c Vatican Fragments and Code of Justinian omit *vel*, “or.” d V.: *publicae*; Mai: *publice*; 15: *vel publ. f.* e Several manuscripts: *ac legi*; 8: *debit*; 10: *debet*. f 19 and Go., in the note: *aliquis sine*; 15 omits *sine*. g Be.’s conjecture is confirmed by the Vatican Fragments and manuscript 15. Likewise 9: *venerit*. The remaining manuscripts and editions, Sich. through Ri*: *vendiderit*, which can be defended. h Vatican Fragments add *et post ab aliquo*; 19: *id ad alium*. i V., Mai, Hollw.: *deferretur*; 8, 9, 19–21, Sich.: *defertur*, not badly; 15: *deferatur*. j 8 and Sich. add *amittat*; 21: *amittit*; from the Interpretation, 18: *possessionem perdat*, “lose possession.” 20 omits *vero*. k 20: *pretio*; Aur., Lugd. omit *pretium*. l Vatican Fragments: *deperdat*.]

§1. It has also seemed proper that no one may enter upon the sale of any property unless, at the time when the contract is formally concluded between seller and buyer, the certain and true ownership is demonstrated by the neighbours.  
[Note: [Col. 0392C] m Vatican Fragments: “We also wish it to be made known to all that it has pleased our clemency that no one ought to seek or enter upon the sale of any property unless …” 20: *cujuslibet liceat acc.*; 21 adds *ut*. n V.: *quom*; 8: *quod*. o 19: *vend. et tempore c.* p W. printed *explicatur* from the Vatican Fragments. All editions and manuscripts have *ut certa et vera*; Go. had already judged that *ut* should be removed as arising from the preceding *explicatur*. q Vatican Fragments: “ownership, with the neighbours present, shall be demonstrated”; 10: *demonstratur*.]

The safeguard of this law extends so far that, even if benches—or, as people commonly say, stools—are sold, proof of the ownership to be displayed must be completed.
