[Note: [Col. 0392C–D] r Vatican Fragments: *currente*; all manuscripts and Sich.–Lugd. likewise; Cuj. 2–W.: *decurrente*; 9: *ratione*. s 6–8, 10, 14, 16, 17, 21 omit *si*. t Several manuscripts: *subsellie*. u 6, 7, 10, 14, 17, 18 omit *ut*. v 10, 18: *agunt*; then 21: *vendentur*, and 19, 20: *ostendite*. x 10, 18: *impleatur*; V., Mai: *completur*.]

§2. Nor shall the formalities between buyer and seller be performed in carefully contrived hidden passages,  
[Note: [Col. 0392D] y 20: *adquisitis*. z 10, 18: *celebrantur se*.]  
but fraudulent sale, utterly buried, shall perish—  
[Note: [Col. 0392D–0393C] aa This paragraph is abridged, retaining a few words, from the longer and wordier discourse preserved for us by the Vatican Fragments: “For from this source many disputes arise; from this source rights of ownership are recklessly violated; from this source trouble is produced for most ancient titles, when, in overhasty blindness and with inquiry into the property neglected, the light of truth omitted and the perpetuity of ownership not considered, the principle of law set aside, they enter upon buying property; all matters omitted, ignored, and neglected, they hurry and hasten to this, that by any means whatsoever FORMALITIES MAY BE PERFORMED IN I KNOW NOT WHAT HIDDEN PASSAGES between buyer and seller. Yet it is far better, as we have said, that a qualified seller should establish the light of truth by trustworthy testimony, public proclamation, and the acclamations of the people, so that the purchaser may thus remain fortunate and secure for a long age. We say this for the tranquillity of the whole succession, lest perhaps some seller claim as his own what is known to belong to another. Thus the purchaser, worse than an evil seller, heedless and credulous, though he ought to inquire into all things with the neighbours testifying, neglects universal investigation, because he thinks he must proceed in such a way that even that should not be investigated which is expressed in law: ‘IF THE THING HAS BEEN SOLD BY THE OWNER.’ Wenckius thinks this a legal formula. Therefore the solemnity of all sales must be conducted in this way: that that deceptive and FRAUDULENT SALE, UTTERLY BURIED, MAY PERISH. Henceforth all must obey this law, so that, after all matters have been investigated with careful circumspection, transactions may pass safely through every succession, and malicious traps may not overwhelm anyone through an unforeseen contingency” [V.: *casum*; see W. on this passage and *Opp.*, p. 425; also Hollw. on Vatican Fragments §35, note 54; Bg. conjectures *casus aut cassum*].]

*[The source breaks off in the middle of the word: “depe-”.]*

[…..][Col. 0393] Given on the day before the Nones of February, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus (337).  
[Note: [Col. 0393C] a 42 adds *id*. b 20: *Felice*; 28 and 40 omit “Felicianus and Titianus, consuls”; 16 omits “and Titianus”; several manuscripts: *Tetiano*. Vatican Fragments: “Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, at the …, to the corrector of Picenum, at Aquileia. Received on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, at Alba, Constantine Augustus consul for the third time (313).” See Hollw., cited place, note 56.]

### Interpretation

Whoever purchases an estate shall know that he has purchased the tax due upon the property itself, as well as the right of possession; for no one may either purchase or sell land without its tax or fiscal payment.  
[Note: [Col. 0393C] c 6, 7, 10, 18 add *homo*, “person.” d 20 adds *quam*. e 20: *agnoscat*. f 6, 7, 9, 10, 42: *nulli*; 20: *agrum nulli*.]

But if anyone, concealing the fiscal payment, has dared to sell or presumed to purchase,  
[Note: [Col. 0393D] g Several manuscripts: “either to sell or to purchase.” h Sich. omits *praesumpserit* through *quod et*.]  
those between whom the contract has been concluded by such a secret transaction shall know that the purchaser loses the price and the seller loses possession.  
[Note: [Col. 0393D] i 20, above the line: *celebrata*. j 6, 7: “the price itself, he who”; 8: “he loses the price itself, he who.”]

For it is ordered that the neighbours of the property sold must be present as witnesses;  
[Note: [Col. 0393D] k 6, 7, 10, 18: “the neighbours are ordered”; Sich. omits “because it is ordered”; 9, 20, 21, 42, and Sich. in the margin: *quia jubet*, “because it orders”; 43 omits “it is ordered … present.” l 6, 7: “be witnesses so that they ought”; 20: “ought to be.”]  
indeed, even if something among ordinary goods is sold for use, it should be shown to the neighbours  
[Note: [Col. 0393D] m 6–8 and other manuscripts omit *in tantum*, “to such an extent.” n 7, 42, 43: *vendito*; 6 according to Ri.: *venditor*; 20: “for use and seller.” o 6–8, 10, 18: *ostendit*. p 20 adds *scientibus*, “with their knowledge.”]  
and so purchased, lest another’s property be sold.  
[Note: [Col. 0393D] q Several manuscripts: *nec*, “and not.”]

## How Civic Obligations Are Imposed

[Col. 0393B]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Council of the Province of Africa.  
[Note: [Col. 0393D] r Go., in the *Chronicle*: “to the council of the provinces of Africa.”]  
We order that perpetual sacerdotales and flamines, as well as duumvirales, be exempt from superintendence of the annona and from inferior public obligations.  
[Note: [Col. 0393D] s 4, Cuj. 1: *flammines*; Til.: *flamines*; Ri*: *sacerdotes*, “priests.” t 4: “we order them to be exempt”; corrected in red ink to “exempt.”]  
And so that this may be established in perpetual observance, we have ordered this law, engraved on bronze tablets, to be published. Posted on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, at Carthage, in the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus (337).  
[Note: [Col. 0393D–0394C] u In A, Ri*, *hanc*, “this,” is absent. a 4, Til.–Cuj. 2*, Ri., Ri*: *Karthagini*; Be.: *Karthagine*; Go.: *Kartagini*; Ri*: “posted on the thirteenth day before …” b 4 and editions before Be.: *Tatiano*.]

## Concerning the Exemptions of Craftsmen

The Emperor Constantine Augustus  
[Note: [Col. 0394C–D] c Code of Justinian: “The Emperor Constantine,” agreeing therefore with C. Th.; nor does it differ in the subscription. Since Constantine died already on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June of this year, Go. thinks either that the inscription must be altered or that the subscription should read “the fourth day before the Nones of April.” Rel. speaks to the same effect, cited place, p. 310. Be. says: “Either the subscription must be changed, or the inscription should read: ‘The Emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, Augusti’; for Constantine the Great had already died in May.” The editor has no doubt that the law was made while Constantine was alive, although published after his death, and does not accept Be.’s proposed inscription, because only on the fifteenth day before the Ides of September were Constantine’s three sons proclaimed Augusti in his place, according to Idatius.]  
to Maximus . . . .  
[Note: [Col. 0394D] d The rank is absent in manuscript 4, in the Code of Justinian, and in the editions; Be., following Go. in the note, adds “Praetorian Prefect.” Go. and Ri. mark the absent rank by six dots, Ri* by seven; elsewhere there is no indication of the lacuna.]

Craftsmen of the arts listed in the brief schedule below, residing in individual cities, we order to be exempt from all public obligations, since leisure must be afforded for learning the arts, so that they may be more eager both to become more skilled themselves and to educate their sons.  
[Note: [Col. 0394D] e Code of Justinian: “since indeed leisure must be afforded in learning”; Go. rightly prefers the reading of the Theodosian Code. f 4: *peritores*, with *i* added above *o* by another hand.]  
Given on the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus (337).  
[Note: [Col. 0394D] g Code of Justinian: *Conss.* And that date is recorded.]

## Concerning All Deserted Land, and When Barren Lands Are Imposed upon Fertile Ones

The Emperor Constantine. If anyone has purchased any property under private law from an emphyteutic or patrimonial possessor, the substance of which had customarily supported other estates, and, as though the sinews of certain powers had been cut, the remaining estates collapse, he shall assume the burdens of those estates which will remain useless in the hands of the impoverished seller. Given on the Ides of December, at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus (337). (From the Code of Justinian.)

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Ursus. The *rationalis* shall decide cases belonging to the fisc, all extortions being prohibited. Given on the Nones of February, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus, 337. (From the Code of Justinian.)

## Enactments without Year

(From the Code of Justinian.)

## Concerning Dignities

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Volusianus, Praetorian Prefect. The gates of office shall not stand open to persons of ill repute and notoriety, to those stained by crime or baseness of life, or to those whom infamy separates from the company of honourable persons.

## Concerning All Deserted Land; Concerning the Assessment of Patrimonial and Emphyteutic Estates

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Proculus, Proconsul of Africa. Emphyteutic possessors, who by the benefit of our clemency are not summoned to extraordinary public obligations as other provincials are, shall render their service in repairing roads. For they ought by no means to be excluded from that which will profit all in common.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Campesius. Since our deified parent Aurelian ordered municipal councils to be summoned concerning deserted estates, and ordered them, after receiving a three-year exemption for those same estates, to satisfy the regular charges for lands which could find no owners: preserving this arrangement, we command that, if the councils are found insufficiently able to take on those same estates, the burdens of those lands shall be apportioned among the estates and territories which they have accepted.

## Concerning Fugitive Slaves

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Probus. If fugitive slaves are caught crossing over to the barbarians, they shall either be disabled by amputation of a foot, consigned to the mines, or subjected to some other punishment.

## Concerning Interest

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the People. If a defendant denies that the handwriting produced in a petition or other document is his own, and is convicted by comparison—that is, by another sample of his handwriting being produced and compared with that in the document—he shall pay the plaintiff twenty-four solidi as a penalty for false denial. But if either the notary before whom the instrument was drawn up is produced, or other witnesses testify to the truth, then, in addition to the penalty of twenty-four gold pieces, he shall not be permitted to raise the defence of money not paid, alleging that, although an instrument was made, what is written in it was nevertheless not given; rather, he shall in every event be condemned, even if in fact nothing at all was paid to him.

§1. These provisions shall prevail when someone is sued upon his own contract. But if he is a tutor or curator of one of those persons customarily under guardianship, whether male or female, administering under the constitutions the guardianship of his own children, and he has denied the handwriting produced in the contract of those under guardianship or curatorship, then, if they are convicted of lying by comparison alone, they themselves shall pay twenty-four gold pieces. But if by production of the notary or witnesses, the defence of money not paid shall not be taken away from those under guardianship or curatorship—for they have committed no wrong—while the tutors or curators themselves shall pay the plaintiff another twenty-four gold pieces as a penalty; those under guardianship or curatorship retaining intact their defence of money not paid. For it is not equitable that they should suffer loss through the wrongs of others.

§2. Having spoken concerning defendants, the constitution also turns to plaintiffs. It orders that, if a plaintiff denies his own handwriting contained in a document produced against him—for example, a document said to record an acknowledgment he made—he likewise, if convicted by comparison alone, shall pay twenty-four gold pieces. But if convicted through production of the notary or witnesses, he shall in every manner be charged with and acknowledge the contents of that document, even if they were not in fact received by him. This applies if he sues in his own name. But if he is a tutor or curator, he shall indeed pay twice the penalty of twenty-four gold pieces; whereas the person under guardianship or curatorship may raise against the proof the defence of money not paid.

## Concerning Eunuchs

The Emperor Constantine to Aurelius, Duke of Mesopotamia. If anyone after this enactment makes eunuchs within the Roman world, he shall suffer capital punishment; and the slave so treated, as well as the place where this was committed, shall be confiscated if the owner knew and concealed it.

## Concerning Patrimonial Estates

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Dracontius. We command that payment of the assessment of a patrimonial estate, whether in gold or grain, omitted within the prescribed period, shall not prejudice the ownership of minors nor operate to defraud their rights, if what is regularly due is paid somewhat later. Provided, however, that while the property of the children remains intact, the judge shall exact from the tutor or curator through whom payment is delayed the penalties for his negligence and abandonment of office, and compel him to make good the losses.

## Concerning Estates of the *Res Privata* and Forest Lands of the Imperial Household

The Emperor Constantine Augustus. Let all know that those properties which they have purchased, or purchase, from our fisc shall never be recovered by us under any claim of right, but shall be left to them as possessions secured by their own title, and to their descendants in the enduring permanence of perpetual ownership.

## Concerning Slaves

[Col. 0396C]

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Bassus, Praetorian Prefect. Whenever a dispute concerning status has arisen, if the person said to be a slave alleges that his master has first seized something from him, it is proper first to consider whether he claims freedom from possession as a slave, or whether he is summoned into slavery from possession of freedom. But if it is established that he seeks freedom from servile services, it is fitting first to decide the case concerning status, and then, if the matter requires it, to hear the issue of the property seized.

But if the person summoned into slavery states that something has been seized from him, all that is established to have been taken should be restored to the person alleged to be a slave only if he has promised through suitable sureties that the property will remain secure. For if he cannot provide such sureties, then the things concerning which the case will be tried should be placed in sequestration until the day on which the dispute is settled, so that from them—if no other resources are available—only such litigation expenses and maintenance for the person may be supplied as the judge in his moderate discretion considers appropriate.

But when things have been seized by someone before litigation concerning status has yet been initiated, and a judgment has been rendered for restoration of possession of the things, and that person, in order not to comply with this judgment, raises a dispute concerning status, he shall be obliged both to restore the same things without security and then to pursue the case of freedom according to the order of law.

## Mandate

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Volusianus, Praetorian Prefect. In a matter entrusted by mandate, not only money—regarding which the action on mandate is most certain—but reputation also is at risk. For everyone is manager and arbiter of his own affairs, and conducts not every business but most according to his own inclination; but another’s affairs are conducted under exact duty, and no neglect or deviation in their administration is free from fault.

## Concerning Fathers Who Have Sold Their Children

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the Provincials, greetings. If anyone, on account of extreme poverty and want, sells for sustenance his newborn son or daughter, still bloodstained from birth, the sale being valid only in this case, the purchaser shall have the right to retain that person’s service. Yet the seller, the person alienated, or any other person may reclaim him or her to original free status, provided that he offers either the price that the person may be worth or a slave in exchange.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Italicus. If anyone considers that he has an action against our tenant, the matter must be referred to the illustrious Count of the Private Estates, lest danger to the judge’s reputation and to the safety of his office arise. Given on the Kalends of February, in the consulship …

## Concerning Interest

The Emperor Constantine to the People. For gold, silver, and clothing, we have ordered that lawful interest may be paid or promised by written acknowledgment.

## Concerning Incestuous and Invalid Marriages

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Patroclus. There can be no lawful marriage with slave women, for slaves are born from such a union; and therefore we command that decurions shall not, led by lust for slave women, flee into the households of the most powerful persons. For if a decurion, secretly and without the knowledge of estate-managers and procurators, joins himself to another’s slave woman, we order both that the woman be sent to the mines by judicial sentence and that the decurion himself be deported to an island. All his property shall be assigned to the city of which he was a curialis, if he has been freed from paternal power and has no children, parents, or relatives called to his succession under the order of law.

But if the estate-managers or procurators of the place where the offence was committed knew of it, or did not wish to disclose the discovered crime, they too shall be consigned to the mines.

But if the owner of the place permitted this to be done, or afterwards concealed the act after learning of it, then, if it occurred on an estate, the estate, with its slaves, livestock, and other things maintained for agricultural cultivation, shall be claimed for the rights of the fisc. But if it occurred in a city, we command half of all his property to be confiscated, increasing the penalty because, within domestic walls, a crime was committed which he did not wish to make public immediately after learning of it.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect. Before our council, or before consuls, praetors, governors, provincial governors, or magistrates of those cities that possess this jurisdiction, diligent service may obtain freedom by the judgment of patrons.

The Emperors Constantine and Licinius Augusti to Euthymius, governor of Cappadocia. We order that all letters of the plaintiff which she sent to Aelius as though to a leading municipal citizen shall be empty and void and recalled; and that an inquiry be made into the free status of the same Aelius. Nor shall it prejudice the woman that she wrote to him as though he were a decurion and leading citizen, or that he himself pretended to be a decurion or leading citizen—especially since not only is his servile condition known through the testimony of witnesses and the servile yoke of his kinship, but Aelius’s own statement before another court had also shown that he appeared to be of servile condition.

## Concerning the Four-Year Limitation

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Orphitus, P. V. [rank abbreviated in the source]. It is known that the fisc may not begin an inquiry after four continuous years concerning vacant property. It is further added that those who rely upon our grant shall not be troubled by any disturbance, nor shall our fisc initiate a controversy against those who have possessed the same things by whatever means or title.

## Concerning the Duties of a Proconsul and a Legate

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Aelius, Proconsul of Africa. Legates shall hear not only civil but also criminal cases, provided that, if they determine that sentence should be pronounced upon defendants, they do not delay in sending them to the proconsuls.

## Concerning the Duties of the Master of Offices

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the *agentes in rebus*. The privileges previously granted to your school, and preserved intact, shall remain; no one shall attain the two-hundred-man command, the one-hundred-man command, or the *biarchia* by favour, but each by service. He shall obtain the chiefship as the roster runs its course, so that those whom the order of military service calls forth, together with the assistant in those labours, may go out to discharge official duties and the postal service. Moreover, the person in whom the standing of the whole school and the security of its master are placed, suitable through uprightness of character and good qualities, shall be presented to our view by the master, so that he may be appointed at our discretion. Posted at Rome, in the Forum of Trajan.

## Concerning Farmers and Slaves of the Imperial Domain, Whether of the Public or Private Fisc

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Constantine, Praetorian Prefect. No original colonus of our private estate shall at all be summoned to any honours or to any other civic duties. For the municipal councils and the others from whom nominations must be made because of their numbers, being in every respect flourishing, ought not through an injurious nomination to descend to these final resources.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Januarius, Praetorian Prefect. We order that our coloni of the private estate who are suitable either for keeping accounts or cultivating fields be recalled and devoted solely to cultivation of our property; indeed, this shall henceforth be observed, that none of them undertake to manage another person’s private estate or administer anything.

The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Equitius, Master of Horse and Foot. Slaves, coloni, their sons, grandsons, and anyone whatsoever who has secretly fled from our estates and possessions to various offices shall be returned, even if they have taken the military oath in armed service. For we order even those who have acquired the title of *protectores* to be stripped of their belts and restored.

### ON NOT PROVIDING *SALGAMUM* TO GUESTS

Emperor Constantine Augustus: Let no one, under the name of Counts, Tribunes, Commanders, or soldiers, extort from the hosts assigned to him, for the sake of *salgamum*, bedding, firewood, or oil; nor, even with the hosts’ consent, take anything from them of the aforesaid kinds. Let our provincials be secure from this imposition, while Counts, Tribunes, or indeed Commanders and soldiers are subject to severe punishment for molestation. Given on the fifth day, at the same place, in October.

### IN WHAT CASES REGISTERED COLONI MAY ACCUSE THEIR MASTERS

[Col. 0399B]

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Vicar of the East. If any colonus is required by his master to render more than was formerly customary, and more than was exacted in previous times [Col. 0400A], let him approach the judge whose presence he can first obtain and establish the offence; so that the person convicted of demanding more than he had customarily received may be prohibited from doing so in future, after first restoring what he is known to have extorted by excessive exaction.

### ON EXEMPTIONS FROM PUBLIC BURDENS

Emperor Constantine Augustus to Catullinus, Vicar. It has seemed proper that dealers in clothing, linen-workers, purple-dyers, and *particarii*, who serve our devotion, should be exempt from every public burden according to ancient custom.

### ON SHIPWRECKS

[Col. 0400B] Emperor Constantine Augustus. Whenever a ship has been driven ashore by shipwreck, or whenever it has reached any land, it shall belong to its owners: my treasury shall not intervene. For what right has the treasury in another’s misfortune, that it should seek profit from so mournful a circumstance?

[Col. 0399]

Second Part. DISCOURSES.

(From Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*.)

## CONSTANTINE’S ADDRESS TO THE SYNOD ASSEMBLED IN THE PALACE, CONCERNING PEACE

[Note: [Col. 0399] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0399]

[Col. 0400B] This, dearest friends, was the fulfillment of my prayers: that at some time I might be granted the enjoyment of the sight of your assembly. Now that I have attained my desire, I give thanks to God, King of all, who, besides innumerable other benefits, has granted me the greatest of all blessings: [Col. 0400C] namely, to behold you all gathered together in one body and of one mind in agreement.

Let no malicious enemy henceforth disturb the happy condition of our affairs; nor, now that the tyranny of those who had declared war on God has been utterly destroyed and removed through the aid of God the Saviour, let the malignant demon again assail the divine law by some other method and contrivance with blasphemies and calumnies. For civil dissension in the Church of God seems to me more terrible and dangerous than every war and conflict; nor do external matters bring so much grief to my mind as these concerns.

At the time when, aided by God’s will and assistance, I had gained victory over my enemies, I thought that nothing remained for me [Col. 0400D] except to give thanks to the divine Majesty and to rejoice in common gladness with those whom God had, through my agency, vindicated into freedom. But when news of your dissension unexpectedly reached me, I judged that matter by no means to be neglected. Wishing, indeed, that a remedy might be applied to this evil through my own service also, I summoned you all without any delay.

I take the greatest delight in spirit when I behold you assembled. But I shall judge that I have fulfilled my desire only when I see the minds of you all joined and blended together, and peace and concord, as it were the common arbiter of all—a concord which it is fitting for you, consecrated as you are to God, [Col. 0401A] to commend and proclaim to others. Therefore, dearest ministers of God and faithful servants of the common Lord and Saviour of us all, exert yourselves: remove as swiftly as possible the causes of your mutual dissension, and dissolve without delay every knot of controversy by the laws of peace. In this way you will both do what is most pleasing to God, supreme over all, and confer an immense benefit upon me, your fellow-servant.

[Col. 0399B] The fulfillment of my prayer, friends, was to enjoy the sight of your company; and, having attained this, I acknowledge my gratitude to the King of all, because, beyond all other things, he has granted me also this blessing, greater than every good: [Col. 0399C] namely, to receive you all gathered together and to behold one common mind of concord among all. Let no envious enemy, then, injure our prosperity; nor, now that the God-defying tyranny of the tyrants has been removed out of the way by the power of God the Saviour, let the evil-loving demon encompass the divine law with blasphemies by another means. For, in my judgment, the civil dissension of the Church of God is more dreadful and grievous than every war and battle; and these matters appear more painful than external ones.

When, indeed, by the nod and cooperation of the Higher Power I had won victories over enemies, I thought that nothing remained except to render thanks to God and to rejoice together with those who had been liberated through us for his sake. But when I learned, contrary to every expectation, of your dissension, I did not treat the report as a secondary matter; and, praying that this too might receive healing through my service, [Col. 0399D] I immediately summoned you all together. I rejoice in seeing your gathering; but I shall judge that I have accomplished my prayer especially when I see all of you united and mingled in soul, and one common peaceful harmony governing all—a harmony which it would be fitting for you, as persons consecrated to God, to advocate also to others.

Do not delay, then, friends; do not delay, ministers of God and good servants of the common Master and Saviour of us all. Begin at once to remove the causes of dissension among you, and resolve every bond of dispute by the laws of peace. Thus you will have done what is pleasing to God who is over all, [Col. 0402A] and will bestow an extraordinary favour upon me, your fellow-servant.

## ADDRESS TO THE ASSEMBLY OF SAINTS

[Note: [Col. 0401C] *Address to the Assembly of Saints.* After the four books on the life and piety of Emperor Constantine, Eusebius had appended two discourses: one by Emperor Constantine to the Assembly of Saints, or to the Church of God; the other composed by Eusebius himself, concerning the construction and offerings of the martyr-shrine at Jerusalem, as Eusebius himself attests in chapters 32 and 46 of Book IV. The latter discourse of Eusebius is no longer extant. The former, however, is so corrupted by errors that it would almost have been preferable had it not survived. Yet, since it is an outstanding monument of a religious prince and an illustrious specimen of his studies and ability, I think I shall perform a worthwhile task if I apply care and diligence to correcting and explaining it.]

[Note: [Col. 0401] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0401]

## CHAPTER I.—THE PROEM MENTIONS PASCHA, AND STATES THAT CHRIST, THOUGH HE HAD BESTOWED MANY BENEFITS UPON ALL HUMANS, WAS EVILLY TREATED BY THOSE SAME PEOPLE

[Col. 0401]

[Col. 0401B] The radiance of sun and day, brighter than usual—the beginning of the resurrection; the new restoration of bodies long dissolved—the foundation of the promise; the path leading to eternal life: the day of the Passion is now present, dearest teachers and all other friends. And you, peoples of believers, far happier than the rest, who devoutly worship God himself, the author of religion, and without intermission praise him, both with inward perception and with tongues and voices, according to the prescriptions of the sacred oracles.

But you, Nature, mother of all things: what have you ever accomplished of this sort for human benefit? Or rather, what work anywhere is yours? For he who is the author of all things was the maker of your substance. He it is who adorned you. For the ornament of nature is life [Col. 0401C] suitably in accordance with nature.

But afterwards that which is wholly contrary to nature prevailed: that no one should venerate God, the author of all, with fitting worship, and that all things should be thought to occur not through the providence of the divine Majesty but by some chance and randomly. Although the prophets, inspired by the divine Spirit, clearly announced this very fact—and their words ought to have been believed—unjust impiety resisted in every way, pursuing the very light of truth with hatred and embracing the impenetrable darkness of error.

Nor was violence and cruelty absent, especially when the authority of rulers supported the rash assault of the populace—or rather, when rulers themselves presented themselves as leaders of untimely frenzy. Thus this manner of life, strengthened by the practice of many generations, brought the people of those times very many calamities.

But when the presence of our Saviour first shone forth, justice immediately arose in place of injustice, serenity in place of the most violent storm, and all that had been foretold by the prophets was fulfilled. For after this same [Col. 0404B] Saviour had been taken up to his Father’s dwelling, and had surrounded the whole inhabited world with the radiant splendours of reverence and moderation, he established on earth his Church as a sacred temple of virtue: eternal and incorruptible, in which worship due both to God the supreme Father and appropriate to himself might be performed with piety.

But what did the mad malice of the nations devise after this? It strove to cast away Christ’s benefits and gifts, to overthrow the Church of God, established for the salvation of all, and to substitute its own superstition in its place. Again dissensions; again battles and wars; again peevishness, luxurious provision for life, and love of wealth. This, though unnatural in human beings—as belongs to wickedness—now entices by hopes adorned with false appearances, now strikes terror by fear. Yet let this lie low, as justice requires, conquered by virtue and tearing and rending itself in repentance. We, however, must now speak of what accords with divine teaching.

[Note: [Col. 0401C]

**Ὁρμαὶ θ᾽ ὑποσχέσεως**—“foundations of the promise.” In Morel’s copy, as also in the margin of the Geneva edition [Col. 0401D], this is corrected to **ὅρμαιον**, a word which I do not recall ever having read anywhere. But Scaliger’s copy corrected it to **ἕρμαιον**, which comes closer to the reading of the manuscripts. Certainly the royal manuscript reads **ἕρμαι**, from which I conjectured that **ἕρμα**, that is, “foundation,” should be written. He elegantly calls the Lord’s resurrection the foundation of the promise. Nor does Christophorson translate badly when he renders it “pledge of the promise,” which amounts to the same thing. For a pledge is given as security; hence the Greeks call it **ἐνέχυρον**. In the Fuk. manuscript and Savile’s copy I found **ἕρμαιον** written.

**Μακαριώτερα δὲ πολλῷ πλήθη**—“but peoples far happier.” I do not agree with the learned men who, joining this with what precedes, read it as **μακαριάτε πολλὰ πλήθη**, etc. For if read thus, the repetition would be pointless, since Constantine had already said, “and all the remaining men, friends.” By these words Constantine greets the whole Catholic populace in the manner of preachers. Therefore the words **μακαριώτερα δὲ πολλῷ πλήθη** [Col. 0402C] begin another period, in which Constantine heightens the blessedness of the Catholic people. Moreover, I would prefer to read **πλήθη τυγχάνετε**, so that Constantine addresses the populace itself. Yet in the Fuk. manuscript and Savile’s copy this passage reads: “and many blessed peoples of worshippers, praising without ceasing God himself, the God of religion, through each person’s inward senses and through utterances, according to what is proclaimed in the divine ordinances.”

**Τῆς σῆς οὐσίας**—“of your substance.” Christophorson followed this reading. But, upon closer examination, I think the received reading ought here to be retained. For Constantine says that nature is not the maker of things, since God created it, and that he is not only the author of nature itself but also of the holiness which is in [Col. 0402D] it. For it is God who adorned nature. The ornament of nature, indeed, is life according to God’s law and ordinance. This is the sense of the passage, which Christophorson failed to notice. I say nothing of de Portes, whom I have found almost everywhere extremely incompetent. Yet in the manuscripts of Fuket, Turnèbe, and Savile, and in the royal papers, **οὐσίας** is written.

**Ἡ κατὰ φύσιν ζωή**—“life according to nature.” It should read **ἡ κατὰ Θεὸν ζωή**, “life according to God,” as is clear from the preceding note: in one word, **θεοσέβεια**, that is, religion, is nature’s ornament. In the received reading, however, I do not see what sense lies beneath it. Thus our Eusebius entitled his books on the life of Emperor Constantine *Concerning the Life according to God* (**περὶ τοῦ κατὰ Θεὸν βίου**). In the royal papers is written **ἡ κατὰ κόσμον ζωή**, “life according to the world.”

**Ἐπικεκράτηκε γάρ**—“for it has prevailed.” It should read: **ἐπικεκράτηκε δὲ οὐ μετρίως ὃν παρὰ φύσιν**, etc. Certainly in the Fuk. manuscript it is written: “But the things contrary to nature have prevailed beyond measure: that no one should worship the God of all worthily,” etc.

[Col. 0403C] **Δεισιδαιμονίαν. ἀνόσιος.** In the royal manuscript the final two words are absent, and an empty space sufficient for one word has been left. I do not doubt that one should read **τὴν οἰκείαν δεισιδαιμονίαν ἀντεισάγειν**, “to introduce its own superstition in return,” deleting the word **ἀνέτρεπε**, which is wholly superfluous. In the Fuk. manuscript the passage is written thus: “to lay waste the Church; and it overthrew its own superstition. Again impious …” In the royal papers, however, is written **νςσος αὖθις**, etc. [Col. 0403D]; Savile corrected in the margin of his copy: **ἀνέτρεπε δὲ τὴν οἰκείαν δεισιδ…**. Upon more careful examination, I think the passage should be restored as follows: “to lay waste the Church; but it overthrew its own prosperity. Again disease, etc.” That is, when the Gentiles undertook to ravage and overthrow Christ’s Church, they overturned their own prosperity. “Again diseases and dissensions,” etc. The word **δεισιδαιμονίαν** may also be retained, so that the sense is: while the Gentiles persecuted the Church, they ruined their own religion. For the Church of God, assailed by the persecutions of the Gentiles, overcame the superstition and worship of false deities.

**Δυστραπελία.** Turnèbe corrected in the margin of his copy: **δυστραπελίαι**. Certainly the Fuk. manuscript reads **δυστραπελίας**. But in the royal papers **δύστραπελος** is read, after which several lines are omitted. Perhaps it should be written continuously: **δύστραπελος βίου παρασκευή**, “a peevish provision for life.” Unless we read thus, [Col. 0404C] what will become of the following phrase **βίου παρασκευή**, “provision for life,” which Constantine counts among evils? Musculus apparently read **βίαιος βίου παρασκευή**, for he translates “a violent furnishing of sustenance.” Soon afterward the Fuk. manuscript has: “which, though unnatural, being proper to wickedness, sometimes …”

**Αὕτη μέν**—“yet this.” In Morel’s copy, and likewise in the margin of the Geneva edition, it is corrected to **ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὴ μέν**, etc., excellently, as those skilled in Greek know. [Col. 0404D] The subject understood is **ἡ πονηρία**, “wickedness.” In the Fuk. manuscript and Turnèbe’s copy **ἀλλ᾽ αὕτη** is likewise read.

**Τηρητέον.** The correction of this passage is owed to the Fuk. manuscript, in which **ῥητέον**, “must be said,” is distinctly read. No correction is more certain than this.]

[Col. 0402B] The exceptionally bright radiance of day and sun—the prelude of resurrection; the new fitting-together of bodies once dissolved; the foundations of the promise; and the path leading to eternal life—the day of the Passion is present, dearest teachers, and all you remaining men, friends. But far more blessed are the many peoples of worshippers, who without ceasing praise God himself, the God of religion, through the inward perceptions of each and through utterances, according to what is proclaimed in the divine ordinances.

But you, Nature, universal mother, what such thing have you ever accomplished for the world? Indeed, what work is yours at all, if he who is the cause of all things is also the cause of your substance? For he adorned you, since the ornament is life according to nature. Yet things contrary to nature have prevailed beyond measure: that no one should worship the God of all worthily, and that all things should be thought to exist not through providence [Col. 0402C] but randomly, disorderly, and wrongly. And though divine inspiration announced every detail through prophets, whom it was necessary to believe, unjust and impious wickedness opposed it by every device: at war with the light of truth and embracing the darkness [Col. 0403A] that is difficult to refute.

Nor was this without violence and cruelty, especially because the judgment of those in power joined the unreflecting rush of the vulgar crowds—or rather, that judgment itself led their untimely madness. Therefore, this way of life, having become strong through many generations, became the cause of the greatest evils for those people. But when the Saviour’s manifestation immediately shone forth, justice arose from unjust deeds, serenity from every kind of surge, and all that had been foretold through prophets was fulfilled.

Accordingly, after being lifted on high to his ancestral dwelling, and having surrounded the inhabited world with the splendours of reverence and temperance, he established on earth the Church, a certain sacred temple of virtue—eternal and incorruptible—in which were performed with piety both the things due to God the supreme Father and those proper to himself. But what did the senseless wickedness of the nations devise after this? It undertook to cast away Christ’s gifts [Col. 0403B] and to ravage the Church established for the salvation of all; and it overthrew its own superstition. Again impious dissension, wars, battles, peevishness, provision for life, love of wealth: which, though unnaturally, as belongs to wickedness, sometimes charms with embellished hopes and sometimes overwhelms with fear. But let this lie on the ground, conquered by virtue, as is right, tearing and rending itself through repentance. We, however, must now speak what belongs to the divine Word.

## CHAPTER II.—AN ADDRESS TO THE CHURCH AND HEARERS, ASKING THEM TO FORGIVE AND CORRECT HIM IF HE HAS SAID ANYTHING LESS THAN RIGHTLY

[Col. 0403]

[Col. 0404C] Hear, then, helmsman possessed of purity and virginity; and you, Church, nurse of tender and inexperienced age, whose concern is truth and kindness, from whose perennial spring the saving stream flows. You too who sincerely worship God, and for that reason are his concern, listen favourably. Attend not so much to the wording as to the truth of the things said; look not at me who speak, but at the pious service of devotion.

For what grace or usefulness could speech possess if the disposition of the speaker had not first been examined? Perhaps I venture upon great things. Yet the love implanted in me toward God is the cause of my boldness, for it does violence to shame. Therefore, I ask you, who are more fully instructed than others in the knowledge of divine mysteries, to assist me, so that if I happen to err in speaking, you may follow my steps and correct me. Do not expect from me a finished system of teaching; rather, kindly approve the earnestness of my faith.

Moreover, may the unique aid of Father and Son breathe upon us now, as we utter what it commands and suggests to our mind. For if anyone professing rhetoric or [Col. 0405B] any other art hopes to complete his undertaking fully without the help of divine majesty, he is found inexperienced and imperfect in both himself and his undertaking. Yet those upon whom the aid of divine majesty has once breathed ought by no means to cease or grow sluggish. Therefore, having asked your pardon for the length of the proem, we shall attempt to approach the head and substance of our purpose.

[Note: [Col. 0404D]

**Ναύκληρε**—“helmsman.” Constantine calls the bishop thus, by a metaphor no less elegant than when they are called shepherds. Since the Church is customarily compared to a ship, bishops who govern it and are successors of the Apostles are rightly called shipmasters: Christ made them, from fishermen, pilots of the Church. He calls him endowed with purity and virginity because such were Christian priests: **ἁγνοὶ καὶ παρθενίαι**, “pure and virginal.”

**Σωτήριον νᾶμα**—“saving stream.” The Fuk. manuscript and the royal papers, along with Turnèbe’s copy, have **πόμα**, “drink.” Soon afterward, where **προσέχοντες τὸν νοῦν**, “applying the mind,” is read, the Fuk. manuscript writes **προσέχεται τοίνυν**. [Col. 0405C] **Ἅπερ ἂν αὐτῷ φράσει**—“whatever it may declare to him.” It should read **αὕτη**, the implied subject being “the inspiration of the Father,” as Christophorson reads it. Certainly in the Fuk. manuscript it is written: “as we utter these things which it itself may say and attach to our understanding.”

[Col. 0405D] **Τὸ μῆκος τῆς ἀναβολῆς παραιτησάμενοι**—“having asked pardon for the length of the *anabolē*.” Christophorson translated both this and the preceding period very badly. He thought **ἀναβολή** here meant delay and postponement, whereas in this place it means a proem. Constantine excuses himself for having used a longer proem. Strictly speaking, an *anabolē* is the opening of a song which a chorus was accustomed to sing first. Aristophanes, in the *Peace*, p. 685, says of dithyrambic poets: **ξυνελέγοντ᾽ ἀναβολὰς πετόμεναι**; the scholiast notes that *anabolai* are “the beginnings of songs” and cites a verse of Homer. Isocrates, in the *Panathenaicus*: “These are the things which I wished, both about myself and about others, to set forth beforehand like a chorus before the contest.” Thus the term was afterwards transferred from singers to orators; and they used **ἀναβάλλεσθαι** for **προοιμιάζεσθαι**, “to make a proem,” as Hesychius testifies. Ulpian, on Demosthenes’ speech *On the Chersonese*: “**ἀναβαλλόμενος**, with one lambda, means ‘having made a proem’; and **ἀναβολαί**, ‘proems.’” [Col. 0406C] Thus Aristophanes in the *Peace*, p. 717, used **προαναβάληται** and **ἀναβαλοῦ** in the same sense. Moreover, this passage shows that the proem of this discourse extends as far as these words.]

[Col. 0403C] Hear, then, helmsman who has attained purity and virginity, and Church, nurse of immature and unlearned age, to whom truth is a concern and kindness a concern, from whose ever-flowing spring a saving stream trickles. And may you too listen favourably, you who sincerely worship God and therefore are his concern, attending your minds not more to the diction [Col. 0406A] than to the truth of what is said, not to me the speaker but to the piety of consecration. For what grace could words have if the disposition of the speaker were left unexamined?

Perhaps, then, I venture upon great things; but I attribute my boldness to the inborn affection toward the divine, for it even compels modesty. Therefore I especially enlist as my helpers those knowledgeable in divine mysteries, so that, should any lapse occur in the discourse, you may accompany me and correct it, seeking not consummate instruction but approving the faithful character of my undertaking. May the greatest inspiration of the Father and of the Son be present with us in this work, as I utter what it may declare and attach to my mind.

For if anyone, pursuing rhetoric or any other discipline without God, supposes that he can sufficiently perfect his work, he is found incomplete, both himself and the undertaking to which he is devoted. Yet those who have ever obtained divine inspiration must neither grow weary [Col. 0406B] nor neglect their task. Therefore, having sought pardon for the length of the proem, let us attempt to bring our purpose to its completion.

## CHAPTER III.—THAT GOD IS FATHER OF THE WORD AND MAKER OF ALL THINGS, AND THAT THINGS COULD IN NO WAY SUBSIST IF THEIR CAUSES WERE DIVERSE

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405B] The good for which all things strive, being by its own nature always God, has no generation and therefore no beginning. Yet he himself is the beginning of all things that come to be. He who has his reference from him is again united and joined with him; for in him separation and conjunction occur not spatially [Col. 0405C] but intellectually alone. For the begotten one did not come to be through any loss to the Father’s inward parts, as things born from seed do, but by the ordinance of providence the Saviour was brought forth, to preside over this perceptible world and the works and products fashioned in it.

Thus, from him comes to all things encompassed by the world the cause of being and living; from him come soul, every sense, and the organs through which the things signified by the senses are accomplished. What, then, does this argument show? That there is one ruler of all beings, and that all things are subject to his sole dominion: the heavenly and earthly things, and both natural and organic bodies.

For if the dominion over these innumerable beings belonged not to one but to many, allotments and divisions of the elements, the old myths, envy, and grasping ambition striving with all their force to prevail, would disturb the harmonious concord of all things, since many would administer differently the portion allotted to each. But the fact that the entire world is always in the same condition and behaves in the same manner proves sufficiently that this occurs not without providence and has not come about by fortuitous chance.

Who could ever have known the maker of all created existence? To whom should prayers and supplications be addressed first, or last? In choosing to worship one of them according to my preference, how should I not be impious toward the others? Or if I were to ask for something necessary for this life, should I not thank the god who helped me and reproach the one who opposed me? Whom should I entreat to reveal to me the cause of my distress and obtain my release from it?

Let us suppose that an answer has been given to us through oracles and prophecies: that this lies not within their own power but pertains to another God. What mercy, then, what providence of God toward a human being is there? Unless perhaps one among them, being somewhat more humane, were violently moved against another who had no benevolent disposition toward humankind and offered assistance. Wrath, moreover, [Col. 0408C] faction, reproach, and finally the confusion of all things would follow, because each failed to mind his own affairs and, not satisfied with his allotted portion through greed, invaded another’s. What then would follow? Clearly the discord of heavenly beings would destroy the things beneath heaven and the earthly things: the ordering and succession of seasons, the benefit of fruits accustomed to arise at each season of the year, day itself, and the nocturnal rest that follows day would all be removed. But enough of this. Let us return to arguments which cannot be refuted.

[Note: [Col. 0406D]

**Οὗπερ τὴν οὐσίαν**—“whose essence.” I think one should read **ὁ ὑπὲρ τὴν οὐσίαν θεός**, “God who is above essence.” For the highest good is nothing other than the supreme God. Thus below, in chapter IX: “he first set forth God, who is above essence.” In the Fuk. manuscript and Savile’s copy **ὅπερ** is written, wrongly.

**Ὀργανικὰ σώματα**—“organic bodies.” Christophorson rendered this “artificial,” that is, things produced by some instrument rather than generated by nature; but I do not agree. Since Constantine is philosophizing throughout this entire discourse, in this place too he speaks, in the philosophers’ manner, of natural and organic bodies: bodies furnished with organs or instruments suitable for action. Aristotle speaks thus when he defines the soul as the actuality of an organic body. Moreover, “organic” is more extensive than “natural.” Some natural bodies lack organs—for example, stones and things of that kind.

[Col. 0407C] **Κλῆροι**—“allotments.” He alludes to the division of the world among the brothers Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto, as the Greek theologians imagined in myth.

**Διοικονουμένων.** In Fuket’s manuscript **διοικουμένων** is written.

[Col. 0407D] **Οὐκ ἀμελῶς ἔχειν**—“not to be without care.” Learned men added the negative particle, I suppose by conjecture, as also the immediately following words: “and proves that it did not come about of itself.” These words are not found at all in the royal manuscript, the old papers, or Robert Estienne’s edition; nor do they cohere in any way with what precedes. For Constantine is not now discussing providence, but only maintains that there is one first principle of all things. He proves this thus: if there were several gods, each would govern his own part; but for the whole world always to remain in one and the same order, they would be insufficiently attentive. Yet we see the contrary; therefore there are not several gods. This is Constantine’s first argument against the theology of the Gentiles. Therefore I read: “But if the whole world is always in the same and like condition, while they are careless …” The sense is then wholly clear. Yet because the very words set forth above are found in the Fuk. manuscript and in the copies of Savile and Turnèbe, our correction is unnecessary.

**Θεραπεύων ἐξ αἱρέσεως**—“worshipping by choice,” that is, at one’s discretion. It may also be read **ἐξαιρέτως**, “in a special manner.”

[Col. 0408D] **μὴ εἶναι δὲ τῆς ἑαυτῶν ἐξουσίας**—“that it is not within their own power.” This passage seems very obscure to me. Christophorson translates: “Suppose answers are given us through oracles; yet that these are performed not by their own and proper power, but pertain to some god.” But I do not see what this means. Having examined everything more carefully, I have finally discovered the true sense. Constantine says: If there are many gods, when I fall into misfortune, which of them shall I approach to explain the cause of the evil and free me from it? Let us suppose, he says, that Apollo, for example, replies that it is not in his power to free me, but that this belongs to another god. What could be clearer than this sense? Therefore one should write: **Ἄλλῳ δὲ ταῦτα ἀνήκειν Θεῷ**, “but that these matters pertain to another God.” Many such oracles are found in Greek histories, where Apollo replies to inquirers that they must appease Bacchus or Saturn if they wish to be freed from their affliction.]

[Col. 0406B] The Good toward which all things strive, whose essence is that he is always God, has no generation and therefore no beginning; but he himself is the beginning of all things in generation. He who has his reference from that One is again united with him, separation and conjunction in that One taking place not locally but intellectually. For the begotten being was not constituted through any loss of the Father’s inward parts, as indeed things from seeds are; rather, by the ordinance of providence, the Saviour was manifested as ruler over both the perceptible world and the things fashioned in it.

Therefore, for all things encompassed by the world, the cause of being and living comes from there; from there come soul, every sense, and the organs through which what is indicated by the senses is effected. What, then, does the discourse declare? That there is one ruler of all beings, and that all things are subject to his sole lordship: heavenly things, earthly things, and natural and organic bodies.

For if sovereignty over these innumerable [Col. 0407A] beings belonged not to one but to many, allotments and divisions of the elements, old myths, envy, and grasping ambition, prevailing according to their power, would disrupt the harmonious concord of all things, because many would administer differently the share allotted to each. Yet the fact that the entire world always remains in the same and identical condition proves that it is not uncared for and has not come about by chance. Who, then, could know the maker of all created existence? To whom should prayers and supplications be directed first or last? By worshipping one according to my choice, would I not be impious toward the rest? Or perhaps, if I needed something necessary for life, would I thank the one who helped and blame the one who thwarted me?

To whom, praying, would I ask to know the cause of my misfortune and obtain deliverance from it? Let us suppose that replies have been given us through sacred utterances and oracles, but that these matters are not within their own power and instead pertain to another God. What mercy, then, or what providence of God toward humanity exists? Unless perhaps the more humane one, violently disposed against the one who has no benevolent inclination, should bring help. But anger, faction, reproach, and finally a confusion of all things would follow, since they would not mind their own affairs and, through greed, would not be content with what fell to their share. What would follow thereafter? Clearly the discord of heavenly beings would destroy what lies under heaven and what is on earth: the ordering of seasons, changes of times, enjoyment of the fruits that grow in their seasons, day, and the night’s rest that succeeds it. But enough of these matters; let us return again to the unanswerable argument.

## CHAPTER IV.—ON THE ERROR OF THOSE WHO VENERATE IMAGES

[Col. 0407]

[Col. 0408C] Everything that has a beginning must also have an end. A beginning in time, moreover, is called generation. Everything arising from generation is subject to decay. Further, length of time itself effaces form and appearance. How, then, could those who originate from perishable generation be immortal?

Yet a certain opinion has spread among unreasoning crowds: that marriages and begetting of children occur among the gods. But if those who are begotten are immortal, and new ones are always being begotten, that race must necessarily overflow. Once this increase has occurred, what heaven or what earth could contain such a swarm of gods coming into being? And what shall we say about those people who join heavenly brothers to sister goddesses in the bond of marriage and charge them with adultery and licentiousness?

We declare boldly that the honours themselves and the tributes bestowed upon them by human beings are mingled with outrage and lewdness. For some sculptor, highly trained in his art, first conceives a certain form in his mind, then produces the work with artistic skill; and shortly thereafter, as if forgetfulness had overtaken him, he flatters his own creation and worships it as [Col. 0410B] an immortal god, while acknowledging that he himself, the statue’s father and maker, is mortal. They themselves point out the tombs and coffins of those supposedly incorruptible beings, and honour the departed with immortal honours, not knowing that what is truly blessed and incorruptible, being visible to the mind and comprehensible by thought, has no need of honour bestowed by perishable beings. For it requires neither a form by which it might be recognized nor endures a shape as an image or likeness. All these things occur for the sake of the departed; for they were human beings while they lived, partaking of a body.

[Note: [Col. 0409C]

**Ἀνάγκη τὸ γένος**—“the race must necessarily …” In the Fuk. manuscript, after the first word, there is a lacuna large enough for one word. I therefore write: **Πλημμυρεῖν ἀνάγκη αὐτῶν τὸ γένος**, “their race must necessarily overflow.”

[Col. 0409D] **Τίς οὖν οὐρανός**—“what heaven, then?” It should read **τίς ἂν οὐρανός**, as I found corrected in the margin of Morel’s copy. In the Fuket manuscript **τίς οὐρανός** is read without the particle.

**Ἤδη γάρ τις**—“for already someone.” I would prefer to read **ἤδη γοῦν τις**, “for certainly someone,” etc. A little later, where **διανοίᾳ προσλαβών**, “having conceived in mind,” is read, Morel’s copy corrects it in the margin to **προλαβών**, as does Gruter’s copy.

**ἑαυτὸν πατέρα**—“himself father.” The Fuk. manuscript more correctly reads **ἑαυτὸν τὸν πατέρα καὶ δημιουργόν**, “himself the father and maker,” etc.]

[Col. 0407C] Everything having a beginning also has an end. A beginning according to time is called generation; all things from generation are perishable, [Col. 0410A] and time obscures their form. How, then, could those from perishable generation be immortal? But such an opinion has become widespread among irrational crowds: marriages and procreation were thought to occur among the gods. If those born are immortal and are always being born, the race must necessarily overflow. And when such an addition has arisen, what heaven or what earth could contain so great a swarm of gods coming into being?

What would one say of men who join heavenly brothers in marital union and accuse them of adulteries and licentiousness? We say boldly that the honours themselves and the distinctions bestowed on them by people are mingled with outrages and wantonness. For someone trained in argument, a maker of statues, having conceived a form in his mind and fashioned it with technical skill, then, as though forgetfulness had come upon him, flatters his own creation, worshipping it as an immortal god [Col. 0410B] while acknowledging that he himself, the father and maker of the statue, is mortal. Yet they display tombs and coffins of those incorruptible beings themselves, and honour the departed with immortal honours, not knowing that what is truly blessed and incorruptible has no need of honour from perishable beings. For that which is visible to the mind and grasped by thought neither seeks a form by which it may be recognized nor admits a shape as image or type. All these things occur for the sake of the departed: for they were human beings when alive, partaking of body.

## CHAPTER V.—THAT CHRIST, THE SON OF GOD, CREATED ALL THINGS AND FIXED A DEFINITE TERM OF LIFE FOR EACH

[Col. 0409]

[Col. 0409C] But why, when about to praise the true God, do I stain my tongue with polluted words? I therefore resolve first to wash away that bitter drink with a pure draught. The pure draught is drawn from the perennial fountain of the virtues of the God whom we praise. I regard it as my own particular duty to praise Christ by holiness of life and by the thanksgiving owed by us to him in return for many and very great benefits.

I say, then, that he established the principles of this universe and devised the creation of human beings according to a definite law and measure. He immediately transferred those newly brought into the light to a certain blessed place, flourishing with flowers and abundant in every kind of fruit, and initially willed them to be ignorant of good and evil. Later, however, he established on earth a dwelling suitable for rational animals; and only then disclosed to them, as rational beings, knowledge of good and evil. He then commanded the human race to increase and that all the region, healthful and free from disease, bounded by the circuit of Ocean, should begin to be inhabited.

As the human race thus increased, arts necessary for the use of this life were discovered. The irrational animals likewise increased, since in each kind there was found a certain proper power and capacity implanted by nature. In tame animals there was a mild disposition, obedient [Col. 0412B] to humans; in wild animals, strength and swiftness, and a certain natural foresight by which they escape dangers. God assigned to human beings the care and protection of all tame animals, while establishing, as it were, a contest against wild beasts. After this he formed the race of birds, numerous indeed in number but diverse in nature and species, endowed with a remarkable variety of colours and a certain natural knowledge of music. Having likewise arranged most beautifully all other things contained within the compass of the world [Col. 0411B], and fixed for all a fated boundary of life, he completed the fabric of the universe, adorned with every ornament.

[Note: [Col. 0409D]

**Καὶ τὸν ταῦτα λόγῳ νομοθετήσαντα**—“and him who established these things by reason/law.” The first three words were added by learned men from the manuscripts. Yet they are found neither in the royal manuscript nor in the old papers. After **νομοθετήσαντα** I have placed a stop on the authority of the royal manuscript, the Fuk. manuscript, and the old papers. Christophorson, failing to notice this, joined the period with the following one. But the sense of the passage is this: “I say,” he says, [Col. 0410C] “that humanity and the other things in the world are the workmanship of the one who established all these things by reason,” that is, of the supreme God. Therefore one should write **φημὶ δὴ τοῦτον τὰς ἀρχὰς**, etc., [Col. 0410D] as in Savile’s copy and as Christophorson appears to have read. Then I read **τὸν καὶ ταῦτα λόγῳ νομοθετήσαντα**, by a wholly certain correction. In the Fuk. manuscript it reads: **καὶ τὸν λόγῳ ταῦτα νομ…**. Thus **λόγῳ νομοθετήσαντα**, “establishing by reason/law,” is the same as what he elsewhere calls **λόγῳ διατάξαντα**, “ordering by reason/law.”

**Εἰς μακάριόν τινα καὶ εὐανθῆ**—“into a certain blessed and flourishing [place].” Here Constantine seems to locate the Paradise in which God placed Adam outside the earth. Most ancient writers held this view. Stephen Gobarus addressed this problem in chapter XI: “That Paradise is neither in heaven nor upon the earth, but between them.” The title of chapter XII was: “That Paradise is the heavenly Jerusalem and is in the third heaven; that the trees there are endowed with intellect and knowledge; and that Adam, after his transgression, was cast down from there to earth.” Then follows the contrary assertion: that Paradise is not in the third heaven but on earth.

Certainly [Col. 0411C] Tatian, in his *Address to the Greeks*, says that the Paradise in which Adam was placed by God was not on this earth that we inhabit, but on another far more excellent one. His words are these, which Stephen Gobarus undoubtedly cited to confirm that view: “The demons were moved away; the first-created humans were exiled. The former were cast down from heaven; the latter from earth, indeed, but not from this earth—from an ordering superior to that found here.” Tertullian too seems to have held the same view. Thus he writes of Adam in *On Patience*: “He was innocent, a close friend of God, and an inhabitant of Paradise. But when he once fell through impatience, he ceased to have understanding of God; he ceased to be able to endure heavenly things. From that point the human being was given to earth and cast away from the sight of God,” etc.

The same may be inferred from Book II of his *Against Marcion*, chapters II and X, where he uses the same metaphor as Tatian: “What wonder if, restored to his own material and relegated to the prison-house of cultivating earth, he was exiled” (**ἐξορισθείς**)? If the book which Tertullian wrote on Paradise were extant today, it would be possible to know more clearly that this was the opinion I have stated. Finally, Clement of Alexandria, in the *Excerpts of Theodotus*, or books of *Hypotyposeis*, p. 341 of the Commelin edition, places the earthly Paradise in which Eve was made in the fourth heaven: “Therefore in Paradise, the fourth heaven, she is formed,” etc. Origen, however, placed the Paradise of which Adam was an inhabitant in the third heaven, as Methodius teaches in his work *On the Resurrection*, preserved in Epiphanius, p. 572. And before all these, Valentinus placed above the third heaven the Paradise in which Adam sojourned and asserted that it was intelligible, according to Irenaeus, Book I.

“Abounding in various fruits.” Grammatical rules require us to write καρποῖς τε διαφόροις (“with various fruits”). And so it is written in the Fuk. manuscript.

“Howsoever much of the uninhabited land.” It seems one should write: ὅσον τε ἄνοσον ὑπὸ τῆς ὠκεανοῦ περινοστήσεως διοριζόμενον οἰκῆσαι, “to inhabit as much uninhabited land as is bounded by the circuit of the Ocean” [Col. 0412D]. It could also be written thus: Τοιγαροῦν ὅσον ποτὲ τὸ ἄνοσον, etc., without any alteration.

“Being useful.” After this word learned men added the words καὶ ἐπιστῆμαι, “and sciences,” which I also found written in the margin of Moraeus’s copy. They are absent, however, not only from the Royal manuscript and the loose sheets, but also from the manuscripts of Fuket and Savile. “By participation in an innate harmony.” I write μέτοχον, “a participant,” as it is read in the Fuk. manuscript. A little earlier, where the text reads φύσει δὲ καὶ ἔθνεσι διάφορον, “diverse in nature and nations,” the same manuscript more correctly has καὶ ἔθεσι, “and habits,” as I also found written in Turnebus’s copy.

[Col. 0410C] Why then do I stain my tongue with defiled words, when I am about to hymn the God who truly is? First I wish, as it were, to wash away a briny draught with a pure drink. And the pure drink flows through the ever-flowing spring of the virtues of the God whom we hymn; and it is my own particular task to hymn Christ throughout my life, and to render him the gratitude owed to him for his many and greatest benefits.

I say that he established the beginnings of all these things: that he discovered the foundation of humankind, and that he who ordained these things by reason immediately settled those newly brought into being in a certain blessed and flourishing region [Col. 0411A], abounding in various fruits; and he willed that at the beginning they should be ignorant of good and evil. In the end he assigned the earthly dwelling, befitting a rational living creature alone; and then, as was appropriate for rational creatures, he opened up the knowledge both of good and evil. Then also he commanded the race to increase, while it inhabited as much uninhabited land as was bounded by the circuit of the Ocean.

As the human race thus multiplied, arts useful for life were discovered. Nor did the breed of irrational animals multiply any less; in every kind there being found some distinctive natural faculty: in tame animals, gentleness and obedience to humankind; in wild animals, strength and swiftness, and a certain natural provision for safety from dangers. He assigned humankind a certain care of all tame creatures [Col. 0411B], but ordained for it a certain contest with the wild ones.

After these things he constituted the race of birds, great in number, diverse in nature and habits, distinguished by its variety of colours and by participation in an innate harmony of music. Having distinguished also everything else that the world embraces and contains, and having assigned to all these an ordained law of life, he adorned the most perfect completion of the whole universe.

## Chapter VI.—On Fate, and That What Is Said about It Is False; Demonstrated Both from Human Laws and from Created Things, Which Move Not at Random but in Order, Thereby Declaring the Command of Their Creator

[Col. 0411]

[Col. 0412C] But most people, being less prudent, attribute the cause of this ordering and adornment of all things to nature; others assign it to fate or chance, reckoning the power over such things to fate. Nor do they understand that, when they name fate, they utter indeed a name, but designate neither an action nor any subsisting substance. For what can fate itself be in its own right, if nature has brought forth all things? [Col. 0413A] Or what should we judge nature to be, if the ordinance of fate cannot be violated?

Moreover, the very statement that there is a law of fate sufficiently shows—since every law is the work of some lawgiver—that fate itself, if indeed it is a law, is the work and contrivance of God. All things, therefore, are subject to God, and nothing is without a share in his power. Nor indeed do we reject the view that fate is and should be considered the will of God. But how can justice, temperance, and the other virtues exist by fate? And whence come the vices opposed to them—namely injustice and intemperance? For wickedness arises from nature, but not from fate; while virtue consists in right actions of character and conduct.

But if the failings, or again the right actions, which arise from good and upright intention have different outcomes at different times, whether according to chance or according to fate, how can everything involving justice, and the due allotment to each according to worth, be according to fate? Laws [Col. 0413B], exhortations toward virtue, deterrents from improper things, praise and blame, punishments, and everything that urges people toward virtue and leads them away from wickedness—how can these be said to arise not from justice, which is proper to God’s providence, but from chance or accident?

For according to the quality of human life, what is deserved also comes to pass: at times plagues, civil disorders, barrenness, and abundance following in turn; and all such events speak almost with an audible voice, openly and plainly declaring that they are fitted to our manner of life. For the divine substance delights in good dispositions, but turns away from all impiety. As it receives a modest frame of mind favourably, so it hates audacity and arrogance exalted beyond what befits a living creature.

Although the proofs of these matters are especially clear and lie before our eyes, they shine forth more plainly whenever [Col. 0413C] we gather ourselves into ourselves, as it were draw our mind together, and consider within ourselves their cause. Therefore, I say, we must live moderately and gently, not raising our thoughts above our nature; and we must take to heart that God, the overseer of our actions, is always present with us.

Let us also test in this manner whether the assertion is true: if the ordering of all things consists by chance and accident, must we believe that the heavenly bodies and stars, earth and sea, fire and winds, water and air, the changes of seasons, and the periods of summer and winter have come about irrationally and at random rather than having been created? Some people, devoid of understanding, say that human beings devised most such things for their own use. Since nature supplies all resources abundantly, let this opinion have some appearance of reason concerning earthly and perishable things. But are immortal and unchangeable things also human discoveries?

For of these and all similar things, which are removed from our perception and can be grasped by intellect alone, the begetter is not human life embodied in matter, but the intelligible and eternal substance of God [Col. 0415B]. The order itself is also the work of providence: that day shines when illumined by the sun; that night succeeds when the sun sets, and, having succeeded, is not left altogether without light because of the choir of stars. What, moreover, might one say about the moon? It is filled out because of its position opposite the sun at a great distance, and wanes because of its close conjunction with it. Do not these things declare God’s inward reason and keen intelligence?

The suitable heat of the sun’s ray ripens fruits; the breaths of winds produce a favourable year; the cooling of rains; the harmony of all these things, by which everything is administered reasonably and in good order; and the perpetual arrangement of the planets, returning to the same place at their appointed and regular seasons—do these not plainly testify to God’s command and to the perfect service of the stars in obedience to the divine law?

Do the heights of mountains, the hollow depths of valleys, and the level expanse of open plains appear to exist without God’s providence? [Col. 0415C] Their sight is not only delightful, but their use also delightful. And do not the measures and separations of water and land, suitable both for agriculture and for transporting needed goods from foreign regions, plainly demonstrate God’s precise and measured providence? For mountains contain water; and when the level ground receives it and is sufficiently watered for the renewal of the land, it discharges the remainder into the sea. The sea in turn delivers it to the Ocean.

And do we still dare to say that all these things happen automatically and at random, without declaring in what sort of shape or form the accidental is characterized? It has no subsistence, either intelligible or perceptible; it is merely an unsubstantial sound of a name buzzing about the ears [Col. 0418A].

> **Note: [Col. 0412D]**
>
> “The power of these things.” Before these words Musculus placed a stop. For he translates thus: “Those who attribute the power of these things to fate do not even understand this,” etc. Christophorsonus followed Musculus.
>
> “Or what might nature be?” It seems one should write: ἢ τί ἂν εἶναι φύσις νομίζοιτο, “or what might nature be thought to be?” In the manuscripts of Fuket and Savile it is written: ἢ τί ἂν ἡ φύσις νομ. In the Royal loose sheets, however, I found: ἢ τί μέν εἶναι ἡ, etc.
>
> [Col. 0413C] “For wickedness would be…” I read: εἰ γὰρ ἥ τε πονηρία, etc. Further, this passage is mutilated, as is evident, and it would be difficult to restore it without manuscripts. Constantine’s argument nevertheless seems to be this: “If,” he says, “the virtues are from fate, then so are the vices. But vices cannot be from fate. For wickedness is either from nature or from will. Therefore it is not from fate. And if someone should say that virtue and vice are indeed from will, but that whether the will acts rightly or otherwise is from fate, by what reasoning, then, can justice—which is nothing other than the constant and perpetual will of assigning to each his due—be from fate?” In the Fuk. manuscript one reads ἥ τε γὰρ πονηρία. But Savile notes in the margin of his copy that perhaps one should write εἴτε γὰρ, etc.; and he immediately emends to ἔσται κατορθώματα.
>
> “Having all that is just.” The last word was added by learned men from manuscript codices, though I cannot approve it at all, even though it is read in the Fuk. manuscript. I therefore write: πᾶν τὸ δίκαιον καὶ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἀπονεμόμενον ἑκάστῳ, πῶς καθ’ εἱμαρμένην; “how can all justice and what is allotted to each according to worth be according to fate?” The sense is what I have stated above. Yet the transmitted reading can be accepted, if πάντα τὸ δίκαιον ἔχοντα refers to the matters shortly to be enumerated by Constantine: laws, rewards, punishments, exhortations, and the other such things which contain justice.
>
> “The quality.” Write ποιόν, with the accent on the final syllable, as I found noted in the margin of Moraeus’s copy. Shortly afterward [Col. 0414C] I read καὶ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἀπαντᾷ, from the manuscripts. Certainly the Fuket manuscript presents it thus: Διὰ γὰρ τὸν ποιὸν τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίον καὶ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἀπαντᾷ, “For according to the quality of human life, what is deserved comes to pass.”
>
> “Why all such things.” I read ὅτι πάντα, “that all,” as I found emended in the margin of Moraeus’s copy. So certainly the Fuket manuscript.
>
> “Although their proofs are especially…” After the first word in the Fuket manuscript there is a lacuna capable of containing one word. It seems that it should be supplied thus: ὧν πάντων εἰ καὶ, etc.
>
> [Col. 0414D] “Then, as often as…” The final word should be deleted, since it occurs neither in the Royal manuscript, nor in the loose sheets, nor in Stephanus’s edition. Rather it should be emended thus: Ὅμως τηνικαῦτα ἡμῖν φανερώτερον ἐκλάμπουσιν, “Nevertheless, at that time they shine forth more plainly for us.” That is: although it is certain and confirmed by many examples that famine, plague, and similar calamities are sent from heaven to punish human wickedness, this shines forth much more manifestly whenever such calamities occur. For then, turning to ourselves, we recognize the causes of these events. Yet the Fuk. manuscript reads τηνικαῦτα τοσάκις.
>
> “Whenever indeed.” I think one should write τοσάκις, or, if preferred, τοσαυτάκις. In the Fuket manuscript one reads ὁσάκις ἂν … συναγείραντες; and at the end of the period λογιζόμεθα, very well. One should therefore write ὁσάκις ἂν ἡμεῖς συναγείραντες.
>
