> [Col. 0415D] “Consists by chance and accident.” I would prefer συνέστηκεν or συνέστη. Moreover, in the manuscripts of Fuket and Turnebus the passage reads thus: Ὡς εἰ ἡ πάντων … διάταξις ἐκ τύχης, etc.
>
> “Not material life in human beings.” Write: οὐκ ἔνυλον ζῶον ὁ ἄνθρωπος, “not a material animal, man.” Christophorsonus, however, read οὐκ ἔνυλος ζωὴ ἀνθρώπων, “not material human life,” which I do not reject. Yet the earlier emendation is more pleasing. Thus Eusebius at the end of chapter 7. Nevertheless, the excellent Fuket manuscript clearly supports Christophorsonus.
>
> “Not without a share in it.” Supply τοῦ φωτός, “of light.” Therefore there is no need for the conjecture of Christophorsonus and Savile, who emends ἄμαυρον, “dark.”
>
> “The suitable…” I read τὸ δὲ ἐπιτήδειον, as is emended in the margin of Moraeus’s copy. Then write ἀνέμων τε πνεύματα, “the breaths of winds.” And again below: τό τε ἀΐδιον τῆς διατάξεως εἰς τὸν αὐτὸν ἀποκαθισταμένων τόπον, “the perpetual ordering of those returning to the same place.” Thus indeed I found it written in the Fuket manuscript, except that it has ἀνέμων δέ.
>
> “The sight is delightful.” Delete here the word ἐπιτερπής, “delightful.” Here he was proving that they knew nothing, and attacking them with their own weapons—that is, the arguments of dialectic.
>
> “And for the transport of foreign necessities.” I read κᾷκ τῆς ἀλλοδαπῆς τῶν ἐν χρείᾳ παρακομιδὴν, etc., than which nothing is more certain. In the manuscripts of Fuket and Turnebus it is written: καὶ τῆς ἀλλοδαπῆς χρείας παρακομιδὴν. I translated διαστάσεις as “separations,” following the authority of Ammianus Marcellinus, who speaks in this manner somewhere. Christophorsonus also correctly translates it “divisions of lands.”
>
> “Levelness, moreover.” One should write ὁμαλότης τε, as a learned man had noted in Moraeus’s copy. So certainly it is read in the Fuket manuscript.
>
> “Not declaring.” In the manuscripts of Fuket and Turnebus this passage reads: οὐ νοοῦντες ἐν ποίῳ τινὶ σχήματι καὶ μορφῇ χαρακτηρίζεται τὸ αὐτόματον, “not understanding in what shape and form accident is characterized.”

## Chapter VII.—That in Things We Cannot Attain by Understanding We Must Proclaim the Wisdom of the Creator, and Must Not Suppose Chance or Any Cause Other than God

[Col. 0417]

[Col. 0417B] For “chance” is truly an expression invented by people who think at random and without reason. Since they cannot grasp the explanation itself, through the weakness of their understanding they suppose that those things for which they cannot provide an explanation have been arranged without explanation. There are indeed certain things possessed of a wonderful nature, the true comprehension of whose reality lies hidden in depth; such is the nature of hot waters. For no one can readily state the cause of so great a fire. Yet it is wonderful that, though surrounded on every side by cold water, it does not at all depart from its innate heat.

These things seem a rare and scanty phenomenon throughout the whole inhabited world, so that, as I am persuaded, the power of providence may become readily recognizable to people: providence ordains that two utterly contrary natures, heat and cold, should flow from one and the same root [Col. 0418C].

Many and innumerable things have been bestowed by the Higher Power upon humankind for consolation and enjoyment, especially the fruit of the olive and of the vine. The one serves to restore and cheer the soul; the other is suitable, besides enjoyment, for the treatment of bodies. The continuous and unceasing flow of rivers, by night and by day, is also an extraordinary wonder, a symbol of perpetual and uninterrupted life. The succession of night likewise has equal force.

> **Note: [Col. 0417D]**
>
> “Serves the purpose.” Learned men emended this passage thus: τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἀνακτήσεως ψυχῆς καὶ φαιδρότητος ἐπέχειν λόγον, “for the one serves the purpose of restoring and cheering the soul.” But since the particle γάρ is found neither in the Royal manuscript nor in Stephanus’s edition, I would prefer to read ἐπέχον, “serving,” which the following words fully confirm. For there follows: τὸ δ’ ἕτερον πρὸς τῇ ἀπολαύσει καὶ θεραπεία τῶν σωμάτων κατάλληλον, “the other is suitable, besides enjoyment, for the treatment of bodies.” Yet the manuscripts of Fuket, Savile, and Turnebus fully confirm the learned men’s emendation. [Col. 0418D] The same Fuket manuscript correctly marks a colon after ἀπολαύσει, “enjoyment.”

## Chapter VIII.—That God Supplies Human Beings Abundantly with What Is Necessary for Use, but Moderately with What Serves Pleasure, Dispensing Both for Our Benefit

[Col. 0417]

[Col. 0417D] Let all this have been said by us to establish that nothing has come to be without reason and understanding, and that reason and providence are God: he who also apportioned in fitting measure the nature of metals—gold, silver, bronze, and the rest. Those things whose use was to be great and manifold he commanded to be supplied abundantly; but those serving only adornment, luxury, and abundance, he supplied generously yet sparingly, midway between frugality [Col. 0419A] and profusion.

For if the same abundance had been permitted also for things made for ornament, miners, through greed, would have despised such materials as are useful for agriculture, building, and the construction of temples—iron and bronze, for example—and neglected their collection; whereas they would have devoted themselves to things suited to luxury and the useless excess of wealth. Therefore, they say, the discovery of gold and silver is harder and more laborious than that of all other metals, so that the severity of labour may be set against the vehemence of desire.

How many other works of divine providence can be enumerated, which, in all the things abundantly bestowed upon us, urge human life openly, though not in so many words, toward temperance and all other virtues, and lead it away from untimely greed? To trace out the reason for all these things is a greater task than accords with humanity [Col. 0419B]. For how could the understanding of a perishable and weak creature attain exact truth? How could it comprehend God’s pure will from the beginning?

> **Note: [Col. 0418D]**
>
> “That providence is God.” In Moraeus’s copy it is emended τοῦ Θεοῦ, “of God,” as Christophorsonus reads; and so it is expressly written in the Fuk. manuscript.
>
> “For delight, adornment, and abundance.” The word ἀφθονία, “abundance,” is corrupt; in its place I would prefer ἀσωτία, that is, “luxury.” Nevertheless, the received reading can be retained.
>
> [Col. 0419D] “Might attain truth.” One should write ἐφίκοιτο, “might attain,” as I found written in the Fuk. manuscript, having long before conjectured that it should be written thus. I also punctuate the entire passage as follows: πῶς γὰρ ἄν τῆς κατὰ ἀκρίβειαν ἀληθείας ἐφίκοιτο ἡ, etc.; πῶς ἂν τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς, etc.

## Chapter IX.—On Philosophers Who, Seeking to Know Everything, Fell into Opinions, and Some of Whom Underwent the Peril of Death; Also on Plato’s Teaching

[Col. 0419]

[Col. 0419B] Therefore we must undertake what is possible and what accords with our nature. For the plausibility arising in dialogues commonly leads most of us away from the truth of things that are. This also happened to many philosophers, while they exercised their ingenuity upon arguments and the investigation of the nature of things. Whenever the magnitude of realities overpowers their inquiry, they conceal the truth by various methods [Col. 0419C]. Hence it happens that they hold contrary opinions and fight against one another’s doctrines, while pretending to be wise.

From this arose uprisings among peoples, harsh judgments by rulers who believed ancestral custom was being destroyed, and often the philosophers’ own destruction. For Socrates, exalted by dialectic, making weaker arguments stronger, and continually playing with contentious arguments, was put to death through the envy of his fellow countrymen and citizens. Nor was Pythagoras exempt: though professing especially to practise temperance and silence, he was convicted of lying. For, having visited Egypt, he proclaimed to the Italians as revelations made privately to himself by God those things formerly foretold by the prophets [Col. 0422A].

Plato himself, gentlest beyond all others, first habituated human minds to rise from sensible things to intelligible realities that always remain the same; he looked up toward the heights and taught others to do so. First, he set forth God as beyond substance; and in this he did well. But he subordinated a second to him and divided substance into two numerically, although the perfection of both is one, and the substance of the second God has its existence from the first. For the first is the maker and governor of all things, having manifestly ascended above all; whereas the one after him, ministering to the commands of the former, refers the cause of the constitution of all things back to him.

According to exact reasoning, therefore, there would be one God who takes care of all things and provides for them: the divine Logos, who ordered all things. And the Logos, being God himself, is also the Son of God. For what name could anyone bestow upon him besides the designation “Son” without committing the gravest error? For the Father of all things may justly also be thought the Father of his own Logos [Col. 0422B].

Up to this point Plato was sound-minded; but in what follows he is found to have departed from the truth, introducing a multitude of gods and assigning forms to each. This became a contributory cause of greater error among irrational people, who do not look to the providence of the highest God but worship images of them transformed into likenesses of humans and other animals. Thus it came about that a nature and learning of the greatest excellence and worthy of great praise, mixed with such errors, became impure and insincere [Col. 0422C].

The same Plato seems to me, correcting his own statement, expressly to declare that the rational soul is the Spirit of God. For he divides all things into two classes, intelligible and sensible: the one uncompounded, the other composed from the joining of bodies; the former apprehensible by intellect, the latter apprehended by opinion joined with sensation. Thus the former, participating in the Holy Spirit and being unmixed and immaterial, is eternal and has obtained everlasting life. But the sensible, being wholly dissolved in the same manner in which it was constituted, is without a share in everlasting life.

He also teaches wonderfully in what follows that those who have lived well—that is, the souls of holy and good men—are consecrated in the most beautiful regions of heaven after their departure from the body. This is not only admirable but also beneficial. For who, persuaded by him and expecting this happiness [Col. 0422D], would not pursue the best life, practise justice and temperance, and turn away from wickedness? He then adds that the souls of the wicked wander, borne like shipwrecked remains upon the streams of Acheron and Pyriphlegethon [Col. 0423A].

> **Note: [Col. 0419D]**
>
> “Arising in dialogues.” It is more correctly written γινομένων in the manuscripts of Fuket and Turnebus. In the Royal loose sheets the word is omitted. I would also prefer to write τὸ γέ τοι πιθανὸν τῶν ἐν τοῖς, “the plausibility indeed arising in…”
>
> “They prattle.” In the sacred books this verb is used in the sense of exercising one’s ingenuity, as Jacobus Tusanus noted long ago.
>
> “Making weaker arguments stronger.” The sense requires the addition of these words: καὶ τοὺς βελτίους χείρονας, “and stronger arguments weaker.” This was the invention of Protagoras, who promised young men that he would make the stronger argument weaker, and conversely the weaker stronger: τὸν κρείττονα λόγον ἥττω ποιεῖν, καὶ ἥττονα τὸν κρείττω. Socrates continually disputed against the Sophists who professed these things, in order to prove that they knew nothing, attacking them with their own weapons—that is, with dialectical arguments.
>
> “Things formerly foretold by prophets.” One should write πάλαι ποτε, “long ago,” from the Fuk. manuscript. By the same error τόσα is written for πόσα above at the end of chapter 7. Constantine’s statement that Pythagoras, on arriving in Egypt and receiving what had formerly been foretold by prophets, afterward publicized it in Italy as though revealed to him by God, seems to me not very plausible. That Pythagoras came to Egypt and there received secret rites and sacred ceremonies from priests is attested by Porphyry in his *Life* of Pythagoras and by many others. Aristobulus, with Clement and Eusebius, also relates that Pythagoras received much from the books of Moses. But, so far as I know, no ancient author said that he learned Jewish prophecies in Egypt and afterward promulgated them to Italians. Perhaps, therefore, this passage should be understood not of Jewish but of Egyptian prophets. For there were prophets among the Egyptians, as I noted on Book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*; perhaps this fact led Constantine into error. Having read that Pythagoras learned many secrets from Egyptian prophets—that is, priests—he understood this of Hebrew prophets.
>
> “And having taught.” The connective particle is absent from the Fuket and Savile copies and from the Royal loose sheets. I therefore write, with Savile: ἀναβλέψαι τ’ ἐπὶ τὰ μετάρσια διδάξας, “having taught [men] to look up toward the heights.”
>
> “A nature worthy of the greatest praise.” He means Plato himself [Col. 0422D], whose extraordinary genius all the ancients, and now Christians as well, have admired.
>
> “Dividing all things.” Christophorsonus seems to have read διϊστῶν τε. The passage of Plato indicated by Constantine is found in the *Timaeus*, p. 28.
>
> “But also beneficial.” Before these words, after καθιεροῦσθαι, “to be consecrated,” the Geneva edition reads: τοῦτο δὲ οὐ μόνον θαυμαστόν, “this is not only admirable,” supplied by Christophorsonus, Scaliger, Bongarsius, and Gruterus, as is noted in the margin of that edition. I found the same emendation in the copies of Moraeus, Turnebus, and Savile, and in the Fuk. manuscript, which also has βιωφλεῖς.
>
> [Col. 0423D] “Like shipwrecks.” I translated this as “shipwrecked remains,” that is, tackle; for these are tossed here and there at sea after a shipwreck. Christophorsonus translates “wares,” which does not seem fitting in this place. Wares, after a shipwreck, are for the most part submerged.

## Chapter X.—On Those Who Reject Not Only Sacred Scripture but Also the Doctrines of Philosophers; and That Either Poets Must Be Believed in All Things or in None

[Col. 0423]

[Col. 0423A] Yet there are some whose understanding is so damaged that, whenever they encounter these very teachings, they neither give heed nor feel fear, but despise and ridicule them as though hearing fabricated myths [Col. 0423B]. They praise the variety of eloquence, but reject the firmness of doctrine. Yet they believe poetic myths and fill all Greece and every barbarian land with stale and false tales.

For poets say that after death certain human beings, children of gods, judge souls; they celebrate judgments and tribunals and appoint them as overseers of those below. The same poets report battles of daimons and certain laws of war, and proclaim their fates. They declare that some are naturally harsh, others unconcerned with the care of human beings, and some difficult and ill-tempered. They even introduce them lamenting the slaughter of their own children, as though unable to aid not merely strangers but not even those dearest to them. They represent them as subject to human emotions, singing of their wars and wounds, joys and lamentations; and, saying such things, they are deemed trustworthy.

For if they undertake poetry under divine inspiration, it is fitting that we believe and obey them concerning the matters of which they speak while inspired. But they speak of the sufferings of gods and daimons; therefore the sufferings of these beings partake in every manner of truth. But someone will say that poets may lie: for it is proper to poetry to charm the souls of hearers, whereas truth exists when the things said are not otherwise than they are said to be. Let it be the property of poetry sometimes to conceal the truth. Yet those who speak falsehoods do not lie in vain: they do so either for gain and advantage, or because, conscious as they seem to be of some evil deed, they conceal it because of the danger imposed by the laws. They could, I think, when relating nothing concerning the higher nature except the truth, refrain from lying and from impiety [Col. 0423D].

> **Note: [Col. 0423D]**
>
> “And they believe myths.” I read μύθοις δέ, “but they believe myths.”
>
> “False tales.” Christophorsonus wrongly translates “they celebrate with praises,” since φῆμαι here means nothing other than tales by which poets filled the whole world. Thus shortly afterward he says concerning the same poets, εἱμαρμένας τε αὐτῶν διαφημίζουσι, “they proclaim their fates”; and likewise at the beginning of chapter 11, where he inveighs against blasphemy or impiety.
>
> “Partake in every kind of truth.” I think one should write παντοίως, “in every manner,” which I followed in my translation.
>
> “For it was possible.” I would prefer to read ἦν δὲ ἄρα δυνατόν, “but surely it was possible.”

## Chapter XI.—On the Bodily Coming of the Lord: What It Was Like and Why It Occurred

[Col. 0425]

## CHAPTER XI.—ON THE LORD’S BODILY ADVENT: WHAT IT WAS AND FOR WHAT REASONS IT OCCURRED

[Col. 0425A] Moreover, whoever is unworthy of a good manner and discipline of life, and is himself conscious of a life ill and wickedly spent, should at last come to his senses; and, having cleansed the eye of his mind, should look toward the divine power, detesting his former way of life. Yet he ought to be content if, even at an advanced age, he attains wisdom. But for us no instruction proceeding from men has ever been of assistance. Rather, whatever in human life and character deserves praise in the judgment of the wise are gifts and benefits of God.

Besides, against those poisoned darts forged by the evil demon I possess no feeble shield to set in opposition: namely, the knowledge of those things acceptable to God. From this knowledge and teaching, selecting what is suited to the present discourse, [Col. 0425B] I shall undertake to praise the Father of all. But do thou, O Christ, Savior of all, favoring the purpose of our devotion, be present; adorn the discourse begun concerning thy power, prescribing for us the manner and rule of praise.

Let no one suppose that he will hear a discourse polished with some exceptional elegance of words. For I know well that a speech which is soft and fashioned for pleasure and allure does not please prudent men, when its speaker pursues applause rather than a sober manner of discussion. Certain impious and senseless persons assert that our Christ was justly condemned to punishment, and that he who is the author of life was himself deprived of life for those who live. And indeed it is hardly surprising that those [Col. 0428A] who have once ventured into impiety, and have determined neither to fear nor to be ashamed of their crimes, should say this. But this surpasses every form of folly: that they seem to have persuaded themselves that the immortal God suffered violence from men, and not from his own kindness and goodwill toward humankind. Nor do they observe that greatness of soul and endurance are not altered by insult, nor displaced from their proper station by abuse, but break the rage of those who assail them hostilely by deliberation and loftiness of spirit.

Divine clemency had indeed resolved to remove injustice from the midst, and to advance orderliness and equity. Therefore, having gathered together the wisest of men, it established a teaching most beautiful and most beneficial to the human race, so that good and blessed men might emulate his providence in administering the affairs of this world. What greater good than this could be named: that God prescribes the laws of justice, and makes those who have merited to be his disciples like himself, so that, when virtue has been handed down and spread among all, everlasting blessedness may be secured for humankind? This is the splendid victory; this is true power; this is the greatest work and the work most fitting for God: namely, the correction and reformation of all peoples. And we offer to thee, O Savior of all, the glory of this triumph with praises and acclamations.

But thou, wicked and detestable blasphemy, who art wont to exalt and glory in falsehoods, rumors, and widely circulated reports—thou, I say, deceivest the young; thou leadest astray boys and men endowed with a certain childish disposition by flattering persuasion, [Col. 0428C] drawing them away from the worship of the true God and setting up images for them to adore and to which they may address prayers, so that, deceived, they receive the recompense of their own senselessness. For they malign Christ, the author of all good things, who is both God and the Son of God.

[Col. 0429A] Is not this God, I ask, rightly and deservedly worshiped by peoples and nations of the greatest sobriety and wisdom? Though he has obtained every power, he remains always steadfast in his purpose and has diminished nothing of the clemency implanted within him. Depart then, you impious people—for this is permitted you, since no punishment is now imposed for your sin—depart, I say, to the slaughter of victims, feasts, festival days, and drinking bouts. In these, under the appearance of religion, you indulge pleasure and intemperance. You pretend indeed to celebrate sacred rites, but in truth you satisfy your lusts. For you know nothing good, not even the first commandment of the supreme God, who prescribes laws of life to the human race and commanded his Son to shape human life and morals, so that those who have lived rightly [Col. 0429B] and temperately may, by the judgment of his Son, attain a second life that is blessed and happy.

I have set forth God’s decree concerning human life, not wandering in ignorance, as many do, nor led by opinion or conjecture. But perhaps someone will say: “Whence this designation of Son, or what manner of begetting is this, if God is one and alone and wholly removed from all mixture and intercourse?” One must understand that there are two modes of begetting: one by childbirth, familiar to all; the other from an eternal cause. The mode and rationale of this generation, by the favor of divine providence, is discerned among men by one who is dear to God. For every wise person understands the cause of the ordering of the universe. Now, since there is nothing without a cause, the cause of all things that exist must necessarily have existed before them all.

[Col. 0432A] Therefore, since the world and everything in it exist, and since their preservation exists, the Savior of all things must necessarily have existed before all things. Thus Christ himself is the cause of all things, and preservation is the effect; just as the Father is indeed the cause of the Son, while the Son is the thing caused. We have already sufficiently shown that Christ existed before all things. But how did he descend to earth and come among human beings?

The purpose itself, as the prophets foretold, proceeded from the care and concern which he bore for all things. For the maker must necessarily care for his works. But when he was about to approach an earthly body and, since necessity so required, to remain among men for a time, he devised for himself a certain new mode of birth. For there was [Col. 0432B] conception without marriage, childbirth from chaste virginity, a maiden who was mother of God, a temporal beginning of an eternal nature, sensation of an intelligible substance, and matter of incorporeal splendor. Everything then seen was consistent with these things.

A most radiant dove, flying forth from Noah’s ark, descended into the Virgin’s bosom. The other events also accord with that marriage which was undefiled, purer than every form of chastity, and indeed surpassing continence itself. There was the wondrous Wisdom of God from the very swaddling clothes; the Jordan, which supplied the waters for baptism, receiving him reverently; and royal anointing joined with knowledge of all things. There were also teaching and power, accomplishing marvelous works and healing incurable illnesses; and finally, astonishing readiness in hearing human prayers [Col. 0432C] without impediment. In sum, his entire life served human benefit: a teaching that imparted not mere prudence but wisdom, while its hearers learned not civic virtues but the way leading to the intelligible world, laboring in contemplation of that nature which always remains in one and the same state, and in continual exercise of the knowledge of the supreme Father.

Nor were the benefits insignificant: in place of blindness, sight; in place of paralysis and bodily weakness, sound bodily health; and, finally, in place of death, life restored anew. I pass over the abundant provision in the wilderness of necessities for sustenance, and the few foods sufficient for a vast multitude of people over a long period.

To thee, Christ, God and Savior, supreme Providence of the great Father, who both deliverest from evils and impartest most blessed teaching, we render this thanksgiving according to our ability. For I say these things not in order to celebrate thy praises, but to give thanks. For who among men could ever praise thee worthily? For thou art said to have created things from nothing, to have kindled light for them, and to have ordered by arrangement and measure the confused mass [Col. 0433B] of the elements.

This is the chief gift of thy kindness: that thou hast made human beings of good natural endowment imitators of the divine and blessed life, and hast provided that, having become merchants of the best things, they might impart their wisdom and blessed fortune to many others, while themselves receiving the immortal fruit of virtue. They are freed from intemperance and made participants in kindness; keeping compassion before their eyes, hoping for the promises of faith, and embracing modesty and every kind of virtue in place of the injustice which the former life of mortals had infused into human character, so that it might be uprooted by him who exercises care and providence over all things. For no other physician adequate for so many evils and for the injustice prevailing in that age [Col. 0433C] could have been found.

[Col. 0433] Therefore Providence, extending even to earth, easily restored all things that had been disordered through insult and intemperance; and it did this not secretly or obscurely. For he knew that some human beings contemplated his power and might with the eye of the mind, while others, resembling irrational animals in nature, clung rather to the senses. Therefore, openly and plainly, so that no one—whether good or wicked—might doubt, he set blessedness and marvelous healing before the eyes of all: restoring life anew to the dead, and commanding those deprived of their senses to recover their former use of them; making the sea firm, and commanding calm to arise in the midst of a storm. Finally, after accomplishing marvelous works and leading human beings from unbelief to the strongest faith, he flew up to heaven. Whose work was this, if not that of God and of some supreme power?

Nor did the time immediately adjacent to the Passion lack those marvelous spectacles: then the darkness of night, obscuring the brightness of day, wholly hid the sun. For terror had seized all peoples everywhere; they believed that the end of the world had now come and that all things would return to the primordial chaos such as existed before the creation of the world. The cause of so great a calamity was sought, and what great offense against the divine power had been committed by human beings. Until God, in tranquil greatness of soul, despised the insults of the impious, restored all things, and adorned the whole heaven with the accustomed course of the stars. Thus the face of the whole world, which had been in some manner confounded with mourning and grief, recovered its former brightness anew.

> **Note: [Col. 0425C]**
>
> **Σύνοιδέ τε τῷ.** It should be written, **σύνοιδέ τε ἑαυτῷ** (“and is himself conscious”), which surprises me that it did not occur to learned men. Moreover, the beginning of this period—that is, the words **οὐκοῦν εἴ τίς ἐστιν ἀνάξιος** (“therefore, if anyone is unworthy”)—belongs to the preceding chapter. We have placed it as in the manuscript sheets and in the Fuk. codex. In the Fuk. codex, in which titles are prefixed to individual chapters, the heading of this chapter is: “On the Lord’s coming according to the flesh, what it was and for what reasons it occurred; and on those who did not know the mystery,” etc. In the Royal manuscripts and in Robert Estienne’s edition, followed by Christophorson, this chapter is divided into two, and “On those who did not know” is the title of a new chapter.
>
> **Τὴν σοφίαν εὐτυχῶσιν.** Without doubt one should write **εὐτυχήσῃ**, or **εὐτυχήσειεν**, “may attain wisdom,” which surprises me that neither Christophorson nor Scaliger nor others noticed; they emended it to **τῆς σοφίας εὐτυχήσωσιν**. But Greek does not say **εὐτυχεῖν τῆς σοφίας**, but **εὐτυχεῖν τὴν σοφίαν**. Yet the Fuk. codex reads **τῆς σοφίας εὐτυχήσωσι**.
>
> **[Col. 0425D] Δηλητηρίων ἄντικρυς.** It should certainly be written **δηλητηρίων ἄντικρυς**, that is, “against poisoned darts.” Here **ἄντικρυς** is a preposition, which Scaliger, Bongarsius, Gruter, and others did not see when they wrote **δηλητήριον**. Thus below, in chapter 15, Constantine says: “having taught them faith and righteousness, against the envy that comes from the opposing nature.” Yet the Fuk. and Turnebus codices have, as we do, **ὡς κατὰ δηλητηρίων ἀντικρύς**.
>
> **Ἐξιστᾷ πρὸς τὸν προκείμενον.** Who would not marvel that Scaliger, Bongarsius, and the rest, from whose books emendations are noted in the margin of the Genevan edition, did not see the true correction of this passage, although it is obvious and easy? For, separating words that had run together, one should write **ἐξ ἧς τὰ πρὸς τὸν** etc. “from which [knowledge] the things relating to…” The word **γνώσεως** (“knowledge”), which occurred shortly before, is understood. Christophorson, however, translates the passage thus: “Therefore I have selected these things as suited to the discourse which I have begun.” From this it appears either that he followed the emendation found in the books of Scaliger, Bongarsius, and Gruter—and which I also found in Morel’s book—or, more probably, that Scaliger and the others claimed to have emended the text following Christophorson’s translation. But that emendation cannot be accepted. First, it departs too far from the traces of the common reading if, in place of **ἐξιστᾷ**, one writes **τὰ τοίνυν**. Yet the Fuk. and Savile codices have **τὰ τοίνυν**, etc.
>
> **Αὐτοῦ τε συναιρόμενος.** In Morel’s book a learned man emended **αὐτός** in the margin. I think the whole passage should be read continuously as follows: **Αὐτὸς δὲ συναιρόμενος τῇ τῆς καθοσιώσεως σπουδῇ πάριθι, Χριστέ** etc.: “But thou thyself, joining in the zeal of devotion, be present, O Christ,” etc. This emendation is confirmed by the Royal codex, in which a stop is marked before the word **αὐτοῦ**. Chapter 12 ought therefore to begin with these words, although in the Royal codex and Estienne’s edition a new chapter begins with **[Col. 0426D] πάριθι** (“be present”). Our conjecture is fully confirmed by the Fuk. codex, where one reads **αὐτός τε συναιρόμενος τῇ τῆς καθοσιώσεως σπουδῇ, πάριθι** etc. In the Royal manuscript sheets, however, I found written **αὐτοῦ τε συναιρομένου**, as Christophorson reads it. In the same sheets a new chapter begins from the immediately following words, **φασί δή τινες** (“certain persons say”). But there is no need to establish a new chapter here, since it had begun shortly before with **οὐκοῦν εἴ τίς ἐστιν ἀνάξιος**, both in the sheets and in Fuket’s codex.
>
> **Τοὺς ἀσεβεῖν ἅπαξ τολμήσαντας.** It must certainly be written: **τοὺς δ᾽ ἀσεβεῖν ἅπαξ τολμήσαντας, καὶ μήτε δεδιέναι, μήτ᾽ ἐγκαλύπτεσθαι τὴν ἑαυτῶν πονηρίαν κατανοοῦντας, οὐδὲν θαυμαστόν, τοῦτο λέγειν**—“it is not surprising that those who have once dared to be impious, and who have resolved neither to fear nor to conceal their own wickedness, say this”—as is written in the excellent Fuk. codex, supported by the Savile and Christophorson copies.
>
> **[Col. 0427C] Ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ φιλανθρωπία.** Gruter adds **καὶ ἀνεξίκακον τοῦ Θεοῦ**, “and God’s forbearing disposition,” words also written in the margin of Morel’s book. But since they occur neither in the Royal and Fuk. codices nor in Estienne’s edition, nothing compels us to add them here. Perhaps one should write **τὸ ἀνεξίκακον τῆς φιλανθρωπίας**, “the forbearance of kindness.” Moreover, Constantine’s argument here appears to me to be directed against Porphyry, or certain other Greek philosophers, who objected to Christians that they said Christ had been crucified and killed by human beings. Thus they argued against Christians: “If Christ is God, how could violence be inflicted on him by human beings, when it is agreed that human beings can do nothing against God?”
>
> **Τοὺς σοφωτάτους τῶν ἀνδρῶν.** Constantine calls the Apostles “the wisest of men,” although they are known to have been unlettered and unlearned. Likewise, in chapter 12 he calls those same Apostles **εὖ πεφυκότας**, that is, “endowed with excellent natural ability.” Constantine evidently thought that the Apostles, whom the Church so greatly venerates, ought to be regarded honorably. But the holy Fathers speak very differently of the Apostles, especially John Chrysostom. He acknowledges that the Apostles were thoroughly unlearned and untrained, and derives from this a most powerful argument for confirming the Christian faith: that unlettered men, fishermen from insignificant Judaea, drew the Romans, masters of the world, to the worship of one crucified. Constantine repeats this point at the beginning of chapter 15.
>
> **[Col. 0428C] Ζηλοῦσα.** This verb appears to be used in place of **ζηλωτὰς ποιoῦσα**, “making imitators.” The sense of this passage should be derived from chapter 12, where Constantine says: “The special excellence of kindness consists in making human beings of good natural endowment imitators of the divine and blessed life.” These two passages shed light upon one another. In the Fuk., Turnebus, and Savile codices **ζηλῶσαι**, not **ζηλοῦσα**, is written.
>
> **[Col. 0428D] Συ δ᾽ ὦ πονηρά.** A new chapter begins with these words in Robert Estienne’s edition and in the Royal codex, where they are separated from the preceding words by a small interval. In the excellent Fuk. codex, however, no division is marked here; we have followed it.
>
> **Τοῦ ὄντος Θεοῦ.** I should prefer to write the adverbial **τοῦ ὄντως**, “the truly existing [God].” And that is precisely what I found written in the Fuk. codex.
>
> **Μένειν τὰ ἐπίχειρα.** Here **μένειν** is used as Latin *manet*, as when one says *te manet Capitolina palmata*—“the Capitoline palm-decorated robe awaits you,” that is, it is prepared for you. Greeks use **μένειν** in the same manner. Thus in the letter of Constantius to the Alexandrians, reported by Athanasius in the *Apology to Emperor Constantius*: “But that noble and splendid man did not await judgment against himself.” Learned men, however, long ago emended from their manuscripts **ἀναμένειν**, an emendation which I find also in the books of Turnebus and Savile. The Fuketian codex has **ἀναβαίνειν**, “to go up.”
>
> **[Col. 0429C] Ἐγὼ μὲν οὖν τὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ δόγμα.** He means God’s decree concerning the assumption of human nature, or the Incarnation, through which human life was restored. It is therefore apparent that the chapters have been correctly arranged by us. Unless someone perhaps wishes to extend chapter 10 as far as these words; I would readily grant this.
>
> **Ὃς ἐκείνῳ φίλος ὑπάρχει.** Robert Estienne, in the variant readings noted at the end of his edition, reports that this passage is read thus in certain manuscripts. That is undoubtedly the true reading. Constantine says that the mode of natural generation is known to everyone, while very few know the rationale of divine generation—those whom God has favored with special goodwill. Certainly, the Royal codex reads **φίλος**. In the manuscript sheets, however, it is written **ὃς ἐκείνων φίλως**. But the Fuk., Turnebus, and Savile codices exhibit the true reading.
>
> **[Col. 0429D] Οὔσης τε αὐτῶν τῆς σωτηρίας.** The Genevan editors unwisely read **τὴν αἰτίαν αὐτῶν τῆς σωτηρίας**, “the cause of their salvation,” from Scaliger’s conjecture, as is noted in the margin. But it is sufficiently apparent that this must be rejected. For it disturbs the entire meaning of the passage and does not occur in the manuscripts.
>
> **Τὴν δὲ σωτηρίαν τὸ αἴτιον.** Christophorson saw nothing in this passage. Yet it was very easy to observe that one ought here to read **τὸ αἰτιατόν**, “the effect.” Constantine compares the Son with preservation and the Father with the Savior. As the Father is the cause of the Son, and the Son the effect or **τὸ αἰτιατόν**, so the Savior is the cause of the preservation of all things, while preservation is the effect or **τὸ αἰτιατόν** of the Savior.
>
> **Αἰτία μὲν υἱοῦ ὁ πατήρ, αἰτιατὸν δὲ ὁ υἱός.** Ancient theologians, especially among the Greeks, said that one person in the Trinity—namely God the Father—is cause, while two, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit, are caused. Thus Athanasius, in the second *Questions*, chapters 11 and 12: “The Son is not cause, but caused.” So too John of Damascus, in Book I *On Images*, not far from the beginning: “The Son himself is the image of the invisible God; he bears the Father in himself, and is in all things the same as he, except in one thing: that he is from him as from a cause. For the Father is the natural cause, from whom the Son proceeds.” Gregory Nazianzen also, in Oration 29, which concerns doctrine, expressly declares that the Father is the cause of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Among Latin writers, Marius Victorinus speaks similarly in the first book *Against Arius*: “But the Father is greater, because he has given all things to the Son, and is the cause to the Son that he is, and that he is in this manner.” Earlier, Victorinus had said that the Son is indeed the principal cause of all things, [Col. 0430D] but that the Father is the pre-cause, because he is the cause of the Son.
>
> **Ἡ μὲν προαίρεσις τῆς καθόλου.** Our manuscripts change nothing here. I should nevertheless prefer to read **τῆς καθόδου**, “of the descent”; that is, of the Lord’s advent.
>
> **Ἀσωμάτου φανότατος ὕλη.** It seems one should write **φανότητος**, “of splendor,” as Christophorson reads. Constantine alludes to the passage of the Apostle Paul in which Christ is called the radiance of the glory of God the Father. Certainly, **φανότητος** is written in the Fuk. and Savile books.
>
> **Αἰγλήεσσα περιστερά.** In the Royal codex **λαμπρά**, “bright,” is written in the margin; it is a scholium on **αἰγλήεσσα**. Scaliger and the other emenders therefore read **αἰθρήεσσα** without reason. Moreover, Constantine’s narrative is drawn from apocryphal books which reported that the Holy Spirit descended into Mary’s bosom in the form of a dove, as the angel had foretold to her. Perhaps this was narrated thus in the Gospel of the Hebrews. Christophorson, however, understood the dove here as the one Noah formerly released from the ark, and took it as a figure of the Holy Spirit who would one day descend upon the Virgin Mary. But I should prefer to read: **αἰγλήεσσα περιστερὰ οἷα ἡ πάλαι ἐκ τῆς Νῶε λάρνακος ἀποπταμένη** etc., “a radiant dove, like that which formerly flew out from Noah’s ark,” etc. Thus the sense will be clear and elegant.
>
> **[Col. 0431D] Ὑμέναιον.** After this word I have placed a stop on the authority of the Royal codex. Since Christophorson did not notice this, he corrupted the whole sense of the passage by adding several words. For he reads: **ὑμέναιον, οἰκονομοῦσα ἡ ἐκ σπαργάνων σοφία τοῦ Θεοῦ θαυματουργεῖ**—“marriage; the Wisdom of God from swaddling clothes, administering things, works wonders.” Yet the Fuk. codex fully confirms Christophorson’s reading and punctuation, except that it has **τοῦ Θεοῦ σοφία**, “the Wisdom of God”; so too does Turnebus’s book.
>
> **Τὰς πολιτικὰς ἀρετάς.** Philosophers distinguish two kinds of virtues: practical virtues, which Constantine here calls **πολιτικαί**, “civic”; and contemplative virtues, which lead our mind to contemplation of God. Hence, among Pythagoras’s disciples, some were called **πολιτικοί**, “civic,” and others **σεβαστικοί**, “reverent,” as the ancient author on the life of Pythagoras teaches in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, chapter 259. The Fuk. codex here reads: “teaching disciples, not causing them to learn the so-called civic virtues, but the paths leading to the intelligible world, and [those] of the contemplation of what always remains in the same condition and in the same way,” etc. The books of Turnebus and Savile read likewise. But I agree with Savile, who, after writing this reading in the margin of his book, subsequently erased it and added this note: “The common reading may be retained with a few alterations.”
>
> **[Col. 0432C] Ἀντὶ μὲν τῆς ῥώσεως.** One should certainly write **τῆς πωρώσεως**, “of blindness.” Soon afterward I emended from the Royal codex **ἀντὶ δὲ [Col. 0432D] παρέσεως**, “in place of paralysis”; the Savile codex reads likewise. A little earlier I should prefer to write **τά γε τοι τῶν εὐεργετημάτων** etc., “the benefits, indeed…”
>
> **τὸ δὲ φῶς αὐτοῖς ἀνάψαι.** I read **τό τε φῶς**, “and to kindle the light.” In the Royal sheets and Savile’s book one reads **σὲ δὲ φῶς**, “but thee, light,” etc. The Fuk. codex has **σέ τε**.
>
> **Κατανοεῖν τε.** Christophorson here supplies the verb **ποιῆσαι**, “to make,” from the common construction. Though I do not reject this, it does not seem necessary. The Fuk. codex reads the passage thus: “embracing virtue, which the former life had driven out of human character; for no one…” without the words **τὴν ὑπὲρ πάντων ποιουμένῳ πρόνοιαν**, “the providence exercised over all.”
>
> **Ἁσπαζόμενοι.** Some words appear to be lacking after this verb. For the sense cannot stand unless you add: **ἀντὶ τῆς ἀδικίας ἣν ὁ προτοῦ βίος** etc., “in place of the injustice which the former life…” I followed this reading in my translation.—Either the most learned man is mistaken, or he had a text different from ours: for the meaning is plain with the verb **ἐκβεβλήκει**, “had cast out,” and we believe the passage is both excellently and very easily translated: “Embracing every virtue which the former life had expelled from human character.” —Editors.
>
> **[Col. 0433D] Τὴν ἑαυτῶν θεωροῦντας δύναμιν.** I do not doubt that one should read **τὴν ἑαυτοῦ δύναμιν**, “contemplating his power.” This is plainly proved by what follows. Constantine gives the reason why Christ, who came to heal human illnesses and vices and to proclaim blessed and happy life in heaven, wished to perform so many miracles on earth—giving eyes to the blind, health to the sick, and life to the dead. He says that Christ did this for the sake of those of slower understanding, so that they might not doubt his strength and power when they saw so many miracles performed. These are those whom he shortly afterward calls **φαύλους**, “base” or “ordinary.”
>
> **Διὰ φανέρωσιν ἃ μηδείς.** I think I have successfully restored this passage, when Scaliger, Bongarsius, and the others whose corrections appear in the margin of the Genevan edition saw nothing in it. With virtually no alteration, I restored the passage to its former clarity thus: **Διὸ φανερῶς, ἵνα μηδεὶς ἀμφιβάλλοι**: “Therefore openly, so that no one might doubt.” Nothing could be truer than this reading. The Fuk. codex agrees with the reading of Scaliger and Bongarsius. But I have already discovered from many passages that the reliability of this codex sometimes falters; and this one passage alone sufficiently proves it.
>
> **[Col. 0434D] Ἕως ὅτε ἠπίως.** I write **ἕως ὅτε ἠπίῳ μεγαλοψυχίᾳ** etc.: “until, with gentle greatness of soul,” etc.
>
> **Τοιγάρτοι ποσῷ.** There was no need for the learned men’s emendation, who correct it to **ποσῶς**, since **ποσῷ** may also be used adverbially for **ἐπὶ ποσόν**, “to some extent.” Yet the Fuk. and Turnebus codices read **ποσῶς**.

[Col. 0426A] Therefore, if anyone is unworthy of a good life, and is conscious in himself that he has lived improperly and disorderly, let him change and look toward the divine, once the eye of his soul has been cleansed and he has become estranged from his former most evil mode of life. Yet it is welcome if he should attain wisdom even in the age of his prime. But no education derived from human beings has ever aided us. Rather, all gifts—whatever wins esteem in character and conduct among those possessing understanding—belong to God. Against all the poisoned weapons which the evil one contrives, I have set before myself no moderate shield: the knowledge of things pleasing to God. Selecting from it what is useful for the proposed discourse, I shall hymn the Father of all. And do thou, joining in the zeal of devotion, be present, Christ, Savior of all, and adorn the discourse concerning thy power, directing the manner [Col. 0426B] of solemn speech.

Let no one expect to hear words and expressions embellished with some elegance. For I know exactly that relaxed public speaking, crafted for pleasure, displeases those of sound judgment when speakers seek applause rather than sober discourse. Certain foolish and impious people say that our Christ was vindicated [i.e. condemned as guilty; the Greek reading is contextually problematic], and that he who is the cause of life for the living was himself deprived of life. It is not surprising that those who have once dared to be impious and have decided neither to fear nor to conceal their own wickedness should say this. But this surpasses all absurdity: that they seem to have persuaded themselves that the incorruptible God suffered violence from a human being, and not solely from his own love of humankind. They do not consider that greatness of soul is neither changed [Col. 0427A] by insult nor driven from its natural firmness by abuse, but always breaks and repels the savagery of assailants by the spirit of reason and magnanimity.

God’s love for humankind had resolved to wipe out injustice and exalt orderliness and justice. Therefore, having gathered together the wisest of men, it established a teaching most beautiful and most beneficial for life, making good and blessed men emulate his providence in worldly things. What greater good could anyone name, when God dispenses justice and makes those worthy of his instruction like himself, so that, once goodness has been distributed among all, human beings may attain blessedness throughout all eternity? This is the solemn victory; this is true power; this is the greatest fitting work: the correction of all peoples.

We accordingly offer thee the prizes of victory with acclamation, O Savior of all. But thou, O wicked and disgraceful blasphemy, exalting thyself through falsehoods, rumors, and public reports, deceivest youths, persuadest boys and those men who have a boyish disposition; drawing them away from the worship of the true God and setting up fashioned images for them, that they may pray to and worship them, so that, being deceived, the recompense of their own insensibility awaits them. For they accuse Christ, who is the cause of all good things, both God and God’s Son.

[Col. 0427B] Is not this God worshiped as he deserves by the most temperate and prudent nations and peoples? Though possessed of every power, he remains in his own purpose and has diminished nothing of his inborn love for humankind. Depart, then, impious people: this is permitted you because of your unpunished sin. Go to the slaughter of sacrificial victims, banquets, feasts, and drunkenness; pretending religion while pursuing pleasures and licentiousness; feigning to offer sacrifices while serving your own pleasures. For you know no good thing, not even the first command of the great God, who gives orders to the human [Col. 0430A] race and commands his Son to guide their life, so that those who have lived well and temperately may receive, according to the judgment of the Son, a second life, blessed and happy.

I have therefore expounded God’s decree concerning human life, not in ignorance as most people do, nor from conjecture or inference. Yet perhaps someone will say, “Whence comes the designation ‘Son’? What sort of generation is this, if he is one God alone, wholly alien from every mixture?” But one must conceive a twofold generation: one from birth, which is commonly acknowledged; another from an eternal cause. Divine providence contemplates the reason of this latter generation, and so does the man who is a friend of God; for a wise person will understand the cause of the ordering of the universe. Since nothing is without cause, the cause of existing things must necessarily pre-exist them.

[Col. 0430B] Therefore, since the world and the things in it exist, and since their preservation exists, the Savior of existing things must necessarily pre-exist. Thus Christ is the cause of preservation, and preservation is the effect concerning existing things; just as the Father is the cause of the Son, and the Son is the effect. His pre-existence has already been sufficiently shown. But how did he descend to human beings and earth? The purpose of the universal descent—as the prophets foretold—arises from care for all things; for the creator must care for his works.

Since he was about to approach a worldly body and dwell on earth, necessity requiring this, he devised for himself a certain irregular [or “unusual,” *nothēn*] generation. For there was conception without marriage; the midwifery of pure virginity; a maiden, mother of God; a temporal beginning of eternal nature; sensation of intelligible substance; matter of incorporeal brightness. Consequently, the other features of the appearance were consistent with these: a radiant dove, flying forth from Noah’s [Col. 0431A] ark, descended upon the Virgin’s bosom. Consistent too were the things after the marriage undefiled, purer than every form of purity and greater than continence itself: the Wisdom of God from the swaddling clothes; the Jordan, provider of the waters of washing, reverently receiving him; royal anointing united with understanding of all things; teaching and power accomplishing extraordinary deeds and healing incurable things; swift and unhindered confirmation of human prayers; and, in general, the whole life devoted to human beings.

There was a teaching imparting not prudence but wisdom; its students learned not the so-called civic virtues, but the paths opening onto the intelligible world, laboring at the contemplation of the kind that is always in the same state, and practicing the conception of the greatest Father. The benefits, indeed, were not moderate: instead of blindness, sight; instead of paralysis, sound bodily vigor; instead of death, restoration once more to life. I pass over the abundant provision of necessities in the wilderness, and the abundance for a long time, from scant food, for great multitudes of every kind.

[Col. 0431B] To thee, Christ God and Savior, greatest Providence of the great Father, who savest from evils and teachest the most blessed doctrine, we render this thanksgiving according to our ability. For I say this not in praise, but in gratitude. For who among human beings could hymn thee worthily? For report declares that thou didst bring existing things into being from non-being, kindle light for them, and order the confused mixture of the elements with arrangement and measure. But the special excellence of love for humankind consists in making those human beings of good natural endowment imitators of a divine and blessed life, and in enabling them to see that, once they have become merchants in truly good things, they may share their own wisdom and good fortune with many others and themselves receive the eternal fruit of virtue.

[Col. 0431C] Freed from licentiousness and sharing in love for humankind, keeping pity before their eyes, hoping in the expectation of faith, and embracing modesty and every kind of virtue—which the former life had driven out of human character—they [follow] the providence exercised over all. For no physician adequate to so many evils and to the injustice that had prevailed in that life could be found.

Providence, then, extending down to this world, most easily ordered everything that had been disordered by insult and licentiousness. Nor did it do this secretly. For it knew that some human beings contemplate its power by intelligence and mind, while others, inasmuch as their nature resembles irrational animals, apply themselves more to the senses. Therefore, by manifestation, so that no one, diligent or base, might doubt, it brought blessedness and marvelous healing before their eyes: restoring life a second time to those who had ceased from life, and commanding those deprived of their senses to perceive soundly again; making the sea firm and commanding calm out of storm. And after undertaking marvelous works [Col. 0434B] and calling human beings forth from unbelief into strong faith, he flew up to heaven. Of whom other than God and the most exalted power could this be the work?

Nor was the time close to the Passion without those marvelous sights, when nights covering the light of day made the sun disappear. Fear had seized peoples everywhere: they thought that the end of all things had arrived and that chaos, such as held sway before the ordering of the world, would prevail again. The cause of so great an evil was sought, and whether any offense had been committed by human beings against the divine. Until, gently, in greatness of soul, having despised the insult of the impious, he restored the whole heaven, adorning it with the dance of the stars. Thus, to some extent, the darkened appearance of the world was restored again to its own brightness.

## CHAPTER XII.—ON THOSE WHO DID NOT KNOW THIS MYSTERY; THAT THEIR IGNORANCE IS VOLUNTARY; AND WHAT GREAT BLESSINGS AWAIT THOSE WHO KNEW IT, ESPECIALLY THOSE WHO DIED IN CONFESSION

[Col. 0435]

[Col. 0436A] But someone among those accustomed to speak impiously will say that God could have made the human will better and more gentle. What, I ask, is a better way, what method more effective for reforming wicked people, than for God himself to address them openly? Did he not, present and exposed to the sight of all, form them to moderation? But if the instruction of God present did no good, what could that of one absent and unheard have achieved? What obstacle, then, stood in the way of that most blessed preaching? Human savagery and cruelty. For whenever we receive with hostile minds things rightly and beneficially commanded, the sharpness of our minds is then obscured by something like darkness. Moreover, it pleased them to disregard the commandments and to lend unwilling ears to the law that was proclaimed. For if [Col. 0436B] they had not neglected them, they would surely have gained a reward worthy of their hearing, not only in this life but also in the future life, which should truly be considered life.

For the reward of those who obeyed God’s commandments is immortal and eternal life. Those alone can aspire to it who have known God and have proposed their own life as a kind of perpetual model for imitation to those who have undertaken to shape their lives in emulation of what is best. For teaching was entrusted to the wise for this purpose: that what they have commanded might be diligently kept by their companions with a pure mind, and that the sincere and firm observance of the divine command might thus endure. From such observance, from uncorrupted faith and sincere piety toward God, there arises contempt for death.

[Col. 0436C] Such a spirit therefore stands resolutely against the storms of the age, fortified by the invincible strength of divine power and directed toward martyrdom. When it has nobly overcome the gravest terrors, it is crowned by him to whom it steadfastly bore witness. Yet it does not therefore boast. For it knows that it is God’s gift both that it endured torments and that it joyfully fulfilled the divine commandments. Such a life is followed by immortal remembrance and everlasting glory, and rightly so. For both the martyr’s life itself is found full of moderation and religious observance of the divine commandments, and his death full of courage and noble character.

Accordingly, after these things hymns, psalms, and praises are sung to God, the inspector of all. A certain sacrifice of thanksgiving is performed in their memory, free from every kind of blood and violence. Nor is the fragrance of incense required, nor a burning pyre, but only pure light, sufficient to illuminate those who pray to God. Sober banquets are also celebrated by many, both to relieve the poverty of beggars and that of persons deprived of homeland and possessions. Whoever judges these things burdensome appears to think contrary to divine and most holy teaching.

> **Note: [Col. 0435C]**
>
> **Ἀλλ᾽ ἐρεῖ τις.** Chapter 12 should begin with these words: [Col. 0435D] “On those who did not know this mystery, and that their ignorance is voluntary,” etc. For up to this point Constantine discussed the Lord’s advent and the reason Christ descended to earth. Now he discusses those who did not know this mystery.
>
> **Τί δὲ ὅτι προσφιλὲς ἦν.** I should prefer to write **ἔτι δὲ ὅτι** etc., “and further, because…” For Constantine gives two reasons why the Gentiles did not accept Christ’s preaching.
>
> **Τοῖς πρὸς ἅμιλλαν ζῇν προῃρημένοις.** Greeks elegantly say **πρὸς ἅμιλλαν ζῇν**, “to live in emulation,” of those who shape their life in imitation of what is best. For those wishing to make great progress in virtue ought to set someone before their eyes as a model to imitate. Thus the emperor Julian shaped his actions and conduct in emulation of Emperor Marcus, as Ammianus Marcellinus says.
>
> **Παραφυλάσσηται καθαρὰ ψυχὴ.** It should be written **καθαρᾷ [Col. 0436C] ψυχῇ**, “with a pure soul,” as is read in the Fuk. codex, in which **ἀληθής τε ᾖ**, “and may be true,” is also written most appropriately.
>
> **Πεφραγμένη πρὸς τὸ μαρτύριον.** In the books of Scaliger, [Col. 0436D] Bongarsius, and Gruter this passage was read: **ἀνανταγωνίστῳ θείας ἀρετῆς μάχῃ φερομένη πρὸς τὸ μαρτύριον**, “borne toward martyrdom in an irresistible contest of divine virtue.” I found this reading also in the Fuk. codex. Savile, however, emended his book thus: **ἀνανταγωνίστῳ τε θείας ἀρετῆς μάχῃ φέρεται πρὸς** etc., and Christophorson reads likewise. But the common reading, found in the Royal codex and the manuscript sheets, is in my judgment much superior.
>
> **Ὃς γενναίως ἐμαρτύρησε.** I do not doubt that one should write **ὃν γενναίως ἐμαρτύρησε**, “to whom he nobly bore witness,” which surprises me that Christophorson and others did not observe.
>
> **Ἡ τελευτὴ πλήρης.** Without doubt one should write **ἥ τε τελευτὴ πλήρης**, “and the death [is] full,” so that the sense may be complete. Moreover, this is a most elegant passage concerning martyrs.

The sacrifice of thanksgiving. This passage too is especially to be noted concerning the sacrifice of the Mass, which was offered to God in commemoration and honor of the martyrs. For these words, “A sacrifice is performed for the men,” must be explained thus [Col. 0437C]; Christophorson did not understand them. Christians did not offer sacrifice to the martyrs [Col. 0437D], but to God alone, giving Him thanks because He had endowed them with the crown of martyrdom, as Augustine writes in Book VIII of *The City of God*, in its final chapter. This is the sacrifice which Constantine here calls “the sacrifice of thanksgiving.” But because Christians offered this bloodless sacrifice to God at the memorials and tombs of the martyrs, in order to give Him thanks for the martyrs’ rewards, crowns, and victories, Constantine says that this honor was rendered to the martyrs.

And the banquets. Augustine himself speaks of these Christian feasts, held at the tombs of martyrs, in the passage cited, as follows: “Those also who bring their own meals thither—which indeed is not done by the better sort of Christians, and in most lands no such custom exists—yet all who do so, after setting them out, pray and remove them in order to eat them, or even distribute some of them to the needy; they wish them to be sanctified there through the merits of the martyrs,” etc. At first these feasts [Col. 0438C] were sober and restrained. Later, as license advanced into worse excesses, they degenerated into drunkenness and wantonness. [Col. 0438D] Therefore they were entirely abolished in many places, as Augustine testifies in Epistle 64. In the Fuk. manuscript it is written: “and the banquets, most temperate beyond many others,” etc., not “of many,” as the common editions have.

[Col. 0435A] “But,” someone who delights in blasphemy will say, “being God, He could have made human disposition better and gentler.” What method, then, would be better? What undertaking more effective for correcting the wicked than His own address? Did He not Himself, being present and visible, teach the orderly life? If God’s command achieved nothing when He was present, what benefit could it have brought when He was absent and unheard? What, then, became an impediment to the most blessed teaching? The boorishness of human beings. For when we receive in anger what is commanded rightly and fittingly, then the sobriety of the mind is obscured. Or what of the fact that they found it agreeable to neglect the commands and to make their ears unreceptive to the law that had been laid down? For, had they not neglected it, they would have received the rewards worthy of obedience, not only immediately [Col. 0435B] but also in the life to come—which is life in truth. For the reward of obeying God is incorruptible and eternal life. Those who know God may lay claim to it: those who make their own life worthy of imitation, and, as it were, an eternal example for those who have chosen to live in emulation.

For this reason teaching was entrusted to the wise: so that whatever they command may be guarded with care by their own people, in a pure soul; and so that the keeping of God’s command may be true and steadfast. For from this there grows fearlessness in the face of death, born of pure faith and sincere devotion toward God. Such a soul withstands worldly storms, fenced about for martyrdom by the unconquerable struggle of divine virtue. Having overcome the greatest fears through greatness of soul, it is deemed worthy of a crown from Him whom it nobly confessed as a martyr [or: “whom it nobly bore witness to”; Greek text uncertain]. And it is in no way exalted by this; for it knows, I think, that this too has been given from God, enabling it to endure and willingly fulfil the divine commands.

A lasting remembrance and eternal glory rightly succeed such a life, if indeed both the martyr’s life is temperate and his end, mindful of the commandments, is found full of greatness of soul and nobility. There follow hymns, psalms, and acclamations; and praise directed to the Overseer of all. Thus a sacrifice of thanksgiving is performed for the men: pure from blood [Col. 0438A] and pure from every violence. Neither the smell of incense nor a pyre is desired, but pure light, sufficient to shine upon those who pray. The banquets too are most temperate, being held for the relief and restoration of those in need and for assistance to the fallen—things which no one who thinks in accordance with the divine and most blessed teaching would judge burdensome.

## Chapter XIII.—That Distinction among Created Things Is Necessary; and That the Inclination toward Good and Evil Arises from Human Will, and Therefore God’s Judgment Is Necessary

[Col. 0437]

[Col. 0437B] Some, moreover, presumptuously display youthful audacity even in reproaching God. “For what reason,” they ask, “did He not fashion one and the same nature and disposition for all beings, but will that many different—and indeed mostly contrary—natures should be born?” Hence arises the diversity of our characters and choices. Perhaps it would have been better, with respect to obedience to God’s commands, accurate apprehension of Him, and the establishment of each person’s faith, for all human beings to be of like character.

But it is altogether absurd and ridiculous to demand that all people should be alike in character, without reflecting that the ordering of the world is not the same as that of the things in the world; that natural things are not of the same substance as moral things; or that the affections of the body are not identical with the passions of the soul. For the rational soul surpasses the whole world by a vast interval, being happier than mortal and earthly living creatures insofar as it is more august and divine; and the human race is not without a share in divine goodness. Yet not all people, simply and indiscriminately, share it; rather, those who have traced out the divine nature and have chosen as the chief pursuit of life the knowledge of divine things.

> Note [Col. 0438D]
>
> “Even in reproaching.” I would prefer to write *in this matter* (*ἐν τούτῳ*), as I found corrected in the margin of Moraeus’s copy. Thus it is also written in the Fuk. manuscript.
>
> “According to each person’s faith.” It seems that one should write: “the faith concerning each person” (*τὴν καθ᾽ ἑκάστου πίστιν*).
>
> “The ordering concerning the world.” I would prefer: “the ordering of the world itself is not also that of worldly things” (*οὐχ ἥ περ ἡ τοῦ κόσμου διάταξις, αὕτη καὶ τῶν κοσμικῶν*).
>
> “For the whole world.” Much is missing after these words, as is clear from the title of the chapter. We preferred to draw whatever sense we could from the corrupt and mutilated passage rather than, with Christophorson, erase it all. Savile likewise deleted in his copy this entire period down to the words “of divine goodness.” Certainly, the entire period is absent from the Fuk. manuscript.

[Col. 0438B] Some now even play the bold youth in reproaching God: Why, having so willed, did He not fashion one and the same nature for existing things, but command diverse and, for the most part, opposite natures to be produced? Hence too the difference of our characters and choices. For perhaps it would have been better, both for obedience to the commands of God, for exact understanding of Him, and for each person’s faith to be made firm, that all people should be alike in character. But to demand that all people be alike in character is utterly ridiculous, and not to consider that the ordering of the world is not also that of worldly things; nor are natural things of the same substance as moral things, nor are the affections of the body the same as the passions of the soul. For the whole world [text defective] in happiness above corruptible and earthly living creatures, insofar as it is more august and divine; [Col. 0438C] and the human race is not without a share in divine goodness. Yet this is not true simply of all, nor indiscriminately, but of those who have traced out the divine nature and have chosen as the foremost pursuit of life the knowledge of divine things.

## Chapter XIV.—That Creation Is Separated from Uncreated Substance by an Immeasurable Interval, and That through Virtue Man Draws Nearest to God

[Col. 0437]

[Col. 0437C] Moreover, to compare things which have come into being with eternal things is truly the height of madness. The latter have neither [Col. 0440A] beginning nor end; but the former, being planted and generated, and having received at a certain time a beginning both of existence and life, necessarily also have an end. How could generated things ever be made equal to Him who commanded them to be generated? For if these things are equal to Him, the command by which He ordered them to be generated could not fittingly apply to Him. Not even heavenly things may rightly be compared with Him, just as neither the sensible world with the intelligible world, nor images with their archetypes. And is not the confusion and mingling of all things utterly ridiculous, when the dignity of the divine is concealed by comparing human beings—and even beasts—with God?

The desire for power that rivals and equals God’s power—is this not the mark of utterly mad people, alien from a temperate [Col. 0440B] and virtuous life? For if we claim any share at all in divine blessedness, we must live according to God’s command. Thus, having lived according to the law established by God, we shall spend our life in immortal and ageless dwelling-places, superior to every fate. For the only human power corresponding to God’s power is sincere and guileless worship of God; conversion to Him; contemplation and learning of the things pleasing to the Higher Power; and not bending downward toward the earth, but raising the mind, so far as possible, toward upright and lofty things. For from this pursuit comes victory in place of many goods, he says. The cause, then, of the diversity of things, both in their difference of worth and in their difference of capacity [Col. 0440C], is this. Those who think soundly willingly accept this reasoning [Col. 0439C] and give thanks exceedingly; but the ungrateful, being foolish, receive the punishment deserved by their arrogance.

> Note [Col. 0439C]
>
> “Things which have come into being.” Christophorson appears to have read “things which are generated” (*γεννώμενα*), which is preferable.
>
> “For if madness.” I think this passage should be corrected thus: “For if these things are equal to Him, then the command that they be generated could not fittingly apply to Him” (*εἰ γὰρ ὅμοια ταῦτα ἐκείνῳ, οὐδὲ πρόσταξις τοῦ γεννᾶσθαι, προσηκόντως ἂν ἐκείνῳ ἁρμόζοιτο*). That is: if generated things are equal to God, the command by which He ordered them to be generated would certainly not apply to Him. For an equal cannot possess right and authority over an equal. Let the emendation of learned men therefore be dismissed, an emendation which I also found in the Fuk. manuscript and Moraeus’s copy: “For if it is madness to make these things equal to Him, the command that they be generated,” etc. But if one reads it thus, there is no sense, nor will what follows cohere with what precedes. Christophorson had indeed found it thus in his books, as his translation shows. But the common reading is supported by the authority of the Royal manuscript and the old notes.
>
> “The confusion of all things.” Musculus seems to have read “comparison” (*σύγκρισις*), which I strongly approve, for he translates: “But how is the comparison of all things not ridiculous?” Certainly it must either be read thus or understood thus. Constantine calls that making-all-things-equal a confusion.
>
> “If even beasts [are] compared.” Without doubt one should write *συγκρίνοιτο*. For Constantine’s argument is this: “Not even heavenly things can be compared with God. How much less earthly things and brute animals.” This is the sense of the passage. Yet the manuscripts of Christophorson, Savile, Gruter, and Fuk. give the text thus: “when the dignity of the divine is concealed by comparison with human beings and even beasts.” This reading seems to me better and more elegant.
>
> “He says, victory in place of many goods.” He seems to allude to what is read in Revelation, chapters II and III, where God says: “To the one who conquers I will give a crown,” etc. Certainly the life of a Christian is commonly compared with that of athletes, as frequently occurs in Paul’s epistles. The word *φησί* (“he says”) is superfluous in Greek fashion, as those skilled in the Greek language know.
>
> “Worth.” The Royal manuscript has “well-being” (*εὐεξία*), as Robert Estienne also noted in his variant readings. I therefore read “worth” (*ἀξία*) with Christophorson, Scaliger, Gruter, and others; or “desert” (*ἐπαξία*), which comes closer to the traces of the written reading. The Fuk. manuscript reads: “and worth.”

[Col. 0438C] To compare things which have arisen by generation with eternal things is truly the most complete madness. For the latter have neither beginning [Col. 0439A] nor end, whereas the former, being planted and generated, and having received at a certain time the beginning both of being and living, necessarily also have an end. How can things which have been generated be made equal to Him who commanded that they should be generated? For if [it is] madness [to make] these things equal to Him, then the command that they be generated could not fittingly apply to Him [the Greek is corrupt]. But not even heavenly things could be compared with Him, just as the sensible world cannot be compared with the intelligible, nor images with archetypes. And how is the confusion of all things not ridiculous, when the dignity of the divine is concealed through comparison with human beings, if even beasts are compared? The desire for power, matching God’s power, how is it not the mark of mad people, who have turned away from the temperate and virtuous life? For if we lay claim at all to divine blessedness, we must pass our life according to God’s command. Thus, in immortal and ageless dwelling-places [Col. 0439B], superior to every fate, we shall live, having lived according to the law ordained by God. For the only human power corresponding to God’s power is sincere and guileless worship toward God, conversion to Him, contemplation and learning of what is pleasing to the Higher Power, and not inclining toward the earth but raising the mind, so far as possible, to upright and lofty things. For from this pursuit comes, he says, victory in place of many goods. Therefore the cause of the difference among beings, both in worth and in difference of capacity, has this explanation: those who think well are persuaded by it and give thanks exceedingly, while the ungrateful, being foolish, receive the punishment deserved by their arrogance.

## Chapter XV.—What Commands the Savior Gave, What Miracles He Performed, and How Greatly He Benefited His Subjects

[Col. 0439]

Moreover, the Son of God exhorts all people to virtue, presenting Himself to the wise as teacher of the commands of salvation [reading uncertain; perhaps “of the Father’s commands”]. Unless, through the greatest folly, we fail to recognize that He travelled throughout the earth for our benefit—that is, for the blessedness of all people—and, having summoned to Himself the best men of that time, taught a most beneficial instruction, a medicine, as it were, for a temperate life. He instructed them in faith and justice against the envy of the hostile nature, which delights in enticing and deceiving the inexperienced.

Accordingly, He visited the sick and relieved the infirm of the evils that oppressed them. He comforted those reduced to the utmost poverty and want. He especially commended moderation of mind joined with reason, and commanded us to bear every kind of insult and contempt nobly and patiently, teaching that such things are a visitation of the Father, so that those who bear what befalls them with greatness of soul always conquer. For He declared this to be the most extraordinary [Col. 0441B] and excellent strength: firmness of mind joined with philosophy, which is the knowledge of truth and goodness. This habituates those who possess wealth with justice to share what they have with poorer persons through humane distribution.

He utterly forbade domination, declaring openly that, just as He came to help the humble, so He would cease to show favor to those who had despised the humble. Having tested the faith of the peoples subject to Him by such great and such extensive proof, He made them not only despisers of terrible and fearful things but also the truest disciples of hope in Him. On one occasion, moreover, He rebuked and restrained with words one of His companions who had yielded excessively to anger. That man was advancing upon someone with a sword, having stripped his own soul of the Savior’s aid, as though to help the Savior. He ordered him to remain still [Col. 0441C] and to let go the sword, rebuking him because he had despaired of recourse to Him.

He expressly laid down this law: whoever undertakes to strike another, or tries to harm one who is striking, and in general whoever uses a sword, shall perish by a violent death. This truly is heavenly wisdom: to choose being wronged rather than wrongdoing; and, when necessity arises, to be ready to suffer harm rather than inflict it. For since wrongdoing is the greatest evil, it is not the person wronged, but the wrongdoer, who is encompassed by the greatest punishment [Col. 0444A]. One obedient to God may neither do wrong nor suffer wrong, provided he trusts in the protection of God, who is present and aids him, so that none of those obedient to Him may suffer harm.

How, trusting in God, could he himself come to his own aid? For there would be a contest between two persons, and the outcome of victory would be doubtful. No one of sound mind chooses uncertainties before certainties. And how could one who has undergone such great dangers, and has always easily been delivered from calamities by God’s nod alone, doubt God’s presence and help? He who travelled through the sea when, by the Savior’s command, it had been spread out and furnished a firm road to the peoples crossing the sea? This, I think, is the manifest foundation of faith, this the ground of confidence: when we observe these wondrous and incredible events coming to pass and being accomplished at the command of the providential God. From this comes also the refusal to repent of one’s faith [Col. 0444B], whenever someone encounters an experience of evils, and the possession of an unchanging hope toward God. For when this disposition has entered into the soul, God is established in the mind; and since He is unconquered, the soul that possesses the Unconquered One in its own mind can never be overcome by surrounding dangers.

Further, we have learned this from God’s victory: He who made providence for all, having been outrageously treated by the injustice of the impious, received no injury from His suffering, but won the greatest triumphs and an eternal crown over wickedness [Col. 0444C], bringing to fulfilment the purpose of His own providence and affection toward the righteous, and crushing the cruelty of unjust and impious people.

> Note [Col. 0440D]
>
> “The commands of the Savior.” It appears that one should write “the commands of salvation” (*τῶν τῆς σωτηρίας …*), as is noted in the margin of the Geneva edition. One might also write “of the Father.” The error seems to have arisen from abbreviated writing. Certainly the Royal and Fuk. manuscripts and the notes have *σρς* at this point.
>
