> [Col. 0441C] “Of those beneficial to life at that time.” Christophorson translates: “And having summoned to himself the very best among those who at that time assisted human life.” But who ever spoke thus: “the best of those beneficial to life” (*τοὺς ἀρίστους τῶν βιωφελῶν*)? Therefore I do not doubt that the passage should be punctuated and corrected thus: “and having summoned to himself the best men of that time, he taught a beneficial instruction” (*καὶ καλέσας ὡς ἑαυτὸν τοὺς ἀρίστους τῶν τηνικαῦτα, βιωφελῆ παιδείαν ἐπαίδευσε*). That is: “having summoned to Himself the best men of that time, He delivered a most beneficial instruction.” The books of Fuket and Turnèbe read *τῶν τηνικάδε*.
>
> “Which delights in enticing.” In the books of Turnèbe and Moraeus it is corrected: “to entice and deceive,” etc. But the Fuk. manuscript correctly writes: “which delights in enticing and deceiving” (*ᾗ δελεάζειν καὶ ἐξαπατᾶν*).
>
> “The moderation joined with reason.” Thus it is printed in Robert Estienne’s edition; this reading is confirmed by the Royal manuscript, the Fuk. manuscript, and the notes. But in Moraeus’s copy I found “with plausible reason” (*μετ᾽ εὐλόγου*) corrected in the margin; I do not know why the Genevan editors introduced this correction into the text. “The measure of prudence” means the same as “to be moderate-minded.” The Apostle Paul says: “to think soberly.”
>
> “A certain command of the Father.” I would prefer “visitation” (*ἐπίσκεψιν*), as is noted in the margin of the Geneva edition [Col. 0442C]. For such calamities as sometimes happen to good people we commonly call visitations of God. Christophorson, however, following the common reading, translated “command.”
>
> “Of truth and goodness.” In Moraeus’s copy a learned man corrected this in the margin to “of the good” (*τἀγαθοῦ*), which is not displeasing. For much in this discourse is Platonic.
>
> “Advancing upon someone with a sword.” Thus in the Fuk. manuscript. Elsewhere it was wrongly read: “advancing upon someone sword-bearing.”
>
> “Everyone who begins unjust violence.” This passage should be restored from the Fuk. manuscript and Turnèbe’s book thus: “openly laying down the law, everyone who begins unjust violence,” etc. As for what follows—“or who attempts to commit injustice against one who has begun it”—I myself would prefer to write: “attempts to retaliate unjustly” (*ἀνταδικεῖν ἐπιχειρήσαντα*).
>
> “For wrongdoing being the greatest evil.” In Moraeus’s copy a learned man noted in the margin: “Socratic, concerning injustice.” Certainly much in this discourse is drawn from Platonic philosophy, as an educated reader will be able to recognize for himself.
>
> [Col. 0443C] “For one obedient to God it was permitted.” The Fuk. manuscript and Turnèbe’s copy read *ἐξόν*.
>
> “To come to his own aid.” Scaliger, Gruter, and others corrected this to “trusting in God, could he aid God?” This correction I also found written in Moraeus’s copy. One might also write “was he going to come to his own aid?” omitting the final two words, which everyone sees are scarcely necessary here. But the Fuk. manuscript fully agrees with the books of Scaliger and Gruter.
>
> “But there was a contest.” I do not doubt that one should write: “for thus there would be a contest between two” (*οὕτως γὰρ μάχη μὲν ἦν μεταξύ δυοῖν*), where *ἦν* is used for *εἴη*, or for “would be.” But the translator who translated this discourse of Constantine into Greek was not very skilled in Greek and was not sufficiently careful, as is apparent from many passages. Constantine here gives the reason why worshippers of the supreme God never wish to avenge themselves or repel force with force. If they did so, he says, they would indeed fight their opponent, but their victory would be uncertain. But if they did not defend themselves at all, they then possess the most certain victory, God fighting for them. This is the sense of the passage, which I am surprised neither Christophorson nor Musculus perceived [Col. 0444C].
>
> “By God’s nod alone.” One should write “by the nod of God alone” (*μόνῳ*), as I found corrected in Moraeus’s copy. And shortly afterward I read “providing a road,” as in the same copy [Col. 0444D]; for “the sea” is understood. The Fuk. manuscript and the old notes read “by the nod of God alone.”
>
> “From this comes the refusal to repent of faith.” The Fuk. manuscript reads “not to repent.”
>
> “Whenever someone encounters an experience of evils.” I would prefer *πεῖρα* in the nominative, for this seems much more elegant. Shortly afterward one must undoubtedly read “and to have the unchanging [hope],” etc., since the verb “comes” is understood from the preceding clause. The Fuk. manuscript and the notes read: “whenever an experience of evils encounters someone, and he has unchanging hope,” etc.
>
> “The unconquered.” In the margin of Moraeus’s manuscript it is corrected: “possessing the Unconquered One.” Christophorson followed this reading. Thus it is written in the Fuket manuscript.
>
> “But besides.” I read: “Moreover, we have learned this” (*πρὸς δὲ τοῦτο μεμαθήκαμεν*), where *πρός* is used adverbially for “besides.”

[Col. 0439C] Moreover, the Servant of God exhorts all people to virtue, making Himself, for those who think well, the teacher of the Savior’s commands; unless perhaps we are unaware of ourselves, wrongly ignorant that He travelled through the earth for what benefits us—that is, for human blessedness. Having summoned to Himself the best men of that time, He taught an instruction beneficial to life, a remedy for a temperate life; having taught them faith and righteousness against the envy of the opposing nature, which delights in enticing and deceiving the inexperienced. Accordingly, He visited the sick; He relieved the infirm of the evils that surrounded them; and He comforted those who had advanced to the furthest extremity of poverty and need. He praised moderation of mind joined with reason, and commanded people to endure every kind of insult and every kind of contempt nobly and with patience, teaching that such a thing was a visitation of the Father, so that those who bear what happens to them with greatness of soul always conquer. For He declared this to be a surpassingly excellent strength: firmness of mind together with philosophy, which is knowledge of truth and goodness, and which habituates even those who are rich with righteousness to share their possessions with poorer persons through humane distribution.

Forbidding domination in every way, He showed that, just as He came to the moderate, so He would leave the moderate whom they had abandoned, granting them favor. Having tested by such and so great an experience the faith of the subject peoples, He made them not merely despisers of dreadful and fearful things, but also most genuine disciples of hope in Him. And once, reproving one of His companions who had given way too greatly to anger, He restrained him with words. That man happened to be advancing sword in hand against someone, having stripped his own soul of the Savior’s assistance. He ordered him to remain quietly and [Col. 0442C] let go the sword, reproaching him as one who had despaired of recourse to Him. And He expressly legislated that everyone who begins unjust violence, or attempts to commit injustice against one who has begun it, and uses the sword, shall perish violently.

This truly is heavenly wisdom: to choose being wronged rather than doing wrong; and, when necessity arises, to be ready to suffer ill rather than inflict it. For wrongdoing being the greatest evil, it is not the one wronged but the wrongdoer who is encompassed by the greatest punishment. To one obedient [Col. 0443A] to God it was possible neither to do wrong nor to suffer wrong, if he trusted in the protection of God, who is present and assists him, so that none of those obedient to Him should suffer harm. How could he himself come to his own aid, trusting in God? For there would be a contest between two, and victory would be uncertain; and no sensible person chooses doubtful things in preference to things firmly established. How, moreover, was one who had encountered so many dangers, and who had always easily been delivered from calamities by God’s nod alone, to doubt the presence and help of God? One who had travelled through the sea, when by the Savior’s command it had been spread out and offered a firm path to the peoples passing across it?

For this, I think, is the obvious basis of faith and the foundation of confidence: when we observe these marvellous and incredible things happening and being accomplished at the command of the providential One. From this also comes not repenting of faith whenever someone is met by an experience of evils, and having unchanging hope toward God. For when this disposition comes into the soul, God is established in the mind; and He is unconquered. Therefore the soul which has the Unconquered One in its own mind will not be overcome by surrounding calamities. Moreover, we have learned this from God’s victory: He, exercising providence for all, when He had been outrageously treated by the injustice of the impious, received no harm from His suffering, but won the greatest triumphs and an eternal crown over wickedness, bringing to completion the purpose of His own providence and affection toward the righteous, and crushing the cruelty of the unjust and impious.

## Chapter XVI.—That Christ’s Coming Was Foretold by the Prophets, and That It Was Ordained for the Destruction of Idols and of the Cities That Worshipped Idols

[Col. 0443]

Moreover, His suffering had long ago been proclaimed by the prophets, and His bodily birth had likewise been proclaimed. The time of His incarnation was also foretold [Col. 0445A]: that the offspring springing from injustice and licentiousness, which harm righteous deeds and ways of life, might be removed; and that the whole inhabited world might share in prudence and temperance, since the law ordained by the Savior had prevailed in almost all souls, reverence toward God had been strengthened, and superstition had been wiped out. Through this superstition not only the slaughter of irrational animals but also sacrifices of human victims and the defilements of impious altars were devised; for according to Assyrian and Egyptian laws, innocent people were slaughtered before bronze-wrought or molded images.

They therefore received a reward fitting for such religion: “Memphis and Babylon shall be laid waste, and they shall be left uninhabited with their ancestral gods.” I say this not from hearsay, but as one who was personally present, observed it, and became a witness of the pitiable fate of the cities. Memphis lies desolate, once the seat of Pharaoh, then the mightiest king, whom Moses, at God’s command, struck down when pride had exalted him; and he destroyed Pharaoh’s army—victorious over many and very great nations, fortified and fully armed—not with flights of arrows or showers of spears, but by holy prayer alone and gentle supplication.

> Note [Col. 0445C]
>
> “And how the offspring of injustice.” In Moraeus’s copy it is corrected in the margin to: “and how the things of injustice,” etc.; Christophorson expressed this reading in his translation. This phrase seems to me insufficiently Greek. I would therefore prefer to write: “in which the things of injustice,” etc. The Fuk. manuscript nevertheless has “and how the things of…”
>
> “Having become a witness.” Constantine says that he personally saw the destruction and desolation of two cities once extremely powerful, namely Memphis and Babylon. We must therefore inquire when Constantine travelled to those places. He did travel to Egypt when still very young, serving in Diocletian’s retinue and being held by him almost as a hostage. For Diocletian waged war in Egypt for many years against Achilleus, who had rebelled there, as Eutropius writes. Later Constantine came from Egypt to Syria with Diocletian and passed through the province of Palestine, where Eusebius first saw him, as Eusebius himself testifies. Diocletian had come into Syria in order to assist Caesar Galerius, who was waging war against the Persians, with his forces. He remained for a long time in Syria to settle peace with the Persians, as we learn from the history of Peter the Patrician. Constantine could therefore at that time have viewed Babylon’s ruins and remains.
>
> “Or Moses.” I think this passage has been corrupted only through transposition. For its meaning is perfectly clear if the words are restored as follows: “Memphis lies desolate, the glory of Pharaoh, then the mightiest ruler; Moses, at the divine command, shattered him,” etc. What could be clearer than these words? Here *ὑπεροψία* means “glory,” the boast by which Pharaoh exalted himself. Let the conjecture of Christophorson, Gruter, and others therefore be dismissed. This was once our own conjecture concerning the reading of this passage. But afterward, having obtained the Fuket manuscript, we discovered the true and genuine reading. For it reads thus [Col. 0446C]: “Having become a witness of the pitiable and unfortunate Memphis among the cities: Moses, at the divine command, laid waste the land of Pharaoh, then the mightiest ruler,” etc. This is exactly how it is read in Turnèbe’s and Gruter’s manuscripts, except that the punctuation which we have supplied belongs to the Fuk. manuscript, in which a full stop is placed after “Memphis.” The translator of this discourse therefore used *Memphis* in the genitive when he should have said *of Memphis*; and *pitiable* is used for “most pitiable.” According to this reading, Constantine says that he saw Memphis alone; this I judge more likely. For he could never have seen Babylon, since he never penetrated Assyria. The Royal notes read the passage thus: “of the pitiable fate of the cities; Memphis was laid waste,” etc., as in the common editions. But the Royal manuscript has “lies desolate,” as Estienne printed it. Savile corrected the passage in his copy thus: “the fate of the cities: Memphis lies desolate; Moses laid waste,” etc. But “Memphis lies desolate” would be flat and would not cohere with what follows. Indeed, Christophorson did not retain those words in his translation.
>
> “Whom pride shattered.” Christophorson translates: “Whom insolence, once it had exalted him, destroyed.” This shows that he supplied “having been lifted up,” or something similar. But there is no need for this correction, since *ὑπεροψία* may be taken in the nominative. Certainly in all our manuscripts—the Royal, the Fuk., and the notes—it is read without an iota subscript. So below, in chapter 19, he says: “Ignorance shattered the souls of human beings,” etc.
>
> “Fully armed.” It seems one should write: “and fully armed.” Shortly afterward, where “gentle supplication” is read, I would prefer “quiet supplication.” The Fuk. manuscript and the Royal notes read: “fortified and fully armed.” Savile’s conjecture, “fortified and fully armed,” is not displeasing either.

[Col. 0443C] But His suffering had already been proclaimed by the prophets; His bodily birth too had been proclaimed. The time of the incarnation had also been foretold: that the offspring springing from injustice and licentiousness, which harm righteous deeds and ways of life, might be removed; that the whole inhabited world might partake of prudence and temperance; that the law ordained by the Savior might prevail in nearly all souls; that reverence toward God might be strengthened; and that superstition might be wiped out. Through this superstition, not only the slaughter of irrational animals, but also the sacrificial immolation of human victims and the abominable defilements of altars were devised, as Assyrians and Egyptians slaughtered righteous lives before bronze-wrought or molded images according to their laws. They therefore reaped the fruit fitting for such religion: “Memphis and Babylon shall be made desolate, and they shall be left uninhabited together with their ancestral gods.” I say these things not from hearsay, but as one present and having observed them, becoming a witness of the pitiable fate of the cities. Memphis lies desolate—or Moses, at the divine command, [laid waste] that of Pharaoh [text corrupt], then the mightiest ruler, whom pride shattered; and his army, victorious over many and very great nations, fortified and fully armed, he overthrew not by flights of arrows nor showers of javelins, but by holy prayer alone and gentle supplication.

## Chapter XVII.—On the Wisdom of Moses, Which the Sages of the Gentiles Imitated; Also on Daniel and the Three Young Men

[Col. 0445]

[Col. 0445B] No people was ever, or would ever be, more blessed than that people, unless it withdrew its mind from the divine Spirit. Who could praise Moses according to his merits? Having arranged the formerly confused multitude of the Jews into fixed orders and adorned their minds with obedience and modesty, he gave them freedom in place of slavery and joy in place of sorrow. He raised their spirits so greatly that, because of the unexpected change of their affairs for the better and their prosperous successes and victories, they were carried away by a certain pride and insolence. He surpassed all who had preceded him in age so greatly in wisdom that those among the gentiles most celebrated either as sages or as philosophers became imitators of his wisdom. Pythagoras certainly emulated his wisdom and was so celebrated for moderation that Plato, a most moderate man, proposed Pythagoras’s abstinence to himself as an example for imitation.

Daniel also—he who foretold the future, gave proof of exceptional greatness of soul, and excelled in holiness of character and of his whole life—what cruelty, and how harsh a cruelty, of the tyrant then ruling in Syria did he overcome? His name was Nebuchadnezzar. When his entire line had been utterly destroyed, that vast and formidable power was transferred to the Persians. The wealth of that king was on everyone’s lips, as it is still celebrated in the speech of many people to this day; likewise his importunate zeal for unlawful religion, his immense abundance of every kind of metal for making images of gods, the rooftops of temples reaching, so to speak, to the very sky, and finally religious laws dreadful and designed for cruelty.

Yet Daniel, despising all this because of his sincere piety toward God, foretold that the tyrant’s importunate enterprise would become the cause of a very grave evil. He did not, however, persuade the tyrant. For abundance of wealth is a very great impediment to sound judgment. At last the king revealed the savagery of his mind, ordering the righteous and innocent man to be cast out to be torn apart by wild beasts. The noble unanimity of those brothers in undergoing martyrdom was likewise especially remarkable. Later generations imitated them and gained immense glory through faith toward the Savior. They suffered no injury at all from the fire, the furnace, and the other tortures devised to consume their bodies, but by the opposition and contact of their chaste bodies drove back the flames enclosed on every side within the furnace.

Then, when the Assyrian empire had been destroyed by God’s vengeance and bolts of lightning, Daniel, through divine providence, went to Cambyses, king of the Persians [Col. 0449A]. Here too envy troubled him, along with the deadly plots of the Magi and the unbroken succession of many and great perils. Easily delivered from all these by Christ’s providence, he shone forth conspicuous in every kind of virtue. For when he offered prayers to God three times daily and performed great and unusual miracles of memorable deeds, the Magi, moved by envy, began to calumniate this efficacy of prayer. They whispered into the king’s ears that such power in a man was exceedingly dangerous; and at length persuaded him that the man who had been the author of so many and such great benefits to the Persian state should be exposed to be devoured by savage lions.

Thus Daniel was condemned and cast into the pit—not to perish, but to attain everlasting glory [Col. 0449B]. While he lived among the beasts, he found them gentler and milder than those by whom he had been thrust into the pit. For prayer, bringing the help of modesty and temperance, tamed all those beasts, though rabid by their own nature. When Cambyses heard this—for such stupendous miracles of divine power could not be concealed—he was struck by wonder at what had been reported and felt remorse that he had lent such ready ears to the Magi’s calumnies. Nevertheless, he wished himself to be an eyewitness of the matter. When he saw Daniel with uplifted hands praising Christ, while the lions crouched low and in a manner worshipped the man’s footprints, he immediately ordered the Magi who had persuaded him to this to be cast to the lions. The beasts which shortly before had caressed Daniel at once rushed upon the Magi and tore them all to pieces with the savagery of their nature.

> Note [Col. 0447D]
>
> “And philosophers.” A particle appears to have been omitted here; when added, the sentence becomes much more elegant. I therefore write: “either sages, or philosophers as well” (*ἢ τοι σοφοὺς ἢ καὶ φιλοσόφους*), that is, “whether one prefers to call them sages or philosophers.”
>
> “But Daniel.” Having spoken of the Egyptians and the destruction of Memphis, he passes to the Assyrians and Babylon’s desolation. Taking occasion from the Egyptians, he inserted a praise of Moses. Now, in speaking of the Assyrians, he recounts the praises of Daniel, who lived as a captive among the Assyrians or Babylonians.
>
> “Daniel, having despised.” After these words, the copyist who transcribed the Royal manuscript, offended by the multitude of errors with which his exemplar abounded, here ceased writing. He attested this by adding at the foot of the page: “… before the sea of errors in the book, I withheld my hand from writing, because there was nothing sound in the original, as readers may infer from what has been written.” [Col. 0448D]
>
> “Destroyed by bolts of lightning.” I do not know from where Constantine drew this assertion that the Assyrian kingdom was destroyed by bolts of lightning; I do not recall reading it elsewhere. Nor do I sufficiently understand it. People, citadels, and cities can be destroyed by lightning strikes, as poets fabled about the Phlegyans. But how a kingdom can be abolished by lightning, I do not see. The Fuk. and Turnèbe manuscripts and the Royal notes read “by bolts of lightning.”
>
> “Extraordinary virtues.” Constantine had said *virtutes* in Latin; everyone knows that in sacred books this word is commonly used for miracles. The translator of this discourse translated it badly as *ἀρετάς* (“virtues”), whereas he should rather have translated it as *δυνάμεις* (“powers,” “miracles”).
>
> [Col. 0449C] “Exceedingly dangerous.” In the Fuk. manuscript the passage is punctuated thus: “They calumniated it as dangerous; and then, “exceedingly, the so great …,” etc.”

“Persuaded him.” I write *and they persuaded him*, as is corrected in the margin of Moraeus’s book. Moreover, this narrative conflicts with Holy Scripture. For in the sacred books it is not the Magi who are said to have accused Daniel, but the satraps [Col. 0449D]; nor is the man who ordered Daniel thrown to the beasts called Cambyses, but Darius the Mede, concerning whom chronologists hold differing opinions. For most wish him to be Cyaxares, son of Astyages. Scaliger, however, maintains that he was Nabonidus; our Petavius supports this view. I attach great weight to their agreement. For although they usually disagree in most matters, wherever we see them concur, it is a very great indication of the truth.

Yet Abydenus, in his history of the Assyrians, seems to oppose their opinion. For he writes that Nebuchadnezzar, shortly before his death, inspired by divine power, foretold to the Babylonians that their city would soon perish. For a Persian mule would come, who would impose the yoke of slavery upon them. And a Mede, the glory of the Assyrians, would be his helper in the capture of the city. Thus I interpret Abydenus’s words, *of whom indeed a Mede will be a joint cause* (*οὗ δὴ συναίτιος ἔσται Μήδης*). The Greek words certainly mean nothing other than what I have said. But if the Mede was Cyrus’s associate and helper in [Col. 0450C] capturing Babylon and reducing it to slavery, the Mede surely was not Nabonidus. Scaliger, however, who wishes Darius the Mede to be Nabonidus, explains Abydenus’s words thus: that this disaster would befall the Babylonians through the fault of the Mede. But Abydenus did not say *because of whom the cause* (*οὗ δὴ αἴτιος*), but *joint cause* (*συναίτιος*): a word signifying partnership and participation with another in some action. Thus the Son of God is called a joint cause [Col. 0450D], because together with the Father he is the author of all things. It is therefore established from Abydenus’s words that the Mede was not Nabonidus.

“For all by prayer.” I would prefer to write in the nominative: “For prayer, joined with the virtue of orderliness and temperance, made them all tame.” That is: so great is the power of prayer that it made even the fiercest beasts gentle. Certainly, in the Fuk. manuscript one reads: “Prayer, joined with the virtue of orderliness and temperance,” etc.

“And seeing the man.” In the Fuk. manuscript and in the papers is written “and to see.”]

[Col. 0446B] No one among that people has ever been, or ever could be, more blessed than he—unless they willingly renounced their souls to the Holy Spirit. And what could one say worthy of Moses, who led a disorderly people into order and adorned their souls with persuasion and reverence; who, instead of captivity, [Col. 0447A] bestowed freedom upon them; instead of gloom, made them cheerful; and raised their souls to such a point that, through their extreme change to the contrary and the success of their achievements, the men’s disposition became more boastful? He so surpassed those before him in wisdom that even those praised among the nations as wise men and philosophers became emulators of his wisdom. For Pythagoras, by imitating his wisdom, became so renowned for temperance that he set his own self-control as an example even for Plato, most temperate of men.

Daniel, who foretold future things, who practised the most eminent greatness of soul, and who was distinguished by beauty of character and of every manner of life—how great and cruel a hardship did he overcome from the tyrant then ruling Syria! That man’s name was Nebuchadnezzar. When his whole line had been wiped out, [Col. 0447B] that solemn and exceedingly mighty power passed to the Persians. For renowned, and renowned even now, were the tyrant’s wealth; his untimely zeal for an improper worship; the heaven-high elevations of mines of every kind; and the terrible laws established for that worship, tending to cruelty. Daniel, despising all these things through his undefiled piety toward the true God, prophesied that the tyrant’s untimely zeal would become the cause of some great evil. But he did not persuade the tyrant; for abundant wealth is an obstacle to sound judgment.

At length the ruler displayed the savagery of his own mind, ordering the righteous man to be torn apart by wild beasts. Noble, indeed, was also the brothers’ unanimity in martyrdom. Those who later emulated them won surpassingly great glory through their faith in the Saviour [Col. 0447C]: fearless amid fire and furnace, and amid the terrible things appointed to devour them, repelling by the pure contact of their bodies the fire enclosed in the furnace.

Then Daniel, after the destruction of the Assyrian kingdom, annihilated by bolts of lightning, passed by divine providence to Cambyses, king of the Persians. Here too came envy, and, besides envy, the deadly plots of the Magi; and a succession of dangers, great and many. Saved easily from all these by the assistance of Christ’s providence, he shone forth through experience of every kind of virtue. For the Magi, when the man prayed three times a day and accomplished great and extraordinary miracles of memorable deeds, maliciously denounced the very success of his prayers. [Col. 0450A] Representing his so great power to the ruler as extremely dangerous, they persuaded him to condemn to a feast of wild lions the man who had publicly become the author of so many benefits to the Persians. Condemned, Daniel was confined not for destruction but for eternal renown. And, tested amid the beasts, he found them gentler and tamer than those who had confined him. For through prayer, joined with the virtue of orderliness and temperance, he made tame all those naturally raging creatures.

When these things became known to Cambyses—for achievements of such great and divine power could not be obscured—he himself was overwhelmed with amazement at the miracle reported. He repented, then, of having readily yielded to the Magi’s accusations. Nevertheless, he dared to become an eyewitness of that sight. And when he saw the man [Col. 0450B] praising Christ with both hands raised aloft, and the lions crouching down and, as it were, worshipping the man’s footsteps, he immediately condemned the Magi who had persuaded him to the same punishment and shut them up in the lions’ enclosure. But the beasts which shortly before had fawned upon the man attacked the Magi, and destroyed them all according to their nature.

## Chapter XVIII.—On the Erythraean Sibyl, who, in the acrostic of the verses in which she prophesied, indicates the Lord and the Passion. The acrostic is: Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour, Cross.

[Col. 0449]

[Col. 0449C] I should also like to mention another testimony to Christ’s divinity, drawn from foreigners. For from these witnesses those accustomed to assail him with slanders and curses will recognize that he is God and the Son of God, if only they are willing to give credence to their own authorities. The Erythraean Sibyl, then, who says that she lived in the sixth generation after the Flood, was a priestess of Apollo. Wearing a crown upon her head [Col. 0452A], like the god whom she worshipped, and tending the tripod around which a serpent was coiled, she gave oracles to those who consulted her. She had been devoted by foolish parents to that cult, from which nothing honourable and virtuous is produced, but a madness devoid of modesty. Such are the things recounted concerning Daphne.

Thus, once when she had entered the inner sanctuaries of that untimely superstition, impelled altogether by the divine Spirit, she began to foretell in verse all the things that would come to pass concerning God, most clearly declaring in the initial letters of the verses—this form being called an acrostic—the history of Jesus Christ’s coming. The acrostic is this: JESUS CHRIST, SON OF GOD, SAVIOUR, CROSS. And these are the verses:

> The earth shall sweat, when the sign of judgment comes.  
> From heaven shall come a king, who shall be for everlasting ages,  
> [Col. 0452B] Present in flesh, to judge all flesh and the whole world.  
> Both faithful and faithless mortals shall behold God,  
> The Most High, in the flesh, with the holy ones at the end of time;  
> He shall judge the souls of men before his tribunal.  
> Then the whole world shall become a desolate wilderness and thorn-brake;  
> Mortals shall cast away idols and all wealth.  
> Fire shall burn up earth, heaven, and sea,  
> Searching; and it shall burst the gates of Hades’ prison.  
> Then all flesh of the dead shall come into free light;  
> Everlasting fire shall convict the holy and the lawless.  
> Whatever anyone did in secret, then all shall speak aloud.  
> For God shall open dark breasts to lights.  
> From all there shall be lamentation and gnashing of teeth.  
> The sunlight shall fail, and the choruses of stars;  
> [Col. 0453A] Heaven shall be rolled up, and the moon’s radiance shall perish.  
> Valleys shall be raised, and the heights of hills destroyed.  
> No lofty height shall any longer appear among humankind.  
> Mountains shall be level with plains, and every sea  
> Shall no longer be navigable; for the earth, scorched by lightning,  
> And rivers bubbling with their springs, shall fail.  
> From heaven the trumpet shall utter a voice of much lamentation,  
> Crying aloud the vain evil and the sufferings of the world.  
> The earth, gaping open, shall one day reveal Tartarean chaos.  
> All kings shall come before God’s tribunal.  
> From heaven there shall flow a river of fire and brimstone.  
> Then there shall be for all mortals a conspicuous sign—  
> The wood, the desired horn among the faithful—  
> The life of pious men, and an offence to the world,  
> Illuminating believers through waters in twelve fountains;  
> A shepherding rod of iron shall rule.  
> This God, now inscribed in acrostic verses, is our  
> Saviour, immortal king, who suffered for our sake.

These things, plainly, were announced beforehand to the virgin by God. I judge her blessed, because the Saviour chose her as a prophetess of his providence toward us [Col. 0453B].

[Note: [Col. 0450D]

“A testimony from foreigners.” The Fuk. manuscript and the papers read *testimonies* (*μαρτυριῶν*), more correctly. For Constantine does not offer only one testimony, but two.

“A priestess of Apollo.” I accept the learned men’s emendation, which I also find in Moraeus’s book: “she was a priestess of Apollo” (*ἱήρεια ἦν τοῦ Ἀπ.*). This is certainly the reading of the Fuk. manuscript and the papers.

[Col. 0451B] “And truly filled with divine inspiration.” Whoever among Christian writers produced the Sibyls’ oracles in confirmation of the Christian faith necessarily had to say of the Sibyls the same thing as Constantine: namely, that inspired by some divine spirit they had foretold Christ. Thus Justin, in his exhortatory discourse to the Greeks: “It will be easy for you to learn in part the true worship of God from the ancient Sibyl, who, through oracles, teaches you under some mighty inspiration,” etc. Augustine writes in agreement with this in Book XVIII, chapter 23, of *The City of God*, and Jerome in Book II against Jovinian. Jerome indeed writes that the gift of prophecy was granted to the Sibyls by God on account of the merit of their virginity. Augustine, however, does not hesitate to enroll them in the City of God.

But Gregory Nazianzen, in his poem addressed to Nemesius, says that Hermes Trismegistus and the Sibyl, in whatever they foretold concerning God, did not prophesy by divine inspiration, but received these things from the sacred books of the Hebrews, which they had read in passing:

> Not from God, but by looking through my books.

That is, Gregory Nazianzen and those most holy Fathers of the Church believed that those poems had actually been composed by the Sibyls [Col. 0451D], although they were invented by idle persons and published under the names of Sibyls around the time of Emperor Hadrian. Certainly no one earlier than Justin mentioned them. And Celsus, whom we have shown above to have lived under Marcus Antoninus, declares that Christians falsely inserted many things into the Sibylline poems. Origen reports his words in Book VII: “But now they are able to insert arbitrarily many false and blasphemous things into her verses” (*νῦν δὲ παρεγγράφειν μὲν εἰς τὰ ἐκείνης πολλὰ καὶ βλάσφημα εἰκῆν δύνασθαι*).

I know, indeed, that Origen flatly denies this. He responds to Celsus that he ought to have produced older copies of the Sibylline poems in which the verses that he said Christians had inserted were not read. It would surely have been easy for Celsus to do this and thereby prove those verses false. Yet other arguments are also available by which this may be demonstrated. For if the Sibyl had foretold Christ so clearly, why did Paul in his epistles, and when speaking at Athens, not use her testimony—especially as he did not disdain to cite Aratus and other pagan poets? Certainly, if the Sibyl wrote this acrostic concerning Christ, there is no reason why we should hesitate to number her among the prophets, indeed in the first place. [Col. 0452B] For none of the ancient Hebrew prophets wrote concerning Christ as clearly and expressly as these Sibylline verses adduced by Constantine. Yet neither Origen nor any of the holy Fathers ever conceded that Sibyls should be counted among the prophets; rather, they held those who believed this to be heretics, and called them Sibyllists, as Origen teaches in Book V against Celsus. Responding there to Celsus, who had objected that Christians were divided into various sects—some being psychics, others spirituals; some worshipping the God of the Jews, others not; some being Sibyllists, and so forth—Origen says: “He said that there were some Sibyllists, perhaps because he had heard some people accusing those who thought the Sibyl to have been a prophetess, and calling such people Sibyllists.”

“Searching.” A verse had been omitted here. From Moraeus’s book, the Fuk. manuscript, the Royal papers, and Sebastian Castellio’s edition of the Sibylline poems, it must be supplied thus:

[Col. 0452D]

> Fire shall burn up earth, heaven, and sea,  
> Searching.

Although I would rather read *searching* (*ἰχνεῦον*) in the neuter. That this verse was omitted is shown by the ancient translation in Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, which reads:

> Fire shall burn the lands, the sea, and the sky,  
> Searching.

Moreover, they had deleted the Greek verse because the whole acrostic seemed able to stand without it. They did not observe that in the acrostic Christ’s name is written with a diphthong, *Chreistos* (*χρειστὸς*), the reason for which I do not know. The Latin acrostic in Augustine nevertheless retained it. The ancient Greeks, indeed, made the name of Christ eight syllables, writing *Chreistos* with a diphthong, as Irenaeus teaches in Book I, chapter 10.

[Col. 0453C] “And rivers bubbling.” Thus it is read in the Fuk. manuscript.

“He shall roll up heaven.” Thus it is read in the standard edition of the Sibylline poems. The ancient translation also confirms this reading: “Heaven shall be rolled up,” etc. Yet I do not doubt that *to roll up* (*εἱλίξειν*) ought to be written. For *shall fail* is understood, as it has occurred shortly before.

“Crying aloud the evil,” etc. In Castellio’s edition this verse is written thus; the ancient translation in Augustine confirms the reading:

> But then the trumpet shall send forth a mournful sound from the high  
> Sphere, lamenting wretched sin and diverse sufferings.

In the Fuk. manuscript is written: “crying aloud a song and the sufferings of the world” (*ὠρύουσα μέλος καὶ πήματα κόσμου*).

“Tartarean chaos.” More correctly, the edition of the Sibylline poems reads: “Then the earth, gaping open, shall reveal Tartarean chaos” (*ταρτάρεον δὲ χάος τότε δείξει γαῖα χανοῦσα*).

[Col. 0453D] “Illuminating believers in twelve fountains.” The edition of the Sibylline poems reads *those called* (*κλητοὺς*), which is preferable: both because it has already used the word *believers* (*πιστοὺς*) shortly before, and because believers would not correctly be said to be illuminated through baptism. For believers are not illuminated by baptism; rather, the Gentiles called to faith are illuminated. But after they have been illuminated through the sacred washing, only then are they called believers. The twelve fountains signify, I suppose, the twelve Apostles.

“A shepherding rod.” Betuleius rightly noted that the Sibyl here alludes to Psalm II, where it is said: “You shall shepherd them with a rod of iron” (*ποιμανεῖς αὐτοὺς ἐν ῥάβδῳ σιδηρᾷ*). From this it appears true, as we observed above from Gregory Nazianzen [Col. 0454C], that the Sibyl—or whoever composed the Sibylline poems—drew many things from the sacred books. Therefore I do not doubt that these verses, as Cicero long ago observed, were not uttered by a Sibyl driven by prophetic frenzy, but composed attentively by someone under the Sibyl’s name.]

[Col. 0450C] It occurs to me also to recall some testimony from foreigners to the divinity of Christ. For from such testimony, surely, even the minds of those who blaspheme him may know that he is God, the Son of God, if indeed they believe their own words. The Erythraean Sibyl, then, who declares that she existed in the sixth generation after the flood, was a priestess of Apollo. [Col. 0451A] Wearing a crown like the god worshipped by her, attending the tripod around which the serpent coiled itself, and uttering Apollo’s oracles to those who consulted her, she had been given over by the folly of her parents to such worship, through which shameful passions arise and nothing reverent comes to be—just as in the accounts concerning Daphne.

Thus once, having entered within the sanctuaries of that untimely superstition, and having truly become filled with divine inspiration, she foretold in verse future things concerning God. Through the arrangement of the initial letters, called an acrostic, she clearly disclosed the history of Jesus’ coming. This is the acrostic: Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour, Cross. Her verses are these:

> For earth shall sweat when the sign of judgment comes;  
> A king shall come from heaven, the one who is to be for ages,  
> [Col. 0451B] Present in flesh to judge all flesh and the entire world.  
> Faithful and unfaithful mortals shall see God,  
> The Most High, in flesh, with the holy ones at time’s end;  
> He shall judge men’s souls at the tribunal.  
> When the entire world becomes a desolate land and thorn-brake,  
> Mortals shall throw away idols and all wealth;  
> Fire shall burn earth, heaven, and sea,  
> Searching; and it shall burst the gates of Hades’ prison.  
> Then all the flesh of the dead shall come into free light;  
> Fire shall test the holy and the lawless for ages.  
> Whatever anyone did in secret, then all shall speak aloud.  
> For God shall open dark breasts to lights.  
> From all shall come lamentation and gnashing of teeth.  
> The sunlight shall fail, and the bands of stars;  
> [Col. 0454A] Heaven shall be rolled up, and the moon’s brightness shall perish.  
> Valleys shall be raised, and the heights of hills destroyed.  
> No mournful height shall any longer appear among humankind.  
> Mountains shall be level with plains, and every sea  
> Shall no longer permit sailing; for earth, scorched by lightning,  
> And bubbling rivers with their springs shall fail.  
> From heaven the trumpet shall utter a voice of much lamentation,  
> Crying aloud the vain evil and the sufferings of the world.  
> The earth, gaping open, shall one day reveal Tartarean chaos.  
> All kings shall come to God’s tribunal.  
> From heaven shall flow a river of fire and brimstone.  
> Then there shall be for all mortals a conspicuous sign:  
> The wood, the desired horn among believers, shall be  
> The life of pious men and an offence to the world,  
> Illuminating believers by waters in twelve fountains;  
> A shepherding rod of iron shall rule.  
> This God, now inscribed in acrostics, is our  
> Saviour, immortal king, who suffered for our sake.

And these things were plainly communicated to the virgin by God, that she might proclaim them beforehand. I count her blessed, whom the Saviour chose as prophetess of his providence toward us.

## Chapter XIX.—That this prophecy concerning Christ was not invented by any Christian, but composed by the Erythraean Sibyl, whose books Cicero rendered into Latin verse before Christ’s coming; and that Virgil mentions her and likewise the virginal birth, obscurely celebrating the mystery through fear of the powerful.

[Col. 0453]

[Col. 0453B] Many people, however, discredit this prediction, although they acknowledge that the Erythraean Sibyl was truly a prophetess. They suspect that someone belonging to our religion, not unacquainted with poetic art, composed these verses, and that they are adulterated and falsely attributed to the Sibyl as oracles. For they contain maxims very useful for human life, which restrain the excessive licence of pleasures and lead toward a modest and ordered life.

But the truth is manifest: the diligence of our men has assembled the chronology with such accuracy that no one can now suppose that the poem was composed after Christ’s coming and condemnation [Col. 0453C], and falsely proclaimed as though the verses had been uttered by the Sibyl long ago. For it is agreed by all that Cicero, having read this poem, translated it into the Roman tongue and incorporated it in his own writings. Antony subsequently killed him after gaining supreme power. Antony, in turn, was later defeated by Augustus, who ruled for fifty-six years. Tiberius succeeded him; in his time the coming of the Saviour shone forth upon the world, the mystery of the most holy religion prevailed, and a new succession of the people was established. I think the most eminent poet of Italy speaks of this when he says:

> Then there appeared a multitude of new men.

And again in another passage of the *Eclogues*:

> Sicilian Muses, let us sing a great utterance.

What could be clearer than this? For he adds:

> The utterance of the Cumaean prophecy has reached its end.

He clearly means the Cumaean Sibyl. Nor was he content with these words, but proceeded further, as though necessity itself desired his testimony. What, then, does he say again?

> This sacred course of ages now rises for us;  
> The virgin comes again, bringing the beloved king.

Who then is this virgin who comes back? Is she not the maiden who was made full and pregnant with the divine Spirit? And what prevents one pregnant with the divine Spirit from always being a maiden and remaining a virgin? He will return a second time and, when he comes, will relieve the inhabited world. The poet adds:

> Do thou, bright-bearing moon, honour  
> The child newly born,  
> Who brings in a golden race instead of an iron one.  
>   
> Under this ruler, all mortal woes  
> And the groanings of sinners will be lulled to rest.

We understand that these words have been said both openly and obscurely through allegory. [Col. 0455C] To those who examine more deeply the force of the verses, they set Christ’s divinity before their eyes. But lest any of the rulers in the imperial city should have grounds to accuse the poet of writing contrary to ancestral laws and overturning the beliefs concerning the gods handed down long ago by forefathers, he veils the truth. For, I think, he knew the blessed and saving rite of the Saviour. But in order to avoid the savage cruelty of his hearers, he led their minds toward their own accustomed practices. He says that altars should be erected [Col. 0458A], temples built, and sacrifices performed for the newly born child; and he adds the remaining details consistently for those who held such views. For he says:

## Chapter XX.—Other verses of Virgil Maro concerning Christ, and their interpretation, in which it is shown that the mystery was indicated obscurely, as is poets’ custom.

[Col. 0457]

[Col. 0457A]

> He shall receive divine life, and shall see heroes mingled with the gods,  
> And shall himself be seen by them—

that is, by the righteous:

> And he shall rule a peaceful world with his father’s virtues.  
> But for you, child, without cultivation, the earth shall first pour forth  
> Wandering ivy everywhere with baccharis,  
> And colocasia mingled with smiling acanthus.

The man, moreover, admirable and accomplished in every kind of learning, knowing the cruelty of those times, added this:

> The goats themselves, their udders swollen with milk, shall bring it home;  
> Nor shall the herds fear the great lions.

He spoke the truth, certainly. For faith would not fear the magnates of the palace.

> Your cradle itself shall pour forth tender flowers for you;  
> The serpent shall perish, and the deceitful poisonous herb  
> Shall perish; everywhere Assyrian amomum shall spring up.

Nothing could be said more true, nor more fitting to the Saviour’s power. For the cradle of God itself, through the power of the divine Spirit, brought forth, as it were, most radiant flowers for the new people. The serpent indeed perished, and the serpent’s poison was removed: that serpent, namely, who first led the first human beings into deceit and diverted their minds from their native temperance to the allurements of pleasures, so that they might not understand the evil [Col. 0457C] hanging over their heads.

For before the coming of our Saviour upon earth, that serpent had overthrown the minds of men—blinded by ignorance of the immortal life of the righteous and sustained by no hope of good things. But after our Lord’s Passion [Col. 0460A], when the body which he had assumed had for some time been separated from the fellowship of the most holy soul, the possibility of resurrection was disclosed to human beings. And if any stain of human sins remained, it was wholly wiped away by the most sacred washing. Only then Christ commands his subjects to take courage, and, from his venerable and glorious resurrection, to hope for like things.

It was therefore rightly said that the whole race of poisoners had perished. Death itself also perished, and the resurrection was confirmed. The Assyrian race also perished, those who had been the leaders and authors of faith in God. When he says that amomum will spring up everywhere, he calls the multitude of Christians by this name. Like innumerable branches adorned with most delightful flowers and watered by a gentle dew, it springs from one root. [Col. 0460B] Therefore these things were learnedly said by you, O Maro, wisest of poets. And the remaining words agree with them:

> But when you can now read the praises of heroes and the deeds of your father,  
> And can know what virtue is.

By the praises of heroes he means the works of righteous men; by the father’s virtues, the constitution of the world and its enduring construction. Perhaps he also means the laws used by the Church beloved of God, which orders its life by precepts of justice and temperance. The advancement to higher things of human life, standing in an intermediate condition between good and evil, is also worthy of admiration, although such a life does not admit sudden change.

> Little by little the field shall turn golden with soft ears of grain.

That is, the fruit of the divine law shall be produced for human benefit.

> And on uncultivated brambles shall hang the reddening grape.

Such things were not at all seen in the unjust and depraved life of humankind.

> And hard oaks shall sweat dewy honey.

[Col. 0461A] This indicates the dullness and hardness of mind among men of that age. Perhaps it also intimates that those who have endured labours for God’s sake will receive the sweet fruit of their endurance:

> Yet a few traces of the old deceit shall remain,  
> Which shall bid men tempt Thetis with ships, surround  
> Cities with walls, and cleave furrows in the earth.  
> There shall be another Tiphys, and another Argo to bear  
> Chosen heroes; there shall also be other wars,  
> And a great Achilles shall again be sent to Troy.

Rightly so, most wise prophet. You carried poetic licence as far as was fitting. For you had not set out to utter oracles, since you were no prophet. Present danger also stood in the way, I suppose—the danger hanging over the heads of those who wished to refute the rites established by their forefathers. Thus, cautiously and safely, as far as possible, setting forth the truth for those who understood, [Col. 0461B] while attributing to towers and wars, which are still seen in human life, the cause of such things, you describe the Saviour as setting out for the Trojan War. By Troy, however, he means the whole world. For Christ waged war against the hostile ranks of utterly wicked demons, sent to earth partly by the decision of his own providence and partly at the command of the supreme Father.

But what does the same poet say afterwards?

> Hence, when firm-set age has made you a man.

That is, after you have entered manhood, removed all the evils which afflict human life, and established the whole world under laws of peace:

> Even the sailor shall leave the sea, and the merchant pine  
> Shall no longer exchange wares: every land shall bear everything.  
> The soil shall not suffer rakes, nor the vine the pruning-hook,  
> Nor shall wool learn to counterfeit its colours.  
> But in the meadows the ram himself shall change his fleece, now with sweetly reddening  
> [Col. 0461C] Purple dye, now with saffron mud.  
> Of its own accord scarlet shall clothe the grazing lambs.  
> Enter upon great honours; now the time shall be at hand,  
> Dear offspring of the gods, great increase of Jupiter.  
> Look upon the world wavering beneath its rounded weight,  
> The lands, the expanses of sea, and the deep heaven.  
> Look how all things rejoice at the age to come.  
> O, may the last portion of life remain for me so long,  
> And may so much breath remain as will suffice to tell your deeds.  
> Neither Thracian Orpheus nor Linus shall surpass me in song,  
> Though the latter has his mother and the former his father at hand.  
> Even Pan of Arcady, if he competed with me while you judged,  
> Even Pan of Arcady would say himself defeated while you judged.

“Look,” he says, “upon the joy of the wavering world and all the elements.”

[Note: [Col. 0457C]

“Barley.” In Moraeus’s book a learned man corrected this in the margin to *ivies* (*κισσοὺς*), corresponding to Virgil’s “wandering ivies.” But the Greek translation is freer and in most places departs far from Virgil’s meaning.

“To you, O child.” I do not doubt that it should be written: “For you, goats weighed down with swelling udders.” This emendation is altogether necessary, since without it the sense does not stand. In the Fuk. manuscript and Turnebus’s manuscript one reads: “For you, child, with flourishing growth,” etc. In the Royal papers: “For you, child, he says, flourishing udders,” etc.

[Col. 0457D] “The flowers themselves.” The Fuk. manuscript has, in place of these words, “shall sing a reproach”; the papers read “shall eat a reproach” [both readings uncertain in sense].

“The poison perishes.” With Scaliger and Bongarsius, I read *herb* (*ποίη*). For it corresponds to Virgil’s words, “the deceitful poisonous herb.” But in Moraeus’s book the margin corrects it to “delusion perishes” (*ὄλλυται ἄτη*). If, however, one prefers *herb*, then *perish* (*ὄλλυτε*) must be written in order for the verse to scan. The Fuk. manuscript reads *of making* (*ποιήσεως*); the Royal papers, *of pitch* (*ποίσσης*).

“Nothing of these.” I write, at my own risk: “But nothing of these is truer,” etc. In the Fuk. manuscript and Turnebus’s manuscript is written simply: “Nothing of these.”

“He bestowed upon the new generation.” Thus it is written in Moraeus’s book and the Fuk. manuscript. In the papers, however, it is “upon the newly blessed generation.” The meaning of this passage is very obscure. Musculus translates it thus: “For to God’s very cradle the power of the Holy Spirit gave certain blazing flowers—namely, a new generation.” Christophorson, however, translates: “For the cradle of God itself, through the power of the Holy Spirit, produced blazing flowers for a new offspring.” Musculus therefore read “to the very swaddling clothes, a new generation”; Christophorson read only *power* (*δυνάμει*) in place of *power* (*δυνάμις*), which I prefer. By “new offspring” Constantine means the new people of Christians, of whom he said above that Virgil speaks in the line, “Now a new generation is sent down from high heaven.”

“How they might know.” Here I added the negative particle: “so that they might not know” (*ὅπως μὴ γνοῖεν*), an emendation plainly confirmed by what follows. Yet if anyone wishes to retain the standard reading [Col. 0458D], I shall not strongly object, since either can be defended.

“From the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.” Constantine had used *spirit* to mean soul. The translator, however, seems to have understood it of the Holy Spirit, as though Christ had had divinity in place of a soul, which was the heresy of Apollinaris. In the Fuk. manuscript, a comma is placed after *separated*. One must therefore consider whether the words “through the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” should be joined to what follows: “The possibility of resurrection was disclosed to human beings,” so that the meaning may be: through the communication of the Holy Spirit, whom Christ poured out upon human beings after the Passion, the power of resurrection was disclosed.

“The possibility of resurrection.” I do not approve Christophorson’s translation, who rendered this passage: “The power of resurrection was disclosed to human beings.” Nor does John Portesius differ. I do not doubt, however, that *what is possible* (*τὸ δυνατὸν*) means what I expressed in my translation.

[Col. 0459C] Constantine therefore says that after Christ’s death it was disclosed to human beings that bodies could rise again. For belief in the resurrection had previously been obscure, even among the Jews. Accordingly, they feared death so greatly.

“But the Assyrian race also perished.” Christophorson interpolated this passage, deleting the two preceding words. Savile likewise deleted the words “but it perished” in his book, as Christophorson did. But both are greatly mistaken. For Constantine, being unskilled in grammar, had construed Virgil’s verse thus:

[Col. 0459D]

> The Assyrian shall perish; amomum shall spring up everywhere.

This is demonstrated both from this passage and from the Greek translator’s rendering of Virgil’s line: “The Assyrian is gone; amomum blossoms throughout the valleys.” Thus it is read in the excellent Fuk. manuscript, and correctly according to Constantine’s meaning.

As for Virgil’s entire poem, Christians consistently maintained that it had been translated from Sibylline verses and should be understood of Christ’s birth. For they held that these words could be said of no one but Christ:

> Under this leader, if any traces of our sin remain,  
> They shall become void and free the lands from perpetual fear.

Thus Constantine, Augustine in his Letter to Volusianus, and in Letter 155. In the Letter to Volusianus Augustine interprets Assyrian amomum as the doctrine of Pherecydes the Assyrian, who first declared the soul to be immortal. But Augustine’s interpretation cannot be accepted, since Pherecydes was not Assyrian but Syrian—that is, from the island Syros. Therefore Constantine’s interpretation is preferable: he says that by the name *amomum* are indicated the faithful or Christians, because they are *amōmoi* (*ἄμωμοι*), that is, without reproach. They are called Assyrian because the beginning of faith arose from the Assyrians. For Abraham was an Assyrian and was the first to believe God; hence he was also called the father of believers.

“He calls it a multitude of worshippers.” I accept Henry Savile’s conjecture, who noted in the margin of his manuscript that perhaps *he calls beforehand* (*προαγορεύει*) should be written.]

[Col. 0460D] “The increase toward that which is kindled.” The preposition must be added, having been wrongly omitted in Robert Estienne’s edition: “toward that which is raised up” (ἐπὶ τὸ ἀνημμένον). Thus it is written in the royal sheets and in the books of Turnebus and Moraeus. Yet I prefer the reading proposed from the books of Scaliger and Bongars, and found in the Fuk. manuscript: “toward that which leads upward” (ἐπὶ τὸ ἀνηγμένον). For ἀνάγειν, “to lead upward,” is a verb proper to Platonic philosophy, from which many things are drawn throughout this discourse. Hence Proclus’s “anagogical sense,” and that saying of Plotinus celebrated by Synesius: “One must raise up the divine element within us toward that which is truly divine.”

“Those who hear of the labours of God.” In the Fuk. manuscript it is written: “those hearing of the labour for God” (τὸν ὑπὲρ τοῦ Θεοῦ πόνον ἀκούοντας). I therefore write, by a most certain emendation, “those undertaking the labour for God” (τὸν ὑπὲρ τοῦ Θεοῦ πόνον ἀσκοῦντας). Constantine explains that verse of Virgil:

> And the hard oaks shall sweat dewy honey.

[Col. 0461C] He therefore says that this verse signifies that those who undergo the gravest labours for God’s sake shall receive the sweetest fruit of their labours.

[Col. 0461D] “For poetic licence.” I approve more highly the translation of John Portesius, who renders it “poetic licence,” than that of Christophorson, who renders it “poetic capacity,” as Musculus had rendered it. For the Greeks use ἐξουσία in the sense which Latins call poetic licence, as I remember reading more than once in Themistius. Moreover, the old sheets begin a new chapter here from the words, “Well done, most wise poet,” and rightly so, in my opinion. Chapter 20 should therefore be placed here.

“He fought directly against the opposing [power].” In the Fuk. manuscript and in Turnebus’s book this passage is written thus: “He fought directly indeed with the opposing and wicked power” (Ἐπολέμησε γοῦν ἄντικρυς μετὰ τῆς ἀντικειμένης καὶ πονηρᾶς δυνάμεως). Savile, however, had emended in his manuscript: “He fought directly indeed against the opposing [power]” (ἐπολέμησε γοῦν ἄντικρυς κατὰ τῆς ἀντικειμένης).

“Not holy for them.” Who does not see that one should write, “It is not holy for sailors,” etc. (οὐχ ὁσίη ναύτῃσιν)? In the third verse from this I read, “and the earth herself, untilled” (αὐτὴ δ’ ἄσπαρτος); for γαῖα, “earth,” is understood.

“He will shine beside streams.” I would rather write “will be fittingly arrayed beside streams” (παραπρέψει), [Col. 0462C] as it stands in the sheets. For πρέπειν τῇ ἐθῆτι, “to be fittingly arrayed in clothing,” is elegantly said. I also write πάρα separately, as in the Fuk. book. A little later I would prefer “behold the well-fastened foundations” (ὄρα εὔπηκτα θέμεθλα) in the imperative. [Col. 0462D] For it is a translation of Virgil’s verse, “Behold the convex…” See a little below, where this verse is repeated.

“May gentle strength preserve me alive.” In Moraeus’s book a learned man emended: “may it preserve me alive indeed” (ζῶντα γ’ ἔχε). But not even thus does the verse stand. I would therefore rather read, “may it keep me living” (ζῶντα σχῇ). For these words are in the optative mood. In the following verse I write “your excellence” (σὴν ἀρετὴν), from Moraeus’s book. This emendation admits no doubt whatever. But concerning the earlier passage further thought is required. The place may seem capable of restoration with less difficulty if one merely changes the punctuation as follows:

> The joy of the boundless age; may gentle strength keep me,  
> Old though I am, alive, with a shaggy heart,  
> To sing of your excellence, etc.

Nothing is more certain than that ἔχε is used for ἔχοι, “may it keep.” In the Fuk. manuscript it is written: “gentle strength [may keep] me alive indeed, [to sing] your excellence,” without the verb ἔχε. Moreover, the reader should be warned that all [Col. 0463C] these verses of Virgil, both in the Fuk. manuscript and in the sheets, are not written from the beginning of the line; rather, only the first words of each verse are set apart by a small space from what precedes. This is done because the verses are not recited continuously, but with Constantine’s frequent interjections.

[Col. 0458A]

> He shall receive the life of the immortal God, and shall behold  
> The heroes gathered together with Him—namely, the righteous—and himself also  
> Shall appear to his native land and to the blessed,  
> Guiding the reins of the world by the virtue bestowed by his Father.
>
> For you, child, the earth shall first produce her gifts:  
> Barley and cyperus together with colocasia, [and] with thorn.

A marvellous man, and adorned with every kind of learning, who knew exactly [Col. 0458B] the harshness of the times then prevailing:

> For you, child, fertile udders, heavy with milk,  
> Of their own accord shall yield sweet streams of milk;
>
> Nor is it right to fear grim lions among the herds.

He speaks truly; for faith will not fear the potentates of the imperial court.

> Naturally fragrant are the swaddling-clothes—the flowers themselves;  
> The nature of the venom-bearing serpent perishes; the pestilence  
> Of deadly poison perishes. Assyrian amomum flourishes in the valleys.

Of these things one could say nothing truer, nor anything more appropriate to the excellence of the Saviour. For the very swaddling-clothes of God—the power of the Holy Spirit—bestowed upon the youthful generation certain fragrant flowers. But the serpent perishes, and the venom of that serpent which first deceived the first-created human beings, drawing their thoughts away from their innate moderation [σωφροσύνη] to enjoyment of pleasures, so that they might know the destruction hanging over them. For before the Saviour’s descent, [Col. 0458C] through ignorance of the immortality of the righteous, he shattered the souls of human beings, which rested upon no good hope. But when He had suffered and for a time been separated from the body that had been put around Him, the possibility of resurrection was revealed to human beings through communion with the Holy Spirit. And if any mire [Col. 0459A] of human wrongs remained, all of it was washed away in holy baths. Then indeed he exhorts his subjects to take courage; and from His own holy and renowned resurrection he commanded them to hope for like things.

Accordingly, the race of venomous things rightly came to an end; death too came to an end; the resurrection was sealed; and the race of the Assyrians also perished—the race which became the secondary cause of faith in God. In saying that Amomum grows everywhere, he designates the multitude of worshippers; for, as a multitude of branches flowering with fragrant blossoms springs from a single root, watered with a due measure of dew, so it sprouts. Learnedly indeed, most wise poet Maro; and all that follows is also consistent and coherent.

> Immediately he shall learn the virtues of heroes and all the deeds  
> Of the greatest Father, adorned with lofty excellence.

By the praises of the heroes he signifies the deeds of righteous men; by the virtues of the Father he means the ordering of the world [Col. 0459B] and the establishment of its everlasting continuance—perhaps also the laws by which the God-beloved Church lives, practising a life joined with justice and moderation. Admirable too is the gradual increase in the life between good and evil, leading upward, since he rejects the suddenness of an abrupt change.

> First, fields of yellow asphodels shall come forth.

That is, the fruit of the divine law shall come into use.

> And on red brambles the hanging cluster shall redden.

Things which were absent under the lawless way of life.

> From the tough bark of pines a stream of honey shall flow.

He sketches the stupidity of the people of that time and their hardened character. Perhaps also, in speaking of the labours undertaken for God, he teaches that they shall receive some sweet fruit from their own steadfastness.

[Col. 0459C]

> Yet a few traces of former error shall remain:
>
> To tempt the sea, to surround cities with walls,  
> And to cleave the earth with furrows by dragging ploughshares;
>
> Another Tiphys there shall be, and a Thessalian Argo, rejoicing  
> In heroic men; and Achilles shall again attempt war  
> Against Trojans and Danaans.

[Col. 0462A] Well done, most wise poet! You have exercised poetic licence only to the proper extent. For it was not incumbent upon you to prophesy openly, since you were not a prophet; and, I think, a certain danger also restrained you—a danger hanging over those who expose the beliefs established by their ancestors. Thus, cautiously and safely, as far as possible presenting the truth to those able to understand, and using towers and war as his subject, things which in truth are even now experienced in human life, he portrays the Saviour setting out for the Trojan War, and Troy as the whole inhabited world. He fought openly against the opposing wicked power, having been sent by His own providence and by the command of the greatest Father. What then does the poet say after this?

[Col. 0462B]

> But when the age of manhood and its fruit shall come,

That is, when, having become a man, He removes from the roots the things encompassing human life, and indeed adorns the whole world with peace:

> It shall not be right for them, most guilty though they are, to wander;
>
> Things springing abundantly from the rich earth in full measure.
>
> And it itself shall be unsown and unploughed; nor shall, I think,  
> The vine still desire the edge of the sharp sickle.
>
> Nor shall a mortal need woolly fleece; but the ram of himself  
> Shall shine beside Tyrian streams,
>
> Changing his rough wool into purple scarlet.
>
> But receive the honoured sceptre of royal rule  
> From the right hand of the thundering Father.
>
> Behold the well-fastened foundations of the teeming world.
>
> The rejoicing of earth and heaven and sea, [Col. 0462C]  
> The joy of the boundless age, with a shaggy heart.
>
> Would that gentle strength might keep me alive when old,  
> To sing your excellence as long as my powers endure;
>
> Neither the divine singer of Thrace would surpass me,  
> Nor Linus, nor Pan himself, whom Arcadian earth bore;  
> But not even Pan himself will contend for victory.

“Behold,” he says, “the teeming world and the rejoicing of all the elements.”

## Chapter XXI.—That These Things Cannot Be Said of a Mere and Ordinary Human Being; and That Unbelievers, through Ignorance of Divine Worship, Do Not Even Know the Cause of Their Own Birth

[Col. 0463]

[Col. 0464A] Perhaps someone among those of less sound understanding might suppose that these things are said concerning the birth of a human being. But what sense is there in saying that, when a human child has been born into the light, the earth requires neither plough nor sowing, nor the vine sickle or further cultivation? How can such things be understood as said concerning human offspring? For nature is the servant of the divine will, not the worker of human commands. Add to this that the rejoicing of all the elements indicates God’s advent, not the conception of some human being.

Further, the poet’s prayer that his life be prolonged is plainly the mark of one invoking God. For we are accustomed to seek life and salvation from God, not from a human being. The Erythraean Sibyl indeed addresses God thus: “Why, Lord, do you impose upon me the necessity of prophecy, rather than preserve me, [Col. 0464B] lifted aloft from the earth, until the day of your most blessed advent?” But Virgil, after the verses cited above, adds these:

> Begin, little child, to recognize your mother by her smile.  
> Ten long months have brought your mother weariness.  
> Begin, little child, at whom your parents have not smiled;  
> Him neither god has deemed worthy of table, nor goddess of couch.

For how could his parents have smiled upon him? His Father is God, a power without quality. He Himself is devoid of every form, yet exists within the circumscription of others; nor is He endowed with a human body. Who does not know that the divine Spirit is free from a couch? For what desire or appetite could be present in the disposition of the highest good, toward whose desire all other things are drawn? And what, in short, can wisdom have in common with pleasure?

Yet let those be permitted to speak thus who imagine some human generation of Christ, and do not endeavour to keep their minds free from every impious deed and word. Here I call upon you, piety; I implore your aid for what is being said. You are nothing other than a law of purity and holiness, the most desirable of all good things, the teacher of most holy hope, the sure promise of immortality. I worship you, O piety and loving-kindness. For the benefit of your healing, of which we stood in need, we owe you thanks. But the common crowd of humankind, deprived of your aid, because of the inborn hatred with which it burns against you, turns away from God Himself and does not understand that the cause of its own life, and of that of the other impious, depends upon worship and obedience to the divine Majesty. For the entire world and whatever it contains are His possession.

[Note: [Col. 0463C]

“What sense, then, is there?” I would rather write: “What sense could there be?” (ποῖος ἂν ἔχοι λόγος).

“For nature indeed.” In the books of Fuk. and Turnebus it is written: “and for nature” (ἥτε γὰρ φύσις).

“Begin, looking upon [her] smiling.” Robert Estienne first printed this verse thus, I suppose from conjecture. For both the royal sheets and the Fuk. manuscript read: “Begin, smiling, as though seeing…” (Ἄρχεο μειδιῶν ὡς ἄν ὁρῶν), etc. From these witnesses it was very easy to restore the genuine text of this passage. I therefore emend it as follows:

> Begin, seeing your dear mother smile,  
> To recognize [her].

Nothing is more certain than this emendation.

“Your parents did not at all…” Constantine, and the Greek translator, did not correctly understand Virgil’s words. For he understood Virgil as though he had said that the child’s parents had not smiled upon him, nor had a god granted him a table or a goddess a couch. Constantine evidently thought Virgil’s verse—

> Begin, little child, at whom your parents have not smiled—

was to be read continuously, without any division; whereas a stop must be placed after “child,” as even boys know. Since Christophorson did not observe this, he interpolated Constantine’s following words, adding a negation contrary to the author’s meaning and contrary to the authority of all manuscripts. Moreover, the Fuk. manuscript reads “smiled briefly” (ἐφημερίως ἐγέλασαν), more correctly, unless I am mistaken. The sheets certainly read “briefly” (ἐφημερίους).

[Col. 0464C] “For his…” It is clear to anyone that one should write: “For his Father is God,” etc. (ὁ μὲν γὰρ αὐτοῦ πατὴρ θεὸς). In the Fuketian manuscript it is written: “For one of them is God, a power without quality” (ὁ μὲν γὰρ αὐτῶν ἂν θεὸς, ἄποιός ἐστι δύναμις).

“The Holy Spirit.” By “Holy Spirit” Constantine seems to mean the Godhead or divine nature, as we noted already in the preceding chapter. For he explains the words translated from Virgil, “nor did you touch couches” (οὐδ’ ἥψω λεχέων), which are said of Christ, not of the Holy Spirit. I therefore preferred in this place to translate it “Spirit of God,” rather than “Holy Spirit,” as Portesius and Christophorson do.

“But let these things be permitted to be said.” From these words it appears that the error noted above was not committed by Constantine himself, but by the Greek translator, who misunderstood Virgil’s final verses. Constantine himself correctly understood those verses, as is evident here. For after he had cited Virgil’s words:

> At whom your parents have not smiled;  
> Him neither god has deemed worthy of table, nor goddess of couch,

[Col. 0464D] he immediately adds, as though reproving the poet: “How,” he says, “could his parents smile upon him, since his Father is God, devoid of body and form? And how can couch and table suit God, who is clearly wholly free from a couch and unaffected by the pleasure of food?” He then adds words from which what I have said is manifestly clear, namely, that Constantine understood Virgil’s verses very well: “But let those who set forth some human generation be permitted to speak thus.” By these words he excuses Virgil, since Virgil was ignorant of Christ’s divine generation. But in the Greek translation, where Virgil’s verses are incorrectly interpreted, this period does not cohere with what precedes.

“But they [prepare] their soul…” I accept the conjecture of learned men, which I also found noted in Savile’s book: “nor [do they prepare] their soul…” (οὐδὲ τὴν ψυχὴν).

[Col. 0465B] “Being a certain pure law.” The rules of grammar require ὑπάρχουσαν, as in the Fuk. manuscript. Moreover, this is a most elegant definition of the Christian religion, though badly corrupted by faulty punctuation. I therefore read: “the most desirable of all good things, teacher of most holy hope, unfeigned promise of immortality” (πάντων τε ἀγαθῶν εὐκταιοτάτην, ἐλπίδος ὁσιωτάτης διδάσκαλον, ἀθανασίας ὑπόσχεσιν ἀκίβδηλον). Nothing is more certain or more elegant than this reading. Constantine calls religion the teacher of most holy hope, because it teaches us to hope for heavenly things and to place all our hope not in earthly and perishable goods but in God. The Fuk. manuscript reads: “teacher of holiness, unfeigned promise of immortality.” The same punctuation is found in the sheets.

“Those who stood in need.” It seems altogether necessary to write “those who were healed” (οἱ ἰαθέντες). For it is elegantly said: “healed by your treatments,” that is, “healed by your remedies.”

“His possession.” I would rather write κτίσμα, that is, “a work” or “creation.”]

[Col. 0463A] Someone of those who do not think rightly might suppose that these things are said concerning the birth of a human being. But when a human child has been born, what sense can there be in the earth being unsown and unploughed, and in the vine not desiring the edge of the sickle, nor indeed any other cultivation? How could this be understood as said of human birth? For nature is the servant of divine command, not the worker of human bidding. Moreover, the rejoicing of the elements portrays the descent of God, not the pregnancy of some human being. And the poet’s prayer that the end of his life be lengthened is a sign of divine invocation; for we are accustomed to ask God for life and salvation, not a human being. The Erythraean Sibyl, at any rate, says to God: “Why then, Master, do you impose upon me the necessity of prophecy? Why do you not rather preserve me, lifted aloft from the earth, until the day [Col. 0463B] of your most blessed coming?” Maro adds also the following to what has been said:

> Begin, looking upon your dear mother as she smiles,  
> To recognize her; for she bore you through many revolving years.  
> Your parents did not smile upon you merely for a day;  
> Nor did you touch couches, nor know a splendid feast.

For how could the parents have smiled upon him? One of them is God, a power without quality; without form indeed, yet within the circumscription of others, and not possessing a human body. And who does not know that the Holy Spirit is free from couches? What desire or longing could there be in the disposition of the Good, toward which all things aspire? And what in general is common to wisdom and pleasure? But let those who introduce some human generation be permitted to say these things; they prepare their soul to be pure from [Col. 0466A] every evil thing and word. Yet I call upon you yourself, O reverence for God, as an ally in what is said: you who are a certain pure law, the most desirable hope of all good things, teacher of holiness, unfeigned promise of immortality. I worship you, piety and love of humankind; and we who have been in need owe everlasting gratitude to your healings. But the ignorant crowd, deprived of your aid, turns away even from God because of its inborn hostility toward you; nor does it know at all that the cause of its own living and being, and of that of the other impious persons, depends upon its duty toward what is better. For the whole world is His possession, and all things that are in the world.
