## Chapter XXII.—The Emperor’s Thanksgiving, in Which He Ascribes His Victories and Other Benefits to Christ; and Refutation of the Tyrant Maximinus, Who Increased the Glory of the Christian Religion by the Cruelty of His Persecution

[Col. 0465]

[Col. 0465A] I ascribe my own good fortune and all that is mine to piety. The outcome of all things that have met my prayers bears witness: deeds of valour, victories over enemies, and trophies. The Great City also knows this and praises it with acclaim. The people of my most beloved city likewise wills it, although, deceived by false hopes, it chose a protector unworthy of itself; he was shortly [Col. 0466B] taken and met an end fitting and deserved according to the deeds he had dared. It is not lawful to recall these things, especially for me who address you and take every care to address you with pure and honourable words.

Yet I shall perhaps say something neither shameful nor unbecoming. A war exceeding in madness and cruelty, an implacable war, was waged by tyrants against you, O reverence for God, and against all your most holy churches. Nor were there lacking some in Rome who rejoiced in such great public evils. A field was also prepared for battle. But you came forth and gave yourself up, resting upon faith in God. [Col. 0467A] The cruelty of impious mortals, raging without ceasing like fire and consuming all before it, bestowed upon you a wonderful glory, sung everywhere for ever. For on this account awe took hold even of those who beheld you.

One could see the executioners and torturers, who stretched the bodies of the pious, growing weary and despairing before the dreadful task; while the bonds were slackened, the very tortures relaxed, and the fires applied were extinguished. Yet the boldness of the pious did not give way even for a little while. What then did you gain by daring these things, most impious man? What was the cause of this frenzy of mind? You will say: “It was for the honour of the gods.” But what gods? Or what conception worthy of the divine nature do you entertain? Do you think the gods angry, like yourself? If they were such, you ought rather to wonder at their purpose than obey their shameless commands [Col. 0467B] which unjustly prescribed the slaughter of righteous men. Perhaps you will say that you acted because of the customs established by your ancestors and human opinion. I grant it. For the accepted customs are akin to the deeds performed, and both spring from one and the same folly. Perhaps you thought that some exceptional power resided in anthropomorphic images fashioned by builders and craftsmen. Therefore you tended these things, taking every care that they might never be defiled—images of the greatest and most eminent gods, who require human care.

[Note: [Col. 0465D]

“Of all things according to prayer.” One might not without reason conjecture that it should be written: “of all things meeting [me] according to prayer” (πάντων κατ’ εὐχὰς ἀπαντώντων). But since the sense stands without this emendation, I judge that nothing should be altered.

“The Great City.” The Greeks customarily called Rome thus, as may be proved by innumerable examples. Thus Tatian, in his Oration against the Greeks, speaks of the shrine of Jupiter Latiaris, and Porphyry in his work On Abstinence. [Col. 0466B] Eusebius also calls Rome by this name in his Tricennial Oration in Praise of Constantine, as we shall see there.

“And against all the most holy…” Before these words Robert Estienne’s edition places an asterisk, indicating that something is lacking here in the manuscripts. [Col. 0466D] Yet the Geneva edition removed all the asterisks that Robert Estienne had carefully marked, especially at the end of this book. In this place, however, only a few words are missing; I supply them thus: “against you and all your most holy churches,” etc. For he addresses the Christian religion.

“And a field.” He means the field in which martyrs were subjected to capital punishment. It was then customary among Greeks and Romans alike to punish criminals outside the gates, as I have often noted in my commentary on Ammianus Marcellinus. Hence persons led to execution were said to be led “to the field.” Thus Augustine, Against the Letter of Parmenianus, book I, chapter 8.

“You gave yourself up, resting…” It should be written: “You gave yourself up, resting…” (σαυτὴν ἐπερειδομένην), that is, “you voluntarily offered yourself.” Constantine alludes to the courage of martyrs who voluntarily presented themselves to judges and ran to death, not under compulsion but of their own accord. For ἐπιδιδόναι is used only of one who does something voluntarily; for example, of Christ, who gave Himself up of His own will for the salvation of humankind. Christophorson therefore wrongly translates the passage: “you set yourself against your adversaries.” Our conjecture is confirmed by the Fuk. manuscript, where it is written: “you gave up yourself, resting…” (ἐπέδωκας σεαυτὴν ἐπερειδομένη).

“The cruelty of impious mortals.” I think I have discovered a happy emendation of this passage. Since the word πίστει, “faith,” occurs immediately before these words, I restored the passage by repeating the last two letters of that word: “Then the cruelty of the impious…” (εἶθ’ ἡ τῶν [Col. 0467D] δυσσεβῶν ὠμότης), etc. Nothing is more certain. Let the conjecture of Gruter and Christophorson therefore be dismissed, who read “the cruelty of impious mortals…” (θνητῶν δὲ δυσσεβῶν). Who can endure this expression? The Fuk. manuscript nevertheless confirms Gruter’s reading. But I have already observed that many secondary corrections occur in that manuscript.

“The bodies of the pious.” Christophorson, Scaliger, and others add after these words, “it was possible to see” (ἦν εἰδεῖν), as I also found in the books of Fuk. and Moraeus. But there is no need to add it here, since the word “beholding” (θεωμένους) has preceded, to which all these things should be referred. I grant, however, that the speech would be clearer if these words were added.

“O most impious man!” He addresses one of the persecutors—namely Maximinus, as the chapter title states. For he persecuted Christians more cruelly and bitterly than the others.

[Col. 0468C] “The slaughter of righteous men.” It seems one should write “against righteous [men],” unless the error lies in the word ἐπαράντων.

“Images of care.” The final word should be deleted, which Christophorson, Scaliger, and Gruter wrongly added. I found the same word added in the books of Fuketius and Moraeus. But it is unnecessary: a comma should merely have been placed after “might be defiled.” John Portesius understood the passage thus, and indeed interpreted it more happily than Christophorson: “All that care of yours, all that zeal lest they be filled with filth. Thus great and principal gods sustained themselves by human help; they required that diligence.” Musculus also renders it thus.]

[Col. 0466A] I ascribe the cause of my prosperity and of all that is mine to nobility of character; and the outcome of all things according to prayer bears witness: feats of courage, victories over enemies, trophies. The Great City knows and praises it with honour; and the populace of my most beloved city desires it, although deceived by treacherous hopes, it chose a patron unworthy of itself. He was immediately captured and met a fitting end, worthy of the deeds he had dared—deeds which it is not lawful to recall, especially for me who speak to you and take every care to address you with pure and honourable discourse. But perhaps I shall say something neither shameful nor improper: against you, O reverence for God, and against all your most holy churches, tyrants waged a war implacable, excessive in madness and cruelty. Nor were there lacking some in Rome who rejoiced at such great public calamities; a field also was prepared for the contest. You came forth and gave yourself up, resting upon faith in God. [Col. 0467A] The cruelty of impious mortals, spreading incessantly like fire, bestowed upon you a marvellous glory sung for ever. For this reason awe seized the very spectators. One could see the executioners and those torturing the bodies of the pious weary and despairing in the face of terrible things; the bonds slackened, the tortures themselves relaxed, the fires applied dimmed, while their boldness did not bend even a little. What, then, did you gain by attempting these things, most impious man? What was the cause of your madness? You will say, “For honour toward the gods.” Which gods? Or what conception worthy of divine nature do you hold? Do you think the gods are angry like yourself? If indeed they were such, you ought rather to marvel at their purpose than obey shameless commands [Col. 0467B] that unjustly ordered the slaughter of righteous men. Perhaps you will say, “Because of the institutions of our ancestors and the opinion of men.” I concede it; for the accepted institutions resemble the deeds being done and arise from one and the same folly. Perhaps you believed that some exceptional power existed in anthropomorphic objects made by builders and craftsmen. For that reason you cared for them, taking every precaution that they might never be defiled: images requiring human care, though they belong to the greatest and most eminent gods.

## Chapter XXIII.—On Christian Institutions; That God Loves Those Who Pursue Virtue; and That One Must Hope for Judgment and Recompense

[Col. 0467]

[Col. 0468C] Compare, if you please, our religion with your rites. Is there not among us genuine concord and enduring love of humankind? Is not our rebuke of fault such as brings correction rather than destruction, and our treatment directed toward salvation rather than cruelty? Is there not among us sincere faith—first toward God, and then toward the natural fellowship of human beings? Is there not mercy toward those whom fortune’s calamity has assailed? Is there not a simple way of life, not concealing wickedness beneath any variegated craftiness, and knowledge of the true God and of monarchy? This is truly reverence for God; this is sincere religion, wholly unstained. This is the wise way of life; those who pursue it travel, as upon some august highway, toward everlasting life. For no one who has undertaken such a life, and who keeps the soul pure from the body, dies altogether; rather, he fulfils the service appointed to him by God than dies.

He who has confessed God does not become an incidental victim of insult or anger; but, nobly enduring necessity, he has the proof of his steadfastness as provision for God’s favour. For it is not doubtful that the divine embraces human virtue. Indeed, it would be most absurd if persons possessing power and persons of lower station, when those who do them good happen to honour or benefit them, should respond gratefully and return benefits, while He who is above all, the ruler of all things and the Good itself, should neglect recompense. He accompanies us throughout our whole life and is present with us whenever we do anything good; immediately accepting our courage and obedience, He benefits us, but postpones our complete recompense. For then the entire reckoning of life is assessed; and if these things are well ordered, the reward of eternal life follows, while fitting punishment overtakes the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0468D]

“And treatment…” I read “and treatment also” (θεραπείαν τε). The verb “bringing” (φέρων), which occurred shortly before, is understood. One could also read “and treatment” (θεραπεία τε), and a little later “and sincere faith” (καὶ πίστις εἰλικρινὴς), perhaps more correctly.

“And sincere faith.” It appears from what follows that one should write “a disposition of love” (διάθεσιν ἀγάπην). For love is first toward God and then toward one’s neighbour; faith, however, concerns only one God. Thus πίστιν, “faith,” cannot fit here in any way. Add that, since this passage treats of rebuke, love is eminently suitable. For benevolent rebuke and correction produce love. Yet it is preferable to read “and sincere faith,” as I have said. Musculus read thus, as is clear from his translation.

[Col. 0469C] “He does not become an incidental victim of insult.” The translators have entirely failed to grasp the force of this expression, though it is easy in this passage. Christophorson renders: “He who frankly confesses God does not voluntarily yield to insult or anger.” From these words everyone necessarily derives this meaning: the one who confesses God is neither angry nor abusive. Yet the Greek words have an altogether different sense: namely, that one who confesses Christ’s name before a judge does not yield to the insults and rage of persecutors.

“Provision for God’s favour.” Christophorson seems to have read “goodwill” (εὐνοίας), which I do not approve. No sense can be extracted from that reading. I translated ἐφόδιον as “means,” in the manner of Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, p. 393: Caesar the Dictator said that recollection of cruelty was a wretched means for old age. See what I formerly noted there. One may also translate “provision for the journey.” Musculus renders it not inappropriately: “He considers the experience of endurance a means of winning favour.”

“Nor is it doubtful.” A learned man wrote in the margin of Moraeus’s book: “Platonic, from the Republic,” that is: “This passage is drawn from book X of Plato’s Republic.” Plato certainly discusses in that book the rewards granted by God to just men both in this life and after death. But the argument by which Constantine establishes this point is not found in Plato, so far as I know.

“Those who possess power.” I do not doubt that one should write: “It would be most absurd if those who possess power and those of lower station, if some people happened to honour them or confer benefits upon them, should respond gratefully…” [Col. 0470C] The phrase “to honour” refers to powerful people, just as “to receive benefits” refers to lower and humbler people; Christophorson did not see this. The Fuk., Turnebus, and Savile manuscripts read: “even if those doing good should not happen to be honouring [them],” which I do not approve. Musculus, however, reads: “even if those doing good should happen to be attendants,” not badly.

“He accompanies.” Without doubt it should be written “who accompanies” (ὃς συμπαρομαρτεῖ). For it refers to “Him who is above all,” that is, the supreme God. Although Constantine called Him “the Good itself,” ὃς, the masculine relative, must nonetheless follow.

[Col. 0470D] “Obedience.” Christophorson translates this “inclined will,” Musculus “goodwill.” I preferred to translate it “obedience.” For εὐδοκεῖν means “to comply,” “to obey the divine will.” Thus εὐδοκία literally means “pleasure in what is approved.” It has this sense in Luke’s hymn of the heavenly host after the Lord’s birth: “among human beings, good pleasure” (Ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία). This expression occurs frequently in both Testaments, as others have already observed. The excellent Fuk. manuscript reads: “courage and right judgment” (ἀνδρείας τε καὶ εὐθυδικίας).]

[Col. 0467C] Compare our religion with your own practices. Is there not here genuine concord and lasting love of humankind? Rebuke of error bringing admonition, not destruction; treatment bringing not cruelty but salvation; and sincere faith, first toward God and then toward the natural fellowship of human beings; mercy [Col. 0470A] for those whom fortune has attacked; a simple life, not covering wickedness with some manifold cunning; and knowledge of the God who truly exists and of His sole rule. This is truly reverence for God; this is sincere religion, altogether unstained. This is a prudent life, and those who pursue it proceed as by some noble highway toward everlasting life. For no one at all dies who has adopted such a life and keeps the soul pure from the body; rather, he fulfils the service commanded him by God than dies. For one who has confessed God does not yield to insult or anger; but, nobly enduring necessity, he has the test of steadfastness as a provision for divine favour. Nor is it doubtful that the divine embraces human virtue. For it would be among the most absurd things if those who hold power and those who are inferior [Col. 0470B] should, when people who benefit them happen to honour them, respond gratefully and return benefits, while He who is above all, ruler of all and the Good itself, should neglect recompense—He who accompanies us throughout all our life and is present with us whenever we do something good. Immediately receiving courage and obedience favourably, He does good; but He delays our full recompense. For the whole reckoning of life is then called to account; and, if these things are well, the reward of eternal life follows, while fitting punishment pursues the wicked.

## Chapter XXIV.—On the Wretched End of the Lives of Decius, Valerian, and Aurelian Because of Their Persecution of the Churches

[Col. 0469]

[Col. 0469C] I now ask you, Decius, who once mocked the sufferings of the righteous, persecuted the Church with hatred, and subjected men endowed with the utmost holiness of life to punishment [Col. 0472A]. What are you now doing after this life? Under how great and how grievous afflictions are you oppressed? The interval between your life and death sufficiently revealed your misfortune, when you fell on the Scythian plains with your entire army and exposed the Roman Empire, so greatly celebrated everywhere, to the contempt and mockery of the Goths.

You too, Valerian, after displaying the same cruelty toward the servants of God, set the just judgment of God before every eye: captured by enemies and led about in chains, with purple cloak and the rest of the imperial attire, and finally, by order of Sapor, king of the Persians, having your skin removed and preserved, you furnished a perpetual trophy of your calamity [Col. 0472B] for all to behold. You likewise, Aurelian, torch [Col. 0471B] of every vice—by what immediate and manifest vengeance of the divine Majesty, while you were rushing madly through Thrace, were you slain in the middle of the public highway and filled the furrows of the public road with impious blood?

[Note: [Col. 0470D]

“What grievous thing are you doing?” I write, at my own risk, “What then are you now doing?” (τί δὴ νῦν πράσσεις), just as I found it emended in the margin of Moraeus’s book. The Fuk. manuscript is written no differently. The sheets, however, read τί δὴ τῷ.

[Col. 0471B] “Having been ordered to be flayed.” Moraeus’s book rightly emends this to κελευσθείς, “having been ordered.” Other writers also speak of the skin of Emperor Valerian being stripped by the Persians and preserved with salt. Thus certainly Peter the Patrician, in the Excerpts on Embassies, where Galerius reproaches the Persians because they held Valerian, deceived by treachery, captive until extreme old age; and after his death, impiously preserving his skin, they subjected his dead body to immortal disgrace.

“Running through and madly.” The Geneva editors unwisely inserted καί, “and,” from the manuscripts of Scaliger, Bongars, and Gruter, as they say; I also found it added in Moraeus’s book. But because that conjunction disturbs the sense and is not found in the royal sheets or Estienne’s edition, I judge it must be removed entirely. The Fuk. manuscript nevertheless retains it.]

[Col. 0470C] I now ask you, Decius, who once trod upon the sufferings of the righteous, hated the Church, and inflicted punishment on those who had lived holy lives: what grievous thing are you undergoing [Col. 0471A] after life? By what circumstances, and how difficult, are you constrained? The interval between life and death showed your prosperity, when you fell with your whole army in the Scythian plains and exposed the famous Roman power to contempt among the Getae. But you, Valerian, having displayed murderous cruelty toward the subjects of God, made the righteous judgment manifest: captured as a prisoner and led away bound, with your very purple robe and the rest of the imperial regalia; and at last, by command of Sapor, king of the Persians, flayed and embalmed, you set up an everlasting trophy of your own misfortune. And you, Aurelian, flame of every injustice: how openly, running wildly through Thrace, you were struck down in the middle of the public road and filled the furrows of the road with impious blood.

## Chapter XXV.—On Diocletian, Who Shamefully Abdicated the Empire and Who, Because of His Persecution of the Churches, Was Struck by Lightning

[Col. 0471]

[Col. 0472B] But Diocletian, after the bloody savagery of persecution, condemned by his own judgment, paid the penalty for the defect of madness, shut up in some mean dwelling. What profit, then, did he gain by making war upon our God? Namely, that he might pass the remainder of his life in continual fear of a lightning stroke. The city of Nicomedia bears witness to these things; nor are those silent who saw the event with their own eyes, among whom I too am numbered. The palace was being ravaged, and Diocletian’s own chamber, as lightning and a certain heavenly fire consumed it.

The outcome of these events had been predicted by prudent men. For they could not keep silent, nor conceal their groaning amid such monstrous circumstances; but openly and plainly they uttered among themselves, with complete freedom, these words: “What madness is this? What such insolence of power, that human beings dare to make war upon God and insult the most holy and most just religion; that they do not hesitate to contrive slaughter and destruction for so great a multitude, indeed for people entirely innocent, without any fault of theirs? O admirable teacher of moderation for all subjects! O admirable instructor in the care and concern that soldiers should show for their fellow citizens! These men pierced the breasts of their fellow tribesmen, though they had never seen the backs of enemies in battle.”

At last the providence of the divine Majesty exacted from them the penalty for such impious deeds, though not without harm to the commonwealth. For so many and so great were the slaughterings of our people that, had as many barbarians ever been slain, this would have sufficed to establish perpetual peace for us. The whole army of the emperor mentioned above, when it had come under the power of an indolent man who had seized the Roman Empire by force, was finally utterly destroyed in many and very great battles, when God restored liberty to the Roman city. And the cries of those calling upon God as helper while they were being oppressed, [Col. 0475A] and desiring with all their prayers the liberty natural to them; likewise the praises offered to God with thanksgiving after the evils had been driven away, when liberty and fairness in agreements had been restored to them—do not all these things declare in every way God’s singular providence and fatherly love toward humankind?

[Note: [Col. 0471C]

### “On the Harm Caused by Folly”

For what reason Diocletian laid down the empire is not agreed among authors. Some write that Diocletian, being an inquisitive investigator of future events, voluntarily relinquished the empire when he learned from the responses of the haruspices that very great disasters threatened the commonwealth. Aurelius Victor attests this. Others write that Diocletian, as age weighed upon him, perceiving himself to be less fit for administering the commonwealth—both on account of old age and because of feeble health—adopted this resolution. So Eutropius, a most reliable and elegant author. The same is written by the anonymous author in the panegyric delivered for Maximian Herculius and Constantine: “Yet, however lawful it may have been for that prince, whom years compelled and health failed, to sound a retreat; as for you, in whom those powers are still whole and sound,” etc. There are those who write that Diocletian, seeing that the Christians could not be overcome by him, resigned the empire out of grief and impatience, as may be read in Zonaras. But Constantine here expressly affirms that Diocletian voluntarily abdicated the empire because of mental derangement. Who, moreover, would dare to dispute Constantine’s testimony, since he lived at Diocletian’s court and none of these matters could have been unknown to him? Eusebius likewise relates this in Book VIII of his *History*.

Yet many considerations lead us to doubt this matter. First, since Diocletian lived for a long time after abdicating the empire, he never gave any indication whatever of a disturbed mind. Is not even that one reply which he made to Herculius and Galerius, when they urged him to resume the empire, proof of great wisdom? “Would that you could see at Salona the vegetables planted by our own hands.” Accordingly, in that retirement he was always honored by all the emperors of that time, who reverently regarded him as a father. Hear Eumenius in the panegyric which he delivered to Constantine: “But that divine man, who was the first both to share the empire and to lay it down, does not repent of his counsel and deed. Truly happy and blessed is he, whom your obedience—the obedience of such great princes—honors in private life.” Would Diocletian have been honored so earnestly by the four Augustan emperors if he had been insufficiently master of his mind? Or would Eumenius have called him a divine man, principally because he had first laid down the empire, if he had done so through madness and delirium?

Finally, Diocletian had adopted the plan of abdicating the empire long before the persecution—namely, when he celebrated at Rome his triumph over the Persians and other barbarian peoples. There, in the temple of Capitoline Jupiter, he exacted an oath from his colleague Herculius that both would lay down the empire on one and the same day. Eumenius teaches this in the panegyric already cited: “He therefore was ashamed not to imitate him whom he had taken as his brother; he regretted having sworn to him in the temple of Capitoline Jupiter.” Diocletian celebrated his triumph at Rome with his colleague Herculius in the eighteenth year of his reign, as Jerome writes in the *Chronicle*—that is, one year before the persecution of the Christians occurred. Certainly the author of the panegyric delivered for Maximian and Constantine testifies that Diocletian adopted this plan long before his abdication and communicated it to Herculius, in these words: “Such, Emperor, is that which you were pleased to do while we all mourned with stifled groaning: not indeed led by neglect of the commonwealth, flight from labor, or desire for idleness, but by constancy in a plan long since, as is the fact, agreed between you,” etc.

This being so, how can Constantine’s assertion stand—that Diocletian, after the persecution of the Christians, fell into madness and therefore voluntarily abdicated the empire? I would readily believe that Diocletian, after the persecution had begun, was seized by illness and for some time disturbed in his mental condition, especially since Constantine and Eusebius steadily affirm it. For this often happens to sick persons, and especially to melancholics, such as Diocletian may be inferred to have been from his coins. But I deny that he laid down the empire for this reason.

Moreover, in the Fuketius and Turnebus manuscripts this entire passage is read as follows:

> “Having condemned himself, and because of the injury arising from derangement, having committed himself to the confinement of a single contemptible dwelling, so that, I suppose, fearing the stroke of lightning, he might pass the remainder of his life. What, then, did it profit him to undertake war against our God? He speaks,” etc. [Col. 0473B]

[Col. 0473C] “The imperial residences were being devastated.” He means the palace at Nicomedia, which, shortly after Diocletian had stirred up persecution against the Christians, was consumed by an accidental fire. The emperors themselves and the other pagans accused the Christians of having caused this fire and therefore raged against them with harsher punishments, as our Eusebius writes at the end of Chapter 6, Book VIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*. But Constantine testifies that that palace was consumed by a fire sent from heaven. His testimony has all the greater authority because he himself was present when these things occurred at Nicomedia.

Diocletian seems, however, to have been so struck with terror by this lightning stroke that thereafter he remained thunder-stricken (*embrontētos*, ἐμβρόντητος) until his death, continually fearing that he would be struck by lightning. Constantine’s account here seems certainly to imply this. From these things it is clear how greatly Christophorson erred in translating the title of this chapter. For he thought Diocletian’s palace had burned after Diocletian had abdicated the empire, whereas it happened while Diocletian still held the empire and resided in the Nicomedian palace. [Col. 0473D]

“Teacher of moderation.” The final word is absent from the Fuketius manuscript.

“Those who had never seen the backs of their enemies.” This may refer either to recruits, recently enlisted and not yet having encountered an enemy, or to cowardly and idle soldiers accustomed to flee from the battle line and never to have defeated enemies. Certainly Diocletian’s army is said to have accomplished nothing worthy of memory, except that it captured Achilleus at Alexandria by a long siege.

Moreover, it is unclear what Constantine means when he says that those soldiers pierced the breasts of their fellow citizens—that is, the Christians. It is credible that Diocletian, hostile to the Christians, whom he suspected of having burned his palace, commanded his soldiers to slaughter whatever Christians they found in city or countryside. Certainly many thousands of Christians are reported to have been killed at Nicomedia under Diocletian and Maximian; the Greeks commemorate them on 4 September and 28 December. [Col. 0474B]

“So many slaughterings therefore took place.” This period has been displaced from its proper location. It ought to have been placed immediately after the word “having seen” [Col. 0474C], thus:

> “Those who had never seen in battle the backs of their enemies. So many slaughterings therefore took place that, if they had occurred against barbarians, they would have been sufficient for everlasting peace. At last, therefore,” etc.

That is: “Those who had never seen in battle the backs of their enemies pierced the breasts of their fellow countrymen. So many and such great slaughterings occurred that, if they had occurred in battles against barbarians, they might have sufficed to secure perpetual peace for us. At last, however, divine providence exacted from them punishment for such impious deeds—though not without injury to the commonwealth. For the whole army of the aforesaid emperor,” etc. What could be clearer or more explicit than this? Indeed, one must be exceedingly obstinate to deny that these things should be restored thus.

“If they had occurred against barbarians.” This passage can have two meanings. It may either be translated as Portesius translates it: “Certainly the amount of slaughter and bloodshed was so great that, if it had been that of barbarians, it would suffice for a perpetual treaty.” Or, with Christophorson, it may be translated thus: “So many slaughterings plainly occurred as, had they been inflicted upon barbarians, might have seemed more than enough for establishing eternal peace.” This latter sense pleases me more. Lucan expresses exactly the same thought at the beginning of the *Pharsalia* when he says:

> Alas, how much of land and sea might have been gained  
> By the blood which civil right hands have shed.

Instead of ὅσαι, however, ὥστε would be better written, for ἱκανὰς εἶναι follows.

“Of a certain worthless man.” He means Maxentius, as appears from what follows. It is not difficult to conjecture how Diocletian’s army passed into Maxentius’s power. After Diocletian’s abdication, Galerius Maximian received his forces, part of which he assigned to Caesar Severus for the defense of Italy. Shortly thereafter, when Maxentius had seized imperial power at Rome, Galerius sent Severus with his forces against him. But Maxentius corrupted Severus’s army with stratagems and promises and drew it over to his own side. After this, Galerius himself marched against Maxentius with larger forces and was likewise deserted through a similar betrayal by his soldiers. Thus Diocletian’s soldiers came into Maxentius’s power. [Col. 0475C]

“By the providence of God freeing the great city.” In the Fuketius and Turnebus manuscripts the passage reads: “and the great city, not prospering through the providence of God.”

“But indeed also.” It should be written, “But indeed the outcries to God,” etc.; the Fuketius manuscript has “but indeed also the.”

“And contracts accompanied by justice.” Constantine boasts that, having overthrown Maxentius’s tyranny, he restored liberty and lawful contracts to the Romans. For after the tyrant’s death, everything done by him or by his judges was invalidated. Thus, if anyone had been advanced in rank by him, he returned to his former status and was compelled to submit the credentials of his acquired office to the lawful emperor. Sentences and decrees issued by judges at that time were likewise removed from the public archives and record offices. [Col. 0475D] Finally, that entire period of tyranny was treated as nonexistent, as though it had never been; consequently it did not count even toward prescription by long possession. Agreements, conventions, and contracts of every kind entered into between private persons during that period were similarly invalidated, and this by strict law.

But after lawful emperors had won victory over tyrants and invalidated all their acts, they customarily confirmed agreements, sales, gifts, manumissions, and similar acts of private persons through the indulgence of a public constitution, lest, if all these things became void, the peace and security of private persons should be disturbed. The laws of the emperors in Book XV of the Theodosian Code, “On Invalidating Things Done under Tyrants,” teach this. From them we understand why Constantine says that he gave contracts back to the Romans. In the Fuketius manuscript συμβόλων is written, not συμβολαίων. Rufinus seems to allude to this practice at the end of Book IX, when he says: “For by frequent edicts posted everywhere, he had not only abolished the tyrannical laws against Christians, but had restored civil law,” etc. [Col. 0476C]

[Col. 0471B] But Diocletian, after the blood-pollution of the persecution, having himself condemned himself because of the harm of his folly, was punished by confinement in one contemptible dwelling [Col. 0474A]. What, then, did it profit him to undertake war against our God? So that, I suppose, in fear of the stroke of lightning he might pass the remainder of his life. Nicomedia speaks, and those who have recorded these events are not silent—among whom I myself happen to be. The imperial residences and his house were being devastated, lightning striking and heavenly fire consuming them. The outcome of these things had indeed been foretold by those of sound judgment; for they neither kept silent nor concealed their lamentation over what was happening undeservedly, but openly and publicly speaking freely, they said to one another:

“What is this great madness? How vast the arrogance of power—to dare, being human, to wage war against God; to wish to insult a religion most pure and most just; and, with no prior cause whatever, to devise the destruction of so great a people and of righteous human beings!”

[Col. 0474B] O teacher of moderation for all subjects! O guardian of an army toward its own citizens! They wounded the breasts of those of their own race—men who had never seen in battle the backs of their enemies. At last, therefore, divine providence exacted vengeance for their impious deeds, yet not without public harm. So many slaughterings took place that, if they had occurred against barbarians, they would have been sufficient for everlasting peace. For the entire army of the aforementioned emperor, having been subjected to the authority of a certain worthless man who had violently seized Roman rule, was destroyed in many and various wars, when [Col. 0475A] God’s providence was freeing the great city. But surely the cries to God of those oppressed and longing for their inborn liberty, and the praises of thanksgiving to God after release from evils, when liberty and contracts with justice had been restored to them—how do these not in every way portray God’s providence and his affection toward human beings?

## Chapter XXVI.—That God Was the Cause of the Emperor’s Piety; and That We Ought to Ask God for Prosperous Outcomes and Attribute Them to Him When Received, Whereas Adverse Events Ought to Be Imputed to Our Own Negligence

[Col. 0476B] When they praise my service, which had its beginning from God’s inspiration, do they not openly affirm that God was the cause of my brave deeds? Most certainly. For it is God’s distinctive work to accomplish whatever is best; human beings’ work is to obey God. And, I think, the fairest and best service is this: before one undertakes an enterprise, to prepare beforehand for the security of what is to be done.

All human beings know that the most sacred service of these hands is owed to God with a pure and wholly sincere faith; and that, joined with the work of the hands, prayers and supplications cause every undertaking for what is beneficial to be successfully accomplished, since benefit has thereby accrued, privately and publicly, in such measure as each person had prayed for himself and those dearest to him. They have also recorded the battles and witnessed the war, when God’s [Col. 0475C] providence awarded victory to the people; and they saw God assisting our prayers. For righteous prayer is an unconquerable thing, and no one who offers supplication reverently fails of his aim. There remains no pretext for failure except where faith alone falters. For God is always graciously present, receiving human goodness with favor.

Therefore, although it is human sometimes to stumble, God is not responsible for human failings. Accordingly, all who pursue reverence toward God ought to give thanks to the Savior of all for our own salvation and theirs, and for the prosperity of public affairs; and by holy prayers and unceasing supplications to render Christ propitious to us, that he may preserve his benefits. For he is the unconquered helper and defender of the righteous—the same, the best judge, leader into immortality, and giver of eternal life. [Col. 0478A]

[Note: Col. 0476C]

“Most of all.” It should be written πάντως, “altogether” or “certainly”; and a question mark should be placed before this word, as Christophorson seems to have read it.

“The most sacred service of these hands.” I cannot approve Christophorson’s interpretation, who translates: “the worship of hands raised to heaven.” I have no doubt that λατρεία here means the same as *ministerium*, “service.” Constantine says that people owe God the service of their hands, and this with a pure and sincere faith. Above he had used διακονία and ὑπηρεσία in the same sense. Certainly I do not see how χεῖρες, “hands,” can mean hands lifted toward heaven, or prayers. What follows most clearly refutes Christophorson’s translation. Constantine adds καὶ σὺν γε ταῖς χερσίν, etc.: that is, “with prayers and supplications joined also to the work and service of the hands, whatever has been done for human benefit has been successfully accomplished.” Having said that people ought to offer God the service of their hands, Constantine adds that not only must hands be put at God’s disposal, but prayers and supplications must also be employed, in order that the undertakings we undertake may succeed. This is what the Greeks commonly expressed in the proverb: “Move your hand along with Athena” (σὺν Ἀθηνᾷ καὶ χεῖρα κίνει), by which they indicated that one should put one’s hand to work together with prayer. Moreover, when Constantine says “the service of these hands,” he speaks of himself, in the manner in which Aeneas says in Virgil:

> If Pergam could have been defended by this right hand,  
> It would have been defended by this right hand.

“Of benefit that has accrued.” It should be written as one word, προσγενομένης, which I wonder Scaliger and others did not notice. Thus certainly reads the Fuketius manuscript.

“Awarding victory to the people.” He means the Roman people, who, oppressed by Maxentius’s tyranny, made vows for Constantine against Maxentius. This sense can indeed be tolerated. Yet, upon more attentive examination, I suspect some textual defect here. Perhaps one should read: “awarding victory to my army,” τὴν νίκην τῷ ἐμῷ στρατεύματι βραβευούσης. [Col. 0477B]

“There remains a κόσμος.” Here κόσμος means “pretext”; the translator, not understanding the word in Constantine’s Latin speech, translated it in this way. He would have done better to use πρόφασις. Portesius and Christophorson therefore wrongly translate it “world.”

[Col. 0478B] “Not responsible for human affairs.” It should be written πταισμάτων, “stumbles” or “failings,” as I find corrected in Moraeus’s book. The Genevans had already noted this from the books of Scaliger and Bongarsius, with which the Fuketius manuscript agrees.

“For our own salvation.” I do not agree with Scaliger, Bongarsius, and Gruter, who emend this passage thus: “for the salvation of ourselves.” I would prefer to read: “for our salvation and for that of themselves,” τῆς ἡμετέρας καὶ σφῶν αὐτῶν σωτηρίας, which reading I have followed in my translation. The Fuketius manuscript reads τῆς, τε ἡμῶν αὐτῶν; the notes, however, have τῆς τε ἡμέρας αὐτῷ, etc.]

## Part Three. Letters

### A.D. 313. Letter of Constantine to Melchiades

(Conc. vol. I, col. 1429, Coleti edition.) He requests that a council be assembled at Rome in the case of Caecilian and the Donatists.

[Note: Col. 0477. The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Constantine Augustus to Melchiades, bishop of Rome [Note: Col. 0477C. “And to Marcus” is added in the edition of John Christophorson, whose translation follows.], hierarch.

[Col. 0477C] Since several letters of this kind have been sent to me by Anulinus, most distinguished proconsul of Africa [Note: Col. 0477C. (2) In Eusebius it is written in Greek Ἀνυλῖνος; the form Ἀνιλῖνος is sometimes used less correctly.], in which it is stated that Caecilian, bishop of the city of the Carthaginians, is accused on many matters by certain bishops, his colleagues established in Africa; and since it appears to me exceedingly grievous that in those provinces which divine providence has of its own accord entrusted to my authority, and in those places where a large population gathers, not only should the multitude turn toward worse things and be divided by dissensions, but bishops themselves should also maintain disagreement among themselves: it has seemed good to me that Caecilian himself, together with ten bishops who appear to accuse him, and ten others whom he himself judges necessary for the adjudication of his case, should cross by ship to Rome, so that there, in your presence, and also in that of your colleagues Rheticus, Maternus, and Marinus—whom I have ordered for this purpose to hasten to Rome—he may be heard, as you know to be appropriate to the most holy law of God.

Moreover, so that you may have the fullest and most exact knowledge of all these matters, I have sent to your aforementioned colleagues copies of the letters sent to me by Anulinus, attached to my own letter. When your firmness has read them, it will carefully consider how and by what method the aforesaid dispute ought to be settled most diligently and rightly, and finally concluded according to the prescription of justice. For your diligence is not unaware that I bestow such reverence upon the holy and catholic Church that I do not at all wish you to leave any schism or division in any place. May the divinity of the great God preserve you for many years, most honored men.

### Another Copy of the Letter of the Emperor Constantine, Ordering a Council of Bishops to Be Held at Rome for the Unity and Concord of the Churches

[Col. 0479B] Constantine Augustus to Miltiades, bishop of Rome, and Marcus. Since several memorials of this kind have been sent to me by the most distinguished man Anulinus, proconsul of Africa, in which it is contained that Caecilian, bishop of the city of the Carthaginians, is accused on many grounds by certain colleagues of his established throughout Africa; and since it seems exceedingly grievous to me that in these provinces, which divine providence handed over to my devotion by voluntary surrender, and in which there is a very great multitude of people, the populace should turn toward worse things, as though divided into two parties, and bishops should disagree among themselves: it has pleased me that Caecilian himself, together with ten bishops who seem to accuse him and ten others whom he himself judges necessary for his case, should sail to Rome, so that there he may be heard in your presence and in the presence of your colleagues Rheticus, Maternus, and Marinus, whom I have ordered to hasten to Rome for this purpose, as you know best to accord with the most holy law.

Furthermore, in order that you may gain the fullest knowledge of the entire affair, I have transmitted to your aforementioned colleagues copies of the memorials sent to me by Anulinus, attached to my letter. Once these have been read, your gravity will weigh by what means the aforementioned controversy is to be adjudicated with the greatest care and concluded according to the prescription of justice. For neither is your diligence unaware that I show such reverence to the most holy catholic Church that I wish no schism or dissension anywhere at all to be left by you. May the divinity of the supreme God preserve you for many years, dearest one.

## First Letter of Constantine and Licinius to Anulinus

(Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, chapter 5.) The emperors declare that the favor granted by them belongs to the catholic Church alone.

[Note: Col. 0479. The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0480C] Greetings, Anulinus, most dear to us. This is the practice of our beneficence: that things belonging to another’s right we wish not merely to be free from disturbance, but also to be restored, Anulinus most dear to us. Therefore we command that, as soon as you have received this letter, if any of the things belonging to the catholic Church of Christians in the several cities or in other places are now held by decurions or by any others, you shall immediately cause them to be restored to their churches. For we have resolved that whatever those same churches formerly possessed should altogether be restored to their right.

Therefore, since your devotion sees that this order of ours is perfectly clear, you shall take care that gardens, buildings, or whatever else belonged to the right of those same churches, all be restored to them as quickly as possible, so that we may know that you have rendered the most exact obedience to this command of ours. Farewell, Anulinus, most honored and most desired by us. [Col. 0479D]

## Letter of Anulinus the Proconsul to Constantine, Submitted to the Emperor Together with the Donatists’ Memorial

(Conc. vol. I, col. 1428, Coleti edition.)

[Col. 0479D] Having received and reverently honored the heavenly writings of Your Majesty, the devotion of my lowliness took care to inform and exhort Caecilian and those acting under him, who are called clerics, that, unity having been achieved through the consent of all, and since the catholics appear to have been freed from every burden by the indulgence of Your Majesty, they should preserve the sanctity of the law and serve divine matters with the reverence due to them.

But after a few days certain persons appeared, having gathered a multitude of the people with them, who thought that Caecilian ought to be opposed. They offered my office a packet sealed in leather and an unsigned memorial, and urgently requested that I send them to the sacred and venerable imperial court of Your Name. While Caecilian remained in his position, my lowliness took care to send these things, together with their attached proceedings, so that Your Majesty might be able to take cognizance of the whole matter. [Col. 0482A]

## Second Letter of Constantine to Anulinus

(Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, chapter 7.) He orders that the heads of the churches be exempt from public obligations.

[Note: Col. 0477. The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0481A] Greetings, Anulinus, most dear to us. Since many facts establish that the religion in which reverence for the supreme divine Majesty is preserved, when despised, brought the greatest dangers upon the commonwealth, but when rightly embraced and preserved, bestowed the greatest prosperity upon the Roman name [Col. 0481B] and, through divine beneficence, exceptional happiness upon all human affairs: it has seemed proper that those persons who, with due holiness and continual observance of this law, render their service to the worship of divine religion should receive the recompense of their labors, Anulinus most dear to us.

Accordingly, we wish those persons who, within the province entrusted to you, serve this most holy religion in the catholic Church over which Caecilian presides, and who are customarily called clerics, to remain entirely exempt from all public obligations, lest through some error or sacrilegious contingency they be drawn away from the worship owed to the highest Divinity; but rather that they may serve their own law without any disturbance. For when they render the highest veneration to the divine Power, very great benefit seems thereby to accrue to the commonwealth. Farewell, Anulinus, most dear and most desired by us. [Col. 0481C]

## Letter of Constantine to Caecilian

(Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, chapter 6.) The emperor grants money to the churches.

[Note: Col. 0481. The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Constantine Augustus to Caecilian, bishop of Carthage.

[Col. 0481C] Since we have decided that a certain sum should be granted for necessary expenses to certain ministers of the lawful and most holy catholic religion throughout all the provinces of Africa, Numidia, and the two Mauritanias, I gave letters to Ursus, the most distinguished *rationalis* of Africa, and instructed him [Col. 0481D] to arrange for three thousand folles to be paid to Your Gravity. Therefore, once you have received the aforesaid amount, you shall take care that this money is distributed among all the persons mentioned above according to the list sent to you by Hosius.

If, however, you learn that anything is lacking in order to fulfill my purpose toward all of you in this matter, you must without hesitation request from Heraclides, procurator of our estates, whatever you find necessary. For I also personally ordered him that, if Your Gravity requested any sum of money from him, he should see that it was counted out to you without any delay. And since I have learned that certain persons of unsound mind are attempting to corrupt the people of the most holy and catholic Church by a wicked and counterfeit deception, know that I have personally issued such orders to Anulinus the proconsul and to Patricius, vicar of the prefects, that among all other matters they should take especially appropriate care of this matter and should not tolerate overlooking or disregarding anything of the sort.

Therefore, if you observe any persons of that kind persisting in this madness, approach the aforementioned judges without any hesitation and report the matter to them, so that they may take action against them, as I personally commanded them. May the divinity of the supreme God preserve you for many years. [Col. 0484A]

### A.D. 314. Letter of Constantine to Aelafius

(Conc. vol. I, col. 1445, Coleti edition.) That the disputing parties of the Donatists ought to be summoned to a council at Arles.

Constantine Augustus to Aelafius [Note: Col. 0483D. (1) Elafius—or, according to others, Ablabius or Ablavius, and no less correctly Aelianus—who was proconsul, as is evident from the proceedings of Caecilian’s vindication, to be reported shortly, and from the letter to his successor Probianus. More on this matter in the notes.].

[Col. 0483B] Previously, when it had been brought to my knowledge that in our Africa several persons, in mad frenzy, had begun to disagree with one another by vain accusations concerning the observance of the most holy catholic faith (variant: “to depart”), it had seemed good to me, for the purpose of ending such dissension, that both Caecilian, bishop of Carthage—against whom all had repeatedly appealed especially to me—and some of those who believed they had charges to bring against him should present themselves in our city of Rome.

I had also ordered certain bishops from Gaul to go to our aforementioned city of Rome, so that these men, by the integrity of their lives and their praiseworthy character, together with seven of the same communion, the bishop of Rome, and those who would investigate the matter with them, might bring a fitting conclusion to the affair which appeared to have been stirred up. Whatever was done in their presence, they reported in full to my knowledge through proceedings which were drawn up; they additionally declared that their judgment had been rendered in accordance with the equity of the facts, and stated that those were rather liable in the case who thought to raise certain objections against Caecilian, so much so that they reported that these men had returned to Africa after the judgment had been given.

For all these reasons I had hoped, on a reasonable assessment of the facts, that a fitting end had been put to every disturbance and contention which these persons appeared suddenly to have raised. But when I read your letters, which Your Gravity had thought should be sent to Nicasius and the others concerning these same pretenses, I clearly recognized that they were unwilling to set before their eyes either regard for their own salvation or, what is greater, reverence for God Almighty. For they persist in actions that pertain not only to their own disgrace and infamy, but also give opportunity [Col. 0484B] for reproach to those people who are known to have turned their minds far away from observance so holy. [Note: Col. 0484D. (1) See Augustine, Letters 68, 162, and 165, and Book I against Parmenian’s Letter, chapter 8.]

You should also know that some of these same persons have come, asserting that Caecilian is held unworthy of the worship of the most holy religion (variant: “most sincere religion”). Against this I replied to them that they were making the assertion in vain, because the matter had been settled at Rome by suitable and most approved men, bishops. But they judged that they should respond insistently and stubbornly that their whole case had not been heard; rather, that these bishops had shut themselves away in some place and had judged as they saw fit.

Therefore, seeing that these many and very great disagreements were being prolonged so obstinately that no end could possibly be given to them unless both Caecilian himself and three persons from those who dissent from him should come to the town of Arles for the judgment of those who agree and ought to be in concord with Caecilian, I thought it necessary to enjoin your diligence that, as soon as you receive this letter, you should cause the aforesaid Caecilian, together with some whom he himself selects—and also persons from the provinces of Byzacena, Tripolitania, the Numidias, and the Mauritanias, each of whom must bring several of their own whom they think fit to choose—as well as certain persons who disagree with the same Caecilian, to sail, supplied with public transport, through Africa and Mauritania and thence by a short crossing to Spain.

From there likewise give each of these bishops individual travel warrants, so that they may reach the aforesaid place by the Kalends of August. You shall promptly notify them that, before setting out, they must make arrangements so that, during their absence, proper discipline may be maintained and no disturbance or quarrel of any persons, tending to the greatest disgrace, may arise. Thereafter, when full examination has been undertaken, an end may be imposed. For once they have appeared in person, all the matters now known to be in dispute must rightly receive a prompt conclusion, so that they may immediately be decided and settled.

Since it is certain to me that you too are a worshiper of the supreme God, I confess to Your Gravity that I would in no way judge it lawful for us to disregard disputes and quarrels of this kind, through which perhaps the supreme Divinity might be stirred against not merely the human race but also against myself, to whose care he has committed by his heavenly will the governance of all earthly things, so that in his anger he might determine something adverse. For then I shall truly [Col. 0486A] and completely be able to be secure, and always to hope for every most favorable and best thing from the ready goodwill of the most powerful God, when I perceive that all venerate the most holy God with the due worship of the catholic religion, in the harmonious observance of brotherhood (variant: “in the brotherhood of harmonious observance”).

## Letter of Constantine to Chrestus, Bishop of Syracuse

(Conc. vol. I, col. 1446, Coleti edition.)

Constantine Augustus to Chrestus, bishop of Syracuse. [Col. 0485A]

Constantine Augustus to Chrestus, bishop of Syracuse.

Already before this, when certain persons had begun, through an unworthy and perverse zeal, to dissent concerning the worship of the holy and heavenly divinity and the Catholic faith, I had determined to cut short disputes of this kind among them as follows: after sending several bishops from Gaul, and ordering to appear also those from Africa who belonged to the opposing parties and were contending with one another most vehemently and stubbornly, the entire matter that seemed to have been stirred up might, with the bishop of Rome also present, be settled by careful deliberation in the presence of the parties themselves. But because certain persons, as commonly happens, forgetful alike of their own salvation and of the reverence owed to the most holy faith, do not cease even now to pursue their private animosities, since they refuse to acquiesce in the judgment already pronounced, and allege that the decisions were rendered by only a few persons, who themselves had proceeded too hastily and precipitately to give judgment without carefully examining everything that ought previously to have been investigated: the result is that those very persons who ought to preserve a fraternal and harmonious agreement of mind are divided by a shameful—or rather, an impious—dissension, and furnish men alienated from the most holy religion with an occasion for mockery.

For this reason I had to take diligent care that these matters, which after judgment had been pronounced ought to have been resolved by voluntary assent, might at last, even now, receive their conclusion in the presence of many. Therefore, since we have commanded a great number of bishops from several different places to assemble in the town of Arles by the Kalends of August [1 August], we have thought it necessary to notify you also by letter: obtain public transport from Latronianus, *corrector* of Sicily, a most illustrious man; take with you two others of the second rank, whom you yourself judge fit to select, and three servants to attend you on the journey; and proceed to the designated place on the day stated. Thus, through your gravity and the unanimous and concordant prudence of the others who will assemble, this dissension—which has thus far persisted disastrously through certain disgraceful disputes—may, when all the matters are heard which will be laid before the assembly by those now in disagreement with one another, whom we have likewise ordered to be present, at last, though late, be recalled to the proper religion and faith and to fraternal concord. May almighty God preserve you unharmed for many years.

Constantine Augustus to Chrestus, bishop of the Syracusans.

Already earlier, when some persons had begun, in a base and perverse manner, to separate themselves concerning the religion of the holy and heavenly power and the Catholic confession, wishing to cut short such contentions of theirs, I had arranged matters so that, after certain bishops had been sent from Gaul, and also those summoned from Africa who, belonging to opposite parties, were suitably, vehemently, and persistently struggling against one another, and with the bishop of Rome also present, that matter which seemed to have been set in motion might, through their presence and after every careful discernment, be brought to a successful settlement. But since, as happens, certain persons, forgetting both their own salvation and the reverence owed to the most holy confession, do not cease even now to prolong their private hostilities, unwilling to agree with the judgment already rendered, and asserting that a few persons had issued their opinions and decisions—or that, without all matters which ought first to have been investigated having been carefully examined, they hastened with great speed and sharpness to pronounce judgment—the result of all this is that these very men, who ought to maintain a fraternal and like-minded unanimity, shamefully, or rather foully, separate themselves from one another; and they give men whose souls are estranged from the most holy religion an occasion for derision.

Accordingly, I had to provide that the matter which ought, after the judgment already rendered, to have ceased by voluntary agreement, might even now at last reach its conclusion in the presence of many. Since, therefore, we have ordered very many bishops from diverse and innumerable places to gather in the city of Arles before the Kalends of August, we considered it right to write to you as well: receive public transport from the most illustrious Latronianus, *corrector* of Sicily; associate with yourself two persons of the second rank whom you yourself judge suitable to choose, and also take three attendants able to serve you on the road; and be present at the aforementioned place by that same day. Thus, through your firmness and through the unanimous and like-minded understanding of the others assembling, this matter which has persisted badly until now through certain shameful contests may, after all that is to be said by those now separated from one another has been heard—for we have likewise ordered them to be present—be recalled, even if belatedly, to the proper religion and faith and to fraternal concord. May God Almighty preserve you in health for many years.

Another copy of the letter of Emperor Constantine to Chrestus, in which he orders a second synod of bishops to be held, so that every dissension among bishops may be removed.

Constantine Augustus to Chrestus, bishop of the Syracusans.

Already before this, when certain persons had begun, with a depraved and perverse mind, to dissent from the holy religion, the heavenly power, and the judgment of the Catholic Church, wishing to cut short such contention of theirs, I had made this determination: certain bishops were to be sent from Gaul; those were also to be summoned from Africa who, divided into two parties, contended stubbornly and obstinately with one another; and, with the bishop of the city of Rome likewise present, that which appeared to have been disturbed might be settled under their presence by a most diligent examination. But since certain persons, as generally happens, forgetful both of their own salvation and of the veneration owed to the most holy faith, do not cease to prolong their private enmities even now, unwilling to acquiesce in the sentence already pronounced and maintaining that exceedingly few bishops delivered the judgment—and that these had hastened to pronounce judgment without first carefully examining all matters that ought to have been investigated—the result is that persons who ought to have been of harmonious and fraternal mind toward one another dissent in a shameful, or rather detestable, separation; and an occasion for mockery is given to those whose minds are alienated from the most holy religion.

Therefore I had to provide diligently that these matters, which after the judgment had been rendered ought already to have been concluded by voluntary agreement, might at last be able to receive an end through the intervention of many. Since, therefore, we have ordered a great number of bishops from diverse and almost innumerable places to gather in the city of Arles before the Kalends of August, we have thought it necessary to write to you also: receive public transport from the most illustrious Latronianus, *corrector* of Sicily; add to yourself two persons of the second order whom you judge suitable to select, likewise three servants able to attend you on the journey; and arrive at the designated place by the same day. Then, through both your gravity and the unanimous and concordant diligence of the others gathering together, this controversy, which has endured until this time through a most disgraceful altercation, may, after all the allegations of those now in disagreement with one another have been heard—whom we have also ordered to be present—at long last be recalled to an appropriate observance of religion and faith and to fraternal concord. May almighty God preserve you unharmed for a very long time.

## Letter of Constantine to the Bishops after the Council of Arles

(Conc. I, col. 1454, ed. Col.)

[Note: (1) This survives in the appendix to Optatus of Milevis, in the Paris edition, from the library of Pierre Pithou. Binius, following Baronius, referred it to this Roman council. Sirmond, however, referred it to Arles I. The royal collector published it twice and appended it to each council in an unnecessary repetition.]

Constantine Augustus to the Catholic bishops, most beloved brothers: greetings.

The eternal, religious, and incomprehensible piety of our God does not permit the human condition to wander any longer in darkness; nor does it allow the hateful wills of certain persons to proceed so far that, by once again opening the way of salvation with its most splendid lights, it should not bring them back to the rule of justice. For I have learned this by many examples; I measure these same matters from myself. For there were formerly in me things that seemed to lack justice, nor did I suppose that any higher power observed what I carried within the secrets of my heart. Indeed, as I have said, these things ought to have received a fitting fortune, one overflowing with every evil; but almighty God, dwelling in heaven through the ages, granted what I did not deserve. Certainly the things which, by his heavenly benevolence toward me, his servant, he has granted cannot now either be spoken or enumerated, most holy bishops of Christ the Savior, most beloved brothers.

Therefore I rejoice especially; I rejoice that, after a most just adjudication has at last been held, you have recalled to better hope and fortune those whom the malice of the devil seemed, by its wretched persuasion, to have turned away from the most splendid light of the Catholic law. O truly victorious providence of Christ the Savior, which has also provided for those who, now withdrawing from the truth and in some fashion arming themselves against him, have joined themselves to the nations: for if even now they are willing, with true faith, to render obedience to the most holy law, they will be able to understand how greatly God’s will has provided for them.

And this indeed, most holy brothers, I had hoped could be corrected even in those whose hardness of mind is inborn and extreme; but right adjudication was of no benefit with them, nor did the propitious divinity enter into their understanding. Truly, and not without reason, Christ’s mercy has withdrawn far from those in whom it is manifestly apparent that they are such that we see them hated even by heavenly providence. Such madness persists in them that, with incredible arrogance, they persuade themselves of things which it is neither lawful to say nor hear, withdrawing from the right judgment given—the judgment which, by heavenly providence, I found they had sought from me. Such is the force of malice persisting in their hearts.

How often have they already been overwhelmed by a fitting reply from myself against their most wicked additions? Had they been willing to keep this before their eyes, they would by no means have introduced this very claim. They seek my judgment, though I myself await the judgment of Christ. For I say, as the truth stands: the judgment of priests ought to be regarded as though the Lord himself were seated in judgment. For they are permitted neither to think nor to judge anything other than what they have been taught by Christ’s instruction. What then do these malicious men—agents, as I have truly said, of the devil—think? They seek worldly things, abandoning heavenly ones. O rabid audacity of madness! As usually happens in the cases of pagans, they have lodged an appeal. Pagans, indeed, sometimes rejecting lesser judgments, where justice may swiftly be discovered—or perhaps, reproved—customarily resort to greater courts by lodging an appeal under authority. What did these detractors from the law, refusing heavenly judgment and thinking that they ought to seek mine, think of Christ the Savior? Behold, now they stand revealed as betrayers; behold, without any more searching inquiry, they have themselves disclosed their crimes. What humanity can be recognized in persons who have violently risen up against God himself?

Nevertheless, most beloved brothers, although these things appear to have been found in them, you who follow the way of the Lord Savior should exercise patience. If, after this has been granted them, you see them persist, immediately depart with those whom the Lord has judged worthy of his worship, return to your own sees, and remember me, so that our Savior may always have mercy upon me. Moreover, I have sent my men to bring those same unspeakable deceivers in matters of religion immediately to my court, that they may live there and there look upon a death worse than death. I have also given appropriate letters to the man who holds the vicariate prefecture in Africa, ordering him, whenever he finds any persons resembling this madness, to send them at once to my court, lest under the great splendor of our God they should any longer commit acts capable of provoking the greatest wrath of heavenly providence. May almighty God grant you, most beloved brothers, safety in accordance with my prayers and yours for all ages.

## Letter of Constantine and Licinius to Probianus

(Bal. *Misc.*, I, p. 21.)

The emperors Caesars Flavius Constantine Maximus and Valerius Licinianus Licinius to Probianus, proconsul of Africa.

Your predecessor Aelianus, rightly, while the most perfect man Verus (or Verinus), vicar of the prefects, was then prevented by ill health from exercising his office in our Africa, acted in his place and judged that, among other matters, this business—or accusation—which appears to have been raised concerning Caecilianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, ought to be referred to his investigation and decision. For after he had caused Superius the centurion, Caecilianus the magistrate of the people of Aptunga, Saturninus (or Saturianus) the *excurator*, Calibius Junior, curator of the same city, and Solon, public slave of the aforesaid city, to be present, he granted a suitable hearing. Caecilianus had been accused of having received the episcopate from Felix, against whom betrayal and burning of the divine Scriptures appeared to have been alleged; yet Felix was established to be innocent in that matter.

Finally, when Maximus (above, Apronianus) maintained that Ingentius, decurion of the city of Ziqua, had forged Caecilianus’s letter, we found that Ingentius himself had been suspended, according to the acts available, and for that reason had not been tortured, although he asserted that he was a decurion of the city of Ziqua. We therefore wish you to send that same Ingentius, under suitable escort, to my court, that before those who are currently active and do not cease their accusations day after day, and in their hearing and presence, it may be shown and made known that they have vainly sought to create an accusation against Bishop Caecilianus and to rise violently against him. For in this way, when such disputes have been set aside as they ought to be, the people will serve their own religion with due reverence and without any dissension.

## Letter of Constantine to the Donatist Bishops

(Conc. I, col. 1431, ed. Col.) He summons them to Brescia to establish peace.

Constantine Augustus to the bishops.

A few days ago, indeed, in accordance with your request, it had pleased me that you should return to Africa, so that there the entire case which you seem to have against Caecilianus might be heard by friends of mine whom I should select, and might receive its proper conclusion. But after long reflection, and not without reason turning the matter over in my mind, this seemed preferable: since I know that some among you are sufficiently turbulent and, in an obstinate spirit, pay no attention whatever to right judgment and the reasoning of uncorrupted truth, and since it might consequently happen that, should the matter be heard there, it would not receive a conclusion as propriety and the principle of truth demand, and that through your excessive obstinacy something might occur that would displease the heavenly divinity and greatly impair my reputation, which I wish always to remain unstained, it has pleased me, as I said, that Caecilianus should instead come here in accordance with the earlier arrangement; I believe that, in accordance with my letters, he will soon arrive.

I promise you that, if, with him present, you yourselves prove even one charge or offense of his, that shall count with me as though all the charges you bring had been proved. May almighty God grant perpetual security.

## Letter of Constantine to Celsus

(Conc. I, col. 1471, ed. Col.)

Your latest letters to your gravity have testified, most beloved brother, that Menalius persists in the madness he undertook long ago, as do the others who have departed from the truth of God and given themselves over to the most depraved error. In those letters, adhering to our command, you reported that you had restrained them in view of the deserved penalty for their sedition and the disturbance they were preparing. Since it has thus become evident that they have conceived impious designs—because, when I had determined to inquire most fully into the various accusations between them and Caecilianus, they labored to evade the summons to my presence by flight—by this most shameful act itself they confessed that they were hastening back to the things which they had done before and persist in doing now.

Yet since it is established that no one wholly gains from his own offenses, even if their restraint has been delayed for a little while, I have thought it necessary to command your gravity that, for the present, you should leave them alone and understand that they are to be overlooked. But upon reading this letter, make it publicly known to both Caecilianus and these men that, when by the favor of divine piety I come to Africa, I shall show most fully, in a clear and open judgment, to all alike—to Caecilianus and to those who seem to proceed against him—what reverence, and of what kind, must be rendered to the supreme divinity, and by what worship it seems to be pleased. After conducting a diligent examination, I shall most fully discover and bring to light those things which certain persons now suppose they can conceal by the allurements of their minds and their ignorance.

I shall destroy and disperse those very persons who stir up and carry out affairs of this kind, so that the supreme God is not worshiped with the reverence required. And since it is sufficiently clear that no one can seek the blessed rewards of a martyr by a manner which appears alien to the truth of religion and unsuitable, I shall, without any doubt, exact the deserved punishments of madness and rash obstinacy from those whom I find guilty of acting against law and religion itself and guilty of violent violation of the due reverence. Know with certainty, therefore—calling salvation itself as witness to fullest faith—that I shall investigate with the utmost care both the people and those clergy who are foremost, and shall render the judgment which is manifestly most true and most religious; I shall also demonstrate to them what worship, and what kind of worship, is to be rendered to the divinity.

For I believe that I cannot otherwise escape the greatest guilt than by judging that this wicked conduct must in no way be ignored. For nothing is more fitting for me to do, according to my own settled purpose and the office of a ruler itself, than that, after errors have been examined and every rashness cut away, I should accomplish the presentation to all of the true religion, harmonious simplicity, and worship due to almighty God.

## Fragment of a Letter of Constantine to Eumalius, Vicar

(Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book III.)

In this matter I found Caecilianus to be a man endowed with every innocence, preserving the obligations due to his religion and serving it as he ought; no crime could be found in him. It appeared that the charge against him, even while he was absent, had been fabricated by the contrivance of his opponents.

## Letter of Constantine to the Catholic Church

(Conc. I, col. 1472, ed. Col.)

Constantine the emperor to the bishops and people of Africa, that they should tolerate the Donatists.

You know very well that I have tried, through every office of humanity and moderation, what faith required, what prudence could accomplish, and what purity permitted, so that, according to the teachings of our law, that peace of most holy brotherhood, the grace of which the supreme God has mingled into the hearts of his servants, might be maintained in the stability of complete concord. But because the power of that infused wickedness, although it clings only to the minds of a few, has adhered obstinately, and because the principle of our purpose could not subdue it, while this perversity still found patronage for itself so that they would not allow themselves to be wholly torn away from the thing in which they rejoiced to have sinned, we must wait until the mercy of almighty God softens into the people what has been stirred up by a few. For from that source we ought to hope for a remedy, when every good prayer and action is directed there.
