But while the heavenly remedy proceeds, our counsels must so far be moderated that we cultivate patience and endure with the strength of tranquility everything that their insolence, in accordance with its accustomed intemperance, attempts or does. Let no injury be repaid in return; for it is foolish to usurp in human hands the vengeance which we ought to reserve for God. Especially because our faith ought to trust that whatever it suffers from the fury of persons of this kind will be able to count with God as the grace of martyrdom. For what else is it in this world to conquer in the name of God, than to endure with steadfast heart the ungoverned assaults of men attacking the people of the law of peace?

If your sincerity observes this, you will soon see, through the grace of the supreme divinity, that, when the institutions or habits of those who present themselves as standard-bearers of most wretched contention have lost force, all will know that they ought not, perishing through the persuasion of a few, to consign themselves to everlasting death, but that, after their errors have been corrected, they may be restored through the grace of repentance, always unto eternal life. Farewell, most beloved brothers, for all ages, in accordance with our common prayer, by God’s command.

## In the Year of the Lord 323: First Letter of Constantine to Eusebius

(Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book II, ch. 46.) On the Building and Restoration of Churches. [Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Since until this day impious presumption and tyrannical violence have persecuted the servants of our Savior, I am certain, and fully persuade myself, that the buildings of all the churches have either been ruined through neglect or, through fear of the impending injustice of the times, have been built less worthily, Eusebius, most beloved brother. But now that liberty has been restored, and that dragon has, by the providence of God most great and good and through our agency, been removed from the administration of public affairs, I think that the divine power has become altogether manifest to all, and that those who have fallen into certain sins either through fear or unbelief, once they recognize him who truly is, will return to the true and right order of life.

Therefore, remind all whom you know—whether churches over which you yourself preside, or bishops, presbyters, and deacons presiding in individual places—that they should devote every zeal and diligence to the works of the churches: so that those still standing may either be repaired, or enlarged, or, wherever necessity requires, new ones built. Whatever may be necessary, you yourself and the others, through your intervention, shall request both from the provincial governors and from the office of the praetorian prefecture. For they have been instructed by letter to comply with every diligence with what your holiness shall say. May God preserve you, most beloved brother.

Letters of this kind were sent, accordingly, to the heads of the churches in each province. The governors of the provinces were likewise commanded to execute the measures appropriate to these letters. Thus, with the greatest speed, the commands of the law were being fulfilled in actual deed.

[Note: *Axios gegenēsthai* (“to have been made worthily”). In Moraeus’s copy the margin corrects this to *mē axiōs gegenēsthai* (“not to have been made worthily”). Another marginal correction in the Genevan edition reads *elattona tēs axias gegenēsthai* (“to have been made inferior to what was fitting”). One might also suspect that the passage should be read and construed as *axiōs tēs epikeimenēs adikias* (“worthily in view of the impending injustice”). But the reading *mē axiōs* is truer, and the manuscript of Fuket confirms it.

*Tou drakontos ekeinou* (“that dragon”): I think Licinius is meant, whom Constantine calls thus because of his cunning and old age. Certainly, the words that follow, *apo tēs tōn koinōn dioikēseōs* (“from the administration of public affairs”), clearly show that these things are said of Licinius. From this it may also be inferred that this letter was written shortly after Licinius’s removal from office.

*Ē phobō ē apistia* (“either through fear or unbelief”): at the beginning of this letter, instead of *apistia* Constantine used *ameleia* (“neglect”). Moreover, *phobō* concerns Christians who had neglected the churches through fear of persecution or had denied the faith. But *apistia* concerns pagans or unbelievers, who had damaged the sacred buildings and persecuted Christians in various ways.

*Kai tēs eparchikēs taxēos* (“and from the prefectural staff”): in my notes on the first book of that work, I observed that *taxis* means the same as *officium*, or staff/retinue—that is, a fixed body of soldiers attending magistrates. The *eparchoi* are praetorian prefects, so called because they are *epi tois archousi*, that is, over provincial governors and rulers. Thus the *eparchikē taxis* is the office of the praetorian prefecture, concerning which the *Notitia Imperii Romani* should be consulted. The office of the praetorian prefect excelled the staffs of all other magistrates. For just as the praetorian prefect surpassed all other judges, civil and military alike, in rank, so his officials surpassed all other attendants. Hence in the third session of the Council of Chalcedon, the office of the praetorian prefects is called *megistē taxis* (“the greatest staff”).

*Phēmi dē ton aïdesimon Theodōron, ton ek tēs megistēs taxēos* (“I mean the reverend Theodore, one of the greatest staff”): the interpreters did not understand these words; I would rather suppress their error in silence than refute it ostentatiously. In the Fuket manuscript I find written *kai tōn tēs eparchikēs taxēos* (“and [those] of the prefectural staff”), as also in Savile’s copy.

*Toutois gar epestalē* (“for instructions were sent to these persons”): Christophorson translates, “For this was communicated to them by me in writing,” adding “by me,” which I do not approve. For the emperor himself did not generally issue letters of this kind; the praetorian prefects did.

*Tauta mēn oun* (“these matters, then”): a new chapter begins from these words in the royal manuscript. Moreover, from these words it appears that Constantine issued letters of the same form to the other bishops of the East.]

“Until the present time, while the servants of the Savior have been persecuted by impious purpose and tyranny, I have believed and fully persuaded myself that the works of all the churches have either been destroyed by neglect or, through fear of the impending injustice, have not been built worthily, most beloved brother. But now that liberty has been restored, and that dragon has been driven from the administration of public affairs by the providence of God most great and through our service, I consider the divine power to have become manifest to all; and I consider that those who through fear or unbelief have fallen into certain sins, when they recognize him who truly is, will come to the true and upright order of life.

“Therefore, remind all those whose churches you yourself oversee, or whose local leaders you know to be bishops, presbyters, or deacons, to take care concerning the works of the churches: either to restore the existing buildings, or to enlarge them, or, wherever need requires, to construct new ones. You yourself, and the others through you, shall request whatever is necessary from both the governors and the prefectural staff. For they have been directed to render, with every readiness, assistance in the matters stated by your holiness. May God preserve you, beloved brother.”

These things, then, were written to the heads of the churches in every nation; and the rulers of the nations were commanded to carry out what followed from them. With great speed, the enacted measures advanced into practice.

## Letter of Constantine to Bishop Alexander and Presbyter Arius

(Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book II, chs. 64–72.) [Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Victor Constantine, greatest Augustus, to Alexander and Arius.

I. God himself, as is fitting—the helper of my undertakings and Savior of all—do I make witness that I was impelled by two causes to undertake in deed the task of these things.

Victor Constantine, Greatest Augustus, to Alexander and Arius.

I. I call God himself, as is fitting, the helper of my undertakings and Savior of all, to witness that two causes arose for me to undertake in action the duty of these matters.

### How He Continually Labored for Peace

II. For first, it was my purpose to bring the inherited conception of all nations concerning God into a single, as it were, disposition and form; second, to restore the body of the inhabited world, oppressed as though by a grave disease of tyranny, to its former health. Having proposed these two matters to myself as aims, I investigated the one with the hidden eye of thought, but sought to accomplish the other by military force and power. For I understood that, if I could establish the common concord of all worshipers of God, as I desired, the administration of the commonwealth would undergo a change corresponding to the pious sentiments of all.

II. “First, I was eager to unite the disposition of all nations concerning the divine as a single established condition; second, to set right the body of the common inhabited world, which was grievously afflicted as though by some severe disease. Considering these aims, I reflected upon one with the secret eye of my mind, while I attempted to accomplish the other through the authority of military power; knowing that, if I should establish a concord shared by all servants of God, in accordance with my prayers, then the business of public affairs too would reap a change harmonious with the pious judgments of all.”

### How He Suppressed the Questions Raised in Africa

III. Therefore, when a certain intolerable madness had seized all Africa, because some persons had dared, in rash levity, to divide the religion of the peoples into various sects, I, wishing to calm this malady, found no other remedy suitable to cure it than to remove from the midst the common enemy of humankind, who had set his impious judgment and command against your most holy synods, and to send some of you as ministers and helpers for restoring concord among those in disagreement.

III. “For when an unbearable madness had seized all Africa, through those who had dared in purposeless frivolity to divide the religion of the peoples into diverse sects, I, wishing to restrain this disease, found no other treatment sufficient for the matter than, after removing the common enemy of the inhabited world, who had opposed his unlawful judgment to your sacred synods, to send certain of you as helpers toward concord among those in discord with one another.”

### That Religion Began from the Eastern Regions

IV. For since the power of the true light and the law of the most holy religion, through God’s benefit, had gone forth from the bosom, so to speak, of the East and had simultaneously illuminated the whole world with sacred rays, I labored, trusting that you would be authors and leaders of salvation for all nations, to seek you with the desire of my mind and the sight of my eyes. Therefore, immediately after that great victory and the most certain triumph over my enemies, I determined before all else to investigate anew the matter which I judged to be chief and of the greatest importance.

IV. “For since the power of light and the law of sacred religion, through the benefaction of the higher power, had gone forth as though from certain bosoms of the East and illumined the whole inhabited world with a sacred lamp, I reasonably believed that you would be, as it were, leaders in the salvation of the nations; and I sought you both with the inclination of my soul and with the activity of my eyes. Thus, immediately upon the great victory and true triumph over our enemies, I chose first to investigate the matter which I considered first and most precious of all.”

### How, Grieved by Sedition, He Urged Peace

V. But, O excellent providence of God! What a report, and what kind of report, most painfully wounded my ears—or rather my very soul—when it was told to me that dissensions had arisen among you far more serious than those which remained in Africa! So that your own party, from which I had hoped healing might be supplied to others, now requires greater treatment. As I carefully reflected on the beginning and origin of these matters, the cause appeared to me exceedingly slight and unworthy of so great a contention of minds. Therefore, compelled to write this letter, and writing to the concordant diligence of you both, having invoked the aid of divine providence for this task, I rightly place myself as arbiter of your disagreement and, as it were, director of peace. For even if a graver cause of discord lay beneath it, yet, with God’s help, by setting the matter before the pious minds of my hearers, I could not with difficulty recall each person to sounder counsels. Since the cause that now obstructs the agreement of the whole body is so slight and trifling, why should I not promise myself a correction of this affair much easier and more expeditious?

V. “But, O most excellent and divine providence! What a grievous wound struck my hearing—or rather my very heart—by indicating a dissension among you far more severe than those matters left there; so that your own party already needs greater healing than those from whom I hoped healing would come to others. As I reflected upon the beginning and subject of these things, the cause was found to be altogether trivial and in no way worthy of such contention. Therefore, impelled to write this letter and writing to your united intelligence, having summoned divine providence as helper in the matter, I rightly present myself as mediator in your dispute with one another, as though a president of peace. For, with the higher power assisting, even if there were a greater cause of discord, I could without difficulty, by committing the argument to the pious minds of those hearing it, bring each person over to what is more advantageous. Since the cause is small and exceedingly trivial, and stands in the way of the whole, how could I fail to promise myself a correction of the affair that is easier and much more readily accomplished?”

### The Origin of the Controversy between Arius and Alexander, and Why Such Matters Ought Not Be Investigated

VI. I learn that the beginning of the present controversy arose as follows. When you, Alexander, asked your presbyters what each of them thought concerning a certain passage of the law—or rather, questioned them concerning some aspect of an empty question—and when you, Arius, imprudently put forward what you ought either never to have conceived in the first place or, if you had conceived it, to have consigned to silence: discord was stirred up between you; communion was denied; and the most holy people, split into two parties, withdrew from the unity of the whole body. Therefore let each of you grant the other reciprocal pardon, and let him embrace what your fellow servant most justly urges upon you. And what is that? It was not fitting from the beginning either to ask questions about such matters or, when asked, to answer them.

For questions of this kind are not prescribed by any necessity of law, but are put forward by the contentiousness of useless leisure. Even if they are undertaken for the exercise of intellectual ability, still we ought to keep them within the inner chambers of our minds, neither readily bringing them out into public assemblies nor rashly entrusting them to the ears of the populace. For how many persons are capable either of comprehending accurately the force and nature of matters so great and difficult, or of explaining them worthily? And even if someone is judged able to achieve this easily, to what portion of the people will he finally be able to persuade it? Or who can hold firm in the subtle and exact discussion of questions of this kind without danger of a most serious fall? Therefore in such questions loquacity must be restrained, lest either we should be unable, through the weakness of our nature, to explain what is proposed, or the hearers, through slowness of understanding, should fail to grasp what is said; and the people, through one or the other of these causes, should fall under the necessity either of blasphemy or of schism.

VI. “I learn, therefore, that the foundation of the present question arose from this source. For when you, Alexander, asked the presbyters what each one of them thought concerning some passage among the things written in the law—or rather questioned them about some point of a vain inquiry—and when you, Arius, carelessly introduced what you ought either not to have conceived from the outset or, if conceived, to have handed over to silence, discord arose among you. The synod was refused, and the most holy people, divided into two, was separated from the harmony of the common body. Therefore let each of you grant an equal pardon in turn, and let each accept what your fellow servant rightly counsels you.

“And what is this? Neither was it fitting at the outset to ask about such matters, nor to answer when asked. For inquiries of this sort are not commanded by the necessity of any law, but are proposed by the contentiousness of unprofitable idleness. Even if undertaken for the sake of a kind of intellectual exercise, nevertheless we ought to confine them within the mind, neither bringing them readily into public assemblies nor heedlessly committing them to the ears of the populace. For how many persons are capable of accurately understanding the force of matters so great and exceedingly difficult, or of interpreting them worthily? And even if someone should be thought capable of doing this easily, what proportion of the people, pray, will he persuade? Or who could stand firm amid the precise discussions of such questions without perilous slipping? Therefore one must restrain prolixity in matters of this kind, lest either, because of the weakness of your nature, you be unable to explain what has been proposed, or, because of the slower understanding of the hearers, they fail to arrive at an accurate comprehension of what has been said; and from either of these circumstances the people might fall under the necessity of blasphemy or schism.”

### Exhortation to Concord

VII. Therefore let both the incautious question and the inconsiderate answer grant each other mutual pardon in each of you. For no contention has arisen between you concerning the chief and supreme command of our law, nor has any new doctrine concerning the worship of God been introduced by you. Rather, you hold one and the same opinion, so that you can readily come together in fellowship of communion.

VII. “Therefore let the unguarded question and the unconsidered answer mutually grant one another equal forgiveness in each of you. For the occasion of your contention has not been kindled concerning the chief command among those in the law; nor has some new teaching concerning the worship of God been introduced among you. Rather, you hold one and the same judgment, so that you are able to come together in the bond of communion.”

### That One Ought Not Persist in Contending over Certain Trifling Words
[Col. 0497C] VIII. For when you contend stubbornly among yourselves over small and utterly trivial matters, it is not fitting that so great a multitude of God’s people should be governed by your judgment, especially amid such discord of minds; indeed, this is judged to be not only unbecoming but altogether impious. And, to remind your prudence by a lesser example, you know that even philosophers themselves are all united with one another by the profession of a single school; yet they sometimes differ in some part of their assertions. But although they disagree concerning the very perfection of knowledge, nevertheless, because of their school’s communion, they again join together in one accord. If this is so, how much more just would it be for you, who have been appointed ministers of the greatest God, to remain unanimous in the profession of the same religion.

But let us, if you please, weigh more carefully and attentively what I have just said: whether it is right that, because of disputes among you over slight and empty words, brothers should stand opposed to brothers as though in battle line, and that the venerable assembly should be divided by impious discord through you who quarrel over matters so minute and altogether unnecessary. These are vulgar matters, more suited to childish ignorance than to the wisdom of priests and prudent men. Let us voluntarily withdraw from the devil’s temptations. Our great God and the Saviour of all has extended a common light to all. Under his auspices and providence, grant me, I pray, his servant and worshipper, to bring this undertaking to its conclusion: so that by my address and service, and by the urgency of admonitions, his people may be recalled to the unity of the assembly.

For since, as I have said, you have one and the same faith and one judgment concerning our religion; and since the commandment of the law, in both its parts, binds all together into a single concord of minds: let that matter which has stirred up a slight contention among you, since it does not pertain to the whole substance of religion, by no means cause division or sedition among you. And I say this not as compelling you to agree altogether concerning that exceedingly foolish question—whatever it may be called. For the dignity of the assembly can remain wholly preserved among you, and one and the same communion can be maintained among all, although you differ from one another in some matter of the slightest importance.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] “Communion can be maintained.” These words and those which follow must necessarily be said to have issued from the Arian workshop. For how can Alexander and Arius be said to hold one and the same view concerning the faith, so that disagreement between the two might easily be reconciled, when Alexander affirmed that the Son of God is coeternal with the Father, whereas Arius stubbornly denied it? Likewise, how can a controversy be considered utterly trivial when the divinity of Christ, which is the sum of the whole catholic faith, is under debate? Hence it is more clearly evident that what I said above is true: these things which issued from the Arian workshop were either added to this letter, or at least altered, by Eusebius of Caesarea; or were persuaded upon the emperor by that more wicked and lethargic serpent, Eusebius of Nicomedia. SEVERUS BINIUS.]

For we do not all desire the same thing in every respect, nor does one nature or opinion prevail in all.

Therefore, concerning divine providence, let there be among you one faith, one understanding, one agreement concerning God. But whatever you discuss minutely with one another concerning these most trivial questions, even if you do not come together in a single opinion, you ought to keep it within the inward thought of the mind and store it away in the secret recess of the breast. Let the special privilege of common friendship, faith in the truth, and observance of God and of the law remain firm among you. Return to mutual affection and charity; restore to the whole people their proper embraces. And you yourselves, having, so to speak, cleansed your souls, recognize one another again. For friendship, once reconciliation has returned after enmity has been laid aside, often becomes more delightful.

[Col. 0498C] VIII. For when you contend with one another over small and altogether trifling matters, it is not fitting that so great a people of God should be directed by your judgments because you are divided in mind; rather, this is believed to be neither becoming nor at all lawful. To remind your understanding by a small example, I shall say this: you surely know that the philosophers themselves all agree in one doctrine, yet often, when they disagree in some part of their propositions, although they are separated in the excellence of knowledge, they nevertheless again breathe together toward one another through the unity of their doctrine. If this is so, how much more just is it that you, established as servants of the great God, should be of one soul with one another in such a purpose of religion?

Let us therefore examine the saying with greater reflection and fuller understanding: whether it is right, because of a few vain disputes over words among us, for brothers to be set against brothers and for the honour of the council to be divided by impious discord through us, who contend with one another over matters so small and in no way necessary. These things are common and popular, more fitting for childish foolishness than appropriate to the understanding of priests and prudent men. Let us willingly depart from diabolical temptations. Our great God, the common Saviour of all, has extended a common light to all. Under his providence, permit me, a servant of the Higher One, to bring this effort to its end, so that through my address, service, and insistent admonition I may bring his very peoples back to the communion of the council.

For, as I said, there is for you one faith and one understanding of the doctrine among us, and the commandment of the law, through its own parts, brings the whole into one disposition of soul. Let not that which raised a slight contention among you with one another, since it does not concern the force of the whole, produce any separation or faction among you. And I say this not as forcing you altogether to agree with that exceedingly foolish inquiry, whatever it may be. For the honour of the council can be preserved intact among you, and one and the same communion maintained for all, even if at some point disagreement should arise among you concerning a very slight matter. For neither do we all will the same things in all matters, nor is one nature or judgment present among you.

Concerning divine providence, then, let there be among you one faith, one understanding, one agreement concerning the Higher One. But the matters which you scrutinize among yourselves concerning these slightest inquiries, even if you do not converge upon one opinion, ought to remain within your reasoning, preserved in the secret place of the mind. Yet let the excellence of common friendship, faith in truth, and reverence concerning God and the law remain unshaken among you. Return, then, to one another’s friendship and favour. Restore to the whole people its proper embraces. And, as though cleansing your own souls, recognize one another anew; for friendship, having returned again to reconciliation after the occasion of enmity, often becomes sweeter.

## How, affected by grief, he shed tears out of piety and restrained the journey which he intended to make to the East for this reason

[Col. 0500C] IX. Restore to me, therefore, tranquil days and nights free from care, so that the delight of pure light and the joy of a peaceful life may also be preserved for me hereafter. But unless I obtain this, I must groan and be wholly overwhelmed with tears; nor shall I pass the remaining time of my life peacefully. For so long as the people of God—I mean my fellow servants—are torn apart by an unjust and ruinous contention, how can I thereafter remain composed in mind?

Moreover, that you may understand the greatness of my grief in this matter: recently, when I had come to Nicomedia, I immediately resolved to make a journey to the East. And when I was pressing forward with my departure and was already for the greater part among you, news of this affair turned my purpose back, lest I be compelled to see with my own eyes things which I thought I could not endure even to hear. Therefore open for me by your concord the road into the East which you have blocked by your mutual contentions. Grant me this: that I may see you and all other peoples cheerful and rejoicing as soon as possible, and may offer to God the thanks due for the common concord and liberty of all, with one harmonious chorus of praise.

[Col. 0499C] IX. Restore to me, then, serene days and nights without care, so that for me too there may remain the delight of clear light and the gladness of a peaceful life. Otherwise, I must groan, be entirely suffused with tears, and not even endure gently the span of life. For when the peoples of God—my fellow servants, I say—are thus separated by unjust and harmful contention against one another, how can I henceforth stand firm in my judgment?

And that you may perceive the excess of my grief at this, when recently I arrived at the city of the Nicomedians, I immediately hastened in purpose toward the East. While I was hastening toward you and was for the greater part already with you, news of this letter checked my intention and turned it back, lest I be compelled to see with my eyes what I thought I could not even receive through my ears. Therefore now open for me, through the concord among you, the road to the East which you have shut off by your contentions with one another. Allow me quickly to see you together with all other peoples rejoicing, and, with harmonious words of praise, to acknowledge to the Higher One the thanks due for the common concord and liberty of all.

## In the year of the Lord 325. Letter of Constantine to the Church after the Council of Nicaea

(Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book III, chapters 17–20.)

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0501]

### Constantine Augustus to the Churches

[Col. 0501A] I. Having learned from the prosperous condition of the commonwealth how great has been the kindness of almighty God toward us, I judged that I ought above all to labour for this: that among the most holy peoples of the catholic Church there should be maintained one faith, sincere charity, and harmonious devotion toward almighty God. But since this could not be established firmly and securely unless all, or at least the greater number, of the bishops had assembled in one place and first examined each matter pertaining to the most sacred religion, for this reason, as many priests as possible having been gathered together, I too was present as one among you—for I shall not deny that the thing in which I most rejoice is being your fellow servant—and everything was examined by fitting inquiry until the judgment acceptable to God, the inspector of all, was brought to light for the concord of unity, so that no room at all might remain for disagreement or controversy concerning the faith.

### Constantine Augustus to the Churches

[Col. 0502A] I. Having received proof from the prosperity of public affairs of how great is the grace of divine power, I judged this to be, before all things, the aim proper for me: that among the most blessed multitudes of the catholic Church there should be maintained one faith, sincere love, and concordant piety toward the all-powerful God. But because this could not receive an unshaken and firm ordering unless all together, or at least the greater number, of the bishops assembled in one place and an examination took place of each of the matters appropriate to the most holy religion, for this reason, when a very great number had assembled, I myself was present with them as one of you—for I would not deny the thing in which I especially rejoice, that I am your fellow servant. Everything accordingly underwent the appropriate examination until the judgment pleasing to God, the overseer of all, was brought forth into the light for the harmony of unity, leaving nothing further for discord or dispute concerning faith.

## Concerning agreement in the celebration of the feast of Easter, and against the Jews

[Col. 0501C] II. When inquiry had also been made concerning the most holy day of Easter, it was decreed by the common judgment of all that this feast ought to be celebrated by everyone everywhere on one and the same day. For what could be more beautiful or more honourable for us than that this feast, from which we received the hope of immortality, should be observed by all without offense in one and the same order and according to a fixed rule?

First, indeed, it seemed to everyone entirely unworthy that in celebrating this most holy solemnity we should follow the custom of the Jews. Since they have defiled their hands by a wicked crime, those impure people are deservedly afflicted with blindness of mind. Once their custom has been rejected, we can extend to future ages also the rite of this observance by the more correct order which we have kept from the first day of the Passion down to the present time. Let us therefore have nothing in common with the most hostile multitude of the Jews. For we have received another way from the Saviour. A lawful and honourable course has been set before our most sacred religion. Holding to this with unanimous agreement, let us separate ourselves from that most shameful association and complicity, most honoured brothers.

For it is surely most absurd that they should boast greatly that we cannot suitably observe these things without their instruction. What sound judgment can those possess who, after the murder of the Lord, after that parricide, have been driven mad and are carried not by reason but by reckless impulse wherever their inborn fury impels them? Hence they do not perceive truth even in this matter, so that, wandering very far from the proper correction, they celebrate two Easters in one and the same year. Why, then, should we follow those who are acknowledged to suffer from the gravest disease of error? We shall certainly never tolerate the observance of a double Easter in one and the same year.

But even if the points I have mentioned did not exist, your diligence ought nevertheless by every means to take care and desire that the purity of your souls should not appear to be joined and mingled, in any resemblance whatever, with the customs of the most wicked people. Moreover, it must be considered that it is impious for disagreement to be found in a matter of such importance and in a religious solemnity of this kind. For our Saviour has left us one feast day of our liberation, that is, the day of his most sacred Passion, and he has willed that there should be one catholic Church. Although its members are scattered through diverse places, they are nevertheless cherished by one Spirit, that is, by the will of God.

Let the prudence of your Holiness, I pray, consider how grievous and unbecoming it is that on the same days some should be occupied with fasts while others celebrate banquets, and that after the days of Easter some should be engaged in festivities and relaxation while others devote themselves to appointed fasts. Therefore divine providence wills, as I think you all understand, that this should be corrected by an appropriate reform and reduced to one and the same form.

[Note: Col. 0501D]

“By common judgment it was decided” (*edoxe koinē gnōmē*). Athanasius appears to have had these words of Constantine in view when, in his book *On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia*, p. 873, he notes that the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea spoke differently in their exposition of faith and in defining the day of Easter. In this matter they used the word *edoxe*, that is, “it seemed good” or “it was decided.” But in the exposition of faith they did not at all say “it seemed good,” but rather, “Thus the holy and universal Church believes.” Certainly, the word *edoxe* reported by Athanasius is not found in the Synodical Letter, but only in this Letter of Constantine [Col. 0502D]; and one may reasonably suspect that it was regarded as a synodical letter.

“Of that nation” (*tou ekeinōn ethnous*). I read “custom” (*ethous*) with Christophorson and Gruter. We have noted the same error in the *Ecclesiastical History*. Certainly, in the Royal manuscripts and in Savile’s book, *ethous* is written.

“And both lawful and fitting” (*kai nomimos kai prepōn*). In Gelasius and Nicephorus one reads “and a fitting law” (*kai nomos prepōn*). Socrates and Theodoret, however, support the received reading.

“From that shameful complicity” (*aischras ekeinēs syneidēseōs*). For those who celebrate the Lord’s Easter with Jews seem to be complicit in the crime which the Jews committed against the Lord; but Christophorson translates *syneidēsis* as “opinion,” which I do not accept.

“From the proper correction” (*tēs prosēkousēs epanorthōseōs*). Socrates, Theodoret, Gelasius, and Nicephorus have “instead of the proper correction” (*anti tēs prosēkousēs epanorthōseōs*), which I do not approve. For it is correctly said, “wandering from correction” (*planōmenous tēs epanorthōseōs*).

“To celebrate Easter a second time in the same year” (*tō autō etei deuteron to pascha epitelein*). Since the Jewish paschal new moon could begin on the fifth day of March and end on the third of April, it sometimes happened that their Easter began before the equinox. Thus they celebrated a double Easter in the same year. Yet this repetition which Constantine charges against the Jews does not seem to me to be of great importance. For the Jews could have retorted the same thing against Christians: namely, that they celebrated Easter twice in one and the same year, if by “year” we understand a revolving year. Suppose, for example, that Easter is celebrated this year on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April]; it must be celebrated earlier in the following year. Thus a double Easter occurs among Christians within the course of a single revolving year. See Epiphanius, *Heresy* 70, that of the Audians, p. 824, and the observations of D. Petavius. To this add chapter 3 of Aegidius Bucherius, *On the Paschal Cycle of the Jews*.

“Why?” (*tinos charin*). In Theodoret and Nicephorus one reads, “Why then?” (*tinos oun charin*). So too Socrates and Gelasius. From these the following should be corrected thus: “your acuteness” (*tēn hymeteran anchinoian*), and shortly afterward, “in no resemblance whatever” (*en mēdemiā homoiotēti*). Although among those writers whom I have mentioned one reads, “in resemblance to nothing” (*en mēdenos homoiotēti*); in the Fuketian manuscript it is written, “on no pretext” (*en mēdemiā prophasei*). Moreover, the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book V, chapter 16, seems to allude to these words. Anyone who compares that passage with these words of Constantine will surely admit it.

“Some occupied with fasts” (*heterous men tais nēsteiais scholazein*). He means the beginning of the fast, which was commenced at one time by the Quartodecimans and at another by the remaining Christians. If, however, anyone prefers to understand this of the end of the Lenten fast, I shall not object. See Chrysostom, in the Homily against Those Who Fasted at the First Easter, p. 714.

[Col. 0502C] II. When inquiry had also been made concerning the most holy day of Easter, it was resolved by common judgment that it was fitting for all everywhere to celebrate on one day. For what could be more beautiful or more venerable for us than that this feast, from which we have received the hopes of immortality, should be kept without error by all according to one order and a manifest rule?

First, it seemed unworthy to celebrate that most holy feast by following the custom of the Jews, who, having stained their own hands with an unlawful transgression, rightly have their impure souls blinded. For, once their custom has been rejected, it is possible to extend into future ages the fulfilment of this observance according to a truer order, which we have kept from the first day of the Passion until the present. Therefore let us have nothing in common with the most hostile multitude of the Jews; for we have received another way from the Saviour. A course both lawful and fitting lies before our most sacred religion. Let us agreeably embrace this and separate ourselves from that shameful complicity, most honoured brothers.

For it is truly most absurd that they should boast that apart from their teaching we are incapable of observing these things. What right judgment can those have who, after the murder of the Lord and that parricide, have departed from their senses and are carried not by any reasoning but by unrestrained impulse wherever their innate madness leads them? Therefore, even in this matter, they do not see the truth, so that, for the most part wandering from the proper correction, they celebrate Easter a second time in the same year. Why do we follow them, who are acknowledged to suffer from grievous error? For we shall never tolerate celebrating it a second time in one year.

But even if these considerations were not before us, our intelligence ought always, both by earnest care and by prayer, to ensure that the purity of your soul does not appear to share in any resemblance whatever with the customs of utterly wicked people. Besides, it must also be seen that it is unlawful for disagreement to arise in a matter so great and in such a feast of religion. For our Saviour handed down one feast—the day of our liberation, that is, of the most holy Passion—and he willed his catholic Church to be one. Although its members are divided into many different places, they are nevertheless warmed by one Spirit, that is, the divine will.

Let the intelligence of our holiness consider how grievous and unseemly it is, on the same days, for some to devote themselves to fasts and others to hold banquets; and after the days of Easter, for some to engage in feasts and relaxations, while others give themselves over to the prescribed fasts. Therefore divine providence wills that this should receive the appropriate correction and be brought to one pattern, as I think all perceive.

## Exhortation that they should be willing to follow the greater part of the inhabited world

[Col. 0504C] III. Therefore, since this ought to be corrected in such a way that we have nothing in common with the custom of those murderers of the Lord and parricides, and since this is the most becoming order, which all the Churches of the western, southern, and northern regions of the world, and also some of those in the East, observe, everyone judged it right and proper—and I promised that it would also please you—that what is observed with one harmonious judgment in the city of Rome and throughout Italy, Africa, Egypt, Spain, Gaul, Britain, Libya, all Achaia, the Asian and Pontic dioceses, and finally Cilicia, should also be embraced willingly by your prudence.

You should surely take into account not only that the number of churches in the places mentioned above is greater, but also that it is most equitable that all should desire in common what strict reason appears to demand, and that there should be no fellowship with Jewish perjury. And, to state the matter briefly and summarily, it was decided by the common judgment of all that the most holy feast of Easter should be celebrated on one and the same day. For it is not fitting that there should be any discord in so great a sacred observance; and it is better to follow that judgment in which there is no association or communion with another’s error and crime.

[Note: Col. 0505D]

“Exact reasoning” (*akribēs logos*). In Theodoret and Gelasius of Cyzicus one reads *logismos*, which certainly does not displease me, so that *logismos* has the same meaning as *psēphismos*, that is, “careful calculation”; hence the paschal computation is so called.

[Col. 0503C] III. Therefore, since this ought to be corrected in such a way that there be nothing in common with that nation of parricides and murderers of the Lord, and since there is a fitting order which all the Churches in the western, southern, and northern regions of the inhabited world observe, together with certain churches in the East, everyone has judged it good at present. I myself also promised that it would please your understanding: namely, that what is observed by one unanimous judgment in the city of the Romans, Africa, all Italy, Egypt, Spain, Gaul, Britain, Libya, the whole of Greece, the Asian and Pontic dioceses, and Cilicia, should be gladly accepted by your understanding as well. Consider that not only is the number of churches in the aforesaid places greater, but that it is also most holy for all to desire in common what exact reasoning appears to require, and to have no communion at all with the perjury of the Jews.

And, to put the principal point briefly, it pleased the common judgment of all that the most holy feast of Easter be celebrated on one and the same day. For it is not fitting that there should be any difference in so great a sacred observance; and it is better to follow this judgment.

## Exhortation that all should assent to the decrees of the Synod

[Col. 0505B] IV. Since these things are so, gladly receive the heavenly grace and truly divine command. For whatever is done in the holy councils of bishops must wholly be referred to the divine will. Therefore, once you have made known what has been done to our beloved brothers, you ought to accept and establish the aforementioned rule and observance of the most holy day, so that when I come into the presence of your affection, which I have long desired, I may be able to celebrate the holy feast with you on one and the same day; and so that I may rejoice with you over all things, seeing that the cruelty of the devil has been removed by divine power through our efforts, while your faith, peace, and concord flourish everywhere on earth. May God preserve you, most beloved brothers.

The emperor sent this letter, written in the same form, into every province, so that those who read it might behold, as in a mirror, the sincerity of his piety toward God.

[Note: Col. 0505D]

“For whatever is done in the holy councils of bishops” (*pan gar, ei ti d’ an en tois hagiois tōn episkopōn synedriois*). This judgment of Constantine concerning the authority of synodal decisions should be noted. A similar passage occurs elsewhere in a letter of the same Constantine to the bishops after the Council of Arles.

[Col. 0506D] “You ought to establish” (*diatattein opheilete*). From this passage it is plainly inferred that this letter of Constantine was written to bishops who had not attended the Synod. It is indeed addressed to the Churches; but under the name “Churches,” their bishops are to be understood.

“Your disposition” (*tēs hymeteras diatheseōs*). This is a distinctive expression of Christians, who, when they addressed one of the brethren either orally or by letter, customarily said “your charity” or “your affection.”

[Col. 0506B] IV. Since these things are so, gladly receive the grace of God and what is truly a divine command. For whatever is done in the holy councils of bishops has reference to the divine will. Therefore, once you have made known what has been done to all our beloved brothers, you ought now to receive and establish the aforementioned ruling and observance of the most holy day, so that, when I arrive at the sight of your disposition, which I have long desired, I may be able to celebrate the holy feast with you on one and the same day and may rejoice with you in all things, seeing that the devil’s cruelty has been destroyed by divine power through our actions, while our faith, peace, and concord flourish everywhere. May God preserve you, beloved brothers.

The emperor sent an equivalent copy of this letter into each province, offering those who read it an opportunity to behold, as in a mirror, the utmost purity of his mind and of his piety toward the divine.

## Letter of Constantine to the Churches

(Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter IX.) The emperor commands that Arius’s books be handed over to the fire.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0505]

### Victor Constantine, greatest Augustus, to bishops and peoples

[Col. 0505C–D] Since Arius has judged malicious and impious men worthy of imitation, it is right that he should bear the same disgrace as they. Thus, just as Porphyry, the enemy of divine piety, having composed wicked books concerning religion, found a fitting reward by which he will be subject to the reproach of all future ages and overwhelmed with the greatest infamy, while, moreover, his impious writings were abolished: so now it has pleased us that Arius and the supporters of Arius should be called Porphyrians, so that those whose conduct they have imitated may also supply their name.

Moreover, if any writing composed by Arius is discovered, it is to be consigned to the fire, so that not only his wicked teaching may be removed, but not even any memorial of him may remain. I further decree this: if anyone is discovered to have concealed any book composed by Arius and has not immediately produced and consumed it by fire, he shall be punished with death. For, when apprehended in such an offense, he shall immediately suffer capital punishment. May God preserve you, beloved brothers.

And when the emperor had written other, more rhetorical letters against Arius and those who agreed with him, he posted them everywhere in the individual cities.

### Victor Constantine, greatest Augustus, to bishops and peoples

[Col. 0506C–D] Arius, having imitated wicked and impious men, deserves to undergo the same dishonour as they. For just as Porphyry, the enemy of piety toward God, by composing certain unlawful treatises against religion, found a fitting reward—such that he should become disgraceful for time to come, be filled with the greatest ill repute, and have his impious writings obliterated—so it has now seemed good that Arius and those of like opinion with him should indeed be called Porphyrians, so that they may bear the designation of those whose ways they have imitated.

In addition, if any treatise composed by Arius is found, it is to be handed over to fire, so that not only the vile things in his teaching may disappear, but no memorial of him at all remain. I nevertheless proclaim beforehand that, if anyone is caught concealing a treatise composed by Arius and does not immediately bring it forward and consume it with fire, death shall be his penalty; for when he is seized in this matter, he shall immediately undergo punishment of the head. May God guard you, beloved brothers.

And the emperor, having written other letters in a more public and celebratory style against Arius and those who held the same doctrines, posted them everywhere, city by city.

## Letter of Constantine to the Church of Alexandria

(Councils, vol. II, p. 62, Labbe edition.)

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0507]

### Constantine Augustus to the catholic Church of the Alexandrians

[Col. 0508A] Greetings in abundance, most beloved brothers. It is indeed a very great and singular benefit bestowed upon us by divine providence that, having been freed from every error, we acknowledge one and the same faith. Certainly no place has henceforth been left for the devil’s snares directed against us; for whatever he plotted against us by deceit has been uprooted completely. The brilliance of truth, in accordance with Christ’s injunction, has utterly overwhelmed and destroyed dissensions of mind, schisms, those tumults, and the deadly poisons, so to speak, of discords. Therefore we all venerate one God in name and believe that he exists.

In order to bring this about, at God’s prompting I summoned a great multitude of bishops to the city of Nicaea. With them I also, who am one of your number and who rejoice greatly that I am your fellow servant, laboured that the truth might be carefully investigated. Accordingly, all matters which seemed capable of furnishing an occasion for controversy or dissension were carefully examined and debated. What great and execrable reproaches—O good God, be gracious and merciful to us!—did some men wickedly and impiously hurl against the great Saviour, against our hope and life, uttering with shamelessness things contrary to the divinely inspired Scriptures and to the most holy faith, and openly professing that they believed them!

For when more than three hundred bishops, men admirable for their moderation and intelligence, confessed with one voice one and the same faith—which is established as true faith by truth and by the exact testimonies of the divine law—Arius alone was found to have fallen away from it utterly, defeated by the power and deceit of the devil. Stirred by an impious impulse of mind, he first spread this stain of error among you and then among others.

Let us therefore embrace the doctrine which the Almighty has handed down. Let us return to our most beloved brothers, from whom some wicked and shameless minister of the devil has separated you. Let us return with all our heart, as the saying is, to the common body of the Church and to our genuine members. For it is especially consonant with your prudence, faith, and holiness that, once the error of him whom you have now recognized to be an enemy of truth has been entirely driven away, you should receive yourselves again into God’s grace.

For what has pleased three hundred bishops is nothing other than God’s judgment, especially since the Holy Spirit dwelt in the minds of men so great and distinguished and disclosed to them the divine will. Therefore let none of you hesitate, let none delay; rather, let all return willingly to the way of truth, so that, as soon as I come to you, I may render due thanks together with you to God, who rules all things, because he has revealed to us the sincere faith and has thereby restored the charity desirable for all. May God preserve you safe for a long time, most beloved brothers.

### Constantine Augustus to the catholic Church of the Alexandrians

[Col. 0507A] Greetings, beloved brothers. We have received complete grace from divine providence, so that, freed from every error, we may recognize one and the same faith. Nothing remains possible for the devil against us; everything whatever that he attempted by evil craft has been destroyed from its foundations. The splendour of truth, according to Christ’s command, has conquered dissensions, schisms, those tumults, and, so to speak, the deadly drugs of disagreements. Therefore we all worship one [God] in name and have believed him to exist.

To bring this about, at God’s prompting I summoned the greater number of bishops to the city of Nicaea. Together with them, I also—one of you, your fellow servant, rejoicing exceedingly to be so—undertook the examination of truth. Thus everything which seemed to generate an occasion for doubt or dissension was exposed and precisely examined. May the divine Majesty spare us! How great and dreadful were the unbecoming blasphemies uttered by some concerning the great Saviour, our hope and life, while they spoke and professed belief in things contrary to the divinely inspired Scriptures and to the holy faith!

When more than three hundred bishops, admired for moderation and intelligence, affirmed one and the same faith—the faith established as faith by truths and exact proofs from the divine law—Arius alone was found defeated by the devil’s activity. By impious judgment he scattered this evil first among you and then among others.

Let us therefore accept the judgment which the Almighty has bestowed. Let us return to our beloved brothers, from whom some shameless servant of the devil separated you. Let us go with all zeal to the common body and to our genuine members. For it accords with your intelligence, faith, and holiness that, after the error of him who has been shown to be an enemy of truth has been refuted, you should return to divine grace.

For what pleased the three hundred bishops is nothing other than God’s judgment, especially since the Holy Spirit, abiding in the minds of men so great and such as these, illuminated the divine will. Therefore let no one doubt, let no one delay; but return eagerly, all of you, to the truest path, so that when I come to you very shortly, I may acknowledge together with you the thanks due to God, who oversees all things, because, having displayed the sincere faith, he has restored to us the love for which we prayed. May God preserve you, beloved brothers.

## Letter of Constantine to Arius and the Arians

(Councils, vol. II, p. 269.)

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0509]

### Constantine Augustus to Arius and the Arians

[Col. 0509A]

## Constantine Augustus to Arius and the Arians

A bad interpreter is in truth a likeness and image of the devil. For just as skilled artists fashion him as a lure for deception, contriving for him, though by nature utterly foul, an appearance of beauty and comeliness, in order that he may destroy wretched mortals by setting error before them, so also, I think, does this man act, to whom this alone seems worthy of zeal: to pour forth without restraint upon all the poisonous drugs of his own insolence and audacity. Accordingly, he introduces a new faith of unbelief, never seen since human beings came into existence. Therefore that saying long ago set forth by the divine utterance does not seem at all remote from the truth: that they are wise for evil.

What else could one say of a man who has lost the faculty of deliberation, and no longer seeks to find any help toward relief? Why, then, O Christ, Christ! Lord, Lord! Why does this band of robbers wound us daily? A certain terrible and violent audacity stands opposed to us, roaring and gnashing its teeth, hideous through disgrace and wounded by innumerable accusations. In the law and the proclamation concerning your name, as though tossed by storms and threefold waves of evils, it belches forth destructive words; and, writing them, publishes those things which you—who coexist with the eternal Father, the source of your own being—never defined in your knowledge of yourself. It gathers together and heaps up altogether grievous and lawless impieties: now brandishing tongues, now again puffed up by the zeal of the wretched, whom it deceives and corrupts while they are present in false security.

But I now wish to examine the character of its leader. For what does he say? “Either let us retain what we have now obtained, or let it be as we ourselves wish.” “He has fallen—and fallen while being killed. Whether by deceit,” he says, “or by some terrible cunning of trickery, makes no difference.” He regards as important only that which, through wicked contrivance, has come upon him. “We have a multitude,” he says.

I too shall go a little farther forward, so that I may become a spectator of the wars of madness. I myself, I say, shall go forward—I who have been accustomed to stop the wars of the foolish. Come then, Ares—Arius—there is need of shields. Do not do this, I beg you; let intercourse with Aphrodite at least restrain you. Yet would that, just as you seem to be most loudly applauded by crowds, so you flourished in piety toward Christ.

Behold, I come again as a suppliant; although strong with every abundance of arms, I do not wish to fight. Armed with the faith of Christ, I wish both to heal you and to cure the others. Why, then, do you say that you do things which do not suit your character? But with what tranquillity, tell me—or surrounded by what resources, or rather, driven to what excess of recklessness? O audacity worthy to be struck down by thunderbolts! Hear what he recently declared to me in writing, his pen dripping poison: “Thus,” he says, “we believe.” Then, adding I know not what, elaborately and very precisely contrived in a luxurious manner, he advanced farther and omitted no bitterness; rather, as one might say, he opened the whole treasury of madness.

“We are driven out,” he says, “and every permission for our reception is taken away.” Yet these matters are still irrelevant. Attend to what follows; for I shall use his own words: “We request that, if the bishop of Alexandria remains of the same opinion, permission may henceforth be granted us, according to the ordinance of the law, to perform for God the lawful and necessary services.”

O dreadful shamelessness, which ought to have been refuted by zeal for truth! For what pleased him expressed itself in the brevity of the phrase. What do you say, absurd man? Do you devise to erect against us a seemingly respectable schism—the rotten ulcer of your savage mind against me—and do you hasten to destroy those entangled with you in evil? “What then,” you say, “am I to do if no one considers me worthy of reception?” For you often cry this from your impious throat. But I shall ask you the opposite: where have you displayed a clear mark and testimony of your own mind? You ought to have unfolded and made it clear both to things divine and to human beings, especially since venomous creeping creatures are naturally fiercer precisely when they perceive themselves hidden in the deepest recesses of their dens.

And indeed this is especially amusing in him: that he earnestly feigns silence as though under some mask of modesty. You publicly display yourself as gentle and tame, while inwardly full of countless evils and plots, and you deceive many. But, alas for the misery! As the Evil One wished, so he made Arius for us a workshop of lawlessness. Come now, tell me the evidence of your faith; do not be silent at all.

You who have a twisted mouth and a nature sharply inclined toward wickedness: do you say there is one God? You have me as a fellow-voter; think so. Do you say that his Word is without beginning and without end, being of his essence? I approve this; believe so. If you attach anything further, I reject it. If you add anything toward an impious separation, I confess that I neither see nor understand it. If you admit the foreign lodging of a body for the dispensation of divine operations, I do not reject it. If you say that the Spirit of eternity was begotten in the surpassing Word, I accept it. “Who has known the Father except he who came from the Father?” Whom has the Father known except him whom he has begotten from himself eternally and without beginning?

You think that a foreign hypostasis must be subordinated—certainly believing wrongly. But I recognize the fullness of the supreme and all-pervading power of Father and Son as one essence. If, therefore, you take away from him—from whom nothing could ever be separated, not even in the thought of contentious persons—and make room for marks of addition, and in general define signs for inquiries, in him to whom he gave from himself entire eternity, an incorruptible conception of immortality through himself, and the faith of the Church: cast down, then, cast down this foolish impiety, you clever and melodious man, chanting evils to the unbelief of the foolish. With good reason the Evil One has overthrown you by his own wickedness, and perhaps this seems pleasant to some; for thus you have persuaded yourself. But the evil is altogether destructive.

Come then, having departed from your occupation with absurdities, listen, wretched Arius; for I am speaking with you. Do you not perceive that you have been expelled from the Church of God? Know well that you have perished, unless, looking to yourself, you condemn the madness now present in you. But you will say that crowds cooperate with you and remove your anxieties. Listen then, bending your ears a little, impious Arius, and understand your own madness.

And you, O God, guardian of all, be propitious to what is said, if it contains faith. For I, your servant, relying upon divine providence, shall clearly demonstrate from Greek and Roman writings, and from very ancient ones, that the madness of Arius was foretold and prophesied by the Erythraean some three thousand years ago. For she said:

> Woe to you, Libya, situated in coastal regions; for a time will come upon you in which, together with your peoples and your daughters, you will be compelled to undergo a terrible, harsh, and altogether grievous contest. By this a criterion will be set for all, and the faith and piety of all will be judged. But you incline toward the final ruin; for you have dared to tear up the receptacle of heavenly flowers and rend it with a bite; indeed, you have defiled it with iron teeth.

What then, crafty man—of what land do you now confess yourself to be? Of that land, plainly. For I possess your letters, which you inscribed to me with the pen of madness, in which you say that the entire Libyan people votes with you, presumably for salvation. If you deny that these things are so, I call God to witness that I shall send to Alexandria the most ancient Erythraean copy, written in Greek, so that you may perish more swiftly.

Then are you sinless, you gallows-bearer? Then have you not plainly perished, wretched man, surrounded by so great an evil? We know, we know your undertaking. What care, what fear disturbs you, has not escaped us, unhappy and miserable man. O dullness of your mind! You do not restrain the disease and helplessness of your own soul, impious man; you pierce the truth with varied words. And, being such a man, you are not ashamed to blame us—now refuting us, as you imagine, now again admonishing us as surpassing us in faith and reasoning—he from whom, of course, the wretched desire to procure aid for themselves.

Indeed, one ought neither to associate with such a man nor to address him at all, unless someone supposes that in this man’s deceitful utterances the hope of right living lies concealed in verses. But this is not so—far from it. The truth is rather: O your folly, all of you who associate with him! What frenzy has compelled you to endure this man’s harsh speech and countenance?

But I shall now direct my argument against you yourself: you who are foolish in soul, garrulous in tongue, and faithless in mind. Give me for discourse not a broad and chariot-roaded plain, but one well bounded by a circle—not a rotten one, but one naturally strong and solid, O impious, utterly evil, and deceitful man. I am driven to say these things; rather, having placed a noose around you and hampered you by argument, I shall set you before the public, so that all the people may observe your depravity.

But I shall proceed to the matter itself. The hands have surely been washed; let us proceed to invoke God in prayer—or rather, wait a little. Tell me, most ardent man, what God will you invoke for your aid? Yet I cannot remain calm.

O Lord possessing authority over all, O Father of solitary power: because of this impious man your Church suffers reproaches, griefs, indeed wounds and pains. Arius now assigns you a place—and very ingeniously—upon which, establishing, as I think, a synod for himself, he claims and holds as an adopted son, by a law of appointment, your Christ, the one from you, the leader of our aid. Hear, I beseech you, this remarkable faith. He thinks that you, Lord, are moved according to place; he dares to circumscribe you within the boundaries of a limited seat. For where is your presence not? Or where do not all perceive your operation through your laws that pervade all things? For you yourself contain all things, and outside you it is not lawful to conceive either place or anything else. Thus your power, together with its operation, is infinite.

You, O God, hear; and all you people, attend in mind. For this shameless and worthless man, who has advanced equally to the furthest point of wickedness and lawlessness, pretends piety. “Away with it,” he says, “I do not wish God to appear subject to the experience of insults.” And for this reason he posits and invents, wonderful in faith, that God, when he made the newly generated and newly created substance of Christ, prepared aid for himself, as it seems to me. “For whatever,” he says, “you take from him, you have made less.”

Then is this your faith, destroyer and pest? Do you take as a hypothesis and fabrication him who condemned the fabrications of the nations? Do you call as an intruder and, as it were, a servant of functions, him who, without thought or calculation, because he coexists with the eternity of the Father, has accomplished all things? Apply now, if you dare, apply to God caution, fear, and hope of what will occur; and further, thought, calculation, the forming and articulating of a considered judgment; and indeed pleasure, laughter, and sorrow.

What, then, do you say, most miserable of all miserable men? O consummate contriver of wickedness, understand, if you can, that in your very own cunning you will be consumed as an evil man. “Christ,” he says, “suffered for us.” But I have already said in advance that he was sent in bodily form. “Yes,” he says, “but there is danger lest we appear to diminish him in some respect.” Then, interpreter of beasts, when you say this, are you not mad and plainly raging?

For behold, the world is a form or figure, and the stars display their marks; and indeed the spirit of this spherical circuit is a kind of form of existing things, as though an image. Yet God is present everywhere. Where, then, are insults in God? Or in what respect is God diminished? You murderer of equity! Reason from yourself and consider whether it seems a sin for God to be present in Christ. He saw the dishonor of the saying and did not delay in inflicting punishment.

Besides these things, sins occur in the world every day; yet God is present, and the penalties of judgment are not delayed. In what, then, is the greatness of his power diminished if he is present everywhere? In nothing, I think. For the mind of the world is through God; through him is all continuance, through him all judgment. But the faith of Christ is from him without beginning. In every respect Christ is the law of God, having through him both infinity and endlessness.

But you seem to reason according to yourself. O extraordinary madness! Turn now the sword of the devil to your own destruction. See, all of you, see how he now puts forward mournful cries, having been wounded by the bite of the viper; how his veins and flesh, seized by venom, mingle terrible pains; how his whole body has wasted away, emaciated and full of squalor, filth, lamentation, pallor, horror, and countless evils, and has become dreadfully dried up; how hideous and filthy is the thicket of his hair; how he is wholly half-dead, with sight already failing, face bloodless, and consumed by anxiety; how all things that have run together upon him—frenzy, madness, and vanity—have, through the duration of the suffering, made him savage and beastlike.

At once, not even perceiving in what evil he is, he says, “I am lifted up with pleasure; I leap and skip with joy, and take wing.” And again, very youthfully: “Well then,” he says, “we have perished.” This indeed is true; for to you alone wickedness has lavishly provided its own pursuits, and what it bought at a great price it has most easily given you. Come now, tell us where your solemn commandments are. Wash yourself in the Nile, if possible, man full of extraordinary insensibility. Yet you have zealously sought to disturb the whole inhabited world by your impieties.

Do you understand that I, the servant of God, already know everything? But I am uncertain whether I ought to remain or depart. For I can no longer endure even to look upon such things, and I am ashamed for the sin, Arius. You have placed us in the light, but cast yourself into darkness, wretched man. This has appeared as the end of your labors.

But I return again to that matter. You say that there is a multitude of those wandering around you. It is likely, I think; receive them, receive them, I say, for they have given themselves up to be devoured by wolves and lions. Yet every one of them, burdened with an addition of ten heads and with their consequences, will soon sweat, unless, running as quickly as possible to the saving Church, he receives again the peace of love through the affection of concord.

For those condemned by an evil conscience will no longer be deceived by you; nor will they endure to perish utterly, entangled in your polluted inquiries. For hereafter your sophistries will be clear and known to all. Nor will you yourself accomplish anything; you will vainly feign, pretending fairness and mildness of speech and outwardly putting on, as it were, the mask of simplicity. Your entire artifice will be vain; for truth will soon surround you, and the shower of divine power will soon extinguish your flames, so to speak.

Moreover, the cares of public services will seize your companions and fellow-minded associates, who have made themselves liable to the council, unless they swiftly flee association with you and exchange it for incorruptible faith. But you, iron-minded man, give me some proof of your purpose, if you trust yourself, are strong in the firmness of faith, and possess a wholly pure conscience. Come to me; come, I say, to the servant of God. Believe that by my questions I shall investigate the secrets of your heart. And if anything mad appears to remain in you, invoking divine grace, I shall heal you more effectively from the bite. But if you appear sound in soul, having recognized the light of truth, I shall give thanks to God for you and rejoice with myself because of piety.

—And in another hand: May God preserve us, beloved ones.

These things were conveyed through the magistriani Syncletius and Gaudentius, when Paterius was prefect of Egypt, and were read in the palace.

## Letter of Constantine to the Nicomedians, against Eusebius and Theognis

(Conc. vol. II, p. 277, ed. Lab.)  
[Note: [Col. 0519] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0519]

Constantine Augustus to the Catholic Church of the Nicomedians.

[Col. 0520A]

You all know accurately, beloved brethren, that the Lord God and Savior Christ is Father and Son: Father, I say, without beginning and without end, the begetter of the age itself; Son, that is, the will of the Father, which was neither assumed through some act of thought nor acquired for the completion of his works through some externally sought substance. Whoever understands—or will understand—this will possess tireless endurance for every kind of punishment.

But Christ, the Son of God, the creator of all things and giver of immortality itself, was begotten, insofar as this pertains to the faith in which we have believed; he was begotten—or rather, himself proceeded forth—while always being in the Father, for the ordering of the things made by him. Therefore he was begotten by an indivisible procession. For the will, being at once fixed in its dwelling-place, acts upon and administers those things which require diverse care, according to the quality of each.

What then is there? What is between God the Father and the Son? Nothing, plainly. For this completion of things has received through perception the command of the will; it has not, being divided from the Father’s essence, separated the will. And what follows from these things: who is there that fears Christ, the Son of my Lord, more from reverence than from folly? Does the divine then suffer when the dwelling of the august body hastens toward the knowledge of its own holiness? Or does what is separated from the body fall under touch? Has not that which is removed from the body’s lowliness been separated? Or do we not live, even if the glory of the soul summons the body toward death?

What, then, has innocent and sincere faith here encountered that is worthy of doubt? Do you not see that God chose a more august body, through which he intended to display proofs of faith and examples of his own power; to shake off the already confused and destructive error—the ruin of the human race; to give a new teaching of religion as a remedy for ignorance; to cleanse the unworthy acts of the mind; then to loosen the torment of death and proclaim beforehand the rewards of immortality?

But you, whom the fellowship of love rightly causes me henceforth to call brothers—you know that I am your fellow-servant; you know the bulwark of your salvation, the care of which I have sincerely undertaken, and through which we have not only overcome the arms of our enemies but have also compelled them, while still alive, to confess the true faith of humanity. I rejoiced in these blessings especially because of the renewal of the inhabited world. For it was indeed truly worthy of wonder to bring so many nations into concord and agreement, nations which a short time before were said not to know God.

Yet how were those nations to know things which they had undertaken no care to understand without contentiousness? What, then, do you think, beloved brethren? That I accuse us ourselves? We are Christians, and we disagree with a pitiable disposition. Is this our faith? Is this the teaching of the most holy law? What, then, is the cause for which the destruction of the present evil has been stirred up? O absurdity! O excess of hatred surpassing the magnitude of every indignation! What atrocity has been revealed in this band of robbers? Does it deny that the Son of God proceeded from the indivisible essence of the Father?

Is not God everywhere? And yet we perceive him always to be present with us. Has not the order of the universe been established through his power and been deprived of the dissension of separation? Therefore, beloved brethren, consider now, I ask, the tests of this present grief, lest something has been done by us. You promise that you will be confessors of him whom you deny to exist, because the utterly destructive teacher persuades you. I beseech you: who has taught such things to so innocent a multitude? Eusebius, plainly—the fellow initiate of tyrannical cruelty.

For it can be seen from every direction that he was everywhere a watchman for the tyrant. The slaughter of bishops—of true bishops—testifies to this; the most grievous persecution of Christians proclaims it openly. I shall say nothing now concerning the insults done to me, through which he arranged as far as possible the attacks of the opposing party. He sent out eyes as spies against me and all but supplied the tyrant with armed services. Let no one suppose that I am unprepared to prove these things. For there is exact proof that I openly apprehended the presbyters and deacons who attended Eusebius.

But I pass over these matters. I have introduced them now not out of indignation but for their shame. I fear only this; I reflect only upon this: that I see you being summoned to share in the accusation. For through Eusebius’s training and perversion you have received a conscience estranged from truth. Yet the remedy is not slow, if, now at least, having obtained a faithful and upright bishop, you look again toward God. This is now within your power; indeed, it should long ago have depended upon your judgment, if the aforesaid Eusebius had not rashly rushed here with the wicked counsel of those who helped him and shamelessly disturbed the right order.

But since I ought to say a few words to your love concerning Eusebius himself, your forbearance remembers that a council was held in the city of Nicaea.
