I myself attended it, in accordance with the service required by my conscience, desiring nothing other than to produce concord among all and, above all, to refute and cast off this matter which took its beginning through the madness of Arius of Alexandria and was immediately strengthened through Eusebius’s absurd and destructive zeal.

With what eagerness, most beloved and honored brethren, do you suppose this Eusebius—convicted by his own conscience—set about, and with what shame, exposed on every side by proven lying, first sending various persons to me to plead on his behalf, then seeking aid from me, lest, convicted of such great wrongdoing, he should be cast out from the honor he possessed? God himself is my witness in this—may he continue favorably disposed toward me and toward you—that Eusebius perverted my judgment and shamefully drew me away from the truth, as you also will recognize.

For everything was then done as he desired, while he concealed every evil whatsoever in his own mind. But lately—passing over the other deeds of his perversity—hear, I beseech you, what he has done with Theognis, whom he has as a partner in madness. I had ordered that certain Alexandrians who had withdrawn from our faith be sent here, since through their service the torch of discord had been raised. But these excellent and good bishops, whom the truth of the council had once reserved for repentance, not only received those men and secured them with themselves, but also shared with them their depravity of character.

For this reason I decided to act thus toward these ungrateful men: I ordered that they be seized and exiled as far away as possible. It is now yours to look toward God in that faith in which it is fitting that you have always existed, continue, and remain, and to act accordingly. Thus we rejoice when we have bishops who are pure, orthodox, and humane. If anyone should rashly dare to become inflamed either in memory or praise of those destroyers, he shall immediately be restrained for his audacity through the agency of God’s servant—that is, myself.

May God preserve you, beloved brethren.

## Letter to Theodotus

(Conc. vol. II, p. 283, ed. Lab.)  
[Note: [Col. 0523] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0523]

Victor Constantine Augustus to Theodotus.

[Col. 0524B]

How great is the force of divine wrath, you too may easily learn from what Eusebius and Theognis have suffered. In raging against the most holy religion, they polluted the name of God the Savior with the company of their own band of robbers even after receiving pardon. For precisely when, after the like-minded agreement of the council, they ought to have corrected their former error, they were found persisting in the same absurdities.

For this reason divine providence expelled them from its own people, since it could not bear to see innocent souls corrupted, however little, by that madness. And now it has exacted from them deserved punishment; greater punishment it will exact thereafter throughout the whole age. I considered that this should be made known to your prudence, so that if any evil exhortation from such persons—though I do not think so—has seated itself in your purpose, you may remove it from your soul and zealously offer to God the Savior a pure mind, sincere consecration, and undefiled faith, as is fitting. For this is appropriate to one who determines to be considered worthy of the incorruptible rewards of eternal life.

May God preserve you, beloved brother.

## Letter of Constantine to Macarius

(Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, III.30–32.) On the construction of the martyrion of our Savior.  
[Note: [Col. 0524] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0524]

Victor Constantine, Greatest Augustus, to Macarius.

[Col. 0524C]

I. So great is the grace of our Savior that no abundance of speech seems sufficient for the account of the present miracle. For that memorial of his most sacred passion, hidden long ago beneath the earth and concealed through the course of so many years, should shine forth after the removal of the common enemy of all and the liberation of his servants, surpasses every wonder in truth.

For even if all those considered wise throughout the whole world were gathered together and undertook to say something worthy of this matter, they seem to me unable even to approach its smallest part. The credibility of this miracle exceeds every capacity of human reasoning by as much as divine things surpass human things. Therefore this is always my one and principal aim: that, just as the faith of truth becomes illustrious through new miracles every day, so also the minds of us all may be stirred to observe the most holy law with every modesty and harmonious eagerness.

Since I trust that this is wholly evident to all, I especially wish you to be persuaded of this: nothing is more important to me than that we adorn with the beauty of buildings that sacred place which, by God’s command, I have relieved of the most shameful addition of an image, as though of a heavy burden; which was holy from the beginning by God’s judgment, but was made much holier when it brought to light the proof of the Lord’s passion.

[Note: [Col. 0523D]

“Not even one remedy of words.” In Socrates, Theodoret, and Nicephorus one reads “an abundance of words,” which I think is more correct.]

By the destruction of the common enemy of all. Here Constantine calls Licinius the public enemy; after whose death, he says, the sacred sepulchre of the Lord, which had previously lain hidden, came forth into the light and the sight of men [Col. 0524D]. Licinius was killed in the year of Christ 326, as is written in the Chronicle of Idatius. In the same year, when Helena arrived at Jerusalem, the Lord’s sepulchre was discovered. One might also understand the devil here by “public enemy,” were it not that the words which follow oppose this. For the devil was not only then conquered and crushed, when the Lord’s sepulchre was uncovered after the debris had been cleared away [Col. 0525C]. Add that ἀναίρεσις—that is, “slaying”—is more aptly said of Licinius than of the devil.

“By so great an extent, the whole …” I think it should be written, ἐπεὶ τοσούτῳ [Col. 0525D] πᾶσαν, etc. In the Fuk. manuscript it is written ἐπὶ τοσοῦτο γὰρ, etc.

“Which, then …” This passage has been corrected from Socrates and Theodoret.]

I. So great is the grace of our Saviour that no ministry of words seems adequate to the present miracle. For the token of that most holy Passion, long concealed beneath the earth, having remained hidden through so many cycles of years until, after the destruction of the common enemy of all [Col. 0523D], it was destined to shine forth when His servants had been set free [Col. 0526A]—this truly surpasses every astonishment. For if all those who are thought to be wise throughout the whole inhabited world came together into one and the same place and wished to say something worthy of the matter, they would not be able even to approach its smallest part. To such an extent does this miracle transcend every nature capable of human reasoning, by as much as heavenly things are established more powerfully than human things.

For this reason, then, this has always been my first and only aim: that, just as the faith of truth daily displays itself through ever-newer miracles, so also the souls of us all may become more earnest concerning the holy law, with every temperate virtue and harmonious zeal. Since I think this is evident to all, I especially wish you to be persuaded of this: that above all things I am concerned that we adorn with the beauty of buildings that sacred place which, by God’s command, I relieved of the foulest additions of an idol, as though of some weight lying upon it; a place made holy from the beginning by God’s judgment [Col. 0526B], but shown to be holier still from the time when it brought the faith of the saving Passion into the light.

That he wished this church to surpass other churches in the beauty of its walls, columns, and marbles.

[Col. 0525]

[Col. 0525B] II. It is therefore fitting for your sagacity to make such arrangements and provision for every necessary thing that not only may the basilica itself be more beautiful than all those anywhere, but its remaining parts also may be such that all the finest structures in each city are surpassed by this building. Concerning the erection and adornment of the walls, know that I have entrusted the care of it to our friend Dracilianus, who is acting in the place of the praetorian prefects, and to the governor of the province. For my Piety has ordered that craftsmen, workmen [Col. 0525C], and everything else which your sagacity may learn to be needed for the construction, be sent at once through their care.

But concerning the columns and marbles, whatever you may judge more precious and more useful, once a design itself has been made, take care to write to us, so that, once we have learned from your letter how many and of what kind are required, these may be brought together from every quarter. For it is proper that the place most admirable beyond all places in the whole world should be adorned in a manner worthy of its dignity.

[Note: [Col. 0525D]

“Dracilianus, who administers the regions of the provinces.” This passage too must be corrected from Socrates, Theodoret, and Nicephorus as follows: τὰ τῶν λαμπροτάτων ἐπάρχων μέρη: “the functions of the most distinguished praetorian prefects.” There are certainly two laws of Constantine in the Theodosian Code, one under the title *On Interest*, the other *On Heretics*, addressed to this Dracilianus. The former bears this superscription: “Emperor Constantine Augustus to Dracilianus, acting in the place of the Praetorian Prefects.” It was promulgated at Caesarea in Palestine on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus. The latter is said to have been promulgated on the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Generastus, Constantine Augustus for the seventh time, and Constantius Caesar—that is, in the year of Christ 326. In the same year Constantine wrote this letter to Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem [Col. 0526C].

Furthermore, it should be noted that the praetorian prefects are here called *clarissimi* (“most distinguished”). They had not yet received the rank of *illustrissimi* (“most illustrious”). In other laws of Constantine as well [Col. 0526D], as is found in these books, praetorian prefects are called *clarissimi*. Moreover, just as the praetorian prefects were only *clarissimi* in Constantine’s age, so the vicars of the praetorian prefecture were only *perfectissimi* (“most excellent”) in Constantine’s time, as the Letter to Probianus, proconsul of Africa, shows. In Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, p. 794: “To Antoninus, *biarchus*, centenarius of the most distinguished prefects of the sacred praetorium.”

“Once a plan has been made.” In this passage σύνοψις means the plan and delineation of the future building. It is used in the same sense in the letter of Himerius, *rationalis* of Alexandria, to the prefect of Mareotis, reported by Athanasius in the *Apology*, p. 803. After saying that Augustus and the Caesars had allowed Ischyras to build a church in his village, he orders the official in charge of that village to draw up the plan of the future work as soon as possible and send it to his office: “Take care, therefore, to prepare the plan promptly and submit it to the office.”]

[Col. 0526B] II. It is fitting, therefore, for your sagacity to arrange matters in this way and to make provision for each necessity: that not only may the basilica be superior to all those everywhere, but that its other parts too may be such that everything finest in each city is surpassed by this building. As for the raising and ornamentation of the walls, know that the responsibility has been entrusted by us to our friend Dracilianus, who administers the functions of the provincial prefects, and to the governor of the province. For my Piety has ordered that craftsmen and workers [Col. 0526C], and all things which your sagacity might ascertain to be necessary for construction, be dispatched at once through their care. But concerning columns or marbles, whatever you may judge to be more valuable and more useful, once a plan itself has been made, make haste to write to us, so that, once we learn from your letter how many and what sort are needed, these may be brought from every quarter.

That Macarius should write to the governors concerning the beauty of the ceiling, the artisans, and the materials.

[Col. 0527]

[Col. 0528A] III. Further, I wish to learn from you whether you think the ceiling of the basilica should be coffered, or made by some other kind of workmanship. For if it is to be coffered, it may also be ornamented with gold. It remains for Your Holiness to make known as swiftly as possible to the aforementioned officials how many workmen, craftsmen, and expenditures will be needed; and to make a prompt report to me, not only concerning the marbles and columns, but also concerning the coffering, if you judge this work to be more beautiful. May God preserve you, beloved brother.

[Note: [Col. 0527D]

“The ceiling of the basilica: whether it should be *lacunar* …” The ceilings of basilicas were generally arranged in two ways. They were either adorned with coffering or decorated in mosaic work. Constantine’s passage testifies to coffering; Procopius, in Book I of *The Buildings of Justinian*, testifies to mosaic work, where he describes the church of Holy Wisdom.

Coffering, moreover, was customarily ornamented in two ways: it was either gilded or painted. The latter practice was first introduced by Pausias, of whom Pliny writes in Book 35, chapter 11: “He was also the first to introduce painted ceilings; before him it had not been customary for ceilings to be decorated in this fashion.” Isidore, in Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, says: “*Laquearia* are those things that cover and adorn a ceiling; they are also called *lacunaria*, because they have certain square or round compartments painted in wood, plaster, or colours, with figures gleaming between them” [Col. 0528D]. Salmasius unjustly criticizes this passage of Isidore in his notes on Flavius Vopiscus, p. 303, where he denies that coffering was ever placed beneath vaulted ceilings. Yet Pliny expressly affirms the same thing, as does Constantine in this letter. The ancient author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, Question 106: “For it belongs to the adornment of a house if its ceiling has coffering marked out in gold,” etc.

“May be ornamented. What remains …” Here I have followed the punctuation of Theodoret and Nicephorus, who place a full stop after καλλωπισθῆναι, “may be ornamented.” All translators before us did likewise, except Musculus. But if anyone prefers to place the punctuation after λειπόμενον, “what remains,” then it should read πλὴν ἡ σὴ ὁσιότης, etc., as in the manuscripts of Fuket and Savile.]

[Col. 0527A] III. As for the ceiling of the basilica, whether you think it should be coffered or made by some other form of workmanship, I wish to learn from you. For if it is to be coffered, it can also be adorned with gold. What remains is that Your Holiness shall quickly make known to the aforementioned officials how many workmen, craftsmen, and expenditures are required; and shall hasten to report directly to me, not only concerning the marbles and columns, but also concerning the coffering, if indeed this should be judged more beautiful. May God preserve you, beloved brother.

NOTICE ON THE LETTERS OF HELENA AND CONSTANTINE.

[Col. 0527]

[Col. 0527A] The Acts of St Sylvester in Greek occur in two Nannian manuscripts, insofar as I find this noted by Bonjoanni [Col. 0527B]. In one of them, marked G, no. XVII, the above-mentioned letters occur only on p. 8. A later hand added the title found here, p. 120, and stated that they had been drawn from Eusebius’s *Life of Pope St Sylvester and Constantine the Great*. Indeed, Acts of Sylvester attributed to Eusebius circulate widely in Latin editions—for example, in Mombritius, Lipomano, and Surius—besides others derived from Metaphrastes. Combefis also reproduces from the Acts he edited in the *Bibliotheca Concionatoria* a certain portion of the disputation held by St Sylvester with the Jew Zambre, in Constantine’s presence, against those same Jews; and he does so as if from its primary and ancient Acts, published from the Mazarin manuscript.

Nevertheless, the decree of Pope Gelasius leaves us no room to doubt that such Acts are spurious and wrongly attributed to Eusebius [Col. 0527C]: “Acts of Sylvester, written by an uncertain author,” as Baronius also notes in the *Martyrology* under 31 December. Yet it does not seem necessary to deny that in that work, however supposititious—and it is very ancient—some true material may be found because of the antiquity of its author. He could have mixed truth with falsehood, received either from rumour or from reliable records, in order to lend credibility and force to his wares. This appears to be why Pope Hadrian I and certain other writers of the seventh and eighth centuries drew authority from it, and why some churches, reverencing ancient custom, made use of it.

When Nicephorus deals with Constantine, he repeatedly reports matters which, if they were true and genuine, would lend full authority to our fragments [Col. 0527D]: namely, that letters passed back and forth between Helena [Col. 0528A] and her son Constantine; that the emperor suffered from a most severe illness; [Col. 0528B] and that he ordered circumcised men to assemble at Rome to dispute before him concerning religion. But Nicephorus drew these matters, in his usual manner, from those adulterated Acts. Therefore, since Nicephorus burdened his history with every kind of rubbish, in the judgment of Casaubon and Cave, nothing of weight can be added from the credit of that man to establish the genuineness of these documents.

Only this may lend some slight support: Eusebius wrote that Constantine made his mother Helena, who had previously been by no means imbued with piety, very devout. From this it is not implausible that she might at some time have been deceived by Jewish calumnies. Add that those worn-out men do indeed everywhere blaspheme in their pandects that our Christ was punished by crucifixion because of evil deeds. Then again [Col. 0528C], since the more genuine Acts of Sylvester extant so far, whether printed or handwritten, either contain those letters or at least relate the very matter contained in them, one can scarcely be persuaded that that ancient writer—the first originator of the Acts themselves—fabricated the whole story by his own invention. He must certainly have lived not very far removed from Constantine’s own age, as the decree of Gelasius sufficiently suggests.

If, therefore, any credit is due to such conjectures in support of the genuineness (γνησιότης) of these letters, we may also determine their date. For it appears that they were written during the early years of Constantine’s reign. Yet we have not been so concerned about the authenticity of these documents that, whatever they may ultimately be held to be, we should allow them to perish altogether [Col. 0528D].

LETTER OF HELENA TO CONSTANTINE.

(*Bibliotheca Gallica*, vol. XIV, Appendix, p. 120.) [Note: [Col. 0529] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0529]

Helena, eternal Augusta, to Constantine her son, victor, triumphator, eternal Augustus.

[Col. 0529A]

Wise reason does not reject truth, nor can right faith ever suffer loss. Therefore, the divine goodness must be credited with your having been deemed worthy to withdraw from the vanity of idols; but error must be blamed for your having believed Jesus of Nazareth to be the true God, and him to be the Son of God in heaven. Though he was a Jew, condemned for magical practices, and sentenced to the punishment of the cross, he died.

Health was granted to your piety for this reason: because you were the first among emperors to renounce idols. For the true and eternal God, wishing to show that those whom you renounced are in no way true gods, granted you health, so that, laying aside every fear of idols, you might know that when appeased they can neither give health nor, when angered, take it away. Illness left your piety when it abandoned the error of this superstition. But now, as you return to Almighty God, a power incapable of ever being overcome will overtake you. Once you begin to worship it, you will gain mastery over the kingdom of David and of most wise Solomon. For the prophets to whom God spoke will be with you, and whatever you ask through them you will receive. Farewell, venerable lord, eternal Augustus, most honoured son, flourishing in happy outcomes.

Having received and read his mother’s letter, Emperor Constantine, fully understanding the cunning of the Jews that sought to deceive [Col. 0529C] his mother, replied in writing in these words.

Helena, eternal Augusta, to Constantine her son, victor, triumphator, eternal Augustus.

[Col. 0530A]

Wise reason does not reject truth, nor can right faith ever suffer any loss. Therefore, divine loving-kindness must be credited with your having been deemed worthy to depart from the vanity of idols; but error must be charged with your having believed Jesus the Nazarene to be the true God, and him to be the Son of God in heaven. Though he became a Jew, was condemned for magical practices, and condemned by sentence to the cross, he died.

Health was granted to your piety for this reason: because you were the first among rulers to renounce idols. For the true and eternal God, wishing to show that those whom you denied are not true gods, granted [Col. 0530B] you health, so that, putting aside all fear of idols, you might be able to know that, when propitiated, they cannot grant health, nor, when made hostile, take it away. Illness left your piety when it abandoned the error of this superstition. But now, as you return to Almighty God, power, which can never be overcome, will come upon you. Having begun to worship it, you will become master of David’s kingdom and of that of most wise Solomon. For the prophets to whom God spoke will be with you, and whatever you ask through them, you will receive. Farewell, venerable lord, eternal Augustus, most honoured son, flourishing in auspicious outcomes.

Therefore Emperor Constantine, having received his mother’s letter, read it, and learned precisely the perversity of the Jews in deceiving [Col. 0530C] his mother, wrote this reply, in the following form.

CONSTANTINE’S REPLY TO HELENA.

(From the same source.) [Note: [Col. 0529] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0529]

Constantine, eternal Augustus, son, to his lady and mother, Helena, eternal Augusta.

[Col. 0529C]

God, who presides over all ages, governs, rules, and gives life to us all. By his power he supplies life and breath to all; but he has deigned to command rulers to distribute justice to humankind. The higher, therefore, the place we hold among human beings, the greater are the expectations of human beings that we receive. Accordingly, the eyes of all people, the minds of all people, and the purposes of all people desire what seems good to us and reject what we do not wish.

For this reason, eternal lady and Augusta, our will ought to be not only beyond reproach but also praiseworthy; indeed, nothing at all ought to be honourable that we do [Col. 0529D] not will. But the things which I have mentioned lie within our administration; to comprehend God lies beyond our understanding.

Therefore let the boldness of our presumption be idle. Rather, let the overseers of the Jews come together in our presence and dispute among themselves concerning these matters, so that by their arguments and reasonings we may be able to recognize the clarity and truth of right faith. Thus from the holy Scriptures they will be able to assure both themselves and us concerning the truth, and exhort the whole world [Col. 0532A] to right and firm faith. Farewell, lady and mother, eternal Augusta, flourishing in happy outcomes.

Lady and mother, Helena, eternal Augusta: Constantine, eternal Augustus, son.

[Col. 0530C]

God, who presides over all ages, governs, rules, and gives life to us all: by his own power he gives life and breath to all, but has deigned to command rulers to apportion justice to humankind. Therefore, by as much as we hold a higher place among human beings, by so much do we receive the expectations of human beings. Accordingly, the eyes of all people, the minds of all people, and the intentions of all people desire what appears good to us and cast off what is unwelcome to us. For this reason, eternal lady and Augusta, our will ought to be not only irreproachable but praiseworthy; and truly nothing ought to be honourable that [Col. 0530D] we do not will. But the matters which I have stated lie in our own administration; to understand God is beyond our understanding.

Therefore let the boldness of our self-will cease; rather, let the overseers of the Jews come together, while we listen, and dispute with one another concerning these matters, so that by their justifications we may be able to recognize the clear and true character of right faith. Thus, from the holy Scriptures, they will be able to assure both themselves and us concerning the truth, and exhort the whole [Col. 0531A] world to right and steadfast faith. Farewell, lady and mother, eternal Augusta, flourishing in auspicious outcomes.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 330. LETTER OF CONSTANTINE TO THE BISHOPS OF NUMIDIA.

(*Councils*, vol. I, col. 1472, Cologne edition.) Concerning a basilica taken from the Catholics.

[Col. 0531]

[Col. 0531A] Since it is evident that the will of the supreme God, author and father of this world—by whose favour we enjoy life, behold heaven, and delight also in human society—is that the whole human race should agree in common and be united by an affection of fellowship, as though by mutual embraces, there is no doubt that heresies and schism have proceeded from the devil, who is the head of wickedness [Col. 0531B]. Therefore there is no doubt that whatever is done by heretics is done at his prompting, since he possesses their judgments, minds, and thoughts. For, having brought people of this sort under his power, he rules them altogether.

But what good can one insane, faithless, irreligious, profane, opposed to God, and hostile to the holy Church accomplish—one who, departing from the holy, true, just, supreme God, Lord of all, who created us and brought us into this light, who gave the spirit for the life we enjoy, and who made us what he willed us to be, and accomplished all things by his will—rushes headlong in error into the devil’s party? But because a mind once possessed by evil must necessarily devote itself to the works of its teacher and perform things which seem contrary to equity and justice, those possessed by the devil comply with his falsehood and wickedness [Col. 0531C].

It is no wonder, moreover, that wicked persons depart from the good. For the proverb rightly says that like gather with like. Those infected by the evil of an impious mind must dissent from our fellowship. For, as Scripture says, an evil person brings evil things out of an evil treasury, while a good person brings good from a good one. But since, as has been said, heretics and schismatics, abandoning good and pursuing evil, do things displeasing to God and are approved to cling to the devil, their father, your gravity acts most rightly and wisely: by refraining from their perverse disputes in accordance with the holy precept of faith, and by relinquishing to them what they strive to usurp as though it were theirs, though it is neither owed nor belongs to them [Col. 0531D]. Otherwise, such is their malicious and faithless perversity that they might burst forth even into seditions, stirring up among crowds and assemblies others like themselves; and something might thus arise which should not need to be calmed.

For their criminal purpose always seeks to accomplish the devil’s works. Therefore, when God’s priests conquer them through patience, together with their very father, those who worship the supreme God gain glory for themselves, while the others gain condemnation and deserved punishments. For the judgment of the supreme God becomes greater and more just in this: that he bears them with equanimity and condemns them by patience, enduring all that proceeds from them. For God promised himself as the avenger of all. And therefore, when vengeance is left to God, punishment is exacted more severely from enemies.

I have learned that you, servants and priests [Col. 0532A] of God, have now gladly done this; and I have greatly rejoiced that you seek no vengeance upon impious and criminal, sacrilegious and profane, faithless and irreligious persons, ungrateful to God and hostile to the Church, but ask instead that they themselves should receive pardon. This is truly and fully to know God; this is to follow his precepts; this is to believe happily; this is to think rightly; this is to know that a greater vengeance is called down upon the adversaries of the Church when they are spared in this world.

Having therefore received the letter of your wisdom and gravity, I learned that heretics or schismatics, in their customary wickedness, thought to seize the basilica of the Catholic Church which I had ordered to be built in the city of Constantina; and that although frequently warned, both by us and by judges at our command, they refused to surrender what was not theirs. But you, imitators of the patience of the supreme God, have with tranquil minds yielded what is yours to their malice, and instead requested for yourselves another site—namely, one belonging to the fisc. I have gladly embraced this petition in accordance with my established practice, and immediately gave instructions to the *rationalis* concerned to transfer a building of our estates, with all its rights [Col. 0532C], to the property of the Catholic Church, which I have granted with ready liberality, and ordered to be handed over to you at once.

I have nevertheless ordered a basilica to be erected at public expense on that site, and have commanded that the consular governor of Numidia also be written to, so that he himself may assist Your Holiness in every respect in the construction of that Church. I have decreed that readers of the Catholic Church, subdeacons, and others who, through the instigation of the persons mentioned, have for certain reasons been summoned to compulsory public services or to the decurionate, are not, in accordance with the provision of my law, to be summoned to any public duty. We have also ordered that those who were drawn in by the instigation of the heretics be released immediately from burdensome obligations. Moreover, I have ordered that my law concerning Catholic ecclesiastics be observed henceforth. All these matters have been set forth in the testimony of this letter, so that they may be known openly to your patience [Col. 0532D].

And would that heretics or schismatics might at last sometime provide for their own salvation; that, their darkness wiped away, they might open their eyes to the sight of the true light; that they might depart from the devil and, even late, flee to God, who is one and true, the judge of all. But since it is plain that they wish to remain in their wickedness and die in their crimes, our warning and the earlier constant exhortation are sufficient for them. For if they had obeyed our commands, they would be freed from every evil. We, however, brothers, should follow what pertains to us, persist in the commands, observe the divine precepts, and, defending our life against errors by good deeds, direct it along the straight path through the favour of God’s mercy.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 332. LETTER OF CONSTANTINE TO THE ANTIOCHENES.

(Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book III, ch. 60.) The emperor exhorts the people of Antioch not to remove Eusebius from the episcopal see of Caesarea. [Note: [Col. 0533] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0533]

Constantine the Victorious, Greatest Augustus, to the people of Antioch.

[Col. 0533A]

How welcome and delightful to all prudent and wise men of this age is your concord! I have certainly resolved, brothers, to embrace you with everlasting goodwill, prompted alike by your religious profession, your manner of life, and your zeal and favour. This is surely the true fruit of good things: to conduct everything with a sound mind and prudent counsel. For what could be more fitting for you?

Do not be surprised, therefore, if I say that the faith of truth has been for you a cause of salvation rather than of hatred. Certainly, among brothers whom one and the same disposition of soul, and a course along the straight and just path, promises, under God’s guidance, to enrol in a pure and holy dwelling, what could be more honourable than to rejoice concordantly in all the good things of all [Col. 0533B]? Especially since the instruction of the divine law urges your purpose to greater perfection, and we desire that your judgment be confirmed by excellent decrees.

Perhaps, however, you may wonder what this beginning of my discourse means. I shall neither be burdened nor refuse to explain the reason. For I confess that I have read the proceedings in which, from your honourable testimonies and praises of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea—whom I too have long known well for his learning and moderation—I learned that you are favourably inclined toward him and wish to claim him for yourselves. What then do you think came into my mind as I strove to investigate what was right and true? How great a care and anxiety do you think I took upon myself on account of that desire of yours [Col. 0533C]?

O holy faith, which through the words and precepts of our Saviour displays to us, as it were, a living image of life: how grievously would you yourself resist those who go astray, if you utterly refused to serve gain and favour. It seems to me [Col. 0536A] that the person who seeks peace most earnestly has conquered victory itself. For where what is honourable is concerned, though you may find no one who does not take the greatest delight in it, I ask you, dearest brothers: why do we adopt a course from which injury flows to others? Why do we pursue and bring upon ourselves things that will overthrow confidence in our own judgment?

I greatly praise that man whom you judge worthy of both honour and goodwill. Yet what ought to have remained fixed and firm for each person should not be so despised that individuals are not content with their own boundaries, nor all enjoy their own possessions; and that, in seeking persons equally worthy of the episcopate, not merely one or two but very many equal to Eusebius are not put forward. For when harshness and violence cause no trouble in ecclesiastical honours, all are alike among themselves and should be held in equal esteem [Col. 0536B]. Nor would it be consistent with reason for an inquiry of this kind to result in injury to others, since the minds of all—whether those of a smaller city or of a greater one—receive and observe the divine decrees equally; so that some are in no way inferior to others in what concerns the common faith.

If we wish to state the truth plainly, one might rightly say that this is not holding a man, but snatching him away; and that what is done is a work of violence rather than justice. Whether the multitude thinks this way or otherwise, I plainly and boldly affirm that the matter furnishes cause for accusations and stirs up a storm of great tumult. Even lambs display the force and strength of their teeth whenever, through the deterioration of their shepherd’s care and vigilance, they see themselves deprived of their former governance [Col. 0536C].

If this is so, and we are not deceived in our judgment, consider first of all, brothers—for many and very great goods will arise for you immediately from the beginning—whether sincere charity and love among you will suffer any loss. Then consider that the man who came to you for the sake of sound counsel should receive, by divine judgment, the honour due to him, since he has received no ordinary benefit in your rendering so honourable a vote concerning his virtue. Finally, let it be your custom to employ, in accordance with prudent counsel, care and diligence in seeking such a man as you need, putting far away every seditious and immoderate outcry. For cries of this sort are always unjust, and sparks and conflagrations are accustomed to arise from the collision of diverse persons with one another.

May I please God and you in this way; may I live in accordance with your prayers: I love you, and I cherish the tranquil harbour of your gentleness. Having cast out that defilement, bring concord into its place together with upright character, and set a firm sign upon the ship, directing the heavenly course of navigation toward the very light with, so to speak, iron rudders. Therefore load incorruptible merchandise aboard the ship. For everything that could corrupt the ship has been drained away as though from the bilge. Accordingly, take care to enjoy all these goods in such a way that you may not appear hereafter either to have resolved anything, or to have undertaken anything from the beginning, through unconsidered and useless zeal. May God preserve you, dearest brothers.

Constantine the Victorious, Greatest Augustus, to the people of Antioch.

[Col. 0534A]

[Note: [Col. 0533C]

“I would not, therefore, be surprised …” This passage is corrupt; I have recovered its sense as best I could. First, I think it should be written θαυμάσετε, “you will wonder.” Then write: “Those whom one and the same course through a straight and just path promises to God,” as it is written in the excellent Fuket manuscript, with which the manuscripts of Savile and Turnebus partly agree.

“What could be more honourable?” After these words Scaliger and others inserted τοῦ δι’ εὐτυχίας, which I also found written in the margin of Morel’s book. But I cannot approve their conjecture. For what does δι’ εὐτυχίας mean? I should much prefer to read: “than to rejoice concordantly in the good things of all.” For Constantine says that Christians should not envy the prosperity of others or draw bishops of neighbouring cities away from their own churches because they excel in learning and virtue. This was what the Antiochenes wished to do: after deposing Eustathius, they asked that Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, be appointed their bishop. In the Fuket manuscript a full stop stands after γένοιτο, “could be.” Then it reads: τοῦτο δι’ εὐτυχίας τοῖς, etc.; nor is it otherwise in the manuscript of Turnebus. Savile, however, corrected the margin of his own book thus: τοῦ δι’ εὐτυχίας τῆς πάντων καλῶς ὁμ. Whether that reading came from conjecture or from a manuscript, I cannot approve it. I would certainly prefer: “What could be more honourable than, prospering well, to agree in the good things of all,” so that the sense may be the one given above.

“Your purpose.” Christophorson did not understand this passage correctly. For he understands Constantine to mean the impetuous desire by which the Antiochenes proposed to acquire Eusebius as their bishop, just as later, by κρίσις, “judgment,” he understands the decision by which they chose him. I therefore read: “and that our judgment also may be confirmed by good things,” etc., as it is written in the Fuket and Turnebus manuscripts.

“Pressing on, claiming for yourselves.” In the old papers of the Royal Library it is written ἐγκειμένως, “urgently,” which greatly pleases me. But the Fuket, Savile, and Turnebus manuscripts offer another reading: ἐγκειμένους καὶ σφετεριζομένους, “pressing on and claiming for themselves.”

“An inquiry arising.” I do not doubt that it should be written: ἐπειγόμενον ἐντεθυμῆσθαι, “to consider urgently.” In the Fuket manuscript I found written: ἐπιγενόμενον διεντεθυμῆσθαι. It might also be written ἐπεγειρόμενον.

“To overcome victory itself.” A most elegant saying, which Christophorson did not understand. “It seems to me,” says Constantine, “that he who most seeks peace has conquered victory itself.” Therefore a full stop should be placed after ἀντιποιούμενος, “seeking,” as the Royal manuscript, the Fuket manuscript, and the old papers have.

[Col. 0535C] “That each should be content with his own judgments.” That is, each should be content with his own boundaries. For γνώμη means a boundary of fields; hence the agrimensorial writers are so called, since they wrote about boundaries of fields. In the same way, ὅρος among the Greeks is used indifferently for both an opinion and a boundary. As a boundary delimits fields, so an opinion brings lawsuits and controversies to an end. Moreover, it seems that ἑκάστους, “all individually,” should be written [Col. 0535D]. For the text continues: “and that all enjoy their own possessions.” Although the Fuket and Turnebus manuscripts have πάντων ἀπολαύειν, “enjoy all things.”

“To the advantage of another.” It should be written εἰς ἑτέρων πλεονέκτημα, “to the advantage of others.” Constantine says that such a deliberation about choosing a bishop in Eustathius’s place ought not to bring injury to others. Nor should you despoil other churches. A little later I agree with Scaliger and Christophorson, who corrected τῆς πάντων διανοίας, “the minds of all.” I found this written likewise in the Fuket and Savile manuscripts and in the old papers.

“Whether lesser or greater”: that is, whether they are inhabitants of a smaller city, such as Caesarea, or of a greater city, such as Antioch. All, he says, both citizens of small towns (*mikropolitai*) and citizens of great cities, are equal before God. Therefore smaller towns ought not to be deprived of their bishops. Constantine had said the same thing a little earlier: ecclesiastical honours are all alike and are to be held in equal esteem [Col. 0536C].

“If, indeed, we wish to speak the truth.” These words can be referred to the preceding period. Thus a full stop should be placed after ἀποφαινόμεθα, and the passage translated: “so that others are in no way inferior, insofar as the common faith is concerned, if indeed we wish to speak the truth plainly. Therefore this is not holding a man, but snatching him away,” etc. The passage is punctuated this way in the old papers.

“He came through sound counsel.” From these words it is inferred that our Eusebius came to Antioch together with the other bishops who condemned Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, at the synod; and that after Eustathius’s deposition the Antiochenes wished to retain him among themselves. This is what Constantine said above: “not retention, but rather removal.” Theodoret reports the same thing in Book I, chapter 21.

“That which belongs to your custom.” I think it should be written: “that it belongs to your custom to bring forward with good judgment the diligence for seeking …” For the verb “consider” must be supplied in common. But if anyone wishes to defend the received reading, I shall not resist very strongly.

“And from the comparison of differences.” Better, if I am not mistaken, would be: τῆς τῶν διαφορῶν συγκρούσεως, “from the clash of different persons.” That is, sparks and flames are accustomed to arise from the collision of many people. The Fuket manuscript finally confirmed our conjecture [Col. 0537B], for it expressly reads τῆς τῶν διαφορῶν συγκρούσεως.

“From which, having cast off that defilement …” Christophorson translates this passage: “From that harbour, after the defilements of the past sedition have been cast out, introduce concord in their place with a peaceful disposition of mind.” There is much in that translation which I cannot approve. First, I do not agree that “that defilement” means the filth of sedition. Constantine seems to me to allude to the charge for which Eustathius was deposed: namely, the sexual violation of a certain woman, of which Theodoret speaks in Book I of his history. Constantine signifies the same thing shortly afterward when he says: “Everything that was corrupting the ship has been drained away as though from the bilge.” Yet Christophorson again interprets this as the filth of sedition. But I do not see how “filth” can be said of sedition. No one can doubt, however, that it is most aptly said of the alleged sexual violation. This is a metaphor from harbours, which are customarily cleared whenever they are choked with mud and all kinds of debris.

Now someone might interpret those words ἐξ οὗ, “from which,” adverbially; and thus one should read ἀντεισενέγκατε, which certainly does not displease me. “Thus,” Constantine says, “may I please God, as I love you and cherish the harbour of your gentleness, after you have cast out that defilement and introduced concord together with upright character.” Certainly this sense appeals to me far more than the received reading. For the Antiochenes were already united, and the sedition had been calmed when Constantine wrote this letter, as is clear from its beginning.

“Having run a favourable course toward the light.” I think one should write “a fair-voyaging course” (*dromon ourion*). For the metaphor is taken from navigation. Thus in Sophocles *ourios dromos* means a prosperous voyage; and a ship borne by a favourable wind is called by the Greeks an *ouriodromous naus* [Col. 0538B].

“You regard the incorruptible as corruptible.” This entire letter is corrupt in many places, but this closing passage especially teems with errors. For what can these words mean? I do not doubt that one should read, “Carry an incorruptible cargo” (*aphtharton phorton agete*). Constantine here employs a sustained nautical metaphor and compares Christians to merchants sailing for trade. “Continue,” he says, “on a favourable course toward the eternal light, with the standard of the cross raised on your ships, and load uncorrupted goods aboard. For whatever could damage the ship has now been pumped out.” Thus, with a slight and almost negligible alteration, an elegant and clear meaning results.

“Of all things” (*tou tōn hapantōn*). It seems that this should be written as one word, *toutōn*, as Savile also corrected it in his manuscript. The Fuketius manuscript reads, “enjoyment of all things” (*apolausin tōn hapantōn*). The conclusion of this letter, however, seems to require restoration as follows: “lest you should think it expedient either to undertake anything at all, or to attempt the beginning, with thoughtless and unprofitable zeal.” I followed this reading in my translation [Col. 0538C]. Constantine calls “thoughtless zeal” (*aboulos spoudē*) the effort which the Antiochenes had displayed toward Eusebius when they sought to obtain him as their bishop. It may also refer to the Antiochenes’ attachment to Eustathius: grieving at his deposition, they had stirred up a sedition. In the Fuketius, Savile, and Turnebus manuscripts, the passage is written thus: “to undertake what we think not advantageous.” But clearer is the wording found in the older papers: “to undertake—we think it not advantageous.”

> How welcome to the understanding and wisdom of the world is the concord that comes from you! And I, brethren, have come to know that you love an undying friendship, prompted by the law, by your manner of life, and by your earnest efforts. This, then, is truly to enjoy good things rightly: to employ an upright and sound mind. For what could suit you better? I would not, therefore, be surprised if I were to say that truth is for you rather a cause of salvation than of hatred.
>
> Among brethren whom one and the same disposition, in the course of an upright and just path, commends to God, what could be more honourable than to be enrolled in a pure and holy household, and, through good fortune, to agree in all that is good? Especially since the instruction derived from the law leads your purpose toward a better correction [Col. 0534B], and since we desire that our own judgment also be confirmed by sound principles.
>
> Perhaps this seems strange to you. “What, then, is the purpose of this preamble to my discourse?” I shall neither evade nor refuse to state the reason. For I acknowledge that I have read the memorials in which I saw you earnestly commending, with splendid praises and testimonies, Eusebius, bishop of the Caesareans—whom I myself have long known well for his learning and moderation—and claiming him for yourselves.
>
> What, then, do you suppose that I, in seeking precise knowledge of the better course, reflected upon? What concern did I derive from your zeal? O holy faith, which through the word and judgment of our Saviour gives us, as it were, an image of life! How difficult it would be for you yourself to withstand sins [Col. 0534C], unless you renounced service directed toward gain. And it seems to me that he who seeks rather the possession of peace gains victory itself. For wherever what is fitting is permitted to someone, no one who does not delight in it could be found.
>
> I ask you therefore, brethren: why do we reason thus—so as to bring reproach upon others by what we choose? [Col. 0535A] Why do we pursue things that will overthrow the credibility of our own reputation? I praise the man who is judged worthy both of honour and of your favour. Yet it must not be the case that what ought to remain authoritative and secure among each community has become so weakened that each person is content with his own opinions and everyone enjoys what belongs to his own community.
>
> In a rival deliberation, not one candidate only, but several, ought to be brought forward for comparison with this man. Therefore no disturbance, whether from astonishment or harshness, should attend ecclesiastical honours; rather, these should be alike and equally welcome to all. Nor is it reasonable to make this consideration an advantage for one person over another, when the minds of all alike—whether they seem lesser or greater—receive and preserve the divine doctrines.
>
> Thus the others are in no respect to be diminished under the common law [Col. 0535B], if indeed we plainly declare what is true: that this would be called not an acquisition, but rather a removal, of the man; and that what is done would be an act of force, not of justice. Whether the multitude thinks thus or otherwise, I plainly and boldly declare that this provides grounds for accusation and provokes no ordinary disturbance of faction.
>
> Even lambs indicate by the nature and power of their teeth that, when the accustomed care and tending of their shepherd deteriorates, they are deprived of their former way of life. If this is so, and we are not mistaken, consider this first, brethren; for from the outset many great consequences will confront you. First of all, the genuineness and mutual goodwill existing among you, provided that it is perceived to have suffered no diminution. Next, when he arrives through right counsel, he will receive from divine judgment the reward corresponding to his worth [Col. 0535C].
>
> You have received no small favour in having cast so favourable a vote concerning him. Moreover, as your accustomed good judgment requires, bring appropriate diligence to the search for the man you need, excluding every factious and disorderly outcry. Such outcry is always unjust; and from the collision of disputes sparks and flames arise.
>
> Thus may I please God and you [Col. 0538A], and live in accordance with your prayers: I love you, and I love the harbour of your gentleness, since, having cast off that filth [the transmitted Greek is corrupt: *ton rbpon*], you have brought in concord with good character, setting the firm sign in place, and, having run a fair-voyaging course toward the light, as one might say, with iron rudders. Therefore carry the incorruptible cargo; for everything damaging the ship has, as it were, been pumped out from the bilge. Therefore now take care to enjoy all these things in such a way that we may not think it expedient a second time, through thoughtless and unprofitable zeal, either to establish anything at all or to undertake the beginning of anything. May God preserve you, beloved brethren.

## LETTER II OF CONSTANTINE TO EUSEBIUS

(Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book III, ch. 61.) The holy bishop is praised for refusing Antioch.  
[Note: [Col. 0537] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0537]

Victor Constantine, Greatest Augustus, to Eusebius.

[Col. 0537A]

I have read your letter repeatedly, and I have learned that you have observed with the utmost exactness the rule of ecclesiastical discipline. Indeed, to persist in the judgment that seems both acceptable to God and consonant with apostolic tradition is an act of the highest piety. You ought, moreover, to regard yourself as fortunate in this very respect: by the testimony, so to speak, of the entire world, you have been judged worthy of the episcopate of the whole Church [Col. 0540A]. For when all desire to have you as bishop among themselves, they unquestionably increase this happiness of yours.

But your prudence acted most rightly in resolving to keep the commandments of God and the apostolic and ecclesiastical rule, by refusing the episcopate of the Church of Antioch and desiring rather to remain in the office which you had received from the beginning by God’s command. On this matter I have written to the people and to your fellow ministers, who themselves had written to me concerning these matters. When your holiness has read those letters, it will readily recognize that, because justice seemed to oppose them, I wrote to them at the prompting of the divine power. Your prudence must also be present at their deliberation, so that this may be established in the Church of the Antiochenes [Col. 0540B]. May God preserve you, dearest brother.

Victor Constantine, Greatest Augustus, to Eusebius.

[Col. 0538A]

[Note: [Col. 0538C]

“Worthy to be bishop of the whole Church.” Baronius, under the year of the Lord 324, no. 145, explains these words as follows: Constantine, he says, calls care for the Church of Antioch “the episcopate of the whole Church,” because Antioch was the metropolis of the entire East. But, with all respect to that eminent man, these words seem to have another meaning [Col. 0539C]. Since, as Constantine testifies shortly afterward, all cities wished to have Eusebius as bishop, Eusebius was, by universal consent, worthy of the episcopate of the whole world.

“That is, the commandments.” The Fuketius and Savile manuscripts read, “if indeed the commandments.” I would nevertheless prefer to write, “which both the commandments,” etc. A little earlier, where the text reads “seem consonant,” the Fuketius and Savile manuscripts add “godly.”]

> I have read your letter very fully, and I have observed that the rule of ecclesiastical learning has been kept with exactness. To remain, therefore, in those things which seem both pleasing to God and consonant with apostolic tradition is godly. Therefore consider yourself fortunate in this very matter: by the testimony, so to speak, of the whole world, you have been judged worthy to be bishop of the whole Church.
>
> For if all desire that you should be among them, they will beyond dispute add to this happiness of yours. But your prudence, resolving to preserve both the commandments of God, the apostolic rule, and the rule of the Church, has acted exceedingly well in declining the episcopate of the Church at Antioch, while earnestly desiring to remain in that Church in which, from the beginning, by God’s will, it received the episcopate.
>
> On this matter I have composed a letter to the people and to the other fellow ministers, who themselves had happened to write to me concerning these matters. When your purity has read it, it will readily recognize that, because justice spoke against them, I wrote to them at the urging of the divine power. Your prudence must also be present at their council, so that this may be established in the Church of the Antiochenes [Col. 0539B]. May God preserve you, beloved brother.

## LETTER II OF CONSTANTINE TO MACARIUS

(Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book III, chs. 52–53.) Concerning the place in Palestine called Mamre.  
[Note: [Col. 0539] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0539]

Victor Constantine, Greatest Augustus, to Macarius and the other bishops of Palestine.

[Col. 0540B]

### I

This is, among other things, a very great benefit which my most holy mother-in-law has conferred upon you: by letters sent to us, she revealed the impious audacity of certain wicked persons, hitherto concealed among you, so that a crime long neglected might at last, though late, nevertheless receive from us the necessary and fitting remedy and punishment. For it is indeed a most grave impiety for holy places to be polluted with detestable sacrileges. What is this, then, dearest brethren, which escaped your vigilance, but which, out of reverence for the divine worship, our aforementioned mother-in-law could not keep silent?

Victor Constantine, Greatest Augustus, to Macarius and the other bishops of Palestine.

[Col. 0539B]

[Note: [Col. 0539C]

“My most holy mother-in-law” (*tēs hosiōtatēs mou kēdestrias*). All the translators—Portus, Musculus, and Christophorson—have erred in interpreting this expression as “care” and “solicitude,” as though the text read *kēdemōnias*. Constantine, however, speaks of his mother-in-law, namely Eutropia the Syrian, mother of Fausta, Constantine’s wife. For *kēdestria* in Greek means “mother-in-law,” as the ancient glosses teach: “*kēdestēs*: father-in-law; *kēdestria*: mother-in-law” [Col. 0539D].

Certainly the words following openly confirm our explanation: “by the letters sent to us.” He means the letter which Eutropia, his mother-in-law, sent him. Thus Christophorson’s alteration of “to us” into “to you” must be rejected. The immediately following words indicate the same thing sufficiently: “the aforementioned woman, on account of her reverence toward the divine,” etc. For who would say of care and solicitude, “the aforesaid care and solicitude”? That would be altogether flat and absurd.

But in our translation everything is plain and clear. The “aforementioned woman” is the aforesaid mother-in-law; in her piety and religious devotion, she could not pass over so great a crime in silence, but informed Constantine, her son-in-law, by letter, that he might at last remedy the evil. Eutropia, therefore, was a Christian, as we learn from this passage [Col. 0540C]. Her daughter Fausta also professed the Christian faith and was buried with her husband Constantine in the church of the Apostles.

Moreover, what I found written in the margin of the Royal manuscript should not be omitted. There, opposite the word *kēdestrias*, “mother” (*geneteira*) is added by way of scholium, as though Constantine meant his own mother Helena. I do not approve this. Sozomen certainly says that it was Constantine’s mother-in-law who, when she came to the oak of Mamre and discovered pagan sacrileges there, reported the matter to Constantine. See him, Book II, ch. 3.

“A benefit to us.” I would prefer “to you,” though the received reading can stand. I would also prefer to read the beginning of this letter, with a slight transposition of words: “This one thing also, and a very great thing,” etc.]

### I

> This too has become one very great benefit to us from my most holy mother-in-law: she made known to us by letters the audacity of impious persons, hitherto concealed among you; so that the sin which had been overlooked might receive, though late, yet necessarily through us, the fitting correction and remedy.
>
> For it is truly an impiety of the greatest magnitude that holy places should be defiled by unholy pollutions. What, then, is this, dearest brethren, which escaped your acuteness, but which the aforesaid woman, because of her reverence toward the divine, was unable to pass over in silence?

That our Saviour appeared there to Abraham.

[Col. 0539]

[Col. 0540C]

### II

That place which is called “by the oak of Mamre,” where we learn that Abraham had his dwelling, is said to be defiled in every way by certain superstitious persons [Col. 0541A]. For it has been reported to us that images worthy of every kind of destruction have been set up beside that tree; that an altar has been erected nearby; and that impure sacrifices are continually performed there.

Since this appears both alien to our times and unworthy of the holiness of the place itself, let Your Gravity know that by letter we have instructed Acacius, the most distinguished count and our friend, that, without any delay, every image found in the aforesaid place is to be consigned to fire and the altar utterly overthrown. All persons who, after our command, dare to commit any impious act in that place [Col. 0544A] are to undergo the punishment they deserve.

We have ordered that the place itself be adorned with a pure basilica building, so that it may become a fitting assembly-place for holy men. If anything should be done contrary to our command, you must immediately report it to our Clemency by letter, so that whoever is found guilty may suffer the extreme penalty as one liable for violating the law.

For you do not fail to know that there the Lord and God of all first appeared to Abraham and conversed with him. There the observance of the holy law first began. There the Saviour himself first granted Abraham the presence of himself together with two angels. There God first began to appear to human beings. There he foretold to Abraham concerning his future offspring and immediately fulfilled the promise. There, long before, he announced that Abraham himself would become father and progenitor of very many nations [Col. 0544B].

Since these things are so, it seems right that the place should, through our care and diligence, both be preserved free from every sacrilege and restored to its former holiness, so that henceforth nothing may be done there except worship fitting for almighty God, our Saviour, and the Lord of all. It is proper that you should observe this with due diligence, if, as I trust, Your Gravity desires to fulfil my will, which depends especially upon the worship of God. May God preserve you, dearest brethren.

[Note: [Col. 0540D]

“The place by the oak of Mamre.” This place was also called the Terebinth, about thirty Roman miles from the city of Jerusalem, as the author of the *Itinerary of Jerusalem*, who lived in the age of Constantine the Great, teaches: “From there to the Terebinth, nine miles, where Abraham lived and dug a well beneath the terebinth tree, conversed with angels, and took food. There a basilica of wonderful beauty was built by Constantine’s command. From the Terebinth to Hebron, two miles, where there is a quadrangular memorial of stones of wonderful beauty, in which Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, etc., were laid.”

Sozomen also writes in Book II, ch. 3, that this place was called the Terebinth. It received this name from the terebinth tree, which was said to be the oldest of all trees there, dating from the very beginning of the world, according to Josephus in Book V of the *Jewish War*. Others, however, said that it was the staff of one of the angels who appeared to Abraham, from which, when planted in the ground [Col. 0541B], the terebinth sprang up. Thus George Syncellus in his *Chronicle*. Yet it is strange that, though the oak under which Abraham pitched his tent stood there, as is read in Genesis 18, the place itself received its name from the terebinth rather than the oak.

“Images worthy of every kind of destruction.” I understand images of the angels who appeared there to Abraham. For the pagans worshipped these images. The same pagans also venerated the terebinth itself, as Eusebius teaches in Book V, ch. 9 of the *Demonstration*. Scaliger wrongly understood that passage in his *Eusebian Observations*, p. 192. He thought that Christians had worshipped the terebinth with the highest honour and cited Eusebius as his authority. But Eusebius in that passage speaks of pagans, not Christians.

For, after saying, “Therefore even now the place is worshipped among those living nearby as divine, and the terebinth is seen to remain there still,” he adds: “Those entertained by Abraham are represented in a painting: two stand on either side, and in the middle is the superior one, surpassing the others in honour; this would be the Lord himself, our Saviour, whom those who do not know him nevertheless worship” [Col. 0541C].

“The terebinth is seen there, still remaining; and the angels entertained by Abraham are painted there on a panel; and in the middle, far superior to and more honoured than the others, is the Lord and our Saviour himself, as I said above—whom they worship in ignorance.” You see that Eusebius here plainly speaks of pagans who did not know Christ. This cannot be said of Christians.

Sozomen confirms our view in Book II, ch. 3, where he discusses at length that market at the Terebinth. He writes that every year in summer Jews, Christians, and pagans came there from Palestine, Phoenicia, and Arabia, some for trade and some for religion, and each observed the festival according to his own custom. “The pagans,” he says, “worshipped the angels, offering them victims and libations.” There were therefore images of angels there, to which pagans sacrificed victims [Col. 0541D].

Jerome, in his work on Hebrew places, writes concerning Arboc: “The oak of Abraham, also called Mamre, was still shown there until the time of King Constantine, and his mausoleum is now visible. Since a church has now been built there by us, the terebinth is superstitiously worshipped by all nations round about because Abraham once entertained angels beneath it.” Jerome has added much here of his own. For Eusebius himself, in the book on Hebrew places, has only the following:

> Arboc: this is Hebron, now a very large village, formerly the metropolis of the foreigners, a dwelling-place of giants, and afterward the royal city of David. It fell by lot to the tribe of Judah and was a priestly city, one of the cities of refuge; it lies from Aelia toward the south, twenty-two milestones away. There are seen there the oak of Abraham and his tomb; and the terebinth is conspicuously worshipped by our enemies, as are the angels entertained by Abraham. Formerly called Arboc, it was later called Hebron, after Hebron, one of the sons of Caleb, as in Chronicles. [Col. 0542B]

This is an outstanding passage, entirely overturning Scaliger’s view and excellently confirming our explanation. For Eusebius says that the terebinth itself and the angels are superstitiously worshipped there by “our enemies,” by which he means pagans and Jews. John of Damascus also cites this passage of Eusebius in Book III on Images.

“It is said to be defiled.” The Royal manuscript, the Fuketius manuscript, and the Royal papers more correctly read, “she says it is defiled,” for “the mother-in-law” is understood.

“And she reported an altar.” Supply “the mother-in-law.” Constantine says that his mother-in-law reported to us that there was an altar there upon which impure sacrifices were offered. Eustathius speaks of this altar in his *Hexameron*, saying that it and the terebinth itself still stood in his time. It follows that Eustathius wrote this work before Constantine ordered that altar overthrown.

In Sozomen’s age, neither the altar nor the terebinth tree remained. Nevertheless pagan superstition persisted in that place, as Jerome testifies. So difficult is it to eradicate completely the roots of superstition. What Antoninus Martyr writes about this should not be omitted [Col. 0542C]: “From Bethlehem to the root of Mamre are twenty-four miles. In that place Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Sarah, and also Joseph’s bones rest. There is a square basilica and, in the middle, an uncovered courtyard; Christians enter through the middle screen from one side, Jews from the other, bringing much incense. For the burial commemoration of Jacob and David in that land is celebrated with the greatest devotion on the first day after the Nativity of the Lord, so that a multitude of Jews gathers from every land, bringing incense and lights. They give gifts and serve there.” Add Jerome’s *Epitaph of Paula*.

“Alien to the authority of our times.” Christophorson deleted the first four words; they are absent from the Royal, Fuketius, and Savile manuscripts. But if the matter were left to my judgment, I would rather delete the following words, “to our authority,” which seem to me to have been added by way of scholium to explain the preceding words. Greeks elegantly use *kairoi* for the time of an emperor’s reign [Col. 0542D]. Emperors especially sought to have the prosperity and clemency of their times celebrated. Nothing occurs more frequently among Latin historians and in imperial laws.

In Philostratus, Book II of the *Lives of the Sophists*, where he speaks of Heliodorus, this expression is corrupt. When Heliodorus began to speak before the emperor, Philostratus says that the emperor suddenly rose and cried out: “O man, whose like I have never yet seen! O glory and ornament of my times: *tōn emautou kairōn heurēma*—the discovery of my own times!” That is how it should be read. Constantine employs the same expression in his Letter to the Heretics, printed at the end of this book. Therefore I judge that the received reading should be retained. The words “to our authority” have been transposed and should be placed after “since.”

“And our friend.” The Fuketius manuscript and the Royal papers read “our own friend.”

“Worthy of punishment.” I read, “may be worthy of punishment”; that is, “let it be a capital offence.” Thus Christophorson’s emendation is unnecessary. Yet the Fuketius, Savile, and Turnebus manuscripts are written differently, and here it is preferable to follow them. A little later, write from the Fuketius manuscript: “which we have ordered to be adorned with a pure imperial building,” etc.

“It was proper for you to observe.” I read “it was proper,” or “it is proper,” as Christophorson seems to have read. In the Royal papers I found “it was proper,” as I had conjectured.]

### II

> That place which is called by the oak of Mamre, where we learn that Abraham had his dwelling, is said to be defiled in every way by certain superstitious persons. For images worthy of every kind of destruction are said to have been set up beside it; and she reported that an altar stood nearby and impure sacrifices were continually performed.
>
> Since this appears alien to the character of our times and unworthy of the holiness of the place, I wish Your Reverence to know that we have communicated by letter with Acacius, the most distinguished count and our friend: without any delay, all images whatever found in the aforesaid place are to be given to the fire, and the altar overthrown from its foundations.
>
> Any who dare, after our command [Col. 0543A], to perform something impious in such a place are to be liable to punishment. We have ordered it to be adorned with a pure imperial building, so that it may become an assembly worthy of holy men. If anything should occur contrary to what has been commanded, it must without delay be made known to our Clemency by letters from you, so that we may order the offender, as a lawbreaker, to undergo the severest penalty.
>
> For you do not fail to know that there the Lord God of all first appeared to Abraham and conversed with him. There the worship of the holy law first received its beginning; there the Saviour himself first abundantly granted Abraham his manifestation together with the two angels; there God began to appear to human beings; there he foretold to Abraham concerning the offspring that would come to him and immediately fulfilled the promise [Col. 0543B]; there he proclaimed beforehand that Abraham himself would become father of exceedingly many nations.
>
> Since this is so, it seems fitting to me that, through your care, this place should be preserved pure from every pollution and restored to its ancient holiness, so that nothing else may be done there except the worship fitting for God almighty, our Saviour, and Lord of all. It is proper for you to observe this with due diligence, if, as I am persuaded, Your Reverence desires that those wishes of mine which are especially dependent upon piety toward God should be fulfilled. May God preserve you, beloved brethren.

## LETTER OF CONSTANTINE TO THE SYNOD OF TYRE

(Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book IV, ch. 62.) The emperor urges the bishops not to remove Eusebius from Caesarea.  
[Note: [Col. 0543] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0543]

Victor Constantine, Greatest Augustus, to Theodotus, Theodore, Narcissus, Aetius, Alpheus, and the remaining bishops at Antioch.

[Col. 0544C]

### I

I have read the letter written by Your Holiness and have greatly approved the prudent intention of Eusebius, your fellow minister. Having learned all that was done, partly from your letters and partly from the letters of the most distinguished men, the counts Acacius and Strategius, and having carefully considered the matter as was fitting, I wrote to the people of Antioch what was acceptable to God and appropriate to the Church.

I ordered a copy of that letter to be appended to this letter, so that you too might know why I wrote to the people of Antioch when prompted by the reasoning of justice. For your letter contained a request that, in accordance with the vote and desire of the people and of Your Prudence, Eusebius, the most holy bishop of the Caesareans [Col. 0544D], should preside over the Church of Antioch [Col. 0545A] and assume care of it.

Eusebius’s letter itself seemed highly consonant with ecclesiastical law. Yet it is proper that my judgment too should become known to Your Prudence. For it has been reported to us that Euphronius, a presbyter and citizen of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and George, likewise a presbyter and citizen of Arethusa, whom Alexander promoted to this rank in Alexandria, are men most approved in their doctrine of faith.

I have therefore resolved to inform Your Prudence that, after bringing forward these men, and any others whom you judge worthy of the episcopate, you should decree those things that accord with the apostolic tradition. With these matters thus prepared, Your Prudence will be able, according to the rule of the Church and apostolic tradition, to direct this election as the principle of ecclesiastical discipline requires [Col. 0545B]. May God preserve you, dearest brethren.

Victor Constantine, Greatest Augustus, to Theodotus, Theodore, Narcissus, Aetius, Alpheus, and the remaining bishops at Antioch.

[Col. 0543C]

[Note: [Col. 0543D]

“Theodotus.” This Theodotus was bishop of Laodicea in Syria; Narcissus bishop of Neroniadis in Cilicia; and Aetius bishop of Lydda in Palestine: all supporters of the Arian party. When they came to Antioch with Eusebius of Nicomedia and Eusebius of Caesarea, they deposed Eustathius, as Theodoret writes in Book I, ch. 21 of his history. Aetius later joined the orthodox party, according to Philostorgius, Book III, ch. 12, and Athanasius. Alpheus, bishop of Apamea in Syria, and Theodore, bishop of Sidon in Phoenicia, are named among the bishops who subscribed to the Nicene synod [Col. 0544D]. Athanasius also speaks of Theodotus in his book on the synods of Ariminum and Seleucia.

“Acacius and Strategius.” Constantine refers, I think, to Acacius, Count of the East, mentioned above in the letter to Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem. Strategius is the man also called Musonianus, concerning whom I have made many notes on Book XVI of Ammianus Marcellinus. He had been sent to Antioch by Emperor Constantine to quiet the disturbance, as Eusebius said above.

“Prompted by the reasoning of justice.” I would prefer to write “prompted.”

“The understanding of the intention.” I would rather read “the intention of their shared decision.” Moreover, from these words, badly understood by Christophorson, it appears that the bishops assembled at Antioch had requested in writing that Constantine transfer Eusebius to the see of Antioch in accordance with the will of the people of Antioch and of the bishops themselves [Col. 0545C]. Thus the words, “in accordance with the intention and will of the people and of your shared decision,” are drawn from the letter sent to Emperor Constantine by the bishops assembled at Antioch.

“But the letters concerning life.” The conjecture of learned men who emended this to “but Eusebius’s letters,” etc., is not displeasing. The passage might also be corrected thus: “Eusebius’s letters were sufficient for you,” etc. But the former reading is confirmed by the authority of the Fuketius and Savile manuscripts. Only the postpositive article should be deleted, since it is not found in the Fuketius manuscript.

“For Euphronius has come to my attention.” The Fuketius and Savile manuscripts read: “For it happened to come to my attention that Euphronius,” etc.; Christophorson followed this reading. But the received reading is far better: “It has come to me,” that is, “it has reached me,” as Musculus translates, or “it has been reported to me.”

“George, the Arethusian.” Supply “citizen,” which must be repeated by common construction; Christophorson entirely failed to notice this. Moreover, *politēs* means not merely someone who is native to a city, but rather someone domiciled in and enrolled among the citizens of a city, whether born there or elsewhere [Col. 0545D].

“Whom Alexander appointed to this rank.” Athanasius writes the same in his book on the synods of Ariminum and Seleucia: namely, that this George, who afterward became bishop of Laodicea, was first made presbyter by Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, and was afterward deposed by that same Alexander on account of impiety. Athanasius also writes in his *Apology against Constantius*, p. 728, that the same man was deposed by Alexander; and the Fathers of the Council of Sardica expressly confirm this in their synodical letter. The same Athanasius, in the same book on the synods, p. 886, testifies that this George lived at Antioch [Col. 0546C].

I have punctuated this passage from the Royal papers as follows: “whom Alexander appointed to this rank in Alexandria, [they are] most approved in the faith”; Musculus does the same.

“Those whom you have brought forward.” This passage seems mutilated to me and should, I think, be supplied thus: “It was therefore well to make these men known to your prudence, and for you, having brought forward these and others,” etc. I followed this reading in my translation. “These men” means the aforesaid Euphronius and George. Euphronius later became bishop of Antioch immediately after Eustathius, as Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodore of Mopsuestia in Nicetas’s *Treasury of the Orthodox Faith* write. George, as I said, afterward became bishop of Laodicea.
