The Fuketius manuscript reads, “both those whom you have brought forward.” It should further be noted that Constantine here praises Arian men as orthodox—either because they still concealed their error or because the Arians had gained control of his ears and mind. “Brought forward” [Col. 0546D]. Christophorson saw nothing here. In elections, *procheirizesthai* means to propose or bring forward someone’s name for consideration as to whether that person is worthy of the office in question. Constantine calls this *ekphēnai*, “to bring forth,” in his Letter to the People of Antioch.

Examination followed nomination (*procheirismos*), then election, and finally ordination or consecration. Certainly *procheirismos* is openly distinguished from laying on of hands (*cheirothesia*) in the Letter of the Fathers of the Nicene Council to the Bishops of Egypt. They decree concerning Meletius: “that he is to have no authority either to nominate or to lay hands.” A little later, concerning bishops ordained by Meletius, they prescribe: “that these are to have no authority to nominate persons pleasing to themselves or to put forward a name.” But concerning Catholic clergy who had kept themselves pure from Meletius’s schism, they decree: “that they have authority both to nominate and to select by name persons worthy of the clergy.”]

### I

> I have read what Your Prudence wrote, and I have approved the sensible intention of Eusebius, who ministers as priest with you. Having learned all that was done—partly from your letters, partly from those of the most distinguished Acacius and Strategius—and having made the necessary examination, I wrote to the people of Antioch what was pleasing to God and fitting for the Church. I ordered a copy of the letter to be appended to this letter, so that you also might know whatever it was that, prompted by the reasoning of justice, I chose to write to the people.
>
> For your letters contained this: that, in accordance with the intention and will of the people and of your own judgment, Eusebius, the most holy bishop of the Church of Caesarea [Col. 0546A], should preside over the Antiochene Church and undertake its care. Yet the letters concerning his conduct seemed to observe especially the ordinance of the Church. It was necessary, however, that my own opinion should be made known to Your Prudence.
>
> For it has come to my attention that Euphronius, the presbyter, a citizen of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and George, likewise presbyter of the Arethusians, whom Alexander appointed to this rank at Alexandria, are most approved in the faith. It was therefore right to make known to Your Prudence those whom you have brought forward and such others as you may judge worthy of episcopal rank, in order that you may determine whatever would be consonant with the tradition of the apostles.
>
> For when such matters have been properly prepared, Your Prudence will be able, according to the rule of the Church [Col. 0546B] and apostolic tradition, to regulate the ordination in such a way as the principle of ecclesiastical discipline directs. May God preserve you, beloved brethren.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 333: LETTER OF CONSTANTINE TO SAPOR, KING OF THE PERSIANS

(Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book IV, chs. 9–13.) The pious emperor confesses God and Christ with the highest devotion.  
[Note: [Col. 0545] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0545]

[Col. 0545B]

### I

I, keeping the divine faith, partake of the light of truth; and, following the faith of truth as my guide, I attain knowledge of the divine faith. By this means, as the facts themselves confirm, I recognize the most holy religion, whose worship I profess to be my teacher for attaining knowledge of the most holy Deity [Col. 0548A].

Therefore, supported by the help of this God, I have advanced from the farthest boundaries of Ocean and raised the whole inhabited world to a firm hope of salvation. Thus all provinces, enslaved under so many tyrants and worn down by continuous calamities until they had almost perished, have at last found a defender of the commonwealth and have been restored, as it were, by the healing application of medicines.

I proclaim this God, whose standard my army, consecrated to God, carries upon its shoulders and bears wherever justice requires; and for these very reasons it immediately wins most renowned victories as its reward. I profess that this God is honoured by me in everlasting remembrance; I contemplate him, set in the highest seat, with a pure and radiant mind.

[Note: [Col. 0547C]

“With firm hopes of salvation.” Without doubt one should write “of salvation,” though in Theodoret, Book I, ch. 25, the word is absent. Epiphanius Scholasticus nevertheless recognizes the word, as his translation in Book V of the *Tripartite History* shows.

“They had become effaced.” Everyone sees that this passage is mutilated. In Morel’s book I found it supplied in exactly the same way as in the Geneva edition: “that these should receive, through me, an improvement toward the better.” But whoever corrected the passage in this way was surely a bad and unskilled conjecturer. Who has ever spoken thus: “an improvement toward the better”? How much easier and safer it would have been to supply this lacuna from Theodoret, in whom Constantine’s Letter to Sapor is read more complete and better corrected.

The Fuketius and Savile manuscripts nevertheless supply the lacuna in the same manner as the Geneva edition [Col. 0547D]. Nor should it trouble us that this expression is barbarous. For this letter of Constantine was first written by him in Latin and afterward rendered into Greek by an unskilled translator. The same happened with Constantine’s other letters and speeches.]

### I

> Keeping the divine faith, I receive a share in the light of truth. Guided by the light of truth, I come to know the divine faith. Therefore, as events confirm these things, I recognize the most holy religion. I confess that I possess this worship as teacher of the knowledge of the holy God.
>
> Having the power of this God as my ally, beginning from the bounds of Ocean, I have successively raised the entire inhabited world to firm hopes of salvation; so that all things, enslaved under so many tyrants and yielding to daily disasters, having become effaced—[“that these should receive, through me, an improvement toward the better”]—I profess to honour this God with immortal remembrance; and with an unalloyed and pure mind I contemplate him as existing in the highest places.

Against images, and concerning the glorification of God.

[Col. 0547]

[Col. 0548A]

### II

I invoke him on bended knee, shunning every abominable blood-sacrifice, foul and detestable odours, and every earthly brilliance. Polluted by all these things as though by filth, the impious and unspeakable error of superstition has cast many of the nations—and indeed entire peoples—down into the lowest Tartarus [Col. 0548B].

For those things which the supreme God of all, in his kindness and providence toward human beings, has brought into light for common use, he in no way tolerates being seized for the gratification of each person’s desire. Rather, he requires from human beings only a pure mind and an unstained soul, weighing in these, as on a balance, deeds of virtue and piety. For he delights in works of moderation and gentleness, loving the mild and hating the turbulent. He loves faith and punishes unbelief. He destroys every dominion joined with arrogance and punishes the insolence of the proud. Those exalted by arrogance he overturns from their very foundations, as one might say; but he rewards the humble and those patient under injuries according to their merits [Col. 0548C].

For this reason, esteeming a just kingship highly, he strengthens it with his aid and preserves royal wisdom in the calmness of peace.

[Note: [Col. 0547D]

“Earthly brilliance.” Christophorson interprets this as the flame of sacrifices; Camerarius, more rightly, as the little fires of incantations. For in pagan mysteries certain fires were employed, and a kind of light flashed forth after darkness. Priests of demons produced this by magical art and certain tricks, in order to win authority and reverence for their rites.

Apuleius, Book II: “I approached the boundary of death; having crossed Proserpina’s threshold, I was borne through all the elements and returned. At midnight I saw the sun shining with brilliant white light,” etc. An elegant passage of Themistius in Stobaeus, ch. 274, concerning this rite deserves quotation here:

> The experience undergone is like that of those initiated into great mysteries. Hence the very word resembles the word, and the act the act, of dying (*teleutan*) and being initiated (*teleisthai*): first wanderings and circuits, wearying and anxious journeys through a certain darkness, unfinished; then, before the very end, all the terrors—shuddering, trembling, sweat, and amazement. But from this point a wondrous light meets one, or pure places and meadows receive one, containing voices and dances, solemnity of sacred utterances, and holy visions. Among these, the one now perfected and initiated, become free and released, walks about crowned and celebrates the mysteries, etc.

This passage of Themistius is drawn from his book on the immortality of the soul. There Themistius argued that the soul is immortal by many other arguments as well, and also because Greeks call death *teleutē*, as though it were *teletē*, that is, a mystery. As these two names are very similar, so the things signified by them have a remarkable resemblance. For in the mysteries there are first wandering errors and troublesome circuits, fearful entrances through dark places, and very long journeys attended with fatigue. Then, before the end is reached, come all terrifying things: trembling, horror, and astonishment with amazement. At the end a certain marvellous light appears, and pleasant, pure places in which sacred voices are heard and divine images are seen, etc. To the same rite belong Origen’s words in Book IV against Celsus: “He compares us to those who introduce visions and terrors beforehand in Bacchic initiations.”

“He cast down entire peoples.” In the Fuketius manuscript I found “he threw down,” which is preferable. The same copy reads “many among the nations.”]

### II

> I invoke him, bending the knee, while fleeing every abominable blood-sacrifice, foul and detestable odours, and avoiding every earthly brilliance. Polluted by all these things, the unlawful and unspeakable delusion has cast down many among the nations [Col. 0547B] and whole peoples, delivering them to the lowest regions.
>
> For the things which the God of all, through his own love for humanity and his providence for human beings, brought forth into public view for the sake of use, he does not at all tolerate being drawn toward each person’s desire. Rather, he demands from human beings a pure mind alone and an unstained soul, weighing in this the deeds of virtue and piety.
>
> For he is pleased with works of moderation and gentleness; he loves the mild and hates the turbulent; he loves faith and punishes unbelief; he breaks down every dominion accompanied by arrogance and exacts punishment for the insolence of the proud. Those raised up by vanity he destroys from their foundations, but he apportions deserved rewards to the humble-minded and patient under wrongs. Thus, esteeming a just kingdom highly, he strengthens it by his own assistance and preserves royal wisdom in the calm tranquillity of peace.

Against tyrants and persecutors, and concerning the captivity of Valerian.

[Col. 0549]

[Col. 0549A] III. Nor do I myself seem to be mistaken, my brother, in professing this one God, the author and father of all things. Many of those who have held imperial power among us, carried away by mad error, have indeed attempted to deny him. But a retributive end of such a kind overwhelmed them all, that now the whole human race holds up the calamities of those rulers as an example for those who may seek to imitate them. One of these, I think, was the man whom divine vengeance, descending like a thunderbolt, drove from our regions and delivered over into your lands; and who, through his own disgrace and ignominy, made that trophy so much boasted of among you famous.

[Note: Col. 0549C]

**Τοῖς παρὰ τούτους.** This passage is read quite differently in Theodoret, as follows: **ἐπαράτους τοῖς τὰ ὅμοια ζηλοῦσι τίθεσθαι**—“to pronounce curses upon those who emulate like things.” In my judgment, this is decidedly preferable. Nor had Constantine written otherwise. “All the former emperors,” he says, “who persecuted the faith of Christ were so overwhelmed by a ruinous end that the whole human race now customarily invokes the calamities of those rulers as a curse, instead of every punishment, upon those who seek to imitate them.” What could be clearer or more elegant than this sense? Here **παράδειγμα** therefore signifies a punishment, in which sense that word is frequently used by the Greeks, as Agellius observed. Moreover, **ἐπαράτους τίθεσθαι τὰς συμφορὰς** [Col. 0549D] is elegantly said in the sense of what the Latins call *imprecari*, “to invoke as a curse.” Thus the Greeks say **εὐχὴν θέσθαι**, “to make a prayer,” as I noted above. Epiphanius Scholasticus translates this passage thus: “But a destructive end overtook them all, so that the whole race of men arising after them seems to set forth their disasters as an example of malediction.”

**Τῆς ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν αἰσχύνης.** In Theodoret’s History the more correct reading is: **Τῆς ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ αἰσχ[ύνης] … τὸ παρ᾽ ὑμῖν τρόπαιον ἀποφήναντα**: “having rendered famous among you the trophy by the disgrace that befell him.” He means Valerian, who, captured by the Persians, grew old among them in ignoble servitude and ennobled the Persians’ triumph by his private disgrace. That is, by his own ignominy he made the Persians’ victory over the Romans exceedingly celebrated. This is the meaning of the passage, which neither Epiphanius nor the other interpreters grasped. In the Fukelmann and Turnèbe manuscripts one reads **ἀποφήνασα**, which is not bad.

[Col. 0550A] III. I do not think that I am mistaken, my brother, in confessing this one God, the originator and father of all things. Many of those who have reigned here, led astray by frenzied errors, attempted to deny him. But a retributive end of such a kind consumed them all, so that the entire human race after them sets their calamities forth as a curse upon those who imitate the same things. I consider one of these to have been the man whom divine wrath, like a thunderbolt, drove out from these regions and delivered into your territories, making famous among you the widely spoken-of trophy through the disgrace suffered by him.

### That he has seen the downfall of the persecutors, and now rejoices in the peace of Christians

[Col. 0549B] IV. Indeed, it appears to have turned out well that in our own age the punishment of such men has been displayed most conspicuously. For I too saw the end of those who lately, by most unrighteous commands, had harassed the people consecrated to God. Therefore I give the greatest thanks to God, because by his perfect providence the whole human race that worships the divine law rejoices and exults, since peace has been restored to it. From this I am myself fully persuaded that all things are in the best and safest condition when God deems fit, through their pure and approved religion and through concord concerning the divine being, to gather all men to himself.

[Col. 0550B] IV. But this has advanced to a good end: that in our age the punishment of such men has been made manifest. For I myself beheld those who lately disturbed the people dedicated to God by unlawful commands. Therefore great thanks are due to God, because, by perfect providence, all mankind that serves the divine law rejoices and exults when peace has been restored to them. From this I too have become convinced that all things are in the best and safest condition, whenever, through their pure and approved worship and through agreement concerning the divine, he deems fit to gather all to himself.

### An exhortation to embrace benevolently the Christians living in Persia

[Col. 0549C] V. How great, moreover, do you think is my delight when I hear that the noblest places of Persia far and wide are adorned by a multitude of these people—Christians, that is, for it is of them that I am now speaking? I therefore wish that your affairs may be in the most flourishing condition, and likewise theirs: [Col. 0552A] that is, yours as well as theirs. For in this way you will have as gracious and propitious the God who is lord and father of all. Therefore, since you are such a great man, I commend these persons to you. Since you are distinguished for piety, I place these same persons in your hands. Embrace them in accordance with your humanity. For thus, by this faith of yours, you will confer an immeasurable benefit both upon yourself and upon us.

[Note: Col. 0549D]

**Τούτου τοῦ καταλόγου.** Theodoret [Col. 0550C] more correctly reads **τούτῳ τῷ καταλόγῳ**, “by this class,” for these words refer to **κεκόσμηται**, “has been adorned.” Shortly afterward write **ὑπὲρ γὰρ τούτων**, following Theodoret and Nicephorus.

**Ὅ, τι σοι κᾀκείνῳ.** Theodoret and Nicephorus read **ὅ ἐστι σοι κᾀκείνοις**, “that is, for you and for them.” In Jacobus Sirmond’s edition one reads **ὅ τι ἐστὶ**, etc. Epiphanius Scholasticus translates these words into Latin thus: “You will therefore govern most excellently, if you are as they are and have in common what they have.” Joachim Camerarius, who translated Theodoret’s History into Latin, renders it thus: “Therefore affairs go best with you, and likewise best with them, because they are common to both.” John Langus gives nearly the same translation. Yet this sense does not satisfy me. Formerly I thought it should be written: **ὅτι σὺ κᾀκείνοις, κᾀκεῖνοί σοι**, “that you [may fare well] with them, and they with you,” and I had followed that reading in my translation. But now, on more careful examination, I judge that the reading of Theodoret and Nicephorus should be retained, and I interpret the whole passage thus: “I wish, then, that both your affairs may be in the most flourishing condition and theirs likewise; that is, equally for both of you.” Thus the sense is quite plain, and the following words agree excellently; only **ὑπάρχοι** must be written in the optative. Musculus certainly reads **ὑπάρχοι**, for he translates: “May this therefore turn out best for you, and likewise for them: for you, I say, and for them.” In the Fukelmann manuscript one reads **ὅτι σοί**, without the word **κᾀκείνῳ**.

**Πατέρα Θεὸν.** Theodoret and Nicephorus read **πρᾷον, ἵλεω τε καὶ εὐμενῆ**, “gentle, propitious, and well-disposed.” Epiphanius Scholasticus read no differently, as is evident from his translation.

[Col. 0550C] V. Concerning this class of people—I mean the Christians, for it is about these that all my present discourse is—how do you suppose I rejoice to hear that the foremost parts of Persia too, in the greatest abundance, as I desire, have been adorned? May the best things be granted to you, then, and likewise to them: namely, to you and to them alike. For in this way you will have the God, lord and father of all, gracious and favorably disposed. Therefore, since you are so great, I commend these people to you; and since you are renowned for piety, I entrust these same people to you. Love them as befits your own humanity. For by your faith you will bestow an unbounded favor upon him and upon us.

## Notice concerning the reciprocal letters of Constantine and Saint Anthony the monk

*(Works of St Athanasius, book I, p. 855.)*  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0552A] Moreover, Anthony’s fame reached even the emperors. For when Constantine Augustus and his sons Constantius and Constans, both Augusti, learned these things, they wrote to him as to a father, earnestly desiring to receive letters in reply from him. But he did not at all regard those letters as a great matter, nor did he rejoice upon receiving the emperors’ epistles; rather, he remained such as he had been before they wrote to him. [Col. 0552B] When letters of this kind were brought, however, he summoned the monks and said: “Do not marvel that the emperor writes to us, for he is a man; but marvel rather that God wrote the law to men and has spoken with us through his own Son.”

He did not wish to accept the letters, saying that he did not know how to reply to such communications. But when the monks urged him, saying that the emperors were Christians and that they might take offense at being so slighted, he allowed them to be read. He replied, commending them because they worshipped Christ, and gave them counsels directed toward salvation. He also warned them not to esteem present things highly, but rather to remember the day of judgment and to know that Christ alone is the true and eternal emperor. He entreated them to cultivate humanity, [Col. 0552C] and to care for justice and the poor. When they received this, they rejoiced. Thus he was welcome and dear to all, and everyone desired to have him as a father.

[Col. 0551A] Anthony’s fame reached even kings. For when Constantine Augustus and his sons Constantius and Constans, both Augusti, learned these things, they wrote to him as to a father and prayed to receive letters in return from him. But he neither made much of the letters nor rejoiced at the epistles; he remained the same as he was before the emperors wrote to him. When [Col. 0551B] the letters were brought to him, he summoned the monks and said: “Do not marvel if an emperor writes to us, for he is a human being; marvel rather that God has written the law to human beings and has spoken to us through his own Son.”

He wished not to receive the letters, saying that he did not know how to reply to such communications. Yet, persuaded by the monks that the emperors were Christians and that they should not be offended as though rejected, he allowed them to be read. He wrote back, approving them because they worship Christ; he advised them concerning the things that lead to salvation, not to account present things great, but rather to remember the future judgment and know that Christ alone is the true and eternal king. He asked them to be humane and to care for justice and the poor. And they, receiving the letter, [Col. 0551C] rejoiced. Thus he was beloved by all, and all asked to have him as a father.

## Letter III of Constantine to Eusebius

*(Eusebius, Life of Constantine, book IV, ch. 35.) The emperor praises Eusebius’s discourse concerning Pascha.*  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

**Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus, to Eusebius.**

[Col. 0552C] It is indeed an arduous undertaking, exceeding every power of speech, to explain worthily the mysteries of Christ, and to expound fittingly the controversy concerning Pascha, its origin, and the full achievement, both laborious and beneficial. For even those able to apprehend divine matters in thought are insufficient to relate them according to their worth. Nevertheless, I have admired beyond measure [Col. 0552D] your outstanding learning and earnestness of study; and I read your book with the greatest pleasure. As you desired, I directed that it should be circulated and made known to many who sincerely profess the observance of divine religion. [Col. 0553A] Therefore, since you understand with what pleasure we receive offerings of this sort from your intellectual acuteness, take care henceforth to delight our mind with more frequent discourses, in which, as you profess, you have been nurtured. We encourage you, as the saying goes, while you are running, toward your accustomed pursuits. For the great confidence in question sufficiently shows that you have found a translator into the Latin language who is not unworthy of your works. Yet such a translation cannot in any way attain the worth of works so distinguished. May God preserve you, dearest brother.

Such was his letter on this subject. But concerning the provision of divine books for ecclesiastical readings, his letter was as follows.

**Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus, to Eusebius.**

[Note: Col. 0551D]

**Τοῦ πάσχα ἀντιλογίαν.** One should write **αἰτιολογίαν**, “explanation of the cause,” as I also found corrected in the margin of Morel’s copy; the following words confirm this. For he adds: **Καὶ γένεσιν, λυσιτελῆ τε καὶ ἐπίπονον τελεσιουργίαν**—“and its institution, and its beneficial and laborious completion.” Certainly **γένεσις**, “origin,” cannot be said of the origin of a controversy. It is better, then, to translate **γένεσιν** as “institution.” **Τελεσιουργία** is the completion of the Paschal feast accomplished by Christ, who by the miracle of his resurrection instituted the true Pascha for Christians.

**Λόγοις εὐφραίνειν.** After these words, the Royal manuscript and Robert Estienne’s edition continue with: **κᾂν τὰ μάλιστα τῶν καλῶν ἔργων**, etc. But Scaliger, Bongarsius, and others supplied this passage from manuscripts unknown to me. I found the same supplement also in the Fukelmann manuscript and in Morel’s copy, and it is somewhat more correct than in the Geneva edition. [Col. 0553D] For first it reads: **οἵς ἀντετράφθαι σαυτὸν ὁμολογεῖς**. Yet one should write **ἀνατετράφθαι**, or **ἐντετράφθαι**.

**Καὶ τὸν εἰς τὴν.** After these words Morel’s copy leaves a blank space. Certainly the word **ῥωμαϊκὴν**, “Roman,” is missing. The passage should therefore be supplied thus: **τὸν εἰς τὴν ῥωμαϊκὴν τοὺς σοὺς πόνους μεταῤῥυθμίσοντα γλῶτταν**, or rather **εἰς τὴν ῥωμαίαν**, as Eusebius says above in chapter 32. Certainly the Fukelmann manuscript reads **εἰς τὴν ῥωμ… τοὺς σοὺς πόνους μεταρυθμίζοντα**.

**Ἠ τοσαύτη πεποίθησις.** He means the boldness of the person who had translated Eusebius’s book on Pascha at Constantine’s command; or at least **πεποίθησις** means the emperor’s own opinion and judgment. The translator, indeed, understood it as Eusebius’s own confidence, which cannot fit here at all. Here **πεποίθησις** can only be understood as the judgment and conviction both of Constantine himself and of the other persons who highly praised Eusebius’s treatise on Pascha when it had been translated into Latin at Constantine’s order. “This,” he says, “the great opinion held by all sufficiently shows: that a translator not unworthy of your writings has fallen to your lot.” The words **τῶν συγγραμμάτων**, “of the writings,” may be construed in two ways: either with the adjective **ἀνάξιον**, “unworthy,” or with **πεποίθησις**, “conviction.”

The undertaking is great and surpasses every power of speech: to set forth worthily the mysteries of Christ, and to explain in a fitting manner both the account of the cause and institution of Pascha, and its beneficial and laborious completion. For the divine cannot be expressed according to its worth by human beings, even by those who are able to understand it. Yet, having exceedingly admired your love of learning and your zeal for honor, I myself read the book with pleasure and ordered it, as you wished, to be published for the benefit of many who sincerely devote themselves to the worship of the divine. [Col. 0554A] Since, then, you see with how much delight we receive such gifts from your keenness of mind, endeavor to delight us with more frequent discourses, in which you acknowledge that you have been nurtured. For we urge you, running as you are, as the saying goes, toward your accustomed studies. Indeed, the great confidence in question shows that you have found a translator into the Roman language for your labors who is not unworthy of your writings. Although such a translation is unable to do justice to the worth of such excellent works. May God preserve you, beloved brother. Such, then, was the letter concerning this matter; but the letter concerning the preparation of the divine books runs in this manner.

## Letter IV of Constantine to Eusebius

*(Eusebius, Life of Constantine, book IV, ch. 36.) Concerning the production of sacred codices.*

**Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus, to Eusebius.**

[Col. 0553A] In the city which has received its name from us, through the assisting providence of our Savior God, a very great multitude of people has attached itself to the most holy Church. Since all things there are receiving great increase, it appears especially fitting that more churches should also be built in that city. Receive therefore with ready willingness what I have resolved to do. For it has seemed right to make known to your prudence that you should arrange for fifty codices of the divine Scriptures—whose preparation and use you know to be especially necessary for the Church—to be copied on well-prepared parchment by skilled scribes, highly practiced in elegant writing, so that they may be easily read and conveniently transported for every use. Letters have also been sent by our clemency to the financial officer of the diocese, directing him to ensure that all things necessary for the production of those books are supplied. It will be your care that the written codices be made ready with all speed. [Col. 0553C] Moreover, by the authority of this letter you will receive the use of two public conveyances. For thus the books, elegantly copied, will be carried most conveniently to our sight, one of the deacons from your Church performing this service. When he arrives with us, he will experience our humanity. May God preserve you, dearest brother.

**Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus, to Eusebius.**

[Note: Col. 0554D]

**Διοικήσεως καθολικὸν.** Here **διοίκησις** means the Diocese of the East. The ancient Romans used this term for a definite number of provinces collectively subject to the vicar of a praetorian prefecture. For a praetorian prefect had several dioceses under his administration, whereas vicars each had one. Moreover, this word began to be used in this sense around Constantine’s time, as is evident both from Constantine’s letters cited above and from several laws of the Theodosian Code.

In the city named after us, by the cooperation of the providence of Savior God, a very great multitude of people has devoted itself to the most holy Church. Since all things there [Col. 0554B] are receiving great increase, it seems very fitting that more churches should also be constructed in it. Therefore receive most eagerly what has seemed good to our intention. For it appeared fitting to make known to your understanding that you should order fifty volumes of the divine Scriptures—whose provision and use you know to be especially necessary for the Church—to be written on prepared parchments by expert calligraphers thoroughly acquainted with their craft, readily legible and easily transportable for use. Letters have been sent by our gentleness to the financial officer of the diocese, that he may take care to provide all things suitable for their preparation. For it will be the work of your diligence to ensure that the written volumes are prepared as quickly as possible. [Col. 0554C] You should also receive, under the authority of this letter of ours, permission to use two public conveyances for transport. In this manner the finely written books will most easily be conveyed even to our own sight, one of the deacons of your Church performing this duty. When he comes to us, he will experience our humanity. May God preserve you, beloved brother.

*(Athanasius, Apology, vol. I, p. 177.)*

[Col. 0556A] But if I learn that you have prevented any who desire to join the Church, or have barred them from entry, I shall immediately send someone who, by my command, will depose you and remove you from your see.

## Letter II of Constantine to Athanasius

*(From the same source.)*  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

**Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus, to Pope Athanasius.**

[Col. 0556A] Having read the letters of your prudence, I came to the conclusion that I should exhort you by my reply to lead the people of God toward moderation and mercy. For I hold these matters among the chief concerns of my mind: to cultivate truth, to preserve justice always in my thoughts, and above all to take pleasure in those who walk the straight path of life.

But concerning those Meletians worthy of every execration—those savage and impious persons, who, as though stricken by madness, are stupefied and are moved to wicked deeds only by envy, rivalry, and turmoil, thereby displaying their impious disposition—I think the following must be said. You see that the men whom they themselves claimed had been killed by the sword are living openly and enjoying life. What evidence could ever be more damaging, or press their case more plainly, than that those whom they asserted had been killed are alive and enjoying the light, and can themselves speak in their own defense? Then this also was added to the accusations of the Meletians: that you had burst in with impious violence, seized the chalice deposited [Col. 0556C] in the most sacred place, and broken it. No accusation could truly be more serious than that crime, if it had indeed been so committed and established.

But what sort of accusation is this? What is this shifting and changing diversity of persons, so that they transfer the charge now to one person, now to another? The fact itself is clearer than light: they were eager to lay snares against your prudence. Finally, who henceforth would wish to follow people who invent so many things for harm, especially when they lead themselves into destruction and it is plain that they are accusers concerning fabricated and false matters? To say again: who would wish to follow them and enter the precipitous road of ruin, in which they alone among mortals suppose that they have hope of salvation and help? For if they wished to approach with a clean conscience, to remember a right disposition, [Col. 0556D] and to take on a sound mind, they would readily understand that no assistance is to be expected for them from divine providence, since they offer themselves as imitators of such conduct to their own destruction. This, therefore, which I announce, I shall rightly call not harshness but severity.

Finally, we add this also: make every effort that what we have written should frequently be read aloud to the people, so that the matter may come to everyone’s knowledge, and especially so that those who act and conduct themselves in this manner may be able to recover their senses, since what is now said by us for the sake of correction will be shown true in fact and deed. Thus, since there is such an outrageous degree of wickedness in this affair, let them know that I have decided and am resolved as follows: if they stir up anything of this sort again, I myself shall undertake the hearing of the case, not according to the custom of the churches but according to public laws. Then they will learn that they are brigands not only against the human race but also against divine teaching. May God preserve you, beloved brother.

**Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus, to Pope Athanasius.**

[Col. 0555A] Having read the letters from your understanding, I came to this opinion: that, in replying to your firmness, I should urge you to endeavor to lead God’s people toward good order and compassion. For I especially hold these foremost in my own soul: to cultivate truth, always to preserve justice in my mind, and above all to rejoice in those who travel the straight road of life.

But concerning those worthy of every curse—the Meletians, that is, those most wicked and lawless people, who have now become numb with madness and stir up enormities only through envy, agitation, and tumult, displaying their lawless disposition—I shall say the following. For you see how the men whom they said had been slain by the sword are now among us and enjoy life. What more damaging proof could there be, brought so manifestly and clearly against their case, than that those whom they claimed had been slain are alive and enjoy life, and plainly are able to speak for themselves? This too was added by those Meletians: they strongly maintained that you had unlawfully entered by force, seized a chalice laid up in the holiest place, and broken it. [Col. 0555C] There truly was no greater charge or such great offense as this, if it had actually happened and been committed in this way.

But what is this accusation? What is this change and variation of the affair, that they now transfer the accusation of this crime to one person and now to another? The matter itself is, as it were, brighter than light: they zealously sought to plot against your understanding. After this, who would wish to follow those people who have invented so many things for injury, especially when they themselves lead themselves to destruction and see that they are accusers concerning fabricated and false matters? As I have said, then, who would follow them and go down the steep path of destruction—indeed, that path in which they alone think that they have hope of salvation and assistance? For if they wished to come to a clean conscience, remember the best disposition, [Col. 0555D] and come to a sound mind, they would readily recognize that they have no assistance from providence, since they are imitators of such things and make trial of them to their own destruction. This, therefore, I should rightly call not any harshness, but truth.

Lastly I add this also, which we desire should often be publicly read by your understanding: so that by this means it may come to the knowledge of all, and especially may reach those who act and conduct themselves in this way, so that what is said by us in the language of correction may be shown by the reality of truth to have been spoken. Since, then, there is so great an enormity in this affair, let them know that I have so judged and am of this resolve: if they should stir up anything of this kind again, [Col. 0558A] no longer according to ecclesiastical procedures but according to public laws, I myself shall hear the matters in person, and they will thereafter discover that they are not merely brigands against the human race but also appear to be against divine teaching itself. May God preserve you, beloved brother.

## Letter of Constantine to John the Meletian

*(Athanasius, Apology, p. 186.)*  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0557] The letters of your prudence were very welcome to me. From them I learned what I especially wished to know: namely, that you had laid aside every animosity, had communicated with the Church as was fitting, and had come into full agreement with the most reverend bishop Athanasius. Know, therefore, that for this reason we have greatly praised you: because, abandoning all contention, you have done what is pleasing to God and have sought fellowship with the Church. Therefore, that you may attain what you desire, [Col. 0557B] I have thought it right to permit you to board a public conveyance and hasten to the camp of my clemency. It will henceforth be your part to delay in nothing. Since this letter gives you the use of a public conveyance, come to us as soon as possible, that you may attain your desire and, after seeing us, enjoy fitting joy. May God preserve you, beloved brother.

This was the outcome of that conspiracy. After it had been accomplished, the Meletians turned away from their purpose. But the Eusebians did not cease even then, for it was not the Meletians but the Arians about whom they were concerned; they feared, evidently, that if the others ceased their activity, actors—agents capable of introducing the scheme which they wished to bring forward—would no longer be available to them. Therefore, stirring up the Meletians again, they urged the emperor to order a synod to be convened once more at Tyre. Then Count Dionysius [Col. 0557C] was sent, a military escort was given to the Eusebians, Macarius was brought in chains to Tyre under military guard, and the emperor compelled me by his letters to go there even against my will.

But the whole sequence of the conspiracy may be learned from the letters of the bishops of Egypt. It will be worthwhile, however, to recount the plan by which it was begun, so that from this each person may observe their malice and cunning against us. In Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis there are nearly a hundred bishops. None of them accused us; no presbyter charged us; no one of the people spoke against us. Rather, the Meletians, long ago expelled by Peter, and the Arians had divided the plot between themselves, so that the former claimed for themselves the role of accusers and the latter that of judges. Yet we rejected Eusebius and his associates, because they were our enemies on account of heresy. Then we showed, by the following argument, that the man said to be the accuser was not a presbyter at all. When Meletius was admitted to communion with the Church—would that it had never happened—the blessed Alexander, knowing his cunning, demanded from him a catalogue of the bishops whom he claimed to have in Egypt, and likewise of the Alexandrian presbyters and deacons belonging to his party, or of any whom [Col. 0560A] he had in the Alexandrian district. Pope Alexander did this so that Meletius, emboldened by the authority of the Church, might not sell many ordinations or daily impose new persons according to his pleasure by his lies. He therefore produced this brief list of those of his party in Egypt. (See this list in Athanasius, *Apology*, p. 187.)

The letters from your understanding were very pleasing to me, for from them I learned what I most longed to know: that you had put aside all faint-hearted resentment, had communicated with the Church as was fitting, and had come into the fullest agreement with Athanasius, the most reverend bishop. Know, therefore, that for these reasons I have greatly praised you, because, abandoning every quarrelsome contention, you have done what was pleasing to God by embracing union with the Church. Therefore, in order that you may seem to have attained what [Col. 0558B] you desire, I judged it fitting to permit you to board a public conveyance and hasten to the camp of my gentleness. Henceforth let it be your part to delay in nothing.

[Note: Col. 0557D (1)] Thus the Royal manuscript; the printed editions wrongly read **μελῆσαι**.

Rather, since this letter grants you the use of a public conveyance, come immediately to us, so that you may fulfill your own desire and, having seen us, enjoy the fitting gladness. May God preserve you,

[Note: Col. 0557D (2)] The Royal manuscript reads **διαφυλάξει**, “will preserve.”

beloved brother.

Thus the conspiracy came to an end, and the Meletians, put to shame, withdrew. But those around Eusebius did not remain quiet even in this way. For they were concerned not with the Meletians but with those around Arius, and feared that, should the former cease, they would no longer find persons playing a part through whom they could introduce this scheme. They therefore incited the Meletians again and persuade the emperor to order a synod to be held again at Tyre. [Col. 0558C] Count Dionysius is sent, and military guards are assigned to those around Eusebius. Macarius is sent to Tyre a prisoner under military escort; but to me he writes and imposes necessity, so that we too are sent even unwillingly.

[Note: Col. 0557D (3)] Thus the Royal manuscript; the printed editions read **ἐπιστέλλεσθαι**, less correctly.

The entire conspiracy may be known from what the bishops of Egypt wrote. But it is necessary to state how it was contrived by them from the beginning; for from this one may observe their malignity and their craftiness directed against us. There are nearly a hundred bishops in Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis. None of them accused us, no presbyter found fault with us, and no one of the people spoke against us. But the Meletians expelled by Peter and the Arians were those who had divided the conspiracy: the former arrogating to themselves the role of accusers, the latter that of judges. We, therefore, objected to those around Eusebius as enemies on account of heresy. Then we showed in this way that the supposed accuser was not a presbyter at all. When Meletius was received—would that it had never happened—the blessed Alexander, knowing his cunning, demanded from him a **βρεβίον**, [Col. 0558D]

[Note: Col. 0558D (4)] The Royal manuscript reads **βρευίον**, that is, “a catalogue.” Saint Benedict, *Rule*, ch. 32: “From which things the abbot should keep a *breve*, that is, a catalogue.” Below, likewise, **βρευίον** occurs in the same manuscript; more commonly, however, it is written **βρεβίον**.

of the bishops whom he said that he had in Egypt, of the presbyters and deacons in Alexandria itself, and of any whom he had in its territory. Pope Alexander did this so that Meletius, having obtained the Church’s authority, might not [Col. 0559A] sell many persons [i.e. ordinations] and daily deceive by putting forward whomsoever he wished. He therefore made this catalogue of those in Egypt.

## Letter of Constantine to the Catholics of the Alexandrian Church

*(Council, vol. II, p. 441.)*  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

**Constantine Maximus Augustus, to the people of the Catholic Church at Alexandria.**

[Col. 0560A] Beloved brothers, I greet you, calling upon God, the supreme witness of my will and creator of our law, who presides over the life of all and hates dissensions. But what especially shall I say? That we are well? Indeed; but we might fare far more happily if you loved one another after shaking off hatred. [Col. 0560B] For we must confront the storms raised by contentious persons, because the harbor of love has been abandoned by you. What an absurd thing! Alas, how many disasters arise each day through envy that confuses all things! Thus it comes about that the people of God suffer reproach. Where, then, has confidence in justice gone, when we are enveloped in such a mist of darkness? And this results not so much from the many-sided error as from the faults of malicious people, while we endure those who champion shamelessness and think that those who overthrow fairness and truth are to be disregarded, even though we perceive this with our senses.

What a terrible kind of perversity is ours, if we do not rebuke enemies but make ourselves companions in brigandage? Thus most destructive deceit has easily made a path for itself, because no one resists it. Is there then no feeling left, not even by the gifts of the common nature shared by all, if we consider the commands of the law to be despised? But someone will say: “At least love is found, in accordance with the prompting of nature.” Certainly: we who are furnished both with God’s law and with good natural capacity nevertheless tolerate enemies kindling, as it were, fires with the torches of disturbance and tumult; and though endowed with eyes we do not see it, nor, though instructed by the judgment of the law, do we perceive it. How great, therefore, is the stupor that has assailed our life, when we are so negligent even of ourselves, although God admonishes us!

What then? Is this an insignificant or tolerable evil? Should they not be regarded as enemies? Do not those wicked people rage savagely and cast reproaches upon the house and people of God before our eyes? I leave it to you yourselves to consider with how much madness [Col. 0560D] they do this. For those fools have malice lodged in their tongue; they carry about with them leaden angers, so that they strike themselves in mutual exchange and draw us with them to increase their own punishment. Meanwhile, the person who teaches rightly is judged an enemy; while the person who displays the vice of envy attacks, devastates, and consumes a gentle people—which ought least of all to occur—and willingly ruins himself, glories, exalts himself, overthrows truth, and deceives faith until, by searching, he finds a cave and hiding place for his conscience.

Thus rustic savagery makes those miserable who so rashly exalt themselves though unworthy, crying: “Alas for these wrongs! Is that man a presbyter, or is that man a boy? My standing is attacked; this is owed to me; it has been taken from that man. Therefore, after despoiling everyone, I shall do harm to the utmost of my power.” You would call it a brilliant outcry of madness if you saw the battle-lines, gatherings, or assemblies of those most troublesome factions. [Col. 0561A] O the perversity in our Church of God; a spectacle of a malicious and deranged mind! Will they never at last be ashamed? Will they never condemn themselves? Will they never feel a sting in their souls, so that at least now they may conceive something worthy against imposture and strife and seem to think it?

Envy is a force relying solely upon its own disguises and pigments. Yet these evil people could accomplish nothing against your bishop. Believe me, brothers: they seek nothing else than, after wearing out our time, to leave themselves no room in this life for repentance.

Therefore assist yourselves. I beseech your love: love one another, and with every power pursue those who seek to destroy the favor of your concord. Keep God before your eyes and stand firm in mutual love. For I gladly received your bishop Athanasius and addressed him as a man of God. But it is for you, not for me, to judge in this matter. As regards, however, the office of greeting and conversing with the most reverend Athanasius, I judged him suitable and necessary to minister sacred things to you. Such is the man’s diligence in maintaining equity; it is certainly neither unworthy nor unsuited to our peaceable religion, since it always cherishes the gifts of a saving judgment and follows the exhortations of reason. May God preserve you, beloved brothers.

**Constantine Maximus Augustus, to the people of the Catholic Church at Alexandria.**

[Col. 0559A] Beloved brothers, I greet you, calling upon God as the greatest witness of my will and the sole creator of our law, who presides over the life of all and hates dissensions. But what shall I say? That we are well? Yet we could have enjoyed a better condition of health if you yourselves loved one another in return after casting off hatreds, through which we have abandoned the harbor of love amid the triple waves of contentious persons. [Col. 0559B] Alas for this absurdity! How many disasters are set in motion every day by confused envy! Thus reproaches have been transferred to the people of God. Where, then, has the confidence of justice withdrawn, when we are wrapped in so great a mist of darkness—not only because of manifold error but also because of the faults of ungrateful people? We endure those who award folly, while, perceiving those who beat back fairness and truth, we disregard them.

What is this terrible feature of our wickedness? We do not expose our enemies, but follow brigandage, through which the deceit of destruction, as I may put it, has easily made itself a path when no one opposed it. Is there no perception at all, not even through the gift of the common nature of all, if we have neglected the commands of the law? But someone will say: “Love is found according to nature.” Why then, though we have God’s law as well as natural capacity, do we tolerate the enemies of disturbance and tumult being kindled, as it seems, by certain torches? Though we have eyes, we do not see; though fenced about by the perceptions of the law, we do not perceive. How great, then, is the dismay that has seized our life, when we neglect ourselves so greatly, even while God gives warning?

And is the evil not intolerable? Should we not regard these people as enemies? Do not those utterly destructive men riot against and accuse the house and people of God in our presence, attacking us from the opposite side? I ask you yourselves to consider with how great recklessness they do this. For fools have malice lying upon their tongue. They carry about certain leaden angers, striking themselves in return and drawing us away as gain for their own punishment. [Col. 0559D] The one who teaches rightly is judged an enemy, while the one who has put forward the wickedness of envy seizes the gentleness of the people—though there is no justification for this—ravages and consumes it, wills evil for himself, adorns and composes himself with praise, overturns truth, and deceives faith until he finds, after searching, a den and hiding place for his own conscience.

This perversity, then, makes them miserable when they rashly approve themselves though unworthy, saying: “Alas for these evils! Is that man a presbyter, and that man a child? My honor is affected; it is owed to me; let it be taken away from that man. Since I myself have seized everything for myself, I shall try to destroy everyone by my power.” It is a conspicuous cry of madness, if one sees the ranks and gatherings—or, as I may say, the assemblies of chief priests—of these absurd [Col. 0562A] factions. O our perversity in the Church of God, as I may put it: it is a display of folly. Are they not ashamed? Do they not censure themselves? Do they not sting their own souls, that even now they might seem to think something worthy against deceit and contentiousness?

Envy is force alone, resting upon its own drugs. These wicked men achieved nothing against your bishop. Believe me, brothers: they have sought nothing else than, by wasting our time, to possess not even one place for repentance in this life. Therefore help yourselves, I beseech our beloved ones: love one another, pursue with all strength those who desire to extinguish the favor of our concord, and, looking toward God, love yourselves. For I gladly received Bishop Athanasius and addressed him, convinced that he was a man of God. [Col. 0562B] It is your part to understand these things, not mine to judge. For I judged it necessary that the most reverend Athanasius should minister to you after being greeted by me, considering his care for fairness; this care is not unworthy of my peaceful faith, since it is continually devoted to the good of saving judgment and will have reason urging it forward. May God preserve you, beloved brothers.

## Letter of Constantine summoning Arius honorably to himself

*(Council, vol. II, p. 443.)*  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0561C] Long ago it was made known to your gravity that you should come to my camp, so that you might enjoy the sight of us. We can scarcely sufficiently wonder why this was not done by you immediately. Therefore now board a public conveyance and hasten to come to our camp, so that, after experiencing our kindness and care for you, you may be able to return to your homeland. May God preserve you, dearest one. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

**Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus.**

[Col. 0562C] Long ago it was communicated to your firmness that you should come to my camp, so that you might be able to enjoy our presence. But we greatly wonder that you did not do this at once. Therefore now, having mounted a public conveyance, hasten to come to our camp, so that, having received our favor and care, you may be able to return to your homeland. May God preserve you, beloved one. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

## Letter of Constantine concerning the holding of the Synod of Tyre

*(Council, vol. II, p. 449.)*  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

**Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus, to the holy synod assembled at Tyre.**

[Col. 0561C] It was perhaps fitting, and especially suited to the opportunity of the present time, that the Catholic Church should be free from all contention and that Christ’s servants should be released and free from every quarrel. But since certain persons, impelled by the frenzy of a wicked contention and—lest I say something more serious—living a life unworthy of their profession, have attempted to throw everything into disturbance and confusion, a crime which seems to me to exceed every calamity, therefore I exhort you, running of your own accord, as the proverb says, to assemble in one place without any delay and with all possible speed, to convene a synod, to bring help to those in need, to apply medicine to brothers in danger, to restore divided members to agreement, and to correct meanwhile all errors, while the time permits, so that you may restore to these great provinces the concord which is most fitting, [Col. 0564A] and which the arrogance of a few people has destroyed.

For I judge that this will be pleasing both to God, lord of the whole universe, and to us more delightful than anything however desirable, and that it will be a source of great glory to you yourselves in the judgment and agreement of all mortals, if you restore concord and peace. Do not therefore delay, but with the keenest zeal define the present controversies by the terms that are fitting, since you have assembled with all purity and faith, which our Savior, whom we serve, almost with a loud voice demands above all in every assembly. Nor will anything belonging to our part and prudence be lacking. For I have attended to all matters which you made known to me in your letters; I wrote to the bishops whom you wished, that they should support your concerns and anxieties by their presence and labors.

[Col. 0564B] I have also sent Dionysius, a former consul, to remind all who should attend your synod of the matters to be done, and especially to observe and guard the preservation of impartiality and order. If anyone—though I do not think that this will happen—shall refuse to be present after rejecting and disregarding our command, we shall dispatch someone to teach him, by his expulsion into exile under imperial authority, that it is wholly unfitting for a man to oppose the commands of the supreme emperor issued for the defense of truth.

For the rest, it is the task of your Holiness, without hatred or any favor, but with concordant purpose, according to the ecclesiastical and apostolic rule, to apply the appropriate remedy to all offenses committed through any error, so that you may free the Church from every alien reproach, relieve my concerns, and, after bringing disturbed matters into order through yourselves, obtain the greatest glory for yourselves. May God preserve you, beloved brothers.

**Constantine Augustus, to the holy synod at Tyre.**

[Col. 0562C] Perhaps it was fitting, and especially suitable to the favorable occasion of the times, that the Catholic Church should be free from faction and that the servants of Christ should now have been released from every quarrel. But since certain persons, driven by the gadfly of unhealthy contentiousness—I would not say that they live unworthily of themselves—attempt to throw everything into confusion, a thing which seems to me to have gone beyond every calamity, for this reason I urge you, running, as the saying goes, without any postponement to come together in one place, fill out the synod, bring aid to those needing assistance, heal brothers in danger, restore to agreement the members that have been separated, and correct offenses as the time permits, so that you may restore to so many provinces the concord fitting for them, which—alas for the absurdity!—the arrogance of very few people has destroyed.

For I judge that this is pleasing to God, lord of all, more desirable to us than every prayer, and worthy of no ordinary glory for you yourselves if you call back peace, all human beings agreeing in this. [Col. 0563A] Therefore delay no longer; rather, now intensifying the eagerness of your efforts, make haste to impose the fitting settlement on the matters set before you, having assembled with all sincerity and faith—the sincerity and faith which the Savior whom we serve most insistently requires everywhere, almost uttering them with a voice.

Nothing will be lacking from us in those things that come within my concern. I have done everything that you stated in writing. I sent to those bishops whom you wished, so that, when present, they might share your concerns. I have sent Dionysius, one from among the former consuls, who will remind those who ought to come to the synod with you and will be present as an overseer of the proceedings, particularly of good order. But if anyone, as I do not suppose will occur, should now also attempt to evade our command and should refuse to be present, [Col. 0563B] someone will be sent from us who, expelling him under an imperial command, will teach him that one ought not resist the ordinances of an emperor issued for truth.

It will henceforth be the work of your holiness, by a unanimous judgment, neither from hostility nor from favor, but in accordance with the ecclesiastical and apostolic rule, to devise the fitting remedy for offenses committed, whether they have occurred through some error. Thus you will free the Church from every blasphemy, relieve my anxieties, restore the favor of peace to those now in faction, and procure the greatest honor for yourselves. May God preserve you, beloved brothers.

[Col. 0563]

He then sent letters to Dalmatius, censor at Antioch, entrusting to him the hearing of the homicide case.”

## Confession of Faith Presented by Arius and Euzoius to the Emperor Constantine

(*Councils*, vol. II, p. 464.)

> [Note: [Col. 0563] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0563]

To our most religious and most holy lord, the emperor Constantine: Arius and Euzoius.

[Col. 0564C]

As your singular piety toward God, lord emperor, commanded, we have committed our faith to writing; and we confess that both we ourselves and those who are with us believe concerning God as follows:

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, and in the Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, God the Word, begotten from him before all ages, through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who came down, was incarnate, suffered, rose again, ascended into heaven, and is coming again to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit. In the resurrection of the flesh. In the life of the age to come. In the kingdom of heaven. In one catholic Church of God, extending from one end of the world to the other.

[Col. 0565A] We received this faith from the most holy Gospels, the Lord himself saying to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” But if we do not believe these things as the entire catholic Church and the Scriptures teach, to which indeed we give complete credence, let God be our judge, both now and at the judgment to come. Therefore we beseech your piety, most holy emperor: since we are ecclesiastical men and hold both the mind of the Church and that of the sacred writings, unite us, through your holiness, which both establishes peace and reverently worships God, to our mother, namely the Church, after all disputes and empty subtleties have been removed; so that both we and the Church, living peacefully, may all together offer our customary prayers for the peaceful and pious condition of your reign and for the whole human race.

To our most devout and God-loving lord, Emperor Constantine, Arius and Euzoius.

[Col. 0563C]

As your God-loving piety commanded, lord emperor, we set forth our faith and confess in writing that both we and those with us believe concerning God as follows:

We believe in one God, Father almighty, and in the Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, God the Word, begotten from him before all ages, through whom all things came to be, both those in the heavens and those upon the earth; who descended and was made flesh, suffered, rose again, ascended into the heavens, and is coming again to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit; and in the resurrection of the flesh; and in the life of the age to come; and in the kingdom of heaven; and in one catholic Church of God, [extending] from end to end. And we say that we received this faith from the holy Gospels, the Lord saying to his own disciples: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0566A]; as the entire catholic Church and the Scriptures teach, in which we wholly believe. God is our judge, both now and in the judgment to come. Therefore we beseech your reverence for God, most God-loving emperor, that, since we are churchmen and possess the faith and understanding of the holy Scriptures, we may be united through your peace-making and God-revering piety to our mother, namely the Church, once disputes and superfluous arguments have been removed; so that both we and the Church, being at peace, may together all offer the customary prayers for your peaceful reign and for your entire race.

[Col. 0565]

# Appendix to the Works of Constantine

## Letter Falsely Attributed to Melchiades

> [Note: [Col. 0565C] **Letter.** That the things written in this letter concerning Constantine’s donation to Melchiades and Sylvester are true is most firmly confirmed not only from this source but also by the authority of Optatus of Milevis, an exceptionally trustworthy writer. For in Book I against the Parmenians he writes that, under the third consulship of Constantine and Licinius—that is, in the year of Christ 313—a synod of nineteen bishops was held at Rome, in the Lateran, in the house of Fausta, which was the seat of the Roman pontiff, in the case of Caecilian and the Donatists.
>
> He does not expressly write that this house was given by the emperor to Melchiades. Yet, since no reason appears why a gathering of only nineteen bishops should have required more spacious premises outside Melchiades’ own house, no prudent person can any longer doubt that the Lateran house, or house of Fausta, in which the aforesaid synod was assembled, was given by the emperor to Melchiades, Roman pontiff. It was called Fausta’s because the house, formerly the palace of a very wealthy man named Lateranus and confiscated to the fisc under Nero, was occupied at Rome by Fausta, daughter of Maximian. This is especially so since the uninterrupted possession of the said buildings for thirteen centuries down to the present indicates, or permits one to infer, nothing else.
>
> Since it has therefore been evidently proved that the most august Lateran buildings were granted by the emperor to Melchiades and his successors, the Roman pontiffs, for residence, it may with the strongest evidence be inferred that the emperor wished the same prelate of the Christian religion, by imperial munificence, to be transferred into imperial quarters—like the chief pontiff of pagan superstition who occupied public buildings—and to be endowed and honored by him with equal honor and glory to that possessed by the heads of the various colleges. When this happened, however, we shall say below in the notes on Constantine’s edict.]

## Falsely Attributed to Melchiades

> [Note: [Col. 0566C] **Falsely attributed to Melchiades.** That this letter was ascribed to Melchiades is evident from canon *Futuram*, 12, question 1; likewise from canon *Decrevit*, distinction 88. These bear Melchiades’ name and contain, for the most part, the matters written here; and this is also evident because the letter was commonly appended hitherto after the decrees of Pope Melchiades in earlier editions of the councils.
>
> That it was falsely furnished with the title and name of Melchiades is clear from the fact that it mentions the Council of Nicaea. Almost all historians agree, as will appear below, that this council was held, by universal consent, after the death of Pope Melchiades and after the emperor’s baptism, not under Melchiades but under Pope Sylvester, in the year of Christ 325, the twentieth year of Constantine.
>
> It may therefore perhaps be truer to regard Isidore himself, the compiler rather than collector, as the author of this letter. It is evidently compiled from the third canon of the Council of Chalcedon, a certain fragment of Letter 24 in Book I of Pope Gregory, and the history of the Council of Nicaea. Baronius, year 312, no. 80.]

Or, a testimony concerning Constantine’s munificence toward the primitive Church.

(*Councils*, vol. I, p. 1562.)

[Col. 0565]

[Col. 0565B] No one who reads the divine Scriptures is ignorant that, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, the disciples were assembled as one with the multitude of believers, among whom there was one heart and one soul. They sold their lands and possessions, brought the proceeds, and distribution was made to each according to his need. For the apostles foresaw the future Church among the nations, especially because the Lord had foretold: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel.” Or because they knew that they would be driven from Judaea and dispersed among the nations, and that the Church was to be gathered from an uncultivated people, they acquired no estates in Judaea, but only funds for the support of the needy.

But when, amid the storms and adversities of the world, the Church grew [Col. 0566B], it came so far that not only the nations but even Roman rulers, who held the monarchy of almost the entire world, flocked to faith in Christ and to the sacraments of baptism. Among them, the most religious man Constantine, the first openly to embrace the faith of truth, granted permission throughout the world to those living under his rule not only to become Christians but also to build churches, and he decreed that they might bestow estates.

Finally, the aforesaid ruler made immense gifts and established the construction of the church of the first see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; indeed, he left the imperial seat which Roman rulers had occupied and granted it to be of benefit to blessed Peter and his bishops. Likewise, when presiding over the holy synod assembled at Nicaea [Col. 0567A], seeing before him a complaint brought by certain persons, he said: “You cannot be judged by anyone, because you are reserved for God’s judgment alone. For you have been called gods; therefore you cannot be judged by men.”

From that time onward, moreover, most religious men consecrated to the Lord not only the possessions and estates they had held, but also themselves, building basilicas on their own lands in honor of the holy martyrs in the cities, and countless monasteries in which gatherings of those serving the Lord might convene. Finally, kings, governors, and magistrates not only granted this permission but themselves gave from their own property throughout the kingdoms of the earth, so that the needy, who possessed nothing in the world, might be fed [Col. 0567B], the churches of God built and restored, and supplies provided to those duly serving God and his Church and to his servants, so that they might be free from need. Receiving these things, they might, according to the apostle’s injunctions, offer prayers, petitions, supplications, and thanksgivings for all people, for kings, and for those in high position, that they might lead a quiet and tranquil life.

And the same teacher of the Gentiles, on whom rests the care of all the churches, testifies that this is good and acceptable before God, since through the Holy Spirit he established bishops to govern the Church of God. To them he says: “Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for shameful gain, but voluntarily.” And he also said to them: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs.”

What secular affairs are, the holy canons make clear and prohibit, when they explicitly teach that certain persons who appear to have been chosen for the clergy [Col. 0568A] become tenants of others’ properties for shameful profit and undertake secular business under their own management, making little of the Lord’s ministry, running through the houses of secular people, and, through avarice, assuming the care of estates. The aforesaid holy synod therefore decreed that henceforth no cleric should lease properties or involve himself in secular affairs, unless it be for the care of minors, orphans, and widows, or unless perhaps the bishop of the city should command him to undertake the care of ecclesiastical matters. Here it is plainly evident that secular affairs are one thing and ecclesiastical affairs another.

Was not Moses in the world when he repeatedly entered and left the tabernacle? Within, he was caught up in contemplation; without, he was pressed by the affairs of the weak. Within, he considered God’s mysteries; without, he bore the burdens of the fleshly. Priests in the Church ought to enact his type: when they go out to conduct affairs for the needs of those under them, they should return inwardly to themselves through contemplation of the commandments. So too Paul, who is admitted into heavenly secrets, nevertheless searches out the bedchamber of the fleshly through the bowels of condescension. Thus Jacob saw angels ascending and descending, because the rulers of the Church not only seek the things above by contemplating God, but also descend in compassion to his members below. The Lord’s priests imitate these deeds: they guard themselves and bear the burdens of those under them, and they are seen to be such as that eminent preacher commanded [Col. 0568C]: “those who use this world, as though not using it; those who rejoice, as though not rejoicing; and those who buy, as though not possessing.”

## Edict

> [Note: [Col. 0567D] a In Justel’s manuscript codex the title reads thus: “Here begins a copy of the constitution of Lord Constantine the emperor.” In Greek it is called **Θέσπισμα Κωνσταντίνου**, “Ordinance of Constantine.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0567D] **Edict.** The things here related concerning dominion and temporal kingdom bestowed upon the Roman see are likely, apart from the matters we said above in the notes on the preceding letter. The emperor’s own munificence, never sufficiently admired, his piety toward the Christian religion, and his proper emulation of pagan superstition attest this plainly enough.
>
> That the most Christian rulers of the Franks declared in their own diplomas that they were restoring to the Roman Church those things taken from the Lombards is surely a great argument for the gifts bestowed upon the Roman Church by Constantine. For if, before the privileges bestowed by Frankish kings, the Roman Church already possessed dominion over property, it could have claimed this right from no other source. For it is most certain that this did not occur through force of arms or violent seizure—a fact to which the eastern emperors, who were by no means favorably disposed to the Roman Church and attempted to reduce it to tribute, not only did not object or oppose, but rather confirmed by very extensive privileges.
>
> The following reasons plainly show that this edict was mutilated and deceitfully corrupted by the Greeks, from whose “treacherous donation,” in accordance with Vergil, *Aeneid* II, “I fear Greeks, even when bearing gifts,” it is said to have been received. First, it traces the primacy of the Roman Church to Constantine the emperor, a layman, whereas it is most plainly evident from what we have said above in the notes on the life of Peter and frequently elsewhere that it was conferred upon Peter by God himself and our Lord Jesus Christ. For to Peter and Peter’s successors was spoken that saying in Matthew 16: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven,” etc.
>
> “This,” says Epiphanius in the *Anchoratus*, “is he who heard, ‘Feed my sheep,’ to whom the fold was entrusted.” Therefore Christ the Lord himself gave his sheep to Peter and Peter’s successors to feed and govern: not the sheep of one city or kingdom, but of the whole world; not those of one age alone, but those also which will exist until the consummation of the world. Thus, not without deceit and fraud, what ought to be attributed to God as author is attributed to a human being.
>
> Second, this same edict relates that the same emperor bestowed patriarchal rank upon the Church of Constantinople. If this is true, how is it written that Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, claimed this patriarchal dignity for himself after the Council of Chalcedon had concluded, despite the objections of Leo, Gelasius, and other Roman pontiffs? How could the Church of Constantinople have been patriarchal at a time when the name Constantinople had not yet been given to Byzantium? Therefore one may believe, with the same degree of credence, that the Church of Constantinople was endowed by the emperor with the honor and dignity of a patriarchate and the Roman Church with the honor and dignity of primacy. See what we said above in the notes on Letter 3 of Anacletus.
>
> Theodore Balsamon first published this edict concerning Constantine’s donation from the acts of Pope Sylvester, falsely written in Greek under the name of Eusebius of Caesarea—not to do something pleasing to the Roman Church, but to show that the patriarchate of Constantinople was most ancient. For it is established that two sets of acts of Sylvester are found. The first are Latin, and these were also conveyed to the Greeks, as those found in most ancient codices, received from the Latin, and summarized by Metaphrastes, Zonaras, Cedrenus, Hadrian I in Letter 1 to the emperors Constantine and Irene, and Letter 3 to Charles king of the Franks. The others, known only after the year 1000 of Christ, were invented by some Greek after these; issued under Eusebius’ name from a book on martyrs; and, as is known, augmented by this edict of Constantine, written in Greek by Greeks and quoted by Theodore Balsamon in his commentary on Photius’ *Nomocanon*, to the hatred of the Roman Church and for their own advantage.
>
> To the hatred, I say, of the Roman Church, so that it might be said to have received what it possesses not from Christ—as will be seen below that the most holy Roman pontiffs Gelasius, Nicholas, and others often maintained when arguing against the Greeks—but from the emperor Constantine. And for their own advantage, because this edict affirms that the Church of Constantinople was already patriarchal in antiquity under Constantine—a claim which, as we shall learn under the succeeding pontiffs, was opposed by St Leo, Gelasius, and other pontiffs.
>
> Let heretical innovators, who with great effort and empty zeal attack this edict of Constantine translated from Greek into Latin, know that in these matters they are advancing our case rather than fighting against us. For with Irenaeus, Cyprian, and other holy Fathers, Greek as well as Latin, we profess that the privileges of the Roman Church were conferred not by human beings but by Christ upon Peter, and transferred from Peter to his successors.
>
> The dominions over temporal property bestowed upon the Church are proved by the original diplomas of the emperors who made the donations, and the Church itself quietly possesses them.
