But St Leo, Felix, Romanus, Gelasius, Hormisdas, Gregory, and other successor pontiffs who flourished from Constantine’s time onward always defended the rights granted to the Roman Church against their assailants, not by the authority of this Constantinian edict but rather by divine and evangelical authority. Of all those who presided over the Church before the year 1000, many of whom saw and cited the genuine acts of Sylvester mentioned above, none is read to have made any mention of this edict, since the fabricated edict had not yet been added by Greek impostors to those acts.
>
> Among those who in good faith received from the East into the West the acts of Sylvester, corruptly altered by Greek malice and bad faith through the addition of this fabricated edict, and who defended them as genuine, legitimate, and free of every imposture and fraud, Pope Leo IX is found to have been the first. In his letter to Michael of Constantinople and Leo, bishop of Acrida, in the year of the Redeemer 1054, he mentions this Constantinian edict concerning the donation made to Sylvester. Because it thereby acquired much credit and authority, I believe that very many of the later writers, even the most weighty and learned, read and accepted it in good faith without any suspicion of fraud or imposture.
>
> In the time of Pope Benedict XII, namely in the year of Christ 1339, a certain diploma in the name of Emperor Otto III emerged and was printed in full by Baronius, vol. 12. It states that this same Constantinian edict concerning the donation was fabricated and devised by its author John the Deacon. But since Baronius attacks that diploma there with many and very strong arguments, thereby invalidating its authority, I add, for more fully overthrowing this often-mentioned edict of Constantine, leaving aside that spurious diploma of Otto, that Gregory VII, Alexander III, and other later pontiffs, most vigorous defenders of the Church’s rights, did not mention this edict as a thing truly done. Likewise Pepin and Charles before Otto, Henry, and other emperors—most munificent donors in their diplomas by which they gave cities and regions to St Peter—did not touch upon this Constantinian edict even in a word; nor did the recipient pontiffs lodge any complaint on this account. These facts render the credibility of this edict highly suspect. It does not, and cannot, derogate from the rights and privileges of the Church founded upon the firm rock.]

## Constantine to Pope Sylvester

(*Councils*, vol. I, p. 1530.)

[Col. 0567]

[Col. 0567C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—Emperor Caesar Flavius Constantine: faithful in Christ Jesus, one of the same holy Trinity, our Lord God and Savior; gentle, beneficent, conqueror of the Alemanni, Goths, Sarmatians, Germans, Britons, and Huns; pious, fortunate, victorious and triumphant, ever Augustus—to the most holy and most blessed father of fathers, Sylvester, bishop and pope of the city of Rome; to all his successors, the pontiffs who shall sit in the see of blessed Peter until the end [Col. 0568C] of the age; and also to all the most reverend and God-beloved catholic bishops subject to that same most holy Roman Church by this our imperial constitution throughout the whole world, those now established and all who shall be established in time to come: grace, peace, love, joy, patience, and mercy from God the Father almighty, Jesus Christ his Son, and the Holy Spirit, with you all (Gal. 5; 1 Tim. 1).

> [Note: [Col. 0567D] b These words are absent from certain codices; Pope Leo IX does not have them in his letter to Leo of Acrida, chapters 12, 13, and 14; nor do Ivo, *Decree*, book 5, chapter 49; Gratian, distinction 96, under the title *Palea*; Balsamon; and others. Yet they survive entire in the collection of Isidore Mercator, said to have appeared about the year of Christ 800; and they were published by Merlin, Crabbe, Surius, Nicolinus, Binius, and others.]

The things which our Savior and Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0569A], Son of the Most High Father, through his holy apostles Peter and Paul, and through the intervention of our father Sylvester, supreme pontiff and universal pope, has deigned wondrously to accomplish, our most gentle serenity has taken care to make known, by a plain narrative on the page of this our imperial ordinance, for the knowledge of all peoples throughout the entire world.

First, setting forth in the inward confession of our heart, for the instruction of the minds of you all, our faith which we learned from the aforementioned most blessed father and our intercessor, Sylvester, universal pontiff, and then proclaiming the mercy of God poured out upon us, we wish you to know—as we indicated through our previous sacred pragmatic command—that we have departed from the worship of idols, mute and deaf images, things made by hands, demonic contrivances, and every pomp of Satan, and have come to the complete Christian faith, which is the true light and everlasting life.

We believe, according to the instruction given us by that same grace-bearing, supreme father and teacher of ours, Pontiff Sylvester [Col. 0571A], in God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible; and in Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, our Lord, through whom all things were created; and in the Holy Spirit, Lord and giver of life to the whole creation. We confess Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in such a way that in the Trinity is perfect fullness of divinity and unity of power. God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit: and the three are one in Jesus Christ. There are, therefore, three forms, but one power.

For God, ever wise from before time, brought forth from himself the Word, through whom the ages that were always to be generated existed. And when, by that same Word alone of his wisdom, he formed the whole creation from nothing, the Word was with him, ordering all things by his hidden mystery. Therefore, having completed the powers of heaven and all the materials of earth, by the gracious decision of his wisdom he first formed man from the clay of the earth in his own image and likeness, and placed him in the paradise of delight. The ancient serpent and envious enemy, the devil, made him an exile from those same joys through the most bitter tasting of the forbidden tree. And after he had been expelled, the devil did not cease [Col. 0571B] to hurl his poisonous darts in many ways, drawing the human race away from the way of truth in order to persuade it to serve the worship of idols—that is, the creature rather than the Creator—so that by this means he might cause those whom he could entangle in his snares to be burned with him in eternal punishment.

> [Note: [Col. 0571D] a Read: “whom.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0571D] b Perhaps better: “does not cease.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0571D] c Another reading: “having taken pity, he directed his creature, sending his holy prophets, through whom …”]

But our God, taking pity on his creature, sent his holy prophets, announcing through them the light of the future life—that is, the advent [Col. 0571C] of his Son, our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ—and sent that same only-begotten Son of his and Word of wisdom. Descending from heaven for our salvation, born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. He did not lose what he had been, but began to be what he had not been: perfect God and perfect man; as God accomplishing wonders and as man enduring human sufferings. Thus, as our father Sylvester, supreme pontiff, proclaims, we understand the Word as man and the Word as God, so that we do not doubt in any way that he was true God and true man.

Having chosen twelve apostles, he shone forth in miracles before them and an innumerable multitude of people. We confess that the same Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0571D] fulfilled the law and the prophets, suffered and was crucified according to the Scriptures, rose from the dead on the third day, was taken up into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead; and of his kingdom there shall be no end. This is our catholic orthodox faith, declared to us by our most blessed father, Sylvester, supreme pontiff.

Therefore we exhort all people and the diverse nations of the Gentiles to hold, worship, and proclaim this faith; to receive the grace of baptism in the name of the holy Trinity; and with devoted heart to worship our Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, who lives and reigns with the Father and Holy Spirit through infinite ages, and whom our most blessed father Sylvester, universal pontiff, preaches.

> [Note: [Col. 0571D] **For he himself.** Pope Hadrian, in his letter to Constantine and Irene included in the Second Council, recounts this whole history in almost the same manner and thus confirms the truth of this edict. See what we said above in the notes on the life of Sylvester.]

For our Lord himself, having mercy on me, a sinner, sent his holy apostles to visit us and shone upon us with the light of his splendor, so that you may rejoice that I have been drawn away from darkness and have come to the true light and knowledge of truth. For when a severe and foul leprosy had invaded all the flesh of my body [Col. 0572B], and the care of many assembled physicians had been employed, yet I had obtained health from the care of none, the priests of the Capitol came to me. They said that a pool ought to be made on the Capitol and filled with the blood of innocents, and that, if I were washed in it while it was warm, I could be cleansed.

> [Note: [Col. 0572D] d Another reading: “and did not attain health from the care of even one.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0572D] e Another reading: “and [that] I, warm in that place …”]

In accordance with their words, many innocent infants having been gathered, when the sacrilegious priests of the pagans wished to slaughter them and fill the pool with their blood, our serenity saw the tears of their mothers and immediately recoiled in horror from the crime. Taking pity on them, we ordered their own sons restored to them; and, vehicles having been provided and gifts granted, we dismissed them rejoicing to their homes.

When that day had passed and the silence of night had come upon us, as the time for sleep approached [Col. 0572C], the holy apostles Peter and Paul appeared and said to me: “Because you have put an end to your crimes and recoiled from the shedding of innocent blood, we have been sent by Christ, our Lord God, to give you counsel for the recovery of your health. Therefore heed our instructions and do whatever we tell you. Sylvester, bishop of this city, fleeing your persecutions, is concealed with his clergy in caves among the rocks on Mount Soracte. When you have brought him to yourself, he will show you the pool of piety; and when he has immersed you in it three times, all this disease of leprosy will leave you. When this has been done, render this return to your Savior: by your command, let churches be restored throughout the entire world. Purify yourself in this respect also, that, leaving every superstition of idols, you may worship and serve the living and true God, who alone is God and true, so that you may attain his will.”

Rising from sleep, therefore, I immediately carried out what I had been instructed by the holy apostles. Having summoned that same chief and magnificent father and illuminator of ours, Sylvester, universal pope, I told him all the words commanded me by the holy apostles [Col. 0573A]. We asked him who those gods Peter and Paul were.

> [Note: [Col. 0573D] **Who those gods Peter and Paul were.** Just as Manoah, Samson’s father, when he had seen the angel of the Lord, said to his wife, “We shall die, because we have seen the Lord” (Judg. 13); and as the woman concerning Samuel’s soul said, “I saw gods ascending from the earth” (1 Sam. 28): so the emperor calls the chief apostles, whom he knew to be human beings, “gods,” either because he conceived something beyond the human in his mind concerning their appearance, or because he judged them to be such gods as those of whom Scripture says in Psalm 81: “God stood in the assembly of gods; I said, You are gods, and all are sons of the Most High.” In this sense the same Emperor Constantine called gods the bishops assembled for the council at Nicaea. See Baronius, year 324, no. 39.]

He answered that they were not truly called gods, but were apostles of our Savior, the Lord God Jesus Christ. We then began again to ask that same most blessed pope whether he had portraits of those apostles, so that from the painting we might learn that these were those whom the revelation had shown. Then that venerable father ordered the images of those apostles to be brought forth by his deacon.

> [Note: [Col. 0573D] **Then that venerable father [ordered] images of the apostles.** Eusebius testifies, at the end of Book VII, chapter 14, that venerable images of Peter and Paul, and above all of our Savior Jesus Christ, were preserved in the Church even to his own times and that he himself had seen them, in these words: “We too have seen preserved images of the apostles Peter and Paul, and of Christ himself, represented in paintings by a variety of colors,” etc. If they remained and were seen in Palestine, devastated by so many wars, how much more could the same images, accurately representing their unaltered and genuine faces, have been preserved at Rome, where the same apostles lived longer and were finally martyred?]

As I looked at them and recognized in those images the features of the faces of those whom I had seen in my sleep, I confessed with a loud cry before all my satraps that these were those whom I had seen in my sleep. Thereupon our same most blessed father Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, prescribed for us a time of penance within our Lateran palace [Col. 0573B], clothed in a single hair-shirt, so that by vigils, fasts, tears, and prayers I might obtain from the Lord our God Jesus Christ the Savior forgiveness for all things that I had done impiously and ordained unjustly.

Then, through the laying on of hands by the clergy, I came to the bishop himself. There, renouncing Satan, his pomps and works, and all idols made by hands, I publicly professed before all the people, of my own free will, that I believed in God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible; and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary.

The font having been blessed—

> [Note: [Col. 0574D] **The font having been blessed.** Namely, the baptistery, which still remains and is called the “Constantinian bath” by Marcellinus, a pagan writer of that age, in Book XXVII of his *History*. By these words he provides noteworthy testimony to the emperor’s baptism, besides the testimony of many other writers.]

—he cleansed me there with the saving water by triple immersion.

> [Note: [Col. 0573C] a Another reading adds *verbi* (“of the Word”) after *mersione* (“immersion”).]

When I had been placed in the bosom of the font—the Constantinian baptistery or bath—I saw with my own eyes a hand from heaven touching me. Rising cleansed from it, know that I was cleansed from all the foulness of leprosy.

> [Note: [Col. 0573C] b Another reading: “I recognized.”]

When I had been lifted from the venerable font and clothed in white garments, he administered the sealing of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit by the anointing of blessed chrism, and anointed my forehead with the sign of the holy cross, saying: “May God mark you with the seal of his faith, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0574A], in the sealing of faith.” And the whole clergy answered: “Amen.” The bishop added: “Peace be with you.”

Thus on the first day after receiving the mystery of sacred baptism and after the healing of my body from the foulness of leprosy, I recognized that there is no other God than the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, whom blessed Pope Sylvester preaches: Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity. For all the gods of the nations whom I worshipped until now are shown to be demons, works made by human hands.

For that same venerable father made very clear to us how great a power our Savior bestowed upon his apostle, blessed Peter, in heaven and on earth. Finding him faithful in his response, he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” [Col. 0574B] (Matt. 16). Consider, you powerful ones, and attend with the ear of your heart to what the good teacher and Lord added to his disciple, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (*ibid.*). It is exceedingly wonderful and glorious to bind and loose on earth, and to have what is bound and loosed also in heaven. And when, through the preaching of blessed Sylvester, I came to know these things, I found that through the benefits of blessed Peter himself I had been restored in complete health.

[Note: [Col. 0573C] c Certain manuscripts begin after the title as follows: “After I had learned that, under the instruction of blessed Sylvester, I had been purified by threefold immersion in the word of salvation and cleansed from every defilement of leprosy through the benefits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul: ‘It is useful,’ etc.”]

We have judged it useful, together with all [Note: [Col. 0574D]

“We have judged it useful, together with all.” These words occur in Greek and Latin in the Nomocanon of Photius, bishop of Constantinople. See what we said above, and the notes added by order of Gregory XIII to the canon *Constantinopolitan*, distinction 96, and many others. St Gregory I frequently mentions the patrimony of St Peter in his letters.]

our satraps, and the whole senate, and my nobles, and likewise all the people subject to the empire of Roman glory, that, just as Saint Peter appears to have been appointed on earth as vicar of the Son of God, so also the pontiffs who are successors of that prince of the apostles (or, who exercise the office of that prince of the apostles [Col. 0574C]) should obtain, by grant from us and our empire, a power of primacy greater than that which the gentleness of our earthly imperial serenity appears to possess; choosing for ourselves that same prince of the apostles and his successors as steadfast patrons before God.

And just as we have decreed that our earthly imperial power (or, our power is earthly and imperial) be reverently honoured, so we have decreed that his most holy Roman Church be honoured, and that the most sacred see of blessed Peter be gloriously exalted above our [Col. 0575A] empire and earthly throne, granting to it power, the dignity of glory, strength, and imperial honour; and we decree and enact [Note: [Col. 0575D]

“We decree and enact.” We have said above, at the beginning, that the matters added below concerning the primacy of the Roman Church and the patriarchal honour conferred upon the Church of Constantinople are false and interpolated.]

that it shall hold primacy over the four chief sees—Antioch, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0575D] a In Justellus’s manuscript this is placed before the preceding see and is numbered third, unlike in Justinian, *Novella* 3, at the beginning, and in the Council of Chalcedon, canon 28, and elsewhere, where, after Rome, it is placed before all the others.]—and likewise over all the Churches of God throughout the whole world. And the pontiff who at any given time presides over that most holy Roman Church shall be higher than, and chief of, all priests in the whole world; and by his judgment all matters that must be ordered for the worship of God or for the stability of the Christian faith shall be arranged.

For it is just that the holy law should possess the headship of primacy in the place where the founder of the holy laws, our Saviour, commanded blessed [Col. 0575B] Peter to occupy the chair of the apostleship; where, also, bearing the gibbet of the cross, he drank the cup of blessed death and showed himself the imitator of his teacher and Lord. And there let the nations bend their necks in confession of Christ’s name, where their teacher, the blessed apostle Paul, with his neck outstretched for Christ, was crowned with martyrdom. There, until the end, let them seek a teacher, where the holy body of the teacher rests; and there, bowed down and humbled, let them perform the service of the heavenly King, God our Saviour Jesus Christ, where they had served the dominion of a proud earthly king.

Meanwhile, we wish all peoples of every race and nation throughout the whole world to know that we have built within our Lateran palace [Note: [Col. 0576D]

“We have built within our palace.” Concerning churches built by the emperor, see the tract concerning Constantine’s beneficence and the notes written upon it above.]

a church from its foundations for that same Saviour of ours, the Lord God Jesus Christ, with a baptistery; and you should know that we ourselves carried upon our own shoulders twelve baskets laden with earth from its foundations, according to the number of the twelve apostles. We decree that this most holy church be called, honoured, venerated, and proclaimed the head and summit of all churches throughout the whole world, as we have established by our other imperial decrees.

We have also built churches for the blessed Peter and Paul, the foremost [Note: [Col. 0575D] b Or: princes.] apostles, which we enriched with gold and silver; and there, depositing their most sacred bodies with great honour, we constructed their shrines of electrum [Note: [Col. 0575D] (1) Ado, in his chronicle, calls Cyprian bronze five feet thick.]—against which no force of the elements prevails—and placed upon each of their shrines a cross of purest gold and most precious gems, fastening them with golden nails. [Col. 0575D] For the fitting-out of lights in those churches, we bestowed landed estates and enriched them with [Col. 0576A] diverse possessions [Note: [Col. 0575D] c Or: adorned them.]; and by our sacred imperial command, in the East as in the West, and likewise in the northern and southern regions—namely, in Judaea, Greece, Asia, Thrace, Africa, and Italy, and in diverse islands—we have granted them liberty through our generosity, on this express condition: that everything be administered through the hands of our most blessed father, the pontiff Sylvester, and his successors.

Therefore let all the people rejoice with us, as also the nations of the peoples throughout the whole world; and, exhorting them, we urge all to render immense thanks with us to our God and Saviour Jesus Christ, because God himself, who is in heaven above and on earth below, visiting us through his holy apostles, has made us worthy to receive the sacrament of holy baptism and bodily health.

[Col. 0576B] For this reason we grant to those holy apostles, my most blessed lords Peter and Paul, and through them likewise to blessed Sylvester, our father, supreme pontiff and pope of the universal [Note: [Col. 0575D] d Perhaps one should read *universalis*, “of the universal.”] city of Rome, and to all his successor pontiffs who shall sit in the see of blessed Peter until the end of the world, and we hereby transfer to them our Lateran imperial palace, which is preferred to and surpasses all palaces in the whole world; next, the diadem, namely the crown of our head, together with the *phrygium* [Note: [Col. 0576D] e Or: *frigium*. Note that the *phrygium* was made from peacock feathers.], that is, the mitre; also the shoulder-band, namely the *lorum* which customarily encircles the imperial neck; moreover, the purple cloak and scarlet tunic, and all imperial garments; and also the rank [Col. 0576C] of the imperial presiding horsemen. We likewise confer the imperial sceptres together with all the standards, and also the *banta* [Note: [Col. 0576D] f Or: “spears and standards, and also bands.” See Albericus de Rosate, under *baltheum*.], and the various imperial ornaments, and all the ceremonial procession of the imperial eminence, and the glory of our power.

For the most reverend clergy serving that same most holy Roman Church in its diverse orders, we decree that they shall possess that eminence in distinction, power, and pre-eminence with which our most ample senate appears to be adorned [Note: [Col. 0576D] g Read: “adorned.”], that is, that they be made patricians and consuls; and we further enact that they be decorated with the other imperial dignities. And just as the imperial soldiery is adorned, so we decree that the clergy of the holy Roman Church be adorned. And just as imperial power is arrayed with diverse offices—namely, chamberlains and doorkeepers, [Col. 0576D] and all the watchmen [Note: [Col. 0576D] h Perhaps “watches” should be read.]—so we wish the holy Roman Church also to be decorated.

And that pontifical splendour may shine forth most fully, we decree this also: that the horses be adorned with the *manipuli* [Note: [Col. 0577D] a Read: *mappulis*, “napkins.”] and linen cloths of the clerics of the same holy Roman [Col. 0577A] Church—that is, with the brightest white colour—and that they ride in this manner. And just as our senate uses footwear embellished with *udones*, that is, white linen, so let the clergy use it also; and thus let heavenly things, like earthly things, be adorned for the praise of God.

Above all, we grant permission to our most holy father Sylvester, bishop and pope of the city of Rome, and to all most blessed pontiffs who shall come after him in succession and for all time, for the honour and glory of Christ our God, that in that great Catholic and Apostolic Church of God, by our decree [Note: [Col. 0577D] b Add: “of the senate.”], he may, according to his own clerical counsel [Note: [Col. 0577D] c Perhaps read: “the clerical order.”], choose whomever he wishes and enroll him in the number of religious clerics, with no one at all presuming arrogantly to interfere.

We have [Col. 0577B] therefore decreed this also: that our venerable father Sylvester, supreme pontiff, and all his successor pontiffs, may use a diadem—namely, the crown that we granted him from our own head—of purest gold and precious gems, and may wear it upon the head for the praise of God and for the honour of blessed Peter. But the most blessed pope himself did not at all permit himself to use that crown of gold over the crown of the clerical office which he bears for the glory of blessed Peter. We, however, placed with our own hands upon his most sacred head a *phrygium* of brilliant whiteness [Note: [Col. 0577D] d Or: “a *Phrygium* shining with white brilliance”; or, as Justellus’s manuscript has it, “a *frigium* gleaming with pure splendour.” Others read *antifrygium*.], signifying the splendid resurrection of the Lord; and, holding the bridle of his horse out of reverence for blessed Peter, we performed for him the office of groom. We decree that all his successors shall use this same *phrygium* distinctively in processions, in imitation of [Col. 0577C] our empire.

Therefore, lest the pontifical apex be diminished in esteem, but be adorned even more than the rank and glorious power of earthly empire: behold, we grant and leave, as has been said, both our palace and the city of Rome, and all the provinces, places, and cities of all Italy and the western regions, to our aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0577D] e Or: oft-mentioned.] most blessed pontiff Sylvester, universal pope [Note: [Col. 0578D] f Or, adding: “transferring and leaving.”], and to the authority and dominion of his successor pontiffs. By firm imperial decree, through this our sacred and pragmatic divine constitution, we enact that these be administered by them, and we grant that they shall remain forever under the right [Note: [Col. 0578D] g Or: “rights.”] of the holy Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0578D] h Better: “shall remain.”].

Accordingly, we have judged it fitting that our empire and the power of our kingdom be transferred and moved to eastern regions, and that in the province of Byzantium [Note: [Col. 0577D]

“To the province of Byzantium.” Shortly after his baptism Constantine proposed to build a new Rome, free from every form of idolatry. Therefore, in the year 324 after Christ’s birth, from the restoration of Ilium, being forbidden by divine providence, he went to Byzantium; he splendidly adorned that city and honoured it with his own name and with the imperial seat. Indeed, it seems not to have occurred without great providence of God that, after the imperial seat had been transferred to Constantinople, no emperor, eastern or western, ever transferred the seat back to Rome. Zonaras says of Constans, nephew of Heraclius, that he indeed contemplated transferring the empire to the city of Rome, but by no means succeeded; so that we may understand that not without the prompting of the divine will Rome, the chief city, was destined for the supreme head of the Church. See what we shall say below concerning the First Council of Constantinople.]

a city be built in a fine location in our name, and our empire established there; because where the primacy of priests and the head of the Christian religion has been established by the heavenly Emperor, it is not just for an earthly emperor to exercise power.

We decree that all these things, which we have established and confirmed both by this [Note: [Col. 0578D] i Or: “all these things which we have established and confirmed by this our sacred imperial decree and by other”] our imperial sacred decree and by other divine decrees, remain inviolate and unshaken until the end of the world. Therefore, before the living God, who commanded us to reign, and before his dreadful judgment, through this our imperial constitution we solemnly charge all our successor emperors, all nobles and satraps, likewise the most ample senate and the whole people throughout the [Col. 0578B] world, now and in all future times subject to our empire, that none of them may in any way oppose, break, or impair in any respect those things which have been granted by us through imperial sanction to the most holy Roman Church or to all its pontiffs.

But if anyone—which we do not believe—should prove a violator or despiser in this matter, let him be bound under eternal condemnations; let him experience the holy princes of God’s apostles, Peter and Paul, as adversaries in this present and future life; and, burned in the lowest hell, let him perish with the devil and all the ungodly.

Confirming with our own hands the document of this our imperial decree, we placed it upon the venerable body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, there promising the same apostle of God that we would preserve all these things inviolate and leave commandments to our successor emperors that they must preserve them; and, with the assent of the Lord God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, we hand over [Note: [Col. 0578D] j Perhaps better: “handed over.”] to our blessed father Sylvester, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and to all his successor pontiffs, for perpetual and happy possession.

And the imperial subscription: “May the Divinity preserve you for many years, most holy and most blessed fathers.” Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth consulship of our lord Flavius Constantine Augustus and the consulship of Gallicanus, men of highest rank. [Note: [Col. 0578D]

“Constantine Augustus for the fourth time, and Gallicanus, consuls.” There is a double error in the chronology of these consuls. First, it is erroneous that Constantine had Gallicanus, rather than Licinius, as colleague in his fourth consulship. Second, it is erroneous that the events narrated above are dated to this consulship, which fell in the year 315 after Christ, since it is certain from what precedes that Constantine was not initiated by baptism before the year 324 after Christ’s birth.

A certain Bartholomew Picernas of Monte Arduo asserted, from a Greek exemplar, that he had translated into Latin the edict of this famous donation; and on this matter he addressed a letter to Julius II, Roman pontiff, in these words:

“While I was reading in this most celebrated library of yours—most blessed Father, I suppose he means the Vatican—I came upon a certain Greek booklet containing the Donation of Constantine. It seemed right to me to translate it from Greek into Latin and to dedicate it to you, most holy Father, who are the vicar of Christ and successor of Peter and Sylvester. For there are many who have asserted that Constantine’s Donation is false; among them is Lorenzo Valla, a man by no means unlearned, who dared to write a book on the false Donation of Constantine. The most reverend Cardinal of Alexandria, most learned in both laws, most effectively refutes his opinions and most diligently answers his objections. That man perhaps thought that what he himself had not read could not be found among others. Nor is it surprising, since he was of such biting temperament that he did not hesitate to criticize Aristotle, prince of philosophers, and to censure all authors in the Latin tongue so that he spared no one. But lest I be too long, let us hear Constantius himself. These are his words.”

He then appends his own elaborate translation of the edict, as he boasts—or, as others think, merely an interpolated version, with the older Latinity altered in some places. Ortvinus Gratius of Deventer, a priest, reprinted this translation by Picernas at Cologne in 1535. We have faithfully presented the Greek fragments that we found in Balsamon, of which there are two translations, one by Henry Agylaeus and the other by Gentian Hervet; we shall add the rest also when they come into our hands. Indeed, Augustine Steuchus, who himself wished to contend in this arena, affirms that he saw four Greek exemplars in the library of the same supreme pontiff. While these pages were already at press, we received a letter from Rome, dated 4 June, from the most learned theologian and our most dear friend, Father Peter Possinus of our Society, stating that a complete text is still preserved in Vatican manuscripts 614, folio 76; 789, folio 185; 973, folio 39; 1416, folio 127; and perhaps in others also. I wished you not to be unaware of this.]

[Col. 0579A]

## Autograph Covenant of Love and Concord between Emperor Constantine, Saint Pope Sylvester, Tiridates King of Armenia, and Saint Gregory, Illuminator of the Armenians

(From Mansi’s Collection of Councils.)

By the will and power of the consubstantial Holy Trinity—the incomprehensible Father, his only-begotten Son, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and the life-giving and liberating Holy Spirit—this our Caesarean testament, firm and immutable in God, has been committed to the memorial of letters by the mighty and independent command of us, Constantine, ever-victorious and glorious Augustus, great king of kings and ecumenical emperor of the Romans, whose invincible dominion extends throughout the whole [Col. 0579B] world; who, by the power of the true God and the strength of Christ’s glorious cross, rule victoriously over the whole world from the bounds of the vast Ocean to the rising of the sun. It has likewise been committed by our command as supreme pontiff of the Romans, Sylvester, successor of Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, who possess the power, by the keys of the kingdom of heaven, to bind and loose in heaven and on earth over all Christian nations from west to east, and who preside over the whole Church of Christ.

Therefore, by these documents we leave testimony before all that, called by the Holy Spirit, the great king of the Armenians John, also called Tiridates, and the living martyr of Christ and valiant confessor, Lord Gregory, illuminator of the East and North—our most beloved brothers in [Col. 0579C] Christ, and chief friends and most faithful leaders of this our sublime dominion, participants in our counsels—have arrived here to see this city, mistress of West and East, heir of the holy princes of the apostles, their venerable successor the pope, the glorious emperor devoted to the newly received Christian faith, and the great and most powerful empress Helena.

For this reason, while all our empire confirmed in God [Col. 0580A] exulted and overflowed with the highest joy, we went out with a most noble retinue to meet such great men. Having greeted one another reciprocally and rendered each other due honour, we offered worship to our immortal King Jesus Christ. Then, entering the Church of the holy apostles, we venerated their sacred relics, blessing Christ, the glorifier of his saints.

(Then, after many other matters, the following occurs:)

By divine will, through the mediation of the Mother of God, the holy apostles, and all the saints, we, the most valiant Latins and the invincible Turcomans—namely, each king, each pontiff, and both the Roman and Armenian peoples—have unanimously sworn ourselves into fraternal union and concord. Before the glorious standard of Christ’s cross we have confirmed this pledge and perpetual covenant of friendship between us; and, as a pledge of this same firm and indelible covenant, we have inscribed this brotherhood of the western and eastern peoples with the dreadful and most precious blood of Jesus Christ. Thus we ought to owe one another faith, love, and concord, just as we owe them to him who became our brother, Christ God: defending one another unto death, and most gladly dying for one another; being friends to one another’s friends and enemies to one another’s enemies. Let none of these two peoples dare to draw the sword against the other; and let the sword of those who violate this enter their own hearts, and their bow be broken.

Let this covenant between these two peoples remain firm until the [Col. 0580C] consummation of the age. But whoever withdraws himself from it, let him be cut off from the holy Christian faith and incur the curse of Cain, Judas, and the priests who slew Christ. Let angels and human beings say: “So be it.”

(Then it again has the following:)

But we, Sylvester, supreme pontiff of Rome and of the whole world, after we saw that our most illustrious son, Emperor Constantine, had exalted to the utmost of his ability King Tiridates of Armenia, crowned, together with the whole Armenian people and country, and had bestowed upon them the highest honours, also readily inclined our mind to advance the honour of the valiant confessor of Jesus Christ and our fellow bishop Gregory. [Col. 0581A]

(And after other matters it adds:)

Therefore, in the name of the most holy Trinity, we blessed him, placing upon his head the venerable right hand of the divine apostle Peter and the sacred linen cloth of Jesus Christ; and we appointed him, together with his successors, supreme patriarch of all Armenians. We will that henceforth the pontiff of Armenia shall ordain the patriarch of the Georgians and have power to establish other bishops over those Armenians who are found dispersed everywhere among other Christian peoples. Then let the region of the Albanians be brought under the obedience of its own patriarch; he, having been elevated from the Albanian king, shall be consecrated by that same Armenian [Col. 0581B] pontiff.

Moreover, when the three patriarchs—namely those of Alexandria, Antioch, and [Col. 0582A] Jerusalem—initiate a new patriarch, this shall be done by the will and concurrence of the pontiff of Armenia. And the profession of faith which the newly elected patriarch ought to communicate to us, let him communicate to the pontiff of the Armenians; for we appoint him our vicar in that central region of Asia.

(After other matters, the same holy Sylvester finally concludes thus:)

Accordingly, by this our sublime mandate, power is granted to the pontiff of the Armenians to bind and loose in heaven and on earth whomever he wishes in accordance with the apostolic canons. Those blessed by the same pontiff of the Armenians are blessed also by Christ the Lord, by the holy apostles, by the other saints, and by us ourselves; and those excommunicated by him shall remain under the same excommunication until they turn to repentance. [Col. 0582B]

## In the Year of the Lord 321: Nazarius

[Col. 0581]

## Panegyric of Nazarius, Delivered to Constantine Augustus

(From the Old Panegyrics, La Baume edition.)

## Notice

[Col. 0581B]

This speech was delivered, as is evident from its opening, in the year of Christ 321, on the Kalends of March, the birthday of the Caesars Crispus and Constantine, when, at the beginning of [Col. 0581C] their fifth year, they paid their five-year vows and undertook ten-year vows. At this time Constantine the Great’s fifteenth anniversary coincided, and vows were made for his twentieth anniversary. Constantine was absent, although Nazarius nevertheless directs his speech to him: “I seem,” he says, “to address one present to me, who, though absent from sight, cannot nevertheless be torn from our minds.”

This speech is without controversy ascribed to Nazarius. Concerning him Eusebius says in the *Chronicle* for the year of Christ 325: “Nazarius is regarded as a distinguished rhetorician.” And Jerome, for the year 337: “The daughter of the rhetorician Nazarius equals her father in eloquence.” Arnaldus Pontacus calls her Eunomia, a Christian virgin, in his *Chronicles*, relying, as he himself says, upon the authority of four Vatican manuscripts. Nazarius is also mentioned by Ausonius in the fifteenth epigram of the *Professors of Bordeaux*. Whether this Nazarius of ours was the same man whom the clergy of Marseilles, among whom he performed the office of reader, delegated by vote with Bishop Oresius to the synod at Arles, is doubted by our Jean-Baptiste Guesnayrus in his annals of the province of Marseilles.

## Synopsis of the Panegyric

In the exordium: He proves that the joy of that day, on which the five-year celebrations of Constantine and the Caesars are likewise observed, cannot be matched by an orator’s eloquence.

Division: It appears to be: I. Concerning the Caesars Crispus and Constantine; II. Concerning Constantine Augustus.

[Col. 0582C] Part I. Crispus had already crushed the Franks and Germans by following his father’s example. Constantine was already holding his second consulship, §3. How great each was may be judged, both because they resemble their father Constantine in bodily appearance and virtues, and because they have been formed by his illustrious deeds, §4. He congratulates both on this formation.

Part II. As he is about to pass to Constantine, he seizes upon the first thing that occurs amid the great variety of his splendid achievements, §5. Having subdued Maxentius, Constantine is gentle and merciful in victory, §6–7. He is compared with that cruel tyrant, §8, whom Constantine had wished to soften by clemency and therefore offered terms of alliance, §9. He rejected the conditions of peace, §10, and fastened Constantine’s images [Col. 0582D] to the ground, §12. Constantine takes up arms, remembering not so much this insult as that inflicted upon his country, §13. Soldiers appear to him as if suddenly fallen from heaven, §14. He had long before experienced heavenly help when, beginning his reign auspiciously, he captured and put to death the most ferocious kings Ascaric and Regaisus, §16; when he routed in one assault the Franks, §17, Bructeri, Chamavi, Herusci, Vangiones, Alamanni, and Tubantes, who had been gathered for war; and when, disguised, he advanced into the midst of the [Col. 0583A] battle-line and engaged hand-to-hand with two barbarians, §18. Thus, intending to cross the Alps to free Italy, §19, he takes Segusium, §21; the Taurini, §22; Brescia and Verona, §25; Aquileia and Mutina, §27; and at last, after routing Maxentius’s army and overwhelming Maxentius himself in the collapse of the Milvian Bridge, §28, he enters Rome victorious, §30. The report of this victory is spread everywhere, §32. Through generosity and wisdom he restores Rome’s splendour, §35. What, further, ought the city not to expect from the Caesars? The courage and goodness of both are wonderfully praised, §36.

At the end: After so many things wisely arranged by Constantine, he says that this one thing should be desired: that they be perpetual, §38.

## The Panegyric Begins

[Note: [Col. 0583C]

I.—“As much as other rulers [surpass private persons].” Gregory the Great said the same thing concerning the kings of Gaul, book V, letter 6, to Childebert, king of the Franks: “By as much as royal dignity surpasses other men, by so much does the summit of your kingdom unquestionably excel the kingdoms of other nations.”

“The five-year celebrations of the Caesars.” Those of Crispus, Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, whom their father Constantine had designated Caesars five years earlier. From this passage it is clear that, as we have observed, not only emperors’ five-year anniversaries but also those of Caesars were customarily celebrated.

“And this is not.” Nor is it necessary to search the innermost recesses of the mind.

“The hidden things of minds.” As “the bitter things of cares,” “the hidden things of lands”; shortly afterwards, “the wished-for things of vows”—as I have already observed once and again.

“And indeed this is not.” Indeed, those rejoice in the highest goods who set no measure to their joy.]

I. As I am about to speak of the most august praises of Constantine, who rises above the rulers of all ages by as much as other rulers have withdrawn from private persons; and as I am about to speak amid a gathering of exultant joys and eager gladness, made more abundant than usual by the first five-year celebrations of the most blessed Caesars, I perceive that no eloquence can either be desired or conceived which may bring a grace worthy of the occasion, abundance worthy of the subject, or capacity worthy of your enthusiasm.

For at this very moment the cheerful and blessed devotion of all displays itself. There is no need to probe the hidden things of minds; the splendour of public gladness is manifest upon everyone’s face, and the judgments of their souls are read beforehand in their serene brows. For the greatness of overflowing joy cannot contain itself; disdaining the hiding-places of breasts, it projects itself outwardly in so many bright forms that it is understood to be no greater [Col. 0584A] than it is genuine. Nor indeed do those rejoice in moderate blessings who know no measure in exultation.

[Note: [Col. 0583D]

II.—“We enjoy.” We do indeed enjoy present blessings most delightfully; but the anticipated hope of future things adds delight to them, joining by the mind’s anticipation things separated by an interval of time.

“Separated.” Or perhaps “disparate,” as the Vienna edition has it.

“The fifteenth year.” Constantine’s fifteenth year coincided with the Caesars’ five-year celebrations. It was customary at five-year celebrations to offer public vows for ten-year anniversaries, and in the fifteenth year to offer vows for the attainment of twentieth anniversaries, as the poet Porphyry expressly testifies in the panegyrical poem which he delivered in Constantine’s presence in this very year, 321 after Christ; fragments of it were published through the efforts of Pithou. Thus in that poem:

> Holy Father, ruler of those above, may joyful twentieth anniversaries  
> Increase for Augustus, and tenfold festivities for his sons.

The same is established by hundreds of coins bearing *VOTIS X MULT.* and *VOTIS XX*, that is, “many vows for ten-year anniversaries,” “vows for twenty-year anniversaries.”

“And this concerning things to come.” We judge from the prosperity of earlier times what we ought to hope for in the future.

“Let us do this.” Read with Acidalio: “We do this not more generously than securely”; that is, our vows are not futile. We desire these things, not more because of our favourable disposition toward the ruler than because we are induced by certain hope that we shall obtain them.

“Unrestricted,” etc. That is, unimpeded liberty.

“And the things which.” Both those animated by memory of past prosperity and those which an eager mind anticipates will one day be received abundantly.

“Timorous.” That is, the speech which will fall below the unspoken thought of each individual comes forth timidly. Indeed, those who formally undertake public encomia of great deeds, though they appear to wish to magnify them, reasonably fear that they may diminish things which are so great that they cannot be amplified.

[Col. 0585C] “Formal praise.” Παθητικῶς (*pathētikōs*, “in an emotive sense”), as in Ovid:

> And confessed guilt alone makes one ugly, etc.

“With a desire to magnify.” Thus restored after Acidalio in place of “than to magnify.”]

II. We indeed enjoy the greatest pleasure in present things, but the prospect of the future now lends them charm; and things separated in time are joined by the anticipation of our minds. The greatest prince is passing the fifteenth year of his saving reign, but we already foretell his twentieth anniversary and confirm trust in the future by the felicity of the past. The five-year celebrations of the most blessed Caesars hold us absorbed in joy, but in their destined tenth years, swiftly moving vows and flying hopes have already taken their stand. Once we have attained these, we shall extend the sequence of the blessings we desire.

Thus all things that come prosperously from [Col. 0584B] our rulers bear uninterrupted fruits, and what is received delights us no more than what is expected aids us. But what are we doing, limiting by twenty or now by thirty years things which we perceive as eternal? The merits of our rulers are greater than the aspirations of our vows. Rather, let the course of this happy empire extend into immensity, and let those who always contemplate divine things take no heed of human limits. Certainly we are not disappointed in what we desire, since, though we pray for the greatest things, we do so more generously than securely; for, owing to the heavenly favour resting upon him, the hope of attaining them is as certain as the freedom to desire them is unrestricted.

Who among all men, then, can satisfy by speech the most ardent enthusiasm of his hearers in these congratulations which are aroused by present things, strengthened by the memory of earlier things, and eagerly fed by reflection upon what seems destined to overflow into the future? And when I wish to embrace only public benefits, while each individual privately reflects upon his own, a timorous speech must be brought forth, one that must be overcome by silent reflection. Even in public affairs, a formal [Col. 0585A] encomium of great deeds, though it bears before itself a desire to magnify, rightly gives rise to fear of diminution where their greatness has removed the hope of amplification.

[Note: [Col. 0585C]

III.—“Though you are absent from sight.” Therefore this speech was not delivered in Constantine’s presence.

“Torn away.” That is, you cannot nevertheless be withdrawn from our thoughts.

“Who, I say.” That is: who, I say, is there who, when celebrating your praises, acts rather so as not to be silent than in hope of being able to equal them in speech?

“To aspire to praises.” A highly unusual form of expression.

“Or crushes their magnitude.” Perhaps one should read: “or is crushed by their magnitude.”

“Afflicted.” By the brigandage and violence of Maxentius’s followers.

“And although the other.” Against the Germans and Franks, whose kings Regaisus and Ascaric he captured in war and punished with death.—“And although the other,” etc. That is, although in your other most successful expeditions, earlier and later, you undertook nothing less than rescuing Rome from impending ruin.

“Of whom,” etc. That is, in whose tender years the first seeds of virtue that would someday emerge are apparent.

“One already for crushing.” Crispus, attacking the Franks and Alamanni by inaccessible routes in the harshest season of a most bitter winter, routed them in the year 320 after Christ. The poet Porphyry attests this in his panegyric of Constantine: “but the powers of Crispus for brave deeds prepare without doubt to protect the farther banks, the Rhine and the Rhone,” etc.

“The other already [holds] the consulship.” Namely Constantine Caesar, the eldest of all the children whom Constantine Augustus had by Fausta, daughter of Maximian, in the same year, 320 after Christ.

“He shows,” etc. That is, since he is already brave beyond his age.

“When the coverings,” etc. That is, when his noble nature shines through the coverings of childhood.]

III. Who, I ask, most mighty Constantine? For I seem to myself to be addressing you in person: though you are absent from sight, you cannot be torn from our minds. Who, I say, could aspire to praise you, relying more on the hope of equalling you than on the merit of not keeping silence? Who is so powerful in speech, whose abundance is so ample and fortunate, that, when it has touched upon your virtues, it is not either overwhelmed by their number and stunned by the hopelessness of the undertaking, or worn down by their magnitude, or so dimmed by their brilliance as to retain only so much lustre as it has gathered from the light of your deeds?

When your divine excellence, with mercy as its companion and victory as its attendant, received the city of Rome not as she was rushing to ruin, but, when she was afflicted and wholly prostrate [Col. 0585B], awakened, revived, and raised her; and when your other most fortunate campaigns, both before and afterwards, embraced no less a task than the rescue of Rome from the very jaws of fate: what can be conceived or spoken worthy of your greatness, when, among your praises, that is not the greatest which is foremost in the whole world?

To wish to recount also the praises of your most noble Caesars is indeed a delightful undertaking, but not one of moderate difficulty. In their youthful years there appears not the swelling bud of a virtue that will one day break forth, nor the flower that heralds a good disposition, more joyous than fruitful; rather, it is already fruit-bearing, and there is a harvest of the greatest fruits mature beyond what their age would permit. One of them has already begun, by crushing enemies, to divert to his own name the grave paternal terror at which all barbarism has always trembled [Col. 0585C]. The other, already conscious of the consulship, already of the reverence paid to himself, already of his father—if his parent or brother leaves anything untouched—shows that he will soon be a conqueror, since in spirit he already surpasses his age. For every outstanding nature is carried away toward likeness to its own; nor does it gradually and slowly give proof of its goodness when a vigorous genius bursts the wrappings of infancy [Col. 0586A]. For whence comes the most mighty prince’s such overflowing affection for his children, unless because he already sees in them an image of himself?

> **Note [Col. 0586C]**
>
> **IV.** “Commendet,” etc.: that is, among those whose station is below yours, the sole bond of nature makes their own children dear to them; and they love them, whatever they may be, because they see that none of their own virtues is lacking in them.
>
> **“Ductae lineae”**: He who undertakes to paint a panel first draws an outline and, as it were, prescribes boundaries to his work within which to exercise his art.
>
> **“Quippe indole similes”**: Acidalius reads otherwise: *Quibus indoles similis, sed*, etc.
>
> **“Sed,” etc.**: That is, happier than his father in this respect: that he has his father himself as a teacher from whom to learn.

IV. Let the mere tie of nature commend their children to inferiors, and let those who do not find in them what they desire from themselves love them, whatever they may be. But the most excellent prince is especially helped by this: that, in their earliest years, the outlines have already been drawn within which the image of his virtues may be enclosed. And the best of fathers, yet a better emperor, rejoices not so much for himself as for the commonwealth when he looks upon children like himself. To bring to perfection the good qualities implanted in them, instruction—the active craftsman of virtues—is joined, not sluggishly; so that the hope of equalling their father [Col. 0586B] is assured. Alike in disposition, but happier in fortune because they learn under the same teacher. From tender years they look upon him; their eyes and minds are fixed upon him; they turn aside from no contemplation of him, uncertain whether they admire or love him—except that both must necessarily occur together in mingled union. For love commends deeds, and from this admiration arises; and deeds, when they are admirable, in turn create love. Thus, as the children watch whatever he does most nobly, it is pleasing to them chiefly because of himself, and at the same time grows within them through eagerness to imitate it.

Indeed, in your education, best Emperor, not everything was set before you which you might wish to follow. Yet you, the keenest observer of right actions, whenever anything was done otherwise, withdrew your modest eyes from the care of looking upon it. Your clemency will grant pardon if truth makes me bolder [Col. 0586C].

> **Note [Col. 0586C]**
>
> **V. “Existimare quidem”**: Perhaps because princes possess something divine, as in Pacatus, *Panegyric* 27: “If it is lawful and reverent for mortals to judge of heavenly things.”
>
> **“Nam”**: That is, the majesty encountered at the very entrance repels one who examines too curiously.
>
> **“Propius adegerunt”**: Read *adhibuerunt* or *adjecerunt*.
>
> **“Quod”**: That is, what happens to those who gaze at the sun with fixed eyes.
>
> [Col. 0587C] **“Non terror”**: That is, terror is not an obstacle, nor does there appear a proud display in concealing virtues, which are for the most part hidden, or in withholding one’s appearance.
>
> **“Intrinsecus latent”**: Thus Livineius restores it for *extrinsecus*.
>
> **“Prohibetur”**: Perhaps *perhibetur*.
>
> **“Benignus,” etc.**: You admit men graciously.
>
> **“In te reserata”**: We venerate them disclosed in you.
>
> **“Ad eumdem”**: That is, they tend to the same end of glory.
>
> [Col. 0587D] **“Ut verenda,” etc.**: That is, so that those proceeding need not fear having to turn back at some loss.
>
> **“Sed”**: I am surrounded by that very abundance of material.
>
> **“Specie,” etc.**: That is, equal in beauty, alike in greatness.

V. It is indeed unlawful for anyone to form a judgment concerning princes: for reverence placed before one at the very threshold repels the inquirer; and if any have pressed their mind nearer, they have suffered what happens to eyes striving toward the sun: their sight has been dazzled [Col. 0587A], and they have lost the power of seeing. But you, greatest of princes, cause what was formerly obstructed to seem open; you desire as much to be wholly seen as others refused it. Terror does not bar the gaze, nor does a specious display prevent the disclosure of those things which generally lie hidden within or delay the sight of them. You graciously receive the eyes of men, and no hostile radiance blunts the beholder; rather, a serene light invites him. Now at last we understand what had been lacking in former rulers, after venerating in you, openly disclosed, those things which we had feared as concealed in others.

Therefore, most blessed Caesars, proceed securely, as you do, through all the paths of your father’s praises. His virtues do not advance by one simple road, but all lead to the same issue of glory. There are no turnings of desire, no winding paths of error [Col. 0587B], so that those proceeding need not fear a costly retreat. Thus you have undertaken a swifter course, since you have no delay in considering the road. But I, surrounded by this very abundance of material, am uncertain which path ought especially to be taken, or by what entrance I may enter: so many things offer themselves, equal in appearance and corresponding in magnitude.

> **Note [Col. 0587D]**
>
> **VI. “Interiorem,” etc.**: That is, the character of a house’s interior adornment is judged from its very threshold.
>
> **“Praedicationis,” etc.**: That is, the entrance to praise or embellishment.
>
> **“Tyrannidis impiae”**: Under Maxentius.
>
> **“Majestatis”**: That is, Rome made the splendour of her former dignity serve to make her seem more worthy of pity.
>
> **“Quod,” etc.**: That is, because those whom we love greatly we honour no less when they experience adverse fortune.
>
> **“Quae,” etc.**: That is, services rendered with regard not so much to the recipients’ misery as to their dignity.
>
> [Col. 0588C] **“Connexio virtutum”**: This was the opinion of the Stoics, as Cicero and Horace report in various places.
>
> **“Sic,” etc.**: That is, for thus they render one another mutual service.
>
> **“Juvant”**: I have restored this from an old manuscript in place of *juvat*. Claudius Puteanus likewise reads differently: *sic enim mutua se opera juvant*—“for thus they aid one another by mutual services.”
>
> **“Onus Urbis”**: Which you had assumed along with the title Augustus. Others read *honos Urbis*, “the honour of the City,” for above it says: “they came not out of pity but out of honour.”
>
> [Col. 0588D] **“Cum stirpe”**: Understand Maxentius together with his son Romulus, slain in that disaster.

VI. But just as, in great houses, the vestibules themselves reveal the interior ornament, so Rome ought to afford us, as we approach the wondrous inner chambers of immense virtues, an entrance to praise and a gateway of panegyric. Once submerged beneath the evils of impious tyranny, and, the greater she was, the more pitiable, she made the splendour of her former majesty contribute to the appeal of compassion. Yet to you, greatest Constantine, she was venerable even in that condition; for our reverence for those whom we love deeply remains undiminished even when their fortune has collapsed [Col. 0587C]. Services bestowed upon the fallen are more welcome when they come not from pity but from honour.

But surely the wise rightly establish a harmonious connection [Col. 0588A] among virtues. For they aid one another by mutual service and share the fruit of their labour, so that their inseparable and undivided intermingling is easily apparent. You waged war, greatest Emperor, because the burden of the City laid it upon you no less than her distress persuaded you to it. Thus no more praise was granted from it to your courage than was paid to your dutiful devotion, because, while pursuing the wicked, you freed the wretched. For Rome was established and founded for eternity, all those who could have shaken her condition having been destroyed with their stock.

> **Note [Col. 0588D]**
>
> **VII. “Fortunae,” etc.**: That is, fortune added some adversity—what it is accustomed to mingle with prosperous circumstances—and marred the victors’ joy.
>
> **“Ut,” etc.**: That is, so that victory must be attributed not so much to courage as to integrity.
>
> **“Servatura”**: Watching over or observing. Below, §26: “No one would *servaret* the combatant,” that is, observe him. Others nevertheless read *scrutatura*, “searching.”
>
> **“Nec,” etc.**: That is, nor does it distinguish between the souls of those whose interests it promotes.
>
> **“Fandi”**: That which judges what is lawful and unlawful.
>
> **“Tot,” etc.**: That is, inflamed in a full heart by the consciousness of so many victories.
>
> **“Ut horrendas,” etc.**: That is: so that your soldiers, like lightning, might overthrow the unknown force of hostile arms and bodies, and that in a single engagement you might happily destroy whatever strength long-continued crime had amassed [Col. 0589C].

VII. Mars did not wander uncertainly, as the outcomes of wars commonly do, through various and shifting chances; nor did fortune’s reversal, which for the most part fastens something sad onto prosperity, wound the victors’ joy. Rather, so great and extensive was the slaughter of the enemy, so fortunate and bloodless the victory, that one might believe not that a doubtful war had been fought, but that the punishments of the impious alone had been exacted. So greatly does a good conscience claim its due even amid arms, that victory has now begun to belong not more to valour than to integrity.

For God, the arbiter of events, watches us from on high; and although human minds possess deep recesses of thought, nevertheless the divinity that watches over us wholly makes itself known. Nor can it be that, while the divine power grants us the breath we draw and all the benefits by which we are nourished, it has withdrawn from care for the earth and does not distinguish between the lives of those whose interests it governs. That power, therefore—that majesty which distinguishes what may and may not be spoken, which weighs, balances, and examines every measure of deserts—that protected your dutiful devotion; that shattered the mad wickedness of that tyrant [Col. 0588C]; that aided your unconquered army, burning in full hearts with the consciousness of so many victories, with such additional strength as either God could grant or your affection ought to deserve; so that the lightning-like soldier might overthrow terrifying battle-lines and unfamiliar strength of iron and bodies, and that you might consume in a fortunate encounter whatever the long contrivance of prolonged crime had prepared [Col. 0589A].

> **Note [Col. 0589C]**
>
> **VIII. “Gravate”**: That is, it grieves you that the wicked perish; you were reluctantly brought to battle.
>
> **“Non imperando habilem”**: Maxentius.
>
> **“Quod,” etc.**: That is, because his spirit was too narrow to be equal to the great office wrongly entrusted to him.
>
> **“Ubi,” etc.**: That is, once a weak mind, overwhelmed by so great a burden of fortune, grants itself licence to do what it cannot prevent [Col. 0589D].
>
> **“Sermo,” etc.**: That is, lest such discourse corrupt.
>
> **“Adeptae felicitatis”**: *Adeptae* is used passively (παθητικῶς), as in Ovid, *Tristia* IV.8.19:
>
> > “Lest he fall and dishonour the many palms already won.”
>
> And Cicero: “All desire to attain old age; they criticize it once attained.” Some read *adepti* instead of *adeptam*, but wrongly, as Henri Estienne observes in the preface to his book *On Latinity Wrongly Suspected*. Many examples of verbs of this kind occur in authors, which I refrain from citing here.

VIII. O Emperor, yours is a clemency to be proclaimed no less than a victory! Even the evil death of the wicked weighs heavily upon your mind. You fought unwillingly, though you conquered so easily. For you had long foreseen that the man was unfit to rule and incapable of such great majesty: the greatness of an office wrongly entrusted overflowed the narrow limits of his mind. Those who cannot preserve what they possess, when weakness has fallen beneath so great a burden of fortune, turn their power into licence. Why should I recount the most shameful massacres of the unfortunate, the insatiable feeding of lusts, the wretched plundering of inheritances? Let these things indeed be passed over—not only lest my speech revive the memory of evils that has been laid to rest, but lest such discourse, while bringing forth the vices of another, defile the most sacred praises of the prince [Col. 0589B].

The recollected removal of evils is indeed an increase of attained prosperity. Yet, as in fields, although industry must uproot many things that have occupied the soil, those who behold the crops produced do not recognize the labour of the cleansed ground; so it is enough for Constantine’s praises that we see the good things now blossoming, without rehearsing the evils cut down.

> **Note [Col. 0589D]**
>
> **IX. “Remedia molliora”**: By sending envoys to him, in case he might be willing to make a treaty with him; Maxentius arrogantly refused it, having cast down and overthrown Constantine’s statues in utter mockery.
>
> **“Quin,” etc.**: That is, indeed you compel yourself to seek a meeting and concord with him—if it is more proper to call it concord than pardon.
>
> **“Concordiam quam veniam”**: For *magis quam veniam*, “rather than pardon,” as in Plautus, *Rudens*: “It is certain to die rather than to suffer,” etc.
>
> **“Quam”**: That is, so that he may not subject it to himself.
>
> **“Concordia,” etc.**: That is, you wished to come to conference not in order to give him permission to harass the City with impunity.

IX. Yet, Emperor, you endured him sporting amid so many evils; and although you knew everything, by overlooking and enduring you wearied out men’s wishes. Thus, even though you had not yet been provoked by the man, you did not take up arms unjustly, being already the enemy of his vices. But, as was fitting for your clemency, you tried gentler remedies, so that a milder cure might heal what you preferred to soothe rather than cut away [Col. 0589C]. Indeed, you even wrested from your own mind the desire for a meeting and the will for concord—if it is lawful to call it concord rather than pardon when one who can conquer wishes to forgive.

And I do not doubt that your heavenly wisdom adopted this course because, by joining herself to him, it might either entirely extinguish or moderately restrain the man’s most burning desires. For no lust is so senseless that it does not yield when temperance enters into partnership with it. Shameful cowardice casts down its eyes when the beauty of virtue is set before it. You may see insolence, confused by gravity, moderation, and decorum, hesitate and cling back. Thus it is clear that, best Emperor, when you commanded concord, you intended not to give him immunity for harassing the City, but to seek a gentler victory, preferring to conquer his vices rather than his arms [Col. 0590A].

> **Note [Col. 0590C]**
>
> **X. “Nec”**: Nor is any bond so tight that it can hold together, by binding, things tending in different directions [Col. 0590D].
>
> **“O quam,” etc.**: That is, oh, how painfully those who have already advanced along the path of wickedness recall themselves to honour.
>
> **“Appetitum tuum”**: That is, what you sought. Others read *affectum tuum*, “your affection”; others, *amicum tuum*, “your friend.” — “He rejects your desire.”

X. But surely things divided by a natural separation cannot unite by any force; nor is there any bond so faithful that it can hold in its embrace things tending in opposite directions. Your outstanding prudence, with dutiful devotion always joined to it, evidently considered all the benefits of concord: that it is the foundation and root of peace, the seedbed of civic goods, the crop of public tranquillity [Col. 0590B], and the nourishing mother of peace. But oh, how painful is the return to honour for those who have once taken a step from wickedness! You summon him to fellowship; he recoils from, opposes, and shrinks from your desire. He thinks that nothing is shared between you, because nothing is alike. Certainly, virtue is no longer free to remain at rest. For to wage war in the mind while abstaining from arms is not a plan for concord but cowardly dissension.

> **Note [Col. 0590D]**
>
> **XI. “Mirari tamen nequeo”**: *Non* or *vel satis* is missing.
>
> **“Cum id,” etc.**: That is, because he did not accept what you offered him.
>
> **“Sed natura affert”**: Perhaps *fert*.
>
> **“Ejus,” etc.**: That is, injuries inflicted upon one whom you love.
>
> **“Quod,” etc.**: That is, what either hope might anticipate or fortune promise.
>
> **“Dolis”**: The tricks which he had used against Severus, Galerius, and Maximian.
>
> **“Sed non,” etc.**: That is, prudence need fear no more being deceived in a conference than valour need fear joining battle with an enemy unsuccessfully [Col. 0591C].
>
> **“That Lynceus”**: Similar accounts occur in Pliny, *Natural History* VII.21; Strabo’s *Geography*; Aelian, *Various History* II.13; Plutarch; Cicero, *Academica* IV; and Valerius Maximus IV, final chapter. To avoid excessive length, I do not quote their words.
>
> **“Non tantum”**: Read *non tanta ut*, as Gruter emends from an old manuscript after Acidalius.
>
> **“Cum spes,” etc.**: That is, after every hope ought to have been broken and the intention of making peace abandoned.

XI. Although one ought not to look for reason in those who, once begun, rush headlong from the path, I nevertheless cannot but wonder that he did not embrace what would have been shameless for him to dare to hope for. Did he suppose that you would endure Rome’s deadly laceration slowly and indifferently? But nature brings it about that injuries to one whom you love, even if grave in reality, become still graver through love. Or [Col. 0590C] did he believe that he was not inferior in joining battle? How impossible this was for him to suppose, the outcome showed, since, although standards had so often been brought together, there had never been anything which either hope might seek or fortune promise.

Perhaps he thought you could be deceived by tricks. But your valour is no less secure in an encounter than your prudence is against fraud. For who is keener in foreseeing? Who more vigilant [Col. 0591A] in seeing? Who considers present things more sharply, future things more extensively, doubtful things more surely, deceptive things more successfully? Not even that Lynceus could contend with you in this regard, who, as poets relate, easily pierced with his sight the partitions of walls and trunks of trees; nor even that other man of whom the same antiquity spoke, who, stationed on a Sicilian lookout, was accustomed to discern ships approaching the harbour of Africa, though the vision of man was hindered neither by the surrounding air, made thicker by the exhalation of the sea, nor by the great distance of separated regions.

> **Note [Col. 0591C]**
>
> **XII. “Habes”**: Perhaps *habet*.
>
> **“Quam,” etc.**: That is, an insult inflicted by one inferior to another in rank [Col. 0591D].
>
> **“Venerandarum imaginum”**: Constantine’s images, conveyed to Rome according to custom, were cast down by Maxentius, as has been stated above in the life of Constantine.
>
> **“Divini,” etc.**: That is, the divine countenance disfigured with mud.
>
> **“In quo lumen mundi”**: Read with Acidalius: *cum lumen mundi*, etc.
>
> **“Commovere,” etc.**: That is, Emperor, let your virtue, conscious of itself, at last arouse you.
>
> **“Nec permittas furori”**: Do not allow him, whose spirit is insufficient to do anything against you, to vent his rage upon your image.

XII. Since every hope ought to have grown cold and the will to make peace had been alienated, who can doubt that he was delivered by divine power into your arms, when he advanced to such madness as even voluntarily to provoke one whom he ought to have courted? O how sharp are the stings of grief which an insult imposed by an inferior gives you! [Col. 0591B] For behold—alas! words scarcely suffice—the bitter overthrow of your venerable images and the shameful defacement of your divine countenance. O impious hands! O savage eyes! Were you not thus darkened? While you obscured him in whom was the light of the world, did you not yourselves drink in the deserved darkness? At last, O virtue conscious of itself, rouse him, and do not leave this to a madness to which nothing else against you was possible.

But what, blind madness, will you finally achieve? This countenance cannot be obliterated. It is fixed in the hearts of all; it does not endure through the recommendation of wax or the dyes of pigments, but blossoms through the longing of minds. The one final oblivion of Constantine is the setting of the human race. Yet now your injury will make his patience more worthy of praise; men will seek him more eagerly whom the picture does not restore. The longings of minds burn more fiercely when they have lost the consolations of the eyes [Col. 0591C].

> **Note [Col. 0591D]**
>
> **XIII. “Ingestos,” etc.**: That is, you bore new causes of grief every day, as though you were drawing a kind of callus of endurance over yourself.
>
> **“Dolor,” etc.**: That is, grief revealing itself.
>
> [Col. 0592C] **“Et male clausi,” etc.**: You could not conceal your grief for afflicted Rome; and although she preferred the wrongs done to herself to those done to you, you were nevertheless induced by her grief rather to declare war on Maxentius.
>
> **“Ambo”**: Rome, whom he addresses, and Constantine, of whom the speech is made.
>
> **“Ratiocinatores,” etc.**: That is, good assessors of your respective duties, you did something alike: you, Rome, through longing—the one thing you could do; he, both by wishing you well and by securing that good for you.
>
> **“Nec illa divinitas”**: Nor did that divinity which obeys you in all things fail to obey your wishes, when it caused Maxentius not to accept the offered treaty, thereby granting you a richer harvest of praise.

XIII. Surely, Rome, you suffered nothing more grievous, nothing more miserable. Although you lamented more deeply in secret, and [Col. 0592A] bore the daily accumulated griefs with a kind of callus of hardened endurance, your grief, less prudent than you, confessed itself; it did not fear detection, and signs of ill-concealed sorrow came forth through the telltale face. For this, Rome, wounded by so many blows, you desired to be avenged, although the most excellent prince, disregarding his own injury, preferred to avenge yours. Thus you both, kindly assessors of duties, did equal things: you by your wish, with which alone you had power; he by love and ability alike, so that he might grant you as many goods as he recognized that you wished for him. Therefore, Emperor, you fought under compulsion; but you especially deserved victory because you did not desire it. You desired peace, but forgive us if the wishes of all prevailed more strongly. Nor did the divinity accustomed to favour your undertakings oppose you in this matter; rather, something did not accord with your wish so that it might yield a greater return in proportion to your deserts [Col. 0592B]. Concord was denied to one for whom victory stood ready.

> **Note [Col. 0592D]**
>
> **XIV. “In ore denique”**: Is this to be understood of the Labarum? Or of what he says shortly afterwards befell the Romans of old—that cavalrymen or even whole legions came from heaven to Constantine? Eusebius indeed says nothing of this matter. But Nazarius affirms that it was on the lips of all Gaul, in Constantine’s own presence and before peoples of various nations.
>
> **“Inconcreta,” etc.**: That is, without bodily substance.
>
> **“Audirique patientes”**: Thus Horace, *Odes* I.2: *patiens vocari Caesaris ultor*, “willing to be called Caesar’s avenger”; and I.19: *vultus lubricus aspici*, “a countenance slippery to behold”; likewise, *Art of Poetry* 163: *cereus in vitium flecti*, “wax ready to be bent into vice.”
>
> **“Ubi meritum,” etc.**: That is, after they had borne witness to your virtue, they withdrew themselves from human sight.
>
> **“Flagrabant,” etc.**: That is, some majestic quality shone forth from them as their shields flashed.
>
> **“Et coelestia,” etc.**: That is, ambition indeed extends even to heavenly beings.
>
> [Col. 0593C] **“Qui,” etc.**: That is, he who recognized that he had been surpassed by you in earthly triumphs.
>
