> **“Ampliorem,” etc.**: That is, he experienced himself as made more glorious by your favour; and he who could now confer benefits on others received glory from you in place of a benefit.

XIV. Finally, it is in the mouths of all the Gauls that troops were seen who declared themselves sent from heaven. And although heavenly beings are not accustomed to come beneath human eyes, because the simple and incorporeal substance of subtle nature eludes our gross and dim sight, yet those helpers of yours endured to be seen and heard; once they had borne witness to your merit, they fled the contaminating contact of mortal vision. But what appearance are they said to have had? What vigour of body? What stature of limbs? What eagerness of purpose? Some awful majesty blazed from their flashing shields, and the terrible light of heavenly weapons burned; for they had come in such a manner that they might be thought yours. This was their own speech; this they declared among the hearers: “We seek Constantine; we go to Constantine’s aid” [Col. 0592C].

The divine indeed possess their boastfulness, and ambition touches even heavenly beings. Those who had fallen from heaven, those sent by divine power, gloried that they served under you [Col. 0593A]. Constantius your father, I suppose, led them: he who had yielded to you in earthly triumphs as his superior was now conducting divine campaigns, being himself divine. This too is a great fruit of your dutiful devotion: that, although he had become a sharer in heaven, he perceived himself made greater through your favour; and although his gifts could now flow to others, your gifts flowed back upon him himself.

> **Note [Col. 0593C]**
>
> **XV. “Restricte, compteque”**: Strictly and sparingly, as Livineius thinks—that is, frugally. Plautus, *Asinaria*, scene I, act I: “His mother keeps him tightly and sparingly.”
>
> **“Duos juvenes”**: Castor and Pollux. Horace, *Odes* I.12: “One famed for horses, the other for surpassing in boxing.” Both, sons of Jupiter by Leda, are most celebrated among poets. “Such was the severity of the battle that report handed down that two gods, Castor and Pollux, on white horses, had been present as spectators; no one doubted it. Therefore the general reverenced them, promised temples in return for victory, and fulfilled the promise, plainly as wages to gods who had fought beside him.” Florus, I.11.
>
> **“Ad remunerandam,” etc.**: That is, as a reward for their valour.
>
> **“Neque enim,” etc.**: As though he said: nor should history be thought in this matter to have falsified the truth, nor does it idly boast that it reports antiquity.
>
> **“Ne apud,” etc.**: That is, lest the prodigy fail to win credence among posterity.
>
> **“Estote,” etc.**: That is, do not fear that you may seem to have described the matter insufficiently faithfully.
>
> **“Hoc certe,” etc.**: That is, this is certainly greater, and no less true.

XV. Let antiquity yield to you—not only that of recent ages, but the memory of all time—although it seeks what is right and, never corrupted in its duty, boasts that the reputation of holiness has rested with it. Yet human panegyrics are not read where divine judgments are sought. Those men of old, then, praised as guides of life, who lived strictly and sparingly in restraining desires, whose whole life was spent in arms—when did they receive, as the reward of their integrity, so great a divine aid in battle? Let them, who are far removed from your virtues, at least be placed near in the rank of justice [Col. 0593B].

In a certain Roman war, it is related, two youths on horseback, remarkable alike in beauty and strength, because they had been conspicuous above the rest in fighting, were sought by the general in order to reward their service. When none could be found, it was believed that they had been divine, because, having zealously shared the labour, they had rejected its reward. For my part, I willingly agree with the history. For it ought not in this matter to be considered a falsifier of truth, since it promises itself as no vain messenger of antiquity. Yet those who bound this account into the records of the annals feared that belief in the miracle might falter among posterity [Col. 0593C]. Be secure, most weighty authors, about the conscientiousness of your writings: we believe deeds, having now experienced greater ones. The greatness of our prince gives credibility to ancient deeds, yet takes away their miraculous character. The scale of aid must be measured by the nature of the need. Once two youths were seen, but now an army. This is certainly more abundant, and no weaker in truth. Faith stands supported by a double proof. Thus Constantine deserved to be helped; thus Rome ought to be saved.

> **Note [Col. 0593D]**
>
> **XVI. “Quae te,” etc.**: That is, we conjectured in our minds what might surround and defend you, although this had not yet been confirmed to our eyes [Col. 0594C].
>
> **“Ubique,” etc.**: That is, he omits nothing by which he might make God favour him.
>
> **“Non ingrato”**: That is, not by an unpleasant digression.
>
> **“Ut nec inhumane”**: That is, so that I may neither pass over his other actions too inhumanely nor linger upon the present matters to the envy of some.
>
> **“Aevi immaturus”**: Yet if Eusebius, Sozomen, and Eutropius are to be believed, who say that he died at sixty-five years of age and had then reigned thirty-two years, he was in fact above thirty-two. But he calls him immature in age by comparison with Maximian and Diocletian, whom he had seen as aged emperors.
>
> **“Et comite”**: That is, Regaïsus, whom he names in more than one place.
>
> **“Duos angues”**: Sent into Hercules’ cradle by Juno, his stepmother. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.288:
>
> > “When, as a child, he crushed in his hand  
> > The twin serpents, monsters sent by his stepmother.”
>
> **“Infantulo immicaret”**: I prefer, with Acidalius, *in infantulo emicaret*, “might shine forth in the infant.”
>
> **“Ludebas”**: Perhaps *praeludebas*, “you were making a prelude,” as Acidalius reads.

XVI. This is great, greatest Emperor, yet not surprising in view of your dutiful devotion. We had grasped by conjecture of mind that the supreme Majesty was present with you in all things, surrounding and protecting you, although it was not yet evident to the testimony of our eyes. For when your mind, removed from mortal contamination, wholly pure and fundamentally sincere, everywhere devotes itself to winning God’s favour; when your glory has surpassed the human measure, what man is there who would not believe that God helps you, since both your life deserves it and the greatness of events bears witness to it?

Let us therefore depart for a while from the established [Col. 0594B] course by a not unwelcome digression. I shall maintain this manner of discourse, so that it may neither be silent inhumanely concerning the rest nor speak spitefully of the matters at hand. You, best Emperor, when you entered upon rule, still immature in years but already mature for empire, showed that in the haste of virtue the course of life need not be awaited. Thereafter, equally good at home and in war, you never advanced a step without glory following you everywhere as though it were your shadow. Having captured the fiercest kings, Ascaricus and his companion, you inaugurated your military achievements with such glory that we already held a hostage of unheard-of consequence.

As they say that Hercules, still tender and nursing, crushed two serpents in his hand, so that even in infancy the indication of his future strength might shine forth, so you, Emperor, in the very cradle of your reign, as though slaying twin dragons, were making sport through the famous punishments of most savage kings [Col. 0594C].

> **Note [Col. 0594D]**
>
> **XVII. “Ultra ipsum Oceanum”**: He touches upon the times of the Emperor Probus, under whom a band of Franks, who were held captive at Pontus, “having seized ships, ravaged Greece and Asia; and, after descending upon many shores of Libya not unpunished, finally captured Syracuse itself, famed of old for naval victories. Having travelled an immense distance, they reached the Ocean where it breaks the lands” [Col. 0595C]—that is, the Strait of Gades, and consequently Spain—“and thus by the outcome of their rashness they showed that nothing is closed to piratical desperation where ships can gain access.” Vopiscus says the same in his *Probus*.
>
> **“Fortissimo Caesari”**: Crispus, who conquered and destroyed the Franks in A.D. 320.
>
> **“Cum memoria”**: That is, fighting with the memory of the defeat it had suffered sharpened rather than dismayed.
>
> **“Segusiensium civitatem”**: Segusium, a city of Cisalpine Gaul beside the River Duria, at the foot of the Cottian Alps, etc.

XVII. The Franks themselves, more savage than the rest, whose force, boiling over for war and carried beyond the Ocean by the swell of its fury, had rendered even the coasts of Spain hostile with arms [Col. 0595A]—they fell so completely beneath your arms that they could have been utterly destroyed, had you not, by the divine inspiration with which you govern all things, reserved for your son to finish those whom you had yourself crushed. Yet, fertile for your glory in its own misfortunes, the nation grew up again so swiftly and was restored so vigorously that it furnished the bravest Caesar with the first fruits of a great victory, fighting with the memory of its received defeat not weakened but sharpened.

Let us defer for a while the Italian campaigns, in which you shattered with force and courage, as though a gate of war, the city of the Segusians, which, after the Alps have been crossed, stands as Italy’s barrier; and from there the unhindered force of your victories ran through battle-lines thrown in your way and armies encountered, all the way to the walls of Rome.

> **Note [Col. 0595C]**
>
> **XVIII. “Bructeros”**: The Bructeri, a people of Germany, mentioned also in another panegyric [Col. 0595D].
>
> **“Chamavos”**: He also speaks elsewhere of these German peoples.
>
> **“Cheruscos”**: Dwelling beyond the River Weser, where the Duchy of Brunswick is now.
>
> **“Vangionas”**: On the Rhine, above Mainz, where Worms now is.
>
> **“Tubantes”**: Some hold that they lived in Transisalania, near the borders of Frisia and Westphalia; others, in that part of Germany now called Westphalia.
>
> **“Publico submittit”**: That is, he performs a common duty. You come to a conference and stir their hope.
>
> **“Versas credulitatem”**: Better than *crudelitatem*: that is, you deceive men who are excessively credulous when you deny that you are present.
>
> **“Invictos ducis”**: That is, you lead unconquered soldiers with you, and you alone are feared more than all. Livineius’ edition reads, “You do not fear unconquered leaders, and you alone are feared,” which is not so acceptable.
>
> **“Quem credit absentem”**: That is, while it thinks you absent.
>
> **“Tibi tamen”**: That is, your praise nevertheless increases from this, because the number of enemies increases; and you crush gathered enemies with greater glory, though it would be more difficult to pursue them while scattered.
>
> **“Dum collativam”**: That is, while they concentrate their forces into one.
>
> **“Dies integer conderetur”**: See Pliny, *Panegyric* 80: “When a whole day was spent, to our greatest benefit and to your greatest praise”; where see several further examples of this kind.

XVIII. Why should I mention the Bructeri? Why the Chamavi? [Col. 0595B] Why the Cherusci, Vangiones, Alamanni, Tubantes? Their names resound with war, and the savagery of barbarism itself brings horror in their very appellations. All these, armed first separately and then together, had blazed forth in the conspiracy of an allied confederacy. Yet you, Emperor, when you saw so great a mass of war, feared nothing more than that you might be feared. You approach the barbarians, and, concealing the bearing of a prince, come as near as possible with two companions. Never is sovereignty loftier than when it submits itself to public duty. You address them, stir their hopes, and deceive their credulity: you deny that you are present. O truly blind barbarism, which did not see in that countenance the marks of a prince—which did not recognize, even thus, that it was Constantine, when he stood secure of himself within range of a missile! Can anyone who was able not to fear this doubt that you proceed in all things upheld by God? You lead the unconquered, and you alone are feared. So many kingdoms, so many peoples, and the gathering of nations so great, deem themselves unequal to your strength when they believe you absent. Yet for you the increase [Col. 0596A] of terror is an increase of praise: you crush them more gloriously when assembled, whom you would pursue with greater difficulty when scattered. Countless nations, gathered together for war but routed by one onset of yours, provided a swift victory while they were mustering their united strength.

[Note: [Col. 0596D]

XIX. “The speech fell short” (*cecidit oratio*). Others read “touched upon” (*tetigit*).

“Would not unfold the totality” (*non summam evolveret*). It is better, if transposition is made, to read: “would not unfold the ornaments, but display the totality” (*non ornamenta evolveret, sed summam monstraret*).

“For the public good” (*e re publica*). That is: from public advantage.

“Fortune might limp” (*felicitas claudicarit*). That is, might falter. Above, §15: “lest among posterity the credibility of the miracle should limp.”

“But only then” (*sed tum demum*). That is: but then at last they may seem to have become manifest.

“Yet in you” (*in te tamen*). That is: your willingness to fight would nevertheless be for you a pledge of victory.

“For one to whom,” etc. That is: since he has entered upon more battles than he has received years of service.]

XIX. In this one war alone, if there were leisure to dwell upon it with the praise it deserves, an entire day would be consumed. Now my speech, flying over everything so rapidly, has fallen short, so that it has not unfolded the full sum of your victories but displayed their ornaments. Since these deeds have always been done for the public good, with such force and such success that your courage has never trembled, your prudence hesitated, or your good fortune faltered, it has, I think, been sufficiently demonstrated that the aid of gracious Majesty flows perpetually toward you; so that the heavenly forces of your army may seem not to have been sent for the first time on that occasion, but only then at last to have been recognized. [Col. 0596B] Thus you approached the liberation of Italy so confidently and so securely that, although warfare has blind contingencies, you held your resolve to fight as a pledge of victory, even if divine assistance had been absent. For there was present an army robust and flourishing, full of strength and spirit, rejoicing in its arms and performing military duties more from zeal than necessity—an army whose periods of service were fewer than its battles. When I say “battles,” I mean victories; and it was besides as devoted to you as it was dear to you. Forgive me, proud valour: however much confidence and spirit you possess, love for the prince makes the soldier braver.

[Note: [Col. 0596D]

XX. “King Eropus.” The story is known from Justin, Book VII, Ammianus, Book XXVI, and Polybius.

“On their side” (*secundum illos*). That is: it went favourably for them, but only until the Macedonians returned to battle.

[Col. 0597C] “Was changed,” etc. That is: the outcome of the war was changed.

“Received,” etc. That is: remembrance of a benefit received confirms love more strongly than hope of a future one.]

XX. The event which I shall relate is very ancient, but not unworthy of remembrance. Once the Illyrians, despising the infancy of King Eropus, challenged the Macedonians to war. [Col. 0596C] The first encounter indeed went in their favour; but when the Macedonians renewed the war, they carried their king to the battle-line in his cradle. While anger inflamed the former and pity the latter, while the sound of standards stirred the former and the wailing of the child [Col. 0597A] the latter, the character of the contest was changed: those who fought from love prevailed. Therefore, by as much as remembrance of a benefit received is a more faithful source of love than expectation of one to come—since there possession delights there, while here anticipation allures—by so much more courageously did your men fight: not as men to whom a child offered the hope of favour, but as men repaying to a most beneficent prince, after men had been born, the debt owed for benefits received.

[Note: [Col. 0597C]

XXI. “The city-state of the Segusians.” Segusium: Susa.

“The first.” That is, the first city encountered on the route.

“Whose resistance.” That is, by resisting obstinately.

“Was sought by force and arms” (*vi manu quaereretur*). Most interpreters introduce the word *vi* (“by force”), which they think was admitted into the text from a gloss.

“Whose,” etc. That is: whose easy spread from adjoining places grew through the origin of a new conflagration.

[Col. 0597D] “By a destructive birth” (*partu pestifero*). Others read *pastu* (“feeding”), but I do not think emendation necessary here. For he speaks of the fire as of a human being, which grows, ages, and dies.

“Not only.” That is: not only that the fire might diminish when its fuel had been removed, but that, once overwhelmed, it might be extinguished.]

XXI. Therefore, the first city of the Segusians upon which the road led was embraced by an easy victory. Its obstinacy in resistance turned the Emperor’s force against itself, yet did not alienate his mercy. For when entrance was being sought by force of arms, and the burning of the gates had spread fire far and wide, its easy contagion through connected places gaining strength by a destructive birth, the chief concern of the most beneficent Emperor was not merely that the fire, [Col. 0597B] lacking assistance, might grow old, but that, overwhelmed, it might die. His clemency was seen to require far more effort than his courage, since there was more labour in preserving the city than in taking it. Accordingly, when he departed, he made it so eager for him that it was disposed to every obedience not by fear of victory, but by admiration for his gentleness.

[Note: [Col. 0597D]

XXII. “From another’s calamity.” That familiar little verse:

> Happy is he whom another’s dangers make cautious.

“Discrimination of the good” (*dilectum boni*). It is not suited to forming a judgment about what is good.

“The Taurini.” Augusta Taurinorum: Turin.

“Because neither,” etc. That is: because Constantine is so strong that he cannot be resisted, and so gentle that there is no reason to resist him.

“By a covering,” etc. That is: horses and men covered on every side with iron.

“Clibanarii.” Cataphract cavalrymen—that is, men who sat upon horses enclosed everywhere in iron, while they themselves too wore iron armour. [Col. 0598C] Claudian says of them:

> By art, a flexible plate is joined,  
> And hooked upon the limbs which it encloses;  
> Terrible to see. You would think iron images moved,  
> And men breathed with metal akin to their own.

For *klibanos* (κλίβανος) in Greek is an iron cuirass.

“Protection” (*noxa*). That is: it rendered them safe against wounds.]

XXII. They say that the best remedies are those which arise from another’s calamity for the correction of ourselves; but a mind hindered by perversity as though by disease has no capacity to choose the good. Behold: at Turin a graver battle already awaited your arrival; nor did the devastation of the Segusians warn them to guard themselves; nor did they reflect that their affair would be with a prince whose strength allowed no hope of resistance and whose gentleness supplied no reason for it. So great a body of soldiers filled the broad-lying plain that anyone who saw them drawn up would not condemn their confidence. For what spectacle was that said to have been—how dreadful to behold, how terrifying—horses and men alike enclosed in a covering of iron? In the army they are called *clibanarii*. With the chests of the horses wholly [Col. 0598A] covered from above, a cuirass hung down to their legs and, without hindering movement, protected them against the harm of wounds.

[Note: [Col. 0598C]

XXIII. “According to the exigency.” That is: courage exercises its force according to what the situation requires.

“Because from itself.” That is: because it regulates and adapts its measure to circumstances.

“Because imbued.” That is: because prompted.

[Col. 0598D] “You yourself choose for yourself.” Supply: those to be attacked.

“They have rammed the battle-line” (*aciem arietaverint*). They have broken through it. The metaphor derives from battering rams, by which city walls were demolished.

“Maintain the course of their attack.” That is: remain steadfast in the fierce assault they have undertaken.

“Proof against,” etc. That is: being secure against wounds, they break through without delay whatever is placed before them.]

XXIII. Yet you, Emperor, were not frightened either by armour which doubled terror with so great a number, or by a number which added force to weapons. For it is certain that courageous valour adjusts its strength to the demands of the occasion: in small matters it is relaxed almost to confidence; in moderate matters it is somewhat more tense; when great matters arise, it lifts itself according to the magnitude of the task to be accomplished. That display of arms and army covered in iron, which might have wounded unwarrior-like eyes, stirred unconquered minds; for, imbued with the Emperor’s example, his soldier burns with all his heart when he finds an enemy whom it is fitting to conquer. You yourself select for attack the cataphract cavalry, [Col. 0598B] in which the greatest strength of the battle had stood. Their discipline in fighting is this: after they have rammed the battle-line, they maintain the course of their attack, and, immune to wounds, break through without hesitation whatever opposes them.

[Note: [Col. 0598D]

XXIV. “Because,” etc. That is: first, in evading the enemy’s attack, wherein there is the greatest safety; then, in enduring that same attack, wherein there is the greatest difficulty.

“Into an irreversible charge.” You spread out the line in such a way that, by suddenly closing in your ranks, you trap and crush the enemy when they are eager to advance and dare to overextend themselves.

“You let loose” (*effundis*). That is: you allow them to rush forward.

“Those whom,” etc. That is: those whom you had admitted for mockery.

“To be mocked” (*ludificandos*). Passive in sense; or perhaps it should be read *ludificando*, “by mocking.”

[Col. 0599C] “The Emperor Antoninus.” Antoninus Pius, adopted by Hadrian, governed the Roman state in A.D. 138. He died at the age of seventy, after twenty-three years of rule; he was succeeded by his son-in-law Marcus Antoninus Verus.]

XXIV. But you, most prudent Emperor, who knew every method of warfare, found through ingenuity assistance in what is safest—to evade—and in what is most difficult—to endure. Having spread out your battle-line, you let the enemy rush into an irreversible charge; then, having drawn back your ranks, you enclose those whom you had received in order to mock them. It was of no use to strain against you when your men deliberately gave way. Iron rigidity did not permit them to turn aside for pursuit. Thus our men attack them, betrayed to their maces; these, wearing them down with repeated blows, battered the enemy whom their heavy iron fastenings made inaccessible to wounds, and, striking chiefly at their heads, compelled to fall those whom they had confused by the blow. Then they rushed headlong, slipped backward, staggered half-dead, or, dying, were held fast in their saddles; entangled amid the mixed ruin of horses, they lay there—men who, finding a place to wound, everywhere threw the cavalryman down in unbridled pain. [Col. 0599A] With every one of them slain and all your men unharmed, they transformed the terror of their armour into the miracle of victory, because those thought invulnerable had perished without wounds among your men. The Emperor Antoninus, eminent in the toga and neither inactive nor ineffectual in war, when he tested arms against the Parthians and saw the cataphracts, became so wholly afraid that he voluntarily sent conciliatory letters of peace to their king. When that king, excessive in spirit, rejected them, the barbarian’s insolence was indeed overcome; but it was revealed that such force resides in these arms that even one who was to be conquered could have confidence, while one who was to conquer might fear.

[Note: [Col. 0599C]

XXV. “At Brescia.” Brixia, a city of Italy among the Cenomani, formerly under the dukes of Milan and now in Venetian territory: Brescia. To the east it has Verona; to the south, Bergamo; to the west, Cremona and Mantua.

“More cunning in its flight than in appearance.” Read with Livineius: “safer by its force” (*quam vi sua [Col. 0599D] tutior*).

“Because those who flee are excused,” etc. That is: because those who flee in order to yield to you have an excuse for their flight.

“Indeed rather,” etc. That is: rather let something worthy of proclamation befall miserable fearfulness—namely, a flight which has dignity.

“How readily.” That is: how readily weakness collapses when, at an unfavourable moment, it has raised itself more boldly.

“As day was now declining.” That is, as it was inclining. *Aeneid*, Book II, 8:

> And now humid night falls headlong from heaven.

“But the outcome.” Ruricius knew what his audacity deserved, yet hoped for a good result from the battle. In this he was deceived; thus the outcome disappointed him more than his deserts did.

“The reasoning of the circumspect.” Neither the reasoning of a circumspect or prudent man, nor the fear which sometimes comes upon men.]

XXV. Why should I relate that, after so great and grave a battle, there was at Brescia a cavalry force indeed large and fierce, more cunning in flight than in appearance, which, routed by your first onset, fled all the way to Verona for stronger defences? Nor was it disgraceful that those flee who are excused because they yield to you. Let some display-worthy thing indeed be granted to miserable timidity: a flight that possesses dignity. Verona itself, however, relying on the immense forces which fear of your arrival had gathered into one place, after it had already suffered the destruction of many men, became for a while more cautious through fear, not more fortunate through judgment. It protected itself from attack by its walls. Ruricius was there, most experienced in war and the pillar of tyrannical commanders. Throughout the whole circuit of the walls was a great multitude of men, most of whom had already been broken at Brescia. As, when some part of the body is ill, the whole health is commonly infected, so a portion of that multitude, affected by evil, had scattered the entire army through contagion of fear. [Col. 0599C] How readily weakness is liable to collapse when untimely audacity stirs it was demonstrated often on other occasions, but especially in that siege. The besieged made an attack; and those who had for some time defended themselves from death by hiding, once given an opportunity to fight, paid the penalty for their reckless sortie. Ruricius too, driven back within the walls with great slaughter among his men, his hope already [Col. 0600A] exhausted but his mind still deranged, hurled himself into Verona, brought new forces into the same place, and, as day was now declining, did not decline battle—more eager for combat than for safety. But the outcome disappointed him more than his deserts did. For death subdued the madness which neither the reasoning of a circumspect man nor the fear of one defeated had been able to cure.

[Note: [Col. 0600C]

XXVI. “A battle in dense darkness.” That is: the whole issue of the contest would soon be at Fortune’s disposal—that the entire outcome would rest with Fortune. Accordingly, the passage, which in the judgment of all interpreters is exceedingly corrupt, should, I think, be emended in place of “in coils and darkness” (*spiris tenebrisque*), as it appears in the common editions.

“You pressed.” Read *instare*, “to press,” and shortly thereafter *ducere*, “to lead.”

“The gift of night.” That is: you might suppose that you received from night, as a benefit, the fact that no one would observe you fighting.

“Those whom you strike down unrecognized.” For they do not know that they perish by your unconquered hand.

[Col. 0600D] “Or valour,” etc. That is: valour either despises these things, or military heat and ardour does not even feel them.

“Darkness has no pity.” Since slaughter is not seen in the night-time, there is no occasion for pity.

“By piety,” etc. That is: when your piety was restrained by nothing and your majesty was safe.

“At the watches of the siege.” The word *vigiliae* (“watches”) here appears to mean those very persons who were on guard duty.]

XXVI. O night to be entrusted to eternal ages and monuments! When, in dense darkness, the whole contest was at Fortune’s disposal, yet you, Emperor, no safer because of the time than more protected by God, pressed fiercely upon the most savage enemy in great numbers; and, exulting in freedom to kill, regarded it as the gift of night that no one would preserve you while fighting. You went undaunted through hostile battle-lines, broke through, cast down, and trampled underfoot all the densest masses. Those whom you strike down unrecognized lose the glory of death—except that your very force compels you to be recognized. [Col. 0600B] For the broken sounds of trumpets, the dreadful cry of soldiers, wounds abandoned to chance, swords clashing at close quarters, the heavy groans of the falling, widely resounding arms, and confusion driven into a single sound from clashing noises of every kind move you not at all; for valour either disregards all these things, or anger does not feel them. Night itself, the most just cause of terror for combatants, had made you fiercer in inflicting slaughter. For darkness has no pity, the sole impediment to your valour; so that one may understand how much your force achieved in that battle, when piety did not hold it back and your majesty was secure. When the battle was scarcely ended after much of the night, weary with slaughter, breathless from battle, stained with blood—but enemy blood—you returned to the watches of the siege. O Fortune! O all-powerful Rome! What gratitude will you ever render for these great labours? Only this: the most indulgent prince, as though he owed you this very service, holds you dearer because he saved you by greater labour.

[Note: [Col. 0600D]

XXVII. “Whither long ago.” That is: whither it was already hastening in an eager course.

“Aquileia.” The capital of the Carni on the shore of the Adriatic Sea; once a most celebrated emporium: Aquilée.

“Mutina.” A city formerly of Cisalpine Gaul, now Italy, fifteen Roman miles east of Forum Lepidi and twenty west of Bologna: Modena.

[Col. 0601C] “On account of,” etc. That is: because of the benefits which followed.

“To a sound course.” That is: to be restored to a flourishing condition.

“Of which there is.” That is: both to pursue them severally is a burdensome task, and to heap them all together is more burdensome still. For to lift upon one’s shoulders things which one could not carry separately is the mark of a hope more daring than confidence ready.]

XXVII. And since some chance has led me to the mention of the City, rather than the order of events, and since it is not permitted to call my speech back from the place toward which it had long been hastening eagerly, I pass over you, Aquileia; you, Mutina; [Col. 0601A] and the other regions to which the injury of the very siege was most welcome because of the benefits of incredible good fortune which followed. For, when the helm of their fortunes had been transferred to the bravest prince, they realized how easily all things might return to a sound course which had been borne along in such a way that they would soon either strike upon the rocks of every evil or stick fast in the shallows of misery. I pass over these, I say, and many others, of which each separately is a burdensome mass, and the heap of all together more burdensome. For to undertake them gathered together when you cannot bear them spread apart is the mark of hope more excessive than confidence more ready. Italy having therefore been recovered, this was the first step toward freeing the City and an easy ascent to victory: divine force dislodged from its accustomed hiding-places the man who had always clung to the very entrails of the City in order to devour them. [Col. 0601B] In this there was indeed so much importance for the ease of accomplishing the task that, most excellent Emperor, it is not so much necessary to glory in your valour because you conquered him as to congratulate your good fortune because you were able to summon him to battle.

[Note: [Col. 0601D]

XXVIII. “His spirit.” That is: his mind already driven from its course by terror.

“Desirable.” That is: greatly to be wished.

“If the contest.” That is: if the ready hope of flight makes the uncertain issue of battle precarious.

“The ranks have slackened.” If by chance the ranks have relaxed somewhat in eagerness to fight, or the front of the army, etc.

“In its position.” That is: deprived of the means of flight, it is made immovable.

“Indeed so.” That is: they made up so great a multitude that the battle-line extended beyond the range of sight.

“Not because the front.” Not because the front of the army was broader, [Col. 0602C] and therefore weaker; rather, the army was so numerous that it was broad although tightly packed, and strong and robust although extended in a long line.]

XXVIII. For let us not suppose that it was by chance or confidence that he even brought out his army voluntarily against one whose very approach he dreaded with a shudder, unless a hostile god, a mind already driven astray by fear, and ripeness for destruction had compelled him. The very method of deploying the army showed that he had lost his mind and that his plan was confused: he took up a position for battle so that, escape being blocked, he imposed on himself the necessity of dying when he had no hope of victory. This, indeed, was greatly to be wished for by our Emperor, who is most displeased when the ready prospect of flight makes the contest uncertain. [Col. 0601C] If the battle-line slackens or the front, once struck, wavers, confidence passes from the hands to the feet. You do not love wars, Emperor, unless the enemy, burning with ardour, is held in position by escape cut off, so that he either falls by the sword or is spared through pity. He accordingly drew up his men beside the Tiber, placing them so near the bank that the fatal wave washed the footprints of the rearmost ranks, as though by a foreknowledge of the slaughter to come. Yet he had such an abundance of men that the extended battle-line reached beyond the furthest range of sight—not because the front was weak by being drawn out over a feeble stretch, but with such reinforcement and strength of reserves and ranks [Col. 0602A] that the battle-line presented a wall on either side, not more extended than robust; neither close packing had compressed it nor length weakened it.

[Note: [Col. 0602C]

XXIX. “For to pursue this.” Perhaps here “for,” etc., as Gruter thinks.

“But you,” etc. That is: no slower to fight than to command.

“They overshadow.” A *hypotyposis*—a vivid depiction—of Constantine fighting fiercely in the battle-line.

“Those whom,” etc. That is: those thrown down by the mighty spear are trampled beneath the feet of their own horses.]

XXIX. I shall pass over here, greatest Constantine, the astonishing and incredible method by which you arranged your soldiers; for I should like to pursue this point, and say what place the heavenly army held. Yet I do not think that they stood anywhere except with you; for you choose for yourself the most difficult part of battle, and, as though a measure of valour ought to be owed to one’s degree of fortune, so among your own men you do not wish to excel more in rank than in labour. It is indeed the fullest duty of a prince, if his hand is idle, not to have been idle in counsel; but you are no slower in action than in command, governing your armies by instruction, aiding them by deed, and inflaming them by example. This you do even more readily here [Col. 0602B] than in other battles, because the present contest had so great a reward: Rome immediately became the prize of its distinguished victor. When I begin to form the image of this event, I shudder at what I am about to say. You attack the battle-line first; you break in alone. Futile flights of missiles overshadow you as you advance; your shield-boss rings, secure beneath the blows. Those whom the beam-like spear throws down are trampled by a fierce rider leaping upon them. Your noble helmet shines, and the flashing radiance of its gems reveals the divine head beneath it. Shield of gold and arms of gold gleam. O how great is the force you possess, valour, when in this array you display more terror than ornament! The bravest soldiers followed this ardour, proving themselves worthy of his leadership and command; each man laboured as though the whole issue rested upon his individual hand.

[Note: [Col. 0602D]

XXX. “Worthy of cowardice.” Thus restored from an old manuscript after Acidalus and Livineius, in place of *dignum ignavia*.

“And because also formerly.” Read with Acidalus and Livineius *pridem* (“formerly”) in place of *pridie* (“on the preceding day”). From this passage, likewise from the affinity of style, Claudius Puteanus is led to believe that this and the preceding panegyric are by Nazarius. In this I agree with him strongly: for what Nazarius says here appears rightly to belong to the preceding panegyric, where the defeat of Maxentius is described at length.]

XXX. I shall not recount here the banks covered by unbroken slaughter, the Tiber filled with heaps of bodies and, amid the high-piled masses of corpses, emerging with sickly effort and scarcely struggling free through its whirlpools; nor how that tyrant himself was betrayed not by a manly death but by shameful flight, and how the blood-stained waves killed him with an end worthy of his cowardice and cruelty. It is enough to touch upon these matters, because I spoke of them more fully before, because there is no opportunity to treat them according to their dignity, and lest a battle conducted swiftly should seem to have been narrated more slowly than it was completed. O, if I were now granted the power to shape my speech in proportion to the dignity of the events! I would employ every flower of expression and lavish a certain exquisite charm and grace [Col. 0603A] of speech. Already the tumult of Mars, already the sounds of trumpets, are changed by joyful cries into echoing applause. The Emperor’s entrance into the City must be described; and, in expressing the supreme joy of Senate and Roman People, the speech itself would be ungrateful unless it too gave itself to celebration. Since the founding of the City, no day has dawned upon Roman rule whose rejoicing was, or ought to have been, so overflowing and so remarkable; no triumphs whose memory the antiquity of annals has consecrated in writing were so joyful.

[Note: [Col. 0603C]

XXXI. “Men of consular rank led out from prison.” Relevant is that passage of Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, Book I, 552, addressed to Rome:

> When Maxentius oppressed you with his pestilential court,  
> You mourned a hundred fathers condemned to a long prison,  
> As you yourself know.

[Col. 0603D] “They seemed to be led before all.” Constantine’s triumphal entry into the City after Maxentius had been killed.

“The tyrant.” Maxentius.

“Conceived,” etc. That is: by heaping insults upon slain Maxentius, they crushed the terror which they had conceived while he was alive.]

XXXI. There were indeed no commanders in chains being driven before the chariot; but at last the nobility went forth freed. No barbarians were cast into prison; but men of consular rank were led out from prison. No foreign captives gave honour to that entrance; rather, Rome herself was now free. She received nothing from an enemy, but recovered herself; she was not enlarged by booty, [Col. 0603B] but ceased to be booty; and, than which nothing greater can be added to the magnitude of glory, she recovered empire while she had endured slavery. All seemed indeed to see led before them the conquered battalions of vices which had grievously besieged the City. Crime was subdued, treachery conquered, audacity distrustful of itself and importunity chained; frenzy bound, and bloody cruelty snarled in empty terror. Pride and arrogance were overthrown, luxury restrained, and lust was held bound with an iron chain. The most hideous head of the tyrant himself followed this retinue of his; and, if there is any credit in those who report it, savagery still remained in it, and not even death had conquered the threats of that dreadful brow. The most insulting cries were cast at it by the crowd. For it was pleasing both to inaugurate liberty by mocking their oppressor and, with wonderful delight, to crush by insults at his death the terror conceived from him while he lived.

[Note: [Col. 0603D]

XXXII. “All whom.” I prefer *qua* (“by which”), as Bongarsius approves; or *omnes quos* (“all whom”), as Acidalus wishes.

“They come more sluggishly.” Horace:

> Things conveyed through the ears stir minds more slowly  
> Than things entrusted to the faithful eyes . . .

“Shone forth.” Perhaps “shone out” (*eluceret*), Acidalus suggests.

“Had afflicted while alive.” In another panegyric addressed to the same man: “For all Africa, which he had resolved to destroy, was exhausted.” Zosimus, Book II, gives the reason why Maxentius raged so fiercely against Africans: “Because African soldiers had prevented his image, sent into Africa, from being carried about, and because they had moreover supported Alexander, who, from being praetorian prefect, had assumed the imperial purple. After Alexander was killed through Volusianus, all who in Africa were prominent either by birth or wealth, as adherents of Alexander’s faction, were either killed or stripped of their property.”

[Col. 0604D] “With the sea not yet sufficiently seasonable.” For Maxentius’ defeat occurred on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September].

“And not as soon as.” That is: it is not immediately pure and cleansed as soon as it becomes permissible to rejoice. For just as pipes, when they have long been closed, once their passage is opened, discharge water the more turbid the thicker it is; so human desires, suspended by fear, show something tumultuous when they burst forth in full flood.]

XXXII. What triumph more illustrious? What spectacle more beautiful? What procession more fortunate? Therefore I shall say, Emperor, that by one thing alone I seem sufficiently to express your divine glory: as many marks of disgrace as you had erased there, so many fillets of praise shone upon you. The most indulgent prince wished that no one should be deprived of this favour: that all whom the tyrant’s hatred had permeated might be purified by the spectacle of his funeral. Everywhere [Col. 0604A] swift report had already spread the joy of the deed, and winged victory had added speed to the announcement; yet the actual sight followed with fuller joy, because things that enter the mind through the avenue of the ears reach it more sluggishly than those which are taken in by the eyes. Thus through Italy such gatherings of people were aroused, such crowds poured out from the towns, that the testimony of past terror could easily shine forth in present exultation. With equal zeal the head of that same tyrant was sent to Africa to give satisfaction, mangled, to the land which he had afflicted most grievously while alive. Though the sea was not yet sufficiently seasonable, favourable breezes and following waves nevertheless attended the sailors, and the elements themselves aided that most blessed victory. The Tiber yielded up the head, in which the title of so great praise was carried about; the winds escorted it, the seas preserved it. In what manner, mighty Africa, with what roar of joy, with what unrestrained delight did you exult? Nothing, indeed, is more excessive than sudden joy after long sadness. It seethes by its own momentum; nor, as soon as it is free, is it immediately settled and at once pure. For just as pipes, when they have long been blocked, once an outlet has been given, discharge water the thicker the more abundantly they flow, so human desires, blocked by fear, acted with a certain turbulence when they burst forth in their accumulated fullness.

[Note: [Col. 0604D]

XXXIII. “But how much.” But by as much as the Emperor’s prudence contributed to the splendour of the City while it devised methods for its liberation, by so much, etc.

“Each in its own way.” Similar is *Aeneid*, Book XII, 552:

> Each man exerts himself with the full force of his resources.

It is tiresome to produce more examples of this kind.

“To be exhausted.” Add “by calamity.” Without this word, which has somehow dropped out, the sense is mutilated.

[Col. 0605C] “To scatter what had been seized.” Others read “to scatter what had been acquired” (*dissipare parta*).

“Care of almost two months.” Constantine seems to have remained at Rome for two months to set everything in order, and then gone to Milan and afterwards to Germany.

“I say, healed.” That is: why do I say “healed”? Restoration to the former condition suffices to soothe grief, not to summon joy; nor can you demand more than that a man should not be displeased with himself when, having recovered what he lost, he has achieved only that he should not grieve, not that he should rejoice in acquiring new things.

[Col. 0605D] “And not of summoning.” Is this not sufficient to earn congratulations for our Emperor?

“In a solitary manner.” In the sense of “only”; a word of the later age.

“Because speech scarcely,” etc. That is: speech is unequal to recounting the public benefits which he bestowed. Yet, since the state is composed of individuals, etc.]

XXXIII. Such were the congratulations for the victories. Nor were the fruits of his other virtues less abundant. Tireless force and exceptional courage disentangled and freed the City, entangled and overgrown with the gravest evils; but how much good did prudence devise, and benevolence [Col. 0604C] and clemency confer? It is difficult to judge which helped more. For to those besieged by calamity, deliverance from misery is the fulfilment of desire; and soon freedom from miseries is of little satisfaction unless joy follows. Thus, each performing its own office, the Emperor’s courage and generosity made the City’s blessedness complete by exhausting its miseries and accumulating its advantages. The way of doing harm is always easier and much more downhill than that of doing good: to wound the sound is easier than to heal the wounded, to scatter [Col. 0605A] what has been seized than to restore what has been torn apart. Yet this condition of affairs yielded to our Prince. For whatever evil that deadly domination had inflicted throughout six whole years, the care of almost two months healed. I say “healed”: restoration to the former condition is sufficient to soothe grief, but not also to summon rejoicing; and you should demand no more than that a person should not be dissatisfied with himself who has achieved only this: having recovered what he lost, he does not grieve, but does not also rejoice at the acquisition of new things. I pass over the estates restored privately to all those whom that monstrous ruin had driven from their homes; I pass them over, I say, because speech scarcely suffices to explain what was done publicly. Yet since the commonwealth is put together from individuals, and whatever is contributed to it flows proportionally to all, it must in turn be that what all individuals acquire separately [Col. 0605B] flows back into the commonwealth.

[Note: [Col. 0605D]

XXXIV. “A more distinguished beauty.” That is: outstanding, exceptional. Cicero, *On Friendship*: “improved morals,” etc.; and Horace, Book I, Epistle 16, to Quintius:

> When you allow yourself to be called wise and improved.

“She regretted her own good.” She regretted her own beauty.

“May judge.” Thus I restore it for *arbitremur* (“we may judge”); without this emendation, as Acidalus notes, *suarum* is barbarous.

“Smiling” (*renidentem*). Or perhaps “resisting” (*renitentem*)? In Horace, Book III, Ode 6: *adjecisse praedam renidet* (“he smiles at having added booty”). Similarly in Virgil.]

XXXIV. I scarcely dare now to mention, concerning so great a prince, that no matron whose beauty was more distinguished regretted her own beauty, since under an Emperor most abstinent in sexual matters conspicuous beauty was not an incitement to licence but an ornament of modesty. This is doubtless great—or rather divine—praise, often vaunted even among philosophers, not so much displayed in deed as in discussion. But let us leave this to our Prince, who desires to instil self-restraint into all so completely that he judges it to be attributed not to the splendour of his own virtues, but to the honourableness of nature itself. What of his easy accessibility? What of his most patient ears? What of his gracious replies? What of his very countenance, venerable in the gravity of august dignity mingled with cheerfulness, smiling with something [Col. 0605C] at once venerable and lovable—who could worthily describe it? By the wonder of these things all were so bound to him that they grieved not so much because they had endured that tyrant for so long, as because they had come to enjoy such a prince [Col. 0606A] so late.

[Note: [Col. 0605D]

XXXV. “In a circuit.” That is: returning without end in a circuit, yet connected through his goodness, etc.

“By oblivion.” That is: bringing forgetfulness of gratitude.

“Of the senate-house,” etc. That is: you have bound them to yourself.

“To the image.” That is: restored to the appearance of antiquity, it does not revel in unbridled licence.

“Obedient,” etc. That is: it is governed not by his terror, but by his benevolence.

“There is leisure.” That is: it is permitted to enjoy the pleasures of peace with a freer mind.

“Unseemly,” etc. That is: they condemn the dishonourable frugality of our ancestors.]

Porticoes. It is universally known that Rome possessed a very large number of distinguished porticoes [Col. 0606D]: some of them double, as Suetonius says in his *Claudius*, others triple; or, in Greek terminology, called tetrastyle and pentastyle from their respective numbers of rows of columns. Above all, Pompey’s Portico is renowned.

“So that thither,” etc. That is, so that the gathering there may be no less for viewing the place than for the spectacle.]

XXXV. It would take long to enumerate in detail the benefits of the emperor, which, returning throughout the world without limit and linked together by his kindness, shone forth—countless in number and great in their advantages—so that neither the multitude of them all nor the usefulness of each individually will ever cast gratitude into oblivion. At last, Rome, you have felt yourself to be the citadel of all nations and queen of the lands, when you have taken as pledges for your senate-house eminent men from every province; so that the Senate’s dignity has become more illustrious in reality than in name, since it consists of the flower of the whole world. That venerable power and greatness of the Roman people, restored to the likeness of antiquity, neither exults in unbridled license nor lies abjectly in languor; but it has been so regulated by the constant admonitions of the divine emperor that, while it is pliant and yielding at his nod [Col. 0606B], it renders itself obedient not to his terror but to his kindness. For conquered nations have established a tranquil repose of affairs and profound peace for the City. It is permitted, with minds more relaxed, to enjoy the delights of peace. Every most celebrated part of the City shines with new works; nor are things merely made obsolete by age marked out with revived adornment, but those very works formerly thought most magnificent now gleam with the light of gold and expose the unseemly frugality of our forefathers. The lofty porticoes and gold-glittering columns of the Circus Maximus itself have supplied so much unprecedented ornament that people gather there no less eagerly for the site’s sake than for the pleasure of the spectacle.

[Note: [Col. 0606D]

XXXVI. “Most noble Caesars.” Crispus and Constantine.

“And their brothers.” Understand Constans and Constantius, whose very names we already venerate, although our prayers are deferred—that is, although they have not yet been admitted among the Caesars.

“Not even to the Lacedaemonians.” Among the Lacedaemonians there were two royal families: one of the Eurysthenidae, from its founder Eurysthenes; the other of the Proclidae, from Procles. Both descended from Hercules and were therefore called Heraclidae.

[Col. 0607C] “By so much from more [persons].” Supply: peoples.

“Unless he had begun, and his father.” Unless it should occur to the mind that these were the beginnings of his father. Or, if we read *partem* rather than *patrem*, the sense will be: unless it should occur to the mind that it is only a part, when someone begins in this fashion.

“By enthusiasms.” In an old manuscript there is *alacritati*. I should gladly read *alacritati eius*: “Nothing is difficult for his vigorous spirit [Col. 0607D], since he first possessed that will so energetic as he demanded from his soldiers.”]

XXXVI. Rome, possessed of such great blessings—blessings indeed shared with it by the whole world—draws in addition an immense fruit of hope from what it has set before itself in the most noble Caesars [Col. 0606C] and their brothers, whose very names we already venerate, though for the moment our prayers are put forward. Not even the Lacedaemonians were more able [Col. 0607A] to preserve their state by this institution, since they had no king except from the stock of Hercules. Your children, most great Constantine, and thereafter your grandchildren, it desires to request together with you, by so much from more peoples as they are born for greater things. See how the deeds of Crispus, greatest of the Caesars, declare both the ground and the eagerness of these prayers: in him swift virtue, not delayed by the hindrance of age, has occupied his boyish years with triumphal glories. His praises already gush forth so abundantly that they might seem complete, were we not to reflect that he has only begun, and to think of his father. He, indeed, now as most noble Caesar enjoys the sight of his venerable father, brothers, and all his own kin, and offers himself for all to enjoy. While winter was still harsh, he completed with incredible speed a journey made impassable by frost, immense in extent and menaced by snows; so that we may understand that nothing is arduous for such alacrity [Col. 0607B], in one who himself first formed that will, so laborious, which he demanded from his own men.

[Note: [Col. 0607D]

XXXVII. “To see [him] victorious.” Not “victory,” as in the Putean edition. Crispus, however, who is in question here, defeated the Alamanni in A.D. 320.

“For his own favor.” Some read *sui*; others *tui*, others *tuam*: that is, in order to gratify you.

“Brother.” Constantine.

“Even for himself,” etc. That is, he also drew some joy to himself from this, because from Crispus’ years—he being nearest to him in age—he perceived how close he was to such great glory.

“Let him only restrain his right hand.” Let him be like you in all things, provided that, soldier-like, he does not join battle hand-to-hand with the enemy; in this matter we hope that henceforth he may not wish to imitate you again.

“As much as you promise by your name.” An allusion to Constantine’s name, which seems derived from *constantia*, constancy.

“Already fortunate.” That is, your fortunate hand is already employed upon beneficial subscriptions [Col. 0608C].

“Grants through you.” Gruter reads *per se concedit*, “grants of himself”; choose either reading.

“To be referred,” etc. That is, he prefers it to be credited to you.]

XXXVII. What joy flooded your gentle heart, most great Constantine, when after so long an interval you were permitted to see your son—and to see him victorious? He surely recounted the wars he had brought to an end, and did so to win your favor, not to display himself: how he had been in receiving the enemy, how vehement against resistance, how gracious to supplication. His brother listened attentively, and bright hopes and gentle joys stirred his boyish mind; and, while he admired his brother, he also rejoiced for himself, because from their respective years he recognized how near he was to such great glory. Now, most great Constantine, we all ask you, when you have praised him in his presence, when you restore him to the urgently demanding state and to the Gauls who long for him, again and again to admonish him as he returns [Col. 0607C]. For it can scarcely be persuaded that, if barbarism, crushed by your arms, should at some time nevertheless make a movement, he should be like you in spirit and in counsel. Let him only restrain his right hand, spare his hand; let there be something, we beg, in which he may not wish to imitate you again. And you, Constantine Caesar, the greatest increase of the common good—with what prayers does Roman prosperity embrace you! How much it expects from you, equal to what you promise by your name! And although your age still calls you back from imitation of your father’s virtue [Col. 0608A], yet nature already leads you toward his dutifulness; already, with ripened zeal, you are fitted for letters; already your fortunate right hand rejoices in fruitful subscription. Your most indulgent parent entrusts much to you, and what he grants through you he prefers to be referred to your favor.

[Note: [Col. 0608C]

XXXVIII. “So early.” When Constantine was in his fifth year and Crispus in his fifteenth.

“With their greatest benefits.” Benefits which we now receive beforehand, as though early fruits; and, when they reach mature age, there will remain for us the benefits which are normally received from that age in their entirety—as though we had received nothing beforehand.

“At the side of Gaul.” That is, beside the Rhine; shortly afterwards, “in your bosom,” that is, in central Germany. Others read “in its bosom.”

“The Persians themselves.” The Persians sent envoys to Constantine to seek his friendship.

“The deceitful evasions cut away.” Aurelius Victor and Eusebius report this concerning Constantine.

“Nor does anyone,” etc. That is, one who abounds in resources does not fear, but rather, amid such a great abundance of goods, it is shameful to lack them.

“Of maintaining [prosperity].” That is, it is more to be desired that we retain perpetual prosperity than that we possess a greater measure of it.

“When the interest of the state.” That is, when the advantage of the state has compelled you to depart from there.]

XXXVIII. What, then, is more fortunate than these times, when through the beneficence of greatest Constantine, who gave us Caesars so early, we enjoy their greatest benefits while their full age remains still before us? Nothing is diminished, and much is received; thus, although resources are abundantly supplied, hope nonetheless remains undamaged. Therefore, now that the five-year celebrations have happily begun, how earnestly we ought to ask and pray for the decades of the most noble Caesars, to be extended beyond our descendants, is impressed upon us by the very blessings of the times and by the advantages of the state. [Col. 0608B] Barbarism lies prostrate at the side of Gaul, or dispersed in your bosom; even the Persians, a powerful nation and second on earth after Roman greatness, sought your friendship, most great Constantine, no less anxiously than affectionately. There is no nation on earth so fierce that it does not fear or love you. All things abroad are peaceful, at home prosperous: there is abundance of grain and plenty of produce. Cities have been adorned in a marvelous fashion and almost founded anew from the beginning. New laws have been established to regulate morals and break vices. The deceitful evasions of old have been cut away and have lost their snares for entrapping simplicity. Modesty is safe; marriages are protected. Secure possessions rejoice in their own abundance, and there is no fear in anyone of possessing as much as possible; rather, amid so great an abundance of goods, there is great shame in not possessing. Finally, such [Col. 0608C] is the condition of affairs that we entertain a prayer for maintaining prosperity rather than a desire for increasing it. There is only one thing by which Rome could become happier—indeed a very great thing, but still the only one: that it may see Constantine, its preserver; that it may see the most blessed Caesars; that it may have the opportunity to enjoy them according to the measure of its longing; that it may welcome you eagerly, and, when the interest of the state has made you depart, dismiss you in the expectation of receiving you back.

# APPENDIX TO NAZARIUS. ANCIENT PANEGYRICS DELIVERED TO CONSTANTINE BY OTHER SPEAKERS.

[Col. 0609]

[Col. 0609]

# PANEGYRIC DELIVERED TO MAXIMIAN AND CONSTANTINE BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR.

## PREFATORY NOTICE.

[Col. 0609A]

This panegyric, as is immediately clear to the reader, was delivered at the celebration of the marriage of Constantine and Fausta, daughter of Maximian, in A.D. 307, when Maximian, having left his retirement in Lucania in order to resume the empire which he had relinquished with reluctance, and to plot against Constantine, came to Trier, where Constantine was; there Constantine received Fausta as his wife together with the title of Augustus. The author is unknown. Sigonius thinks that he was an Aeduan, but upon what evidence he relies does not appear.

## SYNOPSIS OF THE PANEGYRIC.

In the exordium.—Since the marriage of Constantine, now Augustus, with Fausta, daughter of Maximian, should according to custom be celebrated in an address, the speaker says that he especially ought to do so in the name of the whole state [Col. 0609B], since he enjoys this present joy.

The arrangement appears to be: I. the praises of Constantine; II. the praises of Maximian, §2.

Part I. What moved Maximian to wish that the man who was already his grandson by right of adoption and his son by rank of majesty should also be his son-in-law: namely, because he represented his father Constantius not merely in appearance but in self-control, courage, justice, and prudence, §3. He pursues the individual points of this comparison, §4. That Constantine, content with the title of Caesar, preferred to wait until he should be declared Augustus by the same man by whom his father had been so declared, §5. That Maximian had long before intended him as his son-in-law, when he had ordered a painting to be displayed in the palace at Aquileia in which Fausta, while Constantine was still a boy, offered him a helmet, §6.

Part II. [Col. 0609C] He passes to Maximian, whom he praises for pacifying Gaul, for carrying Roman standards beyond the Rhine against barbarian peoples, for subduing [Col. 0610A] the Quinquegentian tribes in Mauretania, and for triumphing at Rome after so many and such great victories, §8. Ingeniously, he complains that Maximian laid aside the care of the state for a time, §9.

At the conclusion.—He addresses both emperors, from whose new kinship, he says, everything is to be hoped: for henceforth the empire is to be founded upon the virtue of the younger man and the maturity of the elder, §13. He turns his address toward Constantius, enjoying heaven: although he has been taken away, Maximian still has a son, and Constantine does not lack a father. Finally, he prays for numerous offspring for Constantine, §14.

[Note: [Col. 0609C]

I. “Whether you wish it or not.” Said flatteringly, as though Maximian had resumed the purple, which he had laid aside four years earlier, unwillingly and only in obedience to the gods. Yet Eutropius, Victor, and others relate that he did this from desire to rule and weariness of solitude. That Maximian was Augustus at the time of this marriage seems, as Antonius Schonovius observes, contrary to the evidence of history.

“Rising emperor.” For when the oration was delivered, Constantine was for the first time called Augustus instead of Caesar.

“Name of empire.” In some copies the reading is *nomen imper.* This leads me to suspect that *nomen imperatoris*, “the title of emperor,” should be read rather than *imperii*, “of empire.” Indeed, below in §2: “And to you, Constantine, through your father-in-law the title of emperor has been increased.”

“Marriage festivities.” Of Constantine and Fausta, Maximian’s daughter by Theodora. Eusebius, Sozomen, Zonaras, etc.

[Col. 0610C] “To this vow.” The author seems to have wished this oration to be entitled a *votum*, “vow.” For in §13: “As befits this vow,” that is, this speech of mine. Since emperors were worshipped like gods and everything pertaining to them was sacred, it is not surprising if he calls a *votum* the oration which he perhaps had promised to them. Below, in §7: “Thus shall I speak, that the truth of my devotion toward you may appear.”

“Whithersoever Fame.” That is: in whatever direction Fame has spread abroad, beyond nature, in which she is depicted under the form of a flying bird.

“Flying courses.” Read with Acidalus: *discursu volucris incitata*, “urged on by the course of a bird,” and “more than,” etc.

“A pledge has been added.” That is, Maximian’s daughter; below, §3, “when you sought from him a pledge most dear to himself.”

“But nevertheless.” That is: nevertheless, it is fitting that we rejoice more than all others.]

I. Though many may say, and many will say, those things by which all your deeds and the merits of your highest virtues are praised, most sacred princes—Maximian, Augustus forever, whether you wish it or not, and Constantine, rising [Col. 0610B] emperor—yet I have resolved in this speech especially to embrace those matters which belong to this particular joy: the joy in which the title of empire has been added to you as Caesar, and the festivals of this heavenly marriage are celebrated. For your other benefits to the state may be proclaimed on many occasions in different times; to this vow an address proper to it is now owed, since what has been done once will endure forever. I know indeed that the zeal of those rejoicing now flourishes throughout the whole world, wherever Fame has spread abroad—endowed beyond nature, as she is imagined, with the swift courses of a winged creature and sounding with more than a thousand voices—so that it is consecrated by the congratulations of all nations. For what could have happened to human affairs either more noble for glory or more certain for safety than this: that to your former harmony and perpetual loyalty this pledge too has been added, venerable through the closest union of the highest names, namely, that one emperor has bestowed his daughter upon another emperor? Yet we ought to surpass all men [Col. 0611A] in exultation, we who behold this great blessing of the state in person and perceive, through contemplating your very faces, that you have so come together, so joined not merely your right hands but all your feelings and minds, that, if it were possible, you would desire to pass into one another’s hearts.

[Note: [Col. 0611C]

II. “May youth be renewed.” For Maximian had then reached his sixtieth year.

“By prolonging.” Others, from an old manuscript, read *propagando*, “by extending.” Indeed, shortly afterward: “you extend the state by an imperial line.”

“May grow together.” Below, §13: “That kinship will surely grow together through perpetual lines, which has always joined the foremost men in the state in concord.” “The pleasure of preserving.” Acidalus reads more aptly *voluntas*, “the will.”

[Col. 0611D] “Since it is immortal.” While some people succeed others, even though individuals are mortal, the state nevertheless becomes as though always whole and the same; and so, through propagated posterity, it is as though immortal.

“In the thousandth year.” Under the two Philips, when the son succeeded his father.

“That is, for all.” Read with Gruter *idem*, “the same,” or with others *id*, “this.”]

II. For what could you have given more dearly, or what could you have received more dearly, than that through this kinship, Maximian, your youth has been renewed through your son-in-law, and, Constantine, the title of emperor has been increased for you through your father-in-law? Therefore, eternal princes, we offer you the greatest thanks in the name of the public, because by receiving children and hoping for grandchildren, by prolonging the succession of your line, you provide for all future ages that the Roman state, long tossed about by the diverse characters and fortunes of its rulers, may at last grow firm in the perpetual roots of your house, and that its empire may be as immortal as the everlasting offspring of emperors. This is true filial devotion; this is the pleasure of preserving the human race: to give nations an example that they should seek marriage more earnestly and rear children, so that, in supplying successors for individuals, the fact that each person is mortal may be no obstacle, since the state is immortal through posterity. Therefore, if those laws which marked unmarried persons with a penalty and honored parents with rewards are rightly called the foundations of the state because they supplied Roman armies with a nursery of youth and, as it were, a perennial source of human bodies, what worthy name can we assign to this service of yours to the state? You who extend the state not by a plebeian stock but by an imperial line [Col. 0611C], so that what we had at last rejoiced to have occurred in the thousandth year after the City’s foundation—namely, that the helm of our common safety should not be handed over by succession to new families—may endure for all ages: emperors always Herculian.

[Note: [Col. 0611D]

III. “Younger.” If compared with sixty-year-old Maximian; Constantine himself was in his thirty-fourth year.

“But indeed.” He is on slippery ground, uncertain which emperor’s praises to pursue first.

“Both of your father and of yourself.” For Maximian had made Constantius, Constantine’s father, Caesar and Augustus.

“Nature stamped.” He confirms the same point elsewhere in these words: “This is why so great a likeness of form passed from him to you [Col. 0612C], that nature seems to have been imprinted upon your faces in the act of stamping them. The same expression, the same gravity on the brow, the same calm in the eyes and mouth; so blushfulness is an indicator of modesty,” etc.]

III. What order, then, shall I establish for praising and venerating each of you? For I have so far spoken generally of the desires of you both that concurred in this bond [Col. 0612A]. I perceive, senior Augustus, that you take precedence in majesty; you follow, younger Emperor. But indeed, just as divinity was first won for your father-in-law, Constantine, before you sought from him the pledge most dear to him; so now too, in this congratulation, those matters ought first to be spoken which that great man, author of both your father’s and your own imperial power, considered in you and rejoiced that you had sought. O divine judgment of yours, Maximian: you wished that this man, your grandson by right of adoption, your son by rank of majesty, should also be your son-in-law! I mean the son of divine Constantius, into whom his father’s early youth poured itself, in whose face nature stamped that heavenly countenance, and who suffices, for us still longing for him who has been transported to the assemblies of the gods, in place of two persons. For in you, Constantine, not only your father’s appearance [Col. 0612B], but also his self-control, courage, justice, and prudence present themselves to the hopes of nations.

[Note: [Col. 0612C]

IV. “At the first entrance upon youth.” An important passage for establishing the self-control of both Constantius and Constantine; but we have discussed this in the life of each.

“He [killed] many thousands of Franks.” Of Constantius’ expedition another panegyric writes thus: “Not content with conquering them, he transferred the nations themselves into Roman territory, so that they were compelled to lay aside not only their arms but also their ferocity.” In the same place, concerning Britain, at last recovered after the tenth year.

“Their kings.” Ascaric and Regaisus, who, immediately after Constantius’ death, began to stir up disturbances. Constantine crushed them, led them into the theatre as captives of war, to be torn apart by beasts. Eutropius.

“By being born there.” Those who think Constantine was born in Britain rely especially on these words. Although they can be twisted into another sense, we have observed in his life that they should nevertheless be understood of Constantine’s native birth.

“To you, all [enemies].” That is, after you crushed all enemies terrified by your courage.]

IV. For in what way could you more closely equal your father’s self-control than by submitting yourself immediately, from the very end of boyhood, to the laws of marriage, so that at the first entrance upon youth you might form a husband’s mind and admit into that sacred breast nothing of wandering desires, nothing of pleasures permitted to your age—a new wonder even then, a youth devoted to his wife? But, as things were, with prescient mind you trained yourself in every observance of modesty, because you were later to take such a wife. You likewise attained his courage already at its beginnings. He killed, expelled, captured, and carried away many thousands of Franks who had invaded Batavia and other lands on this side of the Rhine [Col. 0612C]; you began with their very kings, and at once both punished their former crimes and bound the fickle loyalty of the whole people with fear. He freed Britain from servitude; by being born there, you made even its inhabitants noble. He subdued many barbarian nations by victory and softened them by pardon; for you, with all enemies cowed by terror at your zeal, there is meanwhile a lack of material for conquest.

[Col. 0613A] [Note: [Col. 0613C]

V. “The elder African.” That is, Scipio Africanus the Elder; see Pliny’s *Panegyric*.

“And Pompey.” While still seventeen years old, he served under his father Pompeius; in his twenty-third year he himself led three legions to Sulla, and three years later, after recovering Italy and Nicomedia, celebrated a triumph. For his other victories see Plutarch.

“You surpass [them] by assuming empire early.” Nazarius, §16: “You, best Emperor, when you entered upon your principate still immature in years, yet already mature for empire, showed that the course of age is not to be awaited in the haste of virtue.”

“And of such great affairs.” That is, and that in this first age you should excel in the glory of the greatest achievements [Col. 0613D].

“The greatest tribuneships.” That is, as a very great tribune.

“Content with the title.” Eutropius, Zosimus, Victor, and others agree with this passage.]

V. You imitate and follow your father’s justice and devotion in such a way that, when all who flee to you seek various forms of aid, whether against others’ injuries or for their own advantage, you seem to discharge your father’s legacies; and you yourself rejoice to have it proclaimed publicly that whatever you have done justly and generously has necessarily been done by Constantius’ son. For what shall I say of that prudence by which we almost believe you will surpass your father himself? You surpass, by taking on imperial power so early, those ancient leaders of the Roman state—Scipio Africanus the Elder and Pompey the Great—who outstripped the course of age by virtue, and you bear the burden of such great affairs while your virtue is still beginning. For although you will have performed many brave and many wise deeds while completing your first military service through the greatest tribuneships, it is necessary that you recognize the omens of such great fortune, young Emperor. Yet why do I apply to you the term of your age rather than of your gravity? Your maturity is so great that, when your father had left you the empire, you were nevertheless content with the title of Caesar and preferred to wait until the same man who had declared him Augustus should declare you so. For you judged that imperial power itself would be more glorious if you did not increase it as an inheritance by succession but earned it as due to your own virtues from the highest emperor.

[Note: [Col. 0613D]

VI. “That image.” So far as I know, this image is mentioned nowhere except in this passage; but it is doubtless too slight a matter to have a place in history.

“In the palace at Aquileia.” Aquileia, in Italy, the metropolis of the Carni, lies between Concordia to the west, Tergeste to the east, and the Adriatic Sea to the south, from which it is scarcely nine miles distant. Aquilée.

“Of a beautiful bird.” He calls the peacock a beautiful bird because of the varied brilliance of its feathers.

“Apelles.” Apelles was an outstanding painter, a native of Cos—Cos being one of the Cycladic islands. He alone contributed almost more to painting than all the rest. He flourished in the time of Alexander of Macedon, who esteemed him so highly that he wished to be painted only by him. Dying, Apelles left unfinished his Coan Venus, which he had begun; yet even in this state it was so excellent that no painter dared to complete it. Ovid:

> Had Apelles never painted the Coan Venus,  
> She would lie hidden beneath the waters of the sea.

“Parrhasius.” Parrhasius too was a most celebrated painter, a native of Ephesus. When he competed with Zeuxis for the praise of painting, Zeuxis deceived birds with grapes aptly and artfully painted; Parrhasius, by spreading out a cloth, deceived not only birds but the rival of his own renown. He lived somewhat before Apelles.

[Col. 0614D] “The form of each most especially.” Read with Acidalus *praecipuae*, that is, outstanding and exceptional; shortly afterward, read *similitudo autem*, “but likeness.”]

VI. There is no doubt that he was already then building up for you that sacred summit of divine power, since long ago, before you could even ask, he of his own accord chose you as his son-in-law.
