For this, as I hear, is shown by that painting in the palace at Aquileia, placed directly [Col. 0613C] in view of the banquet: there a girl, already venerable in divine beauty but still unequal to her burden, holds up and offers to you—then still a boy—a helmet gleaming with gold and gems and rising with the feathers of a beautiful bird, so that a betrothal-gift may make you more beautiful, a thing which scarcely any ornaments of dress [Col. 0614A] can accomplish. Fortunate was that painter, whoever he was; and though he surpassed Apelles and Parrhasius themselves in skill, he was nevertheless more fortunate in the subject of the image than in his art. For although painters themselves maintain that the imitation of each outstanding form is most difficult, because ugliness is quickly expressed by definite marks of its own, while the likeness of beauty is as arduous as beauty is rare, nevertheless he undertook not so much labor in transferring divine features from your faces as he drew divinity from seeing you close at hand—observing you intently and carefully, drawing from the cheerfulness of that age fixed and serious expressions, and finally bringing forth the silent forebodings of your love—so that in the painting you might freely behold one another in what modesty denied you between yourselves.

[Col. 0614B] [Note: [Col. 0614D]

VIII. “In mind.” That is, you had conceived it in spirit beforehand.

“In the most delightful seat of joy.” In the place where Bacchus, giver of joy, reigns; and *Aeneid* I.738.

“You were predestining.” A non-Ciceronian word for “you were conceiving beforehand in your mind.”

“So that at the same time.” That is, so that, while in that image you watched your little daughter Fausta and the boy Constantine growing up together, you might nourish yourself with the pleasing expectation of your desire, which you confirmed by their marriage.

“For what.” That is, for what could be more fitting?

“You had admitted by kinship.” When he gave his stepdaughter Theodora in marriage to Constantius.

“Generosity.” That is, munificence.

[Col. 0615C] “Always”—that is, nevertheless, he remains whole in the distribution of his waters.]

VII. But indeed, Maximian, you had already then foreseen this with divine mind; when the age allowed it, you had desired to be asked, when in that most delightful seat of joy you were appointing beforehand the pleasures of this marriage. Thus, while watching her as a little girl and him as he grew up, you might long enjoy the expectation of the desire which you confirmed by this union. For what could you have done more fittingly, what more worthy of your foresight, than to entrust from your inmost affections the pledge of supreme empire to the son of the man whom you had long before both admitted into kinship and associated in majesty? This, Maximian, is your generosity peculiar among all princes. Others have bestowed riches, honors, or even empires themselves, but have bestowed them alone; you, with a spirit greater than the rest [Col. 0614C], grant together both what your devotion holds dearest and what fortune holds most preeminent. Nor, Maximian, is this greatness of spirit in you to be wondered at, upon whom the immortal gods have heaped such great goods of nature and ornaments of fortune that, although you give away the greatest things [Col. 0615A], everything remains with you as though you alone possessed it. For just as Ocean, who supplies all waters to heaven and earth, nevertheless always remains entire in his flows, so you, Maximian, can give away empire but cannot cease to possess it. When I have reached the proper point, I shall speak of this in such a way that I may perhaps seem too bold to some; yet the truth of my devotion toward you will be apparent.

[Note: [Col. 0615C]

VIII. “Matched.” That is, by equal virtues.

“At the very rising of his divine power.” As soon as Maximian was made Caesar, he subdued Gaul, made savage by the injuries of Carinus Caesar in former times and contemplating rebellion, and restored it to obedience to the state.

“Which was now falsely.” That is, what was reported of ancient emperors—Caesar, Tiberius, Trajan—that they had carried arms against barbarians beyond the Rhine, was considered a fabrication in Maximian’s time, since nothing similar had been seen from those times until he, first of all men, renewed these examples of courage.

“With his brother.” Diocletian.

“Either takes it well.” Pacatus remarkably admired this panegyric, from which he has almost transcribed one or two passages, §22: “Whatever barbarian nation has ever been formidable to you in strength, ferocity, or numbers, either accepts it willingly that it should be at peace, or rejoices like a friend if it serves.”

“Either takes it well.” That is, partly it bears this with equanimity so as to have peace; partly, being subject to us, it rejoices as though it bore the yoke voluntarily.

“The people welcomed [you].” He alludes to the triumph which Maximian celebrated with Diocletian in A.D. 298, when he returned to Rome after subduing the Moors. Victors were led up to the Capitol.

[Col. 0616C] “By their throng.” That is, you could scarcely enter the gates of the city, so great was the multitude of people crowding around you.

“You again in the twentieth year.” Maximian abdicated the empire with Diocletian in A.D. 304, the nineteenth year after his tenth of imperial power—certainly, at least, if the calculation begins from the year in which he was made Caesar.]

VIII. It now follows that, since I have praised your virtues, Constantine Augustus, to your father-in-law, you too, although you know it very well, should hear how great an emperor’s kinship adorns you. This is the man who gave you the name which he received from the god who was founder of his race, who proved that he was the offspring of Hercules not by flattering fictions but by matched virtues. This is the man who, at the very rising [Col. 0615B] of his divine power, restored to obedience to the state the Gauls made savage by the injuries of earlier times, and restored them to themselves for their own safety. This is the man who first carried Roman standards beyond the Rhine against barbarian peoples, a deed which was now thought falsely reported of ancient emperors. When Germany had been repeatedly and often subdued by campaigns with his brother, it either accepts it willingly that it should be at peace, or rejoices like a friend if it obeys. You conquered, recovered, and transferred the most ferocious peoples of Mauretania, settled on inaccessible mountain ridges and protected by natural defenses. At your first arrival the people welcomed you with such joy and in such numbers that, eager to bear you, if only with their eyes, to the bosom of Capitoline Jupiter, they scarcely allowed you to enter the city gates because of their own crowding. Rome itself wished again to hold you, emperor in your twentieth year and consul for the eighth time, in a sort of embrace [Col. 0615C], so that it seemed already to foresee and fear what came to pass. For there is one matter, eternal Emperor, in which you almost deserved the state’s complaint.

[Note: [Col. 0616C]

IX. “Hear the unrestrained voice of our grief.” A passage full of artifice, in which he removes from Maximian the stigma of fickleness.

“Groaning with [our grief] enclosed,” that is, hidden in the innermost breast.

[Col. 0616D] “As things were.” We have noted above that this formula of speech is characteristic of this age.

“Lest even that man’s.” Read *neve illius*, Acidalus. That is, lest you should be inferior to him in that new praise, whatever sort of praise it was.

“In you.” Read *inter vos*, “between you,” Acidalus; or *vobis*, Langius.

“Must be declined.” Others read *abeundum*, “must be departed”; I prefer *abstinendum*, “must be refrained from,” or *absistendum*, “must be desisted from,” as Acidalus conjectures.

“Constantine’s children and our grandchildren.” Thus I read with Rhenanus and Daniel, rather than the reading of the Putean edition.

“For what else?” The sense is: What else was the reason why we granted Diocletian, your partner in empire, leave to rest because he preferred repose to imperial labors, except that he thereby made it possible for you to administer the empire in place of two?]

IX. Hear the free voice of our grief. For when we complain that the gods themselves generally neglect human affairs while hailstorms fall, the earth gapes open, and cities are swallowed up, they forgive us: they may seem to happen not because the gods wish cities to be swallowed up, but because the gods are looking elsewhere or because the fated course of events presses onward while they attend to other matters. Such, Emperor, is the thing which you chose to do, to the grief of us all as we mourned with a suppressed groan—not because you were led by neglect of the state, flight from labor, or desire for idleness, but by constancy in a plan, as things were, agreed between you, and by brotherly devotion: lest you should abandon in participation in any act the man whom you had always had as companion of your whole life and of the highest affairs, and lest you should yield even to his—whatever it may have been, certainly a new—distinction. Yet the reason for declining or enduring labor was far different between you. Even if you had offered the whole excuse of your age, still you ought not on that account to have refused the cares of the state [Col. 0616B]. Or if every helmsman of greatest age is the surest safeguard, is not the best commander the one most experienced through practice? Or will Constantine’s children and our grandchildren ever allow you, even when you have reached the height of old age, to draw in the sails of the state which, even as a young man, you have filled with such favorable winds? Yet, however permissible it may have been for an emperor whom years compelled or health failed to sound retreat, we marvel that you, in whom these powers are still whole and sound, in whom there is this vigor of the whole body, this imperial fire of the eyes, should have hoped for an untimely leisure. For what other grant of repose could be given to your partner in majesty than that you should succeed him in imperial authority on behalf of two?

[Col. 0616C] [Note: [Col. 0617C]

X. “In these regions,” that is, in Gaul, where this oration was delivered. Shortly afterward, “there indeed,” that is, in Italy, where Maxentius raised extraordinary disturbances.

To rule emperors. That is, Rome commands Maximian, as is her right, to resume the empire he had laid aside. She withdrew the same army from Maximian when, as a private person, he retired into Lucania, and restored it to him when he advanced with forces against Maxentius.

[Col. 0617D] To calm the spirits. Of the Praetorians rebelling with Maxentius.

Stretching out suppliant hands to you. Note the ingenious personification of the city of Rome, most aptly devised to avert from Maximian whatever envy or charge of fickleness might have attached to his resumption of imperial power.

Or rather. Acidalius thinks these two words ought to be deleted. Yet they occur in all editions.]

X. But surely the very changeability and nature of Fortune required this, since she had been permitted to alter nothing while you held the empire: that the unbroken prosperity of those twenty years should be marked by some interval. Or perhaps the immortal gods wished to demonstrate that the commonwealth had stood firm by reliance upon you, since it could not stand without you. Yet in these regions [Col. 0617A] it did not lack its former stability; but there it nearly collapsed from the foundations, where you, Maximian, had departed. So great had been the firmness it derived from your support there where, once abandoned, it most severely wavered. For just as the earth, when its solidity is disturbed by winds or by waters admitted beneath it, is accustomed to tremble, so all Italy—and Rome herself—when the hand that had supported her was suddenly withdrawn, shook and almost sank down.

I pass over this hastily. For why should we even recall adversity, when we see that everything has been restored by your return? Rome herself acted in a manner worthy of the majesty of her name, to show that she too could rule emperors. She withdrew her armies and restored them to you; and when you had brought the authority of a private prince to calm their emotions, she stretched out suppliant hands toward you—or [Col. 0617B] rather, in complaint cried aloud:

[Note: [Col. 0617D]

XI. To the deified Augustus. For he died in the seventy-sixth year of his life and the fifty-sixth of his reign. Suetonius.

That you. That is, that you should withdraw from me the strength which you had dedicated to me.

“Through you he shall have stood by you.” A corrupt passage. Perhaps: “Such a great emperor shall have cost you [something]”; namely, restoring peace to the commonwealth, so that this glory must be purchased at the cost of some injury to yourself. It touches upon what Eutropius says of him: Hercules Maximian [Col. 0618C] afterwards tried, in an assembly of the army, to strip his son Maxentius of power, but endured mutiny and the soldiers’ insults.

Asked by his brother. That is, by Diocletian; commanded by his mother, that is, by his native country.

More easily. That is, it would have been easier to have held the empire without any interruption.

Interrupted. That is, if there is nevertheless some interruption, fresh strength must be applied.]

XI. How long, Maximian, shall I endure this: that I am shaken while you rest; that liberty is taken from me while you claim for yourself an unlawful discharge? Was what was denied to the deified Augustus after seventy years of life and fifty of rule granted to you so quickly? Did that Hercules, to whom heaven gave so many altars, so many temples, so many names, give you to me in order that you might sit idle on a country estate and lose the use of the strength dedicated to me? Return yourself to my helm; and since you hastened to enter harbor upon a calm sea, go out upon the waves—anxious indeed out of love for me, but secure in your own majesty. And yet—[corrupt text; perhaps: “an emperor will have cost you so much”]—you will suffer injury in restoring me. Long ago you ruled when asked by your brother; rule again when commanded by your mother.

O heavenly devotion, eternal Emperor, which alone conquered that spirit of yours always unconquered! You could not resist the command of that holy parent; and, though unwilling, you obeyed and restored yourself to those vigils and cares which you had experienced for twenty years. With what benefits, mistress of nations, can you compensate this obedience of your emperor? Knowing from so great experience how heavy is the burden of command, for your sake he does not avail himself [Col. 0618A] of that pleasure which he had tasted, but takes up the great burden of the commonwealth after repose. It would have been easier to rule continuously; for custom does not perceive even very great labor, whereas interruptions demand new powers.

[Note: [Col. 0618C]

XII. That god. The comparison of Maximian and Apollo is highly ingenious. Apollo had necessarily to take up and guide again the reins which had been abandoned and badly entrusted to an errant driver, namely Phaethon, so as to restore peace to the disordered world.

“I do not take it back.” Not permanently, but I preserve it, to be restored to you shortly at that very time.

“Have subsided.” *Aeneid* VII.27:

> … When the winds have subsided, and every blast  
> Has suddenly fallen still.

In more distant lands. He indicates the disturbances raised by Maxentius in Italy.

Some. That is, there are certain tumults, and the remnants of the aroused tempest still roar.

Before your nods. Read: “at your nods.”]

XII. How great was the foresight required of you, eternal Emperor, how great the authority, to raise the fallen supports of the commonwealth, revive what had lost its breath, gather up what had been scattered! We wondered that you were a private man after being emperor. It is far more astonishing to bear the empire after leisure. Only that god, it is said, could do this—the god to whom we owe our life and sight: to take back the reins badly entrusted, and the course of a tranquility disturbed by an errant driver, and to guide them once more. You too, Emperor, readily accomplished what was like this. Nor is this surprising, since when the empire departed [Col. 0618B] from you, and though you wished to be called a private man, inborn majesty clung to you. All your armies and all the provinces endured with some equanimity your repose after such great labors; they never believed that you had ceased to rule.

What, Maximian, do you suppose Jupiter himself answered you when you said with lofty spirit: “Take back, Jupiter, what you lent”? Surely he answered thus: “I did not entrust it to you as a loan, but for eternity. I do not take it back; I preserve it.” Therefore, as soon as you checked the rushing commonwealth and took back its wavering helm, the hope of safety dawned upon all. The winds subsided, the clouds fled, and the waves sank. Even if somewhere in more distant lands some darkness still hangs about, or the remaining beat of the waves murmurs, nevertheless it must grow bright and fall silent at your [Col. 0618C] nods.

[Note: [Col. 0618D]

XIII. You have renewed. For a little earlier Maximian Augustus was the father-in-law of Constantius Augustus; now he says that this same relation has been renewed by the immortal gods. For Maximian is again emperor and Constantine’s father-in-law.

[Col. 0619B] “This one [supports] the elder.” This passage had to be emended in accordance with Livineius’s conjecture. Previously it read *iste senior* (“that elder”), in which, I think, no one fails to recognize a corruption.

“Surely through perpetual…” In the Putean edition: “Let this affinity surely grow together through perpetual devotions,” etc. With Gruter I have erased the word *pietatibus* (“devotions”), which is absent from the Langian manuscript. Others read, in place of *pietatibus*, “this devotion and affinity,” etc.

Gracchus and Cornelia. Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, as praetor, subdued Gaul; as consul in A.U.C. 576, Spain; and in a second consulship, Sardinia. He celebrated two triumphs. He had serious enmities with Scipio Africanus the Elder, but laid them aside for the sake of the commonwealth and married Scipio’s daughter Cornelia.

The Actian victory. At Actium, A.U.C. 724, reported on the fourth day before the Nones of September. Actium is a city and promontory of Epirus at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, opposite Nicopolis, where Antony was defeated in a naval battle.

Agrippa, the son-in-law. He married Julia, Augustus’ daughter, and was consul three times. The conduct of the Actian war was entrusted to him. *Aeneid* VI.682:

> Elsewhere, with winds and gods propitious,  
> Agrippa stands aloft, etc.

Undertook it as a young man. When he was twenty-four years old.

Hannibal. Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, at nineteen years of age, brought by his father to the altars, swore perpetual hatred toward the Romans. Thereafter he destroyed Saguntum, allied with Rome; crossed into Italy; and defeated P. Scipio at the Ticinus, Sempronius Longus at the Trebia, Flaminius [Col. 0620B] at Lake Trasimene, and Paullus and Varro at Cannae. Enervated by the pleasures of Campania, he was first overcome by Fabius, then by Valerius Flaccus, again by Galerius, Gracchus, and Scipio; finally, lest he be surrendered to the Romans, he was killed by poison which he kept beneath his ring. Aurelius Victor.

Marius. After Jugurtha had been led before his chariot, after the Teutones had been defeated in Gaul and the Cimbri in Italy, after a triumph and several years spent in exile, Gaius Marius, already an old man, entered the City with Cinna and Sertorius, rescued it from Sulla’s faction, and became consul for the seventh time in A.U.C. 668. Aurelius Victor.]

XIII. I have said, most sacred Princes, what the occasion required concerning those qualities which you ought, as you do, to admire and love in one another. It remains to unite at the end of my speech, as suits this prayer, those very things which I have spoken separately concerning your virtues. How much have you renewed for the Roman empire, immortal gods—things which, as matters stood, [Col. 0619A] had already yielded to age! Constantine, the new emperor, has begun to be more than a son to Maximian, the eternal emperor. The one favors the growing man; the other stands by the elder. May this affinity surely grow together through perpetual generations, this affinity which has always joined the greatest men in the commonwealth in concord. For if the marriage of Gracchus and Cornelia restored to favor families however divided; if Agrippa, Augustus’ son-in-law, achieved the Actian victory for the deified Augustus alone—what ought we to hope when the bond of marriage has fastened even the everlasting affection of father and son?

And if Publius Scipio undertook the Punic War as a young man, destined later to overcome Hannibal himself; if Marius, as an old man, recovered the City from Sulla’s faction—and it is memorable that this occurred after a great interval of time—how easily may the Roman commonwealth now [Col. 0619B] lay aside all fears, defended as it is by the two ages of a united empire, and enjoying alike the valor of youth and the maturity of age!

[Note: [Col. 0620C]

XIV. Father. He addresses Maximian; soon afterwards he directs his speech to Constantius: “you, young man.”

Making peace. A word either never or rarely used in the plural in the classical period of good Latin; but several similar usages occur repeatedly among writers of this age, as I observed above.

Where the Roman… That is, in that part of the Roman empire which lies close to barbarian nations.

In a chariot almost visible. This had to be restored from an old manuscript in place of “in a chariot and almost visible, while the sun, rising nearby….” The sense is: the setting sun itself, hastening toward its neighboring risings, received him upon its chariot to carry him up to heaven; as though Constantine had risen for the whole world when Constantius set. It alludes to a coin, on whose reverse Constantius is borne in a chariot, steering four horses with his left hand and joining his right [Col. 0620D] to the hand extended from heaven.

The same father. Maximian.]

XIV. It is fitting, father, that from the very summit of empire you survey the common world and, with a heavenly nod, decree destinies for human affairs, give auspices for wars to be waged, [Col. 0620A] impose laws for peaces to be made. It is fitting for you, young man, tirelessly to travel along the frontiers wherever the Roman empire presses upon barbarian nations, frequently to send laurels to your father-in-law, to seek instructions, and report accomplishments. Thus it will come about that you both possess the counsel of a single breast, and that each has the strength of two.

Happy in empire, and happier after empire, you surely hear and see these things, deified Constantius: you whom the sun himself, almost visible in his chariot, while returning at sunset to neighboring risings, received to carry up to heaven. With what joy will you now be filled, with what delight will you rejoice, when that same father, the same father-in-law, the same emperor has introduced this your son—who first made you a father—into possession of your empire? This is your immortality peculiar to you above all other deified men, which we behold: a son like you in appearance, like you in spirit, equal in imperial power. [Col. 0620B] Though they may have envied us, the fates have nevertheless been unable to take anything from your house. Nor does Maximian lack a son such as you were, nor Constantine a father. Indeed, so that your family connection may be renewed in every way, this man is again father-in-law, again son-in-law, so that the most blessed emperor may always be enlarged in descendants and grandsons from your stock.

[Col. 0619]

EUMENIUS’ PANEGYRIC TO CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS.

PREFACE. The life of Eumenius.

[Col. 0619]

Eumenius, Greek by origin, was born at Augustodunum in Gaul. [Col. 0619D] In that city, then flourishing exceedingly and, as it were, a seat of liberal arts, he says that his grandfather had once taught, although he was more than eighty years old: a man born at Athens, long famous at Rome, and later detained in that very city because he had observed and approved its people’s love of learning and their reverence for this very work.

He himself, while he was *magister sacrae memoriae* in the court of Constantius Chlorus Caesar—that is, responsible for drafting memorials and letters and for authenticating rescripts—performed that distinguished office of the palace with such excellence of intellect and eloquence that Constantius appointed him to the place of the deceased director of the schools of the Aedui. In the record of this appointment Constantius commends Eumenius’ eloquence and seriousness; and, doubling his salary, assigns him six hundred thousand *nummi* (that is, 26,250 French livres) as pay. Obedient to Caesar, he accepted this sum of money, as he himself says, insofar as honor was concerned; but he requested, in this most elegant speech, that authority be granted him to expend it upon restoring the schools of the Aedui.

He testifies somewhere that he had many children, when, turning his speech to Constantine the Great, he says: “I give the greatest thanks to your divinity, and I commend to you my children who remain, especially the one already administering the highest protections of the treasury, into whom devotion has transferred my whole self…. Yet what I said of all my children was, Emperor, a broad ambition. For besides those five whom I begot, I also count among them those whom I have advanced to the guardianship of the forum and to offices of the palace.”

The year of his birth and death is uncertain. Certainly, he cannot have been very young in A.D. 296, when this speech was delivered, since his son was already then holding a highly distinguished magistracy. [Col. 0621C] Elsewhere he says that an extemporaneous faculty of speaking does not suit him well, since he was now beyond middle age. And elsewhere, wishing Constantine would someday come to Augustodunum, he says: “But that happiness must see whether it is still owed to my lifetime.”

Four panegyrics are commonly attributed to Eumenius. One is that which he delivered at Augustodunum for the restoration of the schools of the Aedui, before a *vir perfectissimus*, that is, before the governor of Lugdunensis Prima—Rictiovarus, I think, as I show in the notes—in 296. This is clear from the victories of the emperors and Caesars briefly reviewed in section 21, which can fall only in that year, as I observed in the lives of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian Augustus and of Constantius Caesar. The fifth [panegyric], which he delivered at Trier before Constantius Caesar, is shown by these words from the preceding speech: “The time must be considered: Caesar is standing by while we speak.” The two Augusti and Galerius Caesar were absent, as is clear from the preceding passage, in which, briefly recounting their glorious deeds, he says: “I shall celebrate these at other times, in the presence of those who performed them.” It was delivered at the end of A.D. 296, after Allectus had been killed and Britain recovered, before Constantius’ victory near Langres, of which there is no word, while Maximian Augustus was attacking the Moors.

Although some assign this to an uncertain author, and Rhenanus assigns it to Mamertinus or to some Belgian, perhaps because the author of this panegyric says at the beginning that he had long been silent, though Eumenius delivered a panegyric in that very year; and because he says that he had delivered an oration before Maximian, which is no longer extant. Yet I attribute this and the following two panegyrics to Eumenius both because of the similarity of style and because he frequently discusses the education of boys and service in the palace.

Another was delivered at Trier before Constantine on the birthday of that city, in A.D. 310, shortly after his birthday, which, if the old calendar in Bucherius is correct, fell on the third day before the Kalends of March. At the end of this speech he invites the emperor not to hesitate to come to the city of the Aedui. When, in the following year, the emperor entered that city, ordered its public buildings restored, and relieved its citizens by remission of taxes, the Aedui at once sent Eumenius himself as ambassador to the emperor at Trier. There, amid the notable assembly of envoys who had come from every quarter to celebrate the emperor’s quinquennial festival, he delivered another panegyric, intending to thank Constantine in the name of the Flavians.

NOTICE.

We have spoken above, in the Life of Eumenius, about the author of this panegyric and the place and time at which it was delivered.

SYNOPSIS OF THE PANEGYRIC.

IN THE EXORDIUM.—He shows that, in praising emperors and Caesars, it is difficult to meet human expectation; but that he will give his speech such a form as chiefly to dedicate it to Constantine.

[Col. 0622C] The arrangement may be:

I. Constantine’s election to the empire.  
II. His various victories.

Part I. Constantine’s lineage: that he received as an inheritance the empire from his grandfather Claudius and father Constantius, §2. That he earned this inheritance itself by military service, especially because while still a youth he joined battle hand-to-hand with a Sarmatian leader, §3. That Constantine was preferred above his other brothers, in order to succeed his father Constantius, to whom he resembled in all respects, §4. An outstanding comparison of the two: Constantius captured Boulogne with incredible speed; while a fleet was prepared to cross into Britain, he liberated Batavia and Frisia, occupied by different Frankish kings; transplanted the captives to deserted regions of Gaul; finally recovered Britain in the tenth year, §5. He exercised clemency in victory. Again he defeated the Franks in their own settlements. Near Langres he killed sixty thousand Alamanni. He filled the fields of Vindonissa with enemy slaughter; and compelled those same peoples, who had dared cross the Rhine when it was frozen, to surrender, §6. He advanced as far as the land of the Caledonians and Picts, Thule, and the Fortunate Islands, §7. He left Constantine as heir to the empire before him, §8. The speaker returns to Constantine. He congratulates Britain for many reasons, especially because she first saw him as Caesar, §9.

Part II. After his father’s death Constantine, now Augustus, restores security to Gaul by punishing Ascarius and Ragaissus, kings of the Franks, whom he had captured in war, §10. Having entered the territory of the Bructeri, he destroys them completely, §12. He so terrifies the rest by building the Agrippine bridge that, while it has scarcely been properly begun, they seek peace as suppliants and offer hostages, §13. He briefly touches upon Maximian’s faults, especially his ungrateful attitude toward Constantine, §14. He praises the steadfastness of Diocletian, who was still living privately at Salona, in his resolution, §15. Again he returns to Constantine: how dear he was to the soldiers, whom Maximian’s promises and gifts could not draw away from him, §16. With what eagerness they hastened against Maximian, first to Arles and then to Marseille, §17. The siege of Marseille, §18. Constantine’s mercy toward the conquered, §21. After Constantine’s departure for Italy, barbarians meditating an incursion were restrained by his sudden return; he attributes these victories to Apollo.

In conclusion.—He wishes that Constantine may turn aside to see Apollo’s temple [Col. 0623B] among the Aedui; thus he will at the same time see the city restored, §22. The orator commends his children to the emperor, §23.

THE PANEGYRIC BEGINS.

[Note: [Col. 0623C]

I. “A day in that city.” Other copies have *diem dicto in ista civitate* (“a day appointed in that city”); but I have deleted the word *dicto*, which Livineius says is absent from the old exemplar and which in fact obscures the meaning.

“In that city.” I think Trier, whose birthday, as he will say in §22, was then being celebrated.

“A man of middle age.” That is, a man already of advanced and mature age, such as I am, ought not to employ extemporaneous speech. Middle age is that which lies between youth and old age. It is reckoned approximately from the thirtieth to the fortieth year. Cicero calls it in *On Old Age* 76 “a settled age”; others call it ἀκμή (*akmē*), “the prime” or vigor of life.

[Col. 0623D] “Unless long written.” In his customary manner Eumenius looked back to a passage of Cicero, *For the Manilian Law*, §2: “For since formerly I had not yet dared, on account of my age, to approach the authority of this place, and had determined that nothing should be brought here unless perfected by talent and elaborated by industry,” etc.

“I prefer my speech rejected.” Some read “my speech desired,” others “sought,” others “brief”; but “which I prefer rejected” means “which I refuse,” because it may cause you weariness. Others read *respici* (“to be esteemed”).

“Therefore first.” That is, for this reason I shall first compress my speech into that part which, etc.

“Most unconquered princes.” Constantine, Licinius, and Maximinus.

“To celebrate him who is present.” These words show that this speech was delivered before Constantine.]

I. I would do, most sacred Emperor, what several persons advised me shortly before: since your Majesty had granted to my modest ability this most celebrated day in that city for speaking, I would take the opening of my address from that very subject—were I not called away from it by a twofold consideration. I reflected that a man of middle age should not parade an impromptu power of speech, and that nothing but what has long been written and often handled ought to be brought before the ears of so great a divinity. For one who speaks extemporaneously before the emperor of the Roman people does not perceive how great [Col. 0623C] the empire is.

Moreover, there are already quite enough people who think that I shall say far too much. I suppose they measure this not from my talent, which is modest, [Col. 0624A] but from the abundance of your praises. I shall disappoint their expectation—though unwillingly—by the brevity of my speech. In truth, I had considered many more things to say; but I prefer my speech to be rejected. Therefore I shall make this first abridgment: although I regard with due reverence all of you, most unconquered Princes, whose majesty is harmonious and shared, yet I shall dedicate this small speech, such as it is, to your divinity alone, Constantine. For just as we worship the immortal gods themselves collectively in our minds, yet at times venerate each in his own temple and shrine, so I declare it lawful for me, while remembering the devotion of all princes, to celebrate with praise him who is present.

[Note: [Col. 0623D]

II. “Perhaps they do not know.” It is no wonder that today learned men dispute whether Constantine was born in Britain [Col. 0624C] or Bithynia, and whether he was born from Eutropia, daughter of the emperor Claudius or of Claudius’ brother. For Eumenius says that even in Constantine’s own time this was unknown to many.

The Gothic forces. Claudius utterly destroyed an enemy army composed of various nations, and a fleet of more than a thousand ships. Three hundred and twenty thousand Goths were killed in that war. Trebellius Pollio; and the coins of Claudius Augustus Gothicus.

“Would that he had been longer-lived.” For he ruled only about two years, namely from the Kalends of April A.D. 304 to the Kalends of August A.D. 306. Idatius.

“Although that…” The meaning is: although that most fortunate day of your inauguration was celebrated with great procession and acclamation of the peoples, and is considered the birthday of your empire because you first appeared adorned in imperial dress on that day, nevertheless you had already received from your father Constantius the right and fortune of ruling. Barthius reads, with an inserted word, “a day celebrated with devotion second only to that owed to the gods.” *Adversaria*, book XIV, chapter 9.

“Indeed.” Indeed, the ancient prerogative of the imperial house advanced your father himself to that rank, so that after two princes of your family—namely Claudius and Constantius—you became the third emperor.

“Because you are Emperor.” That is, because you are in fact emperor and because you possess by nature the quality of being emperor. I would gladly add the word which Livineius and Acidalius suspect is missing: “because you were born emperor.” For shortly afterward: “You earned the empire by being born.” But the authority of the old manuscript is lacking.

[Col. 0625C] “To your divinity.” That is, to grant you it as if it were a benefit. Perhaps it should be read *numini suo*, “to its own divinity,” so that Fortune may not ascribe to herself what was already yours and was owed to your birth, without canvassing and popular votes.]

II. I shall begin, then, from the divine power of your lineage, which perhaps many still do not know, but which those who love you know exceedingly well. For from that deified Claudius [Col. 0624B] an ancestral kinship flows down to you. He first restored the relaxed and ruined discipline of the Roman empire, and on land and sea destroyed the monstrous forces of the Goths, bursting forth from the mouths of the Pontus and the Danube. Would that he had lived longer as the restorer of humankind than he was swiftly made companion of the gods. Therefore, although that most fortunate day, celebrated with a devotion second only to that owed to the gods, is considered the birthday of your empire because it first adorned you with that garb, nevertheless the fortune of empire had already descended into you from that founder of your line. Indeed, the ancient prerogative of the imperial house advanced your own father, so that you now stood at the highest rank and above the vicissitudes of human affairs: the third emperor after two princes of your family.

Among all those who share your majesty, Constantine, you have this distinctive privilege: that you are emperor; and your lineage possesses such nobility that empire has added no honor to you, nor can Fortune [Col. 0625A] attribute to your divinity what is yours, with canvassing and voting set aside.

[Note: [Col. 0625C]

III. “The outcome of popular favor.” Or perhaps “the wind of popular favor,” as Bongarsius prefers; certainly Cicero has *ventum popularem* (“a popular wind”) and *ventos contionum* (“the winds of public assemblies”).

“Although indeed.” Said as a compliment to Diocletian, who was then living privately at Salona; for he had been raised to the empire in this way.

“In single combat.” With a Sarmatian leader whom, after defeating him, he brought on foot to Galerius, under whom he was serving. Zonaras.

“To seek from the plain.” I have followed Livineius’ emendation. The meaning is: it is a great thing for a man distinguished by birth to rise to the highest ranks; greater for a man from the common people to raise himself to the highest honors. The Putean edition reads *patere plano* [materially uncertain reading].]

III. No chance agreement of men, no sudden result of popular favor, made you prince. You earned the empire by being born. This seems to me both the first and greatest gift of the immortal gods: to come immediately into the light under a fortunate destiny and, to receive at home, already acquired, what others scarcely attain through the labors of an entire life. For however great and admirable is the good fortune which, after earning service-pay and passing through the grades of military service, ascends to that summit of majesty and, relying upon the roots of virtue alone, grows strong into such power—this too you attained as far as your age allowed. And although Fortune had placed you above all delays in acquiring glory, [Col. 0625B] you wished to grow through military service; by facing the dangers of war and joining hand with enemies even in single combat, you made yourself better known to nations, though you could not become more noble.

It is great, I say, to have advanced from one’s own resources to the highest things; yet it is quite another thing to struggle through steep paths and seek mountain ridges from the plain, and another to hold Fortune’s summit, supported by the loftiness of one’s very birth, and not to hope for what is highest but to possess it.

[Note: [Col. 0625D]

IV. “You entered as designated.” Constantius had already designated you as his heir, whether he summoned you to himself from Italy or you yourself hastened to him.

“The emperor’s first son.” The first son he had by Helena, while he was in the first flower of his age, before he married Theodora, Maximian’s daughter.

Vindonis. Below, Vindonissa. Vindonus or Vindonissa was a city in Helvetia, near the district of Ambronicum and the River Arola, now Windisch.]

IV. You entered that sacred palace not as a candidate for empire but as one designated; and at once those paternal household gods saw in you their lawful successor. For there could be no doubt that the inheritance belonged to him whom fate had granted as the emperor’s first son. For he, both emperor on earth and a god in heaven, begot you [Col. 0625C] alone in the first flower of his age, while his whole body was still vigorous and he possessed that energy and courage with which he waged many wars, especially on the fields of Vindonis. Hence such great likeness of appearance has passed from him into you that nature seems to have stamped itself upon your faces. For it is the same countenance that we worship again in you; the same dignity on the brow, the same calmness in eyes and mouth. Thus blushing is the sign of modesty; thus speech is the witness of justice.

Receive, Emperor, receive the confession of our feelings. We grieve that Constantius has departed from us, but when we behold you, we do not believe that he has departed. Yet why do I say that he has departed, whose immortal deeds live and are present in the mouths and before the eyes of all humankind?

[Note: [Col. 0626C]

V. “He shut off the Ocean.” By fixing stones and beams at the harbor entrance, so that the fleet of Carausius, which controlled that coast, could not come to the aid of the people of Boulogne.

“With the same army.” That is, the garrison forces which Carausius had placed at Boulogne.

“The land of Batavia.” Not “Batavian land,” as some emend. For Catullus similarly says “Celtiberian land,” and Tibullus “Campanian land”:

> Not if Campanian land were given you as a price.

“His own fosterling.” Carausius was born among the Menapii, not in Hungary but in Flanders.

“He transplanted [them] into Roman nations.” Into the Gauls subject to Rome, namely to cultivate the territories of Amiens, Beauvais, Troyes, and Langres.

“Thus, on a calm sea.” After recovering Britain at last in the tenth year, he enters here as victor.]

V. Who, indeed, not merely remembers but still in some manner sees the greatness of the achievements by which he enlarged and adorned the commonwealth? On being admitted to the empire, at his first arrival he shut off the Ocean, boiling with an innumerable hostile fleet; and he enclosed on land and sea that army which occupied the shore of the town of Boulogne, having divided the recurrent movements of that element by barriers cast amid the waves, so that those whose gates the waters washed had lost both the sea and what they touched. Having captured that same army by valor and preserved it by clemency, while the recovery of Britain was being prepared by the construction of fleets, he cleared the land of Batavia—once occupied under his own former fosterling by different Frankish nations—of every enemy. Not content with victory, he transplanted the nations themselves into Roman territories, so that they were forced to lay aside not only their arms but also their savagery.

Why should I speak of the recovery of Britain? He sailed to it on so calm a sea that the Ocean, awestruck by so great a passenger, seemed to have lost its own movements; he crossed over in such a manner that Victory did not accompany him but awaited [Col. 0626C] him.

[Note: [Col. 0626D]

VI. “He was moderate toward the conquered.” Read: “He showed moderation toward the conquered.” Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XIV, chapter 9.

“He offered himself to them in such judgment.” The word *judicio* (“judgment”) appears superfluous; if it is removed, the meaning is: “He showed and proved himself such that….” Others read *se ejusmodi judicem* (“he offered himself as such a judge”), or rather *se ejusmodi vindicem* (“as such an avenger”).

[Col. 0627C] “From their own original…” Constantius defeated the Franks not only in Gaul and Batavia, where they were ravaging, but also in the northern part of the Germanic Sea, that is, in the place of their origin, and transferred them into deserted regions of Gaul, so that they might cultivate those lands and follow Roman standards.

The victory near Langres. Constantius was at first routed near Langres by a very numerous Alamannic army. Later that same day, after inflaming the courage of his own men, he renewed battle with such force that sixty thousand of the enemy fell. Eutropius.

“Which…” That is, which the Rhine, frozen hard with ice, had invited them to cross.

“By its division.” The island of Batavia, which once, according to Pliny, extended almost one hundred Roman miles in length but is now much narrower, is encircled on every side by the Rhine dividing itself into two branches. The same river is called Rhine on one side and Waal on the other. Constantius besieged the Franks who had dared to break in there and compelled them to surrender. “So that…” That is, so that, which is worse than if they had endured a common fate, they chose which hostages to give.]

VI. What shall I say of his mercy, by which he was moderate toward the conquered? What of his justice, by which he restored what had been lost to the despoiled? What of his foresight, by which, after joining allies to himself, he offered himself in such a judgment that recovered freedom might help those who had endured slavery, while impunity might call back to repentance those conscious of guilt? [Col. 0627A] What shall I say again of the most remote Frankish tribes, now torn away not from those places which the Romans had once occupied but from their own original homes and the furthest shores of barbarism, in order that, settled in the deserted regions of Gaul, they might support the peace of the Roman empire through cultivation and its arms through conscription?

What shall I recall of the victory near Langres, glorious even by the wound of the emperor himself? Of the fields of Vindonis filled with the slaughter of enemies, yet still covered with their bones? Of the immense multitude from diverse German peoples which the Rhine, hardened by ice, had invited to cross on foot into the island embraced by that same river in its division—and which, when the river was suddenly released, was enclosed and immediately besieged by launched vessels, and so compelled to surrender that it chose, which is more difficult than a common fate, and delivered over equally to captivity [Col. 0627B] those [of its members], bringing back with its survivors the disgrace of betraying its own people?

[Note: [Col. 0627D]

VII. That expedition. Against the Picts.

“Begetter of the gods.” Homer calls Ocean thus in *Iliad* XIV.201:

> Ὠκεανόν τε θεῶν γένεσιν καὶ μητέρα Τηθύν.  
> “Ocean, source of the gods, and mother Tethys.”

And: “Tethys, mother of the gods, and Ocean, their father.” Perhaps because Ocean nourishes with its waters the sun, the common parent of all things, which the Stoics considered fire.

“Day almost continuous.” Because of the obliquity of the sphere and the sun’s declination. Juvenal, *Satires* 2.161:

> “The Britons content with the shortest night.”

Tacitus, *Life of Julius Agricola*: “Night is bright and, in the furthest part of Britain, brief, so that you can distinguish the end and beginning of daylight by only a slight difference,” etc. [Col. 0628C]

**“Extending his right hand.”** There survives a coin of Constantine, represented ascending to heaven in a four-horse chariot, with a hand extended from heaven above him. Constantius must have had a similar coin.

**“Pious Constantius.”** He gave the answer becoming a pious emperor. Constantius also seems to have been called *Pius* by a particular designation in chapter 8: “Good gods, with what good fortune you endowed pious Constantius even in his departure!” Another panegyric: “He was set in Maximian’s place; you are the son of pious Constantius.”

**“You were chosen.”** This must be restored for the integrity of the sense, in accordance with the old manuscript.

**“To your filial devotion.”** For nothing is so pleasing to you as to have been chosen emperor by your father. [Col. 0628D]

**“Prescribed by authority.”** That is, by the force of a kind of irrevocable prescription.

VII. The day will fail me before my speech does, if I run through all your father’s deeds, even with this brevity. Even that final expedition of his did not, as is commonly supposed, seek British trophies; rather, when the gods were already summoning him, he approached the innermost threshold of the world. For after accomplishing so many and such great things, he did not deign—I do not say—to acquire the forests and marshes of the Caledonians and other Picts, but not even nearby Ireland, remotest Thule, or the Islands of the Blessed themselves, if any such islands exist. Rather, as he was about to go to the gods, he looked out upon that father of the gods, Ocean, which nourishes the fiery stars of heaven, so that, about to enjoy perpetual light thereafter, he might already see there a day that was almost continuous. [Col. 0627C; 0628A]

For truly, indeed, the temples of the gods above stood open to him; he was admitted into the assembly of the heavenly gods, Jupiter himself extending his right hand. Indeed, when immediately asked for his decision as to whom he assigned the empire, he spoke as befitted pious Constantius: you were manifestly chosen emperor by your father’s decision. Since truth bids us say this, I see that it is most welcome to your filial devotion. But why should we flatter only your private feelings, when this was the decision of all the gods, and one long before prescribed by authority, although it was then confirmed by their full counsel? For already at that time you were being called by heavenly votes for the salvation of the commonwealth, when, at the very time when your father was crossing over to Britain, your sudden arrival shone upon the fleet as it was already setting sail: so that you seemed not to have been conveyed by the public post, but to have flown there by some divine speed. [Col. 0628B]

[Note: [Col. 0628D]

VIII. **“Of the Cydonians,” etc.** The Cydonians were a people of Crete; their city is called Cydonia by Strabo, Cydonis by Ptolemy, and Cydon by others.

**“All his cares.”** Eusebius says the same in his *Life of Constantine*. Zonaras adds that, when Constantius was ill and distressed by the unsuitable character of his other sons, an angel appeared and commanded him to leave the empire to Constantine.

**“The army agreed.”** At the urging of Crocus, king of the Alamanni, who had come to his aid against the Pictish peoples of Britain. Victor.

**“And although you.”** I follow Rhenanus’s edition. In others there is: “and although you [referred] to the senior emperors concerning the supreme affairs of the commonwealth”—corrupt, in my judgment.

[Col. 0629C] **“For it was not.”** For Constantius, bestowed upon heaven and consecrated, ought not to have been mourned longer.

**“You spurred on your horse.”** Schott’s Victor reports that Constantine spurred on his horse while fleeing Rome, where Galerius held him as a hostage to guarantee his loyalty, and hastening to his father in Britain after disabling the post-horses behind him. But that he did this in order to withdraw himself from the wishes of an army demanding him as emperor—no one, I think, would say except this panegyrist.

**Cyllarus.** Castor’s horse, which Juno received from Neptune and gave him. Poets everywhere speak of its swiftness. Propertius, II.7:

> Castor’s horse could not go fast enough for me.

Virgil, *Georgics* III, says that it was Pollux’s horse. [Col. 0629D]

> Such Cyllarus, tamed beneath the reins of Amyclean Pollux.

But here poetic licence has substituted brother for brother, as Servius notes along with the other interpreters of Virgil.

**Arion.** The horse given by Neptune to Adrastus; Statius, *Thebaid* VI, and other poets everywhere celebrate its equal swiftness.]

VIII. No missiles of Persians or Cydonians, however surely aimed, ever struck their intended marks as certainly as you, at the fitting moment, stood beside your father when he was about to leave the world; and by the security of your presence you relieved all the cares that he revolved in his foreknowing and silent mind. Good gods, with what good fortune you endowed pious Constantius even in his death! As the emperor was about to cross into heaven, he saw the heir whom he was leaving behind.

For as soon as he had been removed from the earth, the entire army united in you; the minds and eyes of all marked you out. And although you referred to the senior emperors what they judged should be done concerning the supreme interests of the commonwealth, they anticipated their judgment by their zeal—a judgment which those emperors soon approved. As soon as you first came forth and made yourself available to the soldiers, they threw the purple upon you while you wept, serving the public advantage more than your own wishes. [Col. 0628C; 0629A] For it was not right that an emperor consecrated to heaven should be mourned any longer.

You are even said, unconquered emperor, to have tried to flee the ardour of the army demanding you, spurring on your horse. Yet, to tell you the truth, you did this through the error of youth. For what Cyllarus or Arion could carry you off, when empire followed you? That majesty—yes, that majesty—which is subject to Jupiter’s nod, and which is entrusted not to Iris, messenger of the gods, but first to Victory, attended you as easily as things sent from heaven swiftly reach the earth. Thus it displayed both your modesty and piety and your attempts to defer the empire; but the good fortune of the commonwealth prevailed.

[Note: [Col. 0629D]

IX. **“You first beheld.”** Does this mean Constantine at his birth, as those infer who make him British? Or when he became emperor? Or at least when he was distinguished by the title Caesar, as others contend? That this occurred at York, a British city, is doubted by no one.

**“In which neither the severity…”** The author of the panegyric looked to the passage in Tacitus’s *Life of Agricola*, where he says the same in his account of Britain’s location, climate, and fertility.

**“Because of which.”** Not *quod propter ut*, as in the common editions. [Col. 0630C]

**“What, etc.”** That is: new gods always come from some farthest part of the world to be worshipped by the entire world.

**“Mercury from the Nile.”** There were several Mercuries. One was born on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, concerning whom see *Aeneid* VIII.138. Another was born on Mount Corycius in Boeotia, not far from Tanagra. The present passage concerns the one born in Egypt; but he is too well known for me to recount his deeds.

**“Liber from the Indians.”** Yet he was Theban, though he also marched against and subdued the Indians. Returning victorious from there, he was received with divine honours.

**“The river’s source is unknown.”** Concerning the source of the Nile, consult Isaac Vossius’s commentary on that subject.

**“Near those aware [of the rising sun].”** That is, nearly in that region where the sun rises.]

IX. O Britain, fortunate and now happier than all lands, which first beheld Constantine Caesar! [Col. 0629B] Nature deservedly endowed you with every good thing of heaven and soil: there is neither excessive harshness of winter nor summer heat; the crops are so fertile that they suffice for the gifts of both Ceres and Liber; the forests are without savage beasts, the land without harmful serpents. In contrast, there is an innumerable multitude of gentle livestock, swollen with milk and laden with fleeces. And surely, as regards that for which life is prized, your days are exceedingly long and no night is wholly without some light. Since the extreme flatness of the shores raises no shadows, the sight of heaven and the stars passes beyond the boundary of night: thus the sun itself, which seems to set for us, appears there merely to pass by.

Good gods, what is this—that new divine powers always descend from some supreme limit of the world to be worshipped by the whole world? Thus Mercury came from the Nile, whose source is unknown; thus Liber came from India, near those aware of the rising sun, revealing themselves to nations as gods present among them. [Col. 0629C; 0630A] Places near heaven are surely more sacred than inland places; and an emperor is sent from the gods more directly from where the earth ends.

[Note: [Col. 0630C]

X. **“An obscure [band], I suppose…”** He alludes to Maximian’s victory over the Bagaudae, which he minimizes in order to flatter Constantine. Maximian [Col. 0630D] seems by then to have died.

**“The kings themselves of the Franks.”** Ascaricus and Ragaïsus, who had risen in violation of the treaty made with Constantius. Constantine brought them into the theatre to be torn apart by beasts (Eutropius).

**“Your clemency.”** Others read, “Clemency is foolish”: that is, it is foolish to spare enemies out of fear and to look to one’s own interests rather than forgive others from a certain pious disposition. Gruter reads, “Clemency is safer,” that is, more cautious; choose whichever reading you prefer.

**“True courage.”** True courage consists in bringing it about that even those who do not love you obey you peacefully.

**“The one Perseus.”** Perseus, king of Macedon, in A.U.C. 576, succeeded his father Philip. In the eleventh year thereafter he was defeated by Lucius Aemilius Paullus and led before the triumphal chariot of his conqueror (Livy XL; Justin XXXIII; Plutarch, *Aemilius Paullus*; Velleius Paterculus; etc.).]

X. Therefore, the son of an emperor—and of so great an emperor—and himself having attained the empire so prosperously: how did you begin to vindicate the commonwealth? I suppose some obscure band of barbarians attempted the omens of your accession by a sudden assault and unforeseen brigandage. You punished for their rashness the very kings of the Franks, who had violated the peace during your father’s absence. You did not hesitate to inflict the last tortures, fearing neither the lasting hatred nor the inexpiable anger of that nation.

For why should an emperor reckon any offence arising from just severity, when he can defend what he has done? It is your clemency that spares enemies and looks more to its own security than to forgiveness. But you, Constantine—however much your enemies may hate you, let them fear you. [Col. 0630B] For this is true courage: that they may not love you, yet remain quiet. Though the man who holds hostile enemies bound by pardon may be more cautious, he is nevertheless stronger who tramples them while angry.

Emperor, you renewed that ancient confidence of Roman rule which took vengeance by death upon captured enemy leaders. When captive kings had honoured the triumphal chariot from the gates to the Forum, they were dragged off to prison and killed as soon as the emperor began to turn his chariot toward the Capitol. Perseus alone, through the entreaty of Paullus himself, who had received his surrender, escaped the law of that severity. All the others, deprived of light in chains, offered other kings a lesson: they should prefer to cultivate Roman friendship rather than provoke Roman justice. So greatly does punishment inflicted upon enemies contribute even this good: not only do enemies not dare to rage, but friends too show more devoted reverence.

[Col. 0631A] [Note: [Col. 0631C]

XI. **“The fame of valour.”** Following Acidalinus, I have restored this in place of *fama virtuti*.

**“They know that they can,” etc.** I have added *se* on Livineius’s conjecture. The sense seems to require it.

**“The power having been ascertained.”** That is, after they have understood what you can do. Gruter prefers *coepto ponte*, “with the bridge begun”; since the manuscript had *pote* for *ponte*, ignorant scribes took it as *potestate*. [Col. 0631D] This conjecture seems supported by chapter 13: “Moreover, by building the bridge at Cologne you insult the remnants of the afflicted nation . . . so that no one doubts what those who already serve the bridge begun will do when it is completed.”

**“Fortlets.”** Various fortlets were placed along the Rhine bank to prevent German incursions.

**“The two-horned river.”** They bathe in the Rhine. Virgil, *Georgics* I.272:

> And plunge the bleating flock in the healthful river.

**“Once, in battle, etc.”** You conquered them once in battle, but by this example of just severity you subdue them permanently.

**“Enemy leaders.”** The statement may seem excessive at this point; but evidently it softens, by this device, an action that was somewhat too harsh.]

XI. This, therefore, Emperor, is the peace that we enjoy. We are now protected not by the Rhine’s whirlpools but by terror of your name. Whether it dries up in heat or stands fast with ice, the enemy will dare use neither ford. For nature has closed off nothing with so impregnable a barrier that boldness will not penetrate it, if any hope of attempting it remains. That is the unconquerable wall which the fame of courage builds.

The Franks know that they can cross the Rhine—and you would gladly admit them to their destruction—but they can hope for neither victory nor pardon. From the tortures of their kings they measure what awaits themselves; and therefore, so far are they from planning a crossing of that river that they despair when they have learned your power. Where now is that fierceness? Where is that ever faithless instability? You no longer dare even live near the Rhine, and scarcely drink the inland rivers in safety. [Col. 0631B]

By contrast, the fortlets positioned at intervals on this side adorn the frontier more than they protect it. An unarmed farmer ploughs that bank once terrible, and all our flocks are immersed throughout the two-horned river. This, Constantine, is your daily and everlasting victory arising from the punishment of Ascaricus and Ragaïsus, to be preferred to all former successful battles. Once they are defeated in battle; without end, by an example. The common people, though many perish, do not know their own defeat; it is a short way to subdue enemies when their leaders have been removed.

[Note: [Col. 0632C]

XII. **“The Bructeri.”** The Bructeri were a people of Germany, placed by some in East Frisia and by others in Westphalia, where the county of Mark now lies.]

XII. Yet, that the barbarian savagery might be crushed in every way, and that the enemy should not mourn only the punishments of their kings, unconquered emperor, you also brought devastation upon the Bructeri. The first principle of your plan was to attack them unexpectedly after crossing over with your army suddenly—not because you distrusted open warfare, since you would have preferred to meet them openly, but so that this nation, accustomed to evade war by refuge in woods and marshes, might lose the time to flee. [Col. 0631C]

Accordingly, countless numbers were slain and very many captured. Every head of livestock was either taken or slaughtered. All villages were consumed by fire. Those of military age who fell into your hands—whose treachery did not suit military service and whose fierceness did not suit slavery—were given over as a spectacle for punishment, and by their multitude exhausted the savage beasts. This, [Col. 0632A] Emperor, is to trust in one’s own courage and fortune; this is not to purchase peace by sparing, but to seek victory by provoking.

[Note: [Col. 0632C]

XIII. **“By the bridge at Cologne.”** Agrippina Colony—Cologne—formerly Agrippina of the Ubii, was the homeland of Agrippina, Nero’s mother. It is a most renowned city of Lower Germany [Col. 0632D] on the Rhine, free and a commercial centre, midway between Trier and Münster; its archbishop is an Elector of the Empire.

**“The Persian king.”** Xerxes, son of Darius Hystaspes, heir to his father’s kingdom and hatred of the Greeks, joined the Hellespont with ships and, to use Eutropius’s term, planked it over, in the seventy-fifth Olympiad. Herodotus, Diodorus, Justin, Plutarch, etc.

**“The third Caesar.”** Caligula. Suetonius, chapter 19: “He joined the middle distance from Baiae to the Puteolan moles with a bridge of nearly three thousand six hundred paces,” etc.

**“At the beginning of his.”** Supply: *reign*.]

XIII. Moreover, by building a bridge at Cologne you insult the remnants of that afflicted nation, so that it may never lay aside fear, may always tremble, may always stretch out suppliant hands—although you do this more for the glory of your empire and the adornment of the frontier than to make it possible to cross into enemy territory whenever you wish. For the entire Rhine is equipped with armed ships, and soldiers are stationed threateningly along every bank as far as the Ocean.

But it seems beautiful to you—and truly it is most beautiful—that the Rhine should be trodden by a new bridge not only in its upper reaches, where it is shallow either through breadth or because it is small near its source, but also where it is wholly itself: where it has already swallowed many streams, which this great river of ours, the barbarian Nicer (Neckar), and the Main have carried into it; [Col. 0632B] where, already fierce in its enormous course and intolerant of a single channel, it strains to overflow into its own branches.

Nature herself surely serves your divinity, greatest Constantine, when foundations of such great structures are laid in that depth of whirlpools, destined to possess secure and stable firmness. Let the most powerful king of the Persians once have joined the narrows of the Hellespont with a connected fleet: that crossing was temporary. Let the third Caesar after Augustus have paved the Bay of Baiae by a similar continuity of ships: it was the luxurious conveyance of an idle prince. This work is both difficult to accomplish and destined for everlasting use.

Certainly, already at its beginning, it has moved your enemies to obedience: they have sought peace as suppliants and offered the noblest hostages. [Col. 0632C] Hence no one doubts what those who already serve while the bridge is being begun will do when it has been completed.

[Note: [Col. 0632D]

XIV. **“That man.”** Maximian, whom Constantine had received most generously at Trier after Maxentius drove him from Italy; Constantine had also taken Maximian’s daughter Fausta as his wife.

**“Although, etc.”** That is, although your filial devotion [Col. 0633C] has just cause to complain of him, a private person nevertheless ought to restrain his speech.

**“Compels [us] to regard him.”** The passage is badly corrupt and has been restored in different ways by different editors. Langius: “We must still be compelled to behold him, and you, though angry, must reverence [him].” Livineius: “Your contemplation still compels [us], so that, though angry, they may reverence [you].” [Col. 0633D] Acidalinus reads, “Let us reverence.”

**“I shall employ,” etc.** That is: I shall use that common defence of crimes which even the wise often employ.

**“Unless by fate.”** Note the cunning perversity of the Stoics, who, in order to make it safe for themselves to be wicked, ascribed the cause of their crimes to some sort of fate.

**“But I think that he…”** Following Acidalinus, I have removed the negation, so that the sense is: when your soul, Constantine, was to enter a mortal body, the decrees of the stars shaped you such that you could not be cruel. But Maximian obtained that lot which brought destruction both upon himself and upon many others. This language of allotment is taken from Epicurean doctrine.]

XIV. While you were intent upon such matters for the benefit and dignity of the commonwealth, new disturbances of that man turned you aside to himself—a man who ought above all to have favoured your successes. I still almost hesitate how to speak of him, and I await counsel from the nod of your divinity.

For although he may deservedly be accused by the complaints of your filial devotion, a private voice must nevertheless restrain itself, especially [Col. 0633A] since he who proved ungrateful to you despite your so many benefits and so great a bond of relationship still compels us to regard him with such reverence that, though angry, we must revere him. What then shall I do, in order to handle such deep wounds with a suspended hand?

I shall surely employ those common defences of all crimes which are, nevertheless, often asserted even by philosophers: that no human being sins except through fate; that the crimes themselves of mortals are acts of fortune; but that virtue is a gift of the gods. Rejoice, Constantine, in your nature and character: pious Constantius begot you such; the decrees of the stars shaped you such that you cannot be cruel.

But I think that he, when about to enter the light and receive a choice of the life he would lead, encountered a lot to be avoided—a lot that brought undeserved destruction upon many men and, finally, voluntary destruction upon himself. For, to pass over other matters, was it not the necessity of fate itself that made him return this recompense to your filial devotion—him whom you received into your provinces, your resources, and your palace after he had been driven from the City, expelled from Italy, and rejected by Illyricum? [Col. 0633B]

[Note: [Col. 0633D]

XV. **“You had sat beside him at the rings.”** I follow the old editions. The sense is that, as a mark of honour, you had sat at his left, on which Greeks and Romans are attested to have worn the ring [Col. 0634C] (Aulus Gellius X.10; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VII.13). The Puteanus edition reads *ad annula foederas*: perhaps one should read, “you had bound yourself by the ring at the altar,” whether when you made a treaty with him or when you took his daughter in marriage. For the Romans observed both customs. [Col. 0634D] Others read, “you had sat on the left”; others, “you had sat by the mules,” etc.

**“That divine man.”** Diocletian, who, while living privately at Salona, was invited by Maximian in a letter to resume the empire. “If only,” he said, “you could see at Salona the vegetables planted by my own hands, you would surely never judge that this ought to be attempted.”]

XV. What, I ask, did he mean? What did he desire? What more could he have gained than what he had obtained from you? You had given him the highest and most diverse goods: private leisure and royal wealth. When he departed, you had sat beside him at the rings; you had instructed our service to attend him even more earnestly than it attended you; you had decreed obedience to all his commands in such a way that the outward rank of empire rested with you, its power with him.

What, then, was that mighty impulse? It was not a lust for power—for what could he not do while you ruled?—but the delusion of an age already losing its reason, that, though so old, he should undertake the gravest cares and civil war. No gifts of fortune, as matters stand, satisfy those whose desires reason does not limit; and so thankless prosperity flows beneath them, so that, always full of hopes and empty of advantages, they lack what is present while they look toward what is to come. [Col. 0633C]

Yet that divine man, who was the first both to share and to lay down the empire, does not repent of his counsel or deed, and does not think that he has lost what he voluntarily transferred. Truly happy and blessed is he, whom the services of you—so great emperors—honour as a private person. [Col. 0634A] And, supported by a many-yoked rule, he too rejoices beneath the shelter of your empire; he knows that you have grown from his stock, and he justly claims your glories for himself.

Thus he was ashamed to imitate the man who had been adopted by him as brother; he regretted having sworn to him in the temple of Capitoline Jupiter. It is no wonder that he also broke faith with his son-in-law.

[Note: [Col. 0634D]

XVI. **“Laid down twice.”** The first time was at Milan, where, induced by the example and authority of Diocletian, whom he regarded as a father, he laid down the purple. Then, having resumed the empire, he abdicated it a second time at Trier. Finally, he usurped the empire a third time.

**“Securely, of course.”** Ironically (*eirōnikōs*, εἰρωνικῶς): for it is not safe to employ an army which one has taught to have purchasable hands.

**“And not only.”** That is, not only those whom reason, education, and a quieter life had made gentler, but even soldiers of more ardent spirit disregarded profit for your sake.

[Col. 0635D] **“From the memory of [your] father.”** Among writers of that age, the preposition *de* is almost used in the sense of *propter*, “because of.” Thus in Tertullian, Cyprian, and other writers of their age. “From the memory [of your father],” that is, because of the remembrance of your father.]

XVI. Is this the loyalty, this the religious reverence, owed to the inner sanctuary of the palace—so that, slowly and reluctantly, after those plans for war had already been made, after the journey had been completed and the resources of the stopping-places exhausted so that no army could pursue him, he should suddenly sit down in purple within the walls, usurp for a third time the empire twice laid down, send letters to solicit armies, and try to shake the soldiers’ loyalty by displaying rewards—securely, [Col. 0634B] of course, intending to use an army whose hands he had taught to be purchasable?

Yet by that error of his it was shown, Emperor, how great was the love in which your soldiers held you: they preferred you to every gift he had promised and every offer of honours. That rare virtue of self-restraint, scarcely preserved at any time even by a few teachers of wisdom, has become common to all men because of you, Constantine. Not only those whom reason, letters, and a quiet life have softened, but even that ardour of military spirits has, out of regard for you, despised gain.

There may have been armies like yours in eagerness and strength; to you alone has it fallen to possess a wise army. Many perverse leaders of old, unequal to war, perhaps competed by lavish gifts; but their popularity was brief and perishable, since anyone who imitated them easily surpassed them. [Col. 0634C] This is the firm, this the everlasting guardian of the commonwealth: one whom the soldiers themselves love for his own sake, whom neither flattering nor purchased servility obeys, but simple and sincere devotion.

Your gifts, Constantine, are manifestly pleasing to the soldiers, but this is more pleasing—that they are yours. Whatever you offer becomes more welcome by your hand. Who can compete with you in this kind of favour-seeking? It is an unsurpassable kind of generosity when the emperor himself is the soldier’s reward. Thus you do indeed grant your armies more than they desire; but your own name, [Col. 0635A] the authority arising from remembrance of your father, the grace of your age, and finally that venerable appearance of yours commend you still more.

[Note: [Col. 0635D]

XVII. **“That great king.”** Alexander, whom historians report to have been no less handsome than brave.

**“The Thessalian man.”** Achilles, whose beauty Homer praises in many passages.

**“Nature herself.”** Yet sometimes an elegant and distinguished soul lies hidden in an ugly dwelling—that is, in a foul body. The old saying concerning Galba, a man as intelligent as he was ugly: “Galba’s talent dwells badly.”

**“To measure out.”** That is, to prepare.

**“How great [a spirit] entered them.”** Acidalinus reads *quantus illo*.]

XVII. Beautiful indeed, good gods, and a heavenly miracle: an emperor still young, in whom that courage which is already supreme nevertheless continues to grow; in whom this brilliance of the eyes, this majesty at once venerable and gracious, both dazzles and invites the gaze. Such do I imagine that great king, such the Thessalian man, to have been: men whose supreme courage is celebrated as joined to beauty.

For not without reason do the most learned men say that nature itself prepares bodily dwellings worthy of great minds, and that from a man’s face and the beauty of his limbs one can infer how great a heavenly spirit has entered them as inhabitant. [Col. 0635B] Therefore, when the soldiers see you entering, they marvel and love; they follow you with their eyes, hold you in their minds, and believe that they obey a god, whose form is as beautiful as his divinity is certain.

[Note: [Col. 0635D]

XVIII. **“That sluggish river.”** The Arar or Araris—the Saône—a river of Gallia Comata, separating the Sequani from the Aedui and joining the Rhône at Lyon. It rises from [Col. 0636D] the Vosges Mountains on the border of Lorraine. Claudian: “Slow Arar and swift Rhône,” etc.

**“The banks receding slowly.”** For those putting out from harbour, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* III.72, see the land as receding. But because they were not moving forward quickly enough, the banks seemed to them to recede more slowly than they wished.

**“They bent to the oars.”** *Aeneid* VI.294:

> Now, chosen band, bend to the mighty oars,  
> Companions of Hector . . .

**Arelate.** Arles, a city of Gallia Narbonensis, an archbishopric on the Rhône. Ausonius writes of it in his *Catalogue of Famous Cities*.]

XVIII. Therefore, as soon as they heard of that foul crime, they themselves asked you for the signal to depart. When you offered travel-money, they said that this very thing delayed them and that they already possessed from your largesses more than sufficed. Then they seized their arms and made for the gates. They completed without any rest the journey of so many days from the Rhine to the Saône; their bodies were weary, their spirits aflame, and their passion for vengeance grew daily as they came closer.

Then indeed your care, Emperor—by which you had provided vessels at the harbour of Chalon to restore their strength—almost displeased those in haste. That sluggish [Col. 0635C] and lingering river seemed never to have been slower. As the hulls glided silently and the banks receded slowly, they cried that they stood still rather than went forward. Then, employing their hands in place of feet, they bent to the oars; by pressing it, they overcame the river’s nature. And when at last they had struggled free of the Saône’s delays, they were scarcely content even with the Rhône itself.
