It seemed to them not to rush swiftly enough, not to hasten toward Arles as quickly as usual.

Why say more? It must be confessed, Emperor, that with this vigour of body and this ardour of mind, you sometimes laboured so that you might follow the army which you led. For all were carried forward with such impetus that, when they learned that he had abandoned Arles and gone to Marseilles, they at once flew from their ships; in their headlong course they outstripped not only the currents of the Rhône but, as it were, even the gusts of wind themselves. [Col. 0636A] So great a love of your divinity had inflamed them that, although they knew they would have to assault a most strongly fortified city, they believed it sufficient merely to arrive.

[Note: [Col. 0636D]

XIX. **Marseilles.** Marseille, on the Mediterranean coast.

**“Greeks and Italians there.”** Greeks and Italians first introduced from their own shores all arts and letters into this most ancient city of Gaul.

**“For an older leader.”** Pompey. This indeed proved fatal to them. See Caesar’s *Commentaries on the Gallic War*. [Col. 0637C]]

XIX. For Marseilles, as I hear, projects into the deep sea and is enclosed by a most secure harbour, into which a gulf of the Mediterranean flows through a narrow entrance. It is connected to the mainland only by fifteen hundred paces, where a very strong and tower-filled wall confronts approach. Long ago, Greeks and Italians who gathered there, being powerful in arts and ingenuity, were taught by the place itself to expend more liberally upon every means useful for war on the side that could be approached, since nature had spared them the expense of construction on the others.

Thus, when in that grave destiny it closed its gates against Caesar in favour of its older leader, it was attacked repeatedly by land and sea, [Col. 0636B] with siege engines brought up, embankments built, and naval engagements; yet it was more often attacked than frightened, and scarcely opened its gates even after a long siege. Greekling magistrates repelled Caesar himself, then his commanders and forces, not so much by their own strength as by their walls.

But at your first arrival, Emperor, and the first charge of your army, neither the height of Marseilles’ walls, nor its very frequent towers, nor the nature of its location delayed you from taking both the harbour and, if you wished, the city immediately. For the soldiers assaulted the entire wall with such confidence that they would without doubt have climbed it at once, had the height not deceived their visual estimate while they prepared the ladders they had brought up.

Yet even so, many, deceived by the ladders’ shortness, made up by stretching their bodies the height remaining for the ascent; raised on the shoulders of those following, they had already seized the spaces between the battlements with hooked hands. [Col. 0636C] They feared no danger in carrying out vengeance, so that they seemed to themselves not to be scaling a wall but to be engaging on equal terms.

[Note: [Col. 0637C]

XX. **“If at the first [assault].”** That is, if opportunity to break in had been afforded at the first assault.

**“Those whom he had received.”** Perhaps “those whom he had deceived”; Acidalinus prefers this. The conjecture is supported by what occurs above: “so that soldiers misled into treachery might be given time to repent.”

**“But forgive the remark.”** A remarkable passage, full of artifice if any passage is. Since Constantine either truly ordered Maximian strangled or was believed to have ordered it, the speaker ascribes the death to the gods’ vengeance and says that it happened against Constantine’s will. Pacatus almost copied this passage in his panegyric of Theodosius, chapter 44: “But it is well that you cannot do everything: your own people avenge you even against your will.”]

XX. But, Constantine, O your singular filial devotion, always observing its own obligations even amid arms! You gave the signal for retreat and delayed victory, so that you might be permitted to forgive all, lest an angry soldier should do anything harsher than the nature of your clemency could endure. Although, by the concern of the best emperor, you took precautions that soldiers led into treachery might receive time to repent and voluntarily seek pardon, we who behold your most gentle feelings—for nothing is as evident as the goodness in your heart—[Col. 0637A] understand that you spared the man whom no one could have rescued from the sword, if the first assault had afforded an opportunity to break in.

Thus, so far as your filial devotion was concerned, Emperor, you preserved both him and all those whom he had received. Let anyone who did not wish to use your benefit and judged himself unworthy of life, when through you he was allowed to live, attribute it to himself. You spared even those undeserving of it, insofar as suffices for your conscience. But—forgive the remark—you cannot do everything: the gods avenge you even against your will.

[Note: [Col. 0637C]

XXI. **“From the frontier.”** From the Rhine frontiers.

**“With which.”** That is: with what terrifying threats those faithless barbarians displayed themselves to us, while they considered this among themselves.

**“The barbarians.”** The Franks.

**“When will he conquer?”** Flatteringly said, as though for Constantine arriving somewhere and conquering there were one and the same thing.

[Col. 0637D] **“More than one [night].”** That is, it kept you anxious for more than a single night.

**“Temple.”** The very famous temple of Apollo at Autun; see the *Oration for the Restoration of the Schools*, chapter 9.

**“Your Apollo.”** Constantine seems to have worshipped Apollo especially, as several coins confirm, in which he is represented in the form of Apollo. The inscription is “To the Unconquered Sun.” Yet he most happily renounced this superstition, the first Christian of all emperors.

**“Pylian old age.”** That is, Nestor’s old age, so called from Pylos, his homeland, a town of Messenia in the western Peloponnese where he ruled. When Nestor is so often said by authors to have lived through three generations, Muretus says this should not be understood as though he had lived three hundred years, as all those wrongly suppose who take *genea* (γενεά) always to mean one hundred years; rather, he was more than eighty years old, since *genea* often signifies only thirty years (*Various Readings*, X.8). [Col. 0638C] Plautus, Propertius, Ovid, Juvenal, and others think otherwise, explicitly saying in more than one passage that Nestor lived three hundred years. Indeed, there would be no reason for Nestor’s old age to be celebrated so greatly if he had reached only ninety years.]

Whose waters are hot. Many authors relate accounts of waters that avenge perjury. At the sanctuary of the Palici in Sicily there was, they say, a spring into which, according to Aristotle, *On Marvellous Things Heard*, 55, a person about to swear an oath would cast a tablet inscribed with the oath: the tablet floated if he meant to keep faith; otherwise it sank, and the perjurer was burned. Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, V.19: “This water is pleasant to upright men, but deadly to perjurers.” Diodorus Siculus reports the same thing of the same spring in Book XI; Solinus, however, chapter 4, locates it in Sardinia. Salmasius and others thought him mistaken, maintaining that it was in Sicily, and that it inflicted not death upon perjurers, as others maintain, but only blindness. Philostratus likewise relates, in the *Life of Apollonius*, of a spring near Tyana, a city of Cappadocia, sacred to Jupiter [Col. 0638D], which was said both to bubble up cold and, while harmless to others, to produce livid pustules and grievous ulcers in perjurers. The same account occurs in Pliny, Book XXXI, chapter 2. Ovid, *Fasti* V, treats of a spring of another kind, in which perjured merchants, while washing themselves, asked Mercury that the water might wash away not only past but future perjuries:

> “Wash away,” he says, “the perjuries of time gone by;  
> Wash away faithless words spoken against faith.”
>
> …
>
> “Let not the gods above care for whatever I shall have said.”

XXI. This indeed is always to be desired for us: that you may enjoy successes prosperous even beyond our prayers, since we place all hope in the bosom of your majesty and seek your presence everywhere—as though it could be granted. For behold: while you had withdrawn for a little from the frontier, by what terrors had the treachery of the barbarians vaunted itself [Col. 0637B]—namely, while they asked themselves: “When will he arrive? When will he conquer? When will he lead back his wearied army?” Yet suddenly, upon hearing of your return, they collapsed as though thunderstruck. Nor did concern for your vow on behalf of the commonwealth touch you for more than a single night. For on the day after receiving that report, when you had undertaken a doubled exertion of travel, you learned that every surge had subsided and that all the tranquillity which you had left behind had returned. Fortune herself so ordered this, that there the good fortune of your affairs might remind you to render to the immortal gods what you had vowed, where you had turned aside to the most beautiful temple in the whole world—or rather, to a god present in person when you arrived.

For you saw, I believe, Constantine, your Apollo, Victory accompanying him, offering you [Col. 0638A] laurel crowns, each bearing the omen of thirty years. For that is the number of human lifetimes, which are surely owed to you beyond Pylian old age. Or rather—why do I say “I believe”? You saw him, and recognized yourself in his appearance: him to whom the divine songs of seers proclaimed that the kingdoms of the whole world were due. I judge that this has now at last come to pass, since you are, like him, young, cheerful, life-bringing, and a most beautiful emperor. Rightly, therefore, did you honour those most august shrines with such great gifts that they need no longer seek the old things. Now all temples seem to call you to themselves, and especially our Apollo, whose hot waters punish perjuries—perjuries which it especially behooves you to hate.

[Note: [Col. 0638D]

XXII.—The god most truly present: Constantine.

The groves of Apollo: Augustodunum, where all these things are located.

“Your divinity”: that is, Apollo’s.

“But such,” etc.: that is, as pure in taste and smell as cold springs are pure.

“My native city”: from this it is clear that this speech is by Eumenius, or at least by [Col. 0639B] some Aeduan rhetor.

“This most fortunate city”: Trier, where he was delivering this speech.

“Gifts of your presence”: perhaps “gifts of your presence” (*praesentiae tuae*).

“Jupiter and Juno”: this is taken from Homer, *Iliad* ξ [14].347, where, speaking of the two:

> “Beneath them the earth sent up fresh grass,
> 
> Lotus, fragrant crocus, and gloomy hyacinth,
> 
> So that a most abundant woodland rose into the soft air.”

“It will at once be restored”: he invites Constantine to turn aside to Augustodunum and see to the restoration of that city, as he has done for Trier.]

XXII. Immortal gods, when will you grant that day on which this god, most truly present, after establishing universal peace, [Col. 0638B] may also visit those groves of Apollo, the sacred precincts, and the steaming mouths of the springs? Their bubbling sources, misty with gentle warmth, seem, Constantine, to smile upon your eyes and to wish to press themselves upon your kisses. You will surely admire that seat also of your divinity, and its hot waters without any indication of a blazing sun; their taste and vapour have no unpleasantness, but they possess a purity in draught and scent like that of cold springs. There too you will bestow gifts, establish privileges, and finally restore my native city through reverence for the place itself.

The ancient nobility of that city, once proud of the fraternal title of the Roman people, awaits the aid of your majesty, so that there also its public places and most beautiful temples [Col. 0639A] may be repaired by your generosity. For I see here this most fortunate city, whose birthday is celebrated by your devotion, rising again in all its walls, so that it somehow rejoices to have once fallen, having become greater through your benefits. I see a circus maximum, a rival, I believe, to that of Rome; I see basilicas and a forum, royal works, and the seat of justice raised to such a height that they promise themselves worthy of and near to the stars and heaven. Certainly all these are gifts of your presence. For wherever your divine power most often gives distinction, there everything increases—in people, walls, and benefactions. Nor did the earth, with Jupiter and Juno reclining, bring forth new flowers more abundantly than cities and temples rise around your footsteps, Constantine.

Therefore this is sufficient for my prayers: that, with devotion as guide, you may see [Col. 0639B] my native city; for it will be restored at once if you see it. But whether that happiness is still owed to my lifetime, that remains to be seen.

[Note: [Col. 0639C]

XXIII.—“The duties of leisure and of the palace”: for he had been *magister memoriae* (“master of records”). Moreover, Constantius had placed him in charge of the Maenian Schools, an office which he calls a duty of leisure.

“To your ears”: “I might dedicate this speech, delivered in your presence, to your ears.”

“Advocacies of the fisc”: to manage the highest advocacies of the fisc means simply to perform the office of advocate of the fisc, or to be its advocate and patron; the two offices were sometimes held by one and the same person. In fiscal cases he acted for the fisc: at court, before the Count of the Treasuries, that is, of the Sacred Largesses; in the city, before the prefect of the treasury; and in the provinces, before Caesar’s procurator. The latter, indeed, could decide nothing without first hearing the advocate of the fisc (*Code*, “On Advocates of the Fisc,” final law).]

XXIII. Meanwhile, since through your condescension I have attained the fulfilment of my prayers, so as to dedicate to your ears this voice of mine, such as it is, exercised in the diverse duties of leisure and of the palace, [Col. 0640A] I give the greatest thanks to your divinity. And, for what remains, I commend my children to you—especially the one now managing the highest advocacies of the fisc, into whom affection has transferred my whole self. If ever you look favourably upon him, his happy service will be especially suited to your age.

Yet the claim I have made concerning all my children is, Emperor, a broad ambition. Besides the five whom I begot, I count as almost mine those whom I have advanced to the guardianship of the forum and to offices of the palace. For many not undistinguished streams flow forth from me; many of my followers even administer your provinces. I rejoice in their success and regard the honour of them all as my own. And if perhaps today I have spoken below what might be expected of me, I trust that in them I have found favour. But if your divinity grants me this also—that from this speech [Col. 0640B] I may offer evidence not of eloquence, which would be too much, but of whatever little prudence I possess, and of a mind devoted to you—then let the undistinguished concerns of private studies give way. An emperor who has approved me will furnish me with an everlasting subject for speech.

[Col. 0639]

## Synopsis of the Speech for the Restoration of the Schools at Augustodunum

[Note: [Col. 0639D] (1) Although publishing the text of this speech does not belong to our purpose, since it is not addressed to Constantine, it is nevertheless fitting to set out its synopsis, for the sake of elucidating the following panegyric, in which that very speech is alluded to.]

In the exordium he says that, as much fear as the unfamiliarity of the place brings him, so much is he refreshed by the cause of learning.

Division.—I. The schools at Augustodunum must be restored.—II. How this may be done without public expense, §3.

Part I. The intention of the emperors and Caesars is that not only temples and public works, but still more the Aeduan schools—brought down by the incursions of the Bagaudic faction [Col. 0639D]—should be restored for the education of the Gallic nobility, §4. Never had letters been such a concern to any rulers, §5. This was understood when, upon the death of the director of these schools, they themselves undertook the task of appointing his successor, and, to commend this profession, selected a man holding a most distinguished office in the palace, §6. If the ancients erected temples to the virtue whose pursuit guided them, Constantius, because of his love for letters, wishes these schools to be raised up, §7. From their very location he proves that they should be restored: both because they stand in the middle of the city and because they lie between the temples of Apollo and Minerva, §9.

Part II. He will contribute to this work the six hundred thousand sesterces given him by Constantius as the salary of his teaching office, §11. In this way he will prove himself worthier of the ruler’s generosity, by devoting it itself to the use of his native city; for his glory it is enough that this sum has been decreed for him there [Col. 0640D]. Thus everyone will understand that he undertook that office not from avarice, §12. He values letters above any price, since Constantius has entrusted to him the education of the Gallic nobility, §13. Letter of Constantius, §14. By the Caesar’s kindness he is encouraged to restore the schools, §15. He gladly gives to the schools the money that was given him on their account, and in which his own grandfather had once taught. He wishes, insofar as his means permit, to imitate the devotion of the emperors in restoring public works, §17. It is fitting that eloquence—or rather, the sacred places of eloquence—should flourish again through the ruler’s generosity no less than the other regions of the world, §17.

[Col. 0641A] In conclusion, he asks the governor to lend his assistance with the emperors and Caesars, so that he may both celebrate this new benefaction toward letters and [Col. 0642A] show boys, depicted in the porticoes, the victories of those same rulers, which he briefly recounts, §20.

[Col. 0641]

## Eumenius’ Thanksgiving to Constantine Augustus, on Behalf of the Flavians

### Notice

[Col. 0641A]

Concerning the author of this panegyric, and the time and place at which it was delivered, we have spoken in the Life of Eumenius.

## Synopsis of the Panegyric

[Col. 0641B] In the exordium, he gives his reason for preferring to offer thanks to the emperor on behalf of the Flavians at Trier rather than at Augustodunum, while the emperor was in that city.

Division.—I. How deservedly Constantine aided the Aedui.—II. How greatly he acted on their behalf, §2.

Part I. The Aedui were first among all peoples to be called brothers of the Roman people by the senate; they were devoted to the commonwealth beyond other peoples; so far as lay in their power, they were defenders of Gaul against tyrants. Therefore, having experienced Constantius’ generosity, §3, they preferred to endure a most severe siege of seven months and, finally—because Emperor Claudius, whose help they had sought, was occupied in the Gothic campaign, and all hope of aid had vanished—to surrender their city to be plundered by the enemy rather than violate their allegiance, §4. Thus far, how well he aided the deserving Aedui; now, how severely afflicted they were. They were burdened by the harshness of a new assessment, §5. The unkindness of the soil was added, §6. In great part their lands were devastated and desolate, their roads precipitous.

Part II. Constantine enters their city amid the extraordinary eagerness of the crowds rushing together, §7. He graciously asks each person what they most wish should be done for their sake, §9. He eases their anxiety, sets a fixed number for the taxes, intending to remit the remaining arrears; he asks how much they owe his fisc, remits seven thousand tax-units—more than a fourth part of their assessments—and asks whether this would suffice, §10. He remits the arrears of taxes for five years.

In conclusion, he praises that five-year period and then turns his speech to praise of the ruler’s *Quinquennalia*, §13.

## The Speech Begins

[Col. 0641A]

[Note: [Col. 0641D]

I.—“By an eternal name”: he means Augustodunum, a city Eumenius calls Flavia. I suppose this is to flatter Flavius Constantine rather than because it is historically true. Why else is there no mention of this name in Ammianus Marcellinus, especially since he wrote under an emperor of the Flavian family? Or should we say it received this name as Rome did, which, although once called Commodiana after the Emperor Commodus, has left no trace of that name?

“To move herself utterly,” etc.: very like Cicero, *In Pisonem*, §52: “Rome herself seemed almost to have been shaken from her foundations and to go forth to embrace her saviour,” etc.

“In that city above all”: Trier, where emperors customarily stayed when they were in Gaul, [Col. 0642D] and where Livineius and Rhenanus accordingly maintain that this speech was delivered.

“But since,” etc.: that is, since in fact she cannot fall at your feet, she at least longs in spirit to do what he acknowledges to be beyond nature and condition.

“Letters of private study”: recognize Eumenius, whom Constantius had placed in charge of the Aeduan schools.

“Your palace”: below he describes how Constantine, upon entering Augustodunum, was received in the palace, §8.

“Divine”: that is, by your divine and humanity-filled voice you raised them up.

“Cohiberet”: perhaps *cohibere* (“restrain”), or, as Acidalius emends, *praeparari et cohiberi* (“prepare himself and restrain himself”).

“How it suited you”: that is, how it suited your majesty.]

I. If Flavia of the Aedui, at last called by an eternal name, had been able, most sacred Emperor, to move herself utterly and come here, she would surely, all at once and in your presence, speak with a single voice of your very great and most beautiful benefits toward her [Col. 0642B]; and she would give thanks to you, her restorer—or rather, to speak more truly, her founder—in that city above all, to which you have begun to make her similar. But since she cannot do this, in her spirit she longs for what nature does not permit; and the distance between you does not allow you to hear the cries with which she daily raises your praises to heaven. I have willingly undertaken the duty that was proper: to be the messenger of my native city’s joy, and now the orator not of the letters of private study but of public thanksgiving.

For, most sacred Emperor, when, in the entrance of your palace, you raised up the rank lying prostrate at your feet by the divine utterance of your indulgence and by the extension of that unconquered right hand, I did not wish to give thanks to your name. Nor would words, however unprepared, have failed me. For who could either prepare himself for benefits so unexpected, or restrain himself from such great rejoicing? Yet I had regard for place and time, lest that ardour of my spirit and zeal for speaking might indeed meet with your approval—which would suffice for my immortality—but, because of the small number present, spread among the people less than was worthy of you; and lest a speech which, owing to the greatness of your merits, could not be hurried should delay you while you were handling many matters concerning our welfare in a single day.

[Note: [Col. 0642D]

II.—“A rival in prosperity”: emperors repeatedly resided at Augustodunum.

[Col. 0643C] “Present and not in need”: Livineius thinks *gratiam* (“favour”) was written instead of *coram* (“present”): then, *indigentes*, “not in need of favour”; from this word, he says, *coram* was formed. Acidalius reads *etiam non indigentes*, “even those not in need.”

“Severely affected”: perhaps “severely afflicted,” as below, §5: “I have said how well you aided the deserving Aedui, Emperor; it remains for me to say how severely afflicted they were.” Certainly all manuscripts and editions have *affectis*, and the word is used in this sense.

“With so much greater desire”: no emendation is needed here, as some suppose. For Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.787:

> “The more she rages, and grows fierce with mournful flames,
> the more the battles grow cruel with blood poured forth.”

So Lucretius, Plautus, Terence, and others use it for *tanto magis*, “so much the more”; and Cicero, *For Deiotarus*, §8: “By that right hand I beseech you … not so much firm in wars and battles as firmer in faith.”

[Col. 0643D] “Monstrous and barbarous”: was this said by a Gaul congratulating a Roman emperor, or did provinces other than those of the Aedui seem barbarous to him?

“To recover the Gauls”: occupied by the tyrant Tetricus.

“Your father”: Constantius.]

II. Now therefore, while in this city—which still enjoys your presence more constantly than the rest, for our Flavia will have a rival in prosperity—your whole retinue of friends and all the apparatus of empire attend you, and while men from almost every city, either publicly deputed or petitioning on their own behalf, stand before you, I shall say, Emperor, things which you will gladly acknowledge [Col. 0642D], and which others would not believe had been granted to us unless I spoke them [Col. 0643A] in your knowledge.

First, most sacred Emperor, in giving thanks one must show that what has been granted was the result not of chance prosperity but of just clemency. For while it is the act of a good ruler to help all persons present who are in need, it is the act of a wise one especially to assist those who have deserved well and are severely afflicted. When I have shown this—not so much from zeal to praise my native city as from the duty of demonstrating your providence—I shall then set forth the greatness of your benefits, with a desire far greater than my ability.

What people in the whole world may claim precedence over the Aedui in love for the Roman name? They were the first of all among those monstrous and barbarous peoples of Gaul to be called brothers of the Roman people by numerous decrees of the senate. While among the other peoples from the Rhône [Col. 0643B] as far as the Rhine not even peace could be hoped for without suspicion, they alone took pride in the name of kinship. And, to pass over intermediate events, they alone recently summoned the deified Claudius, your ancestor, to recover the Gauls; and, a very few years ago—what is especially to be proclaimed—they rejoice in the many benefits of your father: some received in deeds accomplished, others indicated in intention.

[Note: [Col. 0643D]

III.—Saguntum: today Morvedre, once a most celebrated town of Hispania Tarraconensis in the territory of the Edetani. It was destroyed by Hannibal; its people preferred to burn themselves and their possessions on a lit pyre rather than surrender to him.

Massilia: a city of Gallia Narbonensis on the coast of Provence, by the Mediterranean Sea, once most renowned not only for the distinction and prestige of its schools but also for upright character. Thus in Plautus’ *Casina*, [Col. 0644C] “Massilian morals” are proverbial for the most upright conduct.

The Mamertines: a people originally from the island of Samos. Received as guests by the Messanians, they seized the city and named it Mamertine; hence Cicero, *Against Verres*, Acts 4 and 7: “Messana, a Mamertine city,” and the people of Messana are called Mamertines.

The Ilians: inhabitants of ancient Ilium. Ilium, also Troy, is the celebrated city of Lesser Phrygia, between Mount Ida to the east and the Aegean Sea to the west.

The Aedui: concerning the Aedui.

“An Aeduan chief”: the leading magistrate of the Aedui, if Julius Caesar is to be believed, was called *Vergobret*—a Gallic term, but corrupted. Whether an Aeduan chief was distinct from this official I do not know. Certainly Julius Caesar often calls Diviciacus an Aeduan chief, but never magistrate of the Aedui.

“On this side of the Rhône”: the Rhône, the great river of Gallia Narbonensis, rises from Mount Adula, opposite the Rhine; after receiving the Arar at Lyons, it flows past Vienne, Valence, Avignon, and Arles. “Le Rhône.”

“Pyrenean Mountains”: the Pyrenees separate Gaul from Spain. See Pliny’s panegyric on them.]

III. Saguntum was once allied with Rome; but when all Spain, already weary of the Punic War, desired to change its sovereignty, it was allied. Massilia was friendly and rejoiced to be protected by Roman majesty. In Sicily, the Mamertines, and in Asia, the Ilians, pleaded a fabulous origin. The Aedui alone, not frightened by fear nor compelled by flattery, but through a free and simple affection, were deemed and deserved to be called brothers of the Roman people [Col. 0643C]—a name which, beyond the other terms of connection, displays both a mutuality of affection and an equality of dignity.

Then, when neighbouring nations, envying not their glory but that Roman brotherhood itself, and driven by their hatreds even to their own destruction, called in Germans as auxiliary masters, an Aeduan chief came into the senate and explained the matter. When an audience was offered him, he claimed less for himself than was granted; leaning upon his shield, he delivered his speech. When assistance was ordered, he was the first to lead the Roman army and Caesar across the Rhône. For until that time the passage into Gaul had been called Transalpine Gaul. But the Aedui delivered to Roman rule all that region contained by the Rhine, Ocean, Pyrenean Mountains, and the whole chain of Alps, providing winter quarters hospitably, furnishing supplies abundantly, manufacturing arms, [Col. 0644B] and assisting with forces of infantry and cavalry. Thus, after all the Celtic and Belgic peoples had been joined in one peace, they wrested from the barbarians whatever they joined to the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 0644D]

IV.—“With age”: perhaps “from age.”

“Great in years”: thus restored from Acidalius. The Putean edition has “great in year.”

“What we saw as boys”: if Eumenius was a boy under Claudius II, namely in AD 269, it seems plausible to me that he was born under Gallienus, around AD 261.

“To recover the Gauls”: from the tyrant Tetricus.

[Col. 0645] “Gallic rebels”: the Bagaudae, concerning whom see above. Bartholomaeus of Chasseneux, doctor of law and also advocate of the Aeduan fisc, in this very speech, which he inserted into his *Catalogue of Glory*—a work printed at Paris in Gothic type 150 years ago—adds to the text: [Col. 0645C] “And although they had at all times deserved well of the Roman people, they nevertheless saw their children carried off into safety and their fields laid waste.”

“If fortune had favoured you”: the Flavian family.

“Could have aided”: he was occupied in the Gothic war. In this war, if Trebellius is to be trusted, 320,000 barbarians fell, and 2,000 ships were sunk. In that disaster the Peucini, Trutungi, Ostrogoths, Virtingui, Sigipedes, Celts, and Heruli were killed, etc.

“Without the Catalaunian disaster”: when Aurelian, in AD 274, utterly defeated the army of the tyrant Tetricus—Tetricus himself having surrendered it, according to Vopiscus, Victor, Pollio, Zosimus, and Zonaras. Catalaunum is a large city of Gaul on the river Matrona, twenty leagues south of Troyes and as many east of Verdun: Châlons-sur-Marne.

“At the Kalends”: Livineius explains that Constantius, in his generosity, gave a large sum of money to the Flavian commonwealth, which they might lend at interest on the Kalends, as was customary. Horace, *Epode* II:

> “Soon to become a rustic,
> he gathers in all his money on the Ides
> and seeks to put it out at interest on the Kalends.”

Gruter reads *ad Caldaria*, that is, “for restoring the baths.”

*Metoeci*: that is, resident aliens or colonists: “Μέτοικοι are those who have moved from one city and dwell in another”—that is, metics are persons inhabiting another city after leaving their former one (Suidas, from Aristophanes’ *Knights*).]

IV. Someone will say: “Those things are ancient”—and indeed holier for being ancient. For good services acquire dignity and weight with age. As we revere and honour parents advanced in years more and more every day, while the equality of brothers and the offspring of children touch our minds with an affection gentler indeed but less weighty, so ancient benefits are more substantial, though present ones may seem more pleasing.

But if those services have grown obsolete with age, what of these recent events which we saw as boys? Consider, I pray, Emperor, how great it was that they were the first to urge the deified Claudius, your ancestor, to recover [Col. 0644C] the Gauls. Awaiting his aid, shut in for seven months and enduring every pitiable hardship of want, [Col. 0645A] they only then abandoned their gates to be broken through by the Gallic rebels, when exhaustion made them unable to keep watch. If fortune had favoured you and the efforts of the Aedui, and if that restorer of the commonwealth had been able to help us when we appealed to him, the brotherhood of the Aedui would, without any loss to Roman strength and without the Catalaunian disaster, have brought a speedy peace through the reconciliation of the provinces.

For these ancient and recent merits, therefore, your deified father wished to raise up the fallen city of the Aedui and revive it when ruined—not only by giving money to be lent at the Kalends and rebuilding the baths that had collapsed, but also by transferring metics from every side, so that this city might be as it were the one mother of the provinces, since it had in some sense first made the other cities Roman.

[Note: [Col. 0645D]

V.—“Exceedingly much”: Cicero likewise, *Orator*, §87: “Those who are exceedingly powerful in speaking”; some also read *mirum quantum*, “wonderfully much,” in both places.

“Except those,” etc.: a corrupt passage, which I restore with Acidalius. Others read *nisi pro quo tuis gratuleris*; others, *nisi quos pro tuis gratuleris*.

[Col. 0646B] “Enjoin”: that is, command this of your mind.

“Without experience of compassion”: I would prefer *miseriae*, “misery”: that is, unless you hear and recognize another’s misery, you can neither be merciful nor be considered merciful.

[Col. 0646C] “Not so much supported by the Romans”: that is, this city did not stand so much because of its inherent alliance with the Romans as it lay prostrate through exhaustion of strength caused by the new tax imposed on it.

“The Gallic assessment”: assessments were made in two ways: by heads, or households; or by lands, which for that reason were registered by the censors, so that the tax was greater or less according to the number and size of the estates. The meaning, therefore, is: we are indeed exhausted by the harshness of the new assessment, since we cannot equal the resources of the other provinces. Yet there is no reason for us to complain, since we possess the lands that have been registered, and nothing is demanded of us except what is due under the common formula of the Gallic assessment.]

V. I have said, Emperor, how well you aided the deserving Aedui [Col. 0645B]; it remains to say how severely afflicted they were. This topic would furnish me with exceedingly much more material for speech, if it were permissible, while you listen, to linger over sadder matters. Therefore, just as modesty set a limit in praising the merits of my native city, lest I rise too arrogantly, so both my own grief and what your ears are accustomed to will restrain me in recounting its misfortunes. For you willingly hear nothing except those whom you may congratulate as your own.

Nevertheless, I pray, Emperor, impose patience upon your mind, so that, just as physicians eminent in knowledge do not disdain to inspect the wounds they heal, [Col. 0646A] so you may now listen for a little while to the hardships of the Aedui which you have removed. For you cannot attain the praise of clemency without experience of compassion. That city lay low—not so much supported by its ties with Rome as cast down by the exhaustion of its strength—ever since the harshness of a new assessment had drained it of life. Yet it could not justly complain, since we possessed the lands that had been registered and were bound by the common formula of the Gallic assessment, though we could equal no one in resources. All the more, Emperor, do we thank your clemency: by remedies freely granted you have made us seem to obtain justly what we could not claim by right.

[Note: [Col. 0646C]

VI.—Remus: the Remi, a people whose city was Rheims, or Durocortorum, in Gallia Belgica, on the river Vidula.

Nervius: the Nervii, a people of Gallia Belgica, those of Hainaut, near Tournai on the river Scheldt.

[Col. 0646D] “Whose”: that is, whose revenues equal their labours.

“Whom”: that is, those burdened by debt.

“Thus”: thus that land which had once been at least somewhat good, etc.

The district of Arebrignus: *pagus* signifies not merely a little village where the cottages of several rustics stand together; it also denotes an entire jurisdictional district. In this sense Caesar, *Gallic War* I, writes that all Helvetia was divided into forty *pagi*; today thirteen are counted, which we call cantons. Dionysius likewise says that Roman territory was distributed into certain districts. Arebrignus, however, is a district of the Aedui around the river Arar.

“It is sown by a grudging hand”: this reading occurs in several old manuscripts, meaning “it is sown with extreme difficulty.” The Putean edition reads *inani fertur invidia*.

“It is exceedingly small”: Acidalius reads this for *perspicua est*, “it is clear.”

[Col. 0647B] Arar: the Araris, the Saône.

“The extended plain”: Augustodunum is elevated by wooded mountains on the east and south; on the north and west it descends into valleys—at least around its middle, from which a most pleasant plain extends northward for twelve thousand paces, surrounded on every side by springs and streams. This is according to Bartholomaeus of Chasseneux in his *Catalogue of the Glory of the World*, XII.60. More on the origin, rank, and location of the Aeduan city may be seen in Peter of Saint-Julian and John Munerius, both of whom wrote commentaries on that city.

“Changed”: supply “has been.” The meaning will be: now everything which, owing to the low-lying position of the place, had been better watered by these waters, and hence richer and more fruitful, has all been changed into a kind of black and muddy abyss.

“Which the ignorant admire”: that is, vineyards admired by people who attend only to a certain luxuriance of leaves and to a useless forest of shoots, unaware of the defect concealed in them.

[Col. 0647D] “For the roots”: roots repeatedly trenched a thousand times had produced so dense a mass of fibres and shoots that pits could not be dug to the proper depth. Thus the very propagation of the vines, insufficiently covered, was either damaged by rains or burned by the heat of the sun. For *ipsam propaginem non debitam, sed obtectam*, read *ipsam propaginem non obtectam*, “the growth itself, uncovered.” The word *debitam* has undoubtedly crept into this line from the preceding verse, as the learned Puteanus observes—unless perhaps, with Livineius, one reads *non diditam, sed obtectam*, “not diffused, but lightly covered,” etc.

“Aquitanians”: the peoples inhabiting that part of Gaul bounded by the Garonne, the Pyrenees, and the Ocean: Guyenne.]

VI. For, as I have said, we have both the number of persons recorded and the measure of land—but both are worthless: the people through idleness and the land through treachery. [Col. 0646B] For where among us is there a Remus, a Nervius, or even the neighbouring territory of the Tricassini, or a farmer, whose revenues contend with his labour? Yet anyone may rightly excuse the cultivators themselves, who are reluctant to labour without profit. A field which never repays its costs is necessarily abandoned, especially amid a shortage of country people; and those who totter under debt have been unable either to channel waters or cut down forests. Thus whatever soil had once been at least tolerable has either been spoiled by marshes or blocked by thickets.

Indeed, the very district of Arebrignus is sown by a grudging hand; in one place alone its vineyard is of exceedingly small cultivation. For beyond it all else, pathless through woods and rocks, is the lair of beasts safe from axes. The plain below, extending as far as the Arar, was, I hear, once pleasant, when continuous cultivation through each person’s boundaries raised the courses of springs through open valleys. But now, their channels blocked by desolation, whatever had been more fertile because of its low position has been turned into an abyss and marshes. Finally, the very vineyards, which the ignorant admire, have grown so old that they scarcely feel cultivation any longer. For the roots of the vines, whose age we now do not know, heaped together by being turned over a thousand times, prevent pits from being dug to the proper depth and expose the growth itself—not properly, but insufficiently covered—to be washed away by rains and scorched by the sun. Nor can we, as is customary among the Aquitanians and other provinces, mark out space everywhere for new vines, [Col. 0647B] since above lie unbroken rocks and below frost-bound low ground.

[Note: [Col. 0647D]

VII.—“The other cities”: Augustodunum was the capital of the Aeduan territory, to which other cities were subject, as we have shown above from Tacitus.

[Col. 0648B] *Navigera*: that is, rivers suitable for navigation.

“Muta”: that is, full of silence and darkness.

“The military road is rugged”: Livineius reads *via situ confragosa*, “the road rugged from neglect.” Since military roads are ordinarily level everywhere and easy for transporting supplies, even the military road among the Aedui was rugged, which strongly contributes to emphasizing the misery of that region.

“Alternis”: that is, because of interposed mountains.

“May be slow”: so that whenever the demands of our service require us to bring you food and supplies, this can occur only with difficulty and slowly, later than we should wish.

“Since”: that is, since it is more difficult for us to transport a little food than for others to transport far more.

“For others, of very many”: it does not seem irrelevant to append here what Chasseneux adds from a manuscript: “Emperor, the nature of these places is such that all will acknowledge it as a supreme benefit that you did not shudder at their sight, and as an act not of a human being but of a god that you restored them; we, in particular, shall honour it with everlasting goodwill.”

“Itinerum”: perhaps this word is superfluous.

“Now”: that is, the course of the speech has now reached the point at which I recount the remedies your majesty brought to these evils.

[Col. 0648D] “Which received you”: that is, which city seemed to receive you in its curved embrace, and, with towers projecting on either side, as though embracing you.]

VII. For why should I speak of the other cities of that region, for which, as you yourself confessed, you wept? For you saw—not, as when travelling through the territories of other cities, nearly everything cultivated, open, flourishing, with easy roads and navigable rivers washing the very gates of the towns—but, immediately from that bend where the road turns back toward Belgica, all things desolate, uncultivated, squalid, silent, and dark. Even the military road was broken and, by alternating mountains, steep and precipitous, so that it could scarcely convey half-loaded carts, [Col. 0648A] and at times empty ones. Hence it often happens that our services are slow, since the transport of a few crops is more difficult for us than that of very many for others. All the more, Emperor, do we thank your compassion: though you knew the approach to and sight of the roads and districts of our country to be so foul and harsh, you nevertheless deigned to turn aside there and to honour with your presence that city which lived solely in expectation of your aid. It is the mark of a good ruler gladly to see his people prosperous; but of a better one to visit even those who suffer. Good gods! What a day then dawned upon us—now indeed the course of my speech has duly reached the proclamation of the remedies supplied by your divine power—when you entered the gates of the city itself, which seemed to receive you in an embrace, its form bent inward into a bosom and its towers projecting on either side [Col. 0648B].

> [Note: [Col. 0648D]  
> VIII.—“Poured themselves forth to meet [you].” Constantine’s entry into the city of Augustodunum.
>
> “For the prolonging [of years].” Anton Schonovius adds *annos*, “years.”
>
> “By the customary fashion of words.” Such acclamations varied. Thus in Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, the people cry: “Jupiter, from our years increase your years.” In Seneca, *Epistles* 31 and 71: “So much the better: arise and breathe”; and in Book VI of the *Natural Questions*: “Go bravely, go prosperously.”
>
> “We pray without anxiety.” It is safe to pray for you a long life; for our wishes will undoubtedly be fulfilled, since even without our prayers a long lifetime is owed to you as the best ruler.
>
> [Col. 0649C] “Grew warm.” That is, the mind leapt with joy.
>
> “As though already.” That is, as though we were already enjoying the favour which we were to receive.
>
> “The emblems of all the associations.” I am readily inclined to think that emblems and images were customarily preserved in the associations of learned persons. These, indeed, were brought out to adorn Constantine’s ceremonial entry.]

VIII. You wondered, Emperor, whence so great a multitude poured itself forth to meet you, when you had seen desolation from the neighbouring hill. For people of every age flocked in from all the fields, in order that they might see him whose survival they gladly wished for themselves. For what, according to the customary form of words, is sworn for the prolonging of other rulers’ years is vowed to you alone, Constantine, who will outlive the destinies of us all; we pray without anxiety for one to whom so long a life is owed in his own right. Great indeed is the force of joys arising after prolonged sickness and grief. Our spirits glowed with joy beyond our strength; and, raised by a certain foreknowledge of future prosperity, we received you with such exultation as though we already possessed the favour which you were to grant. We adorned the roads by which one comes to the palace with poor equipment indeed; but we brought forth the emblems of all associations, the images of all our gods, and very few instruments for renowned musical strains; we displayed them at convenient intervals, so that they might meet you more often. He would have believed us rich who measured reality by devotion. Yet your foresight could not fail to perceive our poverty, however well concealed: you recognized the dutiful and honourable display of the poor.

> [Note: [Col. 0649C]  
> IX.—“The trouble of asking.” The old maxim is that nothing is bought more dearly than what must be bought with entreaties. Indeed, he destroys the grace of his own kindness who does not anticipate the petitioner’s wish. [Col. 0649D] See Seneca, *On Benefits*.
>
> “Before the sight of majesty.” I have inserted Gruter’s emendation into the text, in place of the earlier reading *majestatis affectu*, “by the feeling of majesty.”
>
> “You remitted.” A common manner of speaking among writers of that age. Thus *Panegyric* 11.18: “Do you think it a small benefit, Emperor, that you remitted the danger to me of having to ask?”
>
> “Enriches.” Read *uberat*, “enriches.”
>
> “To yourself.” That is, by considering the matter with yourself.]

IX. Of your own accord you summon us to approach your divine presence; of your own accord [Col. 0649B] you deigned to address us, of your own accord to ask what assistance we desired. These, Emperor, are true benefits: those which arise not from favours urgently sought through prayers, but from your spontaneous goodness, and which have bestowed the pleasure of obtaining them without any trouble of asking. For it is no small undertaking to petition privately on one’s own behalf the emperor of the whole world: under the gaze of so great a majesty, to rub one’s brow, compose one’s expression, strengthen one’s mind, frame one’s words, speak tremblingly, end appropriately, and await the answer. All these difficulties, Emperor, you have remitted to our modesty, not merely by spontaneously asking what remedy we sought, but even by suggesting to yourself what we left unsaid, while you raised us as we lay at your feet by your most merciful address. With tearful eyes we saw your compassion made manifest. [Col. 0649C] Tears ran down that face—saving to us, glorious to you—and we, our grief now dispelled, wept in turn for joy. For just as a rain long desired enriches fields thirsty from prolonged heat, so your tears watered our hearts with joys; so that, although it would have been impious to rejoice while you wept, rejoicing nevertheless overcame reverence, since those tears were signs of compassion, not of grief.

> [Note: [Col. 0649D]  
> X.—“Sent down from heaven.” Compare *Panegyric* 7.8: “That majesty, I say, that majesty, subject to Jupiter’s nod, and entrusted not to Iris, messenger of the gods, but to the wings of Victory, accompanied you as readily as things sent down from heaven swiftly reach the earth.”
>
> [Col. 0650C] “A more shrewd friend.” That is, if you were to seek advice from some more astute person. I retain the word *amici*, “friend,” absent from the Putean edition.
>
> “Hardens.” Virgil, *Georgics* I.179:
>
> > Then first the threshing-floor must be hardened with tenacious clay.
>
> “Ripens.” Or perhaps *maturat*, “brings to maturity.”
>
> “And store [them] among provisions.” A metaphor taken from reapers, who do not reap and store their harvest in granaries at the same time. It has always been the practice of good rulers to assist cities and provinces worn down by war or another calamity through exemption from, or remission of, fiscal burdens. [Col. 0650D]]

[Col. 0650A] X. And these things might indeed have sufficed for the fullness of our rejoicing, even if you had deferred the hope of our remedies and left uncertain the resources by which you intended to relieve us. But the disposition of goodness in you is so ready that what you conceive in a compassionate mind you immediately declare in speech. Thus generous and abundant springs hasten to flow wherever they may be of use; thus things sent from heaven swiftly reach the earth; thus, finally, that divine mind which governs this whole world immediately accomplished whatever it conceived. In this, however, Emperor, if you admitted the advice of a shrewder friend, there might be something perhaps to criticize: namely, that you disclose too readily what you are about to grant, and without any art quickly bring forth what ought long to be hoped for. You do not know, Emperor, how to enhance the value of your benefits: by the speed of granting them you forestall the time [Col. 0650B] for wishing. Yet by the speed of your generosity you have surpassed, Emperor, the very elements by which we are sustained and live. For a long time the birth of a coming human being is desired; for a long time an infant’s inarticulate cries delay the voice that will speak; for a long time winter restrains crops, spring draws them forth, summer hardens them in flower, and heat ripens them. But you have given us our whole life at once; you have ordered us immediately to reap the fruits of your merits and to store them among our provisions. When intending to reduce the assessment, you fixed the number. When intending to remit the remaining debts, you asked how much we owed. That question was an open promise. For when one who can do all things asks what is owed to him, he does not inquire inquisitively in order to know, but graciously wishes to hear how much he may remit.

> [Note: [Col. 0650D]  
> XI.—“In a medley.” As Festus writes in Book XVII, *satura* was a kind of food prepared from diverse ingredients, or, according to another interpretation, a type of poem in which many matters were discussed jointly and confusedly. Hence a *lex satura*, a “medley-law,” was formerly said to be one packed with many other laws; or νόμος πολλὰ περιέχων, that is, “a law containing many things,” a law which speaks of several matters. It was named from an abundance of matters, as though from fullness (*saturitas*). Hence the name *satire*, because it attacks every kind of vice; hence also *saturum carmen*, a “full poem.”
>
> “Seven thousand heads.” *Capita*, “heads,” are poll-tax assessments levied upon individual heads. The ancient glosses: *Tributum capitulare, ἐπικεφάλαιος φόρος*—“a capitation tax, a head-tax.”
>
> “Generosity.” That is, we imposed moderation upon your liberality as it poured itself forth abundantly.
>
> [Col. 0651C] “How useful.” That is, how useful also for rendering whole the services by which we are devoted to you.
>
> By this remission, twenty-five thousand persons paid one hundred [units]. Thus, when he remitted more than a fourth part of the assessment to this same number, he gave strength to twenty-five thousand, and ensured that thereafter they paid the tax with less hardship to themselves.
>
> “And you obtained more thereby.” You gained more for yourself by relieving the others and enabling them more easily to pay the assessment than you took away from yourself by remitting the tax of seven thousand.
>
> [Col. 0651D] “Four times as much,” etc. He rounds off the number: for four times seven makes twenty-eight, whereas the assessments of Augustodunum amounted to only twenty-five thousand heads. Others read this passage differently, but badly in my judgment.
>
> “Overburdened.” Others read *exacervata*, “heaped up,” others *exacerbata*, “aggravated.”]

XI. I shall therefore speak of each separately; for such great benefits must not be confused as though in a medley. [Col. 0650C] You remitted seven thousand heads, more than a fourth part of our assessments; and yet you repeatedly asked whether this would suffice for us. Should I call us excessively modest, or sufficiently grateful, who kept silent, hesitated, and set a limit to your generously overflowing liberality? You wished to grant still more, had we dared to request it. How great a benefit this is, Emperor—[Col. 0651A] how necessary for us, how useful even for the duties of devotion—I cannot say sufficiently. By this remission of seven thousand heads, you gave strength to twenty-five thousand; you gave assistance; you gave salvation. And you gained more by what you strengthened than you cut away by what you remitted. Four times as much was rendered secure and certain to you as had been demanded in vain. For despair of bearing the debt prevented even the payment that could have been made; nor was there any reason to attempt it when there was no hope at all of completing it. O divine remedy, Emperor, which you have applied to heal the city! Just as diseased bodies, oppressed by the numbing torpor of their limbs, are healed by the cutting away of some part of themselves, so that what has been diminished flourishes, though what was overburdened lay inert; so we, pressed down by an excessive mass, rise when the burden is lightened.

> [Note: [Col. 0651D]  
> XII.—“To assess.” That is, to estimate.
>
> “Seven thousand.” That is, that he embraced seven thousand persons by his benefit. You embraced all those whom you rendered able to meet the tax payment.
>
> “Since not all is borne.” The Putean edition reads: *quia nemo vicino praefertur*, “because no one is preferred to his neighbour.” Others, removing *nemo*, read: *quia nemo praefertur*, “because no one is preferred.” Acidalius: *quia non omnis porro feretur*, “because not all will henceforth be borne.” Others: *quia non perferetur*, “because it will not be borne through.” From all these conjectures, this is how the passage seemed to me to require restoration to integrity.
>
> [Col. 0652C] “Of being relieved.” In a passive sense—*exonerandi*: that is, the assured confidence that the burden will be lightened.
>
> “Long exhausted.” Earlier, “oppressed.”
>
> “When more [persons].” That is, when a multitude of heads lessens each individual burden.
>
> “The remitted [amounts].” That is, after remission of what remained to be paid, there is nothing to be feared or looked back upon.
>
> “That something.” That is, something which in some degree diminishes the ability to pay the future tax.
>
> “One.” Namely, the present time, and that the least.
>
> “May be.” That is, and may be divided from the past.
>
> [Col. 0652D] “And of both.” That is, lying midway between the limits of both periods.
>
> “Bordering.” Others think *confiniis* or *confinium* should be read.]

[Col. 0651B] XII. He does not know how to assess your generosity who thinks that you bestowed only seven thousand heads. You bestowed everything that you enabled to stand. For although we still stagger under our former burden, it nevertheless seems lighter because it is not all borne: the expectation of being relieved gives patience to endure. Certainly, even now children hold their parents dearer; husbands maintain their wives without reluctance; and parents do not regret their grown children, whose burdens they rejoice to have remitted to themselves. Thus the affection of all, long exhausted, takes breath again; and each person is glad to count his own family without anxiety, when more persons assist the obligations of fewer. Accordingly we are all the more uplifted by hope for the future. The mind is restored by security concerning the past; and, since the remainder has been remitted, there is nothing to be looked back upon or feared which might destroy any part of our strength for future payments. Thus we have been freed from the burden of two periods, which are the greatest; the one remaining period—and that the smallest—we pass through with brief labour. For since past time is long in its own measure, while future time is infinite, and present time is brief and always changeable in either direction, since it both leaves the past and passes [Col. 0652A] into the future: this single year has scarcely any perceptible difficulty, hemmed in by the favours granted concerning the two periods, and set, as it were, as a boundary of prosperity and adjoining both, making us free in respect of the past and secure in respect of the future.

> [Note: [Col. 0652D]  
> XIII.—“For us, therefore.” That is, especially for our sake.
>
> “Equalled the age.” The five-year period of your reign.
>
> “For those [celebrations].” He compares Constantine’s *Quinquennalia* with the five-year remission of tax which he granted severally.
>
> “On the good fortune of his lustrum.” So far as I know, that speech survives nowhere; nevertheless, it is praised by ancient grammarians.
>
> “Flowed abundantly.” Or should it be *large*, “abundantly”?
>
> “Since in no remaining [debts].” Since we are free of concern over paying what remained.
>
> “This is to us.” That generosity of yours is to us like the fruitful abundance of the earth, etc.]

XIII. You have remitted to us the arrears of five years. O five-year period happier than all five-year periods! O five-year period which deservedly has equalled this span of your reign! The gods created you ruler especially for our sake, for each of whom this happiness was born when you began to rule. Your completed *Quinquennalia* too are to be celebrated by us. For those celebrations, undertaken at the beginning of the fifth year, are rightly common to all peoples; these, which are complete, are our own. Cato’s speech *On the Good Fortune of His Lustrum* is said to be splendid. For already in that ancient republic it contributed [Col. 0652B] to the praise of censors if they had completed a prosperous lustrum: if the harvest had filled the granaries, if the vintage had overflowed, if the olive-groves had flowed abundantly. What, then, is fitting for us to celebrate concerning this lustrum of your generosity? A lustrum in which, although no abundance of crops has failed, you have nevertheless made all things seem more abundant than they were. For it avails us as much to have possessed as much as we cease to owe; it avails us that the granaries and store-rooms were full, when we are entangled in no remaining debts. This bounty is to us what the earth, mother of crops, is; what Jupiter, governor of the winds, is. Whatever they had given too sparingly has nevertheless, through your benefaction, been born for us.

> [Note: [Col. 0653A]  
> XIV.—“That companion of your majesty.” Whom he means, says Livineius, I cannot determine; perhaps Faustus, son by Minervina. Acidalius reads: “and that compassion, companion of your majesty,” etc., so that *pietas* denotes the kindness which Constantine had shown toward the Flavienses.
>
> “The affront of our love.” Although this may seem an injury toward you, we shall nevertheless do it out of love for you.
>
> [Col. 0654A] “Bibracte, indeed.” That is, says Valesius in his *Description of the Gauls*, Bibracte among the Aedui, like Pola in Istria and Florence among the Tuscans, received its name from Julius Caesar and was surnamed Julia. But the chief city of the Aedui, namely Augustodunum, is called Flavia after its restorers Flavius Constantine and Flavius Constantius, and its inhabitants Flavienses.]

XIV. What mines of gold and silver in the whole world are so abundant? What Tagus or Pactolus has flowed with so much gold as we have obtained through your liberality? For what we have received from you is no smaller gift. Indeed, by as much as it is harder to have one’s own property extorted than not to acquire what belonged to another, by so much sweeter is release from the necessity of payment than the hoped-for advantage of gain. How many, most august Emperor, whom poverty had compelled to hide [Col. 0653A] in the forests or even to go into exile, emerge into the light through this remission of arrears, return to their native country, cease to accuse their former poverty, cease to hate the barrenness of their lands, regain courage for work, prepare cultivation, strive under better auspices, revisit their homes, and render their vows to the temples! Especially since you, the preserver of us all, have arrived; and, like that companion [Col. 0654A] and partner of your majesty, the entire city will blaze, resound with joys, and perhaps hold you back when you depart. For you will grant pardon; you will bear the affront of our love. Though you may be lord of all cities and all nations, we too have now taken your name, not our ancient one. Bibracte, indeed, has hitherto been called Julia, as have Pola and Florence; but the city of the Aedui is Flavia.

[Col. 0653]

# PANEGYRIC OF AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR, TO THE EMPEROR CONSTANTINE

## PREFACE

[Col. 0653B]

This speech was delivered in the year of Christ 313, after the defeat of Maxentius, I think in the month of January, at Trier, before Constantine departed thence to quell disturbances in Germany. The author is unknown. Yet the distinguished Puteanus attributes it to Nazarius: “This,” he says, “I infer from the style and from a passage in Nazarius’ panegyric addressed to Constantine, which begins thus: ‘I shall not here recall the riverbanks covered by uninterrupted slaughter, nor the Tiber filled with heaps of bodies; it is enough to touch briefly upon these things, since they were more fully recounted by me the day before.’” That is, in this very speech, in which the battle by which Maxentius was defeated by Constantine is described at greater length. Further, this follows from the order in which all the panegyrics are arranged in the ancient manuscripts: for Nazarius’ panegyric follows this one, beginning: [Col. 0653C] “When I am about to speak of Constantine,” etc.

## SYNOPSIS OF THE PANEGYRIC

In the introduction, the speaker says that he would not proceed to praise the emperor, unless it were impious for him—who had often praised him for lesser deeds—not to offer congratulations for the empire recovered.

Division: I. How bravely Constantine undertook war against Maxentius. II. How successfully he completed it.

Part I. Though his friends discouraged him, the omens opposed him, and his fellow-rulers almost despaired, he crossed the Alps with only a fourth part of his army, to march against enemies twice as numerous, heavily armoured, and, because of their consciousness of their crimes, never to cease except in death, §2. Severus, Galerius, and Maximian had attacked Maxentius with huge armies, all unsuccessfully, §3. But justice fought for Constantine. His virtues are compared with Maxentius’ vices, §4.

Part II. He takes Segusium, §5; the Taurini, §6; Milan, §7; Verona, §8; and Aquileia, where he puts some of the more obstinate to death and orders others to be bound with swords converted into chains, §11. After Maxentius is defeated at the seventh milestone from the city and, while fleeing, falls from the Milvian Bridge into the Tiber, §14, Constantine enters the city as victor and triumphant, §19. How unlike Cinna, Marius, and Sulla, §20. How merciful toward citizens and good toward soldiers, whom he will lead with him into Lower Germany as companions in his victories, §21. He surpasses the glory of Constantius, §24. For all these reasons he is granted exceptional honours by the senate, §25.

At the end, he prays Jupiter for the eternity of the Prince, [Col. 0654C] §26.

## THE PANEGYRIC BEGINS

> [Note: [Col. 0653D]  
> I.—“Both in the sacred city.” At Rome. “And here.” I think at Trier, from which Constantine was preparing to depart for Germany.
>
> “It is innate in them.” Those things are called innate in us for which nature seems to have made us, so that they cost us no effort; things are called acquired when we accomplish them only with great exertion.
>
> “Imitation.” That is, by imitating, we divert it to our own uses.
>
> [Col. 0655C] “The city recovered.” After Maxentius’ defeat.
>
> “And at last.” That is, after its prolonged disturbance of many years had been made firm.
>
> “That amid so many.” That is, amid the applause of so many eloquent speakers.
>
> “Trumpets and clarions.” They differ in that the trumpet was straight, the clarion curved; the former belonged to infantry, the latter to cavalry. Yet authors often use them interchangeably.
>
> “Spartan pipes.” Λακεδαιμόνιοι τὰς ἐξόδους etc.—“The Lacedaemonians [their marches] …” The Lacedaemonians entered battle not to the crash of trumpets, but to the measures of pipes, lyre, and cithara. Pausanias, *Laconica*; Plutarch, *On Music*.
>
> “That [you may assess] my speech.” That is, that you may assess my speech more by the zeal to please you than by its own thinness.
>
> “Filled up.” By the speeches of other orators.]

I. Whence comes to me such confidence, most sacred Emperor, that after so many most eloquent men whom you have heard speak both in the sacred city and here again, I should dare to speak—unless I considered it impious, and feared the religious taint of a kind of sacrilege, if I, who had always been accustomed to proclaim the deeds performed by your divine power, should pass over in silence deeds so much greater than the former, through which not some part of the state has been preserved, but the entire commonwealth restored to itself? For I do not fail to know how much inferior our talents are to those of the Romans. For to speak Latin eloquently is innate in them; in us it is acquired by labour. And if we happen to say anything aptly, our imitation derives it from that spring and [Col. 0654D] source of eloquence. Yet, although conscious of my inborn weakness and of an effort merely begun rather than perfected by learning, I cannot restrain myself from silence [Col. 0655A] but must attempt to say something about the City recovered, the Roman Empire, and its stability at last after a long convulsion, so that amid so many sounds of eloquent men even my own slight voice may seem to be heard. For if in military affairs and in battles themselves not only trumpets and clarions, but even Spartan pipes, are said to have had some stimulating effect, I believe it is because great spirits can be sufficiently stirred even by a small melody. Why, then, should I distrust your favour toward me, so as to measure my speech rather by the zeal of my devotion to you than by its own powers? I shall therefore attempt, insofar as I can, although your ears are filled, so to speak, to whisper to you—without confidence in rivalry, but eager to imitate.

> [Note: [Col. 0655C]  
> II.—“For, the indication having passed.” That is, the signification of an adverse omen. Others read *metu*, “fear,” for *nutu*, “indication.” Shortly after, instead of *offenso*, I would read *offensa* or *offensione*, “the offence” or “the displeasure.” Below he says that the war was undertaken contrary to the warnings of the haruspices. Therefore I should suppose that an omen was first drawn which was adverse, and then that the same omen, recalled and repeated, was adverse again. This, and what follows, sheds light upon a passage which has greatly troubled interpreters.
>
> “Having passed.” That is: for, disregarding both the fear inspired by the unlucky omen and the offence caused by its repetition.
>
> “The partners in your rule.” The Augusti Galerius and Licinius; the Caesars Severus and Maximinus.
>
> “Counts and commanders.” Counts were governors of one city; commanders, of many cities, each of which had its own count.
>
> “Muttering silently.” *Aeneid* XI.346: “but they mutter to speak”; *Aeneid* XII.657: “King Latinus himself mutters.”
>
> “Contrary to the warnings of the haruspices.” The haruspices were seers, either Etruscans or trained by Etruscans in haruspicy; their art consisted chiefly in foretelling the future through inspection of sacrificial victims. Those who derive the word from *hara*, “pen,” or from a victim taken in a pen, with Donatus, write *haruspices*; those who derive it from *arae*, “altars,” with Isidore, write *aruspices*. What is said here concerning the unlucky omen, the haruspices, and the adverse auspice may perhaps refer to the Labarum, seen by Constantine at the beginning of this expedition. For no one, I suppose, is ignorant that the cross was regarded by the Romans as an evil omen. On that portent, see the *Life of Constantine*, under the year 307.
>
> “You had left.” He had left the greater part of his army at the Rhine to guard against the Franks.]

II. First I shall take up the point which I think no one has yet dared to address: that I may speak of the resolve of your expedition before the praise of your victory. For, once the indication of the adverse omen had passed and the offence of its repetition had been overcome, I shall exercise toward you the freedom of our affection, which at that time we held in suspense between fear and prayers for the commonwealth. Did you, Emperor, dare to conceive so greatly in your mind as to attack first a war formed with such resources, such united greed, such contagion of crimes, and such desperation of pardon, while the partners in your rule were then inactive and hesitant? What god, what majesty so immediately present, urged you that, while nearly all your counts and commanders not merely muttered silently but openly feared, you yourself should perceive—contrary to human counsels and contrary to the warnings of the haruspices—that the time had come for you, through yourself, to liberate [Col. 0656A] the City? You surely possess, Constantine, some secret understanding with that divine mind which, having entrusted care for us to lesser gods, deigns to reveal itself to you alone. Otherwise, most brave Emperor, even after your victory, give an account of this. You had indeed left the Rhine secure, with armies posted along its whole frontier; but we conceived greater fears on your behalf because you provided for us rather than for yourself, and had strengthened our peace more than the war which you undertook.

> [Note: [Col. 0656C]  
> III.—“Who did not.” That is, who did not lead all his forces with him.
>
> “Arms.” Forces, armies.
>
> “With forces divided.” Some were left at the Rhine, others led into Italy.
>
> “What escaped us.” That is, what we, trembling from love for you, did not recognize.
>
> “His enemy.” Maxentius. Against him Caesar Severus had been sent by the Augustus Galerius; betrayed by the treachery of his own men through Maxentius’ artifices, Severus was forced to flee almost alone, and was subsequently killed either at Ravenna or at Rome on the Appian Way by Maxentius himself.
>
> “He too, stripped by deserters.” Maximian Herculius considered himself fortunate to have escaped Maxentius’ hands, having lost almost all his forces, which had likewise gone over to Maxentius.
>
> “Who was believed to be his father.” This passage strongly supports those who think Maxentius was not Maximian’s true son; as does §4: “to omit that he was a substituted son of Maximian,” and again: “that we may not begrudge the false son-in-law,” and Victor’s statement: “They report that Maxentius, substituted by a woman’s device, held the heart of his husband, who was troubled by the omen of the most wicked undertaking, from a boy,” that is, from male offspring. Then Anonymous Valesianus: “When the origin of Maxentius, whose mother was questioned, was investigated, she replied that he had been fathered by a certain Syrian.”
>
> [Col. 0657C] “For one thousand and sixty years.” For Maxentius’ war fell in the year 1060 from the founding of the City.
>
> “Besides this, others’ [wives].” That is, moreover, by granting other men’s wives, the lives of innocent persons, and their property indiscriminately to murderers, he had bound them so closely to himself that they devoted their very lives to him.]

III. Surely, Emperor, in your excessive love for us you failed to provide truly for our security, since you did not move all your forces with you when your preservation is our safety. And what need had the Rhine itself of soldiers and fleets stationed there, when the terror of your courage had long barred it to barbarian nations? Did you wish to display your diligence, with your forces divided between guarding peace and prosecuting war; or even, boastfully and gloriously, to prove that you were sufficient with few men for the liberation of the City? For you crossed the Alps with scarcely a fourth part of your army against one hundred thousand armed enemies, so that those who considered more deeply might perceive what escaped us in our trembling love: that you sought not a doubtful victory, but one promised by divine power. Severus had led a great army and, deserted through treachery, had armed his own enemy. Later Maximian had brought up greater forces, and he himself, stripped of deserters, seemed fortunate to have escaped. Finally, he who was believed to be Maxentius’ father, when he attempted to tear from his shoulders the rent purple robe, felt that his destiny had passed into that disgrace. That monster had amassed riches gathered from the whole world for one thousand and sixty years, and had lavished them upon hands bought for civil brigandage. Besides this, by giving away other men’s wives, the lives of innocent persons together with their goods indiscriminately, he had bound murderers to himself in devotion unto death. He punished those who laid snares for him, or openly attempted anything for freedom; he crushed them by arms. And meanwhile he made use of the majesty of the city he had seized; he filled all Italy with hireling guardsmen ready for every crime.

> [Note: [Col. 0657C]  
> IV.—“In deliberation.” Others read *in consilium*, “into deliberation.”
>
> “Each person’s own god.” An allusion to *Aeneid* IX.185:
>
> > Or does each person’s own dreadful desire become his god?
>
> “In so unequal a contest.” For above, in §3, addressing Constantine: “You crossed the Alps with scarcely a fourth part of your army against one hundred thousand armed enemies.”
>
> “He was.” An elegant contrast between Maxentius and Constantine. For Maxentius’ character, cruelty, lusts, sexual violations, proscriptions, false accusations, and magical practices, see Eusebius, Zonaras, Eutropius, etc.
>
> “Pious Constantius.” A coin exists in Tristan’s historical commentaries bearing the inscription: *D. Constantio pio principi*, “To the divine Constantius, the pious ruler.”
>
> “With his name mutilated.” He seems to indicate that Maxentius was called by Maximian with his name cut short and mutilated.
>
> “Devoted to marriage alone.” Therefore he held Minervina, by whom he had Crispus, in the position of a wife. See the *Life of Constantine*.
>
> “Of abolished accusations.” Victor Schotti says of him: “He was most beneficial in many respects, suppressing accusations by very severe laws,” etc. Eusebius says the same, as does *Panegyric* 6.38.]

IV. When you considered, knew, and saw all these things, Emperor—and neither your father’s seriousness nor your own nature allowed you to be rash—tell me, I pray, what did you have in [Col. 0657B] your deliberation except the divine power? Or did this reasoning guide you—for each person’s prudence is his god—that in so unequal a contest the better cause could not fail to prevail, and that, though he might set countless forces against you, justice nevertheless fought for you? For, to omit matters which it is not fitting to compare—that he was the substituted son of Maximian, while you were the son of pious Constantius; that he was of the most contemptible depravity, with limbs twisted and slack, his very name mutilated by a spurious appellation, while you are, enough said, so great and such a man—to omit these things, I say: you, Constantine, were accompanied by filial devotion; he, lest we begrudge the false son-in-law, by impiety. You by clemency; he by cruelty. You by chastity devoted to marriage alone; he by lust defiled by every sexual violation. You by divine precepts; he by superstitious sorceries; he, moreover, by the expiatory guilt of temples plundered, a senate slaughtered, and the Roman people destroyed by famine; you by the abolition of false accusations, the prohibition of informers, preservation, and rejoicing at the blood of murderers. In so divergent [Col. 0658A] a balance of causes, Emperor, by divine judgment—that is, by your own—you counted not the multitude of soldiers but the merits of the parties.

> [Note: [Col. 0658C]  
> V.—“All Greece.” Greece had different boundaries at different times. Thus, in a broad sense, it includes Epirus, Macedonia, and Thessaly; in a stricter sense, only Achaea, the Peloponnese, and the islands.
>
> “All Illyricum.” Illyricum lies between Macedonia on the east, Istria on the west, Pannonia on the north, and the Adriatic Sea on the south. “All Illyricum”: that is, though he could have assembled countless forces from all Illyricum, he never raised more than forty thousand soldiers, judging anything above that number useless to a commander.
>
> [Col. 0658D] “Light Medes.” The Medes dwell by the Caspian Sea, bordering Persians, Parthians, and Assyrians.
>
