> “You had soldiers to conquer.” He diminishes Alexander’s victories as much as possible, so that Constantine’s courage may appear greater.
>
> “Armed in the fashion of the first class.” That is, cataphracts.
>
> “The town.” Segusium.
>
> “By driving tunnels.” Observe the method then employed for taking cities. See Lipsius, *On the Roman Military System*.
>
> “Undertaken and accomplished together.” Sallust, *Jugurtha*: “In one day a war between two kings was begun and completed.”]

V. Great Alexander, though he could, in addition to his Macedonians, levy an innumerable force from all Greece and all Illyricum, never led an army greater than forty thousand, judging whatever exceeded that number unfit for a commander and a crowd rather than an army. But you undertook a far greater war with even fewer forces, superior in your personal courage by as much as he was better supplied in numbers. He indeed fought against light Medes, unwarlike Syrians, the shifting arms of the Parthians, and Asians eager to exchange one servitude for another, and conducted his campaign by the outcome of a single battle. But you had to conquer soldiers—heaven forbid!—Romans only shortly before, armed [Col. 0658B] in every respect in the manner of the first class, and, from consciousness of their crimes, never to cease except in death. Their first obstinacy proved this: they who held a town under the very ridges of the Alps, fortified by a very strong wall and by its position, dared, though you were approaching, to resist and close the gates. They did not, indeed, as I hear, believe that you yourself were present: for who would have believed that an emperor had flown from the Rhine to the Alps so swiftly with an army? Yet they ought to have yielded not only to your presence as a divine power, but even to the announcement of your name. They immediately paid the penalty of their madness, when they refused the pardon offered by your clemency. For no siege by rampart and trench was begun; they were not tested and shaken by tunnels driven, engines brought up, or the impact of a battering ram. Instead, torches were immediately hurled against the gates and ladders set against the battlements; and they were attacked not merely from afar with slings and missiles, but with spears and swords. Thus the undertaking and accomplishment were simultaneous, and their attempt at rebellion was joined to its outcome.

VI.—Gomphi. Gomphi, a city of Thessaly on the borders of Epirus, and the first encountered by travellers coming thence; neighbouring Gonnoi; more than forty Roman miles west of Larissa [Col. 0659C]. Statius, *Silvae* IV: “And to break the journey repeatedly at Gomphi.”

“Destroyed in one day.” On this expedition of Caesar see Dio, book XLI.

“In the Taurinian plains.” In the plains around Taurinum. Taurinum was a city of Subalpine Italy, the capital of Piedmont; today Turin.

“Whom fortune …” That is, men whom adverse fortune ought to have restrained.

“But,” etc. That is: the army was formed as a wedge, its flanks receding backwards into depth, so that while the front of our army fought vigorously, the extended flanks of the enemy might surround our men engaged in combat. But you, foreseeing this, sent forward men to meet them and at the same time to discover whether some ambush [Col. 0659D] lay concealed. You yourself, after putting that stubborn point to flight and opening the face of the wedge, inflicted so much greater slaughter as the engagement advanced, inasmuch as, etc.

“Drawn up in the form of a wedge.” That is, with the army arranged in wedge formation. A wedge is a mass of infantry narrower at its front and then broader, which breaks the enemy’s ranks. Soldiers call the outermost part of the wedge the “boar’s head.” VEGETIUS.]

VI. Gaius Caesar destroyed Gomphi, a city of Thessaly, in one day because it refused obedience [Col. 0659A]. But he attacked paltry Greeks; you, Subalpine peoples. He attacked inhabitants alone; you, a military garrison as well. He could not protect the captured from plunder; you were able to impose clemency upon your victorious troops. The disaster of the Gomphians was indeed a warning to the rest; but shortly afterward you fought another battle in the Taurinian plains—not against rebels frightened by your victory, but against men angry and inflamed with the desire for vengeance, whom the adverse turn of fortune ought to have restrained. Nor were the enemy wandering haphazardly and scattered, so that they could easily be cut down while dispersed; rather, their line was formed in the shape of a wedge, with its sides descending backward into depth, so that, while its foremost part engaged greedily, its bent-back sides might encircle men hampered by the fighting. But foreseeing this, you sent forward [Col. 0659B] men on either flank to meet them and at the same time to search out any hidden ambush. You yourself broke that resolute point and threw the battle-line into rout; and as the slaughter progressed, you made it all the greater because it had stood equipped with larger reserves. Thus they were routed and cut down as far as the walls of Taurinum; and, finding the gates barred by the inhabitants, they even closed them with the mass of their own bodies.

[Note: [Col. 0659D]

VII.—“Most shameful.” That is, a prodigy so monstrous and shameful awaited him.

“What a day was that?” Constantine’s triumphal entry into the city of Milan.

“An omen of victory.” From the happy beginning of the victory they inferred its completion.]

VII. What else could you have hoped for, unhappy soldier, when you devoted yourself then to that most shameful portent? I no longer reproach you; I grieve for you. You compelled Constantine to shed so much blood. Since he could not obtain your safety from yourselves, victory itself almost displeased him. Yet the Taurinians and the other cities of Italy were not of the same mind as you. Rejoicing with delight, they competed in calling you to themselves, Emperor. Embassies were sent by all [Col. 0659C], and supplies were offered from every quarter, so that it became clear how long they had desired the man to whom they so readily entrusted themselves while war still remained.

What a day was that [Col. 0660A] on which you entered Milan! What congratulations from the leading men of the city! What applause of the people! What confidence among mothers and maidens as they looked upon you! With what twofold delight they rejoiced, when they saw the form of a most beautiful emperor and did not fear licence! All displayed themselves and danced for joy, with no fear whatever of what remained of the war; and they took the auspices of your victory as its consummation. It seemed not that the province beyond the Po had been recovered, but that Rome herself had been recovered. For who could believe that, after successes so great, any obstacle remained to prevent all armies from surrendering themselves to your clemency, once they had learned the proof of your courage? You had taken walls by force; you had openly conquered in battle. Who seemed so mad as to dare either to endure siege or to engage in battle? Especially since, by remaining some days in Milan, you had given everyone time to consider [Col. 0660B] and to hope concerning you.

[Note: [Col. 0659D]

VIII.—“Long ago, in our middle age.” That is, about thirty years earlier, when Sabinus Julianus, who had seized the imperial power, was killed by Carinus in the plains of Verona [Col. 0660C]. VICTOR SCHOTTI.—Accordingly, the author of this panegyric was then sixty years old when he delivered this speech. Certainly, when he says that this happened in his own middle age—that is, while he was in the flower of life—this is the period called middle age. No. 1, note 3. Verona is a city on the river Athesis, between Tridentum and Mantua: Verona.

“Most obstinate prefect.” Ruricius, a most energetic man.

“Colony.” Of that colony Tacitus, *Histories* III: “The question was then raised what position should be selected for the war. Verona seemed preferable, since the open plains around it favoured the cavalry battle in which they were superior; and at the same time they saw that a colony strong in resources would serve both the practical need and their reputation.”

“Pompeian.” Does he mean Ruricius, perhaps born in the town of Pompeii? Or perhaps Carinus, as belonging to the family of Pompey [Col. 0660D]? Or finally Constantine?

“Athesis.” A river flowing from the territory of the Raeti past Tridentum and Verona and emptying into the Adriatic Sea: the Adige. Virgil mentions it, *Aeneid* IX.680.

“Whirlpools.” That is, swift with frequent eddies.

“For transporting supplies.” By bringing in provisions. Below, no. 18: “You, nourisher of your Rome by conveying supplies,” at the Tiber. Seneca, *On Benefits* VI.7: “Nor do we give thanks to rivers, although they admit great ships and run on in a broad, unfailing channel for carrying supplies.”

“Sent across.” Or “carried across”? Schonovius.

“Worse things.” That is, to endure a worse fate.

“Who had attempted a sortie.” Or: “at which a sortie had been attempted.” Thus Lipsius and Livineius read it. Not “which had attempted a sortie,” as in the Putean edition.

“Commander.” Namely Ruricius.

[Col. 0661C] “You preferred to meet him as he returned”—that is, as he was returning to Verona after making his incursion—with only that part of your army which was equipped for battle, in which there was no small danger, rather than interrupt the siege by leading out all your forces and give the besieged an opportunity either to recover breath, escape, or pursue you.]

VIII. But Verona—wretched city, long before stained in our own middle age with civil blood—was held by a very large army of enemies, by most vigorous commanders, and by a most obstinate prefect; so that the colony which Gnaeus Pompeius had once established might be destroyed by a Pompeian. O pitiable calamity of the Veronese, oppressed not so much by your siege as by the internal siege of their own minions! For that Athesis, rough with rocks, swirling with eddies, and fierce in its current, prevented attack and kept the whole region behind it secure and defended for conveying supplies. Yet, lest it assist the enemy longer, your foresight brought this about: at points farther upstream, where the river was gentler and the enemy unsuspecting, you sent part of the army across, at double risk [Col. 0660C], and compelled those shut in and besieged to experience worse things in battle. You cut down so completely all who had attempted a sortie that even their commander withdrew beyond the walls with part of his forces to summon [Col. 0661A] assistance—poor man, intending to bring back a larger army so that he might die amid a larger retinue of disaster. At that moment, indeed, your exceptional care and greatness of spirit appeared, Emperor: you preferred to engage him as he returned with the smaller army, rather than interrupt the siege, lest the confined enemy should be allowed to recover breath, escape, or threaten your rear.

[Note: [Col. 0661C]

IX.—“Then, having ascertained.” That is, after having reconnoitred the enemy’s numbers.

“From your own,” etc. That is, judging the courage of all your men from your own courage, and believing that the mass of the enemy army, though heavier, could be broken through by the force of the fewer.

“I complain again.” Or perhaps, “I ask again”? For, as Acidalius observes, he had not complained before but had asked why the war had been undertaken.

“With your whole force.” Compare Panegyric 2, no. 5: “You were borne through the entire battle, no otherwise than a great river, swollen with winter rains and clouds.”

“What have you to do?” According to Acidalius’ view, this entire phrase should be moved in position—an emendation that, I trust, everyone will approve. In the Putean edition: “What have you to do, Emperor, with adverse fortune? For you were borne on with your whole force, like a torrent,” etc.]

IX. At first, as I hear, you had drawn up a double battle-line. Then, after the enemy’s numbers had been observed, you immediately ordered the ranks to be deployed into a front and the arms extended more widely, measuring, no doubt, the spirit of all your men from your own, and judging that the heavier mass on the other side could be shattered by the assault of fewer men. Do you suppose, Emperor, that I intend to praise everything you did in that battle? On the contrary, I complain again. You had foreseen everything, arranged everything [Col. 0661B], and performed the duties of the greatest commander: why did you fight in person? Why did you mingle yourself among the densest masses of the enemy? Why did you expose the safety of the commonwealth to such great dangers? Or do you think we do not know that, when you were swept away by excessive ardour, you entered the midst of the enemy’s missiles and would have disappointed the hope and prayers of the whole human race unless you had opened a way for yourself by slaughter?

You were borne onward with your entire force like a rushing torrent, followed by forests torn up from their roots and rocks wrenched away from their foundations. What have you to do, Emperor, with adverse fortune? It is right for those to fight who must, according to each man’s lot, either conquer or fall; but can you, on whose life the fortunes of all depend, approach any danger? Can you move among so many missiles and swords? Who demands this of you? Or who could endure that anything should be allowed to the hazards of war in your case [Col. 0661C]? Does it become you, Emperor, to strike an enemy? No: it does not become you to toil.

[Note: [Col. 0661D]

X.—“From a high mountain.” Xerxes watched the naval engagement from Mount Aegaleus, opposite Salamis; the Greek forces utterly destroyed his fleet. Herodotus VII; Justin III; Diodorus Siculus.

“Occupied elsewhere.” Perhaps he takes the Actian war for the Sicilian one, in which Augustus, through Agrippa and other commanders of armies, defeated Pompey between Mylae and Naulochus, in A.U.C. 718. Augustus himself was so deeply bound in sleep that his friends had to awaken him to give the signal … Nor did he rise and appear before the soldiers until Marcus Agrippa had put the enemy ships to flight. Suetonius, *Augustus* 16. For in the Actian war Marcus Larius held the right wing of Caesar’s ships, Arruntius the left, while Agrippa had the entire direction of the naval engagement. Caesar was assigned to the sector to which fortune summoned him and was everywhere present. Velleius, II.85.

“Lifted up on ladders.” Who this person was, I have nowhere discovered.

“Companions.” On the *comites*, see above, no. 2, note 3.

“You had exposed.” Or “you had exposed us”?

“What need have you of our hands?” Or: “Why do you demand our hands?”

“Greatly.” Or “more greatly,” as Acidalius prefers.

“From their swords.” He ordered the soldiers’ swords to be forged into shackles.

“Double [shackles] from swords.” That is, restraints suited to binding two hands were forged.]

X. Xerxes watched a naval battle from a lofty mountain. Augustus, occupied elsewhere, won at Actium. There was also a man who, lifted upon ladders joined to one another, saw two armies meeting from afar, so that he was neither involved in danger [Col. 0662A] nor absent from its outcome. “These examples,” you will say, “are cowardly.” But they are safe; and fear for your danger is weightier than joy in your victory. Did not your companions and tribunes themselves, after the enemy had been slain and routed and even their commander killed, seize you in tears and embrace that panting breast of yours, your bloody hands, and whatever had emerged from the blood of the deep slaughter? Did they not cry out on every side: “What have you done, Emperor? To what fates had you exposed us, had your divine courage not protected you? What is this impatience? Or what need have you of our hands, if, with the roles reversed, you fight in person for us?”

I would not say these things, Emperor, nor recall that others said them, unless through the benefit of your gentleness our boldness in words were safer than your boldness in arms. For by a certain new diversity of nature and a blended harmony [Col. 0662B] of virtues, you are at once most fierce in battle and, once security has been gained, most gentle.

XI. For when you had granted the besieged time to repent, and had received Aquileia also through its envoys and suppliants, and all those whom you had saved by besieging them had surrendered to you, you forgave all and restored the life they had despaired of. You did indeed order them to lay down their arms, that they might be protected much more safely by the victor’s mercy; yet, that they might feel what their obstinacy deserved, you ordered them arrested and bound—not for punishment, but for life—lest they flee through fear of conscience, commit grave offences, and deserve no second preservation if they had not been saved. But from where could there come, for so great a number of men, enough bonds to restrain hands that were military and had been armed so recently? The soldiers who had undertaken to lead them away were bewildered [Col. 0662C]; they declined responsibility for guarding them and did not know at all what to do. Even those in your council, and the prefect himself, were at a loss, when you, prompted by divine inspiration, ordered double hand-restraints to be made from their swords, so that their own swords might preserve the surrendered men whom they had not defended while resisting.

[Note: [Col. 0663C]

XII.—“The great poet.” Virgil, *Georgics* I.508.]

[Col. 0663A] XII. O most beautiful triumph of your courage and clemency, one which ought to have been placed before the eyes of all! For whose power was it to take weapons from enemies, it was also whose humanity to bind the surrendered to impunity with their own weapons, and thus bind them so that they might daily repent of that iron which they had borne against you. The sword which the hostile enemy had drawn against you itself held its master’s hands; ready for slaughter, it became a guardian for safety. The great poet, while describing the movement and preparation of wars rising throughout the world, says: “And why are curved sickles forged into the rigid sword?” A sad time indeed, when tools prepared for tending flocks were turned to the slaughter of human beings. But now those rigid and deadly blades are bent into life-preserving bonds; they do not kill the disarmed man [Col. 0663B], but restrain him. And the surrendered enemies are protected by their own swords, blunted and battered, though those swords, whole and sharp, had been unable to benefit them at all.

[Note: [Col. 0663C]

XIII.—“Now sad, now joyful.” This passage recalls Seneca, *Natural Questions* II.41: “Three kinds of thunderbolt are assigned to Jupiter: the first warns, the second benefits, and the third is sent forth after the gods have been consulted.” Festus confirms this in almost the same words.

“Lest anyone give himself up to grief.” The meaning will be clearer if it is read, as in the Pithoean manuscript, “lest anyone, overcome by grief, give himself up [to it],” or, as Puteanus conjectures, “lest anyone give himself up to grief beyond the battle-line.”

“For human life,” etc. That is: human life, procured through long labour, must be preserved permanently so far as possible; iron, on the other hand, is easily found and applied to any use whatsoever. Therefore, you transformed by forging the iron that could be restored to its former form; but you preserved that which could not be restored—namely, life.

“That is.” As though you said: the iron was formerly a cause of fear, now a cause of security.

“Because security.” *Quod* here is a conjunction.

“Splendour”—that is, it lost its splendour through this transformation.]

XIII. Therefore all the functions of weapons serve different effects at your will, Emperor: swords conquer for you; they preserve for you. When you fight, they strike; when you forgive, they guard. As that god, creator and lord of the world, sends messengers by the same thunderbolt, now sad and now joyful, so under your divine authority those same weapons distinguish your enemies or suppliants by destruction or preservation. You took swords from your adversaries, Emperor, lest anyone give himself up to grief. You overcame them and rendered them harmless by their own hands, so as to satisfy both your clemency and your vengeance: you broke the weapons of those whose blood you had spared. For human life, acquired with long effort, must always be preserved [Col. 0663C], if possible; iron is easy to obtain and changeable in use. Therefore you melted down what was reparable, but preserved what could not come back to life.

What comparable transformations do fables report? That human bodies were changed into springs, beasts [Col. 0664A], or birds? Such transformation is foul and degrading. A sword changed into manacles: this is what security after fear is, what shade after heat is. The transformation lost its splendour, but blunted its edge.

[Note: [Col. 0663D]

XIV.—“That our exultation.” That is, that by this play upon words we might express our joy.

“Italy on this side of the Po.” The speaker is a Gaul from Trier.

“That portent.” Maxentius.

“Degenerate spirits.” Taken from *Aeneid* IV.13.

“A foolish and worthless animal.” A harsh expression; yet Cicero employs a scarcely more honorable one of a consular man whom he addressed in the Senate. Seneca, *On Benefits* II.16 calls Alexander “the most timid animal.”

“Or fear,” etc. That is, through the fear which omens instilled in him.

“He was warned.” Read “he was moved,” as all interpreters conjecture; or, if this reading is retained, the sense is that the fear which his omens instilled in him warned him to act so.

“Not the duties of men.” I would gladly insert *quidem*: “not even attempting the duties of men.” “Not the duties of men”: that is, not even so much as performing the duty of a man [Col. 0664D] by walking about in that palace whose walls were marble.

“The Gardens of Sallust,” which Gaius Crispus Sallustius, the distinguished historian, a wealthy and magnificent man, laid out beneath the Quirinal outside the *pomerium*, near the Collatine Gate. He lived in Cicero’s time; and there are writers who say that Terentia, wife of Marcus Cicero, after being divorced by him, married Sallust.

“Had besieged the world.” Perhaps one should read “the City.”

“Himself alone.” That is, he boasted that he and they alone were emperors, while the others bore arms on his behalf at the frontiers.]

XIV. Your eagerness and humanity, Emperor, have prompted us thus far to let our exultation play upon words. But now let us return to more important matters. When all Italy on this side of the Po had been recovered, Rome herself was already stretching suppliant hands toward you. That portent had seated itself there, daring to attempt nothing amid so many reports of its own defeats. Indeed, its cowardice held itself under siege within the person of a most contemptible man, and fear exposed its degenerate spirit. That foolish and worthless animal did not dare to go anywhere beyond the walls. For it was warned—or, perhaps, moved—by prodigies or by forebodings of its own fear. Shameful! Within the protection of walls, Emperor [Col. 0664B], he neither dared to breathe the open air, exercise with weapons, nor endure dust. Clever, certainly, in walking amid the marble walls of that palace without attempting even the duties of men. For a journey to the Gardens of Sallust was thought an expedition and a campaign. And throughout the whole period in which he had besieged the world—had shut himself in—such luxuries concealed his most shameful cowardice. He wished to seem not unwarlike but fortunate, not idle but secure. Whenever he called the soldiers into assembly, he boasted that he alone was emperor with them, while others performed military service for him at the frontiers. “Enjoy yourselves,” he said; “scatter it; squander it.” This was the brief and fleeting happiness of wretched men.

[Note: [Col. 0664D]

XV.—“Although,” etc. That is: although he had free passage across the Po and the Apennine mountains.

“Boundary of the Po.” The Po, Italy’s largest river, rises from Mount Vesulus in Subalpine Gaul and flows not far from Augusta Taurinorum; it washes Placentia and Ferraria and pours through many mouths into the Adriatic Sea: the Po.

[Col. 0665C] “Armies brought near.” First by Caesar Severus, then by Galerius himself, and finally by Maximian Herculius; all of whom were betrayed by their own soldiers and compelled to flee.

“Those whom you,” etc. That is: those whom not only your generosity and the sanctity of their oath had bound to you, but also the glory of so many victories won with you.

“Scipio.” On Scipio Africanus, see Pliny’s *Panegyric* no. 13, note 9.

“Caesar.” For the speed with which Caesar came to Rome to fight Pompey, see his commentaries, *On the Gallic War*, and the other writers of Roman history.]

XV. Not even when he had learned of so many adverse battles of his own side did he attempt to go out to resist [Col. 0664C], although he had the boundary of the Po and the ridges of the Apennines at his disposal. Instead, he suppressed letters reporting his disasters. At times he even openly wished that men would come right up to the gates. He did not understand that the majesty of the City—which had once deterred armies brought near it—had now, disfigured by his crimes and driven from its own seat, passed over to your aid; nor that no rewards could corrupt men whom, beyond your generosity and the faith of their oath, the glory of so many victories had dedicated to you [Col. 0665A]. For what soldier, who had fought so often and so successfully under your command and auspices, would sell his wounds to that man? Who would concede to him the outcome of a war already almost completed?

But you, perceiving this very ardour throughout the army, flew to the scene with rapid march and no delay for hesitation, by the shortest route through those regions; and in the energy of your action you represented Scipio’s and Caesar’s speed, especially at the time when Rome most desired it. This is the confidence of an unconquered commander who relies upon the spirit of his own men: not to hesitate or prolong war, but to regard every nearest occasion for battle as victory. Your circumstances were not like those of Quintus Maximus against victorious Hannibal, requiring you to seek an opportunity and a time after adversity; rather, your successes pressed you onward, and you had to continue your victories. Above all, you ought to bring aid to the City as soon as possible. For it is the part of a wise commander to help broken fortunes by delaying, and not to fail fortune when it is favourable [Col. 0665B].

[Note: [Col. 0665D]

XVI.—“Lest he, alarmed.” Lipsius emends this passage thus, I.22: “Lest he, alarmed, with his affairs grievously distressed and reduced to straits, should take counsel by delay.”

“Africa exhausted.” Aurelius Victor says: “Maxentius ordered Carthage, the glory of lands, together with Africa’s more beautiful regions, to be laid waste, plundered, and burned.”

“All islands.” Especially Sicily and Sardinia.

“After six years consumed.” I prefer “six-year period,” as Petavius wishes, *On the Doctrine of Times* II.37; for he held the tyranny for six years, until on the last day of that sixth year, before beginning the seventh, he was defeated and fell into the Tiber, as is said below.

“A household slave arrayed in purple.” Maxentius. Compare Pacatus on Theodosius concerning the tyrant Maximus: “That man, once the most worthless household slave of your house.”

“With his wife.” Magnentia Urbica, daughter of the former wife of Galerius; Tristan records her coins in his historical commentaries.

“And son.” This was Marcus Aurelius Valerius Romulus, of whom there is a coin inscribed *Divo Romulo n. v. filio*—that is, “son of our city.” There are also others reported by Tristan in his historical commentaries.

“Long purged by exhalations.” That is, long before cleansed of its foul breath.

“So completely did he himself,” etc. That is, he himself had so fully foreseen this in his mind.]

XVI. Thus one thing alone was now feared: lest he, alarmed by these forces, grievously distressed and reduced to straits, should choose the wiser course and postpone, by a siege, the punishments owed to the commonwealth. For, having exhausted all Africa—which he had resolved to destroy—and emptied all the islands, he had amassed provisions for an infinite period. But divine providence and the eternal majesty of the City herself took this counsel from the impious man, so that he suddenly burst forth from that inveterate stupor and those foulest hiding places and, after a six-year period [Col. 0665C] consumed in idleness, marked his own birthday by his final slaughter, lest he violate that sacred and religious number seven by entering upon it.

But how did this household slave, purple-clad for so many years, draw up his line? Precisely so that none could escape, none could—as often happens when displaced—retreat and renew the battle: pressed by weapons before him and the river Tiber behind him [Col. 0666A]. In this arrangement, by Hercules, he did not contemplate the necessity of resistance but the nearness of retreat. Unless perhaps, already sensing that his fated day had come, he wished, as consolation for his death, to draw as many as possible with him, so that all who had been accomplices in his crimes might be companions in his end. For what else are we to believe he hoped, when two days earlier he had already left the palace and voluntarily retired with his wife and son into a private house? Thus, shaken by terrible omens and driven out by nocturnal avengers, he made way for you, long awaited, to succeed as occupant of those sacred buildings after they had been purified and cleansed of their long-exhaled foulness. And so truly had he spoken to himself and yielded to your coming that, although he entered battle armed, by leaving [Col. 0666B] the palace he had already abdicated imperial power.

[Note: [Col. 0666C]

XVII.—“By the narrowness.” That is, because they could not all cross at once on account of the restricted space of the Milvian Bridge.

“Milvian Bridge.” A bridge over the Tiber near Rome, famous above all for Maxentius’ disaster.

“That banditry.” He calls that war banditry both because Maxentius’ army consisted of the lowest rabble and because Maxentius himself fought to seize another’s imperial power.

“The place which they had taken for battle.” An allusion to Sallust, *Catiline*: “Each man covered in death the place which he had taken while fighting alive.”

“Some end,” etc. That is, that the hands of your men, wearied with killing, might at last stop the slaughter.

“Lest so hideous.” That is, lest that so disgraceful monster obtain even this praise by the manner of its death: that, etc.

“Lest the joy of the people.” That is, lest their joy remain uncertain for a long time.]

XVII. Therefore, at the first sight of your majesty and the first assault of your entire victorious army, the enemy were terrified and routed. Shut out by the narrowness of the Milvian Bridge, all except the chief instigators of that banditry—who, despairing of pardon, covered with their bodies the position they had taken for battle—plunged headlong into the river, so that at last the Tiber’s swallowing of the impious might afford some curtailment of slaughter to the wearied right hands of your men. The Tiber likewise swallowed that very man, horse and splendid armour included, when he vainly attempted to escape over the steep bank on the farther side; it seized him in an eddy, lest so hideous a portent should leave even this report of his death: that he had fallen by the sword or missile of some brave man. The rushing river rolled away the bodies and arms of the other enemies [Col. 0666C]; but it held him at the very place where it had extinguished him, lest the joy of the Roman people should long remain uncertain if they believed he had escaped somewhere and sought proof of his death.

[Note: [Col. 0666D]

XVIII.—“Sacred Tiber.” *Aeneid*: “Father Tiber.”

“Aeneas’ adviser.” *Aeneid* VIII:

> The god himself of that place, Tiberinus of the pleasant river,  
> appeared to raise himself among the poplar leaves, an old man, etc.

[Col. 0667C] “Romulus’ preserver.” When Romulus and his brother Remus were cast into the overflowing river by Amulius’ command, the river-god Tiberinus restrained the waters lest they engulf both. But that episode is too well known to delay over. Florus, Victor, and others may be consulted.

“The false Romulus.” That is, Maxentius’ son, named Romulus, as stated above. Perhaps also Maxentius himself, whom the speaker jokingly calls a false Romulus, just as the author of the speech against Cicero attributed to Sallust calls Cicero “the Arpinate Romulus.” Lepidus in Sallust, *Histories* I, says of Sulla: “That savage Romulus holds all these things as though snatched from foreigners.”

“Nourisher by the conveyance of supplies.” Nourisher because it carries supplies; above, no. 7, note 5.

“Armed Cocles.” Horatius, called *Cocles* because he lost one eye in battle. When Porsenna, king of the Etruscans, tried to restore the Tarquins to the city, Horatius stood before the Sublician Bridge and alone held the enemy line until the bridge had been cut down. Then he himself leapt into the Tiber and swam, armed, back to his people [Col. 0667D]. Livy II; Florus I; Aurelius Victor.

“Cloelia.” When she was a captive in Porsenna’s camp, she deceived her guards, seized a horse supplied by chance, and crossed the Tiber by night. For the other reports concerning her, see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Livy, and Plutarch.

“Meanwhile.” That is, mockery was made meanwhile, as is customary in the joking of triumphs: the bearer was laughed at through an insult directed at the man whose punishment he was suffering.

“As triumphal jests are.” Dionysius VII notes this Roman custom of soldiers shouting, joking, and hurling witticisms at the triumphing commander: Ἐφεῖται γὰρ, etc. “For those conducting victors in procession are permitted to utter iambic verses and hurl jests at distinguished men, even at the commanders themselves, as at Athens those leading the procession in wagons used to attack bystanders with mockery.” Livy V says of Camillus: “The dictator, having recovered his fatherland from the enemy, returned in triumph to the City; amid the unpolished military jests customarily thrown out, he was called Romulus, father of his country, and second founder [Col. 0668C] of the City, not without reason.” Martial, I.4:

> Even your triumphs have been accustomed to endure jokes,  
> nor is a commander ashamed to be matter for witticisms, etc.]

XVIII. Sacred Tiber—once the adviser of your guest Aeneas [Col. 0667A], later preserver of the exposed Romulus—you did not permit either the false Romulus to live long or the parricide of the City to swim away. You, nourisher of your Rome by conveying supplies; you, defender by encircling its walls: rightly you wished to share in Constantine’s victory, so that he might drive the enemy into you and you might kill him. For you are not always swift and torrential, but measured according to the circumstances of the times. In your calmness you carried armed Cocles back. To your gentle waters the maiden Cloelia entrusted herself. But now, violent and turbulent, you swallowed the enemy of the commonwealth; and you did not betray your obedience to your shores by casting up his corpse.

When the body had therefore been found and mutilated, the whole Roman people blazed up in joy and vengeance. Throughout the entire City, wherever that expiatory head was carried fixed upon a spear, it did not cease to be dishonoured; while meanwhile, as triumphal jests are [Col. 0667B], the injury of its bearer was laughed at, as he endured what the crimes of another head deserved.

[Note: [Col. 0668C]

XIX.—“The very buildings.” A remarkable *hypotyposis*—vivid portrayal—of Constantine entering Rome after Maxentius’ defeat. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.8 and *Life of Constantine*.

“To withdraw from there.” Gruter conjectures that one should read “to climb up to the heights.”

“They recalled to mind how many people,” etc. That is, people marvelled that so many citizens still survived after that six-year slaughter.

“Spirits.” Or read, with Acidalius, *admirabundi* (“wondering”) for *animi* (“spirits”); or, with Lipsius shortly thereafter, *admirabantur* (“they marvelled”) for *memorabant* (“they recalled”).

“Six-year period.” During which Maxentius is said above to have held tyranny in Italy.

“The greatest orator.” Cicero, *Speech after His Return to the Senate*, no. 38: “When the Roman people recalled me, the commonwealth implored me, and all Italy almost carried me back to my fatherland on its shoulders.”

“Longed to bear [you] with their eyes.” Panegyric 6, no. 8: “At your first entry the people received you with such joy and such a crowd that they longed to bear you even with their eyes to the bosom of Capitoline Jupiter.”

“Days.” Such ceremonial entries were customarily celebrated with distributions, games, and spectacles.

“All rejoiced.” That is, they enjoyed the delay occasioned by the spectacles and favoured performers familiar to them solely because they competed in his presence.]

XIX. But why should I continue with these jesting matters? The very buildings, I hear, seemed to move, and the height of their roofs to rise, wherever your divine presence was borne in the slow movement of the chariot. Such a density of people, such a close escort of senators, simultaneously carried you forward and held you fast. Happy were those who saw you from nearer at hand; those farther away called out your name. Those whom you had passed regretted the place they had occupied. In turn, all withdrew from one place and followed from another. An innumerable multitude competed, surged with varied motion, and recalled how many people still survived after that slaughter of six years. Some even dared to ask you to stop [Col. 0668A], complaining that you had gone to the palace so quickly; and once you had entered, they not only followed you with their eyes but almost burst in upon the sacred threshold itself. Then, gathering around everywhere, they waited, looked out, wished, and hoped for you to come out from there—so that they seemed to besiege the man by whom they had been freed from siege.

Let the greatest orator have boasted, and truthfully, that he had been borne on Italy’s shoulders back to his fatherland: you, Constantine, were borne by Senate and Roman people both on that day and on all others when you went abroad, and they longed to bear you with their eyes. During the days of public gifts and sacred games, people could look upon nothing other than you yourself: the brightness of your eyes, the majesty spread over your whole body, the dignity of your face. All rejoiced in the delay of the shows and favoured performers familiar to them for this reason alone: that they competed in your presence [Col. 0668B].

[Note: [Col. 0668D]

XX.—“Safety.” That is, you did not wish them to regard the life you had saved for them as a benefit received from you.

“Happy through civil …” That is, blessed Rome because of its civil victory.

“Mad Cinna.” Lucius Cornelius Cinna, in his first consulship, proposed a law for recalling exiles. Prevented by his colleague Octavius and deprived of office, he fled the city. After summoning slaves to freedom and calling upon Gaius Marius, Carbo, and Sertorius, he entered the City, besieged and captured by four armies, in A.U.C. 667; he killed Octavius [Col. 0669C] and slaughtered his enemies. He made himself consul again and a third time. In his fourth consulship, while preparing war against Sulla, he was stoned by the army at Ancona because of excessive cruelty. Appian, *Civil Wars*; Plutarch, *Marius*; Aurelius Victor.

Marius enraged. After holding six consulships, defeating Jugurtha and leading him before his triumphal chariot, and subduing the Teutones in Gaul and the Cimbri in Italy, he was defeated by Sulla and would have perished after being thrown into prison, had he not deterred the Gaul sent to kill him by the authority of his countenance, and immediately fled to Africa. Returning from that exile to the City with Cinna and Sertorius, he filled everything with slaughter. Livy, Velleius, Victor, Plutarch, *Marius*.

Before the Colline Gate. The Colline Gate at Rome, so called from the town of Collatia, to which the road through that gate led. Festus.

Sulla. When, by the proposal of Sulpicius, his command was transferred to Marius, he returned to Italy and, having corrupted the armies of his opponents, drove Carbo from Italy; after gaining possession of the City, he killed Sulpicius, put Marius to flight, and posted lists of proscription. He slaughtered nine thousand surrendered men in the Villa Publica, in the year 672 A.U.C. Three years later, having laid down the dictatorship, he withdrew to Puteoli and died of the disease called phthiriasis. Appian, Plutarch, Aurelius Victor.]

XX. For why should I speak of your opinions and actions in the senate, by which you restored to the senate its former authority; did not claim credit from them for the safety they had recovered through you; and promised that its memory would remain forever in your heart? I should say more about your divine speeches, about kindness offered rather than obtained, if I did not prefer to be silent about words while I hasten to praise deeds. However well known to us may be the words you spoke in the senate, what manner of words they were has been proclaimed by the glory of your clemency. O Rome, at last fortunate in civil victory! Once frenzied Cinna and enraged Marius burst upon you. They were not satisfied with the head of the consul Octavius alone; after extinguishing the lights of the state, they left you examples which you have now endured for a full six years. Sulla again conquered for you before the Colline Gate—fortunate, had he avenged himself more sparingly; but in truth he filled the Rostra with many heads. Constantine set a limit to the licence of victory by the end of the battle: he did not permit swords to be drawn even against the blood of those whom men were demanding for punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0669D]

XXI.—“But also conqueror of his own victory.” This is taken from Cicero, *For Marcellus*, §12: “You seem to have conquered victory itself, when you remitted to the conquered the very things which it had gained.” Pacatus, *Panegyric on Theodosius*, §45: “Victor over victory itself, you so laid aside all wrath together with your arms.”

Against the barbarians. The Germans, against whom he set out in the following year after putting affairs in the City in order.

Forgetful of luxuries. Luxuries in which they had wallowed under the leadership of Maxentius.

The Theatre of Pompey. Gnaeus Pompey was the first of all to build a permanent theatre, as Tacitus says (*Annals* XIV.20), made of squared stone [Col. 0670C], after the model of that which he had seen at Mytilene during the Mithridatic War. It was in the form of a semicircle; at each extremity were stages, with separate altars, one of Bacchus and the other of the god in whose honour the games were held.

The renowned baths. The baths of Trajan, Titus, Agrippa, the Syrian Baths, those of Commodus, Severus, Antoninus, Alexander, Nero, and Diocletian were famous at Rome.

“Are extended.” Perhaps *praetendunt* (“they stretch themselves out”), as Livineius prefers. Pacatus, *Panegyric*, §10: “You had scarcely seen your Iberus, when you were already extending yourself toward the Ister,” that is, advancing; as *Aeneid* II.29: “Here fierce Achilles was advancing.”

“With the victors.” That is, they join them, about to fight alongside them against the common enemies, so that those conquered before in civil war may in wars against enemies show themselves in no way inferior to others.

From the Etruscan Albula. That is, the Tiber, according to Pliny: the most famous river of Etruria, flowing through Rome, so called from the whiteness of its waters. It says of itself in Ovid, *Fasti* V.645:

> Alcides came, attended by an Achaean throng.  
> Albula, if I remember, was then my name.

Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.332:

> It lost its true old name, Albula, etc.

] XXI. Sulla slaughtered in the Villa Publica a legion that had surrendered to him and been disarmed; and when the senate was appalled by the groans of the dying, he warned it not to be afraid, since he himself had given the order. But this conqueror, not only of his enemies but also of his own victory, preserved for you whatever soldiers survived the war. For they now serve you: men whom their commander, after stripping them of arms, armed again against barbarian enemies. Now forgetful of the luxuries of the Circus Maximus, the Theatre of Pompey [Col. 0669B], and the famous baths, they are stationed along the Rhine and Danube; they keep watch, suppress brigandage, and finally contend with the victors, so that men defeated in civil war may prove equal to enemies in war. Nor can this seem surprising, when by your example, Emperor, you make every sort of soldier most brave.

For, not wearied by battles and sated with victories, as nature requires, you have not given yourself to leisure and repose; rather, with the same impetus with which you had returned to your Gauls, you proceeded to the lower frontier of Germany. After an annual campaign, with, to be sure, a great interval of time and a short distance of place, you immediately inaugurated war, carrying the empire from the Tiber to the Rhine—or rather, that there may be an omen and resemblance of name, and as the greatness of your spirit, Emperor, promises, from the Etruscan Albula to the German Albis [Col. 0669C].

[Note: [Col. 0670D]

XXII.—“The earth rests.” That is: the ground rests during the fallow season.

“Rests by night.” That is: it rests through the nights.

“A fickle and slippery race.” Thus he calls the Franks, in order to flatter the Roman emperor, as I observed above.

“Chosen leaders for an incursion.” That is: word was brought that a mobile and deceitful nation had taken up position on the Rhine, having selected leaders for making an incursion.

“Also.” Read: “And now.”

“By a feigned report.” That is, pretending that news had been brought to you of a more serious uprising stirred up in the upper regions of the empire.]

[Col. 0670A] XXII. What is this unbroken ardour? What divinity ever vigorous in continual motion? All things have intervals. The earth rests in its fallow fields; rivers too, they say, sometimes stand still; and day itself rests by night. You alone, Constantine, indefatigable in wars, prolong wars and heap victories upon victories. As though past achievements were erased if you ceased, you do not think that you have conquered unless you are conquering.

The fickle and slippery nation of barbarians had broken faith; and it was reported that, with chosen instigators of an incursion distinguished for strength and boldness, they had taken up position on the Rhine. At once you were there to meet them, and by your presence frightened them from daring a crossing. And now you seemed to have acted contrary to your wishes, because, with the incursion checked, there would be no material for victory. But employing an unexpected plan—for by departing, under a feigned report of a greater disturbance on the upper frontier [Col. 0670B], you gave their foolish and bestial minds an opportunity to come into our territory—you left leaders concealed to attack them when off their guard. When they arrived, fortune followed your plan. With the whole channel of the Rhine filled with ships, you were conveyed downstream and ravaged their lands and homes, desolate and mourning; and you inflicted such slaughter and devastation upon the perjured nation that after that it will scarcely retain a name.

[Note: [Col. 0671C]

XXIII.—“The spectacle,” etc. That is: he increases the magnificence of the distributions from barbarian spoils.

“To be thrown to beasts.” Constantine in fact ordered the Frankish kings Regaisus and Ascaricus, captured in war, to be brought into the theatre at Trier to be torn apart by beasts; and in Panegyric 7, §12: “The grown men who fell into our hands, whose treachery fitted them neither for military service nor whose ferocity fitted them for slavery, were handed over to punishment as a spectacle and exhausted the raging beasts by their multitude.”

“To defer their end.” Perhaps *exitium*, “destruction,” that is, death.

“So lavish of themselves.” For none are equally to be feared in war as those who are unconcerned for their own safety.]

XXIII. Go now, all barbarian nations, if you please, and undertake designs fatal to yourselves: you have an example. For although our emperor accepts the services of friendly kings—and it itself contributes to the praise of victory that he is feared and honoured by the most noble kings—yet he rejoices whenever challenged that the glory of his valour may be increased. For what is finer than this triumph [Col. 0670C], which employs the slaughter of enemies even for the pleasure of us all [Col. 0671A], and heightens the splendour of public games from the remnants of barbarian ruin: so great a multitude of captives is thrown to beasts, so that the ungrateful and faithless suffer no less pain from the mockery made of them than from death itself? Hence it is that, although they may defer their end, they hasten to perish and offer themselves to mortal wounds and death. From this very fact it appears how great an achievement it is to have conquered men so prodigal of themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0671D]

XXIV.—“Scarcely a light cloak.” Pacatus took this passage from Panegyric §33: “Those shining through their thin clothing and scarcely enduring a light linen garment while avoiding the sun,” that is, in order to avoid the sun.

“Whomever and whatever kind.” Perhaps *quem qualemcumque*, as Livineius conjectures: that is, whatever sort of man he may be, military discipline both makes him brave and gives him order.

“The fierce Frank.” By whom the Romans had often been badly treated.

“For the cheapness of his food,” etc. That is, they are reared in so mean a fashion.

“In Italy.” After the defeat of Maxentius’s men.

“In sight of barbarism.” On the German frontier.

[Col. 0672C] “Your father.” Constantius.

“From recent times.” Such as Numerian, Carinus, Carus, Probus, Florianus, Tacitus, and the other emperors of that age in succession, not much more illustrious.]

XXIV. It is easy to conquer the timid and unwarlike, such as pleasant Greece and the luxuries of the East rear: men who scarcely endure a light cloak and silken folds while avoiding the sun, and who, if they ever come into danger, forgetful of liberty, pray that they may be allowed to serve. But how great a task it is to overcome or capture a Roman soldier—whatever sort military discipline orders, and the sanctity of his oath strengthens—or a fierce Frank, swollen only with wild flesh, who despises life because of the cheapness of his fare! Yet this, Emperor, you did recently in Italy and a little earlier in the very sight of barbarism.

Thus, without any distinction, every kind of war, arms, and enemies yields to you alone; even the written memorials of valour from all recorded memory yield. Nor have you surpassed only those ancient achievements of dictators, consuls, and subsequently great emperors; you have also surpassed the most upright and beautiful deeds of your deified father. For it is beneath the occasion to compare others from recent times: I mean that you have already, in the first five-year periods of your reign, surpassed in the glory of deeds even the deified Constantius himself.

[Note: [Col. 0672C]

XXV.—“Unwilling.” That is: perhaps you hear this unwillingly.

“Long ago.” Seven years earlier, namely in A.D. 306.

“From the furthest barbarism.” He subdued the Franks, who had rebelled against the treaty made with his father.

“The islands of the African sea.” Perhaps Sardinia and Sicily, where we read that Maxentius committed depredations. He calls the Mediterranean Sea, in which they lie, “African” because of its proximity to Africa.

“Africa.” There survives a coin: *SALVIS AVGG. ET CAES. FEL. KARTH.* That is, “With the Augusti and Caesars safe: Fortunate Carthage.”]

XXV. Perhaps, Emperor, you receive this unwillingly; but while we speak, he rejoices in heaven, and, called long ago to the stars, still grows in his son and ascends by the steps of your glories. He cleared Batavia by driving out the foreign enemy; native peoples surrendered themselves to you from the furthest barbarism. He crossed Ocean by fleet; you crossed the Alps on foot and seized Italian harbours with fleets. He recovered Britain; you, the most noble islands of the African sea, which had been provinces of the Roman people. May the deified Constantius himself forgive me: what have I that I can compare with Italy, Africa, Rome?

Rightly, therefore, Constantine, the senate recently gave you an image of a god, and Italy shortly before dedicated a shield and crown, all of gold, that they might in some measure relieve the debt of gratitude. For to divinity is due also a golden image; to valour, a shield; and to piety, a crown.

[Note: [Col. 0672D]

XXVI.—“As many names as the languages of peoples.” For it is well known that among different peoples not only Jupiter but individual gods have different names.

“You are mingled with the elements.” He alludes to *Aeneid* VI.726:

> A Mind, poured through all its limbs,  
> sets the whole mass in motion and mingles itself with the great body.

“Your offspring.” Constantine, whom he had already begotten by Fausta, daughter of Maximian.]

XXVI. Therefore, highest creator of things, whose names are as many as you have willed there to be languages of peoples—for we cannot know by what name you yourself wish to be called—whether you are a certain divine power and mind, poured throughout the whole world so as to be mingled with all its elements, and moving yourself through yourself without any impulse of force coming from outside; or whether you are some power above all heaven, looking down upon this work of yours from a higher citadel of nature: you, I say, we pray and beseech to preserve this prince through all ages. For it is too little to wish for so great a valour and so great a piety one whom life allows so long a course.

Surely there is in you supreme goodness, and piety also; and therefore you ought to will what is just. Nor is there any reason for refusal when you can grant it. For if there is anything withheld by you from those who deserve well, either power has failed or goodness. Grant, therefore, that what you have given as best to humankind may remain forever, and that Constantine may live out every age upon earth. Although, invincible Emperor, your divine offspring has already succeeded to the hopes of the commonwealth, and is still expected to become more numerous, that posterity will nevertheless be truly blessed when, having brought your children to the helm of the world, you are the greatest emperor of all.

[VARIOUS WORKS.]

[Col. 0673]

ANCIENT DOCUMENTS RELATING TO THE HISTORY OF THE DONATISTS, FROM A.D. 303 TO A.D. 350. (C, S)

A.D. 303.

The origin of the Donatist schism. [Note: [Col. 0673C] (1) From Saint Augustine, vol. IX, col. 774.]

[Col. 0673A]

First hear who the *traditores* were, and learn more fully who were the authors of the schism. It is agreed that in Africa two evils, and the worst possible evils, were committed: one in the handing over [of sacred books], the other in schism; yet both evils seem to have been committed at one and the same time and by the same authors. You must therefore learn, brother Parmenianus, what you are understood not to know.

For about sixty years ago and more, the storm of persecution spread throughout all Africa. It made some martyrs and others confessors; it struck down some in a baleful death [Note: [Col. 0673C] (2) The old Germanensis codex: “struck down in a baleful death.”], while leaving those who lay hidden unharmed. Why should I mention the laypeople, who then held no rank in the Church [Note: [Col. 0673C] (3) The word *suffulti*, “supported,” is absent from the Germanensis codex.]? Why the many ministers? Why deacons in the third, or presbyters established in the second priesthood? The very peaks and leaders of all, certain bishops of that time, in order to exchange the brief delays of this uncertain light for the loss of eternal life, impiously handed over the instruments of the divine law.

Among them were Donatus of Masculita, Victor of Rusiccada, Marinus of Aquae Tibiltinae, Donatus of Calama, and the murderer Purpurius of Limata [Note: [Col. 0673C] (4) In the same manuscript, “of Liniata.”]. When questioned about his sister’s sons—because he was said to have killed them in prison at Milevum—he confessed, saying: “I killed, and I kill—not them alone, but whoever acts against me.” [Note: [Col. 0673C] (5) From Optatus, book I, revised and corrected according to the old Germanensis codex.] Also Menalus [Note: [Col. 0673C] (6) “Menalius” in the Germanensis manuscript. See Constantine’s letter [Col. 0673D] to Celsus.], who, lest he should be proved by his fellow citizens to have burned incense, tremblingly avoided appearing before his colleagues by feigning an ailment of the eyes.

These men and the others, whom we shall shortly show to have been your leaders, after the persecution [Col. 0673C] assembled at the city of Cirta—because the basilicas had not yet been restored—in the house of Urbanus Carisius on the third day before the Ides of May, as the writings of Nundinarius, then a deacon, testify [Note: [Col. 0673D] (8) See the proceedings before Zenophilus, consular governor.], and as the antiquity of the parchments bears witness; these parchments we shall be able to produce for doubters. We have appended their full text [Note: [Col. 0673D] (9) In printed editions of Optatus, *rerum* (“of the matters”) is added. It is absent from the Germanensis [Col. 0674C] codex, so that “of the parchments” is to be understood.] at the end of these little books [Col. 0674A], to establish the facts.

When Secundus of Tigisis questioned them, these bishops confessed that they had handed things over. And when Secundus himself was reproached by Purpurius because he too had long been with the police officers [Note: [Col. 0674C] (1) Germanensis manuscript: “with the police officer,” singular.], had not fled, but had been released—and, it was said, had not been released without reason, unless because he had handed things over—all rose and began to murmur [Note: [Col. 0674D] (2) Printed editions: “all the heretics.” Corrected from the Germanensis manuscript.]. Secundus, fearing their spirit, took counsel from his nephew, the younger Secundus, that he should reserve such a case for God. Those who remained were consulted: Victor of Garba, Felix of Rotarium, and Nabor of Centurion [Note: [Col. 0674D] (3) Germanensis manuscript: “Victor of Gabra, Felix of Rotarium, and Nabor of Centurionis.”]. They said that such a case ought to be reserved for God. Secundus said, “Sit down, all of you”; then all said, “Thanks be to God,” and they sat down.

You have, therefore, brother Parmenianus, those who were manifestly *traditores*. Then, not long afterward [Col. 0674B], these same *traditores*—so many and such men, incense-burners [Note: [Col. 0674D] (4) Printed editions: “conspirators.” More aptly the Germanensis manuscript: *thurati*, or “incense-burners.”], murderers—went to Carthage and ordained Majorinus, whose chair you occupy, after the ordination of Caecilianus, thereby making a schism. Since it has been shown that your leaders were guilty of handing things over, it will follow that they were also the authors of schism.

That the matter may be plain and manifest to all, it must be shown from what root the branches of error have extended themselves down to the present day, and from what spring this little stream of malignant liquid, creeping secretly, has flowed down to our times. It must be said whence, where, and by whom this second evil is known to have arisen; what causes came together, what persons acted, who were the authors of this evil, and who nourished it; by whom judgments were sought from the emperor between the parties [Col. 0674C], who sat as judges, where the council was held, and what sentences were delivered.

The issue is division. In Africa, as in the other provinces, there was one Church before it was divided by the ordainers of Majorinus, whose hereditary chair you occupy. It must be seen who remained at the root with the whole world, who went outside, who occupied another chair which had not existed before, who raised altar against altar, who performed an ordination while the other ordinand remained in place, and who lies under the sentence of the Apostle John, who said that many antichrists would go out: “They were not ours,” he says, “for if they had been ours, they would have remained with us” (1 John 2:18–19). Therefore, whoever refused to remain in unity with the brethren, following heretics, went out as an antichrist.

No one is unaware that this took place at Carthage after the ordination of Caecilianus, namely through some Lucilla, a factious woman. Before the peace, shaken by the storms of persecution, while the Church was still tranquil, she could not endure the rebuke of Caecilianus, then archdeacon. Before receiving spiritual food and drink, she was said to kiss the mouth of some martyr—if indeed he was a martyr. And because she preferred to the saving cup the mouth of some dead man, even if a martyr, yet not as yet vindicated, she was rebuked and departed in anger and disgrace.

To this angry and grieving woman, lest she submit to discipline, the suddenly arising storm of persecution came to her aid [Col. 0675B]. At the same time, a certain deacon Felix, who had been accused on account of some notorious letter, I know not what, then written about the tyrant-emperor, is said, fearing danger, to have hidden with Bishop Mensurius. When Mensurius publicly denied that Felix, who had been demanded, was with him, a report was sent. A rescript came back ordering that, if Mensurius did not surrender Deacon Felix, he should be sent to the imperial court.

He was undergoing no slight pressure. For the churches possessed very many ornaments of gold and silver, which he could neither bury in the ground nor take with him. He entrusted them, as if to faithful elders, drawing up an inventory which, it is said, he gave to an old woman, on the condition that, if he himself did not return after peace had been restored to the Christians, the old woman should give them back to whomever she found sitting in the episcopal chair [Col. 0675C]. He departed, stated his case, and was ordered to return; but he could not reach Carthage.

The storm of persecution was completed and ended. By God’s command, and through the indulgence granted by Maxentius, liberty was restored to Christians. Botrus and Celesius [Note: [Col. 0675D] (1) The old Germanensis codex consistently has “Coelestius”; likewise Augustine himself in the alphabetical psalm against the Donatists.], wishing, it is said, to be ordained at Carthage, took pains that, in the absence of the Numidians, only neighbouring bishops should be sought to perform the ordination at Carthage. Then Caecilianus was elected by the vote of all the people and, with Bishop Felix of Aptunga laying hands upon him, was ordained bishop. Botrus and Celesius were cast down from their hope.

Then the schedule of gold and silver [Note: [Col. 0675D] (2) Something appears to be lacking here.] was handed over to Caecilianus as he sat, according to Mensurius’s instruction, witnesses being present. The aforementioned elders were summoned; they had swallowed the entrusted treasure down the throat of avarice [Col. 0675D]. When compelled to restore it, they withdrew themselves from communion [Note: [Col. 0675D] (3) Thus the Germanensis manuscript. Printed editions: “they withdrew the people from communion,” less correctly, since he will shortly say that the entire civic population was gathered with Caecilianus against the schismatic Donatists.]. So too did the office-seekers, to whom ordination had not fallen; likewise Lucilla, who had long been unable to bear discipline. With all her household, a powerful and factious woman, she refused to join the communion. Thus, by the concurrence of three causes and persons, wickedness achieved its effect [Col. 0676A]. The schism, therefore, was produced at that time by the anger of an affronted woman; ambition nourished it; avarice strengthened it.

From these three persons accusations were fabricated against Caecilianus, so that his ordination might be called defective. A message was sent to Secundus of Tigisis [Note: [Col. 0676D] (1) The Germanensis manuscript reads: “it was written.”] that he should come to Carthage. All the aforementioned *traditores* set out; they were received as guests by the avaricious, the ambitious, and the angry—not by the Catholics, at whose request Caecilianus had been ordained. Meanwhile, none of those mentioned above approached the basilica where the whole civic multitude had been gathered with Caecilianus [Note: [Col. 0676D] (2) Thus the Germanensis manuscript. Printed editions: “the whole city was present in the crowd.”].

Then Caecilianus sent word: “If there is anything that can be proved against me, let an accuser come forth and prove it.” At that time nothing could be fabricated against him by so many enemies; but he deserved to be defamed concerning his ordainer, because that ordainer was falsely called a *traditor* by them [Col. 0676B]. Caecilianus again sent word that, if Felix had conferred nothing upon him, as they thought, they themselves should ordain Caecilianus as though he were still a deacon. Then Purpurius, relying on his customary malice, spoke as though Caecilianus were his sister’s son: “Let him come out here, as if a hand were to be laid upon him for the episcopate, and let his head be shaken in penance.”

When these things became known, the whole Church held Caecilianus back, lest he surrender himself to brigands. At that time either a guilty man ought to have been expelled, or an innocent man ought to have remained in communion. The Church was crowded with people; the episcopal chair was occupied; the altar stood in its place, the altar on which, in former times, peaceful bishops had offered—Cyprian, Carpophorus [Note: [Col. 0676D] (3) “Carpophorus” is added from the Germanensis manuscript; it had been omitted in the printed editions.], Lucianus, and the rest.

Thus they went out, altar was raised against altar, an unlawful ordination was performed [Col. 0676C], and Majorinus—who had been a reader in Caecilianus’s diaconate and a member of Lucilla’s household—was ordained bishop through her support by the *traditores* who, in the council of Numidia, as we said above, confessed their crimes to one another and granted one another indulgence. It is therefore manifest that both the ordainers who handed things over and Majorinus, who was ordained, went out from the Church.

Meanwhile, from the fountain of their own crimes, which among them had overflowed from veins of many wicked deeds, they thought that a single charge of handing things over should be diverted onto Caecilianus’s ordainer. Foreseeing that public report could not speak of two similar matters at the same time, they tried to consign their own crimes to silence by defaming another’s life. Though they themselves could have been accused by the innocent, they strove to accuse the innocent, sending everywhere letters written at envy’s dictation, which we retain among the other documents for future use [Col. 0676D]. While still at Carthage, they went before themselves with their letters, so that false reports might implant their lie in everyone’s ears and spread rumour among the people. And while falsehoods about one man were publicized, the wholly true crimes of those mentioned above lay concealed in silence.

Men often blush for a crime; but at that time there was no one before whom they could blush, because, apart from a few Catholics, everyone had sinned [Col. 0677A], and a crime committed among many was, as it were, an image of innocence [Note: [Col. 0677A] (1) Printed editions: “and because it was an image.” Corrected from the Germanensis manuscript.]. The crime of handing things over, known to have been committed by Donatus of Masculita and the others named above, was not enough: they also joined to it the enormous outrage of schism. You see, therefore, Parmenianus, that these two crimes, so evil and so grave—handing things over and schism—belong to your leaders.

Petition of the bishops of Majorinus’s party to Constantine.

[Col. 0678A]

We beseech you, O Constantine, best of emperors: because you are of a righteous stock, whose father, among the other emperors, did not carry out persecution, and Gaul is free from this crime. For there are disputes in Africa between us and the other bishops. We ask that Your Piety command judges to be given us from Gaul. Submitted by Lucianus, Dignus, Nasutius, Capito, Fidentius, and the other bishops of Donatus’s party.

TEXT OF THE EDICT ISSUED AND PROMULGATED AGAINST CHRISTIANS BY DIOCLETIAN AND MAXIMIAN.

(See Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, vol. VII, chapters 12 and 13, cols. 213–214, and Baluze’s notes on those chapters, cols. 316–317 of the same volume.)

TEXT OF THE SAME EDICT.

(From Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 2.) On the destruction of churches. [Note: [Col. 0677] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0677B] All these things were fulfilled in our own times, when we saw with our own eyes houses of prayer cast down from their height to the ground, together with their very foundations, and the sacred and divinely inspired books consigned to fire in the middle of marketplaces; when we saw the shepherds of churches, some shamefully hiding themselves here and there, others disgracefully seized and exposed to the mockery of enemies. Then, as another prophetic utterance had foretold, “contempt was poured out upon their rulers, and he caused them to wander in a trackless waste, not in a way” (Psalm 106 [107]).

But I judge it impious to recount in speech the grievous calamities that befell them at the end, since it is not fitting for us even to commit to memory the dissensions and outrages by which they contended mutually with one another before the persecution. Therefore [Col. 0677C] we have resolved to relate of them only those things by which we may perceive the equity of divine judgment. Accordingly, I have decided to make no mention either of those shaken by the persecution or of those who made utter shipwreck of their salvation and, of their own accord, plunged themselves into the abyss of the waters’ deep. I shall henceforth put into this universal history only those things which may be useful first to myself and then to those who come after us.

Let us therefore begin from this point to set down, in summary, the sacred contests of the witnesses to the divine word. It was the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, in the month of Dystrus—called March by the Romans—when the feast of the Saviour’s Passion was approaching, that imperial edicts were posted everywhere. They commanded that churches be razed to the ground [Col. 0677D], sacred codices consumed by fire, persons of rank marked with infamy, and household servants deprived of liberty if they persevered in their profession of Christian faith. Such was the first edict against us. But not long afterward other letters arrived, commanding that all presidents of churches, everywhere, first be committed to chains and then by every means compelled to sacrifice to the gods.

[Col. 0678B] Thus all these things were fulfilled among us, when we ourselves saw with our own eyes the houses of prayer cast down from their height to the ground, together with their very foundations; the divinely inspired and sacred Scriptures given over to fire in the midst of marketplaces; the shepherds of the churches shamefully hiding themselves here and there; and others disgracefully captured and mocked by their enemies. Then also, according to another prophetic saying, “contempt was poured out upon their rulers, and he caused them to wander in a pathless place, not a way.”

But it is not our task to record their grievous calamities at the end; since it is not fitting for us to commit to memory even their former dissensions and absurdities against one another before the persecution. Therefore we resolved to relate nothing further about them except what might vindicate the divine judgment. Accordingly [Col. 0678C], we were not moved to make mention either of those tested by persecution or of those who utterly made shipwreck of salvation and, by their own decision, cast themselves into the depths of the storm. We shall add to the universal history only those things that may be useful first to ourselves and then to those after us.

Let us now proceed from here to describe briefly the sacred struggles of the witnesses of the divine Word. This was the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign: the month was Dystrus, called March by the Romans. As the feast of the Saviour’s Passion approached, imperial letters were published everywhere, commanding churches to be brought to the ground and the Scriptures to be destroyed by fire; declaring that persons holding rank should be made dishonoured, and those in household servitude deprived of freedom if they persisted in their profession of Christianity [Col. 0678D]. Such was the first document against us. But, shortly thereafter, other letters arrived, ordering that all presidents of churches in every place should first be handed over to bonds and then, afterward, compelled by every device to sacrifice.

A.D. 304.

EXECUTION OF THE PRECEDING EDICT IN AFRICA.

[Col. 0679A]

ACTS OF SAINT FELIX, BISHOP.

(From Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. II, p. 77.)

BALUZE’S NOTICE ON THE ACTS OF SAINT FELIX, BISHOP OF TUBYZACA.

Surius was the first to publish these Acts, but in a very corrupt and mutilated form. Later, the most distinguished Lucas D’Achery gave us a fuller text in the twelfth volume of his *Spicilegium*, from the papers—as he himself states—of the equally distinguished Pierre-François Chifflet. We carefully compared it [Col. 0679B] with four ancient and excellent manuscripts in the Colbert Library and added it here for that reason as well.

Moreover, since from this text—as also from the history of the passion of Saints Saturninus and Dativus, and from the proceedings of the purification of Felix, bishop of Aptunga, and Caecilianus of Carthage—we understand that the origin of the *traditores*, a name than which none was more common or more insulting in the African Church, is to be sought from the beginning of the persecution described by Lactantius, we judged it our duty to join to that account such genuine ancient documents of that age as could be found, corrected in accordance with the evidence of ancient copies.

[Note: [Col. 0679C]

“The passion begins.” Thus codices 59 and 930 of the Colbert Library. But codex 401 reads: “The passion of Saint Felix, bishop of Bituzaca, begins, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January.” Codex 316 is briefer: “The Passion of Saint Felix, Bishop.”

“Diocletian consul for the eighth time.” Thus all ancient copies and D’Achery’s edition correctly read. Incorrectly in Surius, where it is written: “Diocletian consul for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth.” For it is certain that the edict was posted in the year when Diocletian and Maximian were consuls for the eighth and seventh times respectively.

“Then.” That is, when Diocletian and Maximian were consuls for the ninth and eighth times. These events must be assigned to the year following the beginning of the persecution, since these Acts took place at Carthage [Col. 0679D] and in Africa in January.

“Tubyzacan.” Thus codices 59 and 930. But codex 401 has *Tubizocense*; codex 316 and D’Achery’s edition, *Tubzocense*. I pay no attention to Surius’s edition, which the agreement of so many ancient copies proves corrupt at this point. This city is called *Tupuza* for *Tubyza* in codex 930, without distinction; interchange of letters is well known.

I think Tubysa was a city of Numidia, perhaps the one whose bishop Frumentius, called Tubusicensis—as Abraham Ortelius found the reading in Victor of Vita—appears among the bishops who came to Carthage by royal command to give an account of their faith in the sixth year of Huneric, king of the Vandals. But the editions of Sirmond and Chifflet read *Tubursicensis*. Moreover, in the first Conference of Carthage, chapter 121, mention is made of Bura, servant of God and bishop of Turbursica; in chapter 142, Maurentius, bishop of the church of Tubursica; and in chapter 202 [Col. 0680C], Januarius, bishop of Tubursicu, or Tubursico, in Numidia.

Certainly the difficulty of establishing the true names of African cities, owing to their mutual similarity and affinity, is so great that I would not venture to affirm whether Victor should here read *Tubusicensis*, as Ortelius saw in his manuscript, or *Tubursicensis*, as others have it. For example, in that list of African bishops Rusticus, bishop of Tipasa, is named among the bishops of Numidia, while Reparatus of Tipasa is named among the bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis. Again, among the bishops of Byzacena is placed Felix of Forontonia, and shortly afterward Boniface of Frontonia. These examples [Col. 0680D] suffice. Meanwhile it should not be omitted that, in the same Conference of Carthage, chapter 187, Martinianus is named as bishop of the place Tibuzabeta.

“Magnilianus.” Thus it is consistently written in the old books of the Colbert Library. Ado and D’Achery’s edition have *Magnellianus*; Surius’s edition and the Roman Martyrology, *Magdellianus*.

“Where is?” This entire passage, not found in codices 401 and 930, is presented by codices 59 and 316 and by D’Achery’s edition. Surius’s edition also has it.

“Hand them over to be burned by fire.” That this command of Magnilianus the curator and the martyrs’ reply were absent from Chifflet’s old copy can be inferred from their omission in D’Achery’s edition. Yet all our old copies, except 316, and Surius’s edition contain them. Indeed, the sense is plainly incomplete in the copies which lack that pronouncement of the magistrate and the clerics’ reply.

[Col. 0681C] **“In his Acts.”** This is the true and genuine reading. Incorrectly in codices 59, 401, and 930: “with him in the act.”

**“At the examination.”** Thus codices 401 and 930. The others have “at the examination” (*examinatione*).

**“Then he addressed his own men.”** It is astonishing how a most corrupt reading could have crept in here in codices 59, 401, and 930, where one reads: “And so his wife addressed her husband with these words.”

**“By no means.”** In these same three codices it is written, “on no account.”

[Col. 0681D] **“That by you, Lord.”** This is the reading of those same three ancient exemplars.
