But codex 316 and the Dacherian edition have: “Attend, Lord, as you have deigned to promise us, that I may deserve to receive immortality with you.” We have retained the reading which seems more genuine and which rests upon the authority of a greater number of ancient exemplars.

**“Never against me.”** Here too we have followed the authority of the ancient books. For Dacher’s edition has: “the enemy shall never have power against me.”

**“Sixteen.”** Colbert codex 401 has “twelve.”

**“I did not ask you about the designation.”** In four ancient Colbert codices one reads: “I did not seek from you the designation of your profession.”

**“To the prefect of the praetory.”** The Surian edition adds “on the Ides of July” [Col. 0682C]—quite absurdly. For since these matters were taking place in January, it is ridiculous to say that the martyr was sent to the prefect of the praetory on the Ides of July. Nor indeed could this have fallen even on the Ides of February. Felix the bishop was arrested on the day after the Nones of January; then, having been kept in prison for three days so that he might deliberate with himself whether he would surrender the divine Scriptures, he was sent on the fourth day to the proconsul; sixteen days after he had arrived at Carthage he was brought before the proconsul, and then sent to Rome to the prefect [Col. 0682D] of the praetory. This makes twenty-one days. Add several days for the journey from Tubyza to Carthage. Felix was therefore sent to Rome toward the end of January.

**“Twelve.”** Thus the four exemplars in the Colbert Library. The Dacherian edition has “fourteen”; the Surian, “nine.”

**“After the emperors.”** That is, to Maximian Herculius, who held Italy, and who is therefore certainly known to have been in Campania at that time.

**“Subsanium.”** Thus three ancient exemplars. The fourth has *subsannium*; the Dacherian edition, *subsanno*. Surius: “and he was in the chest of the ship for four days.” From this it is clear that by *subsanium* or *subsannium* one must understand the lowest part of a ship.

[Col. 0683D] **“I order him to be punished with the sword.”** That passage troubles me. For above, the prefect sent Felix to Herculius, plainly so that Felix’s case might receive its conclusion in the emperor’s presence. Yet the investigator of the city of Nola arrogates judgment to himself and orders Felix to be executed. But this must be understood as meaning that the investigator undertook to judge this case in accordance with an order, as is said below—that is, by delegation from Maximian, who was then present.

**“Unconquered and abiding.”** Thus three ancient Colbert codices. The fourth has, “living, you remain”; Dacher’s edition, “living and abiding.”

[Col. 0684D] **“At Nola.”** Surius’s edition teaches that these events took place at Venusia, a city in Apulia.

**“On the eighteenth.”** This is the reading of three ancient exemplars. In the fourth and in Dacher’s edition one reads “on the nineteenth”; in Surius, “on the third day before the Kalends of September.” But in the ancient martyrologies the passion of Saint Felix is assigned to the ninth day before the Kalends of November.

**“To noble Carthage.”** These words have been added from the manuscript codices. It is an epithet of the city of Carthage, as is also clear from the Acts of the Conference of Carthage between Catholics and Donatists. Elsewhere it is called “most splendid,” as in the acts of the vindication of Felix of Aptunga, and “most exalted,” as in the acts of the Conference of Carthage.]

## The Passion of Saint Felix, Bishop of Tub[y]za, who was beheaded for the law of the Lord, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, begins.

[Col. 0679C] In those days, when Diocletian was consul for the eighth time and Maximian [Col. 0680A] for the seventh, the Augusti, an edict of these same Caesars or emperors went forth over the whole face of the earth. It was posted throughout the colonies and cities for the governors and magistrates, each in his own place, that they should extort the divine books from the hands of bishops and presbyters.

Then a public proclamation was posted in the city of Tub[y]za on the day of the Nones of January. Then Magnilianus, curator of that city, ordered the presbyters to be brought before him. Because Bishop Felix had gone to Carthage, he ordered the presbyter Januarius and the readers Fortunatus and Septiminus to be brought before him.

Magnilianus the curator said to them: “Do you have a bishop?”

The presbyter Januarius replied: “We do.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “Where is he?”

The presbyter Januarius replied: “I do not know.”

Magnilianus said: “Do you have the divine books?”

[Col. 0680B] Januarius replied: “We do.”

Magnilianus said: “Hand them over to be burned by fire.”

The presbyter Januarius and the readers Fortunatus and Septiminus said: “Our bishop has them with him.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “You shall therefore remain under official custody until you render an account to Anulinus the proconsul.”

But on the following day Bishop Felix came from Carthage to Tubyza. When Magnilianus learned of his arrival, he immediately ordered him to be presented before him by the officials. When he arrived with greater speed than words could tell, Magnilianus the curator said to him: “Are you Felix, bishop of this city?”

Bishop Felix said: “I am.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “Give up the books, or whatever parchments you have in your possession.”

Bishop Felix said: “I have them, but I do not surrender the law of the Lord my God, whom I worship.”

Magnilianus said: “Then [Col. 0680C] is your God greater than our gods?”

Bishop Felix said: “Great and fearful is our God, [Col. 0681A] who made heaven and earth, the sea and everything in them. For your gods are stones, made by human hands, concerning whom it is written: ‘They have eyes and shall not see; they have ears and shall not hear; they have a mouth and shall not speak. May those who make them become like them, and all who put their trust in them.’”

Magnilianus the curator said: “What the emperors have commanded comes first; what you say amounts to nothing. Therefore hand over all the books you have, so that they may be burned by fire, as has been decreed.”

Bishop Felix said: “It is better that I surrender my body to the fire than that the Scriptures of the Lord should be seen to be burned through me; for it is good to obey God, the eternal and immortal king, rather than the emperor of this age when he commands what is unjust.”

Magnilianus said: “I have already told you that what the emperors have commanded comes first, rather than the things you say.”

[Col. 0681B] Bishop Felix said: “The command of God is to be kept before obedience to men.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “Meanwhile, reflect with yourself during these three days; for if you neglect to carry out in this your own city what has been commanded, you shall go to the proconsul, and before his official records you shall pursue the things you now say.”

But after the third day Magnilianus the curator ordered holy Bishop Felix to be presented before him. When Bishop Felix had been brought before him, Magnilianus said: “Have you considered with yourself what better course you seem able to adopt?”

Felix said: “My word is one: where it began, there too, with God as my guide, it shall end. For the things I spoke at first, those same things I now say; and before the proconsul I shall say nothing whatever different.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “You shall therefore now go [Col. 0681C] to the proconsul, and there you will render an account at the examination.”

Then he addressed his own men with these words: “Since Bishop Felix has by no means hastened to do, in accordance with the decrees of the emperors, those things which they have deigned to command us, let him be conducted to Carthage with you accompanying him.”

Bishop Felix said: “Thanks be to God.”

Then Vincentius, a decurion of the city of Tub[y]za, was appointed to escort him. Bishop Felix set out [Col. 0682A] for Carthage. When he arrived there, he was brought before the legate of the proconsul.

The same legate said to him: “Why do you not surrender the superfluous Scriptures?”

Bishop Felix said: “I do indeed have them, but I do not give them up. The Scriptures which we possess are not superfluous, nor can they by any means be surrendered by us.”

Then the legate ordered him to be placed in the lowest part of the prison. When Bishop Felix entered it, he prayed to the Lord his God, saying:

“Lord God, creator and maker of all things, Lord Jesus Christ, do not abandon me, because I suffer these things for your sake and for the sake of your testament. Have mercy on me; receive my spirit; and leave my mortal body in this world, so that by you, Lord, as you have deigned to promise, I may deserve to receive immortality with you. For while I live always in you, Lord, [Col. 0682B] death shall never have power against me.”

After sixteen days, at the fourth hour of the night, Bishop Felix was brought out of prison and immediately presented to the sight of Anulinus the proconsul.

Anulinus the proconsul said to him: “What is your name?”

Bishop Felix said: “I am a Christian.”

Anulinus the proconsul said: “I did not ask you about the designation of your profession, but I asked by what name you are called.”

Bishop Felix said: “As I have already told you, so now I say again: I am a Christian and a bishop.”

Then Anulinus the proconsul, angered because he would not tell him his name, said to him: “Do you have superfluous Scriptures?”

Bishop Felix said: “I have Scriptures; but they are not, as you assert, superfluous. Know that I shall by no means surrender them.”

Then Anulinus the proconsul sent him [Col. 0682C] to Rome to the prefect of the praetory. When Bishop Felix had arrived there and had been presented to that prefect, he ordered him to be received into prison and bound with heavier chains.

But after twelve days the prefect of the praetory ordered him to sail after the emperors. Then Bishop Felix boarded a ship, bound in the harsh fetters of chains, and lay in the *subsanium*—the lowest part—of the ship for four days and four nights, beneath the feet of horses, [Col. 0683A] eating no bread and drinking no water at all. He arrived at Nola fasting.

Then the investigator of that city ordered the arriving Bishop Felix to be presented before him, bound with still heavier chains. The investigator said to him: “Felix, how did you come here?”

Bishop Felix said: “As God willed.”

The investigator said: “If in your own city or at Carthage you had surrendered the divine Scriptures, you would never have come here to me.”

Bishop Felix said: “I do indeed have the divine Scriptures; but, as you well know that I have answered various questioners, so now too, being present before you, I make most certainly plain that I do not surrender them in any way.”

The investigator said: “If you refuse to surrender the divine Scriptures, you will be punished by beheading.”

Bishop Felix said: “I am more ready to be beheaded than sacrilegiously to surrender the books [Col. 0683B] of the Lord.”

Then the said investigator ordered the imperial mandates to be read aloud. When the decrees had been read by Vincentius the clerk, the investigator said: “Since this man has persisted so greatly in that same confession, in accordance with the command I order this same Bishop Felix to be punished with the sword.”

Bishop Felix, raising his eyes to heaven, said:

> “God, I give you thanks, because for fifty-six years in this world you have deigned to preserve my virginity within me. Lord God of heaven and earth, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, for your sake, for the sake of your law, and in fear of you I suffer this, and I bend my neck for the sacrifice. Receive my spirit from this mortal world. For you alone are the living God, unconquered, abiding, [Col. 0683C] glorious for everlasting ages of ages. Amen.”

When this prayer had been completed, he was led away by soldiers and beheaded there—that is, at Nola—on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February. There at Nola his body was laid, and his relics were conveyed by devout servants of God and sons of Mother Church to noble Carthage and deposited on the road called that of the Scillitans. In that same venerable place many wonders occur, and every sickness is healed in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with God the Father, belong honor, praise, and glory in the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## THE SAME ACTS

From the old Surian edition, compared with the editions of Mombritius, Baronius, Cotelerius, Baluzius, and Acherius; and [Col. 0683D] with the manuscripts: Ursicampum I; Saint Cornelius of Compiègne I; Saint Victor of Paris I; the Celestines of Paris I; Saint Marianus of Auxerre I; [Col. 0684A] as published by the most learned Thierry Ruinart, priest and Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, among the Genuine and Selected Acts of the Early Martyrs, p. 374 and following.

## Thierry Ruinart’s Notice on the Acts of Saint Felix, Bishop and Martyr

1. Since the enemies of the Christian religion perceived that the reading of the divine Scriptures was exceedingly effective in confirming the minds of the faithful in their resolve, they declared war on the sacred codices, ordering that they be consumed by flames everywhere in the world. This edict, promulgated throughout all the provinces of the Roman Empire, produced many martyrs of the Church, especially in Africa, where several suffered death on this account. Others, terrified by fear of punishments, surrendered [Col. 0684B] the sacred codices and gave rise to the notorious name of the *Traditores* (“Surrenderers”). And when the Donatists applied that name to Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, and to the other Catholics, the African Church was agitated by many disturbances.

Among the others who suffered martyrdom in Africa for the defense of the sacred books, Bishop Felix is listed first. We have taken his Acts, which are transmitted in various forms, from the old Surian edition, because there they seem to be more genuine and pure; although I do not deny that several passages ought to be restored, or at least clarified, with the aid of other editions and manuscript codices. These must be considered individually.

2. First, one must inquire over which city Felix was bishop. Of the four manuscript codices in the [Col. 0684C] Colbert Library, from which the learned Baluzius prepared his edition of this martyr’s Acts in volume II of the *Miscellanea*, two call Felix’s see Tubizacensian. They agree with other manuscript codices: namely, one from the library of Saint Victor at Paris, another belonging to the Celestine Fathers of that city, and a third of Saint Melanius at Rennes, as we learn from several slips transcribed before the burning of that library, which are in our possession.

But the other two Colbert codices and one of Saint Cornelius at Compiègne, together with Mombritius and the Acherian edition of volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, offer Tubizocensian, Tubzocensian, or Tubzuzensian; several ancient martyrologies agree with them. The old Surian edition, however, calls him Tibiurensian; Cardinal Baronius substituted Thibarensian for this name under the year 302, no. 118, [Col. 0684D] and this name entered the Acts of the new Surian edition.

Which of these readings should be preferred is uncertain, since no city under any of these names is found in any African geographical register. The city of Thibaris or Tibaris is indeed known: Cyprian wrote Epistle 58 of the new edition, formerly 56, to the people of that city; and at the Council of Carthage on Baptism Vincentius of Thibaris delivered his judgment. But Baronius substituted the name Thibaris conjecturally, for he cites no manuscript codex in proof; nor is it established whether it belonged to the proconsular province. The Oxford editor, in notes on the cited letter, considers that it should be assigned to Zeugitania, although he had previously said in notes on the Council of Carthage on Baptism that it seemed to him to be Tabora in Mauretania Caesariensis.

Hence it is no more certain that Felix was bishop of Thibaris than that he was bishop of Tubursicum, as the most distinguished Baluzius suspects, or of Tuburbo, as our Acherius noted in the margin of his [Col. 0685B] edition. Yet the former opinion has this difficulty: Tubursicum was a city of Numidia, whereas Felix seems to have belonged to the proconsular province, since he was sent by the curator of his city to the proconsul. Indeed, his see must be said to have been not far from Carthage if credence is given to the Surian Acts, in which Felix is said to have set out for Carthage in one day and to have returned to his see the next day.

3. The second point on which the Surian Acts differ from the others concerns Felix’s clergy. Surius calls them Aper the presbyter, and Cyrus and Victor the readers; the other editions, with the manuscripts, call them Januarius the presbyter, and Fortunatus or Fortunatianus and Septiminus the readers. Ancient martyrologies agree with the latter: they add to Felix as companions Audactus and Januarius, presbyters, and Fortunatianus and Septimius, readers. But the same martyrologies favor Surius in identifying the place. With unanimous agreement they report that Felix consummated his martyrdom at Venusia in Apulia, though the Baluzian and Acherian editions, with all the manuscripts which I have been able to inspect, state that he suffered at Nola.

4. The published Acts disagree no less in assigning the time at which Saint Felix suffered martyrdom. The Acherian and Baluzian editions, with the manuscript codices, report that it occurred on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February; the Surian edition assigns it to the third day before the Kalends of September. We judge the latter opinion preferable.

For since the edict concerning the burning of books was promulgated at Nicomedia in March of the year 303, scarcely anyone could persuade himself [Col. 0685D] that it did not reach Africa until the following year. Yet those who embrace the first opinion must say this. For it is certain from the Acts that Felix was arrested immediately after this edict was promulgated in Africa. The very context of the Acts also favors the Surian edition: “When Diocletian was consul for the eighth time . . . the edict went forth,” etc.; “Then the proclamation was posted,” etc. In the other opinion, the words “Then the proclamation” cannot be understood of the year designated by the words “When Diocletian was consul for the eighth time,” etc.

All these details, however, agree very well [Col. 0686A] with the Surian or Baronian reading. For when Diocletian was consul for the eighth time and Maximian for the seventh—that is, in 303—the first edict against Christians concerning the burning of books and the like was issued at Nicomedia in March. That edict, transmitted to the different provinces of the Roman Empire, reached Africa in June. When it was promulgated in the city over which Felix was bishop and he steadfastly refused to surrender the sacred books, he was brought before various tribunals, even across the sea; finally, on 30 August, at Venusia, a city of Apulia, he completed his martyrdom by the sword.

Nevertheless, the martyrologies of Usuard, Ado, the Roman Martyrology of Rosweyde, Galesinius, and Baronius celebrate his feast in October; while on the preceding day he is commemorated in the martyrologies of Florus and Notker. But above all these must be preferred the authority of Bede’s genuine martyrology. I set down here its words, which splendidly confirm the Surian reading:

> “On the third day before the Kalends of September, in the city of Venusia in Apulia, the natal day of Saints Felix, bishop of Tubzocum, and Audactus and Januarius, presbyters, and Fortunatianus and Septiminus, readers, who in the time of Diocletian, having been seized in their own city by the curator Magnelianus, were long afflicted by many chains and prisons, both in Africa and Sicily, and were finally consummated by execution with the sword. Felix died a virgin at the age of fifty-six. There are thirty-five Roman miles between Carthage and Tibzoca [manuscripts: in the margin, Tibiuca, perhaps Tibiura].”

[Col. 0686B] The same words down to “There are,” etc., are found in a very ancient manuscript codex of Queen Christina of Sweden in Florentinius, and in Lucas Holstenius’s annotations on the Roman Martyrology for 30 August, except that Januarius is not listed among Felix’s companions; but the day on which they were seized is stated: the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July. Moreover, the commemoration of our Felix is celebrated also among the Greeks, who observe his feast on 16 April.

# ACTS OF SAINT FELIX, BISHOP AND MARTYR

From manuscript codices and printed editions.

> **Note: [Col. 0685D]**
>
> **I. “Diocletian and Maximian.”** The Surian edition erroneously has Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII. Baronius, also erroneously and without any manuscript authority, has Constantius Chlorus and Galerius Maximian IV.
>
> **“On the same day.”** These words are absent from the other editions and manuscripts.]

I. In the consulship of Diocletian for the eighth time and of Maximian for the seventh, the Augusti, an edict of the emperors and Caesars went forth over the whole face of the earth; and it was posted throughout colonies and cities for the governors and magistrates, each in his own place, that they should demand the divine books from the hands of bishops and presbyters.

Then a public proclamation [Col. 0686D] was posted in the city of Tibiura on the day of the Nones of June. Then Magnilianus (otherwise Magnellianus) ordered the elders of the people to be brought before him. On the same day Bishop Felix had gone to Carthage. He ordered Aper the presbyter, and Gyrus (Baronius: Cyrus) and Vitalis, readers, to be brought before him.

Magnilianus the curator said to them: “Do you have the divine books?”

Aper said: “We do.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “Hand them over to be burned by fire.”

Then Aper said: “Our bishop has them with him.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “Where is he?”

[Col. 0687A] Aper said: “I do not know.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “You shall therefore remain under official custody until you render an account to Anulinus the proconsul.”

II. But on the following day Bishop Felix came from Carthage to Tibiura. Then Magnilianus the curator ordered Bishop Felix to be brought before him by an official.

Magnilianus the curator said to him: “Bishop Felix, give up the books or whatever parchments you have.”

Bishop Felix said: “I have them, but I do not give them up.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “What the emperors have commanded comes before what you say. Hand over the books, that they may be burned by fire.”

Bishop Felix said: “It is better for me to be burned by fire than for the divine Scriptures to be burned; for it is good to obey God rather than men.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “What the emperors have commanded comes before what you say.”

[Col. 0687B] Bishop Felix said: “The command of the Lord comes before that of men.”

Magnilianus said: “Reflect with yourself.”

III. But after the third day the curator ordered Bishop Felix to be brought before him and said to him: “Have you reflected with yourself?”

Bishop Felix said: “The things I spoke before, I speak now also, and I shall say them before the proconsul.”

Magnilianus the curator said: “You shall therefore go to the proconsul, and there you will render an account.”

Then Vincentius Celsinus, decurion of the city of the Tibiurans, was assigned to him.

> **Note: [Col. 0687D]**
>
> **IV. “He was conducted.”** Other editions and manuscripts add “to Carthage.”
>
> **“The proconsul.”** In the other editions and manuscripts this examination is said to have occurred before the proconsul’s legate. Hence perhaps above one should read, “The legate ordered him to be cast into prison”; and here, “the proconsul’s legate: Why,” etc.
>
> **“He ordered.”** Other editions and manuscripts: “He sent him to Rome.” Yet from what follows in both editions, this prefect seems then to have been in Africa.]

IV. Then Felix set out from Tibiura. On the eighth day before the Kalends of July he was led away bound; and the bound man was ordered to be thrown into prison. But on the next day Bishop Felix was brought out before dawn. The proconsul said to him: “Why do you not surrender the superfluous Scriptures?”

[Col. 0687C] Bishop Felix said: “I have them, but I shall not give them up.”

Then he ordered him to be sent, bound, into the lowest part of the prison. But after sixteen days Bishop Felix was brought from prison in chains at the fourth hour of the night before Anulinus the proconsul. Anulinus said to him: “Why do you not surrender the superfluous Scriptures?”

Bishop Felix replied: “I shall not give them up.”

Then Anulinus the proconsul ordered him to be sent to the prefect of the praetory on the Ides of July. Then the prefect ordered him to be received into his prison and bound with heavier chains. But after nine days the prefect ordered him to sail to the emperors.

> **Note: [Col. 0687D]**
>
> **V. “He arrived at the harbor.”** Other editions and manuscripts: “He arrived at Nola, where he was questioned by the investigator of that city and condemned to death.” It is remarkable, however, that this martyr, sent to the emperors, should have been condemned by an investigator or anyone else, unless perhaps they acted under a special command of the emperor, who was then staying in that region.
>
> Moreover, some codices assert that Felix’s body was transported to Carthage.
>
> **“Agrigento.”** Agrigentum, Catana, Messana, and Taurominium are very well-known cities of Sicily, formerly episcopal sees under the metropolitan of Palermo; now only Agrigentum is subject to him, for Messana has been elevated to a metropolitan see, Catana recognizes the archbishop of Monreale, and the episcopal see of Taurominium has been suppressed.
>
> **“Rulo.”** The name of this city is not found in geographical records of Italy. Lucania, however, was formerly a large part of Magna Graecia, comprising much of present-day Basilicata, a province of the Kingdom of Naples, together with several neighboring regions. Venusia is an episcopal city under the metropolitan of Acerenza, at the foot of the Apennines, distinguished by the title of principality.]

V. Then Bishop Felix boarded the ship in great chains and remained in the ship’s chest for four days. Rolled about beneath the feet of horses, he tasted neither bread nor water. Fasting, he arrived at the harbor and was received by the brethren with the highest honor in the city [Col. 0688A] of Agrigentum. From there they came to the city called Catana; there likewise they were received. From there they came to Messana; then to Taurominium, where likewise they were received. Afterwards they sailed across the strait to Lucania, to a city called Rulo. From there they proceeded to Venusia, a city of the region of Apulia.

Then the prefect ordered Felix to be taken from his chains and said: “Felix, why do you not give up the Scriptures of the Lord? Or perhaps you do not have them?”

He replied: “I do indeed have them, but I do not give them up.”

The prefect said: “Kill Felix with the sword.”

Bishop Felix said in a clear voice: “I thank you, Lord, because you have deigned to set me free.”

VI. And he was led to the place of his suffering—when the moon itself also was turned into blood—on the third day before the Kalends [Col. 0688B] of September. Bishop Felix, lifting his eyes to heaven, said in a clear voice:

“God, I give you thanks. I have spent fifty-six years in this world. I have kept virginity; I have observed the Gospels; I have preached faith and truth. Lord God of heaven and earth, Jesus Christ, to you I bend my neck for the sacrifice, you who endure forever; to whom belong splendor and majesty for ages of ages. Amen.”

# ACTS OF THE MARTYRS SATURNINUS THE PRESBYTER, FELIX, DATIVUS, AMPELIUS, AND OTHERS

From Baluzius, *Miscellanea*, vol. II, p. 56, from a manuscript codex of the Colbert Library.

## BALUZIUS’S NOTICE ON THE ACTS OF THE SAINTS SATURNINUS, DATIVUS, AND THEIR COMPANIONS

[Col. 0688C] We have added this title from codex 930 of the Colbert Library. It was absent from the editions of Surius and Henschenius. Since this codex is ancient and contains certain matters pertaining to the history of the holy martyrs which are not found in the Acts themselves, it seemed worthwhile to publish it as we find it in the ancient codex.

These things were certainly written, as cannot be denied, by some Donatist, but by one learned and educated; and they seemed to me worthy to be joined with Lactantius, both because of the likeness of their subject and because of the elegance of their style. Although they are not the very Acts of the martyrs cited in the Conference of Carthage, as is clear from Saint Augustine, they are nonetheless the work of an ancient writer who was not very far removed from the age of Diocletian.

Those, therefore, are greatly mistaken who misuse Augustine’s authority to prove that these are the very proconsular records taken down by notaries. On the contrary, Augustine’s testimony establishes that those records do not survive today, but only the history which that Donatist compiled from those same records. For Augustine, in the *Breviculus* of the third day, chapter 17, teaches that the acts of the martyrs were recorded when Diocletian was consul for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth, on the day before the Ides of February. Yet in this book it is written simply, without any indication of time, that the war from which the *Traditores* arose was stirred up in the time of Diocletian and Maximian.

Moreover, the matters said in chapter 16 and following concerning Mensurius and Caecilian plainly do not belong to proconsular records; and Baronius rightly observed that they were not read at the Conference of Carthage.

## The Confessions and Acts of the Martyrs Saturninus the Presbyter, Felix, Dativus, Ampelius, and the Other Persons Written Below Begin

They confessed the Lord at Carthage, under Anulinus, then proconsul of Africa, on the day before the Ides of February, on account of their assemblies and the Scriptures of the Lord; and, separated in diverse places and times, they poured forth their most blessed blood.

> **Note: [Col. 0689C]**
>
> **I. “In the archive of memory.”** Below, chapter 9: “And committing his confession to memory together with the confessions of the others.” There Baronius notes that *memoria* was said to be the place in which proconsular records were preserved. But since this is established by no testimony of the ancients, and the matter is obscure, I have not yet been persuaded that this interpretation is correct.
>
> It is known that in the imperial palace there were *magistri memoriae*, masters of memory, who dictated “to memory”; Salmasius, in his customary fashion, said much about them in his notes on the writers of the *Historia Augusta*, pp. 207 and 480. But that *memoria* was different from the one mentioned here.
>
> I think that *memoria* here signifies the public registers in which cases conducted in the forum were written, lest their memory be effaced. But at the beginning of this history, where one reads that the Acts of the martyrs were written in the archive of memory so that the glory of the martyrs might not become obsolete as ages passed, I think that the word is used in a different sense and refers not to public registers, whose custody was not in the hands of clergy, but to ecclesiastical books in which the deeds of the martyrs were written for the everlasting remembrance of all.]

I. Whoever exults and glories in Christ through faith in the most holy religion, and rejoices in the truth of the Lord, having condemned error, in order that he may hold fast to the Catholic Church and distinguish holy communion from what is profane, should read the Acts of the martyrs. They were necessarily committed to writing in the archive of memory, lest, as ages passed, [Col. 0689C] the glory of the martyrs and the condemnation of the *Traditores* should become obsolete.

Accordingly, I undertake to write from the public records the heavenly combats and new contests performed by the bravest soldiers of Christ, unconquered warriors, glorious martyrs. I undertake this, I say, not so much endowed with talent as joined to them by the civic affection which I bear them; and I do so deliberately in a twofold way: both that we may prepare the minds of their imitators for martyrdom, and that, while we set down in writing the battles and victories of their confession of those whom we trust live forever and reign with the Lord Christ, we may consign them to eternal memory.

But, most beloved brethren, I cannot find what beginnings I should use, or with what opening of praise I should approach the most fortunate confession of the most holy martyrs. For I am carried away by great deeds and great virtues; and whatever I see in them, I admire as wholly divine and heavenly: faith in their devotion, holiness in their life, constancy in their confession, victory in their suffering. The more these things shine alone in their respective virtues, the more brightly are they all displayed in each individual martyr.

It therefore pleases me at the beginning to treat the cause of this war itself and to survey, necessarily but briefly and with all speed, the crisis of the whole world, so that, once the truth is known, one may know both the rewards of the martyrs and the punishments of the *Traditores*.

> **Note: [Col. 0690C]**
>
> **II. “Testaments.”** In the Colbert codex it is written “sacraments,” that is, mysteries; which comes to the same thing.
>
> **“Alutinensis.”** Thus Surius and the Colbert codex. Henschenius’s edition has “Abitinensis,” from two ancient codices, as he himself says. Certainly in the Conference of Carthage we read of Maximus and Victor, bishops of Abitinae; and at the Council of Carthage under Cyprian, Saturninus, bishop from Abitinae, was present. Nevertheless, knowing how dangerous any alteration of proper names is, especially of the names of African cities, I have retained the ancient reading.
>
> **“Occani.”** In the Colbert codex one reads *octavi* (“eighth”). Henschenius notes that the same reading stood in the Trier codex.
>
> **“The trumpet of war.”** Lest anyone should suppose that these words were spoken in the manner of rhetoricians rather than in a simply historical style, a notable passage from the Acts of Saint Euphemia the martyr must be produced. She was taken to God at Chalcedon while this very persecution was raging. It is written there that in that city there was a temple of Mars and a conspicuous image of him. The edicts summoned the citizens to the festival, together with those dwelling around Chalcedon. Death and punishments were threatened to those to whom they were directed if they could not be persuaded to worship demons. Trumpets sounding clearly and terribly were the signal to assemble at the temple.
>
> The Acts of Saint Alexander the martyr, who was taken away in this same persecution, in Surius under 13 May: “Accordingly, all, having heard the voice of the heralds and the blast of the trumpet, were ready to be present with the emperor in the temple of Jupiter.”]

## II.

[Col. 0690B] In the times of Diocletian and Maximian, the devil declared war upon Christians in this manner: he demanded the most holy testaments of the Lord and the divine Scriptures for burning; he overthrew the Lord’s basilicas; and he forbade sacred rites and most holy assemblies to be celebrated for the Lord. But the army of the Lord God did not endure this monstrous command, and recoiled in horror from the sacrilegious order. At once it seized the weapons of faith and descended into battle, intending to fight not so much against human beings as against the devil.

And although some fell away from the pivot of faith by handing over to the gentiles the Scriptures of the Lord and the divine testaments to be burned in profane fires, yet very many acted bravely by preserving them and willingly shedding their own blood for them. Filled with God, having conquered and cast down the devil, [Col. 0690C] bearing the victorious palm in their suffering, all the martyrs ratified with their own blood the judgment against the *traditores* and their associates, by which they had rejected them from the communion of the Church. For it was not lawful that martyrs and *traditores* should be together in the Church of God.

Accordingly immense companies of confessors hastened from every direction to the field of contest; and wherever each one encountered the enemy, there he established the Lord’s camp. Thus, in the city of Alutina, in the house of Occanius Felix, when the trumpet of war sounded, the glorious martyrs raised the Lord’s standards. While they everywhere celebrated, according to custom, the Lord’s sacraments, they were arrested by the magistrates of the colony and by the stationing soldier himself: the presbyter Saturninus with his four children—namely, Saturninus the younger and Felix, readers; Maria, a consecrated woman; and the child Hilarianus—as also Dativus, who was likewise a senator; Felix; another Felix; Emeritus; Ampelius; Rogatianus; Quintus; Maximianus; Thelica; Rogatianus; Rogatus; Januarius; Cassianus; Victorianus; Vincentius; Caecilianus; Restituta; Prima; Eva; Rogatianus; Guinalius; Rogatus; Pomponia; Secunda; Januaria; Saturnina; Martinus; Elautus; Felix; Margareta the elder; Honorata; Regiola; Victorianus; Pelusius; Faustus; Dacianus; Matrona; Caecilia; Victoria; Herectina; a second Matrona; [Col. 0691B] and Januaria.

## III.

Those who had been arrested were led cheerfully to the forum. Dativus went first into the first field of contest, he whom his holy parents had begotten as a stainless senator for the heavenly court. The presbyter Saturninus went also, surrounded by his many children: one portion of that offspring he destined to share martyrdom with him; another he left to the Church as a pledge of his own name. The Lord’s company followed them, in which shone the splendor of heavenly armor: the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, and the two-edged sword, the word of God. Strengthened by this protection, they promised their brethren hope of victory.

But now they came to the forum of the aforesaid city. There, entering their first encounter, they won the palm of confession by the magistrates’ charge. For in that [Col. 0691C] forum heaven had already fought for the Scriptures of the Lord when Fundanus, once bishop of the city, handed over the Lord’s Scriptures to be burned. When the sacrilegious magistrate applied them to the fire, suddenly rain poured down from a clear sky; the fire brought to the holy Scriptures was extinguished; hail was added; and the whole region itself was devastated on account of the Scriptures of the Lord as the elements raged.

From this city, therefore, the martyrs of Christ received their desired first chains. Sent on to Carthage, cheerful and rejoicing, throughout the whole journey they sang hymns and psalms to the Lord. When they reached the official court of Anulinus, then proconsul, and stood in line steadily and bravely, by the Lord’s steadfastness they repelled the assault of the raging devil. But since diabolical fury could not prevail against all the soldiers of Christ at once, it summoned them individually to contests. The battles of these contests I shall recount not so much in my own words as in those of the martyrs, so that both the audacity of the raging enemy may be known in the tortures and in the sacrilegious invective itself, and the power of Christ the all-powerful Lord may be praised in the martyrs’ endurance and in their confession itself.

> **Note [Col. 0692D].**  
> “In the very lacerations.” This is precisely the reading of the Colbert manuscript. Here the word *in* has the force of “among” or “amid”; as below, chapter 11: “placing his life amid the tortures of prison.”

## IV.

When therefore they were brought from the official staff before the proconsul, [Col. 0692A] and it was reported that Christians sent by the magistrates of the Alutinenses had celebrated the Lord’s assembly contrary to the prohibition of the Emperors and Caesars, the proconsul first questioned Dativus as to his rank and whether he had held an assembly. When he professed himself a Christian and stated that he had been at the assembly, the author of that most holy gathering was demanded from him; and immediately the officials were ordered to raise him upon the rack and prepare him, stretched out, for the claws.

But while the executioners fulfilled their cruel orders with savage speed, and stood raging at the words spoken, and, with the martyr’s sides bared for wounds, threatened him with raised claws, suddenly the most valiant martyr Thelica thrust himself into the midst and offered himself to the tortures. He cried out: “Because we are Christians, we assembled.” Immediately [Col. 0692B] the proconsul’s fury blazed up; groaning, grievously wounded by the spiritual sword, he battered the martyr of Christ with most severe blows, stretched him when suspended upon the rack, and tore him with the scraping claws.

But, amid the very frenzy of the executioners, the most glorious martyr Thelica poured out prayers such as these to the Lord with thanksgiving: “Thanks be to God. In your name, Christ, Son of God, deliver your servants.” As he prayed thus, the proconsul said, “Who is the author of your congregation with you?” He answered the executioner, raging more cruelly, in a clear voice: “The presbyter Saturninus—and all of us.”

O martyr, giving primacy to all! For he did not set the presbyter above the brethren, but joined the brethren to the presbyter in the fellowship of confession. Therefore, when the proconsul sought Saturninus, he pointed him out—not because he betrayed him, [Col. 0692C] whom he saw fighting alongside himself against the devil, but in order to make it fully clear that he had celebrated the assembly, since the presbyter too had been with them.

Thus blood flowed together with the voice of the man praying to the Lord; and, mindful of the precepts of the Gospel, the martyr sought forgiveness for his enemies amid the very lacerations of his body. Indeed, amid the most grievous agonies of his wounds, he rebuked both the torturers and the proconsul in these words:

> “You act unjustly, unhappy men; you act against God. Most high God, do not allow them in these sins. You sin, unhappy men; you act against God. We keep the commandments of the most high God. You act unjustly, unhappy men; you tear innocent persons. We are not murderers; we have committed no fraud. God, have mercy. I give you thanks. For your name, Lord, [Col. 0692D] grant endurance. Deliver your servants from the captivity of this age. I give you thanks, nor am I sufficient to give you thanks.”

And while the sides, violently shaken by the blows of the claws, were more deeply furrowed, and the flowing flood of blood streamed out under their violent pulls, he heard the proconsul say to him: “You will begin to feel what you must suffer.” He added: “For glory. I give thanks to the God of kingdoms. The eternal kingdom appears, the incorruptible kingdom.”

[Col. 0693A]

> “Lord Jesus Christ, we are Christians; we serve you. You are our hope; you are the hope of Christians. Most holy God, most high God, almighty God, we offer you praises for your name.”

When through the judge the devil said to one praying such things, “You ought to have kept the order of the Emperors and Caesars,” then, his body already exhausted, he proclaimed victoriously with a strong and steadfast spirit: “I care for nothing except the law of God, which I have learned. I keep it; for it I shall die; in it I shall be consumed; apart from it there is nothing else.”

By such words of the most glorious martyr, Anulinus himself was more tortured in the martyr’s torments. At last, his rage fed full by savagery, he had the martyr shut up in prison and reserved him for suffering worthy of his passion.

## V.

[Col. 0693B] After him, Dativus was strengthened by the Lord in the contest; he was joined close at hand to Thelica in the most valiant battle. While he hung stretched out upon the rack and repeatedly declared in a firm voice that he was a Christian and had held an assembly, the brother of the most holy martyr Victoria came forward—a man indeed wearing the toga, but at that time estranged from the most holy worship of Christian religion. He accused the martyr hanging on the rack with profane words:

> “This is the man, lord, who, during the absence of our father, while we were studying here, seduced our sister Victoria and brought her from the most splendid city of Carthage all the way with him to the colony of Alutina, together with Secunda and Restituta. He never entered our house except when he lured girlish minds there with certain [Col. 0693C] persuasions.”

But Victoria, the most illustrious martyr of the Lord, could not bear for her colleague and fellow-martyr, the senator, to be falsely attacked. Immediately breaking forth in Christian freedom, she said: “I set out at no one’s persuasion, nor did I come with him to the colony of Alutina. I can prove this through citizens. I accomplished everything of my own accord and will. For I was at the assembly, and I celebrated the Lord’s rite with the brethren, because I am a Christian.”

Then the shameless advocate heaped abuse upon the martyr. Against him the glorious martyr from the rack refuted everything with a truthful answer.

## VI.

Meanwhile Anulinus, burning with rage, ordered the claws pressed upon the martyr. Immediately the executioners found his naked sides, prepared for blows, with bloody wounds. [Col. 0693D] Savage men rushed upon him with swift obedience to their commands; ripping skins and tearing apart entrails, they cruelly exposed the hidden parts of his breast to the abominable gaze of the profane.

Yet the martyr’s mind remained unmoved. Though his limbs were torn, his entrails ripped apart, and his sides mangled, the martyr’s spirit nevertheless remained whole and unshaken. Finally, mindful of his rank, Dativus—who was also a senator—offered this prayer to the Lord while the executioner raged: “O Christ, Lord, may I not be put to shame.”

Having spoken these words, the most blessed martyr obtained from the Lord as readily [Col. 0694A] as he had briefly asked. For immediately the proconsul, his mind shaken, spoke out in a voice inclined to mercy. The executioners ceased. For it was not lawful that a martyr of Christ should be tortured in the cause of his fellow-martyr Victoria.

For when Pompeianus too approached him as a fierce accuser with an unworthy allegation and added a calumnious charge, he was despised and struck by the martyr:

> “What are you doing in this place, devil? What do you still attempt against the martyrs of Christ?”

By the Lord’s senator and martyr, both official power and forensic frenzy were overcome. Yet the most illustrious martyr, though tortured for Christ, when asked whether he had been at the assembly, steadfastly professed that he had come upon the assembly and had celebrated the Lord’s rite with the brethren in fitting devotion of religion, [Col. 0694B] and that there had been one author of that most holy assembly. He again stirred up the proconsul more sharply against himself. As the latter’s savagery broke out anew, the martyr’s dignity was doubled: with the claws again furrowing him, he was inscribed anew.

But amid the most savage agonies of the wounds, the martyr repeated his former prayer: “I ask, Christ, may I not be put to shame. What have I done? Saturninus is our presbyter.”

> **Note [Col. 0693D].**  
> “To sound judgment.” See what was said above on chapter XXXIV of Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, vol. VII, col. 219.

## VII.

While his sides were scraped by hooked claws, as the teaching cruelty of the hard and savage executioner displayed its art, the presbyter Saturninus was summoned to the contest. Considering, in contemplation of the heavenly kingdom, that his fellow-martyrs were enduring matters altogether slight and light, he too began the engagement in this way. For when the proconsul said, “You acted against the order of the Emperors and Caesars in gathering all these persons,” [Col. 0694C] the presbyter Saturninus answered confidently, prompted by the Spirit of the Lord: “We celebrated the Lord’s rite.”

The proconsul said: “Why?” He answered: “Because the Lord’s rite cannot be omitted.”

As soon as he had said this, the proconsul immediately ordered Dativus to be put to the rack again. Meanwhile Dativus regarded rather than felt the laceration of his own body; and because his mind and spirit hung upon the Lord, he attached no value to bodily pain. He only prayed to the Lord, saying:

> “Help, I ask, Christ; have pity; save my soul; guard my spirit; may I not be put to shame. I ask, Christ, grant endurance.”

When the proconsul said to him, “From this most splendid city you ought rather to have called others to sound judgment and not acted against the commands of the Emperors and Caesars,” he cried out more strongly and steadfastly: “I am a Christian.” [Col. 0694D] By that voice the devil was overcome. “Spare him,” he said; and, handing him over to prison, he reserved the martyr for suffering worthy of his passion.

## VIII.

But the presbyter Saturninus, sprinkled with the fresh blood of the martyrs, hanging upon the rack, was admonished to persist in the faith of those in whose blood he stood firm. When he was asked whether he himself was the author and had gathered them all, he said: “Yes, I was present at the assembly.” As the presbyter engaged in battle, Emeritus the reader leapt forth into the contest: “I am the author,” he said, “in whose house the assembly [Col. 0695A] was held.”

But the proconsul, who had already been defeated so many times, recoiled in fear at Emeritus’ onslaught. Nevertheless, turning to the presbyter, he said: “Why did you act against the command, Saturninus?” Saturninus answered: “The Lord’s rite cannot be omitted. The law commands it thus.”

Then the proconsul said: “Still, you ought not to have despised what was forbidden, but rather to have observed it, and not to have acted against the command of the Emperors.” With words long rehearsed against the martyrs, he stirred up the terror of his anger, and it was obeyed with no sluggish compliance. The executioners rushed upon the aged body of the presbyter and, with raging fury, severed and tore apart the connection of his sinews.

You might have seen lamentable punishments and tortures of a new kind devised for the priest of God: the executioners raging in hunger-like fury, as though feeding upon wounds; and, with the entrails exposed, the bones stripped bare showing pale amid the red of blood, to the horror of those who watched. Nor, even amid the delay of the torturers, did the soul, driven out, abandon the body hanging under punishment. Yet with such words the presbyter prayed to the Lord:

> “I ask you, Christ, hear me. I give you thanks, God. Order me to be beheaded. I ask, Christ, have mercy. Son of God, help.”

The proconsul said to him: “Why do you act against the command?” And the presbyter said: “The law commands it thus; the law teaches it thus.”

O answer of the presbyter-teacher, altogether admirable and worthy of proclamation! Even in tortures the presbyter proclaimed the most holy law, for which he willingly endured punishments. At last Anulinus, frightened by the word “law,” said, “I shall spare him”; and, consigning him to prison custody, he reserved him for the desired punishment.

## IX.

But when Emeritus was brought forward, the proconsul said: “Were assemblies held in your [Col. 0695C] house against the commands of the Emperors?” Emeritus, overflowing with the Holy Spirit, answered: “In my house we performed the Lord’s rite.”

The other said: “Why did you allow them to enter?” He answered: “Because they are my brethren, and I could not forbid them.”

“But,” he said, “you ought to have forbidden them.”

“I could not,” he answered, “because we cannot exist without the Lord’s rite.”

Immediately he too was ordered to be stretched upon the rack and tortured while extended. As he endured violent blows from a newly assigned executioner, he said: “I ask, Christ, help. You act against God’s command, unhappy men.” And when the proconsul interjected, “You ought not to have received them,” he answered: “I could not fail to receive my brethren.”

But the sacrilegious proconsul said: “Yet the command of the Emperors and Caesars came first.” Against him the most devout [Col. 0695D] martyr said: “God is greater than emperors. I ask, Christ, praises to you. Christ Lord, grant endurance.”

As he prayed thus, the proconsul cast this at him: “Then do you have some Scripture in your house?” He answered: “I have it, but in my heart.”

The proconsul said: “Do you have it in your house or not?”

The martyr Emeritus said: “I have them in my heart. I ask, Christ, praises to you. Deliver me, Christ, in your name. I suffer briefly; I suffer gladly. Christ, may I not be put to shame.”

O martyr mindful of the apostle, who possessed the law of the Lord written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts. O fitting and diligent guardian of the sacred law, who, recoiling in horror from the crime of the *traditores*, [Col. 0696A] placed the Scriptures of the Lord within the secret places of his breast, lest he lose them. When he learned this, the proconsul said, “Spare him.” And, committing his confession to record together with the confessions of the others, he said: “All of you, according to your confessions, shall pay the punishments you deserve for your merits.”

## X.

But now the bestial frenzy, its bloody mouth sated by the martyrs’ tortures, was growing weak. Yet when Felix—blessed both in name and in suffering—advanced into battle, and the whole line of the Lord stood uncorrupted and unconquered, the tyrant, crushed in mind, subdued in voice, broken in soul and body, said: “I hope that you will choose rather the course by which you may live, so that you may observe the commands.”

Against this the confessors of the Lord, Christ’s unconquered martyrs, spoke as though with one voice: “We are Christians; [Col. 0696B] we cannot but keep the holy law of the Lord, even to the shedding of blood.”

Struck by this voice, the enemy said to Felix: “I do not ask whether you are a Christian, but whether you held an assembly or possess any Scriptures.”

O foolish and laughable question from a judge! “Whether you are a Christian,” he says, “be silent about that.” And he added: “Were you at an assembly?” Felix answered: “As though a Christian could exist without the Lord’s rite, or the Lord’s rite be celebrated without a Christian. Do you not know, Satan, that the Christian is constituted in the Lord’s rite and the Lord’s rite in the Christian, so that neither can exist without the other? When you hear the name, learn the Lord’s gathering; and when you hear ‘assembly,’ recognize the name.”

Thus you are recognized and laughed at by the martyr; by such an answer you are confounded. “We most gloriously celebrated the assembly,” he said; “we always assemble for the Lord’s rite to read [Col. 0696C] the Scriptures of the Lord.”

Severely confounded by this confession, Anulinus had him beaten with clubs. Having completed his passion, he joined the martyr, lifeless and hastening to the heavenly council and the starry tribunals.

## XI.

Another Felix followed Felix, alike in name, confession, and suffering itself. Entering the contest with equal courage, he too was battered by the injury of clubs; placing his life amid the tortures of prison, he was joined to the martyrdom of the earlier Felix.

After them Ampelius, guardian of the law and most faithful keeper of the divine Scriptures, undertook the contest. When the proconsul asked him whether he had been at an assembly, he answered cheerfully and confidently in an eager voice: “With the brethren I held an assembly; I celebrated the Lord’s rite; and I have the Lord’s Scriptures with me, but written in my heart. [Col. 0696D] Christ, I render praises to you. Hear me, Christ.”

After speaking these words, his neck battered, he was joyfully confined, as though already with the brethren in the Lord’s tabernacle. Rogatianus followed him. Having confessed the Lord’s name, he was joined to the aforesaid brethren unharmed. But Quintus Applicitus, having nobly and magnificently confessed the Lord’s name, was beaten with clubs and thrust into prison, reserved for worthy martyrdom.

Maximianus followed him also, equal in confession, similar in engagement, and alike in the triumphs of victory. After him Felix the younger proclaimed that the Lord’s rite is the hope and salvation of Christians. When he likewise was beaten with clubs, he said: “With a devoted mind I celebrated the Lord’s rite; I held an assembly with the brethren, because I am a Christian.” [Col. 0697A] By this confession he too merited association with the aforesaid brethren.

## XII.

Then Saturninus the younger, offspring of Saturninus the presbyter and martyr, eagerly came forward for the desired contest, hastening to equal his father’s most glorious courage. When the proconsul, raging at the devil’s prompting, said to him, “And you, Saturninus, were present?” Saturninus answered: “I am a Christian.”

“I do not ask you that,” he said, “but whether you performed the Lord’s rite.”

Saturninus answered: “I performed the Lord’s rite, because Christ is Savior.”

When he heard the name Savior, Anulinus blazed with rage and renewed the paternal rack upon the son. Once Saturninus had been stretched out, he said: “What, Saturninus, do you profess? You see where you have been placed. Do you have any Scriptures?”

He answered: “I am a Christian.”

The proconsul said: [Col. 0697B] “I ask whether you assembled and whether you have Scriptures.”

He answered: “I am a Christian. There is no other name after Christ which we ought to observe as holy.”

Inflamed by this confession, the devil said: “Since you persist in your obstinacy, you too must be subjected to tortures. Say whether you have any Scriptures.” And he said to the officials: “Torture him.”

The torturers, exhausted by the father’s wounds, went at the young man’s sides; and to the father’s blood still moist upon the claws they added the related blood of the son. You might have seen blood from the father formerly flowing through the furrows of gaping wounds in his sides, and the son’s blood mingled with the father’s streaming from the dripping claws.

But refreshed by the mingling of the two bloods, the youth felt a remedy rather than torments. Strength received amid torture, he cried in a most resolute voice: “I have the Lord’s Scriptures, but in my heart. I ask, Christ, grant endurance. There is hope of life.”

Anulinus said: “Why did you act against the command?” He answered: “Because I am a Christian.”

On hearing this, he said: “Spare him.” And immediately, as the torture ceased, he was confined in fellowship with his father.

## XIII.

Meanwhile, as the hours passed, day sank into night; with the sun the tortures were exhausted; the dark frenzy of the executioners failed, languishing together with the cruelty of its judge. But the legions of the Lord, in which Christ, the eternal light, shone with the flashing splendor of heavenly armor, leapt more strongly and steadfastly into the contests.

But when the adversary of the Lord, conquered in the most glorious battles of so many martyrs and overcome by engagements so great and such as these, abandoned by day and overtaken [Col. 0697D] by night, with the executioners’ frenzy now failing, could no longer continue fighting each one separately to destroy them, he questioned the minds of the entire army of the Lord and assailed the devoted spirits of the saints with this interrogation:

> “You have seen what those who persevered endured, [Col. 0698A] and what they still have to endure as they persist in their confession. Therefore, whoever among you wishes to obtain pardon, so that he may be safe, let him declare it.”

To this the confessors of the Lord, the glorious martyrs of Christ, rejoicing and triumphing together—not inflamed by the proconsul’s words but by the Holy Spirit through the victory of suffering—said more strongly and clearly, as though with one voice: “We are Christians.”

By that voice the devil was cast down; and Anulinus, shaken and confounded, thrust all the saints into prison and reserved them for martyrdom.

> **Note [Col. 0697D].**  
> “To the sanctuary of chastity,” that is, to the temple of God. This is a figurative and elegant manner of speaking, by which it is understood that she wished to dedicate and consecrate her virginity to Christ. Livy, book X, and Festus mention the shrine of Patrician Chastity, which was at Rome in the Forum Boarium, near the round temple of Hercules. P. Victor writes that it stood in the eighth region.
>
> “She preserved her sacred hair.” Victoria therefore did not cut her hair when she consecrated herself to Christ. For formerly Christian women were forbidden to lay aside their hair, even those who chose a profession of perpetual continence. Yet somewhat later, as Jerome writes in Epistle 48 to Sabinianus, this was the custom in the monasteries of Egypt and Syria: both virgin and widow who vowed themselves to God and renounced the world offered their hair to the mothers of the monasteries to be cut.

## XIV.

Lest the most devoted female sex and the most flourishing choir of sacred virgins should be deprived of the glory of so great a contest, all the women, with Christ the Lord helping, joined battle in Victoria and were crowned. For the most holy Victoria, most holy of women, flower of virgins, [Col. 0698B] ornament and dignity of the confessors, noble in birth, most holy in religion, restrained in conduct—in whom the natural good of bright chastity shone forth, while faith more beautiful in mind and integrity of holiness answered to the beauty of her body—rejoiced that she had been restored to a second palm in the Lord’s martyrdom.

For from childhood the clear signs of her chastity already shone, and even in her still unformed years there appeared the most chaste steadfastness of mind and a certain dignity of her future passion. Finally, when full virginity had completed the final stage of youth, and the girl, unwilling and resisting, was compelled by her parents into marriage, while a ravisher urged that she be handed unwillingly to a bridegroom, the girl secretly cast herself down from a height and, borne up by the accommodating air, was received unharmed into the embrace of the earth. She would not afterwards have suffered for Christ [Col. 0698C] the Lord if she had then died for chastity alone.

Freed, therefore, from the marriage torches, and with the bridegroom together with her parents made a mockery, she leapt forth almost from the midst of the wedding crowd to the Church, the sanctuary of chastity and harbor of modesty. There, an untouched virgin, she preserved in unshaken modesty her most sacred hair—of a head consecrated and dedicated to God—for perpetual virginity. Thus hastening to martyrdom, she bore before her in her triumphant right hand the flourishing palm of chastity.

When the proconsul asked what she professed, she answered in a clear voice: “I am a Christian.” And when Fortunatianus, her toga-wearing brother and defender, said that her mind had been captivated by vain arguments, Victoria answered: “My mind is mine; I have never changed.”

The proconsul said: “Do you wish to go with your brother Fortunatianus?” [Col. 0698D] She answered: “I do not wish to, because I am a Christian; and those are my brethren who keep God’s commandments.”

O girl founded upon the authority of the divine law! O glorious virgin, worthily consecrated to the eternal King! O most blessed martyr, most illustrious in evangelical profession, [Col. 0699A] who answered in the Lord’s words: “These are my brethren who keep God’s commandments.”

On hearing this, Anulinus laid aside the authority of a judge and descended to persuading the girl: “Look to your own interest. For you see that your brother desires to provide for your safety.”

The martyr of Christ said: “My mind is mine; I have never changed. For I was at the assembly, and I celebrated the Lord’s rite with the brethren, because I am a Christian.”

As soon as Anulinus heard these words, he blazed up, driven by furies; and, sending the most sacred girl and martyr of Christ to prison with the rest, he reserved them all for suffering.

> **Note [Col. 0699D].**  
> “Hair.” The editions have “neck,” wholly contrary to the proconsul’s meaning. For by these threats he wished to frighten the child, as if he threatened beatings or a fall from a raised but not dangerous place. But cutting off the neck goes beyond this and cannot be counted among childish threats. The Colbert manuscript is therefore better, since it has “hair.” Boys are lovers of their hair. Hence Statius’ poem on the hair of Earinus.

## XV.

But Hilarianus still remained, one of the sons of the presbyter and martyr Saturninus; with immense devotion he surpassed his tender age. Eager to be joined to the triumphs of his father and brothers, [Col. 0699B] he did not so much dread the tyrant’s terrible threats as count them for nothing.

When he was asked, “Have you followed your father or your brothers?” suddenly the youthful voice was heard from his small body, and the narrow breast of the boy wholly opened itself to the confession of the Lord in his answering voice: “I am a Christian, and of my own accord and will I held the assembly with my father and my brothers.”

You heard the voice of Saturninus, the martyr-father, issue through the channels of his sweet son, and a tongue confessing Christ the Lord follow the example of his brother. But the foolish proconsul, not understanding that it was not men but God who fought against him in the martyrs, and because he perceived great spirits in youthful years, thought that the boy could be frightened by the terrors of childhood.

Finally he said: “I shall cut off both [Col. 0699C] your hair and your nose and ears, and so let you go.”

To this the boy Hilarianus, glorious in the courage of his father and brothers, who had already learned from his elders to despise tortures, answered clearly: “Do whatever you wish, because I am a Christian.”

Immediately he too was ordered to be received into prison. And Hilarianus’ voice was heard with great joy saying: “Thanks be to God.” Here the battle of the great contest is completed; here the devil is overcome and conquered; here the martyrs of Christ rejoice in eternal congratulation over the glory of their future suffering.

## Appendix to Those Acts Containing the Accusation of the Donatists against Mensurius and Caecilianus

Concerning this, see Optatus, book I, §§19–20, pp. 18–19. See note 44 there.

> **Note [Col. 0700D].**  
> What follows, because it contains manifest calumnies against Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, and his deacon Caecilianus—who himself later became bishop of Carthage—was omitted in the second edition of Surius and in the Henschen edition.

## XVI.

But since, as we said above, the time of schism [Col. 0699D] has admonished us to join to confessions of martyrs so great and such as these their decrees and most holy ordinances, and to link these with the preceding deeds of God’s friends, I shall necessarily run briefly through all that the martyrs decreed in prison on the authority of the divine law and left to be observed by posterity. Nor shall I, in this haste of mine, pass over the pride of the fallen and the audacity of the *traditores*.

For the truth of the events, love of the law, the state of the Church, public welfare, and common life compelled me to pass over nothing. For by these matters it may be recognized what the Catholic Church is, if the pestilential stain of the *traditores* is declared to every age by their abominable actions and by the martyrs’ judgment.

After the desired prison received the aforesaid martyrs of Christ, the confessors who had earlier been thrust in there joined their triumphant right hands, bearing victorious palms, to those who were coming. Moreover, many other confessors from diverse parts of the province came to the same place. Among them were bishops, presbyters, deacons, and other clerics, who upheld the law of the Lord, celebrated the assembly and the Lord’s rite steadfastly and bravely, and, preserving the Scriptures of the Lord [Col. 0700B] and the divine testaments from flame and fire, offered themselves to cruel fires and diverse torments, after the manner of the Maccabees, for the divine laws.

## XVII.

At that time, therefore, while the dreadful prison and its thick darkness held within themselves God’s most faithful witnesses, while immense weights of chains bound their devoted limbs, while hunger weakened them, thirst exhausted them, cold shook them, the crowd pressed them together, and their very sides burned from the fresh tearing laceration of claws, they celebrated a council amid chains, iron, and instruments of torture. On the authority of divine law they established heavenly decrees—what they would preserve for themselves and for later martyrs. For truly the living Holy Spirit, breathing upon the confessors’ minds, exercised them in eternal [Col. 0700C] and divine conversations.

But after the cruel storm and the terrible threats of persecution by which tyrannical frenzy had assailed the Christian religion, so that a purer and more tranquil eternal peace of the Christian name might again shine forth, there was not lacking the most crafty fraud of all the *traditores*: a conspiracy of destructive wrecks fashioned by diabolical art, which under the pretext of religion attacked religion, overthrew faith, and disturbed the law and divine rights.

Especially since Mensurius, once bishop of Carthage, polluted by his recent handing over of the Scriptures, had begun to make public the madness of his crime with even worse boldness. Although he ought to have sought and implored from the martyrs pardon for the books he had burned, he instead accumulated his offenses with greater crimes, raging against the martyrs with the disposition [Col. 0700D] in which he had handed over the divine laws.

For this man, fiercer than a tyrant and more cruel than an executioner, chose his deacon Caecilianus as a suitable minister of his crime. He stationed thongs and scourges with armed men before the prison doors, so that all who brought food and drink to the martyrs in prison might be driven back from entrance and access after suffering grievous injury. [Col. 0701A] Those who came to feed the martyrs were everywhere beaten by Caecilianus; cups were smashed before the thresholds of the prison while the confessors within their bonds were thirsty; food was everywhere torn apart and scattered for dogs. The martyrs’ most holy fathers and mothers lay before the prison doors; driven away from the last sight of their children, they kept painful vigil at the prison entrance by night and day. There was dreadful weeping and bitter lamentation among all present: pious embraces of the martyrs were forbidden, and Christians were torn away from the duty of affection, while Caecilianus raged as tyrant and cruel executioner.

XVIII. Meanwhile, the martyrs of Christ were moved neither by the squalor of prison, nor by pain in their bodies, nor indeed by any lack of necessities; but, now close to the Lord through their merits and confession, they transmitted to posterity salvation [Col. 0701B] that would separate the common offspring of the Christian name from every renewed communion with the traditors, under this threat: “If anyone communicates with the traditors, he shall have no share with us in the heavenly kingdoms.” They confirmed this judgment of theirs, written with the authority of the Holy Spirit, by the following comparison. “It is written,” they say, “in the Apocalypse: ‘Whoever adds to this book one stroke or one letter, may God add to him innumerable plagues; and whoever removes [anything], may the Lord remove his share from the book of life.’ If, therefore, one added stroke or one letter removed from the holy book utterly cuts off, makes sacrilegious, and destroys its author, it is necessary that all who have handed over the divine testaments and the venerable laws of almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ to profane fires to be burned [Col. 0701C] should be tormented by the eternal flames of Gehenna and by unquenchable fire. And therefore, as we said above, if anyone communicates with the traditors, he shall have no share with us in the heavenly kingdoms.” Thus each of those in communion with this declaration hastened toward the glory of suffering, and every martyr sealed it with his own blood as a final testimony. Thereafter the holy Church follows the martyrs and detests the traditors of accursed treachery.

[Note: [Col. 0701D]

XIX. *Pannus illotus* (“an unwashed cloth”). Thus the Colbert manuscript. The editions have *panis luctus* (“bread of mourning”). This latter reading is also found in Hosea in all editions. I do not know, however, whence this reading arose in the old manuscript. But the following words confirm it [Col. 0702D], where, in place of what is read in the common manuscripts of Hosea, “all who eat it shall be defiled,” the old manuscript has: “everyone who touches it shall be polluted.”]

XIX. Therefore, since these things are so, who is endowed with knowledge of divine law, furnished with faith, distinguished by devotion, holy in religion, and mindful of God the Judge, who would distinguish truth from error, separate treachery from faith, and exclude feigned pretence from certain and unblemished holiness; who would separate the fallen from the steadfast, the wounded from the sound, the guilty from the just, the condemned from the innocent, [Col. 0701D] the betrayer from the keeper of the law, the denier of Christ’s name from the confessor, the persecutor from the Lord’s martyr—and yet suppose that the Church of martyrs and the conventicles of traditors are one and the same? Surely no one; for these things are so opposed and contrary to one another as light to darkness, life to death, a holy angel to the devil, Christ to Antichrist. For the Apostle Paul says: “I speak as to children: be enlarged also yourselves, and do not be yoked with unbelievers. For what participation [Col. 0702A] has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What share has the believer with the unbeliever? And what agreement has the temple of God with idols? But you are the temple of the living God. For he says: ‘Because I shall dwell in them and walk among them; and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. Therefore depart from their midst and be separated,’ says Almighty God, ‘and do not touch what is unclean; and I shall receive you, and I shall be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me,’ says the Lord Almighty” (2 Cor. 6).

For this reason the conspiracy of traditors, the house of hypocrites, and the judgment of the Pharisees must always be fled and avoided by the good and devout. Would that those spiritually born as the adopted sons and daughters of God in the holy Church might worthily succeed, and not, immersed in others’ crimes, [Col. 0702B] acquire darkness for light and death for life, destruction for salvation. For such is the Church of the Lord: always one and unique; it cannot be divided against itself and into two parts. Yet after the dreadful night of persecution and the pestilential storms of tyrants, the devil devised the most cunning artifice of fraud for the deception of the innocent and the plundering of peoples: those whom he had been unable to swallow up in the open ruin of persecution, and whom he had been unable to retain for everlasting destruction in a sacrilegious world, enslaved to the service of idols by the bonds of sins, he might destroy by joining them to himself through polluted acts of handing over, under the pretext of most holy religion.

Thus their false sacred rite and counterfeit mysteries are celebrated not so much for the salvation as for the destruction of the wretched, when a sacrilegious man raises an altar, a profane man celebrates sacraments, a guilty man baptizes, a wounded man heals, a persecutor venerates martyrs, a traditor reads the Gospels, and a burner of the divine testaments promises the inheritance of heaven. The Lord rebukes and reproves such men in the Gospel, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has become one, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves” (Matt. 25). And the prophet, rejecting their polluted sacrifices, says: “Their sacrifices are like an unwashed cloth. Everyone who touches it shall be polluted” (Hos. 9). And likewise through Haggai, most illustrious among the prophets: “Ask the priests concerning the law,” says the Lord. “If a man carries holy flesh in the fold of his garment, and the fold of his garment touches some portion [Col. 0702D] of bread, wine, or oil, will it be sanctified?” And the priests said, “No.” And Haggai said: “If one defiled in soul touches any of these things, will it be defiled?” And the priests said: “It will be defiled.” And Haggai said: “So is this people, and so is this nation before me, says the Lord; and everyone who approaches there shall be defiled” (Hag. 2).

XX. Therefore the corrupt congregation of all who are polluted must be fled and execrated; and the glorious succession of the most blessed martyrs must be sought by all. This is the holy Church, one and true catholic Church, from which the martyrs came and by whom the divine testaments were preserved. For it alone broke the assault of hostile persecution; it preserved the Lord’s law even to the shedding of blood. Within it, through the presence of the Holy Spirit, the powers of the holy people are manifested; baptism is accomplished by the Savior; eternal life is restored. For God is always graciously present with them, the Lord Christ rejoices with them, and the Holy Spirit exults—victor in the confessors, triumpher in the martyrs. Finally, since neither Mensurius nor his agent Caecilianus would cease from this monstrous cruelty, while the proconsul Anulinus and the other persecutors were meanwhile occupied with other affairs, these blessed martyrs, [Col. 0703B] deprived of bodily food, gradually and at intervals of days yielded to their natural condition, compelled by the atrocity of hunger, and passed with the palm of martyrdom into the starry kingdoms, through the grace of our Lord Jesus, who reigns with the Father for ages of ages. Amen.

## THE SAME ACTS FROM THE EDITION OF THEODORIC RUINART
