Collated from one manuscript codex of Saint Cornelius at Compiègne, one of the monastery of Saint Peter at Préaux, one of Saint Benedict at Fleury, one of the Reverend Fathers Celestines of Paris, one of the Reverend Fathers Feuillants, and the editions of Baluze and the Bollandists.

## NOTICE OF THEODORIC RUINART ON THE ACTS OF SS. SATURNINUS AND HIS COMPANIONS

[Col. 0703C]

I. Although the names of Saturninus and the other martyrs of whom we speak here are not expressly found in Saint Augustine, nevertheless no one doubts that they are the very persons whose Acts were produced by the Donatists and were acknowledged and received as genuine by the Catholics at the Conference of Carthage, held in 411 between Catholic and Donatist bishops. The Catholics used these Acts against the Donatists to show that, even during the time of persecution, a council of twelve bishops could have been assembled, since Christians then held *collectae* and sacred gatherings. Augustine reports this in the *Brief Account of the Conference*, day 3, chapter 17: “The Catholics,” he says, “replied that it was much easier for twelve men to have assembled in a house [Col. 0703D] at a time when gatherings of the people were customarily held, even though persecution raged, as was shown by the very records of the martyrs, who confessed in their sufferings that they had held a *collecta* and the *dominicum*.”

II. But these Acts, which at that time were considered pure and genuine, were shortly afterward somewhat corrupted by the Donatists so as to remove the names of the consuls. By adding a short preface at the beginning and a longer appendix at the end, they inserted into them many calumnies against Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, and against other Catholics. Nevertheless, the material recorded from the public examinations by the notaries, or at least that which the compiler there reports as taken from the public Acts, remained whole and untouched; he himself attests: “they were taken [Col. 0704A] [from them].” Since these may, as Baronius says, be read without stumbling, once the Donatists’ additions have been removed, it seemed proper to publish them. Anyone who desires more should consult the most learned Baluze, who in volume II of his *Miscellanea* presents the complete collection of the Donatist author. Moreover, we have prepared this edition of ours by collating the manuscript codices and printed editions together.

III. From Augustine, in the passage cited above, we learn the time when these martyrs suffered. There he reports, in these words, the names of the consuls which the Donatists withheld from us: “The records of the martyrs, which showed the time of the persecution, were made under the consuls Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth, on the day before the Ides of February”—that is, in the year 304, on 12 February. Usuard commemorates these martyrs on that day, whereas the Roman Martyrology entered them on the preceding day, for some reason unknown to me. But the date there designates the examination, not the completion of their martyrdom, as is clear from the Acts. For we know nothing of their death except what the Donatist author reports in these words: “While the proconsul Anulinus and the other persecutors were meanwhile occupied with other affairs, these blessed martyrs, deprived of bodily food, gradually and at intervals of days yielded to their natural condition, compelled by the atrocity of hunger, and passed with the palm of martyrdom into the starry kingdoms, through the grace of our Lord Jesus, who with the Father, etc.” The title of the Acts in the Colbert, Compiègne, and Préaux manuscript codices agrees with this, and for that reason we have prefixed it to the Acts. Indeed, in the Acts themselves the martyrs are repeatedly said to have been shut up [Col. 0704C] in prison and reserved or appointed for a suffering worthy of them.

The Donatist writer is also supported by the fact that these holy martyrs are celebrated in the Carthaginian calendar not on one day but on different days, indeed in different months. For Rogatus is entered on the … day before the Kalends of July; Felix, Eva, and Regiola on the third day before the Kalends of September; Ampelius on the day before the Kalends of the same month; Januarius on the … day before the Kalends of October; and finally Victoria on the … day before the Kalends of November. Yet it may be doubted whether the Januarius mentioned here belongs to the number of these martyrs of whom we are now speaking. He appears rather to be Januarius, bishop of Benevento, who suffered at Puteoli near Naples with Sosius, whose feast is celebrated in the same calendar on the following day. Likewise, several women named Victoria suffered in Africa; Augustine praises one of them among the twenty martyrs who had a most celebrated basilica at Hippo, and names her with Valeriana and Bishop Fidentius in Sermon 325, which is entitled concerning those same twenty martyrs.

IV. Furthermore, from the replies of Secundus, bishop of Tigisis, to Mensurius of Carthage, we learn that several martyrs also died in Numidia because of the sacred books. There, according to the testimony of Saint Augustine in the *Brief Account of the Conference*, day 3, chapter 13, “Secundus recounts what the persecutors did in Numidia, and how those who were arrested, refusing to hand over the holy Scriptures, suffered many evils, were tortured by very severe punishments, and were killed.” These things occurred under Florus, whom Optatus, in book III against Parmenian, calls the persecutor of Numidia.

## ACTS OF THE HOLY MARTYRS SATURNINUS, DATIVUS, AND VERY MANY OTHERS IN AFRICA

Collated from manuscript codices and printed editions.

[Col. 0705A]

Here begin the confessions and acts of the martyrs Saturninus the presbyter, Felix, Dativus, Ampelius, and the others written below, who, because of the *collectae* and the Lord’s Scriptures, confessed the Lord at Carthage under Anulinus, then proconsul of Africa, on the day before the Ides of February; and who poured out their most blessed blood in different places and at distinct times.

I. In the time of Diocletian and Maximian the devil declared war upon the Christians in this manner: he demanded that the most sacred testaments of the Lord (*sacramenta*, Colbert manuscript) and the divine Scriptures [Col. 0705B] be surrendered for burning; that the Lord’s basilicas be destroyed; and that sacred rites and most holy assemblies celebrated to the Lord be forbidden. But the army of the Lord God did not endure so monstrous a command and recoiled from the sacrilegious order. At once it took up the weapons of faith and descended into battle, to fight not so much against human beings as against the devil.

Although some fell from the hinge of faith by handing over to pagans the Lord’s Scriptures and the divine testaments to be burned in profane fires, very many others, filled with God, ended bravely by preserving them and willingly pouring out their own blood for them. Having overcome and laid low the devil, they bore the victorious palm in their suffering; and all the martyrs sealed with their own blood the judgment against the traditors and their associates, by which they had rejected them from the communion of the Church (Préaux manuscript: “would reject them”). [Col. 0705C] For it could not be right that martyrs and traditors should be together in the Church of God.

[Note: [Col. 0705D]

II. “*Reperiebat*” (“found”). Thus the Compiègne codex; other manuscripts and the printed editions have *repererat* (“had found”).

“Abitinensis.” Thus the Compiègne codex with two Henschenian manuscripts. Other printed editions and manuscripts have “Alutinensis”; and so wherever this name recurs in the Acts. But Alutina, if it was ever a city, is unknown; Abitina, however, is an episcopal city in the proconsular province. Its bishops Victor and Maximus are mentioned in the Conference of Carthage. See Augustine, book VII against the Donatists and book III against the letter of Parmenian. Moreover, Saturninus, bishop from Avitinae, was present at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian.

“Octavi.” Thus the Colbert manuscript I, the Trier manuscript in Henschenius, and the Celestine manuscript. The Compiègne manuscript has *Octavii*. The remaining manuscripts and printed editions have *Occani*.

“*Dominicum*.” Thus the Compiègne manuscript with the Bollandists; others have “the Lord’s sacraments.”

[Col. 0706D] “Aeva.” The Bollandists: “Primaeva.” But it should be read “Prima, Eva,” as is clear from the manuscripts and the Carthaginian calendar, where the third day before the Kalends of September reads: “of Felix, Eva, and Regiola.” Baronius and Surius have “Fua” for Eva. The Fleury codex has “Euva.”

“Dantus.” Baronius: “Datus.” Baluze: “Elautus.” The Feuillant and Préaux manuscripts: “Clautus.”

“Major.” Margarita and Major appear to be distinct persons; the latter is not a second Margarita.

“Victorinus.” Baluze, with the Feuillant and Préaux manuscripts: “Victorianus.”

“Herectina.” The Bollandists have “Heredina” here; in the title, “Beredina.” The Préaux manuscript: “Hecretina.”

“*Item*” (“likewise”). Only the Bollandists have *item*. Hence Baluze has “a second Matrona,” as though there were another Matrona.]

II. Therefore immense bands of confessors flew from every direction toward the field of contest; and wherever each found the enemy, there he established the Lord’s camp. Thus, in the city of Abitina, in the house of Octavius Felix, when the trumpet of war sounded, the glorious martyrs raised the Lord’s standards. As they everywhere celebrated the *dominicum* according to custom, they were seized by the magistrates of the colony and by the stationarius soldier himself: Saturninus the presbyter, with his four children—namely Saturninus the younger and Felix, readers; Maria, a consecrated virgin; and the child Hilarion (Bollandists: Hilarian)—and likewise Dativus, [Col. 0706A] also called Senator; Felix; another Felix; Emeritus; Ampelius; Rogatianus; Quintus; Maximianus; Thelica; Rogatianus; Rogatus; Januarius; Cassianus; Victorianus; Vincentius; Caecilianus; Restituta; Prima; Eva; Rogatianus; Givalius (otherwise Guinalius); Rogatus; Pomponia; Secunda; Januaria; Saturnina; Martinus; Dantus; Felix; Margarita; Major; Honorata; Regiola (Bollandists: Regula); Victorinus; Pelusius; Faustus; Dacianus; Matrona; Caecilia; Victoria; Herectina; Secunda; likewise Matrona; and Januaria. When seized, they were brought joyfully to the forum.

[Note: [Col. 0706D]

III. “*Ipsius*” (“his own”). Only the Bollandists have *ipsius*.]

III. Dativus was the first to go to this first field of contest, the noble senator whom holy parents had begotten for the heavenly senate. Saturninus the presbyter also went, surrounded [Col. 0706B] by his numerous progeny; some of his offspring he destined to share martyrdom with him, while others he left to the Church as pledges of his own name. The Lord’s host followed them, in which shone the splendor of heavenly weapons: the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, and the two-edged (variant: flashing) sword, the word of God. Strengthened by their protection, they promised their brothers the hope of victory.

But now they had reached the forum of the aforesaid city. There, at their first encounter, they won the palm of confession by the magistrates’ formal accusation. For in this forum heaven had already fought for the Lord’s Scriptures when Fundanus, formerly bishop of that city, handed over the Lord’s Scriptures to be burned. When the sacrilegious magistrate set them to the fire, suddenly rain poured down from a clear sky; the fire applied to the holy Scriptures was extinguished; hail was unleashed; and the whole region itself was devastated, as the elements raged, on behalf of the Lord’s Scriptures.

IV. From this city, therefore, the martyrs of Christ received their longed-for first chains. Sent on to Carthage, cheerful and glad, they sang hymns and psalms to the Lord throughout the journey. When they came before the tribunal of Anulinus, then proconsul, and stood steadfastly and bravely in battle array, they repelled the devil’s raging assault with the Lord’s constancy. But since the devil’s fury could not prevail against all Christ’s soldiers at once, he summoned them one by one to contests. I shall recount the struggles of these contests not so much in my own words as in the words of the martyrs, so that both the boldness of the raging enemy may be known in the tortures and [Col. 0707A] in the sacrilegious attack itself, and the power of Christ the all-powerful Lord may be praised in the martyrs’ endurance and in their confession itself.

[Note: [Col. 0707D]

V. “*Dominicum*.” Thus the Compiègne codex, correctly, as is clear not only from nos. 7 and 8 below, but from Augustine himself in the *Brief Account of the Conference*, day III, chapter 17: “As was shown by the very records of the martyrs, who confessed in their sufferings that they had held a *collecta* and the *dominicum*.” Tertullian, in *On Flight*, appears to distinguish the two: “But how shall we assemble? How shall we celebrate the Lord’s solemnities?” *Collecta* applies to any gathering; *dominicum*, however, denotes the sacred mysteries. Cyprian, Letter to Caecilius: “Must we therefore celebrate the *dominicum* after supper, so as thus [to celebrate] the mystical cup,” etc. The Bollandists have “a *collecta* or *dominicum*”; other printed editions and manuscripts, “the Lord’s *collecta*.”

[Col. 0708D] “*Praecidi*” (“to be cut/raked”). Thus Compiègne; the other manuscripts and printed editions have *praeparare* (“to prepare”). By the term *officium* are denoted public attendants who served proconsuls, governors, or magistrates in public functions; hence *officiales*.

“Thelica.” Compiègne and the Celestine manuscript: “Tazelita.” Préaux: “Talezita”; and so afterward, although in the general enumeration they have Thelica, like the rest.]

V. Therefore, when they were presented to the proconsul by his staff, and it was reported that the Christians sent by the magistrates of Abitina had, contrary to the prohibition of the emperors and Caesars, celebrated a *collecta* and the *dominicum*, the proconsul first questioned Dativus as to his status and whether he had held a *collecta*. When he professed himself a Christian and declared that he had been at the *collecta*, he was asked who had organized that most holy gathering; and the staff was immediately ordered to raise him upon the rack and cut him while stretched out. But as the executioners carried out their cruel orders with savage speed, and stood raging in their words (Compiègne: “in [Col. 0707B] their fingers”), and with their claws raised over the martyr’s bared flanks for wounding, the most courageous martyr Thelica suddenly threw himself into the midst of the tortures (variant: placed himself beneath them) and cried out: “We are Christians; we,” he said, “assembled.” Immediately the fury of the proconsul blazed up; groaning, grievously wounded by the spiritual sword, he beat the martyr of Christ with very severe blows, stretched him when suspended upon the rack, and tore him with whistling claws.

But, in the very midst of the executioners’ fury, the most glorious martyr Thelica poured out to the Lord prayers of this kind with thanksgiving: “Thanks be to God. In your name, Christ, Son of God, deliver your servants.”

[Note: [Col. 0708D]

VI. “Victor in spirit.” The Bollandists: “his soul victorious.” Baronius and Surius, however: “he proclaimed victoriously in speech.”]

VI. As he prayed thus, the proconsul said: “Who is the organizer of your assembly with you?” While the executioner raged more cruelly [Col. 0707C], he answered in a clear voice: “Saturninus the presbyter—and all [of us].” O martyr giving primacy to all! For he did not set the presbyter above his brothers, but joined the brothers to the presbyter in partnership of confession. Therefore, when the proconsul sought Saturninus, he pointed him out—not because he betrayed one whom he saw fighting side by side with him against the devil, but so as to show him that he had fully celebrated the *collecta*, since the presbyter too had been with them.

Blood flowed with the voice of the man praying to the Lord; and mindful of the Gospel commandments, the martyr asked forgiveness for his enemies amid the very tearing of his body. Amid the most grievous agonies of his wounds, he reproached both torturers and proconsul with these words: “You act unjustly, unhappy men; you act against God. Most high God, do not assent to them in these sins. You sin, unhappy men; you act against God. Keep the commandments of the Most High. [Col. 0708A] You act unjustly, unhappy men; you tear innocent people. We are not murderers; we have committed no deceit. God, have mercy. I give you thanks. For your name, Lord, grant endurance. Deliver your servants from the captivity of this world. I give you thanks, nor am I sufficient to give you thanks.”

And when his sides, struck with the blows of the claws, were more deeply furrowed, and a stream of blood flowed out in violent torrents, he heard the proconsul saying to him: “You will begin to feel what you must suffer.” He added: “Unto glory. I give thanks to the God of kingdoms. The eternal kingdom appears, the incorruptible kingdom. Lord Jesus Christ, we are Christians; we serve you. You are our hope; you are the hope of Christians. Most holy God, most high God, almighty God, for your name we render praises to you, Lord God [Col. 0708B] almighty.”

While he prayed such things, the devil through the judge said to him: “You ought to have observed the command of the emperors and Caesars.” His body now exhausted, yet victor in spirit, he proclaimed in strong and steadfast speech: “I care for nothing except the law of God, which I have learned. I keep it; for it I shall die; in it I shall be perfected; apart from it there is no other.” Thus by the words of the most glorious martyr it was Anulinus himself who was more tormented in his tortures. At last, his fury satiated with savagery, he said, “Spare him,” and, having shut the martyr in prison, appointed him for a suffering worthy of him.

[Note: [Col. 0708D]

VII. “Fortunatianus.” The name is not given in Baronius, Surius, and Baluze, nor in the Feuillant and Préaux manuscripts. Some codices have “Fortunatius.”]

VII. After him Dativus was raised up by the Lord for the contest. He had watched Thelica’s most courageous battle from close by while he himself hung stretched upon the rack. And when, repeatedly proclaiming in a strong voice that he was a Christian [Col. 0708C] and had held a *collecta*, Fortunatianus emerged, brother of Victoria, the most holy martyr: a man indeed in a toga, but at that time estranged from the most holy worship of Christian religion. He thus far assailed the martyr hanging on the rack with profane words: “This is the man, O lord,” he said, “who, during the absence of our father, while we were studying here, seduced our sister Victoria and brought her from the most splendid city of Carthage all the way with him to the colony of Abitina, together with Secunda and Restituta. He never entered our house except when he was there enticing the girlish minds by certain persuasions.”

But Victoria, the most renowned martyr of the Lord, did not endure that her colleague and fellow martyr, the senator, should be falsely attacked; immediately bursting forth in Christian freedom, she said: “I did not depart at anyone’s persuasion, nor did I come with him to Abitina. This I can prove through the citizens. [Col. 0709A] I did everything of my own accord and will. For I was at the *collecta*, and I celebrated the *dominicum* with the brothers, because I am a Christian.”

Then the shameless advocate heaped insults upon the martyr. In response, the glorious martyr, from the rack, refuted everything with a truthful answer. Amid this, Anulinus, blazing with anger, ordered the claws to be pressed into the martyr. Immediately the executioners found his flanks naked and prepared for blows, covered in bloody wounds. Savage hands flew upon him, swifter than the hasty orders; with skins broken and entrails torn apart, they laid open the hidden parts of his breast, by cruelty bent upon offering them to the impious gaze of profane men. Yet amid this the martyr’s mind stood unmoved; though limbs were broken, entrails torn, and flanks laid waste, the martyr’s spirit nevertheless remained whole and unshaken. Finally, mindful of his rank, Dativus, also called Senator, poured out prayers to the Lord in this voice while the executioner raged: “O Christ the Lord, may I not be put to shame.” By these words the most blessed martyr obtained from the Lord what he had asked as easily as he asked it briefly.

[Note: [Col. 0709D]

VIII. “Spare him.” Other editions: “the tongue wishing to spare.” Feuillant and Compiègne codices: “the proconsul … [with] tongue unwilling to spare”; Baluze: “willing.”

“*Inquit*” (“he said”). The Bollandists add: “in accordance with what you profess.” [Col. 0710D] The Compiègne manuscript has “you were able” in place of “you profess.”]

VIII. Accordingly, the proconsul’s mind shaken, the word “Spare him” sprang from his tongue—that is, he said it. The executioners ceased. For it was not lawful that a martyr of Christ should be tortured in the case of Victoria, his fellow martyr. And when Pompeianus too, a cruel accuser advancing against him with an unworthy suspicion, joined a calumnious charge, he was scorned and rebuffed (other codices: “struck”) by the martyr. “What are you doing in this place, devil? What do you still dare against Christ’s martyrs?” By the Lord’s senator and martyr, both authority and the fury of the court had been overcome.

But because that most illustrious martyr ought also to be tortured for Christ, when asked whether he had been at the *collecta*, he confessed steadfastly and said that he had come when the *collecta* was being held, had celebrated the *dominicum* with the brethren in fitting religious devotion, and that the organizer of that most holy gathering was not one person alone (in another text, *non* is absent). Thus he again stirred the proconsul more fiercely against himself. As the latter’s cruelty revived, the martyr’s dignity was doubled, his body being scored again by the claws. But amid the most savage agonies of his wounds the martyr repeated his former prayer: “I beg you, Christ, may I not be put to shame. What have I done? Saturninus is our presbyter.”

IX. While his sides were scraped by hooked claws, as the cruel and savage executioner’s teaching hand demonstrated, [Col. 0709D] Saturninus the presbyter was summoned to battle. Contemplating the heavenly kingdom and considering what his fellow martyrs suffered to be very small and light, he too began the contest in this manner. When the proconsul said, “You acted against the command of the emperors and Caesars in gathering all these people,” the presbyter Saturninus answered, prompted by the Spirit of the Lord: “Securely, we celebrated the *dominicum*.” The proconsul said: “Why?” He answered: “Because the *dominicum* cannot be omitted.” [Col. 0710A]

As soon as he had said this, he was immediately ordered to be made ready beside Dativus. Meanwhile Dativus watched the mangling of his own body rather than felt it; and, with mind and spirit fixed upon the Lord, he reckoned the body’s pain as nothing, but prayed only to the Lord, saying: “Come to my aid, I beg, Christ; have pity; save my soul; guard my spirit, so that I may not be put to shame. I beg you, Christ, grant endurance.” When the proconsul said to him: “From this most splendid city you ought rather to have called others to sound judgment, and not acted against the command of the emperors and Caesars,” he cried out more strongly and steadily: “I am a Christian.” By this utterance the devil was overcome. “Spare him,” he said; and thrusting him into prison, he reserved the martyr for a suffering worthy of him.

[Note: [Col. 0710D]

X. “*Commonuit*” (“he urged on”). Baluze and Préaux: “he stirred up the terror of his wrath.”]

[Col. 0710B] X. But the presbyter Saturninus, sprinkled with the fresh blood of the martyrs (variant: “with fresh martyr’s blood”), as he hung on the rack, was urged to persist in the faith of those in whose blood he stood. When he was asked whether he himself was the organizer and whether he had assembled them all, and said, “Yes, I was present at the *collecta*,” the reader Emeritus sprang forth for the contest. While the presbyter was fighting, he said: “I am the organizer, in whose house the *collectae* were held.”

But the proconsul, who had already been defeated so often, recoiled from Emeritus’s onslaught; nevertheless, turning to the presbyter, he said: “Why did you act against the command, Saturninus?” Saturninus answered: “The *dominicum* cannot be omitted. Thus the law commands.” Then the proconsul said: “Yet you ought not to have scorned what was forbidden, but rather to have observed it and not acted against the command [Col. 0710C] of the emperors.” With a voice long practised upon martyrs, he urged the torturer to rage; and he was obeyed with no sluggish compliance.

For the executioners rushed upon the aged body of the presbyter and, as their rage spread, tore it apart into lamentable punishments and torments of a new kind, exquisitely devised against the priest of God, breaking the connection of his sinews. One might see the executioners raging with ravenous hunger as though toward a feast of wounds; and, with the entrails exposed, the bared bones showing pale amid the redness of blood, to the horror of the onlookers. And lest, amid the executioners’ delays, the expelled soul might abandon the body while it hung under punishment, the presbyter prayed to the Lord in this voice: “I beg you, Christ, hear me. I give you thanks, God. Command that I be beheaded. I beg you, Christ, have mercy. Son of God, come to my aid.”

The proconsul said to him: “Why did you act against the command?” The presbyter answered: “Thus the law commands; thus the law teaches.” O divine answer, greatly worthy of admiration and praise, of the presbyter-teacher! Even in tortures the presbyter proclaims the most holy law, for which he willingly endured punishments. Finally Anulinus, terrified by the word “law,” said, “Spare him”; and returning him to prison custody, appointed him for the desired suffering.

[Note: [Col. 0711D]

XI. “*Memoriam*” (“the record”). Here the word *memoria* appears to mean the register in which legal cases conducted before the proconsul were entered. Hence those who kept instruments of this kind were called *memoriales*. On the *memoriales*, see Du Cange’s Glossary.]

XI. Then, when Emeritus was brought forward, the proconsul said: “Were *collectae* held in your house against the commands [Col. 0711A] of the emperors?” Emeritus, filled with the Holy Spirit, replied: “In my house we celebrated the *dominicum*.” The proconsul said: “Why did you allow them to enter?” He replied: “Because they are my brothers, and I could not forbid them.” “But,” he said, “you ought to have forbidden them.” He replied: “I could not” (variant: “I could”), “because without the *dominicum* we cannot exist.”

He too was immediately ordered to be stretched upon the rack and tortured while stretched out. As he endured powerful blows from a newly assigned executioner, he said: “I beg you, Christ, come to my aid. You act against God’s command, unhappy men!” The proconsul interjected: “You ought not to have received them.” He replied: “I could not but receive my brothers.” But the sacrilegious proconsul said: “The command of the emperors and Caesars came first.” The most devout martyr answered: “God is greater, not the emperors. [Col. 0711B] I beg you, Christ, I offer you praises. Christ the Lord, grant endurance.”

As he prayed thus, the proconsul cast this at him: “Do you then have any Scriptures in your house?” He answered: “I have them, but in my heart.” The proconsul said: “Do you have them in your house, or not?” The martyr Emeritus said: “I have them in my heart. I beg you, Christ, [accept] praises. Deliver me, Christ; I suffer in your name. I suffer briefly; I suffer gladly. Christ the Lord, may I not be put to shame.”

O martyr mindful of the Apostle, who possessed the law of the Lord written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts. O martyr, fitting and most diligent guardian of the sacred law, who, recoiling from the crime of the traditors, placed the Lord’s Scriptures in the hidden places [Col. 0711C] of his breast lest he lose them. When this became known, the proconsul said: “Spare him.” Having entered his declaration into the record together with the confessions of the others, he said: “All of you shall pay the punishments you deserve according to your confession.”

[Note: [Col. 0712D]

XII. “*Confusus*” (“confounded”). The Bollandists: “shaken by that confession.”

“*Ad siderea*” (“to the starry [realms]”). The Bollandists: “near the very tribunals.”]

XII. But by now the beastly rage, having glutted itself with the tortures of the martyrs in its blood-stained maw, was growing faint. Yet when Felix, both in name and in suffering, had advanced into the battle, and the entire battle-line of the Lord remained uncorrupted and unconquered, the tyrant—his mind cast down, his voice subdued, his soul and body broken—said: “I hope that you will choose rather that course by which you may live, so that you preserve the commands.” Against this the confessors of the Lord, the unconquered martyrs of Christ, spoke as if with one voice: “We are Christians; we cannot but keep the holy law of the Lord even to the shedding of blood.” [Col. 0711D]

Struck by this declaration, the enemy said to Felix: “I do not ask whether you are a Christian, but whether you have held an assembly (*collecta*), or possess any writings.” O foolish and laughable question of the judge! “Whether you are a Christian,” he says, “be silent about that; and he added: ‘Have you attended the assembly? Answer!’—as though a Christian could exist without the Lord’s service (*dominicum*), or the Lord’s service be celebrated without a Christian. Do you not know, Satan, that the Christian is constituted in the Lord’s service, and the Lord’s service in the Christian, so that neither can exist without the other? When you hear the name, recognize the Lord’s gathering; and when you hear of the assembly, recognize the name. In short, you are recognized by the martyr and mocked; you are put to shame by such an answer.”

“We have most gloriously celebrated the assembly,” he said; “we always gather on the Lord’s day to read the writings of the Lord.” Confounded deeply by this confession, Anulinus united with the heavenly council the martyr—beaten with clubs until lifeless, hastening, his suffering completed, to the starry tribunals. But another Felix followed the blessed Felix, alike in name, confession, and suffering itself. For having entered the contest with equal courage, he too, shaken by the blows of clubs and committing his soul amid the torments of prison, was joined to the martyrdom of the former Felix. [Col. 0712B]

> **Note [Col. 0712D]**
>
> XIII. *Maximianus.* The Bollandists and the Compendium: *Maximus*.

XIII. After these, Ampelius, guardian of the law and most faithful keeper of the divine writings, undertook the contest. When the proconsul asked whether he had attended the assembly, he answered cheerfully and confidently, in an eager voice: “I held the assembly with the brethren; I celebrated the Lord’s service; and I have the writings of the Lord with me, but inscribed in my heart. Christ, I render praise to you. Hear me, Christ.”

Having said this, bruised about the neck, he was confined with his brethren in prison, as though already in the tabernacle of the Lord’s service (*dominicium*)—joyfully banished there with them (variant: “bound”). Rogatianus followed him: having confessed the Lord’s name, he was joined to the aforesaid brethren unharmed. Quintus, however, being brought forward, made a noble and magnificent confession of the Lord’s name; he was beaten with clubs and thrust into prison, reserved for a martyrdom worthy of him. [Col. 0712C]

Maximianus also followed him, equal in confession, similar in combat, and equal in the triumphs of victory. After him the younger Felix, proclaiming that the Lord’s service was the hope and salvation of Christians, when he likewise was beaten with clubs, said: “With devout mind I celebrated the Lord’s service; I held the assembly with the brethren, because I am a Christian.” By this confession he too deserved to be joined to the aforesaid brethren.

XIV. But the younger Saturninus, the holy offspring of Saturninus the presbyter and martyr, hastened eagerly into the desired contest, striving to equal his father’s most glorious courage. When the proconsul, raging at the devil’s prompting, said to him: “And you, Saturninus, were present?” Saturninus answered: “I am a Christian.” “I do not ask you that,” he said, “but whether you performed the Lord’s service.” Saturninus answered: “I performed the Lord’s service, because Christ is the Saviour.”

Upon hearing the name “Saviour,” Anulinus blazed with anger, and renewed upon the son the rack once inflicted upon the father. Saturninus having been stretched out, he said: “What, Saturninus, do you profess? You see where you have been placed. Have you any writings?” He answered: “I am a Christian.” But the proconsul said: “I ask whether you assembled and whether you have writings?” [Col. 0713A] He answered: “I am a Christian. There is no other name after Christ which it is fitting for us to observe as holy.”

Enraged by this confession, the devil said: “Since you persist in your obstinacy, you must also be subjected to tortures. Say whether you possess any Scriptures.” And he said to the officials: “Torment him.” The executioners, wearied by the father’s wounds, went at the young man’s sides, and, while the father’s blood still moistened the claws, mingled it with the kindred blood of the son. One might see, through the furrows of gaping wounds in the son’s sides, the father’s blood, shed earlier, flowing forth, and the son’s gore, mingled with the father’s, streaming from the dripping claws.

But the young man, strengthened by the mingling of their natural blood, felt remedies rather than torments; and, gaining courage amid the tortures, cried out in most resolute tones: “I have the writings of the Lord, but in my heart. I pray, Christ, grant endurance. My hope is in you.” (Edition: “of life.”) Anulinus said: “Why were you acting contrary to the command?” He answered: “Because I am a Christian.” On hearing this, he said: “Spare him.” And at once the torture ceased, and he was confined in the company of his father.

XV. Meanwhile, as the hours slipped away, the day was sinking (perhaps: “turning”) into night; with the sun the tortures were spent, and the dark rage of the executioners failed (Bollandists: “was wearied”), declining together with the cruelty of their judge. But the legions of the Lord, in whom Christ, the everlasting light, shone with the flashing splendor of heavenly years, leapt forth into the contests more courageously and steadfastly.

But when the adversary of the Lord, defeated in the most glorious battles of so many martyrs and overcome in struggles so great and such as these—abandoned by day, overtaken by night, and with the rage of the executioners now failing—could no longer, utterly defeated, contend with each individual, he questioned the spirits of the whole army of the Lord and assailed the devoted minds of the confessors with this interrogation: “You have seen,” he said, “what those who persevered have endured, and what they still have to endure as they persist in their confession. Therefore, whoever among you wishes to obtain pardon, so that he may be saved, let him make a declaration.”

To this the confessors of the Lord, the glorious martyrs of Christ, joyful and triumphant together, inflamed not by the proconsul’s words but by the Holy Spirit through the victory of suffering, said more boldly and clearly, as if with one voice: “We are Christians.” By that declaration the devil was cast down and shaken (variant: “fell”). And Anulinus, confounded, thrust them all into prison and assigned those holy men to martyrdom. [Col. 0713D]

> **Note [Col. 0713D]**
>
> XVI. *Fugeret* (“might escape”). Baluzius and several manuscripts: “and that the parents might deliver her unwillingly to a bridegroom whom the girl would regard as a robber.”
>
> *Crinem* (“her hair”). From this Baluzius infers that women professing virginity did not then cut off their hair. The same is proved from Optatus, book VI, and Ambrose, *To a Fallen Virgin*, ch. 8. The custom in Egypt and Syria was otherwise, as Jerome relates in his letter to Sabinianus. On this matter see our Menard in his notes on the Gregorian Sacramentary, p. 212, and *History of Eastern Monasticism*, book I, ch. 12.

XVI. And lest the most devout sex of women and the flourishing choir of sacred virgins be deprived of the glory of so great a contest, all the women, with Christ the Lord helping them, joined battle with Victoria and were crowned.

For most holy Victoria among women, the flower of virgins, the ornament and glory of confessors—honorable in birth, most holy in religion, restrained in conduct; she in whom the good of nature shone forth in radiant chastity, while a faith and integrity of holiness more beautiful than bodily beauty answered to the beauty of her body—rejoiced to be restored to a second palm in the Lord’s martyrdom. [Col. 0714A]

For from infancy the bright signs of her chastity already shone forth; even in her tender years there appeared the most chaste rigor of her mind and a certain dignity of her future suffering. Finally, after perfect virginity had filled the mature period of life, when the girl, unwilling and resisting, was being forced by her parents into marriage, and her parents were delivering a bridegroom to her against her will, she secretly cast herself down a precipice, in order to escape the robber; borne up by supporting breezes, she was received unharmed into the bosom of the earth. Nor afterward would she have suffered even for Christ the Lord, had she then died for chastity alone.

Thus freed from the marriage torches, and having at once deceived both bridegroom and parents, she sprang out almost from the very midst of the wedding company and, an untouched virgin, fled to the Church, the sanctuary of chastity and harbor of modesty. There she preserved, in perpetual virginity and with unshaken modesty, the most sacred hair of a head consecrated and dedicated to God. [Col. 0714B] Therefore, hastening to martyrdom, she bore before her the flower of chastity—the palm—in her triumphant right hand.

When the proconsul asked what she professed, she answered in a clear voice: “I am a Christian.” And when Fortunatianus, her toga-clad brother, and her defender said that she had been led astray in mind by empty arguments, Victoria answered: “My mind is my own; I have never changed.” To this the proconsul said: “Do you wish to go with your brother Fortunatianus?” She answered: “I do not wish to, because I am a Christian; and those are my brethren who keep the commandments of God.” [Col. 0714C]

O maiden grounded in the authority of the divine law! O glorious virgin deservedly consecrated to the eternal King! O most blessed martyr, most renowned for her Gospel confession, who answered in the Lord’s own words: “These are my brethren who keep the commandments of God.”

When he heard this, Anulinus put aside the authority of the judge and lowered himself to persuasion of the girl. “Take thought for yourself,” he said. “For you see that your brother wishes to provide for your safety.” The martyr of Christ said to him: “My mind is my own; I have never changed. For I attended the assembly and celebrated the Lord’s service with the brethren, because I am a Christian.” As soon as Anulinus heard this, he blazed up, driven by fury; and, confining the most sacred maiden, the martyr of Christ, in prison with the others, he reserved them all for the Lord’s suffering. [Col. 0714D]

> **Note [Col. 0715D]**
>
> XVII. *Comam* (“your hair”). Thus Baluzius from the Colbert manuscript. The Fulda and Pratellus manuscripts agree. Other editions have *collum* (“your neck”), but how could one be dismissed after one’s neck had been cut off? The Compiègne manuscript: “I shall cut off your nose.”

> [Col. 0716D] *Laetantur* (“they rejoice”). There follows much fabricated by the Donatists against Mensurius and his deacon Caecilianus, later his successor in the see of Carthage; this is therefore omitted.

XVII. But Hilarianus still remained, one of the sons of Saturninus the presbyter and martyr; by great devotion he surpassed his tender age. Hurrying to be joined to his father’s and brothers’ triumphs, he did not so much dread the tyrant’s dreadful threats as count them for nothing. When he was asked: “Have you followed your father or your brothers?” immediately a boyish voice was heard from that small body, and the narrow breast of the child was wholly opened to confess the Lord in his answer: “I am a Christian, and of my own free will and choice I held the assembly with my father and my brothers.” [Col. 0715A]

You could hear the voice of Saturninus the martyr and father issuing through the channels of his dear son, and a tongue confessing Christ the Lord, made fearless by its brother’s example (variant in editions and manuscripts: “following [that example]”). But the foolish proconsul, failing to understand that it was not men but God who was fighting against him in the martyrs, and because he perceived great spirits in childish years, thought that a boy could be terrified by infantile torments.

“I shall cut off,” he said, “both your hair and your nose and your little ears, and thus dismiss you.” To this the boy Hilarianus, glorious through the courage of his father and brothers, who had already learned from his elders to despise torments, answered in a clear voice: “Whatever you wish to do, do it, because I am a Christian.” He too was immediately ordered to be received into prison; and Hilarianus’s voice was heard with great joy, saying: “Thanks be to God.” Here the struggle of the great contest is completed; here the devil is overcome and defeated; here the martyrs of Christ rejoice over their sufferings with the eternal gladness of future glory. [Col. 0715B]

## In the Year of the Lord 314

> **Note [Col. 0715D]**
>
> (1) But the matters narrated there belong to events that took place during the persecution, in the years 303 and 304.

## Proceedings for the Exoneration of Felix, Bishop of Aptunga, Who Ordained Caecilianus Bishop of Carthage, Held at Carthage before Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa, under the Consuls Volusianus and Annianus

Published by Papirius Massonus, also at the end of Optatus, and by Baluzius, *Miscellanies*, vol. II, p. 81, from an old manuscript formerly in the Thuan Library, now in the Colbert Library.

[Col. 0715C]

## Baluzius’s Notice on the Proceedings for the Exoneration of Bishop Felix, Etc.

We possessed one old copy of these proceedings from the Thuan Library, namely the very copy from which Papirius Massonus published the Conference of Carthage and these proceedings near the end of the preceding century. He had indeed placed them after the proceedings concerning Caecilianus’s exoneration, following the order and authority of that same old copy.

But both the chronology and the authority of Saint Augustine oppose this arrangement. For, although he had fallen into the same error, Augustine subsequently taught in *Retractations*, book II, ch. 27, that Felix’s acquittal ought to precede it:

> “We did not place the acquittal of Felix of Aptunga, Caecilianus’s ordainer, in the order which subsequently became clear to us upon careful examination of the consuls, but as though he had been acquitted after Caecilianus, whereas it occurred before.”

It is sufficiently clear that in this passage he refers to these proceedings concerning Felix and Caecilianus. Likewise Augustine himself says in the *Brief Record of the Third Day*, ch. 24:

> “One will find that Caecilianus was acquitted by the Emperor Constantine later than Felix’s case was examined and cleared by Aelianus the proconsul.”

This, however, must be understood of Caecilianus’s second and third acquittals, not of the first, by which Caecilianus was acquitted at the Roman council, as Henricus Valesius rightly observes in his dissertation on the Donatist schism, ch. 11. For Augustine himself teaches us thus in Letter 152, written in the name of the Council of Cirta to the Donatists:

> “For anyone who now carefully observes the order of consuls and days that is set forth will find that first Caecilianus was cleared by episcopal judgment. [Col. 0716B] Then, not long afterward, the case of Felix of Aptunga was examined by Aelianus the proconsul, where he was established to be innocent; in that case Ingentius was ordered to be sent to the imperial court. And long afterward the Emperor himself heard and decided the case between the parties.”

See the same author in *On the One Baptism against Petilian*, ch. 16, and in *To the Donatists after the Conference*, ch. 33.

Moreover, Valesius rightly observes that the greater part of these proconsular proceedings has perished through the injury of time—namely the earlier part, which contained the municipal records and the interrogations and declarations of the curators and the official in charge of the station. These inquiries were ordered by Emperor Constantine so that every opportunity for accusation might be removed from the Donatists, who complained very frequently to Constantine about the Roman synod or the judgment of Pope Miltiades, asserting that the bishops had not heard the whole case there.

For Miltiades had passed over in silence Felix, bishop of Aptunga, and Caecilianus’s other ordainers, whom the Donatists alleged to be guilty of having surrendered the Scriptures. Therefore the emperor, wishing, as I have said, to remove from them every pretext for accusation, ordered Verus—as he is called in Saint Augustine, or rather Lucrinus Verinus, acting as vicar prefect in Africa—to inquire carefully into the charge of surrendering the Scriptures brought against Felix.

But when Verinus began to execute the emperor’s command, he was seized by ill health and, as Constantine writes to Probianus, was subsequently obliged to withdraw from hearing the matter. Therefore Aelianus, proconsul of Africa, acting in his stead, judged that the affair ought to be brought under his own examination and decision, as Constantine says. From these words it is inferred that Aelianus did not assume the functions of the vicar by the emperor’s command, as Valesius thought, but of his own accord, on account, namely, of the vicar’s sudden illness.

Yet the opinion of that most distinguished man might be supported from book I of Optatus, where it is written that Constantine had written to Aelianus the proconsul that, public necessities being set aside, there should be a public inquiry into the conduct of Felix of Aptunga; and from Augustine’s Letter 162, where it is written that Felix of Aptunga was cleared in proconsular proceedings at that emperor’s command.

But these words should be understood thus: since Constantine had written to Verinus the vicar concerning an investigation of the accusations made against Felix, and Verinus had been prevented by illness from obeying the sacred command, Aelianus the proconsul, acting in his stead and undertaking the examination and judgment of this cause, is said to have acted at the command of the same emperor because he performed what the emperor had commanded, even though no special rescripts had been issued to him.

For how could Constantine have been informed soon enough after Verinus’s illness—which, from the first law of the Theodosian Code, *On Curators of the Calendar*, may not unreasonably be inferred to have occurred in the last days of January or at the beginning of February—and how, I say, could a new rescript from Gaul have reached Aelianus before the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March? Therefore, as I have said, the words of Optatus and Augustine must be interpreted generously: that is, Aelianus investigated Felix’s case under the authority of the rescript given to Verinus the vicar, whose functions he discharged because of the exigency of the time. [Col. 0718A]

Later, however, the Donatists criticized the proceedings against Felix because, though he was a bishop, he was cleared by proconsular rather than ecclesiastical judgment. Augustine vigorously refutes this accusation in the same letter. They also held it against him, as Augustine teaches in the *Brief Record of the Third Day*, ch. 24, that he was absent when Aelianus investigated his case; and they said that he ought to have been cleared while present, as is read in the Third Conference of Carthage, ch. 571. Against this, the Catholics replied in ch. 574 that Felix’s being cleared while absent was a greater proof of his innocence.

## Proceedings for the Exoneration of Felix

> **Note [Col. 0717B]**
>
> *Autumnitani.* That is, the Aptungitani or Aptungenses, as frequently in Saint Augustine. But in the old manuscript both here and below those elsewhere called Aptungitani are called Autumnitani. Indeed, the most distinguished scholars who prepared the most recent edition of Saint Augustine’s letters note on Letter 43 (which is 162 in the old editions) that, where Felix of Aptunga is there read, the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus and ten manuscript codices have “Felix of Autumna.”
>
> Aptunga, moreover, was a municipality in the proconsular province, as is clear from this passage of Augustine in the *Brief Record of the Third Day*, ch. 16, where he says that it is the custom of the Catholic Church that the bishop of the Church of Carthage be ordained not by bishops of Numidia but by those nearer at hand.
>
> *Aelii Paulini.* There is no doubt that this passage is seriously corrupt. For at the time when these proceedings took place, Aelius Paulinus was not vicar of Africa, as is clear even from Constantine’s letter to Probianus. Certainly Paulinus had been invested with that office much earlier, namely in the year of Christ 303, when persecution was raging in Africa and Alfius Caecilianus was duumvir of Aptunga, as is written below, p. 20, col. 2, in these same proceedings.
>
> That Verinus was vicar of Africa at the beginning of the year 314, under the consuls Volusianus and Annianus, when these proceedings took place, is inferred from the same letter of Constantine. For from Saint Augustine’s *To the Donatists after the Conference*, ch. 33, we learn that the examination of Felix’s case began on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March. Indeed, that he held the vicar prefecture at the very beginning of the year appears to be proved by the first law of the Theodosian Code, *On Curators of the Calendar*, which was promulgated by him on 30 January under the same consuls Volusianus and Annianus.
>
> I wholly agree with the most learned men Franciscus Juretus and Jacobus Gothofredus that the vicar of Africa whose illness Constantine discusses in his letter to Probianus was Verinus; consequently, his name should be corrected in that same letter, where through scribal error he is called Verus. For it should not seem strange that here he was changed into Verus, when in Augustine, *To the Donatists after the Conference*, ch. 33, he degenerated into Valerius and Valerianus, as we shall say below.
>
> Therefore, in place of the name Aelius Paulinus, which has crept into these proceedings, must be substituted the name of Verinus himself. He is found to have held the vicar prefecture of Africa even some years later in Saint Augustine’s *Brief Record of the Third Day*, ch. 22:
>
> > “They added another great support for convicting their falsehood, by reading letters of Constantine himself, written to Verinus the vicar, ordering him to leave them to their free choice and declaring that he had commanded them to return from exile.”
>
> Likewise in Letter 152, written in the name of the Council of Cirta to the Donatists:
>
> > “Third, they produced letters of the same Constantine addressed to Verinus the vicar, in which he severely denounces them and therefore says that they are to be released from exile and abandoned to their own madness, because God had already begun to take vengeance upon them.”
>
> Saint Augustine took this from the proceedings of the Third Conference of Carthage, ch. 548, where the editions of Massonus, Pithoeus, and Binius read:
>
> > “Where the letter of Constantine addressed to the vicar, the vicar, is read aloud, by which he grants the Donatists liberty of action.”
>
> Juretus saw that there was an error here and, in his *Miscellanies on Symmachus*, p. 312, rightly conjectured that it should read “to Verinus the vicar”; Henricus Valesius adopted this emendation in his *Dissertation on the Donatist Schism*, ch. 17. Certainly, in the most ancient copy from which Massonus published the proceedings of that Conference, it is expressly written: “to Verinus the vicar.”
>
> Those who supervised the edition of the works of Optatus, bishop of Milevis, in 1631, after the death of the most illustrious bishop of Orléans, Gabriel de L’Aubespine, had not seen Augustine, nor these miscellanies of Juretus, nor finally the old copy. Had they seen them, they would doubtless have refrained from that dangerous and excessively rash emendation which they applied to this passage. Thinking that the word *Vicarium*, twice written here, was redundantly repeated through scribal error, they retained it only once, contrary to the authority of the proceedings and the old book, and also contrary to Saint Augustine.
>
> This error was retained by the recent editor of the works of Optatus and in the most recent Paris edition of the Councils. I am still more surprised at the edition issued in 1644 from the Royal Press. Although it is said to have been prepared by most learned men, and indeed in Paris, where the old manuscript could easily have been consulted in a difficult and obscure passage, they rejected the reading found in earlier editions and retained the rashness of the editor of Optatus’s works.
>
> These matters having been established, since it is certain that Constantine’s letter reported in the index of the Third Conference is the one which Augustine, at the beginning of ch. 33 of *To the Donatists after the Conference*, says was written by Constantine to Valerius the vicar (or Valerianus, as the old Colbert manuscript reads), under the consuls Crispus and Constantine for the second time, it is likewise certain that Augustine’s text here is corrupt and that Verinus must be restored in place of Valerius.
>
> Again, since it follows that Verinus was vicar of Africa under the consulship of the same Caesars, falling in the year of Christ 321, and since various constitutions contained in the Theodosian Code show that he administered the same vicar prefecture also in the years 318 and 319, it is evident not only that he recovered from the illness by which he was detained at the time of Felix’s acquittal, but also that his authority was continued.
>
> Yet Augustine himself causes me difficulty here. For in the same ch. 33 of *To the Donatists after the Conference*, he says that Constantine wrote to Eumalius the vicar concerning Caecilianus’s exoneration on 10 November, under the consuls Sabinus and Rufinus—that is, toward the end of the year of Christ 316. Augustine quotes a fragment of this letter in *Against Cresconius*, book III, ch. 71; and in the *Brief Record of the Third Day*, ch. 19, he teaches that it was read at the Third Conference of Carthage, where he reports its substance.
>
> Earlier, moreover—that is, in the preceding year—the inscription of the sole law of the Theodosian Code, *On Those Who Steal Others’ Children*, dated 1 August under the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and Licinius, teaches that Domitius Celsus was vicar of Africa. Verinus must therefore have been removed for some time, allowing room for Celsus and Eumalius, and then restored to Africa. So too, after Aelianus, we find in the Theodosian Code that Catullinus was proconsul of Africa in the years 315, 317, and 319; that in the last of those years Proculus also held that office; that afterward Aelianus recovered it in the year 320; that in 324 Hilarianus possessed this proconsular authority; and that again Aelianus shone in the proconsulship of Africa in the year 326.

[Col. 0718B] Very much is missing. … in the municipality of the Autumnitani, Gallienus the duumvir said: “Since you are present, Caecilianus, hear the letter of my lord Aelius Paulinus, the most distinguished man acting as [Col. 0719A]

> **Note [Col. 0719C]**
>
> *Cum scriba tuo* (“with your clerk”). The old manuscript reads *cum scripta tua* (“with your writing”). Massonus emended this, entirely correctly, as what follows shows.
>
> *Ut veniret et acta.* In the old copy and Massonus’s edition it reads *venit ut acta*. We have emended it. The correction is certain.
>
> *Inquirit, quoniam.* In the old book and Massonus’s edition: *inquirit et quoniam*. We have removed the particle *et*, which divided and confused the sense.
>
> *Anni sunt undecim.* Thus Caecilianus had held the duumvirate in the municipality of Aptunga in the year of Christ 303, namely the year when the edict for demolishing basilicas and burning the sacred Scriptures was promulgated in Africa, as the following passages also show.
>
> *Suppleto anno.* That is, “when the year was completed,” “ended.”
>
> *Si mei in cera.* This is our emendation, which I think will please learned men. For the old manuscript had previously been read, without sense: *sed in ei in cera possit*. Massonus changed *sed* to *si*. The sense of the passage seems to me capable of being established thus: the magistrate took the public records home after the year of his office had ended; therefore they are not with me. I have only wax tablets, on which the proceedings were first entered; and I investigate whether the records requested by the proconsul may be found in them.
>
> For, as Priscian says in the first book of his *Grammar*, the ancients commonly wrote on wax tablets and then erased what they had written. This was the work of notaries and clerks, who took down on wax tablets what was dictated. Jerome, Letter 140 to Principia: “The stylus writes on wax; the reed-pen writes either on paper or parchment, or on any material suited for writing. But my tongue, in the likeness of a swift scribe—whom we may understand as a notary—has inscribed, by a certain abbreviated method of signs, the compressed and concise discourse of the Gospel upon tablets of fleshly hearts.”
>
> The Sixth Synod, Act 12: “Our most holy Patriarch sent us to the most holy Patriarch of Constantinople, bearing for rereading the notes.” Hence Possidius, *Life of Saint Augustine*, ch. 6: “The discussion began after the notaries’ tablets had been opened.” Notaries used wax tablets because of their ease of erasure, as Priscian teaches. Jerome, Letter 44 to Chrysogonus: “You have so wholly forgotten our bond of friendship that you have erased that letter which the Apostle says is written in Christians’ hearts—not with a slight blotting, but, as they say, from the deepest wax.”
>
> *Aelianus proc.* Aelianus the proconsul, frequently mentioned in Augustine and in the Third Conference of Carthage, and also in the Theodosian Code, as we have seen above. Therefore, since it is established that he held the rank of proconsul in Africa at precisely the time when Volusianus and Annianus were consuls, under whom the Council of Arles was held in the Donatist controversy, I am readily led to believe the opinion true of those who suspect that Constantine’s letter concerning the dispatch of African bishops to Arles before the Kalends of August was addressed to him; and that in place of Aelasius, to whom it is addressed in the old Thuan manuscript and in the common editions, Aelianus should be restored.
>
> There can be no other reason why it was written to the proconsul rather than the vicar than that at that time the vicar was detained by ill health, as Constantine Augustus teaches in his letter to Probianus, Aelianus’s successor. Hence it is clear that the heading of that letter in the volumes of the Councils should be corrected, where it is said to have been written to the vicar of Africa. Nor is it surprising that Aelianus’s name was changed into Aelasius in the exceedingly corrupt Thuan manuscript, from which alone all editions of that letter published to this day have proceeded.

“...acting as vicar prefect, what he has deigned to command according to the letter given to us: it compels you to produce a statement, and also the clerk whom you had during the administration of your term, and the archives. But since the archivist of that time has died, and according to the tenor of the letter of that same lord of mine you must take with you all the records of your administration, it is necessary that you travel to the colony of Carthage with your clerk. The curator is present, before whose presence we compel you to appear. What do you answer to this?”

Caecilianus said: “As soon as you brought me the letter of Aelius Paulinus, the most distinguished man acting as vicar prefect, I immediately sent to the clerk Miccius, asking him to come and bring me the completed records of that period. Even now he is searching, because it is no small time since I administered the duumvirate: it has been eleven years. Therefore, when he has found them, I shall obey so great a command.”

Gallienus the duumvir said: “It concerns you to obey the command, for you see that the command is sacred.”

Caecilianus said: “I am devoted to so great a command.” [Col. 0720A]

Then, shortly afterward, when the clerk Miccius arrived, Fuscius the duumvir said: “You too, Miccius, have heard that you are required, together with Caecilianus, to go to the office of the most distinguished vicar and take with you the documentary material from that period. What do you say to this?”

Miccius answered: “When his year was completed, the magistrate took all his records to his house. I am investigating whether mine can be found on wax [tablets].”

While he was searching, Quintus Sisenna the duumvir said: “He has answered what the office has learned.”

Apronianus said: “If the magistrate had taken all his records, whence are the proceedings that were issued or completed at that time?”

And when he spoke, Aelianus the proconsul said: “Both my interrogation and the reply of each individual are contained in the proceedings.” [Col. 0720B]

Agesilaus said: “There are besides other letters necessary for this matter; it is important that they be read.”

Aelianus the proconsul said: “Read them with Caecilianus listening.” [Col. 0721A]

> **Note [Col. 0721B]**
>
> *Volusiano.* Here a blank space had been left in the old copy and in Massonus’s edition. We have added the name Volusianus from the consular lists and the Theodosian Code, but especially from Augustine, who, in *To the Donatists after the Conference*, ch. 33, treating this very matter, says: “Aelianus the proconsul heard Felix’s case under the consuls Volusianus and Annianus, on the Kalends of March.” Thus this exoneration of Felix occurred in the year of Christ 314.
>
> *XIIII Kal.* Thus the old copy, whereas Massonus published *XIII*. But where the text here says that these proceedings occurred on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, Augustine, as we saw shortly above, places this inquiry on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March. Baronius therefore says that the proceedings for Felix’s exoneration must be corrected accordingly, otherwise pronouncing them sufficiently corrupt and faulty.
>
> But Valesius criticizes Baronius on this point in his *Dissertation on the Donatist Schism*, ch. 11, among other arguments on the ground that within the space of one day so many documents of proceedings could not have been read and so many persons examined; and therefore he says that the hearing of so great a case must have been extended over several days. Accordingly, he maintains that Aelianus began it on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, but, on account of public necessities and provincial business, interrupted it and finally concluded it on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September—that is, in the sixth month after the beginning of the proceedings.
>
> For my part, while I readily grant that this question was debated over several days, I would be very reluctant to believe that an inquiry which Augustine in Letter 72 calls “a most careful examination” and “a diligent and formidable investigation” remained pending before a judge for so long; especially since Optatus in book I teaches that Constantine the emperor wrote into Africa that, public necessities being set aside, a public inquiry should be held concerning the conduct of Felix of Aptunga.
>
> And since it is necessary to suppose an error either in Augustine’s *To the Donatists after the Conference* or in this passage of the proceedings, and since it is established that what Augustine reports is free from error—because he says that Aelianus undertook the examination of Felix’s cause approximately four months after the judgment of Miltiades, which had occurred at the beginning of the previous October—I do not see how Baronius’s opinion can be rejected: he held that this passage of the proceedings must be corrected from Augustine’s book *To the Donatists after the Conference*.
>
> *Duumvirium splendidae.* In the old book and Massonus’s edition it reads: *Duoviru recitavit. Splendidae.* We have removed the word *recitavit*, which was entirely superfluous here and disturbed the sense.
>
> *Apud Max. Imperatores.* Constantine and Licinius, who were then governing the commonwealth.
>
> *Cum persecutio esset indicta.* In the year of Christ 303, as we have repeatedly said above. From this arose the designation *traditores* (“those who surrendered [the Scriptures]”) in Africa.

By proconsular command. That is, by the command of Anulinus, who is shown to have been proconsul of Africa at that time by the acts of the martyrs then persecuted in Africa for the name of Christ.

“Secundus sens est.” Thus the old manuscript. Masson printed, “Secundus is an old man,” which makes no sense. For the matter here is not Secundus, but Alfius Caecilianus, former duumvir of the Aptungitani.

Letters of greeting. Below: “that he brought forth letters of greeting from the basilica.” It is difficult to explain what is meant here by “letters of greeting.” Nor am I so far persuaded by those who infer from this passage that letters of greeting are those by which someone conveys greetings to another. For it is manifestly a question here of a certain venerable codex, which the duumvir Alfius Caecilianus removed from the basilica of Aptunga, doubtless in order to burn it. For, after the episcopal chair and the letters of greeting had been removed, all the doors too were burned, in accordance with the sacred command.

Ingentius, clerk. He afterwards became a decurion of the city of the Ziquenses, and was then convicted of having forged and interpolated the letter which Alfius Caecilianus had written to Felix, bishop of Aptunga. Augustine, *Letter* 152, written in the name of the Council of Cirta to the Donatists: “Ingentius had confessed in the investigation of Aelianus the proconsul that he had committed a forgery against Felix, Caecilian’s ordainer.” The same, in the book to the Donatists after the Conference, ch. 32: “Ingentius, who in the same trial confessed that he had committed a forgery against Felix.” See Constantine’s letter to Probianus, mentioned in these passages of Augustine.]

“that he may ascertain whether he himself dictated it.” Agesilaus read it aloud. “In the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, in court before Aurelius Didymus Speretius, priest of Jupiter Best and Greatest, duumvir, it was read aloud. Maximus of the splendid colony of the Carthaginians said: ‘I speak in the name of the elders of the Christian people of the Catholic law. Before the most great emperors a case is to be conducted against Caecilianus and Felix, who attempts to usurp every primacy of that same law. Evidence of their crimes is being gathered against them. For when persecution had been proclaimed against Christians—that is, that they should sacrifice, or commit to the flames whatever Scriptures they possessed—Felix, who was then bishop at Aptunga, had given his consent that the Scriptures should be surrendered from the hand of Galatius, so that they might be burned by fire; and at that time the magistrate was Alfius Caecilianus, whom you deem worthy to see present. And since the duty of that time lay upon him—that, by proconsular command, all should sacrifice and, if they possessed any Scriptures, should surrender them in accordance with the sacred law—I ask that Secundus is [an old man?], as you see, and cannot proceed to the sacred imperial court: let him place on record whether he has already given letters concerning an agreement made with him by the same Secundus, and whether the things which he has stated in the letters are true, so that the acts and good faith of these persons may be disclosed in the sacred judgment.’”

As Caecilianus stood by, Speretius the duumvir said: “You hear what has been placed on record.” Alfius Caecilianus said: “I was at Zama with Saturninus in order to procure lines. And when we arrived there, the Christians themselves sent to me at the praetorium to ask: ‘Has the sacred command reached you?’ I said: ‘No, but I have already seen copies.’ At Zama and at Furni I demolished basilicas, and I saw Scriptures burned. Therefore produce whatever Scriptures you have, so that the sacred command may be obeyed. Then they sent to the house of Bishop Felix, to remove the Scriptures from there so that they could be burned in accordance with the sacred command. Thus Galatius went with us to the place where they had been accustomed to hold prayers. From there we took the chair and the letters of greeting, and all the doors were burned in accordance with the sacred command. And when we sent to the house of the same Bishop Felix, the public officials reported that he was absent. For later, when Ingentius, clerk of Augentius, with whom I had held the aedileship, arrived, I dictated a letter to that colleague of mine, which I made to the same Bishop Felix.”

Maximus said: “He is present; let that same letter be offered to him, so that he may acknowledge it.” He replied: “It is the very one.” Maximus said: “Since he has acknowledged his letter, I read this, and request that it be inserted in full into the acts.” And he read aloud:

[Note: Col. 0723D

“My colleague.” Previously the reading was *collega meus* [“my colleague”], not only in printed editions but also in the old handwritten manuscript. But since these words must refer to Augentius, who was Alfius Caecilianus’s colleague, the correction which we have made in this passage appeared necessary.

“This sign.” This passage is also cited below, p. 21, col. 1, but differs greatly.

Paulinus administering the vicariate of the prefect. In the year of Christ 303, when the persecution began in Africa, as we said above.

The appearance of a courier. The old codex and Masson’s edition have *modicum* [“a small amount”], by an evident error. He said *modum cursoris*, that is, form or appearance. It is a Latin expression.

[Col. 0724D] “Write to him.” That is, “to him.” So most ancients wrote, who also frequently wrote *alio* for *alii*. Thus Commodian, bk. I, ch. 30: “you believe in one who is to perish”; and ch. 33: “Believe in one God.”

“His sides.” I have retained the reading of the old manuscript. Masson’s edition has “his letters,” which is perhaps more correct.

“Let him be suspended.” Constantine, in his letter to Probianus: “We have inspected the same Ingentius, suspended, together with the records which lay beneath him.” Optatus, book I: “Ingentius, a public clerk, hung under fear of the impending tortures.”]

“Caecilianus to Father Felix, greetings. When Ingentius met my colleague Augentius, his friend, and inquired whether, in the year of my duumvirate, any Scriptures of your law had been burned in accordance with the sacred law . . . [whether] Galatius, one of your law, had publicly brought forth letters of greeting from the basilica. I wish you good health. This sign, which the Christians had sent to me as a petition, and he himself whose petition it is; and you said: ‘Take the key, and take whatever books you find in the chair and codices upon the stone; but see to it that the officials do not take oil and wheat.’ And I said to you: ‘Do you not know that, where Scriptures are found, the house itself is demolished?’ And you said: ‘What then shall we do?’ And I said to you: ‘Let one of your people take them into the courtyard where you hold prayers and place them there; and I shall come with the officials and take them.’ And we went there and removed everything in accordance with the sacred command.”

Maximus said: “Since the reading of his letter has been entered in the acts, which he himself acknowledged that he sent, we request that the things he has said be attached to the acts.” Speretius the duumvir said: “What you have said has been written down.” Agesilaus said: “He has acknowledged the present letter; he says that the remaining portion, now read, is false.” Caecilianus said: “My lord, I dictated as far as the words that stand there: ‘I wish you, dearest father, good health.’”

Apronianus said: “It has always been thus: falsehood has been perpetrated by intimidation, by theatrical display, by an irreligious mind, by those who refused to agree with the Catholic Church. For when Paulinus here administered the vicariate of the prefects, a certain private person was suborned, who had the appearance of a courier, to come to Catholic unity and to persuade and frighten them. The plot was therefore exposed. For it was contrived by falsehood against the most religious Bishop Felix, so that he might seem to have surrendered and burned the Scriptures. Ingentius indeed, because all that he was doing was detrimental to the holiness and religion of Caecilianus, was suborned to come with letters supposedly from Bishop Felix to Caecilianus the duumvir, and to fabricate for him a mandate from Felix. Let him state the very words by which this was fabricated.”

Aelianus the proconsul said: “Speak.” Apronianus said: “‘Tell my friend Caecilianus that I have received eleven precious divine codices, and since I am now asked to restore them, say that in the year of your magistracy you burned them, so that I may not return them.’ Therefore Ingentius must be examined, to determine to what extent these things were schemed and fabricated, and to what extent he wished to entrap the magistrate into a lie, so as to stain Felix with infamy. Let him say by whom he was sent; nevertheless, [let him say] this scheme against Felix’s conscience, by which he might detract from Caecilianus’s honour and standing. For there is a certain man who has been sent as envoy through Mauritania and Numidia by the opposing party.”

And as Ingentius stood by, Aelianus the proconsul said: “On whose command did you undertake the acts alleged against you?” Ingentius said: “Where?” Aelianus the proconsul said: “Since you pretend not to understand what you are being asked, I shall speak more plainly: who sent you to Caecilianus’s magistracy?” Ingentius said: “No one sent me.” Aelianus the proconsul said: “How then did you come to Caecilianus’s magistracy?” Ingentius said: “When we had arrived and the case of Maurus of Utica, a bishop who had purchased a bishopric for himself, was being conducted, Felix, bishop of Aptunga, went up to the city to negotiate, and said: ‘Let no one communicate with him, because he has committed a forgery.’ And I said to him in reply: ‘Nor with you, nor with him, since you are a *traditor* [surrenderer of sacred books].’ For I grieved for the case of Maurus, my guest, because I had communicated with him while abroad, since I had escaped the persecution. Thereupon I went into Felix’s own country and took with me three elders, to see whether he had really surrendered [the Scriptures] or not.”

Apronianus said: “That is not how he came to Caecilianus, to inquire about Caecilianus.” Aelianus the proconsul said to Caecilianus: “How did Ingentius come to you?” Caecilianus replied: “He came to me at home. I was dining with workmen. He came there and stood at the door. ‘Where is Caecilianus?’ he said. I answered: ‘Here.’ I said to him: ‘What is it? Is everything all right?’ ‘Everything,’ he says. I replied: ‘If you do not disdain to dine, come, dine.’ He said to me: ‘I shall return here.’ He came back there alone and began to say to me: ‘Look, I have been charged to investigate and inquire whether Scripture was burned in the year of your duumvirate.’ I said to him: ‘You are troublesome to me; you are a man sent in for this; get away from me.’ And I dismissed him from me. And he came there again with my colleague, with whom I had been aedile. My colleague said to me: ‘Our Bishop Felix has sent a man here, that you should make him a letter, because he has received precious codices and has refused to restore them: write to him that they were burned in the year of your duumvirate.’ And I said: ‘Is this the faith of Christians?’”

Ingentius said: “My lord, let Augentius come. I am an honourable man; let my honour perish, and we have his sides [i.e., his testimony?].” Aelianus the proconsul said to Ingentius: “You are convicted on another charge.” Aelianus the proconsul said to the staff: “Bind him.” And when he was bound, Aelianus the proconsul said: “Let him be suspended.” And when he was being suspended, Aelianus the proconsul said to Caecilianus: “How did Ingentius come to you?” He replied: “‘Felix, our [bishop], sent me here,’ he said,

[Note: Col. 0725D

Constantine. A blank had been left in this passage in the old codex and in Masson’s edition. Yet there is no doubt that the name of Constantine ought to have been written.

Decurion. The old codex and Masson’s edition read “a worshipper of God”; and although this reading can be tolerated in view of what precedes, we preferred to adopt Baronius’s conjecture, because in Constantine’s letter to Probianus we saw that Constantine had inferred from these acts that Ingentius was not tortured because he asserted that he was a decurion of the city of the Ziquenses. [Col. 0726D] For this was the privilege of decurions: they could not be tortured, as we said in our note on Lactantius.

“From Caecilianus’s declaration.” These words, and those which follow to the end of the sentence, also occur in Augustine, book III against Cresconius, ch. 70.

“But Felix.” Optatus copied this part of the judgment in book I, adding: “Accordingly, the accusation having been driven away and erased, he departed from that judgment with great praise.”]
