“that you may write to him, because there is some ruined man or other who has in his possession precious codices belonging to me, and I do not wish to restore them. Therefore make a letter [saying] that they were burned, so that I may not reclaim them.” And I said: “Is this the faith of Christians?” And I began to rebuke him. And my colleague said: “Write to him, to our Felix.” And so I dictated the letter, which is genuine as far as I dictated it.”

Aelianus the proconsul said: “Hear the reading of your letter without fear. Acknowledge how far you dictated.” Agesilaus read aloud: “I wish you, dearest father, many years of good health.” Aelianus the proconsul said to Caecilianus: “Did you dictate as far as this?” He replied: “As far as this; the rest is false.” Agesilaus read aloud: “By this sign, which you sent to me as a petition, unless I and you and he whose petition it is; and you said: ‘Take the key, and take whatever books you find in the chair and codices upon the stone; but see to it that the officials do not take oil and wheat.’ And I said to you: ‘Do you not know that, where Scriptures are found, the house itself is demolished?’ And you said: ‘What then shall we do?’ And I said to you: ‘Let someone among you take them into the courts where you hold prayers and place them there; and I shall come with the officials and take them.’ And we went there and removed everything according to the arrangement, and burned it in accordance with the sacred command.”

Maximus said: “Since the tenor of his letter has also been read aloud in the acts, which he said he acknowledged and sent, we request that this be attached to your acts.” Speretius said: “What you have said has been written down.” Caecilianus replied: “That is false from that point onward; my letter goes only as far as the words: ‘Farewell, dearest father.’” Aelianus the proconsul said: “Whom do you say added to the letter?” Caecilianus said: “Ingentius.”

Aelianus the proconsul said: “Your declaration is attached to the acts.” Aelianus the proconsul said to Ingentius: “You shall be tortured, so that you do not lie.” Ingentius said: “I erred; I added to this letter myself, grieving over the case of Maurus, my guest.” Aelianus the proconsul said: “Constantine, greatest and perpetual Augustus, and the Caesars Licinius, deign to show such piety toward Christians that they do not wish discipline to be corrupted, but rather that this religion be observed and worshipped. Do not therefore flatter yourself that you can tell me that you are a decurion and therefore cannot be tortured. You shall be tortured, so that you do not lie—a thing which appears alien to Christians. Therefore speak plainly, that you may not be tortured.” Ingentius said: “I have already confessed without torture.”

Apronianus said: “Deign to inquire of him by what authority, by what deceit, by what madness he went through all the Mauritanias and also the Numidias, and by what device he stirred up sedition against the Catholic Church.” Aelianus the proconsul said: “Were you in the Numidias?” He replied: “No, my lord; let whoever can prove it do so.” Aelianus the proconsul said: “Nor in Mauritania?” He replied: “I went there to trade.” Apronianus said: “In this too he lies, my lord—for one cannot go to the region of Mauritania except through Numidia—when he says that he was in Mauritania but not in Numidia.”

Aelianus the proconsul said to Ingentius: “What is your status?” Ingentius replied: “I am a decurion of the Ziquenses.” Aelianus the proconsul said to the staff: “Take him down.” When he had been taken down, Aelianus the proconsul said to Caecilianus: “Are the things you said false?” Caecilianus replied: “No, my lord. Order the man who wrote the letter to come. He is his friend. He will say how far I dictated the letter.” Aelianus the proconsul said: “Who is this man whom you wish to come?” Caecilianus said: “Augentius, with whom I was aedile. I cannot prove it except through Augentius himself, who wrote the letter, how far I dictated to him; he can say.” Aelianus the proconsul said: “Then is it established that the letter is false?” Caecilianus replied: “It is established, my lord; I do not lie on my own blood.” Aelianus the proconsul said: “Since you held the duumvirate in your native city, one ought to have faith in your words.”

Apronianus said: “Nor is it new for them to do this. Moreover, they have added to the acts whatever they wished. It is now their craft.” Aelianus the proconsul said: “From the declaration of Caecilianus, who says that the acts have been falsified and that very much has been added to the letter, it is manifest with what intent Ingentius did these things; and therefore let him be received into prison. For he is needed for closer examination. But it is manifest that the devout Bishop Felix is free from the burning of divine documents, since no one has been able to prove anything against him—that he surrendered or burned the most sacred Scriptures. For the foregoing examination of all persons makes manifest that no divine Scriptures were either found, altered, or burned. The acts contain that the devout Bishop Felix, at that time, was neither present, nor lent his knowledge or consent, nor ordered anything of the kind to be done.”

Agesilaus said: “What does Your Authority command concerning those who have come to furnish information for your authority?” Aelianus the proconsul said: “Let them return to their homes.”

Here end the acts of the vindication of Bishop Felix of Aptunga, ordainer of Caecilianus of Carthage.

# ACTS OF THE VINDICATION OF CAECILIANUS

## PREFACE TO THE ACTS OF THE VINDICATION OF CAECILIANUS

The old manuscript of these acts, from which Masson published them, survives in the Thuan Library, but is exceedingly corrupted and contaminated, as the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius observed before me. Optatus of Milevis mentions them in book I, where he also states that he appended them to his work. “For,” he says, “in the final part of these little books we have added the full account of these matters, in order to furnish complete proof.” Certainly, in the old book the following words are written after the collection of these and certain other acts: “Here end the seven books of holy Optatus the bishop, or the acts of the vindication of Bishop Caecilianus and Felix, his ordainer.” Augustine likewise mentions them in Letter 162, where he notes that they were not read at the Conference of Carthage because there was no time. See also Letter 165 and book III against Cresconius, ch. 29, where some fragments of these acts are copied.

[Note: Col. 0727B

“He ordained Majorinus,” to whom Donatus—from whom the Donatists take their name—succeeded in the see of Carthage. Accordingly, the party of Majorinus was first so called, and afterwards came to be called the party of Donatus, as is read in Letter 68 of Saint Augustine. Third Conference of Carthage, ch. 220: “The petition of the Catholic Church concerning Caecilianus’s crimes, submitted by the party of Majorinus.” Saint Augustine also copied those words in the same letter. Therefore I judge most true the opinion of Henri Valois, who in his dissertation on the Donatist schism, ch. 4, declares that those words from book I of Optatus—“submitted by Lucianus, Dignus, Nassutius, Capito, Fidentius, and the other bishops of Donatus’s party”—should be corrected by removing Donatus’s name and restoring here the name of Majorinus.

Constantine. I agree with the same Valois, who in the same dissertation, ch. 3, proves against Baronius that these acts belong not to the year of Christ 306 but to 320.

[Col. 0727C] Of Thamugadi. The old book and Masson’s edition read *Thamugudiensis*. The acts of the Council of Carthage under Cyprian confirm our correction, for in them one reads the name “Novatus of Thamugadi.” With Saint Augustine, moreover, the name of Gaudentius, Donatist bishop of Thamugadi, is well known; Augustine wrote two books against him, which he himself mentions in *Retractations*, book II, ch. 59. Likewise, in Letter 61 he writes: “I owe the Thamugadians such a service of charity.” Further, the second law of the Theodosian Code, *On Honorary Codicils*, which is of Constantius, is said to have been issued at Thamugadi; there Jacobus Gothofredus notes that the city was in Mauretania Tingitana, and that its name is corrupted in the *Notitia Imperii* and in both *Itineraries*. In the first Conference of Carthage, ch. 128, Faustinianus is named as bishop of the people of Tamogadi; and in the *List of the Bishops of Africa*, Secundus Tamogaziensis is listed among the Numidians.

[Col. 0727D] Nundinarius. He was the author of this entire inquiry, in order to avenge himself against Silvanus, bishop of Cirta, by whom he had been wronged. Augustine, Letter 162: “There are acts before Zenophilus the consular, in which a certain deacon Nundinarius, deposed by Silvanus, bishop of Cirta, insofar as may be understood from the acts themselves, after he had vainly attempted to satisfy him through letters of other bishops, disclosed much in anger and brought it before public judgment. Among these things it is also recorded that, through Lucilla’s money and corrupt bishops, in the Church of Carthage, the capital of Africa, altar was raised against altar.” The same, Letter 165: “Read to him the acts before Zenophilus the consular, in which a certain deacon Nundinarius, angry with Silvanus because he had been excommunicated by him, disclosed all these things before the courts, which were established more clearly than light by definite documents, the replies of witnesses, the reading of acts, and many letters.”

“Most distinguished man.” These two words are usually written in old books as V.C. But in this place they occur in the old manuscript as we have printed them. Since the copyist did not understand these abbreviations, he subsequently wrote *vicarius* [“vicar”] for *vir clarissimus*, by a foolish error, which Masson’s edition nevertheless retained in some places. Others thought that those abbreviations should be expanded as “consular man,” an interpretation rightly criticized by the very learned François Juret in his *Miscellanies on Symmachus*, p. 282. Certainly, if that interpretation held, Zenophilus would here consequently be called *consularis* twice. Nothing could be imagined more absurd. By the same reasoning, the abbreviations in Gruter, p. 193, in the inscription where Postumius Lampadius is called V.C., Cons. Camp., would have to be expanded in that way; yet another inscription in Gruter, p. 283, proves that they must mean *vir clarissimus*, for it reads: “Decimius Geminianus, most distinguished man, consular of the province of Baetica.” Indeed, even the ordinary consuls themselves and the prefects of the City, whose rank was above that of consulars, would nevertheless be found called consulars if the interpretation we refute were true. For several inscriptions survive in Gruter, p. 193, in which Tiberius Fabius Titianus is called V.C., ordinary consul, and prefect of the City. It follows that the Gemeticensis codex of Saint Augustine’s letters is corrupt, when it expands those abbreviations as “consular man” in the report of Anulinus, proconsul of Africa, to Constantine, preserved in Letter 88 of Saint Augustine in the new edition. In the third Conference of Carthage, however, where the same report is inserted, they are expanded as “most distinguished man,” entirely correctly. For this is not, as Juret says, a designation of fame and celebrity but one of honour and rank; it was joined to the titles of those to whom letters were written, and those who were themselves *clarissimi* adorned themselves with this name. Thus once the kings of our first dynasty called themselves “illustrious men” in their titles, as everyone knows, and as Sirmond also observed in his notes on Ennodius, p. 19.

Of Constantina, or of Cirta. For the city that had formerly been called Cirta was then called Constantina. See Valois, dissertation on the Donatist schism, ch. 3.

Bishop Secundus. The bishop of Tigisis, who then held the primacy in Numidia, as Augustine says in Letter 162. He also held the presidency of the Council of Cirta, as Augustine writes in the same passage: there he left those *traditores* who were present and confessed to be judged by God, and allowed them to remain in their episcopal sees. See the same author, book I against the letter of Parmenianus, ch. 3; *Brief Record of the Third Day*, ch. 13; and book I against Gaudentius, ch. 37.]

Here begin the acts in which it is established that Silvanus was a *traditor*, he who, with the others, ordained Majorinus, to whom Donatus succeeded.

In the consulship of Constantine, greatest Augustus, and Constantine the younger, most noble Caesar, on the Ides of December, Sextus of Thamugadi having been brought in and Victor the grammarian summoned, with the deacon Nundinarius also in attendance, Zenophilus, most distinguished man and consular, said: “What are you called?” He replied: “Victor.” Zenophilus, most distinguished man and consular, said: “What is your status?” Victor said: “I am a teacher of Roman letters, a Latin grammarian.” Zenophilus, most distinguished man and consular, said: “What is your rank?” Victor said: “My father was a decurion of Constantina; my grandfather was a soldier and had served in the imperial retinue. For our origin descends from Moorish blood.” Zenophilus, most distinguished man and consular, said: “Mindful of your faithfulness and integrity, state simply what was the cause of the dissension among Christians.” Victor said: “I do not know the origin of the dissension. I am one of the Christian people. For when I was at Carthage, Bishop Secundus, when he had at length come to Carthage,

[Note: Col. 0729B

Caecilianus, the Catholic bishop of Carthage and successor of Mensurius, endured so many storms from the party of Donatus that his name consequently became very celebrated. The history of his calamities is very well known.

“They appointed another.” Majorinus, to whom Donatus succeeded, as we said above.

“Our city has one Church.” That is, we Cirtensians know no division. For we do not have two bishops, as most cities of Africa do: one of Donatus’s party and another of Caecilianus’s party. We have only one, but he communicates with Donatus and does not communicate with Caecilianus. Later, however, the Cirtensians had two bishops, namely Fortunatianus and Petilianus, as is clear from the first Conference of Carthage, chs. 65, 138, and following.

“Silvanus, bishop of Cirta,” who, with Secundus of Tigisis, primate of Numidia, and the others, ordained Majorinus against Caecilianus.

“Passing over him.” The most learned Henri Valois, in the dissertation cited above, ch. 3, interprets these words of Caecilianus, whose innocence had then been proved by many indications. But this interpretation is not without difficulty. For these things were not said at Carthage but in Numidia, of which Zenophilus was consular. Moreover, Victor had not yet said that he did not communicate with Caecilianus. It is therefore doubtful whether these words should be understood of Caecilianus or rather of Felix of Aptunga.

“Vindicated.” Thus the old codex. Masson’s edition has “proved.” That our correction is legitimate is also shown by the third Conference of Carthage, ch. 571, where it reads: “The Donatists’ prosecution, in which they say that Felix, being present, ought to have been vindicated.” And ch. 574: “The Catholics’ prosecution: that it is a greater proof of innocence that Felix was vindicated while absent.” Saint Augustine, Letter 162: “Nor did negligence result concerning the case of Felix of Aptunga; rather, at the command of that same Emperor, he himself was also vindicated by proconsular acts.” And below, of the same Felix: “A bishop ought not to have been vindicated by proconsular judgment.” The same, book III against Cresconius the grammarian, ch. 61: “Public records proclaim that the case was heard and brought to its due conclusion, as far as the vindication of Felix of Aptunga.”

*Traditores* were those who, during persecution, had surrendered the divine Scriptures and church furnishings to officers of the state. The Donatists made much complaint on this point, commonly calling Catholics—that is, those who communicated with Caecilianus—*traditores* and offspring of *traditores*. Conversely, Catholics charged the Donatists with betrayal, calling them heirs of *traditores* and schismatics, so much so that Optatus of Milevis says it is manifest that their leaders were *traditores*.

“Whether.” The old codex reads *non*. Masson substituted *nam*. Both readings are false; the reading we have retained is correct.

“Mount Bellona.” Near Cirta.

“Lest you be examined more strictly.” That is, lest you be tortured. Acts of the Vindication of Felix, p. 21, col. 2: “For he is needed for closer examination.”

“Diocletian VIII.” That is, the year of Christ 303, when the persecution began.

“XIV Kalends of June.” This is precisely the reading of both the old manuscript and Masson’s edition; it is also found in Augustine, book III against Cresconius, ch. 29. Yet in Letter 165, when mentioning these acts, Augustine states that they were conducted on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June—certainly, in my judgment, by error. For both in the acts which we have published here and in the manuscript which, as we noted, survives in book III against Cresconius, the day is expressly and consistently marked as the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June. This correction escaped the very learned men who recently usefully devoted their efforts to revising and correcting Augustine’s letters for publication. But the conjecture of the most distinguished Jean Broc of Bourges is certainly false: in his dissertation on the date of the Council of Cirta, he writes that June in this passage of Augustine should be changed to January, so that the matters here reported concerning Munatius Felix would have occurred in the January immediately following the beginning of the persecution. This is futile, I say, since all the old books and all editions unanimously give the month of June, and this matter has nothing in common with the acts of the Council of Cirta.

“Munatius Felix.” Letter 165 of Saint Augustine reads *Numatius*, but this was corrected from book III against Cresconius in the latest edition. Sirmond, however, in his notes on Ennodius, p. 95, preferred the reading containing the name Numatius. Valois, in his annotations on Eusebius, p. 161, preferred Munatius to Numatius—correctly, in my opinion. For the name Munatius is frequent in ancient inscriptions, and such persons are also very often called Felix, as may be seen in Gruter, pp. 66 and 1124.

“Perpetual flamen.” The old codex reads “prefect,” because the copyist, not understanding the abbreviation PP., expanded it by the word *praepositi*. But the true reading was found in Augustine, book III against Cresconius, ch. 29, and book IV, ch. 56. Of the flamines appointed throughout the provinces, some were temporary and others perpetual, as has been observed by the most learned men.]

they say that he found Caecilianus the bishop not rightly established for some reason or other; they in turn appointed another. From this dissension began there at Carthage. I cannot fully know the origin of the dissension from there, because our city has always had one Church; and if it had a division, we know nothing at all of it.”

Zenophilus, most distinguished man and consular, said: “You are in communion with Silvanus.” Victor replied: “With him.” Zenophilus, most distinguished man and consular, said: “Why then, passing over him whose innocence has been vindicated?” And he added: “Furthermore, it is asserted that you certainly know another matter: that Silvanus is a *traditor*. Confess concerning this.” Victor replied: “I do not know this.” Zenophilus, most distinguished man and consular, said to Nundinarius the deacon: “Victor denies that he knows that Silvanus is a *traditor*.” Nundinarius the deacon said: “He himself knows whether he surrendered the codices.” Victor replied: “I had fled that storm; and, if I lie, may I perish. When we suffered the onset of the sudden persecution, we fled to Mount Bellona. I was sitting with the deacon Martius; and Victor the presbyter, when all the codices were demanded of him by that same Martius, denied that he had them. Then Victor gave the names of all the readers. They came to my house. While I was absent, the magistrates went up and my codices were removed. When I returned, I found the codices removed.”

Nundinarius the deacon said: “You therefore answered in the acts that you handed over the codices. Why are these things denied, when they can be produced?” Zenophilus, most distinguished man and consular, said to Victor: “Confess simply, lest you be examined more strictly.” Nundinarius the deacon said: “Let the acts be read.” Zenophilus, most distinguished man and consular, said: “Let them be read.” And Nundinarius handed them over, and the recorder read aloud:

“In the eighth consulship of Diocletian and the seventh of Maximian, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, from the acts of Munatius Felix, perpetual flamen and curator—”

[Note: Col. 0731C

Paulus, bishop of Cirta, who was convicted of surrendering the Lord’s documents, including those which had been carefully concealed, as Augustine says in Letter 165.

“By command and order.” The old book and Masson’s edition read: “as it has been commanded, as to the order,” etc. It has been corrected from what follows.

“Afterwards in the libraries.” This is precisely the reading of the old manuscript. Augustine, however, citing this passage in book III against Cresconius, ch. 29, writes: “After it had been opened into the library.” But in book IV, ch. 56, he has: “After they had come to the library.” Masson composed his text from this double Augustinian recension and wrote: “After they had come into the library.” I think the reading of the old book is true. In these acts, *bibliothecae* means the book-cupboards in which books were enclosed. Thus a little later Silvanus, then a subdeacon, says: “Nothing remained; we threw all this out.” Valerius, *Life of Saint Pontius the Martyr*, ch. 2: “pouring into his small body the abundance of volumes and books which the libraries could not carry.” Possidius, *Life of Saint Augustine*, ch. 31: “He left the monasteries of continent men and women, with their superiors, full for the Church, together with libraries containing books and treatises, whether his own or those of other saints.”]

Capitulatam arg. The old copy has: “a silver *capitulata* and a silver lamp.” In place of this Masson substituted: “silver plaques and silver lamps,” entirely wrongly. For in various passages of these proceedings and in Augustine there is mention of only one lamp. Augustine indeed cites this very passage several times, and in two places writes “a silver *capitulata* and a silver lamp,” as we have restored it. Therefore Augustine himself must be corrected in *Against Cresconius*, IV.56, where “a little box” [Col. 0732D] is read instead of *capitulata*. Below, p. 24, col. 1, “a plaque” is read instead of *capitulata*. Thus either this passage is corrupt, or by *capitulata* a plaque is meant.

“Had you died.” Augustine cites this passage in Epistle 167, *Against Cresconius* III.29, and IV.56.

*Orca.* In Augustine “chest” is wrongly read. An *orca* is an earthenware vessel, as the most distinguished Charles du Fresne demonstrates with numerous testimonies in his Glossary.

“Felix the *sarsor*.” That is, a worker in marble. [Col. 0733B] Hence *opus sarsorium* in Ennodius, when various pieces of differently coloured marble are joined together so as to form one body and, as it were, one picture; as Sirmond notes there.]

of the colony of the people of Cirta. When they had come to the house in which the Christians assembled, Felix, perpetual flamen and municipal curator, said to Bishop Paul: “Produce the writings of the law, and whatever else you have here, so that you may comply with the command and order.” Bishop Paul said: “The readers have the Scriptures; but what we have here, we give up.” Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said to Bishop Paul: “Show us the readers, or send to them.” Bishop Paul said: “You all know them.” Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said: “We do not know them.” Bishop Paul said: “The public office knows them, that is, Edusius and Junius, recorders.” Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said: “While the inquiry concerning the readers remains, whom the office will identify, give up what you have.” While Bishop Paul, [Col. 0731B] Montanus, Victor, Deusatelius, and Memorius, presbyters, were seated; while Marte together with Helius and Marte, deacons, Marcuclius, Catullinus, Silvanus, and Carosus, subdeacons, Januarius, Meraclus, Fructuosus, Migginus, Saturninus, Victor son of Samsuricus, and the other grave-diggers were standing by; Victor son of Aufidius recording for the opposing side, the following was briefly entered:

Two gold chalices; likewise six silver chalices; six silver pitchers; one silver kettle; seven silver lamps; two *cereofala*; seven short bronze candles with their lamps; likewise eleven bronze lamps with their chains; 82 women’s tunics; 38 *mafortea*; 16 men’s tunics; 13 pairs of men’s stockings; 47 pairs of women’s stockings; 19 rustic coverlets.

Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said to the grave-diggers Marcuclius, Silvanus, and Carosus: [Col. 0731C] “Produce what you have.” Silvanus and Carosus said: “Everything that was here, we have thrown out.” Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said to Marcuclius, Silvanus, and Carosus: “Your answer is entered in the proceedings. Afterwards, in the bookcases, cupboards were found there empty.” There Silvanus produced a silver *capitulata* and a silver lamp, saying that he had found them behind an *orca*. Victor son of Aufidius said to Silvanus: “You would have died, had you not found them.” Felix, perpetual flamen [Col. 0732A] and curator of the municipality, said to Silvanus: “Search more carefully, lest anything remain here.” Silvanus said: “Nothing remains; we have thrown everything out.”

And when the dining-room had been opened, four jars and six *orcas* were found there. Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said: “Produce the Scriptures which you have, so that you may comply with the emperors’ commands and order.” Catulinus produced one very large codex. Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said to Marcuclius and Silvanus: “Why have you handed over only one codex? Produce the Scriptures which you have.” Catulinus and Marcuclius said: “We have no more, because we are subdeacons; but the readers have codices.” Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said to Marcuclius and Catulinus: “Show us the readers.” Marcuclius and Catulinus said: [Col. 0732B] “We do not know where they live.” Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said to Catulinus and Marcuclius: “If you do not know where they live, state their names.” Catulinus and Marcuclius said: “We are not betrayers. Here we are; order us to be killed.” Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said: “Let them be taken back.”

And when they had come to Eugenius’s house, Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said to Eugenius: “Produce the Scriptures which you have, so that you may comply with the command.” He produced four codices. Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said to Silvanus and Carosus: “Show us the other readers.” Silvanus and Carosus said: “The bishop has already said that Edusius and Junius, the recorders, know them all. Let them show you their houses.” Edusius and Junius, recorders, said: “We [Col. 0732C] will show them to you, my lord.”

And when they had come to the house of Felix the marble-worker, he produced five codices. And when they had come to Victorinus’s house, he produced eight codices. And when they had come to Projectus’s house, he produced five larger codices and two smaller ones. And when they had come to the grammarian’s house, Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said to Victor the grammarian: “Produce the Scriptures which you have, so that you may comply with the command.” Victor the grammarian offered [Col. 0733A]

[Note: [Col. 0733B]

“Bovus, public slave.” An official, an apparitor.

“The bishops’ letters written on behalf of Nundinarius [Col. 0733C] to Silvanus, bishop of Cirta, and to the clergy and people of the same city.” Saint Augustine mentions these letters in Epistles 162 and 165.

“From Fortis.” It is true that Fortis too wrote on behalf of Nundinarius. Nevertheless, his name must here have been placed out of position, or else some words are missing afterwards to show that the bishops’ letters were composed by Fortis and the others.

“Copy of the petition handed to the bishops.” These words are absent from the old copy, evidently through the carelessness and inattentiveness of the scribe. They have been supplied from Book III of Saint Augustine’s *Against Cresconius*, chapter 29.

“Thief of the poor’s property.” Silvanus is called a thief of the poor’s property because he kept for himself twenty *folles* which Victor the fuller had given in order to become a presbyter, and no part of them reached the people, among whom were the poor, as is read below, p. 25, col. 1. Moreover, he, together with the other bishops—whom for this reason Saint Augustine in Book I of *Against Parmenianus*, chapter 3, calls “thieves of church silver”—divided among themselves four hundred [Col. 0733D] *folles* which Lucilla, a woman of senatorial rank, gave in order that Majorinus might become bishop. No part of these is written to have reached the poor, p. 24, col. 2, and p. 25, col. 1.

“Concerning the four hundred *folles*.” This passage has been restored from Augustine. For the old copy wrongly reads: “You yourselves know, and Lucilla consul Felix, for which to you,” etc. In the older codex there stood *Lucilla C. F. pro quod*. Since the scribe did not understand those abbreviations, he interpreted them incorrectly.—“*Folles*.” A kind of coin. See the Glossary of du Fresne and Jacob Gothofredus’s Notes on the Theodosian Code. See also Sirmond on Sermon 39 of Saint Augustine, where he conjectures that the value of the *follis* and of our solidus is the same or similar.

“Lucilla.” She was a wealthy and partisan woman. Before the peace was shaken by the storms of persecution, as Optatus says—while the Church was still at peace—she was said to take into her mouth, before the spiritual food and drink, the mouth of some martyr, if indeed a martyr; and, when she preferred to the saving cup the mouth of some dead man, even if a martyr, but not yet vindicated, she was rebuked. In shame and anger she departed. As she was angry and grieved, lest she submit to discipline, the storm of persecution suddenly arose to meet her. Saint Augustine mentions this passage in Book I of *Against Parmenianus*, chapter 3, and in Epistle 162.

“From this the schism arose.” Optatus, shortly after the passage quoted here: “Thus the anger of a humiliated woman gave birth to the schism at that time; ambition nourished it; avarice strengthened it.” Charges against Caecilian were fabricated by these three persons so that his ordination might be called defective: namely, Botrus, Celesius, and Lucilla. Therefore anger must without doubt be ascribed to Lucilla; ambition to Botrus and Celesius, who had desired to be ordained at Carthage; avarice to the bishops who ordained Majorinus, divided among themselves the four hundred *folles* given by Lucilla, and through love of money raised up a bishop against Caecilian. Majorinus, moreover, was Lucilla’s household servant, as Optatus himself teaches.

“Bishop Purpurius.” Of Limata, whom Optatus calls a murderer because, when questioned concerning his sister’s sons, whom he was said to have killed in prison at Milevum, he confessed, saying: “And I killed not only them, but also anyone who has acted against me.” Optatus took this from the proceedings of the Council of Cirta, extant in Saint Augustine’s *Against Cresconius*, III.27. Limata, therefore, was a city of Numidia.

“Stoned.” That is, deposed, as Augustine says, and thus subjected to disgrace. Below, p. 23, col. 1: “by whom they might be stoned for the truth.” See du Fresne’s Glossary.

“It is not right.” That is, equitable. Livy, Book XXXII: “Moreover, that the requests of the allies should be heard was right.” In Saint Ambrose, Epistle 70, one reads: “That tributaries should be ruined is by no means just and equitable.” In place of this, I saw *verum* written in the very ancient manuscript codex of the Church of Beauvais.

“Without spiritual blood.” This is a passage of uncommon elegance. He says that spiritual blood is shed when the sword of discord rages against the Church, when bishops disagree with clergy, when these dissensions burst out among the populace and provide matter for talk.]

two codices and four quires. Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said to Victor: “Produce the Scriptures; you have more.” Victor the grammarian said: “Had I possessed more, I would have handed them over.” And when they had come to the house of Euticius of Caesarea, Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said to Euticius: “Produce the Scriptures which you have, so that you may comply with the command.” Euticius said: “I have none.” Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said to Euticius: “Your declaration is entered in the proceedings.”

And when they had come to Coddeo’s house, his wife produced six codices. Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said: “Search, lest you have more; produce them.” The woman replied: “I have none.” Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said to Bovus, public slave: “Go in and search, lest she have more.” The public slave said: “I searched and [Col. 0733B] found nothing.” Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the municipality, said to Victorinus, Silvanus, and Carosus: “If anything has been omitted, the danger will fall upon you.”

After these had been read, Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Victor: “Confess plainly.” Victor replied: “I was not present.” Nundinarius the deacon said: “We have read letters of bishops written by Fortis,” and he read a copy of the petition handed by Nundinarius the deacon to the bishops:

“Christ and his angels are witnesses that those with whom you have communicated handed things over; that is, Silvanus of Cirta is a betrayer and thief of the poor’s property. All of you—bishops, presbyters, deacons, and elders—know this concerning the four hundred *folles* of Lucilla, a woman of senatorial rank, for which you conspired that Majorinus might be made bishop; and from this the schism arose. For Victor the fuller too, in your presence and that of the people, gave twenty *folles* that he might be made presbyter, as Christ and his angels know.”

And a copy of the letter was read:

“Purpurius, bishop, to Silvanus, fellow-bishop, greeting in the Lord. Nundinarius the deacon, our son, came to me and asked that I send this letter of intercession from myself to you, most holy one, so that, if possible, peace might be between you and him. For this is what I want to be done: that no one may know what is taking place between us. If you wish, by your written word [let it be arranged] [Col. 0734B] that I too may come there alone in the present matter and cut off the dissension itself between you. For he personally handed me a petition concerning the affair for which, by your command, he was stoned. It is not right that a father should punish a son contrary to truth; and I know that what is written in the petition handed to me is true. Seek a remedy by which this malignity may be extinguished there before a flame rises which afterwards cannot be extinguished without spiritual blood.” [Col. 0735A]

[Note: [Col. 0735D]

“Bishop Purpurius.” These words are not extant in the old codex or in Masson’s edition, where a blank space was left. We have therefore added them because the context of the following letter shows that the same author wrote both it and the preceding one.

“To Silvanus.” We have added this word also. For here a blank space was left in the old copy and in Masson’s edition. It is certainly written to Silvanus, since it concerns the disagreement between him and Nundinarius the deacon.

“Fortis.” A bishop already mentioned above. I have not ascertained of what see he was bishop. In the first Conference at Carthage, chapter 163, Fortis, bishop of Cedia, is mentioned.

“Celebrate peace.” Read: “celebrate Easter,” as the following proves. P. 23, col. 2: “that we may celebrate Easter in peace”; and below: “Let Nundinarius celebrate Easter in peace with you.”

“Brothers and sons.” That is, the clergy and elders of the Church of Cirta, as above.

“Is judged, but before.” Thus the old codex. Masson printed: “contends in judgment, and this before.”

“Sabinus to brother Silvanus.” We have added these words also; they occur neither in the old book nor in Masson’s edition. But the restoration is certain.—Sabinus, a Numidian bishop.]

“Bring in your fellow-clerics and the ecclesiastical elders of the people, and let them investigate carefully what these disagreements are, so that what is done may be done according to the precepts of faith. You shall not turn to the right or to the left. But do not willingly lend your ear to evil advisers who do not want peace. You are killing us all—and, in another hand, Farewell.”

Likewise a copy of a letter:

“Purpurius, bishop, to the clergy and elders of the people of Cirta, eternal greeting in the Lord. Moses cries out to the whole council of the children of Israel and says to them what the Lord commands to be done; nothing was done without counsel of the elders. Thus you also, most beloved, whom I know to possess every heavenly and spiritual wisdom, use all your strength to discover what this disagreement is and bring it to peace. For Nundinarius the deacon says [Col. 0735B] that nothing is hidden from you concerning the source of this disagreement between our most beloved Silvanus and himself. For he handed me a petition in which everything is written. He said also that it was not hidden from you. I know that there is no ear [to hear]. Seek a good remedy whereby this affair may be extinguished without peril to your souls, lest suddenly, by showing partiality, you come into judgment. Judge a just judgment between the parties, in accordance with your seriousness and justice. Take care not to turn to the right or to the left. God’s cause is at stake; he searches each person’s thoughts. Strive that no one may know what this conspiracy is. What the petition contains is true; it is not good. For the Lord says: ‘By your words you shall be condemned, and by your words you shall be justified’ (Matt. XII).”

Likewise another letter was read:

“Fortis, eternal greeting in the Lord to Silvanus, most beloved brother. Nundinarius the deacon, our son, came to me and reported what had happened between you and him through the intervention of an ill-wisher, who wishes to turn righteous souls from the way of truth. When I heard this, I was overcome in mind that such disagreement had arisen between you. For that a priest of God should come to this is not advantageous for us. Therefore now ask him that, insofar as it is possible, the peace of the Lord, Christ the Saviour, may be with him. Let us not come before the public and be condemned by the Gentiles. For it is written: ‘See that, while you bite and contend with one another, you are not consumed by one another’ (Gal. V). I therefore ask the Lord that this scandal be removed from our midst, so that God’s affair may be celebrated with thanksgiving, the Lord saying: ‘My peace I give you; [Col. 0735D] my peace I leave you’ (John XIV). What peace can [Col. 0736A] exist where there is discord, where there are rivalries? For when I was separated from the soldiers [reading uncertain: *a milites essem ass. … separatus*] and had come there, with such an injury, I entrusted my soul to God and forgave you, because God sees the minds of men and theirs, whether I was brought from you to them; but God delivered us, and we serve with you. Therefore, as it has been forgiven us, you too be reconciled to peace, so that in Christ’s name we may celebrate Easter with joy. Let no one know.”

“To the brothers and sons, clergy and elders, Fortis, eternal greeting in the Lord. Nundinarius your deacon, my son, came to me and reported concerning what has been done against you; and indeed it ought to have been settled by you, so that it should not come to this—that, having suffered such madness, they might be stoned for the truth—something which both you and we know, as you reported to us. And it is written: ‘Is there no one wise among you who can judge between brothers? But brother is judged with brother, and before unbelievers’ (1 Cor. VI). Just as you do not press your case in court, so it has come to this: shall we give the Gentiles such an example that those who believed in God through us themselves curse us when we come before the public? Therefore, lest this occur, you who are spiritual must act so that no one may know, that we may celebrate Easter in peace; urge them to be reconciled to peace, and let there be no disagreement, lest, when the matter comes before the public, you too begin to be endangered if this is done, and afterwards blame yourselves. Give very great assistance—you, Donatus the presbyter, holder [of property?], and each of Valerius and Victor, who know all that has been done—see that peace may be among you.”

Likewise another letter was read:

“Sabinus, eternal greeting in the Lord to brother [Col. 0736C] Silvanus. Nundinarius, your son, came to us—not only to me, but also to our brother Fortis—bringing a strong and grave complaint. I am astonished at your gravity, that you have acted thus toward your son, whom you nurtured and ordained. For if an earthly building be constructed, nothing heavenly is added to it, which is built through the hand of the priest. But you ought not to be astonished, Scripture saying: ‘I shall destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent’ (1 Cor. I). And again it says: ‘Men loved darkness rather than light’ (John III). So too do you. Let it suffice for you to know everything concerning which our brother Fortis has written to you. Now I ask of your charity, most kindly brother, that you fulfil the saying of the prophet Isaiah: ‘Cast out wickedness [Col. 0736D] from your souls, and come, let us reason together,’ says [Col. 0737A]

[Note: [Col. 0737D]

“In these days.” The Paschal days.

“What office did he hold?” This passage is corrupt in Saint Augustine, where it reads thus in *Against Cresconius*, III.29: “Who was administering? Then Silvanus in the clergy replied, ‘Under Paul.’” And in IV.56: “Who was administering? Then Silvanus in the clergy Victor replied: ‘Under Paul.’” Augustine must therefore be corrected in both places.

“Silvanus was a subdeacon.” Augustine mentions this passage in Epistle 165. Therefore, from being a subdeacon under Paul, bishop of Cirta, he was afterwards placed in Paul’s episcopal chair.

“Our fellow-citizen.” That is, Donatus, as is clear from the end of the following page.

“A plaque.” We have already observed above that this passage is either corrupt, or that *tabula* must mean the *capitulata* mentioned both here and in Augustine.

“Vinegar.” Or a vinegar-vessel. See du Fresne’s Glossary.

“Superius.” The old copy and all editions have “Lucianus,” certainly in error. We have substituted the name Superius because below, when these matters are repeated, Superius’s name is always given in place of Lucianus. Lucianus was only a deacon, as is immediately stated.]

the Lord’ (Isa. I). And again: ‘Cast evil out from your midst.’ Do so yourself as well. Subdue and turn away the sedition of those who have not wished there to be peace between you and your son. But let your son Nundinarius celebrate Easter in peace with you, lest the affair come before the public and thus become known to all of us. I ask you, most kindly brother, fulfil the request of my humble self. Let no one know.”

Likewise another letter was read:

“Sabinus, eternal greeting in the Lord to brother Fortis. I am certain what love is due toward all fellow-colleagues; yet I am especially certain that you have honoured Silvanus according to God’s will, who said: ‘Some I love above my own soul.’ Therefore I did not hesitate to give you these writings, because I caused your writings to him to be delivered on account of Nundinarius’s name; and one who acts vigorously always advances God’s affair with force. Do not put forward an excuse. For our occupation presses us in these days and urgently moves us concerning these matters until before the most solemn day of Easter, so that through you the fullest peace may be achieved, that we may be found worthy co-heirs of Christ, who said: ‘My peace I give you; my peace I leave you’ (John XIV). And again: ‘I ask that you do it.’ And in another hand: ‘I wish that you may be well in the Lord and remember us. Farewell. But I ask you, let no one know.’”

After these had been read, Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “Both by the proceedings and by the letters which have been read, Silvanus is established to be a betrayer.” And he said to Victor: “Confess plainly whether you know that he handed anything over.” Victor said: “He handed it over, but not in my presence.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “What office did Silvanus hold in the clergy at that time?” Victor [Col. 0737C] replied: “Under Bishop Paul the persecution arose, and Silvanus was a subdeacon.” Nundinarius the deacon replied: “When it came to the point, he says, that he should be made bishop, the people answered: ‘Let another be made; hear us, God.’” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Victor: “Was it said by the people, ‘Silvanus is a betrayer’?” Victor said: “I myself contended for a bishop.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Victor: “Then you knew him to be a betrayer? Confess concerning this.” Victor replied: “He was a betrayer.” Nundinarius the deacon said: “You elders were shouting: ‘Hear us, God; we want our fellow-citizen; that man is a betrayer.’” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Victor: “Then you shouted with the people that Silvanus was a betrayer and ought not to be made bishop?” Victor said: “Both I and the people shouted. For we were seeking our fellow-citizen, an upright man.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “For what reason did you think him undeserving?” Victor said: “We were seeking an upright man, and our fellow-citizen. [Col. 0737D] For I knew the emperors’ case [perhaps: “that we would come before the emperors”] would bring us to this, since matters are entrusted to such men.”

Likewise, after Victor son of Samsuricus and Saturninus, grave-diggers, had been brought in and presented, Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “What is your name?” He replied: “Saturninus.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, said: “What is your status?” Saturninus replied: “A grave-digger.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “Do you know Silvanus to be a betrayer?” Saturninus said: “I know that he handed over a silver lamp.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Saturninus: “What else?” Saturninus replied: “I know nothing else, except that he brought it out from behind an *orca*.” After Saturninus had been removed, Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to one standing by: “And you, what is your name?” He replied: “Victor son of Samsuricus.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “What is your status?” Victor said: [Col. 0738B] “I am an artisan.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, said: “Who handed over the silver plaque?” Victor replied: “I did not see it. What I know, I say.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Victor: “Although it has already been established from the answers of those questioned above, nevertheless confess whether Silvanus is a betrayer.” Victor said: “When he asked a second time how he had allowed this, so that we were led to Carthage, I heard it from the bishop’s own mouth. A silver lamp and a silver *capitulata* were given to me, and I handed them over.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, said to Victor son of Samsuricus: “From whom did you hear this?” Victor said: “From Bishop Silvanus.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Victor: “Did you hear from him himself that he had handed them over?” Victor said: “I heard from him himself that with his own hands he had handed them over.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, said: “Where did you hear it?” Victor said: “In the basilica.” Zenophilus, [Col. 0738C] *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “At Constantine’s?” Victor said: “There he began to address the people, saying: ‘On what account do they say that I am a betrayer—on account of the lamp and the *capitulata*?’”

Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Nundinarius: “What else do you think should be investigated from these matters?” Nundinarius said: “Who took the jars of the treasury?” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Nundinarius: “Which jars?” Nundinarius said: “They were in the temple of Serapis, and Bishop Purpurius took them; Bishop Silvanus, Presbyter Dontius, and Lucianus took the vinegar which they had.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Nundinarius: “Do those present know this was done?” Nundinarius replied: “They know.” Deacon Saturninus said: “Our elders said that they were removed.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “By whom are they said to have been removed?” Saturninus [Col. 0738D] said: “By Bishop Purpurius; and the vinegar by Silvanus, Dontius, and Superius, presbyters, and Lucianus the deacon.” Nundinarius said: “He gave twenty *folles*, and [Col. 0739A]

[Note: [Col. 0739D]

“Before the bishops’ chair.” Therefore, even then the location of the episcopal chair in the Church was certain and fixed.

“The bishops themselves.” Therefore several bishops ordained Victor the fuller as presbyter.

“By the arena-workers.” Not by the clergy or by persons of rank, but by the common rabble, among whom there were arena-workers—what sort of men those persons were at last. Hence a little later it is said that prostitutes were there, to show that the election of the bishop had been made by force and sedition. This passage proves that the constitution of the Synod of Laodicea, which decreed that crowds should not be permitted to make episcopal elections, was altogether most just.

“They carried him.” That is, they lifted and bore the bishop’s throne.

“The court of the martyrs.” Most interpret *area* as a cemetery, on the authority of Tertullian’s *To Scapula*, where he says that under the governor Hilarianus our opponents shouted concerning the areas of our burials: “Let there be no burial-grounds.” But in this passage *area martyrum* cannot mean a cemetery, since it is certain that it was a building in which the raging rabble shut up the people of God, or citizens of rank, so that they might have freedom to appoint whomever they wished as bishop. Hence below, p. 25, col. 1, when Crescentianus the subdeacon was questioned by Zenophilus whether he had been present when Silvanus was made bishop, he replied: “I was present with the people, shut up in the large house.” Thus we now have that the court of the martyrs and the large house of the city of Cirta were the same thing.

“I have no rank.” Zenophilus’s question, therefore, concerned not ecclesiastical rank but civil status.]

Victor was made presbyter?” Saturninus said. And when he said this, Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Saturninus: “To whom did he give it?” Saturninus said: “To Bishop Silvanus.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Saturninus: “Then, in order that he might become a presbyter, he gave Bishop Silvanus twenty *folles* as a reward?” Saturninus said: “He did.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “Was it placed before Silvanus?” Saturninus said: “Before the bishops’ chair.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Nundinarius: “By whom was the money taken?” Nundinarius said: “The bishops themselves divided it among themselves.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Nundinarius: “Do you wish Donatus to be produced?” Nundinarius said: “Certainly, let him come—the one concerning whom, two days afterwards, the people shouted equally: ‘Hear us, God; we want our fellow-citizen.’” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, [Col. 0739B] said to Nundinarius: “The people certainly shouted this?” He replied: “They shouted it.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Saturninus: “Did they call Silvanus a betrayer?” Saturninus said: “Certainly.” Nundinarius said: “When he was made bishop, we did not communicate with him, because he was said to be a betrayer.” Saturninus said: “What he says is true.” Nundinarius said: “I saw that Mutus, an arena-worker, carried him on his shoulders.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Saturninus: “Did it happen thus?” Saturninus said: “Thus.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “Are all the things Nundinarius says true—that Silvanus was made bishop by arena-workers?” Saturninus said: “They are true.” Nundinarius said: “Prostitutes were there.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Saturninus: “Did arena-workers carry him?” Saturninus said: “They themselves carried him, and [Col. 0739C] the people. For the citizens had been shut up in the court of the martyrs.” Nundinarius the deacon said: “Was the people of God there?” Saturninus said: “They were shut up in the large house.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “Are all the things Nundinarius says certain and true?” Saturninus said: “True.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “What do you say?” Victor said: “Everything is true, my lord.” Nundinarius said: “Bishop Purpurius took one hundred *folles*.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Nundinarius: “Whom do you think should be questioned concerning the four hundred *folles*?” Nundinarius said: “Let Lucianus the deacon be produced, because he knows everything.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Nundinarius: “Do these men know?” Nundinarius said: [Col. 0739D] “They do not know.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “Let Lucianus be produced.” Nundinarius said: “These men know [Col. 0740A] that the four hundred *folles* were received; but because the bishops divided them among themselves, they do not know [the details].” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Nundinarius and Victor: “Do you know that *folles* were received from Lucilla?” Saturninus and Victor said: “We know.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “Did the poor not receive them?” They said: “No one received anything.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Saturninus and Victor: “Was nothing taken from the shrine of Serapis?” Saturninus and Victor said: “Purpurius took the jars, and Bishop Silvanus, and Presbyters Dontius and Superius, and Deacon Lucianus took the vinegar.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “From the answer of Victor the grammarian, Victor son of Samsuricus, and Saturninus, it has become clear that all the things Nundinarius alleged are true. Let them be removed and leave.”

Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* [Col. 0740B] and consular governor, said: “Whom else do you think should be questioned?” Nundinarius said: “Castus the deacon, so that he may say whether Silvanus is not a betrayer. He himself ordained him.” And when Castus the deacon had been brought in and presented, Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “What is your name?” He replied: “Castus.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Castus: “What is your status?” Castus said: “I have no rank.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Castus: “Although now, through Victor the grammarian as well as through Victor son of Samsuricus and Saturninus, the matters which Nundinarius charges have come into confession, nevertheless you too confess whether Silvanus is a betrayer.” Castus replied: “He said that he had found the lamp behind an *orca*.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Castus: “Confess also concerning the jars removed from the shrine of Serapis and the vinegar.” [Col. 0740C] Castus replied: “Bishop Purpurius took the jars.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said: “Who took the vinegar?” Castus replied that Bishop Silvanus and Presbyters Dontius and Superius took the vinegar from there. Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Castus: “Confess how many *folles* Victor gave in order to become a presbyter.” Castus said: “He offered, my lord, a little shrine, and what it contained I do not know.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Castus: “To whom was the little shrine given?” Castus said: “That man carried it into the large house.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Castus: “Was the money not divided among the people?” Castus replied: “It was not given, nor did I see [it].” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus* and consular governor, said to Castus: “Of the *folles* which [Col. 0740D] Lucilla gave, did the common people receive nothing?” Castus said: “I did not see anyone receive [anything].” [Note: [Col. 0741D]

“Campenses.” The old codex reads *Campeses*, by the same principle by which *Monteses* is frequently written for *Montenses*. By *campenses* are meant those who live in fields and countryside, as the word itself indicates. There are other Campenses in Jerome, Epistle 57, who are associated both with Arians and with Tarsensian heretics. Again, there are other *Campitae*, as the edition of Marianus Victorius has it, or *Campates*, as John Andrew, bishop of Aléria, and Desiderius Erasmus printed, in Jerome at the end of the dialogue *Against the Luciferians*. These were identical with the Montenses, that is, the Donatists. Erasmus and Victorius are mistaken in thinking that the Montenses were so named from the heresy of Montanus. They are mistaken, I say, as is clear also from Epistle 133 of Jerome.

“The remainder is missing.” Except for the final part of these proceedings, which is wanting, the proceedings of the Council of Cirta were read before Zenophilus the consular governor, as Optatus of Milevum teaches in Book I: “These men and the others, whom we shall shortly show were your leaders, after the persecution sat down at the city of Cirta in the house of Urbanus Carisius on the third day before the Ides of May, because the basilicas had not yet been restored, as the writings of Nundinarius, then a deacon, testify.” Incidentally, I should note that the most illustrious Gabriel Albaspinaeus, bishop of Orléans, erred in his interpretation of this passage by referring the persecution mentioned here to Maxentius, when the proceedings of the Council of Cirta show that the persecution at issue was that of Diocletian. This is also plainly inferred from Augustine, *Breviculus* of the Third Day, chapter 17. Moreover, the proceedings of the Council of Cirta are found, as we have noted, in Augustine.]
the consular Castus said: “Where, then, did they end up?” Castus said: “I do not know.” Nundinarius said: “Surely you either heard or saw whether it was said to the poor: ‘Lucilla gives you too something from her own property.’” Castus said: “I did not see anyone receiving anything.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said: “Castus’s confession is clear: he did not know that the bags of coins which Lucilla donated had been distributed among the people; therefore let him be removed.” And when Crescentianus the subdeacon had been brought forward, Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said: “What is your name?” He replied: “Crescentianus.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “Simply, as did the others, confess whether you know Silvanus to be a *traditor*.” Crescentianus said: “The earlier clergy reported the individual particulars.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “What did they report?” Crescentianus [Col. 0741B] said: “They reported that he was a *traditor*.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “Did they call him a *traditor*?” And he added: “Who said this?” Crescentianus said: “Those who associated with him among the people said that he had at some time handed [the Scriptures] over.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “Were they speaking of Silvanus?” Crescentianus said: “Certainly.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “Were you present when he was made bishop?” Crescentianus said: “I was present with the people, shut up in the larger hall.” Nundinarius the deacon said: “The country people and the sand-workers made him bishop.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “Mutus the sand-worker certainly elevated him?” He said: “Plainly so.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “Do you know that casks were taken from the temple of Serapis?” [Col. 0741C] Crescentianus said: “Many said that Bishop Purpurius himself took away the casks and the vinegar, which came into the possession of our old man Silvanus; and the sons of Aelio said so.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “What did you hear?” Crescentianus said: “That vinegar was taken by the old man Silvanus, by Dontius and Superius the presbyters, and by Lucianus the deacon.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “Out of the four hundred bags of coins which Lucilla donated, did the people receive anything?” Crescentianus said: “No one received anything from it; I do not know, nor do I know who disbursed them.” Nundinarius said: “Did the old women never receive anything from it?” Crescentianus said: “Nothing.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said: “Certainly, whenever anything of that kind is donated, all the townspeople publicly receive something from it.” [Col. 0742A] Crescentianus said: “I neither heard nor saw that he gave anything to anyone.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “Then nothing of the four hundred bags was given to the people?” Crescentianus said: “Nothing. Certainly some little part would have reached us.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said: “Where, then, were they taken?” Crescentianus said: “I do not know. No one received anything.” Nundinarius said: “How many bags did Victor give in order to be made presbyter?” Crescentianus said: “I saw baskets brought in with money.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Crescentianus: “To whom were the baskets given?” Crescentianus said: “To Bishop Silvanus.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said: “They were given to Silvanus?” Crescentianus said: “To Silvanus.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said: “Nothing was given to the people?” He replied: [Col. 0742B] “Nothing. We too would necessarily have received something if they had been distributed as usual.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said to Nundinarius: “What else do you think ought to be asked of Crescentianus?” Nundinarius said: “That is all.” Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said: “Since Crescentianus the subdeacon has frankly confessed concerning everything, let him be removed.” Likewise, when Januarius the subdeacon had been introduced and brought forward, Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, consular, said: “What is your name?” He replied . . . . . The rest is missing.

## A.D. 304

## TEXT OF THE LETTERS OF MENSURIUS TO SECUNDUS OF TIGISIS, AND OF SECUNDUS TO MENSURIUS, CONCERNING MENSURIUS’S HANDING OVER [OF THE SCRIPTURES]

(From Augustine, *Brief Record of the Conference*, Day 3, ch. 13, no. 25, vol. IX, col. 638.)

[Col. 0742C]

Then the Donatists stated at some length that Mensurius, who before Caecilianus had been bishop of the Church of Carthage, had, during the persecution, handed over the holy Scriptures to the persecutors. To prove this, they read his letter addressed to Secundus of Tigisis, who at that time held the primacy among the bishops of Numidia. In that letter Mensurius seemed, as it were, to confess his own crime. Yet he had not written that he had handed over the sacred codices, but rather that he had removed and preserved them so that they should not be found by the persecutors; while in the basilica he had left whatever disreputable writings of heretics there were. When the persecutors found and removed these, they demanded nothing further from him. [Col. 0743A]

> **Note: [Col. 0743D]**
>
> *Ecbola.* This term denotes cast-off items, or things of no use. Relevant here is the statement of Silvanus in the acts related above, in Book III, chapter 29, *Against Cresconius*: “Nothing remains here; we threw all this out.”

Nevertheless, some men of the Carthaginian municipal council later represented to the proconsul that those who had been sent to seize and burn the Christians’ Scriptures had been deceived, because they had found only certain things which did not concern them; but that the Scriptures themselves were kept in the bishop’s house and should be produced from there and burned. The proconsul, however, was unwilling to agree to this.

It was also read in the same letters that Mensurius disapproved of those who, without having been arrested, offered themselves for persecution and voluntarily declared that they possessed Scriptures which they would not hand over, although no one had demanded this of them; and he forbade Christians to honour them. Certain criminals and debtors to the treasury were likewise censured in the same letter: under the pretext of persecution, they either wished to escape a life burdensome through many debts, or thought that they might cleanse themselves and, as it were, wash away their crimes, or else obtain money and enjoy luxuries in custody through the attendance of Christians. [Col. 0743B]

Yet the Donatists brought no accusation against Mensurius except that of handing over codices. They said, indeed, that he had lied because those were not sacred codices; and that he had wished to conceal his sin, though they charged even this very contrivance as a crime.

They also read Secundus of Tigisis’s reply, sent peaceably to the same Mensurius, in which he too recounted what the persecutors had done in Numidia: those who had been arrested and had refused to hand over the holy Scriptures suffered many evils, were tortured by most severe punishments, and were killed. He commended them as worthy of honour because of the merit of their martyrdom, praising them for not handing over the holy Scriptures, following the example of the woman [Col. 0743C] who in Jericho (Joshua 2), in whom the two Testaments, Old and New, were prefigured, refused to hand over the two spies to the persecutors.

If that example is to be understood under this figure, it rather supported Mensurius. For in his own letter Mensurius censured those who, although they did not hand over the holy Scriptures, nevertheless admitted that they possessed them. That woman did not do this: she did not confess that the spies being sought were with her, but denied it.

Secundus also wrote that a centurion and a *beneficiarius*, sent to him by the curator and the municipal council to demand divine codices for burning, had come to him; and that he had replied to them: “I am a Christian and a bishop, not a *traditor*.” When they wished to obtain from him some *ecbola*, or anything whatever, he had not given them even that—following the example [Col. 0743D] of Eleazar the Maccabee (2 Macc. 6:24), who would not even pretend to eat pork, lest he provide others with an example of apostasy. The Catholics patiently heard these letters of Mensurius and Secundus until their reading was finished, although they declared that they were private letters and irrelevant to the case of the Church. [Col. 0744A]

And no. 27. But what Purpurius alleged against him—that he had been detained by the curator and the council in order that he might give up the Scriptures—Secundus himself almost confessed in the letter he had written in reply to Mensurius. For there he says that a centurion and a *beneficiarius* had been sent to him by the curator and council, that Scriptures—or any *ecbola* whatever—had been demanded of him, and that he had not handed them over. Yet, after he had there commemorated so many martyrs who, because they refused to hand them over, were tortured and killed, how could he, though detained and convicted and unwilling to hand over anything, have suffered nothing and been released? He neither wrote this to Mensurius nor answered it to Purpurius. For he did not tell the centurion and the *beneficiarius* that he had no Scriptures; he replied that he would hand over nothing whatsoever. How they could have reported this after releasing him [Col. 0744B] without endangering themselves is not apparent, especially since this same Secundus stated that not merely insignificant persons but even householders had been killed by the cruellest deaths after giving this same answer to the persecutors.

## THE SAME, FROM THE SAME WORK

(*Against Gaudentius*, Book I, ch. 37, no. 47, col. 735.)

Moreover, Secundus himself unambiguously admitted this in his letter addressed to Mensurius, which you yourselves produced and read: he did not hand [the Scriptures] over, but persecutors sent by the curator and municipal council came to him—the same men whom Purpurius of Limata alleged had demanded that he hand over the Scriptures. When they asked him for them, he replied, “I am a Christian and a bishop, not a *traditor*,” and he wished to hand over absolutely nothing to them. You wish us to believe this, although you yourselves see how incredible it is that, while that persecution raged, a bishop detained or summoned to hand over the Lord’s Scriptures could have been released without handing anything over.

Indeed, you maintained that bishops could not assemble in the city of Cirta during the persecution in order to ordain a bishop. How, then, did that persecution rage if a bishop could be held for the purpose of handing over Scriptures and released with impunity after handing over nothing?

## A.D. 305

## ACTS OF THE COUNCIL OF CIRTA

Mentioned by Optatus, Book I, §14, p. 14.

(From Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, Book III, ch. 27, no. 30, vol. IX, col. 510.)

[Col. 0744D]

> **Note: [Col. 0743D]**
>
> *Diocletian for the eighth time.* In the copy that was examined more carefully during the Carthaginian Conference, these acts of the Council of Cirta were dated in the year after the consulship of Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth time, on the third day before the Nones of March—that is, A.D. 305—as Augustine testifies below in the *Brief Record of the Conference*, Day 3, ch. 17. In Optatus, Book I *Against Parmenianus*, this same meeting at Cirta is noted as having been held after the persecution, on the third day before the Ides of May. There “persecution” is to be understood, not as Maxentius’s persecution, as Albaspinaeus wished, but as that concerning the handing over of codices, as you will learn from Augustine at the end of the preceding chapter. This persecution ceased in the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII.
>
> *They sat in a house.* Optatus, Book I: “Since,” he says, “the basilicas had not yet been restored, they met in the house of Urbanus Carisius.”
>
> *“They were discarded items.”* In the manuscripts: *delititia fuisse*.
>
> *“And God forgives me too.”* Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “And God will forgive me.”
>
> *From Limata.* A Corbie manuscript of the best quality reads *a Liniata*. In Augustine, Letter 43, some codices have *Liniacensem* in place of *Limatensem*.
>
> *Felix from Rotaria, [and] the centurion.* The same Corbie manuscript reads *a Rotoria Centurionis*. Other manuscripts also have *Centurionis* in the genitive. Optatus read it very differently; in discussing the same Cirtan assembly in Book I, he says: “Those who remained were consulted, namely Victor of Garba, Felix of Rotarium, and Nabor of Centurion,” etc.

When Diocletian was consul for the eighth time and Maximian for the seventh, on the fourth day before the Nones of March, at Cirta, Secundus, bishop of Tigisis, having taken his seat in the first chair [Col. 0745A] in the house of Urbanus Donatus, said: “Let us first examine ourselves, and then we shall be able to ordain a bishop here.”

Secundus said to Donatus of Mascula: “It is said that you handed [the Scriptures] over.” Donatus replied: “You know how greatly Florus sought me out so that I might burn incense, and God did not hand me over into his hands, brother. But because God forgave me, you too preserve me for God.” Secundus said: “What then are we to do about the martyrs? Because they did not hand [the Scriptures] over, they were crowned.” Donatus said: “Dismiss me to God; there I shall render an account.” Secundus said: “Stand apart.”

Secundus said to Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae: “It is said that you too handed [the Scriptures] over.” Marinus replied: “I gave the records to Pollus, for my codices are safe.” Secundus said: “Stand apart.”

Secundus said to Donatus of Calama: “It is said that you handed [the Scriptures] over.” Donatus replied: “I gave medical codices.” [Col. 0745B] Secundus said: “Stand apart.”

And elsewhere: Secundus said to Victor of Rusiccada: “It is said that you handed over the four Gospels.” Victor replied: “Valentianus was curator; he compelled me to cast them into the fire. I knew that they were discarded items. Forgive me this offence, and God forgives me too.” Secundus said: “Stand apart.”

And elsewhere: Secundus said to Purpurius of Limata: “It is said that you killed the two sons of your sister at Mileum.” Purpurius replied: “Do you think I am frightened by you, as were the other men? What did you do, you who were detained by the curator and the municipal council in order to hand over the Scriptures? How did you free yourself from them, unless you gave, or ordered to be given, something or other? For they did not simply let you go. As for me, I killed and I kill those who act against me. Therefore do not provoke me to say more. You know that I make no account of anyone.” [Col. 0745C]

Secundus the Younger said to his paternal uncle Secundus: “Do you hear what he says against you? He is ready to withdraw and make a schism—not only he, but also all those whom you accuse. I know that they will abandon you, pass sentence against you, and you will remain alone as a heretic. Therefore, what concern is it of yours what anyone has done? He must render an account to God.”

Secundus said to Felix of Rotaria, the centurion, and Victor of Garba: “What seems right to you?” They replied: “They have God, to whom they must render an account.” Secundus said: “You know, and God knows. Sit down.” And all replied: “Thanks be to God.”

## A.D. 311

## SUMMARY OF THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE CARTHAGINIAN COUNCIL OF SEVENTY NUMIDIAN BISHOPS, WHO CONDEMNED CAECILIANUS AND ORDAINED MAJORINUS

Concerning it, Optatus, Book I, §19, p. 18.

(From Augustine, *Brief Record of the Conference*, Day 3, ch. 14, no. 26, vol. IX, col. 639.)

[Col. 0745D]

> **Note: [Col. 0745D]**
>
> *Colleagues of Caecilianus.* Among Caecilianus’s colleagues there mentioned by name in connection with the charge of handing over [the Scriptures] were Novellus of Tyzica and Faustinus of Tuburbo, according to the book written after the Conference against the Donatists, ch. 22.

And the Donatists read out a council of approximately seventy [Col. 0746A] bishops held at Carthage against Caecilianus. There they condemned him in his absence because he would not come to them, as having been ordained by *traditores*; and because, when he was a deacon, he was said to have forbidden food to be brought to martyrs held in custody. Certain colleagues of Caecilianus were also named, who were asserted to be *traditores* on the evidence of public records, though those records were not read. Felix of Abthugni, however, was accused with particular bitterness among them, so that he was called the source of all evils. Then judgments were pronounced individually, first by Secundus of Tigisis, who was their leader, and then by the others; in these they declared that they would not communicate with Caecilianus and his colleagues.

## JUDGMENT OF MARCIANUS, ONE OF THE BISHOPS [Col. 0746B] PRESENT AT THIS CARTHAGINIAN COUNCIL

(From the author of the book *Against Fulgentius the Donatist*, wrongly ascribed to Augustine, ch. 26, in the Appendix to vol. IX of Augustine, col. 774.)

Your Marcianus, among the others, delivered the following judgment, which assuredly the seventy who were present did not disapprove:

“In his Gospel, the Lord says: ‘I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman; every branch in me which does not bear fruit, he will cut off and cast out, and every branch which remains in me and bears fruit, he cleanses’ [cf. John 15:1–2]. Therefore, just as unfruitful branches are cut off and cast away, so those who have sacrificed incense, *traditores*, and those ordained in schism by *traditores*, cannot remain in the Church of God unless, having acknowledged their own lamentation, they are reconciled through repentance. Hence one ought not to communicate with Caecilianus, ordained in schism by *traditores*.” [Col. 0746C]

## LETTER OF EMPEROR CONSTANTINE

[Col. 0747B]
