## CONCERNING THE ROMAN COUNCIL UNDER MILTIADES

> **Note: [Col. 0747D]**
>
> (1) From Optatus, Book I.

Judges were appointed [Note: (2) In the Germanensis manuscript, *principes*—“leading men”—is read in place of *judices*], Maternus from the city of Agrippina, Rheticius from the city of Augustodunum, and Marinus of Arles. The three Gauls and fifteen other Italians came to the city of Rome. They assembled in Fausta’s house in the Lateran, in the consulship of Constantine for the third time and Licinius for the third time, on the sixth day before the Nones of October, Friday [Note: (3) In the same codex: “Constantine for the fourth time and Licinius, on the sixth day before the Nones of October.” In Augustine’s book written after the Conference, no. 56: “in the consulship of Constantine for the third time and Licinius for the second time, on the sixth day before the Nones of October.” Note: (4) A.D. 313].

When Miltiades, bishop of the city of Rome, Rheticius, Maternus, and Marinus, Gallican bishops, [Col. 0747C] and Merocles of Milan, Florianus of Caesena, Zoticus of Quintianum, Stemnius of Ariminum [Note: (5) Germanensis manuscript: “Florianus of Sinna, Zonticus of Quintianum, Stennius of Ariminum”], Felix of Florence in Tuscany, Gaudentius of Pisa, Constantius of Faenza, Proterius of Capua, Theophilus of Benevento, Savinus of Terracina, Secundus of Praeneste, Felix of Tres Tabernae, Maximus of Ostia [Note: (6) The same manuscript: “Maximus of Tres-Ostia”], Evandrus of Ursinum, and Donatianus of Forum Claudii had taken their seats—these nineteen bishops—the case of Donatus and Caecilianus was brought before them.

Judgments were pronounced individually against Donatus [Note: (7) Donatus of Casae Nigrae, from Augustine, *Brief Record of the Conference*, Day 3, chs. 12 and 17]: that he had confessed to rebaptizing and to imposing hands upon lapsed bishops, which is alien to the Church. The witnesses introduced by Donatus confessed that they had nothing to say against Caecilianus. Caecilianus was declared innocent by the unanimous judgment of those mentioned above, including the judgment of Miltiades, which concluded the proceedings [Note: (8) The same manuscript has “sealed” (*coagulatum est*)] in the following words:

> “Since it has been established that Caecilianus is not accused, in accordance with their own declaration, by those who came with Donatus, and since it has not been established that he has been convicted by Donatus in any respect [Col. 0748A] [Note: (1) The same codex: *in aquila professione constiterit*, apparently corrupt], I judge that he ought rightly to be retained in his ecclesiastical communion with his status unimpaired. It is therefore enough that Donatus has been struck by so many judgments and Caecilianus cleared by so great a judgment.”

Yet Donatus thought that an appeal ought to be made by the bishops [Note: (2) In the same codex, *ab episcopis* is absent. The Germanensis codex reads: “the bishop thought that an appeal ought to be made,” and so forth]. Constantine the emperor answered this appeal as follows: “O rabid audacity of madness! They have lodged an appeal, as is customary in cases of pagans.” [Note: (3) These words of Constantine occur in a letter written to the bishops after the Council of Arles. They were therefore uttered by Constantine when the Donatists appealed to him from the judgment at Arles. Compare Augustine, Letter 43, no. 20.]

Eunomius and Olympius, bishops sent to Africa, declared to the Carthaginians, against Donatus’s party, where the Catholic Church was, and confirmed the judgment delivered by the Roman council in favour of Caecilianus [Note: (4) From Optatus, Book I].

[Col. 0748B] At the same time this same Donatus requested permission to return, provided that he did not approach Carthage [Note: (5) Thus we restore this passage on the authority of the Germanensis manuscript. For the printed editions of Optatus read: “that it might befall him to return to Carthage.” That this Donatus, already condemned—the bishop not of Carthage but of Casae Nigrae—would have dared request permission to return to Carthage, where he had created a schism, will scarcely be believed by anyone, as we have already observed above, in the *Brief Record of the Conference*, Day 3, ch. 20].

Then his supporter Filuminus represented to the emperor that, for the good of peace, Caecilianus should be kept at Brescia; and this was done. Then two bishops, Eunomius and Olympius, were sent to Africa. They came and stayed at Carthage for forty days in order to declare where the Catholic Church was. Donatus’s seditious party would not allow this to be done. Daily uproars arose from partisan zeal. The final judgment of the same bishops Eunomius and Olympius is read as follows: they declared that the Catholic Church was that which was spread throughout the whole world, and that the judgment already given by nineteen bishops could not be annulled. Thus they communicated with Caecilianus’s clergy and returned. [Col. 0748C] We possess volumes of the proceedings concerning these matters. Whoever wishes may read them in their final portions.

Meanwhile Donatus himself, unbidden and first, returned to Carthage. Upon hearing this, Caecilianus hastened to his own people. Thus the parties were renewed once more. Nevertheless, it is established both that Donatus was struck by so many judgments and that Caecilianus was declared innocent by just as many judgments.

## A.D. 321

## RESCRIPT OF CONSTANTINE TO VALERIUS OR VERINUS

In the index to the Conference, Day 3, ch. 549, a letter [Col. 0749B] of Constantine sent to Verinus, vicar, is read, by which he grants the Donatists freedom of action.

There, ch. 550: The Catholics’ prosecution, which says that Constantine’s letter makes rather for their case, because nothing was adjudicated concerning Caecilianus, but they themselves were surrendered to their own madness.

Augustine, in the book written after the Conference, ch. 33, testifies that these letters, addressed to Valerius or Verinus, vicar—concerning the lifting of their exile and leaving their madness to God the avenger—were issued in the consulship of Crispus and Constantine for the second time, on the third day before the Nones of May; that is, after approximately four years and nearly six months had elapsed from the date of the rescript directed to Eumalius. Compare *Brief Record of the Conference*, Day 3, ch. 22, and Letter 141, no. 9, vol. II of Augustine’s works.

## LETTER OF CAECILIANUS TO FELIX

CAECILIANUS TO HIS FATHER FELIX, GREETINGS.

[Col. 0749D]

Since my colleague pressed his friend Augentianus more urgently and asked, in the year of my duumvirate, whether any documents of your law had been burned in accordance with the sacred law—[the connection of the following clause is uncertain:] Galatius, one of your law, had publicly produced letters of greeting from the basilica. I pray, dearest father, that you are well.

PETRONIUS, ANNIANUS, AND JULIANUS TO DOMITIUS CELSUS, VICAR OF AFRICA.

Since His Dignity ordered Lucianus, Capito, Fidentius, and Nasutius, bishops, and Mammarius, presbyter—who, in accordance with the heavenly command of our lord Constantine Maximus, unconquered and ever Augustus, had come to Gaul with other [Col. 0750A] men of his law—to return to their own homes, we have supplied them, brother, with official transport and the appropriate grain allowance as far as the port of Arles, in accordance with the command of the eternity of that same most merciful prince, so that from there they may sail to Africa. It is fitting that you learn this through our letter. We pray, brother, that you remain in the happiest good health. Hilarius, *princeps*, presented [this] on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, at Trier.

### Concerning Constantine’s judgment held at Milan, where Caecilianus was again acquitted

In the index to the Carthaginian Conference, Day 3, ch. 516, one reads: “Reading of Constantine’s judgment, by which the emperor indicates that Caecilianus was cleared before him also after the Council of Arles.” There, ch. 521: “Interlocutory ruling that the emperor pronounced judgment between the parties.” There, ch. 523: “Interlocutory ruling expressing the same point from the imperial rescript read above.”

Augustine cites this rescript to Eumalius, vicar of Africa, in the *Brief Record of the Conference*, III, no. 37, and in the book written after the Conference, no. 56, where he says that it was issued in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus, on the fourth day before the Ides of November [Note: [Col. 0750D] (1) 10 November, A.D. 316]. He also quotes Constantine’s very judgment in favour of Caecilianus from the same rescript in *Against Cresconius*, Book III, no. 82: “I further insert,” he says, “the words of Constantine from his letter to Eumalius, vicar, in which he testifies that he investigated the matter between the parties and found Caecilianus innocent.” After recounting in what he had said above how the parties had been brought to his judgment after episcopal judgments, Constantine says: “In this [case] I found [Col. 0750C] Caecilianus to be a man endowed with every innocence and observing the obligations of his religion, and discharging them as was proper; and it clearly appeared that no crime could be found in him, such as had been fabricated in his absence by the pretence of his adversaries.” Compare Letter 43, no. 20, vol. II.

Some time after that judgment he issued a most severe law against Donatus’s party, as Augustine testifies in Letter 105, no. 9: “He was the first to enact many measures against their error and ordered their basilicas to be taken away.” From Book II *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, no. 205: “He ordered that the places of their assemblies should be claimed for the treasury.” Augustine, Letter 88, no. 3. Constantine’s law against the Donatists is mentioned by Gratian in Book II of the Theodosian Code, title *That Holy Baptism Is Not to Be Repeated*.

## A.D. 340

## SERMON OF A CERTAIN DONATIST CONCERNING THE HARASSMENT OF THE DONATISTS IN THE TIMES OF LEONTIUS AND URSATIUS

Now first published from a manuscript codex of the library of the Most Illustrious and Reverend Bishop of Châlons, approximately five hundred years old; the work of a very ancient author.

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING SERMON

Although the following document, which had not previously been published, contains no few calumnies against Catholics, it ought nevertheless not to have been omitted, since it sheds much light both upon Optatus’s statements and upon Donatist history. The sermon was delivered on 12 March, at the solemn annual commemoration of certain Donatists who were regarded by their own party as martyrs. In the manuscript it is entitled: “On the Passion of Saints Donatus and Advocatus.” Yet the name of neither occurs in the sermon itself. There is only mention of Honoratus, bishop of Sciliba, or rather Siciliba, in the proconsular province, who had come to Carthage from the town of Advocatum. Therefore it should be called not the Passion of Donatus or Advocatus, but rather the Passion of Honoratus.

There is described there a military operation carried out against several Donatists at Carthage, in which their basilica was taken from them. [Col. 0751B] Nothing is certain about the date, except that it is said there that the affair took place while Caecilianus Eudinepisus was then pressing it, with Leontius concurring, Ursatius serving as duke, and Marcellinus then as tribune. Caecilianus Eudinepisus is none other than the bishop of Carthage. For this persecution is later also called the Caecilianian persecution, and memorial inscriptions are said to have been erected for the martyrs lest the parricide should at some later time deceive others, by the title of bishop, who had not shared in the deed. By these words Caecilianus of Carthage is plainly designated.

Since he died during the time of the Council of Sardica, that is, in A.D. 347, and Gratus, his successor, attended that council, these events must have occurred before that year. Leontius and Ursatius, as agents of unity raging against the Donatists, are mentioned in more than one place. In our Optatus, Book III, §1, pp. 50–51: “Many harsh acts indeed were performed by the agents of unity; but why do you impute them to Leontius, Macarius, or Taurinus?” And in the same book, §10, pp. 66–67: “You disapprove of the times—I know not whose—of Leontius, Ursatius, Macarius, and the others . . . . There was first a storm under Ursatius . . . . there followed rain under Gregory . . . . after the rain came stones under the agents of unity.”

Cresconius, cited by Augustine, says that Silvanus of Cirta refused communion with Ursatius and Zenophilus while they were persecuting, and for that reason was sent into exile. Petilianus the Donatist likewise, recalling the officials hostile to the Donatists, mentions Ursatius among them: “Macarius perished,” he says; “Ursatius perished, and all your officials likewise perished by God’s vengeance. For Ursatius, having been struck down in barbarian battle, was torn to pieces by birds with savage talons and by the bites of ravenous dogs.” [Col. 0751D]

In the Acts of the Carthaginian Conference, Day 3, ch. 258, a letter of Januarianus and other Donatist bishops is reported, in which they enumerate the persecutors of the Donatists as follows: “For, to omit how much Christian blood was shed through Leontius, Ursatius, Macarius, Paulus, Taurinus, Romanus, and the other executioners whom they obtained from the rulers of this world for the slaughter of the saints: very many venerable priests were killed, others relegated into exile, [Col. 0752A] Christianity was widely harassed, sacred virginity violated, the rich proscribed, the poor despoiled, basilicas taken away, and fugitive priests driven into flight.” These charges resemble those recited in the present document.

We have nothing concerning Marcellinus the tribune in Africa; for he certainly differs from the man who presided over the Carthaginian Conference. It is established that these things occurred during the reign of Emperor Constans, even before Paulus and Macarius were sent to Africa. In all the places just cited, Leontius and Ursatius are named before Macarius, Paulus, and Taurinus; and Optatus openly shows that Ursatius was earlier than the others. It is established from this present document that Leontius, who is always named before Macarius, was contemporary with Ursatius, since it states that at the same time Leontius was *comes* and Ursatius *dux*. It is also established that Ursatius had contended for the Catholic side from the times of Silvanus of Cirta and Zenophilus. Zenophilus heard Silvanus’s case in A.D. 320, as is clear from the acts related above.

The events reported here therefore seem to have happened about A.D. 340, or a little later—certainly before Macarius was sent to Africa around A.D. 348. The Donatus mentioned in the title seems to be the same as Donatus of Bagaia, who suffered with Marculus, concerning whom see Optatus, Book III, §4, p. 63. He is also mentioned in Usuard’s martyrology under 1 March, where he is said to have suffered under Ursatius the *dux* and Marcellinus the tribune, which agrees with our acts. But that Donatus, according to Augustine, Homily XI on John, is said to have been thrown into a well—a circumstance that cannot fit any of the martyrs mentioned here, since all were killed by soldiers in the basilica. The title is therefore unrelated to the sermon itself, as has already been observed.

Moreover, this work is by an African writer of no mean ability. Although he inveighs notably against the Catholic Church, he is nevertheless neither unlearned nor ignorant; indeed, he is a man not moderately versed in the sacred writings and in the precepts of Christian doctrine, who offers many excellent things—would that they had been offered for a better cause. His style plainly proves the writer’s antiquity, and it is evident that the sermon was delivered when the Donatist sect flourished in Africa. The author’s name is unknown.

## 12 March: Sermon on the Passion of Saints Donatus and Advocatus

> **Note: [Col. 0751D]**
>
> I.—“The crafty deceits and snares of flattering deception.” This writer accordingly admits that the persecution of the Donatists was not like the persecution of Christians by pagans. He says that the records of the latter are clear, whereas those of the former are obscure and less known. On the difference between the two, read Optatus, Book III, §8, p. 64.

[Col. 0752D] I. If the manifest records of persecutions have not been written down idly, nor read without deliberation, in annual solemn observance, for the honour of the martyrs and the edification of believers, why should the subtle deceits and snares of flattering deception not likewise be written down and read—those which, under the pretext of religion, overthrow souls by fraudulent entrapment? Instruction is all the more necessary where there is no openly declared hostility, because a hostile fellowship is easy and close at hand for deceiving; “and a man’s enemies,” it says, “shall be those of his own household” (Matt. 10:36 [Col. 0753A]). Therefore it would be foreign to the duty of religion and piety not only to suppress the glories of martyrs in a kind of envious silence, but also, under the protection of that silence, to conceal by deceptive subtlety what is salutary. For what is so perilously kept silent by the prudent as it is uselessly unknown by the simple? For just as the unwary are easily deceived by impostors through invocation of Christ’s name, so it is necessary to flee from the ministers of Antichrist who bear this name. Thus, by the exposure of wolves hidden in sheep’s clothing, those whom ignorance had deceived will either be set free, or, being obstinate, will perish through their own fault, without blame or danger to the preachers. The Christian reason, then, for recounting what was done is full both of usefulness and of justice: for the faithful are strengthened by commemoration, the inexperienced are stirred to endure temptations [Col. 0753B], and enemies are condemned by being exposed. Let the pious mother Church therefore proclaim the most patient faith of her children. Let the den of most cruel robbers also recognize the fruit of its work. Let us now, then, come to the causes.

> [Note: Col. 0753D]  
> **II.—Caecilian.** This is undoubtedly Caecilian of Carthage; for this persecution is afterwards called Caecilianic, and its author is a bishop. These events therefore occurred in the time of Bishop Caecilian, who attempted, through Ursatius, to recover the basilica held by the Donatists.  
>   
> **Eudinepisus.** This appears to have been Caecilian’s cognomen.  
>   
> **Open persecution.** Namely, that of the pagans against Christians.  
>   
> **To retain anew, unlawfully, ecclesiastical offices after their lapse.** The Donatists had separated from the Church on the pretext that Catholics had promoted to the episcopate, or retained in it, persons guilty of handing over the Scriptures and of idolatry [Col. 0754D].

II. The affair took place at Carthage, while Caecilian Eudinepisus was then pressing for it, Count Leontius consenting, Ursatius acting as commander, and Marcellinus then serving as tribune—though the Devil was the counsellor of them all. First—for it is the habitual way of the ancient dragon—as though he had not long since shown himself an assailant of the Christian name through overt persecution, he sought to entrap by cunning fraud those whom he had been unable to overcome by open persecution, so that deception might succeed the more readily because its author lay concealed. But those for whom the divine precepts are always victorious weapons understood the snares of one who flattered no less than they had not been terrified by the threats of one then raging.

But when he had not deceived those who were watchful and wary by flattery, that envious artificer, knowing that those whom he had formerly struck down in the public carnage could return by repentance to him whom they had denied, and that the Lord himself is ready to receive the confession of those who grieve, since he does not will the death of one dying so much as that he should return and live—he raised up by blandishments, in the time of peace, minds that he had subdued amid the contest of tortures by fear. Removing humility, by which alone the wrath of the offended God could be appeased, he instilled pride, by which he knew God would most certainly be more gravely offended; he suggested that those who had fallen might unlawfully retain anew ecclesiastical honours—those who then held them, deserters of the heavenly sacraments [Col. 0753D]. Now he rejoiced equally in their false betrayal as he had recently rejoiced in their weakness of faith.

[Col. 0754A] Indeed, he was now more secure when they were called, as it were, bishops or Christians than when they fell through denial of the Name: so long as he had his own enemies called by that name, provided that through such fraud he might more safely hold those whom he mocked with a false designation—as we have said—not only delighting the wretched with empty glory, but also ensnaring the greedy with royal friendship and earthly gifts.

> [Note: Col. 0754D]  
> **III.—“Let unity therefore be established.”** Hence Leontius, Ursatius, Paul, and Macarius were called workers for unity, because they compelled the unwilling Donatists into the unity of the Church.  
>   
> **Calling it Catholic.** That writer cannot deny that the Church in communion with Caecilian was called Catholic.  
>   
> **He sends money.** The Emperor Constans had not at first sent Paul and Macarius to establish unity, but with alms, as Optatus testifies, book III, §3, p. 55. The author of this writing teaches the same concerning Leontius and Ursatius.

III. Yet the insatiable plunderer, distressed that he had not gained possession of all by this device, the enemy of salvation found a subtler argument for violating the sincerity of faith. “Christ,” he says, “is a lover of unity; therefore let unity be established.” Before a people always excessively compliant with him, and therefore forsaken by God, he called it “Catholic,” so that those unwilling to communicate with it might be called heretics on the prejudice of the name. He sent money, by which he might either capture faith [Col. 0754B] or make profession of the law an occasion for avarice. But when, against all these alluring trials, the firm and inflexible tenor of justice resisted with greater devotion, judges were ordered to intervene; the powers of the world were compelled that they might compel; houses were surrounded by detachments of troops; threats of confiscation were held out against the wealthy; sacred rites were profaned; a crowd of pagans having been brought in, sacred assemblies became splendid banquets.

IV. What was said or done there amid the feasts of licentious youths, and wherever there were at hand the scornful actions of women, it would be a crime, most faithful brethren, to recount. What a sudden change of circumstances! The basilica was turned into a tavern—or, lest I say something more shameful. What anguish it was to see so great an abomination in the house of God: that place accustomed to chaste prayers and vows profaned with incestuous acts [Col. 0754C] and illegitimate voices! What man, I ask, even of the lowest condition, would permit such things to be done within his own walls? No one would wish this except one who could also do it.

Who denies either that such acts were done by the instigation of the Devil’s children, or that those who instigated the deed should be called Christians, unless he wishes either to excuse the Devil himself or thinks otherwise concerning Christ the Lord? How great was the serpent’s industry! How intensely he laboured to bring about these evils: that his own household, marked by a divine name, might conceal itself by means of the name, just as it disgraced the Name by its works! O venerable power of divine patience! Though enduring the extension of so great a wickedness, it suffers the deeds of the subtle enemy to be imputed to itself or to its Name.

Let no one think it a slight matter what happens whenever schisms and heresies arise: by their profane ministry and adulterous work Satan’s transformation slanders God and Christ [Col. 0754D].

[Col. 0755A] V. But lest we wander too far from our subject, let us pass over the violations of consecrated virgins; I leave unmentioned the killings, insults, robberies, and plundering inflicted upon God’s priests, so that they themselves may understand that we intentionally select a few matters out of many, and set them forth briefly and modestly. We do not seek to exact vengeance upon enemies, but to free wretched souls from the jaws of the ravening wolf and from the very mouth of the dragon itself.

The destroyer of salutary discipline could therefore violate the chastity of faith under the name of unity—that is, compel unity to himself rather than to God. Nor did the rulers of this world and of these darknesses order this to be done in such a way that the character of what was commanded might reveal the person commanding it. What and how great were the glorious examples of the Church of God and Christ displayed amid these events? What marks of Christian profession? What exiles? What public proofs of true faith and uncorrupted devotion? Once these had been openly displayed, truth could remain hidden from none, unless one had resolved, against his own conscience, according to the Prophet’s saying, to place his hope in falsehood [Col. 0755B].

VI. Let us come to those final events, when deceptions had failed and the engines of intrigue were exhausted, and they burst forth into open threats and manifest furies. Then one could see bands of soldiers serving the madness of the traditores, hired by the payment of the persons mentioned to perpetrate so great a crime. At length they stood around with most scrupulous watchfulness, observing lest mercenary cruelty might be permitted to act there with any greater mildness. Their intentness upon so curious a spectacle declared not so much the defense of a perverse assertion as the exaction of blood for which they had been hired [Col. 0755C].

But the people of God, although they had heard the report of the slaughter to come and recognized it from the very preparations, were not driven away by fear of the impending death that would bring destruction. Rather, with the desire for suffering, they ran all the more courageously to the house of prayer. There faith is nourished by sacred readings, commanded fasts are strengthened by continual prayers, and through prayer itself the souls handed over to wicked hands are commended into God’s hand. Behold: from the camp, in imitation of the Lord’s Passion, a cohort of soldiers advances to kill Christians, sent by new Pharisees. Right hands are armed with clubs against hands innocently outstretched to the Lord—as though they were saying that those butchered not by swords but by an impious beating with clubs suffered a lesser martyrdom.

> [Note: Col. 0755D]  
> **VII.—Honoratus.** This is the proper name of a bishop, sufficiently common among Africans. These acts are therefore incorrectly entitled *The Passion of Donatus and Advocatus*; they ought rather to be called *The Passion of Honoratus, Bishop of Sicilibensis*.  
>   
> **Scilibensis.** Read *Sicilibensis*. At the Council of Carthage under St Cyprian, Satius of Siciliba gave his opinion. At the Council of Carthage of 419, Praetextatus of Sicilibensis was present, one of the bishops of the proconsular province. A bishop of Sicilibensis, named Quadratianus, also attended the Carthaginian conference. The town is known from the Itinerary of Antoninus [Col. 0756D], where it is called Sicilibra; in the Anonymous Cosmography of Ravenna, Siciliba. It was situated in the proconsular province and looked obliquely toward both Tuburbos, being eighteen Roman miles distant from the greater one.

[Col. 0755D] VII. Although the sword of the tribune did not pierce the throat of the most holy Honoratus, bishop of Scilibensis, it nevertheless wounded it. Thus both the fury of the Devil’s ministers was exposed there, and the patience of the glorious bishop revealed [Col. 0756A] Christ’s Church. For no one was shown to be a servant of Christ the Lord except the one who suffered these same things which the Lord himself suffered: “The servant,” he says, “is not greater than his lord. If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20).

Therefore, if these servants of God who are loved by the world have been beaten, let them show that the Lord himself was loved by the world. But if the world loves only those who belong to it, it must hate those whom the Lord Jesus chose out of the world. “If you were of the world,” he says, “the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (ibid. 15:19).

> [Note: Col. 0756D]  
> **VIII.—Titulationes.** Concerning such inscriptions on the tombs of martyrs, see what we said in note 78 to book III, p. 61.

VIII. Finally, the outcome of this hatred has always been marked by the shedding of blood. So now too they consummated their pact and agreement in crime only by the sealing of blood [Col. 0756B], when persons of every age and sex were slaughtered in the midst of the basilica, with their eyes tightly shut. The basilica, I say, within whose walls numerous bodies were both killed and buried; and there, from the inscriptions of names, the memory even of the Caecilianic persecution is prolonged to the end, lest at some later time the parricide should deceive others, inexperienced in what happened, by the name of episcopal office.

> [Note: Col. 0756D]  
> **IX.—A religious annual day.** The Donatists observed a feast day in commemoration of those who had been killed or harshly punished on that occasion.

IX. And this annual day is deservedly celebrated with religious devotion. For it is a day to be honoured, on which the whole Church of God confessed, and afterwards was crowned at the right hand of Christ the Lord, the eternal Judge. Let supreme mercy determine why it did not permit all to be slaughtered; nevertheless, seeing the hearts of all, it rewarded with the prize of martyrs [Col. 0756C] those whom it saw had wished to suffer with complete devotion—for he seeks not blood but the faith of believers. But the man who hired the whole people to be killed must necessarily be held guilty of all their blood.

X. Furthermore, what was an act of greater madness: even after so wicked a deed, the murderer thought that he should possess the same basilica, as though they would yield to attachment to a place. The other Christians who escaped—men from whom he saw that the very life of the present world was despised—he thought, I suppose, would be pleased with him after the stain of blood, though he had coveted their blood; after the ruin of betrayal, though he persecuted them precisely because they avoided the contagion of his communion. He promised himself that they would communicate with him after the murder had been perpetrated. O [Col. 0756D] imprudence mingled with vanity and madness! Blinded by this, that most wretched robber thought that he ought to adopt the very plan by whose own arrangement he was, unknowingly, prevented.

> [Note: Col. 0757D]  
> **XI.—“Help,” he says, “my catechumen,” etc.** An excellent sentiment, if it were put forth for a good cause.

XI. The violence of that authority which was then seen must now be set before our eyes and reconsidered in the mind [Col. 0757A]. When God’s priest was being slain before the altar of the sacred Name, and when a catechumen boy, uninitiated in the discipline of the sacraments, almost lifeless, most eagerly begged for the grace of the saving washing, “Help,” he said, “my catechumen.” His soul, plainly, was already near to God; with his final voice he showed that he greatly desired this to happen to him: that, in the likeness of the Lord’s Passion, water might be joined to blood.

> [Note: Col. 0757D]  
> **XII.—The bishop mentioned.** Namely Honoratus, bishop of Sicilibensis. The statement that he came to Carthage from the town of Advocatus must not be understood of the city of which he was bishop; for there is no African episcopal city of this name, but of some nearby town from which he had set out for Carthage.  
>   
> [Col. 0758D] **“Where whatever is condemned by public law is committed with impunity.”** This is sarcasm and wordplay on *Catholic*, which means “universal.” The Church is called catholic because it is universal; but this writer, mocking the Catholic Church, twists the word into another sense, so that it is called “catholic” because there whatever is condemned by public and common law is committed with impunity. The allusion is certainly feeble and ridiculous.

XII. But the bishop mentioned, arriving at Carthage as a guest from the town of Advocatus, was received with such humanity of this “catholic” hospitality that, after the exertion of so great a journey, he took not even a little water before satisfying the most avid throats of the traditores with the cup of his own blood. Hence, I think, one must ask what sort of apostasy this can be, if such a thing is worthily called “catholic.” For the enemy took great pains also to bring injury upon the name, causing it commonly to be called catholic where whatever is condemned by public law is committed with impunity [Col. 0757B].

XIII. Meanwhile, after the tribune had prepared to comply with the wishes of the traditores, and after abundance of blood had sated the ardour of his cruelty, some brethren entered the basilica again and rendered such services to the martyrs as circumstances allowed. What disturbance of souls there was then! What floods of tears! What groans of lamentation! What piety, running among the bodies of the slaughtered, hastened to recognize the face of each one lying there! When children found the prostrate bodies of parents, and parents those of children, you could see some clinging to the embraces of their own people [Col. 0757C], others struck by the sudden sight and sitting down half-dead, and some applying pious hands to gather the bodies. They covered the bodies of both sexes, lying otherwise than decency allowed; they restored limbs shattered by savage blows, if not through the rites due to them, at least to their proper places.

The evening hour was now attempting to shut out the daylight; and so the numerous bodies were at once carried away hastily from different places. Yet the Spirit enriched those labouring in devotion in such a way that where the shepherd lay wounded, there also the flock of sheep was gathered from its suffering. The event itself testified that this was divinely done: so that those who had offered themselves as a sacrifice to God might crown the altar of God in a circle about it; and so that the bishop, to whom services had been rendered by a people while he exercised his priesthood, might, having been advanced also by martyrdom [Col. 0757D], enjoy the company and service of his fellow-martyrs.

XIV. O truly divine wisdom, and far different from human wisdom, as the Lord himself says through the prophet: “My thoughts,” he says, “are not like yours, nor yours like mine; for as heaven is distant from earth, so [Col. 0758A] are my ways distant from your ways, and your thoughts from my understanding” (Isa. 55:9). On the battlefield of nations, to kill an adversary is victory; in our contest, to be killed by an enemy is triumph. For he wins most wretchedly who lives after victory as a murderer.

Rejoice and exult, pious mother Church, you who, instructed in heavenly disciplines, contend in an irreproachable and unstained struggle. For if resistance is required, you resist with the mind, not with weapons; you fight not with the hand but with faith. This difference in your battles tests you in the world, crowns you in heaven, and commends you to Christ the Lord. Thus that person conquers who does not know how to be conquered after victory; thus that person triumphs whose triumph does not end. To you alone it is permitted to contend piously, to gain a benefit through another’s wrongdoing, and to be crowned through Christ with a pure and virginal conscience—to whom be glory and dominion unto ages of ages. Amen.

## A.D. 348

# Passion of Marculus, a Donatist Priest, Who Was Killed under Macarius and Was Regarded by the Donatists as a Martyr

*(From Mabillon’s* Analecta, *vol. IV, p. 105; collated with a Corbie manuscript approximately five hundred years old.)*

## Mabillon’s Note on the Passion of Marculus

Just as the Catholic Church gloried in having its own martyrs, so the Donatists also gloried in having theirs. Among the more distinguished were Donatus, bishop of Bagaï, and Marculus, a presbyter, whom they asserted had been driven by the Macarians—or traditores, as [Col. 0758C] they called Catholics—from the brow of a steep mountain and killed by being cast headlong. The matter stands thus.

The Emperor Constans, urged by Gratus, bishop of Carthage, because of the most lamentable condition of the African Church, initially sent Paul and Macarius not to make unity, as Optatus of Milevis testifies in book III, but with alms, so that poverty, relieved throughout the individual churches, might breathe again, be clothed, fed, and rejoice. While these two were performing their office admirably, distributing aid to the poor everywhere and exhorting individuals to unity, the two Donatuses were foremost in resisting: one, of Carthage; the other, of Bagaï, bishops of the Donatist faction. The former indeed heaped insults upon the emperor himself; the latter armed the Agonistici, as he called them—that is, the Circumcellions—against Paul [Col. 0758D] and Macarius.

The envoys obtained from Count Taurinus armed soldiers to restrain their fury. Very many were killed and many mutilated; the Donatists regarded them as martyrs. One of these was Marculus. At the Carthaginian conference, chapter 188, Dativus, Donatist bishop of Nova Petra, says: “I have no adversary, because Lord Marculus is there, whose blood God will require on the day of judgment.”

The Catholics, in Augustine near the end of Tractate II on John, deny that they cast Marculus down, but say that he threw himself down:

> “The Donatists produce for us I know not what martyrs of their own in the persecution. ‘Look: Marculus was thrown down from a rock; look: Donatus of Bagaï was cast into a well.’ When did Roman authorities decree punishments of this sort, that people should be thrown headlong? But what do our people answer? ‘I do not know what happened.’ Yet what do our people hand down? That they threw themselves down and defamed the authorities. . . . But those who wished to be worshipped as dead men found no more notorious death.”

Optatus in book III seems to indicate the same thing in these words [Col. 0759B]:

> “Thus Donatus of Bagaï found a means of hiring a mad crowd against Macarius. Among them were persons who, in desire for a false martyrdom, hired assailants against themselves for their own destruction. Hence also those who, casting their worthless lives from the summits of high mountains, hurled themselves headlong.”

By these words Optatus seems to indicate Marculus. Nevertheless, later on the same author does not deny that Marculus and Donatus were killed by Macarian soldiers:

> “I am compelled, though unwillingly, at this point to mention even those persons—whom I do not wish to mention—whom you count among martyrs, and by whom, as by the one religion, the people of your communion swear. I should indeed like to pass them over in silence, but the principle of truth does not allow itself to be silenced. Even from their names envy barks thoughtlessly against unity; and some, in their scorn, judge unity to be accused or avoided because Marculus and Donatus are said to have been killed and to have died. As if in God’s vengeance no one at all deserved to be killed,” etc. [Col. 0759C]

Finally, the same author removes from the aforesaid persons the title of martyr because they had experienced no war against Christians; because they had not loved peace, in which lie the first foundations of martyrdom; and because they had possessed no charity, without which martyrdom is empty.

Nevertheless, when we found these acts in the library of St Gall, we decided, on the advice of friends, to publish them in order to illustrate antiquity. Another manuscript, containing the same acts, was graciously lent to us for use by Antoine Faur, a man distinguished for learning and scholarship, a doctor of the Sorbonne, and an especially devoted student of ecclesiastical antiquity [Col. 0759D], above all African antiquity. This manuscript had been granted in the year 921 by Adelelmus, bishop of the Church of Laon. The same manuscript contains a fragment of a letter of Macrobius concerning Isaac and Maximian, Donatist martyrs, to be appended shortly after these acts.

Moreover, Rabanus had read the acts of Marculus and enters him in his Martyrology on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, with a brief summary of these acts. The day varies in the manuscripts: that of St Gall has the third day before the Kalends; that of Laon, the eighth day before the Kalends of the same month. Baronius assigns the year 348 to these Macarian disturbances.

In Molanus’s additions to Usuard, drawn from the spurious Martyrology of Bede, mention is made of a certain Marculus on the sixth day before the Kalends of December in these words [Col. 0760A]: “At Nicomedia, of blessed Verculus, priest and martyr, who in the time of the tyrant Constans endured most severe persecutions; at last he was thrown down from a high cliff.” In the appendix to the second edition of Usuard, the same author suspects that this is Marculus, the Donatist pseudo-martyr.

Baronius denies this in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, where the following occurs on the same day: “At Nicomedia, of St Marcellus, presbyter, who in the time of Constantius was thrown down from a cliff by Arians and died a martyr.” A certain learned man, favouring Molanus’s conjecture, thinks that *in Numidia* should be read in place of *at Nicomedia*; that the name Marculus should then be retained; and that *by Macarians* should be written instead of *by Arians*. This is highly plausible.

Yet in the additions to Bede’s Martyrology among the Bollandists [Col. 0760B], Marcellus, a martyr at Nicomedia, is mentioned more than once on the fifth day before the Kalends of December. First, from two manuscripts, in these words: “At Nicomedia: Marcellus, Peter, Serena, Victorinus.” Then from two others: “At Nicomedia, the feast of the holy Peter, Marcellus, and Serenus, one of whom was crucified for the faith of Christ, the other was beheaded”; in one of the two manuscripts, the name Marcellus is absent. But in two others, three names alone are read thus: “At Nicomedia: Peter, Marcellinus, and Serenus.”

It is probable that a certain Marcellus suffered at Nicomedia. But because some read that the Donatist Marculus was killed at almost the same time, they thought he was the same person as Marcellus, and consequently attributed Marculus’s manner of death to Marcellus.

# Here Begins the Passion of the Blessed Martyr Marculus. The Eighth Day (Alternatively, the Third Day) Before the Kalends of December

[Col. 0760C]

Because the passions and glories of many martyrs, long ago arranged in discourse and preserved in exalted remembrance, contribute greatly to the benefit of peoples while they are continually recited to their ears as an incentive to virtue and praise of the Church, the honour of so great a martyr and the advancement of the common devotion of all have also moved me to recount, in an unworthy but loving discourse, the Passion of glorious MARCULUS—resplendent also with priestly honour (variant: “of one resplendent”)—recently consummated by the crime of the traditores (Corbie: *consummatum*). For it is just and altogether fitting that the virtue of later martyrs (Corbie: “earlier martyrs”) should be joined and bound together with the praises of ancient witnesses [Col. 0760D]. For just as pagan cruelty, obedient to the Devil, sent the former to the kingdom, so the fury of the traditores, serving Antichrist, sent the latter to heaven. And since the memorable course of his earlier life must not be passed over, something must be said, if only a little—though not everything can be said because of their multitude—about the virtues of glorious Marculus (variant: “glorious virtues”), for the sake of his testimony.

For he, long ago chosen and predestined by the Lord, as soon as he first received the rudiments of blessed faith, immediately rejected worldly letters, trampled underfoot forensic practice and the false dignity of secular learning, his mind fixed upon heaven; and passing from the slanderous enclosures of the law courts to the most holy school of the Church, because he chose Christ as his true teacher, [Col. 0761A] he deserved thus to be honoured among Christ’s principal disciples.

What integrity of conscience there was in him, what inborn modesty of distinguished character, what spiritual grace in his countenance—I do not think one needs to labour long and greatly over it, since this fact proves his earlier life: that he deserved the priesthood. And how he exercised that priesthood is made clear by the fact that the Lord deigned to grant him martyrdom as its reward.

Accordingly, while he was living praiseworthily in these offices of the heavenly precepts (Corbie: “having lived”), while, established as high priest, he enjoyed with the other saints his goodness and priesthood, behold: suddenly there rang out from the tyrannical house of King Constans and from the citadel of his palace the polluted rumour of the Macarian persecution. Two beasts were sent into Africa—namely Macarius and Paul—and a wholly execrable and dreadful conflict was declared against the Church [Col. 0761B], so that the Christian people might be compelled into union (Corbie: “unity”) with the traditores by the soldiers’ drawn swords, the present standards of dragons, and the shouts of crowds.

But Macarius, who was the more hideous of these two beasts, had long pursued this bloody business by subtle means in the remaining provinces (Corbie: “had already pursued it”); yet in Numidia, and against glorious Marculus, he openly displayed proofs of barbarous cruelty and unheard-of ferocity. For when the most holy company of the most ancient fathers and the assembled council of priests had sent to him, as an embassy, ten bishops approved from their own number (Corbie: plural, “had sent”), so that they might call him back by salutary admonitions from so great a crime, or else—what occurred—might themselves be the first to rush forward into the field of most devoted struggle and into the battle line of faith [Col. 0761C], the care of the noble shepherds was divinely directed such that whatever cruelty threatened the sheep might first tear their own limbs.

Among these came also the most holy Marculus. When they found him on an estate named Vegesela, they were immediately received with the humanity of the man who presided over the sacrilegious unity: they were bound to individual columns, their priestly bodies publicly stripped, and beaten with harsh strokes of clubs (variant: “ropes”). Who could now sufficiently recount the constancy of glorious Marculus? Who could adequately set forth, by the powers of eloquence, either the unheard-of madness of the insane persecutor or the present and wondrous protection of Christ the Lord toward his martyr?

For the inhuman ferocity was stirred against him with more severe cruelty because the Devil’s envy prompted it against the future martyr, and the malice of the forerunner of Antichrist was not hidden from the Holy Spirit [Col. 0761D]. Since he could not overcome a mind strengthened by divine constancy, he imposed upon bodily frailty a contest of pain. Thus bloody bands of robbers and barbarous companies of soldiers, suddenly turned into executioners, surrounded Christ’s bravest warrior. And when they tried to fasten him to a column with hard bonds, he at once eagerly seized so great an opportunity to display God’s power. For he voluntarily bound himself to that very column with the bonds around his arms and with knots of his fingers, in such a way [Col. 0762A] that no punishment could tear him away from it and no cruelty could separate him. By this deed the persecutor could understand that God’s servant desired rather than feared tortures for God’s name; that those whose spirit embraces Christ and whose hope already possesses the kingdom cannot feel bodily pain.

Accordingly, a manifold host of executioners raged against one man, and the harsh punishment of clubs tore his consecrated limbs to pieces [Note: Col. 0762D (1): Thus corrected from the Corbie manuscript; the alternative reading, *confitentis* (“confessing”), is erroneous]. As the torment alternated, insofar as the blows of punishment were inflicted from behind, the hardness of the column struck his breast from the front. Cruelty assailed his body on every side, but his illustrious tongue uttered nothing except God’s praise. Rage panted; now, worn down by the exhaustion of the torturers and the steadfastness of the sufferer, ferocity languished in defeat [Col. 0762B].

Then Christ, clothed in the limbs of his martyr, displayed such a miracle that he not only allowed no pain to reach him, but even wiped from his body every mark of cruelty and every sign of execution. Defeated and subdued in this contest, the enemy, no longer satisfied by any cruelty of punishments (variant: “of execution”), destined him for a sentence and a suffering as atrocious, in his own judgment, as possible and altogether manifest. Then, leading him through certain cities of Numidia as a spectacle, as it were, of his own cruelty (Corbie omits “as it were”), the ferocity, without knowing it, provided amazement to pagans (variant: “nations”), confusion to Christ’s enemies, and an incentive to glorious struggle for God’s faithful servants.

But after he had devised an elaborate and savage [Col. 0762C] kind of death, he immediately brought him, under the closest military escort, to the fortress of Nova Petra, which is linked in name and proximity with the precipice of a steep mountain. In that place the Lord granted his martyr such great joy, and bestowed such gladness over his approaching Passion, that the four days in which he was delayed there from the impending crown ought now to be counted not among the afflictions of worldly pressures but among the triumphs of the heavenly kingdoms. For how greatly could he exult, who, after the toilsome pilgrimage of flesh and world, hastened, his journey completed, to see God and Christ; who, setting out for the fellowship of angels and the embrace of the saints, was already almost entering the threshold of paradise?

His prayer was constant and unceasing; his meditation, born of devotion, continuous [Col. 0762D]. He had the Gospel on his lips, martyrdom in his thoughts (variant: “contradiction”); and, devoted both in speech and mind to divine powers, he uttered with his mouth what he bore enclosed in his breast. Still thirsting for spiritual righteousness, and wholly serving God in order to win His favour, he concluded the final day of those four by fasting: namely, so that at the dawning of the Lord’s Day—on which his own passion was also to be consummated—the devout soul of the priest might become more acceptable to God in offering a twofold sacrifice. Thus the high priest, separated not only from the enticements of the age but even from its food [Col. 0763A], might approach to lay victims upon Christ’s altars with such purity that he himself might deserve to become a victim for Christ.

Indeed, so much did that fast avail with the Lord, so greatly did that purification summon Christ’s presence within him [Note: [Col. 0763D] (1) In Corb.: “the purification of Christ’s presence within him summoned [it].”], that before his passion the reward of his passion was shown to him in a heavenly revelation. For when the greater part of the night had passed and the time near daylight arrived—a time whose suitability has always been welcome for prayers and all divine matters, because it is already assigned to the dawning day (Corb.: *quo*, “by which”), though human works and business still rest—then, at this time, the priest rose to celebrate the sacraments. He was not so much awakened from sleep [Note: [Col. 0763D] (2) *tam* absent in Corb.] as (Corb.: “was”) fired to pray to God by the joy of a recent vision. Yet before proceeding to the mysteries themselves, he disclosed in faithful speech, for the joy of the brethren present [Col. 0763B], what had been divinely shown to him.

“I saw,” he said, “these three gifts offered to me from the eternal treasures of the Lord who bestows them: a cup made of most gleaming silver; a crown shining with ruddy gold; and a most lofty palm, which, full of joy, would complete the number of preceding triumphs” (Corb.: “the triumphs of gifts”).

Great confidence in imminent glory did the Lord grant to His martyr, brethren; great assurance did He give of His future favour toward him. For nothing seems obscure or ambiguous in this revelation: he received the cup which he was to drink in his passion; he took the crown due to him once martyrdom was accomplished; and he deserved the palm through which, hoping for victory [Col. 0763C], he was already secure concerning the contest.

After these things, when the customary solemn rites had been completed and some moments of the night still remained (Corb.: “dreams”), suddenly there arrived the wakeful messenger of wickedness, bearing Macarius’s deadly commands (Corb.: *pervigilis*, “ever-watchful”). He carried the explicit sentence of a most cruel death and was to consummate both the martyr’s innumerable glories and the abominable crime of the persecutors. When the care of the guards had opened the still-closed doors for him, and they learned what his untimely arrival had brought, their hearts immediately turned to weeping.

O how great was that man’s grace! How universal the love felt for him by all! How common the grief, that in his passion even the savagery of the guards and military hardness should be moved to pious tears [Col. 0763D]. Yet amid the tears and disturbance of all, he alone remained fearless, rejoicing that the hour of his consummation had drawn near. For he could neither be troubled nor sad, whom faith had made joyful and divine revelation peaceful.

There then was one among the soldiers, a most foul executioner; while the others feared, he alone had been prepared by the devil to accomplish the illustrious man’s death. Anticipating his deed in speech, he began to recount to all who heard the martyrdom (Corb.: “to all”)—what sort of dream he himself too had seen (Corb.: “how all things”). “While I was held in the repose of the night,” he said, “I saw you suddenly appear to me as though bound in very hard chains, altogether burdened by heavy fetters (Corb.: “very greatly”); and afterward I saw those same bonds unfastened by my own hand. Therefore hope for pardon and forgiveness to follow.”

Accordingly, the executioner’s absurd dream was not without an appropriate vision; nor was it without cause that he related what he had seen. He followed, that is, the example of the sacrilegious Caiaphas: the man who was himself to kill the Lord likewise prophesied concerning His passion. He had rightly seen the martyr bound, for while he still dwelt in the body and was shut within the twofold prison of world and flesh, he was constrained by the narrowness of temporal life. For he feels the body’s bondage and the world’s prison who is troubled by their temptations [Col. 0764B]. Nor without reason had he dreamed that he was released by him whose cruel hands were destined, through the intervention of death, to separate him from the body; through whose agency, after the grievous bonds of worldly oppression, he was in his passion to make his way to the freedom of the heavenly kingdoms.

That we are released from great bonds when, freed from this world, we hasten to the Lord, the Apostle proves when he says: “To depart and to be with Christ is far better.” The same point was demonstrated by that most righteous Simeon, who, stirred by the assurance of approaching death, rejoiced that he would escape the troubles of this life: “Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, Lord, in peace, because mine eyes have seen thy salvation.” He would surely never have testified with all joy that he was to be dismissed [Col. 0764C], unless he was held, as it were, in certain bonds by the condition of the body.

At last no delay, no interval of time intervened before the most cruel executioner immediately set about fulfilling what he had seen in a brigand-like attack before dawn [reading of *lucano latrocinio* uncertain]. For he pressed fiercely that the witness of God should be brought from custody to the sheer height of a natural rock and the precipice of a most harsh cliff. This had been the most savage kind of death chosen by that bloody and barbarous enforcer of profane unity, and by the treacherous cruelty detested in every age.

Thus glorious Marculus went forth from the house, surrounded by the sentries of guards and the ranks of soldiers, and honoured by his very persecutors. He went forth, raised upright by the constancy of Christian vigour, leaving behind human lodgings [Col. 0764D] and hastening to the dwellings of angels. He went forth with a joyful face and hurried step, thinking not so much of the present punishment as of the glory to come. Even the route by which he was led to execution had been arranged for him in such a manner that, as masses of earth were heaped up everywhere and embankments gradually rose in height, he came to the lofty eminence marking his passion, nature herself upon the mountain serving him. Treading first the low ridges of the hill and then its steep peaks, as though climbing certain steps into the height, he drew near even in his body to heaven and the stars; so that, still placed in the world, he might stand higher than the world and rejoice that whatever seemed precious or exalted in this age lay beneath his feet [Col. 0765A]. But once the summit of the rock had been reached, all the soldiers withdrew, some through fear and some through sorrow: though their consciences participated in so unheard-of a crime, they would not participate in its execution.

Then the most savage executioner, armed with a double cruelty—with both precipice and sword—and carrying a double death in his hands, thrust the martyr headlong with his cruel right hand. He believed that he had plunged into a grim abyss the man to whom the heights of heaven were due. But the most holy body, as the firmness of the earth fell away beneath it, descended from the height to the depths [Note: [Col. 0765D] (1) Emended from codex Corb. The reading *alma* is erroneous.], borne through the empty spaces of liquid air. Finding no obstruction in that void, it doubled the speed of its course through its very momentum.

Yet in that swiftness of travel, amid the rushing noises of disturbed air [Col. 0765B], a moderation so great was divinely provided that the limbs, immune to every roughness (Corb.: *immunita*, “protected”), were laid upon the very hardness of rocks as though upon the softest cushions (Corb.: “a very soft bed”) and most tranquil bosoms. Then the victorious soul sought heaven more swiftly in its natural course than the body had descended to earth: so that, when the passion was completed, each substance might be restored to the most ancient principles of its origin by the hands of almighty God, acting mercifully toward His whole martyr. He commanded the spirit, assisted by angels, to be placed in eternal abodes; and the untouched body, encircled by caressing breezes and gently supported by serving winds, to be laid upon a ledge amid the rocks.

Thus the contrived devices of the persecutors [Col. 0765C] and the wicked counsels of the traitors were confounded by Christ’s powers. They had devised such a punishment in order that the martyr’s memory might never be honoured by God’s peoples as testimony against them. “[For they had thought that in that precipice the body would be torn limb from limb and mangled upon sharp crags, so that he from whom they had taken life might not even retain burial]” [Note: [Col. 0765D] (2) These words are absent from codex Corb.]. They had thought that nothing could reach the earth which pious brethren might gather and bury. They thought that each crag amid the shattered places of that steep mountain would seize a limb for itself; or at least that the intact body, once swallowed in some cleft among the fissures of rocks or in the gaping recesses of rugged crags, would disappear.

But behold: hard stones and rough cliffs spared the consecrated limbs; and him whom the traitors had not feared to kill, the mountains feared to harm. For, apart from those men, every creature venerates its Creator [Col. 0765D]; and in this cause intelligence could not be lacking to the mountains for winning God’s favour, since Scripture granted them even a voice for His praise.

Meanwhile, that glorious Marculus had completed the blessed victory of his contest was concealed within the knowledge of the soldiers alone. They had consummated their stealthy crime in the silence of night so that neither strangers nor brethren in the fortress where he had been kept could know it (Corb.: “no one could know”), unless divine powers (Corb.: “divine power”) and heavenly signs had revealed the deed. For as soon as the entrance of whitening day poured pallor upon the orb of night, and the conflict of darkness and light diversified the variegated face of heaven, a shining cloud immediately appeared in the hollow of that same mountain. At times, with flashing brightness (Corb.: *fulgure*, “lightning”), it testified by gentle light that it had knowledge of the martyr’s body [Col. 0766A].

It was not a cloud heavy with morning dew, shadowing the living (variant: “suddenly appearing”) hills beneath a dark covering; rather, gleaming wholly with a white fleece, it so covered the blessed limbs that, while human services were briefly absent, it seemed itself meanwhile to supply, in some fashion, the covering of burial. At times it was split open at its trembling boundary (variant: “mound”), and through winding openings it shot forth flashing fire [Col. 0766B], either to remind those ignorant of so great a passion by wondrous marvels, or, since some darkness from the neighbouring night still remained, to show the way to those devoutly seeking the body.

Warned by these marvels of God, the fervour (variant: “ardour”) of the brotherhood was kindled; and the whole place was suddenly filled with exultant cries, while they announced their shared vows to one another as they hurried in religious devotion. Then, leaving their homes, every sex and age hastened forth and rushed together toward mountain and cloud in longing for the martyr. Neither the weakness of old age, nor the frailty of childhood, nor the weakness of sex could delay any soul there. For all had been fired by the ardour of one faith.

When the hurrying crowd had reached the places beneath the precipice, those whom one intention of running had gathered together [Col. 0766C] were soon scattered across the whole mountain by the care of seeking the body. There one might see works of piety apportioned among individuals. Some swiftly searched by hand the thickets of briars densely grown from hard stems; others thrust watchful eyes into the winding hollows of fissured rocks; others, lest their haste be deceived, carefully examined by lamplight even the rocks they had already looked upon. Finally—because this too could not be without the Lord—the lightning sent for this purpose revealed the desired place, and the whiteness of the cloud, serving as guide, showed the brethren the longed-for body.

What mingled weeping with joy was then there among all! What embraces around those illustrious limbs! At last, when all had scarcely taken their fill, the brethren’s final offices were celebrated with immense joy, and the religious (variant: “glorious”) honour of burial was restored amid the greatest triumphs [Col. 0766D]. For the Lord had restored wholly to the glory of His name whatever the enemy had tried to deprive Him of.

O memorable and illustrious martyrdom of blessed Marculus! O example of unshaken courage, to be desired by all the devout! O instruction necessary for every rank of the Church: through it the merit of his praiseworthy life attained the palm—renouncing the world at the beginnings of faith; showing himself worthy of the priesthood in its apprenticeship; receiving in the priesthood the honoured gifts of martyrdom; and, in martyrdom, the testimony of divine powers! To Him be honour and glory and dominion unto ages of ages. Amen. The end.

## THE PASSION OF MAXIMIAN AND ISAAC, DONATISTS, BY MACROBIUS

Part of this work had been published by the most reverend Father Jean Mabillon in *Analecta*, vol. IV, p. 119; it now appears complete and in a more corrected form from the Corbie manuscript.

[Col. 0767A]

[Note: [Col. 0767D]

The Passion begins. Its author was Macrobius, a Donatist and hidden bishop of his party in the city of Rome; Gennadius discusses him in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 5. Cresconius charged Catholics with the killing of three others besides Marculus by the Macarians. Without doubt they are these two martyrs, Maximinian and Isaac; Donatus must be added as a third. Augustine’s words are these, *Against Cresconius*, book III, ch. 49: “But concerning the other three, whose deaths you have variously charged [upon us], I confess that I did not inquire what happened, or how, from those whom I suppose to know.” Cresconius had charged [them with] these three because accounts of their passion circulated. Macrobius wrote this letter to the people of Carthage, as is evident from the conclusion of this document.

Here at Carthage the savagery of persecution had fallen silent. Optatus too, book III, §4, observes that no armed man was seen in the proconsular province.]

The Passion of the Holy Martyrs Isaac and Maximian begins, observed on the seventh day before the Kalends of September [26 August].

A timely and joyful ardour to write a glorious exhortation to you, brethren, kindles me; and the occasion is illustrious, since I, an unworthy witness of Christ’s witnesses, have written this letter, so that I who am less fit to bear martyrdom for the Lord might at least be admitted to give testimony concerning His martyrs. Indeed, I would not dare to put forth in writing, even as a final word to such persons, something about such persons [Col. 0767B], unless I might announce such things to you through another—unless I might, by the blameless emulation of a devoted heart, begrudge them to you.

For I know that no one can report anything more fully unless he himself has been able either to suffer or to do it. But he who has deserved neither commits only the fault of reporting it inadequately; yet joy reveals another and more frequent reason: they incur no penalty for whatever they have boldly done for Christ’s praises. Therefore, brethren, I believe that the example of sudden courage was suitably provided for you: the Lord snatched to heaven together the two martyrs of the Church at Carthage, Isaac and Maximian—or Maximinian—and Isaac. I believe it as difficult for anyone to recount their triumphs in due order as it is for not only earthly proclamations [Col. 0767C], but even heavenly ones, to count whatever Christ has done.

For they ran through the deeds of the entire contest so suddenly and swiftly that I do not know what was first, second, or third. With such headlong speed did they at once blend together all their immeasurable glories that they almost completed them before they began—or rather, as I should say more truly, both things were born in them at once. From where, then, shall I begin? By what threshold shall I enter into such great praise? From where shall I in turn close the exit of that same threshold? I am troubled to open it and wearied to close it. If I begin to recount the conduct of their whole life, I shall seem to do injustice to the martyrdom that returns to mind; if I direct my steps toward proclaiming their martyrdom, I shall be held guilty as one who despises so great a life. I am pressed to survey all things, and I know that I cannot survey all. On every side the burden of devoted labour comes upon me [Col. 0767D]; but against this, one relief comes to my aid in the remembered saying of the Gospel: once he has seen the Lord Jesus Christ praise the end of life, let him now confidently undertake to set forth the memorial of martyrdom.

Here at Carthage the savagery of persecution had been silent [Col. 0768A], that by a longer cessation it might nourish worse ambushes. While the enemy raged everywhere, fears and terrors alone were quiet here, so that one might say the powers of this world themselves would now stir nothing. No first reports were already shaking ears and hearts with terror; only the comfort furnished by the boundless report of you martyrs in Numidia sustained the spirits of the brethren. Among all, rejoicing in your glories was frequent as though it were their own; just as you too now rejoice with them, as though over your own martyrdom.

Then suddenly the devil again roared, rekindled the sleeping flames of fury in punishments, and set in motion the mad weapons of his violence. I think he had therefore ceased so long because he believed he had enslaved all Christ’s armies to himself. But when he discovered that the Church of the Lord grew stronger than all others through daily exercise, he immediately perceived that he was mocking his own hopes by frauds. Aroused by fiercer goads, he sought whose heart of a judge he might choose as suited to himself. Nor was the proconsul slower: he made himself equal to the devil’s desires, and by edicts of deadly purpose commanded that the covenant of sacrilegious unity should again be celebrated with established tortures [Col. 0768B]. He even added the law of the traitors: that those whom Christ commanded to be received by all for His sake should be expelled for ever, and should not, as it were, devise resistance against the covenants of unity.

But Christ, unwilling to endure delay in the triumphs of His own people, did not permit His soldiers to be divided while the enemy provoked them. He immediately chose from among strong men the mighty soldier Maximian, to make him glorious in such a contest—not because the rest were unequal, but so that the whole war might be overthrown in one man by a single combat. Knowing him already to be great-hearted from his first confession, He brought him forth armed with accumulated strength, so that what the Lord deigned to show him before the day of passion should not prove empty or vain.

For on the preceding day he had been dining with certain brethren at the house of a praiseworthy man, at a banquet marked by Christian temperance. When he took the cup to drink and then mixed it, behold, a crown immediately descended and spread itself within the rim of the cup. Enclosed within it, clinging to both sides and mingled with the drink, it enclosed the cup itself; it shone with such a bright and blood-red colour as to reveal, in both blood and splendour, the likeness of his future passion and heavenly dignity [Col. 0768C]. Rejoicing, he showed this miracle to all present, urging all to reckon it henceforth with a spirit of love, and wishing whatever had occurred to be shared by all.

But when he himself began to drink, the circle of the crown by no means broke. Instead, mingled with the drink, it gradually shortened—indeed, rather gathered itself—by withdrawing itself, as the quantity of drink was taken away and he strove to drink it, so that it might make crowned within the heart to which it had come. Thus he, immediately sustained by such assurance, breathed out on the following day the intoxication of the previous day’s cup; and with great-heartedness enclosed in the marrow of his fruitful breast, he seemed to hope for victory.

But why say more? With the swiftness of an astute mind, and without delay of foot, he went up to provoke the contest voluntarily, and with a quick hand scattered the deadly notices, as though he were tearing apart there the limbs of the devil. He was at once seized and brought before the tribunal; by the proconsul’s command he was immediately surrounded in an enclosure by a savage troop of torturers. Who, then, can recount Christ’s power or the savagery of the mutilators, the executioners’ punishments or Christ’s victories, the enduring madness of insane fury or the persistence of Christian endurance? [Col. 0769A]

Horrible torturers rose to strike, doubling with their efforts the force of the leaded scourges; they bore the judge’s anger in their hands and competed in savagery to see who might prove stronger. But Christ was present against them, clothed in the limbs of His soldier; from within He blunted whatever the mad executioner inflicted from without [Col. 0769B]. They inflicted torments almost more fiercely, angry that they had imposed so great a cruelty in vain; and the Lord in His strength restored and strengthened endurance. They exchanged executioners for newer and crueler instruments of madness; and so many changed bands of harsh men were insufficient to commit murder upon one innocent man. Nor, on the other side, did the Lord cease to transform the steadfastness of His endurance into something better.

The force of the heavy punishment did not abate until he was ordered to be beaten with rods and afterward torn apart by laceration, so that the later wounds, rending his limbs, might open what that violent battering had raised into swelling [Col. 0769C]. These wounds had so lacerated his whole body that all the mutilation of his limbs formed a single wound. Yet he did not yield to these things; as though estranged from his own body, he triumphed over all.

Thus there was waged a battle between body and punishments, between the sacrilegious and the devout man, between strength of spirit and mutilators, between Christ’s soldier and the devil’s soldiers, between the sufferer and the judge. One afflicted man sufficed to fight more gloriously against so great a multitude of punishments and enemies, so that in a single contest he carried off not one victory alone. There he could have reached the culmination of supreme suffering (Corb.: “in the ordeal”), since he was sent to death with triumph (Corb.: “might be sent”); but he had to be delayed meanwhile for the companion whom Christ had assigned him.

For then the illustrious Isaac, unable to contain his joy over his companion’s struggle, was borne among the brethren’s crowds in public exultation of the Holy Spirit. Filled with heavenly constancy, he cried more freely: “Traitors (Corb.: ‘to the traitors’), come, save the madness of your unity” (Corb.: “satisfy the madness of your cruelty”). At his cry, the furious proconsul ordered his staff urgently to seek the author of the shouting [Col. 0769D].

But traitors who had gone before the soldiers were not lacking. Immediately those sacrilegious ministers, not at all satisfied with one victim, delivered up another to be slaughtered by their own hands, so that the measure of those fathers might more openly be fulfilled through them [Col. 0770A] (Corb.: “by them”; variant: “might” rather than “might be”). The judge, violently inflamed, removed the man whom he had tortured a little earlier and turned upon this one more fiercely the rage that burned in him—as though he had not yet digested one anger and were conceiving another.

The exhausted torturers renewed their frenzy; cruelty alone made their already weary arms stronger. Again and again that band of butchers unleashed the violence of leaded scourges, and, applying their entire strength in spent efforts, raged with groaning fury as though it itself suffered what it inflicted. What must have been the endurance of the sufferer where the violence of the assailant groaned! Yet the devil was not allowed to prevail in the second case, since it was not lawful for Christ’s victorious power, which was aflame, to fail in anyone.

Accordingly, after the leaded scourges had again accomplished nothing, furious savagery likewise applied rods, so that the heavenly standard-bearers might differ in no unequal kind of endurance, and the enemy might nowhere appear softened by a gentler punishment [Col. 0770B].

Isaac was torn by the breaking rods—the name, indeed, of a victim—imitating the patience of his name; and though the blows of his executioners were repeated again and again, the devotion of the confessor remained unshaken. Every joint lay exposed, soaked as its connexions were ruptured; and as though it found an outlet through so many wounds, the voice seemed to ring out the proclamations of confession. Let no one suppose that the rod-strokes then were a light chastisement: they certainly surpassed the tearing of the claws, so much so that the judge himself had already grown weary of the claws.

There were no longer wounds, but the hidden parts of the body exposed; and no one could call him merely beaten when he had been weakened into dripping fragments [Col. 0770C]. The bundles of rods had yielded; one might almost have thought that axes or sickles would be blunted if they chopped such a man to pieces. The grim ministers now gasped with feeble blows, the languid openings of their defeated savagery; yet they still gaped ravenously for every punishment to chew and devour.

Then there his body defied the torments and his mind the raging men. Though one man was tortured by so many torturers and condemned by the judge, the judge did not delay the sentence, but joined both men in an equal lot and consigned them to exile. Once they had been thrust into prison, Isaac immediately achieved the consummation of martyrdom; and, what is more, in one act he left behind all prisons, body, and world, lest the revelation of his vision should fail in any respect [Col. 0770D].

For he had run through everything in order (Corb.: “had run ahead”), so that in the revelation itself he had already almost undergone what he was to suffer (Corb.: “had suffered”). While he was held briefly in the slumber of rest, he seemed to be in conflict with the emperor’s ministers—precisely in the manner in which he endured his passion. And this was plainly nothing other than a sign of devotion: what he considered in desire while awake, he underwent even while sleeping; so that what the Prophet declared of himself might be fulfilled in him: “I sleep, and my heart wakes.”

Thus that devotion kept watch, already practising the efforts of courage, and more steadfastly repelled the ministers of wickedness with the commands of the king [Col. 0771A] (Corb.: “practising courage in the contest, and [repelled] the ministers,” etc.) as they boldly resisted. After overcoming them in a long contest, he also suddenly saw the emperor himself approach.
