When the latter compelled him to fulfil the command, he more strongly rejected the authority of the sacrilegious command and the savage punishments of the threatener (Corb.: “of one threatening”). He in turn repeatedly and terribly promised that he would tear out the other’s eye. As they fought one another fiercely for a long time in these struggles, he did not permit himself, though victorious, to be delayed any longer. He thrust in his hand boldly, broke through the delay of his threat, and violently plucked out the eye, leaving the face bereft (Corb.: “faces”) and emptying the seat of sight.

Immediately after this victory, a young man of wondrous brightness appeared triumphing and placed a radiant crown upon his head [Col. 0771B]. In its rays appeared fixed the faces of many brethren and sisters. As he joyfully gave it to him as a reward (Corb.: “was giving”), he also mocked the adversary with great reproaches and derision. Then the enemy, driven by violent pain, ordered him to be torn by raging punishments, as though he might avenge his own punishment. But the victor now saw himself carried upward in the hands of those bearing him and lifted, flying swiftly, to the heights of heaven. As he ascended joyfully, he heard from above the voice of a certain old man crying: “Woe to thee, world, because thou hast perished.” With this cry repeated three times, the vision reached its end; afterward he repeated in action what he had seen.

What, then, could be clearer than this vision? What could have been expressed more plainly in daylight, when what had been seen was set out in deeds? In the night he saw himself fighting alone against the king’s ministers in the very manner in which he afterward showed us by day; he saw himself tear out the emperor’s eye, and in conquering blind him; he received the crown’s rewards and was publicly crowned. He had seen many faces adhering to the crown’s rays, just as the whole people was to keep vigil over his passion. He flew to heaven, just as he deserved swiftly to attain martyrdom [Col. 0771C].

Only this, plainly, is known still to await fulfilment among his utterances: that he prophesied the world’s destruction. Since we all know that he did not lie, perhaps some brother may be afraid and call Maximian unequal to him because, though he confessed first, he was preserved alive for a short time. Far be it, brethren, that they should be divided, since they fought an equal battle. For if the Lord made equal in the agreed wage those who came to the vineyard at different hours, how does He judge unequal those whom He found labouring at the same time? Rather, because Isaac seems to depart first, I say that the Lord thereby made them more equal: just as Isaac had supplied Maximian with an incentive to confession, so Maximian might likewise summon him to the crown. The Lord wished both to be teachers of one another, so that by the reciprocal exchange of instruction He might make them equals, lest one should precede in everything and the other seem in everything merely to follow him. Now, however, both preceded one another and both followed one another [Col. 0771D].

Meanwhile, when the prison’s confinement had been opened, a ship was prepared for exile. I believe that this was arranged not by human counsel but, as became evident, by the provision of heavenly favour [Col. 0772A]. For the Lord chose to confine them together by the delay of one day in order that, in accordance with the vision of His martyr, they might be honoured by the people’s vigils. For once Isaac had consummated his perfect martyrdom, the news had filled the ears of all. The whole brotherhood immediately hastened in joyful throngs to his body. When burial of the body was refused by the executioners, they all kept watch with great rejoicing lest the unburied body be cast away. There the people triumphed through the whole day and night, gloriously singing psalms, hymns, and songs as a testimony to all; and every age and sex rejoiced with ardent desire to share in so great a celebration.

What a thing was this, brethren, which the Lord deigned to arrange for the honour of His martyrs: that on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, a Sabbath day [15 August], the people should be permitted to celebrate vigils in imitation of Easter [Col. 0772B]. Thus the day was completed and the night spent. As soon as the following day rose and the proconsul, expected to order burial of the body, came—what might that wretched man perhaps grant, which no judge is accustomed to deny even murderers or adulterers? Unless, on the contrary, the savage destruction wrought by the traitors was awake to devise plans of cruelty. At their prompting, the proconsul was then compelled to order the people driven from the prison [Note: [Col. 0772D] (1) The reading *populos* is emended from codex Corb.; the printed editions incorrectly read *protinus*.] and both the living man and the dead man drowned in the waves of the sea, lest he should seem to permit them to venerate the martyrs’ dignity.

What foolish cruelty, which wished to deny the bodies to our hands as though it could take veneration from our minds! Or if they were not buried in the earth, could they not otherwise enter the heavenly kingdoms? Yet this too was added as proof of their blessedness: after earthly tortures they, though dead, should be harassed for Christ even by the sea’s assaults, so that no place might remain in the world where they had not mocked the enemy [Col. 0772C]. The Lord had provided this for the increase of their triumphs: that they might suffer under a greater hatred of the world and that He might display His power in their dead bodies as in the living.

Thus soldiers and reserve troops came to the prison, laden with clubs; driving the people back by a path of slaughter, they wounded nearly everyone. So much, indeed, was granted to the martyrs’ dignity that others too might deserve to confess on account of their burial. Once they had scarcely managed to exclude everyone, an unequal number of soldiers led away the dead man and the survivor, one on either side [Col. 0772D]. Unknowingly, vain savagery mocked itself by rendering them the services which it had denied to others.

They had now reached the shore; the ship bore away the martyrs it was to drown. But when it swiftly entered the depth of the deep sea, Satan’s servants were no less swift in fulfilling their orders. They bound them with ropes and fastened two jars (*orcae*) filled with sand to the neck and feet of each man; then, separated by no small interval from one another, they released them beneath the sinking weight (Corb.: “drowned them”). When the sea received into its bosom those cast into it (Corb.: “as it received them into itself”), it immediately could not hold the most holy limbs, as though the whole sea were burning with heavenly flames [Col. 0773A]. Rolling waves downward from above, it scraped away utterly the sand driven down to cast out the bodies; overturning the lower depths to its upper surface, it removed it with rebounding waves.

The searching waves plunged from their highest masses with vast force toward the bottom to seize them from below; and the sea, driven back from the depths, was again stirred by the stronger piled-up force, labouring to bring forth the holy limbs. At length the whirlwind of rushing waters shook loose the submerged bodies, lifted their immense weight, and, having carried off the bodies, the victorious wave finally emerged. The masses of water then rose more violently, raised into mountains of solid water, so that their gathered heap might more securely bear up the burdensome limbs, lest, once defeated again [Col. 0773B], they should struggle. Beneath the united masses of the sea on every side, the wave formed a vault and fought against the weight, lest the sea’s strong floor yield before the violent burden [Note: [Col. 0773D] (1) Emended from codex Corb.; final syntax uncertain.].

But there still remained the task and exertion of another labour: to gather into one swift assemblage those whom an infinite interval had separated, lest that alien sacrilege should remain owing to its negligence. From this side the waters drew them, from that the masses of water, bending in twin horns; and by an equal coming-together of themselves (Corbie MS.: “restraint”) they eagerly received the bodies borne toward them at close range (Corbie MS.: “the common [course] entered”). Already the meeting of the advancing waters from either horn had begun to shorten the middle space; and, as each approached from its side, the length of the interval, diminishing by their convergence, had come into a narrow compass. When at last, with the full spaces on either side exhausted, the entire intervening distance had been consumed, all were brought together, and a harmony of waves and bodies was celebrated.

The brethren therefore kept watch upon these shores, as though some report had already preceded the martyrs who were now more certainly approaching; and, day and night, anxiously at every moment, with fixed eyes they hoped for that which they believed would at some time come from God’s customary power. Then, suddenly, after six days, they rejoiced that the temples of Christ were coming; and all ran to meet them, hanging upon the sight as best they could with exultant eagerness (Corbie MS.: “opening” rather than “hanging”). The hastening wave, as though sounding forth in joy, delivered up the longed-for limbs with their trophies into their outstretched hands; and the devoted brotherhood, their desire attained, received them in joyful embraces.

Thus the blessed martyrs received their due burial and rendered to the brethren the service they had desired; and Christ showed the counsels of the Traditors to have been frustrated, neither permitting the bodies of such great men to remain unburied, nor allowing the people’s devotion to be defrauded in any respect, nor looking on unmoved while the impious fulfilled the vows of their cruelty amid blasphemy against his name (Corbie MS.: “while the cruelty of the impious was fulfilled”).

Let now the demented—

> [Note: [Col. 0773D] (2) Absent from Corbie MS.]

—cruelty of the faithless lament, which would not remember the Lord’s mighty works. It did not fear that he could free bodies from the sea, though it knew that he could also—

> [Note: [Col. 0773D] (3) Absent from Corbie MS.]

—draw souls from the underworld. Or, if it received no other lesson—not even from the whale that had vomited him forth—it lost, wretched cruelty, what it believed it had discovered as a great design, for which not even the sea consented to lend its support. [Col. 0774A] It poorly commended its own desires, since it could not make the sea deny its Creator. What now can human fury do, where the sea does not pursue the martyrs? (Corbie MS. reads *humiliando*, “by humbling,” in place of *humana*, “human.”) What can the savagery of criminals do, where the cruel seas call them back for burial? Or what sort of men are judged by persecutors to be those whom even the elements themselves feared to violate? O memorable glory of blessed suffering, in which Christ deigned to display so many mighty works! O happy end that befell such men, which he adorned with such great powers for their merits! Constancy in devotion; endurance in suffering; victory in death; a miracle in burial.

> [Note: [Col. 0774D] (1) Corbie MS.: “wondrous”; printed editions: “mighty works.”]

To you now, brethren, all those things return which [Col. 0774B] have led you to the heavenly kingdoms. These examples urge you on—examples which first urged them, through you, toward these glories. The frequency of your confessions had made you their teachers through repeated reports, and now they themselves instruct you concerning martyrdom. Likewise, your own examples exhort you, examples which exhorted others. They now stretch out their arms to you from heaven, awaiting the time when they may come to meet you. Hasten earnestly; run together steadfastly. They await your attaining dignity together with them. Come then, brethren; make haste as quickly as possible, that we too may rejoice over you in no different way. May our return find among you something in which to glory, just as our departure has obtained from these men the joys of glory. But let us go forth toward your trophies, so that, just as we have announced to you their victories, so afterward we may announce yours here at [Col. 0774C] Carthage to those others who follow.

Here ends the letter of the most blessed martyr Macrobius to the people of Carthage concerning the suffering of the martyrs Isaac and Maximian.

> [Note: [Col. 0774D] (2) The remainder is absent from the Corbie manuscript.]

Thanks be to God. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 348 or 349

## From the Council of Carthage

When Gratus, bishop of Carthage, had taken his seat in council with his colleagues, and those who had assembled from the various African provinces . . . Gratus, the same bishop, said: “Thanks be to almighty God and to Christ Jesus, who has put an end to evil schisms and has looked upon his Church, so as to raise up into her bosom all her scattered members; who commanded the most devout Emperor Constans—

> [Note: [Col. 0774D] (3) Printed editions: “Constantine.”]

—to fulfil the desire for unity and to send the servants of God Paul and Macarius, ministers of the holy work.”

### From the First Council of Carthage

> [Note: [Col. 0774D] (4) In the year of Christ 348, or thereabouts.]

Gratus, bishop, said: “Thanks be to almighty God and to Christ Jesus, who has put an end to evil schisms and has looked upon his Church, so as to raise up into her bosom all her scattered members; who commanded the most devout Emperor Constans to fulfil the desire for unity and to send the servants of God Paul and Macarius, ministers of the holy work.”

[Col. 0775A] This council contains two canons against the Donatists: I, that baptism received in the Trinity is not to be repeated; II, concerning martyrs’ tombs and the honour due to them.

The following two canons of this council concern the Donatists.

### I

“Therefore, if it pleases you, let us first consider the heading of rebaptism. Accordingly, I request your holinesses to declare the judgment of your minds concerning one who descends into the water, is questioned concerning the Trinity according to the faith of the Gospel and the doctrine of the Apostles, and confesses a good conscience toward God concerning the resurrection of Jesus Christ: whether it is lawful for him to be questioned again in the same faith and immersed again in water.”

All the bishops said: “Far be it, far be it. We decree [Col. 0775B] that rebaptisms are unlawful, and that they are wholly alien to sincere faith and Catholic discipline.”

Gratus, bishop, said: “Great blessedness has been granted by God the Father through the Lord Christ in our time: that it is permitted to impress ecclesiastical discipline upon devout minds, so that hearers, receiving a rule that is upright and pleasing to God, may receive the rewards of good merits, and that in them God may be honoured in all things and for all things. The necessary heading of rebaptism has been examined, a matter in which the frenzy of schism lay especially concealed; and, moderation having been observed, the force of the law and the authority of the faith have been preserved. Certainly I endeavour to impress this upon your most wise understandings, although your prudence is instructed and taught by God and deserves to obtain from above abundant gifts in peace and unity; nevertheless, I too am one of you, and bear [Col. 0775C] an equal concern with you, and will take care to set this before you for the sake of ecclesiastical order.”

### II

“Let no profane person disparage the dignity of martyrs, nor extend it to—

> [Note: [Col. 0775D] (1) “To” is absent in certain manuscripts.]

—bodies that have merely suffered death and have been ordered to be committed to burial solely through the mercy of the Church: those, that is, who have died by hurling themselves down in madness, by some such compact, or for some other sinful reason, are not to be called by the name of martyrs without a fitting ground or outside the fitting time at which martyrdoms are celebrated. But if anyone, to the injury of martyrs, joins infamy to their renown, it is resolved that, if he is a layman, he shall be reduced to penance; but if he is a cleric, after admonition and investigation, he shall be deprived of his rank.”

All said: [Col. 0775D] “Your holiness has rightly decreed. This too has been decreed at individual councils.”

## On the Indulgence and Freedom of Choice Granted to the Donatists by Constantine

> [Note: [Col. 0775D] (2) In the year 321.]

In the index to *Collation* III, chapter 544, one reads: “The Donatists’ prosecution, by which they assert that their own predecessors gave Emperor Constantine a petition, and that, moved by it, the emperor granted them freedom to act.” In the same work, chapter 549: “A letter of Constantine addressed to the vicar Verinus is read aloud, by which he grants the Donatists freedom to act.” In the same work, chapter 550: “The prosecution of the Catholics, which says that Constantine’s letter makes more strongly for them, because nothing was adjudged concerning Caecilian, but the Donatists were left to their own frenzy.” In the same work, chapter 552: “The Donatists request that the judge, Marcellinus, pronounce upon the freedom of choice granted to them by Constantine.”

Augustine, in the book written after the *Collation*, §56, testifies that these letters were given to Valerius, or Verinus, the vicar, concerning the ending of their exile and the committing of their frenzy to God as avenger, when Crispus and Constantine were again consuls, on the third day before the Nones of May; that is, about four years and almost six months after the time when the rescript was sent to Eumalius. Compare *Breviculum Collationis* III, §40, and Letter 141, §9.

## On the Persecution by Paul and Macarius: How Unjust Was the Donatists’ Complaint

> [Note: [Col. 0776D] (1) From Optatus, Book III.]

Many harsh acts were indeed committed by the workers for unity [Col. 0776B]; but why do you charge these against Leontius, Macarius, or Taurinus? Charge them against your own predecessors, and so forth: first, against those who divided God’s people and erected superfluous basilicas. Then against Donatus of Carthage, who provoked the attempt to bring about unity shortly thereafter. Thirdly, against Donatus of Bagai, who had assembled a mad multitude, and, lest Macarius should suffer violence at its hands, requested the assistance of armed soldiers to protect himself and the things he was carrying. Then armed men with quivers came; every city was filled with shouting men. When unity was announced, you all fled, and so forth. Therefore all the bishops fled with their clergy; some died; those who were stronger were captured and banished far away. Yet none of all these things was done by our wish, our counsel, our knowledge, or [Col. 0776C] our action, and so forth.

Who can deny the fact, to which all Carthage is chiefly a witness: that Emperor Constans at first sent Paul and Macarius not to effect unity, but with alms, by which poverty, relieved through every individual church, might breathe, be clothed, be fed, and rejoice?

> [Note: [Col. 0776D] (2) Constans governed Italy, Africa, and several other parts of the Empire from the year of Christ 337, when his father Constantine died, until 350. The event dealt with here is assigned to about the year 347.]

When they came to Donatus, your father, and stated why they had come, he burst out, inflamed with his customary fury, in these words: “What has the emperor to do with the Church?” From the fountain of his frivolity he poured forth many insults, no less than he had formerly done against Gregory, to whom he did not hesitate to write: “Gregory, stain of the senate, disgrace of prefects,” and other such things. The Prefect replied to this Donatus with episcopal patience, and so forth. For the Emperor had sent ornaments [Col. 0776D] for the houses of God; he had sent alms for the poor; he had sent nothing to Donatus. Why then did he rage? Why was he angry? Why did he reject what had been sent? And when those who had been sent said that they would go through each province and give to those who wished to receive, he said that he had sent letters everywhere in advance, ordering that what had been brought should nowhere be distributed to the poor, and so forth.

Paul and Macarius were coming, to distribute alms to the poor everywhere and to exhort each individual to unity. [Col. 0777A] When they were approaching the city of Bagai, then the other Donatus, as we have said above, bishop of the same city, wishing to place an obstacle and a barrier in the path of those aforementioned men who were coming, sent heralds through the neighbouring places and through every market, calling the Circumcellions *Agonistici*, and invited them to assemble at the appointed place. At that time the gathering was demanded of men whose madness a little before had seemed to be wickedly inflamed by the very bishops themselves. For when, before unity, people of this sort roamed through all the regions with Maxidus and Fasir, and were called by those madmen “leaders of the saints”—

> [Note: [Col. 0777D] (1) Germanensis manuscript: “under Axidus and Fasirab, by those madmen.”]

—no one was permitted to be secure in his possessions. Written acknowledgements of debts had lost their force; no creditor at that time had power to exact payment. All were terrified [Col. 0777B] by the letters of those who boasted that they were leaders of the saints, and so forth.

Accordingly, when jealousy was then stirred up against Paul and Macarius by bishops of your party—

> [Note: [Col. 0777D] (2) From the German manuscript we have added the particle “by,” because it concerns the hostility which Donatist bishops bore toward Paul and Macarius.]

—they are said to have written at that time to Taurinus the count, declaring that persons of this kind could not be corrected within the Church, so that they might receive discipline from the aforementioned count. Then Taurinus, in response to their letters, ordered armed soldiers to go through the markets where the frenzy of the Circumcellions was accustomed to roam. In the place called Octavensis—

> [Note: [Col. 0777D] (3) The same manuscript: “Octaviensis.”]

—very many were killed and many mutilated. Their bodies could be counted even to the present day by the whitewashed altars or tables. When some of their number began to be buried in basilicas, the presbyter Clarius at Subbulensis—

> [Note: [Col. 0777D] (4) The same manuscript: “Clarus, presbyter at Subbulensis.”]

—was compelled by his bishop to undo the burial and leave them unburied. From this it became known that what was done had been ordered, when not even burial in the house of God was permitted. Later their multitude regained strength. Thus Donatus of Bagai found a means of hiring a frenzied crowd against Macarius. From this same class came those who, through desire for false martyrdom, hired men to strike them down, to their own destruction; from it also came those who cast away their worthless lives by throwing themselves headlong from the summits of high mountains. See what sort of bands the other Donatus, the bishop, had formed for himself. Frightened by this danger, those who were carrying treasures for distribution to the poor found, in so great an emergency, the expedient of requesting armed soldiers from Count Silvester—

> [Note: [Col. 0777D] (5) In the German manuscript, “Silvestre.” The man whom he previously called Count Taurinus he now calls Silvester, perhaps to soften an insulting word by this interpretation. For Leontius, Ursacius, and Taurinus seem to be names attached to the judges or commanders who corrected the Donatists, while they compared their own punishments to persecutions of martyrs—“the first,” says Optatus in the same third book, “was like a lion; the second, like a bear.”]

—not that they might use force against anyone, but that they might prevent the violence arranged by the aforementioned bishop Donatus, and so forth.

[Col. 0777D] You set down in order the complaints that very many were wronged under Leontius, [Col. 0778A] under Ursacius; that some were killed under Paul and Macarius; and that some persons, I know not whom, were temporarily proscribed by their successors. What has this to do with us? What with the Catholic Church? Whatever you allege, you yourselves did it, because you were unwilling gladly to receive the peace commended by God, and so forth. Some think unity to be blameworthy or to be shunned because Marculus and Donatus are said to have been killed or to have died—as though no one could ever deserve to be killed under God’s vengeance, and so forth.

For we read in the prophet Ezekiel of a whitewashed wall, against which God threatened a storm, rain, stones hurled as missiles, and accusations (Ezekiel 13:13), and so forth. These four things could not occur at one time. First came the storm under Ursacius—

> [Note: [Col. 0778D] (1) On the authority of the German manuscript we restore here “under Ursacius,” and below “under Gregory,” and shortly afterward “under the workers for unity”; all of which are entirely absent from the printed editions. Optatus enumerates in order the three persecutions of which they complained: first, that of Ursacius, also mentioned in Book III against Cresconius, §34; second, that of the prefect Gregory, praised above; and third, that of Paul and Macarius. Here he passes over Leontius, whom at the beginning of Book III he joined to Macarius, and afterwards joined or set before Ursacius.]

—the wall was shaken, but did not fall, so that the rain might have somewhere to work. [Col. 0778B] Rain followed under Gregory: the wall was wetted, but did not become soaked through, so that the stones might have somewhere to work. After the rain, stones followed under the workers—

> [Note: [Col. 0778D] (2) Paul and Macarius.]

—for unity: the wall was scattered, but rebuilt itself once more upon its foundations. Now three things have been accomplished, and so forth.

## Fragment of a Letter of the Donatist Macrobius, Concerning the Suffering of the Donatists Maximian and Isaac, to the People of Carthage

*(From Mabillon, **Vetera Analecta**, p. 185.)*

. . . nevertheless he yielded, who, as though estranged from his own body, triumphed over all things. Thus there a war was waged between body and punishments, between sacrilegious men and the devout man, between the powers of the soul and those who tore him, between the soldier of Christ and the soldier of the devil, between the sufferer and the judge; and one afflicted man [Col. 0778C] was sufficient to contend more gloriously against so great a multitude of torments and enemies, so that in one contest he won not one victory only. He could there have undergone the final ordeal of supreme torture, which sends a man to death in triumph; but it was necessary that he should meanwhile wait for the man whom Christ had assigned him as a companion.

For then, in that place, the illustrious ISAAC, unable to restrain his joy at the struggle of his companion, was borne among the brotherly congregations in the public exultation of the Holy Spirit. Filled with heavenly constancy, he cried out more freely: “Traditors, come, save the madness of your unity.” At his cry the raging Proconsul urgently threw the staff of his office into disorder, demanding that they seek out the author of the outcry.

But there were no lack of Traditors who had gone ahead of the soldiers. [Col. 0778D] At once these sacrilegious agents, not at all satisfied with one victim, delivered up the other also to be sacrificed by their own hands, so that the measure of their fathers might more openly be fulfilled upon them. Immediately the judge, violently enraged, set aside the man whom [Col. 0779A] he had shortly before been torturing and turned upon this man more sharply the fury that possessed him, as one who had not yet digested one anger and was conceiving another. The exhausted executioners again repeated their mad assault; their weary arms were made stronger by cruelty alone. Again and again that band of butchers unleashed the violence of leaded scourges, and, expending all its strength in repeated efforts, savaged him with groaning rage, as though it itself suffered what it inflicted. How great was the endurance of the sufferer, when the assault of the raging men groaned!

Yet even in the second martyr the devil was not permitted to prevail, because Christ’s victory, burning brightly, could not rightly be allowed to succumb in anyone. Accordingly, when the leaded scourges again accomplished nothing, frenzied savagery likewise applied tortures, so that the heavenly standard-bearers might not differ in any unequal kind of endurance, and the enemy might not seem to be softened by a milder punishment in either case.

Isaac—the name, of course, of the victim—was torn by breaking rods; imitating the endurance implied by his name, the confessor’s devotion remained unshaken, though the blows were delivered again and again. All the joints had been opened, their connections broken and soaked; and, as though it could find an outlet through so many wounds, that voice seemed to sound out the proclamations of confession. Let no one suppose that those strokes of rods were a slight chastisement: they certainly surpassed the laceration of the claws, so completely that the claws had become distasteful even to the judge himself. They were no longer wounds, but the hidden parts of the body laid bare; nor could he be called merely beaten, who had been reduced to weakness by dripping fragments of flesh. Already bundles of rods had yielded; axes or sickles would almost have been blunted if they had shattered so great a man. Already the grim agents, drawing painful breaths, gasped through the languid mouths of defeated savagery, and still their hungry limbs gaped for every torment to be chewed and devoured.

Then the body mocked its tortures, and the mind rejoiced amid their raging. Amid so many tormentors, one man was both tortured and condemned; no postponement now delayed the sentence—the transmitted syntax is difficult—but the judge, joining both men in the same lot, bound them over for exile. When they had been thrust into prison, Isaac at once completed the effect of martyrdom; and, what is more, at one stroke he left behind every prison, body, and world, so that the revelation granted to him might not prove false in any respect. For he had run through everything in due order, so that almost what he underwent afterward had already been undergone in the revelation itself. For when [Col. 0779D] he was held a little while in the sleep of rest, he seemed to himself to be struggling with the emperor’s agents, plainly in the very matter in which he endured his suffering. This was nothing other than a token of devotion: what he pondered while awake in longing, he also suffered while asleep, so that the saying which the prophet confessed of himself might be fulfilled in him: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.”

That devotion therefore kept watch, already exercising its attempts at courage, and more steadfastly repelled the ministers of wickedness as they boldly resisted with the king’s commands. When, after a long contest, he had overcome them, he saw the emperor himself suddenly approaching. Though the emperor pressed him to carry out the command, [Col. 0780A] Isaac all the more resolutely rejected the authority of the sacrilegious order and its cruel threats of punishment. Isaac in turn repeatedly made the terrible promise that he would tear out the emperor’s eye. While they fought fiercely with one another in these prolonged contests, Isaac did not permit himself to be delayed so long as victor. With a strong hand he broke through the delay of his threat and violently tore out the emperor’s eye, emptying the seat of light and leaving his face bereft.

Immediately after this victory, a young man of marvellous brightness was seen triumphing and placing upon his head a radiant crown. In its rays the faces of many brothers and sisters seemed fixed. As he joyfully gave him that crown as his reward, he mocked and derided the adversary also with great reproaches. Then the enemy, driven by violent pain, ordered him [Col. 0780B] to be torn by raging punishments, as though he might thereby avenge his own pain. But Isaac, already victorious, saw himself drawn upward by the hands of those who bore him and swiftly raised as he flew to the heights of heaven. As he joyfully ascended, he heard from above the voice of an old man crying: “Woe to you, world, for you have perished.” When this cry had been repeated three times, the vision reached its end; and later he repeated in action what he had seen.

What, then, could be clearer than this vision? What could be more plainly set forth as to what was to happen by day, when it had been arranged in a vision? In the night he saw himself alone fighting against the king’s ministers, just as he afterward displayed it to us by day; he saw himself tearing out the emperor’s eye and blinding him as he conquered; he received the rewards of the crown and was publicly crowned. He saw many faces clinging to the rays of the crown, just as the whole people would keep vigil at his suffering. He flew to heaven, just as he deserved swiftly to attain martyrdom.

Only this is known still to await fulfilment among his sayings: that he prophesied the world’s destruction. Since, as all know, he did not lie, perhaps some brother may fear and call MAXIMIAN unequal to him, because, though he confessed first, he was kept alive for a short time. Far be it, brethren, that they should be thought unequal, for they fought an equal battle. If the Lord made equal in the agreed wage those who came into the vineyard at different hours, how does he judge unequal those whom he found labouring at one time? But Isaac’s seeming to depart first was rather the means, I say, by which the Lord made them equal: just as Isaac had supplied Maximian with an incentive to confess, so Maximian might in turn summon him equally to the crown. The Lord willed that both should be teachers to one another, so that he might make them equal by reciprocal instruction, lest one should precede in everything and the other seem in everything merely to follow him. But now both preceded one another, and both followed one another.

Meanwhile the prison guards were withdrawn, and a ship was, of course, prepared for exile—an arrangement which I believe was not made by human counsel, since it was plainly provided by heavenly favour. For if the Lord willed them to be shut up together for the delay of one day, so that, in accordance with the vision of his martyr, they might be honoured by the vigils [Col. 0781A] of the people, then, before Isaac’s perfect martyrdom was complete, news had filled the ears of everyone. The whole brotherhood immediately hastened with joyful running to his body. When the executioners refused burial for the body, they all maintained a great and joyful vigil, lest it should be cast away unburied. There, all day and night, the triumphing people sang psalms, hymns, and canticles, as testimony to all of the Lord’s glory; persons of every age and sex rejoiced to take part in such congratulations with burning desire.

What a thing was this, brethren, which the Lord deigned to provide for the honour of his martyrs: that on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, a Saturday, the people were permitted to celebrate vigils after the pattern of Easter. Thus the day was spent and the night likewise passed. As soon as the following day arose, they waited to see what the proconsul would order concerning the burial of the body, or what the wretch might perhaps grant—something which no judge is accustomed to deny even murderers or adulterers—unless, on the contrary, the cruel destructive designs of the Traditors were awake to devise measures of cruelty. At their suggestion, the proconsul was then compelled immediately to order that the living man be expelled from the prison together with the dead and drowned in the waves of the sea, lest he should seem to permit honour to be paid to their rank as martyrs.

How foolish was that cruelty, which thought to deny their bodies to our hands as though it could remove veneration from our minds; or as though, if they were not buried in the earth, they could not otherwise enter the heavenly kingdoms. But an increase of blessedness was added to them: after earthly sufferings for Christ, they were also buffeted in death by the sea, so that no place might remain in the world where they had not mocked the enemy. The Lord had provided this addition to their triumphs, so that they might have suffered under a greater hatred of the world, and so that he might display his power in their dead bodies, as in the living.

Accordingly, all the soldiers and the *trivarii*, armed with clubs, came to the prison; driving the crowds back with a path of slaughter, they wounded almost everyone. So much was granted to the dignity of the martyrs, that others too were counted worthy to confess for the sake of their burial. Afterwards, since they could scarcely exclude all the people, they led away the dead man and the survivor, with unequal numbers of soldiers on either side. In its blindness, vain savagery deceived itself: it provided them with the services [Col. 0781D] which it had denied them at the hands of others.

Now they had reached the shore of the sea; now the ship was carrying the received martyrs in order to drown them. But when it had swiftly entered the depths of the deep sea, the satellites of Satan hastened no less eagerly to carry out their commands. Binding them with ropes, they fastened to the neck and feet of each man two jars filled with sand; then, separated by no small distance from one another, they let them sink beneath the water under the weight. When the sea recognized those bodies cast into its bosom, immediately, as though it were wholly burning with heavenly flames, it could not hold their most sacred limbs. With waves rolling downward and upward, it stripped away from its depths the sand pressed down for the purpose of casting out the bodies, overturning it from the lowest bottom to the upper surface and removing it in rebounding waves.

The searching waves plunged from their highest crests to seize what lay below, descending with vast force to the bottom. And the sea, driven back from below by the stronger mass thrown up, was again urged on as it laboured to bring forth the members of the saints, until the whirl of rapid waves shook loose their sunken limbs and, lifting the immense weight away, escaped at last victorious with the bodies carried off. The crests then rose more violently, elevated as solid mountains of water, so that their united mass might bear up the heavy limbs more securely, lest they should be overcome and sink again. Under the dome formed by the sea’s masses gathered on every side, the wave contended with the weight, lest the strong back of the sea should open and admit the violent burden.

But there still remained the task and exertion of another labour: to gather into one swift assemblage those whom an infinite interval had separated—at this point the transmitted text adds the corrupt phrase *in quo quinquies unum*, “in which five times one” [Col. 0782B]—lest that alien sacrilege should remain owing to its negligence. From this side the waters drew them, from that the masses of water, bending in twin horns; and by an equal coming-together they eagerly received the bodies borne toward them at close range. Already the meeting of the advancing waters from either horn had made the middle space short, and as each approached from its side, the length of the interval, diminishing by their convergence, had come into a narrow compass. When at last, with their full courses run, the whole intervening space had been consumed, all were brought together, and a harmony of waves and bodies was celebrated.

The brethren therefore kept watch upon these shores, as though some report had already preceded the martyrs who were now more certainly approaching; and, day and night, anxiously forewarned, with fixed and expectant eyes they hoped for that which they believed would at some time come from God’s customary power. Then, suddenly, after six days, they rejoiced that the temples of Christ were coming—“doubled, that is, after the pattern of [the] number” (the transmitted wording is corrupt)—and all ran to meet them, hanging upon the sight as best they could with exultant eagerness. The hastening wave, as though sounding forth in joy, delivered up the longed-for limbs with their trophies into their outstretched hands; and the devoted brotherhood, their desire attained, received them in joyful embraces.

Thus the blessed martyrs received their due burial and rendered to the brethren the service they had desired; and Christ showed the counsels of the Traditors to have been frustrated, neither permitting the bodies of such great men to remain unburied, nor allowing the people’s devotion to be defrauded in any respect, nor looking on unmoved while the impious fulfilled the vows of their cruelty amid blasphemy against his name.

[Col. 0782D] Let now the demented cruelty of the faithless lament, which would not remember the Lord’s mighty works. It did not fear that he could free bodies from the sea, though it knew that he could also draw souls from the underworld. Or, if it received no other lesson—not even from the whale that had vomited him forth—it lost, wretched cruelty, what it believed it had discovered as a great design, for which not even the sea consented to lend its support. It poorly commended its own desires, since it could not make the sea deny its Creator. What now can human fury do, where the sea does not pursue the martyrs? What can the savagery of criminals do, where the cruel seas call them back for burial? Or what sort of men are judged by persecutors to be those whom even the elements themselves feared to violate? O memorable glory of blessed suffering, in which [Col. 0783A] Christ deigned to display so many mighty works! O happy end that befell such men, which he adorned with such great powers for their merits! Constancy in devotion; endurance in suffering; victory in death; mighty works in burial.

To you now, brethren, all those things return which have led you to the heavenly kingdoms. These examples urge you on—examples which first urged them, through you, toward these glories. The frequency of your confessions had made you their teachers through repeated reports, and now they themselves instruct you concerning martyrdom. Likewise, your own examples exhort you, examples which exhorted others. They now stretch out their arms to you from heaven, awaiting the time when [Col. 0784A] they may come to meet you. Hasten briskly; run together steadfastly. They await your attaining dignity together with them. Come then, brethren; make haste as quickly as possible, that we too may rejoice over you in no different way. May our return find among you something in which to glory, just as our departure has obtained from these men the joys of glory. But let us go forth toward your trophies, so that, just as we have announced to you their victories, so afterward we may announce yours here at Carthage to those others who follow.

Here ends the letter of the most blessed martyr Macrobius to the people of Carthage concerning the suffering of the martyrs Isaac and Maximian. Thanks be to God. Amen.

[Col. 0783]

City of Neapolis — 15 miles.

There is Mount Agazaren. There the Samaritans say that Abraham offered sacrifice; and there are three hundred steps ascending to the summit of the mountain.

From there, at the foot of that mountain, is a place named Sechim. There is situated the tomb in which Joseph was placed, on the estate which his father Jacob gave him. There Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, was carried off by the sons of the Amorites.

From there, one thousand paces away, is a place named Sechar, from which the Samaritan woman came down to the same place where Jacob dug the well, in order to draw water from it; and [Col. 0790C] our Lord Jesus Christ spoke with her there. There are plane-trees which Jacob planted, and a bath supplied from that well.

From there, 28 miles on the way to Jerusalem, on the left is the estate called Bethar. A thousand paces from there is the place where Jacob, as he was going to Mesopotamia, fell asleep; there is an almond-tree, he saw a vision, and an angel wrestled with him. There King Jeroboam was; to him a prophet was sent, that he might turn to the Most High God. The prophet had been commanded not to eat with the false prophet whom the king kept with him. Because he was deceived by the false prophet and ate with him, a lion met the prophet as he was returning on the road, and the lion killed him.

From there to Jerusalem: 12 miles. From Caesarea in Palestine [Col. 0790D] to Jerusalem there are 116 miles, 4 posting-stations, and 4 change-stations.

In Jerusalem are two large pools beside the Temple, one on the right and the other on the left, which Solomon made. Within the city, however, are twin pools having five porticoes, called Bethsaida. There persons sick for many years were healed. These pools have water disturbed to the appearance of scarlet. There is also a crypt there in which Solomon tortured demons. There is also the corner of a very high tower, to which the Lord ascended, and he who tempted him said to him. [Note: [Col. 0790D] (1) Here is lacking what you will find in Matthew, chapter 4, verse 6.] [Col. 0791A] And the Lord said to him: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God, but shall serve him alone.” There is also the great cornerstone, of which it was said: “The stone which the builders rejected.” Likewise, at the head of the corner and beneath the tower’s pinnacle, are many chambers where Solomon had his palace. The chamber also survives in which he sat and wrote wisdom; it is covered by a single stone. There are also great underground water-collectors and pools constructed with great labour; and in the very sanctuary where the Temple stood, which Solomon built, you might say that, in the marble before the altar, the blood of Zechariah is still shed today.* [Note: [Col. 0791D] (1) The asterisk marking these words indicates that something is missing; although, if one removed the word *ibi* (“there”), they could appear sound. (Note of Father Wesseling.)]

The marks of the nails of the soldiers who killed him are also visible over the whole area, so that you would think they had been impressed in wax. There are also two statues of Hadrian there. Not far [Col. 0791B] from the statues is a pierced stone, to which the Jews come every year; they anoint it, mourn with groaning, tear their clothes, and so depart. There is also the house of Hezekiah, king of Judah. Likewise, on leaving Jerusalem in order to ascend Zion, on the left and down in the valley beside the wall, is the pool called Siloam; it has four porticoes, and outside is another large pool. This spring flows for six days and nights. On that same ascent to Zion, the place where the house of Caiaphas the priest stood is visible; and the column is still there at which they struck Christ with scourges. But within the wall of Zion is visible the place where David had his palace, and the seven synagogues which were there; only one remains, while the others are ploughed and sown, as Isaiah the prophet said. From there, when those going from Zion outside the wall [Col. 0791C] proceed to the Neapolitan Gate, on the right and down in the valley are walls where the house, or praetorium, of Pontius Pilate stood. There the Lord was heard before he suffered. On the left is the little hill of Golgotha, where the Lord was crucified. From there, about a stone’s throw away, is the crypt where his body was laid and where, on the third day, he rose again. There too, now by order of Emperor Constantine, a basilica has been made—that is, a church of wondrous beauty—having beside it reservoirs from which water is drawn for washing, and behind it a bath where infants are washed. Likewise, for those leaving Jerusalem by the gate facing east and ascending the Mount of Olives, the valley called Jehoshaphat is on the left, where there are vineyards. There is also the rock where Judas Iscariot betrayed Christ. On the right [Col. 0791D] is the palm-tree from which children took branches and spread them out at Christ’s coming. Not far from there, about a stone’s throw away, are two tombs,* [Note: [Col. 0791D] (2) The asterisk seems to indicate a lacuna. Otherwise, if one punctuates after the word *pulchritudinis* (“beauty”), the words cohere tolerably well. (The same.)] monuments of marvellous beauty. In one lies the prophet Isaiah, which is truly monolithic; and in the other Hezekiah, king of the Jews. From there one ascends the Mount of Olives, where the Lord taught the apostles before the Passion. A basilica was built there by Constantine’s command. From there [Col. 0792A] not far away is the little hill where the Lord went up to pray, and Moses and Elijah appeared there when he took Peter and John with him. From there, 1,500 paces eastward, is the estate called Bethany. There is a crypt where Lazarus was laid, whom the Lord raised.

Likewise, from Jerusalem to Jericho: 18 miles. As one descends the mountain, on the right, behind the tomb, is the sycamore-tree which Zacchaeus climbed in order to see Christ. At 1,500 paces from the city is the spring of the prophet Elisha. Previously, if any woman drank from that water, she did not bear children. Beside it is Elisha’s earthen vessel: he put salt in it, came and stood over the spring, and said: “Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters; from now on, if any woman drinks from it, [Col. 0792B] she will bear children.” Above the same spring is the house of Rahab the prostitute, into which the scouts entered; she concealed them when Jericho was overthrown, and she alone escaped. There was the city of Jericho, whose walls the children of Israel circled with the Ark of the Covenant, and the walls fell. Nothing is visible there now except the place where the Ark of the Covenant stood and the twelve stones which the children of Israel lifted from the Jordan. There Jesus son of Naveh circumcised the children of Israel and buried their circumcisions.

Likewise, from Jericho to the Dead Sea: 8 miles. Its water is exceedingly bitter; there is absolutely no kind of fish in it, nor any ship; and if anyone enters it to swim, the water itself turns him over.

From there to the Jordan, where the Lord was baptized by John: 5 miles.

[Col. 0792C] There is a little hill on the bank above the river where Elijah was taken up into heaven. Likewise, from Jerusalem to Bethlehem: 4 miles. Above the road, on the right, is the tomb where Rachel, Jacob’s wife, was laid. Two miles from there, on the left, is Bethlehem, where our Lord Jesus Christ was born; a basilica was built there by Constantine’s command. Not far from there are the tombs of Ezekiel, Asaph, Sobbe, Jesse, David, and Solomon; and in the crypt itself, as one descends, the names written above are inscribed in Hebrew at the side.

From there to Bethazsora: 14 miles.

Where there is the spring in which Philip baptized the eunuch.

From there to the Terebinth: 9 miles.

Where Abraham lived and dug a well beneath the [Col. 0792D] terebinth-tree, spoke with angels, and took food. A basilica of marvellous beauty was built there by Constantine’s command.

From the Terebinth to Hebron: 2 miles.

Where there is a square memorial made of stones of marvellous beauty, in which Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Sarah, Rebecca, and Leah are laid.
