From the same distinguished man, on Gallic words.

Lugdunum: “Desired Mountain.”

Armorici: “before the sea”; for they say *are* for “before,” and *mor* for “sea,” hence *marini* (“maritime”).

Arverni: “before the obstacle.”

Rhône: “violent”; for *rho* means “excessively.”

*Dan*, “judge,” is said both in Gallic and in Hebrew.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 333. POPE ST SYLVESTER.

[Col. 0795]

[Col. 0795]

PROLEGOMENA.

§ I.—Historical notice from the *Liber Pontificalis* of Pope Damasus.

[Col. 0795]

[Col. 0795C] [Note: [Col. 0795D]

**Sylvester.** After the Roman episcopal see had been vacant through the death of Miltiades not merely for seventeen days (as the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*, forgetful of himself, maintains), but for a whole month, on the very Kalends of February, in the year of Christ 314, the ninth of Emperor Constantine, Sylvester, a Roman by birth, was ordained priest by Marcellinus—not, as the Acts of Sylvester have it, by Miltiades—and obtained the pontificate. After Maximinus and Licinius, enemies and persecutors of the eastern Church, had been defeated, and after the Jews, who had stirred up sedition, had been happily suppressed by Constantine, who cut off their ears and imprinted upon their bodies a mark of rebellion, peace and tranquillity were granted to the whole world and especially to the whole Church. Once this had been secured, ruined churches immediately began to be rebuilt, and most holy laws began to be promulgated by the rulers of the ecclesiastical and secular empires for the correction of corrupt morals. Finally, in order to curb the obstinacy of the Donatist schismatics, who appealed three or four times in the case of Caecilian; to extinguish the blaze of the Arian heresy that had arisen in Alexandria; and to confirm Athanasius’s election against the faction of the Arians and Meletians, councils were convened, assembled, and held at various places and times: at Arles, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Alexandria, Laodicea, Rome, Nicaea, and many others.

Among the laws which the Emperor, still a catechumen and not yet baptized, most devoutly decreed and promulgated, especially worthy of notice are those by which he restored to freedom freeborn persons subjected to slavery by the tyrant; prohibited sodomitical intercourse with boys; relieved the poverty of parents in feeding and bringing up their offspring; [Col. 0797A] abolished the punishment by which the faces of unfortunate persons were branded; after Licinius’s defeat recalled exiled Christians and those condemned to the mines; restored those degraded from their rank and stripped of all their property; repealed the Julian and Papian laws, once enacted against shameful, fictitious, and barren celibacy and turned against the true, holy, and fruitful celibacy of Christians; and finally wrote to Maximus, prefect of the City, concerning soothsayers, that they should not enter private houses, since on that pretext they instilled the poisons of clandestine idolatry.

But when he saw that this decree of his had grievously exasperated many minds and had almost provoked a sedition, under the appearance of allaying the sedition he issued to the same Maximus a rescript contrary to the earlier one. By it he decreed that, if lightning struck any building, soothsayers should be consulted, and that what they answered should be reported to himself. Wherefore, in order that the Emperor himself might learn, and teach others by his example, how great an offence against God it is to disguise religion for the sake of temporal advantage, God’s avenging judgment permitted his previously most fortunate empire to relapse into the utmost misery, and something like a revival of the age of Nero to be seen.

For, after he had killed the younger Licinius on suspicion of rebellion, he then most cruelly put to death the excellent Christian Caesar Crispus—renowned for splendid victories, truly great through his courageous exploits, and distinguished for chastity and other virtues—as though Crispus had attempted the violation of his stepmother; together with his own wife Fausta and, moreover, many men of proven virtue. For these crimes the Emperor was struck by God with leprosy. When, on consulting the responses of the soothsayers, who advised him, in order to cure the leprosy, to add the blood of innocents to blood innocently shed, he was deterred by the cries of mothers and infants, he returned to his senses, abhorred the deed, and sought expiation both for the crime [Col. 0797C] and for its penalty. From Hosius, bishop of Corduba, and from an apparition of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, he learned that Sylvester must be recalled from his hiding-place in exile and that he must seek from him the washing of baptism. They promised the Emperor that, if he did this, he would be cleansed from the pollution both of mind and body. He obeyed the admonitions of the apostles and bishop, recalled Sylvester from exile, and, after being instructed in the faith by him for several days, was baptized and suddenly cleansed of leprosy.

Mindful of this benefit received, in order to make known his disposition toward God and the Church, he immediately destroyed the shrines of the pagan gods, built very many churches to be consecrated to divine worship, and most generously adorned them with exceedingly ample gifts. And because he judged it unworthy that the city in which the monarch of the whole Church and Christ’s vicar on earth resided should be subject to the authority of a secular prince, he most generously bestowed upon Sylvester and his lawful successors in the chair of Peter temporal lordship and jurisdiction not only over the city of Rome but over nearly all Italy and other provinces as well. By what means he exalted the Lord’s cross, which had lain hidden and buried in the earth for three complete centuries; by what miracles he distinguished it from the crosses of the thieves; what churches he built in God’s honour; and what other illustrious deeds he performed, we have in part stated above in the notes to the third letter of Eusebius and shall in part recount below.

He sat for 23 years, 10 months, and 11 days. Sylvester, having sat for 21 years, 11 months less one day, departed this life on the day before the Kalends of January, in the year of Christ’s birth 335. Others indeed say otherwise; but since, in the book *On the Roman Pontiffs*, his accession is placed under the consulship of Volusianus, in Constantine’s time (for this is how it must be read here), whereas the appointment of his successor Mark is placed under the consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus, which fell in the year of Christ 336, Sylvester plainly cannot have died in 335. Baronius, appendix to volume 10, under the year 324, no. 8.]

Sylvester, a Roman by birth and son of Rufinus, sat [Col. 0795D] for twenty-three years, ten months, and eleven days. [Col. 0796C] He lived in the times of Constantine and Volusianus, [Col. 0796D] from the day of the Kalends of February until the day of the Kalends [Col. 0797A] [Note: [Col. 0798A]

**He was in exile on Mount Soracte.** Besides his own Acts, Zosimus, book 2, and Sozomen, book 1, chapter 5, probably indicate that Sylvester, fearing the Emperor’s cruelty, went into exile from the city, since Constantine, seeking expiation for his crime, consulted not the Roman bishop but a foreigner—namely Hosius, bishop of Corduba. “Conscious of these deeds,” Zosimus says, “and therefore of his contempt for the religion of the sacred rites, he approached the priests and sought purifications for his crimes. They replied that no mode of purification had been handed down which could wash away such [Col. 0798B] foul abominations. A certain Spaniard, whose name was Aegyptius” (thus he calls Hosius, bishop of Corduba—both because he had returned from Egypt after undertaking an embassy and because, like nearly all Egyptians and all Christian priests in pagan estimation, he was thought to be a magician), “came to Rome and was admitted to an interview with Constantine; he affirmed that the teaching of Christians had the power to abolish whatever sin,” etc. Baronius, year 324, nos. 17 and 27.

**Returning with glory.** For, at the command of the blessed Peter and Paul, who appeared to the Emperor by night in repose and sleep, he was recalled from exile and returned to the city. *Acts of Sylvester*, recited by Pope Hadrian in the First Session of the Second Council of Nicaea; likewise in volume 2 of the Decretal Letters.

Baptized the Emperor Constantine. The Roman council held under the above-mentioned consuls most clearly proves that Constantine was baptized in the year of Christ 324, when Crispus and Constantine were consuls for the third time. For at the beginning of that council the following is narrated: “At the same time” (namely, when Crispus and Constantine were consuls for the third time, as is evident from the subscription), “while many nobles rejoiced that Constantine had been baptized by Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, and cleansed of leprosy, on account of this benefit which he received from our Lord Jesus Christ through Bishop Silvester, he began to preach the Lord Jesus Christ wholeheartedly and to confess his benefits,” etc. By the authority of that same council, Anastasius the Librarian, in the very brief chronicle which he wrote, records that Constantine’s baptism took place at Rome in the eighteenth year of his reign, namely, A.D. 324, the year of Christ’s birth in which Constantine’s eighteenth year ended and his nineteenth began. These same things are confirmed by the testimony of Zosimus, Book II, and of other pagans, whom Sozomen mentions in Book I, chapter 5. For all of them share one and the same judgment: that, after the murder of his son Crispus, Constantine, repenting of the crime committed and anxiously seeking its expiation, learned from pagan and Christian authorities [Col. 0798D] that pardon for parricide could not be obtained except through baptism duly and lawfully administered; and that, therefore, upon receiving Christian baptism, he would be washed clean from every contamination of body and soul.

There is also the fact, accepted by the common consensus of almost all historians, that the emperor attended the universal Council of Nicaea, where debate concerned not only morals but also faith, and hence had been initiated by baptism beforehand. For, as Severus testifies in Book II, Constantius, still a catechumen, was not permitted to attend the Council of Milan. Baronius, in the aforesaid year, no. 17 and the following numbers through 30; likewise under the year 355, no. 11.

The assertion of Eusebius Pamphilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, in Book IV of the Life of Constantine, chapters 61 and 62, that Constantine, at the very end of his life, many years after the Council of Nicaea had been held, was baptized in the suburbs of Nicomedia by Eusebius of Nicomedia, leader of the Arians, and departed this life impious and wholly alien from the Catholic Church—this is a fabrication devised in favor of Constantius, the Arian emperor, by the standard-bearer of the Arians (as Jerome calls him in the Chronicle). The Greeks enrolled Constantine among the saints in their Menologion; the whole Church, as Nicholas testifies in his letter to Emperor Michael, has customarily recited the name of this most pious emperor from the Diptychs. The Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon acclaimed Marcian, a most pious and religious man, as “a New Constantine.” How, then, if someone whom Eusebius deceitfully writes to have been baptized by an Arian died impiously, could the Catholic Church so greatly commend him?

By your own testimony, Eusebius, it is established that the emperor took part in the sacred mysteries at the most holy season of Easter, and that he had a seat among the bishops in the sacred assembly at Nicaea. [Col. 0799B] How do you suppose that these things, forbidden to all other catechumens and sinners, were granted to an emperor liable for many sins and still a catechumen? Moreover, in Book III, chapter 3, you say that many years before the end of his life the emperor displayed himself in a painted panel for all eyes to behold, and depicted in the painting above the head of his image the saving emblem of the Passion; and that he caused that hostile and enemy beast which had attacked the Church of God through the tyranny of the impious to be represented as sunk in the depths, in the form and likeness of a dragon. How can these things be applied to Constantine if he had not yet been baptized? For every catechumen is an energumen, or possessed person; and so far is he from slaying the serpent himself that he is rather possessed by it. For the serpent is expelled from a catechumen only through baptism, which is that sea into which the slain serpent is plunged.

But you will say that he was baptized at the very end of his life, as Saint Ambrose testifies in the funeral oration delivered for Theodosius, where he says: “Although the grace of baptism, bestowed upon him when he was at his last, forgave all his sins, nevertheless, because he is believed to have been the first of the emperors and to have left to rulers after him an inheritance of faith, he found a place of great merit.” I reply: unless you understand this of that illness from which, abandoned by the aid of all physicians, he was delivered through Silvester, Ambrose himself will have spoken contrary things in the same sequence of words. For how, as he says, is Constantine of great merit if he died baptized by Arians?

And what is written in the Chronicles of Jerome—that Constantine at the end of his life was baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, and inclined toward Arian doctrine—is spurious, inserted by another rather than by Saint Jerome. Finally, the objection that the synodical letter of the Council of Rimini written to Constantius—which Theodoret, Book II, chapter 29, Socrates, Book II, chapter 29, and Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 17, reproduce—plainly testifies that the sacrament of baptism was administered to Emperor Constantine shortly before his death, is not so much written there mendaciously as falsely, through the fault of authors or copyists. [Col. 0799D] For Saint Athanasius, in the commentary which he wrote on the synod, reproduces that very letter of the bishops addressed to Constantius, and where the other text has “Constantine,” he has “Constans.” For he writes there: “And we were firmly persuaded that it was unjust, when Emperor Constans—worthy of all remembrance after his death—had promulgated this faith, composed with every care and diligence, only after he, having been baptized, had passed from among men into the rest due to him” (namely, having been killed by the tyrant Magnentius shortly after receiving baptism). Baronius, in the year of the Lord 324, nos. 18, 27 and following, through no. 55. See below the first letter of the Council of Rimini under Liberius.

[Col. 0800A] More correct Acts concerning the baptism relate this history: that, at the command of Pope Silvester, Constantine spent seven days in solitude and penitence after laying aside the imperial crown; and that the faithful observed public prayers and a fast proclaimed for this reason. When Saturday came, the font having been blessed with prayers according to custom, Constantine entered it and was baptized; a divine splendor shone from heaven, and, because he had been cleansed of leprosy of soul and body, Christ appeared to him in that radiance and, extending his hand, congratulated him. These things are proved from the most approved Acts of Silvester, cited by Hadrian in a decretal letter and in the first session of the Second Council of Nicaea. Baronius, no. 41 under the preceding year.]

In January, under the consuls Constantine and Volusianus. He was in exile on Mount Soracte (struck by Constantine’s persecution [Col. 0798A]), and afterward, returning with glory, baptized the Emperor Constantine, whom [Col. 0799A]

[Note: [Col. 0800A]

Whom the Lord cured of leprosy. Constantius, son of Constantine, wished with the greatest zeal that the history in which his father, on account of the exceptionally atrocious crimes committed by him, had been struck with leprosy should be obliterated. Therefore, I think it came about that Eusebius, performing the office of a flatterer rather than of a historian, deliberately suppressed the history of the leprosy, just as he falsely and deceitfully narrated that the emperor received baptism at the end of his life, so that the fictions he had written might please the son. But because Liberius had circulated among the public certain Acts written by himself stating that Constantine had been cleansed of leprosy through Silvester, Emperor Constantius was on that account not only greatly angered against him but also made grave threats against him; of these, below in their proper place.

Lest you suppose that the Acts of Silvester, filled with many errors, waver and lack credibility on this point, know that the same thing is confirmed by the Fathers of the Roman Council held under Silvester, immediately at the beginning of the synodal proceedings. For there one reads: “While many nobles rejoiced that Constantine had been baptized by Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, and cleansed of leprosy, on account of this benefit,” etc.

Whom the Lord cured of leprosy. That in subsequent centuries the leprosy of Constantine and the cure effected through baptism were believed and accepted without hesitation is attested by Gregory of Tours, when he deals with the baptism of Clovis, king of the Franks, in these words: “A new Constantine approaches the washing, to destroy the sickness of old leprosy and to wash away in fresh water the foul stains of ancient deeds.” The same is found in the Life of Saint Remigius written by Hincmar. What is more, did even pagan historians remain silent about the wondrous history of this matter? Among others, Michael Glycas, in Book IV of his Annals, wrote the following concerning Constantine: “After this, when he again strayed through his wife Fausta into the worship of deities, God drew him back through leprosy,” etc.

Thus, strengthened by the testimony of Christian and pagan writers, true are the things narrated in the Acts of Silvester concerning Constantine’s leprosy: namely, that Emperor Constantine, while still following his ancestral religion, stirred up persecution against the Church of God; that, to avoid this, Silvester with some of his followers sought the secluded places of Mount Soracte; and that Constantine, struck with leprosy by God because of his crimes, in accordance with a response received from the haruspices, did indeed command infants of the lowliest rank to be sought out for slaughter, so that he might be cured by their blood. Yet, moved to pity by the lamentation of their mothers, he ordered them spared from death and ordered the mothers to be sent away with their little children, endowed with gifts. Finally, while he lay in bed, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul appeared to him and instructed him to summon Silvester, hidden on the mountain, and to be baptized by him; upon receiving baptism, he was suddenly cleansed and cured of bodily leprosy. See the Acts of Silvester, fragments of which are found recited in the Council of Nicaea and produced by Hadrian against the Iconoclasts: the first letter of Pope Hadrian I to Constantine and Irene; likewise the third letter to Charles, king of the Franks; likewise the first session of the Second Council of Nicaea. Also confirmed by Baronius under the year of the Lord 324, no. 32 and following.]

the Lord cured of leprosy, fleeing at first from whose persecution he is known to have been in exile. He built in the city of Rome [Col. 0800A] a church on the estate of one of his presbyters, surnamed Equitius, near the Baths of Trajan; [Col. 0801A]

[Note: [Col. 0801C]

Where he also bestowed these gifts: a silver paten, etc. The following confirms what we said above: that it is not unlawful for the Church to possess goods contributed for the worship and honor of God and for the support of ministers. On this, see what we said above in the notes on the second letter of Pius I, at the words “lest estates”; likewise in the Life of Zephyrinus, at the words “as for patens”; and in the Life of Urban, at the words “He made the ministries,” etc.; and the notes on that same letter of Urban, at the words “We know that you are not ignorant.”

[Col. 0801D] In his times a council took place. Concerning it, see below.

He also decreed that chrism should be prepared by a bishop. It is established by Christ’s institution that a bishop alone is the minister of blessing chrism, as we said in the notes on the letter of Urban and on Fabian II. Thus it will be clear how these matters are to be understood.

He also decreed that a presbyter should anoint the baptized person. These words must be understood not of the sacramental anointing with chrism on the forehead, but of that ceremonial anointing which, at solemn baptism, takes place on the crown of the person being baptized. This is attested by Hugh of Saint Victor, Book II on the Sacraments, page 7, chapter 3. Recounting this decree of Silvester, he says: “In the earliest times every anointing with chrism was performed by bishops alone; but after it was decreed that the priest should anoint the baptized person on the crown of the head, the signing of the forehead was nevertheless reserved to bishops alone.” Hence it is clear that this ceremony was once forbidden to presbyters and was exercised by them only with the bishop’s permission. The same is confirmed by the twentieth chapter of the First Council of Toledo, where it is said: “It has been decreed that a deacon is not to administer chrism, but a presbyter may do so in the bishop’s absence; in his presence, however, not unless commanded by him,” etc. See Suárez, On the Sacrament of Confirmation, Disputation 36, section 2, and the notes on canon 20 of the First Council of Toledo.

That deacons should use dalmatics. What a dalmatic is, we said above under Eutychianus. The use of the dalmatic, once granted only to bishops, was authorized by Silvester and prescribed in canon 6 of the Roman Council. Now, however, deacons and subdeacons use them. Suárez, vol. III, disputation 82, section 2.

That the sacrifice of the altar should not be on silk. This decree of Pope Silvester confirms what had been established by his predecessor Eusebius: that the consecration of the body of the Lord should be performed upon a certain consecrated cloth of linen, not silk. This was received in the Church by common agreement and custom, as Bede and Burchard testify, and was confirmed by the third chapter of the Council of Rheims. In the canon *Sacratas*, distinction 24, it is called the sacred cloth (*palla sacra*), because it is like a mantle and garment of Christ upon the altar. It is commonly called the corporal, because it represents the shroud in which Christ’s body was wrapped, or because the body of the Lord is placed upon it. See Alcuin, Durandus, and many others who wrote on the divine offices. Suárez, vol. III, disputation 81, section 6.]

he established this as a Roman title, and to the present day it is called the Title of Equitius. There he also bestowed these gifts: a silver paten weighing 20 pounds, from the gift of the Emperor Constantine. He also donated two silver cups, each weighing ten pounds; a gold chalice weighing two pounds; five service chalices, each weighing two pounds; two silver *amae* [vessels], each weighing ten pounds; a silver chrismal paten, set in gold, weighing five pounds; ten crowned lamps, each weighing eight pounds; twenty bronze lamps, each weighing ten pounds; twelve bronze wax-lamps (*canthari cerostroti*), each weighing 30 pounds; the Valerian estate in Sabine territory, yielding 80 solidi; the estate of Stations in [Col. 0801B] Sabine territory, yielding 80 solidi; the estate of Stations in Sabine territory, yielding 55 solidi; the estate at the Two Houses in Sabine territory, yielding 40 solidi; the Percilian estate in Sabine territory, yielding 20 solidi; the Corbian estate in Sorano territory, yielding 60 solidi; a house with a bath in the city, in the Sicunini district, yielding 85 solidi; a garden within the city of Rome, in the district of the Two Lovers, yielding 15 solidi; a house in the Orpheus district within the city, yielding 58 solidi and one tremissis. He also issued a decree concerning the whole Church.

In his times a council was held, with his consent (alternative reading: “by his command”), at Nicaea in Bithynia. And 318 Catholic bishops assembled and set forth the [Col. 0801C] whole, holy, Catholic, and undefiled faith. And they condemned Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius, and their followers. In the city of Rome he himself, with the counsel of the Emperor, assembled 277 bishops, and again condemned [Col. 0802A] Callixtus, Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius. And he decreed that a presbyter should not receive an Arian who repented unless the bishop of the place (alternative reading adds: “appointed”) designated him. He also decreed that chrism should be prepared by a bishop. And he granted bishops the privilege of signing the baptized, because of heretical persuasion.

He also decreed that a presbyter should anoint with chrism the baptized person lifted from the water, because of the contingency of approaching death. He likewise decreed that no layperson should dare to bring an accusation against a cleric. And he decreed that deacons should use dalmatics in church and that their left side should be covered with a linen mantle (*palla linostima*). He likewise decreed that no cleric should enter the curia for any cause or plead a case before a girded judge, except in the church. He also decreed that the sacrifice of the altar [Col. 0802B] should not be consecrated (celebrated) on silk or dyed cloth, but only on linen produced from the earth, just as the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud (John XIX) (alternative reading adds: “thus masses should be celebrated”).

He nevertheless decreed that, if anyone desired to serve or advance in the Church, he should be a doorkeeper for ten years, a reader for thirty years, an exorcist for thirty days, an acolyte for five years, a subdeacon for five years, guardian of the martyrs for five years, a deacon for seven years, and a presbyter for three years; having been tested in every respect, so that he might also have a good testimony from those outside. He must be the husband of one wife, whose wife had been blessed by a priest; and then he should ascend to the order of the episcopate. He should not seize the place of anyone greater or prior to himself, unless in the order of time he should modestly ascertain the favorable wishes (alternative reading: “votive favors”) of all the clergy, [Col. 0802C] with absolutely no cleric or faithful person objecting. He held seven ordinations in the month of December: 42 presbyters, 36 deacons (alternative reading: 25), and 66 bishops in various places and at various times (alternative reading: 65).

From the booklet on Constantine’s munificence.

[Col. 0803A]

[Note: [Col. 0803D]

In his times he built. The matters that follow were transferred here from the booklet on Constantine’s munificence, which Anastasius the Librarian published from the archives of the holy Roman Church. Baronius, under the year 324, nos. 55, 63, and 67.

The Constantinian Basilica. It is otherwise called the Lateran Basilica because it was built by Constantine, its founder, on the Caelian Hill in the very extensive buildings of Lateran; these buildings Constantine had first yielded to the Empress Fausta and then to Pope Miltiades. For that council which, as we said above, was held under Miltiades in the case of Caecilianus, was held at the Lateran, in the house of Fausta. See Baronius under the year 312, no. 8 and following; likewise under the year 324.

[Col. 0804D] The Savior seated. An image of the Savior five feet high; from the celebrated image of the Savior, to whom the basilica was also dedicated, it was called the Basilica of the Savior rather than the Constantinian Basilica, to distinguish it from another basilica of the same name devoted to public business, situated in the third region near the Temple of Peace, as Sextus Rufus and Publius Victor report. Baronius, in the aforesaid year, no. 68.

Where 200 pounds of balsam burn, etc. Balsam is a most precious oil, which the lavishest of emperors, Heliogabalus—as Lampridius writes in his *Heliogabalus*—used in lamps; Constantine is found to have applied it to the worship of sacred religion. Baronius, no. 56.]

In his times the Emperor Constantine built and adorned these basilicas. The Constantinian Basilica, where he placed the following gifts: a silver pediment, having on its front the Savior seated in a chair, five feet high, weighing 120 (310) pounds; and the twelve apostles, each five feet high, weighing 90 pounds, with crowns of the purest silver. Likewise, on the rear, facing into the apse, the Savior seated on a throne, five feet high, of the purest silver, weighing 140 pounds; and four angels of silver, each five feet high, each weighing 115 pounds, with Alabandine gems. The pediment itself weighs 2,025 pounds; four crowns of the purest gold, with twenty dolphins, each weighing [Col. 0803B] 15 pounds; a lamp of the purest gold, with five hundred (fifteen) dolphins, with a chain, weighing 25 pounds; the ceiling of the basilica of gold, weighing 50 pounds in length and breadth; seven altars of the purest silver, weighing 200 pounds; seven gold patens, each weighing thirty pounds; sixteen silver patens, each weighing thirty (three) pounds; seven cups of the purest gold, each weighing ten pounds; one exceptional cup of metal, adorned with coral and on every side with green and hyacinth-colored gems, enclosed throughout in gold, weighing twenty pounds and three ounces; twenty silver cups, each weighing fifteen pounds; two vessels (*amae*) of the purest gold, each weighing fifty pounds and each holding [Col. 0803C] three medimnoi; twenty silver vessels, each weighing ten pounds and each holding one medimnus; forty smaller chalices of the purest gold, each weighing one pound; five hundred smaller service chalices, each weighing two pounds.

Ornaments in the basilica: a lamp-cup (*pharus cantharus*) of the purest gold before the altar, in which pure nard oil burns, with eighty dolphins, weighing three pounds; a silver lamp-cup with twenty dolphins, weighing forty pounds, in which pure nard oil burns; forty-five silver lamp-cups in the body of the basilica, each weighing thirty pounds, in which the aforesaid oil burns; forty silver lamps on the right side of the basilica, each weighing twenty pounds; twenty-five silver lamp-cups on the left side of the basilica, [Col. 0803D] each weighing twenty pounds; fifty silver wax-lamps in the body of the basilica, [Col. 0804A] each weighing twenty pounds; three measures (*metretae*) of the purest silver, each weighing three hundred pounds and holding ten medimnoi; seven candelabra of orichalcum, ten feet high, with silver ornamentation and set with seals depicting the prophets, each weighing three hundred pounds. He built a basilica for the Apostle Blessed Paul. Because the Basilica of Paul had been built where his body was placed, between the Ostian Way and the Tiber, it could not, owing to the narrowness of the intervening site, be built on a scale as large as was fitting. At the same time he built a basilica in the Sessorian Palace. That this basilica was built after the discovery of the Cross in A.D. 326 is clearly shown by the portion of the Cross set there for most reverent veneration. But why, I ask, in the Sessorian court, by the Temple of Venus and Cupid? Namely, in order that he might justly avenge the monstrous crime perpetrated by pagans in hatred of the Cross: for, on holy Golgotha, on the rock of the Cross—as Saint Jerome testifies in Letter 13—an indecent statue of Venus had been placed, and the place of the Cross itself, so glorified by its title, had been called the Shrine of Venus by those same people. Therefore the Temple of Venus, which at Rome was more celebrated than others, was judged worthy to be demolished with disgrace and to yield to the most holy Cross, which, trampling underfoot indecencies, would shine with the splendor of every virtue. The other Constantia mentioned here was Constantine’s sister and the surviving wife of Licinius. This Sylvester held six ordinations in the month of December: forty-two priests, twenty-six deacons, and sixty-five bishops for various places. He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, near the city of Rome, at the third mile, on the day before the Kalends of January [31 December]. He died a catholic and confessor. The episcopal see was vacant for fifteen days. These are the words of Damasus.

## § II.—WHEN AND FOR HOW LONG HE HELD THE SEE

*(From D. Coustant.)*

[Col. 0812C]

The time during which this pope held the pontificate is accurately recorded in the Bucherian Catalogue as follows: “Sylvester, twenty-one years, eleven months. He lived in the time of Constantine, from the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, from the day before the Kalends of February, until the day of the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Constantius and Albinus.” That is, from 31 January 314, which was a Sunday, until the final day of the year 335. For that phrase, “until the day of the Kalends of January,” is plainly to be understood so that the day of the Kalends of January itself does not belong to his pontificate. This is established not only by the Hieronymian Martyrology but also by the frequently cited catalogue of the depositions [Col. 0812D] of Roman pontiffs, likewise published by Bucher, in which Sylvester’s death is entered thus: “On the day before the Kalends of January: the deposition of Sylvester in Priscilla”—that is, in Priscilla’s cemetery.

## § III.—OTHER WRITINGS RELATING TO POPE SYLVESTER

*(From D. Coustant.)*

### I. Letter of Alexander of Alexandria to Sylvester

Around the year of Christ 319, when Alexander, bishop of the church of Alexandria, had condemned Arius and his associates in a council, he informed bishops everywhere of the matter by encyclical letters. Among others, he wrote to Pope Sylvester. Liberius, in Letter 4 to Constantius, no. 4, cites this letter as follows: “There remain letters of Bishop Alexander, formerly sent to Sylvester of holy memory, in which he reported that, before the ordination of Athanasius, he had expelled from the Church eleven presbyters and deacons alike because they followed the heresy of Arius.” Socrates, Book I, chapter 6, has preserved for us a copy of encyclical letters of this kind, in which the names of the aforementioned eleven are listed, whom Alexander struck with anathema together with Arius and declared alienated from the Church and from the catholic faith. It seems beyond doubt [Col. 0813B] that this letter of Alexander, the issue of the Arian heresy, and the Council of Nicaea consequent upon it, gave Sylvester occasion for writing and receiving many letters, although none, at least no genuine letter, has come down to us.

### II. Sylvester, accused by sacrilegious persons, pleaded his case before Constantine

The fathers of the Roman council, in Sirmond’s appendix to the Theodosian Code, p. 88, petitioning the emperors Gratian and Valentinian that, if his case was not entrusted to a council, Damasus might defend himself before an imperial council, testify that Damasus was asking for nothing new in this matter but following the examples of his predecessors. “For Pope Sylvester too,” they say, “when accused by sacrilegious persons, pleaded his own case before your ancestor Constantine.” Who those sacrilegious persons were, and at what time or on what charge Sylvester was accused by them, cannot easily be guessed. The Donatists did indeed allege against him at the Conference of Carthage in 411 that, when he was a presbyter of Marcellinus, he had surrendered the sacred books together with Marcellus and Miltiades. But we have already observed, in discussing Miltiades, that this calumny was then fabricated by them for the first time, and that nothing had previously been heard of such an accusation. Indeed, had Sylvester pleaded his case before Constantine on that charge, the Catholics would have possessed, in the proceedings by which he had been acquitted, grounds for more forcefully rebutting the Donatists as they raised and repeated the same calumny. Yet Augustine, as we have seen, offers against their calumnies no other reply than that the allegation collapses of itself, having no witness and no support from the authority of any document whatsoever. Therefore Sylvester must be understood to have pleaded his case before Constantine concerning some other matter which has escaped us.

### III. Writings falsely attributed to Sylvester

Among the works of John of Bosco published in the library of Fleury is a letter of Pope Sylvester to all bishops throughout Gaul and the Seven Provinces. Likewise, editions of the councils circulate Sylvester’s decree issued in a Roman council, the letter of the Nicene Synod to Sylvester, Sylvester’s reply to that synod, and the second Roman council held by Sylvester after the Nicene Synod. We shall present each item in the appendix to this volume, preceded by an assessment of it. But the decrees attributed to Sylvester in the *Liber Pontificalis*, having been excerpted from the aforesaid *Constitutum*, need not detain us here with their recital or evaluation.

[Col. 0814A] IV. Isidore inserted in his collection both extracts from the Acts of Sylvester and the constitution of the lord Emperor Constantine. For the completeness of this collection, we did not begrudge transcribing them, to be published in their proper place with the remaining writings of this impostor.

[Col. 0814A]

## WORKS EXTANT. (S)*

### FRAGMENT OF AN UNKNOWN WORK AGAINST THE JEWS

*(Mai, vol. VIII, part II, p. 26.)*

**SYLVESTER**

If it seems impossible to some that someone can be two in one, and that he may at once be held fast and crucified, while one of these undergoes the outrage, I shall attempt to demonstrate this through a human analogy. The imperial purple garment was wool; the blood of the shellfish, mingled with it, gave it a purple colour. When, therefore, it was placed upon the fingers and wound round, having become thread, which then endured the twisting—the wool or the dye? Clearly, the wool. Thus one must compare the human being to the wool, and God the Word to the purple colour. He was united in the Passion on the Cross, yet did not in any way undergo the Passion.

If the analogy stated is insufficient, I shall add another. A tree which contains within itself a ray of the sun may be cut down. In the cutting, we observe that the ray first receives the blow of the cutting iron before the wood receives it. Yet the brightness, although present there, can neither be cut nor severed. Thus also the divinity could neither be separated nor cut nor suffer; but that which was subject to suffering was what, like wood, could be bound and held fast.

These analogies [Col. 0814C] have been offered—humble ones, by a humble and mortal human being—because it is fitting to present to believers some faint conception of the dread economy. Yet it is not possible to attain the whole, since created nature cannot comprehend that uncreated and incomprehensible essence of the Word, who for this reason deigned to assume flesh from our human substance, so as to make us partakers of nature and unite our nature to himself—an union, I say, without confusion, without change, without alteration, and known to him alone.

### ANOTHER FRAGMENT

*(Mai, Spicilegium.)*

Sylvester, one of the earliest bishops of Rome, in a disputation with Jews concerning our Saviour Jesus Christ, says:

[Col. 0814D] “If someone wished at noon, when the sun was shining, to cut down a tree, would not the axe then strike the tree, wholly surrounded by the sun?” “Certainly,” Noah replied. Sylvester then added: “Can the sun, which on every side completely encompasses both axe and tree, be struck or cut?” Thus, in Christ, the body is the tree, the axe is the Passion, and the sun is the divinity. Christ suffered, while the divinity suffered no diminution whatsoever on account of the Passion.

## LETTERS RELATING TO POPE SYLVESTER I

[Col. 0814D]

### NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

*(Coustant, p. 341.)*

[Col. 0814D]

In the year of Christ 314, the first year of Pope Sylvester, a council was held at Arles. Constantine, having been petitioned by the Donatists, had convoked it in that city during the same year, before the Kalends of August. Since Sylvester could not leave Rome, he sent in his place the presbyters Claudianus and Vitus, together with the deacons Eugenius and Cyriacus, to Arles. The fathers assembled there were not content merely to pronounce judgment in Donatus’ case; they also issued canons concerning ecclesiastical discipline, knowledge of which they considered should, through Sylvester’s agency, be communicated to all. Accordingly, they took care to send him the canons addressed to himself. A little later, after Constantine, angered by the Donatists’ appeal, had permitted them to return to their respective sees, they wrote another letter to the same pope before leaving Arles. At its end [Col. 0815B] they set out a summary of the principal canons they had issued. The first document is transmitted by several manuscripts. The second letter, however, neither sufficiently complete nor purged of errors, has been copied from an old manuscript containing the privileges of the church of Arles, now preserved in the Colbert Library.

## LETTER I. THE SYNOD OF ARLES TO POPE SYLVESTER

*From the same source.*

To the lord, most holy brother Sylvester [Note: [Col. 0815C] (1) The sixth-century Corbie manuscript, as well as that of the monastery of Murbach in the diocese of Basel, reads: “To the lord, most holy brother Sylvester, the assembly of six hundred bishops who gathered,” omitting the words “Marinus or,” which are likewise absent from the Colbert exemplar that formerly belonged to the Church of Arles. Moreover, the preliminary index of the said Corbie manuscript reads similarly: “Letter of six hundred bishops to Pope Sylvester concerning various ordinances.” At the end of the letter itself: “Here end the canons made by six hundred bishops in the city of Arles.” Constantine, in his letter to Chrestus reported by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, chapter 5, writes that he had summoned bishops from nearly countless different provinces. The Second Synod of Arles, canon 18, says that this council was assembled from all parts of the world over which Constantine held authority. Accordingly, Augustine calls it, in *On Baptism against the Donatists*, Book II, chapter 9, a plenary council and a council of the whole Church; and in *Against Parmenian*, Book III, chapter 4, no. 21, and chapter 6, no. 31, observing its judgment against the Donatists, says that they had been overcome and convicted by the judgment and authority of the entire world.] Marinus, or the assembly of bishops gathered in the town of Arles. What we have decreed by common counsel we communicate to your charity, so that all may know what they ought to observe in the future.

[Col. 0815C] First, concerning the observance of the Lord’s Pascha: that it be observed by us throughout the whole world on one day and at one time, [Note: [Col. 0815D] (2) The Nicene Synod likewise approved this, as Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book III, chapter 19, testifies in these words: “It pleased the judgment of all bishops that the most holy festival of Pascha should be celebrated on one and the same day; as it is observed by harmonious agreement in the city of Rome and throughout all Italy, Africa, Egypt, Spain, Gaul, Britain, Libya, all Achaea, and the Asian and Pontic dioceses, and finally in Cilicia.” Hence one may infer that there were then only very few who differed from the view upheld by Victor and other Roman pontiffs.] and that, according to custom, you send letters to all. [Note: [Col. 0816A] (1) Innocent, Letter 14 to Aurelius; Cyril of Alexandria in Bucher, p. 48; and Leo, Letter 88, mention this custom. Epiphanius, however, *Heresies* 70.10, suggests that from the age of the Apostles until Hadrian’s time the entire Christian world learned from the bishop of Jerusalem on what day Pascha was to be celebrated. Yet in the Apostolic Constitutions upon which he relies, as may be seen in Book V, chapter 16, nothing of this kind is decreed.] Then follow the remaining canons, which may be read in editions of the councils.

Somewhat later, and with several short works intervening, the Corbie manuscript reads: “Here begin the names of the bishops with their clergy, and the number and provinces from which they came together at the Synod of Arles under Bishop Marinus, in the time of Constantine, to settle schisms and the perverse designs of men, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus [A.D. 314].” There follow the names of bishops and clergy in the order in which Sirmond appended them to the canons of Arles. But in the Colbert manuscript no. 3368, immediately after canon 22 of the same synod—which is called canon 21 in that manuscript—there follows: “Synod of bishops held in the city of Arles, with Marinus bishop of the Catholic Church, in the time of Constantine Augustus, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus [the same year].”

They assembled from the province of Sicily, from the city of Syracuse: Chrestus, bishop, and Florus, deacon.

From the province of Campania, from the city of Capua: Protinus, bishop; Agrippa and Pinus, deacons.

From the province of Dalmatia, from the city of Aquileia: Theodorus, bishop; Agathon, deacon.

From the province of Apulia, from the city of Alpium (*read Arpi*): Pardus and Crescens, deacons.

From the city of Rome, those whom Bishop Sylvester sent: Claudius (Sirmond: Claudianus) and Vitus, presbyters; Eugenius and Quiriacus, deacons.

[Col. 0816C] From the province of Italy, from the city of Milan: Merocles, bishop; Severus, deacon.

From the Viennese province, from the city of Marseille: Horesius, bishop; Nazarius, reader.

From the province of the Viennenses, from the city of Arles: Marinus, bishop; Salamas, presbyter; Nicasius, Afer, Ursinus, and Peter, deacons.

From the aforementioned province, from the city of Vienne: Verus, bishop; Bedas (Corbie manuscript: Beflas), exorcist.

From the aforementioned province, from the city of Orange: Faustinus, presbyter.

[Col. 0816D] [From the city of Apt: Romanus, presbyter; Victor, exorcist.] [Note: [Col. 0816D] (2) The material enclosed in brackets is omitted in the Colbert manuscript but supplied from the Corbie manuscript.]

From the province of Gaul, from the city of Reims: Imbittausius, bishop; Primogenius (Sirmond: Imbetausius … Primigenius), deacon.

From the city of Autun: Reticius, bishop; Amandinus (Sirmond: Amandus), presbyter; Filomatius, deacon.
