[Col. 0818A] Thus far the Colbert manuscript 3368. We have judged it worthy of transcription here, not because we consider it more genuine than the Corbie manuscript published by Sirmond in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*, but so that, through the addition of new readings, those already published may either be illuminated or confirmed.

## LETTER II. THE SYNOD OF ARLES TO POPE SYLVESTER

*(Coustant, p. 345.)*

### Concerning its proceedings and the canons established by it

To the most beloved Pope Sylvester: Marinus, Agraecius, Natalis, Theodorus, Proterius, Vocius, Verus, Probatius, Caecilianus, Faustinus, Surgentius, Gregorius, Reticius, Ambitausus, Termatius, Merocles, Pardus, Adelfius, Hibernius, Fortunatus, Aristasius, Lampadius, Vitalis, Maternus, Liberius, Gregorius, [Col. 0818B] Crescens, Avitianus, Dafnus, Orientalis, Quintasius, Victor, Epictetus: eternal salvation in the Lord.

### The Donatists condemned or rejected

Bound by the common bond of charity and unity of the mother Catholic Church, and brought to the city of Arles by the will of the most devout emperor, we salute you from there, most glorious pope, with the reverence deserved by your merits. There we encountered persons violent, pernicious to our law and tradition, and of unrestrained minds—the Donatists—whom the present authority of our God, and the tradition and rule of truth, rejected in such a way that in them no basis for speaking remained, no admissible form of accusation against Caecilian, and no proof. Therefore, with God and the mother Church—who knows and approves her own—as judges, they were either condemned or rejected. And would that, most beloved brother, you had thought it worth your while to be present at so great a spectacle: we surely believe that a harsher sentence would have been pronounced against them, and that our assembly, with you judging together with us, [Note: [Col. 0818C] (1) Those bishops thus consider the head of the Apostolic See worthy of every honour, yet do not hesitate to claim for themselves a partnership with him in judicial decisions.] would have rejoiced with greater gladness. But since [Note: [Col. 0818D] (2) That *since* is superfluous.] you were wholly unable to depart from those regions in which the Apostles also [Note: [Col. 0818D] (3) That is, they do not cease to preside over the Church and, in their successors, to exercise care for it. From this it is clear why the Roman see is called the Apostolic See.] sit, and their blood unceasingly bears witness to the glory of God.

II. Yet these alone did not seem to us, dearest brother, to require consideration—the matters for which we had been summoned; rather, we judged that we must also take counsel for ourselves. And since the provinces from which we have come are diverse, so too various circumstances occur which we think ought to be observed. It therefore pleased us, in the presence of the Holy Spirit and His angels, that from among the matters which moved each individual we should give judgment concerning the present peace. It also pleased us that, before anything else, what has been judged and defined by us should be communicated through you especially to all, since you hold the larger dioceses. What we have decided, however, we have appended in writing from our humble station.

III. But first consideration had to be given to our life and welfare: that, since one died and rose again for many (Rom. V), that very season might be observed by all with such religious devotion that divisions or disagreements could not arise in so great an act of devoted service. Therefore, we decree that the Lord’s Pascha be observed throughout the whole world on one day. Concerning those ministers who have been ordained in whatever places: let them remain in those same places. Concerning those also who lay down arms in time of peace, it has pleased us that they be excluded from communion. Concerning circus-drivers who are believers, it has pleased us that they be separated from communion for as long as they drive. Concerning those who are in illness and wish to believe, it has pleased us that hands be laid upon them. Concerning governors who are believers and aspire to a governorship, it has pleased us that, when promoted, they receive ecclesiastical letters of communion; provided, however, that in whatever places they conduct themselves, the bishops of those places shall exercise care concerning them; and if they begin to act contrary to discipline, then at last they shall be excluded from communion. The same applies to those who wish to engage in public administration.

But concerning Africans, who follow their own custom of rebaptizing: it has pleased us that, if any heretic comes to the Church, he be questioned concerning the Creed; and if it is ascertained that he has been baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, hands only shall be laid upon him [for the reception of the Holy Spirit]. But if, when questioned concerning the Creed, he does not answer with this Trinity, he should rightly be baptized, etc. Then, wearied, he ordered all to return to their sees. Amen.

[Col. 0819]

## APPENDIX. VARIOUS WRITINGS OF DOUBTFUL AUTHORITY. (S)

### CHAPTER OF SAINT POPE SYLVESTER.

*(Collection of Councils, Mansi.)*

[Col. 0819D]

If anyone takes in marriage a daughter or sister [in spiritual kinship] through the sacred font or chrism, let them be separated; let them do penance for five years.  
[Note: [Col. 0819D] (1) From additions to Burchard in a Lucchese manuscript codex.]

### DECREE OF SAINT POPE SYLVESTER.

*(From the same source.)*

We establish, and by this present decree of the year 324 determine, that first they are to be summoned paternally and awaited for seven days, without any permission concerning ecclesiastical matters being forbidden. To this period of waiting another seven days shall again be added, during which permission to enter the church and to hear all divine offices is forbidden. Thereafter two days shall be added, during which they are suspended from the peace and communion of the holy Church; then, during another two days under the same waiting period, let the accused persons be brought forward. When one day has been added to these, all expectation being, as it were, abandoned as hopeless, the guilty person shall immediately be struck by the sword of anathema.  
[Note: [Col. 0820D] (1) In Vatican Palatine codex 574, containing a certain collection of councils, the following is also read under this title: “A constitution of the Apostolic See. ‘Sylvester, bishop, to all bishops throughout Gaul and the seven provinces. It has pleased the Apostolic See that, if anyone from whatever ecclesiastical rank,’” etc. This is the entire first chapter of Pope Zosimus’s fifth letter; but “Metropolitan of Autun” has been substituted for the Metropolitan of Arles, as it is read there, and “Reticius” for Patroclus. By similar fraud the same letter of Zosimus is attributed to Sylvester in a manuscript of Saint-Florentinus and transferred to the Church of Vienne, in Father Constantine, *Appendix*, vol. I, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 35. Thus the brothers Ballerini, *Dissertation on Ancient Canonical Collections*, part II, ch. 10, §3.]

## ASSESSMENT OF THE TWO FOLLOWING LETTERS.

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 51.)*

[Col. 0821A]

I. Those two letters were first published by Peter Crabbe from an old Cologne book. Baronius says that he found both together in two copies of the Cresconian collection; but he judged only the first worthy of insertion in his *Annals* under the year 325, no. 171, content to append the following concerning the next:

> Attached to this is a letter of Sylvester to the synod, but a most corrupt one, which, because the consuls are wrongly stated, is judged fictitious; for it is said to have been sent and received under the fourth consulship of Constantius with the eighth or seventh of Constantine, which is the fifth year from this one.

Yet in the fifth year after the Nicene synod—that is, 329—it was not Constantius, but his elder brother Constantine, fourth time consul with his father Constantine eighth time; whereas in 325 Constantius entered upon his first, not fourth, consulship with Constantine seventh time consul. Concerning the same letter Labbe, vol. II of the *Councils*, p. 58, judges as follows: “This reply is not genuine; I should call it truly fictitious and most corrupt, and not merely almost so, as Binius does.”

II. Nor did Labbe regard the first as more genuine, since, he says, its style together with its chronological indication betrays forgery. That it is in fact unworthy of so great a council is evident from reading alone; and each reader will be ever more convinced when he compares it with the other genuine letter of the same council to the Alexandrian and other churches. In the latter, indeed, the bishops assembled at Nicaea and summoned to the great and holy council first simply offer greeting, and then explain what they have done and determined. In the former, however, Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem, offers greeting after Hosius, while Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, and Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, who ought to have been addressed first, are not named at all; nor afterward is anything explained about the matters decreed. This was all the less to be omitted in this letter because it is fictitiously represented as written by the synod in order to seek confirmation of its proceedings.

Baronius indeed says under the year 325, no. 171: “It is certain that the decree of faith and the rest of the synod’s proceedings were sent with these letters.” Dionysius Exiguus and other compilers of canons no later than Dionysius’s age partly support this assertion, insofar as they note that it pleased the Nicene synod that all matters enacted should be sent to the bishop of the city of Rome. But we cannot agree with one who maintains that all these things were sent with letters in which no dispatch is mentioned; for custom teaches that this is not normally left unmentioned in letters of this kind.

[Col. 0822A]

III. Nor are signs lacking by which this letter of the Nicene synod and Sylvester’s reply may be recognized as having issued from the same workshop as the *Constitutum* discussed above. We encounter in them the same barbarity of language; and certain expressions are common to them, expressions which, the more singular they are, the less they permit us to doubt that they have sprung from the same mind. Thus, just as the *Constitutum*, as its title itself declares, determines how ranks or religion are to be maintained by Sylvester, and then in chapter 3 says of this pope, “He made RANKS,” so in the letter to Sylvester we read that it is fitting for him to establish the RANKS or orders of the city.

Again, the same letter, where it has “As mystical truth teaches,” agrees with chapter 3 of the *Constitutum*: “Thus mystical truth is given.” Likewise, in the aforementioned letter of the Nicene synod we observe “FIXED ranks”; in Sylvester’s reply, “I confirm and fix that you have received the holy grace of chrism”; in the *Constitutum* of the same pope, no. 4, “FIXED curtains”; and in chapter 11: “Whatever I shall FIX by speech, let it be confirmed by your signed document.” From this passage, where *chirographus* means a subscription, one may understand the phrase in Sylvester’s reply to the Nicene synod: “I offer my signed document and that of my disciples.”

Finally, in the same letter, as in the *Constitutum*, Victorinus is blamed for the same cause and in the same words: because he pronounced the Paschal cycles erroneous. Thus the parent of those malformed productions cannot remain wholly concealed, since his very diction makes him evident. We have already more than once put forward our conjecture that he lived in the time of Pope Symmachus.

## LETTER OF THE NICENE SYNOD TO POPE SYLVESTER.

*(From the same source.) That whatever is established may be confirmed by him. (S)*

To the most blessed Sylvester, pope of the city of Rome, to be honored with all reverence: Hosius, bishop of Cordoba, a city of the province of Spain; Macarius, bishop of the city of Jerusalem; Victor and Vincent, presbyters of the city of Rome, ordained at your direction; and the other 318 bishops, greeting in the Lord.  
[Note: [Col. 0822D] (1) Thus Baronius. In other books the greeting or superscription ends here.]

Since we acknowledge that all matters concerning the divine mysteries, for the ecclesiastical benefit, which pertain to the strengthening of the holy catholic and apostolic Church, have been confirmed, explained to your Roman see, and translated from Greek into writing, we now hasten to be strengthened for the increase of the true faith.  
[Note: [Col. 0822D] (2) In Baronius: “are strengthened by divine mysteries for the sake of ecclesiastical utility.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0822D] (3) In editions of the councils: “for the purpose of your see.”]

Therefore let your apostolic teaching determine that the bishops of your whole apostolic city assemble together and hold your council; as mystical truth teaches, let it confirm our enactments, so that our rule may have fixed ranks joined to the ordering of your holiness, because it is fitting to learn from you how to establish the ranks or orders of the city, of the number of the said fellow-bishops.  
[Note: [Col. 0822D] (4) Thus Baronius. Other books: “that our holiness and the fixed ranks or texts of your ordination may be strengthened.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0823D] (1) In Baronius: “to ascend ranks conformed to the Word.”]

Whatever we have established in the Council of Nicaea, we pray may be confirmed by association with your voice. May your blessedness pray for the whole council. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of July; received on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, under the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, the most eminent consuls.

## LETTER OR REPLY OF SYLVESTER TO THE NICENE SYNOD.

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 54.)*

Sylvester, bishop of the Apostolic See and of the holy catholic Church of the venerable religion of the city of Rome, to the brothers and fellow-bishops who assembled in the Nicene council: greeting in the Lord.

I rejoice that you maintain ready goodwill. For I confirm and establish, against those who oppose your teaching concerning the mystery or unity of the Trinity, that according to the sayings and evangelical teaching you have received the holy grace of chrism; and I approve upon examination that the things which flowed into your and our mystery were true and will remain so. I offer my signed document and that of my disciples, giving one equal consent to whatever you established in your holy council.

Moreover, in the bosom of your synod I shall attach certain brief precepts for the discipline of the Church, concerning Victorinus, who on his own authority asserted whatever he wished and declared the Paschal cycles false; and may the whole body of your holy council deign to receive the unity examined with the bishops of all the city of Italy.  
[Note: [Col. 0823D] (2) That is, against those who protest and resist your teaching concerning the mystery or unity of the Trinity. Further, in place of “chrism,” “anointing”—that is, spiritual anointing—would be preferable.]

And in another hand: May the blessedness of your holy council of 318 pray for us, that the increase of charity given to you by our Lord Jesus Christ may be preserved. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of November; received on the fourth day before the Ides of February, under the consulship of Constantine for the seventh time and Constantius Caesar for the fourth time.

## ANOTHER LETTER OF ST. SYLVESTER TO THE NICENE SYNOD.

*(Councils, vol. II, p. 721.)*

### COLLECTOR’S PREFACE.

In Vatican codex 1342 these two apocryphal letters are contained; a third is also joined to them, which stands there in second place. Since no one has hitherto inserted it in collections, it must therefore be added here, as it is produced by the Ballerini in the work often cited, p. 190.

Here begins the letter of Bishop Sylvester directed to the Council of Nicaea through Abundantius the presbyter and Abundantius the deacon, under the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.

To the most blessed holy brothers and fellow-bishops, or fellow-presbyters, assembled in the Nicene council: Sylvester, bishop and prelate of the apostolic and catholic city of Rome, greeting in the Lord.

When our most glorious and most pious son Constantine Augustus learned through his own hearing of the enactments of your holiness, we receive them together with affection, our Lord Jesus Christ commanding; and he makes known to the whole world the entrance of the right and declared faith. We believed that this ought to be communicated to your charity: that a council has been assembled by us in our diocese against Victorinus the bishop and Hippolytus the deacon, who distinguished themselves by fellowship with the Manichaeans, and against Jobianus and Calixtus, who in their arrogance said that Pascha does not come on its proper day or month, but must be observed on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. Let the whole world know that they have been condemned, cast out beyond the Church, and excommunicated.

Those who, in the council of the Apostolic See, with the inquiry made public, failed rightly to acknowledge their defiled opinions and were condemned for perpetrating criminal acts by the execrable defilement of innocent penitents. And because, in their fatal withdrawal, they themselves, forestalled by death on their last day, dared by their own ordination to leave behind a defilement of the priesthood which we command to be condemned and invalidated by holy men and fellow-priests through our preaching and apostolic teachings: we condemn, as if confirming with your voice, those struck with anathema—especially Photius, Sabellius, and Arius [reading uncertain: *percussus*, perhaps *percussos* or *percussum*]; and whatever you established in the Council of Nicaea, city of Bithynia, for the regulation of the true [perhaps “universal”] Church, we preserve in equal form: you determine by the balance of weighing. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of January. And in another hand: May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to preserve you, holy brothers and fellow-bishops.

## ASSESSMENT OF THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK.

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 5.)*

[Note: [Col. 0825D]

**Council.** After the emperor, recently baptized, had most generously enriched the Church with gifts, this council, convened by Pope Sylvester, was piously advanced by him with the necessary expenses, to the end that it might offer God a public thanksgiving for the benefit received and that the first Christian emperor might celebrate the dedication-festival (*encaenia*) of Christian piety with the greatest joy of all. Two hundred and eighty-six bishops, summoned by the pontiff, brought by the emperor in vehicles, and sustained by the most generous provision of food, assembled at Rome in the Baths of Trajan, a place which Pope Sylvester had recently made into a titular church and which the emperor adorned with many gifts. This occurred, as is evident from the final chapter, under the consulship of Crispus and Constantine III, in the 224th year from Christ’s birth, the eleventh of Sylvester and the nineteenth of Emperor Constantine.

Accordingly, the statement openly written at the beginning of the epilogue by an unknown author—that this synod was held in Rome in Constantine’s presence after Nicaea had concluded—is spurious. And the placing of Priscus in the twentieth canon instead of Crispus as Constantine’s colleague is demonstrably erroneous from the consular lists. The purpose of assembling was that the Church might be kept free from the assault of heretics and enemies, and that matters necessary for preserving ecclesiastical discipline and peace might be established. Therefore, at the beginning of the first session, they condemned Hippolytus the deacon, a follower of the Valentinian heresy; Calixtus, tainted with Sabellius’s heresy; and Victorinus the bishop, who had presumed to criticize the Paschal cycles accepted by the Church.

Almost all the matters established in the remaining canons concern the hierarchical order of clerics. That in this synod no mention is made of Arius and the Arian heresy, which had greatly troubled the Eastern Church for several preceding years, seems to have occurred because the pontiff and emperor had decided in the following year, with greater ceremony and a larger number of bishops from the entire world, to convene by common agreement an ecumenical council at Nicaea in the East, so that where the Arians had fought with undying hatred and obstinate persistence, there the assembly of holy bishops might firmly station the sacred camp of God to attack their impiety. See Baronius, year 324, no. 123 and following.

**Roman.** We have said above that the 284 Fathers assembled in the Baths of Trajan, where Sylvester established a titular church splendidly endowed by Constantine. What sort of city Rome was in ancient times, and still is in our own time, Rome which is rightly called the head of the world, is explained very well and learnedly by the Reverend Lord Georg Braun in his celebrated and distinguished theatre of cities, in these words:

> Rome, mistress and queen of cities, and head of the whole world, which had truly subjected the entire world to her dominion through the most outstanding exploits of the bravest men. As many and varied opinions are found regarding her first founders as there are different writers.

And below:

> The more common opinion of almost all is that Rome is called after Romulus.

And shortly afterward:

> Its entire area attained such vastness that its circuit is said to have contained twenty thousand paces, which make approximately five German miles. It was once divided into fourteen regions. Pliny says that the suburban and urban gates together numbered twenty-four; Livy, however, gives thirty-seven. While the empire flourished, there were 734 towers around the city, in which garrisons were stationed as circumstances required. Now only 365 towers remain; there are twenty-five gates, etc.

It is reported of Emperor Constantius that, as he surveyed the Campus Martius with admiration—the tomb of Augustus Caesar adorned with so many bronze and marble statues, the Roman Forum, the shrines of Jupiter on the Tarpeian Rock, baths, porticoes, the amphitheatre, the Pantheon formed in immense masses of marvelous height, the Temple of Peace, Pompey’s theatre, the Circus Maximus, so many triumphal arches, so many aqueducts, so many statues placed throughout the city for ornament—he was astonished and finally said that nature had poured out all its powers into one city.

The River Tiber enters the city from the north and flows out on the southern side toward Ostia. But why should I say more concerning so great and magnificent a city? In it resides the lawful and ordinary successor of Saint Peter, the supreme pontiff of the catholic Church; there are seen the venerable relics of the holy apostles and martyrs; there law is prescribed for the Christian world. There finally the most delightful Muses, abandoning all Greece, found a seat and dwelling; so that Cicero most truly transmits in book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*: “As nothing in the whole nature of things is better or more excellent than the world, so on earth nothing better or more excellent than Rome can be found.” These are Georg Braun’s words concerning Rome, dean of Blessed Mary at the Steps, Cologne.]

This council Peter Crabbe attached after the two preceding letters, but placed before the *Constitutum* above, which is fictitiously said to have been issued in a Roman council held before Nicaea. He does not state whether he copied those four documents from one and the same exemplar. The difference in style suggests that the fabricator of this text was different from the architect of the others. For here neither the same barbarity nor the same obscurity appears. Nor is there disagreement only in style: there is also some discrepancy between this and the other Roman council in the decrees themselves, as is shown by the provisions in each regarding the time a cleric must remain in each grade before being promoted to another.

This latter council was unknown both to the author of the *Book of the Popes* and to Isidore Mercator. It becomes suspect even from its title itself, in which it is said to have been held in Constantine’s presence, although Baronius and learned scholars agree that Constantine was then absent from Rome. Baronius considers it a scribe’s error: the scribe, he thinks, imprudently referred to this council what is mentioned in chapter 1 concerning the Nicene synod. Who could also persuade himself that 275 bishops, summoned by Sylvester, assembled at that time, when this was neither easy nor necessary?

Moreover, the title of chapter 3 indicates that a decree had been attached there establishing that councils should be held three times a year. If this is so, who would consider that council admissible which, though said to have been assembled chiefly in order to confirm whatever was established at Nicaea, nevertheless immediately departs from Nicaea’s own determination that synods be assembled twice yearly? Therefore, although we may freely grant that Sylvester convened a synod immediately after the celebration of the Nicene council, in which he confirmed the acts of that council, and that perhaps the decrees set forth here were collected from that synod, we must nevertheless in turn concede that the collection itself, in the form in which it has reached us, bears some mark of adulteration. This prevents it from receiving a place among the genuine and authentic writings of the supreme pontiffs that provide proof, until it is corrected and supported by suitable authority.

## LETTER OR REPORT OF THE COUNCIL CELEBRATED BY HOLY POPE SYLVESTER, IN THE PRESENCE OF CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS, IN THE CITY OF ROME WITHIN THE BATHS OF DOMITIAN, WITH 275 BISHOPS WHO HAD ASSEMBLED IN THAT SYNOD AT THE SUMMONS OF BLESSED SYLVESTER.

*From the same source.*

### I. Whatever was done at Nicaea is confirmed.

SYLVESTER, bishop and prelate of the holy and apostolic see of the city of Rome, said: Whatever was established at Nicaea in Bithynia for the strengthening of the holy mother, the catholic and apostolic Church, by the 318 holy priests, we likewise confirm by our voice. We anathematize all who dare to dissolve the definition of the holy and great council assembled at Nicaea under the presence of the most pious and venerable prince Constantine Augustus. And all said: It pleases us.  
[Note: [Col. 0825C] (1) The word *praesul* (“prelate”) is omitted in the editions of the councils by Luparinus and Labbe.]

### II. Concerning the solemnity of Pascha.

All bishops and presbyters are commanded to keep the observance of Pascha from the fourteenth moon through the twenty-first, so that the Lord’s Day may shine forth. And the bishops said: It pleases us.  
[Note: [Col. 0825C] (2) Innocent I rather clearly teaches that this decree was unknown to him, since, writing to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, on this matter, he found it sufficient to say: “Because we know that no Pascha has ever occurred on the twenty-third moon before this Pascha.” Otherwise he should have said that Pascha must by no means be celebrated on the twenty-third moon, since by Sylvester’s prescription the feast ought not extend beyond the twenty-first moon. Dionysius Exiguus, Letter I, in Bucherius, p. 487, attributes to divine authority the command to celebrate Pascha from the fourteenth through the twenty-first moon, or, what is the same, from the fourteenth through the twenty-first day: “It was made clear by so great a divine authority that the Paschal feast ought to be celebrated in the first month from the fourteenth day at evening until the twenty-first.”]

### III. Concerning councils to be held three times yearly.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] (3) In the editions of the councils by Luparinus and Labbe this title was suppressed without manuscript authority, and the next chapter was joined with the preceding one, since apparently nothing is said there concerning the holding of synods. We think the title should be restored, so that the reader may be warned that the following chapter is incomplete.]

Sylvester the bishop said: We have judged it a more robust counsel, if it please you, that every bishop who comes to the council confirm his faith by a signed document, so that thereafter, on returning to his parish, he may make known to his people the bond of our greeting, in order that, with the council’s faith declared, the undefiled order may be preserved. And the bishops said: It pleases us.  
[Note: [Col. 0826C] (1) In a certain catalogue of Roman pontiffs in our possession, Xystus I is said to have established that any bishop summoned to the Apostolic See of Rome should not be received upon returning to his parish unless he brought from the Apostolic See a confirmed greeting for his people. The fabricator of this council seems rightly to be regarded as having imitated these words.]

### IV. No cleric may examine a case in public.

Sylvester the bishop said: No cleric whatsoever may examine any case in public, nor may any cleric stand before a lay judge. And the bishops said: It pleases us.  
[Note: [Col. 0826D] (2) In the preceding pseudo-Roman council, or Letter XI—where two chapters, namely 15 and 16, are made from this single chapter—there is added here: “except in church”; there *public* is used for a secular court, and *church* for an ecclesiastical court.]

### V. Concerning appointments to orders and advancement.

If anyone desires to merit—or be promoted to—the clergy, it is just that he be a doorkeeper for one year, a reader for twenty years, an exorcist for ten years, an acolyte for five years, a subdeacon for five years, and a deacon for five years; and then [the text perhaps reads *si*] let him proceed to the honor of the presbyterate. Having spent six years in that order, if he enjoys the freely given favor of all, not through payment, not through an ambitious seizure, and taking no rank before another, then let him be chosen by the whole Church for consecration as bishop, with no member of the Church objecting and with the whole Church assembled. And the bishops said: It pleases us.

### VI. Concerning ordinations, and that neophytes are not to be ordained.

Let no bishop be permitted, without the whole church, to ordain a neophyte from the lowest rank up to the first. And the bishops said: It pleases us.

Sylvester the bishop said: Beginning with ourselves, we admonish and declare, with the moderation of gentleness, that no bishop may ordain or consecrate anyone to any clerical rank unless the whole church is assembled, if it please you. And the bishops said: It pleases us.

[Note: [Col. 0828C]

**Brief epilogue of the following Roman council.** Some believe, on the authority of this epilogue, that two councils were held at Rome under Sylvester after Nicaea. But since the same matters established by 284 Fathers in twenty canons are recounted summarily and briefly by the author of this epilogue, and since what is written concerning the condemnation of the Photinians by this synod is plainly false, as will be evident below from the notes on the Council of Sirmium, we judge it more correct that this passage contains the proceedings not of some fourth council, but solely of the second Roman council held under Sylvester, described here by an unknown author. Baronius, year 325, no. 201. In the collection of Isidore Mercator this title occurs: “Here begin certain extracts from the synodal proceedings of holy Pope Sylvester.”

[Col. 0828D] **Photinus.** Since it is certain from the acts of the Council of Sirmium that Photinus was condemned much later than these times, the beginning of this epilogue—which the unknown author placed as a preface before the genuine Second Roman Council, down to the words “and he decreed that the presbyter”—is rendered suspect by its falsehood. What follows is drawn from that same genuine Roman council and reduced to compendium.]

## ANOTHER BRIEF EPILOGUE OF A ROMAN COUNCIL HELD UNDER POPE SYLVESTER.

*(Councils, vol. I, col. 1542.)*
In the times of Pope Saint Sylvester and the most devout Augustus Constantine, a great council was held at Nicaea in Bithynia; and, having been duly summoned by the same Pope Sylvester, three hundred and eighteen Catholic bishops assembled together. They set forth the whole, Catholic, undefiled faith, and condemned Arius, Photinus, Sabellius, and their followers. At the same time also, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July [19 June], when the aforementioned great council had assembled at Nicaea, he himself, following the canonical summons of the pope, convened at the city of Rome, together with the council of the aforesaid Augustus Constantine, two hundred and sixty-seven bishops. He again condemned Callistus, Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius; and decreed that no one should receive an Arian presbyter who had come to his senses unless the bishop of that same place reconciled him and, by episcopal laying on of hands and the most sacred chrism, confirmed him with the grace of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be bestowed by heretics.

In that council, by the agreement and subscription of all, it was decreed that no layperson should dare bring an accusation against a cleric (2, question 7); that a presbyter should bring no accusation against a bishop, a deacon against a presbyter, a subdeacon against a deacon, an acolyte against a subdeacon, an exorcist against an acolyte, a reader against an exorcist (likewise, 2, question 7), or a doorkeeper against a reader. Nor shall a prelate be condemned except upon seventy-two witnesses (2, question 3). Nor shall the supreme prelate be judged by anyone, because it is written: “A disciple is not above his master.” A cardinal presbyter, moreover, shall not be condemned except upon forty-four witnesses. A cardinal deacon established in the city of Rome shall not be condemned except upon twenty-six [indeed, thirty-seven] witnesses. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, or doorkeeper shall not be condemned except, as it is written, upon seven witnesses. The witnesses and accusers, moreover, must be free from every infamy, have wives and children, and in every respect preach Christ. Let no one receive the testimony of a layperson (11, question 1) against a cleric (law: “cleric against layperson”).

[Col. 0828B] Let no one presume publicly to examine any cleric, except in the Church. For no cleric, deacon, or presbyter may enter a court on account of any cause, nor presume to plead a case before a girded judge, because every court is so called from bloodshed and the sacrifice of images. And if any cleric accusing a cleric enters a court, let him incur anathema.

Here, among the other matters aforesaid, it was decreed in the synod by the counsel of all that no one should presume to celebrate the sacrifice of the altar upon a silk or dyed cloth, but upon pure linen consecrated by a bishop—linen, that is, produced from the earth and woven—just as the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean shroud.

> **Note [Col. 0829C] (1).** On consecration, distinction 1, in Gratian, where the *sindon* is called linen.

And if anyone desired to serve in the Church or to advance, he was first to be a doorkeeper, then a reader, and afterwards an exorcist, for such periods as the bishop should establish; then an acolyte for five years, a subdeacon for five years, guardian of the martyrs for five years, a deacon for five years, and a presbyter for three years. He was to be approved by every father to such a degree that he also had a good testimony from those outside; namely, he was to be the husband of one wife, who nevertheless had been blessed by a priest. And if he had been found worthy, and the wishes of the people and clergy concurred, he was to be canonically consecrated bishop; thereafter neither cleric nor people ought to disturb him. For bishops, who are called thrones of God, are not to be torn to pieces, but rather supported and venerated.

Concerning them blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Do not rebuke an elder, but exhort him as a father.” For we read the Lord himself saying that a disciple is not above his master; that is, no one ought, to the injury of teachers, to vindicate doctrine for himself, nor by any contrivance disparage or defame the disciples of the Lord—that is, the successors of the apostles—because injury done to teachers pertains to Christ, in whose stead they perform an embassy. How they grieve the Lord who presume to do this, the Lord’s discourse in the Gospel testifies (Matthew 18). For the Savior himself says that it is expedient for one who causes one of these little ones to stumble to be drowned in the depths of the sea, with a millstone hung about his neck.

[Col. 0830A] If, therefore, such punishment is here promised to those who scandalize the disciples of the Lord, what ought to come upon them in the future must be considered with the greatest seriousness. For no small danger may await before God those who refuse to render these things to his ministers. This may at last be proved if those who do not fear to do such things fear God, and, imposing upon themselves a wholesome silence, henceforth keep themselves from such acts; for it profits a person nothing to do other good deeds unless the mind is recalled from wickedness and the tongue restrained from detractions. Hence the prophet says (Psalm 33): “Restrain your tongue from evil, and let not your lips speak deceit. Turn away from evil and do good.” For no one who does good wishes to harm another by word or deed. And the rest.

Here, in the aforementioned synod, it was decreed with the agreement of all that no presbyter should presume to celebrate Masses (On consecration, distinction 1, “No presbyter shall celebrate Masses”), except in places consecrated by a bishop who thereafter wished him to share in his priesthood.

And this most holy pope, in compassionate concern, by synodal proceedings restored by apostolic authority to communion many who had been excommunicated by other bishops and expelled by tyrants; he restored them to the churches to which they had formerly been appointed, received them when purified under the satisfaction of a written declaration, and gave future generations an example of rescuing priests from the hands of persecutors. He also decreed that no person from overseas should be received among us into a clerical rank, unless designated by the written attestations of five bishops (five or more bishops).

### Forewarning to the Reader concerning the Following Synod

[Col. 0830C] The following canons have been transcribed word for word from two ancient exemplars. In many places, because of the corruption of the exemplars, they can scarcely, or not at all, be understood. Let the kindly reader pardon this, and, if he can offer anything more certain, communicate it.

[Col. 0829]

## Canon, or Constitution, of Sylvester, Bishop of the City of Rome, and of the Lord Augustus Constantine, concerning How Ecclesiastical Ranks or Religion Are to Be Observed

> **Note [Col. 0829D] (1).** These twenty chapters, which Isidore wove into his collection, appear spurious to Hincmar and to most learned men.

*(Councils, vol. I, col. 1544.)*  
> **Note [Col. 0829].** In the following work, the “First Edition” and “Second Edition” of the First and Second Sessions are printed in parallel in Migne.

*(C, S)*

### Titles of the Canons

[Col. 0829]

I. Concerning the assembly of bishops and deacons.  
II. Concerning the condemnation of Callistus, Victorinus, and Hippolytus.  
III. That no one bring an accusation across the successive ranks.  
IV. That the revenues of the Church be divided into four parts.  
V. That no presbyter make chrism.  
VI. Concerning diocesan deacons and cardinal deacons of the city of Rome.  
VII. That all persons from the subdeacon down to the reader be subject to the cardinal deacon of the city of Rome.  
VIII. That no subdeacon enter into marriage.  
IX. That no reader or acolyte touch sacred vessels.  
X. That no bishop bless a consecrated virgin for marital union.  
XI. That no one from lay status be elevated from the office of acolyte to the episcopate, except through each successive rank.  
XII. No one is to give penance except at forty years of age.  
XIII. Concerning a certain mystery.  
XIV. Let no one receive the testimony of a cleric against a layperson.  
XV. Let no one examine a cleric publicly.  
XVI. That no cleric, deacon, or presbyter enter a court on account of his own case.  
XVII. That no one strike a sinful cleric.  
XVIII. That no deacon bring an accusation against a presbyter.  
XIX. That no presbyter contract marriage from the day of his presbyterate.  
XX. That no one judge the first see of justice.

## First Edition

### First Session

[Col. 0829]

#### Chapter I

[Col. 0829C]

The establishment of the canons, ranks, or manner in which religion is to be observed, by Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, and the lord Constantine. At that time, when many nobles rejoiced that Constantine had been baptized by Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, and cleansed of leprosy, he began, because of the benefit he had received from our Lord Jesus Christ through Bishop Sylvester, to preach the Lord Jesus Christ fully and to confess his benefits.

Sylvester, therefore, bishop of the city of Rome, gathering together the brethren—his fellow presbyters, fellow bishops, and deacons, Roman citizens—and since Mother Church had begotten her most beloved son Constantine, desired wholly to order her affairs with his own men, frequently to nourish her children, and to establish the ranks of her order and custom. He assembled the entire synod of bishops with the counsel of the Augustus and his mother, and caused preparations to be made in the city of Rome at the Baths of Domitian, now called the Baths of Trajan.

He assembled in the precinct of his see 284 bishops, to whom Augustus Constantine ordered vehicles and provisions to be supplied everywhere; also fifty-seven bishops of the region of Rhinocorura, whose written attestation is declared in their council; sixty-two presbyters of the city of Rome; deacons and acolytes appointed by his counsel; twenty-two exorcists; and ninety readers of the city of Rome, whose presence was heard. There were fourteen notaries of the Church, who received and recounted in order the acts of various martyrs. While he gathered all these in the aforesaid baths under one examination of holiness, this was so arranged that no layperson appeared to preside.

There follow 139 bishops from the city of Rome or from not far from it.

[Col. 0831]

Castus, Cyprus, Peter, Abundius, Severinus, Lucianus, Capax, Herculanus, John, Himilus, Andrew, Peter, Renovatus, Cresconius, Ambrose, Luke, Hermogenianus, Augustus, Felix, Barbarus, Secundinus, Citonatus, Reparatus, Gaudentius, Sebastianus, Graeces (otherwise Cresces), Renatus, Irenaeus, Laurentius, Valerianus, Botudorus, Leo, Abundantius, Almachius, Honestosus, Victor, Plenus, Delphinus, Amabilis, Paul, Constantius, Sixtus, Concordius, Nepotianus, Bedandulus, Deutherius, Amabilis, Syrus, Quadratus, Mirabilis, Audacius, Turcilianus, John, Marcus, Fidelis, Symmachus, Probianus, Asellus, Crispinus, Rusticus, Faustus, Turdus, Mojorianus, Jobianus, Exonosus, Sanctulus, Coricosus, Nepus, Tiburtius, Peter, Sylvestrianus, Turturanus, Leontius, Anastasius, Agapitus, Verustimilus, Asellus, Jacob, Felicissimus, Quadratus, Alexander, Philip, Exuperantius, Hypolitus (Hippolytus), Jordianus, Archidamus, Lollius, Martia-Caritosus, Concordius, Januarius, Felicianus, Redus, Auxibus, Timothy, Boniface, Tranquillinus, Calbulus, Sixtus, Catellus, Epiphanes, Victor, Habet Deum (“God Has”), Contentus, Apronianus, Probus, Repostibus, Paul, Fidelissimus, Homobonus, Luminosus, Vitalis, Carpilio, Volusianus, Peter, Probinus, Honestosus, Ariston, Bacanda, Peter, Marinus, Priscillianus, Carito, Gattus, Januarius, Caecilius, Epiphanius, Laurentius, Humanianus, Urbanus, Micinus, Caecilius, Priscus, Tiburtius, Nonnonus, Anthimus, Agapitus, Vindemius.

And these are from Greece.

[Col. 0831]

Peter, Anastasius, Hermes, Nicostratus, Quod vult Deus (“What God Wills”), Vitalis, Renatus, Vinulus, Andriphorus, Irenaeus, Olympius, Demeter, Theodolus, Anastasius, Thespias, Firminus, Cleopatris, Honorius, Simplex, Exitiosus, John, Timothy, Hermes, Paul, Metronius, Stephen, Alexander, Constantine, Andrew, Exuperantius, Firmus, Quirillianus, Anastasius, Hermogenius, Severus, Aconcius, Thomas, John, Caecilianus, Theodolus, Theophilus, Prispilius, Festus, Almacus, Andecius, Concordius, Deutherinnus, Thomas, Quadratus, Timothy, Potestas, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Victorinus, Severianus, Domanicus, Eulogius, Demeter, Nepotianus, Albinus, Peter, John, Exuperius, Theodolus, John, Exuperantius, Sebastianus, Theodorus, Claudius, Demetrianus, Rufinus, Spes in Deo (“Hope in God”), Reparatus, Peter, Asellus, Archanus, Eufemius, Crisolatus, Lazarus, Leo, Anthimus, Andrew, Catharon, Vultibus, Anastasius, Hermes, Sempervivus, Titus, Orifensis, Epiphanius, Anastasius, Leo, Ultius, Fortunatus, Caecilianus, Nicostratus, Audax, John, Rufinus, Honorius, Felix, Petronius, Andrew, Requisitus, Bacauda, Terfilius, Zeno, Caritosus, Majoranus, Leo, Hermes, Demeter, Andrew, Spes in Deo (“Hope in God”), Timothy, Jacob, Zeno, Quadratus, Fusilis, Marcus, Paulinus, Oyfensis, Concordius, Priscus, Herculanus, Leoninus, Androtilus, Eufimius, Squiro, Martin, Anastasius.

[Col. 0831C] When all these and others, whose written attestations and reputation for holiness had been circulated, had come to the synod, they sat before the aforesaid baths. [Col. 0833A] But all the Roman presbyters and deacons—

> **Note [Col. 0833D].** “But all the Roman presbyters and deacons.” The account here says that only the bishops sat with Pope Sylvester, while the presbyters and deacons, together with all the remaining clergy, stood behind the seated bishops. This must be said to have occurred, at least then, for the sake of modesty; for otherwise, as Jerome testifies in Letter 85 to Evagrius, it was accepted in the Roman Church that only deacons stood before bishops, while presbyters sat. That letter says: “Moreover, even in the Church of Rome, presbyters sit and deacons stand. Although, as abuses gradually multiplied, I have seen a deacon sit among presbyters in the bishop’s absence.” Indeed, at the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 34 enacted concerning this matter provides that a bishop sitting in any place is not to allow a presbyter to stand.

—and the clergy and the ranks following them stood behind the bishops. No one sat in the same place except the bishops alone and Sylvester, bishop and pontiff of the city of Rome. There was also Calphurnius, prefect of the city, first a pagan and afterwards a Christian.

Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, gave the following explanation: “Hear me, brothers and fellow bishops, and the whole order of the Roman Church. It is good for the Church to have fixed curtains, so that royal churches may not utter oracles [reading uncertain: *non vaticinentur*], but may be firm, shut their door because of the persecutor, and have a strong wall from which they may overcome their adversaries.”

#### Chapter II

“I speak what is known, and I prove [the case against] Callistus and Victorinus, who by their own judgment made a creature, and Jobinianus, who in his arrogance said that one should observe not the month but the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April]. For I, as the law states, submit the matter to your judgment: let these three be brought forward, and let the examination first confirm the condemnation of Callistus, who thus taught himself to be Sabellian, so that by his own judgment he held that the Trinity was one person. For Victorinus, chief prelate of religion, did not make the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit coequal; and in his arrogance he affirmed to people whatever he wished and proclaimed false Paschal cycles. Therefore let what he decreed, namely the observance of the tenth day before the Kalends of May, be annulled by your declaration, as truth requires, condemned by your judgment, and let the authority of our sons, the Augusti, proceed to condemn Bishop Victorinus.”

He condemned Hippolytus, the Valentinianist deacon; Callistus, who in his arrogance divided the Trinity; and Bishop Victorinus, who, ignorant of the calculation of the moon, through obstinate adherence to his own judgment shattered the truth. In the presence of the aforesaid bishops and presbyters, he condemned Hippolytus, Victorinus, and Callistus, pronounced anathema upon them, and condemned them outside their cities.

#### Chapter III

Afterwards he established the ranks in the midst of the synod: that no presbyter should bring an accusation against a bishop, no deacon against a presbyter, no subdeacon against a deacon, no exorcist against an acolyte, no reader against an exorcist, and no doorkeeper against a reader. A prelate shall not be condemned except upon seventy-two witnesses; nor shall the supreme prelate be judged by anyone, because it is written: “A disciple is not above his master.” A presbyter shall not be condemned except upon forty-four testimonies. A deacon bound to the cardinal office of the city of Rome shall not be condemned except upon thirty-six. [Col. 0835A] A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, or reader shall not be condemned except, as it is written, upon seven testimonies—[witnesses] having children and a wife and wholly preaching Christ—as mystical truth declares.

#### Chapter IV

I remind you, my fellow members, that the revenues of the Church are to be divided into four parts: that the Church shall take the first part, one part for the pontiff and the relief of the brethren, half for the churches, and half for presbyters and deacons together with all the clergy and pilgrims. He established this order: if any member of the clergy or presbyter of the whole place—that is, of the community—should depart from this world and have no partner from his own family, whatever property his poverty possessed should be given to the Church; and from it four parts should be made, as has been said.

#### Chapter V

Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, also decreed aloud that no presbyter should make chrism, saying that Christ is named from *chrism*.

#### Chapter VI

That there should not be more than two deacons in each parish district, and seven cardinal deacons of the city of Rome; nevertheless, they were to use dalmatics, and *linostima* [uncertain garment term] pallia were to cover their left side.

> **Note [Col. 0835D].** “Cardinal deacons.” Those called cardinal deacons here were so called because, although they served in different places, they were nevertheless attached to the hinge (*cardo*) of one Church, and that Church the principal one. Above, in the Life of Fabian, they are called regional deacons, because by office each was required to preside over two districts of the city and care for the poor living in them. For this purpose seven cardinal deacons were appointed over the city’s fourteen districts, so that, each diligently caring for two districts, provision might be made well for all the city’s poor. See our notes on the Lives of Evaristus and Fabian.

#### Chapter VII

Sylvester further said aloud to the fellow bishops that all, from the subdeacon down to the reader, should be subject to the cardinal deacon of the city of Rome, representing honor only in the Church; but presbyters, subdeacons, deacons, acolytes, and exorcists should render service in every place to the pontiff, whether in public or within the bosom of the Church, the reader representing this service only to the pontiff. [Text syntactically corrupt.]

#### Chapter VIII

We decree that none of the subdeacons shall enter into marriage, lest he presume some transgression.

#### Chapter IX

No reader or doorkeeper shall touch the sacred vessels. No acolyte shall pass on to another a sacred object received from a presbyter, but shall merely carry what the priest places upon him and blesses orally.

#### Chapter X

[Col. 0835D] No bishop, moreover, shall seek to bless a consecrated virgin for marital union unless he has proved that she has reached seventy-two years of age. When judgment and chastity have been proved—so that, for seventy-two years seeking the true Christ and preserving chastity—she may be anointed on the head and introduced into marriage with Christ, wearing a veil upon her head, not upon her heart.

And the aforesaid bishops subscribed to this while Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, preached. Calpurnus, prefect of the city, subscribed last; Augustus Constantine subscribed, with his mother Helena Augusta. Then, seated in the same place, he delivered an address, and they departed.

### Second Session

[Col. 0837]

On another day all the presbyters of the city of Rome and all the 284 deacons came to the Baths of Domitian, now called the Baths of Trajan, and he took his seat in the same place. There he made seven districts and apportioned them among the deacons. These deacons were Fabian, Marcus, Liverius, Archidamus, and Julius. He appointed two others, Priscus and Theodore. The entire body—presbyters, deacons, and clergy—asked Bishop Sylvester to appoint them. There in the baths he subordinated these two, Priscus and Theodore; he did not ordain or consecrate them except in the precinct of the basilica, where he consecrated them, contrary to the synod’s decree.

#### Chapter XI

That no person from lay status should be raised to the rank of acolyte and onward to the episcopate unless he had first been a reader for thirty years; then an exorcist for one day; afterwards he should take on the burden of the acolyte and serve in that rank for ten years, so that he might receive the burden of the subdiaconate; he should remain in the subdiaconate for five years, then attain the fixed honor of the diaconate, upon the petition and examination of thirty presbyters, so as to be a cardinal deacon, because it was established by the first see [Col. 0837C] that he should serve for seven years.

For if anyone desired the order of presbyterate, this was to be required: that for seven years he be deprived, by all the Roman clergy, of learning, birth, family standing, and counsel; that he seek no gain from any reputation; and that all the presbyters declare and confirm him as of clear and firm repute. Thus he should approach the order of presbyterate and remain in that order for three years. If the order, arrangement, care of piety, or holiness required that he advance to the burden of the episcopate, the whole clergy should petition for his ordination with one enduring vote. This was so enacted, and no one opposed the words of Bishop Sylvester; rather, they confirmed them by petition.

Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, also said: “Hear, holy ones and fellow bishops. Let no one conceal what he thinks justice requires to be reproved.” All the bishops answered and, crying out with all the presbyters and clerics, said: “May justice remain in you and may piety not depart from you, for nothing shall be judged by us contrary to the authority of your words, because wisdom does not exist unless it has been built upon patience.” Sylvester, bishop, then said: “Since wisdom does not exist except in patience, whatever I establish by word, let it be confirmed by your written attestation.”

#### Chapter XII

Let no one give penance to one seeking baptism unless he is forty years old; for preach to all, “give,” Matthew at the end. [Text corrupt.]

#### Chapter XIII

[Col. 0839A] No one who has not first received the heavenly veil of marriage through the hand of a priest shall approach the honor of the clergy. For he is feigned [or: dissembling].

#### Chapter XIV

Let no one receive the testimony of a cleric against a layperson.

#### Chapter XV

Let no one publicly examine any cleric, except in the Church.

#### Chapter XVI

No cleric, deacon, or presbyter shall enter a court on account of any cause of his own, because every court is called from bloodshed and is a sacrifice of images. If any cleric enters a court, [Col. 0839B] let him incur anathema, never returning to Mother Church. Yet let him not be deprived of communion on account of the troubled times.

#### Chapter XVII

Let no one strike any cleric who has sinned; no presbyter, deacon, or bishop shall inflict blows upon a cleric or servant of the Church. But if the cleric’s case so requires, let him be deprived of rank for three days, so that penitents may return to Mother Church.

#### Chapter XVIII

Let no deacon bring an accusation of indecency against presbyters.

#### Chapter XIX

[Col. 0839C] Let no presbyter contract marriage from the day on which he assumes the burden of the presbyterate. If anyone, disregarding this, enters into it, we say that he is to be deprived of rank for twelve years. If anyone has acted publicly contrary to this present written attestation, let him be condemned forever.

> **Note [Col. 0839D].** “From the day on which he assumes the burden of the presbyterate, [let no one] contract marriage.” By *marriage* in this place understand cohabitation with a woman. Taking a wife was prohibited by this council not only to presbyters but also to subdeacons. Thus, under the penalty added, the avoidance of cohabitation with a suspect woman is earnestly enjoined.

#### Chapter XX

Let no one judge the first see, desiring justice to be moderated; neither by the Augustus, nor by all the clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people shall its judge be judged.

> **Note [Col. 0839D].** “Let no one judge.” Pope Nicholas of Rome appears to have cited this canon when, among other things by which he reproved the rashness of Emperor Michael, he said: “Saint Sylvester, baptizer of the great Constantine, agrees with this necessary judgment, saying: ‘Neither by the Augustus, nor by all the clergy, nor by the people shall the judge be judged’”—without doubt, an ecclesiastical judge.

And 284 bishops, forty-five presbyters, five deacons, and the two following persons subscribed, as did Augustus Constantine and his mother Helena. Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, established this canon and sprinkled all the bishops. Done in the Baths of Trajan, on the third day before the Kalends of June [30 May], in the third consulship of the lord Augustus Constantine and the consulship of Priscus.

## Second Edition

### First Session

[Col. 0829]

#### Chapter I

[Col. 0830C]

At the same time, when many nobles rejoiced that Constantine had been baptized by Sylvester of the city of Rome and cleansed of leprosy, through this benefit which he received from the Lord Jesus Christ through Bishop Sylvester, he began fully to preach the Lord Jesus Christ and to confess his benefits.

Sylvester, therefore, bishop of the city of Rome, gathered his brethren, fellow presbyters, fellow bishops, and deacons, his Roman citizens. And since Mother Church had begotten her beloved son Constantine, Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, desired with his own men to order her affairs, frequently nourish her children, and establish the ranks of her order and customs. He assembled the whole synod of bishops with the counsel of the Augustus and his mother, and caused preparations to be made in the city of Rome within the Baths of Domitian, now called the Baths of Trajan.

He assembled in the precinct of his see 284 bishops, to whom Augustus Constantine ordered vehicles and provisions to be supplied; also fifty-seven bishops from the region of Rhinocorura, whose written attestation is declared in their council; 142 presbyters of the city of Rome; six deacons; six subdeacons; forty-five acolytes appointed by his council; twenty-two exorcists; and ninety readers of the city of Rome, whose parents were heard as present. There were fourteen notaries of the Church, who, receiving the acts of various martyrs, recounted them in order. While he gathered all these in the aforesaid baths under one examination of holiness, this was so arranged that no layperson appeared present.

There follow 139 bishops from the city of Rome or from not far from it.

[Col. 0831]

Castus, Cyprus, Peter, Abundius, Severinus, Lucianus, Capax, Herculanus, John, Himilus, Andrew, Peter, Renovatus, Cresconius, Ambrose, Luke, Hermogenianus, Augustus, Felix, Barbarus, Secundinus, Citonatus, Reparatus, Gaudentius, Sebastianus, Graeces (otherwise Cresces), Renatus, Irenaeus, Laurentius, Valerianus, Botudorus, Leo, Abundantius, Almachius, Honestosus, Victor, Plenus, Delphinus, Amabilis, Paul, Constantius, Sixtus, Concordius, Nepotianus, Bedandulus, Deutherius, Amabilis, Syrus, Quadratus, Mirabilis, Audacius, Turcilianus, John, Marcus, Fidelis, Symmachus, Probianus, Asellus, Crispinus, Rusticus, Faustus, Turdus, Mojorianus, Jobianus, Exonosus, Sanctulus, Coricosus, Nepus, Tiburtius, Peter, Sylvestrianus, Turturanus, Leontius, Anastasius, Agapitus, Verustimilus, Asellus, Jacob, Felicissimus, Quadratus, Alexander, Philip, Exuperantius, Hypolitus (Hippolytus), Jordianus, Archidamus, Lollius, Martia-Caritosus, Concordius, Januarius, Felicianus, Redus, Auxibus, Timothy, Boniface, Tranquillinus, Calbulus, Sixtus, Catellus, Epiphanes, Victor, Habet Deum (“God Has”), Contentus, Apronianus, Probus, Repostibus, Paul, Fidelissimus, Homobonus, Luminosus, Vitalis, Carpilio, Volusianus, Peter, Probinus, Honestosus, Ariston, Bacanda, Peter, Marinus, Priscillianus, Carito, Gattus, Januarius, Caecilius, Epiphanius, Laurentius, Humanianus, Urbanus, Micinus, Caecilius, Priscus, Tiburtius, Nonnonus, Anthimus, Agapitus, Vindemius.

Peter, Anastasius, Hermes, Nicostratus, Quod vult Deus (“What God Wills”), Vitalis, Renatus, Vinulus, Andriphorus, Irenaeus, Olympius, Demeter, Theodolus, Anastasius, Thespias, Firminus, Cleopatris, Honorius, Simplex, Exitiosus, John, Timothy, Hermes, Paul, Metronius, Stephen, Alexander, Constantine, Andrew, Exuperantius, Firmus, Quirillianus, Anastasius, Hermogenius, Severus, Aconcius, Thomas, John, Caecilianus, Theodolus, Theophilus, Prispilius, Festus, Almacus, Andecius, Concordius, Deutherinnus, Thomas, Quadratus, Timothy, Potestas, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Victorinus, Severianus, Domanicus, Eulogius, Demeter, Nepotianus, Albinus, Peter, John, Exuperius, Theodolus, John, Exuperantius, Sebastianus, Theodorus, Claudius, Demetrianus, Rufinus, Spes in Deo (“Hope in God”), Reparatus, Peter, Asellus, Archanus, Eufemius, Crisolatus, Lazarus, Leo, Anthimus, Andrew, Catharon, Vultibus, Anastasius, Hermes, Sempervivus, Titus, Orifensis, Epiphanius, Anastasius, Leo, Ultius, Fortunatus, Caecilianus, Nicostratus, Audax, John, Rufinus, Honorius, Felix, Petronius, Andrew, Requisitus, Bacauda, Terfilius, Zeno, Caritosus, Majoranus, Leo, Hermes, Demeter, Andrew, Spes in Deo (“Hope in God”), Timothy, Jacob, Zeno, Quadratus, Fusilis, Marcus, Paulinus, Oyfensis, Concordius, Priscus, Herculanus, Leoninus, Androtilus, Eufimius, Squiro, Martin, Anastasius.

[Col. 0832C] When all these had come to the synod, and the written attestations and reputation for holiness of some had been circulated, they sat before the aforesaid baths. [Col. 0834A] But all the Roman presbyters, deacons, clergy, and the ranks following them stood behind the bishops. No one sat in the same place except the bishops alone and Sylvester, bishop and pontiff of the city of Rome. There was also Calphurnius, first a pagan, then a Christian, and prefect of the city.

Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, gave the following explanation: “Hear me, brothers and fellow bishops, and the whole order of the Roman Church. It is good for the Church to have fixed curtains, so that the royal Church may not be shaken, but may be firm, shut its door because of the persecutor, [Col. 0834B] and have a strong wall from which it may overcome its adversaries.”

#### Chapter II

“I speak what is known, and I prove [the case against] Callistus and Victorinus, who by their own judgment made a creature, and Jovianus, who in his arrogance said that Easter does not come on its proper day or in its proper month, but is to be observed on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April]. For I, as the law states, submit the matter to your judgment: let these three be brought forward, and let the examination first confirm the condemnation of Callistus, who taught himself to be Sabellian, so that by his own judgment he maintained that the Trinity was one person, not making the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit coequal.

“Victorinus, therefore, chief prelate and bishop of the region, in his arrogance proclaimed to people whatever he wished and announced false Paschal cycles. Thus let what he decreed, namely the observance of the tenth day before the Kalends of May, be annulled by your declaration, as truth requires, condemned by your judgment, and let the authority of our sons proceed to condemn Bishop Victorinus.”

And all entered so that they might be condemned by their own declaration in judgment. He condemned Hippolytus, the Valentinianist deacon; Callistus, who in his arrogance divided the Trinity; and Bishop Victorinus, who, ignorant of the calculation of the moon, by obstinate adherence to his own judgment shattered the truth. In the presence of the aforesaid bishops, presbyters, and other ranks, he condemned Hippolytus, Victorinus, and Callistus; pronounced anathema upon them; and condemned them outside their cities.

#### Chapter III

Afterwards he established the ranks in the midst of the synod: that no presbyter should bring an accusation against a bishop, no deacon against a presbyter, no subdeacon against a deacon, no acolyte against a subdeacon, no exorcist against an acolyte, no reader against an exorcist, no doorkeeper against a reader, and no layperson should bring any accusation. A prelate shall not be condemned except upon seventy-two witnesses; nor shall the supreme prelate be judged by anyone, because it is written: “A disciple is not above his master.” A presbyter shall not be condemned except upon forty-four testimonies. A deacon attached to the cardinal office of the city shall not be condemned except upon thirty-six. [Col. 0836A] A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, or reader [shall not be condemned] except, as it is written, upon seven testimonies, [of persons] having children and wives and wholly preaching Christ. Thus mystical truth is given.

#### Chapter IV
I remind you, fellow guardians, that the revenues of the Church are to be divided into four parts, and that a fourth part is to be claimed from the Church: one part for the pontiffs; half for the brethren, for the relief of the churches; and half for presbyters and deacons together with all the clergy and strangers. He established this order: if any member of the clergy or any presbyter of the whole place—whose possessions are common—should depart from this world, and should have no partner from his own family, whatever his poverty possessed should be given to the Church; and from it four portions should be made, as was said above. [Col. 0836B]

## CHAPTER V

For Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, established in a clear voice that no presbyter should make chrism, saying that Christ is called from chrism.

## CHAPTER VI

And there were to be no more deacons, nor any additional ones, through the examination of the parishes, save two; and the cardinal deacons of the city of Rome were to be seven.

## CHAPTER VII

Yet Silvester said in a clear voice to his fellow bishops that all ranks from subdeacon down to reader should be subject to the cardinal deacon of the city of Rome, representing [him] only in the Church. But presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, and readers, representing service in every place, whether in public or in the bosom of the Church, are [subject] to the pontiff alone. [Col. 0836C]

## CHAPTER VIII

We command that none of the subdeacons proceed to marriage, lest he incur some transgression.

## CHAPTER IX

Let no reader or doorkeeper touch the sacred vessels; let no acolyte hand over a sacred thing from one presbyter to another, except that he may carry only what the priest places upon him, blessed by his mouth.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0836D] Let none of the bishops seek to bless a consecrated virgin for the partnership of marriage unless he has proved that she has reached the age of seventy-two years. There she shall be approved by the judge for true chastity; or, having sought Christ as her husband for seventy years, with chastity preserved, anointed upon the head, she shall be brought in to the marriage of Christ, bearing a veil upon her head, not upon her heart. And the aforesaid bishops subscribed to this, Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, proclaiming it. [Col. 0838A] Calphurnius, prefect of the city, subscribed last. Augustus Constantine subscribed with his mother Helena Augusta. Then, seated in the same place, he delivered an address, and they departed.

# SECOND SESSION

[Col. 0837]

On another day all the presbyters of the city of Rome came, together with the deacons and all the bishops, two hundred and eighty-four in number, within the Baths of Domitian, now called those of Trajan; and he sat upon his seat in that same place. There he made seven regions and distributed them among the deacons. These were the deacons: Fabianus, Marcus, Liberius, Archidamus, Julius. He also appointed two others, Priscus and Theodore. The entire body of presbyters, deacons, and clergy requested of Silvester the bishop [Col. 0838B] that he ordain them. There in the baths he subordinated those two, Priscus and Theodore; he did not ordain and consecrate them except within the precinct of the basilica, and he appointed them apart from the synod.

## CHAPTER XI

Let no one from the lay condition be raised to an office from acolyte up to the episcopate unless he had first been a reader for thirty years, then an exorcist for one day, and afterwards undertook the burden of acolyte; and let him remain in that rank of acolyte for ten years, so that he may undertake the burden of subdeacon, and let him be in the subdiaconate for five years. Then let him attain the rank of deacon, established by the examination requested by thirty presbyters, so that he may be a cardinal subdeacon, because it had been established by the first see [Col. 0838C] that he should serve for seven years.

For if anyone desired the order of presbyter, this was required: that during seven years he should be approved by the whole Roman clergy in doctrine, birth, noble lineage, and counsel; that, seeking no gain from anyone, all the presbyters should declare and confirm him as established in good repute; and thus he should approach the order of presbyter, and remain in that rank for three years. And if order or arrangement, or care for piety or holiness, required it, he should proceed to the burden of the episcopate, so that all the clergy should ask that he be ordained by one enduring vote. This was so enacted that the synod raised no objection to the words of Silvester the bishop, but rather confirmed them by prayer.

Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, also said: “Hear, holy men and fellow bishops. Let no one conceal what justice seems to him to rebuke.” [Col. 0838D] All the bishops answered and cried out together with all the presbyters and clergy: “May justice prevail, and may piety not depart from you. For nothing shall be judged by us contrary to the opinion expressed in your words, since wisdom does not exist unless it has been founded in patience.” Silvester the bishop said: “Since wisdom does not exist except in patience, whatever I establish by speech, let it be confirmed by your written attestation.”

## CHAPTER XII

Let no one grant penance except to one requesting it who is forty years old. But give baptism to all.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0840A]

Let no one approach the dignity of the clergy unless he has first received the heavenly veil of marriage through the hands of a priest. The testimony of a cleric against a layman is not to be admitted, for he is a pretender.

## CHAPTER XIV

Let no one receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman.

## CHAPTER XV

Let no one publicly examine any cleric except in the church.

## CHAPTER XVI

Let no cleric, deacon, or presbyter enter the curia on account of any cause of his own, because every curia is so called from bloodshed, and is the sacrifice of images. [Col. 0840B] For if any cleric enters the curia, let him incur anathema, never returning to mother Church. Yet let him not be deprived of communion because of a troubled time.

## CHAPTER XVII

Let no one strike a cleric who has sinned; let neither presbyter nor deacon nor bishop bring a cleric or servant of the Church to a beating. But if the cleric’s case so requires, let the two be deprived of office, so that they may be penitents returning to mother Church.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Let no deacon bring an accusation of indecency against a presbyter.

## CHAPTER XIX

Let no presbyter, from the day on which he assumes the burden of the presbyterate, contract marriage; and if he acts in disregard of this, we say that he is to be deprived of office for ten years. But if anyone acts publicly against this present written decree, let him be condemned forever. [Col. 0840C]

## CHAPTER XX

Let no one judge the first see, because all sees desire that justice be moderated by the first see. Nor shall it be judged by Augustus, by all the clergy, by kings, or by the people. And two hundred and eighty-four bishops, forty-five presbyters, five deacons, and two followers subscribed, together with Augustus Constantine and his mother Helena. And Silvester the bishop established this canon in the city of Rome and sprinkled it upon all the bishops. Acts in the Baths of Trajan, the third day before the Kalends of June [30 May], in the third consulship of the lord Constantine Augustus and the consulship of Priscus. [Col. 0840D]

> **Note [Col. 0840D].**  
> “In the consulship of Constantine Augustus III and Priscus.” Here, as the consular fasti themselves show, one must read: “in the consulship of Crispus and Constantine III.” It is not surprising that the text is corrupt at this point, since one can scarcely find a single complete line into which an error has not crept. The fact that Crispus was killed by his father at the beginning of the year 324 does not conflict with the time at which this synod was held. For the consuls with whose names the year opened and began to be designated continued to designate it until its end, even if, having died or otherwise resigned, others had been substituted in their place.

# CENSURE OF THE PRECEDING *CONSTITUTUM*

(*Constantine’s Appendix*, p. 37.)

[Col. 0841A]

I. This *Constitutum* survives in an old manuscript of the Colbert Library, written in Lombardic majuscule letters, and in another no less ancient copy in the same library; it also occurs in the collection which Baronius, under the year 324, no. 124, calls Cresconian. Benedict III and Nicholas I, Epistle 8 to Emperor Michael, cite it. Having obtained two very ancient copies of it, Peter Crabbe presented a threefold edition, placing three versions opposite one another in columns. “Because of the intolerable and excessive difference and corruption of the copies,” he says, “so great that at times one cannot understand what they mean, the text of each copy has therefore been set forth syllable by syllable, without any alteration of a letter.” [Col. 0841B] Between the two he placed a third edition, corrected by conjecture and, so far as possible, restored to the rules of grammar.

Later editors suppressed this version, since it has no authority, content to retain the twofold text. Yet all agree that, owing to the corruption of the copies, both can scarcely, or cannot at all, be understood in many places. And according to Baronius, no. 123, one can scarcely find a line into which an error has not crept. Nevertheless, they imposed the venerable name of Silvester upon every part, so that, moved by reverence for antiquity, they considered it almost sacrilegious to alter even a single character, even in the more obscure places.

But this defect of barbarous diction, alien to ordinary understanding, which this *Constitutum* shares with the two following letters, seems rightly to be attributed less to corruption of the copies [Col. 0841C] than to the incompetence of the person who forged these writings. We would not deny, however, that scribes too, because of that unfamiliar barbarity of style, may perhaps, while trying to remove errors, have introduced new ones, or at least repeatedly departed from the fidelity of the archetype. Hence arose those variations among the copies, for displaying which a double edition initially seemed necessary. We have nevertheless thought it sufficient to note those variants in the margin at their respective places. But the inelegance of the language alone removes all credibility from a writing to which not only so many bishops and other distinguished men, but also the greatest and most cultivated Emperor, are alleged to have subscribed.

II. Later Labbe, judging that one ought by no means to endorse this little work, although Binius, Baronius, and others accepted it, noted opposite the title of this *Constitutum*: [Col. 0841D] “These twenty chapters, which Isidore inserted into his collection, appear to be supposititious, according to Hincmar and most learned men.” By these words Labbe undoubtedly indicates Hincmar’s little work 48, no. 21, vol. II, p. 793:

> “For it is written in a certain discourse, without the name of the excerptor, excerpted from the acts of St. Silvester, which Isidore, bishop of Seville”—he would more accurately have said Isidore Mercator—“collected together with the letters of the pontiffs of the Roman see from St. Clement to Blessed Gregory, that this same St. Silvester decreed: that no cleric should dare bring an accusation against a layman; and that no presbyter [should proceed] against a bishop, nor deacon against a presbyter, etc., as below, chapter 3, down to ‘having wives and children and altogether preaching Christ’; with this added immediately thereafter: ‘Let no one receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman.’”

After setting this forth, Hincmar reveals what he thinks of that excerpted discourse in no. 22 in these words: “No one doubts how mutually contradictory these statements are and how different from the holy canons and sacred laws.” And he adds in no. 23: “Therefore it is not to be believed that the same holy man established such things as are written in the aforesaid discourse.” Nor is there any other passage in which Hincmar rejects the inserted twenty chapters.

III. But it is clear that in the cited passage Hincmar is recalling not the following *Constitutum*, but another little work which Isidore entitles *Certain Excerpts from the Synodal Acts of St. Silvester Pope*, and which, in Labbe, vol. I of the councils, p. 1542, is entitled *Brief Epilogue of the Following Roman Council*. [Col. 0842B] Hincmar does not mention the acts of St. Silvester themselves, but a discourse excerpted or extracted from the acts of St. Silvester.
