He also observes that the excerpted discourse bore no name of its excerptor, just as the excerpts from the synodal acts of Silvester in Isidore likewise bear no author’s name. Yet, since they are ascribed to no one else, Isidore himself may rightly be judged to have excerpted them.

Moreover, the passage cited by Hincmar is found in these excerpts complete, in precisely the same words and in the same order of words. In contrast, in the following *Constitutum*, the final words of that passage—namely, “Let no one receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman”—are separated by twelve chapters from the preceding words which Hincmar immediately joins to them; and the earlier words, “that no cleric should dare bring an accusation against a layman,” you would seek throughout the whole *Constitutum* in vain. [Col. 0842C]

IV. One may also doubt whether Isidore inserted the twenty chapters contained in the following *Constitutum* into his collection. They are indeed inserted in an old manuscript of the College of Navarre; but in the manuscript of Noyon, in the Colbert manuscripts, and in others older than the Navarre manuscript, they appear nowhere. Indeed, it would have been wholly superfluous for Mercator to compose excerpts from these twenty chapters had he inserted the chapters themselves into his collection.

V. Yet, although Hincmar saw and noted only those excerpts, what he judges concerning their conflict with ecclesiastical rules applies equally to the *Constitutum* itself. Certainly it conflicts with them that chapter 1 relates that presbyters at the Roman council stood behind seated bishops, and that no one sat there except bishops. [Col. 0842D] For, as Baronius observed, the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 34, decrees that a bishop sitting in any place should not allow a presbyter to stand. And there is no doubt that this rule also prevailed at Rome. For, according to Jerome, Epistle 85 to Evagrius, in the church of Rome presbyters sit and deacons stand—even in the presence of bishops, as is clear from the subsequent words. Thus in the Council of Elvira we read that bishops sat together, while twenty-six presbyters also sat and deacons stood by. The same was always done in Roman councils.

Again, it conflicts with ecclesiastical rules that chapter 2 prescribes the number of witnesses. For, as Hincmar rightly observes, canons concerning the judgment of bishops or clerics who fall into some crime are useless if this decree prevails. [Col. 0843A]

VI. Why, then, do so many canons take care that consecrated virgins not be violated and decree penalties for those who violate them, if, as chapter 10 sanctions, a virgin were permitted to be consecrated only at the age of seventy? Certainly this canon would have eliminated that great number of consecrated virgins with which the Church has always been adorned; and, if any had remained, the merit of consecrated chastity would thereafter have been slight.

But that another custom prevailed in the Church is proved by the judgment of Syagrius, so strongly disapproved by Ambrose in Epistle 5: when a consecrated virgin named Indicia was accused of violated chastity, he ordered that she should be examined by midwives. It is proved both by the treatise *To a Fallen Virgin*, by Ambrose or another writer no later than he, and by Basil’s letter on the same subject. It is proved again by Ambrose’s books *On Virgins*, addressed to his sister Marcellina and written thirteen years after the death of Liberius, who had consecrated her. It is also proved by the command of King Huneric, who ordered consecrated virgins to be assembled and sent midwives to investigate their chastity, and by the impious cry of the same virgins: “Say that the bishops lie with you, and your clerics.” [Col. 0843B] Finally, innumerable other cases prove it, for none of these would have had any place if no virgin were to be consecrated unless she had reached seventy-two years. But more genuine canons, already mentioned elsewhere, oppose this fictitious canon: some forbid virgins to be consecrated before their twenty-fifth year, others before their fortieth.

VII. This same *Constitutum* also contradicts itself when, in chapter 1, it condemns Callistus as a Sabellian, one who holds the Trinity to be a single person, and at the same time as one who separated the Trinity. For one who separates the Trinity follows a heresy opposed to Sabellianism. The latter consisted in confounding, not separating, the Trinity. [Col. 0843C]

VIII. Here, moreover, one is led to wonder why, in so celebrated an assembly, with Constantine present, in the very year in which the Emperor was devoting all his effort to extinguishing the fires of the Arian heresy, and for that reason had sent the great Hosius to Alexandria with letters, no word at all is made of Arius; while only Callistus, Jovianus, Hippolytus the deacon, and Victorinus—names unknown in ecclesiastical records—are condemned, unless Victorinus is someone other than Victorius, the inventor of the Paschal cycles, as we shall shortly examine.

The conjecture of Binius and Baronius, who suppose that Arius’s case was then reserved for the ecumenical Council of Nicaea, does not adequately answer this objection. For it is far more probable that Silvester and Constantine, in May of the year 324, had not yet contemplated convening the Council of Nicaea. But grant that they had already determined this in their minds: what prevented matters to be treated and defined at the ecumenical council from being prepared at the Roman assembly? Certainly it later became the practice of Roman pontiffs, after holding synods at Rome, to anticipate general councils: in the former they pre-condemned the heresies to be condemned in the latter. [Col. 0843D]

Moreover, it is not easy to guess how fifty-seven bishops from the region of Rhinocorura are listed; and it is still harder to understand why so many Egyptian bishops would then have come to Silvester, unless to complain of Arius’s perverse teaching and of the crimes of the Arians, or how they could have allowed silence to be kept concerning a matter so grave and necessary. [Col. 0844A]

IX. Who would not also find suspect the many purely Latin names in the catalogue of Greek bishops—such as Quodvultdeus, Spesindeo, Exsuperantius, Exitiosus, Fortunatus, Potestas, Sempervivus, and so forth? Greeks do indeed sometimes borrow Latin names, but Greeks do not commonly do so on such a scale.

X. The discussion would run too far if we pursued individually every mark of falsehood occurring in the work under examination. Its spurious character is sufficiently and more than sufficiently proved from the beginning by the fabulous account of Constantine’s leprosy and cure, and is confirmed, as though by a seal, by the erroneous consular date at the end.

XI. From the aforementioned reference to Constantine’s leprosy and to his baptism administered by Silvester, it follows that the following *Constitutum* is later than the false acts of Silvester. At the least, it cannot be denied that the architect of this *Constitutum* knew those false acts of Silvester, since he drew from them the aforesaid fable concerning Constantine’s leprosy and baptism. [Col. 0844B]

Conversely, from what Hincmar long ago observed (*Opusc.* 48, no. 23, p. 792)—namely, that nothing resembling the matters found in the *Constitutum*, or in the excerpts consonant with it, is read in the acts of Silvester, but that these matters are mentioned only in the books of the pontiffs—we rightly infer that the author of those acts was unaware of the aforesaid *Constitutum* and of the pseudo-Roman council. For who could persuade himself that he would have passed over in silence, in those acts, a matter so celebrated?

XII. When we consider who this Victorinus is, whose condemnation is sought in chapter 1 because he affirmed to men whatever he wished and declared the Paschal cycles false, a further argument will be supplied by which we may confirm that this *Constitutum* is much later than the time of Silvester. First, incidentally, we observe that the same Victorinus is likewise blamed in the following Epistle 13 because, by his own judgment, he affirmed whatever he wished and declared the cycles of Easter false; thus everyone may perceive in advance from what source this little stream flowed.

Now, when one investigates who this Victorinus is, blamed in both writings for new Easter cycles, no one other than Victorinus of Aquitaine occurs: he is called Victorius by most writers and Victor by some, and, at the request of Hilary—then archdeacon and later pope—composed Paschal cycles in the year of Christ 457. [Col. 0844C] Although Pope Leo approved these cycles and the Fourth Synod of Orléans, held in 541, canon 1, accepted them, many later rejected and sharply criticized them.

In particular, Victor, bishop of Capua, wrote a book against Victorius himself in the year 550. In the course of it, according to Bede (*On the Reckoning of Time*, ch. 49), he said: “Now, I say, the order of the discussion requires that I reveal the errors of the cycles which Victorius published, since he does not know how to determine the lawful day of Easter.” Nor did Columbanus, at the end of the sixth century, think more favorably of the same cycles. His letter to Pope Gregory I (*Gregory*, book III, Epistle 132, new edition) testifies to this in these words:

> “Know that Victorius has not been accepted by our masters and the ancient Irish philosophers, most wise calculators in the composition of the computus; rather, he has been considered worthy of laughter or pardon than of authority.”

After some intervening remarks, he adds: “Therefore either excuse or condemn your Victorius.” The remainder of the letter shows how greatly the Irish abhorred Victorius’s calculation. Nor were the Western Britons more favorably disposed toward him. For, as Aldhelm writes in St. Boniface, Epistle 44, they did not decree that the course of Victorius’s Paschal table should be followed by posterity. [Col. 0845A]

XIII. Nor should anyone be moved by the fact that, although many writers—such as Gennadius of Marseilles, Isidore of Seville, Gregory of Tours, Fredegar, Aldhelm, Honorius of Autun, and others—wrote about Victorius, who devised the Paschal cycles in the time of Pope Leo, not one of them calls him a bishop; whereas Victorinus mentioned in the *Constitutum* of Silvester is repeatedly called a bishop.

For it is certain from Columbanus’s quoted words to Gregory, “Therefore either excuse or condemn your Victorius,” that the Victorius criticized by Columbanus is the Victorius whose cycles Rome had accepted and was even then following, and thus Victorius himself, who had composed the cycles in Leo’s time. That this Victorius was a bishop, Columbanus himself makes clear beyond doubt in the same letter, where he says:

> “After so many authors whom I have read, the single opinion of those bishops does not satisfy me, saying only: ‘We ought not to celebrate Easter with the Jews.’ Bishop VICTOR said this long ago; but no Oriental accepted the invention.”

[Col. 0845B] No one who examines what precedes and follows will doubt that here he refers not to Victor, bishop of Capua, but to Victorius himself, who is sharply criticized throughout the whole letter. Indeed, as we have said, the man called Victorius by most is called Victorinus by Isidore, *Origins*, book VI, chapter 17, and Victor by Fredegar, chapter 108.

Let each person therefore judge as he pleases concerning the episcopal status of Victorius, whose cycles Rome accepted. Certainly it is no more remote from the truth that the architect of this *Constitutum* could have believed him to be a bishop than that Columbanus and others, who rejected the same cycle with no little indignation, could have done so. If this is so, no one can deny that this *Constitutum* is later than the middle of the sixth century. We have already proved by another argument, in the general preface, § 3, that it belongs to the time of Pope Symmachus. [Col. 0845C]

# NOTICE CONCERNING ANOTHER ROMAN COUNCIL, ALSO HELD AT ROME UNDER POPE SILVESTER BEFORE THE TWO PRECEDING ONES

(*Councils*, vol. I, col. 1490, Labbe edition.)

[Col. 0845D]

At this council at Rome, in the presence of Emperor Constantine, the celebrated disputation between the Jews and Silvester was held. At the urging of the Emperor and his mother Helena, most learned men from both sides assembled with the purpose that the defenders of each party might prove and manifest the truth of their religion by Scriptures and miracles alike.

Concerning its outcome, the acts of Silvester are cited in the third letter written by Hadrian, Roman pontiff, to Charlemagne, in the following words:

> At the very beginnings of the Christians, when Emperor Constantine was being converted to the faith, his mother Helena Augusta came to him in the city of Rome with twelve scribes, Pharisees, teachers, and leaders of the Jews; and she, together with her son Constantine Augustus, decided that a council of Jews and Christians should be held. In it holy Pope Silvester presided with very many most holy bishops; enlarging the Christian faith to a more extensive condition, they became victors both through sacred Scripture and through miracles, the Lord protecting them, according to the judgment of Craton the philosopher and Zenophilus, *vir clarissimus*, whom they had chosen for this purpose. [Col. 0846A]

These acts of Silvester at greater length had such authority before Gelasius that they were read both at Rome and in many other churches; indeed, even after Gelasius they were cited as authentic by Pope Hadrian in the aforesaid third letter to Charlemagne. Yet in the form in which they survive today, they abound in many falsehoods that entered from elsewhere. For their statements that Constantine was a Christian before Helena; that Constantius and Constans, Caesars and Augusti, were living in the East at this time; that Isaac held the high-priesthood among the Jews; that Helena was of Bithynian origin; that the Sabbath fast was abolished by Silvester; that Sunday was instituted by him; that Silvester himself was ordained pontiff by Miltiades; and many other things, are wholly foreign to the truth. Besides Baronius’s fine demonstration of this under the year 315, no. 12 and following, the apostolic canons themselves and the notes which we have written upon them openly demonstrate it. [Col. 0846B]

The acts of Silvester and Law 1, *Concerning the Jews*, in the Theodosian Code, dated by these consuls, testify that this assembly was held when Constantine and Licinius were holding their fourth consulship: namely, in the year of Christ 315, Silvester’s second and Constantine’s tenth year. For, when the Jews were confounded in this disputation, they not only inflicted insults and grievous injuries on Christians, but even stirred up sedition against the Emperor himself in order to repel the injury from the heads of Christians. By the cited law promulgated against them, he decreed that, if they harassed with stones or any other cruel punishment any Christian who had abandoned their sect, they should immediately be committed to the flames.

To suppress their rebellion and sedition, he had the ears of the seditious cut off, a mark impressed upon their bodies, and led them about through every place as runaway slaves and ruffians. Chrysostom, *Homily 2, Oration against the Jews*; Baronius, in the aforesaid year, nos. 9 and 10. [Col. 0846C–D]

# CENSURE OF THE FOLLOWING LETTER

(*Constantine’s Appendix*, p. 35.)

I. In the library of Fleury, the forged seventh letter in the name of Cornelius is followed by the present letter, of no greater authority. It consists of the same words as the first letter of Pope Zosimus, with the names Vienne and Paschasius substituted for Arles and Patroclus, and with additions, in place of what Zosimus explains in chapters 1 and 2, of the matters contained in no. 2. Therefore either this letter of Silvester or that of Zosimus must be declared false.

But the truth of Zosimus’s first letter is proved not only by two other letters of the same pontiff, the seventh and tenth, which assert the same right of granting *formatae* to Patroclus, bishop of Arles, but also by several other letters of Zosimus’s successors to Patroclus’s successors confirming it. For we still possess letters of Pope Symmachus and Vigilius in which they state that, following the custom of their predecessors, they granted this right to Caesarius, Auxanius, and Aurelian, bishops of Arles. [Col. 0847A]

The architect of the second letter of Zosimus, to Simplicius, bishop of Vienne—later to be placed in its proper location—whom we suspect to be none other than the maker of this very letter, freely acknowledges the authenticity of Zosimus’s letters written in favor of the bishop of Arles. Indeed, he supposes this letter of Silvester unknown to that pope; yet Zosimus could not have copied it unless he had had it before his eyes.

And when we compare the words of Zosimus’s first letter, “But this privilege of *formatae* we have granted to our brother and fellow bishop Patroclus, in special consideration of his merits,” with these words in Silvester’s letter, “But this privilege of *formatae* we have granted to our brother and fellow bishop Paschasius and HIS POSTERITY, in special consideration of his merits,” we discover that it is not Zosimus copying Silvester’s words, but pseudo-Silvester tastelessly interpolating Zosimus’s statement. [Col. 0847B]

What, after all, does this “and his posterity” mean? Is this said of Paschasius’s children and grandchildren? Silvester should surely have said “and his successors.” Nor ought he to have said “in special consideration of his merits” if he wished the same privilege to extend to Paschasius’s successors. We omit the facts that none of those successors is recorded as having used it; that, in the controversy between the churches of Arles and Vienne concerning the privileges of their sees, which burned with such partisan zeal, no Roman or Viennese bishop ever thought to mention this letter of Silvester; that, in granting the privilege of *formatae* to Patroclus, Zosimus speaks as though he certainly knew it had previously been granted to no one in Gaul; and, finally, that the same privilege is known to have been granted to other successors of Patroclus. [Col. 0847C]

II. Furthermore, in a manuscript of canons written more than eight hundred years ago, preserved by the celebrated monastery of Murbach in the diocese of Basel, we read the privilege, or part of the privilege, inserted under this title: “Here begins a constitution of the Apostolic See: Silvester, bishop, to all bishops throughout Gaul and the seven provinces.” Then follows the whole of chapter 1 of the first letter of Pope Zosimus, except that in this manuscript “metropolitan of Autun” is substituted for “metropolitan of Arles,” and Reticius for Patroclus.

Yet we never read that the title metropolitan was granted to the bishop of Autun, much less in the age of Reticius. For Gregory, after granting Syagrius the use of the pallium, wished him to regard it as a very great favor that “we have likewise taken care to grant this also: with every rank and honor of its metropolitan preserved, the church of the city of Autun … shall be after the church of Lyons, and may claim this place and order for itself by the indulgence of our authority.” It is therefore evident that those who sought to establish the antiquity of a church’s privileges more than once adopted as a model the privilege granted by Zosimus to Patroclus. [Col. 0847D–0848A]

The Murbach manuscript itself proves the integrity of that privilege. After its first chapter, adapted in the manner described to Pope Silvester and Reticius of Autun, it adds the remaining two chapters of Zosimus’s letter, inscribed not to Reticius but to Zosimus himself—or, as the name is corruptly written there, Ozimus.

# LETTER CONCERNING *FORMATAE* TO BE RECEIVED FROM THE BISHOP OF VIENNE; THE SEVEN PROVINCES BELONGING TO THE CHURCH OF VIENNE

(From the same source.)

[Col. 0848A]

Silvester, pope, to all bishops throughout Gaul and the seven provinces.

[Col. 0848B]

1. It has pleased the Apostolic See that, if anyone from any part of Gaul, in whatever ecclesiastical rank, strives to come to us, or [Note: **[Col. 0848D] (1)** In Zosimus: “to go elsewhere.”] intends to go to other lands, he is not to set out otherwise than after receiving *formatae* from the metropolitan of [Note: **[Col. 0848D] (2)** In the Murbach manuscript: “of Autun.” In Zosimus: “of Arles.”] Vienne, by which, through the attestation of his writings, his priesthood or the ecclesiastical position which he holds may be made manifest. [Note: **[Col. 0848D] (3)** Murbach manuscript, with Zosimus: “may make fully known.”]

We have established this for the reason that very many persons, pretending to be bishops, presbyters, or ecclesiastics, enter under the name of reverence and obtain undeserved [Note: **[Col. 0848D] (4)** In the same books: “reverence.”] honor, because there is no documentary proof of *formatae* by which they may be refuted. Therefore, whoever, dearest brethren, disregarding the aforesaid [Note: **[Col. 0848D] (5)** Zosimus: “aforesaid”; Murbach manuscript: “above-mentioned.”] *formata*, whether he be bishop, presbyter, deacon, or [Note: **[Col. 0848D] (6)** In the Murbach manuscript and thereafter: “or be in a lower rank, [and] come to us.” Zosimus: “or be in a lower rank, [and come] to us.”] be established in a lower rank, should thereafter come to [Col. 0848C] us, let him know that he cannot be received at all.

It is evident that this authority has not been sent everywhere, so that all these regions may know that what we have established is in every respect to be observed. But if anyone should presume of his own accord to violate [Note: **[Col. 0848D] (7)** Murbach manuscript, with Zosimus: “attempt.”] these salutary provisions, let him know that he has separated himself from our communion. This privilege of *formatae* we have granted to our brother and fellow bishop [Note: **[Col. 0848D] (8)** In Zosimus: “Patroclus.” In the Murbach manuscript: “Reticius,” and thereafter “special” for “specially.”] Paschasius and his posterity, in special consideration of his merits. [Note: **[Col. 0848D] (9)** In the Murbach manuscript, the constitution attributed to Silvester ends here with the words: “Fare well happily.”]

2. The seven provinces belonging to the church of Vienne, as the Roman catalogue testifies, are these: First Vienne; First Narbonensis, which is second; Second Narbonensis, which is Aquae [Aix], third; First Aquitania, which is Bourges, fourth; Second Aquitania, which is Bordeaux (added: fifth); [Col. 0848D] Novempopulana, which is Auch, sixth; and the Maritime Alps, which is Embrun, seventh. Farewell.

# IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 334: SAINT POPE MARK

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849]

# PROLEGOMENA

## § I.—LIFE OF POPE MARK

From Labbe, vol. II of the Councils, p. 467.

[Col. 0849A]

Mark. [Note: [Col. 0849B]

Marcus. In the year of Christ 336, the thirty-first of Constantine, after an interregnum of fifteen days, Marcus, a Roman by birth, was appointed in place of the pontiff Silvester, who had died piously and holy. During his pontificate the Church was shaken by a great commotion of the Eusebians. Athanasius, on the fresh accusation that he had allegedly threatened to prevent grain from being conveyed from Alexandria to Constantinople, and having been convicted of a new charge of treason by false witnesses suborned by the Eusebian party, was banished to Gaul by the emperor without a hearing, amid the great grief and mourning of all Catholics. Maximinus the bishop received him at Trier, not as a fugitive or exile, but as a confessor triumphing over impiety; and he held him in great honour as an outstanding athlete of the faith [Col. 0849C]. Hence the story that he composed the Creed while hiding in a well is demonstrably fabulous.

After Athanasius’ exile, the Arians, petitioning for Arius’ restoration to the city of Alexandria, did indeed obtain it. Yet, although fortified by letters from the Eusebians and the emperor, he was barred by the Alexandrian citizens from entering the city itself, because he was alien to the Catholic faith. He returned to Constantinople; and there, at an assembly of evildoers convened on the occasion of Marcellus of Ancyra, as we shall say below, he presented himself before the emperor. Questioned concerning the faith, he professed the Catholic faith orally and in writing, swearing to it with the utmost pretence. When Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, refused to receive him into the communion of the Church contrary to the emperor’s command, and feared that he would be forcibly imposed, he himself, together with the people, devoted himself to fasting and prayer, and obtained from Christ, the avenger of Arian impiety, that, while Arius was being led with great pomp by the Eusebians [Col. 0849D] to the church, he was compelled by the need to evacuate his bowels to turn aside to a more secluded place, and there, by a divine miracle, poured out his entrails together with his excrement and died miserably.

Thus the Arian heresy having been divinely condemned, very many of those previously deceived were converted. Great fear and consternation seized the Eusebian party, as the report of the event spread through almost the entire world. Moved by so great a prodigy, the emperor utterly detested the Arians and Eusebians, whom, deceived by their artifices, frauds, and simulated piety, he had hitherto considered the most zealous defenders of the Nicene faith and the most faithful guardians of ecclesiastical discipline. And he would himself have recalled Athanasius [Col. 0850B], whom he had rashly relegated into exile after he had been ensnared by Arian calumnies, as he had resolved to do, had he not been overtaken by death. These matters are taken by Baronius, under the year 336, nos. 2, 3, 4, and many following, from Athanasius, Rufinus, Socrates, and Sozomen.

A Roman by birth, the son of Priscus, he sat for two years, eight months, and twenty-one days.

> **Note [Col. 0850B].** “He sat for two years, eight months, and twenty-one days.” It is clear from Baronius, Appendix to vol. X, that he sat for nine months less nine days. This is what Jerome expressly says in the *Chronicle*: that he sat for only eight months. So too Sozomen, book II, chapter 19, says that he held the see for a short time. Indeed, the testimony of the author himself of the *Liber Pontificalis* establishes that Julius began to sit in the consulship of Felicianus and Maximus, namely in the year of Christ 337. How, then, could Marcus, who began his pontificate under the consuls Nepotianus and Facundus in the year of Christ 336 [Col. 0850C], have sat for more than two years? Marianus Scotus, Onuphrius, and many other modern writers, rightly following our view, abandoned the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*. Baronius, in the aforesaid year, no. 61.

He lived in the time of Constantine Augustus and of the consuls Nepotianus and Secundus (otherwise Facundus), from the first day of the Kalends of February until the first day of the Kalends of October.

> **Note [Col. 0850C].** “Of the consuls … Secundus.” H. reads *secundo*, “for the second time,” or “again,” consul.

> **Note [Col. 0850C].** “From the first day of the Kalends of February.” If Silvester, Roman pontiff, fell asleep holy in the Lord on the day before the Kalends of January in the year of Christ 335, and if from then until the beginning of Marcus’ pontificate the episcopate was vacant for fifteen days, as you assert in the Life of Silvester, how is Marcus’ beginning deferred to the Kalends of February?

> **Note [Col. 0850C].** “Until the first day of the Kalends of October.” It is more probable that he died on the seventh day of October, on which his annual commemoration has from ancient usage been observed in the Church. Baronius, in the place cited.

He decreed that the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates the bishop of the City, should then use the pallium, and that the bishop of the city of Rome should be consecrated by that same bishop.

> **Note [Col. 0850C–D].** “He decreed that the bishop of Ostia.” The custom by which the bishop of Ostia ordinarily consecrates the bishop of Rome seems older than this time; for Pope Dionysius is said to have been consecrated by Maximus, bishop of Ostia. Saint Augustine, in the *Breviculus of the Conference*, day 3, chapter 16, writing against the Donatists, mentions this rite as very ancient. Baronius.

> **Note [Col. 0850D].** “Should use the pallium.” The word *pallium* is used here differently from its use in canon 12 of the Council of Gangra. There it denotes the garment worn by those who professed a stricter monastic life and had renounced the flesh and the world, as is clear from the notes written there. Here, however, it denotes the vestment and insignia of the supreme Roman pontiff [Col. 0851C], by which his highest honour and full authority are signified, and which the pontiff was accustomed at times to impart to metropolitan bishops for grave and reasonable causes. Elsewhere it is called the *Phrygium*, perhaps because it was customarily embroidered with crosses by Phrygian workmanship.

> Baronius, under the year 336, no. 63; Theodore Balsamon in the *Nomocanon*; Photius, title 8, chapter 1; and Baronius, under the year 430, no. 26, write that Pope Celestine conferred the *Phrygium* upon Cyril of Alexandria when he acted as the pope’s representative at the Council of Ephesus, and that Cyril used it at that council and in sacred solemnities according to the custom of the Roman pontiff. Jerome Rubeus’ assertion that the use of the pallium was granted by a privilege of Emperor Valentinian to John and his successors, archbishops of the Church of Ravenna, is refuted by the admission of those archbishops themselves, preserved in Gregory, book II, letter 54: they ascribe the use of the pallium [Col. 0852C] not to the emperor but to the Roman pontiff. Baronius, under the year 432, nos. 92–95, shows that the edict alleged by Jerome is fictitious and fabricated by schismatics.

> The use of the pallium during a fast seems to have been prohibited by letter 54 of book II of Pope Gregory, in which he rightly reproaches John of Ravenna for wearing the pallium through streets and lanes during a fast. Baronius, under the year 451, no. 63. Add that the name *pallium* denoted every covering used in sacred matters, as Venantius Fortunatus explains in book II, epigram 3, where he calls the veils offered to the holy cross *pallia*. See Baronius, under the year 336, no. 64.

And he enacted regulations concerning every ecclesiastical order. He built two basilicas: one on the Ardeatine Way, where he rests; and another in the city of Rome, near the Palatine. At his suggestion, Constantine Augustus bestowed upon the basilica—or cemetery—that he established on the Ardeatine Way, the estate of Roses, with all its open land, yielding forty solidi. In the basilica in the city of Rome he bestowed the following: a silver paten weighing thirty pounds; two silver *amae*, each weighing twenty pounds [Col. 0851A]; one silver cup weighing ten pounds; three silver service chalices, each weighing two pounds; a silver crown weighing ten pounds; the Antonian estate on the Clodian Way, yielding thirty solidi; the Baccanas (otherwise Vaccanas) estate on the Appian Way, yielding forty solidi and two tremisses (otherwise trimisia); and the Morrea (otherwise Orrea) estate on the Ardeatine Way, yielding fifty-five solidi and one tremissis (otherwise one trimisium).

He held two ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: twenty-five presbyters, six deacons, and twenty-seven bishops for various places.

> **Note [Col. 0852C].** “He held two ordinations during the month of December.” How much credit should be given to these statements of the author is evident from what precedes.

He was also buried in the cemetery of Balbina, on the Ardeatine Way, which he himself established and made, on the day before the Nones [Col. 0851B] of October (otherwise, the second day before the Nones); and the episcopate was vacant for twenty days.

## § II.—WHEN AND HOW LONG HE SAT

*(From D. Coustant)*

The beginning and death of this pope are set out thus in the Bucherian Catalogue: “Marcus, eight months, twenty days. And he lived in the time of Constantine, under the consuls Nepotianus and Facundus, from the twenty-fifth day before the Kalends of February to the day of the Nones of October under the consuls named above.” That is, he entered upon the pontificate in the year 336, on 18 January, a Sunday, and departed to heaven in the same year, on 7 October, on which day his commemoration is still observed in the Church.

Here the artificer of the *Liber Pontificalis* manifestly reveals his unreliability. Carelessly copying the Bucherian Catalogue [Col. 0851C], he writes: “He lived in the time of Constantine Augustus and of the consuls Nepotianus and Secundus, from the Kalends of February until the Kalends of October” [Col. 0852A], thus placing Marcus’ pontificate as not extending to any December; and nevertheless he was not ashamed to add: “He held two ordinations during the month of December: twenty-five presbyters, six deacons, and twenty-seven bishops for various places.”

## § III.—ON THE DECREE ATTRIBUTED TO HIM

*(From the same source)*

We know of no writings of Marcus except those fabricated by Isidore Mercator; the others are to be reserved for another volume. Yet if faith is to be placed in the *Liber Pontificalis*, he decreed that the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates the bishop of the City, should then use the pallium, and that the bishop of the city of Rome should be consecrated by the same bishop.

The privilege of the bishop of Ostia by which he consecrates the Roman pontiff is indeed ancient. Augustine is a witness in the *Breviculus of the Conference with the Donatists*, no. 29, where the custom is mentioned that not the bishops of Numidia but nearer bishops should ordain the bishop of the Church of Carthage; just as no metropolitan bishop ordains the bishop of the Roman Church, but the bishop of nearby Ostia does. But since no mention of the pallium in the sense in which it is used here occurs in authentic monuments before Pope Symmachus, this decree rightly appears suspect, indeed forged. For although I would not wish to attribute the first use of this ornament to Pope Symmachus, still the profound silence concerning it in the writings of so many predecessors is a very strong argument that not long before then it began to be granted to certain bishops as a special privilege [Col. 0852C].

[Col. 0851]

# WRITINGS OF DOUBTFUL AUTHORITY (S)

## LETTER OF SAINT ATHANASIUS AND THE EGYPTIAN BISHOPS TO POPE MARCUS

*(Councils, vol. II, col. 466, ed. Labbe.)*

[Col. 0851D]

### On the number of the Nicene canons; requesting copies of the Council of Nicaea, because the Arians had burned their copies

To the holy lord and venerable pope of apostolic eminence, of the holy Roman and apostolic see and of the universal Church: Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt.

We do not doubt that the extent and character of what we suffer daily from heretics, and especially from Arians, have reached you [Col. 0852D]: for we are persecuted by them to such an extent that we are now weary even of living. For at a critical moment they suddenly and unexpectedly rushed upon us; and, as we fled from them in accordance with the precept of the Lord, who says, “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10), avoiding them because of the disaster threatening the people, they were unable to seize us, but they devastated everything. Indeed, they ravaged our possessions to such a degree

> **Note [Col. 0852D].** These things occurred under Liberius, in the year 355.

that they left us neither books nor ecclesiastical vestments, nor other ornaments, nor remaining implements [Col. 0853A]. They burned our books down to the smallest item, leaving not even one iota. For hatred of the truth, they even burned the Nicene synod, by which clergy and people were then being instructed, and indeed had already been especially instructed, to the insult of us and of all Christians.

Therefore we beseech you, most blessed father, because we do not doubt that complete copies of the Council of Nicaea are in your possession, to send us, under secure guarantee, those which belonged to your predecessor Silvester of holy memory. For when we attended the aforesaid synod with Alexander of blessed memory, our bishop worthy of God—that is, bishop of the great city of Alexandria—in the office of the diaconate, seventy chapters, under the testimony of our presence, were sent to the aforesaid Pope Silvester through the blessed men Victor and Vincent, presbyters [Col. 0853B] and *apocrisiarii* (envoys) of the Apostolic See, with an attached attestation.

> **Note [Col. 0853C].** Read *subnixa* (“supported/attached”), as is evident from innumerable medieval diplomas.

Certainly, in our presence eighty chapters were discussed at the aforesaid synod: namely, forty issued by the Greeks in the Greek language, and forty issued by the Latins likewise in the Latin language. But it seemed good to the 318 fathers, filled with the Holy Spirit and assembled in the aforesaid council—especially to Alexander already mentioned and to the *apocrisiarii* of the Apostolic See—that ten chapters should be united with the others and inserted in suitable places; and that, after the model of the seventy disciples, or rather of the languages of the whole world, there should be seventy chapters of so great and excellent a council, which would instruct the whole Christian world, so that one faith and one priestly and clerical rule might govern all living under the priestly and Christian name [Col. 0853C], and no one might dissent from his head (St Leo, letter 84).

Now therefore, since, as stated above, we are attacked, crushed, and oppressed daily by the enemies of the holy Church of God, and especially by the Arians, the aforesaid seventy chapters of the Council of Nicaea—which, once the aforesaid synod had been held, I brought by command of my lord Alexander and by decree of all the bishops, which I also recited and copied before all—have been burned by fire. We desire to receive them from the authority of your see, which is the mother and head of all churches [Col. 0854A], through these present legates, for the correction and restoration of orthodox believers. Thus, supported by your authority and strengthened by your prayers, we may be able to escape unharmed from the aforesaid enemies of the holy Church of God and of ourselves, and to rescue those entrusted to us.

We truly know, from the Council of Rome under Gregory II in the year 721, that the heart of your apostolate is so kindled by the grace of the Holy Spirit that you aid all who are oppressed. How much more, then, should you aid us, who, though of lowly rank, are nevertheless yours, obedient to you with all committed to us, and both are and always wish to be so. Therefore it is fitting and necessary that you grant us without delay what we request, and whatever else you know, according to the wisdom bestowed upon you by the Most High, to be necessary [Col. 0854B], so that the foulness of so great a misery may be wiped from the minds of believers, and that—as though a wound had been inflicted upon the body—the harm caused by hearing of so great a misery,

> **Note [Col. 0854C].** “When the entrance to so great a misery has been closed,” as the manuscript of C. Justel has it.

may be healed by a saving antidote. Thus, relying on divine help and strengthened by your authority and assistance, we may escape the evasions of our opponents and, with unshaken countenance, not struck down by anyone’s deceit, be counted worthy to stand before the eternal Judge and hear him saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

And the subscription: May the Lord preserve your holy apostolate, which prays for us, through long-lasting years (Pope John II to Justinian).

## RESCRIPT [Note: [Col. 0853D]]

> **Note [Col. 0853D].** A letter of Marcus to Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and to the other bishops of Egypt, is said to have been written on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, under the consuls Nepotianus and Facundus. Its subject, as understood from the letter of Athanasius and the other bishops of the same province to Marcus, was this: the Egyptians, harassed by a savage Arian persecution, had requested in letters sent to Pope Marcus, among other things, a copy from the Roman Church of the Nicene canons, which, together with all their other books, had been burned by the same Arians.

> By these letters, both Marcus’ and the others’, the number of Nicene canons is determined: namely, that seventy chapters were established by that great synod, according, as they say, to the number of the disciples. Baronius, no. 58. That this is spurious and fabricated by someone is evidently demonstrated by five arguments. The first is that, in the controversy over the number of Nicene canons between the African Church and the Roman pontiffs Zosimus and Boniface, this letter was entirely unknown to them. The second is that Athanasius, as is evident from the foregoing, was exiled in Gaul at this time and therefore could not have written from Alexandria to the Roman pontiff about this matter. The third is that that assault upon the Church of Alexandria occurred many years later under Constantius, when, after Athanasius had been expelled, a certain Arian Gregory was ordained in his place, as Athanasius testifies in his letter to all the orthodox. The fourth is that Marcus died on the Nones of October in that year while Constantine the emperor was still alive; therefore it cannot but be suspect that he is said to have written this letter on the tenth day before the Kalends of November under the consuls Nepotianus and Facundus. Fifth: if Pope Marcus had sent a copy to the Alexandrians from the Roman archive, thereafter the Roman and Alexandrian copies would certainly have agreed; how then were those three canons concerning appeals, which occurred in the Roman copy, absent from the copy sent by Saint Cyril from Alexandria to the Africans?

> It is therefore thought that the same person who, to support the assertion of Zosimus and Boniface concerning a Nicene canon cited beyond the number twenty, fabricated Pope Boniface’s letter to Eulalius, bishop of Alexandria, concerning the restored communion of the African Church, also fabricated and composed these letters of Marcus to Athanasius and of Athanasius to Marcus. Baronius, under the year 336, nos. 59–60; Bellarmine, book II, *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 25.

# OF POPE MARCUS TO ATHANASIUS AND ALL THE BISHOPS OF EGYPT

*(From the same source.) On the transmission of the chapters of the Council of Nicaea.*

[Col. 0854C]

To the venerable lords and brothers Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt: Marcus, bishop of the holy Roman and apostolic see and of the universal Church.

I grieve, brothers, and am deeply saddened by your affliction; but I am greatly comforted because you are not a reed shaken by the wind (Matt. 2), but remain unwaveringly upright in the faith amid all the struggles of storms and whirlwinds [Col. 0855A]. Having read, therefore, the letter of your brotherhood (St Leo, letter 85), we have recognized the vigour of your constancy which we knew of old. We rejoice with you because, in guarding Christ’s flock, you diligently pursue your pastoral care, lest wolves who have crept in under the appearance of sheep tear to pieces the simple with beastly savagery. They did not creep in in order to improve through any correction, but in order to corrupt what is sound.

Therefore I admonish and exhort your charity (the same St Leo, letter 2) to strive to bring the good which you have begun, by the help of divine grace, to its end; for the voice of truth admonishes: “Blessed is he who perseveres unto the end” (Matt. 24). For whence comes blessed perseverance except from the virtue of patience? (St Leo, letter 92) [Col. 0855B]. For, according to the Apostle: “All who desire to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). Nor is persecution to be reckoned only where action is taken against Christian piety by sword, fire, or whatever punishments; for varieties of conduct, the obstinacy of the disobedient, and the weapons of malicious tongues likewise supply the cruelty of persecutions. By these struggles the common members are always assailed, and no portion of the godly is free from conflict, so that they lack neither dangers nor leisure nor labour.

For these things, and every increase (Celestine I, letter to the Gauls, chapter 11) of worthy endeavours, perseverance in them unto the end, and the growth of good will, must always be referred to Christ’s grace, so that in all that [Col. 0855C] we do, God may be perfectly praised at every time.

As to the truth and number of the chapters of the Council of Nicaea, at which your fraternal letter stated that you were present, we made more careful inquiries among our own men who were present together with you. Just as your letter attests, they laid out the entire sequence of events for us and testified that your letter was wholly true—not because we suspect any perversity on your part. But we wished that we, you, and they might be of one mind in the future without any wavering, and that the holy Roman Church, which has always remained undefiled and, with the Lord’s providence and the assistance of the blessed apostle Peter, will remain so in the future, might stand firm and immovable at all times without any insult from heretics [Col. 0855D].

Having therefore completed these matters, and carefully searching in the holy archive of our apostolic see, we found intact the same seventy chapters—as you indicated—which had been sent to my predecessor Silvester of holy memory. We did not send you those very copies, because of the authority and subscription of so many fathers and [Col. 0856A] of that great council. But in their place, before your *apocrisiarii*, we took care to write back and send you other identical copies, containing the same number, the same words, and the same subscription, under certain guarantee and confirmation.

And who would dare deny such things to his brothers? (Atticus, letter from Constantinople to the African Fathers.) For the Lord taught us through the grace of the Holy Spirit that these things are not to be neglected but faithfully practised, handed down to brothers, and taught. This is the living tradition of the apostles (Agatho to Emperor Constantine, act IV of the Sixth General Council); this is true charity, which is to be preached and especially loved and cherished, and confidently held by all.

This is the holy and apostolic Church of Christ, mother of all churches, which by the grace of Almighty God has proved never to have strayed from the path of apostolic tradition, nor succumbed to corruption by heretical novelties. Rather, just as at the beginning it received the rule of Christian faith from its founders, the chief apostles of Christ, so it remains unblemished unto the end, according to the divine promise of the Lord and Saviour himself, who said in his Gospels to the chief of his disciples: “Peter,” he said (Luke 22), “behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like one sifts wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when once you have turned, strengthen your brothers.”

Let, therefore, your excellent prudence consider how good it is to persist in the stewardship entrusted to you and in the right faith, to resist heretics and enemies of Christ, and never to depart from the path of truth. For the Lord and Saviour of all, whose faith it is, did not hesitate to die for us and redeemed us with his own blood; he promised that the faith of blessed Peter would not fail and commanded him to strengthen his brothers [Col. 0856C]. It is known to all that the apostolic pontiffs, predecessors of my lowliness, always did this confidently. Although unequal and weak, my own insignificance nevertheless wishes, in the ministry received through divine condescension, to follow in their footsteps.

For woe will be to us who have undertaken the burden of this ministry if we neglect to preach the truth of the Lord Jesus Christ which the apostles proclaimed. Woe also will be to us if we suppress the truth by silence, since we are commanded to distribute it to the bankers—that is, to instruct and teach Christian peoples. What shall we say at Christ’s future judgment if we are ashamed to preach the truth of his word? What will become of us when Christ our God, the just Judge, strictly demands an account of the souls entrusted to us and of the office we have undertaken? Therefore, brothers, I exhort, entreat, and admonish [Col. 0857A] your charity (St Leo, letter 2) to keep watch with all the care you owe and can exercise, in order to seek out heretics and enemies of the holy Church of God, and to uproot them from sound minds with such severity as you can command, lest this plague spread more widely.

For just as one who has diligently carried out what advances the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive from God the reward of worthy recompense, so anyone who has refused to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will not be able to excuse himself from the guilt of negligence before the tribunal of the Lord [Col. 0858A].

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, under the most illustrious consuls Nepotianus and Secundus.

> **Note [Col. 0858A].** Facundus, in the year 336. But Marcus had already died on the Nones of October in that same year. Some, among them Sigonius, book IV of the *History of the Western Empire*, substitute October in order to create a false appearance.

# A.D. 337–352: SAINT POPE JULIUS I

[Col. 0857]

# HISTORICAL, CRITICAL, AND LITERARY NOTICE ON SAINT POPE JULIUS

## § I.—ON THE LIFE OF POPE JULIUS I

*From the Pontifical Book of Pope Damasus.*

[Col. 0857B]

Julius.

> **Note [Col. 0857B].** On 26 October in the year of the Lord 336, the final year of Emperor Constantine, Julius, a Roman citizen, obtained the pontificate of the Church. At the beginning of his pontificate, Emperor Constantine, confessor of the Catholic and orthodox faith, departed this life, leaving his three sons—Constantine, Constantius, and Constans—as heirs of his empire. As he was dying, he commanded them to restore Athanasius safely to his former position and dignity, since he had not so much exiled him as temporarily withdrawn him from the eyes of bloodthirsty enemies.

> Constantine the younger, with Constantius’ permission, carried out his father’s will and restored Athanasius, together with the other exiled bishops and presbyters, to their sees and churches. When the Arians and Eusebians saw their heresy collapsing, they not only burdened Athanasius with fresh calumnies, but also laboured to alter the formula of the Nicene faith by omitting the term *consubstantial*, and to introduce Arius’ heresy into the Church. To accomplish this more easily, they relied on the help of a certain Arian presbyter. At the persuasion of his sister Constantia, Constantine the Great had entrusted to this man the documents of his will for delivery to Constantius upon his return. They gained the grace and favour of the ambitious ruler; then, having proclaimed most savage war against the Catholic bishops, especially Athanasius of Alexandria, Eustathius of Antioch, and Paul, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, they hurled bloody weapons and missiles against them, invented fresh calumnies, and, after holding assemblies of evildoers, expelled the innocent bishops from their sees as condemned men; finally, they destroyed them by exile or violent death and, most shamefully, maliciously corrupted the Creed of the Nicene faith by removing the term *consubstantial*. To repel this injury from the head of the divine majesty and from its bride, the Church, Pope Julius showed himself such that his whole pontificate was spent in defending the Nicene faith and protecting Catholic bishops, especially Athanasius [Col. 0858B]. This will be apparent below from the notes on the letters and councils held under Julius.

A Roman by birth, son of a rustic, he sat for fifteen years, two months, and eighteen days.

> **Note [Col. 0858B].** “He sat for fifteen years, two months, and eighteen days.” Since he departed this life to the Lord in the year of Christ 352, on the day before the Ides of April, he is found to have sat for fifteen years, five months, and seventeen days. So Baronius, following the Vatican registers, no. 1 here.

> That Jerome’s *Chronicle* places Liberius’ accession in this year confirms what we said a little earlier concerning Julius’ death.

He lived in the time of Constantius the heretic, son of Constantine, beginning from the consulship of Felicianus and Maximinus. After many tribulations he was in exile for ten months.

> **Note [Col. 0858B–C].** “After many tribulations he was in exile for ten months.” It will be clear below in many places that Pope Julius expended much labour in restoring the exiled bishops—Athanasius, Marcellus, and many others. But, apart from Platina, who follows the error of the *Liber Pontificalis*, no one, so far as I know, has yet asserted that Julius himself endured exile for any time. Nor can the claim that he was released from exile after the death of Constantius be sustained. For all Christian writers, as also the pagan Ammianus, plainly write that while Constantius was still alive and reigning, Liberius governed the Roman Church and, after many attacks, was exiled by him.

> If this is true, let the imprudent compiler consider how he can extricate himself from this snare. In the year of Christ 350, Constans, emperor of the West—the great patron of the Catholic Church and of the holy bishops, the terrible enemy of the Arians, the prince of most uncorrupted faith, and defender of bishops exiled from the East—held the western empire. I do not see on what grounds Pope Julius could have been banished while this defender was still alive [Col. 0858D]. After Emperor Constans was killed, the tyrant Magnentius possessed the City and the whole western empire. Therefore either Julius must have been banished at Magnentius’ instigation—which no one is recorded to have written—or it must be conceded that he was by no means removed from the City and sent into foreign regions under Constantius’ rule. See Baronius, under the year 352, nos. 2–3.

After the death of Constantius he returned in glory to the see of the blessed apostle Peter. He built two basilicas, one near the Forum and the other on the Flaminian Way; and three cemeteries, one on the Flaminian Way, another on the Aurelian Way, and another on the Portuensian Way. He decreed that no cleric should conduct any case in public except in the church; that public instruments which establish proof for all should be collected by notaries; and that the preparation of all documents in the Church should be carried out through the chief of the notaries—namely, that bonds, instruments, donations, exchanges, transfers, testaments, compilations, or manumissions of clerics should be executed in the Church through the holy archive (*scrinium*, perhaps *scrutinium*) [Col. 0859A].

He held three ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: eighteen presbyters, three deacons, and nine bishops for various places. He was also buried on the Aurelian Way, in the cemetery of Calepodius, on the day before the Ides of April (August). And the episcopate was vacant for twenty-five days.

## § II.—WHEN AND HOW LONG HE SAT

*(From D. Coustant)*

[Col. 0859B]

In the old Corbie manuscript he is said to have sat for twenty-five years, two months, and eight days; but in the *Liber Pontificalis*, for twenty-five years, two months, and six days. Accordingly, the reading in the Bucherian Catalogue—“Julius, twenty-five years, one month, eleven days”—seems to require correction from that book, especially since the following statements in the same catalogue demand this correction:

> “He lived from the time of Constantine, who died in the fourth month after Julius’ ordination, from the consulship of Felicianus and Tilianus, from the eighth day before the Ides of February until the day before the Ides of April, under the consuls Constantius V and Constantius Caesar.”

For from the eighth day before the Ides of February to the day before the Ides of April, not one month and eleven days, but two months and six days intervene. It follows [Col. 0859C] that Julius was ordained on 6 February 337, a Sunday, and departed to heaven on 12 April 352, the day on which he is also commemorated.

## § III.—ON THE LETTERS CONCERNING POPE JULIUS

*(From D. Coustant)*

I.

1. Letters of the Eusebians to Julius.—We have already observed that in the year 339 the Eusebians arranged for Pistus to be made bishop of Alexandria. Having done this, they lost no time in sending to Pope Julius the presbyter Macarius, together with the deacons Martyrius and Hesychius, bearing letters. [Col. 0859D] Athanasius, in his *Apology against the Arians*, no. 1, ascribes those letters to Eusebius alone—the Eusebius who had transferred himself from Berytus to Nicomedia, and thence to Constantinople, contrary to law and canon, as the Alexandrian synod says: “Eusebius having written” (Εὐσεβίον γράψαντος). In this Socrates, book II, chapter 1, and Sozomen, book III, chapter 7, agree with him. Julius himself also seems to support this view in Letter 1, no. 4, where he writes that Macarius was sent by Eusebius (παρὰ Εὐσεβίου) together with Martyrius. Yet Julius himself, ibid., no. 8—indeed Athanasius both in *Apology against the Arians*, no. 20, and in the *Letter to the Solitaries*, no. 9, as well as Theodoret, book II, chapter 4—speak of them in such a way that they appear to have been composed not by Eusebius alone but also by his associates. Therefore they are sometimes attributed to Eusebius, with his companions unmentioned, because he was the leader and standard-bearer of the party, although he did not send them without the cooperation of his faction. The Synod of Sardica, in Hilary, fragment [Col. 0860A] II, no. 2, recalls that letters had formerly been sent to Julius, bishop of Rome, by Eusebius, Marius, Theodorus, Theognis, Ursacius, and Valens; to these Menophantus and Stephen are added by Theodoret, book II, chapter 8.

2. What they contained.—Those letters were written, as the Synod of Sardica testifies in Hilary, fragment II, no. 2, against Athanasius and Marcellus, and, according to the letter of that same synod as presented by Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, no. 49, and Theodoret, book II, chapter 8, against Asclepas, bishop of Gaza. In the same letters, as Athanasius says in the passage just cited, no. 49, the Eusebians asked that a synod be convened and that Julius himself, if he wished, should act as judge. Sozomen, book III, chapter 7, puts this as follows: Eusebius [Col. 0860B] wrote to Julius asking that he himself should be judge of the matters decided against Athanasius at Tyre. Here, certainly, this writer is not faithful in rendering Athanasius’s words. Yet if we adhere to Julius’s words in Letter 1, no. 2, it was not Eusebius, nor the Eusebians themselves, but their envoys Martyrius and Hesychius who requested Julius to convene a synod. Thus they sought this not in person, but only through their envoys. Indeed, the passage from Julius just cited would seem to require that, if they themselves had asked this in their letters, the pontiff would not have passed it over in silence. Yet it is easier to grant that the Eusebians’ chief concern in the aforesaid letters was to obtain from Julius letters of communion for Pistus, whom they had recently ordained.

3. Documents brought by the envoys.—Moreover, Julius, Letter 1, no. 10, states that Martyrius and Hesychius brought records of the inquiries that had been conducted against Athanasius in the [Col. 0860C] Mareotis. that had been conducted against Athanasius in the Mareotis. Hence we may suspect that other documents of similar proceedings were likewise entrusted to them.

II.

4. Letters of the Egyptians to Julius.—In the year 340, not long after the Eusebians’ envoys had arrived in Rome, Athanasius’s presbyters also came there. No one can doubt that they too brought letters in support of their bishop. At least it is nearly beyond doubt that the letter of the Alexandrian synod, most recently assembled from Egypt, the Thebaid, Libya, and Pentapolis—which, according to Athanasius’s testimony in *Apology against the Arians*, no. 20, was addressed to all bishops and to Julius, bishop of Rome—was delivered to Julius by these presbyters. [Col. 0860D] Julius seems to refer to this letter in Letter 1, nos. 9 and 11, where he recalls having received letters in Athanasius’s favor from all the bishops of Egypt and of the other provinces. Nor do we think Hilary speaks of other letters in fragment 4, no. 2, where he says: “Such letters as were formerly sent from all Egypt and Alexandria to Julius concerning the restoration of communion to the exiled Athanasius, such letters have now been given to Liberius concerning its preservation.” Liberius himself, Letter 4, no. 2, mentions letters written to him in Athanasius’s favor by eighty bishops of Egypt. It follows that, if those previously sent to Julius were altogether like them, they too were composed by eighty bishops. Certainly, those letters which Julius reports as having been sent to him by all the bishops of Egypt must be understood as written by no smaller [Col. 0861A] number of bishops. In any case, it is certain that bishops of Egypt and the other provinces wrote to Julius in Athanasius’s favor, and that their letter had been delivered to Julius before he summoned the Eusebians or other Easterners to a synod. But since it is highly probable that this letter was none other than the letter of the Alexandrian synod which Athanasius inserted in full at the beginning of his *Apology against the Arians*, there is no reason to seek another. Although, according to Athanasius’s testimony, it was expressly addressed to Julius, we refrain from reproducing it here because it contains nothing peculiar to this pontiff.

III.

5. Letters of Julius to Athanasius and the Eusebians.—Martyrius [Col. 0861B] and Hesychius, sent by Eusebius and his associates to Julius, having been unable to withstand Athanasius’s presbyters, asked Julius to convene a synod and to send letters to Athanasius at Alexandria and to the Eusebians, so that a just judgment might be pronounced before all. Acceding to these requests of the envoys, Julius sent letters near the end of the year 340 both to Athanasius and to the Eusebians. In them, as Athanasius says in the *Letter to the Solitaries*, no. 9, “he indicated at what place we wished the synod to be convened, so that they might prove their accusations true, while we might confidently refute those brought against us.” Julius himself notes, in Letter 1, no. 13, the letters he then wrote to Athanasius in these words: “For he [Athanasius] did not come here of his own motion, but having been summoned and having received our letters, as we informed you also by our letters.” [Col. 0861C] Since Athanasius began to make his way from Alexandria to Rome in 341, shortly after the feast of Easter, which fell on 19 April, it follows that these letters of Julius must have been delivered to him by April of that same year at the latest. Nor should it be doubted that the Eusebians received similar letters at the same time. Indeed, Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 4, expressly teaches this when he says: “Julius, following ecclesiastical law, ordered the Eusebians themselves to come to Rome and summoned Athanasius to plead his cause. Athanasius, obeying the summons, immediately set out.” No one has indicated by whom these letters were conveyed; yet it may be conjectured that Julius’s letters to Eusebius and his associates were entrusted to their envoys Martyrius and Hesychius as they returned to the East, [Col. 0861D] while those directed to Athanasius and the other Catholics were given to Athanasius’s own presbyters.

IV.

6. Other letters of Julius to the same Eusebians, and an embassy.—When Athanasius, summoned to Rome, had arrived and no one appeared on behalf of Eusebius, Julius sent new letters to Eusebius and his associates through his presbyters Elpidius and Philoxenus. These are commonly confused with the earlier letters; but Athanasius, if we are not mistaken, clearly distinguishes the two in his *Letter to the Solitaries*. For in no. 9 he says: “Julius, bishop of Rome, indicated in his letters at what place we wished the synod to be convened.” Then in no. 10 he recounts the arrival and impious deeds of Gregory, [Col. 0862A] who had been intruded into the see of Alexandria. Finally, in no. 11, he continues the narrative thus: “Athanasius, before these things had taken place, sailed to Rome at the first report of the matter, because he had fully perceived the fury of the heretics, so that the synod might also be held there, as had been decided. Julius then sent the presbyters Elpidius and Philoxenus with letters, and appointed them a time within which they were to come to Rome, or know that they would be regarded as suspect in every respect.” It is therefore evident that the mission of Elpidius and Philoxenus to the Easterners was later than Athanasius’s arrival in the city, and accordingly that the letters which those envoys carried must be distinguished from those by which Athanasius and the Eusebians had previously been summoned together to the synod.

[Col. 0862B] It may also be inferred that in his earlier letters Julius had fixed neither the time nor the place at which the synod was to be held, but had left them free to agree upon a place; whereas both were fixed by him in the later letters. Unless, perhaps, we say—though this seems less likely—that after the Eusebians’ envoys had requested that letters be written jointly to Athanasius and the Easterners, Julius first wrote to Athanasius alone, leaving to his discretion the place where he wished the synod to assemble; and that after Athanasius had arrived in Rome, Julius fixed the time and place of the synod with him, and by sending an embassy to the East notified in letters those who had previously written to him against Athanasius. This much is certain: Elpidius and Philoxenus departed for the East about June 341, carrying letters of Julius in which the bishop [Col. 0862C] stated that Athanasius had come to Rome after receiving his letters, summoned them to a synod to be held there on an appointed day, and warned them that if they failed to attend they would be considered suspect in all the charges they had brought against Athanasius.

V.

7. Letter of the Easterners to Julius, full of complaints and threats.—Eusebius and his associates detained Julius’s presbyters Elpidius and Philoxenus beyond the agreed day on which the synod was to be held at Rome—that is, until January 342. Then, from Antioch, where they had gathered with certain others for a year, they in turn wrote a letter to Julius and gave it to the aforesaid presbyters to deliver. Sozomen seems rightly to have seen this letter in the collection of Sabinus, the Macedonian bishop. [Col. 0862D] in the collection of Sabinus, the Macedonian bishop. Therefore, although in the preliminary Notice to Julius’s first letter we have already read not a little from it as recalled by Julius himself, it will not be irrelevant to present here also what the writer just mentioned, book III, chapter 8, sets out summarily concerning it.

First, he observes that the letter “was composed with exquisite elegance of language and in an oratorical manner, yet was full of quibbling and not without the gravest threats.” He then adds the following concerning it: “They admitted that the Church of the Romans was illustrious among all, since from the beginning it had been the seat of the Apostles (φροντιστήριον, ‘center of instruction’) and the teacher and metropolis of piety, even though teachers of the faith had come to it from the East. Yet they did not think it fair that they should therefore be held inferior [Col. 0863A] because they were surpassed in the size and multitude of their Church, since they themselves were superior in virtue and purpose of mind. Then, making it a charge against Julius that he had communicated with Athanasius, they expressed indignation as though their synod—namely, that held at Tyre—had been insulted and its judgment annulled; and they condemned this act as unjust and inconsistent with ecclesiastical laws. Having thus complained of these matters, they promised Julius peace and communion if he would accept the arrangement concerning those whom they had expelled and the ordination of those substituted in place of the former; but if he resisted their decrees, they threatened the contrary. For they asserted that the bishops of the East had in no way objected when Novatian was expelled from the Roman [Col. 0863B] Church.”

Sozomen adds: “Concerning the things they had done contrary to the decrees of the Synod of Nicaea, they wrote him nothing in reply, indicating indeed that they had many necessary reasons by which they could defend their action, but judging for the present that it was superfluous to undertake a defense of these matters, since they were generally accused of having acted unjustly in everything.” From Julius’s words, Letter 1, no. 6, it follows that this letter was written at the beginning of 342.

VI.

8. Whether Julius wrote now-lost letters in support of bishops expelled by the Eusebians.—If Socrates, book II, chapter 15, and Sozomen, book III, chapter 8, are to be trusted, [Col. 0863C] Athanasius, Marcellus, Paul, Asclepas, and Lucius, bishops, after explaining their case to Julius, obtained from him letters under whose authority they recovered their churches. Yet Athanasius mentions no letter written at that time by Julius in his own favor or in favor of the bishops just named, except the letter in which that pontiff replied to those assembled at Antioch. If the whole narrative of Socrates and Sozomen is examined and weighed more closely, it will be found that they have inserted some matters foreign to the truth of the events; but it will not escape notice that they had before them no other letter than the aforementioned fourth letter of Julius. Certainly Athanasius returned to his own Church not after the Roman synod held in 342, but after the Synod of Sardica celebrated in 347. The acts of the Council of Sardica teach us the same concerning the other bishops mentioned above. [Col. 0863D] concerning the other bishops mentioned above. Julius then wrote to the Alexandrians the letter, still extant, in Athanasius’s favor. But we have no documentary evidence that he did the same in favor of the other bishops. Nor did he have an equal reason or opportunity for writing on their behalf. Socrates and Sozomen, therefore, not sufficiently distinguishing the periods in which Julius’s first and fourth letters were written, and reasoning from the fact that the same pontiff wrote to Athanasius’s Church in Athanasius’s favor that he had also done the same simultaneously in favor of the other bishops, constructed a narrative which the truth does not permit us wholly to accept.

VII.

9. Julius’s letter to the Synod of Sardica.—[Col. 0864A] In 347, when Julius sent legates to Sardica, he wrote a letter to the bishops assembled there in which he testified that, though separated from them in body, he was present with them in harmony of mind and will. At the same time he excused his absence on the ground that the condition of his own Church, threatened by heretics, schismatics, and blasphemers or unbelievers, did not permit him to go farther away. The Synod of Sardica itself cites this letter.

VIII.

10. Writings falsely attributed to Julius by the Apollinarians.—The Apollinarians fabricated several writings under Julius’s name, [Col. 0864B] including a letter to Dionysius, another to Docius or Prosdocium, and a fragment of a discourse on the *homoousion*; the appendix to this volume presents them in Greek and Latin.

IX.

11. By Isidore Mercator.—Isidore too was not ashamed to sell his wares under Julius’s name. From his workshop emerged the acts of a Roman synod under Julius, this pope’s letter to the Easterners, the Easterners’ letter to him, and finally Julius’s reply to the Easterners, in which twenty-four canons of Nicaea, in addition to the customary twenty, are cited. We reserve these matters for another volume.

§ IV.—ON DECREES ATTRIBUTED TO JULIUS.

(From D. Coustant.)

[Col. 0864C] I.—1. What is disgraceful gain.—The editions of the councils, from the compilations of Gratian and Ivo, have gathered other decrees also which are attributed to this pope. The first of these defines that the person who buys for less in order to sell for more pursues disgraceful gain. Although Gratian, Distinction XIV, question IV, chapter 9, ascribes it to Julius, and Ivo, part 6, chapter 201, after Burchard, book II, chapter 127, cites it as from the decrees sent by Pope Julius concerning usurers, chapter 131, Ivo himself, part 13, chapter 21, following Regino, book I, chapter 125, cites it as from book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 125, where it in fact appears, copied from the Capitular of Noyon, held in 806, chapter 18.

[Col. 0864D] II.—2. That penance is not to be denied to the dying.—The second decree, reported under Julius’s name by Gratian, question XXVI, question VI, chapter 12, as well as by Ivo, part 15, chapter 43, and Burchard, book XVIII, chapter 21, is as follows:

“If a presbyter denies penance to those who are dying, he shall be guilty of souls; because the Lord says: ‘On whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die.’ For true confession—or conversion—may occur at the end; because the Lord examines not only time but also the heart, just as the thief, by the penance of a single moment, deserved to be in paradise at the hour of his final confession.”

3. Yet it is not obscure that this is a crude and rather inelegant summary of what Pope Celestine wrote in a more polished style in Letter 4, no. 3:

“Therefore the person who refuses to grant penance in the time of [Col. 0865A] death takes salvation away from a human being; and the person who does not believe that God’s mercy can suffice, even for a moment, to aid one who is dying, has despaired of that mercy. The thief hanging on the cross at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward if the penance of one hour had not helped him. Though he was under punishment, he repented, and by the profession of a single utterance he merited, through God’s promise, a dwelling in paradise. Therefore the true conversion to God of those at the end of life must be assessed by the mind rather than by time, as the Prophet declares thus: ‘When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved.’ Therefore, since the Lord examines the heart, penance must not be denied at any time to one who requests it.”

III.—4. That the brother of a deceased brother may not marry his betrothed wife.—The third [Col. 0865B] is cited by Gratian, question 27, question II, chapter 15, as follows:

“Pope Julius. If anyone has betrothed a wife or given her earnest-money, and, whether death should come first or other circumstances intervene, has not consummated the union with her, neither his surviving brother nor anyone of his kin may take that same woman as wife at any time whatsoever.”

Quite similar is another passage which Gratian immediately precedes under Gregory’s name:

“If anyone has betrothed a wife or given her earnest-money, even though afterwards, because death came first, he could not take her as wife, nevertheless no one of his kin may take her in marriage. If this is found to have been done, they shall be separated without qualification.”

The same decree is cited a third time there, chapter 11, in this form: [Col. 0865C] “Likewise it is found in the Canons: If anyone has betrothed a woman to himself and, because the hour of death came first, could not consummate the union with her, his brother cannot take her as wife.”

The final editors of Gratian note that the very words above attributed by Gratian to Julius are presented in Polycarp as from the Council of Tribur, confirmed by Julius; they rightly observe that this is an error, for the councils of Tribur are much later than Julius. Relevant here is what may be read in Anselm of Lucca’s compilation, book II, chapter 92:

“Chapters of the blessed Doctor Gregory concerning the line of consanguinity, issued under Emperor Maurice because of a certain count who was accused of having taken as wife the betrothed virgin of his deceased nephew. Let him who has taken in marriage the betrothed woman of his kinsman be anathema.”

Although these words are framed with adjuncts that make them appear credible, they nevertheless smell of the age of Gregory II [Col. 0865D] rather than Gregory I. We may reasonably judge this question and decision concerning the betrothed woman of a deceased brother to be later than the decree found in the First Council of Orléans, canon 18:

“Let not a surviving brother ascend the bed of his deceased brother, nor let anyone dare to join himself to the sister of his lost wife. If they do so, let them be punished by ecclesiastical severity.”

For once this had been determined concerning a wife, the question concerning a betrothed woman could easily arise.

IV.—5. That the marriage is lawful when a man marries as wife a slave woman whom he has freed.—The fourth decree, [Col. 0866A] which Gratian, question 29, question II, chapters 1 and 3, divides into two and reports out of order, is presented jointly by Ivo, part 8, chapter 156, and Burchard, book IX, chapter 18, as from the decrees of Julius, chapter 4:

“If anyone has granted freedom to his slave woman and united her to himself in marriage, some have doubted whether such a marriage ought to seem lawful or not. We, therefore, resolving this ancient ambiguity, judge such unions lawful. For if all marriages arise from affection, and nothing impious or contrary to the laws can occur in such a union, why should we judge the marriages mentioned above to be forbidden?”

“There is one Father for us all in heaven, and every rich person and poor person, free person and slave, will alike render an account for himself and for their souls. Therefore we do not doubt that all persons, of whatever condition, have one law in respect to God.”

Gratian adds: “But if all [Col. 0866B] have one law, then, just as a freeborn person who has been joined in marriage cannot be dismissed, so neither can a slave be dismissed thereafter.”

The first and principal part of this decree, from the words “If anyone has granted freedom to his slave woman” through “There is one Father for us all,” is copied from the Code of Justinian, book V, title 4, *On Marriages*, law 26; and the additions which follow are therefore also much later than Julius’s age.
