V.—6. That no one may marry a wife from among relatives of his own blood or of his wife’s blood to the seventh degree.—The fifth is presented from Gratian, question XXXV, question II, chapter 7:

“We permit no one of either sex to take as wife anyone related by his own blood or by that of his wife as far as the seventh degree of descent, or to be joined under the stain of incest.”

[Col. 0866C] “Furthermore, we have added this: just as it is not permitted to any Christian to take a spouse from among his own blood relatives, so neither is it permitted to take one from among the blood relatives of his wife, because of the unity of the flesh.”

7. Again, the two parts of this decree must be distinguished. Burchard, book VII, chapter 14, and Ivo, part 9, chapter 49, ascribe the first part to the Council of Orléans, chapter 10, on the same basis on which we have just separated it from the latter part. Yet although canon 10 of the Third Council of Orléans legislates against incestuous unions, it appears there in very different wording. The latter part of the decree, however, is attributed to Gregory by Gratian himself, question XXVII, question II, chapter 12, §2, with Anselm of Lucca, book XI, chapter 92, supporting this attribution.

[Col. 0866D] 8. It is evident that the whole decree is a fuller interpretation of this other text, which Burchard, book VII, chapter 7, and Ivo, part 9, chapter 43, again cite as from the decrees of Pope Julius:

“A man is equally not joined in marriage to his own blood relatives and to the blood relatives of his wife.”

That is, just as a man may not unite himself with his own blood relatives, so neither may he unite himself with the blood relatives of his wife. But this decree is reported in a more concise form in the *Penitential* of Theodore of Canterbury, chapter 11, in Petit, vol. I, p. 12. Thus there is scarcely any doubt that its fuller explanation was added after Theodore’s time.

9. Marriages between the sons and daughters of brothers permitted until the end of the fourth century.—Certainly [Col. 0867A] the opinion of theologians does not permit the fuller decree to be ascribed to Pope Julius. They maintain that during the first four centuries of the Church marriages between first cousins—that is, between the sons and daughters of brothers or sisters—remained valid and lawful, until they were prohibited by a constitution of Theodosius the Elder. Augustine gives explicit testimony on this point in book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 16, no. 2:

“Even in our own times, we have experienced in marriages between first cousins how rarely that which was legally permitted occurred in practice, because of the degree of relationship so near to that of siblings; for neither divine law forbade it, nor had human law yet forbidden it. Yet even what was lawful, because of its proximity, was regarded with the horror proper to something unlawful; and what takes place with a first cousin was judged almost to take place with a sister.”

Examples taken from the family of Constantine the Great confirm [Col. 0867B] the same opinion of the theologians.

10. Ambrose writes thus concerning the law of Theodosius the Elder just mentioned, Letter 60 to Paternus, no. 8:

“Emperor Theodosius also forbade paternal cousins, brothers, and first cousins to enter into a marriage union with one another, and imposed a most severe penalty if anyone should dare to violate the sacred pledges of brethren.”

Augustine likewise refers to the same law both in the passage cited and in the following chapter, no. 2, where he says: “Who would doubt that, in the present age, even marriages of first cousins have more honorably been forbidden?” For the same law Theodosius is also praised by Aurelius Victor, as one who assigned so much weight to modesty and continence that he forbade the marriages of first cousins as though they were those of sisters. Yet Theodosius’s praise would have been far less [Col. 0867C] if a decree of the Apostolic See had already existed on the matter, prohibiting marriage not only between first cousins but also between relatives of more remote degrees. I pass over the fact that Emperor Arcadius, in 396, excluded from marriage no degrees of kinship other than those to which Diocletian had earlier forbidden marriage; indeed, he repealed by another law issued in 405 and inserted in the Code of Justinian, book V, title 4, law 19, the earlier law of Theodosius.

11. Yet this is certain: even by the law in which Theodosius forbade marriages of first cousins, he left marriages of more remote degrees untouched and permitted them just as before. The decrees of Pope Julius which forbid marriage to the seventh degree of kinship are therefore falsely peddled. On this subject, the *Penitential* of Theodore, chapter 11, p. 11, prescribes: [Col. 0867D]

“In the third degree of blood relationship marriage is permitted according to the Greeks, as it is written in the law; in the fifth according to the Romans. Yet in the third degree, if it has taken place, the union is not dissolved. [Note: Perhaps: ‘after it has taken place.’ Rabanus seems to have read: ‘if it was done earlier through ignorance.’] Therefore they are to be united in the fifth. If it is found to have taken place in the fourth, they are not separated. Yet in the third it is not permitted to take another’s wife after her death. A man is equally joined in marriage to those who are related by blood to himself and to the blood relatives of his wife after the death of his wife.”

Rabanus observes on these words of Theodore in his letter to Humbert (*Regino*, book II, chapter 200):

“This Theodore, born at Tarsus in Cilicia, was ordained bishop at Rome [Col. 0868A] by Pope Vitalian—who began to occupy the see in 656—and sent to Britain. Hence he had been fully instructed in the customs of both Eastern and Western Churches. Nothing could have escaped him concerning what the Greeks or Romans observed at that time in legal observances, especially since he was perfectly learned in both languages. But the fact that writings of Roman pontiffs in recent times contain that the use of marriage must be postponed to the sixth or seventh generation ought to be understood as something they prescribed more from human custom than from divine law.”

[Col. 0868B] 12. Rabanus adds that “Isidore in his *Etymologies* [Isidore, *Origins*, book IX, chapter 7; consult the passage] asserted that one must abstain to the sixth generation of consanguinity, and then enter into lawful marriage.” What he himself thinks of the question he discloses at the end of the letter:

“Therefore, because you wished me to write back what I thought concerning this matter, owing to the frailty of the present age I judge that what Bishop Theodore, proceeding in the middle between Gregory and Isidore, determined in his chapters ought rather to be followed: namely, that marriage becomes lawful in the fifth generation, because neither divine law contradicts this nor the sayings of the holy Fathers prohibit it.”

By “Gregory” he undoubtedly means Gregory the Great’s letter in reply to Augustine’s questions, in which we read:

“A certain law in the Roman commonwealth permits a brother and sister, [Col. 0868C] or the son and daughter of two sisters, to unite. But we have learned from experience that offspring cannot flourish from such a marriage; hence it is necessary that already in the fourth or fifth generation the faithful may lawfully be united.”

[Col. 0868D] 13. Hence the letter bearing the name of Gregory the Great to Felix, bishop of Messana, has the odor of Isidore Mercator’s workshop. Gregory is there made to write:

“You are to know with certainty that what I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English people, namely your pupil as you will recall, concerning unions of consanguinity, I wrote specifically for him and for the English people, who had recently come to the faith, lest they should withdraw in fear from the good work they had begun because of more stringent requirements; I did not write it generally. Therefore, as the whole Roman city is my witness, I did not write these commands to them with the intention that, once they had been strengthened with a firm root in the faith, they should not be separated if they were found within their own consanguinity, or that they should be joined within the line of affinity, that is, up to the seventh generation.”

Certainly, if this had then been Gregory’s meaning, or if the custom had already prevailed that marriages were to be contracted only in the seventh generation, that prudent pontiff would not have failed to add some exception in the letter itself to Augustine. But Isidore of Seville and Theodore of Canterbury, cited above by Rabanus, knew neither that custom nor any such exception; Rabanus himself did not know it; nor did Gregory II, who shortly before Rabanus’s time, having been asked by Boniface of Mainz in what generation marriages between relatives might be contracted, replied to that bishop in 726: [Col. 0869A]

“We say that, so long as persons know themselves to be related by affinity, they ought indeed not to enter into partnership of this union. But because moderation, especially among so barbarous a people, is more pleasing than the strictness of discipline, it should be permitted that they marry after the fourth generation.”

14. From what has been said, we learn that marriages of relatives were lawful from the fourth degree onward during the first four centuries of the Church; that, as the fourth century ended, the fourth degree was forbidden by Theodosius the Elder but shortly thereafter again permitted by Arcadius; that thereafter, until the end of the sixth century, the custom remained that marriages were contracted in the fourth or fifth generation; that after the middle of the seventh century Theodore [Col. 0869B] of Canterbury prescribed that marriages should be contracted in the fifth, although unions made in the fourth should not be dissolved; and that Gregory II, before the middle of the eighth century, held the same view, to which Rabanus, later in that same century, judged that one should adhere: “Because neither divine law contradicts this nor the sayings of the holy Fathers”—and therefore not those of Julius—“prohibit it.” Rabanus does indeed note certain “writings of Roman pontiffs which contain that the use of marriage must be postponed to the sixth or seventh generation”; but he simultaneously teaches that those pontiffs wrote this only in recent times. Those times must indeed have been very recent, since they plainly were later than the age of Gregory II. Hence it follows that Isidore Mercator, who represents Gregory the Great [Col. 0869C] as forbidding marriages of relatives until the seventh generation, is both a forger and not much earlier than Rabanus. In this alteration of discipline there is evident in the Church a constant horror of unions in marriage between close relatives; and the rule gradually prevailed that marriages should be deferred until the seventh generation, when the memory of affinity ordinarily disappears.

15. The sixth item brought forward from Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter XXIV—“concerning the rebuilding of any church if it has been destroyed,” etc.—does not concern Julius at all, but Pope Vigilius, whose words are copied from the letter to Profuturus.

[Col. 0869D] 16. The seventh, beginning “when every crime,” etc., which Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter VII, after Ivo, part 2, chapter XI, and Burchard, book V, chapter I, cites as from decrees of Julius sent to bishops throughout Egypt, is canon 2 of the Fourth Council of Braga, held in 675.

17. The eighth, “Church is a Greek name,” etc., is noted as taken from Ivo’s decree. Ivo in fact, part 3, chapter III, following Burchard, book III, chapter 1, cites it as from the decrees of Pope Julius, chapter V. Yet it is excerpted from Isidore of Seville, *Origins*, book VIII, chapter 1.

18. The ninth is stated thus: [Col. 0870A] “If anyone burns a church, let him do penance for fifteen years, restore it diligently, and distribute its value to the poor.” It is copied from Ivo, where, part III, chapter 127, as in Burchard, book III, chapter 204, it is prefaced as from the decrees of Pope Julius, with Anselm of Lucca, book V, chapter 18, supporting this. But Gratian, question XVII, question IV, chapter 4, attributes it to Hyginus. It has no more the flavor of Hyginus’s age than of Julius’s. See what we have observed concerning this at the end of the decrees attributed to Hyginus.

19. The final item, “If anyone has granted freedom to his slave woman,” etc., repeated from Ivo, part 8, chapter 156, is the first part of the fourth decree itself, which above, no. 5, we observed belongs to Emperor Justinian. Perhaps Julius’s name slipped into Ivo in place of that of the earlier Julian, from whose interpretation the decree was excerpted.

20. Moreover, Julius is said in the standard *Liber Pontificalis* to have decreed: [Col. 0870B]

“That no cleric should plead any case whatsoever in public, except in the Church; that official record, which establishes credibility for all, should be collected through notaries; and that the drawing up of all documents in the Church should be carried out through the *primicerius* of notaries—that is, that sureties, instruments, donations, exchanges, transfers, testaments, bonds, and manumissions of clerics should be executed in the Church through the holy archive.”

21. But, first, in the ancient copy of this book, which Bolland’s continuators judge to have been written in the age of Emperor Justinian, as likewise in the Fossatensis copy, nothing of this sort is said to have been established by Julius. Secondly, it must be admitted that the Roman pontiff could not, without the consent of the emperors, have prohibited every cleric from conducting any cause in public. [Col. 0870C] Thirdly, it is certain that no such concession was made generally by the emperors. Valentinian II and Theodosius I did indeed later enact “that the name of bishops, or of those who serve the needs of the Church, should not be dragged before the courts, whether of ordinary or extraordinary judges”; and they held that the bishops themselves were their judges, and that “they had nothing in common with public laws.” Yet they immediately append to this privilege the following limitation and exception: “so far, however, as ecclesiastical causes are concerned, which ought to be decided by episcopal authority.” Therefore, shortly afterward they say to the prefect Optatus, to whom this constitution is addressed: “Your praiseworthy authority, exercising moderated discretion, shall determine whatever matters arise from elsewhere.” If, therefore, clerics even at that time had civil causes, their cognizance belonged to the public judge, unless perhaps they were referred to episcopal judgment by agreement of the parties. For then the bishop was permitted, in the manner of an arbiter, as Emperors Arcadius and Honorius state in the Code of Justinian, book I, title IV, law 7, to pronounce judgment concerning them. Moreover, Gregory I often speaks of endowing churches, oratories, or monasteries; but he regularly provides that such donations be entered in municipal records, never commanding that they be transacted before the sacred chancery.

§ V.—On the writings of Pope Julius (from Schoenemann).

The bishop of Rome, appointed in place of Marcus on 6 February 337. At that time the anger of the Arian faction against Athanasius had again been stirred up, because the emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Constans had in that year permitted him to return from Trier, where he had lived in exile, to Alexandria; where they had recently, in 339, ordained a certain Pistus bishop in his place. Therefore they strove not only to alienate the emperors’ minds from him, but also to make him odious to the newly appointed Bishop Julius. Through the presbyter Maximus and the deacons Martyrius and Hesychius they sent Julius letters against Athanasius, and also against Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, whom they had likewise deposed, and Asclepas, bishop of Gaza, with the gravest accusations, at the same time urging him to communicate with Pistus. To overthrow their malevolent designs, Athanasius himself also sent certain presbyters to Julius; before Julius they so thoroughly blunted the slanderous tongues of their opponents [Col. 0871B] that the latter, lest they should immediately bear the charge of calumny, appealed for a council to be convened by Julius.

Julius, won over by this ambitious request, summoned Athanasius to Rome and wrote to the Eusebians concerning a council to be held at Rome in June 341. Those bishops evaded the Roman bishop’s invitation. Having themselves assembled a council at Antioch, they deposed Athanasius and appointed another bishop, named Gregory, in his place; they sent him to Alexandria accompanied by military force, and soon sharply reproached Julius by letter for claiming the authority of a judge in a matter already adjudicated, threatening to exclude him from their communion. Meanwhile, when a council had been held at Rome, Athanasius, his case having been reconsidered, was acquitted and freed from every accusation of his adversaries.

Julius, however, having for some time withheld the bitter letters of the Eusebians because he expected a more moderate disposition through their envoys, at last, disappointed in that hope, ordered them to be read in the council and, at the exhortation and command of the assembly, undertook to answer them—in words indeed most gentle, but with solid reasoning. Having achieved nothing, he and other bishops sought the help of Emperor Constans; through his intervention Constantius allowed an ecumenical council to be convened at Sardica, in Illyrian Dacia, in 347. But because the eastern bishops denied that Athanasius and the other bishops condemned by their decrees should be admitted to the session, and yet could not prevail against the opposition of the western party, they immediately returned to their sees. The remaining western bishops approved Athanasius and the bishops who had been driven from their sees on account of his case, and declared that they should be restored; those whom the Arians had meanwhile ordered to occupy their sees were condemned and held apart from the communion of the Church.

In the decrees of this council, some have thought that bishops hostile to the Arian faction, excessively zealous for their own party, conceded too much authority to the Roman pontiff; for they judge it owing to their reverence for the see of the apostle Peter that the priests of the Lord from every province should report to him, and they commit the matter to his care, so that through his letters the brethren in Sardinia, Sicily, and Italy might learn what had been done and decided. [Col. 0872A]

> [Note: The letter of this council to Julius survives in Latin in Hilary, Fragments II, no. 9. But anyone who reads with a mind free from all bias, understanding the mode of interpretation and adhering to the tenor of the whole, must judge that the earlier passage, beginning “For this will seem best and most fitting, that from every province the priests of the Lord should report to the head, that is, to the see of the apostle Peter,” has been stitched in by another hand.]

Meanwhile Athanasius did not dare return to the Alexandrian see until Constantius, frightened by his brother’s threats, had granted full peace to Athanasius and the bishops who supported him. When Athanasius departed, Julius gave letters of recommendation to the presbyters, deacons, and people of Alexandria. Shortly afterward Ursacius, bishop of Singidunum, and Valens, bishop of Mursa—who had also been especially hostile to Athanasius—recanted their formulations before the Council of Milan, came to Rome, and, that their fraud might lie more plausibly concealed, confirmed the same things before Julius. Not long afterward, on 12 April 352, Julius died, having held the episcopal see for fifteen years, two months, and six days.

Two of his letters survive in Greek. One answers the Antiochenes in September 342, in accordance with Constantius’s judgment; the other, written in 349, commends Athanasius to the Alexandrians as he leaves Rome.

Among the lost writings must be counted the letters written in 340 to Athanasius and the Eusebians, summoning both parties to Rome; likewise those which he afterward sent through envoys to the Eusebians about 341, when Athanasius had waited for them in vain at Rome; and also his letter to the Synod of Sardica.

The letters to Dionysius of Alexandria and Prosdocium are spurious, having been written by Apollinarians; so are various fragments from a discourse on the *homoousion* and the Letter to Cyril of Alexandria on the Nativity of the Lord, together with the letter of Cyril and Juvenal of Jerusalem to Julius; as well as many other items [Col. 0872C] from the workshop of Isidore Mercator, and the Decrees attributed to him.

The two letters of Julius were published with Athanasius, who preserved them in the *Apology against the Arians*, nos. 21–35, in Montfaucon’s edition (Paris, 1698), vol. I, part I, pp. 141, 154, and nos. 52–53, pp. 171–172. One also survives in Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* II.23, p. 108, and in Nicephorus IX.22, and in Latin in the *Tripartite History* IV.29. From there they were received among the pontifical letters by Pierre Coustant, pp. 350–387 and 399–405, with learned summaries and notes. As was his custom, Coustant inserted various items concerning affairs between Julius, Athanasius, and the Arians: for example, the letter of Marcellus of Ancyra, p. 388, from Epiphanius, *Heresies* 72.2; that of the Synod of Sardica, p. 395; and those of Valens and Ursacius from Athanasius’s *Apology*, no. 58, vol. II, p. 176. He then discusses, from p. 406 onward, other letters concerning Julius, and from p. 411 onward the Decrees attributed to him. Finally, in the appendix, p. 69, he presents the spurious writings noted above.

[Col. 0873]

## GENUINE MONUMENTS. (S)*

### Of the blessed Julius, Archbishop of Rome: On the unity in Christ of the body with the Godhead

[Col. 0873A]

The Lord is rightly confessed to be a holy offspring from the beginning, also according to the body; and in this respect he differs from every body. For he was not at all conceived in a womb apart from Godhead, but united with it, as the angel says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore also the holy thing that is born shall be called the Son of God.” And the heavenly descent is not merely the birth from a woman; for it is said not only, “made from a woman, made under the law,” but also: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.”

Nor is it proper to call the body, considered in itself, a creature, since it is in every respect inseparable from him whose body it is; rather, it shares the designation of the uncreated and the title of God, because it is joined to God in unity—as it is said: “The Word became flesh”; and, in the Apostle: “The last Adam became a life-giving spirit.” But just as we ascribe to the body the glorious things arising from the divine conception and the unity with God, so we must not deny the inglorious things deriving from the body: namely, being born from a woman according to the Apostle; being formed from the womb as a servant of God according to the prophet; being called altogether man and Son of Man; being counted, with Abraham, through many generations after which he became man. Yet one must speak and hear these things in a human sense.

Just as, when he is called wholly man, no one should deny [Col. 0873C] the divine essence indicated by that name together with the body; and when he is named servant according to the body, no one should deny the lordly nature indicated by the name of servitude together with the body; so again, when he is proclaimed the heavenly man who descended from heaven, no one should deny the body’s conjunction from earth with Godhead. For when the Lord is called servant, and the uncreated is named formed, he is not divided either in reality or in name, because of the conjunction with the form of a servant and with the body being formed. Rather, it is confessed in him that the created is in unity with the uncreated, and the uncreated in mixture with the created: one nature constituted from each part, the Word contributing a partial operation to the whole along with divine perfection.

This is unlike the common human being, who is made from two incomplete parts [Col. 0873D] completing one nature and designated by one name. For the whole is even called flesh, without thereby excluding the soul; and the whole is called soul, without thereby excluding the body, although it is something other than the soul.

Therefore God, the Lord who became human and who existed before birth—though he was born from a woman; being Lord, though he was fashioned in the form of servants; being Spirit, though through the union with flesh he is shown to be flesh; not being man according to the Apostle, though by that same Apostle he is proclaimed man—in short: the invisible God transformed into a visible body; the uncreated God manifested in a created covering; having emptied himself according to the form, yet remaining unemptied, unchangeable, and undiminished according to the divine essence. For there is no change in divine nature: it is neither diminished nor increased.

When he says, “Glorify me,” the utterance comes from the body, and the glorification concerns the body, though it is said of the whole; because the whole is one. And when he continues, “With the glory which I had with you before the world existed,” he declares the ever-glorious Godhead, though this belongs properly to Godhead, and yet is said commonly of the whole. Thus he is consubstantial with God according to the invisible Spirit, flesh also being included under the designation because it is united to the Word consubstantial with the Father. Again, he is consubstantial with human beings, Godhead also being included with [Col. 0874B] the body, because it has been united with what is consubstantial with us. The nature of the body is not diminished in its consubstantial union with God and in its sharing of the consubstantial name, just as the nature of Godhead is not changed by its communion with the human body and by the designation of flesh consubstantial with us.

For Paul, in saying, “Of the one who came from the seed of David according to the flesh,” says that the Son of God received this birth; he does not name the flesh separately and say, “The flesh came from the seed of David.” And when he says, “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as something to be seized,” he does not separate matters and say: “He whose Godhead, existing in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as something to be seized.” Yet the Godhead was neither called Jesus before the birth from the Virgin [Col. 0874C] nor received an anointing in the Holy Spirit, since the Word of God is giver of the Spirit and is not sanctified in the Spirit.

And he says concerning them: “I sanctify myself for their sake, that they themselves may be sanctified in truth,” without separating and saying, “I sanctify myself.” Yet, upon exact consideration, it is impossible for him to sanctify himself. For if the Word sanctifies, what is sanctified? If the whole is sanctified, what sanctifies? Nevertheless, preserving the one person and the indivisible designation of a single living being, he has placed both sanctifying and being sanctified in reference to the whole, so that it may be exact and clear to us that he does not sanctify another in the prophetic or apostolic manner, as the Spirit sanctifies prophets and apostles. Thus Paul says concerning the whole Church: “Those called saints and sanctified in Christ Jesus.” And the Savior himself says concerning the apostles: “Sanctify them in truth.”

For all human nature is in need of sanctification; and the angelic order, as also every creature, is sanctified and enlightened. The Spirit sanctifies and enlightens; the Word sanctifies and enlightens through the Spirit, but is in no way sanctified, for he is Creator and not creature. But here being sanctified is where being embodied also is. The realities are distinguished, yet they are united by the union of flesh with Godhead, so that the sanctifier and the sanctified are not set apart as different persons. [Col. 0875A] And this, altogether, is the sanctification of the incarnation.

For to those saying, “You, being a man, make yourself God,” the Savior gave the account of his own humanity, saying: “Do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” What sanctification does he mean here other than that of the flesh by the Godhead? Thus the body lived through the sanctification of Godhead, not through the constitution of a human soul.

> [Note: Leontius read this passage and from it argued that this writing was by Apollinaris, whose well-known error was to deprive Christ of a soul and suppose the divinity to function in its place. Julius will shortly contradict this error.]

And, generally speaking, the whole lived in conjunction. Here too, when he says, “He whom the Father sanctified and sent,” he says that the sanctifier and the sanctified are sanctified together, joining the sanctifier to that which is sanctified. Elsewhere he interprets this sanctification as birth from a virgin: “For to this end I was born, and for this end I came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth.”

For the common human being is endowed with soul and life through a will of flesh and a will of man, the emitted seminal matter bringing life-giving power into the receptive womb. But through the visitation of the Spirit and the overshadowing power, the holy infant is constituted from the Virgin: not because seminal matter produces the divine work, but because spiritual and divine power grants the Virgin divine conception and bestows divine childbirth.

Thus, according to the mode of unity, it is said both that Christ is exalted and that the name above every name was granted to him, although exaltation properly belongs to the flesh ascending from below. But because it does not ascend separately, the whole is commonly said to be exalted; and the phrase “was granted to him” concerns the flesh glorified out of ingloriousness. For glory is not added by grace to the Word who always possesses glory. What he was and remains, he existed in the form of God and was equal with God. According to John, he says even in the flesh that he is equal with God, calling God his own Father and making himself equal with God. Therefore equality with God did not change; rather, the Godhead remained unchanged in identity.

What it possesses cannot receive; just as the flesh receives what it does not possess: impassibility from sufferings, heavenly status from earthly sojourn, royal status from servitude under human beings, and being worshipped by all creation from worshipping. Of the whole it is said that the name above every name was granted to him. If anyone dares to separate the language of grace from the name above every name, neither statement will be said properly. For if it was granted to the Word as one who did not possess it, the name above every name is never given by grace; and if he possesses it not by gift but by nature, as he possesses it according to Godhead, it cannot be given to him. Hence both what is bodily and what is divine are necessarily spoken of universally. Whoever cannot discern, in the united but different things, what belongs properly to each will fall discordantly into contradictions; but one who knows the proper characteristics and preserves the union will neither falsify the nature [Col. 0875D] nor fail to recognize the union.

> [Note: The manuscript reads “the nature.” But St Cyril, as Leontius also testifies, read “the natures.” At this point the manuscript of Leontius has in the heading “according to it,” but one should nevertheless read “at Ephesus,” if indeed we believe both other witnesses and Leontius, *Against Nestorians and Eutychians*, book I, p. 552, who say that this passage of Julius was read at the Ephesian synod, as in fact it is read there. Severus likewise read “the natures”; finally Ephraemius too, in Photius, codex 329, col. 829.]

### Encyclical of Julius, Archbishop of Rome

To the beloved brothers everywhere, bishops of the catholic Church: Julius, grace in Christ.

[Col. 0876A]

I am persuaded, beloved brothers, concerning our faith in the Lord, God, and King, from ecclesiastical history, beginning with Hosea the prophet concerning God the Word and the Father as Lord: “I will not utterly abandon Jacob to destruction; for I am God and not a man in your midst, the Holy One; and I will not enter into a city. I shall go after the Lord.” By these words and others like them, God the Word, having become human, says to those who confess him to be merely a holy man and not God: “I am God and not a man.”

I believe in the Trinity glorified and worshipped in one Godhead and essence—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and in the descent from heaven, the incarnation from the holy Virgin Mary, and the manifestation of God the Word and our Savior Jesus Christ; and in his manifestation among human beings as God and man. He is not one God and another man, but one hypostasis and one person [Col. 0876B] of God the Word and of the flesh from Mary: from God and from woman; the same one passible and impassible—suffering in the flesh and receiving our suffering, but in Godhead dissolving suffering, and through salvific death destroying our death; enlightening and granting life and incorruption to believers, enjoyment of future impassible things, and the inheritance with glory of the heavenly and divine kingdom.

> [Note: Here one person, not one nature, is stated.]

*(Mai, Collectio, vol. VII, p. 165.)*

### Of Julius, Archbishop of Rome, against those who contend against the divine incarnation of the Word under pretext of the *homoousion*

[Col. 0876C]

> [Note: Ephraemius also read this title, according to Photius, codex 229, col. 813.]

Let no one disparage the lordly and saving flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ under pretext of the *homoousion* (“consubstantial”). For neither we, nor our synod, nor any person possessed of human reason, calls or conceives a body by itself to be consubstantial. Nor do we say that the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ is from heaven; rather, we confess that God the Word was made flesh from the holy Virgin Mary. Nor do we divide him from his flesh. Rather, there is one person, [Col. 0876D] one hypostasis, wholly man and wholly God.

> [Note: Again, correctly “one person”; but below, “one nature.” Julius thus speaks without strict distinction.]

If, therefore, we believe that our Master Jesus Christ came in the likeness of a human being, then from that very virginal conception—by which the Virgin is demonstrated to be *Theotokos*, God-bearer, and which is the mystery of our salvation, namely that God the Word was made flesh—he is inseparable and indivisible from his own flesh. And by its union with God the Word, his flesh, endowed with a rational soul, shares in the designation belonging to the Word’s consubstantiality by nature with the Father, since it is his flesh. For we truly confess that God the Word became flesh. If it does not share in this, it is wholly alienated. For no salvation from the incarnation would follow for believers if it existed outside the divine Trinity; for nothing outside the divine Trinity is worshipful or saving.

Instead, the incarnation would prove superfluous and untimely for them, and the statements of the divine Scriptures would, according to them, be found false: for example, “The Word became flesh,” and “Today Jesus Christ was born for us in the city of David.” “Mighty God,” “Child,” and all similar expressions would likewise be false. Nor would the Virgin still be believed to be *Theotokos*—which is unlawful and impious, alien to every God-fearing soul. For every hope of Christians would be overthrown for them, and Christianity itself would be reckoned as nothing. For even the great and precious gift of Christians—the washing administered into Christ’s death—would not be reckoned divine but human, if the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ were not numbered within the divine Trinity.

But we must confess as Son of God and true, before the ages, our Lord Christ Jesus, consubstantial with the Father, whom the Virgin bore as Savior and Redeemer; and we rightly offer worship to him. Nor is his flesh excluded from worship. For where the divine life is not delimited, the objects of worship cannot be delimited. Whoever does not worship a person’s flesh does not worship that person. Therefore, in the union of the Word with his animate and rational [Col. 0877C] flesh, one worship is offered by us to the one Son.

> [Note: Therefore the author of this writing acknowledged a rational soul in Christ, unlike what is said above, col. 879.]

Thus the Evangelist proclaims one life of the Word and flesh: “The Word became flesh.” Therefore, if the Word became flesh, one who worships the Word worships the flesh; and one who worships the flesh worships the Godhead. The apostles, worshipping Christ Jesus and worshipping his body, worshipped God the Word. The angels too ministered to him as to their own Lord, approaching the body. The Virgin, from the beginning bearing flesh, bore the Word and was *Theotokos*. The Jews, crucifying the body, crucified God.

And no division of the Word and his flesh is set forth in the divine Scriptures. Rather, there is one nature, one hypostasis, one operation, one person: the same one wholly God and wholly man. His essence, according to the invisible, is Godhead; according to the visible, flesh. Therefore the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ is neither alienated from nor divided from the divine Trinity. For in enumerating the Trinity he established baptism, which gives remission of sins and resurrection of flesh; this is a work of Godhead and not of created nature. For the body and the God whose body it is are one and the same—not because the flesh has been changed into the bodiless, but because it retains both its own character derived from us through birth from the Virgin and what is above us through the mixture, or union, of God the Word.

*(From the same source.)*

## Notice concerning the Letter to the Antiochenes

*(From Coustant.)*

[Col. 0878A]

I. For a fuller understanding of this letter, it will be helpful briefly to recall the preceding events. Among the presbyters of Mareotis whom Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, together with an Egyptian synod, deposed from the rank of presbyter about the year of Christ 320, there was a certain Pistus. Although condemned both by the judgment of that synod and by the subscription of the Mareotic and Alexandrian clergy, and additionally expelled from the Church in 325 by the decision of the Council of Nicaea (see Epiphanius, *Heresies* 69.8), the Eusebians nevertheless appointed him bishop of Alexandria about 339, lest the Arians should lack their own bishop in that city.

They then sent to Julius the presbyter Macarius and the deacons Martyrius [Col. 0878B] and Hesychius, with letters written in favor of Pistus against Athanasius, and perhaps also against Marcellus of Ancyra and Asclepas, bishop of Gaza. Athanasius states, *Apology against the Arians*, no. 1, that these letters were written by Eusebius, who had unlawfully transferred from Berytus to Nicomedia and thence to Constantinople. But Julius, Letter I, no. 8, implies that Eusebius wrote them with only a few associates participating. Meanwhile, as Athanasius’s envoys arrived at Rome, Macarius the presbyter secretly fled, fearing to be refuted by them. The Eusebian envoys who remained, namely Martyrius and Hesychius, met with Athanasius’s presbyters and, being unable to resist them, requested that a synod be convened. On this point the parties then agreed. Accordingly, summoned by Julius’s letter, Athanasius immediately went to Rome.

After Athanasius’s arrival, Julius sent his presbyters Philoxenus and Elpidius to the Eusebians with letters summoning them on an appointed day to a synod. But, as Athanasius relates, *Letter to the Monks*, no. 11, the Eusebians detained those envoys beyond the agreed day of the synod—namely, as Julius says below in no. 6, until January 342—and then dismissed them to Julius with a letter.

II. In this letter they complained that Julius dealt insultingly with them, because he had summoned them, as they said (no. 2), to render an account of matters decided by them before his own synod; and they alleged (no. 3) that every synod’s authority ought to be firm, and that a judge is wronged when his judgment is examined by another. They then appealed (no. 5) to what had occurred in the times of Novatus, or Novatian, and Paul of Samosata; according to them, easterners had accepted the western judgment concerning Novatus or Novatian, and westerners the eastern judgment concerning Paul of Samosata. They added (ibid.) that bishops’ honor was equal—indeed, the same—and that their dignity should not be measured by the size of their cities. Refusing to come to Rome, to which they had been invited, they pleaded (no. 6) that neither the shortness of the appointed time nor the state of eastern affairs, that is, the Persian war, allowed it. They also indicated (no. 8) that they were disturbed because Julius had addressed letters only to Eusebius and a few of his associates, not to all of them. [Col. 0879A]

Above all, they charged that same pope (nos. 9 and 20) with having granted communion to Athanasius and Marcellus, concerning whom they wrote, in no. 16, that he was impious toward Christ. They said, as though Julius were influenced by party spirit: “You have chosen the communion of Marcellus and Athanasius rather than ours.” Among these things there were indeed testimonies by which they seemed to honor Julius (no. 1); but their accompanying remarks, by which they reproached him (no. 5) with kindling the flame of discord, showed that this honor was fictitious and wholly insincere.

III. When Julius received this letter, fearing that, if it were made public, everyone would be offended by such insolence, he kept it with him as long as there remained hope that at least some of the Eusebians would come to him. But when he began wholly to despair of this, he finally produced the letter before a synod assembled at the place where the presbyter Vito held meetings (Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, no. 20), and undertook the task of answering it, entrusted to him by the synod itself, which consisted of more than fifty bishops. The date of his reply depends upon when Athanasius came to Rome. For, when the appended letter was written, this bishop is said below, in no. 13, to have been awaiting his opponents at Rome for eighteen months. Yet Athanasius had not left Alexandria when Gregory, sent to that city from the Antiochene council held in 341 at the Encaenia [Col. 0880A] and forcibly installed in his place shortly before Easter, arrived there. Only then did Athanasius go to Rome; he could not have reached it before May. If, therefore, we begin from that month and count another eighteen months, during which Athanasius is reported to have remained in the City, it follows that the appended letter should be dated to September 342, or thereabouts.

It is addressed to those who had gathered at Antioch and written to Julius. Socrates, book I, chapter 12, and Sozomen, book III, chapter 8, also mention this synod and its letter; but they seem to have departed from the truth in suggesting that the easterners assembled there not to reply to Julius’s letters summoning them to the Roman synod, but rather to those accusing them of failing to come—namely, the appended letter. This letter was sent through Count Gabianus, but could not be delivered to Eusebius. For Socrates, book II, chapter 12, and Sozomen, book III, chapter 7, state that he died shortly after the Council of Antioch and before learning Julius’s decision. Athanasius agrees with them: after transcribing this whole letter in the *Apology against the Arians*, nos. 21–36, he adds at the end of no. 36: “Meanwhile Eusebius died.”

## Letter of Julius to the Antiochenes

*(Coustant, p. 353.)*

Julius to Danius,

> [Note: In the latest edition of Athanasius it has been observed that neither should “the Deacon” be read here with Nannius, nor should Danius, as with most modern writers, be understood as Dianius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, although that bishop attended the Antiochene synod. Rather, it is Theognius of Nicaea, who is repeatedly called Diognius by Athanasius and Diognitus by Hilary, *Fragments* II.2. The documents reported by Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, pp. 192, 193, and 195, establish that after Eusebius he customarily held first place among the Arian leaders. Further, from the Council of Sardica, III, where, as in Hilary, *Fragments* II.2, letters forged by Theognitus against Athanasius and Marcellus were read, it is inferred that this famous Theognius had played a notable role in composing letters promoting the Arian cause. Thus he might seem the architect of the letter to which Julius now replies, and for that reason to have had his name placed before the others. Nevertheless, the fact that below, no. 6, the Nicene bishop is called not Danius but, according to customary usage, Diognius, prevents us from unhesitatingly accepting this conjecture.]

Flacillus,

> [Note: He was bishop of Antioch; he is again mentioned in the memorial of the Egyptian bishops to Count Dionysius and in the reply of the same Dionysius in Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, pp. 196–197. Sozomen, III.6, calls him Plaketos; Socrates, II.9, Plaketos; and Theodoret, I.22, Plakeitios.]

Narcissus, Eusebius, Marius, Macedonius, Theodore, and their associates who wrote to us from Antioch: beloved brothers in the Lord, greetings.

> [Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### I. The easterners at Antioch replied in a contentious spirit

[Col. 0880C]

I have read the letter

> [Note: It does not survive.]

brought to me by my presbyters Elpidius and Philoxenus, and I was amazed that, while we had written in love and with a consciousness of truth, you replied contentiously and not as was fitting. For the pride and arrogance of the writers showed themselves through the letter; and these things are alien to faith in Christ. What had been written in love ought to have received an equal return in love, not in contention.

Is it not a mark of love to send presbyters to sympathize with those who suffer, and to urge those who had written to come, so that everything might quickly receive a resolution and be set right, and so that our brothers might suffer no longer and no one might slander you? But I do not know why you thought fit to be so disposed as to make us suppose that even the words by which you seemed to honor us were uttered with a certain disguise and mockery. For the presbyters who were sent, and who ought to have returned with joy, returned instead distressed by what they had seen done there. After reading the letter and reflecting on many things, I kept it with me, thinking that at least some of you would nevertheless come and that there would be no need for the letter, lest, when made public, it should grieve many here.

But since no one came and it became necessary to produce it, I confess to you that everyone was astonished and nearly disbelieved that such things had been written by you at all. For the letter displayed contention rather than love. If the person who dictated it wrote so for the sake of rhetorical display, such an undertaking belongs to other pursuits.

> [Note: Or, “it pertains to other affairs”; the Greek term permits either meaning.]

For in ecclesiastical matters there must be no display of eloquence, but apostolic canons, and a concern that not even one of the little ones in the Church be caused to stumble. It is better, according to the ecclesiastical saying, that a millstone be hung around one’s neck and that one be drowned in the sea than that even one of the little ones be caused to stumble (Matt. 18:6). If, however, such a letter came about because certain persons, exasperated by mutual ill-feeling—for I would not say that this was the mind of all—were grieved, they ought either not to have been offended at all or not to have let the sun go down upon their anger; at any rate, they ought not to have been carried so far as to set it forth in writing.

### II. There was nothing in their letter of which they could justly complain

[Col. 0881B]

For what was done that deserved complaint? Or at which words in my letter was there reason for you to be angry? Was it because we urged you to attend a synod? But this ought rather to have been received with joy. Those who have confidence in what they have done—or, as they themselves say, judged—do not take offense if their judgment is examined by others; rather, they are confident that what they themselves judged justly can never become unjust.

For this reason, the bishops gathered at the great Synod of Nicaea, not without God’s will, permitted the acts of an earlier synod to be examined in another synod, so that those judging, keeping before their eyes that a second judgment would follow, might investigate the matter with every precaution, and those judged might believe that they were judged not from the hatred and enmity of the earlier judges but according to the rule of justice.

> [Note: Baronius and others think that an otherwise missing Nicene decree is indicated here, and therefore suppose that, besides the received twenty canons, other canons were issued at Nicaea. But what prevents our understanding Julius to refer here to the fifth canon of that council? It ordains that if anyone is expelled by his own bishop, he is not to be received by others until his case is examined in a provincial synod; and if the synod approves the bishop’s just sentence, he is to be held separated by all until an assembly of bishops sees fit to pronounce a more lenient judgment in his favor. By these latter words the Nicene Fathers seem to permit another assembly of bishops to revoke, and therefore reconsider, the sentence pronounced by the earlier synod. Augustine’s well-known statement is relevant: “Councils held in individual regions or provinces unquestionably yield to the authority of plenary councils held from the whole Christian world; and even earlier plenary councils are often corrected by later ones, when experience reveals what was closed and discovers what was hidden” (*On Baptism against the Donatists*, II.3).]

If you do not wish such an ancient custom, mentioned and recorded in the great synod, to retain force among you, such a refusal will be unbecoming. For it is least fitting that a practice once established in the Church and confirmed by synods should be abrogated by a few. In any event, they could not be thought justly offended in this matter. For those sent by you Eusebians with letters—Macarius the presbyter, Martyrius, and Hesychius the deacons—came here and were unable to withstand the presbyters of Athanasius who had come here; they were refuted and convicted in every respect. Then they requested us to convene a synod and to write both to Athanasius, bishop at Alexandria, and to the Eusebians, so that in the presence of all a just judgment might be rendered. For they then promised to prove every accusation brought against Athanasius.

Martyrius and Hesychius were publicly refuted by us, and Athanasius’s presbyters, bishop of Alexandria, opposed them confidently; Martyrius and his associates, to speak the truth, were refuted in everything. Hence they were compelled to request a synod.

> [Note: No associate of Martyrius in requesting a synod seems to have been present except Hesychius, as is expressly stated shortly below. Although Macarius the presbyter is joined to them above, Julius says below, no. 4, that as soon as he heard Athanasius’s presbyters were pressing the matter, he fled by night; consequently he was absent from Rome when Martyrius and Hesychius, refuted by Athanasius’s presbyters, began to demand a synod. Martyrius and Hesychius were deacons, not presbyters. Yet Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*, no. 9, says that presbyters sent by the Eusebians requested the synod when they perceived themselves convicted. Has *presbyteroi*, “presbyters,” entered there in place of *presbeutai*, “envoys”? Or perhaps were they called presbyters because the head of the embassy was a presbyter, although he had fled shortly before?]

If, then, Martyrius and Hesychius had not requested that a synod be held, and I had urged those who wrote to undergo the inconvenience of travel

> [Note: Namely, so that those summoned might come to the synod.]

for the sake of our brothers who complained that they had suffered injustice, the exhortation would even then have been reasonable and just, since it is ecclesiastical and pleasing to God. But when those whom you Eusebians yourselves considered trustworthy asked us to convene it, it was appropriate that those summoned should not take offense but should come eagerly. Therefore the indignation of those who seemed to be offended was rash; and from this their refusal, by those unwilling to come, is shown to be unbecoming and suspect. Does anyone blame another for doing what he himself approves when he does it?

> [Note: Indeed, Athanasius states in the *Apology against the Arians*, no. 20, that the Eusebians themselves, in letters written to Julius, asked for a synod to be convened and that he himself, if he wished, should be judge. It is surprising that Julius omitted this here, unless Athanasius there attributes to the Eusebians themselves what their envoys did; Sozomen, III.7, also testifies: “Eusebius wrote to Julius, asking him to be judge of the matters decided against Athanasius at Tyre.”]

### III. They object that a synod is dishonored when its judgments are overturned; they themselves are convicted of overturning the acts of the Synod of Nicaea

[Col. 0884B]

For if, as you write, every synod possesses unshaken authority, and a judge is dishonored when his judgment is examined by others, consider, beloved, who they are that dishonor a synod and who overturn what their predecessors have judged. And lest, by examining each case now, I should seem to burden certain persons, the most recent occurrence alone—which one might shudder to hear—is sufficient to prove everything else that I omit.

The Arians, expelled for impiety by Alexander, of blessed memory, formerly bishop of Alexandria, were not merely rejected by the churches of individual cities; they were also anathematized by all who assembled together at the great Synod of Nicaea. For their offense was no ordinary one: they had sinned not against a human being, but against our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the Son of the living God. Yet those rejected by the whole inhabited world and publicly branded in every Church are now said to have been received; and I judge that even you ought rightly to be indignant on hearing this.

Who, then, are those who dishonor the synod? Are they not those who set at naught the votes of three hundred bishops and prefer impiety to piety? For the heresy of the Ariomaniacs was convicted and rejected by all bishops everywhere. But Athanasius and Marcellus, the bishops, have more persons speaking and writing in their defense. For we were given testimony concerning Marcellus that he opposed those who held Arius’s views in the Synod of Nicaea. Concerning Athanasius, witnesses testified that he was not convicted at Tyre, nor was he present in Mareotis, where the documents against him are said to have been prepared.

> [Note: This passage caused much difficulty for Nannius, who translated it into Latin as: “Nor was he condemned at Tyre.” They vainly attempted to reconcile this with the acts of the Synod of Tyre, from which it is most certain that Athanasius was condemned there. Their effort would have been more successful had they observed that *katagignōskein* is commonly used, both by other authors and by Athanasius, in the sense “to convict.” Julius himself, or his translator, uses the same word below, no. 14, when he observes that, if Athanasius had in fact been convicted at Tyre, another bishop should have been appointed in his place; he employs it in the same sense three times in nos. 20 and 21.]

You know, beloved, that proceedings conducted by only one side have no force, but are suspect. Yet although this was so, for the sake of exact investigation, and without prejudging either you or those who wrote for them, we urged those who had written to come, so that, since more persons had written in their defense, everything might be examined in a synod—so that neither the innocent might be condemned nor the guilty reckoned pure.

Therefore the synod is not dishonored by us, but by those who casually and heedlessly received the Arians condemned by all, contrary to the judgment of those who had judged them. For most of these judges have already departed to be with Christ; but those still surviving in this life are indignant that some people have annulled their judgment.

### Greek Version (parallel text)

**I.** I read the letter brought to me by my presbyters Elpidius and Philoxenus, and wondered how, when we had written in love and with a consciousness of truth, you had replied contentiously and not as was fitting. For the haughtiness and arrogance of the writers were displayed through the letter; and these things are alien to the faith in Christ. What was written in love ought to have received an equal return in love, and not in contention. Is it not a mark of love to send presbyters to sympathize with those who suffer, and to urge those who wrote to come, so that all things, quickly receiving a resolution, might be set right, and neither our brethren continue to suffer nor anyone slander you?

But I do not know why you thought fit to be so disposed as to cause us to suppose that, even in the words in which you seemed to honor us, you spoke with a certain disguise and irony. For the presbyters who were sent, who ought to have returned with joy, returned instead in distress because of what they had seen done there. When I had read the letter and reflected on many things, I kept it with me, supposing that at least some would nevertheless come and that there would be no need for the letter, lest, once made public, it should grieve many here. But since no one came and it became necessary to produce it, I confess to you that all were astonished and were almost incredulous that such things had been written by you at all. For the letter was one of contention rather than love. If the person who dictated it wrote for the sake of display in words, such a pursuit belongs to other matters. For in ecclesiastical affairs there is no display of words, but apostolic canons and care not to cause even one of the little ones in the Church to stumble. For, according to the ecclesiastical saying, it is better for a millstone to be hung about one’s neck and for one to be drowned than to cause even one of the little ones to stumble. But if such a letter came about because certain persons were distressed through mutual petty-mindedness—for I would not say that this was the opinion of all—they ought not to have been distressed at all, nor to have let the sun set upon their distress; in any event, they ought not to have been carried so far as to display it in writing.

**II.** For what occurred that was worthy of distress? Or in what that we wrote was there reason for you to be distressed? Was it because we urged you to attend a synod? But this ought rather to have been received with joy. For those who have confidence in what they have done—or, as they themselves say, judged—are not indignant if their judgment is examined by others; rather, they are confident that what they judged justly can never become unjust. For this reason the bishops assembled at the great Synod of Nicaea, not without God’s will, permitted the acts of an earlier synod to be examined in another synod, so that those judging, keeping before their eyes the second judgment that was to come, might examine with every safeguard, and those judged might believe that they were judged not through hostility on the part of the earlier judges but according to justice.

If you do not wish such an ancient custom, mentioned and recorded in the great synod, to retain force among you, such a refusal is unbecoming. For what has once acquired customary force in the Church and has been confirmed by synods ought not reasonably to be set aside by a few. Besides, they could not justly appear to have been distressed in this matter. For those among you who belong to Eusebius and were sent with letters—Macarius the presbyter and Martyrius and Hesychius the deacons—when they arrived here and could not withstand Athanasius’s presbyters who had come here, but were refuted and convicted in all things, then requested us to convene a synod and to write both to Athanasius, the bishop at Alexandria, and to those belonging to Eusebius, so that a just judgment might be rendered in the presence of all; for then they promised to prove all the charges against Athanasius.

For Martyrius and Hesychius were publicly refuted by us, while the presbyters of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, opposed them confidently; and Martyrius and his associates, to speak the truth, were refuted in everything. Hence they requested that a synod be held. If, therefore, even without Martyrius and Hesychius requesting a synod, I had urged those who wrote to undergo the inconvenience for the sake of our brethren who alleged that they had suffered injustice, the exhortation would still have been reasonable and just; for it is ecclesiastical and pleasing to God. But when those whom you yourselves, the adherents of Eusebius, considered trustworthy also requested that we convene it, it was fitting that those summoned should not be distressed, but rather should come eagerly. Accordingly, the apparent indignation of those who were distressed is rash; and the refusal of those unwilling to come is thereby shown to be unbecoming and suspect. Does anyone blame what he himself approves when he does it, if he sees it done by another?

**III.** For if, as you write, every synod possesses unshaken authority, and the judge is dishonored when his judgment is examined by others, consider, beloved, who are the persons dishonoring a synod and undoing the judgments of those who judged earlier. And lest I seem to burden certain persons by now examining each case, the latest occurrence alone—at which one might shudder on hearing it—is enough to prove all that I omit. The Arians, expelled for impiety by Alexander of blessed memory, formerly bishop of Alexandria, were not merely rejected by those in each city, but were anathematized by all who assembled together at the great Synod of Nicaea. For their offense was no ordinary one, nor had they sinned against a human being, but against our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the Son of the living God. Yet those rejected by the whole inhabited world and publicly branded throughout every Church are now said to have been received; and I judge that even you ought rightly to be indignant on hearing it.

Who then are those who dishonor the synod? Are they not those who set the votes of three hundred bishops at nothing and prefer impiety to piety? For the heresy of the Ariomaniacs was convicted and rejected by all bishops everywhere; but Athanasius and Marcellus, the bishops, have more persons speaking and writing in their defense. For concerning Marcellus testimony was given to us that he had opposed those who held the views of Arius in the Synod of Nicaea. Concerning Athanasius testimony was given that he was not convicted at Tyre and was not present in Mareotis, where the documents against him are said to have been prepared. You know, beloved, that proceedings conducted by one side have no force, but are suspect. Yet, although these things were so, for the sake of exactness, without prejudging either you or those writing on their behalf, we urged those who wrote to come, so that, since more persons had written in their defense, all things might be examined in a synod, in order that neither the innocent be condemned nor the guilty be reckoned pure. Therefore the synod is not dishonored by us, but by those who casually and as chance had it received the Arians condemned by all, contrary to the judgment of those who had judged them. For most have already departed to be with Christ; but those still living are indignant that some have annulled their judgment.

### IV. They violate the Nicene Synod in the affair of the Eusebian Pistus; Julius preserves it inviolate.

[Col. 0885B]

We learned that this was so from what occurred at Alexandria. For a certain Carpones, expelled by Alexander on account of the Arian heresy, together with some others likewise expelled for the same heresy, came here, sent by a certain Gregory. [Note: (2) He is listed among those who deserted the Church by Alexander in Athanasius, new edition, p. 397, and by Socrates, book I, ch. 6. Epiphanius, *Heresies* 69, likewise reports that he administered one of the Alexandrian churches.] We learned the same thing also from the presbyter Macarius and the deacons Martyrius and Hesychius. Before Athanasius’s presbyters arrived, they urged us to write at Alexandria to a certain Pistus, at a time when Athanasius too, the bishop, was residing at Alexandria. But when the presbyters of Bishop Athanasius arrived, they showed that this Pistus was an Arian, formerly expelled by Bishop Alexander and by the Synod of Nicaea, and that he had been ordained by a certain Secundus, whom the great synod had expelled as an Arian. [Note: (3) “The same thing” does not refer to the matter immediately narrated, but to that which Julius undertakes to prove at the beginning of this section: namely, how little account the Eusebians made of the decrees of the Nicene Synod. He first proves that he learned this from the example of Carpones and his companions, sent by Gregory to Rome, and now from that of Pistus and Secundus.] [Note: (4) Namely, the bishop of Ptolemais, whom first a council of Egyptian bishops around the year 320, and then the Nicene Synod, condemned by anathema, as the records reported by Socrates, book I, chs. 6 and 9, attest. Therefore Sozomen’s statement, book I, ch. 21, cannot stand, where he says that Secundus, bishop of Ptolemais in Libya, together with Theognis, Maris, and others, approved the creed composed at the Council of Nicaea. Nor does the explanation devised by Valesius to reconcile Sozomen with Socrates avail: namely, that Secundus and his companions at first wholly rejected the Nicene formula of faith, but later approved it out of fear of the emperor, who threatened exile to those who dissented. For the Nicene Fathers themselves, in their synodal letter sent to the Alexandrian Church and into Egypt, announce that Secundus had been expelled from the Church; and Julius himself confirms this same fact seven years later, without denial from the Eusebian delegates. Thus at least this is certain concerning Secundus: he held the Nicene faith neither at the council nor afterward.]

Neither Martyrius himself nor his companions disputed this, nor did they deny that Pistus had received ordination from Secundus. Consider therefore from these facts who are justly liable to blame: we, who could not be persuaded to write to Pistus the Arian; or those who urged us to despise the great synod and to write to the impious as though they were pious?

For Macarius himself, the presbyter sent by Eusebius together with Martyrius, when he heard that Athanasius’s presbyters had arrived, departed by night, though physically ill, while we were awaiting his appearance before us together with Martyrius and Hesychius. Thus we reasonably inferred that he had withdrawn because he was ashamed that he would be refuted in the matter of Pistus. For the ordination of Secundus the Arian could not possibly have force within the Catholic Church. It would truly be an insult to the synod and to the bishops assembled in it if the things which they had done with such earnestness and reverence, as though God were present, were annulled as though of no value.

[Col. 0886B]

**4.** We learned this also from the things which occurred at Alexandria. For a certain Carpones, expelled by Alexander on account of Arius’s heresy, together with some others likewise expelled for the same heresy, came here, having been sent by a certain Gregory. We learned this same thing also from the presbyter Macarius and the deacons Martyrius and Hesychius. For before Athanasius’s presbyters arrived, they urged us to write at Alexandria to a certain Pistus, at a time when Athanasius the bishop too was in Alexandria. But Athanasius the bishop’s presbyters, when they arrived, demonstrated that this Pistus was an Arian, expelled by Bishop Alexander and by the Synod of Nicaea, and ordained by a certain Secundus, whom the great synod expelled as an Arian. Neither those associated with Martyrius disputed this, nor did they deny that Pistus had received his ordination from Secundus.

Consider therefore also from these facts who are justly subject to blame: we, who did not yield so as to write to Pistus the Arian; or those who advised us to dishonour the great synod and to write to the impious as though they were pious? For Macarius the presbyter too, sent by Eusebius with those associated with Martyrius, when he heard that Athanasius’s presbyters had arrived, departed by night, though ill in body, while we were awaiting his appearance with those associated with Martyrius and Hesychius. Consequently, we reasonably inferred that he withdrew because he was ashamed of the refutation concerning Pistus. For it is impossible for the ordination of Secundus the Arian to have force in the Catholic Church. It is indeed an affront to the synod and to the bishops assembled in it, if what was done with such earnestness and reverence, as though God were present, should be annulled as of no account.

### V. Their feigned concern for synodal decrees.

[Col. 0888A]

If, then, as you write, the decrees of synods ought to remain in force by the example of what was done in the case of Novatian and Paul of Samosata, it was much more fitting that the decision of the three hundred should not be annulled, and that the universal synod should not be dishonoured by a few. For the Arians are heretics just as those men were, and similar decisions were issued against these as against them. [Note: [Col. 0887B] (1) Socrates, book II, ch. 15, elucidates this passage, whose sense the earlier Latin translations have not adequately expressed. He says that Julius was answered by the Orientals assembled at Antioch that it did not belong to him to investigate whether they wished to expel anyone from their churches; for they had not objected when Novatian was expelled from the Church. The Eusebians themselves explain their meaning more plainly in Hilary, fragment III, II.26, repeating the same calumny at Philippopolis, not merely against Julius but also against the Westerners, as follows: “They were attempting to introduce this novelty, which the ancient custom of the Church abhors: that whatever Eastern bishops might perhaps decide in a council should be reconsidered by Eastern bishops, and likewise whatever bishops of the Western regions might decide should be undone by Easterners.” Yet the acts of our forebears establish that the decrees of all councils conducted justly and lawfully are to be affirmed. For a council held in the city of Rome concerning the heretics Novatian, Sabellius, and Valentinus was confirmed by the Easterners; and again, what was decided in the East concerning Paul of Samosata was subscribed by all. I note in passing that in all those passages the word “Novatian” should have been substituted for “Novatus.” The Eusebians now invoke in vain what was done in Novatian’s case, in order to establish that what has been decided by one council ought not to be examined at all by another. For, as Eusebius himself testifies, when a synod had assembled at Rome on this matter, and the bishops in the provinces had separately deliberated what should be done, the following decree was promulgated to all: that Novatus [read Novatian] and those who, together with him, had arrogantly exalted themselves were to be regarded as outside the Church. Accordingly Cyprian writes to Pope Stephen, Letter 1, no. 2, that Novatian had recently been checked and refuted and excluded throughout the whole world by the priests of God—who, as Eusebius was shortly to say, had deliberated separately in councils. Nor is their assertion more credible that the judgment of the Council of Antioch against Paul of Samosata was accepted without prior examination. For, as Eusebius himself relates in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, ch. 30, after Paul had been condemned by the council, he refused to leave the house of the church at Antioch and therefore appealed to the emperor. Aurelian ordered the house to be delivered to those to whom the bishops of the Christian religion in Italy and the bishop of Rome should write; Eusebius himself testifies that this was most rightly decided. But how could the Roman bishop and the other bishops have written to Domnus, appointed in Paul’s place on that occasion, and awarded him the house of the church at Antioch, unless they had first reviewed the judgment of the Council of Antioch in Paul’s case—especially since they knew that they would have to render an account of their decision before a pagan emperor? Nor is what the Eusebians again objected at Philippopolis concerning Sabellius’s case any more consistent with truth or equity. For the preceding Letter 1, to Xystus II, no. 2, shows that Sabellius’s heresy arose at Ptolemais in Pentapolis, and thus in the East, and was first refuted and condemned by Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, who likewise belonged to the East. It follows that the Eastern judgment concerning Sabellius was confirmed at Rome, rather than that the judgment of the Roman council concerning the same heretic was ratified by the agreement of the Easterners. Or at least, if Dionysius of Alexandria, content to refute Sabellius’s emerging heresy, sent to Xystus the letters by which he refuted it, awaited what the Roman council would decide concerning it, and finally approved the Roman synod’s judgment together with the other Easterners, the authority of the Roman bishop in the East will nevertheless be evident from this.]

When such deeds have been dared, who has kindled the flame of discord? In your letter you accused us of having done this. Did we introduce discord, we who sympathize with afflicted brothers and have done everything according to the canon? Or rather, did those who contentiously and contrary to canon annulled the decision of the three hundred and in every respect dishonoured the synod? For not only were Arians admitted, but bishops also have contrived to transfer themselves from place to place. [Note: (2) He attacks Eusebius, who, abandoning the see of Berytus, seized that of Nicomedia and finally, rejecting this also, occupied Constantinople. Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, had reproved the first transfer even before the Nicene Synod, whose canon 15 forbids such translations, in his encyclical letter in Athanasius, new edition, vol. I, p. 397, and in Socrates, book I, ch. 6. The Alexandrian synod of 340 likewise condemned both transfers, in Athanasius, ibid., p. 129: “He did not observe Paul’s precept: ‘Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release.’ And if this was said concerning a wife, how much more concerning the Church and the episcopal office itself, to which someone bound ought not seek another, lest he be found from the sacred Scriptures to be an adulterer.” In 347 the Synod of Sardica, desiring to extirpate this evil custom entirely, refused even lay communion to such a man. Damasus subsequently judged him worthy of anathema once and again.]

If, therefore, you truly regard the honour of bishops as equal and the same, and do not, as you write, judge bishops according to the size of cities, then he entrusted with a small city ought to have remained in the one entrusted to him. He ought not, despising that which had been entrusted to him, to pass over to another not committed to him—thus scorning what God had given him and pursuing the empty glory of men.

[Col. 0887A]

**5.** If then, as you write, the decrees of synods ought to remain in force by the example of the case of Novatian and Paul of Samosata, it was all the more necessary that the decision of the three hundred should not be annulled, and that the catholic [universal] synod should not be dishonoured by a few. For the Arians are heretics just as those men were, and the decisions against these are similar to those against them.

When these things have been dared, who are those who have kindled the flame of discord? For, writing, you blamed us as having done this. Did we produce discord, we who suffer with afflicted brothers and have done everything according to the canon? Or did those who, contentious and contrary to canon, annulled the decision of the three hundred and in every respect dishonoured the synod? For not only were Arians received, but bishops have also devised transferring from place to place.

If, therefore, you truly consider the honour of bishops equal and the same, and do not judge bishops from the size of cities, as you write, then he who had been entrusted with a small city ought to remain in that entrusted to him; he ought not to despise what had been entrusted to him and transfer to that which had not been committed to him, so as to disdain what was given by God and love the vain glory of men.

### VI. In vain they plead the shortness of the appointed time as a reason for not coming to Rome.

[Col. 0889A]

Therefore, beloved, you ought to have come here and not declined, so that the affair might be brought to an end; for reason requires this. But perhaps the appointed time prevented you; for in your letter you complained that we had fixed too short a period for convening the synod.

But this, beloved, is a mere pretext. For if that day had overtaken persons already on their journey, they could rightly have alleged that the appointed interval was too short. But if those unwilling to come detained even their presbyters until the month of January, [Note: (1) Some believe that June should be preferred to “January,” but the manuscript copies and the history itself oppose this. Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*, 11, says only that Julius’s delegates were detained beyond the appointed time. Either reading indicates that the day fixed for holding the council fell at the end of the year 341.] it is the mere excuse of persons lacking confidence in their case.
