For they would have come, as I said before, had they hoped well concerning their cause—not considering the distance of the journey or looking to the appointed time, but trusting in the justice and equity of their cause.

[Col. 0890A]

**6.** Therefore, beloved, you ought to have come and not excused yourselves, in order that the matter might reach its conclusion; for reason requires this. But perhaps the deadline impeded you; for, writing, you complained that we had fixed too narrow a time for the synod.

But this too, beloved, is a pretext. If the day had shut out some who were coming, then the interval of the deadline could have been shown to be short. But if those unwilling to come detained even the presbyters until the very month of January, this is the excuse of those who lack confidence. For they would have come, as I said before, if they had confidence, looking neither to the length of the journey nor to the deadline, but speaking boldly on the basis of what was just and reasonable.

### VII.

[Col. 0889B]

But perhaps they did not come because of the circumstances of the times. For this also you again indicated in writing: namely, that we ought, upon observing the present state of affairs in the East, not to have urged you to come. [Note: (2) Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*, 11, explains this state of Eastern affairs of which they spoke: “They invented the futile excuse: ‘Because of the Persian war, we cannot now come.’” He mocks the excuse in these words: “What has war to do with bishops? And why are they hindered by the Persian war from coming to Rome, a distant city beyond the sea, when at that time they ranged like lions through Eastern places bordering on Persia?” Julius, however, seems to have understood their pretext concerning the Eastern situation as though they spoke of the grievous and mournful division of the Eastern churches, from which bishops ought not then to be absent.]

If you did not set out because of such a condition of affairs, as you say, then above all you ought, having considered this state of affairs, not to have become the authors of schism, lamentation, and tears in the churches. [Note: (3) They became the authors of schism and mourning when, while Athanasius was alive, they ordained Gregory bishop and intruded him by force and many outrages into the Alexandrian see.] But those who did such things have shown that the state of affairs was not the cause, but rather the deliberate purpose of those who were unwilling to come.

[Col. 0890B]

**7.** But perhaps they did not come because of the circumstances. For, writing, you indicated again that we ought, after considering the state of affairs in the East, not to have urged you to come. If, then, you did not come because the circumstances were such, as you say, you ought first, having considered these circumstances, not to have become causes of schism, lamentation, and mourning in the churches. But those who did these things have shown that the cause was not the circumstances, but the intention of those who did not wish to come.

### VIII. They complain unjustly that Julius alone wrote only to the Eusebians.

[Col. 0889C]

I am also astonished at that part of your letter in which you complained that I alone wrote to Eusebius and his companions alone, and not to all of you. [Note: (4) A conjecture has been made that one should read here “to Eusebius alone,” and below: “Therefore either Eusebius ought not alone, apart from all of you, to have written,” and so forth. Thus expressions made in the plural would be understood as said singularly of Eusebius alone. Julius is speaking here of the letter delivered to him by Martyrius and Hesychius. Above, section 4, he recalls that Martyrius and Hesychius were sent by Eusebius (*para Eusebiou*). Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, 1, likewise ascribes the letter which Martyrius and Hesychius brought Julius to Eusebius alone: “Eusebius wrote.” Socrates, book II, ch. 11, and Sozomen, book III, ch. 7, agree with Athanasius. Theodoret, book II, ch. 4, while discussing the same letter, retains Julius’s phrase, saying not simply “Eusebius,” but “those around Eusebius”; Epiphanius, *Tripartite History*, ch. 6, and Valesius understand this phrase to mean Eusebius and his associates—the Eusebians—as the writers of the letter. The Synod of Sardica, in Hilary, fragment II, 2, identifies the associates, if it is speaking of these earlier rather than later Eusebian letters: Eusebius, Maris, Theodorus, Diognitus, Ursacius, and Valens; Theodoret, book II, ch. 8, adds Menophantus and Stephen.]

For in those who complained one finds sophistry rather than truth. Since I had received letters against Athanasius from no one except Martyrius and Hesychius, I necessarily replied to those who had written against him. Therefore either the Eusebians ought not to have written alone, apart from all of you, or you, to whom I did not write, ought not to be offended that a reply was sent to those who had written. For if it was fitting to send letters to all of you, it was equally fitting that you should have written with them.

But now, considering what was appropriate, we wrote to those who had informed us and sent letters to us. If you were disturbed also because I alone wrote to them, it is consistent for you to be indignant that they wrote to me alone. But here too, beloved, the excuse is plausible indeed, but not equitable.

Nevertheless, it is necessary to make known to you that, although I wrote alone, this judgment is not mine alone, but that of all the bishops in Italy and in these regions. I did not wish to make all of them write, lest the burden be onerous and troublesome to many. Indeed, the bishops have now assembled at the appointed time and have held the same judgment which I again make known to you in this letter. Therefore, beloved, although I write alone, recognize that this is the judgment of all.

These points are sufficient to show that some among you advance excuses which are not reasonable, but unjust and suspect.

[Col. 0890B]

**8.** I am astonished also at that part of the letter—how it was written at all by you—in which you say that I alone wrote only to those around Eusebius, and not to all of you. For one would find in those who complained facility rather than truth. Since I received letters against Athanasius from no source other than through those associated with Martyrius and Hesychius, I was necessarily obliged to write to those who had written against him.

Therefore either those around Eusebius ought not to have written alone, apart from all of you; or you, to whom I did not write, ought not to be grieved if a reply was written to those who had written. For if it was necessary to write also to all of you, it was necessary for you too to write together with them. But now, observing what was consequent, we wrote to those who had informed us and sent things to us. If you were disturbed because I alone wrote to them, it is consistent that you should be indignant because they too wrote to me alone.

But in this too, beloved, the excuse is plausible but not reasonable. Yet it is necessary to make known to you that, even if I wrote alone, this is not my judgment alone, but also that of all the bishops in Italy and in these regions. I did not wish to cause all of them to write, lest they should bear a burden from many. Indeed, at the appointed deadline bishops assembled and adopted this judgment, which I again make known to you in writing. Therefore, beloved, even though I write alone, know that this is the judgment of all.

These things, then, suffice concerning the fact that some among you have procured excuses not reasonable, but unjust and suspect.

### IX. Athanasius and Marcellus were rightly received into communion.

[Col. 0892B]

That we did not rashly or unjustly receive our fellow bishops Athanasius and Marcellus into communion is sufficiently clear from what has already been said. Nevertheless, it will be worthwhile to show you briefly.

The Eusebians and their associates first wrote against Athanasius; you too have now written. But very many bishops from Egypt and from other provinces wrote on Athanasius’s behalf. [Note: (1) Athanasius inserted this Egyptian letter entire at the beginning of his *Apology against the Arians*, and at section 20 expressly states that it was sent to all bishops and to Julius, bishop of Rome.]

First, it must be observed that your letters against him conflict with one another. The earlier letters agree in no respect with the later; rather, in many points the first are refuted by the second, and the second are charged with falsehood by the first. Where letters do not agree among themselves, no credence is due to what they say.

Further, if you demand belief for your letters, it is consistent not to deny belief to those who wrote in his defence—especially because you write concerning matters that occurred far from you, whereas they write while being in the very places where they saw the man himself and the events done there. [Note: (2) Julius undoubtedly here sets Eusebian testimony against the testimony of the Mareotic clergy in Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, 74, p. 191: “We bear witness, for we are not far from the bishop, but accompany him throughout Mareotis as he visits all places: whatever has been alleged is sheer calumny.”] They bear witness to the integrity of his life, affirming that in every matter he suffered a conspiracy against him.

Again, a certain Arsenius, said to be a bishop, was once alleged to have been murdered by Athanasius; but we learned that he was alive, indeed that he was Athanasius’s friend. [Note: (3) In the letter Arsenius wrote to Athanasius, reproduced in Athanasius’s *Apology against the Arians*, 69, he calls himself bishop of the Hypselites, who had formerly belonged to Meletius. Socrates, book I, ch. 32, seems to assign him a bishopric of the Meletian sect distinct from that of the Hypselites, saying: “He had formerly been bishop of the Meletian sect; then, at the Council of Tyre, he subscribed to Athanasius’s deposition as bishop of the city of the Hypselites.” But Socrates did not sufficiently grasp Arsenius’s words, which mean only that the Hypselites, whose bishop he calls himself, had formerly adhered to Meletius’s sect. Rufinus errs no less in writing that Arsenius was a presbyter of the Alexandrian clergy; later Greek biographers of Athanasius say that he was a reader of that same church.]

[Col. 0891B]

**9.** Concerning our having received our fellow bishops Athanasius and Marcellus into communion neither lightly nor unjustly: although what was said before is sufficient, it is nevertheless reasonable to demonstrate it briefly to you.

Those around Eusebius first wrote against those around Athanasius, and you have now written as well. But very many bishops from Egypt and other provinces have written on Athanasius’s behalf. First, then, the letters from you against him conflict with one another; the later have no agreement with the earlier, but in many matters the earlier are undone by the later, and the later are charged with falsehood by the earlier. Since the letters disagree, there is no credence in what is said.

Then, if you think that what is written by you should be believed, it follows that those who wrote on his behalf should not be disbelieved—especially because you write from afar, whereas they, being in the places and knowing the man and the affairs taking place there, write in testimony to his life and affirm that he suffered conspiracy in every matter. Again, a certain Arsenius, a bishop, was once said to have been murdered by Athanasius; but we learned that he lives and is also friendly toward him.

### X. The Mareotic records are invalid in themselves, since only one party was present.

[Col. 0893A]

He—Athanasius—affirmed that the records drawn up in Mareotis had been made with only one party present. For we learned not only from his own words, but also from the actual records of the inquiries, which Martyrius and Hesychius brought us, that neither Macarius the presbyter, who was accused, nor his bishop Athanasius himself was present there. Reading them, we found that the accuser Ischyras was there, but neither Macarius nor Bishop Athanasius; moreover, Athanasius’s presbyters were refused permission when they requested to be present. [Note: (1) Athanasius incorporated their petition into his *Apology against the Arians*, 73, p. 189.]

But, beloved, if the judgment had been conducted sincerely, not only the accuser but also the accused ought to have been present. For just as at Tyre Macarius the accused and Ischyras the accuser were present, and nothing was proved there, so also in Mareotis not only the accuser but the accused ought to have gone there, so that, being present, he might either be convicted or, if not convicted, publicly expose the calumny.

But since this did not occur, and the accuser alone went there with those whom Athanasius had objected to, those proceedings certainly appear suspect. Athanasius also complained that those who went to Mareotis had gone there contrary to his wishes, saying that Theognis, Maris, Theodorus, Ursacius, Valens, and Macedonius—men who were suspect to him—had been sent.

[Col. 0894A]

**10.** He affirmed that the records made in Mareotis were made with only one party present. For neither Macarius the presbyter, who was accused, nor Athanasius his bishop was present there; and we learned this not only from his own words, but also from the records which those associated with Martyrius and Hesychius brought us. For, on reading, we found that Ischyras the accuser was there, but neither Macarius nor Bishop Athanasius; moreover, Athanasius’s presbyters, though requesting to be present, were not permitted.

But, beloved, if the tribunal was conducted truthfully, not only the accuser but also the accused ought to have been present. For just as at Tyre Macarius the accused and Ischyras the accuser were present, and nothing was proved, so it was necessary also in Mareotis that not the accuser alone should go, but the accused as well, so that, being present, he might either be convicted or, if not convicted, show the calumny.

But since this did not happen, and the accuser alone went with those whom Athanasius had rejected, the proceedings appear suspect. Athanasius also accused those who went to Mareotis of having gone contrary to his judgment; for he said that Theognis, Maris, Theodorus, Ursacius, Valens, and Macedonius, being suspect, were sent.

### XI. The falsehood of those same records is refuted by numerous witnesses.

[Col. 0893B]

He demonstrated this not only from his own words, but also from the letter of Alexander, formerly bishop of Thessalonica. He produced Alexander’s letter, written to Dionysius, the count at that synod, in which he declared that an evident conspiracy against Athanasius had been formed. (See Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, p. 197.)

He also produced an authentic document, written wholly in the hand of Ischyras himself, the accuser. (See Athanasius, ibid., p. 181.) In it, invoking God Almighty as witness, Ischyras declared that neither a cup had been broken nor a table overturned, but that he himself had been suborned by certain persons to fabricate this accusation.

When the presbyters of Mareotis arrived, they firmly affirmed that Ischyras was not a presbyter of the Catholic Church and that Macarius had committed no such offence as Ischyras alleged against him. The presbyters and deacons who came here bore testimony, not in a few matters but in very many, to the innocence of Bishop Athanasius, affirming that nothing alleged against him was true, but that a conspiracy had been fabricated against him.

Indeed, all the bishops of Egypt and Libya testified in their letters both that his ordination had been lawful and ecclesiastical and that all the allegations brought against him by you were false: no murder had occurred, no one had been killed on his account, no cup had been broken; all these things were contrary to truth. [Note: (2) Athanasius places these letters before Julius’s letter in his *Apology against the Arians*. In them the bishops of Egypt and Libya defend the canonical character of Athanasius’s ordination at section 6, and from the beginning of their letter utterly demolish the other calumnies concerning murder, the broken cup, and so forth.]

[Col. 0894B]

**11.** He demonstrated this not only from his own statements, but also from the letter of Alexander, formerly of Thessalonica. For he produced a letter of Alexander written to Dionysius, the count at the synod (*Reg. ms.*: *kymita*), in which he declares that an open conspiracy had been formed against Athanasius.

He also produced the authentic autograph document of Ischyras himself, the accuser, in which, calling God Almighty as witness, he said that neither a breaking of a cup nor an overturning of a table had occurred, but that he had been induced by certain persons to fabricate this accusation.

When presbyters from Mareotis arrived, they firmly affirmed that Ischyras was neither a presbyter of the Catholic Church nor had Macarius committed any such offence as he alleged. The presbyters and deacons who arrived here bore witness, not in a few matters but in many, on behalf of Bishop Athanasius, affirming that nothing of what was said against him was true, but that he had suffered a conspiracy.

All the bishops from Egypt and Libya also, writing, firmly affirmed that his ordination had been lawful and ecclesiastical, and that everything said against him by you was false: neither had a murder occurred, nor had any persons been killed on his account, nor had the breaking of a cup occurred; rather, all was false.

### XII. Their falsehood is demonstrated from the records themselves.

[Col. 0893D]

[Col. 0896A] Indeed, from the very records of the inquiries conducted in Mareotis with only one party present, Bishop Athanasius demonstrated that a certain catechumen, when examined, said that he had been inside with Ischyras at the time when, as they alleged, Macarius, Athanasius’s presbyter, entered that place. Other persons, likewise examined, said that Ischyras, then sick, lay in a small cell according to one account, and behind the door according to another, at the time when they say Macarius came there.

From these statements we consequently observe: how could one lying sick behind the door then have stood, performed the liturgy, and made the offering? Or how could an offering have been set forth while catechumens were inside? For if catechumens were inside, it was not yet the time for the offering.

As stated, Bishop Athanasius said these things and made them evident from the records themselves. Those with him affirmed that Ischyras had never been a presbyter in the Catholic Church, nor had he ever occupied a presbyter’s place in ecclesiastical assemblies. [Note: (2) That is, the Mareotic presbyters and deacons, whose affirmation is found in *Apology against the Arians*, 74.]

Moreover, when Alexander, with the great synod’s indulgent permission, received those of the Meletian schism, they affirmed that Ischyras had not at all been named by Meletius among his presbyters. This is the strongest evidence that he was not even one of the Meletian presbyters; for had he been one, he surely would have been numbered among them. [Note: (3) Athanasius likewise does not neglect this argument, but develops it in his *Apology*, 71–72.]

Besides these matters, Athanasius also exposed other lies of Ischyras from those records. For in the accusation in which he alleged that books had been burned when Macarius, as they say, burst in, he was convicted of falsehood by the very witnesses whom he had produced. [Note: (4) That is, as Athanasius says in *Apology*, 83, even the suborned witnesses testified that nothing of the kind had occurred and that Ischyras was lying.]

[Col. 0894D]

**12.** From the records made in Mareotis with only one party present, Bishop Athanasius demonstrated that one catechumen, when examined, said that he was inside with Ischyras when Macarius, Athanasius’s presbyter, as they say, came to the place. Others, when examined, said that Ischyras lay sick at that time: one said in a small cell, another behind the door, when they say that Macarius came there.

From these statements, then, we reasonably infer: how was it possible that the man lying sick behind the door should then have stood, performed the liturgy, and offered? Or how was it possible for an offering to have been set forth while catechumens were inside? For if the catechumens were inside, it was not yet the time for the offering.

As has been said, Bishop Athanasius stated these matters and demonstrated them from the records; and those with him affirmed that Ischyras had never at all been a presbyter in the Catholic Church, nor had ever assembled in the church as a presbyter. They also affirmed that, when Alexander received those from Meletius’s schism through the clemency of the great synod, Ischyras had not been named by Meletius among his own. This is also the strongest proof that he was not even Meletius’s man; for had he been, he would certainly have been counted with them.

Moreover, Athanasius showed from the records that Ischyras had lied in other matters also. For, having accused Macarius of burning books when, as they say, he came there, Ischyras was convicted of lying by the witnesses whom he himself produced.

### XIII. Athanasius’s innocence is shown by the confidence with which he awaits his adversaries at Rome.

[Col. 0896C]

When these things were being said, when so many witnesses stood for him and he himself produced so many proofs of his innocence, what, I ask, were we to do? What else did ecclesiastical rule require than that we should not condemn the man, but rather receive him and regard him as a true bishop—as indeed we did?

For besides all this, he remained here for one year and six months, awaiting your arrival or that of any who wished to come. By his presence he put all to shame, since he would not have been present unless he had confidence in his cause. [Note: (5) Athanasius was still at Alexandria in 341, and remained there at least until Easter, which that year fell on 19 April, as is clear from his encyclical letter to the bishops, section 5. Therefore the beginning of these eighteen months can scarcely be placed earlier than the end of May 341. Bernard de Montfaucon refutes at length, in observations 14 on the life and writings of St Athanasius, the opinion of those who begin to count them from 340.]

For he did not come of his own initiative, but came when summoned, having received our letters, as we also informed you in our letter. [Note: (6) That is, after Martyrius and Hesychius, the Eusebians’ delegates, had been refuted and convicted in every respect by Athanasius’s presbyters, who had likewise come to Rome, they requested of Julius that a synod should be convened and letters sent both to Athanasius and to the Eusebians, as was narrated above, section 2. These letters must therefore be distinguished from those which Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, 20, recalls as having been sent by Julius through his presbyters Elpidius and Philoxenus to the Eusebians. Athanasius testifies that these were first sent into the East when he himself had arrived at Rome. The distinction between the letters is also clear in Athanasius’s *Letter to the Solitaries*, 10–11.]

Yet, after so many and such great acts by us, you accused us of acting contrary to the canons.

[Col. 0895B]

**13.** Since these things were thus said, so many witnesses existed on his behalf, and he himself brought forward so many proofs, what were we to do? Or what does the ecclesiastical canon require, except that we should not condemn the man, but rather receive him and hold him to be a bishop, as indeed we did?

For besides all this, he remained here one year and six months, awaiting your presence or that of those willing to come; by his presence he put all to shame, because he would not have been present unless he had confidence. For he did not come of himself, but was summoned and received letters from us, just as we wrote to you. Yet after so many things, you reproached us as though we had acted contrary to the canons.

### XIV. The unlawful ordination of Gregory, and the actions connected with his entry into office.

[Col. 0896D] [Col. 0897A]

Consider, therefore, who have acted contrary to the canons: we, who, after so many proofs of his innocence, received the man; or those who, thirty-six stages distant, appointed at Antioch a certain foreigner as bishop and sent him to Alexandria escorted by military force? This was not done even when he had been banished to Gaul; for it ought to have been done then, if he had truly been convicted. Certainly, upon his return he found the church vacant and awaiting him. But now I do not know on what grounds these things have been done. First, to speak the truth, after we had written to convene a synod, no one ought to have anticipated the judgment of the synod. Next, such an innovation ought not to have been introduced against the Church. For what ecclesiastical canon, or what apostolic tradition, permits this: that while the Church is at peace, and so many bishops are in agreement with Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, Gregory should be sent—a stranger to the city, neither baptized there nor known to most, requested neither by presbyters, nor bishops, nor people—appointed at Antioch and dispatched to Alexandria, not with the presbyters or deacons of the city, nor with the bishops of Egypt, but with soldiers? For this is what those who came here said and complained of.

[Note: [Col. 0897C] (1) Antoninus’s itinerary agrees with the statement concerning July: for travelers proceeding from Antioch to Alexandria it in fact assigns thirty-six stopping-places [Col. 0897D]. That the ancients customarily measured the distance between places, or the length of journeys, by the number of stopping-places is confirmed by Augustine, *On the Unity of the Church*, ch. 10, no. 31: “Ascertain how many stopping-places there are from Jerusalem, by overland routes, round about as far as Illyricum.” On this matter see the observations in the new edition of Hilary, p. 270, note e, and p. 271, note a.]

Even if Athanasius had been found guilty after the synod, it was not right for an appointment to be made thus unlawfully and contrary to the ecclesiastical canon; rather, in that very church, from its own priesthood and clergy, the bishops of that province ought to have appointed someone, and the canons handed down from the Apostles ought not now to have been violated. [Note: [Col. 0897D] (2) There is no reason why protection and authority should be derived from the canons circulated under the Apostles’ name. In them you would look in vain for the rules which are here noted as having been disregarded. Athanasius explains how these “canons of the Apostles” are to be understood in the encyclical letter which he sent to the bishops as soon as Gregory had been intruded. In no. 2 he says: “If any accusation against us had force, it was proper that neither an Arian nor a man of the Arian sect should be ordained, but that, according to the ecclesiastical canons [Col. 0898C] and according to the words of Paul, when the people had assembled and the spirit of those ordaining was present with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, all matters should be investigated and carried out according to ecclesiastical laws, with the people and the clergy who sought him present.” Thus the rules mentioned by Julius are called canons of the Apostles because they derive their authority either from Paul’s expressed words or from apostolic tradition. Accordingly Cyprian, *Epistle* 68, writes to the people of Emerita that the divine tradition and apostolic observance must be carefully maintained; he teaches that it is observed throughout Africa and almost [Col. 0898D] throughout the provinces, that, for ordinations to be duly celebrated, the nearest bishops of the same province should assemble before the people over whom the candidate is ordained, and that the bishop should be chosen in the presence of the people, who know each person’s life most fully. Cyprian’s latter words also seem to indicate the practice commended by Julius: that the bishop to be ordained should be chosen from the clergy itself of the church for which he is to be ordained; otherwise, how could he be most fully known to the people placed under him? In the same work, pp. 163–64, Cyprian, in proving that Cornelius was legitimately ordained, lucidly explains the rules of canonical ordination. I pass over what the Council of Laodicea, canon 12, and Nicaea, canon 4, decree on this matter. The Fourth Council of Toledo, in 633, canon 19, renewed the various precepts which the Apostles and Fathers had handed down for observance in episcopal ordinations. But in those various passages nothing occurs that favors Gregory’s ordination, and nothing that does not openly oppose it.]

For if such a thing had been done against one of you, would you not have cried out? Would you not have demanded redress for the violation of the canons? Beloved, as in God’s presence, we speak and say with truth: this is neither pious, nor lawful, nor ecclesiastical.

Moreover, the things said to have been done by Gregory at his entrance show the character of his appointment. For in such peaceful times, as those who came from Alexandria themselves reported, and as the bishops also stated in their letters, the church suffered arson; virgins were stripped naked; monks were trampled underfoot; presbyters and many of the people were maltreated and subjected to violence; bishops were imprisoned; many were dragged about; and the holy mysteries—concerning whose violation they accused Macarius the presbyter—were plundered by pagans and cast upon the ground, in order that some might accept Gregory’s appointment. [Note: [Col. 0899D] (1) Athanasius, in the letter sent to the bishops on this matter, vividly describes the same outrages and others; in particular, no. 3 recounts that the church with its sacred baptistery was burned, holy virgins stripped naked, and monks trampled underfoot. But he says nothing about the mysteries being plundered and thrown to the ground. Since, however, he composed that letter immediately after his flight, he was not yet able to learn all that the Arians had perpetrated. Julius, moreover, recounts these matters not on Athanasius’s authority, but on that of those who had come from Alexandria and of the bishops who had written to him. That sacrileges of this sort were customary with the Arians is also proved by what Hilary, *Against Constantius*, no. 11, reports that they committed in the city of Toulouse; he himself protests against them [Col. 0900D] as follows: “Clerics beaten with clubs, deacons crushed with lead, and hands laid upon Him Himself—upon Christ Himself, as the saints understand with me.” Thus Hilary does not hesitate to call the sacred mysteries of which Julius speaks “Christ Himself,” because Christ is truly present in them, though hidden; indeed, he is Himself those mysteries.]

Such things show who are violating the canons. For if the appointment had been lawful, it would not by unlawful means have compelled obedience from those who lawfully refused obedience to him. And yet, after such things had occurred, you write that great peace had existed in Alexandria and Egypt. Unless, perhaps, the meaning of peace has been altered, and you now call such things peace.

[Note: [Col. 0900D] (2) So that works which until now we judged to belong to war may be said to suit it exceedingly well.]

**XV. Other reprehensible features of the proceedings in Mareotis.**

I also thought it necessary to inform you that Athanasius affirmed that Macarius had remained at Tyre under military guard; that the accuser alone had gone away with those proceeding to Mareotis; that, although the presbyters requested permission to be present at the investigation, this had been refused; and that the examination concerning the cup and the table had taken place before the prefect and his troop, with pagans and Jews present. At first this seemed incredible, unless it had been demonstrated from the official records themselves. [Note: [Col. 0900D] (3) This confession of faith, unless we are mistaken along with learned men, is the very one preserved for us by Epiphanius and appended to this letter.]

What caused us astonishment will, I think, also astonish you, beloved: presbyters, though they are ministers of the mysteries, are not permitted to be present, yet before a secular judge, catechumens being present, and—what is worse—in the presence of pagans and Jews, hostile and ill-disposed toward Christianity, an inquiry concerning Christ’s blood and Christ’s body is conducted. For even if some offense had indeed been committed, such matters ought to have been examined lawfully in the Church by clergy, and not by pagans who abhor the Word and do not know the truth. How great and what kind of sin this is, I am persuaded that both you and all others perceive. Such, then, are the matters concerning Athanasius.

**XVI. Marcellus is declared to hold right belief.**

With regard to Marcellus: since you also wrote concerning him as one impious toward Christ, I hastened to inform you that, when he came here, he firmly maintained that what you had written about him was untrue. Nevertheless, when we required him to state his faith, he answered with such confidence in his own person that we recognized that he professed nothing outside the truth. For he confessed that he held as pious a belief concerning our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ as the catholic Church holds; and he firmly stated that this was not a new opinion of his, but one held from long ago.

Likewise our presbyters, who had then been present at the Synod of Nicaea, bore witness [Note: [Col. 0901D] (4) That is, Vito and Vincentius, legates of Pope Silvester. See the following letter, no. 1, where Marcellus recalls that the Arians were convicted by him at the Synod of Nicaea.] to his orthodoxy. For he maintained that both then and now he had held a position opposed to the heresy of the Arians. Accordingly, it is right to remind you that no one should accept such a heresy, but should abhor it as alien to sound teaching. Since, therefore, he held right beliefs and had testimony to his orthodoxy, what else were we to do concerning him, I ask, except to regard him as a bishop—as indeed we did—and not exclude him from communion?

**XVII.**

I have written these things not as though defending their cause, but in order to persuade you that we received these men justly and canonically, and that you are contending in vain. It is right, however, that you should take pains and exert every effort to correct what has been done contrary to the canon, and that the churches may enjoy peace; so that the peace of the Lord which has been given to us may remain, the churches may not be divided, and you may not incur blame as authors of schism. For I confess to you that what has been done bears the appearance not of peace but of schism.

**XVIII. Many who came to Rome report the abominations committed by the Arians.**

For not only the bishops Athanasius and Marcellus came here, complaining that injustice had been done to them, [Note: [Col. 0901D] (1) Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*, no. 5, lists several bishops driven by the Arians from their cities, but does not say which of them withdrew to Rome. If Socrates, book II, ch. 15, and Sozomen, book III, ch. 8, are to be believed, besides Athanasius and Marcellus those who fled there were Paul, bishop of Constantinople, Asclepas of Gaza, and Lucius of Hadrianopolis.] but also very many other bishops from Thrace, Coele-Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine; likewise not a few presbyters, some from Alexandria and others from elsewhere. They came to the synod assembled here, and before all the bishops gathered together, besides the other matters which they presented, they complained that the churches had suffered violence and injustice. They maintained, not merely in words but by the facts themselves, that things like those done at Alexandria had occurred in their own and other churches.

Moreover, presbyters who recently came again from Egypt and Alexandria with letters testified, not without complaint and groaning, that many bishops and presbyters who wished to come to the synod had been prevented. They said that from Athanasius’s departure until the present time confessing bishops had been battered with blows, others imprisoned, [Note: [Col. 0901D] (2) Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*, no. 12, relates that this occurred as soon as the Eusebians had dismissed Elpidius and Philoxenus [Col. 0902D], Julius’s legates through whom they had been invited to the Roman synod. They then sent letters to Philagrius directing him to traverse Egypt with Gregory. “Hence,” says Athanasius, “bishops are scourged and harshly bound in chains; Sarapammon, bishop and confessor, is driven into exile; while Potammon, likewise bishop and confessor, is struck so long upon the neck that they thought the man dead.”] and even aged bishops—men who had spent very many years in the episcopate—handed over to public services; that almost all the clergy and people of the catholic Church were plotted against and persecuted. They also said that certain bishops and brethren had been exiled for no other reason than that, even unwillingly, they might be forced to communicate with Gregory and the Arians associated with him.

We also heard from others, and Bishop Marcellus confirmed by his testimony, that at Ancyra in Galatia not small matters, but again the very same things as had occurred at Alexandria, had taken place. [Note: [Col. 0902D] (3) Perhaps the acts which the Arians, in Hilary, fragment III, no. 9, impute to Marcellus himself. It was customary for them to charge Catholics with the outrages of which they were the authors and perpetrators, thereby stirring up hostility against them. Thus in the aforementioned fragment of Hilary, no. 8, they are not ashamed to write of Athanasius: “By force, slaughter, and war he plunders the basilicas of the Alexandrians. After a holy and blameless priest (Gregory) had already been appointed in his place by the judgment of a council, like a barbarian enemy and a sacrilegious pest, bringing in populations of pagans, he burns God’s temple, shatters the altar, and secretly leaves the city and flees.” Thus they accuse Athanasius of what they themselves perpetrated by installing Gregory in his place [Col. 0903D].]

Besides this, those who came here brought such accusations, and accusations so dreadful, against certain among you—whose names I do not mention—that I myself shrank from writing them, though perhaps you too have heard them from others. This, indeed, was the chief reason why I wrote and urged you to come: that you might hear these things in person, and that everything might be corrected and healed. In these circumstances those summoned ought to have come all the more readily and not declined, lest, by failing to appear, they should now be regarded as suspects concerning what was alleged, as persons unable to prove what they had written.

**XIX. The authors of discord are the Eusebians, not Julius.**

Since these things have been reported, and since the churches suffer and are assailed by such grievous evils, as those reporting them firmly maintained, who are those who have kindled the flame of discord? Are we, who grieve at such things and suffer with afflicted brethren, or those who have perpetrated them? For I wonder how, when such great disorder existed there in every church—and it was because of this that those who came here had come—you nevertheless write that harmony existed in the churches. Such things tend not to the building up of the Church but to its overthrow; and those who rejoice in them are not sons of peace but of disorder. Our God is not a God of disorder but of peace.

Therefore, as God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ knows, while caring for your reputation and praying that the churches may not be in disorder but may remain as the Apostles established them, I considered it necessary to write these things to you, so that at last you may prevail upon those who, through mutual hostility, have brought the churches to such a condition. For I have heard that there are only a few who are responsible for all these things. Take pains, having hearts of compassion, to correct, as I have said, what has been done contrary to the canons, so that if any evil has been undertaken beforehand, it may be remedied through your diligence.

**XX. Athanasius and Marcellus were received into communion without partisan preference.**

And do not write: “You have chosen the communion of Marcellus and Athanasius rather than ours.” Such language is a mark not of peace but of contentiousness and hatred of brethren. I therefore wrote the foregoing, so that, having learned that we did not receive them unjustly, you might cease from such strife. For if, when you came here, they had been convicted, and if they had not appeared to possess reasonable defenses for themselves, you would rightly have written such things. But since, as I have said, we have had communion with them canonically and not unjustly, I entreat you for Christ’s sake: do not permit the members of Christ to be torn apart; do not believe preconceived judgments, but give preference to the Lord’s peace. For it is neither holy nor just, because of the petty-mindedness of a few, to reject those who have not been convicted and thereby grieve the Spirit.

**XXI. If they consider them guilty, let them come to Rome and convict them in person there.**

But if you think that anything can be proved against them and that they can be convicted face to face, let those who wish it come. For they themselves have promised that they are ready both to demonstrate and thoroughly refute the charges concerning which they informed us. Inform us, therefore, beloved, concerning this, so that we may write both to them and to the bishops who ought to assemble again, in order that, with all present, those liable to accusation may be convicted and disorder may no longer arise in the churches.

For what has happened is enough; it is enough that, while bishops were present, bishops were driven into exile. There is no need to speak at length about this, lest those who were then present seem to be burdened. For, if the truth must be told, matters ought not to have reached such deeds, nor should these resentments have advanced so far. Let it be that Athanasius and Marcellus, as you write, were removed from their own places; [Note: [Col. 0905C] (1) “Justly” seems to be understood here. Athanasius did not omit this sort of argument: thus in his *Letter to the Solitaries*, no. 3, he says, “Let it be that they accused Athanasius; but what wrong did the other bishops commit? What charge was brought against them? With which of them was Arsenius found dead? With which was Macarius the presbyter, or the broken cup? Which Meletian accused them?”] but what can one say concerning the other bishops and presbyters who came here from various places, as I said before? For they too said that they had been seized and had suffered such things.

**XXII. Judgments not conducted according to the Gospel. The bishop of Alexandria ought not to have been judged without Julius’s knowledge.**

O beloved, judgments of the Church are no longer according to the Gospel, but are now for the infliction of exile and death. [Note: [Col. 0905C] (2) Supply: “after the manner of the age,” from whose severity evangelical and ecclesiastical clemency is absent.] For even if, as you say, some offense had indeed been committed by them, judgment ought to have been conducted according to the ecclesiastical canon—and in that manner. It was necessary to write to all of us, so that what was just might thus be determined by all. [Note: [Col. 0905C] (3) What can “to all of us” mean except Julius and those who had assembled with him at the convoked synod? Julius above, no. 2, recalls that a synod was requested so that a just judgment might be rendered before all; in no. 18 he reports that bishops harassed from many regions presented their complaints before all the assembled bishops; and in no. 21 he indicates his readiness to summon them again so that the accused might be convicted with all present. It therefore cannot be concluded from this that any bishop could not be judged without the consent of the Roman pontiff. The judgment of the bishop of Alexandria must, however, be viewed differently. When Julius speaks expressly of him, he says that the custom is first to write to us, and does not add “to all”; and shortly thereafter: “It was necessary to write to this church.”] For bishops were suffering, and the churches suffering were not insignificant ones, but churches which the Apostles themselves personally guided. [Note: [Col. 0905D] (4) This applies especially to the Alexandrian church. Leo, *Epistle* 94 to the bishops of Gaul, ch. 4, writes that “at the very beginnings of the Gospel it had as founder blessed Mark, disciple of the most blessed apostle Peter, in every respect conforming to his teacher’s instruction.” Hence Gregory I, book VII, indiction XV, epistle 37, replies to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, who had said of Peter’s chair that he himself still sits in it through his successors: “He speaks to me of Peter’s chair who sits in Peter’s chair,” plainly teaching that the Alexandrian see is likewise Peter’s chair. Furthermore, Julius may seem to have said this also because of Ancyra, of which Marcellus was bishop. For that city was the head of Galatia, to which we have the Apostle’s epistle addressed. Paul, in Augustine’s judgment (*Epistle* formerly 161, now 49, no. 2), established and founded the churches whose names his epistle bears. Tertullian too, book IV, *Against Marcion*, ch. 5, considers them churches of the Apostles. For after teaching that what was sacred among the apostolic churches had been handed down by the Apostles, he immediately explains which churches are apostolic: “Let us see what milk the Corinthians drew from Paul, by what rule the GALATIANS were corrected, what the Philippians read.”]

Why, then, was nothing written to us especially concerning the church of Alexandria? Or do you not know that it has been the custom first to write to us, and then for what is just to be determined from here? [Note: [Col. 0906C] (5) Socrates, book II, ch. 17, undoubtedly had this passage in view when he writes that Julius, in a letter sent to those assembled at Antioch, complained first of all that, contrary to the canons, they had not invited him to the synod, since ecclesiastical rule forbade the Church to decree anything apart from the judgment of the Roman pontiff. Sozomen, book III, ch. 10, agreeing with Socrates, states that what was done apart from the judgment of the bishop of Rome must be regarded as invalid. Epiphanius, *Tripartite History*, book IV, ch. 9, with their words somewhat changed, indicates that the Antiochene synod was invalid because Julius neither attended it nor appointed someone in his place, since ecclesiastical rule commands that councils must not be held apart from the judgment of the Roman pontiff. Hence Isidore Mercator, in a writing falsely composed under Julius’s name to the Easterners, no. 3, asserts that the canons of the Council of Nicaea command that councils must not be held and bishops must not be condemned apart from the judgment of the Roman pontiff. In another equally false letter of Julius to the same Easterners, no. 4, he adds that it had long ago been decreed in the aforesaid ancient statutes by the holy Apostles and their successors—which the holy and universal apostolic Church has held until now—that councils must not be held, nor a bishop condemned, apart from the judgment of the Roman pontiff. Who would have believed that Julius’s view, as handled by different persons who delight in interpolating the same words, could have been presented with so different an appearance? Nevertheless, it must not be denied that, given circumstances as they then were—namely, when the Eusebians’ legates had requested a synod from Julius, Julius had granted their request and summoned the bishops to Rome, and very many had already arrived—the Eusebians were not permitted to hold councils, enact decrees on disputed matters, or condemn accused bishops apart from the judgment of the Roman pontiff. Socrates and Sozomen are mistaken, however, in interpreting Julius’s words, “Do you not know that it has been the custom first to write to us, and then for what is just to be determined from here?”—said by him of the Alexandrian church alone—as applying to all churches. The custom which Julius here vindicates is supported by the case of Dionysius of Alexandria: when he fell under suspicion of heresy and was reported to Dionysius of Rome, he did not delay to clear himself. This special right of the Roman pontiff over the Alexandrian church may be referred to that church’s origin: it had as founder, through the agency of Mark, Peter’s own disciple, Peter who was already established at Rome; or, if one prefers Leo’s phrasing, Mark, in every respect conforming to the teaching of his master Peter.]

If any such suspicion had fallen upon the bishop there, it was necessary to write to the church here. But now, without informing us, they acted as they wished, and afterward wish us—though we have not condemned him—to be fellow voters with them. The ordinances of Paul are not so; the Fathers have not handed down such a practice. This is another pattern; this proceeding is new. [Note: [Col. 0907D] (1) Julius alludes here to the form of judgment exemplified by Paul in condemning the guilty party of incest, 1 Cor. 5:4: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled and my spirit is present,” etc. Athanasius testifies in his encyclical letter—whose words were cited above, col. 901, note 2—that the Church derived not only judicial proceedings but also the establishment and ordination of bishops from the same apostolic words.]

I beseech you, receive this with good will. What I write serves the common good. For what we have received from blessed Peter the Apostle, these things I also make known to you. I would not have written, since I considered them evident to all, had not what has happened disturbed us. Bishops are seized and driven from their places; others from elsewhere are put in their stead; still others are assailed by plots. Thus people mourn those who have been seized, while being compelled to receive those sent to them; so that they may not seek those whom they desire, but receive those whom they do not wish. [Note: [Col. 0907D] (2) That is, they are deprived of the right to seek those whom they desire. As Julius teaches above, no. 14, and as Cyprian’s words cited there confirm, ecclesiastical laws required that the bishop to be ordained be sought by clergy and people. It is no less contrary to the canons that people should be compelled unwillingly to receive bishops they do not want. Accordingly the Fifth Council of Orléans, in 549, canon 11, providing that “a bishop is not to be given against their will,” adds expressly: “as the ancient canons decreed.” See Celestine I’s letter to the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne, nos. 4–5.]

I ask that such things no longer occur. Rather, write against those who attempt such acts, so that the churches may suffer such things no longer, and that no bishop or presbyter may suffer insult or, against his own judgment—as has been reported to us—be compelled to do anything. Let us not incur mockery among the nations, and above all let us not provoke God to anger. For each of us shall render an account on the day of judgment for what he has done here.

May it be granted that all may think according to God, so that the churches, having received back their bishops, may rejoice forever in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom be glory to the Father unto ages of ages. Amen. I pray that you may be well in the Lord, beloved and most longed-for brethren.

[Note: [Col. 0908C] (3) As Athanasius himself relates, *Apology against the Arians*, no. 51, after the Council of Sardica had dissolved, while he was staying at Aquileia he received three letters in which Constantius urged him to return home with all speed. At last, in the year 349, he returned to Rome to take leave of its bishop and church. On this occasion Julius gave him this letter, which Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, no. 52, appended after the aforesaid three letters of Constantius, omitting out of modesty the things recounted in praise of himself throughout no. 2 [Col. 0908D]. Socrates, book II, ch. 23, and Epiphanius Scholasticus, drawing from him, *Tripartite History*, book IV, ch. 29, likewise transmitted the entire letter to us.]

**LETTER OF POPE JULIUS I TO THE PRESBYTERS, DEACONS, AND PEOPLE OF ALEXANDRIA. JULIUS CONGRATULATES THE ALEXANDRIANS ON THE RETURN OF ATHANASIUS, TO WHOM THEY HAD ALWAYS CLUNG WITH FAITH AND LOVE, AND PRAYS FOR THEIR WELL-BEING.**

**[LETTER OF JULIUS I.]**

**JULIUS TO THE PRESBYTERS, DEACONS, AND PEOPLE DWELLING AT ALEXANDRIA.**

[Note: [Col. 0908D] (4) Socrates here adds in Greek *episkopois kai* (“to bishops also”), which the edition of the councils retains. Yet it is clear that this letter was written to the Alexandrians alone, over whom Athanasius presided and who acknowledged no bishop but him. Epiphanius Scholasticus seems to have read the Greek *Ioulios episkopos* (“Julius, bishop”); but he did not adhere consistently even to this reading, for in Latin he has “Julius archbishop.” Valesius retained the Greek word *episkopois* but translated it in Latin not “to bishops,” but “bishop.” There is all the more reason to suspect that Socrates interpolated the title rashly because Julius does not add the name “bishop” to himself here in Athanasius, nor in the preceding first letter.]

[Note: [Col. 0908D] (5) In the *Tripartite History*: “and to the people dwelling in Alexandria, beloved brethren in the Lord, greeting”; supported by Socrates’s Greek text: *kai laō paroikounti Alexandrian, agapētois adelphois en kyriō chairein*.]

[Col. 0908C] I. I too congratulate you, beloved brethren, because [Col. 0909A] you now at last behold before your eyes the fruit of your faith. For it is plainly evident to anyone that this has indeed come to pass in my brother and fellow-bishop Athanasius, whom God has restored to you both because of the purity of his life and because of your prayers. From this one may certainly perceive that you have always offered to God prayers pure and full of love. For, mindful of the heavenly promises and of the discipline leading to them, in which you were instructed through the teaching of my aforesaid brother, you have truly known—and, according to the right faith planted in you, have understood—that he would by no means be separated from you forever, whom you always held as present in your most devout souls.

Therefore, as I write to you, I have no need of many words. For whatever might be said to you by me, your faith [Col. 0909B] has anticipated, and through God’s grace has fulfilled the common desire of us all. [Note: [Col. 0910D] (1) Epiphanius: “and divine grace has fulfilled the desires of our common prayer.” In Socrates, Valesius’s edition: καὶ πεπλήρωται κατὰ Χριστοῦ χάριν τὰ τῆς κοινῆς ὑμῶν πάντων εὐχῆς, “and, according to Christ’s grace, the things of the common prayer of all of you have been fulfilled”; but Epiphanius’s preceding rendering shows that he read, as in our manuscripts, πεπλήρωκε, not πεπλήρωται; θεοῦ, not Χριστοῦ; and ἡμῶν, not ὑμῶν. Certainly Valesius’s preferred reading coheres less well with what precedes, where Julius writes that he needs no many words, not because what the Alexandrians had desired in common prayers had been fulfilled, but because they themselves had already anticipated and fulfilled by their faith whatever Julius might have desired from them.]

I therefore congratulate you—for I shall say it again—because you have kept your souls unconquerable in the faith. Nor do I less congratulate Athanasius himself, my brother, because, although he endured many distresses, he was never for an hour forgetful of your love and your longing. For although in body he seemed for a time to have been drawn away from you, in spirit he nevertheless dwelt continually among you as present; he returns more illustrious than when he departed.

Julius, to the presbyters and deacons, and to the people dwelling at Alexandria.

[Col. 0907B]

I. I too rejoice with you, beloved brethren, because you now behold before your eyes [Col. 0910A] the fruit of your own faith. For anyone may truly see this to have occurred in my brother and fellow-bishop Athanasius, whom God restores to you because of the purity of his life and because of your prayers. From this, then, it is possible to see that you have always offered up to God prayers that are pure and full of love. For, being mindful of the heavenly promises and of the training leading toward them, in which you were instructed through the teaching of my aforesaid brother, you have truly known and, according to the right faith present in you, have understood that this man will not be cut off from you to the end—the man whom you have always possessed in your most God-fearing souls as though present. Therefore I need no many words in writing to you. For whatever may be said to you by me, your faith has anticipated and has fulfilled [Col. 0910B], by God’s grace, the matters of the common prayer of us all. I therefore rejoice with you—for I shall say it again—because you have preserved your souls unconquerable in the faith. And I rejoice no less with Athanasius himself, my brother, because, though suffering many grievous things, he has never for a single hour become forgetful of your love and your longing. For even if in body he seemed for a time to have been dragged away from you, nevertheless in spirit he lived continually among you as though present.

[Col. 0909B] II. And I, beloved brethren, judge that all the trials which he endured were not without glory. For both your faith and his have become known and have been tested by all. Had so many and such things not occurred, who would have believed either that you possessed such judgment and such love toward so great a bishop, [Col. 0909C] or that he was clothed with so many and such virtues, through which he is not estranged from the hope laid up in heaven? Thus, in every respect, both in this present age and in the age to come, he has obtained the glorious testimony of confession.

For, having suffered many and varied trials by land and sea, he trampled underfoot every intrigue of the Arian heresy. Often assailed through envy and brought into peril of life by plots, he despised death, guarded by the protection of almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ; trusting both that he would escape the plots and that he would be restored to you for your consolation, bringing you from your own [Note: [Col. 0910D] (2) For “your,” Epiphanius reads “most steadfast”; this reading is especially pleasing. Hence, in Socrates’s Greek text [Col. 0911C], we suspect καρτερᾶς, “steadfast,” should be restored in place of ὑμετέρας, “your.”] conscience greater trophies—trophies in which he became gloriously known even to the furthest bounds of the whole earth, approved by the integrity of his [Col. 0909D] life. He was confident in the purpose of his mind and in heavenly teaching; and you have demonstrated, by your enduring and steadfast judgment, that he is loved by you continually.

[Col. 0910B] II. And I, beloved brethren, consider that every trial which came upon him was not inglorious. For both our faith and his have become known to all and have been tested. For if so many things had not happened, who would have believed either that you have such judgment and such love toward so great a bishop, or that he had been clothed with so many [Col. 0910C] virtues, through which he might not be estranged from the hope in heaven? Thus, by whatever means, both now and in the future, he attained a glorious testimony of confession. For, having suffered many trials in diverse ways by land and sea, he trampled down the entire machination of the Arian heresy. Often plotted against through envy and brought into danger, he despised death, being guarded by almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ; hoping at once to avoid the plots and to be restored for your consolation, while bringing you from your own conscience greater trophies, in which he became glorious and known even to the ends of the whole earth, having been approved through his life. Having spoken boldly through his resolution and heavenly teaching, he was shown by you to be loved with an undying judgment.

[Col. 0909D] III. Therefore he returns to you now far more illustrious than when he left you. For if fire tests precious materials—gold, that is, and silver—for purity, what might anyone say worthy of so great a man, who, having overcome the dangers of so many afflictions, is restored to you, declared pure and innocent not only by our judgment but also by that of the whole synod? Receive, therefore, beloved brethren, with every glory and joy according to God, your bishop—with the Greek text of Socrates supporting: “and to the people dwelling at Alexandria, beloved brethren in the Lord, greetings”—[Col. 0912A] Athanasius, together with those who shared in so many of his labours. And, having obtained the objects of your prayers, rejoice—you who, when your shepherd hungered and thirsted, so to speak, for your piety, fed and gave him drink through salutary writings. For you were his consolation while he lived in a foreign land; you cherished him in persecution [Note: [Col. 0911C] (1) In Athanasius καὶ ἐπιβουλευόμενον, “and while plotted against,” is lacking; we borrow its Latin rendering from Epiphanius Scholasticus.] and dangers with your most faithful souls and minds.

Indeed, it now delights me to consider and foresee in thought the joy of each of you at his return, the most devout welcoming processions of the multitude, and the glorious festival of those running together. What a day, and what a day will that be for you, when my brother returns, the previous evils cease, and that most precious and longed-for return joins all together in a certain exuberance of fullest joy! Such joy also reaches us to a very great degree, since it is established that God has granted us this gift as well: that we might be able to come to know so great a man. It is fitting, then, to close the letter with prayer.

[Col. 0910D] III. Therefore he returns to you now more splendid than when he went away from you. For if fire tests precious [Col. 0911A] materials—gold and silver—for purity, what could anyone say worthily concerning so great a man, who, having conquered the dangers of so many afflictions, is restored to you, received as innocent not only by us but also by the whole synod? Receive, therefore, beloved brethren, with all glory and joy according to God, your bishop Athanasius, together with those who have become partners with him in these many labours. And rejoice as you enjoy the fulfillment of your prayers—you who fed and gave drink, through saving writings, to your shepherd, who, if I may say so, longed and thirsted for your piety. For you became a consolation during his stay abroad, and you warmed him, while persecuted and plotted against, with your own most faithful souls and minds.

And it already gladdens me to consider and to foresee in thought [Col. 0911B] the joy of each of you at his return, the most God-fearing welcome of the multitude, and the glorious celebration of those gathering together. And what a day will that day be for you, and of what sort, when my brother returns, the things that went before cease, and the very precious and prayer-desired return joins everyone in an overflowing joy of fullest gladness! Such joy reaches us also in the greatest degree, to whom it has been granted by God even in this matter that we may be able to come to know so great a man. It is good, therefore, to finish the letter with prayer.

[Col. 0911B] IV. May God almighty, and his Son, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, grant you abiding grace, rendering a reward for your admirable faith, which you displayed toward your bishop in a glorious testimony; so that to you and to your descendants, in this life and in the age to come, he may grant the good things which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the human heart—things which God has prepared for those who love him (1 Cor. 2:9)—through Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom be glory to almighty God unto ages of ages. Amen. I pray that you may fare well in the Lord, beloved brethren. [Col. 0912C]

[Col. 0911B] IV. May God almighty, and his Son, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, grant you perpetual grace, giving a reward to your admirable faith, which you showed toward your bishop through glorious testimony; [Col. 0911C] that he may dispense better things to you and to those after you, here and in the age to come—things which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which have not ascended into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him—through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom be glory to almighty God unto the ages of ages. Amen. I pray that you may be well in the Lord, beloved brethren.

## Letter of Valens and Ursacius to Pope Julius

This letter, [Note: [Col. 0911C] (2) Socrates, Book II, chapter 24, mentions this letter and teaches that it was written by Ursacius and Valens after they had learned the acts of the Synod of Jerusalem, held in 349. Hilary, Fragment II, no. 20, and Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*, nos. 25 and 26, confirm this. Accordingly, Athanasius places it in *Apology against the Arians*, no. 58, immediately after the aforesaid Synod of Jerusalem. Athanasius again testifies, both in the cited place of the *Apology* and in the *Letter to the Solitaries*, no. 26, that it was written in Latin and then translated into Greek from the Latin text. In both places he declares that it was sent to him by Paulinus, bishop of Tibur, according to the old manuscripts, as our editors observed in no. 13 of the Life of St Athanasius prefixed to his works—not “Triberon,” but “Tiberon.” Thus it is more probable that Paulinus of Tibur, as Nannius also interpreted him in the *Letter to the Solitaries*, rather than Paulinus of Trier, is intended. For a bishop of Tibur, being near the city, could more conveniently and swiftly transmit a document delivered in Rome to Alexandria than could a bishop of Trier. Hence the opinion is not sufficiently secure of those who, relying on this passage alone, report that Maximinus, bishop of Trier and predecessor of Paulinus, died in 349. Yet one should not therefore subscribe to Baronius’s opinion, under the year 350, no. 8, that the bishop Maximus, whom Athanasius in *Apology to Constantius*, no. 9, recalls as having been sent with Servatius as an envoy from Magnentius the tyrant to the emperor Constantius, was Maximinus of Trier himself. For it is known from elsewhere that this Maximus must be distinguished from Maximinus of Trier. Leaving aside that Maximus and Maximinus are not one name, Athanasius himself, in no. 14 of the same *Apology to Constantius*, confesses that he could not invoke the testimony of Maximinus, since he was already dead; but in no. 9 he calls Maximus, Magnentius’s envoy, as a witness still living, from whom Constantius might more certainly learn and verify the truth of the matter. We present the Latin text of this letter or memorandum, with the preceding annotation, from Hilary, Fragment II, no. 20; and the Greek from Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, no. 58, where it bears the heading “On the repentance of Ursacius and Valens.”] after the Eastern bishops had reported [Note: [Col. 0912D] (3) Namely Maximus and the other bishops who assembled at Jerusalem and informed the Alexandrians and all bishops throughout [Col. 0913B] Libya and Egypt by letter of the decisions they had made concerning the restoration of Athanasius, as Socrates, Book II, chapter 24, records.] that Athanasius was not guilty, was written out in Rome in Valens’s own hand and subscribed by Ursacius.

(From Hilary, Fragment II, no. 20.) [Note: [Col. 0911] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.] (C, S)

[Col. 0911]

To the most blessed lord Pope Julius, Valens and Ursacius.

[Col. 0912C]

Since it is established that we previously represented in our letters many grave accusations concerning the name of Bishop [Col. 0913A] Athanasius, and that, having been summoned by letters of your Holiness [Note: [Col. 0913C] (1) The rules of grammar require *conventos*, “having been summoned.” No letters of Julius are indicated here other than those which he sent in 341 through the envoys Elpidius and Philoxenus to the Eusebians, summoning them to the synod held at Rome in 342. Ursacius and Valens were bound in alliance and fellowship with the Eusebians, of whom the Sardican Synod writes to Julius in the preceding Letter 3, no. 2: “Although summoned by your presbyters and by letter to come to the synod that was to be held in Rome, they refused.” Nor should those letters, in which Valens and Ursacius confess that they had made many grave allegations against Athanasius, be understood as written in their private names; for the Sardican Synod, in its letter to all the churches in Hilary, Fragment II, no. 2, says: “Formerly, when Eusebius, Marius, Theodorus, Diognius, Ursacius, and Valens wrote to Julius, our fellow-priest, bishop of the Roman church, against our aforesaid fellow-bishops—that is, Athanasius and Marcellus.” Liberius also teaches by name in the dialogue to be presented below after Letter 7 of Liberius himself that they begged pardon for proceedings which they had carried out, by calumny and with one side only present, against Athanasius at Mareotis.], we were unable to render an account of the matter concerning which we had written, we declare before your Holiness, with all our brother presbyters present, that everything which previously reached your ears concerning the name of the aforesaid Athanasius was falsely alleged by us and possesses no force whatsoever. Therefore we most willingly embrace communion with the aforesaid Athanasius, especially since your Holiness, according to the benevolence innate in you, has deigned to grant pardon to our error.

We further declare that if ever the Easterners, or Athanasius himself, should wish maliciously to summon us to trial concerning this matter, we shall not appear without your knowledge. But Arius the heretic, together with his adherents—those who say, “There was a time when the Son was not,” who say that the Son is from nothing, and who deny [Note: [Col. 0913D] (2) The Greek reading, by adding that Christ is God, attacks the Arians more explicitly. Nor does this less oppose Photinus, on whose account the Synod of Milan, shortly to be mentioned, had been convened; concerning that synod see the observations on Hilary.] that the Son of God existed before the ages—we have anathematized, now and always, just as in our earlier memorandum which we submitted at Milan. These things we declare in our own handwriting, and again say that we have condemned forever the Arian heresy, as stated above, and its authors. And in Ursacius’s hand: I, Bishop Ursacius, have subscribed to this our profession. [Note: [Col. 0913D] (3) From Athanasius’s Greek text there ought here to be added: “likewise Valens.” Yet this ending agrees with the notice prefixed to the letter, in which Hilary teaches that this letter was written out in Valens’s own hand and subscribed by Ursacius. Thus in Greek “and in Ursacius’s hand” ought rather to have been expressed.]

To the most blessed lord Pope Julius, Ursacius and Valens.

[Col. 0911C]

Since it is established that we formerly submitted, by letters, many grave accusations concerning Athanasius the bishop, and, having been summoned by letters from your kindness, were unable to render an account concerning the matter of which we had given notice, we confess before your kindness, with all our brother presbyters present, that everything which previously came to your ears concerning the name of the aforesaid Athanasius is false and fabricated, and is entirely foreign to him. Therefore we gladly claim communion with the aforesaid Athanasius, especially because your piety, according to its innate goodness and nobility, has deigned to grant pardon to our error.

We also confess this: if ever the Easterners, or Athanasius himself, should maliciously wish to summon us to judgment concerning this, we shall not go apart from the knowledge of your [Col. 0914B] disposition. But Arius the heretic and those who defend him—those who say, “There was a time when there was no Son,” that the Son is from what is not, and those who deny that Christ, God and Son of God, existed before the ages—we anathematize now and always, just as we submitted in our earlier memorandum at Milan. Having written these things in our own hand, we again confess that we have condemned the Arian heresy, as we said before, and all its authors forever. I, Ursacius, being present, subscribed to this my confession; likewise Valens.

## Notice on the Letter of Marcellus of Ancyra to Julius

[Col. 0913]

(Coust. p. 387.)

I. We have this letter from Epiphanius, *Heresies* 72, no. 2. Marcellus declares that he delivered it at Rome to Julius himself, after waiting in that city for his opponents for a full year and three months, although they had refused to come to the synod despite being summoned by Julius’s presbyters Philoxenus and Elpidius. From this it is reasonably inferred that it was written only after those envoys had returned [Col. 0914C] from the East, and while the synod was being held from which Julius sent the preceding letter to the Eusebians—therefore in 342.

Nevertheless Baronius, under the year 341, no. 2, doubts whether this is the exposition of faith which Julius, in the preceding letter, no. 16, testifies that he requested from Marcellus and, when Marcellus gave it, approved, because, he says, the name *consubstantial* is not used in it, though this was especially required of a professor of the catholic faith. “But there was no reason why an explicit profession of this term should be required from a bishop in no way suspect of the Arian heresy, indeed its hostile opponent, who at the Synod of Nicaea, as the legates of the apostolic see themselves testified, had especially displayed his zeal against it. Certainly Julius nowhere says that he received from him two expositions of faith; and the circumstances of place, time, and other particulars by which he indicates that the exposition praised in the preceding letter to the Eusebians was given to him agree preeminently with this one. Why, then, should we suppose another?”

II. Epiphanius, about to bring this letter forward, prefaces it thus: “I shall set forth the exposition which Marcellus himself wrote to the blessed Julius, bishop of the Romans, in order to clear himself. From this defence and memorandum it will appear that he held some views besides the sincere faith. For if he held nothing different from it, for what reason would he undertake this self-vindication?” Yet, with the reverence due to so great a man preserved, this ground for his judgment appears exceedingly slight. For it follows from this only that some accused Marcellus of unsound doctrine; it does not likewise follow that he held unsound views—especially since those who charged Marcellus with heresy were his enemies, and enemies precisely because they were devoted to the Arian sect which he opposed.

Or, if Marcellus is to be thought at some time to have held views contrary to the sincere faith because he was compelled to set forth his faith in self-defence, then it will likewise follow that neither Hilary of Poitiers nor the other Gallican bishops of his age possessed sound faith. For, as Sulpicius Severus testifies, Book II of his *History*, when Hilary came to Seleucia, “the first question put to him was what was the faith of the Gauls; because, when the Arians were then spreading false reports about them, the Easterners suspected them of believing, according to Sabellius, in a three-named union of the solitary God. Hilary, having expounded his faith according to what had been written by the fathers at Nicaea, bore witness for the Westerners.” Is Athanasius to be called suspect in faith because he composed an *Apology against the Arians*? Or Dionysius of Alexandria, because even Catholics denounced him to the Roman pontiff and compelled him to send an apology in his own defence?

Moreover, Epiphanius himself, in the cited passage, no. 4, testifies that he does not dare pronounce whether or not there is any defect in this letter or memorandum of Marcellus, but leaves judgment on the matter free to each person. As for Julius, his judgment in Marcellus’s favour is plain.

## Letter of Marcellus of Ancyra to Pope Julius

Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, sets forth to Julius what the Arians believe and what he himself believes.

(Ibid.) [Note: [Col. 0915] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.] (S)

[Col. 0915]

To the most blessed fellow-priest Julius, Marcellus greets you in Christ. [Note: [Col. 0915C] (1) Petavius renders συλλειτουργῷ as “colleague,” others as “fellow-minister”; but Hilary, whom we judged worthy of imitation, rendered the Greek words of the Sardican Synod concerning the letters of the Eusebians sent to Julius συλλειτουργῷ—letters to be read in Theodoret, *History*, Book II, chapter 8—as follows in Latin: “to Julius, our fellow-priest.”]

[Col. 0916B]

I. Since certain persons who were formerly condemned for not believing rightly, and whom I refuted at the Synod of Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0915D] (2) Julius observed in his letter to the Antiochenes, no. 16, that this was confirmed by the testimony of his presbyters who had attended the Synod of Nicaea.], have dared to write against me to your Piety, alleging that I do not think rightly or according to the doctrine of the Church, while striving to transfer their own charge onto me: for this reason I considered it necessary to come to Rome and remind you, so that you might summon those who wrote against me; that, when they came, I might refute them on two counts—namely, that what they wrote against me is false, and that even now they persist in their former error and have dared to devise grievous things against the churches of God and against us who preside over them.

But since they refused to come, [Col. 0916C] although you sent presbyters to them, and though I myself had remained at Rome for a year and three complete months, [Note: [Col. 0915D] (3) Just as in the letter mentioned above, no. 13, where Athanasius is said to have remained at Rome for a year and six months awaiting the arrival of his opponents, it is plain that the term of those eighteen months is reckoned from the time of the synod from which Julius wrote that letter, so Marcellus doubtless reckons these fifteen months from his arrival at Rome up to that same synod.
