It follows that he arrived in the city three months after Athanasius’s arrival.] I considered it necessary, before leaving here, to give you in writing, inscribed in my own hand with all sincerity, the profession of my faith which I have learned and have been taught from the divine Scriptures; and at the same time to remind you of the false assertions made by them, so that you might understand by what words they seek to conceal the truth while deceiving their hearers.

To the most blessed fellow-minister Julius, Marcellus greets you in Christ.

[Col. 0915B]

I. Since certain persons formerly condemned for not believing rightly, whom I refuted at the Synod of Nicaea, dared to write against me to your Piety, as though I did not think rightly or ecclesiastically, while striving to transfer their own accusation to me: for this reason I considered it necessary, having come to Rome, to remind you that you should summon those who wrote against me, in order that, when they came [read: “when they come”], they might be refuted by me on both points: both that what they wrote against me is false, and that even now they persist in their former error and have dared grievous things against the churches of God and against us who preside over them.

Since, therefore, they were unwilling to come, although you had sent presbyters to them, and although I had spent a year and three full months at Rome, I considered it necessary, being about to leave here, to give you in writing my own faith, written in my own hand with all truth—the faith which I learned and was taught from the divine Scriptures—and to remind you of the things wrongly said by them, so that you may know by what arguments they wish to conceal the truth while deceiving their hearers.

[Col. 0916C] II. For they say that the Son of almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ, is not his proper and true Word, but that there is another Word of his, and another wisdom and power; and that he, after being made by him, was called Word, wisdom, and power. From this opinion of theirs it follows that they also declare there to be a substance distinct from the Father. [Note: [Col. 0915D] (4) That is, they declare the substance of Father and Son to be different, contrary to the explicit profession of the Nicene Creed, which strikes with anathema those who say that the Son is from another substance or essence: ἐξ ἑτέρας ὑποστάσεως ἢ οὐσίας φάσκοντας εἶναι, “who say that he is from another hypostasis or essence.” Here the word ὑπόστασις (*hypostasis*) is plainly used both by the Nicene Council and by Marcellus in the sense in which teachers of secular letters taught it should be used. For Jerome says, in Letter 57 to Damasus: “The whole school of secular literature knows no other meaning of *hypostasis* than *ousia*.” Therefore Valesius correctly rendered Socrates, Book I, chapter 8, the aforementioned words of the Nicene Council, ἐξ ἑτέρας ὑποστάσεως ἢ οὐσίας φάσκοντας εἶναι, in Latin: “who say that he is from another substance or essence.” Accordingly Petavius must be corrected in Epiphanius, *Heresies* 72, no. 11, where he renders the same words of the Nicene faith professed by Marcellus’s disciples: “who say that he existed from another person or essence.” For the Nicene Council was far from denying that the Son exists from another person.]

Furthermore, by what they write they plainly declare that the Father existed before the Son and that he is not truly Son from God. Yet, though they say that he is from God, they say this in the same sense in which all other things exist from him. Moreover, they dare to affirm that there was once when he was not, that he is a created and made thing, and they separate him from the Father. Therefore I am persuaded that those who assert these things are outside the catholic Church.

[Col. 0915C] II. For they say that the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, is not the proper and true Word of almighty God, but that there is another Word of his, another wisdom, and another power; and that, having been made by him, this one was called Word, wisdom, and power. Because they think in this way, they say that there is another hypostasis distinct from the Father. Furthermore, through what they write, they declare that the Father existed before the Son and that he is not truly Son from God. And even if they say that he is from God, they say it in the same way as all things. They also dare to say, “There was once when he was not” [the text has ὅτι, “that,” for ὅτε, “when”], and that he is a creature and a made thing, separating him from the Father. I am persuaded, then, that those who say these things are alien to the catholic Church.

[Col. 0917B] III. But I, adhering to the sacred Scriptures, believe that there is one God, and his only-begotten Son, the Word, who always exists with the Father and never had any beginning of existence; who is truly from God, not created, not made, but always existing and perpetually reigning together with God and the Father, and whose kingdom, as the Apostle testifies, will have no end (Luke 1:33). [Note: [Col. 0918D] (1) The words cited are from the Gospel according to Luke; [Col. 0919C] consequently Marcellus seems to have been among those who attributed Luke’s Gospel to Paul, concerning whom Jerome writes in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 17: “Some suppose that whenever Paul says in his letters, ‘according to my Gospel,’ he means the volume of Luke.” Yet below he cites it under Luke’s own name.]

This Son, this Power, this Wisdom, this proper and true Word of God—our Lord Jesus Christ—is the indivisible power of God, through whom all things that were made came to be, as the Gospel teaches when it says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1 etc.). This is the Word concerning whom Luke the Evangelist testifies, saying: “As they delivered them to us, who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word” (Luke 1:2). David also said concerning him: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Psalm 44:2). Thus our Lord Jesus Christ also teaches us in the Gospel, saying: “I came forth from the Father and come” (John 16:28). He is the one who, in the last days, descended for our salvation and, having been born from the Virgin Mary, assumed humanity.

[Col. 0918A] III. I believe, following the divine Scriptures, that there is one God, and his only-begotten Son, the Word, who always coexists with the Father and has never at any time had a beginning of being; who truly exists from God, not having been created or made, but always being and always reigning together with God and the Father, and whose kingdom, according to the testimony of the Apostle, shall have no end. This is the Son; this is the Power; this is the Wisdom; this is the proper and true Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, the indivisible power of God, through whom the things that came to be came to be, as the Gospel testifies, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things came to be through him, and without him not one thing came to be.” This is the Word concerning whom Luke the Evangelist also testifies, saying: “As those who from the beginning became eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word delivered them to us.” David also said concerning him: “My heart poured forth a good word.” Thus our Lord Jesus Christ teaches us through the Gospel, saying: “I came forth from the Father [Col. 0918C] and have come.” This is he who, in the last days, descended for our salvation and, having been born from the Virgin Mary, took humanity.

[Col. 0917B] IV. I therefore believe in God almighty, and in Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, [Col. 0917C] our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, buried, and rose from the dead on the third day; who ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, from where he will come to judge the living and the dead. And I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Church, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life.

We have learned from the divine Scriptures that the divinity of Father and Son is indivisible. For if anyone separates the Son—that is, the Word of almighty God—he must either suppose there are two Gods, which is plainly contrary to divine teaching, or confess that the Word is not God, which likewise is clearly foreign to the right faith, since the Gospel says: “And the Word was God” (John 1). But I have certainly learned that the Son, the Power of the Father, can neither be divided nor separated. For our Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ himself, says: “The Father is in me and I am in the Father” (John 14:10); “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).

[Col. 0918C] IV. I therefore believe in God almighty and in Christ Jesus, his only-begotten Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin; who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, buried, and rose from the dead on the third day; who ascended into the heavens and sits at the right hand of the Father, from where he comes to judge the living and the dead. And I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Church, forgiveness of sins, resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life.

We have learned from the divine Scriptures that the divinity of the Father and the Son is indivisible. For if anyone separates the Son—that is, the Word of almighty God—he must either think that there are two gods, which is held to be foreign to divine teaching, or confess that the Word is not God, which also appears foreign to the right faith, since the Gospel says, “And the Word was God.” But I have learned precisely that the Son, the Power of the Father, is indivisible and inseparable. For our Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ himself, says: “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father”; “I and the Father are one”; and “He who has seen me has seen the Father.”

[Col. 0917D] V. This faith, which I received from the divine Scriptures and learned from my forebears according to God, I both preach in the Church of [Col. 0920A] God and have now set down in writing for you, retaining a copy of it with myself. I ask you to append a copy of it to your letter to the bishops, lest any of those who do not know us well, giving credence to what has been written by them [Note: [Col. 0919C] (1) Namely, by the Arians, whose doctrine he attacks at the beginning of this letter or memorandum, and in particular by Eusebius, of whom five books against Marcellus survive; or also by Acacius, from whose work against Marcellus Epiphanius, *Heresies* 72, no. 6 and following, transcribes some fragments.], should be led into error. Farewell. End.

[Col. 0918D] V. Having received this faith from the divine Scriptures and been taught it by forebears according to God, I proclaim it in the Church of [Col. 0919A] God and have now written it to you, retaining its copy with myself. I ask you to insert a copy of it in your letter to the bishops, lest some who do not know us accurately, giving attention also to those writings of theirs, should be deceived. Farewell. Completed.

## Letter of the Synod of Sardica to Julius, Bishop of the City of Rome

[Note: [Col. 0919D] (2) Restored here from Hilary’s fragments. It is also found in certain ancient collections of canons. We have newly collated it against two manuscripts of the Colbert Library: one appears to be about eight hundred years old, while the other, even older, is written in Lombardic majuscule letters. Nicholas I was not ignorant of it.]

(Coust. p. 395.) The Synod of Sardica informs Julius of the matters it carried out. (C, S)

[Col. 0919]

I. What we have always believed, we also now think; for experience proves and confirms what each person has heard by report. For what the most blessed teacher of the Gentiles, the Apostle Paul, said of himself is true, [Note: [Col. 0919D] (3) These are Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 13:3: “Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” Baronius did not hesitate to restore them to the text; but because they occur neither in the Pithoean archetype nor in the Colbert manuscripts, we judged that they also should be omitted.] although, since the Lord Christ dwelt in him, there can certainly be no doubt that the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0919D] (4) Thus Baronius with the Colbert manuscripts; but the Pithoean codex has *Spiritium sanctum*, “Holy Spirit.”] spoke through his mind and sounded through the instrument of his body.

You also, therefore, most beloved brother, though separated in body, were present in concord of mind and will. And the excuse for your absence was honourable and necessary, lest either schismatic wolves should steal and snatch by ambush, or heretical dogs, stirred to rabid frenzy [the Colbert manuscripts read *excitati*, “aroused”], should bark madly, or indeed the serpent, the devil, should pour out the poison of blasphemers. [Note: [Col. 0919D] (5) Baronius reads *blasphemiarum*, “of blasphemies,” against the manuscripts, which have *blasphemiorum*, occurring elsewhere in place of *blasphemorum*, “of blasphemers.” Here a threefold class of destructive persons is censured: schismatics, heretics, and blasphemers. Therefore *blasphemiarum* has been substituted less correctly.] For it will seem best and most fitting that the priests of the Lord should report the affairs of each province to the head—that is, to the see of the Apostle Peter.

[Col. 0919C] II. Since, then, both the documents and the living voices of our most beloved brothers and fellow-presbyters Archidamus and Philoxenus [Note: [Col. 0919D] (6) The Pithoean manuscript reads *Filioseni*. The two Colbert manuscripts more correctly read *Filoxeni*. This Philoxenus appears to be no one other than the presbyter whom Julius, Letter 1, no. 1, recalls sending to the East with Elpidius in 341 to summon bishops to the synod.] and of our most beloved son Leo the deacon can set forth most truly and faithfully [Col. 0920A] everything done, carried out, and decreed, it seems almost superfluous to insert the same matters into this letter. [Note: [Col. 0920C] (7) The two Colbert manuscripts read *inferre litteris*, “to include in the letter,” which is clear.]

It was evident to all who gathered that those from the Eastern regions who call themselves bishops [Col. 0920B]—though among them are certain authors [Note: [Col. 0920C] (8) These authors of the Arian sect are listed by name in another letter of the same synod to all the churches, in Hilary, Fragment II, no. 7.] whose sacrilegious minds the Arian heresy has stained with its deadly poison—had long resorted to evasions and, because of their distrust, had refused to come to judgment. They also censured your communion and ours, though it had no fault, because we believed alike in Athanasius’s innocence not only on the testimony of eighty bishops [Note: [Col. 0920C] (9) Namely, those who wrote from Egypt to Julius himself, as the other synodical letter to all the churches in Hilary, Fragment II, no. 7, states, and whose letter Athanasius transcribes in *Apology against the Arians*, no. 3.], but also because, although summoned by your presbyters and by letter to the synod [Note: [Col. 0920C] (10) The Colbert manuscripts read *a synodo*, “from the synod”; the Pithoean has *et synodo*, “and the synod.” More correctly in Hilary and Baronius, *ad synodum*, “to the synod”: namely, the synod to which Julius summoned the Easterners through Elpidius and Philoxenus in 341, which was held at the appointed time in 342 and from which Julius wrote the preceding Letter 1, as he states in no. 8.], which was to be held in Rome, they refused to come. And it was sufficiently unjust, when they had shown contempt, to deny fellowship to Marcellus and Athanasius, while so many bishops bore testimony.

III. There were three matters to be discussed. For the most devout emperors themselves permitted that all matters should be debated anew [Col. 0920C] [Note: [Col. 0920D] (11) That is, all the matters transacted at the Council of Tyre and thereafter. For no consideration permits us to understand these words as also said of the Nicene decrees. Rather, this interpretation is wholly excluded by Athanasius, *Tome to the Antiochenes*, §5, who relates as follows: “Although some demanded that something be written concerning the faith, as though the Synod of Nicaea lacked something, and rashly attempted to obtain this, the synod assembled at Sardica nevertheless regarded the matter with indignation and decreed that no further pronouncement concerning the faith should be issued, but that the faith promulgated by the fathers at Nicaea should suffice, since it was deficient in nothing but was full of piety.” Hence he charges with falsehood and warns that the document should be rejected which some were circulating as if it had been composed concerning the faith at the Synod of Sardica. Those heretics would, moreover, have been far bolder if they had understood themselves to be supported even by the authority of the emperors themselves, with the council itself offering no opposition.], and before all else the holy faith and the integrity of the truth, which they had violated. Secondly, concerning the persons whom [Note: [Col. 0920D] (12) One of the Colbert manuscripts reads: “whom they said had been deposed.” Baronius wrongly prefers *delectas* (“chosen”) in place of this latter word. For the persons deposed, concerning whom proceedings were held at Sardica [Col. 0921C], are named below, §5, as also in the synodal letter to all the churches in Hilary, fragment II, §8: Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; Marcellus of Ancyra; and Asclepas, bishop of Gaza. Before the following words, “concerning the unjust judgment,” one must supply *ut* (“that”).] they said [Col. 0921A] had been deposed: concerning the unjust judgment, so that, if they could prove it, a just confirmation might be made. The third question, however—a question truly deserving to be called a question—was that they had inflicted grave and bitter injuries, intolerable and even impious outrages, upon the churches: seizing bishops, presbyters, and deacons; sending all clerics into exile; carrying them off to desert places; killing them by hunger, thirst, nakedness, and destitution; wearing others away, shut up in prison, by filth and stench [Note: [Col. 0921C] (1) The Colbert manuscripts lack: “wearing others away, shut up in prison, by filth and stench.” Then after the words “some with iron chains,” one must supply *stringerent* (“they bound tightly”) or some similar verb. In the synodal letter to all the churches, §3, bishops are said to have attended the synod, one of whom displayed the iron and chains which he had borne around his own neck because of them.]; and binding some with iron chains so tight that their necks were strangled by the closest fetters. Finally, some of these men died while bound under the same unjust punishment; and there can be no doubt that their death was glorious through martyrdom. Even now they dare to keep some in custody; nor was there any ground for accusation except that they resisted and cried out [Col. 0921B], execrating the Arian and Eusebian heresy and refusing communion with such persons. Yet those who preferred to serve the world (rather than to be of service in the Church) [Note: [Col. 0921C] (2) Baronius reads: “but to benefit those who preferred to think with them. And those,” etc., supported by no manuscript. One Colbert manuscript reads “because [they preferred] to be in the world”; the other, “but those who [preferred] to be in the world”; then both read *sevire maluerunt* (“preferred to be harsh/cruel”) in place of *prodesse* (“to benefit”). Pithou reads: “those who preferred to serve the world, to benefit.” From these readings, if “rather than in the Church” is supplied before *prodesse*, the sentence is restored entire and accords sufficiently with the council’s meaning: it complains that those who had chosen to serve the world rather than the Church were promoted to clerical rank. That these words designate Ischyras will be made clear by the following note.], and those previously deposed, were not merely received back but even promoted to clerical rank, and received [Note: [Col. 0921D] (3) In the letter to all the churches, §5, it is written: “As a reward for falsehood they gave that same Scyrus [that is, Ischyras] episcopal honour—a man who was neither presbyter nor even cleric.” Julius’s earlier Letter I, §12, also convicts Ischyras of lies in this matter and others.] the reward of falsehood.

IV. But learn, most blessed brother, what was decreed concerning the impious and unlearned young men Ursacius and Valens. Since it was evident that they did not cease to scatter the deadly seeds of adulterated doctrine [Note: [Col. 0921D] (4) One Colbert manuscript has *eum* (“him”) in place of *hos* (“these men”).], and since Valens, having abandoned his church, had wished to invade another church, and at the time when he stirred up the sedition one of our brethren who could not flee, Viator, was crushed and trampled underfoot and died on the third day in that same city of the Aquileians [Col. 0921C]: Valens was assuredly the cause of his death—he who disturbed, he who incited. But when you have read what we communicated to the most blessed Augusti [Note: [Col. 0921D] (5) This letter is not extant.], you will readily perceive that we omitted nothing insofar as reason permitted; and, lest the long account should be burdensome [Col. 0922A], we indicated who had acted [Note: [Col. 0922D] (6) Two Colbert manuscripts, with Baronius, read “what they had done.” Baronius then omits “and what they had committed.”] and what they had committed.

V. Your outstanding prudence, however, ought to arrange that through your letters our brethren in Sicily, Sardinia, and Italy may learn what has been done and decreed; and that, through ignorance, they may not receive the letters of communion—that is, the *epistolia* [Note: [Col. 0922D] (7) The same manuscripts here read *episcopalia*, but below retain *epistolia*.]—of those whom a just sentence has deposed. Let Marcellus, Athanasius, and Asclepius remain in our communion, for the unjust judgment cannot harm them [Note: [Col. 0922D] (8) The same manuscripts read “could not harm.” Those who withdrew to Philippopolis are here indicated.], nor the flight and evasions of those who refused to come before the judgment of all the bishops who assembled. The full report of the brethren whom your sincere charity sent will further instruct your unanimity concerning the rest, as we mentioned above. [Col. 0922B] We have also taken care to append the names of those who were deposed for their crimes, so that your eminent gravity may know who have been deprived of communion. As we said beforehand, be pleased to admonish by your letters all our brethren and fellow bishops not to receive their *epistolia*, that is, their letters of communion.

## Names of the Heretics

[Note: [Col. 0922D] (9) The names of these heretics are listed in a different order in Hilary, from the Pithou manuscript, fragment II, §14; in another order in the synod’s letter to all the churches, ibid., §7; and in yet another in the Colbert manuscripts which we now follow. Since the order is inconstant, it is evident that nothing can be inferred from it.]

Acacius of Caesarea. Ursacius of Singidunum. Menophantus of Ephesus. Valens of Mursa. George of Laodicea. Narcissus of Hieropolis. Stephen of Antioch.

## The Same Letter from Hilary

*(Councils, vol. II, col. 660, Labbe edition.)*

What we have always believed, we still believe now. For experience proves and confirms what each person has heard by report. For true is what the most blessed [Col. 0922C] teacher of the Gentiles, the Apostle Paul, said of himself: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13). Indeed, since the Lord Christ dwelt in him, there can be no doubt that the Holy Spirit spoke through his mind and gave utterance through the instrument of his body. You also, therefore, most beloved brother, though absent in body, were present in harmonious mind and will (*mente, concordia, voluntate*, according to the Fossatensis and Aniciensis manuscripts); and the excuse for your absence was honourable and necessary: lest schismatic wolves should steal and snatch away by ambush, or heretical dogs, roused in rabid frenzy, should bark madly, or indeed the serpent, the devil, should pour forth the poison of blasphemies. For this will appear the best and most fitting course: that the priests of the Lord from every individual province should report to the head, that is, to [Col. 0922D] the see of the Apostle Peter.

Therefore, since both the written documents and the living voices of our dearest brethren and fellow presbyters [Col. 0923A] Archidamus and Philoxenus, and of our most dear son Leo the deacon, will be able to set forth most truthfully and faithfully everything that has occurred, been done, and decreed, it seems almost superfluous to insert the same matters in this letter (variant: “bring them forward”). It became clear to all who assembled from the regions of the East—those who call themselves bishops, although among them there are certain originators whose sacrilegious minds the Arian heresy has stained with its pestilential poison—that, through distrust, they had long prevaricated and refused to come to judgment; and that they censured both your communion and ours, though it was wholly guiltless. For not only did we alike believe the testimony of eighty bishops concerning Athanasius’s innocence, but, though summoned by your presbyters and by letter to the synod to be held in the city of Rome, they refused to come. And it was sufficiently unjust, when they held the matter in contempt and so many priests bore witness, to deny fellowship to Marcellus and Athanasius.

There were three matters to be discussed. For the most devout emperors themselves permitted all things to be examined and debated anew: first of all, the holy faith and the integrity of the truth, which they had violated; secondly, the persons whom they said had been deposed, concerning the unjust judgment, so that, if they could prove their case, a just confirmation might result; thirdly, the question which truly deserves to be called a question: that they had inflicted grave and bitter injuries, intolerable and even impious outrages, upon the churches, seizing bishops, presbyters, and deacons, sending all clerics into exile, transporting them to desert places, killing them by hunger, thirst, nakedness, and every kind of destitution; wearing others away, shut in prison, [Col. 0923C] by filth and stench; binding some with iron chains so tight that their necks were strangled by the closest fetters. Finally, some of these men died while bound in that same unjust punishment, and there can be no doubt that their death was glorious through martyrdom. Even now they dare to retain some in custody. Nor was there any ground for accusation (variant: “for anyone”) except that they resisted and cried out that they execrated the Arian and Eusebian heresy (variant: “the heresy of Eusebius”) and refused communion with such persons; while benefiting those who preferred to agree with them (variant from the Paris edition or a manuscript: “those who refused to serve the world”; another variant: “those who preferred to serve the world”). And those previously deposed were not merely received back but promoted even to clerical rank (variant: “clerical”), and received the reward of falsehood.

[Col. 0923D] But learn, most blessed brother, what was decreed concerning the impious and unlearned young men Ursacius and Valens. Since it was evident that they did not cease to scatter the deadly seeds of adulterated doctrine, and since Valens, having abandoned his church, had wished to invade another church, and at the time when he stirred up the sedition one of our brethren who could not flee, Viator (variant: Victor), was crushed and trampled underfoot and died on the third day in that same city of the Aquileians: Valens surely furnished the cause of his death—he who disturbed, he who incited. But when you have read what we communicated to the most blessed Augusti, you will readily perceive that we omitted nothing insofar as reason permitted; and, lest the long narration should be burdensome, we indicated who had acted and committed these things.

[Col. 0924A] Your outstanding prudence, however, ought to arrange that through your letters our brethren in Sicily, Sardinia, and Italy may learn what has been done and decreed; and that, through ignorance, they may not receive the letters of communion of those whom a just sentence has declared outside the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0924D] (1) Variant: “whom a just sentence has deposed.”]. Let Marcellus, Athanasius, and Asclepius remain in our communion, because the unjust judgment could not harm them, nor the flight and evasions of those who refused to come before the judgment of all the bishops who assembled. Moreover, as we mentioned above, the full report of the brethren whom your sincere charity sent will fully inform your unanimity. We have taken care to append the names of those who were deposed for their crimes, so that your eminent gravity may know who have been deprived of [Col. 0924B] communion, as we stated beforehand. Be pleased to admonish all our brethren and fellow bishops by your letters not to receive their letters (*epistolia*), that is, their letters of communion.

### Names of the Heretics

Ursacius of Singidunum; Valens of Mursa; Narcissus of Neronopolis [Note: [Col. 0924D] (2) Incorrectly given as Ieropolis or Hierapolis; for Athanasius, *On Flight*, reads: ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως Νέρωνος, “from the city of Nero.”]; Stephen of Antioch; Acacius of Caesarea; Menophanes (Menophantus) of Ephesus; George of Laodicea. Theodore also ought here to have been added, concerning whom St Athanasius writes in his Letter to the Solitaries, p. 635, and the fathers of the Council of Sardica in their letter to all the churches, p. 669, listing them in this order: Theodore, Narcissus, Acacius, Stephen, Ursacius, Valens, Menophantus, and George.

# Appendix: Writings of Suspect Faith

## Notice concerning the Letter of Julius to Dionysius of Alexandria

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 57.)*

[Col. 0925A] I. Time, which commonly consumes so much, has at last restored to us this letter in its entirety and completeness, already well known from many records, and especially from Monophysite writings. One fragment of it had previously been supplied by Leontius’s book *Against the Frauds of the Apollinarians*, and its final part by an old Greek manuscript. Moreover, in the *History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria* compiled by Eusebius Renaudot—a man most distinguished for his learning in Oriental languages and disciplines—p. 360, there is transcribed a synodal letter of John, patriarch of Antioch, who flourished in the middle of the tenth century. In it, words from §3 of this letter are cited as follows:

> “He likewise says in the letter to Dionysius, bishop of Cyprus: ‘While they confess two natures, they are compelled to worship one and not to worship the other. They are baptized in the one who is divine, and are not baptized in the one who is human. But since we are baptized in the name of Christ, we confess one nature: divinity and a passible body, so that our baptism may be in God and in the death of the Lord.’”

There, indeed, these words are presented as though from St Hippolytus of Rome; but other books attribute the same words to Julius of Rome. Earlier, Christianus Lupus in the *Synodicon*, or compilation of letters relating to the Council of Ephesus, republished by Stephen Baluzius, ch. 224, had given us at least its middle portion in Latin. But we owe it to the indefatigable labour and diligence of Antonio Muratori that the whole work was not long ago published in Greek from an Ambrosian manuscript, furnished with a new translation and elucidated by a learned dissertation.

II. The same letter is cited by an Eutychian in the aforementioned [Col. 0925D] *Synodicon*, chs. 222 and 225; by Eutychian disciples in Facundus, book I, ch. 5; and by the Acephali, or Severians, in the Conference held at Constantinople before Emperor Justinian in 533. Gennadius also mentions it in his book *On Writers*, and declares his view of it in these words:

> “Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote one letter to a certain Dionysius on the incarnation of the Lord. At that time it appeared useful against those who maintained that Christ had, through the incarnation, two persons just as he had two natures; but now it is shown to be pernicious, for it is fuel for the impiety of Eutyches and Timothy.”

Here he indicates that this letter requires a competent interpreter, by whom it may be cleansed of the impiety of Timothy—that is, Apollinaris’s disciple. Accordingly Ephraemius of Antioch, who accepts it in Photius at the end of codex 229, [Col. 0926A] takes the expression “one nature” as certainly denoting one hypostasis [Col. 0926B]. Such, indeed, was the opinion of the ancients concerning Julius: deceived by its superscription, they did not doubt that this letter was his, and preferred to adapt its heretical words—as Leontius calls them—“because of the credible authority of the person” to a Catholic sense, rather than accuse, or even suspect, so great a man of heresy.

III. Yet Facundus, book I, ch. 5, and Eulogius of Alexandria in Photius, codex 230, regarded the superscription of the letter as suspect; while Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, Leontius, and many others did not hesitate to declare it false. But they do not agree concerning its authorship. Leontius says that it seems likely to him that those who separated from Julius through schism—that is, those to whose schismatic letter Julius replies in Letter I—placed this letter under his name in order to stir up hatred against him. Diognitus, certainly, who was one of their number, is said in the synodal letter of Sardica to all the churches to have fabricated false letters. But if those schismatics alienated from Julius undertook to stir hostility against him by substituting heretical writings, why should they have behaved with the same intent toward Pope Felix, Gregory Thaumaturgus, and other fathers? Surely it seems more likely that other heretics did this, in order to win authority for their perverse doctrine by those great names.

And indeed Leontius himself proposes another conjecture on this matter. He begins the book which he entitled, *Against Those Who Produce for Us Certain Writings of Apollinaris Falsely Inscribed with the Names of Holy Fathers*, [Col. 0926D] with these words:

> “Certain persons from the heresy of Apollinaris, or Eutyches, or Dioscorus, wishing to confirm their own heresy, inscribed certain discourses of Apollinaris with the names of Gregory Thaumaturgus, Athanasius, or Julius, in order to deceive simpler people; and this they did accomplish.”

It must therefore be investigated to which of those heretics such great fraud ought to be attributed.

IV. There is no ancient writer in whom this letter does not suggest the impiety of Apollinaris. Many, moreover, teach that Apollinaris himself was its genuine author. Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, says expressly in the Conference of Constantinople:

> “For we have clearly shown that that famous letter of the blessed Julius was written to Dionysius.”

But the anonymous author of the *Collectanea against the Severians* in Canisius, vol. 4, part 1, and Leontius devote more labour than others to proving this. In *On Sects*, act 8, Leontius proves that this letter is not Julius’s but Apollinaris’s: “first, because whoever considers it will find in it nothing worthy of Julius’s name; next, because, whenever it mentions the body, it nowhere says that it was endowed with mind or was animate, although it was customary among the fathers of that age, whenever they mentioned Christ’s body, to call it endowed with mind and animate; finally, because Gregory of Nyssa, in his work against Apollinaris, explicitly cites many things contained in this letter and refutes them as erroneous.”

But an irrefutable proof is derived from his same book *Against the Frauds of the Apollinarians*. At its beginning Valentinus, Apollinaris’s leading disciple, adduces many testimonies of “Lord Apollinaris,” and among them one “from the letter to Dionysius, whose opening is ‘To me, a proof of friendship,’” and another from a letter to the same man whose opening is: “I am astonished when I hear that certain persons confess God in flesh, yet fall into the error of the division perversely introduced by the Paulianists.” This is the beginning of the letter attributed to Julius. It follows that Apollinaris was so certainly the genuine author of this letter that he did not wish the fact itself to remain concealed; and thus another contriver of the false superscription must be sought.

V. We have already heard Leontius attribute such fraud to certain persons “from the heresy of Apollinaris, or Eutyches, or Dioscorus.” Evagrius, however, book III, ch. [Col. 0927C] 31, ascribes it to the Eutychians and disciples of Dioscorus, of whom he says:

> “They also falsely attributed many books of Apollinaris to Athanasius, Gregory Thaumaturgus, and Julius.”

Emperor Marcian likewise attributes the same crime to certain Eutychian disciples at the end of his letter to the Alexandrian monks, Council of Chalcedon, part 3, ch. 8:

> “They did not hesitate to disseminate among the people the books of Apollinaris, attaching to them the names of the holy fathers, so that by their falsehood they might altogether deceive the minds of the simple.”

But Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, testifies in the Conference of Constantinople that he suspected not these, but the Apollinarians, of this crime. For when the Acephali had cited the letters of Felix and Julius in support of their heresy, he declared without hesitation that they were false. Then, when they pressed him, saying, “What, then, do you suppose—that we falsified them?” he answered: “We do not suspect you, but the ancient heretics, the Apollinarians.” And indeed Leontius, in the latter part of *Against the Frauds of the Apollinarians*, argues that “the letters said to be Julius’s are Apollinaris’s” from the fact that “the disciples of Apollinaris are older than all who used them.”

Not without reason, therefore, did the ancient compiler of the letters published by Christianus Lupus and reprinted by Stephen Baluzius in the new collection of councils, ch. 224, place before this letter the following title:

> “Copy of Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, as the writings of Eutyches assert, to Dionysius, bishop; guided by its meaning, Eutyches himself fell into error.”

Nor should that unhappy heresiarch be accused of falsehood when, in the same work, ch. 222, he wrote to Pope Leo that he could not depart from the confession of one nature: “For I know,” he says, “that our holy and blessed fathers Julius, Felix, Athanasius, Gregory—most holy bishops—rejected the term ‘two natures.’” Would that he alone had been deceived by the deceptive mask of so many bishops. But even now the devout mother Church laments the ruin of countless persons who, though they anathematize Eutyches, nevertheless believe that they have the holy fathers Julius, Felix, Gregory, and Athanasius as their guides, refuse to be torn away from the confession of one nature, and do not shrink from condemning and detesting the Council of Chalcedon and Leo’s *Tome*.

[Col. 0928B] VI. It remains now to inquire who Dionysius was, to whom Apollinaris wrote this letter. In ch. 9 of the *Collectanea against the Monophysites* by an ancient author, whose Greek copy is preserved in the Paris college of the Reverend Fathers of the Society of Jesus, there occurs this observation on the superscription of this letter:

> For Apollinaris writes thus: “Apollinaris to my lord, the most beloved Dionysius, fellow minister [συλλειτουργός].” But those who fabricated it made: “Julius, bishop, greeting in Christ.”

These words are translated in Canisius, vol. IV, part I, p. 236:

> “For Apollinaris writes thus: ‘Apollinaris to my lord, most beloved Dionysius, fellow minister.’ But the forgers made the superscription: ‘Julius, bishop of Rome, greeting in the Lord.’”

The same writer then asserts that Dionysius was a presbyter, not a bishop. The disciples of Apollinaris, Timothy and Valentinus, seem to favour this opinion insofar as they never call this Dionysius a bishop, but only an intimate of Apollinaris. Nor is he called bishop by Gennadius of Marseilles, Hypatius of Ephesus, or Eulogius of Alexandria. Yet the superscription which the aforementioned author of the *Collectanea* judges original and genuine strongly opposes this view, because Dionysius is called *syllēτουργos* (συλλειτουργός, “fellow minister”); for nothing is more customary than for bishops to call their colleagues *syllēτουργoi*. Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, expressly inscribed his exposition of faith “to Julius, fellow minister,” and the fathers of the Synod of Sardica call Julius himself “fellow minister.”

[Col. 0928D] Moreover, in the aforementioned superscription the preceding word *despotēi* (δεσπότῃ, “my lord”) scarcely permits doubt that the following *syllēτουργōi* denotes a fellow bishop rather than a fellow presbyter. Accordingly, the compiler of the *Synodicon* calls Dionysius a bishop. Others also identify the place of which he was bishop, but disagree among themselves in doing so. Leontius, in *On Sects*, act 8, calls him bishop “of the Corinthians”; John, patriarch of Antioch, in the passage cited above in §1, calls him bishop “of Cyprus”; and the superscription of the Ambrosian manuscript calls him bishop “of Alexandria.” Yet Leontius was gravely mistaken in this matter if by “Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians” he meant the celebrated bishop whose letter to Pope Soter survives. Nor is the Greek superscription that calls him “Dionysius [Col. 0929A] of Alexandria” more genuine. For in the time of Julius or Apollinaris no Dionysius presided over the church of Alexandria. Dionysius of Alexandria, contemporary with Dionysius, bishop of Rome, was indeed very famous; but Jerome’s *Chronicle* reports that he died in 281, whereas Julius began to govern the Roman church only in 336. There is therefore no basis from which to determine this Dionysius’s see.

# Letter of Julius, Bishop of Rome, to Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 61.)* [Note: [Col. 0929] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0929]

[Col. 0930A] I. I am astonished when I hear that certain persons do indeed confess the Lord as God incarnate, yet fall into the division perversely introduced by the Paulianists. For those devoted to Paul of Samosata say that one is he who is from heaven, confessing that he is God, and another he who is from earth, declaring that he is man: the one uncreated, the other created; the one eternal, the other of yesterday; the one Lord, the other servant. They act impiously whether they worship him whom they call servant [Col. 0930B] and created, or do not worship him who redeemed us with his own blood. But those who confess that the God who is from heaven took flesh from the Virgin and is one with the flesh, needlessly stir up disturbances by uttering things that savour of the impiety of those people.

[Col. 0929A] αʹ. I am astonished to learn of certain persons who confess the Lord to be God incarnate, yet fall into the division wrongly introduced by the Paulianizers. For those enslaved to Paul of Samosata say that one is he from heaven, confessing him to be God, and another he from earth, calling him man: the one uncreated, the other created; the one eternal, the other of yesterday; the one master, the other slave. They act impiously, whether they worship the one whom they call slave and created, or fail to worship the one who redeemed us by his own blood. But those who confess that the God from heaven was made flesh from the Virgin and is one with the flesh, vainly create disturbance, giving utterance to the language of that impiety.

[Col. 0930B] **II.** For they too, as I hear, speak of two natures, although John plainly demonstrates that the Lord is one when he says, “The Word became flesh,” and Paul when he says, “One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” If, then, he who was born of the holy Virgin is named one, and he himself is he through whom all things were made, there is one nature; since, possessing one person, he is not divided into two, because the body is not a proper nature, just as the Godhead is a proper nature in the incarnation;

[Note: [Col. 0929C] (1) Here Leontius’s observation has force: he notes that Apollinaris, in this letter, whenever he speaks of Christ’s human nature, nowhere mentions a soul. Another point must be observed here. If that is called a proper nature which stands separately and is set apart from every other, then in Christ neither the body, or humanity, nor the Godhead were proper natures, since they are joined and united to one another. But if a proper nature means that which is entire and preserves its natural properties, then in that sense both the body and the Godhead remained proper natures even after the union, since they retain their respective properties.

Apollinaris, unable to distinguish the person of the Word from its nature, and wishing what is said of the person of the Word—“the Word became flesh”—to be predicated also of the nature of the Word itself, maintained not only that the Word became flesh, but that the nature of the Word likewise became flesh. Hence, in Leontius, *Against the Deceptions of Apollinaris*, vol. VI, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Cologne ed., p. 491, he reasons thus: “If the Word was named flesh because of the union, it follows that flesh too is named Word because of the union.” And shortly before: “It is utterly irrational to name the incorporeal by bodily names, when we say ‘the Word became flesh,’ yet not to name the body by the name of the incorporeal, according to the union which it has with it.”

There is, however, a great difference between the two. For it is rightly said that the Word became flesh, because the person of the Word assumed flesh; but one cannot likewise say that flesh became Word, because the person of the flesh in no way assumed the nature of the Word.]

But as man is one nature, so also is Christ, made in the likeness of men. If, however, they do not acknowledge that which is one according to union, they may also divide him who is one into many parts and speak of many natures; for the body is composite, consisting of bones, sinews, veins, flesh, skin, nails, hair, blood, and spirit. All these differ from one another; yet the nature of man is one. Therefore the reality of the Godhead is with the body and is not divided into two natures.

[Note: [Col. 0930D] (2) Apollinaris, and after him the Monophysites, are accustomed to misuse the example of man, in whom soul and flesh nevertheless do not cease to be two substances when united. Yet even under this illustration Apollinaris concealed the poison of his heresy: as human nature is composed of soul and flesh, so he believed Christ’s nature composed jointly of Word and flesh. In this he agreed with the Arians. Among them Lucius, pseudo-bishop of Alexandria, argues thus in Canisius, vol. IV, part I, p. 238: “How is Christ [Christ], if he is not one person, one composite nature, as we recognize man to be composed of soul and body? But if he had a soul … then the motions of God and of the soul conflict; for each moves of itself and is drawn toward different operations.”]

For the reality of the Godhead is one with the body,

[Note: [Col. 0930D] (3) The old translator reads: “is one with the body.” Hence there is reason to suspect that the word ἕν (*one*) has dropped out here in the Greek.]

and is not divided into two natures. For it would not be possible to call the whole “Son of Man,” descended from heaven, and “Son of God,” born of a woman, if it admitted a division of two natures. Rather, that which descended from heaven would be called Son of God and not Son of Man; while that which was born of a woman would be called Son of Man and not Son of God. And this accords with the Pauline division.

[Note: [Col. 0930D] (4) Rather, this whole could rightly—and ought to—be predicated both “Son of Man” and “Son of God.” For the whole which consists of the united divine and human natures is nothing other than the person; and since that person is one in Christ, even by Apollinaris’s admission, it comprehends in itself whatever belongs to the united natures. Accordingly, Augustine’s rule has force, *Against an Arian Sermon*, bk. I, ch. 8, copied by Leo, Epistle 28, no. 7: “Because of this unity of person, to be understood in both natures, the Son of Man is read to have descended from heaven, although the Son of God assumed flesh from that Virgin of whom he was born; and conversely, the Son of God is said to have been crucified.”

Earlier Hilary, *On the Trinity*, bk. X, no. 52, had taught this to be the faith of the Church: that Jesus Christ is not divided into Word, soul, and body, nor conversely is God the Word absorbed into soul and body. “The Word of God,” he says, “is wholly God for him; Christ is wholly man for him.” Again Leo, Epistle 115, to the monks of Palestine: “It makes no difference from which substance Christ is named, since, with the unity of person remaining inseparably, the same one is wholly Son of Man because of the flesh and wholly Son of God because of the Godhead one with the Father.”

Augustine’s words agree with these, Sermon 293, no. 7: “God himself remains God; man is added to God, and one person comes to be, so that he is not a half-god—as though God in part as God and man in part as man—but wholly God and wholly man.” Moved by this mode of speaking in Augustine, Leo, and other Fathers, theologians subsequently established that, when Christ was under discussion, *whole* should be predicated of the natures and *wholly* of the person. But it has been observed, in the latest edition of this Doctor’s exposition of Psalm II, no. 27, note a, and on *On the Trinity*, bk. X, no. 52, note e, that this rule was unknown in Hilary’s time. Apollinaris’s writings confirm this: in them he is found misusing the word “whole,” customarily used among the orthodox to signify the person, for the purpose of confusing the natures.]

[Col. 0929B] **βʹ.** For they too, as I hear, say there are two natures, though John clearly shows that the Lord is one, in saying, “The Word became flesh,” and Paul in saying, “One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” If, therefore, he born of the holy Virgin has been named one, and he himself is he through whom all things came to be, there is one nature; because, having one person, he is not divided into two; since neither is the body a proper nature, as the Godhead is a proper nature according to the incarnation, but as man is one nature, so also is Christ, made in the likeness of men.

But if they do not recognize that which is one according to union, they can divide the one into many and speak of many natures, since the body is manifold, consisting of bones, sinews, veins, flesh, skin, nails, hair, blood, and spirit. All these have difference from one another, yet man’s nature is one. Thus the truth of the Godhead is with the body and is not divided into two natures. For it could not be that the whole should be called Son of Man, having descended from heaven, and Son of God, having been born of a woman, if it admits a division of two natures. Rather, that which descended from heaven would be called Son of God and not Son of Man; and that which was born of a woman would be called Son of Man and not Son of God. And this follows the Pauline division.

[Col. 0932A] **III.** But the divine Scriptures teach us that, when we hear both the descent from heaven and the birth on earth from a woman, we must understand both of the one Lord. Let those, therefore, who understand thus not go so far as to use the words of those who think contrary things, lest, thinking rightly in mind, they speak perversely with their mouth.

[Note: [Col. 0931C] (1) According to the anonymous author in Lupus, *Synodicon*, ch. 225, and in Baluzius, *New Collection of Councils*, p. 937, Eutyches cited this passage under Julius’s name in defense of his heresy. But an ancient writer in Canisius, vol. IV, part 1, p. 237, comparing it with other unquestioned writings of Apollinaris, proves that this letter falsely bears Julius’s name and belongs to Apollinaris.

First he adduces this passage of that heretic: “How is it not impious to have one substance created or servile, and to render one and the same worship to it and to the Creator and Lord?” Then he adds another: “It is impossible that the same should be worshipful and not worshipful; therefore it is impossible that the same should be God and man, except in the united, commingled nature of the incarnate Godhead.” He had previously set out a third, p. 236, as follows: “It is impious [supply: to say] that one and the same worship belongs to one nature and another—that is, to Creator and creature, God and man. But Christ has one worship; and therefore God and man are understood under one name. God and man, then, are not one substance and another, but one according to composition with a human body.”

That this argument was habitual with Apollinaris is clear from other passages excerpted by Leontius. It is enough to add the passage which he appended near the end of *Against the Deceptions of Apollinaris*: “If man is wholly God and the same person, a pious mind, worshipping God but not worshipping man, will be found both to worship and not to worship the same one—which cannot be. And the same person, as man, will not deem himself worshipful, for he will not be impious; but as God he will know himself worshipful. Yet it is impossible that the same be worshipful and not worshipful. Therefore it is impossible that the same be wholly God and man, except in the sole united nature of the incarnate Godhead.”

But the Catholic faith readily dissolves this alleged Achilles argument. For, as the anonymous author in Christian Lupus, ch. 225, replies: “We who hold the straight path of Catholic faith, leaving aside this confusion of two natures, having been baptized into the Lord’s flesh, worship it because it has been assumed by the Godhead and so united to it that we confess not one person and another but one and the same Son of God, God and man.” Indeed, Apollinaris’s own disciple Valentinus did not conceal how weak it was. He censures his fellow disciples in Leontius, *Against the Deceptions of Apollinaris*, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Cologne ed., p. 489d: “Timothy and his master Polemius, and their followers, failed to understand that the worship of the one person of God the Word and of the flesh fashioned by the Word belongs to the incarnate God, not to the flesh. For the Word is not worshipped on account of the flesh; rather, the flesh is worshipped together with the Word.”]

For those who say two natures must worship one and not worship the other, and be baptized into the divine nature but not into the human. But if we are baptized into the Lord’s death, we confess one nature of the impassible Godhead and passible flesh, so that our baptism may thus be accomplished into God and into the death of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0932C] (2) Baptized into the Lord’s death, we do not confess one nature of impassible Godhead and passible flesh, but one person. Ephraem of Antioch, in Photius near the end of codex 239, wishing to apply these words to a pious and Catholic sense, interprets them of unity of hypostasis. Although the opening words of the following section seem to favor this interpretation, what is attached to them wholly opposes it. For whoever denies that after the incarnation either Christ’s body or Godhead has a proper nature shows that he defends unity not merely of person but also of nature.

Apollinaris himself, or one of his disciples, more shrewdly veiled the heretical intent when, under the names of Gregory Thaumaturgus and Athanasius, he asserted one incarnate nature of God the Word. Deceived by the authority of these names, many Catholics considered it religiously obligatory not to reject that expression. Thus Basil, bishop of Seleucia, at the Council of Chalcedon, act 1, p. 230, urged Eutyches, who affirmed that Christ had one nature after union, to add “incarnate.” “For,” he said, “if you say ‘from two natures, but after union one,’ and do not add ‘incarnate’ and ‘made man,’ you will seem to introduce confusion. But if you add ‘incarnate’ and ‘made man,’ you say the same as our Fathers.”

After the Council of Chalcedon, Epiphanius, bishop of Pergamum, with the synod of Pamphylia, wrote to Emperor Leo: “For it makes no difference whether the unity of two natures is called unconfused, or whether it is said to be from two in the same sense. Nor, if one nature of the Word is named but ‘incarnate’ is added, does it signify anything else; rather, it declares the same thing in more fitting language. For we find that the holy Fathers often spoke thus.” These words are found in Labbe, vol. IV, p. 936.

In the proceedings of the Council of Constantinople, at the first session of the Synod of Chalcedon, read at p. 182, Dioscorus says: “Flavian was condemned because he said there were two natures after union. But I have testimonies of the holy Fathers—Athanasius, Gregory, Cyril—in many places, that one must not say two natures after union, but one incarnate nature of God the Word.” Although he does not lie in asserting that Cyril preached one incarnate nature of God the Word, he is nevertheless not free from falsehood when he insists that Cyril denied two natures after union. For Cyril speaks thus in Epistle I to Successus: “We understand that two natures came together in an indissoluble union without any confusion or alteration. If there is no alteration whatever, they are what they were before union. For,” he immediately says, “flesh is flesh and not Godhead, even though it has become God’s flesh; likewise the Word is God and not flesh, though in the economy he has made flesh his own … We say that it came to be from two natures; but after union we do not divide the natures from one another, nor cut the one indivisible Son into two sons. We confess one Son and, as the holy Fathers say, one incarnate nature of God the Word.”

On this occasion Cyril disclosed no less his orthodoxy than his reverence toward the Fathers. For he knew exceedingly well how to bring back to a Catholic and orthodox meaning the Apollinarian expression which he believed to belong to the Fathers and therefore did not dare reject. For objections made to him as he proclaimed one incarnate nature of God the Word, and for his answers, see his second Epistle to Successus. Basil of Seleucia himself, in the passage cited, told Eutyches: “If you do not say two natures after union, you speak of mixture and confusion.” Soon after, Florentius the patrician, with the entire synod approving, cried: “Whoever does not say ‘from two natures’ and ‘two natures’ does not believe rightly.”]

[Col. 0931A] **γʹ.** But the divine Scriptures teach us to think of both the descent from heaven and the birth on earth from a woman as concerning the one Lord. Those, therefore, who think thus should not proceed to agreement in speech with those who think the contrary, lest while speaking well in thought they speak ill in words. For those who say two natures must worship the one and not worship the other, and be baptized into the divine but not into the human. But if we are baptized into the death of the Lord, we confess one nature of impassible Godhead and passible flesh, so that in this way our baptism is performed into God and into the death of the Lord.

[Col. 0933A] **IV.** For we do not fear slanderers who divide the Lord into two persons, should they revile us—while we maintain the evangelical and apostolic union—as though we said that the flesh is from heaven. For when we say that the Son of God was born of a woman, we cannot be blamed as though we said that the Word is from earth and not from heaven. We say both: the whole is from heaven on account of the Godhead, and the whole is from a woman on account of the flesh; knowing no division of the one person and not cutting off the earthly from the heavenly or the heavenly from the earthly. Such a cutting apart would indeed be impious.

[Note: [Col. 0934D] (1) Supply “which Christ is.” Such a form of speech, used by Hilary and other ancients to explain unity of person, is wholly orthodox; but in Apollinaris, where it is used to introduce confusion of natures, it becomes heretical. Therefore Ferrandus the deacon, in his Letter to Severus, no. 8, carefully distinguishes *wholly* (*totus*) and *the whole* (*totum*). Having asked, “What is the whole Christ?” and answered, “God the Word, rational soul, and flesh,” he immediately adds: “Therefore Christ is wholly everywhere according to the Word; but the whole is not everywhere, since the rational soul and flesh, with which the whole exists, are not everywhere.” As we observed, theologians followed this distinction afterwards.]

Let not, then, those who say two natures give cause or occasion to those who cut apart. For the body, taken by itself, is not a nature in the one Christ, because it is not life-giving by itself and cannot be cut apart or separated from the life-giving Word. Nor, conversely, is the Word, taken by itself, divided into its proper nature, which it possesses insofar as it is without flesh; for the Lord moved about in the world in flesh and not without flesh. Nor does anyone separate the created body from the uncreated Godhead so as to distinguish a created nature; nor did the uncreated Word dwell among us without a body, so that anyone might divide an uncreated nature.

But if both are one according to union, conjunction, and human-like composition, one name also is applied to the composite: from the Godhead it has impassibility; from the body, liability to suffering. And as, when we hear Paul calling Christ passible, we do not understand it in a divided sense, nor suppose the Godhead passible, so “created” and “servant” are neither said in a divided sense nor make the Godhead created or servile. Again, “uncreated” neither makes the flesh uncreated nor is said separately of the Godhead alone.

[Note: [Col. 0934D] (2) Apollinaris’s doctrine entails that he too must call the Godhead passible. For if, on his view, the Word or Godhead becomes flesh through incarnation and, conversely, flesh becomes Word or Godhead, he must concede that the Godhead becomes passible through incarnation. If the name and nature of flesh belong to the Word and Godhead, the property of flesh must also belong to it.

Yet he does not simply deny either a passible Godhead or uncreated flesh; he both denies and attributes these things: he denies them when considered separately, but attributes them when considered conjointly. For when he says, “Uncreated neither makes the flesh uncreated nor is said separately of Godhead alone,” why does he refuse to allow “uncreated” to be said of Godhead alone, unless he wants it said also of the united flesh? How vain are the efforts of this heresiarch, who cannot extricate himself from the labyrinth of error except by returning to the path of right faith from which he departed—now grasping one point, then abandoning it, like a restless, skipping man.

Faith, however, does not divide Christ’s natures, but distinguishes the natures united in the one person of God the Word, so that the nature of the Word is one thing and that of the flesh another, and the properties of the Word are different from those of the flesh. Thus, while confessing that God the Word suffered in the flesh, we proclaim his Godhead impassible; and with respect to Godhead we understand Christ as uncreated, while with respect to flesh we believe the same Christ created. For one nature does not arise from united natures; rather, one divine person subsists, to whom the things proper to each individual nature are attributed.]

[Col. 0934A] **δʹ.** For we do not fear those slanderers who divide the Lord into two persons, if, while we uphold the evangelical and apostolic union, they blaspheme us as saying that the flesh is from heaven. Nor, when we say that the Son of God came to be from a woman, can we be reviled as saying that the Word is from earth and not from heaven. We say both: the whole from heaven because of the Godhead and the whole from a woman because of the flesh, knowing no division of the one person and not cutting the earthly away from the heavenly or the heavenly from the earthly; for the severance is impious.

Let not those who speak of two natures therefore give an occasion to those who sever. For neither is the body by itself a nature in the one Christ, because neither is it life-giving by itself, nor capable of being severed without the life-giving Word; nor is the Word by itself divided into a proper nature which it has as without flesh, because the Lord came into the world in flesh, not without flesh. Neither does anyone separate the created body from the uncreated Godhead, to distinguish a created nature; nor did the uncreated Word come among us apart from a body, to divide an uncreated nature.

But if each is one according to union, conjunction, and human-like composition, one name is applied to the composite, which has impassibility from the Godhead and susceptibility to suffering from the body. And as, hearing Paul call Christ passible, we did not hear it in a divided sense or consider the Godhead passible, so “created” and “servant” are neither said in a divided sense nor make the Godhead created or servile. Again, “uncreated” neither makes the flesh uncreated nor is said in a divided sense of the Godhead alone.

[Col. 0933C] **V.** Let those who think thus remain at peace, avoiding superfluous questions, lest we disagree in judgments for the sake of words. It is therefore agreed and confessed jointly that the body is from the Virgin, the Godhead from heaven; that the body was formed in the womb, while the Godhead is uncreated and eternal; so that, once the Word is united with the body, the Godhead remains undivided.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] (1) Here also “which Christ is” must be supplied. By the usage in which Scripture calls the whole which Christ is now God, now Son of Man, it teaches us not, with Apollinaris, a confusion of natures but unity of person in united natures. Unity of person forbids us to divide the natures; the truth of the natures requires us to distinguish them.

But Apollinaris, unable to understand union of natures without their confusion, admits that Christ’s flesh by its own nature is neither God nor of the substance of which God is; yet after union he does not hesitate to assert that it is consubstantial with God and God. In another letter to the same Dionysius, in Leontius, *Against the Deceptions of Apollinaris*, p. 487h, he explains: “We have always written that the Savior’s flesh is neither from heaven nor of the same substance as God, insofar as it is flesh and not God; but it is God insofar as it is united to the Godhead in one person.”

Hence Polenius, Timothy, and other disciples of Apollinaris taught that one must confess the flesh to be the same by union as God the Word, speak of it as of the Word, and believe it consubstantial with God as Word. Another Timothy, a disciple of Apollinaris, strongly rejects this teaching in Leontius, at the cited place, p. 488f.]

But if it is customary in Scripture to call the whole God and likewise to call the whole man, let us too follow the divine utterances and not divide the indivisible: neither separating the Godhead from the body, as though we then spoke more fittingly when the body is said to have been fashioned from the womb; nor dividing the body from the Godhead, as though we confessed the presence when the uncreated Godhead is glorified.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] (2) That is, a mere presence of the Word such as exists in the prophets.]

[Col. 0934C] **εʹ.** Holding these views, let them remain quiet, avoiding superfluous inquiries, and let us not divide doctrines for the sake of words. It is agreed and jointly confessed that the body is from the Virgin, the Godhead from heaven; the body was fashioned in the womb, while the Godhead is uncreated and eternal, so that, the Word having been united with the body, the Godhead may remain undivided.

If it is customary in Scripture both to speak divinely of the whole and to speak humanly of the whole, let us likewise follow the divine sayings and not divide what is indivisible: neither dividing the Godhead from the body, as though this were fitting speech when the body is called formed from the womb, nor dividing the body from the Godhead, as though this were a confession of the presence when the Godhead is glorified as uncreated.

[Col. 0936A] **VI.** How, then, is it not lamentable that those who rightly confess or think these things, as they have also received them handed down from their forebears, should differ from one another over words? For some use the name of the body when speaking of the Word, just as John says that the Word became flesh (John 1:14); while others take the name of Godhead when they speak of the whole servant, as Paul: “I say, the last Adam became a life-giving spirit” (1 Cor. 8:6).

[Note: [Col. 0936D] (3) The ancients commonly understand by “Spirit” the immeasurable and incorporeal nature of God. Therefore Apollinaris does not without reason infer from this that the name of God is attributed to the last Adam. Yet Paul gave it to Christ not because Christ’s nature is one, but because his person is one.]

According to the flesh Christ confesses that he worships the Father, saying, “We worship what we know” (John 4:22), and the Godhead is not divided. He is worshipped according to the Godhead, and the body is not separated when we worship the Godhead. Nor do we separate the body from the Godhead—for this is impossible—when we worship that body which suffered death; nor is the Godhead separated, for it is united. For death had to be conquered by God, and it has been conquered.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] (4) Not because one nature was made out of Godhead and body, but because those two natures have been united in the one person of the Word.]

[Col. 0935A] **ϛʹ.** How, then, is it not grievous that those who rightly confess or think these things, as they have received them, should hesitate against one another over words? Some use the name of the body concerning the Word, as John says that the Word became flesh; others take the name of Godhead concerning the whole servant, as Paul says: “The last Adam became a life-giving spirit.” Christ confesses that according to the flesh he worships the Father, saying: “We worship what we know”; and the Godhead is not separated. He is worshipped according to the Godhead, and the body is not separated in the worship of the Godhead. Nor do we remove the body—for this is impossible—when we worship the body that suffered; nor is the Godhead separated, for it is united. For death had to be conquered by God, and it has been conquered.

[Col. 0936B] **VII.** Admonish those who vainly disagree over these questions, and let agreement in doctrine be preserved, so that we may not disagree over words. For it is impious to differ in doctrine while pretending agreement in words; but for those who agree in doctrine to disagree over words is vain and foolish.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] (5) In the Rupefoucauld *Parallels*, title 76, where these final words are cited as from Pope Julius of Rome’s letter to Dionysius, the Greek reads διαφωνοῦντας (*disagreeing*), not διαφέροντας (*differing*).]

Holding this agreement—that Christ is God incarnate, both from heaven and from earth, the same one a servant in form and God in power—let them remain in concord and not differ vainly, nor fall into the wrangling over words familiar to heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] (6) In the *Parallels* just mentioned, the following words are inserted here: “let them remain quiet, avoiding superfluous inquiries, and let us not divide for the sake of a word.” They have been transferred here from the beginning of section 5. This example can therefore show that such excerpts are not always reproduced with complete fidelity. In other instances some things are suppressed or mutilated; in this one the words have been moved from their place.]

Rather, let them emulate the simplicity of the Church. Farewell.

[Col. 0935B] **ζʹ.** Admonish those who vainly differ concerning these matters, and let agreement in doctrine be preserved, so that we may not be divided over words. For to differ in doctrines while pretending agreement in words is impious; but for those agreeing in doctrines to differ in words is vain and foolish. Holding this agreement—that Christ is God incarnate, both from heaven and earth, the same one a servant in form and God in power—let them remain in harmony and not differ vainly; let them not fall into the word-wrangling of heretics, but rather emulate the simplicity of the Church. Farewell.

## Old Translation of the Same Letter through the Middle of Section 5, Copied from Chapter 224 of the *Synodicon*

A copy of a letter of Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, as the Eutychians assert, written to Bishop Dionysius; guided by its sense, Eutyches himself fell into error.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] (1) It seems one should read: “Copy of a letter of Julius … written to Dionysius.”]

[Col. 0937A] **I.** I marvel on hearing of certain persons who indeed confess our Lord in the flesh, but fall into the division wickedly introduced by the Paulianists. For they follow Paul of Samosata and understand one person to be he who descended from heaven, confessing him God, while they say that another is the earthly man. They call the former unmade [or “unfabricated”], the latter made; the former eternal, the latter of yesterday; the former lord, the latter servant. They act impiously, whether they venerate him whom they call servant and made, or do not worship him who redeemed us by his blood.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] (2) Following the example of this ancient translator, we would prefer in the preceding translation placed opposite the Greek text: “For they, devoted to Paul of Samosata, say that one is he who is from heaven,” etc., so that *they* refers back to the preceding word “certain persons.”]

But those who confess that God descended from heaven, and that flesh was made from the Virgin [read: “that he became flesh”], and that he is one with the flesh, are vainly troubled [read: “trouble others”], venturing into the words of their impiety.

[Col. 0937B] **II.** For they also say, “as I hear” [OCR/translation uncertain: the text reads *sicut odio*], that there are two natures. Yet John plainly proves our Lord to be one when he says, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), and Paul the apostle when he says, “One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:6). For if Jesus, born of the holy Virgin, is named, and he himself is he through whom all things were made, there is of course one nature [delete *facta est*, “was made”], because there is also one person, not divided into two [“having one person, he is not divided into two”]; since the body is not a proper nature and the Godhead is a proper nature according to the flesh. But as man is one nature, so also is Christ, who was made in the likeness of man.

If they do not recognize that which is one through union, they can also divide the one into many and speak of very many natures, since the body is manifold, consisting of bones, sinews, veins, flesh, skin, nails, hair, blood, and spirit. All these are indeed different from one another, yet man’s nature is one [Baluzius: “their nature is one”]. Hence the nature of the Godhead is one with the body and is not divided into two natures. For the whole could not be called Son of Man when he descended from heaven, and again Son of God when born from a woman, if it admitted the division of two natures. Rather, that which descended from heaven would be called Son of God, not Son of Man; and that which was born of a woman would be called Son of Man, not Son of God. And this is of the Pauline division.

**III.** But the divine Scriptures teach us to think of our one Lord both when he descended from heaven and when he was born on earth. Those, therefore, who think thus do not depart into discord with those who think contrary things, so that while in mind they agree with the divine precepts, they may disagree in speech. For, if they understand [variant: “say”] two natures, they must worship one and not worship the other; and be baptized into the divine, but not baptized into the human. But if we are baptized into the Lord’s death, we confess one nature both of impassible Godhead and passible flesh, so that through this our baptism is received both into God and into the Lord’s death.

**IV.** For we do not fear slanderers who divide the Lord into two persons. Nor, when we preach evangelical and apostolic unity, should they assail us as if we said that the flesh is heavenly, though, on the contrary, we read the divine Scriptures saying that the Son is not from heaven. For when we say that the Son of God was created from a woman, we cannot be censured as though we said that the Word is from earth and not from heaven. For we say both: the whole from heaven because of the Godhead, and the whole from a woman because of the flesh, knowing no division of the one person.

## Muratori’s Inquiry into the Letter to Dionysius of Alexandria Published under the Name of Julius I, Addressed to the Most Learned and Distinguished Antonio Maria Salvini, Professor of Greek in the Florentine Academy

[Col. 0938]

## Synopsis of the Inquiry

Gennadius and the Centuriators wrongly attribute this letter to Julius I, Roman pontiff. Facundus of Hermiane more correctly denies it to him. Leontius of Byzantium does the same, together with Evagrius. There is nothing in it worthy of Julius. Apollinaris the heretic is believed to be its author; certain other works falsely attached to Julius are also his. He denied Christ’s body a soul, or human mind; so too does the author of this letter. Many things condemned in Apollinaris by St. Gregory of Nyssa are likewise taught here. Hypatius, Anastasius, Eulogius, Ephraemius, and others clear St. Julius of this calumny. Who Dionysius was to whom this letter is alleged to have been sent.

You know well, most learned Salvini, how heartily on another occasion you congratulated me for having returned from the more agreeable arts to more serious studies, and especially to sacred learning. Its study yields to none in pleasantness, while it is plainly established that it surpasses all others in usefulness. It has been most gratifying to me that, regarding this decision of mine, I have in you not merely an earnest encourager but also a kindly admirer.
