For although to persons who do not know you intimately you may at times appear to have confined all the force and concern of your talent solely to the more elegant branches of literature, I have ascertained that you possess such abundance of learning of every kind that both your praise and your encouragement will always carry the greatest weight and highest authority with me. And my judgment concerning you has repeatedly been confirmed not merely by the consensus of reputation, but by my own experience. Whenever I consulted you about the various difficulties that presented themselves to me in the vast field of learning, I always found in you such a wealth of knowledge and such mastery of the Greek language and of all antiquity as few attain and as we are accustomed to admire in very few.

Only this one thing—if I may say so with your leave—I could not entirely approve: namely, that you were content almost alone to know, and to sing behind your screen [*in sipario canere*], and that you did not enrich the republic of letters with benefits which you most certainly could have bestowed. But you preferred to enjoy your modesty and the consciousness of your learning rather than publish the fruits of your studies in these most difficult times, when one easily encounters readers who are fastidious or malicious, and when scarcely anyone, scarcely even the author himself, can be pleased—a man desirous of honorable quiet rather than turbulent glory.

If I followed you in this decision, I should do so with even greater reason than you, and should consult more wisely for the fortune and powers of a talent far inferior to yours. Yet I have now resolved to proceed more boldly and to heed your exhortations rather than your example. Therefore, since I have determined to publish these things, to which, through your humanity and learning, you have contributed more than one benefit, I considered nothing more important than choosing some place where I might testify both to my gratitude and to your worthiness of every commendation.

I accordingly wish this inquiry, in which I propose to vindicate the reputation of Julius I, Roman pontiff, against the calumnies of heretics, to bear your name. This we can readily do at present, since that document has been placed before us by which the Eutychians once hoped, under the fabricated name of so great a bishop, to deceive the Catholic Church. For what more clearly displays the truth than to expose the very workshop of falsehood and set the fabrication itself before all eyes?

Certainly this is the letter that made the faith of St. Julius doubtful to some of the ancients, and that seems to have troubled later centuries as well, when uncertain judgments were uttered concerning it precisely because it was unknown. We shall therefore render a service both welcome to the learned and useful to the memory of the holy pontiff if, by publishing this most notorious offspring, we enable everyone henceforth to judge its falsity and the fraud of the heretics.

Among ancient writers, the first to mention this letter is Gennadius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 2, writing as follows:

> Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote one letter to a certain Dionysius concerning the Incarnation of the Lord [Col. 0939D]. At that time it was indeed thought useful against those who, through the Incarnation, asserted in Christ two persons just as they did two natures. But it is now found pernicious; for it is a support of Eutychian and Timothean impiety.

The Magdeburg Centuriators gladly adopted and repeated Gennadius’s words in Century IV, chapter 10. They immediately append the following: “Cyril of Alexandria seems to have drawn from the same letter a testimony concerning Christ’s person in his *Apologetic* in this manner.” They then produce these very words of the letter:

> For the completion of the faith, the Son of God is proclaimed as incarnate from the Virgin Mary, and as having dwelt among men, working energy not in a name [it should have read “in a man”]. For this is found in the prophets [Col. 0940A] and in the epistles: perfect God in flesh and perfect man in spirit; not two sons. One is indeed the true Son, who assumed the man; the other, a mortal man, was assumed by God. But there is one Only-Begotten in heaven, the Only-Begotten upon earth.

Finally, the Centuriators conclude thus: “The Council of Chalcedon likewise cites the same testimony from his Letter to Prosdocimus against Eutyches.”

Yet neither the Centuriators nor Gennadius produced anything displaying an exact knowledge of the matter. First, it is worth observing that this letter was not properly known to Gennadius, a Latin writer, but only known by name. For his manifest mistake is to affirm that it was once thought useful against those who asserted two persons in Christ just as they asserted two natures [Col. 0940B]. No council and no Fathers of the Catholic Church had ever employed the testimony of this letter against the Nestorians, nor did they employ it afterwards.

Gennadius’s error arose because, in Act I of the Council of Ephesus, a passage from a letter of Pope Julius I was cited against Nestorius—the passage recently adduced by the Centuriators. Gennadius, and after him the Centuriators, therefore thought that the letter said to have been sent to Dionysius was the same as that cited in the Ephesian Council. But the letters are wholly different. The one supposedly written to Dionysius is now published by us, and it contains none of the material employed by the Ephesian synod. The other, *πρὸς Δόκιον* or *Δόκιμον*, that is, “to Docius,” whom others also call Prosdocimus [Col. 0940C], has long since perished; it was this letter that the Ephesian Fathers cited. Gennadius therefore confused the two letters, thinking that the letter to Dionysius had formerly been useful because he believed it had been used by the Ephesian Council to confirm the true faith.

Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, living in the century after Gennadius—that is, in Justinian’s time—has several remarks in book I, chapter 5, which support our conjecture and disclose Gennadius’s error more clearly. Writing against the Eutychians and their offspring, the Acephali, who maintained one nature in Christ, he says:

> What assistance against these most evident testimonies of the Fathers can they derive from saying, in support of their utterly vain error, that Julius, bishop of Rome, wrote somewhere in reply that there is one nature of Christ? Whereas in that same holy Ephesian synod only this statement of Blessed Julius was recited against Nestorius, from the letter to Prosdocimus, in which he says: “For the completion of the faith, the Son of God is proclaimed as incarnate from the Virgin Mary,” etc.

After Facundus has quoted the entire passage from Act I of the Council of Ephesus, reproduced above by the Centuriators, he continues:

> Nothing else from the sayings of Blessed Julius was brought forward in that synod besides this letter to Prosdocimus—if perhaps he wrote anything else—nor was anything further taken even from this letter. Why, then, was not that which they circulate as written by Blessed Julius concerning one nature of Christ, or similar matters which they claim other venerable Fathers wrote, recited against Nestorius in the synod [Col. 0941A]? For such things would have appeared more contrary to his doctrine.

From this it is clear that no letter of Julius I other than that written to Docius, or Prosdocimus, was ever used against the Nestorian heretics. Therefore Catholics never derived any benefit from the other letter addressed to Dionysius, as Gennadius lightly asserted. Facundus seems, however, to have taken the Greek title *πρὸς Δόκιον*, “to Docius,” as one word, as though it had read *πρὸς Προσδόκιον*, “to Prosdocimus.”

We next begin to draw a most powerful argument from Facundus’s words for recognizing the falsity and fabrication of this famous letter published by us. For if this letter to Dionysius already existed when [Col. 0941B] the Nestorian heresy began to raise such disturbances in the Church, why did the Ephesian Fathers refrain from citing it against Nestorius? Why, moreover, did Eutyches and Dioscorus never invoke it on their own behalf, never confirm their opinion by its testimony? The authority of Julius, bishop of Rome, would certainly have lent great weight to the Eutychian view.

Nor could a work by so great a pontiff, published in Greek, have lain so hidden as to escape everyone’s notice, since it is sufficiently clear that documents of this kind, scarcely published, customarily circulated through the churches and in learned hands. Therefore either that letter was fabricated and attributed to Julius after the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon, and thus did not exist before those synods; or, if it did exist, no one until then knew or believed that Julius was its author.

For this reason [Col. 0941C] Facundus rightly adds:

> What controversy would then have remained concerning the single subsistence, or person, of that God-Man, if the Fathers were proved to have proclaimed that he also had one nature? Therefore, in order that every question may be removed: if that letter—that is, the one circulated as written to Dionysius—was not later composed [perhaps one should read “fabricated”], either the synod judged that it was not Blessed Julius’s, as is more credible; or, even if it believed it to be his—which I do not say—it judged that the contrary error should be overcome, not from what was carelessly said, by producing another letter of the same holy Julius, rather than this one—namely, the one written to Prosdocimus or Docius—against Nestorius.

But Facundus would not have admitted even this final shadow of suspicion [Col. 0941D]; indeed, he would firmly have denied that Julius I was the maker of that letter, had he himself known what we have learned from Greek writers more directly acquainted with the matter. Let us therefore hear them. Not merely their testimony, but their reasons also, will establish that this famous letter was falsely attributed to Julius by heretics.

Evagrius Scholasticus, from whom we have the *History*, and Leontius of Byzantium, from whom we have the book *On the Sects*—writers commended on many grounds, both flourishing in the sixth century of Christ, when Facundus of Hermiane also flourished—must be called as witnesses. The former, speaking of Nestorian heretics in book I, chapter 31, says:

> They often corrupted the books of the holy Fathers, and attributed many books of Apollinaris, after changing their titles, to Athanasius, Gregory Thaumaturgus, and Julius; by these books they led very many into their impious error [Col. 0942A].

Evagrius’s history is not at hand; I cite it on the authority of Baronius, who himself quotes it under the year of Christ 352, no. 5. Yet I cannot but wonder why Nestorians are said to have been the authors of this imposture. It is more certain than certain that the letter now before us is so full of Eutychian errors that it expresses an opinion wholly opposed to the Nestorians—as Gennadius also observed—and plainly betrays a Eutychian contriver. How, I ask, could both companies of opposing heretics attribute and foist upon one and the same Roman pontiff these contrary monsters of perverse opinions? Evagrius therefore perhaps erred; or, to state the more probable explanation [Col. 0942B], Cardinal Baronius should have considered Evagrius’s passage more attentively. We shall return below to this very issue. For the moment it suffices to have learned that books of the heretic Apollinaris were fraudulently attributed to Julius by heretics.

Let Leontius of Byzantium now be added, than whom no one treated questions of this kind more clearly. In *On the Sects*, action 8, p. 526, he overturns the foundations of the Eutychian heresy. His words, translated from Greek, are these:

> They—the Eutychians—produce another saying, as though proceeding from Blessed Julius, found in a letter written to Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, whose beginning is: “I am astonished at hearing certain persons,” etc. The saying is this: “It is necessary, when they say two natures, that they worship one and do not worship the other; that they are baptized into the divine nature, but not baptized into the human” [Col. 0942C]. And this letter contains many further statements of the same kind.

Here are several words of this letter which, since they are likewise found in the copy now published by us, confirm the authority of the Ambrosian manuscript.

Let us now see how Leontius extricates himself from this difficulty. “But we,” he continues, “prove by many arguments that this letter is not that of Blessed Julius, but of Apollinaris. First, because anyone who examines it carefully finds in it nothing worthy of the name of Julius. Indeed, the seven letters which they claim as his are also by Apollinaris. Secondly, because, whenever it mentions the body, it nowhere says that the body possesses mind or is ensouled. Yet it was customary for the Fathers of that age, whenever they mentioned the body [Col. 0942D], to call it mind-endowed and ensouled. This is so true that, because they feared this accusation and accordingly added thereafter the terms ‘mind-endowed’ and ‘ensouled,’ no books of later writers can be found without this addition inherited from the ancients.

“Further, it is proved not to be Blessed Julius’s but Apollinaris’s also because Gregory of Nyssa, in his work against Apollinaris, openly quotes and refutes as erroneous many things contained in this letter. It can also be proved in another way that it is not Blessed Julius’s. They say that it was inserted in the acts of the Ephesian synod under Blessed Cyril; but they plainly lie. For nothing of the sort is found there in the text. Rather, another letter has been inserted as though written by Julius, and even that is not Julius’s but Timothy’s, as may be understood from many copies [Col. 0943A]. Since, therefore, nothing harms us in their calling it Julius’s, it should plainly be treated as of no account.”

Thus far Leontius, certainly deserving the name of a most exact critic; under his guidance we learn that this letter must in fact be attributed to Apollinaris. Before proceeding, however, it must be observed that Baronius likewise brought forward these pronouncements of Leontius. Having cited the letter’s words, “It is necessary, when they say two natures, that they worship one and do not worship the other,” etc., he says that he wonders how Gennadius could call this letter useful when it contains such monstrous and manifest blasphemies, by which the Nestorian heresy would be confirmed. So speaks the great father of the *Annals* [Col. 0943B]. But he would have spoken differently, had it been permitted him—as it will henceforth be permitted—to read the text of the forged letter itself.

By these words, which also occur in the copy published by us, not the Nestorian heresy but rather the Eutychian is confirmed. For the author of the letter advances them as a necessary and, as he himself implies, utterly absurd consequence of the Nestorian opinion. So far is he from thinking with Nestorius that there are in Christ two divided natures, one to be worshipped and the other not worshipped, that instead he mingles and confuses them both, affirming that they are to be honored with one single worship—wholly agreeing and concurring with the Eutychians in this.

Let us now follow Leontius *κατὰ πόδα*, step by step, and examine individually his reasons and arguments, by which [Col. 0943C] it will readily become clear who was the true author of this letter. He says it was written not by Julius, first Roman pontiff of that name, but by Apollinaris, the heresiarch. He confirms this judgment by the following reasons.

The first is that nothing occurs in it worthy of Julius’s name: that is, the document contains nothing of the gravity, eloquence, wisdom, or pure and ancient doctrine befitting Julius, bishop of the Apostolic See. And indeed, since nothing was of greater concern to Roman bishops, teachers of the whole Church, than always to transmit and defend the most ancient doctrines of Christ, whereas here are found so many seeds of novel teachings unheard of in Julius’s time: who in the fifth century, when the controversy of Eutyches was aflame, could or should readily have believed Julius to be the author of that pernicious letter and novelty? Both Western and Eastern bishops would already have protested, had Julius taught anything of the kind in the fourth century.

Apollinaris could indeed secretly rave and, in furtive little writings among his adherents, pour forth and devise whatever he pleased. But the Roman bishop, head of the whole Church, could not hide himself, especially after writing a letter to a renowned bishop of Greece and publishing it openly. Two genuine letters of Julius, transcribed by St Athanasius, still survive—[Col. 0943D] for I pay no attention to the pseudo-letters of Isidore Mercator—in which one sees a wholly different character of style, doctrine, and prudence.

The anonymous writer from whom we have the collection against the Severians [Col. 0944A] adds, §6, that the superscription of this letter did not accord with the practice of Roman pontiffs. We cannot at present judge this point, because the copy now published by us lacks its superscription.

Leontius’s second argument is that not this letter alone but seven other letters too were falsely attributed to Julius, although they were in fact by Apollinaris. Such were the arts and deceits of the Eutychians. What wonder, then, if, when the Eutychians produced the letter to Dionysius, the fraud was likewise detected there without difficulty? It was exceedingly difficult to invent so many letters for so great a pontiff, who had died only in the preceding century, and to deceive critics and learned men for long. The subject matter, style, occasion for writing [Col. 0944B], persons to whom letters were allegedly sent—of whom there is now no trace—and a thousand other considerations would immediately arise in a matter, so to speak, still recent, exposing the letters as false and restoring them to Apollinaris, their true father. Thus one letter accused another; and all together formed a most powerful argument that this letter too, written to Dionysius, must be attributed not to Julius but to Apollinaris.

Thirdly, Leontius very rightly observes that throughout this letter Christ’s body is indeed mentioned, but no mind or soul is ever ascribed to that body. Nothing could more plainly betray the person of Apollinaris than this affected manner of speech. It is established that among Apollinaris’s errors the principal one was that rejected by St Leo the Great in Decretal 23, where he sets forth the Catholic position: “We do not say that Christ is God only,” etc., “nor man in such a manner that he lacks anything certainly belonging to human nature, whether soul or rational mind,” etc.

Hence St Augustine says in *On Heresies*, chapter 55:

> “The Apollinarists were founded by Apollinaris, who dissented from Catholic teaching concerning Christ’s soul, saying, like the Arians, that God assumed flesh without a soul in Christ. Defeated in this question by Gospel testimonies, they say that the mind, by which the human soul is rational, was not in Christ’s soul, but that the Word itself was in it in place of this.”

Such was Apollinaris’s false doctrine. Since the letter attributed to Julius not obscurely conveys and breathes it, we can immediately understand that the letter must be attributed to Apollinaris [Col. 0944D]. Certainly nowhere in it do you read anything else said of Christ as man than *σῶμα* or *σάρξ*, that is, “body” or “flesh”; there is no mention of a human soul or mind assumed by the Word. Therefore, if you weigh these things rightly, Christ’s body is presented to us as *ἄψυχον, καὶ ἀναίσθητον, καὶ ἀνόητον*: without soul, sensation, and mind. This fiction was condemned in Apollinaris by the Alexandrian synod held in A.D. 362 by Athanasius and other Catholic bishops.

See, moreover, how without evasion this same abominable doctrine is insinuated by the author of that letter:

> *Οὔτε γὰρ τὸ σῶμα καθ᾽ ἑαυτὸ φύσις ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς Χριστοῦ, ἐπεὶ μηδὲ ζωοποιὸν καθ᾽ ἑαυτὸ μηδὲ διατέμνεσθαι δυνάμενον ἄνευ τοῦ ζωοποιοῦ λόγου.*

“For the body in itself is not a nature in the one Christ, because it is not life-giving in itself, nor can it be severed and separated from the life-giving Word” [Col. 0945A].

Here Christ’s body is said not to be life-giving in itself: that is, to lack in itself life, soul, and the operations of life. But whence, one might have asked Apollinaris, did the Savior possess life and its functions insofar as he was man? From the life-giving Word, the heretic replied: Christ’s flesh possessed them because the very divinity supplied and fulfilled in Christ the role of human soul and mind.

This agrees with what the aforementioned Leo the Great writes of Apollinaris in Homily IV on the Nativity [Col. 0945B]:

> “Apollinaris, deprived of the firmness of faith, believed that the Son of God assumed the true nature of human flesh in such a way that he said there was no soul in that flesh, because the divinity itself fulfilled its role.”

Since this is so, and since only Arians, Apollinarists, and Eutychians promoted this impious opinion, discordant with evangelical truth, who can any longer doubt that the author of the letter published by us was Apollinaris or someone else of his party? When were Catholic Fathers, and especially bishops of the Roman See, ever of such an opinion? Rather, who did not abhor it? Who did not attack it—not when it was growing, I say, but when it was scarcely born and heard?

No one has ever even suspected Julius I, supreme pontiff, of agreeing with Arians or with Apollinaris, their contemporary [Col. 0945C]. On the contrary, Julius was the constant hammer and enemy of the Arians. One may therefore wonder at the Eutychians’ shamelessness and lack of judgment in choosing this man upon whom to forge such a spurious letter—a letter as congenial to his character, doctrine, and conduct as whiteness to an Ethiopian.

It cannot therefore be that Julius so often spoke of Christ as man and named his flesh or body without calling it also mind-endowed and ensouled—*ἔννουν καὶ ἐμψυχώμενον*—or at least adding something by which we might be taught that Christ’s human nature does not consist of bare flesh alone. Yet the author of this letter does not blush to affirm this quite plainly against Catholic truth.

Fourthly, Leontius says, it may also be recognized that this letter should be attributed not to Julius but to Apollinaris the heretic because Gregory of Nyssa, in his work against Apollinaris, quotes many matters contained in this same letter and refutes them as erroneous [Col. 0945D]. By good fortune, that excellent work of Gregory of Nyssa, long lost and long desired by scholars, was published a few years ago from a Vatican manuscript transcribed by the distinguished Lorenzo Alessandro Zacagni, prefect of the Vatican Library. Through his service anyone henceforth may compare this letter with fragments of Apollinaris refuted by Nyssenus. We shall meanwhile make the experiment as briefly as possible.

Gregory of Nyssa says of Apollinaris in §35:

> *Ἡμᾶς, φησὶ, δύο πρόσωπα λέγειν τὸν Θεὸν, καὶ τὸν παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ προσληφθέντα ἄνθρωπον. αὐτὸν δέ, φησι, μὴ οὕτως ἔχειν, ἀλλὰ φάσκειν τὸν σαρκωθέντα, καὶ ὄντα οὐχ ἕτερον παρὰ τὸν ἀσώματον, ἀλλὰ τὸν αὐτὸν καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμετέρας ἐν σαρκὶ ζωῆς.*

Zacagni translates this as follows:

> He asserts that we—that is, Catholics—say that God and the man assumed by God are two persons; but he himself, he says, does not think this at all. Rather, he says that Christ was incarnate and is not different from the incorporeal one, but is one and the same, according to the likeness of the life which we live in the flesh [Col. 0946A].

The author of the letter recently published by us has similar, indeed identical, assertions; their harmony reveals the same Apollinaris in both places. He says that he does not fear *τοὺς συκοφάντας τοὺς διαιροῦντας εἰς δύο πρόσωπα τὸν Κύριον*, “the slanderers who divide the Lord Christ into two persons” [Col. 0946B]. By this name, as you see, Catholics are also meant here. For worthy Apollinaris thought Catholics posited two persons in Christ because they posited two natures in him without confusion.

This is certainly false. The Catholic Church acknowledged two natures in the one Christ, but only one person. The heretic, by contrast, departed so far from the Catholic path that he confessed not only one person but one nature too in Christ our Lord—something no orthodox theologian before him had said.

In the words quoted above from Nyssenus, this false opinion of Apollinaris is found where Christ’s corporeal aspect is not distinguished from the incorporeal. But Nyssenus states it more plainly in §13 when he says of Apollinaris [Col. 0946C]:

> *μίαν ἐποίησε τοῦ Θεοῦ τε καὶ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὴν φύσιν*,

that is: “He made one nature of God and man.”

Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, likewise quotes these words of Apollinaris from his book *On the Incarnation*, in Photius, codex 230:

> *Ὦ καινὴ κτίσις, καὶ μίξις θεσπεσία! Θεὸς, καὶ σὰρξ μίαν ἀπετέλεσαν φύσιν.*

“O new creation and divine mixture! God and flesh effected one nature.”

Apollinaris had therefore imagined that human nature and divine nature in Christ were so mingled and confused that no distinction any longer remained between them, as though a third single nature arose from the mixture of two natures. This was also the opinion of the author of the letter now published. He most explicitly denies two natures, *δύο φύσεις*, in Christ, led by the plausible argument that the Apostle calls the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made, one. The obscurantist argues thus:

> *Εἰ γοῦν εἷς ὁ ἐκ τῆς ἁγίας παρθένου τεχθεὶς ὠνόμασται, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐστι, δι᾽ οὗ τὰ πάντα γέγονε, μία φύσις ἐστίν, ἐπειδὴ πρόσωπον ἓν ἔχων εἰς δύο οὐ διαιρεῖται.*

“If, therefore, he who was born of the holy Virgin is called one, and is himself he through whom all things were made, there is one nature; for, having one person, he is not divided into two” [Col. 0946D].

Here you have not only one person in Christ, which the orthodox also affirmed, but one nature as well. This false opinion especially pleased Apollinaris, the father, so to speak, of the Eutychians, although it was novel and utterly lacking the authority of the ancients.

From the words of the *Antirrheticus* quoted above we learned that Apollinaris said that Christ is one and the same according to the likeness of the life which we live in flesh. The author of our letter likewise openly declares:

> *Ὥσπερ ἄνθρωπος μία φύσις, οὕτω καὶ ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος Χριστός.*

“As a human being is one nature, so Christ, made in the likeness of men, is one nature” [Col. 0947A].

I cannot deny that certain holy Fathers also used such an illustration to show that Christ’s one person proceeds from the union of two natures. See Rusticus the deacon in the *Library of the Fathers*, Leontius, Theorianus, and others; see also the Creed attributed to St Athanasius. Yet none of them allowed himself to be carried so far as to prove, from the conjunction of soul and body in one human being, that one nature also arises and results in Christ [Col. 0947B].

Apollinaris was the first to abuse this comparison. Accordingly, this too aptly establishes that the letter should be attributed to him rather than to Julius I, defender of orthodox doctrine. Thus, in the *Antirrheticus*, Gregory of Nyssa argues by various reasons against the illustration drawn from human nature by which Apollinaris supported his opinion.

What made Apollinaris’s doctrine still more absurd was this: he held that Christ had come together from human flesh alone and from God, who occupied the place of mind or soul, just as human nature comes together from soul and body. But how, Gregory of Nyssa asked, was Christ made in the likeness of man, when he is something different from man and wholly unlike our nature? For if man consists of soul and body, and the soul is not found in the man whom Apollinaris invented, how can that be like man in Christ which is foreign to our nature [Col. 0947C]?

Apollinaris gave no other title to his composition than *ἀπόδειξις περὶ τῆς θείας σαρκώσεως τῆς καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν ἀνθρώπου*: “Demonstration of the divine Incarnation according to the likeness of man.” Since these matters correspond quite openly with what is set forth by the author of the letter, they reveal the same Apollinaris in both.

Let us proceed. Gregory of Nyssa refutes another fiction of Apollinaris in the work already cited. The mad heresiarch held that human flesh was not assumed by the Word of God in the fullness of time [Col. 0947D], but before the ages; hence he wrote that the man who appeared in time had existed previously before his manifestation. See §13 of the *Antirrheticus*, and Nazianzen, Oration 46, against Apollinaris.

It followed that he also said that Christ, insofar as he is Son of Man, descended from heaven. And indeed, according to Nyssenus, Apollinaris openly held this view, as may be seen in §6. Having established this opinion, he then inferred:

> *εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου, καὶ ἐκ γυναικὸς υἱὸς Θεοῦ, πῶς οὐχ ὁ αὐτὸς Θεὸς καὶ ἄνθρωπος;*

“But if the Son of Man is from heaven and the Son of God from a woman, how is he not the same God and man?”

The writer of the letter addressed to Dionysius seems to think no differently. First he says that, if a division of two natures in Christ were admitted, it would be improper to call the whole one Son of Man who descended from heaven, and Son of God who was born of a woman:

> *Οὔτε γὰρ οἷόν τε ἦν τὸ ὅλον υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου καλεῖσθαι καταβεβηκότα ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ υἱὸν Θεοῦ γενηθέντα ἐκ γυναικός.*

In both places Christ, insofar as he is Son of Man, is said to be from heaven, just as, insofar as he is Son of God, he is said to be from a woman [Col. 0948A].

The author of the letter continues to babble that a division of two natures in Christ is incompatible because what descended from heaven would be called Son of God and not Son of Man, while what was born of a woman would be called Son of Man and not Son of God. If we believed this inept sophist, that opinion would agree with the heresy of Paul of Samosata. Hence he then says [Col. 0948B]:

> *Ἡμᾶς δὲ αἱ θεῖαι γραφαὶ διδάσκουσιν, ὡς περὶ ἑνὸς τοῦ Κυρίου φρονεῖν κατὰ τὴν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ κατάβασιν, καὶ τὴν ἐκ γυναικὸς ἐπὶ γῆς γέννησιν.*

“But the divine Scriptures teach us, when we hear of his descent from heaven and his birth on earth from a woman, to understand all things as concerning one Lord.”

Below he adds other matters to the same effect, saying that he pays no heed to the slanderers who divide Christ into two persons—that is, Catholics, upon whom he fastened such a belief, as we have seen above—because they revile him as affirming *τὴν σάρκα ἐξ οὐρανοῦ*, “flesh from heaven.” This disguised heresiarch neither disowns nor rejects the expression. He continues:

> We say both: that the whole is from heaven through the Godhead, and the whole from a woman through the flesh, knowing no division of one and the same person, nor severing the earthly from the heavenly or the heavenly from the earthly; for such a severing would be impious [Col. 0948C].

These matters certainly need no greater light. But below other statements occur which wholly confuse the view he has established. For the author of the letter says:

> *Συμπεφώνηται οὖν, καὶ συμφώνως ὡμολόγηται τὸ σῶμα ἐκ τῆς παρθένου, ἡ θεότης ἐξ οὐρανοῦ· τὸ σῶμα πέπλασται ἐν κοιλίᾳ, ἡ θεότης ἄκτιστος αἰώνιος.*

“Therefore it is concordantly said, and concordantly confessed, that the body is from the Virgin and the Godhead from heaven; the body was formed in the womb, while the Godhead is uncreated and eternal.”

In these words the author seems to confess that Christ’s flesh was taken from the Virgin, although above he had indicated that it was from heaven and was said to be from heaven. First, we say that Apollinaris could have advanced discordant and contradictory assertions. Although this is characteristic of almost all who depart from truth, Nyssenus shows in more than one place that it can especially be said of Apollinaris.

Secondly, we suspect [Col. 0948D] that the heretic did not sincerely hold, nor properly intend to affirm, that Christ assumed a body from heaven before Gabriel informed the Virgin of the divine counsel. He called the flesh “from heaven” only because, in his opinion, whatever is said of Christ as Word of God ought likewise to be said of Christ as man. Certainly, in §51 of the *Antirrheticus*, the same Apollinaris says concerning the Word of God:

> *ὅτε σὰρξ ἐγένετο, τότε αὐτὸν ἐν ἡμῖν ἐσκηνωκέναι.*

“When he became flesh, then he dwelt among us” [Col. 0949A].

By these words he indicates that he did not believe the humanity of the Word descended to us from heaven, as Nyssenus observes, though the heretic appeared above openly to have taught and written otherwise. Apollinaris therefore called Christ’s flesh “from heaven” insofar as he had adopted the view that human nature should not be divided or distinguished from divine nature in Christ, and consequently that everything must be proclaimed of the one Christ in such a way that the whole Christ might rightly be said also to have descended from heaven. Thus we may understand that the author of our letter does not differ from Apollinaris even here.

Moreover [Col. 0949B], we saw above that another capital error of Apollinaris consisted in his affirmation that Christ lacked a human soul or mind. Gregory of Nyssa therefore refutes him in §35 of the *Antirrheticus*. We likewise showed that the disguised author of this letter thought the same. You therefore discover the same writer in both places. In addition, Apollinaris abuses in defense of his dreams the Apostle’s words in 1 Corinthians 15, “the last Adam became a life-giving spirit,” as is clear from §§10 and following of the *Antirrheticus*. Our author misuses the same words, as may be seen in the published letter.

Accordingly, you finally understand that the harmony of opinions between Apollinaris refuted by Nyssenus and the author of this letter is so remarkable that Leontius was right to judge him identical with Apollinaris. And indeed, who ever said or heard that Julius, bishop of Rome, taught such most absurd doctrines, which we know were refuted as soon as they emerged from Apollinaris’s mouth and pen [Col. 0949C]? It was impossible for the bishop of the Apostolic See publicly to teach such things without great scandal and outcry among Christians.

Finally, Leontius charges the Eutychians, or Acephali, with falsehood because they say that a passage from this letter was produced and cited by the Fathers of the Ephesian Council. He says that another letter, different from the one alleged to have been written to Dionysius, was cited in the acts of that synod. He adds that even the other letter was not Julius’s, but rather that of Timothy, the Apollinarist heretic, as many copies attested.

Concerning this calumny drawn from the acts of the Ephesian Council, we have seen above what Facundus of Hermiane also left in writing. But Leontius, immediately saying, “since nothing harms us in their calling it Julius’s, it should be treated as of no account,” acted rightly in not trusting only himself and manuscript copies in wholly denying Julius the letter to Docius just mentioned. For, besides the fact that it contained nothing—which Leontius himself admits—unworthy of Julius, bishop of Rome and leader of Catholics, Ephraemius, patriarch of Antioch, in book III of *On the Sacred Laws*, quoted in Photius, codex 229, attributes it to Julius without hesitation and extracts several words from it.

Likewise Anastasius the presbyter, in *Eclogae of Testimonies concerning Divine Theology*, chapter 38, adduces more passages from it as from a genuine work of Julius, except that he has Acacius instead of Docius, writing:

> *Ἰουλίου ἐπισκόπου Ῥώμης ἐκ τῆς πρὸς Ἀκάκιον ἐπιστολῆς*—“Of Julius, bishop of Rome, from the letter to Acacius” [Col. 0950A].

I nonetheless admit that one may rightly doubt whether the letter cited by Anastasius is the same as the earlier letter written to Docius, since it may be one of those letters which Leontius above declared spurious and wrongly attributed to Julius.

And thus far we have brought forward many things capable of persuading even obstinate minds that the letter once given to Dionysius and published by heretics under the name of Julius, Roman pontiff, must be restored to Apollinaris alone, as to its rightful parent. We now add that, in Justinian’s time, Catholics were so certain of its spuriousness, and fought with arguments so powerful in defense of Julius’s reputation, that they openly professed that every ground for doubt on the matter had been removed. Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, in the conference [Col. 0950B] held at Constantinople with the Acephali, as Sirmond, the most eminent man, testifies, said: “We have clearly shown that that famous letter of blessed Julius to Dionysius was written by Apollinaris.” The praised presbyter Anastasius affirmed the same in the *Eclogae of Testimonies*. So too Saint Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, who flourished in the same century as Justinian and Leontius, testifies to the same effect in Photius, codex 230, writing:

> Ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ ἡ χρῆσις, ἢν ἡ αἵρεσις προκομίζει ἐκ τῆς πρὸς Διονύσιον ἐπιστολῆς τοῦ Ἰουλίου ῥώμης, ἀναμφίβολον μὲν οὐκ ἔχει τὸ γνήσιον.

That is: “But the testimony which the heresy produces from the letter of Julius of Rome to Dionysius is unquestionably not genuine.” Eulogius mentions as his argument for this what we indicated above: namely, that Saint Cyril, at the Synod of Ephesus, did indeed employ [Col. 0950C] a certain passage from Julius’s letter to Docium, but made no mention of the other letter addressed to Dionysius—although it contended most explicitly against the Nestorians—for no other reason, surely, than that he either judged, or knew for certain, that it was not a genuine offspring of Julius.

The same Eulogius testifies that the Eutychians, in order to establish one nature in Christ, cited not only the letter now published by us under Julius’s name, but also others which they ascribed to Athanasius and Gregory Thaumaturgus. Eulogius rejects their fabrications, maintaining that those most holy Fathers never committed such things to writing; rather, Apollinaris had been their author, while the followers of Eutyches and Severus subsequently, by a sufficiently evident fraud, attributed them to those most celebrated bishops of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0950D] Leontius and Evagrius report the same, as we observed above. We are therefore now compelled reasonably to judge that Baronius wrote with too little caution when he said that all such inventions originated with the Nestorians—although they plainly supported not Nestorius’s error, but that of Eutyches.

Moreover, it is regrettable that the works of Ephraemius of Antioch, praised above by us and likewise a sixth-century author, have long since perished. For from them it might perhaps easily be established how far the doctrine of our Julius was removed from the opinions of Apollinaris and Eutyches. Yet since Photius not only carefully reviewed but also extensively quoted his books in the *Bibliotheca*, codices 228 and 229, it is worthwhile to gather [Col. 0951A] a few things from there.

In a letter to Zenobius, a scholastic of Emesa, Ephraemius, according to Photius, shows that Saint Leo the Great agreed with the other Fathers in confessing the twofold nature in the one Christ, neither divided nor confused. He then demonstrates that Saint Cyril’s doctrines, especially on this question, agree altogether with the judgment of the same Saint Leo, Gregory of Nyssa, and Julius of Rome, and are *kata panta symphōnounta*—“consonant in all respects.”

The same Ephraemius, in an address to Domnus and John, in order to prove that Christ our true God divided neither the properties of divinity nor those of humanity—as the Nestorians held—but through the uniting, or union (*henōsis*), joined in himself both divine and human things without confusion, “brings forward our God-bearing Fathers [Col. 0951B] as witnesses, Julius the bishop of Rome from his books concerning the union in Christ of the body with the divinity,” together with Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, and Cyril. Finally, whatever passages occur in Julius’s genuine books of which heretics were accustomed to make misuse, Ephraemius explains, proves to contain sound doctrine, and says that Julius, *in the discourse concerning consubstantiality* (*en tō logō tō peri homoousiou*), refuted not only Marcion and Valentinus, but Apollinaris and Eutyches as well.

Therefore I think there can now be no further doubt that what we undertook to prove at the outset is certain: namely, that the once-famous letter now published by us [Col. 0951C] is to be attributed and restored, if not to Apollinaris himself, at least to someone from his school, or that of Eutyches or Severus. It must certainly be wholly taken away from Julius I, Peter’s successor in the Roman see; and in future nothing will better persuade people of this than the letter itself. What is read here differs immeasurably from the teaching and reputation of so great a pontiff, since, in explicit words and with such elaborate effort, the very delusions of Apollinaris and Eutyches are established and the judgment of the Catholic Church rejected.

It remains to say something also about the letter’s title. In the Ambrosian manuscript it is said to have been sent *pros Dionysion tēs Alexandreias episkopon*, “to Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria.” But Leontius of Byzantium, as we have seen, makes this Dionysius not bishop of Alexandria but bishop of the Corinthians. [Col. 0951D] I suspect an error in both places.

First, I must abandon reliance on the Ambrosian manuscript. For while Julius, to whom the letter is affixed, occupied the apostolic see, no Dionysius presided over the Alexandrian Church; Athanasius the Great did. Some uninstructed person, seeing this letter addressed to Dionysius—whom he may perhaps have learned by rumor, or imagined, to have been a bishop—completed the title out of his own invention. Having heard, however, that a Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, had formerly been famous—that is, in the third century of Christ—he supposed, by a patent anachronism, that he was the same person to whom Julius was said to have sent this letter in the immediately following century. It is therefore more pleasant to believe that this scrap was added to the title [Col. 0952A] than that heretics inserted it fraudulently. For who, in the fifth and sixth centuries of Christ, when the letter itself began to be brought into controversy, would not have laughed at this absurd title?

Indeed, among the subscriptions of the Sardican conciliabulum held in the time of our Julius, there is mention of “Dionysius, bishop from the province of Alexandria.” But the editors themselves, by placing an asterisk, warned that some corruption lies hidden in these words. Moreover, he could not have been bishop of Alexandria, both because it is probable that he would have subscribed in a more distinguished place, and because at that time, as we said, Saint Athanasius filled the Alexandrian see on the Catholic side, while on the Arian side it was filled by Gregory, to whom a letter is also recorded as having been sent by the bishops of that same pseudo-synod.

[Col. 0952B] Secondly, the letter’s superscription which Leontius gives seems to me likewise not free from suspicion of error. Just as in Alexandria during the third century of the common era there was one famous bishop Dionysius, so in the preceding century there had been another of the same name, bishop of the Corinthians, a most celebrated man, some of whose canonical letters were once read. If not Leontius himself, a man of assured learning, then certainly the scribes used by Leontius, or those by whom Leontius’s works were later copied, may have been misled by the fame of that Corinthian Dionysius into believing that the letter published by heretics under Julius’s name had been written to him.

For my part, I find in ecclesiastical history no Dionysius who governed the Church of the Corinthians in the age of Julius of Rome. Moreover, that anonymous writer from whom we possess [Col. 0952C] the collections against the Severians calls Dionysius, to whom the pseudo-letter of Julius was addressed, not a bishop but a presbyter. Gennadius calls him simply a certain Dionysius. The other writers who mention that letter—Eulogius, Ephraemius, Hypatius, and any others—nowhere say that this Dionysius was a bishop. Therefore Leontius should not be angry with us if we do not acquiesce even in his testimony on this point.

And these, most learned Salvini, are the things which I had to write concerning the letter fraudulently attributed by heretics to Julius I, in order to place the heretics’ imposture in clearer light. Continue, as you do, to love me—you who are forever to be loved and esteemed by me.

## Notice on the Following Letter

[Col. 0952D] I. We possess a fragment of this letter both in Greek, in the first action of the Council of Ephesus, p. 509; in Cyril’s *Apology against the Orientals*, at Anathema 6; and in Photius, codex 230, p. 845; and in Latin, in Marius Mercator’s extracts from the Council of Ephesus and in Facundus, book I, chapter 5. Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, in the conference with the Severians held in 535, and likewise Eulogius of Alexandria in Photius, codex 230, p. 845, testify that what was produced at the Ephesian Council had been excerpted by Cyril of Alexandria. It is certain that it was read with the Council itself hearing and approving, and was inserted in its acts together with other testimonies of the Fathers. Accordingly Marius Mercator, Vincent of Lérins, [Col. 0953A] Facundus, Hypatius of Ephesus, and Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, regarded it as an authentic work of Julius—until Leontius, in the eighth action of his book *On Sects*, did not hesitate, on the authority of several manuscripts, to assert that the letter from which the passage was copied belonged not to Julius but to Timothy, who had Apollinaris as his instructor and teacher.

II. If the cases were equal, Leontius’s authority would be judged not merely not preferable to that of the Council of Ephesus, but not even comparable with it. But since it is clear that no investigation of the letter’s authenticity preceded the Council, whereas Leontius employed diligence in examining that matter, his judgment does not seem to be lightly dismissed. For perhaps this one letter to Prosdocium, containing nothing openly false, circulated under Julius’s name, and there was no reason for the synod to distrust its superscription. But when, in succession, several others attributed to the same person began to be circulated—containing the manifest impiety of Apollinaris and abused by Eutyches and his disciples—the defenders of the faith were obliged to expend their efforts in uncovering the author of this letter as well as of the others. In this Leontius was more fortunate than the rest, as he was also more diligent.

III. Yet so long as we were allowed to see in this letter only what had been quoted by the Ephesian Synod, we hesitated, out of reverence for that most holy council, to deny entirely that the fragment ascribed to Julius belonged to him and to banish it to an appendix. But after Michael Lequien, well known for his learned edition of Damascene, graciously shared with us [Col. 0953C] the entire letter, recovered from an old English manuscript, we judged that Leontius’s verdict must be fully accepted—unless one prefers to assign it to Apollinaris himself rather than to his disciple Timothy.

Leontius indeed admits, in the eighth action of his book *On Sects*, that there is nothing in it contrary to us—that is, to the orthodox faith—and therefore that the claim that it belongs to Julius is not worth a straw. Yet it must not be denied that beneath Catholic words, like fair coverings, certain seeds of Apollinarian doctrine lie concealed everywhere; examples more suitably set forth in the notes will confirm this.

IV. Moreover, almost all the other arguments by which Leontius [Col. 0954A] and the other ancient opponent of the Severians judged the preceding letter unworthy of Julius and worthy of Apollinaris or his disciple apply to this one. A similar superscription is prefixed at the beginning: “To my most beloved lord,” etc. Indeed, since here, unlike in the preceding letter, the word *syllitourgos* (“fellow-minister”) is not added, this conflicts even more with the custom of Roman pontiffs, because that Prosdocium is called neither bishop nor presbyter. Next, likewise, when the author of this letter mentions the body, he nowhere calls it endowed with mind or soul. Moreover, Athanasius, refuting Apollinaris, quotes certain of his words which we shall show to be contained in this letter, or at least very closely akin to them. Of this letter too we may say what the anonymous author said of the preceding one: “The very phraseology does not suit Julius, as though translated from Latin, since it is excessively Greek.”

V. This writing contains not only the testimony quoted by the Council of Ephesus, but another also, transcribed by Sirmond in his notes on Facundus, book I, chapter 5, from handwritten collections of a certain presbyter Anastasius, preserved in the library of the Jesuit College at Paris. In those collections, however, it is cited not as from a letter to Prosdocium, but as “from Julius’s letter to Acacius.” We shall state in its proper place what is to be thought concerning this variation. The few corrections enabled by this short extract make us desire all the more another manuscript from which the remainder of the letter may be corrected, because we ought to be more certain of the words of a heretic feigning Catholicism, so that we may more easily detect wherein his deceit consists [Col. 0954C] or to what extent he insinuates heretical doctrines.

VI. The argument by which the divinity of the Holy Spirit is established somewhat laboriously at the beginning of this writing indicates that it was composed only after Macedonius began to deny that the Holy Spirit is God, and therefore after the year 360. But just as Basil and Gregory vigorously defended the Church’s teaching concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit in Cappadocia and the churches of Pontus, so also did Apollinaris of Laodicea in Syria, according to Sozomen, book VI, chapter 22. This likewise adds force to the observations we have made concerning the author of this letter.

## Letter of Blessed Julius of Rome to Prosdocium

[Note: [Col. 0953D] (1) In the archetype, as also in the Ephesian Council and in Eulogius of Alexandria, *pros Dokion*, “to Docium”; but the following salutation makes it clear that, with Facundus, Marius Mercator, and the other ancient Latin interpreters of the Council of Ephesus, one must read *pros Prosdokion*, “to Prosdocium,” since even in the Greek archetype itself the salutation is addressed to *Prosdokios*, not *Dokios*.]

What is to be believed concerning the Trinity and the Incarnation of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0953] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0953]

## [Letter of Julius I to Prosdocium]

To my most beloved lord Prosdocium, Julius sends greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0953C]

### I.

Our doctrine, according to the apostolic tradition, is this: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess one true divinity; there is one worship and glorification [Col. 0953D] of the Son toward the Father in the worship of the Holy Spirit. But whoever introduces another divinity, let him be anathema.

Likewise, if anyone adds another confession and praise besides the words with which the Seraphim, singing, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. 6:3), praised the divine Trinity—as John and Paul [Note: [Col. 0954D] (3) That is, the words of the Seraphim crying “Holy,” etc., are referred to the divine Trinity, so that when Isaiah prefaces them with “I saw the Lord,” he indicates that the Son and the Holy Spirit, no less than the Father, were seen by him. The whole passage is most aptly elucidated by Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, chapters 21–22:

> “Thus it stands, Paul saying: ‘The Holy Spirit spoke well through Isaiah to our fathers, saying: Go to this people and say: You will hear with your ears and not understand; and seeing, you will see and not perceive.’”

From Paul’s words, approved and reported by Luke, Ambrose infers:

> “Therefore it is the Spirit who sent Isaiah; if the Spirit sent him, then certainly it was the Spirit whom Isaiah saw when King Uzziah had died, when he said: ‘I saw the Lord of hosts seated,’” etc.,

because in that same chapter he is said to have been sent by the one whom he saw. Moreover, in chapter 22 Ambrose renders the Greek name *doxa* by the Latin term “majesty”:

> “Now one may recognize the unity of majesty and dominion in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For many say that the Father was seen by Isaiah at this time; Paul said it was the Spirit; Luke, in Acts, confirmed it; John the Evangelist referred it to the Son. For it is written concerning the Son: ‘Jesus said these things . . . Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with their eyes and understand with their heart, and I will heal them.” Isaiah said these things when he saw his majesty and spoke of him.’”

Having cited these words, Ambrose reasons thus:

> “John says that Isaiah spoke these very words and that the Son’s majesty appeared to him; Paul, however, records that the Spirit spoke them. Whence, then, this diversity? It is a diversity of words, not of meanings . . . because the Father is seen in the Son, who said: ‘Whoever sees me sees the Father’; and the Son is seen in the Spirit, because just as no one says ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit, so Christ is seen not by the fleshly eye but by spiritual grace.”

In Athanasius’s book *On the Incarnation against the Arians*, which some hold to be by Apollinaris, no. 10, the one divinity of the entire Trinity is proved by the same reasoning:

> “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are Lord of hosts. For there is one divinity and one God in three hypostases. Therefore the things which the Father says in Isaiah, John says were said by the Son, while in Acts Paul says that the Holy Spirit said them.”]

testify: [Col. 0956A] John, indeed, says that the Prophet saw the glory and majesty of the Son, celebrated in the Seraphic hymn; [Note: [Col. 0955D] (1) From the preceding observation it is plain that the words indicated here are John 12:41: “Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory,” namely Christ’s; and therefore *heōrakenai* or *tetheōrēkenai* (“had seen” or “had beheld”) is to be preferred to *peplērōkenai* (“had filled”).] while Paul signifies that the same is the glory and majesty of the Holy Spirit (Acts 28:25), teaching that those words are truly the Holy Spirit’s words, uttered by him who was seen and glorified. For the glory of the Spirit is the glory of the Son, and the glory of the Son likewise the glory of the Father. Therefore the one substance of the Trinity is proclaimed by councils throughout the world. Whoever, therefore, separates the Son and the Spirit from the substance of the one God, as though they existed by will, as we too do, and not from the same substance but [Note: [Col. 0955D] (2) Literally: “in likeness according to the same [substance].”] in likeness to the same substance, let him be anathema.

> Τῷ δεσπότῃ μου τῷ ποθεινοτάτῳ Προσδοκίῳ Ἰούλιος ἐν κυρίῳ χαίρειν.

“To my most beloved lord Prosdocium, Julius sends greetings in the Lord.”

[Col. 0954C]

### I.

> Τὸ φρόνημα ἡμῶν κατὰ τὴν ἀποστολικὴν παράδοσιν· πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ καὶ ἁγίου πνεύματος μία θεότης ἀληθινή . μία προσκύνησις καὶ δοξολογίᾳ υἱοῦ πρὸς πατέρα [Col. 0954D] ἐν τῇ προσκυνήσει τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος . ὁ δὲ θεότητα ἑτέραν ἐπεισάγων, ἀνάθεμα . καὶ ὁ προστιθεὶς ἑτέρα ὁμολογίαν παρὰ τὰς φωνὰς τῶν Σεραφεὶμ, τῶν ἅγιος [Col. 0955A] ἅγιος, ἅγιος κύριος σαβαὼθ, πλήρης πᾶσα ἡ γῆ τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ, ἀνυμνούντων εἰς τὴν θεϊκὴν τριάδα, ὡς ὁ Ἰωάννης καὶ ὁ Παῦλος μαρτυροῦσιν . ὁ μὲν Ἰωάννης υἱοῦ δόξαν πεπληρωκέναι εἰπὼν τὸν προφήτην ὑμνηθεῖσαν· ὁ δὲ Παῦλος πνεύματος ἁγίου τὴν αὐτὴν δόξαν δηλῶν, ἐν τῷ λέγειν, ἁγίου πνεύματος εἶναι τὰς φωνὰς τὰς ἀληθεὶς, ἃς (perhaps **τὰς**) ὑπὸ τοῦ θεωρηθέντος καὶ δόξα σθέντος . ὅτι πνεύματος δόξα υἱοῦ δόξα, καὶ υἱοῦ δόξα καὶ πατρὸς δόξα· διὸ μία αὐσία τῆς τριάδος ὑπὸ τῶν συνόδων διὰ τῆς οἰκουμένης ἀναβοᾶται . πᾶς οὖν ὅς νις σχωρίζει τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ μόνου οὐσίας τὸν υἱὸν καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα, ὡς ἐκ βουλῆς ὄντα καθάπερ καὶ ἡμεῖς, οὐκ ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῆς [Col. 0958A] ὡς ἐν ὁμοιώματι κατὰ τὴν αὐτὴν, ἔστω ἀνάθεμα.

“Our doctrine according to the apostolic tradition: of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there is one true divinity; one worship and glorification of the Son toward the Father in the worship of the Holy Spirit. But whoever introduces another divinity: anathema. And whoever adds another confession besides the utterances of the Seraphim, who sing, ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory,’ in praise of the divine Trinity, as John and Paul testify: John saying that the Prophet had beheld the Son’s glory, which was celebrated; Paul declaring the same glory to be that of the Holy Spirit, when he says that the true utterances are those of the Holy Spirit, utterances [perhaps read **tas**, ‘which’] by the one beheld and glorified. Since the glory of the Spirit is the glory of the Son, and the Son’s glory is also the Father’s glory, therefore the one substance of the Trinity is proclaimed by councils throughout the inhabited world. Therefore everyone who separates the Son and the Spirit from the substance of the one God, as existing by will as we do, not from that very substance but in likeness according to it: let him be anathema.”

### II.

It is proclaimed, moreover (Council of Ephesus, action I; Cyril, *Apology against the Orientals*), for the fullness of faith, that the Son of God was incarnate of the Virgin Mary and dwelt among human beings, not operating in a human being; [Note: [Col. 0955D] (3) Here the heresy is indeed excluded which held that the Word operated in Christ only externally, as though, in Hilary’s words (*On the Trinity*, book X, no. 50), the Word of God had dwelt in him merely as a prophetic spirit; Gregory Nazianzen rejects it in his letter to Cledonius, in Baluze’s *New Collection of Councils*, p. 469:

> “If anyone says that he acted in him by grace, as in a prophet, and was not joined or formed according to substance, let him be deprived of the better operation.”

Augustine also contends against it in *On Christian Combat*, and finally concludes:

> “Of other wise and spiritual souls it may rightly be said that they have within themselves the Word of God through whom all things were made; but of none of them may it rightly be said that the Word became flesh.”

Apollinaris himself, in a letter to the bishops of Diocaesarea, quoted by Leontius near the end of his book *Against the Frauds of the Apollinarians*, rejects this same heresy in such a way as to reveal the poison of his own impiety:

> “We confess that the Word of God, who was in the prophets, did not come to a holy man, but that the Word himself became flesh—not having assumed a human, mutable mind . . . but a divine, immutable, heavenly mind.”]

for this takes place also in prophets and apostles. Perfect God in flesh and perfect human being [Note: [Col. 0956B] (4) The term “Spirit” is here used not for a human soul or mind but, in the usage customary among the ancients and familiar to Apollinaris himself—as observed in the note on the preceding letter, no. 6—for the divine nature. If it is understood in this way, as the mutual and reciprocal indwelling and conjunction of the perfect human being in God and the perfect God in the human being, nothing here is non-Catholic and nothing is contrary to Apollinaris’s impiety. For, as Augustine observes in letter 87 to Dardanus, no. 4, a human being is not perfect if either the soul is missing from the flesh or the human mind from the soul itself.

But the perfidy of a changeable heresy is to be feared even beneath Catholic words. From Epiphanius, *Heresies* 77, no. 23, we learn that Vitalis, Apollinaris’s disciple, first confessed without hesitation: “Christ was wholly a perfect human being.” Then, when asked whether he had assumed a mind, he denied it: “For,” he said, “we call him a perfect human being insofar as we ascribe divinity to him in the place of mind.”

Accordingly Gregory Nazianzen, letter 2 to Cledonius, says of the Apollinarians:

> “For them, the perfect human being is not one who experienced all our conditions except sin in every respect; rather, it is held to be that mixture composed of flesh and God.”

It must therefore be feared [Col. 0956D] that here too Christ is called a perfect human being “in Spirit,” that is, through divinity completing the human being and supplying the place of a human mind. For Apollinaris, in the passage cited in the preceding note, after saying, “The Word became flesh, not having assumed a human mind but a divine [mind],” immediately adds:

> “Therefore the Savior did not have an inanimate body, nor one devoid of sensation and intelligence . . . Being truly the Son of God, he became the son of man . . . Hence he was not one Son of God before Abraham and another after Abraham; rather, he was the one only-begotten of God, perfect with divine perfection and not with human perfection.”

And in another work mentioned in the same place by Leontius, Apollinaris, again abusing the name of Gregory Thaumaturgus, asserts concerning Christ:

> “There is one true one who appeared in flesh without flesh, perfect with true and divine perfection—not two persons, not two natures each perfect in itself, since neither is it permissible to speak of two sons.”

Although, then, Apollinaris [Col. 0957C] and his disciples confess Christ to be not only Son of God but also son of man and a perfect human being, one must not therefore immediately think that they have abandoned their particular error. You may reasonably regard this passage as suspect because of what follows, lest Christ be called perfect God and perfect human being here in the manner which Athanasius, *Against Apollinaris*, book I, no. 16, marks as impious—namely, that divine perfection has been transformed into human perfection. Moreover, Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Right Faith*, no. 16, p. 15, should be consulted.] in Spirit; [Col. 0957A] not two sons—one, namely, the proper Son who assumed a human being, the other a mortal human being assumed by God—but one only-begotten Son in heaven, only-begotten on earth: God in truth, [Note: [Col. 0957C] (1) If it is asked how Christ can be called truly human while Apollinarian doctrine is retained, Apollinaris and his followers explain in Leontius’s frequently cited book what they think concerning the Incarnation:

> “The living Word of God assumed from Mary flesh consubstantial with our flesh, into union with divinity from the beginning of conception in the Virgin, and thus became human; because, according to the Apostle, a human being is flesh and spirit. And this is what it is for the Word to have become flesh: to have been united to flesh as a human spirit [that is, after the likeness of a human spirit]. Flesh like ours is called human, but the Lord is human above us. Therefore he is heavenly because of his own heavenly spirit . . . and we, made participants in this work—by which Christ destroyed sin and death—are saved by faith; and though we are from an earthly father, we are made like the heavenly one.”

That is, for someone to be a human being, the Apostle requires only that there be flesh and spirit. But in Christ there are flesh and spirit; therefore he is truly human. His spirit, indeed, is not human but divine; and therefore, although like us, he is a human being above us. Further, Christ as God the Word, through whom are all things, is said to have formed the flesh which he assumed in his own likeness, according to Genesis 1:26: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”] human by reason of the flesh which he formed in his own likeness, saving the world through participation in his own Spirit, which is bestowed by [Note: [Col. 0958B] (2) He refers either to Genesis 2:7, “Therefore God formed man from the clay of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life,” or to John 20:22, “He breathed on them and said: Receive the Holy Spirit,” or to both. Hence in the aforesaid book *On the Incarnation* attributed to Athanasius, no. 19, it is observed that Scripture sometimes calls the Holy Spirit “God’s breathing” (*emphusēma tou theou*).] breathing. As a human being, in human form, reigning over heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings, he is glorified by all as the one and only Lord, unto the glory of the Father (Phil. 2:10–11). Amen.

[Col. 0958A]

### II.

> Κηρύσσεται δὲ εἰς συμπλήρωσιν τῆς πίστεως καὶ σαρκωθεὶς ἐκ παρθένου Μαρίας ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ υἱὸς καὶ σκηνώσας ἐν ἀνθρώποις, οὐκ ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ ἐνεργήσας τοῦτο γὰρ ἐπὶ προφητῶν ἐστι καὶ ἀποστόλων . τέλειος θεὸς ἐν σαρκὶ καὶ τέλειος ἄνθρωπος ἐν πνεύματι, οὐ δύο υἱοὶ, εἷς μὲν γνήσιος υἱὸς ἀναλαβὼν ἄνθρωπον, ἕτερος δὲ θνητὸς ἄνθρωπος ἀναληφθεὶς ὑπὸ θεοῦ . ἀλλ` εἷς μονογενὴς ἔν οὐρανῷ, μορνογενὴς ἐπὶ γῆς . Θεὸς ἐν ἀληθείᾳ, ἄνθρωπος τῇ σαρκικῇ μορφώσει καθ` ὁμοίωσιν ἑαυτοῦ, σώζων κόσμον κατὰ μετάληψιν τοῦ ἰδίου Πνεύματος, ὃ δωρεῖται δι` ἐμφυσήσεως . ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἐν σχὴματι ἀνθρωπίνῳ βασιλεύων ἐπουρανίων καὶ ἐπιγείων καὶ καταχθονίων, ὑπὸ πάντων ὡς εἷς καὶ μόνος κύριος δοξαζόμενος εἰς δόξαν τοῦ Πατρὸς, ἀμήν.

“But for the completion of the faith, the Son of God is proclaimed as having been made flesh from the Virgin Mary and as having pitched his tent among human beings, not as operating in a human being—for that occurs among prophets and apostles. Perfect God in flesh and perfect human being in Spirit; not two sons, one proper Son having assumed a human being and another, a mortal human being, having been assumed by God; but one only-begotten in heaven, only-begotten upon earth. God in truth; human through fleshly formation according to his own likeness; saving the world through participation in his own Spirit, which he bestows through breathing. As a human being, reigning in human appearance over the heavenly, earthly, and subterranean beings, he is glorified by all as one and sole Lord, to the glory of the Father. Amen.”

[Col. 0957A]

### III.

But if anyone calls the Son born of Mary [Note: [Col. 0958C] (3) If the human being whom God assumed is understood to have existed before being assumed, it is right to deny that a human being was so assumed by God. But the hidden meaning of the Apollinarians must here be guarded against: they wished “God born of Mary” to be said in such a way that they denied that the same one was born human.

When their teacher Apollinaris declared, “We say that he who was born from Mary is God,” Athanasius, *Against Him*, book I, no. 20, sets against this the Church’s doctrine:

> “The Church of God neither received nor handed down this teaching. Rather, as it is written, God the Word, who was with God before the ages, came at the consummation of the ages and was born, from Mary and the Holy Spirit, as Son of Man.”

Unable to grasp this doctrine, the aforesaid heretics, Athanasius reports in book II, no. 4, circulated this calumny concerning Catholics: “They say Christ is a human being who became God.” Yet they themselves never ceased to call the same Christ “God born of the Virgin,” and not “God and human being.” Indeed, since they held that the Word assumed from Mary flesh without a human soul or mind, it followed that they would not permit the Son born of Mary to be called a human being assumed by God, since flesh without a soul or human mind is not a human being.] a human being assumed by God, and two persons united, let him know that he is estranged from divine hope. For God the Word, through whom are all things, as John and Paul taught, did not say that the Word assumed Jesus born from Mary; rather, they said that he himself came into the world, [Col. 0957B] born [perhaps “made”; Gal. 4:4] of a woman. Nor did they say that he who is from heaven dwelt in a human being from the earth, earthly (1 Cor. 15:47), but that he himself is the second, heavenly Adam. For heavenly is the Word who has flesh from Mary; and he makes us, who are truly earthly, heavenly according to likeness through that which is heavenly in him. [Note: [Col. 0958D] (4) Recall what we have already cited from the words of Apollinaris, in the preceding column, note 1: “Though we are from an earthly father, we are made like the heavenly one.” From the kinship of wording and thought, the genuine author of this letter is increasingly identified.] For we have been called into fellowship with the Son of God (Heb. 2:14), who also shared with us our death and the cross owed by human beings, although he was the Lord of glory; not held by death like every human being, but destroying death itself and imparting to us light, life, incorruption, and his own victory.

[Col. 0958A]

### III.

> Εἰ δέ τις ἄνθρωπον ὑπὸ θεοῦ προσληφθέντα λέγει τὸν ἐκ Μαρίας υἱὸν, καὶ δύο πρόσωπα ἑνωθέντα, γινωσκέτω [Col. 0958B] τῆς θείας ἐλπίδος ἀλλότριος ὤν . ὁ γὰρ θεὸς λόγος δι` οὗ τὰ πάντα, ὡς Ἱωάννης καὶ Παῦλος ἐδίδαξαν, οὐ τὸν λόγον ἀνειληφέναι Ἰησοῦν τὸν ἐκ Μαρίας τεχθέντα, ἀλλ` αὐτὸν ἐλθεῖν εἰς τὸν κόσμον γεννώμενον (perhaps **γενόμενον**) ἐκ γυναικός . οὐδὲ κατῳκηκεναι τὸν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ τῷ ἐκ γῆς χοϊκῷ, ἀλλ` αὐτὸν τὸν δεύτερον Ἀδὰμ ἐπουράνιον εἶναι . ὅτε ἐπουράνιός ἔστιν ὁ λόγος ὁ τὴν σάρκα ἔχων ἐκ Μαρίας, καὶ ἡμᾶς δὲ διὰ τοῦ ἐπουρανίου ἐπουρανίους καθ` ὁμοίωσιν ποῖων ὄντως χοϊκούς . ἐκλήθημεν γὰρ εἰς κοινωνίαν υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ, ὃς ἐκοινώνησεν ἡμῖν καὶ τοῦ θανάτου καὶ ὀφειλομένου ἀνθρώπῳ σταυροῦ, κύριος ὢν τῆς δόξης, οὐ κρατούμενος ὑπὸ θανατου ὡς πᾶς ἄνθρωπος . ἀλλὰ καταργῶν τὸν θάνατον, καὶ φῶς καὶ ζωὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν ἡμῖν νικὴν διδούς.

“But if anyone says that the Son from Mary is a human being assumed by God, and that two persons have been united, let him know that he is alien from divine hope. For God the Word, through whom are all things, as John and Paul taught, did not say that the Word assumed Jesus born from Mary; rather, that he himself came into the world, being born [perhaps **genomenon**, ‘having been made’] from a woman. Nor [did they say] that he who is from heaven dwelt in a human being, earthly and from the earth; rather, that he himself is the second Adam, heavenly. Since the Word having flesh from Mary is heavenly, he also makes us, truly earthly as we are, heavenly in likeness through the heavenly one. For we have been called into fellowship with the Son of God, who shared with us both death and the cross owed by humankind, though he was Lord of glory—not held by death as every human being is, but abolishing death and giving us light, life, incorruption, and his own victory.”

[Col. 0957B] 4. Therefore let all those be anathema who do not confess that the Son born of Mary is God the Word incarnate, consubstantial with the Father, existing from the beginning, unchangeable in the Incarnation, and impassible in his sufferings. Likewise, let him be anathema who says that the Saviour’s flesh is not from Mary but from heaven; or who asserts that he who is uncreated by nature is a created thing and from things that do not exist. But whoever, on account of the union with the uncreated God, calls the body divine, and worships, according to the composite whole in which both are together, as one uncreated God, shall be blessed. Let neither the flesh nor his sufferings cause you offence; rather, worship incorporeally him who is worshipped together with his own body, as the one and only Son of God from age to age. Moreover, according to the teaching of holy baptism, we have learned to confess also his second coming. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0958D] (5) In the handwritten collections of the presbyter Anastasius, kept in the library of the Jesuit college at Paris, ch. 38, this anathema is presented as “of Bishop Julius, from the letter to Acacius.” Nor is it inconsistent that a statement of this sort should be repeated in two letters forged under the same name. Leontius, indeed, testifies in *On Sects*, act 8, that he had seen seven letters of Apollinaris inscribed with Julius’s name. Moreover, this passage is more correctly transmitted in those collections than in the English manuscript, where the reading is: “Everyone who does not confess the man from Mary to be God incarnate . . . God existing from the beginning, unchangeable in the . . .” If that reading were admitted, there would be an evident conflict with the preceding words: the man who had previously pronounced anathema upon one confessing the Son born of Mary to be man would now himself confess the Son born of Mary to be man. But this conflict is now removed, and Apollinaris’s doctrine is consistently maintained: he admits “God incarnate,” that is, God made flesh, in such a way that he refuses, with the Nicene Council, also to confess him “made man,” that is, properly made human. He wishes the flesh to have been assumed by the one Word from God, not a human being.]

[Note: [Col. 0959B] (1) After Athanasius, in book I *Against Apollinaris*, §9, has represented Apollinaris as saying, “Certainly, we say that he who was born of Mary is consubstantial with the Father,” he immediately adds: “But this manner of speaking of yours, which you think so splendid, will be proved either superfluous or foolish”; and he shows it to be foolish, teaching that heresy lies hidden beneath Catholic words, because, he says, “you dare to call the flesh consubstantial with the divinity.” This impiety was not that of all Apollinaris’s followers; but Valentinus, Apollinaris’s disciple, reports and refutes it in Leontius, *Against the Frauds of the Apollinarians*, saying that Timothy defended it by various devices: “It cannot happen that a body should become consubstantial with the incorporeal God through union, as Timothy and Polemius, and their followers, madly and impiously say in various ways and by various contrivances.” The impiety of Timothy and his associates lay in this: whereas Catholics believe that he who was born of Mary is consubstantial with God according to the nature of the Word, they wished Christ’s flesh to be consubstantial with us by nature, but divine by union; hence they held that the properties of divinity were common to it and that, through union, that same flesh possessed a difference from ours. Therefore, when Timothy heard that Homonius, a bishop and fellow-disciple of Apollinaris, had written, “If anyone says that the flesh united to the Lord is homoousios—consubstantial—with God in any respect or manner, let him be anathema,” he felt himself attacked and asked him, in the book cited by Leontius: “Have you accused us in this passage as embracing heresy, and anathematized the preacher of piety together with piety itself?”]

[Note: [Col. 0959D] (2) Timothy, on his master’s authority, says in the passage of Leontius cited above that Christ is rightly said to exist “from the beginning” according to the body—falsely, of course, relying on the doctrine that, through union, the properties of the Word had become common even to the flesh itself.]

[Note: [Col. 0959D] (3) Apollinaris writes in the cited book of Leontius: “Let him be anathema who does not say that the flesh is from Mary, and who says that that flesh is of uncreated nature.” Yet he thinks that the same flesh which he admits to be of created nature may be called uncreated by this argument: “If the Word was named flesh because of the union, it follows that the flesh also is named Word because of the union; and, as the Word is, so it is uncreated—not because it was not created, but because through the union it was shown to be the Word.” Timothy, in the aforesaid work of Leontius, praises these words of Apollinaris: “It is not permissible to say separately that Christ’s body is created, since it is necessarily inseparable from him whose body it is; yet the name ‘uncreated’ and the name ‘God’ are communicated to it, because it has been joined with God into unity.” Hence Athanasius addresses Apollinaris in book I *Against Apollinaris*, §4: “But you say that Christ’s flesh became uncreated because it was united with the uncreated.” Athanasius there shows at length how absurd this opinion is; it will suffice to quote: “That which has communion with the uncreated, or which is united to it, has indeed what is proper to the uncreated, but is not itself called uncreated.” This refutes Apollinaris’s teaching in Leontius: “We do not say that the Saviour’s flesh is from heaven, nor consubstantial with God insofar as it is flesh and not God; but [we call it] God insofar as it is united with the divinity into one person.” For flesh thus united with divinity, according to Athanasius’s foregoing statement, is to be called not God but God’s. Thus it also follows that Christ’s body united with the Word is called a divine body, not because, as the Apollinarians think, it is God, but because it is God’s.]

[Note: [Col. 0960C] (4) Or rather, according to the preceding observation, “as [the body] of the uncreated God.” Here more openly than anywhere else the architect of this letter reveals himself as an Apollinarian. To those heretics, who alike said that Christ’s body had through union become uncreated God and repeatedly used this as a pretext, declaring, “We do not worship a created thing,” Athanasius aptly replies in book I *Against Apollinaris*, §6: “O foolish men, why do you not consider that, even if the Lord’s body was made, the worship due to it is not fitting for a created thing? For it became the body of the uncreated Word; and therefore you offer your worship to him whose body it became. The worship due to it is accordingly rendered when it is worshipped and honoured with divine worship, because the Word, whose own body it is, is God.” Holding this with the Church, one neither admits two sons in Christ nor, when worshipping his sacred body, is to be regarded as a worshipper of a human being. Thus Athanasius, at the end of book I *Against Apollinaris*, §21, charges his followers with a twofold calumny: they slander Catholics both as assertors of two sons in Christ and as anthropolaters. The innovators of our age renewed the same calumny, branding us with idolatry when we worship the Crucified One at the presentation of the sign of the cross, or venerate the saints as servants of God.]

[Note: [Col. 0960D] (5) There is a suspicion that Christ is here said to be worshipped in an incorporeal manner, just as the Apollinarians wished him to have lived on earth in an uncreated manner.
