Against them Athanasius asks in book I, §6: “By what reasoning, then, did the Lord die, if, being uncreated, he came to earth in an uncreated manner?” Since they do not know how to distinguish what belongs to Christ’s person from what belongs to his nature, they introduce a startling confusion into Christ’s properties; as Athanasius notes in book I, §2, they sometimes say that Christ’s flesh is uncreated and heavenly, at other times consubstantial with the divinity, and devise many other absurdities, whose shame often compels them either to change their opinion or to conceal it under expressions having a Catholic appearance. But the Catholic, distinguishing Christ’s person and nature, believes there is not one Son of Man and another Son of God, while recognizing one nature of the Word and another of the flesh; he rightly affirms that the Son of Man, even when on earth, is in heaven, and denies that the nature of the flesh is heavenly, uncreated, or consubstantial with the Father, just as he denies that the nature of the Word is affected by sadness, pain, and death.]

[Col. 0958B] IV. Therefore let everyone be anathema who does not confess the Son from Mary to be God the Word incarnate, consubstantial with the Father, existing from the beginning, unchangeable in the incarnation and impassible in sufferings. Likewise let him be anathema who does not say that the Saviour’s flesh is from Mary, but from heaven; or who calls the created thing, which is from non-being, uncreated by nature. But he who, because of its union with the uncreated God, calls the body divine, and worships according to the composite whole as one uncreated God, shall be blessed. Let not his flesh and sufferings cause you offence; but worship incorporeally him who is worshipped with his own body, as one and only Son of God from eternity and unto eternity. We have also learned to confess his second coming in the teaching of holy baptism—in which [read: in the teaching] of holy baptism. Amen.

**WORDS OF NO. 2 OF THE PRECEDING LETTER, FROM THE ANCIENT TRANSLATION OF THE COUNCIL OF EPHESUS IN BALUZE, *New Collection of Councils*, vol. I, p. 467. Of the most holy Julius, bishop of Rome, from the letter to Prosdocium.**

[Col. 0961]

For the fullness of faith, the Son of God is proclaimed both as incarnate from the Virgin Mary and as dwelling among human beings—not as operating in a human being; for this latter occurred in the Prophets and Apostles. Perfect God in flesh and perfect man in spirit are not two sons: one is properly the Son, assuming a human being; the other is a mortal assumed by God. Rather, there is one only-begotten God in heaven, the only-begotten God on earth.

**THE SAME WORDS, FROM THE TRANSLATION OF MARIUS MERCATOR IN THE SAME BALUZE, ibid., p. 613. Letter of the most holy Julius, bishop of Rome, to Prosdocium.**

For the completion of faith, the Son of God is proclaimed as incarnate from the Virgin Mary: he dwelt among human beings, not as acting in a human being; for this latter is said of the Prophets and Apostles. Perfect God in flesh and perfect man in spirit are not two sons: one is the natural Son who assumed a human being; the other, a mortal human being assumed by God. Rather, there is one only-begotten God in heaven, the only-begotten God on earth.

**THE SAME WORDS, FROM FACUNDUS, BOOK I, CHAPTER 5, p. 40. Of the most holy Julius, bishop of Rome, from the letter to Prosdocium.**

[Col. 0961C]

For the supplement of faith, the Son incarnate from the Virgin Mary is indeed proclaimed, and as dwelling among human beings, not as acting in a human being; for this had been the case in the Prophets and Apostles. Perfect God in flesh and perfect man in spirit are not two sons: one is the proper Son, assuming a human being; the other, a mortal assumed by God. Rather, there is one only-begotten God in heaven, the only-begotten God on earth.

## CENSURE OF THE FOLLOWING FRAGMENT

[Col. 0961]

I. Ephraem of Antioch preserved this fragment for us in Photius, codex 229, where its Latin translation is wholly discordant. It is likewise cited in the commonly circulated first book of Leontius *Against Nestorius and Eutyches* as: “Of St Julius, bishop of Rome.” Cyril produced this authority at the Synod of Ephesus. Yet it appears nowhere in the whole Ephesian Council. Nor did Facundus see it there. For although the Acephali, as Leontius himself testifies in *On Sects*, act 8, assert that a pseudonymous letter of Julius to Dionysius was inserted into the Ephesian Synod, and although, as Facundus reports, book I, chapter 5, they say, in support of their utterly vain error, that Julius of Rome wrote somewhere in reply that Christ has one nature, Facundus himself convicts them of falsehood from the fact that, in that same holy Synod of Ephesus, only this passage of Julius against Nestorius was recited from the letter to Prosdocium: “For the fullness of faith, [the Son] is proclaimed.” Having transcribed this testimony, he adds: “No other passage besides this from the letter to Prosdocium was produced at that synod from the sayings of Blessed Julius, if indeed he wrote anything else; nor was anything further produced from this letter.”

Hence we have no slight suspicion that the book of Leontius *Against Nestorius and Eutyches* is not by the same author as the books *On Sects* and *Against the Frauds of the Apollinarians*. The latter was surely too careful to write that an authority of which there is no mention whatever in the Ephesian Synod had been produced there—especially when, in *On Sects*, act 8, he recalls that the letter to Prosdocium alone, under Julius’s name, was cited at that council. He was also too discerning, and too accustomed to distinguish Apollinarian writings, to present as the unquestionable authority of an orthodox pope the testimony of a fierce enemy of Christ’s two natures, who deliberately defends the consubstantiality with God of the flesh united to the Word—so much so that, when intending to adduce it with others, he would not have hesitated first to say: “We have not produced an ambiguous authority, or one capable of a double meaning; nor have we cited obscure Fathers as witnesses. Rather, we have summoned to give testimony the most illustrious men, who were the most splendid lights of the world, and have produced testimonies most manifest and least doubtful.”

But, having proposed this reason for doubting the genuineness of the title by which the book *Against Nestorius and Eutyches* is ascribed to Leontius, we leave its more thorough examination to others. Meanwhile, the work from which the appended fragment was extracted is shown, even by the title attached to it, to be the work of some vapid disciple of Apollinaris—such as Polemius and Timothy—who maintained that Christ’s flesh after the union is consubstantial with God, an error which Valentinus and other followers also devoted to Apollinaris detested. Ephraem of Antioch indeed thinks this fragment plainly shows how St Julius confesses two natures, and judges that it must therefore be established that, in the preceding letter to Dionysius, the same pope took “one nature” to mean hypostasis. Yet, in our judgment, the same heresy manifests itself in both places: it invents one nature in Christ after the union and charges with falsehood those who believe in two.

## FRAGMENTS OF THE WRITINGS OF JULIUS

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0961]

### OF ST JULIUS, BISHOP OF ROME, IN A DISCOURSE ON THE *HOMOOU SION* [CONSUBSTANTIALITY]

[Col. 0961D]

Therefore it is necessary that both the corporeal be spoken of in its entirety and the divine in its entirety. Whoever cannot discern, in things united yet different, what belongs properly to each will fall into discordant contradictions. But one who recognizes the proper attributes and preserves the union will neither falsify the natures nor ignore the union.

Of Julius, bishop of Rome, in the discourse concerning consubstantiality.

[Col. 0962D]

Therefore it is necessary that both the bodily and the divine be spoken of as a whole. Whoever, being unable to know in the united yet different things what is proper to each, will fall into incongruous contradictions. But one who recognizes the proper characteristics and preserves the union neither falsifies the natures nor ignores the union.

### FRAGMENT II

[Note: This fragment, translated into Latin and communicated to us by Eusebius Renaudot out of his great zeal for the advancement of learning, was extracted both from an Arabic apologetic treatise by ‘Isa son of Zura‘ah concerning the position of the Jacobites, or Monophysites, on the mystery of the incarnate Word, and from Royal MS 432, likewise Arabic, in which various patristic testimonies are brought forward in support of the same opinion. ‘Isa died in A.D. 1007. Nor is it surprising that the letter from which this extract is taken is called the fifth, since Leontius says he encountered seven letters ascribed to Pope Julius by Apollinaris’s followers.]

Julius, patriarch of Rome, writes thus in Letter V concerning the union of Christ’s divinity with his humanity:

When he is called God, let no one deny his humanity, which is joined to the divinity; but when he is called by the name of his humanity because of the body which he assumed, let no one call his dignity and lordship into doubt. After the union, let no one divide him as though he were the principle of two natures [Royal MS: “divide him into two natures”]. For just as a human being, consisting of two perfect parts distinct in nature [Royal MS: “of two individual things different in nature”], namely soul and body, is nevertheless after their union of one nature and designated by one name: when he is called corporeal, the soul is not excluded from him; and when he is called ensouled or spiritual, the body is not excluded from him.

[Note: (2) In Christ what is united is not to be divided, but distinguished. For, when the natures are united, their properties remain, by which they are distinguished. But because those natures meet in the one person of the Word, the result of that union is not one nature of Christ but one person, to which the properties of the individual natures are attributed.]

[Note: (3) Soul and body cannot be reckoned as two perfect and complete natures if they are considered as established and fitted by God so as to be joined together. This cannot be said of the Word and the assumed human being. Further, something more perfect exists from soul and body than from body alone or soul alone; but no perfection accrued to the Word by assuming a human being. Nor do Catholics employ the likeness of a human being in order to deny two natures in Christ, but in order to explain the unity of person.]

### FRAGMENT III

[Note: This fragment is found only in Royal MS 432, cited separately from the preceding fragment.]

St Julius.

No distinction is found in the sacred Scriptures between the Word the Son and the body which Christ assumed; rather, he himself is one nature, one person, one hypostasis, wholly God and wholly man, and he is the one who acts.

[Note: (5) The holy Fathers rightly proclaim Christ wholly God and wholly man; see above, p. 63, note 1, from Leo’s Letter 115 to the Palestinians, §6; Augustine’s Sermon 293, §7; and Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book X, §28. But the preliminary phrase in this fragment, “one nature,” indicates that Apollinarian teaching is concealed here beneath Catholic words: it holds that Christ’s flesh itself became God after the union. Although adherents of this doctrine readily proclaim him wholly God, they shrink from and avoid calling him wholly man. For they do not know and reject the distinction which the deacon Ferrandus, in his letter to Severus, made between *totus* (“whole,” masculine) and *totum* (“the whole”), in order to avoid every ambiguity: “The whole Christ was in hell according to the rational soul, but not the whole [of Christ], etc.” If the conjunction *and* is removed from “wholly God and wholly man”—a particle which among Arabs is often said to add nothing to the sense of the words into which it is inserted—there remains the bare doctrine of Timothy, Polemius, and other Apollinarians, who hold that the whole human being became wholly God after the union, so that there are no longer two natures but one divine nature.]

### OBSERVATION: A sacred liturgy received by the Jacobites under Julius’s name

From these fragments and other passages from the letter to Dionysius, often cited in the writings of Jacobite doctors, it is clear how great was the veneration with which this sect received whatever bore the name of Pope Julius. This veneration, however, appears to have passed to them from Apollinaris and his followers. For since Apollinaris presented himself as a vigorous and, in that respect, praiseworthy adversary of the Arians, Julius’s letter—where those same heretics are attacked so wisely and refuted so invincibly—was undoubtedly highly welcome to him. Yet he could not show Julius as agreeing with him in defending the doctrine that he himself had devised, although he rejoiced in Julius’s agreement in attacking Arian doctrine, unless writings of his own were inscribed with Julius’s name. We have shown above, concerning the letter to Dionysius, that this at least was done by his disciples.

Deceived by the authority of so great a name, and of the other Fathers to whom the Apollinarians attributed similar writings, Eutyches could not be moved from the defence of one nature. The Jacobites, or Monophysites, likewise deceived by the same testimonies, though they detest Eutyches in other respects, proved no less obstinate in maintaining the doctrine of one nature. Their reverence for Pope Julius is further evident from the fact that they possess a sacred liturgy also bearing his name. Eusebius Renaudot is preparing its edition, having already rendered good service to the Church by publishing and elucidating several liturgies of this sort.

## CENSURE OF THE LETTERS OF CYRIL TO JULIUS AND OF JULIUS TO CYRIL CONCERNING THE DAY OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

I. Franciscus Combefisius published, from Royal MS formerly 696, now 2428, p. 149, a letter on the Nativity of the Lord written by John of Nicaea, who flourished around the end of the tenth century. In it Cyril’s letter to Julius is cited as follows: “Cyril once wrote—not the Cyril who wrote the letter to Constantine [read: Constantius], but the one who succeeded him in his see—to Julius, bishop of Rome.” Then John, wishing to prove from the same letter how the celebration of the Lord’s Nativity on 25 December was established, adduces this passage from it.

### WORDS OF CYRIL REPORTED BY JOHN OF NICAEA

[Col. 0965]

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following paragraph are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0965A]

“Great toil and loss befall the great and splendid feasts because they are celebrated on one day. For the readings and order of both feasts remain incomplete, since the Nativity and Baptism of the Lord cannot be celebrated together. Since, therefore, we cannot on one day go both to Bethlehem and to the place of baptism—for Bethlehem lies three miles south of Jerusalem, and the Jordan fifteen miles to the east—let your Holiness order an investigation of all the Jewish records which Caesar Titus carried off from Jerusalem to Rome as spoils. Perhaps you will certainly discover the day of the birth of Christ our God.”

[Col. 0966A]

“Great labour and deprivation occur in the case of the great and splendid feasts because they are celebrated on one day. The readings and the order of service of the two feasts remain incomplete, because it is impossible to perform the Lord’s birth and baptism together. Since indeed we cannot on one day go to the place of baptism—for Bethlehem is three miles south of Jerusalem, while the Jordan is fifteen miles eastward—let your Holiness therefore command an examination of all the writings of the Jews, which Caesar Titus, after plundering them, carried from Jerusalem to Rome. Perhaps you may certainly find the day of the birth of Christ our God.”

II. Another writer, however, whose work is entitled *Necessary Narrative* (*Anankaia diēgēsis*), preserved in the said Royal MS 2428, p. 120, cites the same fragment differently, as follows: “The patriarch Juvenal of Jerusalem wrote concerning this matter to Julius, patriarch of Rome.” He then relates it in such a way as to differ from John of Nicaea not only in wording but also in substance. It is presented by him thus.

### THE SAME PASSAGE FROM THE ANONYMOUS ACCOUNT

[Col. 0965]

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following paragraph are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0965B]

“I cannot go on one day both to Bethlehem and to the Jordan. For the Jordan is twenty-five miles east of the city of Jerusalem, while holy Bethlehem is six miles south of the city; nor can I celebrate both feasts on one day. Therefore I beg your Holiness, Father, to search the records and, after making an exact investigation, to inform us in writing, venerable one, on what day Christ the Lord was born and on what day he was baptized. For we know well that the records were originally carried from Jerusalem to Rome by Titus and Vespasian.”

[Col. 0966B]

“I cannot on one day go both to Bethlehem and to the Jordan. For the Jordan lies twenty-five miles east of the city of Jerusalem, while holy Bethlehem lies six miles south of the city; and I cannot complete the two feasts on one day. I beseech, therefore, your Holiness, Father, that you investigate the records, or rather that, after an exact investigation, you give us through your writing, honoured one, knowledge concerning these matters: on what day Christ the Lord was born, and on what day he was baptized. For we have learned with certainty that the original records were brought from Jerusalem to Rome by Titus and Vespasian.”

III. But anyone may observe that these two writers disagree with one another both in words and in substance. Further, as our colleague who prepared the most recent edition of Cyril of Jerusalem observed, the mistake of this anonymous writer is manifest, since Juvenal is separated from Julius’s time by nearly a hundred years. Nor can the Cyril to whom John of Nicaea attributes the same writing be reconciled any better with the lifetime of this pope. For no successor can be imagined to have succeeded Cyril, who wrote to Constantius—that is, the writer of the celebrated letter concerning the cross seen at Jerusalem on Pentecost—and to have occupied the see of Jerusalem while Julius was still alive.

Epiphanius indeed, *Heresies* 66.20, enumerates two Cyrils among the bishops of Jerusalem: one, the successor of Maximus, who wrote the aforementioned letter concerning the cross seen; and another, the son of Hilarion, who governed the church of Jerusalem in the thirteenth year of Valens, that is, A.D. 375. But there is serious reason to fear that Epiphanius took a single and same Cyril, returning from exile to his church, for a second, younger man. Whether, then, the cited letter is attributed to the one and same Cyril after he returned from exile to his church, or to another put in his place, it is falsely addressed to Julius, since this pope died at least four years before Cyril was first expelled from his see.

IV. Therefore it is false that John of Nicaea and the Anonymous writer relate that Julius replied to Cyril at that time. John says: “Then Julius of Rome diligently sought how he might satisfy this request of Cyril. Having assembled all the Jewish writings that had been captured and brought to Rome, he found a certain record of Joseph the chronographer, written by Joseph himself, in which it was stated that, in the seventh month, on the feast of Tabernacles, on the day of Atonement, an angel of God appeared, and that the priest remained mute and voiceless until the time when Elizabeth, his wife, bore a child in old age.” The Anonymous writer, however, relates the matter thus: “When these letters had been received, Julius, patriarch of Rome, investigated the records and discovered that our Lord Jesus Christ was born on 25 December, and that thirty years after his birth he was baptized by John in the river Jordan on the sixth day of January. Therefore, when the Fathers complied with this investigation and divided the feast, a murmur arose among many, etc.”

V. Moreover, the falsity of this narrative may be demonstrated on several grounds. First, it is nearly certain that the feasts of the Lord’s Nativity and Baptism were never separated by Cyril. The most recent editor of Cyril supposes that this may be proved from the words of Basil of Seleucia in his homily on St Stephen, in which Juvenal is praised because “he began to celebrate the glorious and saving Nativity of the Lord.” He thinks the passage observes that the custom of celebrating the Lord’s Nativity on 25 December was first introduced into the Jerusalem church by Juvenal. Yet if we trust the ancient writer under the name of Cosmas, who flourished in Justinian’s reign, the Jerusalemites had not yet adopted this practice in his time, that is, in the sixth century. For he speaks thus, as cited in the most recent edition of Chrysostom, vol. II, p. 353: “The Jerusalemites alone, from a plausible conjecture but not from an exact calculation, celebrate the Nativity at Epiphany.”

Next, the statement in John of Nicaea concerning a discovered record of Joseph was devised after the time of Chrysostom and the aforementioned Cosmas, as may be inferred from what both say regarding the day of the Lord’s Nativity. Taking it as certain, although contrary to the truth, that Zachariah had been high priest, that the angel of the Lord appeared to him when he entered the Holy of Holies, and that the angel promised John’s birth, they concluded that this promise occurred on 10 September, the day on which alone during the whole year the high priest might enter the Holy of Holies; and consequently that Christ, conceived six months later, was born in December rather than January. Chrysostom, while attempting with deliberate effort and much labour to persuade his audience of this, puts it forward not as something already reported by Joseph, but as a new argument which he himself was the first to draw from the Scriptures.

It is likewise evident that Cosmas, when he employs the same argument, took it not from the pseudo-letter of Julius but rather from Chrysostom’s homily: not only because he makes no mention of Joseph, but also because he expressly states that the Jerusalemites had not yet abandoned the custom of celebrating the Lord’s Nativity at Epiphany. Those fabricated letters of Cyril and Julius were thus unknown to him; for that reason we reasonably suspect that they were forged after the fifth century.

VI. Indeed, to pass over the fact that Joseph was not the sort of person who would have counted Zachariah—merely a priest exercising his priestly office “in the order of his course” and entering the temple of the Lord “by lot”—among the high priests: if Cyril, desiring to learn the true day of the Lord’s Nativity and to be relieved of the difficulty of celebrating two feasts on one day, had consulted Julius, that pope would not have satisfied his inquiry from a previously unknown and still no better known record of Joseph, from which at most one might certainly learn the day on which John was promised, but not the day on which he was conceived or Christ was born.

But if Cyril had sought some authority, Julius could readily have produced from the archives of the city of Rome, as Chrysostom observed, the record of the census, on the occasion of which Mary went with her betrothed to Bethlehem and there gave birth to Christ. Yet, setting aside these investigations, it can scarcely be doubted that Julius would rather have urged him to follow the practice which the whole Latin Church preserved by tradition. Januarius recalls this tradition when he asked Augustine: “Why does the anniversary day for celebrating the Lord’s Passion not return to the same day of the year, as does the day on which tradition says he was born?” Augustine answers (*Epistle* 119, now 65.2): “You ought to know that the Lord’s birthday is not celebrated as a sacrament, but only as a remembrance that he was born; and therefore nothing was needed except that the recurring day of the year on which the event itself occurred should be marked by festive devotion.”

At last the eastern churches yielded to the force of this tradition. Thus Chrysostom, preaching at Antioch on the Lord’s Nativity in the first year in which he was made a presbyter, hence in A.D. 386, says in §1: “It is not yet ten years since this very day was plainly made known to us, though it has been known from the beginning to those who live in the West.” And in §2: “The Romans, having celebrated it much earlier and by ancient tradition, transmitted knowledge of it even to us.” It follows that the church of Antioch began to celebrate the Lord’s Nativity on 25 December only in 376 or 377.

Likewise, from the sermon delivered at Alexandria by Paul, bishop of Emesa, on 25 December 432, it is clear that the same custom had then been received in that city. Gregory of Nyssa, in his homily *On the Nativity of the Lord*, says: “Now throughout the inhabited world the harmonious sound of those celebrating the feast-day” of the Lord’s Nativity “is heard.” Chrysostom seems likewise to support this in the homily cited above. We also possess Gregory Nazianzen’s Oration 38, delivered at Constantinople on the Nativity of the Lord, which persuades us that this feast was observed in that city on 25 December. Certainly, after speaking near its conclusion about Christ’s birth, he adds: “And indeed, a little later, you will see Jesus purified in the Jordan by my purification.”

## TEN DECREES OF POPE JULIUS I ACCORDING TO GRATIAN AND IVO

[Col. 0968]

### FIRST. He pursues shameful gain who buys cheaply in order to sell dearly; or, what usury is

Whoever, at the time of harvest or vintage, buys grain or wine not from necessity but from greed—for example, buys one modius for two coins and keeps it until he may sell it for four or six denarii, or more—this we call shameful gain.

### SECOND. A priest who denies penance to the dying is guilty of souls

If a priest denies penance to those who are dying, he will be guilty of their souls, because the Lord says: “On whatever day the sinner turns to repentance, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 18; Luke 23). For a true confession may be made at the last moment, because the Lord is the examiner not only of time but also of the heart; just as the thief, by repentance in a single instant, deserved to be in Paradise at the hour of his final confession.

### THIRD. After someone’s death, no one of that person’s kindred may take his betrothed

[Col. 0969A]

If anyone has betrothed or endowed a wife, and, whether prevented by the day of death coming first or by other intervening causes, has not had intercourse with her, neither his surviving brother nor anyone of his kindred may ever take that same woman as his wife.

### FOURTH. A slave may contract marriage

We all have one Father in heaven (Matt. 23), and every one of us—rich, poor, slave, and free—will equally render an account for himself and for his soul. Therefore we do not doubt that all persons, of whatever condition, have one law, insofar as pertains to God. But if all have one law, then, just as a freeborn person cannot be dismissed, so neither can a slave, once joined in marriage, thereafter be dismissed.

### FIFTH. No one may marry within the seventh degree through relationship by one’s own blood or by one’s wife

We permit no one of either sex to marry, or to be joined in the stain of incest, with a person related either through his or her own blood or through a spouse, to the seventh degree of kinship. We further add this: just as no Christian may marry someone of his own kindred, so neither may he marry someone of his wife’s kindred, because of the unity of flesh.

### SIXTH. When a church once consecrated to God is to be consecrated again

[Col. 0969C]

Concerning the rebuilding of any church, if it has been destroyed, and whether the solemnity of consecration ought to be repeated in a place where the sanctuaries have not been disturbed: we judge that nothing prevents this, if exorcized water is not sprinkled over it, because in the consecration of any church in which the pledge of the Holy Spirit is not placed, we know that there is only the celebration of Masses. Therefore, if any basilica of the saints has been rebuilt from its foundations without moving the altar, then, without any doubt, when the solemnity of Masses has been celebrated in it, the consecration of the entire sanctification will be fulfilled. But if the sanctuaries which it possessed have been removed, it is to receive again the reverence of sanctification through their re-deposition and the solemnity of Masses.

### SEVENTH. Concerning those who erred in various ways while offering sacrifice
When every crime and sin is removed by sacrifices offered to God, what thereafter shall be given to the Lord for the expiation of offences, when error is committed in the very offering of sacrifice? For we have heard that certain persons, held by schismatic ambition, contrary to divine ordinances and apostolic institutions, consecrate milk instead of wine in the divine sacrifices; that others offer the people intinct Eucharist as the completion of communion; that some offer pressed wine in the sacrament of the Lord’s chalice; and that others preserve throughout the whole year a linen cloth soaked in must, and [Col. 0970A] at the time of sacrifice wash part of it with water and so offer it. How contrary this is to evangelical and apostolic teaching, and how hostile to ecclesiastical custom, is not difficult to demonstrate from the very fountain of truth from which the ordered mysteries of the sacraments themselves proceeded.

For when the teacher of truth commended to his disciples the true sacrifice of our salvation, we know that under this sacrament he gave them not milk (variant: “not to them”), but only bread and the cup. For it is read in the truth of the Gospel: “Jesus took bread and the cup, and, blessing, gave [them] to his disciples” (Matt. 26). Let milk therefore cease to be offered in sacrificing (variant: “in the sacrifice”), since the manifest and evident example of Gospel truth has shone forth: nothing other than bread and wine may be offered.

Moreover, concerning their giving the people intinct Eucharist for the completion of [Col. 0970B] communion, they have not received this testimony brought forth from the Gospel, where he commended his body and blood to the apostles. For the commending of the bread and of the cup is recorded separately. We do not read that Christ gave dipped bread to others, except to that one disciple whom the dipped morsel showed to be the Master’s betrayer—not as signifying the institution of this sacrament.

For what is distributed to the people from the pressed cluster—that is, from grape berries—is altogether very confused. But, if necessity requires it, the cluster should be pressed into the cup and mixed with water. For, according to the precepts of the canons, the Lord’s cup ought to be offered mixed with wine and water, because we see that the people are understood in the water, while the blood of Christ is shown in the wine. [Col. 0970C] Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the cup, the people are united with Christ, and the congregation of believers is joined and bound to him in whom it believes. This union and conjunction of water and wine is so mixed in the Lord’s cup that the mixture cannot be separated. For if anyone offers wine alone, Christ’s blood begins to be without us; but if water alone is present, the people begin to be without Christ. Therefore, when the cluster alone is offered, in which only the efficacy (variant: “effect”) of wine is signified, the sacrament of our salvation, which is signified by water, is neglected. For the Lord’s cup cannot be water alone or wine alone unless both are mixed.

And therefore, since from this matter there has already flowed forth a very extensive and manifold judgment of the elders, every such error and presumption must henceforth cease, lest the perverse and disorderly assemblage [Col. 0970D] weaken the stability of truth. Therefore henceforth no one shall be permitted to offer anything else in divine sacrifices except, according to the judgment of ancient councils, bread alone and a cup mixed with wine and water. Whoever henceforth acts otherwise than has been commanded shall abstain from offering sacrifice until, corrected through lawful penitential satisfaction, he returns to the function of his rank which he has lost.

OCTAVE.

(Taken from the decree of Ivo of Chartres.) What the Church is.

Church (*Ecclesia*) is a Greek name rendered in Latin as “assembly” (*convocatio*), because it calls all persons to itself. It is called Catholic—that is, universal—[Col. 0971A] because it is established throughout the whole world. Or because “Catholic,” that is, general, is in the same teaching for instruction.

NINTH.

(From the same source.) Concerning those who burned churches.

If anyone burns a church, let him do penance for fifteen years, diligently restore it, and distribute its value to the poor.

TENTH.

(From the same source.) That a freedwoman may lawfully marry her master.

If anyone grants freedom to his female slave and joins her to himself in marriage, some doubted whether such a marriage should be considered lawful [Col. 0971B] or not. We, therefore, settling the ancient uncertainty, have judged such unions to be lawful. For if all marriages arise from mutual affection, and nothing impious or contrary to the laws can be done in such a union, why should we think that the aforesaid marriages ought to be prohibited?

EPISTLE I [Note: [Col. 0971D] (1) This epistle, together with those following, rightly appears to Baronius and other learned persons to be spurious, no differently from the other wares of Isidore, first originating from Spain, as they suppose.] OF REBUKE BY JULIUS [Note: [Col. 0971D] Epistle of rebuke by Julius. On the following grounds it may reasonably be judged sufficiently evident that this epistle was given under the consuls Felicianus and Titianus, in the year of Christ 337, and was written by the Roman pontiff from the first Roman synod held under Julius. First, this epistle and the Roman synod bear the date of the same consulship of Felicianus and Titianus. Second, those who openly declare in the acts of the synod that they had assembled for this purpose are reproved for the unjust condemnation and banishment of Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra, in these words: “Let us labor, dealing with the oppression of our brethren; for while they are so grievously afflicted, we are unable either to breathe or to rest.” In the year of Christ 336 they had repeatedly condemned and banished Athanasius in their conventicles; since this had occurred without the knowledge and consent of the Roman pontiff, they are rightly reproved for the nullity of the act and the violation of ecclesiastical constitutions.] POPE I, TO THE EASTERN BISHOPS, CONCERNING THE CAUSE OF ATHANASIUS AND OFFENCES AGAINST THE ROMAN CHURCH.

(Councils, vol. II, col. 475.)

I. That only the Roman pontiff may convene a general council and judge bishops.

II. Councils ought not to be held, nor bishops condemned, apart from the judgment of the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 0971C] III. That accusers and accusations not admitted by secular laws should be rejected.

IV. If anyone condemns a bishop apart from the authority of the Apostolic See, or expels him from his see, he is to be deprived of his rank and excommunicated; and the expelled bishops are to be restored.

Julius, to all his venerable brethren, the eastern bishops.

It was fitting, brethren, that you should instruct others in ecclesiastical disciplines, not accuse them with such contrivances; as John the Baptist says: “Extort from no one, and make no false accusation” (Luke 3), and the rest. On this matter the Apostle Paul also instructs us, saying: “Brethren, even if a person is caught in some transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, [Col. 0971D] considering yourself lest you too be tempted” (Gal. 6), and the rest. And elsewhere the Apostle Peter says (1 Pet. 3): “Be all of one mind [Col. 0972A] in prayer, compassionate, lovers of the brotherhood, merciful, modest, humble; not rendering evil for evil or curse for curse, but, on the contrary, blessing, because to this you were called, that you might inherit a blessing. For whoever wishes to love life and see good days, let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. Let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue” (variant: “follow”) “it. For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears upon their prayers; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 33).

What is worse, brethren, than that priests of the Lord—who ought to remain free from every evil defilement and from injury to all Christians, and all the more from injury to brethren and fellow bishops, whom they ought to protect and support against snares, and [Col. 0972B] whom they ought especially to cherish and love—should persecute them and strive to deprive them of communion? Do you not remember Wisdom, which says: “Perverse thoughts separate men from God” (Wisdom 1)? If perverse thoughts separate men from God, how much more do wicked deeds? For what is more wicked than that anyone should endeavor to turn aside, persecute, and destroy those of whom the Lord says: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zech. 2)?

Proved virtue bears, protects, and consoles the oppressed, and teaches the ignorant. For God is witness of the heart of man (variant: “the human heart”), the true searcher of individual consciences, and the hearer of every tongue; because “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which holds all things has knowledge of speech” (Ps. 17). [Col. 0972C] And elsewhere that same author says (1 John 4): “God is love. In this the love of God was manifested in us: that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. In this is love: not as though we had loved God, but because he first loved us and sent his Son as the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we too ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us. In this we know that we remain in him and he in us: because he has given us of his Spirit. And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son, the Savior of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God; and we have known and believed the love which God has [Col. 0972D] in us. God is love; and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him. In this God’s love is perfected with us: that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world. There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts fear out, [Col. 0973A] because fear has punishment. But whoever fears is not perfect in love. Therefore let us love God, because God first loved us. If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God: that whoever loves God should also love his brother.”

For Wisdom itself also says (Prov. 15): “The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge; the mouth of fools pours forth folly. In every place the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil. A healing tongue is a tree of life, but an immoderate one crushes the spirit. In the house of the righteous is abundant strength, but in the fruits of the impious there is disturbance. The lips of the wise scatter knowledge; the heart of fools will be unlike it. [Col. 0973B] The victims of the impious are abominable to the Lord, but the vows of the righteous are pleasing. Whoever follows righteousness is loved by the Lord.” Again elsewhere (Prov. 10): “The lips of the righteous consider what is pleasing, but the mouth of the impious [speaks] perversities. The uprightness of the righteous will direct them, but the deceitfulness of the perverse will lay them waste; the righteousness of the upright will deliver them, and the wicked will be caught in their own snares. The righteous will be delivered from distress, and the impious will be handed over in his place. A dissembler deceives his friend with his mouth, but the righteous will be delivered by knowledge. In the prosperity of the righteous the city will be exalted” (variant: “rejoice”), “and in the destruction of the impious there will be praise. By the blessing of the righteous the city will be exalted.”

And you who do not cease to persecute brethren do not consider what the most patient Job says among other things at the beginning (Job 29): “The hearing ear called me blessed, and the seeing eye bore witness to me, because I had delivered the poor man crying out and the orphan who had no [Col. 0973C] helper. The blessing of one about to perish came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow. I clothed myself in righteousness, and I put on my judgment like a garment and diadem. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor; and I investigated with utmost care the cause which I did not know. I broke the jaws of the wicked and plucked the prey from his teeth.” And a little later: “If,” he says, “I denied the poor what they desired, and made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone and the orphan did not eat from it—for compassion grew up with me from my infancy, and came forth with me from my mother’s womb.”

For if anyone considers all these things with an upright eye, he will by no means hasten to harm brethren (variant: “the brethren”), but to deliver them; because nothing is worse than citizens envying citizens, brethren laying snares for brethren, or bringing false accusations. [Col. 0973D] Desiring to oppose such snares, the holy Fathers assembled a general synod at Nicaea, wishing to reform the life of persons living in the Church. Although many ordinances of holy Fathers had long been written down, they established laws which we call sacred canons; by these many things most necessary for the condition of God’s holy Church, and for the support of its pillars—that is, the bishops, who bear it upon their own shoulders—were decreed, and injuries to them were prohibited. Thus, those attempting such deeds or presuming to harm them were, if clerics, to fall from their own rank; but if monks or laypersons, to be anathematized.

Armed with these examples, we have judged, inspired by almighty God, that we ought by apostolic [Col. 0974A] authority to extinguish this kindled flame of discord, and not permit it further to devour human souls. Therefore, together with all [who are subject to] the apostolic rule, we decree that henceforth no Christian should presume to perpetrate such things or rashly harm bishops, since the teacher of the gentiles also forbids this, saying: “Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father” (1 Tim. 5), and the rest.

For it is undoubtedly good, and desirable to all who fear God, to restrain dissensions and disputes, to assist brethren, and not to envy but to help one another. Hear, I say, the synod already held in the city of Nicaea, to which I too rendered due observance of conscience [Note: [Col. 0974D] (1) Constantine the Great, in the letter to Alexander, *Tripartite History* III.27, from Socrates I.6.], desiring nothing other than to produce concord among all and, above all, to condemn and remove this contentiousness of plotters. Foreseeing these snares and illicit disputes, the holy Fathers unanimously decreed in the aforesaid Nicene synod that no bishop accused of certain charges should be heard—that is, judged or condemned—except in a lawful synod convened at the proper time by apostolic authority. But if some persons presume otherwise, what they have done shall be rendered void (variant: “shall be rendered”), and shall in no way be counted among ecclesiastical acts.

I.

To the Church of the First See itself were granted, by evangelical, apostolic, and canonical institutions, through a singular privilege, the rights of convening general synods and the judgments of bishops, because [Col. 0974C] greater causes have always been commanded by many authorities to be referred to the Apostolic See. And in no way can a greater be judged by a lesser. For it is greater than and set above all churches, and it obtained a singular primacy not only by decrees of the canons and holy Fathers but by the voice of our Lord and Savior himself: “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16), and the rest. “And whatever you bind upon earth and loose shall be bound and loosed in heaven and on earth.”

II.

Moreover, long ago, by the holy apostles and their successors, it had been decreed in the aforesaid ancient statutes—which the holy, universal, apostolic Church maintains to this day—that councils ought not to be held apart from the judgment of the Roman [Col. 0974D] pontiff (Socrates II.8 and 17), nor a bishop condemned, because they willed the holy Roman Church to be the primatial (variant: “principal”) church of all churches. And just as the blessed Apostle Peter was first of all the apostles, so too this church, consecrated in his name by the Lord’s institution, is made first and head of the rest. All greater causes of the Church and the judgments of bishops should have recourse to it, as to a mother and summit, and should receive their final determination by its just judgment (variant: “and according to its judgment”). Nothing in these matters should be decreed outside the Roman pontiff, so that metropolitan bishops, as they had been accustomed to do, might not so rashly and at anyone’s whim [Col. 0975A] be permitted, by their own private judgment and without consulting the Roman pontiff, either to overthrow greater causes of the Church or to condemn bishops. Rather, by the common counsel of the bishop of the holy Roman See [Note: [Col. 0975D] (1) Hadrian, collection 43. This occurs below in the decree of Pope Julius, “To the Eastern Bishops concerning Athanasius.”] and united action, let them unanimously arrange whatever must be done with zeal for Christ, judge rightly, and accomplish what they have judged—not disagreeing among themselves, but doing what pleases God.

III.

It was also unanimously decreed in the aforesaid Nicene synod that accusers and accusations not admitted by secular laws should be wholly removed from causing injury to priests. “Behold,” says the Prophet, “how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132). [Col. 0975B] But those do not dwell in unity who withdraw themselves from the consolation of brethren or prepare snares for brethren. Do not suffer yourselves, brethren, to be burdened by another’s sin (St Leo, Epistle 25), because what we are obliged to say, we are reluctant to say: namely, lest indignation be provoked by the ruin of anyone’s religion. Keep before your eyes and reverently behold with the full attention of your minds the glory of blessed Peter, and with him the common crowns of all the apostles and the palms of all martyrs, who suffered for the strengthening—not the destruction—of brethren, and for truth in Christ.

IV.

[Col. 0975C] We, therefore, who desire both to be called and to be disciples of the Lord, ought to bear Christ’s cross, suffer with brethren, and not persecute them. Withdraw, we entreat you, your acts and thoughts from such injuries, if you do not wish to incur that very vengeance yourselves; for he who prepares a pit for his brother deserves retaliation. And know that we shall henceforth not endure this arrogance (African Fathers, in their letter to Boniface): that you should, without consulting us, seize matters which belong especially to this holy See, such as the judgments of bishops and the greater causes of the Church, as was touched upon a little above—without danger to your own standing.

But if, from this day onward, anyone presumes to condemn a bishop apart from the judgment of this holy See or drive him from his own see, let him know that he is irrecoverably condemned and shall forever lack his own honor. And know that those expelled or condemned apart from the judgment of this See receive, by the authority of this holy See, their former communion and are restored [Col. 0975D] to their own sees. For these things were granted to this holy See earlier, namely from the time of the apostles; and afterwards, in the aforementioned Nicene synod, they were unanimously confirmed by all because of the assaults of wicked persons, the persecutions of heretics, and the schemes of brethren who lay snares. Thus may each person take greater care (variant: “forethought”) not to dare perpetrate such acts; and let them beware, if not for God’s sake and for fraternal love (variant: “love of brethren”), then at least because of human reproach, their own shame, and canonical punishment. Restrained by fear and modesty, let such deeds [Col. 0976A] be suppressed in silence, with every excess of usurpation cut away (St Leo, Epistle 84), because no one ought to presume what does not appear to have been granted to him.

You could in no way have incurred this fault (St Leo, Epistle 4, ch. 7), if you took from the source whence you receive the consecration of honor the law of complete observance; and if the See of blessed Apostle Peter, which is the mother of your priestly dignity, were also your teacher in ecclesiastical reasoning. Therefore, just as those things which you have done piously and rightly give us great joy, so the things done wrongly cause us excessive grief, because after the experience of many such cases it is necessary henceforth to provide more carefully and guard more diligently, so that those things established by the apostles and their successors are [Col. 0976B] neglected by no sloth, violated by no dissension, and disturbed by no contention.

For as we have many members in one body, but all members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another (Rom. 12). The connection of the whole body produces one health and one beauty; and this connection of the entire body requires unanimity, but especially demands concord among priests. Although their dignity is not common, yet their order is general; for even among the most blessed apostles, in the similarity of honor there was a certain distinction of authority. Though the choice of all was equal, it was nevertheless granted to one that he should take precedence over the rest. From this model arose a certain distinction among bishops; and by great ordering it was provided [Col. 0976C] that not all should claim all things for themselves, but that in each province there should be individuals whose judgment held first place among their brethren; and, again, that certain persons established in the greater cities should undertake a more extensive care, through whom the care of the universal Church might flow to the one See of blessed Peter, and nothing anywhere might dissent from its head.

Therefore, whoever knows himself to be set over some persons should not resent that another is set over him, but should himself render the obedience that he demands. Do not therefore err, my beloved brethren. “Do not be led away by various and strange teachings” (Heb. 13). Behold, you have the institutions of the apostles and apostolic men, and the canons (Distinction II, *Nolite errare*); use them, surround yourselves with them, delight in them, arm yourselves with them, so that, relying on, surrounded by, delighted in, and armed with them, [Col. 0976D] you may be able to stand against all the darts of enemies.

For it is sufficiently unworthy (Gelasius, Epistle 9, ch. 10) that any of the pontiffs or subordinate orders should reject this rule which he sees the See of blessed Peter both follow and teach. For it is most fitting that the entire body of the Church should agree with itself in this observance, which has authority from that source where the Lord established the primacy of the whole Church, Scripture saying: “Set love in order within me” (Song 2). And again: “Let all things be done in order” (1 Cor. 14). And again the Psalmist proclaims: “Surround Zion and embrace her; recount [her glory] in her towers. Set your hearts upon her strength, that you may tell it to later generations, because this is God, our Lord” (variant: “God”), “for ever, and he himself will rule us through the ages” (Ps. 47).

For, having considered our office, we have no liberty to dissemble or to be silent (variant: “we are not free”), since zeal for the Christian religion, greater than all else, rests upon us; nor should we appear by silence either to favor or to consent to injuries against brethren. Given on the Kalends of October, under the most illustrious consuls Felicianus and Maximianus (perhaps Titianus), in the year 337.

EPISTLE [Note: [Col. 0977D] (1) Fictitious, according to Baronius and other learned persons; stitched together from various fragments of other Latin writings.] OF THE EASTERNERS [Note: [Col. 0977D] Epistle of the Easterners. From the epistle of Julius to the Easterners, recited by Athanasius in *Apology* 2 and printed above at col. 883, it is most certain that the Arians wrote after the Council of Antioch more bitterly, and with greater arrogance, pride, and contentiousness than was proper. For it begins thus: “I read your letter, which my presbyters Elpidius and Polyxenus brought to me,” etc. That the true and genuine letter does not survive is confirmed, besides the authority of Baronius under the year 341, no. 54, by what I noted above at the beginning of Julius’s epistles. The letter placed here in second position, bearing the heading “of the Easterners,” appears to have been compiled by an unknown author from Sozomen and Socrates. For, if you compare it carefully with Julius’s reply recited by Athanasius in *Apology* 2, you will observe that much is missing and that some matters and names expressed in it also vary.] TO POPE JULIUS I.

(Councils, vol. II, col. 481.) They complain that he received Athanasius and the others whom they had condemned into communion. (S)*

[Col. 0977B]

To the most blessed and honorable lord and father Julius, venerable bishop of the Apostolic See: Eusebius, Theognis, Theodorus, and [Note: [Col. 0977D] (2) Theodorus was bishop of Perinthus, or Heraclea, whom the forger divides into two persons.] Berinthus, together with the rest of our brethren and fellow bishops gathered at Antioch [Note: [Col. 0977D] (3) In the year 341. This epistle reveals that those who wrote it were heretics.].

Although we know that the Roman Church is generous toward all, has apostolic care, and always exists as the mother of piety—although preachers of piety had come to it from the East (Tripartite History IV.16; Sozomen III.7)—yet we would wish you to agree with us: that those whom we suspend from communion should be suspended by you, and those whom we confirm in the rank of bishops should be confirmed by you; and that we should not be held in second place, since the apostles who taught doctrine reached you from these regions.

For we did not oppose your actions, although we could have done so, when Novatian was expelled from the Roman Church; for, to speak according to common usage, “everyone who wishes to withdraw from a friend seeks enmities” (Prov. 28). Nor can a person be without fault if he receives into communion another’s excommunicated person without permission from the one by whom he is known to have been deprived of communion; since the canons command that one excommunicated by some persons should not be received by others while those by whom he was deprived of communion remain alive.

And you inflict insult upon us not only in these matters, but also by dissolving our councils and not permitting them to stand as valid. For Athanasius of Alexandria, Paul of Constantinople, Marcellus of Ancyra, Asclepius of Gaza, and Lucian [Note: [Col. 0978D] (1) Athanasius, in 335 at Tyre; Marcellus, in 336 at the synod of Constantinople; Paul, in 340. Correct: Asclepas and Lucius, concerning whom see Athanasius, Sozomen, Socrates, Theodoret.] of Hadrianopolis have been condemned by us, and especially by the bishops of the entire East, [Col. 0978A] for definite crimes, concerning which accusations have been filed against them among us. We do not fail, through the present bearers of this letter, to make all these matters known to your holiness by a precise report.

When you have learned these things, if you choose to agree with our decisions rather than with their schemes, and to establish bishops appointed in place of the condemned (Tripartite History IV.16), we wish to have peace and communion with you. But if you act otherwise and judge that you ought to agree with them more than with us, we shall act contrariwise, and henceforth we do not wish either to assemble with you, obey you, or favor you and yours; but we shall endeavor, by ourselves, to do whatever we choose as better.

For there is no adult in this part of the world who does not know the designs of the aforesaid deceivers. Because of them many evils have been committed, many councils held in diverse and difficult times, many seditions and many intrigues (variant: “deceptions”), and many reproaches inflicted upon us [Col. 0978B] [Note: [Col. 0978D] (2) Observe how they acknowledge the primacy of the Roman pontiff.], besides many other things too numerous to recount. For if you choose to agree with them, it is evident that you wish to destroy us, rather than cherish us as a father cherishes sons.

For both their fellow citizens and their priests say and affirm that you wish to support these men as murderers (Athanasius, *Apology* II and *To the Solitaries*; Hilary, *Fragments*), destroyers of sacred temples, violators of virgins, burners of sacred books, plunderers of sacred vessels and other sacred ministries, [Col. 0978C] neglecters of duties, faithless toward emperors, betrayers of their people and country, and producers of the greatest discord among priests, because they had introduced into the teaching of faith the term “consubstantiality,” which is not found written.

Why need more be listed, when, because of them, as we and all inhabitants of this region know, so great a slaughter of men was perpetrated that more than a thousand people were struck down? What else is it to favor such persons than to consent to their crimes, when sacred Scripture forbids this, saying: “Not only those who do such things are held guilty, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. 1)? You must resist such persons with all your strength, lest you be entangled in their sins; and you must not receive their excommunication. Cast such persons far away from you, lest, because of the violence of such [Col. 0978D] persons, weak souls and an ignorant people perish through sacrilegious dissension.

[Col. 0979A] Therefore you ought (Martin I, Second Lateran Council) to resist the wicked rightly. Hence, if you neglect to overthrow the perverse, it is clear that you protect their error. Nor is anyone free from the suspicion of a hidden partnership who ceases to oppose manifest (variant: “manifestly committed”) crimes (Felix III, in the letter to Acacius). It is fitting that you sharpen your tongue to rebuke their insolence, and drive them from you as poisonous persons, lest you and yours be wounded in some way by their poison.

Therefore (the same Martin), the complaints brought against them suffice for us, because time would fail us if, as the Apostle says, we wished to set forth all the complaints offered against them by every opponent; especially since [Col. 0979B] the matters stated above suffice for us. Nor is it necessary for us to publish their evils again, since they reveal themselves, and especially since all easterners are witnesses concerning their evils. For “by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matt. 18); how much more by the multitude of so many priests and peoples, abbots and monks, who daily cry aloud to us, in writing and without writing, against the perversity of these men?

We indeed waited for them a long time in great patience, that they might produce grapes; but they did the opposite and produced wild grapes. You therefore must no longer neglect or delay concerning such persons, lest—God forbid—you be subjected (variant: “subdued”) to their aforementioned crimes by irrationally appointing them bishops. For unless they are quickly corrected, according to the protest of the blessed Apostle, [Col. 0979C] through their hardness and impenitent heart they “store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2). They need correction, lest, while you lend them assent through temporal pleasure (St Gregory), and through their lies and inventions, they lose the eternal rewards which they could have obtained by true penitence.

Nor do we bring the aforesaid charges against Athanasius and his followers alone, but also [the charge] that he acted contrary to the rule which we had decreed: because he had received the priesthood not by decree of a common council of bishops (Tripartite History IV.9 and 16; X.17, from Socrates and Sozomen), but had entered the church by arrogating it to himself and had seated himself in the see, though it had long [Col. 0979D] [Note: [Col. 0979D] (1) Rather, only in the year 341: canon 12 of the Council of Antioch [Col. 0980D]. Julius testifies in the following epistle that this was a decree of heretics.] been decreed that no one should be restored by a smaller number [Col. 0980A] than the number by which he was known to have been deposed.

Further, because a disturbance arose at his arrival and very many died in sedition; and not only were these things done by him and on his account, but some persons said to have been struck by the aforesaid Athanasius have already been handed over to judges. These and countless other things have been shamelessly perpetrated by him and his followers; and, as we have heard, you have joined to communion, contrary to rule and to the insult of all easterners, those who were excommunicated.

Having therefore rendered the due office of greeting (Letter of the Africans to Pope Celestine I) for the honor of blessed Peter, we request that henceforth you do not so readily admit to your hearing persons coming from here, nor choose to receive any longer those excommunicated by us, lest you be found transgressors of the canons [Col. 0980B]; but rather, preserving fraternal love, do not allow this error in the future.

And the subscription: “May the Lord preserve your apostolate, praying for us, through a longer age, most blessed father” (Letter of Tarragona to Pope Hilary). Amen.

## LETTER II

*[Note: Col. 0980D (1): Spurious, no less than the two preceding letters.]*

OR RESCRIPT OF JULIUS I

*[Note: Col. 0979D: Rescript of Julius. This rescript of Julius agrees in part, but differs very greatly in most respects, from the reply-letter which Athanasius recites above, col. 883. Since both report that the Eusebians and Athanasius were summoned to the Roman council convened in 340; both further relate that Athanasius appeared on the appointed day while the Eusebians obstinately remained away; and both finally mention the letter written by them after the celebration of the Antiochene synod and after Gregory of Cappadocia was introduced in A.D. 342 amid the great and terrible slaughter of the Alexandrians—a letter described as proud, boastful, and contentious—both ought to be one and the same letter of Julius. There is no doubt that this one is faulty, corrupt, and compiled by someone from diverse materials (or rather, fabricated at will), whereas the one reproduced below from Athanasius is the genuine copy of Julius’s rescript to the eastern bishops. That this one is faulty and corrupt is plainly demonstrated by the consulship of Felicianus and Maximianus appended below at its end. For if it was written under those consuls, it must necessarily have been written at the beginning of Julius’s pontificate, in A.D. 337; and thus its references to the Roman synod convened and to the Alexandrian sedition cannot stand.]*

AGAINST THE EASTERNERS, ON BEHALF OF ATHANASIUS AND THE OTHERS.

*(Compare vol. II, col. 483.)*

I. On the summons of the eastern bishops before Julius, and on the restoration by him of bishops condemned by them.

II. That accused bishops should appeal to the apostolic see.

III. On the same matter.

IV. If anyone considers himself aggrieved by his own metropolitan.

V. On accusers, or accusations, not admitted by secular laws. [Col. 0980C]

VI. That no bishop may retain or ordain a member of another’s diocese, etc.

VII. If anyone has a dispute against a bishop or the administrators of the Church.

VIII. On bishops stripped of their possessions or driven from their sees.

IX. On accusers and witnesses.

X. If an accused or condemned bishop appeals to the apostolic see; and concerning those who take up arms against the Fathers or associate with enemies.

XI. On accusations against clerics.

XII. Which metropolitan sees are called primatial sees.

XIII. Who are infamous.

[Col. 0981A] XIV. On the cases of bishops.

XV. That those in error, those who depart from their profession, or those disobedient to the canons, may not be admitted as accusers.

XVI. On foreign tribunals.

XVII. That no one be summoned outside his province for judgment, or if anyone has suspect judges.

XVIII. That persons confessing concerning themselves are not to be believed regarding another’s crime.

XIX. On matters not to be judged when uncertain.

XX. On accusations against persons of greater age.

XXI. On a provincial synod to be reconsidered by the pope.

XXII. If anyone appeals to judges of greater authority.

XXIII. That a metropolitan is to do nothing without the counsel of the bishops, nor they without his, except insofar as their own dioceses are concerned.

[Col. 0981B] XXIV. That judges may not pronounce sentence against an absent person, and that an informer is not to be heard.

XXV. On accusations against clerics.

XXVI. On accused bishops.

XXVII. On the unjust condemnation of bishops.

XXVIII. Slanderers and supporters of enemies must be excluded from accusation; a superior must not be attacked by an inferior; no certain judgment is to be given in a doubtful matter; and on irregular judgments.

XXIX. Whether a bishop can be restored by a smaller number of bishops than had condemned him.

XXX. Whether bishops may flee because of persecution, and on the privileges of the apostolic see.

XXXI. How great caution is required in judging; and that no one is to be condemned before he has his accusers present [Col. 0981C] and has been granted opportunity to defend himself.

XXXII. The right of accusation is not to extend beyond the boundaries of a province.

XXXIII. Who ought not to be admitted to accusation.

XXXIV. That no one is bound by the sentence of a judge other than his own, and what such judges ought to be.

XXXV. On bishops stripped of their possessions or driven from their sees.

XXXVI. That excommunicated persons cannot accuse bishops, nor those who do not receive them into their accusation; and that a superior cannot be condemned or judged by an inferior.

Julius, bishop of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, to Eusebius, Theognis, Theodore, Berinthus *(read: Theodore of Perinthus)* [Col. 0981D], and the other eastern bishops.

You ought to have spoken in polished fashion, and not ironically, against the holy Roman and apostolic Church (Tripartite History III.7), since our Lord Jesus Christ himself addressed it fittingly, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16). For it possesses the power, granted it by a singular privilege, of opening and closing the gates of the heavenly kingdom for whom it wills. If you have not refused to disparage it—which has been consecrated by the Lord’s mouth and exalted from above *(variant: if you have not feared)*—it is no wonder that you do not cease at all to inflict injuries upon the brethren.

Therefore, those things which were turbulently [Col. 0982A] decreed in your council amid storm and disorder cannot now be passed over in silence.

*[Note: Col. 0982D (1): Tripartite History III.7, from Socrates and Sozomen: Constantine’s words in his letter to the Council of Tyre.]*

For it is apparent that truth has been suppressed by a certain tumultuous lack of discipline: since, without considering what pleases God, because of the quarrels which you have against your neighbors, you insist that our prayers (*vota*) are invincible. Yet divine providence must ensure that these things, once openly exposed, may be annulled *(variant: and that this contention, once openly exposed, may be annulled)*, and that whatever you assembled there accomplished without any grace, out of hatred or enmity, may be utterly rejected.

Accordingly, I wish all of you to hasten with all speed to show reverence for this holy see, so that you may personally demonstrate the integrity of the proceedings conducted among you. For I believe you do not doubt that Athanasius [Col. 0982B], a teacher of the sacred law, was proved to be a worshipper of the true faith not only by us, but also by the Nicene synod.

*[Note: Col. 0982D (2): From the same authorities, IV.2: words of the Emperor Constantine II to the Alexandrians. See also Theodoret, *History* II.2, and Athanasius, *Apology* 2.]*

After the death of Alexander, that remarkable old man who had overthrown Arius’s blasphemies, he assumed the episcopate of the Alexandrian Church five months after the Nicene council. Weaving many lies and wholly groundless calumnies against him and his party, and fashioning them as though they were true accusations, you represented to us that he was the cause and head of many evils; and in your writings you declared him to be a disturber not only in Egypt, but also in Palestine, Phoenicia, and neighboring peoples.

For this reason, following ecclesiastical rule, we summoned you and them regularly to judgment at Rome on an appointed day, by letters and envoys—not with a short interval of time [Col. 0982C], so that no excuse might find place.

*[Note: Col. 0982D (3): Theodoret II.3, translated by Epiphanius, friend of Cassiodorus.]*

They accepted the summons and came on the appointed day; but you delayed coming, lest you should be caught in your lies and your calumny exposed. Nor were you content with these machinations alone: seeing the sheep deprived of their shepherds, you set wolves over them in place of shepherds.

You should therefore have come to the regular summons, in order to give a true account concerning these matters and your other presumptions. For truth would come forth, if falsehood displeased you (Celestine, Letter 1 to the Gauls); and no one doubts that the guilty person thus evades judgment (Boniface, Letter 2 to the Gauls), whereas the innocent seeks it in order to be acquitted. Nor is he free from suspicion who maliciously alleges that another has said false things, when he himself, summoned to judgment to prove what he has charged, has delayed coming.

I would rather that you had come to the aforementioned canonical summons, in order to give account before the universal [Col. 0982D] council.

*[Note: Col. 0982D (4): There were about fifty, according to Athanasius, *Apology* 2.]*

[Col. 0983A] You should have explained why you held a synod at Antioch to overthrow the condition of the churches and brethren (Tripartite History IV.9; Socrates II.8) and to destroy the great Nicene council; or why, without consulting us, you summoned bishops to it—although neither Maximus of Jerusalem came, nor was our delegation present, and although the canons of the Nicene synod prescribe (Tripartite History IV.19) that councils must by no means be held, nor bishops condemned, apart from the judgment of the Roman pontiff. Or why did you install other, adulterous bishops in place of the aforementioned brethren before their case had been canonically examined by us or our envoys and had received its proper conclusion?

Those who regularly came to the said summons, seeing that you withdrew from the aforementioned calumnies, report many grievous and tearful matters against you, accusing you and saying that they have suffered many unbearable things from you. Since you flee from appearing, while they persist [Col. 0983B] in the true account and protest against your calumnies—and the bishops of Egypt also attest in letters sent to us (Tripartite History IV.19; Socrates II.17) that the charges contrived against Athanasius and his followers are false, and that all the Arian contrivances *(perhaps: “machinations”)* are full of blasphemies and such fabrications—it is clear (Tripartite History IV.15, from Sozomen III.7) that they are blameless and you guilty. For if you trusted in genuine innocence, you would not in any way have withdrawn from the said canonical summons, which was announced not suddenly but with ample time; rather, setting aside every defense, you would have hastened to come without delay and give account.

After these events, I wrote to you (Tripartite History IV.9) and to all who had assembled at Antioch against apostolic and canonical rule without consulting us [Col. 0983C], reproving you first for the injuries in your letter, and then asking why you had summoned Athanasius and his followers to your council. The canons command, namely, that nothing be decided apart from the Roman pontiff, to whom these and greater affairs of the churches have been entrusted by the Lord himself and by all the brethren of all councils through a special privilege, as has already been said.

But since you fled and, though summoned so often to the council, refused to appear; and since they persisted in their protest and just cause; and since, recognizing your crimes and examining their just case, we found all of them obedient to the Nicene council and to our apostolic commands, it seemed good to us and to the entire council—being instructed by divine precepts and apostolic admonitions [Col. 0983D] (St Leo, Letter 4), and being obliged to keep unwearied watch over the condition of all churches—that, if anything anywhere were found liable to censure, we should promptly recall it from the unskilfulness of ignorance or the usurpation of presumption.

### I

Having considered and distinguished these matters in this way, and bearing the care of all (Tripartite History IV.15), we received them into communion because of the dignity of our see, together with each of their people [Col. 0984A], and, by the authority of this holy see, restored to each of them his own church together with its possessions. For because of the snares of wicked persons, this holy see has always had—and, with the Lord’s help, will have forever—the right, instituted by the Lord himself and confirmed through every council by the holy apostles and their successors, to do this.

Hence, whoever knows himself to be set over others should not take it badly that someone is set over him (St Leo, Letter 84); rather, he too should gladly render the obedience which he requires from others. Therefore I write in rebuke to you (Tripartite History, same passage), because you treated without justice men who were blameless and not examined by us, driving them from their churches after depriving them of communion; and because, inflicting injury upon ecclesiastical discipline and by no means observing the decree of the Nicene council, you did not fear to act with such disorder [Col. 0984B].

Since you long ago refused to come when summoned, we now again summon you regularly by letters and envoys for a fixed day, namely the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October], so that before you we may show that we rendered a just sentence concerning them, and that henceforth we shall not tolerate such acts. For it is decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that whoever seizes what belongs to another shall not go unpunished but shall restore it with increase. Thus it is written in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” *(Vulgate: “If I have defrauded anyone”)* (Luke 19). The Law also provides: “Cursed is everyone who removes the boundary-mark of his neighbor.” And all the people shall say: “Amen” (Deut. 27).

Why, then, I wonder that you have been so bold and have acted so shamelessly, invading the boundaries and rights of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 0984C]. For it belonged to his jurisdiction, as was demonstrated a little above, that without the authority of his holy see no one ought to hold councils, summon bishops to a synod, condemn them, drive them from their own sees, or ordain others in their places (Socrates and Sozomen, cited above). Yet you did not fear to violate all these things.

What else, then, is such presumption except transgressing the decrees of the apostles and their successors and not fearing to incur the curse set forth above in the Law—a curse which all the people confirmed with one voice and harmonious response by “Amen,” that is, “let it be”? For, as I think, bound by such cords of transgression, you avoided our examination lest your misdeeds should be exposed, and delayed coming to the aforementioned [Col. 0984D] summons.

Certainly, it is manifest that those confess their own crime who, repeatedly summoned, delay coming without unavoidable cause and do not avail themselves of the opportunity to clear themselves (Boniface, Letter 2). For if you trusted your own assertions, you would not have delayed to prove them face to face (Tripartite History IV.24, from Theodoret II.8, reporting the synodical letter of the Council of Sardica). Foreseeing in spirit such plotters, the holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea established laws (Tripartite History IV.14, from Socrates I.22), which we call canons, so that upright persons might not easily be condemned by the wicked. We judged that certain of their decisions should be inserted here, so that our letter might be strengthened by the authority of such great Fathers and that eastern bishops, or bishops of other regions, hearing these things, may not fall into so great a pit and incur the condemnation decreed by the Fathers.

The following chapters, namely 18, 19, 21, 23, 26, 27, 28, 33, 41, 45, 47, 49 *(variant: 48)*, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 63, and 66 *(variant: 67)*, follow from the aforementioned Council of Nicaea.

*[Note: Col. 0983D (1): Julius’s letter which St Athanasius recites in *Apology* 2. (2): That these canons are spurious is shown, according to Contius, even by the fact that no one—not even Gratian himself—dared cite them.]* [Col. 0985A]

### II
