That all bishops who are assailed or accused in certain more serious cases may, whenever necessary, freely appeal to the apostolic see (2, question 6, *All Bishops*) and flee to it as to a mother, that they may be piously supported, defended, and freed by it—as has always been the case (Council of Sardica, canon 7). Ancient authority of the apostles and their successors and of the canons has reserved to its disposition all major ecclesiastical cases and the judgments of bishops. For bishops who act otherwise toward their brethren than the pope of that see judges proper are blameworthy. [Col. 0985B]

### III

It has seemed good (3, question 6, *Accused*, Council) that a bishop accused or judged by fellow-provincial bishops in any case may freely appeal and approach the pontiff of the apostolic see, who shall arrange for his case to be reconsidered either personally or through his representatives (Sardica, canons 4, 5, and 17). While the pontiff hears his case in a renewed judgment, no other bishop is to be installed or ordained in his place. For although fellow-provincial bishops may investigate the case of an accused bishop, it is nevertheless not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff [Col. 0985C], since the Lord said to the blessed apostle Peter—and to no one other than him—“Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16).

### IV

If anyone considers himself aggrieved by his own metropolitan (2, question 6, *If Anyone Considers*; Council of Chalcedon, canons 9 and 17; Hadrian, cols. 6, 18, 26), he is to be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pope of the universal apostolic Church.

### V

We unanimously exclude accusers and accusations (3, question 5, *Accusers*) which secular laws do not admit (Hadrian II, from canon 2 [Col. 0985D] of the Seventh Council of Carthage). Nor may impiety enter into strict proof, when the judgment’s decision in election is right (Ennodius, Letter 18, book I).

### VI

No bishop may presume to retain, ordain, or judge a parishioner of another bishop without that bishop’s consent (Hadrian 16), while apostolic authority is preserved in all matters. For just as his ordination will be invalid, so also will his judgment be; since we hold that no one is bound by the judgment of a judge other than his own (Annianus, on Constitution I, title 16, book IV of the Theodosian Code). For one who could not ordain him cannot in any way judge him.

### VII

[Col. 0986A]

If anyone believes that he has a personal dispute with a bishop or with the administrators of the Church (2, question 7, *If Anyone Has*; and in the Decretals of Pope Alexander), he should not first approach judges, but should have recourse to them in a spirit of charity (Hadrian II, from canon 17 of the Fifth Council of Orléans), so that, admonished by familiar conversation, they may heal the matters brought forward as a complaint. If he acts otherwise, let him be deprived of communion.

### VIII

Henceforth no pontiff may presume to excommunicate or judge a bishop stripped of his possessions or driven from his see (2, question 2, *No One Can Be Summoned*), because there is no legal warrant by which a person already stripped naked can be further despoiled (from the Fifth Roman Synod under Symmachus).

### IX

[Col. 0986B]

By the same tenor we decree that no credence be given to an accuser (Annianus on Constitutions IX and XIII, title 39, book XI of the Theodosian Code) who presents a case while his adversary is absent, before a hearing of both parties; nor are accusers or witnesses who are unsuitable to be accepted.

### X

It has seemed good (6, question 1, *A Sacred Person Who*) that, if an accused or condemned bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff (Hadrian 21, from canon 7 of Sardica), whatever that pontiff judges justly is to be established. We judge infamous all who take up arms against the Fathers (from Proclus to Domnus); nor are those who associate with enemies (sentence 1, title 15, book V of Paulus) to be received for accusation or testimony.

### XI

[Col. 0986C]

It has seemed good that in accusations against clerics the character, faith, life, and conduct of those making blasphemous allegations should always first be examined (Hadrian 4). For faith must precede all a person’s actions, because one doubtful in faith is unbelieving (Sayings of Sixtus 5 and 156). They are not to be believed at all, because they do not know fidelity to truth and do not live a life of upright conduct; for such people readily and indiscriminately tear apart and accuse those living rightly and piously. Therefore their suspicion must first be investigated and corrected; nor are suspect accusers, or persons coming forth from the household of enemies (sentence 1, title 15, book V of the same Paulus), to be believed.

### XII

[Col. 0986D]

No metropolitan churches or primatial sees are to be recognized except those which were primatial first and, after Christ’s coming, deserved to hold primacy by apostolic and synodal authority. The others, however, are not to be called primatial sees but metropolitan sees; and their bishops are to bear the title not of primates (Hadrian 23), but either of metropolitans or archbishops.

### XIII

We judge infamous all who violate their own law or the Christian law, or who set aside canonical authority.

### XIV

Saving in all respects the privilege of the Roman Church [Col. 0987A], no metropolitan may hear the cases of any persons without the attendance of all his fellow-provincial bishops (Hadrian 34, from Apostolic Canon 35, translated by Dionysius Exiguus); for the proceedings shall be invalid, and indeed he shall answer in synod for the act.

### XV

We cannot receive one allied with others’ errors (3, question 4, *Allied with Others’ Errors*), one departing from the path of his profession, or one disobedient to the sacred canons; nor do we permit such a person to attack those who rightly believe or obey the decrees of the holy Fathers.

### XVI

We prohibit foreign tribunals by a general enactment (3, question 7, *Foreign Tribunals*), because it is unworthy that persons should be judged by outsiders when they ought to have as judges fellow-provincials and persons chosen by themselves [Col. 0987B] (Hadrian 17, from the Theodosian Code).

### XVII

Saving the authority of the apostolic Church (Hadrian 18), no bishop is to be summoned outside his province for judgment. Rather, once he has been canonically summoned *(perhaps: “once he has been summoned”)*, he is to be heard at a place suitable for all, at the time of a synod, by all the bishops of his province, who must pronounce upon him a unanimous and canonical sentence. For if this is granted to lesser persons, clerics as well as laypeople, how much more ought it to be observed with regard to bishops? If, however, he regards the metropolitan or the judges as suspect, or perceives them as hostile, he is to be judged before the primates of the diocese or before the pontiffs of the Roman see.

### XVIII

[Col. 0987C]

No one can be believed, when confessing concerning himself, regarding another’s crime (15, question 3, *No One*; Ennodius, Letter 4, book I), because his confession—and confession concerning any matter—is dangerous (Hadrian 64, from Annianus; in the Decretals of Pope Sixtus II) and must not be admitted against anyone.

### XIX

No pontiff may ever presume to judge uncertain matters. Even if they are true (Isidore II, Synod 16), they are not to be believed unless established by manifest indications, proved by manifest judgment, and made public in judicial order.

### XX

Accusations against persons of greater age (2, question 7, *Accusations*) are not to be brought through others, but only by those themselves who make the accusation [Col. 0987D] (Second Council of Carthage, canon 6), provided that they appear worthy and irreproachable and have demonstrated in public records (First Council of Arles, canon 13) that they are free from every suspicion and enmity and lead an irreproachable life of faith and conduct.

### XXI

A provincial synod is to be reconsidered through the representatives of the bishop of Rome (Hadrian 39), if he decrees it.

### XXII

It has seemed good that, whenever appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where there is greater authority, a hearing is not to be denied (also in the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 10; 2, question 6, *It Has Seemed Good That, Whenever*).

### XXIII

[Col. 0988A]

If a metropolitan bishop, apart from what pertains solely to his own diocese, attempts to do anything without the counsel and consent of all fellow-provincial bishops (Hadrian 43, from Apostolic Canon 35), he shall be liable to loss of his rank, and whatever he has done shall be regarded as invalid and void. Whatever must be done or arranged concerning the cases of fellow-provincial bishops and the needs of their churches, clerics, and laypeople is to be done with the full consent of the fellow-provincial pontiffs—not in any haughty spirit of domination, but through the humblest and concordant administration, as the Lord says: “I came not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20); and elsewhere: “Whoever is greatest among you shall be your servant” (Mark 10), and the rest.

Likewise, fellow-provincial [Col. 0988B] bishops themselves are to act with his counsel, except insofar as their own dioceses are concerned (Antioch, canon 9; Ephesus, act 6; Chalcedon, canon 12), according to the enactments of the holy Fathers, so that the holy Trinity may be glorified harmoniously, with one voice and one mind, forever.

### XXIV

Let judges of the Church beware (3, question 9, *Let Judges Beware*) lest they pronounce sentence while the person whose case is under discussion is absent (Hadrian 49, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 10), for it shall be invalid. Indeed, they shall render account in synod for their action; and afterwards, like the calumny of an informer, not even their voice is to be heard (from Annianus and the Theodosian Code). For no one can know a debtor more fully than the one who bears his injury and wickedness.

### XXV

[Col. 0988C]

If anyone believes that a cleric should be accused of any crimes whatever (3, question 6, *If Anyone, a Cleric*), he must pursue his action in the province where the accused person resides (Hadrian 8). Nor may the accuser imagine that the accused should be dragged elsewhere or farther away for judgment. If the accused person considers the judges suspect, he may appeal.

### XXVI

When primates investigate an accused bishop, they shall not pronounce a sentence of condemnation (Hadrian 55) before, relying on apostolic authority, either the accused confesses himself guilty or he is regularly convicted by innocent witnesses canonically examined.

### XXVII

[Col. 0988D]

We decree *(or: judge)* (3, question 6, *Invalid*) that an unjust condemnation of bishops is invalid and must therefore be reconsidered by a synod (Hadrian 54), so that aid may be given in every case and in all things to those oppressed.

### XXVIII

We exclude from episcopal accusation slanderers (3, question 4, *Slanderers Also*; 2, question 7, *Any of the Greater*), who must be uprooted by divine authority, and supporters of enemies. Likewise, no superior is to be attacked or ruined by accusations of inferiors; no judgment is to be given in a doubtful matter (St Gregory, Letter 30, book VIII, and Letter 52, book XI); and no judgment is to stand unless it has been conducted in due order.

### XXIX

[Col. 0989A]

We do not insert more on these points here (see Hincmar, book LV, chapter 20), lest we seem to render the aforementioned synod empty or worthless, or lest the lengthy letter create weariness for readers and hearers. But if anyone wishes to know fuller and more abundant material on these matters, he will be able to find in the sacred archive of the see of our Church both these matters and those we have stated. Yet the Deity is witness that I have spoken (Ennodius, book I, Letter 20).

Concerning the recovery of his see, priesthood, and honor, which you said Athanasius had assumed without a decree of a council, we have not found matters as you slanderously alleged. Rather, by the counsel and decree of certain bishops he recovered the priesthood which he had unjustly lost and sat again in his see (Tripartite History X.17, from Socrates, Sozomen, etc.). What you wrote [Col. 0989B]—that he could not be restored by a smaller number of bishops than had deposed him—is not so; nor is this the rule of the orthodox bishops of the holy Church. Rather, it is an invention of the Arians, your associates, devised for the destruction of orthodox bishops.

For, as truthful witnesses have reported to us, when you assembled at Antioch for the condemnation of the faith concerning consubstantiality, out of hatred for the aforementioned Athanasius you produced this rule. It has no force and cannot have any, because that council was neither conducted by orthodox bishops nor attended by a delegation of the Roman Church; and the canons prescribe that councils must not be held without its authority (Tripartite History IV.9 and 19). No council which is not supported by its authority is, or ever shall be, valid. [Col. 0989C]

### XXX

Accordingly, you do not act well *(variant: rightly)* in reproaching Athanasius for his flight.

*[Note: Col. 0989D (1): He fled only in the year 342, driven out by Gregory; see his *Apology* 2 and Tripartite History VI.22.]*

The Lord himself gave us this command: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10). The Lord himself also showed us an example in his own person *(variant: showed)*: when the Pharisees took counsel against him in order to kill him, “Jesus, knowing this, departed from there” (Matt. 12). Elsewhere: “The Jews took stones to cast at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple” (John 8); and, “passing through their midst, he went away and thus departed” (Luke 4).

The disciples also withdrew for fear of the Jews, concealing themselves. Paul likewise (2 Cor. 11) [Col. 0989D], sought at Damascus by the ruler of that people, was lowered from the wall in a basket and escaped the hand of his pursuer. And very many, indeed innumerable, other saints are recorded to have fled, both in the Old Testament and in the New.

If, then, you reproach those who flee for their flight, blush rather at persecuting and cease your plots; then those who flee will immediately cease. For whether you kill them, death always cries out against you; or whether you impose exile upon them again, you are known everywhere to send forth against yourselves the memory of evil, while they benefit themselves by enduring. Thus the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10).

[Col. 0990A] We have known many to be unjustly deposed by most wicked machinations. Therefore I *(variant: for me)*, to whom the care of the universal Church has been entrusted in the place of the prince of the apostles, must take the greatest care, with the assistance of that highest apostle, that such things may not happen henceforth. For this reason the aforesaid privileges were specially granted to this holy see (2, question 6, *For This Reason to This Holy See*)—both concerning the calling of councils, judgments, and restorations of bishops, and concerning the supreme affairs of the churches—that all oppressed persons may receive help from it and those unjustly condemned may receive restoration; and that such acts may not be presumed by the wicked without punishment nor performed without condemnation [Col. 0990B] *(variant: their own condemnation)* (Third Roman Council under Symmachus).

Therefore you did not act rightly in slandering the aforementioned brethren, since the Lord says: “You shall not bring a false accusation against your neighbor, nor oppress him by force” (Lev. 19). You did not act rightly in holding a council without consulting us, summoning them to the council, and presuming to condemn them, although the canons, as stated above, command (Tripartite History IV.9) that none of these things be done without the authority of this holy see. You did not act rightly in delaying to come after we had regularly summoned you to the council. You did not act rightly in failing to come and give account against them, so that your judgment regarding them might either be proved right or shown wrong; nor did you send a rational explanation of why you refused these things.

When all this has been weighed, it is manifest that you stand guilty [Col. 0990C] and they remain innocent; that you have rightly been excommunicated and they justly freed. The Lord did not will his ministers to be treated so lightly as you treat them, or to be condemned by you, but—as has been said—to be reserved either for judgment by this holy see, to which they are entrusted, or for his own judgment. For he says: “Whoever grieves you grieves me” (Luke 10). “Whoever commits injustice against you will receive what he has done unjustly” (Col. 3). The Gospel sufficiently explains what punishment awaits those who cause the Lord’s disciples to stumble, where it speaks concerning those who cause disciples to stumble.

That they must not be condemned by you but either be reserved, as stated above, for this holy see or for himself, he plainly provides an example when he expelled from the temple, not through another but by himself, the priests who sinned, whose place bishops now hold in the holy Church, as they bought and sold; overturned with his own scourge the tables of the money-changers; and expelled them from the temple (Matt. 21; Mark 2; Luke 19; John 2). Elsewhere he says: “God stands in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Ps. 81 [82]), and other such and similar things. Elsewhere the same one says: “Do not judge, that you may not be judged; do not condemn, that you may not be condemned” (Matt. 7). “For with the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged” (Luke 6). [Col. 0990D]

### XXXI

Therefore no one should rashly, as you do, presume to spew forth his own wickedness (30, question 5, *The Work of a Judge*; and in the Decretals of Eleutherius); rather, whoever judges [Col. 0991A] ought to investigate everything.

*[Note: Col. 0991D (1): Pope Hadrian, 24, from Constitution I, title 18, law II of the Theodosian Code, with the interpretation of Anianus; also in Ivo’s *Decretum*, book IV.]*

He must examine the order of events through a full inquiry and must by no means presume to render judgment upon matters not entrusted to him; he must afford opportunity for questioning, presenting, and adding material, so that the parties’ pleadings may there be fully delimited. Nor should he wish to anticipate the litigants with his own judgment until, all things having been completed, they have nothing further to advance in the controversy. No one should be judged or condemned before he has his accusers present and is granted ample opportunity to defend himself and wash away the charges (Hadrian XX).

### XXXII

Likewise, it was decreed in the aforesaid synod (2, question 6, *Beyond the Provinces*) that the right of accusation may not proceed beyond the boundaries of a province [Col. 0991B] (Hadrian X, from the Theodosian Code), unless appeal has been made to this apostolic see, to which all who wish must be free to come and resort without any impediment imposed by certain persons in the pursuit of their case.

### XXXIII

Likewise, in the aforementioned synod (3, question 5, *Likewise in the Aforesaid*) it was decreed that suspect, infamous, criminal, flattering [Col. 0991D] *(gratiosi: “flatterers,” as the gloss on the cited chapter explains)*, calumniating, related, or readily litigious persons are not to be admitted as accusers (Hadrian XV), but only persons free from every suspicion; for the Lord willed his pillars to stand firm and not be shaken by just anyone.

### XXXIV
Likewise, the aforesaid synod decreed that no one should be bound by a sentence pronounced except by his own judge. Nor ought judges to be any others [Col. 0991C] (1, question 1, *Judices autem alii*) than those whom the person accused has himself chosen [Note: [Col. 0991D] (3) Hadrian 37, from the Theodosian Code, book IV, title 16, constitution 2, in Gregory, epistle 56 of book XI.], or whom this holy see, or its primates by the authority of this holy see, has delegated with his consent. Yet from these and other provisions established both in this holy see and by the apostles and their successors, you granted nothing to the aforesaid bishops; rather, employing force against them and unjustly condemning them (as was mentioned above), you expelled some while absent—an act hostile to the whole Christian religion. In these matters it is apparent—and certainly hidden from none of the wise—that you neither preserved the Lord’s rights nor those of this holy mother and apostolic Church, which, as stated above, wished them to be reserved for its own judgment or for that of this see, lest they be condemned or expelled by men as depraved as yourselves; and that in all these things [Col. 0991D] you are fools and transgressors of the Gospels and canons.

XXXV.

Nor, in your transgression, were you content with these things (2, question 2, *Nullus potest convocari*). Rather, after first expelling them and stripping them of their property, you purported to summon and condemn them; although no one can regularly be summoned or judged before he has been regularly restored and [Col. 0992A] all his possessions have been restored to him in their fullest integrity according to the laws (Third Roman Council under Symmachus). For in the often-mentioned holy synod it was unanimously decreed and confirmed by apostolic authority that, if any bishop (2, question 2, *Si episcopus suis fuerit*; and, decisively, in the decretal of Pope Eusebius) has been despoiled of his possessions and assailed by an accusation, the holy purpose requires and befits, by ordinance of the pontiffs, that the action be set aside at the outset, so that everything which he had lost through the allegations of his enemies may first be lawfully restored to his control by an honorable council; that the prelate be regularly restored first to his former condition; and that he himself, once his affairs have been arranged and set in order, then appear at the appropriate time to answer the case and, if this seems just, respond to the accusations of his accusers.

Why, therefore, did you overstep the boundaries of the Fathers, judging and condemning those whom you ought not to have judged? Why did you judge those whom you had not regularly found guilty? You did not observe (Pope Anastasius II, in his letter to Emperor Anastasius, ch. 2) what is written in the Book of Kings: “God does not see as man sees; for man sees the face, but God sees the heart” (1 Kings 16). And in Chronicles: “God searches all hearts and knows every thought” (2 Chronicles 28). And elsewhere it is written: “He whom God has reserved for His own judgment cannot be condemned by human examination” (Hadrian, ch. 55). All these matters must be guarded against with the greatest care, and an accusation against bishops is not lightly to be received; for the Lord says: “You shall not accept a lying report” (Exod. 23). And the Apostle says: “An accusation against an elder is not to be received except [Col. 0992C] upon two or three suitable witnesses” (1 Tim. 5). If these precautions must be observed in the case of presbyters or other faithful persons, how much more in the case of bishops?

Since these matters are known, it is clear (St Leo, epistle 84, ch. 1) that you wish to exercise lordship rather than to take counsel for, or support, your brethren: for honor swells into pride, and what was provided for concord tends toward injury. For it would have been fitting for you, in accordance with the aforesaid rules, if they had done anything contrary to their order, to report it to us and await what we might reply to your consultations—so much so that, even if they had committed something serious and intolerable, our judgment should have been awaited. Nor should you have decided anything beforehand or otherwise than what you had learned to be pleasing to us, so that you might depart from the established rules neither through negligence nor presumption. Let presumption of this kind cease, our authority having been suppressed (Boniface, [Col. 0992D] epistle 3); let harms of this kind be avoided. For we cannot patiently endure such contrivances, since it is fitting that we be diligent guardians of paternal enactments. Rightly indeed (St Celestine, epistle 1) the matter concerns us if by silence we give support to error.

XXXVI.

Moreover, in the aforesaid holy Synod of Nicaea it was decreed (1, question 7, *In sancta Nicaena*) that no person under anathema should be received in an accusation against us; nor should those who refuse to receive us in their complaint or accusation be received, since we know that we have been appointed by the Lord over them, not they over us. And just as (Gelasius, *On the Bond of Anathema*) [Col. 0993A] a greater person cannot be judged by a lesser, so neither can he be bound; for everything that is great is rare (Zosimus, ch. 1, epistle 1). We bear the burdens of all who are burdened (Siricius, epistle 1); indeed, blessed Apostle Peter bears these burdens in us, whose office of representation we discharge and by whose rule we are instructed, so that, [Col. 0994A] supported by his aid, we may be protected from all adversities now and forever.

Given on the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Felicianus and [Note: [Col. 0994A] (1) “Titianus” should be corrected; thus the year is 237, which makes the fabricator’s fraud evident.] Maximianus, most illustrious men.

A.D. 362–372—C. F. MARIUS VICTORINUS AND CANDIDUS THE ARIAN.

(Galland, *Bibliotheca*, pp. VII–IX, 133, 199; Mai, *Collection*, vol. III, part II, pp. 1–163.)

[Col. 0993]

PROLEGOMENA.

[Col. 0993]

[Col. 0993B]

NOTICE CONCERNING VICTORINUS THE AFRICAN.

I. C. Fabius Marius Victorinus, a man of clarissimate rank, African by birth, according to the testimony of St Jerome [Note: [Col. 0993D] (1) Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 101.], taught rhetoric at Rome under Emperor Constantius and, in extreme old age, embraced the faith of Christ. This seems to have occurred not long before A.D. 362, when Julian the Apostate held power. For St Augustine, addressing God, says the following concerning Victorinus [Note: [Col. 0993D] (2) Augustine, *Confessions*, book VIII, ch. 5, no. 10.]:

> “In the time of Emperor Julian, Christians were forbidden by an enacted law to teach literature and rhetoric. Victorinus embraced that law and preferred to abandon his school of eloquence rather than Thy word, by which Thou makest the tongues of infants eloquent.”

That he attained such distinction through the great praise of his eloquence and devotion to learning [Col. 0993C] as to deserve a statue in Trajan’s Forum is attested by the greatest Doctor [Note: [Col. 0993D] (3) Jerome, *Chronicle*, at year 2370.]. On this matter it is better to hear Augustine again addressing God [Note: [Col. 0993D] (4) Augustine, cited work, ch. 2, nos. 3 and 4.]:

> “That most learned old man, most skilled in all the liberal disciplines—for he had read, judged, and elucidated so many philosophers—a teacher of many noble senators, who, on account of the distinction of his eminent teaching, had deserved and received a statue in the Roman forum, was, even to that age, a worshipper of idols. . . . Yet he was not ashamed to become a child of Thy Christ and an infant at Thy font, bending his neck beneath the yoke of humility and subduing his brow to the reproach of the cross.”

After inserting some intervening remarks, the holy Doctor adds: “He read Holy Scripture and investigated and searched out all Christian writings with the greatest zeal.” Finally compelled by this sacred reading, [Col. 0993D] he gave his name to Christ. Consequently, the words of St Jerome should be understood more mildly when he says [Note: [Col. 0993D] (5) Jerome, preface to the commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians.] that Victorinus, occupied with the learning of secular literature, was wholly ignorant of the Holy Scriptures.

II. How long this great man survived after embracing the faith, about A.D. [Col. 0994B] 360 or 361, is not sufficiently established for anything certain to be determined. Yet, if one considers the literary monuments that remain—writings both against the Manichaeans and against the Arians, as well as commentaries on the Apostle which St Jerome mentions and read [Note: [Col. 0994D] (1) Jerome, cited passages.] and which Sirmond testifies still lie hidden in a manuscript at Hérivaux [Note: [Col. 0994D] (2) Sirmond, *Works*, vol. I, p. 345, §5.]—one may reasonably infer that Victorinus, though converted to Christ in old age, did not fail either in strength or intellect, and thus lived for some considerable time after A.D. 360 or the following year, diligently applying himself to learning Christian doctrines and writing so many and such important works for faith and religion.

I am led especially to this conclusion because St Jerome himself, in composing his apology for his books against Jovinian, addressed to Pammachius, writes as follows [Col. 0994C]: “If the same person is regarded as both virgin and wife, why could Victorinus not hear at Rome the reproachfulness of this expression?” I am certainly not unaware that this passage of Jerome was first altered by Martianay [Note: [Col. 0994D] (3) Martianay, edition of Jerome’s works, vol. IV, epistle XXX, p. 229.], who omitted Victorinus’s name and rewrote it thus: “Why could Rome not hear?” Vallarsi likewise followed the Benedictine editor [Note: [Col. 0994D] (4) Vallarsi, Jerome’s works, vol. I, epistle XLVIII, p. 210.]. Yet earlier editions—especially those of Erasmus [Note: [Col. 0994D] (5) Erasmus, Jerome’s works, vol. II, epistle L, p. 101a.] and Marianus Victorius [Note: [Col. 0994D] (6) Marianus Victorius, Jerome’s works, vol. II, epistle L, p. 388b.]—supported by not a few manuscripts, consistently preserve the reading just cited, which retains Victorinus’s name. It therefore does not seem that it should be lightly rejected. Once this ancient reading is accepted and confirmed by manuscript authority, Victorinus was still living [Col. 0994D] in A.D. 382. For scholars agree that Jovinian the heretic, whom Jerome attacks in that passage, [Col. 0995A] did not establish himself at Rome before that year. But in what subsequent year he ended his life is not clearly known.

III. Having thus discussed the year of Victorinus’s death, we must now infer from the literary monuments that survive how great the author’s learning was and what place he deserved to hold among writers of the Church. First, therefore, we have included in our collection of Victorinus’s ecclesiastical works two short treatises. One is entitled *To Justinus the Manichaean, against the Two Principles of the Manichaeans, and on the True Flesh of Christ*; the other, *On the Words of Scripture: “Evening Came and Morning Came: One Day.”* Sirmond published them at Paris in 1630, having copied them from the Hérivaux manuscript [Col. 0995B] and warning at the same time that he had devised the titles, which the manuscript treatises lacked.

Launoy doubts whether these two little works should be ascribed to Victorinus the African [Note: [Col. 0995D] (3) Launoy, *On Victorinus*, works, vol. II, part I, p. 648.], because Jerome does not mention them. Yet elsewhere we have sufficiently demonstrated how weak is an argument drawn from Jerome’s silence, by which certain writings are denied to this or that author [Note: [Col. 0995D] (4) Prolegomena to vol. I of the *Library of the Fathers*, ch. 1, §12, p. 22.]. Moreover, if the harsh, obscure, and involved style of these same treatises is compared with the author’s manner of writing in the other surviving works mentioned by Jerome, it is conclusively shown that their author was Victorinus, as Tillemont rightly argues [Note: [Col. 0995D] (5) Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. X, p. 405.].

Add to this what the author of the Appendix to Isidore [Col. 0995C] and Ildefonsus records [Note: [Col. 0995D] (6) Ch. 7, in Fabricius, *Ecclesiastical Library*, p. 69.]:

> “Bishop Victorinus also composed in verse two very brief treatises: one against the Manichaeans, who reject the God of the Old Testament and deny Christ’s true incarnation; the other against the Marcionites, who invent two principles, that is, two gods.”

Miraeus rightly remarks on this passage: “The two treatises against the Manichaeans and Marcionites mentioned here appear to be those of Victorinus the African rhetor, of whom Jerome speaks in ch. 101. Sirmond published at Paris in 1630 two treatises by this Victorinus. Yet García Loaysa thinks that the two little works mentioned in this chapter should be ascribed to Victorinus, the rhetorician of Marseilles, of whom Gennadius speaks in ch. 60. Be that as it may, the reader should note that our Victorinus is called bishop in this chapter—a title which neither Jerome gives to his Victorinus the African nor Gennadius to his Victorinus of Marseilles.” Thus Miraeus. Indeed, that anonymous author of the Appendix recorded without much care what he says there concerning Victorinus; yet it is sufficiently opportune, at least in some measure, for establishing the point which we chiefly intend to prove.

IV. The two works just mentioned are followed by another [Col. 0996A] of the same Victorinus, *On the Generation of the Divine Word*, or *Refutation of Candidus the Arian on the Same Subject*. Before it stands a treatise by that same Arian, Candidus, *On Divine Generation*, to which, as we have indicated, Victorinus opposed his own work. Jacob Ziegler first published both little works at Basel in 1548, together with his own conceptions on Genesis and Exodus [Note: [Col. 0996D] (1) Ziegler, *Conceptions on Genesis and Exodus*, pp. 232, 237.]. Thereafter Johann Herold included them in the same city, in 1555, among the *Orthodoxographa*. In the middle of the following century Andreas Rivinus incorporated them among the writings of the two Victorini. Finally Mabillon made these works public as though still unpublished [Note: [Col. 0996D] (2) Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. IV, p. 155, and p. 1 of the new edition.].

The most learned man published Victorinus’s work complete, but Candidus’s without its beginning and indeed greatly truncated. For the codex of St Ulrich at Augsburg, from which he copied both, was in no other condition and was also covered with very numerous errors. Yet Mabillon’s edition yielded this advantage: by collating Victorinus’s treatise with earlier editions, we have not only supplied quite a few passages and restored to integrity various readings once corrupted, but also—what is the chief point—where formerly very many things had been dislocated, wrongly transposed, and shamefully inverted, whether through scribes’ ignorance or, more probably, through the fault of badly assembled exemplars, we have arranged everything in its proper place from Mabillon’s edition, where all runs correctly. The reader will ascertain this from the notes appended below [Note: [Col. 0996D] (3) See below, p. 144, note 6; p. 145, note 12; p. 146, note 1.].

V. It is worth observing that, near the end of the aforesaid treatise *On the Generation of the Divine Word*, Victorinus mentions his books *On the Trinity against Arius*. For he says [Note: [Col. 0996D] (4) Victorinus, *On the Generation of the Divine Word*, §31, near end, below p. 150.]:

> “It has been sufficiently stated by us, I believe, in other books from whom the procession and descent come; the return of the promised Holy Spirit has been explained; and likewise the threefold unity and the one Trinity.”

After some intervening remarks, he says: “But concerning those three, another discussion is ours.” Yet I would not have you infer from this that Victorinus completed or even published the four books *On the Trinity* before this treatise, and therefore that the treatise of which we are speaking ought to be placed after those four books and that the author’s works have here been arranged in the wrong order. Victorinus himself removes this difficulty at the very beginning of Book I, where, addressing Candidus the Arian, he says [Note: [Col. 0996D] (5) Same author, book I *Against Arius*, §1, below p. 152.]:

> “In the first discourse of this work, O friend Candidus, you set forth and discussed many matters, including some stronger points among these; though they have been refuted as was fitting. Do you hear?”

He says, “In the first discourse.” By these words the author clearly indicates both Candidus’s treatise *On Divine Generation* and his own refutation of it. Accordingly, when Victorinus above says, “It has been sufficiently stated by us,” etc., he seems properly to mean that his four books were underway, though not yet completed.

[Col. 0997A] VI. We have therefore placed after the aforementioned treatises the four books *Against Arius*, written in dialectical fashion and very obscure, in Jerome’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0997D] (1) Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 101.], so that only learned persons understand them. They are prefaced by a short letter of Candidus addressed to Victorinus, in which that Arian inserted Arius’s letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, reproduced by Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0997D] (2) Epiphanius, *Heresies* 69, §6.], Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0997D] (3) Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, ch. 5.], and Nicephorus [Note: [Col. 0997D] (4) Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 9.]. It is surprising that learned men who assembled libraries of the ancient Fathers failed to recognize this: they prefaced Victorinus’s four books with the same letter, but made no distinction and attributed it to no certain author.

We learn from Victorinus himself that he requested this Arian letter from his friend Candidus, and for what purpose. For, addressing Candidus, he says [Col. 0997B] [Note: [Col. 0997D] (5) Victorinus, book I *Against Arius*, §1.]:

> “Although the matters you set forth and discussed, O friend Candidus, have been refuted as was fitting, yet we wished for this reason to hear these things from *their letters*: that, while we overcome these matters by every refutation, we may also overcome the others through the refutation of those men.”

It remains our duty to note that, in the title of these four books and that of the preceding *Refutation*, we followed the old editions, in which Victorinus is incorrectly called a man of consular rank; whereas the manuscript abbreviation V.C. must be understood as *vir clarissimus*, “most illustrious man,” and by no means as *consularis*, “a consular,” as Tillemont rightly observes [Note: [Col. 0997D] (6) Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. X, p. 401, note 1.]. We have accordingly corrected this both at the head of the collection of this author’s works and elsewhere.

Nor should we omit here the warning of Brasichellensis [Note: [Col. 0997D] (7) Brasichellensis, *Index of Expurgated Books*, vol. I, p. 121.]: namely, that these books must be read cautiously, since in them one finds certain statements somewhat harsh and insufficiently weighed against the Catholic rule; and that their author may, as Petavius says [Note: [Col. 0997D] (8) Petavius, *On the Trinity*, book I, ch. 5, pp. 30 and 103.], be called *skoteinos* (σκοτεινός, “obscure”) with no less right than that Heraclitus. Yet on this point I especially wish you to read what learned men wrote in defense of Marius Victorinus against Petavius’s criticism—the men who illustrated with learned dissertations the sermons of St Zeno, bishop of Verona [Note: [Col. 0997D] (9) Ballerini, on St Zeno, Dissertation II, ch. 1, §8, p. 85.].

Nevertheless, no one will deny that the printed exemplars are everywhere marred by errors, removable only through some older manuscript, such as the seven-hundred-year-old Clairmont manuscript mentioned by Simon [Note: [Col. 0997D] (10) Simon, *Critical Study of the Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. I, p. 64.]. In seeking to remedy this evil, the first publisher of these books placed several corrections in the margin [Col. 0997D]; we have added these in our customary manner at the foot of the page, together with a few of our own. On the more important passages of the New Testament cited by Victorinus, Johannes Mill will provide more, besides the Simon already cited [Col. 0998A] [Note: [Col. 0998D] (1) Mill, *Prolegomena to the Greek New Testament*, p. 74, no. 778.].

VII. We are instructed by Victorinus himself as to the time when the same books *Against Arius* were written. In them, speaking of the Council of Nicaea, he says [Note: [Col. 0998D] (2) Victorinus, book II *Against Arius*, §9, at end.]: “That council was approved by the father of our emperor, Constantine.” The author was therefore writing those books while Constantius was still in power; and above, from Jerome, we have learned that Victorinus still flourished as a pagan under that emperor. Victorinus also indicates another chronological point in the same place, where, again mentioning the Council of Nicaea, he says that it was held forty years before [Note: [Col. 0998D] (3) Same author, same work, book I, §28.]. Since that council was held in A.D. 325, the author was thus writing in A.D. 365, during the reign of Valentinian, if he calculated the years correctly [Col. 0998B].

Baronius carefully noted both passages of Victorinus. Speaking of the latter, he says [Note: [Col. 0998D] (4) Baronius, at the year 362, §301.]:

> “If anyone wishes to refer the number of forty years to an exact calculation, it must be said that Victorinus wrote those books only in the sixty-fifth year after three hundred, when that forty-year number from the said Council of Nicaea is completed. It therefore seems possible to understand that he expressed the number in this way not because, treating the matter incidentally, he wished to record an exact number of years, but because after the third decade of years the fourth was already running.”

Thus the eminent man. Gothofredus, however, judges otherwise [Note: [Col. 0998D] (5) Gothofredus, *Theodosian Code*, vol. VI, part I, p. 275, new edition; otherwise p. 251.]: he thinks that Victorinus’s words, “forty years before,” are so far from signifying a number short of, or less than, forty that they rather suggest a number beyond it. Tillemont makes some observations on this question [Note: [Col. 0998D] (6) Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. X, p. 799, note 4, on St Simplician.], but, unwilling to undertake the labor, did not consult the passage of Victorinus cited by Baronius. For he says: “For the first book on the Trinity, from which Baronius cites him, it is too long to seek those forty years there.”

The reader should further be informed that the sound reading “forty years before” occurs in Johannes Herold’s *Haereseologia* alone [Note: [Col. 0998D] (7) Herold, *Haereseologia*, p. 186, Basel edition of 1556.], where the author’s four books *Against Arius* appear; Baronius drew it from that edition. In the other editions that followed, in the two Parisian libraries of the ancient Fathers [Note: [Col. 0998D] (8) *Library of the Fathers*, Paris, 1624 and 1644, vol. IV, part I, p. 198b.], the erroneous reading is “two years before.” The latest Lyons edition likewise gives the number written out as “eleven” [Note: [Col. 0998D] (9) *Library of the Fathers*, Lyons, vol. IV, p. 261h.], as does our own [Note: [Col. 0998D] (10) *Library of the Fathers*, Venice, vol. VIII, p. 162d.], modeled on those editions, since Herold’s *Haereseologia* was then unavailable. The number “forty” should therefore be restored; with failing eyes, it could easily have been changed into “eleven,” from which there subsequently arose both the Arabic number 11 and the other form written out syllabically, *undecim*.

But to return to our course: one must further observe regarding this work of Victorinus that Book I perhaps ends with the profession of faith found in chapter XLVII and closed by these words: “Grace and peace from God the Father and from his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, unto all ages of ages, to one so confessing.” This conjecture seems capable of confirmation from what the author says near the beginning of chapter 54 of the same Book I: “These matters,” he says, “have been spoken of in the book which is before this one.” Yet we have not departed from the printed editions, being content merely to note the point.

VIII. After the four books *Against Arius*, we place the short work [Col. 0999B] *On Receiving the Homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον, “of one substance”). The aforementioned Gothofredus seems, with excellent reason, to have judged it nothing other than an epitome of the said four books, and therefore written later by the author; nevertheless, it is wrongly placed in earlier editions after Hymn I. There follow three hymns on the Trinity, without metre or rhythm; they must indeed be read cautiously, for in some places, in Launoy’s judgment [Note: [Col. 1000A] (1) Launoy, *On Victorinus*, works, vol. II, part I, p. 648.], they require a sympathetic interpreter, as may be seen in Brasichellensis [Note: [Col. 1000A] (2) Brasichellensis, *Index of Expurgated Books*, vol. I, p. 122.].

As for the poem concerning the seven Maccabean brothers, formerly attributed to our Victorinus, we have thought it should be omitted, with the learned Johannes a Bosco [Note: [Col. 1000A] (3) Johannes a Bosco, *Florentine Library*, vol. II, p. 198.], Barthius [Note: [Col. 1000B] (4) Barthius, *Adversaria* III.23.], Labbe [Note: [Col. 1000B] (5) Labbe, *Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 468.], Oudin [Note: [Col. 1000B] (6) Oudin, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 1230.], and the Ballerini [Note: [Col. 1000B] (7) Ballerini, on the works of St Leo, vol. II, p. 343, no. 4.]. Guided by the authority of several manuscripts, they believe that poem should be attributed to St Hilary, bishop of Arles, rather than to Victorinus the African.

[Col. 0999]

THE BOOK OF MARIUS VICTORINUS TO JUSTINUS THE MANICHAEAN, AGAINST THE TWO PRINCIPLES OF THE MANICHAEANS, AND ON THE TRUE FLESH OF CHRIST. (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0999C] I. To speak to one who has long possessed, through much reading and the unwearied vigils of continual labor, what he ought to confess concerning the faith of the Law is the act, Justinus, of one mistaken—but one who loves. Therefore I preferred to disclose how highly I value you; and I gladly accepted the labor I undertook with you, that you might understand beforehand that you still had to seek what Manichaeus—and, as Andrew speaks in the *Acts*, also the *Treasury*—has disclosed. Confronted by this, I carefully inquire whether you truly say these things or not: that things diverse and contrary to us derive from one principle. Since I wished, as I undertook the discussion, not to reject the same matters, I respond.

I want you, brother, to consider this labor worthwhile. Read the treatise addressed to you repeatedly; and yourself, by turning over what is said, penetrate or investigate the secret of the deeper inquiry. For inward vision surpasses words and overwhelms and blinds the conjectures of even the immense mind itself [Col. 0999D]; when such matters are sought piously and reverently, they are understood as delightful rather than terrifying. For each man wishes to prevail when the intention of a holy mind asks whether there is one principle; and this flesh of ours, together with the hidden herbs and grasses which you love, venerates one and the same author—its own author and that of the whole world—according to its capacity to act.

But I myself, wondering and astonished at the obstinacy of your judgment—that you hate flesh and revere grasses—do not yet know whether you confess these things to derive from one source or from different sources. If you say, “from one,” you see into what you fall. If “from another,” it is inconsistent to praise the maker of one thing because of other things, while blaming and reproaching one’s own maker because of what exists in oneself. But lest I seem, in saying this, to rebuke rather than answer, if these points move you, they shall be stated later. For now, receive what you asked.

II. To be able and permitted to inquire into things beyond ourselves and the world, when we ourselves are almost unknown to ourselves, is madness and insanity; and it is a real danger to be uncertain whence, how, or from whom you are, when you do not dare doubt that you exist and possess flesh, and when you plainly see that you live in the world and are delivered through the help of your Creator, insofar as you obey him. You acknowledge that there is one Savior, yet shrink from confessing that you come from one maker, dividing the maker of flesh from the creator of the soul.

We say, then, imagining that each rules the world and preserves his own work in the human being: each alike striving that what he has made from his own kingdoms should not perish. The bright sun rejects this, as do chaste virginity, the glorious choir of stars, and the entire fabric of the whole world; they reject and cast away the notion that their origin comes to them from two distinct and two unbegotten principles. For the understanding is violated by clouds of profane thought if so great a splendor of immeasurable radiance should consist in earlier darkness and in a portion of it. For it follows that the sun itself is from those darknesses, if the whole world received its existence from two principles.

Certainly, because it is not ours to hold understanding fixed in such matters or to remain in this wandering of perception, we flee from and dread confessing that he is from himself—even he whom we ourselves conquer. Finally, I ask you to grasp how it is possible to say that flesh exists apart from him from whom all things received their beginning, and that it dwells in the higher kingdoms, where are that virginity, glory, and proclaimed light of which mention has been made. Since it descended thence into Christ, it cannot be thought not to be there. For Christ has flesh from there, since your reverence does not allow you to say that it is from Mary. Shall we then say that what God assumed is from another? What was he who was to assume it to do, if the Creator did not fashion it? And if he fashioned it, is it not worthy to merit [uncertain: the sense of *numquid est digna mereri?* is elliptical]?

III. Here, as I see, the inventor and creator is praised if eternity deemed it worthy to dwell in it. But if that flesh in Christ is another flesh, God the maker is nevertheless later, not earlier. If it is earlier, why is it not itself in the world, and why is it in heaven, where no one is fleshly? And if the flesh in Christ is not itself in the world, whence does the creature come into foreign kingdoms from external regions? Or how is it joined here to souls? Or why is it so often able to take souls captive, so that it appears almost more powerful in foreign kingdoms? And why does the author of the inner realm labor to free this inner being from flesh? Or why did he permit him to enter that from which he had to be freed, in order to be enclosed?

Certainly all that is here—the world—is the kingdom of truth and light, and its maker rules it. If, throughout this whole kingdom that is peculiarly his own, there is one thing belonging to another, which is called flesh, and if this alone can have such power and force that the soul, driven by it, is tossed about, fluctuates, and grows weary through exhaustion, we may see how great in his own kingdoms the maker of flesh can be. For if we understand that this kingdom, which is the whole world, belongs to him from whom we believe flesh to be his servant, then we shall say that the sun, that choir, and the singular virgin have shone forth from the source of hidden places. This I indeed gladly embrace, and with exalted joy rejoice to profess: that all these things have one Creator, and that he—whom it is permitted to understand as light, truth, and the whole—should be reverently worshipped as known through the hidden cause of a pious and penetrating inquiry.

Thus the recollection of a rejoicing soul raises the senses, and the better origin consoles all the cares of the wavering spirit by the festal grounds of reason. Whatever are called ages, whatever are counted as kingdoms or regarded as worlds, whatever precedes everything ancient—all this is gathered into the fact that there is one being, singular in existence, and that it is understood to be immeasurable because it is the whole, though called one.

IV. In one way, Justinus, is what he himself is; in another, what is from him. What he himself is, is one; and whatever he is, is wholly one. But what is from him is innumerable. These are the things by which all that is enclosed and encompassed by the one whole is filled. Yet because the things which are from him who is from himself and is one are varied, it is fitting that he rule over them in varied ways. And, so that he may appear omnipotent, he had to be found to be the source even of opposites.

This is plainly already the case with that forest which distinguishes every tree by the material of its species, unlike and dissimilar in kinds of trees; yet the whole forest, and the confused multiplicity of its distinct parts, is perceived and seen as timber in the material of innumerable thousands upon thousands, but its nature is not thereby characterized. You remember, as you consider with me, that these are matters of likenesses and of things decreed, and that it befell them to come into being from another.

But those realities—those immense realities existing from themselves—are themselves devoid of likeness, deprived of comparison, and lacking an example. No one will doubt this. Thus the advance of our inquiry is compelled to confess and pressed into a confined course: to enter those hidden heights stretching onward with unwearied bounds; to penetrate to the more secret object of veneration among the secrets of things; and, by nature alone—yet only insofar as it can—by speech insofar as it suffices to utter, to approach, reach, or attempt it. And therefore I now ask: what can be like the immeasurable?

V. Tell me, if you can—you who, granting credence to comparisons, believe that through the shadows of images you have attained truth. But, as I see, it is not you, Justin, who fail things, but things that fail you. And if, as you are accustomed to say and now say, there is another kingdom, is this other kingdom some unknown kingdom which is also immense? [Col. 1002B] Yet I do not see how it can rightly be called limitless if existence is not denied to another. For where the one begins to exist, there the limit of the other ends, and neither is infinite. But if this is so, that it is finite, I reject—or misuse—the claim that either of them exists of itself.

Nevertheless, since we are from another, and the world is not from itself, and however great it may be, it is nevertheless finite—if not in relation to other things, then at least in relation to its maker—it is altogether sacred to confess its maker as infinite. Therefore I perceive and know that all things which are in the world, and whatever the world itself is, are from that principle which alone and solely exists from itself, in itself, for itself; which is immeasurable and extends infinitely as a whole, and proceeds until it is not and fails wherever another has being or existence. Nor can there be another which is external [Col. 1002C] or divided, becoming a rival or standing as an enemy, which, established and remaining within its own domain, may admit defeat and afterward be taken captive, then be drawn into the victor’s kingdoms; and, having been transferred there, cease to exist where it existed before the war.

Certainly, if it is still in that realm, it has not yet been conquered; and if it exists, perhaps it may be restored. In what number of cases will this happen? Through how many ages will that struggle endure? When will it cease? If it has been extinguished, or if it has already been conquered, it is no longer in its own realm; and where is it? Indeed, it now lacks being and has ceased. Thus all things that belonged to it have perished and been removed together with their source. If they have perished, they are never its own; and the flesh which exists belongs not to it, but rather to him who conquered.

VI. Perhaps you prefer to say that this victor bore away into [Col. 1002D] his own kingdoms, as a trophy, certain things from those which the defeated one possessed. Let it be so: even if these things exist, they are not hostile—the victor has carried them off as spoils. Yet you confess even today that flesh is hostile to God. O the idleness of the triumphant one! O the leisure of the beaten! O the numbness of the injured! O the sluggish strength of the provoked! O the authority of the lord lying at rest! You are wearied by your captives in your own kingdom; and you who were able to conquer by fighting grow accustomed, by sparing them, to be overcome.

Let these things be held in such an order that this suspicion may collect its errors far back, before the world existed. Certainly you say that both are from themselves, those whom you recount as having entered into war: equal is the power of those in whom origin from themselves and one eternity are found. Shall I dare here to call one better, and suppose greatness in one above the other? Shall I not [Col. 1003A] fall or rush into guilt and be arraigned and condemned against eternity itself, which is always one? Shall I not fear to profess that what is eternal can be overcome, and that what is from itself is not one? And while we confess one omnipotent, shall I assert that he does not at some time rule over another?

A blind thing is disclosed, darker than every darkness: the error of sacrilege. A mad concern, in saying that what is from itself is conquered, agitates even the victor who is from himself with fear that the captive, which is unbegotten, may be subjected. Thus the omnipotent victor has enlarged himself from conquered kingdoms, and you inquire whether that which is unbegotten can be destroyed or removed. Indeed, that which is from itself will be destined not to be, if it yields to the victor’s power and is either slain or led away.

VII. Next, which shall we say was not content with its own possessions, so that the war you recount arose: [Col. 1003B] light or darkness? If light, it lacked darkness and took delight in gloom. Where is that which is called omnipotent, that which is understood as the whole, if something was not in it but was outside it, possessed in other kingdoms, and was a reality for itself, since it existed, though the dominion of the omnipotent did not yet possess it? But now let us suppose that darkness began the war, and let us establish that the shadow of unbegotten radiance, existing in its own proper solidity, conspired against it.

If that light is fire, darkness must have come to the conflagration, so that its solidity—belonging to itself—might, coming from outside into conflict, be burned. But if darkness is empty and therefore has no solidity, where, I ask, is there a joining of solid things with emptiness? To think these things, and in one’s mental course to have reached such inner matters, is plainly bold and mad. To imagine a conflict [Col. 1003C] of emptiness with solidity, depth with height, finite with infinite, darkness with light, false with true, and something tiny with the whole? I cannot allow, brother, that these discordant things, having arisen in equal fashion, should be affirmed, remembered under one eternity, and so located that each of them has being. Rather, I assign being to the one who is from himself; of the other I would maintain that it is not possessed at all.

For if you reject this, teach what substance there is in emptiness; what is outside the infinite; what is earlier than the eternal; what is equal in extent to the whole. Then I shall understand that it exists and is possessed in reality, and I shall not deny two principles of things. If some Indian says these things, or a Persian recounts them, let him prescribe them to his own people and grow old beside his own pole. For there they have another way of thinking about divine things, as they have another manner of living under law. Although they are human beings by nature, nevertheless, as they are separated by language, so also are they distinct in reason; [Col. 1003D] nor is it otherwise with such people, whose bodies are nourished differently, whose dress is fitted differently, whose appearance is shaped differently by their manner of life, who preserve themselves differently, and many of whom are even born with another form; and, as I say, there are nations beyond number.

Have you not therefore seen how many Manes, Zoroasters [Note: [Col. 1003D] (1) In pronouncing the name of this man, the inventor of the Magi and of magic, there was much variation; Cotelerius discusses this at greater length in his notes on the *Recognitions of Clement*, book IV, chapter 27.], or Buddhas have deceived people by teaching these things? Let us return to the inquiry.

VIII. What we are, Justin, we are from him who is omnipotent and is manifestly established as existing from himself; for him, not to be is not to be what he is. [Col. 1004A] Thus there is not even another being that might stir up battle. But the fact that two forms are recognized, contrary or diverse—good and evil, solid and empty, high and deep, true and false, light and darkness, eternal and temporal, life and death, and all opposites—does not teach or reveal that the order of things proceeds from two principles.

For if to perceive two eternal beings and observe them as enemies is to think this, then it belongs to outcomes to have held them so. Perhaps it was permitted to the Parthians—whom anxious fear, innate in a trembling dread, disturbed with sad concern over kingdoms about to fight—to establish the principles themselves and invent what events would befall the combatants. They might invent what terms and agreements were made, what end checked the war, and what lord the more secure outcome set over the two. But because danger is, as I see, being considered for both the unbegotten and the victor, therefore, brothers, that which is from itself is conquered, and that which is without beginning will end and not be—or has already ended. [Col. 1004B]

I have escaped; I breathe again. There is no other who is called my maker. Or, if he is still perishing and nevertheless remains, he dwells in his own kingdoms, and he will not be my maker in this world. My creator is he who is also the maker of the world: from whom are established chaste virginity, the glorious company of stars, and the splendid sun in heaven, or, as you are accustomed to say, placed in the vessels above. Therefore let us rejoice in triumph; flesh, no longer to perish, rejoice. For you are from your Christ the savior—whether you are in Adam and Mary, or whether, taken up in the higher vessels, you have deserved to be eternal. No longer, desolated by the hope of promise, cast down into the depths, do you decay in old age; now restored by the price of the cross, you shall be clothed with the glory of immortality.

[Col. 1004C] IX. And this is worthy of you, who, having entered, have encompassed all that eternity and immensity are. Here indeed it is now pleasing to mark the magicians of Babylon and the Ctesiphontine singers of their secrets by their mysteries: whose power is now to raise spirits by a chant, now to summon them. Yet it is better, and truly divine, that our Savior raised flesh buried in tombs. For no one doubts that what could be buried was dead; and if death clung to flesh coming down from above after it had been wounded, then in Christ our flesh rose again.

What cause, nevertheless, was there for taking flesh if that flesh itself was not raised? But if it was another flesh, the flesh which can be killed is certainly mortal. This is immense and beyond estimation: that he dwelt in human limbs. Unless he were from eternity, he would not be omnipotent. Recognize in that same eternal being those things which are called contraries [Col. 1004D]. To him whose Father is found unbegotten, and whose age and eternity are found, it belonged also to die; and that he might truly be known as omnipotent, his birth from a virgin is not denied.

What now is omnipotent, eternal, infinite, and the whole; what is immeasurable and loftier than every height and eminence; what it is from which everything that exists in things remains and comes to be—I perceive, instructed by the saying of the Savior of all, who, teaching himself to be the Son, deigned to show that he had a Father. Revealing whom God is, Jesus, marveling that he is all things, disclosed as much as the measure of the world permitted. Therefore God is one sole principle, and God alone is truth; truth itself is light, and light is always eternal. Everything true is solid, always exists, remains manifest, and endures [Col. 1005A].

But what is true from itself is never conquered; what is solid has no emptiness; what is light does not admit darkness and does not know it. And if it admits darkness and darkness comes into it, darkness ceases to be for itself. Rather, things which have ceased to be for themselves are not for others. But if they are still in their own domain, they are outside this world and are still being fought against; and it is uncertain whether they will be overcome or truly perish at some time. But if this is still uncertain, then neither the world nor flesh received being in it as from another; rather, it came to that one from whom the bright sun was also established as minister to the world.

For if you imagine darkness to be that which is called evil, you will grasp and understand it—not by taking darkness to be granted being in the way that light and brightness possess being, but as something produced or appearing from the activity of another which truly exists. [Col. 1005B] For there is, both among heavenly things and in the air, and even among our own things, something which finds its being from the activity of another: as heat from the sun’s ray; as cold from the wind’s breath, which freezes rivers and splits the earth through frost. Thus the earth is opened by the sun’s heat, and the flowing waters of rivers are bound by ice.

X. These matters must be understood thus: one thing is produced by the activity of another, so that one may see in things that exist that something not inherent in them by quality arises from the activity of another. But it is otherwise when something is said to come about from the reality of the eternal—which is the whole—through the activity of another. Darkness is not established, not solid, not penetrating; it is rather an emptiness that perishes through light and has no being for itself when light shines.

For it happens to darkness not to exist through light’s activity, because darkness is not substance; it admits the substance of light and perishes [Col. 1005C]. If, therefore, darkness perishes from light, from that same source it receives its appearing—in the way that depth comes from height, and nothingness from the whole. For although the whole is eternal, there is also nothingness, wherever there is no substance at all. Height exists, but its counterpart is depth: for unless there were height, depth could not appear. Unless you knew solidity, you would not perceive emptiness.

Therefore there are things which are substance, and there are things which do not possess their own substance. Since those things which are substance exist, it happens that those things which are not substance appear through them, as hoarfrost and ice do. They appear; but because they do not possess their own substance, they receive their being from the activity of cold, then melt and perish when dissolved. Yet ice is from water, though it is congealed by the coldness of the air. Therefore I see two states of water: liquid [Col. 1005D] and ice. Thus what is substance is the liquid; but what happens to it through an activity is the freezing of that same liquid into ice. Since ice itself has no substance, it perishes and is removed; yet the liquid of water, remaining substance, endures.

XI. These, indeed, are worldly things, either from the Creator or from nature. But those higher, final things—and first without beginning—which lack likeness, fail of comparison, are not formed by the example of images, have nothing equal or prior to them, beyond which no estimation can go, and are comprehended only in this: that they are known as incomprehensible—do not possess activity from the same cause or form as the things mentioned, which this composite world contains [Col. 1006A].

But as belongs to things unmade, unbegotten, infinite, and whole, so consider or attend to their being: there is one sole being, omnipotent, which contains all things of the whole, is perceived as infinite, and itself exists and stands; extending beyond its own invisible solidity, it rules and reigns, employing the wondrous substance of its own majesty by that divine activity of its own whereby it is either moved or unmoved. Yet that very being falsely affords an origin to the whole; for, when the omnipotent is the whole, it comes about through him that even nothingness appears. For the omnipotent would not be the whole unless, besides him, there were some other thing which was nothing.

Therefore what is called nothing exists, but it has no substance; and what is called the whole exists and has substance. For the latter, to be is to exist; for the former, to be is not to be [Col. 1006B]. God, therefore, is truth: he is the whole and stands infinite. Since nothingness cannot exist outside the whole, Justin, that which is understood as being without place and is held to be outside boundaries is rightly called false—if indeed reason can admit that you understand a boundary anywhere for him whom you perceive and investigate as the whole.

For if the whole is occupied by the eternal, nothingness has nowhere to be; and if the omnipotent is all things, nothingness can be understood only in this way: as that which is outside the whole, not as something having being. Finally, if you measure the omnipotent so that there is also another who is not omnipotent, there will be said to be a place greater than God, greater than both of them—if distinct unbegotten principles possess their own kingdoms and stand as rivals.

XII. To understand or maintain that anything is greater than the eternal omnipotent is the barbarous thought of heedless confusion. [Col. 1006C] To hold that what fights is coeternal, and suppose that one of the eternal beings is conquered, belongs to one who says that light itself will not exist in some age; but if you listen to that claim, you will then understand that the sun will not exist. And since for it to be is to have begun, if danger of perishing comes also upon what exists from itself, then the unbegotten fights, and that which is unbegotten is overcome by the unbegotten.

Do you dare determine which of the unbegotten began first? Or perhaps do you conceal this merely by order and invent that they began equally? Can you judge greater and lesser among eternal unbegotten beings? If you place darkness first, you give it every principle and make it greater. If you confess light as older, you confess everything from it. If you perceive both as equally coeval, either neither will be conquered [Col. 1006D], or something will remain to the one whom the other has overcome. And where then will the omnipotent or eternal be? Will the victor be one of the two, and in equal existence will a dissimilar cause arise? Will chance govern the war of unbegotten beings, or will it receive an outcome?

Far be it from the mind to consider this error; let human hope cast away the confession of so mad an understanding. One unbegotten being exists; from one Lord all things have proceeded. But because diverse things are from the same cause, he is found omnipotent by all creatures, before principles and ends.

XIII. Thus false being also proceeds from what is true, as shadows proceed from solid things. [Col. 1007A] For unless the solid exists, neither does a shadow exist. This is the true mystery of truth. For things which are not appear from things which are true, so that he may himself be from himself, and from himself establish others in order that they may be—not by his works, not by labor, not by matter, not by nature, nor by substance. For if it belongs to the omnipotent to be the whole, whatever is outside is his. But if anything happens without him, neither is omnipotent, and the principles grow by accident and activity when things are added to them, diminished indeed insofar as additions have made them so.

What matter or nature does a shadow have, which does not appear without another and is not possessed in darkness? Yet because it has no substance of its own and is not from itself, it vanishes and perishes; while the solid thing from which there is sometimes a shadow remains and endures in its own strength. Marvel, Manes of Babylon, at these mysteries and these riches of the omnipotent. Confess that nothing is not his whom you venerate as eternal, whom you confess as Lord, before whom nothing is earlier. And how can anything be not his or not from him, before whom you understand that there is no other?

But you are troubled by the anxious care of wandering error—or rather, confused by the labor of vain pursuit, deceived by dull understanding—you have wounded the first beginnings of a soul setting out toward greater inquiry with madness. Recall your unruly concerns to their first footsteps, and cease to believe that one eternity has taken on two kingdoms, testing themselves against one another, as you say.

XIV. If one of two eternal beings is to be conquered, eternity will remain severed. Therefore light and darkness have equal things, though diverse within themselves—indeed, contrary things. One power belongs to both, but in one it will at some time cease. It is no longer the same if, wherever it is hoped, one of them will fail first. Justin, you will have to confess one principle if one is victor from the two.

Certainly, what I understand in the upper heights and beyond every ultimate altitude is that nothing called evil dwells there—that realm which reverent human devotion, fearing, contemplates beyond Angels and Archangels. It is sacrilegious speech to say that evil dwells in such places; or, if it has its seat there and is itself acknowledged as creator, then the devil rules over every creature, and over the sun itself. For if he is coeternal, he is there; but if he is not there, he is in some kingdom of his own, I know not what. I suppose that other realm has no sun, no heaven, no world, no light, no truth. And if he has a kingdom elsewhere, it has nothing in common with us; but if he is in this world, he is already conquered, already subject to the sun, already has no strength. If you confess this, you understand that what you perceive as captive to a ruler cannot be called a principle.

Can two highest things, two lowest things, two infinities be suitable to reality? Two infinities cannot be called such, because where one begins, the other ends. The highest is highest because there is nothing beyond it; and likewise the lowest, because there is nothing within it. The whole is then possessed when no other thing is possessed. If one sole God is highest, infinite, the whole, omnipotent, and all-containing, then he alone is the one sole principle.

XV. Do not be disturbed; do not, anxiously terrified by amazement at so venerable a truth, be struck dumb or blinded because evil cannot arise from a good author. I rightly inquire about such matters in creatures: created things do not emit from themselves something other than what they are—bitterness from sweetness, water from fire, the offspring of the lower world from shadow, a human being from wood, flesh from what is fleshless, and all the other things which the whole world enumerates [Col. 1008A].

But these things cannot be ascribed to the omnipotent. It is a doctrine that sets a law for him as to what can be from him, what cannot be, what is from him and what through him. You rightly draw and press these conclusions if you do not confess the omnipotent. But if his power and eternity are diffused through the whole, and his being did not come to him from another, then all things either are from him, or of him, or through him, or come about, or are created. Therefore evil also received its being from him.

Yet this evil is what is called a demon; for all other things which you may call evil have neither substance nor nature. A demon, however, is an angelic creature, now good, now evil, as the expression of Attic speech teaches, saying: ἈΓΑΘΟΣ ΔΑΙΜΩΝ, “a good daimon,” and ΚΑΚΟΣ ΔΑΙΜΩΝ, “an evil daimon.” And later we shall say that even the one called *kakos* (“evil”) is good [Col. 1008B]. But the other things which you call evil, if the faults of errors come to rest, will have no origin of birth.

XVI. Do not indeed be worn down by the impulse of evil as though there were some existing, born, or made substance that precipitates one into vices. It is the soul which, standing in freedom, has violated through the license of free choice the dominion granted to it. It is deceived by a curious desire and concupiscence rather than by pride.

Then you set before us a lord ruling two substances, or human kingdoms ruling peoples without number through a twofold—or rather many-formed—nature. You take such delight in examples that you love to perceive eternal and perpetual things through mortal and perishable ones. You deny flesh in Christ and confess a human being; you do not wish him to have been born, yet you do not deny that he lived; you proclaim that he was killed by the Jews [Col. 1008C], yet judge that what was wounded did not exist. Thus you maintain that the limbs of the condemned men tortured at the right and left died, so that Christ’s own destruction was fulfilled; and you refuse a true human being with flesh where you find a true burial.

Behold, Justin: you attempt to assert that what truly exists did not exist, and you strive to prove that what neither is nor was persists. Yet, instructed by you yourself as teacher, I speak firmly: was it possible for the eternal one to die, but impossible for him to have flesh? Was it possible for him to establish what did not exist, but impossible to grant the world two natures, of light and darkness? Would he who is from himself, in order to exist, not be by power the source of opposites?

Cease, Justin, cease diligently pursuing the barbarity of this vanity; and strive, as a Roman man, to remove yourself from Persian or Armenian sacrilege [Col. 1008D]. For it is by no means fitting, O Mani, that one whose authors are darkness or the devil should dwell in the kingdoms of the glory of eternal life and of true light.
