And in vain, until now, you have worn down the limbs of allegedly hostile flesh by continual fasting, supposing that the juices of a nourished body impede the soul’s merits and nature, burdening it with the growth of swollen fat and the weight of the very belly—if, after this labor of fasts, you return to your creator, whom you call either the devil or outer darkness.

I judge it better, and plainly declare, that you confess almighty God to be your creator, so that you may truly be God’s temple, as the Apostle Paul says: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3:16). But if you are deprived of this honor [Col. 1009A], so that you are neither God’s temple nor his Spirit dwells in you, Christ came not as the savior of humanity but as its abductor—something which divine law forbids one to say, and the eternity of his majesty does not admit.

For if we are not his temple and his Spirit is not in us, what relation is there between him and us? But if we are his, we are his in both respects, in soul and body. And this is true and catholic, uttered by a holy mouth: “God, all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28)—he who alone and solely is the principle, omnipotent without beginning, the whole of the universe, infinite through all things. To him be honor and glory.

[Col. 1009]

## VICTORINUS, ON THE WORDS OF SCRIPTURE: “AND THERE WAS EVENING AND THERE WAS MORNING, ONE DAY.” DID THE DAY BEGIN FROM EVENING OR FROM MORNING? (C, G, S)*

I. If the divine Scriptures were read simply, the reading of any chapter would never be wrongly understood by anyone; rather, as they stand, they would unanimously be received piously and rightly. Philonic disputation would cease; syllogistic argument would cease; every superstitious [Col. 1009B] invention would cease; and no dark comparison would ever be recognized in any person. All would think one thing, agree with one another, and profess the same things, as the most lucid reading declares itself.

For our dear friend has raised for us the question whether the whole world has its corresponding hours or not. “In short,” he says, “I say that if it is the first hour here, the whole world has the first hour. For it seems absurd to me to hear that different hours are said to be contained in the four regions of the earth. Since, I say, all regions are inhabited, how can it be proved to me that one hour is not possessed by all people? And since it is day here, show me in what region you assert that it is night, when all the quarters of heaven are illuminated by day. For Moses taught us no differently in the book of Genesis than that day should be day throughout the whole world, and night should hold the entire globe in darkness.”

Therefore, friend, if these things which you have said suffice for the question, I ask you to grant us patience and hear from us what is true—not so that you may catch human inventions, but rather approve things spoken by God. Thus, if an authoritative reading is found, you must yield us room to speak, so that you may learn more plainly in what manner the most blessed Moses briefly indicated day and night. For Solomon too teaches us, saying: “Your good Spirit is in all things; therefore you correct little by little those who err, and remind them of the things in which they sin, speaking to them, so that, abandoning ignorance, they may believe in the words of God” (Wis. 12:1).

For every Scripture inspired by the Spirit of God, says the Apostle Paul, requires interpretation (2 Pet. 1:20). Apollos too was “mighty in the Scriptures” (Acts 18:24), and exceedingly fervent in spirit; nevertheless Aquila and Priscilla took him aside and explained the way of the Lord to him more carefully. For the wise are readily corrected. “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain.”

II. We therefore unfold each point taught by the reading of Genesis. But it would be lengthy to speak of what was said above; and let us postpone disputation concerning heaven and earth, darkness and the abyss, water and spirit, since it is not yet time to say anything about these matters, but rather to answer and satisfy this present question [Col. 1010A].

It is indeed the case that darkness possessed the whole world, as the reading in the preceding passage declares. For it was thus said: “Let there be light; and there was light” (Gen. 1:3). The wise ask where this light was made. For darkness was not a substance, as philosophers say, nor was there in it some material configuration: it is nothing. Yet far be it from us to think anything with them, since divine Scripture says that God created darkness and made heaven. Therefore whatever is made by God is believed to be substantial. Hence, if darkness is substantial, it was not reduced to nothing when light was made. [Col. 1010B]

Nor were light and darkness mixed together, because both are substances, contrary to one another even today, as heat is to cold or sweetness to bitterness. Yet, when they are tempered with one another, they are recognized as necessary to each other for the generation of creatures and for rest from all works. Let calumny therefore cease if we have called them contrary according to substance, but necessary in the generation of creation and in rest from all works.

We show, however, that when light was made darkness was not removed; rather, Scripture teaches that it was confined to one region—that is, condensed in the middle of the globe—so that the light which was made illuminated the middle part of the world [Col. 1010C]. For the worldly light which was made, that it might possess the whole globe, is not God’s substance. There is another light, the true light, which can illuminate the whole world, of which the Evangelist says: “There is the true light, which illuminates every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9).

The true light, therefore, illuminates the whole world because darkness yields place to its author; just as the sun too will be obscured by the true light and covered in darkness. But the light which is not yet that true light could not—indeed, ought not—illuminate the entire world at a single summit, lest the day be judged fixed and limited, rather than established by the rapid course of hourly moments. The weakness of the creature is manifest in its inability to surround the entire world; and thus it is recognized even now as traversing it in portions [Col. 1010D].

III. But if it possessed the whole globe with its light, it would not show any hour in the day; for when it illuminated the whole world, there would be nothing for it to traverse. According to this reasoning which we have discussed, we can rightly understand the prophet Moses saying: “And God separated between the light and the darkness” (Gen. 1:4). What is separation but the making of a distance between these things?

If he established distance and set one against the other, decreeing that they should be in division itself, so that he called the light day and the darkness night, we now hear one thing named differently from another. [Col. 1011A] Why then was the first designation not sufficient and pleasing, if afterward he called it day as though the thought had occurred to him? But far be it from us not to inquire why, while the preceding name remains, it is called day: the consequence is that he indicated a span enclosed by twelve hours.

For even today, if a day is called Sunday, it is not defined without its proper hours. When, therefore, you say “day,” you establish some definite hour up to evening. Thus my lord Moses says that the light was called day, so that we might recognize that it was said in reference to the daily usage not lacking the office of twelve hours. Finally he adds: “And there was evening, and there was morning, one day” (Gen. 1:5). If he calls evening and afterward day made, he indicates the completed hours of that creation. For Solomon asks in the book of Ecclesiastes: “What is that which has been made? The same that shall be; and what has been, the same is what shall be” (Eccl. 1:9).

IV. Therefore, friend, if a day is defined in this way today, why should we not believe the prophet saying that what happens today was made in the beginning itself: [Col. 1011B] that there is nothing new under the sun, nor anything added or diminished? Evening remains until morning, completing the hours of night; and thus one day is called defined, in which the morning is said to belong not to the first day but is found to be the beginning of the second.

But we ask whether our Lord worked in the day or in the night. Certainly, if in the day, this morning is not judged to belong to the first day, since the firmament of heaven is commanded to be made in it. But if the firmament was made on the second day, it becomes clear that the morning belongs to the second day. For the balance of day and night had been fixed; for this reason one day had been named in the number.

Again Scripture says: “Let the water be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear” (Gen. 1:9); and immediately afterward he commanded it to produce fodder-bearing grass according to its kind, and fruit-bearing trees. Concerning these things, “there was evening, and there was morning, the third day.” Therefore, if you take this morning as belonging to the third day, why does Scripture say: “Let two lights be made in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth at the beginning of day and night, and divide between day and night, and be for signs, days, seasons, and years” (ibid., 14)? No person who knows the law would agree with you that the sun and moon were made on the third day.

V. Perhaps, if I ask you yourself, you will answer me that they were made on the fourth day, and contend that this morning belongs to the third day [Col. 1011D]. If this morning truly belonged to the third day, our predecessors would never have professed that the sun and moon were made on the fourth day. But if they were made on the fourth day, this morning belongs not to the third but to the fourth, on which the sun, moon, and other things were made.

Finally, they divide day and night in their beginnings. For their maker balanced them in this manner: they should occupy and traverse an equal extent of the world—not so that, when their task was completed, they might have a resting-place for repose, but rather that they run unceasingly within their own limits. For the sun’s yearly course is traversed by the moon in thirty days. Having traversed the circuit of the globe, they return to the first point from which they set out [Col. 1012A].

Therefore they do not rest when they have run the whole circuit; or show me that this is written, and I shall be silent. But you cannot show it, because you do not find it, as Solomon says: “The sun rises, and the sun sets, and returns to its place. It rises and goes toward the south, and, circling, goes about unto the north” (Eccl. 1:5). If you think that the sun sets, give us an explanation of how it returns to its place.

Therefore, if the inclination to invent falsehoods escapes you, believe Solomon, who says that the rising sun goes toward the south and, circling, reaches the north: “For the wind goes round and round, and returns upon its circuits” (ibid., 6). What more plainly can we argue, when the prophet has in few words delineated our question: that it is a spirit which, circling and turning, unceasingly traverses the whole globe? Thus one day is defined, and one passes to another morning; for this reason days, months, and years were established.

VI. Henceforth be satisfied with yourself, and agree with our earlier fathers who handed down the matters we mentioned above: that this light does not occupy the whole world, but its middle part. Thus, wherever the sun has looked, day and its hours come to be. Accordingly, as it travels through the circuit over the space allotted to it, it changes the hours. If this is true, wherever morning has arisen, morning cannot remain there for long; for as the sun moves on to other places, the hours continually change, and so evening is reached. What follows is the service of night, which the hours supply. But when we see morning arise, we recognize that darkness has failed; and when evening [Col. 1012C] comes, day undergoes its setting.

For it thus divided the regions of heaven between day and night: wherever the sun makes its course, there is morning; and wherever the moon has travelled, evening is recognized, which is called that of the following day. For it is foolish to hear that night came first with evening, and that morning afterwards arose. If evening had come first, our lawgiver would not have hesitated to designate that one night in the number of nights. No one neglects to state what is first and principal, while allowing what follows to be named. Therefore, if nothing of the kind is found among men, how is it reckoned by you that one day is called after morning has come later? Why do you not declare what you first read: that light was made and called day, and afterwards darkness was called night? Therefore night was not made before day. Nor, then, should you believe that evening was made before morning, which you understand to be the first part of the day.

VII. But Scripture’s silence concerning morning discloses its rationale when it commanded light to come to be. What else could the rising of light show, unless it defined it as morning? For day could not be called day apart from morning; and we rightly say that, when God called the light day, he enclosed morning within it. For when day was finished, evening began to arise; working throughout the entire night, it would arrive at the morning of the second day, on which the firmament was made.

And although we have discussed the third and fourth days, on which he fashioned the sun and moon, let us inquire more fully on which day the human being was made—whether on the fifth or the sixth—so that it may be discovered whether evening precedes morning. For God said: “Let us make humankind according to our image and likeness.” And God made humankind; according to God’s image he made him; male and female he made them, and gave them every herb for food. “And evening came to be, and morning came to be: the sixth day” (Gen. 1:26, 27, 31). Hence, if this morning belongs to the sixth day, then the human being was made on the fifth day. For if he was made on the sixth day, it is established that this morning belongs to the seventh day, on which God rested. If not, show me here where the works of the sixth day are, on which all the things he said were made on the sixth day were completed.

But on the fifth day I find that the waters brought forth creeping things and [Col. 1013B] birds—not the human being, who was made from earth together with quadrupeds and beasts of the earth. If the human being was made on the fifth day together with the things mentioned above, we find neither the things which the waters brought forth nor those completed on the sixth day. And how does Scripture say that on the seventh day God rested from all his works, when I find that after the human being, and the things made with the human being, every work which God had begun to make was completed?

Therefore, if the human being and the things mentioned above were made on the fifth day, we find that everything was completed on the fifth day, so that we must conclude that on the sixth day [Col. 1014A] God rested from all his works. But if you understand evening after the creation of the waters, you will be able to find not the beginnings of the fourth day, but the beginnings of the fifth night. If this is true, this morning, which is named after evening, belongs not to the fifth day but to the sixth, because Scripture teaches us in it that the human being was made. Hence after the making of that human being it says that evening came to be, and morning—which truly is the beginning of the seventh day. For in that very morning God rested from all his works which he had begun to make, not in the evening, which was subsequent to the sixth day.

Now, friend, consider the reading more clearly and satisfy your mind that night cannot be placed before day, nor likewise [Col. 1014B] evening before morning, in which the day’s action and work are shown to have been completed, and then evening is said to follow. Finally, after the evening of the sixth day it ceased to mention evening itself, as it did morning, which the prophet plainly and clearly declared to be the seventh day itself. Therefore, if it is not itself, now kindly show the seventh evening, so that morning may follow it. But if you do not find it, believe the reading: the seventh day itself is that which, after evening, was called morning.

[Col. 1013]

# Candidus the Arian, Book on Divine Generation, to Marius Victorinus the Rhetorician. (C)

[Col. 1013C] I. Every generation, my Victorinus, sweet old friend, is a kind of change. But everything divine—namely, God—is immutable. God is Father in all things and is the first cause of all things. Therefore, if God is irreversible and immutable, then what is irreversible and immutable is neither begotten nor begets anything. If this is so, God is unbegotten.

For generation is generation through conversion and change. Before God there neither was nor could be any substance or substantiality, any existent or existent-ness, any existence or existentiality, any potency. For who is more powerful than God? Is it potency, existence, substance, or being (*ὄν*)? For all these things either are what God himself is or come after him. For he supplies all things.

But suppose these existed beforehand. How could they, when they willed, generate God? For they were neither perfect nor self-subsisting. They were therefore imperfect. How, then, by their own and their own potency, did they either beget or make God, who is perfect, when they were imperfect? But if God is imperfect, it is pointless to generate what already was. The same reasoning applies if perfect things generated the perfect. Therefore, whether they were perfect or imperfect, to generate God is either pointless, superfluous, or impossible.

First, potency is said to be older than everything that is; but potency itself does not attain actual being through itself without act and operation, since it is potency, not action. Potency, not made actual, does not proceed to the generation [Col. 1014C] of anything, still less to that of God. For potency remains in what it is to be potentially, without action. From where, then, was God born?

II. Let us see, then, whether perhaps substance or substantiality existed before God existed; whether existence or existentiality existed. But substance, since it is a subject, is subject to something else—to that which is in it—and, as being something other, is distinct from that which is in it. Yet “one thing and another” is not admitted in relation to God. For God is not in another thing as something other. God is not one thing and God’s being another. For God is something simple; therefore he is not from pre-existing substance. God, then, is unbegotten.

For God supplies substance rather than substance having pre-existed before God—substance which is indeed a subject, made the subject and receptacle of another, as something other; and that of which it is the receptacle is more powerful, and therefore comes later as an accretion. The same must be understood of existence and existentiality.

Existence differs from existentiality because existence is already in the condition that being already belongs to it; but existentiality is potency, so that what does not yet exist may be able to exist. Existence differs still more from substance: for existence is being itself, and being alone; it is not being in another or the subject of another, but is one being itself and alone. Substance, however, not only has being but is also something qualified and determinate; for it underlies the qualities placed in it, and is therefore called a subject. How, then, was God born when existence, existentiality, [Col. 1015A] existential potency, or existence itself pre-existed—these being in bare being and not having action or the power and force to act?

III. Thus, if these things stand as stated, neither being (*ὄν*) nor beingness (*ὀντότης*) existed before God; for beingness is multiple and composite, made up of substance and quality. Therefore, if neither potency nor existence nor existentiality existed—things which bear an image of simplicity—much less did being and beingness, substantiality and substance. For they were generated later from existentiality and existence. If all these things were generated later, they were generated; and if they were generated, something else existed from which they were generated. Therefore that from which all these things were generated is unbegotten. What is that but he from whom all things come—God? God, then, is unbegotten, since God is the cause of all these things.

But what is God’s being? Of what kind is it? Or by what cause is God himself? For he is the first cause, and cause to himself—not one thing being cause of another, but that very thing which he himself is is cause of his being. He is his own place; he is his own inhabitant. Not so that an image of two things arises: he is one and alone. For he is being alone.

Indeed, being itself is the same as living itself and understanding itself. For according as he is, he also lives and understands; according as he lives, he also is and understands; and according as he understands, he also lives and is. Thus, according to one, there are three; and according to three, one: simple quality and simple one. But what is simple is the principle of composites; and the principle is without a principle, for it precedes and has no principle before itself, and for that reason is principle. This is God.

Therefore God is without origin and unbegotten. What is unbegotten is without origin; what is without origin is without end. For an end belongs to what has begun. But if he has these two attributes, he is infinite; and if infinite, incomprehensible, unknowable, invisible, irreversible, immutable. For reversal and change are a beginning and an end: for one thing, indeed, a beginning; for another, an end. But none of these is God. Therefore God is irreversible and immutable. But if God is such, he neither begets nor is begotten. For to be begotten and to beget are a kind of reversal and change.

To this is added that to beget is to give to the one born either the whole or a part of the begetter. If he gives the whole, the begetter perishes; if a part, he is diminished. Therefore, if God always remains the same, he does not beget.

[Col. 1015D] IV. The same will be evident if someone says that generation from God occurs in any of these ways: by radiance, by emission of a ray, by the flowing-out of a point, by emanation, by image, by character, by procession, by what is superabundant, by motion, by action, by will, by the named “type”—or by any other mode there may be. For none of such things exists without reversal.

First, radiance is motion, assigns time, and involves a certain recession withdrawing into its own substance. Even if that radiance always remains, it is a distinguishable part from the whole. But if the generation is not empty, it proceeds from what always is to what [Col. 1016A] does not always exist. Further, is not radiance a reversal? For it is a brightness, as though fleeing and belched forth from a luminous substance. Radiance is substantial, not substance; and if it is substance, it is not the same substance. Thus already there is a reversal of the former into what is subsequent.

V. Let us examine generation through the emission of a ray. A ray is connected, then, and is connected to that from which the ray has proceeded. Nevertheless, if it is begotten it is reversed; or there is no generation if the ray always remains in it. If there is generation through the flowing of a point, how can that be? For a point is immovable and is the limit of a line, having neither part nor being part of another. If, then, it is such, it will not proceed from itself; for if it proceeds, it is no longer a point, but already a line. Thus it is changed.

But God is invisible [Note: [Col. 1016D] (1) “Or indivisible?”]. Therefore God is not a point. But if the point remains, the line does not come from it. For the point is immovable, whereas a line is in motion or arises from motion; and according to this mode there is no generation in God or from God.

What next, by emanation? How can generation be in God in that way? For if something is emitted from himself, something primary is diminished—whether in substance, divinity, or action. Then, what is emitted is either of his own potency or not of his own potency. If it is of his potency, how are there two gods and equals? And what need is there of two, if they are equals? What one can do, the other can do likewise; and a perfect fullness in one need not be multiplied. But if what proceeds is not of the same potency, God is changed and the whole has suffered from a part—which is incongruous with God. Therefore there is no generation in God in this sense either.

VI. The same applies to image. For image differs greatly from what can be imaged: the latter is as substance; the former is a shadowy appearance delineated only according to quality. An image has its substance in some other thing and does not subsist from itself; nor, in any respect, is it that in which it is. Therefore what is begotten from God is not an image. For an image is a sort of consequence of that of which it is the image.

The same reasoning holds with character. For character is an impress of substance; by itself it is nothing, and it is in another thing which is given form. Therefore nothing of this sort is in God. For what is generated from God must be consubstantial. But a character is not consubstantial. Therefore generation in God is not according to character.

But is generation from God according to procession and motion? Procession differs from motion. For every procession is from motion and in motion, yet not every motion is procession: motion inwardly is not procession but motion only. For procession is motion proceeding outward. What then are we to say: that generation from God is according to procession? Once, often, or always? If once, what use is it? And if what proceeds is good, why is God poor in proceeding? If often or always, what new thing has he generated? And the first procession is necessarily imperfect if another was needed for its perfection.

[Col. 1017A] VII. From these points it is evident that what is generated is neither consubstantial nor generated from God without conversion. But if this is incongruous with God, there is no generation from God. It appears still more incongruous to us if generation is by motion. For motion is either inward or proceeding: if inward, there is no generation; if proceeding, the same objections apply. Therefore there is change. And if motion proceeds, it is not consubstantial.

Then, if it proceeds, it proceeds into its own substance or into the production of another. In the first case, God has undergone motion into motion, and this is reversal. Then, if he proceeds into his own substance, he did not possess substance; if into the substance of another, something other than God existed which was made by God. This is more a production than generation from God. Therefore it is not consubstantial, and is a conversion of the former into [Col. 1017B] what is subsequent. Thus there is no generation from God.

Some, however, say that generation from God is according to superabundance—that superabundance is generation from God. By “superabundance” they mean, as when a bubbling spring possesses an overflow, pours it out, and is always full. So also, they say, from God: as from a spring comes that which remains over and is poured out [Note: [Col. 1017D] (1) “Which is poured out.” The relative pronoun seems to need deletion.]. And this is generation from God.

But the reasoning returns again to the same point. For if he is superabundant and always full, generation from God is always occurring, since the spring does not fail. What increases is poured out. Or does what is increased remain? Surely, then, what is superabundant is poured out, since it is incongruous that what remains over should not be poured out. But it pours out, and always pours out, for it is always overflowing. Therefore there are also new angels and new worlds. For it is incongruous that what continually flows out should not be poured out.

But if God was superabundant once only, there is then a double change and reversal of God; this too is incongruous. Therefore there is no generation in God according to this view either. But if it is according to superabundance, moreover, what is poured out is not consubstantial with God himself: God is superabundant, whereas what is poured out is merely what has been poured out, not itself always abundant. Therefore something else is superabundant after that; hence one thing after another, and another.

VIII. Some speak of generation according to will and according to action. Yet especially in God these two—will and action—are taken as the same. For in God acting and willing are simultaneous. Nevertheless there is a difference, even in him, between willing and God’s act; for willing, precisely as willing, is the cause of action. [Col. 1017D] Action is the effecting of will. Therefore will is other than action; and in terms of expression, one is prior and the other subsequent. It is impossible for both to be the same. In God, then, will is first and action subsequent. I do not mean in time, but as one is the cause of the other’s being.

It is thus admitted that will is not substance, nor action. Then the work itself is something other than action and will. For a work is the work of a worker, but the work is not the worker himself. Therefore the work is not consubstantial with the worker; consequently it is not generation. Nor is what has been made begotten; and it is a work, not generation, nor sonship, nor son, nor only-begotten, nor consubstantial—especially since substance itself does not yet exist before God wills to generate something. For every substance is an effect of God [Note: [Col. 1018D] (1) “Every substance is [an effect] of God.” Here Mabillon’s edition begins in the *Analecta*, p. 21, fol.].

Therefore God is not substance. For substance is through God. How, then, since substance is subsequent, do we call God substance? For if we call God substance, reason compels us to confess that substance is prior to God. For substance truly is a kind of subject. But what is a subject is not simple: the mind simultaneously understands that something else exists in the subject when it hears it called a subject. But God is something simple; therefore God is without substance. If, then, God is without substance, nothing is consubstantial with God, even if it appears to be born from God or has been born.

IX. Some, however, say that generation from [Col. 1018B] God is according to the named “type.” For God is spirit. Spirit, when it directs itself toward its own nature, rests in itself. They call a motion of this kind a type. What then? From a motion of this kind, a certain sonship suddenly bursts forth; and this is generation from God. But how? As an outflow, an emanation, radiance, or some other thing among these? Further, is it as a part from a whole, or a whole from a whole?

But whichever of these it is, it is either imperfect, if it pours forth a part—so that a certain diminution of the Father occurs, since the Son is a part—or else the generation is empty. But if the whole appeared from the whole, there is no reason why the same thing should be generated from that very same thing. And if there was a necessity for a double generation, both are imperfect: both what is prior and what is subsequent in the conversion.

But when the spirit rises [Col. 1018C] into itself [Note: [Col. 1018D] (2) “Into itself,” Mabillon; “in itself,” [the other edition] has “spirit.”], something other merely appears, without any radiance. It is clear, then, that what is subsequent belongs to things which at some time did not exist. Therefore it was made, not born, and for that reason is not consubstantial. Therefore there is no generation from God.

X. What, then, follows from all these things, my sweet Victorinus? That the Lord Jesus Christ (John 1:1, 3), who is the *Logos* (*λόγος*) with God, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made, is not from God by generation but by operation: the first and principal work of God. To him God gave the name above every name (Phil. 2:9), calling him Son and Only-Begotten, because he alone made his works. He made them from things that are not, because the power of God brings what is not into being (Rom. 4:17).

Jesus too, through whom all things were made, did this: he made the things that are from things that are not. But what God makes differs in this: it is perfect in every way; Jesus, however, made other things, not in the same manner, although perfectly. In what respect, then, is Jesus the maker through operation of the things which are from the things which are not? He is in the Father, and the Father is in him (John 14:9, 11), and both are one (John 10:30). But in what respect one cannot do the same as the other, he is understood as other. For he cannot make another thing altogether perfect.

Nor does he operate by his own operation or his own will, but wills the same things as the Father. And he also [Note: [Col. 1019B] (1) “Also.” Mabillon; the other edition: “even if.”] has a will, yet says: “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26:39). And he does not know many things in the Father’s will [Note: [Col. 1019B] (2) “In the Father’s will.” Thus rightly Mabillon. The word “Father’s” is absent in the *Orthodoxa* of Joannes Herold, p. 461, Basel ed. 1555, which we use.], such as the day of judgment (Mark 13:32). He is passible, whereas the other is impassible; the latter is the one who sent, and the former the one who was sent; and there are other matters of this kind: that this one put on flesh [Note: [Col. 1019B] (3) “That this one put on flesh,” Mabillon; the other edition: “in that he put on…”], that he died, that he rose from the dead. All these happened to the Son. They are incongruous with the Father, but not incongruous with his work, since it is a work in substance [Note: [Col. 1019B] (4) Mabillon: “Since it is a work”; perhaps one should read, “since indeed it is a work.”], which is receptive of diverse qualities, and especially of contrary ones.

XI. That God made Jesus Christ is stated by the sacred reading in the Acts of the Apostles: “Let all the house of Israel know most certainly that God made for us [Col. 1019B] the Lord Jesus Christ, whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36). Likewise in Solomon: “You made me [Col. 1020A] set over all the ways” (Prov. 8:22). The Gospel according to John also signifies this when it says: “And what was made, in him was life” (John 1:3–4). If, therefore, something was made in him, he too was made—still more so if he himself is life.

Let no one, then, take it as offensive that Jesus Christ is God’s work, perfect in every respect by God’s power; whereas God is unbegotten, unbegotten Spirit above all spirits; but the Only-Begotten, by operation and power, is a Son made substance, not from substance. For Jesus is every substance, including the first substance; every action, every *Logos* (*λόγος*); beginning and end of all things that are—bodily and incorporeal, intelligible and intellectual, knowing and known, sensible things and senses; pre-principle, pre-cause, preeminence, maker, capacity, fullness. Through him all things were made, and without him nothing: our Savior, the restorer of all things [Note: [Col. 1020B] (1) “Restorer,” Mabillon; “restoration,” [the other edition].], as servant for our salvation, but as Lord for the punishment of sinners and impious persons, and as glory and crown of the righteous and saints. Amen.

[Col. 1019]

# Victorinus, Book on the Generation of the Divine Word, to Candidus the Arian. (C)

[Note: [Col. 1019D]

I.—*Nous ethikos* (*Νοῦς ἠθικός*), “moral intellect,” and spirit. Thus the Basel edition. But Mabillon: *nous patrikos* (*νοῦς πατρικός*), “paternal intellect,” and spirit.

“Jesus Christ.” Thus Mabillon. But the *Orthodoxa*: “Jesus Christ, Savior of all believers, God’s Only-Begotten.” [Col. 1020D] “David says,” etc.

“God was.” Mabillon: “If he was God, he did not lie. Therefore Christ is the Son of God. But if he lied…”]

[Col. 1019C] I. Who has bewitched your great intelligence, noble Candidus? To speak about God is a boldness beyond the human. But because a moral intellect (*νοῦς ἠθικός*) has been implanted in our soul, and a spirit sent from above, toward the forms of understandings inscribed from eternity in our soul, it moves ineffable matters toward the investigable mysteries of God’s wills and operations—as though it were an elevation of our soul’s mind. For it wishes to see, even while situated in such a body, what is difficult merely to understand and impossible to express.

For blessed Paul says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are God’s judgments, and his ways beyond tracing out!” (Rom. 11:33). Isaiah too says: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Isa. 40:13). You see, then, how great a matter knowledge concerning God is.

But since you write so boldly concerning divine generation, we too shall first show you from the Scriptures that the generation of the Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, is eternal. Do you suppose that the Scriptures which we read are empty? If anyone is a Christian in reality as well as in name, he must venerate the Scriptures, which proclaim the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, if it is necessary for you to accept the Scriptures, it is also necessary to receive and believe the things said in them concerning Christ exactly as they are said.

They say that Jesus Christ is the Only-Begotten Son of God, as David the prophet says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten [Col. 1020C] you” (Ps. 2:7). And the apostle Paul: “Because he did not spare his own Son” (Rom. 8:32). And again: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. 1:3). Then Jesus Christ himself frequently says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); “Who sees me sees my Father” (John 14:9); and “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (ibid. 10–11). In saying these things he was God, if he did not lie; but if he lied, he is not a work of God perfect in every respect. These things are said often, by many, a thousand times: does it not appear to you that they are everywhere said in this way?

[Note: [Col. 1020D]

II.—“Omnipotent.” Mabillon: “omnipotent power.”

“And he supplies by ineffable generation.” These words are in Mabillon, p. 22, but absent from the *Orthodoxa*, p. 462.

“Whole.” We add this word from Mabillon. And shortly afterward, likewise from him: “Jesus, however, is this whole *being* (*ὄν*) itself.”

“In every way.” Thus Mabillon. But the *Orthodoxa* has “in all things,” less correctly. Soon afterward Mabillon has “perfect” for *teleion* (*τέλεον*) or *teleion* (*τέλειον*). A little later it has: “This is the Son, this is every *Logos*,” omitting what precedes.

“Truly.” Mabillon: “true.”]

II. Hear something else from us. We say that God is our Father, and most truly so. What is the cause, and in what respect? Because, I say, “in love he predestined us for adoption through Christ” (Eph. 1:5). Does God also have Christ as Son by adoption? No one has dared say this; perhaps not even you. Do you see what blasphemy arises from this assertion?

We say that we are heirs of God the Father, and through Christ heirs—sons by adoption; and that Christ is the true Son, through whom we are made sons and co-heirs in Christ himself. You have said many things about Christ, and they are true and as they stand: that he is God’s power, omnipotent, the universal *Logos* (*λόγος*), every operation, every life, and very many other things. Has he, then, attained goods of this kind, having been made from things which are not? And is blessed that which is not from what truly is? A mind that conceives thus is without God, sacrilegious, and full of blasphemy.

The Lord himself is above all things that are and all things that are not. If, as you say, he has been made from things that are not, will he himself be able to make from things which are not all the things that are? Yet we believe God to be that which is and always is, not that which at some time did not exist. Therefore he surpasses what is; through ineffable generation he surpasses existence, intellect (*νοῦς*), and life—not as one who is these things, but as above these things and always above all things.

Therefore, if God is not what is not, but is above what is, truly the One Who Is (*ὢν*), the power of the One Who Is (*τοῦ ὄντος*), roused by operation into generation, begot by an inexpressible motion the One Who Is (*τὸν ὄντα*), perfect in every way: the whole from the whole of power. God, then, is the whole pre-being (*πρόον*); Jesus, however, is this whole [Col. 1021B] being (*ὄν*) itself, but now in existence, life, and intelligence—universal being (*ὄν*) perfect in every way (*τέλεον*).

He is the end; he is the beginning; he is the Son; he is every *Logos* (*πᾶς λόγος*), he who is the *Logos* with God and in God; he is Jesus Christ, before all things that are and that truly are: the first and universal existence, the first and universal intelligence, the first being (*ὄν*), perfect in every way, the very first being; the name before all names, for all names are from him, as will be shown.

[Note: [Col. 1021C]

III.—“Being.” This word is absent from the *Orthodoxa*, but Mabillon has it.

“And by this very fact,” etc. Mabillon: “But let it be by this very fact that the cause is above true being (*ὄν*).” This seems less correct, as do the words immediately following.]

III. But I want to hear, my sweetest Candidus, what you judge that which is not to be. For if God is the cause of all things, God is the cause both of that to which being belongs and of that to which being does not belong. But if he is cause, he is not what is not. For the cause is being (*ὄν*), since from it and through it comes that to which being (*ὄν*) will belong. And by this very fact the cause is [Col. 1021C] truly above being (*ὄν*). Therefore that which is not yet being (*ὄν*), that is, which is not, has being (*ὄν*) as its cause toward becoming such. For this reason it is called pre-being (*πρόον*); and according to this account God is cause both of the things that are and of the things that are not.

[Note: [Col. 1021D]

IV.—“Wholly, in every way.” Thus Mabillon. But the *Orthodoxa*: “according to negation, so that it may be the privation of what exists, so that being is denied in every way.”

“And can be.” These words occur in Mabillon but are lacking in the *Orthodoxa*.

“Is.” Perhaps “to be.”

“Of the things,” etc. Mabillon: “to call being (*ὄν*) the cause because they are.” It would seem more correct from what precedes, if the wording were restored as follows: “to call being (*ὄν*) the cause of the things that are.” Yet perhaps nothing should be changed, because of what immediately follows.

[Col. 1022C] “Supreme,” etc. Thus Mabillon, whom we have preferred to follow. The *Orthodoxa*, however, reads: “God, then, is above being (*ὄν*); and according to that above which he is all things, God is called not-being (*μὴ ὄν*): not through privation of the whole of what is, but so that being (*ὄν*) itself is another thing, which is not-being (*μὴ ὄν*) in relation to not-being (*τοῦ μὴ ὄντος*), the things that are not (*τὰ μὴ ὄντα*), and not-being, and not truly not-being (*μὴ ἀληθῶς μὴ ὄντα*).”]

IV. What is not must therefore be defined. It is understood and named in four ways: by absolute negation in every respect, so that it is the privation of what exists; according to one nature in relation to another nature, so that this is not that; according to not-yet-being, which will be and can be; according to that which has being above all things that are, since it is none of these things and does not accord with any of them.

What, then, do we call God? Being (*τὸ ὄν*) or not-being (*τὸ μὴ ὄν*)? Surely we call him being (*ὄν*), because he is the Father of the things that are. But the Father of the things that are is not being (*τὸ ὄν*) if those of whom he is Father do not yet exist. One may not say this; it is impious to understand not-being (*μὴ ὄν*) as the cause of the things that are. For the cause is prior to those of which it is the cause.

God, therefore, is supreme being (*ὄν*); and because he is supreme, God is called not-being (*μὴ ὄν*)—not through privation of the entirety of that which is, but as another being (*ὄν*) itself, which is not-being (*μὴ ὄν*) in relation to the things that will be; not-being (*τὸ μὴ ὄν*) insofar as he is cause toward the generation of the things which are [Col. 1022B] being (*τὸ ὄν*).

[Note: [Col. 1022C]

V.—“It is true, therefore.” Here, toward the end of p. 462 of the *Orthodoxa*, several passages occur in a wrongly transposed order; they are known to concern §9, as we shall note at that place. In Mabillon’s edition, however, all proceeds correctly: the passages found here occur on p. 22; in the *Orthodoxa*, on p. 463, about the middle.

“Of being” (*τοῦ ὄν*). Thus the *Orthodoxa*. Perhaps “of the one who is” (*τοῦ ὄντος*). But I make no change. Mabillon, moreover, reads: “It is true, therefore, to say that God is Father, and by way of cause is also [Father] of the things that are. By will,” etc.

“And they both are and are called, and before generation.” These words are absent in Mabillon, p. 23, through a copyist’s error, evidently because of the repeated word “generation.” What immediately follows there is likewise represented less correctly.]

V. It is therefore true to say that God is father of *that which is* (τοῦ ὄν), as cause both of the things which are and of those which are not. By God’s will, therefore, both the things which are and those which are not come into generation. Do not suppose that the things which are not are so through a privation of the things which are. For none of these either exists or is conceived. For if the world and all things above are subsistent, all things are. There is no *non-being* (μὴ ὄν) in the sense of privation; rather, there is a certain conception by which, from the things which are, one conceives their privation—not a subsistent privation, not even a conception itself subsisting, nor existing in the manner of the things which are. Yet certain things which are not are in a certain way: such as those things which now indeed are, which after generation both are and are called such, but before [Col. 1022C] generation existed either in their potentiality or in their idea. But from where, or from what, were they generated? Namely, according to those modes: according to another nature, and according to that which is not yet, which will be and can be.

[Note: [Col. 1022D]

VI.—“Generator,” etc. Thus Mabillon. But the *Orthodoxa*: “He is generator and father, insofar as he is cause.”

“Production.” We preferred Mabillon’s reading to the other reading of the *Orthodoxa*, “producer.”

[Col. 1023C] “Other things which are not truly non-existent.” Thus Mabillon’s edition: μὴ ἀληθῶς μὴ ὄντα, “things not truly non-existent,” as the author himself says below. The *Orthodoxa* has: “other things which are not truly existent.” Shortly afterward Mabillon less correctly reads: “Into those things—fullness did not receive being.—For, insofar as it is being and being in some manner, [it is] fullness.”

Τῇ μόνῃ ἐμφάσει ὑπάρχοντος. Mabillon: “existing by the sole emphasis of existence.”

[Col. 1023D] “Subjection.” The *Orthodoxa*: “subjectio.” Or perhaps “subject”?]

VI. Thus God is first both above the things which are and above the things which are not, since he is their generator and father insofar as he is their cause. Then, according to the generation from God, or according to production, the things which are appeared. [Col. 1023A] But things which are not (μὴ ὄντα) also appeared. Of the things which are, some truly are; some are; some are not truly non-existent; others are not. But the fullness of God does not admit into being those things which truly are not. For the fullness of God is according to that which is being and that which is being in some manner. For this fullness exists, by a sole presentation, in the conception of those things which truly are not—things which, in accordance with subjection, arise from those which are not truly existent. Yet mind (νοῦς), initiating all things in some manner, has imagined something concerning that which truly is not.

[Note: [Col. 1023D]

VII.—“Yet in some manner.” Here Mabillon’s copyist was plainly blind.

“Judgment.” Mabillon: “existence.” And this kind of reading seems confirmed by what follows, akin to the preceding: namely, “existentiality,” “vitality,” “intellectuality.”

“Being.” We have borrowed this word from Mabillon, although in his text the following “we understand” is absent.

“For.” Incorrectly present in the *Orthodoxa*.

“Intellectualizes.” Mabillon: “gives a countenance.” Perhaps the latter is more correct; for below, §8, the author likes to say: “it is figured and given a countenance.”

“To something.” Mabillon: “somewhere,” which is unsatisfactory. Shortly afterward he likewise has only “to mind” and “to spirit,” omitting the remaining Greek.

“Thus the soul is substance.” These words occur in Mabillon but are absent from the *Orthodoxa*.]

VII. Hear how I speak. There are certain things of this sort which are manifest by nature, such as the things which are and all supercelestial things: spirit (τὸ πνεῦμα), mind (ὁ νοῦς), soul (ἡ ψυχή), thought (τὸ νόημα), instruction (ἡ παιδεία), virtue (ἡ ἀρετή), reason (ὁ λόγος), opinion, [Col. 1023B] perfection, judgment, life, understanding; and still higher: existentiality, vitality, intellectuality; and higher still than all these, being alone (ὂν μόνον), and that which is “one alone being” (ὅ ἐστι ἓν μόνον ὄν). If our mind (ἡμῶν νοῦς) enters rightly into these, it comprehends them and is formed by them; and understanding stands firm, no longer existing in the confusion of inquiry. But because such understanding is of another, a certain comprehension and definition results.

We understand other beings (ὄντα) to be merely beings, because whatever is such is another’s and other—like the intellectual in relation to the intelligible. Therefore the intelligible things are those which truly are; other things, which merely are, are intellectual things. Now all these are in the nature of intellectual souls which do not yet possess intellect: they are, but are fitted for understanding. For when mind (ὁ νοῦς) is awakened in the soul, [Col. 1023C] it brightens and illuminates the soul’s intellectual capacity, intellectualizes it and gives it form; and understanding and perfection are born in the soul. For this reason the soul is also called substance, because every substance is a subject. But a subject lies beneath some other thing; and the existence of the soul (ἡ ὕπαρξις τῆς ψυχῆς) lies beneath mind (τῷ νῷ) and the Holy Spirit (πνεύματι ἁγίῳ). Thus the soul is substance.

[Note: [Col. 1024C]

VIII.—“Therefore all things … not those which truly are.” This is Mabillon’s reading. But the *Orthodoxa* has: “Therefore all things which are and souls are merely beings, which are not truly [beings].” Shortly afterward Mabillon has: “The soul therefore does not apprehend the cause.”

“And beings.” Mabillon: “and beings, that is, those very intellectual things.” A little later the *Orthodoxa* reads: “But other things, and those which are not, from these,” etc. We follow Mabillon.

[Col. 1024D] “For,” etc. This passage is mutilated and corrupt in Mabillon, where it runs: “For it does not understand non-being (τὸ μὴ ὄν). Therefore it takes non-being as though it were an expulsion of being (τοῦ ὄντος). Expulsion …”

“And it is not as being.” Mabillon: “but nevertheless it is, though not as being is.” Shortly afterward likewise: “both in existence and in quality.”

“Unfigured.” Mabillon varies somewhat; shortly afterward he has: “and therefore those things are which are not truly non-existent.”

“A certain natural [order].” Mabillon: “this natural order of being: beings [from] being; non-beings [from] non-being; non-beings.”]

VIII. Therefore all things which belong to soul are merely beings [Col. 1024A], not those which truly are. The soul, therefore, comprehends those things which truly are; for if mind (νοῦς) enters into an intellectual soul, it also comprehends beings (ὄντα), and the soul understands truly existing things (ὄντα ἀληθῶς), since it is soul. Thus from those things which truly are (ἃ ἀληθῶς ὄντα εἰσί) arises understanding of the things which are.

But the other things which are not truly non-existent, and those which are not, receive understanding from these through the turning of the understanding of being (τοῦ ὄντος). For non-being (τὸ μὴ ὄν) is not understood insofar as it is non-being; rather, non-being is understood in relation to being (τὸ ὄν). Thus non-being is taken as a kind of expulsion of being (τοῦ ὄντος). But expulsion is something unfigured, and it is not as being is. For every being (τὸ ὄν), whether in existence or quality, is figured and given a countenance. But the unfigured is something; therefore non-being is in some manner something. [Col. 1024B] Therefore non-beings (τὰ μὴ ὄντα) are; and therefore things which truly are not are also. And, with regard to being, things which are not truly non-existent are prior to things which are non-beings. Hence a certain natural order arises among beings: from being (τοῦ ὄντος), beings (τὰ ὄντα).

[Note: [Col. 1024D]

IX.—“We have said,” etc. Thus continuously in Mabillon. But in the *Orthodoxa* the passages occur incorrectly transposed at the end of p. 462, as we noted above at §3.

“And in potency.” These words are absent from Mabillon.

“In nature,” etc. Mabillon: “in nature and in matter (ὕλη).” And shortly afterward: “and they have being.” Perhaps better.

[Col. 1025C] “Simply.” Mabillon: “simple.” And immediately: “Therefore those parts of this world which participate in intellectual soul are, in potency and in nature, among those things which are truly not.” This appears less correct, both in the distinction and in the text.

“But when the soul,” etc. Thus Mabillon. But the *Orthodoxa*: “But although it is substance, it is nevertheless changeable. How is this so? When the soul receives and understands animated and animal things,” etc.]

IX. We have therefore spoken of the things which are, and also of those which truly are. Let us now say what things truly are not, and what things are not.

Since God’s essence and potency are intelligible and intellectual, all things which are appeared through understanding. But understanding operates in two ways: through its own intellectual potency, and, by the limitation of understanding, also through sense. Again, since sense is an image of what is understood and a limitation of understanding, if it perfectly receives the operation of understanding [Col. 1024C] which strengthens it in working and acting, sense becomes close and neighboring to pure understanding. And it is this which comprehends heavenly things, things in the ether, and things generated and regenerated in nature and in matter (ὕλη), and other such things whose potency lies in sensible understanding. Such being is in some manner both being and non-being.

For heaven, everything in it, and the whole world consisting of matter [Col. 1025A] and form, exist in mixture; therefore it does not exist simply. Thus those parts of this world which participate in the potency and nature of the intellectual soul belong by nature among those things which are not truly non-existent. For they use understanding, but understanding according to sense; and according to sense they are changeable and mutable, whereas according to understanding they are unchangeable and immutable. But how does sense apprehend this? It apprehends only qualities; substance—that is, the subject—it neither perceives nor apprehends. For qualities are changeable, whereas substance is unchangeable. Yet although soul is substance, it is nevertheless changeable. How is this so? Understand it thus.

[Note: [Col. 1025D]

X.—“Changeable.” The *Orthodoxa* omits this word.

“Not truly non-existent” (μὴ ὄντως μὴ ὄντα). We have restored this reading, following the author, who elsewhere said μὴ ἀληθῶς μὴ ὄντα, “things not truly non-existent.” Both editions are erroneous. Mabillon has μὴ ὄντος μὴ ὄντα; the *Orthodoxa*, merely μὴ ὄντος. And immediately the same *Orthodoxa* manuscript, p. 463, about the middle, after the words μὴ ὄντος adds: “those things which will be and of which he is cause. But with respect to generation,” etc.—words found above at the end of §4. But the Mabillon manuscript which we follow inserts after μὴ ὄντα: “But when we understand,” etc., which occurs in the *Orthodoxa*, p. 464, final line and following. Clearly everything has been confused, whether through faulty assembly of manuscripts or scribal incompetence.

[Col. 1026C] “Which.” Perhaps another, rather than Victorinus, wrote this. A little later Mabillon has: “And the first qualities are fire, air, water, earth, each in itself without mixture.”

“Union.” Thus from Mabillon, in place of the *Orthodoxa*’s “one.”

“For quality cannot be.” The words found in Mabillon are absent from the *Orthodoxa*, perhaps because of the repeated word “quality.”

“The same [is] substance … and matter.” Here [Col. 1026D] we depart from Mabillon, who has: “the very same thing is the substance both of soul and of matter,” perhaps “of matter.”

“Wholly intelligent.” I would prefer “wholly not intelligent.” Mabillon: “wholly, altogether intelligent.”

“When it alone,” etc. Mabillon’s manuscript is very poor here.]

X. When the soul receives and understands the things which are in the world, if it understands those things which are animals and animate, [Col. 1025B] then insofar as they possess soul, they are things which are not truly non-existent. For in one manner they are non-beings (μὴ ὄντα), insofar as they possess soul; in another manner they are non-beings, insofar as they possess changeable matter (ὕλη) and changeable qualities. And these are what we called “not truly non-existent” (μὴ ὄντως μὴ ὄντα).

But when we understand matter under soul—by “matter in soul” I mean whatever exists without an intellectual soul, with sense extended around it—the soul comprehends, in relation to qualities, things which are as if non-beings. For qualities are changeable and, in this respect, non-beings. Indeed, the subject itself, which is called matter, is indeterminate and is therefore called without quality. But if it is determined, it is called quality and not qualified matter.

But there are primary qualities in primary bodies—fire, air, water, earth—which exist each by itself, without mixture or [Col. 1025C] union with anything. For if these are qualities and these are matter, qualities are therefore matter. For quality does not happen to matter (τῇ ὕλῃ) as an accident; rather, matter itself is quality. For quality cannot exist through itself, but through that which it is; by this very fact it is matter. And because it is always material (ὑλική), it is nothing other than matter.

Likewise, insofar as soul is intellectual, it is soul; and insofar as it is always moved and moves itself, not by duplication or [Col. 1026A] accident, it is soul. Rather, the fact that these are its qualities means that soul is substance. So also matter itself is quality; matter itself is substance. Yet soul differs from matter (ὕλη). For some say that soul is matter: that subject and quality are the same substance, and that soul and matter are the same substance. But it differs, as I said, because, being intellectual, soul understands itself. Matter, however, being wholly intelligent [probably “wholly not intelligent”], possesses neither understanding nor any sensation in sense. Therefore soul belongs to the things which are: when it is alone and pure, it belongs among the things which are; but when mixed with matter (τῇ ὕλῃ), it belongs among the things which are not truly non-existent. Matter (ἡ ὕλη) alone is the nurse of all things which are not. But soul and matter are nurse of all things; yet soul, by its own power, is nurse of all things and begetter of life, while matter [Col. 1026B], without soul, rendered barren and dense, remains forever, receiving animation from soul. These things, therefore, are and are called non-beings (μὴ ὄντα). Such is the case concerning the things which are not.

[Note: [Col. 1026D]

XI.—“The combination of these names.” Thus correctly Mabillon. But the *Orthodoxa*, p. 465, around the middle, after “combination,” has “and the only-begotten Son,” etc., which appears below in §15. But the words “of these names” and what follows occur there, p. 464, near the beginning. Clearly everything has been shamefully inverted.

“They differ.” This verb is absent from Mabillon.

“According to privation.” Both editions read thus, although something appears to be missing.]

XI. You have, then, four categories: things which truly are, things which are, things which are not truly non-existent, and things which are not. But through reversal and combination of these names, two further modes are understood: things which are not truly existent, and things which truly are not. Yet things which are not truly existent signify only things which are: for only those things are which are not truly existent. But things which truly are not have no place for being. For since all things are full of God, it is impious and impossible that things which truly are not should either be said to be or be. By understanding alone, as we have explained, things which truly are not differ not from things which are not, but arise in the soul from things which are according to privation, being established neither in their own substance nor in understanding.

[Note: [Col. 1027C]

XII.—“Made similar.” Mabillon incorrectly has “feigned,” it seems.

“And not itself that one.” Mabillon: “not that one itself.”

“Of which two … the others.” We have reconstructed this passage from Mabillon, whose *Orthodoxa* text is defective.

[Col. 1027D] “According to another [nature].” Mabillon: “according to a nature toward another, and according to that which is not yet; which is potential being, not yet actual being.”]

XII. Let us therefore proceed to see what God is and in what things he is. Is God in the things which are truly first and more honorable? Yet he is their cause, giver, and father. Nor may one say that he is those things to which he himself gave being. For, since he is one [Col. 1027A] and alone, he willed that things made similar should exist, but not that they should be that one himself. Rather, he willed that the fact of being one should be many things.

Perhaps you will say, O Candidus: “This is my argument; and according to this reasoning I say that the Son of God was born from things which are not, by election rather than generation.” But the non-beings (μὴ ὄντα) which we said to be—are they things that are altogether not? But it has already been agreed that they are not; and it has also been agreed that “things which are not” are spoken of in four modes: two according to absolute nothingness and according to being above all things; the others according to another nature and according to that which is not yet, though it is in potentiality toward being and is not yet actual being.

[Note: [Col. 1027D]

XIII.—“And beings of all beings” (πάντων ὄντων ὄντα). Mabillon: “and beings of being” (ὄντος; perhaps ὄντως, “truly”) “beings.” Shortly afterward: “without intellectual [faculty] … and that which is above all things, nothing of the things which are.” This seems less correct.

“And because [he is] above the things which are.” Thus Mabillon. But the *Orthodoxa*: “because he is above the things which are.”]

XIII. What, then, is God, if he is neither even the One nor the things which truly are, nor the things which are, nor the things which are not [Col. 1027B] truly non-existent, nor the things which are not? For God, as cause, grants all these things. But it is impious to suppose that God is among the things which truly are not.

Necessarily, therefore, we speak of God in priority and transcendence over beings (τῶν ὄντων): above every existence, above every life, above every knowing, above every being (ὂν), and as being of all beings (πάντων ὄντων ὄντα)—for he is unintelligible, infinite, invisible, without intellect, unsubstantial, unknowable; and although above all things, he is nevertheless nothing of those things which are. And because he is above the things which are, he is nothing of those things which are. Therefore God is non-being (μὴ ὄν).

[Note: [Col. 1027D]

XIV.—“May be understood.” Mabillon: “may not be understood.” Perhaps the latter is more correct from what follows.

“What then [is] God, who … produced beings?” Mabillon punctuates: “What then [is] God? He who … produced beings.”

“From nothing? But how?” Mabillon: “Therefore from nothing. And how [is this] from God?” A little later: “he generated being, although from nothing”—incorrectly.

[Col. 1028C] “For that which,” etc. Mabillon: “For what is first above being? It is hidden being.” Shortly afterward: “it is in generation.”

“He is cause also of being,” etc. Here we have reproduced Mabillon’s reading. The *Orthodoxa*, omitting “he is cause,” has only “and of being.” “For in generation, since he is above being, [he is] near to being, being both its father and generator.”

“And by generation … in potency.” Thus Mabillon. But the *Orthodoxa*: “and by generation being comes into manifestation, and by operation that which had already been from potency.”

“Being already.” The *Orthodoxa*: “which already”—without sense.]

XIV. But what is this non-being (τὸ μὴ ὄν) which is above being (τὸ ὄν)? It is neither to be understood as being, nor altogether as non-being, but as intelligible in ignorance, because it is being and [Col. 1027C] because it is non-being; and by its own power alone it brought being into manifestation and generated it. Now the account is as follows.

How did God, who is above being, produce beings (ὄντα) from what he himself is, as he himself is? From another? Or from nothing? From another? But from what other? For nothing existed before God. Nor did he produce them from another as God, because nothing is equal to him. From nothing? But how? For if he produced being (τὸ ὄν), it is more true to say that he who is above being generated [Col. 1028A] being from himself than from nothing. For that which is first above being is hidden being. But the manifestation of the hidden is generation. Indeed, being in potency generates being in operation; for nothing is in generation without a cause. And if God is cause of all things, he is also cause of being in its generation, since, being above being, he is nearer to being and is both its father and generator.

For a pregnant woman has hidden within her what she is about to bear. The fetus is not nonexistent before birth, but hidden; and by generation it comes into manifestation as that which it was in operation through having been in potency. And, to state what is true, being in operation is [the operation] of being; for it generates outwardly by operation. But what does it generate? What was within. But what was within God? Nothing other than being—indeed, true being; or rather [Col. 1028B] pre-being (πρόον), which is above every being: the genus, I say, which is being above the beings of being, being already as potency operates. This is Jesus Christ. For he himself said: “If [someone] asks, ‘Who sent you?’ say, ‘He Who Is’” (ὁ ὤν; Exod. 3:14). For that being alone, always being, is “He Who Is” (ὁ ὤν).

[Note: [Col. 1028D]

XV.—“The beings” (τὰ μὲν ὄντα). Thus the *Orthodoxa*, p. 464, final line, where it appears that τοῦ μὲν ὄντος, “of the being,” should be read. Mabillon does not recognize these words. What follows immediately—“and the only-begotten Son”—appears likewise in the *Orthodoxa*, p. 465, around the middle, with many passages inappropriately inserted. See the observations above on §11. In Mabillon everything proceeds properly, p. 24, near the end.

“Before all things … perfect being.” These words are absent from the *Orthodoxa*.

“This being was born in potency.” Conversely, these words are missing in Mabillon.]

XV. Therefore the Son, Jesus Christ, [is] “the beings” (τὰ μὲν ὄντα) and the only-begotten Son, because that pre-being (πρόων) generated nothing other than being before all things and being perfect in every respect. Such being cannot exist with another; and that which is perfect in every respect has no need of another. For universal being, being alone, the one, and the being which is the general genus above genus, is one and being alone.

But because this being is not that being which possesses perfect potency, that being was born in potency before all things which truly are and which are primordial beings (ἀρχαῖα ὄντα), from which [Col. 1028C] all things are (ἀφ᾽ ὧν πάντα εἰσί). He, I say, is he from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things which are. On this account being in operation is the image of that being which is in potency, remaining always in itself without any progression.

[Note: [Col. 1029D]

XVI.—“Again,” etc. Mabillon: “But again we have said that Jesus, not the Logos, is about God.”

“Then,” etc. This is the reading of the *Orthodoxa*. But Mabillon: “The thing itself cries out through the neck of John: the Aeons also confess that this is so.” Both are certainly corrupt.

“From an aeon” (ἐξ αἰῶνος). Mabillon: “from eternity.”

“The Logos was about God.” Here Victorinus undoubtedly alluded to John 1:1; but he appears less correctly, both here and frequently below, to have rendered the Scriptural words πρὸς τὸν Θεόν as “about God.” Yet below, §20, he acknowledges the Vulgate reading “with God” (*apud Deum*), and in §26 rejects “about God.”

“Because Jesus Christ.” Mabillon: “because God is being.” Shortly afterward: “is in the bosom of God.”

“The being or coming forth of Jesus.” Mabillon: “the being of God.”]

XVI. What next? We say that Jesus is the first being (τὸ ὂν), being before all things, through whom are all things which are. For this is the name above every name: being (τὸ ὄν) is the principle of names and the principle of substances, as [Col. 1029A] I have frequently made clear in many places.

Again, we say that Jesus Christ, being (τὸ ὄν), is naturally about God, and more especially that in the beginning he is Logos (λόγος), and that this Logos itself is God. Then, through John, we confess three “kerouchidia” (κερουχίδια; term uncertain) as eternal, and say that this is so. For it has been said that Logos is in the beginning; and, as you say, there is no principle which precedes another principle. For a principle without a beginning is called a principle, if indeed it is. Therefore he who was in the beginning is from an aeon (ἐξ αἰῶνος), whether in God or about God (John 1:1). For Logos was about God and in the beginning. Therefore he always was. If he always was, he must be, not among the things which are not, nor made.

John says (ibid., 18): “No one has ever seen God.” Again (ibid.): “The only-begotten Son of God, [Col. 1029B] who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared [him].” We therefore have these same things: that Jesus Christ is being (ὂν), that he is Logos, that he was in the beginning, that he was about God, that he was and is in the bosom. Do not all these things plainly and clearly signify that the Son of God—to whom these are attributed—is being and being before all things, if God the Father, before being is, is understood as being in potency of that which is being? This being sprang forth from its potency in its Father, receiving manifestation, though it had been hidden; and this is the divine and ineffable generation. Therefore the doctrine that Jesus is or proceeded from things which are not must be rejected.

[Note: [Col. 1029D]

XVII.—“Unmoved.” Mabillon incorrectly has “in motion” here and shortly afterward. A little earlier he correctly has “paternal” or “of the Father,” for which the *Orthodoxa* incorrectly has “fatherland.”

[Col. 1030D] “Potency.” Mabillon: “in potency.”

“God is Logos.” Thus Mabillon. The *Orthodoxa* incorrectly: “God and Logos.”]

XVII. Let us consider another point. Jesus is Logos (λόγος). What then is Logos? I say that it is a certain paternal [Col. 1029C] active power, unmoved, and constituting itself so as to be in act rather than in potency. If this is so, why was Logos about God? Necessarily, so that through the Logos itself (αὐτὸν λόγον) all things might be generated, and without him nothing.

God therefore works through Logos, and Logos always works. Logos is therefore an unmoved active potency, always working, and constituting that what was in potency may be in operation. This, then, is what we say was in the beginning. But being in the beginning signifies not being generated. And truly for this reason God is Logos: because he was in the beginning as God, and was about God. [Col. 1030A] Logos was not begotten, since God himself is Logos, but Logos at rest and silent. Thus you may see the necessity of recognizing that Logos was not begotten, far more than [of recognizing] that he himself came to be from things which are not.

[Note: [Col. 1030D]

XVIII.—“How is it moved?” Mabillon punctuates thus: “How is it moved? According to Logos?” Shortly afterward he reads “because” for “as if.”

“Cause.” Mabillon: “by causing,” which is unsatisfactory. Shortly afterward: “constitutive” for “constituted.” This is excellent, in my judgment.

“Of itself.” Mabillon: “to itself … from itself both Logos and God.”]

XVIII. What next concerning our knowing? How is it borne? How is it moved with respect to Logos? It does not see Logos as though it either exists for something else or belongs to another insofar as it is. It exists in order to constitute another being, and for no other purpose whatever. Therefore Logos is the father and generator of all things, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made.

But the power of Logos itself—the power to constitute and make another—must not be understood and heard as [being] like the cause of all things. For it is also constituted by Logos itself (αὐτοῦ τοῦ λόγου). If it is the first cause, it is not only cause of all other things, [Col. 1030B] but is cause of itself. Therefore God is from himself, and is God.

[Note: [Col. 1030D]

XIX.—“Because.” With Mabillon I prefer this reading to the *Orthodoxa*’s “that.”]

XIX. But because being itself—that is, moving and understanding—is acting, it is first potency; and constitutive potency, I say, is first. Therefore being itself necessarily precedes. Thus understanding, moving, and acting derive from that which is being. But being in act is according to what it is; that is, it is to be Son. Indeed, this is more [properly said] than that being itself which is Father: being is acting and working. For there, being is not one thing and working another. For that One is simple, one, and alone always. Therefore in the Father is the Son, and in the Son the Father.

[Note: [Col. 1030D]

XX.—“But this,” etc. Mabillon incorrectly has: “if this must be sought?” Shortly afterward: “Let us speak insofar as is permitted.”

“Romans,” etc. Thus Mabillon, though “as if inwardly” is absent there. The *Orthodoxa*: “The Romans say πρὸς τὸν ὄντα, ‘with the being,’ as if inwardly,” etc.

[Col. 1031D] “And this is God.” These words are absent from Mabillon, perhaps through a copyist’s carelessness.

“Principle.” This word too is absent from Mabillon. Shortly afterward he reads merely “unto action.” A little later: “but is generated by generation”—incorrectly.]

XX. How, then, did this come about? How are Son and Father [so], if they are simultaneous? Not only are both simultaneous, but [they are] one, alone, and simple. Yet this need not be asked; for it is enough to believe. Let us speak, then, insofar as permitted.

First, it is clear that Logos is neither something else nor from another, but about God. For the Gospel says: “In the beginning was Logos, and Logos was about God” (John 1:1). Again it says: “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (ibid., 18). How do you receive or understand these sayings? The Romans render πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, “with God,” as though inwardly, or wholly within—that is, in God’s existence—and this is true. For in being is inherent working. For Logos is in God, and thus the Son in the Father. [Col. 1031A] For being itself is cause for action: being must be first, and working inheres in it; and this is God. These two, then, are two, I say, according to power; but according to the understanding of simplicity, I call [them] one alone. Therefore, if being itself is the principle and cause of operation and action, acting is generated from being. But being is Father; therefore working is Son.

[Note: [Col. 1031D]

XXI.—“Of generation.” Mabillon: “of action.” Shortly afterward: “nor the presentation”—incorrectly.

“Into itself.” Mabillon: “to be into itself.” Shortly afterward, “preserves” for “preserved.”

“In every [thing].” Thus, excellently, Mabillon. But the *Orthodoxa*: “in man”—very badly.]

XXI. What then is generation, or the appearance of generation? First—if it is necessary to say this—lest anyone understand a temporal presentation (ἔμφασιν temporis). “First,” I say, according to understanding. We therefore say first that [God is] turned into himself, and that he moves and understands the blessedness set within in repose, preserved as perfect in every way. But the very blessedness [Col. 1031B] and greatness of God is both within and without, and moves and works. For everything which is all is both within and without. How this can be both within and without, while God exists in every thing and in the whole, must be said later.

[Note: [Col. 1031D]

XXII.—“Wholly absent.” Mabillon omits these words; shortly afterward he has “and eternal.” Neither is satisfactory.

“Perfect.” This reading of the *Orthodoxa* seems better than Mabillon’s alternative, “perfected.”

“Are.” This word is absent from Mabillon, apparently without justification. Shortly afterward he has: “but all other things without action.”

[Col. 1032D] “Into that which is acting.” Thus Mabillon. But the *Orthodoxa*: “into which is acting.”

“Thus this acting has both acting and being.” These words are absent from the *Orthodoxa*; we have taken them from Mabillon.]

XXII. Now receive the grounds for understanding that every implication of time is altogether absent, provided that all things are effected according to prior and subsequent without time. For all things are from eternity. Therefore God, in every respect perfect and beyond all things that are in every respect perfect—he who created all things and is the cause of all things—was not merely that very thing which was one and alone; but he was also the many and all things which are potentially capable of being, and he willed all things to be.
