But how could the other things exist without action? Therefore action sprang forth by God’s will; and that action itself was God’s will. For everything there is simple [Col. 1031C]. Therefore the Logos [Λόγος] who is in God is God himself, is will itself, is intelligence itself, is also life itself, is action itself. By a motion begotten from himself, it proceeded from that which is being into its own proper being—that is, into that in which acting consists. Acting itself appeared, and it indeed effected all things. Yet it was itself born from that which is being into that which is acting, having, in that which is acting, both being and existence. Just as that being has both acting and existence, so this acting has both acting and existence. Acting itself, however, is being; just as that being is that which acts. Therefore these two are one and simple.

[Note: [Col. 1032D]

XXIII.—“And this was.” Mabillon: “and it was in it.”

“And is not, etc.” Mabillon: “nor is it not consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον], because the being that is substantial is one for both, and indeed the action is one,” etc.

“Who is altogether the same as he.” These words are absent in Mabillon.]

XXIII. If this is so, Jesus is not from nothing: he who appeared as action from that which is being, since action itself was also that which is being. Nor, on account of [Col. 1032A] these two, is consubstantiality [τὸ ὁμοούσιον] absent; for that which belongs to one and the same substance is the same. Certainly one thing is one action, since acting itself and being are one. This is the Son; this is from the Father; this is with God; this is he who is in the Father’s bosom; this is within; this is without. For in operation he is without, while in that which is being he is within; and in the Father he is God himself in God, altogether identical with him; but as action he is the Son. And wherever he is, there are both being and action. In this way, then, there is both Father and God, and Son and Logos [λόγος].

[Note: [Col. 1032D]

XXIV.—“Has a place.” These words seem redundant if the interrogative is admitted. Mabillon’s reading is preferable: “Where is there room for anything else to be, and to be from another—and, still more, for Jesus Christ and the Son to be from nothing?”]

XXIV. Where, then, is that wicked and blasphemous conception? Where is there room for something else to be, and where is there room for it to be from another? Where is what it further says: that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is from nothing? Where is that which is nothing? How can that which is nothing enter into God or into God’s thought? [Col. 1032B] For a true conception proceeds from true things. But what truly is not is false. Therefore God does not conceive what truly is not. Yet we deceive ourselves, because we believe God’s power to be greater in this respect if he produces things which truly are from things which truly are not. But insofar as God’s power can do all things, so far, according to what belongs to power, it generates nothing other than things whose potentiality is to be. But for things which in every respect truly are not, there is absolutely no potentiality at all.

[Note: [Col. 1032D]

XXV.—“Things that are” [ὄντα]. We have taken this word from Mabillon; it is lacking in the Orthodox edition.

“And the restorer, etc.” Mabillon: “and the restorer into the angelic virgin did he not send forth from within?”

[Col. 1033D] “And again, etc.” Mabillon: “and again, from water, the living soul of birds and of other things in the water; and this from one thing into another; and this is from things which are not. But Jesus,” etc.

“Every spirit.” Mabillon: “I sent forth every spirit by breathing.” If he himself breathed: the Son is from God and was born Son; God did not make him.

“First of all.” Mabillon: “That the Word is first, and that the universal Word exists by God’s generation—the Word in every respect, the perfect Word—which,” etc.

“As the Hebrews.” Mabillon: “and the Hebrews: whether ‘in the head’ or ‘in the beginning,’ God made in Christ.”

“Whence then Christ?” Here we follow Mabillon’s reading and punctuation.

“We know.” Mabillon: “we are.” The rest is either corrupt or badly punctuated.

[Col. 1034D] “But as though existing.” Mabillon: “but as though existing, neither existing as being [ὄν], but as being [ὄν].” Thus, etc.

“And his essence.” Mabillon: “and we call his being essence [οὐσία], as having a different relation to that which is his being. Likewise,” etc.

“That . . . or man.” Mabillon: “because Christ was made.”

“This one.” With Mabillon we read thus. Orthodox edition: “Jesus.”

“Of existing substance.” Mabillon: “existing substance.”

“Consubstantial” [ὁμοούσιον]. Mabillon: “consubstantial” [ὁμοούσιος]. Thus, a little earlier, “consubstantial, substance” [ὁμοούσιος, substantia] also seems to require restoration.

“If the Son, etc.” These, according to Mabillon, are words of Candidus the Arian. For there it reads: “If Jesus is Son by generation; but if generation, then motion,” etc. See above, Candidus’s treatise, §7.

[Col. 1035C] “But whom did you lead around?” Thus, with Mabillon, we read. Orthodox edition: “But what did you lead around?” Perhaps “yourself,” but more likely “I mean yourself.”

“Begets.” Mabillon: “Therefore Jesus is by generation, because Jesus is Logos.”

“How, etc.” Mabillon: “how God and Logos [λόγος] are Father and Son.” And shortly afterward, “of living creatures” in place of “of a living creature.”

“Sanctification.” Mabillon: “signification.” And shortly afterward: “who indeed is himself Spirit.”

“And not to worship with one voice.” Mabillon: “and not to worship with a human voice as divine, but to wish to declare.” But, etc.

“Who, etc.” These words are absent in Mabillon.]

XXV. How, then, when there is no potentiality for things which truly are not, was action effected for things which are? For if God has the power to bring into being things which cannot be, then, according to potentiality, those very things which are altogether non-being [εἰσὶ μὴ ὄντα] already have being or are beings [ὄντα]. Therefore we said that those things are not [Col. 1032C] which, placed in concealment and in potentiality, have not yet appeared in action. For all things were in God. For the Logos [λόγος] is the seed of all things that are. Since the Logos is in God, all things that were made appeared in operation, that is, in the power of God, who is the Son of God.

XXVI. But certain sacrilegious persons say: “If the Logos was with God and the Son existed above God’s bosom, he is understood not to be within the bosom but outside it.” But what then? Did God breathe the soul into a human being from himself, from within; yet did he not bring forth from within the creator, deliverer, and sanctifier of that very soul, the redeemer and restorer of the whole body? Did he not send forth the angelic nature from within? When [Col. 1033A] he formed man from earth, and then cattle and quadrupeds, and again all living creatures from water, and those others in the air—each from one thing into another, and that first from things which are not—from where, then, do you say that Jesus came? For the Son is before all things. Is he then from emptiness, and altogether from nothing? Further, he formed his body. Did he not have a soul or spirit without a body before he entered the world? Did he have a soul? Then he breathed it forth, or breathed it out; for he did not breathe it into him. For how could he breathe it into him, when he did not yet have a body? But if that which he breathed out was the Son himself, then the Son is from God; and so too is the Spirit. For the Spirit is not from nothing. For God says (Isa. 42:5): “I myself sent forth every spirit.” Therefore, by breathing, God breathed upon himself, and [Col. 1033B] thus the Son was born. Therefore God did not make him. Thus he is not with God or above the bosom, outside, but within. David bears witness to both when he says (Zech. 12:1): “My heart uttered a good Word.” Therefore that which is the Son was not made as all things were, contrary to what God says. For if he was made, then before he was made, the Word of God was not.

XXVII. What, then, do we say? Must we not confess that, if the Word made all things, the Word is first of all things—as Word in every respect, the Word whom we, the prophets, and the evangelists call Logos [λόγος] and Son? Moses says thus (Gen. 1:1): “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Aquila renders the same passage thus: “In the head God made.” As the Hebrews pronounce Moses’ saying: whether “in the beginning” [Col. 1033C] or “in the head,” God made it in Christ. Therefore Christ is beginning and head. And this is frequently said: “He created all things in Christ.” For Christ, as Logos [λόγος], is the seed of all things. Therefore Christ is first, for he was before every creature. From where, then, is Christ? If he is Word, he is from God; if will, from God; if motion or action, from God. And if acting itself is being, then, with respect to being itself, the Father is; but the Son is action. And because being itself is action and acting is being, therefore the Father and the Logos himself [αὐτὸς λόγος] are consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον].

XXVIII. But how is there consubstantiality [ὁμοούσιον], when substance did not yet exist? Names, however, were devised and adopted from things which came later and from things which are after God. And because no name worthy of God can be found, we name God from things that we know, [Col. 1034A] while understanding that we do not name or call him properly. Thus we say, “God lives,” “God understands.” Accordingly, we name God’s actions from our own actions, though he exists above all things—not merely existing, but existing as though existing, “not truly subsisting, but being a little subsistent” [οὐδὲ ὄντως ὑπάρχοντος, ἀλλὰ ὄντος μικροῦ ὑπάρχοντος; reading uncertain]. In this same way we apply substance, existence, and other such terms to God; and we call his essence being [οὐσία] in one way, while created substance has another relation to what inheres in it, and also to its own being.

XXIX. Likewise, when we say that God became Christ or man, we do not mean that he truly came to be, but that he is one and is in all things and all things are in him. Therefore he is said to have become all things to all people [Col. 1034B] so that they might be—not that he became in order to be, but that he was made effective for their being thus. For it is not said, “The Son of God was made,” but (Acts 2:36) that he was made Lord for us; as Solomon says (Prov. 8:22): “And he made me above your ways.” For immediately afterward he posits eternal and divine generation (ibid., v. 25): “Before all, the Lord begot me.” And John says (John 1:3–4): “What was made, in him was life.” What next? Did not God make the creation, and in the creation first heaven and earth? Therefore he did not make Christ. Christ, then, was born, not made. For whenever he is said to have been made, after his first and eternal generation, he is said to have come to be after being effected. Thus he is said to have been made from a woman (Gal. 4:4); and in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2:36): “Therefore let the house of Israel know with certainty [Col. 1034C] that God made this Christ whom you bore on the wood of the cross.” All these things, I say, are said after the one, holy, and ineffable generation. They are not said with reference to his existence, but to the acts and administration of his power and might. Therefore, concerning the generation which is the Son of God, it is evident also that his substance is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον], in majesty, in its proper signification and understanding, when understood according to the being of existent substance. And thus it has been demonstrated how he is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον].

XXX. You have, my dear Candidus, what remains to be said. If Jesus is the Son of God, he is Son by generation. For you say: “If generation is motion, and motion is change, but it is impossible to conceive change in God, then it is necessary to say impiously that something [Col. 1035A] can be begotten from God. Therefore Jesus is not Son by God’s generation.” You have argued in good order—but whom have you led astray? Perhaps me? Rather, yourself. For you said that Jesus made God. What follows? Is making not motion, no less than acting is? For to act is to make, just as to make is to act. Therefore, since both are in motion, change must follow; and, as has been shown, it is incongruous to posit this in God. Therefore one must confess either that making is not motion, or that not every motion is change. But making is motion, and God made in accordance with motion; yet it cannot in any way happen that he is changed, and it is altogether unfitting for him to receive an accident in any manner whatsoever. Therefore it remains that not every motion is change. If not every motion is change, what [Col. 1035B] should rather be chosen concerning Jesus: that he exists according to generation or according to production? According to divine understanding, according to generation. For although God simultaneously says and does what he does, yet saying is motion, since silence precedes it; therefore, for one who is silent, speaking is change. But if God made through the Word, the Word existed before making. If the Word existed before making, then he existed before according to generation. For intellect [ὁ νοῦς] begets the Word. Therefore Jesus, who is Logos [λόγος], is generated.

Those knowledgeable in these matters say that Jesus is Son in three modes: by truth, by nature, and by appointment. He is Son according to truth by this very fact that he is substance; and for this reason he is at once and of the same substance—just as Father and Logos [λόγος], Son and God. He is Son by nature in animal generation. [Col. 1035C] He is Son by appointment in adoption. There are also other modes: by character, age, or instruction; as the apostle Paul says (1 Cor. 4:15), “I begot you.” Therefore the mode according to truth is the higher mode and [Col. 1036A] the most divine of all. But what the mode of his generation or sonship is, whether according to the meanings indicated or according to other modes, I entrust to God, by whose power this was accomplished.

XXXI. In other books, I believe, we have sufficiently said from whom there is procession and descent; and the return of the promised Holy Spirit has been explained; as also the threefold unity and the one Trinity. I cannot bear to hear your doctrine about the Holy Spirit, full of blasphemy: “That this Spirit is for sanctification, and only sanctifies and teaches; and that he was made, just like every creature.” Yet the Spirit himself differs from the Son in his proper action, though he is always present to him; just as the Son himself differs in action from his Father, who is Father [Col. 1036B] with respect to being. And thus, since these three are one and the same, there is one divinity and not a manifold majesty; nor is there either opposition or atheism [οὐδὲ ἀντίθεια μήτε ἄθεια], but three are one and one is three; and, set forth three times, the one is the same and alone. But another discourse of ours concerns these three.

XXXII. Save us now, Father; grant us our sins. Indeed, to say what God is is sin; to say how he is is sin; and it is sin not to worship, so far as is possible, with a single sober voice, but to wish to make declarations. Yet because you have given us, holy Lord and Father, the Spirit (1 Cor. 12:11), who apportions to us as he wills, grant us also knowledge. For we have faith, and we speak, though we possess every kind of ignorance concerning you. Nevertheless, always confessing you as God the Father, and the Son Jesus Christ our [Col. 1036C] Lord, and the Spirit in every word, who lives forever with you and the same Son. Amen.

[Col. 1035]

THE LETTER OF CANDIDUS THE ARIAN TO MARIUS VICTORINUS, RHETOR. (C, G)*

[Note: [Col. 1035D]

Letters.—Arius. Arius wrote this letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia; it is quoted by Epiphanius, *Haereses* LXIX, §6; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 5; and Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 9. The same letter exists in Latin in the *Tripartite History*, book I, chapter 15.

“Common.” It seems that *commonitam* should be read. In Greek, [Col. 1036D] ὁμοῦ τε ὑπομνῆσαι τὴν ἔμφυτόν σου ἀγάπην: “and at the same time to remind you of your inborn love.”

“And moves every evil.” Greek: καὶ πάντα κάλων κινεῖ, and thus it should be translated, “and employs every device.” In place of κάλων the translator read κακόν.

“Without God.” Greek: ἀθέους; Valesius translates it “impious.”]

[Col. 1035D] I. Although you may assemble many arguments and examples, my friend Victorinus, by which you may attempt to prove that Christ was born and not made, nevertheless Arius, a man of keen intellect, his disciples, and the outstanding Eusebius among them, have set forth their opinions on this matter in their letters; and we now append those letters.

From Arius to Eusebius:

“To the most desired lord, the faithful man of God, right in opinion: Arius, who suffers persecution unjustly from Pope Alexander because of the all-conquering truth [Col. 1036D] for which you too contend, greeting in the Lord. When my father Ammonius came to Nicomedia, it seemed fitting to send you greetings through him and at the same time to recall to you the love born within you and the affection that you have for the brethren because of the Lord and his Christ. For the bishop treats us harshly and persecutes us, and employs every evil device against us, so as to drive us from the city as men without God, because [Col. 1037A]

[Note: [Col. 1037B]

“Begotten-unbegotten.” Greek: ἀγεννητογενής ἐστιν.

“The Son coexists unbegottenly with the Father.” These words are badly punctuated in the editions. Greek: συνυπάρχει ἀγεννήτως ὁ υἱὸς τῷ Θεῷ, “the Son coexists unbegottenly with God.”

“Always begotten.” Theodoret: ἀειγεννής; Epiphanius and Nicephorus, however: ἀειγενὴς, with a single ν.

“Neither in thought.” Greek: οὔτε ἐπινοίᾳ οὔτε ἀτόμῳ τινί. Valesius: “Neither in thought nor by any instant of time.” Candidus the Arian’s version, “nor by anything minute,” is preferable. For mention of time, where the Son’s eternity is under discussion, seems less suitable.

“Always Son . . . Son from God.” The words “always Son,” stated a little earlier, are redundant here and absent from the text, which reads only: ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἑστι τοῦ Θεοῦ ὁ υἱὸς, “the Son is from God himself.” Moreover, all these matters are arranged differently in the Greek texts.

“Athanasius.” The printed editions incorrectly read “Anastasius.” Epiphanius, Theodoret, and Nicephorus have Ἀθανάσιος. Arius is evidently here naming Athanasius, bishop of Nazarborum [uncertain place-name], who undertook the Arians’ defense against Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, and who revealed his heresy more openly when he said that the Son of God was one of the hundred sheep—as the great Athanasius teaches us, *On the Synods*, §17.

“God exists before the Son without beginning.” Candidus adheres closely to the Greek, which reads: προϋπάρχει ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ υἱοῦ ἀνάρχως. Valesius more clearly: “The bishops throughout the East maintain that God, free from every beginning, exists before the Son.”

“To whom it has not sounded.” Greek: ἀκατήχητων, “those not instructed in the faith.” Shortly afterward the translator renders the Greek συναγέννητον, “co-begotten,” as *simul ingenitum*, “simultaneously unbegotten.”

“Sacrileges.” Greek: καὶ τούτων τῶν ἀσεβειῶν οὐδὲ ἀκοῦσαι δυνάμεθα: “But we cannot even hear these impieties.”

“We say and think.” Greek: τί λέγομεν καὶ φρονοῦμεν, “what we say and think.”

“Thought.” Greek: βουλῇ, “counsel.” Shortly afterward, “and aeons”: Greek πρὸ αἰώνων, “before the ages.”

“We are persecuted.” Greek: διὰ τοῦτο διωκόμεθα, “therefore we suffer persecution.” A little earlier in the text: οὐκ ἧν. ἀγέννητος γὰρ οὐκ ἦν: “He was not; for he was not unbegotten.” [Col. 1038B]

“The Son has a beginning, but God is without beginning.” This is indeed what the Greek says; but Valesius the translator omitted it, perhaps because the printer, seeing the repeated words “therefore we suffer persecution,” omitted it. [Col. 1038C]

“Now you know, etc.” This passage is badly transmitted in the editions: “Now you know, be strengthened in the Lord. Offer prayers (or, I offer), remembering our tribulations, truly fellow-Lucianist Eusebius.” Greek: λοιπὸν σὺ οἶδας. ἐῤῥῶσθαί σε ἐν Κυρίῳ εὔχομαι, μεμνημένον τῶν θλίψεων ἡμῶν, συλλουκιανιστὰ ἀληθῶς Εὐσέβιε. Valesius translates: “You know the rest. I pray that you may be well in the Lord, remembering our troubles, truly a fellow-Lucianist, truly Eusebius.”

“Because, etc.” Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 6, quotes this letter of Eusebius of Nicomedia to Paulinus of Tyre.

“Universal, etc.” Greek: καθόλου τῆς φύσεως τῆς ἀγεννήτου μὴ μετέχον, “not in any way a participant in the nature of the unbegotten.”

“Disposition.” Greek: διαθέσεως. Valesius translates “nature.” The ancient lexicographers discuss this word extensively; Hesychius above all: Διάθεσις, σχῆμα, ἀγάπη, ἀπόδοσις, προαίρεσις: “Disposition: condition, love, rendering, choice.”

[Col. 1038D] “And we do not READ these things, substituting them for ourselves.” Perhaps the translator wrote, as he often does elsewhere, λογισμοὺς, “reasonings,” for *legimus*, “we read.” For the text reads: καὶ ταῦτα οὐχὶ λογισμοὺς ἑαυτῶν ὑποθέμενοι. Valesius: “And these things are not conclusions reached by our own reasoning.”

“And made in substance.” Theodoret indeed has: καὶ γεννητὸν τῇ οὐσίᾳ. But our translator read γενητὸν, with a single ν. And Valesius himself would prefer this spelling, for, he says, it agrees better with the Arians’ doctrine, who said that the Son of God was made and created.

“To the maker.” Thus in the *Haeresiologion*, Basel edition of 1556. Incorrectly in the Paris *Bibliotheca Patrum*, 1644, “for making.” Greek: πρὸς τὸν πεποιηκότα, “to the maker.” Shortly afterward, “before the aeon”: Greek πρὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος, “before the age.”]

we do not agree with him when he publicly says: ‘He is begotten-unbegotten; always God, always Son; simultaneously Father, simultaneously Son; the Son coexists unbegottenly with the Father; he is always begotten; neither in thought nor by anything minute does God precede the Son; the Son is always Son from God himself.’ And because your brother Eusebius, who is in Caesarea, and Theodotus, and Paulinus, and Athanasius, and Gregory, and Aetius, and all who throughout the East say that God exists before the Son without beginning, have been made anathema—except only Philogonius, Hellanicus, and Macarius, heretical men, to whom it has not been made known that some call the Son an utterance, others an emission, others co-unbegotten. But we cannot even hear these sacrileges, even if the heretics threaten us with ten thousand deaths. [Col. 1037B] But we say and think, and have taught and do teach, that the Son is not unbegotten, nor a part of the Unbegotten in any manner, nor from any underlying subject; but that, by will and counsel, he subsists before times and aeons as full God, only-begotten, and immutable. And before he was begotten or created or determined or founded, he was not; for he was not unbegotten. We are persecuted because we have said: the Son has a beginning, but God is without beginning. Therefore we are persecuted also because we have said that he is not from existing things. We said this because he is neither a part of God nor from any underlying subject. Now you know. [Col. 1038A] I pray that you may be strengthened in the Lord, remembering our tribulations, truly a fellow-Lucianist, truly Eusebius.’ These are the words of Arius.

II. And Eusebius wrote such things to Paulinus in this manner concerning them:

“Since we have neither heard nor said nor believed, lord, that there are two unbegotten beings, or that one is divided into two, or anything corporeal that suffers; but one indeed unbegotten, and another who is truly from him, yet not made from his substance, in no way participating in the nature which is unbegotten, nor from his substance, but made altogether other in nature and power, to the perfect likeness both of the disposition and the power of him who makes what has been made. We have believed that his beginning is not only inexpressible in speech, but also incomprehensible in thought—not only for human beings [Col. 1038B] but altogether also for those who are above human beings. And we do not say these things by advancing reasonings of our own, but have learned them from holy Scripture. We have learned that he is created, founded, and made in substance, and that he has immutable and ineffable nature and likeness toward the maker; as the Lord himself says (Prov. 8:22–23): ‘God created me as the beginning of his ways, and before the aeon he founded me; before all hills he begot me.’ But if he were from him—that is, from him—as a part of him or from an outflow of substance, he would not be said to be created or founded; and you do not fail to know this, lord. [Col. 1039A]

[Note: [Col. 1039B]

“But also IN things unlike . . . naturally.” Read “OF things unlike.” Greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνομοίων αὐτῷ κατὰ πάντα τῇ φύσει. Valesius: “but also of other things which differ from him in every respect by nature.” Thus shortly afterward the Arian translator renders ἐπ᾽ ἀνθρώπων as “in human beings”; more correctly, “of human beings.”

“Clods of dew.” Theodoret follows the Septuagint of Job 38:28: τίς ὁ τετοκὼς βώλους δρόσου; Vulgate: *Quis genuit stillas roris?* “Who begot drops of dew?”

“To his likeness through him.” The words “through him” and several others are redundant here. The complete Greek passage reads: τὰ δὲ, πρὸς ὁμοιότητα αὐτοῦ λόγῳ ὅμοια ἐσόμενα, τὰ δὲ καθ᾽ ἑκουσιασμὸν γενόμενα. τὰ δὲ πάντα δι᾽ αὐτοῦ ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ γενόμενα, πάντα δὲ ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ. That is: “Those things which were to be like him in likeness by the Word were made by his will. But all things were made by God through him; and all things are from God.”

“And refuting . . . grace.” Greek: καὶ ἑξεργασάμενος κατὰ τὴν προσοῦσάν σοι θεόθεν χάριν: “and, working it through according to the grace given you by God.”]

For that which exists from the Unbegotten, if it was unbegotten from the beginning, truly could not have been created or founded later by another or by itself. But if to call it born is to posit some substance—as though it were from the paternal substance itself and possessed identity of nature from him—we recognize that Scripture has said not that he was born from God alone, but uses such language also of things naturally unlike him in every respect. For even of human beings it says (Isa. 1:2): ‘I begot and exalted sons, but they rejected me.’ And (Deut. 32:18): ‘You have forsaken the God who begot you.’ And elsewhere (Job 38:28): ‘Who,’ he says, ‘gave birth to clods of dew?’ This does not set forth nature from nature, but the generation, by his will, of the nature [Col. 1040A] proper to each of the things that have been generated. For nothing is from his substance; rather, all things were made by his will, each according to the way it was made. And he indeed is God. But some things, being to become like him, are like him through the Logos [λόγος]; some things are made according to participation in substance; but all things were made by God through him, and all things are from God. Receive these points and refute them according to the grace given you from God, and take care to write to my lord Alexander. For I believe that if you write to him, you will put him to shame. Greet all who are in the Lord. May divine grace preserve you safe, lord, and praying for us.”

[Col. 1039]

VICTORINUS AGAINST ARIUS (C)

BOOK ONE

[Col. 1039]

[Col. 1039B] I. In the first discourse of this work, my friend Candidus, you also advanced and discussed many points, including some stronger than these. Although they have been refuted as they ought to have been, we nevertheless wished to hear these things from their letters, so that, while we convict these by every refutation, we may also overcome the former arguments by refuting these men themselves. First the opinions of Arius and Eusebius must be defined: in what they agree with us, in what they differ, and in what they seem to disagree with themselves.

Arius says that the Son is not unbegotten. Eusebius says likewise that there are not two unbegotten beings. This too is our view. Arius says that the Son is not a part of the Unbegotten and is not from some underlying subject; Eusebius says these same two things. And he adds: “nor is the one divided into two,” which means that the Son is not a part of the Unbegotten. But Eusebius says: “He is neither a part nor an outflow.” We likewise deny this; for the Son is neither a part of the Father [Col. 1039D] nor an outflow which, flowing from him, would diminish that from which it flowed. But we cannot accept that he is not from a subject—not because we say that he is from some subject, but because he is from the Father as Son.

Arius says that the Son subsists by God’s will before times and aeons. Eusebius says likewise: “Before all aeons and before all times”; but we say that he was begotten, not made, not created, not founded. Arius says that the Son was made—namely, full God, only-begotten, immutable—who was not before he was created, because he is not unbegotten. Eusebius says the same, adding that the Son is like the maker of all things. We, by contrast, say not that he is like, but that he is the same, since he is from the same substance.

Moreover, Eusebius adds that the Son’s beginning cannot be known by a human being [Col. 1040B] nor by any higher power or thought; and yet he dares to say that the Son is a product of fabrication, subsisting by the Father’s will and determination, without existing from any source. Is this not to state the Son’s beginning? For if he says this, the Son is from non-existent things; he is neither of the Father, nor a part, nor an outflow. He knows not only the beginnings but also the rational principles [τοὺς λόγους] of the beginnings. But if he does not, what audacity is it to say: “This is God; this is Christ; this is Father; this is Son”? We, however, speak of the Father as Father and of the Son as Son.

II. And first, just as he believed that he had established in five little verses what he asserted—that the Son was made and not born—so we shall first teach, from all sacred reading, that the Son was born. Then, with the permission of God’s Spirit, we shall establish as far as we can that this very Son is substantial. Let this be our first beginning.

Paul writes to the Ephesians (Eph. 3:14–21): [Col. 1040D] “For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened in power through his Spirit in the inner person; that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, rooted and founded in love; that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth; and also to know Christ’s love, which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God. To him who is able to do above all things more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power working in us—to him be glory in Christ Jesus and in the Church [ἐκκλησίαι], through all generations of the ages.”

What appears from these words? That it is possible to know God and God’s Son—and how he is Father and how he is Son. There is also this in the Gospel according to John (John 1:18): “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the Father’s bosom, has made him known.” Therefore it is possible to speak of God, and hence also of the Son. For who made the Father known? The Son. Who is this? He who is in the bosom. Therefore the Son not only proceeded, but is always in the bosom, a sufficient teacher concerning the Father.

What did he declare? How God is. Jews and pagans had declared things beforehand; what, then, did he declare? That God is Father, that he himself is Son, that he is from the same substance, and that he came forth from the Father. For he says (John 8:19): “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.” He would never have said, “You would know,” unless he were Son, and Son substantially: “If you knew me, you would know my Father.” For if he were a product of fabrication, [Col. 1041B] the Father would not be known from him; rather, as Paul said (Rom. 1:20), God’s power and divinity would be known: “For his invisible things, understood through the things that have been made from the creation of the world, are known—his eternal power also and divinity.”

The Holy Spirit also declared Christ, as the Savior says in the Gospel according to John (John 16:16): “The Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things.” If these things are so, then we have learned both Father and Son in the holy Scriptures and from the Spirit, whom the holy person has as teacher through faith.

III. Let us, then, speak from the Scriptures, and first from John. For he says (John 1:1) how the Logos [λόγος] was in the beginning, was with God, and was God. Does he speak of another Logos? Entirely of the Son. What then is the Logos, if he is from no underlying subject? How does the Logos have the power for all things to be created through him, if he himself is from no underlying subject? For it is impossible that that which was made from nothing should be the seed of all things that are.

Further, if he was in the beginning, how is he beginning? Insofar as he is beginning, he is without beginning; he who was in the beginning was always. What audacity, then! What blasphemy, to say “There was a time when he was not,” when John says so often: “The Logos was in the beginning, was with God, and the Logos himself was God. He was in the beginning with God.” Although *was* has the signification of past time, it frequently signifies not being without beginning; but here it must be understood as without beginning, because he said: “In the beginning he was.” You yourselves also signify this when you say “before times” and “before aeons.”

He says (John 1:3): “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” For what is there that does not receive, through the Logos [λόγος], that it may be? The Logos alone, precisely as Logos, is being both for himself and for others, and himself bestows [Note: [Col. 1041D] “Himself bestows.” It seems one should read either “he bestows” or “when he himself bestows.”] being upon all things that are. Therefore he is equal to the Father. For the principal cause is cause both for itself and for other things, in power and substance, being cause. But the Father is prior to the cause. The Son differs from him in this: that he moves and acts in manifestation, while the Father acts unknowably for us because of his great divinity. For the Father is above blessedness [Col. 1042A] and therefore is repose itself. For acting, even if it effects imperfection, involves the strain of motion; this blessedness is perfect insofar as it acts.

IV. Hear, then, something further. That which is being is the Father; that which is acting is the Logos. And prior is that which is being; second, that which is acting. Being itself indeed has action implanted within it; for if by motion—that is, by action—there is life or intellect, then it is not merely being, but is itself that which is primary being. Therefore it is proper to it to rest, being solely itself. In this manner that which is acting also is, though it is second; since it is called “acting” not when it acts within, but when it acts outwardly. For when action becomes manifest, it both is and is called action, and is reckoned and is as a generation of itself [Col. 1042B].

Thus that very thing which is acting has being—or rather, does not have it: for acting itself is being. For to be and to act are simultaneous and simple, such being the nature assigned to the things above: according as it rests, being and substance; but according as it is in motion, action and operation. Yet this being-in-motion is the manifestation of that which is being in respect of action.

And therefore [John 1:9], “There was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world.” Therefore the Logos is the true light; and therefore [John 1:3–4], “What was made, in him was life, and the life was the light of human beings.” And the Logos himself, the true light [John 1:19], “was in the world, and the world was made through him”; he is the Son of God, of whom it says [John 1:18]: [Col. 1042C] “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the Father’s bosom, himself has made him known”—concerning the Logos.

V. Above, he has stated and joined together all things concerning the Son, declaring no other Son than the Logos. Thus the Son was with God, and was in the beginning, and was himself God, and through him all things were made, and he is the only-begotten. And, as it were, proceeding from the Father, he was with the Father in respect of acting; but, in respect of being, existing in the Father’s bosom, he made the Father known, having become the manifestation of the Father according as he acts. Pre-eminently, the Logos himself is the Son, himself the light, himself the life.

That the Son is God, John says thus [John 1:1]: “And the Logos was God.” And again [John 3:13]: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven.” That the Son is life [John 3:15]: “That whoever believes in him may not perish”; and again: “But may have hope, eternal life.” That he is the Son [John 3:16]: “Thus he delivered up his only-begotten Son.” He called him Son, his own, and only-begotten. What more is needed for a true Son? That he himself is life: “that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but may have eternal life.” That the Son himself is Christ [John 3:17]: “For God did not send the Son to judge the world, but that he might save the world.” That he is light, he says of him [John 3:19]: “Because the light came into the world.”

John was not the true light, and therefore he says [John 1:20]: “I am not the Christ, but [Col. 1043A] I have been sent.” Therefore John was sent. But Christ, the Son [John 3:31], “who comes from above is above all.” And again: “Coming from heaven.” It is indeed said that he was sent by God—as [John 3:17]: “For God sent the Son.” But these two expressions, “coming” and “sent,” signify that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. For Christ says to the Samaritan woman concerning life [John 4:10]: “You would ask him, and he would give you living water.” And again [John 4:13–14]: “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water which I shall give him shall not thirst for ever; rather, the water which I shall give him will become in him a spring bubbling up into eternal life.” That Christ is Savior [John 4:42]: “And we know that this is the Savior of the world.”

That he is the Son of God [John 5:17]: “My Father works until now.” Who says this? Christ. What blasphemy would it be for him to call one Father who was not Father? What would be the wrath of the Jews [John 5:18], who heard God called Father and were angry with one who said that he was God’s Son, if he were not God’s Son? For if he had not been, he would not have said it. But he did say it, and he said it as a worshiper of God; therefore he said it in truth, and for this reason the unbelief of the Jews is punished.

VI. After these things, his entire reply to the Jews declares both Christ as Son and God as Father [John 5:19–21]: “What the Father does, I also do. The Son does nothing from himself, unless he sees the Father doing it; for the Father loves the Son. The Father raises from the dead; the Son also raises.” [John 5:26]: “The Father has life in himself; the Son also has it.” And then throughout.

That the Logos is Son and the Son is Christ [John 5:38]: “And you do not have his Logos abiding [Col. 1043C] in you, because you do not believe him whom he sent.” That he is Son [John 6:32]: “My Father gives you the true bread from heaven.” That Christ is not a human being from a human being [John 6:33]: “For the bread is from God, which descends from heaven.” That he is life: “And gives life to the world.” And afterwards he says [John 6:35]: “I am the bread of life.” That he is from God [John 6:46]: “No one has seen the Father except the one who is from the Father.” That Father and Son are one in the other [John 6:58]: “As the living Father sent me.”

If the Son is life and the Father living, the Son is in the Father. For just as that which is prior is followed by its quality, so God, who is living, is first, and then life. For he who generated life is living; life lives from the living Father. Life is not prior, and then God living; rather, God living is prior. Thus there is life, and thus living life. And therefore he then says [John 6:57]: “And I [Col. 1043D] live because of the Father.” Therefore the Father too is in him. That he is both bread and life: “And whoever receives me shall live because of me” [John 6:59]. “This is the bread descending from heaven: not as your fathers ate and died; whoever eats this bread shall live for ever.”

VII. Does a human being who is merely human say these things concerning himself? If a human being says them, he blasphemes; and [John 9:31] “God does not hear sinners.” But Christ says that God hears him. Therefore he is neither sinner nor merely human. And it has been said [Ps. 108:3]: “Vain is hope in a human being.” And it is said [Ps. 19:8]: “But we hope in our God.” Therefore Christ is God, not of another substance [John 6:58]: “The Father is living, and I live because of the Father.” And [John 6:35, 48]: [Col. 1044A] “I am the bread of life”; [John 6:59], “whoever eats this shall live for ever.”

All these things signify one substance. Therefore Jesus, who says these things, says that he is from above [John 6:63]: “If, then, you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?” That God is spirit has been said [John 4:24]: “God is spirit.” And that the Son is life-giving spirit—and that this faith in Christ is perfect—Peter says [John 6:69–70]: “You have the word of eternal life, and we have believed in you, Lord, because you are Christ, the Son of God.” What is “the word of eternal life”? That whoever hears you shall live eternally. That he is from God [John 7:29]: “I know him, because I am from him.” That Christ is the Father’s substance [John 14:10–11]: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” This is not through dignity alone, but through substance.

[Col. 1044B] For if only through dignity, how does he himself say [John 14:28]: “My Father is greater than I”; and how does the Father send and the Son get sent? Again, dignity is given to the Son by the Father. Accordingly, in this respect the Father is in the Son. Does the Son also give dignity to a Father who does not possess substance? Therefore both the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father.

VIII. But enough of these matters. Again, that Christ himself, who is the Father’s Son, is himself also the Holy Spirit [John 7:37–38]: “Jesus stood and cried out: If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water flow from his belly.” That saying indeed concerns the person who receives the Spirit: the one receiving the Spirit becomes a belly, pouring out rivers of living water. But Christ gives this Spirit; he also gives living water, as he himself says. Scripture spoke this concerning the Spirit.

Therefore the belly which receives the Spirit—and the Spirit himself—is a belly from which rivers of living water flow; as Scripture says [John 7:39]: “But he said this concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were about to receive; for the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.” Yet again, the rivers are of the Spirit, while the belly from which the rivers flow is Jesus; for Jesus is Spirit. Thus Jesus is now the belly from which rivers of Spirit flow. For as the Son is from the Father’s bosom and in that bosom, so the Spirit is from the Son’s belly. Therefore the three are ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, of one substance); and therefore in all things there is one God.

That he is not from the world [John 8:3]: “I am the light of the world”; for through him the world lives, and will live so long as it obeys him. That all three are spirit has already been said [John 4:24]: “God [Col. 1044D] is spirit.” And when some said [John 8:19], “Where is your Father?” he said: “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you could know my Father also.” But the Holy Spirit is manifestly Spirit; and all these things are both Father and from the Father. Therefore they are ὁμοούσιον. For they are not spirit as other things are: those are from God, not from God’s own being. Therefore these three are ὁμοούσιον.

That the Son is true [John 16:27–28]: “For I came forth from God,” as from the Father’s bosom, “and I come into the world.” That Christ existed before he was in flesh [John 8:56, 58]: “Abraham, your father, rejoiced to see my day; and he saw it and rejoiced.” And again: “Before Abraham, I am.” That he is not merely human [John 9:5]: “While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” Who gave sight to the blind man? [Col. 1045A]

> **Note [Col. 1045D]**
>
> “And I.” Perhaps: “but I.”
>
> “Before Abraham.” We have judged that the printed codices, which read “before Adam,” should be corrected thus.
>
> “You will believe.” Perhaps: “you may believe.”
>
> “That he himself does, and will do, all things.” This seems the reading required [Col. 1046D]: “That he himself does,” for it refers to [John 14:12], “The works which I do, he also will do … because I go to the Father.” Thus immediately afterwards, “and what you rise in my name” should plainly be read “what you ask,” since he is citing John 14:13 here.

A human being? Impossible. And that he is the Son of God [John 9:35–37]: “Do you believe in the Son of God? He answered: Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him? Jesus said to him: You have both seen him, and he who speaks with you is he.” That he is of the same substance and power [John 10:30]: “I and the Father are one.” And again [John 14:10–11]: “The Father is in me, and I in him.”

IX. Hence it is said in Paul [Phil. 2:6]: “Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God.” These things therefore signify both one substance and one power. For how can he say, “I and the Father are one,” and “The Father in me and I in the Father,” unless he had substance and power from the Father, generated wholly from the whole? And how, “He did not consider it robbery to be equal with the Father”? [Col. 1045B] For he did not say, “He did not consider himself equal,” but “He did not consider equality robbery.” He therefore wishes to be inferior, not wishing to regard being equal as robbery. For in these words, to consider or not consider equality robbery concerns things that are equal.

But we thought that “equal” was said with respect to power. First, this is not Arius’s doctrine, that the Father is greater in dignity, power, splendor, divinity, and action; for he said “equal.” And if they are equal in this respect, it is impossible for them to be equal in this respect unless they also have the same substance. For in God, power, substance, divinity, and action are themselves one and the same. For all things are one, one simple reality.

Add to this: if the Son were from another substance, and especially if from nothing, what substance could receive these divinities and powers? [Col. 1045C] Equality is joined to equality, and like to like. Therefore Son and Father are equal; and for that reason the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, and both are one.

X. But enough of these matters for the moment. Let us consider those words of John. The Savior himself says [John 11:25]: “I am the resurrection,” because he himself is life. But who is this? Martha says [John 11:27]: “You are Christ, the Son of God, who came into the world.” He is not Son in the way that we are: we are sons by adoption; he by nature. Christ too is in a certain sense Son by adoption, but according to the flesh [Ps. 2:7]: “Today I have begotten you.” For if this were all, he would have only a human being as Son; but by saying [John 8:58], “Before Abraham, I am,” he made clear that he was Son by nature first. Therefore the Photinian doctrine is not true.

Further, we are sons not only as nations, but also as those who have been scattered [Col. 1045D]. Christ, then, is God’s Son, and we too are sons; but we are sons through adoption, through Jesus Christ, as scattered sons. Is Christ Son in that same manner? Jesus is therefore Son by nature; we are sons by adoption. That he is Son by nature, he himself often says [John 11:41]: “Father, I give you thanks that you heard me”; and [John 12:27]: “Father, save me from this hour”; and again [John 16:28]: “I proceeded from the mouth of the Father.”

These things are not said, as we say, merely with reference to God as Father. For God is neither a liar nor impious, calling himself Son and calling God Father when he was not at all Father. Rather, on account of the body he introduced suffering, so that all things might be fulfilled in the mystery. That Christ existed before he was in the body [John 12:28]: “I have glorified, and I shall glorify again”; for in the mystery, in flesh, he humbled himself. Therefore Jesus was glorified before this and after this. That he is represented as fearing and asking certain things on account of the mystery [John 12:30]: “This voice came not because of me, but because of you.” Likewise, I do these same things not because of myself, but because of you.

XI. That Christ himself, the Son of Man, is light in the world and Son of God [John 12:34–35]: “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains for ever; and how do you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is the Son of Man?” Jesus said to them: “For a little while longer the light is among you.” And then [John 12:36]: “While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become children of light.”

That he is ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*, of the same substance) with God [John 14:6–7]: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. If you have known me, you will know my Father also; and from now on you know him and have seen him.” And again, to Philip [John 14:9–10]: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” And again, these and such sayings, in which it is evident that the Father is according to what he is, and the Son is according to what he is, and therefore they are two. But because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, they are ὁμοούσιοι (*homoousioi*, of one substance).

One should therefore not say “two persons, one substance,” [Col. 1046C] but “two, Father and Son, from one substance”: the Father giving the Son substance from his own substance in that by which he generated the Son; and both are ὁμοούσιοι.

“That he himself does, and will do, all things, because I am from the Father” [John 14:13]: “And whatever you ask in my name, this I shall do, that the Father may be glorified in me.” That the Paraclete and Christ [John 14:15–16]: “If you love me and keep my commandments, I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you for ever.” But who is the other Paraclete? [John 14:17]: “The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot see,” because it does not see him. But they saw another Paraclete, namely Christ, who was in flesh; they did not believe in him. That the Paraclete is Christ’s power [ibid.]: “But you know him, because he remains with [Col. 1046D] you.” Therefore Christ gave him to them; for he said: “He remains in you and is in you.”

XII. What is evident from these things? If God is spirit, and Jesus is spirit, and the Holy Spirit is spirit, the three are from one substance; therefore the three are ὁμοούσια (*homoousia*, of one substance). That the Holy Spirit is from Christ, as Christ is from God, and therefore the three are one [John 14:18]: “I shall not leave you orphans; I shall come to you.” And again [John 14:20]:

> **Note [Col. 1047D]**
>
> “Christ, God, sent [him].” The Basel edition reads, “God sent Christ.” That is, “that which is.” Thus the Paris and Lyons editions; but the Basel edition reads, “into that which is.” And immediately: “but the Holy Spirit, acting operation, is regeneration into that which is.”

“You will know on that day that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.” These things are according to spirit. That the Paraclete is from the Son [John 14:26]: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things which I have said.”

From these things it is evident that God is in Christ and Christ in the Holy Spirit: Christ is the first Paraclete; the Holy Spirit is the Paraclete. Then Christ, God, sent [him]; the Holy Spirit says the very things Christ spoke. But Christ spoke in parables and performed signs: therefore all things were hidden because he was in flesh; as he himself was inward, so too the truth was inward in parables and signs. But the Holy Spirit teaches all things. For the Holy Spirit speaks to the human spirit; he speaks that which is, and speaks what is without any figure. Therefore [Col. 1047B] he will teach you.

And what does he speak? “Whatever I shall have said,” Christ said. “I shall have said” is future. Of what future? Not of what is now, but of what is after ascending to the Father. And if this Paraclete, coming from God in Christ’s name, teaches the things Jesus says, then is Jesus himself in him—or is he another Jesus? Or does Jesus dwell in that other Paraclete, that is, the Holy Spirit, as God dwells in Jesus?

In this sequence, with three existing, the three are one and ὁμοούσιον; for Christ says [John 14:28]: “I go and come to you.” Another Paraclete will be given to you by God, who has from me whatever he has; and the Father handed over all things to me that he has. For this is the whole mystery: the Father, inoperative operation; the Son, operative operation, that is, regeneration; but the Holy Spirit, operative operation in the regeneration into that which is [Col. 1047C].

XIII. But these things have indeed been said elsewhere too. That the Logos—that is, Jesus or Christ—is equal to the Father and inferior [John 14:28]: “I go to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.” Paul also says [Phil. 2:6]: “He did not consider it robbery to be equal with God.” And it has been said [John 10:30]: “I and the Father are one.” And both the Father and the Son are operation; and he would not have said, “The Father is greater than I,” unless he were equal. Furthermore, if he is wholly from the whole, light from light, and if the Father has given the Son all that he has—all things being substance, power, and dignity—then the Son is equal to the Father, but the Father is greater, because he gave him all things and is the cause of the Son’s being and of his being in this manner.

But the Father is greater in this respect: he is action without active exertion, more blessed because he is without trouble, impassible, the resting source of all things that are, perfect from himself and lacking nothing. But the Son received being; and, proceeding from action into acting, coming into perfection, fullness is effected through motion. Yet because all things are generated in him, into him, and through him, he is always fullness and always a receptacle; in what sense he is both impassible and passible. Therefore he is equal and unequal: the Father is therefore greater.

That the Paraclete is from God and from Christ [John 15:26]: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who comes from the Father.” That the Logos has a twofold power in relation to God: one manifest, Christ in flesh; the other hidden, the Holy Spirit. Therefore, while the Logos—that is, Christ—was present, the Logos in hidden form—that is, the Holy Spirit—could not come [John 16:7]: “For if I do not depart, the Paraclete will not come to you.” Thus these too are two, one from another: the Holy Spirit from the Son, rationally as the Son from God, and the Holy Spirit from the Father.

That all three are one: the Father is not silent silence, but a voice in silence; the Son is now voice; the Paraclete is the voice of the voice [John 16:13–14]: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth; for he will not speak truth from himself”—for Christ is truth—“but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will tell you things to come. [Col. 1048B] He will honor me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” Then he adds [John 16:15]: “All things which the Father has are mine.”

Therefore he says, “He will receive from what is mine,” because there is one motion—that is, one acting action—Christ and the Holy Spirit. And first is living, and from living comes understanding: Christ is living; the Spirit is understanding. Therefore the Spirit receives from Christ, Christ himself from the Father, and therefore the Spirit also from the Father.

XIV. Therefore all things are one, but from the Father. That Christ proceeded from the Father—that is, that God sent him, that is, that he proceeded from God—he says [John 16:27–28]: “For I proceeded from God; I proceeded from the Father.” It should be noted that he also said: “And I came forth.” But he placed first, “I proceeded from God,” which signifies that God sent him. Believe, then, this first: “I came forth from God.” But from what God, and as who? From that God who is my Father: “I proceeded, then, from the Father and came into the world.”

The natural order of this statement is: “I proceeded from the Father, I came forth from God, I came into the world.” But the order of effect and speech is determined by the hearers: “Because you loved me and believed that I came forth from God”; for this is first in faith. Then he says, “I proceeded from the Father,” explaining from what source he was, whence they too say [John 16:30]: “We believe that you came forth from the Father.”

Why, above, did he omit “God” and “Father”? For he does not say [John 8:16], “I am not alone, because the Father is with me”; and it is not to be understood that the Father suffered, for it was not he, but his human being. That he came for the resurrection of the flesh [John 17:1–2]: “Glorify the Son, that the Son may glorify you, as you gave him authority over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you gave him.” Therefore Christ is not merely human, but God in a human being. That to have life is to believe in the Lord and in his Son [John 17:3]: “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” That he was before the world [John 17:5]: “And now, Father, glorify me with yourself by the glory which I had before the world was.”

That human beings are from God, but not from God’s own being [John 17:6–7]: “I have manifested your name to the human beings [Col. 1049A] whom you gave me.” From this it is evident that not all were yours, and you gave them to me, and they kept your word. “Now they have known that all things which you gave me are from you.” And what is remarkable if human beings are from God, when flesh also is from him, since he formed it? What then? Is Christ from him in this same way? Far be it. The whole passage establishes this: human beings are from God, but not all in the same way.

And again this: that Christ was before the foundation of the world; that the Father handed everything over to the Son, if he gave even the name. For he says [John 17:12]: “I kept them in your name, whom you gave me.”

XV. Therefore we have that Christ has the Father’s name, that he is life, and that he has power to give life. That he himself is life and the Father is life has been said [John 6:58]: “The living Father sent me.” This is the substance of God and Christ; therefore they are ὁμοούσιοι. Then it has been said that Christ is light and God is true light; these things concern understanding. Is the Holy Spirit something else? Nothing. Then light is not substance; thus they are ὁμοούσια. And the Son has all things which God has; therefore they are ὁμοούσια. But more on this later.

That he was born [John 18:11]: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, that I might reign.” That the Holy Spirit is from Christ [John 20:21]: Christ breathed and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” All these things are according to John’s Gospel. Let us consider a few things also according to Matthew, for I pass over the similar passages.

That Satan too confesses that Christ is God’s Son, for he says [Matt. 4:3, 6]: “If you are the Son of God.” And he says this three times. But in the second instance, confessing concerning the Son of God, he tested whether he himself was Christ, saying: “You are the Son of God; throw yourself down. For it is written that he will command his angels concerning you.” He confesses: one who says “concerning you” confesses God’s Son, and confesses this one. Then demons also confess again [Luke 4:41]: “Demons went out from many, crying and saying: You are the Son of God.”

Hear, Arius; hear, Eusebius; and all you Arians, hear—especially you who say that Christ is “from him who is being,” but in the serpent’s sense: because the Father is ὤν (*ōn*, “the one who is”), who made Christ; hence you call the Son from that which is being. Hear, then: Satan calls him God’s Son—Satan, to whom the kingdom of the world was promised, who knows all things in the heights, for from there he is. What else does it mean, after the third temptation, that the devil departed, having confessed that he was God’s Son? The demons too said that he was God’s Son [Col. 1049D] [Mark 1:24]: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come?”

That one ought not doubt concerning Christ [Matt. 11:6]: “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized in me.” That the Son possesses all things of the Father [Matt. 11:27]: “All things have been handed over to me by the Father; no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” What is the reason that only the Son knows the Father, or that the Father knows the Son, unless no one else has his substance? For all things in splendor, divinity, power, and action both know the Father and worship him. But since knowing—that is, knowing God himself—is what it is for him to be, namely his substance, therefore no one knows God except the Son, who has the same substance and has it from him.

In no other way could anyone see, as it has been said [John 1:18]: “The only-begotten, who is in the Father’s bosom, has made him known.” What is it to be God? For in the bosom and in the μήτρα (*mētra*, “womb”) of substance, both are ὁμοούσιον, existing alike in substance and divinity; each is in the other, and each knows the other.

XVI. What then, Valentinus, do you say? The first αἰών (*aiōn*, “aeon”) proceeded, and, wishing to see the Father, could not. John says that the Son is in the Father’s bosom and is always so. Therefore he not only sees the Father, but is also always in the Father.

That it is a great sin to speak against the Holy Spirit [Matt. 12:31–32]: “Every blasphemy and sin will be forgiven human beings. And if anyone speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy [Col. 1050B] Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” First, one must observe that the Holy Spirit is God’s Spirit. For he said [Matt. 12:28]: “In the Spirit of God I cast out demons.”

Then, concerning the blasphemy and sin which the Jews committed, as he said, of what sort it is against the Holy Spirit: first, blasphemy and sin against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven anyone. Sin is to speak blasphemously with intention. But this does not suffice. Second, he said that even if someone unwillingly speaks any sort of word—which is not sin—it will not be forgiven him in any age.

Therefore, if the Holy Spirit is God’s Spirit, and the Holy Spirit has all things from God’s Son, the three are one substance from the Father’s substance, ὁμοούσια. Therefore the three are, that is, substance together. For if the Spirit is the Father’s substance, and the Son is Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is the Father’s Spirit, [Col. 1050C] in what order is the Holy Spirit placed? He both precedes, if he is the Father’s Spirit, and follows, if he has what he is from the Son. And again, the Son, according as he is Spirit, is one with the Father; and the Father is in the Son, and all exist reciprocally in one another. Therefore they are ὁμοούσιοι, possessing one and the same substance, and always together ὁμοούσιοι, possessing their proper subsistence according to action by divine affection.

XVII. But the matters stated in the Gospels are again sufficient for us. That Christ is God’s Son, the Savior himself says [Matt. 22:43, 46]: “How do they say that Christ is David’s son, when David himself says in the book of Psalms: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand’? David, therefore, calls him Lord; how then is he his son?” In this he shows that Christ existed before he was in my flesh [reading uncertain: “my flesh”], that he is God’s Spirit, and that he is God.

Let us also consider the Apostle. He says concerning Christ to the Romans: that Christ is God [Rom. 2:5], “on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God.” Without doubt this is about Christ, for he himself will judge; because before God τὸ μὴ ὄν (*to mē on*, “that which is not”) is nothing. Paul adduces an example from Genesis [Rom. 4:17]: “I have made you father of many nations before the God in whom you believed, who makes the dead alive and calls those things which are not as though they were.”

That the Spirit of God is the Spirit of Christ, and the same Spirit is the Holy Spirit [Rom. 8:9]: “But you are not in flesh but in spirit, if indeed the Spirit [Col. 1051A] of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person is not his.” The power of the whole mystery is in baptism; its power lies in receiving the Spirit. If this is so, it has been said: “You are in spirit,” which the Holy Spirit has given you. Who is this Spirit? He adds: “If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.” Who is he? “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ.” Therefore the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are the same.

Here one must also observe that the Spirit of Christ is the same as Christ himself. For it follows [Rom. 8:10]: “But if Christ is in you.” Hence the Spirit of God is God. Therefore there is one substance, because the Spirit is the same; but it is in three, and therefore ὁμοούσιον. Hence not similar substance, because the Spirit is the same. Yet for that reason the affections are not the same in the Father, because the Spirit is one; for such affections are, as it were, in only two, because they are now proceeding spirits.

XVIII. But these matters more fully later (Rom. 11:36): “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.” “From him” is said with reference to the Father; “through him,” with reference to Christ; “in him,” with reference to the Holy Spirit. Elsewhere, however, he says thus: “In him, through him, unto him.” That Christ is God (Rom. 9:5): “From whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed through all ages of ages.” In the First [Epistle] to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 2:8): “For had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” That Christ, like God, is incomprehensible, or scarcely comprehensible, is also shown by what was said (ibid., 9): “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him.” [Col. 1051C] Then he says that these things are understood (ibid., 11): “As the spirit of a human being [knows] the things that are in the human being, so also the Spirit of God [knows] the things of God.” If he says these things concerning Christ, it is apparent from them that it is not easy to know the generation of the Son. For neither *nous* (νοῦς, intellect) apprehends God’s Son, nor can it know the manner of his generation. But if he speaks of his presence, this too is above eye, above hearing, above *nous*. But if, as some understand it, he says these things of what God has prepared for those who love him, the generation is much more wonderful and scarcely comprehensible.

If these things are thus beyond understanding, what can you say on their basis—that Christ is from things which are not, or that Christ is of similar substance? Those things are comprehensible and definable. But to be *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιον, of one substance) is not only incomprehensible, but involves many apparent contradictions. For if he is *homoousios*, he too is unbegotten; if *homoousios*, how is he another? How is one Father and another Son? If *homoousios*, how did one suffer and the other not? From this arise the Patripassians. But since the Spirit who dwells in us searches all things by God’s will, even the things of God, the manner of divine generation will be found, according to which *homoousios* will also be made manifest and those objections will be eliminated (1 Cor. 2:12): “For we have received not the spirit of the world, but [the Spirit] of God.”

That the same Spirit is God and Christ and the Holy Spirit, and that he is one and the same Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3–6): “Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus be accursed’; and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit. Now there are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; [Col. 1052A] and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all.”

Therefore, if no one says, “Jesus be accursed,” in the Spirit, he is the Spirit both of God and of the Holy Spirit. Of him he says this same thing: “And no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” Further, he says that the divisions of gifts are from the Spirit: the gifts indeed are from God, but the divisions are from the Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is one mode of existence in action, but in substance he is *homoousios*, since the Holy Spirit is as is also the Lord’s ministry: for he himself divides ministries, working in the operation of life, and he himself is in his substance according to the operation of life. But in substance he is *homoousios*.

That the Spirit and operations are from God. The operations are many, [Col. 1052B] but in all [is] the same God. God differs in that he himself makes the divisions of operations, yet he himself works all things in all. For, since being itself is the cause of operation, he makes divisions of operations; and since God himself is, according to substance, Spirit, *homoousios* with action, therefore all three are *homoousioi* in action and *homoousioi* in substance. That all three are Spirit, and that the Spirit is from the Father: from the Father in substance.

XIX. That Christ is life and that he is Spirit has been said (John 6:63): “The Spirit gives life.” And again there he says (2 Cor. 3:17): “But the Lord is Spirit.” That Christ is from God, not from things which are not (2 Cor. 4:4): “That the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, might not shine upon them.” If Christ is the image of God, Christ is from God. For image is the image of that which is image-forming. [Col. 1052C] But God is image-forming; therefore Christ is image. Yet image is the image of the image-forming, and what is image-forming is primary. The image, however, is second, and is other in substance from that which is image-forming.

But we do not understand image here as in sensible things. For there we do not understand the image as substance: it is a certain shadow in air or in water, a figure produced by the reflection of a corporeal light and corporeal emanation; in itself it is nothing, has no movement of its own, and possesses only the substance of that which is image-forming—neither body, nor sensation, nor intelligence. When that in which it has been figured is removed or disturbed, it is altogether nothing and nowhere.

In another way, therefore, we say that Christ is the image of God: [we say] that he is first being, and exists through himself; that he is intelligent being; and [Col. 1052D] we call the image living and life-giving, and the seed of all things that are. For he is the *logos* (λόγος), through whom all things [exist], and without him nothing [exists]. But all these things are also attributed to God; therefore God and the *logos* are *homoousioi*.

And why is the *logos* the image of God? Because God is hidden, for he is in potency; but the *logos* is manifest, for he is action. This action, possessing in potency all things that are, brings forth and manifests all things by life and knowledge according to motion. Therefore action is the image of all things that are in potency, perfecting the form of each of those things which are in potency, and existing through itself; for no substance is from nothing. For every being has an inseparable form; rather, form itself is substance—not because form is prior to that which is being, [Col. 1053A] but because form makes determinate that which is being, namely, the form. For that which is being is the cause of the form’s being in that which is. And therefore that which is being is Father; that which is form is Son.

Again, because being itself bestows upon form being itself, the being of form is the image of that which is being. This is according to causality: the first being is *homoousios*, therefore being belongs to the two themselves; and the second being is the image of the first being without time. I call them first and second according to causality. One is other than the other with reference to being itself: Father and Son. But because the cause is not reversed, the Father is Father and the Son Son. Yet in that which is being both are together, and both always [are together], *homoousioi* according to being; but according to potency and action, the Father is potency, the Son action.

Therefore the Son is begotten, possessing being in action and potentially, just as potential being has action-being in itself potentially. “Has,” however, understand according to conception: for he does not have it, but is it. For all things there are simple. Yet I spoke according to the Gospel (John 16:15): “Whatever the Father has, the Son also has.” According to this account, the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father; both are *homoousioi*, and the Son is the image of the Father, for the being of the two is *homoousios*. But inasmuch as one is from the other, there is image-forming and image. And again, inasmuch as one is other than the other, one is unbegotten and the other begotten. Yet these are without time: they are in the beginning, and from eternity unto eternity. Therefore neither those who call Christ a human being, nor those who say that he is from nothing, nor [Col. 1053C] those who assign him some time, nor others of this kind, have any place in this consideration.

XX. Let us also consider this. Moses records God’s saying (Gen. 1:26): “Let us make the human being according to our image and according to [our] likeness.” God says this, “Let us make,” to a co-worker—necessarily Christ—and he says, “according to [our] image.” Therefore the human being is not the image of God, but [made] according to the image. For Jesus alone is the image of God; the human being, however, is according to the image, that is, an image of the image. But he says, “according to our image.” Therefore Father and Son are one image. If the Son is the image of the Father, and the Father himself is image-forming, they are *homoousioi* in respect of image. For image itself is substance: there, being and acting are one and simple; and so too are substance and form.

But since substance [Col. 1053D] is image, Father and Son are *homoousioi*: the Father is, according to being, also acting; the Son is, according to acting, also being; each has that by which he is, according to that in which he most especially is—being being prior to acting. The Father, however, is being, and most especially the Father is being itself, in whom action is present potentially. Again, since acting is later, the Son is later than being, having sonship in acting from the first being. Therefore there is one Father according to being, one Son according to acting, each existing together in the other, as has been demonstrated: therefore they are *homoousioi*.

Let us then say: “Let us make the human being”; and what is “according to the image”? And what is “according to our [image]”? Then what is “according to likeness”? For this wording signifies a difference both of image and of likeness. Although there is much question as to what he meant when he said, “Let us make the human being according to our image,” we may now grant that it concerns the human soul, or both [soul and body]; for, whether it concerns the soul alone, nothing else is understood except the soul. For it alone is according to the image of God and according to likeness.

We say that Christ, the *logos* itself, is the image of God. Therefore we call the mind (*animus*) according to the image of God, calling it rational. For the soul is not *logos*, but rational; and Christ is wholly life, whereas the soul lives because life has substance. Therefore the soul is according to God’s image, but Christ is God’s [image]. What then do we understand by “according to likeness”? [Col. 1054B] Just as the *logos* is substance, as has been explained—for to be *logos* is itself being, and being itself; and *logos* is acting and is being in motion, and, because all this there is simple, being and acting are the same, which there is substance—so too, what the soul is as soul is being and is substance. But that it moves itself is the image of substance; rather, it is substance itself according to the form of substance. Thus, when in defining the soul we say, “What is the soul?” we properly and substantially say: “That which moves itself.”

It is also clear from this that the substantial image—or rather the substance—of the soul is that which moves itself. This is rationality: to be rational according to the image of the *logos*. Therefore it is one thing to be according to the image, which belongs to substance; another to be according to likeness, which is not substance but a name declarative of quality in substance. But just as we have understood God, and also the image—that is, Christ—as substance, so we understand perfection as signifying “according to quality.”

And if “similar” necessarily signifies quality, how do we say that the soul is rational and perfectly rational according to the likeness of perfection in God?
