We say that the soul is perfect according to the image, therefore even now and in the world; but according to likeness, later, through faith in God and in Jesus Christ—such as it would have been had Adam not sinned. Thus, in so far as it is rational, it is according to the image with respect to reason; in so far as it is to be perfect, it is according to likeness. Therefore it is one thing to be an image, another [Col. 1054D] to be according to the image, and still more another to be according to likeness. What blasphemy, then, is there in calling the Father and Son *homoousioi*, when the Son is image according to substance, not according to likeness? But enough of this for now.

XXI. Let us proceed to other matters. That there is creation in Christ, but not one [single creation]. For there are three creations: one, indeed, when all things were created through Christ; a second creation of us in Christ according to baptism; but in Christ another transformation also takes place. Hence (2 Cor. 5:17), “If anyone [is] in Christ, [there is] a new creation.” It is said that before Christ was in flesh (ibid., 21): “Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us.” At what time did he not know sin? Before he was in flesh. To the Ephesians: [Col. 1055A] that before Christ was in flesh (Eph. 1:3–4): “Blessed [is] the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, according as he chose us before the foundation of the world.” That Christ was before he was in flesh (Eph. 2:12): “For you were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel.” That Christ is God (ibid.): “Having no hope, and without God.” This means, without Christ.

That he is Spirit who binds all things together (Eph. 4:3–6): “Desiring to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one Spirit. One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all, who is in all, and through all, and in all.” To the Galatians, that Christ is God (Gal. 1:1): “Paul [Col. 1055B] an apostle, not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.” And again (ibid., 11–12): “The Gospel which was preached by me is not according to a human being; for neither did I receive it from a human being, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.” To the Philippians, that Christ is Spirit (Phil. 1:19): “And through the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.”

That the Son is *homoousios*, and together with the Father (Phil. 2:5–7): “Have this mind in yourselves which [was] also in Christ, who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of a human being, and found in appearance as a human being.” First, let Photinus, and those with him and before him who call Jesus a human being and say he was made only from a human being, recognize their impious blasphemy in “[Christ], who existed in the form of God.” When did he exist? Before he came into a body; for he said that he emptied himself and took the form of a servant. Therefore he existed before becoming human. And what was he? God’s *logos*, the form of God.

What is this, “existing equal to God”? [It means] that he is of God’s very own substance and power; for he said that he was equal. For “equal” is declarative both of magnitude and of quantity; but magnitude is the magnitude of a substantial mass. Quality has no magnitude, nor does it possess being from substance. Only that which is quantitatively substantial is quantitative in magnitude. Therefore blessed Paul, declaring God’s substance, speaks of all the dimensions (Eph. 3:18): “That you may know God’s height, length, breadth, [and] depth.”

[Col. 1055D] XXII. Accordingly, Christ exists equal to God. For he did not say “similar to God,” which does not signify substance but something other in substance, similarity being according to an accident—as the human being is according to likeness to God, since the substance of God is one thing and that of the human being another. Hence it is impious to say that a human being is equal to God. Therefore if Christ is the form of God, and form is substance—for form and image are the same—and if the *logos* is the form and image of God, and the *logos* is always with God, the *logos* is *homoousios* with God, with whom the *logos* is in the beginning and always.

That being image and substance, and being together with substance, is what is called *homoousios*, is apparent from this. For the Apostle said: “He emptied [Col. 1056A] himself, taking the form of a servant.” Did he take merely the form of a human being, and not also human substance? For he put on flesh, was in flesh, and suffered in flesh; and this is the mystery and our salvation. Therefore, if he emptied himself, and Christ emptied himself, Christ existed before he was in flesh. And if he existed before this, since he emptied himself, he himself put on flesh. For why did he empty himself if, as you say, O Marcellus or Photinus, he assumed a human being as though it were a fourth [entity]? For the *logos*, remaining what it was, ought to have assumed a human being and in some fashion breathed spirit into [that human’s] actions. But he said, “He emptied himself.” Rightly so: he who was to put on a human being.

What then is “he emptied himself”? [It means] that the universal *logos* was not universal in that in which he is *logos*, [but became] flesh, and became [Col. 1056B] flesh. Therefore he did not assume a human being, but became human. Thus form is substance, together with the substance in which form is; therefore it is *homoousios* with the primary substance and with that which is prior in potency, which bestows on form both being and substantial being, and [bestows that] they are always together; for without one the other is not.

Therefore, inasmuch as form is from substance, substance is the form belonging to substance: this is God’s Son. That form is substance, and that substance is always with form: [therefore] the Father is always [Father], the Son always [Son] in relation to the Father—that is, the *logos* with God—and this is always so. But since this form is substance, image, and *logos*, which we call the Son of God, it is *logos* inasmuch as it is the *logos* of all things that are. For the universal *logos* is the Son of God, by whose power all things proceed, come forth into generation, and subsist.

Therefore his power, proceeding and at the same time existing with the Father, makes and generates all things. And that same power, in its advance—which is called action—suffers, if it suffers anything, according to the materials and substances to which it gives what is proper to their being; while the universal *logos*, who is always with the Father and *homoousios*, remains unchangeable and impassible. [Col. 1056C] Therefore it is said of the Son that he is impassible and passible; but passion belongs to the procession, especially to the furthest point of the procession, that is, when he was in flesh. For those things are not called passions: generation from the Father, the first motion, and being creator of all things. For these are substantial, or rather are substances, since the *logoi* of existing things are their substances according to potency. Therefore they are not passions.

XXIII. But enough of this. Again, what then do the Photinians say? If the Son is *homoousios* with the Father, how did God have as Son a human being born from Mary? And what do the Arians say? If the Son is *homoousios* and *logos*, and substance together with the Father? For it is impious to say: “There was [a time] when he was not.” And this too is impious: that he is from things which are not.

Those, again, who say that the Son is *homoousios* with the Father are impious. For substance, in so far as it is substance, is not another [substance] such that it may be similar to another: it is the same in two, and is not similar but itself. But when it is another, it is called similar not in respect of what it is as substance but in respect of a certain quality. Therefore it is impossible and incongruous that anything should be *homoousios*. Furthermore, [Col. 1057A] what is similar, being in otherness, is either in the same [substance], divided into two parts, or in another [substance]. For what is capable of being dissimilar is capable of being similar. But substance, in so far as it is substance, does not admit similarity or dissimilarity; rather, in so far as it admits [such predicates], it is said to be similar or dissimilar in quality, while substance remains in its own potency or existence, either the same or different.

But is that substance of God or of the *logos* capable of dissimilarity, so that it may be called similar? But this is impossible; therefore it is not similar, and therefore not *homoousios*. Let us also consider this: if similar substance is in the same genus, as [the genus] of human being or animal—for a human being is similar to a human being and an animal to an animal—or in another genus, as a stone to a human being, or a statue to a horse, [Col. 1057B] how do they say that these two are *homoousioi*? If in the same genus, as in animal, substance takes precedence. But if in substance itself, either [it is] divided, or born from another, higher substance. Yet either case is subordinate, and one is subject; but if divided, [it yields] neither unequal nor equal [things], nor does one possess another as perfect, but there are two perfect [things], and perfect from perfect. Therefore [they are] not in similarity itself, since similarity too [is something distinct]. If this is so, it must necessarily be in another genus. From where, then—is it something else? Therefore [is it] from nothing? Or [are there] two principles? But none of these [is true], since there is one principle and the cause of all things that are: the Father according to the *logos* who was in the beginning and therefore always was. Therefore he was not from nothing. But if this too [is granted], neither [is there] similarity in the sense of another genus.

But how does he say not that Jesus considered himself equal to God, but that he did not consider equality with God a seizure? For those things which are equal by nature are not equal through a divinity of their own; but things made equal by fortune are equal, as though by seizure. Therefore there is great confidence, and a truly natural divinity, in not considering equality with God a seizure.

XXIV. But enough of this. And again, what does he say to the Colossians: that Jesus is first before all things (Col. 1:17)? For his generation is twofold: one into divinity and sonship, hidden, divine, and understood by faith; the other, his coming into flesh and bearing flesh. The former is only generation from God, a manifestation of power; the latter is rather an assumption of flesh, not [Col. 1057D] generation.

Therefore, if he is prior, the Savior is not from a human being; if [it] is generation, he is not a fabrication; but if generation is from God, [he is] not from nothing. If Jesus is the image of God, he is *homoousios*: for image is substance together with the substance whose image it is and in which the image is. And that image is substance, generated from the substance in which it is or subsists, declares the power within: hence the Father, who is within; hence the Son, who is without.

Again, because the Son is *logos*, he is substance hastening into action. For life is *logos* and intelligence is *logos*; it proceeds into the substance of intelligible and material things. Therefore the action of the *logos*, because of the weakness of those receiving it, is passible—or rather is called passible. For blessed Paul says of Christ [Col. 1058A] (Col. 1:13–20): “Who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption and remission of sins; who is the image of the invisible God, firstborn before every creature. For in him were created all things, those in the heavens and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers: all things have been established through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things consist in him. He is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, firstborn from the dead, so that he might become first in all things; because it pleased [God] that all fullness should dwell in him, and through him to reconcile and restore all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven.”

The whole mystery is set forth in this exposition: that he is *homoousios*, [shown] from “who is the image of the invisible God”; that the Son is firstborn; that he did not say “created before every creature.” For if he too had been created, he would not have said “before every creature”; and he properly said “firstborn,” which concerns the Son. Let us then join the meaning: “firstborn before every creature.” Therefore he is begotten as Son; that creation is as what has been created. But [this does] not [mean] that he afterward begot another, but that he is firstborn before every creature.

Now every creature includes things in heaven and things on earth, visible and invisible. Therefore the Son is outside creation; therefore he is Son by nature and generation. That Christ is *logos*, and that the *logos* is the cause to all things that are of their being: hence it was said that all things were created in him [Col. 1058C] and through him. For *logos* is both the cause of being to things that are and the receptacle of those things which are in him. But because all things are in him, this receptacle itself is filled with all things that are, and it itself is fullness. Therefore (Rom. 11:36), all things are through him, all things unto him, and all things in him.

XXV. Therefore if the Son were from nothing, how could these things be? Thus without faith it is impossible for such things to be so. Again, if he is not *homoousios*, how are both Father and Son fullness? For all things together are fullness. Or is fullness *homoousios* in the way souls and other created things are? This is wholly impossible. For *homoousios*, as has been said, is in otherness: for another cannot be said to be of similar substance unless it is not in that [substance]. But if it is another substance of that power, and all things that are have from it what they are, [Col. 1058D] it is impossible that all should be one.

But now, since God the Father and the Son, the *logos*, are *homoousioi*, because all things are called into one through the *logos*, all things are from God, and God is all things in all, the Father remaining without passion, as has likewise been shown. Jesus, however, is the *logos*, who is also the life-giving Spirit of all things, the fountain of eternal life; according to the mystery he came into flesh, conquered death in the death [brought by] sins, and raised the dead unto eternal life.

God is the power of that fountain of eternal life; and therefore the Son is the *logos*, the fountain of eternal life, existing as the Father’s power, firstborn from the dead. Hence all things, turned toward him, will become one—that is, spiritual. Therefore the Son of God is *homoousios*, because he is the fountain of eternal life, just as the Father is his power; and because all things will become one through the Son, since all things are through him.

That Jesus, that is, the *logos*, is seed and, as it were, the element of all things that are—especially now in the *energeia* (ἐνέργεια, actuality/operation) and manifestation of things that are—is [shown] by this: “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2:9), that is, substantially in operation; for in the Father all things dwell potentially. Therefore Jesus the *logos* is the image of God the Father: what he himself is is potency, now [becoming] that which is action. For everything that comes forth into action is the image of what is potentially, and what is in action is son of what is potentially; in these, Son and Father are *homoousioi*.

That all things are from Jesus, and therefore all things are from God—all things, I say, whatever things are—and [that one is] “not holding fast the head, from which the whole body, supplied and brought forth through joints and connections, grows with the growth of God” (ibid., 19). For all things are one, even though the things that are differ. For the body of the whole universe is not like a heap, which becomes a body only by the mutual contact of its grains; but rather [it is] like a chain, a body held together by its parts being interwoven with one another. For the chain is: God, Jesus, Spirit, *nous*, soul, angels, and then all bodily things supplied. Therefore fullness has indeed been brought forth.

XXVI. Therefore, if all things are one in substance, much more are God and the Son [one], not merely insubstantiated but consubstantiated. For all beings (*onta*, ὄντα) are insubstantiated in Jesus, that is, in the *logos*, as has been said [Col. 1059C]: “All things were created in him” (Col. 1:16). Yet these are not *homoousioi*. For that first being which is God is not *ousia* (οὐσία, substance) in the same way, nor is the image, which is the Son, [an image] as a substance; rather, the being of divinity in respect of causality is simultaneously only their [being], [and] the being of things that are. Therefore God and the *logos* alone are *homoousioi*.

To Timothy, first [epistle]: “And confessedly great is the mystery of godliness: which was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, believed in the world, received into glory” (1 Tim. 3:16). This is not about the first generation but the second. For this is the great mystery: that God emptied himself while existing in the form of God; then that he suffered—first, that he was in flesh and possessed the fate of human generation, and that he was lifted up upon the cross. These things would not be wonderful if they had been either from a human being alone, or from nothing, or from God by way of manufacture. For what did he empty if he did not exist before he was in flesh? And what was that of which he said [that he was] equal to God? How, moreover, was he equal if he were a fabrication from nothing?

Therefore the mystery is great: “which was manifested in flesh.” Therefore he existed before he was in flesh, but it says that he was manifested in flesh. For he existed intelligibly and intellectually; but then he was manifested sensibly and in flesh. For the power of the *logos*, according to its own substance, is life, always substance; inasmuch as it is life, it gives life and restores life and does not permit to remain in death whatever it gives life to. Therefore in the first movement it brought all things into life, and this is the [Col. 1060A] descent of the *logos*: because, proceeding from the Father, it gave to those who are in heaven—to angels, thrones, glories, and beings of this sort—its own life, the Father’s power. For it is the *logos* of all things, through whom all things were made.

Again, because life-giving would not exist unless there were matter capable of being made alive, dead matter of nature was made; having been made alive, it emitted its hosts through divine vivification and corrupted the human being. But the *logos*, perfect life, completed the mystery and appeared in matter, that is, in flesh and in darkness. For how could that which had existed possibly appear unless it appeared in flesh, that is, in sense? Therefore the *logos* accomplished all things, is in all things, generated all things, saved, and reigned, being eternal life in Spirit. Therefore he was justified, appeared to angels, and, having come, was preached among the nations.

Therefore he existed before he came. “He was believed in the world”; for Isaiah too confesses this in prophecy: “Egypt has labored, and the merchandise of Ethiopians and Sabeans; men of great height shall walk in you, and shall be your servants; they shall follow behind you bound with manacles, and shall worship you and entreat you, [saying], ‘God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know [it], God of Israel’” (Isa. 45:14). Therefore he was preached in the world, received into the glory of divinity from the beginning, and in the beginning, and afterward, and always from everlasting things, and unto ages of ages. Amen.

XXVII. Observe also how, with reference to the *homoousion*, the Spirit says through Isaiah: “In you is God, and there is no God apart from you.” This is said to the Son, our Lord: God is manifest in you; that is, what was said: “The Father is in me.” [Col. 1060C] The further statement, “and there is no God apart from you,” foretells in this one phrase all heresies. What do all the Jews say to this, and those who say that Jesus is a mere human being, and those who say that he is from nothing and that “there was when he was not”? For God was, and God was always one God. If Jesus is the *Logos*, and the *Logos* is always with God; and the *Logos* is one God, and there is no other: therefore God is *homoousios*. And again, if the *Logos*, being God, is that which is—to be (*esse*), and Jesus, that is, the *Logos*, is the power and wisdom of this God and of that which is—to be: one God, and no other. Therefore the *Logos* and God are one unity (*unalitas*), and that which is—to be itself, and the being of the *Logos*, subsisting together as the same in that which is—to be; and therefore *homoousios*. But for the *Logos* to be is to be life and *nous* (intellect); for these are the power and wisdom of God, which is Jesus the Savior: procession and generation, [Col. 1060D] procession into sonship with respect to substance, and effulgence and radiance with respect to activity. This was not “when he was not,” but always was. Therefore the Father always is, and the Son always is.

The Father is Father only, and the Son Son only. Yet with respect to the Father, because that which is—to be, which is God and Father, is the cause for the *Logos* of its being what it is, and not conversely: it is proper to him who is first being to rest; while it is proper to the *Logos* to move and act—not to move locally, nor by a change of place, but by a movement more excellent and more divine, such as belongs to soul, which by its own movement gives life and, subsisting in itself, produces intellects, without being divided from its own power in operation.

XXVIII. But enough of this. Again: there are other things [Col. 1061A] in Holy Scripture—that Jesus is God; that he is before the ages; that he is Son, Son by nature, and Son in the flesh; and especially that he is called Son in the flesh, because then he saved all beings (*onta*) and then conquered the enmities against divinity and every death; and that he himself suffered according to movement, whereas the Father did not suffer according to cessation.

If these things are so, only this remains: how is *homoousion* to be understood, or how is the Son *homoousios* with the Father? For this doctrine has now been awakened, though long ago tossed about in rumors: namely, that one ought not to say *homoiousion* but rather *homoousion*. This doctrine, they say, has now been discovered. They even dare to say that it was long ago—not, I say, how long ago; for it is enough for me if it was handed down not from eternity nor from the presence of Jesus, but long ago, a hundred years ago; I grant even more. [Col. 1061B] Where was it hidden? Where did it sleep until eleven years ago, when, at the city of Nicaea, the faith was confirmed by more than three hundred bishops, excluding the Arians? In that synod these men were lights of the Church throughout the whole world.

Thus this old doctrine had fled away. If it did not exist, it was convicted [note: “Convicted”: perhaps “fabricated,” or “now made”] and has only now begun. If it did exist, either it was silent through contention, or it was driven away by the judgment of knowledge and truth. Perhaps then, patron of this doctrine, you were not only alive but a bishop: you too were silent, along with your associates, disciples, and fellow teachers; and throughout the time afterward, until the emperor was at Rome, you heard many contrary things while you were a table-companion of those men whom you now anathematize—angry, perhaps, because they drew up the creed without you. Or were you sent by your masters as an envoy to defend betrayal?

But what difference does it make [Col. 1061C] whether thirty, seventy, or more times, and repeatedly, the same faith has been established for the destruction of other *haireseis* (heresies), since it is one faith, proceeding from one source and active until now? Yet you write and say that Paul of Samosata, Marcellus, Photinus, and now Valens and Ursacius, together with others found religiously engaged in this sort of heresy, were overthrown. Were they overthrown for saying *homoousion*? No. How then were they blasphemers? Samosata was like Arius: he said “from nothing,” “there was when he was not,” that the Son was a creature, and altogether, in every respect, unlike the Father. What of Marcellus and Photinus? They held Jesus to be merely a human being from a human being, and the Trinity to exist apart from Jesus. And now Valens and Ursacius are remnants of Arius. Therefore it was for their own blasphemy that they were expelled. But you defeated them then because you say *homoousion*; for they did not say *homoousion*, and so were defeated.

XXIX. Let us therefore consider also what you say, and how you say it: “The Africans and all the Orientals think thus.” Why, then, do you write to them that they should cast *homoousion* out of the holy Church? They say this: There was no need to write to them; if there was need to write, you ought also to persuade them—not by command alone, but by arguments and Holy Scriptures. For you ought not only to destroy *homoousion*, but also to establish *homoiousion*.

But now, above and below, in your distortion of *homoousion*, you say nothing else than that those who affirm it must confess a pre-existent substance, and that thus Father and Son are excluded. First, [Col. 1062A] this is not necessary. For God is both substance and cause of substance; he pre-exists all things that are, all existence and all essentiality. For from him are all things that are, and their names. Therefore from this God, who is the principle of substance, and who is therefore substance, the *homoousios* Son is in him and with him. For he is the form, image, and χαρακτήρ (*character*, impress) of him who is; without these God is neither understood nor attained by understanding. Yet this does not mean that the simple God is not what he is; nor that these are, as though another thing, in him as accidents; rather, this itself is to be God. Thus that which is—to be and the Father, who is that which is—to be, are *homoousios*.

But the Son is being in this manner. For God is that which is—to be; and the *Logos* is being in this manner. This is always what he means when he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and: “The Father is in me, and [Col. 1062B] I in the Father” (John 14:10); and: “If anyone has seen me, he has seen the Father”—for they are *homoousia* (ibid., 9).

What then does he mean in saying: “Substance pre-exists; therefore there is *homoousion*”? What if, when there is *homoousion*, it is not necessary to understand that substance pre-exists, from which these two similar substances were made? By your own reasoning, you too fall into the very thing which you fear in *homoousion*. Or is it permitted to you alone to understand *homoousion* as the Father giving substance to the Son, whereas we may not conceive *homoousion* as the Father being cause of the Son’s being, while substance is God? Yet you yourself confess *homoousion*, for you say that Father and Son exist. Who is similar to whom? Is the Son similar to the Father according to rank and the dignity of their names? Yet the Father is also similar to the Son; for all such things are relative. If this is similarity, and we say *homoiousion*, we say that the Son is similar to the Father. And how then shall we receive Isaiah’s saying: “Before me no other God was, and after me there shall not be one like me” (Isa. 43:10)?

XXX. What then is the *Logos*—before God, after God, or with God? If before God, God is neither unbegotten nor Father, nor the principle of principles. But if after God, he is not *ouk homoios* (“not like”) but another similar God. But if you call this impious—not only in power, dignity, and divinity, but also in substance—what is a similar substance? From this very substance, insofar as it is this very substance, it is the same, not similar. For similarity is produced by quality: similarity in color, disposition, affection, power, or form. But Jesus, that is, the *Logos*, is the image of God, not a similarity.

He is called the image of God. God is not an image; but God is God by image and substance—not as two, for substance is one and image is one; hence one God and one *Logos*, one Father, one Son, and these are one. For this too is one—not two; and therefore simultaneously substance itself is the other one. Thus it is not another one, but rather, and solely, one.

But enough of this. Again, what do we call substance, as the wise and ancient philosophers defined it? That which is subject, which is something, which is not in another. They distinguish existence from substance: existence and essentiality are pre-existent subsistence [Col. 1063A] without accidents, with only those pure realities which are in it—that is, merely to be that which subsists. But substance is the subject together with all its accidents, existing in it separably; yet in usage we employ “existence” and “substance,” wherever they signify in the same manner that something is.

Let it be so, whether in eternal or worldly things. For it is permissible to call either existence, substance, or that which is truly substance. There is movement, and not merely movement, but first movement, which is genus and itself a state; and therefore itself substance. But this belongs to a longer and another inquiry.

For the present, however, we confess that there is there a substance having, according to its proper signification, this meaning: to be something that is (*on*). This is against those who say that the name “substance” is not found in Holy Scripture. Perhaps the noun “substance” itself is not found, but terms derived from substance are. From what else is *epiousion* derived but from substance? (Matt. 6:11): “Give us *epiousion* bread,” that is, daily bread. Since Jesus is life, and his body is life, while his body is bread, as it was said: “Give us bread from heaven,” *epiousion* signifies bread from, or in, substance—that is, bread of life.

Likewise Paul, in the Epistle to Titus (Titus 2:14), says: “a *periousion* people,” “a people around substance,” that is, a people established around life; as is also said in the offering: “Cleanse for yourself a people about life, zealous for good works, approaching around your substance.” The same thing seems to me to be signified in Jeremiah the prophet, where he says (Jer. 23:18, LXX): “For who has stood in [Col. 1063C] the substance of the Lord and has seen his word? Who has given ear and heard?” And shortly afterward he says (ibid., 22): “And if they had stood in the substance.” But they write *in substantia* (“in substance”) as two words, not *insubstantia*.

If anyone truly understands the meaning, he finds nothing else than this: if anyone stands in that which is God’s being—that is, in substance, in which the *homoousios* Son is—he immediately sees his *Logos*. For we must make the intellect (*nous*) stand within, in the divine substance—that is, in substance; and immediately we comprehend both God and the *Logos*, for they are *homoousios*, and together both are one.

XXXI. But you seem [to object]. Let us suppose that we say that the substance of God is that which is—to be, and that the being of Jesus is God; this is both piety and confession. What then is God’s substance? If substance is spoken of in worldly terms—as animal or human being—then it is necessary to say that in eternal realities God is substance. But you see God himself, according to what we say, to be light, spirit, being itself, the power of that which is—to be, universal intellect, the power of universal intellect, universal life or action, or something else of this kind—in which he is the fountain of all things that truly are, or that are.

But the Scriptures say that God is light and spirit. These signify substance, not accident. For to what does that which is—to be first happen as an accident, if this is an accident? To nothing; for it is impossible that anything should exist beyond that which is—to be. Therefore, substance, insofar as it is—to be, [Col. 1064A] is light and spirit—simple and uncompounded, where light and spirit are the same.

Now light and spirit have an image, not from the necessity of nature but by the will of the Father’s greatness; for he has delimited himself. Therefore it is said: “You understand yourself,” yet you are also intelligible to the Son. Therefore the Son is in the Father as image, form, *Logos*, and will of the Father; and, insofar as he is the Father’s will, the Son is other than the Father. For every will is offspring; and insofar as it is universal will, it is the Only-begotten. For once the *Logos* of the whole fullness sprang forth from God’s power. This power, existing as *Logos*, generated the *Logos*—that is, brought him into manifestation and operation.

Thus, by the will of the Father, the will appeared: the *Logos* himself, the Son. Therefore God’s will is the *Logos*, together with him who always is; and this will’s relation to him is sonship. Thus the Father is he whose will it is; the Son is the will; and the will is the *Logos* himself. Therefore the *Logos* is the Son.

For the *Logos* is not a certain utterance, but the power for creating something, conferring upon those things that are to be, according to their being (*ontotēs*), the power and proper substance of each; and the *Logos* himself is form, which is God’s self-knowledge. For knowledge is effected through the *Logos* alone. For this reason it was said that the *Logos* is with God. The *Logos* is Word: light from light, spirit from spirit, substance from substance—not first and second according to time, but according to one being cause for the other in order that it may be power. They are always together: the effulgence of light is not severed, but is always in the light; and, itself existing as light, the *Logos* does all things, [Col. 1064C] moving from himself and always moving, possessing abundance—that is, the Father’s omnipotence.

XXXII. What similarity, then, is there here—a similarity effected and generated by deliberation, as you say, for the generation of the Son? The Father moves from himself; the Son generates himself from himself; yet the Son, who generates himself, is the Father’s power. For the Son is will. For if will itself does not generate itself from itself, it is not will. But because it is God’s will, it is itself that which generates and is generated in God. Therefore God is Father and will is Son; both are one—or rather, they are one, and only one—not by conjunction but by simplicity. The will has indeed proceeded into active power, yet has not departed from its proper substance and the same movement. For these three there are one: substance, movement, and will. Substance is Father; movement and will are the same thing. Again, the Son is movement and will, and likewise substance; and this is *homoousion*.

Let us take as an example what I now say. For we must now speak thus, since many say that the body is in the soul; but according to ordinary usage let the soul now be in the body. The soul is in the human body. Insofar as it is soul, it is substance, just as matter (*hylē*) or body is substance. For these are the two worldly substances. And as matter has form—that is, species—such as body or some other thing, one thing is concreted materially (*hylikōs*) into a mass. For something must have a certain quantity; therefore whatever is material [Col. 1065A] is so. For matter is defined by quantity, so that it subsists and becomes substance, now existing as something.

In this same way the soul, being incorporeal substance, has definition and image: vital and intellectual power; for it has two powers and a double light. For it both gives life, enlivening animals, and has the *nous* conjoined and *homoousios* with it; and therefore all these are *homoousia*. For substance and movement are together the same, with the soul as subject, insofar as it lives and gives life; and insofar as it understands, it is intellect in a single movement. Since it is one and the same thing, which is its species, it is defined by movement and exists as one being (*on*) with two powers in one movement: life and intellect.

These are impassible in themselves, but in activity two, in one movement; that is, what is generated is the soul’s only-begotten Son, himself life and himself *nous*, and the first power together with that whose being is life. For what it is, that is what is life. For that being is to it both substance and life, and is above life: it does not enliven another thing, nor itself; for it does not receive from another as though it were another thing. Its being is its own moving and being movement; and what is movement is life, and what is life is intellect.

I call these substantial: movements, life, and intellect; I mean no movement of sensible things, nor transition from place to place. Therefore these two, life and intellect, are *homoousia* with that which is—to be, that is, with the soul. These two are one movement, which is indeed life’s first power; for life is the form of that which is—to be. It defines [Col. 1065C] infinite being, which is the first power of movement; the movement itself is the second power, because what is defined is comprehended by intellect from life, as intellect is innate in substance and subsists insofar as it is intellect, being led forth through itself from the substance of life.

These two are one, and, with respect to movement, are the soul’s only-begotten Son, suffering nothing passively insofar as it belongs to the soul. But the soul is either mother or father of the only-begotten Son, while movement proceeds into a double power, which alone suffers. For movement is passion, and passion is by movement: in movement are movement and rest; but for rest to be in movement is passion, and for movement to arise from rest is passion, and hence movement. Therefore every passion is through movement.

This passion is twofold, according to life and intellect. According to life, passion consists in still needing another whom it wishes to enliven, and therefore, insofar as it participates in that other, it suffers other passions even unto death. According to intellect, because it too needs that which is intelligible in order that intellect may subsist, it encounters rather passions and weaknesses, is whirled about among insensible things, and through imagination is led around into false subsistence. Yet while these things exist and suffer, the soul remains according to substance, preserving in the seed of movement the power of life and intellect. While that always remains, life and intellect are kindled—or rather raised up—if the soul, having been raised, rises again to fontal life, that is, Christ, and to fontal intellect, that is, the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1066A] XXXIII. But this is by way of analogy. Concerning God, the *Logos*, that is, the Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, let us, using a more divine understanding, apprehend the unity of their *homoousion*. First we must inquire whether God and God’s being are the same, or something different. If they are the same, then being and acting are already one. But if God’s being is one thing and being God another, then God’s being is pre-existent to God, existing in potency toward that which is—to be, which is more truly that which is—to be; for power pre-exists all things and is their principle, and is prior to that which truly is (*on*).

But they reckon this blessed reality to be, in every way whatsoever, at rest; only in movement is it cause of all things that exist in any sort of movement. And they say that it is conceived by foreknowledge, which in itself is nothing, but receives through conception what pre-exists.

But Scripture and all intelligence say that this God both is and has being, and that before him nothing exists; he is both that which is—to be and that which acts. This God we confess and worship, the principle of all things that are. For things that are exist by action; before action they are not yet. We understand God as active, just as “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” and made angels, humankind, and all things in heaven and on earth.

This, therefore, is the true and only God, because he is God both in power and in action, though in the eternal order; just as Christ is in power and in action, though now outwardly and openly. Therefore God the Father is first action, first existence and substance, and the principal *on*, who by his own action generates himself from himself without beginning, always existing from himself, infinite, in every respect perfect, omnipotent, immutable, [Col. 1066C] always existing thus and in the same manner, substantial in himself: existing as *Logos* so that all things may exist—not as some other thing or as another, but coexisting simultaneously by simplicity and being one by unity. For what the *Logos* is, that itself is what is—to be; and through being that which is—to be, it is *Logos*. For the *Logos* himself is God: therefore one and *homoousios*. For God is not without action, but acts, as was said.

XXXIV. But God’s substance is image, action, and Son; through it God is understood and what he is is declared: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). And it itself exists as substance, possessing being and being from itself. But because that in which it is has causality for it, the image itself is Son of him in whom it is, by an ineffable generation—and especially by an unbegotten generation, or rather by a generation eternally generating, as Alexander also said. And he is called always Father, the Son always existing simultaneously. Therefore he also always coexists consubstantially, being one: the Son is in the Father; but when he acts, he proceeds, and when he proceeds, the Father is in the Son.

How do we say this? God and the *Logos* are one and united, and therefore *homoousios*. Yet God, insofar as he is God, is cause of the *Logos*, insofar as he is the power both of being and of all things that are, with respect to the *Logos*’ being what it is. The *Logos* is the Father’s power, bringing into subsistence that which is—to be itself: that which is—to be in the primary sense, its principle and perfection. For from universal being, and from that which is above every universal being, every universal being—according to genera, species, [Col. 1067A] and individuals—has its being.

If, therefore, the *Logos* has being—for the *Logos* is that which is—to be for itself and is *Logos—*then it has being from that which is above universal being. But the universal that is—to be is the *Logos*; God is that which is above universal being, while the Son is that which is universal being. Therefore the Father is that which is—to be above the universal; therefore they are *homoousios* in respect of being: that which is—to be and that which is—to-be above the universal in relation to universal being. This too is procession: for universal being goes forth from that which is above universal being; or, more accurately for one who understands, it both goes forth and remains, for universal being is not abandoned.

Therefore universal being both subsists through itself and is within that which is above universal being. It is connected and inseparable. This is called the radiance of light: possessing all that belongs to light, yet not received or sprung up, but connatural, always *homoousios*. Thus there is no local movement or change; for Father and Son are immutable, and Father always is Father, Son always Son, even if the Son is believed to be the image in the Father and the form of being, as has been said, or, according to procession, the radiance of light.

Since these things are so, and are even more one—for radiance is the splendor of light, and itself possesses light in itself from the Father, and is in the light and outwardly—therefore the Son is in the Father. Since the splendor of light is conjoined, splendor is said rather to be of the light than in the light; though it shines forth from the light, it is in the light. This is the meaning of John 1:1: “In the beginning was the *Logos*, and the *Logos* was with God.” Therefore Son and Father are *homoousios*, always thus, from eternity and unto eternity.

XXXV. We say other things as well. That the *Logos* is with God is acknowledged. What is the *Logos*? He through whom all things are, in whom all things are, and unto whom all things are. That this is Jesus is acknowledged. That the *Logos* is the Son of God—and that the Son is Jesus—Paul says of him (Col. 1:13): “He has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.” Who then is this Son? “He,” he says (ibid., 14), “in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our sins.” Who is this? He who was born from Mary.

What then? Is this all? Is it chiefly only what was in him who was from Mary? He was also before he was from Mary. What does Paul introduce [Col. 1067D] next (ibid., 15)? “Who is the image of God.” Is this only from Mary? No; for the image of God is image from eternity. If, therefore, we have hope in the Son and he redeemed us through his blood, and he is the image of God, then the image is Son of God. Do I say this? Not I alone, but Paul also. For how does he say it? “Firstborn of all creation.” Who is firstborn? The Son. Which Son? The Son from Mary. Which Son from Mary? The firstborn of all creation. Who is the firstborn of all creation? He who is the image of God. For the image of God must be firstborn before every creature.

Who is the image? The *Logos*. Which *Logos*? He who was in the beginning. For how can God be without an image? And which *Logos*? [Col. 1068A] He who was with God and through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1:2–3). How is the image the *Logos*, and the *Logos* the Son, and he the one from Mary? Rather, he is in the one who is from Mary. From these things it is clear: if the Son of God redeemed us through his blood, and he is the Son from Mary, and he is the image of God, then he is God’s Son. For if he is firstborn of all creation, he is necessarily Son. Is he another? Far be it; for he is the only-begotten Son of God.

Therefore the Son, the image, and he who is from Mary must be one and the same. For how is the image of God Son if he is not firstborn of all creation? And how is he the image of God if the Son from Mary was born after all things had been made? It is therefore clear that he himself is the firstborn. But what was born from Mary is not a creature; rather, if the Son of God, the image of God, was born before every creature, he himself is in him who was born from Mary. It is therefore clear that he is the only-begotten.

XXXVI. After this we must see how the same one is image, Son, and *Logos*. It is acknowledged that the image is Son; for Paul said (Col. 1:15): “The Son of God is the image of God.” I say that he is the *Logos* of whom it was said: “In the beginning was the *Logos*.” For Paul explains how the Son is firstborn of all creation: [Col. 1068B] “In him were created all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers. All things have been created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things subsist in him” (ibid., 16–18).

You see what he says of the Son: that he is firstborn because all things were created from him, through him, and in him. Thus he states three things, among which is what was said, “all things through him,” which has always, by confession, been attributed to the *Logos*. If Paul attributes “through him” to the Son, while John, the first apostle and evangelist, attributes “through him” to the *Logos*, their statements agree before all others. What doubt can remain that the Son is the *Logos*?

And the other two things which he attributes to the Son—whose are they more properly than the *Logos*’? For his power is the subsistence of all things that are. And if this too is so, that all things are in him—as it was said, “all things were created in him,” and therefore all things are in him because all will become spiritual—Paul also signifies this at the consummation of the world: “For when all things have been subjected to him, then [Col. 1068D] he himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28). What is this, and how does it come later? It is now in the manner in which things are spiritual.

Therefore it is true that the Son from Mary is Son of God, and that he himself is the image and the *Logos*, before the ages and before every creature; and that every creature was created through him, in him, and from him, together with the consequences already stated.

XXXVII. Who, then, is so devoid of sense—who is so sacrilegious as Arius—that he does not see who Jesus is and whence comes the Only-begotten Son? That God and the *Logos* are *homoousios*, that is, Father and Son, is clear from these things. What Paul has attributed to the Son, he has attributed also to the Father: these three things, with paternal dignity, in one, so that the unity of divinity, substance, and paternal power might be made manifest.

To the Colossians [Col. 1069A] Paul spoke this concerning the Son. But to the Romans he says the same things concerning the Father (Rom. 11:34–36): “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, and shall be repaid? For from him, through him, and in him are all things.” You see how he has given the same things—thus the same things—to both Father and Son, in *homoousion*: first three and three, then the same things to Father and Son.

Now “through whom are all things” is attributed both to Father and Son, because the Son is the *Logos*, the active power of all things that are. And because the Father is in the Son, the Father too exists in him as active power. For the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son simultaneously. Therefore there is one power, that is, one substance; for power is substance there, and power is not one thing and substance another. Therefore the same is true of Father and Son.

But the Son himself is also from him, from whom are all things; this, then, belongs properly to the Father. “In whom are all things” belongs to the *Logos*, who is also place; for he himself is the receptacle of things made and works through himself. Since all things that are exist there, fullness comes to be. For Jesus too is father of all works, those which are through himself. Therefore Father and Son are one.

But works do not enter from without. From where could they? For nothing is outside. Therefore all things are in him; he himself is both receptacle and inhabitant. And because the Father is in the Son, and the Father is the inhabitant, “in whom are all things” is proper to the Son. What remains, therefore—“in him,” I mean—is common to both. For at the consummation all things are one. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 8:6): “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things, and we through him.”

Or how is “in him” otherwise? For in other passages it is likewise stated of the Father: from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things. But of the Son: in whom are all things, through whom are all things, unto whom are all things. Therefore Paul has attributed all things equally to Son and Father. Rightly: Father and Son are *homoousios*, and therefore it was said: “Then he himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all.”

### XXXVIII

See the force of his statement: for he establishes (perhaps, concludes) *homoousion*. The Son subjects all things to the Father by his own power, as it seems, but in truth by paternal power. For he says: “He will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him.” To whom will he be subjected? To God. Who will be subjected? The Son, to whom God subjects all things. Therefore both Father and Son are action. Where, then, is substance? In [Col. 1069D] that in which action itself is—and indeed is action all the more—which is substance. Therefore, *homoousion*.

Paul says this also: “when he has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Cor. 15:24). Therefore he himself now reigns, and Christ, according to his own action, subjects all things and destroys both hostilities and death itself. Therefore he himself subjects them, as Paul says, “when he has abolished every power.” Thus he says that the Son accomplishes these things by his own power. And he adds this: “For he must reign” (ibid., v. 25). God indeed is king of all things; but since the Son is *homoousios*, and even more, the *Logos*—that is, the power and wisdom of God—it is necessary that wisdom should reign first, through which all things will be subjected. For by the *Logos* all things both subsist and will be subjected [Col. 1070A]; since it is both said, and has been said, that the *Logos*, that is, the Son, subjects all things. And therefore Paul added: “until he puts all his enemies beneath his feet” (Heb. 10:13). Who? Whose enemies? Manifestly, those of the Father’s Son.

But since the Father is in the Son, the Father therefore subjected all things to the Son; and for this reason the Son, rather than the Father, especially has enemies. And since both are involved—that is, this is a good ambiguity of understanding—and therefore are *homoousioi*: “the last enemy to be abolished is death” (1 Cor. 15:26). For if Jesus is life, and eternal life, death will be abolished by life. Therefore Jesus—that is, the Son—subjects all things to the Father.

But because he is *homoousios* with the Father, both in substance itself and in power itself: insofar as it is primary to be Father, and primary being is; whereas acting, living, and understanding come second; and because that which is primary is the cause of both [Col. 1070B], it is necessary to say that the Father subjects to the Son. Thus, when he says, “when he has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father,” it necessarily means the Son; and when he says, “when he has abolished every rule and power,” it necessarily means the Son. Again he says: “But when all things have been subjected, it is manifest that he is excepted who subjected all things to him” (ibid., v. 27). This is no small insight.

### XXXIX

But let us now leave this. What does he wish us to understand by saying that God, who is cause, all-powerful, and the pre-principle of power, himself made all things, when the Son makes them? And if the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, the Father himself makes in the Son those things which the Son has made; and “what the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19). Therefore all things—whether operations or repose—are attributed either to the Father or to the Son. For in the one they are toward the other, and there is nothing other in that [Col. 1070C] in which the other is in the one.

Therefore there is one alone, and nothing other; but Father and Son are each a proper subsistence, from the one substance which is from the Father. The Son, that is, the *Logos*, is active power: power which makes, vivifies, and is intellectual. Therefore he both begets all things justly, makes them according to life, and regenerates them according to the understanding of truth and of God—an understanding which Jesus, being the *Logos*, gives to all: the *Logos* of all things, of intellects, and universally of all things that are.

If, then, he begets and regenerates all things, if he subjects all things—not human beings alone, but also, as Paul says, every rule and every power—does he do these things as man or as *Logos*? For this act of subjecting belongs not only to the time from which the Son is from Mary, but both before and afterward. For if the flood occurred, if Sodom and Gomorrah were burned, if these [Col. 1070D] and many such things took place; if at the first advent he triumphs over enemies in himself; if at the second advent the last enemy, death, will be abolished: the Son, the *Logos*, does these things, but by paternal power.

Therefore the Spirit accomplishes all spiritual things; then he too will be subjected to God, who subjects all things to him. For when all things have been abolished, active power rests; and God will be in him according to what it is to be, and according to what it is to rest; while in all other things he will be spiritually present according to both his power and his substance. And this is what is meant by “that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28): not that all things are in each individual, but that, since God exists in all, God will therefore be all things, because all things will be full of God.

[Col. 1071A] ### XL

Let us say other things also. “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel of God” (Rom. 1:16). Paul calls Christ Jesus virtue and power; for the Gospel says this, and says of him: “Christ, therefore, the wisdom and power of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). What, then, are the wisdom and power of God? Are they not God himself?

For it is not as in bodies or bodily things, where the eye is one thing and sight another; or, in fire, fire one thing and its light another. For the eye and fire require something else: the eye requires another light, in order that sight may arise from it and be in it; fire requires air, in order that light may arise from it. But just as the power of sight has sight in itself, which exists outwardly when the power of sight operates, and sight is begotten by the power of sight—its own only-begotten—for nothing else is produced from it; and sight is related to the power of sight not merely inwardly [Col. 1071B], but inwardly in the power and, more in action, outwardly: therefore sight, being sight, is *homoousios* with the power of sight, and the two are one whole.

The power indeed is at rest, while sight is in motion; through sight all visible things come to be perceived, and affections belong to sight, while the power of sight remains impassible and begets sight without affection. Thus also the virtue and wisdom of God are God himself: a whole which is simple, one, of one and the same substance; existing simultaneously from eternity, always, and from the Father, who is their generator from himself.

Wisdom and virtue are those of operation—for this is the sense of “virtue” here; he has joined wisdom and virtue. God, therefore, is their power, and for that reason Father, because they are from him. For he begets them for action and impassibly [Col. 1071C]; and power, action, God, God’s virtue, and wisdom are *homoousia*. Since they are active, attending to things outside, they are directed toward God, always imparting wisdom and always vivifying—not God, but every creature made by God through themselves. And if there is any affection, the affection belongs to action.

In this way, whether Jesus is *Logos*, light, radiance, form, image, virtue and wisdom, χαρακτήρ (*character*, “impress”), or life, the *Logos* and God the Father, the Son, Spirit, and Christ will appear *homoousioi*.

### XLI

Let us bring forward these same points further. If we call Christ life, how is he *homoousios* with God? John says: “What was made, in him was life” (John 1:3–4). And again: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in [Col. 1071D] himself” (John 5:26). What could be more simultaneous? What more identical? The Father has life in himself; the Son too has life in himself.

What is it to have life in oneself? It is to be life to oneself: not to receive life from another, but to have it from oneself and give it to others. Someone says that they are of similar substance, but not *homoousioi*. This has already been answered: “similar” is not predicated of substance. For a thing is not similar with respect to that whereby it is substance; rather, if it is of the same substance, it is called identical in substance, not similar. Similarity concerns qualities. Thus fire is substance, and air is the same in substance—for both are matter (*hylē*)—but they are similar or dissimilar in their qualities, according to the conception of their powers, and similar in other respects. Say likewise that earth and water are similar in heaviness and density, or [Col. 1072A] in other such features; in these cases it also happens that things which are in some way similar are dissimilar, being different in this or that quality.

For similar is not identical; nor is identical one, but identical in duplicate. Even this “one” is not one in substance, but one in number. We are now investigating substance: whether, in God and the Son, it is itself or the same; or whether in some manner it is both itself and the same.

How, then, can it be itself, when the Son comes, accomplishes such great things in heaven and on earth, and enters into flesh? How can Jesus be the Son, who signifies the Father? How can there be three substances—God, *Logos*, and Holy Spirit? For one must not say, nor is it lawful to say, that there is one substance and three persons. For if that very substance both did all things and suffered, then we too are Patripassians—far be it.

What then? It is the same, not itself [Col. 1072B]. But if this is so, either the two arise from a pre-existent substance, or the same substance has become itself the same through division or through the loss of a part of itself. Yet the Son was born neither by a letting-go nor by a diminution; rather, the Father is perfect and always perfect, always Father; the Son is perfect and always perfect, Son from eternity and unto eternity. How, then, are they the same? For in what two things is there sameness? Yet Father and Son are one; and he who is Father is Father, and he who is Son is Son. The Father is not the same as the Son, nor is the Son the same as the Father whose Son he is.

Therefore they are not one: the substance is neither itself nor the same. It remains, then, that in some manner it is both itself and the same. For it is not lawful to say that the Father and Son are of different substance. For we shall say what it is for it to be itself, whether we speak of God and *Logos*; God and God’s virtue and wisdom; [Col. 1072C] being and life; being and understanding, or intelligence; being and living understanding; Father and Son; light and effulgence; God and χαρακτήρ; God and form and image; substance and species—though not here as there; substance and motion; power and action; silence and utterance. One must confess that it is substance itself.

For if we call God being and the Son life, how do we separate life from being, whether in the Father or in the Son? For the Father has life in himself, and so does the Son, except that the Son received from the Father what he has. Thus understand “having” as I say: Father and Son have their origin from themselves and power for life from themselves, just as the Gospel says that the Father has life in himself. Therefore “to have” is not as though life were another thing, but it is life itself—yet this is a distinction in understanding [Col. 1072D].

### XLII

We have said these things. If, then, the Father has life in himself, he is life, and his substance is life; and so is the Son. For he says: “I am life” (John 14:6). Therefore the Father is life, and the Son is life.

Every life, precisely as life, is motion, vivifying those which can be vivified. Hence this is the definition of soul and life: that which moves itself. And if this is said to be its substance, this is so much more the case in God and the *Logos*. What, then, did we say? The Father is life and substance, self-moving substance; and self-moving motion is nothing other than life itself—therefore both substance and life.

But because in motion intelligence is conceived as if it were something else, though not perfectly other, [Col. 1073A] living itself, as it were by a mutual intermingling of the two, is one thing insofar as it is life and motion. Again, insofar as it is life, it is one with that other itself; and therefore it is the same substance. But whether it is itself or the same, it is necessarily and simultaneously *homoousion*, because the two are simultaneous: neither has ever been without the other. Therefore these are one and one.

Thus, to be life and to be motion through oneself is the Father. To be moved and to be life through oneself is the Son. For life is the cause of motion. The Father, therefore, is life in the more principal sense, having motion at rest in concealment and moving inwardly within himself; but the Son is motion made manifest, and is therefore Son, because he proceeded from that which is within. Indeed, existing more as motion, he is that which is manifest. In this way the Son is life from the Father, who receives life as being from the pre-principial principle [Col. 1073B].

The universal is born from the universal, the whole from the whole. Therefore he says: “The living Father sent me, and I live because of him” (John 6:58). If, then, the begetter is life, and the Son is Son according to motion, while according to being moved he is life; if the Father gives life to the Son unto motion, generation, and simultaneously life; and if he is *homoousios* in himself: then Father and Son are always one, the Son is born from eternity, each is in the other, and there is an inseparable separation: the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son.

Most especially, the Son is action, because the Son is life with action; but the Father, according to being, is life, and according to being life, is action. The Father therefore remains and remains impassible. The Son operates and brings things into manifestation. And God operates inwardly, action existing according to power. Both in Father and in Son, action is action according to action [Col. 1073C].

### XLIII

Such statements must be referred back to all those analogies we set forward: whether God is *Logos*; light and effulgence; silence and utterance; or other things by which their oneness and simultaneous *homoousion* and unbegotten generation appear.

Where, then, is there room for saying that what is similar is *homoousion*? For what reason is this said? This whole mystery is always this: one God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one God. How, then, can “similar” be one God? But *homoousion* necessarily is one God. For if they are, as it were, not simultaneous, necessarily there are two; but if that which is similar is other, *homoousion* is necessarily other; therefore necessarily of another substance.

These Arians, Lucianists, Eusebians, Illyrians—by rejecting some things, taking away [Col. 1073D] some things, and changing others—are all heretics of differing opinion. Add this: if Father and Son are *homoousioi*, how does the Savior say, “I am truth” (John 14:6)? If what has been said is true, since the Son is truth, the Father is inferior: he is similar to truth, not truth. What blasphemy this is! But if God is truth, and the Son is truth, as the Son himself says—and says truly—the Son is God, *homoousios* with God. Therefore truth is not twofold but always one; and what is similar to truth is very far outside and very far below: perhaps it is the likeness of truth which exists in the world, where there are error, corruption, and every affection.

To be truth itself, then, is substance. For substance is not one thing and truth another. What is simple is truth; God is simple, [Col. 1074A] the Son is simple; God is truth, the Son is truth, and God and Son are one truth. For truth is truth in itself.

Again, if the Son is similar to truth, that is, if the similar guides, where does it guide? But if he is truth, he guides into truth. Yet he guides to God, and God is truth; therefore he guides into truth. But it is impossible to guide into truth unless he himself is truth. Therefore both Father and Son are truth, as it is also said: “Whom the Father sends to me, that one will come to me” (John 6:37).

From all these things it is not merely concluded, but made manifest, that motion in God is outside change. For generation there is neither local nor accompanied by affection, corruption, increase, diminution, or any alteration. For there, to move and to be moved are being itself, simultaneous and identical, simple and, in understanding, one in one—as in power and action [Col. 1074B]. Always *homoousion* in being; but in acting, Son from being and Father. Yet, as has been said, the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father.

### XLIV

Does the fear arise from this that, in saying these things, we are somehow Patripassians? The serpent-like doctrine differs greatly from the truth. For they say that God alone exists—him whom we call Father—as the sole being and maker of all things; and that he came not only into the world but also into flesh, and did all the other things which we say the Son did.

But if we say Father, then Father; and Son, then Son; while saying that they are one—and therefore *Logos*, that which is one—not merely saying “one,” but “one and one”: the one is impassible, the other suffered. How, then, are we Patripassians? For God neither [Col. 1074C] proceeds from himself nor is action in manifestation, nor is he, as it were, in motion; for inward motion is, as it were, not motion. But the *Logos*, who is in the power of motion, is more properly motion and action; by his power he is borne toward the production of things which are. For insofar as he is *Logos*, he is their cause; and insofar as he is cause, he does not always remain in himself, though he exists in that whereby he is *Logos*.

And in this respect he is unchangeable and immutable, yet he is active among things which exist according to their kinds—things which are this and that—while, precisely as universal *Logos*, he remains the same in the Father. Where, then, are the affections? Neither in Father nor in Son, but in those things which, according to their kind, are capable of receiving them: each thing receiving the whole power of the universal *Logos* in its own way, while he distributes to each its own proper quality—to angels, Powers, Thrones [Col. 1074D], Dominions, Authorities, souls, sensible things, and flesh itself. Affection, therefore, is in these things and belongs to them, not to the *Logos*, that is, not to the Son.

Thus the Savior suffered according to the flesh; according to the Spirit which he was, he was without suffering. This is the difference between our doctrine and that of the Patripassians. For to be Son is not suffering, as has been said; nor is doing or speaking anything suffering. For all things are done by divine power without affection; and this is rather its own substantial and divine motion, not passion.

Further, the Patripassians were not so called because of this, but because of the cross: sacrilegiously declaring that the Father was crucified, involving the impassible in suffering and failing to understand that, if there is something which suffers, something else must necessarily be impassible. We nevertheless call even the Son [Col. 1075A] impassible, though, insofar as the *Logos* became flesh, passible.

But mercy, anger, joy, sorrow, and other such things are not passions there, but nature and substance. If, then, the Spirit is benevolence, himself good through himself, he is life to some and death to others—not because his nature has changed, but because of the matter and will of those who undergo the effect. Divinity, immutable in its character, is said to be affected or to suffer for those receiving it, either as they ought or otherwise, because we judge divine things from our own perceptions. For among sensible things, insofar as an animal is an animal—that is, a soul using a body, or an ensouled body—it is said to suffer according to sensation. Yet truly passions do not belong even to soul by itself; much less do they belong to the Spirit of the *Logos* and of God. For the divine nature is impassible [Col. 1075B].

### XLV

Let the Patripassians depart, therefore, because we name both Father and Son, and call the latter alone passible according to motion in matter (*hylē*). Let the Arians depart, because we call the Son natural, begotten before every creature. Let those also depart who say that Christ is “from being” (*apo tou ontos*), because he was made by God, who is Being (*ōn*). For we call the Son nature, and say that he is from the Father and in the Father.

Let the disciples of Marcellus and Photinus depart. For we say that the Word himself was in flesh; not that one Word exists and another man, in whom, they say, Christ exists; rather, the *Logos* himself put on flesh. For they say that there are God, *Logos*, and Spirit, but a fourth—the Son, that is, the man from Mary—whom the *Logos* assumed and governed as a servant; and they say a seat has been prepared for that man. They have therefore fallen away from the Trinity [Col. 1075C].

But if the Trinity alone remains, the man himself is the *Logos*—which *Logos*, as we showed above, is Son. Nor does “the *Logos* became flesh” mean that the *Logos* was corrupted or changed into flesh. Rather, the *Logos*, through whom all things were made, and who made all things, became flesh, so that, being in flesh, he might purchase the whole human being through his suffering and death, according to the sufferings of the body. For if he himself was not the man from Mary, why did he empty himself? What does “taking the form of a servant” mean (Phil. 2:7)? And again, what is meant by “the *Logos* became flesh” (John 1:14)?

Let the Basilians, who call themselves *homoousioi*, depart also. For we say *homoousion* in truth and according to the Synod at Nicaea. Thus Father and Son are both one, always and simultaneously [Col. 1075D] both, because they are *homoousion*. But although these people say *homoousion* and confess that the Son has substance from the Father, they nevertheless posit something different: they say that the Son exists from God neither by generation nor by making, but by a striking together of these two, generation and making—as when a stone and iron are struck and flame is emitted from them. Those who say this are hidden Arians.

First, in denying that the Son of God exists by generation but saying that he exists by manufacture, they propound Arius’ doctrine. For what leaps out through striking is a product and is from nothing. Flame is not from iron or stone—this is precisely Arius’ mad thinking. If a collision occurred, there was a time when it was not. And if the Son was made by a compulsion of making and generation, making and generation existed before the Son. But these are later things [Col. 1076A].

How, then, can there be compulsion? This too is Arius’ doctrine. Further, what kind of collision is this, and of what things and in what? Is there a collision of wills in God? Of passions, or of differences—especially of opposed motions? And if the Father, who is without passion, suffered this, and the Son did not appear from his substance: for through the collision of two wills or passions neither a will nor a passion is made, much less a substance from the Father’s substance; rather, some external substance would arise from nothing, from the *Logos* toward the Father. To entertain such notions is impious blasphemy.

### XLVI

We have spoken of *homoousion*, and spoken sufficiently; for this was our purpose. But how, if the Son is *homoousios* and always with the Father, does he proceed, [Col. 1076B] descend, ascend, get sent, and do what belongs to the Father’s will? How, being the image of God, does he sit at God’s right hand? What is the right hand, and what is sitting? What is meant by “through whom all things were made,” and how were all things made through him? What is meant by “nothing was made without him”? How does he himself have a will, and do what he does by the Father’s will? How is he perfect, and yet, from the perfect Father, as though imperfect, receives a body and now bears a body—even if it is holy and spiritual, and like those human beings who will afterward be holy? And how is he always moved, begotten from himself by the Father’s power? All these things define *homoousion*.

Whoever is worthy to understand will find in this book that the Faith is such. And, with God, Jesus Christ our Lord, and the Holy Spirit permitting, we say this lest anyone, understanding my doctrine blasphemously, should speak against it. For all these things are both said by Holy Scripture and are so. We shall say especially that point from which many heresies arise: the Gospels, the Apostle, and all the Old Scripture say all things concerning God and concerning Jesus Christ—that is, concerning the incarnate *Logos*. For he accomplished the mystery of our salvation; he made us free and redeemed us. In him we believe as our Savior according to the cross and according to his resurrection from the dead. Therefore Paul says: “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2) [Col. 1076C].

### XLVII

Therefore we confess God the Father almighty; we confess the only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ [Col. 1076D]: God from God, true light from true light; the form of God, having substance from God’s substance; nature, generation, Son consubstantiated with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion*; firstborn before the constitution of the world, and firstborn before every creature—that is, before the substance of coming-to-be, generation, and revivification; firstborn from the dead, the *Logos* who is the universal *Logos* of all things; *Logos* toward God; *Logos* incarnate in the last times; by the cross conquering death and every sin; our Savior; judge of all; always substantial with and *homoousios* with the Father; active power from the paternal power; begetting and making all things; the substance [Col. 1077A] of the existence of all things, and generation and revivification. For he is eternal life, the power and wisdom of God; himself unchangeable and immutable (variant: “changeable”) insofar as he is *Logos* and always is *Logos*; but, insofar as he creates all things—and especially insofar as he acts in matter (*hylē*)—impassibly undergoing affection.
