As a fountain of waters is immutable, impassible, and outside every motion, yet when it flows and becomes a river is thought to undergo effects according to the riverbed and the kinds and qualities of the earth, always preserving its own power of water; and as a river irrigates the earth, suffering no diminution in being water: so that Christ is the river of whom the Prophet says, “who waters and pours over the whole earth” (Gen. 2:6). But Christ wholly irrigates all things, visible and invisible; by the river of life he irrigates with the substance of all things that are [Col. 1077B].

He in whom there is life is Christ; he in whom the Holy Spirit irrigates is he in whom is the power of vitality, the Father and God. Yet the whole is one God. Therefore we also confess the Holy Spirit, who has all things from God the Father, the *Logos*—that is, Jesus Christ—handing over to him all things which Christ has from the Father.

And in this such manner we confess at once that these three exist from this one source; that they are one God, *homoousia*, always simultaneous—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, by ineffable power and inexpressible generation, is *Logos*, God, image, form, χαρακτήρ, radiance of the Father, virtue, and wisdom of God. Through these God appears and is revealed in the power of all things, existing, remaining, and doing all things according to [Col. 1077C] the action of the Son, that is, Jesus Christ—whom, incarnate, crucified, risen from the dead, ascended into heaven, seated at the right hand of the Father, and destined to come as judge of the living and the dead, we confess always, in voice and with the whole heart, as Father of all creation and Savior. Amen.

Grace and peace from God the Father and from his Son Jesus Christ our Lord to one who confesses these things unto all ages of ages.

### XLVIII

Spirit, *Logos*, intellect (*nous*), wisdom, substance: are they all the same, or are they different from one another? And if the same, are they so by some communion or by universality? If by some communion, what is primary, what derives from another, and by what communion? If by universality, what then are the [Col. 1077D] differences and what the communion? If they are wholly different from one another, are they related as subject and accident, or in some other manner?

If they are in every way different, they are heteronymous (*heterōnyma*) and of different substance. But nothing is wholly of different substance from anything else; for Being (*on*) is the genus of things which are, and is more especially genus in respect of being. Yet being is twofold, and Being itself (*to on*) is twofold: there is true being, and there is merely being.

If, then, true Being and merely Being are predicated of all beings and merely beings, whether synonymously (*synōnymōs*) or homonymously (*homōnymōs*), they are not wholly different. Therefore all things that are are related to one another by participation in a certain communion. For that which is not being is opposed to Being (*to on*) as a contrary by privation, without any mutual participation; therefore it is not “other” either [Col. 1078A].

If, then, things which are also differ and are different, nevertheless by some communion they are the same; and in this manner they are both same and different, in two ways: either different in identity, or the same in otherness. But if they are the same in otherness, they incline more toward otherness; if different in identity, identity appears most strongly. What agrees with these points must therefore be discerned from this.

### XLIX

By God’s permission enough has been said concerning God and the *Logos*, that is, concerning Father and Son, because the two are one. It has also been said concerning the *Logos*, that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit, that they are in one. If, therefore, the two are one and the two are in one, that one in which the two are—because it is with [Col. 1078B] that one and always with it from eternity—makes the two, which are simultaneous and the same to one another, one. Therefore they must be the same.

How this is so, hear as I say. Before all things which truly are, there was the One, or the One itself, before there was for it the being-one. For that One must be spoken and understood as having a single conception of otherness: one alone, simple one; one by concession; one before all existence, before all existentiality, and especially before all inferior things, before Being itself. For this One is before Being.

Before every essence, substance, subsistence, and even all things more powerful than these: without existence, without substance, without intelligence. For it is above these—immeasurable, invisible, universally indistinguishable, both from those things which are in it [Col. 1078C] and from those which come after it, even from those which are from it. Yet it is discernible and defined for itself alone by its own existence—not as an act, so that subsistence might be something other than itself; and its knowledge of itself is indivisible in every respect; without figure, without quality, nor even qualifiedness; qualified without quality; without color, species, or form; lacking all forms.

Nor is it the form itself by which all things are formed, both all universals and all particulars which are. It is the first cause of all principles, the principle of all intelligences, the pre-intelligence of all powers, strength itself more renowned than motion, more stable than stability itself. For by ineffable motion it is stability; by ineffable stability it is supereminent motion. Denser than every continuity, higher than every distance, more bounded than every body, greater than every magnitude [Col. 1078D], purer than every incorporeal thing, more penetrating than every intelligence and body, most powerful of all, power of powers; greater than every genus, power, and species; itself being the whole of all things, yet greater than every whole, corporeal and incorporeal; more a part than every part, by an unutterable power, pure, existing before all things which truly are.

### L

This is God; this is the Father: pre-intelligence, pre-existent and pre-existence, preserving his own blessedness and himself in immovable motion. For that reason he does not need others: perfect above the perfect, threefold-powerful in unity, perfect Spirit and above spirit. For he does not breathe, but is simply Spirit; in him, [Col. 1079A] what it is for him to be is Spirit breathing into himself, so as to be Spirit. For he is Spirit inseparable from himself, himself both place and inhabitant, remaining in himself, alone in the alone, existing everywhere and nowhere by simplicity; one, uniting three powers—every existence, every life, and blessedness.

But all these are one, a simple one, and especially in the power of what it is to be—that is, the power of existence, life, and blessedness. For the power by which he is and exists, which is the power of existence, is itself also the power of life and blessedness through itself; and therefore he is also his own *Logos*, living and acting, possessing according to himself the existence of himself existing in himself: an indistinguishable union of Spirit, divinity, substantiality, blessedness, intellectuality, vitality, goodness, and universally [Col. 1079B] all things in every way; purely unbegotten pre-being (*proon*), unity of union, subject to no union.

Therefore, since this One exists, one then sprang forth from one: one in substance, one in motion—for motion is existence, since existence is motion. This One, then, is existentially one, but not one as the Father is non-existentially one, who is existentially one according to power. For he has power—or rather, he has that which will be according to operation; and in truth he does not have it but is it. For power, since it is an active compulsion toward all things, is without strain and truly in every way without need; it is power from this, that it is all things. For that power which can give birth needs action; action itself, being unity, acts.

LI. Therefore, according to this One which we call being [Col. 1079C], the One is life: an infinite movement, productive of others—whether of those which truly are or of those which are—an existent Word (*logos*), moving toward being the things that are, moving all things from itself, ever in motion, possessing motion within itself—or rather, itself being motion. For thus the divine Scripture says: “The Father God himself gave him to have life in himself” (John 5:26). This Son is the Word (*logos*) who is with God; this is he through whom all things were made; this Son, and the whole sonship of the whole fatherhood, is ever Son and Son from eternity. The Son, moreover, is by self-moved motion, since power proceeds, as though from an immovable pre-existence, and is unmoved insofar as it was power.

This motion nowhere rests; arising from itself, it hastens into every kind of movement. For it is infinite life, and in vivification itself it has, as it were, appeared outwardly [Col. 1079D]. Therefore life was necessarily begotten; but life is the Son, life is motion—life from vital pre-existence, existence in constitution and in the manifestation of all wholes—which, according to power, is the Father, just as pre-intelligence appears from the intelligence of those things which truly are. Therefore this existence is the life of all existence; and, insofar as life is motion, it has received, as it were, a feminine power, that which it desired to vivify.

But since, as has been shown, this motion, though one, is also life and wisdom, wholly turned toward wisdom—and rather toward paternal existence—yet more toward the paternal power of motion turned back; and, vivified by it, life returns to the Father, becoming male [Col. 1080A]. For descent is life; ascent is wisdom. And this too is Spirit. Therefore Spirit is both: two in one. And just as, with life being the first existence, it was necessary to enter into virginal power and for the Son of God, a man, to be generated by the masculine birth of a virgin.

For in the first motion—I mean the first to come into manifestation—life seemed, as it were, to have departed from the Father’s power; and, with an implanted desire to vivify, though existing inwardly as life, yet existing outwardly as motion, it returns into itself. Again, turned back into itself, it comes to its paternal existence, made and perfected by power (or: “having been made through omnipotent power, it became perfect Spirit, its inclination turned toward the higher things, that is, inward”). Thus, according to the type, the order had to be so: when Spirit is in the body—that is, in Christ the Son—and seems [Col. 1080B] to suffer diminution and to be born from the Virgin, it rises again and is renewed through that very apparent diminution into its paternal power, that is, into a more divine and primal existence; and it returns to the Father, that is, to paternal existence and power.

LII. How this is, I still dare to say, so that our subject may be made clear by a fuller exposition. Let us posit intelligence. In this manner God is the power of these three powers: existence, life, blessedness—that is, of being, living, and understanding. That there are three in each of these is evident: first, being; and secondly, according to being itself, living and understanding—without any unification, but simply simplicity. And this too is evident, as has been shown: that being, of such a kind, is manifestly God; and, as has been shown, God is power, able to grant being to all things—not giving “being” from himself as a part, but bestowing the paternal and productive power proper to each thing’s being.

This occurs through the ministering Word (*logos*), that is, through life, which grants life to all; and then anyone receives being insofar as he receives life. If, therefore, God’s being is not derived from that by which he grants being to all, but from the ministry of that which is life; and if being life itself in him is one and the same as the Father’s being in repose, then the being of life, according to identity, is motion, dependent through its own power on paternal power [Col. 1080D].

And because every natural power is will, life willed to move itself, by motion implanted according to substance, impassibly and directly toward being. For natural will is not passion. Therefore, according to God’s being—in which is the power of existence, paternal substantiality—according to power, being itself is also life. If, then, life moved itself, and motion is will, motion is paternal and will is paternal, because paternal power is life. But if life, according to what it is, is motion, then motion belongs properly to life.

But because motion is borne from one thing to another—as though from that which is within to what is without—this is life and power and nature and [Col. 1081A] will; and above all it is its own existence. Therefore it is called an effulgence, or procession, or manifestation of the exalted Spirit, operative in vivifying all that is wholly of essence. Thus, since life exists inwardly, insofar as life itself is motion, life is the offspring of the Father according to motion.

But since motion, insofar as it is motion, possessing no elevation of its own, proceeds outward from what is inward—as sensation receives fontal and universal power from *nous*—it is both within and without according to motion. For motion is *nous*. Thus life also, insofar as it is motion, has become Son: manifest motion from paternal motion, which is hidden and which, according to primal power, is existence. Again, life, insofar as it is motion, proceeding [Col. 1081B] from paternal motion, is both within and without. Yet life is motion; therefore life is within and without. Thus God lives; life itself lives; therefore God and life are one. Therefore these two are in each, both other and the same: in the Son, therefore, is the Father; and in the Father, the Son.

LIII. Truth therefore cries out that these are *homoousia*—consubstantial—united in identity with distinction. Again, if the Father is life and the Son is life, because the Son, being life insofar as he is motion, is both within and without, God lives, the Son lives, and all things live outwardly, the Son being everywhere. And because the Father is in the Son, the Father too is everywhere.

Again, because the Father is in the Son: when you see the Son and understand him, you will see and understand the Father. “Whoever sees me sees the Father.” This was said for that reason. For the Son is the form of the Father [Col. 1081C]. “Form” is not here understood as something outward and outside substance, nor as a countenance attached to substance, as in our case; but as a subsisting substance in which what is hidden and veiled in another appears and is displayed.

God is, as it were, something veiled: for no one sees God. Therefore the Son is form, in whom God is seen. For if God is existence, power, substance, motion, and life, then God is hidden, as though without form. Thus, if life is manifest, and manifest according to the power of motion, then life according to motion—which is hidden in appearance—is understood, proclaimed, and seen in existent motion.

Further: being is the Father, whereas life is the Son; and since it is impossible to comprehend being—for it is hidden—life, insofar as it is life, is already also being [Col. 1081D]. Therefore in life being appears; life is consequently the life of being. But the Father, God, is being, and the Son is life. Therefore the Son, life, is the form of Father God, in which paternal power is contemplated.

We must therefore believe in the Son of God, so that life—which is both true and eternal life—may arise in us. For if we have faith in Christ the Nazarene, incarnate from Mary, we shall have faith in the Son of God, who both was and became incarnate Spirit. How I have understood this, I shall say.

LIV. But first we must see whether the other things are to be attributed to the Father or to the Son. I mean Spirit, Word (*logos*), *nous*, Holy Spirit, wisdom, substance. First, Father and Son are the same; but Son and Holy Spirit are also the same. Therefore existence and life are the same; hence [Col. 1082A] existence and blessedness are the same. Again, being and life are the same, and life and understanding are the same.

This has been said concerning these matters in the book preceding this one and in others: there are three in one, and therefore the three are the same. “Therefore the three are synonymous” (*synōnyma ara ta tria*), according to the name by which each of them possesses its own power. For being, life, and intelligence are so; and likewise each in relation to the others. Therefore they are the same and synonymous, the same and co-generated; thus they are also consubstantial.

Yet a certain distinction seems to appear in them; and especially for this reason, although they are the same, they are not simply identical. For a certain power of theirs is hidden, while others are manifest, both in being and in understanding. Yet existence, in the same power, is at once power and consubstantiality; and in these alone there is one being, the same. In other things, however, they are other in identity and the same.

LV. Now we must examine what the other names set down at the beginning signify. I mean Spirit, Word (*logos*), *nous*, Holy Spirit, wisdom, substance. Spirit is a name of substance or existence; it signifies being, and is named and understood in terms of what it is. If you wish to know what God is: Spirit signifies that he is being. Therefore God and Spirit signify being.

Again, what is life? That which is Spirit. Therefore Spirit and life signify being. Thus Holy Spirit too, by this very name, signifies being, with a distinction from the first two, which are named by one term. Since this distinction is substantial, it signifies what it is. From these matters it already appears that substance, in each instance, signifies being. Therefore Spirit is substance in these three; they are thus *homoousia*, consubstantial [Col. 1082C].

For Spirit is not divided Spirit: being one in the three. Since paternal existence is one in nature, power, and action, and since it possesses the three which generate themselves, substance is omnipotence. Nor, therefore, did existence pre-exist. For the Father is the generator of his own substance, and is, at the summit, the fontal existence of the others. Nor is existence itself divided. Existence and the power in being are, in each of these three, according to all majesty, omnipotence, and every mode of perfection: generating itself, establishing itself from itself, moving itself, ever moving itself; consubstantial, at once powerful, both this being which is so and the being which the Father gives.

The Savior says: “All things that the Father has are mine; therefore I said, ‘He will receive from what is mine’” (John 16:15); “for he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak” (ibid. 13). Therefore if the Holy Spirit speaks, he speaks from the Son; and the Son himself speaks from the Father. Voice, Word (*logos*), and uttered Word are therefore three; and for this reason, three are one. The Father indeed speaks in silence, the Son manifestly, and the Holy Spirit speaks in speech not manifestly, but speaks spiritually what he speaks.

LVI. These three, therefore, are true lights—rather, one light; truly, one Word (*logos*), one voice, one uttered Word—that is, one active power, harmonious before it brings anything into being. It is manifest, however, that the soul is another substance: made by the three-powered Spirit, it is neither pure voice nor uttered Word, but, as an echo (*ēchō*), hears in order to speak; it is more an image of voice than voice itself [Col. 1083A].

And this is John’s voice crying in the wilderness: “Make straight the way of the Lord” (Matt. 3:3). For the soul cries in the wilderness—that is, in the world—because it belongs to the Lord God and desires to be purified, so that it may enjoy God the Lord. It bears testimony concerning God and was sent beforehand into the world for the testimony of testimony. For the testimony of God is Jesus Christ; therefore Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and John the son of the Lord. For John was not the light, but came to bear testimony concerning the light (John 1:8).

Therefore Word and voice are the Son: he himself is life, Word (*logos*), motion, *nous*, wisdom, existence, and first substance; he himself is potential action; he himself is the first Being (*on*), from whom are all beings (*onta*), through whom and in whom they are. He stands in the middle in the Angel of the Trinity: he declares the pre-existent Father and brings the Holy Spirit to perfection. For, as blessed Paul says, “The Gospel is the power of God and wisdom” (Rom. 1:16), signifying the Son through “power,” because all things are through him: for all things come to be by the word of power, and all things are made perfect by the wisdom of the Holy Spirit.

If, then, God is these things, these three are simultaneous. And because one is two, all things exist simultaneously in the simultaneous knowledge that is life in the Father, in which the Holy Spirit too is according to existence, because the three were one and always are. Therefore, if eternal life, the Son, is the effulgence of pre-eternal life, and life itself is perfect knowledge and eternal life—for then it is perfect when it knows both what it is and whose it is, since it is both itself and by the Father’s command—then, existing in itself, it does not become infinite, saving and saved [Col. 1083C] by itself. It is necessary to understand and say that God’s power is in it, that is, the Father is in the Son, while it itself was infinite through itself.

And this signifies: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). For life descended by infinite motion into the lower regions and vivified corruption. For this purpose the universal Word and power of life became flesh, as the angel said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). Therefore Jesus Christ was born according to the flesh from Mary and from the Holy Spirit, by the power of the Most High.

LVII. Therefore Christ our Lord is all things: flesh, Holy Spirit, power of the Most High, Word (*logos*). He fulfilled the mystery so that all life, with the flesh, might return from every corruption into heaven, through eternal light, to what has been fulfilled [Col. 1083D]. Therefore our Lord Jesus is not flesh alone, nor Holy Spirit alone, nor Spirit alone, nor Word alone, but all things together.

Thus the Holy Spirit, all blessedness, in the first unbegotten generation—the only generation which is and is called generation—was himself Father and himself Son. For when Spirit moved itself—that is, when perfect life, existing in motion, wished to see itself, namely its own power, that is, the Father—there came about the manifestation of itself which is and is called generation; and thereby it existed outwardly. For all knowledge, insofar as it is knowledge, is outside that which it desires to know. “Outside,” however, I mean as in the act of beholding itself: this is to know or see that pre-existent paternal power [Col. 1084A].

Thus in that time without temporal understanding, as though departing from what was being in order to behold being itself—because there every motion is substantial distinction—it swiftly returns into identity. For this is not an effulgence in a backward direction; rather, like lights or faces looking at one another, by reciprocal vision, the same one thing subsisted in the same way, whole and perfect. Lights are everywhere like faces beholding one another; they have no back. Yet God is said mystically to be seen “from behind.” Therefore, without any diminution, the whole always remained one, above all by the most potent union of paternal power.

The Holy Spirit is therefore the first inward motion, which is paternal thought—that is, knowledge of itself; for foreknowledge precedes knowledge. According to this natural mode of knowledge, intelligence was made outward, and the Son was born, becoming life: not because he had not been life, but because outward life is more fully life, since life is in motion. This is the Word (*logos*) called Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made: the seed of all things for their being; for without life it is impossible for anything to be, among things that are or among things that are not, which are consequences.

LVIII. But since we have said that motion is one and the same, and that the Word (*logos*) and the Holy Spirit are one and the same—the Word insofar as it is life, and the Holy Spirit insofar as it is being, knowledge, and intelligence—and since we have said that life and knowledge are the same thing, and that intelligence was moved in the first motion: for this order, being natural and divine power [Col. 1084C], it was necessary that intelligence be moved toward knowledge of itself.

The Son was born, who is the Word, that is, life by paternal power, with intelligence generating him—that is, the being of all things that are, as it were an eternal fountain. Therefore no one will err if he understands the Holy Spirit to be the mother of Jesus, both above and below: above in the manner stated; below in this manner. For the sake of liberation, it was necessary that all that is divine—that is, the seedbed of all spirits existing universally, and primal being, that is, the universal Word—be incarnate from lower matter (*hylē*) and all corruption, for the destruction of all corruption and sin.

For the darkness and ignorance of the soul, despoiled by material powers, needed eternal light as an aid, so that the Word of the soul and the Word of the flesh, corruption having been thrust down through the mystery of death, might raise souls and bodies, through the Holy Spirit as minister, into divine and life-giving intelligences by knowledge, faith, and love [Col. 1084D].

Therefore the angel answered Mary and said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). These two in motion, the Word and the Holy Spirit, came so that Mary might become pregnant, so that flesh might be fashioned from flesh—the temple and dwelling of God. The Holy Spirit is power in motion, for motion is the principle of generation; but the power of the Most High is the Word itself. For Jesus the Word is “the power and wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). But concerning the Word, that is, the Son, he said, “will overshadow you.” For human nature cannot receive what is perfect, divine, and resplendently clear. This signifies: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). More particularly, the overshadowing signifies what was said: “He emptied himself” (Phil. 2:7).

LIX. Therefore, according to the order set forth, we have God the Father, the Son consubstantial (*homoousios*) with him, and the three consubstantial according to identity in substance. For Spirit is one substance: it is being itself. But being itself is life and understanding. These three are in every individual thing, and therefore there is one divinity and one God, because Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one—distinction appearing only according to power and action.

God, in power and hidden motion, moves and commands all things as in silence; but the Word, the Son [Col. 1085B], who is the Holy Spirit, converses by voice for the generation of all things according to life and according to intelligence, establishing them in being. From these things it is apparent that the Word himself and the Holy Spirit are *nous* and wisdom. For Paul himself said this divinely: “Who has known the *nous* of the Lord?” (Rom. 11:34). And again, concerning him: “the power and wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24).

Solomon also speaks of wisdom in reference to him; many names are referred back to the Son. Paul, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, also calls him substance: “the image of his substance” (Heb. 1:3). Jeremiah likewise calls the people consubstantial: “For who has stood in my substance and seen my Word?” (Jer. 23:18, LXX); and again: “If they had stood in my substance and heard my words” (ibid. 22). And the Gospel according to Matthew: “Give us today our consubstantial bread” (Matt. 6:11). In Luke’s parable, the younger son says to his father: “Give me the fitting portion of the substance” (Luke 15:12); and again: “There he squandered his substance” (ibid. 13). For when he descended from there, he did not retain his powers.

These are matters concerning the soul, but I have said this against those who deny that the name *ousia*, “substance,” occurs in the sacred Scriptures. Moreover, God made the soul—that is, the human being—in his own image and likeness.

LX. Hear what these things signify, as I say. The supreme *nous* and perfect wisdom, that is, the universal Word (*logos*)—for this is one and the same thing in eternal motion—was circular motion, existing circularly from the first point (*sēmeion*) and at the highest summit, with the cyclical cause inseparably turned, so that it exists from the Father, in the Father, with the Father, proceeding with him, existing simultaneously. Thus the Son was in the Father and the Father in the Son [Col. 1085D].

First substance, and already substance in substance: spiritual substance according to *nous*, generative and productive substance, the pre-principle of all intelligible, intellectual, psychic, and material substance in matter (*hylē*). If, then, primal motion is life and intelligence—for these are that perfect, sole One—this motion is not merely circular but spherical; rather, it is a sphere, a sphere truly perfect in every way.

For if being, living, and understanding are one, and if life itself is being and intelligence; and if each has extremities and a middle, then so too has intelligence. Therefore these three of the one are circled within themselves and participate mutually in one another [Col. 1086A]. Or rather, existing together without any interval, they are the first, perfect, and sole sphere; other things are spheres only more or less by spherical likeness.

By this reasoning, necessarily, the point (*sēmeion*) is power, and the line (*grammē*) and the point producing the line are one. It goes forth from itself, and yet does not always go forth; it is at once in rest and in motion, always at once, circling itself all around in a circle (*kyklō*), so that God, being everywhere, is a sphere. For, since he is the point from which and to which all motion is brought back by turning, he is God: wholly Word, wholly *nous*, wholly wisdom, omnipotent substance—the substance whom we fear, whom we worship, seeing by Spirit alone and, by his nod and will, raised toward him through the grace of the cross, our Lord Jesus Christ having mercy on us. Amen.

LXI. With the cyclical motion raised upright—I mean the straight motion, which goes from point to point, that is, from Father to Father—there exists, in the manifestation of this motion and of the whole divinity, by God’s command, an image of the Word (*logos*) and of the Son according to the image and likeness of God: the image of the image, that is, of the Son. For the Son is the image of the Father, as has been shown. This means that the Son is life. Therefore the soul, made an image of life, is, together with its *nous*, an intellectual power of life from him who is *nous*; it is not *nous*, though, insofar as it looks toward *nous*, it is as though *nous*. For there vision is union.

But turning downward and away from *nous*, it drags both itself and its own *nous* downward. Made merely capable of understanding, no longer as intelligible being, if it persists thus it is the mother of the things above heaven: light, though not true light [Col. 1086C], and indeed light together with its proper *nous*. But if it looks toward lower things, being wanton, it becomes a power of vivifying, which will produce life in the world and in the things in the world, down to stones in the manner of stones; it too is then made together with *nous*.

For though the soul is *logos*, it is not the Word (*logos*). And being between spirits, intelligible things, and matter (*hylē*), turned by its own *nous* toward either, it either becomes divine or is embodied. For it is directed toward understanding by its own freedom; and, deprived of the true light, it is again called back because of the slender spark of its own *nous*. For it is indeed alone; but, when darkened below, it is said to be darkness. Indeed the purer summits of matter (*hylē*), possessing the power of animation, are the cause why light, as it were, descends into its own realm. Why then, someone says, is it stated that it discerns these things, if the soul is such? How is it said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26)?

LXII. We must first examine what man is; then what image is; what differs between image and likeness; how man was made according to image and likeness, rather than made image and likeness; and what “according to our [image]” means.

“Man” is understood in two ways, according to common usage: as composed of body and soul. Some think him composed of body and a threefold soul; others, of body and a soul possessing three powers. Others again say that he consists of body, partial *nous*, soul, and spirit, by which the flowing body is held together. Still others speak of a body fourfold by the four elements, a twofold soul, and twofold *nous*.

My understanding is this [Col. 1087A]. The body, as has been shown: God took dust and fashioned Adam. That is, with the earth already fashioned, we have the highest parts and flower of the earth as principles of the body. The Gospel according to Matthew and Luke also declares a double *nous* and a double soul. For they say: “So shall be the coming of the Son of Man. Then two shall be in the field: one shall be taken and one left; two women grinding at the mill: one shall be taken and one left” (Matt. 24:40–41). Luke adds two with respect to the body: “That night two shall be in one bed; one shall be taken and the other left” (Luke 17:34); and the other statements likewise.

Therefore, since there are two in the field, these are either *logos* or *nous*: one heavenly and the other material. And the two women grinding are two souls, heavenly and material. Thus the heavenly *nous*, or heavenly *logos* of the soul, shall be taken; but the material *logos* and soul shall be left. Hear how this is.

One must confess that the human being consists of soul and body. Since the body is composed from earth, earth therefore has a material soul; and Adam was made, according to the body, an animate being, like an animal from water and earth. Other animals are made into a living soul, but Adam was not made thus: for God breathed into his face all sensory power, to which *nous* is joined for the discernment of sensation. Thus there is another and more divine soul with its own *nous*; for a material *nous* is implanted in sensory power and is consubstantial with the material.

If this is so, the heavenly Word (*logos*), that is, divine *nous* or Spirit, is in the divine soul; the divine soul itself is in the material spirit; the material spirit is in the material soul; and the material soul is in the fleshly body. All three must be purified with the body, so that it may receive eternal light and eternal life. This faith in Christ accomplishes [Col. 1087C].

LXIII. Let us therefore say how such a soul was made according to God’s image and likeness, and whether the soul alone is the human being. For Paul says that one human being is earthly, another animal, another spiritual; and all these are in one human being. Yet he especially and often speaks of the inward human being. Thus the soul is such: for it embraces *nous* and the divine soul, and calls this the heavenly human being, while the remainder is the earthly human being.

If this is so, our soul is according to the image of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. For if Christ is life and Word (*logos*), he is the image of God, in which image Father God is discerned: namely, that God is being in life. For this is image, as has been said. And if Christ is life, while living is Word (*logos*), and life itself is being, and being is the Father; and if life itself is understanding, while this is the Holy Spirit; and if these three are all things, the three being in each and the one being three and altogether consubstantial (*homoousia*): then the soul, insofar as it is soul, and its being, living, and understanding, is the soul of the higher Triad as image of image.

For, insofar as it is soul, it possesses being, gives life, and possesses understanding together before its act of understanding: consubstantial in one, each existing as its own substance—not by severance, division, effusion, extension, or a birth cut off, but as three eternal realities, one existing in another, and this substantially. Thus it is according to the image [Col. 1088A].

And just as the Father is being, while the Son is the two in motion and act, so the soul, insofar as it is soul, is like paternal power; but vivification and intelligence are in motion. Therefore this is the soul’s being according to the image of Father and Son; and this is to be according to likeness. Thus it too is consubstantial in its unity and of similar substance: in threefold power, generating itself, therefore moving itself and always in motion in the world of motions; the fountain and principle, as Father and Son are creator, pre-cause, and pre-principle of the soul’s own motion.

LXIV. I shall say further, concerning a great mystery hidden within: just as the more divine Trinity, in unity, through its own effulgence made the soul in the intelligible world into substance—indeed, into its proper substance, which we properly call substance—so the second, united trinity of the soul unfolded an image in the sensible world, the soul itself, which is always above, generating worldly souls. Thus this too is according to image and likeness.

Let us consider, therefore, whether they speak of the flesh too, in advance by divination, because Jesus was to put on flesh. I say, perhaps, that in this respect also the Word (*logos*) is Word of flesh, God both bodily and said to be above every body. For God is the power of the universe and of all things; therefore it is not without purpose that human beings are according to the image of body.

For if our body and flesh are to rise again, put on incorruption, and become spiritual flesh—as our Savior also was in all respects, rose, ascended, and is to come—and if, after the resurrection, we shall be changed, receiving spiritual clothing [Col. 1088C], nothing prevents the human being from having been made according to the image of the flesh of the higher Word (*logos*).

For this purpose the Prophet gives testimony, saying: “And God made man according to the image of God” (Gen. 1:27). If God made according to the image, the Father made according to the image of the Son. But if it says, “He made him male and female,” as was said before, “He made man according to the image of God,” it is evident that this applies also, very greatly and mystically, according to body and flesh: the Word (*logos*) being male and female, because he was Son to himself in the first and second birth, spiritually and carnally.

Thanks be to God the Father and to his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, from eternity unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## BOOK TWO
I. We all confess that Christ [Col. 1088D] Jesus is almighty God now; presently, however, all will confess it who have faith in Christ the Son. Concerning both, that they are both and individually [God]: for the Father is God, the Son Jesus Christ; this is our whole religion, our whole hope, and in this is faith for us. Yet when we confess two individually, we nevertheless call them one God, and both one God, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Others call the Father alone one God, but the Son a man; let us for the moment pass these over. For when we call Jesus Son, we confess that he was Son even before he was born of Mary. For if (John 1:1–3) in the beginning was the Λόγος [Word], and the Word was with God, and the Word itself was God, and this was in the beginning—then, when the Word later became flesh, being the Word and being Jesus are the same. For if in the beginning [Col. 1089A] was the Word, in the beginning was the Son, who later was Jesus in the flesh, on account of the mystery which he fulfilled by the Father’s command.

Therefore it must be confessed that the Son was from the beginning. Do we say that he is of the Father’s substance, or outside it? But this must be examined. Do we not confess that God is being? We do confess it. Do we then call this being ἀνούσιον or ἐνούσιον—that is, without substance, or substance? “Ἀνούσιον,” they say. I accept this, but ask: in what sense ἀνούσιον? Is it that he has no substance whatever? Or that he is above substance, that is, ὑπερούσιον? Who, while confessing that God is, would say that he is without substance? For his being is his own substance—not that substance known to us, but he himself, what he is, is being itself: he is not from substance, but is substance itself; the begetter of all things, granting being to himself from himself; the first substance, universal substance, substance before substance.

[Col. 1089B] Therefore, because he is ὑπερούσιος [beyond substance], he is called ἀνούσιος by some—not because he is without substance, since he truly is. Let us therefore reverence God and call him being, that is, ἐνούσιον [substantial], he who established all things: heaven and earth, the world, spirits, angels, souls, living creatures, and man according to the image and likeness of their image. What then, since he is ἐνούσιος? He is certainly called God the Father—as we confess—and Father of the Only-Begotten; this is the faith of all. Does the Word mislead the understanding through its ambiguity? For God said even of human beings, “He begot you.” If, therefore, “I begot” means “I created,” as [one creates] a creature, [does it not also mean], “I begot naturally from my own substance”? What applies more [properly] to the Only-Begotten? What to him who is Son? What to him who is one and alone? What to him in whom the Father is? What to him who is in the Father? What to him who is the Λόγος, who was in the beginning, [Col. 1089C] and was with God, and is God, and through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1:1–3)?

And what does it mean that Christ is Only-Begotten? If God is Father of all according to creation, how is he Father of this Only-Begotten unless in another way—out of substance, not out of nothing? Before all things there was no substance other than the Father’s. Therefore Christ is from the Father’s substance.

II. Come then: we confess that Christ now is. Let us inquire in the same way whether this being is ἐνούσιον or ἀνούσιον. It was said above that that which has being cannot be ἀνούσιον. What then? From where is this being? ἐκ τοῦ ἀνουσίου or ἐκ τοῦ ἐνουσίου—that is, from that which is being, or from that which is non-being? “God,” they say, “is being; Christ likewise is being, but nevertheless he began.” This [last] is true. But that being which began began from that which in some manner had been, since all divine things, and those originating from the divine, always are and have been in potency; their procession, however, is their activity, and their manifestation comes from movement—and indeed it is a birth. For what of God is born, when God is unbegotten? Or is it credible, or permissible to say, that Christ was born out of nothing—he whom we call God’s Son, the Lord of majesty, and the other things which we have said above and in other books?

This, indeed, is finally what heresy asserts—both that heresy which says that Christ began from Mary, and that which says not that the Λόγος himself put on flesh, but that he assumed a human being, in order that the Λόγος himself might govern him. The latter is Marcellus; the former, Photinus. Let us therefore exclude [Col. 1090A] all who hold these and similar views concerning Christ. Let us speak with those who call Christ God’s Son, and the Son born—for they confess him to be Only-Begotten, certainly begotten and not made. This is too little, they add: the Son from the Father, God from God, true light from true light; likewise, consequently, Spirit from Spirit; and the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son. They confess these things without any rational plan, rather from fear than from truth.

Some deny that “substance” ought to be named here; others name it, but wish to call it similar, not the same. They must first consider what the prophet Isaiah said (Isa. 43:10): “Before me no God existed, and after me no God like me shall be.” If Christ is the Son, Christ is certainly after God; but after God no Christ similar [to God] exists. Therefore Christ is not similar to God; or, if not after God, certainly with God—for in no way before God is there ὁμοούσιον [consubstantial]. And David likewise says (Ps. 70:19): “None is like you.”

Next, as we have taught extensively, substance, precisely as substance—especially if it is of the same kind and is found in two or more—is called the same substance, not a similar substance. Thus soul is substance: although there are many souls, insofar as they are souls they have one and the same substance. Not because that substance preceded and pre-existed them, but because it always exists simultaneously [with them]; and so too in other cases. How much more so in God, since he is the source of substance, and the Son, receiving substance from the Father through a certain divine birth, is always with him and in him: other and yet the same, of the same substance. There is no diminution in the one, nor any completion [Col. 1090C] of unity through the other’s consubstantial reception; rather, God and his power have always been and always existed—namely, God and the Λόγος, God and his form, Father and Son, God and Jesus Christ, God and power and wisdom: ὁμοούσιον.

Therefore, if ὁμοούσιον is said as ὁμοούσιον, when things coexist in the same species, they are ὁμοειδεῖς, of the same time and age. Here, however, ὁμοηλική signifies the consubstantial: simultaneous substance, without composition or separation, yet always together, though distinct in the powers and activities of things.

III. Here questions arise. First: that Scripture makes no mention of substance, and still less is ὁμοούσιον found there. Second: that, if this is so, the Father suffered together with the Son. Third: that, if this is so, neither is the Father greater nor the Son lesser, [Col. 1090D] nor is one sender and another sent. And other such matters.

Let us first consider that question concerning substance: “There is no substance in God, nor in Christ.” Is it not read? If it is not, then, as we said above, do we take this to mean that God does not exist at all? Or that he is altogether above substance? It is impious for us to say that God is not. For substance is what God is, what Spirit is, what Light is. Why indeed do we add “true light”? In divine matters and in God, therefore, we shall understand “substance” as bodies among material things and mind among bodily things. For that is substance there: being above substance. All confess that God is, since he is the power of substance and therefore above substance, and from this is substance; for being inheres in power.

[Col. 1091A] Certainly God is almighty; and he himself is, by power and in a certain manner, all those things of which he is source or cause. Hence Paul said (1 Cor. 15:28): “That God may be all in all.” Therefore he is ὤν [being], existent, and substance. Since he is all these things, because he is the begetter of all things, he is all things in power. Therefore one should not hesitate to speak of God’s substance. For when proper words fail us regarding the first or highest things, we appropriately adapt terms available to our understanding; thus here we rightly call God’s being “substance.”

In the same manner, let us understand Christ both as being substance and as having substance from the Father, since he too is light from light, God from God, Spirit, Λόγος, through whom all things were made. And since it is so, he willed that his substance should come even to the bodily mystery, concerning which the Apostle said (Col. 2:8–9): “And not according to Christ, because in him dwells bodily all the fullness of divinity”—that is, οὐσιακῶς, “substantially.” For God is power and the Λόγος activity; in each, both are present. For power is what can be, and what is can be. Power itself, therefore, is activity, and activity itself is power. Thus the Father too is activity; the Son acts, and the Father acts. He is Father because power begets activity; and he is Son because activity is from power. Therefore the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, but both are in each individually, and for that reason they are one.

They are two, however, because what is more prominent makes the other appear. The Father is more prominently power and the Son activity; and [Col. 1091C] activity is more prominently activity because it is activity outwardly. If this is so, both Father and Son are substance: one substance, substance from the Father, simultaneous substance; and Father and Son are always and eternally together, the same and simultaneous substance. This is ὁμοούσιον.

Is it not read in the divine Scriptures? The first person to deny it concedes the reality, but seeks Scripture’s authority. Yet how is it not unjust to refuse the reality because the ancients perhaps omitted it, whether by some contingency or reason, when reason has defeated you? But what do they deny has been read: substance? Or substance concerning God and Christ? Or ὁμοούσιον itself? Substance concerning God and Christ has been read. Concerning God it is read in the prophet Jeremiah (Jer. 28:18 LXX): “Who has stood in the substance of the Lord and seen his Word? Who has given ear and heard?” Again shortly afterwards (ibid. [Col. 1091D] 22): “And if they had stood in the substance and heard my words.” Substance is likewise read in the prophet David (Ps. 138:15): “And my substance in the lower regions of the earth.” Concerning Christ it is read in Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews (Heb. 1:3): “Who is the χαρακτήρ [impress] of his substance.” There are other examples, but I judge these sufficient.

IV. “But,” they say, “the Greek has ὑπόστασις, not οὐσία.” Let us see what the difference is. The Greeks call both things that are eternal and things in the world and earthly things ὄντα [beings]. In eternal things, then, God almighty is the cause of all things, and the fountain and source of all things that are—that is, of all beings, τῶν ὄντων πάντων. What, then, do we attribute to God: that which is being? Or do we attribute being to all things? Indeed, reason is such that God is first being.

But because “being” may be understood without making clear what that being is, when it has become comprehensible it is called ὄν, that is, a certain form coming into knowledge. Such being is then called ὄν and ὕπαρξις [existence]. Every ὕπαρξις has being; but what is being is not immediately also ὕπαρξις or ὄν, except potentially—not manifestly, so as to be called ὄν. For ὄν is a certain figure, that which is being when formed; yet that which is pure is then understood as pure when it is already understood as formed. For form generates understanding and plainly declares that form is one thing and that which has been formed another. That which has been formed is being; form is that which makes that which is being intelligible.

Therefore we attribute being to God, but form to Christ, because [Col. 1092B] the Father is known through the Son—that is, being is known through form. And here it was said (John 14:9): “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also.” Therefore both God is ὕπαρξις and Christ is ὕπαρξις, since ὕπαρξις is being together with form. And because they are always together, form is being and being itself is form. Hence the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. For being is in the Father, who is power, which is prior to that which is form. Likewise, being is again in the Son; but this being, which is proper to him, he has from the Father, so that form may be his being. Thus each is in the other, and both are one.

Therefore God is ὄν and the Son is ὄν; for τὸ ὄν means being with form. Everything that is ὄν is being with form. This is also called existence, substance, and subsistence; for what is ὄν both exists and is underlying. But that which is being without any connection, which is [Col. 1092C] simple, which is one—this is more manifestly called subsistence, existence, and substance. If, then, subsistence is said of God, substance is said of God still more properly; indeed, the former signifies an underlying subject and a primary principle, which befit God. Yet it is not “underlying” as substance is in the world, but in a manner more honorable, more ancient, and in accordance with the fountainhead of the universe.

But the being which God imparts to things that are, so that each thing may be ὁμοούσιος [of one substance], is being possessing form, first, sole, and true. For that being is pure being; and this is substance in the fullest sense. But because form in turn is being and itself substance, it is called ὑπόστασις. For formed being is substance; and formed being is God—God as God and Father—and likewise the Son, as Λόγος and Son. [Col. 1092D] Thus subsistence is properly said of both, which is substance, because primary being together with form is called substance. This too is called substance, and therefore it has been said that there are three subsistences of one substance: so that being itself subsists in three ways—God himself, Christ—that is, the Λόγος—and the Holy Spirit. Therefore ὑπόστασις is rightly attributed to God and rightly to the Λόγος—that is, to the Father and the Son. The Latins call this substantia, because, as we have said, what is being, and more particularly formed being, can also be called substance. Since these things are so, ὑπόστασις has been read; and this is οὐσία, as we have proved.

V. Let us now see whether, in the passages where we read it, ὑπόστασις signifies anything other than οὐσία. [Col. 1093A] Many think that this word, ὑπόστασις, signifies resources and possessions. But if it says, “If they had stood in the ὑπόστασις of the Lord, they would have seen his Word” (Jer. 23:22 LXX), what do we understand here by the Lord’s ὑπόστασις, except that which God is? Now God is Spirit, Light, Power, Almighty, and things of that sort. One who stands and understands—yet there was no one who understands—therefore stands; but one who understands God understands and sees the Λόγος, God’s Son. It is therefore evident that this is God’s ὑπόστασις, because when it is understood, the Word too is understood; for they are together, and this is ὁμοούσιον.

He says this again: “For if they had stood in my ὑπόστασις and heard my word.” Above, [the text said] “seen”; here it has placed both—that by which one understands. For a person understands a thing who stands in the substance of the thing, that is, in the first source of the thing, so as to understand all things that belong to it.

[Col. 1093B] What next? When ὑπόστασις is used and read elsewhere, whether in David or in the Gospel, is anything other than οὐσία understood? “My ὑπόστασις,” David says (Ps. 138:15), certainly concerning God: “My ὑπόστασις [was] in the lower regions of the earth.” For he says: let no one believe himself hidden, because assuredly I am, and all that I am, and my substance, even in the lower regions of the earth. For God, or the Spirit of God—which is God’s substance—is everywhere.

VI. I also wish now to examine that which is set forth in the Gospel through parable and example. A certain householder divided his ὑπόστασις between two sons (Luke 15:12); certainly we understand this as resources and inheritance. But if this must be referred to God, then here too ὑπόστασις will be all power and might. This one son consumes when he withdraws from God. For whoever travels away from God has neither God’s Spirit nor light nor Christ; this person consumes within himself the substance of God.

[Col. 1093C] This is God’s ὑπόστασις, as we have said. Whether here we call it riches or inheritance makes no difference. For thus the Apostle Paul said: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. 11:33). If, therefore, the riches of God are wisdom and knowledge, and if wisdom and knowledge are the very power of God, while the power of God is Christ, and Christ is the Λόγος, and the Λόγος is truly Son, while the Son himself is in the Father: then he himself is the Father’s riches; he himself is ὑπόστασις. Accordingly, it makes no difference whether we understand ὑπόστασις as riches or as οὐσία, provided that what is signified is that by which God himself is.

Therefore either ὑπόστασις or οὐσία has been read concerning God; and this is also understood concerning Christ. It has been said: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10). This was said twice for this reason: the Son could be in the Father without the Father also being in the Son, unless fullness and the same one were in each individually. But if the ὑπόστασις is the same, then [they are] ὁμοούσιον. And it is the same: for Christ is God from God and light from light. Therefore [they are] ὁμοούσιον. And if this is eternally and always necessarily simultaneous, then they are truly ὁμοούσιον.

VII. But ὁμοούσιον itself has been read. For all that we have said has been read. I say this to you who now confess concerning God either that he is light or that he is Spirit. You therefore call God “God from God,” Spirit from invisible Spirit, and true light from true light—things which are God’s ὑποστάσεις. But when you call Christ God from God, light from light, and such things, where [Col. 1094A] have you read them thus? Or are you permitted to speak thus—whereby ὁμοούσιον is all the more proved—while we are not permitted to derive ὁμοούσιον? But if you say “light from light” because both God is called light and Christ is called light, and likewise both the Father is called God and Christ God, this indeed is evident. Yet “light from light” is not read concerning God, though you have been permitted to infer it. Let us therefore be permitted to compose from what has been read that which has not been read.

You deny that ὁμοούσιον has been read; but if similar terms, or terms formed in a similar way, have been read, then by equal right we ought to accept this term as formed in the same way. God’s οὐσία is light; this light is life; and this life is understanding. It has been sufficiently made clear that this is what God is and what Christ is. “The Father lives, and I live” (John 6:58). “The Father has life in himself, and he gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26). “All things that the Father has he gave to me” (John 16:15). By these and other passages [Col. 1094B] we often prove that the same things are in Father and Son, and that this is always and eternal; and therefore it is called ὁμοούσιον.

VIII. But whence comes this word? Hear the Gospel; hear Paul the Apostle; hear the prayer of offering: for God is life, and eternal life. We Christians—that is, those who believe in Christ—are taught in the Gospel (Matt. 6:9) how we ought to pray to God the Father. In that prayer, while we ask many things, we ask for bread; and this bread is life, for it is said (John 6:59): “This is the bread that came down from heaven.” This life, both Christ’s and God’s—that is, eternal life, as he himself calls it—we ask for as ἐπιούσιον ἄρτον, “bread from the same οὐσία,” that is, from God’s life: consubstantial life.

For from where shall we be sons of God except by participation in eternal life, which Christ brought us from the Father [Col. 1094C] and gave us? Thus this is “δὸς ἡμῖν ἐπιούσιον ἄρτον” (Luke 11:3): “Give us bread from the same substance,” that is, life. For if what we receive is Christ’s body, while Christ himself is life, we ask for ἄρτον ἐπιούσιον. For riches dwell bodily in Christ. The Greek Gospel therefore has ἐπιούσιον, a term derived from substance—certainly God’s substance. The Latins, either not understanding it or unable to express it, could not say this, and rendered only “daily,” not ἐπιούσιον.

Therefore both the name has been read, and substance is in God; it may be said in Greek even if it is not expressed in Latin, yet it is said in Greek because it is understood. Therefore we who believe in Christ, because we hope for eternal life from him, because he himself is life, when we follow him and are with him, around him, and around eternal life, are called λαὸς περιούσιος, “a people belonging especially [to him].” Hence the holy Apostle said in Greek in the Epistle to Titus (Titus 2:14): “Ἵνα λυτρώσηται ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ πάσης ἀνομίας, καὶ καθαρίσῃ ἑαυτῷ λαὸν περιούσιον ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων”—“that he might redeem us from every lawlessness and purify for himself a people specially his own, zealous for good works.”

The Latin translator, not understanding περιούσιον ὄχλον, “a periousion people”—περιούσιον, τὸν περιόντα, that is, [a people] around the life which Christ both has and gives—rendered it “an abundant people.” What merit is there in a people being saved by that in which it abounds? But this, again, is a great reason and almost a necessity for [the term] περιούσιος. Hence the prayer of offering asks him, with the same sense: “σῶσον περιούσιον λαὸν, ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων”—“Save a people specially your own, zealous for good works.”

Therefore all these things have been read; terms have been formed from οὐσία. Hence ὁμοούσιον has been compounded concerning God and Christ; nor is it alien to reason. For it has οὔσιον, [Col. 1095A] which the preceding names possess, and it is formed in the same way. This name excludes all heretics; therefore it was necessarily established by the ancients. It must therefore be spoken and always discussed.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] (1) Here there seems to be lacking “signification,” “derivation,” or something similar.]

IX. “But because it is not understood and causes offense, it should be removed from faith and discussion—or at least put into Latin.” They say: “It is not understood.” Therefore it cannot even be said in Latin. “It is not understood”—why then do you fear it? Those who attack it nevertheless fear it. If you fear it, you are heretics: with this excluded, you wish to enter. If you deny οὐσία in God, do you therefore wish ὁμοούσιον removed because they confess οὐσία? Then you understand it and fear it. And if Basil too says ὁμοούσιον, then this name also is against you, and you reject it for the same reason: because once for all you deny οὐσία in God. But if you reject it because [Col. 1095B] you understand it, Basil himself understands it, since he wishes ὁμοούσιον to be said; we shall speak of him later.

Ὁμοούσιον is not a name that is not understood. “Let it be said in Latin,” they declare. You demand this because it is difficult to say; and if it is said, you will follow it. A great marvel! A word makes you heretics—or rather, the sound of a word spoken in Greek. Moreover, if I say it in Latin, since the Church contains Greeks, and since all Scripture, both Old Testament and New, is written in Greek and Latin, what shall we answer when questioned by Greeks if we do not give it in Greek? It must necessarily be said ὁμοούσιον; therefore it must be used.

What then? Do not the Scriptures contain many Greek or Hebrew names, whether translated or untranslated? For example (Matt. 27:46), “Ἠλεὶ, Ἠλεὶ, λαμὰ σαβαχθανεί”—“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”; likewise Golgotha and Emmanuel; likewise (1 Cor. [Col. 1095C] 16:22), “If anyone does not love our Lord Christ the Son, ἀνάθεμα.” There are six hundred other instances: terms translated but still given; terms not translated and given alone; or anathema, which is not rendered either into Latin or Greek, yet is used and employed daily—just as Alleluia and Amen are said unchanged in every language. Thus it is permissible to use ὁμοούσιον in the same way.

Certainly, when a term is to be removed, it is removed either because it is obscure, because it is contrary, because it expresses too little or too much, or because it is superfluous. This term is not obscure: we too have explained its meaning; and because you understand it, you fear it; and Basil, because he understands it, alters it. Nor is it contrary. For since we all now confess substance—God is substance, Spirit, Light, things said of God the Father and Christ—the term ὁμοούσιον, being said of substance, cannot be contrary. But does it express too little or too much? It should be corrected rather than removed. And how can it be superfluous? Because it has already been said—where it has been said? Or because it is not useful, though it chiefly excludes heretics, especially Arians, and was established by the ancients as a wall and bulwark?

“But it was established recently.” That is because the poisonous cohort of heretics erupted recently; nevertheless it was established in accordance with the ancient faith. For even before this discussion, three hundred and fifteen bishops in the city of Nicaea, sending forth the faith decreed for the whole world, had [Col. 1096A] thousands of bishops with them throughout the world, whether of that time or of the years following. Moreover, it was approved by the father of our emperor, an emperor himself.

X. But we wish this to be said in Latin; nor will this be denied you—both you who deny substance in God and are defeated by Basil, and you, Basil, who confess substance. Both of you, by your own statements, confess ὁμοούσιον. Surely you call God, and call that same one Light, that same one Spirit. Whoever says these things affirms God’s substance. For whoever calls the Father almighty, good, infinite, or such things, does not name substance but quality. Likewise, you call the Son Λόγος, Light, Spirit; and these signify substance.

Again, when you call God, you call him God from God, true light from [Col. 1096B] true light. You remove Basil’s argument of fear—that there might be a higher substance from which two derive. For if God is from God and light from light, then the Father’s substance is certainly the Son’s, because God the Father himself is the substance from which the Son is Λόγος, Light, and Spirit. For when he is called Son, likewise Savior, likewise Jesus Christ, he is so called according to quality, not according to substance. So also the remaining terms are attributed either to Father or Son. Therefore you confess substance.

But you, at least, believe Basil, who says the same things about God and Christ: God as Light, Spirit, Λόγος, and who confesses substance. “But ὁμοούσιον is not in these things.” It is so, if you do not understand the same substance in ὁμοούσιον. But when the word is compounded, the same thing in two or more is signified: ὁμοειδής means “of the same species”; [Col. 1096C] ὁμήλιξ, “of the same age”; ὁμώνυμος, “of the same name”; concord, ὁμονοία, “of the same mind”; the same ἔννοια, “conception.” Therefore “consubstantial” means being of the same substance.

But if ὁμοῦ [together] is understood, then ὁμοούσιον will mean in Latin “simultaneously consubstantial,” not from some other thing but from God’s eternal power. For if (John 1:1) “In the beginning was the Λόγος, and the Λόγος was with God,” since the beginning has nothing before it—for if it had, it would cease to be beginning—God is eternal and the Λόγος is eternal. Therefore both are together and always together; neither is ever without the other, nor is the Son from what at some time was not. Here Arius is excluded, who advanced the phrase ἐνίοτε οὐκ ἦ, “there was a time when he was not”; and this too was his proposition, that the Son was ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, “from non-beings,” that is, from nothing.

Ὁμοούσιον signifies simultaneous existence and substance. Against both sacrileges [Col. 1096D] the force of this term, ὁμοούσιον, contends. For whether ὁμοούσιον means “of the same substance,” as ὁμοειδής does, as we taught above, it excludes the assertion that Christ is from nothing: if God and the Λόγος are of the same substance, God and the Λόγος are not only not from nothing, but not even from similar substance. Or if ὁμοούσιον is understood from the sense of simultaneous substantial being, this means simultaneity of substances: God and the Λόγος together, Father and Son together always and eternally.

XI. Thus is excluded the assertion: “There was [a time] when he was not.” If this is so, then by this single word, ὁμοούσιος, the entire poison of Arian doctrine is destroyed. O learned [Col. 1097A] bishops! O holy men! O you who confirm faith by the Spirit! O word, truly God’s Word—by which God and the Λόγος are shown to exist together eternally and always, and to be of one and the same substance!

Therefore ὁμοούσιον has been expressed in Latin; consequently it must also necessarily be used and discussed in Greek. But let us add something further, by which ὁμοούσιον, expressed in Latin through your confession and through the divine reading, may be approved. The divine reading says: “The Father in the Son, and the Son in the Father.” And lest this be insufficient for faith, our Lord Jesus Christ himself says (John 14:10): “I am in the Father and the Father is in me.”

What then? Are these names in one another? Or powers, substances, wisdoms, and authorities? The Father, insofar as he is Father, cannot be in the Son; likewise, the Son cannot be in the Father. But insofar as each possesses the substance of power, [Col. 1097B] that is in the other. Hence each is in the other. One is rendered even though each subsists individually; yet they are one because the same thing is understood and named in both. Therefore the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father—but in this manner.

If this is so, let us consider the remaining points. You say, and rightly say, that Jesus Christ our Lord is God from God and light from light. It is close at hand to say this also in like manner. Let us therefore say—and say truly—light in light in God. This is not said also in reverse because one term is in two [persons]. For Father and Son are two names; therefore they can be reciprocally reversed, so that Father is said to be in Son and Son in Father. But when one name is said of two—God in God—it will likewise be said, when it is said of the other, according to the same reasoning: light in light.

Therefore, by the necessity [Col. 1097C] of the single name, it is indeed said once; but because there are two, Father and Son, it is understood and heard twice. Let us therefore say: Jesus, the Son of God, God from God, light from light. Let us say also: God in God, light in light. For if, as we all confess, the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, while the Father is God and light, and this Son is from the Father, then it is necessary and true to say: God in God and light in light. Is this difficult? Yet it must necessarily be confessed that it is so and stands so.

XII. What if it has also been read, and one thing most plainly set forth from these two, so that it is not an invention of mine but has already been established by sacred reading? The hymn-writer David, in the book of Psalms—called the key of all mysteries—sings thus to God (Ps. 35:10): “[Col. 1097D] For with thee is the fountain of life, and in thy light we shall see light.” Do we judge this to have been said to God, or to Christ, or to both? For it is rightly said to whichever; for the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. But if it is addressed to God the Father, this will be that saying (Jer. 23:22, LXX): “If they had stood in my substance and heard my word.” But if to the Son, it will be that saying (John 14:9): “He who sees me sees also the Father.” Therefore, “in thy light we shall see light.” Light, then, is that in whose light we shall see light. Nor should there be any doubt, since this follows also, when that which is in the same manner has been established both in reality and by reading.

If this is so, let us gather all things together: now *homoousion* will appear, both understood in Greek and expressed in Latin. We believe in God the Father almighty, and in his only-begotten Son [Col. 1098A]. So be it: enough has now been said on this matter. Isaiah speaks thus (Isa. 45:14): “Egypt has laboured, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians and Sabaeans. Men of great stature shall walk in thee, and shall be thy servants; they shall follow behind thee; bound in manacles, they shall worship thee and pray to thee, because God is in thee, and there is no God apart from thee.”

Jesus Christ our Lord: God from God, light from light; consubstantial, simultaneously substantial. Thus, joined to the remaining words of the creeds and to the faith, *homoousion* is set forth and completed in its fullness: “from the same substance,” “in the same substance,” and “always together,” if one wishes, may thus be expressed in Latin. But if it is pleasing to retain the one Greek word—which with great force and great brevity embraces both—let it remain concerning God and our Lord; and let *homoousion* [Col. 1098B] be held ever more firmly, written, spoken, discussed, and preached in all the churches. This is the faith at Nicaea; this is the faith of the apostles; this is the catholic faith. By this all Arians and all heretics are overcome. Peace from God the Father and from Jesus Christ our Lord be with those who think thus. Amen.

## BOOK THREE

The divine *Logos* or *Nous* uses a heavenly soul as its seat, and as a body; but that soul uses the sensory *nous*, or the insensory *Logos* uses the soul, just as the sensory soul itself is in a body, and therefore in whatever sort of body. Everything that comes from divine things is in a sense a part of them, but as an image—as has also been asserted and demonstrated elsewhere. For since, among the divine things themselves, the *Logos* of God is an image, so too are the rest; therefore, they are images of all divine things. For [Col. 1098C] as God’s *Logos* is an image, so every soul of this kind there is an image of the *Logos*; the rest are images. But in sensory nature they should be called not images but rather likenesses and representations.

For the progression of things is such that the shining-forth of light is an image of light. Hence there is the same substance in the highest and eternal things, because the image of light is light. For as from Spirit there is nothing but Spirit, from the true nothing but the true, and from God God, so likewise from substance, substance; for Spirit, the true, and God are substance. Whatever constitutes each thing’s own being is substance.

But this “being” of which we speak must be understood differently in the case of “to be” and in the case of “to be thus,” so that one belongs to substance and the other to quality. Yet this is so among sensible things and in the world. But in divine and eternal things these two are one: for everything there is simple; and God is that which is light, which is good, which is existence, which is life, which is intelligence. But we have spoken of this elsewhere also.

Therefore all things there are substantially simple, unconnected, one with respect to number—and not one in number, but one before number, that is, before the one that is in number: namely, utterly simple, alone, without the phantasy of another. Hence that which is born from it as image is not a division, nor an outpouring, but a shining-forth; not an extension, but an appearing; not a germination of power, but the action of power. For where, or whence, is action except in power and from power? And when or where is power except with action and in action? Therefore it is not one thing in another, nor at any time similar; for it is always the same [Col. 1099A].

And because the shining-forth manifests light, or action manifests power, therefore: “He who sees me sees also the Father” (John 14:9). And because no one sees power itself alone: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). And because power at rest is life and intelligence at rest, while life and intelligence are action: whoever sees God must necessarily die. For God’s life and intelligence are in themselves, not in act; but every act is outward, and our life is precisely outward life. Therefore to see God is death: “No one,” he says, “has ever seen and lived” (Exod. 33:20); for like is seen by like. Therefore outward life must be relinquished, outward intelligence must be relinquished, if we wish to see God; and this is death for us.

II. But since this life and intelligence is the *Logos*, who is Christ: through Christ we too have all things; therefore through him are *Logos*, life, and intelligence. Why? Because all these are movement and addition. Therefore, if we are in Christ the Lord, we see through Christ—that is, true life, namely through the true image. And because it is true, it is of the same substance, because power is also in action. Thus we see God there; and hence comes the saying: “He who sees me sees God” (John 14:9).

But because action is from power, therefore the Son is from the Father, and the *Logos* from Spirit; and because Spirit is from Spirit, therefore God is from God. Thus substance is from the same substance, as we have taught above. God is power—that is, the first universal being of existence, which has life and intelligence with itself, that is, within itself; or rather, it is being itself, namely that which is life and intelligence in an inward movement turned back upon itself. Therefore there is movement in God, and from this also action; whence it is said (John 5:19): “Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son cannot do anything from himself unless he sees the Father doing it; for whatever he does, these things the Son likewise does.”

Therefore the Father too both makes and acts, but inwardly; and since he needs nothing external, he is always full, always whole, always blessed. Yet because life and intelligence are movements, and every life gives life, while whatever is given life is outward; likewise, whatever intelligence understands is outward, and that which it understands inwardly understands by an intelligence drawn forth—whether shining forth or enlightening—and by life. Hence from God and from the same substance are substance, life, and intelligence; and likewise movement, when it is inwardly in itself, is the same as substance. But when it looks outward and stands out, that is, when it works and acts, this is birth, this is nativity [Col. 1099D].

And because the movement is one, the Son is only-begotten; and movement is one, whether that life or intelligence. For life must be movement. For every life gives life; therefore life is movement. If it exists in itself and is turned back upon itself, it is substance unto itself; if it looks outward, it is more properly called movement. For inwardly movement is rest, or moving rest, and resting movement. For God must be both the parent of rest and movement, and substance itself, because through its union and a certain form it is the source of both.
