He himself is simple and one, always one and alone, and, as we said above, [Col. 1100A] whole.

When he is received and understood in resting movement, this is God, and he himself is Father—Father always and from eternity. For movement is always from substance and in substance, or rather is substance itself. But when it looks outward—and to look outward is to be movement or motion—this is to see, understand, and wish to know itself. But when it sees itself, it exists and is understood as twofold: as seeing and as that which is seen; the one who sees and the thing seen are the same, because it sees itself. Therefore this is looking outward, generated or existing outwardly, in order that it may understand what it is. Therefore, if it is outward and generated, it is Son; and if Son, only-begotten, because it alone is all action, and all movement is both universal and one; and movement is the same as substance. Therefore Father and Son are one and the same substance: thus consubstantial, that is, *homoousion* [Col. 1100B].

III. Therefore the Son is all things, as the Father is all things. But because substance is prior in potentiality to act and movement—I said “prior” with respect to force and cause, because substance is the cause of movement; for every movement is in substance—the Father is necessarily generator; and likewise the Son necessarily possesses all that the Father possesses: “All things which the Father has, he gave to me” (John 16:15). And again: “As the Father has life from himself, so he gave the Son to have life from himself” (John 5:26). Therefore, as the Father is life, so the Son is life and life from himself. For life itself is the power of living for itself and for others, not life from elsewhere.

Thus the movement—the principal movement, the one movement, self-moving, only-begotten movement—is the *Logos*; for it is life, through whom all things live. And because it is life, it is he through whom all things were made and in whom all things were made, because all things, purified, return into eternal life. And all things were made in him, because the things made in him are life. For there is nothing that has its own being for which being itself is not life. Therefore all things were made in Christ, because Christ is *Logos*.

Life, however, did not begin, because it is always life from itself for itself; hence it never ceases, is always infinite, and is through all things and in all things—from divine and supercelestial things down through the celestial things and all the heavens, the ether, air, moist and earthly things, all things which arise from the earth, and all other things. Therefore our body and flesh also possess something vital, and all matter is animated, so that the world might exist, from which animals burst forth at God’s command. Therefore life, that is, the *Logos*, is in flesh; and Christ is in life. This is why the *Logos* became flesh [Col. 1100D].

Hence it is not surprising that he took flesh in the mystery, in order to help both flesh and humankind; but when he took flesh, he took the universal *Logos* of flesh. For this is why the power of all flesh triumphed in flesh, and why he aided all flesh, as is said in Isaiah (Isa. 40:5; 52:10; Luke 3:6): “All flesh shall see thee, the salvation of God.” And in the book of Psalms (Ps. 64:3): “All flesh shall come to thee.”

Likewise, he took the universal *logos* of soul. For that he had a soul is evident, when the same Saviour said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:33). And again in the Psalm: “Thou wilt not abandon my soul in hell” (Ps. 15:10). But that he took the universal *logos* of soul is clear from Ezekiel (Ezek. 18:4): “All souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son.” Likewise, the universal *logos* of soul is shown by this also: he becomes angry, when he curses the fig tree and says, “It shall be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah on that day than for you” (Matt. 10:15; 11:23), and similarly in many places. He also desires, when he says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39). There too he reasons: “But rather let thy will be done.”

These and many other matters show the universal *logos* of soul. Therefore the whole human being was assumed, and, having been assumed, was set free. For in him were all universals: universal flesh and universal soul; and they were raised to the cross and purified through the saving God, the *Logos*, universal of all universals. For through him all things were made—he who is Jesus Christ, God, Saviour, and our Lord [Col. 1101B]. Amen.

IV. Therefore the *Logos* is that which exists, what can exist, and what could have existed: as it were the seed and power of existing, the wisdom and power of all substances, from God unto all actions; God as the Father’s power and act, by which the Son himself is one God with the Father.

For, since these existences are living and intelligent, let us observe that these three—being, living, understanding—are three in such a way that they are always one, and one in that which is being. But by “that which is being,” I mean the being that is there. Therefore, in this being, living and understanding are all substantial, and are one subsistence. For living itself is what being is; for in God, unlike in us, that which lives is not one thing and the life which causes it to live another [Col. 1101C].

For if we posit and understand that he himself is life and existence, and that what is his power is itself his being, it will be clear that being and living must be understood as one and the same. The same account and force applies also to his intelligence. Therefore his understanding itself is what his being is, and his being is what his understanding is; this very understanding is intelligence. Therefore being is the being both of life and of intelligence—that is, being is life and intelligence. Thus life is one, and being is the same as intelligence.

If these are one in each singly and in each pair, it follows that living itself is understanding. For if being is living, and being is understanding, living and understanding become one, since for them being is one. Moreover, being itself is nothing other than living; for what does not live loses being itself, so that as long as each thing exists, this is its own life; hence being dies together with life.

But when we speak of eternal things, we understand another kind of living: it is the very knowledge that one lives; and knowing, moreover, is understanding. Therefore knowing is understanding, and knowing that one lives is living; thus understanding will be living. If this is so—if living and understanding are one, and being is one with living and understanding—substance is one, while these are three subsistences. For since they have their own force and signification, and are as they are spoken of, they are necessarily three and yet one, since every individual thing is one, although there are three. This is said thus in Greek: [Col. 1102A] *ek mias ousias treis einai tas hypostaseis*: “from one substance there are three subsistences.”

This being so, being is as a foundation for the rest; for living and understanding, as second and subsequent, seem by a certain natural order either to inhere in that which is being, or somehow to arise from being; and in that which is their own being they preserve that first, fontal being. For being is never without living and understanding, nor living and understanding without being, as has now been demonstrated.

V. Let this be an example for understanding the matter. Let us posit sight or vision, existing potentially through its own power and nature; this is its being. It has the visual power to see, which will be the right or capacity of seeing; and likewise it has the power, in seeing, to distinguish each thing seen, which corresponds to understanding. If these are powers, they are called and remain nothing other than being; and insofar as they are at rest and turned back upon themselves merely in order to exist, vision or sight acts only as existence, and is therefore to be counted only as being.

But when that same vision begins to exercise the activity of seeing, vision, as it were, advances from itself—“as it were,” I say, for it does not advance or depart from itself. Rather, by the intention and force of its own power, which for it is living, it performs the office of living in regard to all things that meet it or that it perceives by encountering them. This is the life of vision itself, which indicates through active movement that vision lives; yet it does so only in what it sees, by a pure sense of seeing, without distinguishing or judging what it sees [Col. 1102B].

We understand this by estimation, as though we could suppose bare seeing without intelligence. But seeing—which is life to vision—is not seeing unless it grasps and comprehends what it has seen. Therefore to see is at the same time to judge what has been seen. Thus, in seeing there is judging; for if it has seen, however it may have seen, it has judged the very thing which it has seen. Therefore, as we say, judging is in seeing; but seeing is in the being of vision. Thus, unconnected and rather simple in what they are, vision, seeing, and discerning are nothing other than one. In the same way, seeing is in discerning, and the being of vision is in seeing; or, to speak truly, they are not “in” one another, but in the fact that it is vision are seeing and discerning. Thus all things are in each individual, or each individual thing is all things as one.

VI. Therefore rise up and be lifted high, my spirit; and by the power through which thou wast inspired in me by God, acknowledge that understanding God is difficult, but not hopeless. For he wished to be known; for this reason he established the world and his divine works, that through all these things we might behold him. Certainly the *Logos*, who is his Son, image, and form, has given a passage from himself toward understanding the Father.

Therefore in what nature, genus, force, or power do we posit, understand, and conceive God? Or by what phantasy of intelligence do we touch him and rise toward him? When we say that he is intelligible, surely there is in us a soul by God’s inbreathing, and from him a part within us—the greatest part in us. Therefore we touch him by that through which we are from him and depend upon him [Col. 1103A].

Certainly after the Saviour’s coming, when in the Saviour we saw God himself, when we were taught and instructed by him, when we received from him the Holy Spirit, the teacher of intelligence, what else would so great a teacher of intelligence give but that we should know God, recognize God, and confess God? Our forebears asked what or who God was; and by him who is always in his bosom the answer was given thus (John 14:9–10): “You see me and seek my Father; I have been with you from long ago. He who has seen me has seen also the Father. I am in the Father and the Father is in me.”

What, then, do we say? God, certainly, is Spirit and the Spirit of life; for it has been said that the Father is life, and likewise that Christ is Spirit. He himself again said of himself: “I am life” (John 14:6). And: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life from himself” (John 5:26). In the same way the Holy Spirit is Spirit and, certainly, is himself life. For Christ received all things from the Father: “I gave him all things”; and again: “What he has is mine” (John 17:7–8, 10). Therefore he has life, and has life from himself.

Why is this so? Because where life is, there life is from itself; and if this is so, there is an understanding that life is from itself, what it is to live, and what life itself is. Therefore all things are joined, all things are one, and there is one substance; and they are truly *homoousia*—either together, which is *homou*, or of the same substance [Col. 1103B].

VII. Therefore the Father is being; for this is the principle and first point for the conception of the others. He is God; he is God together with the other two; he is one God, because that which is living and understanding is precisely that which is being, and because living and understanding derive their being from being. Therefore let no one separate the Holy Spirit or by profane blasphemy suppose him to be some unknown thing, for he too is from the Father, as is the Son who is from the Father.

For after that which is being—that is, existence or substance—or, if you rise to a higher “movement” [the text reads *metu*, perhaps *motu*] on account of familiar names, and say “existentiality,” “substantiality,” *hyparchotēs*, *ousiotēs*, or *ontotēs*: all these are that which I call abiding in itself, giving life by its self-originating movement through its own power, by which all things are vivified and empowered; it is full, absolute, and divine perfection in every way beyond all perfections. This is God beyond *nous*, beyond truth, omnipotent power, and therefore not form. But *nous* and truth are form [Col. 1103D]—not form as inhering inseparably in another, but as inseparably joined, for the manifestation of the power of God the Father, as the same substance, image, or form.

Therefore that first thing which we called being, which is God, is also called silence, quiet, and rest. If this is so, the progression of power—which is not indeed a progression but an appearing, and, if a progression, one that does not leave behind that from which it proceeds but proceeds in connection, or rather is an appearing—could not occur outside anything. For God is everywhere, and God is all things. Therefore the progression of power became act. This act, if God is silence, is called Word; but [the text reads *sed*, perhaps *si*] if rest, movement; if essence, life.

As we have taught, in being and living, in that which is silence there is the silent Word; and in quiet or rest there is movement or hidden action. Therefore movement and action are necessarily born from this rest, Word from silence, life from essence. Thus essence, silence, and rest are the Father—that is, God the Father. But life, Word, movement, or action is the Son, the only Son. For these are nothing other than one thing—life, Word, movement, or action; indeed, all these are more properly movement or action, for life and Word are active, vigorous in movement and operative through movement.

But the universal movement, which is the principal movement, arises from itself. For what is movement unless it is movement from itself to itself? If it is moved by another, then there is some other thing than movement which is moved by another; and if that thing, whatever it may be, which moves it is not movement, it cannot move—for it would not possess the source from which it moves. But if movement is born from movement, movement is born from itself. This is: “The Father gave him life, that life might be in him” (John 5:26) [Col. 1104B].

VIII. Therefore movement is one movement, and self-moving. In one respect it is hidden, and then this manifest movement is movement from the Father. And because movement is from movement, it is self-moving and one movement; hence the only Son. This is the universal *Logos*, in all things, through whom all things were made. This is life for all, because all things made live. This too is Jesus Christ, because he will save all things unto life. Therefore there is one movement, one Son, and only Son, because there is one unique life, a life alone eternal.

Therefore the Son is *homoousios* with the Father. For the Father is life and the Son is life, and life is *ousia*; likewise the Father is movement and the Son is movement, and movement is *ousia*, for nothing there is accidental. Therefore the Father too is Word, though silent Word, yet Word; and the Son is Word, and this too is *ousia*. For whatever either is, acts, or works is *ousia*; and where is *ousia* more truly than in Word? For Word is not like sounding air here, but as something active. Therefore there is one Son because there is one movement; one life, because there is one sole eternal life. For it is not life that at some time dies.

But it never dies if it knows itself. Yet it cannot know itself unless it knows God—the God who is life, true life, and the fountain of life. If this is so, when God is known, it will know all things, because all things are from God, God is in all things, and God is all things. John proclaims this (John 17:3): “This is eternal life: that they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” [Col. 1104D]. Knowledge is life. Further, whether life or knowledge, it is one movement: the same movement produces life, and through life knowledge, and through knowledge life. Thus it is the same movement performing two offices, life and knowledge.

But the *Logos* is movement, and the *Logos* is Son. Therefore the Son is only-begotten insofar as he is Son; but insofar as he is *Logos*, he is twofold. For he is life and he is knowledge, working through both in the mystery of the cross for the salvation of souls: life, because we were to be delivered from death; and knowledge in the mystery through the Holy Spirit, because he was especially given, taught all things, and bore testimony concerning Christ. To produce knowledge as life, and thereby to know God, is to become true life; and this is to bear testimony concerning Christ.

Thus Christ is Son of God, that is, *Logos*, and the Son is life; and because he is also movement and knowledge, he is Son by the work whereby he exists as life, namely Jesus. But by the work whereby he exists as knowledge, he is also the Holy Spirit, so that there are two existences, of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, in the one movement which is the Son [Col. 1105A]. Thus Jesus too is from the Father: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. 24:5). And the Holy Spirit too is from the Father, because the one movement brought both forth into existence.

And because the Father gave all things that he has to the Son (John 16:15; 17:10), the Son, who is movement, likewise gave all things to the Holy Spirit. “All that he has,” he says, “he has from me” (John 16:14–15); for because he too is movement, he has it from movement. The Son did not give it to him; rather, “he has from what is mine.” For principally movement is life, and life itself is knowledge and cognition; therefore whatever cognition has, it has from life. This is the supreme Trinity, this is the supreme Unity: “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16:15) [Col. 1105B].

IX. This therefore will make sufficiently clear that being, which is the Father, and life, which is the Son, and cognition, which is the Holy Spirit, are one and one substance, though three subsistences. From being—which is substance—movement has the power of doubling, because it too, as we have taught, is substance itself, and it doubles in the potency of vitality, wisdom, and intelligence; so that, of course, there are three in every individual thing. Therefore the Holy Spirit is knowledge and wisdom.

Sacred readings prove this (1 Cor. 2:16): “Who has known the mind of God, except the Spirit alone?” “The Spirit himself bears testimony to our spirit” (Rom. 8:16). Who can be a witness without knowledge? And knowledge itself, because it is wisdom, teaches us that we are children of God. Again: Who searches hearts? Who knows the thoughts of the spirit? Again, how are both joined to knowledge? “I speak the truth in Christ” (Rom. 9:1). Where truth is, there is knowledge, because truth is Christ; hence knowledge too, which is the Holy Spirit. And again: “I do not lie, my conscience bearing testimony to me in the Holy Spirit.” For what else is conscience (*conscientia*) than knowledge with another? Now our knowledge is with the Spirit; therefore the Spirit is knowledge. And Christ is knowledge, because he is truth; therefore both Christ and Spirit are knowledge.

But Christ is life. What if the Spirit is life? For, as I have said, there is one movement, and the same life is knowledge. For whatever is taught in Christ is taught by God; and when I say “taught,” I mean from knowledge. Whether it is from Christ or from the Spirit, it is one and the same. For what does Paul say, when he declares both to be the same thing (Rom. 8:6)? “The prudence of the Spirit is life.” Error, imprudence, and ignorance boil, rebel, and struggle against themselves; and this is “the prudence of the flesh,” which is imprudence, and because it does not know God, is death. Therefore the prudence of the Spirit is life and peace. Thus these are now joined and are one [Col. 1106A].

X. Let us show that God is both knowledge and life, although Paul himself says this of him: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. 11:33). The same says: “The manifold wisdom of God” (Eph. 3:10). Hence also the mystery of God; hence Christ is called wisdom; hence also: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth, and to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge” (Eph. 3:18). Thus God too is knowledge, and knowledge frees us, but through Christ nonetheless, because he is knowledge, gate, life, *Logos*, and he through whom all things were made.

Therefore we must know these things and also have love for Christ. These and very many other things make sufficiently clear that God, Christ, and the Holy Spirit are knowledge and likewise life; this is sufficiently proved, if only by one example. For we have demonstrated it more fully in other books: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26). Again he says: “As the living Father sent me, so I live because of the Father” (John 6:58).

These, therefore, are individually such that all three are each individual; thus the Father is one substance, and therefore likewise the Son, the Holy Spirit, God, *Logos*, and *Paraclete* are one: substantiality, vitality, blessedness, silence—but silence speaking within itself—Word, Word of Word [Col. 1106B]. What indeed is the Father’s will except silent Word? In this way, therefore, since the Father is Word and the Son is Word—that is, sounding and working Word—then, I say, since both Father and Son are Word, they are one substance.

Then: “My judgment,” he says, “is just, because I do not seek to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:30). Therefore there is one will, and hence one substance, because will itself is substance. That the Word itself is life is shown thus: “You do not wish to come to me, that you may have life” (John 5:40).

Moreover, the entire mystery that I expound is contained in this: “Everything given to me by the Father I have with me” (John 6:37). But because movement is the same as being, and being is movement; and because, by a certain understanding, being is prior to moving—but prior *kata to aition*, that is, according to cause—the Father gave the Son movement, who also possesses being. Therefore movement as being is *Logos*; and thus he who is movement also has being. But being is life and knowledge; therefore he has all things, because he has the Father’s being. Therefore the Son fulfils the Father’s will.

What is that will, except that, since the Father is life, the movement of his life is to make other things live? This therefore is also the will of the *Logos*, that is, Christ: “And this,” he says, “is the will of the Father who sent me: that I should lose nothing of that which he gave me, but should raise it up on the last day. For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life and rise on the last day” (John 6:39–40) [Col. 1107A].

To see is to know Christ as God’s Son, life, and the God of life; and this is to receive the Holy Spirit, the Word, as that which is life. Hence it has been established: “To whom shall we go? Thou hast the word of life, and we have believed and known that thou art Christ, the Son of God” (John 6:69–70). The whole mystery is Christ, Son of God; Christ, Word; and that Word, the Word of eternal life. Therefore that Word is life; and whoever hears and believes it surely knows God, and therefore has the Holy Spirit.

XI. Here a complete faith is declared, indeed by the disciples. Again he says to the Jews: “If you knew me, you would know my Father. You know neither me nor my Father” (John 8:19). And rightly so. For although the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son—existence or substance in life, and life in substance—substance, being invisible, is not understood except in life. Indeed Christ is more properly life, although he is also substance; therefore the Father is known in the Son. How? Because: “You do not know me or the Father; if you knew me, you would know also the Father.” What is this? You would know that I am from him, because he is also knowledge, which is the Holy Spirit.

Again, because he is Word and the Father is Word, there is one substance: “He who sent me is true, and I speak to the world the things I heard from him” (John 8:26). The Father speaks to the Son, and the Son to the world, because the Father acts through the Son, and the Son does all things by the power of the Father’s Word: that is, the Word speaking within itself does all things through the Word speaking openly. But the Word speaking within itself is God with the Son, because Father and Son are one God [Col. 1107C].

He further says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he shall not see death” (John 8:51). And he again says: “For I know the Father, and I keep his word” (John 8:55). Both are Word, but in the manner I have described.

What, moreover, is the significance of this in John (John 10:17–18)? “Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my soul that I may take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again.” That Christ is never called “soul” is quite clear; nor is God called soul. For the Father is called God and Spirit. Likewise the Son is called *Logos*, is called Spirit, and without doubt is God, since both are one God. Therefore these—*Logos* and *pneuma*—are above soul, by their higher substance; the soul’s substance is far different and lower, since it has been breathed forth and generated by God. It alone is properly called substance, because it underlies its own species within itself, in the same manner as matter (*hylē*) [Col. 1107D].

XII. To this is added that God is life, Christ is life, and life from himself indeed; yet Christ has life from himself as the Father gives it to him. Therefore life is superior to soul. For ζωή and ζωηρίς, that is, life and vitality, are prior to soul; therefore God and the Logos, Father and Son, are homoousios. For just as he is Spirit, so this one is Spirit; and this one is life, and he is life. Likewise, Word and Word, and the rest. Therefore Spirit has power to take up, lay down, and take up again the soul. For life—and life from itself—has power to take up and lay down that which it causes to live by its own power, by participation in itself. For the soul was made in the image of the image of God: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Therefore it is inferior, and derives or is made more from God and the Logos. It is never God himself or the Logos; but indeed it is a logos—not that Logos who is the universal or general Son, and the seed, origin, and source of all things made through him. Rather, soul is the logos of that Logos. How, or of what kind, I recall having said, and shall state in its place.

Therefore the universal [Spirit], because it is Spirit and life, not soul, has power from itself to lay down the soul and again to take up the soul. God, then, and the Logos, whether because they are life or because they are Spirit, live and always live. For they live from themselves. Therefore they are homoousios. But the soul is homoousios when it is assumed by the divine [powers], that is, by the Logos—not indeed by God. For Logos is motion, and soul is motion, and motion is motion from itself; whence soul is the image and likeness of the Logos. Therefore, when it is assumed, nothing is added to life, since the soul’s life is from life—that is, from the power of living.

Accordingly, when Spirit assumes the soul, it as it were carries its power and activities down to lower things, when it fills the world and worldly things. Therefore Spirit—and especially the Logos, the Spirit which is life—has it in its power both to take up and to lay down the soul. When it takes it up, it is as it were born into the world and its power converses with the world; when it lays it down, it withdraws from the world and does not work in the world bodily, nor yet spiritually. This we call his death; and then he is said to be in hell, certainly not without soul. Hence he asks (Ps. 15:10) that God not leave his soul in hell. Therefore, because he is to return to the world, he carries it with him from the lower regions for its activity in the world; thus he as it were takes up again the soul, that is, the activities, and again receives the world. And because the Logos, who is Spirit, performs full and complete activities in the world, he had again taken up soul and body; therefore these too had again to be sanctified. Therefore he went to Spirit and returned sanctified; he dealt with the apostles, and acted after the Holy Spirit.

Who, then, is the Holy Spirit? That is, the Logos; for there is one motion. Therefore it was said: “And if I go away and prepare [a place] for you, I come again.” For who came after Christ’s departure except the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete?

XIII. That what I say is so—that Father and Son are one; likewise that Jesus and the Holy Spirit are one; and consequently that all are one—John made plain by the connected reading. For he began with the Logos: “I am,” he says, “the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). For who comes to that which is being, and true being—which is the Father—except through life? For life which is true life, because it is eternal, is truly being: nothing changes, nothing is corrupted; and these are kinds of death. To be life, therefore, is truly to be. “God lives,” he says (Job 17:2). Therefore God is life. And: “I live” (John 14:19). Whoever comes to Christ comes to life, and thus through life to God. Therefore God and the Logos are united.

Hence too is this: “He who knows me knows also the Father” (John 15:23). And: “He who has seen me has seen also the Father” (John 14:9). Hence also: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me?” (John 14:11). Hence also, mystically: “And if ever you ask anything in my name, I shall do it” (John 14:14). What is it to ask in Christ’s name? To become an eternal soul; to see the light of God; to come to behold him himself; to possess eternal life—not riches, not children, not honours, nothing worldly, but every spiritual thing, and everything by which, united to God, we may be joined to Christ. For this is what it means that he may be glorified in the Son, that is, in eternal life, which I shall give to those who ask.

XIV. Thereupon follows a most complete statement concerning the Holy Spirit: what he is, whence he is, and that he himself is [the same]: “If,” he says, “you love me, keep my commandments. And I shall ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may be with you for all time” (John 14:15–16). What is the Paraclete, who may affirm and establish before the Father all faithful and believing human beings? Who is this? Is the Holy Spirit one alone, or is Christ also the same? For he himself said: “God will give you another Paraclete.” In saying “another,” he identified himself as another; in saying “Paraclete,” he declared a similar service and, in some manner, the same activity. Therefore Spirit too is Paraclete, and the Holy Spirit is another Paraclete, and he himself is sent by the Father.

Jesus, therefore, is the Holy Spirit. For Spirit is motion, whence Spirit too is motion, because “the Spirit breathes where it wills” (John 3:8). And he now says: “the Spirit of truth”; and thus Holy Spirit is its name. Christ too is Spirit, and God is Spirit: therefore all are Spirit. God, however, is Spirit substantially: for both substance and motion are present in that which he is; or rather, he is substance itself, which is motion, yet motion remaining in itself—as we have often said already and shall often repeat for the sake of retention. But Jesus and the Holy Spirit are motion truly moved; hence they operate outwardly. Yet Jesus is manifest Spirit, since he is also in flesh; the Holy Spirit is hidden Spirit.

Jesus, indeed, who infuses understandings—not now one who performs signs or speaks in parables—thus teaches that he himself is [present]: “I shall not leave you orphans; I shall come to you” (John 14:18). But that he himself is hidden in the Holy Spirit he teaches thus: “The world will no longer see me, but you will see me, because I live and you shall live” (John 14:19). This too is granted to the Holy Spirit: that the Spirit of truth may remain with you forever (John 14:16). And of himself he said: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Then he added: “Whom the world cannot see” (John 14:19). And of himself he said: “The world will no longer see me.” Then he added: “Because it neither sees him nor knows him” (John 14:17). But no one knew Christ either: “He came into his own, and the world did not know him” (John 1:11). He added: “You shall know him, because he remains in you and is in you” (John 14:17). And he himself says of himself: “You shall see me” (John 14:19). And since Christ is life, he adds of himself: “Because I live, you also shall live.” And because the Holy Spirit is understanding, both of which the world itself lacks, he adds: “Because he remains with you and is in you” (John 14:17).

But how is the Holy Spirit either in them or already remaining, if he is still to come afterwards and has not already begun to be with them through Christ? Therefore they are united and are from the one who is motion. This is declared more plainly in what follows. For he says: “I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you. But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things which I say” (John 14:25–26). “I,” he says, “remain in you.” For life has been given, and Christ no longer departs from them. Therefore they also have spiritual motion, which is Christ’s remaining in them. Yet they are souls in whom Spirit remains and never departs; nevertheless it was said: “Now I shall go to the Father” (John 16:16).

XV. What this is may easily be understood if it is taken as spoken from the mystery, and from the bodily mystery. For spiritually, since he himself is in the Father and the Father in him, where, or why, will he go? From the same mystery comes the fact that the Spirit, like a dove, came to Christ, and that now the Spirit will be sent by the Father and sent to the Father, Christ going and asking that it be sent. For it is life recalled from death—not life itself, because it is the Logos. For the Logos does not know death; rather, it itself destroys death. It is the life in human beings which rose from death. This he put on together with the body, and took it up again from hell.

Therefore, for the sake of sanctifying this, it was necessary to go to the Father—but bodily and animally, that is, potentially and existentially to penetrate into that which the Father had been in himself. Thus in this manner he went to the Father. Finally, no time of absence is declared; rather, the contrary is said (John 20:1, 17–20, 27, 29): on the night following the Sabbath he appeared to Mary; he would not be touched before going to the Father; Mary announced this to the disciples; that same night he came to them, showing his hands and side, evidently no longer forbidding himself to be touched. Afterwards Thomas handled and touched him, at his own invitation, because Thomas despaired. This signifies that he had already been sanctified. How brief, then, was this interval; yet “I shall go to the Father” was said on account of the mystery. For since he himself is in the Father and the Father in him, where will he go?

By the same mystery, [the Spirit is] “whom the Father sends you,” because the Father sends when Christ sends. Finally, he says: “The Father sends [him] in my name,” that is, for me; or “in my name,” because the Spirit is Christ and he himself is the Holy Spirit; or “in my name,” because the Holy Spirit himself will bear witness concerning Christ. For so it is said: “He bears witness concerning me” (John 15:26). Who is “he”? “Whom I send you from the Father.” Therefore all are joined: I send; I send from the Father; I send the Spirit of truth. Therefore the intermediary Logos—that is, Jesus himself—sends. For the primary and universal motion, which is vital and life, sends the motion of understanding, which, as he taught, is from life and is life itself. For to know what something is, is to live; this is to be. And what is this being, except to be from God’s substance, which is to be Spirit? Hence we are made spiritual, receiving Spirit from Christ, and thereby [receive] eternal life.

Therefore this Trinity is called Spirit. For it is said: “God is Spirit” (John 4:24). Likewise Paul says in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “But the Lord is Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). This is certainly said of Christ. The Holy Spirit, indeed, is so called because he sanctifies saints, that is, makes them holy; and certainly he is the Spirit of God. For he is called prudence, wisdom, and knowledge of all things. Thus he goes on to say concerning him: “He will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John 16:8–10).

“Concerning sin,” he says, “because they do not believe in me”—either that Christ is life, or that he is the Son of God and sent from God, and that he remits sins. “Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father”: for so much was [done] in the mystery of the Passion, because he kept and fulfilled the faithfulness of the commandments. For although he willed otherwise, he said: “Let your will be done” (Matt. 26:42). Likewise, because in leaving them warned, he left them no longer to be seen in the same manner, it was fitting, after all these things had been done, that he should go to the Father—not merely go to the Father, but now be with him. Therefore it is said: “He sits at the right hand of the Father” (Matt. 26:64). “Concerning judgment, because the prince of this world has been judged”: for in the mystery of the cross all powers hostile to Christ were triumphed over by Christ himself. “These things,” he says, “the Holy Spirit will teach.” What conclusion is chosen? Does the Paraclete complete the mystery of salvation and Christ leave it incomplete? Or is it because Christ himself and the Holy Spirit are the same, or because he sends him, or because the Spirit possesses all that belongs to Christ? He possesses all; through Christ he is manifested.

XVI. Yet let us see what the Spirit is to do: he will give knowledge of the events and an imparting of knowledge, as though possessing the force of testimony—and even more, of judgment—whether for repentance or punishment. “Concerning sin,” he says, “because they did not believe in me.” Thus the world may know its punishment now. “Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father.” This can also concern the sin which those did unjustly who raised him upon the cross because he called himself the Son of God. And now he goes to the Father; which will likewise be the lot of all if they believe in God and do God’s commands, so that they too may go to the Father. For they are justified; for “Abraham believed, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6). Then, “concerning judgment, because the prince of the world has been judged.”

These things, as can be seen, do not concern salvation, which has already been completed by Christ, but concern knowledge of the events. For the Father is speaking silence; Christ is voice; the Paraclete is the voice of the voice. Therefore, in this activity, the Holy Spirit is another Paraclete; in the mystery of salvation, a co-worker like Christ; but in the Spirit of sanctification, that which God is.

If, therefore, Christ is Spirit in this manner also, while in the mystery of eternal life Christ is God, and in sanctification the Holy Spirit, and God sanctifies—as it is said, “Sanctify them in truth” (John 17:17), the Son says to the Father—therefore the Father sanctifies. Christ also sanctifies, as it is said: “And for them I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth” (John 17:19). Likewise the Holy Spirit sanctifies, for baptism pertains to sanctification. Therefore it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “John baptized with water, but you shall be immersed in the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1:5). What he poured out upon them was for knowledge, for they had already been sanctified by baptism, God Christ having been invoked. For it was said to the Holy Spirit: “Sanctify them in truth.” And Christ is truth; the Paraclete is also Spirit of truth. Therefore everyone who is baptized, professes belief, and receives the faith of truth—that is, the Holy Spirit—is made holier by the Holy Spirit. Hence it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you” (Acts 1:8)—not for sanctification, but for knowledge and for those things Christ promised in the Gospel concerning the Holy Spirit, that is, concerning the Paraclete.

First, that it may bear witness concerning Christ; for thus he says: “You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem.” But Luke also says (John 7:39): “The Spirit had not yet been sent.” Yet he already bears testimony. What else, however, does Paul do in all his epistles except bear testimony concerning Christ? And after Christ’s departure, he alone saw Christ and Christ appeared to him alone. Therefore Spirit was present through Christ, and Christ through the Holy Spirit.

Likewise John and Peter bear testimony: “What we heard, what we saw, what we touched” (1 John 1:1). And in the Acts of the Apostles, Peter himself—and Luke, who wrote about these things—says thus concerning David: “Being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him by an oath that from the fruit of his loins one would sit upon his throne, he foresaw and spoke concerning Christ’s resurrection: that he was neither left in hell nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus, therefore, God raised up, of which we all are witnesses” (Acts 2:30–32). When do they say these things? “When a sound had already come from heaven, and as though by a great wind the Spirit was borne along, which filled the whole house; and they were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various languages” (Acts 2:2, 4).

Then the apostles speak concerning the sin of the world, because it did not believe Christ, thus in Acts: “As you know, this man, delivered over by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you fastened to the cross and killed through wicked hands; [but] God raised him up” (Acts 2:22–24). Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, Peter reports that David did not ascend into heaven, but said: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at [my] right hand” (Acts 2:34). Paul too said this: “Who rose again, who is at the right hand of God” (Rom. 8:34). Therefore they taught that after the resurrection he went to the Father. Immediately he added: “Who also intercedes with the Father.” Therefore, if Christ intercedes, he too is Paraclete. Likewise, that he went to the Father is attested in Acts: “While they looked on, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes; and as they watched him going into heaven,” and the rest (Acts 1:9–10).

XVII. Three things have now been said concerning testimony to Christ: concerning sin, concerning righteousness, and now concerning judgment. Thus Paul, through the Holy Spirit, spoke to the Romans: “The God of peace will swiftly crush Satan under your feet” (Rom. 16:20). Likewise he says to the Ephesians: “He who ascended on high led captivity captive” (Eph. 4:8). Likewise he said in the Apocalypse: “And I have the keys of death and hell” (Rev. 1:18). Likewise there: “And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon” (Rev. 12:7). And the entire passage shows that the devil has been judged.

Therefore, since it has been demonstrated that these three powers, by common and proper activity and the same substance, constitute unity and deity, not without reason are they reduced to these two, Son and Father. For since the Father himself is as it were twofold—existence and activity, that is, substance and motion, but motion inward, self-generated motion (αὐτόγονος), and that which is substance is motion—necessarily the Son also, since he is motion and self-generated motion, is the same substance. For these are one with one another without conjunction, and simple without duplication, in their proper mode of existing, force, and power; because neither is ever without the other, and they are one and the same only in activity. Yet one is outward and falls into passions, while the other remains ever inward and eternal, since it is original and substantial, and therefore always Father; by the same reasoning, [the other is] always Son.

Paul says in all his epistles: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1:1). Likewise: “Not from human beings, nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and through God the Father” (John 10:30). Likewise in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one; I am in the Father, and the Father in me” (John 10:30; 14:9).

XVIII. We too constantly employ “Father” and “Son” reverently, and rightly according to the reasoning stated above. For motion, as we have taught above, is Son; and this motion is life and knowledge, or wisdom. Certainly Paul expressed most fully what we intended to understand: “I give thanks,” he says, “to my God always for you in Christ Jesus, because you have been enriched in him in every word and in every knowledge” (1 Cor. 1:4–5). We have called Christ Word, that is, life; knowledge, the Holy Spirit; therefore [they are] one. For, he says, “you have been enriched in Christ.”

Since this is so, if God and Christ are one, and Christ and Spirit are one, rightly the three are one in power and substance. Yet the first two are one differently: the Father is actual existence, that is, substantiality; the Son, existential activity. But the other two are two in such a way that Christ and the Holy Spirit are two in one, that is, in motion; and they are two in such a way that one is two. But the first two are two in such a way that two are one. Thus, with two in one and two one, the Trinity exists as one.

For why should I recall many things concerning the Holy Spirit, of whom much has been discussed? From him Christ in flesh is conceived; from him Christ in flesh is sanctified in baptism; he is in Christ who is in flesh; he is given by Christ who is in flesh to the apostles, that they may baptize in God, Christ, and the Holy Spirit; he is the one whom Christ in flesh promises will come, with a certain difference in activity. The same is both Christ and Holy Spirit; and because he is Spirit, therefore he is God; because Christ is Spirit, therefore he is God. Hence Father, Son, and Spirit are not only one, but one God.

# Book Four

I. Are “he lives” and “life” one, the same, or different? One. But why are two names the same, and how? Since to be in act is one thing and to be the action itself another, they are different. Yet how are they different? Since in that which lives there must be life, and in that which is life there must be living: for what lives does not lack life, nor, when it is life, does it not live. Therefore one is in the other; and from this, in either one, there are two. And if as two, not as merely two, since one is in the other and this is in both, they are therefore the same.

But the same is in two and is other than itself. Thus it is both the same and another in either of these. Yet if it is the same, each is the same and one in relation to itself. For, whichever exists as the other which it is, neither is a pair; therefore, if each is both what it is and the other, each will be one in itself. But when each is one in itself, in the other it is the same one; and when it is the same one, both are truly one. For the two differ in nothing: neither in the power of existing, nor in time, perhaps [only] in cause; and in this respect one is prior to the other.

II. In order that this may be judged more easily, let us reconsider these matters more carefully. Living and life are such that living is life, and life is living—not such that one duplicated thing is in the other, nor such that one is with the other. For that is conjunction. Or from this, even if joined inseparably, are they united and not one? But now, when being life is living by the very same operation, and being life is being in the same manner—for we are speaking of these two, living and life, not of that which has life and living in effect—then they are one.

Although that itself is also a third [term], and in that which has life, both as one from the other and yet both as one. From this it appears what self-subsistent existences themselves accomplish in their own realities: while the one and same substance remains, they preserve their own being without any alteration of themselves. For life’s own being is to be moved; and being moved itself is living. Therefore to be is to live, and to be is to be life: therefore [there is] one and the same substance. For to each thing, its own being in that in which it is, is substance.

For in the higher and eternal things—that is, intelligible and intellectual things—there is nothing accidental, no quality, no pair, nor anything with another; but all are living and understanding substances, pure, simple, of one form, by the very fact that they are, live, and understand; and conversely, by the very fact that they understand, they also are. Therefore “he lives” and “life” are one substance.

III. But since intellect unfolds itself thus, and the argument has proceeded thus, that life is in that which is living, and that in that which is life, life is life because it lives, we must consider and inquire by attentive reasoning whether this natural interweaving and twofold mode of existence is pure simplicity and one, or two. If there is no difference—if living is life, and if living is inherent in being life—then rightly and deservedly we shall call these one, not a twofold conjunction, for the existence of their being.

But if, first, living is one thing and being life another; and likewise if there is a difference, such that now life is cause for living, and now living itself is cause for life to be, then these are two, but paired with one another and simply united in themselves. For it pertains to the power of its own divine Logos that these should be paired, as being of the same nature and power: one is that of which [the other is], and from one comes the other. Yet there is some difference, however small; therefore the pairing is not pointless. For action and acting are not the same; nor power and operation; nor, to speak more truly, is cause the same as effect. The former is origin, the latter offspring.

Therefore, since “he lives” and “life” are action and acting, although they are in themselves and together, they must nevertheless be regarded as existing by a different power and nature, so that one is cause of the other and the other exists as effect. But in my understanding, and according to the conclusion I approve, in the primary and natural beginning of the first divinity, first is that which is living, and second that which is life. For reason will teach this, and truth itself will confirm it. Thus living is cause, and life the effect of living; yet living itself is also life. For these are simultaneous and always simultaneous, as is known.

Life is something different in the second, third, and subsequent ordered beings that live: namely, it is at once the same thing as life and living; but this living is second from life, when it is life. That first and primary living, however, is at once life, cause of life, source, and origin of living beings. I know this may appear obscure, not so much because of the matters themselves as because the same words are repeated: these two are linked in such a conjunction that, since living is life and life is living, once either is established, the duplication of the other may seem futile.

IV. Listen, reader—listen to what will astonish you, reader. These things, so difficult, so winding, so closed up in a treatment of God and divine things, we shall unfold by a simple argument. Certainly we all confess God: God almighty, God above all, God before all, God from whom are all things. When we confess him, we also undoubtedly confess that he is. What do we believe this being to be? What do we think? “God is Spirit,” he says, “light”; and God is true light (John 4:24). What is this being believed to be which is called Spirit? Surely we are compelled to understand Spirit as a certain existing, living, and understanding substance. In the higher realms, and especially around God, [the word] seems rather lowly and alien; and in lower things they do not believe “substance” an appropriate name. But why should we avoid this word, when for each thing to be is for it to be substance?

And God, speaking in Jeremiah, says: “If you had stood in my substance, you would have seen my Word” (Jer. 23:22, according to the LXX). So also there not much later, and in many other places. Therefore Spirit is substance—that is, his being. Let us therefore gather together what is said according to John: “God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). “God,” he says, “is Spirit”: that is what God is, namely, being. Therefore the substance of God is Spirit; the same substance is living—not so that substance is one thing and living another, but so that the living itself is substance itself. For if it is said by the same [author], “It is the Spirit that gives life” (John 6:63), certainly the one who gives life lives and is the power of life. Therefore Spirit lives; God lives. Moreover, because it lives, as we said above, it is also life. Therefore Spirit is also life, as John himself says: “Spirit is life.” Therefore God, since he is Spirit, both lives and is life.

Paul also says to the Romans: “There is therefore no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus and do not walk according to the flesh; for the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 8:1–2). “Spirit of life,” he says; for these three are Spirit: God, Jesus, and the Holy Spirit.

V. And concerning God, I think it has been demonstrated that he is Spirit; and that Spirit both lives, makes live, and is life substantially. Thus these matters are understood as simple and one substance, so that to be Spirit is to live and to be life. But this is not the living that belongs to us, to animals, to elements, to things created from elements, to the world, to all things in the world, to angels, demons, or even those whom people in and from the world call gods. No, I say, that is not the living which is in God.

God is that which is the living of any soul, whether an individual soul or that universal and fontal soul; not [life] as it is in angels, nor as it is in thrones, glories, or the other beings existing in eternal things, intelligible things, or intellects. Rather, it is that living from which these receive life and live according to their kind of existence, as it in some manner proceeds and breathes into them, according as they can receive it, the power of living vigour: simple, pure, from itself to itself, through itself, in itself alone, without a beginning of being from which it has been poured forth, proceeded, or born—rather, it is the principle through which the living of all other things might be created.

For living brings forth life; for by natural force the agent is prior to the action. The one acting generates the action, and, as though from it, having himself bestowed both name and reality, he himself receives [them]. Since this is correct, it is also altogether true in reason. Certainly God—to whom, in omnipotence and highest primacy, the name “God” belongs—is first, if anything may be called first in God’s works. Yet human intellect, in order to exert itself and grasp things, ascribes beginnings, distinct beginnings, and as it were time to things existing simultaneously or poured forth simultaneously.

God, I say, first brought forth the existences and substances of universals. Plato calls these Ideas, the principal species of all species existing within [things]. Of this kind are, by way of example, ὀντότης, ζωότης, νόησις; likewise τουτότης (“thisness”) and τερότης (“otherness”) [Note: Col. 1115D (1): Perhaps ταυτότες (“sameness”) and ἑτερότες (“otherness”)]. And there are other things of this kind. Thus genera of genera are poured forth—indeed, universally principal powers of all powers.

Therefore ὀντότης, that is, existentiality or essentiality; and ζωότης, that is, vitality, namely the first universal power of life, the first life and source of all living. Likewise νόησις: the force, faculty, power, substance, or nature of understanding. These three are to be understood severally, but in such a way that they are named and said to be whatever they are pre-eminently in their own mode. For there is none of these which is not all three: being is being if it lives—that is, if it is in life. But living is not living if it lacks understanding. They are therefore as it were mixed and, as the matter stands, simple by a threefold simplicity. For whatever, by the very fact that it is what it is, is also another, must never be called a pair, but always one.

VI. But of these things elsewhere, at greater length. God, then, is living: that supreme, first, fontal, primarily principal living. He generated these three, that is, by the operation of his living he brought them forth so that they might exist. Therefore they came forth by operation, and are offspring; this is generation: that from the agent, act; from that which is essentiality or essence, vitality or life; from the living, νόησις—the universal intelligence of all universal intelligences—should be born.

Therefore living is prior to life, although life is in that which is living. But living, as parent of life, and life, as offspring and that which is generated—since it is generated by the living—stand thus. God therefore is that first living: living from himself, living before every living thing, and before the living of life itself; for he is acting, always acting, acting without any beginning. He is not acting from action, lest action or the appearance of a beginning belong to the agent; rather, action has either been brought forth, come into existence, or poured forth by the agent’s operation.

We place this acting in that which is living. Therefore God is living, and primary living; life, however, is as something generated. Therefore living is Father, life Son. For what was made in him is life, and the Son himself says: “I am the way, I am the truth, I am the life” (John 14:6). This is the life which arose from the Father’s living, and this is the meaning of: “For I came forth from God” (John 16:27).

Likewise he says of himself: “Let him who thirsts come to me and drink. He who believes in me—as Scripture has said—rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:37–38). Hence too is his answer to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me to drink,’ you would rather have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10). Likewise later: “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again” (John 4:13). The Samaritan’s water is the worldly soul. “But whoever drinks of the water which I shall give him will never thirst; but the water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13–14).

By these and countless similar examples, it becomes sufficiently clear that Christ, the Son of God, is life, and eternal life. For he too, like the Father, is Spirit: “For that which is born from Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6). But Spirit breathes, and breathes from itself; and to breathe is to live. Further, what breathes from itself lives from itself; what lives from itself lives from eternity and unto eternity. For that which is its own cause, so that it is itself what it exists as, never abandons itself.

Therefore, since the Father is that which is living, as we have taught above, and living is being life; and likewise since life is that which is generated from that which is living, necessarily life is that which is living. For it lives, and life is life by the very fact that it is life, and is life from itself; for living belongs to it from itself. Yet [it has this] from that first [principle] which is primary living, which is the Father, in whom and from whom life exists. This life, which has living in it and lives from itself, we understand and confess to be the Son, Jesus Christ.

VII. Let us see how all these things which have been said by me are signified and affirmed in the Gospel according to John, through the very words of the Saviour (John 6:58): “The living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father.” And lest anyone should suppose that Christ said this of himself in the flesh, he immediately added [Col. 1118A] (John 6:59): “This is the bread which came down from heaven.” Then he thus testifies and teaches that he is life, and eternal life (ibid. 54–55): “Unless you receive the body of the Son of Man as the bread of life, and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves; but he who eats his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life.” Therefore all that Christ is—whether spirit, soul, or flesh—is eternal life; for he is the Logos. But the principal Logos is life; therefore also those things which he assumed are life. Hence these too, having become spiritual through the Spirit whom Christ gives us, will merit eternal life in us.

And lest anyone should believe that Christ says these things concerning the fleshly Christ, rather than concerning his whole self, who is spirit, soul, and flesh, what does he say? (ibid. 62): “What if you should see [Col. 1118B] the Son of Man ascending?” Who is the Son of Man? Spirit, soul, flesh: for these he had when he ascended, and with these he ascended. What then does he add? That spirit may be understood: “Where he was before” (ibid.); that is, spirit, and life, which are the Father, which are God. Whence these are homoousia, that is, consubstantial: never existing outside themselves at any time; principal in the primary sense; one and the same substance; equal in force, the same in power, majesty, and efficacy; neither prior to the other, except that one is the cause of the other, and for this reason the other. Yet the other is truly the same, because the same one God; but because other, therefore first and second; and because one is the cause of the other, therefore Father, as that which is cause; while that which is from the other is Son. But in substance there is no distance, no temporal distinction, [Col. 1118C] no differentiation; there is one movement, one will, and at times an appearance of another will, but always the same.

VIII. Let us first establish from sacred reading that these things are so; then, as order demands and the necessity of the matters requires, let us consider why, in those whose substance is one and the same, one bears the authority of sender and the other of one sent; one of commander and the other of minister; one, in the movement of acting, free from passions, the other, infinite through infinite acts in creating the ages, and, in the things that are in the ages, subjected to innumerable passions even unto death.

That which is first lives; it lives from itself; it lives eternally; and this is God. That which itself lives, as I have taught, possesses the force of existence or substance, and the nature of life and intelligence; indeed, in its being—that is, in that which we call living, and in that which we call understanding—this is God. Therefore that which God is—his being—is the cause and father of existence. And since in his very being he has life, and in it also knowledge of what he is, he is the fountain both of universal life and of intelligence.

For of these three, which are in God by simple existence—or rather, which are God—God is more properly being: for he has from himself both to live and to be life, or to understand and to be intelligence, as we have taught above and in many places. Let us now understand the remaining two, life and intelligence, as begotten from that which is being, possessing their own being from that which is the first movement of being, and, in accordance with the priority of existence, receiving the force and name of life or intelligence.

For all things are in some sense threefold and are named in an order of these three [Col. 1119A]—not because each of the three does not contain threefoldness, but because by movement they effect what they are said to be. For being is the first movement, which, while at rest, is called movement—movement inwardly. For when it acts upon itself in order to exist, it is rightly called both inward movement and resting movement. Hence we say that movement is that which “lives” and “to live” is.

But when, from that which is “lives” and “to live,” there has in a certain manner been produced and begotten, in the appearance of a disposition, a formed form of that very “lives” and “to live,” this is called life, this is called Son. For just as any form, whether set there where its subject is or elsewhere, leads us to knowledge of that whose form it is, so life causes us to know what living is. For living is an act, and in the act there is a course in every instant; and therefore it was said (John 1:18): “No one has ever seen God.” For who [Col. 1119B] can see living, which is God, without life, which comes together and exists in a certain form through the delineations of its acts, so as to be the form of the living one?

Therefore life is the form of that which is living, through or in which that which is—“lives” and “to live”—is seen, apprehended, and known. This is indicated concerning the Father by the Saviour’s saying (John 14:9): “He who sees me sees also the Father”; for the Son of God is the form of God, that is, life, which is the form of the living one. For Paul said to the Philippians (Phil. 2:6): “Who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized.” Likewise, to the Colossians (Col. 1:15): “Who is the image of the invisible God.” Therefore Jesus Christ is both image and form of God.

Now we have said that in the form that whose form it is is seen; and likewise, in the image, he whose image it is is seen, [Col. 1119C] especially if he whose image it is is invisible, as it is said here: “Image of the invisible God.” In the same way it is said in the Gospel according to John: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who came forth from his bosom.” And Moses likewise was told (Exod. 33:20): “You shall not see my face; for who has seen my face and lived?” Yet he permitted his hind parts to be seen—that is, what is below, and all else besides the face.

IX. How many mysteries are here? How many kinds of questions? How many indications for showing that both God and Jesus Christ are substance, that both are one substance, that together both are one substance, and that the substance is from Father to Son? All these matters, and others of this kind, can in no way be explained, understood, or demonstrated unless the foregoing discussion shines forth through manifest apprehensions.

Let this, therefore, be our settled conviction: that God is spirit; that the Spirit from whom the Son is, is spirit; and that the Holy Spirit is spirit (John 3:6): “For what is born of Spirit is spirit”; and (John 6:63): “The Spirit gives life.” That which gives life surely itself lives. That which lives, because it is spirit, lives from itself; and that which lives from itself is itself that which lives. And because that which lives from itself, being itself that which “lives,” has nothing else that may be called its living—for it has not been made alive, but itself lives, existing as “lives” or “to live”—and because it lives, and to live is to act, it never began in that in which it lives from itself. For it did not await another, so that [Col. 1120A] it has never abandoned itself and never will. From eternity and into eternity, therefore, the principal and universal substance of living lives: not as though it were first substance and then living, but that very thing which is living is itself substance. For since it is itself living, and “lives” and “to live” are being, and in some manner are understood as being, its being is not other than its own substance. This is called spirit both by all sacred reading and by the language of the things themselves.

X. But spirit breathes, and breathes from itself; and God is spirit. To breathe, however, is to live. Therefore the spirit which is God lives from itself and always lives. It lives, I say, and in the act of living, and by life itself as work, when it lives by the work of life, it works. Therefore eternal life was born from the living God; it was generated; and because it lives, [Col. 1120B] it is itself substance. And that which is from him who lives, namely life itself, is also substance—equal and simultaneous by the same considerations—because that which lives is life, and life itself exists by living so as to be life.

Therefore spirit is living, and life is spirit. Each embraces itself, each is in the other; and the other is not twin-like and added on, but, by the simplicity of what exists from itself and in itself, is as it were a duplication of another substance, never separated from itself, because in each there is a double. For living is with life, and life in turn is with that which is living. But living, as we have taught, is God; life is Christ. And because living is the generator of life—for by its act, that which is living generates, as a kind of offspring, life—living becomes [Note: [Col. 1119D] (1) “It becomes” (*fit*). Perhaps thus.] Father, life Son. These very things are indeed each the other; therefore two. For whence are two, unless [Col. 1120C] one is from the other? And whatever is from another is always Son; while that from which the other is, is Father.

But now they are not other in such a manner as to be discrete and diverse, but only other from one another, as maker and made, begetter and begotten: both one through their conjunction of substance, since living is life and life itself is living. Hence Father and Son are one God. And because the natural conversion of existence is only one—for in that which is living life is present, and likewise in that which is life living is present—there is also only one conversion. Hence, since in that which is life living is present, the only-begotten Son is consubstantial with the Father: the Son himself is one, the Father one.

Hence there is one and the same substance, simultaneous and everlasting. For this is *homoousion*: *homou ousian echon*, “having substance together,” and possessing an equal force and power of existing and the same nature of substance, with no temporal priority; this we call “consubstantial.” Yet, through the prior causality of that which is living in relation to that which is life, the former is and is called begetting and Father, while the latter is and is called begotten and Son.

Therefore, because they are in one another, although when the Father is, the Son is not, and conversely, when the Son is—the Son of him whose Son he is—the Father is not, nevertheless by the force of the realities and equality of substance, since living is life and living is one, the divine utterance of the Saviour rightly declares (John 16:10–11): “And I am in the Father, and the Father in me.” Hence also: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). For [Col. 1121A] by the force of things and under the guidance of nature itself, all things are nothing if they do not live; and, empty of vital movement, they cannot be believed to possess either the material mass, or existence, or image, or form. For the unstable and inconstant force of flux and reflux, subsisting without order, does not receive form so as to be said to be something.

XI. Hence, lacking that by which it is something, it nevertheless retains its own being, so that it is rightly said in no way to be. But now, when it is comprehended and whole, standing about in parts, formed and thereby embodied, and, having received some form, is brought to be something, it is believed to be because, by vital movement and being bounded from the infinite by definite delineations, it is brought forward to most certain perceptions.

Therefore it is the vital force and power that makes material things appear to be. Flowing down from that Logos which is life, whom we call [Col. 1121B] the Son, through Archangels, Angels, Thrones, Glories, and the other things above the world, it first runs and descends, in bodies and immaterial things (*aula*), pure and more purified in its natural substance; it undergoes a greater sharing of its own light; then, coming gradually to soul and to the fountain of soul, it receives, because the soul is an image of the Logos, as it were through a certain cognition a fuller course of descent. And because it hastens to animate the soul, it acquires in animating it a more impetuous desire.

Hence, immersed in matter and the elements of the world, and finally entangled in bonds of flesh, mingling itself with corruption and death itself, it furnishes, amid the dregs of matter, an image of living. Thus all earthly, watery, aerial, fiery, ethereal, and heavenly things live—not by that prior Logos, nor by the undiminished light of life, but through a material conjunction and a wounded light of life. Those above the heavens live, and live more fully, which have withdrawn from matter and bodily bonds: such as purer souls, Thrones, and Glories; likewise Angels and the Spirits themselves—some, in one way or another, having life in their own substance; others being life itself: Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit. For we shall teach concerning the latter shortly. Together with God, yet from God, they are life; but they live by universal life, live from themselves, and do not have in another that by which they live. Rather, for them, to be is itself to live, to be life, and to be knowledge—the Father imparting this, that is, existing in the primary sense as that which is living.

Therefore [Note: [Col. 1121D] (1) “These.” Perhaps *cum* (“since”) is missing.] [Col. 1121D] all these enumerated things live, and there is nothing either among eternal things or among worldly or material things which does not live according to its nature, it must surely be acknowledged that there is some force or power by which all things are made to live and, as though by a fountain of living, are raised into living spirits, so that from this they both live and, because they live, have received being.

XII. Who is this, from whom the vital spirit breathes into eternal things and mortals alike, by whom all things flourish, subsist, receive their proper acts, are generated, and advance to generate? God—without doubt God—and, in terms reverent to our mind, the Father of living and the divine power of living. Him, or the power of life, as we have said elsewhere, we shall call the highest and principal life, universally universal, and the origin, cause, head, and fountain of all living things: the Principle [Col. 1122A] of existing things, Father of substances, who, from what he himself is, grants being to other things, regulating, according to the capacity and nature of those receiving it, the power and substance of living.

What is he himself, or in what does he consist? Surely he is living and true: one, insofar as he permits us to speak of him thus. He lives, and from eternity and into eternity he lives, having from himself that very thing which is his substance: he lives. For an act neither ought nor could accrue to him, lest he at some time be less than himself. But he is always perfect, full, and whole; in that which is his being, being thus is also present. The things after God are powers, and acts of powers, which by their own force are now believed to be, so that they may appear both to be and to possess all that, through the mature acts of procession, existence comes to possess here in its operation. They are called actions when, through processes of coming into being, they generate and bring forth outwardly what they can be.

Thus seed is already a potency, and so are stalk and leaves; likewise male and female are an outpouring of sexual desire. But these things belong to the world and beneath the moon. Above, however, in ether and heaven, there are actions, and they live by actions; yet, having also been generated, they have become what they were going to be. For, released from their origin into their proper operations, they run through their own acts by contact with the nature that contains them.

XIII. If, then, the things in the world are acts, how much more are those things which are eternal and above the heavens acts and actions—the things which generated these worldly things? So too the soul, and Angels from souls, and above souls. For the soul is borne by a self-generated motion (*autogonōi kinēsei*), that is, a motion arising from itself; it is called self-moving (*autokinētos*), whence [it is called] unmoved (*akinētos*) [the wording is uncertain]. Therefore it is always in motion; which is always to act, and to be activity (*energeia*) itself, so that that movement may be its substance.

For it was said (Gen. 1:26): “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” Therefore it has self-generated motion (*autogonos kinēsis*), that is, motion arising from itself, as God has it, as Christ has it. But because it is not that first spirit, it is therefore another substance, and created: not existing from itself, but made so as to have movement from itself. For soul is one thing, life another. Life is a disposition of living, and as it were a certain form or state produced by living, containing in itself living itself and being what life is; and both are one substance. For one is not truly in the other, but they are one, doubled in their own simplicity; and therefore in itself because from itself; and therefore from itself because simplicity produces another in itself. For rest generates nothing; but movement and the activity of acting forms for itself out of itself that which it is, or rather, in some manner is.
