For to be is to live; but to be life is a certain movement, that is, the form of the living one, produced by that very thing whose form it is; while that which produces is living. Since it never began, what lives from itself does not begin, because it always lives; hence life also does not begin. For when the producer is without beginning, that which is produced lacks a beginning also. Therefore both are simultaneous and consubstantial. But living is God; life is Christ. And in that which is living there is life, and in that which is life there is living. In this manner each is in the other, because the made and the maker are each in the other. For as the maker is in the thing made, so the thing made is in the maker—especially if these are everlasting. Therefore the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father. For the maker makes the made, and the made is made by the maker. Therefore there is one substance: not one substance belonging to two, and two in one, but because where God is, there also is the Son, that is, one of such a kind. For as God lives, so also the Son lives; in the kind of substance in which the Father is, in that kind is the Son.

XIV. “But,” they say, “if the Father lives, the Son also lives; and therefore both are of the same and such a substance.” Yet the substance of this “lives,” since both are “lives,” is without origin: both are eternal. But this is excluded by the sacred words of the Evangelist, as the Son himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, speaks: “The Father lives” (John 6:58). Here is a fountain without origin. But where is there another principle? “And I,” he says, “live because of the Father.” Therefore, if because of the Father, he received from the Father; and if he received, he was begotten from the unbegotten. And if he lives, there is a definite existence and a force of substance in both, with this “lives” of one kind in each: the same substance in Father and Son, but the Son’s substance is from the Father. For “what is born of Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6); therefore, from such a substance of the Father comes such a substance of the Son.

And, in order that it may be shown more clearly that both substance is given by the Father and that it is one and the same substance, it is said that he lives, and life is substance. Therefore the substance is the same in God and in Christ the Son, and from God to Christ the Son. The Evangelist says this: “For as God has life from himself, so he gave the Son to have life from himself” (John 5:26). Therefore Christ is *homoousios* with God: that is, consubstantial, of the same substance—namely the first, principal, universal substance—from which all things that are and live possess life as something added (*epakton*), that is, imparted, not generated from themselves, nor constituting their own living, as it does in God and the Son.

For all other things have from life only as much as Christ grants. In God, living is the principal producer of life, from one and the same fountain of existence, with no prior time or power—at least with respect to substance. Hence whether we understand *homoousion* to mean that the substance is the same, there is no doubt that it is the same: because he who lives is already life, namely God; and he who is life lives, namely Christ; and in both life is from themselves, as has been said: “As the Father has life from himself, so he gave the Son to have life from himself.”

But if we understand *homoousion* as being *homoousion einai*, “to be simultaneously the same substance,” this is more readily and clearly demonstrated by what I said the Father or the Son is. For living and life are so simultaneous, and always simultaneous, that in that which is living there is life, and again that which is life is living.

XV. Let us take an example—although what I say is rather the thing itself than an example. We have said that God is nothing other than living, but living in the principal sense: that from which is every living of all things, the very activity of other things existing in action and having its being in a movement of this kind, that is, possessing its existence or substance—although it does not even possess it, but is itself existing, namely that which is principally and universally living. But what is produced from this act, and is as it were its form, is life.

As *aiōn* is produced by the ever-present act of all things, so life is produced by living and by the ever-present activity of living itself. Let us put it thus: vitality—that is, the form of life—is generated into its own power and substance. Our own living also consists in ever-present time. For we do not live the past, nor do we live the future, but always make use of the present. For this alone is time; and this alone, because it alone is time, is said to be the image of *aiōn*, that is, eternity. For just as *aiōn* always has all things through present things, and has them always, so we too, because through present time we have all that we can have, have this our time as an image of *aiōn*, because our present is neither always present in the same things nor itself always the same.

Therefore life is produced by living and simultaneously is formed by existing. Formation is appearance; appearance is birth from hidden things, and birth from hidden things is nativity—and the nativity of that which existed before it arose in this manner. Hence in living there is life before life; yet life is subsequent, because life is produced by living; and it is always and from eternity life, because, in that which lives and lives from eternity, life is.

Therefore, since God lives and Christ is life, because life arises in existence from that which lives, necessarily the Father lives and the Son is life, as we have taught above; so that in that which lives there is life, and in life living is present. Therefore the Son is consubstantial with the Father, as we have taught above with examples.

XVI. It now remains to explain what the Holy Spirit is in relation to these. These things have been said and demonstrated concerning God: that God is that which is being; that Spirit is that which is living. Likewise, that light is that which is intelligence and knowledge. For light allows nothing to remain hidden, nothing obscure; it opens, makes clear, illuminates. Therefore God is precisely that which God is: he is being; he is the first and principal being of all things that are, granting being according to the capacity of those receiving it, as we have taught before. This is living; this is understanding; that is, this which is being is spirit, is light.

For these are in one and simple reality—indeed, are one and simple. They are that which is being; rightly we call this existence or substance. Yet, since the principal of these is that which is being, while the other two, living and understanding, are understood as movements, and every movement arises from rest: rest is that which is being; from that which is being, movement is born, and then action. But the movement of that first being is living and understanding. For both are movement, and one movement, bestowing two powers by a twofold office, while remaining one and the same substance. For in them substance is movement: there is not one thing in them to be and another to be moved. So likewise, with regard to substance, it is not one thing to live and another to understand. For it belongs to the living one to understand, and to the understanding one to live, as one movement turns itself through acts. Yet this is so that, while the work and act of living remain, the act of intelligence is set in motion.

Hence, since Christ is life, while the Holy Spirit is knowledge and intelligence, nevertheless the Holy Spirit receives from Christ all that he has, and Christ from the Father—that is, from that which is being. Life has come forth, and from living have come forth knowledge and understanding; [Col. 1125A] nor was there a time when that first being existed without movement also existing.

XVII. Although it is called rest, it is moved inwardly by the movement through which it lives for itself and understands itself. Therefore, from inward movement, movement outside and that which is outside were born: from inward being, and from inward living, outward living; from inward understanding, outward understanding—life and intelligence moving themselves.

For movements exist, in the same manner simultaneously with being, so that this Trinity might be inwardly: God alone and sole outwardly; Jesus Christ inwardly and outwardly; both one God. And since God is consubstantial with Christ, Christ also is necessarily consubstantial with the Holy Spirit, and through Christ with God; for he too came forth from God. For if every movement which is outside is from God’s movement, which is inward movement, then this movement too is from God.

For knowledge and intelligence are the existence of both and the power of knowing; and this very thing is movement, precisely because movement is substance. Therefore the Holy Spirit necessarily is in Christ, or is Christ, and has all things from him, because intelligence subsists from life, which Christ is, and therefore is other. This is what is said: “He has all things from me” (John 16:14–15). But “from me” and “he has” are two: therefore one is other than the other.

But because the Holy Spirit too is movement, and Christ is movement, and because Christ is true life and gives true life—that is, eternal life—to those who believe in him, and because he is present with God to those who believe in him—that he is the Son of God—and this through faith, we are therefore reconciled to God through Christ. Yet because human beings’ memory of themselves and of God is submerged, the Holy Spirit is necessary, when knowledge comes: “that you may understand what is the breadth of God, what the length, what the depth and height” (Eph. 3:18). When love and faith in Christ are confirmed through the Holy Spirit, because he is knowledge, the person will be saved. For the Spirit himself bears full testimony concerning Christ, teaches all things, and is Christ’s inward power, bestowing knowledge and bringing salvation about; hence he is another Paraclete.

For to human beings dead through sins life first had to be given, so that they might be raised toward God through faith: this was already to live from the life of God which Christ brought in the flesh, so that he might also aid the flesh. Therefore, when human beings have been strengthened through faith in Christ the Son of God, knowledge also appears to be given—knowledge concerning Christ and likewise concerning God; likewise concerning the world, in order that he might convict it. Once they understood these things, they might more easily be liberated to God’s light by understanding their human and divine realities, through contempt for earthly and worldly things and through the desire which knowledge of divine things arouses.

XVIII. Therefore the latter came—that is, faith came later in operation. For when Christ, who by miracles and precepts had sown faith that he was the Son of God and gave life to those believing in him, departed, all things were fulfilled by the Spirit, and faith, mature in knowledge concerning Christ, grew up; while Christ himself remained ever present. For he said: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine” (John 16:13–14).

Therefore intelligence is from life, and life itself from living—that is, the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from the Son. For he immediately added: “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine” (ibid. 15). He said, “are mine,” because the things which the Father has are the Son’s: being, living, understanding. The Spirit has these same things; therefore all are consubstantial.

Yet, in order to show his own abiding presence, he speaks thus in Matthew: “Go now, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all things whatsoever I have commanded you; and behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:19–20). From this it is in some manner shown that Jesus and the Holy Spirit are the same, namely in the act of operation, though distinct: the latter teaches intelligence, the former gives life. For he is the same and one movement, the first movement; so that it follows that he who lives truly also truly understands, and he who truly understands truly lives.

And in order that Jesus and the Holy Spirit may be shown to be the same, let us consider this: the Holy Spirit is doctrine, intelligence, and wisdom itself; and wisdom is ascribed both to Christ and to God. Christ is called by this name, because the Gospel defines Christ, the Son of God, as God’s power and wisdom, as Paul says in Romans (Rom. 1:16). Likewise Solomon: “All wisdom is from God, and was with him always before the age” (Ecclus. 1:1). Behold, *homoousion* appears: wisdom is ascribed to God and from God, certainly to Christ and the Holy Spirit. And when it is said that it was always with God, that which is *homoousion* is shown to be together with the Father.

Then, when it is said, “before the age,” Christ is not therefore only then, when in the flesh. Likewise: “Wisdom was created before all things” (ibid. 4); if Christ is firstborn, Christ is wisdom. Then what follows concerns the Holy Spirit: “and the understanding of prudence from the age.” If the Holy Spirit is prudence and understanding, if knowledge and doctrine, then he is undoubtedly Christ, because he is from the age—that is, from eternity—and firstborn, and, more than this, only-begotten.

These matters, and others, treated by me in many books, establish *homoousion* not only for God and Christ, but also for the Holy Spirit. Let us therefore grant or understand that God is that which is first and principally living, which is truly and principally being; for nothing is that does not live. We have made clear that this very living, by its own operation, produces and generates life. But in that which is life, knowledge and intelligence are present. Therefore God lives, and God is life by living; and when he is life, he is intelligence. Yet these three are one and simple; and, insofar as he is principal, that is, insofar as God is living being in principal existence, he necessarily also understands himself. For from this he understands all things, because he understands himself. He is the cause of all existences and therefore all things. Thus life and intelligence, received into that which is inwardly being, always work that which is living. But for God living is being. Therefore the being of all things is the one omnipotent God.

What then? If life and intelligence work within him—or rather work him—how could these things appear as if outside? And what are *on* (“being”) and *logos* (“reason” or “account”), outside or inside? Philosophers and men learned in the Law have asked what these are and where they are: what they are, so that we may explain their substance or existence; where they are, whether therein or outside, and in all other things, or in both and everywhere.

XIX. We have indeed set these matters forth fully and systematically in other books. But now we shall state them briefly and summarily. Before *on* and before *logos* is that force and power of existing which is signified by the word “to be,” in Greek *to einai*. This very being must be understood in two ways. First, as universal and principally principal, so that being is in other things from it, while the being that belongs to other things is different from that of all subsequent genera, species, and things of that kind.

But first being is so unparticipated that it cannot even be called one or alone; rather, by pre-eminence it is before one and before alone, beyond simplicity, pre-existence rather than existence, the universal of all universals, infinite and unbounded—but unbounded for all other things, not for itself. Therefore it is apprehended as formless by a certain understanding, and received, known, and believed as pre-intelligence rather than intelligence. This is that which we have called “living” or “lives”: that infinite reality, that which is above the living of all universals—being itself, living itself; not some being or some living, and hence not even *on*. For *on* is also something determinate, intelligible, and knowable.

Therefore, if not *on*, neither *logos*; for *logos* is determinate and determining—whether it is reason, or the power of existence itself, or those realities which intelligence apprehends, so that each has its being. For one does not know what one does not know unless one attends to and grasps what those things are which bestow substance upon each individual. And this is the Logos of things, through whom all things were created: the universal power, universally containing the realities of all things, and providing to each its own and proper basis for existence. Therefore, because it provides what is proper and its own to each, it defines and delimits; it also makes that *on*. For, by imposing a limit upon the infinite, it forms for each thing the reality of its own existence and subjects intelligence once infinity has been removed. Thus, in that which is the power of things for generating and bringing existences to completion, there is *logos*; but from the fact that it defines and encloses each thing by giving form, *on* is now existent, when there is a determinate form of that which is being.

XX. Since this is so, let us consider whether there is no λόγος [principle, reason, Word] of the first—which is being. If we call it infinite, if we call it immense, undifferentiated, we do not grasp or hold the things in which being consists; therefore it has no λόγος. But since it cannot be that this very existent which is should in any way be and yet be without its own λόγος, it is infinite; beyond doubt it has its own λόγος, but one lying hidden and concealed, so that in that which is being itself, λόγος itself may be; or rather, λόγος itself is nothing other than being itself. This is what I called truly first, and universally universal life, although, as we have taught, it is life itself, and life, and [Col. 1128A] determinate intelligence. For what is determinate and formed belongs to the powers of λόγος; while intelligence is also that which defines. Yet because these things are within and turned back upon themselves, all are ἄγνωστα, ἀδιάκριτα—unknown and undifferentiated. Thus God, who is being, that is, life, is unknown and undifferentiated; and his form, that is, the intelligence of life, is unknown and undifferentiated. For these are nothing other than being, which is life. Since this is infinite, its form too is infinite, remaining there and existing as nothing other than being.

But when it begins to be outside, then the appearing form is the image of God, displaying God through itself; and it is λόγος, no longer λόγος πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, “Word toward God,” in which are life and intelligence, but now ὄν, “being”; for it is determinate knowledge and existence, grasped by understanding and cognition. But [Col. 1128B] how did these things come to stand outside? And is the very form which is within sent forth outwardly, or did it cast itself forth? Yet, since that inner form is undifferentiated and infinite, how is that which is outside known in it? Or is this other? But if it is other, it is not born from that form, whether by emission or by its own motion. And if it is thus other—not a part, not the same, not wholly ὁμοούσιος, “of the same substance”—whence then did it appear?

XXI. Are there then two principles, the one from the other, or is it from nothing? Nothingness is not among the things that are beneath God. Further, if it came forth by God’s power or will, God’s power or will is not nothing. For if God is omnipotent, his omnipotence is the cause of all things and is itself existence. Shall we then dare to say what remains, that this form arose from itself? And how, when it was [Col. 1128C] in the Father—without the Father’s knowing, or at his command? If at his command, then it was not from itself. Or without his knowledge? Then there is something which was not God’s power, or something which existed without him—although concerning the λόγος which is called his form it has been said: “Through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). What is this? What release from such great confusions is there?—if it is not truth, or the life of truth.

Let the Holy Spirit be present. Let the hearer attend while we set forth, in pure simplicity, what has been inspired in us. Meanwhile I offer one warning: these matters ought to be understood without time—always from eternity, with no beginning in time—yet so that both, begetter and begotten, are one principle. First: eternal things, especially divine and most primary things, abiding still and existing in that which they are, have not generated through any change of themselves by motion. [Col. 1128D] God is first; then λόγος, or νοῦς [intellect], or whatever the other may be—or both, as spirit, as living, or life, as intelligence, or knowledge. Soul alone, being moved, has generations.

All these things are so constituted: God is τριδύναμος, “three-powered,” that is, possessing three powers—being, living, understanding—so that in each single one there are three; and he himself, receiving whatever one of the three names by which he makes himself known, is each one of the three, as I taught above and in many places. For nothing is to be said to be unless it understands. Thus there is a threefold singularity in each, and unity in the Trinity. We shall set forth these three by their progression.

XXII. All things which are, which can be, or could have been, have received existence, life, intelligence, and participations in them, according to the capacity of things and substances. For in all things there is their own being, their own living, their own understanding, and their own sensing, so that these may be an image or shadow of the three things that are above all. Therefore God, since he is, as all say, one—and one alone—[Col. 1129A] is one. Yet some have said that God is “one, all things,” and also not one; for he is the principle of all things, whence he is not all things, yet in that manner is all things.

This is the reason why God is first one and one alone. Those three do not subsist by conjunction, but by being what they are in themselves; and what we suppose to be other is necessarily one, and in no way other. But this has often been said. As for the statement “one, all things, and not one, for he is the principle of all things,” it quite openly and clearly declares God to be Father and principle of all things. Since he is not one, he is rather all things, because he is both the cause and principle of all things and all things in all things. Since this is so, God will be all things: all-existing, all-living, all-seeing, and all-understanding.

And since we have said that power is completed by act—for the first principles are so related that, since all things are from divine ἐνέργεια, that is, act and operations—it is necessary that from God, the principle of all powers, there should arise the universal source and origin of universal things. [Col. 1129B] For this is the progression of things: since all things are from God, and powers and acts are from God, who is conceived as above powers and acts, these things are believed to have arisen from him.

XXIII. Yet although we have said that God is a certain act, namely life—but this life which is above every life, from eternity and unto eternity—when living is understood together with understanding, with [Col. 1129C] being, and with understanding itself, yet in such a way that there is not even an image of conjunction: necessarily, through the act of living, as I have taught, there is confessed and brought forth a form which we call universal power, formed in each of those particular things, from all-existence, all-livingness, and all-seeingness. These particular powers are known and determinate.

But when all things are in the one, or the one is all things, or when the one is all things—or neither one nor all things—there arises infinity, the unknown, the indistinguishable, the unknowable, and what is truly called ἀοριστία, that is, infinity and indeterminacy. For he is the being of all, the life of all, and the understanding of all, and is one, one without any image of otherness; whence he is not one, because he is the principle of all things, and therefore also of the one itself. From this we are now compelled necessarily [Col. 1129D] to say such things concerning God: that his being, living, and understanding are incomprehensible; and not merely that his being, living, and understanding are incomprehensible, but that these do not even seem to be, since he is above all things. Therefore he is called ἀνύπαρκτος, ἀνούσιος, ἄνους, and ἄζων—without existence, without substance, without intelligence, without life—not through στέρησις, that is, not through privation, but through transcendence. For all things named by words come after him; hence he is not ὄν, “being,” but rather προόν, “pre-being.”

In the same way, pre-existence, pre-seeing, and pre-knowledge are so called in relation to things which are brought about; while he himself is pre-existing, pre-seeing, and pre-knowing. Yet all these were understood and named only after secondary things appeared. For after knowledge appeared, [Col. 1130A] pre-knowledge too was understood and named; likewise pre-existence and pre-living. These things indeed were, but had not yet been perceived or named. Hence everything which God is is unknowable.

But because something is then held and called knowable when there is knowledge—for these are relative, mutually uphold and generate one another, or mutually destroy one another—that thing was not yet knowable because knowledge did not yet exist. Not because that did not exist which knowledge made knowable to itself, but because there was indeed that which could be knowable, not that which was knowable. It becomes and is conceived as knowable when it is understood that intelligence too can be. In this way, therefore, in God something could be and, for this reason, was knowable, because knowledge too could be and for this reason was.

[Col. 1130B] XXIV. What then follows from this? Since these things were later born, they were in God; and if they were in God, because God is one, these too are one—and what God is, these are one because they are God. Therefore the knowable and knowledge are the same; yet so that what is knowable is itself knowledge. For since the power of these three is one—being is nothing other than living, and living itself understanding, insofar as it is also being understood—the whole force of each lies in knowing, or in being knowledge.

But knowledge cannot be unless there is something knowable. In these first things, however, where being is living and understanding, there cannot be the knowable unless knowledge itself, not yet appearing, holds itself inwardly, remains quiet, rests, and, turned toward itself, renders itself knowable to itself. [Col. 1130C] For when knowledge itself lies hidden and is with itself, entering into itself from without but naturally immersed in that wherein its being abides, it belongs to its form that it may be knowable when knowledge, awakened and as though having gone forth, looks around itself and makes itself knowledge; by knowing itself it becomes its own knowable.

Thus, if it is permitted to say so—thus, I say—that first, that one alone, that God, whether spirit, breathing, light, illuminating, existing, all-existing, existence, all-existence, living, all-living, life, livingness, all-livingness, understanding and knowing, all-understanding, all-knowing, all-intelligence, all-knowledge, omnipotent, perfect in every manner, unbounded, [Col. 1130D] immeasurable—yet bounded and measured to itself by the others—is above all things and therefore none of all things, but rather that from which all things are. Therefore he is one and one alone, for he is the principle of all things.

Accordingly, do not understand “one, all things” as remaining in himself, nor “in himself” in such a way as to make two, hearer; rather, he is himself remaining or abiding, rest at rest—more precisely, resting, because rest comes from that which rests, as we taught above. Therefore he has also been said to sit as it were at the centre τῶν πάντων ὄντων, “of all things that are,” from which, by the universal eye—that is, by the light of his substance, by which he is either being, living, or understanding—he sees the things that are with an unturning gaze; for he is rest, and from the centre there is at once one vision toward all things.

Such is God. But in what way is God Father, and who is the Son, or how is he Son? And afterward, how is Jesus the Son? The principle of the being of all things, existing before all things, is the being of all things—not so much being rest as being rest itself. For everything generated or made is generated or made from motion. But motion itself, insofar as it is motion, is rest before it moves. For the origins of opposites arise from opposites, so that by the opposite origin the opposite from which this arose perishes into non-being—as death from life and life from death. Likewise, from being comes non-being, and from non-being, being. Likewise, from rest comes motion and from motion, rest.

XXV. But let us attend more sharply and, with daring intelligence, behold the force and depth of things. If the matters proposed are carefully considered, one will find a certain existence even in these things [Col. 1131B] whose appearance involves perishing. For since life is that to which being belongs, and death arises from it, there is being also for death if life arises from death. Likewise, if non-being is brought about from being, non-being itself must also be if being arises from it. Likewise, if cessation exists, motion must be cessation, if motion arises from it.

What then? Are not opposites thought either to die or not to be through the origin of opposites? So it seems, but the contrary is true. For both remain and do not perish from their eternal substantial quality. How this is, I shall say; may God be present, and the explanation will become easier. In eternal things, being is living and understanding. We have said and demonstrated this repeatedly. But that being is such that there are living and understanding substances there. [Col. 1131C] Let us understand these, according to the capacity of existing things, as conferring three realities and retaining all things by participation in themselves; in the noetic realm they flourish, alone simple, divine, and eternal; in worldly and material things, however, they are indeed present but are sustained in various and mortal bodies.

Here, therefore, if death exists, it is the death of bodies; and, if closer attention is applied, not even of bodies insofar as they are matter, but a dissolution caused by a certain destruction of these bodies in their present species. Thus, only the bodily species is dissolved; when it is scattered into the elements, those things remain and are from which living things will be restored. For since in the world there is matter, always existing in determinate elements, and since images of those three also present themselves here, that is, in the world, what can death do, when they are eternal even in their images? By images I mean the powers flowing everywhere from the lines of soul.

[Col. 1131D] Since these things are eternal, the elements too are eternal in matter. If death dissolves only composites, it utterly perishes. Hence it is rightly said that death is produced from life: from the vigor of life in any composite body there comes, at a determined point, dissolution; and again from death, with all the same constituents, restoration comes about into another composition. Thus too being in the world must be understood; thus too are rest and motion here. But in divine things, because there are no bodies, there is no death; life too is there in another manner, namely primary and true life. Therefore progression there is not birth, or, if one prefers, is rather an appearing and manifestation of birth. Likewise there are there being and non-being in another manner, and motion and cessation in another manner. For [Col. 1132A] God lives; and this is being and understanding—these three constitute one thing: three powers, existence, life, intelligence.

XXVI. But because I have taught how those three are one: just as any one of the three is three, so these three also are one. In God these three are being; in the Son, living; in the Holy Spirit, understanding. Therefore being, living, and understanding are being in God; but existence, life, and intelligence are form. For in the inner and hidden act of that which is being, living, and understanding, they are inward and hidden; indeed God is more properly above being, above living, and above understanding. Hence he is called ἀνούσιος or ἀνύπαρκτος, and likewise ἄζων and ἄνους, discovered by a certain pre-intelligence and known rather through his form, which is inherent in and consubstantial with [Col. 1132B] him.

And this is what the Son is in the Father. Since this is so, the Son is the same as the Father; hence the Son too is God, because the form is that whose form it is. For since God is being, living, and understanding, while the form is existence, life, and intelligence, I wish you to understand me as saying this in such a way that God is above these things. If this is so, form becomes the same as substance. For in the same way these things have force and are: having or existing, being, living, understanding. Thus, although there are two λόγοι—one by which each thing is, the other by which it is in a certain manner—yet because the manner in which it is and what it is have the same force, necessarily one λόγος results, since form has the same force as substance. Therefore, if form has the same force and is the same as that substance—since the form is substantial—the Son will be the same as the Father; or [Col. 1132C], before the outward going-forth, there is neither Father nor Son, but the one alone itself.

XXVII. Since this is so: since God has understanding and intelligence, and intelligence is the same as life and as being; but since understanding is more a power of acting than being or living; and since being is understanding insofar as it is, and living is understanding insofar as it lives: necessarily God is understanding or intelligence. When God understands, he understands himself; but when he understands himself, not as one other understands another, it follows that intelligence itself understands itself. When this occurs, it makes itself to be and comes forth into existence; it becomes for itself that which is being. In the same way, by understanding it brings forth its own living. Since all these are born from itself—or rather exist from itself—the unbegotten God [Col. 1132D] exists from unbegotten things. And since these are one, one and simple, there is one God. This is intelligence inwardly, which understands itself without any motion; for when it understands, it exists, and when it exists, it understands. This is God, certainly from eternity and unto eternity.

XXVIII. But since we call the Son the image of God, the form has been generated: from that which is being, living, and understanding, existence, life, and intelligence are generated. For there is a certain form in these, through which, as through an image, one understands what being, living, and understanding are. Necessarily, therefore, God is understood through the form, for “no one has ever seen him” (John 1:18). Thus, when the form of God is understood in God, it is God; [Col. 1133A] but when God understands himself, he understands himself through form. Yet the form itself must also understand. For it is intelligent and living existence, understanding nothing other than that these things are God. And I have often already taught this.

But when intelligence itself understands that it is intelligence—for it necessarily follows that intelligence understands itself—it has understood itself as though existing from itself and has made itself outside: what is outside is itself by understanding, that is, by its own motion. Hence there is intelligence outside, and here is the Son; here is λόγος; the Son is born because he is other than God, yet from God—that is, from that which is existing and living, intelligence which is God. And intelligence, inwardly understanding itself, brought itself forth outwardly and came to be for [Col. 1133B] the Father, in whom it was and always is, an image existing through the inner intelligence which is being and existing; and therefore an image begotten from image.

XXIX. There are, therefore, two intelligences: one existing inwardly, which is its being; the other existing, which is its being by understanding. This latter is outside; this is the Son. Since intelligence, by understanding itself, understood God—namely, inward intelligence, which is God—it understood true being and true living, and, by understanding, itself came forth as true being, true living, and true understanding. For whoever understands one thing, possesses one thing, and is one thing according to that thing’s intelligence within him.

Thus the Son—that is, intelligence begotten by intelligence through understanding itself—understood God and all those things which God is unbegotten; and by seeking πλήρωμα, “fullness,” through understanding, and understanding πλήρωμα, [Col. 1133C] came forth as the same as the Father. For since the Father is πλήρωμα, he necessarily has his own infinite χώρημα, “capacity” or “receptacle,” though finite in relation to himself, in which he holds and contains his πλήρωμα. The Son likewise, by receiving and seeking—for to receive χώρημα is to exist—came forth begotten by understanding the whole πλήρωμα which is the Father, himself whole from the whole. And because intelligence understands intelligence, and intelligence is the light of things, light comes forth from light; and because both are intelligence, true light from true light.

Likewise, since God is inward intelligence, this intelligence, by understanding itself, is God from God: therefore ὁμοούσιον in all things—in being, living, and understanding; likewise in that each is χώρημα and πλήρωμα; likewise in that each is image and image, for it is said: “according to our image” (Gen. 1:26); and in that each is light and light, true light and true light, Spirit and Spirit, motion and motion. Yet the Father is motion at rest, that is, inward motion, and nothing other than motion—not motion moved by motion—whereas the Son is motion moved by motion; nevertheless both are motion. Likewise both are action and works; both are life; and both have life from themselves, will and will, the same power, wisdom, Word, God, God, living God and living God, invisible from eternity and invisible from eternity. For Matthew says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son” (Matt. 11:27). Both together: for this is what ὁμοούσιον signifies, in addition to the same οὐσία, “substance.”

[Col. 1133D]

All this may be understood from that complete saying: “All that the Father has, he gave to me,” and, “All that the Father has, I too have” (John 16:15). “All,” he says. If all, the Son is ὁμοούσιος with the Father. Therefore he is the same; and if the same, equal; and if equal, Paul rightly said of Jesus Christ, the Son of God: “Who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as robbery” (Phil. 2:6).

[Col. 1134A]

XXX. Many divine and magnificent mysteries are contained here. First, Christ is the form of God; this shows that he possesses all that God possesses. This is also why he is called the image, as is said of him: “who is the image of God” (2 Cor. 4:4; Col. 1:15). God, then, also has his own image; and the Son is the image of God. For if it is said: “No one has ever seen [Col. 1134B] the face of God” (Exod. 33:20), and it is said: “You shall see my back parts” (ibid. 23), God undoubtedly has a face; the Son has it, or rather the Son is the image of God, as it is said: “being in the form of God.”

Thus it was rightly said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). The Son exists; and if he is other, he exists. For Father and Son are not the same: they are the same in all those respects set out by me above, but “the same” means possessing the same proper existences. Hence they are both the same and other. For when it is said here, “being in the form of God,” certainly one must understand one thing as the form and another as God.

But perhaps there is room for quibbling: perhaps the form of God is form within God himself, so that there is one undifferentiated substance. How then shall we understand what follows: “He did not regard it as robbery to be equal [Col. 1134C] with God”? One who is situated in his own existence may think or say himself equal with another. What, further, does this mean: “He emptied himself and took the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7)? Do we understand this of Christ, who died, or of God? Yet no one has ever said it of God. Further, when it is said of the Father that he raised his Son from the dead, is it not sufficiently clear that Father and Son are different, that the raiser is one and the one raised another?

Therefore: the form of God. Form is one thing, God another. God indeed has form; but the Son is God’s form in manifestation, whereas God’s form is hidden. Thus all God’s existence, life, and knowledge are inward and hidden; in the Son they are manifest. So too are the remaining things: χώρημα, πλήρωμα, image, true light, truth, spirit, motion, action, operation, life, life from himself, will, power, [Col. 1134D] wisdom, Word, God, living God, and all the rest. But these are, as it were, outward and manifest; those are in themselves and about existence—or rather are existence itself. These, however, are in the acting act which is manifest.

Finally, the Son has all these things, but with the Father giving them. This is strongly expressed where it says that the Son has life from himself, yet adds: “The Father gave him to have life in himself” (John 5:26). Therefore he is the true image, and the existence is the same in all things, but with the Father giving. Thus Father and Son are ὁμοούσιοι, but with the Father giving. For from what we have said—that the Father is being, living, and understanding—existence has been generated, as have life and intelligence. This is the form of God; this is the Son. But when the Son is in the Father, the whole is one within: God acting, working, using himself, enjoying himself, fountain and fullness of all things in himself.

[Col. 1135A] XXXI. But since, as we have taught, intelligence by the force of its own power necessarily understands itself while turning itself toward itself, it becomes in some manner twofold; and, as though inward and outward, the Son is begotten from the Father’s existence. For existence is intelligence, which is also life; therefore the appearing and existing one is God from God. And because in any one of the three—being, living, understanding—all things are present: when intelligence has begotten intelligence, the Son is begotten, and the Son has all that the Father has and has it from the Father.

[Col. 1135B] Further, because these are all the things through which all things are created—for whatever things exist receive their own being, their own living, and their own understanding—the Son, being all these things, since he is the Father’s image and is an active act, that is, so as to confer this upon others according to the nature of existing things, is necessarily the λόγος of all things universally and wholly: the λόγος of universals, genera, species, and particulars; that is, the force and power through which things that are come to be, through whom God made and makes all things, and without whom nothing is made.

Others call this active motion, word, operative reason. Yet because, when he works, the Father’s power is in him, he works in himself; hence many things are said in such a way that, although what he does is his own, he nonetheless refers all things to the Father: “The Father sent me” (John 6:58); “I do not do my own will but the Father’s” (John 6:38); and a thousand such sayings. Nevertheless, let us attend to this passage: we shall find him acting as if by himself, of his own accord: “He did not regard equality with God as robbery” (Phil. 2:6); and again: [Col. 1135C] “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”—he who possessed dominion. All these are the actions of one acting by his own will.

Yet one may believe that he acts because the Father is in him; hence also those sayings: “I give eternal life” (John 10:28); “I am the door” (John 10:7); “I am the way, I am life, I am truth” (John 16:6); “For as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21). These true and varied sayings, in all of which the truer intelligence is especially operative, establish both that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, and yet that they are Father and Son—other, yet one; still two, because Father is one and Son another.

For the Father is the source of the Son, the Son like a river running forth from a spring. In the spring, water remains and is still, pure, unstained, without the appearance of bubbling; with a more manifest motion, hidden to itself, it runs abroad through diverse places, is affected by the qualities of the lands which it cuts through, and in some manner suffers. So also the Son, by his own water and his own substance—which is the Father’s—is always pure, unstained, and impassible in the regions and places through which he passes, whether supercelestial, celestial, or intracelestial; now he foams, as against rocks that meet him, which arise from the kinds of souls; now he runs as a quiet plain. [Col. 1135D] He therefore receives passions not in respect of substance, but in act and operation. For when he fulfilled the mystery of his coming, then he endured passion, emptying himself and taking the person of a servant. So too the remaining matters, in all of which there is act and operation.

Although even in the first act of his existence, as we have taught in many books, there was a passion of departure from the Father, from which darkness—that is, matter—followed, though it was not created. But these matters are treated more fully elsewhere.

XXXII. What, then, has now been asserted and demonstrated? That God the Father and God the Son are ὁμοούσιοι, “of one substance”; yet that there is both Father in substance and Son in that same substance, but the Son exists for himself as an acting act, coming forth in the act of passion; that he has never been separated from the Father, and eternally is, was, and will be. He is act because he is within the nature of acting, and because he is with the Father or in the Father. He is said to be both outside this and inside and outside; and because he himself acts, since his act is from the Father, he is said to act while the Father acts, while nevertheless the Father is said to do all things through him.

This one is the λόγος of all things, universally of universals, genera, species, and particulars. And because he is the λόγος of all incorporeal things, he is also the λόγος of corporeal things, according to their own power to become what they can be. Therefore, in the dispensation of the mystery, in the last ages the λόγος—he who is the Son demonstrated above—was incarnate, being shadowed forth in all existing things through the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. He was in a body in the same manner in which the Holy Spirit is in us: not wholly; for as God is everywhere, he is present as a part of the whole. For in all divine things, that which is a part is always the whole, as soul is in bodies, as capacity and instruction are in souls, or as the sun or its light is in eyes.

That λόγος himself, that Son whom we have demonstrated, was in the body: all the Gospels, the whole Apostle, and all the Prophets [Col. 1136B] declare this. For when they foretold that Christ would come, they foretold that he would come in the flesh, since they say that before [Col. 1136C] his coming into flesh he was seen and appeared—to Abraham, to Jacob. And he himself said in the flesh: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

And the Apostle, especially in this sacred passage full of mysteries, declares that the Son of God existed before the flesh and afterward took flesh: “Have this mind in yourselves, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being constituted in the form of God …” (Phil. 2:5–6). This was certainly before the flesh; therefore he existed before the flesh and was such and so great before the flesh. “The form,” he says, “of God.” What is this? Form is the same as the Father. What is form? That in which the Father is seen: “He who sees me sees the Father” (John 14:9). Certainly not in that which was visible, but in that he himself is God, divine substance, λόγος, life.

This, then, existed before the flesh. For what does he add? “He did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God.” He thinks of himself and of God; he therefore makes it clear that he is not equal, but was equal. What does he add next? “But he emptied himself” (Phil. 2:7–8). What did he empty, or from what, if he had not existed? He adds further: “Taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.”

What does this not in every respect declare concerning Jesus Christ and the Son of God? For it is thus said: “God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4), and the one sent, doing all things by the judgment of his own power and also his own will, willed not to be equal, emptied himself, and put on the form of a servant. Therefore he existed who was the form of God; he existed who emptied himself. That same one is Jesus, [Col. 1137A] who took the image of a servant, who was found to be a man, who subjected himself unto death, so that Jesus Christ might be designated still more fully: even unto the death of the cross.

### XXXIII

These points have been sufficiently established for faithful men: that he existed before the flesh, and that in the flesh he was the same Son—he who was begotten before the ages, he who ascended into heaven and descended thence, he who is for us bread from heaven; he who says in the flesh: “Restore to me, Father, my glory which I had with you” (John 17:5)—certainly above the heavens and before the flesh; he is the *Logos* [Word], and “in the beginning was the *Logos*,” and the *Logos* was with God, and the *Logos* was God, and through the *Logos* all things were made and without him nothing was made; he who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9); he who, the *Logos*, became flesh (John 1:14).

You have heard: “In the beginning [was] the *Logos*”; you have heard that the *Logos* himself became flesh. Hear that he himself is the Son of God and begotten of the Father: this is the generation of which we spoke above. The evangelist says: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18). Yet we should better say “in the lap.” The Greeks say *en kolpō*, that is, “in the lap.” But either expression signifies the begotten Son: that he is outside, yet is with the Father, when it is said, “who is in the bosom of the Father.” A diligent and faithful investigator will understand that this is so from every reading.

Moreover, we have set forth in many books that the Holy Spirit is, in another manner, Jesus Christ himself—hidden, inward, conversing with souls, teaching these things, and imparting understandings—and that he is begotten from the Father through Christ and in Christ; for Christ is the only-begotten Son. And what we have demonstrated by very many examples is sufficiently clear.

In this manner and understanding, the Father and God are *homoousios* [of one substance] with the Son, and the Son, because he himself is life, is so with him. But because Christ himself is understanding, the Holy Spirit too is understood as *homoousios*. Thus, when Father and Son are taken together, he is the same as the Holy Spirit, in that mode in which the Son is the same as the Father. Yet, although Father and Son are one, the Father is nevertheless Father and the Son Son, each existing in his own existence, but both one and the same substance. So too, although Christ and the Holy Spirit are both one, Christ nevertheless exists in his own existence, and the Holy Spirit in his own; but both are one substance. From this all are one—that is, the whole Trinity is one—in the same way when Father is joined with Son, and Son with Holy Spirit.

And by this reasoning, when Father is joined with Holy Spirit through Christ, while each exists singly as one, the whole Trinity is; and that *homoousios* exists, since for all there is one and the same substance together from eternity.

This is our salvation, this our deliverance, this the full salvation of the whole human being: to believe thus in God the almighty Father, thus in Jesus Christ the Son, thus in the Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 1137]

## Victorinus, On Receiving the *Homoousion* (C)

### I

[Col. 1137C] I am astonished that the single manner of understanding is still not held among us with settled conviction: we all understand rightly, yet we are not united. Therefore I shall state the whole mystery—the words, meanings, understandings, of all—in brief discourse, so that we may exclude Arius.

The Greeks, whom they call Hellenes or pagans, speak of many gods. The Jews, or Hebrews, of one. We, because truth and grace are later, declare one God against the pagans; against the Jews, Father and Son. Thus we speak of two, Father and Son, but nevertheless of one God; embracing both religions, we resist each of the two by the contrary position of the other.

The pagans indeed fell far: they said that both the elements and their foods were gods. The Jews, through a carnal error, deny Christ, whom in another way they confess. Therefore our doctrine must be demonstrated: it taught truth and corrected error. This will be easy to know if the force of the term established by the elders, called *homoousion*, is known. Nor do I wish anyone to err when I speak only of Father and Son as *homoousion*, since the Holy Spirit is both from the Father and in the Son. This reasoning will prevail especially against Arians and against heretics.

We confess that God exists; this is what it is to exist. Let us confess that Christ exists in this way. I say in this manner: God is; Christ is. But what is this “is”? We confess that light is, Spirit is, God is, *Logos* is. Therefore no one denies these things. The Greeks call this being *ousia* or *hypostasis*; we in Latin call it by one name, substance. Few and rarely use *ousia* among the Greeks; all use *hypostasis*.

### II

[Col. 1138C] There is indeed a difference; but let us now omit it. Divine Scripture often says *hypostasis* in Greek, “substance” in Latin. The prophet Jeremiah says concerning God’s substance: “If these had stood in the substance of the Lord, they would have seen my Word” (Jer. 23:22, according to the Septuagint).

But what is it to stand in the substance? To understand God’s substance: that he is true light, that he is infinite Spirit. Had they understood this, they would have understood the *Logos* of the Lord; that is, they would have seen the Word of the Lord. And in the same way Jeremiah speaks a little later (ibid., 18). David says: “And my substance [was] in the lower parts of the earth” (Ps. 138:15); he speaks also concerning God and uses the word “substance,” and what this is is plain. The Apostle says to the Hebrews: “Who is the χαρακτήρ [impress] of his substance” (Heb. 1:3). For he called the Spirit the χαρακτήρ of God’s substance.

There are many other examples, but what does it matter? We have read that there is, and is called, a substance of God. God’s substance, then, is light, Spirit, God. Likewise Christ’s substance is *Logos*, light, Christ. Hence we all rightly say that Christ is true light from true light, God from God. Therefore he is rightly said to be of the same substance: that is, *homoousion*.

Confess, then, the *homoousion*, when you say “light from light,” “God from God.” Why do you resist? Because it is Greek? *Homo-* has such a force that, when joined to a word, it sometimes signifies that a thing is of the same kind, and sometimes that one thing is together with another. For example, *eidos*, which in Greek means “species”: *homo-* and *eidos* are joined, and it signifies “of the same species”; similarly *homōnymon*, “of the same name.” Therefore, when *homo-* is joined to *ousia*, *homoousion* results: “of the same *ousia*,” that is, “of the same substance.”

By this Arius, who said that Christ was from nothing, is excluded. Again, we have said that *homo-* signifies *homou*, “together,” when joined to a thing: it says nothing other than that a thing exists together with a thing; as *homēlikēs*, “of one and the same age,” and *homotrophous*, *homou traphentas*, “nourished together.” Therefore we shall call *homoousion* “substantial together,” or “consubstantial.” Behold, we have Latin terms as well.

If this is so, Arius, who said, “There was when he was not,” is excluded by this also. For if we say, “always Father, always Son,” and if “in the beginning was the *Logos*, and the *Logos* was with God” (John 1:1), since the beginning is without origination, and God was always without time, the *Logos* always, the Father always, the Son always—if this is so, then, as I said, “There was when he was not” is excluded. Behold: in each respect the *homoousion* is set against Arius and against the whole heresy of Arius.

### III

If these things are true, accept the *homoousion*. For if you will not, you are openly new Arians. Yet, as is clear from your deeds, you do indeed say that Christ is God from God, light from light; but you say that he was made, and thus born—not from God’s substance but from nothing. By your arguments you compel others to say this, so that you may hear it rather than say it yourselves. And why these arguments? O God, O Christ, come to our aid! “If Christ was born from God, God was either divided or diminished.”

You often put forward these and similar unworthy things, as if God were a body, or corporeal, or matter; for in these division or diminution can occur. But we have already said much on this question: how in divine and incorporeal things—and especially in soul, spirit, and mind, and still more in God—there can be motion or generation in every respect. For perfect things cannot be increased or diminished, especially with respect to substance; for, being self-generated (*autogona*) and self-powered (*autodynama*)—I speak of God, of Spirit—they emit such things as they themselves are. There generation is not generation by alteration, nor is there any passion, or even any appearance of passion.

Meanwhile, by these arguments of yours, what do you compel us to confess? That Christ was born from nothing? Is your blasphemy less because you hold the same opinion? Or why is your profession not open, if you think this way? But you do not see that you speak contradictions. For you say, “God from God, light from light.” Is this from nothing, when you state whence he is? Therefore Christ is from God, not from nothing; from light, not from nothing. For “from God” is understood as “from his own substance.” For that which is from God is one thing: all things are from God; but Christ is from God. Christ himself is the *Logos*, or the *Logos* is Christ.

### IV

Finally, inquire what the *Logos* is, and you will find that the *Logos* cannot be from nothing. But those deceive you—those, I say, who, not understanding the manner of generation, say: “Who can declare the Lord’s generation?” (Isa. 53:8). First, this may seem to have been said concerning human beings: “Who?” that is, no one. Yet the Holy Spirit can both intimate and declare it. Hence, by the permission of God the Father and of Jesus Christ our Lord, we too have spoken of it. Certainly this was not said as hopeless, but with wonder.

Further, let the manner of generation be unknown: we speak of substance. If there are Father and Son, there is *homoousion*. But how God is Father and how the *Logos* is Son is difficult to know. At present this does not seem to be the question to pursue. First it must be confessed that the Son is from the Father’s substance, and then how he is Son. This manner is truly difficult and has been treated by us elsewhere.

Therefore now concerning the *homoousion*: certainly, to satisfy you—for we desire peace with all—we have ways of expressing *homoousion*: first, “consubstantial,” or “substantial together.” Then, if we say “God from God, light from light”—and the Father is light and likewise the Son light—when we say that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, let us also say, as we rightly do, “God from God, light from light.” This will be true and complete *homoousion*.

Do you doubt? What if this too is read? It is blasphemy to contradict. David says: “For with you is the fountain of life,” and: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10). Confess this too now, and the *homoousion*.

Likewise this can be objected to one who says “similar substance”: for we say the same substance and substance together. Certainly it is said in Isaiah: “No one before you, O God, and no one after you is like you, O God” (Isa. 43:10); and David: “Who will be like you, O God?” (Ps. 34:10). These points are against those who speak of similar substance. But I pass over much that has been treated more fully and copiously in works against them—works which they themselves sent. For there is no need to speak of those who say “unlike,” nor of those who consider as Patripassians those who treat the matters we are discussing. All these and other heretics have easily been refuted in a fuller treatment.

Be present, God the Father, and God, Lord Jesus Christ, so that in your people there may be *homoousia* through the *homoousion*. Amen.

[Col. 1139]

## Victorinus: Hymns on the Trinity (C, S)

### Hymn I

Be present, true light, almighty God and Father.

Be present, light of light, mystery and power of God.

Be present, Holy Spirit, bond of Father and Son.

When you rest, you are Father; when you proceed, Son.

You who bind all things into one, you are the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1140D] One first, one arisen from itself, one God before the one.

You precede every quantity, known by no limits.

There is no quantity in you, because no quantity is from you.

For the one born from you begets rather than possesses quantity.

[Col. 1141A] Hence the Father is immeasurable; the Son both measured and immeasurable.

But you too, Father, are one, and the Son whom you begot is one.

That which is many, or all things, is the one which the Son begot.

You are the seed of being (*ontos*) for all things, the true power of the seed,

In whom and through whom all things are begotten—the power which God pours forth.

And all things begotten from the seed return again into the seed.

Therefore Christ works all things, he who is the whole power of God.

For Christ in repose is motion, the supreme God.

And motion itself is wisdom and the power of God,

Not at all distant from substance, because what is motion

[Col. 1141B] is substance; and the one who is motion, because he is in it and it in him.

He is called God from God, but begotten because he is motion;

For every motion is a nod, and God, though one,

God’s motion, is one and the same God.

Yet motion itself is being, so that it may be to itself what motion itself is.

But because it is God’s motion, motion has God in itself.

And again, because God himself is motion, God has motion in himself.

Therefore the Father is in the Son, and the Son himself is in the Father.

Thus each exists singly and always in himself, although they are singly existing.

Hence there is one power in the two; hence one substance.

[Col. 1141C] But, because the Father gives it, the Son is the substance which he is to himself.

For being is prior; motion is subsequent.

Not that time belongs to him, but in divine things order is power.

For being precedes motion, prior in reality, not in time.

They call this being in God substance.

But this motion is origination, for motion begets substance.

And what else is the generation of substance than substance?

Therefore motion belongs also to the Father; therefore the Son is the same substance.

The Greeks called this *Logos*: God within the Father,

The cause of birth and of the origin of all things.

For nothing was created without this; through him all things were created.

[Col. 1141D] If this *Logos* is Christ, and if the *Logos* is begotten life,

The *Logos* is from the Father; for he is the living God, in whom,

Since God is substance and life is God’s substance,

The begotten Son is life: the substance is one.

The *Logos* is God, therefore always undivided, and always also another.

Sent together, equal to the sender, yet as a flowing fountain always

He runs abroad, scattering lives—the Son sent as a stream.

Hence both are one substance: God the fountain, the Son the stream.

But in divine things substance is the same as life.

And life itself is wisdom, as being comes first,

To whom first and simple living is inherent and thus present,

Ever understanding and wise, while living comes first.

[Col. 1142A] Not that one other thing precedes another, nor that there is any other thing at all,

But that by progression the other is made threefold.

The Son is life in activity, through whom all things proceed and are created.

He becomes likewise teacher and master, likewise the perfecting Spirit,

Watering souls sown through the ages by the seeds of Sophia [Wisdom; reading uncertain].

But since Sophia is Christ, Christ the Son himself teaches;

The Spirit, proceeding from the Father, teaches Father and Christ.

Hence all things of the Father are Christ’s; hence Christ has all things of Christ.

Thus my Christ, between the begetting Father and himself, fills

The other Spirit with the Father, while he grants being to all things.

[Col. 1142B] And being is life for all things; and this is what was made in Christ.

For he joins and saves all things, and teaches the true God.

The Holy Spirit joins those who follow Christ, reborn in Christ, to Christ.

Therefore Christ is all things; hence Christ is mystery.

Through him all things, in him all things, and into him all things.

His height is the Father, while he himself is wholly

His own progression, the length and height of the Father.

Hence Christ, appearing through the ages, instructed unto the depth, and into the secret,

And, teaching inwardly within, Christ became the hidden Spirit.

[Col. 1142C] Therefore all are one Spirit, all one light.

Hence there is true substance for each; hence one substance for the three.

Proceeding from Father to Son and returning through Spirit,

Because the three exist singly, and the three are singly in the one.

This is the blessed Trinity; this the blessed unity.

### Hymn II

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ; have mercy, Lord, because I have believed in you. Have mercy, Lord, because by your mercy I have known you.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: you are the *Logos* of my spirit, you are the *Logos* of my soul, you are the *Logos* of my flesh.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: God lives, and God always lives; and because nothing is before him, God lives from himself.

[Col. 1142D] Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: Christ lives, and because God, in begetting him, gave Christ to live from himself, Christ lives from himself and always lives.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: if the Father lives from himself, and the Son lives from himself through the Father’s begetting, the Son is consubstantial with the Father, because the Son always lives.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: you gave me a soul, O God; but the soul is an image of life. Since the soul lives eternally, may my soul live.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: if I was made, O God the Father, according to your likeness and according to the image of the Son,

[Col. 1143A] created for life through the ages, because the Son has known me.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: I loved the world because you had made the world. I was held by the world while the world begrudged your own; now I hate the world, because I have now received the Spirit.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: help the fallen, Lord; help the penitent. For, by your divine and holy judgment, that I have sinned is a mystery.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: I know, Lord, your command; I know the return written in my soul. I hasten, if you command, to return, O God, Savior of us.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: for a long time I struggle, for a long time I resist my enemy; but flesh is still in me,

[Col. 1143B] in which the devil, defeated, gave you a great triumph and gave us a bulwark of faith.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: “To will is present with me” (Rom. 7:18), to leave world and earth; but willing without your aid is a feeble feather. Give wings of faith, that I may fly upward to God.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: now I seek the gates of the Spirit, which the Spirit opens, bearing witness concerning Christ and teaching what the world is.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ: Father, ever begotten, who make God manifest, give the keys of heaven, and conquer the devil within me, that I may rest in the seat of light, saved by your grace.

### Hymn III

God, Lord, Holy Spirit: O blessed Trinity.

Father, Son, Paraclete: O blessed Trinity.

Giver, minister, distributor: O blessed Trinity.

Spirit of workings, Spirit of ministries, Spirit of graces: O blessed Trinity.

One principle, and another with another, and always another with another: O blessed Trinity.

The substance from which the Father is, the substance which the Son himself is, and the substance which the Spirit is—but the same substance threefold: O blessed Trinity.

> Note [Col. 1143D] (1): Read “threefold” cautiously, that is, “in three”; otherwise it is certain that substance or nature is not counted, but is one—more simple than one in number.

The Father perfect; the Son perfect from the perfect Father; the perfect Holy Spirit from the perfect Son: O blessed Trinity.

Fountain, stream, irrigation: O blessed Trinity.

Threefold in the three, but one activity: O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1143D] Existence, life, knowledge: O blessed Trinity.

Love, grace, communion: O blessed Trinity.

Love is God, grace Christ, communion the Holy Spirit: O blessed Trinity.

If there is love, there is grace; if there are love and grace, there is communion. Therefore all are in each, and one in the three: O blessed Trinity.

Hence the Apostle Paul: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit [be] with you” (2 Cor. 13:13). O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1144A] Unbegotten, only-begotten—that is, proceeding and begotten: O blessed Trinity.

Begetter, begotten, regenerator: O blessed Trinity.

True light, true light from light, true illumination: O blessed Trinity.

Rest, progression, return: O blessed Trinity.

Invisible invisibly, visible invisibly, invisible visibly: O blessed Trinity.

All power, all action, all knowledge: O blessed Trinity.

Impassible impassibly, passible impassibly, impassible passibly: O blessed Trinity.

Seed, tree, fruit: O blessed Trinity.

From one all things, through one all things, in one all things: O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1144B] One simple one; one and only one; only and always one. Another one; from one, one—the same one; and the one uniter of all things, the power of the one, working one thing, that all things may come to be: O blessed Trinity.

From eternity, unbegotten; from eternity, begotten; begotten, that all things may be eternal: O blessed Trinity.

You command creation; you create; you re-create what has been created: O blessed Trinity.

You, Father, are substance for all things; you, Son, their life; you, Spirit, their salvation: O blessed Trinity.

Substance itself is life; life itself, which is, is eternal salvation. Therefore Father and Son and Holy Spirit are: O blessed Trinity.

You grant being to all things; you grant the Son form; you grant the Spirit reformation: O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1144C] You are Father, O God, of the infinite and the finite: O blessed Trinity.

You, O Son, because you are life, are infinite; because you call life back from the dead, you are finite; you too are Father of the infinite and the finite: O blessed Trinity.

You also, Holy Spirit, because you are salvation, are finite; and because you preserve the definition of what is infinite, you are Father of the infinite and the finite: O blessed Trinity.

Therefore, if unity is Father in three, and every fatherhood is from you, O God: both one God and every fatherhood, O blessed Trinity.

You, God, created the *Logos*—and hence God became Father; and because the *Logos* was created by you, and because you yourself are in him, the *Logos* became God. You anointed these two with the Holy Spirit. Therefore in three you have become simple and one: Spirit, *Logos*, God. O blessed Trinity.

> Note [Col. 1144D] (1): Read cautiously: Victorinus is accustomed to use “create” and “make” in place of “beget” and “bring forth.”

[Col. 1144D] First being (*on*), second being, third being, and the simple is three: O blessed Trinity.

Every *on* is substance; *on* is formed substance. Formed substance is known either to itself alone, or to others, or to itself and others: O blessed Trinity.

Substance is God, form the Son, cognition the Spirit: O blessed Trinity.

You are the first *on*, the true *on*, God; therefore you are all and whole substance: O blessed Trinity.

The second *on*, Christ, is every form. But universal substance, when it is universal, is formed substance; therefore, since he is form, Christ too is God: O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1145A] The third *on* is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the manifestation of all existence. But manifestation never manifests except what is known; and in divine things, knowing is the same as possessing. For knowledge itself is the same substance. Therefore the Holy Spirit possesses God and possesses Christ, whom he manifests: O blessed Trinity.

You are God, immeasurable, infinite, invisible—but immeasurable, infinite, and invisible to others; measured, finite, and visible to yourself. Hence you have form in yourself, and therefore *Logos*. You are the same, because *Logos* is form; and because form is knowledge to you, and knowledge is the Holy Spirit: therefore you are God and *Logos* and Holy Spirit. O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1145B] You, Son, are visible, for you are the universal form and the form of all things. For when you give life to all things, form comes from life. Form, however, is always in substance, and every form is knowledge. Therefore in substance you are God, in form *Logos*, in knowledge Holy Spirit: O blessed Trinity.

You too, Holy Spirit, are knowledge; but every knowledge is knowledge of form and substance. Therefore you know God and possess God’s form. Hence you are God and Son and Holy Spirit: O blessed Trinity.

You are being, God; Christ is the being of Spirit; the Paraclete Spirit is the manifestation of what is: O blessed Trinity.

Hence the Father sent Christ; Christ sent the Paraclete, so that Christ might appear through the Paraclete and the Father through Christ: O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1145C] God is substance, secret and hidden; you are God, form secret and hidden; God is knowledge, secret and hidden. Hence you are God, before being (*pro on*) of these beings (*tōn ontōn*): O blessed Trinity.

> Note [Col. 1145D] (1): Perhaps *proon* here and below.

The *Logos* is now substance made public and appearing; and because public and appearing, and because you are the Father’s form, you are substance to yourself. Therefore the Father is in you, because the Father is substance. But the substance is the same, for there is no other substance. Therefore, if the appearing *Logos* is form, and form itself is substance; and if appearing form and appearing substance are knowledge: you yourself are *Logos*, God, and Holy Spirit. O blessed Trinity.

Every knowledge is cognition, every cognition is substance, and cognition itself is form. Therefore you are the Holy Spirit, form made public and substance appearing, but substance that saves and regenerates, not substance that remains and begets: O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1146A] Therefore God, *Logos*, and Spirit are one substance, remaining in the three and existing threefold in all three. This is also form and cognition. Thus every simple singularity is made threefold: O blessed Trinity.

You, unknowable God, are incomprehensible God; yet you are God of the unknowable and incomprehensible, as though a certain form without form. Hence, when you are called *on* with *on*, you are rather deficiency and rest. Hence the form of knowledge is the knowledge of one who has ceased: O blessed Trinity.

You, *Logos*, since you are form, are the Father’s form; therefore you are also the Father’s image. And because you are the Father’s form, form and substance itself are yours; and because form and substance are the same, the Father is in you and you in the Father.

[Col. 1146B] Likewise, because you are form, knowledge is there; therefore substance is known to you, and thereby the Father is known. Since you are in his bosom, begotten from him, you therefore are true being, *ek tou ontos to on*—being from being. But every being is always in three: O blessed Trinity.

You, Holy Spirit, are connection. Connection is whatever connects two, so that, while you connect all things, you first connect two and are yourself the third comprehending of the two; and that comprehending is not at all distant from the one, when you make two one: O blessed Trinity.

Therefore three are one, and therefore threefold; therefore three times three are one: O blessed Trinity.

Hence the supreme Father sends the *Logos*; being sent, he creates and administers all things, bearing flesh together with the holy cross for our salvation; returning victorious to the Father, he sent another to exist for our salvation: O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1146C] Christ is always with God in respect of substance; for life always is. But since life is action, he begins in order to act: this is that Christ was born. Yet God and Christ act from eternity; therefore God-Christ was born from eternity: O blessed Trinity.

He who ascended into the heavens is Christ; he who descended from the heavens is the same. Therefore Christ is not from a human being, but extends as far as humanity: O blessed Trinity.

This is our God; this is the one God, this the one and only God: O blessed Trinity.
