We all pray to him, and pray to the one—Father and Son and Holy Spirit: O blessed Trinity.

Grant pardon for sins, bestow eternal life, give peace and glory: O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1146D] Deliver us, save us, justify us: O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 1145D]

## Victorinus, Two Books on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians (C, S)

### Book One

[Col. 1145D] The Epistle to the Galatians is said to have been sent by the Apostle from the city of Ephesus. For this reason some place it before the Epistle, and arrange this one after it.

The summary of this Epistle is as follows: the Galatians err because they add Judaism to the gospel of faith which is in Christ, observing in a bodily understanding the Sabbath,

[Col. 1146D] circumcision, and likewise the other works which they had received from the Law. Moved by these matters, Paul writes this Epistle, wishing to correct them and call them back from Judaism, so that they may keep faith in Christ alone and have from Christ the hope of salvation and of his promises—namely, that no one is saved from works of the Law.

Therefore, in order to refute the things which they add, he wishes to confirm his gospel. In order to give authority to his gospel, he begins by saying that he is an apostle not from human beings nor through a human being. By these divisions: that, though a Jew—and a zealous Jew—he received the gospel by revelation; that after three years he came to Jerusalem to Peter; that he was with him for fifteen days; that after fourteen years he returned to Jerusalem—by all these points he shows that he learned nothing from them, whether because of his brief presence or his long absence.

Having therefore established the authority that he received the gospel from God, our Lord Jesus Christ, he adds the actual precepts: namely, that the bodily understanding of Judaism must not be joined to it. He says that he formerly showed and did this, even when he acted against Peter. Then he pursues this very point,

[Col. 1147B] maintaining that the gospel which he taught is one, and that those who add the precepts and observance of Judaism go far astray. How he treats these matters we shall divide in their proper place. Meanwhile, let us return to the beginning of the Epistle.

> Note [Col. 1147D] (1): Thus the manuscripts, without the conjunction “and,” although Paul in the text says, “through Jesus Christ and God the Father.”

## Chapter I
VERS. 1.—Paul, an apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead; and all the brethren who are with me, to the churches of Galatia. The order of the sentence at the beginning is this: “Paul, an apostle, and all the brethren who are with me, to the churches of Galatia.” Here the apostle commends himself as one sent not from men nor through a man, but through the Lord Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead; showing who writes, with whom, and to whom. And whereas Paul the apostle customarily identifies only himself in writing to the Romans and Corinthians [Col. 1147C], in order to burden the Galatians and mark them as being in grave error, he joined to himself also all the brethren who were with him, so that they too might be writing to them, thereby making them ashamed that they think against all the rest.

“Not from men nor through a man,” in order to give greater force to his instructions and to the Gospel which he proclaims. For, intending to correct the Galatians, he says that he is an apostle neither from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. Therefore, I am to be believed and trusted; and the Gospel which I set forth is true, since it is through Jesus Christ and God the Father. “An apostle,” then, he says, “not from men nor through men,” because not through the apostles—of whom he says both that he was with them only a few days and that they gave him the right hand—therefore he learned nothing from them [Col. 1147D].

Nor through a man, or through some prophet, as is ambiguous [Note: [Col. 1147D] (2) Thus the manuscripts read.]; nor through Christ as man, but through Christ who is in man; for Christ is both God and man. “Not from men nor through a man.” When he says “from men,” he seems to signify Matthias, who learned from men; for this man was put in the place of the traitor, and therefore learned from men. But when he says “nor through a man,” he means that he was not sent or taught by a man, but through Jesus Christ, namely God. Thus in saying “not from men,” he alludes to the apostles; because the apostle Paul, as he has shown, learned nothing from any apostle who had been with Christ [Col. 1148A].

Again, lest, since he learned through Christ, he should seem to deny—as some blasphemous heretic does—that Christ was a man, he adds “not through a man,” and then explains what this means by saying, “but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.” Since he denied that it was through a man, and then added “through Christ,” it may be understood as through Christ God. But because he added “through God the Father,” some say that Christ is scarcely called God by Paul. Yet we have shown in many places that Paul too calls him God. Here also it may be so understood: for if it is said “not through a man,” and then added “but through Christ,” it must be understood that Christ too is God.

Nevertheless, because God does what he does through Christ, as we have shown in many places [Col. 1148B], it is said, “through Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.” So that no one might say, “How did you learn through Christ, when you did not follow Christ and Christ died?” he added that God raised Christ from the dead. Therefore Christ taught me, he who was raised from the dead; but he was raised by the power of God the Father. What this mystery of the Son raised from the dead is, we have often explained; and we shall often speak of it when occasion arises.

“And all the brethren who are with me”: Paul the apostle has already shown above the order of this sense: “Paul, an apostle, and all the brethren who are with me.” What follows? “The churches of Galatia.”

VERS. 3, 4, 5.—Keeping the customary formula by which we add either a greeting or something of that sort: “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself” [Note: [Col. 1148D] (1) The Vulgate has: “who gave himself.”] “for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil age” [Note: [Col. 1148D] (2) Vulgate: “rescue us from this present wicked age.”], “according to the will of God and our Father, to whom be glory unto ages of ages.”

Let us remember what the Apostle is doing in this Epistle: he reproves the Galatians and wishes to correct them, so that they may have faith in Christ and expect from him alone the hope of salvation, the hope of eternity, and the remission of sins; and, altogether, that they may not think the works of the Law, Sabbaths, or circumcision profit them. Therefore, at the outset he prays for them peace and grace from God; and then he adds “from Christ,” because in Christ are all our good things. And he proves that all things are in Christ and through Christ when he says, “who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil age.”

Therefore by his benefit, by his grace, indeed from God the Father but through his passion [Col. 1148D], we are delivered from the present malignant age; and we are delivered through Christ, but by the power of God—God, namely, to whom is glory throughout all eternity. If, therefore, God is eternal, his glory too is eternal. And since Christ, in accordance with God’s will, performed the mystery and gave himself for our sins in order to deliver us all, deliverance is from God’s will through Christ. But if it is through Christ, nothing further is to be sought; and vain are the things which the Galatians add—namely Judaism, works of the Law, Sabbath observance, and circumcision.

VERS. 6.—“I marvel that you are so quickly being transferred” [Col. 1149A] “from him who called you into grace” [Note: [Col. 1149D] (1) The Vulgate gives this verse as: “I marvel that . . . you are being transferred from him who called you into the grace of Christ.”] “to another gospel.” Since the Gospel proclaimed by the apostle Paul is certain—namely, that Christ, the Son of God, is the power of God for salvation [Note: [Col. 1149D] (2) Thus the manuscripts, without a verb.] to all who believe, whether Greeks or Jews—and nothing besides; but that the whole hope of salvation and of God’s grace toward us is in faith concerning Christ: that we believe him to be the Son of God, that he suffered for us, that he rose again, and that we too shall thereafter rise with remission of sins—this is the true Gospel proclaimed by Paul.

If anyone adds anything else—namely Judaism, circumcision, Sabbath observance, and the rest—such a person sins and is alien from the truth. Therefore, since the Galatians supposed that Judaism ought to be added to the Apostle’s Gospel, he says, “I marvel that you are so quickly being transferred” [Col. 1149B]. For first, it is sinful to be transferred quickly; for there is no reason when something is transferred quickly. Then there is the fact that it is transferred, since it is transferred from someone. Let us see, therefore, from whom: “from him,” he says, “who called you into grace.” For Christ, who suffered for us all, called us into grace, if we believe in him. For it is no great matter to attain his grace, provided only that we follow him in faith, believing that he bestowed these things through his mystery—and that freely, without toil and without great works.

Since this has been bestowed upon us by him, it is a great cause for wonder that they should so quickly be transferred from him, preferring to be transferred to another gospel by associating the teaching of Judaism with it. Yet the Gospel is one, and one alone: to believe that Christ is the Son of God; that Christ, by his passion, his coming in the flesh [Col. 1149C], his resurrection, and his passion, has dissolved all sins, conquered death, and destroyed all corruption. This alone is the Gospel. Therefore he adds:

VERS. 7.—“Which is not another.” For that alone is what we said above; there is no other. Nor is salvation to be earned through works, nor is Sabbath observance or circumcision the Gospel—that is, our salvation.

“Except that there are some who trouble you and wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ.” He says, therefore, that the activity of certain persons is not from truth, when they wish to trouble you and, as though you were insufficiently instructed, teach you. They pervert the Gospel of Christ, whereas the Gospel is Christ’s alone. But that which comes from works or circumcision is not Christ’s. For, understood carnally [Col. 1149D], those things are not Christ’s; but if they are understood spiritually [Note: [Col. 1149D] (3) Vulgate: “But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach...”]—so that circumcision is that of the heart, and all things which are in the flesh are understood spiritually—then these, I say, are the Gospel of Christ.

But those who descend to works and to things carnal do not possess Christ’s Gospel. Therefore those who desire and command you to observe either Sabbath, new moons, circumcision, or the other things performed by works, do not possess Christ’s Gospel; hence they wish to turn you away from Christ’s Gospel. But when you have believed in Christ [Col. 1150A], and all hope is to be placed in Christ, they wish to trouble you by urging something else.

VERS. 8.—“But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you” [Note: [Col. 1150D] (1) Vulgate: “as.”] “besides that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema.” With sharper and more forceful language he asserts that all err if they proclaim anything besides Christ’s Gospel. If we ourselves, whom you have already believed, or even an angel—an angel indeed from heaven—should preach otherwise to you, namely otherwise than Christ’s Gospel, which we have preached, let him be anathema. For this is what he said: “besides that which we have preached to you.”

Thus, if I preach otherwise, or if an angel from heaven, he says, proclaims otherwise than we once proclaimed to you, let him be anathema; that is, as we have explained above, let him be rejected, and let him be without reward [Col. 1150B]—indeed rather, subject to punishment for his evil deed.

VERS. 9.—“As we have said before.” It may seem that he had said something of this kind in the preceding words, namely that those who preach the Gospel otherwise are to be anathema. But he said, “as we have said before,” in order to add, “and now I say again,” so that it may be understood concerning this very thing which he had just said: “As we have said before, I now again admonish you.” What? What was said above: “If anyone should preach to you besides that which you received, let him be anathema”; that is, whether I myself should previously say and proclaim the Gospel otherwise, or an angel, or any other person, let him be anathema.

He then adds a stronger reason: that he is not doing this in order to persuade men, but in order to accomplish the mystery entrusted to him. Thus he adds:

[Col. 1150C] VERS. 10.—“For am I now persuading men, or God?” For, he says, I do not do what I do in order to persuade men, but I seek to persuade before the Lord God, whom I wish to please, so that I may carry out what has been commanded. The Greek reads differently: “For now am I persuading people, or God?” (ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ τὸν θεόν;) [Note: [Col. 1150D] (2) Victorinus is not persuaded that the Greek text—as it certainly stands in the manuscript—differs from the Latin.]. That is: I do not proclaim men, nor things belonging to men, but God. For I wish to persuade not men but Christ God. Therefore I have both necessity and fear to speak what is true, and not to say now one thing and now another.

“Or do I seek to please men?” [Note: [Col. 1150D] (3) Vulgate: “or.”] I do not do things that would be for men’s advantage, in order to please men, but in order to please God by rendering obedience and fulfilling commands. Yet he adds more forcefully what he says: “If I were still pleasing men, I would not be Christ’s servant” [Col. 1150D]. For pleasing men, as is shown in many ways, is not earning the grace of God. If someone thinks that life must be conducted by works, he pleases men and does not yet merit grace. “But if I were pleasing men”: therefore, he says, if I wished to please men, I would not be Christ’s servant; that is, I would not have been redeemed by Christ.

For this is to be Christ’s servant: redeemed through his passion, delivered from the world and from the lords of the world and of the flesh, I now have Christ as Lord and am his servant. Accordingly, whoever wishes to please men [Col. 1151A] has not been redeemed by Christ and serves the lords of the world while pleasing men. But one who is redeemed from slavery into freedom becomes Christ’s servant. For this is to be Christ’s servant: to be free from worldly servitude. He is Christ’s servant who, redeemed, as we have said, knows nothing of that slavery; and this is full freedom.

VERS. 11.—“For I make known to you” [Note: [Col. 1151D] (1) Vulgate: “I make known to you, brethren.”] “the Gospel which was preached by me, that it is not according to man.” Just as he said above that he was an apostle not from men nor through a man, so now he says that it is not according to man. For the apostle announces—that is, proclaims the Gospel—which is this: he preaches Christ, the Son of God, Savior of all, through whom all things were made. And I say this not according to man, that is, not as received from man.

Or else, because that very Savior [Col. 1151B] is not merely man, as some suppose [Note: [Col. 1151D] (2) That is, he is not only a man, as certain heretics suppose.]; nor, because he was sent into a man, is he therefore man; but God, taking flesh in the mystery in order to conquer flesh—as has been said and discussed in many places—became man [Note: [Col. 1151D] (3) The words “became man” were added in the margin and afterward deleted.].

Therefore, he says, I did not preach the Gospel to you according to man. Thus I make known, brethren who are in error and are carried away toward man by thinking carnally, observing Sabbaths, circumcision, and the rest: my Gospel is not according to man—that is, it does not concern man, that is, flesh—but according to the power of the soul. For the whole mystery was performed so that we might not think in the way some think according to man, taking everything carnally. But he himself adds what he wishes to be understood by “not according to man.”

[Col. 1151C] VERS. 12.—“For I neither received it from a man, nor was I taught it” [Note: [Col. 1151D] (4) Vulgate: “For I neither received it from a man nor learned it.”], “but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.” Therefore I did not proclaim the Gospel according to man, because I did not receive it from man. If receiving from man is one thing, then “according to man” will be another; and likewise, if “I did not receive from man” is one thing, “not according to man” will be another. Hence it may be understood that “according to man” means to think bodily, since he takes this as his argument: “I did not receive it from man.”

For if a man had handed these things down to me, I would receive them according to man, so as to understand everything according to the flesh. But now what I proclaim must not be received according to man, that is, not carnally but spiritually, since this is the argument: that I did not receive it [Note: [Col. 1151D] (5) “From man” seems to require supplementation.]. For if I received it from the Spirit [Col. 1151D] and was taught by the Spirit, I ought to understand spiritually; and this will be “not according to man.” Finally, what does he add? “But it was revealed to me,” he says, “by Christ Jesus.”

What he calls “revealed” has more credibility than if it had been taught. For men teach and establish something, as it were, by arguments; but revelation is the sight of the realities themselves, and is certainly greater. Who revealed it? Jesus Christ. Those who already follow Christ ought not to receive this as something understood to have been received from man, when it was said, “Jesus Christ revealed it,” and the Galatians have already received both God and the Son of God [Col. 1152A]. The additional things which they add are from man—either from those who persuaded them, or from Moses himself, who gave the Law. Moses indeed received it from God, but they, understanding too little, think of everything carnally. Such is the extent of the evil! For Moses received this Law and believed; but the apostle says that it was revealed to him, and he explains this.

VERS. 13.—“For you have heard of my manner of life formerly in Judaism, because” [Note: [Col. 1152D] (1) Vulgate: “For.”] “beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and attacked it” [Note: [Col. 1152D] (2) Vulgate: “and attacked it.”], “and advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my own nation, being more exceedingly zealous” [Note: [Col. 1152D] (3) Manuscript 1: *dum lator*; 2: *eum lator*, though *eum* is deleted there; 3: *lator*.] “for the traditions of the fathers” [Note: [Col. 1152D] (4) The Vulgate adds: “my.”].

The sum of this narrative about himself is to teach that he did not learn from men nor through a man, but from God and Jesus Christ. This serves to ensure that the Galatians do not think otherwise, nor suppose that anything should be added to the Gospel he proclaimed to them: that faith in Christ must be embraced, that he alone gives salvation and no other; that salvation is not given through works, circumcision, or Sabbath observance; that this is the Gospel; and that they ought to receive nothing further beyond what the Galatians received.

To prove this readily, he adds, as I said, the narrative concerning himself: what he had been, how he was converted; what he did after he was converted from Judaism and began to believe in Christ [Col. 1152C]; and that he learned none of this from men. For, he says, “I did not see Peter except when already prepared and taught, nor any of the apostles.” “For first,” he says, “I was a Jew; therefore I was opposed. Nor did I learn from them, since what is said in the Gospel about Christ is contrary to them. Therefore I was a Jew, doing many things against the Church; therefore I learned nothing from the Jews. But after I was converted, and God through his grace began to reveal his Son in me, I began,” he says, “to proclaim the Gospel among the Gentiles.”

He next shows that he did not spare himself and did not come to Jerusalem, lest perhaps he had learned there from the apostles. “But I departed,” he says, “into Arabia; from there I returned to Damascus” [Note: [Col. 1152D] (5) Vulgate: “But I went away into Arabia and again returned to Damascus.”]; “then after three years I came to Jerusalem.” Behold, he is already proclaiming the Gospel and teaching Christ. Thus he did not learn these things from men, since he came to Jerusalem only after three years [Col. 1152D]. Then he saw Peter and was with him for fifteen days. When, then, did he learn from Peter, or when could he have learned? “Then,” he says, “I saw none of the apostles except James, the Lord’s brother.”

By this he clearly shows that he learned from no one, both because he was with Peter only a few days and because, in seeing James [Col. 1153A], the Lord’s brother, he more strongly established that he could not have learned from James. For Paul has the things found in the Gospel, whereas James does not have these things, as we shall teach later. He then says that he went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia; yet he was already known to all the churches and Jews as one who, though he had been a Jew, now followed and proclaimed the Gospel.

After these things he relates that he came to Jerusalem after fourteen years. From where, then, did he learn the things he proclaims? Not from men nor through a man, but through revelation. “I set before them all,” he says, “the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 1153D] (1) Vulgate: “I conferred with them the Gospel which I had preached among the Gentiles.”]. Then I myself related the Gospel even to the apostles; they did not teach me.

There also he teaches how much he did by dissimulation in order that the Gospel might prevail: namely, that he accepted a small part of Judaism out of necessity, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain; what this means we shall teach in its place [Col. 1153B]. Then he says that there is one Gospel, possessed both by Peter and himself, but Peter’s task is to proclaim it to Jews and his own to the Gentiles; that this was given to him through revelation; and that these offices were apportioned by God and our Lord Jesus Christ, for he worked in both. Peter and John, together with the apostle Paul and Barnabas, confirmed that their teaching was the same; and they agreed that these should proclaim the Gospel to the Gentiles and those to the Jews.

But he adds and recalls the greatest proof of his confidence, knowledge, revelation, and Gospel: he says that Peter acted consistently before certain persons came from James; but after they came, he changed. Paul rebuked him for this and refuted him. He had changed so as not to eat with Gentiles [Col. 1153C], and to use Jewish foods. Paul says that he rebuked this in him, since before those from James came, Peter lived with Gentiles, but afterward, fearing them as though they were James’s envoys, lived with Jews. For James proclaimed Christ with Judaism mixed in, and Paul denies that this should be done.

If, therefore, this has already been rebuked, and Peter, acting thus, has been convicted and overcome [Note: [Col. 1153D] (2) Thus the older manuscript; the other two have “separated.”] and the matter confirmed, then these Galatians too, when they have begun to do this, must be corrected and changed: namely, so that, believing through faith in Jesus Christ, they may be justified by faith and not by works of the Law.

Thus far runs the argument concerning himself. Then comes an admonition and exposition quite useful and fitting for what he wishes to do [Col. 1153D]: to correct the Galatians, lest, by following Judaism, they fail to follow the Gospel—which is one alone: to have true faith in Christ and to be justified by him, not by works of the Law. After this he provides other arguments, that justification comes from Christ, not from the Law or works. This whole passage, as I said above, runs as far as the place beginning thus: “But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves are found sinners, is Christ then a minister of sin?” and the rest.

But now let us return to the narrative concerning his own person, for which we have said [Col. 1154A] why it was undertaken. “You have heard,” he says, “of my manner of life formerly in Judaism.” Lest he seem to be telling a new thing about himself, he says, “You have heard of my life”; for this is what he meant by “manner of life.” You know the course of my life, the manner in which I lived when I was in Judaism, and how I acted: “because beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God.”

“I was not only,” he says, “a Jew and a follower of the Law, but I persecuted and attacked the Church. Therefore, being such a person as to persecute the Church, I cannot now, after conversion from Judaism, persecute the Church which I persecuted. I cannot, I say, approve a course in which I both follow Judaism and persecute the Church. At the same time, as I said above, in Judaism I understood and received nothing that pertained to the Church [Col. 1154B]. Therefore I was not taught by men. I attacked the Church; ‘I attacked it’ is too little. What did he add? ‘And I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my own nation, more exceedingly’: when I had companions, I surpassed them all alike in zeal and profession in Judaism; and I acted more abundantly—that is, I was stronger and more vehement in defending Judaism—being a zealot for ancestral traditions, so that I might expound and hand down the traditions of the fathers, that is, the teachings of Judaism and of the Law, in the same manner.

A zealot, that is, an imitator, and one engaged, as it were, in a certain contest: one who wished to be the same as my fathers, or as the traditions themselves had been.

VERS. 15.—Since this, then, was his life, from where came such a conversion? He adds: “But when it pleased him who” [Col. 1154C] “set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles.” The order is: “But when it pleased God to reveal his Son in me.” What does “it pleased God to reveal his Son in me” mean? It means that I might know Christ; for first comes knowing him, then proclaiming him.

Thus, “he who,” he says, “set me apart from my mother’s womb,” that is, caused me to be born. Likewise, “he called me through his grace,” that is, calling me forth so that I might come to his grace and know God. For no one knows God unless called. Therefore he called me, and it pleased him to reveal his Son in me, so that I, he says, might know him, and then might proclaim him among the Gentiles.

After this pleased him, what followed? “Immediately I did not yield” [Col. 1154D] “to flesh and blood.” Therefore, he says, what I proclaim was revealed to me. And in every respect I labored carnally. For this is not labor. If he announces divine things and those which contain God’s grace, there is no labor of the mind; rather, it is the labor of flesh and blood—that is, traveling about, bearing the hardship of journeying, traversing provinces and nations [Note: [Col. 1154D] (1) Vulgate: “Immediately I did not confer,” etc.].

“But I did not yield,” he says, “to flesh and blood.” For flesh and blood are the entire outward human being. “Nor did I come to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me” [Note: [Col. 1154D] (2) Vulgate: “to those who were apostles before me,” etc.]. For it might have seemed that he learned from men or through men if he went to Jerusalem and lived long with elders [Col. 1155A] and predecessors. “No,” he says, “I did not go to the apostles who were my predecessors; I did not learn from them. But I went away into Arabia and again returned to Damascus.”

This is what he received by revelation from God: that he should proclaim the Gospel among the Gentiles. “I went away,” he says, “into Arabia.” What a long journey! And when he returns to Damascus, how different a place! “Then, after three years, I came to Jerusalem to visit Peter.” Therefore he had already proclaimed the Gospel among the Gentiles for three years. What else could it be but what he had received from God: that he should proclaim Christ, revealed to him, among the Gentiles? “After three years,” he says, “I came to Jerusalem.” Then he adds the reason: “to visit Peter.”

For if the foundation of the Church was laid in Peter, as was said in the Gospel, Paul, to whom all things had been revealed, knew that he ought to visit Peter—as one to whom so great authority had been given by Christ—not in order to learn something from him [Note: [Col. 1155C] (1) A distinguished passage supporting Peter’s authority, which even the wisest teachers in the Church ought especially to revere.]. Finally, what does he add? “And I remained with him fifteen days.” Therefore I remained only that long. Could I, in so few days and in so brief a time, have learned from Peter this great knowledge of God?

“But I saw no other of the apostles except James, the Lord’s brother.” In this also he adds a great teaching and with great ingenuity. First, he said, “I saw no other of the apostles.” For the Symmachians make James an apostle, as though he were a twelfth [Note: [Col. 1155C] (2) This passage of Victorinus concerning the Symmachian heretics is especially noteworthy; it should be added to the few ancient testimonies which Fabricius collected in his scholia on Philastrius, chapter 63, for transmitting knowledge of this heresy.]. They are followed by those who add the observance of Judaism to our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1155C] (3) That James permitted Christians converted from Judaism, at least in part, to observe Mosaic rites is evident from Acts 21:20, where Paul, brought before James and the elders residing in Jerusalem, [Col. 1155D] heard them say: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and all are zealots for the Law.” Nevertheless, in the apostolic council James had followed Peter’s judgment, Acts 15:13, namely that those coming to Christ from the Gentiles should not be subjected to the yoke of the Mosaic Law.].

Although they also confess Jesus Christ, they say that he himself is Adam and is the universal soul, and other blasphemies of this kind. Therefore Paul here denied that James was an apostle [Col. 1155C] [Note: [Col. 1155D] (4) A question long debated among ecclesiastical writers is whether James, the first bishop of Jerusalem and called the Lord’s brother, belonged to the college of the twelve apostles. This question in turn depends on another controversy: whether there were three Jameses or only two. Among others, Florentinius discussed this learnedly in his dissertation on Jerome’s Martyrology, in which he argues that there were three Jameses. Our Victorinus certainly excludes James, bishop of Jerusalem, from the number of apostles and consequently admits three Jameses; for two Jameses are explicitly numbered among the apostles in Acts 1:13.], by saying, “I saw no other of the apostles,” because he said he had seen no other apostle except James. And the reason for adding “the Lord’s brother” is that he was considered his brother according to the flesh. But when he called him “brother” [Col. 1156A], he denied that he was an apostle.

Yet he had to be visited honorably. But he could not learn anything from James either, since James thinks differently. Nor from Peter, both because he stayed with Peter only a few days and because James is not an apostle and is in a heresy [Note: [Col. 1156B] (1) Let no one here take offense without consideration. Victorinus does not call it “heresy” here in an infamous sense, but in a grammatical and natural sense. For in the apostolic council, Acts 15:5, some arose from the sect (*haeresis*) of the Pharisees who had believed, saying that it was necessary to circumcise and to command observance of the Law of Moses.].

He also added James. “I saw,” therefore, “by name what James treats and proclaims in the Gospel; and yet, because this blasphemy is known to me” [Note: [Col. 1156B] (2) The Acts of the Apostles, chapter 15, report that Peter condemned in the apostolic council the opinion that Mosaic rites were to be retained in Christian profession, and that James was the first of all to assent to that decree. Consequently the opinion became blasphemous—namely, if anyone compelled Gentiles coming to baptism to obey Moses. But James was far removed from blasphemy, since, by a certain economy, he allowed only converted Jews to retain their ancestral rites. Does not Jerome also report that the church at Alexandria was Judaizing at its beginning [Col. 1156C], *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 8? And what of Paul himself, who sometimes yielded to necessity—for example, when he circumcised Timothy?], “it has been rejected by me, just as it must be rejected by you, O Galatians. For you cannot say: ‘You deny James and therefore reject what we follow, because you did not see James.’ Therefore he added, ‘I saw James also.’ Nor is there error: the James whom he calls the Lord’s brother is the author of your opinion. Thus he had no influence upon me. Though I did not follow him, I knew his opinion. Therefore, since nothing is unknown to me, and he too could not persuade me, you follow him in vain” [Col. 1156B; Note: [Col. 1156C] (3) This passage stands thus in the older Ottobonian manuscript, from which the other two Victorinus manuscripts were derived. Yet that older manuscript was sometimes subjected to the hand of a corrector, who sometimes wrote in the margins—read these cautiously—and sometimes, although rarely, altered the text itself, deleting ancient portions, all of which, however, remain legible beneath erasure, and inserting different readings in the margin. The two other manuscripts admitted these corrections into their text, so that the one manuscript sometimes supplies the genuine and uninterpolated text, which I have always taken care to reproduce. Yet do not suppose that an interpolation was made in the Vatican Library: for this Ottobonian manuscript was brought into the pontifical library only in 1749 through the favor of Benedict XIV; moreover, the hand of the interpolator is so much older than that date that it seems to me to belong to the beginning of the fifteenth century. Therefore, the person who interpolated the manuscript wrote thus in the margin at this point: “Paul therefore does not here assert that James is an apostle by saying, ‘I saw no other apostle except James.’ Why, then, did he add ‘the Lord’s brother’? Because he was considered his brother; but he had to be visited honorably. Nor could he learn anything from James, since James thinks differently. Nor from Peter, both because he remained with Peter only a few days and because James the apostle holds the view that legal observances should be kept; this view has been rejected by me and must be rejected by you, O Galatians. For you cannot say: ‘You reject what we follow because you did not see James.’ Therefore he added: ‘I saw James too, the Lord’s brother, the author of your opinion.’ Clearly, he had so little influence upon me that I did not follow him, though I knew his opinion. Therefore, since nothing is unknown to me, and he could not persuade me, you follow him in vain.”].

VERS. 20.—“But as to what I write to you, behold, before God” [Col. 1157A], “I do not lie.” Credence had to be given even by an oath. For to those who had already departed from faith he says: “I do not lie in what I write to you; behold, before God I profess that I recount all things as they happened.”

VERS. 21.—“Then I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia,” that is, to proclaim the Gospel among the Gentiles.

VERS. 22.—“But I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea which are” [Note: [Col. 1157D] (1) Vulgate: “were.”] “in Christ.” That is, the Gospel which I proclaimed was already known to almost all the churches of Judea—Judea, however, which is in Christ, not in the Judaism of the Jews. There are many churches in Christ, and to them all the Gospel concerning Christ was known. Yet I myself was unknown by face. What, then, does he show by all this? That he had already persuaded all men of his Gospel, even while absent.

[Col. 1157B] VERS. 23.—“They only heard that he who” [Note: [Col. 1157D] (2) Vulgate: “But they had only heard: ‘He who,’ etc.”] “formerly persecuted us now proclaims the faith.” He says that this was a marvel to all, as indeed it ought to be marvelous. “All heard,” he says, “that I, who had been a Jew, who formerly persecuted Christians and churches, was now proclaiming the faith”—that is, so that all might have faith in Christ, the faith which previously I had denied and formerly attacked. Thus it was a marvel that he now proclaimed the faith which formerly he had attacked, the very thing he himself had done.

VERS. 24.—“And in me,” he says, “they magnified” [Note: [Col. 1157D] (3) Vulgate: “glorified.”] “the Lord.” For all now grasped the power of God and called God great because I had been converted, and because I who had been an attacker was now a preacher. Thus they magnified [Col. 1157C] God in me—that is, they called him great, because, with my mind suddenly changed, I preached the Lord Christ, whom I had previously attacked.

For what could be more magnificent than for the mind to be overcome, to receive the contrary faith, and to preach the faith which one had previously attacked? But if this is so, then you too ought to follow nothing other than that faith of Christ which he proclaims to you.

CHAPTER IV.

VERS. 1.—Then, after fourteen years, I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also with me. For once before, after three years; now, after fourteen years, I went up again, he says. Therefore, the Gospel proclaimed by me to the Gentiles I received by revelation; I did not learn it from men or through a man. With Barnabas, and taking Titus. He has these, certainly, as witnesses, through whom he proves that his Gospel was given him by revelation: for Barnabas, he says, went up with me [Col. 1157D]; he also took Titus, whose faith and Gospel were approved by all.

VERS. 2.—But I went up according to revelation, and set before them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles [Note: Col. 1157D (4): Vulgate: “and conferred with them concerning the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles.”]. By weighty arguments he endeavors to prove that the Gospel given him by revelation, which he preached among the Gentiles, was from God. “For I went up,” he says, “to Jerusalem according to revelation,” so that I might also teach all—even the Jews themselves [Col. 1158A]. “I set before,” he says, “all the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles.” From the fact that no one contradicted or resisted, it is understood that this Gospel is true and one: “for that which I preach,” he says, “among the Gentiles, I set before them in Jerusalem.” But the people might have been unaware. What did he add? “But privately to those who seemed to be pillars” [Note: Col. 1158D (1): Vulgate: “privately to those who seemed to be something.”]. That is, to those through whom the commands of God and the Gospel were handed down, namely the apostles and the rest. “To these,” he says, “I privately set before them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles,” so that, if there were anything which they taught differently, they might correct it; or if I taught anything differently, they might amend it.

This, then, was the reason why I went up to Jerusalem; and for this reason it was revealed to me that I should go up: so that the good character of the Gospel might more readily be recognized, both mine among the Gentiles and theirs among the Jews. But his showing it to them privately was so that they might remove the Jews from the midst and themselves, who knew the mysteries, communicate them among themselves [Col. 1158B]. Since all of them had one judgment and one Gospel, what is he seeking to persuade them of? That nothing new ought to be added, and nothing joined to it. Hence the Galatians now sin in following Judaism and the observance either of circumcision, or of the Sabbath, or of other matters: “lest perhaps I should run, or had run, in vain.” That is, lest I should not preach the Gospel completely. For if I have proclaimed anything deficiently, I have run in vain, or am even now running in vain. For if circumcision, Sabbath-observance, and the other things are beneficial, salvation will not be from the grace of Christ, and one runs in vain.

VERS. 3.—But not even Titus, who was with me, though a Greek [Col. 1158C; Note: Col. 1158D (2): Vulgate: “though he was a Gentile”], was compelled to be circumcised. He explains that nothing at all was accomplished by those who are false apostles—that is, by those who think that to Paul’s Gospel, namely the proclamation concerning Christ, the Son of God, through whom come faith and certain salvation, must be added circumcision, Sabbath-observance, and the rest. These things, he says, were of no force; nor was Titus persuaded—who, he says, was certainly a Greek, that is, a pagan—to be compelled to be circumcised. Accordingly, he was not persuaded, nor indeed did they dare to compel him. Thus the apostle obtained the agreement of all who were at Jerusalem concerning the Gospel. Therefore the Galatians sin, who think that this novelty must be added.

VERS. 4–5.—But because of the false brethren secretly brought in [Note: Col. 1158D (3): Vulgate: “secretly introduced”], who slipped in [Note: Col. 1158D (4): Vulgate: “slipped in to spy out … in Christ Jesus”] to listen in on our liberty [Col. 1158D], which we have in Christ, in order to reduce us to slavery, we yielded in submission for a time.

Some read this thus: “Nor did we yield in submission even for an hour” [Note: Col. 1158D (5): Thus in the common edition of Paul, which gives the text: “To whom we did not yield in submission even for an hour.”]. In that reading the sense is complete with the preceding statement: neither was Titus, a Greek, compelled to be circumcised, nor did we yield in submission even for an hour—that is, so as to give way in any respect.

Yet since in very many Latin and Greek manuscripts [Note: Col. 1159D (1): Wetstein presents this sort of patristically collected variation in his critical scholia on this passage. See also Sabatier.] the reading is, “we yielded in submission for a time,” that is, we bore what seemed to them necessary to do, though not so as to follow it forever, there are many reasons to prove that this reading should be retained. First, because he truly did yield: for he also circumcised Timothy on account of the Jews, as he says in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. XVI, 3). The apostle ought not therefore to have lied. Next, no one would say “not even for an hour” if it were necessary to deny that it happened at all. And surely, if he resisted Peter, what does “we did not yield even for an hour” mean here? Likewise, if it was said above, “not even Titus, who was with me, though a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised,” then it was not in every case, nor always, nor extensively. Finally, this was because of the brethren brought in, who were mixing Judaism [Col. 1159B] with Christianity.

And on this account, because of the Jews, he certainly made known his usual policy: that he would sometimes yield even in matters which are true. For this is the meaning of that saying, “I became a Jew in order that I might gain the Jews,” and the like. Therefore now, because of the false brethren secretly brought in—for there were many false apostles, whom he calls false brethren—some began to add things, to insinuate themselves by their persuasions, and to spy upon the liberty of apostolic teaching; that is, they wished to gain entrance among us. Were they nevertheless true apostles of Christ? Or were they testing our liberty which we have in Christ?

When, therefore, we saw their purpose, namely to bring us into slavery, we indeed yielded in submission for a time—that is, for a brief period, so as to do certain things. We must understand that this is permitted not to just anyone, but to one perfected and strengthened in faith: for Christ’s sake, he may do certain things outside the rule, provided that what he does benefits the law—that is, so that souls may be set free [Col. 1159C]. We shall show from many places, and from Paul’s own conduct, that he yields to a rule which is not the true rule, and then corrects and brings many people to the true rule.

Thus too he permits second marriages, marriage itself [Note: Col. 1159D (2): In the margin of the older manuscript is written: “read cautiously.”], and foods—even all foods. Though he forbids food sacrificed to idols, he nevertheless permits it where there is confidence and assured faith. For when Christ is in the mind, and Christ is nourished in us through faith, there is no danger in yielding for a time to a rule which is not true—provided only that we do this in order that, through this initial association itself, we may be able to bring them to the true rule.

Accordingly he adds: “We yielded in submission, but for a time, that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you” [Col. 1159D]—you who were instructed by us. O Galatians, we did not yield so that you also might do so, but that they might be satisfied and brought to the true rule, and that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you.

VERS. 6.—But from those who seem to be something—what they formerly were is nothing to me; God does not accept a man’s face [Note: Col. 1159D (3): Vulgate: “God does not accept the person of a man,” etc.]—from these [Col. 1160A], as though from those who seem to be something, or from false apostles who had proceeded from them [Note: Col. 1160D (1): The manuscripts read *pseudoapostolis*, “false apostles”; but the final *s* seems erased in the older manuscript.], something nevertheless might be accomplished—that is, they might be changed and now follow the Gospel.

Whoever, then, now seems to be something, and has arisen from such people—so that they were formerly such, but are now sound (for this is what it is “to be something”)—what they formerly were, that is, at some time in the past, “is nothing to me,” he says. For it is enough for me what he is now; I do not care what he was formerly. And he adds the reason: for God does not accept a man’s face, but his mind and faith. Whether Greek, whether Jew, whether he was formerly anything at all—God does not accept that, but what he is now, and whether he has received the faith and the Gospel. For God does not accept a person to the prejudice of truth.

“Nor did those who were said to be pillars add anything to me.” This, then, is what he says: “For those who are thought to be something [Col. 1160B; Note: Col. 1160D (2): Vulgate: ‘those who seemed to be something’] contributed nothing to me.” That is, they taught me nothing and added nothing, but approved my Gospel. Therefore nothing ought to have been added by you to the Gospel which I proclaimed to you.

VERS. 7, 8, 9.—But, on the contrary [Note: Col. 1160D (3): Vulgate: “But on the contrary, when they saw that,” etc.], when they saw that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me, as that of the circumcision to Peter; for he who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked in me [Note: Col. 1160D (4): Vulgate: “worked also in me among the Gentiles”] among the Gentiles; and when they recognized the grace given to me [Note: Col. 1160D (5): Vulgate: “and when they recognized the grace,” etc.], Peter and John [Note: Col. 1160D (6): James must be added. The Vulgate has: “James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave right hands to me.”], who seemed to be pillars, gave their right hands.

The order is this: those eminent men, Peter, John, and James, who seemed to be pillars, gave me their right hands; that is, they offered their agreement, when they saw that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me—that is, entrusted among the Gentiles in the same way as the Gospel of the circumcision had been entrusted to Peter, so that he might proclaim the Gospel among the Jews [Col. 1160C].

Why it was entrusted to me as to them is added: “For he who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked in me among the Gentiles.” That is, one God, the same God himself, worked so that Peter should proclaim the Gospel to the Jews and I should proclaim it to the Gentiles. When the grace given to me was recognized—namely, that I too had become an apostle among the Gentiles in the same manner by God’s grace—Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars, that is, who supported the Church as pillars support roofs and other structures, were compelled to give me their right hands. These men, so great and of such standing, joined me in friendship, peace, and steadfastness, and declared that they possessed one Gospel.

You Galatians, therefore, sin. You follow neither my Gospel nor that of Peter, James, and John, who are pillars of the Church, while you add things which no one has approved. For throughout this entire narrative he is arguing that the Galatians sin by adding to faith in Christ observance of the Jewish law, the Sabbath, and circumcision.

“And to Barnabas, in fellowship” [Col. 1161A]. They gave the right hands of fellowship not to me alone, but also to Barnabas, who was my companion. He added this in order that it might not seem that the trust had been given to himself alone. But Paul’s Gospel is shown to have been approved if Barnabas’s too was approved, since Barnabas was Paul’s companion. He received fellowship through the right hands of those who exercised the apostleship at Jerusalem and proclaimed the Gospel to the Jews. He proves that there is one true Gospel among all, and that the Galatians are in error.

“So that we should preach among the Gentiles [Note: Col. 1161D (1): Vulgate: ‘that we among the Gentiles, but they unto the circumcision’], but they among the circumcision.” For this purpose they gave right hands, giving their agreement concerning the Gospel to both me and Barnabas: that we should preach among the Gentiles, while they should preach the Gospel to the Jews—that is, among the circumcision.

VERS. 10.—Only that we should remember the poor [Note: Col. 1161D (2): Vulgate: “only that [we should remember] the poor,” etc.]. Thus, if anything needed correction, they would correct and admonish me; for whatever they thought ought to be added, I would have added. But what is this, “that we should remember the poor”? Paul argues thus throughout his whole epistle.

When, then, Paul and Barnabas were discussing these matters with John, Peter, and James, the Gospel was accepted in the manner Paul sets out, and was confirmed. But they did not readily listen to this one point in the discussion: that works are not admitted as the basis of salvation. Still, they urged us only to remember the poor [Col. 1161B; Note: Col. 1161D (3): The manuscripts read “they should be.”]. Thus they themselves also agree that the hope of salvation does not lie there if we perform works for the poor [Note: Col. 1161D (4): The manuscripts read “works.”; Note: Col. 1161D (5): Namely, without right faith or without the grace of God. Bellarmine should be read, who treats this question most fully and keenly in *On Justification*, book I, ch. 19 and following.], but they merely admonish us to remember the poor: not so that we should consume all our activity in this, but so that we should share with those who do not have what we are able to have.

“Only that we should remember the poor” [Col. 1161C]. We should not place our care and concern in this, or make it the whole power by which our salvation is preserved. In this respect he was thus almost corrected and admonished, yet he does not concede it: “that we should remember,” he says, not that we should do this as our main activity, but that we should keep it in mind. This is less than applying oneself to it and doing this alone.

“Which very thing I was eager to do.” He adds further that, besides the Gospel which he preached, he also took care to remember the poor and provide whatever he could. Indeed, no one is truly poor if he preserves the faith and believes in God, expecting the riches of his salvation. For present sustenance is small and sufficient, and costs neither giver nor recipient very much.

VERS. 11.—But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he was blameworthy [Col. 1161D–1162A; Note: Col. 1161D (6): Thus the manuscripts; but the common edition gives: “But when Cephas came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he was blameworthy.”]. “Not only,” he says, “was my Gospel approved by those apostles who were at Jerusalem, nor was I only admonished to remember the poor—a good and necessary duty, which we fulfilled and which I was eager to perform—but I also did not keep silence about Peter’s fault.” In this he displays his freedom and confidence in his Gospel, since he rebuked what Peter was doing otherwise.

Further, Peter, being rebuked, would be even more likely to break out in rebuke if there were anything defective in me; if I were not acting rightly concerning the Gospel, he would expose me, and, being injured, would not spare me. “When Peter came to Antioch,” he says, “I did not speak in the assembly or before the people, but I resisted him to his face”; that is, I openly contradicted him. And whence came this confidence? He does not himself rebuke Peter, but charges and accuses one who had been rebuked by all, because he was blameworthy. Therefore Peter too sinned by the judgment of the people [Col. 1162B], and was accused; and the people would likewise rebuke me if there were any sin in me, just as they rebuked him.

VERS. 12.—For before certain men came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew himself [Note: Col. 1162D (1): Vulgate: “he withdrew and separated himself, fearing,” etc.], fearing those who were of the circumcision. And the other Jews also agreed with him, so that Barnabas joined in their dissimulation [Note: Col. 1162D (2): Vulgate: “The other Jews joined in his dissimulation, so that Barnabas was carried away by them into that dissimulation.”].

He openly explains the fault itself, what Peter had done. He says that he rebuked this fault in Peter; perhaps he would now have passed it over in silence, since it was enough that Peter had been corrected by the people’s rebuke and by this open accusation. But because it is useful, and especially necessary to the epistle, it is narrated. Here he does two things. First, he shows that his own Gospel had not privately been reproved, and that he himself, when rebuking Peter [Col. 1162C], heard no rebuke from Peter. Then follows the point which I said was especially necessary: since the Galatians, abandoning the original Gospel, thought that something had to be added to the rule of the Gospel [Note: Col. 1162D (3): The manuscripts have “for life” instead of “something.”]—that they should observe the Sabbath and circumcision and live in the same way as the Jews—because the Galatians were doing this, the epistle is written to them. Thus it is most suitably narrated that Paul rebuked this very thing in Peter and that the people rebuked it; from which it follows that these people also sin.

He continues his narrative by explaining how and what Peter had done. “For before,” he says, “certain men came from James, he ate with the Gentiles,” holding the Gospel and its rule intact: that Christ should be proclaimed equally to Jews and Gentiles, that Jewish food regulations should not be observed [Col. 1162D], but that one should live simply in the manner of the Gentiles. “This,” he says, “Peter did before certain men came from James.” James, the brother of the Lord, who is the originator for the Symmachians [Note: Col. 1162D (4): The manuscripts read “because.”; Note: Col. 1162D (5): Thus the manuscripts. I would prefer: “is the originator for the Symmachians.” James did not produce the Symmachian heresy; rather, the Symmachians slanderously claimed him as their authority.], was the first at Jerusalem to think that he should take this course: preach Christ and yet live as a Jew, doing all that the Jewish law commands—that is, all which the Jews understood themselves to be obliged to observe [Col. 1163A].

When, therefore, certain men came from James to Peter, he withdrew himself, he says, fearing them, lest he should eat with the Gentiles. But he rebukes this: that Peter had previously eaten with the Gentiles and now withdrew himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision, that is, the men coming from James.

Nor was it a small matter that Peter himself did this; his great sin was that others agreed with him. “And the other Jews also agreed with him.” Here we should understand “Jews” as those who had nevertheless already received Christ, so that they agreed with him in receiving Christ and the Jewish discipline and observance. Otherwise, what would “they agreed with him” mean, if they were living in their own manner [Col. 1163B] according to Jewish discipline? Rather, those who had already received the Gospel by believing in Christ acted as Peter had previously acted in eating with Gentiles; later, when Peter withdrew himself and feared those who had come from James—namely the men of the circumcision whom he feared—the others agreed with him, so that they would not live with Gentiles but with the circumcision, that is, with Jews, even though they themselves had formerly been Jews.

“So that Barnabas also joined in their dissimulation.” Thus, he says, they wrongly pretended to live with the Jews, abandoning the Gentiles, so that Barnabas joined them. Above, Barnabas was said to be Paul’s companion and to hold the Gospel intact; nevertheless he joined them and their dissimulation. What, then, do we understand by “dissimulation”? Peter, Barnabas, and the other Jews had truly adopted the Jewish discipline in their manner of life, but temporarily, for the sake of those present, and were pretending; therefore, he says, Barnabas also joined in their dissimulation [Col. 1163C].

This is how it must be understood. Peter and the others had not converted to Jewish discipline, but had consented temporarily; such pretended agreement sometimes occurs. Yet wherein did Peter sin? Not because he had contrived these things in order to win the Jews over [Note: Col. 1163D (2): The manuscripts read, uncertainly, “whence some ‘not’ for ‘because he did not [do this] to win them over.’”], by agreeing with them; for Paul himself did this, and boasts that he did it in agreeing with the Jews, in order to win them. Rather, Peter did pretend, but sinned in that he withdrew himself through fear of those who were of the circumcision [Note: Col. 1163D (3): One manuscript reads “in Peter.”]. Therefore, because he pretended through fear and separated himself from the Gentiles, and Barnabas himself joined in that dissimulation, “I,” he says, “openly resisted him and accused him for having pretended thus wrongly because of that fear” [Col. 1163D].

Then follows VERS. 14.—But when I saw that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel [Note: Col. 1163D (4): Vulgate: “But when I saw that they were not walking rightly,” etc.]. They did indeed hold the Gospel and hold it intact, and understood that one ought not to live in the manner of those of the circumcision. But because they were pretending, they both interpreted the Gospel wrongly and did not proceed by a straight path according to the truth of the Gospel.

When I saw this, I said to Peter before all: this is what he said above, “I resisted him to his face”; I spoke openly, and I spoke before all. “If you, though you are a Jew, live as a Gentile, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” [Col. 1164A]. Paul certainly understood that Peter had pretended from fear, when he would not live with Gentiles. He therefore does not charge him with this, since Peter could have replied, “I was pretending.” What then did he charge against him? “You have lived with Gentiles, and you live with Gentiles.” For if you consent temporarily, you undoubtedly live as a Gentile. Because dissimulation deceives many, you sin: for you compel the Gentiles to Judaize.

Thus he shows that he understood Peter to have agreed with the Jews by dissimulation, yet that Peter sinned: first, because he feared those who had come; then because the others were deceived and compelled to Judaize, not understanding that Peter was pretending [Col. 1164B]. This, therefore, he concludes and recalls having said: “If you, Peter, though you are a Jew, live as a Gentile”—that is, live with Gentiles—“how do you compel the Gentiles themselves to Judaize?” That is, to follow Jewish discipline both in food and in observances.

VERS. 15.—We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from among the Gentiles; knowing that a human being is not justified by works of the law, except through faith in Christ Jesus; and we have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith [Note: Col. 1164D (2): The Vulgate adds “of Christ.”] and not by works of the law; because by works no flesh is justified [Note: Col. 1164D (3): Vulgate: “therefore by works of the law no flesh shall be justified.”].

This is still part of Paul’s speech accusing Peter and addressing him because he had wrongly agreed to Judaism and thus induced the Gentiles to Judaize. “We Jews,” he says—that is, I and you, Peter, and the others—“who are sinners [Note: Col. 1164D (4): A notable wording, showing that Victorinus placed a comma before *peccatores*, “sinners,” in the Pauline text printed above, unlike the Vulgate edition, where ‘sinners’ refers to the Gentiles] but not from among the Gentiles, are Jews.” We have, of course, embraced faith in Christ. Since we were Jews because we knew that a human being is not justified by works of the law, but is justified through faith—faith in Jesus Christ—therefore, knowing this, “we believed and believe in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith and not by works of the law; because by works of the law no flesh,” that is, no human being in the flesh, “is justified” [Col. 1164C].

Therefore, if, knowing this, we believed that justification comes through faith, we surely err if we now return to Judaism, from which we passed over so that we might be justified not by works but by faith, faith in Christ. For faith itself alone gives justification and sanctification [Note: Col. 1164D (5): We know that several other Fathers spoke in this way, whom Bellarmine enumerates and explains in the cited work, ch. 25. I do not wish now to enter the sea of controversy concerning justification. Yet see the holy James, Epistle ch. II: “Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he offered his son upon the altar? You see that faith cooperated with his works, and by works faith was brought to completion. … A person is justified by works and not by faith alone.”]. Thus every flesh, whether Jewish or Gentile [Col. 1165A], is justified not by works or by observance of the Jewish law, but by faith.

VERS. 17.—But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we are found ourselves also to be sinners, then is Christ a minister of sin [Note: Col. 1165D (1): Vulgate: “But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we too were found sinners, is Christ then a minister of sin? Far be it.”]? For if Jews are sinners, though not sinners from among the Gentiles, and, having received faith in Christ, we do what Jews do—although we embraced faith in Christ because we understood that a human being is not justified by works of the law—and if, while desiring to be justified in Christ [Note: Col. 1165D (2): Supply “faith.”], we observe the works of the law, we become sinners, it follows that Christ is a minister of sin. We received him so that we might not sin; now that we have received him, when we return to sins—that is, when we Judaize—has Christ become a minister of sin?

“But far be it,” he says. That is, one ought neither to think nor act in such a way that Christ, who suffered in order that sin might perish, should become a minister of sin [Col. 1165B].

VERS. 18.—For if I build again those things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor. For when I, a Jew, believed in Christ, I destroyed the law and the works of the law. But if, after faith in Christ, I return and perform the works of the law, I build up what I destroyed and am now a transgressor, doing what is contrary to what benefit, power, and reason require. But whose transgressor am I? Not the law’s, but Christ’s. For I turn Christ’s commandments into transgression if I return to Judaism and begin to observe things which I condemned as things to be observed, because I understood that a human being is justified not by them but by Christ.

VERS. 19.—For I through the law died to the law [Col. 1165C], that I might live to God. Paul may seem to have spoken of two laws: one of Christ, the other of Moses. Thus he says that he died to the law given to the Jews through the law given by Christ: “Through the law I died to the law,” that is, through the law of Christ I died to the law of the Jews previously given.

Or it may appear—as Paul frequently says, and the Savior himself also—that he calls two laws here because the same law is, as it were, twofold: one when understood carnally, the other when understood spiritually. Formerly it was understood carnally; and one served the law through works, circumcision, and the other observances understood carnally. But after the Savior, the true and spiritual light, appeared, the law began to be understood spiritually, becoming as it were another law, though it is the very same law.

The meaning, then, will be: through the law now understood spiritually, I died to the law understood carnally. And since this is so, because I understand the law spiritually, I died to the carnal law, that I might live to God. For one lives to God when one understands those precepts set down in the law not carnally but spiritually: that is, what true circumcision is, what the true Sabbath is, and the rest—matters which have been treated, and will be treated, in many places [Col. 1165D].

“I have been crucified with Christ.” This means that I have now received another law, so that the old human being has been fixed to the cross: that is, the whole flesh, the whole old human being, and the desires of the flesh. Christ accomplished this for me by his mystery. Therefore we have been crucified with Christ [Col. 1166A].

VERS. 20.—But I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me. That is, I have now become spirit by understanding God’s commands spiritually. Formerly I gave my whole self to the flesh, either serving or governing its desires, understanding nothing spiritually. Now therefore, because I myself live spiritually, Christ lives in me.

“But what I now live in the flesh, I live in the faith of the Son of God and Christ.” This is truly to live spiritually: that although one lives in the flesh, one does not live for the flesh or from the flesh, but lives to God and Christ in their faith. This is to live spiritually: to think of him, speak of him, believe him, strive toward him in desire, flee the world, and reject from one’s mind all things that are in the world [Col. 1166B]. This is to live by faith: to hope for no good from anyone other than Christ and God. This is to live in the faith of God and Christ, who loved me and bestowed such a benefit as to give himself for us to death and the cross, and thus free us from sins.

Accordingly, VERS. 21 follows: “I am not ungrateful for the grace of God” [Note: Col. 1166D (1): Vulgate: “I do not reject the grace of God.”]. That is, when he himself has made me an heir through Christ, and Christ has given himself for me, I will not abandon every hope which I have in Christ and return to hope in the law, believing that I am justified by works of the law. This is to be ungrateful to him who bestowed so much upon me, exposing himself for me and freeing me from sins by sins punished in himself.

“For if righteousness is through the law [Col. 1166C], then Christ died gratuitously.” This is the full conclusion concerning the errors of the Galatians and of those who add Judaism to Christianity. “For,” he says, “if righteousness is through the law, Christ died in vain.” If Christ died because justification was not obtainable through the law, I must nevertheless follow Christ. But if, after Christ’s coming, I believe that I am justified through the law, Christ did not die for me, and he died gratuitously—that is, without cause.

To believe in Christ and to follow the works of the law conflict and are mutually opposed. Since the law did not justify humanity through its works, Christ came so that justification might come to humanity through his death. But if, after faith in Christ, there is a return to the law, Christ will seem to have died gratuitously, as though he had granted us nothing, since the law already granted this [Col. 1166D]. Yet the law did not grant this; and therefore Christ came, so that he himself might grant it. Therefore Christ did not die gratuitously, but justification comes to us through him. If this is so, righteousness is not from works of the law.

CAP. III.

VERS. 1.—O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you [Note: Col. 1166D (2): The Vulgate has: “Who has bewitched you not to obey the truth?”], before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly proscribed [Note: Col. 1166D (3): Note the reading *proscriptus*, “proscribed,” for *praescriptus*, “set forth,” which other ancient Fathers also attest], and crucified in you? Only those who are distinguished in some good are subject to bewitching, and they suffer it at the hands of malicious and envious persons. Having received good from the true Gospel, believed in Christ, and hoped for his promises, they now began also to add the discipline of Judaism. “Who,” he says, “has bewitched you, that you should depart from your good?”

You are therefore foolish, that is, without understanding. What have they admitted, whereby they are foolish? They have been persuaded to cultivate Judaism. Therefore Christ has been “proscribed”: that is, his goods have been distrained and sold—goods which were certainly in us, but which, through persuasion toward Judaism, have been proscribed, sold, and lost. Therefore you are foolish, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was proscribed, so that these goods might perish in your own presence, as things publicly proscribed perish. You did not resist or contend; and therefore you are foolish.

Accordingly, the statement that Christ “was crucified in you” also belongs to this meaning [Col. 1167B]. The Jews who persuaded you to follow the discipline of Judaism did to Christ in you what was done to Christ when he was raised upon the cross: by persuading you toward Jewish discipline, they also crucified Christ in you. Therefore, foolish Galatians, you have lost Christ and his goods from your souls. I do not know, then, who has bewitched you in your good things.

VERS. 2.—This only I wish to learn from you. I will introduce nothing; I will rebuke nothing. “This only,” he says, “I wish to learn, and learn from you: Did you receive the Spirit from works of the law, or from the hearing of faith, by which you began to become better fitted for the knowledge of God?” Whence, he says, did receiving the Spirit come to you—from works of the law, or from the hearing of faith? When, therefore, I preached the Gospel to you, you received the Spirit from the hearing of faith, not from works of the law [Col. 1167C].

Or, if not from works of the law, why do you now add Jewish discipline, so as to suppose that you receive the Spirit from works of the law, and think concerning God and hope in God through them, when you already received the Spirit from the hearing of faith—that is, from what you heard, that faith in Christ must be followed? But if it was from hearing, it is contrary to faith when you suppose that you receive the Spirit from works of the law, since the Spirit is given—and was given to you—through this faith in Christ alone.

VERS. 3.—Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you will now be brought to completion by the flesh [Note: Col. 1167D (1): The Vulgate has *consummemini*, “be brought to completion.”]? He has explained what “from works of the law” and “from the hearing of faith” mean. For the works of the law do nothing except satisfy the flesh, undergo affection from the flesh, and assist the flesh. Therefore one who believes that he is justified by works of the law has a carnal understanding.

You therefore, he says, are so foolish, so lacking in understanding, while you add works to your justification—which is to think according to the flesh—that, although you began with the Spirit through the Gospel given by me, and received the Spirit from hearing faith in Christ, you will now bring the outcome of your conduct and life to completion in the flesh: that is, through works undertaken for the flesh and according to the flesh?

VERSE 4.—Have you suffered so much in vain? Such speech readily moves one to endurance: it reproves and admonishes, yet in turn reproves its own reproof. For it reproves when it says, “Have you suffered so much in vain?” adding, “if indeed it was in vain.” It admonishes, however, when it says, “You have suffered so much,” so that, having steadfastly endured many things when they received the faith, they might also live spiritually. For whoever begins to live spiritually, casting away worldly things and, with his new person, enduring the hatred of Greeks and nations destined to perish, must necessarily suffer much; and the Galatians, indeed, are said to have suffered such things. But since you have suffered so much, it is all the more grievous that you have suffered so much without cause and have not attained the reward of faith, for which you suffered so much. Yet, lest what he said—“in vain”—should seem to induce despair, he corrects his reproof by saying, “if indeed it was in vain.” For they can be corrected, so that what they suffered may not be in vain, but may have as its ground perseverance in faith, its reward and confirmation being the promises that come from faith in Christ.

VERSE 5.—Does he, then, who supplies you with the Spirit and works miracles among you, do so from works of the law, or from hearing with faith? [The words “do so” are absent from the Vulgate.] Since above he said, “You have suffered so much,” and explained what they seemed to have suffered—or things of that sort and kind—in their endurance they certainly displayed virtues of endurance. He therefore joins together: “He who supplies you with the Spirit works miracles among you”; by these virtues you suffered and endured so much. From this he surely makes them understand that God worked many miracles in them; and if he worked miracles, he supplied them with the Spirit. Therefore, once it has been established that the Spirit was given them, the question properly follows: whether God worked miracles among them from works of the law or from hearing with faith.

Certainly not from works: for no works had proceeded from you; rather, you heard the faith and obeyed the faith, and therefore God worked miracles in you. And if he worked them, he supplied you with the Spirit; moreover, he worked them and supplied the Spirit, since you suffered many and great things. But what is this “without why?”—“without cause”? [Note: *quare* (“why?”) is used substantively; later writers, adopting it from popular Latin, used it frequently in their writings.] Yet he corrected this: they were not without cause, for he hopes that they can be corrected. He therefore returns to the proof that all these things came to them from hearing with faith; and he establishes that nothing wonderful or incredible occurs unless the faith of the Gospel is obeyed.

He therefore gives an analogy from the reading which contains the remarkable sufferings which the Galatians endured and bore through faith, and consequently through the Spirit given them and through the power worked in them by God.

VERSE 6.—Just as Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. In Genesis (15:6) it is stated that Abraham believed God and that it was reckoned to him as righteousness. [Cf. the Vulgate, which has only: “Just as it is written,” etc.] Thus God works miracles when faith arises in human souls, and faith by which they believe in God. “It was reckoned,” he says, “to Abraham as righteousness, because he believed God.” Therefore you too have suffered, endured, and overcome so much; and God has worked, and works, miracles in you because through hearing with faith you believed God. It is understood, therefore, that those who are of faith—

VERSE 7.—These are the children of Abraham. For many promises were made to Abraham’s seed; but Abraham himself was accepted as righteous by faith. Therefore, whoever are of faith, these are Abraham’s children, as we have often reminded you. The whole mystery accomplished by our Lord Jesus Christ seeks faith alone. For it was accomplished for us—for our resurrection and liberation—provided that we have faith in the mystery of Christ and in Christ. For the Godhead foreshadowed and sent this beforehand: that a human being should be justified by faith. Therefore, just as it was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness because he had faith, so we too, if we have faith in Christ and his mystery, shall be children of Abraham; that is, our whole life will be reckoned to us as righteousness. [Victorinus here acknowledges that the life rightly lived after faith has been received is reckoned to us as righteousness.] Finally, he adds this: the mystery concerning Abraham was enacted for this reason, that human beings might be justified by faith—namely, faith in Christ.

VERSE 8.—And Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the nations by faith, foretold to Abraham—[the Vulgate: “announced beforehand”] that is, to the prophet—that what was being enacted concerning one man might be proclaimed concerning others in ages to come. “Foreseeing,” he says—seeing what was to come; “Scripture,” that is, the written prophecy. What did it foresee? That God was to justify the nations by faith; for this reason the same Scripture foretold it to Abraham. And what did it foretell? That the nations would be justified by faith. Finally, he adds the Scriptural example, that they “shall be blessed”: that is, in the manner in which Abraham was reckoned righteous—namely, by faith. This example is from Genesis. [Thus the manuscripts read.] Therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed; that is, it shall be reckoned to them as righteousness, and they shall be blessed by God.
