They shall be blessed by God when justified; and to be justified is to be freed from the law of slavery. Therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed, because Abraham was blessed by faith. Faith, then, is everything.

How is this brought back to the Galatians? Plainly because blessing and justification come solely from faith, not from works. Therefore those persons erred who, in addition to the faith they had received in Jesus Christ our Lord, thought that the law and its precepts must also be added—that is, that justification should be believed to come from works. He therefore adds this in order to teach the opposite as well: what comes from works, lest the Galatians suppose that they retain faith in Christ and nevertheless can benefit themselves still more if they also do something from works.

On the contrary, the Apostle denies that blessing comes from works. But what is still more serious, and contrary to blessing, is that those who act from works are under a curse.

VERSE 10.—For all who are of works of the law are under a curse. [The Vulgate: “under the curse.”] He therefore adds forcefully that those who are of works are not merely not blessed, but that those who are of works of the law are even under a curse. By “works of the law,” moreover, let us understand even works of Christianity [thus the manuscripts read]—especially those which the Apostle often commands, as he says that he himself was commanded: “let us remember the poor,” and the other instructions for living contained in this Apostle, works which the Apostle commands every Christian to perform. [If good works are commanded by the Apostle, it follows that they are necessary for attaining salvation. Moreover, Christ will carry out the judgment of humankind on the basis of works, especially deeds of mercy done or omitted.]

[Jerome comments on this very passage of the Apostle: “The example by which it is proved that the righteous person lives by faith and not by works is taken from Habakkuk, etc. It must therefore be considered that he did not say, ‘a human being’ or ‘a man lives by faith,’ lest he give occasion for contempt of virtuous works; rather, ‘the righteous person lives by faith,’ so that whoever was faithful and was to conquer by faith could not otherwise come to faith or live in it unless he had first been righteous and, by purity of life, had ascended as by certain steps to faith. It can therefore happen that someone is righteous and yet does not live without faith in Christ, etc. Let us also make some similar statements to this saying, ‘the righteous person lives by faith,’ and say: ‘The chaste person lives by faith; the wise person lives by faith; the brave person lives by faith,’ etc.” Certainly, if we speak strictly, theological doctrine does not allow that faith alone justifies. For is not hope also necessary, and above all charity, for justification?]

Let us understand other works of the law to mean observances, sacrifices of the lamb now that the Passover has been fulfilled through Christ, and the remaining practices connected with circumcision and with foods either to be possessed or supplied.

Therefore, though we do not know the works of the law, Christ, who is in heaven and descended even to the flesh, unites and joins the two Churches. He is therefore mediator; and by his mystery, arranged through angels, as it were a mediator he frees this Church—that is, the members of the Church—and recalls it to the higher Church. Therefore Christ is mediator.

VERSE 20.—Now a mediator is not mediator of one; but God is one. Christ is the one who recalls and joins his members to the Church. Does the law, then, do this? Is the law a mediator? If the law is not a mediator—for since the law concerns deeds, it does not join things that are separated, but judges only concerning deeds—then it was inserted, he says, until Christ should come, that is, the seed to whom the inheritance was promised, in whose hand lies what was arranged through angels, and who is a mediator—and a mediator, of course, between two.

And I have said “two”; but God is one. Therefore he cannot be mediator of God alone, because God is one. Thus the law in no way justifies; the law of deeds in no way obtains the inheritance. For heirs are those who draw their origin from that source and receive the Spirit from the source whence the inheritance will come: namely, Christ joining what is separated, freeing that part of the Church which is held here by the errors of the world, and recalling it to the heavenly Church. For he alone is mediator.

But a mediator, as we have taught, is not mediator of one. For all things after God are not one; God alone is one. Therefore, whatever is outside God is many things, which can be joined because they derive from him, or are separated because such was the mystery—and such it is even now, that they may be joined—because they are far apart, divided, hostile, and perishing. Therefore, since God alone is one, the mediator is outside God; yet he is not mediator of one. This mediator reconciles and joins, by a certain mystery, those other things which are distinguished from one another by a certain mystery.

We are among those who were separated through our ancestors and joined again through ancestors indeed, but according to Christ—that is, according to faith. Hence it is apparent that we cannot be freed without a mediator. If this is so, it is a vain hope to believe that justification and salvation come from the law of deeds, which, as we have said, is not a mediator. For Christ alone is mediator, joining those between whom he is mediator. Therefore justification and liberation come through Christ, not through the law of deeds.

## BOOK TWO

This entire Epistle to the Galatians, as we have said, aims at and assails the view which the Galatians thought they should adopt: that together with Jewish discipline and observance they should preserve Christ’s faith and uphold the Gospel. The Apostle teaches both that this is not so and that he did not so command; indeed, that it is altogether futile to hope for justification and salvation from the law. For all things come from faith: the promise of liberation, justification, and inheritance in heaven and above heaven was given to Abraham by faith, and likewise to his seed. If this is so, he teaches altogether that no justification, no liberation, and no inheritance comes from the law and from its works fulfilled according to its precepts. For this reason, since he seems to attack the law, a question is rightly raised.

VERSE 21.—What then, he says: is the law contrary to the promises? [The Vulgate: “Is the law then contrary to the promises of God?”] For if the law accomplishes nothing through its works, and it came later—for the promises were made earlier to Abraham, whereas the law was given through Moses and maintains a righteousness of deeds—it seems in some way either to have been given in vain or to be contrary to the promise. For if works from the law accomplish and confer nothing, the law is contrary to the promises. The promises offer inheritance and justification; but this law of works, in drawing souls away from faith and keeping them occupied with something else, so that the promises are expected not by faith but by something else—that is, by works—is contrary to the promises. Yet it is not plausible that, although God gave the law, that same law should appear to have been given contrary to the promises. It is certainly contrary to the promises if it occupies us otherwise—namely, in fulfilling works prescribed by the law—and prevents us from expecting by faith what was promised: that by faith in God we may attain the inheritance of heaven.

But we shall understand his answer to this objection as follows. First he says generally: “Far be it!” That is, it is not fitting that this should appear to have been done by God: that he gave a law which, while holding a person occupied in other matters, empties the promise and makes merit rather than faith operative—that is, so that, after all works have been performed, we attain justification by merit rather than by faith alone. “Far be it,” he says. Then he supplies the reason: “For if a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly be from the law.”

We have said that the law given by Moses does nothing other than teach which sins have been committed and admonish how they are to be avoided; and Scripture concluded nothing else except that it placed all precepts under sin and concerning sin. [The manuscripts read “and concerning sin”; it is uncertain whether these words perhaps belong with the following sentence.] This law, he says, was not given so that it could give life. For if it had been given in that way, righteousness would truly be from the law. But now it was not given so that life might be sought from it; rather, it was given so that its Scripture [that is, the law’s; perhaps “sacred” should be read] might both teach all sins and show that they must be avoided. Therefore righteousness is not from the law—that is, justification and salvation do not come from it—but from faith, as was promised.

Finally he adds:

VERSE 22.—But Scripture shut up all things under sin, so that the promise from faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. This, he says, was accomplished through Moses: he established a law concerning sin, and all Scripture concerning sin and those under sin was brought to a conclusion, so that what had been promised might come about by faith and the inheritance from faith in Jesus Christ might be given to believers. What, then, does or did he accomplish by all this? That faith in Jesus Christ alone may suffice for our justification and liberation.

VERSE 23.—But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up for the faith which was to be revealed. [The Vulgate: “which was to be revealed.”] This was so that the law might not become empty or opposed to the promises. How does he call it necessary? Because there was expectation of the coming faith and promise through faith. “Before faith came,” he says, “we were kept”—that is, in some manner, guided and guarded by the law, we lived uprightly by avoiding sins and knowing them; so that when Christ came, being, as it were, shut up for that faith which was to come, we might await his advent. Believing in his faith, prepared by the law, avoiding sins and performing works of the law, we could readily receive from his advent what had been promised—namely, faith in Christ.

Therefore we ought not to have faith in the law, but in the advent. For, he says, we were shut up for faith—for that faith, he says, which was to come, namely Christ’s faith—so that the same faith might be revealed when he came.

VERSE 24.—Therefore the law was our pedagogue unto Christ. For just as those who teach children advise them, as far as they can, concerning the way of life and show it to them, yet are not themselves teachers of the complete life, so the law too was like a pedagogue. But it was neither profitable in itself nor a complete pedagogue for teaching life; rather, “unto Christ,” he says—that is, until Christ. Thus the law guarded us by warning us about sins, so that in Christ we might have every hope of salvation and life, that we might be justified by faith. Not by the law but by faith, he says, are we freed—that is, justified—and receive the inheritance and promise.

VERSE 25.—But when faith came—that is, Christ himself (for then faith arose, that is, it began to have its time, so that faith might exist and we might believe in him, in whom is all salvation; whereas the Jews did not believe)—we are no longer under a pedagogue. That is, we no longer live under the law, because we kept the precepts of the law that pertain to faith, we who were being prepared by the pedagogue of the law. When Christ himself came—that is, faith itself—we no longer live under the pedagogue, but live, or shall live, by faith.

VERSE 26.—For you are all children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. [Cf. the Vulgate: “all [are children] through faith which is in Jesus Christ.”] For this is the inheritance: that we attain eternal life. Then, indeed, we are children of God. But from what source? By faith in Christ Jesus. We have faith in Jesus Christ when we believe in him: that he is the Son of God, that he himself saves us, that he accomplished that mystery for us, and all those things which we stated in the Gospel.

But this should be observed here: although he had been speaking about matters, he turns to direct address, where he shows an endearment by which he might persuade them more readily. “You are all children,” he says. Above, “we are under a pedagogue”; now he turns directly to them [the manuscripts read *apostrofat*; Victorinus the African is either an innovator or a writer of less-than-good Latin, as the published works show abundantly]: “You are children,” he says, “of God,” but children by faith in Jesus Christ.

VERSE 27.—For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. [See the Vulgate: “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ,” etc.] That is, in Christ you are children of God. What does “in Christ” mean? Whoever is baptized in Christ is already a child of God; for whoever is baptized is baptized into Christ. But one baptized into Christ puts on Christ. [Thus the manuscripts read, although above and below the text has “in Christ.”] For whoever is baptized has Christ, and, having Christ, is already in Christ; and having Christ, one is a child of God, because Christ is the Son of God.

VERSE 28.—For in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. [The Vulgate omits “in Christ.”] He therefore removes the remaining human distinctions, which can arise from status, human nature, or nationality. By these things we can be divided among ourselves: one may be a Jew, another a Greek; one a slave, another free. The former distinctions are of status or legal standing; the latter, of nature. “There is neither male nor female,” he says. What follows? When all these are removed, he says, “You are all one in Christ Jesus.” Since you are one by receiving the Spirit from Christ, you are Christ. Therefore you are children of God in Christ.

VERSE 29.—Therefore you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise. If this is so, that which was promised to Abraham’s seed has been fulfilled. You too are Abraham’s seed according to faith; you are in Christ and therefore Abraham’s seed. You are heirs according to the promise, because the inheritance was promised to Abraham’s seed. But you, baptized in Christ Jesus, have received Christ and are Christ; therefore you are Abraham’s seed. If the inheritance was promised to the seed, the inheritance will be given to you also, and you are heirs according to the promise.

## CHAPTER IV

VERSE 1.—Now I say: as long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, though he is lord of all. [The Vulgate: “for as much time as.”] By adding this comparison he continues to teach what we were under the law before Christ’s advent, and what we were after he came. For, resolving the question whether the law had been contrary to the promises, he says that the law was given for a time, to keep us under guard. By imparting precepts, it guarded us from sins until the time should come in Christ’s advent when we could be heirs of the promises.

Therefore, he says, when heirs are children—which is the time under the law before Christ’s advent—they differ in nothing from slaves. For although they are to be lords of all, because they are to be heirs, nevertheless, until the time comes in which they exercise the full title of lord, they are held, as it were, in a certain function of slavery. But this is not forever: it lasts until they reach their own age and freedom, and are able to fulfill both the name and the authority of heir. This is what he adds.

VERSE 2.—But he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the father. [The Vulgate: “guardians.”] Every heir, he says, while a child, is under guardians. That law of Moses guarded future heirs—those who already were heirs but were not yet mature because of their age—as though under a guardian and a steward. For they cannot act for themselves or receive the benefit or the full title of heir.

Yet during that period they are not slaves in the sense of truly serving; rather, they live under guard, so that they may be slaves until the time appointed by the father. For a steward, guardian, or tutor has force by the father’s ordinance, until the child reaches maturity and then acts by his own right and free will, governing the inheritance received. This comparison, as I said, refers to those to whom the law was given.

VERSE 3.—So we also, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of this world. [“This” is absent from the Vulgate.] But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son. [The Vulgate: “But when,” etc.] The question had concerned one thing; yet, in returning to the analogy, he adds another thing—something more than what had earlier been set out. For while the matter concerned the law that had been given, as though inserted after the promises, and it was said that the law was introduced before Christ’s advent because we were still children and placed under the law’s guardianship—and just as he himself said, “we were kept under the law,” and “the law was our pedagogue”—although the law, he says, was a pedagogue, yet it was “unto Christ.” The whole preceding discussion had concerned the law, until the time came when, according to the promise, we might be heirs. As I said, while speaking of the law and adding the analogy, he pursued the argument with an unbroken sense.

But now, in the conclusion, he returns not to the law but to the elements: “We also,” he says, “when we were children.” What ought to have followed? “We lived under the law.” But this is not added; rather: “We were enslaved under the elements of this world.” This is either different from the preceding statements or depends upon them. [Thus the manuscripts read.] We must inquire how it is not foreign to them.

Without doubt, this was said above: whoever has been baptized in Christ has put on Christ. But those who have put on Christ are neither Jews nor Greeks. If we who have put on Christ are neither Greeks nor Jews, we no longer belong to the world. For before Christ’s advent the world regarded a human being as either Jew or Greek. Whether Jew or Greek, while living according to their own laws, people lived under the elements of the world. For among the Jews sacrilege, theft, false witness, and the rest are punished. [Thus the manuscripts read. The verb *est* governs τὸ *puniri* (“the ‘to be punished’”). Victorinus writes similarly in his published tract Against the Manichees, ch. 2: “for from it Christ has flesh.”] Likewise among the Greeks—that is, among the pagans [so Victorinus, On the Reception of *homoousios*, ch. 1: “the Greeks whom they call pagans”]—these things were and are punished by laws.

But the elements of the world bring with them their movements and, as it were, certain necessities arising from those movements: as in the stars, by whose revolution human life is drawn into necessity. Thus people serve the elements as the stars command and as the course of the world dictates.

[When he says that pagans are governed by the stars but Christians are not, Victorinus does not yet seem to have discarded every superstition; nor is this surprising. For Nicetas of Aquileia was still writing against astrologers a hundred years after Victorinus, as Gennadius testifies in chapter 22; we regret that Nicetas’s tract has been lost. I myself remember reading long ago, in the Ambrosian Library, a very ancient codex (M. 77, upper shelf), to which three leaves of parchment had been added as an inner covering. On these parchments was writing of the greatest antiquity and of a larger script; but it had been widely scraped away with a knife to make a palimpsest, so that I could transcribe only a few verses, and not without gaps. It is an invective against astrologers and diviners of that sort. Whether this invective belongs to known or unknown writings of the Fathers, there is no leisure to investigate, especially because the fragment is exceedingly small and gaping with lacunae. I once read it thus: “…what [is assigned] to each person at birth, or how the administration of divine providence [works]. Many have thought that many things ought to be attributed to human conjectures. Therefore, conjectured in letters … at the same time something is struck by lightning: such things have only such force as they possess through the presumption of minds, being united, as it were, by a common language with divinations. Yet they are all full of pestilential curiosity, tormenting anxiety, and deadly slavery. For they are not observed because they are certain; rather, through observing and marking them, it came about that they had force. And therefore different things happen to different people according to their thoughts and assumptions. For those very persons who wish to deceive forecast such things for each person as they see him ensnared by his own suspicions and agreements. Just as, for example, one figure, X, marked crosswise, signifies one thing among Greeks and another among Latins, not by nature but by convention of signifying … He who announces an omen must also know the language if he wishes to signify something to a Greek person … For he does not attach it to that meaning when [he hears] a person … with one and the same sound, a letter among Greeks, among Latins … In these two syllables the Greek understands one thing, the Latin another. Therefore, just as all these significations move minds differently, according to the agreement of each community, and people did not agree upon them because they already had force for signification, but they have force because … certain things … must be attributed in part to demons desirous of evils … according to the most beautiful order of providence … for the human race … by which [there are] impiety, curiosity …”]

All of these bonds are dissolved for anyone who has faith in Christ and has received from Christ the Spirit as lord of his life, so that he may escape and avoid every worldly necessity and the power of the elements. Such a person does not serve the world, but serves the Lord Christ and, with the Spirit governing his actions, has freedom. Something more, therefore, than was expected has been introduced: the Galatians are to understand that the Jewish law, its precepts, observances, and works must be abandoned altogether. For they see that even the law of the world itself and of the elements has been overthrown, has no force under Christ, and that the power of the world’s revolution is utterly overturned.

VERSE 4.—But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, brought forth from a woman. [For “brought forth from a woman,” the Vulgate reads, “made from a woman.”] Just as there is fullness in things, so there is fullness in times: each has its own fullness. Christ is the abundant, complete, and copious perfection and fullness of all things; the fullness of times is the consummation of liberation. As Christ, in order that there may be a whole and perfect fullness, gathers the members which have been scattered and becomes fullness, so likewise the fullness of times was then accomplished, when all had matured for faith and sins had risen to their height, and a remedy was necessarily sought against the death of all things. Hence Christ came to aid, the fullness of times having been perfected.

It is said that God sent his own Christ—his own, I say, before he sent him; but afterward, brought forth from a woman. Yet he sent his Son: that is, one who was his Son. And he sent him. How did he send him? Brought forth from a woman. Thus, by his mystery, Christ the Son of God came to the aid of the world and of us all; for we are the world. By putting on flesh—that is, by being brought forth from a woman—he fulfilled all that had to be done in the mystery: that he might be seen, heard, suffer, die, and rise again. Therefore he sent, brought forth from a woman, him who had been his Son, brought forth from a woman.

Some say, “brought forth from a wife,” and they themselves create a question by the word they have used: since the Virgin Mary is or was a virgin, why did he say, “brought forth from a wife”? [The reading *et* (“and”) for *vel* (“or”) is not unusual. In any event, it is the settled authority of the Catholic Church that the Mother of God remained a perpetual virgin, not only before Jesus was brought forth but also afterward. Victorinus also mentioned the Mother of God’s virginity in his Commentary on Cicero’s Rhetoric 1.40.] In customary speech we call *femina* that which the Greeks call γυνή (*gynē*, “woman/wife”). Then, since she brought forth Christ, why should he not call her a *mulier* (“woman, wife”)? For every *femina* who brings forth something is called a *mulier*. Yet the force of the mystery, although hidden and holy, should nevertheless be considered in such a way that it may for the moment be recognized in passing: all things perfect are called male; all things imperfect, female. Thus we find that all perfected, sanctified, and justified persons “come together into a man.” [Ephesians 4:13.] [The manuscripts read *est*.] The saying may therefore be understood thus: while the world—or we ourselves placed in the world—are not most perfect, we live after the manner of females and women.

Therefore, in order that Christ, providing or about to provide salvation for us, might come to us, he was born from a woman: that is, he took also that part which rendered him imperfect and made him like us—namely, either flesh or the world. In this world or in this flesh, having been brought forth, he was indeed from a woman: that is, from imperfect things. The mystery having been fulfilled, after his passion and resurrection he was also sanctified and became male—that is, he had and received the perfect Spirit—so that he might give us an example, that we too might rise into a man from a woman, that is, from this life, which, being corrupted, is rightly called either female or woman. For evil comes from woman; indeed, even in the first human being there was no sin except through woman.

“Made.” Under this word a great error arises, so that from it they understand that the Son was not born but made, because it says: “God sent his Son, brought forth from a woman, made under the law.” But there is a great difference between saying that the Son was made and saying that he was made under the law. For it is one thing that the Son, who was already Son and, indeed, was Son by birth, should be sent; but now, when he was brought forth from a woman, he can be said to have been made in this respect: that he was under the law.

What does “made under the law” mean? That he was born not among the nations but among the Jews, and within the discipline and law of Moses. For correction could be effected there. Israel was called the people of God; Moses received the law from God and gave it to that people, which certainly misunderstood the law. Therefore aid had to be brought to it in its sinning, and its sins removed—if only the same people might recognize the Son of God. For if he had been born elsewhere, that is, among the nations, Israel could on that account have failed to recognize him, because he would not have seemed to be born among its own people.

But this people incurred greater sins precisely because, though he was born among its own people—that is, within Moses’ law, among Israel—he was not recognized, although that people, and David in particular, had been told that inheritance and eternity would be given to David’s seed. Therefore, since David is Israel’s father, Christ was born there so that they might recognize him. Hence their sin is greater because they did not recognize him who was made under the law.

Many things may be said as to why he was made under the Law [Col. 1177D]: either because there the one God was already worshipped; or because they had already received oracles and commandments from God; or because Moses was an image and type of Christ; or because Christ himself, though he was in the condition of those under the Law, nevertheless commanded differently and, for salvation’s sake, departed from the Law by not observing the Sabbath and the other things. From this they might know that salvation was not to be hoped for in works of the Law or from the Law. Hence the Galatians too might understand that they had fallen into error, since the Savior himself in whom they believed, though made under the Law, did not nevertheless serve the Law.

But these and many other reasons why he was made under the Law need not be gathered, because he himself added the reason why he was made under the Law: “that he might redeem those who were under the Law, that we might receive adoption as sons.” This, he says, is the reason why God sent his Son—and indeed sent one already his Son, but now born of a woman—and sent him made under the Law. What is the reason for his being under the Law? That he might redeem those who were under the Law. Therefore, if he was sent in order to redeem us, we are the more bound [to him] if we have been redeemed from the Law. And he himself says likewise elsewhere, when speaking of a woman: “For while her husband lives, she is bound to her husband; but if he dies, she is freed from her husband.” Therefore, since the Law held people as though bound by its commandments, only to integrity of life and not to hope of liberation and eternity, God sent his Son—and sent him under the Law, that is, in Israel—in order to redeem those who had been there and were living under the Law.

This, moreover, is a great thing: that he did not merely furnish them with a way of life [Col. 1178B], nor merely stir them toward eternity by commandments, but, he says, “that he might redeem.” For this was accomplished in the mystery: that he might redeem all who believe in him, so that all who believe in him may become sons by adoption.

Therefore, since so great a benefit—indeed, the whole benefit—is from Christ, nothing further is to be added, nor is the Law to be served. For we have been redeemed: redeemed from the Law, and redeemed from this world, so that we may be sons of God, yet sons by adoption. For we are not sons as the Son himself is, but sons through the Son. This, then, is adoption, which, he says, God sent his Son that we might receive. “But because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts.”

Behold the whole order of these three powers—that is, persons [Note: Victorinus uses *potentia* for “person”; cf. the title *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*.]—through one power and one divinity. For, he says, he who is Father sent his Son, who is Christ [Col. 1178C]. Again, Christ himself, who is the power of God and himself God—“God sent,” he says; for there is now a Trinity. And Christ, especially after the mystery had been sanctified, sent, he says, “the Spirit of his Son,” who is the Holy Spirit, who, descending into our hearts, readily knows the Father.

Thus Jesus Christ, the Son, is sent from God; those who believe believe in him and become sons of God. And from God the Spirit of the Son, that is, the Holy Spirit, is sent into them, so that they may now hasten—make haste—to the Father, and cry out in a manner by inward sanctification and an inward voice. What they cry, he himself adds: “They cry, Abba, Father.” The spirits have words; rather, they have them when they receive knowledge (*cognoscentia*) of the Father. This very knowledge of the Father—that is, when we know the Father—is itself the voice of our spirit to God, the Spirit whom God gave us [Col. 1178D]. Knowledge harmonizing with him whom it knows is, as it were, a certain voice directed toward him whom it knows.

Therefore, since through God and through Christ we know God, we ourselves become sons of God, and through that knowledge itself have a voice to the Father. [Col. 1179A] For just as Christ alone knows God, and from what he knows has knowledge, so he calls upon him and addresses him because he knows him. For this reason Christ is God’s Word. For I have said that every kind of knowledge, since it enables us to understand, designate, grasp, and conceive what we understand, as it were calls that thing—whatever it may be—by knowledge. For we receive, regarding him whom we know, from him whom we know, a word when we name what he is, because we know those things: this is the whole knowledge of the thing we know. [Note: Victorinus’s expression here and elsewhere is admittedly obscure and impeded; Petavius called him, as it were, another Heraclitus, *skoteinos* (“the Obscure”).]

Therefore Christ, because he knows God, is God’s Word; and the Spirit, because Christ is given to us, gives us knowledge of God through himself. Hence it comes about that we too are word, both toward Christ and toward God; and therefore [Col. 1179B] we cry out as knowers. Now when the knower belongs to the one known, it follows that the known one is Father and the knower is Son. If this is so, rightly, when through Jesus we know the Father, through knowledge we become his Word; and consequently, as sons, we cry, “Abba, Father.”

### Verse 7

“Therefore you are no longer a slave, but a son.” [Note: The manuscripts read “you are no longer,” not “he is no longer.”] For one who says “Abba, Father” certainly names God as Father. If he names him Father, he is a son; therefore he is no longer a slave. And if this is so, in Christ there is neither slave nor free, neither male nor female: for we are all one.

But to what does all this lead? “And if a son, then an heir through God.” Therefore, if he is called a son, he will also be an heir; yet an heir not through deeds or his own works, but through God’s mercy and God’s grace. This is what he meant by “through God.” As has been shown in many places, it is not of the one who runs but of the one who shows mercy; and all things are through God’s grace. [Col. 1179C]

### Verse 8

“But formerly, when you did not know God, you served those who are not gods.” [Col. 1179C] [Note: Vulgate: “But then … you served those who by nature are not gods.”] I have often said and reminded you: not to know God is not to know Christ, for God is known through Christ. But now that Christ has appeared—he who taught me, revealed God through himself, revealed himself as God and the Father through himself—it is not permissible not to know God.

“But formerly,” he says, “when you did not know God, O Galatians, you served those who are not gods.” I have often reminded you that “gods” is said in the plural even in the Law; yet God is one. The rest—angels and the other powers—are honored by this title, as in “God of gods.” Would that they had served those! But instead you served those who are not gods: namely, all worldly and other false powers, imaginary, fabricated, and simulated by the devil. [Col. 1179D]

### Verse 9

“But now that you have known God—or rather, have been known by God—how do you turn again to the weak and needy elements of this world?” [Note: Vulgate: “But now that you have known God—or rather have been known by God—how,” etc.]

He either adds another charge against the Galatians, namely that they had also passed into gentile observance; or he persists in the same accusation as before, that they were adding the Jewish Law to Christianity—circumcision, Sabbath observance, and dietary rules. He charges them, then, by saying: after you came to know God through the Gospel given by me, how do you turn again to weak things—which they certainly are? Or understand it as referring either to Jewish observance or to pagans, who likewise are weak.

But when he added “the needy elements of this world,” he seems rather to touch on pagans, who make gods for themselves even from the elements of this world: they worship fire, water, earth, and air [Col. 1180B]. There is no doubt that they call each of these gods, a matter which would require lengthy discussion; provided it is certain that pagans call individual things from the elements gods, or call the discoverers of the elements gods, or fashion gods for themselves from the elements—for example, gods from earth, but gods through fire. Then they call certain demons aerial; others empyrean; others watery (*enydri*); others genii, that is, terrestrial, aquatic, aerial, and fiery beings.

If pagans do these things, he perhaps also rebukes them for having turned to paganism, especially since he had said above: “Before you knew God and did not know God, you served those who are not gods.” This must certainly be understood of pagans in the preceding passage as well.

Nevertheless, since the whole course and treatment of this argument has been undertaken in order to rebuke the Galatians for turning to Judaism, and since all these things are to be understood of Jews, we understand “how do you turn again to weak things” accordingly. Therefore, when he says “the needy elements of this world,” let us understand that those who understand the Law carnally seem to have turned to elements which are needy. For the flesh is always needy and desires to be sustained by foods, drinks, and desires; yet all these things are weak. Therefore, when he says, “You turn to weak and needy elements,” he means those which are always in need; for soul and spirit have no need and desire nothing except what belongs to them.

But when he says, “You have known God—or rather, have been known by God,” he preserves the force of his own teaching: that those come to Christ whom God sends and whom God calls, and that those know the Lord whom God has known. We have said much above on this subject. [Col. 1180D] For those known by God receive the Spirit by which they know God. Yet, in order that they may be known by God and be persons known to God, they are already guided by that ruling Spirit which was given so that the soul might be subject to those divine commandments of its Father. When the soul stirs itself, God knows it; and thus the soul knows God. [Col. 1181A]

When he called them “the needy elements of this world,” he did not mean that there are other elements, so that these are needy elements of this world and there are elements which are needy; although we may also call the things above “elements.” But this is very remote from ordinary usage. [Note: Observe the term.]

“To which you wish to be enslaved again.” Plainly: as he said above, before you knew God you served those who are not gods; now, therefore, you wish to serve them again. He says “you wish,” so that it may be a matter of their will, not of necessity.

But that these things may seem to be spoken to and about Jews—that is, to Galatians who attach Jewish observance to themselves—he adds as follows.

### Verse 10

“You observe days and months and seasons and years.” Since “seasons” is a general term covering all these, why are days, months, and years also inserted? It is as though they are distinct, which indeed they can be. For it is one thing to observe days, as when one rests on the Sabbath; another to observe months, as when one observes the new moon, when the moon ends or begins; another to observe years; and another, truly, to observe seasons: fasting, Passover, Unleavened Bread, and the other things of this kind, which are numerous among the Jews. For these are not years, months, or days, but seasons. [Col. 1181B]

### Verse 11

“I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain.” That is, I greatly fear lest all my labor in the Gospel by which I instructed you to have faith in Christ should come to nothing. For what I taught you will be in vain when you begin to keep Jewish observances and discipline.

### Verse 12

“Become as I am, because I also am as you are.” [Note: The Vulgate has *quia*, “because.”] For, he says, just as I passed over from Jewish discipline, believed in Christ, serve him, and do otherwise—and taught you this, becoming such a person as I made you—so live as I live; and if you live, I live. [Col. 1181C]

### Verse 13

“Brothers, I beseech you: you have done me no wrong. You know that through weakness of the flesh I preached the Gospel to you formerly.” This inserted statement pertains to persuasion, that we may follow Christ in all things. To commend this more readily, he recalls the beginnings of his Gospel. First he commends his labors: though he was weak in body and suffering, he nevertheless imposed labor upon himself and preached the Gospel to the Galatians. He also added “formerly,” that is, long ago. Thus your love toward me and faith toward Christ ought to have been strengthened, since a long time has passed.

“I spared not my body,” he says, “but through weakness of the flesh I preached the Gospel to you, and I preached it long ago. Why, then, do you add other things which I did not preach to you?” When he said, “You have done me no wrong,” he added this: I have withheld nothing from you, I have said nothing less [than I should have said], as one does who has been wronged. And lest they suppose that they had been a burden to him when he preached while weak in body, he says: “You have done me no wrong; though I was weak in body because of you, I preached the Gospel to you long ago—and this you surely know.” [Col. 1182A]

### Verse 14

“And you did not despise or reject your trial in my flesh.” [Note: Observe the division of the sentence, differing from the Vulgate.]

What we should understand by “your trial” is ambiguous to me: whether you tried me, or I tried you. That you tried me has no sense, for they did not try him. But then, did Paul himself try them, when he spoke truth and preached Christ? For to preach the Gospel is not to try.

What then, since there is no third possibility? Should we understand that, when Paul came to the Galatians, they wished to try him—that is, to question him and inquire whether he knew anything about Christ? This might indeed seem a trial, since the Galatians saw Paul as a weak man, weak in the flesh. That is: since he serves God and preaches God, yet is weak in body, perhaps this was their thought: “Let us question him; let us see what this man, weak in body, answers concerning Christ.”

“You did not despise this in my flesh,” he says; “and though you tried me, you did not scorn your trial in my flesh.” For to scorn it would have been not to question him, and to think that what they sought—that is, asked, which is what it means to try—could be falsely heard from him: believing, I say, that a false answer would be given them by one weak in the flesh.

But you persevered and did not scorn your trial in my flesh; rather, you came to me to see whether I remained in my faith and in the Gospel. Thus you tried one weak in body, asking whether my resolve to preach the Gospel remained firm although I was weak in body. That is, you did not reject me as weak in the flesh and therefore less fit to answer, or as someone who might change his view because he was weak in body. In this he also gave the reason why it could not have happened, or did not happen, that his evangelical teaching was different: for I was weak in body, not in mind or spirit.

Thus he says that they had, as it were, considered that he was weak in body but not in spirit; and for that reason they persevered in trying him and neither rejected him nor declined to try him. That is, they did not scorn or despise their trial in his flesh. Finally, that they themselves understood Paul to be weak in body but not in spirit he shows from what follows: “But you received me as an angel, as Christ Jesus.” [Col. 1182C]

Indeed, my bodily weakness was no impediment to you; rather, you received me as an angel of God—that is, as a messenger, a preacher sent from God; for this is an angel of God. And you received me as Christ Jesus, whom I preached to you. Thus you truly received Christ Jesus if you received me as an angel of God; this is how you received Christ Jesus. [Col. 1182D]

### Verse 15

“Where then was your blessedness?” He now shows that they are wretched, since formerly they had possessed blessedness because they had received Jesus Christ and Paul as an angel of God. Great, he says, was your blessedness; it “was,” he says. Now, therefore, the contrary is surely true, since you add things which I did not teach or impart, things outside the Gospel—namely, those things mentioned above.

“For I testify to you that, if it were possible, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me.” [Col. 1183A] You received me so, and had such a disposition and will toward me, that, since nothing is dearer to a human being than the eyes, you would have wished to pluck out even your own eyes and give them to me. Therefore, since you loved me so, and loved me for the Gospel, how has this resolve arisen in you, that you add to the teaching things which I did not preach to you? That is, that beyond Christ you should do something from the Law, rather than, as I delivered it simply, having hope, faith, and belief in Christ, hoping all things, believing that you can obtain all things—remission of sins, sanctification, and the glory of God? [Col. 1183B]

### Verse 16

“Then have I become your enemy by preaching the truth to you?” [Note: Vulgate: “Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?”] For if you have begun to do other things, I have become your enemy to you. But since I foretold and preached to you Christ and the Gospel—that Christ is truly the one Son of God, that all things are through him and in Christ, and that he himself is before all things—since this is true and is truth itself, why have I become your enemy to you? For he ought to be an enemy who, when asked what is true, teaches falsehood. But since I have spoken truth—for one who preaches Christ speaks truth—it is not fitting that I should have become your enemy. [Col. 1183C]

### Verses 17–18

“They are jealous of you, but not rightly; and they wish to exclude you, that you may be zealous for them. But be zealous for better gifts.” [Note: Vulgate: “They are jealous of you, but not rightly; but they do not wish to exclude you, that you may be zealous for them. But be zealous for the good always, and not only when I am present with you.”]

He warns them often to beware of snares: those who persuade the Galatians also to follow the Jewish Law, he says, “are jealous of you,” that is, they envy you. For *aemulari* has two meanings: one, when someone is zealous for something because it pleases him and is good; the other, when people are jealous because they envy. “They are jealous of you,” he says, “not rightly,” thereby showing that they are jealous through envy.

Then he adds, “They wish to exclude you,” that is, from that happiness and blessedness, because by knowing Christ you possess the hope of salvation and heavenly glory. But they desire to exclude you from this. And when he adds, “that you may be zealous for them”—that you too may follow them—he uses the twofold meaning of zeal in different places, since zeal is imitation, especially when it is for good. This is what he says here: “that you may be zealous for them,” that is, that you may follow what belongs to them as though it were good.

But in saying “they are jealous of you,” and then adding “not rightly,” he shows that “jealousy” here means envy. “Be zealous, however, for better gifts”—not for the things the Jews possess, which are not good and are not better, but for things that are good and for better gifts; that is, be zealous for whatever belongs to faith and love in relation to Christ, and follow it. It is good always to be zealous for better things. Not, “To be zealous is good,” but, “To be zealous for better things, and always, is good.” And not only when I am present with you. [Col. 1184A]

### Verse 19

“My children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you.” [Note: Vulgate: “My little children.”] You ought, he says, to be zealous not only while I am present, but always. Therefore, to the word “always” he adds, “and not only when I am present with you.”

As for the addition “my children”: this is said in many ways—now by affection, now by nature, now by blood, and now also by religion, as Paul says here, “my children.” It may be because, through baptism, when regeneration occurs, the one who performs the baptism or receives the baptized person when he has been completed is called father; [Note: Observe the ancient custom of receiving the baptized, and of calling and regarding as fathers those who baptized and received them; this is spiritual kinship in ecclesiastical law.] or because, when he renews them in Christ, he makes them his children. Therefore he adds, “for whom I am in labor,” that is, whom I desire to bring forth into the light, whom with great pains of my soul I desire to be born to life and salvation. For this is what he means by “until Christ be formed in you.”

Every soul can receive Christ: the soul, I say, of a human being, if it uses reason, if it recognizes the world as not its own, if it discerns all things in the world, if it acknowledges its Creator. Indeed, Christ—that is, the Spirit—is formed in that very soul; when implanted and growing through faith, he liberates it, brings it to the heavenly kingdoms, and obtains for it the salvation of eternal light. [Col. 1184C]

Great indeed is the force and power of what he says: “until Christ be formed in you.” The discourse which is now ours gives a simple exposition of the words; and we have said above what we believe sufficient for this. But what Christ is, what it is for Christ to be formed, and for him to be formed in a human being, is unfolded and explained by us elsewhere in a loftier and truer exposition.

### Verse 20

“But I would wish to be present with you now and to change my voice, because I am perplexed about you.” [Note: The Vulgate omits “now,” and reads “to be” for “to be present.”] These precepts, as we see, are given by letter. But he spoke with great indignation when he said, “Would that I were now with you and changed my voice!”—not that I would proclaim the Gospel differently, but that I would express myself in anger.

Now he admonishes them through the letter which he sends. He added the reason for his justified anger when he said, “I am perplexed about you,” that is, I am tormented by shame that you who were quickly converted are losing so great a faith, and are not holding fast to the labor, the Gospel, and the truth that was imparted to you. For this produces great confusion in me concerning you. Finally, though in anger and indeed with agitation, he adds:

### Verse 21

“Tell me, you who wish to be under the Law: have you not read the Law?” From the Law itself, to which they had passed over, he wishes to persuade them. For provided that they read the Law itself, he strives, I say, to persuade them from the Law itself that it was written in such a manner that faith should be placed in Christ, and that faith placed in Christ is the whole liberation, the whole salvation, and all blessedness. [Col. 1185A]

With what indignation, then, he says, “Tell me”? I do not admonish you, but answer me yourselves: you have surely passed over to the Law and wish to be under the Law, yet you have not read the Law, in which this is so written. And he adds what proves what the Law and discipline of the Jews are, what their hope and faith are, what faith in Christ is, and what its hope and blessedness are.

### Verse 22

“For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman.” This example is from Genesis. He wishes to prove that the Law belonging to the Jews, and the whole people, are as it were a son of the slave woman; but the Church and Christians are sons of the free woman. For it is written that Abraham, the father of faith, had one son by a slave woman—that is, Hagar—and another, Isaac, by a free woman—that is, Sarah. This signifies two peoples; but the latter, who is from the free woman, is better, for Isaac is a figure and type of Christ. Thus he adds:

### Verse 23

“But he indeed who was of the slave woman was born according to the flesh; but he who was of the free woman, through promise.” He who was born of the slave woman is a fleshly son; but he who was of the free woman is spiritual, because he was promised by God. For God promised him to the believer, that although he himself and his wife had already reached nearly a hundred years, they would have a son. Therefore, when they came together, whether the seed had died or even the womb had died, they begot the son whom they begot no longer from flesh but from Spirit. And this was the promise: that they would have him. [Col. 1185C]

But we shall compare these two sons, and likewise their mothers, with the peoples and churches of Jews and Christians. Paul, however, adds a different interpretation as follows.

### Verses 24–25

“These things are said allegorically …” Thus we too have interpreted them, as though allegorically. When one thing is said and another signified, this is allegory. Yet Paul himself interprets the allegory, as he adds: “For these are the two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem which now is.”

The Jewish people, he says—or the old covenant—signifies the son of the slave woman; and the slave woman is she who was from Mount Sinai. Since the slave woman was in slavery, this people too is in slavery. And because Mount Sinai was joined to the city which is Jerusalem, he wished the city to be understood from the mountain, and the Jews through the city. Through the mountain, moreover, that slave woman who was from the same Mount Sinai bore children into slavery; therefore Jerusalem too—that is, the people of that city—and the covenant written concerning that same city are in slavery with their children. [Col. 1185D–1186A]

### Verse 26

“But the Jerusalem above is free, the mother of us all.” [Note: Vulgate: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother.”] He returns to that people, that is, the sons of Abraham who are of the free woman, and says that this Jerusalem, which he calls free, is in heaven. This is what he says: “the Jerusalem above,” and above the heavens; surely because it is not in the world, it does not serve.

Therefore Jerusalem is free with its peoples, and he calls it the mother of us all—that is, of Christians; the other, the mother of Jews. What does it mean for Jerusalem to be above the heavens, while Jerusalem also exists on earth? From this one may understand that there is earth here and earth there, above the heavens; [Note: An undoubtedly curious question: whether another earth above the heavens will be discovered. Does Victorinus hint at some millenarian opinion?] for Jerusalem, which is a city, is not without earth. What, then, it means that there is earth here and there, and city here and there, but that one is free and this one enslaved, is another and lengthy discussion. For the moment, let us retain this: that Jerusalem is ours, and that we must hasten toward it. For I now indicate provisionally that the higher Jerusalem is spiritual, while this lower one is fleshly. [Col. 1186B]

### Verse 27

“For it is written: ‘Rejoice, barren woman, you who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for many are the children of the desolate woman, more than of her who has a husband.’”

This example is from Isaiah, intended to exclude what they were especially trying to persuade the Galatians to do: namely, though they had adopted Christ’s worship and faith in Christ, to keep Jewish observance as well. To exclude this, I say, so that they might reject it and hold only the Gospel concerning Christ, he had cited above the example teaching that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman.

The free woman, who was truly a wife, was barren; for she would not have borne a child unless God, by his promise, had granted her a son. Hence it is understood that Abraham had a son not through the bodily union of their bodies but through God’s promise. For this son of the free woman, Isaac, was born of a barren woman—conceived rather by a certain Spirit than by union. [Col. 1186C]

Therefore this barren woman bore Isaac, a son born as an image and type of Christ; he is the one who freed the people. Thus when he says, “Rejoice, barren woman, you who do not bear,” because God makes children for you; and likewise when he says, “Break forth, you who do not travail,” because children are created for you without pain—for to travail is to be in pain when the child is brought forth—this is not in the same manner as with the Church, which bears the image, or whose image was that free wife of Abraham. The Church, I say, has many children, whom it possesses as sons of God and sons of the Spirit more with joy than pain.

These, then, he calls the many children of the desolate woman. For the slave woman, even though she had a son, had him in pain and had him by a man. Therefore, when he says, “many are the children of the desolate woman,” he refers it to the Church, whose image and type she supplied above. Then, when he says, “many are the children of the desolate woman, more than of her who has a husband,” he shows what was said above: that she had a son without a man, but spiritually. For he would never give this woman a husband unless that other woman had received a husband not through union with a man but through a spiritual promise. [Col. 1187A]

And certainly, he says, many are the children of the desolate woman. Since Sarah had one son, this cannot be referred to Sarah but to the Church, which has many children. Thus she who has a husband is the Law and the church of the Jews, which consents bodily; when bodily union is made with it, it cannot have a son spiritually.

### Verse 28

“But you, brothers, are children of promise according to Isaac.” [Note: Vulgate: “But we … are.”] By this comparison he separates them plainly: the Jews appear to be children of the slave woman, whereas Christians are children of the free woman. For just as the son promised to Sarah is spiritual, so you also, who are children of faith, are children of the free woman according to Isaac. That is, Isaac was a son according to faith. Thus every son is [such] who is according to faith; for according to faith he receives a son spiritually, and [is] Isaac, a spiritual son. [Col. 1187B]

### Verse 29

“But just as then, he who was according to the Spirit, so also now.” [Note: Vulgate: “But as then he who had been born according to the flesh, so also now.”] By a full exposition he shows that he who was born according to the flesh—that is, from the slave woman—persecuted him, namely Isaac, who was according to the Spirit, as is read in Genesis. So now those who have a fleshly understanding persecute those who live according to the Spirit—that is, Christians. [Col. 1187C]

Finally, to display the force of the whole argument he has conceived, he adds:

### Verse 30

“But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.’” [Note: Vulgate: “with the son of the free woman.”] From this example in Genesis he declares quite plainly that whoever thinks in this way and receives the Jewish Law carnally is a son according to the flesh. Concerning such a son the Law itself has pronounced and given judgment: “Cast out the slave woman and her son,” because the slave woman’s son cannot be heir with the son of the free woman, Isaac.

Therefore you too, since you have added observance of the Law according to the flesh in order that you may more readily be heirs, be sons of the free woman. That is, receive Christianity alone, the Law of Christ and the Gospel in Christ, and have nothing, as it were, from the son of the slave woman—that is, follow Jewish observance. [The supplied text is internally awkward at this point.] [Col. 1187D]

### Verse 31

“Therefore, brothers, let us not be children of the slave woman, but of the free woman.” [Note: Vulgate: “Therefore, brothers, we are not …”] By adding this, he himself explains it more aptly: you who have now received Christ and my faith are not children of the slave woman—that is, you do not think carnally, because the slave woman’s son is fleshly—but are children of the free woman, that is, children of faith. For Isaac was this: a spiritual son according to faith and promise.

“The freedom by which Christ has set us free”: namely, the freedom by which our mother, the free woman, is free—that is, by faith. For this is true freedom: to preserve faith in God, and to believe God and all God’s promises. Therefore, according to faith Christ has led us back to freedom and has made us free by the freedom of faith.

- [Col. 1177D] (2) The manuscripts read *descenderet* (“should descend”) for *discederet* (“should depart”).
- [Col. 1177D] (3) The manuscripts read *intelligere* (“to understand”).
- [Col. 1177D] (4) The manuscripts read *quoniam non* (“because not”).
- [Col. 1178D] (1) 1 Corinthians 7:39.
- [Col. 1178D] (2) “Merely” also belongs to the preceding clause.
- [Col. 1178D] (3) The manuscripts read *hominem* (“man”) for *hoc* (“this”).
- [Col. 1178D] (4) Victorinus uses *potentia* (“power”) for “person.” Thus, if a recently edited title of a little work by Nicetas, *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*, is to be understood in this way, it means “the Person [of the Holy Spirit].”
- [Col. 1178D] (5) *Cognoscentia* (“knowledge”) is a word not unusual even in Victorinus’s published writings.
- [Col. 1179D] (1) The manuscripts read *in eum vocem* (“a voice toward him”).
- [Col. 1179D] (2) Thus the manuscripts.
- [Col. 1179D] (3) Victorinus’s expression here and elsewhere will certainly seem obscure and impeded to readers; yet that he suffers from this defect in his other writings also is thoroughly established, so that Petavius calls him, as it were, another Heraclitus, σκοτεινός (“the Obscure”).
- [Col. 1179D] (4) The manuscripts read *efficiamur* (“we may become”).
- [Col. 1179D] (5) Thus the manuscripts: *non es* (“you are no longer”), rather than *non est* (“he is no longer”).
- [Col. 1179D] (6) The Vulgate reads, “But if [you are] a son.”
- [Col. 1179D] (7) The manuscripts read *appellatur num superiora erit*. But in the old codex *dum superiora erit* is deleted. I nevertheless retain *erit* (“he will be”).
- [Col. 1179D] (8) The manuscripts read *nunc* (“now”), the Vulgate *autem* (“but”), [whereas the text reads *tunc*, “then”].
- [Col. 1179D] (9) The Vulgate reads: “But then … you served those who by nature are not gods.”
- [Col. 1180D] (1) Compare the Vulgate, which reads here: “But now that you have known God—or rather have been known by God—how,” etc.
- [Col. 1180D] (2) Thus the manuscripts.
- [Col. 1180D] (3) The manuscripts read *agenda* (“things to be done”) for *egena* (“needy”).
- [Col. 1180D] (4) Thus the manuscripts here and elsewhere.
- [Col. 1180D] (5) Victorinus retains his habit of frequently referring to his own writings even in his published works.
- [Col. 1180D] (6) The manuscripts read *scripta* (“written things”) for *subdita* (“subject”).
- [Col. 1181D] (1) Note the word.
- [Col. 1181D] (2) The Vulgate reads *denuo* (“again”).
- [Col. 1181D] (3) The manuscripts read *ut* (“that”) for *cur* (“why”).
- [Col. 1181D] (4) We still use [*tempora*, “seasons”] in ecclesiastical speech.
- [Col. 1181D] (5) The manuscripts read *ut* (“that”) for *aut* (“or”).

- [Col. 1181D] (7) The manuscripts read *infirmis* (“weak persons”).

- [Col. 1182D] (2) The Vulgate reads: “but as an angel … as Christ.”
- [Col. 1182D] (3) The Vulgate reads, “Where, then, is,” etc.

- [Col. 1183D] (2) The manuscripts read *vellitis*, then *factum velitis*. I preferred *velletis*.

- [Col. 1183D] (4) These verses are read in the Vulgate: “They are jealous of you, but not rightly; but they do not wish to exclude you, that you may be zealous for them. But be zealous for the good always, and not only when I am present with you.”
- [Col. 1184D] (1) The Vulgate reads *filioli mei* (“my little children”).
- [Col. 1184D] (2) Note the ancient custom of receiving baptized persons, and of calling and considering as fathers those who baptized and those who received them; this is spiritual kinship in ecclesiastical law.

## Chapter V
VERS. 1.—Stand firm, therefore, and do not again be held under a yoke of slavery. The exhortation was to be added that they should persevere in the same things which they had received from him through the Gospel, and not return again to the servitude of the Law. “Stand,” he says—a thing not permitted to one who is under a yoke; for such a person bends down a lowered neck. Therefore he does not stand. “You, therefore,” he says, “stand”: that is, hold your body upright with free limbs. “Do not,” he says, “again be held under a yoke of slavery,” because formerly you were slaves either to the Law or to paganism. He therefore says “again,” lest we return to the same condition.

VERS. 2.—Behold, I Paul say to you that, if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing. He plainly shows that Christ is of no benefit if anyone places hope in circumcision—and in circumcision of the flesh. Therefore, when you join to yourselves Jewish custom, commandments, and discipline, if you place salvation and deliverance in these things, “I say,” he says, “to you”—and it is Paul, of course, who says it, he who formerly promised you when he called you to God’s Gospel—“I, Paul, deny that Christ benefits you or brings you any assistance, if you are circumcised,” if you place all hope in circumcision.

Although the Galatians seem both to have received Christ and to have joined Jewish discipline to him, nevertheless he affirmed and, as it were, bound his own person to what he says in declaring: “Christ will profit you nothing if you are circumcised.” It may therefore seem that there is something hidden here. For since the Galatians follow Christ, and, following Christ, place their hope of salvation in him, how could Paul affirm that Christ would profit the Galatians nothing if they were circumcised? While preserving their disposition and faith toward Christ, they do something additional; yet they do not abandon Christ or cease to place faith in Christ.

But let us return to their disposition, purpose, and intention. Since they had received Christ from Paul, taken up faith in Christ, and since this is the true Gospel, they necessarily thought that they would receive less from Christ. This is already blasphemy and the attitude of those without faith: after receiving Christ, they wished to be circumcised and to serve the Law and its works. If this is so, there is no faith in Christ. Because something else that may profit is added, rightly does he say: “Christ will profit you nothing.”

VERS. 3.—For I testify to every man who circumcises himself that he is bound to perform the whole Law. The Galatians were not to suppose that they needed to take up only certain elements of the Jewish Law, such as circumcision, while disregarding the rest: matters of food, observance of days, and the kind of union and the things involved in it which the Law prescribes. Among all these, some things are superfluous and some almost abominable; thus they are left aside by the true and most chaste Christian.

I shall mention only one: when, for the purpose of raising up offspring, a brother’s wife is joined to her brother-in-law. Other such things are either done or read as having been done. Likewise, the other matters I mentioned—foods, then observances, and many other things—must also be adopted, he says, by one who is circumcised. If you do not do the other things, you have employed circumcision in vain. For I testify that every man who circumcises himself becomes obligated to perform everything that belongs to the Law.

Thus he makes them sinners also under that Law which they have adopted, because they do not do everything but select what is to be done. And again, with respect to the Law which is Christ’s and to the Gospel altogether, they go astray—and will go still further astray—if they perform all that belongs to the Law. Accordingly, he now adds from this point, since they perform certain things that the Jews do, that in this respect they appear alienated from Christ.

VERS. 4.—You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the Law; you have fallen from grace. For the whole power of one who believes in Christ lies in God’s grace. Grace, moreover, comes not from merits but from God’s mercy. Therefore you have now fallen from grace if you place your justification in the Law: because you serve works, observe the Sabbath, and are circumcised, you have fallen from grace and been emptied of Christ. For you no longer have hope from Christ, nor do you hope for grace through his passion and resurrection, if you believe justification comes to you from the Law.

VERS. 5.—For we await in spirit and faith the hope of righteousness. “We Christians,” he says, “and those who follow Christ, have hope both in spirit and in faith, and in God’s justification—not from works.” The entire power of the mystery has accomplished this: that through grace and God’s mercy forgiveness of sins might be granted to us and eternal life bestowed, as we have often taught, by God’s grace, not by works or merits. This happens through the Spirit. But when justification is hoped for from works, hope is not from the Spirit. This is what we await, and this is to follow Christ’s Gospel.

VERS. 6.—For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor foreskin has any power, but faith working through love. Everywhere he teaches concerning faith in Christ’s Gospel that neither circumcision nor acts concerning the body, from the body, or for the body—such as circumcision, works, and the like—have any force. None of these things, he says, has force in Christ; circumcision is futile.

Nor do we have power in Christ because of foreskin; rather, because we have received faith in him, believe his promises, and because through his resurrection we too rise again. We have suffered all things with him and, through him, rise with him to life. We have sure faith, through which there is activity unto salvation; and we ought to receive it through the love which we have toward Christ and God, and then toward every human being.

For these two things especially reform the whole of life, fulfill the entire force of the Law, and contain all the commandments of the Decalogue. Whoever preserves faith consequently preserves love. These two fulfill all that Christ’s Law commanded. I have discussed these matters very frequently: faith liberates, and love builds up.

VERS. 7.—You were running well; who hindered you? That is, you had sound faith concerning the Gospel. Why have you changed? Why have you been recalled from your unbroken course as if by some spell? For what I taught you through the Gospel was whole and true; this is both false and contrary, and will profit nothing. This is what he adds: “not to obey the truth.” “Who,” he says, “hindered you from obeying the truth?” For truth is in us; you ought to have obeyed it, lest you observe anything else.

Thus at first he seems amazed when he says, “Who hindered you?” Afterwards he admonishes them about what must be done: consent to no one. He fights in every way against their changing their judgment and adding anything beyond what had been commanded them through the Gospel by Paul. “Do not,” he says, “give your assent to others.”

VERS. 8.—Your persuasion is from God, who called us. That is, either what was persuaded to you by me, or what you yourselves have already received as persuasion from God who called you, as was said above: those whom he called, he also predestined; and all the other things said in sequence.

VERS. 9.—Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? All leaven is corruption of bread, and corrupted bread is flour; when a mass of flour is left, it turns sour and thereby becomes leaven. But when a little leaven is put into a lump, the lump is corrupted. “You ought,” he says, “to be unleavened.”

Therefore, what you think you have added only a little of—namely, the observance of circumcision—this little thing, because it is corrupt, corrupts the lump of our Gospel, so that you may not have complete hope in Christ, nor may Christ regard you as his own, as persons hoping in him and from him. For faith liberates; and, as we have said, one who hopes for assistance in any way apart from Christ—even alongside Christ—does not have faith.

VERS. 10.—I have confidence concerning you in the Lord that you will think nothing else. “I now have confidence,” he says, “about the future: that you will hold nothing else in heart and understanding except to have faith in Christ alone according to my Gospel.” But whoever troubles you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be. He frightened both those who were leading them astray and these others by threats of future judgment: “Whoever disturbs you,” he says, “will bear judgment.” It was enough to name judgment, in which it need not have been said that they would suffer punishment, but rather judgment itself. He had already almost expressed fear when he said, “will bear.”

VERS. 11.—But I, brothers, if I preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? In every way he proves himself foreign to the precept which they thought should be added. He suffers persecution from the Jews. For what reason? Unless because he does not preach circumcision. Therefore I did not preach circumcision to you in the Gospel, as is clear from the fact that the Jews persecute me.

He adds another argument to show that he does not preach circumcision. “Then has the scandal of the cross been abolished?” In vain, then, do those deserve punishment who raised Christ upon the cross, and abolished is that evil deed. For this is the scandal of the cross, over which the Jews were troubled. He now refers this not only to his own preaching, but also to the force of the matter itself. “For this reason I do not preach it: because the scandal of the cross remains and has not been abolished. Therefore they ought to suffer punishment. But if the Jews ought to suffer it, since they caused the scandal of the cross, it follows that I too ought not to preach circumcision and that you ought not to follow it.”

VERS. 12.—Would that those who trouble you were cut off! He pursued with a curse those who introduce these new persuasions among them and trouble them. “Let them be cut off,” he says, “from the truth of the Gospel; or let them separate themselves, or be torn by punishments.” With great confidence he launched this curse against them, to show that he did not fear those of whom he had said above that he suffered persecution. Thus: I do not fear persecution because I preach truth and do not preach circumcision; nor do I fear to suffer persecution. “Would that those who trouble you were cut off!” Not merely circumcised, but cut off altogether: so that this word too is so used as to concern circumcision, namely, “cutting off” (*abscisio*).

VERS. 13.—For you, brothers, were called to freedom; only do not misuse freedom as an occasion for the flesh. For Christ’s Law, which is spiritual, gives freedom by which we leave the world and return to the Father and to our origin. But because we are still in the world—that is, in the flesh—we ought not to exercise the freedom we have received in such a way as to walk according to the flesh, as though faith in Christ, by affirming that we are free, provided us an occasion to act in the flesh.

Through love of the Spirit serve one another. We have received granted freedom; nevertheless we ought to serve one another through love, and through love of the Spirit, not of the flesh.

VERS. 14.—For the whole Law is fulfilled among you in one saying. He has often made this point, and we have discussed it: the whole Law and every work of the Law are fulfilled in this saying, namely love. For one who loves another neither commits adultery nor steals; and this is also to love Christ. The things shown by the Decalogue are in a sense fulfilled in this single commandment, as we said above.

He himself adds an example from Exodus: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” We must understand every human being as a neighbor; and then we shall also have Christ as our neighbor. Therefore you too love yourselves—but in the Spirit. Here he now seems, as though leaving aside the preceding question and discussion, to give a precept of exhortation: that they should not love discord but love one another. This can happen if you love one another in the Spirit, not in the flesh, nor in works of the flesh, nor in observances of the flesh. For one who loves another cheats no one, deprives no one, harms no one, despises no one, and rebukes no one.

VERS. 15.—But if you bite and accuse one another, see that you are not consumed by one another. An exhortation to concord is made by showing what evil discord does. For if you accuse and bite one another—that is, if you wish to harm one another or do harm—you will consume one another. Therefore love yourselves and one another, and you will fulfill the Law by love alone, not, as you suppose, by circumcision, works, and other matters in addition.

Accordingly, this statement concerning love is added in keeping with the preceding discussion, in which he taught them that they thought they were observing the Law in circumcision and works beyond the Gospel that Paul himself had proclaimed to them, whereas the Law is wholly fulfilled in this alone: that they love one another.

VERS. 16.—But I say to you: walk in the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desire of the flesh. The whole power of the Gospel is this: to live according to the Spirit, to believe according to the Spirit, and to hold nothing of the flesh in one’s mind, action, or life—that is, not even to receive one’s hope from the flesh. “Walk, therefore,” he says, “in the Spirit,” that is, conduct your life thus. If you do so, you will not fulfill the flesh’s desire; that is, you will admit no sin born from the flesh. For there is no other desire except one from the flesh. Therefore he adds:

VERS. 17.—For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. He teaches these people altogether that they ought to think nothing from the flesh, as occurs in circumcision and the other observances of Jewish discipline, since these things are opposed to one another. The flesh not only desires, but desires against the Spirit. For the flesh has its own motions and perceptions; they are not aroused only by the soul. This may be understood even from things that have no soul: for example, water, which has its own impulses and powers, whether in taste, motion, quality, or quantity; likewise fire, earth, and the other elements, from which there is, as it were, a certain mixture, and the flesh was made from moist elements.

[Note: From this verse, 17, until the beginning of chapter VI, the manuscripts contain no commentary. It is altogether incredible that Victorinus should have left almost ten clauses unexplained. I therefore judge that some leaf fell out of the ancient exemplar from which the Vatican paper manuscripts were derived.
