Later copyists either did not recognize this lacuna or at least did not mention it. We shall shortly encounter another lacuna at the beginning of the Epistle to the Philippians.]

CAP. VI.

[Col. 1193A]

VERS. 1.—Those who are spiritual. As though addressing one of them individually, he expressed it thus, so that each of them might consider lest he too be tempted; and therefore ought to assist and instruct such a person and, through the Spirit given, restore him by admonition to modesty and equality.

VERS. 2.—Bear one another’s burdens. He returns to the plural number, so that every person may bear another’s evils; and may bear, endure, and correct, insofar as possible, what another suffers. For this is to bear burdens: patiently to endure and correct another’s fault. And thus you will fulfill the Law of Christ. For he too was patient, bore our evils, and himself endured for our evils. “You will fulfill,” he says, “the Law of Christ,” not simply the Law.

VERS. 3.—For if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. He now proves by reasoning why the one who boasts in desire for glory must be corrected and instructed in the Spirit: because wretched is the person who leads himself astray, deludes and deceives himself, who thinks himself something when he is nothing. For if this is the sum of the Law—that whoever is humble, lowly, and least is chosen by God from among the lowly, to be raised and made great—then every person who claims something for himself and judges himself to be something is without doubt nothing.

For what in the world is anything, when nothing is in the world? Thus to act as though one were nothing in the world is to be something before God. But if anyone thinks himself something in the world—wise, intelligent, lord, king, rich, or any such thing; in wealth, mind, skill, or strength—then, because the wisdom of the world is foolishness before God, that person is nothing; and, being nothing, he deceives and deludes himself.

[Note: “A most admirable doctrine indeed: that the hinge and summit of religion consist in Christian humility. This teaching is all the more remarkable in a man who had become famous with such great honors and had lived as a pagan into old age. Jerome, *Letter* 108.15, agrees: ‘the first virtue of Christians is humility.’”]

VERS. 4.—But let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another. Great exhortations, and great discipline as well! Let no one, he says, claim anything for himself or hold the opinion that he is something. Let each only test his own work—indeed, let each test his own work by his own judgment, lest, employing a bad judge, he approve himself as having done well when perhaps he has not done well.

Therefore let him test and make his work approved; when the work has been approved, then he will have glory in himself alone, not in another. For one who thinks himself something boasts and seeks glory from another. But one who either himself approves his work or proves it to others has glory from himself and within himself, and does not expect it from another. “For,” he says, “I do not wish to be praised by a human being or approved by human beings, but by God.”

VERS. 5.—For each person will bear his own burden. “Burden” is used indifferently, whether for good or evil. Therefore all will bear their own burden, each his own.

VERS. 6.—Let the one who is instructed in the word share in all good things with the one who instructs. The meaning is this: *katēchizein* [κατηχίζειν] means “to sound around” or “to sound alongside,” which occurs when someone first begins to be a Christian and God and Christ are sounded alongside him, spoken into his ears, and instilled into his mind. This is “one who is instructed in the word”: that is, someone instructed through the word, so that it may sound alongside him through invocation.

The one instructed in the word should share in all good things with the one who instructs: that is, in no matter should he fail to hold things in common with him; rather, he should share all things with the one who instructs in the word—but all things that are good. For since it was said above, “Instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness,” that which he teaches is surely good; and the one who teaches this very good word teaches in good things. Therefore let the one who is instructed in the word share with the one who instructs.

VERS. 7.—Do not go astray; God is not mocked. He adds another precept, general indeed in application to all things, yet pertaining to what was discussed above: that they should not follow anything besides the Gospel—that is, that they should not add Jewish discipline and works as well. “Do not,” he says, “go astray; for all these things taken up outside the Gospel are errors.”

He adds the force of necessity to the precept: “God is not mocked.” He did not say, “For God knows all things,” lest they hope either for pardon of their error or that it can be hidden. “He is not mocked,” he says. Then he adds what will happen to those who maintain life on earth.

VERS. 8.—For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. That is, one who sows wheat will have a harvest of wheat; but if he sows tares, he will reap that. Whoever is a reaper of evil sows evil. Does he sow good? He will receive fruit from good. Thus the harvest is as the seed.

Because one who sows in his own flesh will also reap corruption from the flesh; but one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit. The Galatians thought Jewish discipline should be adopted by them: that they should observe Sabbaths, undertake circumcision, and perform other such things with a fleshly understanding; they had hope in and from the flesh. Therefore, whoever has hope in the flesh and sows his hope with respect to the flesh will have a harvest from the flesh—the fruit of which, however, he calls corruption.

For flesh decays, and its end is to decay, rot, perish, and be destroyed. Everything from the flesh rots and has corruption. No one ought therefore to hope from the flesh or sow in the flesh—that is, place hope in the flesh. For if one places hope there, one will have fruit from the flesh. What fruit? Destruction and corruption. This is the fruit of flesh.

It is better, therefore, to place hope in the Spirit, so that we may have hope from the Spirit. That hope which is from the Spirit, and that fruit which is from the Spirit—this is to sow in the Spirit: namely, eternal life. For this life is life, not eternal life. But one who is in the Spirit lives, acts according to the Spirit, does nothing carnally, sows eternal life for himself; and this will be his harvest: when departing from here, he will receive eternal life.

VERS. 9.—But in doing good let us not grow weary. It is too little merely to do good. Our merit is not at once acceptable to God because we do good, but only if we do not grow weary in doing it. For many begin, many seem to persevere, but afterwards cease, whether weary or led astray. Rightly, therefore, he admonished: “Let us not grow weary” in any way, lest by failing we abandon what we began, after beginning to do good. For in its own time we shall reap, if we do not grow weary.

This is well added. For many, if they suffer something evil in this manner of life called good, think they do good for no reason; exhausted, they stop doing good. What then does he add? “Let us not grow weary,” because although today we do not obtain the fruit of doing good, later, he says, we shall reap: that is, we shall have a harvest of our good deed, if we have not failed in doing good.

VERS. 10.—Therefore, while we have time, let us work. He gave the strongest urgency for doing good: time is imminent, life quickly ends, the world is already at its end. “While,” he says, “we have time”—whether the time of our own life or of this life in the world—“let us do good”; and let us do it toward all, so that there may be no exception of persons and no other kind of action. Let us do good, and toward all let us do good.

For if love builds up, and we ought to hold every human being dear, every good we do we do toward all. But especially toward the household of faith. He said, “Let us do good toward all”; yet he establishes a degree: of the good we do toward all, let us do good especially toward those who are of the household of faith, that is, those who have received faith in Christ and God.

He placed this in exhortation as a great conclusion, since it bore especially on the Galatians. For they, by adding certain things from Judaism, did not act from faith, but thought that through works and fleshly observance they would have fruit. Therefore he added: “Let us do good especially toward the household of faith,” who have received faith alone in the Gospel—that is, in Christ and God.

VERS. 11.—See with how large letters I have written to you with my own hand! To show affection, and lest they be ashamed that others knew they had either sinned or been corrected, “I have written to you with my own hand,” he says, giving them a sign of love. And change of life is easy for you when you are corrected by me, since you owe your conscience to me alone.

VERS. 12.—All who wish to please in the flesh compel you to be circumcised. He plainly states, under a description, precisely what he reproved in the Galatians: their transgression of the Gospel command when they wished to be circumcised. “All,” he says, “who wish to make a good appearance in the flesh persuade you to be circumcised.” This consists only in the act itself of being circumcised, not in any aid toward salvation.

They do it only so that they may not suffer persecution for Christ’s cross. They think, he says, that they will not pay penalties for raising Christ upon the cross and persecuting him, if you add—or if they themselves add—circumcision to the Gospel, that is, to confession concerning Christ. Yet they sin also in this: although all hope is in Christ, and still more in his cross, we—or they—suppose that something lies in circumcision as well. Therefore they persuade you, as though they may thereby avoid suffering persecution for Christ’s cross, that is, for having raised Christ upon the cross.

VERS. 13.—For those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the Law. For in Christ neither foreskin nor circumcision has force. What Law, then, does he mean? Either that which must be understood spiritually, or that which Christ gave, which is without doubt spiritual, teaches spiritual things, and must be practiced spiritually. But they wish you to be circumcised so that they may glory in your flesh.

He reveals the craftiness of those who persuade you, so that they may appear to have persuaded you and may glory in your flesh, though circumcision profits nothing. They seek only glory: that in your flesh they may think they have gained the point that without circumcision there is no hope, so that they may now seem to have won, lest hope rest in Christ alone unless the discipline of the Jewish Law is joined through circumcision as well.

VERS. 14.—But far be it from me to glory in anything. Previously he reproved their glory: for their glory is to glory in the flesh. “But I,” he says, “glory in nothing—neither in flesh, nor in a human being, nor in any such thing, nor in myself.” It has already been said and frequently urged that everyone who glories should glory in God, concerning which we spoke above.

Except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. That is, all hope should be placed there, and from it should come glory and joy, because in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ are our salvation and the eternity we seek. Through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. This is glory: namely, the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. For through that mystery, when he suspended flesh upon the cross and triumphed in it over the power of this world, the whole world was crucified through him.

But since he possessed a universal body for every human being, he made universal all that he suffered: that is, all flesh was crucified in him. Therefore I too have been crucified and fastened to the world. “I,” he says, “that fleshly person who thought according to the flesh, have been fastened to the world,” that is, subjected with the world to punishment.

VERS. 15.—For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision is anything nor foreskin, but a new creation. This is what we touched on above. Although this sense occurs everywhere, he teaches what the mystery has done: in Christ Jesus there is no rank, no distinction. All equally, whoever follow Christ, attain eternal life. Circumcision is not something in Christ merely because it is circumcision; nor is foreskin something in Christ merely because it is foreskin. Rather, in either condition, whoever one may be, provided that one is reborn and made a new person by the mystery, all have power in Christ.

VERS. 16.—And upon all who follow this rule, peace be upon them, and upon the Israel of the Lord. He concludes that this alone is the rule: to hope in Christ and not distinguish Christ’s power by foreskin or circumcision, but by the new creation—whatever it may be—in which through Christ and in Christ there is complete hope of salvation, eternity, and glory.

“Upon those,” he says, “who follow this rule”—not as you Galatians wished to hold it—“let peace be.” And he adds, “upon the Israel of the Lord”: not upon every Israelite who is a Jew, but upon the Israel of the Lord. For Israel is truly the Lord’s if it follows the Lord, so as not to hope for salvation from elsewhere.

VERS. 17.—Henceforth let no one cause me troubles. That is, let no one any longer make me anxious, sad, and subject to troubles by their sins. For at the beginning, we said that he took their sinning grievously and painfully. Therefore in the conclusion of the letter he admonishes them not to turn to any sins, lest they cause him troubles.

For I bear the marks of our Lord Jesus Christ in my body. That is, I bear every suffering, including those things which he endured on the cross: the nails fastening him, the wound of the lance through his side, and the rest—the marks of Jesus Christ our Lord I bear in my body. That is, I too have suffered, and in the mystery I serve Christ; I suffer Christ’s mystery. Therefore you too ought to endure many adversities—indeed, all things—because the one who suffers with Christ will be with Christ, and will himself begin in his own experience to suffer from hostile opponents the things Christ suffered. By this he shows both what he himself suffers, how much he deserves from Christ, and what we also must suffer if we wish to be with Christ.

VERS. 18.—The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. The letter ends with a prayer and blessing that grace may be present: “the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,” he says, “be with your spirit,” so that, because you live in Christ, Christ’s grace may be with your spirit.

[Col. 1197]

VICTORINUS: THE SINGLE BOOK ON PAUL’S EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS. (C)

CHAPTER I.

[Col. 1197C]

Textual and editorial notes:

- VERS. 1, [Col. 1188D] (1): The Vulgate omits “therefore.”
- VERS. 1, [Col. 1188D] (2): The manuscripts have *intellegis* (“you understand”) in place of “to the Law.”
- VERS. 1, [Col. 1188D] (3): The manuscripts read “he casts down [his head] with neck lowered” (*ulla deponit cervice summissa*).
- VERS. 2, [Col. 1188D] (6): *Aliqui* is used for *aliquis*, as has been observed in Cicero.
- VERS. 3, [Col. 1188D] (7): The Vulgate adds “again.”
- VERS. 5, [Col. 1189D] (1): The Vulgate reads “from faith” (*ex fide*).
- VERS. 6, [Col. 1189D] (2): The manuscripts read *conditionem* (“condition”) for “circumcision.”
- VERS. 6, [Col. 1190D] (1): The manuscripts read *continentur* (“are contained”).
- VERS. 6, [Col. 1190D] (2): *Qui* is used for *quis*, just as *aliqui* is used for *aliquis*.
- VERS. 7, [Col. 1190D] (3): The Vulgate has “you” (*vos*) for “to you” (*vobis*).
- VERS. 8, [Col. 1190D] (4): The Vulgate reads: “This persuasion is not from him who calls you.”
- VERS. 9, [Col. 1190D] (5): The Vulgate reads: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.”
- VERS. 10, [Col. 1190D] (6): The Vulgate has “in” (*in*) for “concerning” (*de*).
- VERS. 10, [Col. 1190D] (7): The Vulgate reads, “whoever that person is.”
- VERS. 10, [Col. 1191D] (1): The manuscripts read “by judgment” (*judicio*).
- VERS. 11, [Col. 1191D] (2): The Vulgate adds “still.”
- VERS. 11, [Col. 1191D] (3): The manuscripts read “will be troubled” (*conturbabuntur*).
- VERS. 12, [Col. 1191D] (4): The manuscripts read *abscio* (“I cut off”).
- VERS. 13, [Col. 1191D] (5): The Vulgate reads: “only do not give freedom as an occasion for the flesh.”
- VERS. 15, [Col. 1192D] (1): The Vulgate reads: “But if you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another.”
- VERS. 15, [Col. 1192D] (2): The manuscripts read “exhortation [to] concord” (*exhortatio concordia*). Jerome elegantly writes on verse 13: “Let us serve one another through love, so that the precepts of the fragmented Law may be brought together under one heading of love.”
- VERS. 16, [Col. 1192D] (3): The Vulgate reads “desires” (*desideria*).
- VERS. 17, [Col. 1192D] (4): In place of “against the flesh,” the manuscripts have “to what follows” (*ad subjunctum*).
- VERS. 17, [Col. 1192D] (5): Thus the manuscripts.
- CAP. VI, VERS. 1, [Col. 1193D] (1): The Vulgate reads, “you who are spiritual.”
- CAP. VI, VERS. 3, [Col. 1193D] (3): The manuscripts read “when” (*cum*) for “as though” (*ceu*).
- CAP. VI, VERS. 3, [Col. 1193D] (4): *Si qui* is used for *si quis*.
- CAP. VI, VERS. 6, [Col. 1194D] (1): The Vulgate reads: “But let the one who is instructed in the word share with the one who, etc.”
- CAP. VI, VERS. 7, [Col. 1194D] (2): The Vulgate reads “is mocked” (*irridetur*).
- CAP. VI, VERS. 8, [Col. 1194D] (3): The manuscripts read “from” (*de*) for “in.”
- CAP. VI, VERS. 9, [Col. 1195D] (1): The manuscripts read “to have” (*habere*).
- CAP. VI, VERS. 9, [Col. 1195D] (2): The manuscripts read “when” (*cum*) for “which” (*quod*).
- CAP. VI, VERS. 9, [Col. 1195D] (3): The manuscripts read “obtains” (*consequitur*).
- CAP. VI, VERS. 11, [Col. 1195D] (4): A noteworthy reading: *quantis* (“how large”) for *qualibus* (“of what kind”). Jerome should indeed be read here, since he disagrees with Chrysostom’s interpretation. The Vulgate reads: “See with what kind of letters.”
- CAP. VI, VERS. 13, [Col. 1196D] (1): The Vulgate reads “those who are circumcised” (*qui circumciduntur*).
- CAP. VI, VERS. 13, [Col. 1196D] (2): Thus the manuscripts; the sense is either “circumcision” or “glory.”
- CAP. VI, VERS. 14, [Col. 1196D] (3): The words “in nothing” are absent from the Vulgate.
- CAP. VI, VERS. 14, [Col. 1196D] (4): The manuscripts read “who” (*qui*) for “because” (*quia*).
- CAP. VI, VERS. 15, [Col. 1197B] (1): The Vulgate reads “has force” (*valet*) for “is” (*est*).
- CAP. VI, VERS. 16, [Col. 1197B] (2): The Vulgate reads “of God” (*Dei*) for “of the Lord” (*Domini*).
- CAP. VI, VERS. 17, [Col. 1198B] (1): The Vulgate reads: “Henceforth let no one be troublesome to me.”

**Verse 15.** [Note: “[Col. 1197D] (1) That a portion of the commentary down to verse 15 of chapter 1 is missing is plainly demanded by the matter itself; yet the manuscripts contain no indication of a lacuna.”] He has set forth, as it were, four causes or four kinds of persons who proclaim Christ. Of these, two—the first and the last—do so from malice; the two in the middle do so from good disposition and good will. It must be explained how [Note: “[Col. 1197D] (2) I would prefer quid here and below.”] the first and last differ from one another, and likewise the second and third.

The first is from malice, arising from envy and contempt. For he said that they feel envy [Note: “[Col. 1197D] (3) The manuscripts: ‘but when.’”] because they are rivals of us. The last too is evil: “Some proclaim Christ through contentiousness” (v. 17). [Note: “[Col. 1197D] (4) Vulgate: ‘Some proclaim Christ out of contention.’”] That is, they do so in order to injure us. Since they openly deny Christ, they pretend to proclaim him, so that we, who consider and believe them to be opponents, may grieve that the same things which we proclaim are proclaimed by them. “Through contentiousness,” he says, they proclaim Christ—not reverently or purely, but in order to inflict upon us affliction, groaning, and pain; so that they may show themselves rejoicing in our punishments and chains. Just as it was said to Christ himself when he was placed upon the cross, “If you are the Son of God, save yourself,” so it may be said to Paul: “May your God free you from your chains. That Christ, God, is God; but you nevertheless are in punishments.”

Thus this proclamation by the malicious differs from the preceding one. The earlier kind is not intended to add punishments to the apostle’s chains, but is done because they themselves aspire to the glory of preaching, acting through envy [Col. 1198C] and not through understanding and their own deliberate will.

But the two causes, or two kinds of persons, on the side of good are as follows: some proclaim Christ through good will, others through love. These two good causes correspond oppositely to the individual evil causes. For the second corresponds to the first. If the first proclaim Christ because they envy and contend, then, conversely, some good people proclaim Christ through good will, genuinely holding this conviction, not envying us [Note: “[Col. 1198D] (1) The manuscripts: ‘you.’”], but because what they believe is good and they have good will toward the Gospel.

The third good cause is contrary to the last evil cause. For if the last evil kind is such that some proclaim Christ contentiously in order to bring about our punishment and affliction, then this good kind is its opposite, because some proclaim him from love: that is, following me and being dear to me, not insulting me. “Knowing,” he says, “that I am appointed for the defence of the Gospel.” [Note: “[Col. 1198D] (2) Vulgate: ‘Knowing that I am appointed for the defence of the Gospel.’”] They know that I am engaged in the defence of the Gospel, and consequently that I endure these punishments for the Gospel. Therefore they too proclaim Christ out of love—either love for Christ or love for me—not insulting me like those who preach Christ through contentiousness, not purely, but supposing that they raise up affliction [Note: “[Col. 1198D] (3) Vulgate: ‘pressure.’”] for my chains.

[Col. 1199A] **Verse 18.** “What then? Provided that in every way, whether under a pretext or in truth, [Note: “[Col. 1199D] (1) Vulgate: ‘What then? Provided that in every way, whether through occasion or through truth.’”] Christ is proclaimed.”

Having above set out four persons or causes by which Christ is proclaimed, he declares and shows that he is not at all [Note: “[Col. 1199D] (2) The manuscripts: ‘but in every way’; indeed, from the first hand, ‘but entirely in manner.’”] disturbed by the malicious because they preach Christ. For they vainly suppose that they are arousing affliction for my chains. What then? Why am I troubled? Why am I thrown into affliction, when I rejoice and am glad that Christ is proclaimed in every manner? Whether they proclaim Christ through some pretext of their own [Note: “[Col. 1199D] (3) The manuscripts: ‘some and some.’”], or through some occasion of their own, whether to injure or to envy—provided they preach—or whether they proclaim him in truth.

For the result greatly pleases me: they proclaim Christ; they name Christ and, though with another intention, confess him as God and as the Son of God. When this is celebrated, practiced, and done, Christ is thus proclaimed by all, and we attain what we desire: that Christ should be proclaimed. If this is so, they vainly supposed that I was being cast into affliction.

Accordingly he adds: “And in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice.” [Note: “[Col. 1199D] (4) Vulgate: ‘And in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice.’”] “I rejoice,” he says, “even in this very thing, that Christ is proclaimed.” For even those who proclaim Christ in order to injure me do not deny him; nor do those who proclaim Christ through envy, on account of their inward disposition, secretly and through malicious words. Yet they confess Christ and proclaim Christ. “In this,” he says, “I rejoice and shall rejoice.”

**Verse 19.** “For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the assistance of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.”

It might seem almost rash and reckless that he willingly accepted—and accepted with joy—that Christ should be proclaimed in any way whatever, even by wicked persons, even through contentiousness, even through envy. But I affirm that this will come to pass through confidence in God, goodwill, and, as he himself says, through the assistance of Christ and his Spirit; and I know that it will come to pass. For this proclamation, in whatever manner [Note: “[Col. 1199D] (6) The manuscripts: ‘how.’”] it is made, will be true and will occur as that Paul himself wishes who proclaims truly.

Therefore he says: “For I know that this will turn out for my salvation”—so that what those proclaim for my destruction, whether those who proclaim Christ contentiously or those who proclaim Christ through envy and rivalry, I nevertheless know will all turn out for my salvation, Christ and his Spirit supplying assistance. “According to what I expect,” he says, “and hope, I have such confidence that they will never harm me, even if they proclaim Christ with another purpose, so that I may suffer punishment and torture. Yet because my hope and expectation are in Christ, this will turn out for my salvation.”

[Col. 1199D] **Verse 20.** “Because in nothing shall I be ashamed; but in all confidence, as always, so now Christ shall be magnified in my body.” [Note: “[Col. 1200D] (1) Vulgate: ‘Because in nothing shall I be confounded; but in all confidence, as always, so now Christ shall be magnified in my body.’”]

It followed that this very proclamation by the malicious, by those who preach through envy and through contentiousness, might not immediately turn out for salvation, but might bring him ruin and punishments, so that he should remain always in chains, or even die. Yet it may have either outcome. For the apostle, looking ahead [Note: “[Col. 1200D] (2) The manuscripts: ‘through appearances.’”], says that Christ will be preached whatever the outcome. “I shall never be ashamed,” he says; “but in either case I shall rejoice and exult. As always, so now Christ shall be magnified in my body.” That is, when my body, subjected to punishments, endures everything and preaches Christ, neither ceasing nor being frightened by punishments, nor yielding to any punishment.

What he means by “every punishment” he himself explains when he adds: “Whether by life [Col. 1200B] or by death.” For if, enduring punishments, I live, Christ will be preached; if I die under punishments, he will be preached still more and more, when all see that I was neither deterred by punishments nor recalled by death, but either lived my life in the Gospel amid punishments, or endured punishments unto death and nevertheless persisted in preaching the Gospel.

**Verse 21.** “For to me life [Note: “[Col. 1200D] (4) Vulgate: ‘to live.’”] is Christ, and to die is gain.”

Therefore I do not fear death, because dying is gain to me—not death itself, but dying. Life, moreover, is Christ, because whoever hopes in him always lives, both now and hereafter. For when he has said, “Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death,” referring to this present life: if he overcomes those who plot against him and perseveres in the Gospel, his life will glory [Col. 1200C], because it glories in Christ—not in chains, not in deliverance, not in suffering nothing. But if he is killed, dying is gain, since Christ is his life.

Thus he has assigned one thing to each case: in answer to death, “I do not fear death, since Christ is my life.” Whether I am in life or even bound in chains, Christ is my life; and dying itself is gain, because I attain Christ. Or both statements may be applied to each of the preceding cases: I do not fear death, because Christ is my life and dying is gain; or, when I am alive amid punishment, I do not fear life, because Christ is my life. Therefore they accomplish nothing, whether they deliver me to death or hand me over to torments in life. Neither harms me: for life amid punishment is not, for me, life in torments, because Christ is my life. Or if they kill me, this too is not punishment for me, because Christ is my life and dying is gain.

[Col. 1200D] **Verse 22.** “But if to live in the flesh, this is for me fruit of work.”

Because above he said, “Christ is my life,” and it was uncertain which life he meant—whether this life in the flesh or that which follows—he added concerning this life [Col. 1201A] in the flesh and said that nevertheless, even in this life, while we live here in the flesh, “this is for me fruit of work.” What fruit of work is this? That through my labour and through the Gospel I proclaim Christ and bring many to the hope of life and salvation, once they begin to hope in Christ and to give faith to the Gospel. “This,” he says, “is for me fruit of work: even to live in the flesh.”

“And what I shall choose, I do not know.” For if I die, death is gain, Christ is my life, and I surely attain him when I die [Note: “[Col. 1201D] (1) The manuscripts: ‘measure.’”] here in the flesh. Or if I live again here in the flesh, it is fruit of work for me to proclaim Christ and evangelize. “What I shall choose,” he says, “I do not know”: whether I should desire death or remain still in life.

**Verses 23–24.** “But I am constrained by the two: having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, [Col. 1201B] which is by far [Note: “[Col. 1201D] (2) Thus the manuscripts.”] the better. But to remain in the flesh is necessary because of you.” [Note: “[Col. 1201D] (3) Vulgate: ‘But I am constrained by the two, having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary because of you.’”]

“A twofold necessity and desire,” he says, “draws me in different [Note: “[Col. 1201D] (4) Thus the manuscripts, for diversa, ‘different.’”] directions. For I have the desire to depart—that is, to leave the body—and to be with Christ; to attain that gain, which is certainly best and to be chosen. But again I have the necessity to remain and persevere in the flesh because of you.” Thus to the former alternative he has assigned the desire to depart and to be with Christ, because it is highest, chief, and best; but concerning remaining still in the flesh he speaks rather of necessity: that I may live for this purpose, to instruct you and confirm you in the Gospel.

Therefore, although he has, as it were, two desires, he affirms one: that he will remain still in the flesh. “And this I confidently [Col. 1201C] know, that I shall remain and continue for you, for your progress and the grace of faith.” Truly as a father, truly as a servant of God, he has virtually set aside that one of his two desires which would have benefited himself alone: that he might now depart, now be released, and be with Christ.

**Verse 25.** “I am confident,” he says, “and confidently know that God will cause me still to be here, so that I may remain; and I shall remain, in order to benefit all of you and that you may make progress toward the glory of faith.” [Note: “[Col. 1201D] (6) Vulgate: ‘And being confident of this, I know that I shall remain and continue with you all for your progress and joy of faith.’”]

“I shall remain,” he says, and adds more: “and shall continue,” that is, I shall remain until completion—the completion, however, of your progress, so that you may advance and obtain grace, namely the grace of faith; that is, when you render faith, you purchase grace from God.

**Verse 26.** “That your glory and exultation may abound in Christ Jesus through me, through my presence again [Col. 1201D] among you.” [Note: “[Col. 1201D] (7) Vulgate: ‘That your rejoicing may abound in Christ Jesus in me through my coming again to you.’”]

So that, when I begin to be among you again—that is, through my presence with you anew—your glory may exult, and that exaltation itself may abound in Christ Jesus through me, through my presence again among you. That is, [Col. 1202A] that I, being present, may perceive how your glory exults and abounds in Christ: that you love Christ, serve Christ, and rejoice to serve Christ.

**Verse 27.** “Only conduct yourselves worthily in the Gospel of Christ.” [Note: “[Col. 1202D] (1) Vulgate: ‘Only [conduct yourselves] worthily [of the] Gospel,’ etc.”]

This is the whole sum of Christian life: to conduct oneself in Christ’s Gospel, to proclaim him to oneself and to others, to have hope in him, and to do everything one does according to his commands. This is to conduct oneself worthily in the Gospel of Christ. Yet even this is insufficient; therefore it must be joined to this: before all else, that we conduct ourselves in the Gospel of Christ, and that we do so worthily. To conduct oneself worthily is to live according to his precepts and do what Christ commands.

“Whether I come and see you, or, while absent, hear concerning you that you stand in one spirit, striving together with one soul in the faith of the Gospel.” [Note: “[Col. 1202D] (2) Vulgate: ‘Whether absent, I may hear concerning you that you stand in one spirit, unanimous, cooperating for the faith of the Gospel.’”] He himself explains what it is to conduct oneself worthily in the Gospel of Christ: standing in one spirit, striving together with one soul in the faith of the Gospel. “Standing in one spirit,” he says, because the spirit is one when we now think alike, understand the Gospel, and live accordingly. But it is the work of the soul to repel bodily adversities; therefore, “striving together with one soul in faith”—the faith which the Gospel gave you. Therefore, he says, stand in one spirit and struggle together with one soul in the faith of the Gospel.

But this exposition contains what he said above: “Conduct yourselves worthily in the Gospel of Christ.” We shall observe how the words stand so as to form a complete and connected whole: “Conduct yourselves worthily in the Gospel, so that I may worthily hear concerning you that you stand in one spirit and strive together with one soul in the faith of the Gospel.” I may hear while absent; but there will be faith, so that, when I hear, I may believe when I come to you and see you. Whether I hear concerning you while absent, I shall already have seen you in both ways: that you stand in one spirit.

**Verse 28.** “And do not be terrified in anything by your adversaries.” [Note: “[Col. 1202D] (3) Vulgate: ‘And be terrified in nothing by adversaries.’”] This too belongs to the exposition of what it is to conduct oneself worthily in the Gospel of Christ: never to be terrified by adversaries, nor to be terrified in anything, since for them it is a declaration of destruction, but for us of salvation.

“This,” he says—this not being terrified [Note: “[Col. 1202D] (4) The manuscripts: ‘to terrify,’ and indeed without ‘not.’”] while serving the Gospel—is the whole activity of the Christian directed toward salvation: not to be disturbed by adversities, to believe the faith of the Gospel in Christ, to suffer for Christ, and at the same time to know that this comes through God’s grace. Therefore, he says, this matter—not being terrified in anything by adversaries—is for us unto salvation [Col. 1202D], and for our adversaries a cause of destruction; and yet this also is God’s gift.

“And this from God”: lest we think that it is our own work that not being terrified is a cause of salvation for us. For this too is from God, as I have often pointed out: all things occur by God’s will, mercy, and grace.

**Verses 29–30.** “For it has been granted to you by Christ.” [Note: “[Col. 1202D] (5) Vulgate: ‘For it has been granted to you for Christ.’”]

He joins these precepts together with every exhortation. For it belongs to showing, according to the preceding precepts, what it is to conduct oneself worthily in the Gospel of Christ. And now exhortation is added: that they should believe in Christ, and not merely believe, but also suffer for him. What they are to suffer he adds: “the things which you saw in me and the things which you heard concerning me.” [Note: “[Col. 1203D] (1) The manuscripts: ‘the things concerning me, the things which you heard.’”] For this is to conduct oneself worthily in the Gospel of Christ, and this has been given to us as a gift for Christ, because he completed the mystery and suffered everything for our deliverance. Therefore, for his sake he gave us the gift of believing in him. It is a great gift if, by faith in him alone, we merit so great a grace.

But we must believe in such a way that we also suffer for him; for he adds: “Having the same struggle and contest which you saw in me and now have heard concerning me.” [Note: “[Col. 1203D] (2) Vulgate: ‘Having the same struggle as you saw in me and now have heard concerning me.’”] Thus you too, believing in Christ, may suffer everything for him, that is, on his account. For to do everything [Col. 1203B] and not turn aside to another, and to suffer everything for him, is the struggle. This is the contest—indeed, the striving and exertion—that leads to the palm and the crown. Therefore, lest you be ignorant of this contest: it is the very one which you saw in me, namely in chains, prison, and all the evils which Paul endured. Both of these establish for you the certainty that I suffered, whether you heard or saw.

### Chapter II

**Verses 1–4.** “If, therefore, there is any advocacy [Note: “[Col. 1203D] (3) The Greek word παράκλησις creates an ambiguity: whether it means ‘advocacy’ or ‘consolation.’ Victorinus rightly retains the first sense, because immediately afterwards we have the second sense from the Greek παραμύθιον. The Vulgate, however, gives this passage as follows: ‘If therefore there is any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of spirit, if any bowels of compassion, fulfil my joy, that you all think the same thing.’”] in Christ, any consolation of love, any fellowship of spirit, any bowels and compassions: fulfil my joy, that you all think the same thing.”

As he is about to request a favour—that his joy may be fulfilled, which joy concerns this command, that all think the same thing and that none differ from another, for then there are both love and concord [Col. 1203C], when all think alike; and if there is concord, the apostle will have this joy—therefore, in order to obtain what he wishes to be his joy, through their unanimity, concord, common judgment, and other such things, he sets before them, as it were, the grounds of their obligation: what he deserves from them, namely that his joy should be fulfilled in this, that all think the same thing, and so forth.

The grounds of this obligation are these: because they are jointly called in Christ. For God calls us in Christ; he sanctifies those whom he has called, chosen, and appointed. Calling, therefore, is first. “If,” he says, “there is some calling in Christ among us, because we have been called together and called in Christ, and if there is my claim upon you, then fulfil my joy.” This, therefore, is the first ground of mutual obligation: that they heed one another because they are called [Col. 1203D] in Christ.

From their being called in Christ, moreover, there is also love. Then he adds, “If there is any consolation of love.” Since we are amid evils and toil under the evils of the world, if we love one another, God will be for us the consolation of love. “If, therefore,” he says, [Col. 1204A] “there is this consolation of love—so that, because I love you, you console me in the evils in which I am—then fulfil my joy.” This must thus be added to each point.

Then he adds, “If there is any fellowship of spirit.” This third point is also in good order. For first comes being called in Christ; next comes having love. But when both are present, so that they are called in Christ and have among themselves the consolation of delight [Note: “[Col. 1204D] (1) The word seems to have been written for delectus, ‘delight,’ as in Cicero, Republic 1.34.”] and love, there is without doubt fellowship of spirit. “If,” he says, “there is any fellowship of spirit,” hear again, “fulfil my joy.”

Then he adds, “If there are any bowels and compassions.” For the Church becomes one body when those called in Christ are joined to one another in love; they are joined also in spirit and become the same bowels and the same compassions. “If, therefore, there are any bowels, if there are bowels of compassion,” for the purpose that there may be calling in Christ and fellowship in spirit. Compassion, however, serves the purpose that, if there is any consolation of love, each may console the other, because we are always amid evils in the world. Since we are the same bowels, we ought to show compassion mutually to one another. Thus, “If there are any bowels of compassion, fulfil my joy.”

What joy this is, he adds: “That you all think the same thing.” What does “think the same thing” mean? He explains through what follows, either the matters in which they are to think the same thing or the manner in which they are to do so:

“Exercise the same love, being of one soul, thinking one thing; doing nothing through rivalry or empty glory, but in humility of mind considering one another to be superior to yourselves. Let not each of you look only to his own interests, but each to those of others.” [Note: “[Col. 1204D] (2) Vulgate: ‘Having the same love, being of one soul, thinking the same thing; doing nothing through rivalry or empty glory, but in humility considering one another superior to yourselves, each not considering what is his own, but what belongs to others.’”]

[Col. 1204C] **Verse 5.** “For think this in yourselves which also [is] in Jesus Christ.”

As I said, this is the exhortation which he now pursues with fuller precepts: “Fulfil my joy” in the matters in which it can be accomplished. These precepts, as he has always taught, contain both what must be done and what must not be done. He sets out what must be done thus: “That you all think the same thing, exercise the same love, be of one soul, thinking one thing.” He interposes what must not be done: “Nothing through rivalry or empty glory.” Then he adds again what must be done: “But in humility of mind, considering one another to be superior to yourselves.” Again he adds what must not be done: “Let not each look to his own interests.” Then, what must be done: “But each to those of others.”

He thus proceeds to add what is of the greatest value for the exhortation, and a definite exhortation from these precepts, the conclusion of which is that each person should consider the refreshment of others [Note: “[Col. 1204D] (3) The manuscripts: unus reatu quae ratione; others, ratumque ratione.”]. “This,” he says, “you ought to do, establish, and think in yourselves: what Christ did.” Thinking of others, he thought nothing of himself or his own glory; indeed, as he will teach, he himself laid aside his power [Col. 1205A] in order to aid all others. Thus the point of the exhortation is this: that Paul’s joy may be fulfilled.

Let us, then, consider individually what the precepts are. First he says that all should think the same thing. The right and operation of all Christian power is not to dissent, but to have one and the same thing in mind. For if there is one God, one Son of God, and one Holy Spirit, and if these three are one, so ought we also to have one thing which we think: that all may think the same thing.

Then follows: “Exercise the same love.” This now belongs to moral discipline, that is, to life; the former belongs to knowledge. For, as I have said that there are two kinds in Paul and in every discourse—some matters are learned [Note: “[Col. 1205D] (1) Thus the manuscripts.”] for knowledge, others for actions and life—so here “that you all think the same thing” belongs to knowledge, while “exercise the same love” belongs to life.

What is “the same”? The love which another bears toward you, you bear toward the other; not divided [Note: “[Col. 1205D] (2) Perhaps diversa, ‘different,’ rather than divisa, ‘divided,’ as on p. 54?”] love, but love in Christ. This is the same love. Then he adds: “Being of one soul, knowing one thing.” He seems to me to have repeated, in reverse order, the matters stated above. For “being of one soul” corresponds to exercising the same love; “knowing one thing” to what he said above, namely, “that you all think the same thing.”

Yet there is something further in these two expressions than in the former ones. For “that you all think the same thing” and “knowing one thing” are different, though both belong to knowledge. The former, “thinking the same thing,” means that, while knowledge is not yet confirmed, the capacity for knowing appears nevertheless equal; [Col. 1205C] knowledge is not yet completed, though it is already perfect knowledge [Note: “[Col. 1205D] (3) This is exactly as the manuscripts read; lest a reader perhaps attribute the author’s obscurity to the editor, both here and on the following page and elsewhere. See col. 1211, note 2.”].

In the second precept, therefore, although both expressions concern one understanding, the wording is stronger: “knowing one thing.” Since he says “knowing,” it is now precept itself. But above he said, “thinking the same thing,” that is, having the same perceptions of understanding. The former, therefore, is still in process; this may be seen as perfection. Likewise, “thinking the same thing” with regard to life is still in process: “exercise the same love” in respect of life. But perfection is “being of one soul,” and both concern morals and manner of life. Thus, although the individual expressions may seem the same, the later ones are stronger.

Then he adds: “Doing nothing through rivalry or empty glory.” It was possible to have both sameness of thought and sameness of knowledge, yet still have rivalry. Therefore he adds the manner which ought to be—or rather, which ought not to be—present: “Nothing through rivalry.” Many people have either the necessity or the will to contend. He therefore removes both forms of contention, so that there is neither a necessity nor a desire to contend, since both are defective. Some rush into contention from curiosity; others are by nature contentious. Therefore he adds, “Nothing through rivalry.”

Again, others bring this forward for ostentation: they contend in order to appear equal, or superior through stubborn resistance, or superior in boasting. He wishes this to be removed and says, “Nor through empty glory.” For empty glory is the desire to please through words, through great cleverness, and through argumentative contention. Contention ought rarely to occur among Christians; boasting in speech ought not to occur.

To this latter precept, so stated—that we should do nothing through empty glory—there is necessarily added: “But through humility of mind.” For empty glory can thus be removed if there is humility in one’s perceptions, that is, understandings. For he has used “perceptions” in this sense. Let one put forward whatever he treats in the manner of inquiry, not on assumed authority.

“Considering one another to be superior to yourselves.” This is truly humility: if you consider every other person superior. For this is what it means to consider yourselves surpassed by one another: that none should fail to regard another as superior, as preceding him, and as better. If this is so, it is humility of mind.

Then he adds: “Let not each of you look to his own interests, but to those of others.” From this understanding the following statement is joined. Meanwhile this should be referred to what precedes: then you will fulfil my joy if you also do this, that each person should not look only to his own interests but to those of others, and that each should thus care for others and for their concerns. This is what we think. If we think only of ourselves, we can benefit ourselves and attend only to our own matters—our hope and our deliverance. But this is too little. For then we truly attend to ourselves if we also care for others and hasten to benefit them. Since we are all one body [Col. 1206C], if we provide for others, we provide for ourselves; if we think of others, we think more of ourselves.

Accordingly he adds how great, chief, and forceful is the matter which he urges, when he says: “Let us have this same thing in our minds which [is] also in Christ Jesus.” What is this: “Think in yourselves what you think in Christ Jesus”? He himself sets it out and explains it. For if we think this in Christ Jesus—because he cared more for others, that is, for us, than for himself, and thought not of himself nor of what he himself could, did, or can do, but rather of us—this is what he said above: “Let each person care for others.” For our Lord Christ the Saviour, being indeed the Saviour, brought salvation to others. He did not merely employ kindness, nor did he, radiant in his goodwill, clothe and cover us in his own light, and draw us to himself through poured-out kindness and majesty.

Therefore, so that we might know his benefit more fully and as the greatest, he “emptied himself,” he says, and stripped himself of all majesty; descending into flesh, accepting all that endurance of humility, so that he might benefit us through flesh, he endured injuries in the flesh and then the cross and death. All these things teach and exhort us that, [Note: “[Col. 1206D] (1) The manuscripts: ‘however.’”] likewise imitating the Lord, we should think not more of others than of ourselves. For this is truly to attend to ourselves: to undertake care for others for the sake of their salvation. This, then, is what it means that “you think this in yourselves which you think also in Christ.” You think that he benefited [Col. 1207A] others; therefore think this also in yourselves: think on behalf of others and undertake concern for others, so that you may be able to benefit them.

**Verses 6–8.** “Who, being established in the form of God [Note: “[Col. 1207D] (1) The Vulgate omits constitutus, ‘established,’ and then has ‘to be equal to God’; ‘but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient,’ etc.”], did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but also emptied himself, and took the form of a servant, having been made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.”

He had above given two matters, that is, two precepts: one, that they should love humility; the other, that they should not care only for their own interests but also for those of others. And he said: “Think this in yourselves which [is] also in Christ Jesus.” What, then, do we take from these two things in Christ Jesus? One of them? And which one? Or rather both? For one concerning humility is evident: Christ humbled himself and took the role of a servant. Yet the second precept may also be present here: for he endured thus for the sake of others and thought more of others than of himself.

Here, however, it is briefly expounded what Christ is, both before he descended into flesh and in what power and substance he exists. For it was said that Christ was the form [Note: “[Col. 1207D] (2) Thus the manuscripts: not ‘in the form.’”] of God. But what is the form of God? Not shape, not countenance, but image and power. I have treated this fully here and in the commentary on Ephesians [Note: “[Col. 1207D] (3) Let us note Victorinus’s testimony concerning his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians. When he adds ‘and in other books,’ he undoubtedly refers to his fourth book Against Arius, chapter 30, as will be clear to anyone who compares them. Therefore Victorinus, author of the books Against Arius published long ago, is the same author as these commentaries now published by me.”], and more fully and abundantly in other books: God consists in that which is primary being itself; and being itself is principally to possess being, life, and understanding. But understanding and living are a certain form and image of existence itself.

Since, therefore, God is existence, as is demonstrated in many ways, [Col. 1207C] and indeed rather that which is above existence; and since the form of existence is movement, understanding, and life—for that which is invisible and incomprehensible, namely being, is in some manner shaped and defined, that is, brought into consideration and knowledge, when life and understanding are understood—thus being is the Father; while life and understanding, which are themselves in that which is being, are as it were his form. Therefore Christ is the form of God: for Christ is life, knowledge, and understanding. This, then, is the form and image of God. How great his power, divinity, and virtue are has been explained elsewhere.

Therefore Paul now says: Christ did not consider it robbery—that is, he claimed this for himself and desired to possess so much—that he should be the form of God. Rather, he emptied himself of power so as to descend into the world and into flesh, and to take the form of a human being—that is, the image of one small and humble.

But I think it must be carefully and keenly observed [Col. 1208A] that, although he himself says both that he was sent by God and that he fulfills the Father’s will, the mystery is so stated that his coming, and his taking the form or image of a servant, belong to his own will. For thus he says: “Though he was established in the form of God, he did not judge it robbery to be equal with God; but he emptied himself and took the form of a servant.”

Yet, since we always join these things together and grasp by the necessity of understanding that intelligence and life are present in that which is being—so that God, whose power it is both to be and to furnish being to all things, is nevertheless that intelligent reality, as living or above intelligence and above life, and above existence; and so that Christ, who is life, is life itself proceeding from God, and in that which is life there is existence itself and intelligence itself, equal to God—hence the Father is in the Son and the Son is in the Father. But these matters, as I said, have been treated more fully elsewhere.

Therefore, when the Father willed, the Son willed; and when the Son willed, the Father willed. Hence both statements are correct: that he was sent by the Father, and that it is here said that he emptied himself. We should understand that he emptied himself, not in the sense that he laid aside his power elsewhere or deprived himself of it, but that he humbled himself to every kind of lowliness, descending to the lowest offices. When he fulfilled these things, he emptied himself and his power. For, taking flesh and the form and likeness of a human being, he endured, did, and fulfilled everything that belonged to humanity. This is what he says: “made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man.”

For those who say that he was a phantom are not to be heard merely because it is said here, “in the likeness [Col. 1208C] of men.” Rather, the reference is to God and to the Logos himself, fashioned through the assumption of flesh in the likeness of human beings. For although flesh on earth has diverse forms, and it is manifest that Christ assumed flesh, in what likeness is this said? “In the likeness of men,” that is, not of the other animals [Note: [Col. 1208D] (1) Thus the manuscripts.]; not because there was here in Christ a likeness of human beings [Note: [Col. 1208D] (2) Thus the manuscripts.] rather than humanity itself assumed.

Finally, after “likeness” he added “appearance,” so that he should be in appearance as a man. Thus he joined: “found as a man.” The Greek indeed says σχῆμα, *schēma*, while the Latin calls it *habitus*, “appearance.” Since the Greek has these two terms, “likeness” and “appearance,” let us therefore understand *habitus* as figure, and as the manner in which a human being is constituted. For every human quality is expressed by these two things: likeness [Col. 1208D] and figure. Human likeness might exist on an immense scale, as in giants, or in the faces and limbs which are imagined; therefore he added “and in human figure,” so that, besides human likeness, a definite appearance and measure might be seen to have been assumed.

Moreover, when he says “found as a man,” he does not say “as a man” with uncertainty, as though he were not a man but merely a human phantom. Rather, he says, “found as a man.” This is, of course, a middle mode of expression: he was truly not merely a human being but God [Note: [Col. 1208D] (3) Namely, God and man, in one person, as Victorinus has plainly stated above.], and, having assumed flesh and figure, was as a man.

When he says, “he took the form of a servant,” it is because he himself was the form of God, while the human being is God’s servant; therefore it is said that he took the form of a servant. By this he humbled and emptied himself, “becoming,” he says, “obedient unto death, namely death on a cross.” Observe that when he says “having become obedient”—in Greek, more expressly and fully, ὑπήκοος γενόμενος, *hypēkoos genomenos*, “having become one who obeys”—there is expressed in this very phrase what we said a little earlier: that he was sent by the Father.

For if he became one who obeys, then that saying, “he who sent me here,” and “having become subject,” is true and complete. Certainly both can be received and understood not only according to that reasoning that God is in Christ, the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, but also because in many passages we find something similar: both the authority of the sender and the will of the one who obeys. Thus, among the poets, if a father sends Mercury by his command, and Mercury, obeying his father’s command, composes himself and empties himself in order to fly and undertake the journey—if it is permissible to compare divine things with such matters—we may understand Christ as sent by the command of God the almighty Father. And Christ the Son, precisely because he obeyed the command, emptied himself in order to take human form, come in flesh, and bear the image of a servant, humbling himself and becoming obedient—obedient even unto death.

What death was that? For there are many kinds of death. First, to be in flesh belongs to death [Note: [Col. 1209D] (1) Thus the manuscripts: *mortis*, not *mors*.]; then to take upon oneself all the sins of the flesh is itself death. Therefore he adds, “unto death.” What death? “Death on a cross,” he says. For the Savior did not free us merely by death, but by death on a cross; for the whole mystery lies not only in Christ’s death, but also in death on a cross. Hence Paul said that he had faith in Christ, and in Christ himself crucified.

VERS. 9, 10, 11.—What conclusion follows from all this? Christ, therefore, both provided for others and made himself humble. “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and infernal beings; and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” [Note: [Col. 1209D] (2) Vulgate: “…and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend,” etc.].

What this means—that God therefore exalted his Son and gave him the name above all names; what this name itself is; and why he has now bestowed and granted these things—is a subject of great discussion and great teaching. Nevertheless, we shall briefly indicate its character. Christ, that is, the Logos, who is with God, at God, beside God, and therefore himself God—the Logos proceeds from God’s activity—so that Christ might be Jesus, be exalted, and receive a name above every name: this Logos, insofar as he is Logos, is the form of God; he is truly joined, united, and one, and therefore the Logos too is God, through whom all things were created, and in whom what was made is life. This was from the beginning, and without the Logos [Col. 1210A] nothing was made that was made, he who is united.

Let the ears receive this simply: was the Son not called by that name at that time? It can indeed be understood that, as God himself by God’s power and as the form of God, he himself God, he received this name and title later, after descending into the world—that is, into matter, ὕλη (*hylē*)—cutting through and conquering matter itself and overcoming death, so that death should no longer rule. If such great works of his and such great mercy of God were fulfilled through this gift accomplished by him, then, in his return and reversion, he received this name; thereby he was exalted and received this grace, that he should receive the name Son, which is the name above every name.

But catholic teaching says that the Father has always been and the Son has always been; and so it must be said and understood. Nevertheless, because among us this error has arisen [Note: [Col. 1210D] (1) He speaks of the Arians, whom he also refutes subtly in what follows.]—that it is established that, before the descent into flesh, the Logos was never called Son—and because the present exposition does not proceed in such a way as to maintain its argument, namely: when it has been said that he emptied himself, though he was the form of God, took the form and figure of a servant, was found and made in the likeness of a human being, humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross, and then it was added, “therefore God exalted him,” he seems to have been exalted on account of that very passion and to have received this grace, namely, to receive the name above every name, for this reason, I say. For Paul speaks thus.

If this is so, Paul seems to mean that this name did not exist before: that he was the power of God, was the Logos, was also form insofar as he was Logos, and God, and was with God; and therefore it would seem not fitting that he should then have received the name Son, but only after he was sent. Here we understand, from the fact that he was sent, that the one is Father and this one Son. Then, on account of his works, the mystery, and the passion—by which life is death, through Christ’s very death—he received, through this grace, the name above every name. Thus the name alone was added, while the reality remained the same: previously, that is, Logos and power itself; not that the reality first came to be when he came into flesh.

But when the reality came—that is, power, wisdom, act, and operation—he was nevertheless called Logos and was Logos. Now, however, when the Logos himself put on flesh, as has been said, this Logos himself, after the passion and after death on a cross, by which he conquered every death and all sins, received the title Son, which title is above every name [Col. 1210D]. For what can be received as equal, or compared, with the name Son? Friendship, blood-relationship, siblinghood, and all other names—whether of servants, angels, or whatever else we may mention—are all inferior. Therefore Son is above every name; this name God gave to Christ after the passion, after the cross.

Yet it may seem almost not to be true that Son is above every name. For if “son” is not said unless there is a father, and “father” unless there is a son, is this name too, Son, above that name, Father? Certainly not. How then, when he received the name Son, did he receive a name above every name? It must certainly be understood in relation to all other names: this name, Son [Note: [Col. 1211D] (1) Thus the manuscripts, for *filii*. Ancient manuscripts often exhibit a single *i* in the genitive case.], is above all other names. For Father is joined with Son, and these names are equal with respect to their names; although the name Son is not above the name Father, nor the name Father above the name Son. That power which is called Father is above that power which is called Son [Note: [Col. 1211D] (2) On this matter theologians should be read, especially Petavius, *De Trinitate*, II.2, where he wisely examines similar expressions of other doctors of the Church. He also discusses this passage of our Victorinus from the books Against Arius, whose words, he says, are very frequently exceedingly obscure. Petavius concludes concerning that passage of Victorinus: “But these matters, like many others, are insufficiently weighed according to the catholic rule by that iron writer.”]; nevertheless, the names Son and Father are equal to one another.

If this is so, Son is above every name because Father together with Son is above every name; at this name, and in the name of Jesus Christ, every human being bends the knee and prays—not human beings only [Col. 1211B], but all heavenly things, all earthly things, and all things under the earth, which are called the lower things.

And again, VERS. 11: “Every voice confesses that Jesus Christ our Lord is in the glory of the Father” [Note: [Col. 1211D] (3) Vulgate: “and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”], and always was. This glory, therefore, was given him: that he himself should be the glory of the Father, because the Father also begot him; through him the world was created and saved; and life is death, and salvation and eternity, which were sought through all these things. Those who believe in him have conquered death in Christ’s death.

VERS. 12, 13.—“Therefore, my dearest ones, as you always obey, not as in my presence only but much more now in my absence, work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both willing and effectiveness, according to good will” [Note: [Col. 1211D] (4) Vulgate: “Therefore, my dearest ones, as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence only but much more now in my absence, with fear … work [out your salvation]. For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to good will.”].

After the mystery of the whole dispensation had been set forth—this having been placed so that the command might be confirmed, by which he urged that no one should think of himself or take care for himself, as our Lord Jesus also acted by his mystery—there follows, as I said, an exhortation that they love one another. First, when he called them dear and beloved to himself; then: “As you have obeyed me, so you have always obeyed—not only in my presence, but more and more in my absence—and you have obeyed with fear and trembling.”

Why “more and more”? Either because the days advance, or because in absence the one who gives warning is to be feared more. But what is this that he urges and exhorts: that they do and work out their salvation, acting observantly and obediently, “with fear,” he says, “and trembling”? Fear refers to the mind, trembling to the body.

There is a great mystery here, which we must hear attentively [Col. 1212A]: by giving counsel to others and taking care of them, we work out salvation more fully for ourselves. Then, that it is especially in us to work out our salvation. Thus he says: “Work out your salvation.” But lest anyone return too little grace to God if he seems to work out salvation for himself, he adds: “For it is God who works in you both willing and effectiveness, according to good will.”

“Work out your salvation,” therefore, he says; but the operation itself is nevertheless from God. For God works in you, and works so that you will in this way. And willing is, as it were, ours, whence we work out salvation for ourselves. Yet because he works that very willing in us, it follows that we have from God both operation and will. Thus both are mixed: we have a will, and yet that will itself belongs to God; and because we have a will, effectiveness is present according to good will.

Moreover, he binds the human being more firmly to fear when he says: “For it is God who works in you.” For if it is God who works in them, we must undoubtedly be in fear lest we act contrary to God’s will, either by doing too little or by failing to act with fear and trembling. God works in us both to will and to act, according to good will. Thus one who does not act from God, first, does not have willing; then, even if he has willing, he does not have effectiveness, because he does not have good will.

VERS. 14, 15.—“Do everything without murmurings and hesitations or reconsiderations” [Note: [Col. 1212D] (3) The Vulgate does not have the latter two words.]. These are two warnings: when we undertake something, now trusting and believing in God and carrying out divine commands—apostolic, prophetic, or evangelical—we should not have murmuring, that is, complaints while obeying. “Do nothing,” he says, “either with any hesitation or with calculation and reconsideration as to whether it ought or ought not to be done.” Or, if you act from necessity and complain, there is no good will of obedience.

“So that you may be without complaint”—the Greek says, “so that you may be without blame”—that is, so that there may be no complaint against you. Thus the Latin has said, “without complaint and blameless.” For what follows is: “And sincere, immaculate children of God, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation” [Note: [Col. 1212D] (4) Vulgate: “and sincere, immaculate children of God in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation.”].

For if you live and obey in this way, you will not be stained, says the Latin. Yet the Greek has ἄμωμα τέκνα, *amōma tekna*, “children without reproach.” This is what was said above: “and that you may now be sincere, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation.” What does this mean? If the soul is saved in this way, it becomes a child of God if it lives as it does now while it is in the world, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation—that is, in this life.

Therefore, while we are in this life, we must labor to flee this perversity and the crookedness of this generation, that is, of the creation in which we are; we must live as immaculate, irreproachable, sincere children of God, doing everything without reproach and without reconsideration. It is not enough, therefore, merely to act; one must act in this manner [Col. 1213A], so that there may be among us no reconsideration, murmuring, or complaint in acting.

If we do these things in this life, the mind devoted to God then becomes one among the children of God, if it performs God’s commands willingly, eagerly, without complaint, and does so now while it is in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation. “Among whom you shine as lights in the world.” This is a great exhortation: already in this very condition, in which we are in this world, let us stand out in this crooked and perverse generation; and let us stand out as lights of the world, which are in the world itself—as the sun and moon and the other shining stars.

For Christians who live by faith and knowledge of God according to the divine commands excel, and exist in this world as light and brightness. For if, beyond other people, they overcome every evil thing, crush hidden demons, expose iniquities, and conquer darkness and the works of darkness, they act in this world as lights and provide light to all.

VERS. 16.—“Holding fast the word of life, for my glory [Note: [Col. 1213D] (1) Vulgate: “…holding fast, for my glory.”] on the day of Christ.” It is also your reward that you live in this way, if indeed you are lights in the world; and you will be for my glory on the day of Christ, that is, when Christ comes to judge. I have glory through you because you hold fast the word of life—that is, because you have known Christ, who is the word of life; because in Christ, what has been made is life. Therefore Christ is the word of life.

From this one recognizes how great is the benefit and glory of those who correct the souls of others. “Because I did not run in vain.” This, he says, will be my glory on the day of Christ: that I have delivered you, and that my labor did not labor in vain, nor did I run in vain [Col. 1213C]. Labor is a genus; running is a species of labor. Therefore, having proposed the genus—“I did not labor in vain,” which could refer to bodily labor, speech, admonition, or persistence—he added the specific species: “I did not run in vain.” Here it is either the labor of travel or the labor of zeal, that he might persuade them of this, and persuade them quickly. This is: “I did not run in vain.”

VERS. 17, 18.—“But if I labor in the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and congratulate all of you. Rejoice likewise yourselves with me” [Note: [Col. 1213D] (2) Vulgate: “But even if I am offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and congratulate all of you; and likewise you also rejoice and congratulate me.”]. What was given above as a command is here [Note: [Col. 1213D] (3) The manuscripts read “this” (*hoc*).] set forth in exhortation: that we should take care not only for ourselves, but that each person should also care for others. If this is so, mutual rejoicing [Note: [Col. 1213D] (4) Thus the manuscripts: *et* (“and”); perhaps *haec* (“these things”) should be preferred.] arises from us as well. He says this concerning ourselves and others.

“But if I labor,” he says, “in the sacrifice and service of your faith”—that is, if I am even prepared to die for you, provided that I serve you and confirm your faith—“I rejoice and congratulate all of you.” Therefore you too rejoice with me, so that together we may all care for one another and rejoice mutually concerning one another.

VERS. 19.—“But I hope in the Lord Jesus Christ to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be of good heart [Col. 1214A], when I learn what concerns you” [Note: [Col. 1214D] (1) The Vulgate varies somewhat.]. This concerns the commands. He truly cares for them, since he promises to send another who will provide the same things for them, and through whom he may learn [Note: [Col. 1214D] (2) The manuscripts read *cognoscant*, “may they learn.”] what the Philippians are doing. He promises that his most beloved Timothy will shortly be sent.

Since every action of ours must be ascribed to God, so that it may be completed by God, he says: “I hope in the Lord Jesus Christ that I shall send Timothy to you, and shall send him quickly.” He then gives the reason why he is sending him: “so that I too may be of good heart, learning what you are doing,” or what the situation among you is. When he says, “so that I too may be of good heart,” he means: I hope that you are of good heart because you keep all the commands and have faith in Jesus Christ, from which you are of good heart; therefore I wish to send Timothy quickly [Col. 1214B], so that I too may be of good heart when I learn what concerns you, whether from your conduct or from others.

VERS. 20, 21.—“For I have no one who is of one mind with me” [Note: [Col. 1214D] (3) Vulgate: “For I have no one so like-minded.”]. He shows why he promises Timothy and gives the reasons: he has no one like-minded, that is, one who bears the same mind. You have one reason. He adds another: “who is faithfully concerned for you” [Note: [Col. 1214D] (4) Vulgate: “who will be concerned for you with sincere affection.”]. Such a man should certainly be sent: one who is most dear to me, who cares for you and has concern on your behalf.

“For all seek their own things [Note: [Col. 1214D] (5) Vulgate: “the things that are their own.”], not the things of Jesus Christ.” Since he said, “he alone is [such a person], and I have no one who is like-minded with me,” what reasons does he give concerning the rest? Namely, the second point is devotion. For if Timothy is given [Note: [Col. 1214D] (6) The manuscripts read “given to Timothy,” a reading perhaps capable of being retained.] as one faithfully concerned for you, then he adds the corresponding fault and sin: “all seek their own things,” that is, they are concerned for their own affairs, defend their own affairs, and preserve their own affairs. But this [Note: [Col. 1214D] (7) Thus the manuscripts.] does not belong to a Christian [Col. 1214C]. For what is more proper to a Christian, in any companion or brother, to seek than the things of Christ: faith in Christ, fellowship, love, knowledge? Yet this may also be understood as: “the things of Christ,” that is, to evangelize concerning Christ.

VERS. 22, 23, 24.—“But you know his proven character very well” [Note: [Col. 1214D] (8) Vulgate: “But know his proven character.”]. That is, you have proof concerning him; the Greek puts it thus. You ought to know; perceive and recognize what proof of him I have. For what follows is rightly connected: “because, as a son with a father, he served with me in the Gospel.”

It is therefore clear what it means that they do not seek the things of Jesus Christ. “Timothy served with me in the Gospel,” he says, “as a son with a father.” He briefly shows how Timothy served, although he has said, “he served with me [Note: [Col. 1214D] (9) The manuscripts read *servierit* (“he has/will have served”).] in the Gospel.” But how did he serve? As a son serves a father: Timothy served with me in the Gospel in greater love and service. “He served with me,” he says; he did not say, “he served me.” Therefore I hope to send him soon.

After commending his person, affection, and diligence, he adds that he intends to send such a man. “I hope,” he says, “to send [him].” This is also what he said above: “I hope in the Lord.” What he said here, “soon,” is what he called above “quickly.” “When I see what concerns me, I shall send Timothy”; but only when I see what concerns me. “But I trust in the Lord that I myself also shall come soon.” With great affection and serious exhortation he adds this: though he sends Timothy, he nevertheless promises that he himself will come.

VERS. 25.—“For I trust,” he says, “in the Lord that everything concerning me will turn out well. Yet I considered it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother [Note: [Col. 1215D] (1) The Vulgate adds here: “and fellow-worker.”], fellow-soldier [Col. 1215B], your apostle, and minister of my desire” [Note: [Col. 1215D] (2) Vulgate: “of my necessity.”]. Although he promised that he would send Timothy quickly, yet because [Note: [Col. 1215D] (3) The manuscripts read *qui* (“who”).] there is still some delay before he sends him, he now sends Epaphroditus: “I considered it necessary,” he says, “to send Epaphroditus to you.”

He commends the person, then adds the reason. The commendation of the person is: brother in the law, fellow-soldier in the camp and labor of the Gospel, and “your apostle.” Observe that he calls Epaphroditus an apostle. For everyone who is sent, and who is sent for the sake of the Gospel, can be called an apostle. Accordingly, the Twelve, or Eleven, were called apostles from the ministry for which they were sent to preach. Thus anyone sent for this purpose may be called an apostle.
