When he says “your apostle,” it may mean either because [Note: [Col. 1215D] (4) The manuscripts read *qui* (“who”).] he is sent to you—for others are sent elsewhere—or because you chose him from among yourselves as an apostle; nevertheless, he says, “minister of my desire.” What is my desire? That you may hear; that you may hold fast the word.

VERS. 26.—“Because he was longing and yearning for all of you” [Note: [Col. 1215D] (5) Vulgate: “Because he longed for all of you.”]. He now adds the reason why he sends him. He had said that he would send Timothy quickly so that he might be of good heart when he learned what concerned them. He now sends this man because he longs and yearns for all of them and finds it hard to be absent from them.

He proves that he bears this absence painfully thus: “and he was distressed because you heard that he was ill [Note: [Col. 1215D] (6) The manuscripts read “because” for “was.”]” [Note: [Col. 1215D] (7) “And he was sorrowful because you had heard that he had fallen ill.”]. This, he says, was the distress he suffered: you heard that he was physically ill, that is, sick. Or does “he was distressed” mean that he himself was the cause, because he was ill? And was he distressed by this very cause, and sick because he longed and yearned for you? Therefore I now send him to you.

VERS. 27.—“For he was indeed ill, even unto death; but the Lord had mercy on him, and not on him only but also on me, lest I should have sorrow” [Note: [Col. 1215D] (8) Vulgate: “For he was indeed ill … not only on him, but also on me, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.”]. He shows why [Col. 1216A] Epaphroditus either longed for the Philippians or was distressed: “he was ill unto death.” In such an illness desires and feelings are intense. “He was sick unto death,” he says; “but the Lord had mercy on him.” See that we experience God’s benefit here also in this life.

Further, we ought also to hasten toward death. For although the world is a ministry of sin and is therefore to be fled, nevertheless it is not a sin to desire life in the world. And if life ought to be desired, then the statement “the Lord had mercy on him” is rightly spoken. Further, whatever we do here for life, if we are righteous and benefit both ourselves and others, God rightly has mercy on us and preserves us in life [Note: [Col. 1216D] (1) Thus the manuscripts.].

Thus he adds: “God had mercy not only on him, but also on me, lest I should have sorrow.” For since Epaphroditus was called above “the minister of my desire,” if I lost the minister of my desire, I would be grieved and have sorrow. Therefore many are preserved, and God has mercy upon those through whom something is done that pertains to the ministry of salvation. At the same time, we must pray for people of this kind, lest we have sorrow if we lose those whose help we use in doing, imparting, and declaring divine matters.

VERS. 28.—“Therefore I sent him more promptly.” He distinguishes his missions. Concerning Epaphroditus he says, “I sent”; concerning Timothy, “I hope to send him to you quickly.” Yet above, “I considered it necessary to send to you,” does not concern what he will send, but what has already been sent. Thus he concludes here: “I sent him to you, so that when you see him you may rejoice again, and I may be without sorrow” [Note: [Col. 1216D] (2) The Vulgate gives the entire verse thus: “Therefore I sent him more promptly, so that, seeing him, you may rejoice again, and I,” etc.].

He adds this reason too for having sent him. Above: “I sent [him] because he longed and yearned for you”; now, in relation to the Philippians: so that you may rejoice and congratulate yourselves again when you see him. What does “congratulate yourselves again” mean? Since you had been in sorrow—for it was said above, “you had heard that he was ill [Note: [Col. 1216D] (3) The manuscripts read “because.”]”—now you may again rejoice when you see him. Or “again” because, after hearing that he had recovered from a severe illness, they had already rejoiced; now, when they see him, they will rejoice again.

When he adds, “and I may be without sorrow,” since he had called Epaphroditus the minister [Note: [Col. 1216D] (4) The manuscripts: “ministry.”] of his desire, he might appear sad in sending him. But because Epaphroditus longed for them and they will rejoice when they see him, Paul can be without sorrow.

[Col. 1216D] VERS. 29, 30.—“Receive him therefore in the Lord with every rejoicing; and hold in honor those who are such. For he came near to death for the work of Christ, exposing his life to uncertainty, in order to supply what was lacking from you in service to me” [Note: [Col. 1216D] (6) Vulgate: “Receive him therefore with every joy in the Lord, and hold such persons in honor; for he came near to death for the work … giving over his life, [Col. 1217D] in order to fulfill what was lacking from you in service to me.”].

This is a commendation, that they should receive Epaphroditus [Col. 1217A]. He gives its favor and reason: “Receive [him] in the Lord,” that is, receive him as a minister of the Lord; you who are already in the Lord, love the Lord’s minister, and love him with every rejoicing. He also wishes this to be shown generally to all who are such: “Receive those,” he says, “who are of this kind.” What does it mean, “receive him”? “Hold [him] in honor.”

He also gives reasons why he wishes such things to be shown to such people: “because he came near to death for the work of Christ.” This clearly concerns Epaphroditus: because, in wishing to satisfy the Gospel by labor of mind and body—that is, by preaching the word of the Lord—he labored greatly and, through severe sickness, came near to death. At the same time he shows both what happened to Epaphroditus and what we ought to do.

But [Note: [Col. 1217D] (1) The manuscripts read *aut* (“or”).] how greatly did he labor? “He came near to death,” he says, “placing his life in uncertainty.” Not uncertainty regarding what he was doing among you, but uncertainty because he labored even to danger [Note: [Col. 1217D] (2) The manuscripts: “you labored.”], so that it had become uncertain whether he would survive the labor. What, then, did he accomplish among you? “To supply what was lacking from you in service to me”: that, while I was occupied, he might complete the service that was lacking alongside me.

For indeed, since preaching is one and doctrine is one, only the labor can differ among individual apostles and evangelists; what they teach is one. Finally, what did Epaphroditus himself, the apostle, fulfill [Note: [Col. 1217D] (3) The manuscripts: “Finally, concerning Epaphroditus himself, what did the apostle fulfill?”]? “This service,” he says, “which was lacking from you, he fulfilled.”

CHAPTER III.

VERS. 1, 2, 3.—Finally, brethren, rejoice in the Lord [Note: [Col. 1217D] (4) Vulgate: “Finally, my brethren, rejoice.”]. To write the same things to you is indeed not burdensome for me, but is plain [Col. 1217C] for you [Note: [Col. 1217D] (5) Thus the manuscripts; not “necessary,” as the Vulgate has it.]. “Rejoice,” he says, “in the Lord, brethren; for me it is not burdensome to write the same things to you, while for you it is highly beneficial. What I write is firm and secure.” The Greek text has it so as to mean “firm and secure”; the Latin says “plain.” Beware [Note: [Col. 1217D] (6) Two manuscripts have *caute* [cautiously]; a third, later one, *cavete* [beware].] of dogs; heed evil workers; look upon the mutilation. For we are the circumcision, who serve God through the Spirit and exult in Christ Jesus, not placing confidence in the flesh [Note: [Col. 1217D] (7) Vulgate: “See the dogs, see the evil workers, see the mutilation; for we are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit and glory in Christ Jesus, having no confidence in the flesh.”].

This admonition teaches not what ought to be done, but what ought to be avoided. He warns them to keep away from the Jews: “Beware,” he says [Note: [Col. 1217D] (8) Manuscripts have *caute* and *cavete*, as above.], “of dogs.” There is a discussion of dogs [Note: [Col. 1217D] (9) Thus the manuscripts.]; for divine Scripture also calls those dogs who are useful and defenders of the Church, as David teaches in Psalm LXVIII [Col. 1217D] [Note: [Col. 1217D] (10) That is, LXVIII according to the Hebrews, but LXVII according to the Greeks and the Latin Vulgate. Victorinus thus follows, as is his custom, the older recension.], whom he says are satisfied with the blood of enemies in the temple [Col. 1218A] of God. Here, however, he speaks against dogs, from whom he says one must beware—namely, the Jews, who are such because they are workers, and evil ones: for workers pass their life in works, not knowing God, and hope for salvation for themselves from works. Concerning them it has already been said above that works avail nothing.

“Look upon the mutilation,” he says. Among them there is mutilation, because they cut off a shameful part of the body. “But we,” he says, “are the circumcision.” For we circumcise every evil from our hearts; and we do this because [Note: [Col. 1218D] (1) Manuscripts: *qui* [who].] we serve God through the Spirit, whereas they serve through the flesh. Therefore they are mutilated, not circumcised. “Let us exult,” he says—or rather, “we exult.” But where do we exult? Not in the flesh, as they do, placing confidence in it, but in Christ Jesus. Therefore draw all your understanding away from Jewish discipline, from the works [Col. 1218B] of the Jews, from Jewish circumcision; and have circumcision of the heart, so that we may serve God through the Spirit and exult in Christ. But let them exult in the flesh, having confidence from this—that, because they are circumcised in the flesh, they are able to be saved and to merit eternal life.

VERS. 4, 5, 6, 7.—Although I too have confidence even in the flesh [Note: [Col. 1218D] (2) Vulgate: “Although I have confidence also in the flesh.”]. In many ways it is shown that the Jews place all confidence in the flesh and in circumcision; indeed, the Jews interpreted it thus even when salvation came to circumcised Moses [Note: [Col. 1218D] (3) Thus the manuscripts.]. From this one may understand that the Jews also bear confidence concerning the flesh, and especially in the flesh.

But Paul teaches this: if confidence is in the flesh, he says—that is, in circumcision—it belongs to me more fully; for “I,” he says, “have confidence in the flesh.” Thus it follows: “If anyone else thinks that he has confidence in the flesh [Col. 1218C], I more.” And he teaches why, if anyone has confidence in the flesh, he himself has it more fully. Thus [Note: [Col. 1218D] (4) Manuscripts: *si* [if].] he shows that his own person was wholly Jewish in every respect: in circumcision, descent, tribe, nation [Note: [Col. 1218D] (5) Manuscripts: *tribuente*.], law, administration under the law, and even devotion in his manner of life. Yet, though he had fulfilled all these matters belonging to Jewish discipline, he says that all these things were loss to him for Christ and because of the eminence of His flesh. All these points, therefore, are proved in the proposition as follows.

“I was circumcised on the eighth day”: this is circumcision. “By descent,” he says, “of the race of Israel.” Likewise, “of the tribe of Benjamin.” Likewise, “a Hebrew [Note: [Col. 1218D] (6) Manuscripts: *Hebraei* [Hebrews].] of Hebrews” by nation. Likewise, concerning the law, “a Pharisee according to the law.” Likewise, concerning zeal, “persecuting the Church according to zeal.” Likewise, concerning life, “according to the righteousness which is in the law, when I was without reproach” [Note: [Col. 1218D] (7) Vulgate: “without complaint.”].

[Col. 1218D] By all these things, therefore, he showed that he had greater confidence in the flesh and in circumcision, since he possessed every feature of Jewish discipline—in blood, nation, disposition, and life. When he says, “persecuting the Church according to zeal,” he means that, having great zeal for the synagogue, he persecuted the Church [Col. 1219A]. Likewise, when he says, “according to righteousness,” that is according to conduct and life, by which a person is justified; yet he speaks of the law of the Jews. “When I was without reproach”: that is, I had committed no offense and had done all that the law commanded. For this is righteousness among the Jews, derived from the law.

But since righteousness now comes to us Christians from Christ, and we are justified on His account, “those things,” he says, “which were gain to me, I considered loss” [Note: [Col. 1219D] (1) Vulgate: “But whatever things had been gains to me, these I considered losses for Christ.”]. That is, I understood that those things harmed me, holding all of them cheap for Christ’s sake.

VERS. 8, 9.—But [Note: [Col. 1219D] (2) Manuscripts: *parum* [little].] he added this also: “Because of the eminence of Christ Jesus our Lord” [Note: [Col. 1219D] (3) Vulgate: “because of the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ our Lord.”]. But the Greek has: “because of the eminence of the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ,” in order to show that those former things are small [Col. 1219B] and least, and indeed more contrary, if they stand alone; for they are loss, he says. And this eminence of Christ is what surpasses [Note: [Col. 1219D] (4) Manuscripts: *excellet*.] and conquers all things.

“On account of whom I have suffered loss of all things, and count them as dung” [Note: [Col. 1219D] (5) Vulgate: “on account of whom I have counted all things loss, and consider them as dung.”]. He concludes the thought: that he despises all those things and suffers every loss for Christ, in order that he may gain Christ. But what does “I have suffered loss” mean? All those things which had been glorious to me—my blood, tribe, nation; the fact that I had been a Pharisee under the law; and that I had kept righteousness so as to be without reproach—when all these were cast aside, I endured the loss of all things and considered, or consider, them all as dung.

For we read “I consider” better than “I am considered”; for the Greek also has *hēgoumai* [ἡγοῦμαι] [Note: [Col. 1219D] (6) Manuscripts: ἡγούμενον.], not that he himself should be considered by others, but that [Col. 1219C] he should consider all those former things as dung, cast them away, and by a just judgment gain Christ. He himself continues: “And that I may be found in Him.” For this is to gain Christ: now to be in Him, to be joined to Him by faith, to think Him, to possess Him.

“Not having my own righteousness, which is from the law.” That is, the righteousness which I expounded above, when I lived without reproach; for then righteousness is, as it were, mine or ours, when we suppose that we merit God’s perfect righteousness through our conduct. “But,” he says, “not having this righteousness.” But which? He adds it: “But that which is from the faith of Christ,” which he mentioned before—“righteousness from God, by faith” [Note: [Col. 1219D] (7) Vulgate: “but that which is through faith in Christ Jesus, the righteousness which is from God by faith.”].

This righteousness, therefore, he says, he possesses—not that which is from the law, which, as I said, is in works and in fleshly discipline, but that which proceeds from [Col. 1219D] God. What is it? Righteousness from faith—which faith is faith in Christ, that is, from us [Note: [Col. 1219D] (8) Thus the manuscripts.] toward Christ. And he has fully added what faith in Christ is for us, from which we have righteousness.

[Col. 1220A] VERS. 10, 11.—“To know Him, and the power of His resurrection, and fellowship in His sufferings; sharing the burden of His death; if in any way I may come to meet Him in the resurrection which is from the dead” [Note: [Col. 1220D] (1) Vulgate: “To know Him, and the power of His resurrection, and fellowship in His sufferings, conformed to His death: if in any way I may attain to the resurrection which is from the dead.”].

He expounds the faith which we have in Christ, which he said that he was persuading and proclaiming to the Philippians: righteousness from faith proceeding from God, from the faith [Note: [Col. 1220D] (2) Thus repeated, with a correction written in the margin of an older manuscript.] which he adds for knowing Him—what He is, who He Himself is, whence He is. He then adds these things concerning Christ: “and the power of His resurrection.” Either because He rose by power—for it is a great power to rise from the dead—or because He rose for our salvation: this is the power of His resurrection.

He proves the same by what follows. For, he says, if we have fellowship in His sufferings, since He Himself said that we have been, or are, participants in death, [Col. 1220B] we shall therefore also be participants with Him. This is the power of the resurrection: that we have fellowship in His sufferings. But what is this fellowship? It is that we who believe in Christ endure sufferings—indeed, all sufferings, even to the cross and to death. Through all these, from knowledge and fellowship in sufferings, resurrection results; and thus, when we share the burden of His death, we are in some manner made ready to meet Him, so that we may come to meet Him in the resurrection, which is the resurrection from the dead.

Behold what faith in Christ is; and he says that he teaches this, teaching what must be done in life: namely, that, as companions in Christ’s suffering, we should both believe this and hold this faith—that we shall come in the power of His resurrection, having become participants in the burden of His death, so that for this reason we may in some manner meet Him in the resurrection [Col. 1220C] which is from the dead. That is the reward; this is the labor; that is the life, this the merit and glory.

VERS. 12.—“Not because I have already received, or am already perfected” [Note: [Col. 1220D] (3) Vulgate: “Not that I have already received, or am already perfect.”]. He adds this more forcefully, speaking indeed of himself; but what Paul says concerning himself belongs to us and must be applied to us. What is this? That through those labors and that endurance in fellowship with His death and sufferings, we may be able to go forth to meet Him and to rise together in the resurrection of the dead.

“But I do not do these things,” he says, “because I have already received them or am already perfected.” For as long as anyone lives, he has not yet received these things or been perfected; he is still engaged in fellowship in Christ’s sufferings, since fellowship in those sufferings extends to death. Therefore he has not yet received nor been perfected, but perseveres [Col. 1220D] to the end of life in these very labors, remaining in true fellowship in His sufferings. Then he will be able to go forth to meet Him in His resurrection from the dead.

Yet he also expressed uncertainty when he said, “if in any way I may come to meet Him.” Since he was still alive, he said “if in any way.” For when one perseveres in fellowship in the sufferings, and has become conformed even by death itself, [Col. 1221A] there is no doubt that he will meet Him in the resurrection. But what is it to be made ready to meet Him in the resurrection of the dead? It is the perfect and full life of each person, brought to completion through fellowship in Christ’s sufferings in every way, at the time when the resurrection from the dead takes place—that is, when the dead are raised.

That person of whom Paul speaks concerning himself—that person, I say, who has lived his life in full fellowship in Christ’s sufferings, meets Christ; he is not merely raised, but meets Christ. Others are simply raised; but the perfect, who have suffered in every manner, will meet Christ and go to meet Christ when He comes, as he himself said elsewhere. Rightly, therefore, he says “if in any way,” because he is still in life. And he rightly adds: “not because I have already received, or am already perfected; but I pursue, that I may at some point apprehend that in which I was also apprehended by Christ” [Col. 1221B] [Note: [Col. 1221D] (1) Manuscripts: *sectantur*.].

You see that he says that he is still in life, and therefore had expressed doubt above. For he still pursues [Note: [Col. 1221D] (2) Vulgate: “But I follow, if in any way I may apprehend that for which I was also apprehended by Christ Jesus.”] Christ through every suffering, in order to apprehend Christ—that is, to arrive at Christ, having become a participant in all His sufferings. For Christ, through all His sufferings, has liberated all who follow; and in a certain manner has apprehended all, but those who follow Him. Whoever wishes to follow and apprehend Christ must follow Christ in all His sufferings, in order to apprehend Christ in that in which he has also been apprehended by Christ. For if Christ has liberated all by His sufferings, He has apprehended all by His sufferings; in these sufferings, therefore, we are. That is: having become a participant with Christ through His sufferings, a person apprehends Christ in that in which [Col. 1221C] he has been apprehended by Christ.

VERS. 13, 14.—“Brethren, I do not consider myself to have apprehended.” He continues in the point which I have stated: that he is still alive and therefore has not already received, is not perfected, and has not yet apprehended. For he said, “but I pursue, that in some way I may apprehend.” Therefore, “I consider that I have not yet apprehended,” so that the Philippians may understand how far they are from the benefits of liberation, when Paul himself, who had so often undergone so many of Christ’s sufferings—beaten, imprisoned, exposed to beasts, and burdened with other evils—still does not consider that he has apprehended Christ, since he is still alive and remains.

Great is that participation in suffering through which we are truly joined, if we imitate Christ even in suffering. “But one thing: still casting into oblivion the things that are behind [Col. 1221D], and stretching myself according to the rule toward the things that are first, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 1221D] (3) Vulgate: “But one thing: forgetting indeed those things which are behind, and stretching myself toward those which are before, I pursue toward the goal, to the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.”].

Since, as we have said, he spoke above thus—“if in any way I may meet Him in the resurrection of the dead”—and we have explained why this uncertainty was introduced, namely because he was still alive and many things might happen, especially death itself, he therefore added that he did not yet consider himself to have apprehended Christ. But he shows that he nevertheless has something [Col. 1222A] [Note: [Col. 1222D] (1) Manuscripts: *quidam*.] even now fixed in his mind: “one thing,” he says. What is that? That all things past should be cast into oblivion; that only those things which lie ahead and are first should be pursued—that is, those things which stand before us first and must be pursued according to the rule and discipline of Christ’s precepts—so that we may arrive at the prize of the heavenly calling, yet in Christ Jesus.

There are, therefore, two precepts for the remaining life of one living in Christian order and still living by the rule: first, that whatever one has done, although one does it well and rightly, one should nevertheless not retain in memory as though one thereby merits what one is to attain; but should cast it into oblivion. Then one should always pursue, as though new, the things which remain, nevertheless living according to the rule, continually stretching oneself toward them, and preserving the Christian rule to the end of death [Col. 1222B], so as to be able to arrive at the prize.

For to remember past deeds, even deeds rightly done, is characteristic of one who assigns and claims them to his own merit; whereas these things are not ours, and we do not attain grace by our works. Then, in some way, we become negligent toward the things that are first—that is, those which follow—because of the confidence that we do many things. Hence the Apostle commanded that all things behind should be cast into oblivion.

This may also be understood of the matters we have mentioned, but of the different life we formerly lived: as Paul himself had been a Jew, a persecutor of the law, and so forth. He may thus have said that these things are behind and must be cast into oblivion; just as each of us ought to cast his former life into oblivion. But the stronger meaning is that we should cast even a life formerly conducted well and rightly according to the rule [Col. 1222C] into oblivion, and stretch ourselves toward the things which are first according to the rule, so that we may follow Christ to the prize of the heavenly calling.

For from that point we are Christians, called by God. This is the heavenly calling: for no one is called to God or by God except in Jesus Christ. For He is the door; He Himself is the propitiator and reconciler. We have taught this in many passages. Our life, then, is and ought to be such that, with Christ leading the way—that is, through our faith [Note: [Col. 1222D] (2) Manuscripts: *fides* [faith].] in Christ—we may arrive at the prize.

VERS. 15, 16.—“Therefore, whoever of us are perfect, let us think this; and if you think otherwise in anything, God has revealed this also to you” [Note: [Col. 1222D] (3) Vulgate: “will reveal.”]. From this it may be understood that we [Note: [Col. 1222D] (4) Manuscripts: *vos* [you].] have truly expounded what we said above: namely, that we should cast behind [Col. 1222D] into oblivion the things done by us according to the right rule. For he joins the thought: “Therefore, whoever are perfect, let them cast into oblivion all things done.” For we attain the prize not by our merits but by God’s grace.

Thus he exhorts: “Let us think this.” Who are to think this? “Whoever of us are perfect.” But what are we to think? That we should cast the things behind into oblivion; and the present time too—that is, what we now perform—must be cast into oblivion. If the present, then certainly also the past, and all that we have had [Col. 1223A] in life; and that we should stretch ourselves toward the things which are first, according to the rule. “Let us all think this,” he says, “all of us who are perfect.”

But if what he adds—“and if you think otherwise in anything, God has revealed this also to you”—is a complete thought, standing independently and not joined to what follows, it must be understood thus: if there is anything concerning this very matter which we have said that you receive, understand, or think differently, I grant it to you. For since he speaks of the perfect—for he said, “therefore, whoever of us are perfect”—those who are perfect may think otherwise; he concluded by way of concession: “God has revealed this also to you.” It is good, because both what you think and what I have said are good.

But if this is not concessive, the thought remains suspended, so that the saying is: “If you think otherwise in anything, and yet [Col. 1223B] God has revealed this to you,” he then adds what follows: “Nevertheless, let us think the same thing to which we have attained” [Note: [Col. 1223D] (1) Vulgate: “nevertheless, as far as we have attained, let us think the same thing.”], that is, what we have taught and that to which we have been instructed. For thus he continues: “Nevertheless, in that to which [Note: [Col. 1223D] (2) Thus the manuscripts.] we have attained, let us think the same thing; let us walk in the same way” [Note: [Col. 1223D] (3) Vulgate: “let us remain in the same rule.”].

That is: from the time when I proclaimed the Gospel to you, we have advanced so far in our manner of living and understanding. “Let us think that same thing,” he says, “and walk in the same way”—namely, in that to which we have attained. For by saying “nevertheless” he virtually rejects what precedes. We do not admit the former view; and the sense is this: that is indeed tolerable and may be done, but this is especially to be done. Therefore, even if you think otherwise, and even if God has revealed this to you, whereby [Note: [Col. 1223D] (4) Thus the manuscripts.] you think otherwise, nevertheless, in that to which we have attained, let us think [Col. 1223C] the same thing [Note: [Col. 1223D] (5) Manuscripts: *in ipsum* [the same thing].].

But what is that to which we have attained? What you formerly received from my admonitions, and what is now commanded by me. For we have attained this through every admonition and precept. Yet he says “we have attained,” namely through our precepts: that, casting the things behind into oblivion, we may stretch ourselves toward the things which are first according to the rule, so that we may come to the prize of the heavenly calling in Jesus Christ. “Let us walk in this,” therefore, he says. So clearly the foregoing argument concerns that life and that precept for life. For it was said above: “casting the things behind into oblivion, let us stretch ourselves toward the things which are first.” This is what it means to “walk in this.”

VERS. 17, 18.—“Be imitators of me, brethren.” This is apt to the thought of which we were speaking: that they themselves should do nothing new, even if they think otherwise, even if they have something revealed by God. “Be imitators of me, brethren,” he says, so that what I do, what I command, what I practice in life, what I pursue [Note: [Col. 1223D] (6) Manuscripts: *se quod*.], you too may imitate and pursue. “And observe those who walk thus, as you have us for an example” [Note: [Col. 1223D] (7) Vulgate: “And observe those who thus walk, as you have our pattern.”].

[Col. 1224A] He had given a precept concerning what perfect persons ought to do, and afterward had added that they should not think otherwise, though he had seemingly made a concession; nevertheless, he concluded that they should rather follow him and walk as he himself did. Now, in giving a full exhortation when he said, “Be imitators of me,” he added an example in order to persuade them more readily why it was necessary to act thus—namely, because others did so: “Observe,” he says, “those who walk thus, as you have us for an example.”

He brings together two points: those who walk as we do; and, in that very connection, he briefly establishes both that he himself is an example to them and that others are examples, as they ought to be, for them. Namely, just as they imitate me, you too should have them as an example. “For many walk, of whom I often told you” [Note: [Col. 1224D] (1) Vulgate: “For many walk, of whom I often told you.”]. He adds further that there are few who appear to imitate him: “Many,” he says, “walk thus.” He also adds another argument: lest I should today bring before you an example merely for exhortation, many, he says, walk as we do—many concerning whom Paul has often already told the Philippians that they live thus. Therefore, he did not produce them merely for the moment as persons who walked in this manner, since he had often already spoken of them as walking thus.

VERS. 19.—“But now I say even with tears: enemies of the cross of Christ, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who think earthly things” [Note: [Col. 1224D] (2) Vulgate: “But now I say, even weeping: enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction; whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their confusion, who think earthly things.”].

Exhortation is stronger when it arises from fear; above, indeed, it proceeded from advantages and benefits. For this is [Note: [Col. 1224D] (3) Manuscripts have *cum* [when] for *est* [is].] an exhortation concerning how they should live, directed to the same point which he had commanded above, when he urges and impels the Philippians toward that same life. He had again given another argument [Col. 1224C]: that many already live in the same way, and that Paul had frequently told the Philippians of many who lived thus.

The benefit of the exhortation is confirmed by a stronger consideration: what evil they will suffer if they live otherwise. And, as I said, persuasion from fear is greater. He also adds feeling, since he is about to describe the evils suffered by those who live otherwise, saying: “I say it with tears.” For I grieve and weep because those who are enemies of the cross—that is, those who do not believe this Gospel, namely that they should believe in Christ as man, that is, in Him who was in a human being, who was born of Mary and was crucified—all heretics, therefore, who accept neither the Crucified One nor Christ in a human being, and who are many and various—these, I say, will have destruction as their end.

Some said that He was a man, but not that He was in a human being [Col. 1224D] [Note: [Col. 1224D] (4) The sense is that certain heretics said that Jesus was a mere man, not God with humanity hypostatically assumed to Himself.]. Others deny that He was born at all in flesh; others deny that He was crucified. All such heretics, as I have said, and those like them [Note: [Col. 1224D] (5) Manuscripts: *hujusmodi* [of this kind].] will perish. For this is what he said: “whose end is destruction,” which will surely befall persons of this kind. And he thus enumerates what they will suffer and what they are: what they will suffer—“whose end is destruction”; what they are—“whose god is their belly”; what will follow—“and their glory,” he says, “is in their shame.” He adds how they think: “who think earthly things” [Col. 1225A].

Concerning destruction: their end is destruction because they do not believe these things, that is, because they are enemies of the cross. For this is what he meant by calling them enemies of Christ’s cross: they do not believe in the cross of Christ. These, I say, will perish, and destruction is their end.

But how do those who do not believe—that is, who are enemies of Christ’s cross—have the belly as their god, concerning whom he says, “whose god is their belly”? There are, in a certain sense, two types—one of two sorts—of those who are enemies of Christ’s cross. Some, thinking carnally, mock Christ’s cross because they suppose Christ to be a man [Col. 1225B] raised upon the cross; they do not receive, according to the mystery of the Gospel, Christ crucified in a human being, through which He conquered sin and triumphed over the powers, triumphing through crucified flesh. This cross, I say, we possess in its mystery.

Others, as I have said, understand the cross merely according to the human being, truly receiving Him as only a human being. Therefore they are enemies of the cross; and because they think carnally, they despise the mystery of the cross. These, as I said, think of the flesh and esteem nothing except what concerns the flesh; their god is their belly, their glory is in their shame, and they are those who think earthly things. Nevertheless, their end is destruction.

Or again, there are those who understand Christ as spiritual and do not understand Him in flesh, nor as crucified. Therefore they too are enemies of Christ’s cross, and they also [Col. 1225C] will have destruction as their end. This section concludes concerning them, although it also applies to those who think carnally concerning Christ. Yet the three following statements apply to those who think carnally concerning Christ: that their god is their belly, their glory is in their shame, and they think earthly things.

VERS. 20.—“For our commonwealth is in heaven.” Certainly this is contrary to what preceded; yet it refers to the clause, “who think earthly things,” namely, by judging Christ to be a human being and to have been a human being, and not to have been in flesh but to have come with flesh, as the Jews say He will come, and as the other heretics say. But [Note: [Col. 1225D] (1) Manuscripts: *ad* [to].] we, on the contrary, have our entire life and manner of living in heaven, understanding that Christ came from heaven, put on flesh, and was lifted up on the cross.

[Col. 1225D] Accordingly he adds: “From which also we await the Savior [Note: [Col. 1225D] (2) Vulgate: “Savior.”], our Lord Jesus Christ.” Thus He both came from there and will come from there. For if He is to come from there, He also came from there before. “He who ascended is Himself also He who descended.” Therefore our commonwealth is in heaven, because from there we also await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will come for judgment in the last times; and He will be Savior to us because we believe in Him and await Christ.

VERS. 21.—“Who transformed [Note: [Col. 1225D] (3) Thus the manuscripts here and below, not ‘will transform.’] the body of our humility, that it may be of like form with the body of His glory [Col. 1226A], according to the working of His power, whereby He is able also to subject all things to Him” [Note: [Col. 1226D] (1) Vulgate: “who will reform the body of our humility, configured to the body of His brightness, according to the working by which He is also able to subject all things to Himself.”].

This passage concerns the mystery of resurrection. For what Christ, being in flesh, accomplished in order to save souls—so that immortality might also be given to the flesh through resurrection—He effected by the powers of His cross. We await all these things, and our Lord Jesus Christ Himself, who, he says, by that mystery through which He descended, was crucified, and rose again, transformed the humility of our body, or its form—or rather, transformed the body of our humility.

How is this so? Because when our humble body rises and is changed for the better, Jesus Christ transforms the humility of our body; or He transforms our humble body into a glorious one. He gives it eternity [Note: [Col. 1226D] (2) Manuscripts: *da*.], [Col. 1226B] making for it a heavenly garment, “that it may be,” he says, “of like form with the body of His glory.”

For Christ is Spirit, from whom the body has form and power; form itself, which is power, is the form of glory, the body of divine and eternal reality [Note: [Col. 1226D] (3) Manuscripts: *sps.* [spirit], or *species* [form], or *spiritus* [spirit]. But in what follows the same manuscript has *species*.] [Note: [Col. 1226D] (4) This is how the passage stands in the manuscripts. I do not know whether Victorinus speaks with sufficient theological precision; but he certainly envelops himself in his own obscurity. Compare Petavius’s remark at col. 1211, n. 2.].

When we, however, rise and are changed, and have become spiritual in soul, body, and spirit—for these converge into one human being, and will be one spirit—then also the body of our humility will be of like form, that is, of the same and equal form, with the body of the glory of Christ Himself; so that we too may be spirit, as He Himself is Spirit. This will occur according to the working of His power. For every mystery and every action of Christ effects and completes this by His power: that we may come together into one, when [Col. 1226C] soul, body, and spirit are united, so that [Note: [Col. 1226D] (5) Manuscripts: *et* [and].] we too may be spirit, as He Himself is Spirit.

Likewise, because God is Spirit, all things will be subjected to God when they are reduced to one power; and thus, he says, He will be able to subject all things to Him—namely, to God. The wording may appear continuous yet syntactically unconnected, since he wrote, “that He may be able also to subject all things to Him,” without first stating to whom “to Him” should refer. For if we refer “to Him” to God, God has not been named above; the expression would be obscure and improper, and seems to have been supplied by an interpreter rather than by Paul.

To whom, then, do we refer it? It is certainly established that Christ works in order to subject all things to God; but here there is no indication of God. To whom, then, shall we refer it? We must understand how he nevertheless stated God briefly and plainly [Col. 1226D]. For when he said that Christ, whom we await, transformed the body of our humility so that this body of our humility might be of like form with the body of His glory, here is where God is understood—and God Himself—when he said, “according to [Col. 1227A] the working of His power.”

For Christ did all things in order to provide for souls, to give eternity also to the flesh, and to make our body of like form with the body [Note: [Col. 1227C] (1) Manuscripts: *corpus* [body].] of His glory; but He did this according to the working of His power. He acted, indeed, but the power by which He acted is God; for He acts through the Father. Christ acts, certainly: that is, the Father is in Him and acts through Him. Therefore, where he said “His power,” there God is understood, to whom He subjects all things, and for this He works: that He may also be able to subject all things to Him.

But his saying “also all things” refers to the fact that He Himself is subject to Him. For the Word, which is Christ [Note: [Col. 1227C] (2) The manuscripts continue: “and the Word, which is Christ,” a pointless repetition.], is subject to God; for God is more powerful [Note: [Col. 1227C] (3) Manuscripts: *potentius* [more powerfully / more powerful].]. This has been proved by many considerations [Note: [Col. 1227C] (4) Concerning this teaching of Victorinus, and the following Pauline text, hear Augustine, Question 69 from the *Eighty-Three Questions*: “The rule of Catholic faith is such that, when things are said in Scripture concerning the Son that He is less than the Father, they are to be understood according to His assumption of humanity; but when things are said that show Him equal, they are to be understood according to that in which He is God.” Likewise Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, I.18: “We know that the Father was said to be greater than the Son because the Son was in the form of a servant, and the Son still remains in the human form which He raised into heaven.” Finally Jerome, *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, I.18: “God, to whom the Apostle teaches that the Son is to be subjected according to the dispensation of assumed flesh.” Indeed, many very similar authorities from other Fathers, formerly advanced against the Arians who misused Paul’s words, are also relevant here.].

He is the one who sends [Col. 1227B]; this One is sent. He is the Father; this One is the Son. This One is He through whom the operation is effected; the other is the operator. Therefore, if these things [Note: [Col. 1227D] (5) Manuscripts: *ita* [thus].] are so, Christ acts toward God, so that He Himself may be subject to Him. For thus it is said in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “But when all things have been subjected to Him, then He Himself will be subject to Him who subjected all things to Him, that God may be all in all.”

Or is the meaning of “that He may be able also” that He not only makes the body of our humility of like form, but is also able to subject all things to Him? For when all things that are either fleshly or created have been overcome and changed, all things are rendered subject to the power of God, through which Christ acts.

CAP. IV.

### Chapter IV

**Verse 1.**—“Therefore, my most beloved brethren, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 1227D] (6) Vulgate: “Therefore, my brethren most dearly beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, so stand firm in the Lord, dearly beloved.”] Every virtue among Christians is charity and love; and this cannot exist unless they possess one essence and stand firm in one thing, being of one mind. This is what he now says: “Stand firm in the Lord, O most beloved brethren.” From this one may understand that he wishes them to think one thing when he calls them “most beloved brethren.” For this results: those who think one thing and stand firm in one thing love one another. In what one thing? Clearly, in Christ. For when all equally have faith in Christ, they stand firm in him. And if you Philippians do this, you will be my joy and my crown.

[Col. 1228A] **Verse 2.**—“I entreat Euodia, and I entreat Syntyche, to be of the same mind in the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 1228D] (1) Vulgate: “I entreat Evodia and I beseech Syntyche.”] He wishes even the women to be of one mind in the Lord; that is, believing in Christ, to think and understand those matters concerning Christ which belong to the Gospel. Yet he says, “I entreat,” thereby expressing what would benefit them. For he does not command or order, but entreats.

**Verse 3.**—“Yes, I also beseech you, true yokefellow [*germane unijuge*; Note: [Col. 1228D] (2) Vulgate: ‘companion’], help those women who laboured together with me in the Gospel, with Clement and my other fellow-workers, whose names are in the book of life.” Above we said that Epaphroditus had promised to come to the Philippians; later he showed that he had sent him, when he said, “Therefore I have sent him more hastily.” Thus this is added, as it were, so that he too may have a charge in the letter: Paul asks and entreats him to admonish those women, Euodia [Col. 1228B] and Syntyche, to be of the same mind in the Lord. “Help,” he says, “those who labour with me in the Gospel.” How do they labour in the Gospel? By themselves recognizing, preserving, and keeping the Gospel which I proclaim; or by themselves proclaiming, defending, and evangelizing. For, insofar as they speak of the Gospel—that is, of Christ and of the whole mystery—even women evangelize.

Finally, he adds: “with Clement and my other fellow-workers, whose names,” he says, “are in the book of life.” Thus he refers to the mystery: all who have faith concerning Christ, have faith in him, and speak and instil that very faith in Christ into human beings, are, as it were, fellow-workers of the evangelists. And since this is so, their names are already with God in the book, because [Col. 1228C] they shall be in eternal life. That this person is Epaphroditus, to whom he gives these instructions to help the aforementioned women become of one mind, may be understood from his saying, “I beseech you also, true yokefellow.” For above he had spoken thus concerning him: “Nevertheless, I considered it necessary [to send] Epaphroditus, my brother, my fellow-soldier.” Thus there he called him “brother”; here he calls him “true” or “genuine.” Above he called him “fellow-soldier”; here, “yokefellow.”

**Verses 4–5.**—“Rejoice; let your moderation be known to all men.” This follows: those who are of one mind and have faith in one thing should rejoice in the Lord and always be dear to one another. “Rejoice,” he says, “in the Lord.” This is too little: “Again I say, rejoice.” For when you are joined in heart, you rejoice in the Lord; and when you rejoice in the Lord, you are joined in heart [Col. 1228D] and stand firm in the Lord. “Let your moderation,” he says, “be known to all men.” For it greatly pertains to the merit of the life to come and to the kingdom in heaven if we live moderately. Moderation is the knowledge by which each person keeps his proper measure, neither reaching nor extending beyond himself. Since we are here—indeed, in what belongs to another—let us acknowledge our lowliness and keep the measure of our humility; God will raise us up. “Therefore let your moderation,” he says, “be known to all men.” Why does he urge this? That we may please here? No; but that Christ may recognize our humility, raise us up, and receive our moderation.

[Col. 1229A] For what does he add? “The Lord is near.” This is a great exhortation and a great command, both in truth and in persuasive force. For since judgment is now impending and the end of this life approaches for all, we ought to make haste to live with good character and great moderation; for the judgment and the coming of the Lord are near.

**Verse 6.**—“Reduce nothing to anxiety.” [Note: [Col. 1229D] (1) Vulgate: “Be anxious about nothing.”] That is, do not take care for yourselves, nor think about or be anxious concerning the world and worldly matters. For God provides for you all necessities, both now in this mode of life and, in that life which is eternal, better things. “But in every prayer and supplication, with good thanksgiving [Note: [Col. 1229D] (2) Vulgate: ‘But in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving’], let your petitions be made known to God.” Thus every action of the faithful, good, and perfect Christian, all anxieties being set aside—for this itself is renunciation—[Col. 1229B] should be devoted to prayers and prayer.

Supplications are requests made of the Lord; prayer is also speech when one asks. Prayer itself, indeed, is supplication with prayer. But what will that prayer be? Will it ask for something, or for nothing? What is it that one who has become faithful asks when he prays to God? What prayer or petition, therefore, will he have, since he has renounced all worldly things? He himself instructed us to pray and make supplication “with good thanksgiving,” so that, in all our supplications, our prayer may be thanksgiving: that we may give thanks because, through God’s mercy, we have received so great a gift. This is what he means by “with good thanksgiving.” He added “good,” moreover, lest we do this unwillingly; rather, we should truly give thanks, and then offer good thanks.

For there is prayer in supplications, which may arise from good thanksgiving or from petition. Above, when he had said “with good [Col. 1229C] thanksgiving,” he added, “let our petitions be made known before God.” But whose petition is not honourable? Let him ask that those heavenly things themselves which are promised may be fulfilled. Whoever asks asks, surely, for such things as it is right for one already faithful to ask. For when we consider what we ought to ask, what we wish to make known before God, such things necessarily befit one faithful and hoping for heavenly things and for all divine things. “These,” he says—that is, “your petitions”—“let them be made known before God.”

**Verse 7.**—“And may the peace of God, which possesses [Note: [Col. 1229D] (4) Thus the manuscripts.] all understanding [Note: [Col. 1229D] (5) Vulgate: “which surpasses all understanding”], guard your hearts.” This will be the reward if we pray and make supplication in this way: if we pray with good thanksgiving and make such petitions as are made known before God. Thus it is: there will be, he says, the peace of God which guards your hearts; that peace of God “possesses all understanding.” This is expressed forcefully and acutely. For when the peace of God comes into us, we shall understand God: there will be nothing discordant, nothing divergent, nothing contentious by arguments, nothing admitting of question, as happens to us in worldly matters. Rather, all things are so open when we have the peace of God that all understanding is with us; for it belongs to peace now to rest and now to possess security. When [Note: [Col. 1229D] (6) Manuscripts: “than.”] God entrusts peace to our hearts, then all understanding [Col. 1230A] is with us. For whoever understands God understands all things; and when he understands God, the heart of the one who understands is guarded. “Likewise, your bodies in Jesus Christ.” [Note: [Col. 1230D] (1) Vulgate: “and your minds in Christ Jesus”; the Vulgate reading is more intelligible.] Behold, here too is an indication of the resurrection. This too is set forth or proclaimed as a reward for those who so ask and so pray with good thanksgiving: that they may have God’s peace and their bodies in Jesus Christ.

For he spoke of heart and understanding, which are guarded when peace is given; now he speaks of those very persons, that is, of body and soul: “your bodies,” he says, “in Jesus Christ.” For our bodies are in his majesty and power; at his coming they will rise, come to life again, and receive their rewards. All this will be whole for us if we keep those commands: being of one mind in Christ, rejoicing, moderate, [Col. 1230B] having no anxiety; in every prayer and supplication, with good thanksgiving, making our petitions known before God.

**Verses 8–9.**—“Finally, brethren, whatever is just, whatever holy, whatever lovable, whatever of good report, if there is any virtue, if any praise, think on these things; what you have learned, received, and heard also in me, do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.” [Note: [Col. 1230D] (2) Vulgate: “Finally, brethren, whatever things are true, whatever modest, whatever just, whatever holy, whatever lovable, whatever of good report, if there be any virtue, if any praise of discipline, think on these things; what you have learned, received, heard, and seen in me,” etc.] He taught what sort of supplications we should offer—that is, with good thanksgiving—and likewise what sort of petitions; then what peace, that is, what benefit is given us by God. Thus we should act and ask, so that our understanding and hearts may be guarded, and all our bodies may be in Christ Jesus. Since this is so, “finally,” he says, “brethren, think on these things.”

What does “finally” mean? After you have been corrected, all discord and error having now been removed, since [Col. 1230C] you are of one mind: henceforth think thus. Whatever things are true, receive and think on these. But what are those true things? Those set forth in the Gospel: Christ Jesus, Son of God, and the other things which we have often mentioned. When you think on what is true, it follows that they are chaste; for what is true is not corrupted. This is chastity: what is not corrupted is true. Then those things which are truly chaste are also just, for they are justified by sanctification from God. All things which are just, chaste, true, and holy are also lovable and of good report. For who does not love what is holy? Who does not speak and think well of it? Therefore, he says, think on what pertains to good repute, so that it may be lovable and possess charity, and may not possess discord. For everything lovable possesses concord; likewise, things of good repute do not possess envy and are in concord.

Of all these things, the former pertain to true virtue itself; the latter, to the fruit of virtue. For it is virtue to love what is true, chaste, just, and holy; the fruit of virtue consists in what is lovable and of good repute. Therefore he added these two: “if there is any virtue, if there is any praise.” He carefully attends to the force of the terms. For since all things occur by the grace of God—[Col. 1231A] for he himself, through his Spirit sent into us, both governs [Note: [Col. 1231D] (1) Manuscripts: “was governing.”] and rules, so that nothing is from ourselves—he says, “if there is any virtue.” And again, if the virtue in us is not from us but from God, neither is praise ours; and therefore, “if there is any praise.”

Yet because virtue or praise seems to be ours, he says there [Note: [Col. 1231D] (2) Manuscripts: “to himself.”], “Think on all these things.” What things, then, are they? Those which you learned, with me, of course, teaching; and received, and heard, and saw in me. He first set forth the perfect expression: “you learned.” But whence did you learn? The causes are added: “you received.” Again, whence did you receive, hear, and see? You saw from me, in me; so that Paul is not merely an admonisher, but also furnishes an example of how to follow what is true, how what is chaste, and how the rest. “Do these things,” he says. Above [Col. 1231B] he said, “Think on these things”; now he adds, “Do these things,” so that these goods may exist not only in thought, but also in action. Then, as above, he adds the reward: “and the God of peace will be with you.” This was a reward especially necessary for the Philippians: that there be no discord, that all be of one mind, that there be peace in their church; and that the God of peace, who is the Father, together with his Son Jesus our Lord, may grant peace to every soul turned toward God. This is what he says: “Peace be with you.”

**Verse 10.**—“But I rejoiced greatly in the Lord, because at last you have flourished again, so as to think also concerning me, as you formerly thought.” [Note: [Col. 1231D] (3) Vulgate: “But I rejoiced greatly in the Lord because at last you have flourished again in your care for me, as you also formerly cared.”] The Philippians had fallen into error after being taught the Gospel by the apostle Paul; but now, admonished, they returned to their former understanding, so as to believe the Gospel as [Col. 1231C] it is proclaimed. “And you have flourished again,” he says; that is, you have returned to flower. Therefore I rejoiced in the Lord, and rejoiced greatly. And this is what he says, “so that you think concerning me”: that is, that you think as I taught you; for they had begun to think otherwise.

As for his saying, “so that you think concerning me”: because your understanding and wisdom, which had been one, were not for me, whereas now, since you think as I taught and handed down the Gospel, you think for me—that is, it can benefit me, since I taught you. And what is this: “in which you formerly thought; now you have flourished again and, thinking the same things, now think for me”?

**Verse 11.**—“But you were occupied. I do not say this because of want.” [Note: [Col. 1231D] (4) Vulgate: “I do not say this as though poor through want.”] If this sense is connected with the preceding one, because above it was said, “you also think concerning me,” that is [Col. 1231D] that you should be mindful of me, the meaning will be: send those things necessary to me. But you did send them, and therefore it was said, “I rejoiced greatly in the Lord because at last you have flourished again,” and the fruit of your activity has begun to abound. For later he says, “and you began to think concerning me.” This includes “in which you formerly thought”: that you might send necessities to me. And this is what follows.

How did they think? Formerly they were occupied; formerly they were engaged in these works. Yet Paul says, “I do not say this [Col. 1232A] because of want.” For it is not because of want that I say that I desire you to think concerning me, or that you should return to what you formerly thought and were occupied with, namely, sending things to me; nor do I now wish you to send things because of want. For later too he says, “not because I seek abundance in your prayer.” Therefore I do not seek this because of poverty, but that the fruit may abound in your prayer when you undertake and think of all these things concerning me. For this is to have care; not because I am in need.

“For I also abound,” he says; indeed, I am self-sufficient. Thus he adds: “For I have learned, in whatever circumstances I am, to be self-sufficient.” There is a new sense here: “I know,” he says, “how to be self-sufficient in the circumstances in which I am.” For I have learned to be content with what I have and, in whatever circumstances I may be, to be sufficient to myself. This must not be referred merely to expenses; rather, they ought to offer care, thought, and prayer [Col. 1232B] for Paul. Thus it is to be referred to all things: “that you think concerning me, as you formerly thought.” In general, therefore, either necessary things or prayer and care are to be offered by the Philippians for Paul. Finally, he did not confine this only to fortunes or to whatever things are necessary:

**Verse 12.**—“I know both how to be humbled and how to abound” [Note: [Col. 1232D] (3) Vulgate: “I know how to be humbled; I know also how to abound.”]: this applies also to virtues—“I know both how to be humbled and how to abound in all things”—in the same way, that is, to display every virtue. “And in all things [Note: [Col. 1232D] (4) Vulgate: ‘everywhere and in all things’] I have been trained.” That is, I have been accustomed to all things: to bear thirst, hunger, and cold, and again to rejoice in abundance. So also in virtues and labours, “in all things,” he says, “I have been trained”: I have been trained both to be satisfied and to endure hunger, to be satisfied by plenty and again to endure hunger. Likewise, he repeats the same two points: “I can abound and be in need in all things.” By saying “in all things,” [Col. 1232C] we have said that these words are to be referred not merely to necessities of food, but to everything which lies in action—to labours and virtues. He says that he has been so trained as to be able both to abound and to be in need in all things. It is unusual that he says, “I can be in need in all things”: that is, I endure it when I lack everything, when I have become needy.

**Verse 13.**—And, to speak what is true and nevertheless according to Gospel teaching, he adds: “Through him who strengthens me.” This manner of life ought always to be possessed and maintained: that we too labour, and that it belongs to our training to undertake, fulfil, bear, and endure all these things—yet in such a way that we believe that God has made us strong for all these things. For when he had said, “I can be in need in all things and endure hunger” [Note: [Col. 1232D] (5) Vulgate: “I have been trained both to be full and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want.”], he referred his strength back to God: “through him who strengthens me.” Thus you too, and all who have faith in God, should surely believe yourselves able to become strong in poverty and in other labours. For God never fails those who love him, who have faith and hope in him.

**Verse 14.**—“Nevertheless, you did well in sharing in my tribulation.” [Note: [Col. 1232D] (6) Vulgate: “Nevertheless, you did well, sharing in my tribulation.”] That is, you were participants with me or aided [Col. 1233A] me in tribulation—as sharing is, to be joined equally in a mystery—or rather, one who suffers with another and helps another.

**Verse 15.**—“But you yourselves also know, Philippians, that at the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the accounting of giving and receiving, except you alone.” [Note: [Col. 1233D] (1) The Vulgate differs only slightly.] Here he openly explains what was said above: “you shared in my tribulation,” that is, you gave me help and support by supplying necessities. Finally, he adds: “You know,” he says, “Philippians—and you too know—that at the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed into Macedonia, I evangelized throughout all the churches, but no church,” he says, “shared with me.” In what did it share? “In the accounting,” he says, “of giving and receiving”: that is, in expenses, which are what is given and received. For one who gives has an account with the one who receives; and one who receives has an account with the one who gives, how much the giver gave and how much the receiver received. Not that the receiver himself gave something; but when a gift is given, there is an account of giving and receiving.

For in what could Paul give money? Yet because an account of giving and receiving exists in monetary matters between givers and recipients, the expression is joined in this way. Money is not received in exchange for the Gospel, so that the accounting of giving should consist in money; it is far otherwise.

**Verse 16.**—“You alone,” he says, “shared [with me].” Finally, he adds that they gave: “Because, when I was in Thessalonica, once and twice you sent what was necessary to me.” [Note: [Col. 1233D] (3) Vulgate: “because even to Thessalonica once and twice you sent for my use.”] He most clearly declares what “you shared” means [Note: [Col. 1233D] (4) Manuscripts: “I shared with these.”] and how there is an accounting [Col. 1233C] of giving and receiving. “You alone,” he says, “once and twice sent to Thessalonica what was necessary to me.”

**Verse 17.**—“Not because I seek the gift, but I seek abundant fruit in your prayer.” [Note: [Col. 1233D] (5) Vulgate: “Not because I seek the gift, but I seek abundant fruit in your account.”] “I am not in need,” he says, “nor do I seek these necessities; but you ought to exercise benevolence toward me, so that I may have the fruit of your benevolence, namely, that you abound in benevolence. That is, when I pray concerning you, your benevolence may be fruit to me. Whether I ask God for you or give God thanks for you, I have fruit in the prayer which is for you, while I understand that you abound and are benevolent.”

**Verse 18.**—“For I have all things and abound.” Therefore, he says, I do not seek the gift, for I have all things. Yet many [Col. 1233D] have all things but do not abound; for we can truly still desire something if we possess but do not abound. The one who abounds both has and has more than is necessary. For above he said, “You sent what was necessary to me”; now he says: “These things I have and abound.” Finally, he goes on to show the abundance: “I have been filled, when I received what you sent through Epaphroditus.” Lest that which abounds be alien to them, he says that it belongs to them too, because [Col. 1234A] they sent it: “I have been filled,” he says, “when I received what you sent through Epaphroditus: an odour of sweetness, an acceptable, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God.” [Note: [Col. 1234D] (1) Vulgate: “I have been filled, having received from Epaphroditus what you sent: an odour of sweetness, an acceptable offering, pleasing to God.”]

If above he said that he sought nothing from what is given except abundant fruit, so here, when he says that he has been filled and has received what was sent, he does not rejoice or find fullness in the things sent. Rather, he rejoices in your willingness and care in sending, which is benevolence and the fruit of abundance. Therefore you are an odour of sweetness to me: because you are such persons; and it is a holy sacrifice, pleasing to God, willingly to do what one does, to take care, and to provide another with what must be provided for necessities. This benevolence itself is the sacrifice: holy, acceptable, and pleasing to God.

**Verses 19–20.**—“But may my God fulfil every [Col. 1234B] desire of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus. But to God, even our Father, be glory for ages of ages.” Since he called their deeds righteous and good on account of their willing sending and care, and called this an excellent sacrifice and an odour of sweetness to God, he now wishes to return thanks and makes a prayer: “May God”—but the God of an apostle—“my God,” he says, lest he be common with the rest—“fulfil,” he says, “your every desire, and fulfil it according to his riches.” That is, since you do not seek the things of the world but those things which God bestows and gives out of his riches—that is, heavenly and divine things; for these are the riches of God.

Finally he adds, “glory in Christ Jesus,” so that the riches may be those which are in Christ Jesus: eternal life and sanctification. He adds also what is always joined with religion, devotion, and obedience: “Glory,” he says, “to God, to God the Father; and to our God,” that is, Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1234D] (2) Note the testimony to Jesus Christ’s divinity; compare the commentary on Galatians.], “our Father.” To him be eternal glory—that is, unto ages of ages.

The letter ends. After the admonitions and commands concerning right living, greetings follow. First he himself greets, or directs others to be greeted in his name. But which others?

**Verses 21–22.**—“Greet all the saints in Christ Jesus.” Does “in Christ Jesus” qualify “saints,” or “greet”? “The brethren who are with me greet you.” “I,” he says, “do not greet alone or direct you to greet alone; the brethren too greet you.” He added, “who are with me.” He intended this to be understood of the people and of every Christian who was with him. Finally [Col. 1234D] he adds something else: “All the saints greet you,” those, certainly, whom received faith had sanctified; “but especially those who are of Caesar’s household.” [Note: [Col. 1234D] (3) The Vulgate varies only slightly in these two verses.] Those from Caesar’s household especially greet you. He also displays the power of the Gospel: many from Caesar’s household believed, though they ought, surely, to have been proud and to think of nothing but Caesar. He also displays their humility: they were humble and hospitable, and greeted all the brethren who were elsewhere. [Col. 1235A] From his saying “especially,” one may understand that they made an effort to please by their service, and that this is why he said, beyond the others, that they themselves greet you.

**Verse 23.**—“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” He thought of the Philippians in such a manner that he did not judge them, as in the other letters, to be entangled or to have been led astray by false apostles; rather, the letter was written only in exhortation and prayer. “The grace,” he says, “of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” For if the Spirit is present, they think rightly. What, then, do the apostle’s prayers accomplish? That the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ may be with their spirit in Christ Jesus. Amen.

Here ends Victorinus’ Commentary on the Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Philippians.

[Col. 1235]

## Victorinus’ Two Books on the Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians. (C)

### Book One

[Col. 1235A] The Epistle to the Ephesians has as its subject that which must always be the sum of all instruction: namely, that they should possess knowledge of theology—that is, of God, Christ, the mystery itself and the coming, and the other things which pertain to this [Col. 1235B] knowledge. It likewise contains precepts for Christian life, suitable either to all or to particular persons: what a master ought to do toward a servant, a father toward a son, and a husband toward a wife. Since, then, these matters are twofold, we shall first set forth everything concerning theology; then concerning the manner of life and precepts for living.

Moreover, the issue is similar to that which is dealt with in all the letters: the Ephesians too seemed to have been corrupted by false apostles into joining Judaism to Christian teaching. This letter was therefore written as admonition and correction, so that they might correct and amend those things wrongly instilled in them, preserve what had formerly been handed down to them, and persevere in the same. The main point at the beginning, then, is this: that Christ, the Son of God, existed before the world, always exists, himself came, hope has been placed in him, and his promises are God’s promises. If this is so, Jewish teaching is utterly distinct: it is received, instilled, and understood differently, as we have frequently said and now explain. It therefore must not be joined either to divine knowledge or to the works and actions of life.

### Chapter I—Verse 1

He therefore begins with Christ, in order to make clear both that he professes to proclaim him in the Gospel and that hope is in him alone. At this beginning, according to his custom, he calls himself an apostle of Jesus Christ, as in the Epistle to the Romans: “Paul, servant of Christ Jesus.” Secondly, he adds, “called apostle,” surely called by Christ; and “predestined for the Gospel of God,” predestined by Christ—predestined long ago. And if long ago, then Christ existed long ago; for this is what the Jews deny. In the same way, in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “Paul, called apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God,” which is Christ. For Christ is the will of God, because he does what God wills. Therefore, apostle of Christ and called by Christ: this is the will of God. Likewise in the second [Epistle]: “Paul, apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God.” And now again in the same words: “Paul, apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God.”

But when he says this, “to the saints who are faithful at Ephesus” [Note: [Col. 1235D] (1) The Vulgate gives the end of this verse thus: “To all the saints who are at Ephesus and faithful in Christ Jesus.”], what does he add? “In Christ Jesus.” Thus [Col. 1236A] in every way he confirms that all the power both of the Gospel and of understanding consists in Christ Jesus, and that liberation, promises, and eternal life come from him. Likewise in the other letters, as we shall say later.

“Paul, apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God.” [Col. 1236B] For Christ Jesus is in the body, while in spirit he is the will of God. Therefore, when Jesus Christ chose and made Paul an apostle, he chose through the Spirit, which is the will of God, or the power of acting as it wills; for Christ wills what God wills. Let us understand, therefore, as we have often said, that God is the very power, greatness, and substance of all fullness; while Christ—that is, the *Logos* (λόγος), he who was in Christ—is the will of God. And if anyone [Note: [Col. 1236D] (1) Thus the manuscripts, for “anyone.”] attends to this thoroughly and carefully, he will find God and his will inseparable and yet, as it were, separable. For God is one thing and will another, though they are joined and cohere, and God and God’s will are never divided from each other. Thus the will alone knows what God wills and thinks.

The will of God therefore signifies the Father’s power, and is established in the Father; and again, the paternal power itself is in the Son, because the Son performs God’s will. At the same time, this too must be considered more carefully: how he is Son and how he is Father. It is not by a stirred generation; rather—if a comparison may be taken—will, conceived in thought, springs forth and is poured out like a certain birth of mind. For the thoughts of a soul are, as it were, the soul’s children. But since God has one will by a universal act of thought, therefore the Son is one and only-begotten. For he did not first think one thing and afterward another or something different, much less something contrary. Hence there is one God, one Christ: that is, one Father, one Son.

But, as we have said, this will is always from God and in God: it is power, God’s very own, full also of God’s and the Father’s strength. It is the very will which has often come here into the world in one manner and another, and now in flesh, which it formed for itself by its own power; and it fulfilled the mystery for the sake of the world and the souls that were being drawn about in the world. Paul therefore writes, “to the saints,” he says, “who are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus.” He constrained and bound them to religion and to the remaining rule of life by calling them both saints and, he says, faithful in Christ Jesus. In other epistles, when he writes to a church and a people, he does not add “saints” and “faithful.” But now, because he wished to hold them to the rule of the name, lest they add some new thing outside that name, [Col. 1237A] since they have already been sanctified by this name and are faithful in Christ, he showed, by calling them saints and faithful in Christ, that they ought to think nothing but Jesus Christ, by whose name they are saints and faithful.

### Verse 2

“Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” There are two things which especially remove disputes and impart God’s instruction: grace and peace. Since these people were held in error [Note: [Col. 1237D] (1) Manuscripts: “held.”], grace was therefore wished for them: namely, that they might know God, follow God and Christ fully, place everything in Christ, and admit nothing else. For Judaism is not the same thing, so as not to tear Christ apart; he rejects not the Law, but the understanding of life received from the Jews, as we shall teach later. [Col. 1237B] Therefore, “grace to you,” he says, that you may understand God and live according to God’s precepts. He adds also “peace from God,” because one who dissents is surely discordant: therefore peace from God also be with you, “with God,” he says, “our Father.” See how great is the grace given by God which is wished for the Ephesians: indeed, God is our Father.

Then he adds—and the two are one, as we said above—“and from our Lord Jesus Christ.” He is God; this one is God’s power. He is Father; this one is Son. The whole grace and power of God is supremely in Christ Jesus. For since the mystery of salvation was fulfilled through him, all salvation is in him. Even before Christ, the same Son of God—that is, the *Logos* (λόγος), that is, Christ—both was and always is and will be; and through him all things were made. Yet this same one was in Christ, that is [Note: [Col. 1237D] (2) Manuscripts: “this.”], Jesus; [Col. 1237C] and then he came to the aid of the salvation of all human beings who know God and keep his commands.

### Verse 3

“Blessed is [Note: [Col. 1237D] (3) Thus the manuscripts read “is,” not “God,” which word the Vulgate edition supplies.] the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He takes up a magnificent argument in order to expound that all things were made through Christ and the power of the mystery. He adds this so that people, and especially the Ephesians, might know how greatly Christ—that is, God through Christ—has benefited us; and, knowing this, might not depart from Christ’s name. For above he said, “Grace to you and peace from God our Father.” And when he had said, “and from the Lord Jesus Christ,” what does he add? “Blessed is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Thus, if God is also our Father, how great are we, and how great a grace have we received? For we have been made known through Christ and made Christ’s brethren, since we have one God as Father. [Col. 1237D] But all this is only through Christ.

Accordingly he adds that through Christ we too have God as Father: “who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.” Therefore we become sons, but sons in Christ: that is, if we confess Christ, follow him, conceive him in our mind, understand and venerate his dispensation by which he accomplished all things, and follow him in our manner of life through the precepts given, we become sons. Therefore, “blessed is [Col. 1238A] the Father.” Because he is Father both of us and of Christ, he adds, “the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Then he added the reason why he is blessed—he who, he says, “blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.” Let this pitiable error of men take notice: he said that we are blessed, and blessed with every blessing; therefore one who is blessed ought to suffer no evil. But what did he add? [Note: [Col. 1238D] (1) Manuscripts: *cum* in place of *quid*.] That is, “with every spiritual blessing,” not a carnal one. If we suffer any evils here in the world, or even outside it, let us ascribe them not to God but rather to ourselves. For then we obtain the blessing if we are spiritual, think spiritually, and seek spiritual goods. It may indeed happen that we understand all these things; nor is it an obstacle if, while understanding these and other matters, we nevertheless suffer some adversity in the world [Col. 1238B]. For many who act spiritually and live spiritually endure many adversities—Paul, Peter, and the rest.

But where is that blessing which makes us blessed? It is God’s blessing: not merely a spiritual blessing, but one “in the heavenly places,” that is, when we have departed from this world. Therefore all things must be endured, because what is promised to us from God’s blessing is both spiritual and in the heavenly places, that is, outside the world, above the heavens.
