And yet all these things, as he says, are in Jesus Christ; for he himself is Spirit. And when spiritual things are promised, they are promised in Christ; and we shall then attain spiritual things if we follow Christ.

## Verse 4

“Just as [Note: [Col. 1238D] (2) Vulgate: ‘As . . . before the foundation of the world.’] he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy.”

There has been a discussion of divinity, and a brief exposition of the whole mystery [Col. 1238C], in which these points are set forth: that Christ existed before the world; that the world was made; that souls existed before the world [Note: [Col. 1238D] (3) An opinion false in itself, though also related by certain others. Nevertheless Victorinus, col. 1241, explains with a certain philosophical subtlety in what sense souls may seem to have existed long before bodies.]; that by God’s ordering the world was made; and that by God’s ordering souls either came into the world or are set free from the world. God’s will is everything that occurs; and the reward for those living according to Christ is that sins are forgiven and that we share in God’s glory—a matter also treated in other epistles.

At the same time, what is the sum and cause of the whole mystery is touched upon here: whether the world was made, whether the world was made in Christ or by Christ; whether souls were sent into the world, whether souls existed before the world, and again whether souls were freed from the world. These matters are indeed hidden, yet true and complete. Thus the conclusion is drawn that, with Christ working, and through Christ and in Christ, all things in heaven and on earth are reconciled to God—in Christ, however—so that, when all things have been brought to fullness, all might be one in all. And this nevertheless takes place through the fullness of times; for nothing has occurred prematurely, nothing without order, but all has been accomplished in the fullness of times, as we shall teach in its place.

Descending especially to this fullness, the Apostle adds that the Ephesians too have been called, that they too may be in that fullness [Col. 1239A]. From this he exhorts and warns them that faith in Christ and faith in God must be preserved, so that they may think nothing other than that the entire mystery has been perfected by God, both through Christ and in Christ. If this is so, let them add nothing and suppose nothing else needs to be done; and let them correct the error by which they had joined Judaism to the pure, simple teaching concerning faith in Christ, salvation, and deliverance through Christ and by God’s will.

Let us first consider that he spoke thus: “God chose us”—certainly, when we already existed, he chose us [Note: [Col. 1239D] (1) Namely, in God’s thought, as Victorinus says below at the cited place.]; and he chose us in Christ. Therefore both we and Christ existed beforehand. And what is “beforehand”? Certainly, from eternity. For he said, “before the foundation of the world”: “he chose,” he says, “before the foundation of the world.” He chose only from among those who existed; and then he said “in Christ,” that is, in him. Therefore Christ existed, and we existed in Christ [Col. 1239B]. For it cannot be that Christ existed and we did not. If he chose us in Christ himself, then we were spiritual, if we were in Christ; and if we were in Christ and were spiritual—and, as he adds later, we existed before the foundation of the world—what reason was there for us to come here, and why was the world established?

If Christ himself, by God’s will, made all things, both those in the eternal realm and those in the world, and all things were in him, then they were there substantially: no longer merely in the force or potentiality by which they would later exist, but as things already existing. Therefore all things existed in Christ. Or is a certain lesser perfection involved in the world’s being established, and in the coming here into the world of very many things—souls and the other powers of this sort—which, as I said, were situated in Christ? Unless they experience and know everything that can exist, and thus see and follow what should be followed and chosen—in the Spirit, certainly, who is Christ. Just as souls, in their force and power, are not themselves the same thing as Spirit, but are such as can receive Spirit; yet, inasmuch as they are souls, they are not already Spirit [Note: [Col. 1239D] (2) Manuscripts: *quo*.] [Note: [Col. 1239D] (3) This distinction will shortly be explained.].

Since, therefore, the nature of souls is such that, if a soul conducts itself wholly and with all things perfected—that is, if it knows itself, knows God, and learns those things which are alien in such a way as to reject and exclude them—it rightly becomes perfect. And when it has become perfect, having rejected alien things and known God, when it has received full knowledge of the universe, it immediately becomes spiritual. So too with the human being, and with everything that belongs to the human being.

But though the soul is capable in respect of intellect [Col. 1239D], intellect can be deceived unless it also knows that which imitates intellect but is not intellect. If the soul observes, recognizes, rejects, and flees as an enemy and deceiver that which deceives, lies, and misleads, it will easily retain and know both itself and its own power; and it will be full and perfect in Christ, that is, spiritual. What then produces a likeness of understanding and yet deceives perception? It is found only in worldly things and in matter [Note: [Col. 1240D] (1) Thus the manuscripts; below, however, *materia*.], which the Greeks call ὕλη (*hylē*, “matter”) [Col. 1240A]. For from bodily things, apertures [Note: [Col. 1240D] (2) Thus the manuscripts.], and powers of sensation, there arises a kind of deceptive intellect which, by manifold coloring, deceives uncorrupted understanding and in some way injures truth through images.

Therefore, since it is natural to the soul [Note: [Col. 1240D] (3) Manuscripts: “to the natural soul.”] that it should be capable of understanding, while understanding can easily slip and fall into the neighboring power and the image of understanding—that is, sensation, which is wholly in the world by nature—so that it might apprehend this and never itself be apprehended, the world was made by God’s work and will, and all things were composed in matter. Held fast by these things, the soul might come to know what the senses are and how much they can do. And law and warnings were given by God, so that God might be known and what is not of God might be known [Col. 1240B].

But souls conquered by sensory powers would have in their perception nothing but the world, matter, flesh, and body; they would believe these alone to be true; nor would they be fit to conquer and break the bonds holding the soul by God’s power and will. In order to free them from the senses and from the deceptive world, he sent his Son, our Lord, Savior, Christ, the Holy Spirit, so that, when the mystery was disclosed, he might teach first what the Father is; then what Spirit is; what it is to live spiritually; what the soul should follow; and what is alien, as I have taught. For this is the Christian’s power: to discern and separate these things—which are eternal, which mortal, which lead to destruction, and which to salvation.

Therefore by the mystery which he fulfilled here through flesh, cross, death, and resurrection [Col. 1240C], aid was brought to souls. If faith is received in Christ, he takes up souls of this kind, assists them, and liberates them. For to believe Christ and receive faith in Christ is already to think spiritually and to be lifted above bodily and material desires. From this, as it were, a kinship in understanding joins and associates us with Christ; and, when it has associated us with Christ, it says, with God also. For through Christ we are joined to God, and there is no hope whatsoever of our salvation except in believing Christ.

This is already to think spiritually, to grasp the true understanding, and not to be tossed about by the motions of the world and of matter. Through all this, the whole human being is in true Spirit, and from this point life is already in Christ. When life is in Christ, then, Christ’s mystery having been enacted, we are received; and through Christ we are received by God into the number of the sons, having become spiritual [Col. 1240D], so that we too may rise from the world and from death by God’s will, yet in Christ.

For this is commanded now, often, and everywhere: that our whole life, our whole hope, and our whole labor of understanding should be in Christ. For the whole ground of our eternity, glory, and salvation is both Christ and in Christ, if, casting away all things and thinking spiritually, we separate from ourselves worldly thoughts, worldly affections, in a sense bodily desires, bodily honors, bodily powers, and even the will for the powers or honors of the world. For everything whatsoever that is worldly—even if it is heavenly in the world, etherial, or called by any other divine and eternal name according to the world—is nevertheless worldly; it is neither divine nor eternal, for it is material. And whatever is material is temporal, perishable, and corruptible [Col. 1241A].

Therefore, if, all worldly things being set aside, as I have said, our whole understanding is in Christ, and our whole understanding concerns Christ, and hence through Christ concerns God, then, having become spiritual, we rise again and are joined to God through Christ, and fullness comes about in all things. This fullness is nothing other than that everything belonging to him should be his own. Thus souls, by the grade of their progression, although they were from him and belonged to him, yet because they shone by a lesser light through a certain distance from him [Col. 1241B], were not so perfect. That is, they could slip from understanding the true into things plausible, and from plausible things into false things—that is, into the things of sense; and these are, as I said, either the world, matter, or all things in the world.

The soul would be less perfect through not knowing these things, and would remain of such a nature if, on coming, it recognized and despised them. And so that it might be restored whole and perfect from that by which it could be apprehended, God made the world for the knowledge of the senses. Thus souls, captured by the great enticements of the senses, had now lost that power of their light. Since they had become flesh and thought bodily thoughts, the mystery was fulfilled through the Savior, so that human beings might learn their parent and might attain the power of understanding—having despised, trodden underfoot, and crushed all sensory things [Col. 1241C]. Thus, perfection having been completed in every respect, all things might become one in all things according to Christ, through Christ, and in Christ; and so that fullness, as I said above, might be rendered perfect out of all things.

These matters are treated in these words so as to teach that all things were made, made through Christ, and, through Christ, brought to completion in God’s will: thus, “he chose us; he blessed us in him.” How do you prove this? Because he blessed us “just as,” he says, “he chose.” But when did he choose? Before the foundation of the world. And when did he bless us? When we came to faith and knew the mystery: “just as he chose us in him before the foundation [of the world], that we should be holy.”

I remind you, as I have often reminded you, that our salvation and all eternity are in Christ [Col. 1241D] and through Christ; and that our souls existed even before the foundation of the world, since they have always existed in the eternal realm with their own substance [Note: [Col. 1241D] (1) Victorinus still insists on the eternal pre-existence of souls. He scarcely, if at all, escapes this error shortly afterward when he says that souls existed in God’s thought. For foreseeing a future thing is one thing; for that thing to exist is another. Christian teaching, however, is that individual souls are created by God when they are introduced into the recently formed bodies of human parents. See Legesis, *collect. vat.*, T. I, p. 81 ff.].

God therefore predestined and chose these before the foundation of the world, that they might be sanctified: that is, that the reception of Spirit might be confirmed; that, all vices which could befall them having been laid aside, they might become spirits. For since by nature they are something else, they can fall into sensation, which belongs wholly to the world and worldly things; and again, when their natural power is aroused, they may know God, be near to God, and exist as, so to speak, children of God [Col. 1242A]. Before the foundation of the world God appointed and chose them that they should become holy and be sanctified; and the world was established for their sake, so that through sensation they might receive true understanding of all worldly things, sensation being the deceiver of true understanding, wholeness, and truth. For the just person is proved in adversities, light in darkness, and truth in falsehood. Thus in the world they might readily know God and, through Christ—that is, through Spirit, by understanding spiritually—become spirits. For this is what it is to be sanctified.

God therefore predestined that we should be holy. “He predestined,” then, can refer only to things that exist, so that a certain order may, as it were, be produced. You may consider how one should take this. For they already existed substantially, as I myself judge and believe; or, if they did not exist in the manner in which I believe, in their own substance or existence, they nevertheless existed in God’s thought. Since God’s thought is not nothing but a certain existence, it must necessarily be granted that souls existed in true and proper existence [Col. 1242B]. For our thought is, as it were, empty; but God’s is not [Note: [Col. 1242D] (1) It seemed to me that *non* should certainly be added.]. Yet, according to the reasoning of philosophers, even our thoughts are substantially nothing but the existence of things. But we have elsewhere explained these matters and this same discussion more fully.

“And blameless.” You see, therefore, how much is added, and what blamelessness includes: not merely “that we should be,” he says, but “that we should be holy”; nor merely “that we should be holy,” but “that we should be blameless” [Col. 1242C]. Therefore a stain is something added to substance. Substance existed, then, but a stain could happen to it. God predestined that we should be blameless. For although the world had not yet stained us, nevertheless, because we were of such a nature that we could fall into stain, God therefore predestined us so that, when we had fallen into stain, we might be blameless through his grace—that is, through Christ.

For by knowing Christ, by knowing [him] in the world, by knowing [him] in the senses, by knowing [him] in what is contrary, and by knowing [him] in darkness, then we receive the true light; then we receive Christ, that is, Spirit. Then, bodily stains having been rejected—that is, carnal sensations—we are blameless and holy.

## Verses 5–6

“Before him in love [Note: [Col. 1242D] (2) Vulgate: ‘In his sight in love.’], having predestined us [Note: [Col. 1242D] (3) The Vulgate has: ‘Who predestined us,’ etc.] for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, unto himself, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace.”

What, to whom, why, and through whom does he grant this? What too does he bestow, that he seems to grant us adoption as sons—a great and principal thing, scarcely to be desired even by our prayers: that we should appear as adopted sons? To whom does he grant it? Clearly to souls situated far from God’s power, since they can fall into vices and receive stains. Through whom does he grant it? Through Jesus Christ and unto him. Why, or for what purpose? “To the praise,” he says, “of his glory” [Col. 1243A]—of grace; that is, when he grants a great benefit, God displays from this the preeminent glory of his power: when he not only liberates us, such as we are, placed in vices [Note: [Col. 1243D] (1) Manuscripts: *invitus*, “unwilling.”] and bound by carnal sins, and, sins forgiven, renders us free from crimes, but also adopts us as sons. This, then, is the praise of his glory and grace: of glory, because he has such great power; of grace, because he grants these things to us.

What he said, “for adoption as sons,” is full, certain, and proper. For Christ is Son, truly Son, and truly Son, as I have often taught, because he is the image of God. But souls are far from God’s image; and again souls far removed receive Spirit, and Spirit is Son. Souls therefore become sons in place of the Son; and when souls are made sons in this sense, they are rightly said to be received for adoption as sons [Col. 1243B]—yet through God’s Christ, that is, through Spirit, who is truly Son and the only Son.

If, then, he is true and only Son, when we receive Christ, that is, Spirit, we are adopted sons, not [naturally] sons. For through the power of the Son we become sons; and this is adoption, “in which he graced us in his beloved Son,” that is, he bestowed grace upon us. For this is what “he graced” means. But everywhere he confirms both what grace is and through whom grace comes; for he also adds through whom grace comes: “in his beloved Son.” He likewise adds grace:

## Verse 7

“In whom we have redemption through his blood [Note: [Col. 1243D] (2) The Vulgate places a comma after *eius* (‘his’).], the remission of sins.”

For this is grace: that in Christ, through his blood, we have redemption and remission of sins; that our sins are remitted through the fact that he was crucified under the Law [Col. 1243C]. For this is “through his blood”: he redeemed us from death, that is, from bodily thoughts and desires, and made us his servants—that is, [made us] serve him, which is already to live spiritually. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1243D] (3) Manuscripts: *idem*, “the same.”], it is to do nothing carnally and perceive nothing by sensation, but to turn wholly toward God, tread underfoot all worldly things, and return to our origin. For this is to be redeemed: to be freed from captivity.

Moreover, captivity is nothing other than being led from the origin of freedom into captivity. Therefore we were free—that is, before the world—but the world made us captives; for we were of such a nature that we could fall and be captured. But this captivity came about for our benefit. For once we had known all the evils of slavery and captivity, we were redeemed by Christ; that is, restored to that former nature which we had from God, we now live spiritually [Col. 1243D]. From this we are spirits and therefore sons of God—but by adoption, all our sins, of course, having been remitted. For we did not return to Spirit by our own power; through Christ’s blood we received Spirit.

Therefore our sins are remitted and forgiven through God’s grace; we do not lay them aside by our own power. This alone belongs to our power: to believe Christ and, because of Christ, to live spiritually. But he himself forgives sins, he himself redeems us, and he commends God’s grace, so that we may now possess eternity and unstained holiness.

## Verse 8

[Col. 1244A]

“According to the riches of his grace, which he abundantly bestowed [Note: [Col. 1244D] (1) Vulgate: ‘which superabounded.’] upon us in all wisdom and prudence.”

God is Father; for all things arose from him as from a fountain. How they arose is a matter of great understanding and great teaching; yet the certain confession is that all things are from God. Now “all things” means both those which are highest and those which are weak, those which are not eternal, and others of this kind. For when I say “all things,” things diverse, contrary, and opposed must be understood. In short, all things certainly are whatever they are, however they are, and of whatever sort they are; and being these things, they nevertheless remain in their own manner, substance, reality, and quality.

Thus angels, demons, matter, elements, souls, and all other things of this sort have their own nature; remaining in their condition, they possess the common force and power of origination [Col. 1244B]. Souls, however, which themselves too have force among all things, do not remain in the state in which they came into being and received their substance; rather, by God’s power they are advanced to a better substance, and, though souls, they become spirits [Note: [Col. 1244D] (2) Manuscripts: *sint*, “are.”]. These, then, are the riches of God bestowed upon us: that we become more than we began to be and more than we were, while the rest remain in their own condition and preserve their substance and quality as they arose.

It is God’s magnificent grace, God’s great riches, when he grants souls this gift: that they come to adoption as sons of God through Jesus Christ, that is, through Spirit; that, thinking spiritual things, they may be spirits. These are his riches, and the riches of his grace, which he abundantly bestowed upon us. Rightly, then, did he abundantly bestow upon us. For an angel will remain what it is as an angel; likewise all other things, whether in matter, in the luminaries, or in other things of this kind. All these are prepared and preserved by God [Col. 1244C].

But among all things the soul has merited more from God—a greatest gift and great riches—when, by knowing God, although this is infused into it by God’s will through Jesus Christ, it merits to be received among the sons and to be near to God. And, through Christ himself, it merits to be made, as it were, a co-heir with the Son—that is, Jesus Christ—of eternity, majesty, and power, and merits the name and power of a son. “He abundantly bestowed upon us,” therefore, he says. But how did he abundantly bestow? “In all wisdom and prudence.” For this indeed is all wisdom and prudence: to know Christ and, through Christ, both to understand and see God. All other wisdom may be worldly, or of another such kind, even outside the world [Col. 1244D]; yet without Christ wisdom and all prudence are empty and miserable. For one who knows Christ and receives Christ becomes Spirit; acting in all things spiritually, such a person is received among the sons of adoption and in some way comes to exist as [a son]. In this grace, then, God has abounded toward us—in all wisdom and all prudence: wisdom as the genus, prudence as the species.

## Verse 9

“That he might make known to us the mystery of his will.”

Does “to us” mean to human beings, or to us Christians who have received the Law? For we understand the mystery of God’s will, by which his grace abounded toward us [Col. 1245A], so that through Christ’s blood and remission of sins we might know his riches. This will, as he says, is the mystery of prudence, or the mystery of the will, in Christ Jesus. For he adds: “according to the will which he purposed in him” [Note: [Col. 1245D] (1) Vulgate: “According to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him.”]. It is not merely a will, but a will purposed in him. For all things are through him; and nothing at all, nor anything done in the mystery, is without Jesus Christ. The world, the things in the world, our liberation, and the cause of all things are in Christ and are Christ.

## Verse 10

“And this is the will of God which he purposed in him [Note: [Col. 1245D] (2) These words, ‘And this is the will of God which he purposed in him,’ are absent from the Vulgate.] in the dispensation of the fullness of times.”

He shows that all things have been arranged in order, so that there might be a dispensation. Likewise, all things are, as it were, administered; for whatever will occur has been ordered. In order to occur, it must undoubtedly be dispensed. The world and everything in the world have been arranged, and thus those things occur; and the sum of the dispensation is certainly apparent through each of the things which occur [Col. 1245B]. This is the fullness of times: when, in their respective times, things arrive at the sum that is made up of all things—namely, our liberation and that of all souls, the heavenly ones, certainly. But this takes place in the fullness of times, when the times are fulfilled, while those things are accomplished which have been ordered by God in Christ [Note: [Col. 1245D] (3) Thus the manuscripts. And indeed I have long since grown weary of the most obscure and leaden Victorinus.].

“And through Christ to restore all things to Christ, both those in heaven and those upon earth, in him” [Note: [Col. 1245D] (4) Thus the Vulgate gives this second part of verse 10: “To restore all things in Christ, both those in heaven and those on earth, in him.”].

For not all things which are in Christ are restored, nor those very things which are in heaven and those above the earth; but those things which are in Christ are restored, for there are also other and alien things [Col. 1245C]. Whatever things, then, are in Christ, these are restored and rise again, whether they are in heaven or on earth. For he himself is salvation, renewal, and eternity; in him we have also obtained the allotted inheritance. He added what was necessary. For not all [are restored] at once, as it has also been said elsewhere: Christ first, then we, then the rest. This, therefore, is what he says:

## Verse 11

“We have obtained an allotted inheritance, having certainly been predestined according to his purpose” [Note: [Col. 1245D] (5) Vulgate: “In whom we also were called by lot, having been predestined according to his purpose.”]; that is, who [is allotted a share] at what time, and, as we said above, that we might already be predestined unto perfection. For nothing occurs which has not been predestined by God and in some manner made beforehand. Things which are established spiritually by God are now brought about perceptibly.

“He who works all things [Note: [Col. 1245D] (6) Vulgate: ‘who works everything.’] according to the counsel of his will” [Col. 1245D].

It is certainly God, he says, who works all things. For Christ works by God’s power; and though Christ himself is the worker, God works through him. Therefore God works, and works all things. Every motion, and the motion of all things, is only from God and through God [Col. 1246A]. Thus, since operation is motion, operation is from God because operation is motion. The rest, however, are inert, inactive, defective, sluggish. Thus, for them to come into motion is God’s operation, namely through Jesus Christ.

Therefore it is God who works all things, and he works according to the counsel of his will. The difference, then, is this: when God works and Christ works, Christ works from God’s will; God works according to the counsel of his will. For Christ is God’s will. In other books, I think, we have explained and sufficiently dealt with what God’s will is, what God is, whether they are the same or something different, whether one thing or another, and related questions. Here we must be content with a simple exposition [Col. 1246B], holding in fear and reverence that Christ is God’s will; that God’s will is motion; that God works all things because God is motion; that God’s will is motion; and that God is.

## Verse 12

“That we may be unto the praise of his glory [Note: [Col. 1246D] (1) Vulgate: ‘That . . . we [may be] unto his glory.’].”

For if we believe in him and become spiritual by following Christ, we shall be unto the praise of the glory of God himself, we who hoped beforehand in Christ. He has given the order. Then we shall be unto the praise of his glory when we have hoped in Christ; or, those who hoped beforehand in Christ shall be unto the praise of his glory. Therefore hoping in Christ comes first—that is, following Christ and believing that all that Christ promised can be fulfilled. The consequence will then be that we become unto the praise of God’s glory, because, as I have often said, through Christ eternity—which is our salvation—and God’s glory alike [Col. 1246C] are given to us; hence there will be praise of his glory.

## Verse 13

“In whom you also, having heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation [Note: [Col. 1246D] (2) Vulgate: ‘In whom you also, when you had heard the word of truth—the Gospel of your salvation.’].”

He descends to the particular point, lest he seem to have treated the matter generally, and neither fittingly nor usefully, so that it might be a benefit to others but not to those whom he addresses. He adds something particular: namely, since he sends this epistle to the Ephesians, “this,” he says, “is also yours; for you too are in this.” But what is “in whom you also”? In Christ, certainly. And what is [your being] in Christ? That, having heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, you have followed faith and are now in Christ.

“In whom, believing, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.” This is the very rationale of the exhortation, and often the mystery: to believe in Christ, to believe the Gospel—that is, he says, the word of truth. “In this, you too, believing, were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise” [Col. 1246D], so that you have now received the Holy Spirit of Christ’s promise. But although the Holy Spirit appears to be one thing and Christ another, the consummation, perfection, and complete liberation is the Holy Spirit. “You were sealed,” he says, “in the Holy Spirit of promise concerning the things which were promised,” because the Holy Spirit has been promised and given to us. And concerning him he thus adds:

## Verse 14

“Who is the pledge of our inheritance, unto the redemption of adoption [Note: [Col. 1246D] (3) Vulgate: ‘of acquisition.’], unto the praise of his glory.”

This Spirit, he says, is the pledge of our inheritance; for he sent him to us as a pledge that we shall obtain the inheritance of heavenly things, eternity, and the glory of God [Col. 1247A]. This is what is meant by “unto the redemption of adoption”: that we may be redeemed from these worldly, earthly, bodily, and carnal evils; redeemed unto adoption; and exist as sons, seeking rather the glory of God. And grace is beyond our merit; for a great gift received beyond merit belongs to the glory of the one who grants it, not of the one who receives it.

## Verse 15

“For this reason I also, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1247D] (1) Vulgate: ‘For this reason I also, hearing of your faith, which is in the Lord Jesus.’].”

He descends specifically [Note: [Col. 1247D] (2) Manuscripts: *descendi*, “I descended.”] to exhorting the Ephesians, together with that admonition that they should not think otherwise. In an urbane manner of speaking he says, “having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.” For this is the sum of things, this the power, this the mystery: that faith be in Christ Jesus [Col. 1247B]. This necessarily also entails that all saints who have received faith in Christ and have been sanctified should be loved. Thus one who is faithful in Christ loves the saints—that is, those sanctified by faith in Christ and by the mystery of baptism.

Therefore, having heard of faith in Christ and of the mystery of baptism—therefore, having heard of your faith, I love you; having heard also of your love, love toward the saints, I shall endeavor to give thanks to God for you.

## Verse 16

“I shall not cease [Note: [Col. 1247D] (4) Vulgate: ‘I cease not.’] giving thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers.”

Every prayer which we make to God is either concerned with what we have received or with receiving something. And because everyone who prays first prays for himself [Col. 1247C], then for those whom he loves, Paul says: “In prayer I make mention of you.” Therefore the principal prayer is first for myself, then also for you. And he adds that twofold reason: “giving thanks for you.” This concerns the past. But he adds:

## Verse 17

“May the God [Note: [Col. 1247D] (6) The Vulgate adds ‘that.’] of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, give you a spirit of wisdom.”

This, then, concerns the future: to pray with some petition. Thus, since you believe in Christ, I give thanks to God for you; and again I pray and make mention of you in my prayers, that God—what God? lest they go astray or imagine some other, whether pagan or Jewish god—God, he says, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom, that you may be wise and understand what is true.

It may therefore seem to be separated thus: “the God of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He is Christ’s God; therefore he is also our God, because Christ is our Lord; and he is our God who is the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, wholly distinct from the God of the Jews; he is also the Father of glory [Col. 1247D]. Therefore I make prayer that God may give you a spirit of wisdom, that you may be wise and understand what is true. Here and in very many places it is sufficiently confirmed, certain, demonstrated, and shown that, in order for us to be wise, to understand, and to understand truth, Spirit is given to us by God—but a spirit of wisdom.

Finally, he adds, proving that what we understand, or strive to understand, is not our own doing. For what does he say? “And of revelation in the knowledge of him,”

## Verse 18
the enlightened eyes of your heart, that he may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation. The spirit of wisdom is that the Spirit himself may make us wise, may be in us, and that we may, as it were, seem to be wise through ourselves, when the Spirit makes us wise. But the spirit of revelation is that what we are to understand, receive, and follow may be revealed to us as though from outside ourselves. Thus, in some way, the spirit of wisdom is one thing, the spirit of revelation another.

Let us therefore know that we arrive at truth and at the fullness of the mystery by, as it were, two ways: either when we ourselves understand [Col. 1248B] God and grasp knowledge concerning divine things, or when there is a certain revelation—that is, an admonition, as it were, from without—which shows us God and all divine things. With some, indeed, it is considered especially great and, as it were, close to truth, to apprehend something by revelation; but [the text is uncertain: “either like, or prepared like”] something more like it and more certain [Note: [Col. 1248D] (1) Thus the manuscripts.]. But when we receive wisdom, so as to apprehend divine things by our own intelligence—and, to speak truly, as is also stated here, by the divine Spirit—then we already have discourse within ourselves and with ourselves, and, if one may say so, with the Spirit now, as it were, present.

I pray, therefore, that he may give us the spirit of wisdom and revelation. Concerning this matter he added, namely, *in the knowledge of him*: that this may be wisdom and through these things revelation, namely, that we may know God and have the [Col. 1248C] eyes of our heart enlightened concerning the knowledge of God. “This,” he says, “I pray for you: that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints.” To know God is indeed a great reward; yet I do not know that it is more than a small reward for a human being unless he himself gains something and in some manner becomes better. Therefore, he says, I ask that the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him may be given you, and that you may have the eyes of your heart enlightened.

But because, as I said, the knowledge of God is great indeed, yet small in our estimation unless we receive something from it, he added what you should understand more fully in that very knowledge of God: “that you may know,” he says, “what is the hope of his calling.” First, what hope we possess as those called; then what riches we attain—and riches of glory—which are the riches [Col. 1248D] of the glory of his inheritance: so that we may attain both his glory and an inheritance, and may be numbered among the sons. For when the goodness of God receives us into adoption, into the adoption of his sons, and we are heirs—we are heirs, however, not as in worldly affairs, where the one whose heir someone is perishes, a thought and statement alike impious—but in the sense that we are accounted heirs of good things: that we may enjoy the same goods which God enjoys, may be in glory, may be eternal. This is the inheritance. For we are also co-heirs with Christ, and Christ is God; therefore, with God we are heirs of the riches of his glory.

But all these things are among the saints, [Col. 1249A] that is, among those sanctified by the mystery, by the name of Christ. Therefore I especially ask this: that you may be enlightened and know this great benefit; and that [Paul] may implore and pray that the Spirit may come upon us and teach us these things. We ourselves frequently ask this for ourselves; yet no small benefit is conferred by one who has already earned the Lord’s favor and has been sanctified. He asks that the very thing which we desire and pray for may come to us. Paul recalls that he renders this service to the Ephesians [Note: [Col. 1249D] (1) The manuscripts: “to Ephesus itself.”].

VERS. 19, 20.

“And what is the sublimity of the greatness of his power toward you who have believed, according to the working of the might of his power, which he worked in Christ” [Note: [Col. 1249D] (2) Vulgate: “And what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his power.”]. “This,” he says, “I ask in my prayers: that he may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation. I also ask that you may know what is the hope of the calling, what the riches are; and [Col. 1249B] likewise that you may know what the sublimity is.”

He explains that sublimity itself: “of greatness,” he says. But what is this greatness? He added, “of power.” Again, what is this power? It is that which is in you, or toward you, because he grants it to you. And what is that power which he grants you? That you may believe in him, and believe according to the working of the might of his power. There are many workings of God’s power; for whatever was made through Christ is, as it were, a working of Christ—as are the world and all things which were made through him. Yet the true, certain, and at the same time magnificent working of God is that which he worked in Christ.

He then adds what that working of God is which he worked in Christ: raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in heaven [Note: [Col. 1249D] (3) Vulgate: “Raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places.”].

VERS. 21, 22, 23.

“Above every principality and power [Col. 1249C] and might and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; and he subjected all things beneath his feet and gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body” [Note: [Col. 1249D] (4) The Vulgate adds “and.”], “his fullness” [Note: [Col. 1249D] (5) The manuscripts: “to him.”], “who is fulfilled in all things in all.”

“According to the working of the might of God’s power,” he says, “you believed.” Now there is a working of God’s power. Although at the beginning it was either the sending of Christ, or the making of the world subject on account of souls, since this is lofty and hidden away from matters openly manifest—matters which were done [Note: [Col. 1249D] (6) The manuscripts: “carried out.”], done recently, and are still before our eyes—he draws from this an exposition of God’s power, which he worked in Christ. What is it? It is the resurrection from the dead. For when he raised Christ from the dead—which we certainly saw—this is surely a great working of the might of God’s power. Then there are the consequences following his resurrection from the dead: he set him at his right hand in heaven. Surely it is great to have bestowed such honor, such majesty, that he set him in heaven and set him at his own right hand. This is too little: [Col. 1250A] “Above every,” he says, “principality,” so that no other ruler, whether worldly or above the world, is anything but inferior to Christ. And “above every power,” he says, “and above every might, above every dominion, and above every name.” What name? A name spoken either on earth, that is, in this age, or in this world, or even in the future.

Again, what is it that he granted? That he subjected all things beneath his feet, and that he gave him to be head over the whole Church. He defines this Church, so that we may understand what the Church is which is his body: that is, the Church consists of all the members of Christ, because it is the fullness of him who is fulfilled in all things in all.

Therefore, since God has bestowed such great and magnificent things on Christ and brought them to fulfillment concerning Christ [Col. 1250B] whom he raised, it is surely the great working of the might of his power which [Note: [Col. 1250D] (1) The manuscripts: “which,” feminine.] he worked in Christ. Since the sense and the overall force of the expression are evident, let us now reconsider the individual points.

“Raising him from the dead”: God raised from the dead on the third day Christ Jesus, who was in flesh, died, and was lifted up on the cross—an event openly done and clear by every testimony. Although the rationale of the mystery is magnificent even in a simple understanding, still, that he was raised from the dead, that death—the death human beings suffer either through violence or bodily necessity—accomplished nothing, and that God removed it so that death might have no power: this is surely a great power of God, a great might, a great working.

But since we have often said what Christ is, what it means that he was in flesh, what it means that he was lifted [Col. 1250C] up on the cross, and what it means that he was raised, we briefly offer this reminder. For the fuller account of the mystery has frequently been treated by us in these books and explained more fully elsewhere. Through Christ—that is, through Spirit—souls were renewed and liberated, so that they might return to their own origin and the sins into which souls had fallen might be removed. But because human beings could not live because of the weakness of the flesh, Christ was sent—that is, the Spirit, and intelligence, and the Spirit of revelations, of all divine things, and of eternal life—so that, through his mystery and through bodily death, souls raised again might return to heavenly power; and so that Christ, suffering death on the cross and receiving resurrection from the Father, might through the mystery furnish to all souls an image of resurrection. [Col. 1250D] But these things, as he said, [belong] also to a certain time.

“And setting him at his right hand in heaven.” Since Christ is God’s motion; and motion belongs to operation; while the operation of motion is always at the right hand: therefore Christ is set at God’s right hand [Note: [Col. 1250D] (2) Let us note Victorinus’s ingenious interpretation.] above every principality and power. For Christ’s motion is the first motion of all things. Principalities, powers, mights, and dominions are motions concerning things to be done, whether in divine or secular matters. But since Christ is the source, origin, and principal reality of everything [Col. 1251A] moved, he is set above every principality, as above every power.

Now principality is one thing, power another: principality is in act; power is in the capacity by which something can be, not by which it already is, but by which something can be. But since Christ himself is the origin of all things, and in him is that which is potentiality, he is above every power. Likewise, since he is the source of all acts—and act is principality—he is above every principality. Likewise, because, whether something is or can be something else in relation to it, there is potentiality, and it can, before there is action, be above every action, in all these things—whether in principality or in power—there is might: that is, before the act, so that principality itself may be possible. Therefore, because Christ is above all these things, he is above every might [Col. 1251B]; and therefore above all those powers, whether worldly, heavenly, or beyond, in eternal things; above all principalities; and above all powers which hold dominion over each particular thing [Note: [Col. 1251D] (1) This is read exactly thus in the manuscripts.], for they exercise dominion.

But Christ is the source of all things, for all things are from him, since he is the father of all motion; and all these are motions. Christ is therefore above every dominion also.

“And every name.” All names were indeed invented later, especially by those who are in the world—whether human beings, angels, or powers. For those eternal realities are things themselves, living, eternal, intelligent powers, which are known substantially [Note: [Col. 1251D] (2) The manuscripts: “knowing.”]. There is therefore no name there; names have been added to them by our vocabulary, whether in our language or, as I said, that of angels—yet of angels who are in the world. But [Col. 1251C] although Christ, the divine and holy Spirit and Son of God, receives these names from us, he is nevertheless beyond all these terms which appear to have been imposed.

And in one place we touched upon the point that every name is subsequent to the begotten, and that among names themselves there is a principal name, truly above every name and the source of all names, which in Greek is called ὢν, “the One Who Is” [Note: [Col. 1251D] (3) Exod. III.14.]. But Christ is above ὢν itself; therefore he is also above every name. Yet that ὢν is among eternal things; and if it is among eternal things, and Christ is above ὢν, it was rightly said, “above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the future.”

More sharply and precisely: all names that could be fashioned by the mind for expressing those realities which [Note: [Col. 1251D] (4) The manuscripts: “which.” Unless you prefer to refer it to “names.”] we intelligent beings have apprehended have already been made. But since many things will be [Col. 1251D] new in the future, and more new in that age, the age which is to come, when all things shall be disclosed, names have not yet been imposed by us upon realities not yet known; indeed, they cannot be, since they are not known. Christ is set above even the names that will come to be. Thus he is first and supreme in realities, because he is above all powers, principalities, and the rest. He is above every name because in this age no name can fittingly be applied to him, and all future names lie within his [Col. 1252A] appellation, substance, or whatever declaration or utterance concerning him [Note: [Col. 1252D] (1) Thus the manuscripts.].

“And he subjected all things beneath his feet.” By many different modes the one power which is Christ is understood: whether as motion, as Word, or as Christ the first universal reality, through whom all things are made, have been made, and will be made. God therefore rightly subjected all things beneath his feet. For Christ is the procession from God, and Christ is procession through all things; and all things which have proceeded and which return to God return by his power. Thus [Note: [Col. 1252D] (2) The manuscripts: “the same,” as elsewhere.] all things are subjected under his feet by action.

“And gave him as head over the whole Church.” Many identify the Church with all souls. Therefore Christ, who is Spirit, through whom souls know God, become spiritual, and are liberated from the quality of soul [Col. 1252B], so that they are no longer tempted or fall—since, made spiritual through Christ the Spirit, believing in him they perceive spiritually and thus come to the knowledge of God—Christ is in this way head over the whole Church, which is his body.

The whole Church is likewise every soul, but a soul to be saved and having its substance from eternal things, through which all things thrive; and thus all souls are through Christ, as we have often said. Therefore every body of Christ is every soul which he called Church. “His fullness,” that is, the Church itself, which is his body. It is the fullness of him “who is fulfilled in all things in all.” Christ is fullness, in whom every fullness is fulfilled. But everything that is fulfilled is emptied. Christ too has been emptied, or emptied himself; and again, when all things have been recovered [Col. 1252C] through the mystery and all souls saved, he is fulfilled in all. Therefore he is fullness.

But Paul spoke in this manner so as to say that the Church is his body, “whose,” he says, “fullness it is” [Note: [Col. 1252D] (3) The manuscripts: “of each of whom.”]; and it is the fullness of him who is fulfilled in all things in all. In other books I have explained more distinctly and fully these two terms, fullness and capacity: how God is fullness alone [Note: [Col. 1252D] (4) In the manuscripts “fullness” is repeated.], and how Christ is both capacity and fullness.

All these statements concerning Christ’s magnificence and power serve this purpose and demonstrate this: nothing beyond this is to be received, nothing outside it thought; and consequently the Ephesians err if they add anything further or associate anything from either Jewish or worldly teaching. Therefore he now returns to them and warns those already received into Christ and receiving Christ that they ought to receive [Col. 1252D] nothing other than Christ’s fullness [Note: [Col. 1252D] (5) The manuscripts: “Christ in fullness.”].

CAP. II.—VERS. 1, 2.

“And you, when you were dead in your offenses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who works in the sons [Note: [Col. 1252D] (6) Vulgate: “into the sons.”] of unbelief.”

The whole sense here must be joined together: both that the Ephesians were in sins, and that Paul himself was in desires of the flesh and in carnal counsels [Col. 1253A]. To all these, I say, must be joined the statement that God, who is rich in mercy, saved all—Paul himself and the Ephesians. For thus he concludes: “by whose grace you have been saved,” though you walked dead in offenses; and you also, though you walked dead in your offenses and sins.

I have frequently pointed out that death is understood in two ways: the familiar death in which, at the end of life in the world, the soul is separated from the body; and another death, when, while established in the body itself, a person pursues the desires of the flesh and lives in sins. “You,” he says, “when you were dead”; and he specified the kind of death: “in your offenses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world.” He shows what the sins are: namely, desires in and from the world—of riches, or worldly will or knowledge, or religion derived from the world [Col. 1253B]—and the other things of this world which destroy the soul as it wanders from the knowledge of truth.

Now when he says “the age of this world,” there are also higher ages, those eternal ages; how they are to be understood and what significance they bear I have explained in other books. But the age of this world is every worldly region, or the whole world: within the world, the motion of things producing and unfolding time. In eternal things “age” is not understood in the same manner. Yet that there are ages of eternal things Paul himself and all the prophets have declared; for it is said, and frequently said, “Blessed be God unto ages of ages.” For an age comes to an end; but ages of ages are both from eternal things and unto eternity.

“According to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who [Col. 1253C] now works in the sons of unbelief” [Note: [Col. 1253D] (1) The manuscripts: “difference.”]. Whoever walks according to the age of this world walks according to the prince of the power of the air, who is the spirit of the sons of unbelief [Note: [Col. 1253D] (2) Again, the manuscripts: “difference.” But before and after, “unbelief” is written.].

Since there are two things—light and darkness, truth and falsehood, good and malice—not, however, as though they were equal; for it is not right that anything should be compared to God even by opposition—let us understand likewise two spirits: one of faith, the other of unbelief. Satan and his devil, this spirit, have their substance from air, that is, from *hyle* (matter), and power in matter itself, or over those who think materially. Thus he is the prince of that power which is in the air, that is, in matter: a prince who is spirit, but, as I have said, spirit of matter; and he now works in material things, in the sons of unbelief—that is, he holds their minds and exercises dominion there.

Therefore whoever lives according to [Col. 1253D] the age of this world lives according to the prince of the power of the spirit of the air, who now works in the sons of unbelief. There is, however, a double reading: “the spirit working,” and “the spirit who now works.” We have said that the prince, or spirit, of the air is the prince or spirit of matter; yet there is this powerful rationale: among the elements, air itself is the chief. For fire is agitated air; water is moistened air; earth is dry and solid air. If air contains all things in itself, it is chaos, that is, darkness and the matter of darkness. Fire, however, is purer air and heaven, air shaken into agitation [Col. 1254A] [Note: [Col. 1254D] (1) The manuscripts: “succeeded.”].

For when the poet [Note: [Col. 1254D] (2) Virgil, *Aeneid* I.58.] described the power of the winds, by which they could throw all things into confusion unless they were controlled, he said that all things would be turned into air if the winds possessed free power:

> Otherwise the swift winds would surely bear sea and lands  
> And the deep heaven along with them, and sweep them through the air.

Their separation, each from the other, is the ordering of the world, as Moses taught: at the beginning, by God’s Word, he separated the waters; he also separated the earth and the spirit. Therefore it is rightly called the spirit of matter, the spirit of air.

VERS. 3.

“Among whom we too all once lived.” So that he might not insult the Ephesians, after saying that they were dead in offenses and sins, walking according to the spirit of the air, he added himself and the rest as well: [Col. 1254B] that all once lived according to this life, which he then adds: “in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of our flesh and of [its] counsels” [Note: [Col. 1254D] (3) Vulgate: “Doing the will of the flesh and of thoughts.”].

These are the matters in which the prince of the power of the air exercises activity—but in unbelieving sons—so that they have desires of the flesh, do the will of the flesh, and follow the counsels of the flesh. Whoever has rejected these now both knows and follows God, thinking nothing of the works of the flesh. “And we were by nature [Note: [Col. 1254D] (4) Vulgate: “And we were by nature children of wrath . . .”] children of wrath, like the rest.”

Since we lived by counsels of the flesh and out of its desires [Note: [Col. 1254D] (5) The manuscripts: “living.”], “we were,” he says, “natural children of wrath”: that is, born according to the nature of flesh and matter, for that is nature itself. We do not mean the divine nature, but the worldly one; and wherever there is birth, there is said to be nature. Therefore in the higher realms, because all things are unbegotten [Col. 1254C], when certain things are called begotten, they are understood to be begotten in some mysterious sense, not in the manner in which things are begotten in the world. For where there is nature, there is generation; and generation occurs when something begins to be which previously was not, or when something which existed otherwise begins to be something else—as a human being from seed, shrubs and other things from seed, and other animals besides.

But in eternal things, because all those divine realities begin to appear, as it were, by a certain distinction, they are therefore called, as it were, generated; although they remain in the same power and the same substance in which they were, and thus are not generated in the proper sense. For when God made all things by nature, he did not make those eternal things out of eternal things in the way he had them; rather, he merely, as it were, separated and established each individually. What and how great these things are, we learn from other books.

[Col. 1254D] Now we understand Christ, angels, souls, and all other eternal things as, in the eternal realms, begotten as it were—although generation in the world is something entirely different. “Therefore we were,” he says, “natural children,” that is, made through nature. But children of whom? Not of God, but of wrath; for that adversary, who is wrath, had claimed us for himself from matter. “Thus,” he says, “we were children of wrath, like the rest.” Properly speaking, those are children of wrath who are from [Col. 1255A] this world. Such, he says, are the rest, like us when we lived wickedly out of that world: that is, when we lived according to the flesh, as children of wrath live.

VERS. 4.

“But God, who is rich also in mercy, through his great love had mercy on us” [Note: [Col. 1255D] (1) Vulgate: “But God . . . because of the exceeding love with which he loved us.”].

For God’s riches in mercy are truly great. Since by our sins we had made ourselves strangers [Note: [Col. 1255D] (2) The manuscripts: “had made.”] to God, although we were from the higher world, he, by his grace forgiving sins and pardoning even offenses, redeemed us to himself through his Son. Since he did not spare his Son in order to liberate us, his riches are without doubt great, and so too is his love. For how great is his love for us, when he emptied his Son for our sake in order to redeem us by his passion? Such, then, is this love.

VERS. 5.

[Col. 1255B]

“And when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together in Christ.” Because God’s love remains, he says. This is the love; these are the riches: that, when we possessed substance from eternal things and were dead in sins, he redeemed us through Christ’s passion and made us saved. Since Christ’s passion is the mortification of sins, while Christ’s resurrection is our resurrection, he says, “He made us alive together in Christ”: that is, he restored us to eternal life, but through Christ, “by whose grace you have been saved” [Note: [Col. 1255D] (3) Vulgate: “By whose grace you have been saved freely.”].

He concludes what was especially necessary for everyone and for the Ephesians: that we are to receive nothing outside Christ, since by his grace we are saved. Therefore you also, Ephesians, saved by Christ’s grace, ought to receive nothing outside [Christ], and possess nothing external in religion and faith.

VERS. 6.

[Col. 1255C]

“And he raised [us] together, and placed [us] together in heaven” [Note: [Col. 1255D] (4) Vulgate: “And raised us together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places,” etc.].

This is a holy and complete mystery: we must have faith in Christ, not [suppose] that we now merit resurrection or heavenly kingdoms; rather, when Christ was raised, then we too were raised. This is what he says: “He raised [us] together.” Likewise, “and placed [us] together in heaven.” For when he placed Christ [there], he simultaneously placed there those who are and will be in Christ. In the heavenly places.

VERS. 7.

“So that he might show in the ages to come the overflowing riches of his glory” [Note: [Col. 1255D] (5) Vulgate: “of his grace.”], “in kindness toward us, in Christ” [Note: [Col. 1255D] (6) The Vulgate adds “Jesus.”].

For he did not render to us what we merited, since we receive this not by merits but by God’s grace and kindness. Therefore he raised us together in Christ for the sake of his goodness and the grace which is in Christ, so that he might show his riches to future and coming ages [Col. 1255D]. What riches? The grace of his kindness toward us. But all these things, as he frequently warns and as I point out, are in Christ. There [Note: [Col. 1255D] (7) The manuscripts: “where.”] is the entire mystery of both our resurrection and that of all things. For through Christ all things are reconciled: he is the door, he is resurrection, he is life, and he is the way to the Father.

VERS. 8.

[Col. 1256A]

“For by grace you have been saved through faith” [Note: [Col. 1256D] (1) Vulgate: “For by grace you have been saved through faith.”].

He explained openly that faith is required from us; and only so much is required: that we believe in Christ. If this is so, this alone is ours; we are not saved by our own merit but by God’s grace. Accordingly he adds, “and this not from yourselves: it is God’s gift.”

VERS. 9.

“Not from works, lest perhaps anyone should boast” [Note: [Col. 1256D] (2) Vulgate: “Not from works . . . so that no one may boast.”].

That we are saved, he says, is by God’s grace. Thus you too, Ephesians, are saved not from yourselves: it is God’s gift; nor is it from your works, but it is God’s grace and God’s gift, not our merit [Note: [Col. 1256D] (3) The manuscripts: “by our merit.”]. Works are one thing, our merit another. Hence he distinguished them by saying, “not from yourselves,” “not from works,” apart from works which must be offered daily in duties toward the poor and in other good deeds. [Col. 1256B]

But even where merit may arise from duty and religion, from chastity and abstinence, it cannot be [said to arise] from your works [Note: [Col. 1256D] (4) Thus the manuscripts.]. These are works. Therefore he concluded both points: “not from yourselves,” nor “from works,” and added, “lest anyone boast.” For somehow one who thinks that a reward has been rendered for his own works wishes it to be his own rather than the giver’s; and this is boasting.

VERS. 10.

“For we are his workmanship” [Note: [Col. 1256D] (5) The Vulgate has: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared that we should walk in them.”], “created in Christ.” By a certain mystery he fashioned and formed us in Christ, so that we might rise with him and, believing in Christ, might be able to be heirs with him. “For good works which God prepared.” God prepared, created, and formed in Christ good works [Note: [Col. 1256D] (6) The manuscripts: “for works.”], he says. Does this mean the works which will come to be, or those we now perform here? Yet whether we understand those which will come to be, or those which [Col. 1256C] now are, they are assuredly good and are witnesses in Christ. And he may seem to have spoken of present works, since he immediately adds, “that we may walk in them.”

VERS. 11.

“Mindful in those [Note: [Col. 1256D] (7) Vulgate: “Wherefore, remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh.”] works,” he says: so that we may now live in the same manner and do the same works, which are good. For God has now created us in Christ by his workmanship so that we may be mindful; and therefore, keeping the faith, we may now walk in those works. “And you who were once Gentiles in the flesh.” Since he said, “that we may walk,” he adds that you also must surely walk in the good works which God prepared. “You,” he says, “who were once Gentiles in the flesh”: that is, you thought as Gentiles and consequently lived carnally, that is, fulfilling the desires of the flesh. The opposite is to be in Christ: that is, to live spiritually and think all things according to the Spirit [Col. 1256D]. I have explained this frequently. This is surely to think of God, hope in God, direct the mind toward God, tend toward the Father, know Christ as the way of our eternity, and believe that through his resurrection we have risen.

“You who are called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision [Col. 1257A] in flesh made by hand.” “You,” he says, “were Gentiles in the flesh, called” [Note: [Col. 1257D] (1) The manuscripts have “who” for “called.”] by those who are circumcised—that is, by the Jews—whose circumcision is made by hand. Thus by this circumcision, that is, by the Jews, you are called uncircumcision: that is, persons who are not circumcised.

But when he said that the circumcision made by hand calls you uncircumcision, he intended it to be understood that circumcision made by hand was not given by God [Note: [Col. 1257D] (2) Namely, the discourse is not about that ancient circumcision.], but that there is another circumcision, one of the mind and of every desire and every sin, so that a person may truly circumcise from himself and separate every desire of the flesh. For what advantage is there in circumcising flesh, when every vice increases all the more through the mind from the flesh? Those sins which arise from flesh must therefore be circumcised; and this circumcision will not be made by hand, but [Col. 1257B] by soul and Spirit.

This was said so that they might not be ashamed that they are called uncircumcision. For neither is this [Note: [Col. 1257D] (3) The manuscripts: “from this.”] outside God’s religion nor is it truly said, since it is said by Jews—by that circumcision made by hand—whereas the circumcision wrought by soul and Spirit, circumcising all sins of the flesh, is better and truer.

VERS. 12.

“Because at that time you were without Christ.” For when you were Gentiles, you were surely without Christ. Christ, however, is always [present]; but whoever receives Christ and places faith in him is then, as it were, circumcised, and then will be in circumcision, though not one made by hand. Therefore you were uncircumcision because you were not with Christ. He adds this: “You were not true Jews, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel.” For [Col. 1257C] this is its true commonwealth: that we should think according to the Spirit, live according to the Spirit, and be circumcised by Christ away from carnal desires.

“And strangers to the covenants, without the hope of their promise” [Note: [Col. 1257D] (4) *Eorum*, “their,” is absent from the Vulgate.], “and without God in this world.” That is, you were Gentiles; and because you did nothing with Christ and were without Christ, therefore, he says, you were not in the commonwealth of Israel; therefore you were strangers to the covenants, that is, alienated from the covenant. What is the covenant? You were strangers from the promise of the covenants: that is, without the hope of those things which God had promised through his covenants, that is, through the prophets—their promise, without hope.

For since you were without Christ, you did not promise yourselves the hope of the promise of those covenants; because you were strangers and aliens from them, and were without God—that is, without Christ. For this is how he said it: “when you were without Christ.” See: here also he called Christ God [Note: [Col. 1257D] (5) Note again Victorinus’s illustrious testimony concerning Christ as God; and compare col. 1147.]. Then “without God” may be understood because God is from Christ. But you were in this world without God. Without God lives one who is a stranger to the promised covenants and alien to true Israel, to whom heaven and the kingdoms of heaven have been promised [Col. 1258A] in eternal life and the glory of God [Note: [Col. 1258D] (1) The manuscripts: “God.”].

VERS. 13.

“But now in Christ [Note: [Col. 1258D] (2) The Vulgate adds “Jesus.”] you who were once far off have been made near in the blood of Christ.” Every discourse containing exhortation, after a general discussion, turns its thought back to those to whom the letter is written, namely the Ephesians. Therefore, he says, you too who were once far off—that is, Gentiles—have now been made near in Christ, as it were, through the blood of Christ. For neither we through our works, nor the Ephesians through theirs, are near and in Christ; rather, through the blood of Christ, he says.

VERS. 14.

And he explains what this means: that through Christ’s blood we are in Christ, though through faith. “For he himself is our peace.” Through his mystery we have been reconciled to God, no longer strangers or [Col. 1258B] adversaries. For when we worshiped others and served idols, we were, as it were, at war with the Father—that is, with God. But Christ, standing between, reconciled us to himself through his mystery and passion. Therefore he is our peace, “who made the two one and, dissolving the middle wall of matter, dissolving hostilities in his flesh.”

VERS. 15.

The law of commandments, nullifying it in decrees. “Christ,” he says, “is our peace”; elsewhere he also calls him mediator. For he placed himself between the divided kingdoms, while souls born from the fountain of God are held, or were held, in this world; so that the intervening wall might stand between them, like a hedge and partition, through the allurements of the flesh and worldly desires. By his mystery, flesh, passion, and discipline Christ dissolved this intervening wall; that is, by conquering the flesh and teaching it to be conquered, and by dissolving the desires of the world and teaching them to be dissolved, he removed the intervening wall—yet, he says, “dissolving their enmities in his flesh.”

Therefore it is not our labor, as I often remind you, by which we dissolve these things; faith in Christ alone is salvation for us. For he dissolved all enmities in his flesh. Likewise, he dissolved the law of commandments, nullifying it in decrees, so that it is not through works or sabbaths. For the decrees themselves are in the law, and the commandments themselves; now [Note: Col. 1258D (3): Manuscripts: “not, I say, through things of this sort,” etc.], I say, Christ has nullified precepts of observance of this sort, understood carnally. When these were nullified, the intervening obstacle was removed; and souls are no longer hindered, as though the world had been set before them—that is, worldly desires, notions, and fleshly appetites—so that they cannot see, know, and follow God, even though they are joined with him [Col. 1258D].

For this is what he teaches: “that he might create the two in himself, making peace in one new man” [Note: Col. 1258D (4): But the Vulgate has: “That God might create in himself into one new man, making peace.”]. I have said what the two are: souls, and those higher things, namely the eternal and spiritual. When the Savior himself—who is Spirit and the Holy Spirit—descends into souls, he joins the two higher spiritual realities, makes souls spiritual, and creates them in himself, he says, “in one new man.” What, then, is the new man? The spiritual man; for the old man is animal, and consequently fleshly.

[Col. 1259A] “Making peace,” he says: that is, among things torn apart, separated, and at war—namely, souls that have fallen away to earthly things and pursue earthly things, and therefore resist what is heavenly and spiritual—he made peace by reconciling them with spiritual things and with God, so that they now think one thing in their mind, worship one, and are one: namely, spiritual.

## VERSE 16

“And that he might present and reconcile both in one body to God” [Note: Col. 1259D (1): The Vulgate does not have “that he might present,” but only, “And reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, slaying the enmities in himself.”]. By joining, he says, as we have said, both souls and spirit, he made peace, in order that he might present those formerly separated two as joined, and reconcile them to God. “In one body,” he says; that is, so that the soul itself, now being spirit, and the spirit itself, now claiming the soul as its own, might be one body, though they had formerly been separate.

But here let us take “body” likewise as union, as one substance [Col. 1259B]; this is the heavenly body and is among eternal things. In what sense is “body” spoken of our Lord Jesus Christ? Christ is a bodily substance and bodily majesty. “Slaying enmities in himself through the flesh.” This is the mystery of the cross: that all things hostile to souls and our spirit might be taken away as punishment—worldly desires, fleshly appetites, and even the flesh itself, in a sense corrupted and defective. Therefore Christ slew enmities through the flesh, that is, everything adverse to souls. And where did he slay them? In himself. For this reason he assumed flesh: to conquer flesh in himself; and thus, through flesh, to benefit flesh, slaying the corruption of flesh; and, through the resurrection, assuming pure and eternal flesh and the whole body of divinity, when all things become spirit [Col. 1259C], as Paul teaches in many places and as the matter itself has been made manifest.

Here also is the point which I wish us everywhere to show: our Lord Jesus Christ conquered and overcame this very conflict, in a manner of speaking, between flesh and world. Almost nothing remains for us except simply to believe in him who conquered all things. For this is full salvation: that Christ conquered these things; that Christ was therefore raised upon the cross; that Christ therefore rose again, so that for us who believe in him salvation, eternity, and the glory of heaven might be prepared.

## VERSE 17

“And coming, he preached peace to us who were far off, and peace to those who were near” [Note: Col. 1259D (2): Vulgate: “And coming, he preached peace to you who had been far off, and peace to those who were near.”] . . . He expresses the whole activity and coming of the Lord Savior through the things that are done and are to be done. For the Lord’s coming preached peace: that human beings might be reconciled, and that the whole world, looking toward God through souls, might feel nothing adverse [Note: Col. 1259D (3): Manuscripts: “adversities”], but have peace.

When he says that God—that is, the Savior—coming preached, every utterance that is good and proclaims what is good is called gospel. For to proclaim God, to teach that God may be known, and to announce conversion toward God, is to evangelize; and this is to evangelize peace: that, with souls no longer discordant and corrupted by error, while serving material (*hylic*) powers, we might not in some fashion wage war against God [Col. 1260A].

Again, what he says—“to those far off, and to those near”—must be referred to Jews and Gentiles. The Jews, of course, are near; the Gentiles are far off. But since the Savior himself received the gospel in order to proclaim God among the Gentiles, he placed that first: so that Christ, coming, might truly proclaim peace to those who are far off—that is, to the Gentiles—as is shown by many considerations. Indeed, those who come to faith from the Gentiles are said to be better children than those from the Jews. Yet, lest it be denied to the latter as well, he adds, “and to those who are near.”

## VERSE 18

“For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” [Note: Col. 1260D (1): Vulgate: “For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.”]. Both, as I said—Jews and Gentiles—have access through Christ to the Father [Col. 1260B]. But how? In the one Spirit, which is Christ: while we believe in him, he enters into us, and we perceive God, know God, and worship God. Therefore, that we may come to the Father in that Spirit, both groups will be able to come through Christ. Thus Jews cannot come to the Father except through Christ, just as neither can Gentiles by anything else external—an idol, a power, or any majesty whatsoever, as they themselves call it.

## VERSE 19

“Therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners” [Note: Col. 1260D (2): For *incolae*, “sojourners,” the Vulgate has *advenae*, “foreigners”], “but fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household.” He concludes with reference to the particular case, namely that of the Ephesians: they are no longer aliens, sojourners, or strangers. For those who journey away from God, since they remain in God’s works—that is, in the world—are strangers and sojourners, though they can become members of the household [Col. 1260C]. For even if they sacrifice to demons [Note: Col. 1260D (3): Manuscripts: “indicate”], afterwards, by believing and following God, they are members of the household, though still in the world. But those who do not believe are strangers and sojourners.

Further, as he concludes concerning the Ephesians: if anyone believes God and has recognized through Christ that he belongs to God, he is neither stranger nor sojourner. Therefore, he says, you Ephesians are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household. For all assemble into one city—that eternal city of higher riches, which they call Jerusalem—and are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, because in that same city God is as it were ruler, lord, and prince. Thus they are members of God’s household.

What, then, should we understand by “fellow citizens of the saints”? It might seem that those called fellow citizens are one thing, and the saints another [Col. 1260D]. If so, who are the saints, and who the citizens? I think that he means by “saints” the apostles, prophets, and the rest who either suffered God or saw him; that is, those who, with the Spirit dwelling in them, spoke divine things, or in some manner saw him present. “In some manner,” I say: either through flesh or through spirit—as Abraham, as the apostle, and as the rest, through flesh and spirit, as all the apostles. These, then, are saints. But those who believe in Christ without any such experience are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household.

## VERSE 20

[Col. 1261A]

“Built upon the foundation of the apostles.” He himself sufficiently declared that saints are one thing and citizens another, since he said that these people are built upon the foundation of the apostles. Likewise, they ought either to observe commandments, or to attain knowledge of God, or to worship and religion. Jesus Christ and his commandments are the foundations of the apostles; these foundations already have superstructure from life, morals, manner of living, and discipline. Yet the first foundation is for life; the rest are for adorning and building up. “The first foundation,” he says, “is to believe Christ, to have hope in him, and to place faith in God.” This is what the apostles teach, and it is also the foundation of the prophets—according to the good order set out above, when I said that saints were both those who saw [Col. 1261B] and those who bore the Spirit [Note: Col. 1261D (1): Thus the manuscripts.]. For the apostles saw; the prophets possessed the Spirit. Therefore the proclamation according to the commandments of apostles and prophets—which commandments are Christ’s—is the foundation of all eternity and hope.

“You have been built up,” he says, “upon Jesus Christ himself, the cornerstone.” Every middle position placed between two things always either joins them or separates them. Where there is separation between souls, the world is called *phragmos* (φραγμός), that is, a partition wall. But where there is union between souls, there is Christ, who is called a cornerstone, because he is truly a cornerstone; and he is the one placed first.
