Truly placed as a foundation at the corner, he joins two sides. He called this stone *akrogōniaion* (ἀκρογωνιαῖον): not merely a corner-stone, but the first and highest stone, where the foundation of the corner begins, joining, coupling, and making the two one.

For the two are, as we have said, either the higher souls, which were also with Christ, and those here which are holy and possess Christ in the mysteries; or all those souls of Christ themselves, including souls from the Gentiles, which are joined by that cornerstone, Jesus Christ [Col. 1261C].

## VERSES 21–22

“In whom the structure, fitted together, [grows] into a holy temple in the Lord” [Note: Col. 1261D (3): Vulgate: “In whom the whole building, being fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.”]. For all souls gathered together, and all human beings made spiritual [Note: Col. 1261D (4): Manuscripts: “spiritually.”] through Christ, are built into a place where God may dwell, like a holy temple. Thus, since Christ is in all, and God is in Christ, all are God’s temple through Christ.

“In whom you also are being built together [Col. 1261D] into a dwelling-place of God in the Spirit.” As I have often taught, he directs the matter to the particular case—that is, to the Ephesians—so that they too may be built upon the same corner, that is, in the Spirit of Christ, and so that they too may be a dwelling-place of God. He does so with great moderation, that it may be an exhortation: he does not say that they have already been made so, but that they are still being built, for they lack something; therefore he admonishes and exhorts them. And when he calls them a dwelling-place of God in the Spirit, what else does he do but exclude every other thing from souls [Col. 1262A], saying that Christ alone is still building souls together there, so that they may become God’s temple?

# CHAPTER III—VERSES 1–2

“For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ” [Note: Col. 1262D (1): The Vulgate adds “Jesus,” and has “dispensation” for “arrangement”], “for you Gentiles—if indeed you have heard the dispensation of God’s grace.” It remained, after speaking of these matters—that all hope is in Christ, and that all are so built together in the Spirit as to become a dwelling-place of God—it remained, I say, for him to teach who he himself was: whether he accomplished this building-together through the gospel, and to give an account of his authority so that he might be believed.

Accordingly he adds: “For this reason,” that is, in order that you may be built into a dwelling-place of God in the Spirit. For he says this not only to the Ephesians, but to all: hear it. “For you Gentiles,” he says, “Paul, a prisoner of Christ”; prisoner, either one joined to Christ’s gospel [Col. 1262B], or one who has borne many labors and punishments, and would bear them for you, proclaiming Christ; and I am Christ’s prisoner, who in proclaiming Christ am bound, but for your sake.

To make it clear that he was Christ’s prisoner for the Gentiles, he added assurance regarding the mystery granted to him [Note: Col. 1262D (2): Manuscripts: “granted [to one] having it.”]. “If indeed,” he says, “you have heard the dispensation of God’s grace.” That is, if you have come to know what grace has been arranged: how the gospel has been ordered through me, so that God may be proclaimed through Christ, and Christ’s power, which is God’s power. “Which was given to me for you” [Note: Col. 1262D (3): Vulgate: “in you.”] “according to revelation.”

For, as Paul himself recalls in many places, he did not receive or learn the mystery from human beings or through human beings; rather, all things were revealed to him. This is what he says: grace was given to him, but through revelation. From this it may be understood that a person can become a Christian by revelation—and especially can so become one. Paul indeed was chosen and called a vessel of election; nevertheless, because God’s power dispenses grace in every manner, we should understand that the lawful discipline of the Savior’s commandments is that a person be reborn through Spirit and water and thus receive Christ’s Spirit. But that comes both from human beings and through human beings.

What befell Paul, however—although, in our judgment, he alone merited this—nevertheless, as I have said, such a revelation of God, or one by some similar means, can occur through God’s grace. Therefore one to whom revelation has been given through Christ’s grace, so that he may be filled with the Spirit and, having attained knowledge of Christ through revelation, may serve him, is not to be denied Christ’s grace [Col. 1262C].

## VERSES 3–4

“The mystery was made known to me” [Note: Col. 1262D (4): Vulgate, “sacrament,” “as I wrote above briefly.”], “as I wrote beforehand in brief, so that when you read you may be able to understand my insight into the mystery of Christ” [Note: Col. 1262D (5): Manuscripts: “understanding”; but “when you read” is rightly given below.].

Here also I remind you that the mystery of Christ can be known by revelations. Although in Paul’s case this seems to have been fulfilled by the Lord’s election, nevertheless, because the Lord’s election is free, it can also happen in the case of others that knowledge of true and full divinity is not received from human beings or through human beings. It is indeed a great and unique condescension; perhaps it may be granted in part that this happens today [Col. 1263A]. For since he himself said that if someone is a prophet and another says that something has been revealed to him concerning the same matter, the prophet should be silent and recognize that the person claiming revelation should be heard, it follows that revelation is possible; and what is possible in part is possible in the whole in the same manner.

For the mystery of the Lord and God’s will extends to all his power. We must understand both that he can do all things and that he wills what he can do; but these matters belong to another question. Now he shows that the mystery was revealed to him [Note: Col. 1263D (1): Manuscripts: “and us” for “shows”], when Paul says that he wrote this to the Ephesians: namely, the mystery itself—not the revelation, but that which was revealed, that is, the mystery.

“I wrote,” he says—or rather, I say: “when you read, you are able to understand,” insofar as you are able, “my insight” [Col. 1263B], “insight into the mystery of Christ.” He uses “knowledge” not of that which by its own power foresees what exists, discovers and comprehends what is future by reasoning; but here he calls knowledge “insight.” For he did not attain it through insight; rather, after attaining it, he began to have insight. Accordingly, he says, “insight into the mystery of Christ,” that is, into what I received, what was revealed to me, what was made known to me; that is, into that [Note: Col. 1263D (2): Manuscripts: “made, which is, however, in that.”] by which he was taught insight—into what was revealed to him, whether by memory, knowledge, or understanding. For these are parts of insight. Thus insight has its sphere, though we cannot attain the mystery through insight, but through revelation.

## VERSE 5

“Which was not made known to the children of men in other generations” [Note: Col. 1263D (3): Vulgate: “was not recognized.”]. This can be an argument concerning insight [Col. 1263C]: that God revealed it to him because he was perceptive and could receive the revelation, the mystery; and that he alone merited, on account of insight, to know the mystery which had not been made known to the children of men in other generations.

What are “other generations”? That is, before my time [Note: Col. 1263D (4): Manuscripts: “before my times.”]. For “generations,” as is read in the Gospel, means periods, as it were, through human beings. To none, he says, of those children of men who were before me in their generation—to none, he says—was the mystery made known. We have often spoken of what the mystery is which Paul says was revealed and made known to him.

By adding “to the children of men,” however, he perhaps shows that, before it was revealed to Paul, that mystery could have been revealed to angels—that is, not to children of men—as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles. He teaches fully the harmony of the mystery: that what was revealed to him and to the apostles is one and the same [Col. 1263D]. Lest what was delivered to the apostles through Christ’s presence should differ from, and not appear to be the same as, what he said was delivered to himself through revelation, he joins what was revealed to himself with what was revealed to the holy apostles. This is not enough: he adds, “and to the prophets in the Spirit.”

This is acute and forceful. For the prophet who spoke the mystery had it revealed to him in the Spirit; the prophet himself did not know the mystery. Since he said that the mystery had not been revealed or made known to the children of men, yet it was known to prophets, who are children of men, he adds that it was known “in the Spirit”; that is, when, inspired by the Spirit, they spoke the mystery [Col. 1264A].

## VERSE 6

Yet it was not made known to them that “the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and participants in his promise in Christ through the Gospel” [Note: Col. 1264D (1): Vulgate: “That the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and fellow participants in his promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel.”]. This is what he says was made known to him as a mystery, and likewise to the holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles too are fellow heirs in Christ and members of the same body—that is, as it were, of the same body. He often speaks in this way, saying that all holy and liberated souls [Note: Col. 1264D (2): Manuscripts: “freedom.”], joined to Christ’s Spirit, are one body.

Accordingly, the Gentiles also are participants in his promise in Christ. For not Israel alone, but also the Gentiles who were incorporated in Christ through the gospel [Col. 1264B] are participants in the promise: that they will merit eternal glory, life, remission of sins, and the other things which God and the Savior promised to those who follow him. Thus all are participants in the promise in Christ through the gospel.

## VERSES 7–8

“Of which I became a minister according to the gift of God’s working, which was given to me according to the workings of his power” [Note: Col. 1264D (3): Vulgate: “Of which I became a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which . . . according to the working . . .”]. “I became,” he says, “a minister of that gospel through which both Gentiles and Israel participate in the promise in Christ; and I became its minister by the gift of God’s grace.” For Paul everywhere recalls that we receive this not by our merits but by God’s grace, so that whatever grace is given belongs to the giver, not the recipient.

What he adds—“according to the working of his power”—he also attributes to God [Col. 1264C]: whatever I perform, it is God’s power. For my own power is not at work in me, but God’s. We must consider carefully how he joins these two things and what follows. For he adds: “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given . . .” If there is already the working of one acting, and grace is given according to working, then the merit of one working comes first, and grace afterwards. But above he said that this grace was given according to the gift of God’s grace, so that he might be a minister of the gospel. The grace by which he now works was only later given; he works by God’s power, and the grace is said to have been given because of the working of God’s power.

What then? Was the working given before grace, or was grace given afterwards? But when the working is said to be God’s power, grace has already been given. Again, when Paul is said to have become a minister according to God’s grace [Col. 1264D], we understand that the gift was given before the working, so that he might be a minister; and that his being a minister is God’s gift [Note: Col. 1264D (4): Manuscripts: “God.”]. Now, when he works from the grace he received as minister, it is also grace that his working comes from God’s power. Thus, that he should be a minister was God’s gift; that God’s power should be operative in him was God’s grace.

“To me, therefore, the least of all the saints, this grace was given,” he says. What grace? To evangelize among the Gentiles according to the working of his power [Col. 1265A]. What is to be evangelized, he adds: “not to the least of the apostles, but of the saints,” he says. For the apostles, holy in both faith and Spirit, are those to whom the gospel was entrusted: “the incomprehensible riches of Christ” [Note: Col. 1265D (1): Vulgate: “the unsearchable riches of Christ.”].

What riches could be such, or how can the riches which are Christ’s be comprehended—riches which make us children of God, grant eternal life, remove all corruption, slay death itself, make us to be in heaven, and forgive all sins? These are therefore great riches: in removing evils, forgiveness of sins; and in granting good things, such great goods as I have mentioned, and others of that kind.

## VERSE 9

“And to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation” [Note: Col. 1265D (2): For “dispensation of the mystery,” the Vulgate has “dispensation of the sacrament.”] “of the mystery.” The sequence is this: grace was given to me to evangelize among the Gentiles [Col. 1265B] and to enlighten all. In what respect enlighten? As to what is the dispensation of the mystery: that they should not merely proclaim the mystery, but also enlighten—that is, disclose—what is the dispensation of the mystery.

By saying “to enlighten all,” he included both Israel and the Gentiles. For he undoubtedly received the gospel for the Gentiles; but Jews too can be enlightened, if they follow, if they obey. We must explain what the dispensation of the mystery is, since Paul says that he enlightens. But he made it clear in what follows: “hidden from the ages in God.” “To me,” he says, “grace was given among the Gentiles, to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation of the mystery.” Of what mystery? “Of that,” he says, “which has been hidden from the ages in God.”

Let us briefly explain what “from the ages” and “in God” mean; what “hidden” means, and how it was hidden. [Col. 1265C] From God, who is the first Father, Christ was begotten, who is light from light and God from God [Note: Col. 1265D (3): Victorinus refers to the words of the Nicene Creed. Indeed, in Victorinus’ boyhood or youth, that great council at Nicaea for Christ’s divinity was celebrated.], who is Jesus, who is God from God [Note: Col. 1265D (4): “But you had already said this, my dear Victorinus.”]. Let no one think that I mean a second God; but the order of speaking demands it.

In this Christ, I say, who is God from God, all things have been completed, and through him all things; but what is now necessary is that all things are in him. For it is said both “through him” and “in him.” Therefore, if all things are in him, although all things are through him, God has all things in him [Note: Col. 1265D (5): This is precisely how the manuscripts read.]; this mystery too is in him and hidden in him.

But hidden from whom? From the ages. For Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, and all other things were created by him; that is, God’s works were made through him, with God working in him and creating through him. All ages, therefore, are subsequent to Christ, since they were made by Christ. Nothing, then, is before Christ, nor are the higher things before Christ [Col. 1265D]. Christ was born from God with no beginning in time.

Therefore from these ages, and likewise from them, the mystery was hidden in God, so that in its own times it might be revealed: that Christ, God’s Son, would come, put on flesh, aid and free humankind, forgive sins, raise them to eternal and heavenly things, justify and glorify them [Col. 1266A], and do the other things which follow.

In whom, therefore, was this mystery hidden? In God. In what God? In him who created all things. For if the mystery hidden in him was revealed through him, it was hidden before he came and revealed after he came. Who is this? “He who created all things,” he says. Therefore the Creator may indeed be understood as God, yet God is Creator through Christ. For “Creator” does not properly belong to God [Note: Col. 1266D (1): “Who speaks thus, as Victorinus does here? Surely the designation ‘Creator’ belongs to God. Besides, why creation is more often predicated of God the Son than of God the Father—or rather why the Father is said to create through the Son—is discussed subtly by Photius, whom I recently edited, *Amphilochia* 188; cf. Vatican edition, vol. I, pp. 328 ff.], but belongs to Christ, and thus through Christ to God. For God begot Christ; Christ created all things, with God himself working and creating through him. Thus it is one thing that all things were created, and by one that all things were created; for all the works of God the Father were created through Christ.

## VERSE 10

“So that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known through the Church to the rulers” [Note: Col. 1266D (2): Vulgate, “principalities.”] “and powers in the heavens” [Col. 1266B]. This is the mystery hidden in God—that is, in Christ—which was afterwards revealed not to souls [Note: Col. 1266D (3): Thus the manuscripts. Perhaps “angels”?] but to human beings, and not only to human beings but to all rulers and powers in the heavens; and it was revealed through the Church, namely, that God’s wisdom is through mystery.

When he says “to rulers and powers in the heavens,” it may be understood that this was not revealed to those that are hostile; for, he says, they are “in the heavens.” And by “through the Church,” he means through all God’s members, through Christ’s members, and through every soul clothed in his mysteries [Note: Col. 1266D (4): “I would prefer ‘imbued.’”] and having hope in him. Thus one may understand how much has been granted to humankind. For rulers and powers in the heavens do not themselves declare God’s wisdom to human beings; rather, through the Church—that is, through those who are Christ’s members [Col. 1266C], sanctified in faith—the powers and rulers in the heavens know that God’s wisdom has been set forth through a human being.

That rulers and powers of the world also learn and know God’s wisdom will be readily acknowledged if they have learned and recognized where the human being is and where he has his origin, through the prophet Ezekiel when he speaks of the cherubim; concerning this vision, the passage itself requires a definite exposition. Briefly, then, he touched upon all the parts of the mystery which we mentioned above in saying, “the manifold wisdom of God”: whether that he sent the Son; that such great majesty assumed the form of a servant; that such great signs were performed; that such great promises were made—forgiveness of sins and the promise of heaven; likewise eternal life, glorification, inheritance together with Christ himself [Col. 1266D], resurrection after death, death itself, and other such things. The wisdom of God is manifold.

## VERSE 11

“According to the determination of the ages, which he made in Christ Jesus our Lord.” From this it is apparent what it means for the mystery to have been hidden in God, since he added, “according to the determination of the ages.” [Col. 1267A] For, with particular ages determined and concluded, the mystery was to appear through the presence of the Lord, in whom the mystery was hidden. It had to be revealed through him in whom it was hidden. For he adds: the determination of the ages which he made in Christ Jesus our Lord—when the mystery would appear, when it would be revealed, when salvation and liberation would be shown.

## VERSE 12

“In whom we have freedom and access in confidence through faith in him” [Note: Col. 1267D (1): Vulgate: “In whom we have boldness and access in confidence through faith in him.”]. Although both redemption was accomplished and salvation given in the mystery of the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ, the chief point—and truly, if we attend to it, the sole chief point, certainly the greatest—is that freedom has been given to us. For, oppressed by captivity, we were not able through the law to resist, as he himself says that our bodily weakness could not resist.

Therefore he came [Col. 1267B] to conquer flesh, and death through death. Once these were conquered, he made possible for us what we had thought impossible. Freedom, therefore, was given, and access to confidence was given through faith in him; that is, when we have faith in him. I have reminded you, and often reminded you, that this is the gate of our liberation: if we believe in Christ. For his mystery has freed us, if we follow him. Then his death and resurrection will benefit us if we have faith in him, because he both did and suffered all things for our sake. Therefore let us be confident, as he adds.

## VERSE 13

“For this reason I ask you not to lose heart in my tribulations for you, which are your glory.” He turns to himself the exhortation which he owes to all, in order to strengthen them. “For this reason,” he says [Col. 1267C]—namely, because “to me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given to evangelize among the Gentiles,” and so forth—“for this reason,” that is, because of this cause, “I ask you not to lose heart in my tribulations.”

For those who follow Paul might be greatly wearied in faith when they heard that Paul himself endured tribulations. If he who preaches, who evangelizes, who was chosen by God, bears much, is wearied by dangers, labors, and many other tribulations, those who follow him are, I say, greatly discouraged; they begin to have an almost imperfect faith, since they may think that they too can be endangered and suffer severely, seeing that he who evangelizes and preaches is, despite such great grace, in tribulations [Note: Col. 1267D (2): Thus the manuscripts.].

“Therefore,” he says, “I ask, because of what was revealed to me, that you not lose heart in my tribulations” [Col. 1267D]. Yet I suffer these tribulations neither by my own merit nor for my own cause, but because you are either weak in faith, or still fearful, and somehow add other things. Therefore I undergo tribulations, wishing to call you back to true discipline and observance: that you may not depart from Christ, add nothing to Christ, and have hope in Christ alone. “This is not your glory; it is mine,” he says. Therefore, since the tribulations are for you, “it is your glory,” he says, that through my laboring, working, and being exercised through tribulations for glory, you may attain your glory.

## VERSE 14

[Col. 1268A]

“For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ.” The reason is, of course, that I endure tribulations for you. “For this reason I bend my knees”; that is, I make full entreaty, and I entreat the Father of the Lord, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: Col. 1268D (1): Victorinus repeats himself here in his customary manner.]. Every operation and every action is through Christ; but because, as we have often reminded you, Christ’s Spirit is the spirit of ministries—since he himself is God’s ministry, and God does all things through him—therefore, he says, “I bend my knees to the Father.”

For he must be entreated that he may have mercy and come to aid, direct our faith, work in us through Christ, so that we may follow Christ himself and, having faith in him, may attain the promises. The posture appropriate to prayer and entreaty is bending the knees. For we ought not only to bend in prayer in spirit, but also in body, so that no part of us is higher [Col. 1268B], either in the appearance of height or as though we seemed to possess pride [Note: Col. 1268D (2): Manuscripts: “of pride.”; (3): Note Victorinus’ teaching concerning the bodily posture of those praying.]. Accordingly, elsewhere: God “will preserve for himself so many thousands of people who did not bend the knee before Baal” [Note: Col. 1268D (4): 3 Kings [1 Kings] 19:18; Romans 11:4.].

## VERSE 15

“From whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.” That is, from God the Father, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ: he is Father, he is the first Father, and from him whoever is father has been named father. Yet this title or power flowed down from the first God the Father, as from a fountain. For Christ too is father of all things created, since all things were created through Christ. Likewise, in the mysteries, the initiator is called father [Note: Col. 1268D (5): Namely, the one who initiates is called the father of the initiated. Recall col. 1184, note 2.]. And Paul is in a certain way a father, since he said, “You are my children: I, in Christ Jesus, begot you through the gospel.”

Accordingly, fatherhood in heaven [Col. 1268C] is Christ; fatherhood on earth consists in apostles, or anyone who evangelizes, or anyone who hands on the mystery. For in these ways, and in many others, those who receive faith are called children, and those who hand it on are called fathers. Therefore all fatherhood proceeds from God the Father.

## VERSES 16–17
**VERS. 16, 17**

That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened in power [Note: [Col. 1268D] (6) Vulgate: “to be made strong.”] through his Spirit in the inner person [Note: [Col. 1268D] (7) Vulgate: “into the inner person”]; that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts. He has set forth the prayers he offers for the Ephesians: “that he may grant you,” he says, “the riches of glory.” He identifies these riches with the glory of God: to be strengthened in power through his Spirit, so that they may be strong against the flesh and the desires of the flesh, and against the utterly wicked powers of this world. This comes about and proceeds through the Spirit of God.

But how are they strengthened through the Spirit [Col. 1268D] of God—that is, made strong? “That Christ may dwell,” he says, “in the inner person.” For when Christ begins to dwell in the inner person—that is, in the soul—people are made strong in power through the Spirit; for everything hostile is driven out. He then adds how Christ dwells in the inner person [Col. 1269A]: “through faith,” he says, “in your hearts.” Thus it is an easy and magnificent matter: easy because faith alone fulfills so great an office and so great a benefit, namely, that Christ may dwell in our hearts.

What do we gain when he dwells there? That we may be stronger through the Spirit, and thus possess the riches of God’s glory; that, made strong, we may endure no danger, despise the world, and overcome all the utterly wicked powers. These are the riches of God. Let us also hope for glory and the promise, being rooted and founded in truth [Note: [Col. 1269D] (1) Vulgate: “in love.”]. This is a most important precept, set forth everywhere by Paul and frequently established by me in exhortation: for steadfastness, foundation, and the soul’s entire condition in relation to eternity lie in truth, of which I have often spoken—truth which is love both toward God and Christ and toward human beings. This makes our faith rooted [Col. 1269B] and founded.

**VERS. 18, 19**

That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height [Note: [Col. 1269D] (2) The Vulgate adds “and loftiness.”] and depth; and to know the love of Jesus Christ that surpasses knowledge. As I said, he has explained the sum of his prayers: what he asks God to grant the Ephesians. Yet it should not be understood that Paul prays this only for the Ephesians, but for all who believe in Christ.

Besides the matters discussed above, he prays and asks that God grant the Ephesians also this greatest gift: that they may attain knowledge—height and depth. He also prays that the Ephesians may attain Christ’s love, a love that prevails over and surpasses knowledge, that contributes more to salvation and to the blessed [Col. 1269C] eternity of souls, if anyone receives love for Christ. Thus, having taught that three things fulfill Christian perfection—faith, knowledge, and love—he has here briefly comprehended everything and shown that he includes in his prayers a request that God grant these things to the Ephesians.

For he spoke of faith thus: “that you may have Christ dwelling in the inner person through faith in your hearts.” Likewise, he spoke of knowledge thus: “that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints breadth, length, height, and depth.” Then he adds concerning love: “and to know the love that surpasses knowledge.” He has set down the three things, their order, and shown which has greater power. There are three: faith, knowledge, and love. The order is that faith comes first; for the one who believes comes to knowledge. Thus it has been said: “If you believe, then you will understand.” After knowledge, Christ’s love is set above all things; for love for Christ alone—together with longing, affection, desire, and yearning—raises and frees souls. Therefore love surpasses knowledge.

Now, although he has set down four things which knowledge ought to comprehend, by nature there are three. For bodily extension has three dimensions: length, breadth, and height. Height, however, extends both upward and downward. [Col. 1270A] Length is what is extended, as it were, before us. Breadth is what stretches beside us on both sides. Height, as I said, concerns what is above and what is below. Here, therefore, he has distinguished height and depth. What we called “height” he divided into two, calling that above “height” and that below “depth.” Thus, dividing height, he has set down two things, and four result, though by nature they are three.

Accordingly, this measure, as it were, of bodily understanding is to be impressed upon and discerned by the inner person, so that these matters may be perceived in relation to God. For since God is through all things and in all things, and is all things, and from him are all things, and through him are all things, and above all things, here lies the task of knowledge: to perceive and know what is length, breadth, and depth. [Col. 1270B] How all these are, or can be understood according to this division and understood in God, is a loftier and different inquiry.

Finally, he prays that the Ephesians may understand these things; and, lest there be despair because they may seem wholly impossible to understand, he adds: “that you may be able to comprehend,” he says, “with the saints.” Therefore the saints comprehend them, and they can be expounded. But this, as I said [Note: [Col. 1270D] (1) Manuscripts: “now.”], belongs to another work and to a great and difficult exposition: “to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge.”

It must be observed with great care and precision that Paul prays that the Ephesians may know also this: that Christ’s love surpasses all knowledge. This, I say, he prays that they may know; for one who knows that love surpasses all knowledge fully fulfills love for Christ. He therefore does not pray that they may do it, [Col. 1270C] because that follows; rather, he prays that they may know it.

That you may be filled with all the fullness of God [Note: [Col. 1270D] (2) Vulgate: “into all the fullness of God.”]. All these things for which Paul prays on behalf of the Ephesians—to be strengthened in spirit, strengthened in the inner person, to have Christ dwell through faith, to be rooted in love, to comprehend with the saints breadth, length, height, and depth, and to know also that Christ’s love surpasses knowledge—this is the fullness of God, which the Greeks call *plērōma* (πλήρωμα), that is, perfection lacking nothing. Christ accomplishes, fulfills, and has fulfilled this fullness through his mystery, in order that God may bring this about in all things and through all things. For this is fullness.

**VERS. 20, 21**

Now to him who is able to do above all things more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in me [Note: [Col. 1270D] (3) Vulgate: “Now to him who is able to do all things superabundantly beyond what we ask … that works in us.”], to him be glory in [Col. 1270D] Christ Jesus, and in the Church, and unto all generations of the age of ages.

The order of this sense is: “to him be glory in Christ Jesus, and glory in the Church, and unto all generations, unto ages of ages.” But to whom is glory due? “To him,” he says, “who is able to do above all things more abundantly than we ask or understand.” For we pray these things for you, that you may do these things and understand these things. But if anyone can do more and more abundantly, and can do beyond all these things—namely, beyond what we ask or understand—to him belongs glory.

Now he who can do beyond and more abundantly beyond these things can certainly do so according to the power that works in us, namely, according to the power of God and of Christ our Lord; for I work according to that power. Therefore he too works according to that power which is in us. Thus, to him who is able to do all these things more abundantly than we ask or understand, let glory be in Christ Jesus and through all ages, and in the whole Church. Yet all this can be referred to God. For he himself can do these things superabundantly. And to him be glory.

**CHAPTER IV—VERSE 1**

I beseech [Note: [Col. 1271D] (1) The Vulgate adds “therefore.”] you—I, a prisoner in the Lord—to walk worthily of the calling by which you were called, with all humility, gentleness, and patience. This passage is one of exhortation and admonition, joined with humble prayer and commendation, so that they too might endure, [Col. 1271B] seeing that he himself patiently endures many things.

“I,” he says, “a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling by which you were called.” Since I endure many things—for he endured bonds and various sufferings—therefore, he says, since I am a prisoner in the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s sake, I myself, who exhort you, being patient in many things, exhort you to walk worthily in that calling to which you have been called. We have often said that people are called by God’s grace. Since you have now been called by this calling, because you now know God and Christ the Lord, walk worthily in this calling. He adds how.

**VERS. 2, 3, 4**

With all humility, gentleness, and patience. And he adds great [Note: [Col. 1271D] (2) Manuscripts: “to.”] endurance, lest they be puffed up or proud. First humility is set down, then gentleness. Humility is the lowering of the soul. Gentleness is the restraint of pride and savagery [Note: [Col. 1271D] (3) The manuscripts read corruptly: “that humility is the lowering of the soul, a wild pride and savagery.”].

But the patience which follows concerns their endurance should anything adverse happen. In the former two terms—humility and gentleness—he provides against their fearing to suffer [Note: [Col. 1271D] (4) Manuscripts: “deserving.”]. In what follows, he says what they should be like if they have suffered: patient. Then he adds, “with all magnanimity” [Note: [Col. 1271D] (5) These words, “with all magnanimity,” as well as the following, “bearing all things,” etc., are absent from the Vulgate.]. For magnanimity consists in this: not merely that you bear things patiently [Note: [Col. 1271D] (6) Manuscripts: “carry forth.”], but that you remain always high in spirit.

Finally, he adds this: if you have suffered patiently, bear it also magnanimously, “bearing all things”—whatever happens—“bearing one another in love.” This may also be connected with “bearing one another in love.” Yet the following may stand as a complete sense: “Be eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” [Note: [Col. 1271D] (7) Vulgate: “Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit …”]. I exhort you to be diligent in preserving the unity of the Spirit, or in preserving one Spirit, for the preservation of peace and in the bond of peace.

He gives reasons, however, why they ought diligently to preserve unity of Spirit in the bond: “One body,” he says, “and one Spirit.” For the whole Church is one body and one Spirit. “Just as you also were called in one hope of your calling.” This too is an argument for preserving unity of Spirit in the bond of peace: that they were called in one hope. For those called do not have differing hopes, but all have one hope—the hope of God’s promises. What has been promised is known to all.

**VERS. 5, 6**

One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all things and through all things and in all of us [Note: [Col. 1272D] (1) Vulgate: “Who is above all, and through all things, and in all of us.”]. This discussion is broad in scope and yet simple: one Lord, that is, Christ; one faith, certainly faith in Christ and in God; one baptism. For baptism is not one thing from some and another from others; nor, if it is otherwise administered by others, is it baptism. Rather, it is that baptism administered in God the Father, and in our Lord Jesus Christ the Son, and the Holy Spirit. No baptism is therefore otherwise administered.

Thus, there is one baptism [Col. 1272B] and one God. For even if the Son too is God, yet because God is in the Son and the Father is God, God is one. Likewise, because the Son is in God, God is one. Which God? “God the Father,” he says, because he is through all things, in all things, and above all. Therefore there is one God, who is Father of all, above all, through all, and in all of us.

Let us carefully attend to the connected order. “One Lord”: he begins with him through whom all Christianity and entrance into liberation begin. For when someone has known Christ, faith in him follows, and the rest. There is one faith in Christ; then his consecration—one baptism; then union: one God, Father of all, above all things, through all things, in all things. He has set down four points: God is, because he is cause; Father of all, because beyond [Col. 1272C] him there is nothing; above all things, because he is activity; through all things, because he is unity and connection in all things.

**VERSE 7**

But to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift. He adds this because impatience may arise from it, or injury be done. Since he exhorts them to humility, patience, and the rest, he gives the reason why each person ought to be patient and magnanimous: because grace has been given to each of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.

Therefore, since different gifts have been given to different persons, there is no place for envy or refusal: one should neither grieve over what another has nor withhold what one has. If, then, Christ’s gift is given according to the measure of grace granted to each [Note: [Col. 1272D] (2) Manuscripts: “grace given to each.”], we ought all to receive one another in love, and to bear all things magnanimously and patiently [Col. 1272D], with gentleness and humility.

**VERSE 8**

Therefore he says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings.” An example is given for what he said, “according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” He proves that the gifts are Christ’s by citing Psalm 67, in which he teaches that Christ, our Lord Jesus, ascended on high and led captivity captive: that is, he made captive the captivity which had made us captive, subdued it, and thus gave gifts to us.

Therefore, if gifts have been given to us by our Lord, [Col. 1273A] who through his mystery led captivity captive, ascended on high, liberated us, and made captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings so that, having received his grace through him, we might perform diverse divine things. As he says later, some would be apostles, others evangelists, others prophets, and so forth. These, therefore, are the gifts.

But since this grace has been given by Christ to each person according to the measure of his gift, no one ought to envy either another’s grace or his own; rather, all should mutually give and regard all things as equal [Note: [Col. 1273D] (1) Manuscripts: *patria*, “native lands,” for *paria*, “equal.”], and bear everything humbly, with gentleness, patience, and magnanimity, for the preservation of unity in the spirit of unity and in the bond of peace, so that we may have concord and preserve peace, with no discord disturbing our souls.

**SECOND BOOK**

[Col. 1273B]

It is now necessary to carry through and complete the interpretation we are presently employing in the words which Paul adds—and necessarily adds—because above he taught by the example that, “ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings.” On account of this example, I say, he discusses the fact that the one who ascended surely descended. This mystery has a broad scope and involves other discussions in its explanation.

What it is to ascend, how he descended into the lower regions of the earth, and how he ascended above all the heavens—which is the more forceful point—must all be examined with every care and diligence. “He ascended,” he says, “that he might fill all things.” What is the coming, and what is the return? As I said, this is a great discussion; and so also is the question how he filled all things, and how, in returning, he filled all things more fully.

If I wished to embrace and expound it, the magnitude of the work does not permit this section to be included in this part, where we are making a simple commentary. I think that a book should be completed on this meaning and discussion; with God’s permission, I shall now undertake it [Note: [Col. 1273D] (2) Let us note Victorinus’ promised work, which does not appear among the published works.], so that, freed from the necessity of commentary, we may develop everything necessary for this kind of understanding. For now, then, we shall state these matters simply, by way of brief admonition.

**CHAPTER IV—VERSE 9**

But that he ascended—what is it except that he also descended into the lower regions of the earth [Note: [Col. 1273D] (3) Vulgate: “But that … [means] that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth.”]? In the psalm it is written, “ascending on high”; from this expression we derive the understanding that the one who ascended is the one who descended. For the nature of the matter is such that no one can ascend into heaven except one who descended from there.

This applies to heavenly matters. In other earthly matters of this kind, someone can ascend who has not descended; but into heaven and the heavens no one ascends except one who descended from there. Thus the Savior said in the Gospel: “Unless one is born again, he cannot possess the kingdom of God.” Then he added that what is born of flesh is flesh, [Col. 1274A] but what is born of Spirit is spirit. Now Spirit is from above; therefore spirit returns to what is above.

For when the resurrection takes place, all things will be spirit; and the whole person, made spirit, will ascend to heaven, namely through spirit. Therefore it necessarily follows that the one who ascends into heaven is himself the one who descended. Thus Christ, of whom it is said that he ascended into heaven, is understood to have descended; and if he descended, he surely descended into the lower regions of the earth—not only into the earth but into its lower regions.

For it has been read that the Savior descended into hell through that suffering of the cross, in order to free every soul and redeem his members from all places.

**VERSE 10**

He who descended is the same one who ascended. He repeats the same sense, because the two are mutually connected: the one [Col. 1274B] who ascends descended, and conversely, the one who descended ascended. Yet, as the preceding sense shows, since our Lord descended into the lower regions of the earth, he further adds that he is the one who ascended—but he ascended above all the heavens.

What heavens? Many say there are three; others, more. But my judgment is that there are three. For Paul himself says that he was caught up above the third heaven. Thus some also teach that waters above the earth are, as it were, the first heaven; then the firmament itself, which is called heaven; then again other waters, the third heaven [Note: [Col. 1274D] (1) This doctrine of Victorinus is noteworthy. When he says that he has elsewhere written much on this matter, understand, I think, a commentary composed by him on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, in which Paul is said to have been caught up into the third heaven.], concerning which discussion we have already said much previously.

But what difference does it make? Christ, who ascended, ascended above all the heavens. [Col. 1274C] For there now are eternity, that incorruptible life, and all things living from Spirit. These things, however, stood otherwise until Christ’s descent. After the mystery had been accomplished, through Christ’s passion they received salvation in his ascension and were made complete.

For this is what he adds: “that he might fill all things,” that is, render them perfect and full, so that nothing might be lacking. Therefore Christ’s passion, resurrection, and ascension are the perfection of all things that could be saved in the world, as well as of eternal things and things above all the heavens. We have treated that mystery very fully in the exposition of one book.

Or do we understand “that he might fill all things” to mean that he fulfilled everything entrusted to him, as though he corrected nothing there and rendered nothing perfect? Rather, he ascended above the heavens in order to fulfill every mystery; and he descended in order to fill them with majesty, perfection, God’s light, and love. For his descent and ascent illuminated all things. Yet he illuminated them more when he ascended, perfected and sanctified by the Father. By his return he makes all things holy: both that from which he returns and that to which he returns.

**VERSE 11**

And he gave some indeed as apostles, others as prophets. Here he begins to enumerate the various gifts [Col. 1275A] of which he said above that God gave gifts to human beings, so that all might possess God’s gifts and no one envy another. These gifts are apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers, and ministers; all of whom he enumerates. Yet he places apostles first, then prophets.

It seems surprising that, although it was said that prophets existed only until Christ, Christ himself should have made prophets. After the apostles he places prophets and evangelists. What, then, do we understand? That “prophets” are not only those who, having received the Spirit of God, spoke concerning Christ and his coming—the prophets of whom it was rightly said, “until Christ.” For when he came, concerning whom the prophets had prophesied, there was undoubtedly no longer any reason why there should be prophets.

Which prophets, then, do we understand? Those whom he says are prophets by Christ’s gift: namely, [Col. 1275B] those who discourse on God and, filled with the Spirit, expound divine teaching. We have said this also above.

**VERSE 12**

Others indeed as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers [Note: [Col. 1275D] (1) Vulgate: “and doctors.”], for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of Christ’s body. There are five kinds of speech concerning the law of grace: speaking in tongues, speaking by revelation, speaking by knowledge, speaking by prophecy, and speaking by teaching. These are fully discussed in the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

But besides these, it is another thing to be an evangelist: that is, to narrate what Christ did and proclaim that Christ is to be worshiped. For this is to be an evangelist. Christ therefore made evangelists by his gift; he also made pastors and teachers, who govern the people of the Church. He called those who administer “pastors” [Col. 1275C]; and those who teach, “teachers.” For “pastors” here should not be referred to feeding or food, but to governing: bishops are called pastors, and Christ himself is a pastor because the souls were reckoned as sheep. By “teachers,” however, as we have said—although pastors themselves may also be called teachers of a flock, as persons set over it—we should understand those called teachers to be instructors.

He says that all these things have been established by God’s gift so that there may be the perfecting, that is, the completion, of the saints. I have often taught what “saints” signifies: those who have received faith and have been sanctified by the Spirit. Therefore, in order that these may be perfected, such mysteries and ministries have been established by Christ’s gift, through which comes the perfection and completion of all the saints.

For apostles can perform these things—teach and evangelize—[Col. 1275D] but others too can do them without being apostles. Therefore a distinction is made: some are apostles, others prophets, others evangelists, others leaders and teachers. Yet through all these comes the perfection and completion of the saints, through what they themselves do and through what others do.

For the mystery is what we ourselves do; but the building up of Christ’s body is what we do in relation to others. Therefore all these things were instituted through Christ’s gift for two reasons and with two effects [Note: [Col. 1275D] (2) Manuscripts: “and two effects.”]: that they may preside over the mysteries, act themselves, and be ministers, as stated above; and that they may build up Christ’s body—that is, the Church—and strengthen all souls [Col. 1276A] in faith. For this is Christ’s body.

**VERSE 13**

Until we all meet in the unity of faith and the knowledge of Christ, into a perfect man, into the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness. He has fully explained what mystery has been accomplished, for what reason it has been accomplished, and what will come to pass [Note: [Col. 1276D] (1) Manuscripts: “is.”]. What has been accomplished is that Christ descended and ascended, and that he himself gave apostles, prophets, and the rest. Then he adds the reason: “for the perfecting,” he says, “of the saints.”

What is that perfection? What follows: that, with all saints made perfect, there may be unity of faith, one faith among all, and knowledge of Christ, so that we may all acknowledge Christ; for in him is all salvation. Then comes what will occur: that we may meet and come together into a perfect man. For the soul perfected through faith [Col. 1276B] and through knowledge of Christ becomes a perfect man [Note: [Col. 1276D] (2) Manuscripts: “may become.”].

Thus the prophet David also spoke in the first Psalm of this same perfected soul: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.” He calls him both blessed and a man; and this is the measure of the age and the fullness of Christ. When all the members have been gathered and the complete man restored, Christ’s entire fullness is restored in each individual.

**VERSE 14**

So that we may no longer [Note: [Col. 1276D] (3) Vulgate: “so that now we may not be.”] be little children, tossed by waves. For when we are not perfect, we are little children; and when we were little children, we were tossed about. But when we are strengthened in faith, we are not tossed about. When we know Christ, we become men.

And no longer are we children, carried about by every wind of teaching, through the wickedness of people, through craftiness, toward the remedy [Note: [Col. 1276D] (4) Victorinus’ reading is noteworthy, since the Greek has ἐν τῇ κυβείᾳ or κυκείᾳ, while the Latin Vulgate has *ad circumventionem*, “for deception.” From Victorinus’ exposition, this term seems now to require the explanation that “deception of error” is a remedy against error.] of error. For when we are not perfect, we slip and waver even in faith, [Col. 1276C] and many things unsettle us, as we range through many teachings and are driven by the changing wind of understanding.

Such teaching is the wickedness, cunning, and craftiness of people, and, as it were, certain remedies for error: so that you may think what you think is thought by the judgment and understanding of certain wise persons, and another person’s understanding becomes a remedy for your error. All these things must be abandoned, so that we may be renewed through those two things and attain the perfect man: faith, namely, and knowledge of Christ.

These two things—faith in Christ and knowledge of Christ—make one blessed. The blessed man does not fluctuate or is not carried about by teaching amid human wickedness. The blessed prophet David touched upon this in the same first Psalm: “Blessed,” he says, [Col. 1276D] “is the man”—whom we say is made so through faith and the knowledge of Christ—who does not know teachings, wickedness, and errors. David enumerates these errors and teachings thus: “who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence.” To sit in the seat of pestilence is to teach heretical doctrines; to walk in the counsel of the ungodly is to engage in human wickedness [Col. 1277A]; to stand in the way of sinners is to engage in craftiness toward the remedy of error.

**VERS. 15, 16**

But, doing truth in love, let us grow [Note: [Col. 1277D] (1) Vulgate: “Let us grow in him in all things,” etc.] in all things into him who is the head, Christ. This is an exhortation, because he wishes the Ephesians to be in love, to do all things according to truth, and to increase still more in what they do. This is “let us grow in all things”; but let us grow in all things into Christ himself, so that nothing may be done outside the strengthening of faith in Christ, who, he says, is the head.

For as all the members are governed from the head, so the whole Church is governed by Christ—that is, every holy and faithful soul. Therefore Christ is the head, from whom the whole body is fitted and joined together through every joint of supply, according to the measure of each [Col. 1277B] part, making the body grow [Note: [Col. 1277D] (2) Vulgate: “According to the working in the measure of each member, it makes the body grow,” etc.] for its own building up in love.

We have said that he is the head, from whom the whole body is connected and fitted together. Therefore, if Christ is the head, the beginning, the source, and the one from whom all the members of the body are governed through every joint, this must be understood precisely: just as individual members, adhering by joints and differing in their functions, make up the measure of the whole body, so also in the Church each individual member of the ministries provides joints in relation to the sanctification of the mystery and faith in Christ, and binds and builds up its body in love.

So too our limbs, naturally joined, as it were, and adhering to one another by genuine affection, provide growth to the body through their parts. In the same way, all the ministries in the Church are Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 1277D] (3) Manuscripts: “is,” for “are.”], if they love one another in love while serving the head—that is, Christ.

**VERS. 17, 18**

Therefore I say this and testify in the Lord: that you no longer walk as the Gentiles also walk [Note: [Col. 1277D] (4) There are certain variant readings here in the Vulgate; see it there.]. As I have always taught, exhortation is twofold: above he stated what must not be done; now he adds what must be done. What must not be done? “Do not,” he says, “walk as the Gentiles.” “I say this,” he says, “and I testify to this; and I testify in the Lord,” that is, I invoke the Lord’s testimony for my admonition. Here there is also fear, for fear mixed with exhortation makes persuasion easy.

When he said “that you no longer walk,” he showed that they had walked for a long time and had lived as Gentiles. He himself adds the manner in which they walked as Gentiles: in the vanity of their mind [Note: [Col. 1277D] (5) Vulgate: “in the vanity of their understanding.”], darkened in understanding [Note: [Col. 1277D] (6) Vulgate: “having their understanding darkened by darkness.” In what follows, for “in themselves” it has “in them,” and for “their” it reads “their own.”], alienated from the life [Col. 1277D] of God through the ignorance which is in them, through the blindness of their heart.

He explains what the life of the Gentiles is: that they are vain, he says, do not think with their mind, and darken [Note: [Col. 1277D] (7) Manuscripts: “dark.”] their understanding. This is to think nothing concerning God with their understanding, to be led by sensation and by the things in [Col. 1278A] the world. For if the world is darkness, so is whatever is understood from the world.

Then he adds: “alienated from the life of God.” This life is the life of Christians, who both worship and understand God. He means the life owed by us to God. And he adds, “through ignorance”: for this is why we are alienated from God’s life—because we do not know God. But when we know him, we live God’s life and merit from God that life which is truly God’s life, which Christ promised us.

“But this,” he says, “is in them through the blindness of their heart”: when their heart has been blinded by darkness, it thinks and lives amid darkness, and considers this worldly wisdom, which is wisdom of darkness, to be wisdom.

**VERSE 19**

Finally, he shows what follows from such an understanding [Col. 1278B]: “They, despairing, gave themselves over to licentiousness, for the practice of every impurity and covetousness” [Note: [Col. 1278D] (1) Vulgate: “unto covetousness.”]. He speaks of the Gentiles, whose heart is blinded and who hope for nothing: that is, they both confess and prove themselves mortal, and believe nothing concerning their eternity. Therefore they seize the life of this world, wishing, as it were, to enjoy it; they live lustfully, pursuing pleasure through licentiousness, as they suppose, avid to possess, and in their mode of life driven by every most shameful pleasure.

**VERS. 20, 21**

But you have not so learned Christ—if indeed you have heard him and believed in him [Note: [Col. 1278D] (3) Vulgate: “and have been taught in him.”]. In contrast, he teaches the Ephesians not to live as the Gentiles do, since they have learned Christ. For Christ, in order to make us immortal, performed the mystery, was present [Col. 1278C] in flesh, taught us so that we might know the Father and have faith in him; and eternity belongs to us if we live according to his commandments.

You, therefore, have not learned in the manner of the Gentiles, since you have heard Christ—if indeed you have heard him—that is, understood and believed. For this is what he adds: “you who believed in him.” As we have said and always say, to believe in Christ is to attain immortality and merit eternal life; for he is life, he is light, he is eternity, he is the one who conquers and has conquered death, and conquered it for us through the mystery which he fulfilled.

**VERSE 22**

As truth is in Jesus, put off, according to your former manner of life [Note: [Col. 1278D] (4) Vulgate: “to put off, according to your former manner of life.”], the old person, which is corrupted according to the desires of error. Before Christ’s coming, all error and empty wisdom consisted in this worldly outlook [Col. 1278D]: in judging temporal things eternal, living according to the flesh, and believing the ruler of this world to be God. This is the old person.

“Put this off,” he says, “as truth is in Jesus,” because in others there is no truth. But truth is in Jesus: what Jesus taught is true, and he is the new person according to whom we ought to live. Therefore let that old person [Note: [Col. 1278D] (5) That is, “person.”], and the former manner of life, be put off. For he is corrupted according to the desires of error. Turned wholly toward the body, he judged everything bodily and [Col. 1279A] fleshly.

From this came errors and a kind of worldly wisdom, since everything in the world is not done according to Spirit—before Christ’s coming, however. But now, after he has taught us those eternal things, we understand what is spiritual. This is, as I said, the new person, who lives and thinks in this manner.

**VERS. 23, 24**
But be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who has been created according to the spirit [Note: [Col. 1279D] (1) Vulgate: “who has been created according to God.”] in righteousness and holiness of truth . . . As I have said, the new human being is one who thinks according to the spirit. This is what he says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” . . . Thus the soul is better, pure, whole; but the mind is a stronger spirit [Note: [Col. 1279D] (2) Victorinus has already distinguished soul from spirit according to a certain subtlety of his own.]. Therefore, he says, be renewed in the spirit of your mind; and put on the new human being, so that you may now live according to him. He is spiritual, since he thinks from [Col. 1279B] the spirit; and this very spiritual human being has been created according to God, that is, in conformity with God—as it was said: “Let us make a human being according to our image and likeness.” God does not, however, have a countenance or face [Note: [Col. 1279D] (3) Victorinus recalled this passage of his in his commentary on Philippians.]; but, just as God is spirit, so we too have been created according to God, in order that we may think according to the spirit—that is, nothing carnally, nothing in relation to the world. Finally, he himself has said what it is for the human being to have been created according to the Lord: “in holiness and righteousness and truth”; that is, that he should be righteous, holy, and true. For one who thinks world-wise [Note: [Col. 1279D] (4) I would prefer *mundum*, “the world.”] thinks according to the flesh; and one who thinks according to the flesh does not think what is true, nor what is righteous, nor what is holy. Therefore, since the spirit sanctifies, gives life, and justifies—the spirit which truly is, always is, and is more especially alone—is itself truth. Understanding all these things in this way, they put on the new human being, renewed in the spirit of their mind.

VERS. 25.

Therefore, putting away falsehood, let each one speak truth with his neighbor, since we are members one of another [Note: [Col. 1279D] (5) The Vulgate has *invicem*, “of one another,” for *alter alterius*.]. He concludes the exhortation concerning all the preceding matters: both that he had taught the diverse graces, and that every person ought to bear the other as a companion, to be patient with all magnanimity, and to bear one another in charity. Therefore here, he says, put away falsehood: let no one deceive another; speak truth; and let each person deal, act, and speak with his neighbor what is true—nothing through deceit, nothing through trickery. And after saying “with his neighbor,” he added, “since we are members one of another.” [Col. 1279D] Thus also above: “one body and one spirit,” and likewise the rest. For since the Church is one body, and all in the Church make one body, individual persons are parts of the Church. Therefore each is another’s member, and thus one body is made [Note: [Col. 1279D] (6) The manuscripts have *efficiatur*, “may be made.”], as he says, of the Church—of that Church, that is, of all souls having faith in God—whose head, I say, is Christ. Therefore [Col. 1280A] we are the body, and individually members of the body; therefore we are members one of another.

VERS. 26.

Be angry [Note: [Col. 1280D] (1) The Vulgate does not have *autem*, “but.”], and do not sin. He adds many admonitions, yet takes, by way of example [Note: [Col. 1280D] (2) The manuscripts have “from the example.”], what is placed in the fourth Psalm, taking from it the beginning of his precepts. But he divides these matters: first, he admonishes the man of the Church, that is, the Christian, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; then he admonishes what husbands and wives ought to do toward one another; then what fathers and children ought to do toward one another; then slaves and masters; and afterward comes an exhortation concerning what all ought generally to do. But as the order itself unfolds, so we too shall enumerate the admonitions individually and give their respective reasons and interpretations.

First he gives these admonitions to the ecclesiastical, Christian man: that he should not become angry; or, if he has become angry, that he should not sin through anger. Then, that he should not hold anger for long, but bring his anger to an end within the day. Then, that he should not live by theft or devote himself to thefts, but rather work with his hands for his livelihood, and from this also assist others in need. Then, that he should utter no evil words, but rather good ones; that he should build up another and not grieve another; that there be no bitterness in the soul, no anger, no indignation, no outcry, no blasphemy; that they should kindly love one another, be merciful, and forgive one another’s sins, just as God in Christ forgave us our sins; that they should love one another, be chaste, and keep themselves apart from every worldly thing, from avarice, indecency, shameful speech, and buffoonery; that they should rather give thanks. For those of such character—that is, those set in vices and sins—will not possess the kingdom of Christ, nor [Col. 1280C] an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ. Then he warns them not to be seduced by others through words—that is, either by heretics, irreligious persons, or those whom he calls children of temptation and unbelief—and terrifies them by saying that the wrath of God will come upon them. Then, that we should not participate in evil and unfruitful works; but rather rebuke those who sin and live with evil morals, disclose their sins, live as wise persons rather than unwise, abstain from wine, speak much more in the spirit, in psalms, hymns, and songs, and do these things more in the heart; give thanks to the Lord, and give thanks for all things in the name of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and be subject to one another in the fear of Christ. These are all the precepts given to the ecclesiastical man. Afterwards he adds what women are to observe—that is, husbands and wives.

[Col. 1280D] Let us now return to the individual points. “Be angry, and do not sin.” If God is angry, as it is said [Note: [Col. 1280D] (3) Rom. 1:18.], “for the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety,” and likewise in many passages, then anger is rightly granted also to the human being [Note: [Col. 1280D] (4) Read Lactantius’ treatise *On the Anger of God*, vol. VII of our edition.], that is, that he may be angry. But the person sins in anger who is angry not in order to correct, but to punish. Therefore, “Be angry, and do not sin; let not the sun go down upon your wrath.” He shows both the measure and the time of anger: anger once conceived ought to be put away within the day. [Col. 1281A] Many imitate this precept and place it among their own rules. For if each day has its own care and evil, that is enough for it; nothing from the preceding day ought to be added to another [Note: [Col. 1281D] (1) The manuscripts have *aeternum*, “eternal.”] day. Therefore:

VERS. 27.

Let not the sun go down upon your wrath, nor give place to the devil [Note: [Col. 1281D] (2) Vulgate: “Do not give place to the devil.”]. For if anger remains, he finds an opportunity to lead us into sins and make us do something that ought not to be done; and this is to sin by the devil’s will. Thus this precept shows that it lies in our power both to be angry and not to be angry; and to give the devil access through anger, so that, when we are angry, he has an opportunity to make us do something [Note: [Col. 1281D] (3) Thus it is read in the manuscripts.]. This must be considered concerning every passion of the soul and every action of the devil: he can do nothing concerning us unless we ourselves, through ourselves, give him the opportunity. Thus we are masters of our own will, [Col. 1281B] receive good rewards for good acts and punishments for evil acts, because through our own fault an opportunity is given to the devil [Note: [Col. 1281D] (4) A notable teaching of Victorinus on human freedom in the devil’s temptations.].

VERS. 28.

Let the one who was stealing steal no longer. To sin altogether is sin [Note: [Col. 1281D] (5) That is, sin without pardon, sin which makes a person perpetually guilty.], but to persevere in sin is [such] sin; for room is given for repentance, room is given for correction. Therefore, let the one who was stealing steal no longer. Yet we ought not to understand this as applying to this sin alone, but to all sins: whoever sinned in any matter should sin no longer. For every sin, when committed secretly, is theft. But since God knows everything that is done, we ought not to sin as though we believed we could steal our sins, since all things are manifest. “But rather let him labor, working with his hands.” From this it may be understood that above he truly spoke of ordinary theft, when he added, “but rather [Col. 1281C] let him labor, working with his hands.” For one who labors by working with his hands has the means of living; therefore he should not steal.

Moreover, let us observe that working with the hands is described simply as labor; other means are by skill, talent, speech, or any other way. Where there is no work of the hands, there are more likely thefts than sustenance acquired by labor. This is good: that he may have something to share with one who is in need; that from work by his own hands he may obtain what he himself has and share it with the needy; and that he may distribute from his own labors whatever benefit he has obtained.

VERS. 29.

Let no evil word proceed from your mouth. This precept also concerns what ought not to be done. I have said that there are two kinds of precepts concerning what is to be done. Let no one, he says, utter a word [Col. 1281D] out of malice. For from this comes great sin; as it is said [Note: [Col. 1281D] (6) Matt. 15:11.], “Not what enters the mouth, but what comes out of the mouth, does the greatest harm.” But if there is any good word for the building up of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear—let a word come forth which is good. But what is a good word? One for the building up of faith. For then it will give grace to the hearer, when what it says builds faith.

VERS. 30.

[Col. 1282A]

And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God: whether your own Spirit, who is in you, or the Spirit who is in another, who will be grieved by your evil word. “Do not,” he says, “grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you have been sealed”: that is, you have certainly been sealed in that Spirit by the sealing of the Holy Spirit. Do not grieve him, either in yourselves when you speak an evil word, or in those who hear. “For the day” [Note: [Col. 1282D] (1) Vulgate: “unto the day.”] “of redemption.” The order is: you were sealed for the day of redemption; for through him your redemption was accomplished. This redemption has a definite day, namely that of God’s judgment. For we are sealed in the Holy Spirit on the day when we are redeemed and set free.

VERS. 31.

For let all bitterness and indignation [Note: [Col. 1282D] (2) Vulgate: “and anger.”] and outcry and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice. He has briefly brought together five things: bitterness, anger, [Col. 1282B] indignation, outcry, blasphemy; although he also added the general category, “with all malice.” For bitterness appears both in envy, in evil speech, and in other actions. Likewise anger is a movement of the soul with a desire for vengeance and punishment. Indignation is a boiling and exalted movement of the soul beyond what is deserved. Outcry is a voice uttered in some frenzy. Blasphemy is now either a voice directed against God and injuring God, or a wicked thought. “Let all these things,” he says, “be taken away from you”—meaning, “take them away from yourselves”; but the sense is the same: “let them be taken away from you.” He rightly said, “with all malice,” because it can happen that some of these things occur without malice: we may blaspheme unknowingly, cry out unknowingly, or be indignant without malice. Let all these things be taken away with all malice. For thus, as we said above, “Be angry, but do not sin.”

VERS. 32.

But be kind to one another. Those things above, as I said, are not to be done; these are the things which are to be done: that you should be kind to one another—not one person toward another, but each toward each, and thus all toward all. And be merciful, forgiving one another. Above he also used “one another”: “be kind to one another.” He likewise said, “forgiving one another”; hence we must understand “merciful to one another.” What is forgiven is, of course, sins. Finally, that this was said concerning sins is made clear by what follows: “just as God in Christ forgave you”—certainly, your sins. And “in Christ,” as we have often said, because Christ died for us; therefore in Christ sins were forgiven us. For that mystery, as we have often said, is for our sins: because [Col. 1282D] we could not conquer sins, our Lord came, who conquered sin and thus forgave us our sins, when, believing in him, we are freed from sins.

CHAPTER V.—VERSE 1.

Therefore be imitators of God, as most beloved children of God. You are imitators of God precisely in this: when you too forgive each other your sins, as God forgave us our sins in Christ. Therefore live as imitators of God, and live in such a way as children of God and most beloved children. For indeed he did not spare his own Son for you, and gave him over to sin for your sins, that he might conquer sin, as the mystery is understood.

VERS. 2.

[Col. 1283A]

And walk in love. This is a great precept and assuredly one to be retained, for it includes all things; charity is sufficient, since the whole law is in it, and the whole mystery of Christianity: love and charity. “As Christ also loved you” [Note: [Col. 1283D] (1) The Vulgate has “us,” “for us.”]. This is what was said above: “imitators of God,” so that you also may love one another, as Christ loved you. But what does “loved” and “gave himself up for you” mean? The same substance, one [Note: [Col. 1283D] (2) The manuscripts have *utrum*, perhaps “either.”] also in will; and likewise, “I and the Father are one.” Here he gave himself up for you, that is, for another; he did not spare his Son, so that in this manner we too may give what is ours for one another and love one another even to this point—that is, even to suffering for another.

“And gave himself up for you, an offering and sacrifice to God in an odor of burning fragrance” [Note: [Col. 1283D] (3) Vulgate: “of sweetness.”]. He offered himself to God, so that through this mystery all things might become spirit and [Col. 1283B] sacrifice. For this is the odor of good fragrance. He said that its substance was spirit, and that its odor was good fragrance. There is a certain book which expounds this matter: what spirit is, and what intelligible character it has, so that its substance may be understood [Note: [Col. 1283D] (4) Let us note the work here named by Victorinus, whether his own or another’s, concerning the substance of spirit.].

VERS. 3.

But indecency [Note: [Col. 1283D] (5) Vulgate: “fornication.”] and every uncleanness and avarice must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints. These too are precepts concerning what is not to be done: that indecency, uncleanness, and avarice should be absent. These three are to be excluded from souls to such an extent that they should not even have a name or mention among them, especially among those who are saints. For even naming these things is sin; how much more possessing or admitting them? For the name, mind, and conscience of saints require [Col. 1283C] that the tongue too be pure. For if one who is pure in conduct [Note: [Col. 1283D] (6) Thus the manuscripts, with *tmesis* for *siqui* or *siquis*, “if anyone.”] names vices, he nevertheless sins, because in what he says he shows that he knows the very vices.

VERS. 4.

Or shamefulness, or foolish speech, or buffoonery. He adds also three others which differ from the foregoing. For indecency is far different from uncleanness. Where there is no shame, there is indecency; but this is not immediately shamefulness. Shamefulness is a disgraceful deed and sin; indecency, however, is the absence of shame. Likewise, uncleanness can be in speech, life, or conduct. Avarice, moreover, is a desire to possess. Thus the following three are far different: shamefulness, foolish speech, and also speaking vainly. Even if what you say does no harm, still, if it is foolish, neither wise nor useful, it is alien to saints. Buffoonery, then, is jesting [Col. 1283D] speech which injures another for the sake of a joke, and is therefore insulting.

These things are irrelevant. For buffoonery can also be used in rebuke, so long as it is not foolish speech. But if these things are relevant, they should be admitted. They are sins if they occur when they are irrelevant. For if they either admonish or correct, then, being relevant, they must be done. “But rather thanksgiving.” Having said what should not be, he adds what should rather be [Col. 1284A] done: namely, let us give thanks—undoubtedly to God, though also to human beings—and therefore it is expressed without qualification.

VERS. 5.

For know this [Note: [Col. 1284D] (1) The Vulgate adds “understanding,” and has “fornicator” for “indecent person.”]: that every indecent person, or unclean person, or avaricious person—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Having set down the three things mentioned above, and added the three following things, he frames this precept so as to teach that the former three are most grave. Indeed, he spoke in such a way that those three should not even be named among saints. Therefore they are grave. How grave? “Know,” he says, “that these things—namely, indecency, uncleanness, avarice—have no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.”

He called avarice idolatry, either because the avaricious person serves idols, believing that the things which are in the world are supplied to him by them—things in regard to which [Note: [Col. 1284D] (3) The manuscripts read uncertainly: “which [things] the unclean . . . in which the avaricious,” etc.] he is avaricious. For God supplies [Col. 1284B] the things which are future; but the avaricious person is certainly avaricious concerning the present life, and therefore serves idols. Or was this said—that avarice is service of idols—because, although there is one God, it belongs to avarice to worship many, adore others, and wish to serve others? Such a person, then, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. For Christ has a kingdom in the heavens, and the one who follows Christ will have an inheritance in Christ’s kingdom. The kingdom of Christ is God’s kingdom. Therefore one who serves idols has no inheritance in God’s kingdom either.

VERS. 6.
