Let no one seduce you with vain words [Note: [Col. 1284D] (4) The Vulgate has “empty words.”]. For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. This too is among the precepts of which I spoke to you, things which ought not to be done. For many recommend through their words worldly advantage and the worship of idols—that is, the desire to possess. But these are vain words. When he says, “for because of these things the wrath of God comes,” this is evidently because persons of this sort have no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. “Because of these things,” he says, “they also have punishment”: they are deprived both of the good things of eternal life and of the coming of wrath upon themselves. Whom did he call [Note: [Col. 1284D] (5) Thus the manuscripts.] [Col. 1284C] children of unbelief? Many think vain the promise of kingdoms in heaven [Note: [Col. 1284D] (6) The manuscripts have *se*, “themselves.”], saying, “What human being has ascended into heaven?” Therefore they do not trust and do not believe. Thus the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Unbelief, however, is that devil whom those who do not trust serve, and therefore they are his children.

VERS. 7, 8, 9.

Therefore do not become participants with them. After treating the matter generally above, he returns to the precept and to the Ephesians, that they should in every way keep themselves apart from persons of this sort [Col. 1284D] and not participate with them. “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.” Therefore, that they may separate themselves in every way from the children of unbelief, he says what they formerly were when they lived as Gentiles. “You were darkness.” But the one who follows Christ is light; for everyone baptized in Christ receives light. “Walk as children of light” [Note: [Col. 1284D] (7) The Vulgate has *ut*, “as,” for *sicut*.]. Therefore, because you are light in the Lord—for you are not light in yourselves, but light in the Lord—and because you too are children [Col. 1285A] of light, live as those who are children of light ought to live.

What it is to live as a child of light, he himself adds: “For the fruit of light is in all goodness and righteousness and truth.” For this is both to be light and to be a child of light: to excel in goodness, righteousness, and truth. These three things themselves are light. Their opposites are darkness: malice, injustice, falsehood. All these belong to the devil; but the former belong to light, because Christ is light. Therefore, goodness, righteousness, and truth: live with these dispositions.

VERS. 10, 11.

But prove what is pleasing to God [Note: [Col. 1285D] (1) Vulgate: “proving what is well-pleasing to God.”], and do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness. I said that he turns through the same precepts to what is to be followed and what is not to be followed: that one should live in goodness, righteousness, and truth. Likewise here: “Prove,” he says, “the things which please God.” Then he adds what ought not to be followed: “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness”—that is, avarice, indecency, and other things of this sort, and idolatry. These are works which yield no fruit. For the one who desires these things gains nothing; therefore they have no fruit, and are darkness, because they show nothing of light, nothing of fruit. “But rather rebuke them” [Note: [Col. 1285D] (2) Vulgate: “rather reprove them.”]. Thus we must not only separate ourselves from evil practices and not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness, but also rebuke and accuse these same works—that is, the persons who live in this manner.

VERS. 12.

For it is shameful even to speak of the things which are done by them in secret [Note: [Col. 1285D] (3) Vulgate: “For the things which are done by them in secret, it is shameful even to speak of.”]. He has almost stated openly what they do, when he shows that it is shameful to speak of those things. Therefore do not participate; therefore rather rebuke.

VERS. 13.

But all things which are rebuked [Note: [Col. 1285D] (4) Vulgate: “are reproved.”] are made manifest by the light. Because he gave the precept that they should also rebuke evildoers, he added how great a gift rebuke is: since those sins done in secret are, as it were, made manifest by light when they are rebuked. For the person who rebukes shows how great is the evil which he rebukes; and in showing it, he as it were illumines the evil. When the person who commits it understands this, he dispels darkness and comes to the light. For everything that is made manifest is light. He himself demonstrates what we have explained: whatever is understood is both manifested and light, is seen and open.

VERS. 14.

[Col. 1285D]

Therefore he says: “Rise from the dead, and you will touch Christ” [Note: [Col. 1285D] (5) Vulgate: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.”]. He gives an example of how one who is rebuked for his sins receives light and understands that he sins. When he understands that he sins, he is enlightened—that is, he rises from the dead; he abandons darkness and touches Christ, that is, receives light and begins now both to avoid sins and to have hope of eternal life.

VERS. 15, 16.

See [Note: [Col. 1286D] (1) The manuscripts have *vide*, “see.” Compare the Vulgate, which admits some variants.] therefore how carefully you walk, [Col. 1286A] not as unwise persons but as wise. In one precept he has included both things, admonishing how they should walk: not as unwise persons but as wise, namely with that wisdom which is from God, not with that which is of the world. “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” All these days which are in the world are evil, for in what belongs to them they work evil against us; and everything good is from the future. “Let us redeem this time,” he says; that is, by our virtue, patience, and obedience, let us make the time our own and, as it were, purchase it by our labors and patience. Let this time, which is against us, become ours. This is “redeeming the time.”

VERS. 17.

Therefore do not become [Note: [Col. 1286D] (2) Vulgate: “Therefore do not become.”] imprudent, but understanding. By the same admonition we are again warned [Col. 1286B] toward understanding of the world and worldly matters. In this we were [Note: [Col. 1286D] (3) The manuscripts have *erimus*, “we shall be.”] imprudent; but “be,” he says, “understanding” [Note: [Col. 1286D] (4) The manuscripts have *sumus*, “we are.”]. He then adds what it is to be understanding: “[Understand] what is the will of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1286D] (5) Vulgate: “of God.”]. Let us understand what the Lord has willed and wills: that we live in integrity, righteousness, and faith; place our hope in him; and think of nothing except God. “This,” he says, “is the will of the Lord.”

VERS. 18.

And do not become drunk with wine, in which is licentiousness. This too concerns things not to be done: that we should use very much wine, from which arise many vices. Then he adds what is to be done: “But be filled with the spirit, speaking to one another” [Note: [Col. 1286D] (6) The Vulgate adds “Holy,” and has “speaking to yourselves.”]. This is a great precept. For all the former matters—abstaining from drunkenness, not walking unwisely, and the things [Col. 1286C] said above—are in our will and our effort. This, however, would be understood as belonging only to God’s will, unless here he admonished us that being filled with the Spirit belongs to our own will. For thus we cleanse the soul of all vices and sins: if we are filled with spirit, so that we make Spirit for ourselves and are filled with spirit [Note: [Col. 1286D] (7) The manuscripts have “in spirit”; but shortly before, “with spirit.”].

VERS. 19, 20.

Speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. Let them speak to one another of nothing except psalms, hymns, and songs [Note: [Col. 1286D] (8) The manuscripts have *canticos*, “songs.”]. We shall state elsewhere precisely what the difference among these is; yet all resound with God’s praise and declare that a human being must have hope in God. For these will truly be spiritual, if they are such. Therefore let us sing these things, and sing them in our hearts, as he himself adds: “singing and making melody.” “Giving thanks always for all [persons], in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to the Father [Col. 1286D] and God” [Note: [Col. 1286D] (9) Vulgate: “to God and the Father.”].

“Singing” [Note: [Col. 1286D] (10) Before *cantantes*, “singing,” the manuscripts read “that all these things . . .”] concerns what is uttered by the voice; “making melody” means striking and moving either the lyre or other instruments, as the prophet David also says, “with strings and cymbals.” But do these things, he says, in your hearts, giving thanks; giving thanks always [Col. 1287A] and for all [persons]—not only for ourselves, but also for others whom we see corrected. And to whom should we give thanks? To the Father and God; but let us give thanks to the Father and God in the name of the Lord. For then we rightly give thanks if we give thanks to God not in our own name, but in Christ’s name. It is necessary, indeed, that we give thanks to God both because we have been delivered and because we receive the Spirit; but we do so rightly when we give thanks to God in Christ’s name.

VERS. 21.

Being subject to one another in the fear of Christ. “To one another,” that is, one for another; “in the fear of Christ,” in that we fear Christ—as it is said, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of understanding” [Note: [Col. 1287D] (1) Ps. 110:10. For “understanding,” the Vulgate has “wisdom.”].

VERS. 22, 23, 24.

Let wives be subject to their own husbands as to the Lord. Precepts are also given to women: what [Col. 1287B] they ought to do and how. What they ought to do, he said: “Let them be subject to their own husbands.” How? “As to the Lord,” or as to Christ: so that their husbands may be to them as their lord. Finally, he gives the reason why this is so: “Because the husband is the head of the wife” [Note: [Col. 1287D] (2) Vulgate: “of the woman.”], “as Christ also is the head of the Church, he himself the savior of the body” [Note: [Col. 1287D] (3) The Vulgate adds “its.”]. Thus the husband too is the head of the wife. “And as the Church is subject to Christ, so also let wives be subject in all things” [Note: [Col. 1287D] (4) Vulgate: “But as the Church is subject to Christ, so also wives [should be subject] to their husbands in all things.”], modest and restrained in all things.

VERS. 25, 26.

Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself up for her, in order that he might sanctify her, cleansing [her] in the washing of water by the word [Note: [Col. 1287D] (5) *Vitae*, “of life,” is lacking in Victorinus here and below; compare the Vulgate because of Victorinus’ variants.]. He turns to husbands, that he may prescribe in like manner what husbands should do toward wives. “Love,” he says, “your wives.” He gives the reason from the same example: “as,” he says, [Col. 1287C] “Christ loved the Church.” For the husband is the head of the woman, and Christ the head of the Church; and as Christ gave himself up for the Church so that he might sanctify her, so the husband too ought to endure everything patiently for her, that he may sanctify her.

Yet he continues to show what Christ bestowed: that he gave himself up in order to cleanse the Church in the washing of water and in the word. We must certainly understand “Church” as every believer and everyone who has received baptism; for one is received in faith, namely through the washing of water and the invocation of the word. How these things are to be referred to the husband in relation to his wife is not very clear. Yet it may seem that what he offered by way of likeness in the preceding section belongs there, while this section is completed in the account of the mystery. Nevertheless, if we refer even this to the husband’s [Col. 1287D] patience—that he give himself up for his wife, bear everything of hers, and endure even sufferings—she will be cleansed by washing and word; that is, she will have purification before the Lord, when he renders her pure and by patience makes her fit to be sanctified through washing and word.

VERS. 27.

That he might present to himself a glorious Church. Christ, he says, gave himself for the Church in order to make his Church glorious to himself, also pure, [Col. 1288A] without spot and without wrinkle. For these bring ugliness—spot and wrinkle; when the body lacks them, it is vigorous, flourishing, and beautiful. But beyond these he added, “or anything of the sort,” that is, if there is anything else of this kind that has a name; but [his purpose was] that she should be holy and immaculate. Christ accomplished this so that the Church might be holy and immaculate: holy in this, that she is cleansed through washing of water and word; immaculate, in that she is without spot and without wrinkle.

VERS. 28.

Thus husbands also ought to love their wives as their own body [Note: [Col. 1288D] (1) Vulgate: “as their own bodies.”]. Equal precepts are given to the husband also: that he should love his wife “as,” he says, “his own body.” For the history of creation shows that the woman was made from the man’s rib. Therefore let him love his wife as his own body. “He who loves his wife loves himself.” He repeats the same point: for if the wife is from our body, [Col. 1288B] he who loves his wife loves himself. And so afterwards he adds the example: “and the two shall become one flesh.”

VERS. 29.

For no one ever hates his own flesh [Note: [Col. 1288D] (2) Vulgate: “has held [it] in hatred.”], but nourishes and cherishes it. He confirms that this love is according to nature: that we love our own flesh. But if the woman is our flesh, and the first woman was from the flesh of the man, and was so a woman that she was also his very wife, then, since no one hates his own flesh but rather nourishes and cherishes it, he ought also to love his wife as his own flesh, as Christ [loves] the Church. The precepts concerning the husband are the same as those concerning the wife. For religion and reverence have been so ordained: the wife serves the husband because the husband is the wife’s head, as Christ is the Church’s; so now this precept is also given to the husband, that he should love his wife as Christ [loves] the Church.

VERS. 30.

[Col. 1288C]

Because we are members of his body. Above it was likewise said that the Church is all the holy faithful, who are Christ’s members; and the Church becomes the one body of Christ, whose head is Christ. “Of his flesh and of his bones.” We are all members, he says, of his very flesh and of his bones. This is not to be understood as though we have a share in that flesh which he put on and in which he appeared, [Note: [Col. 1288D] (3) The manuscripts have “to have.”] or in his bones, which were the bones of the flesh in which Christ appeared. Rather, let us understand the whole of his deity, which is in spirit, where above all heaven and in heavenly things he possesses the power of his deity, in relation to spirit, to mind—which the Greeks call *nous* (νοῦς)—and to soul. Therefore, since we too have these same things, [Col. 1288D] it must be understood thus: that we are members of Christ, that is, in spiritual substance; “of his flesh,” that is, of soul; and “of his bones,” that is, of what is called *nous* in Greek. For in the higher realm all these things are spirit by God’s power, as the same Paul says in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians [Note: [Col. 1288D] (4) Ch. 5:23.]: “May the very God of peace sanctify you wholly, so that [Note: [Col. 1288D] (5) The manuscripts have “and.”] your whole spirit and soul and body may be preserved.”

VERS. 31.

“For this reason a man shall leave” [Note: [Col. 1288D] (6) The manuscripts have “leaves.”] his father [Col. 1289A] and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.” This example is from Genesis, by which it is proved that love ought to be so great—or that a man should hold his wife so dear [Note: [Col. 1289D] (1) Note the Hellenism from εἶναι ἔχοντα.]—that he leaves both father and mother, cleaves to his wife, and they become two in one flesh. In many ways he teaches that a husband is joined to his wife, and establishes that it ought to be so: that the husband should love his wife [Note: [Col. 1289D] (2) The manuscripts have *liberet*, “should free.”] and the wife her husband. This is so simply, as the matter itself stands, and has been stated thus both by us and by Paul. Nevertheless, what follows shows that this statement has a deeper scope; for he adds:

VERS. 32.

This mystery [Note: [Col. 1289D] (4) The Vulgate has “sacrament” (*sacramentum*) for “mystery” (*mysterium*).] is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church. Beyond what the plain sense itself indicated [Note: [Col. 1289D] (5) The manuscripts read “will indicate” (*indicabit*).], Paul shows that there is something more when he says, “This mystery is great” [Col. 1289B]; yet he did not make clear what he meant. He merely added another interpretation: that by “husband and wife,” here [Note: [Col. 1289D] (6) The manuscripts read *hoc* for *hic*.], Christ and the Church are to be understood for the present. But because he called it a great mystery, it must be understood more deeply. What, then, do we suppose? I think it is to be understood thus: husband and wife are spirit and soul joined to one another. For this is Adam and Eve: the spirit is Christ; the soul is the Church. But Paul interpreted this as requiring to be understood of the Church and Christ, provided that the same relation is that of spirit and soul. Yet this was easier, and more readily reached the people: “I speak,” he says, “in Christ and in the Church.” He did not say, “Christ and the Church,” but “in Christ and in the Church.” For Christ has the Church in his members, and the Church has Christ as head in her members. [Col. 1289C] Therefore the Church is in Christ; in whatever one flesh, the two are to be.

### Verse 33

Nevertheless, let each one of you love his own wife as himself. [Note: [Col. 1289D] (7) The Vulgate: “Let him love his own wife as himself.”] Although above he had given precepts generally to husbands concerning wives, and to women concerning husbands, he now directs the same precepts specifically to the Ephesians: “and you,” he says. This is because he had explained figuratively that the saying, “This mystery is great,” meant that both wife and husband were in one flesh; and he wished this to be understood of the Church and Christ. Therefore he added “nevertheless,” so that, although he wished that saying to be understood truly of Christ and the Church, as being in one body, nevertheless you too should observe and imitate this same thing, so that each man may love his own wife. And likewise he adds concerning wives: “but let the woman” [Note: [Col. 1289D] (8) The Vulgate: “wife.”] “fear her husband.” Here there is love in fear, and affection is preserved together with honour: husbands are to love their wives; [Col. 1289D] women are to fear their husbands.

## Chapter VI

He likewise passes to other persons: children and parents. Afterwards he was about to add concerning slaves . . . [Note: [Col. 1289D] (9) “No one doubts that there is a lacuna here, although the manuscript gives no indication of it; something we have observed elsewhere as well.”] and grieve over how much they provide, yet how much more they entangle the mind than free it, and bind it within the world. I have set forth, handed down, and taught this with full arguments there [Note: [Col. 1290D] (1) “The passage must be conjectured.”], showing that spiritual wickedness chiefly works through worldly power even up to heaven [Note: [Col. 1290D] (2) Thus the manuscripts read.], while it promises wretched souls that they may become, as it were, certain names. [Note: [Col. 1290D] (3) Thus the manuscripts read. The sentence appears broken off or corrupted.]

### Verse 11

Therefore take up the weapons of faith, that you may be able to resist in the evil day. [Note: [Col. 1290D] (4) The Vulgate: “Put on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.”] Since all the matters mentioned above involve great difficulties—against the rulers of this world and of these darknesses, and, what is greater, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavens—it was necessary, since resisting all these requires great strength, to add the means by which it might be done: “Take up,” he says, “the weapons of faith.” For faith in Christ alone fortifies us, so that no temptation of these worldly powers can prevail against us. Thus what seemed difficult—to resist—has become easy, if the means by which we resist lies in our power. [Col. 1290B] And it does lie in our power: to have faith in Christ, and to have full faith, involves no labour and no difficulty; it requires only a willing and believing disposition of mind. [Note: [Col. 1290D] (5) Thus the manuscripts read.] Therefore it becomes easy to resist so many evils, if we have faith. Faith alone suffices; faith alone withstands; faith alone fortifies—but full faith. Even he himself said that, if we have a grain of faith like a mustard seed, we can command even mountains. Therefore sincere and pure faith—faith, I say, in Christ, and faith in God—will furnish us with weapons against all those powers. “Now take up,” he says, “the weapons of faith, that you may be able to resist.” When are you to resist? When temptation comes; when something begins to tempt you. This is what he means by “the evil day.” The day is evil when we are tempted.

### Verse 14

And, having accomplished everything, stand; having girded [Col. 1290C] your loins with truth. [Note: [Col. 1290D] (6) Thus the manuscripts read. The Vulgate, at the end of v. 13: “And, having accomplished everything, to stand: stand therefore, having girded yourselves,” etc.] He knows that above he has urged many things to be done: either with reference to particular persons—masters and slaves, husbands and wives, fathers and sons—or with reference to what must be done and what must not be done, such as “do not become drunk” and “do everything in the name of the Lord,” and the other matters mentioned above. Therefore he says: “And, having accomplished everything which I have commanded and prescribed above, stand,” that is, be prepared and equipped. For every exertion, if there is labour, falls upon the loins; or, if there is to be labour and exertion, it comes from our loins. [Note: [Col. 1290D] (7) The manuscripts read “your.”] From there comes every strength and all material for blood; hence we call persons weak and “unloined” (*elumbes*). Therefore, that strength both of body and mind may prepare itself, he says, “having girded your loins.” “Stand in truth,” he says: for what we exhort you to is truth; the rest, which is taught and debated from the wisdom of the world, is false. [Col. 1290D]

And having put on the breastplate of righteousness. He adds another command besides faith: that we should preserve righteousness. Although what was said above—namely faith in Christ [Note: [Col. 1290D] (8) The manuscripts read *ipsum*, “itself,” for “in Christ.”]—is the chief thing of all (for righteousness does not avail as much as faith, since “the righteous person lives by faith”), [Col. 1291A] nevertheless this disposition too must be fulfilled, so as to be most righteous. For then faith will benefit us, and then faith will be true, if we are most righteous; and righteousness will benefit us if faith is added. Therefore after faith he added: “Put on the breastplate of righteousness.” Above he said, “Take up the weapons of faith”; now, “Put on the breastplate of righteousness.” For “weapons” include both that which protects and that which resists and overcomes the adversary, whereas in a breastplate there is nothing other than our protection. Faith, however, also resists; and for that reason he spoke of “weapons of faith.” How does faith resist? Clearly, if when the enemy begins to tempt us we do not follow him, and, preserving faith in God and in the Lord Christ, we are not moved from our conviction. Therefore resist, as one who has missiles and swords resists. “Put on,” he says, “the weapons of faith, that you may resist.” Righteousness, on the contrary, exists only in deeds; it does not resist an adversary, [Col. 1291B] but itself proves good and gentle. Therefore, he says, the breastplate of righteousness, by which, pursuing what is good, one displays a good mind and a good heart.

### Verse 15

And your feet shod in preparation for the gospel of peace, because the gospel is carried abroad and preached among the nations. Therefore, wherever it is preached, it must be heard. But in order that we may hear, we must go, hasten, hurry. “Therefore,” he says, “your feet shod in preparation for the gospel.” Of which gospel? “Of peace,” he says. For whoever hears the gospel and is prepared in the gospel becomes the Lord’s, believes Christ, receives the promises, bears confidence, and is hostile to no one. Therefore it is the gospel of peace: that is, of the peace [Note: [Col. 1291D] (1) The manuscripts read “peace which.”] which belongs to souls. In order to receive this, then, our feet must be shod—that is, we must be ready to run forth, range about, and listen. What, then, is accomplished by all these things? [Col. 1291C] We shall easily resist the powers, the spiritual rulers of wickedness.

### Verse 16

In all things, having taken up the shield of faith. [Note: [Col. 1291D] (2) The Vulgate: “in all things. Taking up the shield of faith.”] He returns to that chief point which encompasses everything and fulfils all things. For we cannot otherwise wage a strong fight and resist all those powers unless we are fortified with a shield, so that with faith’s protection we repel all the blows and assaults of every power.

Finally he adds: “whereby you may be able to extinguish all the fiery arrows of the most wicked one.” [Note: [Col. 1291D] (3) The Vulgate: “whereby you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one.”] We very often read of arrows in the Gospel, in Paul, in the prophets, and in David; these we understand to be arguments, words, and discourses. But they are the arrows of the most wicked one: that is, they give evil counsel and wound our understanding, soul, and spirit evilly. Therefore he called them fiery, because they burn; and the shield of faith—faith itself—extinguishes them all, so that they have no force within us. For when faith is present in souls, that fire which is sent through the tongue, persuading us of all malign worldly things, is quenched and grows cool. For every such persuasion of the evil one, because it speaks carnally and insinuates itself carnally, has power through the blood. Therefore it stirs up the blood itself by novel conceptions; and when stirred, the blood becomes fiery. Thus those arrows become fiery, which faith suppresses and extinguishes, because faith receives [Col. 1292A] all things spiritually. Spirit is light, not fire. Accordingly, spirit, while it imitates light, is not fire; but every fire harms. Therefore spirit does not harm. Yet when faith is in Christ, it receives light from the light in Christ; thus the light of faith conquers fire, because fire has force and works around the flesh, and is itself worldly, material from matter. It has no force against the eternal light of God, Jesus Christ. Thus this fire is extinguished by that light. I have said that this fire is especially stirred up by discourses; and because such discourses run forth and fly, they have been called arrows.

### Verse 17

And the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Since above he said, “having put on the breastplate of righteousness,” here too one should understand: “Put on the saving helmet and the sword of the Spirit.” Whether “sword of the Spirit” should be taken independently, and “the saving helmet” added independently—the Spirit is both saving and a helmet—and “put on the sword.” [Note: [Col. 1292D] (1) Thus in the manuscripts.] But if the sword is truly and certainly referred back to “which is the word of God,” it is separate: “Put on the sword of the Spirit.” What then does “put on the helmet of salvation” mean? Christ, in that he descended here and redeemed us by his mystery, is saving; he himself is our head, for he guards the head of the Church. Hence he is the helmet of salvation. Furthermore, the word is that by which adverse powers are conquered and crushed, as it is said: “He will destroy the devil by the spirit of his mouth.” [Note: [Col. 1292D] (2) 2 Thess. 2:8.] Therefore Christ, who is the Word of God, was sent in order to conquer every corruption, every malignity, and death itself. For this reason it is said: the sword is the Spirit, the Word of God.

### Verse 18

[Col. 1292C]

Praying through every prayer and supplication, at every time, in the Spirit. [Note: [Col. 1292D] (3) The Vulgate: “supplication.”] To drive out the things mentioned above—that is, to conquer the powers of the world, the rulers of darkness, and the spiritual forces of wickedness—he adds this too: that we should pray and make supplication daily, and through every supplication pray at every time in the Spirit. How numerous and how hidden are the precepts here concerning what we ask! First, he said, “through every prayer.” Prayers are many: now for ourselves, now for others; now for matters of the present life, now for those of the future; now for matters of the soul, now for those of the body, as we desire certain things. “In every prayer,” he says, “let us pray in the Spirit and at every time.” Let us pray in the Spirit—that is, let us not merely say, utter, or recite certain words in prayer, as if rehearsed or written; but, he says, let us pray in the Spirit at every time: that is, let us bring feeling to it, and let the inward spirit—the inward person—owe and possess prayer at every time in full desire, so that even when one does not pray, one may pray in the Spirit. Then what does he mean when he says, “through every prayer and supplication”? I think the distinction is this: prayer includes when we speak God’s praises, recount his great works, give thanks, and do other such things; supplication, however, is when we pray to God for forgiveness [Col. 1293A] and our sins, or for grace, that he may grant it to us. This, I say, is supplication; and when we pray to God, these two modes should be present, both prayer and supplication. “Through every prayer,” therefore, he says, “and through every supplication.” Let us not be satisfied merely to utter certain words by habit, but pray from the inward soul and mind—indeed, to speak plainly, from the very spirit and in the very Spirit—so that even when prayer or supplication is absent in words, we may pray in the Spirit.

And in it, watching always in every prayer. [Note: [Col. 1293D] (1) The Vulgate does not have “always”; and instead of “prayer” reads “persistence and supplication.”] He also added a definite time. For when he said “at every time,” this could be understood as the time granted to a human being, namely the day. But what did he add in order to make “at every time” fuller? “Watching always.” Yet this may be understood as referring to attentiveness of mind: “watching always in every prayer,” so that we should not be like persons asleep, as those suffer who recite, read, or pronounce from memory things with which they are familiar, scarcely sensing what they say or how they say it. Therefore he says: “watching always in prayer for all the saints.” [Col. 1293B]

### Verse 19

And for me. This too is an important admonition, which we have often touched upon and said should be noted: we ought not to pray only for ourselves, but also for others. Here and in many places I remind you that this precept is twofold: both those saints themselves—bishops, apostles, and superiors—ought to pray for the faithful, catechumens, and all other inferiors, just as he frequently declares here that in every prayer of his he makes mention [Col. 1293C] also of all his own people. Likewise here again those who are inferior should pray in every prayer for the saints, for bishops, and, he says, “for me.” This should be attended to and regarded as remarkable: that he seeks, as it were, help from those whom he himself admonishes, instructs, and announces the gospel to, in order that he may obtain something by their prayer. What he says they should ask for him, he himself adds: “that utterance may be given to me in the opening of my mouth, with confidence to make known the mystery.” [Note: [Col. 1293D] (2) The Vulgate: “That utterance may be given to me in the opening of my mouth with confidence, to make known the mystery of the gospel.”] He exhorted the Ephesians to pray both for the saints and especially for himself. What they should ask for himself—that is, for Paul—he added: not health, not any desires, but that Paul himself might have speech and open discourse, that is, confidence in expounding the gospel and the mystery. Indeed, this should also be sought by the prayer of those whom it can benefit: since Paul proclaims the mystery and the gospel, those who are to receive it should pray that his discourse may abound, that his mouth may speak more openly, and that he may expound the mystery confidently and without any trembling. [Col. 1293D]

### Verse 20

For which I discharge an embassy in a chain. That is: I am Christ’s ambassador, though placed in a chain; nevertheless I disclose the mystery and the gospel. In this [Col. 1294A] he shows what he suffers and how he perseveres, so that he may not be frightened by adversities or overcome by pain, but may fulfil the assigned office of apostleship. “That I may act confidently in it.” [Note: [Col. 1294D] (1) The Vulgate: “So that in it I may dare, as I ought to speak.”] Well does he say here also, “confidently” and “with confidence.” For what else ought he to ask or promise against threats and imposed punishments, except that he might have confidence in expounding? “That utterance may be given to me in the opening of my mouth with confidence”—that is [Note: [Col. 1294D] (2) The manuscripts read “here” for “that is.”] in acting—“that I may act confidently in it”: in it, that is, in the gospel and mystery. “As I ought to speak”: that is, evangelizing itself is acting; to speak, and to speak as one ought, is to speak confidently, lest I fulfil my office inadequately, or chains produce some effect in my mind and I fail to fulfil it as I should by expounding the mystery.

### Verse 21

But that you too may know the things [Col. 1294B] concerning me, what I am doing, Tychicus, the most beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make known to you. [Note: [Col. 1294D] (3) The Vulgate: “He will make all things known to you . . .”] He properly chose not to communicate in the letter about the things he suffers, but only through a messenger, so that the Ephesians might learn what he had commanded, what he was doing, and what concerned him. For there are two matters: chains and other injuries concern him; but what he is doing is persevering, disclosing the mystery, evangelizing, and opening it. He commends the person: “Tychicus,” he says, “the most beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord”—not a minister to me, but a minister in the Lord, concerning the gospel and the mystery.

### Verse 22

Whom I sent to you for this very purpose. For it was not that, as he was going, I gave him instructions; rather, I sent him for this reason. Thus I care also for you and want you to know everything. Therefore I sent him for this very purpose, that you might know what is happening concerning us. And that he may comfort your hearts. Here he adds more, since he has joined one thing to the two: “what is happening concerning us,” that is, what punishments and chains we endure. Therefore he added, “and that he may comfort your hearts,” so that you may not labour under concern and anxiety about me, but he may be a consolation to you when he explains with what disposition and confidence I am.

### Verses 23–24

Peace to the brethren, and love with faith. Grace to those [Note: [Col. 1294D] (4) The Vulgate: “all.”] who love our Lord Jesus Christ in eternity. Amen. The final part of the letter is a prayer: he prays and wishes peace for the brethren; likewise love, then faith. For above he had said that discord was among them. He then adds grace for those who show faith and love [Col. 1294D] our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus everything is concluded: peace against discord, love for concord, faith toward God; and grace is granted from faith—the Lord’s grace to those who have love and peace among themselves, and faith in him. He adds “in eternity,” so that these wishes may not be only for the present life, but also for the future life, which is in hope and promise for Christians. Amen.

[Col. 1295]

# Victorinus’ Book on Natural Things (*De Physicis*)

(Mai, *Collections*, vol. III.) (C, G, S)*

Notice prefixed by Mai to the book *On Natural Things*.

[Col. 1295A]

For preparing this edition of the commentaries, I used three manuscripts from the Vatican Library: namely, Ottobonianus 328 A, of the fourteenth century, from which Ottobonianus 3288 B, of the sixteenth century, was copied; and finally Vaticanus 3546, likewise of the sixteenth century, derived almost from one or the other Ottobonian manuscript. Consequently, in these unpublished commentaries there is almost no variation in readings. The same lacunae occur in all the manuscripts, as do the same corruption, ambiguity, and obscurity of a great many passages. Otherwise, the orthography is somewhat older in the former 3288 A, which later copyists evidently repeatedly altered in the other exemplars.

Moreover, the contents of all the manuscripts are the same, namely, writings of Victorinus both published and unpublished. First comes Victorinus’ commentary on the Apocalypse (or *commentarium*, as it is more frequently written in these manuscripts), preceded by Jerome’s letter. This work is extant under the disputed name of Victorinus of Petavium in the great Lyons Library of the Fathers, vol. III, p. 414 ff. There follow Victorinus’ hitherto unpublished commentaries on the Epistles to the Galatians and to the Philippians. Then two short works of Victorinus are written: namely, on the words of Genesis, “there came to be evening and morning, one day”; and against the two principles of the Manichaeans. Sirmond first brought both into print, taken from a manuscript of the monastery of Hérival; in that manuscript there were also concealed Victorinus’ commentaries on several Pauline epistles. Sirmond indeed mentioned them and said that they were fuller and clearer in Victorinus’ customary style (*Works*, vol. I, p. 345, fol. V), but did not publish them, whether prevented by varied occupations, by someone’s wish, or by some other circumstance.

Yet in the Vatican manuscripts the short work against the Manichaeans lacks the first chapter, which the printed text has; conversely, the printed text lacks the conclusion which I shall now present. The edition stops at “to whom be honour and glory.” But the Vatican manuscripts have: “to whom be [Col. 1295C] honour and glory from all creatures, and before beginnings and after ends. Thus, then, from the true—which is—there proceeds also the false being, as shadows from solid things: for if there is no solid thing, neither does a shadow arise.” In the manuscripts there follows the hitherto unpublished commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians. Last in the manuscripts is the short work entitled *On Natural Things*, which certainly has not been published under Victorinus’ name; whether it perhaps exists under another name, I do not know. To me it certainly seems wholly Victorinus’, both because of the similarity of style and because, in these three Vatican manuscripts, there is no writing that is not Victorinus’. If Victorinus’ name is not prefixed to this work, I maintain that it is not prefixed even to the two short works in these manuscripts which I said were published by Sirmond and which are undoubtedly Victorinus’. Therefore I have not allowed Victorinus’ writing *On Natural Things* to be absent from this volume of mine.

## The Book *On Natural Things* Begins

[Col. 1295D]

### I

Human perception recognizes God, the maker of all things, by natural judgment and movement. [Note: [Col. 1295D] (1) The manuscripts read “Lord,” owing to an earlier misunderstanding of the abbreviation of the word.] But [Note: [Col. 1295D] (2) The manuscripts read “of course” (*scilicet*).] the natural philosophers, admiring the things themselves—indeed, stupefied and blinded by the force of their own marvel [Note: [Col. 1295D] (3) The manuscripts read “by their marvel.”]—have forgotten him, the maker of all creation. Some maintain, with the boldest motion, that there is no God, but that nature generates all things from itself without God. [Col. 1296A] Others, while acknowledging both God and nature, make the nature of things equal to God. They say indeed that he did violence [Note: [Col. 1296D] (1) The manuscripts read *ei*, “to it.”] to nature because he is said to have fashioned by appropriating from it; and conversely that he suffers violence because nature dissolves the things which he established.

Against these two opposed classes, both of which blaspheme, an answer must be given—first, I think, to those who are more audacious, whom we have said deny God, though he is made manifest through his whole creation. For who doubts that the order which exists in the nature of things was established by someone, not by itself? Times yield measures and succession to one another; and the sun, although brighter, more effective, and possessed of the greatest power, yields at night to the lesser moon and choir of stars, nor can it always preserve day itself in the same interval. The stars and moon relinquish the very interval of power which they possess. Spring, autumn, winter, and summer are expected and arrive, ordered within a fixed interval. Yet violence is at times even done to the seasons, so that they do not always do what is expected but, something preventing them, exceed their proper limit. Why should one prolong the discussion about the sea, rivers, earth, mountains, the other elements, or the crops that grow from them? Let us now approach the promised matters.

### II

Creation itself declares that it has some maker. For it does not, by generating itself, also consume itself; for making has one purpose and consuming another. And if the nature of things had always brought forth the whole from itself, it would also have preserved the whole—especially since those who attribute eternity and beginninglessness to nature are compelled also to attribute eternal power to it. Since that power is found in the things it generates, the things generated must also be eternal and without beginning—a claim disproved by the daily birth of things.

And if it is said that things themselves always exist because they succeed one another, nevertheless the limit of birth and dissolution in each individual thing shows that, since each is constrained by this defect, the defect is fitted to all through their very individuality. [Note: [Col. 1296D] (2) The manuscripts read *coaptatur*, “is fitted.”] Thus none of the things that have been made can exist without limitation: for they begin and are completed, grow and diminish. From all these things it is found that there is someone who imposes force upon nature, so that it always suffers this very defect.

### III

Since, then, this has been recognized from physical arguments themselves, which even human perception has always acknowledged, we must now answer those who posit such a needy maker that he did not fashion from what was his own, but by appropriating what belonged to another; so that he is found not only needy but unjust. For what has he to do with another’s matter, if he could have had his own? Thus they seem compelled to acknowledge God, yet do not understand God’s power or marvel at him; they imagine him, like a human being, fashioning from matter [Col. 1297A] set before him. They so far diminish his dignity, as they suppose, that they make matter equal to God by nativity: matter which suffers force from him and acts upon him. For it suffers when it generates; it acts when it dissolves; and both are reduced to nothing.

Next, one must ask them whether each preserves the characteristic of its own nativity. For if God is overcome, he has lost the power proper to his nativity. Conversely, if matter is refashioned by God, it has lost the form of its nativity. Further, when, in the work undertaken, it did what it had never [Note: [Col. 1297D] (2) Supply: “done” or “would have done.”] done before, so that, compelled by the maker, it generates, it received from him for a time some power of bringing forth. But if it received what it did not have, the power of eternity is now excluded by the power which it received. Therefore I ask: from what is that shown to be innate which did not remain in the form [Col. 1297B] of its own nativity? What changes in power, heat, form, quality, and every force cannot remain either in its power or in the same substance; what succumbs to so many defects and necessities cannot be innate. Since it is and is shown not to be innate, it remains that what it is should be recognized as born and made.

### IV

Nor is it recognized that many gods, but one, made it. The diversity of things or powers does not allow reason to posit many gods, since in one earth diverse kinds of herbs, crops, and trees are produced—brought forth in diverse bodies, adorned with diverse colours, strengthened by diverse powers. Indeed, though our soul is one, it establishes diverse technical contrivances, teachings of disciplines, forms of institutions, numbers of measures, elevations of sounds, effects of things, thoughts, and judgments of reason. If, in matters so small, so many effects are granted to one substance, [Note: [Col. 1297D] (3) The manuscripts read “one substance.”] how much more is that one divinity, the progenitress of these very things, [Note: [Col. 1297D] (4) Thus the manuscripts read.] recognized as one, since diversity of things could neither inflict force upon nor remove power from such great majesty?

Next, one must ask on what grounds they introduce many gods: are all of them creators of all things, or [Note: [Col. 1297D] (5) The manuscripts read “or.”] of individual things? They cannot all be makers of everything, because one is sufficient, as has been said. But if many gods are thought to do this, it is necessary that every one contribute to each thing what they bestow. Hence what is contributed by one is imperfect, and the contribution of the rest to matter is lacking, because what it received from [Col. 1297D] one is not sufficient. Matter is now the better, because it alone has received into itself the powers of all.

### V

Further, it is not shown that individual things are constituted by all the gods. A stone does not subsist from the same elements as a tree, nor a tree from those of cattle, nor the genus of fish from those of wild beasts, nor serpents or beasts from those of humankind. Rather, it is necessary to acknowledge that they possess less and more. Hence they are known neither to be makers of every individual thing nor to rule in all things. Since they have not contributed to all things, and since the contributions made to diverse kinds are not all equal (for one differs from another), they must be recognized to contribute less and more. From this contribution, one is found greater and another lesser by his power. This difference does not allow one divinity by nativity to be established for all; therefore beginninglessness again belongs to one alone, the rest being excluded from beginninglessness, whence they must be born. Moreover, being born, they are shown not to possess from themselves what they are, nor to possess power from themselves, but to have received it. If they are not from themselves and use a granted power, how will they be called makers of all things, when they are manifestly creatures? [Note: [Col. 1298D] (1) A Hellenism.]

All this applies if all contribute to each individual thing. [Col. 1298B] But if not all do so, but individual gods rule individual things, and one does not use another’s creation, then the whole world would collapse, each drawing its own works to itself and defending them. Nor would we ourselves be allowed to use another’s creation; and how could living creatures live, each separated from the rest? But if, for the harmony of their goodness, they permit this, they themselves are weak, since they could not make their own being stand unless by means of another’s creation; [Note: [Col. 1298D] (2) Victorinus writes in this harsh fashion, by no means unlike his other writings. Understand: “could not bring their own essence into existence.”] nor do they themselves rule their own being, but only its use. But if use holds it, that god does not rule; from this he is recognized not to exist. [Note: [Col. 1298D] (3) Supply: *stare*, “to stand,” that is, “being” or “essence.”]

### VI

And the world itself refutes these people’s madness, showing its maker, ruler, governor, and administrator. For who, by sending rains upon what belongs to another, nourishes another’s things by his own operation? Who has joined together for usefulness all the harmful oppositions of the seasons by the interposition of temperateness? Who supplies the blasts of winds, for the sake of breathing, to the formations of things coming into being? God [Note: [Col. 1298D] (4) The manuscripts read “who?” for “God.”] is indeed recognized from all creation, as it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands.” Here is found the maker, ruler, governor, and administrator of all things.

Once he is recognized, some people, in perverse contention, not comprehending the order of things because of the weakness of their minds, and not even understanding that which they do not know, cunningly bring accusations against God. They say either that things ought not to have been made so as to fall, or that, because they fall, ignorance or malice must be attributed to him. For he made them in order that they might be; but if it happens that they are not, then either he did not know when making them what would happen, or, knowing it, he could not free them though he wished to do so, or, though able, he gave them over through malice. None of these alternatives is admissible concerning divinity. For it is not lawful to say that divinity did not know future things, that he was unable to free them though willing, or that malice should be attributed to him. He who willed and made is free from malice in neglecting, because the will to make excludes the malice of neglecting. When these charges are removed, they bring a third charge against God: incapacity. All these matters must be explained. For he is not evil who willed and made, [Col. 1299A] and who made because he willed. He who can do all things, or can do what he wills, is not weak. Nor is he subject to ignorance: since he always is, future things cannot come to be without him.

### VII

Let us now seek the cause of things, lest by prolonging the discussion we allow room for error to deceivers. He made all things in order that they might be: this we unquestionably confess. It happens that they are not: nor can we deny this. But contraries cannot exist in the same thing, so that both being and not-being should at once befall his will. For if he made them that they might be, he always wills that they be; and if he wills that they not be, he ceases to will what he willed—which defect cannot fall upon God.

But since two persons are involved in the question, maker and made thing, and since the maker is free from blame, it remains that the thing which was made is itself the cause of its own injury, and could not have fallen into non-being without some fault. Again, if the fault of the made thing nullified God’s will, then the fault itself is stronger than the maker. Therefore it is necessary that we be reborn, so that, coming to him as what we were, we may nullify what happened through fault; and so that God’s will—that we should be—may prevail. Hence, though condemned for fault, we are recalled, while God’s justice and power remain the same: his justice, in that he judges; his power, in that he recalls. He is not prevented from saving, who is able, from that which fell, to recall what he himself had made from nothing; and he who made from nothing will all the more recall from something. When the condemned person fell by God’s just judgment, so also by the utterance of his mercy he rises again. Nor is he excluded from recalling, who always is. His power obeys his will, and justice his power; and, as power accomplishes its work, it does what it wills at the time it wills—indeed, at the fitting time. The death of condemnation will not harm his power, nor does condemnation overcome the purpose of his will. But his mercy is not empty, nor is the grace of renewal without reason: for it is given to those who ask, just as they were condemned when they did not ask.

VIII. This was the reason why pardon was not granted to the first sinners: when, by his questioning, he summoned them to repentance and saw that they rejected their own salvation, he condemned them. But he had mercy on those born from them and on those who fled to him. For it is just that those who are willing and repentant, fleeing to him who can bestow aid, should obtain it; while the ungrateful and resistant, who cast the blame of their deed upon God and make themselves the cause of their condemnation, should be abandoned. Justice did not allow this grace to be given to the first-created humans; it was not that he who condemns was unwilling to grant it. He was the same before as he is now and will be: good now and good before; merciful now and merciful before; always abiding in himself, who is unchangeable. Since he condemned them because of fault, it is necessary to recognize the fault itself [Note: [Col. 1299D] (1) The manuscripts read *miscere* (“to mingle”), instead of *dinoscere* (“to recognize”).], rather than again inquire into physical explanations.

Man was made not in order to confer anything upon his Creator [Note: [Col. 1299D] (2) That is, he was not made in order to be useful to God, who needs no one.], but in order that he himself might possess the world. Formed from the better elements, he was rightly made rational; and the order of creation itself required this: since diverse things had been created in the world and constructed through the interaction of all the elements, this being, who is better than all the rest [Note: [Col. 1300D] (1) The manuscripts read “by all the rest.”], should have authority over the others. Yet he was not thereby to forget his Creator, but, subject through a command to his Lordship, was to hold the rest subject to himself.

The subjection of this rational being requires a law, lest he himself should be the god of all, free from law. Since reason demands such a law, it is necessary to see to what it should be applied. Reason teaches that the law should be imposed concerning those things which he enjoyed [Note: [Col. 1300D] (2) Thus the manuscripts.]. Since food is found to have been given at that time above all else, reason required that the law be given concerning this; and it is made clear that the sin concerned this.

IX. In investigating the cause, reason has brought us thus far. As we inquire what food it was, for what use, and in what manner the law was given [Note: [Col. 1300D] (3) Thus the manuscripts, instead of *caeterum*.], we need a history consonant with these physical explanations already investigated by us. Since there is no other history than that which we have learned in the divine Scriptures—and since these same physical explanations themselves lead us to it—let us ask whether it agrees with reason that a law was imposed on man to abstain from one tree while he freely enjoyed all the rest.

Scripture teaches that, after transgressing the command, he was punished with death. Some indeed accuse this severely, saying that a law was given which could not be kept; that he himself, foreknowing the future, gave the command because he knew they would not preserve it; that he commanded abstinence from food whose desirability would overcome the command. They also allege many other objections: either, they say, he ought not to have given a command which he gave knowing that they would not observe; or he ought not to have placed this tree there as an occasion for transgressing the command. He could have commanded concerning the other things, in which desire did not arise; or he could have given a precept which man was able to observe. If he could not preserve him by his aid from sinning, he was powerless; or else he ought not to have allowed the tempter to approach, by whose persuasion he fell into fault.

But now, they say, everything is contrary: by making him such, he made him liable to defeat; he planted a harmful tree; concerning this tree he gave a command which he knew they would not observe; foreseeing by his prescience that man would sin, he let him go; he did not restrain the adversary who approached to overthrow man; and, moved by anger, he himself condemned to death him whom he had appointed for life. Yet now you say that he came to liberate him and would suffer for him, though at that time he was unwilling to pardon. The inertia of their own minds advances such empty words; all of which must be answered.

X. We have already rightly proved that a law had to be given: he to whom so many things were subject had to be subject to God through a law. We teach that this law was not burdensome, as they say, but rather light and easily kept. For, while he enjoyed all things, he was commanded to abstain from one. If he had been commanded to use only one thing and had been forbidden all the rest, would it not seem just to you that he should keep the command of him who had granted permission to enjoy it? Yet he who gave the command did not do this—although this too is shown to be possible. Do we not [Note: [Col. 1301D] (1) The manuscripts read *aut non* (“or not”).] also in this world abstain from many things because of the danger of death or disease? Thus the command is shown to be possible. And if this is possible, how much more possible is it, for one enjoying everything, to restrain himself from one thing?

And how could a law have been given if authority to command is not allowed even in one matter? Therefore, because a law had to be given, and because it had to be given concerning the things which he enjoyed, it is rightly understood that it was given concerning these very things. Yet the tree was not an occasion of offence, nor should the command have concerned another tree rather than this one; for whichever tree had been made the subject of the command, desire would have attached itself to that very one. The tree was not the cause of desire [Note: [Col. 1301D] (2) The margin corrects this to “cause.”], but man himself was the author of it, because he chose to desire.

Let there therefore be no complaint now as to why he chose, since, being made rational, he had power over himself. The law itself requires that the person upon whom it is imposed should have this power over himself. A law is vain for one who has no power to act; and if a person is naturally constrained by someone else, and then seems to be restrained by that same person through an imposed law, the law is given less to the person not prohibited than to the ruler who has constrained himself. Therefore power over himself was fittingly given; and because man used this fittingly bestowed power in a matter over which he had no authority, he is justly condemned.

XI. By the Lord’s sentence, announced beforehand concerning transgression, he had also been given aid [Note: [Col. 1301D] (3) Let us note the teaching of the most ancient author Victorinus concerning the assisting grace of God.], so that he might know both what he ought to avoid and what he would suffer through negligence if he did not avoid it. Nor was his nature powerless. For when the serpent approached the woman in order to persuade her, the woman overcame it when she wished; and at the beginning of its speech she recognized it as a liar and repelled it, as Scripture says:

> And the serpent said to the woman: “What? Did God really say, ‘You shall not eat from every tree that is in paradise’?”

It believed it could deceive her by a lie, supposing her also to have forgotten the divine command. But she immediately drove it away by answering thus:

> And the woman said to the serpent: “We shall eat from every tree that is in paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of paradise, God said: ‘You shall not eat from it, nor touch it, lest you die.’”

Most wisely [Note: [Col. 1301D] (4) The marginal gloss reads “most wisely.”] preferring the divine command, she convicted it. It then turned to another device, saying:

> “You shall not die by death; for God knew that, on the day when you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

Then, seized by a desire for divinity [Note: [Col. 1301D] (5) The manuscripts read “more.”], she cast aside [Note: [Col. 1301D] (6) Namely, she cast aside.] what she had previously foreseen, now seeing through desire something other than what she had seen before. For then the woman said that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes. She saw from desire, not from the judgment of the mind, so that even before eating she pronounced it good for food. It was not the tree’s natural appearance or its usefulness that attracted her—although she had previously seen it and abstained—but the desire for divinity enticed her.

XII. Nor need one ask why he allowed Adam [Note: [Col. 1302D] (1) The discussion now concerns Adam.] to be tempted, when by foreknowledge he had protected him with his aid so that he would not be deceived. But Adam, forgetting his salvation and unmindful of God’s words, was deceived by preferring the woman’s persuasions. She certainly made her husband a participant in sin. Moreover, without questioning, her husband received and took it [Note: [Col. 1302D] (2) That is, he ate.]. For Scripture says: “She herself ate, and gave to her husband, and they ate.”

Thus the condemnation and the judgment of death were more justly imposed: though admonished, he had not observed the command; and when summoned to repentance, he not only rejected it but even imputed the fault of his deed to God, saying: “The woman whom you gave me, she gave it to me, and I ate.” He ascribed the sin to the Lord of all things because he had given the woman. Yet he knew that she was a very small portion of his own body, to whom he himself had given a name; he ought not to have been subject to her, knowing that she was subject to him in every respect, and recognizing himself as author of her body, origin, procreation, and even her very name. Since he ought not to have preferred her to himself, still less ought he to have preferred her [Note: [Col. 1302D] (3) Namely, Eve, who had been overcome. This is a Hellenism from ἐχομένη, “the following one.”] to the Lord God who had given the command. One sentence was pronounced for so many offences.

Yet he did not judge when moved by anger, as they say. This defect cannot be attributed to God [Note: [Col. 1302D] (4) That is, insofar as anger is a defect. For Lactantius’s teaching on this matter, see his treatise *On the Anger of God*.], so as to make him appear subject to passions, as though, stirred by anger, he imposed the condition of death. Anger moves one who pronounces sentence because he has been provoked by sin; but one who proclaimed the judgment of the deed before the offence cannot be called angry when he warned. Admonition is not anger, but protection.

XIII. Next, let us consider what sentence he gave in the event itself. By condemning the one who ate, God judged that he should not become eternal, as God himself is—the very thing man had imagined would happen. Since all food serves to strengthen the substance, this food instead served to dissolve the substance. Thus he neither foretold with hostility when he warned, nor afterward condemned in anger, by dissolving what man had presumptuously sought.

Nor did envy prohibit him from eating, nor did envy take divinity away by forbidding food that harmed him. For one who could not preserve himself from evil ought not to know evil. Knowledge of evil arose from transgression of the command; and he would not have fallen into this if he had not chosen to eat. By following the Lord without discrimination, he found good itself; by passing over the command, becoming conscious to himself, he knew evil. Therefore, simply to follow the command is good; to pass beyond it by desiring more is shown to be evil. For by distrusting the Lord’s words, he passed over the precept. The knowledge of good and evil had already begun, as he reflected upon what he had done. The command freed him from this entanglement [Note: [Col. 1302D] (5) The manuscripts read “this.”].

Thus, reason showing him the matter, conscious of his own evil, he fled. From the highest wisdom he was reduced to such folly that he imagined he could hide beneath a tree from God, the Creator of all, to whom the leaves of all trees and the blades of grass are numbered, and who said of us that even our hairs are numbered. Into so great an evil did he fall who began to have knowledge of evil and good! From so great an evil God was freeing him at the very time when he prohibited him.

XIV. Now that it has been made clear that he did not prohibit eating through envy, it remains to show that he did not take divinity away through envy. This is easily demonstrated, because we show that it was restored. From the beginning of creation until the condemnation of death, we have recognized that God did everything rightly. Yet man’s deed seems to have excluded God’s purpose: for he made them in order that they might exist, but through fault it happened that they would not exist. If matters stood thus, so that they should not exist, the purpose of him who made them would have been defeated. But if there is a return, sin is overcome through restoration, and the thing is restored to that for which it was made, so that the Lord may overcome man’s deeds and not be overcome.

His power also requires this, so that he may be shown omnipotent. For if there is anything that he could not do, the diminution of his power excludes omnipotence; but omnipotence prevails over all things, and, if it prevails over all things, it must prevail even in this: that he who made from nothing should restore from death.

XV. Therefore we had to return to what we had been. But let us ask how. That first ungrateful man was condemned because, when summoned to repentance, he did not obey. Yet after the sentence he lived for some time, because by his presence God provided that righteous persons should be begotten from those same people; nor was it just immediately to destroy what had the hope of producing righteous persons. Those who are born righteous show that it was not nature but will that sinned, since, established from the same parents [Note: [Col. 1303D] (2) The older manuscript reads *iisdem* instead of *isdem*.], they themselves keep the commandments. Will is not a part of natural substance but a movement—a movement, however, that in some way joins as an indicator [Note: [Col. 1303D] (3) The manuscripts appear to read *judex*, “judge.”] of thoughts [Note: [Col. 1303D] (4) Thus exactly the manuscripts.].

These righteous persons of whom we have spoken were the same as their parents in nature but unlike them in character, through repentance. Justice requires that the unrepentant be passed by and the repentant pardoned. The order of repentance proceeds so that it has an effect by which, pleasing God and hoping in his power, one asks for grace. The petition calls upon its Creator for absolution [Note: [Col. 1303D] (5) The manuscripts read “in absolution.”], and it follows no one else as the giver of restoration but him who made it. For if he himself made them to exist, but it came about that they did not exist, the one who repairs them unto eternity would be better than the one who made what fell away.

Therefore it belongs [Note: [Col. 1303D] (6) That is, it is fitting.] to God the Creator himself to renew; and he who made from nothing also restores from death. He is invoked to grant this, and is about to teach how the grace to be granted may be preserved, lest so great a gift be lost. Again, this is so that the person who perceives himself to have been liberated by the present sentence, just as he had previously been condemned, may differ in conduct; and by this conduct, imitating God, may come to divinity. Thus he may receive from God that very divinity which he previously thought he had usurped for himself through the tree, without God:

> “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’; but you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.”

He who laments that they lost what he said is thereby shown not previously to have taken divinity away through envy; and he who lamented came, when asked, to grant precisely what we lost—by showing himself, speaking, giving, and restoring.

XVI. Yet some are offended that he came in a body. But he could not otherwise have been seen by human beings than in a body, nor could they see their own preservation except in a body. Indeed, he ought not to have liberated them from the condemnation of death otherwise than in a body, so that he might show that this very thing had been freed which had perished [Note: [Col. 1304D] (1) The manuscripts read *ipsud*.]. But let us see how.

The first woman sinned, and she sinned while a virgin. This caused all subsequently born persons to be mortal. For the virgin received the sentence, and, having thereby been made mortal, produced other mortals. Through this virgin death reigned. Therefore he who would give life had to come through a virgin. The occasion of death entered through wood, but the woman came from the side of the man. Hence the Lord’s side is struck by wood, so that he might suffer also for the woman. The woman was not the whole side, but a portion of the side; for she was built from one of the ribs. Therefore not the whole side is opened, but the very place of the side from which she was taken is pierced. The earth produced thorns and thistles through the sentence of condemnation; therefore he is crowned with thorns and thistles. The substance of thorns is a curse. The crown was the form of victory; thus, by passing through the very things through which sin began, the Lord triumphed.

XVII. To those who consider human things, it appears impossible that what is said should be so: that he who had to be born is proclaimed to have been born from a virgin contrary to nature. Human reason cannot admit that, unlike all others, he should be thus born and be a son from a mother without a father. Yet this especially befitted him: he who has a heavenly Father should not have an earthly father. Nor had he come to deny his own Father by being born from another; rather, because something was lacking in the nature of the one giving birth [Note: [Col. 1304D] (2) The manuscripts read *gignantis* here and below.], his mother was to be a virgin. The begetter of all ought not to have been bound under this condition of our generation, since even the first parents were not generated by sexual intercourse.

There are also many kinds of beings in the world that secretly generate in many ways without mating. Moreover, the rationale of conception, to one who considers it chastely, is possible. He who is holy is proclaimed to have been born from the Holy Spirit: nothing is incredible in this. Yet his holiness seems to be defiled by mixture, although there was no mixture. For when the virgin asked and inquired into the cause of conception, the angel Gabriel said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.” He did not name a mixture of the two; rather, by the coming of the Spirit and the power of the Most High, nature is coagulated, so that what seed accomplishes in others, being joined in a holier manner befitting God, might be born through the undefiled body of the virgin.

XVIII. This is not incredible, since we know that many things in the world itself are thus congealed. When the Jews crossed the sea, the sea, struck by the rod, was indeed forcibly divided; yet the wind, the spirit of the world, compressed the waves, as Scripture shows when it says:

> “Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the Lord brought the sea in a strong south wind throughout the whole night, and made the sea dry.”

It was not emptied of water, but compressed. For it says: “And the water was divided; and the children of Israel entered through the midst of the sea on dry ground; and the water was a wall to them on the right and on the left.” Thus what was effected by the south wind is taught to have been compressed.

Moreover, the psalm-writing prophet David, interpreting this very sign, says:

> “He broke open the sea and brought them through; he made the waters stand like a wineskin.”

And if anyone, through the weakness of his own mind, hardening his heart, does not believe these proofs, let him observe the force of the winds and understand that the atmospheric currents accomplish this very thing: they so compress falling rains into drops that they freeze in their descent. Why need we enumerate the other things that, composed of moisture, are solidified by the force mentioned above? Nor need we linger long, since the effects of things cry out more loudly than our assertions. Since these things occur in nature under God’s ordering, how much more, in his advent so necessary for the fashioning of the body he was to assume, could the body of the virgin, from which a flow was expected, be compressed through the Holy Spirit?

XIX. What seems unclean to some is, to those who consider rightly, proved clean. Before the body’s flow, while it is still a part of the body, mixed and concreted with the whole, it does not receive the name “unclean” while it lives. But when it has flowed out and has become dead from that body, then it is unclean and dead, because it is now alien from nature and cannot be vivified. While it remains in nature, it generates what is compacted and coagulated, not what is unclean. Thus truth finds that this was not unclean.

Even if we allow those who call it unclean, still it is made clear that holiness could not be contaminated by what is unclean. We see the sun—which we cannot deny to be his creature—draw foul filth, marshy cesspools, and decaying mud upward to itself; yet, though it sends forth its power through its rays over these things, it is not polluted. If a creature is not polluted by such filth, much less is divinity itself polluted in a living, holy body [Note: [Col. 1305D] (3) The manuscripts read “more.”] [Note: [Col. 1305D] (4) Thus the manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 1305D] (5) The manuscripts read *que*.].

XX. Now that the necessary [Note: [Col. 1305D] (6) The manuscripts read *necessaria*.] holy and undefiled birth through bodily form has been shown—a form in which the logic of our salvation required him to be present—it remains to prove why, in likeness to us, he was born a little child, grew, hungered, ate, thirsted, and undertook the other functions of the body, so that he suffered even death, and so shameful a death; after which death, though this is incredible to opponents, he is said to have been buried and to have risen.

Certainly, since the savior of flesh came in flesh, it is manifest that he ought to assume our flesh, not another’s; for if another flesh had been assumed, salvation would not concern us. Having assumed our flesh, he had to be born as a little child from a virgin. A fully grown man ought not to be born through a virgin; this is so taught. He would have been said to have been born, but his birth would not have been proved. For how could a fully grown man be born through a virgin? Thus, if you do not believe him born as a little child, you would still less believe that a grown man had been brought forth.

XXI. Let us nevertheless recognize how divine was his infancy. He was conceived as a human being, but without the origin of human seed. He was born like a human being, but from a virgin, which is holy. He was lowly and uncomely, but glorious: by nature an infant laid in a cradle, yet proclaimed by angels as King and Son of God, Savior of the human race, uniter of heaven and earth in glory, and maker of peace. The shepherds are taught this most explicitly. For it is written thus:

> It happened, while they were there—namely in Bethlehem—that her days were fulfilled, that is, Mary’s days, for her to give birth; and she bore her firstborn son, wrapped him, and laid him in a manger, because there was no room in the inn. Now shepherds were in that region, keeping watch through the night and guarding their flocks. And an angel of the Lord stood by them, and radiance shone around them; and they feared with great fear. And the angel said to them: “Do not fear; for behold, I announce to you great joy, which is for all the people: because today there has been born to you a savior, who is Christ Jesus, in the city of David. And this shall be a sign for you: you shall find an infant wrapped in swaddling-clothes and lying in a manger.” And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will.”

One angel announces the birth: that this one, who was a little child, was born before the world but is born for us today, because it was then that he began to exist for human beings. And lest he appear to have been announced as King only of those to whom “today there has been born to you” was said, the host of angels gathers and says: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will.” His glory appeared in heaven, and peace on earth to people of good will is announced by angels. Do you see whether or not he appears similar to our infancy? [Note: [Col. 1306D] (1) The manuscripts read “or.”]

XXII. Is it surprising that angels announced as King one whom the Magi also knew while dwelling in a distant land? When a sign from heaven appeared to them, they understood that he had been born; they found him after seeking long, and, having found him, they worshipped him. The sign of his star surpassed the marks of all other stars. For the star that indicated the Lord’s birth did not shine in darkness like the others, but shone by day in the sun, surpassing both sun and day in splendor. It was not fixed in heaven like other stars; rather, in a marvelous appearance it went before those journeying to seek the Lord, showing them the way on their journey.
