Finally, it stood above the house where it showed that the one it announced was.

Scripture testifies:

> Now when Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the east to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east and have come to worship him.”

When the Magi saw the little child, they worshipped him as King, as human being, and as God; and they offered gifts, by which also his future suffering was signified. For they offered incense as to God, gold as to a king, and myrrh to one who would suffer. Such was the divine infancy that is recognized, nourished, and brought up—yet knowing all things without a teacher. The Jews marvelled at this when they saw him knowing letters without instruction, saying: “How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?” They acknowledged that he knew, and did not deny that he had not learned, but did not understand from where he had this knowledge.

When he speaks with the teachers of the Jews, he is found to be the teacher of teachers. While still almost twelve years old, sitting in the midst of the teachers, the teachers marvelled with astonishment at his teaching. For Scripture says: “And all who heard him marvelled at his understanding and his answers.” These things are proved from the Scriptures, and are further discovered through physical reasoning: for God, born in a human being, ought to have displayed such marks of his infancy.

XXIII. But if you ask the reason for his advent, a human being had to appear again. So great a divinity had to remain hidden, not from those who believed [Note: [Col. 1307D] (1) The manuscripts read “believe.”], but from the prince of the world, for whose overthrow [Note: [Col. 1307D] (2) The manuscripts read “overthrow.”] he had descended, and this for the sake of our liberation. For that prince held mankind not by his own authority but by the Lord’s sentence, because God had commanded the sinner who did not repent to die. Yet the merciful one ought to free the repentant. Justice and divine power required this: if the one who held the guilty person by sentence should seize one who was not guilty, he would lose his power by passing beyond the sentence.

No one is without guilt, since all are descended by origin and birth from mortals. But he who was born was proved to be the one who had pronounced the sentence; and he himself is not held guilty under that sentence, because, though he assumed flesh, he lived among human beings without sin. As it is written:

> “This is our God, and no other shall be counted beside him. He found every way of understanding and gave it to Jacob his servant. After this he was seen upon earth and lived among human beings.”

[Note: [Col. 1307D] (3) Baruch 3:36 ff. And let us note our Victorinus’s most ancient authority for the divine prophecy of Baruch.]

This is he who lived without sin, as it is again written:

> “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

[Note: [Col. 1307D] (4) 1 Peter 2:22.]

He produced this sinless flesh. The prince of this world foresaw it as opposed to himself and not inclined to his desires; yet, considering him merely human, he dared to assail him when he permitted it. The Lord permitted this so that the prince himself might be the cause of losing his power. Having claimed the guilty as his own by sentence, when he usurped this one who was not guilty, he acted contrary to the sentence by which [Note: [Col. 1308D] (1) The manuscripts read “through which.”] he held them and thereby lost [Note: [Col. 1308D] (2) The manuscripts read “admitted.”] his power.

Thus it was reasonable for him to perform the functions of the body: he showed that the flesh he had assumed was the same flesh that had previously been condemned; but the other, seeing the body’s functions, did not understand the divinity and thus, acting contrary to God’s sentence, lost his power, because he dared to attack one whom he perceived to be without fault.

XXIV. For this reason, then, he displayed the functions of flesh without being subject to those functions themselves. To prove that his flesh was real, he hungered; not because fasting overcame him and he had to eat. Thus, after fasting for forty days and forty nights—beyond the capacity of nature, in order to prove our flesh—he is indeed found to have hungered, but not to have eaten. Scripture says: “And when forty days and forty nights had been completed, afterward he hungered.” Yet he did not eat, though he hungered.

This plainly happened [Note: [Col. 1308D] (3) The manuscripts read *ad* instead of *ob*.] for this reason: during the forty continuous days in the wilderness, in which the devil, fighting against the Lord with his temptations, had been overcome, he had not begun to eat [Note: [Col. 1308D] (4) That is, he had not begun to take food.]; and, lest the devil should flee on recognizing God, lest the benefits of his passion, so necessary, should perish, he hungered. Thinking him weak, the devil immediately attacked him again as a human being, telling him, if only because of the need of his body, to turn stones into bread; but he neither did this nor ate [Note: [Col. 1308D] (5) I would prefer “who indeed.”]. Thus he hungered for a reason, yet was not subject to that reason.

And not only there: when the disciples offered bread to him while he was hungry and said, “Rabbi, eat,” he answered: “I have food to eat which you do not know. My food is to do the will of him who sent me, that I may complete his work.”

XXV. He thirsted in order to demonstrate the nature of the body, not because he needed drinks, since he himself is the fountain of living water. Thus, when he is found thirsty with the Samaritan woman, after he had asked for water and she, regarding him as a Jew, had not given it, he offered the woman water by which she might permanently satisfy thirst. As it is written:

> Jesus was sitting beside the well, and it was about the sixth hour; and a certain Samaritan woman came to draw water. And Jesus, sitting there, said to her: “Give me a drink.” For his disciples had gone into the city to buy food. But the woman answered Jesus, saying: “How do you, being a Jew, ask a drink of me, who am a Samaritan woman?” And Jesus answered her: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who said to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would rather have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” And the woman said to him: “Lord, you have no bucket, and the well is deep; from where do you have living water to give me? Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well, from which he drank with his sons and his cattle?” And Jesus answered her: “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water which I shall give him will never thirst; rather, it will become a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.”

Therefore, he did not thirst in order to receive, but in order to give—he who gave by promising divine [Note: [Col. 1309C] (1) Either understand “water,” or read *divina*, “divine.”] water. Thus the woman, leaving her water-jar behind and forgetting her former thirst, proclaimed his advent to the other Samaritans of Samaria. The Lord thirsted to teach the woman, whom he already knew to be ready; he did not seek earthly water, but through his request gave living water, which made a fountain springing up into eternal life.

XXVI. Jesus thirsted again upon the cross and cried, “I thirst.” But this was the reason for his thirst. They had crucified him, yet were not thereby satisfied: they still had sins to commit. Even to evil persons under punishment, compassion is due through the common feeling of human nature; but toward him whose benefits they had experienced in healing infirmities, whom they had attacked despite his innocence, they hurled insults even after the cross, contrary to the natural impulse of mercy. They were so filled with a spirit of rage that they gave vinegar to one who thirsted.

He who willingly undertook the passion did not receive even this unwillingly. As they were more audacious in inflicting punishments, so he was gentler in suffering injury. Seeing that the works of their malice were not yet complete, he cried, “I thirst.” They gave vinegar to add to the injury. Yet he did not provoke them to offer vinegar; he voluntarily received what they gave him. Such was the Lord’s thirst. Finally, after receiving it, he cried: “It is finished.” And immediately he gave up the spirit.

Jesus also slept, not as though overcome by sleep, but so that there might be an order for the miracle to be performed. He slept so that the sea might be stirred, so that the frightened disciples might ask for help, and so that David’s prophecy, uttered in the one hundred and sixth psalm, might be fulfilled:

> “Let his works be proclaimed in exultation. Those who go down to the sea in ships, who conduct business in great waters, these saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep. He spoke, and the spirit of his power stood fast, and its waves were lifted up.”

But that he completed the entire dispensation by conducting it thus through death, and was about to ascend into heaven, David immediately adds: “They ascend as far as the heavens and descend as far as the depths.”

XXVII. Although this must be believed because it was spoken by the divine Spirit, let us nevertheless, as with the rest, confirm it also by a few physical explanations [Note: [Col. 1310C] (2) The manuscripts read “we confirm.”]. Having freed us from death by the Lord’s passion, he brought us again to the state of immortality; and, though formerly unequal to heavenly beings, he has now joined us to them.

Yet this seems unjust to some—not because God cannot do it, but because it seems not to accord with his justice. They say that, when the first-created man was still free from fault and untouched by sin, God had made him merely lord of paradise, judging that gift of God appropriate; but now, after sin and offence, when man has been restored, it was not enough to return him to what he had been, but God also granted him the heavenly kingdoms. Yet this is shown to be altogether just.

For if at first, by his grace, when man had earned nothing through acts of devotion, he granted him a dwelling in paradise, then surely now, when he struggles against the infirmity of the flesh and the desires of iniquity already aroused, against the prince of the world and his powers, trampling down the world, a heavenly reward had to be rendered. Thus the one who, in imitation of God, lived a divine life on earth while established in a body, might dwell in heaven with that same body now made immortal, earthly things having been removed.

Further, for the reason of this gift, it is fitting to bring human flesh into heaven, since God deigned to be its inhabitant. Nor can a human being be regarded as made an inhabitant of heaven contrary to merit, when the Spirit, God himself, did not disdain to take his body as a sheath. It was just that the body in which God, by dwelling in it, deigned to visit the earth—and through which, becoming a participant in our condition, he brought our race to immortality—should also be placed in heaven. For where ought God’s dwelling to be, except in the kingdom of God? And where is his kingdom except in heaven?

ANNO DOMINI CCCLVI–CCCLVII. OSIUS, BISHOP OF CÓRDOBA.

[Col. 1309]

PROLEGOMENA.

[Col. 1309]

## Historical Notice Concerning Hosius, Bishop of Corduba

*(From Galland, Prolegomena, chapter X.)*

[Col. 1309C] We know that Hosius, a Spaniard by birth, governed the church of Corduba in the province of Baetica for almost seventy years. The encomia of Hosius found among the ancients are nearly countless. Eusebius [Note: [Col. 1309C] (1) Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book III, chapter 7.] says: [Col. 1310C] “He was a man celebrated in the speech of all,” ὁ πάνυ βοώμενος, “the man much spoken of.” Nor does Theodoret speak differently [Note: [Col. 1310C] (2) Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 15.], calling him “the old man by far most illustrious of all,” πάντων [Col. 1311A] μάλιστα περιφανὴς ὁ γέρων, and thus “worthy of honor and reverence both because of the prerogative of his age, because of his confession of faith, and because of the many and great labors he had undergone.” In the same sense, the fathers of the Council of Sardica [Note: [Col. 1311D] (2) In Hilary, *Fragments*, II, §2.] proclaim Hosius to be “of most venerable old age, who, both because of his age and confession, and because of his faith proved over so long a time, has borne, at that age, so great a labor for the benefit of the Church that he is to be considered most worthy of every reverence.”

But, to include everything, let us hear Athanasius [Note: [Col. 1311D] (3) Athanasius, *Apology concerning His Flight*, §5, works, vol. I, p. 322.]:

> “It would be superfluous to speak of the great man, the man of blessed old age, and confessor—Hosius, indeed.... For he is no obscure old man, but the most illustrious of all. What council has there been over which he did not preside? When did he not, by his wise sayings, bring all men over to his own judgment? What church does not preserve most beautiful memorials of his protection? Who came to him sorrowful and did not leave him joyful? Who asked anything of him in need and did not depart having obtained what he desired?”

Thus far Athanasius, whose distinguished words Theodoret copied out [Note: [Col. 1311D] (4) Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 15.].

Moreover, among these statements of Athanasius, the point which above all deserves notice, as Baronius observes [Note: [Col. 1311D] (5) Baronius, under the year 305, §§19–20.], is that this great Hosius, on account of his singular excellence in learning and virtues, and his admirable skill and prudence in conducting affairs, occupied, in the famous Council of Nicaea above all others, the first seat in the name of Pope Sylvester, among the many councils over which he is said to have presided; and that he was the foremost of the colleagues serving as legates, as we learn from Gelasius [Note: [Col. 1311D] (6) Gelasius of Cyzicus, *History of the Council of Nicaea*, book II, chapter 5.]:

> “That Hosius from Spain, distinguished by the renown of his name and reputation, holding the place of Sylvester, bishop of greatest Rome,” ἐπέχων καὶ τὸν τόπον τοῦ τῆς μεγίστης Ῥώμης ἐπισκόπου Σιλβέστρου, “also holding the place of Sylvester, bishop of greatest Rome,” [Col. 1311C] “sat in that assembly together with the Roman presbyters Vitus and Vincentius and very many others.”

Other writers, Greek as well as Latin, agree with Gelasius. Indeed, does not Eusebius, much earlier than Gelasius, also assert this rather plainly? [Note: [Col. 1311D] (7) Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book III, chapter 7.] For Theodoret [Note: [Col. 1311D] (8) Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 7.], Socrates [Note: [Col. 1311D] (9) Socrates, book I, chapter 8.], and Sozomen [Note: [Col. 1311D] (10) Sozomen, book I, chapter 17.] understood the sense of his words in no other way. From these sources one may understand what should be thought of Cave’s judgment [Note: [Col. 1311D] (11) Cave, *Historia Litteraria*, under the year 316, vol. I, p. 185.], who rather cheaply calls the claim that Hosius was honored as legate of the Roman pontiff “an empty dream of Baronius and others.” The exceedingly critical man, no doubt, preferred the pseudo-Dexter chronicle and its commentator Bivarius to the authority of the ancient writers. Basnage too makes use, once and again, of this same pseudo-chronicle with no dissimilar skill [Note: [Col. 1311D] (12) Basnage, on Prosper’s Chronicle, vol. I; *Thesaurus Canisianus*, p. 292 ff.]. But let us return to Hosius.

[Col. 1312A] II. The Arians, therefore, made every effort before Constantius to draw such a great man, especially conspicuous for the glory of his confession, over to their opinion [Note: [Col. 1312D] (1) Athanasius, *History of the Arians*, §42 ff., works, vol. I, pp. 368–369.]. The emperor, caught by their deceits and artifices, summoned that venerable and distinguished old man, more than a hundred years old. When Hosius came, Constantius asked him and urged him with gentle words to communicate with the Arians and condemn Athanasius. But that excellent old man, who could scarcely endure even hearing of such a thing, indignantly reproved the emperor for having dared to utter anything of the kind, and so struck him by his words that he turned him from his purpose. Thus, with matters still unchanged, Hosius returned to his homeland and his church.

But scarcely had he departed when, behold, the Arians renewed their complaints, revived their lamentations, and unceasingly assailed the very fickle mind of Constantius with every sort of contrivance. Accordingly, yielding to their demands, he sent Hosius letters full of threats; reviling him, he threatened dangers, deportation, and punishments; then, in repeated letters, he gently sought to move the old man’s mind. But Hosius, moved not even in the slightest either by fear of shameless evils or by the enticements of flattery, remained firm in his resolution. Indeed, he wrote back to the emperor a letter full of steadfastness and truly worthy of so great a bishop, declaring that long before, under Maximian, he had suffered for Christ’s name, and that he was ready, when necessary, to endure any hardships for the truth. We reproduce this sole surviving letter [Col. 1312C] from the great Athanasius: it is plainly a splendid monument of Hosius’s faith [Note: [Col. 1312D] (2) Athanasius, ibid., §44, p. 370 ff.].

III. Yet Constantius, continually intent upon forcing Hosius from his firm purpose, kept the old man away from his homeland at Sirmium for a whole year [Note: [Col. 1312D] (3) Athanasius, ibid., §75, p. 372.]. He dared to afflict him not only with exile but also with insults, beatings, and blows [Note: [Col. 1312D] (4) Athanasius, *Apology concerning His Flight*, §5, p. 322.], fearing neither God nor, impious man that he was, respecting either the gray hair or the dignity of the man. At length, overwhelmed by these miseries, being an old man and physically weak, Hosius yielded to the Arians for a time, εἶξεν αὐτοῖς πρὸς ὥραν, “he gave way to them for an hour”; [Note: [Col. 1312D] (5) Athanasius, ibid.] and he was brought to enter into communion with Ursacius and Valens, though he never cast his vote against Athanasius.

But the old man did not at all neglect his lapse. “For when death was imminent,” Athanasius testifies [Col. 1312D] [Note: [Col. 1312D] (6) Athanasius, *History of the Arians*, §45, p. 372.], “as though making a testament, he declared the violence done to him, anathematized the Arian heresy, and commanded that no one should accept it.” Μέλλων γὰρ ἀποθνήσκειν ὥσπερ διατιθέμενος ἐμαρτύρατο τὴν βίαν, καὶ τὴν Ἀρειανὴν αἵρεσιν ἀνεθεμάτιζε, καὶ παρήγγελλε μηδένα ταύτην ἀποδέχεσθαι: “For, being about to die, he testified to the violence done to him as though making a testament; he anathematized the Arian heresy and directed that no one accept it.” Augustine says no differently: he acknowledges that Hosius ended his last day in the communion of the Catholic Church [Col. 1313A] and at the same time defends him from the calumny of the Donatists [Note: [Col. 1313D] (1) Augustine, *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, book I, chapter 4, §7.].

Moreover, this “Abrahamic old man and great father of bishops,” as Athanasius calls him [Note: [Col. 1313D] (2) Athanasius, *History of the Arians*, §§45–46, pp. 371 and 373.], seems to have died, at the earliest, as the year 357 was ending. For it is established that Athanasius wrote his *History of the Arians to the Monks*, in which Hosius’s death is related, in the following year, 358, as the most learned Montfaucon [Note: [Col. 1313D] (3) Montfaucon, on Athanasius’s works, vol. VII, p. 340.] and Tillemont [Note: [Col. 1313D] (4) Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. I, p. 321.] report. Besides, his memory is commemorated in the Greek Menaea on 27 August. Would that Fassonius, most distinguished gentleman, might someday publish what he has stored in his notebooks: namely, material prepared to clear and defend Hosius, bishop of Corduba, from every stain of impiety, notwithstanding the protests of historians and all theologians, as we learn from Fassonius himself [Col. 1313B] [Note: [Col. 1313D] (5) Fassonius, *Dissertation on Greek Sacred Literature*, edit. §24, p. 35.].

## Judgments of Hosius Delivered at the Council of Sardica

*(Council, vol. II, col. 625.) (C)*

### Proem — History of the Council of Sardica

After the fathers of Nicaea—whose authority had been a shield of orthodox faith, a terror and grief to the impious, and a bond and repose for the churches—had nearly all been summoned from the bonds of the body to receive the rewards of their contests, the Arian heresy returned, as it were, by a criminal restoration after banishment. It began again to gather strength and to grow considerably stronger, under the leadership of Eusebius of Nicomedia, Theognis of Nicaea, Asterius the Sophist, Macedonius of Constantinople, Ursacius of Singidunum in Moesia, Valens of Mursa in Pannonia, and other Arian bishops of that sort [Col. 1313C] (Socrates, book I, chapter 18 ff., book II, chapter 2 ff.; Theodoret, book I, chapters 21, 26 ff., and book II, chapter 3; Sozomen, book II, chapter 20 ff.).

Relying upon the support both of Constantius—who, after the death of his father Constantine, ruled the entire East—and of many governors, who, surrounded by military forces, were a terror to all [Socrates, book II, chapter 2 ff.; Athanasius, *On the Synods*; Theodoret, book II, chapter 3 ff.; Sozomen, book III, chapter 1], they attempted secretly, through repeated councils, to assail the faith of the Nicene synod, which they did not dare openly to overthrow [Socrates, book II, chapter 7]. They strove to terrify Catholic pastors by threats, chains, confiscation of property, removals from office, and exile [Athanasius, *On the Synods* and *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*; Socrates and Theodoret, cited above]—above all Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. It would take long to recount how many snares they laid for him, the strongest champion of the Church and most vigorous defender of the divine *homoousion*, not only after Constantine’s death but even during his life.

When a council was convened at Tyre [Socrates, book I, chapter 21; Theodoret, book I, chapter 30; Sozomen, book II, chapter 24; Athanasius, *Second Apology*], they accused Athanasius of cutting off Arsenius’s hand for magical [Col. 1314A] practices. By this fraud, rejected by the emperor, and by other accusations, they obtained through a most shameless calumny that Athanasius be ordered into exile at Trier in Gaul, on the ground that he had forbidden Alexandrian grain to be transported to Constantinople [Socrates, book I, chapter 23; Theodoret, book I, chapter 31]. Then, after being restored to Alexandria by a letter of Constantine the Younger, he was again deprived of his episcopate by gross injustice at a gathering of ninety bishops in Antioch. Various charges were fabricated, especially that, having returned from exile without a common council of bishops, he had seized the church of Alexandria [Socrates, book II, chapter 2; Sozomen, book III, chapter 2; Socrates, book II, chapter 5; Sozomen, book III, chapter 5; Athanasius, *On the Synods*].

Athanasius [Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, *Second Apology*, and *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*; Socrates, book II, chapter 11; Sozomen, book II, chapter 7], together with Paul, who had been expelled from the see of Constantinople; Marcellus of Ancyra, then regarded as Catholic [Athanasius, *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life* and the letter of the Council of Sardica in his *Second Apology*]; Asclepas of Gaza; Lucius of Hadrianopolis; and the other bishops whom the Arians had expelled from their sees because of the orthodox faith, fled to the Roman Church, as mother of all churches and rock of the right faith, over which Pope Julius then presided.

To intimidate them, the Arians sent Julius letters from their Antiochene conventicle, feigning obedience and piety; and, referring the judgment of the whole matter to him, they requested that he convene another synod in which the truth might be examined more carefully [Athanasius, *Second Apology*; Theodoret, book II, chapter 4]. Julius convened one, and, sending the presbyters Elpidius and Philoxenus to the East, ordered them to appear at Rome on a specified day [Athanasius, *Second Apology* and *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*; Theodoret, book II, chapter 4]. But they were dismayed by this decree, seeing that Athanasius and his companions, as most steadfast defenders of the Nicene faith, had been admitted to Roman communion, and that the matter was to be decided in the city not by the hands of assassins in whom they trusted, but by the judgments of bishops. They first pleaded the disturbances of war, then the shortness of the appointed time [Athanasius, *Second Apology*]; and while they added delay upon delay and pretext upon pretext, a full year and six months passed.

Throughout this time Julius received various letters from Egypt [Socrates, book II, chapter 13; Sozomen, book III, chapter 9] and very weighty episcopal testimonies concerning Athanasius’s innocence. Having convened at Rome a council of fifty bishops [Athanasius, *Second Apology* and *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*], and openly rejected the charges falsely made against the Catholic bishops, he pronounced, with the entire synod approving, that Athanasius and his companions were free from every accusation and worthy to recover their churches [Col. 1314D].

The Arians bore this grievously [Socrates, book II, chapter 11; Sozomen, book III, chapter 7; Julius’s letter in Athanasius, *Second Apology*]. Returning again to the hiding places of the Antiochene assembly, they attacked both Athanasius and Julius, in letters full of insults, for usurping the power to annul what their synod had decreed. Since their audacity daily tended toward more serious disturbances, especially because, having promulgated two creeds against Nicaea, they were throwing everything into utter confusion [Athanasius, *On the Synods*; Socrates, book II, chapters 14–15; Sozomen, book III, chapters 9–10], Julius referred the affair to Constans in order to provide for these afflicted circumstances [Sozomen, book III, chapter 9; Theodoret, book II, chapter 5].

Constans wrote to his brother Constantius, ruler of the East, advising that a synod be assembled [Socrates, book II, chapter 16]. By the authority of the pontiff—for some Eastern bishops accused him regarding the shortness of the time appointed for the council [Athanasius, *Second Apology* and *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*]—and with the consent of the emperors [Socrates, book II, chapter 16; Sozomen, book III, chapter 11], a general synod was convened at Sardica, a city of Illyricum, in the consulship of Rufinus and Eusebius, the eleventh year after Constantine’s death [Athanasius, *Second Apology*; Theodoret, book II, chapter 7; Socrates, cited above]. About 280 bishops from the West and seventy-six from the East came there [Athanasius, *Second Apology*]. Hosius, Archidamus, and Philoxenus presided in Julius’s name [Athanasius, the same *Second Apology* and *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*; Socrates and Theodoret, cited above]. Athanasius too was present with his companions [Athanasius, cited passage], to answer the charges for which they had been summoned.

But the Easterners, full of Arius, understood that business would be transacted without Musonianus, Hesychius, and Castritius [Socrates, book II, chapter 16; Athanasius, *Second Apology*], by whose armed attendants they had been accustomed to trample the bishops’ freedom. Distrusting their cause and dismayed by the consciousness of their crimes, they openly refused to appear before the synod unless Athanasius and his companions were first removed from the way [Athanasius, *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life* and *Second Apology*]. Since the fathers at Sardica refused to decide this concerning innocent and most holy men, already received into Roman communion, and repeatedly urged the Arians to emerge from the palace in which they had shut themselves up [Athanasius, cited above], and prove the accusations they had brought against Athanasius—otherwise they themselves would be treated as defendants—the Arians, not daring to entrust their cause to such incorruptible judicial seats, secretly fled to Philippopolis in Thrace [Socrates, book II, chapter 16; Sozomen, book III, chapter 10].

There they published a new formula of faith, as though to supply what Nicaea lacked [Sozomen, book III, chapter 10]; condemned the *homoousion*; confirmed their decrees against Athanasius and his companions; and pronounced an anathema upon Julius, Hosius, and the other supporters of Athanasius, depriving them of the episcopal name [Augustine, book III, *Against Cresconius*, chapter 34, and Letter 263]. To give all this more authority and weight, they turned to the devices of heretics: as acts transacted at the Council of Sardica, whose name they abused, they sent these things in writing to Donatus [Letter of the Council of Sardica in Athanasius, *Second Apology*; Athanasius, *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*; Socrates, book II, chapter 16; Sozomen, book III, chapter 11], then a most bitter enemy of the Catholic Church in Africa, so as to unite him with their party. Yet this deception did not deceive the African fathers at all. For long afterwards, when the Donatists wished to misuse that council, convened by the Arians, in defense of their cause, Blessed Augustine immediately discovered from the most unjust condemnation of Julius and Athanasius, which was recited as though made in that council, that the work had issued from an Arian workshop.

[Col. 1316A] Moved by the disgracefulness of these acts and the singular shamelessness of these men [Letter of the Council of Sardica in Athanasius, *Second Apology*; Athanasius, *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*; Socrates, book II, chapter 16; Sozomen, book III, chapter 11], the fathers of Sardica proclaimed a most just anathema against them as deserters of their cause, accusers of all godly men, and adversaries of the orthodox faith. They removed Stephen of Antioch, Menophantus of Ephesus, Narcissus of Neroniadis, Theodore of Heraclea, Acacius of Caesarea, Ursacius, and Valens from the episcopal rank; above all Gregory, who had burst into the see of Alexandria surrounded by armed soldiers. They adorned Athanasius and his companions with honorable judicial sentences and decrees, and commanded them again to assume the governance of their churches.

They approved the *homoousion* and Nicene doctrine with most devout acclamations, as requiring no addition [Athanasius, *Letter to the Antiochenes*], but complete in every respect. They abolished and annulled as spurious and forged the schedule and new formula which their opponents had fabricated and issued in the synod’s name. Finally, they enacted twenty canons in Greek and Latin for the common benefit of the Church [Nicholas I, Letter XI to Photius; Dionysius Exiguus, preface to the canons]. They carefully set down in writing the order in which everything had been done: first to Julius, Roman pontiff [in Cresconius], and to the other bishops [in Athanasius, *Second Apology*], so that they might provide consolation and refuge for those unjustly harassed by the Arians; then to the Church of Alexandria, which had such great interest in knowing whatever concerned Athanasius’s case; and then to the Emperor Constans, who shortly afterward communicated by letter with his brother Constantius [Socrates, book II, chapter 18], asking that he order the churches to be restored to Athanasius and his companions, who had been expelled contrary to every principle of divine and human law. This was also what the holy synod requested, having sent to him Euphratas, bishop of Agrippina, and Vincentius, bishop of Capua [Athanasius, *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*]. Such was the outcome of the Council of Sardica.

Since nothing new concerning the faith was enacted in this synod, nor any new article of faith expounded [Athanasius, *Letter to the Antiochenes*], but only those things established and confirmed by new votes which the fathers had delivered at Nicaea, the Council of Sardica, though gathered from nearly the entire world, was always considered a part and appendix of the Nicene Council, since all its definitions concerning faith concerned the preservation of the Nicene decrees. Therefore, although this synod was distinct from Nicaea, yet because it did not undertake new questions of faith or of the Church, but only the defense and protection of Nicene faith, and—as the Council of Chalcedon says (Act XVI)—opposed the remnants of the Arians; and because the Sardican and Nicene fathers had one judgment, one mind, and one spirit, many include the Council of Sardica under the name of Nicaea, just as a city and the fortification of the city are customarily reckoned and named as one thing.

For this reason Innocent [Letter to Victricius, chapter 3] and Zosimus [Carthage VI, chapters 3 ff.] call the Sardican canons Nicene, as appears from the Sixth Council of Carthage. For the same reason Saint Gregory [book II, letter 10], Isidore [*Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 16], Bede [*On Time*, chapter 65], and other fathers, when they enumerate the first four councils, pass over Sardica in silence, though truly general, as included within Nicaea.

How great the authority of this synod is may be proved by many weighty arguments. First, it is shown to be general both by the great number of bishops who assembled there, as appears from Athanasius’s *Second Apology* and others who have given the number of the fathers; and because it was convened by the authority of Pope Julius [Socrates, book II, chapter 16], whose legates presided over it. To this is added the authority of the emperors Constans and Constantius, who made every effort to bring together bishops from nearly all provinces. There is, moreover, the testimony of Socrates and—what is more important—of Emperor Justinian, who in his edict concerning the Three Chapters writes:

> “Because certain of those who gathered in the holy Council of Nicaea and subscribed to the definition or creed of faith set forth by it [Note: [Col. 1317D] (1) Perhaps: ‘are found to think contrary things.’], were afterward found to hold opinions opposed to it, some while living and others after death were anathematized by Damasus, pope of holy memory of elder Rome, or by the universal Council of Sardica, as Saint Athanasius testifies.”

Thus Justinian. Since Julius himself, in his letter to the Alexandrians [in Athanasius, *Second Apology*], rejoices that his judgment concerning the restoration of Athanasius had been approved by the synod, it is clear that it was approved by him, especially since Hosius and the others wrote to him and requested him [Sozomen, book III, chapter 11; Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 12] to confirm the synod’s judgment by his authority. Thus, if all things are carefully considered, it will be established that this synod was general, since nothing belonging to a general council can be found lacking in it.

The Apostolic See also always held the Council of Sardica in honor: it placed the Sardican canons in the body of canons which it especially used in former times for deciding ecclesiastical controversies; and Leo IV, in his letter to the bishops of Britain, taught that disputes of the Church should be resolved through the canons of this council. Gratus, bishop of Carthage, likewise confirms this in the First Council of Carthage. His words are these: “I remember that it was decreed in the most holy Council of Sardica that no one should appropriate a person belonging to another people; but if he should happen to be necessary, he shall ask his colleague, and have him with his consent.” This was decreed at Sardica, canon 15. Nicholas I also settled the cause of Rhotad by the authority of this synod in Letter 4; and the letter to the clergy of Constantinople testifies that the Council of Sardica was received by the whole Church.

## Judgments, or Canons, of Hosius and of the Holy and Blessed Fathers Who Assembled at Sardica

*Translated by Gentian Hervetus.*  
[Note: [Col. 1318] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1317C] The holy synod assembled at Sardica from different provinces decreed the following.

### I

Hosius, bishop of the city of Corduba, said: An evil custom—or rather, a most pernicious corruption of affairs—must be utterly uprooted from its very foundations: no bishop should be permitted to transfer from a small city to another city. For the pretext that causes such attempts is obvious. No bishop has yet been found who has endeavored to move from a larger city to a smaller one. It is therefore clear that such men are inflamed by a burning desire to possess more, and serve pride more readily, so that they may appear to have greater power. Does it please all that such wickedness should be punished more severely? For I think that such persons ought not even to have lay communion.

All the bishops said: It pleases all.

[Greek text: “The holy synod assembled at Sardica from various provinces decreed the matters set forth below.”]

αʹ. Hosius, bishop of the city of Corduba, said: It is not so much evil custom as the most harmful corruption of affairs that must be uprooted from the very foundations, so that no bishop may be permitted to transfer from a small city to another city. For the pretext for this cause, through which such things are attempted, is evident. For no bishop has ever been found able to be one who has made haste to transfer from a greater city to a very small city. Hence it is established that such persons are inflamed by a fiery manner of covetousness and are more enslaved to arrogance, in order that they may seem to possess greater authority. If, therefore, this pleases all, so that such perversity may be punished more strictly? For I judge that such men ought not even to have lay communion.

All the bishops said: It pleases all.

### II

Hosius the bishop said: But if anyone should be found so mad or bold as to seem to offer some excuse concerning these things, alleging that letters have been brought to him by the people, it is clear that a few persons, corrupted by payment and reward, could stir up sedition in the Church, in order, supposedly, to demand that they have the same man as bishop. Therefore I judge that such frauds and schemes must altogether be punished, so that no such person may be considered worthy even at the end of lay communion. Answer, then, whether this judgment pleases you.

They answered: What has been said pleases us.

βʹ. Hosius the bishop said: If anyone should be found so mad or bold as to seem to bring some excuse concerning such matters, affirming that letters were brought to him from the multitude, it is evident that a few persons, corrupted by wages and price, have been able to create faction in the Church, as though demanding that they have the same man as bishop. I therefore judge that such knaveries and schemes must absolutely be punished, so that no such person should be deemed worthy even at the end of lay communion. If, therefore, this judgment pleases you, answer.

They answered: What has been said pleased us.

### III

Hosius the bishop said: This too must necessarily be added: no bishop shall cross from his own province into another province in which bishops are present, unless he is called by his own brothers, lest we seem to close the doors of charity. Likewise, provision must be made that, if in any province one bishop has a dispute against his brother and fellow bishop, neither of them [variant: “not one of the two”] may call bishops from another province as judges.

But if a bishop seems liable to condemnation in some case, and thinks that his cause is not bad but good, so that the judgment should be reopened, then, if it pleases your charity, let us honor the memory of the Apostle Peter: let those who gave judgment write to Julius, bishop of Rome, so that, through the bishops neighboring the province, the trial may, if necessary, be renewed, and that he himself may provide the judges. But if it cannot be proved that his case is such as to require a rehearing, let what has once been judged not be overturned, but let the judgment rendered stand.

γʹ. Hosius the bishop said: It is necessary to add this also: no bishop may pass from his own province into another province in which bishops are established, unless he is summoned by his own brothers, so that we may not appear to close the gates of love. Likewise, provision must be made that, if in some province one bishop has a matter against his brother and fellow bishop, neither may summon from another province bishops as adjudicators. But if a bishop seems to be condemned in some matter and supposes that his cause is not unsound but good, so that the judgment may be renewed, then, if it seems good to your charity, let us honor the memory of Peter the Apostle; and let those who judged write to Julius, bishop of Rome, so that, through the bishops neighboring the province, the tribunal may, if necessary, be renewed, and he may provide adjudicators. But if it cannot be established that his case is such as to require a rehearing, let matters once judged not be undone, but let what exists remain firm.

### IV

Hosius the bishop said: It has pleased us that, if a bishop is accused and the assembled bishops of the same region remove him from his rank, and he appeals, as it were, and takes refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, and wishes him to hear the case, and that bishop judges it right to renew the investigation, he should deign to write to the fellow bishops nearest the province, so that they may carefully and accurately investigate each point and render judgment concerning the matter in accordance with the assurance of truth.

But if anyone requests that his case be heard again and, in response to his petition, the bishop of Rome judges [variant: “is moved”] that presbyters should be sent from his own side, it shall be in that bishop’s power to determine whatever he finds proper. And should he decide that persons ought to be sent to judge together with the bishops, possessing the authority of the one by whom they have been sent, this too shall be established. But if he thinks that the examination of the matter and the bishop’s judgment are sufficient, he shall do whatever seems proper to his most prudent counsel.

The bishops answered: What has been said pleased us.

δʹ. Hosius the bishop said: It has pleased us that, if a bishop is accused, and the bishops assembled from the same district remove him from his rank, and he, as though making an appeal, flees to the most blessed bishop of the church of the Romans and wishes him to hear the case, and that bishop judges it right to renew the examination of his affair, he should deign to write to the fellow bishops nearest the province, so that they may investigate each matter diligently and accurately, and render a vote concerning the matter in accordance with the certainty of truth.

But if anyone asks that his case again be heard and, by his own petition, seems to move the bishop of the Romans [variant: “seems to decide that he should send”] presbyters from his own side, it shall be in the authority of that bishop whatever he judges proper and determines—perhaps [variant: “and even if”] that those judging with the bishops should be sent, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent; and this must be established. But if he judges the examination of the matter and the bishop’s decision sufficient, he shall do whatever seems proper to his most prudent counsel.

The bishops answered: What has been said pleased us.

### V

Hosius the bishop said: If it happens in one province, in which there are very many bishops, that one bishop remains absent and, through some negligence, refuses to come together and consent to the ordination and election of bishops, while the assembled multitude of people urges that the bishop whom they seek should be ordained, that absent bishop must first be reminded by letters from the primate of the province—that is, the metropolitan bishop—that the people request that a pastor be given to them. I think it proper that he also be awaited, so that he may be present. But if, having been requested by letter, he neither comes nor even writes back, the people’s wish should be satisfied.

Bishops from the neighboring province also must be summoned for the ordination of the metropolitan bishop. But it is not permitted simply to establish a bishop in any village or small town for which one presbyter is sufficient; for there is no need to establish a bishop there, lest the name and authority of bishop be held cheap. Rather, as I have said before, the bishops of the province must establish bishops in those cities where bishops have also previously existed. But if some city is found to have grown so populous that it is judged worthy of a bishopric, let it receive one.

Does this please all?

All answered: It pleases us.

εʹ. Hosius the bishop said: If it happens in one province, in which there are very many bishops, that one bishop remains behind, and he, through some negligence, refuses to assemble and consent to the appointment of bishops, while the assembled crowds ask that the appointment be made of the bishop they seek from them: first, that remaining bishop must be reminded by letters of the head of the province, namely the bishop of the metropolitan city, that the crowds request that a pastor be given them. I judge it proper to wait also for this bishop, so that he may appear. But if, when invited by letters, he does not appear and does not even reply, the desire of the multitude must be satisfied.

Bishops from the neighboring province must also be summoned for the appointment of the bishop of the metropolitan city. But it must not be permitted simply to appoint a bishop in a village or a small city where one presbyter alone is sufficient. For there is no need to appoint bishops there, lest the name and authority of bishop be depreciated. Rather, as I have said, the bishops of the province must appoint bishops in those cities where bishops had previously existed. But if some city is found to be increasing to such a great number of people that it is judged worthy even of a bishopric, let it receive one.

Does this please all?

All answered: It pleases us.

### VI

Hosius the bishop said: Our importunity, excessive persistence, and unjust petitions have caused us not to possess as much favor and freedom of speech as we ought to possess. For many bishops do not cease to go to the imperial court, especially Africans, who, as we have learned from our beloved brother and fellow bishop Gratus, do not accept salutary counsels but despise them so far as to bring, through one man, to the court many and various petitions that cannot benefit the churches. And instead of bringing aid and assistance, as should and ought to be done, to the poor, laypeople, or widows, they seek secular offices and public functions for certain persons. This perversity therefore brings us discredit, not without scandal and condemnation.

I thought it more fitting that a bishop should provide his help to one who suffers violence from someone; or if some widow is wronged; or if an orphan is deprived of what belongs to him—provided, indeed, that these persons have a just cause and petition. Therefore, beloved brothers, if this seems good to all, decree that no bishop ought to go to the imperial court except those summoned by letters of our devout emperor. But since it often happens that persons needing mercy flee to the Church, having been condemned for their sins either to confinement, deportation to an island, or any other sentence, assistance must not be denied such persons; rather, pardon must be sought for them without delay or hesitation.

Therefore, if this also pleases you, all of you give your vote together.

All answered: Let this also be decreed.

ϛʹ. Hosius the bishop said: Our untimeliness, our great persistence, and unjust requests have made us possess not as much favor and frankness as we ought to have. For many bishops do not cease from coming to the imperial court, especially the Africans. As we have learned from our beloved brother and fellow bishop Gratus, they do not accept wholesome counsels but despise them so greatly that they carry by one man to the court very many and diverse petitions, unable to benefit the churches; and instead of helping and assisting the poor, laypeople, or widows, as is required and fitting, they devise worldly dignities and offices for certain persons. This perversity, therefore, brings us ruin, not without some scandal and condemnation.

But I judged it more fitting that a bishop should provide his own assistance to one who is oppressed by someone; or if one of the widows is wronged; or again if some orphan is deprived of what belongs to him—if indeed these cases have a just petition. Therefore, beloved brothers, if this seems good to all, determine that no bishop should come to the imperial court except those whom our most devout emperor summons by his own letters. But since it often occurs that persons needing mercy flee to the Church, having been condemned for their sins to confinement or to an island, or delivered over by any kind of judgment, assistance must not be denied to such persons; rather, pardon must be requested for them without delay and without hesitation. If, therefore, this also pleases you, all vote together.

All answered: Let this also be decreed.

### VII

Hosius the bishop said: Let your prudence judge this also. Since it has been decided that no bishop should, by coming to the imperial court, incur condemnation, if any of them have petitions of the kind mentioned above, let them send them through their own deacon. For the person of a minister is not subject to envy, and whatever is granted can be conveyed more quickly.

All answered: Let this also be enacted.

ζʹ. Hosius the bishop said: Let your intelligence judge this too. Since it has been decided, in order that a bishop coming to the imperial court may not fall under some condemnation, that if any of them have petitions of the sort we mentioned above, they should send them through their own deacon. For the person of the servant is not liable to envy, and the things to be granted will be able to be conveyed more swiftly.

All answered: Let this also be decreed.

### VIII

Hosius the bishop said: I also judge this to follow: if bishops in any province send petitions to their brother and fellow bishop, the bishop who is in the larger city—that is, the metropolis—should himself send his minister and the petitions, furnishing him with letters of recommendation as well. He should also, accordingly, write to our brothers and fellow bishops who at that time reside in the places or cities in which the most devout emperor administers public affairs.

But if any bishop has friends at the court of the palace and wishes to obtain something honorable and just, he should not be prevented from making his request through his own minister and from instructing those friends to be willing to provide him with their good assistance. Those who go to Rome, however, as stated above, ought to present to our beloved brother and fellow bishop Julius the petitions which they have to submit, so that he may first examine whether any of them are improper, and then, granting his help and care, send them on to the imperial court.

All the bishops said that this pleased them and that this counsel was most fitting.

[Col. 1322D] **VIII.** Osius the bishop said: “I also think this is consequent: that, if bishops in any province send petitions to their brother and fellow-bishop, the bishop who is in the greater city—that is, the metropolis—should himself send both his deacon and the petitions, furnishing him also with letters of recommendation and, accordingly, writing likewise to our brothers and fellow-bishops, if any happen at that time to be residing in the places or cities [Col. 1323A] in which the most pious emperor administers public affairs. But if any bishop has friends at the court of the palace and wishes to make a request concerning something more fitting, he should not be prevented from making the request through his own deacon and instructing these persons to provide him, at his request, with their assistance. Those who come to Rome, as I have said before, ought to present to our beloved brother and fellow-bishop Julius the petitions which they have to submit, so that he may first examine whether any of them are shameless; and thus, providing his own protection and care, may send them to the imperial camp.” All the bishops replied that this pleased them and that this counsel was most fitting.

[Col. 1324A] **IX.** Osius the bishop said: “I also consider this necessary: that it should be examined with every care and diligence [Col. 1324B] whether any man from the forum—whether wealthy or trained in civil law—should be deemed worthy to become a bishop; and that he should not be appointed until he has performed the ministry of reader, deacon, and presbyter, so that at each rank, if judged worthy, he may be able to ascend by advancement to the height of the episcopate. The grade of every order must, plainly, have a duration of no small length, through which his faith, uprightness of conduct, steadfastness, and moderation may become known; and he himself, being judged worthy of the divine priesthood, may attain the greatest honor. For it is neither fitting, nor does learning or good conduct admit, that one should approach this office rashly and lightly, so that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon should be appointed readily and easily (1 Tim. III). For otherwise he would rightly be considered a novice (1 Tim. V), since the most blessed Apostle, who was also the teacher of the Gentiles, plainly appears to have forbidden hasty ordinations. For probation over a very long period can fittingly bring out both a man’s conduct and the character of each individual.” All said that this pleased them and that these provisions ought by no means to be overturned.

[Col. 1323A] **IX.** Osius the bishop said: “I also consider this necessary: that, with every exactness and care, it should be examined whether a wealthy man or a lawyer from the marketplace seeks to become a bishop; and that he should not be appointed before he has completed the service of reader and presbyter [the Greek text appears to omit “deacon”], so that at every rank, if he is judged worthy, he may by advancement be able to pass to the summit of the episcopate. The rank of each order must plainly have a duration of no very short time, through which his faith, excellence of character, steadfastness, and moderation may be recognized; and he himself, judged worthy of the divine priesthood, may enjoy the highest honor. For it is neither fitting, nor does knowledge or good conduct permit, to proceed to this rashly and lightly, so that one should appoint a bishop, presbyter, or deacon offhand. Nor would he rightly be regarded as a novice, especially since the most blessed Apostle, who became the teacher also of the Gentiles, appears to have forbidden appointments from being made hastily. For a probation of the longest time will be able fittingly to portray a man’s conduct and each person’s character.” All said that this pleased them, and that these things should not at all be overturned.

[Col. 1324C] **X.** Osius the bishop said: “We must also determine this: when a bishop has come from one city to another city, or from one province to another province, in pursuit of self-display and serving his own praises, or for the sake of religion, and wishes to stay there for a longer time, while the bishop of that city is not skilled in teaching, he must not despise him by preaching more frequently and striving to disgrace [Col. 1324D] and demean the person of the bishop—for this pretext commonly gives rise to disturbances—nor should he seek by such craftiness to win over and draw to himself another’s see, not hesitating to leave the church entrusted to him and move to another. A limit of time must therefore be determined for this. For refusing to receive a bishop has been judged inhumane and uncivil. Remember, moreover, that our fathers formerly decided that if a layman living in some city does not assemble on three Lord’s Days within three weeks, he should be removed from communion. If, therefore, this has been decreed concerning laymen, it is neither right nor fitting nor useful that a bishop, if he has no graver necessity or more difficult business, should remain away from his own church for too long [Col. 1325A] and grieve the people entrusted to him.” All the bishops said that this opinion too was most fitting.

[Col. 1323C] **X.** Osius the bishop said: “We must also determine this: that when a bishop comes from another city into another city, or from another province into another province, for the sake of display, attending to his own praises, or under the pretext of religious devotion, and wishes to remain for a longer time, while the bishop of that city is not skilled in teaching, he must not despise him, speaking more often and striving to shame and disparage the person of the bishop there. For this pretext is accustomed to cause disturbances. Nor should he, by such craftiness, endeavor to betroth to himself beforehand and draw away another’s see, without hesitation leaving the church entrusted to him and transferring himself to another. A period must therefore be fixed concerning this, since it has also been judged inhuman and rude not to receive a bishop. Remember, moreover, that in former times our fathers decided that if a layman living in a city did not assemble on three Lord’s Days in three weeks, he should be removed from communion. If, then, this has been decreed concerning laymen, a bishop ought not, nor is it fitting or beneficial, unless he has some graver necessity or difficult business, to remain away for the longest time from his own [Col. 1326A] church and grieve—or, according to another reading, leave—the people entrusted to him.” All the bishops said: “We determine that this opinion too is exceedingly fitting.”

[Col. 1325A] **XI.** Osius the bishop said: “Since nothing ought to be omitted, let this too be determined. Some brothers and fellow-bishops seem to possess very little private property in the cities in which they are appointed bishops; but in other places they have large estates, from which they are able also to assist the poor. I judge, therefore, that they should be permitted thus: if they are to go to their own estates and gather their produce, they may remain upon their estates for three Lord’s Days, that is, three weeks; and in the nearby church, in which a presbyter gathers the people, they should assemble and perform the divine offices, lest they appear to be without the assembly, [Col. 1325B] and they should not be present too frequently in the city in which there is a bishop. In this way their own affairs will suffer no loss from their absence, and they will appear to avoid the charge of arrogance and pride.” All the bishops said: “This provision also pleases us.”

[Col. 1326A] **XI.** Osius the bishop said: “Since nothing ought to be omitted, let this too be determined. Some of our brothers and fellow-bishops, in the cities in which they are appointed bishops, appear to possess very little private property; but in other places they have large estates, from which they are able to aid the poor. I judge, therefore, that they should be permitted to do this: if they are going to visit their own estates and gather their fruits, they may remain for three Lord’s Days—that is, three weeks—on their own estates; they should assemble and perform the liturgy in the neighboring church, in which a presbyter gathers the people, so that they may not appear to be apart from the assembly; [Col. 1326B] and they should not come too frequently to the city in which there is a bishop. In this way their private affairs will suffer no loss through their absence, and they will avoid the charge of boastfulness and vanity.” All the bishops said: “This ordinance too pleases us.”

[Col. 1325B] **XII.** Osius the bishop said: “Let this too please all: if a deacon, presbyter, or any member of the clergy has been excommunicated and flees to another bishop who knows him and knows that he has been removed from communion by his own bishop, that bishop ought not, by doing an injury to his brother bishop, to grant him communion. But if anyone dares to do this, let him know that, when the bishops meet, [Col. 1325C] he himself will have to answer the charge.” All the bishops said: “This judgment will preserve peace forever and safeguard the concord of all.”

[Col. 1326B] **XII.** Osius the bishop said: “Let this too please all: if a deacon, presbyter, or any cleric becomes excluded from communion and flees to another bishop who knows him, knowing that he has been removed from communion by his own bishop, that bishop must not, in insulting his brother, grant him communion. But if anyone dares to do this, let him know that, when the bishops have assembled, he makes himself liable to answer a charge.” All the bishops said: “This judgment will always preserve peace and maintain the concord of all.”

[Col. 1325C] **XIII.** Osius the bishop said: “I ought not to keep silent about what moves me in every respect. If any bishop is found prone to anger—which ought to be absent from such a man—and, being quickly provoked against a presbyter or deacon, wishes to cast him out of the church, provision must be made that the latter is not suddenly condemned and deprived of communion.” All the bishops said: “The person expelled shall have the right to flee to the bishop of the metropolis of the same province; or, if the metropolitan is absent, to have recourse to the neighboring bishop and request that his case be examined carefully. For those who make a request must not be denied a hearing. The bishop too who expelled him, rightly or wrongly, ought to bear it with equanimity that the matter be examined, so that his judgment may either be confirmed or corrected. Before every point has been diligently and faithfully examined, however, the person who lacks communion ought not, before the case has been heard, to claim communion for himself. If some clerics assemble and perceive his pride and arrogance, because it is not fitting to endure insult or unjust complaint, they ought to correct him with harsher and weightier words, so that they may serve and obey the one who commands what is fitting. For just as the bishop ought to show sincere love and affection to his ministers, so likewise [Col. 1328A] those subject to him ought to render bishops an unfeigned ministry and obedience.”

[Col. 1326C] **XIII.** Osius the bishop said: “I ought not to keep silent about what continually moves me. If some bishop is found to be quick-tempered—which ought not to characterize such a man—and, swiftly angered directly against a presbyter or deacon, wishes to cast him, or another person according to another reading, out of the church, provision must be made that such a person is not suddenly—or, according to another reading, innocently—condemned and deprived of communion.” All said: “The person expelled shall have authority to flee to the bishop of the metropolis of the same province; but if the metropolitan is absent, to run to the neighboring bishop and request that [Col. 1326D] his case be examined exactly. For those who make a request must not be denied a hearing. The bishop who expelled such a person, whether rightly or wrongly, ought also to bear it nobly that the case be examined, and that either his decision be ratified or corrected. But before each point has been carefully and faithfully examined, the person who does not have communion ought not, before judgment in the case, to assert communion for himself. If, moreover, some of the clergy gather and observe his haughtiness and arrogance, since it is not fitting to endure insult or unjust reproach, they ought to correct such a person with more severe and weightier words, so that they may serve and obey the one who commands what is fitting. For just as the bishop ought to offer his ministers sincere [Col. 1327A] love and goodwill, in the same way those subject to him ought to perform, without guile—or, according to another reading, conspicuously—the duties of ministry for bishops.”

[Col. 1328A] **XIV.** Osius the bishop said: “Let us all determine this too: if any bishop wishes to appoint into some rank a minister belonging to another diocese without the consent of that minister’s own bishop, such an appointment is to be considered null and invalid. If any persons permit themselves to do this, they ought to be admonished and corrected by our brothers and fellow-bishops.” All said: “Let this decree too stand firm and immovable.”

[Col. 1327A] **XIV.** Osius the bishop said: “Let us all determine this too: if any bishop wishes to appoint to some rank a minister belonging to another parish, without the consent of his own bishop, such an appointment is to be considered null and invalid. If anyone permits himself to do this, he ought to be admonished and corrected by our brothers and fellow-bishops.” All said: “Let this ordinance also stand—or, according to another reading, remain standing—unshaken.”

[Col. 1328A] **XV.** Osius the bishop said: “This is the judgment of my moderation: because we ought to be peaceable and patient, and to have enduring mercy toward all, those who have once been advanced to ecclesiastical clerical rank by some of our brothers, if they are unwilling to return to the churches to which they were appointed, should henceforth not be received. Eutychianus, moreover, must not even claim for himself the title of bishop; nor is Musaeus to be considered a bishop. But if they request lay communion, it ought not to be denied them.” All said: “It pleases us.”

[Col. 1327A] **XV.** Osius the bishop said: “This is the decision of my moderation: since we ought to be peaceable and patient and have lasting mercy toward all, those once promoted by some of our brothers to ecclesiastical clerical rank, if they are unwilling to return to the churches to which they were designated, should no longer be received. Eutychianus must not claim for himself even the title of bishop, nor must Musaeus be regarded as a bishop. But if they demand lay communion, it ought not to be refused them.” All said: “It pleases us.”

## THE COUNCIL OF HOSIUS OF CORDUBA

(Conc. vol. II, col. 91.)

[Col. 1327]

[Col. 1328B] Therefore the most holy Hosius, bishop of Corduba, having summoned in his own city a divine and holy synod of bishops, made manifest the divinely wrought doctrine: condemning those whom the Synod of Sardica had rejected, and receiving those whom it had in turn acquitted.

[Col. 1327B] Therefore the most holy bishop of Corduba, having called together in his own city a divine and sacred synod of bishops, made clear the divinely wrought teaching: condemning those whom the Synod of Sardica had rejected, and receiving those whom it had again vindicated.

[Col. 1327]

## LETTER OF THE BISHOP OF CORDUBA TO THE AUGUSTUS CONSTANTIUS

In Athanasius, *History of the Arians Addressed to the Monks*, §XLIV, *Works*, vol. I, pt. I, p. 370, Benedictine edition, Paris, 1698.

(Gall. vol. V, p. 81.)

[Note: [Col. 1328] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.] (S)

Hosius to the Emperor Constantius, greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 1328C]

I confessed the faith long ago, when persecution raged under your grandfather Maximian; and if you too persecute me, I am still ready to endure anything whatsoever rather than shed innocent blood and betray the truth. I by no means approve of your writing and threatening in this manner. Therefore cease writing such things; do not hold Arius’s views, do not listen to the Easterners, and do not put faith in Ursacius and Valens. For what they babble is spoken not on Athanasius’s account but for the sake of their own heresy.

Believe me, Constantius: by age I could be your grandfather. I attended the Synod of Sardica, when both you and your brother Constans, of blessed memory, summoned us all. I myself summoned Athanasius’s enemies when they came to the church in which I was staying, so that, if [Col. 1328D] they had anything to allege against Athanasius, they might state it. I gave my pledge and promised them security, that they should expect nothing but a just judgment in every respect. I did this not once only but twice, urging them that, if they did not wish to bring the matter before the whole synod, they should at least bring it before me alone. I also promised this: if the man were found guilty, he would certainly be rejected by us; but if he were found innocent and proved you to be slanderers, then, if you nevertheless rejected him, I would persuade Athanasius to go with me to Spain [Col. 1329A]. On these terms Athanasius obeyed without resistance. But they, wholly distrustful of their case, refused equally to do so.

Again, when Athanasius came to your army, summoned by your letters, he requested that his enemies, then at Antioch, be called, either all together or individually, so that they might either convict him or themselves be convicted; and that they might either prove in his presence that he was what they said, or cease slandering him in his absence. Yet you did not comply with this request; indeed, they refused it. Why, then, do you still listen to his detractors? Why do you tolerate Ursacius and Valens, although they repented and confessed their slander in writing? They confessed, I say, not under compulsion, as they allege—not with soldiers pressing upon them, nor with your brother’s knowledge. For nothing such as is done in these times, far be it, was done under him. Rather, of their own accord, they went to Rome and wrote this in the presence of the bishop and presbyters, having previously sent Athanasius a friendly and peaceful letter.

If they plead that force was used against them, let them acknowledge that force to have been unlawful. And if you do not approve of force, cease using force: send neither letters nor imperial officers, but restore the exiles, lest, while you condemn force, they themselves inflict still greater violence. What of this sort was done by Constans? What bishop was exiled? When did he intervene personally in ecclesiastical trials? What court official under him compelled anyone to sign against another, so that Valens and his associate might utter such things?

I beseech you: cease, and remember that you are a mortal human being. Fear the day of judgment; [Col. 1329C] keep yourself innocent for that day. Do not involve yourself in ecclesiastical affairs, nor issue us commands concerning them; rather, learn these matters from us. God entrusted imperial power to you; to us he entrusted the affairs of the Church. And just as the person who usurps your imperial authority resists God who ordained it, so fear lest, by drawing ecclesiastical matters to yourself, you become liable for a great crime. “Render,” it is written [Note: [Col. 1327D] (1) The Royal manuscript has Σερδικήν, “Sardican.”], “the things of Caesar to Caesar, and the things of God to God.” Therefore we are not permitted to rule on earth, nor do you, Emperor, have authority to offer incense.

I write these things because I care for your salvation. But concerning the matters on which you wrote, this is my judgment: I do not join myself to the Arians; indeed, I condemn their heresy with anathema. Nor do I write against Athanasius, whom we, the Church of Rome, and indeed the whole [Col. 1329D] synod declared innocent. Since you had ascertained these things, you summoned the man and allowed him to return with honor to his country and his church. What then was the cause of so great a change? For his enemies are the very same as they were before; and the things they now whisper—for they do not utter them in his presence—they were already saying against him before you summoned Athanasius. They were muttering these things when they came to the synod. And, as I said above, when I demanded proofs, they could not produce them; for if they had possessed them, [Col. 1332A] they would not have fled so shamefully.

Who induced you, after so long a time, to forget both your letters and your words? Restrain yourself, I beseech you, and do not comply with wicked men, lest you make yourself liable for the sake of reciprocal advantage. For concerning what you now grant them, you alone will have to render account on the day of judgment. They want, under your auspices, to injure their own enemy; and they want you to become the minister of their malice, so that with your assistance they may disseminate their accursed heresy in the Church. It is not prudent, for the pleasure of others, to cast oneself into manifest danger. Cease, I beseech you, and obey me, Constantius. For it is fitting that I write these things, and fitting that you should not despise them.

Hosius to Constantius the Emperor, greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 1327C]

I confessed the faith at the first, when persecution occurred under your grandfather Maximian. But if you also persecute me, I am ready even now to endure anything whatsoever rather than drain innocent blood and betray the truth. I do not approve of your writing and threatening such things. Cease writing such things; do not think the thoughts of Arius, do not listen to the Easterners, and do not trust those about Ursacius and Valens. For what they say, they do not utter on account of Athanasius but because of their own heresy.

Believe me, Constantius: by age I am your grandfather. I was myself at the Synod [Note: [Col. 1329D] (1) After this letter is read, Athanasius adds: “These were the thoughts and writings of that Abrahamic old man, truly Hosius—that is, Holy.”] of Sardica, when you and your brother Constans of blessed memory gathered us all together. I summoned Athanasius’s enemies personally when they came to the church in which [Col. 1327D] I lived, that they might say whether they had anything against him. I promised them confidence and that they should expect nothing other than a righteous judgment in all things. I did this not once, but a second time also, urging them that, if they did not wish to do so before the whole synod, they should do so at least before me alone. I promised again that if he were shown guilty, he would certainly be rejected even by us; but if he were found blameless and proved you slanderers, then, if you rejected the man, I would persuade Athanasius to come with me to Spain. And [Col. 1330A] Athanasius accepted these terms and did not object. But they, lacking confidence in every respect, perhaps declined.

Athanasius again came to your camp when you summoned him by writing to him. He requested that the enemies who were present in Antioch itself should be summoned, all or each individually, so that they might either convict him or be convicted, and so that they might either prove in his presence that he was as they alleged, or not slander him in his absence. But neither did you endure to hear him speak [Note: [Col. 1330D] (1) Thus the Royal manuscript, and so it should be read. Printed editions: ἠνέσχον, “they endured.”], nor did they consent. Why, then, do you still listen to those who malign him? How do you tolerate Valens and Ursacius, though they repented and admitted their slander in writing? For they admitted it not after suffering violence, as they themselves allege; not with soldiers pressing them, nor without your brother’s knowledge. For under him such things as now occur did not happen—may it never be so! Rather, willingly and of their own accord, they went up [Col. 1330B] to Rome and wrote in the presence of the bishop and presbyters, after first having written a friendly and peaceful letter to Athanasius [Note: [Col. 1330D] (2) Thus the Royal manuscript. Printed editions: πρότερον, “previously.”].

But if they plead violence, they know that this too is evil; and you do not approve of it either. Cease from using force; neither write nor send imperial officers [Note: [Col. 1330D] (3) The Royal manuscript has κόμιτας, “counts” or imperial officers; in accordance with usage.]. Rather, release the exiles, lest, while you accuse them of violence, they commit greater acts of violence. For what such thing occurred under Constans? What bishop was exiled? When did he personally intervene in an ecclesiastical judgment? Which court official of his forced someone to subscribe against another, so that those around Valens might say such things? Cease, I beseech you, and remember that you are mortal. Fear the day of judgment; keep yourself pure for that day. Do not involve yourself in ecclesiastical matters, nor command us concerning them; [Col. 1330C] rather, learn these matters from us. God committed imperial rule to you and entrusted us with the affairs of the Church. And just as one who steals your authority resists the one who established it, so fear lest you too, by drawing the affairs of the Church to yourself, become liable to a great accusation. “Render,” it is written, “the things of Caesar to Caesar, and the things of God to God.” Therefore we are not permitted to rule upon earth, nor do you, Emperor, have authority to offer incense.

I write these things [Note: [Col. 1330D] (4) In the Royal manuscript, οὖν, “therefore,” is absent.] because I care for your salvation. But concerning what you wrote, I hold this opinion: I do not assent to the Arians, but I anathematize their heresy; nor do I write against Athanasius, whom we, the Church of the Romans, and the whole synod acquitted. Since you recognized these things, you summoned the man and allowed him to return with honor [Col. 1330D] to his native country and church [Note: [Col. 1330D] (5) The Royal manuscript has ἀπελθεῖν, “depart,” less correctly.]. What, then, has caused such a great change? For the enemies he had before are the same ones he has now; and what they now whisper—for they do not speak it in his presence—they were saying before [Note: [Col. 1330D] (6) Thus the Royal manuscript; printed editions have πέμψῃ, “you send.” Then the Royal manuscript has διεθρύλουν, with one lambda, in accordance with usage.] you summoned Athanasius, and they were spreading the same things when they came to the synod. When, as I said, proofs were demanded of them by me, they were unable to provide them; for if they had possessed them, they would not have fled so shamefully [Col. 1331A].

Who, then, persuaded you after so long a time to forget your own writings and words? Restrain yourself, and do not yield to evil men, lest through your obligation toward one another you make yourself liable. For you now grant them this favor [Note: [Col. 1331A] (1) Thus the printed editions. The Royal manuscript has καθικεύεις.
