Elsewhere the same manuscript has καθηκούειν; printed editions have καθικετεύειν.], but at the judgment you will be the only one required to answer. They wish through you to wrong their own enemy, and they want you to become the servant of their wickedness, so that through you they may sow their abominable heresy in the Church. It is not wise, for the pleasure of others, to throw oneself into evident danger. Cease, I beseech you, and obey me, Constantius. For it is fitting that I write these things and that you not despise them.

# A.D. 353–363. POPE LIBERIUS

[Col. 1331]

# PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 1331]

## § I.—HISTORICAL NOTICE

(From the *Liber Pontificalis*.)

[Col. 1331]

[Col. 1331A]

[Note: [Col. 1331B]

**Liberius.** After an interregnum of twenty-five days, in the year of Christ’s birth 352, the sixteenth of the Emperor Constantius, Liberius, of holy memory, reluctantly accepted the pontificate of the Church, according to the testimony of Ambrose, the most blessed bishop. Besides many letters of his, there are found written accounts concerning the cure and leprosy of the Emperor Constantine. In Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book III, there survives an entire sermon by him, which he delivered at the consecration of his sister.

He was so great a defender of Athanasius and enemy of the Arians that the Emperor Constantius, elated by his victory over Magnentius, commanded by public edict, under penalty of exile, that no one thereafter should defend Athanasius or exclude Arians from the communion of the Church. When the pontiff, secretly brought from Rome to Milan, refused to comply with the emperor’s unjust edict, he was deported to Thrace after many others had been banished by the conciliabulum of Milan. After two years of exile, induced by force and fear of torments, weariness of exile and calamities, and finally hope of recovering his former see and dignity, he unhappily fell into error: subscribing to the First Sirmian Confession, condemning the innocent Athanasius, and finally communicating with the Arians. Thus he branded himself with a most shameful stain upon his life and conduct.

Valens and Ursacius, by the emperor’s authority, introduced him into the city after his release from exile and removed Felix from the pontifical see. But lest a pontiff suspected in faith should defile Peter’s chair, it happened by God’s singular providence that, while the true Catholic pontiff fell by communicating with the Arians and forfeited the pontificate, Felix—during Liberius’s exile a schismatic and defiled by communion with the Arians—broke off that bond, excommunicated Constantius, Valens, Ursacius, and all Arians as heretics, and by God’s just judgment began to be the true pontiff. The Catholics could not be removed from his communion after Liberius’s restoration from exile, even by force and martyrdom; nor, so long as Felix lived, could they unite with Liberius, stained and defiled by the blemish of Arian communion.

But after Felix’s martyrdom, when, by a greater divine benefit, Liberius in turn severed communion with the Arians, rejected the formula of the conciliabulum of Rimini, and again raised the standard of faith, he began not merely to be regarded by the Roman clergy as lawful bishop and pontiff, but also completely washed away that most shameful blemish on life and conduct which he had previously incurred. At last, in the year of the Lord 367, he departed this life most holy. Hence Ambrose, Epiphanius, and Basil everywhere call him a most blessed man; and the pontiff Siricius, in his letter to Himerius, calls him his predecessor of venerable memory.

It is false that Liberius, as heretics slanderously allege, was infected with the Arian heresy, since he wrote and taught nothing contrary to orthodox faith. We willingly concede that, by communicating with Arians, unjustly condemning Athanasius, and subscribing to a formula of faith lacking the term *consubstantial*, however Catholic it might have been, he sinned, incurred a just suspicion of heresy in the external forum, and was for just cause avoided by Catholics. See Baronius, year 355, nos. 53 ff., and 357, nos. 46 ff.; Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book IV, ch. 9.

Under his pontificate there arose the heresies of the Anomoeans, who taught that the Son of God is unlike the Father; the Macedonians, who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit; and the Messalians, who arose from monks and taught that, all else being neglected, one must devote oneself continually to prayer alone. Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, who several times served as papal legate, rejected the decree of the Synod of Alexandria concerning the reception of fallen bishops and became—alas for sorrow—a schismatic.

The Donatists, restored from exile by Julian’s edict, perpetrated those most disastrous demolitions of altars, seizures and plunderings of chalices, slaughterings of very many clergy and laypeople, abductions of virgins and matrons, and finally horrible violations of every sacrament, which Optatus recounts in book II. Among these was the memorable event that, after the sacred Eucharist had been thrown to dogs, the same dogs, inflamed with madness, tore their own masters with their teeth as though they were thieves guilty against the holy body, strangers and enemies. Likewise, when a vessel of chrism was thrown through a window so that it might break, an angelic hand held it in such a way that it settled unharmed among the stones. These matters are taken from Optatus or others by Baronius in the *Annals*.]

Liberius, a Roman by birth, son of Augustus, sat [Col. 1332A] for six years, three months, and four days. He lived, however, in the times of Constantius, son of Constantine, until the eighth consulship of Constantius Augustus (better: the third). He was deported into exile by Constantius because he would not consent to the Arian heresy; and he was in exile for three years. And the priests, assembling a council—or, according to another reading, Liberius, assembling the priests with his council—ordained …

[Col. 1333A]

[Note: [Col. 1333A]

**He sat for six years, three months, and four days.** It can certainly be inferred from the dates at which Liberius began and ended that he held the pontificate for fifteen years, four months, and one day. Having obtained the pontifical see on 8 May 352, as appears from what precedes, he thereafter held it until 9 September 367. For since, according to Ammianus, book XXVII, the fierce schism of Ursicinus against Damasus arose during the prefecture of Viventius, and since it is established from law XII, *On Punishments*, of the Theodosian Code that that prefecture occurred during the consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus, namely A.D. 367, it is certain that Liberius died and ceased to be pontiff in that year [Col. 1333B], and that Damasus succeeded him. The author of the *Liber Pontificalis* reports that he was buried on 9 September. These points being firmly established, the statement made above concerning the time of Liberius is evidently true.

**He lived, however, in the times …** The author of the *Liber Pontificalis* is mistaken. Liberius presided over the Church under the emperors Constantius, Julian, Jovian, Valentinian, and Valens, until the year 367, the fourth year of Valens.

Constantius, a supporter of the Arians, still a catechumen and on his deathbed, was baptized by Arians. At the same time at which, through the Arian conciliabulum of Antioch, he had stripped Christ the Lord of divinity, he was deprived of imperial power by Julian. Julian, renouncing the faith of Christ which for ten years he had feigned through fear of Constantius, became an apostate. In order to win over the minds of Christians at the beginning of his reign, he recalled all bishops exiled from their sees.

On this occasion Athanasius, who had been driven for the third time from the Alexandrian see by George of Cappadocia with armed force, returned to Alexandria from exile, the desert, and that dry cistern in which he had hidden for five years, after the said George had been killed by the Alexandrians, who were avenging the wrong inflicted upon them under Constantius [Col. 1333C]. But because, through the activity of the restored Athanasius, all the gods were being condemned, Julian’s rescripts compelled him to go into exile for a fourth time and depart from the city. Having entrusted the church to friends for a short time on this account—“Take courage,” he said, “for it is a cloud and will quickly vanish”—he embarked on a ship. Shortly afterward, learning that certain persons were pursuing him in order to kill him, he turned the ship in the opposite direction, frustrated his pursuers, came to Alexandria, and remained hidden there throughout Julian’s lifetime.

Julian attacked Christians with a new and unheard-of type of persecution. Envious of the glory of martyrdom, he zealously arranged through his agents that no one should be punished for piety but only under the charge of some crime, as a criminal. Since Christians, according to the Gospel commandment, ought in no way to abound in riches but to distribute everything for the sake of perfection, the treasury plundered their property. Those who seized the goods of the poor were either struck with leprosy or possessed by a demon. He removed every privilege from Christians and decreed that persons suffering injury should not be heard in court. He forbade them to teach or learn the liberal arts.

When he learned that at Caesarea Philippi, a city of Phoenicia, there stood a distinguished statue of Christ, placed there by the woman suffering from a flow of blood after she had been healed of her illness—and that from its base grew a certain herb able to cure diseases of every kind—he threw it down and placed his own statue in its place. After this, a violent fire fell from heaven and split that statue around the breast, casting its head and neck together to the ground. To dishonor Christians and erase Christ’s name, he publicly decreed that Christians should be called Galileans. Theodoret reports that Julian, as soon as he received in his body a missile sent against him by an angel, immediately filled his hand with blood, threw it into the air, and said: “You have conquered, Galilean.”

Jovian, renowned under Julian for confessing Christ’s name, was chosen emperor by the commanders of the army at divine prompting in A.D. 363. Before all other bishops, he recalled Athanasius from his fourth exile, as the most vigorous defender of the Catholic faith, and asked him to impart to him the truth of the faith. After Jovian was found dead at night, the other two illustrious confessors—Valentinian and Valens—who under Julian had preferred to lay aside the military belt rather than sacrifice to the gods, obtained the empire by God’s purpose and will in A.D. 364.

The reply Valentinian gave to Hypatianus, bishop of Heraclea, when he requested the calling of a synod, was this noble one: since he was but one of the laity, he was not permitted to involve himself in such matters. “Therefore,” he said, “let the priests and bishops, to whom these matters belong, meet separately among themselves wherever they please.”

Valens, a Catholic emperor for three years, while preparing for the Gothic campaign and wisely seeking saving baptism, was seduced by the caresses of his Arian wife and, through the worst counsel, went over to the Arians. Baptized by Eudoxius, the most wicked of Arians, he was bound by him under oath to persevere in the impious doctrine he had adopted and everywhere expel from the churches those who thought differently. These matters are from Baronius’s *Annals*. See more below in the notes to the letters and councils, and in the Life of Felix.

**He was deported into exile by Constantius.** In this matter the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* is shown to be mistaken by the notes on the conciliabulum of Milan below. Since he refused to condemn Athanasius as commanded, he was banished to Thrace.

**He was in exile for three years.** Since he was banished in A.D. 355 and released from exile in A.D. 357, he must have been in exile for only two complete years, or three years begun.

[Col. 1334C] **The priests, assembling a council, ordained …** The testimonies of the most eminent writers of this period conflict with these words of the *Liber Pontificalis*. Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Acacius, speaking of him, says: “He became so distinguished under the Emperor Constantius that he appointed Felix bishop at Rome in Liberius’s place.” Rufinus, book I, ch. 22: “Felix, his deacon, was substituted by heretics in Liberius’s place, and was defiled not so much by difference of sect as by fellowship in communion and ordination.” Athanasius, in his letter to the solitaries, adds that the same Felix was ordained through the machinations of Epictetus by three Arian bishops. Thus, what the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* writes concerning Felix’s ordination seems wholly untenable.

Moreover, while Liberius still lived and was adorning the pontifical dignity with the title of his glorious confession, a pontiff could not have been created, lest there be two bishops of one Catholic Church and two heads of one body shamefully appear. If it is said that, through Liberius’s arrangement, he was selected by a council of priests merely as fellow-bishop of the Roman Church, I do not strongly dispute it, although neither the testimonies of the aforementioned Fathers permit this to be said nor does it appear that Arians would have allowed it.

That Felix, substituted by the Arians, was not an Arian but Catholic is established especially by Rufinus’s testimony; second, Theodoret testifies to the same in explicit words, book I, ch. 17, when he says: “Liberius was succeeded by a certain faithful deacon of his, named Felix. Although he himself preserved intact the faith set forth by the Council of Nicaea, he nevertheless freely communicated with those who sought to undermine it; and for that reason none of the inhabitants wished to enter the church while he was inside.” Finally Sozomen, book IV, ch. 10, testifying to the same, adds: “Felix, a deacon of that clergy, was appointed to the episcopate of the Roman Church. They say that he always agreed with the faith of the Council of Nicaea and was altogether beyond reproach so far as religion was concerned, and that he was accused solely because he not only ordained Arian ministers of the church, but also used their communion.”

This is how Socrates, book II, ch. 29, must be understood when he says that Felix was devoted to the Arian sect: namely, because he communicated with them and subscribed, at their will, to the judgment pronounced against Athanasius. If, as Rufinus and Theodoret say, Felix was Liberius’s deacon, there can be no doubt that he was Catholic. For it is not credible that Liberius, who always abhorred the Arian name, would have permitted an Arian deacon to minister to him. That Felix is found called “Arian” in Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Acacius, is plainly a textual corruption, as is clear from the *Chronicle*, other more ancient manuscripts, and the Greek text of Sophronius. See Baronius, A.D. 355, no. 54 ff.; Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book IV, ch. 9.]

[Col. 1335A]

[Note: [Col. 1335C]

**Ursacius and Valens, and he condemned them.** Around the time at which Liberius shamefully fell by communicating with the Arians, Felix, previously defiled by communion with them, was raised from his lapse through God’s marvelous counsel and providence. By condemning and excommunicating Constantius, Ursacius, Valens, and all Arians, he broke their communion, lest, when substituted for Liberius, he should defile Peter’s chair even with the suspicion of heresy.

**After a few days.** See the notes on Liberius’s letters to the Easterners.

**He participated in only one communion, apart from a second baptism.** For how these words should be understood, see below under the words: “He agreed with Constantius the heretic, yet was not rebaptized.”

**Liberius agreed to the commands of Augustus.** Namely, induced by force, torments, and weariness of exile, he approved the First Sirmian Confession and the condemnation of Athanasius by subscribing, and communicated with the Arians.

**Returning from exile, he lived in the cemetery of St. Agnes.** What the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* reports concerning Liberius’s dwelling in the suburban cemeteries of St. Agnes is wrongly connected with Liberius’s first exile. For, according to Sozomen, book IV, ch. 10, Liberius was severely harassed by the Arians on two different occasions. The first was when he was secretly taken from Rome to Milan and, refusing to subscribe to the judgment against Athanasius issued by the conciliabulum of Milan, was banished thence to Thrace. The second was when, refusing to approve the formula of Rimini, he was expelled from Rome by Valens, an Arian bishop who had received that authority from the emperor [Col. 1336B].

The former harassment was exile; the latter was only an expulsion from the city. The former took place at Milan in A.D. 355; the latter took place at Rome after the Council of Rimini, in A.D. 359. Released from the earlier harassment, Liberius, according to Jerome’s *Chronicle*, entered Rome as though a victor: for he was introduced into the city with great pomp by Constantius’s officials. Therefore, his alleged residence in the suburbs cannot have occurred except after that second harassment inflicted by Valens. See the notes on the councils of Sirmium and Rimini; also Baronius, A.D. 359, nos. 46, 47, 48.

[Col. 1336C] **He expelled Felix from the episcopate.** Sozomen, book IV, ch. 14, says that it was written to Felix, then bishop of the Roman Church, and to the clergy of the same Church, that they should receive Liberius and that both should together administer the apostolic see and exercise that priesthood by common consent and concord, etc. What the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* asserts here appears more probable.]

From that same day there was a very great persecution of the clergy. This was because the whole Roman clergy rejected Liberius as defiled by manifest communion with the Arians and therefore altogether unfit for the exercise of the pontificate, and joined Felix, who raised the banner of the Catholic faith, as we said above.

That they might be crowned with martyrdom. It seems to have happened then that Eusebius, a Roman presbyter, was shut up in a chamber by the agents of Constantius and, remaining there for seven months, perished from hunger and gave up his spirit. Baronius, notes on the Martyrology, 24 August.

Felix was deposed. Here the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* judges differently concerning Felix’s end [Col. 1336D] from what he judges in Felix’s *Life*.

He agreed with Constantius the heretic, yet was not rebaptized. This seems to indicate that, although Liberius communicated with the Arians, he was not made an Arian by a second baptism, by which they were accustomed to rebaptize Catholics who defected to them. But these words are superfluous and added by someone; for the Arians did not yet rebaptize. Indeed, at this time the Church did not reject Arian baptism, as St Jerome testifies in *Against the Luciferians*; Baronius, year 357, no. 41.

There was a great persecution in the city of Rome, etc. Those who did not communicate with Liberius abstained not only from the Church but also from the public baths, lest they wash with them; for they knew, in accordance with the teaching of John the Evangelist, that one must not participate even in the washing of the bath with heretics. For that reason the magistrates acted cruelly against them. Baronius, year 357, no. 58.]

in his place [they installed] Felix, a presbyter and venerable man, as bishop. Felix held a council and found two bishops—or rather, presbyters—who agreed with Constantius Augustus the Arian, named Ursacius and Valens; and he condemned them in a council of forty-eight bishops. But a few days later Ursacius and Valens, led by zeal, asked Constantius Augustus to recall Liberius from exile, provided only that he participate in a single communion, apart from a second baptism (variant: “that he participate in one communion only, except for rebaptizing”). Then, authority having been sent through Catulinus, an imperial agent, Ursacius and Valens together came to Liberius. Liberius agreed to the commands of Augustus. They then recalled Liberius from exile.

On returning from exile, Liberius lived in [Col. 1335B] the cemetery of Saint Agnes, near the sister of Constantius Augustus, so that Liberius might seem to return to the city through her intervention or request. But Constantia Augusta, who was faithful to the Lord Jesus Christ, would not petition her brother Constantius Augustus, [Col. 1336A] because she had perceived the scheme. At the same time, the emperor Constantius, together with Ursacius and Valens, summoned some men who were the dregs of Arianism; and, as though holding a council, he sent for and recalled Liberius from the cemetery of blessed Agnes, where he had been residing.

When Liberius entered Rome, Constantius Augustus immediately held a council with the heretics, together with Ursacius and Valens; he expelled Felix, who was Catholic, from the episcopate and restored Liberius. From that same day there was a very great persecution of the clergy, so that many presbyters and clerics were killed within the Church and crowned with martyrdom. Felix, deposed from the episcopate, lived on his small estate on the Portuensian Way, where he also rested in peace on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [29 July]. Liberius entered the city of Rome on the fourth day before the Nones of August [2 August] and agreed with Constantius [Col. 1336B] the heretic; nevertheless, he was not rebaptized, but gave his assent. He held the basilicas of blessed Peter and blessed Paul, and the Constantinian basilica, for six years—or rather, seven.

There was also a great persecution in Rome, so that clerics and priests were admitted neither into the church nor [Col. 1337A] into the baths. Liberius adorned with marble slabs the tomb of St Agnes the martyr. Therefore all the years of Felix are counted in Liberius’s reckoning. He built a basilica in his own name near the market of Libya. He performed two ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: eighteen presbyters, five deacons, and nineteen bishops for various places. He was buried on the Salarian Way in the cemetery of Priscilla, on the fifth day before the Ides of September [9 September], alternatively on the eighth—or rather, seventh—day before the Kalends of May [24 or 25 April]. The episcopate was vacant for six days.

## CONCERNING THE SAME MAN

*(From D. Coustant.)*

I. In the Bucherian Catalogue, which ends with this pope and is therefore believed to have been compiled during his lifetime, one reads only this:

> Liberius was [bishop] in the time of Constantius [Col. 1337B], from the eleventh day before the Kalends of June [22 May], until the day . . ., under the consuls Constantius V and Constantius Caesar.

From this we learn that he was ordained in the year 352, on 22 May, a Friday. Or, if one accepts the conjecture of Antoine Pagi—that for “the eleventh day before the Kalends of June” one should read “the eleventh day before the Kalends of July”—his ordination falls on 21 June, which was a Sunday.

> **Note [Col. 1337D] (1).** From this point as far as § II of this *Notice*, we have been compelled to reduce the spacing between lines, so that documents formerly omitted might later be inserted, after the pages had already been fitted together, in order to complete the first paragraph. The reader will undoubtedly agree with us in preferring his own benefit even to typographical elegance. —Ed.

II. Having courageously and steadfastly undertaken many labours for the sake of the faith, he was exiled at the end of 355. After two years, broken and overcome by the weariness of exile, he made some temporary concessions to the Arians. Yet, having returned to Rome about the beginning of 358, he did not abandon the care of the Church. For, after the Council of Rimini had been annulled, as Siricius says in Letter 1 to Himerius, no. 2, he sent general decrees to the provinces. And he confirmed the decision of the synods held at Alexandria in 362 and subsequently in Achaia concerning bishops who had fallen at Rimini: namely, that those who had fraudulently induced others to fall should be condemned, but the rest spared [Col. 1337C]. Toward the end of his life, when the Easterners had professed the Nicene faith and condemned the Arian heresy, he admitted them to his communion.

Marcellinus and Faustinus, presbyters, state in the preface of their petitions to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius that he died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September], under the consuls Gratian and Dagalaifus—that is, in the year 366. His commemoration is observed on that same day in Bede’s martyrology, but in the Hieronymian martyrology and some others on the 23rd of that month. Pagi judges that the former indicates the day on which he died, while the latter indicate that on which he was buried.

## CONCERNING THE SAME MAN

*(From the Gallican Library.)*

I. Liberius, a Roman and successor of Pope Julius, was ordained pontiff in the year 352, on the twenty-second day of May, as we learn from the Bucherian Catalogue.

> **Note [Col. 1337D] (2).** Bucher, *De doctrina temporum*, p. 273.

Hardly had news [Col. 1337D] of his election been received when the Arians vainly tried to draw him to their position against Athanasius. This supreme pontiff sent envoys to Emperor Constantius, requesting above all that the matter of faith and the case of Athanasius be dealt with frankly and thoroughly; and at the same time seeking from him “a true peace, one not fashioned out of words through an inward disposition of deceit, but rationally confirmed by the precepts of the Gospels.”

[Col. 1338A] Constantius bore this most equitable request with the utmost displeasure and is found thereafter never to have ceased planning to harass Liberius. But the holy pontiff, neither broken by imperial threats nor afraid of imperial anger, undertook many labours for the faith with undaunted spirit and was driven into exile. Yet, as Ammianus writes, “only with difficulty, because of fear of the people who burned with love for him, could he be carried away in the middle of the night.”

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (1).** Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV, chapter 7.

Liberius’s exile took place “under the consuls Arbitio and Lollianus,” that is, in the year 355.

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (2).** Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 39.

After Liberius had been expelled and Felix intruded into his see, the Roman citizens could never be induced to enter into any association or communion with such a man. Indeed, matters eventually reached such a point that “Liberius was shortly afterward restored to the City because of Roman disturbances,” according to Sulpicius Severus.

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (3).** Ibid.

Socrates says the same:

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (4).** Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 37.

> “Liberius,” he says, “was recalled from exile not long afterward and recovered his see, when the people of Rome had risen in faction, **τοῦ ἐν Ῥώμῃ λαοῦ στασιάσαντος**, ‘the people in Rome having rebelled’; [Col. 1338B] the Church had expelled Felix, and the emperor, although unwilling, had yielded to them, **ὅ τε βασιλεὺς καὶ παρὰ γνώμην τούτοις ἐγένετο σύμψηφος**, ‘and the emperor, even contrary to his own inclination, joined in their vote.’”

Theodoret agrees with these accounts.

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (5).** Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 17.

Returning from exile at the beginning of 358 and entering Rome as “a distinguished conqueror and vigorous athlete of truth,” **ὁ νικηφόρος τῆς ἀληθείας ἀγωνιστής**, he was received with immense applause and joy from all. Restored now to his own see, he proclaimed yet more splendidly after his return the Nicene faith which he had courageously affirmed while suffering exile. For, as we learn from blessed Pope Siricius, “after the Council of Rimini had been annulled, he sent general decrees to the provinces.”

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (6).** Siricius, Letter I to Himerius, §2.

Thereafter he confirmed the synods convened at Alexandria and in Achaia and their decisions concerning the reception of bishops who had fallen at Rimini. He admitted the Easterners to communion after their profession of the Nicene faith and their condemnation of the acts of the Council of Rimini. Having performed these and other distinguished deeds, as is especially clear from his letters, Liberius was at last taken from human affairs in 366, on 24 September—or, as the presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus report, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, under the consuls Gratian and Dagalaifus.

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (7).** Marcellinus and Faustinus, preface to the *Book of Petitions*.

II. It is now sufficiently clear how greatly this supreme pontiff excelled in faith, holiness, and learning, and how highly his memory was valued by every eminent man. St Athanasius counts him among the celebrated writers of the Church and compares him with apostolic men:

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (8).** Athanasius, Letter to the Bishops of Egypt, §8, *Works*, vol. I, p. 278.

> “If the things which they [the Arians] write were written by orthodox persons—as they would be if written by Julius and Liberius, bishops of Rome—**Εἰ μὲν οὖν παρὰ ὀρθοδόξων ἦν τὰ γραφόμενα, οἷα ἂν ἐγεγόνει παρὰ … Ἰουλίου καὶ Λιβερίου τῶν ἐπισκόπων Ῥώμης**—then certainly there would be no ground for suspicion in their writings; for the character of apostolic men is simple and candid.”

Basil the Great calls him “the most blessed bishop Liberius,” **ὁ μακαριώτατος ἐπίσκοπος Λιβέριος**.

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (9).** Basil, Letter 263, alternatively 74, §3, *Works*, vol. III, p. 406.

Epiphanius calls him “the Roman bishop of blessed memory.”

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (10).** Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 75, §2.

Pope Siricius likewise calls him his “predecessor of venerable memory.”

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (11).** Siricius, Letter I to Himerius, §2.

Addressing his sister Marcellina, St Ambrose says:

> **Note [Col. 1338D] (12).** Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book III, chapter 1, §1.

> [Col. 1339A] “It is time, holy sister, to recall the instructions of Liberius of blessed memory which you are accustomed to discuss with me, so that the holier the man, the more welcome may be his discourse.”

And below, after reciting in full the address in which Liberius consecrated Marcellina by giving her the veil of virginity—which we have placed among the letters of Liberius—Ambrose adds:

> **Note [Col. 1339D] (1).** Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book III, chapter 4, §1.

> “This is what Liberius of holy memory said to you.”

Finally, Theodoret recalls “the boldness and admirable words of the most celebrated Liberius,” **Λιβερίου τοῦ πανευφήμου τὴν παρρησίαν καὶ τοὺς ἀξιαγάστους λόγους**, which he delivered before Emperor Constantius in defence of the truth.

> **Note [Col. 1339D] (2).** Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 15.

He further celebrates him, as we saw shortly before, as “a glorious athlete of truth.”

> **Note [Col. 1339D] (3).** Ibid., chapter 17.

Indeed, calling him back from exile an admirable man, he says: “That wondrous Liberius returned,” **Ἐπανῆκε μὲν Λιβέριος ὁ θεσπέσιος**.

> **Note [Col. 1339D] (4).** Ibid., at the end.

Accordingly, his memory is commemorated in Bede’s martyrology, in the metrical martyrology composed by Wandelbert, in the Hieronymian martyrology, and in additions to Usuard.

[Col. 1339B] III. From the monuments of ecclesiastical antiquity we understand that Liberius committed quite a number of writings to letters for the establishment and confirmation of the Catholic religion. Yet we acknowledge and maintain, on the testimony and authority of the ancient Fathers, that only fourteen surviving letters were truly written by him. We judge that certain others circulated under his name—especially those thought to reveal the fall of this supreme pontiff—ought rightly to be rejected as spurious and forged.

No one is unaware that heretics have often fabricated many writings under false names of holy Fathers, especially Roman pontiffs or bishops of other sees, in order to deceive the Catholic Church, mislead the unwary more safely, and by this means spread and establish their impious doctrines more easily and effectively. We know that this happened especially in the age of Liberius, when it was not unusual to find adulterated writings mixed with genuine ones.

We know, indeed, that the *Exposition of Faith in Detail* (**κατὰ μέρος**) bearing the name of St Gregory Thaumaturgus has Apollinarius as its author, as Eulogius of Alexandria, Leontius of Byzantium, Palestinian monks under Emperor Leo I, and other defenders of the Council of Chalcedon established.

> **Note [Col. 1339D] (5).** Eulogius, in Photius, *Library*, codex 230.  
> **Note [Col. 1339D] (6).** Leontius of Byzantium, *Against the Fraud of Apollinarius*, in the *Thesaurus Canisianus*, vol. I, p. 608.

Learned men also know that the Eutychians praised the Roman pontiffs Julius and Felix, Athanasius, and other Fathers of the Church as asserting one nature in Christ.

> **Note [Col. 1339D] (7).** Lequien, *Dissertation on Damascene*, II, §1 ff., p. 32.

Why should I mention that famous letter fabricated by Apollinarius and falsely attributed to Julius I? The particularly well-qualified witness to that fraud is the aforementioned Leontius.

> **Note [Col. 1339D] (8).** Leontius of Byzantium, *On Sects*, act VIII, vol. XI, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris edition, p. 526.

Moreover, as we learn from Athanasius himself, Arians fabricated letters not only in the names of Athanasius and other orthodox persons, but even in the names of emperors.

> **Note [Col. 1339D] (9).** Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, §§11, 19, 20, *Works*, vol. I, pp. 301, 307.

IV. But, to come more closely to our purpose with that most learned man:

> **Note [Col. 1339D] (10).** Montfaucon, *Observations on vol. II of the Collection of Greek Fathers*, p. 47.

Does not every prudent man now recognize as forged the reciprocal letters of Liberius and Athanasius, which in very ancient manuscripts of Athanasius [Col. 1339D] were regarded as genuine?

> **Note [Col. 1339D] (11).** Athanasius, *Works*, vol. II, p. 667 ff.

Why, then, could not the Arians also have fabricated the four letters prefixed with Liberius’s name among Hilary’s fragments and setting forth his fall?

> **Note [Col. 1340D] (1).** Hilary, *Fragment* IV, no. 1; and VI, nos. 5, 8, and 10.

Certainly, the great Baronius was the first to demonstrate by many arguments that the first of these, addressed to the Easterners and composed against Athanasius, was fictitious and forged.

> **Note [Col. 1340D] (2).** Ibid., Fragment 4, no. 1.  
> **Note [Col. 1340D] (3).** Baronius, year 352, §12 ff.

Most learned men—Coustant, Montfaucon, and others, except Tillemont—followed his judgment.

> **Note [Col. 1340D] (4).** Coustant, on Hilary’s fragments and in the appendix to the letters of the Roman pontiffs, p. 93.  
> **Note [Col. 1340D] (5).** Montfaucon, observations 20 on the collection of Greek Fathers, p. 45.

We are indeed surprised that so great a man went so far as to attempt to establish the authenticity of such a letter.

> **Note [Col. 1340D] (6).** Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. VIII, p. 695, note 65 on St Athanasius.

For anyone may expose the imposture both from the text itself when compared with the chronology of Liberius, and especially from the appendix immediately attached to this letter, where we read: “What is there in this letter that does not arise from holiness, what that does not arise from the fear of God?” From this one plainly understands, to use Baronius’s words, that these are not Hilary’s words proving that Athanasius was condemned by Liberius, but the words of some Arian who desired Athanasius’s condemnation above all else.

> **Note [Col. 1340D] (7).** Baronius, year 352, §14.

Nor does Montfaucon’s conjecture please us, namely that Hilary wrote these things ironically (**εἰρωνικῶς**). Whether one considers the chronological indications of the time when the letter is said to have been written, or the subject with which it is chiefly concerned, both authorize the conclusion that the letter is Arian and that an Arian added its appendix, intending more securely to deceive the simple and imprudent.

V. Since it is certain that the first letter among Hilary’s fragments is spurious and betrays an Arian author, what prevents us from thinking that the three just mentioned were also fabricated by an Arian hand and heaped into that miscellany of *Fragments*? With learned men, I would call those Hilary fragments nothing else than a miscellany. For, although they contain many splendid monuments of ecclesiastical antiquity, no one can rightly deny that their collection presents a monstrous appearance of materials [Col. 1340C] and an unorganized heap. Accordingly, the authority of at least some part of the work appears suspect; for there one finds not only certain false things mingled with true, but also many things corrupted and distorted by heretics.

Hence Rufinus says:

> **Note [Col. 1340D] (8).** Rufinus, *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, in the appendix to vol. IV of Origen’s *Works*, Paris edition, 1759, p. 53.

> “When Hilary had composed in fullest detail an instructional treatise for the correction of those who had subscribed to the perfidy of Rimini, and when that very book had come, without his knowledge, into the hands of enemies and ill-wishers, it was so corrupted by them, while that holy man perceived absolutely nothing, that it was afterward found to be such that he himself did not recognize it.”

So says Rufinus. I would not deny that Rufinus wove some things contrary to the truth into this narrative, and that Jerome therefore rightly rebuked him.

> **Note [Col. 1340D] (9).** Jerome, book II *Against Rufinus*, §19, *Works*, vol. II, p. 512, Verona edition.

Yet “the eventual corruption of Hilary’s work,” to use a learned man’s words, “was the reason why Rufinus invented these things. And indeed the malice of the Arians was such that they begrudged us the integrity of Hilary’s [Col. 1340D] work.”

> **Note [Col. 1340D] (10).** Coustant, preface to Hilary’s *Fragments*, §8.

What then [Col. 1341A] if Hilary himself collected all these fragments, whether Arian or orthodox, in order afterward to weave a history from them, separating the spurious from the genuine—refuting the falsehood of the former, while showing and establishing the truth of the latter?

VI. But you will say: Granted that Hilary’s fragments were altered and corrupted by the evil design of the Arians, and that the letters proclaiming Liberius’s fall were fabricated by Arians—what, then, should be thought of the testimonies of Athanasius, Jerome, and other ecclesiastical writers from which Liberius is understood to have defected?

A man outstanding in learning and scholarship, Monsieur Corgneus, canon of the Church of Soissons, answers these points most aptly. In a recently published special dissertation entitled *Critical and Historical Dissertation on Pope Liberius, in Which It Is Shown That He Never Fell*, guided by the authority of the principal ancient writers and at the same time examining and critically reassessing the passages adduced by others, he demonstrated with the greatest clarity that Liberius’s fall is fictitious [Col. 1341B]. This distinguished man’s judgment was subsequently defended admirably, though concisely, by a cardinal father; and we judge that it is further strengthened by what we have set forth above.

> **Note [Col. 1341D] (1).** Orsi, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VI, p. 201, §72.

This excellent French work, whose author I do not know, first appeared at Paris in 1732; subsequently revised and enlarged by its author, it was published there again in 1736. Whoever reads attentively this dissertation, wrought with the greatest acuteness of intellect and judgment, must surely conclude that Livy’s saying applies most fittingly to the cause of Liberius: “Truth is often sorely assailed, but never extinguished.”

## § II.—NOTICE OF NON-EXTANT OR SPURIOUS LETTERS RELATING TO POPE LIBERIUS

*(From D. Coustant.)*

[Col. 1341C]

I. Letters of the Egyptians to Liberius, sent about the end of 352.

1. From Egypt and Alexandria, letters were given to Liberius at the beginning of his pontificate like those previously written to Julius concerning the restoration of communion to Athanasius in exile: namely, letters concerning the defence of that communion which Julius and then the Synod of Sardica had restored to that bishop. Hilary mentions these letters in *Fragment* IV, no. 2, and promises there to append them; but they have been detached from it. The letters sent from all Egypt by the Alexandrian synod to Julius, as Athanasius testifies in his *Apology against the Arians*, no. 20, survive complete in that same apology, no. 3 and following. From them one may infer the character of those sent to Liberius [Col. 1341D] about the end of 352. Liberius himself mentions these letters in Letter 4, no. 2, where he also says that he recited and communicated them to the Italian bishops.

II. Letters of the Easterners to Liberius, written about the same time.

2. At the same time, as Liberius himself again testifies in Letter 4, no. 2, he received from the Easterners—that is, from the Arians—letters against Athanasius, left for him by a certain Eusebius who was hurrying to Africa. It contained precisely the same accusations [Col. 1342A] which the accused bishop had already refuted, whether in the Roman council in the presence of Julius or at Sardica. Liberius did not suppress these letters, as some have slanderously alleged, but read them to the Church and to the council.

III.—Letter of Liberius to the Easterners, sent in 353.

3. Liberius replied to the aforementioned letter of the Easterners at the very time he received it. He stated that he had received a document of eighty bishops which contradicted their judgment concerning Athanasius, and that it seemed to him contrary to divine law, when the greater number of bishops supported Athanasius, to lend any degree of agreement to their statements against him.

IV.—Letter of Liberius to the Egyptians, written at the same time.

4. It can scarcely be doubted that Liberius, who replied to the Easterners writing against Athanasius, also sent a letter to the Egyptians who had written to him on Athanasius’s behalf, and whose own letter he took care to communicate likewise to the Italian bishops. In it, he would have declared that he would adhere wholly to the course of his predecessor Julius.

V.—Letter of Liberius to Constantius, written in 353.

5. Liberius, having convened many bishops of Italy, sent Vincent of Capua and Marcellus, likewise a bishop from Campania, to Arles to Constantius, bearing a letter in which he asked the emperor to order the assembly of a council at Aquileia, as had formerly pleased the emperor himself. There, after the matter of faith had first been carefully considered, the remaining issues could finally be settled. At the same time, he entrusted to the envoys for delivery to Constantius the documents he had received, both from the Easterners against Athanasius and from the Egyptians for Athanasius, so that the desired council might more readily be obtained.

VI.—Letter of Liberius’s envoys from the Council of Arles.

6. When Vincent and Marcellus, Liberius’s envoys, had arrived at Arles, after preliminary discussion with the bishops there, they declared that, because of the disturbance of all the churches, they were willing to yield to the judgments of the Easterners who had condemned Athanasius—on this condition, however: that those who demanded this of them should first condemn the heresy of Arius. Then, when the agreed document had been ratified, they proceeded to the council. After deliberation, Athanasius’s opponents replied to Liberius’s envoys that they could not condemn Arius’s doctrine; they demanded only that Athanasius be deprived of communion. Vincent and Marcellus immediately notified Liberius of all these matters by letter.

7. These things were done while Constantius was staying at Arles. Ancient records establish that this emperor remained in that city at least from 8 November 353 until the spring of 354. It follows that the Synod of Arles, held then, must be assigned either to the end of 353 or to the beginning of 354.

VII.—Letter of Eusebius of Vercelli to Liberius, sent in 354.

8. Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, was asked by Liberius to join his envoys Lucifer, Pancratius, and Hilary in obtaining a council from Constantius. He replied that he willingly consented to Liberius’s wish. Knowledge of this letter is provided by Liberius’s letter to Eusebius; it was therefore written shortly before that letter in 354.

VIII.—Letter of Liberius to Fortunatianus, sent at the same time.

[Col. 1343B] 9. In the same letter to Eusebius, Liberius mentions a letter which he wrote to Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, asking him, by the sincerity of his heart and by the faith which Liberius knew him to have preserved even at the risk of his present life, to undertake watchful support with the envoys sent to Constantius.

IX.—Letter of Constantius to Liberius, in 355.

10. Shortly after the Council of Milan, held in 355, Constantius sent threatening letters, accompanied by gifts, to Liberius through the eunuch Eusebius. By them he tried to compel Liberius to condemn Athanasius and to communicate with the Arians. Athanasius mentions these letters in *History of the Arians to the Monks*, no. 35; and both Constantius’s innate disposition and the accompanying gifts make it easy to see that flattery was mixed with the threats.

X.—Letter of Liberius to the Roman clergy, written in 357.

11. As soon as Liberius, broken by the weariness of exile and by the emperor’s threats, assented to the emperor’s will, he informed the Roman clergy—before the emperor learned of this assent—that he had withdrawn from the name and communion of Athanasius. Therefore in his Letter to Ursacius, no. 2, he calls his clergy witnesses to this change.

XI.—His letter to Constantius at the same time.

12. At the same time Liberius gave Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, a letter concerning Athanasius’s name to deliver to Constantius, as he himself says in his Letter to the Easterners. The same letter is also indicated in [Col. 1343D] the Letter to Ursacius, no. 2.

XII.—Decretal letter of Liberius sent through the provinces about 362.

13. In Letter to Himerius, no. 2, Pope Siricius strongly disapproves of those who rebaptized persons baptized by Arians, among other reasons specifically because general decrees sent to the provinces by “my predecessor Liberius of venerable memory,” after the Council of Rimini had been annulled, prohibited it. From this it may be inferred that, after the disastrous outcome of the Council of Rimini, Liberius convened a synod, declared that council invalid, enacted various decrees conducive to the benefit of the universal Church, and sent them to the provinces in a synodal letter.

XIII.—Letters of the Synod of Lampsacus and others to Liberius and the Westerners, sent in 365.

[Col. 1344A]

14. The Easterners of the Synod of Lampsacus, and of various councils held in Asia, Pamphylia, Isauria, and Lycia, entrusted letters to the envoys Eustathius, Silvanus, and Theophilus for delivery to Liberius and the Western bishops. As Sozomen, book VI, chapter 11, briefly summarizes them, “they exhorted them to assist their envoys with every resource, to consider with them what ought to be done, and to correct the state of the Church as seemed good to them; since they retained a sound and steadfast faith and ought, above all others, to take care for religion.” Socrates and Sozomen report that the aforementioned envoys delivered these letters to Liberius. Since the Synod of Lampsacus, which first sent the envoys and to which the other synods entrusted their letters in like manner, was concluded about September 365, all these letters must belong to the latter part of that same year.

XIV.—Whether Liberius wrote to the Easterners concerning the Holy Spirit.

15. Noting the controversy raised in the East concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, Sozomen says in book VI, chapter 22:

> “When this question was being debated and the zeal for contention increased more and more each day, the bishop of the city of Rome, having learned of the matter, wrote to the churches of the East that they should confess with the Western bishops the Trinity to be consubstantial and equal in honour and glory. Once this was done, the controversy having been settled by the judgment of the Roman Church, each party became quiet, and the question seemed to have reached its end.”

In chapter 23, Sozomen begins to relate Liberius’s death in these words: “About the same time, Liberius having died, Damasus assumed administration of the Roman see.” Therefore, if Sozomen relates events in precise chronological order, Liberius must be thought to have sent letters to the churches of the East some time before his death, defining both that the Trinity is consubstantial and that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son—unless Sozomen anachronistically attributed to the time of Liberius what Damasus did, which seems more probable.

XV.—Sermon of Liberius.

16. The sermon delivered by Liberius must not be passed over. On the feast of the Savior’s Nativity, “at the Apostle Peter’s,” as he solemnly and publicly consecrated Marcellina, Ambrose’s sister, with the giving of the veil of virginity, he delivered it; Ambrose himself relates it in book III of *On Virgins*, chapters 1, 2, and 3, though, as scholars judge, in altered rhetorical form. In this discourse Liberius first instructs Marcellina in matters pertaining to the faith, and then gives her precepts suitable for virgins. Ambrose says that he recalls these words “so that the holier the man, the more welcome may be his discourse.”

XVI.—Writings falsely attributed to Liberius.

17. Furthermore, the appendix to this volume will present one letter of Liberius to the Easterners forged by Arians, likewise a writing of Liberius to Athanasius and Athanasius’s reply to him [Col. 1345A], as well as ancient but utterly false acts of Liberius.

18. Isidore Mercator also falsely attributed to this pope a letter written in the names of Athanasius and the Egyptians from the Alexandrian synod; he appended to it an equally fabricated reply of Liberius himself to the same persons. We reserve both works with his other fabrications for another volume.

### Assessment of the Decrees Attributed to Liberius

19. Editions of the councils contain three new decrees of Liberius, drawn from ancient codex 16, book XIII, chapters 9, 10, and 12. The same are cited under the same name by Burchard, book XIII, chapters 13, 14, and 18, and by Ivo, part 4, chapters 46, 47, and 50.

The first of these, beginning, “On these days of fasting there shall be no lawsuits,” is chapter 42 of the *Capitulary* of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans.

The second, which begins, “For in these most sacred days one must abstain from one’s spouse,” is the following chapter of the same *Capitulary*.

The third, stated as follows—“If famine, unseasonable weather, pestilence, or any other kind of affliction occurs, the Lord’s mercy should immediately be sought by fasts, alms, and prayers”—is adapted from book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 118, where we read: “Concerning this: if famine, pestilence, unseasonable weather, or any other kind of affliction occurs, let our edict not be awaited; rather, let God’s mercy immediately be sought.”

## EXTANT WORKS

[Col. 1345]

[Col. 1345]

## ADDRESS CONSECRATING MARCELLINA, SISTER OF ST AMBROSE, BY THE GIVING OF THE VEIL OF VIRGINITY

*(From Galland’s Library.) (C, S)\**

[Col. 1345B] I. “You have desired, daughter, a good marriage.

> **Note [Col. 1345D] (1).** St Ambrose, addressing his sister, prefaces this passage as follows: “It is time, holy sister, to recall the instructions of LIBERIUS of blessed memory which you are accustomed to discuss with me, so that the holier the man, the more welcome may be his discourse. For when, on the Savior’s birthday, at the Apostle Peter’s, you were marking your profession of virginity by changing your dress as well, and when many maidens of God stood by, competing with one another for your companionship, he said: ‘You have desired, daughter, a good marriage,’ etc.”

Do you see how great a crowd has assembled for the birthday feast of your Bridegroom, and that none departs unfed? This is he who, invited to a wedding, turned water into wine (John 2:9). He will likewise confer upon you the pure sacrament of virginity, though you were previously subject to the lowly material elements of nature. This is he who fed four thousand people in the wilderness with five loaves and two fish (Luke 9:13 ff.). He could have fed more, had more then been present to be fed. Finally, he has invited more guests to your marriage feast; but now it is not barley bread but the body ministered from heaven.

II. Today indeed, according to his humanity, a man has been born of a virgin; yet before all things he was begotten of the Father: he who represents his mother in body and his Father in power. Only-begotten on earth, only-begotten in heaven: God from God, offspring from a virgin; righteousness from the Father, power from the Mighty One, light from light; not unequal to him who begot him, not separated in power; not confused by an extension or utterance of the Word, as though blended with the Father, but distinct from the Father by the right of generation. He is your brother, without whom neither heavenly things nor things of the sea nor things on land subsist. The good Word of the Father (Song 5:1), which, he says, was in the beginning (John 1:3 ff.): here you have his eternity. And it was, he says, with the Father: here you have a power undivided from and inseparable from the Father. And the Word was God: here you have his unbegotten divinity; for you must draw faith in a concise form.

III. Love him, daughter, because he is good: “For none is good except God alone” (Luke 18:19). For if there is no doubt that the Son is God, and God is good, then surely there is no doubt that the Son, who is God, is good. Love him, I say. He is the one whom the Father begot before the morning star (Ps. 109 [110]:3), as eternal; whom he generated from the womb, as Son; whom he uttered from his heart (Ps. 44 [45]:2), as Word. He is the one in whom the Father was well pleased (Matt. 17:5); he is the Father’s arm, because he is the creator of all things; the Father’s wisdom, because he proceeded from the mouth of God (1 Cor. 1:30); the Father’s power, because in him dwells bodily the fullness of divinity (Col. 2:9). Him the Father so loves that he bears him in his bosom and sets him at his right hand, so that you may learn wisdom and know power.

IV. If, therefore, Christ is the power of God, was God ever without power? Was the Father ever without the Son? If he is always Father, then surely the Son also is always present. Therefore the Son of the perfect Father is perfect. For whoever detracts from the power detracts from him whose power it is. Perfect divinity admits no inequality. Therefore love him whom the Father loves; honor him whom the Father honors: “For whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father.” And whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either (John 5:23). So much concerning faith.

V. Yet although faith is sometimes secure, youth is suspect. Therefore use a little wine, lest you increase the body’s weakness (1 Tim. 5:23), not in order to excite pleasure; for wine and youth alike inflame. Let fasts also restrain tender age, and let moderation in food curb untamed desires with certain reins. Let reason recall, hope soften, and fear restrain. For one who does not know how to govern desires is, like a man dragged by unbroken horses, hurled about, trampled, torn, and afflicted.

VI. This, it is said, once happened to a young man because of his love for Diana. But the story is embellished with poetic falsehoods: Neptune, they say, was stirred by grief at the preference of his rival and sent madness into the horses, so that his great power might be proclaimed; although he overcame the young man not by strength but deceived him by fraud. Hence they renew an annual sacrifice to Diana, so that a horse may be sacrificed at her altars. Yet they call her a virgin, though she was able to love one who did not love her—a thing at which even prostitutes are accustomed to blush. Still, let their tales retain their authority, if they please; for, although both things are wicked, it is nevertheless less grievous that a young man should have burned so fiercely for love of an adulteress that he perished, than that, as they themselves say, two gods should have contended over adultery. Jupiter, moreover, avenged upon the adulterer’s physician the suffering of his daughter as she played the prostitute, because he had healed the wounds of the man who adulterated Diana in the woods—a huntress indeed most skilled, not in hunting wild beasts but lusts; and wild beasts also, so that she might hunt naked.

VII. Let them, then, grant Neptune dominion over frenzy, so as to establish the charge of incestuous love. Let them grant Diana sovereignty in the woods which she inhabited, so as to confirm the adultery she practiced. Let them grant to Aesculapius that he restored a dead man, provided that they admit that he himself did not escape being struck by lightning. Let them also grant Jupiter the thunderbolts which he did not possess, so that they may bear witness to the disgraces which he did possess. But let us return from fables to our purpose.

VIII. I think also that all foods which generate heat in the limbs should be used sparingly; for meats make even flying eagles descend. Within you too, may that inner bird of which we read, “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102 [103]:5), remain aloft and, in the swift flight of virginity, know no desire for superfluous flesh.

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts read thus; some, however, read: “and your youth, like eagles.”]

The festivities of banquets must be avoided, and social calls fled.

IX. I wish even visits to be more limited among younger persons, unless perhaps duty must be rendered to parents or equals. For modesty is worn away by such civilities; boldness flashes forth, laughter steals in, and reserve is loosened while elegance of manner is being cultivated. Not to answer one who questions you is childishness; to answer is conversation. I would therefore rather that speech should be lacking in a virgin than that it should be excessive. For if women are commanded even concerning divine matters to keep silence in church and to ask their husbands at home (1 Cor. 14:34), what precautions, do we suppose, are prescribed for virgins, in whom modesty adorns youth and silence commends modesty?

X. Or is this a slight example of modesty: that Rebecca, when she was coming to her marriage and saw her bridegroom, took a veil (Gen. 24:65), lest she be seen before she was joined to him? And certainly this beautiful virgin did not fear for her appearance, but for her modesty. What of Rachel? How, after the kiss had been forcibly taken, she wept and groaned (Gen. 29:11–12); and would not have ceased weeping, had she not recognized her kinsman? Thus she preserved the obligation of modesty and did not omit the affection of piety.

[Note: The Vulgate and other versions, with the Hebrew text, read: “He kissed her; and, raising his voice, he wept, and told her,” etc. From these words, the account here that Rachel’s modest kiss was followed by weeping is indeed elegant and appropriate to the subject; nevertheless, it ought to be referred to Jacob. And certainly, even if there were some ambiguity in other languages, the Septuagint plainly reads: “and crying aloud, he wept” (καὶ βοήσας τῇ φωνῇ αὐτοῦ, ἔκλαυσε; *kai boēsas tē phōnē autou, eklause*).]

But if a man is told, “Do not gaze upon a virgin, lest perhaps she cause you to stumble” (Sirach 9:5), what should be said to a consecrated virgin, who, if she loves, sins in mind; and, if she is loved, she sins also in deed?

XI. Great is the virtue of silence, especially in church. No saying of the divine readings will escape you if you lend your ear and restrain your voice. Let no word issue from your mouth which you might wish to recall; rather, let your confidence in speaking be sparing. For sin is abundant in much speaking (Prov. 10:19). To the murderer it was said, “You have sinned; be still” (Gen. 4:7), lest he sin further; but to a virgin it must be said, “Be still, lest you sin.” For Mary, as we read, kept in her heart all that was said concerning her Son (Luke 2:19). You too, when something is read by which Christ is announced as to come or shown already to have come, do not interrupt by chattering, but apply your mind. Is anything more unworthy than that divine oracles should be drowned out, so that they cannot be heard, believed, or revealed; that mysteries should be surrounded with confused voices, so that prayer offered for the salvation of all may be hindered?

[Note: All printed editions read “for the salvation of all, when the Gentiles … offer”; but the manuscripts agree strongly with our text. Valerius Maximus, book III, chapter 3, “On Patience,” recounts the following story of this barbarian youth.]

XII. The Gentiles pay reverence to their idols by silence. Hence this example is related: while Alexander, king of the Macedonians, was sacrificing, a barbarian boy who was holding a light for him caught fire in his arm; his body was burned, but he remained motionless, revealing neither his pain with a groan nor the punishment silently by tears. So great was the discipline of reverence in this barbarian boy that nature was overcome. Yet he feared not gods, who were no gods at all, but the king. For why should he fear those who, had that same fire touched them, would have burned?

XIII. How much better is the case of the young man who, at his father’s banquet, is commanded not to reveal his love for prostitutes by shameless signs? And you, virgin of God, in the mystery refrain from groans, spitting, coughing, and laughter. What he can do at a banquet, can you not do in the mystery? Let virginity first be marked by the voice; let modesty close the mouth; let religion exclude weakness; let custom train nature. Let a virgin’s gravity announce her to me before anything else, with modesty meeting me, sober gait, and restrained expression; and let signs of virtue, heralds of integrity, go before her. A virgin is NOT sufficiently approved if she has to be inquired about when she is seen.

[Note: Printed editions read: “What of a certain man?” And below: “in the ministry … refrain from coughing and laughter … cannot you do so in the ministry of God?” The manuscripts, however, agree with the text, except that some read “ministry,” as do the printed editions, in place of “mystery.” The passage points to Terence’s play *Heautontimorumenos*, Act II, near the end of scene III, where the young man Clitipho is admonished to preserve decorum at dinner in his father’s presence. There the words are: “Refrain from groaning, spitting, coughing, laughter.”]

XIV. A common story is told: when the religious ears of the people were disturbed by the very loud croaking of frogs, a priest of God commanded them to be silent and to show reverence for the sacred prayer; then the surrounding noises suddenly ceased. The marshes are silent, and will human beings not be silent? Even an irrational animal recognizes through reverence what it does not know by nature; is human immodesty so great that most people do not know how to render to the religion of minds what they render to the pleasure of ears?

[Note: The holy Doctor concludes this Liberian discourse as follows: “These are the things which Liberius, of holy memory, [said] to you.”]

[Col. 1349]

## LETTERS AND SAYINGS

(Coust., cols. 421–464.) (C,S)

### LETTER OF POPE LIBERIUS TO HOSIUS, BISHOP OF CORDOBA

(At the end of the year 353, or the beginning of 354.) Concerning the embassy and lapse of Vincentius, bishop of Capua.

[Note: This survives among the fragments of Hilary, fragment VI, no. 2, and is also published by Baronius under the year 353, no. 9. Its opening words in Hilary, “Meanwhile,” show that it is not complete. It was written after the recent lapse of Vincentius at the Synod of Arles, and therefore around the end of 353 or the beginning of 354.]

Because I must not pass over your conscience in any respect: many bishops from Italy assembled, who, together with me, had petitioned the most religious Emperor Constantius to order that, as he himself had formerly determined, a council be convened at Aquileia. I inform your holiness that Vincentius of Capua, together with Marcellus, likewise a bishop from Campania, undertook our embassy. Since I had hoped much from him, because he both understood the case extremely well and had often sat as judge in the same case together with your holiness, I had believed that by his embassy the integrity of God’s Gospel could be preserved. Not only did he obtain nothing, but he himself was led into that pretence. After this deed, overwhelmed with a double grief, I determined that I ought rather to die for God, lest I seem the last informer, or to have consented to judgments contrary to the Gospel.

[Note: In Baronius the phrase “the integrity” is missing. In two manuscripts it reads “the entire integrity of the Gospels.”]

[Note: From the words of Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, no. 27, it is inferred that he persisted in this pretence at least until the time when Liberius and Hosius were sent into exile. Yet later he deserved praise from Damasus, writing from the Roman synod to the bishops of Illyricum, as one who had preserved the priesthood unstained for so many years. It should be noted that Athanasius, in the passage just cited, briefly surveys what followed both the Councils of Arles and Milan. Therefore, although, while speaking of Vincentius’s pretence, he joins to him Fortunatianus of Aquileia, Heremius of Thessalonica, and all the western bishops, it by no means follows that all these lapsed at Arles. Likewise, although in the same place he mentions together the exiles of Liberius, Hosius, Paulinus, Dionysius, Eusebius, Lucifer, and others, it does not follow that, because Paulinus was driven into exile by the Synod of Arles, the exile of the others should not be dated later.]

### LETTER OF POPE LIBERIUS TO CAECILIANUS, BISHOP OF SPOLETO

(At the same time.) Concerning the same matter.

[Note: Hilary, fragment VI, no. 2, has transmitted this small portion of the letter. The letter was written at the same time as the preceding one.]

Do not let the action of Vincentius turn you aside from the purpose of the good work, dearest brother.

### LETTER OF POPE LIBERIUS TO EUSEBIUS, BISHOP OF VERCELLI

(At the same time.) Concerning the embassy of Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, to the Emperor Constantius, requesting a council through which the affairs of the Church might be settled; and that Eusebius himself should assist him in obtaining this request.

[Note: Baronius, under the year 353, no. 20, and Stephen Ferrerius, bishop of Vercelli, transcribed and published this from the archive of the Church of Vercelli. In this letter, as in those above, Liberius laments Vincentius’s pretence; but he says nothing in the earlier letters of the consolation which he now remembers having received from the magnanimity of Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari. It is therefore clear that this letter was written somewhat later than those. It appears to belong to the year 354.]

Liberius, bishop, to Eusebius, his beloved brother.

I. Dearest brother, your unconquered faith raises me up for the consolation of this present life: in following the precepts of the Gospels, you have in no way departed from communion with the Apostolic See. I believe that, not without God’s prompting, you have fulfilled with benevolence what he preserves in the priesthood for those worthy of him—or, perhaps, “for the worthy.” Therefore, after the embassy, Vincentius was led into that pretence, and the remaining bishops throughout Italy had been compelled, by a public assembly, to obey the judgments of the eastern bishops. But by God’s providence our brother and fellow bishop Lucifer came from Sardinia. When he had learned the hidden character of the matter and perceived that, under the pretext of the name of Athanasius, heretics wished to attempt these things, he chose, in devotion to his faith, to undertake the righteous labor and to proceed to the court of the religious prince, so that at last, once the entire course of the case had been set forth, he might obtain the examination in an assembly of God’s priests of all matters brought forward.

[Note: The completeness of the sentence requires: “had been led into that pretence,” and the rest. Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, no. 29, may refer to this violence inflicted upon Italian bishops: “The western bishops were subjected to no small force—indeed, to the utmost violence and grievous insults—until they promised that thereafter they would not communicate with us.” To deny communion to Athanasius, therefore, was to obey the decrees of the easterners.]

II. Therefore, because I know that the holy ardor of your faith agrees with his mind, I ask your prudence that, if God grants that he finds you present, you strive, through whomever you can, to keep watch diligently, so that you may be able to lay before the most merciful emperor everything that the Catholic faith requires. Thus at last, having laid aside the indignation of his mind, he may do what can in every respect accord both with our peace and with his own salvation. Moreover, I thought it superfluous to explain in a letter to your honor the ordering of the whole case, since the aforesaid brother of mine or his companions can presently recount everything in their own report. May God keep you safe, most beloved lord brother.

[Note: Namely, Pancratius the presbyter and Hilary the deacon, as is made clear in the following letter.]

### LETTER SENT TO THE EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS BY LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, THROUGH BISHOP LUCIFER

(Year 354.) He seeks to placate Constantius and obtain from him a council to provide for the peace of the churches.

Liberius, bishop, to the most glorious Constantius Augustus.

I. Constantius’s implacable disposition toward Liberius. A council requested.—I beseech you, most serene Emperor, that your clemency grant me gracious ears, so that the purpose of my mind may become apparent to your gentleness. For I deserve without hesitation to obtain this very thing from a Christian emperor and son of Constantine of holy memory. Yet I understand that I labor in this respect: although I have repeatedly made satisfaction, I cannot restore your mind to favor toward me even where the guilty are concerned. For the words of your piety, long ago sent to the people, deeply wound me, who must bear all things patiently. Yet that your mind, ever devoted to gentleness, never retaining anger until sunset, as it is written, should preserve indignation against me is a wonder to me. For I, most religious Emperor, seek true peace with you—not peace made up of words through an inward disposition of deceit, but peace reasonably established by the precepts of the Gospels. Not only the affair of Athanasius, but many other matters have arisen, on account of which I had entreated your gentleness that a council be held: so that, before all else, since your mind’s sincere devotion toward God especially desires it, the matter of faith—in which lies our first hope toward God—might be diligently examined, and the affairs of those who ought to admire our devotion toward God might not be settled. It would have been worthy of a worshipper of God, worthy of your Empire, which is ruled and enlarged through Christ’s piety, that your clemency should grant us this particular favor, for the reverence of the holy religion to which you are prudently attentive.

[Note: Baronius reads “I desire,” and shortly afterwards, “so that I may … set forth,” instead of “so that it may … become apparent.”]

[Note: This alludes to what Athanasius explains in his *History of the Arians addressed to the Monks*, no. 68: while bishops were being sent into exile, some others were convicted, according to the nature of their crimes, of murder, sedition, or theft. After a few months, when petitioned, he absolved these men from punishment, like Pilate with Barabbas; but toward the servants of Christ he showed himself an everlasting evil.]

[Note: Baronius reads “nor their affairs.” It would be preferable to supply “their” before “affairs.” Liberius means here what he repeats below, in letter or section 9, when addressing the eunuch Eusebius: “First every disagreement concerning faith must be cut off; then other affairs must be examined.”]

II. Liberius falsely accused of suppressing the easterners’ letters.—But many hasten to tear apart the members of the Church. They alleged that I had suppressed letters, lest the crimes of the man whom they said they had condemned should be exposed to all. What letters were those? The letters of the eastern bishops and of the Egyptians? Were the same accusations against Athanasius contained in all of them? But it is sufficiently clear to all, and no one denies, that we made known the letters of the easterners, read them in church, read them before the council, and also replied to the easterners that we had not given them our faith and judgment, because at the same time the judgment of eighty Egyptian bishops concerning Athanasius opposed them. We likewise read this aloud and laid it before the Italian bishops. It therefore seemed contrary even to the divine law to give consent in any respect when a greater number of bishops supported Athanasius. These documents Eusebius, who had been sent in haste to Africa, left with us, if he is faithful to God; yet afterwards Vincentius, who had been sent with the others to Arles, carried away all these writings, lest they perhaps be lacking for securing the council.

[Note: In the Pithoean manuscript—that is, in the archetype of Hilary’s fragments—the reading is “as though those letters.” From this passage it is clear that the easterners, that is, the Arians, as soon as they learned that Liberius had succeeded Julius, sent him letters full of accusations against Athanasius; and that the Egyptians, sending letters at the same time, refuted those accusations. Thus each party renewed what had already been attempted when Julius entered upon the pontificate. Hilary, fragment IV, no. 2, testifies expressly concerning the Egyptians: “Such letters as had formerly been written from all Egypt and Alexandria to Julius concerning the restoration of communion to the exiled Athanasius, such now … were given to Liberius concerning its preservation.” Just as Julius, letter I, nos. 3–4, declared that he was prevented from condemning Athanasius on the testimony of the Eusebians because far more Egyptians testified to his innocence, so Liberius now refutes the Arians’ demands on the same ground. Accordingly, the pope shows that the eastern and Egyptian letters did not agree with one another, and were far from containing the same accusations against Athanasius. He could have suppressed letters so plainly full of calumnies on the grounds on which Cyprian, in letters 1 and 2, says that he took care not to have a libellus of schismatics, full of insults, publicly read before the people; but, wishing to leave no avenue for anyone’s complaint, he arranged for the letters of both parties to be read in church.]

[Note: Baronius reads “to this”; the preposition *ad* is superfluous. A little later, “because [we gave] them faith” would be preferable, so that Liberius may here indicate what he answered the easterners.]

[Note: Baronius reads “seventy-five,” contrary to the manuscripts of Hilary and to letter III, no. 2, of the Synod of Sardica to Julius.]

[Note: In the *Bibliotheca Patrum* the text reads *Theosebius*. Baronius has *Theosebius*, with *Theobadius* in the margin. Is the eunuch Eusebius meant, who was later also sent to Liberius with gifts in order to induce him to comply with Constantius’s will?]

III. He clears himself of the charges laid against him.—Your prudence sees, therefore, that nothing entered my mind which it was unworthy of servants of God to contemplate. God is my witness, and the whole Church with its members is witness, that through faith and fear toward my God I have trampled, and continue to trample, all worldly things, as evangelical and apostolic teaching commands. Living also in another ecclesiastical office, I fulfilled nothing required by the law through boasting or desire for glory; and, God is my witness, I came unwillingly to this office, in which indeed I desire, as long as I am in the world, to remain without offence against God. I have carried out not my own ordinances, but the apostolic ordinances, so that they might always be established and observed. Following the custom and order of my predecessors, I have allowed nothing to be added to or taken away from the episcopate of the city of Rome. Preserving that faith which has run through the succession of so many bishops—of whom many were martyrs—I ever desire it to be kept unstained.

IV. Why he cannot communicate with the easterners.—Finally, ecclesiastical concern and devotion itself urge me now to disclose the reason to your piety. The easterners declare that they wish to join themselves to our peace. What peace is this, most merciful Emperor, when there are among their own party four bishops—Demophilus, Macedonius, Eudoxius, and Martyrius—who, eight years ago, when they would not condemn Arius’s heretical teaching at Milan, left the council in anger? Your equity and clemency can judge, if it is lawful to assent to their judgments, what such assent is and what danger it involves. It is not new what is now being subtly attempted under the pretext of Athanasius’s name. There remain letters of Bishop Alexander, formerly sent to Sylvester of holy memory, in which he reported that, before Athanasius’s ordination, he had expelled from the Church eleven persons, both presbyters and deacons, because they followed Arius’s heresy. Some of these now, placed outside the Catholic Church, are said to have found conventicles for themselves, with which even George at Alexandria is asserted by letter to communicate. What peace, then, can there be, most serene Emperor, if bishops, by published edicts, as has now happened throughout Italy, are compelled to obey the judgments of such men?

[Note: After Athanasius, in *On the Synods*, Socrates, book II, chapter 19, relates that the easterners, three years after the Council of Antioch held in 341, drew up a lengthy creed and sent it through Eudoxius, Macedonius, and Martyrius to the bishops of Italy.
