The arrival of these envoys, together with their demand, according to western custom, that the Arian heresy be condemned beforehand, probably gave occasion for holding the Council of Milan; we have already observed this in Hilary at this passage.]

[Note: Namely, the encyclical letters which Socrates incorporated into book I, chapter 9, of his *History*. They are also extant in Athanasius, new edition, vol. I, p. 397. Julius, letter I, nos. 3–4, writes that those whom Alexander recalls in these letters as expelled by him from the Church were condemned with an anathema by all who assembled at the Nicene Synod.]

[Note: Perhaps the bishop of Laodicea. This is certainly a different George from the one who only in 355, and thus long after this letter was written, invaded the Alexandrian see.]

[Note: In Baronius the word “published” is missing. The reference is to the edict issued by the emperor, as Sulpicius relates in book II: those who would not subscribe to the condemnation of Athanasius were to be driven into exile.]

V. On the condition under which Athanasius’s condemnation was proposed at the Synod of Milan.—Hear another matter, because your serenity admits it patiently. There remain the letters of the envoys, Vincentius and Marcellus, who had been sent to your clemency and who arrived recently. They report that, because of the disturbance of all the churches, they had wished indeed to yield first to the judgments of the easterners, but proposed this condition: if the same men condemned Arius’s heresy, then, being so persuaded, they would obey their judgments. The agreement, as they report, was confirmed by a written document. They proceed to the council and, after deliberation, receive the answer that they could not condemn Arius’s teaching, but that Athanasius, which alone they demanded, must be deprived of communion. Let your clemency now consider this also: whether, with the law of the Catholic religion rightly maintained, the cause of a man ought to be carefully and thoroughly examined.

VI. Liberius earnestly seeks a council.—Therefore again and again we entreat your gentleness and your mind devoted to God, by the power of him who showed all mortals how great he is in your defense, that, keeping before your eyes the benefits of him who directs your empire in all things, you cause these matters to be carefully examined with every consideration in an assembly of bishops. Thus, when through you the times have been pacified, with God’s favor and your serenity’s assent, all matters may be discussed in such a manner that those things confirmed by the judgment of God’s priests—when it has been established that all have assented to the exposition of faith confirmed at Nicaea, in the presence of your father of holy memory, among so many bishops—may thereafter be preserved as a precedent. Thus the Savior himself, who from above beholds the purpose of your mind, may rejoice that, amid so great an expedition of affairs, you have deservedly set the cause of faith and peace before even the necessities of the commonwealth.

[Note: Against Magnentius, destroyed in 353.]

VII. He commends the envoys.—Therefore, to entreat your gentleness that you may deign to hear our representations with a favorable mind, I have resolved to send my brother and fellow bishop, the holy man Lucifer, with Pancratius the presbyter and Hilary the deacon. We trust that, through your clemency, they may readily obtain a council for the peace of all Catholic churches. May the clemency of almighty God preserve you for us, most merciful and most religious Augustus.

[Note: Baronius reads “my fellow presbyter,” a phrase which Liberius indeed uses below, in letter 6.]

### LETTER OF POPE LIBERIUS TO EUSEBIUS, BISHOP OF VERCELLI

(Year 354.) That he should join the envoys proceeding to Constantius.

[Note: We owe this letter to the records of the Church of Vercelli; Baronius published it under the year 354, no. 6, and Stephen Ferrerius likewise. It was evidently written after the departure of the envoys, but before they passed through Vercelli on their journey into Gaul; hence it was written not long after the two preceding letters.]

Liberius, bishop, to Eusebius, his beloved brother.

As my son Callepius was returning to his homeland, I judged it best to greet your holiness through him, most beloved lord brother, praying God’s clemency that you may receive my letter safe and cheerful. And because I know that your unconquered mind faithfully does what God commands, I commend to you our brother and fellow bishop Lucifer, and also my dearest sons Pancratius the presbyter and Hilary the deacon. For the state of the Church, with manly courage and God-given power, at an opportune time they have undertaken to confront the enemies of the Church, whom God will destroy by the breath of his mouth. For I know that the fervent Spirit of God is in you, so that you may undertake the struggle together with them, in order that the faith handed down from the Apostles to the Catholic Church may in no way be broken in upon—provided, certainly, that you deign to uphold it if public laws do not forbid the condemnation of one absent. May your faith join their fellowship; and, wherever it may be fitting, may your holiness be present, so that in one conference and one counsel you may do what pleases God and his angels and benefits the Catholic Church. For this labor may Christ our Lord render to you the heavenly reward, the unfading crown, and the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. We greet all who faithfully serve God with you. Greet all the clergy … May God keep you safe, most beloved lord brother.

[Note: Baronius identifies him in the margin as Calepodius. At the Council of Sardica, Calepodius, bishop of Naples, is recorded as a signatory; but Liberius customarily calls bishops “brothers,” not “sons,” in ecclesiastical usage. Nor does he seem here to speak of a bishop returning to his church, but of a layman returning to his homeland.]

[Note: Baronius adds in the margin, “to fight.” The same expression repeated shortly afterward—“that you may undertake [the struggle] together with them”—shows that no word is missing here.]

[Note: That is, they do not forbid an absent person to be condemned.]

### LETTER OF POPE LIBERIUS TO EUSEBIUS, BISHOP OF VERCELLI

How greatly delighted he was by Eusebius’s letter, from which he learned that Eusebius had joined his envoys. He had also written to Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, asking him to keep watch with them and, if necessary, not deny them his presence.

[Note: This was first published from the same archive of the Church of Vercelli by Baronius, under the year 354, no. 8, and then by Stephen Ferrerius. It was written after Eusebius, requested by Liberius to join his envoys, had replied that he would comply with his wish; but before Liberius learned that his envoys had reached the emperor, as is inferred from what he writes concerning Fortunatianus. This letter too therefore belongs to the year 354.]

Liberius, bishop, to Eusebius, his beloved brother.

I. Praise of Eusebius’s piety.—I knew, most beloved lord brother, that, fervent in the Spirit of God in the cause of faith—which can commend us to the Lord—you would deign to offer faithful assistance to our brother and fellow bishop Lucifer and to our fellow presbyter Pancratius, who had set out together with my son Hilary the deacon; nor could you deny yourself to men whom you knew had undertaken so great a labor of travel in devotion to their faith. Therefore my mind received great relief from reading your letter; indeed, with God’s favor, I now confidently hope that the cause itself may advance for the better, because you did not wish to abandon our brothers. Labor, then, as a good soldier who awaits the reward of the eternal emperor; and strive to display—or, perhaps, “bring forth”—the strength of mind by which I know that you have despised the enticements of this world, against those who are blind to the light of the Church. Since you have contempt for this life, show yourself a true priest, so that, while you labor for the state of the Church, a council may be held and all the things which opponents, coming from another direction, have subtly contrived to prejudice the faith may be restored for the better. Eternal rewards accompany this labor, which your excellent faith knows better; and concerning the way in which we ought to apply ourselves to it, even if exhortation were to grow cold, the fervent Holy Spirit who is in you would, at every moment, spur your mind toward greater assistance for the unity of the holy Church.

II. I also sent a letter to our brother and fellow bishop Fortunatianus [Note: [Col. 1356D] (6) Ferrerius has *Fortunianus*, incorrectly. This is Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, who later became the very cause of Liberius’s falling away. Liberius indicates that he was then in the emperor’s retinue, or not far away, or that the envoys had perhaps made some delay at Vercelli or elsewhere on the journey, when he signifies that he had written to Fortunatianus to keep watch with the envoys and, should they so wish, not to withhold his presence from them.], whom I knew neither to fear human persons nor to think more of future rewards, in order that he too, in the sincerity of his heart and in the faith which he knows he has preserved even at the risk of his present life, might now deign to keep watch with you. For I know that, through the holiness of his heart, he will assuredly strengthen your wisdom by his counsel [Col. 1356C] and, if it so pleases you, will in no respect withhold his presence from your charity. May God keep you safe, dearest lord brother.

## LETTER

[Note: [Col. 1356D] (7) It appears in Hilary, fragment VI, from the Remigian and Pithoean manuscripts; likewise in Baronius, under the year 355, no. 32, and in Stephen Ferrerius, copied from the records of the Church of Vercelli and from a Vatican manuscript. It was written not long after the Synod of Milan, held in 355 and, as scholars think, at its beginning; before Liberius himself was summoned to Milan, indeed before he had learned with certainty and precision what had been done in the aforesaid synod; and thus about the middle of 355. Baronius, under the year 355, no. 54, testifies that in the Vatican manuscript it is read as addressed both to Eusebius [Col. 1357C] and to the other exiled bishops, Dionysius and all the rest. It would have been desirable for him to have transcribed the exact words of the manuscript. For I fear that this codex presents nothing other than what is found in Hilary: that, before Liberius went into exile, he wrote this identical letter to the confessors—that is, to Eusebius, Dionysius, and Lucifer, then in exile. If we adhere to the wording of that superscription, it was written not as an encyclical to all confessors exiled in different places, as Baronius writes, but as one identical letter to Eusebius, Dionysius, and Lucifer, or, as was later said by analogy, in three copies of one form. At one time I had considered it probable that the same letter was also sent to the presbyter Pancratius and the deacon Hilary; but since in the letter he addresses those whom he calls at first “most acceptable priests in the Lord,” thereafter “holy priests,” and at the end “lord brothers”; and since it is by no means fitting for a bishop, especially the bishop of Rome, to address his own clerics by these honorific titles, it seems more likely that Liberius wrote a separate letter to Pancratius and Hilary as sons. In the records of the Church of Vercelli the proper superscription addressed to Eusebius has been preserved in this form: “Liberius, bishop, to his beloved brother Eusebius”; but nothing has been altered in the body of the letter.]

## OF POPE LIBERIUS TO EUSEBIUS, DIONYSIUS, AND LUCIFER, IN EXILE  
*(A.D. 355)*

Having congratulated them on the glory of their confession, he commends himself to their prayers and asks that they inform him of everything done at Milan.

### I. Liberius desires exile and glories in the persecution inflicted by false brethren.

Although, under the appearance of peace, the enemy of the human race seems to have raged more violently against the members of the Church, [Col. 1357A] yet you, most acceptable priests in the Lord [Note: [Col. 1357D] (1) Thus Baronius. But the Pithoean manuscript has “most acceptable priests.” Ferrerius: “priests most acceptable to God.”], by your outstanding and singular faith, have shown yourselves here approved by God and have already been marked out as martyrs for future glory. By what proclamation of praise, then, by what exultation of speech, may I set forth the merits of your courage? Placed as I am between grief at your absence and joy at your glory, I cannot discover how—except that I know I shall offer you more fitting consolation if you believe that I have been driven into exile together with you.

Indeed, I am deeply grieved that I still hang in expectation, while harsher necessity meanwhile separates me from your fellowship. For I had wished, most devoted brothers, to be spent before all of you, so that by my example your charity might attain more fully [Col. 1357B] to the example of glory. But let this be the palm of your merits: that you have come first, through perseverance in the faith, to the illustrious glory of confession. I therefore entreat your charity to believe that I am present with you; and not to feel me absent in affection; and to understand that I am greatly grieved because I am meanwhile separated from your fellowship.

Moreover, you can know still more fully how great a glory you have attained from this: those who were crowned in persecution could feel only the blood-stained swords of the persecutor [Note: [Col. 1357D] (2) Ferrerius has: “that those who were crowned in persecution [felt] only the sword of the persecutor’s fruit.” The Pithoean manuscript agrees in these last three words. Baronius, however, prefers: “that those who … [felt] the blood-stained swords of persecution alone.” *Persecutor* should be retained, to be contrasted with the false brethren, from whom to suffer persecution was, in Liberius’s view, more grievous, and from whom to triumph more glorious.]; but you, soldiers of God wholly devoted, having experienced even false brethren as enemies, have won victory over treachery. And in proportion as their violence could increase in the world, rewards of praise are found to be bestowed upon holy priests.

### II. The confessors become nearer to God.

Be therefore secure in the heavenly promise; and because you have become nearer to God, raise me, your fellow priest and servant of God, to the Lord by your prayers, so that we may be able patiently to endure the assaults that come upon us, which, being announced day by day, inflict more grievous wounds; so that, with faith inviolate and the condition of the Catholic Church preserved, the Lord may deign to make me equal to you [Col. 1358B].

And because I desire to know more faithfully what was done in the very assembly [Note: [Col. 1358C] (3) Baronius reads “congregation,” rejecting in the margin “assembly,” which other books prefer—and indeed more aptly.], I beseech your Holiness to deign to make known everything faithfully by letter, so that either my spirit, which is tormented by conflicting reports, or the strength of my body itself, now exhausted, may receive greater reinforcement from your exhortation.

*(In another hand.)* May God keep you safe, lord brothers [Note: [Col. 1358C] (4) In place of this closing, Ferrerius reads: “May God keep you safe, dearest lord brother. Likewise deign to remember me also.” There, that is, the letter is presented as addressed to Eusebius alone.].

## SAYINGS OF POPE LIBERIUS

[Note: [Col. 1358C] (5) We have judged that a place should be given here to these sayings, since they are of the same kind as the letters and reveal the mind and judgment of Liberius no less than those letters do. For the same reason we shall append below the dialogue of Liberius with Constantius. As soon as Liberius’s envoys and the other confessors had departed from Milan for the place of exile, Constantius, hoping that through Liberius he would very soon win all men to his side, sent a certain eunuch named Eusebius with letters and gifts: the gifts were to flatter, [Col. 1358D] while the letters were to threaten. Having gone to Rome, this man first urged Liberius to subscribe against Athanasius and communicate with the Arians, saying that this was the emperor’s wish and command. Then, showing the gifts and touching Liberius’s hand, he said: “Obey the emperor and accept these.” The reply of Liberius which followed the eunuch’s words is given here from Athanasius’s *Letter to the Solitaries*, or *History of the Arians to the Monks*, no. 36.]

## TO THE EUNUCH EUSEBIUS, WHEN HE URGED HIM TO OBEY THE EMPEROR BY SUBSCRIBING AGAINST ATHANASIUS  
*(A.D. 355)*

[Note: [Col. 1358] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1357]

How, I ask, can this be done against Athanasius, as you advise? For how can we condemn one whom not merely one but a second synod, assembled from the whole world, lawfully declared pure and innocent, and whom the Roman [Note: [Col. 1358D] (6) Namely, the synod held in 342 under Julius, consisting of fifty bishops. It was followed in 347 by that of Sardica, gathered from the whole world. This was followed in 349 by the Synod of Jerusalem, which likewise declared Athanasius innocent. Athanasius transcribed the letters of these three synods in his *Apology against the Arians*, nos. 21, 37, and 57, vol. I, p. 365. There is no doubt that Liberius here mentions at least the first two.] synod dismissed in peace? Or who will approve us if we reject in his absence one whom we loved when present [Col. 1357C] and admitted to communion [Col. 1360A]?

That is not an ecclesiastical canon, nor have we ever received such a tradition from the fathers, who themselves received it from the blessed and great apostle Peter. But if the emperor is zealous for ecclesiastical peace, and orders that what was written among us in Athanasius’s favor be annulled, let whatever was done by them against him likewise be annulled; let also what has been done against all others be annulled. Then let an ecclesiastical synod be convened far from the palace, where neither the emperor is present, nor a count comes near, nor a judge makes threats; but where the fear of God alone, together with the ordinance of the apostles, suffices, so that above all the ecclesiastical faith may be preserved in the manner defined by the fathers at the Synod of Nicaea.

Let the adherents of Arian perversity be expelled and their heresy condemned by anathema; and then, after judicial inquiry concerning the accusations brought against Athanasius or any other person, and concerning those charges of which they themselves are accused, let the guilty be expelled, while the innocent live in confidence and security. For it is not lawful that those impious in faith be counted among a synod; nor is it fitting that inquiry into any other business be preferred to inquiry into the faith [Col. 1360B]. For first every disagreement concerning the faith must be cut off; then the other matters must be examined. For our Lord Jesus Christ did not heal the sick before they had shown and declared in words what faith they had toward him. We learned these things from the fathers; report them to the emperor. For they are beneficial both to him and to the edification of the Church. Let Ursacius and Valens not be heard: since they repented of their former actions, whatever they may now say, [Col. 1360C] they are by no means trustworthy [Note: [Col. 1359D] (1) Athanasius adds that the eunuch was angered by these words and, forgetting that he stood before a bishop, departed with grave threats, taking the gifts with him. He then did what Christians abhor: imitating Saul’s transgression, he placed those gifts at the martyr-shrine of the apostle Peter. When Liberius learned this, he was greatly angered with the keeper of the place for not having prevented the man, and threw out the gifts themselves as an unlawful sacrifice.].

[Col. 1358B]

How can this be done against Athanasius? For how can we condemn one whom not only one synod, but also a second synod gathered from all regions, properly acquitted, and whom the Church of Rome dismissed in peace? Or who will approve us if, after loving and admitting to communion one present, [Col. 1358C] we turn away from him when absent? This is not an ecclesiastical canon, nor have we ever received such a tradition from the fathers, who themselves received it from the blessed and great apostle Peter. But if the emperor is concerned for ecclesiastical peace, and orders the annulment of what has been written among us concerning Athanasius, let what has been done by them against him also be annulled, and likewise what has been done against all. Let an ecclesiastical synod then be held far from the palace [Col. 1359A], in which the emperor is not present, no count attends, no judge threatens, but the fear of God alone suffices, together with the ordinance of the apostles; so that, above all, the ecclesiastical faith may be preserved as the fathers defined it at the Synod of Nicaea. Let those who think Arian thoughts be expelled and their heresy anathematized. Then, after a judgment concerning the accusations against Athanasius and anyone else, and concerning the charges against their accusers themselves, let the guilty be expelled, but let the innocent possess freedom of speech. For those who are impious with respect to faith cannot be numbered with a synod; nor is inquiry into a matter to be preferred to inquiry concerning the faith. For every disagreement concerning faith must first be cut off; then an examination of the matters may be undertaken. For our Lord Jesus Christ did not heal sufferers before they showed and declared what faith they had in him. We learned these things from the fathers; report them to the emperor. For they benefit him and build up the Church. Let Ursacius and Valens not be heard [or perhaps, “not be listened to”]: for they repented in former times, and, though they now speak, are not trustworthy.

## DIALOGUE

[Note: [Col. 1359D] (2) Since the eunuch Eusebius accomplished nothing with Liberius, the emperor soon sent letters to the prefect at Rome ordering that Liberius be removed from the city and sent to him. The command of Constantius was carried out, as Ammianus Marcellinus relates in book XV, by Leontius, who is said to have entered upon the office of Prefect of the City on 6 July 355. Liberius, sent—or, as Athanasius says in the *History of the Arians to the Monks*, no. 39, dragged—to Milan, had the following dialogue with the emperor toward the end of 355. Introducing his account of it in book II, chapter 16, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, Theodoret says in chapter 15: “I now wish to commit to writing the celebrated Liberius’s boldness for the truth and the admirable words which he spoke before Constantius. For they were recorded by pious men, competent to urge and stir lovers of divine things to emulation.”]

## OF LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF ROME, AND THE EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS, HELD THREE DAYS BEFORE LIBERIUS WAS DEPORTED INTO EXILE  
*(A.D. 355)*

[Note: [Col. 1360] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1359]

### I. Both the judgment and the subscription condemning Athanasius were unjust.

[Col. 1360C] The Emperor Constantius said: “Since you are both a Christian and bishop of our city, we have judged it fitting to summon and admonish you to renounce communion with the impious Athanasius and his unspeakable madness. For the world has judged this to be right, and by synodal decision has decreed him alien from ecclesiastical communion.”

Bishop Liberius said: “Ecclesiastical judgments, O emperor, [Col. 1360D] must be rendered with the utmost fairness. Therefore, if it pleases Your Piety, order a tribunal to be established; and if Athanasius is found worthy of condemnation, then let sentence against him be pronounced in accordance with the rule of ecclesiastical procedure. For we cannot condemn a man whom we have not judged [Note: [Col. 1361D] (1) Those who recall what Julius writes in Letter I, no. 22—that if any suspicion falls upon the bishop of Alexandria, the Church of Rome is first to be written to, and then what is just is to be decreed—will suppose that Liberius here, and below where he repeats the same reason for not condemning Athanasius, has this custom in view. Perhaps this pope also says simply that Athanasius had not been judged, because he had so far not been condemned in any lawful judgment.].”

The Emperor Constantius said: “The whole world has pronounced judgment on his impiety, and he has been trifling with the times from the beginning.”

Bishop Liberius said: “All who subscribed did not themselves see the proceedings [Note: [Col. 1361D] (2) Not only did those who subscribed against Athanasius at Milan not see them, but neither did those who condemned him at Tyre. Julius addresses them thus in Letter I, no. 9: “If you demand that credit be given to your letters against Athanasius, it is consistent not to deny credit to those who wrote on his behalf—especially since you write concerning things done far away from you,” etc.]; but they subscribed for glory and out of fear, lest they suffer disgrace at your hands.”

The Emperor said: “What glory, what fear, what disgrace?”

Liberius replied: “Those who do not love the glory of God, preferring your gifts, condemned without prior trial one whom they had not seen; and that is foreign to Christians.”

[Col. 1359C]

**I.** Emperor Constantius said: “Because you are a Christian and bishop of our city, we judged you worthy of being summoned; and, having summoned you, we advise you to renounce communion with the unspeakable folly of the impious Athanasius. For the inhabited world judged this fitting and, by the decree of a synod, declared him alien to ecclesiastical communion.”

Bishop Liberius said: “Emperor, ecclesiastical judgments ought to be conducted with great justice. Therefore, if it pleases your Piety, order a tribunal to be established. If Athanasius is found worthy of condemnation, then a verdict against him shall be pronounced in accordance with the rule of ecclesiastical procedure. For it is impossible to condemn a man whom we have not judged.”

[Col. 1362A]

Emperor Constantius said: “The whole inhabited world has condemned his impiety, and from the beginning he has been mocking the present situation.”

Bishop Liberius said: “Those who subscribed were not eyewitnesses of what had happened, but did so for glory, fear, and disgrace from you.”

The Emperor said: “What are glory, fear, and disgrace?”

Liberius said: “Those who do not love God’s glory, preferring the gifts bestowed by you, condemned without judging one whom they had not seen with their own eyes; and this is foreign to Christians.”

### II. Athanasius was judged in absentia.

The Emperor said: “Yet he was judged in person at the Council of Tyre [Col. 1361B], and all the bishops of the world condemned him in the council.”

Liberius said: “He was never judged in person. All who then assembled and condemned Athanasius condemned him irrationally after he had withdrawn from the tribunal.”

The eunuch Eusebius said: “At the Council of Nicaea he was shown to be alien from the Catholic faith.”

Liberius said: “Only five judged, of those who sailed with Ischyras into Mareotis [Note: [Col. 1362D] (3) Liberius, disdaining to reply to this absurd interruption—as below he likewise disdains to answer Epictetus’s similar one—set an example to those who dispute about religion that time should not be wasted on pointless trifles.]: they had been sent to draw up proceedings against the accused. Of those sent then, two have departed from this life, namely Theognis and Theodore; three remain alive, namely Maris, Valens, and Ursacius [Note: [Col. 1362D] (4) If there is no error in the letter of the Alexandrian synod in Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, no. 13, then six rather than five must be said to have judged, and Macedonius must be added to those named below. Yet he is not numbered among those expressly condemned at the Synod of Sardica.]. At Sardica sentence was issued against those who had been sent for this reason. Later, at the synod [Note: [Col. 1362D] (5) Held near the city of Milan, as Valens and Ursacius themselves declare in Letter VII to Julius.], they submitted petitions [Col. 1361C] asking forgiveness for the proceedings which they had made against Athanasius in Mareotis through calumny and with only one side present. We now hold those petitions in our hands. To which of these, emperor, ought we to assent and communicate: to those who had formerly condemned Athanasius and later asked forgiveness, or to those who recently condemned these men at Sardica?”

Bishop Epictetus of Centumcellae said: “Liberius speaks today, emperor, not for the sake of faith nor in defence of ecclesiastical judgments, but in order to boast among the Roman senators that he has overcome the emperor.”

**II.** The Emperor said: “Yet the man was judged in person at the council held at Tyre, and all the bishops of the inhabited world condemned him in the council.”

Liberius said: “The man was never judged in person. For all who assembled at that time and condemned him did so without reason after Athanasius had departed from the tribunal.”

The eunuch Eusebius said: “At the Synod of Nicaea he was proved alien to the Catholic faith.”

Liberius said: “Only five of those who sailed with him to Mareotis judged—the men whom they sent to prepare memoranda against the accused. Of those sent, two have died, Theognis and Theodore; but the three remaining are alive: Maris, Valens, and Ursacius. Because of these delegates, a verdict was delivered at Sardica on this matter. At the synod, they submitted documents seeking pardon for the memoranda which they prepared against Athanasius in Mareotis, by calumny and with only one side present [Col. 1362C]. We now have these documents in hand. To which of these should we, emperor, submit and communicate: to those who first condemned him and afterwards sought forgiveness, or to those who have now condemned these men?”

Bishop Epictetus said: “Emperor, Liberius makes this speech today not for the sake of faith, nor as one concerned with ecclesiastical judgments, but so that he may boast among the senators in Rome that he has defeated the emperor by argument.”

### III. How Liberius wishes provision to be made for the peace of the Church.

The Emperor said to Liberius: “What part of the world are you, that you alone wish to support an impious man and to dissolve the peace of the inhabited world [Col. 1361D] and of the whole world?”

Liberius said: [Col. 1364A] “Even if I stand alone, the cause of the faith is not thereby diminished; for in ancient times only three were found who resisted the king’s command.”

The eunuch Eusebius said: “Do you make our emperor Nebuchadnezzar?”

Liberius said: “Not at all; but you rashly condemn a man whom we have not judged. I demand, however, that first a general subscription be issued confirming the faith set forth at Nicaea; then, after our brothers have been recalled from exile and restored to their sees, if those who now stir up tumults in the churches are found to agree with the apostolic faith, let us all meet at Alexandria, where the accused, the accusers, and his defender are; and, after examining their case, let us deliver a unanimous verdict.”

Bishop Epictetus said: “But the public post will by no means [Col. 1364B] suffice for the transport of the bishops.”

Liberius said: “Ecclesiastical affairs have no need of the public post; for the churches can easily send their bishops at their own expense as far as the sea.”

**III.** The Emperor said to Liberius: “What portion of the inhabited world are you, that you alone take the side of an impious man and destroy the peace of the inhabited world and the whole world?”

Liberius said: “The cause of faith is not diminished because I am alone; for in ancient times three alone were found resisting the command.”

The eunuch Eusebius said: “Have you made our emperor Nebuchadnezzar?”

Liberius said: “No; but you thus irrationally condemn a man whom we have not judged. Yet I demand that an ecumenical subscription first be issued, confirming the faith set forth at Nicaea; so that, once our brothers have been recalled from exile and restored to their own places, if those who now cause tumults in the churches are found to agree with the apostolic faith, then all of us may meet at Alexandria, where the accused, his accusers, and his defender are, and, after examining their case, may reach a common decision.”

Bishop Epictetus said: “But the public post cannot bear [Col. 1363B] the expense of the bishops’ journey.”

Liberius said: “Ecclesiastical matters have no need of the public post. The churches are able to send their own bishops as far as the sea.”

### IV. An absent person must not be accused. It is unworthy of a bishop to avenge a ruler’s private enmities.

The Emperor said: “What has already taken a fixed form can no longer be undone; for the decision of the greater number of bishops must prevail. You alone persist in the friendship of that impious man.”

Liberius said: “We have never heard, emperor, of a judge accusing an absent defendant of impiety as though he maintained a private enmity against him.”

The Emperor said: “He indeed injured everyone generally, but no one as much as me. Not content with bringing about the destruction of my elder brother, he never ceased to incite even Constans, of blessed memory, [Col. 1364C] to enmity with us [Note: [Col. 1363D] (1) Athanasius refutes this calumny at length in his *Apology to Constantius*. He begins his defence against it in no. 3 as follows: “With hand outstretched, as I learned from the Apostle, I call God to witness upon my soul; and, as it is written in the histories of the Kings, ‘The Lord is witness, and his Christ is witness’—and I ask that I too may be permitted to say this—that I never spoke ill of your Piety to your brother Constans, the most pious Augustus of blessed memory, nor incited him against you, as these men slanderously allege.”], had we not with greater gentleness endured the assault both of the inciter and of the one incited. No victory—not even that which I won over Magnentius and Silvanus—do I value as highly as the removal of that criminal from the administration of the Church.”

Liberius said: “Do not avenge your enmities through bishops, emperor. The hands of churchmen ought to be free for sanctifying and blessing. Therefore, if it pleases you, order the bishops to be recalled to their own sees; and if they are found to agree with him who maintains the orthodox faith set forth long ago at Nicaea, then, assembling together, let them provide for the peace of the world, lest a man who has committed no offence be found branded.”

The Emperor [Col. 1364D] said: “One thing is at issue: once you have embraced communion with the churches, I wish to send you back to Rome. Therefore assent to peace and subscribe, and so return to Rome.”

Liberius said: “I have already bidden farewell to the brothers at Rome. For ecclesiastical laws are weightier than residence at Rome.”

The Emperor said: “You therefore have an interval of three days to deliberate whether you wish to return to Rome after subscribing, [Col. 1363D] or to consider to what place you wish to be deported.”

Liberius said: “An interval of three days or of three months does not change my resolve. Therefore send me wherever you will.”

**IV.** The Emperor said: “What has already taken a fixed form cannot be dissolved; for the decision of the greater number of bishops must prevail. You alone claim the friendship of that impious man.”

Liberius said: “Emperor, we have never heard of a judge denouncing impiety when the accused is absent, as though introducing a private enmity against the man.”

The Emperor said: “He wronged all men in common, but none so much as me. Not content with the destruction of my elder brother, he did not cease to provoke even the blessed Constans to enmity with us; had we not with greater gentleness endured the impulse of both the provoker and the provoked [Col. 1363C]. No achievement—not even that against Magnentius and Silvanus—means so much to me as the removal of that foul man from ecclesiastical affairs.”

Liberius said: “Do not avenge your enmity through bishops, emperor. For the hands of churchmen ought to be available for sanctifying. Therefore, if it pleases you, order the bishops recalled to their own places. And if they are found of one mind with him who now maintains the orthodox faith set forth at Nicaea, then, having assembled together, let them provide for the peace of the world, lest a man who has committed no sin be found marked.”

The Emperor said: “There is one issue. Once you have embraced communion with the churches, I wish to send you back to Rome. Therefore be persuaded toward peace and, having subscribed, return to [Col. 1363D] Rome.”

Liberius said: “I have already taken leave of the brothers in Rome. For ecclesiastical ordinances are greater than residence in Rome.”

The Emperor said: “Accordingly, you have three days for deliberation: whether you wish, after subscribing, to return to Rome, or to consider to what place you wish to be transferred.”

Liberius said: “An interval of three days or months does not alter my judgment. Therefore send me wherever you wish.”

### V. He rejects the gifts brought to him.

[Col. 1365A] Two days later the emperor summoned Liberius; and when he did not depart from his decision, he ordered him relegated to Beroea, a city of Thrace. When Liberius had departed, the emperor sent him five hundred gold solidi for expenses. But Liberius said to the bearer: “Go, return them to the emperor; he needs them to provide for his soldiers.”

Likewise the Empress sent him the same amount. Liberius said: “Return them to the emperor; for he needs them for the pay of his soldiers. If the emperor does not need them, let him give them to Auxentius and Epictetus, for they need them.”

When he refused to accept gifts from them, the eunuch Eusebius brought him others. Liberius said to him: “You have emptied and desolated the churches of the inhabited world, and you bring me alms as though I were a criminal [Col. 1365B]. Go; first become a Christian [Note: [Col. 1365C] (1) Theodoret adds: “And after three days he was banished, having accepted nothing.”].”

[Col. 1366A]

**V.** After two days the Emperor, Liberius having been summoned and not having changed his resolve, ordered him exiled to Beroea in Thrace. When Liberius had gone out, the Emperor sent him five hundred solidi for expenses. Liberius said to the bearer: “Go away; give them to the Emperor, for he needs them to give to his soldiers.”

Likewise the Empress sent him the same sum. Liberius said: “Give them back to the Emperor, for he needs them for the provisioning of his troops. But if the Emperor does not need them, let him give them to Auxentius and Epictetus, for they need them.”

When he did not receive anything from them, the eunuch Eusebius offered him other gifts. Liberius said to him: “You have made the churches of the inhabited world desolate, and you offer me alms as to a condemned man. Go away; first become a Christian.”

## LETTER

[Note: [Col. 1365C] (2) Hilary transmitted this letter to us along with the following two, fragment VI, no. 5 and following. Baronius also made them public from two copies of what he calls the Cresconian collection, under the year 357, no. 34. That they had been transferred into the aforesaid collection, whoever its compiler may have been, from no other source than Hilary’s work is plainly shown by Hilary’s own notes, either inserted in or appended to the text; Baronius admits that he found these in his copies in the second editions. Athanasius sufficiently indicates the time when these three letters were written in the *History of the Arians to the Monks*, no. 41: “Liberius, made an exile, was finally broken after two years and, terrified by threats of death, subscribed.” Likewise Theodoret, book II, chapter 17, who, if he did not know of Liberius’s fall, altogether conceals it, reports that, after Liberius had spent two years in exile, he was recalled to the city at the petition of the wives of Roman nobles. It has been shown above that Liberius was banished toward the end of 355 [Col. 1365D]. These letters must therefore be dated about the end of 357. A learned man considers them somewhat later than the letters written to Constantius; but if the addition be admitted which we supply from manuscript evidence in Letter XI, no. 2, it must be acknowledged that the same Fortunatianus delivered at the same time both a copy of this Letter X and Liberius’s letter to Constantius. It is indeed probable that the emperor was then in Pannonia, and that Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius were in his retinue. If that is so, the following letter of Liberius to these leaders of the Arian faction is readily understood to have been sent through the same Fortunatianus. Moreover, throughout this whole affair, as Athanasius observes in the passage soon to be cited, both the violence of the Arians and Liberius’s hatred of that heresy, as well as his support for Athanasius, are established for as long as he retained free power over his own will. For things extracted by the force of tortures contrary to an earlier judgment are the decisions not of those who fear, but of those who afflict.]

## OF POPE LIBERIUS TO THE EASTERNERS  
*(A.D. 357)*

He states that he has abandoned the defence of Athanasius, that he has peace with them, and that he has accepted the faith set forth at Sirmium and offered to him by Demophilus. Let them also work for his release from exile.

To the beloved brothers, presbyters, and fellow bishops of the East [Note: [Col. 1366C] (3) Baronius: “to the brothers and bishops.”], greetings.

### I.

Your holy faith, through the fear of God, is known to God and to people of good will. As the Law says: “Judge justly, sons of men” (Psalm 57:2), I do not defend Athanasius. But because Julius, the bishop of blessed memory, my predecessor, had received him, I feared lest I be judged a transgressor. Yet when I learned, as it pleased God, that you had justly condemned him, I immediately gave my assent to your judgments and gave letters concerning his name [Note: [Col. 1366C] (4) In the manuscripts, as also in Baronius, there is added here: “that is, concerning his condemnation.” Nicolaus Faber judged this to have been inserted from Hilary’s interpretation. Liberius, in Letter 3, no. 1, and again in Letter 11, nos. 1 and 2, recalls his letters “about his name” and “concerning his name” without any interpretation added. In these places, however, *name*—Greek *to onoma*—by itself means rather the person or the case than the condemnation. Certainly no one should interpret this word as “condemnation” in what Liberius himself writes in Letter 12, no. 2: that he had withdrawn from that dispute “from the name of Athanasius.” Similar is what Pope Zosimus says to Caelestius in Augustine, book II, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 4: “You condemn all those things which have been alleged concerning your name”; and Augustine immediately adds: “Among the other things alleged concerning his name.” And shortly afterward: “How then did he reply that he had condemned those things which had been alleged concerning his name …?”] through our brother Fortunatianus [Note: [Col. 1366D] (5) Not at another time, but at the same time. Nor is it unusual for supreme pontiffs, when they write several letters on the same matter to different persons, to inform those to whom they write and whom it concerns of the other letters dispatched at the same time and speaking of the same matter. This Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, is judged detestable by Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 107, because he was the first to solicit and break Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, as he went into exile for the faith, and compelled him to subscribe to heresy.] to be carried to the Emperor Constantius.

Accordingly, with Athanasius removed [Note: [Col. 1366D] (6) Baronius reads: “with Athanasius removed, concerning whom the decisions of all of you are to be accepted together with the Apostolic See, I say,” etc.; and shortly afterward, “unity,” not “unanimity.”] from the communion of us all—and letters from him are not to be received by me—I declare that I have peace and unanimity with all of you and with all the Eastern bishops throughout every province.

II. For, that you may know more truly that I declare these things to you in true faith by this letter, my common lord and brother Demophilus, who in his kindness deigned to set forth your faith and the Catholic faith—a faith discussed, set forth, and accepted at Sirmium by many of our brothers and fellow-bishops—I have accepted with a willing mind; in no point have I opposed it; I have given my assent; I follow it; it is held by me. I therefore thought that I should entreat your Holiness, since you now clearly see that in all things I agree with you, to deign by common counsel and effort to work so that I may now be released from exile and return to the see divinely entrusted to me.

[Note: [Col. 1366D] (7) In the same author: “to declare the true faith through my letter.” After the verb *loqui* (“to speak”), or *proloqui* (“to declare”), the completeness of the sentence requires *quam proposuit* (“which he set forth”), or something similar.]

[Note: [Col. 1367A] (1) Thus the Pithoean manuscript. But the copies of Baronius and Sirmond read: “the true faith.”]

[Note: [Col. 1367B] (2) Between the words “was accepted” and what follows, Hilary inserted: “This is Arian perfidy; I have noted this, not the apostate.” Liberius continues. Supported by this note, some learned men think that Liberius accepted not the formula of faith written at Sirmium in 351 against Photinus, but that published in the same city in 357 under the name of Hosius. Hilary, in *On the Synods*, no. 10, calls the latter by no other name than “the third blasphemy,” and seems to excuse the formula composed against Photinus.

But let them observe, I pray, that Hilary does not here say, “This is the blasphemy of Hosius and Potamius,” but “This is Arian perfidy.” Then let them recall what the same holy confessor asserts in *Against Constantius*, no. 24: “Whatever is besides the one faith is PERFIDY, not faith.” Thus even the first Sirmian formula, as being outside the Nicene faith, was judged by him not to be faith but perfidy.

Nor does the pious bishop contradict himself when, on the one hand, he congratulates the Easterners because they proclaimed that the Son of God was no longer from nothing but like the Father in substance, and, although they did not yet profess the true faith, were nevertheless approaching it more closely and offering hope of a return to it; while, on the other hand, he charges Liberius—departing from the defence of the Nicene faith and yielding to acceptance of Eastern propositions—with perfidy.

Moreover, this was Arian perfidy, because Liberius testifies that he accepted the faith set before him by Demophilus. Demophilus belonged to those who interpreted *homoiousion* heretically; of them Hilary says in *On the Synods*, no. 74: “Nor am I unaware, for example, that there are some who, while confessing likeness, deny equality.” Liberius was therefore considered to have accepted *homoiousion* in the sense in which the man who induced him to accept it understood that term. So too later the fathers of the Council of Rimini, although they subscribed to the faith offered them by the Arians with a Catholic intention and assented to the silence concerning consubstantiality, were everywhere called Arians and deserters of the orthodox faith, as Jerome testifies.

But, in order certainly to know whether Liberius subscribed to the first Sirmian formula or the second, who are called “Easterners,” and what faith they professed, this must be examined; for Liberius repeatedly says that he accepted the faith, peace, and communion of the Easterners. Now Hilary, throughout his whole book *On the Synods*, calls “Easterners” not those who composed the Sirmian blasphemy in 357, but those who embraced the faith set forth at Antioch in 341, at Sardica—or rather Philippopolis—in 347, and at Sirmium in 351, and who finally at Ancyra in 358 vigorously opposed the aforesaid blasphemy and immediately compelled its authors to suppress it. Therefore, when Liberius says that he accepted the faith of the Easterners set forth at Sirmium, he indicates not that blasphemy but the faith composed against Photinus.

Further, the authors of the Sirmian blasphemy are named by Hilary, *On the Synods*, no. 11, as none other than Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius; add also, if you wish, Hosius and Potamius, although there it is said to have been composed by the former not because they composed it, but because they subscribed to it. But when Liberius first writes to the Easterners, he expressly declares that he has accepted and follows their faith. Then, in separate letters sent to Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius, though he omits nothing by which he might win their favor, he does not even by a word indicate that he gave assent to the formula of faith said to have been discussed and debated at Sirmium in their presence. For in those letters his principal object is that, after the letter to the Easterners has been copied out, they may be informed of the peace established with them. Thus Liberius assented to the faith which the Easterners, though not in the same sense, generally professed—not to that which the three Western bishops had issued and which was immediately proscribed and suppressed through the efforts of many Easterners. I refrain from recounting further arguments proving that this pope subscribed only to the first Sirmian formula, because they have been treated extensively by Hilary in this very passage.]

---

[Note: [Col. 1368C] (4) Baronius accepted this letter as genuine under the year 357, no. 53; but later, in the appendix, p. 25, retracting his opinion and misled by a false interpretation of a corrupt passage, as note b will show, he wished it to be spurious and fabricated by the very persons who had forged the other letter which we have relegated to the appendix. Binius adopts this latter opinion, and Labbe does not oppose it. But Hilary’s same notes on this letter as on the preceding one—in which he alike pronounces anathema upon the betrayer—do not permit us to doubt that he believed both to have one and the same author. Indeed, what need was there for forged letters when genuine ones abounded in which Liberius condemned Athanasius? Impatient to see Rome again, he was not content to implore the aid of the Easterners, but also judged it necessary to seek the favor of Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius, who had great influence with the emperor and, as it seems, were then in his retinue.]

## LETTER OF POPE LIBERIUS TO URSACIUS, VALENS, AND GERMINIUS

*(At the end of the year 357.)*

That he is separated from communion with Athanasius and has peace with the Easterners, as also with Auxentius and Epictetus; and that they should arrange for him to be sent back by Constantius to his own church.

Liberius, from exile, to Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius.

[Col. 1368A]

I. Since I know that you are sons of peace and love also concord and the unity of the Catholic Church, I address you meanwhile, dearest lords and brothers, not compelled by any necessity, but, God being witness, for the good of peace and concord, which is to be preferred to martyrdom. Let your prudence therefore know that Athanasius, who was bishop of the Alexandrian church, before I wrote—or something similar—to the court of the holy emperor, in accordance with the letters of the Eastern bishops, was separated from the communion of the Roman church, as the whole presbyterium of the Roman church testifies.

But this was the reason why I seemed slower in sending letters concerning his name to our Eastern brothers: that my legates, whom I had sent from the city of Rome to the court, or the bishops who had been deported, might themselves, together with those legates if possible, be recalled from exile.

[Note: [Col. 1368D] (5) Against Athanasius, as we have already observed from Athanasius himself, *History of the Arians to the Monks*, no. 41: Liberius, terrified by threats of death, subscribed, and thus by no means freely. There is a suspicion that this clause was added not so much at his own prompting as at that of those by whom he was overcome and intimidated. Something similar later befell Pope Vigilius, who, while detained at Constantinople and suffering many things by force, was allowed to write nothing to the bishops of Gaul and Scythia except what pleased Emperor Justinian.]

[Note: [Col. 1368D] (6) In Baronius: “my dearest lords.” Our reading better accords with the style of Liberius. For in the three letters to Eusebius cited above one constantly reads, “dearest lord brother,” not “my dearest lord brother.”]

[Note: [Col. 1369B] (1) There are three different readings available for this passage. Having long and carefully weighed them, we have decided to prefer the corrupt reading published by Nicolaus Faber from the Pithoean archetype to the other two, which seem more complete but are not free from suspicion of interpolation. We have indicated beside the text how it may be repaired.

Baronius presents the other reading thus: “Before I came to the court of the holy emperor, Athanasius was separated from the communion of the Roman church in accordance with the letters of the Eastern bishops.” In this reading nothing is lacking for completeness of expression; but the word *pervenissem* (“I came”), which he seems to have added of his own accord, cannot be reconciled with historical truth. So much so that, when the same Cardinal revised the third volume of his *Annals*, because of that one word—which he had perhaps then forgotten had been added with no authority from ancient manuscripts—he rejected in the appendix to that volume the whole letter which he had inserted in its place as genuine, declaring it spurious.

Certainly, from such a reading it follows that this letter deserves to be accused of fabrication no less than the other letter in which Liberius is made to condemn Athanasius at the beginning of his pontificate. But one who asserts this as certain must still ask whether the word *pervenissem* can in any way cohere with the words that follow. For the subsequent words manifestly indicate the time when the legates of Liberius—Lucifer, Pancratius, and Hilary—as well as the bishops Eusebius, Dionysius, and others, had been deported into exile. Yet around the time of Liberius at which the spurious letter makes him condemn Athanasius, neither these legates nor these bishops were exiles. Therefore the phrase “before I came to the court” belongs to another time: to what time, I ask, except the time when Liberius was working so that he and others banished for the same cause might have an opportunity to return from exile? Hence Baronius’s correction, and the criticism based solely upon it by which he judges this letter fictitious, cannot be approved at all.

More tolerable, and not wholly to be rejected, is the reading which Jacques Sirmond formerly collected from the Remigian copy, which we were unable to obtain, as follows: “Athanasius, who was bishop of the Alexandrian church, was condemned by me before I sent letters of the Eastern bishops to the court of the holy emperor, and was separated from the communion of the Roman church.” We preferred it in the new edition of Hilary’s works, not as indubitable, but because it presents a passage needing a physician’s hand as somewhat healed. Yet there remains a difficulty: Liberius is said there to have sent letters of the Easterners to the court, whereas he himself is silent about this in other letters, and neither the Pithoean nor the Baronian manuscripts support this reading. Indeed, the phrase preserved in these manuscripts, “in accordance with the letters of the Easterners,” seems better to agree with historical truth.]

[Note: [Col. 1370B] (2) In Baronius, “witness.” We retain with the Pithoean manuscript “testifying.” Thus Liberius seems to have used *testis* and *teste* as one now uses “faithful” in masculine and neuter forms. Further, from the sixth letter of Pope Siricius we have already proved that the word *presbyterium* denotes an assembly not only of presbyters and deacons but also of the whole clergy. Therefore, just as Liberius, after his defection, wrote letters to Vincent of Capua and perhaps others, so we understand from this that he wrote to the Roman clergy at that time also, in order to restore their former affection toward himself.

Before his exile, that clergy was so devoted to him that, on the day when he departed for exile, as the presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus relate in the preface to their petitions, the whole clergy—that is, the presbyters, Archdeacon Felix, intruded into his office, Damasus himself, then a deacon, and all the church’s officers—together, in the presence of the Roman people, confirmed on oath that while Liberius lived they would in no way have another pontiff. Jerome briefly summarizes this in his *Chronicle*: “All the clerics swore that they would receive no other.”]

[Note: [Col. 1370C] (3) In the Pithoean manuscript, and thence in Nicolaus Faber: “that the legates and those whom…” Better in Baronius: “that my legates”—namely Lucifer, Pancratius, and Hilary—whom he had sent to Constantius to request a council. Therefore, just as Liberius, before his exile, in the dialogue with the emperor, no. 3, insisted that his brethren be recalled from exile, so even as an exile he did not desist from the same concern for them, wishing, as far as lay in him, not to return to his church without them.]

II. I also want you to know that I asked brother Fortunatianus to carry my letters to the most gracious emperor, letters which I wrote to the Eastern bishops, so that they might know, together with him, that I am separated from communion with Athanasius. I believe that his piety will receive them with rejoicing for the good of peace. I have also sent a copy of them to Hilary, the emperor’s faithful servant.

Let your charity clearly see that I have acted in this matter with a kindly and innocent mind. Therefore by these my letters I address and adjure you through almighty God and Christ Jesus, his Son, our God and Lord, that you may deign to go to the most gracious Emperor Constantius Augustus and ask that, for the good of peace and concord—in which his piety always rejoices—he may command me to return to the church entrusted to me by God, so that in his time the Roman church may suffer no tribulation.

By these my letters you ought to know, dearest brothers, that I have peace with all of you, bishops of the Catholic Church, in an equitable and sincere spirit. For you will gain great comfort on the day of recompense if through you peace is restored to the Roman church. I also wish you to make known to our brothers and fellow-bishops Epictetus and Auxentius that I have peace and ecclesiastical communion with them; I believe that they will gladly receive these things. But whoever dissents from our peace and concord, which by God’s will has been established throughout the world, should know that he is separated from our communion.

[Note: [Col. 1370C] (4) The words enclosed in brackets have been supplied from the manuscripts of Baronius and Sirmond. In their place the Pithoean manuscript has only: “I asked that he should go with my letters to the most gracious Emperor Constantius, to ask.” Although much shorter, this reading seems to leave nothing lacking for completeness of expression. It also agrees sufficiently with the words of the preceding Letter 10, no. 2. But the following phrase, “For great comfort indeed…,” coheres more suitably with our supplement.]

[Note: [Col. 1370D] (5) In Baronius: “received, a copy of which your charity should also deliver to Philagrius, the emperor’s eunuch; these things I…”—corruptly. Athanasius mentions Hilary, the notary employed by Constantius, in the *History of the Arians to the Monks*, nos. 48 and 81.]

[Note: [Col. 1370D] (6) Baronius: “his Son and our Lord and the Holy Spirit, that…”]

[Note: [Col. 1370D] (7) In the same author: “great reward also for you.” The Pithoean manuscript itself preserves: “for great comfort indeed for you,” although nothing precedes to which the particle *enim* (“indeed/for”) can refer, unless we admit the supplement copied from the manuscripts of Sirmond and Baronius.]

[Note: [Col. 1371B] (1) How intimate this Epictetus was with Constantius is shown by the preceding dialogue between the same emperor and Liberius, where each is recorded as having interrupted more than once. Concerning Auxentius, Athanasius writes in the *History of the Arians to the Monks*, no. 75: “Constantius sent a certain Auxentius, more a litigious man than a Christian, from Cappadocia to Milan, namely into the place of Dionysius, whom he had banished.” Liberius therefore tries at the same time to bind Ursacius, Valens, Epictetus, and Auxentius to himself, since, continually present at Milan in the court of Constantius, they possessed great influence with that emperor.]

[Note: [Col. 1371C] (2) In all manuscripts there follows here: “I have pronounced anathema upon the prevaricator together with the Arians.” These words are not Liberius’s, as Baronius thought, but Hilary’s. For that bishop, carried away by constant zeal for the faith, lest he seem to assent to the betrayal—upon which in the preceding letter he had already pronounced anathema upon the betrayer—judged that he must once more pronounce anathema upon one repeating the betrayal. He had learned from Paul, Galatians 1:2, that even an apostle or angel from heaven ought to be anathema if afterward he should proclaim something different from what he had proclaimed before.]

---

[Note: [Col. 1371D] (3) It seems to have been conveyed by the same person whom Liberius employed to send his other letter on the same matter to the presbyterium, that is, his clergy. If this is so, Liberius’s letters to Constantius, to the Easterners, to Ursacius and his associates, to his clergy, and to Vincent were written and dispatched at the same time. For in these, as in the others, mention is made of the letter to the Easterners. Nor is it inconsistent that in the preceding letter, no. 1, he calls his own clergy witnesses that Athanasius had been separated from the communion of the Roman Church before he sent the emperor letters on the matter. He could conveniently call them witnesses if, from letters composed at the same time, he thought those addressed to the clergy should be delivered to them before the others. Perhaps we seem to have examined this point too scrupulously. But I judged that nothing should be neglected that might lessen the fault of a pontiff previously so distinguished in his deeds. That fault will be much lighter if Liberius, at the very time when he was overcome and worn down by the weariness of exile and the threat of death, either himself wrote so many letters unworthy of his name or subscribed letters presented by Demophilus, than if he is supposed to have written repeatedly at intervals—now to the clergy, soon after to the Easterners, later to the emperor, and so forth.]

## LETTER OF POPE LIBERIUS TO VINCENT, BISHOP OF CAPUA

*(A.D. 357.)*

Concerning the comfort he derived from the assistance of Urbicus, which was taken from him; that he has withdrawn from the name of Athanasius and has peace with the Easterners; that Vincent should inform the bishops of Campania of this and, together with them, write to the emperor so that he may be recalled from exile.

Liberius, from exile, to Vincent.

[Col. 1371B]

I. I do not teach but remind your holy mind, dearest brother, that evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33). You know well the snares of evil men, by which I have come to this suffering; pray that the Lord may grant endurance. My most beloved son Urbicus, the deacon, whom I seemed to have as a comfort, has been taken from me through Venerius, the *agens in rebus*.

II. I thought it right to make known to your Holiness that I have withdrawn from that controversy concerning the name of Athanasius, and have sent letters to our Eastern brothers and fellow-bishops concerning his name. Therefore, since, by God’s will, peace is everywhere with you, deign to summon all the bishops of Campania, explain these matters to them, and, from among their number, write together with your letter to the most gracious emperor concerning our unanimity and peace, so that I too may be freed from great distress.

*(In his own hand):* May God keep you safe, brother.

*(Again, in his own hand, on the page written over):* We have peace with all the Eastern bishops, and with you. I have acquitted myself before God; you must see to yourselves. If you wish me to waste away in exile, God will be judge between me and you.

[Note: [Col. 1372C] (4) Labbe, following Baronius: “And therefore to your Holiness…”]

[Note: [Col. 1372C] (5) In Baronius: “that controversy of the name.”]

[Note: [Col. 1372C] (6) Baronius: “peace is with us,” omitting the preceding “therefore, since by God’s will…”—corruptly.]

[Note: [Col. 1372C] (7) Sirmond: “the page written over.” In Baronius: “dearest lord brother. Again, in his own hand, written on the same page.” After the word *perscriptae* (“written over”), “is added” is understood.]

---

## LETTER OF LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, TO THE CATHOLIC BISHOPS OF ITALY

*(A.D. 363.)*

That pardon ought not to be refused to those who lapsed at Rimini; and on what condition they should be admitted.

Liberius, to the Catholic bishops established throughout Italy: eternal salvation in the Lord.

[Col. 1372B]

I. Repentance effaces the fault of ignorance. This is also evident from the Holy Scriptures. We read that godliness is profitable for all things (1 Timothy 4:8), and bodily exercise yields to it, although it too retains some fruit of usefulness; the circumstances of the present time require us to pursue this course.

For if some perhaps, who make it their concern to destroy by a harsher judgment what has prudently been provided, have thought that what has already been established by apostolic authority concerning godliness ought to be changed—when it was said that those who acted ignorantly at Rimini should not be spared, because their not knowing what was unlawful led them into the snare of error, and therefore the severity of discipline must be meted out to them—yet it seemed to me, whose duty it is to weigh everything moderately, especially since all the Egyptians and the assembled Achaeans have accepted the judgment, that pardon should indeed be granted to many of those whom we discussed above; but that the authors should be condemned, who by crooked and malicious subtlety and darkness wounded innocent minds, in order to draw a veil over truth, selling darkness as light and light as darkness.

[Note: [Col. 1372C] (8) This letter has been preserved for us among Hilary’s fragments, indeed covered with errors, but so elucidated in the most recent edition of Hilary that what Liberius states, approves, or condemns is no longer obscure. Some think it is cited in Letter I of Siricius to Himerius, no. 2, where that pope, after the Council of Rimini had been annulled, recalls “general decrees sent to the provinces by Liberius, my predecessor of reverend memory.” But there Siricius praises decrees specifically forbidding anyone to rebaptize Arians returning to the Catholic faith; nothing of that sort occurs in this letter.

It is clear that this letter was written not, as Baronius thought, before the Alexandrian Synod, but after it. For it expressly approves the judgment of the Egyptians assembled at that synod and of the Achaeans who met later. Indeed, it also not obscurely notes the dissent of Lucifer, to whom the moderation of the Alexandrian Synod was displeasing. Hence it cannot be dated earlier than 363.]

[Note: [Col. 1372D] (9) Perhaps: “For if some perhaps, who make it their concern to destroy by a harsher judgment what has been wisely provided, should have thought that they could invalidate—or renew—what has already been established by apostolic authority concerning godliness, contending that those who acted—or erred—ignorantly at Rimini ought not to be spared, since not to know what was unlawful was to fall into the snare—or trap—of error, therefore the severity of discipline must be repaid to them. But it seemed to me, whose duty it is to weigh everything moderately, especially since all the Egyptians and the assembled Achaeans have accepted this judgment, that pardon should indeed be granted to those of whom we have spoken above, namely those who fell into the snare of error in such a way that, with conscience unharmed, they consented to the heretics. Then what is said concerning the authors of impiety must not be understood as though pardon were denied even to them, but because hope of remaining in the clergy has been taken from them.

This is what Athanasius teaches in the Letter to Rufinianus: that it pleased bishops not only in Egypt but also in Greece, Spain, Gaul, and everywhere that, if those who had lapsed were authors of impiety, pardon should be granted them if they repent, but no place in the clergy should be given them; while to those who did not sponsor iniquity but were drawn into it by necessity and force, both pardon should be granted and a place in the clergy given.”]

[Note: [Col. 1373D] (1) Or: “has already been established by the authority of the Apostolic See.” Hence it follows that the decree concerning the reception of the lapsed, first enacted by the Alexandrian Synod and shown in the preceding note from Athanasius’s Letter to Rufinianus to have been approved everywhere, was also received by the Romans. Athanasius’s own letter, as read in the First Session of the Second Council of Nicaea, in Labbe, vol. VII, pp. 75 and 680, expressly attests this. There, after the words of the Alexandrian decree have been reported, it adds: “These things were also written at Rome—or, as the ancient translation in Labbe, p. 680, has it, ‘to Rome’—and were received by the church of the Romans.”

Our colleagues observed that this phrase is lacking in the old Athanasian manuscripts which they examined; nevertheless, the authority of the ancient Greek and Latin copies of the Second Council of Nicaea, which contain it, seems preferable, especially because the ensuing statement of Sabas and the other monks concerning the Alexandrian decree in some way requires it: “It is not the voice of Athanasius alone, but also of synods; for the same father says that both Romans and Greeks received it.” This passage of Liberius persuades us that “Romans” there must include the Roman church. Further, that Liberius and the Roman church adhered to the decree of the Alexandrian Synod concerning bishops who lapsed at Rimini is evident both from this letter itself, from Hilary’s Fragment XII, no. 3, and from Rufinus’s *History*, Book I, chapter 30.]

II. Therefore, if anyone, recovering from the snare of ignorance, has experienced within himself that pestilential, deceitful, and dark poison of Arian doctrine, let him, restored by the very gentle advocacy of our word, now drain it out, condemn it, and rage more vehemently against its authors, whose violence he has experienced in himself; and let him anew devote his entire self to the apostolic and Catholic faith as far as the Council of Nicaea. By this profession, even if it seems slight and lenient to some, let him recover what he had lost through the craftiness of falsehood.

But if anyone of such foolish mind should be found—which I do not believe—who not only refuses to turn back, having received the antidote of healing, but thinks that he ought to claim for himself poisonous venom and destructive infection, he shall be overcome by reason; and, being utterly assigned to the author of perfidy, he shall be punished by the spiritual force of the Catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 1374C] (2) In the Pithoean manuscript, *benissima*, perhaps for *lenissima* (“very gentle”) or *benignissima* (“very kind”). Shortly afterward, the Sirmond manuscript has *latebrosum* (“hidden, obscure”), not *tenebrosum* (“dark”). The sentence will be less obscure if constructed thus: “Therefore, if anyone, recovering from the snare—or from the snare of—ignorance, had experienced that deceitful and dark—or hidden—pestilential poison of Arian doctrine within himself, restored by the very gentle exhortation of our word, let him now drain it out and condemn it.”]

[Note: [Col. 1374D] (3) That is, let him do what the Macedonian bishops in the following letter, at Liberius’s command, profess: “We acknowledge this to be the Catholic and apostolic faith, which remained whole and unshaken down to the Council of Nicaea.” Both passages refute the opinion of those for whom the fathers preceding the Nicene Synod appeared to favor Arius’s doctrines.]

[Note: [Col. 1374D] (4) Perhaps: “But rather he claims for himself the poison and venom.” This passage is clarified by another in the following Letter 15, which Liberius again closes thus: “If after this council they refuse to vomit forth the poison of perverse doctrine, reject all Arius’s blasphemies, and condemn them by anathema, let them know that they, together with Arius and his disciples and the other serpents … are strangers and alienated from the communion of the Church.”]

---

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE TWO FOLLOWING LETTERS

[Col. 1374A]

I. We owe the first of the following two letters to Socrates, Book IV, chapter 12, and likewise to Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 11; the second only to Socrates in the same place, though Sozomen also mentions it. It will be worthwhile here to draw briefly from both the occasion on which they were written.

When Eudoxius, relying on the authority of Emperor Valens, began to harass the Macedonians, they, fearing the evils threatening them, sent embassies among themselves from city to city and judged that it was better to flee to Valentinian and to the bishop of Rome, and join their communion, than to share with Valens and the followers of Eudoxius in the doctrine of faith. They therefore sent three bishops from their number: Eustathius of Sebaste, Silvanus of Tarsus, and Theophilus of Castabala, with letters written to Liberius, bishop of Rome, and to the Western bishops, both from the city of Smyrna in Asia and from Pamphylia, Isauria, and Lycia, where they had held councils.

“Sozomen says that “they urged them to assist their envoys with every effort, deliberate with them what ought to be done, and restore the condition of the Church as seemed best to them; since they retained the sound and stable faith handed down from the apostles and, beyond all others, ought to have a care for religion.” These letters were long and therefore omitted by Socrates. Consequently, they have not reached us at all.

When the envoys arrived in Rome, they could not approach Valentinian, who was detained by war in Gaul, and so presented their letters to Liberius. “At first he refused to receive them, saying that they belonged to the Arian party and could not be received by the Church, since they had abrogated the Nicene faith. But they replied that they had long since repented and acknowledged the truth: that they had already long renounced the doctrine of the Anomoeans; that they confessed the Son to be like the Father in all things; and that ‘like’ does not differ from ‘consubstantial.’”

Liberius then required from them a written profession of their belief. When they presented a document in which, both in their own name and in the name of those whose embassy they were conducting, they professed to condemn the false doctrine of Arius and the other heretics, as well as the acts of the Council of Rimini, and to accept the faith of consubstantiality and of the Council of Nicaea inserted in their petition, they obtained communion from Liberius and the letter which we set forth as transcribed from Socrates.

II. Besides these letters, anyone adhering to the words of Basil the Great, Letter 74 to the Westerners, may easily be led to believe with Baronius, under the year 365, that Liberius sent another letter directing that Eustathius specifically be restored to his see; and that Eustathius, content to produce to the Easterners assembled in the Synod of Tyana the letter favorable to himself, concealed the other letters.

For Basil writes of him in Letter 74: “What terms were proposed to him by the most blessed bishop Liberius, and what he himself agreed to, is unknown to us, except that he brought a letter by which he was restored; and when he produced this in the Synod of Tyana, he was restored to his place.” Accordingly, Basil shortly afterward asks “that the churches be written to, stating on what conditions he was admitted to communion; and that it be added how, now changing his judgment, he renders void the favor received from the fathers then present with Liberius.”

But no place remains for this suspicion when one comes to Letter 82 of the same doctor. There Basil, now more fully informed of what had happened, expressly teaches on p. 153 that “Eustathius of Sebaste brought from Rome to Tyana a document in which he professed the faith of consubstantiality.” What that document was he explains on p. 152, speaking of the same Eustathius and his companions: “They do not consider that their written document, in which they confessed the Nicene faith, is kept at Rome; nor the petition brought from Rome, which they delivered with their own hands to the Synod of Tyana and which is also in our possession, in which that same faith is contained.”

By these words Basil mentions both the petition which Liberius required from Eustathius and his companions, and the letters which the same pope then gave them to carry to the Easterners, to which, naturally, the aforesaid petition was appended. At the same time he records that those letters were delivered to the Synod of Tyana by the very hands of Eustathius and his companions.

Since, therefore, Liberius openly explains in these letters on what condition he was admitted to communion, it is plain that when Basil wrote Letter 74 he had learned the acts of the Synod of Tyana only from uncertain report. Thus those who, relying on one cited passage from that letter, require another letter by which Liberius ordered Eustathius restored to his see rest on a very slight and unstable foundation—especially since Socrates and Sozomen, who wrote rather carefully about this entire affair, are altogether silent about that other letter.

Yet it follows from the words of the said Letter 74 that the Synod of Tyana, when it learned from Liberius’s letters that Eustathius had been admitted to his communion, restored to that bishop both communion and his see. It is also certain, from Basil’s Letters 74 and 82, that Eustathius immediately betrayed the faith he had professed at Rome.

III.
