Nor, for that reason, was Liberius to be blamed as though he had too readily granted communion to those envoys; for he required from them something more than Athanasius, in his Letter to Rufinianus, according to the Alexandrian synod, lays down as necessary from those returning to the Church. For Athanasius considers it sufficient “that they condemn by anathema, expressly naming Eudoxius and Euzoius, their doctrine, and confess the faith declared at Nicaea by the Fathers, setting no other synod before it.” Indeed, Eustathius and his companions had no need to profess anew their repudiation of Eudoxius’ doctrine, since they had openly declared this at the Council of Lampsacus, whose embassy they were discharging.

IV. The learned man wonders that they were not additionally required to profess in more explicit words the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Yet this would be more surprising if the heading prefixed by Socrates to the following Letter 13 were to be accepted: “Letter [Col. 1376C] of Liberius . . . to the bishops of the Macedonians”; that is, if the bishops who sent envoys to Liberius and to whom he replies had already been called Macedonians after the author of the sect which denied that the Holy Spirit is God. But since Sozomen simply calls them “Easterners,” while Liberius addresses his letter “to all orthodox bishops of the East,” it is clear that Socrates called them Macedonians by a kind of anticipation, because many of those whom Liberius names individually later openly attached themselves to this sect.

Nevertheless, it must not be denied—and it is clear from Athanasius’ Tome to the Antiochenes—that from at least the year 362 there were persons who pretended to accept the Nicene faith while maintaining that the Holy Spirit was a created thing. For this reason the Alexandrian synod, in the cited Tome, no. 3, prescribing to its envoys sent to Antioch the terms upon which peace was to be granted, commands:

> “Require nothing further of them than that they condemn the Arian heresy by anathema and profess the faith promulgated by the holy Fathers at Nicaea; further, that they condemn those who affirm that the Holy Spirit is a creature and divided from Christ’s substance . . . For those who pretend indeed to profess the Nicene faith, while meanwhile not hesitating to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, do nothing other than deny the Arian heresy in words but breathe it in heart and judgment.”

Accordingly, at the end of the Tome Paulinus professes:

> “I condemn by anathema those who despise the faith promulgated at Nicaea, and those who deny that the Son is [Col. 1377A] from the substance of the Father and consubstantial with the Father. I likewise condemn by anathema those who say that the Holy Spirit is a creature made by the Son.”

Nor can it be said that this new heresy, having arisen in the East, became known in the West only later. The acts of the Alexandrian synod, in which it is made manifest, were also well known in the West, and were cited by Liberius himself in Letter 13. Moreover, among the chief and principal envoys sent by that synod to Antioch were Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, and Lucifer of Cagliari; and these certainly did not allow Liberius to remain ignorant of what had then occurred.

It remains, therefore, to say that those who wrote to Liberius were not at all suspected by him of this new heresy, and that consequently he judged that nothing further was to be required of them than what he customarily required of bishops of the West requesting his peace [Col. 1377B] and communion. Yet some of them, as soon as they had obtained Liberius’ communion and letters, laid aside all pretence and did not delay to attack the divinity of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1378A]. Basil testifies this specifically concerning Eustathius in Letter 74: “This man is now laying waste the faith into which he was received; he joins those who strike down the *homoousion* with anathema, and is the standard-bearer of the heresy of the Pneumatomachians”—that is, those who attack the divinity of the Holy Spirit.

V. There is no reason to discuss at greater length the date on which the following two letters were written. The first was issued at Rome and presented to Liberius by the envoys sent from the Council of Lampsacus; the second was received from Liberius not long afterward by the same envoys and delivered to the bishops assembled at the Council of Tyana. It follows that they were written during the interval between the two synods. Now the Council of Lampsacus, according to Socrates, book IV, chapter 4, was held in 365—indeed, according to the more expert critics, as autumn approached [Col. 1378B]—whereas that of Tyana was held at the beginning of spring in 367. The aforesaid letters must therefore have been written in the intervening year, 366.

## LETTER

[Note: [Col. 1377D] (1) Socrates indeed calls it a *biblion* (βιβλίον), which properly means a little book or memorandum; but nothing prevents it also being called a letter. Epiphanius, *Heresies* 72, no. 1, applies that name to the similar memorandum which Marcellus of Ancyra presented in person to Julius. Basil the Great, Letter 82, calls the following letter, which Liberius gave the envoys to carry and which they delivered to the Council of Tyana, a *biblion*. Thus *biblion* and *epistolē* (ἐπιστολή), or *gramma* (γράμμα), are in some sense interchangeable terms.]

## OF THE ENVOYS OF THE COUNCIL OF LAMPSACUS TO POPE LIBERIUS

*(A.D. 366)*

**IN THEIR OWN NAME AND IN THE NAME OF THOSE WHO SENT THEM, THEY PROFESS THAT THEY HOLD AND WILL MAINTAIN THE NICENE FAITH; AND THAT, IF ANYONE ACCUSES THEM, THEY WILL PLEAD THEIR CASE BEFORE BISHOPS APPROVED BY LIBERIUS.**

[Note: [Col. 1378] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1377]

To the lord brother and fellow-priest Liberius: Eustathius, Theophilus, and Silvanus, greeting in the Lord.

I. Because of the mad [Note: [Col. 1377D] (2) Valesius translates “opinions”; but we prefer to retain in Latin as well what the Greek word properly means. It is well known that it has always been customary for heretics to defame their opponents with suspicion of some heresy.] suspicions of heretics, who do not cease to bring occasions of offence upon the catholic churches, we, desiring to remove from them every opportunity, profess and affirm that the synod of orthodox bishops held at Lampsacus, Smyrna, and various other places—whose embassy we are undertaking, and on whose behalf we bring letters both to your kindness and to all the bishops [Col. 1377C] of Italy and the West—holds and preserves the catholic faith. This faith was confirmed in the holy Council of Nicaea, in the time of blessed Constantine, by three hundred and eighteen bishops [Note: [Col. 1378D] (3) In place of “bishops,” Sozomen has “God-bearing Fathers” (*theophoroi pateres*, θεοφόρων πατέρων).], and has remained continually whole and unshaken to this day. In it the term “consubstantial” was set forth in a holy and devout manner against Arius’ perversion.

Likewise, we personally declare under our own hand that we, together with those mentioned above, have held, do hold, and will preserve until our last breath the same faith; condemning Arius and his impious doctrine together with his disciples; likewise [Note: [Col. 1378D] (4) In Socrates: “and all who share his mind, and every heresy of Sabellius: the Patripassians, Marcionites, Photinians, Marcellians, and that of Paul.” That is, “those who think the same as he does; likewise every heresy of Sabellius—the Patripassians, Marcionites, Photinians, Marcellians, and that of Paul.” We follow Sozomen. Although Socrates might have suggested restoring “Sabellius” before “Patripassians,” Liberius in the following letter distinguishes Sabellians and Patripassians; we therefore judged that nothing should be added to Sozomen’s text. Or else it should be read with this punctuation: “of Sabellius, the Patripassians.”] every heresy of the Patripassian, Marcion, Photinus, Marcellus, and Paul of Samosata; their doctrine; all who think as they do; and finally every heresy opposed to the aforesaid holy faith, which was devoutly [Col. 1380A] and catholicly expounded at Nicaea by the holy Fathers. Above all [Note: [Col. 1379C] (1) Socrates gives this whole passage as follows: “Anathematizing especially also the creed read at the Synod of Ariminum, as having been enacted contrary…” and subsequently has *prachthēsan* for *eprāchthē*, *komistheisan* for *komitheisi*, and *hypegrapsan* for *hypegrapsamen*. Sozomen, whom we prefer, is supported by Liberius in the following letter. There, when recounting what occurred with the envoys, he represents them as “having anathematized Arius and what had been done at Ariminum against the faith established at Nicaea.”] we pronounce anathema upon Arius and upon everything done at the Council of Ariminum against the aforesaid faith of the holy Council of Nicaea. Deceived by fraud and perjury, we subscribed to these measures after they had been brought to Constantinople from Nica in Thrace [Note: [Col. 1379C] (2) The acts held at Nica in Thrace are dated by Hilary, *Fragments* 8, no. 4, on 10 October 359; they were subscribed at Constantinople by the envoys of the Council of Seleucia on the last day of the same year, 359, as Sozomen relates, book IV, chapter 23. These men were first ensnared by perjury because, as Sozomen recounts in the same place, when they steadfastly affirmed that they would never repudiate the term “substance,” the Acacians, by interposing an oath, persuaded them that they did not at all assert the Son to be unlike in substance and were ready to affirm that he was like in substance.

[Col. 1379D] The Easterners themselves, in Hilary, *Fragments* 10, no. 1, locate the fraud perpetrated by perjury in this: that they assented to the condemnation of Aetius in such a way that Aetius, the author of this heresy, rather than these impious doctrines themselves, seemed to be condemned; and that the judgment seemed to have been pronounced more against a man than against a doctrine. Another of their deceits was that they advertised as the faith of the entire Council of Ariminum the formula which, as Hilary says, *Fragments* 8, no. 4, ten Ariminian envoys had finally subscribed at Nica in Thrace after being worn down and terrified by the emperor’s threats. Hilary reveals other deceits of theirs in *Fragment* 10; but the chief one, by which they first deceived the Westerners and compelled them to silence concerning *ousia* (“substance”), was the most shameless lie: they asserted that the Easterners so shrank from this word that they could never be brought to accept it. Therefore the Council of Paris, in Hilary, *Fragment* XI, no. 1, writes to the Easterners: “The greater number of those who were present either at Ariminum [Col. 1380C] or at Nica [in Thrace] were compelled, under the authority of your name, to silence concerning *ousia*.” Sozomen confirms the same, book IV, chapter 19. They then persuaded the Easterners to accept the formula brought from Nica in imitation of the Westerners; see Hilary, *Fragment* IX.

The Gallic bishops at Paris complained of such fraud; Eustathius and his companions now likewise complain of it—or rather renew their complaint. For, as Basil relates, Letter 82, p. 152, they had already complained in another gathering of the fraud by which they had been led astray into assenting to the Tome composed by Eudoxius’ party. Accordingly, to cleanse themselves of this lapse, they devised this means: they would go to Rome, receive there the faith of the Fathers, and, by introducing the better faith, correct the injury by which they had harmed the churches through fellowship with evil.] Our faith, and that of the persons mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1380C] (3) Sozomen omits the following exposition of the Nicene faith, but indicates that it was appended in these terms: “Having made this profession, they added to their confession, in exactly the same words, the faith set forth at Nicaea.”], whose embassy we discharge, is as follows.

**Greek text, translated:**

To the lord brother and fellow-minister Liberius: Eustathius, Theophilus, and Silvanus, greeting in the Lord.

I. On account of the mad suspicions of the heretics, who do not cease to bring scandals upon the catholic churches, we therefore remove every pretext from them and confess that the synod of orthodox bishops held at Lampsacus and Smyrna and in various other places—whose embassy we are undertaking and for which we bring a letter to your kindness and to all the Italian and Western bishops—holds and keeps the catholic faith. This faith, confirmed in the holy Council of Nicaea under blessed Constantine by three hundred and eighteen bishops, remains even now and continually in an intact and unshaken condition; in it the *homoousion* was devoutly and piously set down against Arius’ distortion.

Likewise, we and those previously named confess under our own hand that we have held, do hold, and shall keep until the end the same faith: condemning Arius and his impious teaching with his disciples; every heresy of the Patripassian, Marcion, Photinus, Marcellus, and Paul of Samosata; their teaching; all who are like-minded with them; and all heresies opposed to the aforesaid holy faith, devoutly and catholicly expounded by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. We especially anathematize Arius and everything done at the Council of Ariminum contrary to this aforesaid faith of the holy Council of Nicaea; deceived by fraud and perjury, we subscribed to those things after they had been brought from Nica in Thrace to Constantinople. Such is our faith and the faith of those mentioned above, whose embassy we undertake.

[Col. 1380A]

II. We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one only-begotten God, the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten of the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made, both those in heaven [Col. 1380B] and those on earth. For us human beings and for our salvation he came down, was incarnate, and became human [Note: [Col. 1380D] (4) Not without divine providence did the Council of Nicaea add, after the word “incarnate” (*sarkōthenta*, σαρκωθέντα), “and made human” (*enanthrōpēsanta*, ἐνανθρωπήσαντα), if indeed Arius had not yet promulgated the erroneous doctrine later professed by his disciples. For Eudoxius, in the collection of an ancient writer against the Severians, in Canisius, vol. IV, part 1, p. 238, declares that he believes in Christ as first among creatures, incarnate and not made human; for he did not assume a human soul, but became flesh. The words of the Arian Lucius of Alexandria are there also appended: “Therefore John cries out, ‘The Word became flesh,’ because it was compounded with flesh, not with a soul.” The Nicene synod had likewise forestalled the heresy of Apollinaris by adding these two terms; but, as Gregory Nazianzen testifies, *Letter* 2 to Cledonius, his disciples, wickedly and craftily employing the word “becoming human” (*enanthrōpēsis*), sought to evade its force.]; he also suffered, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead. And [we believe] in the Holy Spirit. But those who say, “There was once when he was not,” and “Before he was begotten he was not,” and “He came to be from things that were not”; or who say that the Son of God is from another substance or essence, or mutable or subject to change: these the catholic and apostolic Church of God anathematizes.

**Greek text, translated:**

II. We believe in one God, Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one only-begotten God, Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father—that is, from the Father’s *ousia* (“substance”)—God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made, like in substance (*homoiousios*) to the Father, through whom all things came to be, both those in heaven and those upon earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, was incarnate, was made human, suffered, rose on the third day, ascended into the heavens, and is coming to judge the living and the dead; and [we believe] in the Holy Spirit. But those who say, “There was once when he was not,” and “Before he was begotten he was not,” and “He came to be from things that were not,” or who assert that he is from another hypostasis or *ousia*, or that the Son of God is mutable or changeable—these the catholic and apostolic Church of God anathematizes.

III. I, Eustathius, bishop of the city of Sebaste, together with Theophilus and Silvanus, envoys of the synod of Lampsacus, Smyrna, and other places, have written this confession with our own [Col. 1381A] hands and of our own free will. If, after this exposition of our faith, anyone wishes to bring any accusation against us or against those who sent us, let him come with letters from your Holiness before orthodox bishops approved by your Holiness, and let him contend with us before them in judicial proceedings; and if any charge is established, let punishment be inflicted upon its author [Note: [Col. 1381C] (1) Ursacius and Valens had already made a similar promise to Pope Julius in Letter 5, writing: “We also profess that, if the Easterners or Athanasius himself should ever wish maliciously to summon us to trial, we will not appear without your knowledge.” But the envoys, in the name of the Easterners who sent them, promise much more and acknowledge as a qualified judge one who can also appoint judges before whom even bishops of the East ought to appear.

[Note: [Col. 1381C] (2) Socrates adds: “When Liberius had bound the envoys by this memorandum, as by a kind of guarantee, he received them into communion and dismissed them after giving letters of this sort”—namely, those which follow. We have already observed from Basil, Letter 82, that the autograph memorandum itself was preserved at Rome.].

**Greek text, translated:**

III. I, Eustathius, bishop of the city of Sebaste, and Theophilus and Silvanus, envoys of the synod of Lampsacus, Smyrna, and the rest, have written this confession with our own hands and by our own resolve. But if anyone, after the faith set forth by us, wishes to bring any accusation against us or against those who sent us, let him come with letters from your Holiness to such orthodox bishops as your Holiness may approve, and let him have the case tried with us before them. If any charge is established, let vengeance be exacted upon the guilty party.

## LETTER

[Note: [Col. 1381D] (3) In Socrates it bears the heading: “Letter of Liberius, bishop of the Romans, to the bishops of the Macedonians.” Why this heading should not be retained is sufficiently clear from what we said beforehand in the prefatory notice to Letter 14, no. 4.]

## OF LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, TO ALL THE ORTHODOX BISHOPS OF THE EAST

*(A.D. 366)*

**THEIR ENVOYS HAVE PROFESSED THE NICENE FAITH; THE STRENGTH OF THIS FAITH LIES IN THE TERMS “SUBSTANCE” AND “CONSUBSTANTIAL.” THE EFFORTS OF THE ERRING PARTY TO SUPPRESS THESE TERMS AT ARIMINUM. THE ACTS OF THE COUNCIL OF ARIMINUM HAVE BEEN CONDEMNED BY THEIR OWN ENVOYS, AND ARE UNANIMOUSLY CONDEMNED BY THOSE WHO WERE THEN DECEIVED.**

[Note: [Col. 1382] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1381]

[Col. 1381B]

To the beloved brothers and fellow-ministers Evethius [Note: [Col. 1381D] (4) So Valesius. Epiphanius, however, *Tripartite History*, book 7, chapter 25, has “Eustathius.” Baronius reads “Hypatius,” and in the margin, with the early editions of Socrates, “Hythius.” Hence Blondel would prefer “Hypsius,” who was deposed from the episcopate at the Galatian synod late in 375. Finally, Tillemont conjectures that “Hypatianus,” bishop of Heraclea, should be read. No one can doubt that the letters brought to Liberius by Eustathius, Silvanus, and Theophilus were composed and subscribed in the names of the bishops listed here.], Cyril, Hyperechius [Note: [Col. 1381D] (5) Epiphanius: Hypericius.], Uranius, Heron, Elpidius, Maximus, Eusebius, Eucarpus, Heortasius, Neon, Eumathius, Faustinus, Proclinus, Pasinicus, Arsenius, Severus, Didymion, Britannius, Callicrates, Dalmatius, Aedesius, Eustochius, Ambrosius, Gelonius, Pardalius, Macedonius, Paul, Marcellus, Heraclius, Alexander, Adolius, Marcianus, Sthenelus, John, Maceri [Note: [Col. 1382C] (7) Baronius: Macarius, and in the margin, with the early editions of Socrates, Macari. We restore Epiphanius’ reading because it adheres more closely to the Greek letters.], Charisius, Silvanus, Photinus, Antony, Anytus [Note: [Col. 1382C] (8) Epiphanius: Authus. Baronius: Aythus.], Celsus, Euphranor, Milesius, Patricius, Severianus, Eusebius, Eumolpius, Athanasius, Diophantus, Menodorus, Diocles, Chrysampelus, Neon, Eugenius, Eustathius, Callicrates, Arsenius, Eugenius, Martyrius, Hieracius, Leontius, Philagrius, Lucius, and [Note: [Col. 1382C] (9) Epiphanius reads: “Liberius, bishop, and the Western bishops, to all orthodox bishops of the East: everlasting greeting in the Lord,” omitting “Italy,” which indeed seems superfluous because Italian bishops belong to the West. But this greeting exactly answers the words of the envoys in the preceding letter, no. 1: “We affirm that the synod of orthodox bishops . . . whose embassy we discharge, brings letters both to your kindness and to all bishops of Italy and the West.” As these Eastern letters, although addressed to Liberius and the Westerners, are said by Socrates, book IV, chapter 12, and Sozomen, book VI, chapter 10, to have been delivered to Liberius alone, so too the present letter, though bearing the name of Liberius and the bishops of Italy and the West, is attributed by Sozomen in the same place to Liberius alone; and the envoys are said to have returned with Liberius’ letters, without any mention of the Western bishops.] all orthodox bishops of the East: Liberius, bishop [Col. 1381C] of Italy, and the bishops of the West, everlasting greeting in the Lord [Note: [Col. 1382D] (10) Valesius, following Epiphanius, has “greeting in the Lord,” without rendering the word *pantote* (“always”). The Greek might be translated, “Rejoice always in the Lord,” as though said in imitation of Paul’s words, Philippians 4:4: “Rejoice always in the Lord.” We have Hilary’s example, who begins his writing against Auxentius by wishing the bishops “eternal greeting alike in the Lord.”].

**Greek text, translated:**

To the beloved brothers and fellow-ministers Evethius, Cyril, Hyperechius, Uranius, Heron, Elpidius, Maximus, Eusebius, Eucarpus, Heortasius, Neon, Eumathius, Faustinus, Proclinus, Pasinicus, Arsenius, Severus, Didymion, Britannius, Callicrates, Dalmatius, Aedesius, Eustochius, Ambrosius, Gelonius, Pardalius, Macedonius, Paul, Marcellus, Heraclius, Alexander, Adolius, Marcianus, Sthenelus, John, Maceri, Charisius, Silvanus, Photinus, Antony, Anytus, Celsus, Euphranor, Milesius, Patricius, Severianus, Eusebius, Eumolpius, Athanasius, Diophantus, Menodorus, Diocles, Chrysampelus, Neon, Eugenius, Eustathius, Callicrates, Arsenius, Eugenius, Martyrius, Hieracius, Leontius, Philagrius, Lucius, and all orthodox bishops in the East: Liberius, bishop of Italy, and the bishops in the West, greeting always in the Lord.

I. Your letters, radiant with the light of faith, beloved brothers, delivered to us through our most esteemed brothers and bishops Eustathius, Silvanus, and Theophilus, have brought us the joy of peace and concord that we most desired [Col. 1384A]. This was especially so because they both declared and demonstrated that your judgment and doctrine wholly agree and harmonize with my lowliness and with all the bishops of Italy and the West.

We recognize this as the catholic and apostolic faith, which remained whole and unshaken until the Council of Nicaea. Your envoys professed that they hold it; and, with inexpressible joy, removing every trace and spark of absurd suspicion, they set it forth not only orally but also in writing. We judged that a copy of it should necessarily be appended to this letter [Note: [Col. 1383C] (1) Liberius here indicates that he appended to his letter a copy of the preceding letter or memorandum. Basil, Letter 82, testifies that he had such a copy, in which the envoys’ memorandum was attached to Liberius’ letter.], lest we leave heretics any occasion for again laying snares, by which they might once more stir up the kindling of their malice and, as is their custom, ignite fires of dissension [Col. 1384B].

**Greek text, translated:**

I. Your letters, beloved brothers, shining beforehand with the light of faith and delivered to us through the most honorable brothers, the bishops Eustathius, Silvanus, and Theophilus, brought us the joy of peace and concord most desired by us—especially because they affirmed and demonstrated that your judgment and convictions agree and harmonize both with my insignificance and with all those in Italy and the West. We know this to be the catholic and apostolic faith which remained intact and unshaken until the Council at Nicaea. They confessed that they themselves hold this faith and, filled with joy and expelling every trace and live ember of unfitting suspicion, set it forth not only in speech but also in writing. We judged it necessary to append a copy of it to this letter, lest we leave heretics any pretext for plotting again, so that, once more stirring the fuel of their own malice, they might customarily kindle conflagrations through schisms.

II. Furthermore, our most esteemed brothers Eustathius, Silvanus, and Theophilus have professed that both they and your charity have always held, and will preserve until their last breath, the faith approved at Nicaea by three hundred and eighteen orthodox bishops. It contains the perfect truth and confutes and overthrows every host of heretics [Note: [Col. 1383C] (2) Epiphanius: “It stops and destroys the mouth of the whole heretical multitude.” Hilary held the same view of the Nicene faith as Liberius here does, since in *Fragment* II, no. 27, he calls it the faith written by 318 bishops against all heresies. Hilary also, *On the Synods*, no. 86, as Liberius here, compares the number of the Nicene Fathers with the number of servants by whose aid Abraham defeated impious kings. Ambrose, prologue to book I *On the Faith*, no. 5, and the commonly received Paschasius the deacon—or rather Faustus, bishop of Riez—in the preface to book I *On the Holy Spirit*, follow them in this.].

For it was not by chance but by divine providence that so great a number of bishops was gathered against Arius’ madness: the same number by which blessed Abraham overthrew so many thousands through faith. This faith [Col. 1384C], contained in the terms “substance” and “consubstantial,” is like a firm and impregnable fortress: it resists and repels every assault and evil contrivance of Arian madness.

[Note: [Col. 1383C] (3) Valesius did not translate the Greek term *en hypostasei* (ἐν ὑποστάσει) into Latin, but retained it as “in hypostasis.” It is clear that Liberius here refers to the words of the Nicene Council condemning those who say that the Son is “from another hypostasis or essence” (*ex heteras hypostaseōs ē ousias*). Hilary, *Fragments* II, no. 27, renders this in Latin, “from another substance or essence.”

In this place he seems preferable to Basil, who, in Letter 78, contends that *ousia* and *hypostasis* were not synonyms at the Council of Nicaea. Basil thinks that first “from another *ousia*” was said against the Arians, and then “or hypostasis” was added against the Sabellians, who, he says, regarded hypostasis and essence as identical. But that learned man reverses the words of the Nicene Council, for in the Creed, as he himself quotes it in the same letter, the synod first sets down “from another hypostasis” and then adds “or essence.”

This addition was made, not in order to combat a new heresy, but so that whoever had not sufficiently perceived the force of the first word might cease altogether to doubt its genuine meaning. Thus Basil’s argument has no force here: “If those terms had one and the same meaning, what need was there to use both?” Moreover, the heresy of the Sabellians did not lie in affirming that the Son was from another hypostasis, insofar as the word means a subsistence or person, but rather in denying this, since they confused the persons of Father and Son. Therefore, if the Council of Nicaea were to be judged to have condemned Arians and Sabellians together and to have employed *ousia* and *hypostasis* in different senses, it would have had to pronounce anathema both upon those who affirm that the Son is “from another *ousia*” and upon those who deny that he is “in another hypostasis.”

Finally, the Arians, foreseeing that the Nicene faith would be ineffective if the term “substance,” or *ousia*, were suppressed, left nothing untried at Ariminum, at Nica in Thrace, at Seleucia, and at Constantinople to have it wholly rejected. To attain this result more easily, they claimed that they rejected the term because it was foreign to Holy Scripture. Against them the Catholics, and particularly Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book I, no. 18, and his contemporary Phoebadius, bishop of Agen, showed that “substance” was not unknown in the sacred writings. They had no doubt that in Jeremiah 23:22, according to the Septuagint, *ei estēsan en hypostasei* (εἰ ἔστησαν ἐν ὑποστάσει), the words *en hypostasei*, ought to be rendered in Latin “in substance.” This is how they actually rendered it, as had Cyprian before them, *On the Unity of the Church*, and after them the ancient author of *Questions on the Old and New Testament* among the appendices to Augustine, vol. III, p. 91; Ambrose, *On the Faith*, book III, chapter 15; and the bishops of Africa in Victor of Vita, at the beginning of book III.

Gregory Nazianzen, however, in Oration 34, reading *en hypostēsanti* (ἐν ὑποστήσαντι) with Theodotion in the same passage of Jeremiah, added *kai ousia Kyriou* (καὶ οὐσίᾳ Κυρίου), “and in the substance of the Lord.” In this manner he imitated the Council of Nicaea, which took care that heretics might not play upon or deceive the simple with the ambiguous word *hypostasis*. For we have shown above that even some Fathers earlier than the Nicene Council used this same term for subsistence or person. Yet among far more of them its usage to signify substance continued for a long time, and the Council of Nicaea did not depart from it.]

**Greek text, translated:**

II. Our most esteemed brothers Eustathius, Silvanus, and Theophilus also professed this: that both they and your charity have always held, and will keep until the end, this faith—that is, the faith approved at Nicaea by three hundred and eighteen orthodox bishops. It contains the perfect truth and shuts the mouths of, and overthrows, all the multitudes of heretics. For the number of so many bishops was not assembled against Arius’ madness by mere chance but by divine direction, in the same number in which blessed Abraham overthrew so many thousands through faith. This faith, contained in hypostasis and in the name *homoousios* (“consubstantial”), like a strong and unconquerable fortress, overthrows and repels every assault and malicious device of Arian vainglory.

III. Therefore, when all the bishops of the West had assembled at Ariminum, to which the perversity of the Arians had summoned them in order that, either by persuasion or, more truly, under the compulsion of secular power, they might remove or indirectly deny what had been most carefully placed in the faith, their cunning accomplished nothing. For almost all those assembled at Ariminum, who had then been deceived partly by enticements and partly by fraud, have now recovered their senses. They have condemned by anathema the formula issued by the Council of Ariminum, subscribed to the catholic faith promulgated at Nicaea, and, entering into communion with us, are moved by a stronger indignation against Arius and his disciples [Col. 1385B].

Your charity’s own envoys, seeing proof of this, joined you yourselves in their subscription, anathematizing Arius and what was done at Ariminum against the faith established at Nicaea; and you too, deceived by perjuries, subscribed to these things [Note: [Col. 1385D] (1) As their own envoys testify in the memorandum or letter above, no. 1.].

**Greek text, translated:**

III. Accordingly, when all the bishops in the West had assembled at Ariminum—because the malevolence of the Arians had convened them so that, by some persuasion or, to speak more truthfully, by worldly power, they might remove or indirectly deny what had been placed most securely in the faith—their craftiness gained nothing. For nearly all those who were at Ariminum and had then been enticed or led astray have now recovered their understanding. Having anathematized the statement of those assembled at Ariminum, subscribed to the catholic and apostolic faith established at Nicaea, and entered into communion with us, they are more vehemently angered against Arius’ doctrine and his disciples. Recognizing the proof of this state of affairs, the envoys of your charity joined you yourselves to their own subscription; anathematizing Arius and what was done at Ariminum against the faith established at Nicaea, to which you yourselves also subscribed after being deceived by oaths.

IV. For this reason it seemed proper to us to write to your charity and to assist those who make just requests [Note: [Col. 1385D] (2) To understand what that just request was, it must be recalled why the Easterners sent envoys to Rome and came there on embassy. According to Socrates and Sozomen, they sent envoys because fear of the evils threatening them from Emperor Valens and Eudoxius led them to judge that they should flee for refuge to Emperor Valentinian and Liberius. Basil, however, in Letter 82, holds that they devised this means in order to wash away the stain and correct the injury they had incurred by assenting to the Tome composed by Eudoxius’ party; or, as Basil also specifically relates of Eustathius in Letter 74, in order that those previously deposed might be restored to their sees. Liberius thus granted the assistance requested: promising aid against the vexations of Valens and Eudoxius, granting peace and communion to those who had fallen, and restoring the expelled to their sees. Basil, Letter 74, indeed relates that Eustathius, immediately upon presenting Liberius’ letter to the Council of Tyana, was restored to his place.]. This is especially appropriate because from the profession of your envoys we have learned that the Easterners, having recovered their senses, agree with the orthodox Westerners.

We further make known to you, lest you be unaware, that the blasphemies of the Ariminian decision have now been struck down by anathema by those who seemed then to have been deceived through fraud [Col. 1385C], and that all have agreed with one mind upon the Nicene faith. You too ought to make this known to everyone, so that those who have suffered some injury to their faith by force and fraud may at last be able to emerge from heretical darkness into the divine light of catholic liberty.

If, after this council, they should refuse to vomit forth the poison of perverse doctrine, reject all Arius’ blasphemies, and condemn them by anathema, let them know that they are, together with Arius and his disciples, and the remaining serpents—whether Sabellians, Patripassians, or heretics of any other kind—strangers and aliens from the communion of the Church, which does not admit adulterous children [Col. 1385D]. May God preserve you in health, most beloved brothers.

**Greek text, translated:**

IV. Therefore it seemed fitting to us to write to your charity and assist those who ask what is just—especially since, from the confession of your envoys, we have recognized that the Easterners, having returned to right understanding, agree with the orthodox in the West. And we make known to you, so that you may be informed, that the blasphemies at Ariminum, now anathematized even by those who were thought then to have been harmed through being swept away [Col. 1386C], have been condemned, and that all are united in spirit toward the faith of Nicaea.

This must become known to all through you, so that those harmed by violence may now at last be able to return from heretical darkness to the divine light of catholic freedom. If after this synod they should refuse to spit out the poison of false doctrine, abolish all Arius’ blasphemies, and anathematize them, let them know themselves to be excluded from covenant and without communion in ecclesiastical assemblies along with Arius, his disciples, and the remaining serpents—whether Sabellians, Patripassians, or adherents of any other heresy—for the Church does not receive children born of adultery. May God preserve you in strength, beloved brothers [Col. 1386D].

## APPENDIX

[Col. 1387A]

## ACTS OF POPE LIBERIUS

[Col. 1387]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING ACTS

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 87.)*

I. Immediately after the pseudo-constitution of Sylvester in the ancient collection written in Lombardic script are appended the following Acts. Their fabricator reveals himself from the outset to be both a liar and an ignoramus, when he calls the emperor reigning at Rome during the pontificate of Liberius indiscriminately Constantine, Constans, and Constantius, and even styles him “grandson of Constantine the Great,” although it is established that Constantius, the son of that emperor, was then ruling at Rome.

He then repeats the inventions concerning Constantine’s leprosy and baptism found in the false Acts and pseudo-constitution of Pope Sylvester. What Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, records concerning the baptism of Constantine the Great at Nicomedia by Eusebius, bishop of that city, he stupidly interprets as concerning the baptism of this fictitious grandson [Col. 1387B]. No less falsely does he attribute to Constantius the heretical opinion that Mary had several sons.

Who does not perceive that he is shamefully mistaken when he sets out either the reason or the place of Liberius’ exile? For Liberius was not banished by Constantius because he mocked or accused him and said to him, “Your kingdom shall not endure, because you do not fear the Lord”; rather, he was banished because he refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Athanasius. Nor is anyone unaware that he was exiled not at Noella, in a cemetery only three miles from the City, but at Beroea in Syria.

Furthermore, he represents Liberius as living in this cemetery as though he did not know that Felix had been substituted in his place. He falsely states that, when Liberius went into exile, Damasus was a presbyter and had been made his vicar by Liberius before leaving Rome. Yet it is established from the petitions of Marcellinus and Faustinus to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius that Damasus was then only a deacon and Liberius’ companion when he departed [Col. 1387C]. For there, on p. 2, one reads:

> “Damasus, Liberius’ deacon, pretends to set out with Liberius; but fleeing from the journey, he returned to Rome.”

Certainly, he would have had a legitimate reason either not to depart or at least to return sooner, if he had been appointed Liberius’ vicar by Liberius himself. But what is immediately added in the same petitions has an altogether different meaning:

> “On the day when Liberius departed for exile, all the clergy—that is, the presbyters, the archdeacon Felix, and Damasus himself, a deacon . . .—bound themselves by oath that, while Liberius lived, they would in no way have another pontiff. Yet the clergy, contrary to right . . . received Felix the archdeacon, ordained in Liberius’ place.”

It is wearisome to dwell longer on refuting such manifest lies, especially since the remaining assertions are either equally fabricated, drawn from events wrongly understood, or related in a disorderly fashion.

II. We suspect that the contriver of these proceedings was none other than the man who fabricated the earlier Acts of Marcellinus and the pseudo-constitution of Silvester [Col. 1388A]. This is suggested both by the place which they occupy in handwritten copies, by their barbarous manner of expression—though somewhat more tolerable—and also by an equal incompetence in devising falsehoods and an equal shamelessness in presenting them. Therefore it will not be useless to append them to those already mentioned. At any rate, they will serve to establish the source from which were taken the opening portions of the Life of Damasus, copied by Abbot Constantine Cajetan from a manuscript codex of the archive of the Canons of St. Peter's, and printed at Paris in 1672 by Ludovicus Billaine with the other works of Pope Damasus, p. 21. For although the author of that Life was not altogether lacking in eloquence or learning, it cannot be denied that he adhered too uncritically to the statements of those Acts. He corrected many absurd and discordant matters [Col. 1388B], and also brought some things that departed from historical truth into conformity with its standard; yet he did not amend everything so as to leave nothing requiring amendment. For he did not correct what is stated in these Acts concerning Liberius' exile in the cemetery of Noella, three miles from the City. And although he does not conceal that Felix was substituted for him, he nevertheless depicts Liberius as entrusting his functions to Damasus and then summoning to himself “all the Catholic ecclesiastical ranks,” in whose presence he administers baptism, on one occasion and again, to many thousands.

We pass over that the same writer believed the embassy of Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, Pancratius, and Hilary to Constantius, as well as the exiles of that same Lucifer, Eusebius of Vercelli, and Liberius himself—which preceded the Council of Rimini by three or four years [Col. 1388C]—to have occurred after that synod; that he confuses Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, with Hilary the deacon, who adhered to the Luciferian schism; and other like matters, concerning which this is not the place for fuller discussion. It is enough here to observe that this writer plainly appears later than these Acts, which he attempted to recast in a better form.

## THE ACTS OF POPE LIBERIUS BEGIN.

*(From the same source, p. 89.)*

### 1. Confession of faith

In the year of the reign of Constantine [Note: **[Col. 1388D] (1)** In A.D. 327 Flavius Valerius Constantinus held the consulship. It is uncertain whether he was Constantine's brother or his brother's son; but he is nowhere recorded as having held imperial power. It is certain that the account given by Eusebius concerning the baptism of Constantine the Great at Nicomedia is wrongly referred to this nephew.]—the nephew of Constantine the great man—there was a certain priest of the City named Liberius, a pious bishop preaching Christ, as he had also been taught by Mark, bishop of the city of Rome, who ordained him deacon in the city, within the precincts of the Constantinian basilica. Always steadfast [Col. 1388D] in the Trinity, he preached Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and praised “God from God and light from light, whole from whole, full from full; not created but begotten; not from nothing but from the Father, [Col. 1389A] of one substance with the Father. But the Holy Spirit, our God, neither unbegotten nor begotten, neither created nor made, but proceeding from the Father—the Spirit of the Father and the Son—we venerate as eternally coexistent with the Father and the Son. Yet we venerate one God, because from the one Father the Son, born as God, possesses all that belongs to the Father; and the Father begot wholly in the Son all that is in him [one manuscript: “all that is”]. In begetting the Son, the Father neither diminished nor lost the deity of his fullness. And, most devoutly confessing that all that God the Father is, that also the Son is, we most certainly confess one God with the Holy Spirit. We believe in Jesus Christ our Lord, the Son of God, through whom all things were made, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible; that for our salvation he descended from heaven, [Col. 1389B] though he never ceased to be in heaven, and was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. The Word made flesh did not lose what he was, but began to be what he was not: not changed, but remaining God, he was also born man—not seemingly but truly, not airy but bodily, not phantasmal but fleshly—having bones, blood, sensation, and soul. Thus, as true man and true God, we do not in any way hesitate to confess him to have been one and the same true man. This same Lord Jesus Christ fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified according to the Scriptures, rose from the dead on the third day, was taken up into heaven, sits at the Father's right hand, and we await his coming thence to judge the living and the dead, and to judge the world by fire.” [Note: **[Col. 1389D] (1)** From the statement of faith found in the Quesnel Codex, ch. 39, and in Augustine, appendix to vol. V, Sermon 235, with certain alterations.]

### 2. Constantine cleansed of leprosy. Constans baptized at Nicomedia. Liberius banished to Noella

[Col. 1389C]

When he had read this from an ancient book, having been instructed by the book of Silvester, bishop of the Romans, he also publicly preached that Constantine, Constans's uncle, had been cleansed of leprosy in the name of Jesus Christ by Silvester. For Constans was not wholly Christian, but was, as it were, a tempter; though baptized in the Trinity, he did not wholly confess the Trinity. He was baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia, at Nicomedia in the estate called Aquilo. This man further said that Joseph had other children by Mary. When Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, heard this, he began to ridicule and accuse him loudly, saying with all his strength: “Your kingdom shall not endure, because you do not fear the Lord your God [Col. 1389D].”

When many reported this to King Constantius [Note: **[Col. 1389D] (2)** The author of the Life of Damasus, mentioned in the Preface, understood this no less falsely of Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, who, after the deaths of his brothers Constantine and Constans, held sole imperial power.], he was exceedingly angry and ordered Liberius to live outside the city. He lived three miles from the city of Rome, as though an exile, in the cemetery of Noella on the Salarian Way.

### 3. Liberius appoints Damasus his vicar. Peter's love after his denial. Chrism in the Lord's name

[Col. 1390A]

When Easter came, he summoned all the Roman citizen-presbyters and deacons, sat in that cemetery, and said: “Do not be afraid because I do not live with you in the city of Rome; rather, you have a vicar. Behold our brother and presbyter Damasus, to whose character you bear witness before me, whom you proclaim with clear voice, in body and mind.” [Note: **[Col. 1389D] (3)** The author of the Life of Damasus so amended and expanded this passage that Liberius’ speech is much fuller and more elegant, and he represents him as saying nothing unworthy of a supreme pontiff. Yet the statements are very much at variance with the Acts. The chief error is that he introduces Liberius the exile as speaking in such a way as to derive the greatest hope of a change of affairs from Arius’s recent death, although Arius died in A.D. 336—twenty years before Liberius was driven into exile.]

Dionysius the presbyter replied to Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, and said: “Holy bishop, undefiled by corruption, mighty champion of Christ, you know well that when the apostle Peter denied, he was ill. A fit came upon him, and again he denied. A fever came upon him for the third time, and he denied. The fever departed, and he wept, both bitterly and sweetly. But the physician had not yet come. The physician came [Col. 1390B] after the third fever; he applied a remedy and healed him. He who had failed by three denials before the Passion was restored after the Resurrection by loving three times. Consider the remedy of chrism, the sacrament of chrism. Let not that dove accuse us, for you make chrism [read: *chrisma*] and do so in the name of him whom you proclaimed in a clear voice. That very voice—because the Lord's voice cannot be repeated and cannot be changed—ought, perhaps, to be heard with trembling.” [Note: **[Col. 1390D] (4)** In the Life of Damasus just mentioned, Liberius’ speech ends thus and Dionysius’ response is appended in such a way that everything coheres suitably; but there is nothing there about Peter’s denial or fall and amendment. Here, however, it seems to serve no purpose other than to exculpate Pope Symmachus, or rather the council by which he had been absolved. By this device, the contriver of these Acts would imply that Symmachus was not innocent. Yet we suspect that a man commended by a certain appearance of goodwill rather than by any prudence concentrated upon one point only: persuading his readers that Symmachus’ rank could have been preserved.]

### 4.

Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, replied and said: “My lords and holy fellow-presbyters, do not be anxious about tomorrow. For so the Master said: ‘Tomorrow will be anxious for itself’ (Matt. 6:34). This is our admonition. John baptized in the wilderness unto repentance. It was wilderness because the author of baptism had not yet come. But when he came, the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained over the waters and over the author of baptism; and the priest administers the sacrament which he has received.”

### 5. Baptism in basin, river, and marsh

Damasus the presbyter replied and said: “Permit us to celebrate Easter. I speak humbly: for the burden which [read: *quod*] you bear upon yourself we cannot lighten, because you do not know where to baptize. Baptize in the basin where the Master did. That basin is not wood, but the whole world.”

Liberius received this speech with great honor, and wept for joy, saying to him: “You shall be a greater minister, just as he who gave us baptism said to the people: ‘Let him who is your lesser [Col. 1391A] become greater.’” [Note: **[Col. 1391C] (1)** In the Life of Damasus this is explained as a prophecy by Liberius that blessed Damasus, owing to the eminence of his humility and vigilance, would someday be raised to the summit of the apostolic see.]

Siricius the deacon replied and said: “Command through my mouth, bishop, and pour forth favor. Our fathers, as a type of baptism, passed through the midst of the sea. Therefore baptism ought to be administered in rivers and marshes.” Liberius the bishop said: “You have spoken rightly.” For not far from the cemetery of Noella was the Ostrian cemetery, where the apostle Peter baptized. At that Easter season he baptized 4,012 persons of both sexes; all were Romans, whether from far away or nearby, or neighbors of the Romans, and desired to be baptized by him.

### 6. Constantius’ expedition beyond the Danube

At the same time, during the octave of Easter, an exceedingly great [perhaps: “very great”] body of barbarians brought war across the Danube. When Constans [read: **Constantius**] heard this [Col. 1391B], he said: “See this sacrilegious man, because he has done what has never been done, the superstition of vanity. Therefore this great plague of a multitude of barbarians has come upon Romania.” He went to war and departed in great bitterness. As he went out through the city gate, he said: “When I go against the beasts of burden of the Danube and cut down the barbarians, I shall return to the city of Rome and offer the flesh of sacrilegious Liberius—who said that my uncle had been leprous, baptized and cleansed by Bishop Silvester—to the birds of heaven and beasts of earth: Liberius alone, and no others, lest they say and assert that I am a persecutor.”

But while he was in the Danubian battle, Constans was fiercely pressed.

[Note: **[Col. 1391C] (2)** The author of the Life of Damasus amended this passage thus: “In those days a multitude of barbarians gathered beyond the Danube to invade Roman territory. Hearing this, Emperor Constantius said: ‘See this sacrilegious man: because he has done what has never been done, this scourge of a multitude has come upon our kingdom.’ And during the Easter days he departed for war, threatening Bishop Liberius as he went that, when he returned victorious, he would offer his flesh to the birds of heaven and the beasts of earth.”]

### 7. Liberius is asked to baptize in the basilica of St. Peter

[Col. 1391C]

When Pentecost came, a very great multitude of both sexes pressed for baptism because of fear of persecution. Dionysius the presbyter said: “Why do you not baptize at our first pontiff, the apostle Peter?” Damasus replied and said: “Do it.” For the thought of Liberius the bishop was obscure, when he said: “His uncle [in the Acts of Damasus: ‘father’] built and constructed this church. Since he has authority to pronounce sentence concerning his uncle. And water does not flow there. People of both sexes desire to be born again, not to die on my account alone.” [Col. 1392A]

Dionysius the presbyter replied and said: “Let them be born again; and if they die after baptism, they will live better in blood.”

[Note: **[Col. 1391D] (3)** In the Life of Damasus, these are Damasus’ own words, and the passage is restored as follows: “When Liberius wished to baptize in the aforesaid Ostrian cemetery, blessed Damasus said to him: ‘Why, when the opportunity is given, do you not baptize at our first pontiff, the apostle Peter?’ Liberius replied: ‘Because I fear—since his father built and constructed this church—that he may pronounce a hostile judgment because of this. For people desire to be born again, not to die.’” As though, if Liberius had been free to approach the church of blessed Peter, this were an adequate reason for declining to baptize there those seeking baptism, merely because the church had been built by Constantius’ father.]

### 8. Damasus promises springs. Liberius baptizes at Pentecost

Damasus replied and said: “Let not your heart be troubled, supreme bishop, because I will provide for you a vein of flowing spring-water.” Liberius was comforted with joy at these words and said to him: “Go; construct it with the Spirit flowing forth. And I, when I come with the brethren, shall worship him whom Christ has left to us, who is shepherd for us.”

On the third day Damasus came; Siricius came; Innocentius, Priscus, and Urbanus, deacons, came [Col. 1392B] to the blessed apostle Peter. For there were memorial tombs there, and things floated upon the water. Damasus took counsel with them [read: *eis*] and said: “Give me your labor for this ministry [the text has *mysterii*, ‘mystery’], that this water may be cleansed of the corpses of people floating above.” He made two channels and emptied the place on the right as one entered the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter. For there was there a spring which [read: *qui*] was insufficient. And Damasus cut through the hill with his own hand; it flowed in more than usual. And he constructed a font. All these men reported to Liberius the bishop what had been done. He ordered all the presbyters, clergy, and persons from every rank, together with the faithful, to assemble. In a clear voice he said: “Peter calls his sheep. Behold, a man keeping the faith, obeying Christ and me a sinner, has made a sheepfold for the sheep and has given sweetness of honey to my speech. Therefore I rejoice, because Peter has not allowed the wolf to enter and lay waste his sheep. Know that I proclaim baptism in the basilica of the apostle Peter.”

All received this with joy. The day of Pentecost was near. He summoned the monasteries and the holy Christian people. With litanies [the text has *laetanea*] he came to the blessed apostle Peter. Upon entering, he offered this prayer: “God, who sent your Son and showed the creature its Creator, [Col. 1393A] look upon this vine and cleanse it of thorns and briars; cause its branches to grow strong, and grant them the fruit of truth through God and our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, who lives with God the almighty Father from everlasting, now, and unto ages of ages.” And all the people responded: “Amen.”

They entered on the Saturday of Pentecost. Liberius approved the font and wept altogether with joy—not bitterly, but, to all, he seemed like a honeycomb. From the ninth hour he catechized them all, and from about the eleventh hour [Note: **[Col. 1393D] (1)** In the Life of Damasus: “from about the eleventh hour onward.”] until sunset on Pentecost Sunday he did not cease baptizing. For many pressed to be baptized [Note: **[Col. 1393D] (2)** There: “they pressed for baptism, so that the Mass of Pentecost Sunday might be celebrated on Saturday.”], so that the Masses of Pentecost Sunday were celebrated on Saturday at about the eighth hour. About 8,810 persons of both sexes were baptized [Col. 1393B]. [Note: **[Col. 1393D] (3)** From the matters that follow, the author of the Life of Damasus took nothing.] At that time many wished to touch the garments of Bishop Liberius.

### 9.

On the following day, which was Monday, all the people heard that Constans had gained a victory. In a voice plainly out of his mind [Note: **[Col. 1393D] (4)** Read: “had gained victory,” spoken “with clear voice but an alien mind.”], he said: “I shall go to Nicomedia.” He proceeded to Nicomedia and, at the estate called Aquilo, where he had been baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia, inclined toward the dogma of the Arians. In the same place Constans died and was buried, in the third consulship of Constans, with Constantius Augustus and Bassus as consuls, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May [23 April]. [Note: **[Col. 1393D] (5)** Constantine the Great—not the emperor by whose command Liberius was banished—was baptized in A.D. 337 in the suburbs of Nicomedia and died there, as Eusebius relates in *Life of Constantine*, book IV, ch. 61 and following. **(6)** Constans’ third consulship fell in A.D. 346, a year to which neither the death of Constantine the father nor that of his son Constantius—and still less that of Liberius—can be fitted.] He held the same see of the apostle Peter for seventeen years, thirteen months, and eight days. In his time an apse was built in the fifth region of the city of Rome, and he rested in peace.

## CENSURE OF THE LETTER TO THE EASTERNERS

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 93.) (C, S)*

### I.

The antiquity of this letter is established for us by the transmitted fragments of Hilary and the commentaries of that same bishop appended to it. Its falsity, however, is betrayed by its opening words. For, if we believe them, when Liberius entered upon the pontificate and received letters from the Easterners concerning Athanasius, he immediately sent envoys to Alexandria, summoned Athanasius to Rome, and separated him from communion with the Roman Church when he refused to come. The genuine letter of Liberius to the Easterners, whose authenticity no one has ever doubted, proves this to be altogether false. The Easterners themselves complained to Constantius that Liberius had placed no confidence in their earlier letter and had entirely suppressed it, “lest the crimes of him whom they said they had condemned should be made manifest [Col. 1394A] to all.” For what room would there have been for this accusation had he actually done what this letter says he did? Liberius could readily have demonstrated the injustice of this complaint if, moved by the Easterners’ letter, he had summoned Athanasius to Rome and then separated him from his communion. It would then follow that he had neither suppressed nor disregarded their letter, but had taken the fullest account of it.

But Liberius, conscious that he was far from the fault either of rashly condemning Athanasius or of suppressing the letters written to him by the Easterners, first testifies that he “made known the letter of the Easterners, read it to the Church, read it to the council, and answered the Easterners themselves.” He then gives this reason why he had refused his assent when they demanded Athanasius’ condemnation: “At the same time, the judgment of eighty Egyptian bishops concerning Athanasius” opposed their petition; and it “appeared contrary to divine law,” since the number of bishops supporting Athanasius was greater than that of those opposing him, to grant the latter “assent in any respect” [Col. 1394B].

### II.

Must we say that the Easterners so forestalled Liberius’ judgment as to induce him to condemn Athanasius before the letter of the eighty Egyptian bishops reached Rome? Yet Liberius himself attests that this letter was delivered to him “at the same time” as he received the Easterners’ letter. Even if we were to suppose that the Easterners had been more prompt than the Egyptian bishops in this matter, no conclusion at all could be drawn unless we simultaneously conceded that, after receiving the Easterners’ letter, Liberius sent envoys to Alexandria and that these envoys returned from Alexandria to Rome before the Egyptian bishops’ letter was delivered to Liberius. Indeed, even then the pope should not have said that he had been prevented by the Egyptians’ letter from “granting assent” to the Easterners, but rather that this letter had induced him to withdraw an assent already granted.

We pass over the fact that Athanasius writes that Liberius, for as long as he was free, could never be bent to condemn him; that the dialogue between Emperor Constantius and Liberius proves that Athanasius had not until then been condemned by him; and finally, that Liberius himself, already shaken from his resolve to defend Athanasius, shows that he had thus far remained steadfast in defending him, giving this reason for his constancy: “Because Julius, bishop of blessed memory, my predecessor, had received him; I feared that someone might judge me a betrayer.” Such arguments are more fully set out, together with certain others demonstrating the falsity of the following letter, in Hilary, Fragment IV. Indeed, in the annotations which he appended, as it were, to this letter, Hilary speaks of it as though he considered it fabricated by Potamius and Epictetus and then sent by Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, to various bishops. It follows that it was published not in A.D. 362, when Liberius entered upon the pontificate, but after the Council of Milan held in A.D. 365, when Fortunatianus fell from his former reputation.

## LETTER IN WHICH ATHANASIUS IS SAID TO HAVE BEEN SUMMONED TO ROME AND SEPARATED FROM THE COMMUNION OF THE ROMAN CHURCH, WHILE HIS EASTERN OPPONENTS WERE RECEIVED INTO LIBERIUS’ COMMUNION

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 95.)*

To all our most beloved brethren and fellow-bishops established throughout the East, Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, eternal salvation. *(C, S)*

Desiring peace and concord among the churches, after receiving the letter of your charity concerning Athanasius and the others, addressed to Julius, bishop of blessed memory, I followed the tradition of the elders and sent from my side Lucius, Paul, and Helianus, presbyters of the city of Rome, to the aforementioned Athanasius at Alexandria [Col. 1395B], that he might come to the city of Rome, so that in his presence that which the discipline of the Church requires [the text: “has existed”] might be determined concerning him. I also gave them letters to the same man, containing the declaration that, if he did not come, he should know himself to be outside communion with the Roman Church. When the presbyters returned, therefore, they reported that he had refused to come. Accordingly, following the letter of your charity which you gave us concerning the aforesaid Athanasius, know from this letter, which I have given to our unanimity, that I have peace with all of you and with all bishops of the Catholic Church; but that the aforesaid Athanasius is outside communion with me and with the Roman Church, and outside the fellowship of ecclesiastical letters.

[Note: **[Col. 1395D] (1)** This letter is spurious and falsely attributed to Pope Liberius. It was devised so that people might not believe, as they say, that Liberius, compelled by force, assented to Athanasius’ condemnation. This is proved by the following reasons. First: whoever approves the exclusion of innocent Athanasius from communion with Catholics and the admission of impious Arians to the bond of communion must be not Catholic but Arian. Therefore, since the man who inserted this condemnatory and excommunicatory judgment against Athanasius among Hilary’s fragments approves it, no sensible person believes that Hilary did this. Secondly, Athanasius’ testimony establishes that Liberius remained steadfast and faithful until the end of his exile, that is, until A.D. 357. How then could he have condemned innocent Athanasius and communicated with Arians at the beginning of his pontificate? Thirdly, in the letter which Liberius wrote and sent to Constantius in A.D. 354 through the second embassy, he defends Athanasius and vehemently rejects communion with Arians; and he could surely not prudently have written this had he already condemned Athanasius at the beginning of his tenure. Moreover, in this very letter written to the Easterners, he admits that he always defended Athanasius, as his predecessor Julius had done before him, until the final year of his own exile. The assertion that Athanasius was deprived of communion with the Catholic Church at the beginning of Liberius’ pontificate must therefore be an invention. These are Baronius’ arguments at the place cited above. Severinus Binius.]

## RECIPROCAL LETTERS

### NOTICE ON THE RECIPROCAL LETTERS OF LIBERIUS AND ATHANASIUS

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 95.)*

### I.

In the latest edition of Athanasius’ works, vol. II, p. 667, our editors observed that these two letters do indeed occur in very ancient manuscripts of Athanasius; but, as may be conjectured from their wording, they appear to be the work of one and the same unskilled Greek writer. Certainly, what they proclaim concerning the Trinity is foreign to Athanasius’ customary forms of expression [Col. 1396A]. Nor is it a slight argument for interpolation that, amid such great disturbances as shook the whole Church when Liberius entered upon the pontificate, no mention is made of the adversity of the times. Finally, the first letter, as the marginal note in the Coislin manuscript indicates—where **Ζήτηι ἀρχήν**, “Seek the beginning,” is written—lacks its beginning; while the other bears no form of a letter at all, but is like some inept and confused exposition of faith.

### II.

We add that the heading and subject placed at the head of both letters is: “That God the Word assumed a perfect human being”; yet in neither letter does the fabricator touch upon that subject. In the first he is content to speak of God the Word “who assumed a perfect, sinless human being” [Col. 1396B], while in the other he does not say even one word about the perfect human being assumed. This confirms that both are mutilated. It is also easy to prove that the argument prefixed to them, by which the Apollinarian heresy is rejected, does not at all suit the times of Liberius: for this heresy began to become known and spread in the West only under Pope Damasus. But even if it had become known earlier, why should a profession concerning the perfect human being assumed by the Word be demanded of Athanasius, who was never suspected of Apollinarian heresy? Indeed, what does this mean: “Write back to me if you think concerning the true faith as we do, so that I may confidently and without hesitation grant what you ask”? For even though Liberius was compelled by force temporarily to abandon communion with Athanasius, he never doubted the soundness of Athanasius’ faith—neither at the beginning of his pontificate, when he had been informed by the acts done under Julius and by the letter of the eighty Egyptian bishops, nor ever afterward. Nor does that elaborate assertion of the divine nature of the Holy Spirit contained in the earlier letter sound like Liberius. For if, at the end of his life, he required of those later called Macedonians no other confession concerning the Holy Spirit than that set forth in the Nicene Creed, how much more would he have been satisfied with that same profession at the beginning of his pontificate?

## LETTER OF LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF ROME, TO ATHANASIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 97.)*

**That God the Word assumed a perfect human being.** [Note: **[Col. 1396]** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.] *(C)*

[Col. 1395]

[Col. 1396C] This, then, is our confession, most beloved Athanasius. The Word, Son of God, begotten according to nature from God and the Father, not created, but always without beginning [Col. 1397A] together with God and the Father, and holding dominion without end through infinite ages. Amen. Likewise, we believe the Holy Spirit to be truly from God according to nature and by nature God, undivided from God according to the Holy Scriptures; so that the Father is truly Father, the Son truly Son, and the Holy Spirit truly Holy Spirit. Under penalty of anathema, it is forbidden to transfer any name from its proper meaning; so that the Trinity is truly Trinity in one deity, one power, one essence, and one substance. For neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit is divided from the paternal substance which fills heaven and earth. Therefore, as I said above, the Trinity is undivided in one substance; and substance is one, deity one, power one, kingdom one, glorification one, image one [Note: **[Col. 1397D] (1)** Namely, because God, when about to create humanity, said: “Let us make man in our image”—not “in our images”—“and likeness.”], Spirit one; for Spirit [Col. 1397B] is not divided. Therefore I pronounce anathema upon the doctrine of Sabellius and Arius, and upon the heresies previously condemned, unto eternal punishment according to the Savior’s word. Therefore, brother Athanasius, if you agree with me in this confession, which alone is the true faith in the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, I ask you before God and Christ the Judge to write back to me whether you think concerning the true faith as we do, so that I may confidently and without hesitation grant what you ask. I also wish you to know, beloved, that the children of truth confess the impassibility of the Godhead and the coming of the Word and God in the flesh, who assumed a perfect [Col. 1397C] human being without sin, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary according to the Gospels, in Christ Jesus. Amen.

[Col. 1395C] Therefore this is our confession, Athanasius beloved by me: the Word of God, the Son, begotten according to nature from God and the Father, [Col. 1395D] not created, but always existing co-eternally from the beginning with God and the Father, [Col. 1398A] and possessing the kingdom without ceasing unto unending ages. Amen. And the Holy Spirit is truly from God according to nature, God by nature, indivisible from God according to the holy Scriptures; so that the Father is truly Father, the Son truly Son, and the Holy Spirit truly Holy Spirit, with each name not transferred, under anathema, from its own designation; so that the Trinity is truly Trinity in one Godhead, one power, one essence, and one hypostasis. For neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit is divided from the paternal hypostasis which fills heaven and earth. Therefore, as I said before, the Trinity is not divided in one hypostasis; it is one in essence, one in Godhead, one in power, one in kingdom, one in glorification, one in image, one in Spirit—for Spirit [Col. 1398B] is not divided. Therefore I pronounce anathema upon the doctrine of Sabellius and Arius and upon the heresies formerly prohibited, unto eternal punishment, according to the Savior’s word. Therefore, brother Athanasius, if in this confession—the only true faith existing in the holy Catholic and apostolic Church—you are of one mind with me, then, as before the judgment of God and Christ, write to me whether you think as we do and likewise hold the true faith, so that I too may confidently, without distinction, grant what you request of me. And you must know this also, beloved: that the children of truth confess the impassibility of the Godhead and the incarnate visitation of the Word and God, because he assumed a perfect human being without sin [Col. 1398C], one born of the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin according to the Gospels, in Christ Jesus. Amen.

## REPLY OF OUR HOLY FATHER ATHANASIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF ROME

*(Coust., Appendix, p. 99.)*

**That God the Word assumed a perfect human being for our salvation.** [Note: **[Col. 1398]** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1397]

[Col. 1397C] One immortal God, who can neither be seen nor touched. For God is spirit (John 4:24). He cannot be contained in any place, nor is there any place from which he is absent. His Word is immortal wisdom, incorruptible, invisible, the firstborn Son, fellow-worker in the works, without beginning, not subject to touch, having neither beginning of days nor awaiting an end of life. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1:3). He is the one who formed humankind; he is the one who showed how the ark was to be constructed; he is the one who gave the promise to Abraham; he is the one who descended in order to save the [Col. 1397D] people, who gave the Law to Moses. This is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; he who spoke in the prophets, who ordained the Old and New Testaments; who in the last days took from the Virgin flesh that was mortal, although he himself was not mortal; [Col. 1400A] weak, although he himself was not weak; liable to death, although he himself was not liable to death; visible, although he himself was not visible.

[Note: [Col. 1397D] (2) This was said in accordance with the opinion of the ancient Fathers, who with considerable agreement taught that the Son had made himself visible in various ways from the beginning of the world. Following them, Leo wrote in Letter 30 to Pulcheria: “For the omnipotence of the Son of God could have appeared for the instruction and justification of human beings, just as he appeared to the Patriarchs and Prophets in a bodily form, when he entered into a wrestling match or held conversation, and when he did not refuse the duties of hospitality,” etc. They evidently held that by the name of the angels seen by the Patriarchs and Prophets the Son of God was to be understood. The Council of Sirmium, assembled against Photinus in 451, canon 13, pronounced an anathema against those who understood otherwise.]

[Col. 1397D] It was that flesh which was suspended, not he; it was that flesh which was buried, not he; it was that flesh which endured all human sufferings as a human being, not he.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] (1) The word *ille* (“he,” like *ego* and *tu*, “I” and “you”) properly denotes a person. But to the person of the Word of God is attributed not only what accords with his own nature, but also what accords with the nature assumed by him; thus the expression here is not exact, by which “he” is denied to have been suspended, suffered, and buried. For the Son of God is truly believed to have been suspended, to have suffered, and to have been buried, namely according to the flesh. But the writer of this letter understood by *ille* not the person, but only the nature of the Word.]

[Col. 1400A] But he is the power of God—that is, God—who, having loosed what was indissoluble in hell and overthrown the dominion of the devil, ascended to the place from which he had descended; who raised his body from the tomb and, after freeing it from the death by which it was held, offered it to the Father. In him we understand the Father; for he too is one and the same thing in divinity, power, essence, substance, glory, and the name of God; and we acknowledge the Son himself in the Father. This is he who, after assuming flesh, was called Jesus insofar as he was human; that is, he assumed [Col. 1400B] a human being into himself, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. We believe him to be separated neither from the Father nor from the Holy Spirit; yet we do not say that the Father descended and was in a human being. Thus one God, the almighty Father, is believed by us. Therefore our faith is in one God, the almighty Father, and in his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit. And indeed, from unity—one power, one substance, one essence, one glorification, one lordship, one kingdom, one image—we believe the consubstantiality of the Trinity to consist; [Col. 1390] through whom all things were made. Thus also we believe in the resurrection of the flesh, that is, of our body, according to the holy Scriptures, when what was corruptible and mortal has been changed by God into incorruptibility and immortality. Amen.

[Col. 1398C] One God, immortal, invisible, untouchable; for God is spirit. He is inseparable (*achōristos*) [perhaps *achōrētos*, “uncontainable”], having no place where he is not. His Word is immortal wisdom, incorruptible, invisible, the firstborn Son, fellow-worker, without beginning, untouchable, having neither beginning of days nor awaiting an end of life. Through him all things came to be, and without him not one thing came to be. He himself formed the human being; he showed how the ark was to be made. He gave the promise to Abraham. He descended in order to save the people; he gave the Law to Moses. He is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.

[Col. 1398D] He spoke in the prophets; he ordained the old and the new covenant; in the last days he took from a virgin flesh that was mortal, though he himself was not mortal; weak, though he himself was not weak; owing death, though he himself did not owe it; visible, though he himself was not visible.

[Col. 1399A] It was this flesh that was suspended, not he. It was this flesh that was buried, not he. It was this flesh that endured all human sufferings as a human being, not he. But he is the power of God, that is, God, who, having loosed the indissoluble things of Hades and destroyed the devil’s might, ascended whence he had descended. Raising that which had been buried, he offered it to the Father, having freed it from the death by which it was held. In him we understand the Father, for this too is one and the same thing in divinity, power, essence, hypostasis, glory, and the name of God; and the Son himself in the Father. This is he who, after taking flesh, was called Jesus, since he was also human; that is, he assumed a human being in himself, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. We hold him not to be separated from the Father or from the Holy Spirit. Nor do we say that the Father descended and became in a human being. Thus one God, the almighty Father, is believed among us.

[Col. 1399B] And for this reason our faith is in one God, the almighty Father, and in his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit.
