But these things are from unity: one power, one hypostasis, one essence, one glorification, one lordship, one kingdom, one image—the consubstantiality of the Trinity; through whom all things came to be. Thus we also believe in the resurrection of the flesh, that is, of our body, according to the holy Scriptures, when its corruptible and mortal state is changed by God into incorruption and immortality. Amen.

## Letter of Pope Liberius to All Bishops in General

(Conc. vol. II, col. 670.) That none, because of persecutions, should abandon his own church while he is able to endure, or choose quiet rather than labor for the people entrusted to him. To the most holy and God-loving lords, all bishops: Liberius, bishop, greeting in the Lord. (S)

Nothing will enable us to stand long (read: may enable us) except the grace of God. But the wickedness of the devil, a contemptible evil full of deadly poison, rages; he goes about above and below, seeking whom he may devour. Therefore we must keep watch and be sober for prayers (1 Peter 5:8), draw near to God, and, with the Lord’s help, reject the foolish [Col. 1399D] snares of men insofar as the Lord has granted us power; follow the Fathers and not overstep the boundaries of the Fathers—that is, not abandon our churches while we are in any way able to remain in them in order to hasten to others—nor neglect the people entrusted to us, seeking repose [perhaps: to rest] more than laboring for them, for whom we ought even to lay down our lives [Col. 1400C]; lest we be found reprobate in God’s sight, but may be able, with his aid, to present to him fruitful sheaves from the flocks entrusted to us.

Although many persecute us and desire to tear apart Christ’s sheep, appearing as if in sheep’s clothing while inwardly they are ravening wolves, we know them by their fruits. At first these seem to be of us, but they are not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us. But when they have vomited forth their impiety, bursting forth with the deceit that is in them, they seize the weaker persons and those whose minds are untrained in the divine sayings; they draw them with themselves into destruction, overthrowing and violating the teachings of the Fathers as well as the holy Scriptures, to their own destruction. [Col. 1400D] They must be guarded against with foresight, lest some, deceived by their malice, be cut off from their own steadfastness. For, according to the prophet’s voice, they sharpen their tongues like serpents; the poison of asps is under their lips (Psalm 139).

Let us not shrink from laboring through temporary sufferings for Christ’s name (St Martin, pope, Letter to St Amandus); rather, let the advantages of future recompense persuade us to endure [Col. 1401A] the afflictions of this age. For it is written: “What shall I repay to the Lord for all that he has repaid to me? I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115). Only as much is required of us as we can offer in the service of our ministry. Hence we must persist in urgent preaching in proportion as the doubled allotment of talents for perfect trading has been entrusted to us, and as the declaration of the Lord’s voice urges us to receive his rest.

For it has been reported to us (7, question I, *Suggestum est nobis*) that, because of past labors and attacks, some of you abandon the congregations assigned and entrusted to you by God, and intend in future to abandon more churches that they ought to protect. [Col. 1401B] They neglect to labor for the sheep entrusted to them; they hasten to consign themselves to the repose of monasteries, choose release from episcopal labors, and desire to pass their lives in silence and leisure rather than remain in what has been entrusted to them. Yet the Lord says: “Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end” (Matthew 10 and 24). Whence is perseverance blessed, except from the virtue of patience? For, according to apostolic preaching, all who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution (2 Timothy 3).

Therefore, dearest brothers, do not let the bitterness of afflictions constrain you to depart from your pious purpose of mind. Consider how much our Creator, Lord, and Redeemer endured for our absolution and deliverance, and to what insults he gave himself, [Col. 1401C] in order to free us from the bonds of the devil’s power. Take heed, therefore, to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired by his own blood (Acts 20). Let there be no one to deceive or seduce you with subtle speech, so that you abandon the congregations entrusted to you (St Martin, Synodical Letter after the Lateran Council), surrender yourselves to repose on account of the reproaches of evil people, save only yourselves, and leave your children orphaned.

For the Holy Spirit openly says through the Apostle that in the last times some will depart from faith and charity, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, having their conscience seared by the hypocrisy of lying words (1 Timothy 4). Therefore watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation (Mark 14; Luke 22). [Col. 1401D] What transgression of mind does this produce in those who do not believe the Lord’s words, who withdraw for their own repose from the service entrusted to them, and submit themselves to their own pleasures? Bound, then, by such and other necessities on behalf of God’s people, we exhort your charity (Pope Martin, in the cited Letter to St Amandus): lest you perish together with all who have been entrusted to you, but may be saved on the day of eternal recompense, be ready in every respect, after the example of him who was willing to suffer for us, to remain in all his services; by no means withdraw from the entrusted charge, but with all your strength persevere courageously in the duties entrusted to you until the end. For blessed is the one who perseveres to the end (Matthew 10): [Col. 1402A] the beginning is not praised, but the end.

Let no one deceive you with empty words. For this reason the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Therefore do not become joint participants in their doctrines, nor share in their unfruitful words (the same author, in the cited Synodical Letter almost to the end); rather, rebuke them. For they are an assembly of transgressors; they have stretched out their tongue like a bow of falsehood and not of truth. “It is fulfilled in them: they have gone from evil to evil, and they have not known me,” says the Lord. “They will not speak truth” (Jeremiah 6). For persecutors of churches and their priests have trained their tongues to speak falsehood. “They labored to act impiously, and refused to know me,” says the Lord.

Stand therefore, beloved ones, upon the ways and look. Ask concerning the ancient paths of the Lord, and see [Col. 1402B] which is the good way of the holy Fathers; walk in it, and you shall find rest for your souls. But if you suffer for Christ, you shall be blessed (1 Peter 3). Do not fear their fear, nor be troubled. Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts, he himself saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. Are not two sparrows sold for an *as*? Yet not one of them falls upon the ground without your Father. But even all the hairs of your head are numbered. Therefore do not fear: you are worth more than many sparrows” (Matthew 10). Remember, then, brothers, him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, lest you become weary and faint in your souls. [Col. 1402C] For we have not yet contended unto blood, struggling against sin (Hebrews 12; variant: “you have contended”).

But we are confident concerning you, dearest brothers, of better things and things nearer to salvation: that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers, neither things present nor things to come, neither strength nor height nor depth nor any other creature, as the Teacher of the Gentiles teaches (Romans 8), will be able to separate us from the love of our Lord Jesus Christ and the right faith that is in him. Therefore do not cast away your confidence, which has great recompense. For patience is necessary for us in the struggles with adversaries, so that, keeping the faith undefiled to the end, we may receive the promise which he promised to those who hasten to contend lawfully. [Col. 1402D] For yet a very little while, and he who is coming will come and will not delay (Hebrews 10). Behold, the judge stands before the door (James 5), cheerfully promising crowns to those who submit to sufferings for him. But if anyone withdraws, his soul will not please him (Vulgate: “my soul”); rather, he will fall from the promise because of denial. But we are not children of withdrawal unto destruction, but of faith unto the gaining of the soul.

Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day against all the enemies of God’s holy Church and your own; put on the breastplate of righteousness, shoe your feet with preparedness for the gospel of peace, and in all things take up the shield of faith, by which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one (variant: “fiery”); receive also the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, [Col. 1403A] which is the word of God, through every prayer and supplication (Ephesians 6), rooted and founded in the consolation of the brethren through Christ Jesus our Lord.

And now, brothers, we commend you all to the Lord and to the word of his grace, who is able to bring you to completion and give you an inheritance with all the saints. May the God of peace and consolation grant you to think the same thing toward one another, so that you may help one another and not be divided; so that, being of one mind, with one mouth and one [variant: “pure”] heart, we may honor him for the concord and consolation of the brethren. He is able to strengthen us according to his Gospel, according to the revelation of the eternal mystery, kept silent through eternal times (Acts 20 and Romans 16), by which gifts of future joys are to be bestowed upon you.

You must also consider most carefully that those who envy the brethren and desire to condemn or lead them [Col. 1403B] destroy their own doctrines by themselves. For the Lord says: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall not stand; and every knowledge and law divided against itself shall not stand” (Matthew 12). Therefore it is necessary that you receive wholesome exhortations harmoniously (St Leo, Letter 87, ch. 2), doing nothing from contention but, united in every pursuit of devotion, obeying the divine and apostolic constitutions. In no respect permit the most provident decrees of the canons to be violated, so that both the ordinances of the Nicene canons and what has been wisely and salutarily decreed by us or our predecessors (Siricius, Letter 1) may remain undefiled in the future.

(In Justellus’s manuscripts, after several scraps of letters wrongly pieced together from Ennodius or another orator of the same period, this subscription is read:)

[Col. 1403C] Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Betius and Julianus, most distinguished men.

## Letter of Athanasius and the Egyptian Bishops to Pope Liberius

[Note: [Col. 1403D] (1) Not only learned writers, but every sort of inferior writer as well, consider this letter and the following one to be among the forgeries.]

(Conc. vol. II, col. 763.) Concerning the oppressions of the Arians. To the most blessed and honorable lord, holy father Liberius, pope: Athanasius and the bishops of Egypt, assembled together synodically at Alexandria. (S)

The prerogatives of your most blessed [Col. 1403D] fatherhood are manifest before God, since, through apostolic preaching and doctrines and the cultivation of the true faith, the whole earth has been filled.

[Note: [Col. 1403D] (2) Compare these fragments from Victor of Carthage’s Letter to Pope Theodore, which appears in session 2 of the Lateran Council under St Martin.]

Yet through instruction in the divine utterances, with your exhortatory admonition providing guidance, the orthodox Church of Christ is built further upon the foundation of apostolic institution and strengthened most firmly by the faithful Fathers. To it all the most blessed apostles, endowed with an equal sharing in honor and authority, converted multitudes of peoples, and by saving precepts and admonitions brought, in piety and holiness, those foreknown by the grace of divine predestination from darkness [Col. 1404A] to light, from falling to the true faith, and from death to life.

Following the venerable merits of those holy apostles and more fully fulfilling their examples, your honored fraternity adorns the Church of God with integrity of character and holiness of deeds. Flourishing in sacred faith and Christian morals, it unceasingly carries out and accomplishes through episcopal zeal what it commands to be pleasing to God, preserving the commands of the divine law; for, as the Apostle relates, it is not hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but doers of the law who will be justified (Romans 2).

Desiring to meditate upon these things, to proclaim what we received from your holy apostolic see through the preaching of the apostles and their successors, and what we have learned was confirmed in the Nicene Synod [Col. 1404B], and desiring to repel the blasphemies of the Arians and other heretics, we are daily persecuted by them, handed over to condemnation, and appointed to death. Therefore we pray that we may be helped by your exhortations, both through yourselves and through your representatives; lest, while they grow and we diminish, the true faith be destroyed and their heresy grow beyond our faith. For we fear that, after iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold (Matthew 24). For this reason, great reward and praise from God and from all believers are stored up for your sacred teaching if these men are cut off by your authority.

We have inserted below the faith which we received from the holy Fathers and which we hold and teach, so that if anyone [Col. 1404C] reports to you—by accusation, whispering, or detraction—that we believe or teach otherwise, or commits it to writing, you may clearly recognize from this that we believe and teach thus.

For we believe in one almighty Father, maker of all things visible and also invisible.

[Note: [Col. 1404D] (3) The Nicene Creed, translated by Rufinus.]

And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten of the Father, only-begotten, that is, from the substance of the Father; God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; *homousion*, that is, of the same substance as the Father; through whom all things were made, things heavenly and earthly. For us human beings and for our salvation he descended from heaven, was incarnate and made human, suffered and rose on the third day; he ascended into heaven and will come from there to judge the living and the dead. [Col. 1404D] And in the Holy Spirit. But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and, “Before he was begotten, he was not,” and that he was made from things not subsisting; or who say that the Son of God is from another substance or essence, or is *trepton*, that is, changeable and mutable—these the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes. This venerable faith three hundred and eighteen Fathers acknowledged and embraced, and, agreeing and unanimous, explained in writing.

But now, since, as you know, such things as ought not arise against these things, come, beloved [Col. 1405A] brothers (St Martin, session 4, Lateran Council), let us with God descend for visitation—that is, for inquiry into their words—and by the truest proof there confound their tongues, raised against knowledge of the only-begotten Son of God and speaking iniquity against the height of his humanity. Let us break their bonds with the spiritual sword, which is the word of God, and cast their yoke from us (Psalm 2), by overthrowing their profane understanding. Then the Lord himself will laugh at them and mock them; then he will speak to them in his wrath and trouble them in his fury (ibid.).

According to blessed Jeremiah, he says: “These prophets prophesy falsely in my name. I did not send them, nor command them, nor speak to them. They prophesy to you a lying vision, [Col. 1405B] divination, fraud, and the deception of their own heart. Therefore the Lord says this concerning the prophets who prophesy lies in my name: They shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem, and all who confess me piously shall be trampled down; and there shall be none to bury them” (Jeremiah 14). For no one can hide himself by certain fabricated deceptions, just as Adam, the ancient transgressor of the command, could not hide himself with fig leaves; through his own tongue he is shamelessly exposed. For a man’s lips are a strong snare; he is captured by his own sayings and by the work of his hands; the recompense of his lips and the rebuke of impiety shall be given him. “I will rebuke you,” he says, “and set you before your face. You wickedly supposed that I would be like you.”

Therefore, as the Lord says to Gideon, let us bring them down to the water of true [Col. 1405C] discernment and test them there by regular examination, as they fall prone in the same manner (Genesis 3; Proverbs 6; Psalm 49; Judith 7), after their perverse understanding has been exposed: whether they are wise in their own eyes while ignorant of the knowledge of the divine Word. For “claiming to be wise, they became fools,” and they changed the glory (Romans 1) of the catholic Church by their own novelty and will, introducing heretical disturbance either by matters unlawfully undertaken in its defense. Let us retain in an appropriate sense that which was well said to Jesus son of Sirach: “Strive for the truth unto death, and the Lord God will fight for you” (Ecclesiasticus 4).

For this purpose the universal Church has been entrusted to you by Christ Jesus, that you may labor for all and not neglect to bring aid to all; for while the strong armed man guards [Col. 1405D] his court, all that he possesses is in peace (Luke 11 [the text has “II”]). Therefore, under such pressing necessity, use your highest authority to restrain the hostile, raise up the oppressed, so that, with the Lord’s help and without grave difficulty, we ourselves may be worthy to offer sacrifice gladly and unharmed at all times. And the subscription: May the eternal Divinity preserve you for many years, most holy Father of Fathers. Amen. (Justinian II, to Pope John V.)

## Responsive Letter of Pope Liberius to Athanasius and the Egyptian Bishops

(Conc. vol. II, col. 765.) Against disturbers of the peace and tranquillity of the churches, and how such persons are to be punished. To his dearest son Athanasius and all the Egyptian bishops assembled together and holding right opinions concerning faith in the Trinity: Liberius, pope.

[Col. 1406A]

Long ago and from the beginning we received from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, such confidence (St Leo, Letter 24) that we possess authority on behalf of the universal Church to defend the right faith, so that no one may be permitted, without jeopardizing his own rank, to disturb the ordinance of the holy Church to the injury of right believers. [Col. 1406B] We had your letter sent to us read before us, and understood the tribulations and persecutions that you suffer for the right faith. In these matters we grieve with you, and are prepared to labor for you as a father for his children.

We found the faith of the Nicene Council in that letter to be right, and for it we rendered most abundant thanks to God. For it we are prepared not only to endure persecutions and sufferings with you but, if necessary, do not refuse, insofar as our frailty permits, even to die for Christ’s name. Therefore, as we read, the aforesaid holy Nicene Council decrees (Maximus of Aquileia, session 4 of the Lateran Council held in 649) that no one may put forward, write, or compose another faith, think or teach otherwise, nor conceive or utter [Col. 1406C] anything concerning the faith that may conflict with these rules of the Fathers. But whoever presumes to compose or set forth another faith, or to teach or deliver another creed to those who wish to turn to the way of truth from whatever heresy, or from Jews or pagans who wish to become Christians: if they are bishops or clerics, bishops are to be removed from the episcopate and clerics from the clergy; if monks or laypersons, they are to be struck with anathema.

For the blessed Apostle testifies (St Martin, session 5 of the same council), saying: “If anyone competes, he is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully.” And again the Lord says: “The one who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (1 Timothy 6; Matthew 10). Since sacred contests have been set before [Col. 1406D] us for the defense of the catholic Church, and great salvation is thereby hoped for from God, giver of all good things, let not our hands, dearest brothers, be weakened and slackened through any occasion of indolence. Rather, let us be made strong by the Lord’s grace and by the might of his power, since he has made our feet like those of deer (Psalm 7), and has more firmly established our understanding upon the heights of his supreme humanity for our salvation, especially since so great a cloud of holy witnesses has been placed upon us.

Therefore, laying aside every burden and the surrounding novelty of adversaries, let us run with patience, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith (Hebrews 12), who may grant us, in the task undertaken for his sake, [Col. 1407A] the Spirit of his truth, speaking in us and testifying to the great things of faith through the teaching of the holy Fathers, whom the adversaries daily calumniate.

For it is written in the prophets (the same St Martin, session 3): “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her righteousness goes forth as brightness and her savior is kindled like a lamp” (Isaiah 62). Certainly the catholic Church, which is the true Zion and the city of Christ the king of heaven, has for so many years been assailed by those who oppose the words of faith, who neither fear God nor respect humankind, but vainly overthrow the pious and canonical doctrines on this subject. Though they have been urged by many and great testimonies, written and unwritten, to correct and expel from themselves their own heresy—as was more clearly demonstrated by prior inquiry, [Col. 1407B] both through written petitions and through the representations of most reverend priests and venerable abbots—and though the Apostle testifies to us that a heretical person must be avoided after a first and second correction, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment (Titus 3), we must by no means henceforth remain silent or rest, lest we somehow be judged wicked for embracing a peace hateful to God.

For it is written: “I was envious of sinners when I saw the peace of sinners”; and it may also be said of us: “My priests despised my law and profaned my sanctuaries; they made no distinction between holy and profane, and did not understand the difference between unclean and clean” (Psalm 72; Zephaniah 3; Ezekiel 22). [Col. 1407C] Instead, let us rise with God and stand ready, putting on the weapons of the Spirit against those who act maliciously against his faith, so that we may wisely test the spirits—that is, their words—whether they are from God. For it is written in Jeremiah: “I have given you as a strong tester among my people; and you shall know and test their way” (Jeremiah 6).

For we need much watchfulness and such investigation of divine wisdom, which reveals the hidden things of darkness, for the examination and scrutiny of this matter. It lies concealed in a manner, and deceitful malice is apprehended with difficulty, because it cunningly flatters itself with an appearance of piety in order to escape the mind of those who investigate it. Knowing this, the blessed Apostle says: “For such persons are false apostles and deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ” (2 Corinthians 11). [Col. 1407D] But this is no wonder, since Satan himself transforms himself as an angel of light. Therefore it is no wonder if his ministers transform themselves as ministers of righteousness, whose end is according to their works. And the Lord, warning us beforehand of this, says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves. You shall know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7).

Therefore, directing our whole heart first of all to prayer concerning such a question, and [Col. 1408A] saying with David: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall behold wondrous things from your law. Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths”—for, as the blessed prophet Daniel says, wisdom and power belong to him: “He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who understand instruction. He reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is set in darkness, and light is with him; you have given me wisdom and strength and shown me what I asked of you” (Psalm 118; Daniel 2)—let us, with divine help, give diligent attention to the written statements of each person accused of devising novelty, brought forth from our venerable archive by those complying with our request and carefully presented to us in due form. Thus those who have presumed to violate these things shall first be subject to the dreadful judgment of almighty [Col. 1408B] God, and then shall fear whatever royal indignation there may be (the *Typos* of Emperor Constans, session 4 of the Lateran Council under St Martin). If they are bishops or clerics, let them in every way be deprived of their priesthood or clerical rank; if monks, let them be segregated and alienated from their places. If they possess rank, a belt of office, or military service, let them be stripped of these. If they are private persons and noble, let them suffer confiscation of their property. If they are of low rank, let them not only be beaten bodily but punished with perpetual exile. Thus may all, restrained by fear of God and reverencing the fitting penalties threatened to them, preserve the unshaken and undisturbed peace of God’s holy churches.

[Col. 1408C] Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Asclepius and Deodatus, most distinguished men (consuls fabricated at will). Glory to Christ Jesus our Lord; peace be with you. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1407D] (1) The consuls added to this letter render its authenticity suspect, since I have been unable to find their names entered anywhere else in the consular lists. I have placed here, in the last position, this sole letter extant in the volumes of councils of the earlier edition, because I placed all the preceding ones according to chronological order. If this was written by Liberius, it must have been written either under Julian or under Valens. For it is a response to Athanasius’s letter, in which he writes that the Arians seek his death daily. Let more learned persons judge whether both Athanasius’s letter to Liberius and, conversely, Liberius’s letter to Athanasius are of suspect authenticity. SEVERUS BINIUS.]

## Decrees of Pope Liberius

Taken from an ancient codex of sixteen books, book XIII, chapter 9. That during days of fasting there should be no quarrels. (S)

During these days of fasting there should be no lawsuits and no disputes; rather, one should persist in the praises of God and necessary work. For through the prophet the Lord rebukes those who engage in disputes and lawsuits during Lent, and those who demand debts from debtors, saying: “Behold, on the days of your fasting your own [Col. 1408D] desire is found, and you exact from all your debtors. Behold, you fast for lawsuits and disputes, and strike wickedly with the fist.”

### Of the Same, Chapter Ten. That married persons should abstain from their spouses on the holy days of fasting.

During these most sacred forty [Col. 1409A] days one must abstain from spouses and live chastely and piously, so that these days may be passed with heart and body sanctified, until one arrives at the holy day of Easter; for the fast which is defiled by conjugal intercourse, and which prayers, vigils, and alms do not commend, is worth almost nothing.

### Of the Same, Chapter Twelve. What is to be done if famine or irregularity of the weather occurs.

[Col. 1410A]

If famine, irregular weather, pestilence, or any such tribulation occurs, the Lord’s mercy should immediately be entreated by fasts, almsgiving, and prayers.

## In the Year of the Lord 366. Potamius, Bishop of Ulyssipona

[Col. 1409]

[Col. 1409]

## Prolegomena: On Potamius, Bishop of Ulyssipona

(Galland., vol. V, Prolegomena, p. XVII.)

[Col. 1409B] 1. In the preceding century Achéry, a Benedictine monk, published from a manuscript of the Abbey of Saint-Evroul [Note: [Col. 1409D] (1) Achéry, vol. II, p. 366, or vol. III of the new edition, p. 299.] Potamius’s letter to Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, concerning the consubstantiality of the Son of God, as its heading, reproduced in the chronological index prefixed to volume I of the new edition, states; there it is also said to have been composed about the year 355. Yet where the same letter is printed, its heading is differently given, apparently drawn from the manuscript itself. For there it reads: “Letter of Potamius to Athanasius, assailed by the Arians, after they subscribed at the Council of Rimini.” To which heading, then, should credit be given, so that we may in some fashion determine who this Potamius, the author of the letter, was? I should certainly judge that no account ought to be taken of the latter heading, since it appears to have proceeded from an unlearned copyist rather than from the author himself. For, since we know of no other Potamius flourishing in Athanasius’s age besides the bishop of Lisbon, he could not possibly have addressed such a letter to Athanasius after the Council of Rimini—that is, in 360, or at earliest 359—he who had plainly crossed over to the Arian camp four or five years earlier and who, especially at the second Synod of Sirmium convened in 357, was numbered among the leading Arianizers.

II. Indeed, as we learn from Marcellinus and Faustinus [Note: [Col. 1409D] (2) Marcellinus and Faustinus, *Libellus precum*, p. 13, Oxford edition, 1678.], this Potamius at first defended the Catholic faith; but afterwards betrayed that faith for the reward of an imperial estate which he coveted. The same writers add that Hosius of Corduba consequently exposed and rejected him among the churches of Spain [Col. 1409D] as an impious heretic. Yet Potamius was not allowed to enjoy the property acquired by so great an impiety: while [Note: [Col. 1409D] (3) The same authors, ibid., p. 17.] hurrying to the estate which he had obtained from the emperor in reward for his impious subscription concerning the faith, he paid a new penalty for the tongue through which he had blasphemed: [Col. 1410B] he died on the road, receiving none of the estate’s fruits, not even the sight of it.

And this was a just judgment of God. For this heretical man, as Phoebadius, bishop of Agen, sufficiently indicates [Note: [Col. 1410D] (4) Phoebadius, *Against the Arians*, §4.], is said to have composed the formula of faith issued at the aforesaid Synod of Sirmium, which Athanasius lists as the seventh [Note: [Col. 1410D] (5) Athanasius, *On the Synods*, §18, *Works*, vol. I, part II, p. 744.], and which was so full of impiety that Hilary called it a “blasphemy” [Note: [Col. 1410D] (6) Hilary, *On the Synods*, §11.]. Moreover, from the presbyters of the Luciferians just cited we learn that it was especially through the agency of this same Arian bishop that the great Hosius was summoned before Emperor Constantius and, terrified by threats, yielded to impiety [Note: [Col. 1410D] (7) Marcellinus and Faustinus, cited passage, p. 14.].

III. Since this is so, Potamius must therefore have written the letter to Athanasius published by Achéry while he was still a vigorous defender of the Nicene faith, [Col. 1410C] namely about the year 355, as the earlier heading indicates. Nor is there any reason why the distinguished Montfaucon should rightly judge the same letter to be under grave suspicion [Note: [Col. 1410D] (8) Montfaucon, preface to vol. I of Athanasius’s *Works*, p. 16, §17.], especially if we observe that Potamius’s own manuscript book *Against the Perfidy of Arius* exists in the library of the monastery of Saint-Vaast at Arras, according to the testimony of Antonius Sanderus [Note: [Col. 1410D] (9) Sanderus, *Bibliotheca Belgica Manuscripta*, p. 63.], as Schoettgen noted [Note: [Col. 1410D] (10) Schoettgen, *Bibliotheca Latina Mediae et Infimae Aetatis* of Fabricius, vol. VI, p. 25.].

Furthermore, Athanasius leaves us no room to doubt that this Spanish bishop wrote this letter in Latin, as it now stands. For, speaking of the Sirmian formula of faith called a blasphemy, of which Potamius is thought to have been author, as we have just recalled, the holy Doctor says: “And they write these things at Sirmium in Latin, and they are translated into Greek”: καὶ γράφουσι ταῦτα ἐν Σιρμίῳ Ρωμαϊστὶ μὲν, ἑρμενευθέντα δὲ Ἑλληνιστί—“And they write these things at Sirmium in Latin, and they are translated into Greek.” Therefore the new editor of Achéry’s [Col. 1410D] *Spicilegium* [Col. 1411A] was less correct when he suggested, more than once, that the letter had been translated from Greek [Note: [Col. 1411C] (1) Achéry, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, in the chronological index under the year 355; and vol. III, p. 299, note (a).].

IV. Before Potamius’s letter to Athanasius we have placed two discourses composed by the same author: one entitled *On Lazarus*, the other *On the Martyrdom of the Prophet Isaiah*. The most learned Ballerini brothers claimed these for their true author, Potamius. They had formerly been inserted among the treatises of Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, but the Ballerini brothers recovered them from the Venetian edition of Zeno and from all the manuscripts by restoring the reading of one passage in Discourse I [Note: [Col. 1411C] (2) Potamius, Discourse I.], and assigned them to Potamius [Note: [Col. 1411C] (3) Ballerini, preface to the appendix of the treatises of St. Zeno, p. 294, §3.]. Nevertheless, they seek another Potamius than the bishop of Lisbon: a bishop of an unknown Latin city. They do so, though hesitantly, by adhering to the later heading of Potamius’s letter. Yet they acknowledge one and the same author for both the letter and the discourses; indeed, the highly obscure and involved style in both points to one and the same writer. We have otherwise followed the careful Veronese edition of these little works and have appended at the same time the Ballerini notes by which they are elucidated.

[Col. 1411]

# TWO TREATISES OF BISHOP POTAMIUS, TO WHICH IS ADDED A LETTER TO ST ATHANASIUS

## TREATISE I. ON [Note: [Col. 1411C] (4) Thus the manuscripts. But the Venetian edition: “On Lazarus Raised.” The Veronese edition adds: “A sermon on the Gospel according to Luke.”] LAZARUS

(Galland, vol. V, p. 96.)

Brothers, I am tormented by immense astonishment and a great miracle, amid ambiguous anxieties, this way and that, in the hollow bosom of a dizzying abyss [Note: [Col. 1411C] (5) Sparaverius would read *voraginis*, “of an abyss.”], by plunging waves. Lazarus is dead—one familiar with God, [Note: [Col. 1411C] (6) “As they report,” omitted from the printed editions, is found in all manuscripts except one manuscript of Sparaverius, which reads “as is reported.” The Zeno, Sparaverius, and Pomp. manuscripts and the Venetian edition write: “with the Gospel as witness, when at John’s [Gospel], after forty…” But copyists transposed *with the Gospel as witness* from its proper place: for John’s Gospel is named here. Unless perhaps one should read: “as they report, with the Gospel as witness, in John, after forty…”], as they report, with the Gospel in John as witness (John 2:24), when he had paid the penalty of the body’s losses by the manner of a forty-year-old will [Note: [Col. 1411D] (7) Sparaverius prefers *vitae*, “of life,” to *voluntatis*, “of will.” The emendation *aetatis*, “of age,” differs less from the received reading.].

For, as his swift-setting end was already drawing near, what was owed to his earthly limbs—namely, to the earth itself [Note: [Col. 1411D] (8) This departs more widely from the Pomp. manuscript and Venetian edition, yet we judged it should be retained, since the discussion concerns burial, which was owed more to the corpse and to the earth than to the man, by that sentence of Genesis whereby it was decreed that man should return to the earth from which he was taken.] than to the man—according to the book of Genesis (Gen. 1), where the finest moisture of clay [Note: [Col. 1411D] (9) Rem. manuscript: “the finest liquid covers”; it is the source of the difficulty. Sparaverius thinks the word *optimus* is superfluous. Below one reads: “the liquid removes or covers the mud of clay.” Should something similar be written here? Sparaverius also thinks that *censente* should be read for *censore*. In the Pomp. manuscript, after the old word, erased by a later hand, some unknown word was overwritten: *censore*. We would rather think *absente*, “being absent,” or *existente*, “being present,” should be read, since Lazarus died and was buried while Christ was elsewhere, indeed far away.] is the cause—while Christ, the arbiter, was far away [Col. 1412A] and was dispensing saving benefits within the borders of Judaea, Lazarus was buried and entombed. That is, he began to be what he had been—clay—when he ceased to be what he was: form, or fable.

Thus, through heavy masses of darkness and the shades of black horror—that is, through the cycles of four days, reborn in the ebbing alternation of increase and decrease—he lay for eight days, so to speak, along with blue-black nights, with the gaping jaws hanging open, teeth broken in his mouth, his mouth foul-smelling [Note: [Col. 1412C] (10) The Pomp. manuscript corrects to *caeruleis*, “blue.” Below, where other codices read *caeruleus*, the same manuscript has *caerulus*. For *rictu*, “gaping,” the Zeno manuscript and Venetian edition have *ritu*, “rite.”]. Truly, since he had been formed from earthly filth, the decaying clod was rotting; and the cords of his sinews, together with the body’s wretched condition, were condemned by the unhappy tomb to corruption. His limbs having been drawn together, the grim skin is stretched over the empty, countable ribs; and the stream of moisture discharged from the deep of the intestines flowed, foul now, through the bottom of the corpse, black and blue-black like a bilge.

Alas! How could a corpse, for four days and four nights, not breathe out through all the channels of the mouth, gall, and [Note: [Col. 1412C] (11) Pomp. manuscript: *fleumatis*; Zeno: *pheumatis*. For *fragranti*, “fragrant,” Pomp. shortly afterward writes *flagranti*, “burning.”] phlegm the stench of a rotting lung, its limbs corrupted? Even the rose itself, more precious—so to speak—in its fragrant petal and in the balsam prepared for it by itself; but if it is plucked from its rose-bed by the sickle of a thumb, it whitens sadly in withering death, so that [Note: [Col. 1412C] (12) “Both,” added from the Pomp., Sparaverius, and Zeno manuscripts and the Venetian edition.] it lacks both the flower’s color and its odor. Water itself, if taken from the river in which it lives, perishes when its nature ceases to be what it had lived as. Therefore, once it is torn from its element and lacks its substance, wherever it lies, the liquid strips off the mud of clay [Note: [Col. 1412D] (13) The Pomp. and Sparaverius manuscripts read *obducit*, “covers,” as the Rem. manuscript notes. The Venetian edition has *obduxit*, “covered.”]; it soon becomes foul with stench.

No one, then, should wonder if the whole body of a human being [Note: [Col. 1412D] (14) In the Pomp., Zeno, and Sparaverius manuscripts and Venetian edition: “of a human being.”], whom the spirit of wisdom, seasoned with salt, had preserved in fragrant [Col. 1412C] breath, and whom the soul had governed with the nectareous vitality of heavenly sweetness [Note: [Col. 1412D] (15) The Tol. manuscript adds “with the life-giving vigor of water,” which agrees with the richness of balsam.] and the honey-sweet richness of balsam [Note: [Col. 1412D] (16) Six manuscripts—Tol., Vat., Pomp., Urb., Sp., and Zeno—add “had governed the body.” The Venetian edition shortly thereafter has *ne faceret*. Sparaverius would prefer *eum*, “him,” to be written for *ne*, “lest.” But no alteration is needed, since this clause can refer to the time when the soul governed the man, as the immediately preceding clause relates.], so that, at the separation caused by the departing spirit, it might not become a mass of clay and inert earth [Note: [Col. 1412D] (17) In the Pomp. manuscript and Venetian edition the particle *et* is absent, perhaps better so, since in that way “the fleeting line of the dead” can be referred to the verb *to become* and understood suitably.]—the fleeting line of the dead resisting the body’s structure—the whole body may be released into the stain of its own stench through decay [Note: [Col. 1412D] (18) Urb., Pomp., and Zeno manuscripts and Venetian edition: *relaxatur*, “is released.”].

[Col. 1413A] Hence it is that, by the [Note: [Col. 1413C] (1) Sparaverius would write *discordiam*, “discord.”] separation of things, the whole nature of the limbs, compacted into one mass, grows numb. When the soul that tended the body’s flower-garden departs, the entire substance, with livid complexion, dissolves into decay; and instead of the corpse’s voice, the foul stench of black gall from the dead [Note: [Col. 1413C] (2) He thinks the word “dead” superfluous.] is inhaled.

The bodily structure, then, composed of earth, moisture, cold, and heat—whose four parts, [Note: [Col. 1413D] (3) The word “always” is not found in the Rem. manuscript.] always at war with themselves, overthrow the body of sins in a storm (heat does not love cold, and cold is tormented by heat; opposites are enslaved to opposites; earth is corrupted by excessive moisture, and moisture is defiled by earth)—the body which stands as a fourfold mass made of these four elements [Note: [Col. 1413D] (4) Tol. manuscript: *dissortiatio*, “dissociation.”], when its charioteer has been separated by the divorce of death—the one who assigned places to these four parts lest any should raise [Col. 1413B] its own movement too violently, and who drove them, with the controlling lash, into concordant union within their respective bounds [Note: [Col. 1413D] (5) Pomp. manuscript: *nobilitatem*, “nobility.”] [Note: [Col. 1413D] (6) Urb. manuscript: “therefore, when these things, as the soul departs, withdraw into four parts…” The same reading is found in Pomp.]—these four parts, I say, when the soul departs, mingle in the mass of the bereft body, their author of fellowship having been expelled.

But because the Lord had loved this young man—I mean Lazarus—in the world, foreknowing the future he told his Apostles that Lazarus had fallen asleep (John 11:11 ff.), and promised that, if he came to that city, Lazarus would immediately be raised. [Note: [Col. 1413D] (7) “This Lazarus,” in the Vat., Pomp., Urb., and Zeno manuscripts and the Venetian edition.] This Lazarus, therefore, whose limbs had wasted away as a livid stiffness wandered through the blue veins; whom, laid in a coffin within the cave of a cut rock, a huge stone cast down by its heavy weight had shut in with an enduring door—this Lazarus, the most holy true mercy of God proclaimed that he could rise [Note: [Col. 1413D] (8) “That Lazarus could,” added in the Tol., Urb., Pomp., and Zeno manuscripts and Venetian edition. Everything, however, is obscure and corrupt. A little later the Pomp. manuscript has *vere Dei*, “truly of God,” for *vera Dei*, “true [mercy] of God.”], if they believed these things.

Immediately the sisters, surrounded [Note: [Col. 1413D] (9) “By the crowd of the miracle,” in the Rem., Tol., Vat., Urb., Pomp., and Zeno manuscripts and Venetian edition. After *nonnulla*, “some,” the Pomp. and Vat. manuscripts have *ebrietatae*, for *ebriatae*, “intoxicated.”] by the crowd, intoxicated with lamentation, anguish, fasting, and abundant tears, cast themselves pitiably at God’s knees, their entire bodies prostrate. And, giving their Hebrew words a Greek inflection, [Note: [Col. 1413D] (10) The word *graecessando*, “speaking Greek,” is added from all manuscripts and the Venetian edition. Sparaverius prefers *complicabant*, “they entwined,” to *expiabant*, “they propitiated,” and would remove the particle *in* before the ablative *laudibus*.], they propitiated the Savior in praises mingled into one with broken sobs.

How great, I ask you, was the hurried gathering of people there? What a crowd of spectators? What a harmony could there have been for so great a miracle, where girls were lamenting, a brother was dead, and Christ promised to raise a human being? Soldiers, Jews, Gentiles, proselytes, most illustrious senators, noble judges [Note: [Col. 1413D] (11) The Vat., Urb., Pomp., and Zeno manuscripts and Venetian edition add [Col. 1414C] “sailors, slaves,” etc. In the first two codices the word “noble” is absent.], slaves—I believe—all the city almost, came running in rivalry to this spectacle, destined for everlasting remembrance, to see whether [Col. 1414A] Lazarus could rise, whose stench was already striking people at a distance from the tomb [Note: [Col. 1414C] (12) “Already” is absent from the Pomp. manuscript, which also reads *populum*, “the people,” for *populus*, “people.”]. On seeing this, the whole city marveled.

What were you like there, Christ Jesus? How golden, how beautiful—purer than a spring, whiter than snow, brighter than the sun, your form clearer than the moon! Alas for me—why do I ask concerning one whom I was not worthy to see then? Yet now I have learned, by your mercy, who and how great you are.

Behold, amid these things Jesus Christ, Savior of humankind, is said to have wept (ibid. 15) [Note: [Col. 1414C] (13) This whole sentence, from “Come, come” to “is said,” has been restored from all manuscripts and the Venetian edition. Why the Veronese editors rejected it, we do not know, unless perhaps because of their preconceived view that this treatise should be regarded as Zeno’s work; whereas this sentence plainly attributes it to Potamius. In the manuscripts, indeed, *Photami* or *Photami* is written with *ph*; but many examples show that Greek φ is often represented by P, or interchangeably by *ph* or *p*. We have preferred P against the manuscripts’ spelling, because these treatises seem to have the same author, Potamius, to whom the letter published by Achéry is assigned among his works, and which has the same style. Therefore either *Photamius* should have been written there, or *Potamius* should have been restored here.]. “Come, come, Potamius, servant of the living God: if you have any strength, tell, if only a little, of the praises of the Lord.”

God wept, stirred by the tears of mortals; and though, relying upon his own power, he was recalling Lazarus from the bond of death, he rendered the office of compassion by the consolation of tears. God wept, not because he knew that the dead man before him had perished, but because he was moderating the sisters’ weeping [Note: [Col. 1414C] (14) Rem. manuscript and Venetian and Veronese editions: “weeping.” The Pomp. codex writes the same, but has in the margin “weeping,” which was adopted in the Paduan edition.]. God wept because the devil, by teaching sin, had made exiles of almost all those to whom God had given everything, subjected everything to their power, and appointed even paradise, flowers, and lilies for them without any labor [Note: [Col. 1414D] (15) Urb. manuscript: “made [them] discover [that they were] exiles.” A little below, all manuscripts and editions read somewhat differently: “made [them] be found guilty.”]. God wept because the devil, through wickedness, had caused those whom God made innocent to be found guilty.

[Note: [Col. 1414D] (16) The following three clauses, omitted in the Veronese edition from “Alas” to “mortal,” are restored from all manuscripts and the Venetian edition. The Rem. manuscript writes *solum tenus* for *tenuis*, “slender.” The Urb. manuscript: *texeras* for *rexeras*, “you had governed.” The Pomp. and Zeno manuscripts: *artubus*, “limbs,” for *artibus*, “arts”; Vat. manuscript: *deferebas* for *deserebas*, “you abandoned.”] Alas, slender breath from heaven, you were abandoning the body which you had governed with failing limbs. Yet neither the Father nor the Son ever despised you. For your death, Christ himself too became mortal.

At their tears [Note: [Col. 1414D] (17) The Pomp. and Zeno manuscripts and Venetian edition lack the particle *et*, “and.”], and at the scattered hair of their pitiable tresses, the Savior, moved by compassion, answered tears with tears [Note: [Col. 1414D] (18) Rem., Vat., Urb., Pomp., Sparaverius, and Zeno manuscripts, along with Venetian and Veronese editions, read *recontabat*, “answered.” But the Paduan edition emended it to *recontrahebat*, “drew back.”]. And because he himself was moved by the sisters’ tears [Note: [Col. 1414D] (19) Pomp. manuscript: *commovebatur*, “was moved.”], the fatherhood of our Savior’s Son was bent among the very heavens by tears [Note: [Col. 1414D] (20) Thus all manuscripts and the Venetian edition. But the Veronese editors [Col. 1415C] substituted *Pater*, “Father,” for *ejus paternitas*, “his fatherhood”; on what evidence we do not know.].

Jesus Christ then approached the tomb of Lazarus. At once, by his command, the stones were rolled away; the secret chamber of horror lay open. The eyes of the groaning crowd, eagerly curious, were cast into the cave [Note: [Col. 1415C] (1) Rem. manuscript: *initebantur*, “were entered into.”]. Lazarus was seen with his face covered and his hands and feet bound; and, as a proof of powers, [Note: [Col. 1415C] (2) The Veronese edition had: “He who had been dead, and still bound hand and foot, was unbound as Christ commanded.” This agrees better with the narrative as the Evangelists indicate, but is absent from the manuscripts and Venetian edition, whose reading we judged should be printed. One Tol. manuscript reads *resolvebatur*, “was being unbound.”] he himself, though dead and still bound at the feet, at Christ’s command unbound himself with his own hands.

What voices, I ask you, brothers [Note: [Col. 1415D] (3) The Tol. and Pomp. manuscripts add “most beloved.”], were there? What pressure of onlookers? How intent the eyes of those who marveled! What a multitude hung upon the necks of those pressing forward! What weeping, what joy, what murmur! What a new and heavenly miracle! Death is conquered; the man is restored; the chains of the underworld are broken. And after four days Lazarus’s tongue moves, his hands are made ready for service, his eyes move in their sockets [Col. 1415B], his feet are freed for walking, hearing is renewed in his ears, his sight is directed toward his parents, his kindred are numbered again by his restored gaze [Note: [Col. 1415D] (4) Thus the Rem., Vatican, and Pomp. manuscripts. The other manuscripts and printed books read *muneratur*, “is endowed.”], something cold is requested, bread is not refused, home is sought, and Christ’s miracles are reported [Note: [Col. 1415D] (5) Rem. manuscript: “The treatise on Lazarus ends happily.” The same stood in Pomp., but was later erased.].

## TREATISE II. ON THE MARTYRDOM OF THE PROPHET ISAIAH

(From the same source, p. 98.)

When Isaiah preached Christ [Note: [Col. 1415D] (6) Thus the Rem., Vat., Urb., Pomp., and Zeno manuscripts and the Venetian edition; elsewhere, “when he foretold.”], or announced to the Israelite people the pronouncement of their future condemnation, the barbarity of blasphemers, aroused to savage ferocity, split him from the head into two pieces, as it were morsels, by a violent punishment [Note: [Col. 1415D] (7) The Urb., Pomp., and Zeno manuscripts and Venetian edition read *bifidarunt*, “they split,” for *bifidavit*, “it split”; the Rem. manuscript agrees, reading *bifaederunt*.]. It ordered his neck to be sawn from his head through his ears down to his shoulders, as though it had been too little if, in mad savagery, it had pierced God’s martyr with a sharp sword [Note: [Col. 1415D] (8) Rem. manuscript: “or in the very butchery of the innocent man.” Venetian edition: *fideculae* for *fidiculae*.], or if the blade itself, of the innocent man, had furrowed by its shrieking stroke through his ribs with the saw’s savage teeth over the width of an acre [Col. 1415C]; unless that brutal violence desired to make of one body two morsels, by the rupture of torn flesh almost two corpses, and to cut out two portions of equal shape and size, as it were [Note: [Col. 1415D] (9) Here *formulae* signifies equal portions, that is, those having equal form and size.].

But in so great a miracle of the heavenly arena, no one, I suppose, can behold him amid that resounding spectacle unless he tries to recount the deeds [Note: [Col. 1415D] (10) Sparaverius emends to *resistente*, “resisting.”] [Note: [Col. 1415D] (11) The Rem., Vat., Urb., Pomp., Sp., and Zeno manuscripts, with the Venetian edition, read “will be able, who [recounts] the deeds.”]. Therefore, with attentive eyes, observe the new solemnity of sufferings in the old discipline [Col. 1416A], and consider what nobility, what splendor, what strength belonged to that martyrdom.

When the saw was making its way through his head—that is, through the navel of gathered sensation—and with reciprocal screeching drew the furrows of its teeth [Note: [Col. 1416C] (13) Rem. manuscript: *duceretur*, “was drawn.” For *labebatur*, “was slipping,” Pomp. has *lavabatur*, “was washed.”], the blade, I suppose, slipped as it set in its teeth and plunged into the Hebrew letters of the head, through the harvest of hair, the thick covering of its veil, and the tough glue of skin, into the woven texture of the skull [Note: [Col. 1416C] (14) Rem. manuscript: *morsit*, “bit.”].

Then, when the anxious cutter had fixed himself, with a fitting effort, at the chamber of the heart [Note: [Col. 1416C] (15) The same Rem. manuscript, with Vat. and Pomp.: *concinenti nisus sector*; Zeno: *concinenti nisu*, “with fitting effort.”], streams from the purple spring poured forth through the released courses of the veins, and a saffron-colored shower drenched him abundantly, lest the profane man should stretch the veins, threadlike, with his thumb [Note: [Col. 1416C] (16) Tol., Pomp., Zeno, Vat., Urb., and Sp. manuscripts: *profanatus*, “having profaned.”]. Thus the painting of the veins, covered with a flood of blood, might not tremble [Note: [Col. 1416C] (17) Rem., Vat., Sp., Pomp., and Zeno manuscripts and Venetian edition: “might not tremble, and might not marvel what that was at which the conquered [man] was compelled to blush” [perhaps *erubesceret*, “might blush”]. “For the…”], nor marvel what that was at which the defeated man was compelled to blush.

For the vaulted chambers of the inward organs of the chaste young man lay open: the sound of the striking trumpet [Note: [Col. 1416D] (18) Rem. manuscript: *buccina*, “trumpet.”], deep vitality, and the dry fasts of pleasures. But Belias, son of Hezekiah [Note: [Col. 1416D] (19) “But Beliab, son of Hezekiah,” in Pomp. and Zeno manuscripts. *Beliab* also in the Rem. manuscript and Venetian edition; the Venetian edition has *Jerechiae*, “of Jeremiah.”], a bloody man and prodigal of genealogy, an astrologer of the *catabolici*, a chief of diviners [Note: [Col. 1416D] (20) Rem. manuscript: *Phisidicorum*; Pomp. and Sp. manuscripts and Venetian edition: *Phiridicorum*.] and [Note: [Col. 1416D] (21) Rem. manuscript: *Ephithonicorum*; Venetian edition: *Phitonicorum*.] pythonic seers, sought within the breastplate of the sacred breast the assembly of faith, the court of the civic letters of preaching.

And although the possession of the body was already divided limb by limb, exposing what was within, revealing what was hidden, bringing forth what was obscure, and showing what it was at which the conquered man was compelled to blush—so that the infamous persecutor might tear apart the man of God with others’ teeth—yet the eminent and illustrious prophet, amid the prostrate cutters and the hanging saws, persisted in the unmoving, unshaken state of his body until two began to be, who would condemn the figures of the nations together with their persecutor [Note: [Col. 1416D] (22) Here likewise all manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *miraretur*, “might marvel,” as a little above in the same sense.] [Col. 1416C] [Note: [Col. 1416D] (23) The Tol. manuscript adds: “who is blessed for ages of ages.” But the Rem. and Pomp. manuscripts read this closing: “The treatise on Isaiah ends happily.”].

[Note: [Col. 1416D] (24) This letter, with its prefixed heading, published by Achéry from manuscripts of the Abbey of Saint-Evroul, is found in vol. III of the latest edition of the *Spicilegium*, p. 299.]

## LETTER TO ATHANASIUS, ASSAILED BY THE ARIANS, AFTER THEY SUBSCRIBED AT THE COUNCIL OF RIMINI

(From the same source, p. 99.)

Potamius to the lord, most glorious and blessed brother Athanasius, bishop.

The pit of so great a prison heaps up the raw filth of a condemnable workshop [Col. 1417A] [Note: [Col. 1417D] (1) The Achéry edition read *concervatam*; we retain the correction of the new edition.], as you rightly write, from the beginning, and from the bloody stench of the dung of dead corpses [Note: [Col. 1417D] (2) Achéry’s first edition, which has *quae magis manus*, “what hand more,” reads thus.]. What hand could disentangle or scrape it away by fiery powers, unless your own enduring titles, won in the holy exile of a crowned head, had excluded that sect of heresy by the curse *anathema maranatha*—“accursed; the Lord comes”?

You have smiled upon us, perfected in Catholic virginity, slaughtering the faithless and condemning the perjured. You conquered with the sword of the one faith striking corrupt minds adulterated and wavering, the lustful commerce of the accursed flock ruinously burdened with venom.

Let the serpent lie, and let the earth that received it grow black with purulent poison. Let the serpent lie condemned by a heavenly blow; let the serpent lie touched by bloody horror [Note: [Col. 1417D] (3) The same first edition has *contractus*, “contracted.”]. Let the serpent lie: let the opened bilge of its three-forked mouth vomit and flow out, its eye-sockets crushed. Let the author of sins be tortured: it was too little for him that he had deprived the first-created man of eternity, unless, more virulent than a hydra, he had also burst forth against the Savior.

He wished to divide our Lord Jesus Christ, as though Christ’s Word could be cut apart, though the clasp of substance is bound together by the unity of the Trinity, as he says (John 10:30): “I and the Father are one.” And (John 14:9): “Who sees me sees the Father.” And (ibid. 5:11): “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” And (John 1:1): “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

A brutal butcher, a parricidal deserter, with hawk-like claws, I think—or with diseased teeth—tried, if he could, to tear this apart. And after these things, what shall I set against their blasphemies? “He who sent me,” they say, “is greater than I” (John 14:28). From whom was the Father begotten? Surely, because the Son confesses it: therefore, is he greater because he is Father to the Son? Order is given precedence; substance is not divided.

What do you say to these things, infamous adulterer? It is well that the antiquity of the fathers, in a most holy synod, pierced you too with chaste missiles, inflated as you were by the impure virulence of a viper’s will. For here too you are shown to have spread snares of calumny because the Savior says (John 6:38): “I did not come to do my own works, but the works of him who sent me.”

What do you say, serpent? Do you pour darkness into this light, into this plain confession, which they regard as a petty question? Time is at issue. The Savior, because he had put on a human body, appeared among men in a body; therefore he said, “I did not come to do my own works.” Did he deny within himself the offices of a human being? He therefore cries out so that he may proclaim in himself as ordainer the Father whom he remembers as his own author within himself. Since the Son follows in title, he who goes before is thus greater; but of sender and sent—because the three are one—there is one substance in the unity of divinity (John 10:30): “I and the Father are one.” And (John 14:9): “Who sees me sees the Father.” And the Savior himself says to the Apostles: “I have been with you so long, and do you not know the Father?”

They also say that the word “substance” is never found written in the divine books. Give back what you have stolen, most thievish tempter: behold, you are defeated when refuted concerning substance. For all the proclamations of the good, ancient companies of holy prophets cry aloud, as he says: “At the voice of substance, from the birds of heaven down to the cattle, they trembled and cried out” (Ezek. 12:11): “I will give Jerusalem into exile.” Behold, when Christ God had not at all been heard by the former people, and those who remained were wasting away, Jerusalem’s pillars fell.

Behold, wretch, although one divine declaration ought already to have sufficed, the holy prophet thundered (Jer. 23:22): “If they had stood in my substance and heard my words, [Col. 1418B] and had taught my people, I would have turned them away from their many pursuits.” Behold, here a blessed hearing of substance broke forth for unhappy peoples, so that the prophet, speaking in Adam’s person, seeks Christ in tears (Ps. 68:3): “I am stuck,” he says, “in the mud of the deep, and there is no substance.” That is, because the substance of the Father had not yet come together with Christ in the flesh.

Likewise, that man in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1418D] (4) Perhaps “in the Evangelist.”] (Luke 15), when, living luxuriously, he had wasted his possessions, “lost all his substance,” as the holy prophet of God wrote (Wis. 1:5): “The Spirit of God will flee deceit.” He therefore lost substance because through luxury he lacked holiness. If this is enough for you, he said; if you now tremble at these things, all is full. If you are still tortured, I press on: we read written (Eccl. 2:8), “For I gathered gold and silver and the substance of kings and regions.”

[Col. 1418C] This is that substance which the prophet remembers when saying (Ps. 61:12): “God spoke once; these two things I heard.” In one voice the prophet testifies that he heard these two things, as David says (Ps. 44:2): “My tongue is the pen of a scribe.” For as a pen is drawn by the divided regularity of its little teeth and is guided by harmonious lines, so the Savior is united with the Father’s works in an indivisible bond. What the Father said, the Son cried aloud; and what the Son spoke, the Father fulfilled.

Justly, he says, “God spoke once; these two things I heard.” Two persons uttered one judgment, just as in the Decalogue one decree is written upon two tablets. Let heresy, condemned beforehand to everlasting silence, struck down by divine blows, and cast into the abyss and Tartarus, be silent. Let the virgin mother alone, ever with her laurels—one with God, to us a dove ever more abundant in fruitfulness—raise her crowned head to the clouds of heaven. May she be blessed, joined with the peoples in the unity of the Trinity in all justice; full of whose praise, from now and for eternal ages of ages may she bless the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1419]

That contention persisted even after these letters of the emperor. 47

**SECOND PART. DISCOURSES.**
Constantine’s Address to the Synod held in Palestine, on Peace. Ibid. ADDRESS TO THE ASSEMBLY OF THE SAINTS. 401 Chapter I. The preface mentions Easter, and that, although Christ had conferred many benefits upon all human beings, he was grievously treated by them. Ibid. Ch. II. An address to the Church and the hearers, asking them to pardon and correct him if he has said anything not quite rightly. 403 Ch. III. That God is the Father of the Word and the maker of all things; and that things could in no way subsist if their causes were diverse. 405 Ch. IV. On the error of those who venerate images. 407 Ch. V. That Christ, the Son of God, created all things and assigned a fixed span of life to each. 409 Ch. VI. On fate, and that what is said of it is false; this is shown both from human laws and from created things, which move not at random but in an ordered manner, thereby declaring the command of the Creator. 411 Ch. VII. That, in matters which we cannot grasp by intelligence, we ought to proclaim the wisdom of the Creator and not suppose chance, or any cause other than God. 417 Ch. VIII. That God abundantly supplies human beings with what is necessary for use, but provides sparingly what serves pleasure, dispensing both for our benefit. Ibid. Ch. IX. On philosophers who, wishing to know everything, fell into mere opinions, and some of whom incurred danger; likewise on Plato’s teaching. 419 Ch. X. On those who reject not only Sacred Scripture but also the doctrines of philosophers; and that either poets must be believed in all things or in none. 423 Ch. XI. On the Lord’s bodily coming: what it was like and why it occurred. 425 [Col. 1429] Ch. XII. On those who did not recognize this mystery, and that their ignorance is voluntary; and how great are the blessings awaiting those who have recognized it, especially those who died in confession. 435 Ch. XIII. That differentiation among created things is necessary, and that the inclination toward good and evil arises from human will; hence God’s judgment is necessary. 437 Ch. XIV. That creation is separated by an immeasurable distance from uncreated substance, and that by virtue a human being comes nearest to God. Ibid. Ch. XV. What precepts the Savior handed down, what miracles he performed, and how greatly he benefited those subject to him. 439 Ch. XVI. That Christ’s coming was foretold by the prophets, and that it was ordained for the overthrow of images and of the cities of image-worshippers. 443 Ch. XVII. On the wisdom of Moses, which the sages of the Gentiles emulated; likewise on Daniel and the three youths. 445 Ch. XVIII. On the Erythraean Sibyl, who in an acrostic of verses by which she prophesied designates the Lord and the Passion. The acrostic is: “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior, Cross.” 449 Ch. XIX. That this prophecy concerning Christ was composed by no Christian, but written by the Erythraean Sibyl, whose books Cicero rendered into Latin verse before Christ’s coming; and that Virgil mentions her and likewise the virgin birth, obscurely celebrating the mystery for fear of the powerful. 453 Ch. XX. Other verses of Virgil Maro concerning Christ, and their interpretation, showing that the mystery was indicated obscurely, as is customary with poets. 457 Ch. XXI. That these things cannot be said of a bare and merely human being; and that unbelievers, through ignorance of divine worship, did not even know the cause of their own origin. 463 Ch. XXII. The emperor’s thanksgiving, attributing his victories and other benefits to Christ; and a refutation of the tyrant Maximinus, who by the cruelty of persecution increased the glory of the Christian religion. 465 Ch. XXIII. On Christian institutions; that God loves those who pursue virtue; and that one ought to hope for the recompense of the Judge. 467 Ch. XXIV. On the calamitous ends of Decius, Valerian, and Aurelian because of their persecution of the churches. 469 Ch. XXV. On Diocletian, who disgracefully abdicated the empire and who, because of his persecution of the churches, was struck by lightning. 471 Ch. XXVI. That God was the cause of the emperor’s piety; that we must seek prosperous outcomes from God and credit them to him, but attribute adverse outcomes to our own negligence. 475

PART THREE.—LETTERS.

Letter of Constantine to Miltiades. He requests that a council be assembled at Rome in the case of Caecilian and the Donatists. 477 Another copy of the letter of the Emperor Constantine, by which he orders a council of bishops to be held at Rome for the unity and concord of the churches. 479 First letter of Constantine and Licinius to Anulinus. Victorinus’s Four Books against Arius.

BOOK ONE. Definition of the views of Arius and Eusebius concerning Jesus: the former says, “Because the Son is not unbegotten”; the latter, that there are not two unbegotten beings. 1039 BOOK TWO. In what Arius and Eusebius agree with Catholics. 1088 BOOK THREE. In what they differ. 1098 BOOK FOUR. In what respects they seem to be opposed to themselves. 1113 Victorinus’s treatise on accepting the word *homoousion* (“of one substance”). 1137 Victorinus’s three hymns on the Trinity. 1139

Victorinus’s Two Books on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians.

BOOK ONE. The first of the two parts into which the author divided the Epistle. The Apostle rebukes the Galatians because they allowed themselves to be led away from the truth they had received from him. Paul explains why and how he opposed Cephas. 1145 BOOK TWO. The other part of the Epistle. Whoever seeks to be justified by works of the law is without the fruit of Christ, in whom neither circumcision nor uncircumcision profits, but living faith. Why one ought to assist one’s neighbor with humility. 1171

Victorinus on Paul’s Epistle to the Philippians.

ONE BOOK. Out of his great affection for the Philippians, the Apostle makes clear to them that his afflictions have resulted in a greater fruit of faith in the Gospel. With remarkable affection he exhorts them to mutual love, concord, and humility of mind. 1197

Victorinus’s Two Books on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians.

BOOK ONE. The first part of the Epistle, divided as it were into two. The Apostle gives thanks to God for the Ephesians’ faith and love toward their neighbors, praying that they may attain perfect wisdom. Formerly dead in sins, they were made alive through Christ, not by their own works. He shows that the Gentiles, formerly strangers to God’s promises, have now through Christ and faith been made fellow citizens of the saints; and that they have the same foundation as the patriarchs and prophets. 1235 BOOK TWO. The second part of the Epistle. The Apostle warns them that, while remaining in this body, they should separate themselves from those whose minds are blinded and who follow the unrestrained desires of the flesh. He wishes wives to be subject to their husbands, and husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the Church. Children should obey their parents, and slaves their masters. 1253 Victorinus’s book on natural philosophy. 1295

Letter, or rescript, of the holy father Athanasius, archbishop of Alexandria, to Liberius, bishop of Rome. 1397. Letter of Pope Liberius to the orthodox bishops of the East, announcing that Athanasius, having refused when summoned by letter to appear at Rome for judgment, was outside his own communion, that is, that of the Roman Church. 1399. Letter of Pope Liberius to all bishops generally: no one, so long as he is able to endure, is to abandon his own church because of persecutions, nor choose repose rather than devote himself to laboring for the people entrusted to him. 1400. Letter of Athanasius and the Egyptian bishops to Pope Liberius, concerning the oppressions inflicted by the Arians. 1403. Replying letter of Pope Liberius to Athanasius and the Egyptian bishops, against disturbers of the peace and tranquillity of the churches, and concerning the manner in which such persons are to be punished. 1406. Decrees of Pope Liberius. 1408.

Potamius, bishop of Olisipo [Lisbon].

Prolegomena.—Concerning Potamius, bishop of Olisipo. 1409. Two treatises by Bishop Potamius.—First treatise, on Lazarus. 1411. Second treatise, on the martyrdom of Isaiah the prophet. 1415. Letter of Potamius to Athanasius, obstructed by the Arians after they subscribed at the Council of Rimini. 1416.
